incorrectas.D: Golgi tendon afferents are sensory (afferent), not motor, and they carry information about muscle tension into the spinal cord as part of a different (inhibitory) reflex arc, rather than serving as the motor output of a reflex.

preguntas.q: Which type of motor neuron provides descending control over spinal reflexes?

e.correcta: Upper motor neurons originate in the motor cortex and brainstem and descend via corticospinal and other tracts to synapse on (and modulate) spinal interneurons and lower motor neurons, providing top-down inhibitory and excitatory control over segmental spinal reflexes. This is why UMN lesions classically produce disinhibited, hyperactive reflexes (hyperreflexia, spasticity, positive Babinski) — the descending inhibitory influence on the reflex arc is lost — in contrast to LMN lesions, which cause hyporeflexia/flaccidity because the reflex arc's effector limb itself is destroyed.

incorrectas.B: Lower motor neurons are the final common pathway that directly innervates skeletal muscle from the anterior horn of the spinal cord (or cranial nerve nuclei) — they execute the reflex rather than descend to control it, so damage to them abolishes reflexes rather than disinhibiting them.
incorrectas.C: Gamma motor neurons innervate intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle to adjust its sensitivity and maintain stretch reflex responsiveness during muscle shortening, but this is a local fine-tuning function of the reflex arc itself, not a descending cortical/brainstem control system over reflexes broadly.
incorrectas.D: Postganglionic sympathetic neurons are part of the autonomic nervous system, innervating smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands — they have no role in modulating somatic spinal stretch or withdrawal reflexes, which are purely a function of the somatic motor system.

preguntas.q: Alpha motor neurons innervate which type of muscle fiber?

e.correcta: Alpha motor neurons innervate extrafusal muscle fibers, the standard contractile fibers that make up the bulk of skeletal muscle and generate the force used for voluntary movement. This is distinct from gamma motor neurons, which innervate the intrafusal fibers within muscle spindles to adjust spindle sensitivity, allowing the stretch reflex to remain accurate across different muscle lengths — a key distinction tested when comparing alpha versus gamma motor neuron function.

incorrectas.B: Intrafusal muscle fibers, found within muscle spindles, are innervated by gamma motor neurons, not alpha motor neurons — their role is proprioceptive (sensing stretch) rather than generating the force of muscle contraction.
incorrectas.C: Cardiac muscle fibers are not innervated by somatic motor neurons at all; the heart has its own intrinsic conduction system (SA node, AV node, Purkinje fibers) modulated by autonomic input, not motor neurons from the spinal cord.
incorrectas.D: Smooth muscle fibers are innervated by autonomic (sympathetic and parasympathetic) neurons, not somatic alpha motor neurons, since smooth muscle contraction is involuntary and regulated differently from skeletal muscle.

preguntas.q: Gamma motor neurons innervate which type of muscle fiber?

e.correcta: Gamma motor neurons innervate intrafusal muscle fibers, the specialized fibers located within muscle spindles (rather than the bulk contractile fibers that generate force); by adjusting intrafusal fiber tension, gamma motor neurons keep the spindle sensitive to stretch across a wide range of muscle lengths, a mechanism called alpha-gamma coactivation that prevents the spindle from going slack during active muscle shortening. This fine-tunes the sensitivity of the stretch reflex during ongoing voluntary movement.

incorrectas.B: Extrafusal muscle fibers are the ordinary contractile fibers that generate the force of muscle contraction and movement, and these are innervated by alpha motor neurons, not gamma motor neurons — this alpha/gamma distinction is a key point tested in motor physiology.
incorrectas.C: Golgi tendon organs are sensory receptors located at the muscle-tendon junction that detect muscle tension (not length) and are innervated by Ib afferent sensory fibers, not by any motor neuron at all, since they are receptor structures rather than muscle fibers requiring motor innervation.
incorrectas.D: Purkinje fibers are specialized cardiac conduction fibers in the ventricles that rapidly propagate the electrical impulse for coordinated ventricular contraction; they are unrelated to skeletal muscle spindle physiology and are not innervated by gamma motor neurons.

preguntas.q: In the muscle stretch reflex, stretch of the muscle increases afferent impulses conducted via which nerve fiber type?

e.correcta: The muscle stretch (myotatic) reflex begins when stretching the muscle elongates the intrafusal fibers of the muscle spindle, activating the primary sensory endings that give rise to Ia afferent fibers — the fastest-conducting, largest-diameter sensory fibers in the body. These Ia afferents synapse directly (monosynaptically) onto alpha motor neurons in the spinal cord, producing rapid reflexive contraction of the same muscle, as classically demonstrated by the patellar tendon reflex. This monosynaptic Ia pathway is what makes deep tendon reflexes so fast and useful for localizing spinal cord level on exam.

incorrectas.B: Ib fibers arise from Golgi tendon organs and signal muscle tension (not length), driving the inverse myotatic reflex that inhibits the contracting muscle to protect against excessive force — this is a different sensory pathway from the stretch reflex being described.
incorrectas.C: Group II fibers do arise from muscle spindle secondary endings and contribute some static stretch information, but they are not the primary, fastest afferent responsible for the classic phasic stretch reflex, which is dominated by Ia fibers.
incorrectas.D: C fibers are small, unmyelinated afferents that carry slow, dull pain and temperature sensation, entirely unrelated to the fast proprioceptive signaling of muscle length used in the stretch reflex.

preguntas.q: In the muscle stretch reflex, Ia afferent fibers directly stimulate which muscles, causing contraction?

e.correcta: In the muscle stretch (myotatic) reflex, muscle spindles detect stretch and their Ia afferent fibers synapse directly (monosynaptically) onto alpha motor neurons innervating the very same muscle that was stretched — the agonist — causing it to contract and resist the stretch (e.g., the quadriceps contracting in the patellar reflex). This monosynaptic reflex arc is the fastest reflex in the body and is the basis of deep tendon reflex testing used to assess spinal cord segment integrity.

incorrectas.B: Antagonist muscles are inhibited, not stimulated, by the Ia afferent — this happens via a separate disynaptic pathway where the Ia afferent excites an inhibitory interneuron that suppresses the antagonist motor neuron (reciprocal inhibition), allowing the agonist to contract unopposed.
incorrectas.C: Synergist muscles are not the primary direct target of the monosynaptic Ia reflex arc described in the classic myotatic reflex; the defining, testable monosynaptic connection is Ia afferent to agonist alpha motor neuron, not a synergist-specific pathway.
incorrectas.D: Contralateral muscles are involved in the crossed extensor reflex (a polysynaptic reflex triggered by nociceptive/flexor withdrawal stimuli, not by simple muscle stretch), which is a completely different reflex arc than the ipsilateral, monosynaptic stretch reflex.

preguntas.q: In the muscle stretch reflex, Ia afferent fibers inhibit which muscles through interneurons, causing relaxation?

e.correcta: In the myotatic (stretch) reflex, muscle spindle Ia afferents synapse directly (monosynaptically) on alpha motor neurons of the same (agonist) muscle to cause contraction, while collateral branches of those same Ia afferents synapse on inhibitory interneurons that hypopolarize the motor neurons of the antagonist muscle — this is reciprocal inhibition. The result is that when the quadriceps is stretched and contracts (as in the knee-jerk reflex), the hamstrings are simultaneously inhibited so the limb can extend smoothly without the antagonist fighting the movement.

incorrectas.B: Agonist muscles are excited, not inhibited, by the Ia afferent in this reflex arc — the monosynaptic connection onto agonist alpha motor neurons is what produces the contraction, which is the opposite of the disynaptic inhibitory pathway being described.
incorrectas.C: The inhibition in reciprocal inhibition targets the specific antagonist of the stretched muscle, not a blanket category of 'ipsilateral flexors only' — whether the inhibited muscle is a flexor or extensor depends entirely on which muscle is antagonistic to the one being stretched.
incorrectas.D: Effects on the contralateral limb belong to the crossed-extensor reflex, a separate polysynaptic reflex triggered by nociceptive withdrawal, not to the simple monosynaptic/disynaptic stretch reflex arc described here.

preguntas.q: In the inverse muscle stretch reflex (Golgi tendon reflex), increased muscle tension increases afferent impulses conducted via which nerve fiber type?

e.correcta: The Golgi tendon organ senses muscle tension (rather than length) and is innervated by Ib afferent fibers; increased tension increases Ib firing, which synapses on inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord to inhibit the alpha motor neuron of the same muscle (autogenic inhibition), protecting the muscle-tendon unit from excessive force/injury.

incorrectas.B: Ia fibers carry afferent information from muscle spindles about muscle length and rate of stretch, driving the monosynaptic muscle stretch (myotatic) reflex — that is a different reflex and a different receptor from the tension-sensing Golgi tendon organ.
incorrectas.C: II fibers are the secondary afferents from muscle spindles that signal static muscle length, contributing to reflexes about stretch and position rather than the tension-based inverse stretch reflex mediated by Ib fibers.
incorrectas.D: A-delta fibers carry fast, sharp pain and temperature sensation from free nerve endings and skin receptors; they are unrelated to proprioceptive feedback from Golgi tendon organs.

preguntas.q: Bisphosphonates have a chemical structure similar to which compound?

e.correcta: Bisphosphonates are synthetic analogs of pyrophosphate, sharing a similar P-C-P (carbon-substituted) backbone instead of pyrophosphate's P-O-P bond, which makes them resistant to enzymatic hydrolysis while retaining high affinity for calcium and hydroxyapatite in bone. This structural mimicry allows bisphosphonates to concentrate at sites of bone remodeling just as natural pyrophosphate does, but with much greater metabolic stability, giving them a long duration of action.

incorrectas.B: Hydroxyapatite is the mineral component of bone matrix that bisphosphonates bind to, not the compound bisphosphonates are structurally similar to — bisphosphonates mimic pyrophosphate's structure to achieve that binding.
incorrectas.C: Citrate is a metabolic intermediate (TCA cycle) and calcium chelator with a completely different chemical structure from bisphosphonates, unrelated to pyrophosphate mimicry.
incorrectas.D: Phosphocreatine is an energy storage molecule used to rapidly regenerate ATP in muscle, structurally and functionally distinct from pyrophosphate and unrelated to bisphosphonate design.

preguntas.q: Bisphosphonates bind to which component of bone, inhibiting osteoclast activity?

e.correcta: Bisphosphonates are pyrophosphate analogs that bind avidly to hydroxyapatite, the calcium-phosphate mineral matrix of bone, concentrating especially at sites of active remodeling. Once incorporated into bone, they are taken up by osteoclasts during resorption and disrupt the mevalonate pathway (for nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates), inducing osteoclast apoptosis and thereby reducing bone resorption — the basis for their use in osteoporosis and Paget disease.

incorrectas.A: Collagen type I is the organic protein scaffold of bone matrix, not the mineral component that bisphosphonates target; bisphosphonates' pyrophosphate-like structure specifically confers affinity for the mineral phase, not collagen fibers.
incorrectas.C: Osteocalcin is a non-collagenous bone protein secreted by osteoblasts that regulates mineralization and serves as a marker of osteoblast activity, but it is not the binding site exploited by bisphosphonates.
incorrectas.D: Osteopontin is another non-collagenous matrix protein involved in cell attachment and biomineralization, but bisphosphonates' pharmacologic mechanism depends on binding the mineral hydroxyapatite crystal, not this matrix glycoprotein.

preguntas.q: When bound to bisphosphonate, which bone cells are unable to adhere to the bony surface, decreasing their activity?

e.correcta: Bisphosphonates bind avidly to hydroxyapatite at sites of active bone remodeling and are then taken up by osteoclasts during resorption; once internalized, they disrupt osteoclast cytoskeletal organization and the ruffled border needed for adhesion to the bone surface, effectively immobilizing and inactivating these cells. This mechanism underlies their use in osteoporosis, Paget disease, and hypercalcemia of malignancy — by preventing osteoclasts from attaching to and resorbing bone.

incorrectas.A: Osteoblasts are the bone-forming cells; bisphosphonates do not target osteoblast adhesion — in fact, by suppressing osteoclast-mediated resorption, they indirectly allow relatively more bone formation activity by osteoblasts to predominate.
incorrectas.B: Osteocytes are mature, embedded bone cells that maintain bone matrix and sense mechanical strain, but they are not the direct target of bisphosphonate-induced adhesion disruption — this occurs at the osteoclast-bone surface interface.
incorrectas.D: Chondrocytes are cartilage cells involved in endochondral ossification and cartilage maintenance, not bone surface remodeling, and are not the target of bisphosphonate action.

preguntas.q: Bisphosphonates decrease the development and recruitment of precursors of which cell type?

e.correcta: Bisphosphonates decrease the development and recruitment of osteoclast precursors, reducing the overall pool of mature, bone-resorbing osteoclasts available at remodeling sites, in addition to directly impairing the function and survival of mature osteoclasts already present. This multi-pronged suppression of osteoclastogenesis and osteoclast activity is central to their efficacy in osteoporosis and other high-bone-turnover conditions.

incorrectas.A: Osteoblasts are bone-forming cells whose precursor development is not the target of bisphosphonate action; bisphosphonates act on the resorptive (osteoclast) side of bone remodeling, not the formative side.
incorrectas.C: Chondroblasts are cartilage-forming cells involved in endochondral ossification, not directly targeted by bisphosphonates, which act specifically on osteoclast lineage cells in bone.
incorrectas.D: Fibroblasts are connective tissue cells involved in collagen synthesis and wound healing, unrelated to bone resorption and not affected by bisphosphonate therapy.

preguntas.q: In addition to decreasing osteoclast activity, bisphosphonates also induce which process in osteoclasts?

e.correcta: In addition to impairing osteoclast adhesion and reducing precursor recruitment, nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates inhibit the mevalonate pathway (specifically farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase), disrupting prenylation of small GTPases essential for osteoclast cytoskeletal function and survival signaling — this triggers apoptosis in mature osteoclasts. Inducing osteoclast apoptosis is a key mechanism by which bisphosphonates achieve durable suppression of bone resorption.

incorrectas.B: Necrosis is an uncontrolled, inflammatory form of cell death rather than the programmed, non-inflammatory apoptotic pathway bisphosphonates trigger via mevalonate pathway inhibition in osteoclasts.
incorrectas.C: Proliferation would increase osteoclast numbers and bone resorption, the opposite of bisphosphonates' therapeutic goal of suppressing osteoclast activity and survival.
incorrectas.D: Differentiation refers to precursor cells maturing into functional osteoclasts, a process bisphosphonates actually inhibit (reducing precursor recruitment) rather than induce; the additional mechanism being tested here is apoptosis of already-mature cells.

preguntas.q: Which two drugs are useful in the acute treatment of hypercalcemia of malignancy?

o.D: Loop diuretics alone and vitamin D

e.correcta: Bisphosphonates (e.g., zoledronic acid) inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption to lower serum calcium over days, while calcitonin acts rapidly (within hours) by directly inhibiting osteoclasts and increasing renal calcium excretion, making the combination useful for acute hypercalcemia of malignancy — calcitonin providing fast, short-lived relief while the slower-onset bisphosphonate produces a more durable calcium reduction. This complementary onset profile is why they're often used together rather than relying on either drug alone.

incorrectas.B: Vitamin D and calcium gluconate would raise, not lower, serum calcium (vitamin D increases intestinal calcium absorption and calcium gluconate directly adds calcium), making this combination counterproductive for treating hypercalcemia.
incorrectas.C: Thiazide diuretics increase renal calcium reabsorption and would worsen hypercalcemia, and PTH itself raises calcium via bone resorption and renal reabsorption, so neither agent is appropriate for lowering calcium in this setting.
incorrectas.D: Loop diuretics alone can promote calciuresis but are not first-line as monotherapy (adequate volume repletion is needed first, and it's an adjunct at best), and pairing with vitamin D (which raises calcium) is directly contradictory to the treatment goal.

preguntas.q: As a result of decreased osteoclast activity, bisphosphonates may cause which electrolyte abnormality?

e.correcta: Bisphosphonates bind hydroxyapatite in bone and are taken up by osteoclasts during resorption, where they inhibit the mevalonate pathway (in the case of nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates) and induce osteoclast apoptosis, sharply reducing bone resorption. Because osteoclastic resorption normally releases calcium from bone into the blood, suppressing this process can transiently lower serum calcium, producing hypocalcemia, especially early in treatment or in patients with inadequate calcium/vitamin D stores. This is why calcium and vitamin D supplementation is often recommended alongside bisphosphonate therapy.

incorrectas.A: Hypercalcemia would result from increased, not decreased, osteoclast activity releasing calcium from bone — since bisphosphonates suppress osteoclasts, they push serum calcium down rather than up.
incorrectas.C: Hyperkalemia is a potassium disturbance unrelated to osteoclast-mediated bone calcium release; bisphosphonates' relevant electrolyte effect is on calcium homeostasis, not potassium.
incorrectas.D: Hypophosphatemia is not the characteristic electrolyte effect of decreased osteoclast activity; bone resorption releases both calcium and phosphate, but the clinically emphasized abnormality with bisphosphonates is hypocalcemia.

preguntas.q: Chronic PTH exposure stimulates osteoblasts to express which ligand, which binds to which receptor on osteoclast surfaces to increase their activity?

e.correcta: Chronic PTH exposure upregulates RANKL expression on osteoblasts/stromal cells, which binds RANK receptors on osteoclast precursors and mature osteoclasts, promoting their differentiation, activation, and survival, thereby increasing bone resorption and releasing calcium into the blood. This osteoblast-mediated coupling mechanism (PTH acts on osteoblasts, which then signal osteoclasts, since osteoclasts lack PTH receptors) is the key concept explaining how PTH indirectly drives bone resorption.

incorrectas.B: OPG (osteoprotegerin) is a decoy receptor that binds RANKL to prevent it from activating RANK, thereby inhibiting osteoclast activity — chronic PTH actually decreases the RANKL/OPG ratio's inhibitory effect by favoring RANKL, not by increasing OPG.
incorrectas.C: M-CSF and its receptor c-Fms are important for early osteoclast precursor proliferation and survival, but the specific ligand-receptor pair upregulated by PTH to drive mature osteoclast activation is RANKL/RANK, not M-CSF/c-Fms.
incorrectas.D: TNF-alpha/TNFR1 signaling can promote osteoclastogenesis in inflammatory contexts (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis), but it is not the classic PTH-driven pathway; PTH's canonical effect on bone resorption is mediated through RANKL/RANK.

preguntas.q: Which peptide hormone directly inhibits osteoclasts, causing decreased bone resorption?

e.correcta: Calcitonin, secreted by parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid in response to hypercalcemia, directly inhibits osteoclast activity by binding calcitonin receptors on osteoclasts, reducing bone resorption and thereby lowering serum calcium. This direct osteoclast-inhibiting action is exploited therapeutically in conditions of excessive bone resorption, such as Paget disease, hypercalcemia of malignancy, and osteoporosis, though its effect is generally modest and subject to tachyphylaxis with prolonged use.

incorrectas.A: Parathyroid hormone actually stimulates osteoclast activity indirectly (via osteoblast RANKL expression) to increase bone resorption and raise serum calcium — this is the opposite action to calcitonin, which is the hormone that inhibits osteoclasts.
incorrectas.C: Vitamin D (calcitriol) primarily increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption and, at high levels, promotes osteoclast differentiation to support bone remodeling and mineralization — it does not function as a direct osteoclast inhibitor the way calcitonin does.
incorrectas.D: Growth hormone stimulates linear bone growth and overall bone turnover via IGF-1, acting on both osteoblasts and osteoclasts to promote remodeling, rather than serving as a targeted, direct inhibitor of osteoclast-mediated resorption.

preguntas.q: Calcitonin promotes which renal handling of Ca2+?

e.correcta: Calcitonin promotes renal excretion of calcium by decreasing tubular calcium reabsorption, complementing its inhibition of osteoclastic bone resorption to lower serum calcium overall; this combined bone-and-kidney action is why calcitonin is used therapeutically for hypercalcemia and Paget disease. Physiologically it counterbalances PTH, which instead promotes renal calcium reabsorption, illustrating the reciprocal hormonal control of serum calcium.

incorrectas.A: Reabsorption is the opposite of calcitonin's true renal effect — that is instead what PTH promotes to raise serum calcium — whereas calcitonin lowers serum calcium partly by increasing, not decreasing, urinary calcium loss.
incorrectas.C: Calcitonin does not act through the aldosterone-mediated sodium/potassium-retention pathway; its calcium-lowering effect operates independently through direct inhibition of osteoclasts and reduced renal tubular calcium reabsorption, not via mineralocorticoid receptor signaling.
incorrectas.D: Calcitonin does have a direct renal effect (increasing calcium excretion by reducing tubular reabsorption); saying it has 'no renal effect' ignores this component of its calcium-lowering mechanism, which works in tandem with its skeletal (osteoclast-inhibiting) action.

preguntas.q: What is a possible adverse metabolic effect of exogenous calcitonin administration?

e.correcta: Calcitonin, secreted by parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid, lowers serum calcium by inhibiting osteoclastic bone resorption and increasing renal calcium excretion, so exogenous calcitonin administration (used therapeutically in Paget disease, hypercalcemia, or osteoporosis) carries the risk of driving serum calcium too low, producing hypocalcemia. This is the expected pharmacologic extension of its mechanism — because its entire job is to oppose PTH and reduce serum calcium, giving too much simply pushes that same effect past the desired therapeutic endpoint.

incorrectas.A: Hyperkalemia (elevated potassium) is not a recognized effect of calcitonin, which specifically targets calcium homeostasis via osteoclast inhibition and renal calcium handling, not potassium transport.
incorrectas.C: Hypercalcemia is the opposite of calcitonin's actual effect; calcitonin is a calcium-lowering hormone (it inhibits osteoclasts and increases renal calcium excretion), so excess dosing would push calcium down, not up.
incorrectas.D: Hypernatremia (elevated sodium) is unrelated to calcitonin's mechanism, which centers on calcium and, secondarily, phosphate handling in bone and kidney, not sodium balance.

preguntas.q: Which leukotriene, along with 5-HETE, is a potent chemoattractant for inflammatory cells, particularly neutrophils?

e.correcta: Leukotriene B4 is generated from arachidonic acid via the 5-lipoxygenase pathway and, together with 5-HETE (an intermediate in the same pathway), acts as a potent chemoattractant that recruits and activates neutrophils at sites of inflammation, promoting their adhesion and migration across the endothelium. This chemotactic role distinguishes LTB4 from the cysteinyl leukotrienes, which instead act mainly as bronchoconstrictors and mediators of vascular permeability rather than as recruiters of neutrophils.

incorrectas.B: Leukotriene C4 is a cysteinyl leukotriene that causes bronchoconstriction, increased vascular permeability, and mucus secretion (important in asthma pathophysiology), but it is not the classic neutrophil chemoattractant that LTB4 is.
incorrectas.C: Leukotriene D4 is also a cysteinyl leukotriene with the same bronchoconstrictive and permeability-increasing effects as LTC4 (targeted by drugs like montelukast), rather than functioning as a chemotactic signal for neutrophils.
incorrectas.D: Leukotriene E4 completes the cysteinyl leukotriene family alongside LTC4 and LTD4, sharing their smooth muscle and vascular effects in conditions like asthma, but it does not share LTB4's specific role in neutrophil chemotaxis.

preguntas.q: Which three leukotrienes increase airway vascular permeability, mucus production, and bronchoconstriction?

e.correcta: Leukotrienes C4, D4, and E4 make up what was classically called slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis (SRS-A); they are cysteinyl leukotrienes produced from arachidonic acid via the 5-lipoxygenase pathway and act on CysLT1 receptors on airway smooth muscle and vasculature. Their effects — bronchoconstriction, increased vascular permeability, and mucus secretion — drive much of the pathophysiology of asthma, which is why leukotriene receptor antagonists like montelukast and zafirlukast specifically block this action to reduce airway symptoms.

incorrectas.B: LTA4 is an unstable intermediate that gets converted into either LTB4 or the cysteinyl leukotrienes, and LTB4 itself is primarily a potent neutrophil chemoattractant rather than a mediator of bronchoconstriction or vascular permeability, so this trio does not match the described effects.
incorrectas.C: LTB4 is a chemotactic factor for neutrophils involved in inflammation and abscess formation, not a bronchoconstrictor, so combining it with LTD4 and LTE4 misattributes its function to the airway effects being asked about.
incorrectas.D: PGE2, PGF2-alpha, and TXA2 are prostaglandin/thromboxane products of the cyclooxygenase pathway (not the lipoxygenase pathway), with different receptor targets and effects such as platelet aggregation (TXA2) and uterine contraction (PGF2-alpha), not the classic cysteinyl leukotriene airway triad.

preguntas.q: Which leukotriene is the most potent bronchoconstrictor?

e.correcta: Leukotriene D4, along with C4 and E4 (collectively the cysteinyl leukotrienes, historically termed 'slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis'), acts on CysLT1 receptors on airway smooth muscle to cause potent, sustained bronchoconstriction — LTD4 is generally regarded as the most potent bronchoconstrictor among them, which is why leukotriene receptor antagonists like montelukast (blocking CysLT1) are used in asthma management.

incorrectas.A: Leukotriene B4 is a potent chemotactic agent for neutrophils, recruiting them to sites of inflammation via a distinct BLT receptor pathway, but it has essentially no bronchoconstrictor activity, unlike the cysteinyl leukotrienes.
incorrectas.B: Leukotriene C4 is a cysteinyl leukotriene and does contribute to bronchoconstriction and increased vascular permeability, but it is generally considered less potent as a bronchoconstrictor than LTD4, which is the specific answer this question targets.
incorrectas.D: Leukotriene E4 is also a cysteinyl leukotriene with bronchoconstrictor activity and is notably used as a urinary biomarker of cysteinyl leukotriene production, but among the cysteinyl leukotrienes, LTD4 is regarded as the most potent bronchoconstrictor, not LTE4.

preguntas.q: Leukotriene D4 exerts its bronchoconstrictive effects by binding to which receptor?

e.correcta: Leukotriene D4 (along with C4 and E4, the cysteinyl leukotrienes derived from arachidonic acid via the 5-lipoxygenase pathway) binds CysLT1 receptors on airway smooth muscle, triggering Gq-mediated bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, and increased vascular permeability — this is precisely why leukotriene receptor antagonists like montelukast, which block CysLT1, are used to control asthma symptoms, especially aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease where COX inhibition shunts arachidonic acid toward the lipoxygenase pathway.

incorrectas.B: The thromboxane receptor (TP) mediates platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction in response to thromboxane A2, a distinct arachidonic acid metabolite produced via COX/thromboxane synthase, not the target of leukotriene D4.
incorrectas.C: EP2 is a prostaglandin E2 receptor subtype generally associated with relaxation/vasodilation effects, an entirely different eicosanoid (prostaglandin, not leukotriene) and receptor system from CysLT1-mediated bronchoconstriction.
incorrectas.D: BLT1 is the receptor for leukotriene B4, which mediates neutrophil chemotaxis and adhesion rather than bronchoconstriction — LTB4 and LTD4 are different leukotrienes acting through different receptors on different cell types.

preguntas.q: Which arachidonic acid pathway metabolite causes neutrophil chemotaxis?

e.correcta: Leukotriene B4 (LTB4) is generated from arachidonic acid via the 5-lipoxygenase pathway and functions specifically as a potent chemoattractant for neutrophils, recruiting them to sites of inflammation and promoting their adhesion to vascular endothelium — this is why it is highlighted as the leukotriene tied to neutrophil chemotaxis, distinct from the cysteinyl leukotrienes that mediate smooth muscle effects. This distinction underlies why 5-lipoxygenase inhibitors (like zileuton) are used in inflammatory/asthmatic conditions where leukotriene-driven inflammation is prominent.

incorrectas.B: LTD4 is one of the cysteinyl leukotrienes (along with LTC4 and LTE4) that causes bronchoconstriction, increased vascular permeability, and mucus secretion — its role is in smooth muscle and vascular effects relevant to asthma symptoms, not in recruiting neutrophils via chemotaxis.
incorrectas.C: PGE2 is a cyclooxygenase pathway product that causes vasodilation, potentiates pain and fever, and helps maintain the ductus arteriosus/protects gastric mucosa — it is not the mediator responsible for neutrophil chemotaxis, which is a lipoxygenase-pathway (LTB4) function.
incorrectas.D: TXA2 (thromboxane A2) is a cyclooxygenase pathway product from platelets that promotes vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation, functions centered on hemostasis rather than the neutrophil recruitment role specifically attributed to LTB4.

preguntas.q: Leukotrienes are synthesized from arachidonic acid by which enzyme?

e.correcta: 5-Lipoxygenase converts arachidonic acid into 5-HPETE and then into leukotrienes (LTB4, and the cysteinyl leukotrienes LTC4/D4/E4), which mediate neutrophil chemotaxis (LTB4) and bronchoconstriction/vascular permeability (LTC4/D4/E4) — the basis for leukotriene receptor antagonists like montelukast in asthma. This is a distinct branch of the arachidonic acid pathway from the cyclooxygenase branch, which is why drugs like zileuton (5-LOX inhibitor) specifically block leukotriene synthesis without affecting prostaglandin/thromboxane production.

incorrectas.A: Cyclooxygenase converts arachidonic acid into prostaglandins and thromboxanes, not leukotrienes; COX and 5-LOX are parallel but separate branches of arachidonic acid metabolism, which is why NSAIDs (COX inhibitors) do not block leukotriene synthesis.
incorrectas.C: Phospholipase A2 acts upstream, releasing arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids in the first place, but it does not itself convert arachidonic acid into leukotrienes — that conversion requires 5-lipoxygenase.
incorrectas.D: Prostacyclin synthase acts within the cyclooxygenase branch, converting the COX-derived intermediate PGH2 into prostacyclin (PGI2), an entirely different product from the lipoxygenase-derived leukotrienes.

preguntas.q: PGI2, PGE1, PGE2, PGF2-alpha, and thromboxane A2 are synthesized from arachidonic acid by which enzyme(s)?

e.correcta: COX-1 and COX-2 (cyclooxygenases) convert arachidonic acid into prostaglandin H2, the common precursor that downstream synthases then convert into PGI2, PGE1, PGE2, PGF2-alpha, and thromboxane A2 depending on the tissue and enzyme complement present. This is why NSAIDs, which inhibit COX enzymes, broadly suppress this whole family of prostanoids, producing both their anti-inflammatory benefits and side effects like reduced protective gastric prostaglandins and altered platelet thromboxane production.

incorrectas.B: 5-Lipoxygenase acts on arachidonic acid through a separate branch of the pathway to produce leukotrienes (like LTB4 and the cysteinyl leukotrienes), not the prostaglandins and thromboxane listed, which are exclusively COX pathway products.
incorrectas.C: Phospholipase C is a signal transduction enzyme that cleaves PIP2 into IP3 and DAG for intracellular calcium signaling; it does not act on arachidonic acid to generate eicosanoids and is unrelated to prostaglandin/thromboxane synthesis.
incorrectas.D: Lipoxin synthase is not the enzyme responsible for prostaglandin and thromboxane production; lipoxins are separate anti-inflammatory eicosanoids formed through interactions between lipoxygenase pathways, distinct from the COX-derived compounds listed in the question.

preguntas.q: Pulmonary blood flow is equal to which of the following?

o.A: Cardiac output of the right heart
o.B: Cardiac output of the left heart only

e.correcta: In a closed circulatory loop, all blood returning to the right heart via the systemic veins must be pumped through the pulmonary circulation before returning to the left heart, so pulmonary blood flow equals the cardiac output of the right ventricle. In the steady state, this also equals left heart output, since the two ventricles are arranged in series and must pump the same volume per unit time to avoid blood pooling in one circuit — a key physiologic principle used to explain shunt calculations and mismatches in conditions like left-to-right shunts.

incorrectas.B: Restricting the equivalence to 'left heart output only' misses the actual anatomic relationship — pulmonary blood flow equals right heart output directly (since the right ventricle ejects into the pulmonary artery), and only equals left heart output secondarily because the two outputs are equal in the steady state.
incorrectas.C: Total blood volume is a static quantity (the total amount of blood in the body at one time), whereas pulmonary blood flow is a dynamic rate (volume per unit time through the lungs) — these are different types of measurements and are not equivalent.
incorrectas.D: Systemic vascular resistance describes the resistance the left ventricle pumps against in the systemic circuit, a hemodynamic parameter unrelated to the volume of blood flowing through the pulmonary circuit, so it cannot be equated with pulmonary blood flow.

preguntas.q: In a standing person, pulmonary blood flow is lowest in which region of the lung?

o.D: It is uniform throughout the lung

e.correcta: In an upright person, gravity causes pulmonary blood flow to be greatest at the base and lowest at the apex, because the hydrostatic pressure gradient in the pulmonary vasculature increases going down the lung, distending basal vessels more and increasing their flow (this is the basis of the West zones model, where the apex is West zone 1 with alveolar pressure sometimes exceeding pulmonary arterial pressure). This gravity-driven mismatch between blood flow and ventilation also explains why the apex has a higher V/Q ratio than the base.

incorrectas.B: The base has the highest, not lowest, blood flow in an upright person because gravity increases hydrostatic pressure in the more dependent pulmonary vessels, distending them and increasing perfusion there.
incorrectas.C: Blood flow increases in a roughly linear gradient from apex to base rather than peaking in the middle zone, so describing the middle as having the lowest flow misrepresents the gravitational gradient that governs pulmonary perfusion.
incorrectas.D: Pulmonary blood flow is distinctly non-uniform due to gravity's effect on the low-pressure pulmonary circulation — this is precisely why the West zone model exists to describe the apex-to-base perfusion gradient.

preguntas.q: In a standing person, pulmonary blood flow is highest in which region of the lung?

o.D: It is uniform throughout the lung

e.correcta: In an upright person, gravity pulls blood toward the lung bases, so both blood flow and vascular distension are greatest at the base and progressively decrease toward the apex. This creates the classic West zones: zone 3 (base) has the highest flow because pulmonary arterial and venous pressures both exceed alveolar pressure, keeping vessels open throughout the cardiac cycle. Ventilation is also higher at the base than the apex, but because blood flow increases even more steeply with gravity, the base ends up relatively overperfused relative to ventilation (lower V/Q), while the apex is underperfused relative to ventilation (higher V/Q).

incorrectas.A: The apex has the lowest blood flow (West zone 1 physiology), because alveolar pressure there can exceed both pulmonary arterial and venous pressure, compressing capillaries especially during conditions like hypovolemia or positive-pressure ventilation.
incorrectas.C: The mid-lung zone (zone 2) has intermediate flow, greater than the apex but less than the base, because pulmonary arterial pressure exceeds alveolar pressure but alveolar pressure still exceeds venous pressure at some points in the cycle.
incorrectas.D: Blood flow is not uniform in the upright lung; gravity creates a clear gradient of increasing perfusion from apex to base, which is the physiological basis of the West zone model.

preguntas.q: What is the term for the volume of air that moves into the lung with each quiet (normal) inspiration?

e.correcta: Tidal volume (TV) is defined as the volume of air inhaled or exhaled during a single normal, quiet breath (typically around 500 mL in an average adult), reflecting resting ventilatory demand without any conscious extra effort. It is the baseline component used to calculate minute ventilation (TV x respiratory rate) and is the volume that changes most directly with exercise or restrictive lung disease. Recognizing TV as the 'normal breath' volume distinguishes it from the reserve volumes, which represent additional capacity beyond a quiet breath.

incorrectas.B: Inspiratory reserve volume is the additional air that CAN be forcefully inhaled after a normal tidal inspiration, representing extra lung capacity beyond quiet breathing, not the quiet breath itself.
incorrectas.C: Vital capacity is the total volume that can be exhaled after a maximal inspiration (TV + IRV + ERV), representing the full functional range of the lungs, not a single quiet breath.
incorrectas.D: Residual volume is the air that remains in the lungs after a maximal forced exhalation and can never be expelled; it is not part of any volume that 'moves' during breathing and is unrelated to a quiet inspiration.

preguntas.q: What is the typical normal value for tidal volume?

e.correcta: Normal tidal volume — the volume of air moved in a single normal, quiet breath — is approximately 500 mL in an average adult, a figure used directly in calculating minute ventilation (tidal volume times respiratory rate) and alveolar ventilation (tidal volume minus dead space, times respiratory rate). This 500 mL benchmark is also the standard starting point for mechanical ventilator settings and pulmonary function test interpretation.

incorrectas.B: 1200 mL is roughly in the range of inspiratory reserve volume territory (well beyond a normal quiet breath) and substantially overstates normal resting tidal volume, which is about 500 mL.
incorrectas.C: 3000 mL approaches the magnitude of inspiratory reserve volume or a large fraction of vital capacity, representing forced maximal inspiration rather than the volume of a single normal resting breath.
incorrectas.D: 150 mL corresponds roughly to anatomical dead space volume (the air in conducting airways that doesn't participate in gas exchange), not the total tidal volume of a normal breath, which is about 500 mL.

preguntas.q: What is the term for the additional volume of air that can be inspired above tidal volume?

e.correcta: Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) is defined as the additional air that can be forcefully inhaled after a normal, quiet tidal volume breath. It represents the lung's capacity to recruit extra volume above resting breathing, which is tapped into during exercise or forced maximal inspiration, and is a major component of the inspiratory capacity.

incorrectas.B: Expiratory reserve volume is the additional air that can be forcibly exhaled after a normal tidal expiration, the mirror-image reserve on the exhalation side, not the inspiration side, of the breathing cycle.
incorrectas.C: Tidal volume is the volume of air moved in a normal, quiet breath itself (about 500 mL), not the extra volume available above and beyond that normal breath.
incorrectas.D: Functional residual capacity is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a normal tidal expiration (ERV + residual volume); it describes lung volume at rest after exhaling, unrelated to the reserve available for additional inspiration.

preguntas.q: What is the term for the additional volume of air that can be expired below tidal volume?

e.correcta: Expiratory reserve volume (ERV) is defined as the additional volume of air that can be forcefully exhaled after a normal, passive tidal expiration, reflecting the reserve capacity of the expiratory muscles (internal intercostals, abdominal muscles) beyond quiet breathing. ERV is reduced in conditions that limit full lung deflation or expiratory muscle strength, such as obesity (due to reduced chest wall compliance) or neuromuscular disease, and it is a component of both functional residual capacity (ERV + RV) and vital capacity (IRV + TV + ERV).

incorrectas.B: Inspiratory reserve volume is the opposite concept — the additional volume that can be inhaled above a normal tidal breath, not the volume that can be exhaled below it, so it describes the wrong direction of respiratory reserve.
incorrectas.C: Residual volume is the air that remains in the lungs even after a maximal forced expiration (i.e., after ERV has already been fully exhaled) and can never be voluntarily expelled, distinguishing it from ERV, which by definition can be exhaled.
incorrectas.D: Vital capacity is a much larger composite measure (IRV + TV + ERV) representing the total volume that can move in and out of the lungs with maximal effort, not the specific volume below tidal volume.

preguntas.q: What is the term for the volume of air remaining in the lungs after maximal forced expiration?

e.correcta: Residual volume (RV) is defined as the air that remains trapped in the alveoli and airways after a maximal forced expiration, because further collapse is prevented by chest wall elastic recoil and airway closure at low lung volumes. RV cannot be measured by spirometry alone (since it can't be exhaled) and instead requires methods like helium dilution, nitrogen washout, or body plethysmography; it is elevated in obstructive lung disease due to air trapping.

incorrectas.B: Expiratory reserve volume is the additional air that can be forcibly exhaled after a normal tidal expiration, on top of tidal volume — it is entirely exhalable and is not the volume left behind at maximal expiration.
incorrectas.C: Functional residual capacity is the volume remaining after a normal (not maximal) tidal expiration, and it is the sum of RV plus ERV — it is a larger, composite value, not the same as residual volume alone.
incorrectas.D: Tidal volume is simply the volume of a normal, quiet breath in and out; it has no direct relationship to the volume remaining after maximal forced exhalation.

preguntas.q: Which lung volume cannot be measured directly by spirometry?

e.correcta: Residual volume (RV) is the air remaining in the lungs after maximal forced exhalation, and because spirometry can only measure volumes that are actually exhaled or inhaled through the mouthpiece, RV (along with any volume that includes it, like FRC and TLC) cannot be directly measured this way — it requires indirect methods such as helium dilution, nitrogen washout, or body plethysmography. This is a classic pulmonary physiology distinction: any lung volume/capacity containing RV is inherently inaccessible to simple spirometry.

incorrectas.B: Tidal volume is simply the volume of a normal breath in and out, which is directly traced and measured on a standard spirometry tracing with no special indirect technique required.
incorrectas.C: Inspiratory reserve volume is the additional air that can be maximally inhaled above a normal tidal inspiration, and since it's bounded by volumes the patient actively breathes in and out, it is fully measurable by spirometry.
incorrectas.D: Expiratory reserve volume is the additional air that can be maximally exhaled after a normal tidal expiration, and like IRV, it involves only air movement through the mouthpiece that spirometry can directly capture, unlike RV which remains trapped in the lungs.

preguntas.q: The sum of tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume is known as which of the following?

e.correcta: Inspiratory capacity (IC) is defined as tidal volume (TV) plus inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) — it represents the total volume of air a person can inhale starting from the resting end-expiratory position (functional residual capacity) up to full lung inflation. This is a clinically useful measure because it reflects how much additional air a patient can pull in above normal quiet breathing, which matters in conditions that limit inspiratory effort (e.g., neuromuscular weakness or restrictive lung disease). Remembering the lung volume/capacity hierarchy (a 'capacity' = sum of two or more volumes) helps distinguish IC from the basic volumes that comprise it.

incorrectas.B: Vital capacity is the sum of IRV + TV + expiratory reserve volume (ERV) — it includes the additional expiratory component that inspiratory capacity does not, making it larger and reflecting the full range of volitional breathing.
incorrectas.C: Functional residual capacity is the volume remaining in the lungs after a normal tidal expiration, equal to ERV + residual volume (RV); it is measured at the opposite end of the respiratory cycle from where IC is calculated and does not include TV or IRV.
incorrectas.D: Total lung capacity is the sum of all four volumes (TV + IRV + ERV + RV) and represents the maximum lung volume achievable, which is larger than IC because it also accounts for the reserve volume that remains even after maximal expiration.

preguntas.q: The sum of residual volume plus expiratory reserve volume is known as which of the following?

e.correcta: Functional residual capacity (FRC) is defined as the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a normal tidal expiration, and it is calculated as the sum of residual volume (air that cannot be exhaled even with maximal effort) plus expiratory reserve volume (the additional air that can be forcibly exhaled beyond a normal breath). FRC represents the lung volume at which the outward elastic recoil of the chest wall balances the inward elastic recoil of the lungs, and it is clinically important because it is reduced in restrictive lung diseases and increased in obstructive diseases like emphysema.

incorrectas.B: Inspiratory capacity is the sum of tidal volume and inspiratory reserve volume — the maximum air that can be inhaled starting from a normal resting expiratory level — which is a completely different combination of volumes than the RV + ERV that defines FRC.
incorrectas.C: Vital capacity is the sum of tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, and expiratory reserve volume (everything except residual volume), representing the maximum air that can be exhaled after a maximal inhalation, not the RV + ERV sum described in the question.
incorrectas.D: Total lung capacity is the sum of all four lung volumes (tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, expiratory reserve volume, and residual volume) representing the maximum air the lungs can hold, which is a larger and different combination than just RV plus ERV.

preguntas.q: What is the term for the volume of gas remaining in the lungs after a normal (quiet) expiration?

e.correcta: Functional residual capacity (FRC) is defined as the volume of air remaining in the lungs at the end of a normal, passive expiration, and it represents the equilibrium point where the outward elastic recoil of the chest wall exactly balances the inward elastic recoil of the lungs. FRC is clinically important because it serves as the baseline lung volume during quiet breathing and determines the oxygen reserve available during periods of apnea (e.g., intubation), and it is reduced in restrictive lung disease and increased in obstructive lung disease (air trapping).

incorrectas.B: Residual volume is the air that remains in the lungs after a maximal (forced) expiration, not after a normal quiet one — it is a smaller volume than FRC and cannot be measured by spirometry alone since it cannot be exhaled.
incorrectas.C: Vital capacity is the maximum amount of air that can be exhaled after a maximal inspiration, representing nearly the entire range of lung volume change, not the resting volume left after a normal breath.
incorrectas.D: Inspiratory capacity is the maximum volume that can be inhaled starting from the end of a normal expiration (tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume), describing how much more air can be taken in, not how much remains in the lungs after quiet expiration.

preguntas.q: The sum of tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, and expiratory reserve volume is known as which of the following?

e.correcta: Vital capacity is defined as the sum of tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, and expiratory reserve volume — essentially the total volume of air that can be moved in a single maximal breath in and maximal breath out, excluding the residual volume that always remains in the lungs. It represents the functional breathing capacity used in clinical pulmonary function testing to assess restrictive versus obstructive lung disease, since it can be measured directly by spirometry (unlike volumes that include residual volume).

incorrectas.B: Total lung capacity is vital capacity plus residual volume (the air that cannot be exhaled), representing the absolute maximum volume the lungs can hold — it includes an additional component (RV) beyond the three volumes listed in the question.
incorrectas.C: Functional residual capacity is the sum of expiratory reserve volume and residual volume — the volume remaining in the lungs after a normal (not maximal) exhalation — which is a different combination of volumes than the one described.
incorrectas.D: Inspiratory capacity is the sum of tidal volume and inspiratory reserve volume only, omitting expiratory reserve volume, so it captures only the inspiratory side rather than the full maximal breath cycle described in the question.

preguntas.q: What is the term for the maximum volume of gas that can be expired after a maximal inspiration?

e.correcta: (Forced) vital capacity is defined as the maximum volume of air that can be forcibly exhaled after a maximal inhalation, calculated as IRV + TV + ERV. It reflects the full usable range of lung volume during voluntary breathing (everything except the residual volume that can never be expelled) and is a key spirometric measurement used to assess restrictive lung disease, where FVC is characteristically reduced due to reduced lung compliance or chest wall/muscular limitations.

incorrectas.B: Tidal volume is only the volume of air moved in a single normal, quiet breath (about 500 mL), far smaller than the total volume achievable with maximal inspiratory and expiratory effort that defines vital capacity.
incorrectas.C: Functional residual capacity is the volume remaining in the lungs after a normal (not maximal) expiration, equal to ERV + RV — it includes air that stays in the lungs and cannot be forcibly expired, unlike vital capacity which by definition is the air that can be expired.
incorrectas.D: Residual volume is the air that remains in the lungs even after a maximal forced expiration and by definition cannot be exhaled — it cannot be measured by spirometry alone and is the volume left over once vital capacity has been expired.

preguntas.q: The sum of tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, expiratory reserve volume, and residual volume is known as which of the following?

e.correcta: Total lung capacity (TLC) is defined as the sum of all four lung volumes — tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, expiratory reserve volume, and residual volume — representing the maximum air the lungs can hold after a full inspiration. Because residual volume cannot be exhaled, TLC (unlike vital capacity) can only be measured indirectly, using techniques like body plethysmography or helium dilution, not simple spirometry.

incorrectas.B: Vital capacity is TLC minus residual volume (TV + IRV + ERV), representing the maximum air that can be voluntarily moved in and out of the lungs, but it excludes residual volume and thus is not the sum of all four volumes.
incorrectas.C: Functional residual capacity is ERV + RV, the volume remaining in the lungs after a normal tidal exhalation, which is only two of the four volumes, not the full sum described in the question.
incorrectas.D: Inspiratory capacity is TV + IRV, the maximum air that can be inhaled after a normal tidal exhalation, representing only two of the four lung volumes rather than their complete sum.

preguntas.q: What is the term for the volume of gas present in the lungs after a maximal inspiration?

e.correcta: Total lung capacity (TLC) is defined as the maximum volume of air the lungs can hold, reached after a maximal inspiration, and it equals the sum of all four lung volumes (residual volume, expiratory reserve volume, tidal volume, and inspiratory reserve volume). TLC is a key spirometric/plethysmographic parameter used to distinguish restrictive lung disease (decreased TLC, as in pulmonary fibrosis) from obstructive lung disease (normal or increased TLC due to air trapping, as in emphysema), making it clinically essential for interpreting pulmonary function tests.

incorrectas.B: Vital capacity is the maximum volume that can be exhaled after a maximal inspiration — it excludes the residual volume that remains in the lungs even after maximal expiration, so it is less than TLC, not equal to the volume present after maximal inspiration.
incorrectas.C: Inspiratory capacity is the maximum volume that can be inhaled starting from the resting end-expiratory position (tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume), which is only a portion of the total lung volume present at maximal inspiration, not the entire capacity.
incorrectas.D: Functional residual capacity is the volume remaining in the lungs after a normal (not maximal) expiration, equal to residual volume plus expiratory reserve volume — this reflects resting lung volume, not the volume at maximal inspiration.

preguntas.q: Which lung capacities cannot be measured directly by spirometry?

o.A: Functional residual capacity and total lung capacity
o.C: Tidal volume and inspiratory reserve volume
o.D: Expiratory reserve volume and vital capacity

e.correcta: Functional residual capacity (FRC) and total lung capacity (TLC) both include residual volume (RV), the air that remains in the lungs after maximal exhalation and can never be exhaled, so it cannot be measured by spirometry, which only detects volumes of air that move in and out of the lungs. These values must instead be measured indirectly using techniques like body plethysmography, helium dilution, or nitrogen washout.

incorrectas.B: Vital capacity and inspiratory capacity are both measurable by spirometry because they represent air that can be actively inhaled or exhaled (VC = IRV + TV + ERV; IC = TV + IRV), containing no residual volume component.
incorrectas.C: Tidal volume and inspiratory reserve volume are both directly measurable by spirometry since they involve air the patient actively breathes in and out during normal and forced inspiration, respectively.
incorrectas.D: Expiratory reserve volume and vital capacity are both spirometry-measurable volumes/capacities because they consist entirely of air that can be voluntarily exhaled, with no trapped residual volume included.

preguntas.q: What is the typical normal value for anatomic dead space?

e.correcta: Anatomic dead space, the volume of the conducting airways (nose through terminal bronchioles) that does not participate in gas exchange, is typically about 150 mL in an average adult, roughly corresponding to 1 mL per pound (or ~2.2 mL/kg) of ideal body weight. This value matters physiologically because it is subtracted from tidal volume when calculating alveolar ventilation (VA = (VT − VD) × respiratory rate), which is the ventilation that actually contributes to gas exchange.

incorrectas.B: 500 mL is the approximate value of a normal resting tidal volume (VT), not the anatomic dead space — confusing these two would significantly overestimate how much of each breath fails to reach gas-exchanging alveoli.
incorrectas.C: 1200 mL is in the range of expiratory reserve volume, a component of the volume that can still be exhaled after a normal tidal breath, and has nothing to do with the fixed anatomic dead space of the conducting airways.
incorrectas.D: 3000 mL approximates inspiratory reserve volume in a healthy adult, the additional air that can be inhaled beyond a normal tidal breath, which is unrelated to the dead space volume of non-gas-exchanging airways.

preguntas.q: The large airways containing the nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, and bronchi belong to which functional zone of the lung?

e.correcta: The conducting zone comprises the nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, and bronchioles down to the terminal bronchioles — airways that have no alveoli and thus perform no gas exchange, instead serving to warm, humidify, and filter air while contributing to anatomic dead space. This is distinguished from the respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli), where actual gas exchange occurs across the thin alveolar-capillary membrane.

incorrectas.B: The respiratory zone is where gas exchange actually takes place (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs), which is distinct from and distal to the conducting zone airways listed in the question, none of which participate in gas exchange.
incorrectas.C: 'Transitional zone' is not one of the two standard functional lung zones taught (conducting vs. respiratory); the respiratory bronchioles are sometimes described as a transition point between the zones, but this is not the term for the large airways listed here.
incorrectas.D: 'Alveolar zone' is not the standard terminology used; the gas-exchanging region is properly called the respiratory zone, and in any case the airways listed in the question (nose through bronchi) are proximal conducting structures, not alveolar structures.

preguntas.q: The small airways that consist of bronchioles further dividing into terminal bronchioles belong to which zone of the lung?

e.correcta: The conducting zone comprises the airways whose sole function is to transport air without participating in gas exchange, extending from the trachea through bronchi, bronchioles, and terminal bronchioles; these airways are lined by epithelium and surrounded by structures (cartilage in larger airways, smooth muscle in smaller ones) suited for airflow regulation rather than diffusion, which is why they contain anatomic dead space. Gas exchange only begins once the airway epithelium transitions to alveolar epithelium in the subsequent respiratory zone.

incorrectas.B: The respiratory zone begins at the respiratory bronchioles and includes alveolar ducts and alveoli, the sites where actual gas exchange with pulmonary capillaries occurs, structurally distinguished from the terminal bronchioles by the presence of alveoli budding off the airway walls.
incorrectas.C: Alveolar zone is not a standard formal division used in this classic conducting versus respiratory zone framework; the alveoli themselves are considered part of the respiratory zone rather than a separately named zone.
incorrectas.D: Exchange zone is not the standard terminology used in this anatomical classification; the correct paired term for the gas-exchanging airway segment is the respiratory zone, not 'exchange zone.'

preguntas.q: Which zone of the lung is responsible for warming, humidifying, and filtering inspired air?

e.correcta: The conducting zone (nose through terminal bronchioles) is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells and a rich submucosal vascular plexus, which together warm, humidify, and filter incoming air before it reaches the alveoli. Because this zone contains no alveoli, it also constitutes anatomic dead space, participating in air conditioning but not in gas exchange.

incorrectas.B: The respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli) is where actual gas exchange occurs across the thin blood-air barrier; it is not specialized for warming or filtering air, which has already been conditioned upstream.
incorrectas.C: "Cortical zone" is not a recognized anatomical division of the respiratory tract (it is a term more associated with organs like kidney or adrenal gland), so it plays no role in air conditioning within the lung.
incorrectas.D: "Perfusion zone" refers to blood flow distribution concepts in the lung (as in the West zones of ventilation-perfusion matching), not to a structural zone responsible for humidifying or filtering inspired air.

preguntas.q: Does the conducting zone of the lung participate in gas exchange?

o.A: No, it only conducts and conditions air
o.B: Yes, it is the primary site of gas exchange
o.D: Yes, but only in the terminal bronchioles

e.correcta: The conducting zone (trachea through terminal bronchioles) has no alveoli and is lined by tissue too thick for effective diffusion, so its job is purely to conduct, warm, humidify, and filter air on its way to the respiratory zone. This anatomic dead space matters clinically because it doesn't contribute to gas exchange volume — it's the reason tidal volume must exceed anatomic dead space to achieve effective alveolar ventilation.

incorrectas.B: Gas exchange occurs in the respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli) where the epithelium is thin enough and surface area large enough for diffusion — the conducting zone lacks these features entirely.
incorrectas.C: The conducting zone's function doesn't change with exercise; what changes is the rate and depth of ventilation and recruitment of additional alveoli/capillaries in the respiratory zone, not gas exchange occurring more proximally.
incorrectas.D: Terminal bronchioles are the most distal part of the conducting zone and still lack alveoli — true gas exchange only begins at the respiratory bronchioles, one generation further along.

preguntas.q: Airway smooth muscle cells extend distally to which structure, becoming sparse beyond this point in the conducting zone?

e.correcta: Smooth muscle wraps the airway walls from the trachea down through the bronchi and bronchioles, but it thins out progressively and becomes sparse at the level of the terminal bronchioles, the last purely conducting (non-gas-exchanging) airways before the respiratory zone begins. This is clinically important because bronchoconstriction in asthma acts on this smooth muscle distribution, so airway narrowing is most pronounced in the small bronchi and bronchioles proximal to this point, producing the wheezing and air-trapping typical of an asthma exacerbation.

incorrectas.B: Alveolar sacs are the terminal gas-exchange structures made of thin squamous epithelium for diffusion, not muscular walls — smooth muscle has essentially disappeared long before air reaches this level, replaced by the thin alveolar septa needed for efficient gas exchange.
incorrectas.C: The trachea does contain smooth muscle (the trachealis muscle posteriorly, connecting the ends of the cartilage rings), but the question asks how distally the muscle extends, and the trachea is the most proximal airway, not the distal limit.
incorrectas.D: The pharynx is upper airway/oropharyngeal tissue proximal to the trachea entirely; it contains skeletal (not smooth) muscle for swallowing and airway protection, and is not part of the conducting zone smooth muscle continuum being described.

preguntas.q: What effect does sympathetic innervation have on the smooth muscle of the conducting airways?

e.correcta: Sympathetic stimulation acts on beta-2 adrenergic receptors on airway smooth muscle, activating Gs protein, increasing cAMP, and causing smooth muscle relaxation and bronchodilation — this is why beta-2 agonists like albuterol are used to relieve bronchospasm in asthma, mimicking sympathetic tone. This is a somewhat atypical sympathetic effect (most sympathetic actions are 'fight or flight' activating), but it makes physiologic sense: dilating airways increases airflow to support increased oxygen demand during exertion.

incorrectas.B: Bronchoconstriction of airway smooth muscle is mediated by the parasympathetic system via vagal M3 muscarinic receptors (Gq, increased IP3/Ca2+), which is the opposite autonomic input from sympathetic stimulation — this is why anticholinergics like ipratropium are also used as bronchodilators.
incorrectas.C: Airway smooth muscle tone is actively modulated by both autonomic divisions with opposing effects; sympathetic input does have a clear physiologic effect (bronchodilation via beta-2 receptors), so 'no effect' misses this well-established mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Increased mucus secretion in the airways is a parasympathetic (muscarinic-mediated) effect on submucosal glands, not a sympathetic one; sympathetic stimulation instead tends to decrease secretions, so this does not describe the correct autonomic pairing.

preguntas.q: What effect does parasympathetic innervation have on the smooth muscle of the conducting airways?

e.correcta: Parasympathetic innervation to the airways, via the vagus nerve acting on M3 muscarinic receptors on airway smooth muscle, causes bronchoconstriction and increased mucus secretion, part of the 'rest and digest' pattern of increased secretory/motor activity. This is the physiologic basis for using anticholinergic bronchodilators (like ipratropium and tiotropium) in obstructive lung diseases such as COPD, since blocking this parasympathetic tone relieves bronchoconstriction.

incorrectas.B: Relaxation (bronchodilation) of airway smooth muscle is mediated by the sympathetic nervous system, specifically beta-2 adrenergic receptor activation (via Gs/cAMP), not by parasympathetic input.
incorrectas.C: Parasympathetic input has a clear, well-defined effect on airway smooth muscle tone (bronchoconstriction via M3 receptors) — 'no effect' contradicts the basis for anticholinergic bronchodilator therapy.
incorrectas.D: Parasympathetic stimulation actually increases mucus secretion from bronchial glands (not decreases it), working alongside bronchoconstriction as part of the same cholinergic pathway.

preguntas.q: The respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveolar sacs together make up which zone of the lung?

e.correcta: The respiratory zone comprises the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveolar sacs — the structures where actual gas exchange occurs across the thin alveolar-capillary membrane, distinguishing this zone functionally from the preceding conducting airways that merely transport air without participating in gas exchange. Recognizing this distinction matters clinically because diseases affecting the respiratory zone (e.g., emphysema, ARDS) directly impair oxygenation, whereas conducting zone pathology (e.g., bronchitis, asthma) primarily affects airflow/resistance.

incorrectas.B: The conducting zone includes the trachea, bronchi, and terminal bronchioles — structures that warm, humidify, and filter air while conducting it toward the respiratory zone, but that contain no alveoli and do not participate in gas exchange themselves.
incorrectas.C: 'Transitional zone' is not a standard formal division of the respiratory tract in this classification; the respiratory bronchioles are sometimes described as transitional in character but the tract is formally divided into conducting and respiratory zones, with the described structures belonging to the respiratory zone.
incorrectas.D: 'Bronchial zone' is not a recognized standard anatomical division of the lung; the named structures (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs) are specifically classified under the respiratory zone due to their gas-exchange function.

preguntas.q: Does the respiratory zone of the lung participate in gas exchange?

o.A: Yes, it is the site of gas exchange
o.D: Yes, but only during forced expiration

e.correcta: The respiratory zone includes respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli — the structures where alveolar walls are thin enough and closely apposed to pulmonary capillaries to allow diffusion of O2 and CO2. This is in contrast to the conducting zone (trachea through terminal bronchioles), which has no alveoli and instead warms, humidifies, and filters air while contributing to anatomic dead space. The distinction matters clinically because diseases affecting the respiratory zone (e.g., emphysema, ARDS) directly impair gas exchange, whereas conducting zone diseases (e.g., bronchitis) primarily affect airflow.

incorrectas.B: "Only conducts air" describes the conducting zone (trachea, bronchi, bronchioles down to terminal bronchioles), which lacks alveoli and does not participate in gas exchange — this is the opposite of the respiratory zone's function.
incorrectas.C: Humidification of air is a function of the conducting zone (aided by nasal turbinates and bronchial mucosa), not the respiratory zone, which is specialized for diffusion rather than air conditioning.
incorrectas.D: Gas exchange in the respiratory zone is continuous throughout the respiratory cycle, not restricted to forced expiration; alveolar diffusion occurs during both quiet and forced breathing as long as ventilation and perfusion are matched.

preguntas.q: Which part of the respiratory zone still contains some smooth muscle?

e.correcta: Respiratory bronchioles are the transitional zone of the lung — they still have scattered smooth muscle and a thin layer of cuboidal epithelium in their walls, but they also bear occasional alveolar outpouchings, marking the start of gas exchange. This retained smooth muscle allows respiratory bronchioles to participate in bronchoconstriction/dilation reflexes (relevant in asthma) even though they are technically part of the respiratory zone where gas exchange begins.

incorrectas.B: Alveolar ducts are distal to the respiratory bronchioles and are lined almost entirely by alveoli with only sparse smooth muscle rings at their junctions with alveolar sacs — far less than the respiratory bronchioles, so they are not the answer being tested here.
incorrectas.C: Alveolar sacs are clusters of alveoli at the terminal ends of the airway tree and consist purely of thin squamous epithelium for gas exchange, with no meaningful smooth muscle component.
incorrectas.D: Alveoli themselves are simple squamous epithelial sacs specialized purely for diffusion of O2/CO2, containing no smooth muscle at all, which is why they cannot actively constrict or dilate.

preguntas.q: Where in the respiratory tract do cilia terminate?

e.correcta: Cilia line the conducting airways to sweep mucus and trapped particles upward toward the pharynx (mucociliary escalator), but they terminate at the respiratory bronchioles, where gas exchange begins and the epithelium starts transitioning to a simpler, thinner lining suited for diffusion. Beyond this point, retaining cilia would impair the thin, low-resistance surface needed for oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange. This is clinically relevant in conditions like primary ciliary dyskinesia, where the mucociliary escalator fails proximal to this transition, causing recurrent infections and bronchiectasis.

incorrectas.B: Alveolar ducts are located distal to the respiratory bronchioles and are part of the gas-exchanging acinus, lined by thin, flattened epithelium (pneumocytes) with no cilia at all, so cilia have already disappeared before this level, not at it.
incorrectas.C: Terminal bronchioles are still part of the purely conducting zone (no alveoli), and they retain ciliated (though not fully columnar) epithelium; cilia persist beyond them into the respiratory bronchioles, so this is too proximal a stopping point.
incorrectas.D: Alveolar sacs are the most distal gas-exchange structures, clustered at the ends of alveolar ducts, and like the ducts they are lined only by pneumocytes with no ciliated cells — cilia are long gone well before reaching this level.

preguntas.q: Do the alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs have cilia?

o.A: No, cilia terminate at the respiratory bronchioles
o.C: Yes, but only the alveolar sacs are ciliated
o.D: Yes, but only the alveolar ducts are ciliated

e.correcta: Ciliated epithelium lines the airway down through the respiratory bronchioles, but as the airway transitions into alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs, the epithelium becomes simple squamous (type I and II pneumocytes) to allow efficient gas diffusion — cilia would physically obstruct the thin diffusion barrier needed for oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange. This is a key structure-function relationship in respiratory histology: mucociliary clearance protects the conducting zone, while the respiratory zone sacrifices cilia for optimal gas exchange.

incorrectas.B: Describing full ciliation of alveolar ducts and sacs contradicts the fundamental need for a thin, unobstructed gas-exchange surface — cilia would impede diffusion and are absent for this functional reason.
incorrectas.C: This reverses the actual histology — ciliated cells are found more proximally (bronchioles), not selectively retained in alveolar sacs, which instead have flattened type I pneumocytes for gas exchange.
incorrectas.D: This is also incorrect for the same reason — alveolar ducts, like alveolar sacs, are part of the respiratory zone and lack cilia to preserve a minimal diffusion distance for gas exchange.

preguntas.q: Which muscle is the most important for inspiration?

e.correcta: The diaphragm is the primary muscle of quiet inspiration, contracting to flatten and descend, which increases the vertical dimension of the thoracic cavity and creates the negative intrapleural pressure gradient needed to draw air into the lungs. It accounts for the majority of tidal volume during normal breathing and is innervated by the phrenic nerve (C3-C5) — a fact clinically relevant because high cervical spinal cord injuries above this level can cause fatal respiratory failure.

incorrectas.B: External intercostals assist inspiration by elevating the ribs (a 'bucket handle' motion that increases the lateral/anteroposterior thoracic diameter), but they play a secondary, supportive role compared to the diaphragm, which is responsible for the majority of resting tidal breathing.
incorrectas.C: The sternocleidomastoid is an accessory muscle of inspiration, recruited only during forceful or labored breathing (e.g., respiratory distress) to help elevate the sternum, and is not active or important during normal quiet breathing.
incorrectas.D: The scalene muscles are also accessory inspiratory muscles that elevate the first two ribs during deep or labored breathing, but like the sternocleidomastoid, they are not engaged during normal resting respiration and are secondary to the diaphragm.

preguntas.q: When the diaphragm contracts during inspiration, in which direction are the abdominal contents pushed?

e.correcta: When the diaphragm contracts, its dome flattens and moves caudally, which pushes the abdominal viscera downward and outward while simultaneously expanding thoracic volume — this drop in intrathoracic pressure is what drives air into the lungs. This is why abdominal wall movement (outward bulge) during inspiration is a clinical sign of diaphragmatic (rather than purely intercostal) breathing.

incorrectas.B: Upward displacement of abdominal contents would occur with diaphragmatic relaxation during expiration (the dome rises back up), not with contraction during inspiration.
incorrectas.C: While the abdominal wall does bulge outward as intra-abdominal pressure rises, the primary displacement described in this classic mechanism is caudal (downward) movement of the diaphragm itself, not purely lateral movement.
incorrectas.D: Abdominal contents are actively displaced with each diaphragmatic contraction — the diaphragm's excursion is the main driver of tidal breathing at rest, so contents are far from unchanged.

preguntas.q: What muscles are normally used for expiration at rest?

e.correcta: At rest, expiration is a passive process driven entirely by the elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall after inspiratory muscles (diaphragm, external intercostals) relax — no active muscle contraction is required to expel air. This is why resting expiration takes longer than inspiration and why increased expiratory effort (using internal intercostals and abdominal muscles) is only recruited during exercise or forced expiration when demand exceeds what passive recoil can achieve.

incorrectas.B: Internal intercostals and abdominal muscles are indeed used for expiration, but only during forced/active expiration (e.g., exercise, coughing), not during quiet resting breathing, which relies solely on passive recoil.
