This vasoactive property, alongside their role in mediating pain and fever, underlies why NSAIDs (which block prostaglandin synthesis via COX inhibition) reduce swelling, redness, and pain in inflamed tissue.

incorrectas.B: Decreased vascular permeability would be an anti-inflammatory effect, but prostaglandins are pro-inflammatory mediators that enhance rather than reduce vessel leakiness during the inflammatory response, which is precisely why blocking their synthesis reduces edema.
incorrectas.C: No effect on permeability would be inconsistent with prostaglandins' well-established role as vasoactive mediators in inflammation; their contribution to redness, warmth, and swelling depends directly on increasing vascular permeability and blood flow.
incorrectas.D: Restricting the effect only to lymphatics misrepresents prostaglandins' primary action, which is on blood vessel postcapillary venules (increasing permeability there), not selectively on the lymphatic system.

preguntas.q: In general, leukotrienes cause which vascular effect?

e.correcta: Leukotrienes, particularly LTC4, LTD4, and LTE4 (the cysteinyl leukotrienes), are potent vasoconstrictors as well as bronchoconstrictors and mediators of increased vascular permeability, produced via the 5-lipoxygenase pathway of arachidonic acid metabolism. This vasoconstrictive action contrasts with prostaglandins like PGI2 and PGE2, which generally cause vasodilation, illustrating how different arachidonic acid metabolites can have opposing vascular effects depending on the enzymatic pathway (lipoxygenase vs. cyclooxygenase) that produced them.

incorrectas.B: Vasodilation is the effect more characteristic of prostaglandins (like PGE2 and PGI2) and histamine, not leukotrienes, which act through the lipoxygenase pathway to constrict vascular smooth muscle rather than relax it.
incorrectas.C: No change in vascular tone misrepresents leukotrienes' well-documented pharmacologic activity; they are potent bioactive lipids with a clear vasoconstrictive (and bronchoconstrictive) effect, not inert with respect to vascular tone.
incorrectas.D: Selective arteriolar dilation only is inaccurate because leukotrienes cause vasoconstriction, not dilation, and their vascular permeability effects extend beyond arterioles to postcapillary venules, unlike a narrowly selective arteriolar dilating action.

preguntas.q: In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), the renal cysts are typically:

o.C: Confined to a single pole of one kidney
o.D: Limited to the renal pelvis only

e.correcta: ADPKD results from mutations in PKD1 or PKD2 (affecting polycystin proteins), which are expressed in tubular epithelial cells throughout both kidneys, so cysts develop bilaterally and progressively enlarge both kidneys over time, often leading to massive bilateral flank masses and eventual end-stage renal disease. This bilateral, diffuse cystic involvement — often with associated extrarenal manifestations like intracranial berry aneurysms and hepatic cysts — is a hallmark that distinguishes ADPKD from acquired or localized cystic kidney conditions.

incorrectas.A: Unilateral cyst involvement is inconsistent with ADPKD's genetic, systemic nature — because the causative mutation (PKD1/PKD2) affects tubular cells throughout the body, both kidneys develop cysts, not just one.
incorrectas.C: ADPKD cysts are not confined to a single pole of one kidney; they are diffusely distributed throughout the parenchyma of both kidneys, ultimately distorting the entire renal architecture bilaterally.
incorrectas.D: ADPKD cysts arise from renal tubules throughout the cortex and medulla of both kidneys, not from the renal pelvis (a collecting structure) — pelvic-confined cystic change is not characteristic of this disease.

preguntas.q: Is polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) an inherited/heritable condition?

o.B: No, it is always sporadic with no genetic basis
o.C: Only rarely, in less than 1% of cases
o.D: It results solely from environmental toxin exposure

e.correcta: ADPKD is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in PKD1 (85% of cases, chromosome 16) or PKD2 (chromosome 4), which encode polycystin-1 and polycystin-2 proteins involved in tubular epithelial cell signaling and cilia function; loss of normal polycystin function leads to progressive cyst formation. Because it is autosomal dominant, each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the disease, making family history a key diagnostic clue.

incorrectas.B: ADPKD is a well-characterized single-gene (PKD1/PKD2) disorder with a clear Mendelian inheritance pattern, not a sporadic condition — the vast majority of cases can be traced through an affected parent, and genetic testing confirms causative mutations.
incorrectas.C: This grossly understates the heritability — ADPKD is the most common inherited cause of kidney failure requiring dialysis/transplant, with the overwhelming majority of cases showing clear autosomal dominant transmission (de novo mutations account for only a small minority).
incorrectas.D: There is no evidence that environmental toxins cause ADPKD; the disease is driven by specific germline mutations in polycystin-encoding genes, distinguishing it from acquired cystic kidney disease seen in some other contexts (e.g., long-term dialysis).

preguntas.q: Is polycystic kidney disease associated with enlargement of the kidneys?

e.correcta: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is characterized by progressive development of numerous fluid-filled cysts (from PKD1 or PKD2 mutations affecting polycystin, which normally regulates tubular epithelial cell growth and fluid secretion) that enlarge the kidneys massively, sometimes to many times normal size, and can be palpable as bilateral flank masses. This distinguishes it from many other chronic kidney diseases, which typically cause the kidneys to shrink as nephrons are lost and replaced by scar tissue.

incorrectas.B: Kidney size is markedly affected in PKD — the hallmark finding on imaging is bilateral, dramatically enlarged kidneys studded with cysts, which is actually one of the classic teaching points that differentiates PKD from most other causes of chronic renal failure.
incorrectas.C: Shrinkage and atrophy describe end-stage kidney disease from chronic glomerulonephritis or long-standing hypertensive/diabetic nephropathy, where nephron loss leads to scarring and a small kidney — this is the opposite of what happens in PKD, where progressive cyst formation enlarges the kidney.
incorrectas.D: PKD is a bilateral, symmetric process — both kidneys develop cysts and enlarge together because the underlying genetic defect (in PKD1/PKD2) is present in all renal tubular cells, not localized to one side.

preguntas.q: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is characterized by cysts located in which two renal regions?

e.correcta: In ADPKD, cysts arise from any portion of the nephron and progressively involve both the cortex and medulla, causing diffuse bilateral enlargement of the kidneys as fluid-filled cysts derived from tubular epithelium (driven by mutated polycystin-1 or polycystin-2) accumulate throughout the renal parenchyma. This diffuse cortical and medullary cyst distribution, seen as massively enlarged kidneys studded with cysts on imaging, is a hallmark distinguishing ADPKD from other cystic kidney diseases with more restricted cyst locations.

incorrectas.B: The renal pelvis and ureter are the collecting/drainage structures of the urinary tract, not sites of cyst formation in ADPKD; cysts in ADPKD originate from nephron tubular epithelium within the renal parenchyma itself, not the pelvicalyceal or ureteral lining.
incorrectas.C: Confining cysts to the glomerulus alone does not reflect ADPKD pathology; cysts in ADPKD arise from tubular segments throughout the nephron and affect both cortex and medulla diffusely, not an isolated glomerular compartment.
incorrectas.D: The renal capsule and hilum are structural/investing and vascular-entry regions of the kidney, not the parenchymal sites where ADPKD cysts form; the disease process is centered on cortical and medullary tubular epithelium, not these peripheral structures.

preguntas.q: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) is characterized by cystic dilation of which renal structure?

e.correcta: ARPKD results from PKHD1 gene mutations affecting fibrocystin, leading to cystic dilation of the renal collecting ducts, typically presenting in infancy with enlarged echogenic kidneys and often associated with congenital hepatic fibrosis and pulmonary hypoplasia (from oligohydramnios due to poor fetal urine output, i.e., Potter sequence). This distinguishes it from ADPKD, where cysts arise from any part of the nephron and clinical disease usually manifests in adulthood.

incorrectas.B: ARPKD is a tubular/collecting duct disease, not a vascular one — the renal artery is not the structure undergoing cystic transformation in this condition.
incorrectas.C: Glomerular capillaries are not the primary site of cyst formation in ARPKD; the pathology centers on the collecting ducts, which is why the presentation includes bilateral, diffusely enlarged kidneys with radially oriented cysts rather than glomerular destruction as the initial lesion.
incorrectas.D: Bowman's capsule is part of the glomerular filtration apparatus and is not the structure that dilates into cysts in ARPKD — the disease specifically targets the collecting duct system derived from the ureteric bud.

preguntas.q: Autosomal recessive PKD presents in infants as worsening renal failure and which additional finding?

e.correcta: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD, due to PKHD1 mutations) presents in infancy with enlarged, cystic kidneys causing progressive renal failure, and is classically associated with hypertension due to renin release from the cystic, ischemic renal parenchyma — this early hypertension, combined with oligohydramnios-related pulmonary hypoplasia (Potter sequence) and congenital hepatic fibrosis, forms the classic clinical picture distinguishing ARPKD from the adult-onset autosomal dominant form.

incorrectas.B: Hyperglycemia is not a recognized feature of ARPKD; the disease's systemic complications relate to renal and hepatic fibrosis and secondary hypertension, not glucose metabolism.
incorrectas.C: Hypocalcemia is not classically associated with ARPKD in infancy; while chronic kidney disease can eventually cause calcium-phosphate derangements, the hallmark early finding paired with renal failure in ARPKD is hypertension, not hypocalcemia.
incorrectas.D: Hyperthyroidism has no established association with ARPKD; the disease's endocrine-adjacent manifestation is renin-mediated hypertension from cystic renal tissue, not thyroid dysfunction.

preguntas.q: Which form(s) of polycystic kidney disease are associated with hepatic cysts?

o.C: Both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive PKD
o.D: Neither form is associated with hepatic cysts

e.correcta: Both autosomal dominant PKD (PKD1/PKD2 mutations) and autosomal recessive PKD (PKHD1 mutations) can produce hepatic cysts, because the same polycystin/fibrocystin pathway abnormalities that disrupt tubular epithelial architecture in the kidney also affect biliary duct epithelium in the liver, leading to cystic dilation there as well. In ARPKD specifically, congenital hepatic fibrosis and biliary dysgenesis are a major part of the clinical picture, while in ADPKD hepatic cysts are a common but usually less clinically severe extrarenal manifestation.

incorrectas.A: Restricting the association to only ADPKD ignores that ARPKD also causes hepatic involvement — in fact, hepatic fibrosis is often the dominant feature determining long-term prognosis in ARPKD, especially in patients who survive the neonatal period.
incorrectas.B: Restricting the association to only ARPKD is incomplete — hepatic (and other) cysts are also a well-recognized extrarenal manifestation of ADPKD, alongside berry aneurysms and cysts in other organs like the pancreas.
incorrectas.D: Saying neither form is associated with hepatic cysts is incorrect — hepatic cystic/fibrotic involvement is a hallmark extrarenal feature of both forms of PKD, just with different characteristic patterns (fibrosis in ARPKD, cysts in ADPKD).

preguntas.q: Which congenital renal defect may cause portal hypertension in an infant?

e.correcta: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) is associated with congenital hepatic fibrosis due to abnormal development of the ductal plate, which leads to periportal fibrosis that can progress to clinically significant portal hypertension (with resulting complications like esophageal varices and splenomegaly) even in infancy. This combination of enlarged, cystic kidneys presenting in infancy alongside hepatic fibrosis and portal hypertension is a classic PKD1L1/PKHD1-related finding that distinguishes ARPKD from its adult-onset autosomal dominant counterpart.

incorrectas.B: Autosomal dominant PKD typically presents in adulthood (30s-40s) with progressive renal cystic disease and is associated with berry aneurysms and hepatic cysts (not the ductal plate malformation/fibrosis that causes portal hypertension), making infantile portal hypertension inconsistent with this diagnosis.
incorrectas.C: A simple renal cyst is typically an incidental, benign finding without an associated hepatic developmental abnormality, and it does not cause any liver fibrosis or portal hypertension.
incorrectas.D: Renal agenesis refers to the complete absence of one or both kidneys during development (associated with oligohydramnios and Potter sequence when bilateral), which has no established link to hepatic ductal plate malformation or portal hypertension.

preguntas.q: Autosomal dominant PKD may present in young adults with which type of pain, along with urinary infection?

e.correcta: In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), progressively enlarging cortical and medullary cysts stretch the renal capsule and collecting system, producing flank pain, and cysts are also prone to hemorrhage, infection, or obstructing stones — all of which classically present as flank pain alongside urinary tract infection symptoms in young adults. This combination of flank pain plus UTI (sometimes with hematuria) is a hallmark early presentation that should prompt renal ultrasound to look for the characteristic multiple bilateral cysts.

incorrectas.B: Suprapubic pain is more typical of lower urinary tract or bladder pathology (e.g., cystitis), not the flank/costovertebral angle pain produced by enlarging renal cysts distending the kidney capsule in ADPKD.
incorrectas.C: Chest pain is not a typical renal symptom of ADPKD; while ADPKD is associated with intracranial berry aneurysms and mitral valve prolapse, the pain classically described alongside UTI in this disease is flank pain from the kidneys themselves.
incorrectas.D: Periumbilical pain is a nonspecific visceral pain pattern (classically associated with early appendicitis) and is not the localization associated with cyst-related distention of the kidneys, which refers pain to the flank/costovertebral region instead.

preguntas.q: Autosomal dominant PKD may present in young adults as worsening renal failure and which urinary finding?

e.correcta: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease causes progressive cyst formation and enlargement in the renal parenchyma, and as cysts expand they can rupture into the collecting system, producing gross or microscopic hematuria along with flank pain — a classic presenting feature in young adults alongside progressive renal failure and hypertension. This finding, combined with a family history and bilateral flank masses, should prompt renal ultrasound to look for the characteristic enlarged kidneys studded with multiple cysts, and screening for associated berry aneurysms given the shared connective tissue/ciliary protein defects (PKD1/PKD2 mutations affecting polycystin).

incorrectas.B: Glucosuria typically reflects hyperglycemia exceeding the renal glucose reabsorption threshold (as in diabetes mellitus) or a proximal tubular defect (e.g., Fanconi syndrome), not the cystic architectural disruption and vascular fragility seen in ADPKD.
incorrectas.C: Pyuria without infection suggests interstitial nephritis or other inflammatory processes, not the vascular disruption from cyst rupture that produces the hematuria classically associated with ADPKD.
incorrectas.D: Ketonuria reflects fat metabolism during states of carbohydrate deprivation (fasting, diabetic ketoacidosis) and has no relationship to the structural cystic and vascular changes of polycystic kidney disease.

preguntas.q: What percentage of patients with autosomal dominant PKD experience progressive renal failure (reaching end-stage renal disease by age 70)?

e.correcta: About 50% of ADPKD patients progress to end-stage renal disease by around age 70, reflecting the gradual replacement of functioning renal parenchyma by expanding cysts (driven by PKD1 or PKD2 mutations affecting polycystin proteins that regulate tubular cell proliferation and fluid secretion) until nephron mass can no longer sustain adequate GFR. This roughly 50% lifetime risk is why ADPKD patients require lifelong surveillance of renal function and blood pressure, since hypertension from cyst-related renin activation accelerates the decline.

incorrectas.B: 10% would understate the true burden of progressive nephron loss in ADPKD; the disease's natural history involves steady cyst growth over decades, making a low single-digit progression rate to ESRD inconsistent with its well-documented course.
incorrectas.C: 90% overstates the proportion who progress to ESRD by this age; genetic variability (PKD1 versus the generally milder PKD2 mutations) and variable rates of cyst growth mean roughly half, not nearly all, patients reach ESRD by 70.
incorrectas.D: 25% underestimates the substantial proportion of ADPKD patients who develop progressive renal failure; this figure is too low given how consistently cyst burden accumulates and compromises renal function over a typical lifespan.

preguntas.q: Autosomal dominant PKD is associated with which vascular abnormality that is an important cause of death?

e.correcta: ADPKD is associated with intracranial (berry) aneurysms, thought to arise from a shared defect in vascular connective tissue related to abnormal polycystin function in vascular smooth muscle and endothelium. Rupture of these aneurysms causes subarachnoid hemorrhage, which is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in ADPKD patients, so many guidelines recommend screening (MR angiography) in those with a family history of aneurysm or rupture.

incorrectas.B: Aortic dissection is classically associated with connective tissue disorders like Marfan syndrome or with severe hypertension causing intimal tears in the aorta — it is not the vascular complication specifically linked to ADPKD's polycystin defect.
incorrectas.C: Deep vein thrombosis is a venous thromboembolic phenomenon related to stasis, hypercoagulability, or vessel wall injury (Virchow's triad), unrelated to the arterial wall weakness caused by polycystin dysfunction in ADPKD.
incorrectas.D: Coronary artery aneurysms are characteristically seen in Kawasaki disease from vasculitis-mediated arterial wall damage, not as a recognized complication of ADPKD's polycystin-related vasculopathy.

preguntas.q: In addition to renal cysts, both autosomal dominant and recessive PKD are associated with benign cysts in which organ?

e.correcta: Both ADPKD and ARPKD are associated with benign hepatic (liver) cysts, since polycystin and fibrocystin proteins are also expressed in bile duct epithelium (cholangiocytes), leading to biliary microhamartomas and cyst formation alongside renal cysts. In ARPKD specifically, this hepatic involvement often manifests as congenital hepatic fibrosis with portal hypertension, while in ADPKD, hepatic cysts are typically asymptomatic incidental findings.

incorrectas.B: Splenic cysts are not a classic extrarenal manifestation of either ADPKD or ARPKD; the well-established extrarenal cystic organ involvement is hepatic, reflecting shared ductal epithelial expression of the disease-causing proteins.
incorrectas.C: While pancreatic cysts can occur in ADPKD, describing this as the primary or 'exclusive' associated organ ignores the much more classic and consistently emphasized hepatic cyst association shared by both ADPKD and ARPKD.
incorrectas.D: Pulmonary cysts are not a typical feature of either ADPKD or ARPKD — pulmonary problems in ARPKD instead relate to hypoplasia from oligohydramnios (Potter sequence), not cystic change in the lung itself, unlike the true cystic organ involvement seen in the liver.

preguntas.q: Which heart defect is associated with autosomal dominant PKD?

e.correcta: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is associated with an increased incidence of mitral valve prolapse, thought to relate to abnormal connective tissue/extracellular matrix effects from PKD1/PKD2 mutations affecting polycystin proteins found not just in renal tubular cells but also in cardiac valve tissue. This association is one of several extrarenal manifestations of ADPKD tested alongside berry (intracranial) aneurysms, hepatic cysts, and diverticulosis, all reflecting the systemic nature of the underlying connective tissue/ciliary protein defect.

incorrectas.B: Tetralogy of Fallot is a congenital cyanotic heart defect resulting from anterosuperior deviation of the infundibular septum during development, a distinct congenital cardiac malformation not part of the classic extrarenal ADPKD association pattern.
incorrectas.C: Atrial septal defect is a structural congenital heart lesion not classically linked to ADPKD; the cardiac association emphasized in ADPKD is specifically mitral valve prolapse.
incorrectas.D: Bicuspid aortic valve is classically associated with other conditions like Turner syndrome and coarctation of the aorta, not with the polycystin-related valvular association seen in ADPKD, which is mitral valve prolapse.

preguntas.q: When patients with autosomal dominant PKD develop hypertension or proteinuria, which medication class is used for treatment?

e.correcta: ACE inhibitors or ARBs are used to manage hypertension and proteinuria in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease because they reduce intraglomerular pressure by dilating the efferent arteriole (via blocking angiotensin II's vasoconstrictive effect), which slows glomerular hyperfiltration injury and proteinuria progression, similar to their renoprotective role in diabetic nephropathy. This makes them first-line antihypertensives in essentially any chronic kidney disease with proteinuria, including ADPKD, unless contraindicated.

incorrectas.B: Thiazide diuretics are not first-line in ADPKD-related hypertension; they lack the specific renoprotective effect on intraglomerular pressure that ACE inhibitors/ARBs provide and are generally reserved as add-on agents rather than initial therapy in this proteinuric, RAAS-driven context.
incorrectas.C: Beta-blockers are not the exclusive or preferred treatment for ADPKD-associated hypertension; while they can be used as adjuncts, they do not address the intraglomerular hemodynamic mechanism that makes RAAS blockade uniquely effective at reducing proteinuria in this disease.
incorrectas.D: Calcium channel blockers are not used exclusively in ADPKD hypertension and, notably, dihydropyridine CCBs can dilate the afferent arteriole and potentially worsen intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria, making them a less ideal choice than ACE inhibitors/ARBs in this setting.

preguntas.q: Is Autosomal Dominant Tubulointerstitial Kidney Disease (formerly Medullary Cystic Kidney Disease) a heritable condition?

o.D: It is caused exclusively by infection

e.correcta: Autosomal Dominant Tubulointerstitial Kidney Disease is, as its name states, an inherited disorder transmitted in an autosomal dominant pattern (caused by mutations in genes such as UMOD, MUC1, or REN), leading to progressive tubulointerstitial fibrosis and chronic kidney disease, often with a family history of unexplained renal failure and, in UMOD-associated cases, hyperuricemia/gout. Recognizing the heritable, dominant transmission pattern is what distinguishes this entity from acquired causes of chronic tubulointerstitial disease and helps guide family screening.

incorrectas.B: Describing it as 'purely acquired' contradicts the disease's defining feature — the 'autosomal dominant' portion of its name reflects a specific, well-characterized inherited genetic transmission pattern, not sporadic acquired renal injury.
incorrectas.C: Autosomal dominant inheritance affects males and females equally, since the responsible genes are on autosomes rather than sex chromosomes, so heritability is not restricted to females.
incorrectas.D: The disease results from inherited gene mutations affecting tubular/interstitial function, not from an infectious process — an infectious cause would not follow the autosomal dominant hereditary transmission pattern implied by its name.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of (Autosomal Dominant Tubulointerstitial Kidney Disease, formerly medullary cystic kidney disease)?

e.correcta: Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (formerly medullary cystic kidney disease) follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, most commonly due to mutations in genes like UMOD (uromodulin) or MUC1, causing progressive tubulointerstitial fibrosis and small kidneys with medullary cysts that lead to chronic kidney disease, often without the massive cyst burden or family screening ease seen in ADPKD. Recognizing the dominant pattern is important because affected families show the disease across generations without skipping, and genetic counseling reflects a 50% transmission risk to offspring.

incorrectas.B: Autosomal recessive inheritance requires both copies of a gene to be affected and typically shows disease clustering in siblings of unaffected parents (as in autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease of infancy), a different pattern from the dominant, multi-generational transmission of this tubulointerstitial disease.
incorrectas.C: X-linked recessive inheritance predominantly affects males, with carrier mothers transmitting to sons, a sex-linked pattern that does not match the autosomal, non-sex-linked transmission of this condition.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance is maternally transmitted to all offspring (since mitochondria come from the egg), a completely distinct pattern from the classic autosomal dominant pedigree seen in this kidney disease.

preguntas.q: Autosomal Dominant Tubulointerstitial Kidney Disease (ADTKD) has the potential to present with cysts in which location?

e.correcta: ADTKD (formerly known as medullary cystic kidney disease) can present with cysts located at the corticomedullary junction and within the medullary collecting ducts, alongside tubulointerstitial fibrosis that leads to progressive, often gout-associated (in UMOD-related disease), chronic kidney disease without significant proteinuria or hypertension early on. This distinguishes it from ADPKD, where cysts arise diffusely from tubules throughout the cortex and medulla and lead to massively enlarged kidneys.

incorrectas.B: ADTKD cysts are not confined to the renal cortex — they classically occur at the corticomedullary junction and within the medulla, which is part of why the historical name was 'medullary cystic kidney disease.'
incorrectas.C: The glomerular tuft is not the site of cyst formation in ADTKD; the disease is fundamentally a tubulointerstitial process, and cysts (when present) arise from tubular structures, not glomeruli.
incorrectas.D: The renal artery wall is a vascular structure, not implicated in ADTKD cyst formation; ADTKD is a tubulointerstitial disease process, not a vascular one.

preguntas.q: In the kidney, renin is synthesized, stored, and released from which structure?

e.correcta: The juxtaglomerular apparatus, composed of granular juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole wall along with the macula densa, is where renin is synthesized, stored in secretory granules, and released in response to decreased renal perfusion pressure, decreased NaCl delivery, and increased sympathetic tone. This integrated structure senses multiple signals and couples them to renin release, making it the key trigger point for the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

incorrectas.B: The macula densa is only one component of the juxtaglomerular apparatus — it senses distal tubular NaCl concentration and signals the adjacent granular cells to release renin, but the macula densa cells themselves do not store or secrete renin.
incorrectas.C: The proximal convoluted tubule is responsible for bulk reabsorption of filtered solutes and water, not for renin production; it has no secretory granules for renin.
incorrectas.D: The renal medulla interstitium is involved in the countercurrent multiplication system that concentrates urine, but it plays no role in renin synthesis or storage.

preguntas.q: Renin catalyzes the conversion of which substrate to which product?

e.correcta: Renin is a proteolytic enzyme released by juxtaglomerular cells in response to decreased renal perfusion, low sodium delivery to the macula densa, or sympathetic stimulation, and it specifically cleaves angiotensinogen (produced by the liver) into angiotensin I, the first and rate-limiting step of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Angiotensin I is subsequently converted to the active angiotensin II by ACE in the lungs, but that conversion is catalyzed by ACE, not renin. Understanding renin's specific substrate and product is essential for understanding why ACE inhibitors and renin inhibitors (like aliskiren) act at different steps of the same pathway.

incorrectas.B: The conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II is catalyzed by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), primarily in the pulmonary vasculature, not by renin, which acts one step earlier on angiotensinogen.
incorrectas.C: Renin cannot directly convert angiotensinogen to angiotensin II in one step; the pathway requires the intermediate angiotensin I, generated by renin, which is then converted to angiotensin II by a separate enzyme (ACE), so skipping this intermediate misrepresents the enzymatic cascade.
incorrectas.D: The conversion of angiotensin II to aldosterone is not a direct enzymatic conversion at all; rather, angiotensin II acts as a signaling molecule on the adrenal cortex (zona glomerulosa) to stimulate aldosterone synthesis and secretion, a receptor-mediated process distinct from renin's proteolytic action on angiotensinogen.

preguntas.q: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) is primarily located in the vascular endothelium of which organ?

e.correcta: ACE is primarily located in the vascular endothelium of the lungs, where it converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II and also degrades bradykinin, making the pulmonary vasculature the principal site of this conversion despite ACE being present in smaller amounts in other vascular beds. This pulmonary localization explains why ACE inhibitor side effects like dry cough and angioedema (from bradykinin accumulation) are clinically prominent, given the drug's major site of action in lung endothelium.

incorrectas.B: The kidneys are the primary site of renin release from juxtaglomerular cells (initiating the RAAS cascade) and are a major target organ for angiotensin II's effects on the glomerulus and tubules, but ACE itself is predominantly located in pulmonary endothelium, not renal vasculature.
incorrectas.C: The liver is the source of angiotensinogen, the substrate that renin cleaves to form angiotensin I, but the subsequent conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II by ACE occurs predominantly in the lungs, not hepatic vasculature.
incorrectas.D: The heart contains some ACE activity in local tissue renin-angiotensin systems, but the major site of systemic angiotensin I to angiotensin II conversion is the pulmonary vascular endothelium, given the large surface area of the lung capillary bed.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, primarily in the lungs?

e.correcta: ACE, expressed abundantly on the luminal surface of pulmonary vascular endothelium, cleaves the inactive decapeptide angiotensin I into the active octapeptide angiotensin II, a potent vasoconstrictor and stimulator of aldosterone release. This pulmonary conversion step is the pharmacologic target of ACE inhibitors (e.g., lisinopril), which block this step to lower angiotensin II levels and reduce blood pressure while also decreasing bradykinin degradation (explaining the characteristic ACE-inhibitor cough and angioedema).

incorrectas.B: Renin is released by juxtaglomerular cells in response to decreased renal perfusion, sympathetic stimulation, or low sodium delivery, and it converts angiotensinogen (from the liver) to angiotensin I — an upstream step, not the lung-based conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II.
incorrectas.C: Chymase is an alternative, ACE-independent enzyme capable of generating angiotensin II in some tissues (notably the heart), which is clinically relevant because it explains why ACE inhibitors don't completely suppress angiotensin II production, but it is not the primary enzyme responsible for the bulk of systemic conversion in the lungs.
incorrectas.D: Neprilysin is a neutral endopeptidase that degrades natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP) and bradykinin, and is the target of drugs like sacubitril in ARNI therapy for heart failure; it plays no role in converting angiotensin I to angiotensin II.

preguntas.q: Angiotensin II is a potent mediator of which vascular effect?

e.correcta: Angiotensin II is one of the most potent endogenous vasoconstrictors, acting via AT1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle to trigger Gq-mediated calcium release and contraction, which raises systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure — this is a central component of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system's role in blood pressure regulation and volume homeostasis. This is precisely why ACE inhibitors and ARBs, which block angiotensin II formation or action, are used to lower blood pressure and reduce afterload in conditions like hypertension and heart failure.

incorrectas.B: Vasodilation is the opposite of angiotensin II's known physiologic effect — vasodilation is instead produced by mediators like nitric oxide, prostacyclin, or bradykinin, several of which are actually increased when ACE inhibitors block angiotensin-converting enzyme (which also normally degrades bradykinin).
incorrectas.C: Angiotensin II is not restricted to venodilation — its predominant, clinically significant effect is arteriolar vasoconstriction, which increases both systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure, distinguishing it from agents that act preferentially on the venous side.
incorrectas.D: Angiotensin II has substantial and well-documented vascular effects (potent vasoconstriction), making 'no significant vascular effect' clearly inconsistent with its established, clinically important role in blood pressure regulation.

preguntas.q: What is the effect of normal (physiologic) levels of angiotensin II on glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?

e.correcta: At normal physiologic levels, angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole more than the afferent arteriole, which raises glomerular hydrostatic pressure and helps maintain (increase/preserve) GFR even when renal perfusion pressure falls, such as in early volume depletion. This is precisely why ACE inhibitors and ARBs can precipitate acute kidney injury in states of renal artery stenosis or volume depletion — removing angiotensin II's efferent constriction drops the glomerular pressure that was propping up GFR.

incorrectas.B: Decreased GFR describes what happens if angiotensin II's efferent constrictor effect is removed (e.g., by ACEi/ARB) in a hypoperfused kidney, or what could occur at pathologically excessive angiotensin II causing severe afferent constriction — but at normal physiologic levels its net effect is to support/increase GFR, not decrease it.
incorrectas.C: Angiotensin II does have a measurable, clinically important physiologic effect on GFR via preferential efferent arteriolar constriction; 'no change' ignores this key renal autoregulatory mechanism that is heavily tested for its pharmacologic implications.
incorrectas.D: GFR does not become 'unmeasurable' under physiologic angiotensin II — this is not a real physiologic outcome and does not correspond to any recognized renal physiology concept.

preguntas.q: Angiotensin II normally constricts which arteriole of the kidney, helping to maintain GFR during decreased renal blood flow?

e.correcta: Angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole of the glomerulus, increasing the pressure gradient across the glomerular capillaries and helping preserve GFR even when renal blood flow (and afferent arteriole pressure) is reduced, such as in states of volume depletion or renal artery stenosis. This is precisely why ACE inhibitors and ARBs can precipitate acute kidney injury in bilateral renal artery stenosis — removing angiotensin II's efferent constriction collapses the compensatory pressure gradient that was maintaining filtration.

incorrectas.B: Afferent arteriole tone is regulated mainly by myogenic autoregulation and tubuloglomerular feedback (via macula densa-released adenosine), not primarily by angiotensin II; constricting the afferent arteriole would actually reduce, not preserve, GFR.
incorrectas.C: Interlobular arteries are larger pre-arteriolar vessels that primarily conduct blood toward the glomeruli and are not the specific angiotensin II-responsive site that fine-tunes glomerular filtration pressure.
incorrectas.D: Vasa recta are the specialized capillaries that follow the loop of Henle into the medulla, maintaining the countercurrent osmotic gradient for urine concentration; while angiotensin II can modestly affect medullary blood flow, this is not the arteriole responsible for the GFR-preserving mechanism described.

preguntas.q: Angiotensin II stimulates the release of which hormone from the adrenal cortex?

e.correcta: Angiotensin II acts on AT1 receptors in the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex to stimulate aldosterone synthesis and release, completing the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Aldosterone then acts on the principal cells of the collecting duct to increase Na+ (and water) reabsorption and K+/H+ secretion, restoring blood volume and pressure when the system is activated by low renal perfusion or low Na+ delivery to the macula densa.

incorrectas.B: Cortisol is secreted from the zona fasciculata under control of ACTH from the anterior pituitary (via the HPA axis), not angiotensin II, and its primary roles are stress response and metabolism rather than volume regulation.
incorrectas.C: Epinephrine is produced by the adrenal medulla (a neuroendocrine tissue derived from neural crest, not the cortex) in response to sympathetic stimulation, not angiotensin II, and mediates the fight-or-flight response rather than sodium handling.
incorrectas.D: DHEA is an androgen precursor synthesized in the zona reticularis under ACTH influence, part of adrenal androgen production, and is not the target of angiotensin II signaling.

preguntas.q: What effect does angiotensin II indirectly have on serum potassium levels (via aldosterone)?

e.correcta: Angiotensin II stimulates the adrenal zona glomerulosa to secrete aldosterone, which acts on principal cells of the collecting duct to increase Na+ reabsorption via ENaC channels while simultaneously increasing K+ secretion into the tubular lumen (to maintain electroneutrality). The net effect of this angiotensin II-aldosterone axis is therefore a decrease in serum potassium, which is why conditions of high aldosterone (e.g., primary hyperaldosteronism) classically cause hypokalemia.

incorrectas.B: Increased potassium is actually the effect of aldosterone deficiency or resistance (e.g., in Addison disease or ACE inhibitor/ARB use), the opposite of what angiotensin II-driven aldosterone secretion produces, since aldosterone promotes potassium excretion rather than retention.
incorrectas.C: No effect on potassium ignores aldosterone's well-established role at the collecting duct, where Na+/K+ exchange is directly coupled — angiotensin II's downstream aldosterone effect reliably lowers serum potassium, not leaves it unchanged.
incorrectas.D: Potassium levels do not become unpredictable; the aldosterone-mediated effect on the collecting duct is a well-characterized, consistent physiological mechanism producing potassium wasting, not a random or variable outcome.

preguntas.q: What effect do ACE inhibitors have on circulating levels of angiotensin II?

o.D: Angiotensin II is converted to angiotensin I

e.correcta: ACE inhibitors block angiotensin-converting enzyme, which normally converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, so blocking this enzyme directly decreases circulating angiotensin II levels. This reduction in angiotensin II decreases aldosterone secretion, arteriolar vasoconstriction, and efferent arteriolar tone, explaining the antihypertensive and renoprotective effects of ACE inhibitors, as well as side effects like hyperkalemia (less aldosterone) and cough/angioedema (from decreased bradykinin degradation, another ACE substrate).

incorrectas.B: Increased angiotensin II would occur with drugs that stimulate renin release without blocking downstream conversion, but ACE inhibitors act specifically to prevent the formation of angiotensin II, producing the opposite (decreased) effect.
incorrectas.C: Claiming no change in angiotensin II ignores the direct enzymatic blockade of ACE inhibitors — ACE inhibitors specifically target the conversion step, so angiotensin II levels do measurably fall, distinguishing them from drugs acting purely on downstream receptors like ARBs (which block the AT1 receptor without lowering angiotensin II levels, and can actually raise them via loss of negative feedback).
incorrectas.D: Angiotensin II being 'converted to angiotensin I' describes a reversal of the normal physiologic pathway that does not occur biologically — ACE converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, not the reverse, and ACE inhibitors block that forward conversion rather than reversing it.

preguntas.q: What effect do ACE inhibitors and ARBs have on glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?

o.D: GFR increases only in diabetic patients

e.correcta: ACE inhibitors and ARBs block angiotensin II's vasoconstrictive effect preferentially on the efferent arteriole (which normally has more angiotensin II receptors than the afferent arteriole), so their net effect is efferent arteriolar dilation, reducing the pressure gradient that maintains glomerular filtration and thus decreasing GFR. This is clinically important because it explains the expected, tolerable rise in creatinine (up to ~30%) when starting these drugs, and also why they must be used cautiously (or avoided) in bilateral renal artery stenosis, where GFR is critically dependent on angiotensin II-mediated efferent constriction.

incorrectas.B: An increase in GFR would be the opposite of the actual pharmacologic effect — by removing angiotensin II's efferent constriction, these drugs reduce, not raise, the intraglomerular pressure that filtration depends on, so GFR characteristically falls somewhat with these agents.
incorrectas.C: Claiming no effect on GFR ignores the well-documented, expected mild GFR reduction (with an accompanying creatinine rise) seen after initiating ACE inhibitors/ARBs, which is actually used clinically as a marker that the drug is working appropriately on the renal hemodynamics.
incorrectas.D: Restricting the GFR increase to diabetic patients only misconstrues the mechanism — while ACE inhibitors/ARBs are specifically favored in diabetic nephropathy for their renoprotective reduction of intraglomerular pressure (slowing progression of kidney disease), the acute hemodynamic effect is a GFR decrease, seen in diabetic and non-diabetic patients alike, not an increase confined to diabetics.

preguntas.q: What effect do ACE inhibitors and ARBs have on aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex?

e.correcta: ACE inhibitors block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, and ARBs block angiotensin II from acting at its AT1 receptor; since angiotensin II is the primary stimulus for aldosterone secretion from the zona glomerulosa, both drug classes decrease aldosterone release. This reduction in aldosterone explains their tendency to cause hyperkalemia (less renal K+ secretion) and their renoprotective effect in diabetic nephropathy by reducing efferent arteriolar constriction and intraglomerular pressure.

incorrectas.B: Increased aldosterone release would occur with unopposed renin-angiotensin activity (e.g., renal artery stenosis before treatment) or primary hyperaldosteronism, which is the opposite of what ACE inhibitors/ARBs achieve by interrupting the RAAS cascade.
incorrectas.C: Asserting no effect ignores the central pharmacologic action of these drugs — interrupting angiotensin II signaling specifically removes a major secretagogue for aldosterone, producing a clinically significant decrease, not a null effect.
incorrectas.D: Aldosterone and cortisol are distinct steroid hormones produced by different adrenal cortex zones (glomerulosa vs. fasciculata) via different terminal enzymatic steps; ACE inhibitors and ARBs do not chemically convert one hormone into another.

preguntas.q: ACE inhibitors can cause what change in serum creatinine within the first few days of starting treatment?

e.correcta: ACE inhibitors block the formation of angiotensin II, which normally preferentially constricts the efferent glomerular arteriole to maintain glomerular filtration pressure; removing this efferent constriction lowers intraglomerular pressure and GFR, causing a modest, expected rise in serum creatinine within the first few days of starting therapy. This small increase (generally accepted up to about 30%) reflects the drug's intended hemodynamic effect and is not a sign of toxicity, though a larger rise should prompt evaluation for bilateral renal artery stenosis.

incorrectas.B: A drop in creatinine would imply improved filtration, but ACE inhibitors reduce efferent arteriolar tone and thus lower, not raise, GFR acutely, making a decrease in creatinine physiologically inconsistent with their mechanism.
incorrectas.C: No change in creatinine would be unusual because ACE inhibition reliably alters glomerular hemodynamics by removing angiotensin II's efferent vasoconstriction, so some change in filtration and thus creatinine is expected in most patients.
incorrectas.D: Creatinine becoming undetectable would imply a dramatic, clinically alarming loss of muscle mass or lab error, not a physiologic effect of ACE inhibition, which produces only a small, self-limited rise, not disappearance, of creatinine.

preguntas.q: What effect do ACE inhibitors have on levels of angiotensin I and renin?

e.correcta: ACE inhibitors block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, so angiotensin I accumulates upstream of the blocked enzyme; because angiotensin II normally provides negative feedback on renin release (and less angiotensin II is now being produced to suppress the kidney), renin secretion also rises via loss of feedback inhibition and reflex activation from lower blood pressure. This combination of increased renin and increased angiotensin I (with decreased angiotensin II) is a classic testable pharmacodynamic signature of ACE inhibitor therapy.

incorrectas.B: Both renin and angiotensin I actually increase with ACE inhibition rather than decrease, because the enzymatic block causes substrate (angiotensin I) to build up and removes the angiotensin II-mediated negative feedback that normally restrains renin release.
incorrectas.C: Renin does not decrease with ACE inhibitors; it rises because angiotensin II-mediated negative feedback on juxtaglomerular cell renin release is lost when ACE is blocked.
incorrectas.D: ACE inhibition clearly changes the renin-angiotensin axis, raising both renin and angiotensin I while lowering angiotensin II, so 'no change' contradicts the core pharmacodynamics of the drug class.

preguntas.q: What effect may ACE inhibitors have on serum potassium levels?

e.correcta: ACE inhibitors block conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, which reduces aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex; since aldosterone normally promotes renal potassium excretion via the principal cells' ENaC/ROMK system, losing this aldosterone drive causes potassium retention and can produce hyperkalemia. This effect is clinically important because it compounds with other hyperkalemia risk factors like renal insufficiency or concurrent potassium-sparing diuretics, and requires potassium monitoring after starting therapy.

incorrectas.B: Hypokalemia is the opposite of what ACE inhibitors cause; drugs that increase aldosterone activity or its downstream effect (like loop or thiazide diuretics causing increased distal sodium delivery) cause potassium wasting, whereas ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone and thus retain potassium.
incorrectas.C: ACE inhibitors do have a clinically meaningful effect on potassium through the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone pathway, so "no effect" ignores this well-documented and clinically monitored hyperkalemia risk.
incorrectas.D: There is no physiologic mechanism by which potassium is "converted" to sodium; ACE inhibitors alter aldosterone-driven ion transport at the distal nephron, affecting the excretion rates of sodium and potassium independently, not interconverting the two ions.

preguntas.q: ACE inhibitors are first-line agents in the treatment of which condition?

e.correcta: ACE inhibitors block conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, reducing afterload (via decreased vasoconstriction) and preload (via decreased aldosterone-driven sodium/water retention), while also blunting the maladaptive cardiac remodeling driven by angiotensin II and aldosterone; this combination reduces mortality and hospitalization in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, making them a cornerstone first-line therapy. Their benefit extends beyond symptom control to a proven mortality benefit, which is why they're recommended even in asymptomatic patients with reduced EF.

incorrectas.B: Hyperthyroidism is treated with agents like thionamides (methimazole/PTU), radioactive iodine, or beta-blockers for symptom control, none of which relate to the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system that ACE inhibitors target.
incorrectas.C: Acute asthma exacerbation is managed with bronchodilators (beta-2 agonists), anticholinergics, and corticosteroids; ACE inhibitors have no bronchodilatory role and are notably associated with cough as a side effect, which would be counterproductive in asthma.
incorrectas.D: Peptic ulcer disease is treated with acid suppression (PPIs, H2 blockers) and H. pylori eradication when present; ACE inhibitors have no role in gastric acid physiology or ulcer healing.

preguntas.q: Do ACE inhibitors reduce mortality in patients with heart failure and myocardial infarction?

o.B: No, they have no mortality benefit
o.C: They increase mortality in heart failure
o.D: They only improve symptoms without any survival benefit

e.correcta: ACE inhibitors reduce mortality in heart failure and post-MI patients by blocking the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, which decreases afterload (via reduced vasoconstriction) and preload (via reduced aldosterone-driven sodium/water retention), and also blunts the maladaptive cardiac remodeling driven by chronic angiotensin II and aldosterone exposure. This mortality benefit, demonstrated in landmark trials like SAVE and SOLVD, is why ACE inhibitors are a cornerstone of guideline-directed medical therapy in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

incorrectas.B: No mortality benefit contradicts robust clinical trial evidence; ACE inhibitors have consistently shown reduced mortality in heart failure and post-MI populations by interrupting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system's contribution to remodeling and hemodynamic overload.
incorrectas.C: ACE inhibitors do not increase mortality in heart failure — by reducing afterload, preload, and pathologic remodeling, they lower the workload on a failing heart, which is the opposite of the harm this option describes.
incorrectas.D: Framing the benefit as symptom relief 'without any survival benefit' misses the core pharmacologic point: ACE inhibitors alter the disease's natural history by blocking maladaptive angiotensin II/aldosterone signaling, producing a genuine survival advantage, not merely symptomatic improvement.

preguntas.q: ACE inhibitors are a first-line agent in the treatment of which condition?

e.correcta: ACE inhibitors block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, reducing vasoconstriction and aldosterone-driven sodium/water retention, which lowers systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure — making them a first-line agent for primary (essential) hypertension, especially in patients with comorbid diabetes or chronic kidney disease due to their renoprotective effect on glomerular pressure. Their efficacy in essential hypertension stems from directly targeting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system that drives blood pressure in the general hypertensive population, unlike secondary hypertension syndromes that require treating the underlying cause.

incorrectas.B: Hyperaldosteronism from an adrenal adenoma is a form of secondary hypertension driven by autonomous aldosterone secretion independent of renin/angiotensin, so the definitive treatment is surgical adrenalectomy or a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone/eplerenone), not an ACE inhibitor, which acts upstream of the autonomously secreting gland.
incorrectas.C: Pheochromocytoma causes hypertension through catecholamine (epinephrine/norepinephrine) excess from an adrenal medullary tumor, so first-line treatment requires alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine) followed by beta-blockade prior to tumor resection — ACE inhibition does not address the catecholamine-driven mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Cushing syndrome causes hypertension via cortisol excess (which has mineralocorticoid-like effects and potentiates vasoconstrictors), so management targets the cortisol source (e.g., surgery for an adenoma or stopping exogenous steroids) rather than the renin-angiotensin system targeted by ACE inhibitors.

preguntas.q: What is the most common congenital renal anomaly?

e.correcta: Horseshoe kidney is the most common congenital renal fusion anomaly, occurring in roughly 1 in 500 people, resulting from fusion of the lower poles of the metanephric kidneys early in development, before ascent; the fused isthmus then gets trapped below the inferior mesenteric artery, preventing normal ascent to the lumbar region. Its high frequency (compared to other renal anomalies) combined with its usually asymptomatic course and known association with Turner syndrome makes it the classic answer for 'most common congenital renal anomaly.'

incorrectas.B: Renal agenesis (absence of one or both kidneys) is a less common anomaly than horseshoe kidney and, particularly when bilateral, is far more clinically severe (incompatible with life via Potter sequence), but it does not occur as frequently as fusion anomalies.
incorrectas.C: Polycystic kidney disease (autosomal dominant or recessive forms) is a distinct genetic disorder causing cystic replacement of renal parenchyma; while clinically significant, it is not more common than horseshoe kidney as a congenital anomaly.
incorrectas.D: Duplicated ureter (ureteral duplication) is a relatively common anomaly of the ureteric bud but is less frequent than horseshoe kidney and represents a different embryologic error (premature ureteric bud branching) rather than fusion of the kidneys themselves.

preguntas.q: As horseshoe kidneys ascend from the pelvis during fetal development, they become trapped under which artery, causing them to remain low in the abdomen?

e.correcta: The horseshoe kidney forms when the inferior poles of the two developing kidneys fuse across the midline; as the fused mass tries to ascend from the pelvis, it gets caught on the inferior mesenteric artery, which originates at the level of L3 and effectively acts as a physical barrier, leaving the kidney abnormally low (usually around L4-L5) instead of reaching its normal position near L1-L2.

incorrectas.A: The superior mesenteric artery arises higher (around L1) and is not the structure that arrests the ascent of a horseshoe kidney — the anatomically lower inferior mesenteric artery is the actual obstacle described in this classic embryologic fact.
incorrectas.C: The renal arteries are typically multiple and variably positioned in horseshoe kidneys because of the anomaly, but they are a consequence of the abnormal position rather than the structure causing the arrest of ascent.
incorrectas.D: The celiac artery arises even higher, near T12-L1, well above where a horseshoe kidney becomes trapped, so it is not the anatomic obstruction responsible for this condition.

preguntas.q: Is kidney function typically normal or abnormal in horseshoe kidney?

o.B: Severely reduced due to fused parenchyma
o.D: Function is present only in one of the fused kidneys

e.correcta: Horseshoe kidney results from abnormal fusion of the lower poles of the two developing kidneys during ascent, but the fused kidneys still contain normally functioning nephrons and typically maintain normal renal function. The clinical significance instead lies in the abnormal position (trapped below the inferior mesenteric artery during ascent) and associated risks like increased susceptibility to trauma, obstruction, stone formation, and infection, plus its association with Turner syndrome. This distinction — normal function despite abnormal anatomy — is a key teaching point tested repeatedly.

incorrectas.B: Severely reduced function due to fused parenchyma is not characteristic of horseshoe kidney; the nephron mass and filtering capacity are generally preserved despite the anatomic fusion, which is why it's often an incidental finding.
incorrectas.C: Horseshoe kidney does not cause absent function or require dialysis; it is a positional/fusion anomaly, not a cause of renal failure, unlike conditions such as bilateral renal agenesis or severe polycystic kidney disease.
incorrectas.D: Function is not restricted to only one side; both fused kidney masses in a horseshoe kidney typically contribute to overall renal function, unlike conditions with unilateral renal dysplasia or agenesis.

preguntas.q: Horseshoe kidney is associated with which complication due to ureteropelvic junction obstruction?

e.correcta: Horseshoe kidney forms when the lower poles of the developing kidneys fuse and become trapped under the inferior mesenteric artery during ascent, leaving the kidney abnormally positioned and its ureters coursing anteriorly over the fused isthmus. This abnormal anatomy predisposes to ureteropelvic junction obstruction, causing back-up of urine into the renal pelvis and hydronephrosis, which is the clinically important complication to screen for.

incorrectas.B: Renal vein thrombosis is typically associated with hypercoagulable states (e.g., nephrotic syndrome, dehydration in infants) rather than the anatomic ureteral obstruction caused by horseshoe kidney's fused, malpositioned structure.
incorrectas.C: Nephrotic syndrome results from glomerular basement membrane pathology causing proteinuria, an intrinsic glomerular disease process unrelated to the structural ureteral obstruction that horseshoe kidney predisposes to.
incorrectas.D: Renal artery stenosis refers to narrowing of the renal artery (often from atherosclerosis or fibromuscular dysplasia) causing renovascular hypertension, a vascular problem distinct from the obstructive uropathy caused by the abnormal ureteropelvic anatomy in horseshoe kidney.

preguntas.q: Horseshoe kidney increases the risk of kidney infection and which other condition?

e.correcta: Horseshoe kidney occurs when the developing kidneys fuse at their lower poles and become trapped under the inferior mesenteric artery during ascent, and this abnormal position and shape lead to urinary stasis and impaired drainage, predisposing to both infection and kidney stone formation. Stasis in an abnormally positioned, poorly draining collecting system is the shared underlying mechanism linking these two complications, making horseshoe kidney a classic congenital anomaly tested alongside its association with Turner syndrome.

incorrectas.B: Renal cell carcinoma is not classically increased by horseshoe kidney; horseshoe kidney is instead more specifically associated with an increased risk of Wilms tumor in children and transitional cell carcinoma, not RCC, and the primary tested complications remain infection and stones.
incorrectas.C: Minimal change disease is a podocyte-related glomerular disease typically idiopathic or associated with conditions like lymphoma, and it has no established mechanistic link to the structural anomaly of horseshoe kidney.
incorrectas.D: IgA nephropathy is an immune-complex-mediated glomerulonephritis often triggered by mucosal infections, unrelated to the anatomic drainage abnormality that predisposes horseshoe kidneys to stones and infections.

preguntas.q: Which sex chromosome disorder is associated with horseshoe kidney?

e.correcta: Turner syndrome (45,X) is associated with horseshoe kidney because during renal ascent from the pelvis to the abdomen, the developing kidneys can fuse at their inferior poles and then become trapped beneath the inferior mesenteric artery, halting further ascent. Turner syndrome carries a range of anomalies from abnormal lymphatic drainage and vascular development (webbed neck, coarctation of the aorta, lymphedema), and horseshoe kidney is one of the classic associated renal anomalies tested alongside these features. Recognizing horseshoe kidney should prompt consideration of Turner syndrome in a female patient, especially if short stature or streak gonads are also present.

incorrectas.B: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is characterized by testicular dysgenesis, infertility, and tall stature with gynecomastia, but it is not classically linked to horseshoe kidney; its pathology centers on hypogonadism rather than the ascent/fusion defect that produces horseshoe kidney.
incorrectas.C: Triple X syndrome (47,XXX) is often clinically silent or associated with mild learning difficulties, and is not part of the classic anomaly spectrum that includes horseshoe kidney, unlike Turner syndrome's broader developmental field defects.
incorrectas.D: XYY syndrome is typically associated with tall stature and normal fertility with a phenotype that is often unremarkable; it does not carry the constellation of midline and renal developmental anomalies seen in Turner syndrome, so it is not linked to horseshoe kidney.

preguntas.q: Which congenital kidney disease is associated with chromosomal aneuploidies such as trisomy 13, 18, and 21?

e.correcta: Horseshoe kidney results from abnormal fusion of the lower (or occasionally upper) poles of the developing kidneys during ascent from the pelvis, and this fusion causes the kidney to become trapped under the inferior mesenteric artery, arresting its ascent at a lower-than-normal position. Because it is a developmental field defect often occurring alongside other malformations, it shows a well-recognized association with aneuploidy syndromes (trisomy 13, 18, 21) and with Turner syndrome.

incorrectas.B: Multicystic dysplastic kidney arises from abnormal metanephric differentiation with disorganized cysts and ducts, often unilateral and linked to ureteral obstruction/atresia in utero, rather than being a classic aneuploidy-associated anomaly.
incorrectas.C: Renal agenesis results from failure of the ureteric bud to develop or interact with metanephric mesenchyme, and while it can occur with various syndromes, it is not the anomaly classically taught as linked to trisomy 13/18/21 the way horseshoe kidney is.
incorrectas.D: Medullary sponge kidney is characterized by cystic dilation of the collecting ducts in the renal medulla, typically presenting later in life with stones or infections, and is not part of the classic trisomy association taught for horseshoe kidney.

preguntas.q: Horseshoe kidney is rarely associated with an increased risk of which malignancy?

e.correcta: Horseshoe kidney carries a rare but recognized increased risk of renal (Wilms) tumor because the abnormal fusion and altered nephrogenic tissue arrangement during development may predispose to aberrant cellular proliferation, and the ectopic, malrotated position of the kidney can also make early tumor detection more difficult on imaging. This association is why any child with a known horseshoe kidney warrants heightened awareness for renal masses, and why horseshoe kidney itself is sometimes discovered incidentally during Wilms tumor workup. The kidney fuses at the inferior poles and becomes trapped under the inferior mesenteric artery, and this abnormal tissue arrangement is the presumed link to increased tumor risk.

incorrectas.B: Hepatocellular carcinoma arises from hepatocyte transformation, typically related to chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, or hepatitis B/C infection, mechanisms entirely unrelated to the renal fusion anomaly and nephrogenic tissue changes that link horseshoe kidney to renal tumors.
incorrectas.C: Bladder cancer is most strongly associated with risk factors like smoking and chronic irritation (e.g., Schistosoma haematobium causing squamous cell carcinoma), not with the renal fusion abnormality seen in horseshoe kidney, so there's no established mechanistic link.
incorrectas.D: Adrenal carcinoma arises from adrenal cortical cells and is not linked to the renal ascent and fusion defects underlying horseshoe kidney; the associated malignancy risk in horseshoe kidney is specifically renal in origin (Wilms tumor), not adrenal.

preguntas.q: Which congenital kidney disease involves unilateral or bilateral absence of kidney and ureter formation?

e.correcta: Renal agenesis occurs when the ureteric bud fails to develop or fails to induce metanephric mesenchyme differentiation, resulting in complete absence of kidney and ureter formation on one or both sides; bilateral renal agenesis is incompatible with life and is the classic cause of Potter sequence due to resulting oligohydramnios (since fetal urine is a major contributor to amniotic fluid). Unilateral agenesis is often compatible with normal life because the contralateral kidney undergoes compensatory hypertrophy.

incorrectas.B: Horseshoe kidney results from abnormal fusion of the two developing kidneys at their lower poles during ascent, and the kidneys are still present (just malpositioned and fused), which is a structural anomaly of formed kidneys, not an absence of kidney/ureter development.
incorrectas.C: Polycystic kidney disease involves formed kidneys that develop multiple fluid-filled cysts (due to genetic defects like PKD1/PKD2 mutations) that progressively destroy renal parenchyma, which is a cystic degenerative process rather than a failure of kidney and ureter formation.
incorrectas.D: Duplex collecting system arises from early or complete splitting of the ureteric bud, producing two ureters draining a single kidney, which is an anomaly of duplication rather than absence of kidney and ureter tissue.

preguntas.q: Renal agenesis is often diagnosed prenatally using which imaging modality?

e.correcta: Renal agenesis is typically detected prenatally by ultrasound, which can show an empty renal fossa and, importantly, oligohydramnios — since fetal urine is the major contributor to amniotic fluid after mid-gestation, its absence (especially in bilateral agenesis) causes the oligohydramnios that leads to Potter sequence (limb deformities, pulmonary hypoplasion, facial anomalies). Ultrasound is favored because it is non-invasive, radiation-free, and routinely performed during prenatal screening, making it the practical first-line modality.

incorrectas.B: CT scan involves ionizing radiation and is not used for routine prenatal screening given fetal radiation risk, making it an inappropriate and impractical choice compared to ultrasound for prenatal diagnosis.
incorrectas.C: MRI can be used as an adjunct in complex prenatal anomaly evaluation but is not the standard first-line or classic modality for detecting renal agenesis prenatally — ultrasound remains the routine screening tool given its accessibility and safety profile.
incorrectas.D: Nuclear renal scans (e.g., MAG3, DMSA) are used postnatally to assess renal function and differential contribution of each kidney, not for prenatal anatomic screening, and are not feasible or indicated in utero.

preguntas.q: In unilateral renal agenesis, what happens to the remaining kidney?

e.correcta: In unilateral renal agenesis, the single remaining kidney undergoes compensatory hypertrophy, with increased nephron size (not number) and glomerular filtration to compensate for the lost renal mass, often allowing near-normal overall renal function. This compensatory mechanism explains why many people live asymptomatically with only one kidney, though the hyperfiltration state can predispose to glomerulosclerosis and CKD over a long lifespan.

incorrectas.B: Atrophy (shrinkage/decreased function) is the opposite of what actually happens; the solitary kidney must work harder to maintain overall renal function, driving hypertrophy rather than atrophy.
incorrectas.C: Cyst development is characteristic of distinct entities like autosomal dominant/recessive polycystic kidney disease or multicystic dysplastic kidney, not the physiologic compensatory response of a normally-formed solitary kidney to the absence of its pair.
incorrectas.D: The remaining kidney does not stay unchanged in size — it actively enlarges via hypertrophy to compensate for the missing nephron mass, since a single kidney at baseline size could not otherwise maintain adequate overall GFR.

preguntas.q: Hyperfiltration of the remaining kidney in unilateral renal agenesis increases the risk of which long-term complication?

e.correcta: When one kidney is congenitally absent (unilateral renal agenesis), the remaining solitary kidney undergoes compensatory hypertrophy and hyperfiltration to maintain adequate overall renal function, but this chronic increase in single-nephron glomerular pressure over decades causes progressive glomerular injury (a process similar to that seen in diabetic nephropathy), predisposing to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and eventual chronic renal failure. This is why patients with a solitary kidney are monitored long-term for proteinuria and hypertension as early markers of this hyperfiltration injury.

incorrectas.B: Renal artery aneurysm is not a recognized consequence of compensatory hyperfiltration; aneurysm formation relates to vessel wall weakness or connective tissue disorders, not glomerular hemodynamic stress from a single functioning kidney.
incorrectas.C: Nephrolithiasis is not the specific long-term complication driven by hyperfiltration; while solitary kidney patients are counseled generally about kidney health, stone formation is not mechanistically linked to the hyperfiltration-induced glomerular injury described here, nor is it exclusive to this condition.
incorrectas.D: Polycystic transformation is a distinct genetic or acquired cystic kidney disease process (as in ADPKD or acquired cystic disease of dialysis), unrelated to the hemodynamic hyperfiltration injury that follows compensatory hypertrophy of a solitary kidney.

preguntas.q: The primary abnormality underlying Potter sequence is which condition?

e.correcta: Potter sequence begins with oligohydramnios — insufficient amniotic fluid, most classically from bilateral renal agenesis or other severe fetal renal dysfunction that prevents adequate fetal urine production, since fetal urine is the major contributor to amniotic fluid in later pregnancy. The resulting fluid deficiency then mechanically compresses the fetus, producing the downstream sequence: pulmonary hypoplasia (from restricted chest wall expansion), limb deformities, and the characteristic flattened facies, illustrating how a single primary insult can cascade into a set of secondary findings.

incorrectas.B: Polyhydramnios is excess amniotic fluid, typically caused by conditions that impair fetal swallowing (such as esophageal or duodenal atresia) or increased fetal urine output — it is the opposite fluid abnormality and not the driver of Potter sequence.
incorrectas.C: Placenta previa is an obstetric complication where the placenta abnormally covers the cervical os, causing painless third-trimester bleeding, but it does not cause the oligohydramnios-driven compression sequence seen in Potter syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Chorioamnionitis is an infection/inflammation of the fetal membranes, associated with preterm labor and neonatal sepsis risk, not with the amniotic fluid volume abnormality that triggers Potter sequence.

preguntas.q: In Potter sequence, oligohydramnios most critically leads to which pulmonary finding, the most common cause of death?

e.correcta: In Potter sequence, insufficient fetal urine output (from renal agenesis or severe renal dysfunction) causes oligohydramnios, and because amniotic fluid volume is essential for adequate space and fluid movement to allow normal lung development, the compressed, fluid-deficient environment leads to pulmonary hypoplasia — underdeveloped, insufficient alveolar tissue that cannot support respiration after birth. This pulmonary hypoplasia, not the renal failure itself, is the proximate cause of death in most affected neonates, making the oligohydramnios-lung development link the key testable mechanism.

incorrectas.B: Pulmonary fibrosis is a chronic scarring process typically from long-term inflammatory or toxic lung injury in postnatal life, not an acute developmental consequence of oligohydramnios in utero, which instead prevents the lungs from developing adequate tissue in the first place.
incorrectas.C: Pulmonary hypertension can occur secondarily in some neonates with lung disease, but it is not the primary, most critical, or most common cause of death in Potter sequence — that distinction belongs to pulmonary hypoplasia, the underlying structural lung deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Pneumothorax is an acute complication that can occur in mechanically ventilated hypoplastic lungs but is not itself the primary developmental abnormality or leading cause of death in Potter sequence — it would be a downstream complication of the hypoplastic, fragile lungs, not the core lesion.

preguntas.q: In Potter sequence, oligohydramnios causes what physical effect on the developing fetus?

e.correcta: In Potter sequence, oligohydramnios (often from bilateral renal agenesis or severe renal dysfunction reducing fetal urine output, a major contributor to amniotic fluid) removes the cushioning effect of amniotic fluid, so the uterine wall directly compresses the fetus, producing the characteristic physical findings of Potter sequence: flattened facies, limb deformities (like clubfoot), and pulmonary hypoplasia due to restricted chest wall expansion needed for normal lung development. This mechanical compression explains why the resulting phenotype is described as a 'sequence' — a cascade of secondary effects from one initiating problem (lack of fluid) rather than a set of unrelated primary malformations.

incorrectas.B: Excessive amniotic distention describes polyhydramnios, essentially the opposite fluid abnormality, which is instead associated with conditions impairing fetal swallowing (such as esophageal atresia or anencephaly), not with renal agenesis or oligohydramnios.
incorrectas.C: Hydrops fetalis refers to abnormal fluid accumulation in fetal body compartments (skin edema, effusions, ascites), typically from severe anemia, heart failure, or immune-mediated causes, not from the mechanical compression caused by reduced amniotic fluid volume.
incorrectas.D: Increased fetal movement would be expected with more amniotic fluid space to move in, but oligohydramnios instead restricts fetal movement due to the tight, compressive uterine environment, contributing to the limb contractures seen in Potter sequence.

preguntas.q: In Potter sequence, compression of the developing fetus from oligohydramnios results in what type of abnormality?

e.correcta: In Potter sequence, oligohydramnios (often from bilateral renal agenesis or severe renal dysfunction reducing fetal urine output) removes the cushioning amniotic fluid, so the uterine wall compresses the fetus directly, producing characteristic limb deformities such as clubfoot and joint contractures, along with the classic Potter facies (flattened nose, recessed chin, low-set ears). This mechanical compression model explains why the abnormalities are positional/deformational rather than true malformations arising from abnormal organogenesis.

incorrectas.B: Cardiac septal defects arise from abnormal septation during early cardiac embryogenesis (e.g., neural crest or endocardial cushion defects), a distinct developmental process unrelated to the mechanical fetal compression caused by low amniotic fluid volume.
incorrectas.C: Neural tube defects result from failure of neural tube closure early in gestation (often linked to folate deficiency), a primary neurulation defect rather than a secondary deformation from oligohydramnios-induced compression.
incorrectas.D: Cleft palate can occur as an isolated malformation from failure of palatal shelf fusion, but it is not the exclusive or defining compression-related abnormality of Potter sequence; the hallmark compression findings are limb and facial deformities, not clefting alone.

preguntas.q: Potter sequence may cause an abnormal positioning of the mandible known as what?

e.correcta: Potter sequence results from oligohydramnios (classically due to bilateral renal agenesis or severe renal dysfunction in utero), which removes the cushioning effect of amniotic fluid and allows the uterine wall to compress the fetus directly. This mechanical compression pushes the mandible posteriorly, producing retrognathia (a receding chin), along with the other classic features of the sequence: flattened facies, low-set ears, and limb deformities such as clubbed feet.

incorrectas.B: Prognathism refers to a protruding, forward-jutting mandible, the opposite deformity to what compression forces produce — oligohydramnios pushes structures inward/backward, not forward, so this is mechanistically the wrong direction.
incorrectas.C: Micrognathia (a small jaw) can be seen in other congenital syndromes but is not the classic mandibular finding taught for Potter sequence, and describing it as 'isolated from sequence' misrepresents that Potter sequence findings all arise from the same underlying oligohydramnios-compression mechanism, not from an isolated process.
