incorrectas.C: Iodine deficiency impairs the gland's ability to synthesize hormone (primary hypothyroidism), so TSH rises appropriately as the pituitary attempts to compensate for low circulating thyroid hormone, not decreases.
incorrectas.D: Peripheral resistance to thyroid hormone typically presents with elevated (not decreased) TSH and T3/T4, because tissues (including the pituitary) fail to sense adequate hormone effect despite high levels, driving continued TSH secretion.

preguntas.q: Hypothyroidism is most appropriately treated with which of the following?

o.B: Thyroid hormone replacement therapy (e.g., levothyroxine, liothyronine)

e.correcta: Hypothyroidism, a state of deficient thyroid hormone production, is treated by directly replacing the missing hormone with exogenous thyroid hormone (levothyroxine, a synthetic T4 that is peripherally converted to active T3, or liothyronine, synthetic T3 itself), restoring normal metabolic rate and negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis. This replacement strategy directly addresses the underlying hormone deficiency, in contrast to hyperthyroidism, which requires the opposite approach of reducing excess hormone synthesis or effect.

incorrectas.A: Propylthiouracil is a thionamide that inhibits thyroid peroxidase to reduce thyroid hormone synthesis, used to treat hyperthyroidism (excess hormone), which is the opposite problem from hypothyroidism and would worsen a hormone-deficient state.
incorrectas.C: Radioactive iodine ablation destroys thyroid tissue to reduce hormone-producing capacity, a treatment for hyperthyroidism (e.g., Graves disease) or thyroid cancer, and would be directly harmful if given to a patient who already has insufficient thyroid hormone.
incorrectas.D: Beta-blockers provide symptomatic control of adrenergic symptoms (tachycardia, tremor) seen in hyperthyroidism by blocking peripheral catecholamine effects, but they do not address a thyroid hormone deficiency and have no role in treating hypothyroidism itself.

preguntas.q: The adrenal medulla secretes which two catecholamines?

e.correcta: The adrenal medulla is composed of chromaffin cells, which are modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons that synthesize and release the catecholamines norepinephrine and epinephrine (with epinephrine predominating, about 80%, due to cortisol-driven induction of phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase, PNMT, in the adjacent cortex). This anatomic relationship — cortisol from the surrounding cortex draining through the medulla before entering venous circulation — is why cortisol is needed to fully convert norepinephrine to epinephrine.

incorrectas.A: Dopamine is a catecholamine precursor synthesized in the pathway but is largely converted onward to norepinephrine and epinephrine in the medulla; serotonin is not an adrenal medullary product at all, making this pairing incorrect.
incorrectas.B: Cortisol and aldosterone are steroid hormones produced by the adrenal cortex (zona fasciculata and glomerulosa respectively), not catecholamines, and are anatomically and biosynthetically distinct from the medullary chromaffin cell products.
incorrectas.D: Androgens (like DHEA) are produced by the adrenal cortex's zona reticularis, and estrogens are not a primary adrenal secretion; neither is a catecholamine, so this pairing does not match the medulla's actual secretory products.

preguntas.q: The adrenal cortex, which makes up approximately 80% of the glandular tissue, occupies which zone of the adrenal gland?

o.C: A scattered zone within the medulla

e.correcta: The adrenal cortex forms the outer, peripheral zone of the adrenal gland, surrounding the inner medulla, and it accounts for roughly 80% of the gland's mass. It is organized into three histologically and functionally distinct sublayers from outside in — the zona glomerulosa (mineralocorticoids), zona fasciculata (glucocorticoids), and zona reticularis (androgens) — all derived embryologically from mesoderm, in contrast to the neural-crest-derived medulla they envelop.

incorrectas.A: The innermost zone of the adrenal gland is the medulla, which is derived from neural crest cells and produces catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine), not steroid hormones, and makes up only about 20% of the gland rather than 80%.
incorrectas.C: There is no scattered cortical tissue distributed within the medulla in the normal adrenal architecture; the gland is organized as a clearly demarcated outer cortex surrounding a distinct inner medulla, not an intermixed pattern.
incorrectas.D: The capsule is a thin fibrous connective tissue covering that surrounds the entire gland; it is not glandular tissue and contributes none of the hormone-producing mass, so it cannot account for the 80% figure describing the cortex.

preguntas.q: Which zone of the adrenal cortex is the middle and widest layer, situated between the zona glomerulosa and zona reticularis?

e.correcta: The zona fasciculata is the middle and widest layer of the adrenal cortex, sandwiched between the outer zona glomerulosa and inner zona reticularis, and it is composed of cells arranged in straight cords (fascicles) that secrete glucocorticoids (primarily cortisol) under ACTH stimulation. Its lipid-rich, vacuolated cytoplasm gives it a pale, "spongy" appearance histologically, correlating with its high steroidogenic activity. Remembering the classic mnemonic "GFR" (Glomerulosa-Fasciculata-Reticularis corresponding to salt-sugar-sex, outer to inner) helps fix both the order and width relationship of the three zones.

incorrectas.A: The zona reticularis is the innermost layer, adjacent to the medulla, and produces mainly adrenal androgens (DHEA), so it occupies neither the middle position nor the greatest width described in the question.
incorrectas.B: The zona glomerulosa is the outermost layer, producing aldosterone under angiotensin II/potassium regulation, and is a thin layer just beneath the capsule rather than the wide middle zone being asked about.
incorrectas.D: There is no "zona medullaris" in adrenal histology — the innermost structure is simply the adrenal medulla, composed of chromaffin cells secreting catecholamines, which is a distinct embryologic and functional compartment from the cortical zones.

preguntas.q: What is the rate-limiting enzyme in the biosynthesis of all adrenocortical steroid hormones?

e.correcta: Cholesterol desmolase (side-chain cleavage enzyme, CYP11A1) catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step of steroidogenesis, converting cholesterol to pregnenolone within mitochondria; this step is upregulated by ACTH (via cAMP-mediated increased cholesterol delivery to the inner mitochondrial membrane through StAR protein) and is required before any downstream glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid, or androgen synthesis can proceed. Because it is upstream of all three steroid pathways, a block here abolishes production of all adrenocortical hormones.

incorrectas.A: 21β-hydroxylase acts downstream in the pathway (converting progesterone/17-OH-progesterone to their 21-hydroxylated products) and is important for glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid synthesis, but it is not the very first, rate-limiting step that commits cholesterol to steroidogenesis.
incorrectas.B: Aldosterone synthase acts far downstream, specifically in the zona glomerulosa to produce aldosterone from corticosterone precursors; it is enzyme-specific to the mineralocorticoid pathway, not the shared rate-limiting entry step for all adrenal steroids.
incorrectas.D: 17α-hydroxylase is a branch-point enzyme needed for cortisol and androgen synthesis (absent in the zona glomerulosa), but it acts after cholesterol has already been converted to pregnenolone, so it is not the initial rate-limiting step of the pathway.

preguntas.q: Which of the following is the major glucocorticoid produced by the human adrenal cortex?

e.correcta: Cortisol (hydrocortisone) is synthesized in the zona fasciculata via the 17α-hydroxylase pathway and is by far the dominant glucocorticoid in humans, exerting major effects on gluconeogenesis, immune suppression, and stress response, and serving as the primary hormone measured/replaced clinically (e.g., in adrenal insufficiency). Its secretion is tightly regulated by ACTH from the anterior pituitary in a classic negative feedback loop.

incorrectas.A: Aldosterone is the major mineralocorticoid, produced in the zona glomerulosa and regulated mainly by the renin-angiotensin system and potassium levels, not the primary hormone responsible for glucocorticoid effects like gluconeogenesis and stress response.
incorrectas.B: Corticosterone does have some glucocorticoid activity and is an important intermediate/end product in rodents, but in humans it is a minor glucocorticoid compared to cortisol, which is the quantitatively and clinically dominant one.
incorrectas.D: DHEA is a weak adrenal androgen produced by the zona reticularis, functioning mainly as a precursor for peripheral sex hormone synthesis, not as a glucocorticoid with cortisol's metabolic and anti-inflammatory actions.

preguntas.q: Which hormone is the major mineralocorticoid produced by the human adrenal cortex?

e.correcta: Aldosterone, synthesized in the zona glomerulosa via aldosterone synthase, is the principal mineralocorticoid in humans, acting on the distal nephron to promote Na+ reabsorption and K+/H+ excretion, thereby regulating extracellular volume and blood pressure. Its secretion is driven mainly by angiotensin II and hyperkalemia (rather than ACTH), which distinguishes its regulatory axis from that of cortisol.

incorrectas.A: Cortisol is the major glucocorticoid, and while it has some mineralocorticoid cross-reactivity at very high concentrations (it can bind mineralocorticoid receptors before being inactivated by 11β-HSD2), it is not the primary physiologic mineralocorticoid — that role belongs to aldosterone.
incorrectas.C: Corticosterone is an intermediate in the pathway with some weak mineralocorticoid activity, but it is not the major, physiologically dominant mineralocorticoid in humans; aldosterone, synthesized further downstream in the zona glomerulosa, holds that role.
incorrectas.D: Testosterone is an androgen involved in male sexual development, produced mainly by the testes (and adrenal androgens like DHEA to a lesser extent), and has no meaningful mineralocorticoid activity.

preguntas.q: If the mineralocorticoid synthesis pathway is blocked below the level of 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC) — such as with 11β-hydroxylase or aldosterone synthase deficiency — can mineralocorticoids still be produced?

o.B: Yes, because DOC and corticosterone both retain mineralocorticoid activity
o.C: Yes, but only via conversion of cortisol to aldosterone
o.D: No, because 21β-hydroxylase is also required and absent

e.correcta: 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC) itself has intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity, and corticosterone (the next intermediate downstream) also retains weak mineralocorticoid activity, so if the pathway is blocked below DOC (e.g., at 11β-hydroxylase or aldosterone synthase), DOC and corticosterone can accumulate and still activate mineralocorticoid receptors, producing a mineralocorticoid excess state (hypertension, hypokalemia) even though aldosterone itself is not made. This is the classic explanation for the hypertensive phenotype seen in 11β-hydroxylase deficiency congenital adrenal hyperplasia, despite low aldosterone.

incorrectas.A: Synthesis is not completely blocked because DOC accumulates proximal to (and includes) the block and retains mineralocorticoid activity itself, allowing continued mineralocorticoid receptor activation despite the enzymatic defect further downstream.
incorrectas.C: Aldosterone itself cannot be made when the pathway is blocked below DOC, and cortisol is not converted to aldosterone; instead, the mineralocorticoid activity comes from the accumulated DOC and corticosterone precursors themselves, not from cortisol conversion.
incorrectas.D: 21β-hydroxylase acts earlier in the pathway (upstream of DOC, converting progesterone to DOC), so a block below DOC (at 11β-hydroxylase or aldosterone synthase) does not implicate a missing 21β-hydroxylase — that enzyme's activity is presumed intact in this scenario.

preguntas.q: If the mineralocorticoid synthesis pathway is blocked above the level of 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC), as in 21β-hydroxylase deficiency, can mineralocorticoids still be produced?

o.A: Yes, corticosterone still retains full mineralocorticoid activity
o.B: No, because there is no precursor beyond the block with mineralocorticoid activity
o.C: Yes, via an alternate zona reticularis pathway
o.D: No, because ACTH secretion is suppressed

e.correcta: In 21β-hydroxylase deficiency, the block occurs before DOC is formed (21β-hydroxylase normally converts progesterone to DOC), so no DOC, corticosterone, or aldosterone can be synthesized — none of the precursors with mineralocorticoid activity accumulate, unlike in 11β-hydroxylase deficiency where DOC piles up upstream of the block. This is why classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes a salt-wasting crisis (aldosterone deficiency) rather than the hypertension seen with 11β-hydroxylase deficiency.

incorrectas.A: Corticosterone cannot be formed at all in 21β-hydroxylase deficiency because the block occurs upstream of DOC (and thus upstream of corticosterone), so there is no precursor with mineralocorticoid activity available to compensate — unlike blocks that occur below DOC.
incorrectas.C: There is no alternate zona reticularis pathway that bypasses 21β-hydroxylase to generate mineralocorticoids; the zona reticularis mainly produces adrenal androgens, and the enzymatic block still prevents mineralocorticoid precursor formation in the glomerulosa.
incorrectas.D: While ACTH-axis feedback dynamics are altered in congenital adrenal hyperplasia (with ACTH actually rising due to low cortisol), the reason mineralocorticoids can't be produced is the enzymatic block preventing precursor formation, not suppressed ACTH secretion (which is, in fact, typically elevated).

preguntas.q: In the absence of 17α-hydroxylase, can glucocorticoids still be produced?

o.A: No, glucocorticoid synthesis is completely abolished
o.B: Yes, the zona fasciculata can still produce corticosterone, which has glucocorticoid activity
o.D: No, because cortisol is the only glucocorticoid and requires this enzyme

e.correcta: 17α-hydroxylase is required to make cortisol (and androgens) in the zona fasciculata/reticularis, but the zona fasciculata can still produce corticosterone via the parallel pathway that does not require 17α-hydroxylation, and corticosterone itself has weak but real glucocorticoid activity. This is why 17α-hydroxylase deficiency causes glucocorticoid insufficiency symptoms that are less severe than a complete block would predict, while also causing mineralocorticoid excess (from DOC/corticosterone accumulation) and impaired sex steroid synthesis.

incorrectas.A: Glucocorticoid synthesis is not completely abolished because corticosterone, made via the 17α-hydroxylase-independent branch of the pathway, still provides some glucocorticoid activity, sparing the patient from complete adrenal glucocorticoid failure.
incorrectas.C: 17α-hydroxylase deficiency actually impairs androgen synthesis (since 17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase is required for androgen precursor formation), so there is no unopposed androgen conversion — if anything, androgen production is reduced, not increased.
incorrectas.D: Cortisol is not the only glucocorticoid; corticosterone, produced via a separate branch not requiring 17α-hydroxylase, retains glucocorticoid activity, which is precisely why glucocorticoid function is preserved (albeit weaker) despite the enzyme deficiency.

preguntas.q: Can glucocorticoids still be produced if there is a deficiency of cholesterol desmolase, 21β-hydroxylase, 11β-hydroxylase, or 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase?

o.A: Yes, corticosterone compensates in all these cases
o.B: No, deficiency of any of these enzymes blocks synthesis of both corticosterone and cortisol
o.C: Yes, but only cortisol synthesis is affected, not corticosterone
o.D: No, but only because ACTH secretion fails

e.correcta: Cholesterol desmolase, 21β-hydroxylase, 11β-hydroxylase, and 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase all act at steps that are shared/required by both the corticosterone and cortisol synthesis branches (unlike 17α-hydroxylase, which is only needed for the cortisol/androgen branch and can be bypassed by the corticosterone pathway), so deficiency of any of these blocks production of both glucocorticoids entirely. This distinguishes them from 17α-hydroxylase deficiency, where the parallel corticosterone pathway can still provide some glucocorticoid activity.

incorrectas.A: Corticosterone itself requires these same shared enzymes (desmolase, 21β-hydroxylase, 11β-hydroxylase, 3β-HSD) for its own synthesis, so a deficiency in any of them blocks corticosterone production just as much as cortisol — it cannot compensate here the way it does for 17α-hydroxylase deficiency.
incorrectas.C: These enzymes lie upstream of and are shared by both the corticosterone and cortisol branches, so their deficiency blocks both pathways equally; only 17α-hydroxylase is branch-specific to cortisol, sparing corticosterone synthesis.
incorrectas.D: The block in glucocorticoid production results directly from the missing enzymatic step needed for steroidogenesis itself, not from a secondary failure of ACTH secretion, which would be a separate (and here, unstated) central process.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme is unique to the zona glomerulosa, making it essential specifically for the mineralocorticoid synthesis pathway?

e.correcta: Aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2) is expressed only in the zona glomerulosa and catalyzes the final steps converting corticosterone to aldosterone, making it the enzyme that uniquely commits this zone to mineralocorticoid production rather than glucocorticoid or androgen synthesis. This zone-specific enzyme expression is why the adrenal cortex is functionally and anatomically divided (glomerulosa for mineralocorticoids, fasciculata for glucocorticoids, reticularis for androgens), a distinction frequently tested alongside the enzyme defects causing various forms of congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

incorrectas.A: 17α-hydroxylase is present in the zona fasciculata and reticularis (not glomerulosa), where it directs steroidogenesis toward cortisol and androgens; its absence in the glomerulosa is actually part of why that zone is restricted to mineralocorticoid production.
incorrectas.B: Cholesterol desmolase (CYP11A1/side-chain cleavage enzyme) is expressed in all three zones of the adrenal cortex as the first, shared step converting cholesterol to pregnenolone, so it is not unique to the zona glomerulosa.
incorrectas.D: 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase is also expressed across all three adrenal cortical zones as a shared early enzyme in steroid synthesis, unlike aldosterone synthase, which is the zone-restricted enzyme unique to the glomerulosa.

preguntas.q: Which enzymes are unique to the zona fasciculata/reticularis, driving the glucocorticoid and androgen synthesis pathways?

e.correcta: 17α-hydroxylase and 17,20-lyase are expressed only in the zona fasciculata and zona reticularis (not the zona glomerulosa), which is precisely why those two zones, and not the glomerulosa, can produce cortisol and androgens — the glomerulosa lacks these enzymes and is therefore restricted to the mineralocorticoid pathway (aldosterone) instead. This zonal enzyme expression pattern explains why 17α-hydroxylase deficiency selectively impairs cortisol and sex steroid synthesis while sparing (and even increasing) mineralocorticoid precursor production.

incorrectas.A: Aldosterone synthase is unique to the zona glomerulosa (not fasciculata/reticularis), and 21β-hydroxylase is expressed across multiple zones; neither is the enzyme pair that specifically distinguishes the fasciculata/reticularis's ability to make cortisol and androgens.
incorrectas.C: Cholesterol desmolase and 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase are expressed in all three adrenal cortical zones as shared early steps of steroidogenesis, not zone-specific enzymes unique to the fasciculata/reticularis.
incorrectas.D: 11β-hydroxylase and 21β-hydroxylase are expressed in multiple adrenal zones (needed for both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid pathways), not restricted to the fasciculata/reticularis the way 17α-hydroxylase and 17,20-lyase are.

preguntas.q: The mineralocorticoids and glucocorticoids (progesterone, deoxycorticosterone, aldosterone, and cortisol) belong to which class of steroids based on carbon number?

e.correcta: Progesterone, deoxycorticosterone (DOC), aldosterone, and cortisol all retain the full 21-carbon steroid backbone (a pregnane-derived structure with an intact C20-C21 side chain), classifying them as 21-carbon steroids, in contrast to androgens (19-carbon, having lost the side chain via 17,20-lyase) and estrogens (18-carbon, further modified by aromatization). This carbon classification reflects the biosynthetic pathway position — mineralocorticoids and glucocorticoids are made before the side-chain-cleaving 17,20-lyase step that generates androgens.

incorrectas.A: 18-carbon steroids refer to the estrogens (estradiol, estrone), which have undergone aromatization of the A ring and loss of additional carbons — a structurally distinct class from the mineralocorticoids/glucocorticoids listed.
incorrectas.B: 19-carbon steroids are the androgens (testosterone, DHEA, androstenedione), formed after 17,20-lyase removes the C20-C21 side chain from 21-carbon precursors — this is a later step in the pathway than the mineralocorticoid/glucocorticoid branch.
incorrectas.D: 27-carbon refers to cholesterol itself, the precursor from which all steroid hormones are derived via progressive side-chain cleavage; none of the biologically active corticosteroids retain this full carbon count.

preguntas.q: Cortisol secretion follows which characteristic pattern?

o.A: Continuous and constant throughout the day
o.D: Triggered only by acute stress, otherwise absent

e.correcta: Cortisol secretion follows a pulsatile pattern driven by episodic ACTH release, superimposed on a circadian rhythm generated by the hypothalamic suprachiasmatic nucleus, producing characteristically high levels in the early morning (peaking around waking) and a nadir in the late evening/early night. This diurnal pattern is clinically important — it's why random cortisol levels are hard to interpret and why tests like the dexamethasone suppression test or late-night salivary cortisol are timed to exploit this expected rhythm.

incorrectas.A: Cortisol secretion is not continuous and constant; it fluctuates substantially over the day (highest in the morning, lowest at night) due to pulsatile ACTH-driven release, which is why single random measurements are often unreliable without knowing the time of day.
incorrectas.C: There is no established month-to-month seasonal secretion pattern that defines cortisol physiology; the well-characterized rhythm is the 24-hour circadian (diurnal) cycle, not a seasonal one.
incorrectas.D: While cortisol is indeed strongly upregulated during acute stress (as part of the HPA axis stress response), it is not "otherwise absent" — there is a robust baseline circadian secretion pattern present even without stress, which is the physiologic rhythm being described here.

preguntas.q: In a person with a typical morning-wake, night-sleep schedule, cortisol levels are highest just before which event and lowest at which time?

o.A: Highest before sleep onset, lowest at midday
o.B: Highest before awakening, lowest in the evening
o.C: Highest at midday, lowest before awakening
o.D: Highest in the evening, lowest before awakening

e.correcta: Cortisol follows a circadian rhythm driven by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, peaking just before awakening (early morning) to help mobilize energy stores and prepare the body for the demands of waking activity, and reaching its nadir in the late evening before sleep onset. This pattern is why cortisol testing timing matters clinically (e.g., interpreting an AM cortisol versus late-night salivary cortisol in Cushing syndrome workups).

incorrectas.A: This reverses the actual pattern — cortisol is lowest around sleep onset/evening and highest before awakening, not highest before sleep and lowest at midday, which does not reflect the true circadian curve of cortisol secretion.
incorrectas.C: Cortisol is not highest at midday; levels are already declining through the day after the early morning peak, and the true trough occurs in the evening before sleep rather than the level being lowest before awakening.
incorrectas.D: Cortisol does not peak in the evening — its peak occurs in the early morning just before waking, with levels progressively falling throughout the day to their lowest point at night, the opposite of what this option describes.

preguntas.q: Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) is secreted by neurons of which hypothalamic nucleus?

e.correcta: The paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus contains parvocellular neurosecretory neurons that synthesize CRH and release it into the hypophyseal portal system at the median eminence, where it travels to the anterior pituitary to stimulate ACTH secretion from corticotrophs. The same PVN also has magnocellular neurons that make oxytocin, but it is the parvocellular population that drives the HPA axis, making the PVN the anatomic hub for stress-induced cortisol release.

incorrectas.A: The supraoptic nucleus is composed almost entirely of magnocellular neurons that produce ADH (and some oxytocin) for release from the posterior pituitary, not releasing hormones for the anterior pituitary like CRH.
incorrectas.B: The arcuate nucleus produces GHRH and dopamine (as prolactin-inhibiting factor) and also contains the neurons central to appetite regulation (NPY/AgRP and POMC neurons), but it is not the source of CRH.
incorrectas.D: The suprachiasmatic nucleus is the master circadian pacemaker that receives direct retinal input and entrains rhythms such as the diurnal cortisol pattern, but it does not itself secrete CRH.

preguntas.q: Through which second messenger does CRH act on corticotrophs in the anterior pituitary to stimulate ACTH secretion?

e.correcta: CRH binds Gs-coupled receptors on anterior pituitary corticotrophs, activating adenylyl cyclase to raise intracellular cAMP, which activates protein kinase A and drives transcription and release of ACTH (via POMC processing). This cAMP-mediated cascade is the same general Gs-PKA mechanism used by many anterior pituitary trophic hormone receptors, distinguishing it from the phospholipase C pathway used by some other hypothalamic releasing hormones like GnRH and TRH.

incorrectas.A: IP3/DAG is the second messenger system used by Gq-coupled receptors such as GnRH and TRH receptors on their respective pituitary target cells, not the CRH receptor on corticotrophs, which signals through Gs/cAMP instead.
incorrectas.B: cGMP is the second messenger for guanylate cyclase-linked receptors, such as those for atrial natriuretic peptide or nitric oxide signaling, and is not involved in CRH receptor signaling in the anterior pituitary.
incorrectas.D: Tyrosine kinase activity is the signaling mechanism used by growth factor receptors like insulin and IGF-1 receptors, not by CRH, which acts through a G-protein-coupled receptor linked to cAMP rather than intrinsic or receptor-associated tyrosine kinase activity.

preguntas.q: CRH binds corticotrophs in the anterior pituitary, prompting them to synthesize which precursor protein and secrete which hormone?

e.correcta: CRH released from the hypothalamus binds Gs-coupled receptors on corticotrophs, activating cAMP/PKA signaling that drives transcription and processing of proopiomelanocortin (POMC), a large precursor peptide. POMC is then cleaved by prohormone convertases into ACTH (along with beta-lipotropin and other fragments), and ACTH is the hormone secreted into the circulation to act on the adrenal cortex. This POMC-to-ACTH relationship also explains why conditions with very high ACTH (like primary adrenal insufficiency) can cause hyperpigmentation, since POMC cleavage also yields melanocyte-stimulating hormone fragments.

incorrectas.A: Prolactin is synthesized by lactotrophs and regulated mainly by dopamine (inhibitory) and TRH, not CRH; oxytocin is made in hypothalamic neurons and released from the posterior pituitary, not by corticotrophs, so neither fits the CRH-corticotroph axis described here.
incorrectas.C: TRH is a hypothalamic peptide that stimulates thyrotrophs to secrete TSH — this is a distinct axis from the CRH-corticotroph-ACTH pathway and involves different cell types and hormones entirely.
incorrectas.D: While corticotrophs do synthesize proopiomelanocortin, the hormone they secrete is ACTH, not growth hormone; GH is produced by somatotrophs under control of GHRH and somatostatin, a completely separate axis.

preguntas.q: ACTH acts on which zone(s) of the adrenal cortex to increase steroid hormone synthesis?

o.C: All three zones, though predominantly the zona fasciculata

e.correcta: ACTH receptors (melanocortin-2 receptors) are expressed on cells throughout all three zones of the adrenal cortex — glomerulosa, fasciculata, and reticularis — so ACTH provides a trophic and steroidogenic stimulus to the entire cortex. However, its dominant physiologic role is driving cortisol synthesis in the zona fasciculata (and androgens in the reticularis), since aldosterone synthesis in the zona glomerulosa is primarily controlled by angiotensin II and potassium rather than ACTH. This is why chronic ACTH excess causes diffuse cortical hyperplasia rather than an isolated single-zone change.

incorrectas.A: Restricting ACTH's action to only the zona glomerulosa ignores its much stronger and more clinically dominant effect on the zona fasciculata, and also ignores that the glomerulosa is actually more dependent on the renin-angiotensin system than on ACTH.
incorrectas.B: While the zona fasciculata is indeed the primary target, saying ACTH acts 'only' there is incomplete — ACTH receptors are present on all three zones and ACTH still exerts trophic effects on the glomerulosa and reticularis as well.
incorrectas.D: Limiting the effect to only the zona reticularis ignores that ACTH's predominant and most clinically important action is on cortisol production in the zona fasciculata, with the reticularis being a secondary target for adrenal androgen synthesis.

preguntas.q: ACTH increases adrenocortical steroid hormone synthesis primarily by stimulating which enzyme?

e.correcta: Cholesterol desmolase (CYP11A1, the cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme) converts cholesterol to pregnenolone, which is the first and rate-limiting step of all adrenal steroidogenesis. ACTH binds its receptor and, via cAMP/PKA, rapidly upregulates cholesterol desmolase activity (and also promotes cholesterol delivery to the mitochondria via StAR protein), making this the key control point through which ACTH increases total steroid output. Because this is the committed step feeding into glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid, and androgen pathways, stimulating it increases synthesis across all three classes of adrenal steroids.

incorrectas.A: Aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2) catalyzes the final steps converting corticosterone to aldosterone in the zona glomerulosa; it is primarily regulated by angiotensin II and potassium, not the main ACTH-responsive rate-limiting enzyme for overall steroidogenesis.
incorrectas.B: 17α-hydroxylase directs steroid precursors toward cortisol and androgen synthesis (versus mineralocorticoid pathways) but acts downstream of the initial rate-limiting conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone, so it is not the primary site of ACTH's stimulatory effect.
incorrectas.D: 21β-hydroxylase converts progesterone/17-hydroxyprogesterone to precursors of aldosterone and cortisol, respectively, but like 17α-hydroxylase it acts further downstream and is not the rate-limiting enzyme that ACTH primarily upregulates.

preguntas.q: What long-term effect does ACTH have on its own receptors in the adrenal cortex?

o.C: No change in receptor number, only acute signaling changes
o.D: Receptor internalization with permanent loss of responsiveness

e.correcta: Chronic ACTH stimulation causes up-regulation of its own melanocortin 2 receptors (MC2R) on adrenal cortical cells, increasing the gland's sensitivity to subsequent ACTH signaling — this is part of why prolonged ACTH stimulation leads to adrenal hypertrophy and increased steroidogenic capacity over time (trophic effect), in contrast to many other hormone-receptor systems that down-regulate with sustained stimulation. This up-regulation helps the adrenal cortex sustain elevated cortisol output during chronic stress or ACTH-secreting states.

incorrectas.A: Down-regulation, where sustained hormone exposure reduces receptor number and blunts responsiveness, is the pattern seen with many other endocrine receptors (e.g., prolonged beta-agonist exposure), but ACTH on the adrenal cortex does the opposite, increasing sensitivity over time.
incorrectas.C: ACTH does not merely have transient/acute signaling effects with unchanged receptor numbers; part of its long-term trophic action is genuinely increasing MC2R receptor expression and adrenal gland growth, not just modulating existing receptor signaling.
incorrectas.D: Receptor internalization with permanent loss of responsiveness would predict adrenal insensitivity or atrophy with chronic ACTH exposure, but the physiologic reality is the opposite — chronic ACTH exposure causes adrenal hypertrophy and heightened, not diminished, sensitivity.

preguntas.q: Chronically elevated ACTH levels produce what structural change in the adrenal cortex?

o.C: Selective fibrosis of the zona glomerulosa

e.correcta: ACTH is trophic to the adrenal cortex — beyond acutely stimulating steroidogenesis, chronic ACTH stimulation upregulates cellular machinery (LDL receptors, steroidogenic enzymes, mitochondrial mass) and promotes cell growth and proliferation. Sustained high ACTH, as seen in Cushing disease (pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma) or conditions of chronic ACTH stimulation, therefore produces adrenal cortical hypertrophy and hyperplasia rather than atrophy, since the gland is being actively driven to work harder rather than being suppressed.

incorrectas.A: Atrophy of the adrenal cortex occurs with chronically low ACTH (e.g., after long-term exogenous glucocorticoid use suppressing the HPA axis), which is the opposite scenario from chronically elevated ACTH described in the question.
incorrectas.C: Selective fibrosis of a single zone is not a recognized consequence of ACTH excess; ACTH's trophic effect is generalized across the cortex, producing hyperplasia rather than a fibrotic, zone-specific process.
incorrectas.D: Calcification of the adrenal medulla is not a feature of ACTH excess and the medulla, being derived from neural crest and responsive to sympathetic input rather than ACTH, is not the tissue affected by this pathway at all.

preguntas.q: Through which second messenger does ACTH exert its actions on the adrenal cortex?

e.correcta: ACTH binds the melanocortin 2 receptor (MC2R) on adrenal cortical cells, a Gs-coupled receptor that activates adenylate cyclase to raise intracellular cAMP; cAMP then activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates and upregulates cholesterol desmolase (the rate-limiting enzyme converting cholesterol to pregnenolone) to boost steroidogenesis. This cAMP-PKA cascade is the same general mechanism used by other peptide hormones acting through Gs-coupled receptors, such as TSH, LH, and FSH.

incorrectas.B: IP3/DAG signaling is used by Gq-coupled receptors such as those for GnRH and TRH, which mobilize intracellular calcium and activate protein kinase C, a different pathway from the cAMP cascade ACTH uses on adrenal cells.
incorrectas.C: cGMP is the second messenger for natriuretic peptides and nitric oxide signaling (via guanylate cyclase), a pathway unrelated to ACTH's action on the adrenal cortex.
incorrectas.D: JAK/STAT signaling is used by cytokine and growth hormone/prolactin receptors that lack intrinsic kinase activity and instead recruit Janus kinases, a mechanism distinct from the Gs/cAMP pathway ACTH employs.

preguntas.q: How does cortisol regulate CRH secretion from the hypothalamus?

o.A: It has no effect on CRH secretion
o.B: It inhibits CRH secretion, both directly and indirectly
o.C: It stimulates CRH secretion via positive feedback
o.D: It inhibits CRH only indirectly via the adrenal medulla

e.correcta: Cortisol exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus in two ways: directly, by binding glucocorticoid receptors on CRH-producing neurons to suppress CRH transcription and release, and indirectly, by inhibiting ACTH secretion from the pituitary (which reduces any downstream signals that might otherwise sustain hypothalamic drive). This dual-level feedback is what keeps the HPA axis tightly regulated under baseline conditions, and it's the basis for why exogenous steroids suppress endogenous cortisol production — the hypothalamus and pituitary sense the elevated glucocorticoid and shut down CRH/ACTH output.

incorrectas.A: Saying cortisol has no effect on CRH ignores the entire principle of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal negative feedback, which is fundamental to endocrine physiology and to understanding conditions like iatrogenic adrenal suppression.
incorrectas.C: Cortisol does not stimulate CRH via positive feedback; positive feedback loops are rare in endocrine axes and would be maladaptive here, since unchecked cortisol stimulation of its own upstream signal would cause runaway hypercortisolism.
incorrectas.D: The adrenal medulla is not part of the cortisol feedback loop on the hypothalamus; cortisol feeds back directly on hypothalamic CRH neurons and also indirectly via suppression of pituitary ACTH, not through the catecholamine-secreting medulla.

preguntas.q: How does cortisol regulate ACTH secretion from the anterior pituitary?

o.C: Has no direct effect, acts only via the hypothalamus

e.correcta: Cortisol acts directly on anterior pituitary corticotrophs to inhibit ACTH secretion, forming a short negative-feedback loop in addition to its longer-loop inhibitory effect on hypothalamic CRH, together keeping circulating cortisol within a controlled range.

incorrectas.A: Cortisol suppresses, rather than stimulates, ACTH secretion; stimulation would produce unchecked positive feedback rather than the homeostatic negative feedback that characterizes the HPA axis.
incorrectas.C: Cortisol has a well-established direct inhibitory effect on the pituitary corticotroph itself, in addition to its indirect hypothalamic effects, so it is not limited to an indirect route.
incorrectas.D: This direct inhibitory feedback on the pituitary operates continuously as part of normal physiologic regulation, not only during acute stress states.

preguntas.q: Chronically elevated cortisol (glucocorticoid excess) leads to decreased levels of which two upstream hormones via negative feedback?

e.correcta: When cortisol is chronically elevated — whether from an adrenal tumor, exogenous steroid use, or ectopic ACTH — it exerts sustained negative feedback at both the hypothalamus (suppressing CRH) and the anterior pituitary (suppressing ACTH synthesis and release from corticotrophs). Over time this leads to atrophy of the corticotrophs and a blunted HPA axis, which is why patients on long-term steroids can develop adrenal insufficiency if the drug is stopped abruptly — their CRH and ACTH have been suppressed and cannot immediately ramp back up to drive adrenal recovery.

incorrectas.A: TRH and TSH are part of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis and are regulated by thyroid hormone feedback, not by cortisol; this axis is anatomically and functionally distinct from the HPA axis being tested here.
incorrectas.B: GnRH and LH belong to the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis; while chronic glucocorticoid excess can have some suppressive crosstalk on reproductive hormones, the direct negative feedback loop described by chronically elevated cortisol specifically targets CRH and ACTH.
incorrectas.D: GHRH and growth hormone are part of a separate somatotropic axis regulated by GHRH, somatostatin, and IGF-1 feedback; cortisol is not the primary negative feedback signal for this axis in the way it is for CRH and ACTH.

preguntas.q: In a normal (non-Cushingoid) patient, what is the expected result of a low-dose dexamethasone suppression test?

o.A: Low-dose dexamethasone fails to suppress cortisol secretion
o.B: Low-dose dexamethasone inhibits ACTH secretion and consequently cortisol secretion
o.C: Low-dose dexamethasone paradoxically increases ACTH secretion
o.D: The test has no effect regardless of dose in normal individuals

e.correcta: In a normal individual, the HPA axis is intact, so even a low dose of exogenous dexamethasone (a potent synthetic glucocorticoid) is enough to bind pituitary and hypothalamic glucocorticoid receptors and trigger the normal negative feedback response, suppressing CRH and ACTH and thus lowering cortisol. This is the physiologic basis of the test: a normal axis responds to even small amounts of exogenous glucocorticoid, whereas autonomous ACTH- or cortisol-producing processes (as in Cushing syndrome) resist this low-dose suppression, which is what makes the test diagnostically useful.

incorrectas.A: Failure of low-dose dexamethasone to suppress cortisol is the abnormal finding seen in Cushing syndrome (due to an autonomous or dysregulated ACTH/cortisol source), not the expected result in someone with an intact, normally feedback-responsive axis.
incorrectas.C: A paradoxical increase in ACTH after low-dose dexamethasone is not a normal physiologic response; it would suggest an abnormality resistant to glucocorticoid negative feedback rather than the expected suppression seen in health.
incorrectas.D: Saying the test has no effect regardless of dose contradicts the entire premise of the test, which relies on the fact that a normal hypothalamic-pituitary axis is exquisitely feedback-sensitive and does respond, even to low doses of dexamethasone.

preguntas.q: A patient with Cushing syndrome due to an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma undergoes a dexamethasone suppression test. What result is expected?

o.A: Neither low nor high dose suppresses cortisol secretion
o.B: Low dose suppresses cortisol, but high dose does not
o.C: Low dose does not suppress cortisol secretion, but high dose does
o.D: Both low and high dose suppress cortisol normally

e.correcta: A pituitary corticotroph adenoma still retains some responsiveness to negative feedback, but it has a higher feedback set-point than normal corticotrophs — low-dose dexamethasone is insufficient to suppress the tumor's ACTH output, so cortisol remains elevated, but a high dose can overcome the adenoma's resistance and suppress ACTH (and thus cortisol) because the tumor cells still express glucocorticoid receptors, just at reduced sensitivity. This 'low dose fails, high dose succeeds' pattern is the classic way to distinguish Cushing disease (pituitary source) from an ectopic ACTH-secreting tumor, which typically does not suppress even at high dose because it lacks meaningful glucocorticoid receptor feedback regulation.

incorrectas.A: If neither low nor high dose suppressed cortisol, this would suggest an ectopic ACTH source (e.g., small cell lung cancer) or an autonomous adrenal tumor, not a pituitary adenoma, which typically retains at least some feedback sensitivity at higher glucocorticoid doses.
incorrectas.B: This pattern is reversed from what actually happens — pituitary adenomas fail to suppress with low-dose dexamethasone but do suppress with high-dose, not the other way around.
incorrectas.D: If both low and high dose suppressed cortisol normally, this would indicate a normal, non-Cushingoid HPA axis, not a pathologic ACTH-secreting adenoma, which by definition shows abnormal (though not completely absent) feedback regulation.

preguntas.q: A patient with Cushing syndrome caused by a cortisol-secreting adrenal cortical tumor undergoes a dexamethasone suppression test. What result is expected?

o.A: Low dose suppresses cortisol, but high dose does not
o.B: Both low and high dose suppress cortisol secretion
o.C: Neither low nor high dose dexamethasone suppresses cortisol secretion
o.D: Only high-dose dexamethasone suppresses cortisol secretion

e.correcta: A cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma or carcinoma produces cortisol autonomously, independent of pituitary ACTH stimulation, so it has no glucocorticoid receptor-mediated feedback loop to be suppressed at all — administering dexamethasone (even at high dose) cannot turn off a tumor that isn't being driven by ACTH in the first place. In fact, in this scenario endogenous ACTH is already suppressed by the tumor's cortisol output (accounting for low ACTH levels), but the adrenal tumor itself keeps secreting cortisol autonomously regardless of exogenous steroid administration.

incorrectas.A: A 'low dose suppresses, high dose does not' pattern doesn't fit any classic dexamethasone suppression test category and specifically does not describe the physiology of an autonomous adrenal tumor, which fails to suppress at any dose since it is independent of ACTH/pituitary feedback altogether.
incorrectas.B: If both doses suppressed cortisol, this would suggest a normal, feedback-responsive axis, not an autonomously functioning adrenal tumor, which by definition escapes pituitary control and thus escapes dexamethasone suppression testing entirely.
incorrectas.D: Only high-dose suppression (with low-dose failure) is the pattern expected for a pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma, not an adrenal tumor; an adrenal source is autonomous and doesn't respond to feedback suppression at either dose.

preguntas.q: What is the effect of somatostatin and opioids on ACTH secretion from the anterior pituitary?

e.correcta: Somatostatin and opioids (endogenous endorphins/enkephalins) act on the hypothalamus and pituitary to inhibit CRH and ACTH release, providing an additional layer of regulatory control over the HPA axis beyond the classic cortisol negative feedback loop. This matters clinically because it explains phenomena like stress-induced analgesia interacting with cortisol regulation, and it highlights that the HPA axis is modulated by multiple neuropeptide inputs, not cortisol feedback alone.

incorrectas.A: Somatostatin and opioids are inhibitory, not stimulatory, on ACTH secretion; describing them as increasing ACTH reverses their actual physiologic role in dampening HPA axis activity.
incorrectas.B: Saying they have no effect ignores their established inhibitory role on CRH/ACTH release, which is a recognized part of the broader neuroendocrine regulation of the HPA axis beyond simple cortisol feedback.
incorrectas.D: There is no established biphasic pattern for somatostatin and opioids on ACTH secretion; their effect is consistently inhibitory rather than an initial increase followed by a decrease.

preguntas.q: Glucocorticoids increase which process in skeletal muscle, providing amino acids to the liver for gluconeogenesis?

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids promote catabolism in skeletal muscle, breaking down muscle protein into amino acids (this is part of their overall catabolic, stress-hormone role). These amino acids are released into circulation and taken up by the liver, where they serve as substrates for gluconeogenesis, helping maintain blood glucose during stress or fasting states; this is also why chronic glucocorticoid excess (Cushing syndrome) classically causes proximal muscle wasting and weakness.

incorrectas.B: Glycogen synthesis is an anabolic process that glucocorticoids do not primarily promote in skeletal muscle; in fact glucocorticoids favor catabolic pathways like proteolysis rather than glycogen storage in muscle.
incorrectas.C: Glucocorticoids actually decrease peripheral glucose uptake (including via GLUT4 in muscle) as part of their anti-insulin, hyperglycemic effect, so increased glucose uptake is the opposite of what they cause.
incorrectas.D: Lipoprotein lipase activity relates to fat storage/uptake in adipose tissue, not to the muscle protein breakdown pathway that supplies amino acids to the liver for gluconeogenesis described in the question.

preguntas.q: What effect do glucocorticoids have on peripheral glucose utilization and adipose tissue insulin sensitivity?

o.A: Increase glucose utilization and increase insulin sensitivity
o.B: Decrease glucose utilization and decrease insulin sensitivity
o.C: Increase glucose utilization and decrease insulin sensitivity

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids act as counter-regulatory, anti-insulin hormones: they decrease peripheral tissue (muscle and adipose) uptake and utilization of glucose while also reducing adipose tissue sensitivity to insulin's signaling actions. This combination raises blood glucose and contributes to insulin resistance, which is why chronic glucocorticoid excess (endogenous Cushing syndrome or long-term steroid therapy) commonly produces steroid-induced hyperglycemia or overt diabetes.

incorrectas.A: Glucocorticoids do the opposite — they decrease, not increase, peripheral glucose utilization and insulin sensitivity, consistent with their overall role as stress hormones that raise blood glucose.
incorrectas.C: While glucocorticoids do decrease insulin sensitivity, they simultaneously decrease (not increase) glucose utilization by peripheral tissues; the two effects work in the same hyperglycemic direction, not opposite directions.
incorrectas.D: Saying there is no change in either parameter contradicts the well-established diabetogenic effect of glucocorticoids, which reliably impair both glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity in peripheral tissues.

preguntas.q: How do glucocorticoids affect insulin resistance, and by what mechanism?

o.A: Decrease insulin resistance by increasing adipose insulin sensitivity
o.B: Increase insulin resistance by decreasing adipose tissue insulin sensitivity
o.D: Increase insulin resistance by directly destroying pancreatic beta cells

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids increase insulin resistance by decreasing adipose tissue's sensitivity to insulin, meaning insulin becomes less effective at suppressing lipolysis and promoting glucose uptake in fat tissue at a given insulin concentration. This mechanism, combined with glucocorticoids' effects on muscle and liver, is central to why chronic glucocorticoid excess (whether endogenous or from steroid medications) predisposes to hyperglycemia and metabolic syndrome-like features.

incorrectas.A: Glucocorticoids increase, not decrease, insulin resistance, and they do so by decreasing (not increasing) adipose tissue insulin sensitivity — this option reverses both the direction of the effect and the underlying mechanism.
incorrectas.C: Claiming no effect on insulin resistance ignores the well-documented diabetogenic, insulin-resistance-promoting action of glucocorticoids that underlies steroid-induced hyperglycemia in clinical practice.
incorrectas.D: Glucocorticoids do not directly destroy pancreatic beta cells (that mechanism describes autoimmune destruction in type 1 diabetes); rather, they act on peripheral tissues like adipose tissue to reduce insulin sensitivity, leaving beta cell mass intact.

preguntas.q: Glucocorticoids increase peripheral lipolysis, which supplies the liver with more of which substrate for gluconeogenesis?

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids stimulate lipolysis in adipose tissue, breaking down triglycerides into free fatty acids and glycerol; the glycerol backbone is then shuttled to the liver where it serves as a direct substrate for gluconeogenesis, complementing the amino acids supplied by muscle proteolysis. This dual mobilization of glycerol (from fat) and amino acids (from muscle) is how glucocorticoids maximize the liver's substrate supply to sustain blood glucose during stress or fasting.

incorrectas.A: Free fatty acids released by lipolysis are used primarily as an alternative fuel source (via beta-oxidation and ketogenesis) rather than as a gluconeogenic substrate, since fatty acids cannot be net converted to glucose in humans.
incorrectas.C: Alanine is an important gluconeogenic substrate, but it comes from skeletal muscle protein breakdown (via the glucose-alanine cycle), not from adipose tissue lipolysis, which is the process specifically referenced in this question.
incorrectas.D: Lactate is a gluconeogenic substrate generated mainly from anaerobic glycolysis in muscle and red blood cells (via the Cori cycle), not from adipose tissue lipolysis, so it doesn't fit the pathway described here.

preguntas.q: In hypocortisolism, decreased levels of which hepatic process lead to hypoglycemia?

e.correcta: Cortisol is a permissive and stimulatory hormone for hepatic gluconeogenic enzyme expression (e.g., PEPCK), so in states of hypocortisolism (such as Addison disease or adrenal crisis), gluconeogenesis is markedly reduced. Because gluconeogenesis is a critical source of glucose during fasting, its impairment in cortisol deficiency leads to hypoglycemia, which is a classic and dangerous feature of adrenal insufficiency, especially during physiologic stress when glucose demand rises.

incorrectas.A: Glycogenolysis is more directly regulated by glucagon and epinephrine rather than being the primary cortisol-dependent pathway; while cortisol has some permissive role, the hallmark hepatic defect in cortisol deficiency causing hypoglycemia is impaired gluconeogenesis.
incorrectas.B: Glycolysis is the breakdown of glucose for energy, which would tend to consume rather than produce glucose; it is not the hepatic pathway whose impairment in cortisol deficiency explains hypoglycemia.
incorrectas.D: Lipogenesis refers to fat synthesis and storage, an anabolic process unrelated to hepatic glucose production; it is not the pathway responsible for hypoglycemia in states of cortisol deficiency.

preguntas.q: What effect do glucocorticoids have on blood neutrophil count, and by what mechanism?

o.A: Decreased neutrophils due to increased apoptosis
o.B: Increased neutrophils (neutrophilia) due to decreased WBC adhesion
o.D: Increased neutrophils due to increased bone marrow production only

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids cause neutrophilia by reducing the adhesion of neutrophils to vascular endothelium (downregulating adhesion molecules), which demarginates neutrophils from the vessel wall pool into the actively circulating pool, increasing the measured blood neutrophil count without necessarily increasing total body neutrophil production. This is a classic pearl: glucocorticoids raise the neutrophil count while simultaneously causing lymphopenia and eosinopenia, and clinicians must recognize this as a pharmacologic effect rather than a sign of infection.

incorrectas.A: Glucocorticoids decrease apoptosis of neutrophils (prolonging their lifespan) rather than increasing it; increased apoptosis would lower the neutrophil count, which is the opposite of the neutrophilia glucocorticoids actually cause.
incorrectas.C: Glucocorticoids do produce a measurable and clinically important change (neutrophilia), so 'no change' is incorrect and would miss an important diagnostic pitfall where steroid use can mimic a bacterial infection picture on a CBC.
incorrectas.D: The neutrophilia from glucocorticoids is mainly due to demargination (redistribution from the vessel wall to the circulating pool) and decreased adhesion/egress from blood, not primarily from increased bone marrow production.

preguntas.q: What effect do glucocorticoids have on circulating eosinophil counts?

o.D: Initial decrease followed by rebound increase

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids decrease circulating eosinophil counts by promoting eosinophil apoptosis and sequestering them out of the peripheral circulation into tissues like lymph nodes, in addition to suppressing eosinophil production. This eosinopenic effect, together with lymphopenia, is part of glucocorticoids' broader immunosuppressive profile, and it is exploited pharmacologically (as well as used diagnostically — a paradoxically normal or elevated eosinophil count in a patient on high-dose steroids can suggest adrenal insufficiency or another disease process).

incorrectas.A: Glucocorticoids decrease, not increase, eosinophil counts; an increase would be inconsistent with their known immunosuppressive and anti-inflammatory actions on this cell line.
incorrectas.C: Saying there is no effect ignores the well-documented eosinopenic action of glucocorticoids, which is actually used clinically as one sign that a patient is under cortisol/stress hormone influence.
incorrectas.D: There is no established biphasic (initial decrease then rebound increase) pattern for glucocorticoid effects on eosinophils; the effect is a straightforward, sustained decrease as long as glucocorticoid levels remain elevated.

preguntas.q: By what mechanism do glucocorticoids suppress the immune response, allowing their pharmacologic use in preventing transplant rejection?

o.A: By inhibiting production of IL-2 and subsequent T-cell proliferation
o.B: By directly lysing mature B lymphocytes
o.C: By blocking MHC class I expression on all nucleated cells
o.D: By inhibiting complement fixation on antibody-coated cells

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids suppress the adaptive immune response largely by inhibiting transcription of IL-2 (and other cytokines) in T lymphocytes, which blunts T-cell activation and clonal proliferation — since IL-2 is the key autocrine/paracrine growth signal that expands antigen-activated T cells. This mechanism is precisely why glucocorticoids are used clinically to prevent and treat transplant rejection (a T-cell-mediated process) and to treat autoimmune and inflammatory conditions driven by lymphocyte activation.

incorrectas.B: Glucocorticoids do not directly lyse mature B lymphocytes; their immunosuppressive action is centered on inhibiting T-cell cytokine signaling (like IL-2) and promoting lymphocyte apoptosis/redistribution more broadly, not a direct cytolytic effect on B cells specifically.
incorrectas.C: Glucocorticoids do not block MHC class I expression; MHC class I presentation is a distinct antigen-presentation pathway unrelated to the cytokine-suppression mechanism by which glucocorticoids prevent T-cell-mediated rejection.
incorrectas.D: Complement fixation is part of the humoral, antibody-mediated immune response and is not the primary mechanism by which glucocorticoids exert their immunosuppressive effect; their main action against transplant rejection is through blunting T-cell proliferation via IL-2 suppression.

preguntas.q: Glucocorticoids are essential in maintaining vascular responsiveness to catecholamines via upregulation of which receptor on arterioles?

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids upregulate the expression and function of α1-adrenergic receptors on vascular smooth muscle, which is essential for arterioles to respond normally to circulating catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine) and maintain vascular tone/blood pressure. This permissive effect is why cortisol is considered necessary for normal vascular reactivity, and it explains why patients with adrenal insufficiency can develop hypotension and vascular collapse even when catecholamine levels are otherwise adequate.

incorrectas.A: β2 receptors on vasculature generally mediate vasodilation (not the vasoconstrictive catecholamine responsiveness being tested here), and they are not the primary receptor whose glucocorticoid-dependent upregulation maintains vascular tone in this context.
incorrectas.C: M3 muscarinic receptors mediate parasympathetic cholinergic signaling (e.g., vasodilation via endothelial nitric oxide release) and are unrelated to the glucocorticoid-dependent catecholamine responsiveness pathway described here.
incorrectas.D: AT1 angiotensin receptors mediate angiotensin II's vasoconstrictive effects and are regulated by the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, not primarily by glucocorticoid-dependent upregulation for catecholamine responsiveness.

preguntas.q: What is the effect of hypocortisolism (e.g., Addison disease) on blood pressure, and why does this occur?

o.A: Increased blood pressure due to increased aldosterone
o.B: Decreased blood pressure due to decreased α1 receptor expression and vasoconstriction
o.C: No significant change in blood pressure
o.D: Increased blood pressure due to catecholamine excess

e.correcta: In Addison disease, cortisol deficiency means arteriolar smooth muscle no longer has adequate α1-receptor expression, so vessels fail to constrict normally in response to catecholamines, leading to decreased vascular tone and hypotension. This is why adrenal insufficiency classically presents with hypotension (and can progress to life-threatening vascular collapse during an adrenal crisis), and it's distinct from mineralocorticoid deficiency, which causes hypotension via volume depletion from renal sodium wasting.

incorrectas.A: In primary adrenal insufficiency, aldosterone is typically also decreased (not increased), since the entire adrenal cortex is failing; increased aldosterone would tend to raise blood pressure via sodium/water retention, which is the opposite of what's seen in Addison disease.
incorrectas.C: Addison disease does produce a significant and often life-threatening change in blood pressure (hypotension), so stating there is no significant change misses a hallmark clinical feature of adrenal insufficiency.
incorrectas.D: Cortisol deficiency reduces, rather than causes excess of, effective catecholamine action at the vessel wall (due to loss of permissive α1-receptor upregulation), so hypocortisolism leads to hypotension, not hypertension from catecholamine excess.

preguntas.q: Glucocorticoid excess decreases fibroblast activity, contributing to which clinical finding?

e.correcta: Glucocorticoid excess impairs fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis, weakening the dermal connective tissue framework; when this thinned, weakened skin is stretched (e.g., over the abdomen in Cushing syndrome, often compounded by central weight gain), it tears at the dermal level, producing the characteristic wide, purplish striae. These striae, along with easy bruising and poor wound healing, reflect the same underlying fibroblast-suppressing, collagen-degrading mechanism of glucocorticoid excess.

incorrectas.A: Hypertrophic scarring results from excessive fibroblast activity and collagen deposition, which is the opposite of the fibroblast-suppressing effect that glucocorticoids actually exert on connective tissue.
incorrectas.C: Keloid formation, like hypertrophic scarring, reflects overactive fibroblast proliferation and excess collagen production, whereas glucocorticoid excess characteristically decreases fibroblast activity and thins connective tissue rather than promoting overgrowth.
incorrectas.D: Glucocorticoid excess decreases, not increases, wound tensile strength because impaired fibroblast function and collagen synthesis lead to weaker, more fragile connective tissue and poor wound healing, which is why steroids are notorious for impairing surgical wound recovery.

preguntas.q: What effect does cortisol have on glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?

o.D: Variable effect depending on time of day

e.correcta: Cortisol increases GFR primarily by increasing renal blood flow and acting permissively to potentiate the vasoconstrictive/vasopressor effects of catecholamines and angiotensin II on renal vasculature, and it also has mild mineralocorticoid activity that promotes sodium and water retention, expanding effective circulating volume. This is part of why glucocorticoid excess (Cushing syndrome) is associated with hypertension and why cortisol's permissive vascular effects are clinically important in states of adrenal insufficiency, where GFR and blood pressure can fall.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in GFR would be more consistent with a hormone that causes vasoconstriction without permissive effects on pressor hormones, or with volume depletion, which is the opposite of cortisol's actual permissive, flow-enhancing effect on the renal vasculature.
incorrectas.C: Cortisol is not neutral on the kidney — it has well-documented permissive effects on vascular tone and mild mineralocorticoid activity, both of which measurably raise GFR rather than leaving it unaffected.
incorrectas.D: While cortisol secretion itself follows a strong diurnal (circadian) rhythm peaking in the early morning, its effect on GFR is a consistent physiologic action of the hormone rather than something that flips direction depending on time of day.

preguntas.q: Cortisol affects sleep architecture by decreasing which sleep stage while increasing total awake time?

e.correcta: Cortisol, which normally peaks in the early morning as part of its diurnal rhythm, suppresses REM sleep while promoting wakefulness; elevated or dysregulated cortisol (as in stress or Cushing syndrome) further decreases REM sleep and increases total time awake, contributing to the sleep disturbances commonly seen in these states. This relationship also underlies why cortisol's circadian peak is timed to coincide with waking, since high cortisol and reduced REM sleep both support the transition to an alert, awake state.

incorrectas.A: Slow-wave sleep (stages 3/4) is more closely tied to growth hormone secretion and is affected differently by various hormones; cortisol's characteristic sleep effect specifically targets REM sleep, not slow-wave sleep.
incorrectas.C: Stage 1 sleep is a light transitional sleep stage and is not the specific stage classically described as being decreased by cortisol; the well-established relationship is between cortisol and reduced REM sleep.
incorrectas.D: Stage 2 sleep is not the sleep stage specifically linked to cortisol's suppressive effect; the clinically and physiologically emphasized association is cortisol decreasing REM sleep while increasing wakefulness.

preguntas.q: Cortisol travels in the blood primarily bound to which transport protein?

e.correcta: About 90% of circulating cortisol is bound to corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG, also called transcortin), a liver-derived carrier protein with high affinity but low capacity for cortisol; a smaller fraction binds albumin (lower affinity, higher capacity), and only a small free fraction is biologically active. This distinction matters clinically because conditions altering CBG levels (e.g., pregnancy, estrogen therapy increasing CBG, or liver disease/nephrotic syndrome decreasing it) can change total measured cortisol without necessarily changing the physiologically active free cortisol.

incorrectas.A: While albumin does bind a portion of circulating cortisol, it is not the primary or exclusive transport protein; CBG is the main high-affinity binder responsible for carrying the majority of circulating cortisol.
incorrectas.C: Thyroxine-binding globulin is specific for thyroid hormones (T4 and T3) and does not bind cortisol; it belongs to a distinct hormone transport system entirely separate from the HPA axis.
incorrectas.D: Sex hormone-binding globulin binds testosterone and estradiol, not cortisol; it is part of the reproductive hormone transport system and is unrelated to glucocorticoid transport in the blood.

preguntas.q: At high concentrations, cortisol can cross-react with and bind which receptor, producing mineralocorticoid-like effects?

e.correcta: At very high concentrations, cortisol can overwhelm the enzyme 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (which normally inactivates cortisol to cortisone in mineralocorticoid target tissues, protecting the mineralocorticoid receptor from cortisol) and directly bind and activate the mineralocorticoid receptor, since cortisol and aldosterone have similar chemical structures and the mineralocorticoid receptor does not intrinsically discriminate well between them. This explains why severe Cushing syndrome or conditions of massive cortisol excess (e.g., ectopic ACTH syndrome) can produce mineralocorticoid-like effects such as hypertension and hypokalemia despite normal aldosterone levels.

incorrectas.A: Cortisol's primary receptor is indeed the glucocorticoid receptor, but the point of this question is that at high concentrations cortisol can also cross-react with a different receptor (the mineralocorticoid receptor) to produce effects beyond its usual glucocorticoid actions.
incorrectas.C: The androgen receptor binds testosterone/DHT and is structurally and functionally distinct from the corticosteroid receptors; cortisol's high-concentration cross-reactivity is specifically with the mineralocorticoid receptor, not the androgen receptor.
incorrectas.D: The estrogen receptor is unrelated to corticosteroid signaling and is not the receptor that cortisol cross-reacts with at high concentrations; the clinically relevant cross-reactivity is with the mineralocorticoid receptor, producing sodium retention and hypertension.

preguntas.q: In adrenogenital syndrome (congenital adrenal hyperplasia), overproduction of adrenal androgens results in increased urinary levels of which metabolites?

e.correcta: In congenital adrenal hyperplasia, enzyme blocks (most often 21-hydroxylase) divert steroid precursors into the androgen synthesis pathway, so the adrenal cortex overproduces weak androgens such as DHEA and androstenedione. These androgens are metabolized and excreted in urine as 17-ketosteroids, so measuring urinary 17-ketosteroids is the classic way to demonstrate adrenal androgen excess in this disease.

incorrectas.A: VMA is a breakdown product of catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine) produced by the adrenal medulla, and is elevated in pheochromocytoma, not in adrenal cortical androgen excess.
incorrectas.C: Metanephrines are also catecholamine metabolites from the adrenal medulla, used to screen for pheochromocytoma; they have nothing to do with adrenal cortex androgen production.
incorrectas.D: 5-HIAA is the metabolite of serotonin and is elevated in carcinoid tumors, an entirely different hormonal axis unrelated to adrenal androgen excess.

preguntas.q: Which classes of adrenal steroid hormones are decreased in primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease)?

o.C: All three classes: glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, and androgens
o.D: Glucocorticoids and androgens only, sparing mineralocorticoids

e.correcta: Primary adrenal insufficiency reflects destruction or dysfunction of the adrenal cortex itself (autoimmune adrenalitis being the most common cause), so all three cortical zones — zona glomerulosa (mineralocorticoids), zona fasciculata (glucocorticoids), and zona reticularis (androgens) — fail together. This is why Addison disease produces the full picture of cortisol deficiency, aldosterone deficiency, and androgen deficiency simultaneously, unlike a lesion confined to the pituitary.

incorrectas.A: Glucocorticoids alone being low would suggest a selective defect (like isolated ACTH deficiency from a pituitary problem), but primary adrenal failure destroys the whole gland, so aldosterone and androgens fall too.
incorrectas.B: Mineralocorticoids alone being low doesn't match Addison disease, which affects the entire cortex; isolated hypoaldosteronism has other specific causes (e.g., renin abnormalities) rather than global adrenal destruction.
incorrectas.D: Sparing mineralocorticoids is actually the hallmark of secondary insufficiency (pituitary ACTH deficiency), because aldosterone is largely driven by the renin-angiotensin system rather than ACTH — the opposite of what happens in primary adrenal destruction.

preguntas.q: What happens to ACTH levels in Addison disease, and why?

o.A: Decreased, because the pituitary is destroyed along with the adrenal gland
o.B: Increased, because low cortisol removes negative feedback on the pituitary/hypothalamus
o.C: Normal, because ACTH is independent of cortisol feedback
o.D: Decreased, because ACTH is co-secreted with cortisol from the adrenal cortex

e.correcta: Cortisol normally exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary to suppress CRH and ACTH release. When the adrenal cortex is destroyed in Addison disease, cortisol levels fall, that feedback brake is removed, and the pituitary responds by markedly increasing ACTH secretion — this elevated ACTH is also why patients develop hyperpigmentation, since ACTH shares a precursor (POMC) with melanocyte-stimulating hormone.

incorrectas.A: The pituitary is intact in primary adrenal insufficiency — it's the adrenal gland, not the pituitary, that is destroyed, so ACTH rises rather than falls.
incorrectas.C: ACTH is very much regulated by cortisol feedback; that's the entire basis of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, so this option misstates the physiology.
incorrectas.D: ACTH is made by the anterior pituitary, not co-secreted from the adrenal cortex alongside cortisol — the adrenal cortex is the target organ that responds to ACTH, not a source of it.

preguntas.q: What effect does Addison disease have on blood glucose levels?

e.correcta: Cortisol is a key counter-regulatory hormone that promotes gluconeogenesis, glycogen synthesis, and insulin resistance to keep blood glucose from falling too low, especially during fasting or stress. When cortisol is deficient in Addison disease, these glucose-supporting effects are lost, so patients are prone to hypoglycemia, particularly during illness or fasting when cortisol demand is highest.

incorrectas.A: Hyperglycemia is what you'd expect with cortisol excess (as in Cushing syndrome), since cortisol raises blood glucose — the opposite is true when cortisol is deficient.
incorrectas.C: Glucose homeostasis is not preserved in Addison disease; cortisol is one of the major counter-regulatory hormones, so its loss directly disrupts glucose maintenance.
incorrectas.D: Addison disease does not cause an alternating pattern; the deficiency is a steady loss of a hormone that raises glucose, producing a persistent tendency toward hypoglycemia rather than swings.

preguntas.q: Which electrolyte abnormality is a clinical feature of Addison disease, and why does it occur?

o.B: Hyperkalemia due to decreased aldosterone levels
o.D: Hyponatremia due to increased ADH secretion only

e.correcta: Aldosterone normally acts on the renal collecting duct to reabsorb sodium in exchange for secreting potassium (and hydrogen ions). In Addison disease, destruction of the zona glomerulosa causes aldosterone deficiency, so potassium secretion falls and patients develop hyperkalemia, often together with hyponatremia, volume depletion, and metabolic acidosis from reduced H+ excretion.

incorrectas.A: Hypokalemia from increased aldosterone is the pattern seen in conditions like Conn syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism), which is the opposite hormonal direction from Addison disease.
incorrectas.C: PTH and calcium regulation are not part of the adrenal cortex's hormone output; hypercalcemia from decreased PTH would reflect a parathyroid problem, not adrenal insufficiency.
incorrectas.D: While ADH can be mildly elevated as a stress response, the hyponatremia of Addison disease is driven mainly by aldosterone deficiency (impaired sodium retention) plus cortisol deficiency, not by ADH acting alone.

preguntas.q: What is the appropriate treatment for Addison disease (primary adrenocortical insufficiency)?

o.C: Replacement of both glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids

e.correcta: Because Addison disease knocks out both the glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid axes (the whole cortex is destroyed), effective treatment must replace both hormone classes — typically hydrocortisone for glucocorticoid activity and fludrocortisone for mineralocorticoid activity. Giving only one class would leave either the glucose/stress-response deficit or the sodium/potassium/volume deficit uncorrected.

incorrectas.A: Glucocorticoid replacement alone would improve energy, glucose, and stress tolerance but would leave the patient hyperkalemic and volume-depleted from unaddressed aldosterone deficiency.
incorrectas.B: Mineralocorticoid replacement alone would help sodium and potassium balance but would not address the cortisol deficiency, leaving the patient at risk for hypoglycemia and inability to mount a stress response (adrenal crisis).
incorrectas.D: ACTH analog therapy would be useless here because the problem is a destroyed adrenal gland that cannot respond to ACTH stimulation — the defect is at the gland itself, not a lack of pituitary signal.

preguntas.q: In secondary adrenocortical insufficiency, which classes of adrenal steroid hormones are decreased?

o.C: Glucocorticoids +/- androgens, with aldosterone relatively spared
o.D: All three classes equally, identical to Addison disease

e.correcta: Secondary adrenocortical insufficiency results from a pituitary or hypothalamic problem causing low ACTH, which drives the zona fasciculata (cortisol) and zona reticularis (androgens) — both ACTH-dependent — leading to their deficiency. The zona glomerulosa, however, is largely regulated by the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system rather than ACTH, so aldosterone production is relatively preserved, distinguishing this from the global hormone loss in primary (Addison) disease.

incorrectas.A: Mineralocorticoids and androgens falling while glucocorticoids are spared is backwards — ACTH deficiency mainly hits cortisol and androgen production, and aldosterone is the one that is relatively protected.
incorrectas.B: Isolated mineralocorticoid loss doesn't fit secondary insufficiency, since aldosterone is the hormone class least dependent on ACTH and thus the one that tends to be preserved.
incorrectas.D: Equating secondary insufficiency to Addison disease ignores the key distinguishing physiology: aldosterone is spared in secondary insufficiency because its regulation is largely independent of the pituitary-ACTH axis.

preguntas.q: What is the level of ACTH in secondary adrenocortical insufficiency, and why?

o.A: Increased, due to loss of negative feedback from low cortisol
o.B: Decreased, because the disease results from decreased pituitary ACTH secretion
o.C: Normal, because the defect is purely at the level of the adrenal cortex
o.D: Increased, due to an ACTH-secreting pituitary tumor

e.correcta: Secondary adrenocortical insufficiency is defined by a defect above the adrenal gland — typically pituitary damage (tumor, surgery, radiation, Sheehan syndrome) or hypothalamic dysfunction — that reduces ACTH secretion itself, so ACTH levels are low rather than compensatorily elevated. This is the key lab distinction from primary (Addison) disease, where ACTH is high because the pituitary is intact and trying to drive a damaged adrenal gland.

incorrectas.A: Increased ACTH from loss of negative feedback is what happens in primary adrenal insufficiency, where the adrenal gland (not the pituitary) is the site of failure; in secondary insufficiency the pituitary itself cannot produce enough ACTH.
