e.correcta: Riedel thyroiditis belongs to the spectrum of IgG4-related systemic fibrosing diseases, in which IgG4-positive plasma cells infiltrate and drive fibrosis in multiple organs, including the thyroid (Riedel thyroiditis), pancreas (autoimmune pancreatitis), retroperitoneum (retroperitoneal fibrosis), and other sites. Recognizing this shared IgG4-mediated mechanism explains why patients with Riedel thyroiditis may also have or develop fibrosis at these other anatomic sites, tying together what would otherwise seem like unrelated diseases.

incorrectas.A: IgA is the antibody class important in mucosal immunity (e.g., IgA nephropathy, celiac disease) and is not the immunoglobulin subclass driving the systemic fibrosing spectrum that includes Riedel thyroiditis.
incorrectas.B: IgE mediates type I hypersensitivity/allergic reactions and parasitic defense, an entirely different immunologic pathway from the IgG4-driven fibrosing disease process linking Riedel thyroiditis to autoimmune pancreatitis and retroperitoneal fibrosis.
incorrectas.C: IgM is the first antibody produced in a primary immune response and mediates complement fixation, but it is not the immunoglobulin subclass implicated in the IgG4-related systemic fibrosing spectrum.

preguntas.q: When a thyroid nodule is discovered, which outcome is statistically more likely?

o.D: The nodule is equally likely to be benign or malignant

e.correcta: The overwhelming majority of thyroid nodules discovered incidentally or on exam are benign, most commonly representing colloid nodules or nodules within a multinodular goiter, with only a small minority (roughly 5% or less) proving to be malignant on workup. This statistical reality underlies the standard evaluation approach (TSH, ultrasound characteristics, and fine-needle aspiration when indicated) rather than assuming malignancy and proceeding straight to aggressive intervention for every nodule found.

incorrectas.A: While malignancy must always be excluded because the consequences of missing thyroid cancer are significant, the statistically more likely outcome for any given newly discovered nodule is that it is benign, not malignant.
incorrectas.C: Metastatic disease to the thyroid is quite rare compared to primary thyroid nodules (benign or malignant), so it is not a statistically likely explanation for a newly found thyroid nodule.
incorrectas.D: Thyroid nodules are not equally likely to be benign or malignant; the base rate strongly favors a benign etiology, which is why risk-stratification tools and FNA cytology are used to identify the minority that are concerning for cancer.

preguntas.q: Which imaging study is used to functionally characterize a thyroid nodule based on its uptake activity?

e.correcta: A 131I radioactive iodine uptake scan exploits the thyroid follicular cells' physiologic uptake and organification of iodine to functionally characterize a nodule based on how much radiotracer it takes up relative to surrounding tissue, classifying it as 'hot' (increased uptake, usually benign and autonomously functioning) or 'cold' (decreased uptake, carries higher relative malignancy risk and warrants further workup). This functional information complements structural imaging and helps guide whether biopsy is needed.

incorrectas.A: Technetium-99m sestamibi scanning is used primarily for parathyroid localization (e.g., in parathyroid adenoma detection) or myocardial perfusion imaging, not as the standard functional study for characterizing thyroid nodule uptake activity.
incorrectas.C: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck provides anatomic/structural detail (size, extent, invasion) and is actually often avoided before radioiodine studies because iodinated contrast can saturate the thyroid and impair subsequent uptake scanning; it does not provide functional uptake characterization.
incorrectas.D: Doppler ultrasound assesses nodule vascularity and structural features (solid vs cystic, margins, calcifications) as part of risk stratification, but it does not measure functional iodine uptake activity the way a radioactive iodine scan does.

preguntas.q: A thyroid nodule demonstrating increased uptake of 131I on radioactive scanning is classified as which type of nodule, commonly seen in Graves disease or toxic nodular goiter?

e.correcta: A 'hot' nodule shows increased 131I uptake because its follicular cells are actively and often autonomously taking up and organifying iodine to produce excess thyroid hormone, independent of normal TSH regulation — this is the mechanism behind toxic adenomas, toxic multinodular goiter, and the diffusely increased uptake pattern seen in Graves disease. Because autonomously functioning tissue is overwhelmingly benign, hot nodules carry a low risk of malignancy and are generally managed based on the resulting hyperthyroidism rather than biopsied for cancer.

incorrectas.A: A cold nodule shows decreased or absent uptake, indicating the tissue is not actively concentrating iodine, and this pattern carries a comparatively higher (though still overall low) risk of malignancy, which is the opposite uptake pattern from what is described in this question.
incorrectas.C: A cystic nodule is a structural/anatomic description (fluid-filled component seen on ultrasound), not a functional classification based on radioactive iodine uptake, so it does not correspond to the 'hot' uptake terminology used here.
incorrectas.D: A calcified nodule refers to a structural ultrasound finding (e.g., microcalcifications raising malignancy suspicion), not a functional uptake classification, and is unrelated to the hot/cold terminology derived from radioactive iodine scanning.

preguntas.q: A thyroid nodule with decreased uptake of 131I on radioactive iodine scanning is classified as which type, and warrants further evaluation?

e.correcta: A cold nodule is one that fails to take up radioactive iodine, appearing as a photopenic area on scintigraphy because the cells within it are not functioning like normal thyroid follicular cells (i.e., not actively concentrating iodine to make hormone). This lack of function is concerning because malignant thyroid tumors are typically non-functional and therefore appear cold, whereas most benign hyperfunctioning tissue lights up; roughly 85-90% of nodules are cold, and of these a meaningful minority harbor carcinoma, so cold nodules require further workup with FNA biopsy.

incorrectas.A: A hot nodule shows increased uptake of 131I, meaning the tissue is autonomously producing thyroid hormone independent of TSH regulation; hot nodules are almost always benign (toxic adenoma) and rarely require biopsy since malignant cells generally cannot concentrate iodine efficiently enough to appear hot.
incorrectas.B: A warm nodule shows uptake similar to surrounding normal thyroid tissue, indicating the nodule is functioning at a baseline level rather than being suppressed or autonomous; this pattern is also generally reassuring and not the classic trigger for biopsy that reduced uptake represents.
incorrectas.D: "Isofunctioning" is not a standard classification used in thyroid scintigraphy terminology; the recognized categories are hot, warm, and cold based on relative iodine uptake, and this distractor does not correspond to any accepted diagnostic category.

preguntas.q: A 'cold' thyroid nodule on radioactive iodine uptake scanning is most indicative of which underlying process, warranting further biopsy?

e.correcta: A cold nodule fails to trap and organify iodine the way normal thyroid follicular cells do, and this loss of differentiated function is a hallmark of neoplastic transformation — both benign adenomas and malignant carcinomas commonly present as cold nodules because the transformed cells lose the normal machinery (sodium-iodide symporter expression, thyroperoxidase activity) needed for iodine uptake. Because carcinoma cannot be excluded on imaging alone, a cold nodule mandates tissue sampling via fine needle aspiration to determine whether it is adenoma or carcinoma.

incorrectas.A: Graves disease is an autoimmune condition where TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies drive diffuse, symmetric hyperfunction of the entire gland, producing diffusely increased (hot) uptake rather than a discrete cold nodule.
incorrectas.B: Toxic multinodular goiter reflects multiple autonomously functioning nodules that concentrate iodine independent of TSH, producing hot or warm areas on scan, the opposite pattern from the cold nodule described here.
incorrectas.D: Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis causes painful gland inflammation with transient hyperthyroidism from stored hormone release, and classically shows globally decreased, not focally cold, uptake due to follicular cell damage throughout the gland rather than a discrete neoplastic nodule.

preguntas.q: Which biopsy technique is used to sample a suspicious thyroid nodule, chosen specifically because the thyroid gland is highly vascularized?

e.correcta: Fine needle aspiration uses a very thin needle (typically 25-27 gauge) to withdraw only cells for cytologic examination, minimizing trauma to the highly vascular thyroid parenchyma and reducing the risk of significant bleeding or hematoma compared to techniques that remove larger cores of tissue. This makes FNA the first-line, safest, and most cost-effective way to triage a thyroid nodule as benign, malignant, or indeterminate before deciding whether surgery is needed.

incorrectas.A: Core needle biopsy uses a larger-bore needle to obtain an intact tissue core for histology, which provides more architectural detail but carries a higher risk of bleeding in a vascular organ like the thyroid, so it is not the preferred first step.
incorrectas.B: Excisional biopsy means surgically removing the entire nodule (or lobe), which is far more invasive than needed for initial diagnosis and is reserved for cases where FNA is indeterminate or malignancy is confirmed and definitive surgical management is planned.
incorrectas.D: Punch biopsy is a technique for sampling skin and superficial soft tissue lesions using a circular blade, not an appropriate or standard method for accessing a deep, vascular structure like the thyroid gland.

preguntas.q: A benign, solitary growth arising within the thyroid gland is best classified as which entity?

e.correcta: A thyroid adenoma is a benign, encapsulated, monoclonal proliferation of follicular epithelium that forms a single, well-circumscribed nodule distinct from the surrounding normal parenchyma. Its defining features — a solitary nature and a benign biologic behavior confined within an intact fibrous capsule without invasion — are exactly what the question describes, differentiating it from carcinoma (which invades) and goiter (which is typically multinodular and hyperplastic rather than a discrete neoplasm).

incorrectas.A: Thyroid carcinoma is malignant and, critically, demonstrates capsular and/or vascular invasion (in the follicular type) or characteristic nuclear features (in the papillary type); the question specifies a benign growth, which rules out carcinoma by definition.
incorrectas.C: Multinodular goiter is a polyclonal, hyperplastic enlargement of the thyroid with multiple nodules arising from fluctuating TSH stimulation over time, not a single discrete neoplasm, so it does not fit the "solitary growth" description in the question.
incorrectas.D: A thyroglossal duct cyst is a congenital remnant of the thyroglossal duct that persists along the path of thyroid gland descent from the tongue base to its final position in the neck; it is a cystic developmental anomaly, not a neoplastic proliferation of thyroid follicular cells.

preguntas.q: Although most thyroid adenomas are nonfunctional ('cold'), autonomous thyroid hormone production by a 'hot' or toxic adenoma can rarely cause which clinical condition?

e.correcta: A toxic (hot) adenoma contains follicular cells that have acquired autonomous, TSH-independent activity (often via activating mutations in the TSH receptor or downstream signaling pathway), causing them to synthesize and secrete thyroid hormone without normal regulatory feedback. Because this excess hormone is not held in check by pituitary suppression, the patient can develop clinical hyperthyroidism — symptoms like tachycardia, weight loss, heat intolerance, and tremor — even though the vast majority of adenomas are non-functional and never cause systemic disease.

incorrectas.B: Hypothyroidism results from underproduction of thyroid hormone, which is the opposite physiologic direction from what a hyperfunctioning "hot" adenoma produces; a hot adenoma oversecretes hormone rather than causing a deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Hypoparathyroidism involves insufficient PTH secretion, typically from surgical injury or autoimmune destruction of the parathyroid glands, and has no mechanistic link to autonomous hormone secretion by a thyroid follicular adenoma.
incorrectas.D: Adrenal insufficiency reflects failure of the adrenal cortex (or pituitary ACTH drive) to produce sufficient cortisol, an entirely separate endocrine axis from thyroid hormone production and not something caused by a functioning thyroid adenoma.

preguntas.q: What is the most common histologic type of thyroid adenoma?

e.correcta: Follicular adenoma is by far the most common histologic subtype of thyroid adenoma, composed of well-formed follicles resembling normal thyroid architecture, all contained within a fibrous capsule without invasion. Recognizing this as the default/most common adenoma type is important because it is precisely this entity that must be distinguished from follicular carcinoma — a distinction that hinges entirely on capsular/vascular invasion rather than cytologic appearance.

incorrectas.A: "Papillary adenoma" is not a recognized standard entity in thyroid pathology — papillary lesions of the thyroid are essentially always classified as carcinoma once the characteristic nuclear features (Orphan Annie eyes, grooves) are present, since there is no benign papillary counterpart analogous to follicular adenoma.
incorrectas.B: Hürthle cell (oncocytic) adenoma is a variant composed of cells with abundant eosinophilic, mitochondria-rich cytoplasm, but it is considerably less common than the classic follicular adenoma and represents a distinct, less frequent subtype.
incorrectas.D: "Medullary adenoma" is not a real entity — medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells and is always considered malignant; there is no benign medullary counterpart in standard thyroid pathology classification.

preguntas.q: What is the key histologic feature that distinguishes follicular carcinoma from follicular adenoma of the thyroid?

o.A: Presence of Orphan Annie eye nuclei
o.B: Follicular adenoma lacks capsular and vascular invasion, which is present in carcinoma
o.D: Follicular carcinoma lacks a fibrous capsule entirely

e.correcta: Follicular adenoma and follicular carcinoma can look virtually identical at the level of individual follicular cell cytology, so the diagnosis rests entirely on architecture: an adenoma remains completely confined within its fibrous capsule with no penetration through the capsule or into surrounding blood vessels, whereas carcinoma is defined by breaching that capsule and/or invading vasculature, giving it access to hematogenous spread. This is why full histologic examination of the capsule (not just cytology from FNA) is required to make the diagnosis — it explains why capsular and vascular invasion is the single most important criterion separating benign from malignant follicular neoplasms.

incorrectas.A: Orphan Annie eye nuclei (with nuclear grooves and pseudoinclusions) are the classic feature of papillary thyroid carcinoma, not a distinguishing feature between follicular adenoma and follicular carcinoma, which are both composed of otherwise unremarkable follicular cells.
incorrectas.C: Psammoma bodies (concentrically calcified structures) are also a hallmark of papillary carcinoma, reflecting dystrophic calcification of necrotic papillary cores, and are not a feature used to separate follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma.
incorrectas.D: Both follicular adenoma and follicular carcinoma are typically encapsulated; carcinoma is defined by invasion through an existing capsule, not by a complete absence of capsule, so this statement mischaracterizes the actual histologic distinction.

preguntas.q: A benign tumor of thyroid follicles is typically surrounded by which structure that helps distinguish it from invasive carcinoma?

e.correcta: A benign follicular adenoma develops its own thin fibrous capsule as it grows, which is formed by compression of surrounding stroma and serves as a physical barrier confining the neoplastic follicular cells; this intact capsule (with no penetration through it or into vessels) is the structural feature that pathologists use to call a lesion benign. In contrast, carcinoma is diagnosed precisely when tumor cells breach this capsule or invade blood vessels, so the presence and integrity of the capsule is the single most clinically important histologic finding in follicular thyroid neoplasms.

incorrectas.A: Psammoma bodies are calcified, laminated structures seen in papillary thyroid carcinoma (and a few other tumors like ovarian serous carcinoma and meningioma), not a feature associated with benign follicular adenomas.
incorrectas.C: A layer of squamous epithelium is not a normal or expected component of thyroid follicular tissue; thyroid follicles are lined by cuboidal-to-columnar follicular epithelium, and squamous elements would be atypical and unrelated to distinguishing benign from malignant disease here.
incorrectas.D: Lymphoid follicles with germinal centers are characteristic of Hashimoto thyroiditis, reflecting chronic lymphocytic infiltration of the gland, not a structural feature that defines or surrounds a benign follicular adenoma.

preguntas.q: What is the most common histologic type of thyroid carcinoma, accounting for approximately 80% of cases?

e.correcta: Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy, accounting for roughly 80% of cases, and is defined by characteristic nuclear features (Orphan Annie eye nuclei, intranuclear grooves and inclusions) rather than by aggressive cytologic atypia. It carries an excellent prognosis overall despite frequent early lymphatic spread to cervical nodes, which is an important teaching point: nodal spread in papillary carcinoma does not carry the same ominous prognostic weight it does in most other cancers.

incorrectas.A: Follicular carcinoma is the second most common thyroid cancer, spreading hematogenously rather than via lymphatics, but it is less common than papillary carcinoma and does not account for the 80% figure described.
incorrectas.B: Medullary carcinoma, arising from parafollicular C cells and associated with MEN 2 syndromes, is a much rarer subtype (roughly 5% of thyroid cancers) and is not the predominant histologic type.
incorrectas.C: Anaplastic carcinoma is a highly aggressive, undifferentiated tumor that is actually one of the rarest thyroid cancer subtypes despite its poor prognosis, representing only a small percentage of cases, far from the 80% majority described in the question.

preguntas.q: Which two gene mutations are most associated with an increased risk of papillary thyroid carcinoma?

e.correcta: Papillary thyroid carcinoma is most strongly linked to RET gene rearrangements (particularly RET/PTC fusions, also seen after radiation exposure such as in Chernobyl-exposed populations) and activating point mutations in BRAF (most commonly BRAF V600E), both of which constitutively activate the MAPK signaling pathway to drive unchecked follicular cell proliferation. Recognizing this RET/BRAF-MAPK axis is useful clinically because BRAF mutation status can inform prognosis and is a target for some therapies in refractory disease.

incorrectas.A: RAS mutations are associated with follicular carcinoma and follicular adenoma, not the classic papillary carcinoma genetic profile, while PTEN mutations are linked to Cowden syndrome and follicular-pattern thyroid neoplasms, not papillary carcinoma specifically.
incorrectas.C: APC mutations cause familial adenomatous polyposis and are linked to an increased risk of papillary thyroid carcinoma in that syndromic context, but TP53 mutations are characteristic of anaplastic carcinoma (representing dedifferentiation), not the primary drivers of typical papillary carcinoma.
incorrectas.D: MEN1 mutations cause multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (parathyroid, pancreatic, and pituitary tumors) and have no established link to papillary thyroid carcinoma, while RET mutations are correctly associated with papillary carcinoma (as fusions) but also, in germline form, with medullary carcinoma in MEN 2 — this pairing does not represent the accepted papillary carcinoma gene signature.

preguntas.q: In addition to 'Orphan Annie eye' nuclei, which nuclear feature is characteristic of papillary thyroid carcinoma?

e.correcta: In addition to the ground-glass, empty-appearing "Orphan Annie eye" nuclei caused by chromatin margination, papillary thyroid carcinoma nuclei characteristically show intranuclear grooves (linear folds in the nuclear membrane) and intranuclear pseudoinclusions (invaginations of cytoplasm that appear as clear round holes within the nucleus). These nuclear features, not cytoplasmic or architectural atypia, are what actually define the diagnosis of papillary carcinoma — a tumor can be diagnosed as papillary carcinoma based on nuclear morphology alone, even without classic papillary architecture.

incorrectas.A: Prominent nucleoli with coarse chromatin describe a pattern of overt malignant atypia seen in many aggressive cancers, but this is essentially the opposite of what papillary carcinoma nuclei look like — the hallmark here is pale, optically clear ("empty") chromatin, not coarse or prominent nucleoli.
incorrectas.C: Binucleation with mitotic figures suggests a highly proliferative, aggressive tumor pattern, which is instead more characteristic of undifferentiated anaplastic carcinoma; papillary carcinoma is notable for its relatively bland-appearing, low-mitotic-rate nuclei despite being malignant.
incorrectas.D: Pyknotic, condensed nuclei reflect cell death or apoptosis (nuclear shrinkage and increased chromatin density), which is essentially the opposite appearance of the pale, open, "empty" nuclei that define papillary carcinoma.

preguntas.q: Papillary thyroid carcinoma most often spreads via lymphatic invasion to which nodal basin?

e.correcta: Papillary thyroid carcinoma has a strong predilection for early lymphatic invasion, spreading preferentially to the cervical (neck) lymph nodes that drain the thyroid gland, and it is not uncommon for a patient to first present with a palpable cervical lymph node rather than a thyroid mass itself. Despite this frequent nodal involvement, papillary carcinoma still carries an excellent prognosis, illustrating that lymphatic spread in this particular cancer does not carry the same negative prognostic implication it does in most other malignancies.

incorrectas.A: Axillary nodes drain the breast and upper extremity, not the thyroid gland, so they are not the expected nodal basin for lymphatic spread of thyroid carcinoma.
incorrectas.C: Inguinal nodes drain the lower extremities, external genitalia, and lower anal canal — anatomically far removed from thyroid lymphatic drainage, which flows to cervical and central neck nodes.
incorrectas.D: Mediastinal nodes can occasionally be involved in more extensive disease, but they are not the primary or most characteristic nodal basin for papillary carcinoma; the classic and most common site of spread is the cervical lymph node chain in the neck.

preguntas.q: What is the general prognosis for a patient diagnosed with papillary thyroid carcinoma?

o.A: Poor, with rapid progression to death
o.D: Variable and unpredictable, with no established prognostic pattern

e.correcta: Papillary thyroid carcinoma has an excellent overall prognosis, with greater than 95% ten-year survival in most patients, even when cervical lymph node metastases are present at diagnosis. This favorable outcome reflects the tumor's typically indolent, slow-growing biology and its general responsiveness to surgical resection with or without radioactive iodine ablation, making it one of the most curable solid organ cancers.

incorrectas.A: Rapid progression to death describes the behavior of anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, an aggressive, undifferentiated tumor with a dismal prognosis, which stands in stark contrast to the indolent, highly curable course of papillary carcinoma.
incorrectas.C: Anaplastic carcinoma prognosis is poor, often measured in months, precisely because it is undifferentiated and rapidly invasive; papillary carcinoma behaves nothing like this and instead has one of the best prognoses among all thyroid and indeed most solid cancers.
incorrectas.D: Papillary carcinoma prognosis is actually quite predictable and well characterized by established staging systems (e.g., age, tumor size, extrathyroidal extension), so describing it as unpredictable with no established pattern misrepresents the extensive prognostic data available for this cancer.

preguntas.q: Thyroid follicular carcinoma is defined by a malignant proliferation of follicles surrounded by a fibrous capsule with which additional finding that distinguishes it from adenoma?

o.A: Presence of psammoma bodies within the follicles
o.B: Invasion through the capsule and/or vasculature
o.D: Diffuse lymphocytic infiltration of the stroma

e.correcta: Follicular carcinoma looks architecturally similar to follicular adenoma — both are encapsulated proliferations of follicular cells — but carcinoma is defined by invasion through the fibrous capsule and/or into blood vessels, showing that the tumor cells have breached their normal confinement and gained access to a route for hematogenous dissemination. This capsular/vascular invasion is the entire basis of the diagnosis, which is why it typically cannot be assessed on FNA cytology alone and requires examination of the full excised specimen and capsule.

incorrectas.A: Psammoma bodies are a feature of papillary carcinoma (from calcified necrotic papillary cores), not follicular carcinoma, so their presence would point toward a different tumor type entirely.
incorrectas.C: Follicular carcinoma typically still has a capsule — the diagnostic issue is that the capsule has been breached by tumor cells, not that a capsule is completely absent; total absence of a capsule would be an unusual and non-specific finding rather than the defining criterion.
incorrectas.D: Diffuse lymphocytic infiltration of the stroma describes an inflammatory or autoimmune process, such as Hashimoto thyroiditis, and is not the histologic feature that separates follicular carcinoma from adenoma, which rests solely on invasion.

preguntas.q: Why can fine needle aspiration (FNA) not reliably distinguish thyroid follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma?

o.A: Both tumors have identical molecular mutations detectable only by immunohistochemistry
o.B: The fibrous capsule and its integrity cannot be visualized with FNA
o.C: FNA cannot sample follicular cells at all
o.D: Follicular neoplasms do not exfoliate cells adequately for cytology

e.correcta: FNA only samples individual cells or small clusters of cells for cytologic review — it cannot preserve or visualize the overall tissue architecture, including whether the tumor's fibrous capsule remains intact or has been breached by invasive cells. Because the sole criterion separating follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma is capsular and/or vascular invasion (a structural, not cytologic, feature), FNA is inherently unable to make this distinction, and definitive diagnosis requires histologic examination of the fully excised, intact specimen.

incorrectas.A: There is no reliable immunohistochemical or molecular marker that definitively separates all follicular adenomas from follicular carcinomas on a cellular level identical between the two; the actual limiting factor is architectural (capsule status), not a shared but hidden molecular profile revealed only by IHC.
incorrectas.C: FNA is actually quite effective at sampling follicular cells and is the standard first-line technique for evaluating thyroid nodules generally; the limitation is specific to distinguishing adenoma from carcinoma within the follicular category, not an inability to obtain follicular cells at all.
incorrectas.D: Follicular neoplasms do exfoliate cells adequately for cytologic evaluation via FNA — that is precisely why FNA is useful for triaging nodules as benign, indeterminate (follicular neoplasm), or malignant; the issue is architectural information being unavailable, not inadequate cell yield.

preguntas.q: Thyroid follicular carcinoma is most strongly associated with which gene mutation?

e.correcta: Follicular thyroid carcinoma is most strongly associated with activating mutations in the RAS family of genes (particularly NRAS and HRAS), which drive constitutive activation of downstream growth signaling pathways in follicular cells; RAS mutations are also found in follicular adenomas, reflecting a shared pathway of tumorigenesis for this follicular-patterned tumor family, with invasion being what separates the benign from malignant lesion. This RAS association contrasts with papillary carcinoma's characteristic RET/BRAF alterations, helping distinguish the molecular signatures of the two most common thyroid cancer types.

incorrectas.A: BRAF mutations, especially BRAF V600E, are the hallmark genetic alteration of papillary thyroid carcinoma, not follicular carcinoma, and reflect activation of the MAPK pathway characteristic of that distinct tumor type.
incorrectas.B: RET mutations/rearrangements are associated with papillary thyroid carcinoma (as RET/PTC fusions) and, in germline form, with medullary thyroid carcinoma in MEN 2 syndromes — not with follicular carcinoma.
incorrectas.D: TP53 mutations are characteristically acquired in anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, often representing a late dedifferentiation event from a pre-existing differentiated carcinoma, rather than being the primary driver mutation of follicular carcinoma.

preguntas.q: Unlike most carcinomas, which typically spread via lymphatics, thyroid follicular carcinoma most commonly metastasizes by which route?

e.correcta: Follicular thyroid carcinoma is unusual among carcinomas in that it preferentially invades blood vessels within and around its capsule rather than lymphatics, giving it direct access to the bloodstream and allowing it to metastasize hematogenously to distant sites such as lung and bone. This vascular invasion is in fact part of the diagnostic criteria for the tumor itself (along with capsular invasion), which mechanistically explains why its metastatic pattern differs from the lymphatic-predominant spread seen in papillary carcinoma.

incorrectas.A: Lymphatic spread to cervical nodes is the classic pattern for papillary thyroid carcinoma, not follicular carcinoma, reflecting a key clinical distinction between the two most common thyroid cancer subtypes.
incorrectas.B: While local invasion can occur, it is not the primary or most characteristic route of spread that distinguishes follicular carcinoma; the defining and clinically important pattern is hematogenous dissemination to distant organs.
incorrectas.D: Transcoelomic seeding (spread across a body cavity, as classically seen with ovarian cancer across the peritoneum) is not a recognized route of spread for thyroid follicular carcinoma, which has no natural coelomic cavity relationship to seed into.

preguntas.q: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells and characteristically secretes which hormone?

e.correcta: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from the parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid, which are neuroendocrine cells embryologically derived from the neural crest rather than from the follicular epithelium that produces thyroid hormone. These C cells normally secrete calcitonin, which acts to lower serum calcium by inhibiting osteoclastic bone resorption, and calcitonin serves as a clinically useful tumor marker for diagnosing and monitoring medullary carcinoma, particularly in the hereditary MEN 2 setting.

incorrectas.A: Thyroglobulin is the protein matrix within thyroid follicles used to synthesize and store thyroid hormone, produced by follicular cells (the cell of origin for papillary and follicular carcinoma), not by the parafollicular C cells that give rise to medullary carcinoma.
incorrectas.B: Parathyroid hormone is secreted by the chief cells of the separate parathyroid glands to regulate calcium homeostasis; it has no relationship to the parafollicular C cells within the thyroid gland itself.
incorrectas.D: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is secreted by the anterior pituitary to regulate thyroid follicular cell hormone production; it is not produced by the thyroid gland itself, let alone by C cells, making it unrelated to medullary carcinoma's hormone secretion.

preguntas.q: High levels of calcitonin secreted by a medullary thyroid carcinoma may lead to which electrolyte abnormality?

e.correcta: Calcitonin, secreted by parafollicular (C) cells and markedly elevated in medullary thyroid carcinoma, acts to lower serum calcium by inhibiting osteoclastic bone resorption and promoting renal calcium excretion, so very high tumor-derived levels can produce hypocalcemia. Medullary thyroid carcinoma is also notable as part of MEN 2A/2B syndromes, and calcitonin serves as a clinically useful tumor marker for diagnosis and surveillance.

incorrectas.A: Hypercalcemia would result from processes that increase calcium release or absorption, like PTH-related peptide from certain malignancies or primary hyperparathyroidism, which is the opposite effect of calcitonin's calcium-lowering action.
incorrectas.C: Hyperkalemia is not a recognized consequence of elevated calcitonin; calcitonin's physiologic role centers on calcium and phosphate homeostasis via bone and kidney effects, not potassium regulation.
incorrectas.D: Hypernatremia relates to free water deficits or excess sodium, governed by ADH and renal sodium handling, not by calcitonin, which specifically targets calcium metabolism rather than sodium balance.

preguntas.q: Thyroid medullary carcinoma is associated with which two multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndromes, both linked to RET mutations?

e.correcta: Medullary thyroid carcinoma is strongly associated with MEN 2A (medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and primary hyperparathyroidism) and MEN 2B (medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and mucosal neuromas/marfanoid habitus), both of which are caused by germline activating mutations in the RET proto-oncogene. Because RET mutations are so tightly linked to hereditary medullary carcinoma, genetic testing for RET mutations in patients (and at-risk family members) guides decisions about prophylactic thyroidectomy, often performed in childhood before malignant transformation occurs.

incorrectas.A: MEN 1 is caused by mutations in the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene and classically involves parathyroid, pancreatic, and pituitary tumors (the "3 P's"), not medullary thyroid carcinoma, so it does not belong in the correct pairing here.
incorrectas.C: MEN 1 alone omits the actual disease association entirely, since medullary thyroid carcinoma is a MEN 2 (not MEN 1) syndrome feature, making this option incorrect on its own terms.
incorrectas.D: While MEN 2B correctly belongs in the pairing, MEN 1 does not include medullary thyroid carcinoma as a feature, so combining MEN 2B with MEN 1 (rather than MEN 2A) misrepresents the actual syndromic associations.

preguntas.q: An elderly patient presents with a rapidly enlarging, undifferentiated malignant thyroid tumor showing large pleomorphic, osteoclast-like multinucleate giant cells and biphasic spindle cells. Which thyroid carcinoma subtype is this?

e.correcta: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is a highly aggressive, undifferentiated malignancy showing marked pleomorphism, including bizarre giant cells with osteoclast-like multinucleation and biphasic spindle cell morphology, reflecting near-total loss of the normal follicular architecture and differentiation markers seen in other thyroid cancers. This extreme dedifferentiation (often arising from a pre-existing differentiated carcinoma that has acquired additional mutations such as TP53) explains both its rapid growth and its very poor prognosis compared to papillary, follicular, or medullary carcinoma.

incorrectas.A: Papillary carcinoma shows characteristic pale, ground-glass "Orphan Annie eye" nuclei and nuclear grooves within a well-differentiated papillary architecture — the opposite of the bizarre, pleomorphic, undifferentiated cells described in this vignette.
incorrectas.B: Follicular carcinoma retains recognizable follicular architecture with relatively bland, uniform cells, distinguished from adenoma only by capsular/vascular invasion, not by the dramatic pleomorphism and giant cell formation seen in anaplastic carcinoma.
incorrectas.D: Medullary carcinoma arises from C cells and typically shows a more uniform, nested or organoid growth pattern often with associated amyloid deposits from procalcitonin, not the highly pleomorphic giant cell and spindle cell morphology described here.

preguntas.q: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is most commonly seen in which patient demographic, distinguishing it clinically from Riedel thyroiditis?

e.correcta: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma classically occurs in elderly women, often arising from a pre-existing, longstanding differentiated thyroid carcinoma (commonly papillary) that undergoes additional genetic hits (such as TP53 mutation) leading to dedifferentiation over years to decades. This age and sex pattern is a useful clinical clue that helps place anaplastic carcinoma on the differential when an older woman presents with a rapidly enlarging neck mass, distinguishing it from other fibrosing or inflammatory neck processes like Riedel thyroiditis, which can mimic its firm, invasive character but follows a much more indolent course.

incorrectas.A: Young men are not the characteristic demographic for anaplastic carcinoma; this aggressive tumor overwhelmingly affects older patients, reflecting its typical origin from years of accumulated mutations in a pre-existing differentiated thyroid cancer.
incorrectas.C: Adolescent girls are far more typically associated with papillary thyroid carcinoma when thyroid cancer does occur at a young age, not anaplastic carcinoma, which is essentially a disease of advanced age.
incorrectas.D: Middle-aged men are not the peak demographic; anaplastic carcinoma skews toward elderly patients and has a female predominance, consistent with the general epidemiology of thyroid disease overall.

preguntas.q: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma often invades local neck structures, leading to which set of symptoms?

o.C: Hoarseness only, with no other symptoms
o.D: Isolated painless neck swelling with no compressive symptoms

e.correcta: Because anaplastic thyroid carcinoma grows extremely rapidly and is locally aggressive, it commonly invades adjacent neck structures such as the esophagus and trachea, producing dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) from esophageal compression/invasion and respiratory compromise (stridor, dyspnea) from tracheal compression or invasion. This aggressive local infiltration, occurring over weeks rather than years, is a key clinical clue that distinguishes anaplastic carcinoma from the far more indolent differentiated thyroid cancers, and it often makes the tumor unresectable at presentation.

incorrectas.A: Diarrhea and flushing are the classic carcinoid syndrome symptoms caused by serotonin and other vasoactive substances released from neuroendocrine tumors (or in some cases medullary thyroid carcinoma via calcitonin/other peptides), not typical of anaplastic carcinoma's mass-effect presentation.
incorrectas.C: Hoarseness alone understates the clinical picture; while recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion causing hoarseness can occur, anaplastic carcinoma's rapid local growth typically produces additional compressive symptoms like dysphagia and airway compromise, not an isolated finding.
incorrectas.D: Isolated painless neck swelling without compressive symptoms describes a more indolent process, such as a well-differentiated carcinoma or benign goiter; anaplastic carcinoma's defining clinical feature is rapid growth causing compressive, often painful, symptoms.

preguntas.q: What is the typical prognosis for a patient diagnosed with anaplastic thyroid carcinoma?

o.B: Good, with long-term survival expected in most patients
o.D: Variable, but generally favorable with surgery alone

e.correcta: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma carries a very poor prognosis, with median survival typically measured in months, because the tumor is undifferentiated, grows and invades extremely rapidly, and is frequently unresectable and poorly responsive to conventional chemotherapy and radiation by the time of diagnosis. This grim outlook stands in sharp contrast to the excellent prognosis of differentiated thyroid cancers (papillary, follicular) and underscores why recognizing red-flag features (rapid growth, compressive symptoms, elderly patient) for early suspicion matters clinically, even though outcomes remain poor even with early intervention.

incorrectas.A: Papillary carcinoma has an excellent prognosis with slow growth and high curability, which is essentially the opposite clinical behavior from anaplastic carcinoma's rapid, lethal course.
incorrectas.B: Long-term survival is not expected in anaplastic carcinoma; most patients succumb to the disease within a year of diagnosis due to its aggressive local invasion and early distant metastasis.
incorrectas.D: Surgery alone rarely achieves favorable outcomes in anaplastic carcinoma because the tumor is frequently unresectable or already has distant spread at diagnosis, unlike differentiated thyroid cancers where surgery can be curative.

preguntas.q: What is the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism?

e.correcta: The most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism is a single parathyroid adenoma, a benign monoclonal proliferation of chief cells that autonomously secretes excess PTH independent of normal calcium-sensing feedback. Because only one gland is typically involved, imaging (such as sestamibi scan) and surgical exploration can often localize and remove the single culprit gland, which is curative — a key clinical distinction from the multi-gland disease pattern seen in secondary/tertiary hyperparathyroidism or MEN-associated hyperplasia.

incorrectas.A: Parathyroid carcinoma is a rare cause of primary hyperparathyroidism, typically associated with markedly elevated calcium and PTH levels and a palpable neck mass, but it accounts for only a small fraction of cases compared to the much more common solitary adenoma.
incorrectas.B: Sporadic four-gland hyperplasia does cause primary hyperparathyroidism and should be considered, especially in the context of MEN syndromes, but it is less common than a single adenoma as the overall cause of sporadic primary hyperparathyroidism.
incorrectas.D: Chronic kidney disease causes secondary (and eventually tertiary) hyperparathyroidism through phosphate retention and decreased active vitamin D synthesis driving compensatory PTH elevation, not primary hyperparathyroidism, which by definition originates from intrinsic parathyroid gland pathology rather than a renal stimulus.

preguntas.q: In primary hyperparathyroidism, what is the expected serum calcium level?

o.A: Decreased, due to increased renal calcium excretion
o.B: Normal, because PTH tightly regulates calcium within range

e.correcta: In primary hyperparathyroidism, an autonomously functioning parathyroid adenoma (or hyperplastic tissue) secretes PTH without regard to the normal negative feedback from serum calcium, so PTH continues driving increased bone resorption, increased renal calcium reabsorption, and increased renal activation of vitamin D — all of which raise serum calcium above normal despite that calcium elevation ordinarily should suppress PTH release. This inappropriate, unsuppressed PTH secretion in the face of hypercalcemia is the biochemical hallmark that confirms primary hyperparathyroidism and distinguishes it from other causes of hypercalcemia.

incorrectas.A: Serum calcium is increased, not decreased, in primary hyperparathyroidism; PTH excess promotes calcium retention and mobilization from bone rather than driving urinary calcium loss to the point of net hypocalcemia (PTH does increase calciuria compared to a normal person at the same calcium level, but the dominant systemic effect is still hypercalcemia).
incorrectas.B: PTH normally regulates calcium tightly, but in primary hyperparathyroidism that regulatory feedback is broken — the parathyroid tissue is autonomous and secretes PTH independent of serum calcium levels, so calcium rises well above the normal range rather than staying regulated within it.
incorrectas.D: Calcitonin, secreted by parafollicular C cells, lowers serum calcium and is not part of the primary hyperparathyroidism pathophysiology; the calcium elevation in this condition is driven by excess PTH, not by any change in calcitonin secretion.

preguntas.q: As a result of hypercalcemia, patients with primary hyperparathyroidism are at increased risk of developing which type of kidney stone?

e.correcta: Primary hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria (since filtered calcium load rises faster than tubular reabsorption can compensate), and the excess PTH also lowers phosphate by increasing renal phosphate excretion. This combination of high urinary calcium with low urinary phosphate favors precipitation of calcium oxalate (and to a lesser extent calcium phosphate) stones, making calcium oxalate the classic stone type seen with hyperparathyroidism-driven hypercalciuria.

incorrectas.A: Uric acid stones form in states of low urine pH and high purine turnover (e.g., gout, tumor lysis syndrome, chronic diarrhea), not from hypercalcemia — hyperparathyroidism does not meaningfully alter urine pH or urate excretion.
incorrectas.B: Struvite stones form from urease-producing organisms (e.g., Proteus, Klebsiella) that hydrolyze urea to ammonia, alkalinizing the urine and precipitating magnesium ammonium phosphate; this is an infection-driven mechanism unrelated to serum calcium.
incorrectas.C: Cystine stones result from a hereditary defect in renal tubular reabsorption of cystine (and other dibasic amino acids, as in cystinuria), a transport defect that has nothing to do with parathyroid hormone or calcium handling.

preguntas.q: A patient with primary hyperparathyroidism develops chronic hypercalcemia leading to calcium deposition within the renal tubules. What is this condition called?

e.correcta: Nephrocalcinosis refers to diffuse deposition of calcium salts within the renal parenchyma itself (tubules and interstitium), which occurs in chronic hypercalcemic states like primary hyperparathyroidism as calcium precipitates directly in the tubular lumen and interstitial tissue, impairing renal function over time. This is distinct from discrete stone formation in the collecting system, even though both processes can coexist in the same patient.

incorrectas.A: Nephrolithiasis refers to discrete calculi (stones) forming within the renal pelvis or collecting system, not diffuse calcium deposition within the tubular parenchyma — hyperparathyroidism causes both processes, but the question specifically describes calcium deposition within the tubules, which is nephrocalcinosis.
incorrectas.C: Papillary necrosis is ischemic/toxic necrosis of the renal papillae classically caused by NSAID overuse, sickle cell disease, diabetes, or pyelonephritis (mnemonic 'POSTCARDS'), a mechanism unrelated to calcium precipitation.
incorrectas.D: Acute tubular necrosis results from ischemic or nephrotoxic injury to tubular epithelial cells with cell death and sloughing (e.g., from contrast dye, aminoglycosides, hypotension), not from calcium salt deposition in the tubules.

preguntas.q: Which CNS/psychiatric manifestation is classically associated with primary hyperparathyroidism, captured in the mnemonic 'psychiatric overtones'?

e.correcta: The classic mnemonic for primary hyperparathyroidism symptoms is 'stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones' — the psychiatric component specifically refers to depression (along with lethargy, fatigue, and anxiety) resulting from hypercalcemia's effects on neuronal excitability and neurotransmission. Depression is the most commonly tested psychiatric manifestation and reflects how calcium acts as a key modulator of neuronal membrane potential and synaptic signaling.

incorrectas.A: Mania is not part of the classic hyperparathyroidism symptom complex; hypercalcemia's psychiatric overtones are characterized by depressive and lethargic features, not manic or elevated mood states.
incorrectas.C: Visual hallucinations are more typical of conditions like delirium tremens, Charles Bonnet syndrome, or certain toxic-metabolic encephalopathies, not the classic psychiatric presentation of hypercalcemia from hyperparathyroidism.
incorrectas.D: Catatonia is a distinct neuropsychiatric syndrome most associated with schizophrenia, severe mood disorders, or certain medical/neurologic conditions, not the depressive picture classically taught for hyperparathyroidism-related hypercalcemia.

preguntas.q: Hypercalcemia from primary hyperparathyroidism can trigger premature activation of pancreatic zymogens, resulting in which complication?

e.correcta: Hypercalcemia can prematurely activate trypsinogen to trypsin within pancreatic acinar cells (calcium is a required cofactor for trypsinogen autoactivation), triggering a cascade of zymogen activation and autodigestion of pancreatic tissue — this is acute pancreatitis. This is why hypercalcemia (along with gallstones and alcohol) is a recognized, testable cause of acute pancreatitis, and clinicians should check calcium levels in unexplained pancreatitis.

incorrectas.A: Chronic pancreatitis results from recurrent or sustained pancreatic injury leading to fibrosis and progressive loss of exocrine/endocrine function over time, not from a single acute event of premature zymogen activation as described.
incorrectas.B: A pancreatic pseudocyst is a walled-off collection of pancreatic fluid and debris that can form as a complication after an episode of acute pancreatitis, but it is not the direct consequence of zymogen activation itself — it's a downstream sequela.
incorrectas.C: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is a malignant neoplasm arising from ductal epithelium, driven by oncogenic mutations (e.g., KRAS) over years, entirely unrelated to acute calcium-triggered zymogen activation.

preguntas.q: A patient with primary hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcemia is more likely to present with which GI symptom?

e.correcta: Hypercalcemia decreases smooth muscle excitability and contractility throughout the GI tract by altering calcium-dependent neuromuscular signaling, leading to reduced peristalsis and resultant constipation. This fits within the 'groans' (abdominal/GI) component of the hyperparathyroidism mnemonic, alongside peptic ulcer disease and pancreatitis.

incorrectas.A: Diarrhea is not a typical feature of hypercalcemia; if anything, hypercalcemia tends to slow GI motility and produce constipation rather than increase stool frequency.
incorrectas.C: Malabsorption implies a defect in nutrient absorption (e.g., from mucosal disease, pancreatic insufficiency, or bile acid deficiency), which is not a mechanism by which hypercalcemia affects the gut — hypercalcemia's GI effect is primarily motility-related, not absorptive.
incorrectas.D: Bloody stools suggest mucosal ulceration, inflammation, or a vascular lesion, which is not a recognized direct consequence of hypercalcemia from hyperparathyroidism.

preguntas.q: In primary hyperparathyroidism, which serum marker is elevated due to increased osteoblastic activity in response to PTH-driven bone turnover?

e.correcta: In primary hyperparathyroidism, chronically elevated PTH stimulates osteoblasts (indirectly, via osteoblast-osteoclast coupling and RANKL signaling) to increase bone turnover, and alkaline phosphatase — an enzyme produced by active osteoblasts during bone matrix formation — rises as a marker of this increased skeletal remodeling activity. Elevated alkaline phosphatase alongside high PTH, high calcium, and low phosphate helps confirm the diagnosis and reflects the degree of bone involvement (e.g., osteitis fibrosa cystica in severe cases).

incorrectas.A: Creatine kinase is a marker of muscle (skeletal or cardiac) injury or breakdown, not of osteoblastic bone activity, so it is not the expected elevated marker in PTH-driven bone turnover.
incorrectas.B: Amylase is a pancreatic/salivary enzyme used to evaluate pancreatitis, unrelated to bone metabolism or osteoblastic activity in hyperparathyroidism.
incorrectas.C: Lactate dehydrogenase is a nonspecific marker of cellular injury/turnover (elevated in hemolysis, tumor lysis, tissue necrosis) and is not the specific enzyme reflecting osteoblastic bone formation activity the way alkaline phosphatase is.

preguntas.q: What is the expected serum calcium level in a patient with primary hyperparathyroidism?

o.D: Variable, depending on vitamin D status

e.correcta: Primary hyperparathyroidism is caused by autonomous overproduction of PTH (often from a parathyroid adenoma), which increases bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption, and intestinal calcium absorption (via activated vitamin D), producing hypercalcemia as the hallmark biochemical finding.

incorrectas.A: Decreased calcium is seen in hypoparathyroidism or secondary hyperparathyroidism (where low calcium is the stimulus for PTH release), the opposite pattern from primary hyperparathyroidism where high PTH drives calcium up.
incorrectas.C: hypercalcemia results directly from the excess PTH acting on bone, kidney, and gut to raise serum calcium; a normal level would be inconsistent with the primary defect of unregulated PTH secretion.
incorrectas.D: the calcium elevation in primary hyperparathyroidism is a consistent, defining feature caused directly by excess PTH, not something that fluctuates based on vitamin D independent of the primary glandular defect.

preguntas.q: What is the expected serum phosphate level in a patient with primary hyperparathyroidism?

e.correcta: PTH decreases renal phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule by downregulating the sodium-phosphate cotransporter, promoting phosphaturia even as it increases serum calcium via bone resorption, increased intestinal absorption (through activated vitamin D), and renal calcium reabsorption. This reciprocal calcium-phosphate relationship (high calcium, low phosphate) is a key lab pattern that helps confirm primary hyperparathyroidism and distinguishes it from other causes of hypercalcemia that don't share this phosphaturic effect.

incorrectas.A: Phosphate is not increased in primary hyperparathyroidism — PTH actively promotes renal phosphate wasting, so an elevated phosphate would actually argue against unopposed PTH excess and might suggest a different etiology such as renal failure with secondary hyperparathyroidism.
incorrectas.C: A normal phosphate level would be atypical for primary hyperparathyroidism, since PTH's phosphaturic effect on the proximal tubule reliably drives phosphate down; the classic lab triad specifically includes low (not normal) phosphate alongside high calcium and high PTH.
incorrectas.D: Phosphate becomes low but not undetectable in primary hyperparathyroidism — PTH promotes increased urinary phosphate excretion causing hypophosphatemia, but the effect is a downward shift in serum level, not complete absence of measurable phosphate.

preguntas.q: What is the expected serum calcium level in secondary hyperparathyroidism?

e.correcta: Secondary hyperparathyroidism arises when a chronic hypocalcemic or hyperphosphatemic stimulus (most often chronic kidney disease, but also vitamin D deficiency or malabsorption) causes the parathyroid glands to appropriately increase PTH secretion in a compensatory attempt to normalize calcium. Because the underlying problem (e.g., failing kidneys, lacking vitamin D) persists, calcium typically remains low or low-normal despite the elevated PTH — this is the key feature distinguishing secondary from primary hyperparathyroidism, where PTH elevation causes hypercalcemia.

incorrectas.A: Increased calcium is the hallmark of primary hyperparathyroidism, where autonomous PTH secretion drives calcium up — in secondary hyperparathyroidism, the parathyroid response is a compensatory reaction to low calcium, not a cause of high calcium.
incorrectas.C: Normal calcium would not be the expected finding, since the entire premise of secondary hyperparathyroidism is a persistent hypocalcemic (or hyperphosphatemic) stimulus driving continued PTH secretion; if calcium had normalized, the compensatory drive would resolve.
incorrectas.D: Calcium level in secondary hyperparathyroidism is directly related to PTH physiology, not unrelated — the low calcium is precisely what stimulates the elevated PTH in the first place.

preguntas.q: What is the most common underlying cause of secondary hyperparathyroidism?

e.correcta: Chronic renal failure is the most common cause of secondary hyperparathyroidism because failing kidneys cannot adequately excrete phosphate (causing hyperphosphatemia that binds serum calcium) and cannot convert vitamin D to its active form calcitriol (via 1-alpha-hydroxylase), reducing intestinal calcium absorption — both effects lower serum calcium and chronically stimulate PTH secretion. This renal-driven mechanism is far more prevalent clinically than other causes of secondary hyperparathyroidism like dietary vitamin D deficiency or malabsorption.

incorrectas.A: Vitamin D toxicity would cause hypercalcemia by increasing intestinal calcium absorption, which would suppress rather than stimulate PTH secretion — this is the opposite of what drives secondary hyperparathyroidism.
incorrectas.C: A parathyroid adenoma is the classic cause of primary hyperparathyroidism, where the gland itself is the autonomously overactive abnormality, not a compensatory response to an external hypocalcemic stimulus as in secondary hyperparathyroidism.
incorrectas.D: MEN1 causes primary hyperparathyroidism (along with pituitary and pancreatic endocrine tumors) due to parathyroid hyperplasia driven by a menin tumor-suppressor gene mutation, which is a primary gland abnormality, not a secondary compensatory response.

preguntas.q: In chronic renal failure, how does the kidney trigger secondary hyperparathyroidism?

o.A: Increased calcitriol production raises calcium absorption, suppressing PTH release
o.B: Decreased phosphate excretion raises phosphate, which binds free calcium and lowers serum calcium, stimulating PTH release
o.C: Loss of erythropoietin directly stimulates parathyroid hyperplasia
o.D: Increased renal calcium reabsorption raises serum calcium, triggering PTH release

e.correcta: In chronic renal failure, declining glomerular filtration reduces the kidney's ability to excrete phosphate, so serum phosphate rises; this excess phosphate binds free ionized calcium (forming calcium phosphate complexes), lowering serum calcium levels. The resulting hypocalcemia is sensed by the calcium-sensing receptors on parathyroid chief cells, which respond by increasing PTH secretion in a compensatory attempt to restore calcium — this is the core mechanism of renal secondary hyperparathyroidism.

incorrectas.A: Failing kidneys actually have decreased, not increased, calcitriol production (due to loss of functional 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity in damaged renal tissue), which contributes to hypocalcemia and stimulates rather than suppresses PTH release.
incorrectas.C: While erythropoietin deficiency does occur in chronic renal failure (causing anemia), it is a separate consequence of lost renal endocrine function and does not itself stimulate parathyroid hyperplasia — the PTH-driving mechanism is specifically the calcium-phosphate disturbance.
incorrectas.D: Renal calcium reabsorption is typically impaired, not increased, in chronic renal failure, and it is the resulting hypocalcemia (via the phosphate-binding mechanism), not renal calcium retention causing hypercalcemia, that triggers PTH release.

preguntas.q: Chronic renal disease can lead to a secondary hyperparathyroidism-driven bone disease characterized by increased bone resorption from elevated PTH. What is this condition called?

e.correcta: Renal osteodystrophy encompasses the spectrum of bone disease seen in chronic kidney disease, including the high-turnover bone changes driven by secondary hyperparathyroidism (increased osteoclastic bone resorption from chronically elevated PTH), as well as contributions from hyperphosphatemia, calcitriol deficiency, and metabolic acidosis. It is the umbrella term specifically used for CKD-associated bone disease, distinguishing it from bone disease due to primary parathyroid pathology.

incorrectas.A: Osteomalacia refers to defective bone mineralization from inadequate vitamin D or phosphate (soft, understructured bone), which can be a component of renal bone disease but is not the specific term for the PTH-driven, high-turnover resorptive process described here.
incorrectas.B: Paget disease of bone is a distinct disorder of dysregulated osteoclast/osteoblast activity causing chaotic bone remodeling, unrelated to chronic kidney disease or secondary hyperparathyroidism.
incorrectas.C: Osteitis fibrosa cystica classically refers to the bone lesions of primary hyperparathyroidism (or severe secondary/tertiary disease) with cystic, fibrous, 'brown tumor' changes, but the broader term for chronic renal failure-associated bone disease as a whole is renal osteodystrophy.

preguntas.q: After a prolonged period of secondary hyperparathyroidism from chronic renal disease, the parathyroid glands can become autonomous, secreting PTH independent of calcium regulation. What is this condition called?

e.correcta: Tertiary hyperparathyroidism occurs when prolonged secondary hyperparathyroidism (usually from years of chronic renal failure) causes the parathyroid glands to undergo hyperplastic, autonomous transformation, such that they continue secreting excessive PTH even after the underlying calcium/phosphate abnormality is corrected (e.g., after renal transplant). This autonomy — behaving like primary hyperparathyroidism but arising from a background of chronic secondary stimulation — is why hypercalcemia (rather than the hypocalcemia of secondary disease) is often seen in tertiary hyperparathyroidism.

incorrectas.A: Primary hyperparathyroidism refers to a de novo autonomous parathyroid abnormality (usually adenoma) as the initial cause, not a state that develops secondarily to years of chronic secondary hyperparathyroidism from renal disease.
incorrectas.C: Pseudohyperparathyroidism is not a standard term in this context; the clinically relevant related entity is humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (PTHrP-mediated), which is a distinct paraneoplastic process unrelated to the progression from secondary hyperparathyroidism.
incorrectas.D: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia results from an inactivating mutation in the calcium-sensing receptor, causing a mildly elevated PTH set point and low urinary calcium excretion, a hereditary condition unrelated to the chronic renal disease progression described here.

preguntas.q: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a (Albright hereditary osteodystrophy) is characterized by shortened stature and shortening of which digits?

e.correcta: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a is caused by a maternally inherited inactivating mutation in the GNAS gene, which encodes the Gs-alpha subunit that couples PTH receptors to adenylyl cyclase; end-organ resistance to PTH causes hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia despite elevated PTH levels. The associated Albright hereditary osteodystrophy phenotype includes short stature, obesity, round facies, and characteristic shortening of the 4th and 5th metacarpals/metatarsals, producing the classic 'knuckle-knuckle-dimple-dimple' sign when a fist is made.

incorrectas.A: The 2nd and 3rd digits are not the digits classically shortened in Albright hereditary osteodystrophy; the disorder specifically targets the more ulnar/lateral metacarpals rather than the radial ones.
incorrectas.B: The 1st and 2nd digits (thumb and index finger) are not affected in this condition — the shortened metacarpals are specifically the 4th and 5th, not the thumb side of the hand.
incorrectas.D: The 3rd and 4th digit combination does not match the classic AHO pattern; the 4th is involved but pairs with the 5th, not the 3rd, digit.

preguntas.q: What is the inheritance pattern of pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a (Albright hereditary osteodystrophy)?

e.correcta: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a (Albright hereditary osteodystrophy) is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern due to a mutation in the GNAS1 gene, which encodes the Gs alpha subunit needed for PTH receptor signaling. Because of genomic imprinting at this locus, the phenotype (end-organ PTH resistance plus the skeletal features) only manifests when the mutant allele is inherited from the mother, since the paternal allele is normally silenced in certain tissues like the kidney.

incorrectas.A: X-linked recessive inheritance would produce a completely different transmission pattern (affecting mainly males, with carrier mothers), which does not match the GNAS1-related, imprinting-influenced autosomal dominant inheritance of this condition.
incorrectas.B: Autosomal recessive inheritance would require two mutant alleles for disease expression, but pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a only requires one mutant allele (dominant), with the phenotype further modified by parental imprinting rather than needing biallelic mutation.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance follows strict maternal transmission of mitochondrial DNA mutations to all offspring, a completely different mechanism from the nuclear GNAS1 gene mutation with imprinting effects seen in this condition.

preguntas.q: Which condition presents with the physical features of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (short stature, short 4th/5th digits) but WITHOUT end-organ PTH resistance or calcium/phosphate abnormalities?

e.correcta: Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism occurs when the same GNAS1 mutation is inherited from the father rather than the mother; because renal PTH receptor signaling requires the maternal allele (paternal allele is imprinted/silenced in the kidney), inheriting the mutation paternally produces the physical Albright hereditary osteodystrophy phenotype (short stature, short 4th/5th metacarpals, round face) without any PTH resistance or the calcium/phosphate abnormalities seen in true pseudohypoparathyroidism. This distinction highlights how tissue-specific genomic imprinting can decouple physical phenotype from biochemical/hormonal phenotype in the same underlying mutation.

incorrectas.B: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a has the identical physical features but occurs when the mutant allele is maternally inherited, which — because the maternal allele is the functionally active one in the kidney — DOES produce end-organ PTH resistance with hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, unlike the biochemically normal picture described in the question.
incorrectas.C: Primary hypoparathyroidism results from insufficient PTH production or gland destruction/absence, leading to hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, but it does not produce the characteristic Albright skeletal features, which are specific to GNAS1-related conditions.
incorrectas.D: DiGeorge syndrome results from a 22q11.2 deletion causing thymic and parathyroid aplasia (with hypocalcemia, immunodeficiency, and cardiac defects), a distinct genetic mechanism unrelated to GNAS1 imprinting or the Albright osteodystrophy phenotype.

preguntas.q: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a occurs due to inheritance of a defective GNAS1 allele from which parent, given that renal tissue only expresses the maternal allele due to imprinting?

e.correcta: Because the GNAS1 gene is imprinted such that only the maternal allele is transcriptionally active in the renal proximal tubule (the paternal allele is silenced there), a defective GNAS1 allele inherited from the mother knocks out the only functional copy of Gs alpha in that tissue. This causes the kidney to become resistant to PTH signaling despite normal or elevated PTH levels, producing the hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia characteristic of pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a.

incorrectas.A: A defective allele inherited from the father would not cause renal PTH resistance, because the paternal GNAS1 allele is normally silenced in the kidney anyway — a paternally inherited mutation only affects the (already largely inactive) paternal copy, producing pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism (physical features only) rather than true hormonal resistance.
incorrectas.B: The parent of origin is not equivalent in this imprinted locus — inheritance is not random or equal between parents, since renal expression comes specifically and exclusively from the maternal allele due to imprinting.
incorrectas.C: Grandparental origin ('skipped generation') is not how imprinting-related inheritance works in this condition; what matters is the specific parent (mother vs. father) transmitting the mutant allele to the affected individual in the current generation, not a generational skip.

preguntas.q: Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism occurs when a defective Gs alpha-subunit (GNAS1) allele is inherited from which parent?

o.D: Neither, it is a de novo mutation

e.correcta: In pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism, the defective GNAS1 allele is inherited from the father; since the paternal allele of GNAS1 is imprinted (silenced) specifically in renal tissue, a paternally inherited mutation does not disrupt the kidney's PTH signaling (the maternal allele there remains normal and functional). The mutation still causes the Albright hereditary osteodystrophy physical phenotype in tissues where imprinting doesn't apply, but without any biochemical PTH resistance.

incorrectas.A: A maternally inherited defective allele would knock out the functionally active copy in the kidney (since only the maternal allele is expressed there), producing true pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a with hormone resistance and calcium/phosphate abnormalities, not the biochemically silent pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism.
incorrectas.B: Inheritance from both parents would imply a different (biallelic) genetic mechanism, but this condition results from a single mutant allele whose phenotypic consequences depend entirely on which single parent transmitted it, due to imprinting.
incorrectas.D: This is a recognized heritable condition tied to parent-of-origin effects on a specific GNAS1 mutation, not a spontaneous de novo mutation with no parental transmission pattern.

preguntas.q: Which type of diabetes mellitus is characterized primarily by an absolute insulin deficiency due to autoimmune beta-cell destruction?

e.correcta: Type 1 diabetes mellitus results from autoimmune (type IV, T-cell-mediated) destruction of pancreatic beta cells, leading to an absolute deficiency of insulin production. Because essentially all beta-cell mass is eventually destroyed, these patients are dependent on exogenous insulin for survival and are prone to diabetic ketoacidosis if insulin is withheld, distinguishing this from type 2 diabetes, which involves insulin resistance with relatively preserved (at least initially) beta-cell function.

incorrectas.B: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is characterized primarily by peripheral insulin resistance with a relative (not absolute) insulin deficiency, and beta-cell destruction is not typically autoimmune in nature — it involves gradual beta-cell dysfunction/exhaustion rather than immune-mediated destruction.
incorrectas.C: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) results from single-gene mutations affecting insulin secretion (e.g., glucokinase mutations), a monogenic cause of a functional beta-cell defect, not autoimmune destruction of beta cells.
incorrectas.D: Gestational diabetes arises from insulin resistance induced by placental hormones during pregnancy, in a mechanism analogous to type 2 diabetes, not from autoimmune beta-cell destruction as in type 1.

preguntas.q: Which type of diabetes mellitus is primarily characterized by peripheral insulin resistance rather than an absolute deficiency of insulin?

e.correcta: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is primarily driven by peripheral insulin resistance (in muscle, liver, and adipose tissue), meaning target tissues respond poorly to circulating insulin despite it initially being present in normal or even elevated amounts; beta cells try to compensate by increasing insulin secretion, but this eventually fails as beta-cell reserve is exhausted over time. This mechanism (resistance rather than absolute deficiency) explains why type 2 diabetes is strongly linked to obesity and metabolic syndrome, and why many patients can initially be managed with lifestyle changes and oral agents rather than insulin.

incorrectas.A: Type 1 diabetes mellitus is defined by an absolute insulin deficiency from autoimmune beta-cell destruction, the opposite mechanism of the insulin-resistant-but-present state that characterizes type 2 diabetes.
incorrectas.B: Diabetes insipidus is an entirely separate condition involving deficient ADH secretion or renal ADH resistance, causing polyuria from an inability to concentrate urine — it has nothing to do with insulin resistance or glucose metabolism.
incorrectas.C: Latent autoimmune diabetes of adults (LADA) is a slowly progressive form of autoimmune beta-cell destruction (similar in mechanism to type 1 diabetes but with a later onset and slower course), so it still involves an autoimmune deficiency process rather than primary insulin resistance.

preguntas.q: Type 1 diabetes mellitus results from beta-cell destruction mediated by which type of hypersensitivity reaction?

e.correcta: Type 1 diabetes mellitus involves destruction of pancreatic beta cells by autoreactive CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and CD4+ T-cell-mediated inflammation (insulitis), which is the defining feature of a type IV (delayed-type, T-cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction. This cell-mediated (rather than antibody-mediated) mechanism explains the characteristic lymphocytic infiltration of the islets seen histologically and why autoantibodies (anti-GAD65, anti-insulin) serve mainly as disease markers rather than the actual mechanism of beta-cell killing.

incorrectas.A: Type I hypersensitivity is IgE-mediated, immediate-onset (e.g., anaphylaxis, allergic reactions via mast cell degranulation), a fundamentally different, antibody-triggered mechanism from the T-cell-driven beta-cell destruction of type 1 diabetes.
incorrectas.B: Type II hypersensitivity involves antibodies directly targeting cell-surface or matrix antigens causing cytotoxicity or dysfunction (e.g., Goodpasture syndrome, autoimmune hemolytic anemia), whereas beta-cell destruction in type 1 diabetes is driven by T lymphocytes, not by antibody-mediated cytotoxicity as the primary killing mechanism.
incorrectas.C: Type III hypersensitivity involves immune complex deposition (antigen-antibody complexes) causing complement activation and tissue damage (e.g., serum sickness, lupus nephritis), a different pathophysiologic process from the direct T-cell infiltration and killing seen in the pancreatic islets in type 1 diabetes.

preguntas.q: Type 1 diabetes mellitus, which manifests with features of insulin deficiency, is most commonly diagnosed in which age group?

e.correcta: Type 1 diabetes mellitus is most commonly diagnosed in children, adolescents, and young adults (generally under age 30), reflecting its autoimmune etiology, which tends to manifest earlier in life as the immune-mediated beta-cell destruction reaches a critical threshold. This early age of onset (formerly called 'juvenile-onset diabetes') is a key clinical clue distinguishing it from type 2 diabetes, which is classically a disease of middle-aged and older adults, though the age distributions of both are shifting somewhat with rising childhood obesity.

incorrectas.B: The 40-60 year age range is more classically associated with type 2 diabetes onset, related to years of accumulating insulin resistance often driven by obesity and sedentary lifestyle, not the earlier autoimmune process of type 1 diabetes.
incorrectas.C: Onset after age 60 is again more typical of type 2 diabetes given its association with long-standing metabolic risk factors, rather than the younger-onset autoimmune destruction seen in type 1 diabetes.
incorrectas.D: While type 1 diabetes can rarely present in infancy, it is not exclusive to neonates — the disease has its peak incidence in childhood/adolescence and can also first present in young adulthood, not being restricted to the neonatal period.

preguntas.q: Type 2 diabetes mellitus most commonly presents in which age group?

e.correcta: Type 2 diabetes mellitus classically presents after age 40, reflecting the gradual accumulation of insulin resistance (often related to obesity, sedentary lifestyle, and genetic predisposition) and progressive beta-cell compensatory failure over years to decades. Although rising childhood obesity has led to more cases in younger patients, the traditional and still-common presentation remains in middle-aged and older adults, contrasting with the earlier-onset autoimmune process of type 1 diabetes.

incorrectas.A: Onset before age 20 is much more characteristic of type 1 diabetes (autoimmune beta-cell destruction manifesting early in life), not the typical presentation of type 2 diabetes, which usually takes years of insulin resistance to manifest clinically.
incorrectas.B: The 20-30 year age range, while it can occasionally show type 2 diabetes (especially with rising obesity rates), is still atypical for the classic presentation, which is more heavily weighted toward middle-aged and older adults.
incorrectas.D: Type 2 diabetes is not exclusive to adolescents — although adolescent cases are increasingly recognized due to obesity trends, the disease remains predominantly a condition of adults over 40, and describing it as exclusive to adolescents misrepresents its epidemiology entirely.

preguntas.q: Compared with type 2 diabetes, type 1 diabetes mellitus has which relative degree of genetic predisposition, as shown by twin concordance studies?

o.A: Relatively strong (90% concordance in identical twins)
o.C: Relatively weak (50% concordance in identical twins)
