e.correcta: Type 1 diabetes shows relatively weak concordance in identical (monozygotic) twins, around 50%, indicating that while genetics contribute (via HLA-DR3/DR4 associations and other susceptibility genes), environmental triggers (such as viral infections) are also required to precipitate the autoimmune process. This is notably lower than type 2 diabetes, which shows much higher twin concordance (often cited around 90%), reflecting type 2's stronger polygenic and lifestyle-driven basis compared to type 1's combination of moderate genetic susceptibility plus environmental triggering.

incorrectas.A: A 90% concordance rate describes type 2 diabetes, not type 1 — type 2's stronger genetic loading (with polygenic contributions reinforced by shared lifestyle/environmental factors in twins) produces much higher concordance than the autoimmune, environmentally-triggered process of type 1 diabetes.
incorrectas.B: Type 1 diabetes clearly has a genetic component, as demonstrated by HLA associations (HLA-DR3/DR4) and family clustering, so 0% concordance would be inconsistent with known epidemiology, even though genetics alone are not sufficient to cause disease.
incorrectas.D: Complete genetic determinism (100% concordance) is not seen in either type of diabetes; the fact that concordance is imperfect in identical twins (who share the same genome) demonstrates that environmental and other non-genetic factors also play a necessary role in disease expression.

preguntas.q: Compared with type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes mellitus has which relative degree of genetic predisposition, based on twin studies?

e.correcta: Twin studies show markedly higher concordance for type 2 diabetes (around 90% in monozygotic twins) than for type 1 diabetes (around 30-50%), reflecting that T2DM is driven predominantly by polygenic susceptibility interacting with environmental factors like obesity and sedentary lifestyle, whereas T1DM requires an autoimmune trigger superimposed on a smaller genetic contribution (largely HLA-DR3/DR4). This strong heritability is why T2DM risk assessment emphasizes family history and lifestyle factors more than autoantibody screening.

incorrectas.B: 50% concordance actually approximates the twin concordance rate reported for type 1 diabetes, not type 2, so labeling this 'relatively weak' misrepresents T2DM's much stronger genetic concordance.
incorrectas.C: T2DM clearly has a heritable component, as demonstrated by high twin concordance and numerous identified susceptibility genes; claiming no heritable component contradicts the well-established genetic epidemiology.
incorrectas.D: This reverses the actual relationship — type 2 diabetes shows stronger (not weaker) twin concordance than type 1 diabetes, making this option the opposite of the correct comparison.

preguntas.q: Histologic examination of the pancreas in type 1 diabetes mellitus classically shows islets with which finding?

e.correcta: In type 1 diabetes mellitus, the pancreatic islets show insulitis — an inflammatory leukocytic infiltrate (predominantly T lymphocytes, along with macrophages) invading and destroying the beta cells as part of the autoimmune attack. This histologic finding is the microscopic correlate of the type IV, T-cell-mediated hypersensitivity process that defines the disease's underlying immunopathology.

incorrectas.A: Amyloid deposits within the islets are the classic histologic finding in type 2 diabetes (from amylin/IAPP co-secreted with insulin accumulating over years), not type 1, which instead shows active inflammatory infiltration rather than extracellular protein deposition.
incorrectas.B: Fibrosis with calcification is more typical of chronic pancreatitis (e.g., from alcohol-related pancreatic damage) affecting the exocrine pancreas, not the specific autoimmune islet inflammation seen in type 1 diabetes.
incorrectas.C: Fatty replacement of acinar tissue is associated with conditions like cystic fibrosis or chronic pancreatic insufficiency affecting exocrine tissue, not the immune-mediated islet pathology that defines type 1 diabetes.

preguntas.q: Histologic examination of the pancreas in type 2 diabetes mellitus classically shows islets with which finding?

o.D: Islet cell hyperplasia only, no deposits

e.correcta: In type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic hypersecretion of insulin (in response to insulin resistance) leads to co-secretion and progressive extracellular deposition of amylin (islet amyloid polypeptide, IAPP) within the pancreatic islets over years, producing visible amyloid deposits on histology. This amyloid accumulation is thought to contribute to progressive beta-cell dysfunction and loss over the course of the disease, distinguishing the chronic, deposition-based pathology of type 2 diabetes from the acute inflammatory insulitis of type 1.

incorrectas.A: A leukocytic infiltrate is the histologic hallmark of type 1 diabetes (insulitis from autoimmune T-cell attack), not type 2, which instead shows amyloid deposition rather than active inflammatory cell infiltration.
incorrectas.B: Granulomatous inflammation is not a feature of either major diabetes type; it is characteristic of conditions like tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, or certain fungal infections involving organized collections of activated macrophages, unrelated to typical diabetic islet pathology.
incorrectas.D: Type 2 diabetes islets do show measurable pathologic change — amyloid deposition and eventual reduction in beta-cell mass — rather than simply hyperplasia with no accompanying deposits, so this option omits the classic amyloid finding.

preguntas.q: In a patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus, how does serum insulin level typically change over the course of the disease?

o.B: Always increased throughout the disease course
o.C: Variable — initially increased, but may decrease later due to beta-cell exhaustion
o.D: Absent from the start, similar to type 1 diabetes

e.correcta: Early in type 2 diabetes, insulin levels are typically elevated (hyperinsulinemia) as beta cells compensate for peripheral insulin resistance by secreting more insulin to maintain normoglycemia; however, over years of sustained overwork, beta cells progressively fail (partly due to glucotoxicity, lipotoxicity, and amyloid deposition), so insulin levels can eventually decline in later disease stages. This variable, biphasic course explains why some type 2 diabetics can eventually require exogenous insulin therapy despite the disease not being a primary insulin-deficient state at onset.

incorrectas.A: Insulin is not always decreased from the start in type 2 diabetes — early in the disease, insulin levels are typically elevated as a compensatory response to insulin resistance, only declining later as beta-cell reserve is exhausted.
incorrectas.B: Insulin does not remain elevated throughout the entire disease course; while early hyperinsulinemia is characteristic, chronic beta-cell stress and exhaustion over time can cause insulin secretion to decline in later, more advanced stages of type 2 diabetes.
incorrectas.D: Insulin is not absent from the start in type 2 diabetes as it is in type 1 — the defining early feature of type 2 diabetes is preserved (often elevated) insulin secretion in the face of resistance, a fundamentally different starting point from the absolute deficiency of type 1 diabetes.

preguntas.q: Type 1 diabetes mellitus shows the strongest HLA associations with which alleles?

e.correcta: Type 1 diabetes has its strongest genetic associations with HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 (class II MHC alleles), which influence how autoreactive T cells recognize beta-cell antigens and contribute to the autoimmune destruction of pancreatic islet cells. Patients carrying both DR3 and DR4 haplotypes have an even higher risk, reflecting a gene-dosage-like effect on autoimmune susceptibility, distinguishing type 1 from type 2 diabetes, which has no strong HLA linkage.

incorrectas.B: HLA-DR2 is not the allele associated with increased type 1 diabetes risk; in fact, HLA-DR2 haplotypes are generally considered protective against type 1 diabetes, essentially the opposite of DR3/DR4's effect.
incorrectas.A: HLA-B27 is a class I allele associated with the seronegative spondyloarthropathies (ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, IBD-associated arthritis), not with type 1 diabetes.
incorrectas.D: HLA-A3 is classically associated with hereditary hemochromatosis, an iron overload disorder, and has no established strong association with type 1 diabetes susceptibility.

preguntas.q: Why do patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus present with weight loss and decreased muscle mass?

o.A: Increased lipolysis and proteolysis occur due to unopposed glucagon from lack of insulin
o.B: Excess insulin promotes fat and protein synthesis uncontrollably
o.D: Increased cortisol secretion causes catabolism independent of insulin status

e.correcta: In type 1 diabetes, the near-total loss of insulin removes its normal inhibitory effect on glucagon and other counter-regulatory processes, leading to unopposed glucagon action that drives increased lipolysis (breakdown of triglycerides in adipose tissue) and proteolysis (breakdown of muscle protein), since insulin normally suppresses these catabolic pathways. This shift toward a catabolic state — with fat and muscle being broken down to supply alternative fuel sources when cells cannot take up glucose — produces the characteristic weight loss and muscle wasting seen at presentation, often before diagnosis.

incorrectas.B: Excess insulin promoting fat and protein synthesis describes the opposite physiologic state (anabolism from hyperinsulinemia, as might be seen in early type 2 diabetes or with excess exogenous insulin), not the insulin-deficient, catabolic state of type 1 diabetes that causes weight loss.
incorrectas.C: Autoimmune enteropathy causing malabsorption is a distinct clinical entity (sometimes associated with other autoimmune conditions) and is not the mechanism responsible for the weight loss and muscle wasting classically attributed to insulin deficiency in type 1 diabetes.
incorrectas.D: While cortisol is a counter-regulatory, catabolic hormone, the classic mechanism taught for type 1 diabetes weight loss is the loss of insulin's anti-catabolic restraint on glucagon-driven lipolysis and proteolysis, not primary cortisol excess acting independently of insulin status.

preguntas.q: Why do patients with diabetes mellitus present with polyuria and polydipsia?

o.A: Excess glucose filtered into the urine creates an osmotic effect that pulls water with it
o.B: ADH secretion is chronically suppressed by hyperglycemia
o.C: Renal tubules develop resistance to aldosterone
o.D: Hyperglycemia directly damages the glomerular basement membrane, causing proteinuria-driven fluid loss

e.correcta: Once plasma glucose exceeds the renal tubular reabsorptive capacity (~180-200 mg/dL, the 'renal threshold'), glucose spills into the tubular lumen and remains there because the SGLT transporters are saturated. This unreabsorbed glucose acts as an osmotic diuretic, holding water in the tubule and driving polyuria; the resulting volume loss and rising plasma osmolarity stimulate thirst, producing polydipsia. This same principle is why SGLT2 inhibitors intentionally cause glucosuria and mild osmotic diuresis as a treatment mechanism.

incorrectas.B: ADH is actually stimulated, not suppressed, in uncontrolled diabetes because the osmotic diuresis causes volume depletion and rising serum osmolarity, both of which are potent triggers for ADH release; the problem is that even maximal ADH cannot overcome the obligate osmotic water loss caused by glucose in the tubule.
incorrectas.C: Aldosterone resistance would cause salt wasting and hyperkalemia (as in type 4 RTA), not the glucose-driven osmotic diuresis seen in diabetes; aldosterone signaling is not the mechanism behind polyuria in hyperglycemia.
incorrectas.D: Diabetic glomerular basement membrane damage (from chronic non-enzymatic glycosylation) causes proteinuria and nephropathy over years, but this is a late microvascular complication, not the acute mechanism producing polyuria/polydipsia at presentation.

preguntas.q: What is the most common type of diabetes mellitus?

e.correcta: Type 2 diabetes mellitus accounts for roughly 90-95% of all diabetes cases and results from a combination of peripheral insulin resistance and a relative (not absolute) insulin secretory defect, typically developing in the setting of obesity and metabolic syndrome. Its high prevalence tracks with rising rates of obesity and sedentary lifestyle worldwide, making it the dominant form encountered in clinical practice and on board exams.

incorrectas.A: Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells and causes absolute insulin deficiency, but it makes up only about 5-10% of diabetes cases, far less common than type 2.
incorrectas.B: MODY is a rare, autosomal dominant monogenic form of diabetes caused by mutations affecting beta-cell function (e.g., glucokinase or HNF mutations); it is a distinct clinical entity but numerically rare compared to type 2 diabetes.
incorrectas.D: Diabetes secondary to pancreatitis (a form of 'type 3c' diabetes) arises from destruction of pancreatic tissue including islet cells, but this is an uncommon secondary cause and does not approach the prevalence of type 2 diabetes.

preguntas.q: Which demographic is most commonly associated with the development of type 2 diabetes mellitus?

o.C: Children with a history of viral infections

e.correcta: Type 2 diabetes classically develops in middle-aged, obese individuals because excess adipose tissue (especially visceral fat) promotes chronic low-grade inflammation and lipid-mediated interference with insulin signaling, leading to peripheral insulin resistance. Over years, beta cells attempt to compensate by hypersecreting insulin until they can no longer keep pace, at which point hyperglycemia manifests clinically — a process that takes decades, explaining the typical middle-age onset.

incorrectas.A: Young, thin patients with an insulin-deficient presentation are more characteristic of type 1 diabetes (autoimmune beta-cell destruction) or MODY, not the insulin-resistant phenotype of type 2 diabetes.
incorrectas.B: Low BMI is essentially the opposite of the classic type 2 risk profile; elevated BMI and central adiposity are the hallmark risk factors, since adipose tissue itself drives the insulin resistance.
incorrectas.C: A history of viral infection in childhood is associated with proposed triggers for autoimmune type 1 diabetes (molecular mimicry theories), not with the insulin-resistant pathophysiology of type 2 diabetes.

preguntas.q: In obese patients, what mechanism underlies the insulin resistance that leads to type 2 diabetes mellitus?

o.A: Obesity causes downregulation of insulin receptors on target tissues
o.B: Obesity triggers autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
o.C: Obesity increases renal clearance of insulin, lowering circulating levels
o.D: Obesity causes a mutation in the insulin gene itself

e.correcta: In obesity, chronically elevated insulin levels (from compensatory hyperinsulinemia) and inflammatory adipokines/free fatty acids from expanded fat stores cause target tissues to downregulate insulin receptor number and post-receptor signaling, reducing the cell's response to a given amount of insulin. This receptor downregulation is a key mechanistic link between obesity and the insulin resistance that eventually manifests as type 2 diabetes once beta-cell compensation fails.

incorrectas.B: Autoimmune destruction of beta cells is the mechanism of type 1 diabetes, producing absolute insulin deficiency; type 2 diabetes in obesity involves resistance to insulin action at the receptor/post-receptor level, not loss of the cells that make insulin.
incorrectas.C: Increased renal clearance of insulin is not a recognized mechanism of obesity-related insulin resistance; in fact, insulin resistance is typically accompanied by compensatory hyperinsulinemia, meaning insulin levels are elevated, not cleared away.
incorrectas.D: A mutation in the insulin gene itself would cause a structurally abnormal insulin molecule, a rare monogenic cause of diabetes, not the acquired, receptor-level resistance that develops from obesity-related metabolic stress.

preguntas.q: Chronic use of which class of drugs can precipitate 'steroid diabetes'?

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids promote hyperglycemia through several mechanisms: they stimulate hepatic gluconeogenesis, antagonize insulin's action at peripheral tissues (inducing insulin resistance in muscle and fat), and can impair beta-cell insulin secretion with prolonged exposure. When this occurs in a patient on chronic steroid therapy (e.g., for autoimmune disease or transplant immunosuppression), it is termed 'steroid diabetes,' and it typically resolves or improves when the glucocorticoid dose is tapered.

incorrectas.B: Thiazide diuretics can mildly impair glucose tolerance by inducing hypokalemia (which reduces insulin secretion), but this effect is far less pronounced and not classically termed 'steroid diabetes'; it is not their primary mechanism of action.
incorrectas.C: Beta-blockers can mask hypoglycemic symptoms and cause modest metabolic effects, but they are not a classic cause of a distinct hyperglycemic syndrome the way glucocorticoids are.
incorrectas.D: ACE inhibitors do not cause hyperglycemia; if anything, ACE inhibitors are used therapeutically in diabetic patients to protect the kidneys from nephropathy, not to precipitate diabetes.

preguntas.q: Which laboratory test is used to diagnose and monitor diabetes mellitus by reflecting average blood glucose over the prior 2-3 months?

e.correcta: HbA1c reflects the fraction of hemoglobin that has undergone non-enzymatic glycosylation, a process proportional to the ambient glucose concentration over the roughly 120-day lifespan of a red blood cell, with more recent weeks weighted more heavily. Because it averages glucose exposure over the preceding 2-3 months, it is far less affected by day-to-day fluctuations than a single glucose measurement, making it the standard test for both diagnosing diabetes and monitoring long-term glycemic control.

incorrectas.A: Fasting C-peptide reflects endogenous insulin secretion (useful for distinguishing type 1 from type 2 diabetes or detecting factitious insulin use), not average glucose control over time.
incorrectas.B: Random urine glucose only indicates whether the renal glucose threshold was exceeded at a single point in time and is affected by hydration and renal function, giving no quantitative information about average glycemia over months.
incorrectas.D: Serum fructosamine reflects glycation of serum proteins (mainly albumin), giving an average glucose estimate over only about 2-3 weeks (albumin's shorter half-life), making it useful for shorter-interval monitoring but not the 2-3 month window that defines HbA1c.

preguntas.q: What HbA1c value meets the diagnostic threshold for diabetes mellitus?

e.correcta: An HbA1c of 6.5% or higher is the American Diabetes Association's diagnostic cutoff for diabetes mellitus, chosen because it correlates with the glucose level above which the risk of diabetic retinopathy rises sharply in epidemiologic studies. This threshold allows diagnosis from a single blood draw without requiring fasting or a glucose challenge, which is part of why it has become a preferred diagnostic tool.

incorrectas.A: An HbA1c of 5.7-6.4% defines prediabetes (impaired glucose regulation), a state of increased future diabetes risk that has not yet crossed the diagnostic threshold for overt diabetes.
incorrectas.C: ≥7.0% is a commonly used treatment target for glycemic control in patients already diagnosed with diabetes, not the value used to establish the initial diagnosis.
incorrectas.D: ≥8.0% would represent poorly controlled diabetes in a patient already diagnosed, but it is well above the actual diagnostic cutoff and does not represent the threshold used to define the disease.

preguntas.q: A fasting plasma glucose above what value (after fasting >8 hours) meets criteria for a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?

e.correcta: A fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL (after at least 8 hours without caloric intake), confirmed on a separate day, meets diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus per ADA guidelines, reflecting a threshold above which the risk of microvascular complications like retinopathy rises sharply in epidemiologic studies. This value is distinct from the ≥100 mg/dL cutoff used to define impaired fasting glucose (prediabetes).

incorrectas.A: A fasting glucose ≥100 mg/dL (but <126) defines impaired fasting glucose, i.e., prediabetes, not overt diabetes — this is an important distinction because management and risk stratification differ.
incorrectas.B: ≥110 mg/dL is not a standard diagnostic cutoff used in current criteria; it falls between the prediabetes and diabetes thresholds without corresponding to an official diagnostic category.
incorrectas.D: ≥140 mg/dL is not the fasting cutoff; rather, 140 mg/dL and above is closer to the 2-hour post-oral glucose tolerance test range used for interpreting glycemic status, not fasting values.

preguntas.q: During a 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test (75 g glucose load), what plasma glucose level at 2 hours is diagnostic of diabetes mellitus?

e.correcta: In the oral glucose tolerance test, a 2-hour plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL after a 75 g glucose load indicates the body cannot adequately dispose of an oral glucose challenge, reflecting either insufficient insulin secretion, insulin resistance, or both. This dynamic test is more sensitive than fasting glucose alone for detecting early diabetes, since it stresses the glucose-handling system directly.

incorrectas.A: A 2-hour glucose of 140-199 mg/dL defines impaired glucose tolerance (prediabetes), a state of increased risk that falls short of the diagnostic threshold for diabetes.
incorrectas.B: 180 mg/dL is close to the renal glucose threshold at which glucosuria begins, but it is not the diagnostic cutoff used for the OGTT; the standard diagnostic value is set higher, at 200 mg/dL.
incorrectas.D: 250 mg/dL is well above the diagnostic threshold and would represent significantly uncontrolled hyperglycemia, but it is not the actual defined cutoff value used for diagnosis.

preguntas.q: What is the normal range for blood glucose levels?

e.correcta: Normal fasting blood glucose is maintained in the range of roughly 70-120 mg/dL (some references cite 70-100 as strictly normal, with up to 125 as impaired fasting glucose) through the tightly regulated balance of insulin and counter-regulatory hormones like glucagon, cortisol, and epinephrine. This range ensures adequate glucose delivery to obligate glucose-using tissues like the brain and red blood cells while avoiding the tissue damage caused by chronic hyperglycemia.

incorrectas.A: 40-70 mg/dL is in the hypoglycemic range, low enough to trigger counter-regulatory hormone release and, if severe, neuroglycopenic symptoms — well below the normal fasting range.
incorrectas.C: 120-180 mg/dL exceeds the normal fasting range and would indicate impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes depending on the clinical context and testing conditions, not a normal baseline value.
incorrectas.D: 180-250 mg/dL is frankly hyperglycemic, at a level associated with glucosuria and osmotic symptoms, far above what is considered a normal physiologic blood glucose range.

preguntas.q: Which acute, life-threatening complication is most feared in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus?

e.correcta: Diabetic ketoacidosis is the classic life-threatening acute complication of type 1 diabetes because the absolute insulin deficiency (from autoimmune beta-cell destruction) removes the normal brake on lipolysis, driving unrestrained free fatty acid release and hepatic conversion to ketone bodies, producing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis alongside severe hyperglycemia and dehydration. It classically arises when insulin is missed or during physiologic stress (infection, illness) that raises counter-regulatory hormones, and it requires urgent treatment with IV fluids, insulin, and electrolyte repletion.

incorrectas.A: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is the analogous severe acute complication of type 2 diabetes, where residual endogenous insulin is usually enough to suppress ketogenesis even as glucose rises to extreme levels; it is not the classic complication associated with type 1 diabetes.
incorrectas.C: Lactic acidosis is a complication most associated with metformin accumulation (used in type 2 diabetes) or tissue hypoperfusion states, not a hallmark acute complication of type 1 diabetes itself.
incorrectas.D: Hypoglycemic coma can occur in any insulin-treated diabetic from excess insulin dosing or missed meals, but it is a treatment complication rather than the disease-intrinsic, feared acute complication that DKA represents in type 1 diabetes.

preguntas.q: Diabetic ketoacidosis is classically precipitated by which type of trigger, such as an infection?

e.correcta: Physiologic stress — most classically infection, but also myocardial infarction, trauma, or surgery — triggers a surge in counter-regulatory hormones (cortisol, catecholamines, glucagon, growth hormone) that antagonize insulin's actions, worsening hyperglycemia and accelerating lipolysis and ketogenesis in a patient with insufficient insulin to compensate. This is why clinicians always search for and treat a precipitating infection or illness when a patient presents in DKA, in addition to correcting the metabolic derangement itself.

incorrectas.A: Excess insulin administration would drive glucose down toward hypoglycemia and suppress lipolysis/ketogenesis, the opposite of what precipitates DKA, which requires insulin deficiency, not excess.
incorrectas.C: Prolonged fasting alone can produce starvation ketosis, but this is typically a mild ketosis without the marked hyperglycemia and severe acidosis of true DKA, which requires the combination of insulin deficiency and counter-regulatory hormone excess seen with stress.
incorrectas.D: Excessive fluid intake would not precipitate DKA and, if anything, would be part of the treatment (volume repletion) rather than a trigger of the ketoacidotic state.

preguntas.q: Which two ketone bodies are chiefly responsible for the ketoacidosis seen in a type 1 diabetic patient in DKA?

e.correcta: In DKA, insulin deficiency unleashes lipolysis, flooding the liver with free fatty acids that undergo beta-oxidation to acetyl-CoA; when this exceeds the Krebs cycle's capacity, acetyl-CoA is instead shunted into ketogenesis, producing acetoacetate, which is then reduced to beta-hydroxybutyrate (favored under the acidotic, NADH-rich conditions of DKA). These two ketoacids are directly responsible for the anion gap metabolic acidosis, while acetone (a third, non-acid ketone) is produced in smaller amounts and is responsible for the characteristic fruity breath odor rather than the acidosis itself.

incorrectas.A: Lactate is not a ketone body and its accumulation reflects anaerobic metabolism or tissue hypoperfusion, a separate process from the ketogenesis that drives DKA; acetone, not lactate, is the third true ketone body alongside acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate.
incorrectas.C: Pyruvate is an intermediate of glycolysis, not a ketone body, and does not contribute to the ketoacidosis of DKA the way beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate do.
incorrectas.D: Acetone is indeed a ketone body (giving the fruity breath smell), but it is a neutral volatile compound that is exhaled and does not significantly contribute to the acidosis; the acid-forming ketones responsible for the acidemia are beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate, not acetone.

preguntas.q: What is the expected serum (extracellular) potassium level in a patient presenting with diabetic ketoacidosis?

e.correcta: In DKA, insulin deficiency and the metabolic acidosis both impair the normal mechanisms (insulin-stimulated Na+/K+-ATPase activity) that drive potassium into cells, causing potassium to shift out of cells into the extracellular space; osmotic diuresis from glucosuria then compounds this by concentrating potassium in the blood before it is ultimately lost in the urine. The result is a serum potassium that is typically normal or elevated at presentation, even though the patient is often severely total-body potassium depleted — a distinction that is critical because insulin therapy will rapidly drive that extracellular potassium back into cells and can precipitate dangerous hypokalemia if repletion is not started early.

incorrectas.A: A decreased serum potassium at presentation would be unusual in untreated DKA; the extracellular shift caused by insulin deficiency and acidosis typically raises or normalizes serum potassium initially, even though total body stores are actually depleted.
incorrectas.B: While serum potassium can sometimes be within the 'normal' range, the classic and testable finding emphasized in DKA is an elevated serum potassium due to the transcellular shift, despite total body depletion — so 'increased' is the better answer than simply normal.
incorrectas.D: Potassium being 'undetectable' does not reflect any real physiologic state in DKA; the extracellular shift makes potassium measurable and typically elevated, not absent.

preguntas.q: What happens to intracellular potassium levels in a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis?

e.correcta: Because insulin normally promotes potassium entry into cells via stimulation of the Na+/K+-ATPase pump, the profound insulin deficiency of DKA causes potassium to shift out of cells and into the extracellular fluid, depleting the intracellular potassium pool even as total body potassium is also being lost through osmotic diuresis. This is why intracellular (and eventually total body) potassium is decreased despite a normal or high serum level at presentation, and why insulin treatment — which restores the intracellular shift — must be paired with careful potassium monitoring and repletion to avoid rebound hypokalemia.

incorrectas.A: Intracellular potassium is not increased in DKA; the lack of insulin action removes the stimulus that normally keeps potassium inside cells, so intracellular stores are depleted, not expanded.
incorrectas.C: Intracellular potassium is not unchanged; the insulin deficiency and acidosis of DKA actively drive potassium out of cells, meaningfully lowering the intracellular potassium pool.
incorrectas.D: Intracellular potassium status in DKA is well characterized physiologically (it is decreased due to loss of insulin-driven cellular uptake and ongoing urinary losses), so it is not an indeterminate value.

preguntas.q: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis is expected to have which acid-base disturbance?

e.correcta: DKA produces a high anion gap metabolic acidosis because the accumulating ketoacids (beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate) are unmeasured anions that consume bicarbonate buffer while raising the calculated anion gap (Na+ - [Cl- + HCO3-]). This pattern, distinct from a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) acidosis, is a key diagnostic clue that points directly to an excess acid production state like ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, or toxic ingestions.

incorrectas.A: A non-anion gap metabolic acidosis results from bicarbonate loss or renal tubular dysfunction with a compensatory rise in chloride (hence 'hyperchloremic'), not from the ketoacid accumulation that defines DKA, which produces an elevated, not normal, anion gap.
incorrectas.B: Respiratory alkalosis would result from hyperventilation blowing off CO2 as a primary process; in DKA, the rapid deep breathing (Kussmaul respirations) is actually a compensatory response to the underlying metabolic acidosis, not a primary alkalotic process.
incorrectas.D: Metabolic alkalosis reflects a primary gain of bicarbonate or loss of acid (e.g., vomiting), which is the opposite acid-base direction from the acid-generating ketogenesis that defines DKA.

preguntas.q: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis is expected to present with which glucose abnormality?

e.correcta: In DKA, insulin deficiency prevents peripheral tissues from taking up glucose while simultaneously driving unchecked hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, causing plasma glucose to rise markedly, typically well above 300 mg/dL. This severe hyperglycemia, combined with the resulting osmotic diuresis, drives the profound dehydration seen in these patients and is one of the three classic diagnostic pillars of DKA (hyperglycemia, ketosis, and high anion gap acidosis).

incorrectas.A: Hypoglycemia is the opposite metabolic derangement from what occurs in DKA; while a rare presentation called 'euglycemic DKA' exists (e.g., with SGLT2 inhibitor use), the classic and far more common presentation involves marked hyperglycemia, not low glucose.
incorrectas.B: Normoglycemia would be inconsistent with the typical pathophysiology of DKA, in which insulin deficiency directly causes glucose to accumulate in the blood; only in the atypical euglycemic DKA variant is glucose near normal, and that is not the classic presentation being tested here.
incorrectas.D: Glucose levels are very much affected in DKA — profound hyperglycemia is a defining and expected feature, not an incidental or unaffected parameter.

preguntas.q: Which fungal infection is a feared complication in patients with diabetic ketoacidosis?

e.correcta: Mucormycosis, caused by Rhizopus and related fungi, is classically associated with DKA because the acidic, hyperglycemic, iron-rich environment favors fungal growth (these fungi have iron-dependent enzymes that thrive when ketoacidosis releases iron from its usual protein-bound stores) while also impairing phagocyte function. It presents as rhino-orbital-cerebral disease with black, necrotic eschars from angioinvasion and tissue infarction, and is a surgical and antifungal emergency because of its rapid, destructive spread.

incorrectas.A: Aspergillosis classically affects immunocompromised or neutropenic patients (e.g., after chemotherapy or in chronic granulomatous disease) and is not the fungal infection specifically linked to the acidotic, hyperglycemic milieu of DKA the way mucormycosis is.
incorrectas.B: Candidiasis is a common opportunistic infection in diabetics generally (e.g., mucocutaneous candidiasis, vaginal yeast infections) due to chronic hyperglycemia, but it is not the specific angioinvasive, life-threatening infection classically triggered by the acid-base and metabolic environment of DKA itself.
incorrectas.D: Cryptococcosis is associated with impaired cell-mediated immunity, such as in HIV/AIDS, and is not the fungal infection classically linked to DKA.

preguntas.q: After correcting volume status, what is the mainstay treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis?

o.A: IV fluids, insulin, and potassium repletion

e.correcta: After initial volume resuscitation, IV insulin is required to shut off lipolysis and ketogenesis and to drive glucose (and potassium) back into cells, but because insulin causes potassium to shift intracellularly, potassium must be repleted concurrently (once levels are known to be safe) to prevent life-threatening hypokalemia and its cardiac arrhythmia risk. This triad of fluids, insulin, and potassium — carefully monitored and sequenced — is the cornerstone of DKA management, alongside treating any precipitating cause like infection.

incorrectas.B: Oral hypoglycemics are inappropriate in the acute setting of DKA because they act too slowly and are not effective substitutes for insulin in reversing ketogenesis; sodium bicarbonate is only used in severe, refractory acidosis, not as mainstay therapy.
incorrectas.C: Glucagon would raise blood glucose further and worsen the hyperglycemia in DKA, making it inappropriate; calcium gluconate is used for cardiac membrane stabilization in severe hyperkalemia, not as standard DKA treatment.
incorrectas.D: Glucocorticoids would worsen hyperglycemia and are not part of DKA management; the actual mainstay after fluids is insulin and potassium repletion, not steroids.

preguntas.q: Which severe acute complication is most feared in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus?

e.correcta: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is the feared acute complication of type 2 diabetes because these patients retain enough residual endogenous insulin to suppress lipolysis and ketogenesis, but not enough to prevent severe hyperglycemia, which — especially when combined with inadequate fluid intake (common in elderly or debilitated patients) — leads to extreme osmotic diuresis, profound dehydration, and dangerously high serum osmolarity that can cause altered mental status, seizures, or coma.

incorrectas.A: DKA requires near-absolute insulin deficiency to unleash unchecked ketogenesis, a state characteristic of type 1 diabetes; type 2 diabetics usually retain enough insulin to prevent significant ketoacidosis, making HHS rather than DKA their classic severe complication.
incorrectas.C: Lactic acidosis can complicate type 2 diabetes (notably with metformin accumulation in renal failure or tissue hypoperfusion), but it is not the disease-defining feared acute complication the way HHS is.
incorrectas.D: The Somogyi effect is a phenomenon of rebound morning hyperglycemia following nocturnal hypoglycemia in insulin-treated patients, a management nuance rather than a severe, life-threatening acute complication like HHS.

preguntas.q: Which patient population is most classically associated with developing hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state?

o.A: Young type 1 diabetics who miss insulin doses
o.B: Elderly type 2 diabetics with limited ability to drink water

e.correcta: HHS classically occurs in elderly type 2 diabetics who have limited access to or ability to drink water — for example, those who are bedbound, cognitively impaired, or in long-term care — because without adequate fluid intake to match the ongoing osmotic diuresis from hyperglycemia, glucose and serum osmolarity climb unchecked to extreme levels. This population is also more likely to have an infection or other physiologic stressor precipitating the hyperglycemia in the first place, while being least able to compensate behaviorally by drinking more water.

incorrectas.A: Young type 1 diabetics who miss insulin doses are the classic population for DKA, since their absolute insulin deficiency unleashes ketogenesis; they are not the typical population for HHS, which occurs in type 2 diabetics with preserved but insufficient insulin.
incorrectas.C: Gestational diabetes is generally well-monitored and rarely progresses to the extreme, prolonged hyperglycemia and dehydration required to produce HHS; this is not the classic population associated with the condition.
incorrectas.D: Children with new-onset type 1 diabetes typically present with DKA due to absolute insulin deficiency, not HHS, which requires the type 2 phenotype of relative (not absolute) insulin deficiency.

preguntas.q: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state classically presents with glucose levels exceeding what threshold, along with a serum osmolarity >320 mOsm/kg?

e.correcta: HHS is defined by extreme hyperglycemia, classically glucose >600 mg/dL, reflecting the prolonged, unchecked osmotic diuresis and dehydration that develop over days as fluid intake fails to keep pace with glucose-driven water loss. This severe hyperglycemia, combined with a serum osmolarity >320 mOsm/kg, is what drives the altered mental status and neurologic symptoms characteristic of the syndrome, distinguishing it from the more modest glucose elevations typically seen in DKA.

incorrectas.A: 300 mg/dL is roughly the glucose level associated with DKA, which typically presents with somewhat lower glucose than HHS because DKA tends to cause symptoms (and prompt treatment-seeking) earlier due to the acidosis and Kussmaul breathing.
incorrectas.B: 400 mg/dL, while clearly hyperglycemic, is well below the extreme threshold that defines HHS; the diagnostic criterion for HHS requires a much higher glucose level reflecting the prolonged, unmitigated hyperglycemia of this syndrome.
incorrectas.D: 1000 mg/dL is higher than the standard diagnostic threshold; while glucose can occasionally reach this level in severe cases, the accepted diagnostic cutoff for HHS is 600 mg/dL, not this even more extreme value.

preguntas.q: Why does hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state typically NOT present with significant ketoacidosis, unlike DKA?

o.B: Because ketone production is inhibited by the presence of residual insulin
o.C: Because renal clearance of ketones is enhanced
o.D: Because these patients lack functional adipose tissue

e.correcta: In type 2 diabetes, the pancreas still secretes enough residual insulin to suppress hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue, preventing the surge of free fatty acid release to the liver that is required to fuel ketogenesis, even though this residual insulin is insufficient to control blood glucose. This is the key mechanistic distinction from type 1 diabetes/DKA, where the near-total absence of insulin removes this brake on lipolysis entirely, allowing unchecked ketone body production.

incorrectas.A: Glucagon levels are typically elevated, not suppressed, in both HHS and DKA as part of the counter-regulatory hormone response to perceived cellular glucose deprivation; glucagon suppression is not the reason ketosis is absent in HHS.
incorrectas.C: Enhanced renal clearance of ketones is not the explanation; in fact, in severe HHS with significant dehydration and often reduced renal perfusion, clearance of any metabolic byproducts would tend to be reduced, not enhanced.
incorrectas.D: Patients with HHS have functional adipose tissue capable of lipolysis; the reason ketones aren't produced is that residual insulin actively suppresses the lipolytic signal, not an absence of fat tissue itself.

preguntas.q: What is the primary treatment approach for hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state?

o.C: Intense IV fluids and insulin therapy

e.correcta: Because the dominant problem in HHS is profound dehydration from prolonged osmotic diuresis, aggressive IV fluid resuscitation is the first and most critical step, followed by insulin therapy to gradually lower the extreme glucose level and shut off ongoing osmotic losses; fluids and insulin must be balanced carefully to avoid overly rapid osmolarity shifts that could cause cerebral edema, particularly in elderly patients.

incorrectas.A: Sodium bicarbonate is used to correct severe acidosis, but HHS characteristically does not present with significant ketoacidosis, so bicarbonate is not part of its standard management the way fluids and insulin are.
incorrectas.B: Oral metformin is inappropriate in the acute, critically ill setting of HHS, both because oral absorption in a dehydrated, altered patient is unreliable and because IV insulin is needed for rapid, titratable glucose control.
incorrectas.D: Emergent hemodialysis is not a standard treatment for HHS; the mainstay is fluid and insulin therapy, with dialysis reserved for other indications such as severe renal failure or refractory electrolyte abnormalities.

preguntas.q: Chronic hyperglycemia in diabetes mellitus leads to which biochemical process affecting vascular basement membranes?

e.correcta: Chronic hyperglycemia drives non-enzymatic glycosylation, in which glucose spontaneously attaches to proteins (such as those in basement membranes) without enzymatic control, forming advanced glycation end-products that cross-link and thicken basement membranes while also generating reactive oxygen species that damage vascular endothelium. This process underlies the microvascular complications of diabetes — nephropathy, retinopathy, and neuropathy — and is the same biochemical process measured indirectly by HbA1c, which itself is glycosylated hemoglobin.

incorrectas.A: Amyloid deposition refers to misfolded protein aggregates (as in AL or AA amyloidosis, or islet amyloid polypeptide in type 2 diabetes' pancreas specifically), a distinct process from the glucose-driven glycosylation that damages vascular basement membranes throughout the body in diabetes.
incorrectas.C: Complement-mediated injury is a feature of immune-complex or antibody-mediated diseases (such as certain glomerulonephritides), not the biochemical mechanism by which chronic hyperglycemia damages vasculature.
incorrectas.D: Fibrinoid necrosis is a histologic pattern seen in malignant hypertension and vasculitis from severe vessel wall injury and plasma protein insudation, not the specific mechanism of glucose-mediated basement membrane damage in diabetes.

preguntas.q: What is the leading cause of death in patients with diabetes mellitus?

e.correcta: Chronic hyperglycemia accelerates atherosclerosis through mechanisms including endothelial dysfunction, dyslipidemia, and non-enzymatic glycosylation of vessel wall proteins, making cardiovascular disease — particularly myocardial infarction — the leading cause of death among diabetics overall. This is why cardiovascular risk reduction (blood pressure control, statins, smoking cessation) is emphasized as heavily as glycemic control itself in long-term diabetes management.

incorrectas.A: DKA is a dangerous acute complication that can be fatal if untreated, but with modern recognition and treatment protocols it accounts for a small minority of diabetes-related deaths compared to the cumulative burden of macrovascular disease over a patient's lifetime.
incorrectas.B: Chronic renal failure (diabetic nephropathy) is a major and serious complication of long-standing diabetes, but cardiovascular disease remains the more common ultimate cause of death, in part because many diabetics die from myocardial infarction before end-stage renal disease fully develops.
incorrectas.D: Sepsis from foot ulcers is a significant morbidity and can be life-threatening, particularly with poor wound healing and peripheral neuropathy/vascular disease, but it is not the leading overall cause of death in the diabetic population compared to cardiovascular events.

preguntas.q: Non-enzymatic glycosylation of medium and large-sized vessels in diabetic patients most classically leads to which complication, a leading cause of nontraumatic amputation?

e.correcta: Chronic hyperglycemia drives nonenzymatic glycosylation of proteins in medium and large vessel walls, forming advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) that cross-link collagen, thicken the intima, and accelerate atherosclerosis. This diffuse macrovascular damage in the lower extremities produces peripheral vascular occlusive disease, which impairs wound healing and perfusion and is the leading driver of nontraumatic amputations in diabetics.

incorrectas.B: Deep vein thrombosis is a clotting disorder related to venous stasis, hypercoagulability, or endothelial injury (Virchow triad), not a direct consequence of AGE-mediated arterial wall glycosylation, and it is not the classic cause of diabetic amputation.
incorrectas.C: Raynaud phenomenon is vasospasm of small digital arteries triggered by cold or stress, typically linked to autonomic dysregulation or connective tissue disease, not to glycosylation-driven atherosclerotic occlusion of medium/large vessels.
incorrectas.D: Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) is a segmental inflammatory vasculitis of small/medium vessels strongly tied to tobacco use, mechanistically distinct from the nonenzymatic glycosylation and atherosclerosis pathway that defines diabetic vascular disease.

preguntas.q: Non-enzymatic glycosylation of small renal vessels in diabetic patients classically produces which pathologic finding, including Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules?

e.correcta: In diabetic nephropathy, nonenzymatic glycosylation of the glomerular basement membrane and mesangial matrix proteins promotes mesangial expansion and deposition of hyaline material, forming eosinophilic, laminated nodules within the glomerulus known as Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules — the histologic hallmark of nodular glomerulosclerosis. This nodular pattern, combined with diffuse mesangial sclerosis, progressively obliterates capillary loops and drives the proteinuria and declining GFR seen in long-standing diabetes.

incorrectas.A: Minimal change disease shows normal light microscopy with only podocyte foot process effacement on EM, typically in children with nephrotic syndrome, and has no relation to glycosylation-driven nodular mesangial deposits.
incorrectas.C: Crescentic glomerulonephritis features crescent formation from parietal epithelial cell proliferation and fibrin deposition in Bowman's space, a rapidly progressive immune/inflammatory process unrelated to the chronic glycosylation injury of diabetic glomerulosclerosis.
incorrectas.D: Membranous nephropathy is characterized by subepithelial immune complex deposits producing a 'spike and dome' pattern on the GBM, a distinct immune-mediated mechanism rather than glycosylation-induced nodular sclerosis.

preguntas.q: Non-enzymatic glycosylation of small renal vessels in diabetic patients can cause which vascular lesion, contributing to chronic renal failure?

e.correcta: Nonenzymatic glycosylation of small renal arterioles causes plasma protein leakage into the vessel wall, producing pink, hyaline (glassy) thickening of the arteriolar wall known as hyaline arteriolosclerosis — classically affecting both afferent and efferent arterioles in diabetics. This narrows the vessel lumen, reduces glomerular perfusion, and contributes over time to ischemic glomerular injury and chronic renal failure.

incorrectas.A: Fibromuscular dysplasia is a non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory condition causing alternating stenosis and dilation ('string of beads') typically in the renal artery of young women, a structural developmental abnormality unrelated to glycosylation.
incorrectas.C: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis shows concentric 'onion-skin' smooth muscle proliferation and is classically associated with malignant hypertension, not the hyaline protein deposition seen with diabetic glycosylation.
incorrectas.D: Polyarteritis nodosa is a necrotizing immune-mediated vasculitis of medium-sized arteries with transmural inflammation and fibrinoid necrosis, mechanistically unrelated to the bland hyaline thickening of diabetic arteriolosclerosis.

preguntas.q: Non-enzymatic glycosylation of hemoglobin produces which clinically useful marker of long-term glycemic control?

e.correcta: Glucose nonenzymatically and irreversibly binds to the N-terminal valine of the hemoglobin beta chain over the roughly 120-day lifespan of the red blood cell, forming HbA1c. Because this glycosylation accumulates proportionally to average blood glucose exposure, HbA1c serves as a reliable marker of glycemic control over the preceding 2-3 months, unlike a single fasting glucose measurement.

incorrectas.A: C-peptide is a cleavage byproduct of proinsulin processing that reflects endogenous insulin secretion, not glucose exposure, and is used to distinguish endogenous from exogenous insulin sources rather than to measure long-term glycemic control.
incorrectas.C: Fructosamine reflects glycosylation of serum proteins (mainly albumin) and only estimates glycemic control over the prior 2-3 weeks because albumin turns over much faster than hemoglobin, making it a shorter-term marker than HbA1c.
incorrectas.D: Carboxyhemoglobin results from carbon monoxide binding to hemoglobin's heme group, an entirely different chemical process from glucose adduct formation, and reflects CO exposure rather than glycemic status.

preguntas.q: A tumor arising from pancreatic alpha cells is called what?

e.correcta: Pancreatic alpha cells, located in the periphery of the islets of Langerhans, normally secrete glucagon to raise blood glucose during fasting states. A neoplasm arising from these cells is termed a glucagonoma, and because it autonomously oversecretes glucagon, it produces a characteristic hyperglycemic, catabolic syndrome.

incorrectas.A: Insulinoma arises from beta cells and secretes excess insulin, causing hypoglycemia rather than the hyperglycemia and catabolic state seen with alpha-cell tumors.
incorrectas.B: Somatostatinoma arises from delta cells and secretes somatostatin, which broadly inhibits other GI/pancreatic hormones, producing diabetes, gallstones, and steatorrhea rather than the glucagon-driven picture.
incorrectas.D: VIPoma arises from non-alpha, non-beta, non-delta islet cells and secretes vasoactive intestinal peptide, causing the WDHA syndrome (watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria), a clinically distinct entity from a glucagon-secreting alpha-cell tumor.

preguntas.q: A patient presents with necrolytic migratory erythema, new-onset diabetes, deep vein thrombosis, weight loss, and depression. Which hormone-secreting pancreatic tumor best explains this presentation?

e.correcta: Glucagonoma classically presents with the '4 D's': dermatitis (necrolytic migratory erythema, thought to result from hypoaminoacidemia and zinc/essential fatty acid deficiency), diabetes (from glucagon's counter-regulatory hyperglycemic effect), DVT (glucagon's prothrombotic state), and depression, plus weight loss from glucagon's catabolic, gluconeogenic, and lipolytic actions. This constellation is a classic board vignette pointing directly to excess glucagon secretion from an alpha-cell tumor.

incorrectas.A: Insulinoma causes fasting hypoglycemia with neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, diaphoresis, palpitations) from excess insulin, not the hyperglycemic, catabolic, rash-associated picture described here.
incorrectas.B: VIPoma causes large-volume secretory diarrhea with hypokalemia and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome) from excess VIP, not the erythema/diabetes/DVT tetrad seen with glucagon excess.
incorrectas.C: Gastrinoma causes recurrent peptic ulcers and diarrhea from gastric acid hypersecretion (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome), a presentation unrelated to necrolytic migratory erythema or glucagon's catabolic effects.

preguntas.q: Besides surgical resection, which medical therapy is used to treat glucagonoma?

e.correcta: Octreotide is a long-acting somatostatin analog that broadly suppresses secretion from neuroendocrine tumors, including glucagon release from glucagonoma cells, and is used medically to control the catabolic symptoms and skin findings when surgical cure is not possible or as a bridge to resection. Somatostatin's inhibitory G-protein-coupled receptor signaling dampens hormone secretion across multiple islet and gut endocrine cell types, making it a useful class-wide tool for functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors.

incorrectas.A: Metformin lowers blood glucose by reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis and improving insulin sensitivity, but it does not address the underlying excess glucagon secretion or the tumor's other catabolic effects.
incorrectas.C: Insulin infusion could help control the hyperglycemia glucagonoma produces but does not suppress glucagon secretion itself or treat the broader syndrome (rash, weight loss, DVT risk).
incorrectas.D: Proton pump inhibitors reduce gastric acid secretion and are the medical therapy for gastrinoma/Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, not glucagonoma, since glucagon excess does not primarily cause acid hypersecretion.

preguntas.q: A tumor arising from pancreatic beta cells is called what?

e.correcta: Pancreatic beta cells, concentrated in the core of the islets of Langerhans, normally secrete insulin in response to rising glucose. A tumor of these cells is an insulinoma, and its autonomous, unregulated insulin secretion causes episodic hypoglycemia even in the fasting state.

incorrectas.B: Glucagonoma arises from alpha cells and secretes glucagon, producing hyperglycemia and a catabolic syndrome rather than the hypoglycemia caused by a beta-cell tumor.
incorrectas.C: Gastrinoma arises from gastrin-secreting cells (often in the pancreas or duodenum, not classic islet beta cells) and causes acid hypersecretion and peptic ulcers, an entirely different hormonal axis from insulin.
incorrectas.D: Somatostatinoma arises from delta cells and secretes somatostatin, inhibiting multiple hormones and producing diabetes (not hypoglycemia), the opposite metabolic direction of an insulin-secreting beta-cell tumor.

preguntas.q: A symptomatic patient with insulinoma is expected to have which combination of blood glucose and C-peptide levels?

e.correcta: Insulinoma cells autonomously secrete endogenous insulin along with its co-secreted cleavage product, C-peptide, so a symptomatic patient shows both low serum glucose (from unchecked insulin action driving cellular glucose uptake) and elevated C-peptide (confirming the insulin is endogenously produced rather than injected). This combination — hypoglycemia with an inappropriately high C-peptide — is the key lab pattern that distinguishes insulinoma from factitious hypoglycemia caused by exogenous insulin injection, where C-peptide would be suppressed.

incorrectas.A: High glucose with low C-peptide would suggest inadequate insulin production or action, essentially a diabetic picture, the opposite of what an insulin-oversecreting tumor produces.
incorrectas.B: Low glucose with low C-peptide is the pattern seen with exogenous insulin administration (factitious or iatrogenic hypoglycemia), since injected insulin suppresses endogenous insulin/C-peptide release rather than accompanying elevated C-peptide.
incorrectas.D: High glucose with high C-peptide would suggest insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinemia (as in early type 2 diabetes), not the hypoglycemic state driven by unregulated insulin secretion from an insulinoma.

preguntas.q: Approximately 10% of insulinoma cases occur in association with which hereditary syndrome?

e.correcta: About 10% of insulinomas occur as part of MEN 1 syndrome, which classically involves tumors of the pituitary, parathyroid, and pancreas ('3 P's') due to inactivating mutations in the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene (menin). Recognizing this association is important because a patient with insulinoma plus hypercalcemia or pituitary symptoms should be screened for the broader MEN 1 syndrome.

incorrectas.B: MEN 2A involves medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and parathyroid hyperplasia due to RET proto-oncogene mutations, a syndrome that does not classically include insulinoma.
incorrectas.C: MEN 2B involves medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and mucosal neuromas/marfanoid habitus, also RET-driven, and likewise does not feature pancreatic islet cell tumors like insulinoma.
incorrectas.D: Von Hippel-Lindau disease causes hemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma, and pheochromocytoma due to VHL gene mutations, a distinct tumor spectrum that does not classically include insulinoma.

preguntas.q: A tumor arising from pancreatic delta cells is called what?

e.correcta: Pancreatic delta cells secrete somatostatin, a hormone that broadly inhibits secretion of insulin, glucagon, gastrin, and other GI hormones as well as pancreatic exocrine and gallbladder function. A tumor of these cells, a somatostatinoma, therefore produces a syndrome of diabetes, gallstones, and steatorrhea by suppressing all of these downstream pathways simultaneously.

incorrectas.A: Insulinoma arises from beta cells and secretes insulin causing hypoglycemia, the opposite hormonal and clinical direction from a delta-cell somatostatin-secreting tumor.
incorrectas.C: VIPoma arises from non-alpha, non-beta, non-delta cells and secretes VIP, causing secretory diarrhea (WDHA syndrome) rather than the diabetes/gallstones/steatorrhea triad of somatostatinoma.
incorrectas.D: Glucagonoma arises from alpha cells and secretes glucagon, producing necrolytic migratory erythema and a catabolic state, a different hormone and clinical picture than delta-cell somatostatin excess.

preguntas.q: Somatostatinoma may present clinically with diabetes due to which mechanism?

e.correcta: Somatostatin is a broad inhibitory hormone that suppresses secretion of insulin (as well as glucagon, gastrin, and other GI hormones) from the pancreas. In somatostatinoma, chronic oversecretion of somatostatin therefore blunts normal insulin release, producing hyperglycemia/diabetes through inhibition rather than through direct destruction of insulin-producing tissue.

incorrectas.A: Direct destruction of beta cells describes the autoimmune process in type 1 diabetes mellitus, not the mechanism in somatostatinoma, where beta cells remain structurally intact but are functionally suppressed by excess somatostatin.
incorrectas.C: Excess cortisol production causing insulin resistance and hyperglycemia describes Cushing syndrome, a distinct hormonal mechanism unrelated to somatostatin's direct inhibitory action on insulin secretion.
incorrectas.D: Autoimmune insulin receptor blockade describes rare conditions like type B insulin resistance syndrome, a receptor-level autoimmune process entirely different from somatostatin's paracrine inhibition of insulin secretion.

preguntas.q: Which diagnostic test may be used to help confirm a diagnosis of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome?

e.correcta: The secretin stimulation test exploits the paradoxical physiology of gastrinoma: in normal G cells, secretin inhibits gastrin release, but in gastrinoma the neoplastic gastrin-secreting cells lack this normal feedback inhibition, so administering secretin causes a paradoxical rise in serum gastrin. This paradoxical increase is highly specific for gastrinoma and helps confirm Zollinger-Ellison syndrome when baseline gastrin is elevated but the diagnosis is uncertain.

incorrectas.B: The water deprivation test assesses the kidney's ability to concentrate urine in response to ADH and is used to diagnose diabetes insipidus, entirely unrelated to gastrin physiology or Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
incorrectas.C: The dexamethasone suppression test evaluates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis's feedback response to exogenous glucocorticoid and is used to diagnose and localize Cushing syndrome, not gastrin-secreting tumors.
incorrectas.D: The TRH stimulation test evaluates pituitary TSH/prolactin response to thyrotropin-releasing hormone and is used in thyroid or pituitary axis disorders, not in confirming a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor.

preguntas.q: In a patient with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, what happens to gastrin levels after administration of secretin during the secretin stimulation test?

e.correcta: In Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, the gastrinoma cells are autonomous and have lost the normal inhibitory response to secretin that healthy G cells exhibit, so administering secretin produces a paradoxical rise in gastrin rather than the expected suppression. This paradoxical increase, rather than a fall, is the diagnostic hallmark that confirms the tumor is responsible for the hypergastrinemia.

incorrectas.A: Gastrin falling to normal levels would be the expected response in a patient without gastrinoma, where secretin's normal inhibitory feedback suppresses G-cell gastrin release — the opposite of the paradoxical rise seen in true Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Gastrin becoming undetectable does not occur in gastrinoma or in normal physiology after secretin administration; secretin causes modest suppression in normal individuals, not complete elimination of gastrin.
incorrectas.D: Unpredictable oscillation is not the characteristic or diagnostically useful pattern; the test's value lies specifically in the reproducible paradoxical rise in gastrin seen with autonomous tumor secretion.

preguntas.q: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is caused by a gastrin-secreting tumor arising from where?

e.correcta: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome results from a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma) that most commonly arises in the 'gastrinoma triangle,' spanning the pancreas and duodenum, rather than from the normal antral G-cell population. The resulting unregulated gastrin secretion drives massive gastric acid hypersecretion, producing severe, often multiple or refractory peptic ulcers along with diarrhea from acid-mediated mucosal injury and enzyme inactivation.

incorrectas.B: The adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines and gives rise to pheochromocytoma, a tumor with a completely different hormonal output and clinical presentation (episodic hypertension, palpitations) than a gastrin-secreting tumor.
incorrectas.C: The anterior pituitary secretes hormones like ACTH, GH, and prolactin, and pituitary adenomas cause syndromes such as Cushing disease or acromegaly, not the acid-hypersecretion and ulcer disease of gastrinoma.
incorrectas.D: The parathyroid gland secretes PTH and its tumors (parathyroid adenomas) cause hypercalcemia, a distinct endocrine syndrome unrelated to gastrin secretion, though parathyroid adenomas can co-occur with gastrinoma in MEN 1.

preguntas.q: A 55-year-old man undergoes resection of a small bowel mass. Biopsy shows nests of cells with prominent rosettes. What is the most common malignancy of the small intestine?

e.correcta: Carcinoid tumors arise from neuroendocrine cells and are actually the most common malignancy of the small intestine, classically showing nests of monotonous cells with rosette formation on histology and potentially secreting serotonin (causing carcinoid syndrome — flushing, diarrhea, bronchospasm — especially once liver metastases bypass first-pass hepatic serotonin metabolism). The rosette pattern described in the biopsy is a hallmark clue pointing to neuroendocrine differentiation rather than glandular (adenocarcinoma) or mesenchymal (GIST) origin.

incorrectas.A: Adenocarcinoma is actually the most common small bowel malignancy in some classification schemes and arises from glandular epithelium forming gland-like structures, not the rosette pattern of nests seen here, which is more classic for neuroendocrine tumors.
incorrectas.C: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal, show spindle cell morphology and stain positive for KIT (CD117), a very different histologic picture from the nested/rosette pattern described.
incorrectas.D: Lymphoma can occur in the small intestine (e.g., MALT lymphoma), showing sheets of monotonous lymphoid cells rather than organized nests with rosettes, making it histologically distinct from the neuroendocrine pattern in this vignette.

preguntas.q: Carcinoid syndrome (flushing, diarrhea, wheezing) typically only manifests once the carcinoid tumor metastasizes to which organ?

e.correcta: Carcinoid tumors of the GI tract secrete serotonin into the portal circulation, but the liver's monoamine oxidase efficiently metabolizes serotonin to 5-HIAA during first-pass metabolism, preventing systemic effects. Only once the tumor metastasizes to the liver (bypassing effective hepatic clearance, as tumor-derived serotonin can then drain directly into the systemic hepatic veins) or arises outside the GI tract does serotonin reach the systemic circulation in sufficient quantity to cause the classic flushing, diarrhea, and wheezing of carcinoid syndrome.

incorrectas.A: The lung is not the site whose involvement classically unmasks carcinoid syndrome from a GI primary; rather, a bronchial carcinoid can cause systemic symptoms without liver metastasis because it secretes serotonin directly into the systemic circulation, bypassing hepatic first-pass metabolism entirely — a different mechanism from the liver-metastasis rule for GI carcinoids.
incorrectas.C: The spleen has no role in serotonin metabolism or in unmasking carcinoid syndrome; it is not part of the portal venous drainage pathway relevant to hepatic first-pass clearance of serotonin.
incorrectas.D: The kidney does not metabolize serotonin via monoamine oxidase in the way the liver does, and renal metastasis is not the classic trigger for systemic carcinoid syndrome symptoms.

preguntas.q: A patient with metastatic carcinoid tumor presents with episodic bronchospasm and recurrent watery diarrhea. Which additional finding is classically part of this triad (carcinoid syndrome)?

e.correcta: Carcinoid syndrome results from vasoactive substances (serotonin, histamine, kallikrein/bradykinin) released by a metastatic neuroendocrine tumor bypassing hepatic first-pass metabolism, and cutaneous flushing is a classic manifestation caused by these vasoactive mediators dilating cutaneous vessels. Along with bronchospasm (from histamine/serotonin-induced bronchoconstriction) and diarrhea (from serotonin's prokinetic GI effects), flushing completes the classic triad taught for carcinoid syndrome.

incorrectas.B: Peripheral edema can occur in carcinoid syndrome due to right-sided valvular heart disease (carcinoid heart disease) from serotonin-induced fibrosis, but it is a later complication rather than part of the classic diagnostic triad of flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm.
incorrectas.C: Jaundice is not a typical feature of carcinoid syndrome; the syndrome itself usually implies that hepatic metastases have already allowed vasoactive substances to escape first-pass metabolism, but liver dysfunction causing jaundice is not a defining triad feature.
incorrectas.D: Hyperpigmentation is characteristic of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) due to elevated ACTH/MSH, not of carcinoid syndrome, which is driven by serotonin and other vasoactive amines rather than pituitary-adrenal hormones.

preguntas.q: Carcinoid heart disease from chronic serotonin exposure classically causes right-sided valvular fibrosis leading to regurgitation of which valve?

e.correcta: Chronic serotonin exposure from carcinoid tumor secretion stimulates fibroblast proliferation and plaque-like fibrous deposition on the endocardium of right-sided heart valves, since blood returning from the gut passes through the right heart before serotonin is inactivated in the pulmonary circulation. This fibrosis most often distorts the tricuspid valve, causing it to become thickened and unable to close properly, resulting in tricuspid regurgitation.

incorrectas.A: The mitral valve is on the left side of the heart, which is typically spared in carcinoid heart disease because pulmonary capillary monoamine oxidase metabolizes serotonin before blood reaches the left heart, protecting it from the same fibrotic injury.
incorrectas.B: The aortic valve, also left-sided, is likewise protected from serotonin-induced fibrosis in the absence of a right-to-left shunt or primary lung carcinoid, unlike the right-sided tricuspid valve that carcinoid-laden blood directly contacts.
incorrectas.D: The pulmonary valve can also be affected by carcinoid fibrosis (classically causing pulmonic stenosis), but the valve most classically associated with regurgitation in carcinoid heart disease is the tricuspid valve, not the pulmonary valve.

preguntas.q: In a patient with carcinoid heart disease, why are left-sided cardiac valvular lesions typically absent?

o.A: The left heart lacks serotonin receptors
o.B: Serotonin is converted to 5-HIAA by pulmonary MAO before reaching the left heart
o.C: The left heart has a thicker endocardium resistant to fibrosis
o.D: Serotonin is degraded by hepatic first-pass metabolism before reaching the left heart

e.correcta: Blood carrying tumor-derived serotonin from a GI carcinoid passes through the right heart first, then travels through the pulmonary circulation where monoamine oxidase in the lung efficiently converts serotonin to inactive 5-HIAA before the blood reaches the left heart. This selective pulmonary detoxification explains why carcinoid heart disease predominantly damages right-sided valves (tricuspid, pulmonic) while sparing the mitral and aortic valves, unless there is a right-to-left shunt or a primary bronchial carcinoid bypassing this filter.

incorrectas.A: The left heart does not specifically lack serotonin receptors; rather, it is protected because serotonin has already been metabolized to 5-HIAA by the lungs before reaching the left-sided valves, not because of receptor absence.
incorrectas.C: Endocardial thickness does not differ in a way that confers resistance to fibrosis; the sparing of the left heart is explained by reduced serotonin exposure after pulmonary metabolism, not by structural resistance of the endocardium itself.
incorrectas.D: Hepatic first-pass metabolism explains why serotonin from GI carcinoids does not cause systemic symptoms until liver metastasis occurs, but it does not explain the right-versus-left heart valve distribution, which is governed by pulmonary (not hepatic) clearance of serotonin before blood reaches the left heart.

preguntas.q: A pancreatic islet cell tumor arising from non-α, non-β, non-δ cells secretes a hormone causing watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome). What is this tumor called?

e.correcta: VIPoma arises from pancreatic islet cells outside the alpha, beta, and delta lineages and secretes vasoactive intestinal peptide, which stimulates intestinal chloride and fluid secretion, activates intestinal smooth muscle relaxation, and inhibits gastric acid secretion. This produces the classic WDHA syndrome: massive watery diarrhea (from VIP-driven intestinal fluid secretion), hypokalemia (from potassium loss in the diarrhea), and achlorhydria (from VIP's inhibitory effect on gastric acid).

incorrectas.A: Glucagonoma arises from alpha cells and secretes glucagon, causing hyperglycemia, necrolytic migratory erythema, and weight loss, a clinical picture distinct from the massive secretory diarrhea of VIPoma.
incorrectas.B: Somatostatinoma arises from delta cells and secretes somatostatin, causing diabetes, gallstones, and steatorrhea (fatty, not watery, stool) through broad inhibition of digestive hormones, not the VIP-driven secretory diarrhea described here.
incorrectas.C: Gastrinoma secretes gastrin and causes acid hypersecretion with peptic ulcers and diarrhea, but it does not cause achlorhydria — in fact it causes the opposite, excess gastric acid, distinguishing it from VIPoma's achlorhydria.

preguntas.q: A patient with a VIPoma presents with large-volume watery diarrhea. Which additional laboratory/clinical findings are classically seen, completing the 'WDHA' syndrome?

e.correcta: VIP acts on intestinal epithelial cells to stimulate chloride-driven fluid secretion, producing large-volume watery diarrhea; the resulting potassium loss in stool causes hypokalemia, while VIP's inhibitory effect on gastric parietal cells suppresses acid production, causing achlorhydria. Together these findings complete the WDHA (watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria) syndrome that defines VIPoma clinically.

incorrectas.A: Hyperkalemia and increased gastric acid are the opposite of what VIP causes — VIP promotes potassium loss through secretory diarrhea (hypokalemia) and suppresses, rather than increases, gastric acid secretion.
incorrectas.C: Hyperkalemia is inconsistent with VIPoma, since the massive diarrhea characteristically depletes potassium rather than raising it, even though achlorhydria correctly reflects VIP's acid-suppressing effect.
incorrectas.D: Increased gastric acid is inconsistent with VIPoma, since VIP inhibits gastric acid secretion (achlorhydria), even though hypokalemia correctly reflects potassium loss from the secretory diarrhea.

preguntas.q: Cushing syndrome is fundamentally defined by a chronic elevation of which hormone?

e.correcta: Cushing syndrome is defined by any cause of sustained excess cortisol, whether from exogenous glucocorticoid intake, an adrenal tumor, a pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma, or ectopic ACTH production. Regardless of the underlying source, it is the chronic elevation of cortisol itself that produces the characteristic clinical features — central obesity, striae, hypertension, hyperglycemia, and immunosuppression.

incorrectas.A: Aldosterone excess characterizes hyperaldosteronism (e.g., Conn syndrome), causing hypertension and hypokalemia through mineralocorticoid receptor activation, a distinct hormonal axis from the glucocorticoid excess that defines Cushing syndrome.
incorrectas.C: ACTH is often elevated in Cushing syndrome (in pituitary or ectopic causes), but the syndrome is fundamentally defined by the downstream cortisol excess it produces, not by ACTH itself — indeed, ACTH is typically suppressed in adrenal- or exogenous-glucocorticoid-driven Cushing syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Growth hormone excess causes acromegaly (or gigantism before epiphyseal closure), a distinct syndrome with different clinical features (bony overgrowth, organomegaly) unrelated to the cortisol elevation that defines Cushing syndrome.

preguntas.q: The term 'Cushing disease' refers specifically to which cause of hypercortisolism?

o.D: Ectopic ACTH secretion from small cell lung cancer

e.correcta: 'Cushing disease' is a specific subtype of Cushing syndrome caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma, which drives excess ACTH release that in turn stimulates bilateral adrenal cortisol overproduction. This terminology distinction matters clinically because it points to pituitary-directed workup and treatment (e.g., transsphenoidal resection) rather than adrenal or ectopic sources.

incorrectas.A: An adrenal adenoma secreting cortisol autonomously is a primary adrenal cause of Cushing syndrome, with ACTH suppressed by negative feedback, distinct from Cushing disease, which specifically requires pituitary ACTH overproduction driving the adrenal glands.
incorrectas.B: Exogenous glucocorticoid administration is the most common overall cause of Cushing syndrome but is unrelated to any ACTH excess or pituitary pathology, so it is never termed 'Cushing disease,' which is reserved for the pituitary-driven form.
incorrectas.D: Ectopic ACTH secretion (e.g., from small cell lung cancer) causes Cushing syndrome through a tumor outside the pituitary, and while it does involve ACTH excess, the term 'Cushing disease' is specifically reserved for pituitary adenoma-driven ACTH excess, not ectopic sources.

preguntas.q: What is the most common overall cause of Cushing syndrome?

e.correcta: Iatrogenic/exogenous glucocorticoid use (for conditions like autoimmune disease, asthma, or transplant immunosuppression) is far more common in clinical practice than any endogenous cause of hypercortisolism, making it the most common overall cause of Cushing syndrome. Recognizing this is clinically important because exogenous steroid use suppresses ACTH via negative feedback, so screening should always include a careful medication history before pursuing an endogenous workup.

incorrectas.A: Ectopic ACTH secretion, most classically from small cell lung cancer, is an important but comparatively rare cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome, far less common overall than exogenous steroid administration.
incorrectas.B: Adrenal adenoma is a recognized endogenous cause of Cushing syndrome but is less common than exogenous glucocorticoid use when considering all cases seen in practice.
incorrectas.D: Cushing disease (ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma) is the most common cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome specifically, but when exogenous causes are included, iatrogenic glucocorticoid use is overall more common than pituitary-driven disease.

preguntas.q: Among endogenous causes only, what is the most common cause of Cushing syndrome?

o.A: Ectopic ACTH secretion from small cell lung cancer
