e.correcta: Both varicocele (dilation of the pampiniform venous plexus) and cryptorchidism (failure of testicular descent into the scrotum) result in the testis being exposed to a higher-than-normal temperature — varicocele through pooled venous blood impairing the countercurrent heat-exchange mechanism, and cryptorchidism because the intra-abdominal or inguinal position is warmer than the scrotum. Since spermatogenesis requires a temperature about 2-4°C below core body temperature, both conditions impair Sertoli cell function (lowering inhibin B) and spermatogenesis, making them important reversible causes of male infertility.

incorrectas.B: Hydrocele (fluid accumulation in the tunica vaginalis) and spermatocele (a cyst of the epididymis) are typically painless fluid collections that do not raise testicular temperature or reliably impair spermatogenesis the way varicocele and cryptorchidism do.
incorrectas.C: Epididymitis and orchitis are infectious/inflammatory conditions that can damage sperm production through direct inflammatory injury, but they are not classically taught as working through the temperature-elevation mechanism described in this question.
incorrectas.D: Testicular torsion causes acute ischemic injury to the testis from twisted vasculature, and hypospadias is a urethral meatus positioning defect — neither works through chronic testicular temperature elevation the way varicocele and cryptorchidism do.

preguntas.q: Which condition involves excess amniotic fluid and may be associated with fetal malformations such as esophageal or duodenal atresia due to impaired swallowing?

e.correcta: Polyhydramnios (>1.5-2L amniotic fluid) classically results from the fetus failing to swallow and absorb amniotic fluid normally, which happens with esophageal or duodenal atresia (mechanical obstruction) or with anencephaly/CNS anomalies that impair the swallowing reflex itself. Because the fetus normally swallows large volumes of fluid daily as part of the balance between production (fetal urination, lung fluid) and clearance (swallowing), any block in that clearance arm lets fluid accumulate. This is a high-yield association: polyhydramnios on ultrasound should prompt a search for a GI atresia or neuromuscular swallowing problem.

incorrectas.A: Oligohydramnios is a deficiency of amniotic fluid, classically caused by poor fetal urine output (e.g., bilateral renal agenesis, posterior urethral valves) or chronic uteroplacental insufficiency — the opposite mechanism (reduced production, not reduced clearance) from what causes atresia-associated fluid excess.
incorrectas.C: Chorioamnionitis is an infection/inflammation of the fetal membranes, usually from ascending bacterial infection, and presents with maternal fever and uterine tenderness rather than an amniotic fluid volume abnormality tied to fetal swallowing.
incorrectas.D: Placenta accreta is abnormal placental attachment into the myometrium due to defective decidua, causing risk of severe postpartum hemorrhage; it has no direct relationship to amniotic fluid volume or fetal swallowing physiology.

preguntas.q: What is the most common gynecologic cancer worldwide, largely due to lack of screening or HPV vaccination in many regions?

e.correcta: Cervical cancer is caused overwhelmingly by persistent infection with high-risk HPV subtypes (16 and 18 in particular), which is why it is both preventable through vaccination and detectable at a precancerous stage through Pap smear screening. In resource-limited regions where HPV vaccination programs and Pap smear screening infrastructure are unavailable or inconsistent, precancerous lesions go undetected and progress to invasive cancer, making cervical cancer the most common gynecologic malignancy worldwide despite being highly preventable where screening exists.

incorrectas.A: Endometrial cancer is more common than cervical cancer in high-resource countries (driven by unopposed estrogen exposure and obesity), but globally it does not surpass cervical cancer, which dominates in regions lacking HPV vaccination and screening.
incorrectas.B: Ovarian cancer, while lethal due to late detection, has a much lower incidence than cervical cancer worldwide and is not primarily driven by a preventable infectious etiology the way cervical cancer is.
incorrectas.D: Vulvar cancer is comparatively rare and, while some cases are HPV-related, it does not approach the global incidence of cervical cancer, which remains the leading gynecologic cancer in unscreened populations.

preguntas.q: What is the most common gynecologic cancer in the United States?

e.correcta: Endometrial cancer is the most common gynecologic malignancy in the United States, largely because unopposed estrogen exposure (from obesity, anovulation, tamoxifen, or estrogen-only hormone therapy) drives endometrial hyperplasia that can progress to endometrioid adenocarcinoma. It typically presents early with postmenopausal bleeding, which prompts prompt endometrial biopsy and generally leads to diagnosis at a treatable stage — contributing to its high incidence but comparatively better prognosis than ovarian cancer. This estrogen-driven pathogenesis is the key concept linking risk factors (obesity, PCOS, nulliparity) to the disease.

incorrectas.A: Cervical cancer, driven mainly by persistent high-risk HPV infection, has become substantially less common in the U.S. due to widespread Pap smear screening and HPV vaccination, making it less prevalent than endometrial cancer.
incorrectas.B: Ovarian cancer, while more lethal due to late-stage detection from vague symptoms, is less common in incidence than endometrial cancer, which is caught earlier because of overt bleeding symptoms.
incorrectas.D: Vaginal cancer is rare, most often occurring as a secondary malignancy from cervical or vulvar spread, and is nowhere near as common as endometrial carcinoma in incidence.

preguntas.q: Among endometrial, cervical, and ovarian cancer, which has the worst prognosis?

e.correcta: Ovarian cancer has the worst prognosis of the three because it is typically asymptomatic in early stages and lacks an effective screening test, so most cases present at an advanced stage (III or IV) with peritoneal spread already present, unlike cervical cancer (detectable early via Pap smear screening) or endometrial cancer (which usually presents early with abnormal uterine bleeding). This is why ovarian cancer is often called a 'silent killer' and carries the highest mortality among gynecologic malignancies despite being less common than endometrial cancer.

incorrectas.A: Cervical cancer generally has a better prognosis than ovarian cancer because it is preceded by a detectable premalignant phase (CIN) and is caught early through routine Pap smear screening, allowing for treatment before extensive invasion occurs.
incorrectas.B: Endometrial cancer usually presents early because abnormal uterine bleeding is a prominent, easily noticed symptom that prompts timely evaluation, so most cases are diagnosed while still confined to the uterus, giving it a comparatively favorable prognosis.
incorrectas.D: The three cancers do not share similar prognoses — ovarian cancer's lack of early symptoms and screening tools gives it a markedly worse overall survival than the other two, which are more often caught early.

preguntas.q: A condition presenting with symptoms of menopause after puberty but before age 40, with decreased estrogen and increased FSH/LH, is known as what?

e.correcta: Premature ovarian failure (primary ovarian insufficiency) occurs when the ovaries stop functioning normally before age 40, leading to depleted estrogen production; the hypothalamic-pituitary axis responds to this low estrogen with loss of negative feedback, driving FSH and LH levels up — the same hormonal pattern seen in normal menopause, just occurring at an abnormally young age. This distinguishes it from other causes of amenorrhea where gonadotropins are low or normal, and it is an important cause of infertility and osteoporosis risk in young women.

incorrectas.A: Polycystic ovary syndrome features anovulation with elevated LH:FSH ratio but typically normal-to-high estrogen states and hyperandrogenism, not the low estrogen/high FSH-LH pattern of ovarian failure described here.
incorrectas.C: Asherman syndrome results from intrauterine scarring/adhesions (often after uterine instrumentation), causing amenorrhea due to a structural/anatomic problem in the endometrium, with normal ovarian function and normal hormone levels — not the hormonal profile described in the question.
incorrectas.D: Turner syndrome (45,X) also causes hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, but it is a congenital chromosomal condition present from birth with associated features (short stature, webbed neck, streak gonads), rather than a condition arising as new-onset ovarian failure after puberty as described here.

preguntas.q: A phenotypic male presents with gynecomastia, female pattern hair distribution, tall stature with long extremities, and a eunuchoid body shape. Which sex chromosome disorder is most likely?

e.correcta: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) results from meiotic nondisjunction giving an extra X chromosome, which produces small, fibrotic, hyalinized seminiferous tubules with low inhibin B and low testosterone. Low testosterone with an aromatizable excess of X-linked gene products shifts the androgen:estrogen ratio toward estrogen, producing gynecomastia, female hair distribution, and a eunuchoid habitus (tall stature, long extremities) from delayed epiphyseal closure. The low testosterone also removes negative feedback on the pituitary, so LH and FSH are elevated — a key lab clue tested alongside the phenotype.

incorrectas.A: Turner syndrome (45,X) occurs in phenotypic females, not males, and presents with short stature, streak gonads, and primary amenorrhea rather than gynecomastia and a eunuchoid male body habitus.
incorrectas.C: Double Y syndrome (47,XYY) males have a normal male phenotype, are typically tall, and have normal fertility and testosterone levels — they do not develop gynecomastia or feminization, distinguishing them sharply from Klinefelter patients.
incorrectas.D: Androgen insensitivity syndrome involves a 46,XY karyotype with a defective androgen receptor, producing a phenotypic female with a blind-ending vagina and absent uterus, not a phenotypic male with gynecomastia and eunuchoid features.

preguntas.q: What is the expected testosterone level in a patient with Klinefelter syndrome?

e.correcta: In Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), dysgenetic seminiferous tubules and impaired Leydig cell function lead to decreased testosterone production, which is the primary driver of the syndrome's clinical phenotype — including small firm testes, decreased facial/body/pubic hair, gynecomastia, and infertility due to seminiferous tubule hyalinization causing azoospermia. The low testosterone triggers compensatory elevation of LH and FSH via loss of negative feedback, and the resulting hormonal imbalance also favors increased peripheral aromatization to estrogen. This decreased testosterone with elevated gonadotropins (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) is the core lab pattern to recognize in Klinefelter syndrome.

incorrectas.A: Increased testosterone is inconsistent with Klinefelter syndrome's pathophysiology, since the dysgenetic testes fail to produce adequate androgen, resulting in low, not elevated, testosterone.
incorrectas.B: A normal testosterone level would not produce the classic clinical features of hypogonadism (gynecomastia, decreased body hair, small testes, infertility) seen in Klinefelter syndrome, which specifically results from testosterone deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Undetectable testosterone is too extreme; while decreased, some residual Leydig cell function typically persists, so testosterone is low but generally still measurable rather than completely absent.

preguntas.q: What is the expected estrogen level in a patient with Klinefelter syndrome?

e.correcta: In Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), dysgenetic seminiferous tubules fail to support normal Leydig cell function, leading to low testosterone; the resulting loss of negative feedback drives elevated LH, which in turn stimulates Leydig cells to increase aromatization of androgens to estrogen, and the relative excess of the extra X chromosome also contributes to a shifted androgen:estrogen ratio. The net effect is an increased estrogen level, which explains the gynecomastia, tall stature with eunuchoid proportions, and reduced facial/body hair seen in these patients. This estrogen-driven phenotype is a key testable feature that distinguishes Klinefelter from isolated primary hypogonadism without altered estrogen levels.

incorrectas.A: Decreased estrogen would be expected in a state of pure gonadal failure without compensatory aromatization, but Klinefelter syndrome actually shows increased estrogen due to elevated LH-driven aromatization, making this the opposite of the true finding.
incorrectas.C: A normal estrogen level does not fit the clinical picture of gynecomastia seen in Klinefelter syndrome, which results specifically from an elevated estrogen-to-testosterone ratio rather than an unchanged hormonal milieu.
incorrectas.D: Undetectable estrogen is inconsistent with the pathophysiology of Klinefelter syndrome, since some testicular and peripheral aromatase activity persists and is in fact increased relative to testosterone, not abolished.

preguntas.q: Klinefelter syndrome is characteristically associated with which testicular finding?

e.correcta: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes primary hypogonadism in which the seminiferous tubules undergo hyalinization and fibrosis due to the extra X chromosome disrupting normal spermatogenic tissue development, resulting in small, firm testes (testicular atrophy). Loss of functional seminiferous tubule tissue leads to low inhibin B and testosterone with compensatory elevation of FSH and LH, producing the clinical picture of tall stature, gynecomastia, and infertility. Testicular atrophy is the classic physical finding that first raises suspicion for this karyotype in an adult male being worked up for infertility.

incorrectas.A: Testicular enlargement would suggest a different process (e.g., a testicular tumor or fragile X-associated macroorchidism), not Klinefelter syndrome, whose seminiferous tubules are damaged and fibrotic, producing shrinkage rather than growth.
incorrectas.C: Normal testicular size is inconsistent with the tubular hyalinization and fibrosis that occurs in Klinefelter syndrome — the extra X chromosome directly impairs testicular tissue, so testes are reliably small rather than normal.
incorrectas.D: Cryptorchidism refers to failure of testicular descent into the scrotum, a distinct anatomic/developmental abnormality unrelated to the chromosomal mechanism of Klinefelter syndrome, which instead causes atrophy of testes that are normally positioned.

preguntas.q: A phenotypic female presents with short stature, a shield chest, and a webbed neck. Which sex chromosome disorder is most likely?

e.correcta: Turner syndrome (45,X) arises from loss of one X chromosome, leading to accelerated atresia of ovarian follicles in utero and streak gonads. Haploinsufficiency of genes that escape X-inactivation impairs lymphatic development, producing the webbed neck (from resolved fetal cystic hygromas), shield chest with widely spaced nipples, and short stature (partly from SHOX gene haploinsufficiency). These physical stigmata plus primary amenorrhea and elevated gonadotropins from ovarian failure are the classic tested triad.

incorrectas.A: Klinefelter syndrome occurs in phenotypic males with an extra X (47,XXY), producing gynecomastia and a eunuchoid body shape, not the webbed neck and shield chest seen in a phenotypic female with Turner syndrome.
incorrectas.B: Double Y syndrome (47,XYY) occurs in phenotypic males with a normal, often tall appearance, and has no association with webbed neck or shield chest, which are lymphatic malformation findings specific to Turner syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Androgen insensitivity syndrome produces a phenotypic female with a 46,XY karyotype due to receptor dysfunction, but presents with normal stature and absent axillary/pubic hair rather than short stature, webbed neck, and shield chest.

preguntas.q: What is the most common cause of primary amenorrhea?

e.correcta: Turner syndrome (45,XO) is the most common cause of primary amenorrhea because the missing X chromosome leads to accelerated atresia of oocytes and streak gonads, resulting in gonadal dysgenesis with minimal to no functional ovarian tissue to produce estrogen and support menstruation. Because these patients never establish a menstrual cycle in the first place (rather than losing one they already had), Turner syndrome is classified under primary rather than secondary amenorrhea.

incorrectas.A: Asherman syndrome is intrauterine scarring/adhesions typically from prior uterine instrumentation (e.g., dilation and curettage), which causes secondary amenorrhea in someone who previously menstruated — it does not explain a patient who has never had a period.
incorrectas.B: PCOS causes oligomenorrhea or secondary amenorrhea due to chronic anovulation from hormonal imbalance, but patients typically do have some menstrual history and reach menarche, making it a less common cause of true primary amenorrhea compared to gonadal dysgenesis in Turner syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Premature ovarian failure describes loss of ovarian function after a period of normal menstrual function (so it is a cause of secondary amenorrhea), whereas Turner syndrome patients typically never develop functional ovaries to begin with, fitting the primary amenorrhea pattern.

preguntas.q: What is the expected estrogen level in a patient with Turner syndrome?

e.correcta: In Turner syndrome (45,XO), streak gonads fail to develop functional ovarian follicles, so the ovaries cannot produce estrogen in normal amounts, resulting in low circulating estrogen. This estrogen deficiency underlies the clinical picture of primary amenorrhea, lack of secondary sexual characteristics, and elevated gonadotropins (FSH/LH) from loss of negative feedback.

incorrectas.A: Increased estrogen would not fit the pathophysiology of Turner syndrome, since the streak gonads lack functional follicles and granulosa cells needed to synthesize estrogen, making elevated estrogen inconsistent with the underlying gonadal dysgenesis.
incorrectas.C: Normal estrogen levels would not explain the clinical features of Turner syndrome such as delayed puberty and primary amenorrhea, which arise specifically because the dysgenetic gonads cannot produce adequate estrogen.
incorrectas.D: Estrogen levels in Turner syndrome are not simply variable by age in a way that offsets the underlying gonadal failure — the streak gonads persistently lack the follicular apparatus needed for estrogen synthesis throughout life, keeping levels low.

preguntas.q: How do males with double Y syndrome (47,XYY) typically appear phenotypically?

e.correcta: 47,XYY arises from paternal meiosis II nondisjunction, giving an extra Y chromosome; because the Y chromosome carries relatively few genes outside the SRY/testis-determining region, testicular function and testosterone production remain essentially normal. This is why affected males have a normal male phenotype, are usually tall (partly due to extra copies of growth-related genes on the Y), and have normal fertility, in contrast to X-chromosome-related syndromes that disrupt gonadal function. It is classically associated with normal intelligence (though sometimes mild learning/behavioral issues), not intellectual disability.

incorrectas.A: Short stature with gynecomastia describes Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), where the extra X impairs testosterone production and shifts the androgen:estrogen ratio — 47,XYY males are tall with normal testosterone and no gynecomastia.
incorrectas.C: Ambiguous genitalia results from disorders of sexual differentiation such as 5-alpha-reductase deficiency or congenital adrenal hyperplasia, not from an extra Y chromosome, which does not disrupt genital development.
incorrectas.D: Webbed neck and shield chest are lymphatic malformation findings specific to Turner syndrome (45,X) in phenotypic females, unrelated to the extra Y chromosome in 47,XYY males.

preguntas.q: Ovotesticular disorder of sex development, also known as true hermaphroditism, is defined by the presence of what?

o.A: Only testicular tissue with ambiguous external genitalia
o.C: Only ovarian tissue with a 46,XY karyotype

e.correcta: Ovotesticular disorder of sex development (true hermaphroditism) is defined by the coexistence of both ovarian tissue (with follicles) and testicular tissue (with seminiferous tubules) in the same individual, either as separate gonads or combined in an ovotestis. This is distinct from other disorders of sex development where the karyotype-gonad mismatch involves only one type of gonadal tissue with abnormal hormone signaling or receptor function. The external genitalia are typically ambiguous because of mixed hormonal output from both tissue types.

incorrectas.A: Only testicular tissue with ambiguous genitalia describes disorders like partial androgen insensitivity or 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, not true hermaphroditism, which requires both ovarian and testicular tissue to be present.
incorrectas.C: Only ovarian tissue with a 46,XY karyotype would describe a form of XY gonadal dysgenesis (e.g., Swyer syndrome), not ovotesticular disorder, which by definition has both gonadal tissue types regardless of karyotype.
incorrectas.D: Absent gonadal tissue bilaterally describes gonadal agenesis, the opposite of ovotesticular DSD, which is defined precisely by the presence (not absence) of both ovarian and testicular tissue.

preguntas.q: Placental aromatase deficiency results in an inability to synthesize estrogens from which precursor?

o.D: DHEA-S from the fetal adrenal only

e.correcta: Aromatase (CYP19A1) is the enzyme that converts androgens (androstenedione and testosterone) into estrogens (estrone and estradiol) by aromatizing the A ring of the steroid nucleus. In pregnancy, the placenta relies on aromatase to convert fetal adrenal-derived androgens (largely DHEA-S) into estrogens for maternal circulation; when aromatase is deficient, these androgen precursors accumulate instead of being converted, since they cannot be aromatized to estrogen. This explains why the deficiency causes both low maternal/fetal estrogen and androgen excess.

incorrectas.A: Cholesterol is the precursor for all steroidogenesis several enzymatic steps upstream of aromatase (via pregnenolone, progesterone, and androgens), but aromatase itself acts specifically on androgens, not directly on cholesterol.
incorrectas.C: Progesterone is produced from pregnenolone early in the steroidogenic pathway and is not the direct substrate for aromatase; estrogen synthesis specifically requires androgens as the aromatizable substrate.
incorrectas.D: DHEA-S from the fetal adrenal is indeed a major precursor that feeds into the androgen pool, but aromatase deficiency is defined by failure to convert androgens broadly (not DHEA-S exclusively) into estrogens.

preguntas.q: Placental aromatase deficiency in a 46,XX female infant classically results in what finding?

e.correcta: In placental aromatase deficiency, fetal and placental androgens cannot be converted to estrogens, so androgens accumulate and cross into the fetal circulation. In a 46,XX female fetus, this androgen excess virilizes the external genitalia (clitoromegaly, labial fusion) even though the internal reproductive organs (ovaries, uterus) develop normally since Müllerian structures are not androgen-dependent. Mothers may also become virilized during pregnancy due to the same androgen excess crossing into maternal circulation.

incorrectas.A: Feminization of external genitalia would require increased, not decreased, estrogen exposure or a defect blocking androgen action (like androgen insensitivity), which is the opposite of what happens when androgens accumulate due to lost aromatase activity.
incorrectas.C: Complete gonadal agenesis is a separate developmental anomaly unrelated to aromatase function; aromatase deficiency does not prevent gonad formation, only the conversion of androgens to estrogens.
incorrectas.D: Isosexual precocious puberty describes early puberty with appropriate (female) secondary sexual characteristics, but aromatase deficiency causes virilization (heterosexual, not isosexual) due to androgen excess, not accelerated normal female puberty.

preguntas.q: In general, sex chromosome disorders such as Turner and Klinefelter syndromes present with which hormonal pattern?

e.correcta: Turner and Klinefelter syndromes both cause primary gonadal failure (streak ovaries or hyalinized seminiferous tubules), so the gonads cannot produce adequate sex steroids despite normal or even elevated pituitary stimulation. With low estrogen/testosterone, negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis is lost, so GnRH drives the pituitary to secrete more LH (and FSH) in a compensatory but futile attempt to stimulate the failed gonads. This low-hormone/high-gonadotropin pattern is the hallmark of primary hypogonadism and is a frequently tested lab pairing.

incorrectas.A: Increased sex hormones with decreased LH would reflect a hormone-secreting source with intact negative feedback (e.g., an exogenous or tumor source), which is the opposite of the gonadal failure seen in Turner and Klinefelter syndromes.
incorrectas.C: Increased sex hormones with increased LH is an inconsistent pattern physiologically, since elevated sex hormones would normally suppress LH via negative feedback; this does not match the failed-gonad, low-hormone physiology of these syndromes.
incorrectas.D: Decreased sex hormones with decreased LH describes secondary (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism, where the defect is at the hypothalamus/pituitary — the opposite of the primary gonadal failure in Turner and Klinefelter syndromes.

preguntas.q: A defective androgen receptor (as in androgen insensitivity syndrome) presents with what testosterone and LH pattern?

e.correcta: In androgen insensitivity syndrome, the androgen receptor is nonfunctional, so target tissues (including the hypothalamus and pituitary) cannot sense circulating testosterone despite normal or even elevated testicular production. Because the receptor-mediated negative feedback loop is broken, the pituitary perceives an androgen-deficient state and increases LH secretion, which in turn drives the testes to secrete even more testosterone — producing the classic combination of increased testosterone with increased LH. This pattern (high androgen, high LH) is a distinguishing lab clue that differentiates AIS from primary or secondary hypogonadism.

incorrectas.A: Decreased testosterone and decreased LH would suggest hypothalamic-pituitary failure (secondary hypogonadism), not a receptor defect — in AIS the testes still make testosterone normally, and LH rises rather than falls because feedback is defective.
incorrectas.C: Decreased testosterone with increased LH is the pattern of primary gonadal failure (e.g., Klinefelter syndrome), where the testes themselves cannot produce hormone — in AIS the testes function normally and testosterone is actually elevated.
incorrectas.D: Increased testosterone with decreased LH would suggest an autonomous androgen source suppressing the pituitary via intact feedback, but in AIS the feedback loop itself is broken, so LH rises rather than falls despite high testosterone.

preguntas.q: A testosterone-secreting tumor or use of exogenous anabolic steroids classically presents with what testosterone and LH pattern?

e.correcta: A testosterone-secreting tumor (e.g., Leydig cell tumor) or exogenous anabolic steroid use raises circulating testosterone independent of pituitary control, and this excess testosterone acts through an intact androgen receptor and intact hypothalamic-pituitary feedback to suppress GnRH and LH secretion. The result is the classic pattern of elevated testosterone with suppressed LH — clinically this also causes testicular atrophy in steroid users because endogenous LH-driven testosterone production shuts down.

incorrectas.A: Decreased testosterone with increased LH describes primary hypogonadism (gonadal failure), the opposite scenario — here an exogenous or tumor source is providing excess, not deficient, testosterone.
incorrectas.B: Increased testosterone with increased LH would only occur if feedback were broken (as in androgen insensitivity), but with a functioning receptor and axis, excess testosterone from a tumor or exogenous source appropriately suppresses LH rather than raising it.
incorrectas.D: Decreased testosterone and decreased LH reflects hypothalamic-pituitary failure (secondary hypogonadism) with a genuinely low androgen state, not the androgen-excess state produced by a secreting tumor or steroid abuse.

preguntas.q: A patient with primary hypogonadism (gonadal failure) would be expected to show which pattern of testosterone/estrogen and LH levels?

e.correcta: Primary hypogonadism means the defect is at the level of the gonad itself (testis or ovary), so the gonad cannot produce adequate sex hormone even though the hypothalamic-pituitary axis is intact and stimulating it normally. Loss of negative feedback from low sex hormone leads the pituitary to increase LH secretion in a compensatory attempt to drive the failing gonad, producing the classic pattern of low sex hormones with elevated LH (and FSH). This pattern is seen in conditions like Klinefelter syndrome, Turner syndrome, and gonadal failure from chemotherapy or radiation.

incorrectas.A: Decreased sex hormones with decreased LH describes secondary (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism, where the hypothalamus or pituitary itself fails to drive the gonads — the opposite defect location from primary gonadal failure.
incorrectas.C: Increased sex hormones with decreased LH would reflect an autonomous hormone source (tumor or exogenous) with intact feedback suppression, not a failing gonad that is unable to produce hormone.
incorrectas.D: Increased sex hormones with increased LH is not physiologically consistent with intact feedback, since high sex hormone would normally suppress LH; it does not describe the low-hormone state of primary gonadal failure.

preguntas.q: Hypogonadotropic (secondary) hypogonadism is characterized by which laboratory pattern?

o.A: Decreased sex hormones with decreased LH and FSH
o.B: Decreased sex hormones with increased LH and FSH
o.C: Increased sex hormones with decreased LH and FSH
o.D: Normal sex hormones with increased LH and FSH

e.correcta: Hypogonadotropic (secondary) hypogonadism arises from a defect at the hypothalamus or pituitary, so insufficient GnRH or gonadotropin (LH/FSH) is released to stimulate the gonads, even though the gonads themselves are capable of normal function. Because both the gonadotropin drive and the resulting sex hormone output are low, labs show decreased sex hormones together with decreased (or inappropriately normal) LH and FSH — the opposite feedback pattern from primary gonadal failure. Causes include Kallmann syndrome, pituitary tumors, and functional suppression from stress, starvation, or excessive exercise.

incorrectas.B: Decreased sex hormones with increased LH and FSH describes primary (hypergonadotropic) hypogonadism, where the gonads fail despite adequate pituitary drive — the opposite defect location from a hypothalamic/pituitary problem.
incorrectas.C: Increased sex hormones with decreased LH and FSH would suggest an autonomous hormone source suppressing the pituitary, not a primary failure of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis to generate gonadotropins.
incorrectas.D: Normal sex hormones with increased LH and FSH would reflect a compensated or mild primary gonadal issue, not the low-hormone, low-gonadotropin state that defines hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

preguntas.q: Which condition is a rare genetic disorder that causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism due to failure of GnRH neuron migration, resulting in incomplete puberty and anosmia?

e.correcta: Kallmann syndrome results from failure of GnRH neurons to migrate from the olfactory placode to the hypothalamus during embryogenesis, since these neurons normally develop alongside and migrate with olfactory neurons. This shared developmental origin explains the syndrome's hallmark combination of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (absent GnRH drive causing incomplete puberty, low sex hormones, and low LH/FSH) plus anosmia or hyposmia from the associated olfactory bulb defect.

incorrectas.B: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is a primary gonadal failure from an extra X chromosome, presenting with elevated (not low) LH/FSH and no association with anosmia or a GnRH neuron migration defect.
incorrectas.C: Turner syndrome (45,X) is also a primary gonadal failure (streak ovaries) with elevated gonadotropins, and has no connection to olfactory system development or anosmia, unlike the shared embryologic defect in Kallmann syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Androgen insensitivity syndrome involves a defective androgen receptor with normal or elevated testosterone and LH, and normal GnRH neuron migration and sense of smell, distinguishing it entirely from the hypothalamic migration defect of Kallmann syndrome.

preguntas.q: In 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, which hormonal pattern of testosterone and LH is typically seen?

e.correcta: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency impairs the peripheral conversion of testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which is required for normal virilization of the external genitalia in utero, but testosterone itself is produced normally by the testes and still supports internal male structures (via Wolffian duct-dependent effects) and pubertal changes like muscle mass and voice deepening. Because testosterone synthesis and testicular function are intact, and testosterone (though not converted to DHT) still provides adequate negative feedback, LH is typically normal or only mildly increased, and testosterone levels remain normal — distinguishing this from a true androgen deficiency state.

incorrectas.A: Decreased testosterone with decreased LH would indicate a defect in testosterone synthesis or in the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, but 5-alpha-reductase deficiency is a peripheral conversion defect with normal testicular testosterone production.
incorrectas.C: Increased testosterone with decreased LH would suggest an autonomous excess androgen source suppressing the pituitary, which does not occur in 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, where testosterone remains within the normal range.
incorrectas.D: Decreased testosterone with increased LH describes primary gonadal failure, not 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, where testosterone production by the testes is normal and only its peripheral conversion to DHT is impaired.

preguntas.q: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH/vasopressin) exerts its main water-reabsorbing action at which segment of the nephron?

o.B: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

e.correcta: ADH binds V2 receptors on the basolateral membrane of collecting duct principal cells, triggering a Gs-cAMP-PKA cascade that inserts aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane. This makes the collecting duct permeable to water, allowing water to be reabsorbed down the osmotic gradient established by the medullary interstitium, which is the final and most important site of ADH-regulated water reabsorption.

incorrectas.A: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs about two-thirds of filtered water and solutes isotonically and constitutively, regardless of ADH — it lacks the regulated aquaporin-2 insertion mechanism that makes the collecting duct the ADH target.
incorrectas.B: The thick ascending limb is water-impermeable by design (no aquaporins) and instead reabsorbs Na+/K+/2Cl- via NKCC2 to build the medullary concentration gradient; ADH acts downstream at the collecting duct to exploit that gradient, not at the thick ascending limb itself.
incorrectas.D: The distal convoluted tubule is also relatively water-impermeable and is the site of thiazide-sensitive NaCl reabsorption; ADH's water channel effect is specific to the collecting duct, which is the final common pathway for concentrating urine.

preguntas.q: Which mood stabilizer used for bipolar disorder is a common cause of drug-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?

e.correcta: Lithium impairs the kidney's ability to concentrate urine by interfering with vasopressin (ADH) signaling in the collecting duct principal cells, reducing aquaporin-2 expression and trafficking so that ADH can no longer promote water reabsorption despite normal or elevated ADH levels — this is the mechanism of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Patients present with polyuria and polydipsia, and the effect can persist even after lithium is stopped if chronic tubular damage has occurred.

incorrectas.A: Valproate is a mood stabilizer known for hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity (neural tube defects), and pancreatitis, but it does not interfere with ADH signaling in the collecting duct and is not a recognized cause of nephrogenic DI.
incorrectas.C: Carbamazepine can actually cause the opposite problem — it can stimulate ADH release or potentiate its action, contributing to SIADH and hyponatremia, rather than causing renal resistance to ADH.
incorrectas.D: Quetiapine is an atypical antipsychotic sometimes used as an adjunct in bipolar disorder, known for metabolic side effects like weight gain and dyslipidemia, but it has no established mechanism causing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

preguntas.q: Which drug-induced diabetes insipidus is amiloride useful for treating, by blocking the causative agent's entry into collecting duct cells?

e.correcta: Lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus by entering principal cells of the collecting duct through epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) and accumulating intracellularly, where it interferes with ADH signaling (impairing aquaporin-2 trafficking to the apical membrane). Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic that blocks ENaC, which prevents lithium from entering these cells in the first place, thereby limiting its nephrotoxic accumulation and improving urine concentrating ability — making it a targeted, mechanism-based treatment rather than a generic antidiuretic.

incorrectas.A: Demeclocycline itself causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (by antagonizing ADH at the collecting duct) and is actually used to treat SIADH, so it is not a cause that amiloride is used to counteract via ENaC blockade.
incorrectas.C: Foscarnet is an antiviral that can cause nephrotoxicity and electrolyte disturbances, but it does not cause diabetes insipidus via ENaC-mediated cellular entry, so amiloride's ENaC-blocking mechanism does not apply here.
incorrectas.D: Cisplatin causes nephrotoxicity primarily through direct proximal tubular cell damage and can cause electrolyte wasting, but it is not associated with lithium's specific ENaC-mediated mechanism of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus that amiloride targets.

preguntas.q: Central diabetes insipidus, caused by inadequate hypothalamic ADH secretion, is best treated with which agent?

e.correcta: Central diabetes insipidus results from inadequate hypothalamic/posterior pituitary secretion of ADH, so the kidney's V2 receptors never receive the signal needed to insert aquaporin-2 channels and concentrate urine — even though the collecting duct itself is fully capable of responding to ADH. Desmopressin is a synthetic ADH analog that directly replaces the missing hormone, binding V2 receptors to restore aquaporin-2 insertion and urine concentration, which is the most logical and effective treatment since the defect is one of hormone deficiency, not receptor resistance.

incorrectas.A: Demeclocycline induces nephrogenic diabetes insipidus by blunting the collecting duct's response to ADH, which would worsen (not treat) a condition already characterized by inadequate ADH signaling in central DI.
incorrectas.B: Tolvaptan is a V2 receptor antagonist used to treat SIADH and hyponatremia by blocking excess ADH action — giving it in central DI, where ADH is already deficient, would further impair water reabsorption and worsen polyuria.
incorrectas.D: Amiloride blocks ENaC channels and is used for lithium-induced nephrogenic DI or as a potassium-sparing diuretic; it does not replace ADH and would not correct the hormone deficiency underlying central DI.

preguntas.q: Besides central diabetes insipidus, desmopressin (DDAVP) is used to treat which bleeding disorder characterized by increased bruisability and mucosal bleeding?

e.correcta: Desmopressin (DDAVP) stimulates V2 receptors on endothelial cells, triggering release of stored von Willebrand factor (vWF) from Weibel-Palade bodies into the circulation. Since von Willebrand disease is characterized by a quantitative or qualitative deficiency of vWF (impairing platelet adhesion and stabilizing factor VIII), desmopressin's ability to acutely boost circulating vWF levels makes it first-line therapy for mild bleeding episodes or prophylaxis before minor procedures in these patients.

incorrectas.A: Hemophilia A is a deficiency of factor VIII itself (not vWF), and while desmopressin can modestly raise factor VIII (since vWF stabilizes it), it is not the primary treatment for hemophilia A, where recombinant factor VIII replacement is standard.
incorrectas.C: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura is caused by autoantibody-mediated platelet destruction, a mechanism unrelated to vWF release; desmopressin does not increase platelet count or address the autoimmune process in ITP.
incorrectas.D: Disseminated intravascular coagulation involves widespread activation of coagulation with consumption of platelets and clotting factors, a complex consumptive coagulopathy that desmopressin's vWF-release mechanism does not treat.

preguntas.q: A hemophilia A patient with hemarthrosis and prolonged bleeding after minor procedures may be treated with desmopressin because it raises levels of which factor?

e.correcta: Desmopressin raises circulating factor VIII levels by stimulating endothelial release of von Willebrand factor, which acts as a carrier protein that stabilizes and protects factor VIII from degradation in plasma. In mild hemophilia A, where some baseline factor VIII synthesis remains, this boost in the stabilizing carrier can transiently raise effective factor VIII activity enough to manage minor bleeding or cover minor procedures without needing factor VIII concentrate.

incorrectas.B: Factor IX is deficient in hemophilia B, not hemophilia A, and desmopressin's mechanism (via vWF-mediated stabilization) specifically affects factor VIII levels, not factor IX.
incorrectas.C: Fibrinogen is a distinct clotting factor involved in the final common pathway of coagulation, but desmopressin's therapeutic effect in hemophilia A works through the vWF-factor VIII axis, not through raising fibrinogen.
incorrectas.D: Factor XI deficiency causes a separate, rarer bleeding disorder (hemophilia C), and desmopressin's vWF-mediated mechanism does not raise factor XI levels or address that deficiency.

preguntas.q: Desmopressin can be used clinically to treat which common pediatric condition involving nighttime urination?

e.correcta: Desmopressin (DDAVP) is a synthetic vasopressin (ADH) analog that acts on renal V2 receptors to increase aquaporin-2 insertion in the collecting duct, concentrating urine and reducing nighttime urine volume — this makes it a first-line pharmacologic option for primary nocturnal enuresis in children when behavioral measures (fluid restriction, bedwetting alarms) fail. It essentially compensates for the normal nighttime rise in endogenous ADH that some enuretic children lack, reducing the volume of urine produced overnight below what would trigger bladder distention and voiding.

incorrectas.A: Vesicoureteral reflux is a structural/functional problem where urine flows backward from the bladder into the ureters/kidneys, predisposing to pyelonephritis; it is managed with prophylactic antibiotics or surgical correction, not desmopressin, since the underlying issue is reflux, not urine concentration.
incorrectas.C: Overactive bladder involves involuntary detrusor contractions causing urgency and frequency, typically treated with antimuscarinics (e.g., oxybutynin) that relax the bladder, a different mechanism from desmopressin's action on renal water reabsorption.
incorrectas.D: Urinary tract infections are treated with antibiotics targeting the causative organism; desmopressin has no antimicrobial action and would not address an active infection.

preguntas.q: Which electrolyte abnormality is an adverse effect of desmopressin (DDAVP) therapy?

e.correcta: Desmopressin (DDAVP) is a synthetic ADH analog that acts on renal V2 receptors to promote free water reabsorption in the collecting duct, and excessive water retention relative to sodium intake can dilute serum sodium and cause hyponatremia. This is why patients on desmopressin (for central DI, nocturnal enuresis, or bleeding disorders like von Willebrand disease) are monitored for water intoxication and counseled to avoid excessive free water intake.

incorrectas.A: Hypernatremia would result from water loss or ADH deficiency/resistance, the opposite problem that desmopressin is often used to treat (as in central DI), not a side effect of giving more ADH-like activity.
incorrectas.C: Hyperkalemia is not a recognized consequence of desmopressin's water-retaining V2 receptor mechanism, which affects free water handling rather than potassium transport.
incorrectas.D: Hypokalemia is similarly not linked to desmopressin's mechanism, since its action is specific to water channel (aquaporin) insertion in the collecting duct rather than potassium secretion or handling.

preguntas.q: Exogenous ADH (vasopressin) is useful in managing which type of bleeding by reducing portal pressure via V1 receptor-mediated vasoconstriction?

e.correcta: Exogenous vasopressin acts on V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle, causing splanchnic arteriolar vasoconstriction that reduces blood flow into the portal system and thereby lowers portal pressure. Since esophageal varices form and rupture as a consequence of portal hypertension, reducing splanchnic inflow directly decreases pressure within the dilated submucosal veins, making V1-mediated vasoconstriction a rational acute treatment for active variceal hemorrhage (often alongside octreotide, which works similarly).

incorrectas.A: Peptic ulcer bleeding arises from mucosal erosion into a vessel (often the gastroduodenal artery) and is managed with acid suppression and endoscopic hemostasis, not portal pressure reduction, since it is not driven by portal hypertension.
incorrectas.C: Diverticular bleeding results from rupture of vasa recta at the neck of a diverticulum in the colon, a local vascular injury unrelated to portal venous pressure, so V1-mediated splanchnic vasoconstriction is not the targeted mechanism for treating it.
incorrectas.D: Hemorrhoidal bleeding arises from engorged anorectal venous cushions, typically related to straining or local venous pressure rather than systemic portal hypertension, so reducing portal pressure via V1 receptors is not the relevant treatment mechanism.

preguntas.q: Treatment of SIADH with a vaptan (e.g., tolvaptan, conivaptan) carries the risk of which electrolyte disturbance?

e.correcta: Vaptans (tolvaptan, conivaptan) are vasopressin V2 receptor antagonists that block ADH's action on renal collecting duct aquaporin-2 channels, producing a selective aquaresis (free water excretion without significant electrolyte loss); this can correct the hyponatremia of SIADH too quickly, risking overcorrection into hypernatremia and, if the sodium rises too fast, osmotic demyelination syndrome. This is why vaptan therapy requires close monitoring of serum sodium during initiation.

incorrectas.A: Vaptans are used specifically to treat hyponatremia in SIADH by promoting free water excretion, so worsening hyponatremia would be a paradoxical, not expected, outcome of appropriate dosing — the actual risk is the opposite, overcorrection to hypernatremia.
incorrectas.B: Hyperkalemia is not a recognized effect of V2 receptor antagonism; vaptans act on water handling in the collecting duct via aquaporin channels rather than on potassium-secreting channels, so significant potassium disturbance is not their typical risk.
incorrectas.D: Hypocalcemia is not associated with vaptan therapy; these drugs are selective for the vasopressin V2 receptor pathway governing water reabsorption, not calcium homeostasis.

preguntas.q: If SIADH-induced hyponatremia treated with a vaptan is corrected too rapidly, which serious and irreversible CNS complication can occur?

e.correcta: In chronic hyponatremia, brain cells adapt by extruding intracellular osmolytes to match the low extracellular osmolality and prevent cerebral edema; if serum sodium is corrected too rapidly (including with vaptans, which cause aquaresis and can raise sodium quickly), the brain cells cannot regain those lost osmolytes fast enough and shrink, damaging oligodendrocytes and stripping myelin, especially in the pons. This produces central pontine myelinolysis (osmotic demyelination syndrome), which can cause irreversible spastic quadriparesis, dysarthria, and locked-in syndrome — hence the rule to correct chronic hyponatremia slowly (generally no more than 8 mEq/L per 24 hours).

incorrectas.A: Wernicke encephalopathy results from thiamine deficiency causing damage to the mammillary bodies and periaqueductal gray, a nutritional mechanism entirely unrelated to rapid sodium correction or osmotic shifts.
incorrectas.C: Cerebral edema is the complication of correcting hyponatremia too slowly or of acute hyponatremia causing water to shift into brain cells, not the result of overly rapid correction, which instead causes cellular dehydration and demyelination.
incorrectas.D: Guillain-Barré syndrome is an autoimmune demyelinating polyneuropathy typically triggered by antecedent infection (e.g., Campylobacter jejuni), a mechanism unrelated to osmotic shifts from sodium correction.

preguntas.q: Which tetracycline-class drug can be used as a second-line treatment for SIADH by inhibiting ADH signaling at the collecting duct?

e.correcta: Demeclocycline is a tetracycline-class antibiotic that, as an off-target effect, antagonizes ADH action at the V2 receptor/collecting duct, inducing a reversible nephrogenic diabetes insipidus-like state. In SIADH, where excess ADH causes free water retention and hyponatremia, this induced ADH resistance is therapeutically useful because it promotes free water excretion and helps correct the hyponatremia when fluid restriction alone is insufficient, making it a classic second-line agent (after vaptans or fluid restriction) for chronic SIADH.

incorrectas.A: Doxycycline is a widely used tetracycline for infections but does not share demeclocycline's specific ADH-antagonist property at the collecting duct, so it is not used to treat SIADH.
incorrectas.C: Minocycline is another tetracycline used mainly for acne and certain infections, but it lacks the distinct nephrogenic-DI-inducing effect that makes demeclocycline useful in SIADH.
incorrectas.D: Tigecycline is a glycylcycline (tetracycline derivative) used for broad-spectrum resistant infections, not for SIADH, as it does not have the collecting-duct ADH-antagonist effect that demeclocycline exhibits.

preguntas.q: A drug used to treat SIADH can paradoxically induce which renal adverse effect due to blunting collecting duct ADH responsiveness?

e.correcta: Demeclocycline (used to treat SIADH) works precisely by blunting the collecting duct's responsiveness to ADH, but this same mechanism can be dose-dependently excessive, producing acquired nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with polyuria and difficulty concentrating urine even when it is not desired. This is the classic paradox tested: a drug used to correct one ADH-related disorder (SIADH, with too much ADH effect) can tip into the opposite disorder (nephrogenic DI, with too little ADH effect) if the collecting duct becomes too resistant.

incorrectas.A: Renal tubular acidosis involves impaired renal acid-base handling (bicarbonate wasting or impaired H+ secretion), a mechanism unrelated to ADH receptor responsiveness, and is not the adverse effect classically linked to demeclocycline.
incorrectas.C: Minimal change disease is a glomerular podocyte disorder causing nephrotic syndrome, typically idiopathic or associated with NSAIDs, and has no relationship to demeclocycline's ADH-blunting mechanism at the collecting duct.
incorrectas.D: Fanconi syndrome is a proximal tubular defect causing wasting of glucose, amino acids, phosphate, and bicarbonate, a different renal segment and mechanism than the collecting-duct ADH resistance caused by demeclocycline.

preguntas.q: The growth hormone receptor belongs to which class of receptors?

e.correcta: The growth hormone receptor is a single-pass transmembrane receptor that lacks intrinsic enzymatic activity; upon GH binding, it dimerizes and recruits a non-receptor (cytoplasmic) tyrosine kinase, JAK2, which phosphorylates itself and the receptor, creating docking sites that activate STAT transcription factors. Phosphorylated STATs dimerize, translocate to the nucleus, and drive transcription of target genes including IGF-1 — this JAK-STAT mechanism is shared by other cytokine-type receptors (e.g., erythropoietin, prolactin) and is a key concept distinguishing GH signaling from receptors with built-in kinase activity.

incorrectas.A: G protein-coupled receptors signal through heterotrimeric G proteins and second messengers like cAMP or IP3/DAG (as with glucagon or ADH V2 receptors), not through JAK-STAT, so this does not describe the GH receptor's mechanism.
incorrectas.B: Receptor tyrosine kinases (like the insulin or IGF-1 receptor) have intrinsic kinase activity built into the receptor itself, whereas the GH receptor has no intrinsic kinase activity and instead relies on an associated, separate JAK2 molecule.
incorrectas.D: Ligand-gated ion channels (like nicotinic acetylcholine receptors) directly open to allow ion flux upon ligand binding, an electrically-mediated mechanism entirely different from the GH receptor's use of JAK2 and STAT transcription factors.

preguntas.q: Growth hormone exerts most of its growth-promoting effects indirectly through which mediator hormone?

e.correcta: Growth hormone stimulates the liver (and other tissues, including growth plate chondrocytes locally) to produce IGF-1, which is the main mediator of GH's anabolic and growth-promoting actions on bone and soft tissue, including stimulating chondrocyte proliferation at the epiphyseal growth plate. This indirect, IGF-1-mediated pathway (the somatomedin hypothesis) also provides negative feedback, since elevated IGF-1 suppresses further GH release from the pituitary, making IGF-1 levels a more stable clinical marker of GH status than pulsatile GH itself.

incorrectas.B: Thyroid hormone is permissive for normal growth and skeletal maturation (its deficiency causes growth failure), but it is not the mediator through which GH itself exerts its growth-promoting effects; the two act through separate pathways.
incorrectas.C: Cortisol generally has catabolic and growth-suppressing effects, particularly on the growth plate and protein metabolism, making it functionally opposite to the anabolic, growth-promoting role that IGF-1 plays for GH.
incorrectas.D: Prolactin regulates lactation and has a different receptor and physiologic role from GH; it is not the intermediary hormone that mediates the skeletal and somatic growth effects of GH.

preguntas.q: The pubertal growth spurt and long bone growth are primarily driven by which hormone?

e.correcta: IGF-1, produced mainly by the liver in response to GH stimulation, directly drives chondrocyte proliferation and hypertrophy at the epiphyseal growth plate, which is the cellular basis of longitudinal bone growth and the pubertal growth spurt. During puberty, sex steroids (particularly estrogen, even in males via aromatization) amplify pituitary GH pulsatility, which increases IGF-1 production and synergistically accelerates growth before ultimately triggering epiphyseal plate closure — so IGF-1 is the proximate mediator even though the timing is set by the sex-steroid surge.

incorrectas.A: Growth hormone acts mainly indirectly rather than directly on the growth plate; while GH does have some direct chondrocyte effects, the dominant driver of longitudinal bone growth is IGF-1 generated in response to GH, not GH acting alone.
incorrectas.C: Testosterone alone contributes to the pubertal growth spurt in males, but its major growth-promoting effect works partly through local aromatization to estrogen and through stimulating the GH-IGF-1 axis, rather than acting as the sole direct driver of bone growth.
incorrectas.D: Estrogen alone is important (including in males via aromatization) for accelerating growth plate maturation and eventual closure, but the direct mediator of the growth spurt at the cellular level in the growth plate is IGF-1, which estrogen helps amplify via the GH axis.

preguntas.q: What is the effect of growth hormone on muscle tissue?

o.D: Anabolic only in the presence of insulin deficiency

e.correcta: Growth hormone is anabolic in muscle, promoting amino acid uptake and increasing muscle protein synthesis, partly directly and partly via IGF-1 generated in response to GH stimulation. This anabolic effect on muscle (along with its lipolytic effect on adipose tissue and anti-insulin/hyperglycemic effect on glucose metabolism) underlies why GH is abused for muscle-building purposes and why GH deficiency in children and adults is associated with reduced lean muscle mass.

incorrectas.A: Catabolic, muscle-breakdown effects are more characteristic of cortisol or prolonged fasting states, not growth hormone, which instead promotes protein synthesis and preserves/builds muscle mass.
incorrectas.C: GH does have a significant, well-documented anabolic effect on muscle protein synthesis; the claim of no significant effect ignores GH's central role (both directly and via IGF-1) in promoting muscle growth.
incorrectas.D: GH's anabolic effect on muscle occurs independent of insulin deficiency; in fact, GH tends to antagonize insulin action (raising blood glucose), and its muscle-building effects are seen under normal physiologic conditions, not specifically requiring insulin deficiency.

preguntas.q: What is the effect of growth hormone on adipose tissue?

e.correcta: Growth hormone (GH) is catabolic on adipose tissue: it activates hormone-sensitive lipase and upregulates lipolytic pathways in adipocytes, releasing free fatty acids and glycerol into circulation. This shifts the body toward using fat as an energy substrate, sparing glucose for the brain, which is part of GH's broader anti-insulin, catabolic profile (alongside increased hepatic gluconeogenesis and decreased peripheral glucose uptake). Clinically this is why chronic GH excess (acromegaly) is associated with insulin resistance and sometimes overt diabetes.

incorrectas.A: GH does the opposite of promoting fat storage — it mobilizes stored triglycerides via lipolysis rather than favoring lipogenesis, which is more characteristic of insulin's action on adipose tissue.
incorrectas.B: GH has a clear and clinically important effect on lipid metabolism; it is one of the classic counter-regulatory (anti-insulin) hormones that increases circulating free fatty acids, so 'no effect' misses a core physiologic action of GH.
incorrectas.D: GH's lipolytic, catabolic effect on adipose tissue persists throughout life, not just childhood — the growth-promoting (anabolic) effects on bone and cartilage are what depend on open epiphyses, but the metabolic effects on fat and glucose continue into adulthood.

preguntas.q: Exogenous growth hormone (somatropin) is administered clinically primarily to treat which condition?

e.correcta: Somatropin is recombinant human growth hormone, and its main clinical use is replacement therapy in patients who cannot produce adequate endogenous GH, such as children with pituitary dwarfism or adults with GH deficiency from pituitary disease or surgery. Giving exogenous GH restores normal growth velocity in children and helps normalize body composition and metabolic parameters in GH-deficient adults. This is a straightforward hormone-replacement strategy, analogous to giving insulin in type 1 diabetes.

incorrectas.B: Acromegaly is caused by GH excess (usually a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma), so administering more GH would worsen the disease; treatment instead uses GH-lowering strategies such as somatostatin analogs (octreotide), GH receptor antagonists (pegvisomant), or surgery.
incorrectas.C: Cushing syndrome results from excess cortisol, not GH deficiency, and is treated by addressing the cortisol excess (surgery, steroidogenesis inhibitors), not by giving GH.
incorrectas.D: Hyperthyroidism is a disorder of excess thyroid hormone and is managed with antithyroid drugs, radioiodine, or thyroidectomy — GH has no role in its treatment.

preguntas.q: Mecasermin, a recombinant IGF-1 analog, carries which important metabolic adverse effect?

e.correcta: Mecasermin is a recombinant IGF-1 analog used to treat severe primary IGF-1 deficiency, and because IGF-1 signaling mimics insulin's metabolic effects (promoting glucose uptake into cells), a key adverse effect is hypoglycemia, especially if the drug is given without adequate food intake. Patients are typically counseled to take it with a meal or snack to mitigate this risk, similar to precautions taken with insulin therapy.

incorrectas.A: Hyperglycemia is the opposite of the expected effect — IGF-1 has insulin-like actions that lower blood glucose by promoting cellular glucose uptake, so mecasermin's characteristic metabolic risk is hypoglycemia, not hyperglycemia.
incorrectas.C: Hyperkalemia is not a recognized characteristic adverse effect of mecasermin; the drug's clinically important metabolic risk relates specifically to glucose homeostasis via IGF-1's insulin-like signaling, not potassium handling.
incorrectas.D: Hypercalcemia is not an established adverse effect of IGF-1 analog therapy; mecasermin's main metabolic concern is hypoglycemia from its insulin-mimetic action, not disturbances in calcium metabolism.

preguntas.q: A growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma causes which condition when it occurs in adults, after the growth plates have already fused?

e.correcta: Once the epiphyseal growth plates have fused after puberty, bones can no longer grow in length, so excess GH in adults causes appositional (width-wise) bone growth and soft tissue overgrowth instead of increased height — this is acromegaly, presenting with enlarged hands, feet, jaw (prognathism), and organomegaly. The same GH-secreting pituitary adenoma occurring before growth plate closure produces gigantism instead, so the distinguishing factor is purely the patient's skeletal maturity at the time of GH excess.

incorrectas.A: Gigantism describes GH excess occurring before epiphyseal closure, causing proportional increased linear growth in children — since this question specifies an adult with fused growth plates, gigantism cannot occur.
incorrectas.C: Dwarfism results from GH deficiency (or resistance, as in Laron syndrome) causing short stature, which is the opposite hormonal problem from a GH-secreting adenoma that produces excess hormone.
incorrectas.D: Cretinism refers to congenital hypothyroidism causing intellectual disability and growth failure in infants, an entirely different axis (thyroid, not GH) and a pediatric rather than adult presentation.

preguntas.q: Which somatostatin analog is used to treat VIPoma and carcinoid syndrome by inhibiting excessive hormone/mediator secretion?

e.correcta: Octreotide is a long-acting somatostatin analog that inhibits secretion of numerous GI hormones and peptides, including vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) and serotonin, making it first-line for symptomatic control of VIPoma (which causes watery diarrhea from VIP excess) and carcinoid syndrome (flushing/diarrhea from serotonin and other vasoactive substances). By suppressing release of these mediators at the level of neuroendocrine tumor cells, octreotide provides symptomatic relief even when the underlying tumor is not resectable. This mirrors somatostatin's natural physiologic role as a broad inhibitor of endocrine and exocrine secretion throughout the gut.

incorrectas.A: Pegvisomant is a GH receptor antagonist used specifically for acromegaly resistant to other therapies — it blocks GH signaling at its receptor rather than suppressing hormone secretion from neuroendocrine tumors like VIPoma or carcinoid.
incorrectas.C: Cabergoline is a dopamine D2 receptor agonist used for prolactinomas and adjunctively in acromegaly by suppressing GH release from lactotroph/somatotroph cells — it has no role in VIPoma or carcinoid syndrome management.
incorrectas.D: Mecasermin is recombinant IGF-1 used to treat growth failure from GH insensitivity or IGF-1 deficiency, which is the opposite pharmacologic goal (promoting growth signaling) rather than suppressing hormone hypersecretion.

preguntas.q: Octreotide, a somatostatin analog, is used in the management of which pancreatic islet cell tumors?

e.correcta: Octreotide broadly suppresses secretion from multiple pancreatic islet cell tumor types because somatostatin receptors are expressed on insulinoma, glucagonoma, and gastrinoma cells alike, and activation inhibits their respective hormone (insulin, glucagon, gastrin) release. This makes octreotide a useful adjunct across the spectrum of functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors for symptom control, particularly when surgery isn't curative or immediately available. The unifying mechanism is somatostatin's general inhibitory tone over endocrine secretion, not a tumor-specific action.

incorrectas.B: Restricting octreotide's use to only insulinoma ignores its well-established efficacy in glucagonoma (reducing glucagon-driven hyperglycemia and necrolytic migratory erythema) and gastrinoma (reducing gastrin-driven acid hypersecretion), where it is also clinically used.
incorrectas.C: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is an exocrine, non-hormone-secreting malignancy, so a somatostatin analog aimed at suppressing hormone secretion has no meaningful therapeutic rationale there.
incorrectas.D: Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting adrenal medullary tumor, managed with alpha- and beta-blockade prior to surgery, not with somatostatin analogs, since it is not one of the islet cell tumors this mechanism targets.

preguntas.q: Octreotide can help manage which type of GI bleeding by reducing portal blood flow and variceal pressure?

e.correcta: Octreotide reduces splanchnic and portal blood flow by inhibiting release of vasodilatory GI hormones (like glucagon and VIP) that normally sustain splanchnic hyperemia in portal hypertension, thereby lowering portal pressure and flow through esophageal varices. This makes it a mainstay adjunct (alongside endoscopic band ligation) in acute variceal hemorrhage, buying time and reducing bleeding severity while definitive endoscopic therapy is arranged. The mechanism is hemodynamic (reducing pressure/flow to the varix), not a direct hemostatic or clotting effect.

incorrectas.B: Mallory-Weiss tears are mucosal lacerations at the gastroesophageal junction from forceful vomiting, and bleeding is typically managed with supportive care or endoscopic therapy rather than portal-pressure-lowering agents, since the bleeding is not driven by portal hypertension.
incorrectas.C: Angiodysplasia bleeding arises from fragile, abnormal submucosal vessels (often in the colon) and is treated endoscopically (e.g., argon plasma coagulation) — it has nothing to do with portal venous pressure, so octreotide's mechanism doesn't apply.
incorrectas.D: Meckel diverticulum bleeding results from ectopic gastric mucosa causing acid-induced ulceration in the diverticulum, a structural/anatomic problem usually addressed surgically, not a portal hypertension-related bleed that would respond to splanchnic vasoconstriction.

preguntas.q: Octreotide commonly causes which category of adverse effects, including nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain?

e.correcta: Octreotide, a somatostatin analog, commonly causes GI side effects such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and steatorrhea/diarrhea because it broadly inhibits GI hormone and enzyme secretion (including cholecystokinin, gastrin, and pancreatic exocrine output) and slows gallbladder motility, which also predisposes patients to gallstone formation with long-term use. Recognizing this side-effect profile matters because octreotide is used chronically for conditions like acromegaly and carcinoid syndrome, where GI tolerability affects adherence.

incorrectas.A: While octreotide can have some hemodynamic effects (e.g., used for esophageal variceal bleeding via splanchnic vasoconstriction), its predominant, most commonly reported adverse effects are gastrointestinal rather than primarily cardiovascular.
incorrectas.C: Neurologic side effects are not the hallmark adverse effect category for octreotide; its mechanism (somatostatin receptor agonism) predominantly affects gut and pancreatic secretory function, producing GI rather than neurologic symptoms.
incorrectas.D: Dermatologic side effects are not the classic adverse effect profile of octreotide; the drug's inhibitory action on GI secretions and motility makes GI symptoms, not skin reactions, the most commonly encountered issue.

preguntas.q: Octreotide can cause steatorrhea through which mechanism?

o.B: Decreased pancreatic secretions and gallbladder contractility

e.correcta: Octreotide, by mimicking somatostatin, inhibits pancreatic exocrine secretion (reducing lipase and other digestive enzymes reaching the duodenum) and also inhibits gallbladder contractility, impairing bile delivery for fat emulsification. The combined loss of pancreatic lipase and adequate bile flow causes malabsorption of dietary fat, which passes through the gut undigested and produces steatorrhea. This is a predictable on-target adverse effect of chronic somatostatin analog therapy, alongside gallstone formation from bile stasis.

incorrectas.A: Octreotide decreases, not increases, pancreatic enzyme secretion — increased enzyme secretion would actually aid fat digestion and would not explain steatorrhea.
incorrectas.C: Octreotide's effect on fat malabsorption is a functional/secretory one (inhibiting enzyme and bile release), not the result of direct cytotoxic damage to the intestinal mucosa itself.
incorrectas.D: Octreotide decreases gallbladder emptying and can promote bile stasis/gallstones, but it does not increase bile acid synthesis — reduced bile delivery to the gut (not increased production) is what contributes to fat malabsorption.

preguntas.q: In addition to treating acromegaly, dopamine D2 receptor agonists like cabergoline and bromocriptine are used to treat which condition?

e.correcta: Dopamine normally acts on D2 receptors on lactotroph cells to tonically inhibit prolactin secretion, so D2 agonists like cabergoline and bromocriptine mimic this inhibitory tone and are first-line therapy for hyperprolactinemia, including prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas (prolactinomas). This same mechanism also suppresses GH release from somatotroph adenomas to a lesser extent, which is why these drugs have a secondary role in acromegaly. The unifying principle is that dopamine agonism directly suppresses anterior pituitary hormone release from lactotrophs (and to a degree, somatotrophs).

incorrectas.A: Hypoprolactinemia (low prolactin) would require a prolactin-stimulating strategy, not a dopamine agonist that further suppresses prolactin — this is the opposite clinical scenario from what cabergoline/bromocriptine treat.
incorrectas.C: Hypothyroidism is treated with levothyroxine replacement; dopamine agonists have no established role in thyroid hormone deficiency, since the underlying defect is in thyroid hormone production, not lactotroph or somatotroph secretion.
incorrectas.D: Adrenal insufficiency requires glucocorticoid (and often mineralocorticoid) replacement, addressing a cortisol deficiency — this is unrelated to the dopaminergic regulation of prolactin or GH that cabergoline and bromocriptine act on.

preguntas.q: Which hormone-secreting pancreatic islet cell tumor is classically associated with necrolytic migratory erythema?

e.correcta: Glucagonoma causes excess glucagon secretion, which promotes catabolism of amino acids and disrupts epidermal protein/lipid homeostasis, classically producing necrolytic migratory erythema — a characteristic migratory, blistering, erythematous rash typically seen with the '4 D's' (diabetes, DVT, depression, dermatitis) and hypoaminoacidemia. This rash is a key board-testable clue that immediately points to a glucagon-secreting pancreatic tumor rather than other islet cell neoplasms. Recognizing this skin finding allows early consideration of glucagonoma even before glucose or glucagon levels are drawn.

incorrectas.A: Insulinoma causes episodic hypoglycemia with neuroglycopenic symptoms (the Whipple triad) rather than a skin rash — excess insulin does not produce necrolytic migratory erythema, which is specifically tied to glucagon excess.
incorrectas.B: Gastrinoma causes Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, with recurrent peptic ulcers and diarrhea from gastric acid hypersecretion, not a dermatologic paraneoplastic rash like necrolytic migratory erythema.
incorrectas.D: Somatostatinoma classically presents with the triad of diabetes, cholelithiasis, and steatorrhea (from suppressing insulin, gallbladder contraction, and pancreatic enzymes respectively) — it is not associated with necrolytic migratory erythema, which is specific to glucagon excess.

preguntas.q: In its unbound (inactive) state, where is the glucocorticoid receptor primarily located within the cell?

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids are lipophilic steroid hormones that diffuse across the plasma membrane and bind their receptor in the cytoplasm, where the unbound receptor is normally held inactive in a complex with heat shock proteins (like HSP90). Upon ligand binding, the receptor undergoes a conformational change, dissociates from the chaperone proteins, and translocates to the nucleus to act as a transcription factor regulating gene expression (transactivation/transrepression). This cytoplasmic-then-nuclear translocation mechanism is a defining feature of steroid hormone receptors as a class, distinguishing them from membrane receptor-based signaling.

incorrectas.A: The receptor is not pre-bound to DNA in the nucleus in its inactive state — it must first be activated by ligand binding in the cytoplasm and then translocate to the nucleus to engage DNA and chromatin.
incorrectas.B: Glucocorticoid receptors are intracellular, not plasma membrane receptors — because glucocorticoids are lipid-soluble, they don't require a membrane-bound receptor and second-messenger cascade the way peptide hormones do.
incorrectas.D: The glucocorticoid receptor is not sequestered in the endoplasmic reticulum; its inactive resting location is the cytoplasm, complexed with chaperone proteins, before ligand-induced nuclear translocation.

preguntas.q: What effect do glucocorticoids have on the production/activity of phospholipase A2?

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids induce synthesis of lipocortin (annexin A1), which inhibits phospholipase A2, the enzyme that liberates arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids. By blocking this very first step of the arachidonic acid cascade, glucocorticoids simultaneously suppress downstream production of both prostaglandins (via COX) and leukotrienes (via lipoxygenase), giving them a broader anti-inflammatory effect than NSAIDs, which only inhibit COX. This upstream site of action is a key distinguishing pharmacologic feature of steroids versus NSAIDs.

incorrectas.A: Glucocorticoids decrease, not increase, PLA2 activity — stimulating PLA2 would promote rather than suppress the inflammatory arachidonic acid cascade, which contradicts the anti-inflammatory action of steroids.
incorrectas.B: Glucocorticoids have a clear and clinically important suppressive effect on PLA2 via lipocortin induction; this is actually one of their core anti-inflammatory mechanisms, not something without effect.
incorrectas.D: There is no established biphasic acute-stimulation-then-chronic-inhibition pattern for glucocorticoid effects on PLA2 — the inhibitory action via lipocortin induction is the consistent, well-described mechanism.

preguntas.q: Glucocorticoids reduce inflammation in part by inhibiting phospholipase A2, thereby preventing production of which molecule?

e.correcta: By inducing lipocortin to inhibit phospholipase A2, glucocorticoids prevent the release of arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids, which is the obligatory precursor substrate for both the cyclooxygenase (prostaglandin/thromboxane) and lipoxygenase (leukotriene) pathways. Blocking arachidonic acid liberation upstream therefore shuts down the entire eicosanoid cascade at its source, rather than targeting one downstream enzyme like NSAIDs (COX) or leukotriene inhibitors (5-LOX) do individually. This is why steroids are more broadly anti-inflammatory than single-pathway-targeted drugs.

incorrectas.A: Thromboxane A2 is a downstream product of the COX pathway acting on arachidonic acid, not the substance whose release PLA2 inhibition directly blocks — thromboxane production is suppressed only as a consequence of losing its arachidonic acid precursor.
incorrectas.B: Prostacyclin, like thromboxane, is a COX-pathway product made from arachidonic acid — it is downstream of the PLA2 step and reduced secondarily, not the direct molecule prevented by PLA2 inhibition.
incorrectas.D: Leukotriene B4 is a lipoxygenase-pathway product derived from arachidonic acid, so its reduced production is a downstream consequence of blocking arachidonic acid release, not the direct substrate PLA2 acts on.

preguntas.q: Glucocorticoids reduce inflammation in part by inhibiting cyclooxygenase-mediated production of which inflammatory mediators?

e.correcta: Prostaglandins are produced from arachidonic acid via the cyclooxygenase (COX) enzyme pathway, and glucocorticoids indirectly suppress this pathway by inhibiting phospholipase A2 (via lipocortin induction), cutting off the arachidonic acid supply that COX would otherwise convert into prostaglandins. Reduced prostaglandin synthesis contributes to decreased vasodilation, pain sensitization, and fever during inflammation, which is part of why glucocorticoids are effective broad anti-inflammatory and antipyretic agents. This distinguishes the 'upstream' steroid mechanism from NSAIDs, which act directly at the COX enzyme itself rather than on substrate availability.
