incorrectas.A: Leukotrienes come from the lipoxygenase pathway, not cyclooxygenase, so while glucocorticoids also reduce leukotriene levels, that occurs via a separate (lipoxygenase) route downstream of the shared PLA2 block, not through 'COX-mediated' inhibition as the question specifies.
incorrectas.C: Thromboxanes are also COX-pathway products, but they are a distinct downstream mediator from prostaglandins (thromboxane A2 specifically drives platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction) — the question is asking about the classic inflammatory mediator group termed 'prostaglandins,' not thromboxanes.
incorrectas.D: Bradykinin is generated from kininogen by kallikrein, entirely independent of the arachidonic acid/cyclooxygenase pathway, so COX inhibition by glucocorticoids has no direct bearing on bradykinin production.

preguntas.q: Glucocorticoids reduce inflammation in part by inhibiting lipoxygenase-mediated production of which inflammatory mediators?

e.correcta: Leukotrienes are synthesized from arachidonic acid via the 5-lipoxygenase (5-LOX) pathway, and glucocorticoids suppress their production by inhibiting phospholipase A2 (through lipocortin induction), which cuts off the arachidonic acid substrate needed for lipoxygenase to act on. Leukotrienes drive bronchoconstriction, increased vascular permeability, and neutrophil chemotaxis, so blunting their production contributes meaningfully to glucocorticoids' efficacy in asthma and other inflammatory conditions. This upstream substrate-limiting mechanism again explains why steroids affect both the lipoxygenase and cyclooxygenase branches simultaneously.

incorrectas.A: Prostaglandins arise from the cyclooxygenase pathway, a separate branch of arachidonic acid metabolism from lipoxygenase — while glucocorticoids reduce both, this question is specifically asking about the lipoxygenase-derived mediator group, which is leukotrienes, not prostaglandins.
incorrectas.B: Thromboxanes are also cyclooxygenase pathway products (like prostaglandins and prostacyclin), so they fall outside the lipoxygenase-specific mediator class the question is targeting.
incorrectas.D: Prostacyclin is generated via cyclooxygenase in vascular endothelium, not via lipoxygenase, so it belongs to the same COX-pathway family as prostaglandins and thromboxanes rather than the leukotriene family being asked about here.

preguntas.q: Glucocorticoids suppress production of proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-2 and TNF-alpha primarily by inhibiting which transcription factor?

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids bind their intracellular receptor, which then translocates to the nucleus and directly inhibits NF-kB (and AP-1) transcriptional activity — largely by inducing IkB, which sequesters NF-kB in the cytoplasm and prevents it from turning on pro-inflammatory cytokine genes. Since NF-kB is a master transcription factor driving expression of IL-2, TNF-alpha, and many other cytokines and adhesion molecules, its suppression broadly dampens the inflammatory and immune transcriptional program. This transrepression mechanism is central to the immunosuppressive power of glucocorticoids beyond their eicosanoid effects.

incorrectas.A: AP-1 is indeed also inhibited by activated glucocorticoid receptor, but NF-kB is the more classically emphasized master regulator for IL-2/TNF-alpha suppression in this context, and the two are often tested together with NF-kB as the primary answer.
incorrectas.B: STAT3 is a transcription factor activated downstream of cytokine receptors (like IL-6) via JAK-STAT signaling, not the primary target through which glucocorticoids suppress IL-2/TNF-alpha transcription.
incorrectas.D: NFAT is the transcription factor targeted by calcineurin inhibitors like cyclosporine and tacrolimus (which block IL-2 gene transcription via a different mechanism), not the direct target of glucocorticoid receptor action.

preguntas.q: Glucocorticoids inhibit production of IL-2, thereby preventing activation of which two lymphocyte populations?

e.correcta: IL-2 is the principal cytokine driving clonal proliferation and activation of both T cells (via autocrine/paracrine IL-2 receptor signaling) and, indirectly, B cells (which depend on T-helper cell cytokine support for full activation and antibody production). By suppressing NF-kB-driven IL-2 transcription, glucocorticoids blunt the expansion and activation of both lymphocyte lineages, which is a major contributor to their immunosuppressive effect in autoimmune disease and transplant rejection prevention. This is distinct from their effects on innate immune cells like neutrophils, which are affected through different mechanisms (demargination) rather than IL-2 suppression.

incorrectas.A: NK cells and macrophages are innate immune cells not primarily dependent on IL-2 for activation in the way adaptive lymphocytes are, so blocking IL-2 does not directly explain suppression of these populations.
incorrectas.C: Dendritic cells and eosinophils are affected by glucocorticoids through other mechanisms (e.g., eosinophil apoptosis), but they are not the classic IL-2-dependent populations whose activation is blocked by this specific mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Neutrophils and mast cells are not IL-2-dependent for their function — glucocorticoids actually increase circulating neutrophils via demargination, the opposite effect from the lymphocyte suppression caused by blocking IL-2.

preguntas.q: Glucocorticoids cause neutrophilia primarily through which mechanism?

o.D: Inhibition of neutrophil extravasation receptors on endothelium alone

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids decrease expression of adhesion molecules on neutrophils and endothelium, impairing margination (the normal adherence of neutrophils to vessel walls); this releases the marginated pool into circulation, causing an apparent neutrophilia despite glucocorticoids actually impairing neutrophil function.

incorrectas.A: While glucocorticoids can have some effects on marrow release kinetics, the classically tested and predominant mechanism for the acute rise in circulating neutrophils is demargination of the pre-existing marginated pool, not new production.
incorrectas.B: Glucocorticoids do not primarily act by preventing neutrophil apoptosis; in fact, they promote apoptosis of lymphocytes, which is the opposite effect seen in lymphopenia, not the mechanism behind neutrophilia.
incorrectas.D: This option isolates only the endothelial side of adhesion, but the overall phenomenon requires impaired neutrophil-endothelial adhesion broadly (demargination), a more complete description than endothelial receptor inhibition alone.

preguntas.q: A patient started on high-dose prednisone develops an elevated absolute neutrophil count on routine labs despite no evidence of infection. What is the most likely explanation?

o.A: Steroid-induced bone marrow stimulation of granulopoiesis
o.C: Glucocorticoid-induced left shift from acute infection

e.correcta: High-dose glucocorticoids impair neutrophil adhesion to vascular endothelium, causing the marginated pool of neutrophils normally adherent to vessel walls to be released into the actively circulating pool — this demargination raises the measured absolute neutrophil count without any true increase in total body neutrophil production or an underlying infection. This is a well-known benign, expected laboratory finding after starting steroids and should not trigger an infectious workup on its own, especially when clinical signs of infection are absent. Recognizing this prevents unnecessary antibiotic use or diagnostic testing.

incorrectas.A: Bone marrow stimulation of granulopoiesis is not the primary or rapid mechanism behind steroid-induced neutrophilia — demargination of the existing marginated pool explains the abrupt rise seen shortly after starting therapy, not increased marrow output.
incorrectas.C: A left shift (bands and immature forms) suggests true infection-driven marrow release of immature neutrophils, which is different from steroid-induced demargination of mature neutrophils and would be an inappropriate conclusion given the stated absence of infection.
incorrectas.D: Eosinophilia is not what glucocorticoids cause — they cause eosinopenia (a decrease in eosinophils) by promoting eosinophil apoptosis and sequestration, so this option describes the opposite effect on the wrong cell line.

preguntas.q: Chronic glucocorticoid therapy has what effect on circulating lymphocyte counts, particularly T-helper cells?

o.A: Increase, due to redistribution from lymphoid organs
o.C: Decrease, due to apoptosis and redistribution into lymphoid tissue

e.correcta: Chronic glucocorticoid exposure decreases circulating lymphocyte counts, particularly T-helper (CD4+) cells, through a combination of inducing apoptosis in susceptible lymphocyte subsets and redistributing lymphocytes out of the blood back into lymphoid tissue (lymph nodes, spleen, bone marrow). This lymphopenic effect is a major part of the immunosuppressive action of steroids and is clinically relevant because it increases susceptibility to opportunistic infections (e.g., reactivation of latent TB or PCP pneumonia) during prolonged therapy. This contrasts sharply with glucocorticoids' effect on neutrophils, which increase due to demargination rather than decrease.

incorrectas.A: Circulating lymphocyte counts decrease, not increase, with glucocorticoid therapy — this is the opposite direction from neutrophils, which do increase via redistribution/demargination, so it's important not to conflate the two cell lines' opposite responses.
incorrectas.B: Glucocorticoids have a well-documented and clinically significant suppressive effect on lymphocyte counts (lymphopenia), which is part of why chronic steroid use increases infection risk — 'no significant change' understates a major, clinically important effect.
incorrectas.D: Glucocorticoids promote, rather than inhibit, apoptosis in susceptible lymphocyte populations, which contributes to the observed decrease in lymphocyte counts, not an increase from inhibited apoptosis.

preguntas.q: Glucocorticoid therapy in a patient with severe asthma exacerbation is expected to have what effect on peripheral eosinophil counts?

o.D: Transient increase followed by rebound decrease

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids induce eosinopenia by promoting eosinophil apoptosis and inhibiting their release from the bone marrow while also enhancing sequestration in lymphoid tissue, so peripheral eosinophil counts fall predictably during steroid therapy. This is precisely the therapeutic goal in a severe asthma exacerbation, where eosinophils are central mediators of airway inflammation — reducing their numbers and activity helps resolve bronchospasm and mucosal edema. Eosinopenia after steroid dosing is actually used clinically as a rough marker of adequate steroid effect/compliance.

incorrectas.A: Eosinophilia would indicate ongoing or worsening allergic/eosinophilic inflammation, which is the opposite of what effective glucocorticoid therapy produces — steroids act specifically to suppress, not increase, eosinophil counts.
incorrectas.B: Glucocorticoids have a robust, well-documented and clinically expected effect of lowering eosinophil counts, so 'no change' contradicts the established pharmacology used as a marker of steroid effect in practice.
incorrectas.D: There is no established transient-increase-then-rebound-decrease pattern for glucocorticoid effects on eosinophils; the expected and consistent response is a prompt decrease (eosinopenia) following steroid administration.

preguntas.q: Glucocorticoids are therapeutically useful for which broad category of disorders, including gout, rheumatoid arthritis, asthma, and IBD?

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids are broadly useful across inflammatory conditions because their core mechanisms — blocking phospholipase A2 (reducing prostaglandins and leukotrienes) and inhibiting NF-kB-driven cytokine transcription — target pathways common to inflammation regardless of the specific trigger, whether crystal-induced (gout), autoimmune (rheumatoid arthritis), allergic/bronchial (asthma), or mucosal (IBD). This shared final common pathway of suppressing inflammatory mediator production and immune cell activation is why one drug class has such wide applicability across seemingly unrelated organ systems. Recognizing inflammation as the unifying thread (rather than the specific organ or trigger) is key to understanding glucocorticoid pharmacology.

incorrectas.A: Glucocorticoids are not chemotherapeutic agents targeting neoplastic cell proliferation broadly (though they are used adjunctively in some hematologic malignancies like lymphoma) — the conditions listed (gout, RA, asthma, IBD) are inflammatory, not neoplastic, disorders.
incorrectas.B: Glucocorticoids have no direct antimicrobial action and, in fact, can worsen infections by suppressing immune defenses — the conditions listed are inflammatory processes, not infections, that benefit from immune/inflammatory suppression rather than antimicrobial killing.
incorrectas.D: While glucocorticoids do have metabolic effects (e.g., hyperglycemia, protein catabolism), these are side effects of the drug rather than the therapeutic rationale for treating gout, RA, asthma, or IBD, which are targeted for their inflammatory, not metabolic, pathology.

preguntas.q: Glucocorticoids are used clinically for what type of therapy in transplant rejection prevention and autoimmune disease treatment?

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids suppress both innate and adaptive immune responses — by inhibiting IL-2-driven T and B cell activation, promoting lymphocyte apoptosis/redistribution, and blocking NF-kB-mediated cytokine transcription — making them classic immunosuppressive agents. This broad dampening of immune activation is exactly what is needed to prevent the host immune system from attacking a transplanted organ (rejection) or from continuing to attack self-tissue in autoimmune disease. Their immunosuppressive potency, though therapeutically valuable, comes with the trade-off of increased infection risk during use.

incorrectas.A: Glucocorticoids have no direct antimicrobial killing action against pathogens — in fact, by suppressing the immune system, they can impair the body's ability to fight infections, which is the opposite of an antimicrobial effect.
incorrectas.C: Glucocorticoids are not anticoagulants and do not act on the clotting cascade or platelets in a way analogous to heparin or warfarin — their relevant action here is immune suppression, not anticoagulation.
incorrectas.D: While high-dose glucocorticoids are used as part of some chemotherapy regimens (e.g., in lymphoma) to induce apoptosis of malignant lymphocytes, in the context of transplant rejection prevention and autoimmune disease, their role is immunosuppression, not cytoreductive chemotherapy of a tumor.

preguntas.q: What effect do glucocorticoids have on peripheral insulin sensitivity?

o.D: Selectively increase hepatic insulin sensitivity only

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids increase insulin resistance by antagonizing insulin's effects at the cellular level — impairing GLUT4 translocation and glucose uptake in muscle and adipose tissue while simultaneously promoting hepatic gluconeogenesis, together raising blood glucose despite normal or elevated insulin levels. This counter-regulatory, anti-insulin action is why chronic steroid use can precipitate or worsen diabetes (steroid-induced hyperglycemia), a well-recognized adverse effect requiring glucose monitoring during therapy. It reflects glucocorticoids' broader catabolic, stress-hormone role in mobilizing energy substrates rather than storing them.

incorrectas.A: Glucocorticoids decrease, not increase, insulin sensitivity — improved insulin sensitivity would lower blood glucose, which is the opposite of the hyperglycemic, diabetogenic effect steroids are known to cause.
incorrectas.B: Glucocorticoids have a clear, clinically significant effect on insulin action (causing resistance), which is why steroid-induced hyperglycemia and new-onset diabetes are recognized complications of chronic therapy — 'no effect' understates a well-documented pharmacologic action.
incorrectas.D: The insulin resistance caused by glucocorticoids is not limited to the liver alone — it also significantly impairs peripheral (muscle and adipose) glucose uptake, which is actually a major contributor to the hyperglycemia seen with steroid use.

preguntas.q: Glucocorticoids can cause hyperglycemia by stimulating which hepatic metabolic process?

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids stimulate hepatic gluconeogenesis by upregulating key gluconeogenic enzymes (like PEPCK) and by providing amino acid substrates through peripheral protein catabolism (breaking down muscle protein into amino acids that the liver converts to glucose). This raises blood glucose levels as part of the stress-hormone response, ensuring adequate glucose supply to the brain during physiologic stress, but chronically it contributes to steroid-induced hyperglycemia and diabetes. This is a distinct process from glycogenolysis, which breaks down existing stored glycogen rather than synthesizing new glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors.

incorrectas.A: Glycogenolysis is the breakdown of stored glycogen to release glucose (classically driven acutely by glucagon and epinephrine), which is a different process from gluconeogenesis — glucocorticoids' major hyperglycemic contribution is through increased gluconeogenesis, not primarily glycogen breakdown.
incorrectas.C: Glycolysis is the breakdown of glucose for energy production, which would lower rather than raise blood glucose — this is the opposite of the hyperglycemic effect being described for glucocorticoids.
incorrectas.D: Lipogenesis is fat synthesis and storage, an anabolic lipid process unrelated to hepatic glucose production — glucocorticoids' hyperglycemic action operates through gluconeogenesis, not through stimulating fat synthesis.

preguntas.q: In addition to stimulating gluconeogenesis, glucocorticoids increase which hepatic storage process?

e.correcta: In addition to driving gluconeogenesis, glucocorticoids promote hepatic glycogen synthesis and storage by activating glycogen synthase, which paradoxically means the liver both makes new glucose and stores some of it as glycogen simultaneously — while peripheral tissues experience reduced glucose uptake and increased catabolism. This dual hepatic effect (increased gluconeogenesis plus increased glycogen storage) is a classic, testable feature distinguishing glucocorticoids' liver-specific actions from their catabolic effects elsewhere in the body (muscle protein breakdown, adipose lipolysis).

incorrectas.B: Glucocorticoids do not primarily promote hepatic triglyceride storage as their signature additional hepatic effect — their well-known combined action alongside gluconeogenesis is increased glycogen storage via glycogen synthase activation.
incorrectas.C: Glucocorticoids promote protein catabolism (breakdown) in peripheral tissues like muscle to supply amino acids for gluconeogenesis, which is the opposite of 'protein storage' — they are catabolic, not anabolic, for protein in peripheral tissue.
incorrectas.D: Ketone body storage is not a recognized hepatic effect of glucocorticoids — ketogenesis relates more to states of insulin deficiency/fasting, and glucocorticoids' distinguishing additional hepatic action paired with gluconeogenesis is glycogen storage, not ketone handling.

preguntas.q: Exogenous glucocorticoids are used as replacement therapy for which condition, which can otherwise progress to circulatory shock, hypoglycemia, and death?

e.correcta: Adrenal insufficiency (whether primary, as in Addison disease, or secondary/tertiary from HPA axis suppression) means the body cannot produce enough cortisol to maintain vascular tone, gluconeogenesis, and stress response; exogenous glucocorticoids (e.g., hydrocortisone) replace this deficit. Without replacement, the loss of cortisol's permissive effect on catecholamine action leads to vasodilation and refractory hypotension (shock), while loss of cortisol's gluconeogenic/glycogenolytic support causes hypoglycemia — together this constitutes an adrenal crisis, which is fatal if untreated. This is why patients with known adrenal insufficiency require stress-dose steroids during illness or surgery.

incorrectas.A: Cushing syndrome is a state of glucocorticoid excess, not deficiency, so giving more glucocorticoid would worsen rather than treat it — management instead involves reducing steroid exposure or removing the source of excess cortisol/ACTH.
incorrectas.C: Hyperaldosteronism is excess mineralocorticoid activity causing hypertension and hypokalemia; treatment uses mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like spironolactone, not glucocorticoid replacement, since cortisol is not deficient here.
incorrectas.D: Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting adrenal medullary tumor causing episodic hypertension; it is managed with alpha- then beta-blockade before surgical resection, and has nothing to do with cortisol deficiency.

preguntas.q: Chronic glucocorticoid use has what effect on peripheral skeletal muscle, contributing to weakness and thin extremities?

e.correcta: Chronic glucocorticoid excess exerts a catabolic effect on skeletal muscle by promoting protein breakdown and inhibiting protein synthesis, which manifests clinically as proximal muscle weakness (steroid myopathy) and thin, wasted extremities — a hallmark exam finding alongside central obesity in Cushing syndrome. This catabolic shift occurs because cortisol mobilizes amino acids from peripheral tissues to supply substrate for hepatic gluconeogenesis, sacrificing muscle mass to maintain blood glucose during stress.

incorrectas.A: An anabolic effect would build muscle mass, which is the opposite of what glucocorticoids do to peripheral skeletal muscle — anabolic steroids (androgens) have this effect, not glucocorticoids.
incorrectas.C: Glucocorticoids clearly do have a significant effect on muscle — the classic Cushingoid habitus of thin limbs with proximal weakness is a direct consequence of chronic catabolism, not an absence of effect.
incorrectas.D: A hypertrophic effect would increase muscle bulk, but glucocorticoid excess instead atrophies muscle by breaking down protein for gluconeogenic substrate, producing weakness rather than growth.

preguntas.q: Glucocorticoids have what effect on peripheral (extremity) fat tissue, in contrast to their effect on central adiposity?

o.D: Effect identical to central fat tissue

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids have a catabolic (lipolytic) effect on peripheral extremity fat, breaking it down and redistributing it, while paradoxically promoting lipogenesis centrally (face, neck, trunk) — producing the classic Cushingoid pattern of thin arms/legs with truncal obesity, moon facies, and a buffalo hump. This differential regional effect is thought to relate to depot-specific sensitivity to cortisol and insulin, with central fat being more responsive to the lipogenic, insulin-resistant state that cortisol excess creates.

incorrectas.A: An anabolic/lipogenic effect on peripheral fat would cause fat accumulation in the extremities, but this is the opposite of what is seen — peripheral fat is broken down while central fat accumulates.
incorrectas.C: Glucocorticoids clearly do affect peripheral fat — the thin extremities of Cushing syndrome result directly from lipolysis in that depot, so 'no effect' is inconsistent with the classic body habitus.
incorrectas.D: The effect on peripheral fat is explicitly opposite to that on central fat (catabolic versus anabolic), which is exactly what produces the characteristic disproportionate fat redistribution seen in glucocorticoid excess.

preguntas.q: Prolonged administration of exogenous glucocorticoids (e.g., for an autoimmune condition) can cause which iatrogenic syndrome?

e.correcta: Prolonged exogenous glucocorticoid use (e.g., prednisone for an autoimmune disease) directly causes iatrogenic Cushing syndrome — cortisol excess from an external source rather than endogenous ACTH or adrenal/pituitary tumor. It produces the same features as endogenous disease (central obesity, moon facies, buffalo hump, striae, hyperglycemia, hypertension, osteoporosis) but importantly suppresses endogenous ACTH and adrenal function via negative feedback, so abrupt discontinuation risks adrenal insufficiency and steroids must be tapered.

incorrectas.B: Conn syndrome is primary hyperaldosteronism from an aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma, causing hypertension and hypokalemia — it is not caused by exogenous glucocorticoid administration and involves a different hormone axis.
incorrectas.A: Addison disease is primary adrenal insufficiency (cortisol deficiency), the opposite state of glucocorticoid excess produced by chronic steroid therapy; exogenous steroids would suppress, not mimic, adrenal failure while being taken.
incorrectas.D: Nelson syndrome is the development of an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma after bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing disease, due to loss of cortisol feedback — a distinct, specific complication unrelated to exogenous steroid administration.

preguntas.q: Chronic glucocorticoid therapy can cause osteoporosis through which mechanism, and what supplementation helps prevent this adverse effect?

o.A: Inhibition of osteoclast activity; prevented with bisphosphonates only
o.B: Inhibition of osteoblast activity; prevented with calcium and vitamin D
o.C: Stimulation of osteoclast activity; prevented with estrogen replacement
o.D: Increased renal calcium reabsorption; prevented with loop diuretics

e.correcta: Chronic glucocorticoids cause osteoporosis primarily by inhibiting osteoblast activity (reducing bone formation) while also decreasing intestinal calcium absorption and increasing renal calcium excretion, tipping bone remodeling toward net loss; calcium and vitamin D supplementation (often with bisphosphonates in higher-risk patients) helps offset this by supporting mineralization and osteoblast-mediated bone formation. This is why patients on long-term steroids are routinely screened with bone density studies and started on calcium/vitamin D prophylaxis.

incorrectas.A: Glucocorticoids do not primarily work by inhibiting osteoclasts — the dominant mechanism is osteoblast suppression, and bisphosphonates (which inhibit osteoclasts) are an adjunct, not the sole preventive measure typically emphasized.
incorrectas.C: Glucocorticoids do not stimulate osteoclast activity as their primary mechanism of bone loss, and estrogen replacement is not the standard first-line prevention for steroid-induced osteoporosis — calcium and vitamin D are.
incorrectas.D: Glucocorticoids actually increase renal calcium excretion rather than reabsorption, contributing to negative calcium balance, and loop diuretics would worsen (not prevent) calcium loss since they also promote calciuria.

preguntas.q: High-dose glucocorticoid therapy can cause a neuropsychiatric adverse effect characterized by hypomania, confusion, and hallucinations. What is this called?

e.correcta: Steroid-induced psychosis is a well-recognized neuropsychiatric adverse effect of high-dose or prolonged glucocorticoid therapy, presenting with mood changes ranging from euphoria/hypomania to depression, along with confusion, agitation, and sometimes frank hallucinations or delusions. The mechanism relates to glucocorticoid effects on limbic structures (hippocampus, amygdala) and neurotransmitter systems, and symptoms typically improve with dose reduction or discontinuation, distinguishing it from primary psychiatric illness.

incorrectas.B: Serotonin syndrome results from excess serotonergic activity (e.g., combining SSRIs/MAOIs), presenting with hyperthermia, clonus, hyperreflexia, and autonomic instability — a distinct toxidrome unrelated to glucocorticoid pharmacology.
incorrectas.C: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is caused by dopamine receptor blockade (typically antipsychotics), presenting with rigidity, hyperthermia, and autonomic instability — it is a dopaminergic phenomenon, not linked to glucocorticoid use.
incorrectas.D: Wernicke encephalopathy results from thiamine (B1) deficiency, presenting with ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, and confusion, classically in alcoholics or malnourished patients — it has no relationship to glucocorticoid administration.

preguntas.q: Chronic glucocorticoid use predisposes to reactivation of latent infections, presenting as cavitary lesions in the upper lung lobes. Which organism is classically implicated?

e.correcta: Mycobacterium tuberculosis classically reactivates from latent granulomas (where cell-mediated immunity had kept it contained) when glucocorticoids suppress T-cell function, presenting as cavitary lesions in the upper lobes due to the higher oxygen tension there favoring this obligate aerobe's growth. This is why patients are screened for latent TB (e.g., with PPD or IGRA) before starting chronic immunosuppressive steroid therapy.

incorrectas.B: Pneumocystis jirovecii causes an interstitial pneumonia in immunosuppressed hosts (classically HIV with low CD4 counts), presenting with diffuse ground-glass opacities rather than focal upper-lobe cavitary lesions.
incorrectas.C: Aspergillus fumigatus can cause invasive or cavitary disease in immunosuppressed patients, but it classically colonizes pre-existing cavities (forming a fungus ball) rather than being the classic organism for primary reactivation causing new upper-lobe cavities in this context.
incorrectas.D: Histoplasma capsulatum can cause cavitary pulmonary disease, particularly in the Ohio/Mississippi River valleys, but it is not the organism classically emphasized for steroid-induced reactivation with upper-lobe cavitation — that distinction belongs to TB.

preguntas.q: A patient on chronic high-dose glucocorticoids develops new hyperglycemia requiring treatment. What is this drug-induced condition called?

e.correcta: Steroid diabetes refers to new-onset hyperglycemia induced by glucocorticoid therapy, which occurs because cortisol promotes hepatic gluconeogenesis, decreases peripheral glucose uptake by antagonizing insulin signaling in muscle and fat, and increases insulin resistance overall. This is a dose- and duration-dependent adverse effect that often resolves or improves when steroids are tapered, distinguishing it from primary autoimmune or genetic forms of diabetes.

incorrectas.B: Diabetes insipidus is a disorder of insufficient ADH action (central or nephrogenic) causing dilute polyuria, unrelated to glucose metabolism or glucocorticoid-induced insulin resistance.
incorrectas.C: MODY (maturity-onset diabetes of the young) is a genetic, autosomal dominant form of diabetes from beta-cell dysfunction, unrelated to drug exposure or steroid-induced insulin resistance.
incorrectas.D: Latent autoimmune diabetes of adults (LADA) is a slowly progressive autoimmune beta-cell destruction process, a distinct entity from the drug-induced insulin resistance mechanism responsible for steroid-induced hyperglycemia.

preguntas.q: Which specific gastrointestinal adverse effect is associated with glucocorticoid use?

e.correcta: Peptic ulcers are a recognized gastrointestinal adverse effect of glucocorticoids, thought to result from impaired mucosal defense (reduced prostaglandin-mediated mucus and bicarbonate secretion) that leaves the gastric epithelium more vulnerable to acid injury, an effect that is compounded when steroids are combined with NSAIDs. This is why patients on chronic steroids, especially with concurrent NSAID use, are often given gastroprotection (e.g., a PPI).

incorrectas.B: Pseudomembranous colitis is caused by Clostridioides difficile overgrowth, typically following antibiotic use that disrupts normal gut flora — it is not a recognized direct effect of glucocorticoid therapy.
incorrectas.C: Achalasia is a motility disorder from loss of myenteric plexus neurons in the esophagus, causing dysphagia to both solids and liquids — it has no established link to glucocorticoid pharmacology.
incorrectas.D: Mallory-Weiss tears result from mechanical mucosal tearing at the gastroesophageal junction, classically from forceful vomiting or retching, and are not a pharmacologic effect of glucocorticoids.

preguntas.q: Which two hormone or hormone-analog agents are used in the acute management of esophageal variceal bleeding?

e.correcta: Octreotide (a somatostatin analog) and vasopressin analogs (such as terlipressin, with desmopressin sometimes grouped here for the underlying vasopressin-analog concept) reduce splanchnic blood flow and portal pressure by causing selective splanchnic vasoconstriction, which decreases flow through the dilated, fragile esophageal varices and helps control acute variceal hemorrhage. This pharmacologic bridge is used alongside endoscopic band ligation/sclerotherapy as first-line acute management of variceal bleeding.

incorrectas.B: Oxytocin promotes uterine contraction and milk letdown, and insulin regulates glucose uptake — neither has any effect on splanchnic vascular tone or portal pressure relevant to variceal bleeding.
incorrectas.C: Glucagon relaxes smooth muscle (used therapeutically for esophageal food bolus obstruction or as an antidote in beta-blocker overdose) and cortisol is a glucocorticoid — neither reduces portal venous pressure or controls variceal hemorrhage.
incorrectas.D: Growth hormone and thyroxine regulate growth and metabolic rate respectively; they have no vasoconstrictive action on the splanchnic circulation and play no role in acute variceal bleed management.

preguntas.q: How does maternal cardiac output change during a normal pregnancy?

e.correcta: Maternal cardiac output increases by roughly 30-50% during normal pregnancy, driven by increased stroke volume (from expanded blood volume) and increased heart rate, to meet the metabolic demands of the growing fetus, placenta, and maternal tissues. This hemodynamic change begins early in the first trimester, peaks around the late second/early third trimester, and is why pre-existing cardiac conditions (e.g., valvular stenosis) can decompensate during pregnancy.

incorrectas.A: Cardiac output does not decrease during pregnancy — it must increase substantially to support the added metabolic and perfusion demands of the fetoplacental unit, making a 50% decrease physiologically incorrect.
incorrectas.B: Cardiac output is far from unchanged in pregnancy; the substantial rise in blood volume and heart rate specifically exists to accommodate increased tissue perfusion needs, making 'no change' an underestimate of the physiologic adaptation.
incorrectas.D: A 10% increase understates the actual physiologic change — cardiac output rises considerably more (approximately 30-50%) to support the significantly increased circulatory demands of pregnancy.

preguntas.q: During pregnancy, plasma volume and RBC mass both increase, but by different amounts. Which pattern is correct?

o.A: Plasma volume increases 30%, RBC volume increases 50%
o.B: Plasma volume increases 50%, RBC volume increases 30%
o.D: Plasma volume decreases, RBC volume increases

e.correcta: In normal pregnancy, plasma volume expands by roughly 50% (driven by estrogen- and aldosterone-mediated sodium and water retention to support the low-resistance uteroplacental circulation), while RBC mass increases by a smaller amount, around 20-30%, because erythropoiesis increases but not proportionally as much as plasma expansion. Because plasma volume outpaces RBC mass, hemoglobin concentration falls, producing the physiologic dilutional anemia of pregnancy that is a normal finding rather than a pathologic one.

incorrectas.A: This reverses the actual relationship — plasma volume increases more (about 50%), not less, than RBC mass (about 20-30%), which is exactly why hemoglobin concentration drops during pregnancy rather than rising.
incorrectas.C: If both increased equally, hematocrit and hemoglobin concentration would stay roughly stable, but pregnancy is well known for producing a mild dilutional anemia, which only happens because the two compartments expand disproportionately.
incorrectas.D: Plasma volume does not decrease in pregnancy — it substantially increases to meet the demands of the expanding maternal-fetal circulation, and RBC mass increases as well, just to a lesser degree.

preguntas.q: The disproportionate increase in plasma volume (50%) relative to RBC volume (30%) during pregnancy results in what clinical finding, and what is its proposed benefit?

o.A: Polycythemia; improves oxygen delivery to the fetus
o.B: Anemia; decreases blood viscosity to reduce postpartum bleeding

e.correcta: Because plasma volume expands more (about 50%) than red blood cell mass (about 30%) during pregnancy, the blood becomes hemodiluted, producing a physiologic (dilutional) anemia — this is a normal, expected finding, not necessarily iron deficiency. The proposed benefit is that the resulting lower blood viscosity reduces cardiac workload and is thought to decrease the relative blood loss (as a percentage of total blood volume) at delivery, protecting against the hemodynamic impact of postpartum hemorrhage.

incorrectas.A: Polycythemia would mean an increase in red cell concentration, but the disproportionate rise in plasma volume relative to RBC mass causes hemodilution (anemia), not polycythemia — this option reverses the actual direction of the hematologic change.
incorrectas.C: While pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state that does increase thromboembolism risk, that increased risk is due to changes in clotting factors and venous stasis, not the physiologic dilutional anemia itself, which is instead framed as protective against hemorrhage.
incorrectas.D: This again incorrectly labels the finding as polycythemia rather than anemia, and incorrectly links it to pre-eclampsia, which is a hypertensive/vascular disorder of pregnancy unrelated to the plasma-volume-to-RBC-mass ratio.

preguntas.q: How does maternal blood pressure typically change during early pregnancy?

o.C: Decreases, then returns to normal near term

e.correcta: Maternal blood pressure typically decreases during the first and second trimesters due to progesterone-mediated systemic vasodilation and decreased peripheral vascular resistance (as the low-resistance placental circulation develops), then rises back toward pre-pregnancy levels as term approaches. This normal dip is important to recognize so it isn't mistaken for pathology, while a rise above baseline with proteinuria after 20 weeks should instead raise concern for pre-eclampsia.

incorrectas.A: Blood pressure does not increase progressively throughout normal pregnancy — a progressive rise, especially with proteinuria or after 20 weeks, is actually a red flag for pre-eclampsia rather than a normal physiologic pattern.
incorrectas.B: Blood pressure is not constant during pregnancy; the mid-pregnancy dip due to progesterone-driven vasodilation is a well-documented physiologic change, not a static state.
incorrectas.D: Blood pressure does not stay persistently low after delivery — it returns toward normal near term and postpartum as the vasodilatory hormonal milieu of pregnancy resolves, rather than remaining suppressed.

preguntas.q: How does minute ventilation change during pregnancy, and what primarily drives this change?

o.A: Increases, mainly due to increased respiratory rate
o.B: Decreases, mainly due to decreased tidal volume
o.C: Increases, mainly due to increased tidal volume
o.D: Remains unchanged despite increased oxygen demand

e.correcta: Minute ventilation increases substantially during pregnancy (up to 30-50%), driven mainly by an increase in tidal volume rather than respiratory rate, largely due to progesterone's stimulatory effect on the central respiratory drive (increasing chemoreceptor sensitivity to CO2). This produces deeper (not necessarily faster) breaths, which helps lower maternal PCO2 and facilitates CO2 transfer from the fetus to the mother across the placenta.

incorrectas.A: While respiratory rate can increase slightly, the dominant driver of increased minute ventilation in pregnancy is increased tidal volume (deeper breaths), not primarily an increased rate, making this option's emphasis backwards.
incorrectas.B: Minute ventilation increases, not decreases, during pregnancy — progesterone increases central respiratory drive, so a decrease in tidal volume contradicts the well-established hyperventilation of pregnancy.
incorrectas.D: Minute ventilation clearly changes (increases) during pregnancy in response to increased progesterone-driven respiratory drive and metabolic demand, so 'unchanged' does not reflect the actual physiologic adaptation.

preguntas.q: The increased minute ventilation of pregnancy leads to what acid-base change in maternal blood?

e.correcta: The pregnancy-induced hyperventilation (increased minute ventilation via increased tidal volume) causes excess CO2 to be blown off, lowering maternal PCO2 and producing a mild, compensated respiratory alkalosis — the kidneys respond by excreting bicarbonate to partially normalize pH. This mild respiratory alkalosis is a normal finding on maternal arterial blood gas during pregnancy and should not be mistaken for pathology.

incorrectas.A: Respiratory acidosis would result from hypoventilation and CO2 retention, which is the opposite of what happens in pregnancy — hyperventilation lowers, not raises, maternal PCO2.
incorrectas.B: Metabolic alkalosis arises from primary bicarbonate excess or acid loss (e.g., vomiting), not from a ventilatory change — the acid-base disturbance of pregnancy originates from the respiratory system (hyperventilation), not a primary metabolic process.
incorrectas.D: There is no mixed acidosis picture in normal pregnancy; the ventilatory changes drive a single, mild respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation, not a combined acidotic disturbance.

preguntas.q: How do maternal PCO2 levels change during pregnancy, and why?

o.A: Increased, due to decreased ventilation rate
o.C: Unchanged, due to compensatory renal mechanisms
o.D: Increased, due to increased metabolic CO2 production outpacing ventilation

e.correcta: Maternal PCO2 decreases during pregnancy because progesterone increases central respiratory drive, causing chronic mild hyperventilation (increased tidal volume) that blows off more CO2 than is produced. This creates a favorable CO2 gradient that promotes diffusion of CO2 from fetal blood into maternal blood across the placenta, aiding fetal waste clearance.

incorrectas.A: PCO2 does not increase in pregnancy — ventilation rises (not falls), which lowers rather than raises maternal PCO2, making this option's direction incorrect.
incorrectas.C: PCO2 is not unchanged in pregnancy; it measurably decreases due to progesterone-driven hyperventilation, and this is a respiratory (not renal compensatory) phenomenon.
incorrectas.D: Metabolic CO2 production does rise somewhat in pregnancy, but ventilation increases even more, so the net effect is a fall in PCO2, not a rise — this option gets the net direction backwards.

preguntas.q: What is the physiologic purpose of the decreased maternal PCO2 seen during pregnancy?

o.B: To facilitate CO2 elimination from the fetus into maternal circulation
o.D: To increase fetal hemoglobin oxygen affinity

e.correcta: The mild decrease in maternal PCO2 (via pregnancy-induced hyperventilation) creates a favorable partial pressure gradient that allows fetal CO2 to diffuse more readily across the placenta into maternal blood, where it can then be exhaled by the mother. This is an elegant adaptation ensuring the fetus, which cannot ventilate on its own, can efficiently offload its metabolic waste product.

incorrectas.A: Reducing maternal oxygen consumption is not the purpose of decreased PCO2 — in fact, maternal oxygen consumption increases during pregnancy to meet higher metabolic demands, unrelated to this CO2 gradient mechanism.
incorrectas.C: Preventing maternal metabolic alkalosis is not the purpose here; the ventilatory change actually produces a mild respiratory alkalosis (with renal compensation), rather than being aimed at preventing a metabolic disturbance.
incorrectas.D: Fetal hemoglobin's high oxygen affinity is an intrinsic property of its hemoglobin structure (different chain composition and reduced 2,3-BPG binding), not something driven by maternal PCO2 changes.

preguntas.q: How does coagulability change during pregnancy, and what is a proposed physiologic benefit of this change?

o.A: Increased (hypercoagulability), which decreases postpartum bleeding risk
o.C: Unchanged, since clotting factors are stable throughout gestation
o.D: Increased, primarily to support fetal iron transport

e.correcta: Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state (increased coagulability), with rises in clotting factors (e.g., fibrinogen, factors VII-X) and decreased fibrinolytic activity, which is thought to serve the physiologic purpose of limiting hemorrhage at the highly vascular placental implantation site during delivery. The trade-off is a clinically significant increased risk of venous thromboembolism, which is why pregnancy and the postpartum period are recognized risk factors for DVT/PE.

incorrectas.B: Pregnancy causes hypercoagulability, not hypocoagulability — a decreased clotting tendency would actually increase bleeding risk at delivery rather than protecting against it, and it would not explain the well-documented increased VTE risk in pregnancy.
incorrectas.C: Clotting factors are not stable during pregnancy; multiple procoagulant factors rise and fibrinolysis is suppressed, producing a measurable hypercoagulable state that has real clinical consequences (increased VTE risk).
incorrectas.D: The hypercoagulable state of pregnancy is related to hemostasis at delivery, not fetal iron transport, which is instead handled by transferrin receptors and active placental iron transfer mechanisms unrelated to clotting factors.

preguntas.q: How does glomerular filtration rate (GFR) change during pregnancy, and what lab findings result?

o.A: Increases, causing decreased BUN and creatinine
o.B: Decreases, causing increased BUN and creatinine
o.D: Increases, causing increased BUN and creatinine

e.correcta: GFR increases substantially during pregnancy (up to 50%) due to increased renal plasma flow and cardiac output, which enhances the kidneys' ability to filter and excrete nitrogenous waste, resulting in lower BUN and creatinine than the non-pregnant baseline. This means creatinine and BUN values considered 'normal' outside of pregnancy may actually indicate renal impairment in a pregnant patient, an important clinical pearl when interpreting labs.

incorrectas.B: GFR increases rather than decreases in pregnancy, so BUN and creatinine actually fall (due to enhanced clearance), not rise — a decreased GFR with elevated retention values would instead suggest a pathologic process like pre-eclampsia.
incorrectas.C: GFR is not unchanged in pregnancy; the substantial rise in renal plasma flow and filtration is a well-established physiologic adaptation that measurably lowers BUN and creatinine.
incorrectas.D: While GFR does increase, this option incorrectly pairs that increase with increased BUN/creatinine — increased filtration should lower, not raise, these markers, making this internally inconsistent.

preguntas.q: How does insulin resistance change during pregnancy, and what hormone primarily drives this change?

o.B: Increases, due to human placental lactogen
o.C: Increases, due to increased cortisol only

e.correcta: Insulin resistance increases during pregnancy, driven primarily by human placental lactogen (hPL), a placental hormone that has anti-insulin (diabetogenic) effects on maternal tissues, shifting maternal metabolism toward increased lipolysis and ensuring glucose is preferentially shunted to the fetus rather than consumed by maternal peripheral tissues. This adaptive insulin resistance is why gestational diabetes can unmask or worsen as pregnancy progresses, typically becoming most pronounced in the second and third trimesters when hPL levels are highest.

incorrectas.A: Insulin resistance increases, not decreases, in pregnancy, and progesterone is not the primary driver of this metabolic shift — human placental lactogen is the key hormone responsible for the anti-insulin effect.
incorrectas.C: While cortisol does contribute somewhat to insulin resistance, it is not the primary driver in pregnancy — hPL is considered the main hormone responsible for the marked insulin resistance seen, especially later in gestation.
incorrectas.D: Insulin resistance clearly changes (increases) during gestation, tracking with rising hPL levels as the placenta grows, so 'unchanged throughout gestation' does not reflect the actual physiologic progression.

preguntas.q: Around which gestational weeks do maternal hCG levels typically peak?

e.correcta: Maternal hCG, produced by the syncytiotrophoblast, rises rapidly after implantation and typically peaks around weeks 8-10 of gestation before declining and plateauing for the remainder of pregnancy. This peak-then-decline pattern is clinically relevant because hCG trends (not just absolute values) are used to assess pregnancy viability and to interpret quad screen results later in gestation.

incorrectas.A: Weeks 2-4 is too early — hCG is just beginning its rapid rise around this time (enough to be detected on a pregnancy test), but it has not yet reached its peak concentration.
incorrectas.C: Weeks 20-22 is well past the peak; by this point hCG has already declined substantially from its first-trimester peak and settled into the lower plateau level characteristic of the second and third trimesters.
incorrectas.D: Weeks 36-38 reflects late third-trimester levels, when hCG is at its stable, lower plateau — far past the early peak that occurs in the first trimester.

preguntas.q: In the GTPAL system used to summarize a woman's obstetric history, what does the "G" represent?

o.D: Total number of deliveries after 37 weeks

e.correcta: In GTPAL, "G" stands for gravidity — the total number of times a woman has been pregnant, regardless of outcome (including the current pregnancy, miscarriages, or abortions), which is distinct from parity (number of pregnancies carried to a viable gestational age). This distinction matters clinically because gravidity counts pregnancies, while the remaining letters (TPAL) break down outcomes of those pregnancies in more detail.

incorrectas.B: Gestational age at first pregnancy is not what any letter in GTPAL represents; GTPAL summarizes counts of pregnancy outcomes, not timing of a specific pregnancy.
incorrectas.C: The number of living children is captured by the "L" (living) at the end of GTPAL, not by "G", which instead refers to total pregnancies regardless of outcome.
incorrectas.D: Total deliveries after 37 weeks relates to the "T" (term deliveries) component of GTPAL, not "G", which counts all pregnancies rather than just term deliveries.

preguntas.q: In the GTPAL obstetric history mnemonic, the letter "T" refers to which of the following?

o.B: Total number of deliveries after 37 weeks (term deliveries)
o.C: Total number of deliveries before 20 weeks

e.correcta: In the GTPAL mnemonic (Gravidity, Term, Preterm, Abortions, Living), the "T" stands for the total number of term deliveries, defined as births occurring at or after 37 weeks gestation. This is distinguished from "P" (preterm deliveries, before 37 weeks) and "A" (abortions/losses before 20 weeks), so an accurate obstetric history requires sorting each prior pregnancy outcome into the correct gestational-age category. Getting T right matters clinically because term versus preterm delivery history informs risk stratification for future pregnancies (e.g., recurrent preterm labor risk).

incorrectas.A: Total number of pregnancies is captured by "G" (gravidity), which counts all pregnancies regardless of outcome, not the specific subset of term deliveries that "T" refers to.
incorrectas.C: Deliveries before 20 weeks are counted under "A" (abortions), which captures spontaneous or induced pregnancy losses prior to viability, distinct from the term-delivery count denoted by "T."
incorrectas.D: Total number of living children is represented by "L" (living), the final letter of the mnemonic, which reflects current survival outcome rather than the gestational timing of delivery captured by "T."

preguntas.q: When using GTPAL to document obstetric history, what does the "P" stand for?

o.B: Preterm deliveries: deliveries after 20 weeks but before 37 weeks

e.correcta: In GTPAL, "P" stands for preterm deliveries — pregnancies delivered after 20 weeks gestation but before completion of 37 weeks — distinguishing them from term deliveries ("T", at or after 37 weeks) and from abortions ("A", losses before 20 weeks). This distinction is clinically important because a history of preterm delivery is itself a risk factor for recurrent preterm birth in future pregnancies.

incorrectas.A: Parity as total pregnancies conflates parity with gravidity; gravidity ("G") already captures total pregnancies, while "P" in GTPAL specifically refers to the subset of deliveries occurring in the preterm window (20-37 weeks).
incorrectas.C: Postpartum hemorrhage episodes are not tracked by any letter in the standard GTPAL system, which is designed to summarize pregnancy outcomes by gestational timing and viability, not delivery complications.
incorrectas.D: Stillbirths are not exclusively what "P" denotes; stillbirths could fall under preterm or term categories depending on gestational age at delivery, and "P" specifically denotes the preterm gestational age window, not fetal viability status.

preguntas.q: In a woman's GTPAL obstetric summary, the letter "A" corresponds to which category?

o.B: Total pregnancies including the current one

e.correcta: In the GTPAL mnemonic, "A" stands for abortions, defined as pregnancy losses (spontaneous or induced) occurring before 20 weeks gestation, which is the standard threshold distinguishing an abortion from a preterm delivery. This obstetric shorthand allows rapid communication of a patient's full reproductive history at a glance.

incorrectas.A: Total number of living children is captured by the "L" (living) component of GTPAL, not the "A," which specifically refers to pregnancy losses before 20 weeks.
incorrectas.B: Total pregnancies including the current one is represented by the "G" (gravida) component, a distinct count from abortions, which specifically tallies losses under 20 weeks.
incorrectas.D: Term deliveries after 37 weeks are captured by the "T" (term) component of GTPAL, separate from the "A" category that counts pregnancy losses before 20 weeks.

preguntas.q: In the GTPAL mnemonic for obstetric history, what does the final letter "L" indicate?

o.B: Number of low birth weight infants
o.D: Number of pregnancy losses before 20 weeks

e.correcta: In the GTPAL mnemonic (Gravida, Term, Preterm, Abortions, Living), the final 'L' specifically tallies the number of children currently alive, which can differ from the total number of pregnancies/deliveries if a child died after birth or in cases of multiple gestation (e.g., twins count as one delivery but two living children). This final tally is clinically important because it captures outcome, not just delivery count, giving a fuller picture of obstetric and family history.

incorrectas.B: Low birth weight infants are not tracked by a specific letter in the standard GTPAL mnemonic; the system focuses on pregnancy timing (term/preterm), losses (abortions), and survival (living), not birth weight specifically.
incorrectas.C: Preterm labors/deliveries are already captured by the 'P' in GTPAL, so the final 'L' does not duplicate this information; it instead refers to the number of children currently living, a distinct piece of data from delivery timing.
incorrectas.D: Pregnancy losses before 20 weeks are captured by the 'A' (abortions, spontaneous or induced) in GTPAL, not by the final 'L', which specifically denotes the count of living children rather than pregnancy losses.

preguntas.q: A pregnancy is classified as "term" if delivery occurs within which gestational age range?

e.correcta: A pregnancy is classified as term when delivery occurs between 37 and 42 weeks of gestation, the window considered to reflect full fetal maturation of organ systems (particularly the lungs) needed for safe extrauterine survival without significant prematurity-related complications. Deliveries before 37 weeks are termed preterm, and those after 42 weeks are termed post-term, both of which carry distinct sets of risks.

incorrectas.A: 34 to 37 weeks falls within the late preterm period, not term — infants born in this window are still at increased risk for respiratory and feeding complications compared to those born after 37 weeks.
incorrectas.C: 20 to 37 weeks spans much of the preterm period (deliveries before 37 weeks are preterm by definition), so this range does not correspond to the term classification, which begins at 37 weeks.
incorrectas.D: 42 to 44 weeks describes post-term pregnancy, which carries its own risks (such as placental insufficiency and macrosomia), and is distinct from and later than the 37-to-42-week term window.

preguntas.q: A pregnant woman undergoes a quad screen. Which combination of results is classically associated with trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)?

o.A: Decreased AFP, decreased estriol, increased hCG, increased inhibin A
o.B: Increased AFP, increased estriol, decreased hCG, decreased inhibin A
o.C: Decreased AFP, increased estriol, decreased hCG, decreased inhibin A
o.D: Increased AFP, decreased estriol, increased hCG, increased inhibin A

e.correcta: The classic quad screen pattern for trisomy 21 is decreased AFP (reflecting relative placental/fetal immaturity of function), decreased estriol (impaired feto-placental steroid synthesis), increased hCG (placental dysfunction leads to compensatory oversecretion), and increased inhibin A — remembered by the mnemonic that AFP and estriol are 'down,' while hCG and inhibin A are 'up.' This combination raises suspicion for Down syndrome and prompts further diagnostic testing such as cell-free DNA screening or amniocentesis with karyotype.

incorrectas.B: This pattern (increased AFP, increased estriol, decreased hCG, decreased inhibin A) does not match trisomy 21; increased AFP with normal/other markers is instead more associated with open neural tube defects or abdominal wall defects, not Down syndrome.
incorrectas.C: While AFP is decreased in trisomy 21, estriol is also decreased (not increased) and hCG is increased (not decreased) in the classic pattern — this option has two of the four markers reversed from the true trisomy 21 profile.
incorrectas.D: This option incorrectly reverses AFP and estriol (showing them increased rather than decreased), while hCG and inhibin A are correctly increased — but the overall mismatched combination does not correspond to the classic trisomy 21 quad screen pattern.

preguntas.q: What effect does a multiple gestation (e.g., twins or triplets) typically have on maternal serum hCG levels?

o.A: No change compared to singleton pregnancy
o.D: Initially increased, then decreased by the third trimester

e.correcta: Multiple gestations involve more placental (trophoblastic) tissue overall, since each fetus has its own placenta or shares an enlarged placental mass, resulting in increased total hCG production compared to a singleton pregnancy. This is one reason markedly elevated hCG for gestational age can raise clinical suspicion for a multiple gestation (or alternatively, a molar pregnancy, which also produces excess trophoblastic tissue).

incorrectas.B: hCG is not decreased in multiple gestations — with more placental tissue producing the hormone, total hCG output rises rather than falls compared to a singleton pregnancy.
incorrectas.A: hCG is not unchanged with multiple gestation; the increased trophoblastic mass from additional placenta(s) drives measurably higher hCG levels than seen in a singleton pregnancy at the same gestational age.
incorrectas.D: hCG does not follow an initial increase followed by a later decrease specific to multiple gestations beyond the normal first-trimester peak-and-plateau pattern seen in all pregnancies — the key feature of multiples is an overall elevated hCG level relative to singleton pregnancies at comparable gestational ages.

preguntas.q: Amniocentesis for prenatal genetic testing is typically performed no earlier than which gestational age?

e.correcta: Amniocentesis is typically performed at 15 to 17 weeks gestation because by this point there is enough amniotic fluid (and enough viable fetal cells shed into it) to safely sample under ultrasound guidance without excessive risk of injuring the fetus or placenta. The fluid obtained is used for karyotyping, AFP measurement (for neural tube defects), and other genetic/biochemical studies, and the mid-second-trimester timing balances diagnostic yield against procedural safety.

incorrectas.A: 10 to 13 weeks is the window for chorionic villus sampling, not amniocentesis — at this earlier gestational age there is too little amniotic fluid to sample safely, which is exactly why CVS (which samples placental tissue instead) is used at this stage.
incorrectas.C: 20 to 24 weeks is later than necessary for amniocentesis; while the fluid volume is certainly adequate by then, waiting this long delays results and narrows the window for decision-making regarding the pregnancy, so amniocentesis is offered earlier once it becomes safe to do.
incorrectas.D: 6 to 9 weeks is far too early for any invasive prenatal diagnostic sampling — at this stage the amniotic cavity and villi are not yet developed enough to sample without a prohibitively high risk of fetal loss.

preguntas.q: Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) can be performed as early as which gestational age range?

e.correcta: CVS can be performed as early as 10 to 13 weeks because it samples chorionic villi (placental trophoblastic tissue) transcervically or transabdominally, which are present and accessible from early in the first trimester — well before there is enough amniotic fluid to perform amniocentesis. This earlier timing is CVS's main advantage, allowing genetic diagnosis (karyotype, specific mutations) early enough to inform first-trimester decision-making.

incorrectas.A: 15 to 17 weeks is the standard window for amniocentesis, not CVS — CVS is specifically valued because it can be done earlier than this, sampling placental villi rather than waiting for adequate amniotic fluid to accumulate.
incorrectas.C: 18 to 20 weeks is even later than the amniocentesis window and offers no advantage over amniocentesis at that stage; it defeats the purpose of CVS, which is to get genetic information earlier in pregnancy.
incorrectas.D: 5 to 8 weeks is too early even for CVS — the chorionic villi have not yet developed sufficiently, and sampling this early carries an markedly increased risk of limb defects and other disruption anomalies.

preguntas.q: How do the risks of fetal loss compare between amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling (CVS)?

o.A: Amniocentesis carries a higher risk (1%) than CVS (0.5%)
o.B: Amniocentesis carries a lower risk (0.5%) than CVS (1%)
o.C: Both procedures carry an equal fetal loss risk of about 2%
o.D: Neither procedure carries any measurable risk of fetal loss

e.correcta: Amniocentesis carries a lower fetal loss risk (about 0.5%, roughly 1 in 200 to 1 in 400 depending on the source) than CVS (about 1%), largely because amniocentesis is performed later in gestation with a well-established, ultrasound-guided needle technique that avoids direct placental disruption, whereas CVS involves sampling placental tissue earlier in a smaller, more vascular uterine cavity. This risk difference is part of the counseling discussion when choosing between early (CVS) versus later (amniocentesis) genetic testing.

incorrectas.A: This reverses the actual risk profile — amniocentesis is the lower-risk procedure of the two, not the higher-risk one, precisely because it is performed later when the uterus and amniotic sac are larger and more forgiving of instrumentation.
incorrectas.C: Neither procedure carries a risk anywhere near 2%; modern ultrasound-guided technique has brought both risks down substantially, with CVS at roughly 1% and amniocentesis at roughly 0.5%, not an equal higher figure for both.
incorrectas.D: Both procedures are invasive and do carry a measurable, quantifiable risk of fetal loss — this is precisely why the choice between them and the decision to pursue invasive testing at all involves careful risk-benefit counseling with the patient.

preguntas.q: Performing chorionic villus sampling before 9 weeks gestation is associated with which fetal complication?

e.correcta: CVS performed before 9 to 10 weeks gestation is associated with limb defects (and oromandibular-limb hypogenesis), thought to result from vascular disruption or embolization of the developing limb bud vasculature during the procedure at a stage when limb formation is still highly sensitive to perfusion insults. This is precisely why CVS protocols restrict the procedure to no earlier than about 10 weeks, giving limb development enough of a head start to reduce this risk.

incorrectas.A: Neural tube defects arise from failure of neural tube closure in the first few weeks of development (around days 21-28) and are detected by elevated AFP or ultrasound findings — they are not a recognized complication caused by early CVS itself.
incorrectas.C: Cardiac septal defects arise from abnormalities in cardiac septation during the fourth to eighth weeks of development due to genetic or teratogenic causes, not as a procedural complication of chorionic villus sampling.
incorrectas.D: Renal agenesis is a primary developmental anomaly of the metanephric system, unrelated to the timing or performance of CVS — it is not among the recognized procedural complications of early sampling.

preguntas.q: Compared to amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling (CVS) has a notable limitation in detecting which type of defect?

e.correcta: CVS samples chorionic villi (placental tissue) rather than amniotic fluid, so it cannot measure alpha-fetoprotein levels or directly visualize the fetus/spine, which means it cannot detect neural tube defects the way amniocentesis (via elevated AFP and acetylcholinesterase in the fluid) can. This is a key practical limitation of CVS that must be supplemented with maternal serum AFP screening or a later anatomy ultrasound if neural tube defects are a concern.

incorrectas.A: Trisomy 21 is readily detected by CVS because chorionic villi share the fetal karyotype, allowing chromosomal analysis just as amniocentesis would — this is one of CVS's core strengths, not a limitation.
incorrectas.B: Sex chromosome abnormalities are also detected via karyotype analysis of the chorionic villi, so CVS performs just as well as amniocentesis for this category of genetic diagnosis.
incorrectas.D: Single-gene mutations can be detected by CVS through DNA analysis of the villous tissue (e.g., PCR-based testing), so this is not a limitation unique to CVS compared to amniocentesis.

preguntas.q: Chorion formation occurs by which day of early embryonic development, such that twinning after this point results in monochorionic twins?

e.correcta: The chorion forms by about day 4-5 post-fertilization as the trophoblast differentiates from the outer cells of the blastocyst, so if a single fertilized egg splits after chorion formation (roughly days 4-8), the resulting twins share one chorion and are monochorionic, whereas splitting before this point (within the first 3-4 days) allows each twin to develop its own separate chorion, yielding dichorionic twins. This timing framework — chorion first, then amnion — is the basis for predicting placentation and amnionicity from the timing of embryonic splitting in monozygotic twinning.

incorrectas.A: Day 8 is closer to the timing of amnion formation, not chorion formation; splitting around this time (after the chorion has already formed but before/around amnion formation) is what produces monochorionic, diamniotic twins, not the chorion-formation cutoff itself.
incorrectas.C: Day 13 is well past both chorion and amnion formation — splitting this late (after the amnion has also formed and the embryonic disc is present) produces monochorionic, monoamniotic twins or, if delayed further, conjoined twins.
incorrectas.D: Day 1 is far too early — at this stage the embryo is only just past the zygote stage undergoing early cleavage divisions, long before trophoblast differentiation and chorion formation occur; splitting this early yields dichorionic, diamniotic twins.

preguntas.q: Amnion formation occurs by which day of embryonic development, such that twinning after this day produces monoamniotic twins?

e.correcta: The amnion forms by day 8 of development. If splitting of the embryonic disc occurs after this point, both twins will be enclosed within the same amniotic sac, producing monoamniotic twins, which carry substantial risk of cord entanglement.

incorrectas.A: Day 4 corresponds to chorion formation, which occurs earlier; splitting after day 4 but before day 8 still allows separate amnions to form, resulting in monochorionic-diamniotic twins.
incorrectas.C: Day 1 is around the time of fertilization, well before either the chorion or amnion has formed; splitting this early yields dichorionic, diamniotic twins (essentially as if from two separate zygotes structurally).
incorrectas.D: Day 13 is beyond the point where monoamniotic twinning would already be established (from splitting between days 8-13); splitting at or after day 13 instead risks incomplete separation and conjoined twins.

preguntas.q: On ultrasound, the presence of a single yolk sac with two fetal poles is most indicative of which type of twin pregnancy?

e.correcta: A single yolk sac with two fetal poles on ultrasound indicates monoamniotic twins, because the yolk sac develops within the amniotic cavity — if there is only one yolk sac despite two embryos, it means both fetuses share a single amniotic sac (the split occurred after amnion formation, around day 8-13). This finding is critical to identify early because monoamniotic twins carry a high risk of cord entanglement and require intensive antenatal surveillance.

incorrectas.A: Dichorionic, diamniotic twins would show two separate yolk sacs (one within each of the two distinct amniotic sacs) along with a thick dividing membrane (the lambda or twin peak sign) and often two separate placentas, not a single shared yolk sac.
incorrectas.B: Monochorionic, diamniotic twins share one placenta/chorion but still have two separate amniotic sacs, so ultrasound would show two yolk sacs (one per amniotic sac) along with a thin dividing membrane (the T sign), not a single yolk sac.
incorrectas.D: Conjoined twins result from incomplete splitting very late (after day 13, once the embryonic disc has formed) and are suggested by inability to separate the fetal bodies or shared organs on ultrasound, not simply by the yolk sac count.

preguntas.q: Cord entanglement on prenatal imaging is a hallmark finding of which type of twin gestation?

e.correcta: Cord entanglement is a hallmark of monoamniotic twins because both fetuses float freely within a single, undivided amniotic sac with no dividing membrane to keep the umbilical cords separated, allowing them to wrap around each other and compress blood flow — a major cause of fetal morbidity and mortality in this twin type. This risk is why monoamniotic pregnancies require close inpatient or intensive outpatient monitoring and typically early, planned delivery.

incorrectas.A: Dichorionic, diamniotic twins each reside in their own separate amniotic sac (and usually have separate placentas), so their umbilical cords are physically separated by the dividing membranes and cannot become entangled with each other.
incorrectas.B: Monochorionic, diamniotic twins share a placenta but still have two distinct amniotic sacs separated by a membrane, which keeps each cord confined to its own sac and prevents entanglement, though this group is instead at risk for twin-twin transfusion syndrome via shared placental vasculature.
incorrectas.D: Dizygotic twins with separate placentas are, by definition, dichorionic and diamniotic (arising from two separately fertilized eggs), so like other diamniotic twins their cords are separated by distinct amniotic sacs and are not at risk for entanglement.

preguntas.q: In twin-twin transfusion syndrome, which twin develops anastomotic vascular connections that lead to anemia, pallor, and growth restriction?

o.D: Neither twin, only the placenta is affected

e.correcta: In twin-twin transfusion syndrome, the donor twin loses blood through abnormal arteriovenous placental anastomoses that shunt blood preferentially to its co-twin, leading to hypovolemia, anemia, pallor, poor perfusion, and consequent growth restriction (and oligohydramnios from reduced renal perfusion and urine output). TTTS occurs specifically in monochorionic twin pregnancies because only they share a single placenta with vascular connections that allow this unbalanced blood shunting between fetuses.

incorrectas.A: The recipient twin is on the receiving end of the shunted blood, developing hypervolemia, polycythemia, and volume-overload heart failure rather than anemia and growth restriction — the opposite physiology from what the question describes.
incorrectas.C: Both twins are affected, but not equally or in the same way — the pathology is discordant by definition, with one twin (donor) losing volume and the other (recipient) gaining it, which is exactly why the syndrome causes such divergent complications in each twin.
incorrectas.D: The placenta is the site of the abnormal vascular connections, but the clinical consequences — anemia and growth restriction in this twin — manifest in the fetus itself, not only in placental tissue, which is why this scenario is attributed to a specific twin's physiology.

preguntas.q: In twin-twin transfusion syndrome, the recipient twin is at risk for which of the following due to receiving excess blood volume?

o.B: Heart failure from volume overload and polycythemia

e.correcta: The recipient twin in TTTS receives excess blood volume through the shared placental anastomoses, leading to polycythemia (from the extra red cell mass) and volume overload that can progress to high-output cardiac failure and hydrops, along with polyhydramnios from increased fetal urine output in response to the volume load. This contrasts directly with the donor twin, who becomes hypovolemic and growth-restricted from the same shunt acting in the opposite direction.

incorrectas.A: Anemia and growth restriction describe the donor twin, who loses blood volume through the anastomoses, not the recipient, who instead becomes volume-overloaded and polycythemic.
incorrectas.C: Limb defects from vascular disruption are associated with early chorionic villus sampling complications, not with the chronic hemodynamic imbalance of twin-twin transfusion syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Neural tube defects arise from failure of neural tube closure early in embryogenesis and are unrelated to the placental vascular shunting physiology that defines twin-twin transfusion syndrome.

preguntas.q: The umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated fetal blood to the placenta, arising as branches of which fetal vessels?

e.correcta: The umbilical arteries arise as branches of the internal iliac (hypogastric) arteries and carry deoxygenated, waste-laden fetal blood back to the placenta for gas and nutrient exchange, running alongside the urachus/median umbilical ligament within the umbilical cord. After birth, the distal portions of these vessels obliterate to become the medial umbilical ligaments, reflecting their fetal circulatory role that is no longer needed once placental exchange ends.

incorrectas.A: The external iliac arteries continue on to become the femoral arteries supplying the lower limbs; they do not give rise to the umbilical arteries, which instead branch from the internal iliac arteries.
incorrectas.C: The common iliac arteries are the parent vessels that bifurcate into the internal and external iliac arteries — the umbilical arteries branch specifically from the internal iliac branch, not directly from the common iliac trunk.
incorrectas.D: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut derivatives (distal transverse colon through rectum) and has no role in fetal-placental circulation via the umbilical cord.

preguntas.q: Total failure of the urachus to obliterate results in which congenital anomaly?

e.correcta: Total failure of the urachus (the allantoic remnant connecting the bladder to the umbilicus) to obliterate leaves a fully patent connection between the bladder and the umbilicus, resulting in a patent urachus that presents with urine leaking from the umbilicus. This reflects the fact that the urachus normally involutes into the median umbilical ligament after birth, and a persistent open lumen along its entire course is what defines this specific anomaly, distinguishing it from partial closure defects.

incorrectas.A: A urachal cyst results from partial obliteration with a persistent patent segment in the middle of the urachus (both ends closed, middle open), not total failure of obliteration along the whole tract.
incorrectas.B: A vesicourachal diverticulum results from failure of obliteration only at the bladder end of the urachus, creating an outpouching from the bladder dome, rather than a fully open communication to the umbilicus.
incorrectas.D: A Meckel diverticulum is a remnant of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct in the ileum, an entirely different embryologic structure unrelated to the urachus or bladder development.

preguntas.q: Partial failure of the urachus to obliterate, resulting in a fluid-filled cavity, is best described as which entity?

e.correcta: A urachal cyst forms when the urachus obliterates at both its bladder and umbilical ends but leaves a persistent patent segment in the middle, which can accumulate fluid or mucoid secretions from the residual urachal epithelium, forming a fluid-filled cavity along the course of the former urachus. Because both ends are closed, it typically presents later in life as a midline mass or becomes infected, rather than presenting at birth with umbilical drainage as a patent urachus would.

incorrectas.A: A patent urachus involves failure of obliteration along the entire tract, creating an open communication between bladder and umbilicus with urine drainage, not an isolated closed fluid-filled cavity.
incorrectas.C: A vesicourachal diverticulum is an outpouching from the bladder itself due to failure of closure only at the bladder end, a different anatomic pattern from a self-contained fluid collection in the mid-urachus.
incorrectas.D: A urachal fistula is not the standard term used for this entity in the classic obliteration-pattern classification; the paired condition characterized by an open lumen at only one end connecting to the umbilicus (rather than a closed cystic cavity) is the umbilical-urachal sinus, which differs from the closed, fluid-filled cyst described here.
