e.correcta: Deamination is the hydrolytic removal of an amino group from a base, and the classic example is cytosine converting to uracil, a base not normally present in DNA, which makes the lesion readily recognizable by uracil DNA glycosylase. This reaction can occur spontaneously at a low background rate, but it is accelerated by heat and by nitrosating/nitrate-derived compounds, which is part of the biochemical rationale for why nitrate-preserved foods have been linked epidemiologically to cancer risk. Deamination lesions like uracil in DNA are corrected by base excision repair.

incorrectas.B: Depurination is the loss of an entire purine base (adenine or guanine) from the sugar-phosphate backbone via hydrolysis of the N-glycosidic bond, leaving an abasic site, rather than a chemical conversion of one base into another like deamination does.
incorrectas.C: Alkylation refers to the addition of alkyl groups (e.g., methyl groups) onto DNA bases by chemical mutagens or certain chemotherapy agents, distorting base-pairing, which is a different chemical modification than the loss of an amino group in deamination.
incorrectas.D: Oxidation of DNA bases (e.g., forming 8-oxoguanine) results from reactive oxygen species attacking guanine, a different chemical mechanism than the hydrolytic amino-group removal that defines deamination, though both are repaired by base excision repair.

preguntas.q: Which DNA repair pathway corrects damage caused by spontaneous or toxin-induced base deamination and oxidation?

e.correcta: Base excision repair specifically targets small, chemically altered bases — such as those produced by deamination (cytosine to uracil) or oxidation (guanine to 8-oxoguanine) — that do not significantly distort the DNA helix. A specific glycosylase recognizes and flips out the abnormal base, AP-endonuclease then nicks the backbone at the resulting abasic site, and DNA polymerase-β and DNA ligase III fill and seal the gap. Because it addresses base-level chemical damage that occurs continuously from normal metabolism, this pathway operates throughout the entire cell cycle.

incorrectas.A: Nucleotide excision repair is reserved for bulky, helix-distorting lesions like UV-induced pyrimidine dimers, which require removal of a larger oligonucleotide segment, unlike the single altered base handled by base excision repair.
incorrectas.B: Mismatch repair corrects base-pairing errors introduced during DNA replication by polymerase, which is a different origin of damage than the spontaneous chemical alteration of an existing base caused by deamination or oxidation.
incorrectas.C: Homologous recombination repairs double-strand breaks using a sister chromatid as template; deamination and oxidation typically produce single-base lesions on one strand, not full double-strand breaks, so this pathway is not the relevant repair mechanism.

preguntas.q: In base excision repair, after a DNA glycosylase removes the damaged base, which enzyme cleaves the DNA backbone to remove nucleotides at the 5' end of the abasic site?

e.correcta: AP-endonuclease (apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease) recognizes the abasic site left behind after a glycosylase removes a damaged base and cleaves the phosphodiester backbone on the 5' side of that site, creating a nick that the rest of the base excision repair machinery can act on. This step is essential because the glycosylase alone only removes the base, leaving the sugar-phosphate backbone intact; AP-endonuclease is what actually opens the backbone to allow removal of the abasic sugar and subsequent gap filling.

incorrectas.B: DNA polymerase-beta fills the gap left after the damaged nucleotide segment is removed, synthesizing new DNA using the intact complementary strand as template — this occurs after the excision step, not during recognition/cleavage at the 5' side.
incorrectas.C: Lyase activity removes the remaining sugar-phosphate residue on the 3' side of the abasic site (often as part of a bifunctional glycosylase/lyase or via polymerase-beta's lyase domain), which is the complementary 3'-side step rather than the 5'-side cleavage performed by AP-endonuclease.
incorrectas.D: DNA ligase III performs the final sealing step, forming the phosphodiester bond that closes the remaining nick after polymerase-beta fills the gap — this occurs at the end of the pathway, not during the initial 5' incision.

preguntas.q: In base excision repair, which enzyme is responsible for removing the abasic sugar-phosphate residue on the 3' side of the site left by the glycosylase?

e.correcta: Lyase activity, often contributed by the same enzyme complex that carries out gap filling (DNA polymerase-beta has an intrinsic lyase domain), removes the remaining deoxyribose-phosphate residue on the 3' side of the abasic site after AP-endonuclease has nicked the backbone on the 5' side. Clearing this residual sugar-phosphate group is necessary to leave a clean 3'-OH end that DNA polymerase can then extend from, completing the excision phase before gap-filling and ligation.

incorrectas.A: AP-endonuclease performs the initial incision on the 5' side of the abasic site, generating the nick that exposes the lesion for removal — it is the complementary step to, not the same as, the 3'-side lyase cleavage.
incorrectas.B: DNA ligase III performs the final sealing of the nick after the gap has been filled by polymerase, which happens at the very end of the pathway, not during the intermediate step of removing the 3'-side abasic sugar residue.
incorrectas.D: The polymerase domain of DNA polymerase-beta synthesizes new DNA to fill the gap once the abasic residues have already been excised; this is a distinct catalytic activity from the lyase domain that actually removes the 3'-side sugar-phosphate.

preguntas.q: Which two enzymes are specifically responsible for filling the gap and sealing the nick during base excision repair?

o.A: DNA polymerase-beta and DNA ligase III
o.B: DNA polymerase-delta and DNA ligase I

e.correcta: Base excision repair specifically uses DNA polymerase-beta to fill the small gap left after the damaged base and its abasic sugar-phosphate are excised, and DNA ligase III to form the final phosphodiester bond and seal the nick. These specific isoforms distinguish base excision repair from other pathways: polymerase-beta lacks proofreading exonuclease activity but is well suited to fill the very short single-nucleotide gaps typical of BER, and ligase III partners specifically with the BER scaffold protein XRCC1.

incorrectas.B: DNA polymerase-delta and DNA ligase I are the main enzymes involved in lagging-strand DNA replication and are also used in long-patch base excision repair variants and nucleotide excision repair, but the classic short-patch BER pathway uses polymerase-beta and ligase III specifically.
incorrectas.C: Primase synthesizes RNA primers for replication initiation, and DNA ligase IV works with the non-homologous end joining pathway to repair double-strand breaks — neither is the enzyme pair used to complete base excision repair.
incorrectas.D: Reverse transcriptase synthesizes DNA from RNA templates (relevant to retroviruses and telomerase) and topoisomerase relieves supercoiling; neither performs the gap-filling or nick-sealing steps characteristic of base excision repair.

preguntas.q: Unlike nucleotide excision repair (G1) and mismatch repair (predominantly S phase), during which portion of the cell cycle does base excision repair occur?

e.correcta: Base excision repair occurs continuously throughout the entire cell cycle because the damage it corrects — spontaneous deamination, oxidation, and other base-level chemical alterations from normal cellular metabolism — arises constantly, independent of the cell's replication status. This is different from repair pathways tied to specific cell-cycle events: nucleotide excision repair mainly occurs in G1 to clear bulky lesions before replication, and mismatch repair acts predominantly in S phase because that is when replication errors are actually generated.

incorrectas.A: G1 is when nucleotide excision repair predominantly operates to remove bulky helix-distorting lesions like pyrimidine dimers before the cell enters S phase, not the cell-cycle restriction that applies to base excision repair.
incorrectas.B: S phase is when mismatch repair predominantly acts because that is when DNA polymerase is actively replicating and generating mismatches; base excision repair is not restricted to this window since its substrate damage occurs independent of replication timing.
incorrectas.D: Mitosis is focused on chromosome segregation, and active repair synthesis is not a hallmark of this phase; base excision repair is characterized precisely by its lack of cell-cycle restriction, working continuously rather than being confined to any one phase including M phase.

preguntas.q: Ataxia telangiectasia, Fanconi anemia, and severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) all share a common underlying defect in the repair of what type of DNA damage?

e.correcta: Ataxia telangiectasia (due to ATM gene mutations), Fanconi anemia (due to FANC gene mutations), and some forms of SCID (due to Artemis enzyme defects) all impair the cell's ability to repair double-strand DNA breaks, which are normally fixed via homologous recombination or non-homologous end joining. Because these pathways are also essential for normal V(D)J recombination in developing lymphocytes and for maintaining genomic stability generally, defects present with a combination of radiosensitivity, cancer predisposition, and (in SCID) profound immunodeficiency from failure to generate functional antigen receptors.

incorrectas.A: Pyrimidine dimers are UV-induced single-strand lesions repaired by nucleotide excision repair, and defects in that specific pathway cause xeroderma pigmentosum, a distinct condition from the double-strand break repair disorders described here.
incorrectas.B: Single-strand mismatches arising from replication errors are corrected by mismatch repair, and defects in that system cause Lynch syndrome/HNPCC — a different mechanism from the double-strand break repair defects seen in ataxia telangiectasia, Fanconi anemia, and SCID.
incorrectas.D: Deaminated bases are corrected by base excision repair, which operates on single, chemically altered bases throughout the cell cycle; this is unrelated to the double-strand break repair machinery whose failure characterizes the three conditions in this question.

preguntas.q: During protein synthesis, in which direction is a polypeptide chain synthesized?

o.D: 5' to 3' relative to the amino acid chain

e.correcta: Protein synthesis proceeds from the N-terminus (amino terminus) to the C-terminus (carboxyl terminus), meaning the first amino acid incorporated (bearing a free amino group) becomes the N-terminal end, and each subsequent amino acid is added by forming a peptide bond between its amino group and the growing chain's terminal carboxyl group. This directionality mirrors the 5' to 3' reading of the mRNA template by the ribosome, since each codon is translated sequentially as the ribosome moves along the transcript, ultimately determining the correct linear order of amino acids in the finished protein.

incorrectas.A: C-terminus to N-terminus synthesis would require adding amino acids to the amino end of the growing chain, which is not how ribosomal peptide bond formation actually works — the growing chain's carboxyl group is what reacts with the incoming amino acid's amino group.
incorrectas.C: Protein synthesis is not random; it follows a strict, templated directionality dictated by the ribosome reading the mRNA codon by codon in a fixed 5' to 3' order, which in turn fixes the N-to-C order of amino acid addition.
incorrectas.D: The '5' to 3'' terminology describes nucleic acid polarity (referring to the mRNA template being read in that direction), not the polarity of the amino acid chain itself, which is properly described using N-terminus and C-terminus terminology.

preguntas.q: Certain antiviral and chemotherapy drugs block DNA replication by acting as chain terminators. What structural modification allows these drugs to prevent addition of the next nucleotide?

o.A: A modified nitrogenous base that cannot pair with its complement
o.D: Removal of the deoxyribose sugar entirely

e.correcta: Many chain-terminating drugs (such as certain antiretrovirals and chemotherapeutic nucleoside analogs) lack a normal, functional 3' hydroxyl group on their sugar moiety. Because DNA polymerase extends a growing strand by catalyzing formation of a phosphodiester bond between the incoming nucleotide's 5' phosphate and the existing strand's 3' OH, a nucleotide analog with a modified or absent 3' OH gets incorporated into the chain but then cannot serve as the acceptor for the next nucleotide, halting further elongation ('chain termination').

incorrectas.A: A modified base that fails to pair correctly would cause a mismatch or miscoding event rather than physically terminating chain elongation — the drugs described here can still be incorporated into the strand, but their sugar defect (not base defect) prevents any further extension.
incorrectas.C: The incoming nucleotide's 5' phosphate is what attacks the existing strand's 3' OH to form the new phosphodiester bond; a modification there would primarily affect that nucleotide's own incorporation, not create the block on the strand's own further extension the way a defective 3' OH does.
incorrectas.D: Complete removal of the deoxyribose sugar would prevent the nucleotide analog from being incorporated into the DNA strand at all, rather than allowing incorporation followed by termination, which is the actual mechanism of the classic chain-terminating drugs.

preguntas.q: Reverse transcriptase, the RNA-dependent DNA polymerase used by retroviruses, requires which of the following to begin synthesizing DNA?

o.A: A DNA template only, no primer needed
o.B: A primer, because it is a DNA polymerase
o.C: A promoter sequence recognized directly by the enzyme
o.D: A pre-existing RNA transcript with a 5' cap

e.correcta: Reverse transcriptase is fundamentally a DNA polymerase (specifically, an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase), and like all DNA polymerases, it can only extend an existing 3' OH end rather than initiate synthesis de novo — so it requires a primer to begin. In retroviruses like HIV, a host-derived tRNA molecule serves as this primer, base-pairing with the viral RNA genome so reverse transcriptase can begin synthesizing the complementary DNA strand. This primer requirement is a defining, testable feature that distinguishes DNA polymerases (including reverse transcriptase) from RNA polymerases, which can initiate synthesis without one.

incorrectas.A: A DNA template alone is not enough, precisely because reverse transcriptase behaves like other DNA polymerases in requiring a free 3' OH to extend from; without a primer providing that starting point, no synthesis can begin regardless of template availability.
incorrectas.C: Recognizing a promoter sequence is a feature of RNA polymerases, which bind promoter regions to initiate transcription without needing a primer; reverse transcriptase, being a polymerase that extends existing strands, does not initiate through promoter recognition.
incorrectas.D: A capped RNA transcript describes a feature relevant to mRNA processing and translation initiation in eukaryotes, not to the priming requirement of reverse transcriptase, which specifically needs a primer (a host tRNA) annealed to the RNA template to begin DNA synthesis.

preguntas.q: DNA polymerase requires a primer to begin synthesis. What does RNA polymerase bind to instead, in order to initiate transcription without needing a primer?

e.correcta: RNA polymerase binds to a promoter, a specific DNA sequence upstream of a gene, which allows it to initiate RNA synthesis de novo without requiring a pre-existing primer, unlike DNA polymerase. This distinction reflects a broader theme: RNA polymerase is inherently able to start a new strand because RNA synthesis does not require the same proofreading fidelity as DNA replication, whereas DNA polymerase's high-fidelity 3'-to-5' exonuclease proofreading mechanism depends on already having a correctly paired 3' end to check and extend.

incorrectas.A: An origin of replication is the site where DNA replication begins and where helicases and primases are recruited to unwind DNA and lay down RNA primers for DNA polymerase — it is relevant to DNA replication initiation, not to RNA polymerase's promoter-based transcription initiation.
incorrectas.C: A centromere is the chromosomal region where sister chromatids are held together and where the kinetochore assembles for mitotic spindle attachment; it has no role in transcription initiation by RNA polymerase.
incorrectas.D: A telomere is the repetitive protective sequence at the ends of linear chromosomes, maintained by telomerase to prevent loss of genetic material during replication; it is unrelated to where RNA polymerase binds to start transcribing a gene.

preguntas.q: During transcription, which strand of double-stranded DNA is actually read by RNA polymerase, being complementary and antiparallel to the resulting mRNA?

e.correcta: The template strand (also called the antisense strand) is the DNA strand that RNA polymerase actually reads during transcription, synthesizing mRNA that is complementary and antiparallel to it. Because the mRNA is built by base-pairing against the template strand, the mRNA sequence ends up matching the other DNA strand (the coding strand) except with uracil substituted for thymine — a key concept for correctly identifying which DNA sequence corresponds to a given mRNA or protein-coding sequence.

incorrectas.B: 'Sense strand' is essentially another name for the coding strand — the strand identical in sequence to the mRNA (aside from T/U) — and is therefore the strand NOT read by RNA polymerase, the opposite of what this question asks for.
incorrectas.A: The coding strand has the same sequence as the mRNA transcript (with thymine in place of uracil) precisely because it is not the strand used as the physical template; RNA polymerase does not read this strand directly during transcription.
incorrectas.D: The leading strand is a concept from DNA replication, referring to the strand synthesized continuously in the direction of the replication fork, and has no direct relevance to which DNA strand RNA polymerase transcribes during gene expression.

preguntas.q: Which strand of double-stranded DNA is NOT used as the template during transcription, but instead has a sequence identical to the mRNA (aside from substituting thymine for uracil)?

e.correcta: The coding strand (also called the sense strand) is not physically read by RNA polymerase during transcription; instead, it has the same 5' to 3' sequence as the resulting mRNA, simply substituting thymine for uracil. This is because RNA polymerase actually transcribes the opposite (template) strand, synthesizing mRNA complementary and antiparallel to it — which, by definition of complementary base pairing, ends up matching the coding strand. Recognizing this relationship lets you quickly convert between a given DNA sequence and its corresponding mRNA sequence on exams.

incorrectas.A: The template strand is precisely the strand that IS used by RNA polymerase as the physical template for transcription, synthesizing mRNA complementary to it — the opposite of the strand described in this question, which asks for the one not used as template.
incorrectas.C: The lagging strand is a DNA replication concept, referring to the strand synthesized discontinuously as Okazaki fragments away from the replication fork; it is unrelated to the sense/antisense terminology used to describe the two strands during transcription.
incorrectas.D: 'Antisense strand' is another name for the template strand — the strand that RNA polymerase actually reads — making it the opposite answer to what this question is asking, since the question seeks the strand not used as template.

preguntas.q: In eukaryotic cells, in which subcellular structure is the majority of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) synthesized?

e.correcta: The nucleolus is a dense, membrane-less subnuclear structure where RNA polymerase I transcribes the ribosomal DNA genes into the pre-rRNA transcripts (28S, 18S, and 5.8S rRNA) that are subsequently processed and assembled with ribosomal proteins to form the large and small ribosomal subunits. These subunits are then exported through nuclear pores to the cytoplasm, where they combine to form complete, functional ribosomes for protein synthesis. Because rRNA synthesis and ribosome assembly are so metabolically demanding, the nucleolus is especially prominent in cells with high protein synthesis needs, and it is also the classic site targeted early in some viral infections and stress responses.

incorrectas.B: The rough endoplasmic reticulum is the site where ribosomes attached to its membrane synthesize proteins destined for secretion or membrane insertion, but it does not itself synthesize rRNA — it merely hosts already-assembled ribosomes during translation.
incorrectas.C: The nuclear pore complex is the structure through which molecules, including assembled ribosomal subunits and mRNA, are transported between the nucleus and cytoplasm; it is a transit conduit, not a site of rRNA transcription.
incorrectas.D: The cytoplasm is where mature ribosomal subunits join to form complete ribosomes and carry out translation, but the rRNA itself is transcribed and initially processed in the nucleolus before export, not synthesized in the cytoplasm.

preguntas.q: In eukaryotic cells, most mRNA and tRNA synthesis occurs in which nuclear compartment?

e.correcta: Euchromatin is the loosely packed, transcriptionally active form of chromatin in which DNA is accessible to RNA polymerases and their associated transcription factors, so the bulk of mRNA and tRNA synthesis occurs there. Its open configuration (less condensed, fewer bound histones relative to heterochromatin) allows the transcription machinery to engage promoters, whereas tightly packed regions are largely silenced. A small additional pool of mRNA and tRNA is also transcribed from mitochondrial DNA, but that is a separate, non-nuclear source.

incorrectas.A: Heterochromatin is densely packed, transcriptionally silent DNA (including regions like the inactive X chromosome/Barr body) — its condensed state physically excludes RNA polymerase, so little to no transcription happens there, the opposite of euchromatin's active role.
incorrectas.C: The nucleolus is the site of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) transcription (by RNA polymerase I) and ribosome assembly, not the primary site of mRNA (RNA pol II) or tRNA (RNA pol III) synthesis, which occurs throughout the nucleoplasm wherever euchromatin is exposed.
incorrectas.D: The nuclear envelope is a structural double membrane separating nucleoplasm from cytoplasm and containing nuclear pore complexes for transport; it has no role in RNA synthesis itself, unlike euchromatin which is the actual DNA template used for transcription.

preguntas.q: When a double-stranded DNA sequence is reported in a genetic database without further specification, which strand is conventionally listed?

e.correcta: By convention, databases report the coding (sense) strand, which has the same sequence as the mRNA transcript (except T is substituted for U). This strand is not physically read by RNA polymerase — it is complementary to the template strand — but it is reported because it directly shows the reading frame and codon sequence that will appear in the mature mRNA, making it far more useful for interpreting protein-coding information at a glance.

incorrectas.A: The template (antisense) strand is the one RNA polymerase actually reads 3' to 5' to synthesize mRNA 5' to 3'; it is complementary to the mRNA, not identical to it, so reporting it would require the reader to mentally complement the sequence to get the actual transcript.
incorrectas.B: Antisense strand is simply another name for the template strand in this context, and is not the strand conventionally deposited in databases for the same reason — it does not match the mRNA sequence directly.
incorrectas.D: Okazaki fragments are short, discontinuous pieces of newly synthesized DNA on the lagging strand during DNA replication, a replication concept unrelated to which strand of a gene's sequence is conventionally reported in a database.

preguntas.q: A DNA template strand reads 5'-TAGC-3' (read 3' to 5' by RNA polymerase). What is the resulting mRNA sequence, written 5' to 3'?

e.correcta: RNA polymerase reads the template strand 3' to 5' and synthesizes mRNA 5' to 3', complementary and antiparallel to the template. Reading the template TAGC from its 3' end (C-G-A-T) and pairing complementary bases (G pairs with C, C pairs with G, U pairs with A, A pairs with T) gives GCUA as the mRNA, written 5' to 3'. Getting the directionality right is the key step students miss — you must flip the template's reading direction before pairing bases, not just complement it in the order given.

incorrectas.A: AUCG is what you get if you complement the bases in the same left-to-right order they were given (T→A, A→U, G→C, C→G) without accounting for antiparallel synthesis — this ignores that RNA polymerase must read the template 3' to 5', so the resulting strand direction is wrong even though the base-pairing itself looks plausible.
incorrectas.B: CGAT simply repeats the template sequence with T swapped in some positions rather than performing true complementary base pairing throughout, and does not represent a strand synthesized antiparallel to a 5'-TAGC-3' template.
incorrectas.D: TAGC is identical to the template strand itself; mRNA cannot be identical to its own template because synthesis is based on Watson-Crick complementary base pairing, not direct copying of the template sequence.

preguntas.q: Which portion of a mature mRNA transcript contains no protein-coding information but is present at both the 5' and 3' ends of essentially every mRNA?

e.correcta: The untranslated regions (5' UTR and 3' UTR) flank the coding sequence of virtually every mRNA and are not translated into protein, though they are transcribed and remain in the mature transcript. These regions contain regulatory elements — for example, sequences affecting ribosome binding efficiency, mRNA stability, and localization — that influence how much and how quickly protein is made from that transcript, even though they don't specify any amino acids themselves.

incorrectas.A: The poly-A tail is a stretch of adenine residues added post-transcriptionally to the 3' end of eukaryotic mRNA that protects it from degradation and aids export/translation, but it is a specific added structure rather than the general untranslated coding-flanking region described, and it is not universally present at the 5' end.
incorrectas.C: Introns are non-coding sequences within the primary transcript that are removed by splicing before the mature mRNA is exported; unlike the UTR, introns are excised entirely and are not part of the final mRNA product, whereas the UTR remains in the mature message flanking the coding sequence.
incorrectas.D: The Shine-Dalgarno sequence is a prokaryotic ribosome-binding sequence found in bacterial mRNA upstream of the start codon; it is a prokaryote-specific element, not the general eukaryotic/universal non-coding flanking region being described here.

preguntas.q: Prokaryotic mRNA characteristically lacks which structural feature commonly found in eukaryotic pre-mRNA?

e.correcta: Prokaryotic genes are generally continuous (uninterrupted) coding sequences without introns, so their mRNA has no intron/exon structure and requires no splicing before translation. This reflects the streamlined, operon-based organization of bacterial genomes, which allows transcription and translation to occur simultaneously (coupled) since there is no need to process the transcript first, unlike eukaryotic pre-mRNA which must be spliced to remove introns before export from the nucleus.

incorrectas.A: Prokaryotic mRNA does have a start codon (AUG) marking the beginning of each coding sequence within the transcript — this is present in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes and is not the distinguishing feature between them.
incorrectas.C: Prokaryotic mRNA does have a ribosome binding site — specifically the Shine-Dalgarno sequence — which is in fact a feature it has that eukaryotic mRNA lacks (eukaryotes use the 5' cap instead), making this option the reverse of what distinguishes the two.
incorrectas.D: Prokaryotic mRNA does have a stop codon terminating translation, just as eukaryotic mRNA does; this is a shared feature of the genetic code and translation machinery in both domains, not something prokaryotic mRNA lacks.

preguntas.q: Compared with eukaryotic mRNA, prokaryotic mRNA undergoes how much post-transcriptional processing before translation?

o.A: Extensive processing, including capping and polyadenylation
o.C: None — it is translated as synthesized

e.correcta: Prokaryotic mRNA undergoes essentially no post-transcriptional processing — no 5' cap, no poly-A tail, and no splicing (since there are no introns) — and translation can begin on the nascent transcript even before transcription is complete. This coupling of transcription and translation is possible because prokaryotes lack a nucleus, so ribosomes have direct access to mRNA as it is being made, a key contrast with the compartmentalized, heavily processed eukaryotic system.

incorrectas.A: Extensive processing with capping and polyadenylation describes eukaryotic mRNA maturation (5' 7-methylguanosine cap and 3' poly-A tail added post-transcriptionally), which is the opposite of the minimal processing seen in prokaryotes.
incorrectas.B: Splicing removes introns from pre-mRNA, a step that is unnecessary in prokaryotes because their genes lack introns in the first place — so prokaryotic mRNA undergoes neither splicing nor capping, not splicing alone.
incorrectas.D: Capping (addition of the 7-methylguanosine cap) is a eukaryotic-specific 5' modification that protects the transcript and recruits the ribosome; prokaryotic mRNA has no such cap, so this option incorrectly attributes a eukaryotic modification to prokaryotic transcripts.

preguntas.q: Ribosome binding to initiate translation in prokaryotes depends on recognition of which sequence upstream of the start codon?

e.correcta: The Shine-Dalgarno sequence is a purine-rich region in the 5' UTR of prokaryotic mRNA that base-pairs with complementary rRNA in the small ribosomal subunit (16S rRNA), positioning the ribosome precisely over the start codon. Because bacterial operons often encode multiple genes on a single polycistronic mRNA, each gene's own Shine-Dalgarno sequence allows independent, separately regulated initiation of translation for each open reading frame within that transcript.

incorrectas.A: The TATA box is a eukaryotic promoter element recognized during transcription initiation (RNA polymerase II binding), not a ribosome-binding site used during translation, and it functions at the DNA level rather than the mRNA level.
incorrectas.B: The Kozak sequence is the eukaryotic analog that helps the ribosome identify the correct start codon in eukaryotic mRNA, but eukaryotic translation initiation actually depends on the 5' cap and scanning mechanism rather than a Shine-Dalgarno-type sequence — this is the eukaryotic counterpart, not the prokaryotic answer.
incorrectas.D: The CAAT box is a eukaryotic promoter element located upstream of the transcription start site that enhances RNA polymerase II binding, a transcriptional regulatory element unrelated to ribosome binding or translation in either prokaryotes or eukaryotes.

preguntas.q: In eukaryotic cells, RNA polymerase II binds to a DNA element unique to each individual gene, called the:

e.correcta: In eukaryotes, each gene has its own dedicated promoter, an upstream DNA sequence where RNA polymerase II and the general transcription factors assemble to form the pre-initiation complex before transcription begins. This one-gene-one-promoter arrangement contrasts with prokaryotic operons, where a single promoter can drive transcription of several genes together as one polycistronic mRNA, reflecting the more individualized regulation of gene expression in eukaryotic cells.

incorrectas.A: An operon is a prokaryotic arrangement in which multiple genes share one promoter and are transcribed together into a single polycistronic mRNA — this is the opposite of the eukaryotic pattern of one promoter per gene described in the question.
incorrectas.B: Enhancers are regulatory DNA elements that increase transcription by binding activator proteins, but they are not the site where RNA polymerase II itself directly assembles to initiate transcription — that role belongs to the promoter, with enhancers acting at a distance to boost that initiation.
incorrectas.D: Silencers are regulatory elements that bind repressor proteins to decrease transcription; like enhancers, they modulate transcription from a distance rather than being the direct binding site for RNA polymerase II, which is the defining feature of a promoter.

preguntas.q: The initial (primary) transcript of a eukaryotic gene contains both coding and non-coding sequences that must be separated by splicing. What are these two sequence types called?

e.correcta: The primary (pre-mRNA) transcript of a eukaryotic gene contains exons (the sequences ultimately retained and translated into protein) interspersed with introns (intervening sequences that are removed). The spliceosome recognizes conserved splice-site sequences at intron boundaries, excises the introns, and ligates the exons together to produce the mature mRNA — a processing step required in eukaryotes but absent in prokaryotes, whose genes lack introns.

incorrectas.A: Promoters and enhancers are DNA regulatory elements that control the initiation and rate of transcription, not the coding versus non-coding segments within the transcript itself that are separated by splicing.
incorrectas.B: Sense and antisense strands refer to the two complementary strands of double-stranded DNA (the coding strand and the template strand), a distinction about the DNA duplex, not about segments within a single RNA transcript that get spliced.
incorrectas.D: The 5' and 3' UTRs are non-coding regions at the ends of the mature mRNA that flank the coding sequence, but they are not the intron/exon distinction — UTRs remain in the final mRNA and are not spliced out the way introns are.

preguntas.q: Initiation of translation in eukaryotic cells depends on ribosome recognition of which mRNA feature?

e.correcta: Eukaryotic translation initiation begins when the small ribosomal subunit, together with initiation factors, recognizes the 7-methylguanosine (m7G) cap added to the 5' end of mRNA during processing, then scans downstream to locate the start codon (often within a Kozak consensus sequence). This cap-dependent scanning mechanism is fundamentally different from prokaryotic initiation, which instead relies on direct base-pairing between the Shine-Dalgarno sequence and ribosomal RNA without a cap structure.

incorrectas.A: The Shine-Dalgarno sequence is the prokaryotic ribosome-binding site that base-pairs with 16S rRNA; eukaryotic mRNA does not have this sequence and instead relies on the 5' cap for ribosome recruitment, making this the wrong-domain answer.
incorrectas.B: The poly-A tail at the 3' end of eukaryotic mRNA promotes mRNA stability and, through interactions with poly-A binding proteins, can enhance translational efficiency, but it is not itself the feature the ribosome first recognizes to initiate translation — that role belongs to the 5' cap.
incorrectas.C: The TATA box is a DNA promoter element recognized by transcription factors and RNA polymerase II to initiate transcription, an entirely different process (and molecule, DNA vs. mRNA) from ribosome binding during translation initiation.

preguntas.q: The eukaryotic promoter region is an AT-rich upstream sequence characterized by which two consensus boxes?

e.correcta: The core eukaryotic promoter contains the TATA (Hogness) box, typically about 25 base pairs upstream of the transcription start site, and the CAAT box, typically about 70-80 base pairs upstream. These regions are AT-rich because A:T base pairs are held by only two hydrogen bonds (versus three for G:C), making the DNA duplex easier to locally unwind — an energetically favorable place for the transcription pre-initiation complex to assemble and begin separating the strands for RNA polymerase II.

incorrectas.A: GC boxes are a separate class of promoter-proximal element (often bound by transcription factors like Sp1) found in many promoters, but they are GC-rich rather than AT-rich; CpG islands are clusters of CG dinucleotides important in gene regulation and methylation, not part of the classic AT-rich TATA/CAAT promoter description.
incorrectas.B: Shine-Dalgarno and Kozak sequences are ribosome-binding elements involved in translation initiation (prokaryotic and eukaryotic, respectively), not DNA promoter elements involved in transcription initiation — a different process and different molecule entirely.
incorrectas.D: GRE (glucocorticoid response element) and CRE (cAMP response element) are examples of specific response elements found within enhancers that bind specific transcription factors, not the general AT-rich promoter boxes bound by general transcription factors for basal transcription.

preguntas.q: A mutation disrupting a gene's promoter sequence most commonly produces what effect on transcription of that gene?

o.D: A shift to a different transcription start site with normal output

e.correcta: Because the promoter is required for RNA polymerase II and general transcription factors to assemble and initiate transcription of that specific gene, mutations that disrupt promoter elements (such as the TATA or CAAT box) typically impair this assembly and cause a dramatic decrease in the gene's transcription level. This is why promoter mutations are an important cause of reduced gene expression in inherited disease (e.g., some thalassemias arise from promoter mutations that lower globin gene transcription) even when the coding sequence itself is entirely normal.

incorrectas.A: No change would only be expected if the mutation fell outside functionally important promoter elements; a mutation that meaningfully disrupts core promoter sequences like the TATA box characteristically has a large effect on basal transcription, not a neutral one.
incorrectas.C: A dramatic increase would be more characteristic of a gain-of-function mutation in a silencer (losing repressor binding) or an unusually strong new element created by mutation, but the typical consequence of damaging a normal promoter is loss of transcriptional machinery binding, which decreases rather than increases output.
incorrectas.D: Promoter mutations do not simply relocate the start site while preserving normal transcription — they typically impair the ability of the transcription machinery to bind and initiate at all, reducing overall output rather than shifting it elsewhere with equivalent efficiency.

preguntas.q: Promoters, present in essentially all nucleated cells and required for basal transcription, serve as binding sites for which category of transcription factors?

e.correcta: Promoters bind general transcription factors (such as TFIID, which recognizes the TATA box) that are required in essentially every nucleated cell to assemble the basal transcription machinery and recruit RNA polymerase II. Because these factors and this machinery are universal necessities for any gene to be transcribed at all, promoters function as the baseline, ubiquitous control point, distinct from the cell-type-specific or signal-specific regulation provided by enhancers and their specific transcription factors.

incorrectas.A: Tissue-specific transcription factors bind enhancer elements (via specific response elements) to drive gene expression selectively in particular cell types or in response to particular signals — this specific, variable regulation is characteristic of enhancers, not the universal general transcription factors that bind promoters.
incorrectas.C: Repressor proteins bind silencers to decrease transcription; promoters are the binding sites for general (activating, basal) transcription factors needed for RNA polymerase II assembly, not specifically for repressors.
incorrectas.D: Hormone receptors (like steroid receptors) act as specific transcription factors binding hormone response elements within enhancers, conferring hormone-responsive, often tissue-restricted regulation — this is a specific enhancer-based mechanism, not the general, ubiquitous promoter-binding factors described in the question.

preguntas.q: Which DNA regulatory element increases gene expression by serving as a binding site for specific transcription factors, and can act at variable distances from the gene it regulates?

e.correcta: Enhancers are stretches of DNA that bind specific activator transcription factors, which in turn stabilize RNA polymerase II and the transcription pre-initiation complex, increasing the rate of transcription of a target gene. Unlike the promoter, which sits immediately upstream of the transcription start site and is required for basal transcription of every gene, an enhancer can be located far upstream, downstream, or even within an intron of the gene it regulates, with DNA looping/bending bringing it into physical proximity with the promoter.

incorrectas.A: The promoter is the core sequence immediately upstream of a gene where general transcription factors and RNA polymerase II assemble for basal transcription; it is required for transcription to occur at all but is not the variable, activator-binding, expression-boosting element described here — that role belongs to the enhancer.
incorrectas.B: A silencer is the functional opposite of an enhancer — it binds repressor proteins and decreases gene expression rather than increasing it, even though structurally it can also act at a distance similarly to an enhancer.
incorrectas.C: An operon is a prokaryotic gene-organization unit consisting of multiple genes under control of a single promoter/operator, a bacterial concept unrelated to the eukaryotic enhancer element that binds activators to boost transcription.

preguntas.q: Which DNA element binds negative regulatory proteins (repressors) and decreases expression of a gene on the same chromosome?

e.correcta: Silencers are DNA sequences that bind repressor proteins, which then interfere with assembly or function of the transcription machinery at the promoter, decreasing expression of the associated gene. Like enhancers, silencers act in cis (affecting only genes on the same chromosome/DNA molecule) and can function at variable distances from the gene, but their functional effect is opposite — dampening rather than boosting RNA polymerase activity at the promoter.

incorrectas.A: Enhancers have the opposite function of silencers — they bind activator proteins that stabilize the transcription machinery and increase gene expression, rather than binding repressors to decrease it.
incorrectas.C: The 5' UTR is a non-coding portion of the mature mRNA transcript itself (not a DNA regulatory element controlling transcription rate); it can influence translation efficiency but is not where repressor proteins bind to reduce transcription.
incorrectas.D: The poly-A signal is a sequence in the 3' region of a transcript that directs cleavage and polyadenylation during mRNA processing — a post-transcriptional processing signal, not a DNA element that recruits repressors to decrease transcription.

preguntas.q: Enhancers increase gene transcription primarily by enhancing the activity of which enzyme?

e.correcta: Enhancers bind activator transcription factors that stabilize RNA polymerase II and the pre-initiation complex at the promoter of protein-coding genes, thereby increasing the rate of mRNA synthesis. RNA polymerase II is the enzyme responsible for transcribing all protein-coding genes into pre-mRNA, so enhancer-driven regulation of gene expression converges on boosting this enzyme's productivity at a given promoter.

incorrectas.A: RNA polymerase I transcribes ribosomal RNA (most rRNA) in the nucleolus; enhancers regulating protein-coding genes act on RNA polymerase II, not RNA polymerase I, which is dedicated to a different class of RNA gene.
incorrectas.B: RNA polymerase III transcribes small RNAs such as tRNA and 5S rRNA; the classic enhancer-activator mechanism described in First Aid-style gene regulation refers specifically to RNA polymerase II-driven mRNA transcription, not RNA polymerase III.
incorrectas.C: DNA polymerase synthesizes new DNA strands during replication, an entirely separate process from transcription; enhancers regulate transcription (RNA synthesis) via RNA polymerase II, not DNA replication.

preguntas.q: Enhancers, unlike promoters, serve as binding sites for which category of transcription factors?

e.correcta: Enhancers bind specific transcription factors — activator proteins whose expression or activity is restricted to particular cell types, developmental stages, or signaling contexts (e.g., steroid hormone receptors binding hormone response elements within an enhancer). This specificity is what allows the same basal transcription machinery at a promoter to be selectively ramped up in some cells/conditions and not others, giving eukaryotic gene expression its combinatorial, context-dependent regulation.

incorrectas.B: General transcription factors (like TFIID) bind the promoter and are needed ubiquitously in essentially every nucleated cell for basal transcription of any gene — this ubiquitous role is the defining feature of promoter-binding factors, in contrast to the cell/context-specific factors that bind enhancers.
incorrectas.C: Sigma factors are prokaryotic proteins that associate with bacterial RNA polymerase to direct it to specific promoter sequences; they are a bacterial transcription-initiation concept, not a eukaryotic enhancer-binding transcription factor category.
incorrectas.D: Histone chaperones assist in nucleosome assembly/disassembly and chromatin remodeling, a structural role in chromatin dynamics, rather than functioning as sequence-specific DNA-binding transcription factors recruited to enhancers.

preguntas.q: Relative to the gene they regulate, where can enhancers and silencers be located?

o.A: Always immediately adjacent, just upstream of the promoter
o.B: Only on a different chromosome from the gene
o.C: Only downstream of the poly-A signal
o.D: Close to, far from, or within the gene itself (e.g., in an intron)

e.correcta: Enhancers and silencers can be located close to the gene, thousands of base pairs away, or even within the gene itself (commonly within an intron), because they act through three-dimensional DNA looping/bending rather than requiring direct linear adjacency to the promoter. This flexibility arises because activator or repressor proteins bound at the enhancer/silencer can be brought into physical contact with the promoter-bound machinery via bending of the intervening DNA, even though the elements may be many nucleotides away in the linear sequence.

incorrectas.A: Being always immediately adjacent to the promoter describes core promoter elements like the TATA and CAAT boxes, not enhancers/silencers, whose defining feature is precisely that they do not need to be immediately adjacent and can act at a distance.
incorrectas.B: Enhancers and silencers act in cis, meaning they regulate genes on the same DNA molecule/chromosome; they do not function in trans from a different chromosome, which distinguishes their mechanism from diffusible trans-acting factors like transcription factor proteins.
incorrectas.C: The poly-A signal is a 3' mRNA processing element unrelated to enhancer/silencer positioning; enhancers and silencers are not restricted to a location downstream of it, and can in fact be found upstream, downstream, or within the gene.

preguntas.q: Within an enhancer, the specific short DNA domains that individual specific transcription factors bind to are called:

e.correcta: Response elements (REs) are the specific short DNA sequences within an enhancer that particular transcription factors recognize and bind, allowing distinct signals to activate distinct sets of genes — examples include the glucocorticoid response element (GRE) bound by the glucocorticoid receptor, the cAMP response element (CRE) bound by CREB, and the estrogen response element (ERE) bound by the estrogen receptor. This modular design lets a single enhancer integrate multiple regulatory inputs by containing several different response elements, each recruiting its own dedicated transcription factor.

incorrectas.B: Poly-A signals are sequences near the 3' end of a transcript that direct cleavage and addition of the poly-A tail during mRNA processing, a post-transcriptional event unrelated to transcription-factor binding within an enhancer.
incorrectas.C: TATA boxes are core promoter elements bound by general transcription factors to position RNA polymerase II at the transcription start site, not the specific, factor-dependent binding domains found within enhancers.
incorrectas.D: Splice sites are sequences at intron-exon boundaries recognized by the spliceosome during pre-mRNA processing, an entirely different step (RNA processing, not transcriptional activation) from response elements within an enhancer.

preguntas.q: By what physical mechanism can an enhancer located thousands of base pairs away from a gene still influence that gene's transcription?

o.A: The enhancer is first transcribed into a separate regulatory RNA
o.B: The enhancer is copied into the promoter region by recombination
o.C: DNA bending/looping brings the enhancer into physical proximity with the promoter
o.D: The enhancer diffuses through the nucleoplasm to reach the promoter

e.correcta: Even though an enhancer may be located far away in the linear DNA sequence, activator proteins bound to it can make direct protein-protein contact with the transcription machinery at the promoter because the intervening DNA bends/loops, physically bringing the two regions close together in three-dimensional space. This looping mechanism explains why enhancers can function regardless of their distance or orientation relative to the gene, unlike the promoter which must be immediately adjacent to the transcription start site.

incorrectas.A: Enhancer DNA is not transcribed into a separate diffusible regulatory RNA to convey its effect in this classic mechanism; the enhancer acts by binding activator proteins directly at the DNA level, then looping to contact the promoter, not by producing an intermediary RNA molecule.
incorrectas.B: Enhancers are not physically relocated to the promoter region via recombination — the enhancer sequence stays where it is in the genome, and its effect is achieved through three-dimensional folding of the DNA, not through cutting and pasting the DNA sequence itself.
incorrectas.D: It is not the enhancer DNA that diffuses; rather, activator proteins bound to the enhancer are brought near the promoter through DNA looping. Free diffusion of the DNA segment itself is not how enhancer-promoter communication is achieved.

preguntas.q: Steroid hormone receptors act as specific transcription factors that bind to which type of DNA element to elicit a steroid-induced transcriptional response?

e.correcta: Steroid hormones (e.g., cortisol, estrogen, testosterone) diffuse into the cell and bind intracellular receptors, which then act as ligand-activated transcription factors that bind specific steroid response elements within enhancers of target genes — for example, cortisol-bound glucocorticoid receptor binds the glucocorticoid response element (GRE). Binding of the hormone-receptor complex to its response element recruits coactivators and stabilizes RNA polymerase II, increasing transcription of genes needed for that hormone's downstream effects.

incorrectas.A: Silencers bind repressor proteins to decrease transcription; steroid receptors acting as activators to increase transcription of target genes bind response elements within enhancers, functionally the opposite of a silencer interaction.
incorrectas.C: Shine-Dalgarno sequences are prokaryotic ribosome-binding sites involved in translation initiation, unrelated to eukaryotic steroid receptor-mediated transcriptional activation, which occurs at the DNA level via response elements.
incorrectas.D: TATA boxes are general core-promoter elements bound by general transcription factors for basal transcription of virtually any gene; steroid receptors bind specific response elements (like the GRE) rather than the universal TATA box.

preguntas.q: Steroid hormone receptors, thyroid hormone receptors, and vitamin A/D receptors all share which common structural motif for DNA binding?

e.correcta: Steroid hormone receptors, thyroid hormone receptors, and the vitamin A (retinoic acid) and vitamin D receptors all belong to the nuclear receptor superfamily, which uses zinc finger DNA-binding domains — motifs stabilized by a zinc ion coordinating cysteine/histidine residues that fold the protein into a shape allowing it to grip the major groove of DNA at specific hormone response elements. This shared structural strategy lets each receptor recognize its own specific response element sequence while using the same general zinc-coordinated binding architecture.

incorrectas.B: The leucine zipper motif is used by transcription factors like CREB, Jun, and Fos, in which a stretch of periodically spaced leucines allows two protein subunits to dimerize into a coiled-coil that grips DNA — a different structural family from the zinc finger receptors used by steroid/thyroid/vitamin A/D receptors.
incorrectas.C: Helix-loop-helix is a dimerization/DNA-binding motif used by transcription factors involved in cell differentiation and development (such as MyoD), not the motif characteristic of the nuclear hormone receptor family described in the question.
incorrectas.D: The homeodomain is a DNA-binding motif encoded by homeobox genes that regulate developmental patterning (e.g., Hox genes), a distinct structural family unrelated to the zinc finger motif used by steroid, thyroid, and vitamin A/D receptors.

preguntas.q: In response to glucagon-stimulated rises in intracellular cAMP, which transcription factor binds cAMP response elements (CREs) to alter gene expression?

e.correcta: CREB is a specific transcription factor that, once phosphorylated by protein kinase A downstream of rising cAMP (as occurs after glucagon or epinephrine signaling through Gs-coupled receptors), binds cAMP response elements (CREs) within enhancers of target genes to activate transcription. This pathway links extracellular hormonal signals to changes in gene expression, illustrating how a second-messenger cascade (cAMP to PKA to CREB phosphorylation) ultimately alters the transcriptional program of the cell.

incorrectas.B: The glucocorticoid receptor is a nuclear (steroid-type) hormone receptor that binds glucocorticoid response elements after direct binding of cortisol, a different signaling mechanism (intracellular hormone receptor, not a second-messenger-activated kinase-phosphorylated factor) from the cAMP/CREB pathway.
incorrectas.C: Sp1 is a general/ubiquitous transcription factor that binds GC boxes in many promoters to support constitutive transcription; it is not the factor specifically activated by the cAMP/PKA pathway in response to glucagon signaling.
incorrectas.D: NF-κB is a transcription factor activated mainly by inflammatory and immune signaling pathways (e.g., through IκB degradation following cytokine or pathogen-associated signals), not by the cAMP/PKA cascade triggered by glucagon.

preguntas.q: CREB (cAMP response element-binding protein) belongs to which class of DNA-binding transcription factor motif?

e.correcta: CREB is a leucine zipper transcription factor, meaning it contains a region with leucine residues spaced every seven amino acids that forms an alpha helix; two such helices (often from two CREB monomers) intertwine into a coiled-coil dimer, positioning adjacent basic regions to grip the DNA double helix at the cAMP response element. This leucine zipper dimerization motif is shared by other important regulatory factors like Fos and Jun (AP-1), making it a recurring theme in signal-responsive gene regulation.

incorrectas.A: Zinc finger motifs, which use a zinc ion to stabilize a DNA-binding fold, are characteristic of the nuclear hormone receptor family (steroid, thyroid, vitamin A/D receptors), a structurally distinct class from the leucine zipper motif used by CREB.
incorrectas.B: Homeodomain proteins, encoded by homeobox genes, are DNA-binding transcription factors central to developmental patterning (e.g., Hox genes), a different structural family from the leucine zipper dimerization motif that defines CREB.
incorrectas.C: Helix-turn-helix is a broader structural motif classically described in many prokaryotic DNA-binding proteins (like repressors) and some eukaryotic factors, but it is not the specific classification used for CREB, which is characterized as a leucine zipper protein.

preguntas.q: Which class of specific transcription factors regulates gene expression patterns during embryonic development, often using the same enhancer sequence to act on different promoters and genes?

e.correcta: Homeodomain proteins, encoded by homeobox (Hox) genes, are transcription factors that bind DNA through a conserved 60-amino-acid homeodomain and coordinate spatial and temporal patterns of gene expression during development, establishing body plan and segment identity along the embryonic axis. Because a shared enhancer sequence and its response element can be recognized by different homeodomain proteins in different tissues or developmental stages, the same regulatory element can drive very different developmental gene programs depending on which homeodomain factors are present at that time and place.

incorrectas.B: Leucine zipper proteins (like CREB, Fos, and Jun) mediate transcriptional responses to signaling pathways such as cAMP/PKA, a role centered on responding to second-messenger signals rather than the classic developmental body-patterning role attributed to homeodomain proteins.
incorrectas.C: Zinc finger nuclear receptors (steroid, thyroid, vitamin A/D receptors) mediate hormone-driven transcriptional responses by binding hormone response elements, a distinct hormone-signaling function rather than the master developmental patterning role of homeodomain/Hox proteins.
incorrectas.D: Sigma factors are prokaryotic proteins that direct bacterial RNA polymerase to specific promoters, a bacterial transcription-initiation mechanism entirely unrelated to eukaryotic developmental gene regulation by homeodomain transcription factors.

preguntas.q: Homeodomain transcription factors that regulate segmental body patterning during embryogenesis are encoded by which two gene families?

e.correcta: HOX and PAX genes both encode homeodomain-containing transcription factors, proteins with a conserved ~60-amino-acid DNA-binding domain that binds enhancer/promoter elements to switch on batteries of downstream genes controlling body segment identity and organ formation along the embryonic axis. HOX genes are clustered and expressed in a spatial and temporal order that mirrors their chromosomal position (colinearity), establishing anterior-posterior identity, while PAX genes direct formation of specific structures like the eyes, kidneys, and vertebral column. Mutations in either family produce characteristic patterning defects, which is why they are grouped together as the classic homeobox gene families in molecular biology.

incorrectas.B: SRY and SOX9 are part of the sex-determination cascade — SRY (on the Y chromosome) upregulates SOX9 to drive testis differentiation — and while SOX proteins contain a DNA-binding HMG box, they are not classified with the homeodomain-containing HOX/PAX family being tested here.
incorrectas.C: WNT and SHH (Sonic hedgehog) are secreted signaling morphogens that act through cell-surface receptors and downstream signal transduction cascades to pattern limbs and neural tube, not homeodomain transcription factors themselves, even though they often act upstream of HOX gene expression.
incorrectas.D: FGF and BMP are also secreted growth factor families that signal through receptor tyrosine kinases and SMAD pathways respectively to guide limb outgrowth and skeletal patterning; they influence HOX expression but are not themselves homeodomain-containing transcription factors.

preguntas.q: A defective PAX3 gene is most closely associated with which syndrome, characterized by pigmentary abnormalities, sensorineural hearing loss, and limb anomalies?

e.correcta: Waardenburg syndrome results from mutations in PAX3 (and related genes), which encode homeodomain transcription factors essential for neural crest cell development. Because neural crest cells give rise to melanocytes, cranial and peripheral structures, and limb-forming tissue, a defective PAX gene produces the classic triad of white forelock/patchy hypopigmentation, heterochromia or bright blue irides, sensorineural deafness, and associated limb abnormalities. This illustrates how a single transcription factor defect can cause a pleiotropic syndrome by disrupting one progenitor cell population that contributes to many tissues.

incorrectas.B: DiGeorge syndrome is caused by a 22q11.2 microdeletion affecting third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development, producing cardiac defects, hypocalcemia, and thymic aplasia — a chromosomal deletion syndrome, not a PAX gene homeodomain defect.
incorrectas.C: Treacher Collins syndrome arises from mutations in TCOF1 (or related ribosomal biogenesis genes) affecting neural crest cell survival, causing mandibulofacial dysostosis, but this is a distinct gene and mechanism from the PAX3 homeodomain defect that causes Waardenburg syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Noonan syndrome is caused by mutations in the RAS/MAPK signaling pathway (e.g., PTPN11), producing short stature, congenital heart disease, and characteristic facies — unrelated to PAX gene homeodomain transcription factor dysfunction.

preguntas.q: A drug once prescribed for morning sickness caused severe limb reduction defects by inadvertently blocking homeodomain proteins from binding enhancer regions. Which drug is this?

e.correcta: Thalidomide was used for morning sickness in the 1950s-60s before it was recognized to cause phocomelia and other severe limb reduction defects. Mechanistically, thalidomide interferes with the binding of homeodomain transcription factors to their enhancer elements, disrupting the normal HOX-gene-driven patterning program that specifies limb bud outgrowth and segmentation, so limbs fail to elongate properly. This became one of the most famous teratogen examples in medical history and prompted the modern era of drug safety testing in pregnancy.

incorrectas.B: Diethylstilbestrol (DES) is a synthetic estrogen that was given to pregnant women to prevent miscarriage, and it causes vaginal clear cell adenocarcinoma and uterine anomalies in exposed daughters — a hormonal teratogenic mechanism, not interference with homeodomain-enhancer binding.
incorrectas.C: Misoprostol is a prostaglandin E1 analog used for cervical ripening/labor induction and peptic ulcer prophylaction; when used as an unsuccessful abortifacient it can cause Mobius sequence and limb defects via vascular disruption, not via blocking homeodomain protein-enhancer interactions.
incorrectas.D: Valproic acid is an antiepileptic that causes neural tube defects by inhibiting histone deacetylase and folate metabolism, a different teratogenic mechanism than the homeodomain-enhancer disruption caused by thalidomide.

preguntas.q: Which class of transcription factors binds peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) to upregulate genes involved in lipid metabolism and peroxisome expression?

e.correcta: PPARs are ligand-activated nuclear transcription factors that, once bound by fatty acids or fibrate/thiazolidinedione drugs, heterodimerize with the retinoid X receptor and bind PPREs in DNA to increase transcription of genes governing lipid storage, lipoprotein metabolism, and peroxisome proliferation. This is the molecular basis for how fibrates (PPAR-alpha agonists) lower triglycerides and thiazolidinediones (PPAR-gamma agonists) improve insulin sensitivity — both work by directly reprogramming gene transcription rather than acting on a surface receptor. Because PPARs are themselves transcription factors, their drugs have delayed onset of action, since new protein synthesis is required.

incorrectas.B: Steroid hormone receptors (e.g., glucocorticoid, estrogen, androgen receptors) are also ligand-activated nuclear transcription factors, but they bind hormone response elements distinct from PPREs and regulate different gene sets tied to their specific hormone signaling, not peroxisome/lipid metabolism genes specifically.
incorrectas.C: Zinc finger transcription factors are a broad structural class defined by a zinc-coordinated DNA-binding motif (e.g., steroid receptors, GATA factors, Sp1) — PPARs actually do use a zinc finger DNA-binding domain, but the category tested here is defined by function and specific ligand/response element (PPRE), which is unique to PPARs.
incorrectas.D: Basic helix-loop-helix transcription factors (e.g., MyoD, myc) dimerize via a helix-loop-helix motif and bind E-box DNA sequences to control cell differentiation and proliferation genes, an entirely different structural and functional family from the nuclear receptor PPARs.

preguntas.q: Which class of antidiabetic drugs improves insulin sensitivity by directly activating PPAR-gamma?

e.correcta: Thiazolidinediones (e.g., pioglitazone, rosiglitazone) bind and activate PPAR-gamma, a nuclear transcription factor expressed predominantly in adipose tissue, which upregulates genes that promote adipocyte differentiation, fatty acid uptake/storage, and adiponectin release, ultimately increasing peripheral insulin sensitivity in muscle and liver. Because this mechanism requires altered gene transcription and new protein synthesis, the clinical effect takes weeks to manifest, unlike drugs acting on ion channels or receptors. Fluid retention and weight gain are notable side effects tied to this same adipogenic transcriptional program.

incorrectas.B: Sulfonylureas (e.g., glyburide, glipizide) close ATP-sensitive potassium channels on pancreatic beta cells to trigger depolarization and insulin release — an insulin secretagogue mechanism entirely independent of PPAR-gamma transcriptional activation.
incorrectas.C: Biguanides (metformin) activate AMP-activated protein kinase to decrease hepatic gluconeogenesis and increase peripheral glucose uptake; they do not act through PPAR-gamma and do not require nuclear receptor-mediated transcription to lower glucose.
incorrectas.D: SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin) block sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 in the renal proximal tubule to promote glucosuria, a mechanism at the level of renal glucose reabsorption, unrelated to PPAR-gamma or adipocyte gene transcription.

preguntas.q: Which class of lipid-lowering drugs decreases serum triglycerides primarily by activating PPAR-alpha and increasing peroxisome-mediated fatty acid oxidation?

e.correcta: Fibrates (e.g., gemfibrozil, fenofibrate) are agonists at PPAR-alpha, a nuclear transcription factor highly expressed in liver and muscle, which upregulates lipoprotein lipase and enzymes of peroxisomal and mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation. The net effect is enhanced clearance of triglyceride-rich VLDL particles, making fibrates the most effective agents for markedly lowering serum triglycerides, which is why they are first-line in severe hypertriglyceridemia to prevent pancreatitis.

incorrectas.B: Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis, which upregulates hepatic LDL receptors and primarily lowers LDL cholesterol — a cytoplasmic enzyme-inhibition mechanism, not PPAR-alpha-mediated transcriptional activation.
incorrectas.C: Bile acid resins (e.g., cholestyramine) bind bile acids in the intestinal lumen to prevent their reabsorption, forcing the liver to convert more cholesterol into bile acids and upregulate LDL receptors; this acts in the gut lumen, entirely independent of nuclear PPAR signaling.
incorrectas.D: Niacin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue, reducing free fatty acid flux to the liver and thereby decreasing VLDL/LDL synthesis while raising HDL; its target is lipolysis regulation, not PPAR-alpha transcriptional activation.

preguntas.q: Which transcription factor binds kB DNA elements and serves as a master regulator of gene expression in the innate and adaptive immune response?

e.correcta: NF-kB is a transcription factor normally held inactive in the cytoplasm by its inhibitor IkB; upon stimulation by cytokines, pathogen-associated molecular patterns, or stress signals, IkB is phosphorylated and degraded, allowing NF-kB to translocate to the nucleus and bind kB elements in promoters/enhancers. This drives transcription of a huge array of pro-inflammatory genes (cytokines, chemokines, adhesion molecules, and anti-apoptotic proteins), making NF-kB a central hub coordinating both innate and adaptive immune gene expression. This is precisely why glucocorticoids, which suppress NF-kB signaling, are such broadly effective anti-inflammatory drugs.

incorrectas.B: STAT3 is activated by phosphorylation downstream of cytokine receptors (like IL-6) via JAK kinases, then dimerizes and translocates to the nucleus to bind different response elements than kB sites, mediating a distinct cytokine-signaling transcriptional program rather than the kB-element pathway.
incorrectas.C: AP-1 is a dimeric transcription factor (Fos/Jun) activated downstream of MAPK signaling that binds TPA response elements to regulate genes in proliferation and stress responses; it cooperates with NF-kB in some contexts but binds a different DNA element and is not itself the kB-binding factor described.
incorrectas.D: NFAT (nuclear factor of activated T cells) is activated by calcineurin-mediated dephosphorylation following calcium influx in T cells and binds distinct NFAT response elements to drive IL-2 transcription; it is the target of calcineurin inhibitors like cyclosporine, not the kB-element-binding factor being asked about.

preguntas.q: Which class of drugs exerts its broad anti-inflammatory effect largely by suppressing NF-kB signaling?

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids bind cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptors that translocate to the nucleus and induce transcription of IkB, the inhibitory protein that sequesters NF-kB in the cytoplasm; the receptor complex can also directly repress NF-kB and AP-1 activity. Because NF-kB is the master switch for so many inflammatory cytokines and adhesion molecules, suppressing it gives glucocorticoids their characteristically broad, multi-pathway anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effect, unlike drugs that block only a single mediator.

incorrectas.B: NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX-1/COX-2) enzymes to block prostaglandin synthesis from arachidonic acid, a much narrower anti-inflammatory mechanism confined to the eicosanoid pathway, with no direct effect on NF-kB-driven gene transcription.
incorrectas.C: Leukotriene receptor antagonists (e.g., montelukast) block the CysLT1 receptor to prevent leukotriene-mediated bronchoconstriction and inflammation in asthma, acting downstream at a single receptor rather than upstream at the transcriptional level like NF-kB suppression.
incorrectas.D: Biologic TNF-alpha inhibitors (e.g., infliximab, etanercept) neutralize a single cytokine, TNF-alpha, before it can bind its receptor and activate downstream signaling (which includes NF-kB activation); they act extracellularly on one mediator rather than intracellularly suppressing the transcription factor itself.

preguntas.q: Which eukaryotic RNA polymerase binds directly to the promoter (e.g., TATA box) to initiate transcription of protein-coding genes into mRNA?

e.correcta: RNA polymerase II is recruited to core promoter elements such as the TATA box via general transcription factors (e.g., TFIID recognizing the TATA box), forming the preinitiation complex that positions the enzyme to begin synthesizing mRNA (as well as snRNA and microRNA precursors). This promoter-binding step is essential for accurate transcription start site selection and is the target of alpha-amanitin poisoning (mushroom toxicity) and actinomycin D chemotherapy. Because it makes mRNA, RNA pol II activity is the rate-limiting step connecting DNA sequence information to protein synthesis.

incorrectas.B: RNA polymerase I is located in the nucleolus and transcribes the large pre-ribosomal RNA (28S, 18S, 5.8S rRNA) from its own distinct promoter, not the TATA-box-driven promoters of protein-coding genes handled by RNA pol II.
incorrectas.C: RNA polymerase III transcribes small, structural RNAs — tRNA, 5S rRNA, and other small nuclear RNAs — using internal promoter elements located within the transcribed gene itself rather than binding a TATA box upstream like RNA pol II.
incorrectas.D: Primase is an RNA polymerase involved in DNA replication, synthesizing short RNA primers to initiate leading and lagging strand synthesis; it is not involved in transcribing genes into mRNA and does not bind promoter elements the way RNA pol II does.

preguntas.q: Which antibiotic exerts its antimycobacterial effect by directly inhibiting prokaryotic DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, thereby blocking bacterial transcription?

e.correcta: Rifampin binds the beta subunit of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and blocks initiation of RNA synthesis, directly halting prokaryotic transcription. This action, along with good tissue penetration, makes it a cornerstone drug for tuberculosis and for prophylaxis against Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae; its well-known side effects include red-orange body fluids and potent induction of cytochrome P450 enzymes (causing many drug interactions).

incorrectas.B: Isoniazid inhibits synthesis of mycolic acids in the mycobacterial cell wall (via inhibition of InhA, an enoyl-ACP reductase, after activation by KatG), a cell-wall-targeted mechanism entirely distinct from blocking RNA polymerase transcription.
incorrectas.C: Ethambutol inhibits arabinosyl transferase, blocking arabinogalactan synthesis in the mycobacterial cell wall; this weakens the cell wall rather than interfering with RNA polymerase or transcription.
incorrectas.D: Pyrazinamide is a prodrug converted by mycobacterial pyrazinamidase into pyrazinoic acid, which disrupts membrane function/energetics in the acidic intracellular environment; its mechanism does not involve inhibition of RNA polymerase.

preguntas.q: Which chemotherapeutic agent inhibits both prokaryotic and eukaryotic RNA polymerase by intercalating into DNA and blocking transcription?

e.correcta: Actinomycin D (dactinomycin) intercalates between DNA base pairs, physically blocking the DNA template from being read by RNA polymerase, and because this mechanism doesn't depend on any bacteria-specific enzyme structure, it inhibits both prokaryotic and eukaryotic RNA polymerases equally. Clinically it is used in pediatric tumors like Wilms tumor, rhabdomyosarcoma, and Ewing sarcoma, and in lab research it is classically used to distinguish transcription-dependent from transcription-independent processes because it shuts down all RNA synthesis broadly.

incorrectas.B: Rifampin also inhibits RNA polymerase, but it is selective for the bacterial (prokaryotic) enzyme's beta subunit and does not meaningfully inhibit eukaryotic RNA polymerases, which is exactly why it can be used safely as an antibiotic in human patients.
incorrectas.C: Doxorubicin is an anthracycline that intercalates DNA and generates free radicals, but its major mechanism of cytotoxicity is inhibition of topoisomerase II (creating double-strand breaks), not direct blockade of RNA polymerase transcription in both kingdoms.
incorrectas.D: Bleomycin induces DNA strand breaks through free radical formation via a mechanism involving iron and oxygen, causing chromosome fragmentation; it does not act by intercalating to block RNA polymerase-mediated transcription.

preguntas.q: How many distinct RNA polymerase enzymes do prokaryotes possess to synthesize all three major classes of RNA (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA)?

e.correcta: Prokaryotes use a single multi-subunit RNA polymerase (core enzyme plus a sigma factor for promoter recognition) to transcribe all three RNA classes — mRNA, tRNA, and rRNA — from their DNA templates. This is a key contrast with eukaryotes, which have evolved three specialized polymerases (I, II, III), each dedicated to a different RNA class; this single-enzyme system in bacteria is also what makes rifampin such a clean antibacterial target, since inhibiting one enzyme shuts down all bacterial transcription.

incorrectas.B: Two polymerases is not correct for prokaryotes; this number would incorrectly split the workload that a single bacterial RNA polymerase actually performs for all RNA classes.
incorrectas.C: Three is the number of distinct RNA polymerases found in eukaryotic cells (RNA pol I, II, and III, each transcribing a different RNA class), not the prokaryotic system, which relies on just one enzyme for everything.
incorrectas.D: Four polymerases does not correspond to either prokaryotic (one) or eukaryotic (three) transcription machinery and reflects a common overestimation of enzyme diversity in bacterial transcription.

preguntas.q: What is the name of the initial, unprocessed primary transcript synthesized directly from eukaryotic DNA before splicing, capping, and polyadenylation occur?

e.correcta: hnRNA is the immediate product of RNA polymerase II transcription in the nucleus — a large, heterogeneous precursor that still contains both introns and exons in the order encoded by the gene. Only after undergoing 5' capping, 3' polyadenylation, and intron splicing does hnRNA become mature mRNA that can exit the nucleus for translation, so hnRNA represents the raw, unedited transcriptional output before eukaryotic RNA processing machinery acts on it.

incorrectas.B: Mature mRNA is the final processed product — after hnRNA has been capped, polyadenylated, and spliced to remove introns — so it is the end result of processing, not the initial primary transcript being asked about here.
incorrectas.C: Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) is transcribed by RNA polymerase I (for the large subunits) as a separate primary transcript in the nucleolus, structurally and functionally distinct from the RNA polymerase II-derived hnRNA that becomes mRNA.
incorrectas.D: Small nuclear RNA (snRNA) is transcribed largely by RNA polymerase III (or II for some) and functions as a structural/catalytic component of the spliceosome that processes hnRNA; it is not itself the primary transcript that becomes mRNA.
