incorrectas.C: Signal peptide cleavage is the proteolytic removal of the N-terminal signal sequence by signal peptidase once a protein has been translocated into the ER, a one-time targeting-related event rather than the broad category of reversible chemical group modifications.
incorrectas.D: Alternative splicing is a pre-mRNA processing event that occurs in the nucleus before translation, generating different mRNA isoforms by including or excluding exons — it is unrelated to the post-translational chemical modifications applied to the finished protein.

preguntas.q: Which phase of the cell cycle is typically the shortest in duration?

e.correcta: M phase, encompassing mitosis (prophase through telophase) and cytokinesis, is typically the shortest phase of the cell cycle, often lasting under an hour, because chromosome segregation and physical cell division proceed relatively quickly once the cell has finished the far lengthier preparatory work of growth and DNA replication. In contrast, interphase (G1, S, and G2 combined) occupies the vast majority of the cycle's total time, since it includes the extensive processes of cell growth, protein synthesis, organelle duplication, and full genome replication. This is why actively dividing cells spend most of their time not visibly dividing at all, but preparing to divide.

incorrectas.A: G1 phase is a growth phase during which the cell increases in size and synthesizes proteins and organelles in preparation for DNA replication; its duration is highly variable between cell types but is generally much longer than the brief M phase.
incorrectas.B: S phase, during which the entire genome is replicated, typically takes several hours since accurate duplication of billions of base pairs requires substantial time for DNA polymerase and associated replication machinery to work through the genome.
incorrectas.D: G0 is not actually a phase of the active cell cycle but a resting state that cells exit the cycle into, sometimes for the remainder of their lifespan (as in neurons) — it is not a timed phase that can be compared for "shortest duration" among the cycling phases.

preguntas.q: Which cell cycle state is characterized by resting, quiescent cells that have exited the active cycle and are not dividing?

e.correcta: G0 is a quiescent, resting state that cells exit into from G1 when they are not actively preparing to divide, allowing them to remain metabolically active and carry out their specialized functions without committing resources to growth and replication. Cells can remain in G0 temporarily (like stable/quiescent cells such as hepatocytes, which can re-enter G1 when stimulated by injury or growth signals) or essentially permanently (like permanent cells such as neurons and cardiac myocytes, which have little to no capacity to re-enter the cycle). Understanding G0 as a true "off-ramp" from the cell cycle, rather than another lap around it, clarifies why terminally differentiated tissues have limited regenerative capacity.

incorrectas.A: G1 is an active phase of the cycle in which a cell is growing and preparing for DNA synthesis, distinct from G0, which represents having left the cycle altogether rather than progressing through one of its phases.
incorrectas.C: S phase is the active DNA synthesis phase, during which the genome is being replicated in preparation for division — a resting, non-dividing cell by definition is not in S phase, since it is not progressing toward mitosis at all.
incorrectas.D: G2 is the active growth phase following DNA replication and preceding mitosis, during which the cell checks for replication errors and prepares its machinery for division — this is part of the active cycle, unlike the quiescent G0 state.

preguntas.q: Which category of cells remains permanently in G0 and can only be regenerated from stem cells, rather than by division of existing mature cells?

e.correcta: Permanent cells — including neurons, skeletal and cardiac muscle cells, and mature red blood cells — exit the cell cycle into G0 and lack the capacity to re-enter it, meaning they cannot divide to replace themselves if lost. Any regeneration of these tissues must instead come from a separate pool of stem or progenitor cells (e.g., satellite cells for skeletal muscle), which is why injuries to permanent tissues like the myocardium after an infarct or neurons after a stroke tend to heal by fibrosis/gliosis rather than true functional regeneration. This concept is central to understanding why certain organs have essentially no capacity for self-repair after significant damage.

incorrectas.A: Labile cells (such as bone marrow, gut epithelium, and skin) are the opposite of permanent cells — they never enter G0 and divide continuously and rapidly throughout life, giving them robust regenerative capacity rather than none.
incorrectas.C: Stable (quiescent) cells, like hepatocytes and renal tubular cells, normally reside in G0 but retain the ability to re-enter G1 and divide when stimulated by injury or a growth signal — unlike permanent cells, they are not permanently locked out of the cycle.
incorrectas.D: Totipotent cells refer to the developmental potential of a cell to give rise to any cell type including extraembryonic tissue (as in early embryogenesis), a concept about differentiation potential rather than about a mature tissue's ability to re-enter the cell cycle.

preguntas.q: Which category of cells normally resides in G0 but can re-enter G1 and divide when stimulated, such as hepatocytes or renal tubular cells?

e.correcta: Stable (quiescent) cells — including hepatocytes, lymphocytes, renal tubular cells, and periosteal cells — normally sit in G0 under baseline conditions but retain the machinery needed to re-enter G1 and proliferate when an appropriate stimulus arises, such as tissue injury or a growth factor signal. This is exemplified clinically by the liver's remarkable capacity to regenerate after partial hepatectomy, as quiescent hepatocytes are triggered to re-enter the cell cycle and restore liver mass. This intermediate regenerative capacity places stable cells between labile cells (which never stop dividing) and permanent cells (which can never resume dividing).

incorrectas.A: Permanent cells (neurons, cardiac and skeletal muscle, RBCs) also reside in G0, but unlike stable cells they cannot be stimulated to re-enter G1 — any repair of these tissues must come from a separate stem cell population rather than division of the mature cells themselves.
incorrectas.B: Labile cells (bone marrow, gut epithelium, skin, hair follicles, germ cells) never enter G0 at all — they divide continuously and rapidly with a short G1, which is the opposite behavior from stable cells that default to a resting state until stimulated.
incorrectas.D: Pluripotent stem cells describe a developmental capacity to differentiate into cells of all three germ layers, a concept about differentiation potential rather than a description of a mature tissue's baseline cell cycle behavior.

preguntas.q: Which category of cells never enters G0 and instead divides continuously and rapidly with a short G1 phase, such as bone marrow and gut epithelium?

e.correcta: Labile cells — including bone marrow hematopoietic cells, gut epithelium, epidermis of the skin, hair follicles, and germ cells — cycle continuously throughout life, moving quickly through a short G1 phase rather than pausing in G0, which gives these tissues their high baseline turnover rate and strong capacity for rapid regeneration. This constant proliferation is exactly why these tissues are especially vulnerable to agents that target rapidly dividing cells, such as cytotoxic chemotherapy, producing classic side effects like mucositis, alopecia, and myelosuppression. Recognizing labile tissues as the most mitotically active helps predict both their regenerative resilience and their chemotherapy sensitivity.

incorrectas.A: Permanent cells (neurons, cardiac/skeletal muscle, RBCs) are the opposite extreme — they remain in G0 indefinitely and essentially never divide again, relying entirely on stem cells for any tissue replacement, unlike labile cells which divide continuously on their own.
incorrectas.C: Stable (quiescent) cells, such as hepatocytes and renal tubular cells, normally rest in G0 and only re-enter the cycle when stimulated by injury or growth signals — this intermittent, stimulus-dependent division contrasts with the continuous, unprompted cycling of labile cells.
incorrectas.D: Senescent cells are cells that have permanently exited the cell cycle due to accumulated damage or telomere shortening and can no longer divide at all, which is essentially the opposite state from the constant, rapid division that defines labile cells.

preguntas.q: Chemotherapy targeting rapidly dividing cells causes the most collateral damage to which category of tissue, exemplified by gut epithelium, skin, and hair follicles?

e.correcta: Labile cells (gut epithelium, skin, hair follicles, bone marrow) continuously divide and cycle through G1, S, G2, and M to replace themselves throughout life. Because chemotherapy agents work by poisoning DNA synthesis or mitotic machinery, they preferentially kill cells that are actively cycling, which is why labile tissues bear the brunt of chemo toxicity — manifesting clinically as mucositis, alopecia, and myelosuppression.

incorrectas.B: Stable (quiescent) cells, like hepatocytes and other parenchymal cells, normally sit in G0 but can re-enter the cell cycle when needed (e.g., liver regeneration); because they are not actively dividing most of the time, they are relatively spared compared to constantly cycling labile cells.
incorrectas.C: Permanent cells, such as cardiac myocytes and neurons, have exited the cell cycle for good and cannot regenerate, so they are essentially resistant to chemotherapy's antimitotic mechanism (though they can be damaged by other drug toxicities unrelated to cell division).
incorrectas.D: Senescent cells have permanently withdrawn from the cell cycle due to accumulated damage or telomere shortening; since they are not synthesizing new DNA or dividing, chemotherapy directed at proliferating cells has little effect on them.

preguntas.q: During which phase of the cell cycle does DNA synthesis and replication occur, doubling the chromatid content while chromosome number stays the same?

e.correcta: S phase is when the cell replicates its entire genome, converting each chromosome from one chromatid to two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. This takes a diploid cell from 46 chromosomes/46 chromatids to 46 chromosomes/92 chromatids — the chromosome number is unchanged because sister chromatids are still counted as one chromosome until they separate in anaphase of mitosis.

incorrectas.A: G1 is the gap phase before S phase in which the cell grows and synthesizes the RNA, proteins, and other building blocks it will need for DNA replication, but no DNA synthesis itself occurs here.
incorrectas.C: G2 follows S phase and serves as a checkpoint where the newly replicated DNA is proofread for errors and the cell prepares the components needed for mitosis; DNA content is already doubled by this point, not being synthesized.
incorrectas.D: M phase (mitosis) is when the already-duplicated sister chromatids are separated and distributed into two daughter cells; no new DNA synthesis happens during M phase itself.

preguntas.q: Which set of cell cycle phases together comprise interphase, the period between successive mitotic divisions?

e.correcta: Interphase consists of G1 (growth and preparation of building blocks like RNA, protein, lipid, and carbohydrate for DNA synthesis), S (actual DNA replication), and G2 (proofreading of newly synthesized DNA and final preparation, including ATP generation, for division). All three phases occur between one mitosis and the next, during which the cell is metabolically active but not dividing.

incorrectas.B: This combination incorrectly includes M phase, which is mitosis itself — the division event that marks the end of interphase, not a part of it.
incorrectas.C: This combination also incorrectly includes M phase alongside S and G2 while omitting G1, but G1 is an essential part of interphase where the cell prepares its synthetic machinery before replicating DNA.
incorrectas.D: G0 is a resting/quiescent state that some cells enter instead of continuing the cycle (e.g., stable cells between divisions); it is not one of the three phases that make up an actively cycling cell's interphase.

preguntas.q: Which phase of the cell cycle is the only one that is NOT part of interphase?

e.correcta: M phase (mitosis) is the actual division event — chromosome condensation, spindle formation, and separation of sister chromatids into two daughter cells — and it occurs between successive interphases rather than being part of interphase itself. Interphase (G1, S, G2) is the growth-and-replication period bookended by rounds of M phase.

incorrectas.A: G1 is the first gap phase of interphase, during which the cell synthesizes proteins, RNA, and other components in preparation for DNA replication.
incorrectas.B: S phase, during which DNA is actually replicated, is squarely part of interphase — it sits between G1 and G2.
incorrectas.C: G2 is the second gap phase of interphase, occurring after DNA replication and before mitosis, used for error-checking the newly copied DNA and final preparation for division.

preguntas.q: Transcription (RNA synthesis) is ongoing throughout which portion of the cell cycle?

e.correcta: Transcription occurs continuously throughout interphase — G1, S, and G2 — because the cell needs a steady supply of mRNA to produce the proteins required for growth, DNA replication machinery, and mitotic preparation. Chromatin is decondensed and accessible to RNA polymerase during these phases, unlike in M phase.

incorrectas.A: Restricting transcription to S phase alone ignores that RNA and protein synthesis are also essential in G1 (to build the machinery needed to even enter S phase) and in G2 (to prepare for mitosis).
incorrectas.B: During M phase, chromatin condenses tightly into chromosomes to allow segregation, which physically blocks RNA polymerase access to DNA, so transcription is largely shut down during mitosis, not ongoing.
incorrectas.D: Limiting transcription to G1 misses that RNA synthesis continues in S and G2 as well — the cell must keep producing proteins needed for DNA replication (S) and for checking/correcting that DNA and preparing for division (G2).

preguntas.q: Which tumor suppressor protein acts at the G1/S checkpoint to prevent cells with damaged DNA from entering S phase?

e.correcta: p53 is activated by DNA damage sensors and halts the cell cycle at the G1 checkpoint (largely by upregulating p21, which inhibits cyclin-CDK complexes) to allow time for repair; if damage is irreparable, p53 triggers apoptosis. This makes p53 the 'guardian of the genome,' and its loss (as in Li-Fraumeni syndrome or many sporadic cancers) allows damaged DNA to be replicated and passed on, promoting tumorigenesis.

incorrectas.A: Rb (retinoblastoma protein) also restrains the G1/S transition, but it does so by binding and inhibiting E2F transcription factors rather than sensing DNA damage directly — its regulation is tied to cyclin D-CDK4/6 phosphorylation status rather than being the primary DNA-damage-response checkpoint protein.
incorrectas.C: BRCA1 is a tumor suppressor involved in double-stranded DNA break repair via homologous recombination; it participates in the DNA damage response but is not itself the master G1 checkpoint regulator that p53 is.
incorrectas.D: APC (adenomatous polyposis coli) is a tumor suppressor that normally promotes degradation of beta-catenin to regulate the Wnt signaling pathway and cell adhesion/proliferation; its loss drives colorectal neoplasia, but it does not function at the G1 cell cycle checkpoint.

preguntas.q: Which organelle is the primary site of synthesis for proteins destined for secretion?

e.correcta: The rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) is studded with membrane-bound ribosomes that translate proteins bearing an N-terminal signal sequence directly into its lumen, where they are folded and can be glycosylated before moving on to the Golgi for further processing and packaging into secretory vesicles. This makes the RER the entry point of the secretory pathway for proteins destined to leave the cell.

incorrectas.A: The smooth ER lacks ribosomes and instead specializes in lipid and steroid synthesis, and detoxification of drugs and xenobiotics via the cytochrome P450 system — it is not where secretory proteins are made.
incorrectas.B: The Golgi apparatus receives proteins after they are synthesized in the RER and further modifies, sorts, and packages them for secretion or trafficking, but it is not the initial site of protein synthesis.
incorrectas.D: Free (cytosolic) ribosomes synthesize proteins that will remain in the cytosol or be imported into organelles like mitochondria and the nucleus post-translationally, not proteins destined for secretion via the ER-Golgi pathway.

preguntas.q: N-linked oligosaccharide addition to nascent proteins occurs in which cellular compartment?

e.correcta: N-linked glycosylation begins co-translationally in the rough endoplasmic reticulum, where a pre-assembled oligosaccharide is transferred en bloc onto asparagine residues of the nascent polypeptide as it enters the RER lumen. This early glycosylation step assists in proper protein folding and serves as a quality-control signal before the protein moves to the Golgi for further trimming and modification.

incorrectas.A: The Golgi apparatus further trims and modifies the N-linked oligosaccharides that were already attached in the RER (and adds O-linked sugars), but the initial N-linked addition itself takes place upstream in the RER.
incorrectas.C: The cytosol is where free ribosomes translate proteins that stay in the cytosol or are imported post-translationally into organelles; it lacks the enzymatic machinery (oligosaccharyltransferase) needed for N-linked glycosylation, which is an ER-lumen process.
incorrectas.D: The nucleus is the site of DNA transcription and RNA processing, not protein glycosylation, which is a post-translational modification occurring in the secretory pathway (RER and Golgi).

preguntas.q: Mucus-secreting goblet cells of the small intestine and antibody-secreting plasma cells are both notably rich in which organelle?

e.correcta: Goblet cells and plasma cells are both dedicated secretory cell types — goblet cells churn out large quantities of mucin glycoprotein, and plasma cells mass-produce immunoglobulins — and both tasks require abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum to translate and initially process these secreted proteins. On histology, this abundant RER appears as basophilic cytoplasm (due to ribosomal RNA), a classic clue for identifying these cells.

incorrectas.A: Smooth ER is prominent in cells specializing in steroidogenesis (adrenal cortex, gonads) or detoxification (hepatocytes), not in cells whose main job is producing secreted proteins like mucin or antibodies.
incorrectas.B: The Golgi apparatus is present in all these cells to package the finished secretory product, but the organelle classically highlighted as abundant and diagnostic in goblet cells and plasma cells is the RER, reflecting their high-volume protein synthesis.
incorrectas.D: Peroxisomes handle fatty acid oxidation and detoxification reactions; they are not the organelle associated with the high-output protein secretion seen in goblet cells and plasma cells.

preguntas.q: Ribosomes that are unattached to any membrane and synthesize cytosolic and organellar proteins are called what?

e.correcta: Free ribosomes float freely in the cytosol rather than docking onto the rough ER, and they translate proteins that will function within the cytosol itself or be imported post-translationally into organelles such as the nucleus, mitochondria, and peroxisomes. This distinguishes them from RER-bound ribosomes, which translate proteins destined for secretion, the membrane, or the endomembrane system.

incorrectas.A: Membrane-bound ribosomes are docked onto the rough ER via the translocon complex and synthesize secretory, membrane, and lysosomal proteins — essentially the opposite population from free ribosomes.
incorrectas.C: Signal recognition particles are cytosolic ribonucleoprotein complexes that recognize the signal sequence on a nascent protein and escort the ribosome-mRNA complex to the RER; they are not ribosomes themselves but a targeting mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Polysomes (polyribosomes) refer to multiple ribosomes simultaneously translating a single mRNA strand — this describes an arrangement of ribosomes, whether free or membrane-bound, not a distinct functional category defined by cytosolic/organellar protein synthesis.

preguntas.q: Which organelle serves as the site of steroid hormone synthesis and detoxification of drugs and poisons?

e.correcta: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum lacks ribosomes and instead houses enzymes for lipid and steroid hormone synthesis as well as cytochrome P450-mediated detoxification of drugs and other xenobiotics. This is why hepatocytes (detoxification) and steroid-producing cells of the adrenal cortex and gonads (steroidogenesis) are especially rich in SER.

incorrectas.A: The rough ER, studded with ribosomes, is dedicated to synthesizing and initially processing secretory and membrane proteins — it is not the site of steroid synthesis or xenobiotic detoxification, which are lipid-handling, ribosome-free processes.
incorrectas.B: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids arriving from the ER for their final destinations; it does not perform steroidogenesis or drug detoxification itself.
incorrectas.D: Peroxisomes break down very-long-chain and branched-chain fatty acids and detoxify certain reactive species via catalase, but the classic organelle for steroid synthesis and P450-based drug/poison detoxification is the smooth ER, not the peroxisome.

preguntas.q: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum can be distinguished microscopically from the rough ER based on which feature?

o.B: It forms a continuous network with the nucleus only
o.D: It is surrounded by a double membrane

e.correcta: The defining structural difference is that smooth ER lacks the studded ribosomes that coat the cytosolic face of rough ER, giving it a smooth appearance on electron microscopy. This absence of ribosomes reflects its different function — rather than translating secretory/membrane proteins, SER handles lipid synthesis, steroidogenesis, and detoxification, none of which require ribosome-based translation at its membrane.

incorrectas.B: Both rough and smooth ER are physically continuous with the nuclear envelope and with each other as parts of one interconnected endomembrane network; continuity with the nucleus is not a distinguishing feature between the two.
incorrectas.C: Neither rough nor smooth ER contains its own DNA — that feature is unique to mitochondria (and, in plants, chloroplasts), which carry their own circular genome from their endosymbiotic origin.
incorrectas.D: Neither type of ER is bounded by a double membrane; a double membrane is instead characteristic of the nucleus and mitochondria, not the endoplasmic reticulum, which is a single continuous membrane-bound tubular/sheet network.

preguntas.q: When a protein is misfolded, tagging it with multiple copies of which small protein marks it for trafficking to the proteasome for degradation?

e.correcta: Misfolded or damaged proteins are recognized by E1-E2-E3 ubiquitin ligase enzymes, which covalently attach chains of ubiquitin (a small 76-amino-acid protein) onto lysine residues of the target. A polyubiquitin chain acts as a molecular 'tag' that is specifically recognized by the 26S proteasome, directing the tagged protein into the barrel-shaped complex for ATP-dependent degradation.

incorrectas.A: SUMO (small ubiquitin-like modifier) is a related but distinct post-translational modifier that typically alters protein localization, stability, or protein-protein interactions rather than serving as the canonical degradation signal for the proteasome the way polyubiquitination does.
incorrectas.B: Clathrin is a structural protein that coats vesicles during receptor-mediated endocytosis, forming the clathrin lattice around budding vesicles — it has no role in tagging misfolded proteins for proteasomal degradation.
incorrectas.D: Actin is a cytoskeletal protein responsible for cell shape, motility, and muscle contraction; it plays no role in marking misfolded proteins for proteasomal destruction.

preguntas.q: Which barrel-shaped protein complex degrades damaged or ubiquitin-tagged proteins into peptide fragments?

e.correcta: The proteasome is a large, barrel-shaped, ATP-dependent protein complex found in both the cytosol and nucleus that recognizes polyubiquitin-tagged proteins, unfolds them, and threads them through its central chamber where internal proteases cleave them into short peptide fragments. This system is the main pathway for regulated turnover of misfolded, damaged, or short-lived regulatory proteins (like cyclins), distinct from the lysosome's role in degrading extracellular and membrane-derived material.

incorrectas.A: The lysosome is a membrane-bound organelle containing acid hydrolases that degrade material delivered via endocytosis, phagocytosis, or autophagy; it operates in an acidic vesicular environment rather than as a cytosolic barrel-shaped complex targeting ubiquitin-tagged proteins.
incorrectas.B: The spliceosome is a ribonucleoprotein complex that removes introns from pre-mRNA during RNA processing in the nucleus — it functions in gene expression, not protein degradation.
incorrectas.D: The ribosome is the machine that synthesizes proteins by translating mRNA, the opposite function of the proteasome, which breaks proteins back down.

preguntas.q: Defects in the ubiquitin-proteasome system, including mutations in Parkin, PINK1, and DJ-1, have been implicated in some cases of which neurodegenerative disease?

e.correcta: Parkin, PINK1, and DJ-1 are genes involved in some familial forms of Parkinson disease, and their protein products participate in the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (Parkin itself is an E3 ubiquitin ligase) and in mitochondrial quality control. When this system fails, misfolded proteins such as alpha-synuclein accumulate rather than being cleared, contributing to the formation of Lewy bodies and the dopaminergic neuron loss characteristic of Parkinson disease.

incorrectas.A: Alzheimer disease is linked to accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques and hyperphosphorylated tau neurofibrillary tangles; while protein clearance dysfunction is relevant broadly to neurodegeneration, the specific genes Parkin, PINK1, and DJ-1 are tied to Parkinson disease, not Alzheimer pathology.
incorrectas.C: Huntington disease results from a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene leading to an abnormal, aggregation-prone protein; it is not the disease classically associated with Parkin/PINK1/DJ-1 mutations.
incorrectas.D: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis involves motor neuron degeneration and has been linked to genes like SOD1 and C9orf72, not to the Parkin-PINK1-DJ-1 ubiquitin-proteasome axis discussed here.

preguntas.q: Inside the proteasome, which class of enzymes cleaves ubiquitinated proteins into peptide fragments?

e.correcta: The inner chamber of the 26S proteasome contains multiple proteolytic active sites (part of the 20S core particle) that function as proteases, cleaving the unfolded, ubiquitin-tagged polypeptide into small peptide fragments once it has been threaded in by the ATP-dependent 19S regulatory cap. These fragments can then be further degraded by cytosolic peptidases into free amino acids or, in some cases, presented on MHC class I molecules for immune surveillance.

incorrectas.A: Kinases add phosphate groups to substrates (e.g., activating cyclin-CDK complexes) — they modify proteins rather than cleaving peptide bonds, so they are not the enzymes responsible for proteasomal degradation.
incorrectas.C: Ligases, specifically E3 ubiquitin ligases, are responsible for attaching ubiquitin to the target protein before it ever reaches the proteasome — they tag the substrate rather than cleaving it once inside the proteasome.
incorrectas.D: Glycosidases hydrolyze glycosidic bonds in carbohydrates and glycoproteins (relevant to lysosomal glycogen and glycoprotein breakdown), not peptide bonds in ubiquitinated proteins within the proteasome.

preguntas.q: Which membrane-bound organelle handles catabolism of very-long-chain fatty acids, branched-chain fatty acids, amino acids, and ethanol?

e.correcta: The peroxisome performs beta-oxidation of very-long-chain and branched-chain fatty acids (which are too long or structurally awkward for mitochondrial beta-oxidation), along with catabolism of certain amino acids and oxidation of ethanol, generating hydrogen peroxide that is neutralized by catalase within the organelle. Its clinical relevance shows up in disorders like Zellweger syndrome and adrenoleukodystrophy, in which defective peroxisomal function causes toxic accumulation of these very-long-chain fatty acids.

incorrectas.A: Mitochondria perform beta-oxidation of most straight-chain fatty acids and generate the bulk of cellular ATP via oxidative phosphorylation, but they cannot handle very-long-chain or branched-chain fatty acids — that job specifically belongs to the peroxisome.
incorrectas.B: Lysosomes degrade macromolecules delivered by endocytosis, phagocytosis, and autophagy using acid hydrolases in an acidified compartment; they are not the site of fatty acid beta-oxidation or ethanol metabolism.
incorrectas.D: The smooth ER is involved in lipid synthesis, steroidogenesis, and cytochrome P450-based drug detoxification, but the specific catabolic functions of very-long-chain/branched-chain fatty acid oxidation and ethanol breakdown described here are peroxisomal, not smooth-ER, functions.

preguntas.q: Which organelle serves as the distribution center that sorts proteins and lipids arriving from the endoplasmic reticulum and sends them to vesicles and the plasma membrane?

e.correcta: The Golgi apparatus receives newly synthesized proteins and lipids from the ER via vesicular transport, further modifies them (trimming and adding sugars, adding mannose-6-phosphate tags for lysosomal proteins, sulfation, etc.), and then sorts and packages them into vesicles destined for secretion, the plasma membrane, or lysosomes. This 'post office' role makes it the central hub of the secretory pathway downstream of the ER.

incorrectas.A: The peroxisome is a self-contained organelle for fatty acid oxidation and detoxification; it is not part of the ER-to-membrane trafficking and sorting pathway.
incorrectas.B: The lysosome is a destination for material sorted by the Golgi (particularly enzymes tagged with mannose-6-phosphate) rather than the sorting center itself — it receives and degrades cargo rather than distributing it.
incorrectas.D: The mitochondrion is largely independent of the ER-Golgi secretory pathway; most of its proteins are synthesized on free cytosolic ribosomes and imported directly, bypassing the Golgi entirely.

preguntas.q: A stretch of 10-15 hydrophobic amino acids on the N-terminal side of a newly synthesized protein forms what structure that directs it to the rough ER?

e.correcta: The N-terminal signal sequence is a short hydrophobic stretch synthesized at the start of translation that is recognized by the signal recognition particle (SRP), which halts translation and escorts the ribosome-mRNA-nascent chain complex to the SRP receptor on the rough ER membrane. Once docked, translation resumes and the growing protein is threaded through the translocon into the ER lumen — the first step in the secretory pathway.

incorrectas.A: A KDEL sequence is a C-terminal (not N-terminal) tetrapeptide that acts as a retrieval signal, retaining or returning proteins to the ER after they have started moving toward the Golgi — a very different function from initially directing translation to the ER.
incorrectas.B: Mannose-6-phosphate is a carbohydrate tag added in the Golgi to target lysosomal enzymes to the lysosome; it is a sugar modification added later in the pathway, not the amino acid signal sequence that initially sends a ribosome to the RER.
incorrectas.D: A nuclear localization signal directs proteins made on free cytosolic ribosomes into the nucleus through nuclear pores, an entirely separate trafficking route from the ER-targeting signal sequence.

preguntas.q: Which abundant cytosolic ribonucleoprotein complex recognizes the signal sequence and escorts the ribosome-nascent chain complex from the cytosol to the rough ER?

e.correcta: The signal recognition particle (SRP) is a cytosolic ribonucleoprotein that binds the emerging N-terminal signal sequence as it exits the ribosome, pausing translation and guiding the entire ribosome-mRNA-nascent peptide complex to the SRP receptor on the RER membrane. This ensures that proteins destined for secretion or the endomembrane system are co-translationally translocated into the ER rather than released into the cytosol.

incorrectas.A: The spliceosome is a distinct ribonucleoprotein complex, but its job is to remove introns from pre-mRNA in the nucleus during RNA processing — it has no role in directing ribosomes to the ER.
incorrectas.C: Telomerase is a ribonucleoprotein enzyme that extends telomeric DNA repeats at chromosome ends using its internal RNA template; it functions in DNA maintenance, unrelated to protein trafficking to the ER.
incorrectas.D: Chaperonins (like GroEL/GroES-type complexes or the eukaryotic TRiC/CCT) assist in the folding of newly synthesized proteins in the cytosol, but they do not recognize signal sequences or ferry ribosomes to the ER the way SRP does.

preguntas.q: If signal recognition particles (SRPs) are absent or dysfunctional, what happens to proteins that should have been targeted to the rough ER?

o.A: They are degraded immediately by the proteasome
o.C: They are secreted directly without processing
o.D: They are mistargeted to the nucleus

e.correcta: Without functional SRP to recognize the N-terminal signal sequence and dock the ribosome onto the RER, translation simply continues in the cytosol and the finished protein is released there instead of being translocated into the ER lumen. This means proteins that should have entered the secretory pathway (secreted or membrane proteins) instead accumulate as free cytosolic protein, where they are likely to misfold since they lack the ER's specialized folding and glycosylation machinery.

incorrectas.A: While misfolded cytosolic proteins can eventually be ubiquitinated and degraded, that is a downstream consequence of quality control, not the immediate, direct effect of losing SRP function — the immediate effect is failure of ER targeting and cytosolic accumulation.
incorrectas.C: Secretion requires the protein to first enter the ER-Golgi pathway; without SRP-mediated delivery to the RER, the protein never enters that pathway at all, so it cannot be secreted, processed or otherwise.
incorrectas.D: Nuclear import is directed by an entirely separate signal (a nuclear localization signal) recognized by importins, not by SRP — loss of SRP function does not redirect proteins to the nucleus.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme in the Golgi apparatus phosphorylates mannose residues on lysosomal enzymes to generate the mannose-6-phosphate tag needed for proper trafficking?

e.correcta: N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase adds a phosphate group to mannose residues on the oligosaccharide chains of lysosomal enzymes within the Golgi, creating the mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag. This tag is then recognized by M6P receptors that package the enzyme into vesicles bound for the lysosome; without it, these hydrolytic enzymes are instead default-routed for secretion out of the cell.

incorrectas.B: Hexokinase phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate as the first step of glycolysis in the cytosol — a metabolic enzyme with no role in Golgi-based lysosomal enzyme tagging.
incorrectas.C: Glycogen phosphorylase cleaves glucose units off glycogen during glycogenolysis; it acts on glycogen storage, not on mannose residues of glycoproteins in the Golgi.
incorrectas.D: Protein kinase A phosphorylates serine/threonine residues on target proteins downstream of cAMP signaling, a completely different phosphorylation event unrelated to the carbohydrate-tagging system that directs enzymes to lysosomes.

preguntas.q: A defect in N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase, causing failure to add mannose-6-phosphate tags to lysosomal enzymes, results in which disease?

e.correcta: I-cell disease results from a defective Golgi phosphotransferase that fails to attach mannose-6-phosphate tags to newly made lysosomal enzymes, so instead of being routed to lysosomes, these enzymes are secreted extracellularly by default. The lysosomes are then left without their normal hydrolytic enzymes and accumulate undigested substrate as dense inclusion bodies (the 'I-cells' that give the disease its name), while serum levels of these lysosomal enzymes are elevated because they end up circulating outside the cell instead.

incorrectas.A: Tay-Sachs disease is caused by a deficiency of hexosaminidase A itself, a specific lysosomal enzyme, leading to GM2 ganglioside accumulation — the enzyme is missing/nonfunctional, not simply mistrafficked as in I-cell disease.
incorrectas.C: Hurler syndrome results from a deficiency of alpha-L-iduronidase, causing accumulation of heparan and dermatan sulfate; like Tay-Sachs, this is a primary enzyme deficiency rather than a Golgi trafficking/tagging defect.
incorrectas.D: Fabry disease is caused by a deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A, leading to accumulation of globotriaosylceramide; again, this reflects loss of a specific enzyme's activity, not a generalized failure to tag and deliver multiple lysosomal enzymes as seen in I-cell disease.

preguntas.q: Which organelle acts as a sorting center for material taken up from outside the cell or arriving from the Golgi, directing it either to lysosomes for destruction or back to the membrane/Golgi for reuse?

e.correcta: Endosomes form as internalized vesicles from endocytosis (early endosomes) mature and become acidified (late endosomes), during which receptor-ligand complexes are sorted: some cargo is directed onward to lysosomes for degradation, while receptors and other components can be recycled back to the plasma membrane or returned to the Golgi. This sorting function makes the endosomal system the traffic hub connecting the outside of the cell, the plasma membrane, the Golgi, and the lysosome.

incorrectas.B: The peroxisome is a self-contained metabolic organelle for fatty acid oxidation and detoxification; it does not participate in sorting endocytosed material or trafficking between the membrane and Golgi.
incorrectas.C: The proteasome degrades ubiquitin-tagged cytosolic proteins into peptides; it is a cytosolic degradation machine, not a membrane-bound sorting compartment for endocytosed or Golgi-derived material.
incorrectas.D: The mitochondrion generates ATP via oxidative phosphorylation and is largely isolated from the endomembrane trafficking system; it does not sort or redirect endocytosed material.

preguntas.q: A child presents with coarse facial features, clouded corneas, restricted joint mobility, and markedly elevated serum levels of multiple lysosomal enzymes, often progressing to fatal dilated cardiomyopathy. Which inherited lysosomal storage disorder is this?

e.correcta: I-cell disease (mucolipidosis type II) arises from a defect in the Golgi enzyme N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase, so lysosomal enzymes never get their mannose-6-phosphate tag and are instead secreted out of the cell rather than delivered to lysosomes. This produces the classic triad of coarse facies, corneal clouding, and joint restriction with high serum (rather than intracellular) levels of lysosomal enzymes, and is often fatal in childhood due to severe dilated cardiomyopathy.

incorrectas.A: Gaucher disease is caused by glucocerebrosidase deficiency, leading to glucocerebroside accumulation in macrophages (Gaucher cells) with hepatosplenomegaly and bone crises — it does not present with the coarse facies/corneal clouding/elevated serum enzyme picture of a generalized trafficking defect.
incorrectas.B: Niemann-Pick disease results from sphingomyelinase deficiency causing sphingomyelin accumulation, presenting with hepatosplenomegaly, foam cells, and a cherry-red macular spot, not the multi-enzyme trafficking failure and corneal clouding seen in I-cell disease.
incorrectas.D: Krabbe disease is caused by galactocerebrosidase deficiency, leading to psychosine accumulation and severe demyelination with globoid cells; it is a single-enzyme deficiency affecting the nervous system, not a generalized failure of lysosomal enzyme trafficking with elevated serum enzymes.

preguntas.q: I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II) is characterized by elevated plasma levels of which class of enzymes, which fail to reach their normal intracellular destination?

e.correcta: I-cell disease results from a defect in GlcNAc phosphotransferase, the enzyme that normally tags lysosomal hydrolases with mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) in the Golgi. Without this M6P tag, the Golgi cannot sort these enzymes into vesicles destined for lysosomes, so they are instead constitutively secreted out of the cell by default, producing the elevated plasma levels of lysosomal enzymes and, conversely, a marked deficiency of enzymatic activity inside the lysosomes themselves. The result is accumulation of undigested cellular debris ("inclusion cell" bodies) and a severe multisystem presentation with coarse facial features, skeletal abnormalities, and restricted joint movement.

incorrectas.A: Proteasomal enzymes degrade cytosolic ubiquitin-tagged proteins and are not packaged through the Golgi M6P-tagging system at all, so a defect in M6P tagging has no bearing on their levels or secretion.
incorrectas.C: Peroxisomal enzymes are synthesized on free ribosomes and imported post-translationally into peroxisomes via a PTS1/PTS2 signal recognized by peroxins, a completely separate trafficking route from the Golgi-dependent M6P pathway disrupted in I-cell disease.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial matrix enzymes are imported directly across the mitochondrial membranes using signal sequences and the TOM/TIM complexes, bypassing the ER-Golgi secretory pathway entirely, so they are unaffected by loss of GlcNAc phosphotransferase activity.

preguntas.q: How do the inclusion bodies of I-cell disease differ from those seen in typical single-enzyme lysosomal storage diseases (e.g., Tay-Sachs, Gaucher)?

o.A: They contain a single accumulated substrate rather than mixed debris
o.B: They are composed of a heterogeneous mixture of accumulated substrates because multiple lysosomal enzymes are simultaneously missing
o.C: They form exclusively in neurons rather than in mesenchymal tissue
o.D: They are membrane-bound autophagosomes rather than lysosome-derived vacuoles

e.correcta: Because I-cell disease knocks out the general M6P-tagging mechanism rather than a single hydrolase, essentially the whole battery of lysosomal enzymes fails to reach the lysosome at once. The lysosome is therefore left unable to degrade many different classes of substrates (glycosaminoglycans, glycolipids, glycoproteins, etc.), so the resulting inclusion bodies are a mixed, heterogeneous "junk drawer" of undigested material rather than one specific accumulated molecule.

incorrectas.A: A single accumulated substrate is the hallmark of classic lysosomal storage diseases like Tay-Sachs (GM2 ganglioside) or Gaucher disease (glucocerebroside), where only one specific enzyme is deficient — the opposite pattern from I-cell disease's global enzyme deficiency.
incorrectas.C: I-cell disease is a systemic disorder affecting connective tissue, bone, and multiple organs broadly (coarse facies, skeletal abnormalities, restricted joints), not a neuron-restricted process, since the trafficking defect affects virtually all cell types that rely on M6P-tagged lysosomal enzymes.
incorrectas.D: Autophagosomes are double-membrane structures that engulf cytoplasmic material for delivery to lysosomes as part of normal autophagy; the inclusion bodies of I-cell disease reflect failure of enzyme delivery to lysosomes, not an autophagosome-specific process.

preguntas.q: Which coat protein mediates retrograde vesicular transport from the cis-Golgi back to the endoplasmic reticulum, as well as transport between Golgi cisternae?

e.correcta: COPI-coated vesicles bud from the cis-Golgi and mediate retrograde transport, returning escaped ER-resident proteins (like those bearing a KDEL retrieval signal) back to the ER, as well as shuttling proteins backward between Golgi cisternae for further processing. This retrieval system is essential quality control: it prevents ER machinery from being permanently swept forward into the secretory pathway and keeps the Golgi's cis-to-trans processing gradient properly stocked.

incorrectas.A: COPII does the opposite job — it coats vesicles budding from the ER to carry newly synthesized proteins forward (anterograde) to the cis-Golgi, making it the functional counterpart to COPI rather than the answer to a retrograde-transport question.
incorrectas.B: Clathrin coats vesicles involved in receptor-mediated endocytosis at the plasma membrane and in trafficking from the trans-Golgi network to lysosomes, a distinct pathway from the ER-Golgi shuttle that COPI and COPII handle.
incorrectas.D: Dynein is a microtubule motor protein that drives retrograde movement of cargo along microtubules (plus-end to minus-end), not a vesicle coat protein — it moves vesicles along tracks rather than defining which Golgi/ER compartment a vesicle buds from or targets.

preguntas.q: Which coat protein mediates anterograde transport of newly synthesized proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum to the cis-Golgi?

e.correcta: COPII coats vesicles that bud from the ER exit sites and carry correctly folded, newly synthesized secretory and membrane proteins forward to the cis-Golgi. This anterograde step is the first leg of the classic secretory pathway (ER to Golgi to secretory vesicle/plasma membrane/lysosome), and its directionality is exactly opposite to COPI, which returns escaped proteins from the Golgi back to the ER.

incorrectas.A: Clathrin mediates a different segment of vesicular traffic entirely — receptor-mediated endocytosis at the plasma membrane and trans-Golgi-to-lysosome transport — rather than the initial ER-to-Golgi export step.
incorrectas.C: COPI is the retrograde counterpart to COPII, moving proteins backward from the cis-Golgi to the ER (and between Golgi cisternae), the reverse direction of the anterograde ER-to-Golgi transport described here.
incorrectas.D: Kinesin is a motor protein that walks vesicles and organelles along microtubules toward the plus end (generally toward the cell periphery), providing the mechanical movement rather than defining the vesicle coat that selects ER-to-Golgi cargo.

preguntas.q: Which coat protein is responsible for vesicular transport between the trans-Golgi network and lysosomes?

e.correcta: Clathrin forms a lattice-like coat around budding vesicles at the trans-Golgi network, packaging mannose-6-phosphate-tagged lysosomal hydrolases for delivery to lysosomes. Clathrin also performs the analogous job at the plasma membrane during receptor-mediated endocytosis, so it is the coat protein associated with both TGN-to-lysosome and cell-surface internalization routes, distinct from the ER-Golgi shuttle handled by the COP coats.

incorrectas.A: COPI operates earlier in the secretory pathway, mediating retrograde transport from the Golgi back to the ER and between Golgi cisternae, not the later TGN-to-lysosome step.
incorrectas.B: COPII mediates the initial anterograde step of the secretory pathway, moving newly made proteins from the ER to the cis-Golgi, well before cargo reaches the trans-Golgi network for lysosomal sorting.
incorrectas.D: Dynein is a microtubule-based motor protein, not a vesicle coat — it provides the force for moving vesicles/organelles toward the microtubule minus end, but it does not define the budding or cargo-selection step at the trans-Golgi.

preguntas.q: Which coat protein mediates vesicular transport between the trans-Golgi network and lysosomes?

e.correcta: Clathrin coats vesicles budding from the trans-Golgi network, packaging mannose-6-phosphate-tagged lysosomal enzymes for delivery to lysosomes. This same clathrin machinery is reused at the plasma membrane for receptor-mediated endocytosis, making clathrin the coat protein for both late secretory (TGN-to-lysosome) and endocytic trafficking, in contrast to the COP coats that operate earlier between the ER and Golgi.

incorrectas.A: COPII mediates the earliest anterograde step of the secretory pathway, moving newly synthesized proteins from the ER to the cis-Golgi, well upstream of the TGN-to-lysosome step that clathrin handles.
incorrectas.B: COPI mediates retrograde transport from the Golgi back to the ER and between Golgi cisternae, a different (earlier, reverse-direction) leg of the secretory pathway than TGN-to-lysosome transport.
incorrectas.D: Dynein is a microtubule motor protein that provides the force to move vesicles along microtubule tracks, but it does not form the vesicle coat that selects and buds cargo at the trans-Golgi network.

preguntas.q: Which cellular structure forms a network of protein fibers in the cytoplasm that supports cell shape, enables organelle and cell movement, and drives cell division?

e.correcta: The cytoskeleton is composed of three main filament systems — microfilaments (actin), intermediate filaments, and microtubules — that together scaffold the cell's shape, anchor organelles in place, generate the mechanical forces for cell and organelle movement, and build the mitotic spindle that segregates chromosomes during division. Each filament type has distinct subunits, polymerization dynamics, and specialized roles, but all three work together as an integrated structural and motility system.

incorrectas.A: The endoplasmic reticulum is a membranous organelle responsible for protein synthesis and folding (rough ER) and lipid/steroid synthesis and calcium storage (smooth ER); it does not form the structural protein fiber network responsible for cell shape or movement.
incorrectas.C: The nuclear lamina is a meshwork of intermediate filament proteins (lamins) that underlies the inner nuclear membrane, providing structural support specifically to the nucleus and organizing chromatin, but it is a specialized subcomponent rather than the general cytoplasmic cytoskeletal network described.
incorrectas.D: The Golgi apparatus is a stack of membranous cisternae that modifies, sorts, and packages proteins for their final destinations; it plays no direct structural or motility role analogous to the cytoskeleton.

preguntas.q: Which cytoskeletal filament type, composed of subunits like actin, is predominantly responsible for muscle contraction and cytokinesis?

e.correcta: Microfilaments are built from polymerized actin monomers and are the thinnest of the three cytoskeletal filament types. They generate contractile force by interacting with myosin motor proteins — this actin-myosin interaction underlies both sarcomeric muscle contraction and the formation of the contractile ring that pinches a dividing cell in two during cytokinesis. Actin also supports microvilli and cell motility structures like lamellipodia, reflecting its role wherever dynamic, force-generating structural support is needed.

incorrectas.A: Intermediate filaments (e.g., desmin, cytokeratin, vimentin, lamins) provide tension-resistant structural support and mechanical integrity to cells and tissues, but they are not the primary contractile machinery for muscle shortening or cytokinesis.
incorrectas.B: Microtubules, built from tubulin, are responsible for forming the mitotic spindle (chromosome segregation) and enabling organelle/vesicle transport and ciliary/flagellar movement, but they are not the actin-myosin-based contractile filaments driving muscle contraction or the cytokinetic ring.
incorrectas.D: Neurofilaments are a specific type of intermediate filament found in neuronal axons that provide structural support to the axon, unrelated to the actin-based contractile apparatus used in muscle and cytokinesis.

preguntas.q: Which cytoskeletal filament type, including proteins such as desmin and cytokeratin, is predominantly responsible for maintaining overall cell structure?

e.correcta: Intermediate filaments are a diverse family of rope-like proteins — including desmin (muscle cells), cytokeratin (epithelial cells), vimentin (mesenchymal cells), glial fibrillary acidic protein (astrocytes), and neurofilaments (neurons) — that provide durable, tension-resistant mechanical support to the cell and anchor it to neighboring cells via desmosomes. Unlike actin or tubulin polymers, they are not directly involved in generating movement or force; their job is largely structural, forming a stable internal scaffold, which is also why specific intermediate filament stains are used clinically to identify a tumor's cell of origin.

incorrectas.A: Microfilaments (actin) are primarily involved in contractile processes like muscle contraction and cytokinesis, and in forming microvilli, rather than serving as the main long-term structural scaffold of the cell.
incorrectas.C: Microtubules, made of tubulin, primarily mediate movement (cilia, flagella, mitotic spindle) and intracellular transport of organelles and vesicles, not the baseline mechanical structural support that intermediate filaments provide.
incorrectas.D: Actin filaments is simply another name for microfilaments, which function in contraction and cytokinesis rather than the durable structural maintenance role of intermediate filaments.

preguntas.q: Which cytoskeletal filament type, forming structures such as cilia, flagella, and the mitotic spindle, is predominantly responsible for cell movement and division?

e.correcta: Microtubules are hollow polymers of alpha- and beta-tubulin heterodimers that assemble into the mitotic spindle to segregate chromosomes during division, form the axoneme core of cilia and flagella for motility, and serve as tracks for kinesin/dynein-mediated organelle and vesicle transport, including axonal transport in neurons. This dual role in both division and movement is why microtubule-targeting drugs (e.g., vincristine, paclitaxel) are used as anticancer agents to halt mitosis in rapidly dividing cells.

incorrectas.A: Intermediate filaments provide durable mechanical structural support to the cell (e.g., desmin, cytokeratin) rather than powering movement or the mitotic spindle apparatus.
incorrectas.B: Microfilaments (actin) drive muscle contraction and the cytokinetic contractile ring at the very end of division, but they do not form cilia, flagella, or the microtubule-based mitotic spindle that separates chromosomes.
incorrectas.D: Spectrin is a cytoskeletal protein that forms a supportive meshwork beneath the red blood cell membrane, maintaining its biconcave shape, but it is not one of the three principal cytoskeletal filament classes and plays no role in ciliary movement or spindle formation.

preguntas.q: Actin and microvilli are structural examples of which type of cytoskeletal filament?

e.correcta: Actin polymerizes into microfilaments, the thinnest cytoskeletal fiber type, which bundle together to form the structural core of microvilli — the finger-like projections that increase absorptive surface area on cells like small intestinal enterocytes and proximal tubule cells. Microfilaments also drive muscle contraction (via actin-myosin interaction) and the cytokinetic contractile ring, making actin dynamics essential wherever a cell needs to generate or support fine, force-bearing projections.

incorrectas.A: Intermediate filaments (like desmin or cytokeratin) provide general structural durability to cells and tissues, but they are not the actin-based scaffold specifically found inside microvilli.
incorrectas.B: Microtubules are built from tubulin, not actin, and form structures like cilia, flagella, and the mitotic spindle rather than microvilli, which are actin-supported projections.
incorrectas.D: A basal body is a microtubule-organizing structure at the base of a cilium (derived from a centriole), not a filament type itself, and is unrelated to actin-based microvilli.

preguntas.q: Cytokeratin and desmin are examples of which type of cytoskeletal filament?

e.correcta: Cytokeratin (found in epithelial cells) and desmin (found in muscle cells) are both intermediate filament proteins, part of a broader family that also includes vimentin, glial fibrillary acidic protein, and neurofilaments. These proteins form durable, rope-like polymers that resist mechanical stress and maintain cell shape and tissue integrity, which is why immunostaining for a specific intermediate filament (e.g., cytokeratin for carcinoma, desmin for rhabdomyosarcoma) is used clinically to determine a tumor's tissue of origin.

incorrectas.A: Microtubules are composed of tubulin, not cytokeratin or desmin, and are involved in cell division and motility (cilia, flagella, spindle), a functionally and structurally distinct filament class.
incorrectas.C: Microfilaments are composed of actin and mediate contraction and cytokinesis; cytokeratin and desmin are intermediate filaments, a separate and thicker filament class with a purely structural (non-contractile) role.
incorrectas.D: Actin filaments is another name for microfilaments, which are built from actin monomers, not from cytokeratin or desmin, and serve a contractile rather than purely structural function.

preguntas.q: Cilia and flagella are structures built from which type of cytoskeletal filament?

e.correcta: Cilia and flagella are built around an axoneme core made of microtubules, classically arranged in a 9+2 pattern (nine outer doublets plus two central singlets), with dynein arms driving the sliding motion between doublets that produces the whip-like beating motion. This tubulin-based architecture is distinct from microvilli, which are actin (microfilament)-based projections without motile capability — a distinction tested because defects in the microtubule/dynein machinery (e.g., primary ciliary dyskinesia) impair ciliary and flagellar motility specifically.

incorrectas.A: Microfilaments (actin) form the structural core of microvilli, which are static absorptive projections, not the motile microtubule-based axonemes of cilia and flagella.
incorrectas.B: Intermediate filaments provide general structural support to the cell body and are not part of the axoneme; they do not contribute to ciliary or flagellar motility.
incorrectas.D: Actin is the monomer that polymerizes into microfilaments (found in microvilli), not the tubulin-based microtubules that form the motile axoneme of cilia and flagella.

preguntas.q: Each alpha- and beta-tubulin heterodimer within a microtubule has two molecules of which nucleotide bound, which stabilizes the polymer?

e.correcta: Each tubulin heterodimer binds two GTP molecules, and as long as the tubulin subunits at the growing (+) end of the microtubule remain GTP-bound, they form a stabilizing "GTP cap" that keeps the polymer growing. Hydrolysis of this bound GTP to GDP destabilizes the lattice, and if hydrolysis outpaces addition of new GTP-tubulin, the microtubule undergoes rapid depolymerization (catastrophe) — the molecular basis of microtubules' characteristic dynamic instability (slow growth, fast collapse).

incorrectas.A: ATP is the energy currency used by motor proteins like kinesin and dynein to walk along microtubules, but the structural nucleotide bound within the tubulin heterodimer itself is GTP, not ATP.
incorrectas.C: GDP is the hydrolyzed, destabilized form of the nucleotide — once GTP is hydrolyzed to GDP within the lattice, that tubulin becomes prone to dissociation rather than being the stabilizing form initially bound.
incorrectas.D: cGMP is a second messenger involved in signaling pathways (e.g., nitric oxide/guanylate cyclase signaling), unrelated to the structural nucleotide that stabilizes tubulin heterodimers.

preguntas.q: What best describes the polymerization dynamics of microtubules with respect to growth and collapse?

o.A: They grow quickly and collapse quickly
o.B: They grow slowly and collapse slowly
o.C: They grow slowly and collapse quickly
o.D: They grow quickly and collapse slowly

e.correcta: Microtubules exhibit "dynamic instability": GTP-tubulin dimers add relatively slowly to the growing plus end, but once GTP hydrolysis to GDP outpaces new subunit addition, the GTP cap is lost and the microtubule undergoes rapid, catastrophic depolymerization. This slow-growth/fast-collapse behavior lets the cell rapidly remodel its microtubule network — for example, during mitotic spindle formation and chromosome capture — explaining why this asymmetric dynamic is a defining and testable property of microtubules.

incorrectas.A: Fast growth paired with fast collapse does not reflect actual microtubule kinetics; polymerization (subunit addition) is comparatively slow, while it is specifically the collapse phase that is fast.
incorrectas.B: Slow collapse is inconsistent with dynamic instability — once the GTP cap is lost, depolymerization proceeds rapidly rather than gradually, which is the key asymmetry tested here.
incorrectas.D: Growth is not fast in microtubule dynamics; the addition of tubulin dimers to the plus end is comparatively gradual, while collapse, once triggered by GTP cap loss, is the rapid process, the reverse of what this option describes.

preguntas.q: Slow axoplasmic transport within neurons relies primarily on which cytoskeletal filament type?

e.correcta: Axoplasmic transport, whether the slow bulk movement of cytoskeletal proteins and organelles down the axon or the fast, motor-driven transport of vesicles, occurs along microtubule tracks that run the length of the axon. Motor proteins like kinesin (anterograde) and dynein (retrograde) use these microtubule tracks to move cargo; slow transport reflects the gradual, less motor-intensive net movement of structural components rather than a fundamentally different track system.

incorrectas.A: Microfilaments (actin) are more concentrated near the axon terminal and growth cone, supporting local motility and structural remodeling, but the long-distance axoplasmic transport machinery runs along microtubules, not actin.
incorrectas.B: Intermediate filaments (neurofilaments in neurons) provide structural, load-bearing support to the axon's caliber and shape, but they are not the tracks along which kinesin/dynein motors move cargo during axoplasmic transport.
incorrectas.D: Neurofilaments are the neuron-specific intermediate filament subtype that reinforces axonal structure, but like other intermediate filaments they do not serve as the transport tracks for axoplasmic flow — that role belongs to microtubules.

preguntas.q: Which motor protein mediates retrograde transport along microtubules, moving cargo from the plus end toward the minus end?

e.correcta: Dynein is a microtubule-associated motor protein that walks toward the microtubule's minus end, which is typically anchored near the centrosome/cell body, producing retrograde transport of cargo (e.g., endocytosed material, signals like retrogradely transported viruses such as rabies and herpes) from the periphery back toward the cell center. This directionality is clinically relevant because certain neurotropic pathogens hijack dynein-mediated retrograde transport to travel from peripheral nerve terminals back to the central nervous system.

incorrectas.A: Kinesin moves cargo in the opposite direction — from the microtubule minus end toward the plus end (anterograde), typically from the cell body out toward the periphery — making it the functional counterpart to dynein rather than the retrograde motor.
incorrectas.B: Myosin is an actin-based motor protein (not microtubule-based), responsible for processes like muscle contraction and some vesicle transport along actin filaments, not the plus-to-minus retrograde movement along microtubules described here.
incorrectas.D: Actin is the filament subunit that myosin walks along, not a microtubule motor protein itself, and is unrelated to the dynein-mediated retrograde transport system on microtubules.

preguntas.q: Which motor protein mediates anterograde transport along microtubules, moving cargo from the minus end toward the plus end?

e.correcta: Kinesin walks toward the microtubule's plus end, which is generally oriented away from the centrosome and toward the cell periphery, producing anterograde transport of vesicles and organelles (e.g., moving synaptic vesicle components down the axon toward the nerve terminal). This complements dynein's minus-end-directed retrograde transport, together allowing bidirectional cargo movement along the same microtubule tracks — a key concept for understanding neuronal transport and diseases that disrupt it.

incorrectas.A: Dynein moves in the opposite direction, toward the microtubule minus end (retrograde), typically back toward the cell body/centrosome, making it the reverse-direction motor compared to kinesin.
incorrectas.C: Myosin is an actin-based (not microtubule-based) motor protein involved in processes like muscle contraction, distinct from the tubulin-track-walking kinesin/dynein system.
incorrectas.D: Tubulin is the structural subunit that polymerizes to form the microtubule track itself, not a motor protein — it provides the road, not the vehicle, for kinesin-mediated anterograde transport.

preguntas.q: The structure at the base of a cilium, situated just below the plasma membrane and consisting of nine microtubule triplets with no central pair, is called the:

e.correcta: The basal body anchors the cilium to the cell and templates its growth; it is structurally derived from a centriole and is organized as nine microtubule triplets arranged in a ring with no central microtubule pair (a "9+0" arrangement). This differs from the axoneme above it, which has the classic "9+2" pattern (nine outer doublets plus two central singlets) responsible for generating the ciliary beat via dynein arm activity.

incorrectas.A: The axoneme is the motile core structure that extends into the cilium itself, arranged as 9 microtubule doublets plus 2 central singlets (9+2), a different microtubule arrangement from the basal body's 9 triplets with no central pair.
incorrectas.B: A centriole pair (forming the centrosome) organizes the mitotic spindle during cell division and is structurally related to (and can give rise to) a basal body, but the specific ciliary base structure with 9 triplets and no central microtubules is termed the basal body, not simply "centriole pair."
incorrectas.D: The kinetochore is a protein complex that assembles on the centromere of a chromosome and attaches to spindle microtubules during mitosis, an entirely different structure unrelated to ciliary anatomy.

preguntas.q: Kartagener syndrome (primary ciliary dyskinesia) results in decreased fertility in both males and females. What is the underlying mechanism in each sex?

o.A: Absent seminiferous tubules in males and absent oocytes in females
o.B: Immotile sperm in males and dysfunctional fallopian tube cilia in females
o.C: Testosterone deficiency in males and estrogen deficiency in females
o.D: Vas deferens agenesis in males and imperforate hymen in females

e.correcta: Kartagener syndrome is caused by a defect in dynein arms (often due to mutations affecting axonemal dynein), which are required for the coordinated sliding of microtubule doublets that produces ciliary and flagellar beating. In males, sperm flagella share this same 9+2 axoneme/dynein architecture, so immotile sperm cause infertility; in females, the cilia lining the fallopian tubes normally help propel the oocyte toward the uterus, and their dysfunction impairs oocyte transport, reducing fertility (and increasing ectopic pregnancy risk).

incorrectas.A: Kartagener syndrome does not involve agenesis of the seminiferous tubules or oocytes — the gonads and gametogenesis are structurally normal; the defect is specifically in the motility apparatus of already-formed sperm and the transport cilia lining the fallopian tubes.
incorrectas.C: This is a dynein/ciliary structural defect, not an endocrine disorder — testosterone and estrogen production are unaffected, since the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and steroidogenic machinery are intact.
incorrectas.D: There is no primary defect in the vas deferens (as seen in cystic fibrosis-related infertility) or in hymenal development in Kartagener syndrome; the reproductive tract structures are normal, but ciliary/flagellar motility itself is impaired.

preguntas.q: A patient presents with bronchiectasis, recurrent sinusitis, and situs inversus (e.g., dextrocardia on chest x-ray). Which developmental/ciliary disorder best explains this triad?

e.correcta: Kartagener syndrome (a form of primary ciliary dyskinesia) results from dynein arm defects that impair ciliary motility throughout the body. In the respiratory tract, immotile cilia fail to clear mucus and pathogens, causing recurrent sinusitis and bronchiectasis; during embryogenesis, nodal cilia normally establish left-right body asymmetry, so their dysfunction produces situs inversus (organs mirrored, e.g., dextrocardia) in about half of affected patients. The combination of chronic respiratory disease with situs inversus is the classic clue pointing to a ciliary motility defect rather than a mucus-viscosity or protease-related disease.

incorrectas.A: Cystic fibrosis causes thick, viscous secretions due to a CFTR chloride channel defect, leading to bronchiectasis and sinusitis, but it does not disrupt the nodal cilia responsible for left-right patterning, so situs inversus is not a feature of CF.
incorrectas.B: Young syndrome presents with bronchiectasis, sinusitis, and infertility due to obstructive azoospermia (not immotile sperm or ciliary dysfunction), and it does not cause situs inversus, distinguishing it from a primary ciliary motility disorder.
incorrectas.D: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes panacinar emphysema (and liver disease) due to unchecked neutrophil elastase activity, a protease-antiprotease imbalance unrelated to ciliary structure, and does not produce situs inversus or the sinusitis/bronchiectasis-plus-organ-mirroring triad.

preguntas.q: Fungal plasma membranes contain which sterol, which mammalian cell membranes lack (cholesterol being the mammalian equivalent), making it a selective target for antifungal drugs?

e.correcta: Ergosterol is the primary sterol component of fungal cell membranes, serving the same membrane-stabilizing role that cholesterol serves in mammalian cells. Because ergosterol is fungus-specific, it is the basis for selective antifungal toxicity: polyenes like amphotericin B and nystatin bind ergosterol directly to form membrane pores, while azoles inhibit lanosterol demethylase (the enzyme that converts lanosterol to ergosterol), depleting ergosterol and disrupting the fungal membrane with relatively less effect on human cells.

incorrectas.A: Cholesterol is the sterol found in mammalian (human) cell membranes, not fungal membranes — it is precisely because fungi use ergosterol instead of cholesterol that antifungal drugs can selectively target fungal membranes.
incorrectas.C: Lanosterol is an intermediate in the sterol synthesis pathway (upstream of ergosterol in fungi and of cholesterol in humans) rather than the main structural sterol embedded in the mature fungal membrane; azoles act by blocking the enzyme that processes lanosterol into ergosterol.
incorrectas.D: Stigmasterol is a plant-derived sterol found in plant cell membranes, not a component of fungal plasma membranes, and is not the target exploited by antifungal drugs.

preguntas.q: Which coat protein mediates transport between the plasma membrane and endosomes during receptor-mediated endocytosis?

e.correcta: Clathrin assembles into a triskelion lattice on the cytosolic face of the plasma membrane, deforming it into a coated pit that pinches off (with help from dynamin) to form a clathrin-coated vesicle carrying receptor-bound cargo to early endosomes. This is the same clathrin machinery used for trans-Golgi-to-lysosome trafficking, reflecting its general role in vesicle budding at both the cell surface and the late secretory pathway, distinguishing it from the COP coats that operate only within the ER-Golgi system.

incorrectas.A: COPII is restricted to the early secretory pathway, coating vesicles that carry cargo from the ER to the cis-Golgi, and plays no role in internalizing plasma membrane receptors.
incorrectas.B: COPI mediates retrograde Golgi-to-ER and intra-Golgi transport, an intracellular trafficking step entirely separate from the plasma-membrane budding events of receptor-mediated endocytosis.
incorrectas.D: Kinesin is a microtubule motor protein that transports already-formed vesicles along microtubule tracks; it does not form the coat that shapes the budding vesicle at the plasma membrane.

preguntas.q: For each ATP hydrolyzed, the Na+/K+-ATPase pump transports how many potassium ions, and in which direction, once the pump is dephosphorylated?

e.correcta: The Na+/K+-ATPase cycles through phosphorylated and dephosphorylated conformations: ATP hydrolysis phosphorylates the pump, driving a conformational change that expels 3 Na+ out of the cell, and then binding of extracellular K+ triggers dephosphorylation, which flips the pump back and releases 2 K+ into the cell. This 3-Na+-out/2-K+-in stoichiometry makes the pump electrogenic (net movement of one positive charge out per cycle) and is fundamental to establishing the resting membrane potential and the ionic gradients that drive secondary active transport and neuronal excitability.

incorrectas.A: 3 Na+ moving out of the cell is the correct stoichiometry for sodium, but it occurs during the phosphorylated state of the pump cycle, not the potassium-transporting, dephosphorylated step being asked about here.
incorrectas.C: Potassium moves into the cell, not out, during the Na+/K+-ATPase cycle — extracellular K+ binds the dephosphorylated pump and is carried inward, the opposite direction from what this option states.
incorrectas.D: The pump moves 2 K+ (not 3) into the cell per cycle; the number 3 corresponds to the sodium ions extruded during the phosphorylated part of the cycle, not the potassium ions brought in during dephosphorylation.

preguntas.q: The Na+/K+-ATPase pump sits in the plasma membrane with its ATP-binding/hydrolysis site facing which side of the membrane?

e.correcta: The Na+/K+-ATPase is oriented so that its catalytic, ATP-hydrolyzing domain faces the cytosol, since ATP is generated and used intracellularly. This cytosolic orientation makes sense functionally: intracellular Na+ binds the pump on the cytosolic side, ATP hydrolysis there drives the conformational change that extrudes Na+, and only after this does the extracellular-facing conformation bind K+ for import, dephosphorylating the pump back to its original state.

incorrectas.A: The extracellular side of the pump is where K+ binds after the conformational change (not where ATP is hydrolyzed); placing the catalytic ATP site there would be functionally impossible since ATP is an intracellular molecule not found in the extracellular space.
incorrectas.C: The catalytic domain must be accessible to cytosolic ATP and ions to function, so it cannot be buried within the lipid bilayer itself — enzymatic domains of transmembrane pumps project into the aqueous cytosolic or extracellular compartments, not into the hydrophobic membrane core.
incorrectas.D: The Na+/K+-ATPase functions at the plasma membrane, not within the endoplasmic reticulum, so it has no orientation relative to the ER lumen; a related but distinct pump (SERCA) handles calcium transport into the ER/SR.

preguntas.q: Ouabain, a cardiac glycoside historically used as an arrow poison, produces cardiac arrest by binding to the K+ site of which membrane transporter?

e.correcta: Ouabain and digoxin are cardiac glycosides that bind the extracellular K+-binding site of the Na+-K+ ATPase, locking the pump and preventing it from extruding Na+ from the cell. The resulting rise in intracellular Na+ reduces the gradient that drives the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, so less Ca2+ is pumped out of the cell — intracellular Ca2+ accumulates and augments myocyte contractility. At toxic doses (as with ouabain used as arrow poison), profound pump inhibition causes membrane depolarization and lethal arrhythmias, i.e., cardiac arrest.

incorrectas.B: SERCA (sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ ATPase) pumps Ca2+ from the cytosol back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum during diastole; it is not the target of cardiac glycosides and its inhibition is not the mechanism by which ouabain raises contractility.
incorrectas.C: The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger is affected only secondarily — its reduced Ca2+ extrusion is a downstream consequence of Na+-K+ ATPase inhibition, not the site ouabain directly binds.
incorrectas.D: The Na+/glucose cotransporter uses the Na+ gradient to import glucose in the gut and kidney; it has no role in cardiac contractility and is not a target of cardiac glycosides.

preguntas.q: Which class of drugs directly inhibits the Na+-K+ ATPase pump, thereby increasing intracellular calcium and cardiac contractility?

e.correcta: Cardiac glycosides such as digoxin directly bind and inhibit the Na+-K+ ATPase, causing intracellular Na+ to rise. This blunts the Na+ gradient that the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger relies on to extrude calcium, so intracellular Ca2+ increases and more calcium is available for excitation-contraction coupling, producing a positive inotropic effect used in heart failure and rate control in atrial fibrillation.

incorrectas.B: Class IA antiarrhythmics like quinidine block cardiac Na+ channels (and some K+ channels) to slow conduction and prolong the action potential; they do not act on the Na+-K+ ATPase and are not positive inotropes by this mechanism.
incorrectas.C: Beta-1 agonists like dobutamine increase contractility through Gs-coupled cAMP/PKA signaling that enhances L-type calcium channel activity, a completely different pathway from ATPase pump inhibition.
incorrectas.D: Phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitors like milrinone raise cAMP by blocking its breakdown, increasing contractility and causing vasodilation, but they do not interact with the Na+-K+ ATPase at all.

preguntas.q: Which protein is the most abundant in the human body and is extensively modified post-translationally?

e.correcta: Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body, forming the structural scaffold of skin, bone, tendon, cartilage, and basement membranes.
