incorrectas.A: The AV node lies upstream in the conduction pathway (between atria and the Bundle of His) and is actually the slowest-conducting tissue in the heart, the opposite of what is needed to rapidly activate the ventricles after the Bundle of His.
incorrectas.B: The SA node is the pacemaker that initiates each heartbeat at the start of the cycle in the right atrium; it has no role downstream of the Bundle of His and does not receive input from it.
incorrectas.D: Atrial internodal pathways conduct the impulse across the atria toward the AV node, functioning entirely before the AV node and Bundle of His, not after them.

preguntas.q: The resting membrane potential of a ventricular myocyte is determined primarily by the permeability of the membrane to which ion?

e.correcta: At rest, cardiac myocyte membranes are highly permeable to K+ through inward rectifier K+ channels (IK1), so the resting membrane potential sits close to the K+ equilibrium potential calculated by the Nernst equation (around -85 to -90 mV). Because conductance to other ions is comparatively low at rest, the cell behaves almost like a pure K+ electrode until a stimulus triggers the next action potential.

incorrectas.A: Na+ channels are largely closed at rest and only open transiently during phase 0 of the action potential to produce the rapid upstroke; Na+ permeability at rest is far too low to set the resting potential.
incorrectas.B: Ca2+ conductance is low at rest and only becomes significant during phase 2 (plateau) via L-type channels; it does not dominate the resting membrane potential the way K+ does.
incorrectas.C: Cl- does contribute modestly to membrane currents in some conditions, but it is not the primary determinant of resting potential in cardiac cells — that role belongs to the high resting K+ conductance.

preguntas.q: In a resting cardiac myocyte, how does membrane conductance to K+ compare with conductance to other ions, and what is the consequence for resting membrane potential?

o.A: K+ conductance is low, so resting potential is far from EK
o.B: K+ conductance is high, so resting potential is close to EK
o.C: Na+ conductance is high, so resting potential is close to ENa
o.D: Ca2+ conductance is high, so resting potential is close to ECa

e.correcta: Resting cardiac cell membranes have high conductance to K+ (mainly via IK1 inward rectifier channels), which allows K+ to flow down its electrochemical gradient until equilibrium is nearly reached. Because K+ dominates the resting conductance, the measured resting membrane potential closely approximates the K+ equilibrium potential (EK), consistent with the Goldman equation weighting the most permeant ion most heavily.

incorrectas.A: This inverts the actual physiology — K+ conductance at rest is high, not low, which is exactly why the resting potential tracks EK so closely rather than sitting far away from it.
incorrectas.C: Na+ conductance is low at rest (Na+ channels are closed), so the membrane potential is far from ENa (~+60 mV); Na+ conductance only spikes transiently during the rapid upstroke of the action potential.
incorrectas.D: Ca2+ conductance is also low at rest, so resting potential is nowhere near ECa; Ca2+ channels only open substantially later, during the plateau phase of the action potential.

preguntas.q: Which membrane transporter is responsible for maintaining the Na+ and K+ concentration gradients across the cardiac cell membrane long-term?

e.correcta: The Na+-K+-ATPase actively pumps 3 Na+ out of the cell and 2 K+ into the cell per ATP hydrolyzed, directly opposing the passive leaks that would otherwise dissipate these gradients over time. This active transport is what ultimately sustains the high intracellular K+ and low intracellular Na+ that make repeated action potentials possible, and it is also the target of cardiac glycosides like digoxin, which indirectly raise intracellular Ca2+ by inhibiting this pump.

incorrectas.A: The Na+-Ca2+ exchanger (NCX) uses the Na+ gradient (already established by the Na+-K+-ATPase) to extrude Ca2+ from the cytoplasm during relaxation; it does not itself generate or maintain the transmembrane Na+ or K+ gradients.
incorrectas.C: SERCA (sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase) pumps Ca2+ from the cytosol back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum for storage between contractions; it has no direct role in the plasma membrane Na+/K+ gradients.
incorrectas.D: Plasma membrane Ca2+-ATPase extrudes small amounts of Ca2+ across the sarcolemma to help restore low resting cytosolic Ca2+, but it does not maintain the Na+ and K+ gradients that define resting potential and excitability.

preguntas.q: The rapid upstroke (phase 0) of the myocardial (non-pacemaker) action potential is caused by the opening of which voltage-gated channels?

e.correcta: Phase 0 in atrial and ventricular myocytes and Purkinje fibers is generated by the rapid opening of fast voltage-gated Na+ channels once the membrane reaches threshold, producing a steep, large-amplitude influx of Na+ that drives the sharp upstroke. This fast Na+ current is what gives non-pacemaker tissue its rapid conduction velocity, in contrast to the slower Ca2+-dependent upstroke seen in the SA and AV nodes.

incorrectas.A: T-type ('transient') Ca2+ channels contribute to the late phase 4 depolarization in pacemaker cells, helping bring the membrane to threshold, but they do not generate the phase 0 upstroke of myocardial cells.
incorrectas.B: L-type Ca2+ channels open more slowly and mediate phase 0 of the SA/AV nodal action potential as well as the plateau (phase 2) of the myocardial action potential, but they are too slow to account for the rapid myocardial upstroke.
incorrectas.D: Delayed rectifier K+ channels open during phase 3 to drive repolarization by allowing K+ efflux; they do not open during phase 0 and would oppose, not cause, depolarization.

preguntas.q: Phase 1 (initial repolarization) of the myocardial action potential results from inactivation of Na+ channels and opening of which channels?

e.correcta: Phase 1 begins immediately after the phase 0 upstroke as the fast Na+ channels inactivate and a transient outward K+ current (Ito) opens briefly, allowing a small K+ efflux that produces the characteristic small downward notch seen on the action potential tracing before the plateau. This brief repolarization sets the stage for the calcium-driven plateau of phase 2 and is most prominent in epicardial and Purkinje cells, contributing to the notch-and-dome morphology.

incorrectas.A: L-type Ca2+ channels open around this time but their sustained influx is what defines phase 2 (the plateau), balancing K+ efflux rather than producing the transient notch of phase 1.
incorrectas.C: Funny (If) channels are pacemaker channels active during phase 4 of SA/AV nodal cells; they are not involved in phase 1 of the ventricular/atrial myocardial action potential.
incorrectas.D: T-type Ca2+ channels contribute to pacemaker phase 4 depolarization in nodal tissue, not to phase 1 repolarization in working myocardium.

preguntas.q: The plateau (phase 2) of the myocardial action potential is maintained by a balance between K+ efflux and influx of which ion through voltage-gated channels?

e.correcta: During phase 2, inward Ca2+ current through L-type Ca2+ channels roughly balances outward K+ current through delayed rectifier channels, producing a sustained plateau near 0 mV rather than immediate repolarization. This prolonged depolarization is essential because the Ca2+ influx triggers additional Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (calcium-induced calcium release), coupling electrical excitation to mechanical contraction, and the resulting long refractory period protects the heart from tetanic contraction.

incorrectas.A: Na+ channels have already inactivated by this point in the action potential (during phase 1) and do not contribute the inward current that sustains the plateau.
incorrectas.B: Cl- currents are not the major inward current balancing K+ efflux during the plateau; the physiologically important inward current at this stage is Ca2+ through L-type channels.
incorrectas.D: Mg2+ is not a significant charge carrier through voltage-gated channels during the cardiac action potential; it plays more of a cofactor/regulatory role in ion channel function rather than generating the plateau current.

preguntas.q: Phase 3 (rapid repolarization) of the myocardial action potential is caused by massive efflux of K+ combined with closure of which channels?

e.correcta: As phase 2 ends, L-type Ca2+ channels close while delayed rectifier K+ channels remain open (and their conductance increases further), producing a large net outward K+ current that rapidly repolarizes the membrane back to resting potential. This closure of Ca2+ channels removes the inward current that had been balancing K+ efflux, so once it drops out, repolarization accelerates sharply — hence phase 3 is markedly steeper than the plateau.

incorrectas.A: Na+ channels inactivated much earlier, during phase 1, and remain inactivated through the plateau; their closure is not what triggers the transition into phase 3.
incorrectas.C: Funny (If) channels are pacemaker channels relevant to phase 4 of nodal tissue, not to phase 3 repolarization of ventricular/atrial myocardium.
incorrectas.D: Cl- channel closure is not the mechanism described for phase 3; the defining event is the closure of the L-type Ca2+ channels that had been sustaining the plateau, unmasking the K+ efflux.

preguntas.q: Which type of action potential, characterized by phases 0 through 4 with a distinct plateau, occurs in the atria, ventricles, and Purkinje system?

e.correcta: The myocardial (fast-response, non-pacemaker) action potential — featuring a rapid Na+-dependent upstroke (phase 0), initial repolarization (phase 1), a Ca2+-dependent plateau (phase 2), rapid K+-driven repolarization (phase 3), and a stable resting potential (phase 4) — is the pattern seen in atrial myocytes, ventricular myocytes, and the Purkinje conduction system. This is distinct from the pacemaker action potential of the SA and AV nodes, which lacks a true resting phase 4 and instead shows spontaneous diastolic depolarization.

incorrectas.A: The pacemaker action potential is specific to the SA and AV nodes; it lacks phases 1 and 2 entirely and instead has an unstable, spontaneously depolarizing phase 4, so it does not match the phase 0-4 pattern described for atria, ventricles, and Purkinje fibers.
incorrectas.C: Skeletal muscle action potentials are much shorter in duration, lack a prolonged Ca2+ plateau, and depend on neuromuscular junction transmission rather than intrinsic cardiac conduction pathways.
incorrectas.D: Smooth muscle slow-wave potentials are gradual, rhythmic fluctuations in membrane potential (e.g., in GI or vascular smooth muscle) that are mechanistically distinct from the fast Na+-upstroke, Ca2+-plateau action potential of cardiac myocytes.

preguntas.q: Phase 0 of the SA node pacemaker action potential is caused by the opening of which voltage-gated channels?

e.correcta: In SA (and AV) nodal cells, the resting membrane potential is relatively depolarized (around -55 to -60 mV), which permanently inactivates the fast Na+ channels needed for a typical rapid upstroke. Instead, once threshold is reached, voltage-gated (mainly L-type) Ca2+ channels open to produce phase 0, giving nodal tissue a comparatively slow upstroke and slow conduction velocity relative to working myocardium.

incorrectas.A: Fast Na+ channels are permanently inactivated in nodal cells because their resting potential is too depolarized to allow these channels to recover from inactivation, so they cannot contribute to phase 0 here (unlike in atrial/ventricular myocardium).
incorrectas.C: Delayed rectifier K+ channels drive phase 3 repolarization in nodal tissue by allowing K+ efflux; they are not responsible for the depolarizing upstroke of phase 0.
incorrectas.D: Funny (If) channels carry the slow inward current responsible for phase 4 spontaneous depolarization that brings the cell to threshold, but the actual upstroke (phase 0) once threshold is reached is driven by Ca2+ channels, not If.

preguntas.q: Compared with a myocardial (ventricular) action potential, the rate of the upstroke (phase 0) in an SA node action potential is best described as which of the following?

o.A: Faster, due to Na+ channel activation
o.B: Identical, since both use the same channels
o.C: Slower, due to Ca2+ channel-mediated upstroke
o.D: Absent, since SA node cells lack a phase 0

e.correcta: SA nodal phase 0 depends on relatively slow-opening L-type Ca2+ channels rather than the fast Na+ channels used by ventricular myocytes, so the nodal upstroke rises much more gradually and with a lower maximal rate of depolarization (dV/dt). This slower upstroke is directly responsible for the SA and AV nodes having the slowest conduction velocities in the heart, which is clinically important because it is exactly the property exploited by AV-nodal blocking drugs like verapamil and beta-blockers.

incorrectas.A: This describes the myocardial action potential, not the SA node — fast Na+ channels are permanently inactivated in nodal tissue due to its more depolarized resting potential, so Na+ cannot mediate a fast upstroke there.
incorrectas.B: The two tissues use fundamentally different channels for phase 0 (Ca2+ in the SA node vs. Na+ in myocardium), so the upstrokes are not identical; this difference in ionic basis is precisely why their conduction velocities diverge so much.
incorrectas.D: The SA node does have a phase 0 (its depolarizing upstroke, just Ca2+-mediated and slower) — what it lacks are phases 1 and 2, not phase 0 itself.

preguntas.q: Which types of calcium channels are present in SA node cells and contribute to their action potential?

e.correcta: SA nodal cells express both L-type Ca2+ channels, which provide the main inward current for phase 0 of the pacemaker action potential, and T-type ('transient') Ca2+ channels, which open at more negative potentials during late phase 4 and help bring the membrane the rest of the way to threshold. This dual expression distinguishes nodal cells from working myocardium, where L-type channels dominate the plateau but T-type channels play little functional role.

incorrectas.A: L-type channels are indeed the primary contributor to phase 0, but this option omits the T-type channels that also participate in late phase 4 depolarization, making it an incomplete description of SA nodal calcium channel physiology.
incorrectas.B: T-type channels do contribute to late phase 4, but they are not the primary channel responsible for the phase 0 upstroke — that role belongs to L-type channels, so T-type alone is an incomplete answer.
incorrectas.D: N-type and P/Q-type Ca2+ channels are predominantly neuronal channel subtypes involved in neurotransmitter release at synapses, not the channels that generate the SA nodal action potential.

preguntas.q: Which phases of the myocardial (ventricular) action potential are absent from the SA node action potential?

e.correcta: The SA node action potential lacks a distinct phase 1 (initial repolarization notch) and phase 2 (Ca2+-mediated plateau) because it does not rely on the fast Na+ current and transient K+ current that create these features in working myocardium; instead, the nodal upstroke (Ca2+-driven phase 0) transitions fairly directly into repolarization (phase 3). This gives the SA node action potential its characteristically smoother, more triangular shape compared to the plateau-containing myocardial trace.

incorrectas.A: Both the SA node and ventricular myocytes have a phase 0 (upstroke, though via different channels) and a phase 4; in fact, phase 4 in the SA node is especially important because its spontaneous slow depolarization is what generates automaticity, so these phases are present, not absent.
incorrectas.B: Phase 3 (repolarization) is present in the SA node action potential, driven by K+ efflux with Ca2+ channel inactivation; it is phases 1 and 2 that are missing, not phase 3.
incorrectas.D: Phase 4 is actually a defining and present feature of the SA node action potential (spontaneous diastolic depolarization driving pacemaker activity) — it is not one of the missing phases.

preguntas.q: Phase 3 (repolarization) of the SA node action potential results from activation of which channels together with inactivation of which other channels?

o.A: Na+ channels activate; K+ channels inactivate
o.B: K+ channels activate; Ca2+ channels inactivate
o.C: Ca2+ channels activate; Na+ channels inactivate
o.D: If channels activate; K+ channels inactivate

e.correcta: Repolarization of the SA node occurs when voltage-gated K+ channels open, producing an outward K+ current, while the L-type Ca2+ channels that had driven phase 0 close (inactivate), removing the inward current that was opposing repolarization. This combination — K+ efflux increasing while Ca2+ influx falls off — drives the membrane potential back toward its most negative value, after which phase 4 (funny current-driven) depolarization begins the cycle again.

incorrectas.A: Na+ channels are not functionally active in SA nodal cells at all (they are permanently inactivated due to the depolarized resting potential), so neither their activation nor inactivation plays a role in nodal phase 3.
incorrectas.C: This is backwards — Ca2+ channel opening is what causes phase 0 (depolarization) in the SA node, and it is Na+ channels, not Ca2+ channels, that are already inactivated at rest and stay irrelevant, not events that define phase 3 repolarization.
incorrectas.D: Funny (If) channels are involved in phase 4 diastolic depolarization, not phase 3; they gradually activate at negative potentials after repolarization is complete, rather than driving the repolarization itself.

preguntas.q: The automaticity and pacemaker activity of the SA node are attributable to which phase of its action potential?

e.correcta: Phase 4 in the SA node is not a stable resting potential as in working myocardium but instead shows slow, spontaneous diastolic depolarization driven initially by funny (If) current and later by T-type Ca2+ current, gradually bringing the membrane from its most negative point up to threshold without any external stimulus. Because this spontaneous drift to threshold happens automatically and repeatedly, it is the basis of the heart's intrinsic automaticity, and its rate of rise directly determines heart rate (which is why autonomic tone modulating If changes heart rate).

incorrectas.A: Phase 0 is the Ca2+-mediated upstroke that occurs once threshold is reached; it is the consequence of automaticity (the point at which an action potential fires), not the phase that generates spontaneous depolarization itself.
incorrectas.B: Phase 3 is the repolarization phase that resets the membrane potential after an action potential; it does not generate spontaneous activity but rather ends one cycle before phase 4 begins the next.
incorrectas.D: Phase 1 (initial repolarization notch) is not even present in the SA node action potential, and even in myocardial cells where it does occur, it plays no role in generating automaticity.

preguntas.q: The slow, mixed Na+/K+ inward current responsible for phase 4 depolarization in the SA node flows through which channels, which are the pharmacologic target of ivabradine?

e.correcta: The funny current (If), carried through HCN (hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated) channels, is a slow, mixed Na+/K+ inward current that activates as the membrane repolarizes and gradually depolarizes the SA node during early-to-mid phase 4, eventually helped along by T-type Ca2+ channels to reach threshold. Ivabradine selectively blocks If channels, slowing the rate of phase 4 depolarization and thus heart rate, without affecting myocardial contractility — a useful property in patients (e.g., with heart failure or stable angina) who cannot tolerate the negative inotropy of beta-blockers.

incorrectas.A: L-type Ca2+ channels mediate phase 0 (the upstroke) of the SA node action potential once threshold is reached; they are not the slow mixed Na+/K+ current of phase 4 and are not what ivabradine targets.
incorrectas.B: T-type Ca2+ channels do contribute to late phase 4 by helping the membrane reach threshold, but they carry Ca2+ specifically, not the mixed Na+/K+ current described, and they are not the ivabradine target — that is the If channel.
incorrectas.D: Delayed rectifier K+ channels mediate phase 3 repolarization (pure K+ efflux), not the mixed inward Na+/K+ current of phase 4, and are unrelated to ivabradine's mechanism.

preguntas.q: Which three cell types function as 'latent pacemakers,' capable of spontaneous phase 4 depolarization but normally suppressed by the faster SA node?

o.A: Atrial myocytes, ventricular myocytes, and papillary muscle cells
o.B: Cells of the AV node, Bundle of His, and Purkinje fibers
o.C: SA node, sinoatrial exit pathway, and internodal tracts
o.D: Endocardial, myocardial, and epicardial layers of the ventricle

e.correcta: Cells of the AV node, the Bundle of His, and the Purkinje fibers all possess intrinsic automaticity (their own spontaneous phase 4 depolarization), but because the SA node depolarizes fastest and reaches threshold first, it 'overdrive suppresses' these slower latent pacemakers under normal conditions. If the SA node fails or conduction from it is blocked, one of these latent pacemakers (typically the AV node, then more distal sites at progressively slower intrinsic rates) takes over to generate an escape rhythm, which is why third-degree heart block still produces a (slow) ventricular rhythm.

incorrectas.A: Working atrial and ventricular myocytes (including papillary muscle) are non-pacemaker, fast-response cells with a stable phase 4 resting potential; they do not have the spontaneous automaticity that defines latent pacemaker tissue.
incorrectas.C: The SA node is the dominant, not latent, pacemaker, and the internodal tracts are simply conduction pathways within the atria, not sites of intrinsic pacemaker automaticity.
incorrectas.D: Ventricular wall layers (endocardium, myocardium, epicardium) refer to anatomic layers with differing action potential morphology and repolarization timing, not to the conduction system's designated latent pacemaker sites.

preguntas.q: What term describes the speed at which cardiac action potentials propagate through cardiac tissue?

e.correcta: Conduction velocity refers to how quickly the wave of depolarization spreads from cell to cell through the myocardium, and it depends largely on the magnitude of the inward current during the action potential upstroke as well as gap junction density (e.g., abundant connexins in Purkinje fibers speed conduction). This property varies substantially by tissue type — fastest in Purkinje fibers, slowest in the AV node — and is clinically manipulated by drugs (e.g., class I antiarrhythmics slow it via Na+ channel blockade).

incorrectas.A: The refractory period describes the interval during which a cell cannot (or can only partially) generate another action potential after one has occurred; it relates to timing between impulses, not the speed of propagation of a single impulse.
incorrectas.B: Excitability refers to a cell's ability to initiate an action potential in response to a depolarizing stimulus, which is a distinct property from how fast that action potential, once initiated, spreads through tissue.
incorrectas.C: Automaticity is the capacity of certain cells (like the SA node) to spontaneously generate their own action potentials via phase 4 depolarization; it does not describe the speed of impulse propagation through tissue.

preguntas.q: Within the cardiac conduction system, in which location is conduction velocity the slowest?

e.correcta: The AV node has the slowest conduction velocity in the heart, largely because its action potential upstroke is Ca2+-channel dependent (slower and lower amplitude than a Na+-dependent upstroke) and its cells have fewer gap junctions. This physiologic delay is actually beneficial: it allows time for the atria to finish contracting and empty into the ventricles before ventricular systole begins, and it is exactly the site targeted by AV-nodal blocking drugs (beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine CCBs, digoxin) to control ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation.

incorrectas.A: Purkinje fibers have the fastest conduction velocity in the heart due to their large diameter and abundant gap junctions, the opposite extreme from the AV node.
incorrectas.B: Atrial myocardium conducts faster than the AV node because it uses the fast Na+-dependent upstroke typical of working myocardium, even though it is slower than the Purkinje system.
incorrectas.D: Ventricular myocardium, like atrial myocardium, conducts via fast Na+ channels and is faster than the AV node, following the overall order: Purkinje fibers > atria > ventricles > AV node.

preguntas.q: Within the cardiac conduction system, in which location is conduction velocity the fastest?

e.correcta: Purkinje fibers have the fastest conduction velocity of any cardiac tissue, owing to their large cell diameter (which lowers internal resistance) and a very high density of gap junctions that allow rapid cell-to-cell current spread. This speed is functionally essential: it lets the Purkinje network deliver the depolarizing impulse to the entire ventricular endocardium nearly simultaneously, producing coordinated, efficient ventricular contraction rather than a slow, disorganized wave.

incorrectas.A: The AV node is at the opposite end of the spectrum — it has the slowest conduction velocity in the heart, providing the physiologic AV delay rather than rapid conduction.
incorrectas.B: Ventricular myocardium conducts faster than the AV node (via fast Na+ channels) but is still slower than the specialized Purkinje fibers, which are optimized purely for rapid impulse transmission.
incorrectas.C: Atrial myocardium conducts at a similar order of magnitude to ventricular myocardium (faster than the AV node) but remains slower than Purkinje fibers, following the sequence Purkinje > atria > ventricles > AV node.

preguntas.q: Conduction velocity in cardiac tissue depends primarily on which property of the action potential upstroke?

o.A: The duration of the plateau phase
o.C: The size (magnitude) of the inward current during the upstroke
o.D: The total duration of the action potential

e.correcta: Conduction velocity is determined mainly by how large and fast the inward current is during the action potential upstroke (phase 0) — a bigger, faster inward current (like the fast Na+ current in myocardium) more rapidly depolarizes adjacent cells through gap junctions, propagating the impulse quickly, whereas the smaller, slower Ca2+-mediated upstroke in nodal tissue propagates much more slowly. This is why class I antiarrhythmics, which block Na+ channels and reduce the upstroke's magnitude, slow conduction velocity as a therapeutic (or sometimes proarrhythmic) effect.

incorrectas.A: The duration of the plateau (phase 2) affects the overall action potential duration and refractory period but does not itself determine how fast the impulse spreads to neighboring cells — that is governed by the upstroke, not the plateau.
incorrectas.B: Resting membrane potential can influence Na+ channel availability, but by itself it is not the direct determinant of conduction velocity; it is specifically the magnitude of the inward current generated once the upstroke begins that sets propagation speed.
incorrectas.D: The total duration of the action potential (from upstroke to full repolarization) does not affect conduction velocity — this is explicitly distinguished physiologically, since a longer action potential does not by itself make impulse propagation slower or faster.

preguntas.q: What term describes the ability of a cardiac cell to initiate a new action potential in response to an inward, depolarizing current?

e.correcta: Excitability reflects the recovery of the channels (chiefly Na+ channels in myocardium) that carry the inward current needed for the upstroke of a new action potential; a cell must have enough of these channels recovered from inactivation to respond to a depolarizing stimulus with a new action potential. Excitability is reduced during the relative refractory period (partial channel recovery, requiring a stronger stimulus) and absent during the absolute refractory period (no channels available, no stimulus can trigger a new action potential), which protects the heart from dangerously rapid re-excitation.

incorrectas.A: Conduction velocity describes how fast an action potential, once triggered, propagates through tissue — a separate property from whether a cell can be triggered to fire a new action potential in the first place.
incorrectas.B: Automaticity is the capacity of specialized pacemaker cells to spontaneously generate their own action potentials without an external stimulus (via phase 4 depolarization), which is distinct from excitability's requirement of an inward depolarizing current triggering the response.
incorrectas.D: Contractility refers to the force-generating capacity of cardiac muscle for a given preload, a mechanical property unrelated to whether the cell's channels can support initiation of a new electrical action potential.

preguntas.q: During which refractory period can no new action potential be initiated in a cardiac cell, regardless of stimulus strength?

o.D: Effective refractory period only in the AV node

e.correcta: The absolute refractory period spans most of the action potential (through phases 0-2 and into early phase 3), during which essentially all fast Na+ channels are inactivated and unavailable, so no stimulus, no matter how strong, can generate a new action potential. This built-in 'dead time' is critical because it prevents tetanic contraction of cardiac muscle and limits how fast re-entrant or ectopic impulses can re-excite tissue, unlike skeletal muscle which can be tetanized.

incorrectas.A: During the relative refractory period (later phase 3), some Na+ channels have recovered from inactivation, so a new action potential can be triggered, but only by a stronger-than-normal stimulus — this is different from the absolute refractory period, where no stimulus works at all.
incorrectas.B: A brief supernormal period can follow the relative refractory period in some tissues, during which excitability is transiently increased above baseline (a weaker-than-normal stimulus can trigger a response) — the opposite of the absolute refractory state.
incorrectas.D: The concept of absolute refractoriness applies broadly across cardiac tissue (nodal and myocardial), not as a phenomenon unique to or defined only within the AV node.

preguntas.q: Which term describes the period of the cardiac action potential during which a second action potential can be triggered, but only by a stimulus stronger than normal?

e.correcta: The relative refractory period follows the absolute refractory period and corresponds to the time when enough Na+ channels have recovered from inactivation that a new action potential can be generated, but membrane potential is still relatively negative and some Na+ channels remain inactivated, so a stronger-than-normal depolarizing stimulus is required. This period underlies why premature beats occurring during it may be smaller or aberrantly conducted, and it sets the physiologic floor on how early a second contraction can occur.

incorrectas.A: The absolute refractory period is the phase during which no stimulus, regardless of strength, can generate a new action potential because essentially all Na+ channels are inactivated — this is fundamentally different from the relative refractory period, where a strong enough stimulus can succeed.
incorrectas.C: A supernormal period refers to a brief window (seen in Purkinje fibers) where a weaker-than-normal stimulus can trigger an action potential due to the membrane potential being closer to threshold; this is the opposite requirement from needing a greater-than-normal stimulus.
incorrectas.D: The effective refractory period is a related but distinct concept encompassing the absolute refractory period plus the early part of the relative refractory period during which a propagated action potential still cannot occur; it is not defined by requiring merely a stronger stimulus for a second AP.

preguntas.q: What term describes the effects of the autonomic nervous system on heart rate?

e.correcta: Chronotropic effects refer specifically to changes in heart rate, mediated by autonomic input to the SA node — sympathetic stimulation via beta-1 receptors is positively chronotropic (increases rate), while parasympathetic stimulation via M2 receptors is negatively chronotropic (decreases rate). Remembering the root 'chrono-' (time) helps distinguish it from the other cardiac 'tropic' terms, which describe different functional parameters.

incorrectas.A: Inotropic effects describe changes in the force or strength of myocardial contraction (contractility), not heart rate — for example, sympathetic stimulation is positively inotropic by increasing intracellular calcium available to the contractile apparatus.
incorrectas.B: Dromotropic effects refer to changes in conduction velocity, particularly through the AV node, not the rate of impulse generation at the SA node.
incorrectas.D: Lusitropic effects describe the rate of myocardial relaxation during diastole, which is a separate autonomic effect from the rate-setting function that defines chronotropy.

preguntas.q: A negative chronotropic effect on the heart has what result?

e.correcta: A negative chronotropic effect decreases heart rate by slowing the firing rate of the SA node, the heart's primary pacemaker. This occurs physiologically through parasympathetic (vagal) input acting on M2 receptors, which hyperpolarizes the SA node and slows the rate of phase 4 diastolic depolarization, thereby lengthening the interval between successive action potentials.

incorrectas.A: Increasing heart rate is the definition of a positive, not negative, chronotropic effect — the sign of the chronotropic effect directly indicates the direction of change in rate.
incorrectas.B: Increased contractility is a positive inotropic effect, a distinct parameter from chronotropy that reflects force of contraction rather than rate of firing.
incorrectas.D: Decreased conduction velocity describes a negative dromotropic effect, which concerns impulse propagation (especially through the AV node) rather than the rate at which the SA node generates impulses.

preguntas.q: A positive chronotropic effect on the heart has what result?

e.correcta: A positive chronotropic effect increases heart rate by speeding up the firing rate of the SA node. Sympathetic stimulation produces this effect via beta-1 adrenergic receptors, which increase cAMP-driven If ('funny') current and calcium current in SA nodal cells, accelerating phase 4 depolarization so the membrane reaches threshold sooner and more action potentials fire per minute.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in heart rate is, by definition, a negative chronotropic effect (mediated by parasympathetic/vagal tone), the opposite of what 'positive chronotropic' describes.
incorrectas.C: Stroke volume is governed by preload, afterload, and contractility (an inotropic parameter), not by chronotropy, which specifically refers to rate of SA node firing rather than the volume ejected per beat.
incorrectas.D: A decrease in AV nodal conduction velocity would be a negative dromotropic effect; sympathetic stimulation (which is positively chronotropic) actually increases AV conduction velocity, making this the opposite pairing.

preguntas.q: What is the effect of sympathetic nervous system stimulation on heart rate?

e.correcta: Sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate (a positive chronotropic effect) by releasing norepinephrine onto beta-1 adrenergic receptors on SA nodal cells, which activates Gs-coupled signaling, raises cAMP, and enhances the funny current (If) and L-type calcium current that drive phase 4 pacemaker depolarization. This is a core component of the fight-or-flight response, allowing cardiac output to rise rapidly to meet increased metabolic demand.

incorrectas.B: Sympathetic activation does not leave heart rate unchanged; the SA node is richly innervated by sympathetic fibers specifically to allow the heart rate to respond dynamically to increased demand.
incorrectas.A: A decrease in heart rate is the parasympathetic (vagal) effect via M2 receptors, which is the physiologic opposite of sympathetic stimulation.
incorrectas.D: The sympathetic effect on heart rate is consistently excitatory (increasing) at the level of the SA node; it is not baseline-dependent in direction, only in magnitude relative to existing vagal tone.

preguntas.q: What is the effect of parasympathetic nervous system stimulation on heart rate?

e.correcta: Parasympathetic (vagal) stimulation decreases heart rate by releasing acetylcholine onto M2 muscarinic receptors on the SA node, which activates Gi signaling to reduce cAMP and open GIRK (IK-ACh) potassium channels. This hyperpolarizes the SA node and slows the funny current-driven phase 4 depolarization, lengthening the time to reach threshold and thus reducing the rate of impulse generation — this is why resting heart rate is normally dominated by vagal tone.

incorrectas.A: An increase in heart rate is the sympathetic (beta-1-mediated) effect, the opposite of the inhibitory action vagal stimulation has on the SA node.
incorrectas.C: Parasympathetic tone is a major determinant of resting heart rate (vagal tone keeps intrinsic SA node rate of ~100 bpm suppressed to ~60-80 bpm), so it is far from having no effect.
incorrectas.D: The ventricles have little functional muscarinic innervation relevant to rate; the parasympathetic effect on rate is exerted at the SA node (and to a lesser extent AV node), not selectively in ventricular tissue.

preguntas.q: Through which receptor does the sympathetic nervous system increase heart rate?

e.correcta: The sympathetic nervous system increases heart rate through β1 adrenergic receptors on SA nodal cells. Norepinephrine (and circulating epinephrine) binding β1 receptors activates Gs protein, raising intracellular cAMP, which enhances the If pacemaker current and L-type calcium current, accelerating phase 4 depolarization and increasing firing frequency — this receptor is also the target of beta-blockers used to reduce heart rate in tachyarrhythmias.

incorrectas.A: α1 adrenergic receptors are Gq-coupled and mediate vascular smooth muscle contraction (vasoconstriction) and mydriasis, among other effects, but they are not the primary receptor driving SA nodal chronotropy.
incorrectas.B: M2 muscarinic receptors are parasympathetic (not sympathetic) receptors that decrease heart rate via Gi signaling — the opposite receptor and opposite effect from what is being asked.
incorrectas.D: β2 adrenergic receptors are Gs-coupled like β1 but predominantly mediate smooth muscle relaxation (bronchodilation, vasodilation) rather than the primary chronotropic drive at the SA node, which is a β1-dominant effect.

preguntas.q: Activation of β1 receptors in the SA node increases the activity of which channel, thereby increasing the rate of phase 4 depolarization and heart rate?

e.correcta: β1 receptor activation raises cAMP, which directly binds and opens If ('funny current') channels — a mixed Na+/K+ inward current unique to pacemaker cells — accelerating the slow phase 4 depolarization that carries the SA node from its most negative potential toward threshold. Because this speeds up how quickly threshold is reached, the SA node fires more frequently, increasing heart rate; the effect is reinforced by a parallel increase in ICa that further steepens the depolarization slope.

incorrectas.A: IK-ACh channels are potassium channels activated by parasympathetic M2 receptor stimulation (via Gi/Gβγ), which hyperpolarize the cell and slow, not speed, phase 4 depolarization — this is the opposite receptor pathway from β1 stimulation.
incorrectas.B: While increased ICa does contribute to the sympathetic chronotropic effect, it is a secondary/reinforcing current; the primary channel responsible for setting the pacemaker's phase 4 slope and named in this mechanism is If, not calcium current alone.
incorrectas.D: Fast Na+ channels drive the rapid upstroke (phase 0) of non-pacemaker cardiac action potentials (e.g., in atrial/ventricular myocytes and Purkinje fibers), but SA nodal cells lack significant fast Na+ channel activity and instead rely on If and ICa-L for their slow upstroke.

preguntas.q: Through which receptor does the parasympathetic nervous system decrease heart rate?

e.correcta: The parasympathetic (vagal) nervous system decreases heart rate through M2 muscarinic receptors on the SA node. Acetylcholine binding M2 activates Gi protein, which inhibits adenylyl cyclase (lowering cAMP, slowing If) and directly opens GIRK/IK-ACh potassium channels via Gβγ, hyperpolarizing the cell and slowing phase 4 depolarization — the combined effect reduces the rate of SA node firing.

incorrectas.A: β1 adrenergic receptors are sympathetic (Gs-coupled) receptors that increase, not decrease, heart rate — this is the opposite arm of autonomic control from the parasympathetic M2 pathway.
incorrectas.C: M1 muscarinic receptors are Gq-coupled and are found mainly in gastric parietal cells and CNS/autonomic ganglia, not as the principal cardiac muscarinic receptor subtype governing SA nodal rate — that role belongs to M2.
incorrectas.D: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors mediate fast synaptic transmission at autonomic ganglia and the neuromuscular junction via ligand-gated cation channels, not the muscarinic G-protein signaling that slows the SA node.

preguntas.q: Activation of M2 receptors in the SA node produces a decrease in which channel's activity, decreasing the rate of phase 4 depolarization and heart rate?

e.correcta: M2 receptor activation reduces If (funny current) channel activity by lowering intracellular cAMP (via Gi-mediated inhibition of adenylyl cyclase), which slows the mixed Na+/K+ inward current responsible for the gradual phase 4 depolarization in SA nodal cells. This delays the SA node's approach to threshold, decreasing firing rate; the effect is compounded by a simultaneous increase in IK-ACh (an outward, hyperpolarizing current) and a decrease in ICa.

incorrectas.A: IK-ACh channel activity actually increases (not decreases) with M2 stimulation — Gβγ subunits released by Gi directly activate these GIRK channels, producing hyperpolarizing outward K+ current that reinforces slowing, but this is a distinct current from If and is not the one that decreases.
incorrectas.C: T-type calcium channels contribute a small early component to pacemaker depolarization but are not the primary channel whose reduced activity, driven by cAMP decline downstream of M2 activation, is classically described in this mechanism — that is If.
incorrectas.D: Fast Na+ channels are not significantly expressed in SA nodal tissue and are not part of the phase 4 pacemaker mechanism modulated by muscarinic signaling; they instead drive rapid depolarization in atrial/ventricular myocardium.

preguntas.q: Atrial repolarization is not visible as a distinct wave on the ECG because it is masked by which structure?

e.correcta: Atrial repolarization is masked by the QRS complex because the two events occur at approximately the same time — by the time atrial myocytes are repolarizing, ventricular depolarization has begun, and the much larger electrical signal generated by the ventricular myocardium (which has far greater muscle mass) overwhelms the smaller atrial repolarization signal on the surface ECG.

incorrectas.A: The P wave represents atrial depolarization, not repolarization — it is the electrical event that precedes atrial repolarization, not the structure that obscures it.
incorrectas.B: The T wave represents ventricular repolarization, which occurs later in the cardiac cycle (after the QRS complex), well after atrial repolarization has already been masked, so it cannot be the structure hiding the earlier atrial repolarization signal.
incorrectas.D: The ST segment reflects the plateau phase of ventricular depolarization when the ventricles are uniformly depolarized (isoelectric baseline), occurring after the QRS complex and thus after atrial repolarization has already been concealed by the QRS itself.

preguntas.q: The duration of the P wave on ECG correlates with what physiologic parameter?

e.correcta: P wave duration reflects how quickly the depolarization wavefront spreads through atrial tissue — that is, atrial conduction velocity. If conduction velocity decreases (as with atrial disease or certain drugs), the impulse takes longer to traverse the atria, so the P wave widens/spreads out on the ECG; faster conduction produces a narrower P wave.

incorrectas.B: The AV nodal refractory period influences how soon a subsequent impulse can be conducted through the AV node and relates more to the PR interval and susceptibility to block, not to the width of the P wave itself, which reflects atrial (not AV nodal) conduction.
incorrectas.C: Ventricular contractility is reflected in mechanical parameters (like ejection fraction) and is not directly represented by any single ECG wave duration — it is not what determines P wave width, which is an atrial electrical event.
incorrectas.D: SA node firing rate determines how frequently P waves occur (i.e., the heart rate/PP interval), not the duration or shape of each individual P wave, which instead depends on the speed of atrial conduction.

preguntas.q: Which ECG interval represents the time from the initial depolarization of the atria to the initial depolarization of the ventricles?

e.correcta: The PR interval spans from the start of the P wave (onset of atrial depolarization) to the start of the QRS complex (onset of ventricular depolarization), capturing the time for the impulse to traverse the atria, pause at the AV node, and enter the His-Purkinje system. This interval is clinically important because prolongation reflects delayed AV conduction, as seen in first-degree AV block.

incorrectas.A: The QT interval spans from the start of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave, representing the entire duration of ventricular depolarization and repolarization — a much later and longer window than the atrial-to-ventricular depolarization gap described.
incorrectas.B: The QRS complex itself represents ventricular depolarization alone; it is a component within, not a measure spanning from, atrial to ventricular depolarization onset.
incorrectas.D: The ST segment represents the isoelectric period between the end of ventricular depolarization and the start of ventricular repolarization, occurring well after the atrial-to-ventricular depolarization interval being described.

preguntas.q: The duration of the PR interval on ECG primarily depends on the conduction velocity through which structure?

e.correcta: The PR interval is dominated by the conduction delay at the AV node, which normally slows the impulse to allow time for the atria to finish contracting and empty blood into the ventricles before ventricular depolarization begins. If AV nodal conduction slows further (e.g., in heart block or with AV-nodal-blocking drugs), the PR interval lengthens; this is the physiologic basis for diagnosing first-degree AV block by a PR interval greater than 200 ms.

incorrectas.A: The SA node sets the rate and location of the initial depolarization (determining the PP interval / heart rate), but it is not the structure whose conduction velocity determines the length of the PR interval, which is dominated by delay downstream at the AV node.
incorrectas.C: The bundle of His conducts rapidly and contributes only a small, relatively fixed portion of the PR interval; it is not the rate-limiting structure whose slowed conduction typically prolongs the PR interval in disease states.
incorrectas.D: Purkinje fibers conduct extremely rapidly to achieve near-simultaneous ventricular depolarization and contribute minimally to the PR interval's duration; delays here would more classically manifest as bundle branch block patterns in the QRS rather than PR prolongation.

preguntas.q: T-wave inversion on ECG may indicate which recent cardiac event?

e.correcta: T-wave inversion reflects altered ventricular repolarization and can be a sign of myocardial ischemia or recent infarction, since ischemic myocardium repolarizes abnormally, reversing the normal repolarization vector. It is also a recognized finding in unstable angina, making it an important but nonspecific marker that should prompt correlation with clinical presentation, troponins, and other ECG changes (like ST depression or elevation).

incorrectas.A: Atrial fibrillation is characterized by an irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves and fibrillatory baseline activity, not by T-wave inversion, which relates to ventricular repolarization rather than atrial rhythm disturbances.
incorrectas.C: First-degree AV block is defined by a prolonged PR interval (greater than 200 ms) reflecting delayed AV nodal conduction, an entirely separate ECG abnormality from T-wave morphology changes.
incorrectas.D: Ventricular hypertrophy can produce secondary repolarization changes including T-wave inversion, but it is a chronic structural finding rather than an acute event, whereas T-wave inversion in the context described classically signals a recent ischemic process like MI or unstable angina.

preguntas.q: Which ECG interval represents the entire period of ventricular depolarization, contraction, and repolarization?

e.correcta: The QT interval extends from the start of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave, encompassing the full duration of ventricular depolarization (QRS), the plateau/contraction phase (ST segment), and ventricular repolarization (T wave). A prolonged QT interval is clinically significant because it increases susceptibility to torsades de pointes, a potentially fatal polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.

incorrectas.A: The PR interval measures conduction from atrial depolarization onset to ventricular depolarization onset, occurring entirely before the events captured within the QT interval, and does not include any ventricular repolarization.
incorrectas.B: The ST segment is only one component representing the plateau phase between ventricular depolarization and repolarization, not the entire depolarization-to-repolarization span that defines the QT interval.
incorrectas.D: The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization alone; it is the initial segment of the QT interval but does not include the subsequent ST segment or T wave that account for contraction and repolarization.

preguntas.q: Which ECG segment is an isoelectric period (horizontal line) occurring while the ventricles are fully depolarized?

e.correcta: The ST segment is isoelectric because it occurs during the plateau phase of the ventricular action potential, when the entire ventricular myocardium is uniformly depolarized and no net voltage gradient exists across the tissue to generate a deflection on the ECG. Deviation of the ST segment above or below baseline is a key marker of myocardial ischemia or infarction (ST elevation or depression).

incorrectas.A: The PR segment (from the end of the P wave to the start of the QRS) is also isoelectric, but it reflects the delay at the AV node before ventricular depolarization begins, not the period of full ventricular depolarization described in the question.
incorrectas.C: The TP segment represents the interval between the end of the T wave and the start of the next P wave, corresponding to ventricular and atrial diastole (electrical resting state), not the plateau of ventricular depolarization.
incorrectas.D: The QT interval is not a single isoelectric segment but a composite measurement spanning the QRS complex, ST segment, and T wave — it includes non-isoelectric deflections and thus does not match the description of a flat line during ventricular depolarization.

preguntas.q: On an ECG, what is the name for the junction between the end of the QRS complex and the start of the ST segment?

e.correcta: The J point (junction point) marks the transition where the QRS complex ends and the ST segment begins, representing the moment ventricular depolarization is complete and the plateau phase starts. J point elevation or depression relative to baseline is used clinically to help identify ST-segment changes, such as in pericarditis (diffuse J point/ST elevation) or ischemia.

incorrectas.B: P wave onset marks the beginning of atrial depolarization, an entirely different and much earlier landmark in the cardiac cycle than the QRS-to-ST transition being described.
incorrectas.C: The T wave peak occurs during ventricular repolarization, well after the QRS complex and ST segment have already occurred, making it unrelated to the junction being asked about.
incorrectas.D: The PR segment is the isoelectric period between the end of the P wave and the start of the QRS complex, representing AV nodal delay before ventricular depolarization — a different landmark than the QRS-to-ST junction.

preguntas.q: Which cardiac pacemaker has the fastest intrinsic firing rate, making it the dominant pacemaker of the heart?

e.correcta: The SA node has the fastest intrinsic rate of spontaneous phase 4 depolarization (approximately 60-100 bpm) among all cardiac pacemaker tissues, which is why it normally sets the heart rate and suppresses (overdrive suppresses) the slower latent pacemakers downstream. The hierarchy of intrinsic rates is SA node > AV node > bundle of His/Purkinje fibers, and if the SA node fails, a slower subsidiary pacemaker takes over, producing a junctional or ventricular escape rhythm.

incorrectas.A: The AV node has an intrinsic rate slower than the SA node (roughly 40-60 bpm) and normally only acts as a pacemaker if the SA node fails, producing a junctional escape rhythm rather than being the dominant pacemaker under normal conditions.
incorrectas.B: The bundle of His has an even slower intrinsic firing rate than the AV node and mainly serves as a rapid conduction pathway from the AV node to the ventricles rather than as the primary rhythm-setting pacemaker.
incorrectas.C: Purkinje fibers have the slowest intrinsic pacemaker rate (around 15-40 bpm) of the conduction system components listed and function chiefly to rapidly distribute the depolarization wave through the ventricles, only becoming the pacemaker as a last-resort ventricular escape rhythm.

preguntas.q: Which cardiac conduction structure is located in the posteroinferior part of the interatrial septum?

e.correcta: The AV node is located in the posteroinferior region of the interatrial septum, near the opening of the coronary sinus, within an area sometimes referenced by the triangle of Koch. Its anatomic position allows it to receive the depolarization wave from both atria and impose a conduction delay before passing the impulse to the bundle of His, coordinating the timing between atrial and ventricular contraction.

incorrectas.A: The SA node is located at the junction of the superior vena cava and the right atrium, an entirely different location from the posteroinferior interatrial septum where the AV node resides.
incorrectas.B: The bundle of His arises from the AV node and travels through the membranous interventricular septum (not the interatrial septum), representing a more distal part of the conduction system.
incorrectas.D: The left bundle branch is a continuation of the bundle of His that runs along the left side of the interventricular septum to depolarize the left ventricle, located well beyond and distinct from the AV node's interatrial septal position.

preguntas.q: A tall patient with lens dislocation and aortic root dilation is found to have a mutation in the fibrillin-1 gene on chromosome 15. What is the mode of inheritance of this condition (Marfan syndrome)?

e.correcta: Marfan syndrome is autosomal dominant, caused by missense mutations in FBN1 (chromosome 15q21), which encodes fibrillin-1, a glycoprotein that scaffolds elastic fibers and sequesters TGF-β in the extracellular matrix. A single mutant allele is sufficient to disrupt the fibrillin matrix (a dominant-negative or haploinsufficiency effect), which is why only one copy of the abnormal gene is needed to produce the full phenotype of lens dislocation, aortic root dilation/dissection, and skeletal overgrowth. Because it's dominant, each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the condition, and family history is often strongly positive.

incorrectas.A: Autosomal recessive conditions require two mutant alleles (one from each parent) and typically appear in individuals with unaffected, carrier parents — this does not match Marfan syndrome, where a single FBN1 mutation causes disease even in the heterozygous state.
incorrectas.C: X-linked recessive conditions (like Duchenne muscular dystrophy or hemophilia) predominantly affect males and are transmitted through carrier mothers; Marfan syndrome affects males and females equally because FBN1 is on an autosome (chromosome 15), not the X chromosome.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance is transmitted exclusively through the maternal line and affects tissues with high energy demand (muscle, CNS); Marfan syndrome instead follows classic Mendelian autosomal dominant transmission from a nuclear gene defect.

preguntas.q: Which type of calcium channel opens during the plateau (phase 2) of the ventricular myocardial action potential, allowing sustained Ca2+ influx?

e.correcta: L-type ("long-lasting") calcium channels open during phase 2 of the myocardial action potential and allow a slow, sustained inward Ca2+ current that balances outward K+ current, producing the characteristic plateau. This calcium influx is essential because it triggers additional Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (calcium-induced calcium release) via ryanodine receptors, which is what actually initiates myocyte contraction. L-type channels are the pharmacologic target of non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers like verapamil and diltiazem.

incorrectas.A: T-type ("transient") calcium channels open briefly at more negative membrane potentials and contribute to pacemaker activity in the SA/AV nodes during early depolarization, but they are not the channels responsible for sustaining the plateau phase in ventricular myocytes.
incorrectas.C: N-type calcium channels are found primarily at presynaptic nerve terminals, where they mediate neurotransmitter release, and play no significant role in the cardiac myocyte action potential plateau.
incorrectas.D: P/Q-type calcium channels are also predominantly neuronal, concentrated at synapses (e.g., the neuromuscular junction and CNS), rather than being the channel type responsible for the sustained calcium current of the cardiac plateau.

preguntas.q: What term describes the effect of the autonomic nervous system on the conduction velocity of electrical impulses through the heart?

e.correcta: Dromotropy specifically refers to changes in conduction velocity, most clinically relevant at the AV node, where autonomic tone determines how quickly impulses pass from atria to ventricles. Sympathetic stimulation (via β1 receptors) increases inward Ca2+ current at the AV node and speeds conduction (positive dromotropy), while parasympathetic stimulation slows it (negative dromotropy) — this is the physiologic basis for why vagal maneuvers and AV-nodal blockers (β-blockers, non-dihydropyridine CCBs) are used to treat SVT.

incorrectas.A: Chronotropic effects refer to changes in heart rate (SA node firing rate), not the speed of impulse conduction through the conduction system — a positive chronotropic drug speeds up the heart rate, but that is a distinct property from dromotropy.
incorrectas.B: Inotropic effects describe changes in the force of myocardial contraction, driven by intracellular calcium handling in the contractile apparatus, and are unrelated to how fast an electrical impulse travels through cardiac tissue.
incorrectas.D: Lusitropic effects refer to the rate of myocardial relaxation (diastolic function), governed largely by calcium reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum via SERCA2a, which is a separate physiologic property from conduction velocity.

preguntas.q: A negative dromotropic effect on the AV node produces which change in conduction velocity?

o.C: Has no effect on conduction velocity

e.correcta: A negative dromotropic effect decreases conduction velocity through the AV node. Mechanistically, this occurs when parasympathetic (vagal) tone predominates, reducing inward Ca2+ current and increasing outward K+ current in AV nodal cells, which slows the rate of phase 0 depolarization and prolongs the time it takes an impulse to cross the node. This is exploited therapeutically — digoxin, beta-blockers, and non-dihydropyridine CCBs all produce negative dromotropy to control ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation.

incorrectas.A: Increased conduction velocity describes a positive dromotropic effect, the opposite of what is being asked — this occurs with sympathetic stimulation via β1 receptors, not the negative dromotropic effect in the question.
incorrectas.C: A dromotropic effect by definition changes conduction velocity; "no effect" would mean the drug or stimulus is not dromotropically active at all, which contradicts the premise that a negative dromotropic effect is present.
incorrectas.D: Automaticity refers to the SA node's (or ectopic focus's) ability to spontaneously generate action potentials, a distinct property from conduction velocity through the AV node — dromotropy and automaticity can be affected independently.

preguntas.q: A positive dromotropic effect on the AV node produces which change in conduction velocity?

o.B: Has no effect on conduction velocity

e.correcta: A positive dromotropic effect increases conduction velocity through the AV node. This happens with sympathetic stimulation, in which norepinephrine acting on β1 receptors increases cAMP-mediated phosphorylation of L-type calcium channels, boosting inward Ca2+ current during phase 0 of the nodal action potential and allowing the impulse to traverse the AV node faster. Clinically, this is why sympathetic surges (exercise, stress) shorten the PR interval and why catecholamines can precipitate rapid ventricular rates in atrial fibrillation by enhancing AV conduction.

incorrectas.A: Decreased conduction velocity is the definition of a negative dromotropic effect, produced by parasympathetic stimulation — the opposite of the positive dromotropic effect described in the question.
incorrectas.B: By definition, a dromotropic effect (positive or negative) changes conduction velocity; stating there is no effect contradicts the premise that a positive dromotropic effect is occurring.
incorrectas.D: SA node automaticity (rate of spontaneous firing) is a chronotropic property, not a dromotropic one — while sympathetic stimulation does affect both, dromotropy specifically concerns conduction speed through tissue like the AV node, not pacemaker firing rate.

preguntas.q: Via increased inward Ca2+ current at the AV node, sympathetic stimulation has what effect on conduction velocity?

e.correcta: Sympathetic stimulation increases AV nodal conduction velocity (a positive dromotropic effect). Norepinephrine binds β1 receptors on nodal cells, activating Gs-adenylyl cyclase-cAMP-PKA signaling that phosphorylates L-type calcium channels, increasing the inward Ca2+ current that drives the upstroke of the nodal action potential — the faster the upstroke, the more quickly the impulse propagates cell to cell through the node. This underlies the shortened PR interval seen with sympathetic activation (e.g., exercise, catecholamine excess).

incorrectas.A: Decreased conduction velocity is what parasympathetic (vagal) stimulation produces via decreased Ca2+ current and increased K+ current — the opposite mechanism and effect of sympathetic stimulation described here.
incorrectas.C: Sympathetic stimulation does have a measurable, well-characterized effect on AV nodal conduction (positive dromotropy) via increased Ca2+ current — there is a direct physiologic and clinical effect, not an absence of one.
incorrectas.D: Wenckebach (Mobitz I) block is a pathologic pattern of progressively prolonging PR intervals until a beat is dropped, typically due to AV nodal disease or excessive vagal/AV-nodal-blocking drug effect — it is not a normal physiologic consequence of sympathetic stimulation, which instead enhances conduction.

preguntas.q: Via decreased inward Ca2+ current and increased outward K+ current at the AV node, parasympathetic stimulation has what effect on conduction velocity?

e.correcta: Parasympathetic stimulation decreases AV nodal conduction velocity (negative dromotropy). Acetylcholine acting on M2 receptors activates Gi signaling (decreasing cAMP) and opens G-protein-coupled inwardly rectifying K+ channels (IKACh), which together reduce the inward Ca2+ current and increase outward K+ current in nodal cells — hyperpolarizing the membrane and slowing the rate of phase 0 depolarization. This is the mechanism by which vagal maneuvers (e.g., carotid massage) slow AV conduction to terminate SVT.

incorrectas.A: Increased conduction velocity describes the sympathetic (positive dromotropic) effect, which works through the opposite mechanism — increased, not decreased, Ca2+ current — making this the wrong direction for parasympathetic stimulation.
incorrectas.B: Vagal tone has a well-documented, clinically exploited effect on AV nodal conduction (this is the physiologic basis of vagal maneuvers for SVT), so "no significant change" understates a real and therapeutically important effect.
incorrectas.D: Conduction velocity through the AV node remains dependent on membrane channel kinetics regardless of autonomic state; parasympathetic input modulates that rate but does not make conduction independent of rate-related properties like refractoriness.

preguntas.q: Slowed conduction through the AV node normally produces an approximately how-many-millisecond delay, allowing time for ventricular filling before ventricular systole?

e.correcta: The AV node normally imposes about a 100-msec delay on the impulse traveling from atria to ventricles. This delay exists because AV nodal cells have small diameter, few gap junctions, and depend on the relatively slow L-type calcium current (rather than fast Na+ current) for their upstroke, all of which slow cell-to-cell propagation. Physiologically, this pause is essential: it allows the atria to finish contracting and complete ventricular filling (the atrial kick) before the ventricles depolarize and contract, optimizing stroke volume — and it corresponds to the PR interval on ECG (normally 120-200 msec, of which AV nodal delay is the major contributor).

incorrectas.A: A 10-msec delay would be far too brief to correspond to the measured AV nodal conduction time reflected in the PR interval, and would not allow adequate time for atrial contraction to complete before ventricular depolarization.
incorrectas.B: 50 msec underestimates the actual physiologic AV delay; while conduction through atrial and ventricular myocardium is fast, the AV node itself is specifically responsible for the majority of the PR interval's duration, which is closer to 100 msec.
incorrectas.D: 300 msec is far too long — a delay of this magnitude would produce a markedly prolonged PR interval consistent with first-degree AV block, not the normal physiologic delay that allows properly timed ventricular filling.

preguntas.q: Serotonin syndrome as a side effect of ondansetron is more likely to occur in patients who are also taking drugs that increase levels of which neurotransmitter?

e.correcta: Ondansetron, though primarily a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist used as an antiemetic, has been associated with serotonin syndrome, especially when combined with other serotonergic agents such as SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, or tramadol. The combined effect drives excess serotonergic activity at multiple receptor subtypes (5-HT1A, 5-HT2A) in the CNS, producing the clinical triad of autonomic instability, neuromuscular abnormalities (clonus, hyperreflexia), and altered mental status. Recognizing this interaction matters because postoperative or chemotherapy patients on SSRIs who receive ondansetron for nausea are at real risk, and the treatment (cyproheptadine, a serotonin antagonist) targets this same pathway.

incorrectas.A: Excess dopamine is implicated in conditions like neuroleptic malignant syndrome's opposite (dopamine agonist withdrawal) or in psychosis, not serotonin syndrome — dopaminergic drugs are not the class that interacts with ondansetron to produce this toxicity.
incorrectas.C: While autonomic instability in serotonin syndrome does involve sympathetic activation, the syndrome's precipitating pharmacologic mechanism is specifically excess serotonin signaling, not norepinephrine excess — drugs that increase norepinephrine (e.g., pure NRIs) are not classically the ones paired with ondansetron to cause this syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Increased GABA activity is sedating and anticonvulsant (as with benzodiazepines or barbiturates), the physiologic opposite of the excitatory, hyperthermic picture of serotonin syndrome — GABAergic drugs do not combine with ondansetron to produce serotonin toxicity.

preguntas.q: Which structure is the basic contractile unit of the myocardial cell?

e.correcta: The sarcomere, the region between two Z discs containing organized arrays of thick (myosin) and thin (actin) filaments, is the fundamental contractile unit of both cardiac and skeletal muscle. Cross-bridge cycling between myosin heads and actin, powered by ATP hydrolysis and triggered by Ca2+ binding to troponin C, generates the shortening that is repeated in series along myofibrils to produce whole-cell and ultimately whole-muscle contraction. Sarcomere length also determines the length-tension relationship (Frank-Starling mechanism at the cellular level) — stretching the sarcomere to an optimal length increases actin-myosin overlap and force generation.

incorrectas.A: A myofibril is a rod-like bundle made of many sarcomeres arranged end-to-end within a muscle cell; it is a larger structural assembly, not itself the basic repeating contractile unit — that distinction belongs to the sarcomere.
incorrectas.B: T tubules are invaginations of the sarcolemma that conduct the action potential deep into the cell interior to trigger calcium release, but they are a conduction/coupling structure, not the contractile apparatus itself.
incorrectas.D: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is an intracellular membrane network that stores and releases Ca2+ to trigger contraction, but it does not generate force directly — the mechanical work of contraction is performed by the actin-myosin sarcomere.

preguntas.q: Which structure of a myocardial cell is responsible for carrying the action potential rapidly into the cell interior to trigger calcium release?

e.correcta: T tubules are deep invaginations of the sarcolemma (plasma membrane) that penetrate into the interior of the myocardial cell, allowing the action potential generated at the cell surface to propagate rapidly to the cell's core rather than relying on slow diffusion. Because T tubules are closely apposed to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, depolarization traveling down them opens L-type calcium channels, initiating calcium-induced calcium release from the SR — this ensures that all myofibrils throughout the cell, not just those near the surface, contract nearly simultaneously.

incorrectas.A: The sarcoplasmic reticulum stores and releases Ca2+ once it is triggered, but it does not itself conduct the action potential from the cell surface inward — that transmission role belongs to the T tubules, which interface with the SR.
incorrectas.C: Intercalated discs are specialized junctions between adjacent cardiac myocytes containing gap junctions and desmosomes; they allow electrical continuity and mechanical coupling between cells, but they do not carry the action potential into the interior of a single cell.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondria are abundant in cardiac myocytes to supply the large ATP demand of continuous contraction, but they play no role in conducting the action potential or triggering calcium release.

preguntas.q: Which structure of a myocardial cell serves as the site of storage and release of Ca2+ for excitation-contraction coupling?

e.correcta: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a specialized smooth endoplasmic reticulum network that sequesters large stores of Ca2+ via the SERCA2a pump and releases it through ryanodine receptors when triggered by a small amount of extracellular Ca2+ entering through L-type channels (calcium-induced calcium release). This SR-derived calcium is what actually binds troponin C and permits cross-bridge cycling, so the amount of Ca2+ stored and released by the SR directly determines the strength of contraction — which is why drugs and diseases that affect SR calcium handling (e.g., in heart failure) change contractility.

incorrectas.A: T tubules conduct the action potential into the cell's interior and house the L-type calcium channels that trigger SR release, but they are not themselves the calcium storage depot — that function belongs to the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
incorrectas.B: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages proteins for secretion or membrane insertion; it has no role in calcium storage or excitation-contraction coupling in cardiac myocytes.
incorrectas.D: The nucleus contains the cell's genetic material and directs protein synthesis via transcription, but it plays no direct role in calcium handling or the contraction cycle.

preguntas.q: During the plateau phase of the myocardial action potential, Ca2+ enters the cell through which type of receptor/channel?

e.correcta: Dihydropyridine receptors are voltage-gated L-type calcium channels located on the T tubule membrane (sarcolemma) that open during the plateau (phase 2) of the action potential, allowing extracellular Ca2+ to flow into the cell. This name comes from their sensitivity to dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (e.g., amlodipine, nifedipine), even though in cardiac muscle the clinically relevant blockers acting here are more often the non-dihydropyridines (verapamil, diltiazem). The small amount of Ca2+ entering through these channels is the trigger for the much larger calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum via ryanodine receptors.

incorrectas.A: Ryanodine receptors are located on the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane, not the sarcolemma/T tubule, and they release intracellular stored Ca2+ in response to the small trigger current — they are downstream of, and distinct from, the dihydropyridine receptors that mediate the initial extracellular Ca2+ entry.
incorrectas.C: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are ligand-gated cation channels found at the neuromuscular junction and autonomic ganglia; they mediate fast synaptic transmission, not calcium entry during the cardiac action potential plateau.
incorrectas.D: IP3 receptors are intracellular calcium release channels found on the endoplasmic/sarcoplasmic reticulum in many cell types, activated by the second messenger IP3 downstream of Gq-coupled receptors — this is not the primary mechanism of calcium entry during the cardiac plateau phase, which relies on voltage-gated L-type channels.

preguntas.q: Entry of Ca2+ into the myocardial cell during the action potential triggers further release of intracellular Ca2+ through which channel?

e.correcta: Ryanodine receptors are calcium release channels on the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane that open in response to the small rise in cytosolic Ca2+ entering through L-type (dihydropyridine) channels during the plateau — this phenomenon is called calcium-induced calcium release. The large amount of Ca2+ released from the SR through ryanodine receptors is what actually reaches the myofilaments and triggers contraction; notably, cardiac muscle depends on this extracellular-to-intracellular trigger mechanism, unlike skeletal muscle, where the L-type channel is mechanically coupled directly to the ryanodine receptor and extracellular calcium influx is not required for contraction.

incorrectas.A: Dihydropyridine receptors are the L-type calcium channels on the T-tubule/sarcolemma that mediate the initial small extracellular Ca2+ influx — they are the trigger, but the question asks about the channel through which the larger subsequent intracellular release occurs, which is the ryanodine receptor.
incorrectas.C: Voltage-gated Na+ channels mediate the rapid phase 0 upstroke of the action potential in most cardiac cells (except nodal tissue) but do not conduct calcium or participate in sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release.
incorrectas.D: The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (NCX) extrudes calcium from the cell (in exchange for Na+ influx) during relaxation to help restore resting calcium levels; it works in the opposite direction from the calcium release process being described here.

preguntas.q: The magnitude of tension generated during myocardial excitation-contraction coupling is proportional to the level of which intracellular ion?

e.correcta: The force of myocardial contraction is directly proportional to intracellular Ca2+ concentration, because Ca2+ binds troponin C, shifting tropomyosin off the actin-myosin binding sites and permitting cross-bridge cycling — the more Ca2+ available, the more cross-bridges can form and cycle, producing greater tension. This principle explains why drugs and conditions that raise intracellular Ca2+ (catecholamines via β1-cAMP-PKA signaling, digoxin via Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition and reduced Ca2+ extrusion) increase contractility, while conditions that impair SR calcium handling (heart failure) reduce it.

incorrectas.A: Intracellular Na+ concentration influences resting membrane potential and, via the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, indirectly affects calcium handling (as with digoxin), but Na+ itself does not bind the contractile apparatus or directly determine tension.
incorrectas.B: Intracellular K+ is the major determinant of the resting membrane potential and repolarization, but it plays no direct role in activating the troponin-tropomyosin contractile mechanism, so it does not correlate with contractile force the way calcium does.
incorrectas.D: Mg2+ serves as a cofactor for ATP (as MgATP) used by myosin ATPase during cross-bridge cycling and has some modulatory effects on channels, but the primary ion whose concentration directly and proportionally drives contractile force is calcium, not magnesium.

preguntas.q: Which structures form low-resistance electrical pathways between adjacent cardiac cells, allowing rapid spread of action potentials throughout the myocardium?

e.correcta: Gap junctions are clusters of connexin protein channels located within intercalated discs that directly connect the cytoplasm of adjacent cardiac myocytes, forming low-resistance electrical pathways.
