e.correcta: Norepinephrine acting on beta-1 receptors in ventricular myocytes raises intracellular cAMP, which activates protein kinase A to phosphorylate L-type calcium channels and phospholamban. This increases calcium entry during the plateau and speeds calcium reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, producing both a stronger contraction (positive inotropy) and faster relaxation — helping raise stroke volume and cardiac output as part of the pressor response.

incorrectas.B: No change would only occur if sympathetic tone were unchanged; the whole point of the reflex is to increase sympathetic drive to the ventricle when pressure falls, and beta-1 receptors are densely expressed there.
incorrectas.D: Contractility is not rate-independent — the same beta-1/cAMP pathway that increases heart rate also increases calcium cycling and contractile force, so rate and contractility rise together under sympathetic stimulation (this is distinct from the intrinsic Bowditch/treppe effect, but both point the same direction here).
incorrectas.A: A decrease in contractility would instead follow parasympathetic or beta-blocker effects reducing cAMP, which is opposite to what increased sympathetic firing produces.

preguntas.q: As part of the baroreceptor reflex response to hypotension, increased efferent sympathetic firing to arterioles causes what change in total peripheral resistance (TPR)?

o.C: No change, since arterioles lack sympathetic innervation
o.D: TPR decreases due to nitric oxide release

e.correcta: Sympathetic nerves release norepinephrine onto alpha-1 adrenergic receptors on arteriolar smooth muscle, triggering Gq-mediated calcium release and smooth muscle contraction. Narrowing the arteriolar lumen raises resistance to flow (TPR), which — combined with increased heart rate and cardiac output — helps restore mean arterial pressure toward baseline when baroreceptors detect hypotension.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in TPR would happen with vasodilation (e.g., beta-2 stimulation in skeletal muscle vessels during exercise or reduced alpha-1 tone), which is the opposite of the reflex vasoconstriction driven by rising sympathetic outflow here.
incorrectas.C: Arterioles are richly innervated by sympathetic fibers acting on alpha-1 receptors; this innervation is precisely what mediates the reflex vasoconstrictor response.
incorrectas.D: Nitric oxide is an endothelium-derived vasodilator released locally (e.g., in response to shear stress or acetylcholine), not a mediator of the sympathetic baroreflex, which acts through norepinephrine/alpha-1 signaling to constrict, not dilate, vessels.

preguntas.q: As part of the baroreceptor reflex response to hypotension, increased sympathetic firing to the venous system produces what change?

o.D: Selective dilation of unstressed volume compartments only

e.correcta: Sympathetic activation constricts venous smooth muscle via alpha-1 receptors, which shifts blood from the unstressed volume (the large-capacitance reservoir that exerts no pressure) into the stressed volume (blood that actually generates venous pressure). This raises mean systemic filling pressure and venous return to the heart, augmenting preload and stroke volume via the Frank-Starling mechanism, and thereby helping restore arterial pressure during hypotension.

incorrectas.B: Venodilation would shift blood into the unstressed volume and lower venous return, which would worsen rather than correct hypotension — the opposite of the reflex response.
incorrectas.C: Venous smooth muscle is sympathetically innervated and quite responsive to catecholamines; venoconstriction is actually one of the fastest and most significant contributors to increasing venous return during acute hypotension (e.g., hemorrhage).
incorrectas.D: Sympathetic stimulation does not selectively dilate the unstressed compartment — it constricts veins broadly, converting unstressed volume into stressed volume rather than expanding the low-pressure reservoir.

preguntas.q: During the strain phase of the Valsalva maneuver, intrathoracic pressure rises and venous return to the heart falls, transiently dropping cardiac output and blood pressure. If the baroreceptor reflex is intact, what happens to heart rate during this phase?

o.D: Heart rate becomes irregular but averages unchanged

e.correcta: The forced expiration against a closed glottis raises intrathoracic pressure, compressing the great veins and reducing venous return, which lowers stroke volume, cardiac output, and arterial pressure. Intact carotid and aortic baroreceptors sense this fall in pressure and reflexively decrease vagal tone while increasing sympathetic outflow, producing compensatory tachycardia to help defend perfusion — a response clinicians use clinically to test autonomic integrity (e.g., in diabetic autonomic neuropathy, this HR response is blunted).

incorrectas.B: No change would suggest an impaired baroreflex arc, which is actually how autonomic dysfunction is detected using the Valsalva maneuver — a normal, intact reflex produces a brisk heart rate increase during strain.
incorrectas.A: A decrease in heart rate would be paradoxical here; that pattern is instead seen with the increased vagal tone at Valsalva phase IV overshoot after release, not during the pressure-drop phase of straining.
incorrectas.D: The heart rate response during straining is a directional, quantifiable rise driven by baroreflex withdrawal of vagal tone, not simply random irregularity.

preguntas.q: On the jugular venous pulse waveform, which wave corresponds to atrial contraction?

e.correcta: The a wave is the first positive deflection of the jugular venous pulse and reflects the rise in right atrial pressure produced by atrial systole just before ventricular contraction begins. Because it depends on coordinated atrial contraction, the a wave is lost in atrial fibrillation (no organized atrial systole) and becomes exaggerated (cannon a waves) when the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve, as in complete heart block or AV dissociation.

incorrectas.A: The c wave reflects tricuspid valve closure and bulging into the right atrium at the very start of ventricular systole, an event that follows atrial contraction rather than representing it.
incorrectas.B: The v wave reflects passive right atrial filling against a closed tricuspid valve during ventricular systole, not atrial contraction itself — it happens later in the cycle and is a filling wave, not a contraction wave.
incorrectas.D: The x descent represents atrial relaxation (and downward displacement of the tricuspid annulus during ventricular systole), which follows atrial contraction rather than representing it.

preguntas.q: Which component of the jugular venous pulse corresponds to right ventricular contraction causing the tricuspid valve to bulge into the right atrium?

e.correcta: The c wave is a small positive deflection that occurs early in ventricular systole, when the tricuspid valve closes and bulges upward (bows back) into the right atrium as right ventricular pressure rises sharply. It immediately follows the a wave and marks the transition from atrial to ventricular events in the cardiac cycle, though it is often subtle on bedside JVP examination compared to the a and v waves.

incorrectas.A: The a wave precedes the c wave and reflects atrial contraction itself, not the tricuspid valve bulging that occurs once the ventricle begins contracting.
incorrectas.C: The v wave reflects passive venous filling of the right atrium later in systole while the tricuspid valve remains closed, a distinct event from the early systolic tricuspid bulge that produces the c wave.
incorrectas.D: The y descent represents right atrial emptying into the right ventricle after the tricuspid valve opens in diastole, occurring well after the c wave rather than describing the valve-closure bulge.

preguntas.q: Which descent in the jugular venous pulse reflects atrial relaxation?

e.correcta: The x descent follows the c wave and represents the fall in right atrial pressure as the atrium relaxes after its contraction, combined with downward pulling of the tricuspid annulus during ventricular systole (atrial diastole plus continued ventricular contraction). It is typically the most prominent descent on the normal JVP tracing and is blunted or absent in conditions like atrial fibrillation or tricuspid regurgitation, where normal atrial relaxation dynamics are disrupted.

incorrectas.A: The y descent instead reflects right atrial emptying into the right ventricle once the tricuspid valve opens in diastole, a later event unrelated to atrial relaxation following contraction.
incorrectas.C: The v wave is a rising pressure wave from passive atrial filling against a closed tricuspid valve, the opposite direction of change (a rise, not a descent) from what atrial relaxation produces.
incorrectas.D: The a wave is the positive deflection caused by atrial contraction itself, occurring before the x descent rather than representing the atrium's subsequent relaxation.

preguntas.q: Which wave of the jugular venous pulse reflects right atrial filling against a closed tricuspid valve during ventricular systole?

e.correcta: The v wave results from continued venous return filling the right atrium while the tricuspid valve remains closed during ventricular systole, causing atrial pressure to rise progressively until it peaks just before the valve opens. Because this wave reflects passive filling against a competent valve, it becomes markedly exaggerated (giant v waves) in tricuspid or mitral regurgitation, where a leaky valve lets ventricular pressure transmit directly back into the atrium during systole.

incorrectas.A: The a wave reflects active atrial contraction occurring earlier in the cycle, before the ventricle has even begun to contract, not passive filling during ventricular systole.
incorrectas.B: The c wave is a brief early-systolic deflection from tricuspid valve closure and bulging, distinct from the gradual pressure rise of ongoing atrial filling that defines the v wave.
incorrectas.D: The y descent is the drop in pressure that follows the v wave, occurring once the tricuspid valve opens and the atrium empties into the ventricle — it represents the resolution of the filling process, not the filling itself.

preguntas.q: Which descent of the jugular venous pulse corresponds to right atrial emptying into the right ventricle?

e.correcta: The y descent occurs when the tricuspid valve opens in early diastole, allowing the right atrium, which had been filling against the closed valve (producing the v wave), to rapidly empty its accumulated blood into the right ventricle. A steep, prominent y descent is characteristic of constrictive pericarditis, where rapid early diastolic filling is followed by an abrupt halt once the stiff pericardium limits further ventricular expansion.

incorrectas.A: The x descent occurs earlier, during ventricular systole, and reflects atrial relaxation and annular descent — not the diastolic emptying of the atrium through an open tricuspid valve.
incorrectas.C: The a wave is a positive pressure wave from atrial contraction, the opposite of a descent, and occurs long before the diastolic emptying event described here.
incorrectas.D: The c wave is an early systolic deflection from tricuspid valve closure, unrelated to the later diastolic opening of the valve and atrial emptying captured by the y descent.

preguntas.q: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies are most strongly stimulated by which combination of changes?

o.C: Increased PCO2 only, independent of PO2 or pH

e.correcta: Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies) are activated by a significant fall in arterial PO2 (typically below about 60 mmHg) and by decreased arterial pH, reflecting their role as sensors of hypoxemia and acidemia that trigger increased ventilation and sympathetic outflow. Unlike central chemoreceptors, peripheral chemoreceptors can directly sense low oxygen tension, which becomes especially important in conditions like chronic lung disease where hypoxic drive may become the dominant respiratory stimulus.

incorrectas.A: Increased PO2 and increased pH would suppress rather than stimulate chemoreceptor firing, since these receptors respond to falling, not rising, oxygen and pH.
incorrectas.C: While peripheral chemoreceptors do respond to rising PCO2, this option incorrectly claims their sensitivity is independent of PO2 and pH; in reality PO2 and pH are the classic, defining stimuli tested for peripheral (as opposed to central) chemoreceptors.
incorrectas.D: Decreased PCO2 and increased PO2 both represent directions that would reduce chemoreceptor firing, the opposite of what stimulates these sensors during hypoxemia or acidemia.

preguntas.q: An increase in which arterial blood gas parameter directly stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors?

e.correcta: Peripheral chemoreceptors respond to rising PaCO2 (hypercapnia), which — along with falling PO2 and pH — increases their afferent firing rate to the medullary respiratory centers via the glossopharyngeal (carotid body) and vagus (aortic body) nerves, driving an increase in ventilation. Although central chemoreceptors are the dominant CO2 sensors overall (via CSF pH changes), peripheral chemoreceptors also contribute a faster-responding component of the ventilatory response to hypercapnia.

incorrectas.A: An increase in PO2 would reduce, not stimulate, chemoreceptor firing, since peripheral chemoreceptors are activated by hypoxemia (falling PO2), not hyperoxia.
incorrectas.B: Bicarbonate is a buffering ion tracked in acid-base status but is not itself the direct stimulus sensed by peripheral chemoreceptors, which respond to PO2, PCO2, and pH rather than bicarbonate concentration per se.
incorrectas.D: Base excess is a calculated metabolic acid-base parameter used to characterize metabolic derangements, not a direct chemoreceptor stimulus in the way PaCO2, PO2, and pH are.

preguntas.q: Central chemoreceptors located in the medulla are stimulated primarily by changes in which two parameters of the brain's local environment?

e.correcta: Central chemoreceptors sense the pH and PCO2 of the brain interstitial fluid/CSF: CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier freely and is hydrated to carbonic acid, which dissociates to lower CSF pH, and it is this local pH change (driven by PCO2) that the chemoreceptors actually detect. This makes central chemoreceptors the dominant long-term regulator of ventilation in response to hypercapnia, since CSF has little protein buffering capacity and pH changes rapidly with PCO2 shifts.

incorrectas.A: Central chemoreceptors do not directly sense PO2 at all — that role belongs to peripheral chemoreceptors — and bicarbonate itself does not cross the blood-brain barrier readily, so it is not the direct local signal being sensed.
incorrectas.C: Lactate is not a recognized direct stimulus for central chemoreceptors; the well-established sensed parameters are CSF pH and PCO2, not circulating lactate levels.
incorrectas.D: Osmolarity is sensed by separate hypothalamic osmoreceptors involved in ADH regulation, not by the medullary central chemoreceptors that govern ventilatory drive.

preguntas.q: During cerebral ischemia, what happens to local brain PCO2 and pH, driving the Cushing reaction?

o.C: Both PCO2 and pH remain unchanged
o.D: PCO2 increases and pH also increases

e.correcta: When cerebral blood flow is compromised, CO2 produced by ongoing brain metabolism is not adequately washed out, so local PCO2 rises and, through carbonic acid formation, local pH falls. This detected hypercapnia/acidosis (sensed by central chemoreceptors and the vasomotor center) triggers the Cushing reaction — a compensatory rise in systemic blood pressure intended to restore cerebral perfusion pressure, classically accompanied by reflex bradycardia and irregular respirations.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in PCO2 with increased pH would reflect hyperventilation or improved clearance of CO2, the opposite physiological direction from what occurs when ischemia impairs CO2 washout.
incorrectas.C: Both parameters do change significantly during ischemia — impaired perfusion allows CO2 to accumulate locally and drives pH down, which is precisely the stimulus that provokes the Cushing reflex.
incorrectas.D: PCO2 and pH move in opposite directions under normal buffering physiology (CO2 accumulation causes acidification), so an increase in both together is not physiologically consistent with ischemia-driven CO2 retention.

preguntas.q: In response to elevated PCO2 in the brain (as in the Cushing reaction), what happens to peripheral vascular tone in order to preserve cerebral blood flow?

o.C: No change in peripheral vascular tone

e.correcta: Rising brain PCO2 and falling local pH during cerebral ischemia trigger a powerful sympathetically mediated peripheral vasoconstriction, which raises systemic arterial pressure substantially. This surge in blood pressure helps drive blood through compressed or compromised cerebral vessels, restoring cerebral perfusion pressure despite rising intracranial pressure — the pressor component of the Cushing reflex, which is often accompanied by reflex bradycardia via baroreceptor-mediated vagal activation.

incorrectas.A: Peripheral vasodilation would lower systemic blood pressure and worsen cerebral perfusion, which is the opposite of the protective, pressure-raising response actually seen in the Cushing reaction.
incorrectas.C: Peripheral vascular tone changes dramatically during this reflex; the whole mechanism depends on a marked rise in systemic vascular resistance to elevate arterial pressure enough to overcome rising intracranial pressure.
incorrectas.D: The vasoconstriction in the Cushing reflex is a generalized systemic sympathetic response affecting peripheral arterioles broadly, not a response limited to the coronary vasculature.

preguntas.q: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) exerts its intracellular effects through which second messenger?

e.correcta: ANP binds a membrane-bound guanylate cyclase receptor, directly increasing intracellular cGMP rather than acting through a G-protein-coupled adenylate cyclase pathway. Elevated cGMP relaxes vascular smooth muscle (mediating vasodilation) and alters sodium channel activity in the renal collecting duct (promoting natriuresis) — the same second messenger used by nitric oxide, though ANP acts through its own particulate guanylate cyclase receptor rather than the soluble guanylate cyclase NO activates.

incorrectas.A: cAMP is the second messenger for many Gs-coupled receptors like beta-adrenergic and V2 vasopressin receptors, but ANP signals through guanylate cyclase and cGMP, a distinct pathway.
incorrectas.B: IP3/DAG signaling is used by Gq-coupled receptors such as alpha-1 adrenergic and angiotensin II AT1 receptors to mobilize calcium and activate protein kinase C, not by the ANP receptor, which is a guanylate cyclase itself.
incorrectas.D: Calcium-calmodulin is a downstream effector in many calcium-signaling cascades (e.g., smooth muscle myosin light chain kinase activation), but it is not the primary second messenger generated directly by ANP receptor activation, which is cGMP.

preguntas.q: Atrial natriuretic peptide generally has what effect on arteriolar tone (with the notable exception of the efferent renal arteriole)?

e.correcta: ANP acts through its guanylate cyclase receptor to raise cGMP in vascular smooth muscle, which relaxes the muscle and produces arteriolar dilation, lowering systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure — consistent with ANP's overall role in counteracting volume/pressure overload. The key clinical exception is the efferent glomerular arteriole, where ANP instead causes constriction, raising glomerular filtration pressure to promote natriuresis even as systemic vessels dilate.

incorrectas.A: Constriction is the effect ANP has specifically at the efferent renal arteriole (to boost GFR and natriuresis), but this is the exception, not the general rule; ANP's dominant systemic effect on arterioles is dilation.
incorrectas.C: ANP has a clear, physiologically important vasodilatory effect on most arterioles via the cGMP pathway; it does not leave vascular tone unaffected.
incorrectas.D: ANP's action is not biphasic in this way — it consistently dilates systemic arterioles while consistently constricting the efferent renal arteriole, rather than showing a time-dependent constrict-then-dilate pattern in the same vessel.

preguntas.q: What effect does atrial natriuretic peptide have on sodium reabsorption at the renal collecting tubule?

o.C: No effect on collecting tubule sodium handling
o.D: Increased reabsorption only in volume-depleted states

e.correcta: ANP is released by atrial myocytes in response to increased atrial stretch (volume overload) and acts at the collecting duct to inhibit epithelial sodium channels (ENaC), directly decreasing sodium reabsorption and promoting natriuresis and diuresis. This action, combined with ANP's suppression of renin, aldosterone, and ADH release, works to reduce circulating volume and blood pressure — a counter-regulatory system to renin-angiotensin-aldosterone.

incorrectas.A: Increased sodium reabsorption at the collecting duct is instead the effect of aldosterone acting on ENaC and the Na+/K+ ATPase, the opposite of ANP's natriuretic action.
incorrectas.C: ANP has a clear and clinically important direct effect on collecting duct sodium channels, reducing reabsorption — it is not without effect on tubular sodium handling.
incorrectas.D: ANP's natriuretic effect is a direct response to atrial stretch/volume expansion, not something reserved for volume-depleted states — in fact ANP secretion and its natriuretic action are suppressed, not activated, during volume depletion.

preguntas.q: Vasopressin (ADH) promotes water reabsorption in the renal distal tubule and collecting duct by activating which receptor?

e.correcta: ADH binds basolateral V2 receptors on principal cells of the distal tubule and collecting duct, activating a Gs-cAMP-protein kinase A cascade that causes aquaporin-2 water channels to be inserted into the apical membrane, increasing water permeability and reabsorption. This water retention expands plasma volume and helps raise blood pressure, which is why V2 receptor antagonists (vaptans) are used to treat hyponatremia from conditions like SIADH.

incorrectas.A: V1 receptors are located on vascular smooth muscle and mediate ADH's vasoconstrictor effect via Gq/IP3-calcium signaling, not the water reabsorption effect in the renal tubule, which is mediated by V2 receptors.
incorrectas.C: AT1 receptors are angiotensin II receptors that mediate vasoconstriction and aldosterone release as part of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, an entirely separate hormonal pathway from ADH/V2 signaling.
incorrectas.D: The mineralocorticoid receptor is activated by aldosterone to increase sodium reabsorption (and secondary water follow) via ENaC and Na+/K+ ATPase upregulation, a distinct mechanism from ADH's direct water-channel effect through V2 receptors.

preguntas.q: The smooth muscle band located at the junction of arterioles and capillaries, which regulates blood flow into the capillary bed, is called the:

e.correcta: The pre-capillary sphincter is a ring of smooth muscle at the terminal end of an arteriole, just before it opens into the true capillary bed, and it contracts or relaxes in response to local metabolic signals (such as low O2, high CO2, or adenosine) to match capillary perfusion to tissue metabolic demand. Because true capillaries lack their own smooth muscle, this sphincter is the main site of local flow regulation into individual capillary beds, allowing intermittent perfusion (vasomotion) rather than constant flow to every capillary at once.

incorrectas.A: The metarteriole is the vessel segment connecting the arteriole to the capillary bed and the thoroughfare channel, containing scattered smooth muscle cells along its course, but the specific sphincter-like structure controlling entry into true capillaries is the precapillary sphincter itself, not the metarteriole as a whole.
incorrectas.C: Post-capillary venules are the vessels downstream of capillaries where blood collects after exchange has occurred; they are a site of leukocyte adhesion/emigration during inflammation, not the flow-regulating sphincter proximal to the capillary bed.
incorrectas.D: An arteriovenous shunt is a direct connection bypassing the capillary bed entirely (important in thermoregulation, e.g., in the skin), which is a different structure from the pre-capillary sphincter that gates flow into the capillary bed itself.

preguntas.q: The effective osmotic pressure exerted by plasma proteins across the capillary wall is known as which pressure?

e.correcta: Oncotic pressure (colloid osmotic pressure) is generated specifically by plasma proteins, chiefly albumin, which are largely too large to cross the capillary wall and therefore create an osmotic force that pulls water back into the vascular space. This protein-driven pressure is one of the four Starling forces (along with capillary and interstitial hydrostatic pressures and interstitial oncotic pressure) that together determine net fluid movement across the capillary wall.

incorrectas.A: Hydrostatic pressure is the physical fluid pressure within the capillary or interstitium generated by blood pressure and volume, not the osmotic force created by dissolved proteins — it favors filtration out of the capillary rather than reabsorption.
incorrectas.C: Interstitial pressure refers broadly to the hydrostatic (or oncotic) pressure in the interstitial fluid compartment, a location descriptor rather than the specific term for the protein-driven osmotic force being asked about here.
incorrectas.D: This is not a standard Starling-forces term; the correct terminology pairs 'hydrostatic' pressure (a physical fluid pressure) separately from 'oncotic' or 'colloid osmotic' pressure (from protein osmotic effects) — the two concepts are not combined into a single named pressure.

preguntas.q: The Starling equation describes capillary fluid flux (Jv). Which expression correctly represents Jv?

e.correcta: The Starling equation states Jv = Kf[(Pc − Pi) − σ(πc − πi)], where Kf is the capillary's hydraulic conductance (how easily fluid crosses), (Pc − Pi) is the net hydrostatic pressure gradient favoring filtration out of the capillary, and σ(πc − πi) is the net oncotic pressure gradient (scaled by the reflection coefficient σ, capillary permeability to protein) favoring reabsorption into the capillary. This equation quantifies why capillaries typically filter fluid at the arteriolar end (where hydrostatic pressure dominates) and reabsorb it at the venular end (where oncotic pressure dominates), and it explains edema formation when any of its terms shift pathologically (e.g., low albumin lowering πc, or heart failure raising Pc).

incorrectas.A: Reversing the signs to addition would imply that both hydrostatic and oncotic gradients always push fluid in the same direction, which is physiologically incorrect — hydrostatic pressure gradients favor filtration while oncotic gradients favor reabsorption, so they must oppose each other (subtraction) in the equation.
incorrectas.C: Placing Kf in the denominator misrepresents its role — Kf is a proportionality constant (hydraulic conductance) that scales the pressure difference to produce a flow rate, so it must multiply the pressure term, not divide by it.
incorrectas.D: Swapping σ and Kf's positions misassigns their physiological roles — σ specifically scales only the oncotic (protein) pressure term as the reflection coefficient, while Kf scales the entire pressure difference as the overall permeability/conductance constant.

preguntas.q: In the Starling equation, when the calculated value of Jv is positive, what does this indicate about fluid movement at the capillary?

o.A: Net fluid movement into the capillary (absorption)
o.B: Net fluid movement out of the capillary (filtration)
o.D: Fluid movement direction cannot be determined from the sign of Jv

e.correcta: By convention, Jv is calculated as the net hydrostatic pressure gradient favoring outward movement minus the net oncotic pressure gradient favoring inward movement; a positive Jv means the hydrostatic forces pushing fluid out of the capillary exceed the oncotic forces pulling it back in, resulting in net filtration into the interstitium. This is the dominant pattern at the arteriolar end of capillaries, where capillary hydrostatic pressure is highest, and pathologic increases in capillary hydrostatic pressure (e.g., heart failure) or decreases in plasma oncotic pressure (e.g., hypoalbuminemia) push Jv further positive, promoting edema.

incorrectas.A: Net absorption into the capillary corresponds to a negative Jv, where oncotic forces pulling fluid inward exceed hydrostatic forces pushing it outward — the opposite sign convention from filtration.
incorrectas.C: A Jv of exactly zero (not merely positive) would indicate the hydrostatic and oncotic forces are balanced with no net fluid movement; a positive value specifically indicates a net outward, not absent, flow.
incorrectas.D: The sign of Jv directly and unambiguously indicates flow direction by the standard convention used in the Starling equation — this is precisely why the equation is useful clinically for predicting edema versus fluid resorption.

preguntas.q: In the Starling equation, when the calculated value of Jv is negative, what does this indicate about fluid movement at the capillary?

o.A: Net fluid movement out of the capillary (filtration)
o.B: Net fluid movement into the capillary (absorption)

e.correcta: A negative Jv means that the oncotic pressure gradient (driven mainly by plasma proteins pulling water back into the vessel) outweighs the net hydrostatic pressure gradient pushing fluid out, so the net effect is absorption of interstitial fluid into the capillary. This pattern is characteristic of the venular end of capillaries, where hydrostatic pressure has fallen along the vessel's length while oncotic pressure remains relatively high, allowing much of the filtered fluid to be reclaimed before it reaches the lymphatics.

incorrectas.A: Net filtration out of the capillary corresponds to a positive Jv, where hydrostatic forces dominate over oncotic forces — the opposite sign and opposite direction of fluid movement from absorption.
incorrectas.C: Equilibrium with no net flow would correspond to a Jv value of zero, not a negative value; a negative Jv specifically signals directional net movement into the capillary, not a balanced state.
incorrectas.D: Lymphatic overflow is a separate clinical concept related to lymphatic drainage capacity being exceeded by filtered fluid (contributing to edema), not something described by a negative value in the Starling equation, which concerns capillary fluid exchange itself.

preguntas.q: When the net movement of fluid at the capillary is out of the vessel and into the interstitium, what is this process called?

e.correcta: Filtration is the net outward movement of fluid from the capillary lumen into the interstitial space, and it occurs whenever the Starling forces favoring outward movement (capillary hydrostatic pressure Pc and interstitial oncotic pressure πi) exceed those favoring inward movement (interstitial hydrostatic pressure Pi and capillary oncotic pressure πc). This is the normal, ongoing process at the arteriolar end of most capillary beds, and it is how plasma-derived fluid initially enters the interstitium before being returned via lymphatics.

incorrectas.A: Absorption is the opposite process — net fluid movement from the interstitium back into the capillary — which happens when the inward-pulling forces (mainly capillary oncotic pressure) dominate, classically near the venous end of the capillary.
incorrectas.C: Osmosis alone does not capture the full picture, because capillary fluid exchange is governed by the balance of both hydrostatic and oncotic (osmotic) pressures on both sides of the capillary wall (the Starling equation), not osmotic force in isolation.
incorrectas.D: Active transport requires ATP-driven pumps to move solutes against a gradient; capillary fluid exchange is a passive, pressure-driven process governed by hydrostatic and oncotic gradients, not an energy-dependent transport mechanism.

preguntas.q: When the net movement of fluid at the capillary is from the interstitial fluid back into the capillary lumen, what is this process called?

e.correcta: Absorption describes net fluid movement from the interstitium into the capillary, which occurs when the inward Starling forces (chiefly capillary oncotic pressure πc pulling water in) outweigh the outward forces (capillary hydrostatic pressure Pc and interstitial oncotic pressure πi). This is classically favored near the venous end of the capillary, where hydrostatic pressure has fallen but oncotic pressure from plasma proteins remains relatively high.

incorrectas.A: Filtration is the reverse process — net outward movement of fluid from capillary to interstitium — driven by the same Starling forces but in the opposite net direction, typically dominant at the arteriolar end.
incorrectas.B: Diffusion refers to the passive movement of individual solutes (like gases and small molecules) down their concentration gradients across the capillary wall, not the bulk, pressure-driven movement of fluid described by absorption.
incorrectas.D: Ultrafiltration is a term more specific to glomerular filtration in the kidney, where a specialized filtration barrier separates plasma from filtrate; it is not the standard term used for the reabsorptive side of systemic capillary Starling forces.

preguntas.q: In the Starling equation for capillary fluid exchange, which variable determines the magnitude (rate) of net fluid movement across the capillary wall for a given pressure gradient?

e.correcta: Hydraulic conductance (Kf), also called the filtration coefficient or water permeability of the capillary wall, is the proportionality constant that scales how much fluid actually moves for a given net Starling pressure gradient. A capillary bed with high Kf (like fenestrated capillaries in the kidney or liver) will filter far more fluid for the same pressure difference than one with low Kf (like continuous capillaries in muscle or brain), and pathologic increases in Kf (from toxins, burns, or inflammation) cause edema even without any change in the pressure gradients themselves.

incorrectas.A: Capillary oncotic pressure (πc) is one of the four Starling pressures that determines the direction and magnitude of the net driving force, but it does not describe how permeable the wall is to fluid — it works by pulling fluid inward, not by scaling the flow rate.
incorrectas.B: Interstitial hydrostatic pressure (Pi) is another of the four Starling pressures, contributing to the net gradient by pushing fluid into the capillary, but like the other pressures it is a force, not the conductance term that converts that net force into an actual flow rate.
incorrectas.D: Capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) sets up the outward-pushing force in the Starling equation, but the actual volume of fluid that moves per unit pressure gradient depends on Kf, not on Pc itself.

preguntas.q: In the Starling equation, the term Kf specifically represents which property of the capillary wall?

o.D: Its surface area available for gas exchange

e.correcta: Kf (hydraulic conductance) quantifies how easily water/fluid crosses the capillary wall for a given Starling pressure gradient — essentially the water permeability of the endothelium and its intercellular junctions. Conditions that damage or open up the endothelial barrier (toxins, infections, burns) increase Kf and cause fluid to leak out even when the pressure gradients (Pc, Pi, πc, πi) haven't changed, which is a key mechanism of inflammatory and septic edema.

incorrectas.B: Protein permeability is a related but distinct property of the capillary wall (reflected in the reflection coefficient, σ) — it governs how much oncotic pressure difference can actually be generated, whereas Kf specifically governs bulk water movement.
incorrectas.C: Resistance to blood flow is determined by vessel radius and blood viscosity (as in Poiseuille's law) and relates to how fast blood flows through the vessel, not to how much fluid crosses the vessel wall into the interstitium.
incorrectas.D: Surface area for gas exchange is a determinant of diffusion capacity for gases like O2 and CO2, a separate physiological concept from the hydraulic conductance that governs bulk fluid filtration across the capillary wall.

preguntas.q: In the Starling equation, Pc refers to which of the following pressures?

e.correcta: Pc (capillary hydrostatic pressure) is the pressure exerted by blood against the capillary wall, and it is the main force pushing fluid out of the capillary into the interstitium. It is highest at the arteriolar end of the capillary (where it can be 30-40 mmHg) and progressively falls toward the venous end, which is why filtration predominates proximally and absorption predominates distally along a typical capillary bed; conditions like heart failure raise venous back-pressure and thus Pc, driving edema.

incorrectas.A: Interstitial oncotic pressure (πi) is generated by protein concentration in the interstitial fluid and pulls fluid out of the capillary, but it is a force from outside the vessel, not the intravascular hydrostatic pressure that Pc represents.
incorrectas.C: Interstitial hydrostatic pressure (Pi) reflects the physical pressure of fluid within the interstitial space pushing back into the capillary, the counterpart to Pc but located outside the vessel rather than inside it.
incorrectas.D: Capillary oncotic pressure (πc) is generated by plasma proteins (mainly albumin) within the capillary and pulls fluid inward, the opposite directional effect of Pc, which pushes fluid outward via hydrostatic force.

preguntas.q: An increase in capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) pushes fluid in which direction across the capillary wall?

o.D: It has no net effect on fluid movement

e.correcta: Capillary hydrostatic pressure is the physical force of blood pushing outward against the vessel wall, so when Pc rises, more fluid is forced out of the capillary lumen into the interstitial space — this is the classic mechanism of edema in conditions like heart failure (elevated venous pressure backs up into capillaries) or localized venous obstruction. It is one of the two outward-favoring Starling forces, along with interstitial oncotic pressure (πi).

incorrectas.A: Fluid movement into the capillary is driven by capillary oncotic pressure (πc) and opposed by Pc, so an increase in Pc would work against, not promote, absorption into the vessel.
incorrectas.C: Lymphatics do pick up excess filtered fluid from the interstitium, but Pc acts directly on the capillary wall, not on lymphatic vessels; the lymphatic role is a downstream consequence of increased filtration, not a direct effect of Pc itself.
incorrectas.D: Pc is one of the four primary Starling forces and directly changes the net filtration pressure, so an increase in Pc absolutely has a net effect — it shifts the balance toward more outward fluid movement.

preguntas.q: Along the length of a typical capillary, where is capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) highest and where is it lowest?

o.A: Highest at the venous end, lowest at the arteriolar end
o.B: Highest at the arteriolar end, lowest at the venous end
o.D: Highest in the middle of the capillary, lowest at both ends

e.correcta: Capillary hydrostatic pressure falls progressively along the length of the capillary because of the resistance encountered as blood flows from the arteriolar to the venous end — it is highest where blood first enters from the higher-pressure arteriole and lowest as it approaches the lower-pressure venule. This gradient is why net filtration tends to dominate at the arteriolar end (Pc high, favoring outward movement) while net absorption can dominate at the venous end (Pc low enough that oncotic pressure pulls fluid back in).

incorrectas.A: This reverses the actual pressure gradient — blood pressure decreases as it travels from arterioles to venules due to the cumulative resistance of the microcirculation, so the venous end has lower, not higher, hydrostatic pressure.
incorrectas.C: Pc is not equal throughout the capillary; the entire Starling framework for capillary exchange depends on the pressure drop along the capillary length to explain why filtration predominates proximally and absorption distally.
incorrectas.D: There is no physiologic basis for a mid-capillary pressure peak — pressure falls in a roughly continuous fashion along the capillary as a function of the resistance to flow encountered from arteriolar to venous end.

preguntas.q: In the Starling equation, Pi refers to which of the following pressures?

e.correcta: Pi (interstitial hydrostatic pressure) is the physical pressure of fluid already present in the interstitial space, and it acts to push fluid back into the capillary (opposing filtration). Under normal conditions Pi is low or even slightly negative in many tissues, but it rises as interstitial fluid accumulates, providing a natural brake that limits further edema formation as filtration proceeds.

incorrectas.A: Capillary oncotic pressure (πc) is generated by plasma proteins inside the vessel and pulls fluid inward, a distinct force from the interstitial hydrostatic pressure that acts from outside the capillary.
incorrectas.C: Capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) is the intravascular counterpart to Pi — it is the blood pressure pushing outward from within the capillary, whereas Pi is the pressure of fluid already in the interstitium pushing back in.
incorrectas.D: Interstitial oncotic pressure (πi) is generated by protein concentration within the interstitial fluid and pulls fluid outward (opposite direction to Pi), rather than being a hydrostatic (physical fluid pressure) force.

preguntas.q: An increase in interstitial hydrostatic pressure (Pi) pushes fluid in which direction across the capillary wall?

o.A: It has no effect on capillary fluid exchange
o.D: Only affects lymphatic flow, not capillary exchange

e.correcta: Interstitial hydrostatic pressure is the physical pressure of fluid within the interstitium, and since it acts on the outside of the capillary wall, an increase in Pi pushes fluid inward, back into the capillary lumen (opposing filtration). This self-limiting mechanism is one reason edema does not progress indefinitely — as interstitial fluid accumulates and Pi rises, it increasingly opposes further outward filtration.

incorrectas.B: Movement of fluid out of the capillary is driven by capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) and interstitial oncotic pressure (πi), forces acting in the opposite direction to Pi, which instead favors movement into the capillary.
incorrectas.A: Pi is one of the four Starling forces in the capillary filtration equation and directly contributes to the net pressure gradient, so it clearly does have an effect on fluid movement, just an inward-favoring one.
incorrectas.D: While lymphatics do drain interstitial fluid and can be affected by interstitial pressure, Pi is a direct term in the Starling equation acting on capillary exchange itself, not merely an indirect influence limited to lymphatic flow.

preguntas.q: In the Starling equation, πc (capillary oncotic pressure) refers to which of the following?

o.A: The osmotic pressure generated by plasma proteins within the capillary
o.B: The hydrostatic pressure of blood within the capillary
o.C: The osmotic pressure generated by proteins in the interstitial fluid
o.D: The hydrostatic pressure of fluid in the interstitium

e.correcta: Capillary oncotic pressure (πc) is generated mainly by plasma proteins (especially albumin) that are largely retained within the capillary lumen, and it exerts an osmotic pull that draws fluid into the capillary (favoring absorption). Because πc depends on plasma protein concentration, anything that lowers plasma albumin — liver failure (decreased synthesis), nephrotic syndrome (urinary protein loss), or severe protein malnutrition — reduces πc and shifts the Starling balance toward net filtration, producing generalized edema.

incorrectas.B: The hydrostatic pressure of blood within the capillary is Pc, a distinct force generated by the physical pressure of blood flow rather than the osmotic pull of dissolved plasma proteins.
incorrectas.C: Osmotic pressure from interstitial proteins is πi, which acts on the outside of the capillary wall and pulls fluid out of the vessel, the opposite location and opposite net effect compared to πc.
incorrectas.D: Hydrostatic pressure of interstitial fluid is Pi, a physical (not osmotic) pressure term that acts from the interstitial side of the capillary wall, distinct from the protein-driven osmotic force that defines πc.

preguntas.q: An increase in capillary oncotic pressure (πc) pulls fluid in which direction across the capillary wall?

o.C: It has no effect unless Pc also changes

e.correcta: Capillary oncotic pressure is generated by plasma proteins retained within the vessel, and this creates an osmotic gradient that draws water into the capillary lumen — an increase in πc therefore pulls more fluid inward (favoring absorption over filtration). This is why conditions that raise effective plasma protein concentration, such as dehydration with hemoconcentration, can transiently favor fluid retention within the vasculature.

incorrectas.A: Fluid movement out of the capillary is favored by Pc (capillary hydrostatic pressure) and πi (interstitial oncotic pressure), both forces acting in the opposite direction from πc, which instead pulls fluid inward.
incorrectas.C: πc directly contributes as an independent term in the Starling equation and changes the net filtration pressure on its own — its effect does not require a simultaneous change in Pc to manifest.
incorrectas.D: πc acts directly across the capillary wall to influence blood-interstitium fluid exchange; it does not act specifically or exclusively on lymphatic vessels, which instead passively drain whatever fluid has already been filtered into the interstitium.

preguntas.q: In the Starling equation, πi refers to which of the following pressures?

e.correcta: Interstitial oncotic pressure (πi) is generated by the small amount of protein normally present in the interstitial fluid, and it exerts an osmotic pull that draws fluid out of the capillary into the interstitium (favoring filtration). Anything that raises interstitial protein content — most notably lymphatic obstruction, which prevents the normal clearance of filtered protein from the interstitium — increases πi and worsens edema by increasing the outward osmotic pull.

incorrectas.A: Capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) is the intravascular blood pressure pushing fluid outward, a physical (not osmotic) force generated within the vessel rather than by interstitial protein.
incorrectas.B: Capillary oncotic pressure (πc) is the osmotic force generated by plasma proteins within the capillary that pulls fluid inward, the opposite location and directional effect compared to πi.
incorrectas.C: Interstitial hydrostatic pressure (Pi) is the physical pressure of fluid already present in the interstitium, distinct from the osmotic pull generated by interstitial protein concentration that defines πi.

preguntas.q: An increase in interstitial oncotic pressure (πi), such as from lymphatic blockage, pulls fluid in which direction across the capillary wall?

o.C: Only affects protein movement, not fluid
o.D: It has no net effect because it opposes Pi

e.correcta: Interstitial oncotic pressure is generated by protein in the interstitial fluid, and because this protein normally exerts osmotic pull from outside the capillary, an increase in πi draws additional fluid out of the capillary into the interstitium (favoring filtration). Lymphatic blockage classically raises πi because lymphatics are the main route for clearing filtered protein out of the interstitium — when that clearance fails, protein (and its osmotic pull) accumulates locally, producing a protein-rich, difficult-to-resolve lymphedema.

incorrectas.A: Fluid movement into the capillary is favored by capillary oncotic pressure (πc), the intravascular counterpart that pulls in the opposite direction from πi.
incorrectas.C: While πi is generated by protein, its physiologic effect in the Starling equation is on fluid movement (via the osmotic gradient it creates), not merely a statement about protein movement in isolation.
incorrectas.D: πi and Pi are different forces that happen to both originate in the interstitium, but they are not simply opposites that cancel out — πi pulls fluid outward (favoring filtration) while Pi pushes fluid inward (opposing filtration), and each contributes independently to the net Starling pressure.

preguntas.q: Excess fluid filtered out of the capillaries into the interstitium is normally returned to the systemic circulation by which route?

o.A: Direct venous absorption at the capillary

e.correcta: The lymphatic system collects excess interstitial fluid (along with any protein that leaked out of capillaries) and returns it to the venous circulation via the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct. This is essential because filtration normally exceeds absorption along most capillary beds, and without lymphatic drainage, this net filtered fluid would progressively accumulate as edema; lymphatic return also prevents interstitial protein buildup, which would otherwise raise πi and worsen fluid accumulation.

incorrectas.A: While some fluid is reabsorbed directly back into the capillary (favored where πc exceeds Pc, typically near the venous end), this does not account for all filtered fluid — the excess that isn't reabsorbed at the capillary must be cleared by lymphatics instead.
incorrectas.B: The kidneys regulate whole-body fluid and electrolyte balance by filtering and reabsorbing plasma at the nephron, but they do not directly retrieve fluid that has already been filtered into peripheral tissue interstitium — that role belongs to the lymphatic system.
incorrectas.D: The hepatic portal circulation carries venous blood from the gut and spleen to the liver for processing, an entirely separate circulatory route unrelated to the return of interstitial fluid from peripheral capillary beds.

preguntas.q: Edema due to conditions like heart failure, arteriolar dilation, or venous constriction is best explained by which change in Starling forces?

e.correcta: In heart failure, backward transmission of elevated venous/right-atrial pressure raises capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc); arteriolar dilation increases the pressure transmitted downstream into capillaries, and venous constriction raises pressure by impeding outflow — all three converge on the same mechanism of elevated Pc, which pushes more fluid out of the capillary than can be reabsorbed or drained by lymphatics, producing edema. This is why loop diuretics and afterload/preload reduction (e.g., in heart failure) are central to treating this type of edema.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in πi would reduce the outward osmotic pull from the interstitium and, if anything, would tend to reduce filtration rather than cause it — the actual cause of lymphatic-blockage edema is an increase, not a decrease, in πi.
incorrectas.B: Decreased Kf would reduce capillary permeability to fluid and thus reduce, not promote, filtration; increased (not decreased) Kf from toxins, infection, or burns is the mechanism that produces edema through this particular Starling variable.
incorrectas.D: Increased πc would pull more fluid into the capillary (favoring absorption) and would actually oppose edema formation; edema from protein loss occurs via decreased, not increased, πc (e.g., in liver failure or nephrotic syndrome).

preguntas.q: Edema seen in conditions such as liver failure, nephrotic syndrome, or protein malnutrition is best explained by which change in Starling forces?

e.correcta: Liver failure impairs albumin synthesis, nephrotic syndrome causes urinary loss of albumin, and severe malnutrition provides insufficient substrate for protein synthesis — all three reduce plasma protein (mainly albumin) concentration and thus lower capillary oncotic pressure (πc). Since πc is the main force pulling fluid back into the capillary, a fall in πc shifts the Starling balance toward net filtration throughout the body, producing generalized (often severe, e.g., anasarca-level) edema even without any change in capillary hydrostatic pressure.

incorrectas.B: Increased Kf reflects a leaky or damaged capillary wall (as from toxins, burns, or infection), a distinct mechanism of edema from the protein-deficiency states in this question, which instead operate purely through lowered oncotic pressure with a normal, intact capillary wall.
incorrectas.C: Increased Pi would oppose further filtration (since it is an inward-pushing force from the interstitial side), so it does not explain edema formation; it is the low πc pulling less fluid in, not a rise in Pi, that drives this type of edema.
incorrectas.D: Increased Pc is the mechanism behind cardiac/venous causes of edema (like heart failure), a separate pathway from the hypoproteinemic states described here, where the capillary hydrostatic pressure is typically normal and the defect lies instead in oncotic pressure.

preguntas.q: Edema resulting from toxins, infections, or burns is best explained by which change in Starling forces?

e.correcta: Toxins, infection, and burns damage the capillary endothelium and widen the intercellular junctions, directly increasing the hydraulic conductance (Kf) — the water permeability of the capillary wall. Because Kf scales how much fluid moves for any given pressure gradient, a rise in Kf causes marked fluid (and often protein) leakage into tissue even without any primary change in the hydrostatic or oncotic pressures, which is why burn and sepsis-related edema can be so severe and rapid.

incorrectas.A: A fall in πc is the mechanism behind hypoproteinemic edema (liver failure, nephrotic syndrome, malnutrition), a different pathway from the direct endothelial injury caused by toxins, infection, or burns, which instead primarily raises Kf.
incorrectas.C: Increased Pc is the mechanism in cardiac/venous causes of edema (like heart failure or venous obstruction), reflecting elevated intravascular pressure rather than the endothelial permeability defect caused by direct capillary injury.
incorrectas.D: A fall in Pi would reduce the inward-pushing force and favor slightly more filtration, but this is not the primary or classic mechanism attributed to toxin/burn/infection-related edema, which is instead explained by a rise in capillary permeability (Kf).

preguntas.q: Edema resulting from lymphatic blockage is best explained by which change in Starling forces?

e.correcta: Lymphatics are the primary route for clearing protein that has leaked into the interstitium during normal capillary filtration; when lymphatic drainage is blocked (as in filariasis, tumor obstruction, or post-surgical lymph node removal), that protein accumulates locally and raises interstitial oncotic pressure (πi). Elevated πi increases the outward osmotic pull on fluid, worsening filtration and producing a characteristically protein-rich, non-pitting lymphedema that is notoriously resistant to diuretics because the underlying problem is a drainage failure, not a pressure or permeability problem.

incorrectas.B: A fall in πc is the mechanism in liver failure, nephrotic syndrome, and malnutrition, reflecting reduced plasma protein production or loss, an entirely separate pathway from the failure of interstitial protein clearance seen with lymphatic obstruction.
incorrectas.C: Increased Pc reflects elevated intravascular hydrostatic pressure (as in heart failure or venous obstruction), not the buildup of interstitial protein caused by impaired lymphatic drainage.
incorrectas.D: Increased Kf reflects direct endothelial damage increasing capillary wall permeability (from toxins, infection, or burns), a different mechanism from lymphatic edema, where the capillary wall itself is normal and the defect is downstream in fluid/protein clearance.

preguntas.q: Capillary injury from toxins or burns has what effect on capillary permeability (Kf)?

o.D: Kf becomes negative, reversing filtration direction

e.correcta: Direct injury to the capillary endothelium — from toxins, thermal burns, or infectious/inflammatory mediators — disrupts the tight junctions between endothelial cells and increases the pores available for water to cross, raising the hydraulic conductance (Kf). Because Kf scales the fluid flux for any given Starling pressure gradient, this increase alone can drive substantial fluid (and protein) leakage into tissue, which is a major contributor to the massive third-spacing seen in severe burns and sepsis.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in Kf would mean a less permeable, tighter capillary wall, which is the opposite of what happens with endothelial injury — damage typically opens up rather than seals the barrier, so permeability rises rather than falls.
incorrectas.B: Capillary injury is specifically defined by structural damage to the endothelial barrier, and this damage measurably increases water and solute permeability; describing it as producing no change would ignore the entire pathophysiologic basis of burn/toxin-related edema.
incorrectas.D: Kf is a proportionality constant (permeability), not a directional term, so it cannot become negative or itself reverse the direction of filtration — the direction of net fluid movement is determined by the balance of the Starling pressures (Pc, Pi, πc, πi), not by the sign of Kf.

preguntas.q: The maintenance of a constant blood flow to an organ despite changes in arterial perfusion pressure is known as what phenomenon?

e.correcta: Autoregulation is the intrinsic ability of an organ's vasculature (notably the brain, heart, and kidney) to keep blood flow relatively constant across a range of arterial pressures by adjusting arteriolar resistance — vasoconstricting when pressure rises and vasodilating when pressure falls. Mechanisms underlying this include the myogenic response (smooth muscle stretch-induced constriction) and local metabolite accumulation, and it is clinically important because organs with strong autoregulation (like the brain) are protected from flow changes across a wide blood pressure range, but this protection can fail at pressure extremes (e.g., in malignant hypertension or severe hypotension).

incorrectas.A: Active hyperemia describes increased blood flow to an organ in proportion to its increased metabolic activity (e.g., exercising skeletal muscle), a response to a change in tissue demand rather than a mechanism for keeping flow constant across varying arterial pressures.
incorrectas.B: Reactive hyperemia describes the transient increase in blood flow that follows a period of reduced flow (such as after arterial occlusion is released), a response to a prior flow deficit rather than a real-time buffering of flow against pressure changes.
incorrectas.D: The baroreceptor reflex is a systemic, neurally-mediated mechanism that adjusts heart rate and vascular tone to regulate overall arterial blood pressure, which is distinct from the local, organ-specific ability to keep flow constant despite pressure fluctuations that defines autoregulation.

preguntas.q: The concept that blood flow to an organ increases in proportion to its metabolic activity, such as increased flow to skeletal muscle during exercise, is known as what?

e.correcta: Active hyperemia is the increase in tissue blood flow that matches an increase in metabolic activity, driven by local accumulation of vasodilatory metabolites (adenosine, CO2, H+, K+, and decreased O2) that relax arteriolar smooth muscle in the active tissue. The classic example is exercising skeletal muscle, where local metabolite buildup causes marked vasodilation to increase oxygen and nutrient delivery precisely where demand has risen, independent of any systemic blood pressure change.

incorrectas.A: Reactive hyperemia is the transient increase in flow that follows a period of ischemia or arterial occlusion once flow is restored — a response to a prior flow deficit, not to an ongoing increase in metabolic demand.
incorrectas.B: Autoregulation is the maintenance of constant blood flow across a range of arterial pressures, a pressure-buffering mechanism distinct from the demand-driven flow increase that defines active hyperemia.
incorrectas.D: Vasomotion refers to spontaneous, rhythmic oscillations in vascular tone/diameter seen in some microvascular beds, a different phenomenon from the sustained, metabolically-driven flow increase of active hyperemia.

preguntas.q: An increase in blood flow to an organ following a preceding period of decreased blood flow, such as after release of arterial occlusion, is known as what phenomenon?

e.correcta: Reactive hyperemia is the marked, transient increase in blood flow that occurs after a period of reduced perfusion (such as arterial clamping or a blood pressure cuff occlusion) is released, and its magnitude and duration roughly correlate with the length and severity of the preceding ischemia. It reflects the buildup of vasodilatory metabolites and local hypoxia during the occlusion period, which cause arteriolar dilation once flow is restored to help repay the accumulated oxygen debt.

incorrectas.A: Active hyperemia is the flow increase that matches a rise in ongoing metabolic demand (as in exercising muscle), a response to increased activity rather than to a preceding period of reduced flow.
incorrectas.C: Autoregulation is the maintenance of stable blood flow across changing arterial pressures through moment-to-moment resistance adjustments, a distinct concept from the transient post-occlusion flow surge that defines reactive hyperemia.
incorrectas.D: The myogenic response is one specific mechanism contributing to autoregulation, in which vascular smooth muscle contracts in response to stretch (from increased pressure), rather than the overall post-ischemic flow-surge phenomenon described here.

preguntas.q: Serotonin released after vascular injury has what effect on arteriolar tone, helping to limit blood loss?

o.C: No significant effect on smooth muscle tone
o.D: Biphasic effect: initial dilation followed by constriction

e.correcta: Serotonin (5-HT) is released from activated platelets at a site of vascular injury and acts on vascular smooth muscle serotonin receptors to cause arteriolar vasoconstriction, which helps reduce local blood flow and limit blood loss as part of the initial hemostatic response, alongside platelet aggregation and the coagulation cascade. This local vasoconstrictive role is distinct from serotonin's better-known functions as a central neurotransmitter in mood regulation.

incorrectas.A: Vasodilation in response to vascular/tissue injury is more characteristic of inflammatory mediators like histamine or the E-series prostaglandins, not serotonin, whose hemostatic role at the injury site is specifically to constrict the vessel and reduce flow.
incorrectas.C: Serotonin has well-documented vasoactive effects on smooth muscle mediated through serotonergic receptors on vascular smooth muscle, so describing it as having no significant effect misses its established role in the vascular injury response.
incorrectas.D: While serotonin can have complex, receptor-subtype- and vessel-dependent effects in some contexts, its classic and tested role after vascular injury is straightforward constriction to help limit hemorrhage, not a biphasic dilation-then-constriction pattern.

preguntas.q: The E-series prostaglandins (e.g., PGE2) have what overall effect on vascular smooth muscle tone?

o.D: Constriction of arterioles but dilation of venules

e.correcta: The E-series prostaglandins (particularly PGE2) act as vasodilators, relaxing vascular smooth muscle largely through increasing intracellular cAMP, and they contribute to local blood flow regulation and to the vasodilation seen in inflammation (contributing to redness and warmth) as well as to the maintenance of ductus arteriosus patency in the fetus, which is why indomethacin (a prostaglandin synthesis inhibitor) is used to close a patent ductus arteriosus.

incorrectas.A: Vasoconstriction is the characteristic effect of the F-series prostaglandins (and thromboxane A2), not the E-series, which instead have the opposite, dilatory effect on smooth muscle.
incorrectas.B: E-series prostaglandins have well-established, potent effects on vascular tone (vasodilation) and are clinically significant enough that drugs targeting prostaglandin synthesis (NSAIDs) have measurable cardiovascular and renal hemodynamic consequences — they are not vasomotor-inert.
incorrectas.D: There is no classic segmental arteriole-versus-venule split described for E-series prostaglandins; their defining vascular effect taught for boards is straightforward vasodilation.

preguntas.q: The F-series prostaglandins (e.g., PGF2alpha) have what overall effect on vascular smooth muscle tone?

e.correcta: The F-series prostaglandins (particularly PGF2alpha) act as vasoconstrictors, contracting vascular (and other) smooth muscle, in contrast to the vasodilatory E-series. PGF2alpha is also notable for its use in obstetrics to induce labor and control postpartum hemorrhage by promoting uterine smooth muscle contraction, a related but distinct smooth-muscle effect from its vasoconstrictive action on blood vessels.

incorrectas.A: Vasodilation is the defining effect of the E-series prostaglandins, the functional counterpart to the F-series, which instead produces vasoconstriction.
incorrectas.B: F-series prostaglandins have clear, clinically exploited smooth muscle effects (vasoconstriction and uterine contraction), so describing them as having no significant vascular effect contradicts their established pharmacologic and physiologic actions.
incorrectas.C: There is no selective arteriole-only dilatory action attributed to F-series prostaglandins; the classic, tested vascular effect is constriction, not dilation of any particular vessel segment.

preguntas.q: Thromboxane A2 released from activated platelets has which effect on vascular smooth tone?

e.correcta: Thromboxane A2 is synthesized by platelet cyclooxygenase from arachidonic acid and acts as a potent vasoconstrictor while also promoting platelet aggregation, which together help stop bleeding at a site of vascular injury. This is why low-dose aspirin, which irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1 and blocks TXA2 synthesis, is used for antiplatelet and mild vasodilatory cardiovascular protection.

incorrectas.A: Vasodilation is the opposite effect of TXA2 and is instead produced by prostacyclin (PGI2) from endothelial cells, which also inhibits platelet aggregation, forming a physiologic balance with TXA2 to regulate clot formation and vessel tone.
incorrectas.C: TXA2 is not tone-neutral; it actively signals through thromboxane receptors on vascular smooth muscle to trigger contraction, making it a key mediator of local vasoconstriction after vessel injury.
incorrectas.D: TXA2 does not produce a biphasic response; its action is a sustained vasoconstrictor and pro-aggregatory effect, distinguishing it from mediators like histamine that can show more complex temporal profiles.

preguntas.q: What is the primary mechanism responsible for autoregulation of coronary blood flow?

e.correcta: Coronary blood flow is autoregulated primarily by local metabolic factors such as adenosine, nitric oxide, CO2, and hypoxia, which are released when myocardial oxygen demand rises or perfusion falls. This metabolic coupling ensures the heart's high and constantly fluctuating oxygen demand is matched by proportional increases in flow, largely independent of systemic blood pressure changes across the autoregulatory range.

incorrectas.A: Sympathetic vasoconstriction has only a minor direct role in coronary vessels because local metabolic vasodilation dominates and typically overrides sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone (functional sympatholysis) during increased myocardial work.
incorrectas.B: The myogenic response, in which vascular smooth muscle contracts in response to stretch from increased pressure, contributes more prominently to autoregulation in vascular beds like the kidney and brain, not as the primary coronary mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Circulating catecholamines act on coronary beta-2 and alpha receptors, but coronary flow regulation is dominated by locally produced metabolites reflecting the myocardium's own oxygen consumption, not by hormonal levels in the blood.

preguntas.q: Which two local metabolic factors are most important for regulating coronary vascular tone, with nitric oxide predominating in larger arteries and the other predominating in small arterioles?

e.correcta: Nitric oxide, released by endothelium in response to shear stress and flow, is the major mediator of flow-mediated vasodilation in large coronary arteries and prearteriolar vessels, while adenosine, generated from ATP breakdown when myocardial oxygen consumption exceeds delivery, dilates the small coronary arterioles that directly control resistance. Together these metabolites (along with CO2 and hypoxia) let coronary flow track myocardial oxygen demand beat to beat, which is why the heart normally extracts nearly maximal oxygen at rest and depends on flow increases, not extraction, during exertion.

incorrectas.B: Endothelin is a potent vasoconstrictor peptide from endothelial cells and angiotensin II is a systemic vasoconstrictor hormone; neither functions as a local metabolic vasodilator matching coronary flow to myocardial oxygen needs the way NO and adenosine do.
incorrectas.C: Prostacyclin and thromboxane A2 are eicosanoids important in platelet-vessel wall interactions and hemostasis, not the principal local metabolic regulators of resting coronary autoregulation.
incorrectas.D: Serotonin and histamine are vasoactive amines involved in platelet activation and allergic/inflammatory responses respectively, not the classic local metabolites (NO, adenosine, CO2, hypoxia) that drive coronary autoregulation.

preguntas.q: Autoregulation of cerebral blood flow is primarily determined by which factor?

e.correcta: Cerebral blood flow is tightly autoregulated by local metabolic factors, chiefly CO2 and H+ (pH), which cause vasodilation when tissue metabolism rises or perfusion falls, keeping flow relatively constant despite wide swings in mean arterial pressure (roughly 60-160 mmHg). This is clinically critical: hyperventilation lowers CO2 and causes cerebral vasoconstriction, which is used therapeutically to acutely reduce intracranial pressure.

incorrectas.A: Sympathetic innervation plays only a minor role in the cerebral circulation compared to skin or skeletal muscle, since the brain's high, constant metabolic demand is instead matched primarily through local metabolic vasodilatory signals.
incorrectas.C: The myogenic response contributes to cerebral autoregulation by adjusting vessel diameter to pressure changes, but the dominant driver highlighted for the brain in this context is metabolic (CO2/H+), not the myogenic mechanism alone.
incorrectas.D: Vasopressin acts mainly on renal water reabsorption and, at high concentrations, systemic vasoconstriction; it is not the primary local regulator of cerebral vascular tone under normal autoregulation.

preguntas.q: Which two local metabolic factors are most important in regulating cerebral blood flow?

e.correcta: CO2 and H+ (reflecting local pH) are the dominant metabolic regulators of cerebral vascular tone: rising CO2 and falling pH (from increased neuronal activity or reduced perfusion) cause cerebral arteriolar vasodilation to increase flow and washout of these metabolites. This mechanism explains why hyperventilating a patient with elevated intracranial pressure lowers PaCO2, causes cerebral vasoconstriction, and transiently reduces cerebral blood volume and ICP.

incorrectas.A: Adenosine and lactate are important local metabolites in skeletal muscle and coronary circulation, but the classic pair driving cerebral autoregulation is CO2 and H+.
incorrectas.C: Nitric oxide contributes to cerebral vasodilation but is not paired with endothelin (a vasoconstrictor) as the primary metabolic regulatory duo; the key pairing tested for cerebral autoregulation is CO2 and H+.
incorrectas.D: Potassium efflux and osmolarity changes can modestly influence local vascular tone in exercising muscle, but they are not the principal metabolic factors governing cerebral blood flow autoregulation.

preguntas.q: What is the major factor determining autoregulation of blood flow to the lungs?

e.correcta: Pulmonary vasculature responds to alveolar hypoxia with vasoconstriction (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction), the opposite response seen in nearly every other vascular bed. This mechanism diverts blood flow away from poorly ventilated alveoli toward better-ventilated regions, optimizing ventilation-perfusion matching, though in conditions like COPD or high altitude, global alveolar hypoxia triggers diffuse vasoconstriction that can lead to pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain (cor pulmonale).

incorrectas.A: Sympathetic innervation is a more prominent regulator of tone in skin and resting skeletal muscle vasculature, not the primary determinant of the lung's unique hypoxia-driven autoregulatory response.
incorrectas.B: The myogenic response to stretch is important in beds like the kidney and brain for maintaining constant flow against pressure changes, but it is not the defining feature of pulmonary vascular autoregulation.
incorrectas.D: In systemic vascular beds, local metabolite accumulation and hypoxia typically cause vasodilation to increase oxygen delivery; the lung is the specific exception where hypoxia instead causes vasoconstriction, which is the point being tested here.

preguntas.q: In most systemic organs, local tissue hypoxia produces which compensatory vascular response?

e.correcta: In virtually all systemic vascular beds, falling local oxygen tension triggers arteriolar vasodilation, increasing blood flow to restore oxygen delivery to the hypoxic tissue — a classic example of metabolic autoregulation matching perfusion to demand. The pulmonary circulation is the important exception: alveolar hypoxia causes vasoconstriction instead, redirecting blood flow away from poorly ventilated lung units to optimize gas exchange.

incorrectas.A: Vasoconstriction in response to hypoxia is the reverse (and exceptional) response seen specifically in the pulmonary vasculature, not the general systemic pattern being described in this question.
incorrectas.C: Vascular tone is not unaffected by hypoxia; systemic vessels are highly sensitive to falling oxygen tension and respond briskly with dilation, since failing to do so would allow tissue ischemia to worsen.
incorrectas.D: Hypoxia does not primarily act by opening arteriovenous shunts in most tissues; the principal compensatory response is arteriolar dilation to increase nutritive capillary flow, not bypass shunting.

preguntas.q: Autoregulation of renal blood flow is maintained primarily by which two mechanisms?

o.A: Sympathetic tone and circulating angiotensin II

e.correcta: Renal blood flow and GFR are kept relatively constant across a wide range of arterial pressures by two intrinsic mechanisms: the myogenic response, in which afferent arteriolar smooth muscle contracts when stretched by increased pressure, and tubuloglomerular feedback, in which increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa (sensed via increased flow/pressure) triggers afferent arteriolar constriction to reduce GFR back toward normal. These two mechanisms work together to protect the glomerular capillaries from damaging pressure swings while keeping filtration relatively stable.

incorrectas.A: Sympathetic tone and angiotensin II are extrinsic regulators that become dominant during severe hypotension or hemorrhage (shifting flow away from the kidney to preserve central perfusion), but they are not the intrinsic mechanisms responsible for renal autoregulation under normal conditions.
incorrectas.B: CO2 and H+ are the key local metabolic regulators of cerebral blood flow, not the primary autoregulatory mechanisms in the kidney, which instead rely on pressure-sensing (myogenic) and flow-sensing (tubuloglomerular feedback) mechanisms.
incorrectas.D: Prostaglandins (e.g., PGE2) help maintain afferent arteriolar dilation especially under stress (which is why NSAIDs can precipitate renal injury), but they are modulators rather than the core two mechanisms of renal autoregulation, which are myogenic and tubuloglomerular feedback.

preguntas.q: What is the major factor determining blood flow to resting skeletal muscle?

e.correcta: At rest, skeletal muscle blood flow is governed primarily by sympathetic adrenergic vasoconstrictor tone acting on alpha-1 receptors in arteriolar smooth muscle, keeping resting muscle relatively vasoconstricted since its metabolic demand is low. This allows blood flow to be redirected to organs with higher priority at rest, and it sets the stage for the dramatic shift seen with exercise.

incorrectas.A: Local metabolites (CO2, H+, adenosine, lactate, K+) become the dominant regulator during exercise, when metabolic byproducts accumulate and override sympathetic vasoconstriction to produce functional hyperemia, but at rest sympathetic tone predominates.
incorrectas.C: The myogenic response, where vessels constrict in response to stretch from increased pressure, is more central to autoregulation in organs like the kidney and brain rather than being the defining regulator of resting skeletal muscle flow.
incorrectas.D: CO2 and H+ are the classic local metabolic regulators of cerebral blood flow, not the primary determinant of blood flow to skeletal muscle at rest, where sympathetic tone dominates instead.

preguntas.q: During active exercise, what becomes the major factor determining blood flow to skeletal muscle?

o.D: Circulating epinephrine acting on beta-2 receptors

e.correcta: During exercise, accumulating local metabolites — remembered by the mnemonic CHALK (CO2, H+, adenosine, lactate, K+) — cause profound arteriolar vasodilation in active muscle, overriding baseline sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone through a process called functional sympatholysis. This metabolic vasodilation is what allows skeletal muscle blood flow to increase many-fold above resting levels precisely in the muscle groups that are working hardest, matching oxygen delivery to the sharply increased demand.

incorrectas.A: Sympathetic innervation dominates skeletal muscle vascular tone at rest, keeping flow relatively low, but during exercise this vasoconstrictor signal is functionally overridden by local metabolic vasodilators in active muscle beds.
incorrectas.C: The myogenic response adjusts vascular tone to changes in intravascular pressure and is more relevant to organs like the kidney and brain; it is not the primary driver of the large flow increases seen in exercising muscle.
