rash. Three weeks ago, she was admitted to the hospital for treatment of Staphylococcal aureus endocarditis. She has 
received 21 days out of a prescribed 42-day course of intravenous oxacillin. Currently, she appears to be in mild 
distress. Temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse is 115/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 120/70 mm 
Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. Physical examination shows a diffuse 
maculopapular rash over the trunk and upper and lower extremities. There is no pus or erythema at the skin insertion 
site of the peripherally inserted central catheter line initially placed on the day of hospital discharge. Results of 
laboratory studies are shown: 
 
Hemoglobin 
11.1 g/dL 
Hematocrit 
33% 
Leukocyte count 
12,100/mm3 
 Segmented neutrophils 
78% 
 Eosinophils 
9% 
 Lymphocytes 
7% 
 Monocytes 
6% 
Platelet count 
341,000/mm3 
Serum 
  
 Na+ 
133 mEq/L 
 K+ 
6.5 mEq/L 
 Cl− 
100 mEq/L 
 HCO3− 
15 mEq/L 
 Urea nitrogen 
65 mg/dL 
 Glucose 
96 mg/dL 
 Creatinine 
5.7 mg/dL 
 
Urine microscopy shows eosinophils and WBC casts. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of 
this patient's condition?

o.B: Glomerular hypertrophy with hemorrhage and necrosis
o.D: Mesangial expansion with glomerular basement membrane thickening
o.E: Proximal tubular dilation with loss of brush border

e.correcta: This patient developed fever, rash, eosinophilia, and acute kidney injury with eosinophiluria and WBC casts about three weeks into oxacillin therapy — the classic picture of acute interstitial nephritis (AIN), a hypersensitivity reaction to the drug. Oxacillin (like other penicillins) acts as a hapten that binds renal tubular proteins, triggering a T-cell-mediated and IgE-mediated allergic reaction with an inflammatory infiltrate (often eosinophil-rich) in the renal interstitium, impairing tubular function and glomerular filtration without directly damaging the glomeruli themselves. Recognizing the triad of fever, rash, and eosinophilia after starting a new drug, along with WBC casts, should immediately suggest AIN.

incorrectas.A: Collapsing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is associated with HIV infection or certain drugs (e.g., interferon, bisphosphonates) and produces heavy proteinuria/nephrotic syndrome from podocyte injury, not the eosinophiluria and systemic hypersensitivity features seen here.
incorrectas.B: Glomerular hypertrophy with hemorrhage and necrosis describes a proliferative or crescentic glomerulonephritis (e.g., rapidly progressive GN), which would show red cell casts and dysmorphic RBCs on urinalysis rather than the eosinophils and WBC casts described in this patient.
incorrectas.D: Mesangial expansion with glomerular basement membrane thickening is characteristic of diabetic nephropathy, a chronic process unrelated to this patient's acute drug hypersensitivity reaction.
incorrectas.E: Proximal tubular dilation with loss of brush border describes acute tubular necrosis, typically from ischemia or nephrotoxins, which presents with muddy brown granular casts rather than the eosinophils and WBC casts pointing to an interstitial allergic process.

preguntas.q:
A 20-year-old woman is brought to the urgent care center because of a 2-month history of progressive weakness of 
her arms. She also has a 1-week history of moderate back pain and headache. Her only medication is ibuprofen as 
needed for pain. Muscle strength is 3/5 in the upper extremities. Sensation to pinprick is decreased over the upper 
extremities. MRI of the spine shows a central syrinx in the cervical spinal cord. It is most appropriate to obtain specific 
additional history regarding which of the following in this patient?

e.correcta: A central syrinx (syringomyelia) of the cervical spinal cord classically damages the crossing spinothalamic fibers near the central canal first (causing bilateral loss of pain/temperature sensation in a cape-like distribution) and can expand to affect the anterior horn cells, producing bilateral upper extremity weakness as seen here. Syringomyelia is strongly associated with prior trauma (post-traumatic syrinx) as well as Chiari I malformation, so asking specifically about a history of trauma (e.g., prior neck injury) is the most relevant additional history to obtain given this MRI finding. This is a key link tested on boards: syrinx formation following spinal cord trauma, often presenting months to years later with progressive weakness and dissociated sensory loss.

incorrectas.A: Dietary history would be relevant if a nutritional myelopathy (e.g., vitamin B12 deficiency causing subacute combined degeneration) were suspected, but that classically affects the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, not a central syrinx.
incorrectas.B: Family illness history would be pertinent for hereditary conditions, but syringomyelia is much more strongly linked to trauma or Chiari malformation than to a specific inherited pattern relevant here.
incorrectas.C: Recent travel history would be useful if an infectious or parainfectious myelopathy were suspected, but the MRI-confirmed central syrinx points toward a structural/traumatic etiology rather than an infectious one.
incorrectas.E: Unintended weight loss would raise concern for malignancy (e.g., an intramedullary tumor causing a syrinx secondarily), but trauma is the far more classic and testable association with syringomyelia, especially in a young patient without other red flags for cancer.

preguntas.q:
A 68-year-old man comes to the office because of a 6-month history of pain and cramping of his right and left lower 
legs. He says the pain is more severe with walking but improves with rest. He has a history of coronary artery disease, 
dyslipidemia, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus with nephropathy. Current medications are aspirin, insulin, 
lisinopril, metoprolol, and atorvastatin. Pulse is 65/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 145/82 mm Hg. 
Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Examination of the lower extremities shows little to no hair, 
atrophic skin, and feet that are cool to the touch. Posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses are absent bilaterally. Which 
of the following is the most likely mechanism causing this patient’s symptoms?

e.correcta: This patient has classic peripheral arterial disease presenting as intermittent claudication (leg pain with exertion relieved by rest) with signs of chronic ischemia (hair loss, atrophic skin, cool extremities, absent pulses) in the setting of multiple atherosclerotic risk factors (diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, coronary disease). The underlying mechanism is atherosclerosis — vascular obstruction caused by lipid-rich (atheromatous) plaques that progressively narrow the lumen of large and medium-sized arteries, reducing blood flow to exercising muscle beyond the point where the demand can be met, producing ischemic pain. This is the same basic pathophysiologic process underlying his coronary artery disease, reflecting the systemic nature of atherosclerosis.

incorrectas.A: Fibromuscular dysplasia is a non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory arteriopathy that typically affects renal and carotid arteries in younger women, causing a string-of-beads appearance on angiography, not lower extremity claudication in an elderly man with typical atherosclerotic risk factors.
incorrectas.B: Giant cell (temporal) arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis of medium and large arteries, classically affecting the temporal and ophthalmic arteries in older adults, causing headache and vision loss, not bilateral lower extremity claudication.
incorrectas.C: Hyaline arteriosclerosis affects small arterioles (typically from chronic hypertension or diabetes), producing luminal narrowing at the arteriolar level (contributing to nephrosclerosis) rather than the large/medium vessel plaque-driven obstruction causing claudication.
incorrectas.D: Segmental inflammation of medium-sized vessels describes vasculitides such as thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) or polyarteritis nodosa; Buerger disease occurs in young smokers and doesn't fit this older patient's classic atherosclerotic risk profile as well as plaque-driven PAD does.

preguntas.q:
A 58-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease comes to the clinic with his wife for a follow-up 
examination. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 35 years. He has tried to quit smoking twice but was 
unsuccessful both times. At today’s visit, when the physician asks the patient about smoking cessation, he says he is 
not ready to do so. The patient’s wife states her husband’s smoking makes her cough and gives her chest tightness. 
Which of the following is the most appropriate physician statement?

o.A: "Are there any reasons why you might want to quit smoking?"
o.B: "Are you aware that your lung condition is chronic at this point?"
o.C: "I'm sure you don't want your wife to suffer as a result of your smoking."
o.D: "The majority of your health issues would improve if you quit smoking."
o.E: "Why haven't you been able to stay off cigarettes?"

e.correcta: This patient is in the not-ready (precontemplation/contemplation) stage of the transtheoretical (stages of change) model, so the most effective communication technique is motivational interviewing — asking open-ended, non-judgmental questions that help the patient explore his own ambivalence and identify his own reasons for change, rather than the physician imposing reasons on him. Asking 'Are there any reasons why you might want to quit smoking?' respects patient autonomy, avoids confrontation, and elicits change talk from the patient himself, which is more likely to move him toward readiness to change than lecturing or guilt.

incorrectas.B: Asking if he's aware his condition is chronic is a closed, somewhat patronizing question that doesn't engage his own motivations and risks sounding didactic rather than exploratory, making it less effective at fostering genuine behavior change readiness.
incorrectas.C: Invoking guilt about his wife's suffering is a manipulative, shame-based tactic that violates patient-centered communication principles and is likely to provoke defensiveness rather than genuine motivation to quit.
incorrectas.D: Stating that his health would improve if he quit is physician-driven advice-giving rather than patient-centered exploration; in the precontemplation stage, this kind of directive statement tends to elicit resistance rather than engagement.
incorrectas.E: Asking why he hasn't been able to stay off cigarettes has a judgmental, blaming undertone (focusing on past failure) rather than exploring forward-looking motivation, and is more likely to make the patient defensive than to build rapport.

preguntas.q:
An 18-month-old girl is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. Her parents say that she has been 
healthy since her last visit at 15 months of age, and they have no specific concerns. Developmental milestones are 
appropriate for age. Her diet consists of two 8-ounce bottles of cow's milk-based formula and small amounts of table 
food. She has consistently been at the 25th percentile for length and weight for the first 12 months of age but is 
currently at the 25th percentile for length and below the 5th percentile for weight. Her mother is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) 
tall, and her father is 183 cm (6 ft) tall. The patient appears thin. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Which 
of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's growth pattern?

e.correcta: This toddler's growth pattern (weight percentile falling from 25th to below 5th while length remains at the 25th percentile) is the classic pattern of failure to thrive due to inadequate caloric intake — weight is affected before height in caloric insufficiency because the body preferentially maintains linear growth at the expense of weight gain when calories are insufficient. Her diet (excess milk, minimal solid table food) is a well-known cause of toddler undernutrition: excessive milk intake displaces more calorically and nutritionally dense solid foods and can also blunt appetite, leading to inadequate total caloric intake for growth.

incorrectas.A: Adrenal insufficiency would typically also impair linear growth over time and often presents with additional signs like hyperpigmentation, vomiting, or electrolyte disturbances (hyponatremia/hyperkalemia in primary insufficiency), none of which are present here.
incorrectas.C: Constitutional growth delay usually presents as short stature with delayed bone age in older children, with growth eventually catching up to genetic potential, not primarily as poor weight gain relative to preserved height in a toddler.
incorrectas.D: Familial short stature would produce proportionate short stature consistent with parental heights (which are not unusually short here, as both parents are average-to-tall) and would affect height, not cause an isolated drop in weight percentile.
incorrectas.E: Growth hormone deficiency classically causes a decline in linear growth (height) with relatively preserved weight, the opposite pattern from what is seen in this patient, who has preserved height but falling weight.

preguntas.q:
Investigators are planning to conduct a prospective cohort study to determine the association between dietary calcium 
consumption and the risk for osteoporosis. A total of 256 women aged 45 to 65 years will be enrolled. Bone mineral 
density will be measured with a DEXA scan. Participants will self-report their dietary calcium consumption with a 
food frequency questionnaire. After reviewing the initial draft of the questionnaire, the investigators notice that yogurt 
is missing from the list of items and add it to the list. Which of the following factors is most likely to be improved by 
including yogurt in the questionnaire?

e.correcta: The food frequency questionnaire is meant to measure participants' true dietary calcium intake, and yogurt is a significant dietary source of calcium; omitting it would systematically underestimate calcium consumption in yogurt eaters, introducing a measurement/misclassification bias that distorts the true association between calcium intake and osteoporosis risk. Adding yogurt improves the accuracy with which the exposure (dietary calcium) is measured, which improves internal validity — the degree to which the study accurately captures the true causal relationship between the exposure and outcome within the study population, free from bias and confounding.

incorrectas.B: Inter-rater reliability refers to the consistency of measurements between different observers/raters, which is not relevant here since this is a self-reported questionnaire completed by participants, not an assessment made by multiple raters.
incorrectas.C: Response rate refers to the proportion of enrolled subjects who actually complete and return the questionnaire; adding a food item to a questionnaire does not directly affect how many people choose to respond, only the accuracy of what they report.
incorrectas.D: Type I error is the probability of falsely rejecting a true null hypothesis (a false-positive finding), which relates to statistical significance thresholds (alpha) and sample size, not to how completely a questionnaire captures dietary exposure.

preguntas.q:
A 40-year-old woman comes to the office after a serum study of her donated blood showed positive results for 
Trypanosoma cruzi. She immigrated to the USA from El Salvador at the age of 20 years. She has no history of major 
medical illness, and she has no cardiac or gastrointestinal symptoms. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical 
examination shows no abnormalities. This patient most likely acquired the organism causing her condition via a bite 
from which of the following?

e.correcta: Trypanosoma cruzi, the causative agent of Chagas disease, is transmitted by the reduviid (kissing) bug, which deposits infected feces near a bite wound on the face during nighttime feeding; the parasite then enters through the wound or mucous membranes when the person scratches or rubs the area. This patient's history of asymptomatic infection found incidentally on blood donor screening, with an origin from El Salvador (an endemic region), is classic for chronic Chagas disease, which can remain silent for decades before potentially causing dilated cardiomyopathy, megacolon, or megaesophagus.

incorrectas.A: Bedbugs are blood-feeding insects that cause itchy bites but are not known vectors for Trypanosoma cruzi or any major systemic parasitic disease transmission in humans.
incorrectas.B: Black flies transmit Onchocerca volvulus, causing onchocerciasis (river blindness), a filarial disease with skin and eye manifestations, not Chagas disease.
incorrectas.C: Mosquitoes transmit organisms such as Plasmodium (malaria), Wuchereria bancrofti (filariasis), and various arboviruses, but not Trypanosoma cruzi.
incorrectas.E: Ticks transmit organisms like Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease), Rickettsia (Rocky Mountain spotted fever), Ehrlichia, and Babesia, but not Trypanosoma cruzi, which requires the reduviid bug vector.

preguntas.q:
A 40-year-old man comes to the office because of a 3-day history of lower abdominal pain. This is his third visit to 
the physician for similar symptoms during the past 6 months. Previous evaluations have been consistent with the 
diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome. He has been drinking herbal tea from his grandmother, which has not improved 
his pain. He does not believe in taking medication and has refused it at the previous visits. Examination discloses no 
abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate physician response?

o.A: "Help me to understand what you are hoping I can do for you today."
o.B: "I'd like to prescribe some medication if you'd reconsider your decision."
o.C: "I'm not sure why you keep coming to see me."
o.D: "Let's talk about the herbal tea you have been drinking."
o.E: "There is nothing I can do for you if you continue to refuse medication."

e.correcta: This patient has a chronic functional condition (IBS) and firm personal beliefs against medication, yet keeps returning for care — the most appropriate response is an open-ended, patient-centered question that explores his actual expectations and goals for the visit, since understanding what the patient truly wants (reassurance, validation, symptom relief through non-pharmacologic means, etc.) is essential before deciding how to proceed. This approach respects patient autonomy and avoids assuming the patient wants medication, while opening a dialogue that can guide a mutually acceptable management plan.

incorrectas.B: Offering to prescribe medication if he'd reconsider pressures the patient to change his stated values and ignores his autonomy, rather than first understanding what he actually wants from the visit.
incorrectas.C: Saying 'I'm not sure why you keep coming to see me' is dismissive and judgmental, damaging the physician-patient relationship rather than exploring the patient's underlying concerns or needs.
incorrectas.D: While the herbal tea use is worth exploring at some point for safety reasons, immediately steering the conversation there does not address the more fundamental need to first understand the patient's goals for this visit.
incorrectas.E: Telling the patient there's nothing that can be done unless he takes medication is an ultimatum that disregards patient autonomy and forecloses other potentially helpful non-pharmacologic interventions for IBS.

preguntas.q:
A 72-year-old man comes to the office because of a 2-month history of increased urinary frequency, frequent nighttime 
urination, and a slow urinary stream. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Temperature is 
37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 66/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 130/78 mm Hg. Physical examination 
shows no abnormalities. Digital rectal examination shows a diffusely enlarged, symmetric prostate gland without 
nodules or induration. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient has which of the following mechanisms 
of action?

e.correcta: This patient has benign prostatic hyperplasia (diffusely enlarged, smooth prostate causing obstructive urinary symptoms), for which first-line pharmacotherapy is an α1-adrenergic antagonist (e.g., tamsulosin, terazosin). These drugs block α1 receptors on prostatic smooth muscle and the bladder neck, causing relaxation of this smooth muscle and reducing the dynamic component of bladder outlet obstruction, thereby improving urinary flow and reducing symptoms like frequency, nocturia, and weak stream without affecting the size of the gland itself (unlike 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors, which shrink the gland).

incorrectas.A: α1-adrenergic agonism would contract prostatic and bladder neck smooth muscle, worsening rather than relieving obstructive urinary symptoms — this is the opposite of the desired therapeutic effect.
incorrectas.C: α2-adrenergic agonism (e.g., clonidine) is used for hypertension and other central sympatholytic effects, not for BPH; it does not address prostatic smooth muscle tone.
incorrectas.D: α2-adrenergic antagonism (e.g., mirtazapine's mechanism in part) is not a treatment strategy for BPH and would not relax prostatic/bladder neck smooth muscle.
incorrectas.E: β1-adrenergic agonism increases heart rate and contractility (used in cardiogenic shock or bradycardia), and has no meaningful role in relieving prostatic obstruction.
incorrectas.F: β1-adrenergic antagonism (e.g., metoprolol) is used for cardiac conditions like hypertension, arrhythmias, and heart failure, not for BPH, and does not relax prostatic smooth muscle.

preguntas.q:
A previously healthy 33-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by the Secret Service for stalking 
the president of the USA for 2 months. She claims to be married to the president's twin brother and states that the 
president just had his twin kidnapped to avoid competition. She speaks rapidly and is difficult to interrupt. Her 
associations are often loose. She says, "I haven't slept for days, but I won't even try to sleep until my husband is 
rescued. God has been instructing me to take over the White House. I can't wait to be reunited with my husband. I 
hear his voice telling me what to do." When asked about drug use, she says she uses only natural substances. She 
refuses to permit blood or urine tests, saying, "I don't have time to wait for the results." Which of the following is the 
most likely diagnosis?

o.A: Bipolar disorder, manic, with psychotic features
o.D: Psychotic disorder due to general medical condition

e.correcta: This patient shows a full manic episode: decreased need for sleep, pressured/rapid speech, flight of ideas (loose associations), grandiosity (belief she is married to the president's brother), and psychotic features (bizarre delusions of kidnapping and auditory hallucinations of God's voice), all occurring together rather than psychosis in isolation. When mood symptoms (mania) and psychotic features occur together and the mood disturbance is the predominant, organizing feature of the presentation, the diagnosis is bipolar disorder, manic episode, with psychotic features — the psychosis here is mood-congruent and occurs squarely within the manic syndrome (elevated mood, grandiosity, insomnia, pressured speech), not as an independent, persistent psychotic illness.

incorrectas.B: Brief psychotic disorder involves psychotic symptoms lasting less than one month with eventual full return to baseline functioning, and does not require or typically feature the pressured speech, decreased need for sleep, and grandiosity that define a manic episode as seen here.
incorrectas.C: Delusional disorder is characterized by one or more non-bizarre delusions lasting at least a month in the absence of other prominent mood or psychotic symptoms (no pressured speech, no decreased need for sleep, no hallucinations as a core feature) — this patient's presentation is far more elaborate and mood-driven than a pure delusional disorder.
incorrectas.D: Psychotic disorder due to a general medical condition requires an identifiable underlying medical cause (e.g., a brain tumor, endocrine disorder) that has not been established here; the constellation of manic symptoms strongly suggests a primary mood disorder rather than a secondary psychosis.
incorrectas.E: Schizophrenia requires at least 6 months of characteristic symptoms (with at least 1 month of active-phase psychotic symptoms) and a decline in function that is not primarily attributable to mood episodes; this patient's 2-month presentation is dominated by manic symptoms (insomnia, pressured speech, grandiosity), making a mood disorder with psychotic features more likely than schizophrenia.

preguntas.q:
A 63-year-old woman with a 2-year history of indigestion and heartburn volunteers for a research study in which a 
variety of drugs are administered and her gastric pH is measured. Which of the following sets of curves best represents 
the results in this patient after administration of cimetidine and omeprazole? 
 
 
Cimetidine 
Omeprazole

o.A: Cimetidine: curve A, Omeprazole: curve D
o.B: Cimetidine: curve B, Omeprazole: curve A
o.C: Cimetidine: curve B, Omeprazole: curve D
o.D: Cimetidine: curve C, Omeprazole: curve A
o.E: Cimetidine: curve C, Omeprazole: curve D
o.F: Cimetidine: curve D, Omeprazole: curve A

e.correcta: Cimetidine is an H2-receptor antagonist that reversibly blocks histamine-stimulated acid secretion from parietal cells, producing a moderate and relatively rapid but incomplete/reversible rise in gastric pH; omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor that irreversibly inhibits the H+/K+-ATPase, the final common pathway of acid secretion, producing a more profound and sustained increase in gastric pH than an H2 blocker. On a graph of pH over time, this translates to cimetidine showing a curve with a moderate pH rise (curve B) and omeprazole showing a curve with a higher, more sustained pH elevation (curve A), reflecting the PPI's greater potency in suppressing acid secretion via its irreversible blockade of the proton pump itself rather than just one of several stimulatory pathways.

incorrectas.A: Assigning omeprazole to curve D would reverse the expected potency relationship — since omeprazole blocks the final common pathway of acid secretion, it should produce a greater, more sustained pH rise than the H2 blocker, not the lesser response implied by curve D.
incorrectas.C: Pairing omeprazole with curve D similarly underestimates the PPI's potency; omeprazole's irreversible inhibition of the proton pump should produce the largest, most sustained pH elevation among the drugs tested, which curve D does not represent if it shows a smaller effect than cimetidine's curve.
incorrectas.D: Assigning cimetidine to curve C would misrepresent an H2 blocker's typical acid-suppressing profile as either too weak or too strong relative to omeprazole's proton pump blockade, inconsistent with H2 antagonists' intermediate potency.
incorrectas.E: This combination places cimetidine on curve C and omeprazole on curve D, which fails to reflect that omeprazole (irreversible H+/K+-ATPase inhibition) should produce a greater and more sustained acid suppression (higher pH) than cimetidine (reversible H2 blockade).
incorrectas.F: Assigning cimetidine to curve D and omeprazole to curve A inappropriately gives cimetidine the more extreme curve; H2 blockers like cimetidine produce a more modest, shorter-acting rise in gastric pH than proton pump inhibitors, which should show the strongest, most sustained effect.

preguntas.q:
A 65-year-old woman comes to the office for a follow-up examination 1 year after she underwent operative resection 
of the right colon and chemotherapy for stage III colon cancer. She reports fatigue. Physical examination shows no 
abnormalities. A staging CT scan of the chest and abdomen shows five new 2- to 3-cm masses in the liver and both 
lungs. This patient's cancer most likely spread to the lungs via which of the following structures?

e.correcta: Venous drainage of the colon flows through the portal venous system to the liver first (explaining hepatic metastases), but the systemic route to the lungs is via the hepatic veins draining into the inferior vena cava, which then carries blood to the right heart and out through the pulmonary arteries to the lungs. This two-step seeding pattern — colon to liver via portal vein, then liver to lungs via hepatic veins/IVC/right heart — explains why colorectal cancer classically metastasizes first to the liver and subsequently to the lungs, as seen in this patient with both new liver and lung masses.

incorrectas.A: The inferior mesenteric vein drains the descending colon, sigmoid colon, and rectum into the splenic vein and then the portal system, directing blood toward the liver, not directly toward the lungs.
incorrectas.C: The left colic vein is a tributary of the inferior mesenteric vein, draining the descending colon into the portal venous system toward the liver, not providing a direct route to the lungs.
incorrectas.D: The middle colic artery is an arterial branch of the superior mesenteric artery supplying the transverse colon; arteries carry blood to tissues, not tumor emboli away from the tumor toward metastatic sites, so it is not a route of venous spread.
incorrectas.E: The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium; it would only be relevant after tumor cells have already reached the lung via the pulmonary artery, not as the route by which cancer initially spreads to the lungs.
incorrectas.F: The superior mesenteric artery supplies arterial blood to the midgut structures including part of the colon; like other arteries, it does not serve as a route for venous metastatic spread to the liver or lungs.
incorrectas.G: The superior vena cava drains blood from the head, neck, and upper extremities into the right atrium and is not part of the venous drainage pathway from the colon, which drains via the portal system and IVC instead.

preguntas.q:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because of a 3-week history of progressively severe itching 
of his hands and inner thighs. Physical examination shows multiple short, thin, elevated serpiginous tracks in the 
superficial epidermis over the axillae, in the webbed spaces between the digits, encircling the waist, and over the inner 
thighs. Small vesicles are seen at the ends of some of these tracks. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

e.correcta: The description of intensely pruritic, thin, elevated, serpiginous (snake-like) burrows in the web spaces of the fingers, axillae, waistline, and inner thighs, with small vesicles at the ends of the tracks, is the classic presentation of scabies, caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei. The female mite burrows into the stratum corneum to lay eggs, and the intense itching results from a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to the mite, its eggs, and fecal matter (scybala) within the skin — the burrows themselves are the visible tunnels the mite creates as it moves through the epidermis, which is why they appear as thin serpiginous tracks rather than discrete lesions.

incorrectas.A: Chickenpox (varicella) presents with pruritic vesicles in various stages (papules, vesicles, crusts) scattered diffusely over the trunk and face, described as dew drops on a rose petal, not as serpiginous burrows confined to web spaces and flexural areas.
incorrectas.B: Ehrlichiosis is a tick-borne bacterial infection causing fever, headache, and myalgias with possible rash, but it does not produce the characteristic burrow tracks seen with a mite infestation.
incorrectas.C: Lyme disease classically presents with erythema migrans, an expanding annular target-like rash at the tick bite site, which is distinct from the multiple thin serpiginous burrows of scabies.
incorrectas.D: Pediculosis (lice infestation) causes itching and visible nits/lice typically on the scalp, body, or pubic area, but does not create the burrow-like serpiginous tracks characteristic of a burrowing mite.

preguntas.q:
An 18-year-old woman with sickle cell disease is brought to the emergency department by her parents because of a 2-
hour history of severe abdominal pain and nausea. Her parents say that she had a cheeseburger, milk shake, and 
chocolate bar for lunch. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Physical examination shows tenderness over the right upper 
quadrant of the abdomen, radiating to the right shoulder. Ultrasonography of the right upper quadrant of the abdomen 
shows gallstones. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's current condition?

o.C: High ratio of cholesterol to bile acids in bile

e.correcta: In sickle cell disease, chronic hemolysis leads to persistently elevated levels of unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin, which is conjugated by the liver and excreted in bile at rates that exceed the solubility of bilirubin in bile, promoting the formation of pigmented (calcium bilirubinate) gallstones. This patient's right upper quadrant pain radiating to the shoulder with ultrasound-confirmed gallstones reflects biliary colic/cholecystitis from these bilirubin stones, a well-known complication of chronic hemolytic anemias like sickle cell disease, distinguishing them from the cholesterol stones typically associated with fatty meals in patients without hemolysis.

incorrectas.A: Decreased hepatic secretion of lecithin would favor cholesterol gallstone formation by altering the bile's ability to keep cholesterol solubilized, which is the mechanism behind cholesterol stones (associated with obesity, rapid weight loss, or fibrates), not the pigmented stones typical of sickle cell hemolysis.
incorrectas.B: Decreased reabsorption of bile salts (e.g., from ileal disease like Crohn's) increases cholesterol saturation in bile and promotes cholesterol gallstones, which is a different mechanism from the hemolysis-driven pigment stones expected in this sickle cell patient.
incorrectas.C: A high ratio of cholesterol to bile acids/lecithin in bile is the classic mechanism of cholesterol gallstones (seen with obesity, oral contraceptives, or rapid weight loss), not the bilirubin-driven pigment stones associated with chronic hemolysis in sickle cell disease.
incorrectas.D: Parasitic infestation with organisms secreting β-glucuronidase (e.g., Clonorchis sinensis, Ascaris) deconjugates bilirubin in bile, promoting pigment stone formation in a manner similar to hemolysis but through a distinct infectious mechanism — this patient's presentation is explained by her underlying sickle cell hemolysis, not parasitic infection.

preguntas.q:
A 34-year-old man comes to the office because of a 1-month history of diarrhea. He has a history of 
pheochromocytoma treated 2 years ago. His mother is being treated for a tumor of her parathyroid gland. He has no 
other history of major medical illness and takes no medications. His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 84/min, 
respirations are 10/min, and blood pressure is 120/75 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation 
of 97%. Physical examination shows a 3-cm, palpable mass on the right side of the neck. A biopsy specimen of the 
mass shows a neuroendocrine neoplasm of parafollicular cell origin. The most likely cause of the findings in this 
patient is a mutation in which of the following types of genes?

e.correcta: The combination of prior pheochromocytoma, a family history of parathyroid tumor, and a neuroendocrine neoplasm of parafollicular (C) cells (medullary thyroid carcinoma) is classic for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2), which is caused by a germline gain-of-function mutation in the RET proto-oncogene. Proto-oncogenes normally promote controlled cell growth and differentiation; when mutated to become constitutively active oncogenes (as with RET in MEN2), they drive unchecked proliferation of specific endocrine cell lineages, explaining the multifocal, multi-organ pattern of endocrine tumors seen in this syndrome (medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and parathyroid hyperplasia/adenoma).

incorrectas.A: Mutations in cell cycle regulation genes (e.g., cyclins, CDKs) contribute broadly to cancer by disrupting checkpoints, but the specific hereditary multi-endocrine tumor pattern in this patient (pheochromocytoma, medullary thyroid cancer, parathyroid tumor) is specifically linked to the RET proto-oncogene, not a general cell cycle regulator.
incorrectas.B: DNA mismatch repair gene mutations cause microsatellite instability and are implicated in Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer), not in the MEN2 endocrine tumor spectrum described here.
incorrectas.C: Metastasis suppressor genes (e.g., NM23) function to limit the ability of tumor cells to metastasize; their loss promotes spread of an already-formed cancer, but they are not the driving mutation behind the multiple endocrine neoplasms in MEN2.
incorrectas.E: Tumor suppressor genes (e.g., RB, TP53, MEN1) require loss-of-function of both alleles to promote tumorigenesis (as in MEN1, which causes parathyroid, pancreatic, and pituitary tumors), but the classic pattern here — pheochromocytoma plus medullary thyroid carcinoma — points to a gain-of-function RET proto-oncogene mutation (MEN2), not a tumor suppressor loss.

preguntas.q:
A 6-year-old girl is brought to the office because of two episodes of vaginal bleeding during the past 2 months. She 
has no history of serious illness and receives no medications. She does not appear to be in distress. She is at the 60th 
percentile for height, 40th percentile for weight, and 35th percentile for BMI. Vital signs are within normal limits. 
Physical examination discloses palpable breast buds and minimal coarse, pigmented hair on the labia. The remainder 
of the examination shows no abnormalities. Results of serum studies are shown: 
 
Thyroid-stimulating hormone 
2.1 mU/mL (N=0.5–5.0) 
Testosterone 
680 ng/dL (N=0.17–0.7) 
Adrenocorticotropic hormone 
18 pg/mL (N=9–52) 
Estradiol 
185 pg/mL (N<20) 
Follicle-stimulating hormone 
15 mIU/mL (N<6.7) 
Luteinizing hormone 
3.0 mIU/mL (N<0.2) 
 
    Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

e.correcta: This 6-year-old girl has precocious puberty with elevated FSH, LH, and estradiol, indicating that the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis has been prematurely activated (central/gonadotropin-dependent precocious puberty) — the elevated gonadotropins (FSH and LH) confirm the pituitary is appropriately driving gonadal estrogen production, meaning the underlying problem is early central activation of GnRH-secreting neurons in the hypothalamus. This central activation prematurely turns on the normal pubertal cascade (GnRH to LH/FSH to estradiol), leading to breast development and other secondary sexual characteristics far earlier than normal, and is the most common cause of precocious puberty in girls, often idiopathic.

incorrectas.B: Ectopic prolactin secretion would elevate prolactin levels and could disrupt normal menstrual/pubertal function by suppressing GnRH, but it does not explain this patient's elevated FSH, LH, and estradiol, which instead indicate a fully activated, appropriately functioning gonadotropin axis.
incorrectas.C: Exogenous sex steroid exposure (e.g., accidental estrogen cream exposure) would raise estradiol but should suppress endogenous FSH and LH via negative feedback, which contradicts this patient's elevated gonadotropins that indicate a centrally driven (GnRH-dependent) process.
incorrectas.D: A germline GNAS activating mutation causes McCune-Albright syndrome, a cause of peripheral (gonadotropin-independent) precocious puberty with autonomous ovarian estrogen production; this typically presents with low/suppressed FSH and LH (due to negative feedback) rather than the elevated gonadotropins seen in this patient.
incorrectas.E: 21-hydroxylase deficiency (congenital adrenal hyperplasia) causes virilization from excess androgens with low cortisol and salt-wasting in severe forms, and would not produce this pattern of elevated FSH, LH, and estradiol with breast development, which points to true central precocious puberty rather than an adrenal source of androgens.

    Question: Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?

o.B: Hypoplasia of hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons
o.C: Inactivating mutation of the follicle-stimulating hormone-receptor
o.E: Nondisjunction of X chromosome during meiosis

e.correcta: This patient has delayed puberty with small testes, low testosterone, and markedly elevated FSH and LH — a hypergonadotropic hypogonadism pattern indicating primary testicular failure rather than a central (hypothalamic-pituitary) problem. Combined with tall stature, long extremities, gynecomastia, and small firm testes, this is the classic phenotype of Klinefelter syndrome, caused by nondisjunction during meiosis producing a 47,XXY karyotype. The extra X chromosome causes seminiferous tubule dysgenesis and hyalinization, leading to low inhibin B and testosterone, which removes negative feedback on the pituitary and drives FSH and LH up.

incorrectas.A: Constitutional delay of puberty is a diagnosis of exclusion in a systemically healthy, often short-for-age child with delayed bone age but eventually normal pubertal progression and normal gonadotropins for the pre-pubertal stage; it does not produce elevated FSH/LH or the tall, eunuchoid body habitus with gynecomastia seen here, which instead points to primary gonadal failure.
incorrectas.B: Hypoplasia of GnRH neurons (as in Kallmann syndrome) causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, with LOW or inappropriately normal FSH/LH in the setting of low testosterone, often accompanied by anosmia; this patient's FSH and LH are markedly elevated, which is the opposite pattern and points to gonadal, not hypothalamic, failure.
incorrectas.C: An inactivating mutation of the FSH receptor would impair spermatogenesis and lower inhibin, but it would not produce the characteristic tall stature, long extremities, and gynecomastia phenotype, and total testosterone (driven mainly by LH acting on Leydig cells) would typically be less severely reduced.
incorrectas.D: 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which in a genetic male typically causes precocious puberty/virilization (or salt-wasting in infancy) from excess adrenal androgens, not delayed puberty with small testes and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.

preguntas.q:
A newborn delivered at 36 weeks' gestation to a 22-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, has difficulty feeding and 
listlessness. The mother received no prenatal care. Spontaneous vaginal delivery was uncomplicated. The mother's 
only medication was a prenatal vitamin. The newborn's length is 49 cm (19 in; 39th percentile), and weight is 3100 g 
(6 lb 13 oz; 30th percentile); head circumference is 33 cm (13 in; 12th percentile). Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), 
pulse is 134/min, respirations are 38/min, and blood pressure is 73/50 mm Hg. Physical examination shows ambiguous 
genitalia. Results of serum studies are shown: 
 
Na+ 
 133 mEq/L 
K+ 
 5.0 mEq/L (N=3.2–5.5) 
Cl– 
 103 mEq/L 
HCO3– 
 17 mEq/L 
Glucose 
 42 mg/dL (N=30–60) 
 
    The most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient targets which of the following receptors?

e.correcta: This newborn has ambiguous genitalia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and a low-ish glucose without prenatal care — classic for salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia (most commonly 21-hydroxylase deficiency), where impaired cortisol and aldosterone synthesis causes shunting of precursors toward androgen production (virilizing a genetic female) and loss of aldosterone's mineralocorticoid effect on the renal distal tubule/collecting duct. Emergency treatment requires immediate mineralocorticoid replacement (fludrocortisone) acting on the aldosterone receptor to restore sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion, alongside stress-dose glucocorticoids and IV fluids/glucose/saline for the acute salt-wasting crisis.

incorrectas.A: ACTH receptor agonism would not address this infant's electrolyte crisis; the problem here is a lack of aldosterone action at the mineralocorticoid receptor, not a deficiency of ACTH signaling, and glucocorticoid replacement (not an ACTH-receptor drug) is what's used to suppress the abnormal ACTH-driven androgen overproduction.
incorrectas.C: The androgen receptor is responsible for the virilization seen in this disorder, but blocking or targeting it does not treat the life-threatening salt-wasting crisis (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension), which is the acute pharmacologic priority.
incorrectas.D: GnRH receptor–targeted therapy is used for central precocious puberty or gonadotropin suppression, which is irrelevant to a neonate in an acute adrenal/salt-wasting crisis from CAH.
incorrectas.E: Growth hormone receptor agonism has no role in treating CAH; growth abnormalities are not the acute concern, and this newborn's presentation is dominated by the mineralocorticoid deficiency, not growth hormone axis dysfunction.

preguntas.q:
A 59-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease comes to the office for a follow-up 
examination. His renal function has gradually deteriorated despite aggressive management. He appears chronically ill. 
Serum studies show a urea nitrogen concentration of 65 mg/dL and creatinine concentration of 4.2 mg/dL. The 
development of which of the following in this patient would most likely necessitate immediate hemodialysis?

e.correcta: Uremic pericarditis, manifesting as a pericardial friction rub, is one of the classic absolute indications for emergent/urgent hemodialysis (along with severe/refractory hyperkalemia, volume overload unresponsive to diuretics, severe metabolic acidosis, and uremic encephalopathy) because it signals that accumulated uremic toxins are directly injuring the pericardium, and it carries a real risk of progressing to hemorrhagic pericardial effusion and tamponade. The mnemonic AEIOU (Acidosis, Electrolyte abnormalities, Ingestions, volume Overload, Uremic symptoms like pericarditis/encephalopathy) captures this: pericarditis is a manifestation of uremia itself, not just a comorbidity, and dialysis is needed urgently to clear the offending solutes.

incorrectas.A: Anemia of chronic kidney disease results from reduced erythropoietin production and is managed with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents and iron, not with emergent dialysis — it's a chronic, correctable problem rather than an acute life-threatening indication.
incorrectas.B: Moderate pedal edema reflects volume overload but by itself (in the absence of refractory overload causing pulmonary edema or hemodynamic compromise) is managed with diuretics and salt restriction rather than triggering emergent dialysis.
incorrectas.D: Hypertension in CKD, even if difficult to control, is managed with escalating antihypertensive regimens; it becomes a dialysis trigger only when it reflects severe volume overload refractory to medical therapy, not simply from being poorly controlled.
incorrectas.E: Hypoglycemia in advanced CKD occurs because the kidney's contribution to insulin clearance and gluconeogenesis is reduced, prolonging insulin's effect; this is managed by adjusting diabetes medications/dosing, not by initiating hemodialysis.

preguntas.q:
A 65-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 10-minute history of chest tightness and 
severe pain of her left arm. Physical examination shows jugular venous distention. Crackles are heard over the lung 
fields. An ECG shows ST-segment elevation greater than 1 mm in leads V4 through V6 and new Q waves. Serum 
studies show an increased troponin I concentration. Which of the following labeled points in the graph best represents 
the changes in cardiac function that occurred during the first 10 seconds after the onset of pain in this patient?

e.correcta: This patient is having an acute ST-elevation MI with signs of acute left heart failure (JVD, crackles) from sudden loss of contractile function in the infarcted myocardium. On a pressure-volume loop, acute ischemia causes a sudden drop in stroke volume and a rise in end-systolic volume because the ventricle can no longer eject normally against the same afterload — this shifts the loop from a normal point (W) to a smaller, more rightward loop with a decreased ejection fraction and elevated filling pressures (point Z), reflecting the immediate loss of contractility (decreased ESPVR slope) within seconds of coronary occlusion. This acute change precedes any compensatory chamber remodeling and is purely a contractility/loading consequence of the infarct.

incorrectas.A: A W→X transition suggests a different, non-ischemic loop change (such as isolated preload/afterload alteration without loss of contractility) rather than the abrupt fall in contractile performance and rise in end-systolic volume expected within seconds of acute infarction.
incorrectas.B: A W→Y shift does not capture the acute reduction in ejection and stroke volume with increased residual ventricular volume characteristic of sudden loss of a large segment of contracting myocardium in STEMI.
incorrectas.D: X→W implies a starting point that is not the patient's baseline (W) before the ischemic insult, so this does not correctly represent the sequence of hemodynamic change caused by the new infarct.
incorrectas.E: X→Y likewise starts from the wrong baseline point and describes a different loop transition, not the specific combination of decreased contractility and increased end-systolic volume from acute infarction beginning at the pre-MI baseline loop (W).
incorrectas.F: X→Z, while ending at the correct low-function loop, again starts from an incorrect baseline (X rather than W), misrepresenting the patient's condition immediately before the onset of pain.
incorrectas.G: Z→W reverses the actual direction of change; the patient is moving from normal function toward impaired function as the infarct evolves, not recovering from Z back to a normal loop W within the first 10 seconds.

preguntas.q:
A 66-year-old man who was recently diagnosed with Parkinson disease comes to the physician for a follow-up 
examination. Carbidopa-levodopa therapy was initiated at the time of diagnosis. The patient tells the physician that he 
still has episodes during which he "freezes." He has a clumsy gait, and there is rigidity of his upper extremities and 
hands. An adjunct therapy designed to inhibit which of the following enzymes is most likely indicated in this patient?

e.correcta: This patient with Parkinson disease has persistent "off" symptoms (freezing, rigidity, clumsy gait) despite carbidopa-levodopa, indicating that dopamine levels in the striatum are still inadequate — an appropriate adjunct is a monoamine oxidase type B (MAO-B) inhibitor such as selegiline or rasagiline, which selectively blocks the enzyme that breaks down dopamine within the CNS, prolonging the action of endogenous and levodopa-derived dopamine and smoothing out motor fluctuations. Because MAO-B is the isoform predominantly responsible for dopamine (rather than norepinephrine/serotonin) metabolism in the brain, these agents provide an extra boost of dopaminergic tone without the tyramine-related pressor crisis risk that follows nonselective MAO inhibition.

incorrectas.A: Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase is the enzyme that converts levodopa into dopamine, and inhibiting it (which is exactly what carbidopa already does peripherally) would reduce, not enhance, the amount of dopamine reaching the brain if it acted centrally — this is not the therapeutic strategy for residual symptoms here.
incorrectas.B: Dopamine β-hydroxylase converts dopamine to norepinephrine in noradrenergic neurons; inhibiting it would not increase striatal dopamine levels and is not part of standard Parkinson disease adjunct therapy.
incorrectas.D: Phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase converts norepinephrine to epinephrine mainly in the adrenal medulla and has nothing to do with striatal dopamine availability or Parkinson symptom control.
incorrectas.E: Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis (tyrosine to L-DOPA); inhibiting it would decrease dopamine production, which is the opposite of what is needed to improve this patient's motor symptoms.

preguntas.q:
A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department via ambulance 15 minutes after he sustained a gunshot 
wound to his back during a robbery. On arrival, he is conscious but appears confused. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), 
pulse is 120/min and weak, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 110/50 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air 
shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. Physical examination shows pale, cold, clammy skin and a single bullet entry 
wound in the posterior 10th intercostal space on the left side. Abdominal CT scan is shown. The bullet is most likely 
lodged in which of the following structures in this patient?

e.correcta: A posterior entry wound at the left 10th intercostal space tracks through a region where the spleen is the most anatomically exposed solid organ, sitting posterolaterally in the left upper quadrant under ribs 9-11, making it highly vulnerable to penetrating trauma at this level. The patient's tachycardia, weak pulse, and pale, cold, clammy skin reflect hemorrhagic shock from a lacerated, highly vascular spleen, which is the most commonly injured intra-abdominal organ in left-sided lower rib penetrating trauma and can bleed briskly given its rich blood supply from the splenic artery.

incorrectas.A: The adrenal gland is a small, retroperitoneal, deeply placed structure that is a far less likely target for a bullet at this trajectory and would not typically produce this degree of hemorrhagic shock if injured alone.
incorrectas.B: The colon (splenic flexure region) could be in the path but colonic injury more typically presents with peritonitis, free air, or fecal contamination signs over time rather than immediate hemorrhagic shock from a solid, vascular organ.
incorrectas.C: The left kidney is more posterior and retroperitoneal; while renal injury is possible with flank trauma, the given trajectory and clinical picture of rapid hemorrhagic shock is more classically produced by splenic injury, and the CT scan findings described point to the spleen.
incorrectas.D: The lung bases can extend low posteriorly, but a wound at the 10th intercostal space is below the typical costophrenic reflection at rest, and the vignette does not describe respiratory findings (like hemothorax or dyspnea) that would suggest a pulmonary injury as the primary lodging site.

preguntas.q:
A 33-year-old man is transferred to the emergency department from an inpatient psychiatric facility because of a 3-
hour history of fever preceded by a 1-day history of confusion and agitation. The patient was admitted to the 
psychiatric facility 5 days ago because of hallucinations and strange behavior. On admission, olanzapine and 
clonazepam therapy were initiated, and the patient's condition initially had been improving. Medical history otherwise 
is unremarkable, and the patient took no medications prior to admission to the psychiatric facility. He has smoked one 
pack of cigarettes daily for 15 years. He typically drank one to two beers daily prior to his psychiatric admission. He 
uses no other substances. He is unemployed. He is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and weighs 83 kg (183 lb); BMI is 27 kg/m2. 
Temperature is 40.3°C (104.5°F), pulse is 127/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 176/109 mm Hg. 
Oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Physical examination of this patient is most likely to show which of the 
following?

e.correcta: This patient on olanzapine (an antipsychotic) develops fever, confusion/agitation, and (as the exam would show) muscle rigidity — the classic triad pointing to neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), caused by dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the nigrostriatal and hypothalamic pathways. The resulting profound dopamine blockade produces "lead-pipe" muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension as seen here), and altered mental status, and it is a medical emergency requiring drug discontinuation, cooling, and dantrolene or bromocriptine.

incorrectas.A: Hyperreflexia is more characteristic of serotonin syndrome (from serotonergic drugs, not typically olanzapine) or conditions with increased neuromuscular excitability; NMS classically produces decreased reflexes with rigidity rather than hyperreflexia, helping distinguish it from serotonin syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Mydriasis is typically seen with sympathomimetic or anticholinergic toxicity/serotonin syndrome, not with antipsychotic-induced NMS, which more classically features normal or reactive pupils alongside rigidity and hyperthermia.
incorrectas.D: A petechial rash would suggest an infectious or hematologic process (such as meningococcemia or a bleeding diathesis), which does not fit the clinical context of a recent antipsychotic start with fever, confusion, and expected rigidity.
incorrectas.E: Unilateral hemiparesis would suggest a focal neurologic lesion like stroke, which does not explain the diffuse, symmetric, drug-induced syndrome of fever and rigidity following antipsychotic initiation.

preguntas.q:
A 68-year-old man with alcohol use disorder comes to the office because of a 3-month history of intermittent blood 
in his urine; he has had no pain. He is a retired laboratory technician from a company that produces naphthylamine. 
He has smoked 1½ packs of cigarettes daily for 45 years. A CT scan of the abdomen shows a mass in the pelvis of the 
left kidney. A photograph of the surgically resected kidney is shown. The neoplastic process in this kidney is most 
likely to be which of the following?

e.correcta: Occupational exposure to naphthylamine (an aromatic amine) and heavy cigarette smoking are classic risk factors for urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma, which arises from the urothelium lining the renal pelvis, ureters, and bladder — these carcinogens are metabolized to reactive intermediates that are concentrated in urine and cause DNA damage to the transitional epithelium. A mass centered in the renal pelvis (rather than the renal parenchyma/cortex) with this risk factor profile is the textbook presentation of urothelial carcinoma, distinguishing it from renal cell carcinoma, which arises from proximal tubular epithelium and is not linked to aromatic amine exposure.

incorrectas.A: Angiomyolipoma is a benign tumor composed of blood vessels, smooth muscle, and fat, classically associated with tuberous sclerosis, and it does not arise from urothelium or have a link to naphthylamine/smoking exposure.
incorrectas.B: Metastatic melanoma to the kidney would show a different clinical context (known primary skin melanoma) and typically produces multiple parenchymal deposits rather than a pelvis-centered mass tied to occupational carcinogen exposure.
incorrectas.C: Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) is a pediatric renal parenchymal tumor arising from nephrogenic blastemal cells; it is not a disease of older adults with carcinogen exposure and does not arise from the renal pelvis.
incorrectas.D: Oncocytoma is a benign tumor of the renal cortex/tubular epithelium (eosinophilic cells packed with mitochondria) and has no established link to naphthylamine exposure or a renal pelvis location.

preguntas.q:
A 37-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of a 3-year history of facial redness that intermittently expands in 
surface area, intensifies in color, and feels warm. She says the rash also sometimes causes a burning sensation. These 
symptoms occur approximately once monthly and are precipitated by stress. She has treated the rash with an over-the-
counter hydrocortisone cream, but she is unsure of whether the cream provided any symptom relief. She previously 
did not seek medical attention for the symptoms because she assumed the condition would resolve spontaneously. 
Medical history is remarkable for type 1 diabetes mellitus. Her only routine medication is insulin administered via 
pump for the past 5 years. She has no known drug allergies. She drinks three glasses of red wine weekly; she does not 
smoke cigarettes or use any other substances. She is 162 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 61 kg (134 lb); BMI is 23 
kg/m2. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination of the skin discloses the findings shown. The remainder of 
the physical examination discloses no abnormalities. At this time, it is most appropriate to obtain specific additional 
history regarding which of the following?

o.A: Effect of alcohol on the condition
o.D: Numbness of the fingers and toes

e.correcta: This patient's recurrent facial flushing and erythema triggered by stress, with a burning sensation, is characteristic of rosacea, and alcohol (a classic vasodilating trigger) is one of the most common precipitants of flare-ups along with heat, spicy food, and emotional stress. Asking specifically about alcohol's effect on her symptoms helps confirm the diagnosis and identify a modifiable trigger she can avoid, since rosacea is fundamentally a disorder of exaggerated cutaneous vascular reactivity rather than a fixed structural lesion.

incorrectas.B: Excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis) is more relevant to conditions like pheochromocytoma or menopausal hot flashes, not the recurrent, stress-triggered facial erythema described, which fits rosacea rather than a hyperadrenergic or hyperhidrotic disorder.
incorrectas.C: Family history of adenomas would be pertinent if considering something like multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes, but the localized, episodic facial flushing pattern described here is classic rosacea, not a paraneoplastic or endocrine tumor syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Numbness of the fingers and toes would suggest a vasospastic process like Raynaud phenomenon or a peripheral neuropathy, which does not fit a facial-only, stress/wine-triggered erythematous rash.
incorrectas.E: Poor wound healing would raise concern for something like Cushing syndrome or diabetes-related skin fragility, but this patient's issue is episodic vascular flushing, not impaired healing, so this line of questioning does not address her presenting complaint.

preguntas.q:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother for an examination prior to attending kindergarten. The mother 
reports no concerns. The child's medical history is noncontributory. At all previous examinations, the mother declined 
all recommended vaccinations for her daughter, saying that she is concerned that vaccines could harm her daughter. 
Physical examination today shows no abnormalities. The mother continues to decline all recommended vaccinations 
today, saying that her daughter has never had a vaccine-preventable illness. Which of the following is the most likely 
explanation for this patient's history of good health?

e.correcta: Herd immunity occurs when a sufficiently high proportion of the surrounding population is immune (via vaccination or prior infection) that transmission chains are interrupted, indirectly protecting unvaccinated individuals like this child from exposure to vaccine-preventable pathogens. This explains why an unvaccinated child can remain healthy despite lacking individual immunity — she is being shielded by the immunity of those around her, not by any innate advantage of her own, which is exactly the phenomenon anti-vaccine reasoning tends to overlook (and why declining vaccination is a free-rider risk to the whole community).

incorrectas.A: Community eradication (complete elimination of a disease, like smallpox globally or polio in most regions) is a much stronger and rarer condition than herd immunity; most vaccine-preventable diseases in this community are merely suppressed by high vaccination rates, not eradicated, so this overstates what is actually happening.
incorrectas.C: Maternal antibodies transferred transplacentally and via breastfeeding wane within the first year of life and would not still be conferring protection in a 5-year-old, so this cannot explain her continued good health at this age.
incorrectas.D: A "normal immune system" is true of most children but is not suffient by itself to prevent infection with pathogens like measles or pertussis without prior immunization or passive protection from herd effects — an unvaccinated, immunologically normal child is still fully susceptible on an individual level.
incorrectas.E: Underdiagnosis would require that the child actually contracted vaccine-preventable illnesses that went unrecognized, but the vignette states she has never had such an illness, making underdiagnosis an unsupported explanation compared to the straightforward herd immunity effect.

preguntas.q:
A 28-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, comes to the office after a home pregnancy test result was positive. Her last 
menstrual period was 12 weeks ago. Laboratory studies performed during her first pregnancy showed that she is blood 
group A, Rh-negative. Her husband is blood group A, Rh-positive. Their first child, a girl, was delivered via 
spontaneous vaginal delivery. Laboratory studies performed after delivery showed an indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) 
titer of 1:32. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 68/min, respirations are 15/min, and blood pressure is 120/75 
mm Hg. Physical examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 12-week gestation. A urine pregnancy test 
result is positive. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy to prevent complications in the newborn has which of the 
following mechanisms of action?

o.A: Binding to the D antigen on fetal erythrocytes
o.B: Blockade of complement binding to fetal erythrocytes
o.C: Induction of class switching by maternal B lymphocytes
o.D: Inhibition of production of fetal blood group A erythrocytes
o.E: Prevention of fetal erythrocytes from entering maternal blood circulation

e.correcta: This Rh-negative mother has an elevated anti-D antibody titer (1:32) already present before this pregnancy, meaning she is already alloimmunized against the D antigen — importantly, this changes management (RhoGAM works prophylactically before sensitization occurs, so an existing high titer actually indicates Rh immune globulin will not prevent hemolytic disease in this ongoing pregnancy, but conceptually the drug's mechanism is still binding to the D antigen on any fetal Rh-positive erythrocytes that enter maternal circulation). Anti-D immune globulin works by opsonizing and clearing fetal Rh-positive RBCs from maternal circulation before the mother's own immune system recognizes the D antigen and mounts a primary antibody (and memory B-cell) response, thereby preventing sensitization in an as-yet-unsensitized woman.

incorrectas.B: Anti-D immune globulin's action is not through blocking complement binding — it works upstream by clearing fetal D-positive cells or masking the D antigen from maternal B cells before an immune response is initiated, not by interfering with complement-antibody interactions.
incorrectas.C: RhoGAM does not induce class switching; rather, it aims to prevent the maternal immune system from ever generating antibodies against the D antigen in the first place, avoiding the entire humoral response including class switching.
incorrectas.D: The concern in Rh alloimmunization is blood group D (Rh) incompatibility, not ABO blood group A production; inhibiting fetal blood group A antigen production is not a real or relevant mechanism, since ABO incompatibility is a distinct (and usually much milder) process from Rh disease.
incorrectas.E: RhoGAM does not physically block fetal cells from crossing into maternal circulation (fetomaternal hemorrhage still occurs); instead it neutralizes/clears the fetal Rh-positive cells that do cross before they trigger a maternal antibody response.

preguntas.q:
A 40-year-old man comes to the office because of a 1-day history of severe pain in his right great toe. He has not 
sustained any trauma to the area. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Three days ago, he 
attended a wedding at which he ate lobster and drank multiple bottles of beer. Vital signs are within normal limits. 
Examination of the right great toe discloses edema, erythema, and exquisite tenderness to palpation. The most likely 
cause of this patient's condition is accumulation of intermediates during which of the following processes?

e.correcta: This is an acute gout attack, precipitated by a high-purine meal (lobster) and alcohol (beer contains purines and also promotes lactate-mediated competition with urate for renal excretion), causing accumulation of uric acid, the end product of purine degradation. When uric acid concentrations exceed its solubility limit, monosodium urate crystals precipitate in joints — classically the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) — triggering an intense acute inflammatory response via NLRP3 inflammasome activation and neutrophil recruitment, producing the exquisite pain, erythema, and edema described.

incorrectas.A: The chylomicron processing pathway relates to dietary triglyceride and lipid transport; defects here cause hypertriglyceridemia and pancreatitis, not joint inflammation from crystal deposition, so it does not fit this acute monoarticular arthritis.
incorrectas.B: The methionine regeneration (methylation) pathway involves homocysteine metabolism; its disruption causes hyperhomocysteinemia and homocystinuria-related complications (thrombosis, lens dislocation), not gouty arthritis.
incorrectas.C: The pentose phosphate pathway generates NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate; defects (like G6PD deficiency) cause hemolytic anemia, not the joint crystal deposition seen in gout.
incorrectas.E: The urea cycle disposes of excess nitrogen as urea; defects cause hyperammonemia with neurologic symptoms, not the peripheral joint inflammation caused by urate crystal deposition seen here.

preguntas.q:
A 34-year-old woman comes to the clinic for a routine examination. She has hypertension. Her only medication is 
lisinopril. She has no known drug allergies. During the interview, she mentions that she is stressed because she recently 
received a citation for driving under the influence and must appear in court. She says she was driving home from an 
office party where she "drank a bit more than usual." Her electronic health record indicates that the patient drinks 
socially. She does not smoke cigarettes or use other substances. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. 
Which of the following is the most appropriate initial response by the physician?

o.A: "Do you have any concerns about your alcohol use?"
o.B: "How has your alcohol use been this week compared to last week: more, less, or about the same?"
o.C: "So you're here because you're concerned about your alcohol use. Is that correct?"
o.E: "Would you be willing to go through a detoxification program?"

e.correcta: The most appropriate opening approach is an open-ended, nonjudgmental question that lets the patient reflect on her own relationship with alcohol without the physician presuming a diagnosis or minimizing/maximizing the issue — this respects patient autonomy and uses motivational-interviewing principles to elicit the patient's own perspective, which is more likely to foster honest disclosure and receptiveness to change than a leading or closed question. Starting broad ("Do you have any concerns...") invites the patient to set the agenda for how much she wants to discuss, which is the recommended first step before moving to more specific screening or intervention.

incorrectas.B: Asking her to compare this week to last week assumes a baseline pattern of problematic drinking and frames the conversation narrowly around quantity comparison rather than exploring her own perception of a problem, which is premature before establishing rapport around the topic.
incorrectas.C: This phrasing puts words in the patient's mouth ("you're concerned...Is that correct?") rather than letting her express her own view, which is a leading, closed-ended question that can feel confrontational and shuts down open reflection.
incorrectas.D: Asking about her last drink is a useful clinical detail for withdrawal risk assessment but does not address the more important step of exploring her insight into and feelings about her alcohol use as an initial response.
incorrectas.E: Suggesting detoxification is a significant, premature intervention for a patient who only reports social drinking and a single citation; jumping to a treatment offer before assessing the severity or her own concerns risks alienating her and is not indicated at this stage.

preguntas.q:
A 4-year-old girl is brought to the office because of a 6-month history of slowly progressive swelling of her right leg. 
She has no history of major medical illness. She is at the 81st percentile for height and 64th percentile for weight. Her 
vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows peripheral edema of the right lower extremity to the 
mid thigh. Lymphoscintigraphy shows anomalous development of the lymphatic vessels. The defect in this patient 
most likely arose from which of the following embryonic tissues during development?

e.correcta: The lymphatic system, like blood vessels, develops from mesodermal tissue — specifically, lymphatic vessels arise from lymph sacs that bud off from developing veins (which are themselves mesoderm-derived), so a primary lymphatic malformation (primary lymphedema, as seen in this child with anomalous lymphatic development on lymphoscintigraphy) reflects a defect originating in mesodermal derivatives. This is analogous to how the entire vascular system (arteries, veins, and lymphatics) is a mesodermal derivative, distinguishing it from ectoderm-derived skin/CNS or endoderm-derived gut/glandular epithelium.

incorrectas.A: Ectoderm gives rise to the epidermis, CNS, and PNS, not to vascular or lymphatic structures, so a defect in lymphatic vessel development would not be attributed to this germ layer.
incorrectas.B: Endoderm forms the epithelial linings of the gastrointestinal and respiratory tracts and associated glands, which is unrelated to the vascular/lymphatic system's mesodermal origin.
incorrectas.D: Neural crest cells (a specialized ectodermal derivative) give rise to structures like melanocytes, adrenal medulla, and craniofacial cartilage/bone, not to the lymphatic vasculature.
incorrectas.E: Neuroectoderm forms the central nervous system and neurohypophysis; it has no role in forming lymphatic channels, which are vascular structures derived from mesoderm.

preguntas.q:
A 50-year-old man comes to the office because of a 2-month history of increasing daytime somnolence. He has 
obstructive sleep apnea for which he has only intermittently used a continuous positive airway pressure device. He is 
170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 181 kg (400 lb); BMI is 63 kg/m2. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 
100/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 135/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a gray-blue tinge 
to the lips, earlobes, and nail beds. Cardiac examination shows no other abnormalities. Arterial blood gas analysis on 
room air shows a pH of 7.31, PCO2 of 70 mm Hg, and PO2 of 50 mm Hg. Which of the following additional findings 
would be most likely in this patient?

e.correcta: This patient has obesity hypoventilation syndrome (Pickwickian syndrome) with chronic hypoventilation, shown by chronic respiratory acidosis (elevated PCO2) and hypoxemia. Chronic hypoxemia is a potent stimulus for renal erythropoietin production, leading to secondary polycythemia (increased hemoglobin/hematocrit) as a compensatory mechanism to improve oxygen-carrying capacity — this also explains the cyanotic (gray-blue) discoloration from a higher absolute amount of deoxygenated hemoglobin.

incorrectas.A: In chronic respiratory acidosis, the kidneys compensate by increasing (not decreasing) serum bicarbonate reabsorption/generation to buffer the persistently elevated PCO2, so a decreased bicarbonate would be inconsistent with this patient's chronic compensated state.
incorrectas.C: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome and obstructive sleep apnea are typically associated with reduced lung volumes (due to chest wall/abdominal mass loading) rather than increased total lung capacity, which is more a feature of obstructive diseases like emphysema.
incorrectas.D: Chronic hypoxemia and hypercapnia from OHS primarily strain the right ventricle via pulmonary vasoconstriction and pulmonary hypertension (cor pulmonale), producing right ventricular hypertrophy, not left ventricular hypertrophy.

preguntas.q:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother because of a 6-hour history of bloody diarrhea. She is 
interactive and in no acute distress. Her blood pressure is 90/55 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows normoactive 
bowel sounds. Stool cultures are obtained, and the patient's mother is advised to give the girl plenty of fluids. Five 
days later, the patient develops decreased urine output and is brought back to the office. Her blood pressure is now 
135/88 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pallor. Laboratory studies show: 
 
Hemoglobin 
8.5 g/dL (N=11–15) 
Hematocrit 
26% (N=28%–45%) 
Platelet count 
45,000/mm3 (N=150,000–400,000) 
Serum creatinine 
3.3 mg/dL (N=0.3–0.7) 
 
    Which of the following infectious agents is the most likely cause of these findings?

e.correcta: This child's bloody diarrhea followed five days later by acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, and hemolytic anemia (schistocytes would be seen on smear) is the classic triad of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), most commonly caused by Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (particularly serotype O157:H7). Shiga toxin damages endothelial cells in the glomerular microvasculature, triggering microthrombi formation that consumes platelets and mechanically shears red cells, producing the thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and renal failure characteristic of HUS — importantly, antibiotics are typically avoided in suspected EHEC infection because killing the bacteria can increase toxin release and worsen HUS risk.

incorrectas.A: Campylobacter jejuni is a common cause of bloody diarrhea and can trigger Guillain-Barré syndrome as a post-infectious complication, but it is not the classic cause of HUS, which is specifically linked to Shiga toxin-producing organisms.
incorrectas.C: Rotavirus causes watery (non-bloody) diarrhea, primarily in young children, and is not associated with Shiga toxin production or the HUS triad of hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and renal failure.
incorrectas.D: Salmonella enteritidis causes bloody diarrhea and can occasionally have systemic complications, but it does not produce Shiga toxin and is not the classic organism associated with HUS.
incorrectas.E: Yersinia pestis causes plague (bubonic/pneumonic/septicemic), not a gastrointestinal illness with bloody diarrhea progressing to HUS; it is an unrelated organism to this clinical picture.

preguntas.q:
