incorrectas.C: Compliance does change measurably with age due to progressive elastin degradation, so it is not preserved unchanged throughout the lifespan.
incorrectas.D: The change in compliance with aging is a gradual, unidirectional (increasing) trend related to elastin loss, not an unpredictable oscillation.

preguntas.q: What is the expected effect of pulmonary fibrosis on lung compliance?

e.correcta: Pulmonary fibrosis decreases lung compliance because deposition of fibrotic (scar) tissue stiffens the lung parenchyma, requiring greater pressure to achieve the same volume change. This is the physiological basis of the restrictive pattern on pulmonary function tests: reduced TLC and FVC with a preserved or even increased FEV1/FVC ratio, since airflow itself is not obstructed, only lung expansion is limited.

incorrectas.A: Increased compliance describes emphysema, where elastic tissue is destroyed and the lung becomes easier to stretch — the opposite structural change from the scarring seen in fibrosis.
incorrectas.B: Compliance is one of the most characteristically altered parameters in fibrosis; the added collagenous scar tissue directly stiffens the lung and reduces compliance, so it is not unchanged.
incorrectas.D: Infinite compliance would mean the lung expands with essentially no resistance to pressure, which is the physiological opposite of the stiff, hard-to-inflate lung seen in fibrosis.

preguntas.q: At the original FRC, in a patient with pulmonary fibrosis, how does the lung's tendency to collapse compare to the chest wall's tendency to expand?

o.A: The lung's collapsing tendency is greater
o.B: The lung's collapsing tendency is less
o.C: The two tendencies remain exactly equal
o.D: The chest wall no longer generates any outward force

e.correcta: In pulmonary fibrosis, scar tissue increases the lung's elastic recoil (decreased compliance), so at the original FRC the lung's inward collapsing pull now exceeds the chest wall's outward expanding pull. This imbalance shifts the new equilibrium to a lower lung volume, explaining the decreased FRC seen in restrictive lung disease.

incorrectas.B: This describes emphysema, where reduced lung recoil (increased compliance) makes the chest wall's outward pull dominate, the opposite of the increased recoil seen in fibrosis.
incorrectas.C: The original balance is disrupted by the fibrotic increase in lung recoil, which is exactly why the resting equilibrium volume shifts downward rather than remaining at the original FRC.
incorrectas.D: The chest wall still generates its normal outward recoil force in fibrosis; it is the lung's collapsing force that has increased and now dominates, not a loss of chest wall force.

preguntas.q: What is the expected effect of pulmonary fibrosis on functional residual capacity (FRC)?

o.D: FRC becomes equal to total lung capacity

e.correcta: Pulmonary fibrosis decreases FRC because the fibrotic lung's increased elastic recoil pulls the resting balance point between lung and chest wall down to a lower volume. This is consistent with the overall restrictive pattern of fibrosis, in which nearly all lung volumes (TLC, FRC, FVC) are reduced, unlike obstructive disease where lung volumes tend to increase.

incorrectas.A: Increased FRC is the pattern seen in emphysema, where loss of elastic recoil raises the resting equilibrium volume — the opposite structural change from the increased recoil seen in fibrosis.
incorrectas.C: FRC is characteristically reduced in fibrosis as part of the restrictive pattern; it is one of the more reliably affected volumes, not one that stays unchanged.
incorrectas.D: FRC remains a distinct, smaller resting lung volume that occurs at end-tidal expiration, well below total lung capacity (the volume at maximal inspiration), even in fibrosis where TLC itself is also reduced.

preguntas.q: A patient develops pulmonary edema secondary to left ventricular failure. What effect does this have on lung compliance?

e.correcta: Pulmonary edema fills the interstitium and alveoli with fluid, which stiffens the lung parenchyma and increases the pressure needed to achieve a given change in volume — this is the definition of decreased compliance. Left ventricular failure raises pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure, driving fluid out of the vasculature and into the alveolar spaces, so the lungs become 'stiff' and harder to inflate, contributing to the dyspnea seen in these patients.

incorrectas.A: Increased compliance is seen in conditions like emphysema, where destruction of elastic tissue makes the lung easier to inflate, which is the opposite of what happens when fluid-filled alveoli stiffen the parenchyma in pulmonary edema.
incorrectas.C: Compliance is not preserved in pulmonary edema; the added interstitial and alveolar fluid physically resists expansion, so compliance falls rather than staying the same.
incorrectas.D: Pulmonary edema does not increase functional residual capacity — it typically causes restrictive physiology with reduced lung volumes, not the hyperinflation seen with increased FRC in obstructive disease.

preguntas.q: In a patient with pneumonia, what is the expected effect on lung compliance in the affected lobe?

e.correcta: Pneumonia fills the alveoli with inflammatory exudate, consolidating the affected lung tissue and making it stiffer and harder to expand, which decreases compliance. This restrictive-pattern change explains why patients with pneumonia often show reduced lung volumes and increased work of breathing on the affected side, similar mechanistically to pulmonary edema.

incorrectas.B: Increased compliance would require loss of elastic recoil or destruction of alveolar septa, as in emphysema — pneumonia does the opposite by filling airspaces with exudate and stiffening the tissue.
incorrectas.C: Compliance is not unchanged because consolidated, fluid-filled alveoli physically resist expansion more than normal air-filled alveoli, actively lowering compliance rather than leaving it unaffected.
incorrectas.D: Pneumonia produces a restrictive pattern with reduced lung volumes, not an increase in total lung capacity, which is more characteristic of obstructive diseases with air trapping.

preguntas.q: Pulmonary surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension. What effect does this have on lung compliance?

e.correcta: Surfactant, produced by type II pneumocytes, is an amphipathic phospholipid (mainly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) that disrupts the hydrogen bonding between water molecules at the air-liquid interface, lowering surface tension. Because collapsing pressure is proportional to surface tension (law of Laplace), reducing surface tension makes alveoli easier to expand for a given pressure change, which is precisely what increased compliance means; this is why surfactant deficiency in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome causes stiff, poorly compliant lungs.

incorrectas.B: Surfactant is not neutral to compliance — its entire physiological role is to lower surface tension and thereby increase compliance, most dramatically demonstrated by the severe restrictive lung disease seen when it is absent.
incorrectas.D: Airway resistance is governed by airway radius and Poiseuille's law, not surface tension in alveoli; surfactant's action is on the elastic recoil properties of the lung parenchyma, not on conducting airway caliber.
incorrectas.A: Decreased compliance is what occurs in surfactant deficiency, not with normal surfactant function — the direction is reversed from what the question describes.

preguntas.q: According to the law of Laplace, the collapsing pressure (P) across an alveolus is best expressed by which relationship, where T is surface tension and r is the alveolar radius?

e.correcta: The law of Laplace for a sphere gives collapsing pressure P = 2T/r, meaning the pressure tending to collapse an alveolus rises with surface tension and falls as the radius increases. This relationship explains why smaller alveoli would tend to collapse into larger ones without surfactant, since they generate a higher collapsing pressure for the same surface tension — surfactant counteracts this by lowering T more in smaller alveoli, stabilizing the lung.

incorrectas.C: P = T x r inverts the actual physical relationship; the correct formula divides tension by radius (with a factor of 2 for a sphere), not multiplies by it, so this does not reflect why smaller alveoli generate higher collapsing pressures.
incorrectas.A: P = T/2r omits the correct factor of 2 in the numerator that comes from the two principal radii of curvature of a sphere, understating the collapsing pressure by a factor of 4 compared to the true relationship.
incorrectas.D: P = 2r/T reverses which variable is in the numerator versus denominator, which would incorrectly predict that larger alveoli have higher collapsing pressure, the opposite of the true physiology.

preguntas.q: Applying the law of Laplace (P = 2T/r) to alveolar mechanics, a large alveolus (with a large radius) will have what collapsing pressure relative to a small alveolus with the same surface tension?

e.correcta: Since collapsing pressure P = 2T/r, radius and pressure are inversely related when surface tension is held constant — a larger radius means the same tension is distributed over more surface, producing a lower collapsing pressure. This is why large alveoli are relatively stable, while their smaller counterparts are at greater risk of collapsing into them if surfactant is insufficient.

incorrectas.A: A higher collapsing pressure would occur in a smaller alveolus, not a larger one, since collapsing pressure varies inversely with radius according to Laplace's law.
incorrectas.B: Collapsing pressure is never exactly zero as long as surface tension exists at the air-liquid interface; a large radius only reduces the pressure, it does not eliminate it.
incorrectas.D: The pressures are not equal between alveoli of different size at the same surface tension — the inverse relationship with radius means differently sized alveoli generate different collapsing pressures, which is exactly why surfactant is needed to prevent small alveoli from emptying into large ones.

preguntas.q: Applying the law of Laplace (P = 2T/r), a small alveolus will have what collapsing pressure relative to a large alveolus at the same surface tension?

e.correcta: Because collapsing pressure P = 2T/r is inversely proportional to radius, a small alveolus generates a higher collapsing pressure than a large one at equal surface tension. Without surfactant to selectively lower the surface tension of smaller alveoli, this imbalance would cause small alveoli to empty their air into larger, lower-pressure alveoli, leading to alveolar collapse (atelectasis) — a key reason surfactant deficiency is so damaging in premature infants.

incorrectas.A: A lower collapsing pressure would describe a larger alveolus, since increasing the radius decreases the collapsing pressure per Laplace's relationship — the opposite of what happens as radius shrinks.
incorrectas.B: Collapsing pressure does not fall to zero in a small alveolus; in fact it rises as radius decreases, which is the underlying danger of instability in small airspaces without surfactant.
incorrectas.C: The pressures are not equal, because collapsing pressure depends inversely on radius; different-sized alveoli at the same tension necessarily have different collapsing pressures, which is the physiological problem surfactant is designed to solve.

preguntas.q: Which equation correctly relates airflow (Q) to the pressure gradient (ΔP) and airway resistance (R)?

e.correcta: Airflow follows an Ohm's law-like relationship, Q = ΔP/R, analogous to current equaling voltage divided by resistance in an electrical circuit. This means airflow increases when the pressure gradient between the atmosphere and alveoli widens, and decreases when airway resistance rises; because resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of airway radius, even small changes in airway caliber (e.g., bronchoconstriction) produce large changes in resistance and thus airflow.

incorrectas.B: Q = ΔP x R would mean airflow increases as resistance increases, which contradicts basic physiology — higher resistance from bronchoconstriction or mucus plugging reduces, not increases, airflow.
incorrectas.A: Q = R/ΔP inverts the true relationship; airflow should rise with a larger pressure gradient and fall with higher resistance, not the reverse implied by placing ΔP in the denominator.
incorrectas.D: Q = R − ΔP is a subtraction relationship that has no physical basis in fluid dynamics; airflow is a ratio of driving pressure to resistance, not a difference between the two quantities.

preguntas.q: Based on the relationship Q = ΔP/R, how is airflow related to airway resistance?

o.D: Proportional to the square of resistance

e.correcta: In the equation Q = ΔP/R, airflow (Q) sits in the numerator relative to resistance (R) in the denominator, making airflow inversely proportional to resistance — as resistance rises (e.g., bronchoconstriction, mucus plugging), airflow falls for a given pressure gradient. This inverse relationship is the physiologic basis for why obstructive diseases like asthma, which increase airway resistance, reduce expiratory airflow.

incorrectas.A: A directly proportional relationship would mean airflow increases as resistance increases, which is physiologically backwards — higher resistance should impede, not enhance, flow.
incorrectas.B: Airflow is not independent of resistance; resistance is one of the two variables (along with the pressure gradient) that directly determines the magnitude of airflow in the Q = ΔP/R relationship.
incorrectas.D: The relationship between Q and R is a simple inverse (first power), not an inverse-square relationship; the fourth-power dependence in this system is actually between resistance and airway radius (Poiseuille's law), not between airflow and resistance directly.

preguntas.q: Based on the relationship Q = ΔP/R, how is airflow related to the pressure gradient (ΔP) across the airway?

e.correcta: Since Q = ΔP/R, airflow is directly proportional to the pressure gradient between the atmosphere and alveoli — a larger pressure difference (generated by greater inspiratory or expiratory effort) drives more airflow for a fixed resistance. This is the same Ohm's-law-like logic used throughout cardiovascular and respiratory physiology, where flow scales with the driving pressure difference.

incorrectas.A: An inverse relationship would mean airflow decreases as the pressure gradient increases, which contradicts the basic physiology of ventilation, where greater respiratory effort (bigger ΔP) produces more airflow.
incorrectas.B: Airflow is not unrelated to the pressure gradient — ΔP is one of the two determinants of Q in this equation, directly setting how much flow occurs for a given resistance.
incorrectas.D: A fourth-power relationship applies to how airway radius affects resistance in Poiseuille's law, not to how the pressure gradient relates to airflow, which is a simple direct proportionality.

preguntas.q: Poiseuille's equation describes airway resistance (R) in terms of air viscosity (η), airway length (l), and airway radius (r). Which expression correctly represents R?

e.correcta: Poiseuille's law gives resistance as R = 8ηl/πr4, meaning resistance increases with the viscosity of the gas and the length of the airway, but falls dramatically as radius increases, since radius is raised to the fourth power. This fourth-power dependence explains why even small amounts of bronchoconstriction or mucosal edema (which reduce radius slightly) cause a disproportionately large rise in airway resistance — the clinical basis for airflow obstruction in asthma and COPD.

incorrectas.A: R = πr4/8ηl inverts the entire equation — it would predict that increasing the radius increases resistance, exactly the opposite of the true inverse fourth-power relationship between radius and resistance.
incorrectas.C: R = 8ηr4/πl incorrectly places radius in the numerator, which would mean wider airways have more resistance, contradicting the physiological principle that larger airways offer dramatically less resistance to flow.
incorrectas.D: R = πl/8ηr4 misplaces the viscosity term and omits it from where it should multiply length in the numerator, distorting the proportional relationships between resistance and each of its true determinants.

preguntas.q: Despite having a smaller individual radius than large airways, which site is actually the major contributor to total airway resistance?

e.correcta: The medium-sized bronchi are the major site of airway resistance because, although each individual small airway (like a terminal bronchiole) has a tiny radius and thus high resistance on its own, the smallest airways are arranged in massive parallel networks that make their combined resistance low. Medium bronchi have fewer parallel pathways relative to their radius, so their cumulative resistance to airflow is greatest — a key concept for understanding why early small-airway disease can be relatively 'silent' before resistance rises detectably.

incorrectas.A: The trachea has a large radius and offers relatively little resistance individually; while it is a single conduit rather than parallel pathways, its large caliber keeps its contribution to total resistance low.
incorrectas.B: Terminal bronchioles have the smallest individual radius and thus the highest resistance per airway, but because there are so many of them arranged in parallel, their combined resistance is actually low — this is the classic 'silent zone' of the lung.
incorrectas.D: Alveolar ducts are involved in gas exchange rather than conducting bulk airflow, and are not the major site of airway resistance; resistance calculations focus on the conducting airways, particularly the medium bronchi.

preguntas.q: What effect does parasympathetic innervation have on airway resistance?

o.D: Increased resistance via mucosal vasodilation only

e.correcta: Parasympathetic stimulation acts through vagal efferents releasing acetylcholine onto M3 muscarinic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, causing bronchoconstriction and thus increasing airway resistance. This is the same pathway targeted therapeutically by anticholinergic bronchodilators like ipratropium, which block this parasympathetic tone to widen the airways in obstructive lung disease.

incorrectas.B: Parasympathetic input has a clear, well-defined effect on airway smooth muscle tone through M3 receptor activation — it is not without significant physiological consequence, as it actively drives bronchoconstriction.
incorrectas.A: Bronchodilation and decreased resistance are the effect of sympathetic stimulation via beta-2 receptors, not parasympathetic stimulation, which produces the opposite effect of bronchoconstriction.
incorrectas.D: While parasympathetic activity does increase bronchial mucus gland secretion and can affect mucosal blood flow, the primary and defining mechanism increasing resistance is direct smooth muscle constriction, not vasodilation alone.

preguntas.q: What effect does sympathetic innervation have on airway resistance?

o.B: No effect on smooth muscle tone

e.correcta: Sympathetic stimulation, largely via circulating epinephrine acting on beta-2 adrenergic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, causes relaxation and bronchodilation, thereby decreasing airway resistance. This beta-2 mediated relaxation is the pharmacologic basis for using beta-2 agonists like albuterol to treat bronchospasm in asthma and COPD exacerbations.

incorrectas.A: Bronchoconstriction and increased resistance describe the parasympathetic (muscarinic) effect on the airway, not the sympathetic (beta-2 adrenergic) effect, which instead relaxes smooth muscle.
incorrectas.B: Sympathetic stimulation does have a clear effect on smooth muscle tone — it activates beta-2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle to produce relaxation, which is far from having no effect.
incorrectas.D: Mucus hypersecretion and increased resistance are more characteristic of parasympathetic/cholinergic stimulation of submucosal glands, whereas sympathetic activation tends to reduce secretions and dilate airways.

preguntas.q: What is the effect of breathing at high lung volumes on airway resistance?

o.A: Increased resistance due to alveolar overdistension
o.C: Decreased resistance due to increased radial traction
o.D: Increased resistance due to airway compression

e.correcta: At high lung volumes, the surrounding lung parenchyma is stretched, exerting greater radial traction on the walls of the airways and pulling them open, which widens airway caliber and lowers resistance. This is why patients with high baseline airway resistance, such as those with asthma, often instinctively breathe at higher lung volumes (dynamic hyperinflation) — it mechanically pulls their airways open to compensate for their obstruction.

incorrectas.A: Alveolar overdistension at high lung volumes does not increase airway resistance; rather, the traction exerted by the stretched surrounding tissue on the airway walls pulls the airways open, lowering resistance.
incorrectas.B: Resistance does change substantially with lung volume — it decreases at higher volumes and rises sharply at low volumes, so assuming no change misses the key elastic-traction mechanism connecting parenchyma and airway caliber.
incorrectas.D: Airway compression from surrounding tissue occurs at low, not high, lung volumes, when reduced radial traction and lower recoil pressures allow smaller airways to narrow or even close (as near residual volume).

preguntas.q: What is the effect of breathing at low lung volumes on airway resistance?

o.A: Increased resistance due to decreased radial traction
o.B: Decreased resistance due to airway widening
o.D: Decreased resistance due to loss of surfactant activity

e.correcta: At low lung volumes, the surrounding parenchyma is less stretched and exerts less radial traction pulling outward on the airway walls, so the airways narrow and resistance rises. This mechanism explains why small airways can close near residual volume, contributing to air trapping in conditions where patients are forced to breathe at low lung volumes.

incorrectas.B: Airway widening and decreased resistance occur at high, not low, lung volumes, when greater parenchymal stretch increases the radial traction that holds airways open.
incorrectas.C: Resistance is not unchanged at low lung volumes — the loss of radial traction on the airway walls is a well-established mechanism that measurably increases resistance as lung volume falls.
incorrectas.D: While surfactant affects alveolar surface tension and compliance, the resistance change at low lung volumes is driven by reduced radial traction on airway walls from the surrounding elastic parenchyma, not by surfactant activity.

preguntas.q: A deep-sea diver breathing gas at increased density experiences increased viscosity of inspired gas. What effect does this have on airway resistance, per Poiseuille's equation?

e.correcta: Poiseuille's equation, R = 8ηl/πr4, places viscosity (η) directly in the numerator, so increasing gas viscosity — as occurs when breathing denser gas mixtures under increased ambient pressure during deep-sea diving — directly increases airway resistance. This is a real physiological concern in diving physiology, which is one reason divers may use helium-oxygen mixtures instead of nitrogen-oxygen to reduce gas density and resistance at depth.

incorrectas.A: Decreased resistance would require lower viscosity, but increased ambient pressure at depth raises gas density and viscosity, which directly raises resistance according to Poiseuille's equation, not lowers it.
incorrectas.B: Resistance is not unaffected by viscosity — viscosity is one of the four variables in Poiseuille's equation, and it has a direct, proportional relationship with resistance.
incorrectas.D: Resistance is never independent of viscosity in this model; the equation explicitly shows resistance scaling directly with viscosity, alongside its fourth-power dependence on radius.

preguntas.q: A patient with severe asthma is given a helium-oxygen (heliox) mixture to breathe. Because helium is less viscous than nitrogen, what effect does this have on airway resistance?

o.D: Resistance increases only in large airways

e.correcta: Since Poiseuille's equation places viscosity (η) directly in the numerator of R = 8ηl/πr4, substituting the less-viscous helium for nitrogen lowers the effective viscosity of the inspired gas mixture and thus decreases airway resistance. This is the physiological rationale for using heliox in severe asthma or upper airway obstruction — it improves gas flow through narrowed airways without needing to change the anatomical radius, buying time for other treatments to reduce bronchoconstriction.

incorrectas.A: Increased resistance would occur with a more viscous gas, but helium is less viscous than the nitrogen it replaces, so resistance falls rather than rises when heliox is used.
incorrectas.B: Resistance does change with gas viscosity because viscosity is a direct multiplier in Poiseuille's equation — switching to a less viscous gas measurably lowers resistance, it does not leave it unchanged.
incorrectas.D: The viscosity effect on resistance is not restricted to large airways; it applies throughout the airway tree wherever gas flows, since viscosity is a property of the gas itself, not of a specific airway segment.

preguntas.q: Which equation is used to calculate pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR)?

o.A: PVR = cardiac output / (mean pulmonary artery pressure - left atrial pressure)
o.B: PVR = (mean pulmonary artery pressure - left atrial pressure) / cardiac output
o.C: PVR = mean pulmonary artery pressure x cardiac output
o.D: PVR = (mean pulmonary artery pressure + left atrial pressure) / cardiac output

e.correcta: Pulmonary vascular resistance is calculated the same way systemic vascular resistance is, as a pressure gradient divided by flow: PVR = (mean pulmonary artery pressure − left atrial pressure) / cardiac output. The pulmonary artery pressure represents the driving pressure entering the pulmonary circulation, and the left atrial pressure approximates the pressure at the outflow end of the pulmonary capillary bed, so their difference is the true perfusion pressure gradient across the lungs, analogous to ΔP/R relationships elsewhere in the cardiovascular and respiratory systems.

incorrectas.A: This formula inverts the true relationship, placing cardiac output (the flow, analogous to Q) in the numerator and the pressure gradient in the denominator, which is backward — resistance should equal pressure difference divided by flow, not the reverse.
incorrectas.C: Multiplying pulmonary artery pressure by cardiac output would actually approximate cardiac work or power output in the pulmonary circulation, not resistance, which requires a pressure difference divided by flow.
incorrectas.D: Adding rather than subtracting left atrial pressure would fail to represent the actual driving pressure gradient across the pulmonary vasculature; the correct calculation requires the difference between inflow and outflow pressures, not their sum.

preguntas.q: During inspiration, how does the volume of air in the lungs change over the course of the breath?

e.correcta: During inspiration, contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles expands the thoracic cavity, which lowers intrapleural and alveolar pressure below atmospheric pressure and draws air into the lungs, so lung volume rises progressively throughout the breath until peak inspiration is reached. This continuous volume increase is paired with a progressively more negative intrapleural pressure and transiently negative alveolar pressure, both of which are the mechanical drivers of airflow into the lung.

incorrectas.A: A progressive decrease in volume describes expiration, not inspiration — during inspiration the chest wall and lungs are actively expanding, increasing rather than decreasing volume.
incorrectas.C: Volume does not stay constant during inspiration; it changes continuously as air flows in response to the pressure gradient created by diaphragmatic contraction, right up until the point of peak inspiratory volume.
incorrectas.D: There is no initial decrease in lung volume at the start of inspiration — volume rises from the very onset of diaphragmatic contraction as air begins entering the alveoli, rather than dipping first.

preguntas.q: How does intrapleural pressure (relative to atmospheric pressure) change during inspiration?

o.D: It stays constant at -5 cm H2O

e.correcta: During inspiration, the diaphragm and chest wall expand outward while the elastic lung tends to recoil inward, and this opposing pull stretches the pleural space further, driving intrapleural pressure to become more negative, typically dropping from about -5 cm H2O at rest to around -8 cm H2O at peak inspiration. This progressively more negative pressure is transmitted to the alveoli and is the mechanical force that keeps the lung expanded and helps draw air in.

incorrectas.A: Intrapleural pressure becoming less negative (moving toward zero) is what happens during expiration, when the chest wall and lung recoil back toward their resting positions, not during inspiration.
incorrectas.C: Intrapleural pressure remains negative relative to atmosphere throughout normal quiet breathing (both inspiration and expiration) and does not become positive except during a forced expiratory maneuver against a closed glottis, unrelated to normal inspiration.
incorrectas.D: Intrapleural pressure is not fixed at a constant -5 cm H2O; it varies continuously through the respiratory cycle, becoming progressively more negative during inspiration and less negative during expiration.

preguntas.q: How does alveolar pressure (relative to atmospheric pressure) change during mid-inspiration?

e.correcta: During mid-inspiration, as the thoracic cavity expands faster than air can flow in to equilibrate, alveolar pressure transiently drops below atmospheric pressure, becoming slightly negative (roughly 0 to -1 cm H2O), which is exactly the pressure gradient that drives air into the alveoli per the Q = ΔP/R relationship. Once inspiration ends and airflow stops, alveolar pressure returns to zero (equal to atmospheric) at that instantaneous point of no flow.

incorrectas.A: Alveolar pressure becoming more positive relative to atmosphere describes mid-expiration, when the chest wall recoils and compresses the alveolar gas, driving air back out — the opposite of the negative pressure needed to draw air in during inspiration.
incorrectas.B: Alveolar pressure is zero only at the very start and very end of each breath when there is no airflow; during active mid-inspiration it becomes transiently negative to create the pressure gradient necessary for airflow.
incorrectas.D: Alveolar pressure does not equal intrapleural pressure — intrapleural pressure is substantially more negative than alveolar pressure throughout the cycle, and their difference (the transpulmonary pressure) is what keeps the alveoli open against their tendency to collapse.

preguntas.q: During mid-inspiration, when alveolar pressure becomes negative relative to the atmosphere, in which direction does air flow?

o.A: Air flows outward, out of the lungs
o.C: Air flows inward, into the lungs

e.correcta: Air always flows down its pressure gradient, from a region of higher pressure to one of lower pressure, following the Q = ΔP/R relationship. Since alveolar pressure drops below atmospheric pressure during mid-inspiration, the atmosphere is now at relatively higher pressure than the alveoli, so air flows inward into the lungs until the pressures re-equilibrate at end-inspiration.

incorrectas.A: Outward airflow would require alveolar pressure to exceed atmospheric pressure, which is the situation during expiration, not during the negative-pressure phase of inspiration described here.
incorrectas.B: Airflow does not cease when there is a pressure gradient present — flow continues as long as ΔP is nonzero, and a negative alveolar pressure relative to atmosphere is precisely the gradient that sustains inward flow.
incorrectas.D: Airflow is unidirectional at any given moment, following the net pressure gradient between the atmosphere and alveoli; it does not move simultaneously in both directions during a single phase of the respiratory cycle.

preguntas.q: During expiration, how does the volume of air in the lungs change over the course of the breath?

e.correcta: During expiration, the inspiratory muscles relax and the elastic recoil of the lung and chest wall (aided by abdominal and internal intercostal muscles in forced expiration) reduces thoracic volume, raising alveolar pressure above atmospheric pressure and pushing air out, so lung volume falls progressively throughout the breath. This passive recoil-driven process is the mirror image of the active, muscle-driven volume increase seen during inspiration.

incorrectas.A: A progressive increase in volume describes inspiration, not expiration — during expiration the lung and chest wall are returning toward their resting position, decreasing rather than increasing volume.
incorrectas.C: Volume does not remain constant during expiration; it falls continuously as air exits along the pressure gradient created by elastic recoil, right up until end-expiratory volume (functional residual capacity) is reached.
incorrectas.D: There is no initial increase in lung volume during expiration — volume decreases from the start of the expiratory phase as elastic recoil begins pushing air out, rather than rising first.

preguntas.q: How does intrapleural pressure (relative to atmospheric pressure) change during expiration?

o.D: It stays constant at -8 cm H2O

e.correcta: During expiration, the chest wall and diaphragm relax and the lung recoils back toward its resting volume, reducing the outward stretch on the pleural space, so intrapleural pressure becomes less negative, typically rising from about -8 cm H2O back toward -5 cm H2O at end-expiration. It stays negative throughout quiet breathing, which is essential to keep the lung from collapsing away from the chest wall, but the magnitude of that negativity diminishes as expiration proceeds.

incorrectas.A: Intrapleural pressure becoming more negative describes inspiration, when the expanding thoracic cage stretches the pleural space further, not expiration, during which the chest wall and lung are recoiling back toward baseline.
incorrectas.C: Intrapleural pressure remains negative relative to atmosphere during quiet expiration and does not become positive; it only becomes transiently positive during a forced expiratory effort against resistance, not during normal passive expiration.
incorrectas.D: Intrapleural pressure is not fixed at a constant -8 cm H2O; it changes continuously through the cycle, becoming less negative during expiration as the lung and chest wall recoil toward their resting positions.

preguntas.q: How does alveolar pressure (relative to atmospheric pressure) change during mid-expiration?

e.correcta: During mid-expiration, elastic recoil of the lung and chest wall compresses the alveolar gas faster than it can escape, transiently raising alveolar pressure above atmospheric pressure (roughly 0 to +1 cm H2O), which creates the pressure gradient that drives air out of the lungs per Q = ΔP/R. This positive alveolar pressure is the mirror image of the negative alveolar pressure generated during inspiration and again returns to zero once airflow stops at end-expiration.

incorrectas.A: Alveolar pressure becoming more negative describes mid-inspiration, when the expanding thorax lowers alveolar pressure below atmospheric to draw air in, not mid-expiration, when the direction of the gradient is reversed to push air out.
incorrectas.B: Alveolar pressure is zero only at the instants of no airflow (end-inspiration and end-expiration); during active mid-expiration it becomes transiently positive to generate the outward-directed pressure gradient.
incorrectas.D: Alveolar pressure does not match intrapleural pressure — intrapleural pressure remains negative throughout the cycle while alveolar pressure oscillates around zero, and the difference between them (transpulmonary pressure) is what keeps the alveoli inflated.

preguntas.q: During mid-expiration, once alveolar pressure becomes positive relative to atmospheric pressure, in which direction does air flow?

o.A: Air flows inward into the alveoli
o.C: Air flows outward, out of the lungs
o.D: Air oscillates back and forth with no net flow

e.correcta: Air always flows down its pressure gradient, from higher to lower pressure. Once the elastic recoil of the lung compresses alveolar gas enough to make alveolar pressure exceed atmospheric pressure (which is defined as zero), gas flows outward from the alveoli to the atmosphere, producing expiration. This is the same principle that drives inspiration in reverse: during inspiration, the chest wall expands the thorax, alveolar pressure drops below atmospheric, and air flows in.

incorrectas.A: Air flowing inward would require alveolar pressure to be lower than atmospheric pressure, which is the condition present during inspiration, not the positive-pressure mid-expiratory state described here.
incorrectas.B: Flow only stops when alveolar and atmospheric pressures are equal (at the very end of inspiration or expiration, when velocity of flow is zero); a positive alveolar-to-atmospheric gradient by definition still drives flow, it does not halt it.
incorrectas.D: Airflow in normal quiet breathing is unidirectional within each phase (in during inspiration, out during expiration) and is governed by the sign of the pressure gradient at that moment, not an oscillating flow with no net movement.

preguntas.q: Intrapleural pressure, which is normally negative throughout the respiratory cycle, can transiently become positive relative to atmospheric pressure during which normal physiologic maneuver?

e.correcta: During forced expiration, contraction of the expiratory muscles (abdominal wall and internal intercostals) actively compresses the thoracic cavity beyond what elastic recoil alone would achieve, driving intrapleural pressure above atmospheric pressure. This is different from quiet breathing, where intrapleural pressure stays negative throughout the cycle (subatmospheric) to keep the lungs from collapsing away from the chest wall. Forced, effort-dependent expiration (as in coughing or a forced vital capacity maneuver) is the classic scenario in which positive intrapleural pressure is generated.

incorrectas.A: During quiet tidal inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and expands the thorax, making intrapleural pressure more negative (more subatmospheric) than at rest, the opposite of the positive pressure seen with forced expiration.
incorrectas.B: Passive quiet expiration relies solely on elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall with no active muscle contraction, so intrapleural pressure rises back toward its resting value but normally stays negative rather than crossing into positive territory.
incorrectas.D: An end-inspiratory pause is simply a breath-hold at full lung volume with glottis and airway open to no flow; intrapleural pressure at that point is still negative (subatmospheric), reflecting the lung's tendency to recoil inward against the chest wall's tendency to spring outward.

preguntas.q: Which equation correctly gives the partial pressure of a gas (Px) in humidified tracheal air, where PB is barometric pressure, PH2O is water vapor pressure at 37°C (47 mmHg), and F is the fractional concentration of the gas?

e.correcta: Once inspired air passes through the upper airway, it becomes fully saturated with water vapor, which exerts its own partial pressure of 47 mmHg at body temperature (37°C) and effectively displaces some of the barometric pressure that would otherwise be available to the other gases. Because Dalton's law states total pressure is the sum of partial pressures, the 'dry gas' pressure available to be distributed among O2, CO2, and N2 is (PB - PH2O), and multiplying that by the fractional concentration F of any given gas yields its partial pressure in humidified air.

incorrectas.A: Px = PB * F is the formula for a dry gas mixture (such as dry inspired air before it reaches the airway), because it does not subtract out the water vapor pressure that is present once air becomes humidified in the trachea.
incorrectas.C: Dividing barometric pressure by the fractional concentration is not a physically meaningful operation here; partial pressure of a gas within a mixture is always a fraction of the total pressure, obtained by multiplication, not division, by F.
incorrectas.D: Subtracting water vapor pressure after multiplying PB by F would incorrectly apply the water vapor correction only to the gas of interest rather than adjusting the total pressure pool available to all gases before partitioning, giving the wrong numeric result.

preguntas.q: In dry expired air (no water vapor correction applied), the partial pressure of a gas (Px) is calculated using which formula, where PB is barometric pressure and F is the fractional concentration of the gas?

e.correcta: For a dry gas sample, where no water vapor is contributing to the total pressure, the partial pressure of a specific gas is simply its fractional concentration multiplied by the total (barometric) pressure — a direct application of Dalton's law of partial pressures. This contrasts with humidified gas (as found in the trachea or alveoli), where water vapor pressure must first be subtracted from PB before multiplying by F.

incorrectas.A: This formula, which subtracts water vapor pressure before multiplying by F, applies specifically to humidified gas (tracheal or alveolar air), not to dry expired gas where no water vapor correction is needed.
incorrectas.C: Px = Px * Solubility is actually the formula for the concentration of a dissolved gas in a liquid (Henry's law), an entirely different physical relationship describing gas dissolved in blood or tissue, not gas partial pressure in a dry air mixture.
incorrectas.D: Adding barometric pressure to a fractional concentration mixes units improperly (pressure plus a unitless fraction) and does not correspond to any physiologically meaningful calculation of partial pressure.

preguntas.q: The concentration of a gas dissolved in a liquid (Cx) is best described by which relationship, where Px is the partial pressure of the gas?

e.correcta: This is Henry's law: the amount of a gas that dissolves in a liquid (such as blood plasma) is directly proportional to its partial pressure in the gas phase it is equilibrating with, and the proportionality constant is the gas's solubility coefficient in that particular liquid. This explains why highly soluble gases like CO2 achieve much higher dissolved concentrations at a given partial pressure than poorly soluble gases like O2, which is clinically relevant for understanding gas transport and diffusion in blood.

incorrectas.B: Px = PB * F (without a Solubility term) describes the partial pressure of a gas within a dry gas mixture using Dalton's law, not the amount of that gas dissolved into a liquid phase, which instead requires Henry's law.
incorrectas.C: This formula corrects barometric pressure for water vapor to get the partial pressure of a humidified gas mixture; it describes gas-phase partial pressure, not the quantity of gas dissolved in solution.
incorrectas.D: Dividing partial pressure by solubility would invert the actual relationship — Henry's law states dissolved gas concentration increases (not decreases) as solubility increases, so multiplication, not division, is the correct operation.

preguntas.q: By what mechanism do respiratory gases such as O2 and CO2 cross cell membranes and capillary walls?

o.A: Facilitated diffusion via a specific transporter

e.correcta: O2 and CO2 are small, nonpolar (or effectively nonpolar) molecules that dissolve readily in the lipid bilayer, allowing them to cross cell membranes and capillary walls purely by simple diffusion down their partial pressure (concentration) gradients, without needing a carrier protein or energy input. The rate of this diffusion is governed by Fick's law, being proportional to the gas's diffusion coefficient, the surface area available, and the pressure gradient, and inversely proportional to membrane thickness.

incorrectas.A: Facilitated diffusion requires a specific membrane transport protein to ferry a solute (such as glucose via GLUT transporters) across the membrane; respiratory gases are small and lipid-soluble enough to cross unaided, so no such carrier is needed or used.
incorrectas.C: Primary active transport uses ATP hydrolysis to move solutes against their concentration gradient (e.g., the Na+/K+-ATPase); gas exchange, in contrast, is a passive process moving gases down their existing partial pressure gradient, requiring no energy expenditure.
incorrectas.D: Bulk flow describes the mass movement of air or blood as a whole down a pressure gradient (such as airflow into the lungs or blood flow through capillaries) rather than the molecular-level movement of individual gas molecules across a membrane, which is a diffusive, not convective, process.

preguntas.q: Compared to oxygen, the diffusion coefficient (DK) of carbon dioxide across the alveolar-capillary membrane is approximately how many times greater?

e.correcta: CO2's diffusion coefficient is roughly 20 times greater than that of O2, primarily because CO2 is markedly more soluble in the aqueous/lipid components of the alveolar-capillary membrane, and diffusion coefficient is proportional to gas solubility (and inversely related to the square root of molecular weight). As a result, CO2 diffuses across the membrane about 20 times faster than O2 for a given partial pressure gradient, which is why impaired diffusion (as in interstitial lung disease) tends to cause hypoxemia before it causes significant hypercapnia.

incorrectas.A: A 2x difference dramatically understates the true disparity in diffusion coefficients between CO2 and O2, which is driven mainly by CO2's much higher solubility, not just a modest difference in molecular properties.
incorrectas.B: A 5x factor is still well below the accepted approximate 20x value used in First Aid/physiology teaching for the CO2-to-O2 diffusion coefficient ratio, and underestimates why CO2 exchange is rarely diffusion-limited even in disease.
incorrectas.D: A 100x factor overstates the difference; while CO2 diffuses much faster than O2, the widely cited teaching value for this ratio is approximately 20-fold, not 100-fold.

preguntas.q: The lung diffusing capacity (DL) is best conceptually understood as being equivalent to which property of the alveolar-capillary barrier?

e.correcta: DL represents how easily a gas can cross the alveolar-capillary membrane overall, integrating the gas's own diffusion coefficient with the membrane's surface area and thickness (DL ~ DK × A / Δx) — conceptually, this is the barrier's 'permeability' to that gas. A higher DL means the membrane is more permeable (thinner, larger surface area, or the gas diffuses more readily), which is why diseases that thicken the membrane (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis) or destroy surface area (e.g., emphysema) reduce DL.

incorrectas.B: Surface area is only one of the three variables that determine DL (along with diffusion coefficient and membrane thickness); DL as a whole is a broader permeability concept, not simply a measurement of surface area by itself.
incorrectas.C: Elastic recoil refers to the lung's tendency to spring back to a smaller volume after being stretched, a mechanical property relevant to lung compliance and breathing mechanics, entirely separate from the diffusive gas-exchange property that DL measures.
incorrectas.D: Airway resistance describes how much the conducting airways impede bulk airflow during breathing (relevant to obstructive lung disease and spirometry), not how readily a gas diffuses across the thin alveolar-capillary membrane once air has already reached the alveoli.

preguntas.q: The lung's diffusing capacity (DL) is clinically measured using which gas because it is exclusively diffusion-limited under normal conditions?

e.correcta: Carbon monoxide is used to measure DLCO because it binds hemoglobin with such extremely high affinity (about 200-240 times that of O2) that essentially none of the CO that diffuses into the capillary remains free in the plasma to raise the partial pressure there; capillary PCO thus stays near zero along the entire capillary length. This means CO uptake never plateaus due to reaching equilibrium with blood — it is limited purely by how fast it can diffuse across the membrane, making it the ideal probe for isolating the diffusion component of gas exchange.

incorrectas.A: Nitrous oxide is the classic example of a purely perfusion-limited gas — it does not bind hemoglobin and equilibrates almost instantly across the alveolar-capillary membrane, so its uptake is governed entirely by how much blood flow (perfusion) is delivered, the opposite of what is needed to test diffusion capacity.
incorrectas.B: Under normal physiologic conditions, O2 is perfusion-limited, not diffusion-limited: O2 equilibrates between alveolar gas and capillary blood well before the blood reaches the end of the capillary, so its uptake reflects blood flow rather than pure membrane diffusing capacity, making it unsuitable for isolating DL.
incorrectas.D: Nitrogen is physiologically inert and is not taken up across the alveolar-capillary membrane in a way that reflects gas exchange at all, so it cannot serve as a marker of diffusing capacity the way a reactive, hemoglobin-binding gas like CO can.

preguntas.q: The DLCO test is used clinically to estimate the extent to which which gas passes from the alveoli into pulmonary capillary blood?

e.correcta: Because CO's uptake is purely diffusion-limited and its transfer characteristics parallel those of O2 (both must cross the same alveolar-capillary membrane and both are taken up avidly by hemoglobin), DLCO serves as a practical surrogate marker for how well O2 itself can diffuse from alveolar gas into the blood. A reduced DLCO (as in pulmonary fibrosis or emphysema) signals impaired O2 transfer capacity, which is why this test is used clinically to evaluate interstitial lung disease and other conditions that thicken or destroy the gas-exchange membrane.

incorrectas.A: CO2 diffuses roughly 20 times faster than O2 across the alveolar-capillary membrane due to its much higher solubility, so CO2 transfer is rarely the limiting step in disease and is not what DLCO is designed to estimate.
incorrectas.B: Nitrogen is essentially inert and not taken up or exchanged across the alveolar-capillary membrane in a way relevant to gas exchange physiology; it is used in other pulmonary function tests (like nitrogen washout for FRC) but not represented by DLCO.
incorrectas.D: Nitrous oxide is used experimentally to demonstrate perfusion-limited gas exchange (since it does not bind hemoglobin and equilibrates instantly), which is the opposite of what DLCO is measuring — DLCO isolates the diffusion-limited behavior relevant to O2 transfer.

preguntas.q: According to the equation DL ~ (DK × A) / Δx, how does lung diffusing capacity (DL) relate to the surface area (A) available for gas exchange?

o.D: Proportional to the square of the surface area

e.correcta: DL is directly proportional to surface area because a larger area of alveolar-capillary membrane provides more parallel pathways for gas molecules to cross simultaneously, increasing total gas transfer per unit time for a given partial pressure gradient. This is clinically important in emphysema, where destruction of alveolar septa reduces the effective surface area and thereby lowers DLCO, even though the remaining membrane itself may not be diseased.

incorrectas.A: An inverse relationship would mean less surface area increases diffusing capacity, which is physiologically backwards — Fick's law of diffusion shows that diffusion rate scales up, not down, as available membrane area increases.
incorrectas.C: Surface area is one of the three core variables in the diffusion equation (alongside diffusion coefficient and membrane thickness) and has a well-defined, direct relationship with DL; it is not unrelated to gas transfer capacity.
incorrectas.D: The relationship in Fick's law is a simple direct (first-power) proportionality between area and diffusion rate, not a squared relationship — doubling the area doubles diffusing capacity, it does not quadruple it.

preguntas.q: According to DL ~ (DK × A) / Δx, how does lung diffusing capacity (DL) relate to the diffusion coefficient (DK) of the gas being transferred?

e.correcta: DL is directly proportional to the gas's own diffusion coefficient, which itself reflects the gas's solubility in tissue and its molecular weight. This is why different gases have different diffusing capacities across the identical anatomic membrane — CO2, with a diffusion coefficient about 20 times that of O2 due to its higher solubility, diffuses much more readily across the same alveolar-capillary barrier.

incorrectas.A: An inverse relationship would imply that gases with a higher diffusion coefficient diffuse more slowly, which contradicts the physical basis of Fick's law, where a higher diffusion coefficient directly increases the rate of gas transfer.
incorrectas.B: The diffusion coefficient is explicitly one of the three multiplicative terms in the DL equation, so it is fundamentally related to (not independent of) the overall diffusing capacity for any given gas.
incorrectas.D: The relationship between DK and DL is a basic physical/chemical property of the gas-membrane system that holds under normal physiologic conditions at any altitude; altitude affects overall barometric and partial pressures, not the fundamental proportionality in Fick's law.

preguntas.q: According to DL ~ (DK × A) / Δx, how does lung diffusing capacity (DL) change as alveolar-capillary membrane thickness (Δx) increases, such as in pulmonary fibrosis?

e.correcta: DL is inversely proportional to membrane thickness because gas molecules must physically traverse a longer diffusion path when the membrane thickens, which slows the rate of transfer for any given partial pressure gradient. This is precisely the mechanism by which pulmonary fibrosis (which thickens the interstitium with collagen deposition) reduces DLCO and causes diffusion-limited hypoxemia, especially evident during exercise when capillary transit time is shortened.

incorrectas.A: A direct (increasing) relationship would mean a thicker membrane transfers gas faster, which is physically backwards — Fick's law shows diffusion rate falls as the path length (thickness) that molecules must cross gets longer.
incorrectas.B: Membrane thickness is one of the three key determinants in the diffusion equation (DL ~ DK × A / Δx); it is not an inert variable, and pathologic thickening (as in fibrosis) has a well-documented, measurable effect of lowering diffusing capacity.
incorrectas.D: There is no physiologic basis for a biphasic (first up, then down) relationship between thickness and diffusing capacity — the relationship described by Fick's law is a simple, monotonic inverse proportionality.

preguntas.q: The partial pressure of oxygen (PO2) in dry inspired room air at sea level is normally approximately how many mmHg?

e.correcta: Dry inspired air's PO2 is calculated as barometric pressure (760 mmHg at sea level) multiplied by the fractional concentration of O2 in room air (approximately 0.21), giving about 160 mmHg. This value represents air before it has been humidified in the airway, and it serves as the starting reference point in the sequence of falling oxygen tensions as air moves from atmosphere to trachea to alveoli to arterial blood.

incorrectas.A: 100 mmHg is the normal PO2 in the alveoli (PAO2) and arterial blood (PaO2), a value already reduced from atmospheric levels by humidification (water vapor dilution) and by the exchange of O2 for CO2 in the alveoli, so it does not represent dry inspired air.
incorrectas.B: 150 mmHg is the PO2 of humidified tracheal air, calculated after subtracting water vapor pressure (47 mmHg) from barometric pressure before multiplying by the fractional O2 concentration; this value differs from the dry inspired air value because of that water vapor correction.
incorrectas.D: 40 mmHg corresponds to the PO2 of mixed venous blood after peripheral tissues have extracted oxygen, a value far downstream from the inspired air stage and reflecting substantial oxygen consumption by tissues, not the initial atmospheric oxygen tension.

preguntas.q: After inspired air becomes fully humidified in the trachea, its PO2 falls to approximately how many mmHg?

e.correcta: Humidified tracheal air's PO2 is calculated as (barometric pressure - water vapor pressure) × fractional O2 concentration, or (760 - 47) × 0.21 ≈ 150 mmHg. The 47 mmHg water vapor pressure at body temperature (37°C) displaces some of the pressure otherwise available to O2 and other gases, so this value is lower than the 160 mmHg seen in dry inspired air, even though no gas exchange with blood has yet occurred at this point.

incorrectas.A: 160 mmHg is the PO2 of dry inspired air before humidification; it does not yet account for the dilutional effect of water vapor pressure that occurs as air passes through the moist upper airway on its way to the alveoli.
incorrectas.B: 100 mmHg is the PO2 in the alveoli and arterial blood, a further reduction from the tracheal value that occurs because alveolar O2 is also being continuously exchanged for CO2 arriving from the pulmonary capillaries, a step beyond simple humidification.
incorrectas.D: 47 mmHg is itself the water vapor pressure at 37°C (the value being subtracted from barometric pressure in the calculation), not the resulting PO2 of humidified air.

preguntas.q: The partial pressure of oxygen in alveolar gas (PAO2) and in arterial blood (PaO2) is normally approximately how many mmHg?

e.correcta: PAO2 and PaO2 normally equilibrate at approximately 100 mmHg because O2 exhibits perfusion-limited exchange under normal conditions, meaning it fully equilibrates across the alveolar-capillary membrane well before blood exits the capillary. This value is lower than the PO2 of humidified tracheal air (150 mmHg) because alveolar gas is a mixture that also contains CO2 diffusing in from the blood, which displaces some of the O2's share of alveolar pressure (formalized in the alveolar gas equation).

incorrectas.A: 150 mmHg is the PO2 of humidified tracheal air upstream of the alveoli; alveolar PO2 is further reduced from this value by the continuous arrival of CO2 from pulmonary capillary blood and ongoing O2 uptake into the capillaries.
incorrectas.C: 40 mmHg is the PO2 of mixed venous blood returning to the lungs (and it is also the normal value for both PACO2/PaCO2 and PvO2), representing a tissue-depleted oxygen level, not the freshly oxygenated alveolar/arterial value.
incorrectas.D: 160 mmHg is the PO2 of dry inspired atmospheric air prior to humidification, well upstream of the alveoli and substantially higher than the equilibrated alveolar/arterial value due to both water vapor dilution and gas exchange.

preguntas.q: The partial pressure of carbon dioxide in alveolar gas (PACO2) and in arterial blood (PaCO2) is normally approximately how many mmHg?

e.correcta: PACO2 and PaCO2 normally equilibrate at approximately 40 mmHg, reflecting the balance between CO2 production by tissue metabolism, its delivery to the lungs in venous blood, and its efficient elimination via alveolar ventilation. Because CO2 has a diffusion coefficient roughly 20 times that of O2, it equilibrates across the alveolar-capillary membrane essentially instantaneously, and PaCO2 is tightly regulated by the respiratory center to stay near this set-point, making it the primary clinical marker of ventilation adequacy.

incorrectas.B: 100 mmHg is the normal value for alveolar and arterial PO2, not PCO2; O2 and CO2 have very different normal partial pressures because atmospheric air contains abundant O2 but essentially no CO2, while metabolism continuously adds CO2 to venous blood.
incorrectas.A: 46 mmHg is the PCO2 of mixed venous blood (PvCO2) before it is delivered to the lungs and CO2 is eliminated by ventilation, representing a slightly higher, pre-gas-exchange value rather than the equilibrated alveolar/arterial value.
incorrectas.D: 47 mmHg is the water vapor pressure at body temperature (37°C), a value used in gas equation calculations for humidified air, unrelated numerically or physiologically to the partial pressure of CO2.

preguntas.q: The partial pressure of oxygen in mixed venous blood (PvO2), i.e., blood returning to the lungs after peripheral tissues have extracted oxygen, is normally approximately how many mmHg?

e.correcta: PvO2 is normally about 40 mmHg, reflecting the oxygen tension remaining in blood after peripheral tissues have extracted O2 for aerobic metabolism as blood traverses the systemic capillary beds. This venous blood then returns to the pulmonary capillaries, where it re-equilibrates with alveolar gas (PAO2 ≈ 100 mmHg) across the thin alveolar-capillary membrane, restoring PO2 to arterial levels before returning to the systemic circulation.

incorrectas.A: 100 mmHg is the PO2 of fully oxygenated alveolar and arterial blood, representing the state before tissues have extracted oxygen — it is the value venous blood is moving away from, not its own resting value.
incorrectas.B: 46 mmHg is the normal value for PvCO2 (mixed venous CO2), a value elevated relative to arterial PCO2 (40 mmHg) because tissues are adding CO2 to venous blood, not the corresponding value for venous O2.
incorrectas.D: 150 mmHg is the PO2 of humidified tracheal air upstream in the airway, a value far higher than any point in the venous circulation, since venous blood has already given up much of its oxygen to metabolizing tissue.

preguntas.q: The partial pressure of carbon dioxide in mixed venous blood (PvCO2) is normally approximately how many mmHg?

e.correcta: PvCO2 is normally about 46 mmHg, slightly higher than arterial PaCO2 (40 mmHg), because peripheral tissues continuously produce CO2 as a byproduct of aerobic metabolism and load it into the venous blood as it leaves the capillary beds. When this venous blood reaches the pulmonary capillaries, CO2 (which diffuses about 20 times faster than O2) rapidly re-equilibrates with alveolar gas, dropping back to the arterial/alveolar value of 40 mmHg before the blood is reoxygenated and recirculated.

incorrectas.A: 40 mmHg is the equilibrated alveolar and arterial PCO2 value, reached only after venous blood passes through the lungs and offloads its extra CO2 into the alveoli; it is lower than the venous value because it reflects the post-gas-exchange state.
incorrectas.B: 100 mmHg is the normal PO2 in alveolar gas and arterial blood, an entirely different gas and an entirely different (much higher, oxygen-specific) normal value, not applicable to venous CO2.
incorrectas.D: 47 mmHg is the water vapor pressure at 37°C used in gas-law calculations for humidified air, a constant physical property of water vapor rather than a measured blood gas partial pressure.

preguntas.q: What is the fundamental driving force for the net diffusion of a respiratory gas across the alveolar-capillary membrane?

o.A: The temperature gradient between alveolus and capillary
o.B: The partial pressure gradient of the gas
o.C: The osmotic gradient across the membrane
o.D: The pH gradient between alveolar gas and blood

e.correcta: Gas molecules move from a region of higher partial pressure to a region of lower partial pressure until equilibrium is reached, and the magnitude of this partial pressure gradient (along with the membrane's diffusing capacity) determines both the direction and rate of net gas transfer, as formalized by Fick's law of diffusion. This is why, for example, O2 with a high alveolar partial pressure (~100 mmHg) diffuses into venous capillary blood with a lower partial pressure (~40 mmHg), while CO2 does the reverse.

incorrectas.A: The alveolar-capillary membrane and adjacent blood are essentially at the same body temperature, and temperature differences are not the mechanism used to explain or drive respiratory gas exchange in normal physiology.
incorrectas.C: Osmotic gradients govern the movement of water and solutes across membranes based on solute concentration differences affecting water movement, a distinct phenomenon from the partial-pressure-driven diffusion of dissolved respiratory gases.
incorrectas.D: While pH affects the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve and bicarbonate buffering of CO2, it is not itself the driving force for gas diffusion across the membrane; that role belongs specifically to the partial pressure gradient of the gas in question.

preguntas.q: When a gas is dissolved in blood, which fraction of that gas actually contributes to its measured partial pressure?

o.A: The fraction bound to plasma proteins
o.D: The total gas content, bound plus dissolved

e.correcta: Partial pressure reflects only the free, physically dissolved gas molecules in solution, because it is this freely moving fraction that exerts pressure and drives further diffusion (per Henry's law); gas that is chemically bound (e.g., O2 bound to hemoglobin, or CO2 as bicarbonate or carbaminohemoglobin) is 'hidden' from the partial pressure measurement even though it constitutes the vast majority of total gas content in blood. This distinction explains why blood can carry large total quantities of O2 and CO2 while their measured partial pressures (PaO2, PaCO2) remain relatively modest.

incorrectas.A: Respiratory gases like O2 and CO2 are not meaningfully carried bound to plasma proteins (unlike, say, bilirubin bound to albumin); the major carrier mechanisms are hemoglobin binding and bicarbonate formation, and in any case bound gas does not contribute to partial pressure.
incorrectas.B: Hemoglobin-bound O2 makes up the large majority of total blood oxygen content, but bound O2 exerts no partial pressure of its own — it is precisely the free, dissolved O2 that determines PaO2, and hemoglobin loading/unloading responds to changes in that free fraction.
incorrectas.D: Total gas content (bound plus dissolved) is what is measured as oxygen or CO2 content of blood (e.g., mL O2/dL blood), a distinct concept from partial pressure, which specifically isolates only the freely dissolved portion of the gas.

preguntas.q: In which type of gas exchange does the gas fail to fully equilibrate between alveolar air and capillary blood by the time blood reaches the end of the pulmonary capillary?

e.correcta: In diffusion-limited gas exchange, exemplified by carbon monoxide, the gas crosses the alveolar-capillary membrane so slowly (due to its chemical binding characteristics, in CO's case its enormous affinity for hemoglobin keeping free plasma PCO near zero) that equilibrium between alveolar and capillary partial pressures is never reached during the normal transit time through the capillary. Because equilibrium is never achieved, increasing blood flow (perfusion) does not meaningfully increase total CO uptake — uptake is capped by how fast molecules can cross the membrane itself, which is exactly what makes CO ideal for measuring diffusing capacity (DLCO).

incorrectas.A: Perfusion-limited exchange (the pattern seen with O2 in health and with N2O) is the opposite situation — the gas equilibrates rapidly and completely well before the end of the capillary, so the only way to increase total gas uptake is to increase the rate of blood flow delivering fresh, unequilibrated blood.
incorrectas.B: Convection-limited exchange is not a standard physiologic term used to classify alveolar-capillary gas transfer; the two classic categories taught are diffusion-limited and perfusion-limited exchange.
incorrectas.D: Ventilation-limited exchange is not the standard term for this phenomenon either; while overall gas exchange does depend on adequate ventilation, the specific distinction being tested here (whether equilibrium is reached across the capillary) is described using the diffusion- versus perfusion-limited framework.

preguntas.q: In which type of gas exchange does the gas equilibrate between alveolar air and capillary blood early along the length of the pulmonary capillary, such that blood flow becomes the limiting factor for total uptake?

e.correcta: In perfusion-limited gas exchange, exemplified by nitrous oxide (N2O), the alveolar membrane poses essentially no barrier to diffusion, so the gas's partial pressure in capillary blood rises rapidly and matches the alveolar partial pressure well before blood reaches the venous end of the capillary. Because equilibrium is reached early, the total amount of gas taken up is determined only by how much blood (perfusion) passes through the capillary per unit time — more blood flow means more total gas uptake, whereas increasing diffusing capacity would have little additional effect since the gas is already at equilibrium.

incorrectas.A: Diffusion-limited exchange (as with carbon monoxide) is the opposite scenario, in which the gas never reaches equilibrium across the membrane during the normal capillary transit time, so uptake is capped by the diffusing capacity of the membrane rather than by blood flow.
incorrectas.B: 'Membrane-limited' is not the standard term used in this classification; the two recognized categories in respiratory physiology are diffusion-limited and perfusion-limited exchange, and this scenario (rapid equilibration limited by flow) corresponds to the latter.
incorrectas.D: While a gas's solubility contributes to its diffusion coefficient and therefore how quickly it can equilibrate, 'solubility-limited' is not the term used to classify this pattern of gas exchange; the accepted terminology is perfusion-limited when equilibrium is reached early.

preguntas.q: In a healthy person at rest, which pattern of gas exchange does oxygen (O2) exhibit across the alveolar-capillary membrane?

e.correcta: In normal health, O2 equilibrates between alveolar gas and capillary blood well before the blood reaches the end of the pulmonary capillary (typically by about one-third of the way along), meaning uptake is limited by how much blood is delivered (perfusion), not by how fast O2 can cross the membrane. This changes in disease states such as severe emphysema, fibrosis, or strenuous exercise with a very short capillary transit time, where O2 exchange can become relatively diffusion-limited, contributing to exercise-induced hypoxemia in those conditions.

incorrectas.A: O2 only behaves as diffusion-limited in pathologic states (e.g., significant interstitial thickening in pulmonary fibrosis) or under conditions that drastically shorten capillary transit time (e.g., high-intensity exercise, especially at altitude); under normal resting conditions, healthy membrane diffusing capacity is more than sufficient for O2 to fully equilibrate.
incorrectas.B: Ventilation-limited is not a standard classification term for alveolar-capillary gas exchange; overall arterial oxygenation does depend on adequate ventilation, but the specific perfusion-versus-diffusion framework is what's being tested here, and O2 falls into the perfusion-limited category.
incorrectas.D: 'Membrane-limited' is not the conventional term used; the accepted dichotomy taught for gas exchange is diffusion-limited versus perfusion-limited, and normal O2 exchange is classified as perfusion-limited.

preguntas.q: Carbon dioxide (CO2) exchange across the alveolar-capillary membrane is normally characterized by which pattern?

e.correcta: CO2 is perfusion-limited, just like O2 under normal conditions, because its diffusion coefficient is approximately 20 times greater than that of O2 (owing to its much higher solubility in tissue), allowing it to equilibrate across the alveolar-capillary membrane even more rapidly and completely than oxygen does. As a result, the amount of CO2 eliminated per unit time depends chiefly on pulmonary blood flow and alveolar ventilation rather than on membrane diffusing capacity, which is why CO2 retention in lung disease usually reflects a ventilation problem rather than a diffusion problem.

incorrectas.A: Diffusion-limited exchange describes gases like carbon monoxide, which never reach equilibrium across the membrane during normal capillary transit; CO2's very high diffusion coefficient makes it the opposite case, equilibrating rapidly rather than being capped by diffusion capacity.
incorrectas.C: 'Solubility-limited' is not a recognized category in the diffusion-versus-perfusion framework; solubility is one factor that helps determine a gas's diffusion coefficient (and thus contributes to why CO2 is perfusion-limited), but it is not itself the classification term.
incorrectas.D: 'Concentration-limited' is not a standard physiologic term used to classify alveolar-capillary gas exchange; the two recognized patterns taught are diffusion-limited and perfusion-limited, and CO2 falls into the perfusion-limited category.

preguntas.q: Nitrous oxide (N2O) has a very low blood solubility. Which pattern of gas exchange limitation does it exhibit across the pulmonary capillary?

e.correcta: Because N2O has low solubility in blood, the plasma partial pressure of N2O rises rapidly and equilibrates with alveolar partial pressure early in the capillary transit, well before the blood reaches the end of the capillary. Once equilibrium is reached, no further net diffusion occurs regardless of how much capillary length remains, so the only way to move more gas is to increase blood flow (perfusion) past the alveolus. This is why N2O (like O2 under normal conditions) is called perfusion-limited.

incorrectas.A: Diffusion-limited gases (like CO, or O2/CO2 in fibrosis/emphysema) never reach equilibrium with alveolar gas during the normal capillary transit time because they are either highly soluble in blood/tissue (CO binds hemoglobin avidly) or the diffusion barrier is abnormally thick; N2O's low solubility means it does the opposite, equilibrating quickly.
incorrectas.C: Gas exchange is not classified by a 'pressure-limited' category in respiratory physiology; the two clinically tested categories are diffusion-limited and perfusion-limited, based on whether equilibrium is reached before blood exits the capillary.
incorrectas.D: There is no standard 'membrane-limited' category either; the actual determinant is whether the gas's solubility allows it to saturate the blood before transit ends, not a fixed property of the alveolar-capillary membrane itself.

preguntas.q: Carbon monoxide (CO) is used to measure diffusion capacity of the lung (DLCO) because it exhibits which pattern of gas exchange?

e.correcta: CO binds hemoglobin with extremely high affinity (about 200-250 times that of O2), so essentially all CO that diffuses into the blood is immediately bound and removed from free solution, keeping the plasma partial pressure of CO very low throughout the capillary. Because equilibrium between alveolar and capillary CO is never reached during normal transit time, CO uptake depends entirely on the rate of diffusion across the alveolar-capillary membrane, not on how much blood flows past — this is exactly why DLCO is used clinically as a measure of the diffusing capacity of the lung.

incorrectas.A: Perfusion-limited gases (like N2O, and O2 under normal healthy conditions) equilibrate with alveolar gas early in the capillary transit, so increasing blood flow is the only way to increase total uptake; CO never reaches equilibrium, so it behaves oppositely.
incorrectas.C: There is no 'facilitated-limited' category in gas exchange physiology; facilitated diffusion refers to carrier-mediated membrane transport of molecules like glucose, not the alveolar-capillary gas exchange classification.
incorrectas.D: Convection describes bulk airflow moving gas through the airways during ventilation, not the diffusion of gas across the alveolar-capillary membrane into blood, so it is not the mechanism being tested here.

preguntas.q: In a patient with pulmonary fibrosis, oxygen transfer across the thickened alveolar-capillary membrane shifts from its normal exchange pattern to which pattern, contributing to hypoxemia?

e.correcta: Normally O2 is perfusion-limited, equilibrating with alveolar gas well before blood exits the capillary. When lung tissue is diseased (fibrosis thickens the membrane, emphysema destroys surface area), the rate of O2 diffusion slows enough that capillary blood no longer reaches equilibrium with alveolar O2 by the time it leaves the capillary — O2 becomes diffusion-limited. Because the blood picks up O2 more slowly and never fully equilibrates, arterial O2 content falls, which is one mechanism driving hypoxemia in these diseases.

incorrectas.A: Perfusion-limited is the normal pattern for O2 in a healthy lung, where equilibrium is reached quickly and blood flow becomes the limiting factor; diseased lung tissue disrupts this by slowing diffusion, converting O2 to the diffusion-limited pattern instead.
incorrectas.C: Osmotic forces govern water movement across membranes based on solute concentration gradients, not the diffusion of a respiratory gas like O2 across the alveolar-capillary interface, so this is not a real gas-exchange category.
incorrectas.D: O2 crosses the alveolar-capillary membrane by simple passive diffusion down its partial pressure gradient, not by an energy-requiring active transport mechanism, so labeling it 'active transport-limited' misrepresents the actual physiology.

preguntas.q: The hemoglobin molecule is a globular protein made up of how many polypeptide subunits?

e.correcta: Hemoglobin is a tetramer composed of four globin chains (in adult HbA, two alpha and two beta chains), each carrying one heme group with an iron atom capable of binding one O2 molecule. This quaternary structure is essential for cooperative binding: oxygenation of one subunit induces a conformational shift (taut to relaxed) that increases the O2 affinity of the remaining subunits, producing the sigmoidal oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve.

incorrectas.A: A two-subunit (dimeric) structure would not permit the positive cooperativity that gives hemoglobin its characteristic sigmoidal binding curve; myoglobin, by contrast, is a true monomer (one subunit) and shows no cooperativity at all, producing a hyperbolic curve instead.
incorrectas.B: Hemoglobin has no three-subunit intermediate form under normal physiology; it functions as an intact tetramer, and partial complexes of three subunits are not the stable, functional unit found in circulating blood.
incorrectas.D: Six subunits would exceed hemoglobin's actual tetrameric structure; some other oligomeric proteins have six subunits, but hemoglobin's two alpha/two beta arrangement is fixed at four.

preguntas.q: In normal, functional hemoglobin, the iron atom within each heme group is maintained in which oxidation state?

e.correcta: Normal hemoglobin holds its heme iron in the ferrous (Fe2+) state, which is the form capable of reversibly binding O2.
