Cellular mechanisms, including methemoglobin reductase (NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase), continuously reduce any iron that becomes oxidized back to Fe2+, preserving the blood's O2-carrying capacity.

incorrectas.A: Ferric iron (Fe3+) is the oxidized state found in methemoglobin, which cannot bind O2 effectively; this is an abnormal state that oxidizing drugs (nitrates, sulfa drugs) or toxins push hemoglobin toward, not the normal resting state.
incorrectas.C: Elemental iron (Fe0) is not a form found in biological heme chemistry; heme iron exists in ionic oxidation states (Fe2+ or Fe3+) coordinated within the porphyrin ring, not as neutral metal.
incorrectas.D: Ferrate (Fe6+) is a highly oxidized, unstable iron species used in some industrial oxidizing agents, not a physiologic form of iron found in hemoglobin.

preguntas.q: Compared to normal ferrous hemoglobin (Fe2+), methemoglobin (Fe3+) binds oxygen how?

e.correcta: Oxidizing the heme iron to the ferric (Fe3+) state distorts its coordination chemistry so that it can no longer bind O2 reversibly the way ferrous iron does; methemoglobin therefore binds O2 much less readily. Additionally, any remaining ferrous subunits within a methemoglobin-containing tetramer have their O2 affinity increased (left-shifted curve), so what O2 is bound is held too tightly to unload at the tissues — compounding the functional hypoxia.

incorrectas.A: Equal affinity would mean methemoglobinemia caused no clinical harm, but the oxidized Fe3+ heme fundamentally loses the ability to coordinate O2 normally, which is exactly why methemoglobinemia causes tissue hypoxia despite a normal PaO2.
incorrectas.C: Fe3+ heme does not bind O2 more readily; the oxidation state change impairs O2 binding rather than enhancing it, which is the opposite of what happens and the reason methemoglobinemia is dangerous.
incorrectas.D: 2,3-BPG modulates O2 affinity by binding the beta chains of normal ferrous hemoglobin to promote O2 unloading; it is not a cofactor required for methemoglobin to bind O2, and methemoglobin's core problem is impaired binding, not a cofactor deficiency.

preguntas.q: Which two drug classes are classically associated with causing methemoglobinemia?

e.correcta: Nitrates/nitrites (e.g., used for angina, or from dietary/well-water sources) and sulfa drugs (e.g., sulfonamide antibiotics, dapsone) are the classic oxidizing agents that convert ferrous (Fe2+) hemoglobin to ferric (Fe3+) methemoglobin, which cannot carry O2 properly. Patients present with cyanosis and a low SaO2 by pulse oximetry despite a normal PaO2, and treatment is IV methylene blue, which helps re-reduce the iron back to Fe2+.

incorrectas.A: Beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors act on adrenergic receptors and the renin-angiotensin system respectively, affecting blood pressure and heart rate; neither class oxidizes hemoglobin iron, so they are not linked to methemoglobinemia.
incorrectas.C: Statins and fibrates are lipid-lowering agents that act on cholesterol synthesis (HMG-CoA reductase) and lipoprotein metabolism (PPAR-alpha); they have no oxidizing effect on heme iron and are not associated with methemoglobinemia.
incorrectas.D: Opioids and benzodiazepines are CNS depressants that act on opioid and GABA-A receptors respectively, causing sedation and respiratory depression; they do not oxidize hemoglobin and are not a recognized cause of methemoglobinemia.

preguntas.q: Ingestion of polluted or high-altitude well water can cause methemoglobinemia due to contamination with which compound?

e.correcta: Nitrites contaminating well water (from agricultural runoff/fertilizer breakdown, particularly in shallow wells at high altitude or in polluted areas) are potent oxidizing agents that convert ferrous (Fe2+) hemoglobin iron to the ferric (Fe3+) state, producing methemoglobin. This is a classic cause of infantile methemoglobinemia ('blue baby syndrome' from well water), since infants have relatively low levels of methemoglobin reductase and are especially vulnerable.

incorrectas.B: Sulfates are inert anions in this context and are not oxidizing agents toward heme iron; sulfa drugs (a different chemical class entirely) cause methemoglobinemia, but sulfate contamination of water does not.
incorrectas.C: Chloride is a common, physiologically important anion (e.g., in the chloride shift) but has no oxidizing effect on hemoglobin iron and is not linked to methemoglobinemia from water contamination.
incorrectas.D: Phosphate contamination of water is not associated with oxidizing heme iron; phosphates are relevant to bone/mineral metabolism and buffering, not to converting Fe2+ to Fe3+ in hemoglobin.

preguntas.q: In a patient with methemoglobinemia, what are the expected SaO2, O2 content, and PaO2?

o.A: Decreased SaO2, decreased O2 content, decreased PaO2
o.B: Normal SaO2, normal O2 content, decreased PaO2
o.C: Decreased SaO2, decreased O2 content, normal PaO2
o.D: Increased SaO2, normal O2 content, normal PaO2

e.correcta: PaO2 measures dissolved O2 in plasma and is unaffected by hemoglobin's ability to bind O2, so it stays normal. However, because Fe3+ heme cannot bind O2 properly, the fraction of functional hemoglobin actually saturated with O2 (SaO2, measured by co-oximetry) falls, and since O2 content depends heavily on hemoglobin-bound O2 (content ≈ 1.34 × Hb × SaO2 + dissolved O2), O2 content falls too — producing tissue hypoxia despite a deceptively normal PaO2 on a standard blood gas.

incorrectas.A: PaO2 reflects only the dissolved O2 driven by alveolar gas exchange, which is unaffected by methemoglobin formation; lungs are ventilating and oxygenating plasma normally, so PaO2 remains normal even though hemoglobin-bound O2 delivery is impaired.
incorrectas.B: PaO2 does not decrease in methemoglobinemia because the lungs still oxygenate the dissolved O2 fraction normally; the defect is in hemoglobin's ability to bind and carry O2, which lowers SaO2 and O2 content, not PaO2.
incorrectas.D: SaO2 falls rather than rises in methemoglobinemia because oxidized Fe3+ heme cannot bind O2 normally; an increased SaO2 would imply enhanced O2 binding, which is the opposite of the pathology.

preguntas.q: How does the O2-binding affinity of fetal hemoglobin (HbF) compare to that of adult hemoglobin (HbA)?

o.A: HbF has much higher affinity than HbA
o.B: HbF has much lower affinity than HbA
o.C: HbF and HbA have identical affinity
o.D: HbF's affinity depends only on 2,3-BPG levels, unlike HbA

e.correcta: HbF (composed of two alpha and two gamma chains) binds 2,3-BPG less avidly than HbA does, because the gamma chains lack some of the positively charged residues that HbA's beta chains use to bind 2,3-BPG. With less 2,3-BPG bound, HbF's oxygen-hemoglobin curve is left-shifted relative to HbA, giving it a much higher O2 affinity — a property that is functionally essential for extracting O2 from maternal blood at the placenta.

incorrectas.B: A lower affinity would work against the fetus, since it needs to pull O2 away from maternal HbA at the placental interface; the actual physiology is the opposite — HbF's affinity is higher, not lower, than HbA's.
incorrectas.C: If HbF and HbA had identical affinity there would be no net gradient favoring O2 transfer from mother to fetus at the placenta; the entire point of HbF's distinct structure is to create a higher-affinity sink for O2 relative to HbA.
incorrectas.D: While 2,3-BPG binding does modulate affinity for both HbA and HbF, HbF's affinity is not solely determined by 2,3-BPG; it is intrinsically higher because gamma chains bind 2,3-BPG poorly compared to HbA's beta chains, and both proteins are affected by 2,3-BPG to differing degrees, not just HbF.

preguntas.q: What is the physiologic reason fetal hemoglobin must have a much higher O2-binding affinity than adult hemoglobin?

o.A: It slows fetal metabolic rate to conserve O2
o.B: It drives O2 diffusion across the placenta from mother to fetus
o.C: It prevents fetal red cells from sickling
o.D: It compensates for a lower fetal red cell count

e.correcta: At the placental interface, maternal HbA must release O2 to fetal blood; because HbF has a higher intrinsic O2 affinity than HbA (due to reduced 2,3-BPG binding by its gamma chains), the O2 partial pressure gradient favors net transfer from maternal to fetal circulation. This higher affinity acts as a 'pull' that drives efficient placental O2 diffusion, ensuring adequate fetal oxygenation even though fetal PaO2 is much lower than adult PaO2.

incorrectas.A: HbF's high affinity is about facilitating O2 uptake at the placenta, not about slowing metabolism; fetal metabolic rate is regulated by other mechanisms unrelated to hemoglobin O2 affinity.
incorrectas.C: Sickling is a property specific to HbS (a beta-globin structural variant), not something prevented or caused by O2 affinity differences between HbF and HbA; HbF's high affinity is unrelated to sickle hemoglobin polymerization, though clinically increasing HbF (e.g., with hydroxyurea) does reduce sickling by a different mechanism (diluting HbS polymer formation).
incorrectas.D: Fetal red cell count and hemoglobin affinity are separate variables; the higher affinity is a qualitative property of the HbF molecule needed for placental gas exchange, not a compensation for red cell quantity.

preguntas.q: Hemoglobin can exist in two structural conformations. What are they, and which is deoxygenated?

e.correcta: Hemoglobin exists in equilibrium between the taut (T) state, which has low O2 affinity and predominates when deoxygenated, and the relaxed (R) state, which has high O2 affinity and predominates when oxygenated. Binding of O2 to one subunit favors a conformational shift of the whole tetramer toward the R state, increasing the affinity of the remaining subunits — this positive cooperativity is what produces the sigmoidal shape of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve.

incorrectas.B: This reverses the correct relationship: the low-affinity taut state is the deoxygenated form (found in peripheral tissues where O2 is unloaded), while the high-affinity relaxed state is the oxygenated form (found in the lungs where O2 is loaded), not the other way around.
incorrectas.C: Cis/trans terminology describes isomerism around double bonds or ring structures in organic chemistry, not the quaternary conformational states of a multi-subunit protein like hemoglobin.
incorrectas.D: Alpha and beta refer to the two types of globin polypeptide chains that make up the hemoglobin tetramer (two alpha, two beta in HbA), not to the taut/relaxed conformational states that each subunit can adopt.

preguntas.q: Which conformational state of hemoglobin predominates in peripheral tissues, where low O2 affinity favors oxygen unloading?

e.correcta: In peripheral tissues, where local CO2, H+, and 2,3-BPG are relatively high and pO2 is low, hemoglobin is stabilized in the taut (T) conformation, which has low O2 affinity. This low affinity is exactly what allows hemoglobin to release its bound O2 to metabolically active tissue rather than holding onto it — the physiologic purpose of the T state.

incorrectas.A: The relaxed (R) state has high O2 affinity and predominates where hemoglobin is picking up O2 (the pulmonary capillaries), which is the opposite of what is needed in peripheral tissue, where O2 must be released, not retained.
incorrectas.C: 'Allosteric state' is not a specific named conformation of hemoglobin; allostery is the general mechanism (cooperative binding via conformational change) that explains the T-to-R transition, not a state itself.
incorrectas.D: 'Fetal state' is not a conformational term; it refers to a different hemoglobin protein (HbF, made of different globin chains) rather than a T/R conformational state that any hemoglobin variant can adopt.

preguntas.q: In the pulmonary capillaries, where hemoglobin is loading up on O2, which conformational state predominates?

e.correcta: In the lungs, high alveolar pO2 and relatively low CO2/H+ favor the relaxed (R) conformation of hemoglobin, which has high O2 affinity. This high-affinity state allows hemoglobin to efficiently bind and load O2 as blood passes through the pulmonary capillaries, then carry that O2 to the periphery where the low-affinity taut state takes over to release it.

incorrectas.A: The taut (T) state has low O2 affinity and is favored in peripheral tissue where O2 is being released, not in the lungs where O2 is being picked up; using the T state in the respiratory tract would impair O2 loading.
incorrectas.C: 'Deoxy state' is essentially describing the taut conformation by another name — it is the low-affinity state associated with deoxygenated hemoglobin in tissues, not the state found in the oxygen-rich pulmonary capillaries.
incorrectas.D: Methemoglobin refers to hemoglobin with oxidized (Fe3+) iron that cannot bind O2 properly at all; it is a pathologic state, not a normal physiologic conformation associated with O2 loading in the lungs.

preguntas.q: Under normal conditions, how much O2 can be bound per gram of hemoglobin?

e.correcta: Each gram of fully saturated hemoglobin can carry 1.34 mL of O2; this constant (Hüfner's constant) is a key term in the O2 content equation: O2 content = (1.34 × Hb × SaO2) + (0.003 × PaO2). It reflects the stoichiometry of O2 molecules binding to heme groups across the roughly 64,500 Da hemoglobin tetramer and is essential for calculating how much O2 the blood can carry given a patient's hemoglobin level and saturation.

incorrectas.A: 0.3 mL O2/g Hb is far too low and does not correspond to the accepted physiologic constant; using this value would grossly underestimate a patient's O2-carrying capacity in the O2 content equation.
incorrectas.C: 3.4 mL O2/g Hb overstates the true binding capacity by roughly 2.5-fold; this number is sometimes confused with the correct constant but does not match the actual established Hüfner's constant of 1.34.
incorrectas.D: 13.4 mL O2/g Hb is off by an order of magnitude from the correct constant and would produce absurdly high, physiologically impossible O2 content calculations.

preguntas.q: What is the approximate normal hemoglobin concentration in whole blood?

e.correcta: Normal blood hemoglobin concentration is approximately 15 g/dL (with typical reference ranges around 13.5-17.5 g/dL in men and 12-16 g/dL in women). This value is a key input into the O2 content equation and, when multiplied by the O2-binding constant of 1.34 mL O2/g Hb, gives the normal O2-binding capacity of blood (~20.1 mL O2/100 mL blood at full saturation).

incorrectas.A: ~5 g/dL would represent severe, life-threatening anemia, not a normal hemoglobin level; a value this low would produce markedly reduced O2-carrying capacity and typically requires transfusion.
incorrectas.B: ~10 g/dL is below the normal range and would indicate at least moderate anemia; while it is not as extreme as 5 g/dL, it still does not represent the normal average concentration of ~15 g/dL.
incorrectas.D: ~25 g/dL is far above even the upper limits seen in significant polycythemia and does not reflect a physiologically typical or even commonly pathologic hemoglobin concentration.

preguntas.q: What is the normal O2-binding capacity of blood, expressed as mL of O2 per 100 mL of blood?

e.correcta: O2-binding capacity is calculated as hemoglobin concentration times the O2-binding constant: ~15 g Hb/dL × 1.34 mL O2/g Hb ≈ 20.1 mL O2 per 100 mL of blood. This represents the maximum O2 the hemoglobin in blood could carry if fully saturated, and it is the ceiling value used alongside actual SaO2 to compute real O2 content.

incorrectas.A: 10.1 mL O2/100 mL blood is roughly half the correct value and would only be seen with a hemoglobin concentration around 7.5 g/dL, corresponding to significant anemia rather than the normal binding capacity.
incorrectas.C: 30.1 mL O2/100 mL blood overstates normal capacity; achieving this would require a hemoglobin concentration well above the normal range (more consistent with significant polycythemia), not the typical ~15 g/dL.
incorrectas.D: 1.34 mL O2/100 mL blood confuses the per-gram binding constant (1.34 mL O2 per gram of hemoglobin) with the total binding capacity of whole blood, which also depends on the actual hemoglobin concentration present.

preguntas.q: Which equation correctly calculates the O2 content of blood?

e.correcta: O2 content = (1.34 × Hb × SaO2) + (0.003 × PaO2) sums the two pools of O2 in blood: hemoglobin-bound O2 (1.34 mL O2 per gram of fully saturated Hb, multiplied by hemoglobin concentration and the fraction saturated) and dissolved O2 (governed by its solubility coefficient of 0.003 mL O2/dL/mmHg times PaO2). The hemoglobin-bound term dominates total content under normal conditions, which is why anemia (low Hb) or hypoxemia (low SaO2) drop O2 content much more than changes in dissolved O2 alone would.

incorrectas.A: This swaps the two constants — 0.003 is the solubility coefficient that should multiply PaO2 (the dissolved O2 term), while 1.34 is the binding constant that should multiply Hb × SaO2 (the hemoglobin-bound term); reversing them produces a nonsensical, physiologically wrong result.
incorrectas.C: Cardiac output × Hb does not calculate O2 content; cardiac output multiplied by O2 content actually gives O2 delivery to tissues, a related but distinct concept from O2 content itself.
incorrectas.D: This omits the hemoglobin concentration entirely and incorrectly multiplies PaO2 by SaO2, which conflates dissolved O2 (dependent on PaO2 and solubility) with hemoglobin-bound O2 (dependent on Hb and SaO2) in a way that does not reflect the real physiology.

preguntas.q: In a patient with decreased hemoglobin (e.g., iron deficiency anemia) but otherwise normal lungs, what are the expected SaO2, O2 content, and PaO2?

o.A: Decreased SaO2, decreased O2 content, decreased PaO2
o.B: Normal SaO2, decreased O2 content, normal PaO2
o.C: Decreased SaO2, normal O2 content, normal PaO2
o.D: Normal SaO2, normal O2 content, decreased PaO2

e.correcta: In simple anemia, the lungs still ventilate and oxygenate normally, so PaO2 (dissolved O2, driven by alveolar gas exchange) is normal, and the hemoglobin that is present still binds O2 normally, so SaO2 (percent saturation of available hemoglobin) is also normal. However, because O2 content = (1.34 × Hb × SaO2) + dissolved O2, and Hb itself is reduced, total O2 content falls even though both PaO2 and SaO2 are normal — there is simply less hemoglobin available to carry O2.

incorrectas.A: SaO2 and PaO2 do not fall in simple anemia because the problem is a quantity deficit (too little hemoglobin), not a gas exchange or hemoglobin-binding defect; the lungs and the hemoglobin present both function normally, so only O2 content (which depends on Hb quantity) drops.
incorrectas.C: SaO2 is normal, not decreased, in anemia — the hemoglobin present binds O2 to its usual percentage; it is the total O2 content that falls because there is less hemoglobin overall, not because each hemoglobin molecule binds less O2.
incorrectas.D: PaO2 remains normal in anemia because it reflects alveolar-to-blood O2 diffusion, which is unimpaired; it is O2 content, not PaO2, that decreases due to the reduced amount of hemoglobin available to carry O2.

preguntas.q: Which equation is used to calculate O2 delivery to tissues?

o.B: O2 delivery = cardiac output × O2 content of blood

e.correcta: O2 delivery (DO2) = cardiac output × O2 content of blood, meaning tissue oxygen delivery depends on both how much blood is pumped per minute and how much O2 each unit of that blood carries. This equation explains why both cardiac failure (low cardiac output) and severe anemia or hypoxemia (low O2 content) can independently impair tissue oxygenation, and why clinical management of shock addresses both variables.

incorrectas.A: PaO2 × SaO2 is not a standard physiologic equation and conflates two different measures of oxygenation (dissolved gas pressure and hemoglobin saturation) without accounting for either hemoglobin concentration or the pump function of the heart, both of which are essential to actual O2 delivery.
incorrectas.C: Hb × 1.34 only calculates the maximum O2-binding capacity per unit of blood (assuming full saturation) — it says nothing about how much blood volume is being circulated to tissues per minute, which is required to determine actual delivery.
incorrectas.D: Stroke volume alone (without heart rate) does not equal cardiac output, and multiplying it by hemoglobin omits both the saturation term and the dissolved O2 term that make up true O2 content, making this an incomplete and incorrect formula.

preguntas.q: On the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, what is the term for the PO2 at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated with O2?

e.correcta: P50 is defined as the PO2 at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated, and it is used as a quantitative marker of hemoglobin's overall O2 affinity. A right shift of the curve (decreased affinity, e.g., from increased CO2, H+, temperature, or 2,3-BPG) necessarily raises the P50, since a higher PO2 is now required to achieve the same 50% saturation, while a left-shifted curve (increased affinity, e.g., HbF, decreased 2,3-BPG) lowers the P50.

incorrectas.B: PaO2 is simply the partial pressure of O2 in arterial blood at a given moment; it is a measured value in an individual patient, not the defined 50%-saturation reference point on the dissociation curve that P50 represents.
incorrectas.C: The A-a gradient measures the difference between alveolar and arterial PO2, used to assess for a gas exchange or shunt problem; it is unrelated to defining a specific saturation point on hemoglobin's oxygen dissociation curve.
incorrectas.D: PvO2 refers to the partial pressure of O2 in mixed venous blood, reflecting tissue O2 extraction, not the specific PO2 value corresponding to 50% hemoglobin saturation defined by P50.

preguntas.q: The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is relatively flat across which PO2 range, allowing tolerance of altitude or ventilation changes without major drops in O2 saturation?

e.correcta: Between roughly 60 and 100 mmHg PO2, the oxygen-hemoglobin curve is nearly flat, meaning hemoglobin remains highly saturated (generally above ~90%) across this whole range. This plateau gives a physiologic buffer: even moderate drops in alveolar PO2 (such as at altitude or with mild hypoventilation) cause only small changes in O2 saturation and content, protecting tissue oxygenation until PO2 falls below about 60 mmHg, at which point the steep part of the curve produces rapid desaturation.

incorrectas.A: 0-40 mmHg lies on the steep, not flat, portion of the curve — small changes in PO2 in this range produce large changes in saturation, which is exactly the region where the body can no longer buffer against desaturation, unlike the plateau at 60-100 mmHg.
incorrectas.C: 100-150 mmHg is above the normal alveolar-arterial physiologic range and, while the curve is also fairly flat here (already near 100% saturation), this is not the clinically emphasized plateau range; the tested range is 60-100 mmHg, which spans the normal-to-mildly-hypoxic zone relevant to altitude tolerance.
incorrectas.D: 20-60 mmHg largely overlaps with the steep portion of the curve, where saturation drops sharply with small PO2 decreases; this is the opposite of a flat, protective range and represents the region of rapid, clinically significant desaturation.

preguntas.q: Unlike the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, the oxygen-myoglobin dissociation curve is hyperbolic rather than sigmoidal. Why?

o.A: Myoglobin has four subunits with negative cooperativity
o.B: Myoglobin is monomeric and shows no positive cooperativity
o.C: Myoglobin binds 2,3-BPG, which linearizes the curve
o.D: Myoglobin has a much lower affinity for O2 than hemoglobin

e.correcta: Myoglobin is a single-subunit (monomeric) protein, so there is no possibility of one subunit's O2 binding altering the affinity of neighboring subunits — the positive cooperativity that produces hemoglobin's sigmoidal curve simply cannot occur. As a result, myoglobin's O2 binding follows simple hyperbolic (Michaelis-Menten-like) kinetics, and its very high, constant O2 affinity suits its role as an O2 storage protein in muscle rather than a transport protein that must both load and unload O2 across a range of tissue conditions.

incorrectas.A: Myoglobin is not tetrameric — it has only one subunit, not four, and it does not display negative cooperativity; negative cooperativity is not the relevant mechanism here, since cooperativity of any kind requires multiple interacting subunits, which myoglobin lacks entirely.
incorrectas.C: Myoglobin does not bind 2,3-BPG in a way that shapes its dissociation curve; the hyperbolic shape arises from myoglobin's monomeric structure lacking cooperative subunit interactions, not from any 2,3-BPG effect.
incorrectas.D: Myoglobin actually has a much higher O2 affinity than hemoglobin (its curve lies to the left of hemoglobin's), which fits its storage function in muscle; the shape difference (hyperbolic vs. sigmoidal) is due to cooperativity, not to a difference in affinity level.

preguntas.q: The phenomenon where increased pCO2 and the resulting decrease in pH enhance the release of O2 from hemoglobin at the tissue level is known as what?

e.correcta: The Bohr effect describes how increased CO2 and the resulting decreased pH in metabolically active tissue shift the oxygen-hemoglobin curve to the right, decreasing hemoglobin's O2 affinity and promoting O2 unloading exactly where it's needed. Mechanistically, CO2 diffuses into RBCs and is converted to HCO3- and H+ by carbonic anhydrase; the H+ is buffered by histidine residues on hemoglobin, stabilizing the low-affinity taut conformation and favoring O2 release.

incorrectas.A: The Haldane effect is the converse phenomenon — it describes how deoxygenation of hemoglobin in peripheral tissue increases hemoglobin's capacity to carry CO2 and H+ (as carbaminohemoglobin and via buffering), rather than describing how CO2/pH changes affect O2 affinity.
incorrectas.C: The chloride shift (Hamburger shift) refers to the exchange of HCO3- out of the RBC for Cl- into the RBC as CO2 is converted to bicarbonate in tissues; it maintains electroneutrality during CO2 transport but is not itself the effect of pH on O2 affinity.
incorrectas.D: 'Hamburger effect' is another name for the chloride shift (named after Hartog Jacob Hamburger), describing the same anion exchange process, not the pH-dependent change in hemoglobin's O2 affinity that defines the Bohr effect.

preguntas.q: 2,3-BPG decreases hemoglobin's affinity for O2 by binding to which part of the hemoglobin molecule?

o.D: The N-terminal valine of the alpha chains

e.correcta: 2,3-BPG binds in the central cavity formed between the two beta chains of deoxyhemoglobin, where its negative charges interact with positively charged residues unique to the beta chains. This binding stabilizes the low-affinity taut (T) conformation, shifting the oxygen-hemoglobin curve to the right and promoting O2 unloading at the tissues — a key adaptive mechanism during chronic hypoxia (e.g., high altitude, chronic anemia).

incorrectas.A: 2,3-BPG does not bind heme iron directly; iron is the actual O2-binding site, and 2,3-BPG instead binds a distinct site in the central cavity between the beta chains, allosterically reducing O2 affinity without touching the heme groups themselves.
incorrectas.B: 2,3-BPG selectively binds the beta chains, not the alpha chains; this beta-chain specificity is exactly why fetal hemoglobin (with gamma chains substituting for beta chains) binds 2,3-BPG poorly and therefore retains a higher O2 affinity.
incorrectas.D: While the N-terminal valines of the beta chains (not alpha chains) do contribute part of the 2,3-BPG binding pocket, describing the site as the alpha-chain N-terminus is incorrect; the beta chains, collectively, form the true binding site for 2,3-BPG.

preguntas.q: At high altitude, how do erythrocyte levels of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) change?

o.D: Transiently increased then normalized within hours

e.correcta: High altitude produces chronic hypoxemia, and the resulting tissue and red cell hypoxia stimulates glycolytic flux, including the Luebering-Rapoport shunt enzyme bisphosphoglycerate mutase, so 2,3-BPG accumulates in red cells. The rising 2,3-BPG binds preferentially to deoxyhemoglobin, stabilizing the low-affinity T (taut) state and shifting the oxygen-hemoglobin curve rightward, which helps unload more O2 to hypoxic tissues even though arterial saturation is reduced.

incorrectas.A: A decrease would blunt the compensatory right shift and worsen tissue oxygen delivery at altitude — this is the opposite of what actually happens; hypoxia is a stimulus that raises, not lowers, 2,3-BPG.
incorrectas.C: 2,3-BPG is not static; it is dynamically regulated by red cell metabolic conditions, and hypoxia is one of the classic triggers that increases its synthesis, so 'unchanged' misses the core physiologic adaptation being tested.
incorrectas.D: The rise in 2,3-BPG at altitude is sustained as long as the hypoxic stimulus persists (days to weeks of acclimatization), not a brief transient spike that resolves within hours.

preguntas.q: An increase in red blood cell 2,3-BPG, such as occurs at high altitude, is classically triggered by which condition?

e.correcta: Hypoxic conditions, whether from high altitude, chronic lung disease, or anemia, drive red cells to shunt more glucose-6-phosphate through the Luebering-Rapoport pathway, activating bisphosphoglycerate mutase and raising 2,3-BPG. The resulting local acidosis and 2,3-BPG accumulation stabilize deoxyhemoglobin, shifting the dissociation curve right so tissues extract more oxygen per unit of blood flow, a key adaptive response to low oxygen availability.

incorrectas.A: Hyperoxic conditions would reduce the hypoxic stimulus for glycolytic shunting, so 2,3-BPG would not be expected to rise — this is essentially the reverse of the trigger being tested.
incorrectas.C: Hypercapnia with normal PaO2 (as in pure hypoventilation without hypoxemia) primarily affects CO2 transport and the Bohr effect acutely, but it is hypoxia specifically, not elevated CO2 alone, that is the classic stimulus for sustained 2,3-BPG synthesis.
incorrectas.D: Alkalosis with normal oxygenation does not represent the hypoxic drive needed to upregulate bisphosphoglycerate mutase; in fact, the acidosis that accompanies hypoxia is part of what stimulates the enzyme, not alkalosis.

preguntas.q: Chronic exposure to high altitude indirectly shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve in which direction, via increased 2,3-BPG?

o.C: No shift, only a change in curve shape (sigmoidal to hyperbolic)

e.correcta: High altitude causes hypoxemia, which raises red cell 2,3-BPG production; 2,3-BPG binds the central cavity of deoxyhemoglobin and stabilizes the low-affinity T state, producing a rightward shift of the O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve. A right shift means hemoglobin releases oxygen more readily at any given PO2, which is adaptive because it improves O2 delivery to tissues despite the lower ambient oxygen tension.

incorrectas.B: A left shift (increased hemoglobin-O2 affinity) is produced by decreased 2,3-BPG, decreased temperature, decreased H+/increased pH, or CO poisoning — the opposite of the altitude-induced 2,3-BPG rise, which impairs rather than aids tissue unloading.
incorrectas.C: The dissociation curve retains its sigmoidal shape (reflecting cooperative O2 binding) at altitude; 2,3-BPG changes the position (right shift) rather than converting the curve to a hyperbolic shape.
incorrectas.D: The physiologic effect described is a horizontal shift in P50 (O2 affinity), not a vertical drop in maximal saturation or oxygen-carrying capacity, which would instead reflect decreased hemoglobin content or CO binding.

preguntas.q: A drop in body/tissue temperature shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve in which direction?

o.C: It has no effect on the curve
o.D: It flattens the curve without shifting P50

e.correcta: Decreased temperature increases hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen by stabilizing the R (relaxed) high-affinity conformation, which shifts the dissociation curve to the left (lower P50). This means hemoglobin holds onto oxygen more tightly and releases less of it at a given PO2 — physiologically relevant in cold extremities, where reduced O2 unloading can occur, and in hypothermic patients where oxygen delivery to tissue may be impaired despite adequate saturation.

incorrectas.A: A right shift (decreased affinity, easier O2 unloading) is instead produced by increased temperature, increased 2,3-BPG, increased CO2, and decreased pH — factors typically increased in actively metabolizing, warm tissue, which is the opposite condition from hypothermia.
incorrectas.C: Temperature is one of the principal physiologic modulators of hemoglobin-O2 affinity alongside pH, CO2, and 2,3-BPG; it is not without effect on the curve's position.
incorrectas.D: Temperature changes the P50 (shifting the curve's position along the x-axis) rather than altering the cooperative sigmoidal shape or slope of the curve itself.

preguntas.q: Compared with oxygen, carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with approximately how much greater affinity?

o.D: About half the affinity of O2

e.correcta: CO binds the same heme iron site as O2 but with roughly 200-250 times greater affinity, so even small partial pressures of CO can outcompete oxygen for binding sites and rapidly form carboxyhemoglobin. This extreme affinity difference is why CO poisoning is so dangerous at seemingly low ambient concentrations and why it takes prolonged high-flow oxygen (or hyperbaric O2) to displace CO from hemoglobin.

incorrectas.A: 20-25 times greater affinity substantially understates the true magnitude; the clinically important and testable figure is 200-250-fold, which explains why trace environmental CO exposure can still saturate a large fraction of hemoglobin.
incorrectas.C: Equal affinity would mean CO and O2 compete on even terms, which does not reflect reality — CO's markedly higher affinity is exactly why it so effectively displaces oxygen from hemoglobin even at low concentrations.
incorrectas.D: CO does not have lower affinity than O2; if it did, it would not pose a meaningful poisoning risk, since oxygen would simply outcompete it for binding under normal physiologic O2 tensions.

preguntas.q: In carbon monoxide poisoning, carboxyhemoglobin formation shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve in which direction?

o.C: No shift occurs, only total O2 capacity falls
o.D: Right initially, then left as CO is cleared

e.correcta: When CO occupies one or more heme sites on a hemoglobin tetramer, it induces a conformational change that increases the remaining subunits' affinity for oxygen, shifting the dissociation curve to the left. This means that even the oxygen that is still bound is released less readily at the tissues, compounding the problem created by reduced O2-carrying capacity — tissue hypoxia in CO poisoning results from both less O2 being carried and the O2 that is carried being held more tightly.

incorrectas.A: A right shift would actually help unload oxygen more easily; this is not what carboxyhemoglobin does — CO does the opposite, tightening O2 binding at unoccupied sites via a cooperative allosteric effect.
incorrectas.C: While reduced O2-carrying capacity is indeed a major consequence of CO poisoning, the question is specifically about the curve's leftward shift, which is a distinct, additional mechanism (increased O2 affinity of remaining sites) beyond just capacity loss.
incorrectas.D: There is no biphasic right-then-left pattern; as long as CO occupies heme sites, the affinity of unbound sites for O2 remains increased (left-shifted), and the curve normalizes only as CO is cleared and displaced by oxygen, not through an intermediate right-shift phase.

preguntas.q: In a hemoglobin tetramer partially bound by carbon monoxide, how is the oxygen affinity of the remaining unbound heme groups affected?

e.correcta: CO binding at one heme group induces an allosteric conformational shift in the hemoglobin tetramer that increases the oxygen affinity of the remaining unbound heme groups. This is the same positive cooperativity mechanism normally seen with O2 itself, but here it works against the patient: it left-shifts the curve and impairs oxygen unloading at the tissues, worsening the hypoxia already caused by CO occupying binding sites and reducing overall O2-carrying capacity.

incorrectas.A: A decreased affinity would promote easier O2 release and be somewhat protective, but this is not what happens — CO binding increases, not decreases, the affinity of remaining sites, which is precisely why CO poisoning is so hypoxia-inducing beyond just reduced capacity.
incorrectas.C: Hemoglobin subunits are allosterically linked (cooperative binding), so occupancy at one site does change the behavior of the others; affinity is not unchanged when CO occupies part of the tetramer.
incorrectas.D: Hemoglobin retains its cooperative, sigmoidal behavior even with partial CO occupancy; it does not become independent, hyperbolic-binding subunits like myoglobin.

preguntas.q: How does carboxyhemoglobin formation affect oxygen unloading at peripheral tissues?

o.C: No change in unloading, only decreased total O2 content
o.D: Unloading increases only in hypoxic tissue beds

e.correcta: Carboxyhemoglobin causes decreased O2 unloading at tissues because the unbound heme groups on the same tetramer have increased oxygen affinity (a left-shifted dissociation curve), so hemoglobin releases less of its bound oxygen at any given tissue PO2. Combined with the reduced number of O2-carrying sites (since some are occupied by CO), this produces tissue hypoxia that is disproportionately severe relative to the measured arterial O2 partial pressure.

incorrectas.A: Increased unloading would be protective and is the opposite of the actual physiology; CO poisoning does not enhance oxygen delivery to tissues — it impairs it via increased O2 affinity of the remaining hemoglobin.
incorrectas.C: While decreased O2 content (from occupied binding sites) is true, the question specifically addresses unloading efficiency at tissues, which is separately and significantly impaired due to the leftward affinity shift, not just a capacity issue.
incorrectas.D: There is no selective increase in O2 unloading confined to hypoxic tissue beds in CO poisoning — the left-shifted curve uniformly impairs unloading throughout the body, which is why CO poisoning causes global tissue hypoxia.

preguntas.q: How does carbon monoxide exposure affect the blood's total oxygen-binding capacity?

o.D: Unchanged, only dissolved O2 in plasma decreases

e.correcta: CO competitively occupies heme binding sites that would otherwise carry O2, effectively removing those sites from the pool available for oxygen transport and decreasing the blood's total O2-binding (carrying) capacity. This lowers oxygen content of the blood even though the PaO2 measured by dissolved gas in plasma remains normal, which is exactly why pulse oximetry (which reads total saturated hemoglobin poorly in this setting) and arterial blood gas PaO2 can both be misleadingly reassuring in CO poisoning.

incorrectas.A: An increased binding capacity would imply more sites are available for O2, which contradicts the basic mechanism of CO poisoning — CO removes usable sites from the oxygen-carrying pool rather than adding capacity.
incorrectas.C: CO poisoning affects both O2-carrying capacity (fewer available heme sites) and the affinity of remaining sites (left shift) — it is not limited to an affinity effect alone, so capacity is also reduced.
incorrectas.D: Dissolved O2 in plasma (which determines PaO2) is unaffected by CO, since CO binds hemoglobin rather than displacing physically dissolved oxygen; the capacity loss instead reflects fewer hemoglobin sites able to bind O2, not a change in the small dissolved fraction.

preguntas.q: In carboxyhemoglobinemia, what is the characteristic pattern of SaO2, O2 content, and PaO2?

o.A: Decreased SaO2, decreased O2 content, decreased PaO2
o.B: Normal SaO2, decreased O2 content, normal PaO2
o.C: Decreased SaO2, decreased O2 content, normal PaO2
o.D: Normal SaO2, normal O2 content, decreased PaO2

e.correcta: In CO poisoning, functional SaO2 (the fraction of hemoglobin actually carrying O2, as opposed to co-oximetry-measured saturation) is decreased because CO occupies heme sites, O2 content falls in parallel since fewer sites carry oxygen, but PaO2 remains normal because PaO2 reflects only dissolved O2 in plasma, which CO does not affect — lungs are still transferring O2 into plasma normally. This dissociation between normal PaO2/normal standard pulse oximetry readings and true tissue hypoxia is a classic diagnostic pitfall in CO poisoning.

incorrectas.A: PaO2 is not decreased in carboxyhemoglobinemia because it measures dissolved oxygen tension in plasma, which is independent of hemoglobin's CO occupancy — pulmonary gas exchange itself is intact, so this option incorrectly extends the O2-carrying defect to the dissolved-gas measurement.
incorrectas.B: SaO2 (true oxyhemoglobin saturation) is decreased, not normal, because CO-bound sites cannot carry O2; conventional two-wavelength pulse oximeters may falsely read normal/high saturation by misinterpreting carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin, but the actual physiologic SaO2 is reduced.
incorrectas.D: O2 content is decreased, not normal, since fewer hemoglobin sites are available to carry oxygen; PaO2 is normal rather than decreased since dissolved plasma O2 is unaffected — this option has both values backwards relative to the true pattern.

preguntas.q: What is the expected hemoglobin concentration in a patient with carboxyhemoglobinemia (CO poisoning) without preexisting anemia?

e.correcta: Hemoglobin concentration (grams of hemoglobin per deciliter of blood) is normal in CO poisoning because CO does not destroy or reduce the number of hemoglobin molecules — it simply occupies some of the existing molecules' binding sites. This is an important distinction from anemia: the problem in CO poisoning is functional (sites are occupied by the wrong gas), not quantitative (the actual hemoglobin mass is unchanged), so total O2 content falls due to reduced functional capacity, not reduced hemoglobin quantity.

incorrectas.A: A decreased hemoglobin concentration describes anemia, a separate condition with normal SaO2 and normal PaO2 but low O2 content due to fewer hemoglobin molecules — CO poisoning does not reduce the number of hemoglobin molecules, only their functional availability for O2.
incorrectas.C: There is no physiologic mechanism by which acute CO exposure would increase total hemoglobin mass; hemoglobin synthesis and red cell mass are unaffected on the acute timescale of CO poisoning.
incorrectas.D: Standard hemoglobin assays (e.g., total hemoglobin measured spectrophotometrically) readily detect the hemoglobin present, including CO-bound hemoglobin — the concentration is measurable and normal, not undetectable.

preguntas.q: In anemia (with normal cardiopulmonary function), what is the classic pattern of SaO2, O2 content, and PaO2?

o.A: Normal SaO2, decreased O2 content, normal PaO2
o.B: Decreased SaO2, decreased O2 content, decreased PaO2
o.C: Decreased SaO2, normal O2 content, normal PaO2
o.D: Normal SaO2, normal O2 content, decreased PaO2

e.correcta: In anemia, the lungs still oxygenate available hemoglobin normally, so SaO2 (percent saturation of existing hemoglobin) and PaO2 (dissolved plasma O2 tension) are both normal, but O2 content is decreased because there is simply less total hemoglobin to carry oxygen. This pattern contrasts with CO poisoning, where SaO2 is reduced because functional binding sites are occupied, illustrating that O2 content depends on both hemoglobin quantity (affected in anemia) and hemoglobin function/availability (affected in CO poisoning).

incorrectas.B: Decreased PaO2 would indicate a separate gas-exchange or ventilation problem (e.g., lung disease, hypoventilation), not simple anemia, where pulmonary oxygenation of the blood that is present remains normal; anemia alone does not lower PaO2.
incorrectas.C: SaO2 is not decreased in isolated anemia — the hemoglobin present is normally saturated by the lungs; it is O2 content, not saturation, that falls, because there are fewer hemoglobin molecules overall to carry oxygen.
incorrectas.D: O2 content is decreased in anemia, not normal, precisely because reduced hemoglobin mass limits total oxygen-carrying capacity even though each individual hemoglobin molecule saturates normally; PaO2 remains normal since gas exchange itself is unaffected.

preguntas.q: How does hemoglobin concentration change in anemia?

o.D: Decreased only in iron deficiency, normal in other anemias

e.correcta: By definition, anemia is a decrease in hemoglobin concentration (or red cell mass) below normal reference ranges, whatever the underlying cause (iron deficiency, chronic disease, hemolysis, marrow failure, etc.). This reduced hemoglobin quantity is precisely why O2 content of the blood falls even though each hemoglobin molecule that is present still saturates normally in the lungs (normal SaO2) and dissolved plasma O2 tension is unaffected (normal PaO2).

incorrectas.A: An increased hemoglobin concentration describes polycythemia, not anemia — these are opposite conditions, and confusing them would invert the expected direction of the core defining lab abnormality.
incorrectas.B: Hemoglobin concentration is by definition reduced in anemia; 'unchanged' would mean the condition does not actually meet the diagnostic threshold for anemia at all.
incorrectas.D: Regardless of etiology, whether iron deficiency, vitamin B12/folate deficiency, chronic kidney disease, or hemolysis, anemia is characterized by decreased hemoglobin concentration; it is not a phenomenon unique to iron deficiency alone.

preguntas.q: Approximately what percentage of CO2 transported in the blood is carried as physically dissolved CO2 in plasma?

e.correcta: About 5% of transported CO2 exists simply as dissolved gas in plasma, a small but clinically relevant fraction because it is this dissolved component (along with dissolved CO2 in equilibrium with carbonic acid) that directly determines PaCO2 measured on a blood gas. The remaining CO2 is carried in the far larger carbaminohemoglobin and bicarbonate pools, reflecting how the body maximizes CO2 transport capacity beyond what simple dissolution in plasma alone could achieve.

incorrectas.B: 25% does not correspond to any of the three classic CO2 transport fractions (dissolved ~5%, carbaminohemoglobin ~5%, bicarbonate ~90%) and overstates the small dissolved-gas contribution.
incorrectas.C: 60% substantially overstates the dissolved fraction; the vast majority of CO2 transport occurs via conversion to bicarbonate in red blood cells, not as physically dissolved gas, which remains a minor pathway.
incorrectas.D: 90% is actually the approximate fraction carried as bicarbonate (HCO3-) after carbonic anhydrase-mediated hydration of CO2, not the dissolved fraction — this option confuses the dominant bicarbonate pathway with the minor dissolved-gas pathway.

preguntas.q: What is the name given to CO2 bound directly to hemoglobin, which accounts for about 5% of blood CO2 transport?

e.correcta: Carbaminohemoglobin (HbCO2) forms when CO2 binds directly to the N-terminal amino groups of the globin chains (not the heme iron), accounting for roughly 5% of CO2 transport. This binding preferentially occurs on deoxygenated hemoglobin, which is part of the Haldane effect — deoxyhemoglobin has a higher affinity for CO2 and H+, facilitating CO2 loading at the tissues where O2 is being released.

incorrectas.A: Bicarbonate (HCO3-) is the dominant CO2 transport form (~90%), generated when carbonic anhydrase converts CO2 and H2O to carbonic acid, which dissociates into H+ and HCO3-; it is a distinct pathway from CO2 binding directly to the globin protein.
incorrectas.C: Carboxyhemoglobin refers to carbon monoxide (not carbon dioxide) bound to the heme iron of hemoglobin, a toxicologically important but entirely separate entity from physiologic CO2 transport.
incorrectas.D: Methemoglobin is hemoglobin with iron oxidized to the ferric (Fe3+) state, unable to bind oxygen normally, and is unrelated to CO2 transport — it results from oxidative stress or certain drugs/toxins, not from CO2 binding.

preguntas.q: The majority (about 90%) of CO2 transported in the blood is carried in which form?

e.correcta: Roughly 90% of CO2 is transported as bicarbonate: carbonic anhydrase within red blood cells rapidly converts CO2 and H2O to carbonic acid, which dissociates into H+ and HCO3-; the bicarbonate then exits the red cell into plasma via the chloride-bicarbonate exchanger (band 3 protein) for transport to the lungs. This pathway vastly increases the blood's CO2-carrying capacity compared to simple dissolution, and it is reversed in the pulmonary capillaries where the process runs backward to regenerate CO2 for exhalation.

incorrectas.A: Dissolved CO2 accounts for only about 5% of transport — while it is what directly determines PaCO2, it is a minor contributor compared to the enzymatically generated bicarbonate pool.
incorrectas.B: Carbaminohemoglobin, CO2 bound to globin's N-terminus, also accounts for only about 5% of transport; it is a real but minor pathway relative to bicarbonate formation.
incorrectas.D: Carbonic acid (H2CO3) is only a fleeting intermediate that rapidly dissociates into H+ and HCO3-; it does not persist as a stable transported form itself, so it is bicarbonate, its dissociation product, that actually carries the CO2 equivalent through the blood.

preguntas.q: CO2 binding to hemoglobin (forming carbaminohemoglobin) stabilizes which hemoglobin conformation, and what effect does this have on O2 affinity?

o.A: Stabilizes the relaxed (R) state, increasing O2 affinity
o.B: Stabilizes the taut (T) state, reducing O2 affinity
o.C: Has no effect on conformation or O2 affinity
o.D: Stabilizes the taut (T) state but increases O2 affinity

e.correcta: CO2 binding at the globin N-terminus stabilizes the taut (T), low-affinity conformation of hemoglobin, which reduces hemoglobin's affinity for O2 — this is part of the Bohr/Haldane effect interplay, producing a rightward shift of the O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve at the tissue level and enhancing O2 unloading exactly where metabolically active tissue is generating CO2. This is physiologically elegant: at the tissues, rising CO2 (and falling pH) both promote O2 release, matching O2 delivery to local metabolic demand.

incorrectas.A: The relaxed (R) state is the high-affinity conformation favored by O2 binding itself, not by CO2; stabilizing R would increase O2 affinity, which is the opposite of what CO2 binding actually does to hemoglobin.
incorrectas.C: CO2 binding does have a conformational and functional effect — it is an allosteric effector that shifts hemoglobin toward the T state, directly influencing O2 affinity, so 'no effect' misses a key physiologic mechanism.
incorrectas.D: While the T state is correctly identified, this option incorrectly pairs it with increased O2 affinity; by definition, the T (taut) state is the LOW-affinity conformation, so stabilizing it reduces, not increases, O2 affinity.

preguntas.q: CO2 binds hemoglobin to form carbaminohemoglobin at which molecular site?

o.D: The C-terminus of the beta chains

e.correcta: CO2 binds the N-terminal amino groups of the globin polypeptide chains, not the heme iron, forming a carbamate linkage (carbaminohemoglobin). This is an important distinction from both O2 (which binds heme iron) and CO (which competitively binds the same heme iron site as O2) — CO2's separate binding site means it does not directly compete with O2 for the same pocket, though it does allosterically influence O2 affinity through conformational changes.

incorrectas.A: The heme iron is the binding site for O2 and CO (competitively), not for CO2; confusing these sites would incorrectly imply CO2 directly displaces O2 from the same pocket, when in fact its effect on O2 affinity is allosteric/conformational rather than site-competitive.
incorrectas.C: The 2,3-BPG binding pocket is a distinct site in the central cavity between the beta chains where 2,3-BPG binds to stabilize the T state; CO2 binds a different location (the N-terminal globin amino groups), even though both molecules ultimately favor the T state.
incorrectas.D: Carbamate formation occurs at the N-terminus (alpha-amino group) of the globin chains, not the C-terminus; the C-terminal residues of the beta chains are instead involved in stabilizing the T state via salt bridges, a separate structural role.

preguntas.q: Carbonic acid (H2CO3) formed from CO2 and H2O within red blood cells dissociates into which two products?

e.correcta: Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes CO2 + H2O to H2CO3, which then rapidly and spontaneously dissociates into H+ and HCO3- (bicarbonate). The H+ generated is buffered largely by deoxyhemoglobin (which has higher H+ affinity than oxyhemoglobin, part of the Haldane effect), while HCO3- is exported to plasma via the band 3 chloride-bicarbonate exchanger, allowing CO2 to be carried to the lungs mainly in this bicarbonate form.

incorrectas.B: While the reverse reaction (regenerating CO2 and H2O from H2CO3) does occur at the lungs when CO2 is expired, the question describes the tissue-level formation and dissociation of carbonic acid, which proceeds forward to H+ and HCO3-, not backward to reform CO2 and water at that stage.
incorrectas.C: Carbonic acid dissociation releases a proton (H+), not a hydroxide ion (OH-); OH- is not a product of this acid-base reaction, which instead follows standard weak acid dissociation to release H+ and its conjugate base HCO3-.
incorrectas.D: Carbonic acid is a diprotic acid, but under physiologic pH and conditions in red blood cells, it dissociates to bicarbonate (HCO3-), not fully to carbonate (CO3^2-); carbonate formation would require a second deprotonation that does not occur to a significant extent at physiologic pH.

preguntas.q: The bicarbonate (HCO3-) generated inside red blood cells is ultimately carried to the lungs in which compartment of venous blood?

o.A: Within the red blood cell cytoplasm
o.D: Bound to carbonic anhydrase in circulation

e.correcta: After carbonic anhydrase generates HCO3- inside the red blood cell, it is exported into the plasma via the band 3 (AE1) chloride-bicarbonate exchanger in a process called the chloride shift, and it is this plasma bicarbonate that is carried to the lungs. This transport strategy is efficient because it keeps intracellular CO2 concentration low (favoring more CO2 uptake from tissues) while allowing the bulk of the CO2-derived bicarbonate to travel dissolved in the larger plasma volume.

incorrectas.A: HCO3- does not remain trapped in the red cell cytoplasm — it is actively exchanged out into plasma in return for chloride ions (the chloride shift), which is essential to prevent intracellular bicarbonate buildup and to maximize CO2 loading capacity.
incorrectas.C: Bicarbonate is a small, freely soluble ion and does not require binding to a plasma protein like albumin for transport; it simply moves as a dissolved ion in plasma after export from the red cell.
incorrectas.D: Carbonic anhydrase is an intracellular enzyme (mainly within red blood cells) that catalyzes the CO2 hydration reaction — it does not circulate freely in plasma binding bicarbonate, and bicarbonate transport does not depend on continued association with the enzyme after it is formed.

preguntas.q: In which location is H2CO3 within the red blood cell reconverted back to CO2 and H2O for eventual exhalation?

e.correcta: In the pulmonary capillaries, the reactions that occurred at the tissues run in reverse: plasma HCO3- re-enters red blood cells (in exchange for chloride, the reverse chloride shift), combines with H+ (released from hemoglobin as it becomes oxygenated, part of the Haldane effect) to reform H2CO3, which carbonic anhydrase then rapidly converts back to CO2 and H2O so that CO2 can diffuse into the alveoli and be exhaled. This completes the CO2 transport cycle that began with CO2 uptake and bicarbonate formation at the tissues.

incorrectas.A: The liver plays no direct role in this CO2 transport/regeneration cycle; hepatic carbonic anhydrase activity is involved in other metabolic and acid-base processes (like bile and gluconeogenesis-related reactions), not in pulmonary CO2 release.
incorrectas.C: Peripheral tissue capillaries are where the forward reaction occurs — CO2 diffuses into red blood cells and is converted to H2CO3, then HCO3- and H+ — the exact opposite direction from the reconversion to CO2 and H2O, which happens at the lungs.
incorrectas.D: The renal tubules handle bicarbonate reabsorption and acid-base regulation over a longer time scale for systemic pH homeostasis, but they are not the site where the CO2 generated by tissue metabolism is regenerated from H2CO3 for exhalation — that occurs specifically in the pulmonary capillaries.

preguntas.q: A somatostatinoma can cause achlorhydria through which mechanism?

o.A: Direct destruction of gastric parietal cells
o.C: Stimulation of H+/K+ ATPase inhibitory pathways in parietal cells only
o.D: Excess secretin release suppressing acid production

e.correcta: Somatostatin is a broadly inhibitory hormone that suppresses secretion of numerous GI hormones, including gastrin from G cells; since gastrin is the primary stimulant of gastric acid (HCl) secretion by parietal cells, a somatostatinoma's excess somatostatin suppresses gastrin and thereby reduces acid output, producing achlorhydria. This fits the broader somatostatinoma triad of diabetes (via insulin/glucagon inhibition), gallstones (via cholecystokinin inhibition impairing gallbladder contraction), and steatorrhea/achlorhydria (via inhibition of pancreatic enzyme secretion and gastrin, respectively).

incorrectas.A: Somatostatinoma does not cause autoimmune or cytotoxic destruction of parietal cells (as seen in pernicious anemia/atrophic gastritis); the mechanism is hormonal suppression of the gastrin stimulus to intact parietal cells, not direct cellular injury.
incorrectas.C: Somatostatin's inhibitory action is not specifically a direct stimulatory pathway on the H+/K+ ATPase pump itself; rather, it acts upstream by inhibiting gastrin release, which normally would stimulate acid secretion, an indirect hormonal mechanism rather than a direct pump-level effect.
incorrectas.D: Secretin does inhibit gastric acid secretion physiologically, but the achlorhydria of somatostatinoma is attributed to somatostatin's suppression of gastrin, not to excess secretin; somatostatinoma is not characterized by secretin hypersecretion.

preguntas.q: The mnemonic "FROM JANE" is used to recall the clinical features of which condition?

e.correcta: FROM JANE recalls the classic findings of infective endocarditis: Fever, Roth spots, Osler nodes, Murmur, Janeway lesions, Anemia, Nail-bed (splinter) hemorrhages, and Emboli. Many of these findings (Roth spots, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, splinter hemorrhages, emboli) reflect immune complex deposition and septic embolization from infected valvular vegetations, which is the underlying pathophysiology tying together this diverse set of clinical signs.

incorrectas.A: Rheumatic fever is instead recalled by the mnemonic JONES (Joint/polyarthritis, carditis (O for heart), Nodules subcutaneous, Erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea) — a distinct set of major Jones criteria related to post-streptococcal autoimmune disease, not endocarditis's embolic/immune-complex findings.
incorrectas.C: Systemic lupus erythematosus has its own diagnostic criteria (e.g., malar rash, discoid rash, serositis, oral ulcers, arthritis, photosensitivity, blood/renal/neurologic/immunologic/ANA criteria), not FROM JANE, which is specific to the peripheral stigmata of infective endocarditis.
incorrectas.D: Kawasaki disease is remembered by mnemonics related to its own diagnostic criteria (fever plus conjunctivitis, rash, adenopathy, strawberry tongue, hand-foot changes), which is a distinct pediatric vasculitis, not the valvular infection described by FROM JANE.

preguntas.q: The anion exchange protein responsible for the Cl−/HCO3− exchange across the red blood cell membrane is known as what?

e.correcta: Band three protein (AE1, anion exchanger 1) is the membrane transporter that mediates the chloride shift — exchanging HCO3- generated inside the red blood cell for extracellular Cl- (at tissues) and the reverse exchange at the lungs. This exchange keeps intracellular bicarbonate concentration low, favoring continued conversion of CO2 to HCO3- via carbonic anhydrase, and it maintains electroneutrality across the red cell membrane during this large anion flux.

incorrectas.B: Spectrin is a cytoskeletal protein that forms a structural lattice beneath the red blood cell membrane, providing shape and deformability (its deficiency causes hereditary spherocytosis); it has no role in bicarbonate/chloride transport.
incorrectas.C: Aquaporin-1 is a water channel protein that allows rapid osmotic water movement across the red cell membrane, unrelated to the anion exchange responsible for CO2/bicarbonate handling.
incorrectas.D: Glycophorin A is a heavily glycosylated red cell membrane protein important for the cell's negative surface charge and serving as a receptor for some pathogens (e.g., Plasmodium falciparum), but it does not function as the chloride-bicarbonate exchanger.

preguntas.q: The pulmonary circulation is normally characterized by which combination of resistance and compliance?

e.correcta: The pulmonary circulation is a low-resistance, high-compliance system, in contrast to the high-resistance systemic circulation, which allows the right ventricle to pump the same cardiac output as the left ventricle while generating far lower pressures (mean pulmonary artery pressure ~15 mmHg vs. systemic ~100 mmHg). This low resistance and high compliance also allow the pulmonary vasculature to accommodate increases in cardiac output (e.g., during exercise) largely through vascular distension and recruitment of previously underperfused capillaries rather than through large pressure increases.

incorrectas.A: High resistance and low compliance describe the systemic arterial circulation, which must generate high pressures to perfuse the whole body against greater vascular tone; this is the opposite hemodynamic profile from the low-pressure pulmonary circuit.
incorrectas.C: High resistance paired with high compliance is not physiologically characteristic of either major circulation; the pulmonary circuit's defining feature is specifically its combination of low resistance with high compliance, not high resistance.
incorrectas.D: Low resistance is correct for the pulmonary circulation, but its compliance is high, not low; low compliance would mean the vessels resist distension, which would require large pressure increases to accommodate rising blood flow, contrary to the actual capacity of the pulmonary vasculature to recruit and distend with minimal pressure rise.

preguntas.q: A decrease in alveolar PO2 in a poorly ventilated region of lung triggers which local vascular response, and what is its purpose?

o.A: Vasodilation, to increase blood flow and washout of CO2
o.B: Vasoconstriction, to shunt blood away from the poorly ventilated region
o.C: No change in vascular tone, since pulmonary vessels are insensitive to PO2
o.D: Vasoconstriction, to increase perfusion to the hypoxic region

e.correcta: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is a unique feature of the pulmonary circulation: unlike systemic vessels, pulmonary arterioles constrict (rather than dilate) in response to low alveolar PO2. Mechanistically, hypoxia inhibits O2-sensitive K+ channels and reduces mitochondrial ROS in pulmonary smooth muscle, causing membrane depolarization and increased cytosolic Ca2+, which drives contraction. This redirects blood flow away from poorly ventilated alveoli toward better-ventilated regions, optimizing overall V/Q matching for the whole lung.

incorrectas.A: Vasodilation in response to hypoxia is what happens in systemic vessels (e.g., coronary or cerebral), which dilate to bring more oxygen to hypoxic tissue. The pulmonary circulation does the opposite, since diverting flow away from unventilated alveoli — not toward them — is what improves gas exchange efficiency.
incorrectas.C: Pulmonary vessels are in fact highly sensitive to alveolar PO2 — this hypoxic vasoconstrictor reflex is a defining physiologic property of the pulmonary vasculature, and its exaggeration or loss underlies conditions like high-altitude pulmonary edema and hepatopulmonary syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Increasing perfusion to a hypoxic, poorly ventilated region would worsen V/Q mismatch by sending blood to alveoli that cannot oxygenate it; the physiologic point of hypoxic vasoconstriction is precisely to prevent this by shunting flow elsewhere.

preguntas.q: Why is fetal pulmonary vascular resistance very high in utero?

o.A: Generalized hypoxic vasoconstriction of the fluid-filled, unventilated fetal lungs
o.B: High fetal hemoglobin affinity for oxygen raising pulmonary arterial tone
o.C: Mechanical compression of pulmonary vessels by amniotic fluid
o.D: Elevated fetal cortisol causing pulmonary arteriolar hypertrophy

e.correcta: In utero, the fetal lungs are fluid-filled and unventilated, so alveolar PO2 is very low throughout the lung. Because hypoxia triggers pulmonary vasoconstriction (rather than dilation, as in systemic vessels), this generalized low-oxygen environment causes diffuse constriction of the pulmonary vasculature, producing high pulmonary vascular resistance. This high resistance is what diverts right ventricular output away from the lungs and across the ductus arteriosus into the systemic circulation before birth.

incorrectas.B: Fetal hemoglobin's high oxygen affinity helps it extract oxygen from maternal blood at the placenta, but it is not the mechanism driving pulmonary vascular tone — the vasoconstriction is a direct smooth muscle response to alveolar hypoxia, not a hemoglobin-mediated effect.
incorrectas.C: Amniotic fluid surrounds the fetus externally and does not fill or compress the fetal pulmonary vasculature; the fetal lungs themselves are filled with fetal lung fluid, but the resistance arises from hypoxic vasoconstriction, not mechanical compression by amniotic fluid.
incorrectas.D: Cortisol surges late in gestation help mature fetal lung surfactant production, not pulmonary vascular tone; the high resistance is a direct consequence of generalized hypoxic vasoconstriction, not a hormonally driven hypertrophic process.

preguntas.q: In the pulmonary circulation, decreased alveolar PO2 (hypoxia) produces what vascular effect?

o.B: No effect on vascular smooth muscle
o.D: Transient vasodilation followed by permanent dilation

e.correcta: Hypoxia causes vasoconstriction in the pulmonary circulation, the opposite response seen in systemic vascular beds. Low alveolar PO2 inhibits potassium channels and reduces reactive oxygen species in pulmonary smooth muscle, raising intracellular calcium and triggering contraction. This hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction serves to redirect blood flow away from poorly oxygenated alveoli, matching perfusion to ventilation across the lung.

incorrectas.B: Pulmonary vascular smooth muscle is exquisitely sensitive to alveolar oxygen tension — this reflex is a defining and clinically important feature of the pulmonary circulation, not an absence of response.
incorrectas.A: Vasodilation in response to hypoxia describes the systemic circulation (e.g., skeletal muscle, brain, coronary vessels), which dilate to increase oxygen delivery to hypoxic tissue; the pulmonary vasculature is unique in doing the opposite so it can shunt blood to better-ventilated alveoli.
incorrectas.D: There is no biphasic dilation-then-permanent-dilation pattern described for pulmonary hypoxic responses; sustained hypoxia (e.g., chronic lung disease, high altitude) produces sustained vasoconstriction and, over time, vascular remodeling with pulmonary hypertension, not dilation.

preguntas.q: Increased PCO2 (hypercapnia) in the pulmonary circulation produces what vascular effect on pulmonary arterioles?

e.correcta: Just as hypoxia does, hypercapnia (elevated CO2, which reflects local acidosis) causes vasoconstriction in the pulmonary circulation. This means poorly ventilated alveolar units — which retain both low O2 and high CO2 — receive a double signal to constrict their local vasculature, reinforcing the diversion of blood flow toward better-ventilated regions of the lung. This is a key mechanism for optimizing overall ventilation-perfusion matching.

incorrectas.A: Vasodilation in response to elevated CO2 or acidosis is characteristic of systemic vascular beds like the cerebral circulation, where it increases blood flow to washout excess CO2; the pulmonary circulation instead constricts under hypercapnia to redirect flow away from poorly ventilated units.
incorrectas.B: Pulmonary vessels do respond to PCO2 changes — hypercapnia acts synergistically with hypoxia to produce vasoconstriction, reinforcing V/Q matching rather than having no effect.
incorrectas.D: There is no described biphasic pattern for the pulmonary hypercapnic response; the vasoconstriction is a straightforward, sustained response as long as the hypercapnia persists in that lung region.

preguntas.q: In the systemic circulation, decreased PO2 (hypoxia) in a tissue bed produces what local vascular effect?

o.D: Constriction of arterioles with dilation of venules only

e.correcta: In systemic vascular beds, local hypoxia causes vasodilation, which increases blood flow to the hypoxic tissue and helps restore adequate oxygen delivery. This is the opposite of what happens in the pulmonary circulation, where hypoxia causes vasoconstriction to redirect flow away from poorly ventilated alveoli. The contrast is a classic USMLE distinction: systemic vessels dilate to bring more oxygen in, while pulmonary vessels constrict to avoid perfusing lung units that cannot oxygenate the blood anyway.

incorrectas.A: Vasoconstriction in response to hypoxia describes the pulmonary circulation's unique behavior, which shunts blood away from underventilated alveoli; systemic tissues do the opposite because increasing local flow (not decreasing it) is the appropriate response to tissue hypoxia.
incorrectas.C: Systemic vascular beds are highly responsive to local oxygen tension — hypoxic vasodilation is a well-established autoregulatory mechanism (e.g., in exercising skeletal muscle or ischemic myocardium), not an absent response.
incorrectas.D: There's no such segmental divergence in the classic hypoxic response; the described physiologic effect is a coordinated dilation of the resistance arterioles supplying the hypoxic tissue to increase overall flow.

preguntas.q: In the systemic circulation, increased PCO2 (hypercapnia) produces what local vascular effect?

o.B: No effect on vascular smooth muscle
o.D: Constriction proportional to CO2 but only above 80 mmHg

e.correcta: In systemic tissues, elevated PCO2 (and the accompanying local acidosis) causes vasodilation, increasing blood flow to metabolically active or poorly perfused tissue and helping washout the excess CO2. This mirrors the systemic hypoxic response and again contrasts with the pulmonary circulation, where hypercapnia instead causes vasoconstriction to divert blood away from poorly ventilated alveolar units.

incorrectas.A: Vasoconstriction in response to hypercapnia is the pulmonary vascular response, which serves to redirect blood flow away from lung regions with poor gas exchange; systemic tissues instead dilate to increase flow and clear the excess CO2 locally.
incorrectas.B: Systemic vessels are quite sensitive to CO2 and pH — hypercapnic vasodilation is a well-recognized autoregulatory mechanism, particularly prominent in the cerebral circulation, not an absent response.
incorrectas.D: There is no described threshold effect limiting this response to PCO2 above 80 mmHg; systemic vasodilation scales with rising CO2 levels across the physiologic and pathologic range.

preguntas.q: In lung zone 3 (the dependent lung base in an upright person), what is the relative ranking of alveolar (PA), arterial (Pa), and venous (Pv) pressures, and what drives blood flow there?

o.A: PA > Pa > Pv; flow driven by alveolar-venous difference
o.B: Pa > PA > Pv; flow driven by arterial-alveolar difference
o.C: Pa > Pv > PA; flow driven by the normal arterial-venous difference
o.D: Pv > Pa > PA; flow driven by venous-alveolar difference

e.correcta: In zone 3, both arterial and venous pressures exceed alveolar pressure (Pa > Pv > PA), so the pulmonary capillaries remain patent throughout the cardiac cycle without being compressed by alveolar pressure. As a result, blood flow through this zone is driven by the ordinary arterial-to-venous pressure difference, just as in most other vascular beds in the body — this is why the dependent lung base (in an upright person) receives the highest blood flow of the three zones.

incorrectas.A: PA > Pa > Pv describes zone 1, where alveolar pressure is highest and can collapse capillaries entirely; flow there (when present) is essentially zero rather than being driven by an alveolar-venous gradient.
incorrectas.B: Pa > PA > Pv, with flow driven by the arterial-alveolar difference, describes zone 2 — the mid-lung region where alveolar pressure compresses the venous outflow, making alveolar pressure (not venous pressure) the relevant downstream pressure for flow.
incorrectas.D: Venous pressure exceeding arterial pressure is not physiologically plausible for driving forward flow, since blood flows down a pressure gradient from artery to vein; this ordering does not correspond to any real West lung zone.

preguntas.q: In which West lung zone can high alveolar pressure compress the surrounding capillaries enough to reduce or abolish local blood flow, as may occur with hemorrhage or positive-pressure ventilation?

e.correcta: Zone 1 is defined by alveolar pressure exceeding both arterial and venous pressure (PA > Pa > Pv). When alveolar pressure is the dominant pressure surrounding the capillary, it can compress and collapse the vessel, cutting off blood flow to that region. This is normally minimal in a healthy upright lung but becomes prominent when arterial pressure drops (e.g., hemorrhage, hypovolemia) or when alveolar pressure rises abnormally (e.g., positive-pressure mechanical ventilation), creating physiologic dead space.

incorrectas.B: Zone 2 has arterial pressure exceeding alveolar pressure (Pa > PA > Pv), so the vessel is not fully collapsed by alveolar pressure — flow still occurs, driven by the arterial-alveolar pressure gradient, though the venous end can be partially compressed.
incorrectas.A: Zone 3, the dependent lung base, has both arterial and venous pressures exceeding alveolar pressure, so capillaries remain open and unobstructed by alveolar pressure — this is the opposite of the zone 1 scenario described.
incorrectas.D: There is no 'zone 4' in the standard three-zone West lung model used to describe regional pulmonary blood flow distribution based on the relationship between alveolar, arterial, and venous pressures.

preguntas.q: In lung zone 2, blood flow through the pulmonary capillaries is driven by the pressure difference between which two compartments?

o.D: Alveolar pressure alone, independent of vascular pressures

e.correcta: In zone 2, arterial pressure exceeds alveolar pressure, which in turn exceeds venous pressure (Pa > PA > Pv). Because the intermediate alveolar pressure compresses the venous end of the capillary, the venous pressure downstream becomes functionally irrelevant to flow — instead, flow is governed by the difference between the arteriolar (upstream) and alveolar (the effective downstream) pressures. This 'Starling resistor' behavior is a distinctive feature that separates zone 2 from the more typical flow physiology of zone 3.

incorrectas.A: Alveolar and venous pressure would be the relevant gradient if venous pressure were the compressing force, but in zone 2 it is alveolar pressure, not venous pressure, that dominates and determines the effective downstream pressure for flow.
incorrectas.B: Arteriolar and venous pressure is the standard driving gradient used in zone 3, where both of these pressures exceed alveolar pressure and the capillary is never compressed; in zone 2, venous pressure is subordinate to alveolar pressure and drops out of the relevant gradient.
incorrectas.D: Alveolar pressure alone does not determine flow — flow always requires a driving pressure difference between an upstream and downstream point; in zone 2 that difference is between arteriolar inflow pressure and the compressing alveolar pressure.

preguntas.q: In lung zone 3 (the dependent lung base), blood flow through pulmonary capillaries is driven by the pressure difference between which two compartments?

e.correcta: In zone 3, both arterial and venous pressures exceed alveolar pressure (Pa > Pv > PA), so alveolar pressure never compresses the capillary and plays no role in limiting flow. Blood flow is therefore driven by the conventional arteriolar-to-venous pressure gradient, exactly as it would be in a typical peripheral vascular bed — this is why zone 3, at the base of the upright lung, receives the greatest blood flow of the three zones.

incorrectas.A: Alveolar and venous pressure would be the relevant driving gradient only if alveolar pressure exceeded venous pressure, compressing the capillary's outflow; in zone 3 venous pressure exceeds alveolar pressure, so alveolar pressure is irrelevant to the flow calculation.
incorrectas.B: Arteriolar and alveolar pressure is the relevant gradient in zone 2, where alveolar pressure sits between arterial and venous pressure and compresses the venous outflow; in zone 3, venous pressure already exceeds alveolar pressure so this gradient does not apply.
incorrectas.D: Alveolar pressure alone cannot drive flow — flow requires a pressure difference between two points along the vascular path, and in zone 3 that difference is simply the normal arterial-venous gradient uncomplicated by alveolar compression.

preguntas.q: A key feature distinguishing hypoxemia caused by a right-to-left shunt from other causes of hypoxemia is that it:

o.B: Cannot be corrected with high concentrations of supplemental oxygen
o.C: Is associated with an elevated A-a gradient that normalizes with oxygen
o.D: Resolves completely once minute ventilation is increased

e.correcta: In a right-to-left shunt, deoxygenated blood bypasses the ventilated alveoli entirely and mixes directly with oxygenated blood, so no amount of supplemental oxygen can act on that shunted fraction of blood since it never contacts an alveolus.
