As a result, PaO2 fails to rise substantially even with 100% inspired oxygen — this poor response to supplemental O2 is the classic bedside/exam clue used to distinguish shunt physiology from other causes of hypoxemia like V/Q mismatch or diffusion limitation, both of which do respond to supplemental oxygen. The larger the shunt fraction, the less effective the oxygen challenge becomes, and the 100% O2 test is actually used diagnostically to quantify and confirm the presence of a shunt.

incorrectas.A: A marked improvement with 100% oxygen is characteristic of V/Q mismatch or diffusion-limited hypoxemia, where at least some gas exchange is occurring and can be augmented by a higher oxygen gradient; shunted blood, by definition, never contacts ventilated alveoli, so oxygen delivery cannot influence it.
incorrectas.C: While shunt does produce an elevated A-a gradient, that gradient does not normalize with supplemental oxygen — in fact, the persistence of a large A-a gradient despite 100% O2 is precisely the diagnostic hallmark that identifies shunt as the mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Increasing minute ventilation improves gas exchange in dead space or V/Q mismatch by increasing overall alveolar ventilation, but it does nothing for shunted blood, which never reaches ventilated alveoli regardless of how much the patient breathes.

preguntas.q: Do left-to-right cardiac shunts (e.g., an uncomplicated ventricular septal defect) typically cause hypoxemia?

o.A: Yes, because oxygenated blood is diluted by deoxygenated blood entering the systemic circulation
o.B: No, because oxygenated blood is instead recirculated through the pulmonary circulation rather than reducing systemic arterial oxygenation
o.C: Yes, but only once Eisenmenger syndrome develops
o.D: No, because left-to-right shunts always occur only in the fetal circulation

e.correcta: In a left-to-right shunt, oxygenated blood from the left side of the heart flows back into the right side (or pulmonary circulation) instead of out to the systemic circulation, meaning systemic arterial blood remains fully oxygenated. This is why uncomplicated left-to-right shunts (VSD, ASD, PDA) do not cause hypoxemia — the extra volume load instead causes pulmonary overcirculation and can lead to pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular strain over time, but does not lower systemic PaO2 until late-stage shunt reversal occurs.

incorrectas.A: This describes the physiology of a right-to-left shunt, where deoxygenated blood bypasses the lungs and mixes into the systemic circulation, diluting oxygen content and producing hypoxemia; in a left-to-right shunt, it is oxygenated blood recirculating into the pulmonary circuit, not deoxygenated blood reaching the systemic circulation.
incorrectas.C: Hypoxemia does appear once Eisenmenger syndrome develops, but that represents shunt reversal to right-to-left flow due to chronically elevated pulmonary vascular resistance — at that point it is no longer a simple left-to-right shunt, which is the scenario the question asks about.
incorrectas.D: Left-to-right shunts are common postnatal congenital heart defects (VSD, ASD, PDA) that persist after birth in structural heart disease, not a phenomenon confined to fetal circulation; the fetal circulation actually has physiologic right-to-left shunting via the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus.

preguntas.q: Chronic pulmonary hypertension leads to right ventricular hypertrophy and, eventually, to which clinical syndrome characterized by jugular venous distention, peripheral edema, and hepatomegaly?

e.correcta: Cor pulmonale is right-sided heart failure caused by pulmonary hypertension: chronically elevated pulmonary vascular resistance forces the right ventricle to generate higher pressures, causing it to hypertrophy and eventually dilate and fail. Because the right ventricle is a low-pressure pump not well-suited to sustained afterload, this failure manifests with signs of systemic venous congestion — jugular venous distention, dependent edema, and hepatomegaly (from hepatic venous congestion) — rather than the pulmonary edema typical of left heart failure.

incorrectas.B: Left-sided heart failure produces pulmonary congestion and edema (dyspnea, orthopnea, pulmonary crackles) because the failing left ventricle backs pressure up into the pulmonary veins and capillaries; it does not typically present with jugular venous distention and hepatomegaly, which reflect systemic venous congestion from right heart failure.
incorrectas.C: Cardiac tamponade is acute compression of the heart by pericardial fluid accumulation, causing impaired diastolic filling and equalization of diastolic pressures across chambers — it is an acute mechanical process, not a chronic consequence of pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular hypertrophy.
incorrectas.D: Restrictive cardiomyopathy is a primary myocardial disease (e.g., from amyloidosis or sarcoidosis) causing impaired ventricular filling due to stiff myocardium, not a condition arising secondarily from elevated pulmonary vascular resistance and right ventricular pressure overload.

preguntas.q: Which physiologic ratio is defined as alveolar ventilation divided by pulmonary blood flow, and is normally about 0.8?

e.correcta: The ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) ratio compares how much air reaches the alveoli (alveolar ventilation) to how much blood flows past them (pulmonary blood flow/perfusion). A normal V/Q ratio of about 0.8 (rather than exactly 1) reflects the fact that resting alveolar ventilation is slightly less than pulmonary blood flow in a normal lung, and it is central to understanding regional lung physiology, since deviations toward 0 (shunt) or infinity (dead space) both impair gas exchange in distinct ways.

incorrectas.A: The tidal volume/dead space ratio (VD/VT) describes what fraction of each breath fails to participate in gas exchange, which is a related but distinct concept from the ratio of total alveolar ventilation to total pulmonary blood flow across the whole lung.
incorrectas.C: Diffusing capacity (DLCO) measures how efficiently gas (typically carbon monoxide, as a surrogate) crosses the alveolar-capillary membrane per unit time and pressure gradient — it assesses the gas exchange surface and membrane properties, not the ratio of ventilation to perfusion.
incorrectas.D: The respiratory quotient is the ratio of CO2 produced to O2 consumed by cellular metabolism (normally ~0.8 as well, coincidentally), a measure of substrate utilization, not a ratio describing lung ventilation relative to pulmonary blood flow.

preguntas.q: What is the normal average value of the ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) ratio across the whole lung?

e.correcta: The normal average V/Q ratio for the lung as a whole is approximately 0.8, meaning alveolar ventilation runs at about 80% of the value of pulmonary blood flow. This is not exactly 1 because ventilation and perfusion are not perfectly matched even in a healthy lung — there is regional variation from apex to base, with both ventilation and perfusion increasing toward the base, though perfusion increases more steeply, producing this slightly-below-1 whole-lung average.

incorrectas.A: A V/Q ratio of exactly 1 represents the theoretical ideal for perfect gas exchange matching, but it is not the actual normal physiologic average measured in the intact lung — 0.8 is the real-world value due to normal regional mismatch.
incorrectas.B: A V/Q ratio of 0.5 would indicate a much more significant degree of perfusion exceeding ventilation than is normally present, more consistent with a pathologic shunt-leaning mismatch than the normal resting state.
incorrectas.D: A V/Q ratio of 2.0 would indicate ventilation substantially exceeding perfusion, more consistent with a pathologic dead-space-leaning process (e.g., pulmonary embolism) rather than the normal average across a healthy lung.

preguntas.q: Compared to the apex of the lung, the base of the lung (in an upright person) has which pattern of ventilation and perfusion?

o.A: Both ventilation and perfusion are lower at the base
o.B: Ventilation is lower and perfusion is higher at the base
o.C: Both ventilation and perfusion are greater at the base
o.D: Ventilation is higher and perfusion is lower at the base

e.correcta: Gravity increases both ventilation and perfusion toward the base of the lung compared to the apex, though perfusion increases more steeply than ventilation does. This differential gradient is why the V/Q ratio is highest at the apex (ventilation relatively exceeds perfusion, favoring a dead-space-like physiology) and lowest at the base (perfusion relatively exceeds ventilation, favoring a shunt-like physiology), even though absolute ventilation and perfusion are both greatest at the base.

incorrectas.B: Ventilation is not lower at the base — it is actually higher than at the apex, just not as dramatically higher as perfusion is; the base's compliance and the weight of the lung above it allow greater alveolar expansion during inspiration compared to the already partially-expanded apex.
incorrectas.A: Both ventilation and perfusion are in fact greater, not lower, at the base — gravity pulls more blood to the dependent regions and the base's alveoli, starting from a less-expanded resting state, expand more during each breath than the apex does.
incorrectas.D: Perfusion is not lower at the base — gravity substantially increases pulmonary blood flow toward the dependent lung regions, making perfusion (not ventilation) the variable that increases most steeply from apex to base.

preguntas.q: What V/Q ratio represents the ideal match between ventilation and perfusion for optimal gas exchange?

e.correcta: A V/Q ratio of 1 represents the theoretical ideal, where ventilation and perfusion to a given lung unit are perfectly matched, allowing maximally efficient gas exchange. In reality, the whole-lung average V/Q is about 0.8 due to normal apex-to-base gradients in ventilation and perfusion, but the physiologic target for any individual alveolar-capillary unit is a 1:1 match, and deviations toward 0 (shunt, perfusion without ventilation) or infinity (dead space, ventilation without perfusion) both represent inefficient gas exchange.

incorrectas.A: 0.8 is the actual measured whole-lung average V/Q ratio in a normal person, reflecting real regional variation between apex and base — it is close to but not the theoretical 'ideal' value of exactly 1 used as the reference point for perfect matching.
incorrectas.C: A V/Q ratio of 0.5 indicates perfusion substantially exceeding ventilation in that lung unit, which is shifted toward shunt physiology and represents inefficient gas exchange, not the ideal.
incorrectas.D: A V/Q ratio of infinity corresponds to pure dead space — ventilation with no perfusion at all — which represents wasted ventilation, the opposite extreme from the ideal matched state.

preguntas.q: Ventilation of lung regions that receive no blood perfusion (V/Q = infinity) is termed:

e.correcta: Dead space refers to ventilation of alveolar units that are not perfused, giving a V/Q ratio approaching infinity. Because no blood flows past these alveoli, no gas exchange occurs there, and the air in these units retains the composition of humidified inspired air (about 150 mmHg O2, 0 mmHg CO2) rather than equilibrating with blood. Physiologic dead space includes both anatomic dead space (conducting airways) and alveolar dead space (ventilated but unperfused alveoli, e.g., from pulmonary embolism).

incorrectas.A: Shunt is the opposite scenario — perfusion of alveolar units that are not ventilated (V/Q = 0) — where blood passes by without picking up oxygen, so it retains a mixed-venous gas composition rather than the fresh-air composition seen in dead space.
incorrectas.B: Diffusion limitation refers to impaired gas transfer across a thickened or damaged alveolar-capillary membrane (e.g., in pulmonary fibrosis) despite adequate ventilation and perfusion being present, a distinct mechanism from a V/Q mismatch caused by absent perfusion.
incorrectas.D: Anatomic dead space (the conducting airways with no gas exchange capacity) is only one component of total physiologic dead space; the question describes the broader concept of ventilated-but-unperfused alveolar units, which is physiologic (alveolar) dead space, a larger category than anatomic dead space alone.

preguntas.q: Perfusion of lung regions that receive no ventilation (V/Q = 0) is termed:

e.correcta: Shunt refers to perfusion of alveolar units that receive no ventilation, giving a V/Q ratio of 0. Because these alveoli never exchange gas with fresh air, the blood passing through them leaves with the same composition as mixed venous blood (about 40 mmHg O2, 46 mmHg CO2), lowering the overall oxygen content of the blood returning to the left heart. This is why shunt-related hypoxemia responds poorly to supplemental oxygen — the shunted blood never contacts an oxygen-rich alveolus to begin with.

incorrectas.A: Physiologic dead space is the reverse scenario — ventilation of alveoli without perfusion (V/Q = infinity) — where air moves in and out without ever exchanging gas with blood, rather than blood passing by without gas exchange.
incorrectas.B: Diffusion limitation involves impaired gas transfer across the alveolar-capillary membrane despite both ventilation and perfusion being present (e.g., thickened membrane in fibrosis), which is mechanistically distinct from a complete absence of ventilation to a perfused unit.
incorrectas.D: Anatomic dead space refers to the conducting airways that carry air but do not participate in gas exchange at all (no capillary contact), a ventilation-only concept unrelated to unventilated but perfused alveolar units.

preguntas.q: A pulmonary embolus classically produces what type of V/Q mismatch in the affected lung segment?

o.D: Uniformly low V/Q throughout the lung

e.correcta: A pulmonary embolus obstructs blood flow to a ventilated lung segment, producing a region with ventilation but no perfusion — physiologic dead space (V/Q approaching infinity) in that area. However, hypoxemia in a PE, when present, actually arises from a decreased V/Q ratio elsewhere in the lung: blood is redirected to other, still-perfused regions, overwhelming their ventilatory capacity relative to the increased flow, effectively creating a low V/Q (shunt-like) state in those areas — dead space itself does not directly cause hypoxemia.

incorrectas.A: Shunt (perfusion without ventilation) is the opposite defect from what a PE produces locally — the embolized segment still receives ventilation but loses its blood supply, making it dead space, not shunt; shunt physiology is more typical of airway obstruction or atelectasis.
incorrectas.B: Diffusion limitation refers to impaired gas transfer across a damaged or thickened alveolar-capillary membrane, which is not the primary mechanism in PE — the embolus mechanically obstructs blood flow to ventilated alveoli rather than impairing diffusion across an intact membrane.
incorrectas.D: A uniformly low V/Q throughout the entire lung would suggest global hypoventilation or diffuse shunt physiology, not the localized dead-space effect of an embolus obstructing a specific pulmonary artery branch, with compensatory flow redistribution elsewhere.

preguntas.q: Airway obstruction classically produces what type of V/Q mismatch in the affected lung segment?

e.correcta: Airway obstruction (e.g., mucus plugging, foreign body, severe bronchospasm) prevents air from reaching the alveoli distal to the blockage, while blood flow to that segment continues — this produces shunt physiology (perfusion without ventilation, V/Q = 0). Because that blood never contacts fresh air, it leaves the lung with a venous-blood gas composition, and this same shunt-like effect can also occur physiologically or pathologically with right-to-left cardiac or vascular shunts.

incorrectas.A: Dead space (ventilation without perfusion) is the opposite pattern from what airway obstruction causes — dead space is more classically produced by a pulmonary embolus, where blood flow (not air flow) is blocked while ventilation continues.
incorrectas.B: Diffusion limitation refers to a problem crossing the alveolar-capillary membrane despite intact ventilation and perfusion (e.g., in interstitial lung disease), whereas airway obstruction prevents ventilation from reaching the alveolus at all, a fundamentally different mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Compensatory hyperventilation of unaffected lung regions may occur physiologically, but the obstructed segment itself does not have elevated V/Q — it has V/Q approaching zero because its ventilation, not its perfusion, has been cut off.

preguntas.q: In a patient with V/Q mismatch due to increased physiologic dead space (assuming less than 100% dead space), does breathing 100% oxygen improve PaO2?

o.A: No, oxygen has no effect since dead space units cannot exchange gas at all
o.B: Yes, because the remaining functional alveolar units can still take up the increased inspired oxygen and raise PaO2
o.C: No, because dead space causes the same fixed hypoxemia as shunt
o.D: Yes, but only if the dead space fraction exceeds 50%

e.correcta: In dead space physiology, the problem is that some alveoli are ventilated but not perfused, wasting part of each breath; as long as some functioning alveolar-capillary units remain (i.e., dead space is less than 100%), those units are still perfused and can respond to a higher inspired oxygen concentration, raising the PaO2 of blood passing through them and thus improving overall PaO2. This responsiveness to supplemental oxygen is what distinguishes dead-space-related hypoxemia from shunt, which does not improve with oxygen because shunted blood never reaches a ventilated alveolus at all.

incorrectas.A: While the dead space units themselves cannot exchange gas, the point of the 100% O2 test is that the remaining, adequately perfused alveolar units are still functional and do respond to increased inspired oxygen, which is why overall PaO2 does improve unless dead space is complete.
incorrectas.C: Dead space and shunt behave very differently with supplemental oxygen — shunt-related hypoxemia classically fails to correct with 100% O2 because the shunted blood bypasses ventilated alveoli entirely, whereas dead space physiology allows correction through the still-functional perfused units.
incorrectas.D: There is no specific 50% threshold; the general rule is that as long as dead space is not 100% (i.e., some functional gas-exchanging units remain), supplemental oxygen will improve PaO2, though the degree of improvement may vary with the extent of dead space.

preguntas.q: In a patient with hypoxemia due to a pulmonary shunt (perfusion without ventilation), does breathing 100% oxygen significantly improve PaO2?

o.A: Yes, oxygen fully corrects shunt-related hypoxemia
o.C: Yes, but only in shunts affecting less than 50% of the lung
o.D: Yes, to the same degree as it corrects dead space hypoxemia

e.correcta: In shunt physiology, blood perfuses alveolar units that receive no ventilation at all, so that blood never has the opportunity to contact the higher oxygen tension provided by supplemental oxygen — raising inspired oxygen concentration cannot influence blood that never reaches a ventilated alveolus. This failure of PaO2 to rise substantially with 100% oxygen is the classic diagnostic feature used to identify a shunt as the cause of hypoxemia, and the larger the shunt fraction, the smaller the observed rise in PaO2.

incorrectas.A: Oxygen does not correct shunt-related hypoxemia in any meaningful way — because the shunted blood bypasses ventilated alveoli entirely, the extra inspired oxygen has no route to reach and oxygenate that fraction of the cardiac output.
incorrectas.C: There isn't a specific percentage threshold like 50% that determines correctability; rather, the degree of PaO2 improvement scales inversely with shunt size in a continuous fashion, and even modest shunts show a blunted oxygen response compared to non-shunt causes of hypoxemia.
incorrectas.D: Shunt and dead space respond very differently to supplemental oxygen — dead space hypoxemia improves with 100% O2 because functional perfused units remain and can take up the extra oxygen, whereas shunt hypoxemia does not improve because the shunted blood never contacts a ventilated alveolus.

preguntas.q: Reactivation tuberculosis characteristically involves which region of the lung, reflecting that organism's preference for a high-oxygen environment?

e.correcta: The V/Q ratio is highest at the lung apex because ventilation decreases less than perfusion does going up the lung, leaving relatively more air than blood per unit lung tissue and thus the highest regional PO2 of any lung zone. Obligate aerobes like Mycobacterium tuberculosis grow best in this oxygen-rich environment, which is why reactivation TB and also primary TB granulomas classically localize to the apices (Simon foci, Ghon complex reactivation).

incorrectas.B: The lung base has the highest absolute perfusion and ventilation of any zone, but its V/Q ratio is actually the lowest (around 0.6) because perfusion outpaces ventilation there due to gravity, giving it a lower regional PO2 than the apex — the opposite of what TB favors.
incorrectas.C: The hilum is where the great vessels, bronchi, and lymphatics enter and exit the lung; it is not a gas-exchanging parenchymal zone and has no defined V/Q ratio in the apex-to-base gradient used to explain TB localization.
incorrectas.D: The middle lobe (right lung) sits between apex and base and has an intermediate V/Q ratio close to 1, but it is not the site classically implicated in TB reactivation — right middle lobe syndrome is instead associated with bronchial obstruction and atelectasis, a distinct clinical entity.

preguntas.q: Afferent signals from pulmonary stretch receptors reach the dorsal respiratory group of the medulla via which cranial nerve?

e.correcta: The vagus nerve (CN X) carries afferent information from pulmonary stretch receptors in the airway smooth muscle back to the dorsal respiratory group (DRG) in the medulla, forming the sensory limb of the Hering-Breuer reflex that prevents lung overdistention. This is consistent with the vagus's broader role as the major visceral afferent pathway for the thorax and abdomen, distinct from its parasympathetic efferent functions elsewhere.

incorrectas.A: CN IX (glossopharyngeal) carries afferent input from the carotid body chemoreceptors and carotid sinus baroreceptors to the medulla, not from pulmonary stretch receptors — a different sensory modality feeding into a different (though related) respiratory reflex arc.
incorrectas.C: The phrenic nerve is the motor (efferent) output of the DRG to the diaphragm, not a sensory input; confusing the two directions of the reflex arc is the key error here — stretch information travels inward via the vagus, and the resulting decreased breathing frequency travels outward via the phrenic nerve.
incorrectas.D: CN V (trigeminal) provides sensation to the face and mucosa of the nasal cavity and sinuses (relevant to reflexes like sneezing), but it does not carry lung stretch receptor afferents to the respiratory centers.

preguntas.q: The dorsal respiratory group sends its motor output to the diaphragm through which nerve?

e.correcta: The phrenic nerve (roots C3-C5, "C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive") carries the motor efferent signal from the dorsal respiratory group of the medulla to the diaphragm, driving the rhythmic contraction that generates inspiration. Lesions or transections above C3-C5 (e.g., high cervical spinal cord injury) can abolish diaphragmatic breathing entirely, which is why this pathway is clinically critical to know.

incorrectas.A: The vagus nerve carries sensory (afferent) information from pulmonary stretch receptors back to the DRG, and separately provides parasympathetic output to thoracic and abdominal viscera — it is not the motor pathway to the diaphragm.
incorrectas.B: Intercostal nerves (from thoracic spinal segments) innervate the intercostal muscles, which are accessory muscles of respiration, not the diaphragm; they matter more when diaphragmatic function is compromised.
incorrectas.D: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is a branch of the vagus that innervates the intrinsic muscles of the larynx (controlling vocal cord movement), entirely unrelated to diaphragmatic motor control.

preguntas.q: Voluntary breath-holding or hyperventilation reflects which structure's ability to temporarily override the automatic brainstem respiratory centers?

e.correcta: The cerebral cortex sends descending corticospinal input that can consciously override the automatic rhythm generated by the medullary respiratory centers, allowing voluntary acts like breath-holding, speaking, or singing. This override is limited, however — as PCO2 rises during breath-holding, the chemoreceptor drive eventually becomes strong enough to force resumption of involuntary breathing regardless of conscious effort.

incorrectas.B: The hypothalamus integrates autonomic and endocrine responses (e.g., temperature regulation, stress response) and can influence breathing via emotional or thermal inputs, but it is not the structure responsible for voluntary override of respiration.
incorrectas.C: The cerebellum coordinates motor timing and balance, contributing to smooth execution of movements, but it is not part of the descending voluntary pathway that consciously controls breathing rate or depth.
incorrectas.D: The pontine respiratory group (pneumotaxic center) fine-tunes the rhythm generated by the medulla, limiting inspiratory duration and increasing respiratory rate, but this is part of the automatic brainstem circuitry being overridden, not the cortical structure doing the overriding.

preguntas.q: Where are the central chemoreceptors that respond to changes in CSF pH located?

e.correcta: The central chemoreceptors are located in the medulla, near the ventral surface, where they are bathed in CSF and respond to changes in CSF H+ concentration that result from CO2 diffusing across the blood-brain barrier. Because CO2 (but not H+ or HCO3-) crosses the BBB freely, the medulla senses hypercapnia indirectly through the resulting drop in CSF pH, making it the dominant driver of minute-to-minute ventilatory control.

incorrectas.A: The carotid bodies are peripheral chemoreceptors located at the common carotid bifurcation; they sense arterial PO2, PCO2, and pH directly in the blood via CN IX afferents, distinct from the medulla's indirect CSF-based sensing.
incorrectas.B: The aortic bodies are peripheral chemoreceptors located near the aortic arch, sending afferents via CN X; like the carotid bodies they respond to blood gas changes directly, not through CSF pH shifts.
incorrectas.D: The hypothalamus is the master regulator of autonomic and endocrine homeostasis (temperature, thirst, hunger) but does not contain the chemoreceptors responsible for CO2/pH-driven ventilatory control.

preguntas.q: Central chemoreceptors increase ventilation in response to rising PCO2 primarily because of which direct stimulus?

o.A: Rising PCO2 itself acting directly on medullary neurons
o.B: Decreased CSF pH resulting from CO2 diffusing into the CSF

e.correcta: CO2 freely diffuses across the blood-brain barrier into the CSF, where it combines with water to form carbonic acid, which dissociates into H+ and bicarbonate — it is this resulting drop in CSF pH that directly stimulates the central chemoreceptors, not PCO2 per se. This indirect mechanism explains why central chemoreceptors respond briskly to acute hypercapnia but why chronic CO2 retention (e.g., in COPD) blunts the response over time as the CSF pH renormalizes via bicarbonate buffering.

incorrectas.A: PCO2 does not act directly on the chemosensitive neurons; its effect is mediated entirely through the pH change it produces in the CSF once it crosses the BBB and is hydrated to carbonic acid — a key distinction tested repeatedly on Step 1.
incorrectas.C: Decreased arterial PO2 is sensed by the peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies), not the central chemoreceptors, which are essentially insensitive to hypoxia directly.
incorrectas.D: Serum bicarbonate does not cross the blood-brain barrier readily, so changes in serum HCO3- have little direct effect on CSF pH or central chemoreceptor activity compared to the freely diffusible CO2.

preguntas.q: Where are the peripheral chemoreceptors that sense arterial blood gas changes located?

e.correcta: Peripheral chemoreceptors are located in the carotid bodies, at the bifurcation of the common carotid arteries, and the aortic bodies, just below the aortic arch. Both sit directly in arterial blood flow, allowing them to sense actual arterial PO2, PCO2, and pH in real time and signal the brainstem via CN IX (carotid) and CN X (aortic) to adjust ventilation.

incorrectas.A: The medulla houses the central chemoreceptors, which sense CSF pH (reflecting CO2) rather than arterial blood directly, and it is also the site of the DRG and VRG respiratory pattern generators — a separate system from the peripheral chemoreceptors.
incorrectas.C: The pontine respiratory group modulates the rate and depth of breathing generated by the medullary centers; it is not a chemoreceptor site but rather a brainstem processing center for respiratory rhythm.
incorrectas.D: The alveolar walls contain juxtacapillary (J) receptors, which respond to pulmonary capillary engorgement (e.g., in left heart failure) and interstitial edema, not to arterial blood gas tensions.

preguntas.q: The carotid and aortic body peripheral chemoreceptors increase their firing rate in response to decreases in which two arterial blood gas parameters?

e.correcta: Peripheral chemoreceptors respond to decreases in both PaO2 and pH, in addition to increases in PaCO2. This dual sensitivity lets them serve as an early warning system for both hypoxemia (e.g., high-altitude exposure, lung disease) and metabolic acidosis, complementing the medulla's CO2-driven regulation via CSF pH.

incorrectas.B: Peripheral chemoreceptors respond to increased PaCO2 (not decreased), and bicarbonate itself is not a direct stimulus for peripheral chemoreceptor firing — the acid-base signal comes from pH changes, not HCO3- levels per se.
incorrectas.C: While both parameters do drive chemoreceptor activity, the direction is opposite for each: decreased PaO2 stimulates firing, but it is increased (not decreased) PaCO2 that does so — pairing PaO2 with PaCO2 here misses the pH-based component of the correct answer.
incorrectas.D: Decreased pH is indeed a correct stimulus, but bicarbonate concentration itself is not directly sensed by peripheral chemoreceptors; it is the resulting pH change from bicarbonate shifts, not bicarbonate itself, that matters.

preguntas.q: Besides responding to decreases in PaO2 and pH, peripheral chemoreceptors also increase their firing rate in response to which change?

e.correcta: Peripheral chemoreceptors also fire more in response to increased PaCO2, giving them a role as a rapid, secondary sensor of hypercapnia that complements the slower, more dominant central (medullary) chemoreceptor response mediated through CSF pH. This peripheral CO2 sensitivity provides a faster initial reflex adjustment before the central mechanism, which depends on CO2 diffusing into CSF, fully engages.

incorrectas.A: Decreased PaCO2 (hypocapnia), as occurs with hyperventilation, would reduce chemoreceptor stimulation and ventilatory drive rather than increase it — the opposite of the stimulus that raises firing rate.
incorrectas.C: Increased PaO2 (hyperoxia) would reduce peripheral chemoreceptor firing, since these receptors are activated by low, not high, oxygen tension; this is why supplemental oxygen can blunt hypoxic drive in some chronic CO2 retainers.
incorrectas.D: Increased bicarbonate would tend to raise pH (make it more alkalotic), which would decrease rather than increase chemoreceptor firing, and bicarbonate itself is not a primary sensed variable at the peripheral chemoreceptors.

preguntas.q: Peripheral chemoreceptors become significantly activated by hypoxia (independent of CO2 or pH) once arterial PO2 falls below approximately what threshold?

e.correcta: Peripheral chemoreceptor firing rises sharply once PaO2 drops below approximately 60 mmHg, which corresponds to the steep, downward-sloping portion of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve where small further drops in PaO2 cause large drops in O2 saturation and content. Above this threshold, PaO2 has relatively little independent effect on ventilatory drive because hemoglobin remains well saturated; this 60 mmHg cutoff is also clinically used as a marker for initiating supplemental oxygen therapy.

incorrectas.A: 100 mmHg is roughly the normal PaO2 in a healthy person at sea level and is far above the threshold at which peripheral chemoreceptors meaningfully ramp up their hypoxic drive.
incorrectas.B: 80 mmHg is still on the relatively flat, well-saturated portion of the oxyhemoglobin curve, so PaO2 in this range has only a minor effect on chemoreceptor firing compared to the 60 mmHg threshold where the curve steepens.
incorrectas.D: 40 mmHg represents severe hypoxemia, well below the threshold at which the chemoreceptor response becomes significant — by this point ventilatory drive would already be markedly increased, not just beginning to activate.

preguntas.q: An isolated rise in arterial H+ concentration (metabolic acidosis, without a change in PaCO2) stimulates which peripheral chemoreceptor site specifically?

o.C: Both carotid and aortic bodies equally

e.correcta: Increases in arterial H+ that occur independently of PCO2 changes (i.e., from a metabolic, non-respiratory acidosis) stimulate only the carotid body chemoreceptors, not the aortic bodies. This is a key distinguishing feature on Step 1: the aortic bodies mainly mediate the circulatory (not ventilatory) response to hypoxia and are less responsive to isolated pH changes, whereas the carotid bodies drive the compensatory hyperventilation seen in conditions like diabetic ketoacidosis.

incorrectas.A: The aortic bodies are not stimulated by an isolated rise in H+ independent of PCO2 — this selective pH sensitivity belongs to the carotid bodies, making this option the reverse of the correct relationship.
incorrectas.C: The two sites are not equivalent in this context; only the carotid bodies respond to isolated increases in arterial H+, while the aortic bodies' role is more centered on hypoxia and circulatory reflexes rather than pure acid-base sensing.
incorrectas.D: The central medullary chemoreceptors respond to CSF pH changes driven by CO2 diffusion across the blood-brain barrier, not directly to arterial H+ from a metabolic acidosis, since H+ itself does not cross the blood-brain barrier well.

preguntas.q: Mechanoreceptors located within the smooth muscle of the airways that detect lung distention are called what?

e.correcta: Lung stretch receptors are mechanoreceptors embedded in the smooth muscle of the airways that respond to distention of the lungs during inspiration. Their vagal afferent signal to the dorsal respiratory group triggers the Hering-Breuer reflex, which decreases breathing frequency to prevent overinflation — most physiologically relevant at large tidal volumes rather than during normal quiet breathing.

incorrectas.A: Irritant receptors sit between airway epithelial cells (not in smooth muscle) and are triggered by noxious inhaled substances like smoke or dust, provoking bronchoconstriction and cough rather than sensing mechanical stretch.
incorrectas.B: Juxtacapillary (J) receptors are located in the alveolar walls near pulmonary capillaries and respond to capillary engorgement or interstitial edema (e.g., left heart failure), causing rapid shallow breathing — a very different stimulus and location than airway smooth muscle stretch.
incorrectas.D: Joint and muscle receptors are located in the limbs, not the lungs, and are activated by limb movement during exercise to help drive the early increase in ventilation seen with physical activity.

preguntas.q: Activation of lung stretch receptors during marked lung distention produces what change in breathing frequency, known as the Hering-Breuer reflex?

e.correcta: The Hering-Breuer reflex causes a decreased breathing frequency (prolonged expiration) when lung stretch receptors are strongly activated by significant lung distention, preventing excessive tidal volumes and overinflation injury. Vagal afferents carry the stretch signal to the dorsal respiratory group, which inhibits further inspiratory drive — a protective reflex most apparent in infants and during very large tidal volume breathing in adults.

incorrectas.A: An increased breathing frequency would be the opposite of what this inhibitory, protective reflex produces; rapid shallow breathing is instead characteristic of juxtacapillary (J) receptor stimulation from pulmonary vascular congestion, a different receptor system entirely.
incorrectas.B: The reflex specifically produces a measurable change (slowing) in respiratory rate; "no change" would defeat the physiological purpose of the reflex, which is to limit further lung expansion once stretch receptors signal that the lungs are already adequately or excessively inflated.
incorrectas.D: Irregular gasping breathing patterns (like Biot's or ataxic breathing) reflect brainstem injury or severe CNS dysfunction, not the coordinated, protective slowing produced by the Hering-Breuer stretch reflex.

preguntas.q: Receptors located between airway epithelial cells that are stimulated by inhaled noxious substances such as smoke or dust are called what?

e.correcta: Irritant receptors are found between airway epithelial cells and respond to noxious stimuli like smoke, dust, and cold air, triggering reflex bronchoconstriction, coughing, and increased respiratory rate to help expel the irritant. This mechanism is a key part of airway defense and also contributes to bronchospasm triggered by environmental irritants in conditions like asthma.

incorrectas.B: Lung stretch receptors are located in airway smooth muscle (not between epithelial cells) and respond to mechanical distention of the lungs, mediating the Hering-Breuer reflex — a different receptor type and stimulus than chemical/particulate irritation.
incorrectas.C: Juxtacapillary (J) receptors sit in the alveolar walls and respond to pulmonary capillary engorgement or edema, producing rapid shallow breathing; they are not triggered by inhaled irritants at the epithelial surface.
incorrectas.D: Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies) sense arterial PO2, PCO2, and pH in the bloodstream, not local airway irritation from inhaled particulates or gases.

preguntas.q: Which pair of receptors, located in the limbs, is activated during limb movement and helps stimulate the early increase in ventilation seen at the onset of exercise?

e.correcta: Joint and muscle receptors are activated by limb movement and proprioceptive input during exercise, and their afferent signaling to the brainstem contributes to the rapid rise in ventilation seen at the very start of exercise — occurring before any measurable change in arterial blood gases, which is why chemoreceptor-independent, feedforward neural mechanisms like this are needed to explain it.

incorrectas.A: Irritant receptors respond to inhaled noxious chemicals and stretch receptors respond to lung distention; neither is located in the limbs nor directly tied to limb movement, so they cannot account for the exercise-onset ventilatory response driven by proprioceptive input.
incorrectas.B: Carotid and aortic body receptors are peripheral chemoreceptors that sense arterial blood gas changes (PO2, PCO2, pH), not limb movement — during early exercise, PaO2 and PaCO2 actually remain unchanged, so chemoreceptors are not the drivers of the initial ventilatory increase.
incorrectas.D: Juxtacapillary receptors sense pulmonary capillary engorgement in the alveolar walls, and stretch receptors sense airway distention; neither pair is located in the limbs or responds to joint/muscle movement during exercise.

preguntas.q: Receptors located in the alveolar walls that cause rapid, shallow breathing in response to pulmonary capillary engorgement, as seen in left heart failure, are called what?

e.correcta: Juxtacapillary (J) receptors are located in the alveolar walls adjacent to the pulmonary capillaries and are activated by engorgement of those capillaries or by interstitial edema, such as occurs in left heart failure or pulmonary embolism. Their activation produces the classic pattern of rapid, shallow breathing (tachypnea) and can also trigger dyspnea sensation, making them clinically relevant to the breathlessness seen in cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

incorrectas.A: Irritant receptors are located between airway epithelial cells and respond to inhaled chemical irritants like smoke, not to vascular engorgement within the alveolar walls.
incorrectas.B: Lung stretch receptors sit in airway smooth muscle and respond to mechanical lung distention (volume), mediating the Hering-Breuer reflex that decreases respiratory rate — the opposite direction of change from the tachypnea caused by J receptor stimulation.
incorrectas.C: Joint and muscle receptors are located in the limbs and respond to movement during exercise, entirely unrelated to alveolar capillary congestion or cardiac pathology.

preguntas.q: During exercise, how does CO2 production by exercising muscle change compared to rest?

e.correcta: Exercising skeletal muscle ramps up aerobic (and, at higher intensities, anaerobic) metabolism to meet increased ATP demand, generating substantially more CO2 as a byproduct of the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. This increased CO2 production is matched by a proportional increase in alveolar ventilation and pulmonary blood flow, which is why arterial PCO2 remains essentially unchanged despite the higher total CO2 output — the body compensates rather than allowing PCO2 to rise.

incorrectas.B: A decrease in CO2 production would imply reduced metabolic activity, which contradicts the fundamentally increased energy demand and substrate oxidation that occurs in contracting muscle during exercise.
incorrectas.C: CO2 production is not unchanged during exercise — while arterial PCO2 stays stable due to compensatory increases in ventilation and perfusion, the actual rate of CO2 generation by metabolically active tissue rises significantly, which is precisely why ventilation must increase to keep pace.
incorrectas.D: There is no physiological basis for an initial decrease in CO2 production at the onset of exercise; metabolic rate and CO2 generation rise promptly as muscle contraction begins and ATP demand increases.

preguntas.q: During exercise, how does O2 consumption by the body change relative to rest?

e.correcta: O2 consumption increases substantially during exercise as skeletal muscle mitochondria ramp up oxidative phosphorylation to generate the ATP needed for sustained contraction. This increased demand is met by a matched rise in cardiac output, pulmonary blood flow, and ventilation, which together keep arterial PO2 essentially unchanged even as total body O2 uptake climbs — the classic teaching point that VO2 rises while PaO2 stays stable.

incorrectas.B: O2 consumption is clearly increased, not unchanged, during exercise; this is the entire physiological basis for the concept of VO2max as a measure of aerobic fitness and exercise capacity.
incorrectas.D: The rise in O2 consumption during exercise occurs in both trained and untrained individuals — training affects the efficiency and maximum capacity (VO2max) of oxygen utilization, not whether consumption increases with exertion at all.
incorrectas.A: A decrease in O2 consumption would be inconsistent with the increased metabolic demand of contracting muscle, which requires more, not less, oxidative ATP production to sustain movement.

preguntas.q: During exercise, how does minute ventilation change in order to meet increased O2 demand?

o.D: Increased only in response to hypoxemia

e.correcta: Minute ventilation increases during exercise to match the rise in O2 consumption and CO2 production by working muscle, driven initially by feedforward neural signals from the motor cortex and joint/muscle proprioceptors, and sustained by chemoreceptor and other feedback mechanisms. This increase is proportional to metabolic demand, which is why arterial PO2 and PCO2 remain stable rather than drifting toward hypoxemia or hypercapnia during exercise.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in ventilation would be physiologically counterproductive during exercise, since it would fail to meet the substantially increased O2 demand and CO2 clearance requirements of working muscle.
incorrectas.C: Ventilation is not unchanged during exercise — it rises briskly and proportionally with workload, which is precisely why arterial blood gases remain normal despite large increases in metabolic rate.
incorrectas.D: Ventilation increases during exercise even though arterial PO2 does not actually drop (it stays essentially unchanged); the increase is driven by feedforward neural and other integrative mechanisms rather than a hypoxemic stimulus, since true hypoxemia does not develop in a healthy exerciser.

preguntas.q: During exercise, how does the ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) ratio gradient from apex to base of the lung change?

o.C: It reverses, becoming higher at the base

e.correcta: During exercise, increased cardiac output raises pulmonary artery pressure, recruiting and distending previously underperfused capillaries, especially at the apex, while ventilation also increases throughout the lung. The net effect is that the normally wide V/Q gradient from apex (high V/Q) to base (low V/Q) narrows and becomes more even, improving overall gas exchange efficiency to support the elevated metabolic demand.

incorrectas.A: The gradient becomes more even, not more uneven, during exercise — increased perfusion pressure recruits apical capillaries that are underperfused at rest, working to equalize V/Q ratios across lung zones rather than exaggerate the mismatch.
incorrectas.C: The gradient does not reverse; the base still has relatively higher perfusion than the apex, and the apex still tends to have higher ventilation relative to perfusion — exercise simply narrows the difference between the two rather than flipping which zone is higher.
incorrectas.D: The V/Q gradient is not unchanged with exercise; the physiological change (equalization due to capillary recruitment from increased pulmonary blood flow) is a well-recognized adaptive mechanism that improves gas exchange during exertion.

preguntas.q: Increased perfusion of pulmonary capillary beds, as occurs during exercise, is associated with what change in pulmonary vascular resistance?

e.correcta: Increased perfusion during exercise decreases pulmonary vascular resistance through capillary recruitment (opening previously closed or underperfused vessels) and capillary distention (widening of already-open vessels). Because the pulmonary vasculature is arranged in parallel, adding more perfused vessels in parallel lowers total resistance — this is the opposite of the systemic circulation's behavior and is key to why the pulmonary circuit can accommodate large increases in cardiac output with only a modest rise in pulmonary artery pressure.

incorrectas.A: Increased resistance would occur with vessel constriction or destruction (as in hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction or pulmonary hypertension), not with the recruitment/distention response to increased flow seen in normal exercise physiology.
incorrectas.C: Resistance does change—it decreases—because the parallel arrangement of pulmonary vessels allows recruitment of additional parallel pathways as flow increases, actively lowering total vascular resistance rather than leaving it static.
incorrectas.D: There is no physiological plateau-then-increase pattern for pulmonary vascular resistance with increasing perfusion in this context; resistance falls progressively as more capillaries are recruited and distended with rising pulmonary blood flow.

preguntas.q: During strenuous exercise, blood pH decreases secondary to which metabolic process?

e.correcta: During strenuous exercise, muscle demand for ATP can outpace oxygen delivery, forcing a shift toward anaerobic glycolysis, which regenerates NAD+ by converting pyruvate to lactate via lactate dehydrogenase. The resulting accumulation of lactic acid lowers blood pH, producing a metabolic (lactic) acidosis that also stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies) to further drive ventilation.

incorrectas.B: Ketoacidosis results from unregulated lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis, typically in the setting of insulin deficiency (as in diabetic ketoacidosis) or prolonged starvation, not from the short-term anaerobic metabolism of strenuous exercise.
incorrectas.C: Respiratory alkalosis results from hyperventilation that lowers PaCO2 and raises pH, which is the opposite acid-base direction from what strenuous exercise produces; exercise-induced acidosis is metabolic in origin from lactate, not from a primary respiratory disturbance.
incorrectas.D: Bicarbonate wasting refers to renal or gastrointestinal loss of bicarbonate (e.g., diarrhea, renal tubular acidosis), an entirely separate mechanism from the anaerobic lactate production that lowers pH during intense muscular exertion.

preguntas.q: In a healthy individual performing moderate exercise, how does arterial PCO2 (PaCO2) typically change compared to resting levels?

o.A: It rises progressively with exercise intensity
o.D: It rises initially, then falls below baseline

e.correcta: In healthy individuals performing moderate exercise, PaCO2 remains essentially unchanged from resting levels because the increase in alveolar ventilation is precisely matched to the increase in CO2 production by working muscle. This tight coupling — mediated by feedforward neural signals and reinforced by chemoreceptor feedback — is a hallmark of normal exercise physiology and is tested specifically because it's counterintuitive that such a large rise in metabolic CO2 production doesn't change arterial CO2 at all.

incorrectas.A: PaCO2 does not progressively rise with exercise intensity in a healthy person; ventilation increases proportionally to compensate for rising CO2 production, keeping PaCO2 stable across a wide range of moderate exercise intensities (only at very high, near-maximal effort might slight changes occur).
incorrectas.B: While ventilation does increase substantially during exercise, it increases proportionally to CO2 production rather than in excess of it, so PaCO2 does not fall the way it would with true hyperventilation (as seen in panic attacks or anxiety, where ventilation exceeds metabolic need).
incorrectas.D: There is no biphasic pattern of PaCO2 rising then falling below baseline during moderate exercise in a healthy person; the well-established physiological finding is a stable, unchanged PaCO2 throughout.

preguntas.q: In a healthy individual performing moderate exercise, how does arterial PO2 (PaO2) typically change compared to resting levels?

o.A: It falls due to increased O2 extraction
o.D: It falls only in untrained individuals

e.correcta: PaO2 remains essentially unchanged during moderate exercise in a healthy person because pulmonary ventilation and perfusion both increase proportionally to O2 demand, and V/Q matching actually improves (becomes more even) with exercise due to capillary recruitment. Although the venous O2 content drops substantially as tissues extract more oxygen, this does not translate into a fall in arterial PO2 because gas exchange at the alveolar-capillary interface remains efficient.

incorrectas.A: Increased O2 extraction by tissues lowers mixed venous O2 content and saturation, but this reflects the arteriovenous difference widening, not a drop in arterial PO2 itself, which stays normal because the lungs continue to fully oxygenate the blood passing through them.
incorrectas.C: PaO2 does not rise with exercise-induced hyperventilation in a healthy person because ventilation increases in proportion to metabolic demand rather than in excess of it, and PaO2 in a healthy lung is already near its ceiling determined by inspired O2 and alveolar gas exchange, leaving little room to rise further.
incorrectas.D: This pattern (PaO2 unchanged) holds true across both trained and untrained healthy individuals during moderate exercise; only at extreme, near-maximal exertion in elite athletes can rare exercise-induced arterial hypoxemia occur due to diffusion limitation, which is a distinct, advanced phenomenon.

preguntas.q: During exercise, how does the CO2 content of venous blood returning from working muscle change?

e.correcta: Venous CO2 content increases during exercise because working muscle produces CO2 at a higher rate as a byproduct of increased aerobic (and anaerobic) metabolism, and this CO2 diffuses into the capillary blood draining the muscle before it returns via the veins. Despite this rise in venous CO2 content, arterial PCO2 remains unchanged because pulmonary ventilation increases proportionally to clear the additional CO2 load at the lungs before the blood re-enters the systemic arterial circulation.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in venous CO2 content would be inconsistent with the increased metabolic CO2 production of exercising muscle; venous blood picks up more, not less, CO2 as it passes through metabolically active tissue.
incorrectas.C: Venous CO2 content is not unchanged during exercise — it rises measurably due to increased tissue CO2 production, even though arterial CO2 stays stable due to compensatory ventilatory changes at the lungs.
incorrectas.D: There is no physiological basis for venous CO2 content initially decreasing before rising during exercise; CO2 production and thus venous content increase promptly and progressively with the onset and continuation of muscular activity.

preguntas.q: During moderate-to-heavy exercise, tissue oxygen extraction increases to meet metabolic demand. What happens to venous O2 content as a result?

o.D: It becomes equal to arterial O2 content

e.correcta: Exercising muscle dramatically increases its metabolic rate and O2 consumption, so it extracts more O2 from each unit of blood that passes through it. Because arterial O2 content stays roughly constant (arterial saturation remains near-normal even during exercise), the increased extraction is reflected as a fall in venous O2 content — the arteriovenous O2 difference widens. This widened A-V O2 difference is one of the classic hemodynamic adaptations to exercise, alongside increased cardiac output and redistribution of blood flow to active muscle.

incorrectas.A: An increase in venous O2 content would imply the tissues are extracting less oxygen, which is the opposite of what happens during exercise when metabolically active muscle pulls more O2 out of the blood.
incorrectas.C: Venous O2 content does not stay unchanged; increased tissue O2 extraction during exercise is precisely what drives the drop in venous O2 content and widens the arteriovenous O2 difference.
incorrectas.D: Venous O2 content falls but does not equalize with arterial content — some O2 always remains in venous blood (venous reserve) even under maximal exertion, which is part of why the body can still increase extraction further during extreme demand.

preguntas.q: At high altitude, the partial pressure of atmospheric oxygen falls. What happens to PaO2 as a direct consequence?

o.B: PaO2 remains normal due to compensation

e.correcta: Barometric pressure falls with increasing altitude, which lowers the partial pressure of inspired oxygen (PiO2) delivered to the alveoli. Since alveolar and arterial PO2 are directly dependent on the inspired PO2, PaO2 falls proportionally, producing hypoxemia. This is the initiating stimulus for the entire cascade of high-altitude physiologic adaptations (increased ventilation, increased 2,3-BPG, polycythemia, etc.).

incorrectas.B: The body does mount compensations (hyperventilation, increased erythropoiesis) but these do not restore PaO2 to sea-level normal — they help maintain adequate O2 delivery despite a persistently lower PaO2, they do not eliminate the hypoxemia itself.
incorrectas.A: PaO2 cannot increase at altitude because the fundamental driving pressure (inspired PO2) is reduced; no compensatory mechanism raises the partial pressure of oxygen in the atmosphere itself.
incorrectas.D: PaO2 decreases but remains measurable and physiologically significant; it does not drop to an undetectable or zero level in typical high-altitude exposure (this would be incompatible with survival).

preguntas.q: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies sense the fall in PaO2 at high altitude. What is the resulting effect on ventilation?

e.correcta: The peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies) are the primary sensors of hypoxemia; when PaO2 falls significantly (typically below ~60 mmHg), they fire more and stimulate the medullary respiratory centers to increase ventilation. This hypoxic ventilatory response increases both rate and depth of breathing, helping to raise alveolar PO2 and partially offset the low inspired oxygen tension at altitude.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in ventilation would worsen hypoxemia and is not the physiologic response; the hypoxic drive from peripheral chemoreceptors specifically pushes ventilation up, not down.
incorrectas.B: Ventilation is not unaffected — the hallmark of the hypoxic ventilatory response is a measurable, sustained increase in minute ventilation that begins within minutes of ascent and persists (with further adaptation) over days.
incorrectas.D: Cheyne-Stokes respiration is a specific oscillating breathing pattern seen in conditions like heart failure or at very high altitude during sleep, not the general daytime ventilatory response to hypoxemia, which is a straightforward increase in ventilation.

preguntas.q: As a result of the hyperventilation triggered by high-altitude hypoxemia, what happens to PaCO2?

o.C: PaCO2 is unaffected because CO2 diffusion is independent of ventilation

e.correcta: Because CO2 is extremely diffusible, alveolar and arterial PCO2 are governed mainly by alveolar ventilation. When hypoxemia at altitude drives an increase in minute ventilation, CO2 is 'washed out' of the alveoli faster than it is produced, so PaCO2 falls. This produces a respiratory alkalosis — the low PaCO2 raises blood pH by the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship, and the kidneys respond over days by excreting bicarbonate to compensate.

incorrectas.A: PaCO2 would rise with hypoventilation, not hyperventilation — the physiologic response to high-altitude hypoxemia is increased ventilation, which does the opposite and lowers PaCO2.
incorrectas.C: CO2 diffusion across the alveolar-capillary membrane is extremely efficient, but the amount of CO2 eliminated per minute depends heavily on alveolar ventilation; PaCO2 is in fact very sensitive to changes in ventilation, which is why it is used clinically as a marker of ventilatory status.
incorrectas.D: PaCO2 changes in a predictable, unidirectional way (it falls) in response to sustained hyperventilation at altitude; it does not oscillate erratically under this steady-state physiologic adaptation.

preguntas.q: Beyond the acute hyperventilatory response, what happens to ventilation with chronic residence at high altitude?

o.A: Ventilation returns fully to sea-level baseline within 24 hours
o.D: Ventilation becomes dependent solely on central chemoreceptors

e.correcta: With prolonged altitude exposure, renal compensation for the initial respiratory alkalosis (bicarbonate excretion) lowers the buffering capacity of CSF and blood, which removes some of the inhibitory brake that a high pH normally places on the central chemoreceptors' response to CO2/H+. This allows ventilation to remain persistently elevated (chronic hyperventilation) even as PaCO2 stabilizes at a new, lower set point — a key acclimatization mechanism that helps sustain higher alveolar PO2 long-term.

incorrectas.A: Ventilation does not fully normalize within a day; acclimatization to altitude is a days-to-weeks process, and the chronic increase in ventilation is a defining feature that persists as long as the person remains at altitude.
incorrectas.C: Ventilation does not fall below baseline with altitude acclimatization — the entire adaptive point is to sustain elevated ventilation to compensate for reduced inspired oxygen, not to reduce it.
incorrectas.D: Central chemoreceptors (responding to CSF pH/PCO2) do become relatively more important as renal compensation proceeds, but peripheral chemoreceptors driven by hypoxemia remain active as well; ventilation is not driven by central chemoreceptors alone.

preguntas.q: A patient with respiratory alkalosis from high-altitude ascent is given a drug that increases urinary bicarbonate excretion to promote a compensatory metabolic acidosis. Which drug class is this?

e.correcta: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., acetazolamide) block the enzyme in the proximal tubule that normally facilitates bicarbonate reabsorption, causing bicarbonaturia. The resulting mild metabolic acidosis counteracts the respiratory alkalosis caused by altitude-induced hyperventilation, and acetazolamide also stimulates ventilation independently, which helps with acclimatization and prevention of acute mountain sickness.

incorrectas.A: Loop diuretics inhibit the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb; they cause volume contraction and can actually promote a mild metabolic alkalosis (contraction alkalosis) rather than the bicarbonate-wasting acidosis needed here.
incorrectas.C: Thiazide diuretics act on the distal convoluted tubule's Na-Cl cotransporter and, like loop diuretics, tend to cause a contraction metabolic alkalosis, not a bicarbonaturic metabolic acidosis; they do not target the carbonic anhydrase pathway.
incorrectas.D: Aldosterone antagonists (e.g., spironolactone) block mineralocorticoid receptors in the collecting duct, reducing potassium and hydrogen secretion; this actually favors retention of acid and would tend toward acidosis via a different, non-bicarbonaturic mechanism, and is not the classic altitude-sickness treatment.

preguntas.q: As part of chronic acclimatization to high altitude, what happens to red blood cell 2,3-BPG levels?

e.correcta: Chronic hypoxemia at altitude stimulates increased production of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) within red blood cells. Higher 2,3-BPG binds preferentially to deoxygenated hemoglobin and stabilizes its low-affinity (T) state, shifting the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right. This facilitates unloading of oxygen to peripheral tissues at a given tissue PO2, partially compensating for the reduced oxygen loading in the lungs.

incorrectas.B: 2,3-BPG is not unaffected — its production is actively upregulated as an adaptive response to sustained hypoxemia, which is part of why altitude acclimatization takes days rather than being instantaneous.
incorrectas.A: A decrease in 2,3-BPG would shift the curve leftward, increasing hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen and impairing peripheral O2 unloading — the opposite of the helpful adaptation the body actually makes at altitude.
incorrectas.D: 2,3-BPG and fetal hemoglobin are unrelated molecules; fetal hemoglobin (HbF) has an intrinsically lower affinity for 2,3-BPG which gives it higher O2 affinity than adult hemoglobin, but adults at altitude do not convert their hemoglobin to HbF as an adaptive mechanism.

preguntas.q: At the cellular level, chronic high-altitude exposure promotes greater efficiency of oxidative metabolism under low oxygen tension. Which organelle increases in number as part of this adaptation?

e.correcta: Chronic hypoxia at altitude induces cellular adaptations including an increase in mitochondrial density in tissues, which improves the efficiency of oxidative phosphorylation and oxygen utilization at the tissue level despite lower arterial oxygen tension. This is one of several coordinated adaptations (alongside increased ventilation, 2,3-BPG, and erythropoiesis) that together allow sustained function in a chronically hypoxic environment.

incorrectas.A: Peroxisomes are involved in fatty acid beta-oxidation and detoxification of reactive oxygen species, but they are not the organelle classically cited as increasing in number in response to chronic hypoxic adaptation.
incorrectas.B: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes for degrading cellular debris and are not part of the oxidative-metabolism adaptation to chronic hypoxia; their numbers are not characteristically increased by altitude exposure.
incorrectas.D: The Golgi apparatus functions in protein modification, sorting, and packaging; it has no established role in the cellular adaptation to chronic hypoxia at altitude, unlike mitochondria which directly relate to oxygen utilization.

preguntas.q: The respiratory alkalosis of high altitude triggers renal compensation. What substance does the kidney excrete in greater amounts as a result?

e.correcta: In respiratory alkalosis, the primary problem is a low PaCO2 with a resulting high blood pH; renal compensation aims to lower the pH back toward normal by excreting bicarbonate, which reduces plasma HCO3- and produces a compensatory (mild) metabolic acidosis. This increased bicarbonaturia also causes an osmotic diuresis and contributes to hemoconcentration during altitude acclimatization, and can be augmented pharmacologically with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor like acetazolamide.

incorrectas.A: In respiratory alkalosis the kidney does not increase net H+ excretion — quite the opposite tendency would be expected if anything, since the compensatory goal is to retain acid (or dispose of base) to correct the alkalemia, which is accomplished chiefly through bicarbonate wasting, not direct proton excretion.
incorrectas.B: Ammonium (NH4+) excretion is the kidney's main mechanism for excreting a hydrogen ion load and generating new bicarbonate in response to acidosis; it is not the primary excretory response invoked to compensate for alkalosis, where the kidney instead needs to get rid of excess bicarbonate.
incorrectas.D: Titratable acid excretion (e.g., as H2PO4-) is another mechanism for eliminating acid and is upregulated during acidotic states, not during the renal compensation for a respiratory alkalosis, which instead calls for bicarbonate loss.

preguntas.q: A patient acutely ascends to high altitude and develops hypoxemia. What happens to their A-a gradient?

e.correcta: At high altitude, both alveolar PO2 (PAO2) and arterial PO2 (PaO2) fall together because the problem is a globally reduced inspired oxygen tension, not a defect in gas exchange across the alveolar-capillary membrane. Since the A-a gradient measures the difference between PAO2 and PaO2, and both decrease proportionally, the gradient itself stays normal — this is a key distinguishing feature of altitude-related (and hypoventilation-related) hypoxemia versus causes like V/Q mismatch or diffusion defects, which do widen the gradient.

incorrectas.A: A markedly increased A-a gradient would suggest a true gas-exchange abnormality (diffusion defect, V/Q mismatch, or shunt), which is not the mechanism at altitude — there, the problem is simply lower inspired PO2 reaching normally functioning alveoli and capillaries.
incorrectas.B: The A-a gradient does not decrease at altitude; it stays essentially at its normal baseline value because both PAO2 and PaO2 fall by similar amounts, keeping their difference unchanged.
incorrectas.D: A negative A-a gradient is not a physiologically expected finding in this context (and would generally reflect a lab/calculation artifact) — the gradient at altitude remains normal (near zero to slightly positive at baseline), not negative.

preguntas.q: A patient with opioid overdose or obesity hypoventilation syndrome develops hypoxemia due to hypoventilation. What is expected of their A-a gradient?

e.correcta: Hypoventilation causes hypoxemia by allowing CO2 to accumulate in the alveoli, which displaces oxygen and lowers both PAO2 and PaO2 in parallel — there is no intrinsic defect in the alveolar-capillary interface itself. Because both alveolar and arterial oxygen tensions fall together, the A-a gradient remains normal, which is the key clue used to distinguish hypoventilation as the cause of hypoxemia from causes like V/Q mismatch, shunt, or diffusion impairment that do widen the gradient.

incorrectas.A: An increased A-a gradient would point toward a true gas-exchange problem (e.g., pulmonary edema, fibrosis, shunt, or V/Q mismatch), which is not what is happening in pure hypoventilation from opioids or obesity hypoventilation syndrome, where the lungs themselves exchange gas normally.
incorrectas.B: The A-a gradient does not decrease with hypoventilation; it stays at its baseline (normal) value because the fall in PAO2 and PaO2 track together, leaving their difference unchanged.
incorrectas.D: The A-a gradient is readily calculated from an arterial blood gas and the alveolar gas equation without needing a separate diffusion study; a diffusion capacity (DLCO) test evaluates a different aspect of lung function and is not required to determine the A-a gradient.

preguntas.q: A patient with pulmonary fibrosis or pulmonary edema develops hypoxemia due to impaired gas diffusion. What is expected of their A-a gradient?

e.correcta: Diffusion defects, such as thickened alveolar-capillary membranes in fibrosis or fluid-filled interstitium in pulmonary edema, impair the transfer of oxygen from alveolar gas into pulmonary capillary blood. Alveolar PO2 (PAO2) remains essentially normal (ventilation itself is not necessarily impaired), but arterial PO2 (PaO2) falls because oxygen cannot equilibrate fully across the diseased membrane, so the A-a gradient widens. A widened A-a gradient is the classic finding that localizes hypoxemia to a true gas-exchange abnormality rather than a purely ventilatory problem.

incorrectas.A: A decreased A-a gradient is not a recognized pattern in these disorders; if anything, worsening diffusion impairment widens the gradient further as the barrier to oxygen transfer increases.
incorrectas.C: A normal A-a gradient would be expected in hypoventilation or high altitude, where PAO2 and PaO2 fall together — but in diffusion defects, PAO2 stays comparatively preserved while PaO2 falls, which is exactly what widens the gradient rather than keeping it normal.
incorrectas.D: The A-a gradient is calculated from arterial blood gas values and the alveolar gas equation, independent of spirometry; spirometry assesses airflow and lung volumes, not the alveolar-arterial oxygen difference.

preguntas.q: In a patient with hypoxemia caused by ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch, what happens to the A-a gradient?

e.correcta: V/Q mismatch means that ventilation and perfusion are not well matched throughout the lung — some units are relatively over-perfused for their ventilation (low V/Q, as in atelectasis or airway obstruction) or over-ventilated for their perfusion (high V/Q, as in pulmonary embolism), and blood leaving poorly ventilated regions is desaturated. Because blood from low-V/Q units cannot be fully compensated by hyperventilating well-matched units (hemoglobin is already near fully saturated there), arterial PO2 falls while alveolar PO2 stays relatively preserved, widening the A-a gradient — this is the most common cause of hypoxemia encountered clinically and, unlike hypoventilation or altitude, it responds only partially to supplemental oxygen.

incorrectas.A: A normal A-a gradient is characteristic of hypoventilation or high altitude, where alveolar and arterial PO2 fall together; V/Q mismatch instead creates a genuine gas-exchange abnormality that widens the gradient.
incorrectas.C: A decreased gradient is not a recognized physiologic pattern — worsening V/Q mismatch, if anything, further widens the A-a gradient as more blood bypasses adequately ventilated alveoli.
incorrectas.D: A negative A-a gradient is not physiologically meaningful in this context; V/Q mismatch produces a widened (increased), not negative, gradient.

preguntas.q: In a patient with hypoxemia due to a right-to-left cardiac or pulmonary shunt, what happens to the A-a gradient?

o.A: It stays normal because gas exchange is unaffected
o.D: It normalizes once 100% oxygen is given

e.correcta: A right-to-left shunt allows deoxygenated blood to bypass ventilated alveoli entirely and mix directly into the arterial circulation, so that blood reaching the systemic arteries is never exposed to alveolar gas. This mixing lowers PaO2 substantially while PAO2 in ventilated regions remains normal, producing a widened A-a gradient — and because shunted blood never contacts alveolar gas, this hypoxemia is characteristically refractory to supplemental oxygen, unlike the other causes of hypoxemia.

incorrectas.A: Gas exchange is very much affected by a shunt — blood is shunted around functioning alveoli altogether, which is precisely what widens the A-a gradient rather than leaving it unaffected.
incorrectas.B: The gradient does not decrease with a shunt; the more blood that bypasses ventilated lung, the larger the discrepancy between alveolar and arterial oxygen tension becomes.
incorrectas.D: This is actually the key clinical clue that distinguishes a shunt from other causes of hypoxemia: giving 100% oxygen fails to substantially raise PaO2 in a right-to-left shunt because the shunted blood never contacts the enriched alveolar gas, whereas hypoventilation, V/Q mismatch, and diffusion defects generally do improve with supplemental O2.

preguntas.q: Which cause of hypoxemia is characteristically NOT significantly improved by administering supplemental oxygen?

e.correcta: In a right-to-left shunt, blood passes from the venous to the arterial circulation without ever perfusing ventilated alveoli, so raising the inspired oxygen concentration cannot enrich that shunted blood — it never contacts alveolar gas in the first place. This makes shunt-related hypoxemia refractory to supplemental O2, a clinically important distinguishing feature used at the bedside (e.g., a patient on high-flow O2 whose SpO2 barely improves should raise suspicion for an intracardiac or intrapulmonary shunt).

incorrectas.A: Hypoventilation-related hypoxemia responds well to supplemental oxygen because increasing the inspired O2 fraction raises alveolar PO2 in alveoli that are still being ventilated, even if ventilation is reduced overall.
incorrectas.B: V/Q mismatch improves with supplemental oxygen because even poorly ventilated alveoli still receive some fresh gas; raising the inspired O2 concentration increases the PO2 delivered to those units and improves oxygenation of the blood that does pass through them.
incorrectas.C: Diffusion defects improve with supplemental oxygen because increasing the alveolar-to-capillary PO2 gradient enhances the driving force for oxygen diffusion across the thickened membrane, allowing more oxygen to cross despite the impaired diffusion capacity.

preguntas.q: A patient in cardiogenic shock has adequate arterial oxygen saturation but develops tissue hypoxia. Which hemodynamic abnormality is most directly responsible?

e.correcta: Tissue oxygen delivery is the product of cardiac output and arterial oxygen content (O2 delivery = CO x CaO2). Even with normal or near-normal oxygen saturation, a severe fall in cardiac output — as occurs in cardiogenic shock — reduces the volume of oxygenated blood reaching tissues per unit time, producing hypoxia despite adequate blood oxygen content. This distinguishes hypoxia (inadequate O2 delivery/utilization at the tissue level) from hypoxemia (low PaO2 specifically).

incorrectas.A: An increased hemoglobin concentration would raise oxygen-carrying capacity and tend to improve, not worsen, oxygen delivery; it is not a cause of hypoxia and is the opposite direction of the anemia-related mechanism that does cause hypoxia.
incorrectas.C: Increased minute ventilation would help maintain or raise PaO2 and is a compensatory response to hypoxemia, not a cause of tissue hypoxia; it does not explain hypoxia occurring with a normal PaO2 in cardiogenic shock.
incorrectas.D: Increased 2,3-BPG shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin curve rightward to facilitate O2 unloading to tissues — this is an adaptive, protective response to hypoxia, not a cause of it, and works in the opposite direction of worsening tissue oxygenation.

preguntas.q: Tissue hypoxia can result from either a reduced arterial oxygen tension or reduced oxygen content of blood despite normal PaO2. Which term describes hypoxia arising specifically from decreased PaO2 lowering hemoglobin saturation?

e.correcta: Hypoxemia refers specifically to a reduced PaO2, which in turn lowers the percent saturation of hemoglobin (via the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve) and thus reduces total blood oxygen content, ultimately causing tissue hypoxia. This is one of several distinct mechanisms leading to hypoxia — the others include reduced blood flow (ischemia), reduced oxygen-carrying capacity independent of PaO2 (anemia, carbon monoxide poisoning), and impaired cellular utilization of oxygen (histotoxic hypoxia, e.g., cyanide poisoning) — recognizing which mechanism is at play guides the appropriate treatment.

incorrectas.A: Ischemia refers to a loss or reduction of blood flow to a tissue (e.g., from arterial occlusion or reduced venous drainage), a mechanical flow problem rather than a defect in arterial oxygen tension or hemoglobin saturation.
incorrectas.C: Anemic hypoxia results from reduced hemoglobin or hematocrit (or a hemoglobin that cannot carry oxygen normally, as in CO poisoning), which lowers oxygen content even though PaO2 and percent saturation of the hemoglobin present may be entirely normal — this is a distinct mechanism from hypoxemia.
incorrectas.D: Histotoxic hypoxia occurs when cells cannot utilize oxygen delivered to them normally, classically from cyanide poisoning inhibiting cytochrome c oxidase; oxygen delivery (PaO2, saturation, content) is normal in this case, unlike hypoxemia where the defect is in oxygen tension itself.

preguntas.q: A patient with severe iron deficiency anemia develops tissue hypoxia despite a normal PaO2 and normal hemoglobin oxygen saturation. What is the underlying mechanism?

o.B: Decreased hemoglobin/hematocrit reducing total O2 content
o.C: Increased A-a gradient from diffusion impairment

e.correcta: In anemia, the amount of hemoglobin available to carry oxygen is reduced, so even though each hemoglobin molecule is fully saturated (normal PaO2 and normal % saturation), the total oxygen content of the blood (CaO2 = 1.34 x Hb x SaO2 + dissolved O2) is diminished because there is less hemoglobin overall. This lowers oxygen delivery to tissues and produces hypoxia despite entirely normal blood gas values for PaO2 and saturation — a good reminder that oxygen content, not just PaO2, determines tissue oxygenation.
