incorrectas.C: Cavitation refers to necrotic tissue destruction forming an air-filled space, typical of certain infections (e.g., TB, necrotizing pneumonia) or tumors, not the diffuse alveolar collapse of ARDS.
incorrectas.D: Emphysematous destruction involves permanent enlargement of airspaces from alveolar wall destruction, a chronic process seen in COPD, distinct from the acute, reversible alveolar collapse driven by surfactant dysfunction in ARDS.

preguntas.q: ARDS classically presents with what appearance on chest X-ray?

e.correcta: ARDS produces diffuse bilateral alveolar filling with protein-rich edema fluid and inflammatory debris, which appears as a diffuse "white-out" of both lung fields on chest X-ray, reflecting widespread alveolar (not just interstitial) opacification. This bilateral, diffuse pattern without cardiomegaly or evidence of volume overload helps distinguish ARDS from cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

incorrectas.B: A honeycomb pattern reflects end-stage pulmonary fibrosis with cystic destruction of lung architecture (as in usual interstitial pneumonia/IPF), a chronic fibrotic appearance quite different from the acute diffuse opacification of ARDS.
incorrectas.C: Kerley B lines are short horizontal lines at the lung periphery reflecting interstitial edema, classically seen in cardiogenic pulmonary edema from elevated hydrostatic pressure, not the diffuse alveolar white-out of ARDS.
incorrectas.D: Tram-track lines refer to thickened, dilated bronchial walls seen in bronchiectasis on CT/X-ray, an airway finding unrelated to the diffuse alveolar process of ARDS.

preguntas.q: Which clinical syndrome is characterized by acute-onset respiratory failure with bilateral lung opacities and no evidence of heart failure or fluid overload?

e.correcta: ARDS is defined by the Berlin criteria as acute onset (within one week of a known insult) of bilateral lung opacities on imaging plus hypoxemia that is not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload, distinguishing it from cardiogenic causes of similar imaging findings. This definition is intentionally exclusionary of a cardiac cause, which is why a normal PCWP and absence of volume overload are part of the diagnostic picture.

incorrectas.B: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema does present with bilateral opacities but is specifically caused by elevated left atrial/left ventricular filling pressures from heart failure, the very entity ARDS is defined in contrast to.
incorrectas.C: A COPD exacerbation typically presents with worsening airflow obstruction, wheezing, and hyperinflation rather than diffuse bilateral alveolar opacities from a permeability-driven edema process.
incorrectas.D: Pulmonary embolism causes acute hypoxemia and respiratory distress through a vascular obstruction/ventilation-perfusion mismatch mechanism, not diffuse bilateral alveolar filling from increased capillary permeability.

preguntas.q: What is the cornerstone of ARDS treatment beyond supportive respiratory care?

o.B: High-dose systemic corticosteroids in all patients
o.C: Prophylactic antibiotics regardless of infection status

e.correcta: Because ARDS is triggered by an inciting insult (sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, trauma, pancreatitis, etc.) that drives the inflammatory cascade causing capillary leak, effective management requires identifying and treating that underlying cause alongside supportive measures like lung-protective mechanical ventilation. Supportive care (low tidal volume ventilation, PEEP, prone positioning) mitigates lung injury, but the disease will not resolve without addressing what triggered it.

incorrectas.B: Corticosteroids are not a universal, first-line treatment for all ARDS and their benefit is inconsistent/controversial in trials; treating the underlying trigger is the more fundamental and universally applicable step.
incorrectas.C: Prophylactic antibiotics without evidence of an actual infectious trigger are not standard of care and could promote resistance; antibiotics are used when an infectious cause is identified, not empirically in every ARDS case.
incorrectas.D: Because ARDS edema is due to increased capillary permeability rather than volume overload (PCWP is normal), routine diuresis to lower PCWP is not the primary therapeutic strategy the way it would be in cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

preguntas.q: Recovery from ARDS may be complicated by interstitial fibrosis/scarring due to loss of which cell type needed for alveolar regeneration?

e.correcta: Type II pneumocytes are the stem-cell-like progenitors that normally regenerate damaged type I pneumocytes and replenish surfactant after alveolar injury; when ARDS destroys type II pneumocytes, the alveolar epithelium cannot properly regenerate and instead undergoes repair by fibrosis/scarring rather than restoration of normal architecture. This repair-over-regeneration outcome explains why some ARDS survivors develop lasting interstitial fibrosis and reduced lung compliance.

incorrectas.A: Type I pneumocytes are the thin cells that make up most of the gas-exchange surface but they are terminally differentiated and cannot regenerate themselves — that job falls to type II pneumocytes, whose loss is what drives fibrotic repair.
incorrectas.C: Alveolar macrophages clear debris and pathogens and participate in the inflammatory response, but they are not the epithelial progenitor cells responsible for regenerating the alveolar lining after injury.
incorrectas.D: Clara (club) cells are secretory progenitor cells found in the bronchioles, not the alveoli, and are not the specific cell type whose ARDS-related loss leads to alveolar fibrosis.

preguntas.q: In a fetus of a mother with poorly controlled diabetes, increased fetal insulin has what effect on surfactant production, raising the risk of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?

o.D: Converts surfactant to an inactive form

e.correcta: Maternal hyperglycemia causes fetal hyperinsulinemia, and insulin delays and decreases surfactant production by fetal type II pneumocytes (it antagonizes cortisol's stimulatory effect on surfactant synthesis), leaving the lungs surfactant-deficient at birth. This is why infants of diabetic mothers are at increased risk for neonatal respiratory distress syndrome even at a gestational age when surfactant would normally be adequate.

incorrectas.A: No effect on surfactant production would not explain the well-documented clinical association between maternal diabetes and neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, which depends on insulin actively suppressing surfactant synthesis rather than being neutral.
incorrectas.B: Increased surfactant production is the opposite of what occurs — insulin actually suppresses surfactant synthesis, which is precisely why maternal diabetes is a major risk factor for NRDS rather than protective against it.
incorrectas.D: Insulin does not chemically inactivate existing surfactant; the mechanism is suppression of surfactant synthesis by fetal type II pneumocytes, not conversion of already-produced surfactant into a nonfunctional form.

preguntas.q: What treatment may be given to an infant after birth to manage neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?

o.C: High-flow supplemental oxygen alone, no surfactant

e.correcta: Once an infant is born with neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, exogenous (artificial) surfactant can be administered directly into the infant's airway to reduce alveolar surface tension, improve lung compliance, and prevent alveolar collapse, directly replacing what the immature type II pneumocytes have failed to adequately produce. This is distinct from antenatal corticosteroids, which are given to the mother before delivery to accelerate fetal lung maturation and surfactant production preemptively.

incorrectas.B: Corticosteroids (like betamethasone) are given to the mother antenatally, before delivery, to stimulate fetal surfactant production in anticipation of preterm birth — they are not a postnatal treatment given to the infant after NRDS has already developed.
incorrectas.C: Oxygen alone treats the resulting hypoxemia but does not address the underlying surfactant deficiency causing alveolar collapse and increased surface tension; surfactant replacement is the more targeted, mechanism-based treatment.
incorrectas.D: Prophylactic antibiotics treat or prevent infection, not the surfactant deficiency that causes NRDS, and are not the standard postnatal intervention for this specific condition unless a concurrent infection is suspected.

preguntas.q: The foam stability index test, using ethanol and amniotic fluid shaken to look for a ring of stable foam, is used to assess maturity of which fetal organ?

e.correcta: The foam stability index test assesses fetal lung maturity by testing whether surfactant in the amniotic fluid is sufficient to generate stable foam when shaken with ethanol at various dilutions — surfactant's surface-tension-lowering phospholipids stabilize the foam, so a stable ring at a high dilution well indicates adequate surfactant and lower risk of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. This is one of several amniotic fluid-based tests (along with the lecithin:sphingomyelin ratio) used to gauge readiness for delivery when preterm birth is being considered.

incorrectas.B: Fetal renal maturity is not assessed via surfactant-related foam stability testing; renal function is instead inferred indirectly through amniotic fluid volume (oligohydramnios/polyhydramnios), not a foam test.
incorrectas.C: Fetal liver maturity is not the target of this test; the amniotic fluid analyzed reflects lung secretions (surfactant phospholipids) rather than hepatic function markers.
incorrectas.D: Cardiac maturity is assessed by other modalities (e.g., fetal echocardiography), not by an amniotic fluid foam stability assay, which is specifically tied to pulmonary surfactant content.

preguntas.q: Which cancer is the most common cause of cancer mortality in the United States?

e.correcta: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the US for both men and women, exceeding colorectal, breast, and prostate cancer combined, largely due to its strong association with cigarette smoking and its tendency to present at an advanced, often unresectable stage. This high mortality despite being only the second or third most commonly diagnosed cancer (behind breast and prostate in incidence) reflects its aggressive biology and the frequent delay in diagnosis until symptoms from local invasion or metastasis appear.

incorrectas.B: Colorectal cancer is a leading cause of cancer death but ranks below lung cancer in overall US cancer mortality, partly because widespread screening (colonoscopy) catches many cases at an earlier, more treatable stage.
incorrectas.C: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in women and a major cause of cancer death in women specifically, but overall (combining both sexes), it causes fewer deaths nationally than lung cancer.
incorrectas.D: Prostate cancer is very common in incidence among men but tends to have a more indolent course in many patients and is screened for, resulting in lower overall mortality compared to lung cancer.

preguntas.q: What is the average age at presentation for lung cancer?

e.correcta: Lung cancer classically presents around age 60, reflecting the decades-long latency between the onset of chronic carcinogen exposure (chiefly cigarette smoking, measured in pack-years) and the accumulation of enough genetic mutations to produce a clinically detectable tumor. This age also overlaps with when smoking-related comorbidities (COPD, cardiovascular disease) commonly emerge, which is relevant when working up new respiratory symptoms in this age group.

incorrectas.A: 40 years old is younger than the typical presentation; lung cancer in someone this young would be somewhat atypical and might prompt consideration of a strong genetic predisposition or unusual exposure history.
incorrectas.B: 50 years old is closer to when screening guidelines (low-dose CT for high-risk smokers) may begin, but the average age at actual diagnosis is later, around 60.
incorrectas.D: 75 years old is older than the typical average age of presentation, though lung cancer certainly can and does present in this age group as part of the broader distribution around the mean.

preguntas.q: Lung cancer risk correlates directly with the duration and amount of smoking, quantified using what unit?

e.correcta: Pack-years (packs of cigarettes smoked per day multiplied by number of years smoked) is the standard metric because it captures both the intensity and duration of tobacco exposure, both of which independently and multiplicatively increase the cumulative mutagenic burden on bronchial epithelium and thus lung cancer risk. This composite measure is more predictive than either intensity or duration alone and is used clinically to determine eligibility for lung cancer screening.

incorrectas.B: Cigarettes per day alone captures intensity but ignores duration of exposure, missing the cumulative risk from years of smoking, which is why pack-years (which incorporates both) is the preferred metric.
incorrectas.C: Total lifetime cigarettes smoked is conceptually similar to pack-years but is not the standardized unit used clinically; pack-years is the specific, universally used metric for risk stratification and screening eligibility.
incorrectas.D: Years since smoking cessation is relevant to how quickly risk declines after quitting but is not itself the measure of cumulative smoking exposure that correlates directly with lung cancer risk.

preguntas.q: Lung cancer often presents on chest X-ray with what classic finding, or a non-calcified nodule on CT, which requires biopsy to confirm malignancy?

e.correcta: Lung cancer classically appears as a solitary rounded opacity on chest X-ray, described as a "coin lesion," or as a non-calcified pulmonary nodule on CT; because benign processes (granulomas, hamartomas) can also produce a similar coin-lesion appearance, tissue biopsy is required to distinguish malignant from benign etiologies rather than relying on imaging appearance alone. This is an important teaching point: imaging can raise suspicion for cancer but cannot substitute for histologic confirmation.

incorrectas.B: "Honeycomb" lung describes the cystic, fibrotic end-stage appearance of interstitial lung disease (like idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis), a diffuse chronic pattern unrelated to the discrete solitary nodule typical of lung cancer.
incorrectas.C: Diffuse "ground-glass" haze is seen in various diffuse parenchymal processes (e.g., atypical pneumonia, some interstitial lung diseases, early ARDS) rather than the focal, discrete coin-lesion appearance classically associated with a lung malignancy.
incorrectas.D: A "water-bottle" silhouette refers to the classic globular enlargement of the cardiac silhouette seen with a large pericardial effusion, an entirely different radiographic finding unrelated to a pulmonary nodule or mass.

preguntas.q: A 'coin lesion' is seen on CXR in a patient from the Midwest. Which benign process is most likely responsible?

e.correcta: A solitary, well-circumscribed 'coin lesion' on chest x-ray is frequently a granuloma, the organized immune response (epithelioid macrophages, giant cells, and often central caseation) to a walled-off infection such as TB or a fungal organism. In the Midwest, Histoplasma capsulatum is a classic culprit because it thrives in soil contaminated with bird or bat droppings, producing calcified granulomas that mimic malignancy radiographically but are benign.

incorrectas.B: Bronchial carcinoid tumor is a low-grade neuroendocrine neoplasm that classically forms a polypoid endobronchial mass rather than a discrete peripheral coin lesion, and it is a true (if indolent) tumor, not an inflammatory granuloma.
incorrectas.C: Pulmonary hamartomas can appear as coin lesions too (often with 'popcorn' calcification), but they are benign neoplasms of disorganized mesenchymal and epithelial tissue, not a granulomatous immune reaction to infection like TB or Histoplasma.
incorrectas.D: Bronchiectasis is permanent bronchial dilation from chronic infection/inflammation and appears as tram-track or cystic airway changes, not a discrete solitary nodule, so it does not produce the coin-lesion appearance described.

preguntas.q: Lung carcinomas are broadly classified into two major histologic categories. Which category comprises approximately 85% of cases?

e.correcta: Non-small cell carcinoma (NSCLC) accounts for roughly 85% of lung cancers and includes adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma. This distinction matters clinically because NSCLC is often amenable to surgical resection and targeted therapies, whereas small cell carcinoma is treated primarily with chemotherapy given its aggressive, early-metastasizing behavior.

incorrectas.B: Small cell carcinoma makes up only about 15% of lung cancers; it is a neuroendocrine tumor strongly linked to smoking, characterized by rapid growth and early widespread metastasis, which is why it is managed differently from the more common NSCLC subtypes.
incorrectas.C: Carcinoid tumors are a separate, much rarer category of low-grade neuroendocrine neoplasms and are not classified under either the small cell or non-small cell carcinoma umbrella, nor do they make up the 85% figure.
incorrectas.D: Mesothelioma arises from the pleura (typically from asbestos exposure) rather than from lung parenchymal or bronchial epithelium, so it is not one of the two categories used to classify primary lung carcinoma.

preguntas.q: Small (oat) cell carcinoma of the lung is most classically associated with which patient demographic?

o.C: Young nonsmokers with a family history of lung cancer

e.correcta: Small cell (oat cell) carcinoma is strongly linked to cigarette smoking and occurs predominantly in male smokers, fitting the classic mnemonic 'small cell, smokers, central, paraneoplastic syndromes.' Its neuroendocrine cell of origin also explains its propensity to secrete ACTH, ADH, and other hormones, producing paraneoplastic syndromes like SIADH and Cushing syndrome.

incorrectas.B: Nonsmoking women are the classic demographic for adenocarcinoma, the most common lung cancer subtype in never-smokers, not for small cell carcinoma, which is tightly tied to heavy tobacco exposure.
incorrectas.C: Young nonsmokers with a family history are not the typical population for small cell carcinoma; this subtype is overwhelmingly a disease of long-term smokers rather than one driven primarily by inherited susceptibility.
incorrectas.D: Asbestos exposure is the classic risk factor for mesothelioma and contributes to some bronchogenic carcinomas, but the demographic most classically tied to small cell carcinoma specifically is smoking, not asbestos exposure.

preguntas.q: Small (oat) cell carcinoma of the lung typically arises in which anatomic location?

o.C: Within the mediastinal lymph nodes primarily

e.correcta: Small cell carcinoma classically arises centrally, near the hilum and major bronchi, consistent with its origin from neuroendocrine (Kulchitsky) cells within the bronchial epithelium. This central location often causes early bronchial obstruction and post-obstructive pneumonia, and combined with its rapid growth, contributes to its typically unresectable presentation at diagnosis.

incorrectas.B: A peripheral location is characteristic of adenocarcinoma and large cell carcinoma, not small cell carcinoma; small cell tumors are centrally located near the major airways rather than out near the pleura.
incorrectas.C: While small cell carcinoma frequently metastasizes early to mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes, the primary tumor itself arises in the central bronchi, not within the lymph nodes.
incorrectas.D: An apical (superior sulcus) location is associated with Pancoast tumors, which are usually non-small cell carcinomas causing Horner syndrome or brachial plexus symptoms, not the classic central location of small cell carcinoma.

preguntas.q: Small (oat) cell carcinoma of the lung is commonly associated with amplification of which oncogene?

e.correcta: Small cell carcinoma is classically associated with amplification of MYC family oncogenes (particularly L-myc), a transcription factor that drives cell proliferation; this genetic alteration helps explain the tumor's characteristically rapid growth rate and high proliferative index. MYC amplification is one of the most consistently cited molecular features distinguishing small cell carcinoma biology from other lung cancer subtypes.

incorrectas.B: RAS mutations (particularly KRAS) are more classically associated with adenocarcinoma of the lung, where they activate downstream MAPK signaling to drive proliferation, rather than being the signature alteration of small cell carcinoma.
incorrectas.C: EGFR mutations are a hallmark of adenocarcinoma, especially in nonsmokers and Asian female patients, and are targetable with tyrosine kinase inhibitors; they are not the classic genetic association for small cell carcinoma.
incorrectas.D: HER2/neu amplification is best known in breast cancer and occasionally in a subset of adenocarcinomas, but it is not the oncogene classically linked to small cell lung carcinoma.

preguntas.q: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung typically arises in which anatomic location?

e.correcta: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung, like small cell carcinoma, arises centrally from the bronchial epithelium, often forming a hilar mass that can cause bronchial obstruction, post-obstructive pneumonia, or atelectasis. Its central bronchial origin reflects squamous metaplasia of bronchial epithelium in response to chronic irritants like cigarette smoke, progressing through dysplasia to carcinoma in situ and then invasive cancer.

incorrectas.B: A peripheral location is characteristic of adenocarcinoma and large cell carcinoma, which arise from more distal airway or alveolar epithelium, in contrast to the central bronchial origin of squamous cell carcinoma.
incorrectas.C: Diffuse bilateral involvement is not typical of primary squamous cell carcinoma, which usually presents as a discrete central hilar mass rather than a diffuse infiltrative process.
incorrectas.D: Primary tumors arising from the visceral pleura itself suggest mesothelioma, not squamous cell carcinoma, which originates from bronchial epithelium rather than mesothelial cells.

preguntas.q: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung commonly presents as a hilar mass arising from which structure?

e.correcta: Squamous cell carcinoma arises from the bronchial epithelium, which undergoes squamous metaplasia and dysplasia in response to chronic smoke exposure before progressing to invasive carcinoma. This origin explains its typical presentation as a hilar mass with central cavitation (from central necrosis outgrowing its blood supply) and its association with obstructive symptoms like hemoptysis.

incorrectas.B: The alveolar septa are the site of gas exchange and are more relevant to peripheral tumors like adenocarcinoma (which can arise from type II pneumocytes), not the central bronchial origin of squamous cell carcinoma.
incorrectas.C: The visceral pleura is the site of origin for mesothelioma, not squamous cell carcinoma, which arises from airway epithelium rather than the serosal lining of the lung.
incorrectas.D: Terminal bronchioles are more peripheral structures associated with adenocarcinoma's origin (via Clara cells and type II pneumocytes), whereas squamous cell carcinoma classically arises from the larger, more central bronchi.

preguntas.q: Adenocarcinoma of the lung typically arises in which anatomic location?

e.correcta: Adenocarcinoma arises peripherally, often from distal bronchioloalveolar structures such as type II pneumocytes or Clara cells, in contrast to the central bronchial origin of small cell and squamous cell carcinoma. Because of its peripheral location, adenocarcinoma is more likely to be found incidentally on imaging and can involve the pleura directly, sometimes producing a desmoplastic reaction that causes chest wall or pleuritic pain.

incorrectas.B: A central hilar location is characteristic of small cell and squamous cell carcinoma, both of which arise from the more proximal bronchial epithelium, unlike the peripheral origin of adenocarcinoma.
incorrectas.C: The trachea is not a typical site of origin for any of the major lung carcinoma subtypes; adenocarcinoma specifically arises from distal airway and alveolar structures far from the trachea.
incorrectas.D: The mediastinum is a site to which lung cancers may metastasize (via lymphatic spread to mediastinal nodes), not the primary site of origin for adenocarcinoma, which begins in the lung periphery.

preguntas.q: Which lung cancer subtype is the most common cause of lung cancer in nonsmokers and in female smokers?

e.correcta: Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer overall in the US and is the leading subtype in both nonsmokers and female smokers, likely reflecting its weaker (though still present) association with smoking compared to squamous cell and small cell carcinoma. It also carries a higher frequency of targetable driver mutations such as EGFR and ALK rearrangements, which are especially enriched in never-smokers, making molecular testing clinically important in this population.

incorrectas.B: Squamous cell carcinoma has one of the strongest dose-dependent relationships with smoking among lung cancers and is far less common in nonsmokers, making it a poor fit for the demographic described.
incorrectas.C: Small cell carcinoma is also very strongly tied to heavy tobacco exposure and is rare in true nonsmokers, distinguishing it from adenocarcinoma's relatively higher occurrence in never-smokers.
incorrectas.D: Large cell carcinoma, while less strongly linked to smoking than squamous or small cell carcinoma, is still less common than adenocarcinoma overall and is not the classic subtype associated with nonsmokers or female smokers specifically.

preguntas.q: Large cell carcinoma of the lung is characterized histologically by which feature?

o.A: Poorly differentiated large cells with no glandular, squamous, or neuroendocrine differentiation
o.B: Well-differentiated glandular structures with mucin production
o.D: Small, round blue cells with scant cytoplasm

e.correcta: Large cell carcinoma is a diagnosis of exclusion within non-small cell lung cancer: it is composed of poorly (undifferentiated) large, pleomorphic cells that lack the glandular formation of adenocarcinoma, the keratinization/intercellular bridges of squamous cell carcinoma, and the neuroendocrine markers of small cell or carcinoid tumors. This high-grade, undifferentiated appearance correlates with its aggressive behavior and generally poor prognosis.

incorrectas.B: Well-differentiated glands with mucin production describe adenocarcinoma, which retains features of its glandular cell of origin — the opposite of the undifferentiated appearance that defines large cell carcinoma.
incorrectas.C: Keratin pearls and intercellular bridges are the defining histologic features of squamous cell carcinoma, reflecting its origin from squamous epithelium; large cell carcinoma specifically lacks these differentiating features.
incorrectas.D: Small, round blue cells with scant cytoplasm describe small cell (oat cell) carcinoma, a neuroendocrine tumor with a very different, much smaller cell morphology than the large pleomorphic cells of large cell carcinoma.

preguntas.q: Large cell carcinoma of the lung may present histologically with which additional finding?

e.correcta: Large cell carcinoma can display pleomorphic giant cells — markedly enlarged, atypical, multinucleated tumor cells — reflecting its highly undifferentiated, high-grade nature. This bizarre cytologic appearance, combined with the absence of glandular, squamous, or neuroendocrine markers, is part of what defines large cell carcinoma as a distinct, aggressive category within non-small cell lung cancer.

incorrectas.B: Psammoma bodies are laminated, calcified concretions classically seen in papillary thyroid carcinoma, serous ovarian tumors, and meningiomas, not a feature associated with large cell carcinoma of the lung.
incorrectas.C: Keratin pearls are whorled structures of keratinization specific to squamous cell carcinoma, reflecting squamous differentiation that is, by definition, absent in large cell carcinoma.
incorrectas.D: Rosette formations (e.g., Homer-Wright rosettes) are associated with neuroendocrine and neural tumors such as neuroblastoma or small cell carcinoma, not with the undifferentiated large cells of large cell carcinoma.

preguntas.q: Is large cell carcinoma of the lung associated with cigarette smoking?

o.A: Yes, it is associated with smoking
o.B: No, it occurs almost exclusively in nonsmokers
o.C: Only in patients with prior radiation exposure
o.D: Only in patients with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

e.correcta: Large cell carcinoma, like squamous cell and small cell carcinoma, is associated with cigarette smoking, distinguishing it from adenocarcinoma, which has a comparatively weaker link and is the more common subtype in never-smokers. This places large cell carcinoma among the smoking-related lung cancers, even though it lacks the specific squamous or neuroendocrine differentiation of the other smoking-associated subtypes.

incorrectas.B: Large cell carcinoma is not confined to nonsmokers — that profile better fits adenocarcinoma, which occurs more frequently (relatively) in never-smokers compared to the other major lung cancer subtypes.
incorrectas.C: While radiation exposure is a recognized general risk factor for lung cancer, it is not the specific or primary association highlighted for large cell carcinoma; smoking is the classic association tested for this subtype.
incorrectas.D: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency predisposes to early-onset emphysema and liver disease, not specifically to large cell carcinoma; it is not the classic risk factor linked to this tumor type.

preguntas.q: Large cell carcinoma of the lung typically arises in which anatomic location?

e.correcta: Large cell carcinoma, like adenocarcinoma, is typically located peripherally in the lung rather than centrally near the hilum. This peripheral location, combined with its undifferentiated, high-grade histology, contributes to its tendency to be diagnosed at a more advanced stage and its generally poor prognosis relative to other non-small cell subtypes.

incorrectas.B: A central hilar location is more classic for squamous cell carcinoma and small cell carcinoma, both of which arise from the proximal bronchial epithelium, unlike the peripheral distribution of large cell carcinoma.
incorrectas.C: Primary tumors within the trachea itself are uncommon regardless of subtype; large cell carcinoma is described as a peripheral lung tumor, not a tracheal one.
incorrectas.D: The carina is the bifurcation point of the trachea into the mainstem bronchi and is not the characteristic site for large cell carcinoma, which arises more peripherally in the lung parenchyma.

preguntas.q: What is the general prognosis of large cell carcinoma of the lung?

o.C: Favorable if surgically resected regardless of stage

e.correcta: Large cell carcinoma carries a poor prognosis, reflecting its highly undifferentiated, anaplastic histology and its tendency to be diagnosed at a more advanced stage due to its peripheral, often silent growth. Because it lacks specific glandular or squamous differentiation, it also tends to behave aggressively with early metastatic potential, similar in aggressiveness to other high-grade non-small cell subtypes.

incorrectas.B: An excellent prognosis with rare metastasis describes bronchial carcinoid tumor, a low-grade neuroendocrine neoplasm, which behaves very differently from the aggressive, poorly differentiated large cell carcinoma.
incorrectas.C: While surgical resection can improve outcomes in early-stage disease, large cell carcinoma's overall prognosis remains poor because of its tendency toward aggressive behavior and later-stage presentation, not a uniformly favorable outcome after surgery.
incorrectas.D: Bronchial carcinoid tumor has an excellent prognosis and rarely metastasizes, the opposite of large cell carcinoma's aggressive course, so equating their prognoses is incorrect.

preguntas.q: Is bronchioloalveolar carcinoma (adenocarcinoma in situ) associated with cigarette smoking?

o.A: No, it is not associated with smoking
o.C: Only in patients who smoke more than one pack per day
o.D: Only in the presence of asbestos co-exposure

e.correcta: Bronchioloalveolar carcinoma, now classified as adenocarcinoma in situ, is notably not associated with smoking, setting it apart from the other major lung cancer subtypes (small cell, squamous cell, and large cell carcinoma), which all show strong smoking links. This lack of a smoking association, combined with its excellent prognosis when fully resected, makes it a favorable outlier among lung neoplasms.

incorrectas.B: A strong smoking association is characteristic of small cell, squamous cell, and (to a lesser degree) large cell carcinoma, but specifically not of bronchioloalveolar carcinoma/adenocarcinoma in situ, which is the exception among lung cancers.
incorrectas.C: There is no dose-dependent smoking relationship described for this tumor because it is fundamentally not a smoking-related malignancy, unlike squamous cell or small cell carcinoma where cumulative pack-years matter.
incorrectas.D: Asbestos exposure is classically linked to mesothelioma, not to bronchioloalveolar carcinoma/adenocarcinoma in situ, which is not defined by any smoking- or asbestos-related risk factor.

preguntas.q: Adenocarcinoma in situ (formerly bronchioloalveolar carcinoma) of the lung typically arises in which anatomic location?

e.correcta: Adenocarcinoma in situ, like invasive adenocarcinoma, is located peripherally in the lung, growing along pre-existing alveolar septa (a pattern historically called 'lepidic growth') without invading the underlying stroma. This peripheral, non-invasive growth pattern is part of why it carries such an excellent prognosis compared to other lung malignancies.

incorrectas.B: A central hilar location is characteristic of squamous cell and small cell carcinoma, which arise from proximal bronchial epithelium, in contrast to the distal, peripheral origin of adenocarcinoma in situ.
incorrectas.C: The trachea is not the site of origin for this tumor; adenocarcinoma in situ arises from distal alveolar structures far from the trachea.
incorrectas.D: Mediastinal lymph nodes are a site of potential metastatic spread for lung cancers in general, not the primary site of origin, and adenocarcinoma in situ specifically is notable for its lack of invasive/metastatic behavior.

preguntas.q: What is the general prognosis of bronchioloalveolar carcinoma (adenocarcinoma in situ)?

o.B: Poor, similar to small cell carcinoma
o.C: Intermediate, similar to large cell carcinoma

e.correcta: Bronchioloalveolar carcinoma (adenocarcinoma in situ) has an excellent prognosis, because by definition it grows along alveolar septa without invading the surrounding stroma or vasculature, meaning it has not yet acquired invasive or metastatic potential. Complete surgical resection is often curative, which is why distinguishing this in situ lesion from invasive adenocarcinoma matters greatly for staging and management.

incorrectas.B: Small cell carcinoma has an aggressive course with early widespread metastasis and a poor prognosis, the opposite of the excellent outcome seen with the non-invasive adenocarcinoma in situ.
incorrectas.C: Large cell carcinoma is a poorly differentiated, aggressive non-small cell subtype with a poor prognosis, quite different from the indolent, non-invasive nature of adenocarcinoma in situ.
incorrectas.D: A uniformly fatal course within a year would describe an aggressive, rapidly progressive cancer, which is the opposite of adenocarcinoma in situ's excellent, often curable prognosis when resected.

preguntas.q: Bronchial carcinoid tumor is characterized by positive immunohistochemical staining for which marker?

e.correcta: Bronchial carcinoid tumor stains positive for chromogranin A, a protein stored in the dense-core secretory granules of neuroendocrine cells, confirming its origin from bronchial neuroendocrine (Kulchitsky) cells. This neuroendocrine identity also explains why carcinoid tumors can secrete bioactive substances like serotonin, occasionally producing carcinoid syndrome when metastatic or when venous drainage bypasses hepatic metabolism.

incorrectas.B: Cytokeratin 20 is a marker more typically used in the workup of certain adenocarcinomas (e.g., colorectal, Merkel cell carcinoma pattern recognition), not a defining neuroendocrine marker for bronchial carcinoid tumors.
incorrectas.C: TTF-1 can be positive in various lung tumors, including some carcinoids, but the defining feature that confirms neuroendocrine differentiation in carcinoid tumors is chromogranin A (and synaptophysin), not TTF-1 in isolation without neuroendocrine markers.
incorrectas.D: CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen) is a nonspecific tumor marker elevated in various adenocarcinomas (e.g., colorectal, some lung adenocarcinomas), not the specific neuroendocrine marker used to characterize bronchial carcinoid tumor.

preguntas.q: Is bronchial carcinoid tumor associated with cigarette smoking?

o.D: Only when combined with alcohol use

e.correcta: Bronchial carcinoid tumor is not associated with smoking, unlike small cell, squamous cell, and large cell carcinoma. This fits with its distinct neuroendocrine cell origin and generally indolent, low-grade behavior, reinforcing that it is a biologically and epidemiologically different entity from the classic smoking-related bronchogenic carcinomas.

incorrectas.B: A strong smoking association is a defining feature of small cell and squamous cell carcinoma, but bronchial carcinoid tumor is specifically the outlier among lung neoplasms that is not linked to tobacco exposure.
incorrectas.C: There is no described threshold of pack-years linking carcinoid tumors to smoking, because unlike the major bronchogenic carcinomas, carcinoid tumors arise independent of smoking history altogether.
incorrectas.D: Alcohol use is not implicated in the pathogenesis of bronchial carcinoid tumors; these tumors arise from neuroendocrine cells without an established smoking or alcohol-related risk factor.

preguntas.q: What is the general prognosis of bronchial carcinoid tumor?

o.A: Excellent, as it is a low-grade malignancy that rarely metastasizes
o.C: Intermediate, similar to squamous cell carcinoma

e.correcta: Bronchial carcinoid tumor has an excellent prognosis because it is a low-grade malignancy that grows slowly and rarely metastasizes, in sharp contrast to the aggressive bronchogenic carcinomas. Even though it can rarely cause carcinoid syndrome (particularly with hepatic metastases or when tumor products bypass first-pass hepatic metabolism), most cases are cured with surgical resection.

incorrectas.B: Early widespread metastasis and a poor prognosis are characteristic of small cell carcinoma, a high-grade neuroendocrine tumor, which behaves very differently from the indolent, low-grade bronchial carcinoid tumor.
incorrectas.C: Squamous cell carcinoma carries a more guarded prognosis tied to its stage at diagnosis and smoking-related biology, which is not comparable to the excellent, low-risk course typical of bronchial carcinoid tumor.
incorrectas.D: The excellent prognosis of bronchial carcinoid tumor is an inherent feature of its low-grade biology, not something contingent on avoiding biopsy; biopsy and resection are, in fact, how the tumor is diagnosed and cured.

preguntas.q: Bronchial carcinoid tumor classically forms a polyp-like mass in which structure?

e.correcta: Bronchial carcinoid tumor classically arises within the bronchus, forming a polypoid, endobronchial mass that can protrude into the airway lumen. This intraluminal growth pattern can cause obstructive symptoms (cough, hemoptysis, recurrent pneumonia) despite the tumor's overall indolent, low-grade behavior.

incorrectas.B: The alveolar sac is the site of gas exchange in the distal lung and is not the classic location for carcinoid tumor growth, which arises from neuroendocrine cells within the larger conducting airways (bronchi).
incorrectas.C: The pleura is the site of origin for mesothelioma and can be a site of metastatic spread for many lung cancers, but it is not where bronchial carcinoid tumors classically form their polypoid mass.
incorrectas.D: The trachea is a separate, more proximal airway structure; bronchial carcinoid tumors are specifically named for and classically arise in the bronchus, not the trachea itself.

preguntas.q: In the TNM staging system for lung cancer, what does the 'T' component represent?

e.correcta: The 'T' in TNM staging describes the primary tumor's size and the extent of its local invasion into surrounding structures (such as the chest wall, mediastinum, or major airways). This component is critical for surgical planning, since larger or more locally invasive tumors are less likely to be amenable to curative resection regardless of nodal or metastatic status.

incorrectas.B: Spread to regional lymph nodes is captured by the 'N' component of TNM staging, which assesses hilar and mediastinal nodal involvement separately from the primary tumor's size and local extension.
incorrectas.C: Distant metastasis is captured by the 'M' component, which specifically addresses spread to sites like the brain, bone, liver, or adrenal glands, distinct from the local size/extension assessed by 'T'.
incorrectas.D: Histologic cell type and tumor grade are important prognostic and therapeutic factors, but they are reported separately from the anatomic TNM staging system, which focuses purely on the extent of anatomic spread.

preguntas.q: In the TNM staging system for lung cancer, what does the 'N' component represent?

o.A: Spread to regional lymph nodes (hilar and mediastinal)
o.D: Number of tumor nodules within the same lobe

e.correcta: The 'N' in TNM staging refers to the extent of spread to regional lymph nodes, specifically the hilar and mediastinal nodal stations that drain the lung. Nodal involvement is a major determinant of prognosis and treatment approach, since spread to contralateral or supraclavicular nodes generally shifts management from surgical resection toward chemoradiation.

incorrectas.B: Tumor size and local extension are assessed by the 'T' component, which evaluates the primary tumor itself rather than its spread to lymph nodes.
incorrectas.C: Distant metastasis is captured by the 'M' component, addressing spread beyond the regional lymphatics to distant organs, which is a distinct concept from regional nodal involvement.
incorrectas.D: Multiple nodules within the same lobe are actually incorporated into the 'T' classification in current staging systems, not the 'N' component, which is reserved specifically for lymph node involvement.

preguntas.q: In the TNM staging system for lung cancer, what does the 'M' component represent?

e.correcta: The 'M' in TNM staging indicates the presence or absence of distant metastasis, such as spread to the brain, bone, liver, or adrenal glands, sites lung cancer classically favors. Any confirmed distant metastasis (M1) generally precludes curative surgical resection and shifts treatment toward systemic therapy, making this the single most important factor separating potentially curable from incurable disease.

incorrectas.B: Spread to regional lymph nodes is assessed by the 'N' component, which is distinct from distant metastatic spread and generally carries a better prognosis than true M1 disease.
incorrectas.C: Tumor size and local extension are assessed by the 'T' component, describing the primary tumor itself rather than spread to distant organs.
incorrectas.D: Mitotic rate is a histologic grading feature assessed under the microscope, not part of the anatomic TNM staging system, which focuses on the extent of tumor spread rather than its proliferative activity.

preguntas.q: Metastasis from lung cancer to which organ is considered an unusual but characteristic site of distant spread, distinguishing it from more common metastatic patterns?

e.correcta: The adrenal gland is a classic and unique site of hematogenous metastasis from lung cancer, along with the brain, bone, and liver. This pattern is tested because adrenal metastases are often clinically silent (found incidentally on staging CT) unless they destroy enough cortex to cause adrenal insufficiency, so recognizing an adrenal mass in a patient with lung cancer should prompt consideration of metastatic disease rather than a primary adrenal tumor.

incorrectas.B: The spleen is relatively protected from metastatic seeding due to its rhythmic contractions and turbulent blood flow, which make it an uncommon site for metastases from any primary tumor, including lung cancer.
incorrectas.C: Skeletal muscle is metabolically active and well-perfused but is rarely a site of metastasis from lung cancer; bone (not muscle) is the classic musculoskeletal target of lung cancer spread.
incorrectas.D: The pancreas is not a classic site of lung cancer metastasis; when pancreatic masses are found, primary pancreatic adenocarcinoma or metastases from other primaries (e.g., renal cell carcinoma) are more typical considerations.

preguntas.q: Why does lung cancer have such a poor overall 5-year survival rate (around 15%)?

o.A: It commonly presents late in its course because no effective screening test exists for the general population
o.B: It is universally resistant to all forms of chemotherapy
o.C: It arises exclusively in patients with pre-existing immunodeficiency
o.D: It metastasizes only after decades of indolent growth

e.correcta: Lung cancer's poor prognosis stems largely from late presentation: the lung parenchyma has few pain fibers and substantial functional reserve, so tumors can grow silently until they invade a structure that produces symptoms (airway, pleura, nerve, or vessel) or until metastases already exist. Unlike breast or colon cancer, there was for a long time no widely implemented population screening test, so a large fraction of cases are diagnosed at an advanced, unresectable stage, which is the main driver of the low survival rate (low-dose CT screening in high-risk smokers has since improved this somewhat).

incorrectas.B: Lung cancer is not universally chemoresistant — small cell lung cancer, for instance, is often initially quite chemosensitive; the poor survival is primarily a staging/detection problem, not an inherent lack of any treatment response.
incorrectas.C: Lung cancer is overwhelmingly linked to smoking and environmental carcinogen exposure, not immunodeficiency; it occurs in immunocompetent hosts far more often than in immunocompromised ones.
incorrectas.D: Many lung cancers, especially small cell and squamous types, are aggressive and metastasize relatively early, not after decades of indolent growth — this is part of why early detection is so difficult and important.

preguntas.q: When a lung nodule is found on imaging, which is statistically more likely to be the underlying process — a primary lung tumor or metastasis to the lung from another primary site?

o.D: Neither; most lung nodules are granulomas

e.correcta: The lungs receive the entire cardiac output through the pulmonary circulation, acting as a natural filter for tumor emboli from virtually any primary cancer (breast, colon, kidney, and many others), which makes metastatic disease to the lung more common overall than a primary lung malignancy. This is why multiple, often bilateral, well-circumscribed nodules on chest imaging should raise suspicion for metastases rather than automatically assuming a new primary lung cancer.

incorrectas.B: Primary lung tumors are extremely common and clinically important (lung cancer is a leading cause of cancer death), but numerically metastatic deposits to the lung from other organs occur more frequently, given how much blood the lungs filter.
incorrectas.C: The two are not equally likely; the pulmonary vasculature's role as a filtering bed for the entire venous return gives metastatic seeding a numerical edge over primary lung carcinogenesis.
incorrectas.D: Granulomas (e.g., from prior tuberculosis or fungal infection) are a common cause of a solitary incidental nodule, but they are not the most common overall explanation when considering all lung masses, and this option does not address the primary-versus-metastatic comparison the question asks about.

preguntas.q: Pulmonary metastases from an extrathoracic primary tumor classically appear on chest imaging as what pattern?

o.A: Multiple well-circumscribed round nodules ('cannon ball' lesions)
o.B: A single cavitary lesion with an air-fluid level
o.C: Diffuse ground-glass opacities in a bilateral peripheral distribution
o.D: A solitary spiculated mass with hilar lymphadenopathy

e.correcta: Hematogenous seeding of tumor emboli through the pulmonary arterial circulation tends to deposit cells simultaneously in multiple sites throughout both lungs, producing the classic 'cannon ball' appearance of multiple discrete, rounded, well-defined nodules — often from primaries like renal cell carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, or sarcoma. Recognizing this pattern helps distinguish metastatic disease from a primary lung cancer, which more typically presents as a single dominant mass.

incorrectas.B: A single cavitary lesion with an air-fluid level is more suggestive of a lung abscess or a cavitating primary squamous cell lung carcinoma, not the multifocal pattern typical of hematogenous metastases.
incorrectas.C: Diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities are a nonspecific finding more associated with interstitial lung disease, atypical infections (e.g., PJP), or pulmonary edema, rather than the discrete nodular pattern of metastatic deposits.
incorrectas.D: A solitary spiculated mass with hilar lymphadenopathy is the classic appearance of a primary bronchogenic carcinoma invading locally and spreading to regional lymph nodes, the opposite pattern from multifocal metastatic seeding.

preguntas.q: Metastatic tumor deposits to the lung typically present radiographically as which of the following?

o.A: Multiple lesions scattered throughout both lungs
o.B: A single dominant mass in one lobe
o.C: A localized area of consolidation confined to one segment

e.correcta: Because metastases reach the lung via the bloodstream, tumor cells are showered simultaneously into many small pulmonary arterioles across both lungs, so metastatic disease characteristically produces multiple nodules rather than one localized lesion. This multiplicity is a key radiologic clue that favors metastasis over a primary lung cancer when a patient with a known extrathoracic malignancy develops new lung nodules.

incorrectas.B: A single dominant mass confined to one lobe is more typical of a primary bronchogenic carcinoma arising from one focus of malignant transformation in the airway epithelium, not the diffuse hematogenous spread seen with metastases.
incorrectas.C: Localized consolidation in one segment suggests a process like pneumonia or a primary endobronchial obstruction with post-obstructive changes, not the bilateral multifocal nodularity of metastatic seeding.
incorrectas.D: A solitary pleural-based lesion could suggest mesothelioma or a pleural-based primary process, but isolated solitary lesions are not the classic pattern for pulmonary metastases, which tend to be numerous.

preguntas.q: Lung cancer is the most common cause of metastasis to which organ?

e.correcta: Lung cancer is the single most common source of brain metastases because tumor cells have direct hematogenous access from the pulmonary veins into the systemic arterial circulation (bypassing the usual portal/hepatic filtering that other primaries must pass through), delivering tumor emboli straight to the brain. This is clinically important because new neurologic symptoms (headache, seizure, focal deficits) in a patient with lung cancer should prompt brain imaging, and multiple well-circumscribed lesions at the gray-white junction on MRI are the classic finding.

incorrectas.B: The kidney is not a preferred site of metastasis from lung cancer; renal cell carcinoma is more often a source of metastases to other organs (including the lung) than a destination for lung cancer spread.
incorrectas.C: The spleen's turbulent blood flow and rhythmic contraction make it a relatively resistant site for metastatic deposits from any primary tumor, including lung cancer, so it is rarely involved.
incorrectas.D: The thyroid is a vascular organ but is an uncommon site for metastases in general; lung cancer's classic distant targets are brain, bone, adrenal, and liver, not thyroid.

preguntas.q: A Pancoast tumor at the lung apex compresses the cervical sympathetic chain, brachial plexus, and thoracic outlet structures. Which constellation of findings — shoulder pain, Horner syndrome, and hand/arm muscle atrophy with edema — results from this local invasion?

e.correcta: Pancoast syndrome results from a superior sulcus tumor invading the C8-T2 nerve roots and brachial plexus (causing arm/hand muscle atrophy and sensorimotor deficits), the cervical sympathetic chain (causing Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), and the thoracic outlet vasculature (causing venous congestion and edema), plus irritation of nearby structures producing shoulder pain and sometimes hoarseness. Recognizing this full constellation as arising from a single apical tumor is what distinguishes Pancoast syndrome from an isolated cranial nerve or peripheral nerve palsy.

incorrectas.B: Superior vena cava syndrome results from compression of the SVC itself (often by mediastinal masses or lymphadenopathy) causing facial plethora and jugular venous distention, a different anatomic complication of lung cancer than the brachial plexus/sympathetic chain involvement seen in Pancoast syndrome, though both can occasionally coexist with an apical tumor.
incorrectas.C: Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) is only one component of the full Pancoast syndrome and results specifically from sympathetic chain disruption; by itself it does not account for the shoulder pain, muscle atrophy, or edema described.
incorrectas.D: Brown-Séquard syndrome is a spinal cord hemisection syndrome producing ipsilateral motor/proprioceptive loss and contralateral pain/temperature loss below the lesion — an intrinsic cord lesion, unrelated to an extrinsic apical lung tumor compressing peripheral structures.

preguntas.q: A lung cancer patient develops new hoarseness. Compression of which structure by the tumor is the most likely explanation?

o.C: Vagus nerve trunk in the neck

e.correcta: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch before ascending back to the larynx, placing it directly in the path of tumors or enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes near the aortopulmonary window; compression or invasion disrupts innervation to the intrinsic laryngeal muscles (via the vagus), producing hoarseness from vocal cord paralysis. This is a classic mediastinal complication of centrally located or left-sided lung tumors and is worth screening for on exam and history.

incorrectas.B: The phrenic nerve innervates the diaphragm, not the larynx; its compression causes diaphragmatic paralysis and shoulder pain (from referred phrenic irritation), not hoarseness.
incorrectas.C: While the recurrent laryngeal nerve is a branch of the vagus, compression of the vagus trunk higher in the neck (above the branch point) would cause a broader range of deficits (including pharyngeal and cardiac autonomic effects), not the isolated hoarseness classically attributed to recurrent laryngeal nerve injury from an intrathoracic mass.
incorrectas.D: The hypoglossal nerve controls tongue movement; its damage causes tongue deviation and dysarthria, not the voice change (hoarseness) that results from vocal cord paralysis.

preguntas.q: Compression of the phrenic nerve by a lung tumor most directly leads to which complication?

e.correcta: The phrenic nerve (roots C3-C5, 'C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive') provides the sole motor innervation to the diaphragm, so a tumor compressing or invading it causes ipsilateral diaphragmatic paralysis, which can be seen as elevated hemidiaphragm on chest imaging and paradoxical upward movement on sniff test. Because the phrenic nerve runs along the pericardium and mediastinum near the hilum, it is vulnerable to invasion by centrally located lung tumors, and irritation of the nerve can also refer pain to the shoulder.

incorrectas.B: Hoarseness results from recurrent laryngeal nerve compression, a different nerve with an entirely different course (looping around the aortic arch) and function (laryngeal innervation) than the phrenic nerve.
incorrectas.C: Horner syndrome results from disruption of the cervical sympathetic chain (as in a Pancoast tumor), not the phrenic nerve, and produces ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis rather than diaphragm dysfunction.
incorrectas.D: Facial plethora is a feature of superior vena cava syndrome from impaired venous drainage of the head, an entirely separate complication caused by SVC compression, not phrenic nerve involvement.

preguntas.q: A lung cancer patient develops headache, dizziness, dyspnea, jugular venous distention, and position-dependent facial edema. Compression of which structure explains this presentation?

e.correcta: The SVC is a thin-walled, low-pressure vessel draining the head, neck, and upper extremities, making it especially susceptible to extrinsic compression by mediastinal masses, right upper lobe tumors, or lymphadenopathy; obstruction impairs venous return causing head/neck/arm venous congestion, edema (worse when lying down), JVD, headache, and dizziness (and if severe, raised intracranial pressure). Most commonly this results from mediastinal masses like lymphoma or thymoma, but lung cancer directly invading or compressing the SVC is also a well-recognized cause.

incorrectas.B: Recurrent laryngeal nerve compression causes hoarseness from vocal cord paralysis, an entirely different mechanism (nerve injury, not venous obstruction) that would not explain JVD or facial edema.
incorrectas.C: Esophageal compression by a mediastinal mass would cause dysphagia, not the venous congestion pattern (JVD, facial plethora, positional edema) described, since the esophagus is not part of the venous drainage system.
incorrectas.D: Pulmonary artery compression would affect blood flow to the lungs (potentially causing pulmonary hypertension or hemoptysis) rather than impairing venous return from the head and neck, so it would not produce facial edema or JVD in this pattern.

preguntas.q: In superior vena cava syndrome, impaired venous drainage of the head produces which characteristic facial finding?

e.correcta: SVC obstruction causes venous congestion in the head and neck because blood cannot drain normally back to the right atrium, leading to facial plethora — a florid, reddish-purple engorgement of the face from pooled venous blood — often accompanied by edema that worsens when lying flat or bending forward. If severe, this venous congestion can raise intracranial pressure and even predispose to cerebral edema or hemorrhage, making SVC syndrome a true medical emergency in advanced cases.

incorrectas.B: Facial pallor suggests reduced blood flow or anemia, essentially the opposite physiology of the venous engorgement and congestion that characterizes SVC syndrome.
incorrectas.C: A malar rash is a classic finding in systemic lupus erythematosus, an autoimmune process affecting facial skin, unrelated to mechanical venous outflow obstruction from a mediastinal mass.
incorrectas.D: Periorbital ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes') classically suggests basilar skull fracture or amyloidosis with periorbital blood vessel fragility, not chronic venous congestion from SVC compression.

preguntas.q: Impaired venous drainage of the neck in superior vena cava syndrome results in which physical exam finding?

e.correcta: When the SVC is obstructed, blood from the jugular veins cannot drain normally into the right atrium, so pressure backs up and distends the internal and external jugular veins, producing visible jugular venous distention that, unlike JVD from heart failure, does not fluctuate normally with respiration or position in the same way and is accompanied by facial/neck swelling. This finding, combined with facial plethora and dyspnea, forms the classic triad clinicians look for at the bedside in suspected SVC syndrome.

incorrectas.B: A carotid bruit reflects turbulent flow through a stenotic carotid artery (usually from atherosclerosis), an arterial finding unrelated to venous congestion from SVC obstruction.
incorrectas.C: Lymphadenopathy may be a cause of SVC syndrome (e.g., from mediastinal lymphoma compressing the SVC) but is not itself the physical finding produced by impaired venous drainage of the neck.
incorrectas.D: Tracheal deviation results from a mass effect shifting the airway (e.g., large mediastinal mass or tension pneumothorax) rather than from venous congestion; it is a separate mechanical finding, not a consequence of impaired jugular drainage specifically.

preguntas.q: In a patient with an indwelling central venous catheter, superior vena cava syndrome can develop due to which mechanism?

o.B: Direct invasion by a mediastinal tumor
o.D: Aortic dissection extending into the SVC

e.correcta: Indwelling central venous catheters are a foreign surface within the SVC and adjacent great veins that promotes local thrombus formation; this thromboembolic material can occlude the SVC directly, producing SVC syndrome even in the absence of a malignant mass, and can also cause thrombosis of the subclavian or axillary veins. Because this presentation constitutes a mechanical venous emergency, catheter-associated SVC thrombosis is an important non-malignant cause to recognize alongside the more classically taught tumor-related causes.

incorrectas.B: Direct invasion by a mediastinal tumor (e.g., lymphoma, thymoma, or lung cancer) is the classic malignant cause of SVC syndrome, but it is a distinct mechanism from catheter-associated thrombosis and does not apply to the scenario of an indwelling line as the culprit.
incorrectas.C: The thoracic duct carries lymphatic fluid into the venous system near the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins; its rupture causes chylothorax, not SVC obstruction, and is unrelated to catheter-induced thrombosis.
incorrectas.D: Aortic dissection extending into the SVC is not a recognized mechanism of SVC syndrome; the aorta and SVC are anatomically distinct structures, and dissections primarily threaten arterial branches and cardiac tamponade, not venous obstruction.

preguntas.q: Severe superior vena cava obstruction can raise which pressure, leading to headaches and dizziness?

o.C: Central venous pressure only, with no downstream effect

e.correcta: When SVC obstruction is severe, impaired venous outflow from the head backs up into the cerebral venous system, raising intracranial pressure; this can produce headache, dizziness, visual disturbance, and in severe cases increases the risk of cerebral edema, retinal hemorrhage, or even stroke. This is why SVC syndrome with neurologic symptoms is treated urgently rather than managed expectantly.

incorrectas.B: Intraocular pressure is regulated by aqueous humor dynamics within the eye (as in glaucoma) and is not the mechanism by which SVC obstruction produces headache and dizziness, even though retinal hemorrhage can occur secondarily from venous congestion.
incorrectas.C: Central venous pressure elevation is indeed part of the pathophysiology, but the question specifically asks about the pressure whose rise causes headache and dizziness — that downstream effect is on intracranial pressure, not an isolated, consequence-free rise in CVP.
incorrectas.D: CSF production by the choroid plexus is not directly increased by venous congestion; rather, impaired venous drainage raises intracranial pressure primarily by impeding outflow/absorption dynamics, not by driving CSF overproduction.

preguntas.q: Which condition is defined by the accumulation of air within the pleural space, causing partial or complete collapse of the underlying lung?

e.correcta: Pneumothorax is defined by air entering the normally negative-pressure pleural space, which eliminates the transpleural pressure gradient that keeps the lung expanded and causes the lung (or a portion of it) to collapse under its own elastic recoil. When both air and fluid (usually blood) accumulate together, the condition is termed a hemopneumothorax, reflecting that pneumothorax specifically denotes the air component of pleural space pathology.

incorrectas.B: A pleural effusion is an accumulation of fluid (transudate or exudate) in the pleural space, not air, and causes compressive rather than the same type of elastic-recoil-driven collapse seen with pneumothorax.
incorrectas.C: A hemothorax is blood accumulating in the pleural space, typically from trauma or vascular injury, distinct from air accumulation, though the two can coexist as a hemopneumothorax.
incorrectas.D: An empyema is a collection of pus (infected fluid) within the pleural space, a complication of pneumonia or thoracic infection, not the presence of air.

preguntas.q: A patient with pneumothorax typically presents with chest pain and decreased chest expansion affecting which distribution?

o.A: Unilateral, on the side of the collapsed lung
o.D: Diffuse pain with no lateralizing findings

e.correcta: Because pneumothorax usually results from a focal process (ruptured bleb, trauma, or iatrogenic injury) affecting one hemithorax, the resulting pain and reduced chest wall expansion are unilateral, localized to the side where air has entered the pleural space and the lung has partially collapsed. This lateralized presentation, combined with dyspnea, is a key clinical clue that helps distinguish pneumothorax from more diffuse respiratory processes.

incorrectas.B: Bilateral pneumothorax can rarely occur (e.g., in severe trauma or with certain connective tissue diseases predisposing to bleb rupture on both sides), but the typical and expected presentation taught for pneumothorax is unilateral, not bilateral, involvement.
incorrectas.C: Pneumothorax is not restricted anatomically to the lower lobes; primary spontaneous pneumothorax classically arises from apical (upper lobe) subpleural bleb rupture, so this description misrepresents the typical distribution.
incorrectas.D: Pneumothorax characteristically produces lateralizing findings (asymmetric expansion, unilateral pain, and unilateral exam changes) precisely because the air accumulates in one pleural space, so a lack of lateralization would be atypical.

preguntas.q: On physical exam, tactile fremitus on the affected side in pneumothorax is typically which of the following?

o.C: Unchanged compared to the unaffected side

e.correcta: Tactile fremitus depends on transmission of vibrations from the vocal cords through aerated, consolidated, or fluid-filled lung tissue to the chest wall; in pneumothorax, air in the pleural space acts as an insulating layer between the vibrating lung and the chest wall, dampening transmission and producing decreased fremitus on the affected side. This mirrors the pattern seen with pleural effusion (also decreased fremitus), in contrast to consolidation/pneumonia, where fremitus is classically increased due to better sound transmission through solid, fluid-filled alveoli.

incorrectas.B: Increased fremitus is the classic finding in lobar consolidation (e.g., pneumonia), where solid, fluid-filled lung tissue transmits vibrations more efficiently than normal aerated lung — the opposite physiology from pneumothorax.
incorrectas.C: Fremitus is not unchanged in pneumothorax; the interposition of air within the pleural space measurably reduces vibration transmission compared to the normal, unaffected side, which is precisely what makes this exam finding useful diagnostically.
incorrectas.D: Fremitus is assessed with sustained phonation (e.g., the patient saying '99') rather than being an inspiration-dependent phenomenon, and the finding in pneumothorax is a persistent reduction, not one limited to a particular phase of the respiratory cycle.

preguntas.q: Percussion of the chest wall on the affected side in pneumothorax classically reveals which finding?

e.correcta: Percussion note depends on the density of the underlying tissue; because pneumothorax replaces normal lung tissue with a pocket of free air in the pleural space, percussion produces an exaggerated, hollow hyperresonant note on the affected side, analogous to why tapping over an air-filled structure sounds different from tapping over solid tissue. This contrasts with pleural effusion or consolidation, where increased density produces dullness or flatness instead.

incorrectas.B: Dullness on percussion indicates increased tissue density beneath the chest wall, as seen with consolidation or a small-to-moderate pleural effusion — the opposite of the air-filled space found in pneumothorax.
incorrectas.C: Flatness is an even more pronounced dull note typically associated with large pleural effusions or massive consolidation, again reflecting increased density rather than the air-filled hyperresonant pneumothorax.
incorrectas.D: Normal resonance would be expected over healthy, aerated lung tissue without pathology; pneumothorax specifically produces an exaggerated hyperresonance beyond normal due to the abnormal free air collection, not simply unchanged resonance.

preguntas.q: Auscultation over the affected hemithorax in pneumothorax typically reveals which finding?

e.correcta: In pneumothorax, air in the pleural space separates the lung from the chest wall and the partially collapsed lung moves less air, so breath sounds transmitted to the stethoscope are diminished or absent on the affected side. This finding, together with hyperresonance to percussion and decreased fremitus, forms the classic triad used to localize pneumothorax on physical exam before imaging confirms the diagnosis.

incorrectas.B: Bronchial breath sounds (harsh, tubular sounds normally heard only over the trachea) appear over consolidated lung tissue that transmits large-airway sounds well, the opposite of the diminished transmission seen in pneumothorax.
incorrectas.C: Coarse crackles suggest fluid within the airways or alveoli (as in pulmonary edema, pneumonia, or bronchiectasis), not the absence of underlying aerated lung tissue against the chest wall that characterizes pneumothorax.
incorrectas.D: Wheezing reflects turbulent airflow through narrowed airways, as in asthma or COPD exacerbation, a bronchospastic process unrelated to the mechanical separation of lung from chest wall caused by pleural air.

preguntas.q: Which type of pneumothorax arises from rupture of apical subpleural blebs or cysts, typically without a preceding traumatic event?

o.D: Secondary pneumothorax due to underlying COPD

e.correcta: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in the absence of clinically apparent underlying lung disease, typically due to rupture of small apical subpleural blebs or cysts, which are thought to form from mechanical stresses at the lung apex; the ruptured bleb allows air from the alveolar space to escape into the pleural space. Classically, this occurs in tall, thin, young males, often smokers, which helps distinguish it clinically from pneumothorax due to trauma or pre-existing structural lung disease.

incorrectas.B: Traumatic pneumothorax results from blunt or penetrating chest injury (or iatrogenic causes like central line placement or thoracentesis) directly disrupting the pleura, a mechanically distinct cause from the spontaneous bleb rupture of primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
incorrectas.C: Tension pneumothorax is defined by a one-way valve mechanism that allows air into the pleural space but not out, causing progressive pressure buildup — this describes a physiologic complication that can occur with any underlying pneumothorax type, not a specific cause tied to apical blebs.
incorrectas.D: Secondary pneumothorax occurs in patients with pre-existing lung disease (such as COPD, where ruptured emphysematous bullae are the source), which is a distinct category from 'primary' spontaneous pneumothorax, precisely because underlying structural lung disease is present in the secondary form.

preguntas.q: Which patient demographic is classically most associated with primary spontaneous pneumothorax?

o.D: Young female athletes with restrictive lung disease

e.correcta: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax classically occurs in tall, thin, young males, often smokers, thought to be related to greater mechanical stress at the lung apices in individuals with this body habitus, predisposing to subpleural bleb formation and rupture. Recognizing this demographic pattern helps clinicians maintain a high index of suspicion for pneumothorax in a young patient presenting with sudden unilateral pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea, even without a history of trauma or lung disease.

incorrectas.B: Obese middle-aged women are not the classic demographic for primary spontaneous pneumothorax; obesity and female sex are not the recognized risk factors — tall, thin body habitus and male sex are.
incorrectas.C: Elderly patients with chronic bronchitis are more at risk for secondary spontaneous pneumothorax related to underlying structural lung disease (e.g., ruptured bullae in COPD), a different category from the primary form seen in otherwise healthy young people.
incorrectas.D: Restrictive lung disease is not the classic association with primary spontaneous pneumothorax, and there is no particular link to young female athletes; the well-established demographic is tall, thin young males.

preguntas.q: Pneumothorax resulting from iatrogenic procedures such as bronchoscopy, subclavian line placement, thoracentesis, or barotrauma from mechanical ventilation is classified as which type?

e.correcta: Traumatic pneumothorax encompasses any pneumothorax caused by direct mechanical disruption of the pleura, which includes iatrogenic causes such as needle or catheter injury during subclavian line placement or thoracentesis, airway injury during bronchoscopy, and barotrauma from high mechanical ventilation pressures rupturing alveoli, in addition to blunt or penetrating external trauma. Grouping these together under 'traumatic' distinguishes them from primary spontaneous pneumothorax, which occurs without any inciting procedural or external injury.

incorrectas.B: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax specifically occurs without trauma or underlying lung disease, due to rupture of apical subpleural blebs — the opposite scenario from procedure- or injury-induced pneumothorax.
incorrectas.C: Tension pneumothorax describes a physiologic complication (progressive air accumulation via a one-way valve mechanism causing mediastinal shift) that can develop from any underlying cause, including traumatic or iatrogenic pneumothorax, but the question is asking about the causative category, not this downstream complication.
incorrectas.D: Catamenial pneumothorax is a rare pneumothorax occurring in temporal relation to menstruation, related to thoracic endometriosis, an entirely different and much rarer cause unrelated to iatrogenic procedures or barotrauma.

preguntas.q: A patient develops a pneumothorax after a gunshot wound to the chest. What type of pneumothorax is this?

e.correcta: Traumatic pneumothorax results from blunt or penetrating injury to the chest wall or lung, such as a rib fracture lacerating the pleura or, as in this case, a gunshot wound directly breaching the pleural space and allowing air to enter. This category also includes iatrogenic causes (line placement, bronchoscopy, barotrauma), but the unifying feature is a direct mechanical disruption of the pleura from an external or procedural cause, rather than spontaneous bleb rupture.

incorrectas.B: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs without any inciting trauma, from rupture of apical subpleural blebs in an otherwise healthy person, which does not match a penetrating gunshot injury.
incorrectas.C: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in patients with underlying lung disease (like COPD) without an external traumatic event causing the air leak — again, this does not fit a gunshot wound mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Catamenial pneumothorax is linked to the menstrual cycle and thoracic endometriosis, a hormonally driven process entirely unrelated to penetrating chest trauma.

preguntas.q: Which type of pneumothorax occurs when air enters the pleural space through a one-way valve mechanism, allowing entry but not exit, and can progressively compress mediastinal structures?

e.correcta: Tension pneumothorax occurs when a tissue flap acts as a one-way valve, letting air enter the pleural space during inspiration but preventing its escape during expiration, so pressure progressively builds with each breath. This rising intrapleural pressure can collapse the ipsilateral lung, push the mediastinum toward the contralateral side, and compress the great veins, reducing venous return and cardiac output — making it a life-threatening emergency that requires immediate needle decompression, regardless of the pneumothorax's original cause (spontaneous or traumatic).

incorrectas.B: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax describes the cause (bleb rupture in a healthy young person) rather than the valve mechanism of tension physiology; a primary spontaneous pneumothorax can become a tension pneumothorax if a one-way valve develops, but the terms describe different aspects (etiology vs. physiologic complication).
incorrectas.C: Catamenial pneumothorax refers to a pneumothorax occurring with menses due to thoracic endometriosis — again a description of cause, not the one-way valve physiology that defines tension pneumothorax.
incorrectas.D: A simple (non-tension) traumatic pneumothorax involves air entering the pleural space from an injury but without a progressive one-way valve effect, so pressure does not escalate and life-threatening mediastinal shift does not occur the way it does with a true tension pneumothorax.

preguntas.q: After immediate needle decompression for a suspected tension pneumothorax, what definitive procedure should follow?

e.correcta: Needle decompression (typically at the second intercostal space, midclavicular line) is a temporizing, life-saving measure that converts a tension pneumothorax into a simple one by releasing trapped pressure, but it does not definitively evacuate the pleural air or prevent recurrence; a chest tube (tube thoracostomy) must follow to continuously drain air (and any blood) and allow the lung to fully re-expand. When placing the tube, it is inserted just above a rib to avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle that runs along the inferior rib margin.
