e.correcta: Essential fructosuria, caused by deficiency of fructokinase, follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, consistent with the other benign and severe inborn errors of carbohydrate metabolism (essential fructosuria, hereditary fructose intolerance, galactokinase deficiency, classic galactosemia). Because it is a loss-of-function enzyme defect, a single functional allele from one parent provides adequate fructokinase activity, so disease only manifests when both alleles are nonfunctional.

incorrectas.B: An autosomal dominant pattern would require only one abnormal allele to produce the phenotype, which does not apply here since heterozygous carriers of a fructokinase mutation have sufficient residual enzyme activity and remain asymptomatic.
incorrectas.C: X-linked recessive disorders are caused by genes located on the X chromosome and disproportionately affect males; the fructokinase gene (KHK) is autosomal, so essential fructosuria does not show this sex-linked inheritance.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance applies to conditions caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA, transmitted exclusively through the maternal line; fructokinase is a nuclear-encoded cytosolic enzyme, so its deficiency follows standard autosomal recessive Mendelian inheritance instead.

preguntas.q: A patient found to have fructose in the blood and urine on routine testing is otherwise completely asymptomatic. Which of the following best describes this presentation?

e.correcta: Essential fructosuria (fructokinase deficiency) is classically asymptomatic because, even without fructokinase, hexokinase can still phosphorylate a portion of the fructose directly to fructose-6-phosphate, allowing it to enter glycolysis; the unmetabolized fructose that remains is simply excreted, producing fructose in blood and urine without any toxic intracellular accumulation. This benign course contrasts sharply with hereditary fructose intolerance, where the enzyme block occurs one step later and does cause toxic buildup.

incorrectas.A: Hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency) is symptomatic, not benign — fructose-1-phosphate accumulates after ingestion of fructose/sucrose and causes hypoglycemia, vomiting, and liver damage, unlike the asymptomatic course described in this patient.
incorrectas.B: Classic galactosemia involves galactose, not fructose, and presents with significant symptoms (vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, cataracts, intellectual disability) starting from the first feeding — it would not present as an incidental, asymptomatic finding of a sugar in the blood/urine.
incorrectas.D: Galactokinase deficiency also involves galactose rather than fructose, and though it is relatively mild, its hallmark clinical finding is cataracts from galactitol accumulation, not an entirely asymptomatic presentation with sugar in the urine.

preguntas.q: Compared to disorders of galactose metabolism, symptoms of fructose metabolism disorders typically present at what point in an infant's life?

o.A: Within the first hours of life, before any feeding
o.C: Months after birth, once fruit, juice, or sucrose-containing foods/formula are introduced
o.D: Only in adulthood after chronic sucrose overconsumption

e.correcta: Fructose (and sucrose, which contains fructose) is not present in breast milk, so infants are not exposed to it until feeding patterns change to include fruits, juices, or sucrose-sweetened foods/formulas — typically months after birth. This is in direct contrast to galactose disorders, which present immediately with the first feeding because lactose (glucose + galactose) is in breast milk and standard formula from day one.

incorrectas.A: No symptoms occur within the first hours of life because no fructose exposure has yet occurred; the fetus and newborn on breast milk are not consuming fructose, so a fructose metabolism disorder would be clinically silent at this stage.
incorrectas.B: Breast milk contains lactose, not fructose, so initiating breastfeeding does not expose the infant to fructose — it is galactose disorders, not fructose disorders, that present with the onset of breastfeeding.
incorrectas.D: While mild forms may go unnoticed for a while, the described timing marker for fructose disorders is the introduction of fructose/sucrose-containing foods in infancy, not a delay until adulthood — significant disorders like hereditary fructose intolerance typically become apparent as soon as fruit or sucrose is introduced in infancy or childhood.

preguntas.q: How does the overall clinical severity of fructose metabolism disorders compare to that of galactose metabolism disorders?

o.A: Fructose disorders are generally more mild
o.B: Fructose disorders are generally more severe
o.C: Both are equally severe and present identically
o.D: Fructose disorders are exclusively fatal in the neonatal period

e.correcta: As a group, fructose metabolism disorders tend to be milder than galactose metabolism disorders — essential fructosuria is entirely benign, and even hereditary fructose intolerance, while it can cause real hepatic and renal toxicity, is generally less devastating than classic galactosemia, which threatens the liver, brain, and can be fatal from E. coli sepsis if untreated in the neonatal period. Part of this reflects that hexokinase provides a partial metabolic backup for fructose that does not exist for galactose in the same way.

incorrectas.B: This reverses the actual comparison — it is galactose metabolism disorders (particularly classic galactosemia) that carry the higher risk of severe systemic disease, not fructose disorders, which tend to be milder overall.
incorrectas.C: The two groups of disorders are not clinically equivalent — galactosemia can cause life-threatening neonatal illness and intellectual disability, whereas even the more severe fructose disorder (hereditary fructose intolerance) is generally more survivable and often diagnosed later without such severe global multisystem involvement.
incorrectas.D: Fructose disorders are not uniformly fatal; essential fructosuria is asymptomatic and hereditary fructose intolerance, while serious if fructose exposure continues, is typically managed successfully by removing fructose/sucrose from the diet rather than being a uniformly fatal neonatal condition.

preguntas.q: What is the pattern of inheritance of hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency)?

e.correcta: Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by deficiency of aldolase B and, like the other carbohydrate metabolism enzymopathies discussed here, follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. Both copies of the aldolase B gene (ALDOB) must be nonfunctional for the disease to manifest, since one functional allele is enough to metabolize fructose-1-phosphate adequately and prevent its toxic buildup.

incorrectas.A: X-linked recessive disorders arise from genes on the X chromosome and predominantly affect males; ALDOB is located on an autosome, so hereditary fructose intolerance affects males and females equally and does not follow this pattern.
incorrectas.C: Autosomal dominant inheritance would require only a single defective allele to cause disease, but heterozygous carriers of an ALDOB mutation have sufficient enzyme activity and remain unaffected, which is the hallmark of a recessive rather than dominant condition.
incorrectas.D: X-linked dominant conditions (e.g., hypophosphatemic rickets) are caused by X-chromosome genes and can affect heterozygous females; since ALDOB is autosomal, hereditary fructose intolerance does not show this sex-linked dominant inheritance pattern.

preguntas.q: In hereditary fructose intolerance, accumulating fructose-1-phosphate causes toxicity primarily by depleting which molecule?

e.correcta: Because aldolase B is deficient, fructose-1-phosphate cannot be cleaved further and accumulates in hepatocytes, sequestering the phosphate that was used (from ATP) to make it. This traps inorganic phosphate in a form the cell cannot readily reuse, so free phosphate becomes unavailable for other essential phosphate-dependent reactions, including those needed for glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis — the basis of the hypoglycemia seen in this disease.

incorrectas.A: ATP is consumed as the phosphate donor when fructokinase first generates fructose-1-phosphate, but the toxic downstream effect is not from ATP being directly used up by mass action — it is the resulting sequestration of inorganic phosphate that causes the cascade of metabolic problems.
incorrectas.C: Glycogen stores are not directly depleted by fructose-1-phosphate accumulation; rather, the phosphate depletion inhibits the enzymes (like glycogen phosphorylase) needed to break down glycogen, which secondarily impairs glucose release, but the primary depleted molecule is phosphate, not glycogen itself.
incorrectas.D: NADH is a reduced cofactor involved in oxidative reactions such as those in glycolysis and the TCA cycle; it is not the molecule sequestered by accumulating fructose-1-phosphate, which is a phosphate depletion problem, not a redox cofactor problem.

preguntas.q: In hereditary fructose intolerance, the resulting phosphate depletion has what effect on glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, explaining the hypoglycemia seen after fructose ingestion?

o.B: Glycogenolysis is stimulated while gluconeogenesis is inhibited
o.D: Neither pathway is affected; hypoglycemia is due to increased insulin release

e.correcta: The inorganic phosphate sequestered within accumulated fructose-1-phosphate is no longer available for phosphate-dependent enzymatic steps in both glycogenolysis (e.g., glycogen phosphorylase requires inorganic phosphate) and gluconeogenesis (multiple ATP/phosphate-dependent steps). With both major glucose-producing pathways shut down simultaneously, the liver cannot compensate for the fructose load, and severe fasting hypoglycemia results — a hallmark clinical feature that distinguishes hereditary fructose intolerance from the benign essential fructosuria.

incorrectas.A: Stimulation of both pathways would raise, not lower, blood glucose, which contradicts the well-documented hypoglycemia seen after fructose ingestion in this disease; the actual mechanism is inhibition due to phosphate trapping, not stimulation.
incorrectas.B: This describes a mixed effect, but the mechanism in hereditary fructose intolerance impairs both pathways simultaneously since both require available inorganic phosphate, which has been sequestered by the accumulating fructose-1-phosphate — glycogenolysis is not spared.
incorrectas.D: The hypoglycemia in hereditary fructose intolerance is a direct consequence of blocked glucose production pathways from phosphate depletion, not from an insulin-driven mechanism; there is no described insulin surge triggering the hypoglycemia in this condition.

preguntas.q: Which foods are natural dietary sources of fructose that can trigger symptoms in susceptible infants with fructose metabolism disorders?

e.correcta: Fruits and honey are natural, concentrated dietary sources of fructose (fruit also contains sucrose, which is hydrolyzed to glucose and fructose), which is why symptoms of fructose metabolism disorders like hereditary fructose intolerance classically emerge once infants begin eating fruit purees or are given honey, rather than at birth. This timing distinguishes fructose disorders from galactose disorders, which present from the very first milk feeding.

incorrectas.A: Milk and dairy products contain lactose (glucose + galactose), not fructose, so they are the relevant dietary trigger for galactose metabolism disorders (e.g., classic galactosemia), not for fructose intolerance.
incorrectas.C: Rice and wheat-based cereals are primarily sources of starch, which is digested to glucose, not fructose; they do not represent a natural dietary trigger for fructose metabolism disorders.
incorrectas.D: Meat and eggs are protein and fat sources with negligible carbohydrate content, and specifically no meaningful fructose, so they would not provoke symptoms in a patient with a fructose metabolism disorder.

preguntas.q: An infant with hereditary fructose intolerance undergoes a routine urine dipstick test after eating fruit. What result would be expected on the standard glucose oxidase dipstick?

o.A: Strongly positive, reflecting elevated urine glucose
o.B: Negative, because the dipstick detects glucose specifically, not fructose
o.D: Positive for both glucose and fructose

e.correcta: The standard urine dipstick uses a glucose oxidase reaction that is specific for glucose and does not react with other reducing sugars like fructose. Because hereditary fructose intolerance causes excess fructose (not glucose) to spill into the urine, the dipstick reads negative despite the presence of a reducing sugar — this is exactly why a more general test, like the Clinitest/copper reduction test, is needed to detect non-glucose reducing sugars in suspected inborn errors of carbohydrate metabolism.

incorrectas.A: A strongly positive dipstick would suggest glucosuria (as seen in diabetes or renal tubular defects), but the metabolic derangement in hereditary fructose intolerance involves fructose accumulation, not glucose spillage into the urine, so the glucose-specific dipstick remains negative.
incorrectas.C: Ketones may appear in other metabolic derangements involving starvation or diabetic ketoacidosis, but a routine glucose dipstick specifically reports glucose status, not ketones, and this question is asking about the glucose-oxidase-based reading of the standard dipstick.
incorrectas.D: The standard dipstick reaction is selective for glucose via the enzyme glucose oxidase; it does not detect fructose, so it cannot read positive for fructose even though fructose is elevated in the urine — this selectivity is precisely why the dipstick is falsely reassuring in this condition.

preguntas.q: Since the standard urine dipstick fails to detect fructose in hereditary fructose intolerance, which alternative laboratory approach can reveal its presence in the urine?

o.B: Testing for reducing substances (e.g., copper reduction/Clinitest)

e.correcta: Because fructose, like galactose, is a reducing sugar, a nonspecific reducing-substance test such as the copper reduction (Clinitest) method can detect it in the urine even though the glucose-specific dipstick cannot. A positive Clinitest with a negative standard glucose dipstick is a classic clue pointing toward an inborn error of carbohydrate metabolism involving a non-glucose reducing sugar, such as hereditary fructose intolerance or galactosemia.

incorrectas.A: A serum electrolyte panel might show secondary abnormalities from the metabolic derangement (e.g., due to vomiting or renal involvement), but it does not directly detect reducing sugars like fructose in the urine, which is what the question is asking about.
incorrectas.C: Urine culture and Gram stain assess for bacterial infection and have no role in detecting reducing sugars like fructose; they would not reveal the biochemical abnormality present in hereditary fructose intolerance.
incorrectas.D: A serum lipid panel evaluates cholesterol and triglycerides and has no bearing on detecting urinary reducing sugars; it is unrelated to identifying fructose in the urine of a patient with hereditary fructose intolerance.

preguntas.q: An infant with hereditary fructose intolerance becomes lethargic and diaphoretic shortly after being given fruit juice. Which metabolic derangement is most likely to be found on labs?

e.correcta: In hereditary fructose intolerance, ingested fructose is phosphorylated to fructose-1-phosphate but cannot be cleaved further because aldolase B is deficient, so it accumulates and sequesters the cell's inorganic phosphate. This phosphate depletion inhibits both glycogen phosphorylase (blocking glycogenolysis) and key gluconeogenic enzymes, so the liver cannot mobilize or synthesize glucose, producing profound hypoglycemia shortly after fructose ingestion — the classic acute presentation that should prompt removal of fructose/sucrose from the diet.

incorrectas.A: Hyperglycemia would suggest impaired insulin action or excess glucose production, the opposite of what happens here — the trapped phosphate specifically shuts down the pathways that would normally raise blood glucose, driving levels down rather than up.
incorrectas.C: Hyperkalemia is not a described feature of hereditary fructose intolerance; the primary electrolyte-related derangement here is depletion of phosphate, not potassium, and there is no direct mechanism linking fructose-1-phosphate accumulation to potassium shifts.
incorrectas.D: Hypercalcemia is not part of this disorder's pathophysiology; the metabolic disturbance centers on trapped intracellular phosphate impairing glucose-producing pathways, not on calcium handling.

preguntas.q: A child with hereditary fructose intolerance who continues to ingest fructose develops chronic liver damage. Which finding reflects this hepatic injury?

e.correcta: Chronic fructose exposure in hereditary fructose intolerance causes repeated hepatocyte injury from accumulating fructose-1-phosphate and the resulting phosphate depletion, which impairs energy metabolism within liver cells. Over time this recurrent injury manifests as jaundice progressing to fibrosis and ultimately cirrhosis (and can also cause renal tubular damage), which is why prompt dietary elimination of fructose and sucrose is essential to prevent permanent organ damage.

incorrectas.B: Painless jaundice from biliary obstruction implies a mechanical block to bile flow (e.g., a pancreatic head mass or gallstone), which is a distinct mechanism from the direct hepatocellular toxicity caused by phosphate depletion in hereditary fructose intolerance.
incorrectas.C: Serum amylase elevation reflects pancreatic injury or inflammation, not the hepatocellular damage seen in hereditary fructose intolerance, which centers on the liver's inability to handle trapped fructose-1-phosphate.
incorrectas.D: Hemolytic anemia with reticulocytosis reflects red blood cell destruction, a mechanism unrelated to the direct hepatotoxic effect of fructose-1-phosphate accumulation and phosphate depletion described in this disorder.

preguntas.q: After ingestion, dietary fructose is taken up and metabolized primarily in which two organs?

e.correcta: Fructose is absorbed from the gut and delivered primarily to the liver and kidney, the two organs that express fructokinase and can efficiently phosphorylate fructose to fructose-1-phosphate for entry into glycolytic/gluconeogenic pathways. This selective organ distribution is exactly why the toxic effects of hereditary fructose intolerance (accumulating fructose-1-phosphate) are concentrated in the liver and kidney, producing hepatic and renal damage rather than injury elsewhere.

incorrectas.A: The brain relies primarily on glucose (and ketones during starvation) for fuel and does not significantly take up or metabolize dietary fructose, and adipose tissue similarly is not a primary site of fructose entry compared to liver and kidney.
incorrectas.C: Skeletal muscle and heart preferentially use glucose and fatty acids for energy and lack significant fructokinase activity, so they are not the major sites where ingested fructose is processed.
incorrectas.D: The pancreas and spleen are not primary sites of fructose uptake or metabolism; the pancreas is involved in insulin/glucagon secretion and digestive enzyme production, and the spleen in blood filtration and immune function, neither of which centers on fructose processing.

preguntas.q: Compared to hereditary fructose intolerance, essential fructosuria is best characterized by which of the following in terms of clinical severity?

o.A: Equally severe, both causing hepatic failure
o.B: Relatively mild, since fructose is not trapped inside cells
o.C: More severe due to greater fructose accumulation

e.correcta: Essential fructosuria results from fructokinase deficiency, meaning fructose is never converted to fructose-1-phosphate in the first place — it simply is not trapped intracellularly, and any fructose that isn't diverted through hexokinase to fructose-6-phosphate is harmlessly excreted. This is why essential fructosuria is benign and asymptomatic, in sharp contrast to hereditary fructose intolerance, where the enzyme block occurs one step later (aldolase B) and does allow toxic fructose-1-phosphate to accumulate and deplete phosphate.

incorrectas.A: The two conditions are not equally severe — hereditary fructose intolerance can progress to significant hepatic and renal damage with continued fructose exposure, whereas essential fructosuria causes no organ damage at all because no toxic metabolite accumulates.
incorrectas.C: This reverses the correct relationship — essential fructosuria does not lead to greater fructose accumulation; if anything, it is hereditary fructose intolerance that traps a toxic phosphorylated intermediate, while fructosuria's unmetabolized fructose is simply excreted without harm.
incorrectas.D: Cataracts are a feature of galactose metabolism disorders (via galactitol accumulation in the lens) mediated by aldose reductase, not a feature of essential fructosuria — fructose is not appreciably reduced by aldose reductase in this condition, so cataracts are not expected.

preguntas.q: Why do disorders of fructose metabolism, unlike disorders of galactose metabolism, not typically increase the risk of cataracts?

o.A: Fructose is efficiently cleared by the kidney before reaching the lens
o.B: Fructose is not appreciably reduced by aldose reductase
o.C: The lens lacks any transporter for fructose uptake
o.D: Fructose is rapidly converted to glucose before it can accumulate

e.correcta: Cataracts in galactose metabolism disorders occur because excess galactose is reduced by aldose reductase to osmotically active galactitol, which accumulates in the lens. Fructose, however, is a poor substrate for aldose reductase, so even when fructose metabolism disorders cause fructose to accumulate in blood and tissues, it is not efficiently converted to a polyol that would draw water into the lens — this is why cataracts are a feature of galactose disorders but not typically of fructose disorders.

incorrectas.A: Renal clearance of fructose is not the reason cataracts are avoided; the relevant distinction is biochemical — fructose simply isn't a good aldose reductase substrate, regardless of how effectively the kidney excretes it.
incorrectas.C: The lens does have some capacity for sugar uptake, and lack of a fructose transporter is not the established explanation for the absence of cataracts in fructose disorders — the key issue is the enzymatic step (aldose reductase) that fructose largely bypasses.
incorrectas.D: Fructose is not simply and rapidly converted to glucose in a way that prevents accumulation; in disorders like essential fructosuria and hereditary fructose intolerance, fructose or its phosphorylated derivative does accumulate to some degree, but this accumulated fructose still isn't turned into a lens-damaging polyol the way galactose is.

preguntas.q: In hepatocytes after a high-carbohydrate meal, which molecule overrides the allosteric inhibition of phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) by ATP, allowing glycolysis to proceed?

e.correcta: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F2,6BP) is produced by PFK-2 when insulin is high (fed state) and acts as the most potent allosteric activator of PFK-1, the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis. It binds PFK-1 at a site distinct from the ATP inhibitory site and increases the enzyme's affinity for fructose-6-phosphate, effectively overriding the energy-charge signal from ATP so that glycolysis can continue even when ATP levels are high after a carbohydrate-rich meal. This is the key control point that lets insulin push hepatocytes toward glucose utilization rather than production.

incorrectas.A: Citrate is actually an inhibitor of PFK-1, not an activator — high citrate signals that the TCA cycle is saturated with intermediates, so it slows glycolysis further rather than overriding ATP inhibition.
incorrectas.C: AMP does activate PFK-1 (signaling low energy charge), but this occurs during fasting/exercise, not after a high-carbohydrate meal — the postprandial override described here is driven by insulin-stimulated F2,6BP production, not a rise in AMP.
incorrectas.D: Acetyl-CoA is a downstream product of pyruvate oxidation that allosterically activates pyruvate carboxylase (promoting gluconeogenesis) and inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase in some contexts, but it does not regulate PFK-1 activity.

preguntas.q: An infant fails to track objects visually and has not developed a social smile. Deficiency of which carbohydrate metabolism enzyme classically presents this way?

e.correcta: Galactokinase deficiency causes accumulation of galactose (and galactitol via aldose reductase) without the toxic buildup of galactose-1-phosphate seen in classic galactosemia. Galactitol accumulates in the lens, causing infantile cataracts, which is why affected infants fail to fixate on objects or develop the expected social smile — the cataracts effectively blind them to visual stimuli. It is a milder condition overall than transferase deficiency because the liver and kidney toxicity from galactose-1-phosphate is absent.

incorrectas.B: Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency causes classic galactosemia, which presents with more severe systemic findings — hepatomegaly, jaundice, vomiting, and hypoglycemia after milk ingestion, along with an increased risk of E. coli sepsis — rather than isolated cataracts from galactitol.
incorrectas.D: Fructokinase deficiency causes essential fructosuria, a benign, asymptomatic condition in which fructose appears in the urine but is not further metabolized; it does not cause cataracts or developmental visual problems.
incorrectas.A: Aldolase B deficiency causes hereditary fructose intolerance, in which fructose-1-phosphate accumulates and causes hypoglycemia, vomiting, and liver failure after fructose/sucrose ingestion — a distinct clinical picture from the ocular findings of galactokinase deficiency.

preguntas.q: Which mitochondrial enzyme complex catalyzes the link reaction connecting glycolysis to the TCA cycle, and is differentially regulated in the fed versus fasting state?

e.correcta: The pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex sits in the mitochondrial matrix and irreversibly converts pyruvate (the end product of glycolysis) into acetyl-CoA, which then feeds into the TCA cycle — making it the critical bridge between glucose breakdown and oxidative metabolism. Its activity is tightly regulated by phosphorylation (inactivating, via pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase, favored in fasting) and dephosphorylation (activating, via pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase, favored in the fed state and stimulated by insulin, calcium, and ADP), allowing the body to shift between carbohydrate oxidation and glucose sparing.

incorrectas.B: Pyruvate carboxylase also acts on pyruvate but pushes it toward oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis (activated by acetyl-CoA during fasting), rather than linking glycolysis to oxidative acetyl-CoA entry into the TCA cycle.
incorrectas.A: Citrate synthase catalyzes the first step within the TCA cycle itself (combining acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate to form citrate), but it does not perform the glycolysis-to-TCA link reaction and is regulated mainly by ATP/citrate feedback rather than fed/fasting phosphorylation switches.
incorrectas.D: α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is a later TCA cycle enzyme structurally similar to PDH (sharing the same five cofactors) but it acts on α-ketoglutarate within the cycle, not on pyruvate at the glycolysis-TCA interface.

preguntas.q: Conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex releases which two products in addition to acetyl-CoA?

e.correcta: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex performs oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate: one carbon is removed as CO2, and the electrons liberated during this oxidation are captured by NAD+ to form NADH. This single reaction requires all five PDH cofactors (thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, and NAD+) and produces one NADH and one CO2 per pyruvate, in addition to the acetyl-CoA that then enters the TCA cycle.

incorrectas.A: FAD is indeed a required cofactor for the PDH complex (it reoxidizes the lipoamide arm), but the electrons ultimately end up transferred to NAD+ to form NADH as the released product — FADH2 is not a direct product of this reaction the way it is in the succinate dehydrogenase step of the TCA cycle.
incorrectas.C: ATP is not produced in this reaction; substrate-level phosphorylation of a nucleotide occurs later in the TCA cycle at the succinyl-CoA synthetase step (producing GTP), not at the PDH step.
incorrectas.D: ATP is not a product of the PDH reaction at all — this step is purely an oxidative decarboxylation generating CO2 and NADH, with no direct phosphorylation of ADP or GDP.

preguntas.q: Citrate synthase, the enzyme that combines acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate to form citrate, is subject to negative feedback inhibition by which molecule?

e.correcta: ATP is the classic negative feedback inhibitor of citrate synthase, the first and a key regulatory step of the TCA cycle. When cellular energy charge is high (abundant ATP), the cell has less need to generate additional reducing equivalents through the cycle, so ATP allosterically slows citrate synthase to throttle flux into the TCA cycle and conserve substrate. This mirrors the broader theme in central metabolism where ATP acts as a stop signal at multiple rate-limiting steps (also inhibiting PFK-1 and isocitrate dehydrogenase).

incorrectas.A: ADP has the opposite effect at the analogous isocitrate dehydrogenase step, where it acts as a positive allosteric activator signaling low energy charge — but it is not the described feedback regulator of citrate synthase itself.
incorrectas.B: Citrate is the product of this reaction and can feed back to inhibit an earlier glycolytic enzyme (PFK-1), but the question asks about regulation of citrate synthase itself, which is governed principally by ATP levels.
incorrectas.D: Succinyl-CoA is a feedback inhibitor further along the cycle, acting on α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, not on citrate synthase at the cycle's entry point.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme of the TCA cycle catalyzes the isomerization of citrate to isocitrate?

e.correcta: Aconitase (cis-aconitase) catalyzes the reversible isomerization of citrate to isocitrate via the intermediate cis-aconitate, repositioning the hydroxyl group so that the subsequent oxidative decarboxylation by isocitrate dehydrogenase becomes possible. This step does not consume or release any cofactors — it is purely a structural rearrangement — and is a favorite mnemonic anchor point in the cycle ("Citrate Is Krebs' Starting substrate...").

incorrectas.B: Isocitrate dehydrogenase acts on the product of aconitase's reaction (isocitrate), catalyzing its oxidative decarboxylation to α-ketoglutarate with release of CO2 and NADH — a distinct, later, and rate-limiting step, not the citrate-to-isocitrate isomerization itself.
incorrectas.A: Succinate dehydrogenase acts much later in the cycle, oxidizing succinate to fumarate while directly reducing FAD to FADH2 and feeding electrons into Complex II of the electron transport chain — unrelated to the citrate/isocitrate isomerization step.
incorrectas.D: Fumarase hydrates fumarate to malate near the end of the cycle, a completely different reaction (addition of water across a double bond) from the isomerization aconitase performs at the beginning of the cycle.

preguntas.q: The oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate by isocitrate dehydrogenase releases which two products?

e.correcta: Isocitrate dehydrogenase removes a carbon from isocitrate as CO2 while transferring the liberated electrons to NAD+, generating NADH. This is the rate-limiting, committed step of the TCA cycle and is positively regulated by ADP and calcium (signaling energy need) while being inhibited by ATP and NADH (signaling energy sufficiency) — the same oxidative decarboxylation pattern seen with pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.

incorrectas.A: FADH2 is generated later in the cycle at the succinate dehydrogenase step, not here — isocitrate dehydrogenase specifically reduces NAD+ to NADH, not FAD.
incorrectas.B: GTP is produced two steps later, at the succinyl-CoA synthetase reaction via substrate-level phosphorylation — the isocitrate dehydrogenase step does not involve nucleotide phosphorylation.
incorrectas.D: ATP is not directly produced by any single TCA cycle enzyme (the cycle generates GTP via substrate-level phosphorylation, and ATP is made later via oxidative phosphorylation), so pairing ATP with NADH misrepresents this reaction's actual products.

preguntas.q: Which molecule acts as a positive allosteric activator of isocitrate dehydrogenase, the rate-limiting enzyme of the TCA cycle?

e.correcta: ADP allosterically activates isocitrate dehydrogenase, signaling a low cellular energy charge (relatively more ADP than ATP) and thus a need to accelerate the TCA cycle to generate more reducing equivalents and ultimately more ATP via oxidative phosphorylation. This is analogous to how AMP activates PFK-1 in glycolysis — both are examples of allosteric sensing of the adenine nucleotide pool to match catabolic flux to energy demand.

incorrectas.B: NADH does the opposite — it is an inhibitor of isocitrate dehydrogenase (along with ATP), since high NADH signals that the electron transport chain is already saturated and further oxidation of isocitrate is unnecessary.
incorrectas.A: Citrate is the substrate several steps upstream (converted to isocitrate by aconitase) and functions as a feedback inhibitor of PFK-1 in glycolysis, but it is not described as the activator of isocitrate dehydrogenase.
incorrectas.D: Acetyl-CoA feeds into the cycle at the citrate synthase step and allosterically activates pyruvate carboxylase during fasting, but it is not the allosteric activator of isocitrate dehydrogenase.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme is the rate-limiting step of the TCA (Krebs) cycle?

e.correcta: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is the rate-limiting enzyme of the TCA cycle, analogous to PFK-1 in glycolysis. It is allosterically activated by ADP and calcium (low-energy signals) and inhibited by ATP and NADH (high-energy signals), so its activity is exquisitely tuned to the cell's real-time energy needs and sets the overall pace at which the cycle turns.

incorrectas.A: Citrate synthase catalyzes the first step of the cycle and is also regulated (inhibited by ATP), but it is not considered the classic rate-limiting enzyme — that designation belongs to isocitrate dehydrogenase, several steps later.
incorrectas.C: α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is regulated similarly (inhibited by succinyl-CoA, ATP, and NADH) and shares cofactors with PDH, but it is a later regulatory point, not the primary rate-limiting step of the cycle.
incorrectas.B: Succinate dehydrogenase is unique in being embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane as Complex II of the ETC, but it is not the rate-limiting enzyme of the TCA cycle — its main role is transferring electrons to FAD while oxidizing succinate.

preguntas.q: The conversion of α-ketoglutarate to succinyl-CoA by α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase releases which two products?

e.correcta: α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase performs an oxidative decarboxylation nearly identical in mechanism to the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction — it uses the same five cofactors (thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, NAD+) to remove one carbon as CO2 and transfer the released electrons to NAD+, forming NADH, while generating succinyl-CoA. This structural and mechanistic parallel to PDH is a commonly tested Step 1 concept, since both enzyme complexes can be inhibited by arsenic poisoning (which disables lipoic acid).

incorrectas.C: FADH2 is not released as a free product here; FAD is used internally within the enzyme complex to reoxidize lipoamide, but the net redox product captured is NADH, not FADH2 — FADH2 is instead generated at the separate succinate dehydrogenase step.
incorrectas.B: GTP is produced at the very next step of the cycle, when succinyl-CoA synthetase converts succinyl-CoA to succinate via substrate-level phosphorylation — not at the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase step itself.
incorrectas.D: ATP is not a direct product of this reaction; like the analogous PDH step, this is purely an oxidative decarboxylation yielding CO2 and NADH, with substrate-level phosphorylation occurring only in the next reaction of the cycle.

preguntas.q: α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is subject to negative feedback inhibition by ATP, NADH, and which additional molecule?

e.correcta: Succinyl-CoA, the direct product of the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase reaction, feeds back to inhibit its own producing enzyme — a classic example of product inhibition layered on top of the energy-charge signals from ATP and NADH. Together these three inhibitors ensure the cycle slows when energy stores and downstream intermediates are already abundant, preventing wasteful overproduction of reducing equivalents.

incorrectas.A: Citrate inhibits PFK-1 in glycolysis (linking TCA cycle intermediate abundance back to glucose breakdown) but is not the product-feedback inhibitor of α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase itself.
incorrectas.C: Oxaloacetate is regenerated at the very end of the cycle and condenses with a new acetyl-CoA at the citrate synthase step; it is not the immediate feedback inhibitor acting on α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
incorrectas.D: GTP is produced later in the cycle by succinyl-CoA synthetase, not at the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase step, and is not described as a feedback inhibitor of this enzyme.

preguntas.q: Succinyl-CoA is converted to succinate by which enzyme of the TCA cycle?

e.correcta: Succinyl-CoA synthetase cleaves the high-energy thioester bond of succinyl-CoA, coupling this exergonic hydrolysis to substrate-level phosphorylation of GDP to GTP (or ADP to ATP in some tissues), producing succinate as the other product. This is the only step in the TCA cycle that generates a high-energy phosphate bond directly, distinguishing it from the oxidative decarboxylation steps that instead generate NADH or FADH2.

incorrectas.A: Succinate dehydrogenase acts on the product of this reaction (succinate), oxidizing it to fumarate while reducing FAD to FADH2 — a separate, later step embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane as ETC Complex II.
incorrectas.C: Fumarase acts two steps further along the cycle, hydrating fumarate to malate, and has no role in converting succinyl-CoA to succinate.
incorrectas.D: Malate dehydrogenase catalyzes the final step of the cycle, oxidizing malate to oxaloacetate with NADH production — unrelated to the succinyl-CoA to succinate conversion.

preguntas.q: Conversion of succinyl-CoA to succinate is coupled to production of which high-energy molecule via substrate-level phosphorylation?

e.correcta: This step, catalyzed by succinyl-CoA synthetase, directly phosphorylates GDP to GTP using energy released from cleaving the thioester bond of succinyl-CoA — the only substrate-level phosphorylation event in the TCA cycle. The GTP produced can be used directly by GTP-dependent enzymes (such as PEP carboxykinase in gluconeogenesis) or can transphosphorylate ADP to ATP via nucleoside diphosphate kinase, making it functionally equivalent to ATP in most energy accounting.

incorrectas.A: ATP is not the direct product of this specific reaction — the enzyme phosphorylates GDP, not ADP; ATP can be generated only secondarily if the GTP transfers its phosphate to ADP.
incorrectas.B: NADH is generated at oxidative decarboxylation steps of the cycle (isocitrate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and malate dehydrogenase), not at the succinyl-CoA synthetase step, which involves no NAD+ reduction.
incorrectas.D: FADH2 is produced at the separate succinate dehydrogenase step (oxidizing succinate to fumarate), not during the substrate-level phosphorylation reaction that converts succinyl-CoA to succinate.

preguntas.q: Which single step of the TCA cycle directly produces a molecule of GTP via substrate-level phosphorylation?

e.correcta: The succinyl-CoA synthetase reaction (succinyl-CoA to succinate) is the sole step in the TCA cycle where substrate-level phosphorylation occurs, directly generating GTP from GDP and inorganic phosphate using the energy of the cleaved thioester bond. Recognizing this as the cycle's only "direct" high-energy phosphate-generating step (as opposed to the NADH/FADH2-generating oxidation steps that require the ETC to make ATP) is a frequently tested distinction.

incorrectas.A: Isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate, catalyzed by isocitrate dehydrogenase, is an oxidative decarboxylation that produces CO2 and NADH — it does not involve any phosphorylation of a nucleotide.
incorrectas.B: Malate to oxaloacetate, catalyzed by malate dehydrogenase, is likewise an oxidation reaction producing NADH, not a substrate-level phosphorylation event generating GTP.
incorrectas.C: Succinate to fumarate, catalyzed by succinate dehydrogenase, transfers electrons directly to FAD (forming FADH2) rather than coupling to nucleotide phosphorylation.

preguntas.q: Succinate is converted to fumarate by which enzyme, which also functions as Complex II of the electron transport chain?

e.correcta: Succinate dehydrogenase is unique among TCA cycle enzymes in being embedded directly in the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it doubles as Complex II of the electron transport chain. It oxidizes succinate to fumarate while directly reducing its bound FAD cofactor to FADH2, and those electrons are fed straight into the ETC via ubiquinone — bypassing Complex I and yielding slightly less ATP per electron pair than NADH-derived electrons do.

incorrectas.A: Fumarase acts on the product of this reaction, hydrating fumarate to malate in the next step of the cycle, and is a soluble matrix enzyme, not a membrane-embedded ETC complex.
incorrectas.B: Malate dehydrogenase catalyzes the final oxidation step of the cycle (malate to oxaloacetate), generating NADH, and has no role in the succinate-to-fumarate conversion or in the ETC directly.
incorrectas.D: NADH dehydrogenase is Complex I of the electron transport chain, which accepts electrons from NADH (not FADH2) and is a distinct membrane complex from succinate dehydrogenase/Complex II.

preguntas.q: The oxidation of succinate to fumarate by succinate dehydrogenase directly produces which reduced electron carrier?

e.correcta: Succinate dehydrogenase uses an enzyme-bound FAD cofactor to directly accept the electrons removed during the oxidation of succinate to fumarate, forming FADH2. Because succinate dehydrogenase is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane as Complex II, these electrons pass directly to ubiquinone without needing a separate diffusible carrier, which is why FADH2-linked electron entry yields less ATP (~1.5 ATP equivalents) than NADH-linked entry through Complex I (~2.5 ATP equivalents).

incorrectas.A: NADH is generated by the other three oxidative steps of the TCA cycle (isocitrate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and malate dehydrogenase), which use NAD+ rather than FAD as the electron acceptor — succinate dehydrogenase is the exception that uses FAD instead.
incorrectas.C: NADPH is not produced by the TCA cycle at all; it is generated mainly by the pentose phosphate pathway and used for reductive biosynthesis, not oxidative phosphorylation.
incorrectas.D: Ubiquinol (reduced coenzyme Q) is indeed formed as electrons move through Complex II, but it results from FAD accepting electrons first and passing them on — the direct product of the succinate oxidation reaction is FADH2, not ubiquinol formed independently of FAD.

preguntas.q: Fumarate is hydrated to form malate by which TCA cycle enzyme?

e.correcta: Fumarase catalyzes the stereospecific addition of a water molecule across the double bond of fumarate, producing L-malate. This hydration reaction requires no cofactors and no redox chemistry — it is purely a hydration step — setting up the final oxidation of malate to oxaloacetate that regenerates the cycle's starting material. Fumarase is also notable clinically as the enzyme deficient in hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC) syndrome.

incorrectas.C: Malate dehydrogenase acts on the product of this reaction (malate), oxidizing it to oxaloacetate with concurrent NADH production — a distinct redox reaction, not the water-addition step performed by fumarase.
incorrectas.B: Aconitase performs an analogous-sounding but earlier and different isomerization, converting citrate to isocitrate via cis-aconitate near the start of the cycle, not the fumarate-to-malate hydration near the end.
incorrectas.D: Succinate dehydrogenase acts one step earlier, oxidizing succinate to fumarate (the substrate for fumarase), and is a membrane-bound redox enzyme rather than the simple hydratase that converts fumarate to malate.

preguntas.q: Malate is converted to oxaloacetate by which enzyme, completing the final step of the TCA cycle?

e.correcta: Malate dehydrogenase catalyzes the final oxidation step of the TCA cycle, converting malate to oxaloacetate while reducing NAD+ to NADH. This regenerates oxaloacetate so it can condense with a new molecule of acetyl-CoA (via citrate synthase) to begin another turn of the cycle, making this reaction essential for the cycle's continuity and a key point where cytosolic and mitochondrial malate/oxaloacetate shuttles (like the malate-aspartate shuttle) intersect with cycle regeneration.

incorrectas.B: Fumarase acts one step earlier, hydrating fumarate to produce the malate that malate dehydrogenase then oxidizes — it performs a hydration, not the oxidation that forms oxaloacetate.
incorrectas.C: Citrate synthase uses the oxaloacetate generated by malate dehydrogenase as a substrate, combining it with acetyl-CoA to form citrate at the start of the next cycle — it does not itself produce oxaloacetate.
incorrectas.A: Succinate dehydrogenase acts much earlier in the cycle (succinate to fumarate) and reduces FAD rather than NAD+, making it mechanistically and positionally distinct from the malate-to-oxaloacetate step.

preguntas.q: The oxidation of malate to oxaloacetate by malate dehydrogenase produces which reduced coenzyme?

e.correcta: Malate dehydrogenase transfers the electrons removed during oxidation of malate's hydroxyl group to NAD+, generating NADH and completing the cycle's fourth and final NADH-producing oxidation (the others being at pyruvate dehydrogenase-adjacent isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase steps within one turn of the cycle). This NADH then feeds into Complex I of the electron transport chain to drive maximal ATP yield (~2.5 ATP per NADH).

incorrectas.A: FADH2 is generated specifically at the succinate dehydrogenase step, which uses a membrane-bound FAD cofactor — a mechanistically distinct enzyme and cofactor system from the soluble, NAD+-dependent malate dehydrogenase.
incorrectas.C: NADPH is not a TCA cycle product; it is generated by the pentose phosphate pathway and malic enzyme reactions for use in biosynthetic and antioxidant pathways, not by malate dehydrogenase in the TCA cycle.
incorrectas.D: GTP is produced earlier in the cycle at the succinyl-CoA synthetase step via substrate-level phosphorylation, an entirely different type of reaction from the NAD+-linked oxidation performed by malate dehydrogenase.

preguntas.q: Which TCA cycle enzyme requires the same five cofactors as pyruvate dehydrogenase (thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, and NAD+)?

e.correcta: α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is structurally and mechanistically homologous to the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, requiring the identical set of five cofactors ("Tender Loving Care For Nancy": Thiamine pyrophosphate/B1, Lipoic acid, CoA/B5, FAD/B2, NAD+/B3) to perform its analogous oxidative decarboxylation of α-ketoglutarate to succinyl-CoA. This shared cofactor dependency explains why conditions affecting one of these cofactors (such as thiamine deficiency or arsenic poisoning, which inactivates lipoic acid) impair both enzyme complexes simultaneously.

incorrectas.A: Citrate synthase simply condenses acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate and requires no B-vitamin-derived cofactor complex — it is a straightforward condensation reaction, unlike the elaborate multi-cofactor decarboxylation machinery of PDH and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
incorrectas.B: Succinate dehydrogenase uses only FAD as its cofactor (bound within the enzyme as it also functions as ETC Complex II) and does not require thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, or CoA in the same combined fashion.
incorrectas.D: Malate dehydrogenase requires only NAD+ as a cofactor for its oxidation reaction and has none of the complex, multi-subunit cofactor requirements that characterize the PDH/α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase family of enzymes.

preguntas.q: In which cellular compartment does the TCA (Krebs) cycle take place?

e.correcta: All eight enzymes of the TCA cycle (with the notable exception of succinate dehydrogenase, which is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane but still catalytically active facing the matrix) reside in the mitochondrial matrix. This compartmentalization allows the cycle's NADH and FADH2 products to be handed off efficiently and directly to the nearby electron transport chain complexes situated in the adjacent inner mitochondrial membrane, maximizing the efficiency of oxidative phosphorylation.

incorrectas.A: The cytosol is where glycolysis and fatty acid synthesis occur, but pyruvate must first be transported into the mitochondria (via the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier) before it can be converted to acetyl-CoA and enter the TCA cycle in the matrix.
incorrectas.C: The endoplasmic reticulum is the site of processes like steroid synthesis, protein folding, and phase I drug metabolism (via cytochrome P450 enzymes), entirely unrelated to the TCA cycle's location.
incorrectas.D: The mitochondrial intermembrane space houses cytochrome c and is where protons accumulate during oxidative phosphorylation to create the proton-motive force, but the TCA cycle enzymes themselves are located in the matrix, not this space.

preguntas.q: For each acetyl-CoA molecule that enters the TCA cycle, how many total molecules of NADH are produced?

e.correcta: One turn of the TCA cycle produces 3 NADH molecules per acetyl-CoA — generated at the isocitrate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and malate dehydrogenase steps. Combined with 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP per turn, and accounting for the ~2.5 ATP yield per NADH (versus ~1.5 per FADH2) through oxidative phosphorylation, this is the basis for calculating the total ATP yield of complete glucose oxidation.

incorrectas.A: Two NADH would undercount the cycle — the three distinct oxidative decarboxylation/oxidation steps (isocitrate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, malate dehydrogenase) each generate one NADH, totaling three, not two.
incorrectas.C: One NADH accounts for only a single oxidative step of the cycle; it misses that isocitrate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and malate dehydrogenase all independently reduce NAD+ to NADH within one turn.
incorrectas.D: Four NADH overcounts the cycle — remember that the succinate-to-fumarate step produces FADH2 via FAD, not an additional NADH via NAD+, keeping the total NADH yield at three, not four.

preguntas.q: For each acetyl-CoA molecule oxidized in the TCA cycle, how many total molecules of FADH2 are produced?

e.correcta: Exactly 1 FADH2 is produced per acetyl-CoA, generated at the succinate dehydrogenase step when succinate is oxidized to fumarate. This is the only FAD-dependent redox step in the cycle, in contrast to the three separate NAD+-dependent steps, and the resulting FADH2 feeds directly into Complex II of the electron transport chain (bypassing Complex I), yielding somewhat less ATP per molecule than NADH does.

incorrectas.A: Two FADH2 would imply a second FAD-reducing step exists in the cycle, but succinate dehydrogenase is the sole site of FAD reduction — the other three redox steps (isocitrate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, malate dehydrogenase) all reduce NAD+ instead.
incorrectas.B: Zero FADH2 is incorrect because the succinate dehydrogenase step does generate one FADH2 per acetyl-CoA — this reaction is a fixed, essential part of every turn of the cycle.
incorrectas.D: Three FADH2 confuses the FADH2 yield with the NADH yield; three NADH are produced per acetyl-CoA, but FADH2 is generated only once, at the succinate dehydrogenase step.

preguntas.q: For each acetyl-CoA molecule metabolized through the TCA cycle, how many molecules of GTP (or ATP-equivalent) are produced via substrate-level phosphorylation?

e.correcta: Exactly 1 GTP is produced per acetyl-CoA, generated at the succinyl-CoA synthetase step when succinyl-CoA is converted to succinate. This is the cycle's only substrate-level phosphorylation event, distinct from the three NADH and one FADH2 that instead require the electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation to yield ATP — meaning most of the cycle's net energy payoff comes indirectly through the ETC rather than this single direct phosphorylation.

incorrectas.A: Two GTP would imply two separate substrate-level phosphorylation events per turn, but only the succinyl-CoA synthetase reaction generates a high-energy phosphate bond directly — all other steps generate NADH or FADH2 instead.
incorrectas.B: Zero GTP is incorrect; the succinyl-CoA to succinate conversion reliably produces one GTP via substrate-level phosphorylation in every turn of the cycle, independent of the electron transport chain.
incorrectas.C: Three GTP confuses the GTP yield with the NADH yield (three NADH per acetyl-CoA); GTP is generated only once per turn, at the succinyl-CoA synthetase step.

preguntas.q: Approximately how much ATP is generated per molecule of NADH oxidized through the electron transport chain and ATP synthase?

e.correcta: Each NADH donates its electrons to Complex I, and as those electrons travel through Complexes I, III, and IV, enough protons are pumped into the intermembrane space to generate approximately 2.5 ATP per NADH once that proton gradient drives ATP synthase. This value (revised down from the older textbook estimate of 3 ATP) reflects modern measurements of the actual P/O ratio and is the figure most current sources and exams use for calculating total ATP yield from glucose oxidation.

incorrectas.A: 1.5 ATP is the yield attributed to FADH2, not NADH — FADH2 donates electrons to Complex II, bypassing Complex I and its associated proton pumping, so it generates less ATP per molecule than NADH does.
incorrectas.B: 3.0 ATP was the traditional textbook estimate used in older sources, but current, more precise measurements of proton stoichiometry have revised the accepted NADH yield down to approximately 2.5 ATP.
incorrectas.D: 1.0 ATP substantially underestimates the energy captured from NADH oxidation; a single NADH contributes enough protons pumped across the inner membrane to generate roughly 2.5 ATP, well above 1.0.

preguntas.q: How much ATP is generated from the oxidation of one molecule of FADH2 through the electron transport chain via ATP synthase?

e.correcta: FADH2 donates its electrons to complex II (succinate dehydrogenase), which feeds directly into the ubiquinone pool, bypassing complex I entirely. Because fewer protons are pumped across the inner mitochondrial membrane per pair of electrons compared to NADH, the proton-motive force generated is smaller, yielding only about 1.5 ATP per FADH2 rather than the 2.5 ATP produced per NADH.

incorrectas.B: 2.5 ATP is the yield from NADH, not FADH2 — NADH donates electrons at complex I, which pumps protons at complex I, III, and IV, generating a larger gradient than FADH2's entry at complex II.
incorrectas.C: 3 ATP is an older, now-outdated teaching estimate no longer used in the more precise modern P/O ratio accounting, which assigns 1.5 ATP to FADH2 and 2.5 ATP to NADH.
incorrectas.D: 1 ATP underestimates the actual proton-pumping capacity of the complexes downstream of complex II (III and IV still pump protons), so the true yield per FADH2 is higher than this.

preguntas.q: Accounting for full oxidative metabolism of its reduced cofactors, how many total ATP equivalents are produced from one complete turn of the citric acid (Krebs) cycle?

e.correcta: One turn of the Krebs cycle generates 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 GTP. Each NADH yields 2.5 ATP equivalents (3 x 2.5 = 7.5), the single FADH2 yields 1.5 ATP, and the GTP is directly equivalent to 1 ATP, giving a total of 7.5 + 1.5 + 1 = 10 ATP equivalents per cycle.

incorrectas.B: 12 overestimates the yield; it does not match the correct arithmetic of 3 NADH (7.5) + 1 FADH2 (1.5) + 1 GTP (1) = 10, and would imply either extra reduced cofactors or a higher P/O ratio than the cycle actually produces.
incorrectas.C: 8 ATP equivalents undercounts the contribution of the three NADH molecules, effectively treating them as if they were producing less than 2.5 ATP each.
incorrectas.D: 6 ATP equivalents is far too low for one turn of the cycle and would only be plausible if just the GTP and FADH2 were counted while ignoring the three NADH molecules generated at isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and malate dehydrogenase.

preguntas.q: In which cellular compartment does the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA occur?

e.correcta: Pyruvate generated by glycolysis in the cytosol is transported into the mitochondrial matrix, where the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex oxidatively decarboxylates it to acetyl-CoA, releasing CO2 and generating NADH. This localization matters because it links cytosolic glycolysis to the mitochondrial TCA cycle and ETC, and it's why mitochondrial pyruvate carrier or PDH complex defects (e.g., thiamine deficiency, arsenic poisoning) cause lactic acidosis from pyruvate backing up in the cytosol.

incorrectas.B: The cytosol is where glycolysis itself occurs (glucose to pyruvate), but the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex that converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA is a mitochondrial matrix enzyme complex, not a cytosolic one.
incorrectas.C: The nucleus houses DNA transcription and replication machinery and has no role in intermediary carbon metabolism such as pyruvate oxidation.
incorrectas.D: The endoplasmic reticulum is the site of protein folding, lipid synthesis, and drug detoxification (via cytochrome P450 enzymes), not oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate.

preguntas.q: In which cellular compartment does oxidative phosphorylation take place?

e.correcta: Oxidative phosphorylation (the electron transport chain coupled to ATP synthase) occurs across the inner mitochondrial membrane, where the ETC complexes pump protons into the intermembrane space to create an electrochemical gradient that ATP synthase then uses to generate ATP. This is why mitochondria are described as the cell's power plant, and why cells with high energy demand (cardiac and skeletal muscle) are packed with mitochondria.

incorrectas.B: The cytosol hosts glycolysis, which produces a net 2 ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation, but it lacks the membrane-embedded electron transport chain complexes required for oxidative phosphorylation.
incorrectas.C: Peroxisomes carry out very-long-chain fatty acid beta-oxidation and reactive oxygen species detoxification (via catalase), not electron transport chain-driven ATP synthesis.
incorrectas.D: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids for secretion or delivery to other organelles; it has no role in generating a proton gradient or synthesizing ATP.

preguntas.q: FADH2 generated from reactions such as the succinate dehydrogenase step delivers its electrons directly to which ETC complex, also known as succinate dehydrogenase?

e.correcta: Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) is unique among the ETC complexes in that it is also a TCA cycle enzyme, directly oxidizing succinate to fumarate while passing the resulting electrons from FADH2 into the ubiquinone pool. Because complex II does not pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane (unlike complex I), the energy yield from FADH2-derived electrons is lower than that from NADH, which is why FADH2 nets only about 1.5 ATP compared to NADH's 2.5.

incorrectas.B: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) is the entry point for NADH-derived electrons, not FADH2, and it does pump protons across the membrane, contributing to the higher ATP yield associated with NADH oxidation.
incorrectas.C: Complex III (cytochrome b/c1, or coenzyme Q-cytochrome c reductase) receives electrons from reduced ubiquinone (produced by complexes I and II) and passes them to cytochrome c; it does not directly accept FADH2 electrons.
incorrectas.D: Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) is the terminal complex that transfers electrons from cytochrome c to molecular oxygen, forming water; it is downstream of where FADH2 electrons initially enter the chain.

preguntas.q: In the electron transport chain, electrons from reduced coenzyme Q (ubiquinone) are next transferred to which complex?

e.correcta: Coenzyme Q collects electrons from both complex I and complex II and shuttles them to complex III, also called cytochrome b/c1 or coenzyme Q-cytochrome c reductase, which then passes electrons onward to cytochrome c while pumping protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane. This convergence point is why coenzyme Q is considered a central hub of the ETC, receiving input from multiple upstream dehydrogenases.

incorrectas.B: Complex I is upstream of coenzyme Q — it oxidizes NADH and passes its electrons to ubiquinone, rather than receiving electrons from it.
incorrectas.C: Complex II is also upstream of coenzyme Q, feeding FADH2-derived electrons into the ubiquinone pool rather than accepting electrons from reduced coenzyme Q.
incorrectas.D: Complex IV acts later in the chain, receiving electrons from cytochrome c (which itself receives them from complex III), not directly from coenzyme Q.

preguntas.q: After passing through complex III of the electron transport chain, electrons are next transferred to which carrier?

e.correcta: Complex III (cytochrome b/c1, also called coenzyme Q-cytochrome c reductase) transfers electrons to cytochrome c, a small, water-soluble heme protein that shuttles along the outer face of the inner mitochondrial membrane to deliver electrons to complex IV. Cytochrome c has additional clinical significance beyond the ETC: its release from mitochondria into the cytosol is a key trigger of the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway of apoptosis.

incorrectas.B: Coenzyme Q is upstream of complex III — it delivers electrons to complex III rather than receiving them from it, so it is not the carrier that comes after complex III in the chain.
incorrectas.C: NAD+ is the oxidized form of the cofactor that accepts electrons in dehydrogenase reactions of glycolysis and the TCA cycle to become NADH; it is not part of the electron relay within the membrane-embedded ETC complexes themselves.
incorrectas.D: FAD similarly is reduced to FADH2 in reactions like the succinate dehydrogenase step and feeds electrons into complex II, but it is not the direct downstream acceptor of electrons from complex III.

preguntas.q: Cytochrome c passes its electrons to which terminal complex of the electron transport chain, also known as cytochrome c oxidase?

e.correcta: Complex IV, composed of cytochromes a and a3 and also called cytochrome c oxidase, is the terminal enzyme of the ETC: it accepts electrons from cytochrome c and uses them to reduce molecular oxygen to water, the final electron acceptor of the chain. This step is why cyanide is so lethal — it binds the ferric iron in complex IV, halting electron flow at the very last step and shutting down oxidative phosphorylation entirely.

incorrectas.B: Complex I is the first complex in the chain, oxidizing NADH at the start of the pathway, far upstream of where cytochrome c acts near the chain's end.
incorrectas.C: Complex II feeds FADH2 electrons into the ubiquinone pool early in the chain and has no direct interaction with cytochrome c.
incorrectas.D: Complex III is the complex that produces reduced cytochrome c (by transferring electrons to it), so it precedes cytochrome c in the sequence rather than being the complex that receives electrons from it.

preguntas.q: The stepwise transfer of electrons through the ETC complexes drives the formation of what type of gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane?

e.correcta: As electrons pass through complexes I, III, and IV, energy released by the redox reactions is used to actively pump protons (H+) from the mitochondrial matrix into the intermembrane space, creating an electrochemical proton gradient (the proton-motive force). This gradient stores potential energy that ATP synthase (complex V) then harnesses, allowing protons to flow back down their gradient through the enzyme and drive ATP synthesis — a mechanism known as chemiosmotic coupling.

incorrectas.B: A sodium gradient is central to processes like the Na+/K+-ATPase in the plasma membrane and secondary active transport (e.g., the SGLT symporter), but it is not what the ETC complexes generate across the mitochondrial inner membrane.
incorrectas.C: Calcium gradients are important in mitochondrial calcium buffering and signaling, and in muscle excitation-contraction coupling, but calcium is not the ion pumped by the ETC to drive ATP synthase.
incorrectas.D: Potassium gradients are largely established by different transporters (e.g., the Na+/K+-ATPase and various K+ channels) and are not the driving force behind oxidative phosphorylation.

preguntas.q: ATP is exported from the mitochondrial matrix to the intermembrane space (in exchange for ADP entering the matrix) via which antiporter?

e.correcta: The ATP/ADP translocase is an inner mitochondrial membrane antiporter that exports newly synthesized ATP out of the matrix while simultaneously importing ADP back in, allowing ADP produced by cytosolic energy-consuming reactions to return and be rephosphorylated. Because ADP availability is what stimulates this exchange and thus oxidative phosphorylation, this translocase underlies the concept of "respiratory control," where mitochondrial respiration is limited by how much ADP is present.

incorrectas.B: The Na+/K+-ATPase is a plasma membrane pump that maintains the resting membrane potential by exporting Na+ and importing K+ using ATP hydrolysis; it plays no role in shuttling ATP and ADP across the mitochondrial membrane.
incorrectas.C: The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger is involved in extruding calcium from cells (e.g., in cardiac myocytes) using the sodium gradient, unrelated to mitochondrial ATP/ADP exchange.
incorrectas.D: The Cl-/HCO3- exchanger (band 3 protein) is found in red blood cell membranes and is central to the chloride shift during CO2 transport, not to mitochondrial nucleotide transport.

preguntas.q: Which class of drugs, when taken in overdose, may bind to and inhibit complex I of the electron transport chain?

e.correcta: Barbiturates such as phenobarbital can inhibit complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) of the ETC at high doses, blocking electron entry from NADH and halting downstream oxidative phosphorylation. This mitochondrial toxicity contributes to the severe cardiorespiratory depression seen in barbiturate overdose, compounding their GABA-A receptor-mediated CNS depression.

incorrectas.B: Benzodiazepines also enhance GABA-A receptor activity (by increasing the frequency of channel opening) but are far safer in overdose because, unlike barbiturates, they do not directly inhibit mitochondrial complex I, so pure benzodiazepine overdose is rarely fatal.
incorrectas.C: Opioids cause respiratory depression through mu-opioid receptor activation in the brainstem respiratory centers, not through direct inhibition of electron transport chain complexes.
incorrectas.D: SSRIs act by blocking serotonin reuptake at the presynaptic transporter to increase synaptic serotonin; they have no recognized mechanism of directly inhibiting complex I of the ETC.

preguntas.q: In cyanide poisoning, which treatment works by inducing methemoglobinemia so that ferric iron can scavenge cyanide away from the electron transport chain?

e.correcta: Amyl nitrite (and related nitrites) oxidizes hemoglobin's ferrous iron (Fe2+) to the ferric state (Fe3+), producing methemoglobin, which has a high affinity for cyanide. This creates a competing sink that pulls cyanide off complex IV of the ETC (where it would otherwise bind ferric iron and halt electron transport) and sequesters it safely in the blood as cyanmethemoglobin, restoring aerobic metabolism.

incorrectas.B: Sodium thiosulfate treats cyanide toxicity by a different mechanism — it donates sulfur groups to rhodanese, the enzyme that converts cyanide to the much less toxic thiocyanate for renal excretion, rather than by inducing methemoglobinemia.
incorrectas.C: Hydroxycobalamin works by directly binding cyanide to form cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12), which is then excreted in urine; it does not act through oxidizing hemoglobin to methemoglobin.
incorrectas.D: Naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist used to reverse opioid overdose and has no role in cyanide toxicity or methemoglobin formation.

preguntas.q: Which cyanide poisoning treatment acts by restoring rhodanese-mediated conversion of cyanide to thiocyanate?

e.correcta: Normally, the mitochondrial enzyme rhodanese detoxifies small amounts of cyanide by transferring a sulfur atom to it, forming thiocyanate, which is water-soluble and renally excreted. In cyanide overdose, the available sulfur donors are rapidly depleted, allowing free cyanide to accumulate and poison complex IV; sodium thiosulfate supplies additional sulfur substrate, effectively re-enabling rhodanese to keep converting cyanide to thiocyanate faster.

incorrectas.B: Amyl nitrite works upstream of this pathway by oxidizing hemoglobin to methemoglobin, which competes for and binds free cyanide directly, rather than supplying sulfur donors to rhodanese.
incorrectas.C: Hydroxycobalamin binds cyanide directly through its cobalt core to form cyanocobalamin, a separate detoxification route that bypasses the rhodanese/sulfur-donor system entirely.
incorrectas.D: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine receptor antagonist used to reverse benzodiazepine overdose or sedation; it has no role in cyanide metabolism.

preguntas.q: Which vitamin can serve as a treatment for cyanide poisoning by directly binding cyanide via its cobalt core?

e.correcta: Hydroxycobalamin, a form of vitamin B12, contains a central cobalt ion that has a very high affinity for cyanide; when administered, it binds free cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, which is then safely excreted in the urine. This makes it an important antidote alongside sodium thiosulfate, particularly favored in settings like smoke inhalation where concurrent methemoglobin-inducing therapy (amyl nitrite) could worsen oxygen-carrying capacity.

incorrectas.B: Thiamine deficiency itself can impair pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (both thiamine-dependent), causing lactic acidosis, but thiamine has no cyanide-binding capacity and is not used as a cyanide antidote.
incorrectas.C: Pyridoxine is a cofactor for transamination reactions and is used clinically to treat isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy, not cyanide toxicity.
incorrectas.D: Ascorbic acid functions as an antioxidant and cofactor for hydroxylation reactions (e.g., collagen synthesis); it does not bind or detoxify cyanide.

preguntas.q: 2,4-Dinitrophenol acts on oxidative phosphorylation as which type of agent?

e.correcta: 2,4-Dinitrophenol is a lipophilic weak acid that inserts into the inner mitochondrial membrane and shuttles protons back into the matrix independent of ATP synthase, dissipating the proton gradient without producing ATP. Because electron transport continues (even accelerates, since the gradient it would normally build against is being dissipated), the energy that would have driven ATP synthesis is instead released as heat.

incorrectas.B: Electron transport inhibitors (such as rotenone, antimycin A, cyanide, and carbon monoxide) block electron flow at a specific complex, which shuts down electron transport entirely — the opposite of DNP, under which electron transport actually continues unimpeded.
incorrectas.C: ATP synthase inhibitors (such as oligomycin) block the flow of protons through ATP synthase itself, which causes the proton gradient to build up (rather than dissipate) and secondarily halts electron transport because the gradient becomes too large to pump against.
incorrectas.D: A competitive substrate inhibitor would compete with a normal substrate at an enzyme's active site; this does not describe DNP's mechanism, which involves physically carrying protons across the membrane rather than blocking any single enzyme's active site.

preguntas.q: Which uncoupling agent of oxidative phosphorylation has historically been used illicitly for weight loss?

e.correcta: 2,4-Dinitrophenol uncouples oxidative phosphorylation by carrying protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, so cells burn through substrate and oxygen to try to maintain the gradient without generating the usual ATP yield — the "wasted" energy is released as heat, which increases metabolic rate and causes weight loss. Its narrow therapeutic window makes it dangerous: overdose leads to severe hyperthermia, and it was banned for medical use after fatalities, yet it persists in the illicit weight-loss supplement market.

incorrectas.B: Oligomycin inhibits ATP synthase directly, which blocks ATP production and backs up the proton gradient rather than dissipating it for weight loss; it is a laboratory tool, not a weight-loss agent.
incorrectas.C: Rotenone is a complex I inhibitor historically used as a pesticide/fish poison and is studied as a model of Parkinson disease in research, not used for weight loss.
incorrectas.D: Antimycin A inhibits complex III and is used experimentally to study the ETC; it is not associated with weight-loss use because it halts respiration rather than uncoupling it.

preguntas.q: In high doses, which common analgesic drug can act as an uncoupling agent of oxidative phosphorylation?

e.correcta: Aspirin (salicylate) in high doses, such as in salicylate toxicity, can uncouple oxidative phosphorylation similarly to 2,4-DNP, dissipating the mitochondrial proton gradient and causing electron transport to continue without efficient ATP synthesis. The resulting surge in cellular metabolism and heat production contributes to the hyperthermia and increased CO2 production seen in salicylate overdose, alongside the classic mixed respiratory alkalosis/metabolic acidosis picture.

incorrectas.B: Acetaminophen overdose causes hepatotoxicity through depletion of glutathione and accumulation of the toxic metabolite NAPQI, a completely different mechanism that does not involve uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation.
incorrectas.C: Ibuprofen is an NSAID that inhibits cyclooxygenase to reduce prostaglandin synthesis; overdose is more associated with GI and renal toxicity, not mitochondrial uncoupling.
incorrectas.D: Morphine acts on opioid receptors to cause analgesia and, in overdose, respiratory depression; it has no recognized effect on the mitochondrial proton gradient.

preguntas.q: What is the typical cause of death in a patient who has overdosed on an uncoupling agent such as 2,4-DNP?

e.correcta: Because uncoupling agents allow electron transport to continue unimpeded while dissipating the proton gradient that would normally drive ATP synthase, the energy from continuous electron flow is released as heat instead of being captured as ATP. In overdose, this uncontrolled heat generation produces severe, often fatal hyperthermia, since the body cannot dissipate heat as fast as it is being produced by runaway mitochondrial respiration.

incorrectas.B: Hypoglycemia is not the primary lethal mechanism; while substrate is consumed rapidly, the acute cause of death is the massive heat production overwhelming the body's thermoregulation, not a critical drop in blood glucose per se.
incorrectas.C: Respiratory alkalosis (from hyperventilation) can be seen in some mitochondrial toxin exposures like salicylates, but it is not the primary mechanism of death in classic uncoupling agent overdose, which is heat-driven.
incorrectas.D: Hypothermia is the opposite of what occurs — uncoupling causes excess heat production (hyperthermia), not heat loss, because the energy that would have gone to ATP synthesis is instead dissipated as heat.

preguntas.q: Electron transport inhibitors (e.g., rotenone, antimycin A, CO, cyanide) cause what change in the mitochondrial proton gradient, along with blocked ATP synthesis?

e.correcta: Electron transport inhibitors block electron flow at a specific complex (e.g., rotenone at complex I, antimycin A at complex III, CO and cyanide at complex IV), which halts the redox reactions that normally pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Without ongoing electron transport, the proton pumps stop working, so the proton gradient decreases (dissipates over time via residual leak) and ATP synthase — which depends on that gradient — can no longer produce ATP.

incorrectas.B: An increased proton gradient is instead the hallmark of ATP synthase inhibitors like oligomycin, which block the outflow of protons through ATP synthase, causing protons to back up and the gradient to build rather than fall.
incorrectas.C: The gradient does not stay unchanged — halting the pumps that generate it while natural proton leak continues means the gradient collapses over time, distinguishing this class from a scenario where transport and pumping continue unaffected.
incorrectas.D: The proton gradient does not reverse direction; protons simply stop being actively pumped into the intermembrane space, so the existing gradient dissipates rather than flipping polarity.

preguntas.q: ATP synthase inhibitors (e.g., oligomycin) cause what change in the mitochondrial proton gradient, along with blocked ATP synthesis?

o.D: Complete loss of the proton gradient

e.correcta: Oligomycin binds and blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase, preventing protons from flowing back into the matrix through this route. Because the ETC complexes continue pumping protons out (at least initially) but the main return route is blocked, protons accumulate in the intermembrane space, increasing the proton gradient until it becomes so steep that it backs up and stalls the electron transport chain itself (since pumping against too large a gradient becomes energetically unfavorable).

incorrectas.B: A decreased proton gradient is instead characteristic of electron transport inhibitors, which stop the pumps generating the gradient in the first place, or uncoupling agents, which actively dissipate it.
