Because of their CNS penetration, they are also used clinically for conditions like motion sickness (meclizine), anxiety/pruritus (hydroxyzine), and nausea (promethazine), beyond simple allergy relief.

incorrectas.A: Second-generation H1 antagonists (like loratadine, cetirizine, fexofenadine) are more selective for peripheral H1 receptors and are far less sedating because they poorly cross the blood-brain barrier, unlike the '-zine' drugs listed, which are classic first-generation agents.
incorrectas.B: H2 receptor antagonists (like famotidine, ranitidine, cimetidine) block gastric acid secretion for peptic ulcer disease and GERD; they act on an entirely different histamine receptor subtype than the H1-blocking '-zine' antihistamines in the question.
incorrectas.D: Leukotriene receptor antagonists (like montelukast and zafirlukast) block leukotriene signaling in asthma and allergic rhinitis, a mechanistically distinct drug class from histamine receptor antagonists altogether.

preguntas.q: Histamine acting on H1 receptors is the principal mediator of which type of hypersensitivity reaction?

e.correcta: Type I hypersensitivity is the classic immediate allergic reaction: antigen cross-links IgE bound to FcεRI on mast cells and basophils, triggering degranulation and release of preformed histamine within minutes. Histamine then acts on H1 receptors on vascular endothelium and smooth muscle to produce the vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and bronchoconstriction seen in allergic rhinitis, urticaria, and anaphylaxis — which is exactly why H1 blockers are first-line symptomatic therapy for these conditions.

incorrectas.B: Type II hypersensitivity is antibody-mediated cytotoxicity, in which IgG or IgM binds directly to antigens on a cell surface and triggers complement activation or ADCC (e.g., autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Goodpasture syndrome) — histamine and H1 receptors play no central role in this mechanism.
incorrectas.C: Type III hypersensitivity involves antigen-antibody immune complexes depositing in tissues (e.g., vessel walls, glomeruli) and activating complement, causing conditions like serum sickness and lupus nephritis; this is a complement- and neutrophil-driven process, not a histamine-driven one.
incorrectas.D: Type IV hypersensitivity is cell-mediated and delayed, driven by sensitized T lymphocytes rather than antibodies or mast cell mediators (e.g., contact dermatitis, PPD skin test, transplant rejection), so it does not depend on histamine release.

preguntas.q: Why do 1st generation H1 receptor antagonists (e.g., diphenhydramine) cause sedation while 2nd generation agents typically do not?

o.A: 1st generation agents are lipophilic and cross the blood-brain barrier
o.B: 1st generation agents have higher plasma protein binding
o.C: 1st generation agents are metabolized faster by the liver
o.D: 1st generation agents have a longer half-life

e.correcta: First-generation H1 blockers are small, lipophilic molecules that readily cross the blood-brain barrier and antagonize central H1 receptors, which are involved in maintaining wakefulness — this central blockade is what produces sedation, along with anti-muscarinic, anti-α1, and anti-serotonergic effects from their relatively nonselective binding. Second-generation agents (e.g., loratadine, fexofenadine, cetirizine) were designed to be more polar and are substrates for P-glycoprotein efflux pumps at the BBB, keeping them largely peripheral and non-sedating.

incorrectas.B: Plasma protein binding affects free drug concentration and distribution generally, but it is not the property that determines CNS penetration or explains the sedation difference between generations; lipophilicity and BBB permeability are the key distinguishing factors.
incorrectas.C: Metabolic rate influences duration of action and dosing frequency, not whether a drug reaches the CNS in the first place — some first-generation agents are actually metabolized relatively slowly, contributing to prolonged sedation, but that's a separate issue from BBB crossing.
incorrectas.D: Half-life determines how long a drug stays in the body and dosing interval, but a long half-life alone would not cause sedation if the drug could not cross into the CNS; it is the ability to penetrate the BBB that drives the central effects.

preguntas.q: A patient takes diphenhydramine for seasonal allergies and reports significant drowsiness. What is the mechanism responsible for this adverse effect?

o.A: Central H1 receptor blockade after crossing the blood-brain barrier
o.B: Peripheral H1 receptor blockade in the nasal mucosa

e.correcta: Diphenhydramine is a first-generation H1 antagonist that is lipophilic enough to cross the blood-brain barrier, where it blocks central H1 receptors that normally help maintain arousal. This central antihistaminic action, compounded by its anti-muscarinic activity, produces the drowsiness and cognitive slowing characteristic of first-generation agents — which is why they are used therapeutically as over-the-counter sleep aids despite being marketed primarily as allergy medications.

incorrectas.B: Peripheral H1 blockade in the nasal mucosa is what relieves the allergic symptoms (itching, rhinorrhea, sneezing) — it does not explain sedation, which is a central nervous system effect requiring the drug to reach the brain.
incorrectas.C: Diphenhydramine has no direct action at GABA-A receptors; its sedating effect is due to H1 (and secondarily muscarinic) receptor antagonism in the CNS, not potentiation of GABAergic inhibitory tone as with benzodiazepines or barbiturates.
incorrectas.D: Diphenhydramine is metabolized by hepatic enzymes, but inhibiting CYP3A4 would alter the metabolism of other co-administered drugs, not directly cause sedation; the sedative effect comes from the drug's own pharmacodynamic action in the brain, not a metabolic drug interaction.

preguntas.q: Adverse effects of 1st generation H1 receptor antagonists are more common and more severe in which patient population?

e.correcta: Elderly patients are especially vulnerable to first-generation antihistamines because these drugs are anti-muscarinic as well as anti-H1, and older adults are more sensitive to anticholinergic toxicity — causing confusion, urinary retention, constipation, dry mouth, and an increased fall risk from sedation and impaired coordination. This is why first-generation H1 blockers are on the Beers Criteria list of medications to avoid in older adults, with second-generation agents preferred instead.

incorrectas.B: Adolescents metabolize and tolerate first-generation antihistamines relatively well compared to the elderly; sedation and anticholinergic effects do occur but are not classically emphasized as more severe in this age group.
incorrectas.C: Pregnancy raises separate safety considerations (teratogenicity, fetal exposure) rather than the exaggerated anticholinergic/sedative burden seen in older adults, and diphenhydramine is not specifically flagged as more dangerous in pregnant patients the way it is in the elderly.
incorrectas.D: Athletes are not a population noted for increased susceptibility to first-generation antihistamine adverse effects; the concern in this group, if any, would relate more to sedation affecting performance rather than heightened physiologic vulnerability.

preguntas.q: Fexofenadine belongs to which drug class?

e.correcta: Fexofenadine is a second-generation H1 antagonist, along with loratadine and cetirizine. These drugs are more polar and are substrates for P-glycoprotein at the blood-brain barrier, so they are largely excluded from the CNS and cause little to no sedation compared to first-generation agents, while still effectively blocking peripheral H1 receptors to relieve allergic symptoms like rhinorrhea and pruritus.

incorrectas.B: First-generation H1 antagonists (e.g., diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine) are lipophilic, cross the BBB, and cause sedation and anticholinergic effects — fexofenadine specifically lacks these properties and was developed as a non-sedating alternative.
incorrectas.C: Leukotriene receptor antagonists like montelukast and zafirlukast block the CysLT1 receptor to prevent leukotriene-mediated bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion; they act on an entirely different mediator pathway from histamine and are not related to fexofenadine's mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Mast cell stabilizers such as cromolyn sodium prevent mast cell degranulation itself, upstream of mediator release, rather than blocking histamine receptors after release — a fundamentally different strategy from fexofenadine's H1 receptor antagonism.

preguntas.q: Why do 2nd generation H1 receptor antagonists (e.g., loratadine, cetirizine) not cross the blood-brain barrier the way 1st generation agents do?

o.A: They are more polar and are substrates for P-glycoprotein efflux transporters
o.B: They have a much shorter plasma half-life
o.D: They selectively bind H2 receptors instead of H1

e.correcta: Second-generation H1 blockers were chemically modified to be more polar and hydrophilic, and they are actively pumped back out of the brain by P-glycoprotein transporters at the blood-brain barrier. This keeps their action largely confined to peripheral H1 receptors, so they relieve allergic symptoms with far less sedation, and also with less anti-muscarinic, anti-serotonergic, and anti-α1-adrenergic activity than first-generation agents.

incorrectas.B: Plasma half-life determines dosing frequency and duration of action, not the ability to penetrate the CNS; some second-generation agents actually have long half-lives allowing once-daily dosing, which is unrelated to their lack of sedation.
incorrectas.C: Second-generation antihistamines are given orally, just like first-generation agents, for systemic relief of allergic symptoms; the route of administration is the same, so it cannot explain the difference in CNS penetration.
incorrectas.D: Both first- and second-generation antihistamines act primarily at H1 receptors, not H2 receptors (which mediate gastric acid secretion and are targeted by drugs like ranitidine); the difference between the generations is BBB penetration, not receptor subtype selectivity.

preguntas.q: Compared to 1st generation H1 blockers, 2nd generation agents like loratadine cause less sedation and also have reduced activity at which additional receptors?

e.correcta: First-generation H1 antagonists are relatively nonselective and also block muscarinic, serotonergic, and α1-adrenergic receptors, producing side effects like dry mouth, urinary retention, and orthostatic hypotension in addition to sedation. Second-generation agents are more selective for the peripheral H1 receptor and largely spare these other receptor systems, which is why they are better tolerated for chronic use in allergic rhinitis and urticaria.

incorrectas.B: Neither generation of H1 antagonists has clinically significant activity at nicotinic or GABA-A receptors; the off-target effects of first-generation agents are specifically anti-muscarinic, anti-serotonergic, and anti-α1-adrenergic, not related to these other receptor classes.
incorrectas.C: Dopamine D2 and opioid receptor activity are not part of the H1 antagonist pharmacologic profile in either generation; confusing these with antihistamine side effects would conflate an unrelated drug class's mechanism with antihistamines.
incorrectas.D: Beta-2 adrenergic receptors are the target of drugs like albuterol and terbutaline for bronchodilation, and leukotriene receptors are targeted by montelukast — neither is part of the off-target receptor profile that distinguishes first- from second-generation antihistamines.

preguntas.q: Second-generation H1 receptor antagonists are primarily used to treat which condition?

e.correcta: Second-generation H1 blockers such as loratadine, fexofenadine, and cetirizine are used to treat allergic conditions like allergic rhinitis, conjunctivitis, and urticaria by blocking peripheral H1 receptors that mediate itching, sneezing, and vasodilation. They are preferred over first-generation agents for routine allergy management because they produce far fewer sedative and anticholinergic side effects while maintaining good symptomatic relief.

incorrectas.B: Peptic ulcer disease is treated with H2 receptor antagonists (e.g., ranitidine, famotidine), which reduce gastric acid secretion by blocking histamine's action on parietal cells — a completely different receptor subtype and clinical indication from H1 antihistamines.
incorrectas.C: Acute bronchospasm in asthma is treated with short-acting β2 agonists like albuterol, not antihistamines; histamine is only one of several mediators of bronchoconstriction, and H1 blockers are not effective rescue therapy for an asthma attack.
incorrectas.D: COPD management relies on bronchodilators (anticholinergics, β2 agonists) and inhaled corticosteroids for inflammation, not H1 antihistamines, since COPD pathology is driven by chronic inflammation and airway remodeling rather than histamine-mediated allergic reactions.

preguntas.q: Classic allergic asthma is driven by which immunoglobulin produced in response to exposure to foreign antigens like dust, dander, and pollen?

e.correcta: In classic (atopic) asthma, allergen exposure drives a Th2-skewed immune response that stimulates B cells to class-switch and produce allergen-specific IgE. This IgE binds to high-affinity FcεRI receptors on mast cells, and re-exposure to the same antigen cross-links the bound IgE, triggering mast cell degranulation and release of histamine, leukotrienes, and other mediators that cause bronchoconstriction, mucus hypersecretion, and airway inflammation.

incorrectas.B: IgG is the most abundant serum immunoglobulin and mediates opsonization, complement fixation, and long-term humoral immunity, but it is not the antibody isotype responsible for triggering mast cell degranulation in type I hypersensitivity reactions like allergic asthma.
incorrectas.C: IgA is the predominant antibody in mucosal secretions (saliva, tears, breast milk) and protects mucosal surfaces from pathogens, but it does not bind FcεRI on mast cells and plays no role in the immediate hypersensitivity mechanism of allergic asthma.
incorrectas.D: IgM is the first antibody produced in a primary immune response and is highly effective at complement activation due to its pentameric structure, but it is not involved in mast cell sensitization or the type I hypersensitivity pathway that drives allergic asthma.

preguntas.q: After being produced in response to allergen exposure, IgE binds to which receptor on mast cells in the airway mucosa?

e.correcta: IgE binds with very high affinity to FcεRI receptors on the surface of mast cells (and basophils) in tissues like the airway mucosa. This binding effectively arms the mast cell; upon re-exposure to the same antigen, allergen cross-links adjacent surface-bound IgE molecules, triggering an intracellular signaling cascade that leads to degranulation and release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators.

incorrectas.B: FcεRII (CD23) is a low-affinity IgE receptor found mainly on B cells, macrophages, and eosinophils, where it participates in regulating IgE synthesis and antigen presentation rather than mediating the rapid, high-affinity mast cell sensitization seen in immediate hypersensitivity.
incorrectas.C: Toll-like receptor 4 recognizes bacterial lipopolysaccharide as part of innate immune pathogen recognition, an entirely separate pathway from IgE-mediated allergic sensitization, and does not bind immunoglobulins at all.
incorrectas.D: Complement receptor 1 binds complement fragments like C3b to facilitate opsonization and immune complex clearance; it has no role in binding IgE or triggering mast cell degranulation in type I hypersensitivity.

preguntas.q: Terbutaline treats bronchoconstriction in asthma by selectively agonizing which receptor?

e.correcta: Terbutaline is a selective β2 agonist that activates β2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, increasing intracellular cAMP via Gs-protein coupling and causing smooth muscle relaxation and bronchodilation. Because it favors β2 over β1 receptors, it produces less cardiac stimulation than a nonselective beta agonist would, though at higher doses some β1 cross-reactivity (tachycardia) can still occur — the same selective β2 mechanism underlies its historical use as a tocolytic to relax uterine smooth muscle.

incorrectas.B: β1 receptors are found predominantly in cardiac tissue, where their stimulation increases heart rate and contractility; activating β1 receptors would not relax bronchial smooth muscle and would instead risk unwanted cardiac stimulation, which is why selective β2 agonists like terbutaline are preferred for asthma.
incorrectas.C: α1 adrenergic receptors mediate vascular and other smooth muscle contraction (vasoconstriction) via Gq signaling, the opposite effect needed in the airway; stimulating α1 receptors would not produce bronchodilation and is not terbutaline's mechanism.
incorrectas.D: M3 muscarinic receptors mediate bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion when stimulated by acetylcholine; blocking (not stimulating) M3 receptors, as anticholinergic bronchodilators like ipratropium do, produces bronchodilation — but this is a distinct mechanism from terbutaline's β2 agonism.

preguntas.q: More severe forms of asthma are characterized by more frequent and severe symptoms during which time period?

o.C: Only in the morning upon waking

e.correcta: Nocturnal symptoms are a key marker of asthma severity classification — more severe persistent asthma is associated with more frequent nighttime awakenings due to symptoms like cough, wheezing, and dyspnea. This pattern reflects circadian variations in airway inflammation, bronchomotor tone, and cortisol levels that tend to worsen airway hyperreactivity overnight, and the frequency of nocturnal symptoms is explicitly used in clinical guidelines to help stage asthma severity and guide step-up therapy.

incorrectas.B: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction is a recognized trigger of asthma symptoms, but it is not the specific pattern used to classify overall disease severity; severity classification instead hinges on daytime symptom frequency and nocturnal awakenings.
incorrectas.C: While some patients report morning symptoms due to overnight bronchoconstriction, the classic severity marker specifically referenced in asthma staging is nocturnal awakening, not simply symptoms confined to the morning.
incorrectas.D: Asthma symptoms are not classically tied to meal timing; postprandial symptom patterns are more relevant to conditions like gastroesophageal reflux-triggered cough, not to the severity staging of asthma itself.

preguntas.q: Which class of drugs can be added as daily inhaled maintenance therapy for persistent asthma?

e.correcta: Inhaled corticosteroids such as budesonide and fluticasone are the cornerstone of daily maintenance therapy for persistent asthma because they suppress the chronic underlying airway inflammation, not just the acute bronchoconstriction. By inhibiting synthesis of virtually all cytokines involved in the inflammatory cascade, they reduce airway hyperreactivity, mucus production, and the frequency of exacerbations over time, making them first-line controller therapy rather than rescue treatment.

incorrectas.B: Short-acting β2 agonists like albuterol provide rapid bronchodilation for acute symptom relief ('rescue' therapy) but do not address the underlying inflammation, so they are not used as scheduled daily maintenance therapy for persistent asthma — overreliance on them without controller therapy is actually a red flag for poor asthma control.
incorrectas.C: Inhaled anticholinergics (e.g., ipratropium, tiotropium) block M3 receptors to reduce bronchoconstriction and are more central to COPD management or add-on asthma therapy in specific cases, but they are not the first-line daily maintenance class for persistent asthma the way inhaled corticosteroids are.
incorrectas.D: Loop diuretics act on the renal thick ascending limb to promote diuresis and have no bronchodilator or anti-inflammatory effect on the airway; they play no role in asthma management.

preguntas.q: Inhaled corticosteroids used in asthma therapy exert their anti-inflammatory effect primarily by inhibiting the synthesis of which mediators?

e.correcta: Inhaled corticosteroids work by binding intracellular glucocorticoid receptors that translocate to the nucleus and alter gene transcription, broadly suppressing the synthesis of virtually all cytokines involved in the asthmatic inflammatory response. Because cytokines are what attract inflammatory cells to the airway and stimulate excess mucus production, blocking their synthesis addresses the root chronic inflammatory process rather than just a single downstream mediator, which is why corticosteroids are more broadly effective than single-mediator-targeted drugs.

incorrectas.B: Leukotriene synthesis is specifically blocked by 5-lipoxygenase inhibitors like zileuton, or leukotriene receptors are blocked by montelukast/zafirlukast — corticosteroids act far more broadly across the entire cytokine network rather than targeting the leukotriene pathway alone.
incorrectas.C: Histamine release from mast cells is targeted by H1 receptor antagonists or prevented upstream by mast cell stabilizers like cromolyn, not by corticosteroids, whose anti-inflammatory action is mediated through broad transcriptional suppression of cytokine genes.
incorrectas.D: Complement proteins are part of the innate immune cascade activated in processes like type II and type III hypersensitivity reactions; they are not the primary target of corticosteroid action in asthma, where cytokine suppression is the key mechanism.

preguntas.q: What is the first-line therapy for chronic (persistent) asthma?

e.correcta: Inhaled corticosteroids are first-line therapy for chronic persistent asthma because they directly target the underlying airway inflammation — suppressing cytokine production, reducing airway hyperresponsiveness, and preventing exacerbations — with minimal systemic absorption when delivered by inhalation. Stepwise asthma guidelines escalate the dose or add other controller agents (like long-acting β2 agonists or leukotriene modifiers) on top of inhaled corticosteroids rather than replacing them, reflecting their central role in disease control.

incorrectas.B: Leukotriene receptor antagonists like montelukast are useful oral alternatives or add-on agents, particularly in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease or in patients with poor inhaler compliance, but they are considered less effective than inhaled corticosteroids and are not first-line for most persistent asthma.
incorrectas.C: Short-acting β2 agonists are reserved for acute symptom relief (rescue therapy), not scheduled daily use; relying on them as a primary strategy for chronic asthma control would fail to address the underlying inflammation and is associated with worse outcomes.
incorrectas.D: Oral systemic corticosteroids are reserved for severe exacerbations or refractory disease because of their significant systemic side effect burden (Cushingoid features, osteoporosis, adrenal suppression); the inhaled route is preferred for chronic maintenance precisely to avoid this systemic exposure.

preguntas.q: Why do inhaled corticosteroids typically avoid the systemic adverse effects seen with oral corticosteroid therapy?

o.A: Minimal systemic absorption when delivered by inhalation
o.B: They are rapidly excreted unchanged by the kidney
o.C: They do not bind the glucocorticoid receptor
o.D: They are converted to inactive metabolites in the lung before absorption

e.correcta: Inhaled corticosteroids are formulated to act locally on the airway mucosa, and only a small fraction is systemically absorbed (largely swallowed drug undergoing significant first-pass hepatic metabolism, plus limited pulmonary absorption). This minimal systemic exposure means patients on standard-dose inhaled corticosteroids generally avoid the classic systemic steroid effects like adrenal suppression, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, and Cushingoid features that occur with oral or systemic administration.

incorrectas.B: Renal excretion is not the reason systemic effects are minimized; the key factor is that very little drug reaches the systemic circulation in the first place due to the inhaled route and hepatic first-pass metabolism of any swallowed portion, not rapid unchanged renal clearance.
incorrectas.C: Inhaled corticosteroids absolutely bind the glucocorticoid receptor — that is precisely their mechanism of anti-inflammatory action in the airway; if they did not bind this receptor, they would have no therapeutic effect at all.
incorrectas.D: Inhaled corticosteroids are not converted to inactive metabolites within the lung tissue itself; rather, they remain active locally in the airway (which is the therapeutic goal), while systemic exposure is limited mainly by low absorbed fraction and hepatic first-pass metabolism of swallowed drug.

preguntas.q: Which adverse effect is classically associated with inhaled corticosteroid use in asthma?

e.correcta: Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush) occurs because inhaled corticosteroids deposited in the mouth and throat locally suppress mucosal immune defenses, allowing overgrowth of Candida species. This local, rather than systemic, adverse effect is specific to the inhaled route and is largely preventable, which is why patients are counseled to rinse and spit after each use to reduce residual drug left in the oropharynx.

incorrectas.B: Acute adrenal crisis results from abrupt withdrawal of long-term systemic (not inhaled) corticosteroids that have suppressed the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis; because inhaled corticosteroids have minimal systemic absorption, they rarely cause clinically significant adrenal suppression at standard doses.
incorrectas.C: Hepatotoxicity is a known adverse effect of the leukotriene pathway drug zileuton (a 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor), which requires liver function monitoring — it is not a characteristic effect of inhaled corticosteroids.
incorrectas.D: QT prolongation is not a recognized adverse effect of inhaled corticosteroids; it is more relevant to certain antiarrhythmics, some antibiotics, and antipsychotics that affect cardiac ion channels, an unrelated mechanism from local steroid action on the oropharynx.

preguntas.q: The risk of oropharyngeal candidiasis after using inhaled corticosteroids is reduced by which simple behavioral measure?

o.A: Gargling water and spitting after each treatment
o.C: Using the inhaler only at bedtime
o.D: Drinking a full glass of milk immediately after use

e.correcta: Rinsing the mouth with water and spitting (rather than swallowing) after each inhaled corticosteroid dose mechanically washes away residual drug particles that would otherwise linger on the oral and pharyngeal mucosa and locally suppress immune defenses there. This simple step significantly reduces the risk of Candida overgrowth without diminishing the drug's therapeutic effect in the lower airways, since the medication has already been delivered to the lungs by the time of rinsing.

incorrectas.B: Taking the medication with food has no established role in reducing oropharyngeal candidiasis risk from an inhaled medication, since the mechanism of thrush is local mucosal deposition in the mouth/throat, not a systemic or gastric interaction that food timing would address.
incorrectas.C: Restricting use to bedtime does not address the mechanism of local drug deposition causing candidiasis; the risk depends on rinsing after each dose regardless of what time of day the inhaler is used.
incorrectas.D: Drinking milk is not a recommended or evidence-based strategy for preventing oropharyngeal candidiasis from inhaled corticosteroids; the established practice is rinsing with water and spitting, which physically clears residual drug from the oropharynx.

preguntas.q: Montelukast and zafirlukast belong to which drug class used in asthma treatment?

e.correcta: Montelukast and zafirlukast are leukotriene D4 (CysLT1) receptor antagonists — they block the receptor that LTD4 (and related cysteinyl leukotrienes) would otherwise activate on airway smooth muscle and mucosal cells, preventing the bronchoconstriction, increased vascular permeability, and mucus secretion that leukotrienes cause. Because they are taken orally, they are a useful option for patients with poor compliance with inhaled therapies, and they are particularly effective in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.

incorrectas.B: 5-lipoxygenase inhibitors, such as zileuton, act further upstream by blocking the enzyme that converts arachidonic acid into leukotrienes in the first place, rather than blocking the leukotriene receptor itself — a related but mechanistically distinct approach from montelukast and zafirlukast.
incorrectas.C: Inhaled corticosteroids (e.g., budesonide, fluticasone) broadly suppress cytokine-mediated airway inflammation via glucocorticoid receptor signaling; they do not act on the leukotriene receptor pathway, which is the specific target of montelukast and zafirlukast.
incorrectas.D: Long-acting β2 agonists (e.g., salmeterol, formoterol) provide bronchodilation through β2 receptor stimulation and cAMP-mediated smooth muscle relaxation, a mechanism entirely separate from leukotriene receptor blockade.

preguntas.q: What is the route of administration of leukotriene D4-receptor antagonists such as montelukast and zafirlukast?

e.correcta: Montelukast and zafirlukast are administered orally, which distinguishes them from most other controller asthma medications (inhaled corticosteroids, long-acting β2 agonists) that require inhaler technique. This oral route makes them a practical option for patients who have difficulty using inhalers correctly or who have poor compliance with inhaled regimens, while still providing meaningful control of leukotriene-mediated airway inflammation and bronchoconstriction.

incorrectas.B: Inhaled administration is the route used for corticosteroids, β2 agonists, and anticholinergic bronchodilators, which act locally on the airway; leukotriene receptor antagonists are specifically formulated as oral tablets, not inhaled formulations.
incorrectas.C: Intravenous administration is not used for chronic asthma controller therapy like leukotriene receptor antagonists; IV medications in asthma management are typically reserved for acute severe exacerbations (e.g., IV corticosteroids or magnesium), a different clinical context entirely.
incorrectas.D: Subcutaneous administration is used for biologic asthma therapies like omalizumab (anti-IgE) or other monoclonal antibodies in severe refractory asthma, not for small-molecule leukotriene receptor antagonists, which are simple oral tablets.

preguntas.q: In a patient with asthma who takes aspirin, COX inhibition has what effect on leukotriene production?

o.D: Leukotriene production is converted to prostaglandin production

e.correcta: When aspirin or other NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase, arachidonic acid can no longer be efficiently shunted down the prostaglandin/thromboxane pathway, so more of it is diverted (shunted) toward the lipoxygenase pathway, increasing leukotriene synthesis. In susceptible asthmatic patients, this surge in leukotrienes causes bronchoconstriction and worsens airway symptoms — the basis of aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (Samter's triad: asthma, nasal polyps, and aspirin sensitivity).

incorrectas.B: Decreased leukotriene production would be the opposite of what actually happens; blocking COX does not reduce the total arachidonic acid substrate available, it simply redirects more of that substrate into the lipoxygenase pathway, raising leukotriene levels.
incorrectas.C: Leukotriene levels are not unaffected — the entire mechanism behind aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease depends on the fact that COX inhibition measurably increases leukotriene synthesis via arachidonic acid shunting, which is why aspirin can precipitate severe bronchospasm in sensitive asthmatics.
incorrectas.D: Leukotrienes and prostaglandins are separate end-products of the same arachidonic acid precursor made via different enzymes (lipoxygenase versus cyclooxygenase, respectively); COX inhibition does not convert one class of mediator into the other, it shifts substrate flow toward the lipoxygenase branch.

preguntas.q: Montelukast and zafirlukast are especially effective in treating asthma triggered by which factor?

e.correcta: Aspirin-induced (aspirin-exacerbated) asthma occurs because COX inhibition shunts arachidonic acid metabolism toward the lipoxygenase pathway, generating excess leukotrienes that cause bronchoconstriction — classically part of Samter's triad along with nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity. Because leukotriene receptor antagonists like montelukast and zafirlukast directly block the receptor these excess leukotrienes would act on, they are particularly effective in this specific subtype of asthma, more so than in general allergic asthma driven mainly by histamine.

incorrectas.B: Cold air-induced bronchoconstriction is thought to involve airway drying and direct irritant effects on airway smooth muscle rather than a leukotriene surge from COX inhibition, so leukotriene antagonists are not specifically highlighted as the preferred therapy for this trigger.
incorrectas.C: Viral infections trigger asthma exacerbations through airway epithelial damage and inflammatory cytokine release, a different inflammatory cascade from the leukotriene-driven mechanism of aspirin sensitivity, so montelukast is not specifically noted as uniquely effective here.
incorrectas.D: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction involves airway cooling and drying with mast cell mediator release; while leukotriene antagonists can have some benefit in exercise-induced symptoms, the classic, specifically highlighted indication for montelukast and zafirlukast's particular effectiveness is aspirin-induced asthma.

preguntas.q: What is the mechanism of action of zileuton in asthma treatment?

e.correcta: Zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase, the enzyme that converts arachidonic acid into leukotrienes (LTA4 and its downstream products). By blocking this conversion step upstream, zileuton reduces the overall production of leukotrienes rather than just blocking their receptor, decreasing leukotriene-driven bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, and inflammation in asthma.

incorrectas.B: Leukotriene D4-receptor antagonists like montelukast and zafirlukast act downstream of leukotriene synthesis, blocking the CysLT1 receptor so that any leukotrienes produced cannot exert their effect — a different point in the pathway from zileuton's enzyme inhibition.
incorrectas.C: Cyclooxygenase inhibitors like aspirin and NSAIDs block the prostaglandin/thromboxane-producing enzyme, which in susceptible individuals actually increases leukotriene production by diverting arachidonic acid toward the lipoxygenase pathway — the opposite effect of zileuton, which directly blocks that pathway.
incorrectas.D: Phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitors, such as roflumilast, work by increasing intracellular cAMP to reduce inflammation, primarily used in COPD, and have no relationship to the arachidonic acid/leukotriene pathway that zileuton targets.

preguntas.q: Which adverse effect requires monitoring in patients taking zileuton?

e.correcta: Zileuton is associated with hepatotoxicity, so liver function tests must be monitored periodically during therapy to detect elevated transaminases or drug-induced liver injury before it becomes clinically significant. This adverse effect, combined with the need for frequent dosing and drug interactions from CYP1A2 inhibition, makes zileuton a less commonly used option compared to leukotriene receptor antagonists like montelukast.

incorrectas.B: Oropharyngeal candidiasis is a local adverse effect specific to inhaled corticosteroids depositing in the oropharynx and suppressing local immune defenses; zileuton is an oral systemic 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor and does not cause this local fungal overgrowth.
incorrectas.C: QT prolongation is not a recognized adverse effect of zileuton; this concern is more relevant to certain antiarrhythmics and other drugs affecting cardiac potassium channels, an unrelated mechanism from zileuton's hepatic enzyme inhibition effects.
incorrectas.D: Nephrotoxicity is not the characteristic monitored toxicity for zileuton; the drug's main organ-specific concern is the liver, given its known potential to cause hepatocellular injury, which is why regular LFT monitoring is recommended rather than renal function monitoring.

preguntas.q: Long-acting β2 agonists (e.g., salmeterol, formoterol) are used for which purpose in moderate to severe persistent asthma?

o.B: Acute rescue therapy during an asthma attack
o.D: Treatment of status asthmaticus in the emergency department

e.correcta: Long-acting β2 agonists provide sustained bronchodilation over roughly 12 hours and are used as prophylactic, scheduled maintenance therapy added on top of inhaled corticosteroids in moderate to severe persistent asthma, helping prevent symptoms rather than treating an acute flare. Because their onset of action is slower than short-acting agents, they are not appropriate for rapid relief of acute bronchospasm and are never used as monotherapy without an inhaled corticosteroid, given the increased risk of asthma-related death when used alone.

incorrectas.B: Acute rescue therapy during an asthma attack calls for a short-acting β2 agonist like albuterol, which has a fast onset of action suited to quickly reversing acute bronchoconstriction — long-acting agents act too slowly to be useful for immediate symptom relief.
incorrectas.C: Anaphylaxis is treated with intramuscular epinephrine, which acts on multiple adrenergic receptors (α1, β1, β2) to reverse hypotension, laryngeal edema, and bronchospasm simultaneously; a selective long-acting β2 agonist would not adequately address the vasodilatory shock component of anaphylaxis.
incorrectas.D: Status asthmaticus is a medical emergency managed with short-acting bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids, and sometimes other emergent measures for rapid effect; long-acting β2 agonists are used for chronic maintenance control, not for the emergent management of a severe acute asthma exacerbation.

preguntas.q: Salmeterol has a much longer duration of bronchodilator action than albuterol despite both being β2 agonists. What property of salmeterol primarily accounts for this?

o.A: High lipid solubility, allowing it to partition into and slowly release from the membrane near the receptor
o.B: Irreversible covalent binding to the β2 receptor
o.C: Renal tubular reabsorption prolonging its plasma half-life
o.D: Conversion to an active metabolite in the liver

e.correcta: Salmeterol's long, highly lipophilic side chain allows the molecule to insert into the plasma membrane adjacent to the β2 receptor, from which it slowly diffuses laterally back to the binding site over many hours, producing repeated receptor activation and a duration of action of roughly 12 hours. This is why LABAs are dosed twice daily for maintenance therapy rather than for acute rescue, since onset is also slower than that of short-acting agents like albuterol.

incorrectas.B: β2 agonists including salmeterol bind reversibly; irreversible covalent receptor binding is not the mechanism used by any clinically used adrenergic bronchodilator and would raise concerns about prolonged receptor blockade rather than sustained activation.
incorrectas.C: Salmeterol's duration of action is a local, membrane-based pharmacodynamic phenomenon, not a pharmacokinetic one dependent on renal handling; its systemic plasma half-life does not explain the sustained bronchodilation seen with a single inhaled dose.
incorrectas.D: Salmeterol itself is the active moiety acting at the β2 receptor; its long action comes from its lipophilic depot effect at the membrane, not from hepatic bioactivation into a different active compound.

preguntas.q: A patient with persistent asthma is prescribed a long-acting β2 agonist (LABA) for daily maintenance therapy. Which additional medication class must always be co-administered with the LABA?

e.correcta: LABA monotherapy in asthma has been associated with an increased risk of severe exacerbations and asthma-related death, so guidelines require that a LABA always be combined with an inhaled corticosteroid, which treats the underlying airway inflammation that the LABA's bronchodilation alone does not address. This pairing (e.g., fluticasone-salmeterol) is a classic step-up regimen for moderate-to-severe persistent asthma.

incorrectas.A: Leukotriene receptor antagonists (e.g., montelukast) are an alternative or add-on controller option but are not the mandatory partner drug for LABAs; the safety requirement specifically concerns pairing with an anti-inflammatory corticosteroid.
incorrectas.C: Short-acting muscarinic antagonists like ipratropium are used for acute exacerbations or as COPD therapy, not as the required daily companion to a LABA in asthma maintenance regimens.
incorrectas.D: Methylxanthines such as theophylline are a second- or third-line adjunct for refractory asthma given their narrow therapeutic index, not a required co-therapy alongside every LABA prescription.

preguntas.q: A patient with moderate persistent asthma remains symptomatic on a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid. What is the appropriate next step in stepwise inhaled corticosteroid management?

o.A: Discontinue the inhaled corticosteroid and switch to a leukotriene inhibitor
o.B: Increase the dose of the inhaled corticosteroid
o.C: Switch to an oral corticosteroid at an equivalent dose
o.D: Add a short-acting muscarinic antagonist in place of the corticosteroid

e.correcta: Asthma management follows a stepwise approach where inadequate control on a given inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) dose prompts escalation to a higher ICS dose (often with addition of a LABA) before moving to systemic therapy. Increasing the inhaled dose maximizes local anti-inflammatory effect on the airway while minimizing the systemic side effects associated with oral steroids.

incorrectas.A: Leukotriene inhibitors are useful adjuncts, especially in aspirin-exacerbated or allergic asthma, but replacing the ICS entirely abandons the most effective anti-inflammatory therapy rather than optimizing it first.
incorrectas.C: Oral corticosteroids carry substantially more systemic toxicity (adrenal suppression, osteoporosis, hyperglycemia) than inhaled steroids and are reserved for acute exacerbations or severe refractory disease, not as a routine step-up from inhaled therapy.
incorrectas.D: Muscarinic antagonists provide bronchodilation but do not address the underlying eosinophilic airway inflammation that inhaled corticosteroids target, so substituting one for the other would undertreat the inflammatory component of asthma.

preguntas.q: Which drug class does theophylline belong to when used as an asthma therapy?

e.correcta: Theophylline is a methylxanthine, a drug class chemically related to caffeine that inhibits phosphodiesterase and antagonizes adenosine receptors, both of which raise intracellular cAMP in airway smooth muscle and promote bronchodilation. It is now a second-line or adjunct asthma agent because of its narrow therapeutic index and numerous drug interactions, but it remains testable as a classic methylxanthine.

incorrectas.A: Leukotriene receptor antagonists (e.g., montelukast, zafirlukast) block the CysLT1 receptor to prevent leukotriene-mediated bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion, a mechanistically distinct pathway from theophylline's phosphodiesterase inhibition.
incorrectas.C: Mast cell stabilizers such as cromolyn sodium prevent degranulation and mediator release from mast cells; they do not inhibit phosphodiesterase or antagonize adenosine the way methylxanthines do.
incorrectas.D: Muscarinic antagonists like ipratropium block M3 receptors on airway smooth muscle to prevent acetylcholine-driven bronchoconstriction, a mechanism unrelated to theophylline's cAMP-based action.

preguntas.q: Theophylline promotes bronchial smooth muscle relaxation and inhibits cytokine release primarily through what effect on intracellular signaling?

o.A: Decreased cAMP due to phosphodiesterase activation
o.B: Increased cAMP due to phosphodiesterase inhibition
o.D: Decreased cGMP due to guanylate cyclase inhibition

e.correcta: Theophylline nonselectively inhibits phosphodiesterase enzymes that normally break down cAMP, so cAMP accumulates in airway smooth muscle cells and immune cells. Elevated cAMP promotes smooth muscle relaxation (bronchodilation) and dampens release of inflammatory cytokines from mast cells and other immune cells, mirroring in a downstream sense the effect that β2 agonists achieve via adenylate cyclase stimulation.

incorrectas.A: Theophylline inhibits, rather than activates, phosphodiesterase; activating phosphodiesterase would accelerate cAMP breakdown and promote bronchoconstriction, the opposite of theophylline's therapeutic effect.
incorrectas.C: Increased intracellular calcium in airway smooth muscle promotes contraction (bronchoconstriction), which is the opposite of the bronchodilatory effect produced by theophylline's cAMP elevation.
incorrectas.D: Theophylline's mechanism centers on cAMP via phosphodiesterase inhibition, not on the cGMP/guanylate cyclase pathway, which is more relevant to nitric oxide signaling and vascular smooth muscle.

preguntas.q: By what route is theophylline typically administered for chronic asthma therapy?

e.correcta: Theophylline is administered orally as a sustained-release formulation for chronic maintenance therapy, allowing steady plasma levels given its narrow therapeutic window; this contrasts with most modern asthma controller drugs that are delivered by inhalation directly to the airway to minimize systemic exposure.

incorrectas.A: Subcutaneous injection is not used for theophylline; oral dosing is preferred because it maintains the steady, predictable plasma concentrations needed to stay within its narrow therapeutic index over a chronic dosing schedule.
incorrectas.B: Unlike albuterol, ipratropium, or inhaled corticosteroids, theophylline is not formulated for inhalation; its systemic oral route reflects its mechanism requiring adequate blood levels to inhibit phosphodiesterase throughout the body, not just locally in the lung.
incorrectas.D: Intramuscular administration is not used for theophylline maintenance dosing; oral therapy is standard for chronic outpatient control of asthma/COPD symptoms.

preguntas.q: Clinical use of theophylline is limited mainly because of which pharmacologic property?

o.D: Rapid renal clearance requiring hourly dosing

e.correcta: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index, meaning the plasma concentration range that provides bronchodilation without toxicity is small; levels only modestly above therapeutic can cause tachyarrhythmias, seizures, nervousness, and tremors. This necessitates monitoring of drug levels and caution with interacting medications, which is a major reason theophylline has been largely supplanted by safer inhaled therapies.

incorrectas.A: Theophylline is actually well absorbed orally; poor bioavailability is not the limiting factor in its clinical use — the danger comes from the small margin between therapeutic and toxic plasma levels.
incorrectas.B: Theophylline does cross into the CNS, which is precisely why toxicity can manifest as seizures and nervousness; it does not lack CNS penetration, and this penetration actually contributes to its toxicity profile rather than limiting its use for another reason.
incorrectas.D: Theophylline's clearance is primarily hepatic (via cytochrome P450) rather than renal, and while its half-life can vary based on enzyme induction/inhibition, the fundamental limitation on its use is the narrow safety margin, not a requirement for hourly redosing.

preguntas.q: A patient on theophylline for asthma develops palpitations. Which cardiac effect is most characteristic of theophylline toxicity?

e.correcta: Theophylline toxicity classically produces tachycardia and tachyarrhythmias, related to its adenosine receptor antagonism (adenosine normally has antiarrhythmic, AV-node-slowing effects) and its sympathomimetic-like stimulation via elevated cAMP. This is one of the key reasons theophylline requires careful therapeutic drug monitoring, along with its CNS effects of nervousness, tremor, and seizures.

incorrectas.B: Complete heart block reflects impaired AV nodal conduction, which is the opposite of theophylline's effect — by blocking adenosine (which normally slows AV conduction), theophylline tends to increase heart rate and rhythm irritability rather than cause conduction block.
incorrectas.C: Bradycardia would be expected from agents that enhance adenosine or vagal tone at the AV node; theophylline does the opposite by antagonizing adenosine, producing tachycardia rather than a slowed heart rate.
incorrectas.D: Torsades de pointes is specifically associated with QT-prolonging drugs; theophylline's arrhythmogenic potential is more broadly tied to generalized tachyarrhythmia from sympathetic-like stimulation, not a specific QT-prolongation mechanism.

preguntas.q: A patient stable on theophylline is started on a new antiepileptic drug and later presents with theophylline toxicity. Theophylline blood levels are especially sensitive to changes in which metabolic pathway?

e.correcta: Theophylline is metabolized by hepatic cytochrome P-450 enzymes, making its levels highly sensitive to CYP inducers and inhibitors — this is captured by the mnemonic 'ATOMS' (Always Think Of Metabolism by cytochromes: antiepileptics, theophylline, oral contraceptives, warfarin among the classic CYP-affected drugs). A CYP-inducing antiepileptic (e.g., phenytoin, carbamazepine) would lower theophylline levels, while a CYP inhibitor could push levels into the toxic range, which is why levels must be monitored closely whenever interacting drugs are added.

incorrectas.A: Theophylline clearance is driven by hepatic oxidative metabolism rather than active renal tubular secretion, so changes in renal transporter activity are not the primary mechanism behind drug-interaction-related toxicity.
incorrectas.C: Glucuronidation is a phase II conjugation pathway used by many other drugs (e.g., bilirubin, some opioids), but theophylline's clinically important interactions arise from phase I CYP450 oxidation, not UGT-mediated conjugation.
incorrectas.D: Plasma esterase hydrolysis inactivates drugs like esmolol or succinylcholine; theophylline is not cleared by esterases, so this pathway is not relevant to its interaction profile.

preguntas.q: Theophylline's bronchodilator effect is partly due to blocking the actions of which endogenous local metabolite?

e.correcta: Theophylline antagonizes adenosine receptors in the airway; adenosine itself promotes bronchoconstriction and mast cell mediator release, so blocking its receptor contributes to theophylline's bronchodilatory and anti-inflammatory effects (in addition to its phosphodiesterase inhibition raising cAMP). This dual mechanism — phosphodiesterase inhibition plus adenosine antagonism — distinguishes methylxanthines from other bronchodilator classes.

incorrectas.A: Histamine causes bronchoconstriction via H1 receptors and is targeted by antihistamines or by preventing its release (e.g., cromolyn), but theophylline's mechanism of action is not through direct histamine receptor blockade.
incorrectas.B: Prostaglandin D2 is a mast-cell-derived mediator that contributes to bronchoconstriction and vasodilation in allergic responses, but it is not the target that defines theophylline's mechanism; theophylline's signature receptor antagonism is at adenosine receptors.
incorrectas.D: Leukotriene C4 (a cysteinyl leukotriene) drives bronchoconstriction and is specifically blocked by leukotriene receptor antagonists like montelukast, not by theophylline, whose relevant receptor antagonism is against adenosine.

preguntas.q: A patient with allergic asthma, elevated serum IgE, and inadequate control despite inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting β2 agonists is being considered for add-on biologic therapy. Which agent is indicated in this setting?

e.correcta: Omalizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds free IgE, preventing it from engaging the high-affinity FcεRI receptor on mast cells and basophils, thereby reducing the allergic cascade that drives bronchoconstriction and airway inflammation. It is reserved for moderate-to-severe allergic asthma with elevated IgE that remains uncontrolled on standard inhaled corticosteroid/LABA therapy, reflecting its role as an add-on biologic rather than a first-line agent.

incorrectas.B: Cromolyn sodium stabilizes mast cell membranes to prevent degranulation and is used prophylactically for mild asthma or exercise-induced bronchospasm; it does not target IgE directly and is not the biologic indicated for IgE-mediated, treatment-resistant allergic asthma.
incorrectas.C: Ipratropium is a short-acting muscarinic antagonist used for acute bronchospasm or COPD; it has no role in targeting the IgE-driven allergic pathway described in this scenario.
incorrectas.D: Zileuton is a 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor that blocks leukotriene synthesis, useful in some asthma phenotypes, but it does not act on IgE and is not the specific biologic indicated for refractory IgE-mediated allergic asthma.

preguntas.q: Cromolyn sodium prevents allergic bronchoconstriction primarily through which mechanism?

o.A: Blocking leukotriene receptors on smooth muscle

e.correcta: Cromolyn sodium stabilizes mast cell membranes and inhibits degranulation, preventing the release of histamine and other preformed inflammatory mediators that would otherwise trigger bronchoconstriction and mucosal edema. Because it works prophylactically to prevent mediator release rather than blocking receptors after mediators are already released, it is most useful when taken before an anticipated trigger (e.g., before exercise or allergen exposure) rather than during an acute attack; nedocromil works via the same mechanism.

incorrectas.A: Leukotriene receptor blockade is the mechanism of drugs like montelukast, which act downstream on smooth muscle receptors rather than upstream at the level of mediator release from mast cells the way cromolyn does.
incorrectas.B: H1 receptor antagonism describes antihistamines, which block the action of already-released histamine on target tissues; cromolyn instead prevents the histamine from being released from the mast cell in the first place.
incorrectas.D: M3 muscarinic receptor blockade is the mechanism of ipratropium and tiotropium, which prevent acetylcholine-driven bronchoconstriction independent of mast cell activity, a distinct pathway from cromolyn's membrane-stabilizing effect.

preguntas.q: A patient presents with an acute, severe asthma exacerbation. Which combination represents appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

o.B: Short-acting β2 agonist ± systemic corticosteroids, or epinephrine
o.D: Omalizumab plus a leukotriene receptor antagonist

e.correcta: Acute severe asthma exacerbations require rapid-onset bronchodilation, provided by a short-acting β2 agonist (e.g., albuterol) with or without systemic corticosteroids to address the underlying inflammatory surge; epinephrine is an alternative rapid bronchodilator, particularly when nebulized SABA is unavailable or in anaphylaxis-related bronchospasm. These agents work quickly, unlike controller medications, which is essential in an acute, potentially life-threatening presentation.

incorrectas.A: LABAs like salmeterol have a slow onset of action and are specifically not used for acute rescue; using a LABA alone in an acute exacerbation would fail to provide the rapid bronchodilation needed and carries safety concerns when used without an inhaled corticosteroid.
incorrectas.C: Theophylline and cromolyn are not first-line acute rescue therapies — theophylline has a slow onset and narrow therapeutic index unsuitable for emergent titration, and cromolyn is purely prophylactic with no role in reversing an ongoing attack.
incorrectas.D: Omalizumab and leukotriene receptor antagonists are both maintenance/controller therapies with delayed onset of benefit; neither provides the immediate bronchodilation required to manage an acute, severe exacerbation.

preguntas.q: In the setting of an acute, severe asthma exacerbation, by which routes are corticosteroids typically administered?

e.correcta: During an acute severe exacerbation, corticosteroids are given systemically — intravenously for the sickest patients or orally when the patient can tolerate oral intake and disease is somewhat less severe — because systemic dosing achieves the rapid, robust anti-inflammatory effect needed to reverse airway edema and mucus plugging, unlike the slower-onset, lower-systemic-exposure inhaled route used for maintenance.

incorrectas.A: Inhaled corticosteroids are the mainstay of chronic maintenance therapy but have too slow an onset and too localized an effect to adequately control the intense systemic inflammatory response of an acute severe exacerbation.
incorrectas.B: Intramuscular corticosteroid administration is not the standard route in acute asthma management; IV access allows more controlled, titratable systemic dosing in the acute hospital setting.
incorrectas.D: Subcutaneous or topical corticosteroids are not used for asthma exacerbations; these routes are relevant to other conditions (e.g., topical steroids for dermatologic disease) but do not provide the systemic anti-inflammatory coverage needed here.

preguntas.q: Which nebulized muscarinic antagonist may be added to treatment for an acute, severe asthma exacerbation?

e.correcta: Nebulized ipratropium, a short-acting quaternary muscarinic antagonist, blocks M3 receptors on airway smooth muscle to reduce acetylcholine-driven bronchoconstriction, and is commonly added to nebulized short-acting β2 agonists in acute severe asthma to provide an additive bronchodilator effect. Its quaternary ammonium structure limits systemic and CNS absorption, making it well suited for inhaled use with a favorable side-effect profile.

incorrectas.B: Atropine is a tertiary amine muscarinic antagonist that crosses into the systemic circulation and CNS, producing more systemic anticholinergic side effects; it is not the inhaled agent used in standard asthma exacerbation protocols.
incorrectas.C: Scopolamine is a tertiary amine anticholinergic primarily used for motion sickness and has significant CNS penetration; it is not used as an inhaled bronchodilator for asthma.
incorrectas.D: Glycopyrrolate is a quaternary anticholinergic used more in perioperative settings (reducing secretions) and for COPD in some inhaled formulations, but it is not the classic agent cited for acute asthma exacerbation management — ipratropium is.

preguntas.q: Besides asthma exacerbations, ipratropium is a standard bronchodilator used in the management of which chronic respiratory disease?

e.correcta: Ipratropium (and its longer-acting analog tiotropium) is a cornerstone bronchodilator in COPD management, where blocking M3 receptor-mediated smooth muscle contraction and mucus secretion improves airflow in a disease driven substantially by cholinergic tone and fixed airway obstruction. This differs from asthma, where muscarinic antagonists are more of an adjunct than a primary controller.

incorrectas.A: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a restrictive lung disease driven by progressive fibrosis, not by bronchoconstriction or cholinergic tone, so bronchodilators like ipratropium do not address its underlying pathology.
incorrectas.C: Pulmonary embolism is a vascular occlusive event treated with anticoagulation or thrombolysis, not with inhaled bronchodilators, since the primary problem is a clot obstructing pulmonary blood flow rather than airway smooth muscle tone.
incorrectas.D: Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous inflammatory disease typically treated with corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants when treatment is needed; it is not a standard indication for muscarinic antagonist bronchodilators.

preguntas.q: Which catecholamine can be administered for an acute, severe asthma exacerbation, particularly when inhaled short-acting β2 agonists are inadequate or unavailable?

e.correcta: Epinephrine stimulates both β2 receptors (causing bronchodilation via increased cAMP in airway smooth muscle) and α1/β1 receptors (providing additional benefits like mucosal vasoconstriction and cardiac support), making it useful in severe asthma exacerbations, especially when the presentation overlaps with anaphylaxis or when nebulized therapy is insufficient. It is typically given intramuscularly or subcutaneously in this context.

incorrectas.A: Dopamine's receptor activity is dose-dependent (dopaminergic, then β1, then α1 at higher doses) and it is used mainly for hemodynamic support in shock, not as a bronchodilator for asthma.
incorrectas.B: Norepinephrine acts predominantly on α1 and β1 receptors with minimal β2 activity, so it lacks significant bronchodilator effect and is used for vasopressor support in shock rather than asthma treatment.
incorrectas.C: Dobutamine is a relatively selective β1 agonist used to increase cardiac contractility in heart failure or cardiogenic shock; its minimal β2 activity makes it ineffective as a bronchodilator for asthma exacerbations.

preguntas.q: Methacholine challenge testing is used to help diagnose asthma by exploiting airway hyperresponsiveness. Methacholine acts as an agonist at which receptor?

e.correcta: Methacholine is a synthetic direct muscarinic agonist that is resistant to acetylcholinesterase breakdown, allowing it to reliably stimulate M3 receptors on airway smooth muscle and provoke bronchoconstriction. In patients with underlying airway hyperreactivity (as in asthma), this triggers a disproportionate fall in FEV1 at low methacholine doses, forming the basis of the bronchoprovocation challenge used when spirometry is otherwise normal but asthma is still suspected.

incorrectas.A: β2 adrenergic receptor agonists (like albuterol) cause bronchodilation, not bronchoconstriction, so they are used to reverse — not provoke — airway narrowing, making them irrelevant to the diagnostic logic of the methacholine challenge.
incorrectas.C: H1 histamine receptor stimulation does contribute to bronchoconstriction in allergic reactions, but methacholine's pharmacologic action is as a cholinergic (muscarinic) agonist, not a histaminergic one.
incorrectas.D: Adenosine A1 receptor activation can contribute to bronchoconstriction in some contexts, but methacholine's mechanism in the bronchoprovocation test is direct muscarinic receptor stimulation, not adenosine receptor engagement.

preguntas.q: What effect does endogenous adenosine have on bronchial smooth muscle tone?

o.C: No significant effect on airway tone
o.D: Bronchodilation via direct smooth muscle membrane hyperpolarization

e.correcta: Adenosine causes bronchoconstriction, particularly relevant in patients with asthma, and this effect is antagonized by methylxanthines like theophylline, which block adenosine receptors as part of their bronchodilator mechanism. This bronchoconstrictive property is also why adenosine (used clinically to terminate SVT) must be used cautiously in patients with reactive airway disease.

incorrectas.A: Adenosine does not act on β2 adrenergic receptors; its bronchoconstrictive effect operates through its own adenosine receptors on airway tissue, a distinct pathway from the β2-receptor-mediated relaxation produced by drugs like albuterol.
incorrectas.C: Adenosine has a clear, clinically important effect on the airway — bronchoconstriction — which is significant enough that adenosine is used cautiously (or avoided) in asthmatic patients undergoing cardiac procedures.
incorrectas.D: Adenosine's airway effect is constrictive rather than relaxing, and it acts through receptor-mediated signaling rather than direct membrane hyperpolarization; theophylline's blockade of this receptor is what produces bronchodilation, not adenosine itself.

preguntas.q: What effect does endogenous acetylcholine have on bronchial smooth muscle tone?

o.A: Bronchodilation via M2 receptor stimulation on smooth muscle

e.correcta: Acetylcholine released from parasympathetic (vagal) postganglionic neurons acts on M3 muscarinic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, activating a Gq-coupled pathway that raises intracellular calcium and produces bronchoconstriction along with increased mucus gland secretion. This is the physiologic rationale for using muscarinic antagonists like ipratropium to counteract cholinergic bronchoconstrictive tone in asthma and COPD.

incorrectas.A: M2 receptors on airway smooth muscle are actually autoreceptors that inhibit further acetylcholine release from the nerve terminal, a negative feedback role rather than the receptor mediating smooth muscle contraction, which is M3; neither M2 nor M3 activation produces bronchodilation.
incorrectas.C: Acetylcholine has a well-established, clinically important bronchoconstrictive effect on the airway, which is precisely why anticholinergic bronchodilators are therapeutically useful — it does not leave airway caliber unaffected.
incorrectas.D: Nicotinic receptors are found at autonomic ganglia and the neuromuscular junction, not on bronchial smooth muscle; the airway smooth muscle response to acetylcholine is mediated by muscarinic (M3), not nicotinic, receptors.

preguntas.q: What effect does theophylline have on bronchial smooth muscle tone?

e.correcta: Theophylline causes bronchodilation, achieved through phosphodiesterase inhibition (raising cAMP) and adenosine receptor antagonism (blocking adenosine's bronchoconstrictive effect), both of which relax airway smooth muscle. This places theophylline among the bronchodilator options for asthma and COPD, though its use is tempered by its narrow therapeutic index relative to inhaled bronchodilators.

incorrectas.A: Bronchoconstriction is the effect of endogenous mediators like acetylcholine, adenosine, and leukotrienes; theophylline works against this tone (via phosphodiesterase inhibition and adenosine antagonism) to produce the opposite effect, dilation.
incorrectas.C: Theophylline has a clear, measurable bronchodilator effect that underlies its historical use as an asthma controller agent; it does not lack a significant effect on airway tone.
incorrectas.D: Theophylline does not produce an initial constrictive phase; its pharmacodynamic effect is bronchodilation from the onset of adequate plasma levels, without a preceding paradoxical constriction.

preguntas.q: What effect do muscarinic antagonists (e.g., ipratropium) have on bronchial smooth muscle tone?

o.B: No effect on smooth muscle, only on mucus glands

e.correcta: Muscarinic antagonists block M3 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, preventing acetylcholine from triggering the Gq-mediated calcium signaling that causes contraction, and the net physiologic result is bronchodilation. This is the basis for using agents like ipratropium and tiotropium in COPD and, as an adjunct, in asthma exacerbations.

incorrectas.A: Bronchoconstriction is the effect of muscarinic agonism (i.e., what acetylcholine itself does); muscarinic antagonists produce the opposite effect by blocking that pathway, resulting in bronchodilation rather than constriction.
incorrectas.B: Muscarinic antagonists act on M3 receptors present on both bronchial smooth muscle and submucosal glands, so their effect extends beyond mucus secretion to include direct relaxation of airway smooth muscle tone.
incorrectas.D: There is no rebound constrictive phase with muscarinic antagonist bronchodilators; their pharmacologic effect is sustained bronchodilation for the duration of receptor blockade, without an initial or delayed constrictive component.

preguntas.q: Guaifenesin is commonly combined with cough suppressants like dextromethorphan in cold formulations. Does guaifenesin itself suppress the cough reflex?

o.A: Yes, by acting centrally on the medullary cough center
o.B: No, it acts as an expectorant rather than an antitussive
o.C: Yes, by blocking peripheral cough receptors in the airway
o.D: No, because it is a decongestant, not a respiratory drug at all

e.correcta: Guaifenesin is an expectorant, not an antitussive — it works by reducing mucus viscosity and increasing respiratory tract fluid secretion, which helps mobilize and clear secretions rather than suppressing the cough reflex itself. This distinguishes it mechanistically from dextromethorphan, which does act centrally to raise the threshold for coughing, which is why the two are often paired in combination products to both loosen and calm a cough.

incorrectas.A: Central suppression of the medullary cough center is the mechanism of dextromethorphan and opioid antitussives (e.g., codeine), not guaifenesin, which has no direct action on the brainstem cough center.
incorrectas.C: Guaifenesin does not block peripheral cough receptors; its expectorant action instead thins mucus so it can be cleared more easily, which may indirectly reduce the urge to cough but is not due to receptor blockade.
incorrectas.D: Guaifenesin is indeed a respiratory-tract-active drug (an expectorant), just not one that suppresses cough; it is not classified as a decongestant, which is a separate drug category (e.g., pseudoephedrine) acting on nasal vascular tone.

preguntas.q: Pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine are used as decongestants that can relieve obstruction of which structure, helping with sinus and ear pressure symptoms?

e.correcta: Pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine are α1 agonists that cause vasoconstriction of the nasal and sinus mucosa, reducing mucosal swelling around the eustachian tube opening and helping relieve obstruction that can cause ear pressure or fullness, such as in upper respiratory infections or barotrauma. This same vasoconstrictive mechanism underlies their use as general nasal decongestants.

incorrectas.A: The cricothyroid membrane is a surgical landmark for emergency airway access (cricothyrotomy) and is unrelated to the mucosal vasoconstriction produced by decongestants.
incorrectas.C: The nasolacrimal duct drains tears into the nasal cavity; while nasal decongestants act in the same general anatomic region, the classic obstruction relieved by these drugs in this context is of the eustachian tube, not the nasolacrimal duct.
incorrectas.D: The thoracic duct is the major lymphatic drainage channel in the chest, entirely unrelated to nasal mucosal vasoconstriction or eustachian tube patency.

preguntas.q: A patient with hypertension takes an over-the-counter cold remedy containing pseudoephedrine and notices their blood pressure readings have risen. What adverse effect explains this?

o.B: Increased blood pressure (hypertension) from α1-mediated vasoconstriction

e.correcta: Pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine stimulate α1 adrenergic receptors, causing vasoconstriction throughout the vasculature, not just in the nasal mucosa; this systemic vasoconstrictive effect increases peripheral vascular resistance and can raise blood pressure, making these decongestants a caution or contraindication in patients with hypertension or cardiovascular disease.

incorrectas.A: Reflex bradycardia can occur as a secondary baroreceptor response to the rise in blood pressure, but the primary adverse effect being tested is the hypertension itself, produced directly by α1-mediated vasoconstriction rather than a bradycardic mechanism.
incorrectas.C: These drugs have little to no β2 agonist activity at typical decongestant doses; they are relatively selective α1 agonists, so hypotension from β2-mediated vasodilation does not occur — the actual concern is the opposite, hypertension.
incorrectas.D: Pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine do not act on renal potassium handling or the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system; their hypertensive effect is a direct pharmacologic consequence of α1 receptor-mediated vasoconstriction, not an electrolyte-driven mechanism.

preguntas.q: A patient presents with lethargy, miosis, and respiratory depression after an overdose of dextromethorphan. Which drug should be administered?

e.correcta: Dextromethorphan is a cough suppressant that, despite not being a classic opioid, acts at sigma and NMDA receptors and can produce an opioid-like toxidrome (CNS depression, miosis, respiratory depression) in overdose, which responds to naloxone, an opioid receptor antagonist. Loperamide, an antidiarrheal that also has opioid-like activity at high doses, is treated the same way, so remembering 'opioid-like toxidrome gets naloxone regardless of the exact drug class' covers both agents.

incorrectas.A: Flumazenil is a competitive benzodiazepine receptor antagonist used to reverse benzodiazepine-induced sedation, not the opioid-like toxidrome produced by dextromethorphan overdose; giving it here would do nothing for the respiratory depression.
incorrectas.C: N-acetylcysteine is the antidote for acetaminophen toxicity, replenishing glutathione stores to detoxify the reactive metabolite NAPQI — it has no role in reversing dextromethorphan's CNS and respiratory effects.
incorrectas.D: Physostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used for anticholinergic toxicity (e.g., from antihistamines or TCAs), which is essentially the opposite clinical picture from the opioid-like depression seen with dextromethorphan overdose.

preguntas.q: Bosentan antagonizes endothelin-1 receptors, producing what effect on pulmonary vascular resistance in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension?

e.correcta: Endothelin-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor that binds ET-A/ET-B receptors on pulmonary vascular smooth muscle, driving the remodeling and vasoconstriction seen in pulmonary arterial hypertension. Bosentan blocks these receptors, preventing endothelin-mediated vasoconstriction and thereby decreasing pulmonary vascular resistance, which is the basis for its use as a first-line oral agent in PAH.

incorrectas.A: An increase in pulmonary vascular resistance is what untreated endothelin-1 signaling itself causes; blocking the receptor with bosentan opposes this effect rather than reproducing it.
incorrectas.B: No change would only occur if endothelin signaling were not contributing to the patient's vascular tone, but endothelin-1 is a major driver of pulmonary hypertension, so receptor blockade produces a measurable hemodynamic benefit.
incorrectas.D: Bosentan is a direct receptor antagonist with a straightforward pharmacodynamic effect; there is no biphasic increase-then-decrease pattern described for its mechanism of lowering pulmonary vascular resistance.

preguntas.q: A patient started on bosentan for pulmonary arterial hypertension requires monthly monitoring of which laboratory parameter due to a known adverse effect?

e.correcta: Bosentan is hepatotoxic, and its endothelin receptor antagonism has been linked to dose-dependent elevations in liver aminotransferases that can progress to serious liver injury. Because of this, patients require monthly LFT monitoring throughout therapy, and the drug carries a black-box warning with a restricted access program in the US.

incorrectas.A: Serum creatinine monitoring is important for many nephrotoxic drugs (e.g., aminoglycosides, calcineurin inhibitors), but bosentan's dose-limiting toxicity is hepatic, not renal.
incorrectas.C: CBC monitoring is relevant for drugs causing bone marrow suppression, such as many chemotherapeutics or clozapine (agranulocytosis), which is not the characteristic toxicity of bosentan.
incorrectas.D: Thyroid function tests are monitored for drugs like amiodarone or lithium that affect thyroid hormone synthesis; bosentan's endothelin blockade does not have a recognized thyroid toxicity profile requiring this surveillance.

preguntas.q: Epoprostenol and iloprost used to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension are synthetic analogs of which endogenous molecule?

e.correcta: Epoprostenol and iloprost are synthetic prostacyclin (PGI2) analogs that act on prostacyclin receptors to promote vasodilation and inhibit platelet aggregation, mimicking the effects of endogenous PGI2 released by vascular endothelium. This makes them useful in pulmonary arterial hypertension, where they counteract the pathologic vasoconstriction and thrombosis in the pulmonary vasculature.

incorrectas.A: Thromboxane A2 has essentially opposite effects to prostacyclin — it promotes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction — so a drug mimicking TXA2 would worsen rather than treat pulmonary hypertension.
incorrectas.C: PGE2 is involved in processes like maintaining ductus arteriosus patency, uterine contraction, and gastric mucosal protection, but it is not the prostaglandin mimicked by epoprostenol/iloprost for pulmonary hypertension therapy.
incorrectas.D: Leukotriene B4 is a potent neutrophil chemoattractant involved in inflammation, structurally and functionally unrelated to the vasodilatory, antiplatelet prostacyclin pathway targeted by these drugs.

preguntas.q: What effect do epoprostenol and iloprost have on platelet aggregation?

o.A: They have no effect on platelets

e.correcta: As prostacyclin (PGI2) analogs, epoprostenol and iloprost activate the IP receptor on platelets, raising intracellular cAMP, which inhibits platelet activation and aggregation. This antiplatelet effect complements their vasodilatory action in pulmonary arterial hypertension, helping prevent the in situ thrombosis that can occur in the remodeled pulmonary vasculature.

incorrectas.A: Concluding these drugs have no effect on platelets ignores their well-established antiplatelet action mediated through IP receptor activation and elevated intracellular cAMP in platelets.
incorrectas.B: Promoting platelet aggregation is the action of thromboxane A2, prostacyclin's physiological counterbalance; epoprostenol and iloprost work in the opposite direction by mimicking PGI2.
incorrectas.D: These drugs do not cause platelet destruction (a mechanism seen in conditions like heparin-induced thrombocytopenia or ITP) — they modulate platelet activation reversibly via receptor-mediated cAMP signaling.

preguntas.q: Epoprostenol and iloprost have what direct effect on pulmonary and systemic arterial vascular beds?

e.correcta: As prostacyclin analogs, epoprostenol and iloprost bind IP receptors on vascular smooth muscle, increasing cAMP and causing relaxation, which produces direct vasodilation in both pulmonary and systemic arterial beds. This systemic vasodilation is clinically relevant because it can cause hypotension and flushing as side effects, in addition to the therapeutic pulmonary pressure reduction.

incorrectas.A: Vasoconstriction is the effect of endothelin-1 and thromboxane A2, the pathways these drugs are meant to counteract, not the direct action of prostacyclin analogs themselves.
incorrectas.C: These drugs do have a direct, receptor-mediated smooth muscle effect (via IP receptor/cAMP signaling) — this is precisely why they are effective in pulmonary hypertension, not an indirect or absent effect.
