o.A: They are excreted into the urine unchanged
o.B: They diffuse into the tubular cell
o.C: They are actively secreted further into the lumen
o.D: They bind to luminal carbonic anhydrase and remain sequestered

e.correcta: CO2 and H2O generated in the lumen by brush-border carbonic anhydrase are small, uncharged, lipid-soluble molecules that diffuse readily across the apical membrane into the proximal tubule cell. Once inside, intracellular carbonic anhydrase reconstitutes them back into H2CO3, which dissociates into H+ (re-secreted into the lumen via the Na+-H+ exchanger) and HCO3- (transported into the blood) — completing the net reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate.

incorrectas.A: If CO2 and H2O were simply excreted rather than reabsorbed, the kidney would fail to reclaim filtered bicarbonate, leading to a bicarbonate-wasting acidosis; this contradicts the entire physiologic purpose of this luminal carbonic anhydrase step, which is to enable bicarbonate reclamation.
incorrectas.C: Secreting these products further into the lumen would move them away from the cell rather than into it, which would abolish the mechanism entirely — the whole point of converting H2CO3 to permeant CO2 and H2O is to let them enter, not exit further into, the tubular fluid.
incorrectas.D: Carbonic anhydrase is an enzyme that catalyzes the reversible hydration/dehydration reaction; it releases its products rather than binding and sequestering them, since an enzyme trapping its own products would halt further catalytic turnover.

preguntas.q: Once CO2 and H2O diffuse into early proximal tubule cells, intracellular carbonic anhydrase reforms H2CO3, which then dissociates into which two ions?

e.correcta: Inside the proximal tubule cell, cytoplasmic carbonic anhydrase catalyzes CO2 + H2O to H2CO3, which spontaneously dissociates into H+ and HCO3-. This regenerates exactly the two species needed downstream: the H+ is recycled back into the lumen via the Na+-H+ exchanger to keep driving bicarbonate reclamation, while the HCO3- exits across the basolateral membrane into the blood, completing net bicarbonate reabsorption.

incorrectas.A: Na+ and Cl- are handled by separate transport systems (the Na+-K+-ATPase and various Na+ and Cl- transporters) and are not products of carbonic acid dissociation; this ion pair belongs to a different transport pathway entirely.
incorrectas.B: K+ is recycled by the basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase and is unrelated to carbonic acid chemistry; only H+ (not K+) is the cation produced when H2CO3 dissociates in this pathway.
incorrectas.D: Cl- is reabsorbed later along the PCT via anion exchange and paracellular pathways, not generated from carbonic acid breakdown; HCO3- is correct here, but pairing it with Cl- misrepresents the dissociation reaction.

preguntas.q: The HCO3- generated inside early proximal tubule cells (from intracellular H2CO3 dissociation) crosses the basolateral membrane into the blood by which mechanism?

o.A: Primary active transport via an HCO3- ATPase
o.C: Cotransport with H+ via an antiporter
o.D: Simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer

e.correcta: HCO3- exits proximal tubule cells across the basolateral membrane via facilitated diffusion, largely through a Na+-HCO3- cotransporter (NBC1) that uses a carrier protein to move the charged bicarbonate ion down its electrochemical gradient into the blood. Because HCO3- is charged, it cannot cross the lipid bilayer unaided, so a dedicated membrane transport protein is required even though no direct ATP hydrolysis drives this particular step.

incorrectas.A: There is no dedicated HCO3- ATPase pumping bicarbonate directly using ATP hydrolysis; the energy for bicarbonate exit ultimately traces back to the Na+ gradient set up by the Na+-K+-ATPase, but the exit step itself is carrier-facilitated rather than a primary active pump.
incorrectas.C: An antiporter exchanging HCO3- for H+ describes a counter-transport mechanism, but basolateral bicarbonate exit in this pathway is not coupled to H+ movement in the opposite direction — that Cl-/base exchange dynamic is more characteristic of other epithelial transport systems.
incorrectas.D: Bicarbonate is a charged, polar ion and cannot cross the hydrophobic lipid bilayer by simple diffusion; it requires a specific membrane transport protein to move across the basolateral membrane, unlike the CO2 and H2O in earlier steps of this pathway.

preguntas.q: The H+ generated inside early proximal tubule cells (from intracellular H2CO3 dissociation) is returned to the tubular lumen by which transporter?

e.correcta: The Na+-H+ exchanger (NHE3) on the apical membrane of the early PCT secretes intracellular H+ into the lumen in exchange for luminal Na+ entering the cell. This step is essential because the secreted H+ combines with filtered HCO3- in the lumen to regenerate H2CO3, which luminal carbonic anhydrase then breaks down into CO2 and H2O — completing the cycle that allows the cell to reclaim filtered bicarbonate while simultaneously reabsorbing sodium.

incorrectas.A: H+-K+-ATPase is found in the intercalated cells of the collecting duct (and in gastric parietal cells), where it actively secretes H+ in exchange for K+ reabsorption as part of distal urinary acidification — it is not the apical transporter used in the early PCT bicarbonate reclamation pathway.
incorrectas.B: SGLT2 is the sodium-glucose cotransporter that reabsorbs filtered glucose alongside Na+ in the early PCT; it moves glucose, not H+, and is unrelated to the bicarbonate reclamation mechanism.
incorrectas.C: The Cl--formate- exchanger operates in the late PCT to help reabsorb chloride by exchanging luminal formate for chloride, a distinct transport process from apical H+ secretion in the early PCT.

preguntas.q: Na+-glucose and Na+-amino acid cotransport in the early proximal convoluted tubule generate what kind of transepithelial potential difference across the tubular cells?

o.D: A potential that oscillates with the Na+-K+-ATPase cycle

e.correcta: As Na+ enters the cell together with glucose and amino acids via cotransport, positive charge is removed from the lumen faster than accompanying anions follow, leaving the lumen relatively negative compared to the interstitium/blood side. This lumen-negative potential difference in the early PCT then provides an electrical driving force that helps pull Cl- and other anions passively into the cell or through paracellular pathways, complementing the concentration-gradient-driven reabsorption happening at the same time.

incorrectas.A: A lumen-positive potential is instead characteristic of the late proximal tubule, where preferential Cl- reabsorption (via the Cl--formate- exchanger) leaves relative negative charge in the peritubular space and positive charge behind in the lumen — the opposite electrical polarity from the early PCT.
incorrectas.C: Cotransport of Na+ with glucose and amino acids does generate a measurable transepithelial voltage; the early PCT is not electrically neutral, since the coupled movement of a cation without matched anion movement necessarily creates a charge imbalance across the epithelium.
incorrectas.D: The lumen-negative potential in the early PCT is a relatively steady feature driven by ongoing cotransport activity, not something that oscillates in phase with individual Na+-K+-ATPase pump cycles, which operate continuously to maintain the underlying Na+ gradient.

preguntas.q: In the late proximal convoluted tubule, Cl- is partially reabsorbed via which luminal membrane transporter?

e.correcta: The late PCT reabsorbs chloride in part through a Cl--formate- exchanger on the luminal membrane: chloride enters the cell in exchange for formate leaving into the lumen, where the formate then recombines with secreted H+ to form formic acid, diffuses back into the cell, and dissociates again, allowing formate to be recycled repeatedly. This mechanism, together with the parallel Na+-H+ exchanger and paracellular Cl- diffusion, allows the late PCT to complete NaCl reabsorption after the early PCT has already preferentially reabsorbed glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate.

incorrectas.A: The Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) is the major transporter of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, targeted by loop diuretics like furosemide; it is not present on the luminal membrane of the proximal tubule.
incorrectas.B: Pendrin (Cl--HCO3- exchanger) functions in the beta-intercalated cells of the collecting duct to secrete bicarbonate in exchange for chloride reabsorption during states of alkalosis, a distal nephron mechanism unrelated to late PCT chloride handling.
incorrectas.C: ENaC is an aldosterone-regulated sodium channel found in the principal cells of the collecting duct, mediating sodium reabsorption (with associated K+ or H+ secretion) far downstream of the proximal tubule, and it transports Na+ rather than Cl-.

preguntas.q: In the late proximal convoluted tubule, sodium reabsorption occurs in part through which apical transporter, working alongside the Cl--formate- exchanger?

e.correcta: In the late PCT, the Na+-H+ exchanger continues to bring Na+ into the cell (in exchange for H+ secretion) even after glucose and amino acids have already been almost completely reabsorbed in the early PCT, so SGLT-mediated Na+ entry is no longer significant here. The combined action of this Na+-H+ exchanger and the Cl--formate- exchanger effectively achieves net NaCl reabsorption, since the H+ and formate that are secreted recombine in the lumen and diffuse back into the cell to be recycled.

incorrectas.A: SGLT2-mediated Na+-glucose cotransport is essentially finished by the late PCT because nearly all filtered glucose has already been reabsorbed in the early PCT (S1 segment); it is not the mechanism responsible for late PCT sodium reabsorption.
incorrectas.B: The Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter is specific to the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, not the proximal tubule, and it moves potassium and two chloride ions alongside sodium rather than pairing with an anion exchanger the way late PCT transport does.
incorrectas.D: ENaC is a channel (not an exchanger) located in the collecting duct's principal cells, regulated by aldosterone, and it operates independently of any paired anion exchange — a very different mechanism from the coupled exchanger system of the late PCT.

preguntas.q: What is the primary driving force for NaCl reabsorption in the late proximal convoluted tubule?

o.A: A high luminal Cl- concentration gradient
o.B: Direct ATP hydrolysis by an apical Cl- ATPase

e.correcta: By the time tubular fluid reaches the late PCT, preferential early reabsorption of HCO3-, glucose, and amino acids (all faster than water) has left the remaining fluid relatively concentrated in chloride compared to plasma. This high luminal Cl- concentration gradient favors Cl- reabsorption via the Cl--formate- exchanger and paracellular diffusion through tight junctions, with Na+ following passively (via the Na+-H+ exchanger and paracellular pathways) to preserve electroneutrality — so it is the chloride gradient, not an active NaCl pump, that drives this segment's reabsorption.

incorrectas.B: There is no dedicated apical Cl- ATPase directly hydrolyzing ATP to pump chloride in the late PCT; chloride movement here is driven by its own concentration gradient and by exchange/diffusion mechanisms rather than by primary active transport of chloride itself.
incorrectas.C: Aldosterone-stimulated ENaC activity governs sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct's principal cells, a distal and hormonally regulated process entirely distinct from the concentration-gradient-driven, aldosterone-independent NaCl reabsorption of the late PCT.
incorrectas.D: ADH-mediated aquaporin insertion controls water permeability in the collecting duct in response to plasma osmolality, and has no role in driving NaCl reabsorption in the proximal tubule, which reabsorbs water passively and constitutively regardless of ADH.

preguntas.q: Cl- is partially reabsorbed by passive diffusion through which structure between cells of the late proximal convoluted tubule?

e.correcta: In the late PCT, part of chloride reabsorption occurs paracellularly — that is, Cl- diffuses down its concentration gradient through the tight junctions between adjacent tubular epithelial cells rather than passing through the cells themselves. Because Cl- movement through this route carries positive charge along with it electrostatically, Na+ follows passively through the same paracellular route, so the net effect is reabsorption of NaCl even though no transcellular NaCl cotransporter is directly involved in this particular piece of the mechanism.

incorrectas.A: The Na+-K+-ATPase is a basolateral transcellular pump that moves Na+ out of and K+ into the cell using ATP; it is not a paracellular route and does not directly transport Cl- through the space between cells.
incorrectas.B: Aquaporin-1 channels are transcellular water channels embedded in the plasma membrane of PCT cells that allow water (not chloride) to cross through the cells themselves, distinct from the paracellular tight-junction route used by Cl-.
incorrectas.C: Gap junctions connect the cytoplasm of adjacent cells to allow direct intercellular communication and small-molecule exchange, but they are not the intercellular junction responsible for paracellular solute reabsorption in the tubular epithelium — tight junctions serve that role.

preguntas.q: In the proximal tubule, does osmotic water reabsorption occur by water following solute, or by solute following water?

o.C: Water and solute are reabsorbed by fully independent, unrelated mechanisms
o.D: Neither water nor solute movement depends on the other

e.correcta: In the proximal tubule, active and secondary active transport of solutes (especially Na+, via the basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase and its many coupled apical transporters) is the primary event, and this creates an osmotic gradient across the epithelium. Water then follows passively through aquaporin channels and paracellular pathways to equalize osmolality, which is why proximal tubule reabsorption is isosmotic — the water reabsorption rate is dictated by how much solute has just been reabsorbed, not the reverse.

incorrectas.B: If solute reabsorption instead followed water, water would need its own independent driving force to move first, but the proximal tubule has no such primary water pump — water reabsorption is passive and secondary to the osmotic gradient solute transport creates, not a leading event that then drags solute along.
incorrectas.C: Describing the two processes as fully independent ignores the well-established coupling in the proximal tubule, where solute transport actively generates the osmotic gradient that water passively follows — the two processes are mechanistically linked, not separate.
incorrectas.D: Water movement in the proximal tubule is highly dependent on solute reabsorption because it is that solute movement which establishes the osmotic gradient driving water flux; claiming no dependency contradicts the basic mechanism of isosmotic reabsorption.

preguntas.q: Na+ is transported out of proximal tubule cells and into the blood primarily by which mechanism?

o.B: Simple diffusion down its concentration gradient

e.correcta: The basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase actively pumps Na+ out of the proximal tubule cell into the interstitium/blood (in exchange for K+ entering the cell), using ATP hydrolysis to maintain a low intracellular Na+ concentration. This low intracellular Na+ is the fundamental driving force for essentially every other apical sodium-coupled transporter in the nephron — without this pump running continuously, none of the secondary active transport processes (SGLT, amino acid cotransport, NHE3) could function.

incorrectas.A: SGLT2 is an apical (luminal) cotransporter that brings Na+ and glucose INTO the cell from the tubular fluid, the opposite membrane location and direction from the basolateral Na+ extrusion this question asks about.
incorrectas.B: Na+ cannot cross the basolateral membrane by simple diffusion in the direction of net reabsorption because that would require moving against significant electrochemical considerations without expending energy; extrusion requires the active, ATP-driven pump rather than passive diffusion.
incorrectas.C: The Na+-H+ exchanger (NHE3) is also an apical transporter that brings Na+ INTO the cell from the lumen (while secreting H+), not a basolateral mechanism for pumping Na+ out into the blood.

preguntas.q: Which Starling force is the major driving force for fluid reabsorption from the interstitium into the peritubular capillaries of the proximal tubule?

o.D: Low interstitial oncotic pressure alone, independent of capillary pressures

e.correcta: Blood entering the peritubular capillaries has just passed through the glomerulus, where a large volume of protein-free fluid was filtered out, concentrating plasma proteins in the blood that remains. This produces a high peritubular capillary oncotic pressure (πc), which pulls the fluid that was reabsorbed across the tubular epithelium into the interstitium onward into the capillaries — making it the dominant Starling force driving proximal tubule fluid uptake into the vasculature.

incorrectas.A: Peritubular capillary hydrostatic pressure is actually relatively low (since these capillaries lie downstream of the high-resistance efferent arteriole), and a high hydrostatic pressure would tend to push fluid OUT of the capillary rather than favor reabsorption into it.
incorrectas.C: High interstitial hydrostatic pressure would oppose, not promote, movement of fluid from the interstitium into the capillary, since fluid moves from high to low hydrostatic pressure — this works against reabsorption rather than driving it.
incorrectas.D: While interstitial oncotic pressure being low does favor capillary uptake, it is the elevated peritubular capillary oncotic pressure (from the concentrated post-filtration plasma proteins) that is specifically identified as the major driving force, not a claim that interstitial factors act in isolation from capillary pressure.

preguntas.q: How does the [TF/P]Cl ratio change as tubular fluid moves along the early portion of the proximal convoluted tubule?

o.B: It remains exactly 1.0 throughout the entire PCT
o.C: It fluctuates randomly with no consistent trend
o.D: It initially increases, then levels out in the late PCT

e.correcta: In the early PCT, water reabsorption (following preferential Na+, glucose, amino acid, and bicarbonate reabsorption) outpaces chloride reabsorption, so the chloride left behind in the shrinking volume of tubular fluid becomes progressively more concentrated relative to plasma, causing [TF/P]Cl to rise. Once tubular fluid reaches the late PCT, the high luminal Cl- gradient that has now been established becomes the driving force for its own preferential reabsorption (via the Cl--formate- exchanger and paracellular diffusion), so the ratio levels out rather than continuing to climb.

incorrectas.A: A steady decrease would mean chloride is reabsorbed faster than water from the very start of the PCT, but early on the opposite is true — glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate are prioritized for reabsorption over chloride, so [TF/P]Cl actually rises initially rather than falling.
incorrectas.B: A ratio pinned at exactly 1.0 throughout would mean chloride and water are reabsorbed in perfect lockstep for the entire PCT, but the mismatch in early reabsorption priorities (other solutes and water outpacing Cl-) causes real deviation from 1.0, particularly the initial rise described in the correct answer.
incorrectas.C: The trajectory of [TF/P]Cl follows a predictable, well-characterized physiologic pattern (initial rise, then plateau) driven by the sequence of solute reabsorption events along the PCT — it is not random or unpredictable.

preguntas.q: How does the [TF/P]inulin ratio change as tubular fluid travels along the proximal convoluted tubule?

e.correcta: Because inulin is freely filtered but never reabsorbed or secreted, its total amount in the tubular fluid stays fixed while roughly two-thirds of the filtered water is reabsorbed along the PCT. With the same amount of inulin dissolved in a steadily shrinking volume of fluid, its concentration relative to plasma climbs continuously, so [TF/P]inulin rises progressively over the length of the PCT — this property is exactly what makes inulin useful for calculating fractional water reabsorption at any point.

incorrectas.A: A progressive decrease would require inulin to be reabsorbed faster than water, but inulin is not reabsorbed at all, so there is no mechanism by which its relative concentration could fall as fluid moves down the tubule.
incorrectas.B: A constant ratio of 1.0 would require inulin and water to be reabsorbed at matched rates, but since water is reabsorbed while inulin is not touched at all, the ratio necessarily diverges from 1 rather than staying fixed.
incorrectas.D: There is no phase of the PCT in which inulin concentration would fall relative to plasma, since neither reabsorption nor secretion of inulin ever occurs; the ratio only trends in one direction — upward — reflecting cumulative water removal.

preguntas.q: How does the [TF/P]HCO3- ratio change over the course of the proximal convoluted tubule?

e.correcta: Bicarbonate reabsorption in the PCT (via the carbonic-anhydrase-dependent mechanism converting filtered HCO3- to CO2/H2O and regenerating it intracellularly) proceeds proportionately faster than water reabsorption — roughly 85% of filtered HCO3- is reclaimed compared to about 67% of filtered water. Because the solute is removed more aggressively than the water it's dissolved in, the remaining tubular fluid becomes progressively depleted of bicarbonate relative to plasma, so [TF/P]HCO3- falls as fluid travels down the PCT.

incorrectas.A: An increasing ratio would require bicarbonate to lag behind water reabsorption (as happens with chloride and inulin), but bicarbonate is actually one of the most efficiently reabsorbed solutes in the early PCT, outpacing water rather than lagging behind it.
incorrectas.C: A ratio fixed at 1.0 would require HCO3- and water to be reabsorbed at exactly matched rates, but the well-documented mismatch (85% HCO3- versus 67% water) means the ratio meaningfully diverges from 1 rather than staying constant.
incorrectas.D: There is no described phase in which [TF/P]HCO3- rises before falling; the mechanism (proportionally faster bicarbonate reclamation compared to water throughout the PCT) produces a straightforward decline, not a biphasic rise-then-fall pattern.

preguntas.q: How do the [TF/P]glucose and [TF/P]amino acid ratios change over the course of the proximal convoluted tubule?

e.correcta: Glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed almost completely (essentially 100% under normal conditions) via Na+-coupled cotransport that is concentrated in the early PCT, a reabsorption rate that considerably outpaces the roughly 67% of filtered water reabsorbed over the same stretch. Because these solutes are cleared from the tubular fluid faster than the water they were dissolved in, their concentration relative to plasma falls steadily, driving both [TF/P]glucose and [TF/P]AA toward zero by the end of the early PCT.

incorrectas.A: An increasing ratio pattern is characteristic of solutes like inulin or (initially) chloride that are reabsorbed more slowly than water; glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed faster than water via dedicated high-capacity cotransporters, producing the opposite trend.
incorrectas.B: A constant ratio of 1.0 would mean glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed at exactly the same rate as water, but their near-complete reabsorption via SGLT and amino acid transporters proceeds much faster than the 67% water reabsorption rate, so the ratio does not stay fixed.
incorrectas.D: These ratios do not plateau above 1; because reabsorption of glucose and amino acids so substantially outpaces water reabsorption, their concentration falls well below plasma levels (toward a ratio near zero) rather than settling above the starting ratio of 1.

preguntas.q: What is the major regulatory mechanism that keeps the fractional reabsorption of water and solute constant in the proximal tubule despite fluctuations in GFR?

e.correcta: Glomerulotubular balance describes the intrinsic ability of the proximal tubule to adjust its rate of solute and water reabsorption in proportion to changes in the filtered load, so that if GFR spontaneously rises, the PCT reabsorbs a proportionally greater amount of filtered water and solute rather than dumping the excess downstream. Because the proximal tubule is the predominant site of nephron water reabsorption, this local mechanism (driven partly by the resulting change in peritubular capillary oncotic and hydrostatic pressures) keeps fractional reabsorption relatively constant and prevents large swings in distal delivery from minor GFR fluctuations.

incorrectas.A: Tubuloglomerular feedback is a distinct mechanism in which the macula densa senses NaCl delivery to the distal tubule and adjusts afferent arteriolar tone to regulate GFR itself, rather than adjusting proximal tubule reabsorption rates in response to a given filtered load.
incorrectas.B: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system is a hormonal cascade that regulates systemic sodium and volume balance over a longer time frame, acting mainly on the collecting duct and distal segments, not the moment-to-moment intrinsic reabsorptive adjustment that defines glomerulotubular balance in the PCT.
incorrectas.D: ADH-mediated aquaporin insertion regulates water permeability specifically in the collecting duct in response to plasma osmolality, an entirely different regulatory axis from the constitutive, GFR-matched reabsorption occurring in the proximal tubule.

preguntas.q: Glomerulotubular balance describes a matching between filtration in the glomerulus and reabsorption in which nephron segment?

e.correcta: Glomerulotubular balance is the phenomenon by which the proximal tubule adjusts its fractional reabsorption of Na+ and water to match changes in GFR, keeping the fraction of filtrate reabsorbed roughly constant despite fluctuations in filtered load. The mechanism is driven by peritubular capillary Starling forces: an increased GFR raises the filtration fraction, which concentrates protein in the efferent arteriolar blood, raising peritubular capillary oncotic pressure (πC) and pulling more fluid into the peritubular capillaries from the proximal tubule. This protects against wide swings in distal Na+ and water delivery whenever GFR changes transiently.

incorrectas.B: The thin descending limb is passively permeable to water and concentrates tubular fluid as it descends into the hypertonic medulla, but it is not the segment classically paired with the glomerulus in glomerulotubular balance, which specifically refers to proximal reabsorption tracking filtration.
incorrectas.C: The thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs Na+, K+, and Cl- via the NKCC2 cotransporter and dilutes the tubular fluid, but its reabsorption is regulated by luminal Na+ delivery (load-dependence) rather than being the site of the classic glomerulotubular balance relationship with GFR.
incorrectas.D: The collecting duct is the site of aldosterone- and ADH-regulated fine-tuning of Na+ and water reabsorption, occurring far downstream of the glomerulus; it is not the segment described by glomerulotubular balance, which centers on the proximal tubule's response to filtered load.

preguntas.q: Which component of tubular fluid is sensed by the macula densa cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus?

e.correcta: The macula densa cells, located in the thick ascending limb where it contacts the afferent arteriole, sense the concentration of Na+ and Cl- (via the NKCC2 transporter) in the tubular fluid delivered from upstream segments. When NaCl delivery is high (as with increased GFR), the macula densa signals the afferent arteriole to constrict, reducing GFR back toward normal — the core mechanism of tubuloglomerular feedback. This same signal also modulates renin release from adjacent juxtaglomerular cells: low NaCl delivery stimulates renin secretion.

incorrectas.A: Glucose is not sensed by the macula densa; it is almost completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule via SGLT2 and SGLT1 transporters well before fluid reaches the thick ascending limb, so it plays no role in tubuloglomerular feedback signaling.
incorrectas.C: Urea concentration is important for the countercurrent multiplication system and medullary concentrating ability, but it is not the signal the macula densa uses to regulate afferent arteriolar tone or renin release.
incorrectas.D: K+ is reabsorbed alongside Na+ and Cl- via NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, but the macula densa's feedback mechanism is specifically tuned to NaCl concentration, not K+, as the sensed variable driving tubuloglomerular feedback.

preguntas.q: As tubular fluid travels down the thin descending limb of the loop of Henle, what happens to its osmolarity?

e.correcta: The thin descending limb is highly permeable to water but relatively impermeable to solutes, so as tubular fluid descends deeper into the increasingly hypertonic medullary interstitium, water passively leaves the tubule by osmosis while solute stays behind. This progressively concentrates the luminal fluid, making it maximally hyperosmotic at the tip of the loop (in juxtamedullary nephrons with long loops) — the key first step in generating the medullary osmotic gradient used later for urine concentration.

incorrectas.A: Fluid entering the loop from the proximal tubule is roughly isosmotic to plasma, but this changes as it descends — the whole point of the descending limb's water permeability is to allow equilibration with an increasingly concentrated interstitium, not to preserve isosmolarity.
incorrectas.C: Hyposmotic dilution of tubular fluid is what happens in the thick ascending limb and early DCT, which actively pump out solute without allowing water to follow — the opposite process and location from the descending limb.
incorrectas.D: The osmolarity change along the descending limb is a smooth, predictable, and physiologically essential gradient (increasing toward the papilla), not random fluctuation, and it directly reflects the corticomedullary osmotic gradient established by the countercurrent multiplier.

preguntas.q: Water reabsorption across the thin descending limb of the loop of Henle occurs by which mechanism?

o.A: Passive movement down an osmotic gradient
o.B: Active transport via aquaporin-driven ATPase pumps
o.C: Secondary active transport coupled to Na+

e.correcta: The thin descending limb expresses aquaporin-1 water channels constitutively, making it freely and passively permeable to water. Water simply follows the osmotic gradient set up by the hypertonic medullary interstitium, moving out of the tubule into the interstitium without any energy expenditure by the cell — this is why the segment is sometimes described as being 'along for the ride' of the countercurrent multiplier rather than actively driving it.

incorrectas.B: There is no such thing as an ATPase pump that actively transports water; aquaporins are simple channels that allow water to move passively down its concentration gradient, and no ATP is consumed to move water itself across this segment.
incorrectas.C: Secondary active transport describes solute movement (like Na+-glucose or Na+-Cl- cotransport) powered indirectly by the Na+-K+-ATPase gradient, not water movement — water transport in the descending limb is purely passive osmosis, unlinked to any solute cotransporter.
incorrectas.D: Facilitated diffusion coupled to glucose describes SGLT-mediated glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule, an entirely different segment and process; the descending limb has no glucose transporters and reabsorbs only water passively.

preguntas.q: As tubular fluid travels up the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, what happens to its osmolarity?

o.C: It remains unchanged from the loop tip
o.D: It matches the surrounding medullary interstitium

e.correcta: The thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs Na+, K+, and Cl- via the NKCC2 cotransporter but is impermeable to water, so solute leaves the tubule while water stays behind. This progressively dilutes the luminal fluid, making it hyposmotic by the time it reaches the early distal tubule — which is why this segment is called the 'diluting segment' and is essential for both diluting urine and building the medullary concentration gradient that surrounds it.

incorrectas.A: Progressive hyperosmolarity is what occurs in the descending limb, where water leaves passively as fluid descends into the hypertonic medulla; the ascending limb does the opposite by pumping out solute while retaining water.
incorrectas.C: The osmolarity changes substantially across the ascending limb precisely because of active NaCl reabsorption without water reabsorption — it does not remain static, and this dilution is a defining physiologic feature of the segment.
incorrectas.D: Because the thick ascending limb is water-impermeable, luminal fluid does NOT equilibrate with the surrounding interstitium the way it does in the water-permeable descending limb; instead a dissociation develops between tubular fluid (increasingly dilute) and interstitium (increasingly concentrated).

preguntas.q: Na+ reabsorption across the thin ascending limb of the loop of Henle occurs by which mechanism?

o.A: Passive diffusion down its electrochemical gradient

e.correcta: The thin ascending limb, unlike its thick counterpart, lacks the energy-dependent NKCC2 machinery and instead reabsorbs Na+ passively, driven by the favorable electrochemical gradient created as the fluid emerges from the concentrated tip of the loop into the less concentrated cortex. Because the interstitium here is less concentrated than the luminal fluid (which was just maximally concentrated in the descending limb), NaCl diffuses passively out of the lumen without requiring ATP.

incorrectas.B: The Na+-K+-ATPase is the basolateral pump that extrudes Na+ from tubular cells into blood in most active-transport segments (like the thick ascending limb and DCT), but the thin ascending limb reabsorbs Na+ passively and does not rely on this active pump for its main transport.
incorrectas.C: NKCC2-mediated secondary active transport is characteristic of the thick ascending limb, which has the metabolic machinery and channel density to actively pump Na+-K+-2Cl-; the thin ascending limb lacks this transporter and instead uses passive diffusion.
incorrectas.D: SGLT2-mediated Na+-glucose cotransport occurs in the early proximal convoluted tubule, an entirely different nephron segment; the thin ascending limb has no meaningful glucose transport and reabsorbs Na+ passively, unrelated to glucose.

preguntas.q: Na+ reabsorption across the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle occurs by which mechanism?

o.A: Passive diffusion down its electrochemical gradient
o.B: Simple osmosis coupled to water flow

e.correcta: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs Na+ via active transport: the luminal Na+-K+-2Cl- (NKCC2) cotransporter brings Na+ into the cell using the energy stored in the Na+ gradient (making it secondary active transport), and that gradient itself is generated by the basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase pumping Na+ out of the cell using ATP. Because the whole process is ultimately powered by ATP hydrolysis, the segment is classified as actively — not passively — reabsorbing Na+, distinguishing it from the passive uptake seen in the thin ascending limb.

incorrectas.A: Passive diffusion down an electrochemical gradient describes the thin ascending limb, which lacks the NKCC2 transporter and basolateral pump machinery found in the thick ascending limb; the thick segment instead relies on active, energy-consuming transport.
incorrectas.B: The thick ascending limb is impermeable to water, so there is no significant water flow across this segment to couple with Na+ movement — this is precisely why the tubular fluid becomes dilute here rather than remaining isosmotic.
incorrectas.D: Facilitated diffusion via uniporters implies passive, single-solute channel-mediated movement down a concentration gradient with no coupling to another ion; the thick ascending limb instead uses the NKCC2 symporter, which cotransports Na+, K+, and 2 Cl- together and is powered indirectly by ATP.

preguntas.q: Approximately what percentage of filtered Na+ is normally reabsorbed by the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle?

e.correcta: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs roughly 10-20% of filtered Na+ via the NKCC2 cotransporter, making it the second major site of Na+ reabsorption after the proximal tubule. This is clinically important because loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide) act here by blocking NKCC2, and because this segment's substantial reabsorptive capacity means blocking it produces a much more potent diuresis than blocking downstream segments that handle a smaller fraction of the filtered load.

incorrectas.A: 65-70% of filtered Na+ is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule, the site of bulk isosmotic reabsorption, which is a much larger fraction than what the thick ascending limb handles.
incorrectas.B: 40-50% does not correspond to any single nephron segment's typical Na+ reabsorption in standard physiology teaching; it overstates the thick ascending limb's actual contribution, which is closer to 10-20%.
incorrectas.D: 3-5% is the amount reabsorbed by the late distal tubule and collecting duct, the fine-tuning segments regulated by aldosterone — a much smaller contribution than the thick ascending limb's 10-20%.

preguntas.q: The Na+ reabsorption mechanism of the thick ascending limb shows which characteristic, explaining why proximal-acting diuretics like acetazolamide cause only mild diuresis?

e.correcta: The thick ascending limb's Na+ reabsorption is load-dependent: the more Na+ delivered to it, the more it reabsorbs, up to its transport capacity. This is why inhibiting proximal Na+ reabsorption with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor like acetazolamide produces only mild diuresis — the extra Na+ that escapes proximal reabsorption is largely picked up by the thick ascending limb downstream, blunting the net natriuretic effect. This principle underlies why loop diuretics acting directly on the thick ascending limb are far more potent than proximal-acting agents.

incorrectas.A: Flow-independence would mean the segment reabsorbs a fixed amount of Na+ regardless of how much is delivered to it; the thick ascending limb does the opposite, ramping reabsorption up or down with delivered load, which is exactly why bypassing the proximal tubule doesn't produce a large natriuresis.
incorrectas.C: Aldosterone-dependence describes the late distal tubule and collecting duct, where aldosterone upregulates ENaC and Na+-K+-ATPase in principal cells; the thick ascending limb's NKCC2-mediated transport is regulated mainly by delivered Na+ load, not by aldosterone.
incorrectas.D: ADH-dependence describes water permeability of the collecting duct (via aquaporin-2 insertion), not Na+ transport in the thick ascending limb, which is water-impermeable and whose Na+ handling is governed by luminal delivery, not ADH.

preguntas.q: In addition to Na+, which two other ions are reabsorbed via the luminal cotransporter of the thick ascending limb?

e.correcta: The luminal Na+-K+-2Cl- (NKCC2) cotransporter in the thick ascending limb moves one Na+, one K+, and two Cl- ions together into the cell, using the energy of the Na+ gradient to drive uphill transport of K+ and Cl-. This transporter is the molecular target of loop diuretics, and its disruption (genetically, in Bartter syndrome, or pharmacologically) causes a salt-wasting picture resembling chronic loop diuretic use, including hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis.

incorrectas.A: Ca2+ and Mg2+ are indeed reabsorbed in the thick ascending limb, but paracellularly (through the lumen-positive potential generated by K+ backleak), not through the luminal NKCC2 cotransporter itself, which specifically carries Na+, K+, and Cl-.
incorrectas.B: H+ and HCO3- handling is characteristic of the proximal convoluted tubule (via the Na+-H+ exchanger and carbonic anhydrase) and the intercalated cells of the collecting duct, not the NKCC2 transporter of the thick ascending limb.
incorrectas.D: Ca2+ is reabsorbed paracellularly in this segment rather than through NKCC2, and pairing it with Cl- misrepresents the actual 1:1:2 stoichiometry of Na+:K+:Cl- carried by the cotransporter.

preguntas.q: What type of transport mechanism is the Na+-K+-2Cl- (NKCC2) cotransporter in the thick ascending limb?

e.correcta: NKCC2 is a secondary active transporter: it does not hydrolyze ATP directly, but instead harnesses the electrochemical Na+ gradient (established by the basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase, which does consume ATP) to move Na+, K+, and Cl- together into the cell against their individual gradients. This indirect coupling to ATP-dependent energy is the hallmark of secondary active transport, distinguishing it from pumps that directly split ATP.

incorrectas.A: Primary active transport describes pumps like the Na+-K+-ATPase itself, which directly hydrolyzes ATP to move ions against their gradient; NKCC2 does not hydrolyze ATP itself, so it does not qualify as primary active transport.
incorrectas.C: Simple diffusion is passive, unassisted movement down a concentration gradient with no protein carrier or energy input; NKCC2 requires a specific transporter protein and moves ions (K+ and Cl-) against their gradients, which simple diffusion cannot do.
incorrectas.D: Facilitated diffusion is passive, carrier-mediated movement strictly down a concentration gradient; NKCC2 moves K+ and Cl- uphill against their gradients by coupling to the downhill Na+ gradient, which requires energy input (indirectly from ATP) rather than being purely passive.

preguntas.q: In the thick ascending limb, Na+ is extruded from the cell into the blood by which transporter?

e.correcta: The basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase actively pumps Na+ out of the thick ascending limb cell into the blood (in exchange for K+ moving into the cell), maintaining a low intracellular Na+ concentration. This low intracellular Na+ is what creates the favorable gradient that drives luminal NKCC2 to bring Na+ (along with K+ and Cl-) into the cell from the tubular fluid — making the basolateral pump the ultimate energy source for the entire reabsorptive process in this segment.

incorrectas.A: The Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) is located on the luminal (apical) membrane and brings Na+ INTO the cell from the tubular fluid; it does not extrude Na+ into the blood, which is the job of the basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase.
incorrectas.C: The Na+-H+ exchanger (NHE3) is the luminal transporter of the proximal convoluted tubule that reabsorbs Na+ in exchange for secreting H+; it is not the mechanism by which the thick ascending limb extrudes Na+ into the blood.
incorrectas.D: The Na+-Ca2+ exchanger is used in tissues like the DCT and cardiac myocytes to handle calcium transport coupled to the Na+ gradient; it is not the basolateral Na+ extrusion mechanism of the thick ascending limb, which relies on the Na+-K+-ATPase.

preguntas.q: In the thick ascending limb, Cl- is extruded from the cell into the blood by which mechanism?

o.C: Diffusion down its electrochemical gradient via membrane channels
o.D: Primary active transport via a Cl- ATPase

e.correcta: Once Cl- enters the thick ascending limb cell via the luminal NKCC2 cotransporter, intracellular Cl- concentration rises above equilibrium, creating a favorable electrochemical gradient for it to exit passively across the basolateral membrane through Cl- channels (and Cl- -K+ cotransporters), requiring no additional direct energy input at that step. This basolateral exit is essential to prevent intracellular Cl- accumulation, which would otherwise stall the luminal NKCC2 transporter.

incorrectas.A: The Na+-K+-ATPase is specific for pumping Na+ out and K+ in; it does not transport Cl- and is not the mechanism by which Cl- crosses the basolateral membrane in this segment.
incorrectas.B: While some basolateral Cl- exit does occur via K+-Cl- cotransport, the classically taught primary basolateral Cl- exit pathway is passive diffusion through Cl- channels down its electrochemical gradient, not an energy-requiring secondary active cotransport step.
incorrectas.D: There is no known Cl- ATPase pump in human renal tubular cells; Cl- transport in this context is accomplished through passive channels and coupled transporters, not through direct ATP hydrolysis dedicated to Cl- movement.

preguntas.q: In the thick ascending limb, K+ is extruded from the cell into the blood by which mechanism?

o.A: Diffusion down its electrochemical gradient via membrane channels

e.correcta: K+ that enters the thick ascending limb cell (both via the basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase and via the luminal NKCC2 cotransporter) exits the basolateral membrane passively through K+ channels, moving down its electrochemical gradient into the blood. This basolateral K+ recycling, together with luminal K+ backleak through ROMK channels, generates the lumen-positive potential that drives paracellular reabsorption of Ca2+ and Mg2+ in this segment.

incorrectas.B: The Na+-K+-ATPase actually brings K+ INTO the cell (in exchange for Na+ leaving) rather than extruding it into the blood; basolateral K+ exit into the blood occurs separately through passive K+ channels, not through this pump.
incorrectas.C: K+-Cl- symport does exist as a basolateral exit pathway for Cl-, but it is not an ATP-hydrolyzing process — it is powered by the ion gradients themselves, and the classic route for K+ exit into blood is simple channel-mediated diffusion, not an ATP-dependent symporter.
incorrectas.D: There is no basolateral K+-H+ coupled active secretion mechanism in the thick ascending limb; H+ secretion coupled to Na+ reabsorption is a proximal tubule and intercalated cell phenomenon, unrelated to basolateral K+ handling here.

preguntas.q: Passage of tubular fluid through the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle results in what net change to the fluid, giving this segment its nickname?

e.correcta: Because the thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs Na+, K+, and Cl- via NKCC2 while remaining impermeable to water, solute leaves the tubular fluid without a proportional loss of water, progressively diluting the fluid. This is why the segment is called the 'diluting segment' — by the time fluid reaches the early distal tubule, its osmolarity is below that of plasma, setting the stage for either further dilution (if ADH is absent) or later reconcentration in the collecting duct (if ADH is present).

incorrectas.A: Concentration of tubular fluid occurs in the descending limb, where water — not solute — moves out passively into the hypertonic interstitium; the thick ascending limb does the reverse by removing solute while retaining water.
incorrectas.C: Acidification of tubular fluid (H+ secretion) is primarily a proximal tubule and intercalated cell function tied to bicarbonate reabsorption and titratable acid excretion, not a defining feature of the thick ascending limb's NaCl transport.
incorrectas.D: Alkalinization is not the characteristic effect of thick ascending limb transport; the segment's hallmark function relates to osmolarity (dilution) via solute reabsorption, not to acid-base changes in the luminal fluid.

preguntas.q: After tubular fluid passes through the thick ascending limb, how do the [TF/P]Na and [TF/P]osmolarity ratios compare to 1.0?

o.D: [TF/P]Na is greater than 1.0 while [TF/P]osmolarity is less than 1.0

e.correcta: Both the tubular fluid-to-plasma (TF/P) ratios for Na+ and osmolarity fall below 1.0 after the thick ascending limb because this segment actively reabsorbs solute (Na+, K+, Cl-) without allowing water to follow, due to its water-impermeability. The result is tubular fluid that is both hyponatremic and hyposmotic relative to plasma at this point in the nephron — a direct consequence of solute reabsorption occurring in the absence of matched water reabsorption.

incorrectas.A: Ratios greater than 1.0 would indicate the fluid is more concentrated than plasma, which is what's seen in the descending limb (where water is reabsorbed without solute) or later in the collecting duct under ADH — not after the diluting thick ascending limb.
incorrectas.C: A ratio of exactly 1.0 would mean the fluid is isosmotic to plasma, as it typically is at the end of the proximal tubule; the thick ascending limb specifically breaks this equality by reabsorbing solute without water, driving the ratio below 1.0.
incorrectas.D: Both Na+ and osmolarity ratios move in the same direction (both fall below 1.0) because Na+ is the major osmotically active solute being reabsorbed here — there is no physiologic mechanism that would decouple these two ratios in opposite directions at this segment.

preguntas.q: Approximately what percentage of filtered Na+ is normally reabsorbed by the early distal convoluted tubule?

e.correcta: The early distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs approximately 5% of filtered Na+ via the Na+-Cl- cotransporter (NCC), making it a relatively minor but clinically important site — it is the target of thiazide diuretics. Because it handles a smaller fraction of filtered Na+ than the proximal tubule or thick ascending limb, thiazides produce a milder diuresis than loop diuretics, but they remain useful for chronic blood pressure control and for reducing urinary Ca2+ excretion.

incorrectas.A: 65-70% is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule, the major bulk-reabsorption segment; the early DCT handles a much smaller fraction downstream.
incorrectas.B: 10-20% corresponds to the thick ascending limb's contribution via NKCC2; the early DCT, working through a different transporter (NCC) further downstream, reabsorbs substantially less.
incorrectas.D: 1-2% underestimates the early DCT's contribution; while it is a relatively small percentage compared to earlier segments, teaching sources place it closer to 5% of filtered Na+.

preguntas.q: In addition to Na+, which other ion is reabsorbed via the luminal cotransporter of the early distal convoluted tubule?

e.correcta: The early distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs Na+ together with Cl- through the luminal Na+-Cl- cotransporter (NCC), which is the molecular target of thiazide diuretics. Unlike the thick ascending limb's NKCC2, this transporter carries only two ions (Na+ and Cl-) in a 1:1 ratio, and it does not carry K+, which distinguishes its pharmacology and electrolyte effects from loop diuretics.

incorrectas.A: K+ is not co-transported with Na+ at the early DCT's luminal membrane; K+ handling here occurs indirectly (e.g., thiazide use leads to increased distal K+ secretion downstream), but the actual luminal cotransporter carries only Na+ and Cl-, unlike the thick ascending limb's NKCC2.
incorrectas.C: Ca2+ reabsorption in the early DCT occurs through a separate apical Ca2+ channel (TRPV5) regulated by parathyroid hormone, not through the same cotransporter that reabsorbs Na+ and Cl-; thiazides actually enhance Ca2+ reabsorption indirectly, but Ca2+ is not part of the NCC cotransporter itself.
incorrectas.D: HCO3- reabsorption is predominantly a proximal tubule function driven by carbonic anhydrase and the Na+-H+ exchanger; it is not carried by the Na+-Cl- cotransporter of the early distal tubule.

preguntas.q: In the early distal convoluted tubule, Na+ is extruded from the cell into the blood by which transporter?

e.correcta: As in essentially every Na+-reabsorbing segment of the nephron, the basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase in the early DCT actively pumps Na+ out of the cell into the blood, maintaining the low intracellular Na+ concentration that creates the driving force for the luminal Na+-Cl- cotransporter (NCC) to bring Na+ into the cell from the tubular fluid. This pump is therefore the ultimate energy source powering thiazide-sensitive Na+ reabsorption at this site.

incorrectas.A: The Na+-Cl- cotransporter sits on the luminal (apical) membrane and brings Na+ INTO the cell from the tubular fluid; it is the target of thiazide diuretics but is not the basolateral mechanism for extruding Na+ into the blood.
incorrectas.C: ENaC is the luminal Na+ channel found in the late distal tubule and collecting duct principal cells (regulated by aldosterone), not in the early DCT, and even where present, it mediates Na+ entry into cells, not basolateral extrusion into blood.
incorrectas.D: The Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter is the luminal transporter of the thick ascending limb, an upstream segment with a different transport profile; it is not present in the early DCT and does not extrude Na+ into the blood in any segment.

preguntas.q: In the early distal convoluted tubule, Cl- is extruded from the cell into the blood by which mechanism?

o.B: Active transport via a Cl- ATPase
o.C: Diffusion down its electrochemical gradient via membrane channels

e.correcta: After entering the early DCT cell via the luminal Na+-Cl- cotransporter, Cl- accumulates intracellularly above its electrochemical equilibrium and then exits passively across the basolateral membrane through Cl- channels, moving down its gradient into the blood without requiring direct additional energy input. This passive basolateral exit step is necessary to keep intracellular Cl- from building up and stalling continued luminal NCC-mediated uptake.

incorrectas.A: The Na+-K+-ATPase moves Na+ and K+, not Cl-; it indirectly supports Cl- reabsorption by maintaining the Na+ gradient that drives luminal NCC uptake, but it does not itself transport Cl- across the basolateral membrane.
incorrectas.B: There is no dedicated Cl- ATPase in renal tubular cells; basolateral Cl- exit in this segment is accomplished by passive movement through channels, not by a primary active transport pump specific to chloride.
incorrectas.D: Cl--HCO3- exchange (via pendrin or AE1) is a mechanism used in intercalated cells of the collecting duct for acid-base handling, not in the early DCT, where basolateral Cl- exit occurs through simple passive channels.

preguntas.q: Passage of tubular fluid through the early distal convoluted tubule results in what net change to the fluid, earning it the nickname 'cortical diluting segment'?

e.correcta: Like the thick ascending limb, the early DCT reabsorbs solute (Na+ and Cl- via NCC) while remaining impermeable to water, so tubular fluid becomes progressively more dilute as it passes through. Because this segment is located in the renal cortex (unlike the medullary thick ascending limb), it is specifically called the 'cortical diluting segment,' and continued dilution here is why urine can become maximally dilute distal to this point when ADH is absent.

incorrectas.A: Concentration would require water reabsorption without proportional solute loss, which is what happens in the descending limb or ADH-responsive collecting duct — the opposite of what occurs in the water-impermeable early DCT.
incorrectas.B: Acidification of tubular fluid is a proximal tubule and intercalated-cell-driven acid-base process tied to H+ secretion and bicarbonate handling, not the defining transport activity of the early DCT, whose hallmark is NaCl reabsorption causing dilution.
incorrectas.D: Osmolarity does change substantially in the early DCT — that's precisely why it earns the 'diluting segment' name; claiming no change ignores the active NaCl reabsorption occurring without accompanying water movement.

preguntas.q: What are the two main cell types found in the late distal tubule and collecting duct?

o.C: Juxtaglomerular cells and macula densa cells
o.D: Proximal tubule cells and Henle's loop cells

e.correcta: The late distal tubule and collecting duct contain two principal functional cell types: principal cells, which reabsorb Na+ (via ENaC) and water (via ADH-regulated aquaporin-2) while secreting K+, and α-intercalated cells, which secrete H+ via an H+-ATPase to acidify the urine and regenerate bicarbonate (a third type, β-intercalated cells, secretes bicarbonate in the opposite direction during alkalosis). This division of labor lets the same tubular segment simultaneously fine-tune volume/electrolyte balance (principal cells) and acid-base balance (intercalated cells).

incorrectas.A: Podocytes and mesangial cells are structural components of the glomerulus involved in filtration and are not present in the late distal tubule or collecting duct, which are downstream tubular segments with entirely different cell populations.
incorrectas.C: Juxtaglomerular cells (renin-secreting) and macula densa cells are part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus located where the thick ascending limb meets the glomerular afferent arteriole, an anatomically distinct site from the late distal tubule/collecting duct.
incorrectas.D: Proximal tubule cells and loop of Henle cells belong to entirely different, more upstream nephron segments with different transport machinery (bulk isosmotic reabsorption and countercurrent multiplication, respectively), not the late distal tubule/collecting duct.

preguntas.q: Approximately what percentage of filtered Na+ is normally reabsorbed by the late distal convoluted tubule and collecting ducts?

e.correcta: The late distal tubule and collecting ducts reabsorb only about 3% of filtered Na+, the smallest fraction of the major nephron segments, via ENaC channels in principal cells. Despite handling a small percentage, this segment is the final and most tightly regulated site of Na+ reabsorption, controlled by aldosterone, which is why it is the target of potassium-sparing diuretics and the physiologic 'last word' on Na+ and volume balance.

incorrectas.A: 65-70% is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule via bulk isosmotic transport, vastly more than the late distal tubule/collecting duct's fine-tuning role of about 3%.
incorrectas.B: 10-20% is the contribution of the thick ascending limb via NKCC2, a much larger fraction than what the late distal tubule and collecting ducts handle downstream.
incorrectas.C: 5% corresponds to the early distal convoluted tubule's NCC-mediated reabsorption; the late distal tubule/collecting duct handles an even smaller final fraction, around 3%.

preguntas.q: In principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct, Na+ is reabsorbed across the luminal membrane through which channel?

e.correcta: Principal cells reabsorb Na+ across their luminal membrane through the epithelial Na+ channel (ENaC), a channel (not a cotransporter) that allows Na+ to move passively into the cell down its electrochemical gradient. ENaC activity is upregulated by aldosterone, which increases channel number and open probability, making this the final hormonally tunable step of renal Na+ reabsorption — and the reason ENaC is the target of amiloride and triamterene (potassium-sparing diuretics) as well as the site of gain-of-function mutations in Liddle syndrome.

incorrectas.A: The Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) is located in the luminal membrane of the thick ascending limb, an upstream segment; it is not present in principal cells of the late distal tubule/collecting duct, which use ENaC instead.
incorrectas.B: The Na+-Cl- cotransporter (NCC) is found in the early distal convoluted tubule, the segment just proximal to the late DCT/collecting duct; principal cells further downstream use the simpler ENaC channel rather than a coupled cotransporter.
incorrectas.D: SGLT-mediated Na+-glucose cotransport occurs in the early proximal convoluted tubule, reclaiming filtered glucose; there is no meaningful glucose remaining in tubular fluid by the late distal tubule, and principal cells do not use this transporter.

preguntas.q: In the principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct, Na+ is extruded into the blood by which mechanism?

e.correcta: As in other Na+-reabsorbing nephron segments, the basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase in principal cells actively pumps Na+ out of the cell into the blood while bringing K+ into the cell, maintaining the low intracellular Na+ that drives passive Na+ entry through luminal ENaC. This same pump activity also supplies the intracellular K+ that principal cells subsequently secrete into the tubular lumen through ROMK channels — linking Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion mechanistically, which is why aldosterone (which upregulates this whole system) simultaneously promotes Na+ retention and K+ wasting.

incorrectas.A: ENaC is the luminal channel that lets Na+ enter the principal cell passively from the tubular fluid; it does not extrude Na+ into the blood, which is the basolateral pump's job.
incorrectas.C: The Na+-Cl- cotransporter is found in the luminal membrane of the early distal convoluted tubule, an upstream segment; it is not present in principal cells and does not mediate basolateral Na+ extrusion anywhere in the nephron.
incorrectas.D: The Na+-H+ exchanger (NHE3) is the luminal transporter of the proximal tubule that reabsorbs Na+ while secreting H+; it is unrelated to basolateral Na+ handling in the late distal tubule/collecting duct, which relies on the Na+-K+-ATPase.

preguntas.q: Aldosterone acting on principal cells of the collecting duct has what effect on epithelial Na+ channel (ENaC) activity?

e.correcta: Aldosterone binds a cytoplasmic mineralocorticoid receptor in principal cells, translocates to the nucleus, and upregulates transcription of ENaC subunits and Na+-K+ ATPase, increasing ENaC activity at the apical membrane. This drives more Na+ reabsorption from the tubular lumen into the cell, which is the first step in a cascade that also promotes K+ and H+ secretion, making aldosterone central to both volume and potassium homeostasis.

incorrectas.A: Aldosterone is a genomic-acting steroid hormone whose entire physiologic purpose in the collecting duct is to change ENaC expression, so "no change" ignores its defining mechanism of action.
incorrectas.B: A decrease would be the effect of mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like spironolactone, which block aldosterone's action, but aldosterone itself does the opposite by upregulating ENaC.
incorrectas.D: Aldosterone's genomic effect is a sustained increase in channel number and activity over hours, not a biphasic response; there is no described phase where aldosterone transiently suppresses ENaC before increasing it.

preguntas.q: In principal cells, aldosterone-driven increases in ENaC activity produce what change in the electrical charge of the tubular lumen?

o.D: Lumen becomes isoelectric with the cell interior

e.correcta: ENaC allows Na+ (a cation) to move out of the lumen into the principal cell without a matched anion following it, so removing positive charge from the lumen makes it relatively more electronegative. This increased lumen negativity is exactly what creates the favorable electrochemical gradient that drives K+ secretion through ROMK channels on the same principal cells, linking Na+ reabsorption to K+ handling.

incorrectas.B: Positivity would result if a cation were being added to the lumen or an anion removed, but ENaC does the opposite — it removes Na+ (a cation) from the lumen, so the lumen becomes more negative, not more positive.
incorrectas.C: A "no change" answer would only apply if Na+ movement were electroneutral (paired with an anion), but ENaC-mediated Na+ transport is electrogenic, so it does change the transepithelial voltage.
incorrectas.D: The lumen does not equilibrate with the cell interior; a persistent negative luminal potential is maintained precisely because ENaC keeps removing Na+ faster than anions follow, sustaining the driving force for K+ secretion.

preguntas.q: The increased lumen negativity generated by ENaC-mediated Na+ reabsorption in principal cells promotes secretion of which ion?

e.correcta: As ENaC pulls Na+ out of the lumen, the lumen becomes electronegative relative to the principal cell interior, creating a favorable electrochemical gradient for the efflux of K+ through apical ROMK channels. This coupling explains why conditions of high aldosterone (or drugs that mimic increased ENaC activity) cause kaliuresis and predispose to hypokalemia, while blocking ENaC (as with amiloride) causes K+ retention.

incorrectas.A: Ca2+ reabsorption in the distal nephron is regulated mainly by PTH and TRPV5 channels, not by the lumen-negative voltage generated by ENaC, so this electrical gradient is not the principal driver of calcium handling here.
incorrectas.B: H+ secretion in the collecting duct occurs via H+-ATPase in intercalated cells and is influenced by aldosterone independently, but the specific electrochemical gradient created by ENaC in principal cells is classically linked to K+ secretion, the topic of this pathway.
incorrectas.D: Cl- movement in this segment tends to follow Na+ paracellularly in other nephron segments, but in the principal cell/ENaC system the lumen-negative potential favors secretion of a cation (K+) into the lumen, not further anion movement out of it.

preguntas.q: Amiloride, spironolactone, and triamterene share a mechanism that inhibits Na+ reabsorption in the principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct. What class of diuretics are these?

e.correcta: K+-sparing diuretics reduce Na+ reabsorption in principal cells either by directly blocking ENaC (amiloride, triamterene) or by antagonizing the aldosterone receptor that upregulates ENaC (spironolactone, eplerenone). Because less Na+ enters the cell through ENaC, the lumen-negative potential that normally drives K+ secretion is blunted, so these diuretics cause a mild natriuresis while sparing K+ — the opposite kaliuresis effect seen with loop or thiazide diuretics.

incorrectas.A: Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) inhibit the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, a completely different nephron segment and transporter, and they cause K+ wasting rather than sparing it.
incorrectas.B: Thiazide diuretics block the Na+-Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, upstream of the principal cells, and like loop diuretics they increase distal Na+ delivery and promote K+ secretion rather than sparing K+.
incorrectas.D: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., acetazolamide) act in the proximal tubule by blocking bicarbonate reabsorption, unrelated to ENaC or aldosterone signaling in principal cells, and they also tend to cause K+ wasting.

preguntas.q: In response to an increase in Na+ intake and ECF volume, what happens to renal sympathetic nerve activity as part of the physiologic response promoting natriuresis?

e.correcta: Volume expansion is sensed by baroreceptors and leads to reflexively decreased renal sympathetic outflow, which dilates the afferent arteriole, increases glomerular filtration rate, and ultimately promotes decreased Na+ reabsorption (natriuresis) to help restore normal ECF volume. This is one of several coordinated pressure-natriuresis mechanisms — alongside decreased renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activity and increased ANP — that the kidney uses to excrete excess salt and water.

incorrectas.A: Increased sympathetic activity is the response to volume depletion (e.g., hemorrhage), where it constricts the afferent arteriole and enhances Na+ reabsorption to conserve volume — the opposite of what is needed when ECF volume is already expanded.
incorrectas.C: The renal sympathetic system is a key effector arm of volume regulation, not a bystander; it actively downregulates in response to volume expansion, so "unchanged" misses the physiologic point of the baroreceptor reflex.
incorrectas.D: The sympathetic response to a sustained rise in Na+ intake and ECF volume is a directional, regulated decrease, not a random oscillation — this is a classic homeostatic feedback loop, not chaotic signaling.

preguntas.q: Increased Na+ intake and ECF volume expansion trigger a change in atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) activity that promotes decreased Na+ reabsorption. What is that change?

o.D: ANP is suppressed while BNP compensates

e.correcta: Atrial stretch from volume expansion directly triggers release of ANP from atrial myocytes; ANP then constricts the efferent arteriole (and dilates the afferent arteriole) to raise GFR, and it also directly inhibits Na+ reabsorption in the collecting duct, together producing a natriuretic and diuretic effect. This makes ANP one of the kidney's key "volume expanded" signals, working in the same direction as decreased sympathetic tone and decreased RAAS activity.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in ANP would occur with volume depletion, when atrial stretch is reduced; that would promote Na+ retention, which is the opposite of the appropriate response to volume expansion.
incorrectas.C: ANP release is exquisitely sensitive to atrial wall stretch, so a significant rise in ECF volume reliably increases ANP secretion rather than leaving it unchanged — this is precisely the stimulus-response pathway being tested.
incorrectas.D: While BNP (from ventricles) responds similarly to volume/pressure overload, ANP itself is not suppressed in this setting — both natriuretic peptides tend to rise together with volume expansion rather than one being turned off while the other compensates.

preguntas.q: Increased Na+ intake and ECF volume expansion lower the plasma protein concentration, causing what change in peritubular capillary oncotic pressure that reduces Na+ reabsorption?

o.D: Increased hydrostatic pressure only, with oncotic pressure unaffected

e.correcta: Volume expansion dilutes plasma proteins and also raises GFR (via afferent dilation and efferent constriction), both of which lower the oncotic pressure in the peritubular capillaries surrounding the proximal tubule. Since the normal reabsorption of tubular fluid across the peritubular capillary depends on a favorable (high) oncotic pressure pulling fluid and Na+ back into the capillary, a fall in this oncotic pressure reduces net proximal Na+ (and water) reabsorption, contributing to natriuresis.

incorrectas.A: An increase in peritubular oncotic pressure would enhance, not reduce, Na+ reabsorption — that occurs in the opposite scenario of volume contraction, where filtration fraction rises and protein concentration in efferent/peritubular blood goes up.
incorrectas.B: The Starling forces in the peritubular capillary are directly linked to plasma protein dilution and filtration fraction changes with volume status, so oncotic pressure does shift meaningfully with volume expansion rather than staying constant.
incorrectas.D: This question specifically concerns the oncotic (protein-driven) pressure change, which is the classic mechanism taught here; while hydrostatic pressure can also change, the physiologically emphasized natriuretic mechanism in this pathway is the fall in oncotic pressure.

preguntas.q: In response to increased Na+ intake and ECF volume, activity of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) changes in a direction that decreases Na+ reabsorption in the proximal tubule and collecting duct. What is that change?

o.D: Selective decrease in renin only, with angiotensin II and aldosterone unaffected

e.correcta: Volume expansion raises renal perfusion pressure and Na+ delivery to the macula densa, both of which suppress renin release from the juxtaglomerular apparatus, leading to less angiotensin II generation and less aldosterone secretion. Lower angiotensin II reduces proximal tubule Na+/H+ exchanger activity, and lower aldosterone reduces ENaC expression in principal cells, so both major RAAS-driven reabsorption sites are down-regulated together to promote natriuresis.

incorrectas.A: Increased RAAS activity is the response to volume depletion, where reduced renal perfusion stimulates renin release to conserve Na+ and water — this is the opposite direction from what volume expansion should trigger.
incorrectas.C: RAAS is one of the most sensitive and rapidly responsive systems to changes in effective circulating volume, so it does not stay static when Na+ intake and ECF volume rise; suppression of renin is a hallmark early response.
incorrectas.D: RAAS acts as a cascade — renin generates angiotensin II, which stimulates aldosterone release — so suppressing renin alone without downstream changes would not occur; decreased renin normally translates into decreased angiotensin II and decreased aldosterone as well.

preguntas.q: A patient given IV insulin and glucose for hyperkalemia experiences a drop in serum K+. What direction does K+ shift and what electrolyte abnormality can result?

o.A: K+ shifts out of cells, causing hyperkalemia
o.B: K+ shifts into cells, causing hypokalemia
o.C: K+ shifts into cells, causing hyperkalemia
o.D: K+ shifts out of cells, causing hypokalemia

e.correcta: Insulin stimulates the Na+-K+ ATPase pump (particularly in skeletal muscle and liver), driving K+ into cells in exchange for Na+ moving out, which is why insulin (with glucose to prevent hypoglycemia) is used as an emergency treatment to rapidly lower dangerously high serum K+. Because this is a redistribution rather than a true loss of total body K+, the effect is temporary and must be paired with definitive therapies (e.g., dialysis, potassium-binding resins) to actually remove excess K+ from the body.

incorrectas.A: K+ shifting out of cells is what happens with insulin deficiency (e.g., diabetic ketoacidosis), not with insulin administration — insulin's whole therapeutic value in hyperkalemia comes from doing the opposite.
incorrectas.C: Insulin cannot cause hyperkalemia through this pathway; driving K+ into cells necessarily lowers, not raises, extracellular (serum) K+ concentration, which is exactly why insulin is used clinically to treat hyperkalemia.
incorrectas.D: K+ moving out of cells would raise, not lower, serum K+, so pairing "out of cells" with "hypokalemia" is internally inconsistent — the direction of the shift and the resulting serum change must move oppositely to what's stated here.

preguntas.q: By what mechanism does insulin drive potassium into cells?

e.correcta: Insulin binds its receptor on skeletal muscle and hepatocyte membranes and signals (via a pathway involving PI3K) the insertion and activation of Na+-K+ ATPase pumps, which actively pump K+ into the cell and Na+ out. This intracellular shift lowers extracellular K+ without changing total body K+ content, which is the basis for using insulin/glucose as rapid, though temporary, treatment for hyperkalemia.

incorrectas.B: H+-K+ ATPase is found in gastric parietal cells and renal α-intercalated cells, where it reabsorbs K+ in exchange for H+ secretion; it is not the pump insulin activates to shift K+ intracellularly in muscle and liver.
incorrectas.C: The Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter is the target of loop diuretics in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle and mediates renal K+ reabsorption from the tubular lumen, not the cellular uptake of K+ driven by insulin signaling.
incorrectas.D: ROMK channels mediate K+ secretion from principal cells into the tubular lumen in the collecting duct, a renal excretory mechanism, not the intracellular redistribution mechanism insulin uses via the Na+-K+ ATPase.

preguntas.q: A patient with new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus and insulin deficiency is found to have an elevated serum potassium. What underlies this finding?

o.A: K+ shifts into cells, causing hypokalemia
o.B: K+ shifts out of cells, causing hyperkalemia
o.C: K+ shifts out of cells, causing hypokalemia
o.D: K+ shifts into cells, causing hyperkalemia

e.correcta: Without adequate insulin, Na+-K+ ATPase activity in skeletal muscle and liver falls, so less K+ is actively pumped into cells; combined with the metabolic acidosis often accompanying insulin deficiency (as in DKA), K+ shifts out of cells into the extracellular space, raising serum K+ despite normal or even depleted total body K+ stores. This is why DKA patients can present with hyperkalemia on labs yet be profoundly total-body K+ depleted, requiring careful K+ repletion once insulin therapy begins and drives K+ back into cells.

incorrectas.A: Insulin deficiency does not drive K+ into cells — it does the opposite by failing to activate Na+-K+ ATPase, so pairing "into cells" with insulin deficiency reverses the actual physiology.
incorrectas.C: K+ shifting out of cells raises, not lowers, serum K+, so labeling this hypokalemia is inconsistent; the extracellular accumulation of K+ from failed cellular uptake is what produces hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia.
incorrectas.D: K+ moving into cells would lower serum K+, which contradicts the premise of insulin deficiency, where the pump that normally moves K+ intracellularly is under-active, leading to a net efflux of K+ instead.

preguntas.q: Hypokalemia is classically associated with which acid-base disturbance?

e.correcta: In alkalosis, the relative excess of extracellular HCO3- (or deficit of H+) drives H+ out of cells to help buffer the extracellular pH, and K+ shifts into cells to maintain electroneutrality, lowering serum K+ and producing or worsening hypokalemia. This same principle also explains why correcting a metabolic alkalosis (e.g., with volume resuscitation) often improves associated hypokalemia, since the transcellular K+ shift reverses as pH normalizes.

incorrectas.A: Metabolic acidosis classically causes the opposite shift — H+ moves into cells and K+ moves out to maintain electroneutrality — producing hyperkalemia rather than hypokalemia.
incorrectas.B: Respiratory acidosis and alkalosis have much less consistent effects on serum K+ compared to their metabolic counterparts, since the H+-K+ exchange is more prominent with metabolic (HCO3--driven) disturbances than with pure CO2-driven pH changes.
incorrectas.D: There is a well-established, testable association between alkalosis and hypokalemia (and acidosis with hyperkalemia) via the H+-K+ exchanger, so saying there is no consistent link ignores this classic physiologic relationship.

preguntas.q: Hyperkalemia is classically associated with which acid-base disturbance?

e.correcta: In acidosis, excess extracellular H+ moves into cells to be buffered, and to preserve electroneutrality K+ exits cells into the extracellular fluid, raising serum K+ and producing or worsening hyperkalemia. This reciprocal H+/K+ exchange is why acidotic patients (e.g., in renal failure or DKA) often present with hyperkalemia even when total body K+ is normal or low, and why treating the acidosis (e.g., with insulin or bicarbonate) can help temporarily shift K+ back into cells.

incorrectas.A: Alkalosis causes the opposite transcellular shift — H+ leaves cells and K+ enters cells — which tends to lower serum K+ and cause hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.
incorrectas.C: The H+-K+ exchanger creates a well-recognized, testable reciprocal relationship between acid-base status and serum K+, so denying any consistent relationship misses a core physiologic mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Respiratory alkalosis, like other respiratory acid-base disorders, has a much weaker and less predictable effect on serum K+ than metabolic acidosis does, and it would tend toward hypokalemia rather than hyperkalemia if any shift occurred at all.
