preguntas.q: Acid-base disturbances affect serum potassium levels primarily by altering the activity and directionality of which transporter?

e.correcta: The H+-K+ exchanger (found on cell membranes throughout the body) moves H+ and K+ in opposite directions to maintain electroneutrality as pH shifts — in acidosis, H+ enters cells while K+ exits, and in alkalosis, H+ exits cells while K+ enters, which is the core mechanism linking acid-base status to serum K+. Notably, not all acid-base disorders cause meaningful K+ shifts through this exchanger — respiratory acidosis and alkalosis have much less impact than their metabolic counterparts, because H+ crosses membranes more readily as CO2 (respiratory) than as fixed acid (metabolic).

incorrectas.A: Na+-K+ ATPase is regulated by hormonal signals like insulin and catecholamines rather than by pH per se, and while it maintains the baseline K+ gradient, it is not the primary transporter responsible for the acid-base-driven shifts described here.
incorrectas.C: The Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb is a renal tubular reabsorptive transporter targeted by loop diuretics, unrelated to the cellular H+/K+ exchange that links systemic pH to serum potassium.
incorrectas.D: The Na+-Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule (target of thiazides) reabsorbs Na+ and Cl-, and has no direct role in the reciprocal H+/K+ exchange that explains acid-base effects on serum potassium.

preguntas.q: A patient with metabolic alkalosis is found to have a low serum potassium. What best explains this finding?

o.A: Alkalosis causes K+ to shift out of cells, causing hyperkalemia
o.B: Alkalosis causes K+ to shift into cells, causing hypokalemia
o.C: Alkalosis has no effect on K+ distribution
o.D: Alkalosis increases renal K+ reabsorption directly

e.correcta: In alkalosis, H+ leaves cells to help buffer the alkalemic extracellular fluid, and K+ moves into cells to maintain electroneutrality, lowering serum K+ via the H+-K+ exchanger. This transcellular shift is one of several causes of hypokalemia in alkalotic states (in addition to renal K+ wasting mechanisms like volume contraction and secondary hyperaldosteronism), and correcting the alkalosis often helps normalize the serum K+.

incorrectas.A: This describes the opposite (acidosis-type) shift; in alkalosis K+ moves into, not out of, cells, so pairing "out of cells" with alkalosis reverses the actual H+-K+ exchange direction.
incorrectas.C: Alkalosis has a well-documented, testable effect on K+ distribution via the H+-K+ exchanger — asserting no effect ignores this classic and frequently tested physiologic coupling.
incorrectas.D: The mechanism being tested here is an intracellular shift of K+, not a change in renal tubular reabsorption; while alkalosis can also secondarily affect renal K+ handling, the direct cellular mechanism is the H+-K+ exchange causing a shift into cells.

preguntas.q: A patient with severe metabolic acidosis is found to have an elevated serum potassium despite normal total body K+ stores. What mechanism explains this?

o.A: Acidosis causes K+ to shift into cells, causing hypokalemia
o.B: Acidosis has no effect on K+ distribution
o.C: Acidosis causes K+ to shift out of cells, causing hyperkalemia
o.D: Acidosis directly increases aldosterone-mediated K+ secretion

e.correcta: In acidosis, excess H+ enters cells to be buffered intracellularly, and K+ exits cells into the extracellular fluid to preserve electroneutrality via the H+-K+ exchanger, raising serum K+ even when total body K+ stores are unchanged. This explains why severely acidotic patients (e.g., in DKA or renal failure) can present with dangerously high serum K+ that improves as the acidosis is corrected and K+ redistributes back into cells.

incorrectas.A: This describes the alkalosis-type shift; acidosis moves K+ out of, not into, cells, so this answer reverses the actual direction of the H+-K+ exchange in acidosis.
incorrectas.B: Acidosis has a well-established, testable effect on K+ distribution through the H+-K+ exchanger, so claiming no effect misses this core and frequently examined physiologic relationship.
incorrectas.D: Acidosis does not act through aldosterone-mediated renal secretion to raise serum K+ in this context; the mechanism tested here is a direct intracellular-to-extracellular shift via the H+-K+ exchanger, not a hormonal renal excretory pathway.

preguntas.q: By what mechanism do β-adrenergic agonists (e.g., albuterol) cause potassium to shift into cells, a property exploited to treat acute hyperkalemia?

o.D: Direct blockade of K+ channels on the cell membrane

e.correcta: β2-adrenergic receptor stimulation activates adenylyl cyclase and increases intracellular cAMP, which in turn stimulates Na+-K+ ATPase activity in skeletal muscle and other tissues, driving K+ into cells and Na+ out. This is why nebulized albuterol is used alongside insulin/glucose as a rapid, temporary measure to lower serum K+ in acute hyperkalemia, working through the same final pump but a different upstream signaling pathway than insulin.

incorrectas.B: H+-K+ ATPase is the pump found in gastric parietal cells and renal intercalated cells that reabsorbs K+ in exchange for H+ secretion; it is not the target of β-agonist signaling for intracellular K+ shift.
incorrectas.C: β-agonists act on cellular K+ distribution (a rapid, temporary intracellular shift), not on renal excretion of K+, which is a slower process governed by aldosterone and distal tubular flow, so this does not describe the described mechanism.
incorrectas.D: β-agonists do not block K+ channels; rather, they actively promote K+ entry into cells via stimulated Na+-K+ ATPase pump activity, a fundamentally different (transporter-driven, energy-requiring) mechanism than channel blockade.

preguntas.q: A patient with a large crush injury develops rhabdomyolysis. What electrolyte disturbance results from the lysis of muscle cells releasing intracellular contents?

o.A: Hypokalemia from K+ shifting into cells
o.B: Hyperkalemia from K+ shifting out of cells
o.D: No significant change in serum K+

e.correcta: Cell lysis, whether from crush injury/rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis syndrome, or other massive tissue destruction, releases the high intracellular K+ concentration directly into the extracellular space, causing hyperkalemia that can be severe and life-threatening. This is a distributional problem superimposed on (and often compounded by) the acute kidney injury that rhabdomyolysis itself can cause via myoglobin-induced tubular damage, further impairing renal K+ excretion.

incorrectas.A: Cell lysis releases K+ from inside cells to the outside, the opposite of a shift into cells; this option describes a redistribution mechanism (like insulin or β-agonists) rather than the destructive release of intracellular contents seen with lysis.
incorrectas.C: While renal K+ wasting is a real cause of hypokalemia in other clinical contexts, it is not the mechanism at play in tissue lysis — lysis causes a direct release of preformed intracellular K+, producing hyperkalemia, not a renal-mediated loss.
incorrectas.D: Cell lysis releases large quantities of intracellular K+ (among other contents like myoglobin, phosphate, and uric acid) which is a major clinical concern precisely because it does change, often dramatically raise, serum K+.

preguntas.q: Strenuous exercise causes potassium to shift in which direction relative to cells?

o.D: Into cells, but only in cardiac myocytes

e.correcta: During vigorous exercise, repeated muscle depolarization opens voltage-gated K+ channels and K+ efflux from contracting muscle cells exceeds the capacity of Na+-K+ ATPase to pump it back in, causing a transient rise in extracellular (and serum) K+. This exercise-induced hyperkalemia is usually mild and self-limited, resolving with rest as the Na+-K+ ATPase catches up, but it illustrates how muscle activity itself is a physiologic determinant of K+ distribution, distinct from hormonal regulators like insulin or aldosterone.

incorrectas.A: Insulin and β-agonists drive K+ into cells via Na+-K+ ATPase stimulation, but exercise itself does the opposite in the short term — repeated depolarization releases K+ from muscle faster than it can be pumped back in.
incorrectas.C: Exercise produces a measurable, often clinically relevant transient rise in serum K+ due to net efflux from muscle, so "no net shift" does not reflect the actual physiology during exertion.
incorrectas.D: This shift is not restricted to cardiac myocytes; it occurs broadly in skeletal muscle undergoing repeated depolarization during exercise, which is the tissue primarily responsible for the K+ efflux seen with exertion.

preguntas.q: Approximately 67% of filtered potassium is reabsorbed in which nephron segment?

o.A: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

e.correcta: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs the bulk of filtered K+ (about 67%) largely passively, following the reabsorption of Na+ and water via the solvent drag/paracellular pathway, mirroring how the PCT handles most other filtered solutes. This makes the PCT a high-capacity, largely unregulated site for K+ reabsorption, in contrast to the more finely tuned, hormonally regulated K+ handling that occurs further downstream.

incorrectas.A: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs a smaller share of filtered K+ (about 20%) via the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2), a distinct transporter and mechanism from the passive, bulk reabsorption that dominates in the proximal tubule.
incorrectas.C: The late distal tubule and collecting duct are where fine, hormonally regulated adjustments of K+ excretion (secretion via principal cells, reabsorption via α-intercalated cells) occur, but they handle a much smaller fraction of total filtered K+ than the bulk reabsorption seen proximally.
incorrectas.D: The collecting duct, like the late distal tubule, is a site of regulated K+ secretion or reabsorption depending on dietary K+ and aldosterone status, but it is not where the majority (67%) of filtered K+ is reabsorbed — that happens far upstream in the proximal tubule.

preguntas.q: Approximately 20% of filtered potassium reabsorption occurs in which nephron segment, mediated by the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter?

o.B: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

e.correcta: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs about 20% of filtered K+ via the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) on the apical membrane, which brings K+ into the cell along with Na+ and Cl-; some of this K+ then recycles back into the lumen through ROMK channels, helping generate the lumen-positive potential that drives paracellular reabsorption of Ca2+ and Mg2+. This is the same transporter blocked by loop diuretics, which is why loop diuretics cause significant K+ wasting — they prevent this reabsorptive pathway entirely.

incorrectas.A: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs the largest share of filtered K+ (about 67%) via a passive, solvent-drag mechanism tied to Na+ and water reabsorption, not via the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter, which is specific to the thick ascending limb.
incorrectas.C: The late distal tubule is responsible for fine-tuned, aldosterone-regulated K+ secretion or reabsorption via principal and intercalated cells, not for the NKCC2-mediated reabsorption that defines the thick ascending limb's contribution.
incorrectas.D: The descending thin limb is primarily permeable to water (via aquaporins) and is not a major site of active K+ reabsorption; it lacks the NKCC2 transporter that characterizes the thick ascending limb.

preguntas.q: Fine adjustments of potassium excretion in response to dietary intake and hormonal signals occur primarily in which nephron segments?

o.A: Proximal convoluted tubule and thin descending limb
o.B: Thick ascending limb and loop of Henle
o.C: Late distal tubule and collecting ducts

e.correcta: While the proximal tubule and thick ascending limb reabsorb the bulk of filtered K+ in a relatively fixed, unregulated fashion, the late distal tubule and collecting ducts are where principal cells (secretion via ROMK, driven by aldosterone and ENaC activity) and α-intercalated cells (reabsorption via H+-K+ ATPase, active during K+ deprivation) fine-tune final urinary K+ excretion to match dietary intake. This makes the distal nephron the key regulatory site for maintaining K+ homeostasis, analogous to how it also fine-tunes Na+ and acid-base balance.

incorrectas.A: The proximal convoluted tubule and descending limb handle bulk, largely passive reabsorption of K+ and water, not the hormonally regulated fine-tuning that occurs distally in response to changing dietary K+ or aldosterone levels.
incorrectas.B: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs a fixed proportion (about 20%) of filtered K+ via NKCC2, a relatively constant process not subject to the same moment-to-moment hormonal regulation seen in the late distal nephron.
incorrectas.D: The glomerulus and Bowman's capsule are involved in filtration of K+ from plasma into the tubular fluid, not in the regulated reabsorption or secretion that determines final urinary K+ excretion.

preguntas.q: In a patient on a low-potassium diet, which cell type in the terminal nephron segments reabsorbs potassium to help conserve it?

e.correcta: α-intercalated cells express an apical H+-K+ ATPase that reabsorbs K+ from the tubular lumen in exchange for secreting H+, allowing the kidney to conserve K+ during states of dietary K+ restriction. This is a key adaptive mechanism distinct from the K+-secreting role of principal cells, illustrating how the same nephron segment houses cells performing opposite functions on K+ handling depending on physiologic need.

incorrectas.B: β-intercalated cells are specialized for bicarbonate secretion and H+ reabsorption (important during metabolic alkalosis), not for K+ reabsorption, which is the specific job of the α-intercalated cell's H+-K+ ATPase.
incorrectas.A: Principal cells are the K+-secreting cells of the collecting duct, driven by ENaC-mediated Na+ reabsorption and aldosterone; they move K+ into the lumen, the opposite function of the K+-reabsorbing α-intercalated cells relevant to a low-K+ diet.
incorrectas.D: Podocytes are specialized epithelial cells of the glomerulus that form the filtration slits and contribute to the glomerular filtration barrier; they have no role in tubular K+ reabsorption occurring downstream in the collecting duct.

preguntas.q: K+ reabsorption in α-intercalated cells during states of K+ depletion occurs through which transporter?

e.correcta: α-intercalated cells reabsorb K+ via an apical H+-K+ ATPase, which pumps K+ from the tubular lumen into the cell while secreting H+ into the lumen, allowing the kidney to conserve K+ when dietary intake is low while also contributing to urinary acidification. This transporter is functionally and structurally related to the gastric H+-K+ ATPase targeted by proton pump inhibitors, which is why PPIs are sometimes discussed as inhibiting a similar type of primary active transport mechanism.

incorrectas.A: Na+-K+ ATPase is the basolateral pump found in nearly all nephron cells (including principal cells) that maintains the Na+/K+ gradient across the cell, but it is not the apical transporter specifically responsible for luminal K+ reabsorption in α-intercalated cells.
incorrectas.C: ROMK is the apical K+ channel in principal cells responsible for K+ secretion into the lumen, essentially the opposite function (and opposite cell type) from the K+ reabsorption performed by α-intercalated cells.
incorrectas.D: The Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter is located in the thick ascending limb and mediates K+ (along with Na+ and Cl-) reabsorption in that segment, unrelated to the H+-K+ ATPase-driven reabsorption specific to α-intercalated cells in the collecting duct.

preguntas.q: The H+-K+ ATPase found in gastric parietal cells and renal α-intercalated cells (and inhibited by omeprazole) uses what type of transport mechanism?

e.correcta: H+-K+ ATPase directly hydrolyzes ATP to move H+ and K+ against their concentration gradients, making it a primary active transporter — the same category as Na+-K+ ATPase and Ca2+ ATPase, all of which use ATP hydrolysis directly rather than relying on an existing ion gradient. This is why proton pump inhibitors like omeprazole, which covalently and irreversibly bind this pump in gastric parietal cells, are said to inhibit a primary active transport mechanism, distinguishing their action from drugs that block channels or secondary transporters.

incorrectas.A: Facilitated diffusion involves passive movement of a solute down its concentration gradient through a channel or carrier without energy input, which does not describe the H+-K+ ATPase, since it actively moves ions against their gradients using ATP.
incorrectas.B: Secondary active transport (like the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter or Na+-glucose cotransporter) uses the energy stored in an ion gradient (typically Na+) established by a primary pump, rather than directly hydrolyzing ATP itself, which distinguishes it from the H+-K+ ATPase.
incorrectas.D: Simple passive diffusion requires no transporter or energy and moves solutes down their gradient across a membrane; this does not apply to the H+-K+ ATPase, which is an energy-consuming pump moving ions against their gradients.

preguntas.q: In a patient with hyperkalemia, K+ is secreted into the tubular lumen in the terminal nephron segments primarily by which cell type?

e.correcta: Principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct express basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase, which pumps K+ into the cell, and luminal ROMK channels through which that K+ diffuses down its electrochemical gradient into the tubular fluid. This is the main regulated site of K+ secretion, and it is upregulated by aldosterone and by high dietary K+ intake, making it the physiologic safety valve that protects against hyperkalemia.

incorrectas.B: Alpha-intercalated cells secrete H+ via an H+-ATPase and reabsorb K+ via an H+/K+-ATPase, a role that becomes prominent during K+ depletion (low K+ diet) rather than during K+ secretion in hyperkalemia.
incorrectas.C: Beta-intercalated cells work in the opposite direction of alpha-intercalated cells, secreting HCO3- and reabsorbing H+ via a basolateral H+-ATPase and luminal Cl-/HCO3- exchanger; they are involved in acid-base handling, not K+ secretion.
incorrectas.D: Proximal tubule cells reabsorb the bulk of filtered Na+, water, glucose, amino acids, and about two-thirds of filtered K+, but they are not the site of regulated K+ secretion — that fine-tuning happens much further downstream in the principal cells.

preguntas.q: What determines the magnitude of K+ secretion by principal cells across the luminal membrane?

o.A: The size of the electrochemical gradient for K+ across the luminal membrane
o.B: The filtered load of K+ at the glomerulus
o.C: The activity of the Na+/H+ exchanger in the proximal tubule
o.D: The concentration of luminal HCO3- in the proximal tubule

e.correcta: K+ secretion in principal cells is a passive, channel-mediated process (through ROMK channels), so its rate is set by the electrochemical driving force for K+ across the luminal membrane — a combination of the K+ concentration gradient (intracellular K+, raised by Na+/K+-ATPase, versus luminal K+) and the electrical gradient (lumen negativity created by electrogenic Na+ reabsorption via ENaC). Anything that raises intracellular K+ or makes the lumen more electronegative increases this gradient and thus increases secretion.

incorrectas.B: The filtered load of K+ at the glomerulus is almost entirely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule and loop of Henle regardless of dietary intake, so it does not directly set how much K+ the principal cells secrete downstream — that is governed by the local electrochemical gradient, not upstream filtration.
incorrectas.C: The Na+/H+ exchanger (NHE3) mediates proximal tubule Na+ reabsorption coupled to H+ secretion and bicarbonate reclamation; it has no direct role in setting the driving force for K+ secretion in the distal nephron's principal cells.
incorrectas.D: Luminal HCO3- concentration in the proximal tubule reflects bicarbonate reabsorption, not the electrochemical gradient across principal cells; while distal luminal anions like HCO3- can affect K+ secretion by altering lumen electronegativity, that is a distinct, downstream phenomenon from this proximal process.

preguntas.q: How does a chronic high-K+ diet affect renal K+ secretion by principal cells?

o.C: It has no effect on K+ secretion
o.D: It shifts K+ handling entirely to the proximal tubule

e.correcta: A high K+ diet raises plasma K+, which is taken up into principal cells via Na+/K+-ATPase, increasing intracellular K+ concentration. This steepens the electrochemical gradient driving K+ out through luminal ROMK channels, so K+ secretion increases — a homeostatic response (reinforced by aldosterone release) that helps excrete the K+ load and keep plasma K+ in a narrow range.

incorrectas.B: A decrease in K+ secretion is what happens on a low K+ diet, when reduced intracellular K+ flattens the electrochemical gradient across the luminal membrane; a high K+ diet moves the gradient in the opposite direction.
incorrectas.C: K+ secretion is highly responsive to dietary intake precisely because the electrochemical driving force across principal cells changes with intracellular K+ content, so diet clearly does affect secretion rather than leaving it unchanged.
incorrectas.D: The proximal tubule reabsorbs a relatively fixed fraction of filtered K+ regardless of diet; it is the distal principal cells, not the proximal tubule, that adjust their secretion rate in response to dietary K+ changes.

preguntas.q: A patient on a chronically low-K+ diet would be expected to show what change in distal nephron K+ secretion, and why?

o.A: Decreased secretion, due to a reduced electrochemical driving force from lower intracellular K+
o.B: Increased secretion, due to compensatory upregulation of ROMK channels
o.C: No change in secretion, because aldosterone maintains a fixed secretion rate
o.D: Decreased secretion, due to loss of principal cell ENaC expression

e.correcta: On a low K+ diet, less K+ enters principal cells via Na+/K+-ATPase, so intracellular K+ concentration falls. This reduces the electrochemical gradient across the luminal membrane that normally drives K+ out through ROMK channels, so secretion decreases. At the same time, alpha-intercalated cells upregulate H+/K+-ATPase activity to actively reabsorb K+, further conserving it — together these responses protect against hypokalemia.

incorrectas.B: ROMK channel number is upregulated by aldosterone and by high K+ states, not by K+ depletion; a low K+ diet does not trigger compensatory secretion — it does the opposite by conserving K+.
incorrectas.C: Aldosterone secretion actually falls somewhat with hypokalemia (since K+ is a direct stimulus for aldosterone release), and secretion rate is not held fixed — it tracks the electrochemical gradient, which drops on a low K+ diet.
incorrectas.D: ENaC-mediated Na+ reabsorption in principal cells is not lost during K+ depletion; ENaC activity is largely driven by aldosterone and volume status, and the change in K+ secretion here is explained by the intracellular K+-driven gradient, not by loss of Na+ channels.

preguntas.q: A patient with primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome) would be expected to develop which acid-base/electrolyte abnormality due to increased principal cell K+ secretion?

e.correcta: Aldosterone stimulates principal cells to increase Na+ reabsorption through ENaC, which drives greater Na+/K+-ATPase activity at the basolateral membrane. This raises intracellular K+ and increases luminal electronegativity, both of which steepen the electrochemical gradient for K+ secretion through ROMK channels — so excess aldosterone chronically drives K+ secretion up, producing hypokalemia, a classic finding in Conn syndrome.

incorrectas.B: Hyperkalemia is the opposite of what aldosterone excess causes — it is instead the hallmark of hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance (e.g., adrenal insufficiency, ACE inhibitors, K+-sparing diuretics), where reduced Na+/K+-ATPase activity impairs K+ secretion.
incorrectas.C: Aldosterone increases Na+ reabsorption, which tends to preserve or expand plasma Na+ and volume (contributing to hypertension in Conn syndrome), not cause hyponatremia; the Na+ effect is essentially the mirror image of the K+ effect.
incorrectas.D: Aldosterone's principal cell actions target Na+ and K+ transport, not calcium; calcium handling is governed mainly by PTH and vitamin D acting on the distal tubule, so hyperaldosteronism does not directly cause hypercalcemia.

preguntas.q: A patient with primary adrenal insufficiency and resulting hypoaldosteronism would be expected to develop which electrolyte abnormality?

e.correcta: Without aldosterone, principal cells have reduced Na+/K+-ATPase activity, so less K+ is pumped into the cell and intracellular K+ falls. This flattens the electrochemical gradient that normally drives K+ secretion through luminal ROMK channels, so K+ secretion decreases and K+ is retained, producing hyperkalemia — a hallmark finding in adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) alongside hyponatremia and hypotension.

incorrectas.A: Hypokalemia is the finding in aldosterone excess (hyperaldosteronism), not deficiency — the two conditions produce opposite K+ derangements because they push principal cell Na+/K+-ATPase activity, and thus the K+ secretory gradient, in opposite directions.
incorrectas.C: Hypoaldosteronism causes reduced Na+ reabsorption via ENaC, leading to natriuresis and volume loss, so plasma Na+ tends toward hyponatremia, not hypernatremia — this is a defining feature of adrenal insufficiency along with the hyperkalemia.
incorrectas.D: Aldosterone deficiency primarily disturbs Na+ and K+ balance through its principal cell actions; calcium homeostasis is regulated separately by PTH and vitamin D, so hypoaldosteronism is not classically associated with hypocalcemia.

preguntas.q: By what additional mechanism, besides increasing Na+/K+-ATPase activity, does aldosterone promote K+ secretion in the late distal tubule and collecting duct?

o.A: By increasing the number of luminal membrane K+ channels
o.B: By inhibiting the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
o.C: By upregulating the H+/K+-ATPase in intercalated cells
o.D: By increasing aquaporin-2 insertion in principal cells

e.correcta: In addition to boosting basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase activity (which raises intracellular K+), aldosterone increases the number and open probability of luminal ROMK K+ channels in principal cells. More channels mean a lower resistance pathway for K+ efflux, so for any given electrochemical gradient, more K+ moves into the lumen — this dual action (more driving force plus more channels) is why aldosterone excess so reliably causes hypokalemia.

incorrectas.B: The Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) is located in the thick ascending limb and is the target of loop diuretics; aldosterone acts on the late distal tubule and collecting duct, not by inhibiting NKCC2, so this is not part of its mechanism.
incorrectas.C: The H+/K+-ATPase in alpha-intercalated cells reabsorbs K+ and is upregulated during K+ depletion, which is the opposite physiologic scenario from aldosterone-driven K+ secretion; aldosterone's action described here is on principal cells' K+ channels, not this intercalated cell pump.
incorrectas.D: Aquaporin-2 insertion into the principal cell luminal membrane is stimulated by ADH (vasopressin) to increase water reabsorption, a distinct hormonal axis from aldosterone's regulation of Na+ and K+ transport.

preguntas.q: A patient started on furosemide develops muscle weakness and is found to have a low serum K+. What effect do thiazide and loop diuretics have on K+ excretion that explains this?

o.A: They increase K+ excretion, causing hypokalemia
o.B: They decrease K+ excretion, causing hyperkalemia
o.C: They have no effect on K+ excretion
o.D: They increase K+ excretion only in the proximal tubule

e.correcta: Loop and thiazide diuretics block Na+ reabsorption upstream (thick ascending limb and distal convoluted tubule, respectively), which delivers more Na+ to the principal cells of the collecting duct. This drives greater Na+/K+-ATPase activity, raising intracellular K+ and the electrochemical gradient for K+ secretion through ROMK channels, so more K+ is excreted — producing the hypokalemia commonly seen with these diuretics and explaining this patient's weakness.

incorrectas.B: Decreased K+ excretion with hyperkalemia is the pattern seen with K+-sparing diuretics (e.g., amiloride, spironolactone), which block ENaC or aldosterone action in principal cells — the opposite mechanism and opposite electrolyte result from loop/thiazide diuretics.
incorrectas.C: Loop and thiazide diuretics have a well-documented, clinically important effect of increasing K+ excretion; this is exactly why patients on these agents are monitored for hypokalemia and sometimes co-prescribed K+ supplements or K+-sparing agents.
incorrectas.D: The increased K+ excretion from these diuretics occurs in the collecting duct's principal cells, not the proximal tubule — the proximal tubule is not the site where diuretic-induced increased distal Na+ delivery translates into extra K+ secretion.

preguntas.q: Thiazide and loop diuretics promote K+ wasting largely because they increase which of the following?

o.A: Delivery of Na+ to the principal cells
o.B: Delivery of Ca2+ to the thick ascending limb
o.C: Delivery of phosphate to the proximal tubule
o.D: Reabsorption of Na+ in the proximal tubule

e.correcta: By inhibiting Na+ reabsorption at upstream sites — NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb for loop diuretics, and the Na+-Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule for thiazides — these drugs prevent Na+ from being reabsorbed before it reaches the collecting duct. The result is increased Na+ delivery to principal cells, which increases Na+/K+-ATPase turnover and thus K+ secretion, the key mechanistic link to diuretic-induced hypokalemia.

incorrectas.B: Ca2+ delivery to the thick ascending limb is not the relevant mechanism here — in fact loop diuretics reduce, not increase, Ca2+ reabsorption in that segment by dissipating the lumen-positive potential that normally drives paracellular Ca2+ reabsorption, leading to increased urinary Ca2+ loss, a separate effect from the K+-wasting mechanism.
incorrectas.C: Phosphate handling occurs predominantly in the proximal tubule under PTH regulation and is not the mechanism by which loop or thiazide diuretics affect distal K+ secretion; phosphate delivery is unrelated to this pathway.
incorrectas.D: These diuretics inhibit, rather than increase, Na+ reabsorption at their respective sites of action; increased proximal tubule Na+ reabsorption would reduce distal Na+ delivery and would work against, not cause, the K+ wasting seen clinically.

preguntas.q: Increased Na+ delivery to the principal cells, as occurs with thiazide and loop diuretics, has what effect on K+ secretion?

o.C: Has no effect on K+ secretion
o.D: Converts K+ secretion into K+ reabsorption

e.correcta: More Na+ reaching principal cells means more Na+ is reabsorbed via ENaC, which in turn increases basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase activity to keep intracellular Na+ low. This raises intracellular K+ concentration and increases lumen electronegativity (since Na+ reabsorption is electrogenic), both of which increase the electrochemical driving force for K+ secretion through ROMK channels — explaining why diuretics that increase distal Na+ delivery cause hypokalemia.

incorrectas.B: A decrease in K+ secretion would require either reduced intracellular K+ or a less electronegative lumen; increased distal Na+ delivery does the opposite by fueling more Na+/K+-ATPase activity and more electrogenic Na+ reabsorption.
incorrectas.C: Increased distal Na+ delivery has a well-established, clinically significant effect — it is precisely the mechanism used to explain why loop and thiazide diuretics, and any condition causing high distal Na+ delivery, promote kaliuresis and hypokalemia.
incorrectas.D: Increased Na+ delivery amplifies the existing secretory pathway (more driving force through ROMK channels); it does not reverse the direction of K+ transport into reabsorption, which is instead mediated by a completely different mechanism (H+/K+-ATPase in intercalated cells).

preguntas.q: A patient on spironolactone for heart failure should be monitored for which electrolyte abnormality, given how K+-sparing diuretics affect K+ secretion?

e.correcta: K+-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone (an aldosterone receptor antagonist) or amiloride/triamterene (direct ENaC blockers) reduce Na+ reabsorption through ENaC in principal cells. Less electrogenic Na+ reabsorption means a less lumen-negative potential and less Na+/K+-ATPase-driven rise in intracellular K+, both of which reduce the electrochemical gradient for K+ secretion — so K+ is retained, producing hyperkalemia, the key adverse effect to monitor for with these agents.

incorrectas.B: Hypokalemia is the expected effect of loop and thiazide diuretics, which increase distal Na+ delivery and K+ secretion — the mechanistically opposite outcome from K+-sparing diuretics, which blunt that same secretory pathway.
incorrectas.C: K+-sparing diuretics act on Na+ and K+ channels/transporters in the collecting duct; they do not have a primary mechanism affecting calcium reabsorption, so hypercalcemia is not a characteristic effect of this drug class.
incorrectas.D: Because these diuretics reduce Na+ reabsorption (hence they are still diuretics, just K+-sparing), they tend to promote mild natriuresis rather than causing Na+ retention, so hypernatremia is not the expected finding.

preguntas.q: Increased delivery of poorly reabsorbable luminal anions (e.g., HCO3-) to the collecting duct, as in a patient with a proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis, tends to cause which electrolyte change?

e.correcta: When poorly reabsorbable anions like HCO3- remain in the tubular lumen, they make the lumen more electronegative because Na+ reabsorption via ENaC continues but there is no accompanying reabsorbable anion to balance the charge. This increased electronegativity adds to the electrochemical gradient favoring K+ exit through luminal ROMK channels, so K+ secretion increases and hypokalemia results — a mechanism relevant in conditions like proximal RTA or with bicarbonaturia.

incorrectas.B: Decreased K+ secretion with hyperkalemia would require a less electronegative lumen or reduced intracellular K+; increased luminal anion delivery does the opposite by making the lumen more negative and pulling more K+ out.
incorrectas.C: This mechanism concerns electrical driving forces for K+ transport, not calcium handling; calcium reabsorption in the distal nephron depends on PTH and the lumen-positive potential of the thick ascending limb, which is a separate process from luminal anion effects on principal cells.
incorrectas.D: Na+ reabsorption via ENaC actually continues (or even increases) in this setting — it's the accompanying anion reabsorption that is impaired, not the Na+ transport itself, so this does not primarily produce hyponatremia through decreased Na+ reabsorption.

preguntas.q: After GTP binds the alpha subunit of a heterotrimeric G protein (Gs, Gi, or Gq) during hormone signaling, what happens to the alpha-GTP subunit?

o.A: It detaches from the beta-gamma subunits and goes on to regulate its effector
o.B: It remains bound to the beta-gamma complex and hydrolyzes GTP immediately
o.C: It is degraded by the proteasome to terminate signaling
o.D: It translocates to the nucleus to act as a transcription factor

e.correcta: Hormone binding to a G protein-coupled receptor causes the receptor to act as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor, prompting the alpha subunit to release GDP and bind GTP. This GTP-bound state causes a conformational change that dissociates the alpha subunit from the beta-gamma dimer, and free alpha-GTP is then able to diffuse along the membrane to interact with and modulate its specific downstream effector (e.g., adenylyl cyclase for Gs/Gi, phospholipase C for Gq) — this dissociation step is essential for propagating the signal.

incorrectas.B: The alpha subunit does not stay bound to beta-gamma after GTP loading — dissociation is the whole point of the activation step, since it is the freed alpha-GTP (and in some pathways the freed beta-gamma dimer) that goes on to activate effectors; GTP hydrolysis back to GDP happens later and terminates, rather than propagates, signaling.
incorrectas.C: The alpha subunit is not degraded as part of normal signal termination — it is inactivated by its own intrinsic GTPase activity (often accelerated by RGS proteins) hydrolyzing GTP back to GDP, after which it reassociates with beta-gamma, not through proteasomal degradation.
incorrectas.D: G protein alpha subunits act at or near the plasma membrane on membrane-bound or cytoplasmic effectors (like adenylyl cyclase or phospholipase C); they do not translocate to the nucleus themselves — nuclear effects of GPCR signaling occur indirectly through downstream second messengers and transcription factors like CREB.

preguntas.q: Approximately 85% of filtered phosphate is reabsorbed in which nephron segment?

o.B: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

e.correcta: The proximal tubule is the dominant site of phosphate reabsorption, accounting for about 85% of the filtered load (roughly 70% in the proximal convoluted tubule and another 15% in the proximal straight tubule) via the sodium-phosphate cotransporter (NaPi-2) on the luminal membrane. This is also the site where PTH exerts its major phosphaturic effect, inhibiting NaPi-2 to increase urinary phosphate excretion and lower serum phosphate — a key part of PTH's role in calcium-phosphate homeostasis.

incorrectas.B: The thick ascending limb is the major site for divalent cation reabsorption (Ca2+ and Mg2+) driven by the lumen-positive potential from the Na+-K+-2Cl- transporter, but it is not where the bulk of filtered phosphate is reabsorbed.
incorrectas.C: The distal convoluted tubule handles a small fraction of Ca2+ reabsorption (regulated by PTH-driven active transport) and Na+-Cl- reabsorption via the thiazide-sensitive cotransporter, but it is not a major phosphate-reabsorbing segment.
incorrectas.D: The collecting duct is primarily responsible for fine-tuning Na+, K+, and water balance under aldosterone and ADH control; it does not reabsorb a significant fraction of filtered phosphate, which is essentially already reabsorbed proximally.

preguntas.q: What percentage of plasma Ca2+ is freely filtered across the glomerular capillaries?

o.B: 60%, because 40% is bound to plasma proteins
o.C: 85%, because only a small fraction is protein-bound
o.D: 100%, because calcium is freely filtered like water

e.correcta: Of total plasma calcium, about 40% is bound to plasma proteins (mainly albumin) and cannot cross the glomerular filtration barrier, while the remaining 60% — comprising ionized (free) calcium plus a small complexed fraction — is filterable. This is analogous to how protein binding limits filtration of other solutes, and it is clinically important because only the unbound, filterable/ionized calcium is physiologically active and available for tubular handling.

incorrectas.A: This reverses the actual proportions — it is 40% that is protein-bound and non-filterable, while 60% is free/filterable, not the other way around; getting the fractions backwards would lead to underestimating the filtered calcium load.
incorrectas.C: 85% filtered would imply a much smaller protein-bound fraction than actually exists; roughly 40% of plasma calcium is bound to albumin and other proteins, so 85% overstates how much calcium escapes protein binding and reaches the filtrate.
incorrectas.D: Unlike freely diffusible water, calcium is subject to protein binding, and only the unbound (ionized plus complexed) fraction is filtered; the size-selective and charge properties of albumin-bound calcium prevent it from crossing the glomerular barrier, so filtration is not complete.

preguntas.q: The majority of filtered Ca2+ reabsorption (about 67%) occurs in which nephron segment, tightly coupled to Na+ reabsorption?

o.B: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

e.correcta: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs about 67% of filtered Ca2+, largely passively via a paracellular route that is driven by the same solvent drag and electrochemical gradients established by bulk Na+ and water reabsorption in this segment. Because Ca2+ handling here is tightly coupled to Na+ transport, conditions or diuretics that alter proximal Na+ reabsorption (like volume expansion) can secondarily change proximal Ca2+ reabsorption as well.

incorrectas.B: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs roughly 25% of filtered Ca2+, a smaller share than the proximal tubule, and does so via a distinct mechanism driven by the lumen-positive potential generated by the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) rather than the bulk-flow-coupled process seen proximally.
incorrectas.C: The distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs only about 8% of filtered Ca2+, and unlike the proximal tubule, this reabsorption is transcellular and actively regulated by PTH, and is not tightly coupled to Na+ transport — in fact thiazide diuretics that block distal Na+-Cl- reabsorption here increase Ca2+ reabsorption.
incorrectas.D: The collecting duct is not a major site of Ca2+ reabsorption; its main regulated transport functions involve Na+, K+, and water rather than calcium, so it accounts for a negligible fraction of the filtered calcium load.

preguntas.q: Approximately 25% of filtered Ca2+ reabsorption occurs in which nephron segment?

o.B: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

e.correcta: The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle reabsorbs about 25% of filtered calcium, via a paracellular route driven by the lumen-positive transepithelial potential difference that is generated when the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) reabsorbs Na+ and K+ recycles back into the lumen through ROMK channels. This is clinically important because loop diuretics, by inhibiting NKCC2, collapse that lumen-positive potential and thereby reduce Ca2+ reabsorption here, which is why loop diuretics can be used to treat hypercalcemia.

incorrectas.A: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs the largest share of filtered Ca2+ (about 67%), well above the 25% attributed to the thick ascending limb, and does so through a different, largely passive paracellular mechanism coupled to bulk Na+/water reabsorption rather than the lumen-positive-potential mechanism specific to the thick ascending limb.
incorrectas.C: The distal convoluted tubule accounts for only about 8% of filtered Ca2+ reabsorption, far less than the thick ascending limb, and its process is active/transcellular and PTH-regulated rather than the passive paracellular process seen here.
incorrectas.D: The descending thin limb of the loop of Henle is primarily permeable to water, not solutes like Ca2+ or Na+, and does not play a significant role in calcium reabsorption.

preguntas.q: In the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, Ca2+ is reabsorbed via which route?

o.C: Transcellular, via facilitated diffusion through basolateral channels only

e.correcta: Ca2+ reabsorption in the thick ascending limb occurs paracellularly — that is, it moves passively between adjacent tubular cells through the tight junctions, driven by the lumen-positive transepithelial potential difference generated by NKCC2-mediated Na+/K+/2Cl- reabsorption and K+ recycling. This is a passive, electrically driven process rather than one requiring active transport machinery within the cells themselves, distinguishing it from the actively regulated transcellular Ca2+ reabsorption seen in the distal convoluted tubule.

incorrectas.B: Active, transcellular Ca2+ transport (requiring luminal channels, calbindin, and a basolateral Ca2+-ATPase or Na+/Ca2+ exchanger) is characteristic of the distal convoluted tubule under PTH regulation, not the thick ascending limb, where the process is passive and paracellular instead.
incorrectas.C: Facilitated diffusion through basolateral channels describes part of an active transcellular pathway, which is not how Ca2+ moves in the thick ascending limb; here Ca2+ bypasses the cells entirely by moving through the paracellular space.
incorrectas.D: SGLT (sodium-glucose cotransporters) mediate glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule and have no role in Ca2+ transport in the thick ascending limb, which instead depends on NKCC2-generated electrical gradients.

preguntas.q: What is the primary driving force for paracellular Ca2+ reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle?

o.C: A steep Ca2+ concentration gradient created by active Ca2+ pumps

e.correcta: The Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) reabsorbs Na+, K+, and Cl- from the lumen, but much of the K+ recycles back into the lumen through apical ROMK channels. Because K+ re-enters the lumen while Na+ and Cl- are retained in the cell, the lumen becomes electropositive relative to the interstitium, and this lumen-positive potential difference is what drives cations like Ca2+ and Mg2+ to passively diffuse through the paracellular tight junction pathway into the blood.

incorrectas.B: A lumen-negative potential (as seen in the collecting duct due to electrogenic Na+ reabsorption via ENaC) would favor secretion of cations like K+ into the lumen, not reabsorption of Ca2+ out of it — this is the opposite electrical configuration from what exists in the thick ascending limb.
incorrectas.C: There are no dedicated active Ca2+ pumps generating a concentration gradient for paracellular transport in the thick ascending limb; the mechanism here is passive and electrically driven, not the result of active transcellular pumping (which instead characterizes the distal convoluted tubule).
incorrectas.D: The thick ascending limb is classically described as impermeable to water (hence its role in diluting tubular fluid), so osmotic water reabsorption via aquaporins does not occur here and cannot be the driving force for Ca2+ reabsorption in this segment.

preguntas.q: A patient with symptomatic hypercalcemia is given furosemide as part of treatment (with adequate volume repletion). What effect do loop diuretics have on serum Ca2+?

o.D: Increase serum Ca2+ only in patients with renal failure

e.correcta: Loop diuretics like furosemide inhibit the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb, which dissipates the lumen-positive potential difference that normally drives passive paracellular Ca2+ reabsorption in that segment. With less Ca2+ reabsorbed, more is excreted in the urine, lowering serum Ca2+ — this is the pharmacologic basis for using loop diuretics (with IV fluids) as adjunctive treatment for severe hypercalcemia.

incorrectas.A: An increase in serum Ca2+ is the effect of thiazide diuretics, which work in the distal convoluted tubule to enhance Ca2+ reabsorption — the opposite segment and opposite calcium effect compared to loop diuretics acting on the thick ascending limb.
incorrectas.C: Loop diuretics have a clear, clinically exploited hypocalcemic effect by blocking the electrical driving force for Ca2+ reabsorption in the thick ascending limb; this is not a neutral or negligible effect, which is why they are used therapeutically in hypercalcemic emergencies.
incorrectas.D: The calciuric effect of loop diuretics is a direct consequence of inhibiting NKCC2 and does not depend on the presence of renal failure; it occurs in patients with normal renal function as well, provided adequate hydration is maintained to allow diuresis.

preguntas.q: Approximately 8% of filtered Ca2+ reabsorption occurs in which nephron segment?

o.B: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

e.correcta: The distal tubule reabsorbs a relatively small fraction (about 8%) of filtered Ca2+, but this segment is disproportionately important because it is the site of active, transcellular, PTH-regulated Ca2+ reabsorption — involving apical TRPV5 channels, intracellular calbindin for buffering/shuttling, and basolateral extrusion via a Ca2+-ATPase and Na+/Ca2+ exchanger. Even though the quantity reabsorbed here is small compared to the proximal tubule, this is where fine physiologic control of calcium balance actually happens.

incorrectas.A: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs by far the largest share of filtered Ca2+ (about 67%) through a passive, bulk-flow-coupled paracellular mechanism, making it quantitatively dominant but not the primary site of hormonal fine-tuning.
incorrectas.B: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs about 25% of filtered Ca2+ passively via the paracellular route, driven by the lumen-positive potential from NKCC2 activity — a larger share than the distal tubule but still not the site of active regulation.
incorrectas.D: The collecting duct is not considered a significant site of calcium reabsorption; its major transport roles involve Na+, K+, and water handling under aldosterone and ADH control, not calcium.

preguntas.q: Although it reabsorbs only a small fraction of filtered Ca2+, which nephron segment serves as the main site of hormonally regulated Ca2+ reabsorption?

o.B: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

e.correcta: The distal tubule is the principal site where Ca2+ reabsorption is actively and hormonally regulated — PTH increases the activity/number of apical TRPV5 channels and upregulates calbindin and basolateral extrusion mechanisms, enabling the fine-tuned control needed to maintain calcium homeostasis. Unlike the proximal tubule, where Ca2+ and Na+ reabsorption move together passively, Ca2+ handling here is largely uncoupled from Na+ transport, which is why thiazides (blocking distal Na+-Cl- reabsorption) can increase Ca2+ reabsorption independently.

incorrectas.A: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs the bulk of filtered Ca2+ passively, tightly coupled to Na+ and water reabsorption, but this coupling means Ca2+ handling here largely follows volume status rather than being independently, hormonally regulated.
incorrectas.B: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs Ca2+ passively via the paracellular route driven by an electrical gradient from NKCC2 activity; while this quantity is substantial (~25%), it is not subject to the kind of direct hormonal (PTH) fine-tuning that occurs in the distal tubule.
incorrectas.D: The collecting duct's regulated transport (Na+ via aldosterone, water via ADH) does not extend to meaningful calcium handling, so it is not considered a regulatory site for Ca2+ reabsorption.

preguntas.q: PTH acts on the distal tubule to increase Ca2+ reabsorption, resulting in what effect on urinary calcium excretion?

o.D: Increased urinary Ca2+ only when PTH is also increasing urinary phosphate

e.correcta: PTH stimulates distal tubule cells to increase apical TRPV5 channel activity and calbindin-mediated Ca2+ transport, enhancing active transcellular Ca2+ reabsorption. Because more filtered Ca2+ is pulled back into the blood, less remains in the urine, producing hypocalciuria — this renal action works together with PTH's effects on bone resorption and vitamin D activation to raise serum Ca2+ overall.

incorrectas.B: Hypercalciuria would occur if Ca2+ reabsorption were reduced or if the filtered load of Ca2+ increased without a matching reabsorptive response; PTH's direct renal effect is to enhance reabsorption, so it lowers, not raises, urinary calcium excretion.
incorrectas.C: PTH has a clear, measurable renal effect on Ca2+ handling via TRPV5 upregulation in the distal tubule; it is not without effect on urinary calcium — this renal action is a key, testable component of PTH physiology.
incorrectas.D: PTH's phosphaturic effect (inhibiting NaPi-2 in the proximal tubule) and its calcium-conserving effect (enhancing distal Ca2+ reabsorption) are two separate, independently occurring actions of the same hormone — the hypocalciuric effect happens regardless of the phosphate effect, not conditionally upon it.

preguntas.q: A patient with recurrent calcium oxalate kidney stones is started on a thiazide diuretic partly for its effect on serum Ca2+. What effect do thiazide diuretics have on serum Ca2+?

o.D: Decrease serum Ca2+ only when combined with a loop diuretic

e.correcta: Thiazide diuretics inhibit the Na+-Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, which lowers intracellular Na+ and enhances basolateral Na+/Ca2+ exchange, pulling more Ca2+ out of the cell and favoring greater apical Ca2+ entry and net reabsorption. This increases serum Ca2+ (and reduces urinary Ca2+ excretion), which is why thiazides are useful in patients with calcium-containing kidney stones — less calcium in the urine means less available to precipitate as stones.

incorrectas.B: A decrease in serum Ca2+ is the effect of loop diuretics, which inhibit NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb and collapse the lumen-positive potential driving Ca2+ reabsorption there — a mechanistically distinct segment and opposite calcium effect from thiazides acting in the distal convoluted tubule.
incorrectas.C: Thiazides have a well-documented and clinically useful hypocalciuric/mildly hypercalcemic effect through their action on distal tubule Na+/Ca2+ exchange; this is not a null effect, and it is specifically why thiazides (not loop diuretics) are chosen for calcium stone prevention.
incorrectas.D: The calcium-retaining effect of thiazides occurs independently of any loop diuretic; combining the two would actually work at cross purposes (loop diuretics increase calciuria while thiazides decrease it), so this effect does not require loop diuretic co-administration.

preguntas.q: Approximately 60% of filtered Mg2+ reabsorption occurs in which nephron segment?

o.B: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

e.correcta: Unlike most other filtered solutes, Mg2+ reabsorption is greatest not in the proximal tubule but in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, which reabsorbs about 60% of the filtered load. This occurs via the paracellular route, driven by the same lumen-positive transepithelial potential difference generated by NKCC2 activity and K+ recycling through ROMK that also drives Ca2+ reabsorption in this segment — which is why loop diuretics, by disrupting this potential, can cause both hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia.

incorrectas.A: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs only about 15-20% of filtered Mg2+, a notably smaller share than for most other solutes (like Na+ and Ca2+, which it reabsorbs in bulk) — Mg2+ handling is unusual in that its primary reabsorptive site is more distal.
incorrectas.C: The distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs a smaller fraction of filtered Mg2+ (roughly 5-10%), via active transcellular transport through TRPM6 channels, which is a site of fine regulation but not the bulk reabsorptive segment.
incorrectas.D: The collecting duct is not a significant site for Mg2+ reabsorption; its major regulated transport functions concern Na+, K+, and water, not magnesium.

preguntas.q: Mg2+ reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle occurs primarily via which route?

e.correcta: In the thick ascending limb, Mg2+ (along with Ca2+ and additional Na+) is reabsorbed paracellularly, passing between tubular epithelial cells rather than through them. This movement is passive, driven by the lumen-positive electrochemical gradient generated by the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter and the K+ backleak into the lumen via ROMK channels. Because this route depends on tight junction proteins (paracellin-1/claudin-16), mutations here cause familial hypomagnesemia with hypercalciuria.

incorrectas.A: Transcellular active transport describes movement of ions through the cell interior via pumps and channels (as with Na+ reabsorption via Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransport and the Na+/K+-ATPase), but the bulk of Mg2+ handling in this segment is not through this route — it moves between cells instead.
incorrectas.C: Facilitated diffusion through basolateral channels would still require the ion to first enter the cell across the apical membrane, which is not how Mg2+ crosses the thick ascending limb epithelium; instead it bypasses the cells entirely via the paracellular pathway.
incorrectas.D: SGLT-mediated glucose cotransport occurs in the proximal tubule, not the thick ascending limb, and has no role in Mg2+ handling — Mg2+ transport here is driven by an electrical gradient, not coupled to glucose.

preguntas.q: What electrochemical force drives paracellular Mg2+ reabsorption in the thick ascending limb?

e.correcta: The Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) brings K+ into the cell along with Na+ and Cl-, but much of that K+ leaks back into the tubular lumen through ROMK channels, making the lumen electrically positive relative to the interstitium. This lumen-positive potential difference is the driving force that pushes cations like Mg2+ and Ca2+ through the paracellular route between cells. It is why loop diuretics, which block NKCC2 and abolish this gradient, cause both hypomagnesemia and hypocalcemia.

incorrectas.A: There is no lumen-negative potential generated by Cl- backleak in this segment — Cl- exits basolaterally via channels, and it is the K+ backleak into the lumen that creates the relevant (lumen-positive, not negative) potential difference driving divalent cation reabsorption.
incorrectas.C: Urea recycling contributes to the corticopapillary osmotic gradient in the inner medulla and collecting duct, but it does not generate the electrical driving force for paracellular Mg2+ transport in the thick ascending limb.
incorrectas.D: The basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase maintains the low intracellular Na+ that powers NKCC2 indirectly, but it does not itself create the lumen-positive charge; that charge specifically comes from K+ recycling back into the lumen through apical ROMK channels.

preguntas.q: A patient started on furosemide for volume overload is at risk for which electrolyte disturbance?

e.correcta: Furosemide blocks the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, which abolishes the K+ backleak that generates the lumen-positive potential difference needed for paracellular Mg2+ (and Ca2+) reabsorption. Without that driving force, Mg2+ reabsorption falls and urinary Mg2+ losses increase, producing hypomagnesemia with chronic loop diuretic use. This is why patients on long-term loop diuretics are monitored for both low magnesium and low calcium.

incorrectas.A: Hypermagnesemia would require increased Mg2+ reabsorption or retention, the opposite of what happens when NKCC2 blockade removes the lumen-positive gradient that normally drives Mg2+ out of the tubular lumen.
incorrectas.C: Loop diuretics cause hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia, because the same lumen-positive potential that drives Mg2+ reabsorption also drives Ca2+ reabsorption in this segment; losing that gradient increases urinary calcium loss (this is the opposite effect seen with thiazides, which increase distal Ca2+ reabsorption).
incorrectas.D: Loop diuretics increase distal delivery of Na+, promoting K+ secretion in the collecting duct and typically causing hypokalemia rather than hyperkalemia; hyperkalemia is more characteristic of K+-sparing diuretics or ACE inhibitors.

preguntas.q: Approximately 30% of filtered Mg2+ is reabsorbed in which nephron segment?

e.correcta: The proximal tubule reabsorbs about 30% of filtered Mg2+, a relatively modest fraction compared to how it handles most other solutes (it reabsorbs ~65-70% of filtered Na+ and water). This is unusual because Mg2+ reabsorption here occurs less avidly than sodium and water, since the majority of Mg2+ handling instead occurs downstream in the thick ascending limb (~65%), which is the primary site of Mg2+ regulation.

incorrectas.A: The thick ascending limb, not the proximal tubule, reabsorbs the majority of filtered Mg2+ (roughly 65%) via the paracellular route driven by the lumen-positive potential difference — this is the dominant regulatory site for Mg2+ balance.
incorrectas.B: The distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs only a small fraction of filtered Mg2+ (about 5%), via active transcellular transport through TRPM6 channels, far less than the proximal tubule's 30% share.
incorrectas.D: The collecting duct plays essentially no role in bulk Mg2+ reabsorption; its main regulatory functions involve Na+, K+, and water handling under aldosterone and ADH control, not magnesium.

preguntas.q: Which nephron segment accounts for only about 5% of filtered Mg2+ reabsorption, via active transcellular transport?

e.correcta: The distal tubule reabsorbs only about 5% of filtered Mg2+, but unlike the thick ascending limb's passive paracellular mechanism, this final portion is active and transcellular, occurring through apical TRPM6 channels. Because this segment represents the last opportunity for Mg2+ reabsorption before excretion, it functions as the primary site of fine-tuned regulation of urinary Mg2+ excretion, even though it handles a small overall percentage.

incorrectas.A: The proximal tubule reabsorbs roughly 30% of filtered Mg2+ passively, following the bulk reabsorption of Na+ and water, which is a much larger share than the 5% attributed to the distal tubule.
incorrectas.B: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs the largest share of filtered Mg2+ (about 65%) via the passive paracellular route driven by the lumen-positive potential, making it quantitatively the dominant segment rather than a minor 5% contributor.
incorrectas.D: The descending limb of the loop of Henle is primarily permeable to water (via aquaporins) and does not meaningfully reabsorb Mg2+; the ascending limb, not the descending limb, is where most tubular Mg2+ handling occurs.

preguntas.q: What is the term for the gradual increase in interstitial osmolarity from about 300 mOsm/L in the renal cortex to about 1200 mOsm/L at the papilla?

e.correcta: The corticopapillary osmotic gradient describes the progressive rise in interstitial fluid osmolarity moving from the cortex (isotonic, ~300 mOsm/L) down through the medulla to the papilla (~1200 mOsm/L in humans). This gradient is what allows the collecting duct, under ADH's influence, to reabsorb water osmotically and concentrate the urine; without it, the kidney could not produce urine more concentrated than plasma. It is established and maintained by countercurrent multiplication in the loop of Henle plus urea recycling in the inner medulla.

incorrectas.A: Glomerulotubular balance refers to the proximal tubule's ability to maintain a constant fractional reabsorption of the filtered load despite changes in GFR, an entirely separate concept from the medullary osmotic gradient.
incorrectas.C: Tubuloglomerular feedback is the mechanism by which the macula densa senses distal tubular NaCl delivery and adjusts afferent arteriolar tone to regulate GFR, unrelated to the axial osmolarity gradient in the medulla.
incorrectas.D: Starling forces govern fluid movement across capillary walls based on hydrostatic and oncotic pressures (as in the glomerulus or peritubular capillaries), not the interstitial osmotic gradient used for urinary concentration.

preguntas.q: The corticopapillary osmotic gradient is established in part through what process occurring in the loop of Henle?

e.correcta: Countercurrent multiplication describes how the hairpin arrangement of the loop of Henle, combined with active NaCl reabsorption in the water-impermeable thick ascending limb and passive water reabsorption in the water-permeable descending limb, progressively amplifies a small transverse osmotic gradient into a large longitudinal (axial) gradient down the medulla. Each cycle of countercurrent flow multiplies the concentrating effect, ultimately producing medullary interstitial osmolarity as high as 1200 mOsm/L at the papilla. This mechanism, together with urea recycling and the vasa recta acting as countercurrent exchangers, underlies the kidney's ability to concentrate urine.

incorrectas.A: Simple diffusion to equilibrium would eliminate a gradient rather than create one; the loop of Henle instead actively maintains disequilibrium between limbs to progressively build, not dissipate, the osmotic gradient.
incorrectas.C: Facilitated glucose transport occurs in the proximal tubule via SGLT and GLUT transporters and has no involvement in generating the medullary osmotic gradient, which depends on NaCl and urea handling in deeper nephron segments.
incorrectas.D: Glomerular filtration produces an isosmotic ultrafiltrate of plasma and occurs upstream of the loop of Henle; it does not itself create any osmotic gradient within the renal medulla.

preguntas.q: In addition to countercurrent multiplication, the corticopapillary osmotic gradient is established in part by recycling of which solute in the inner medulla?

e.correcta: Urea recycling contributes significantly to the corticopapillary osmotic gradient, particularly in the inner medulla. ADH increases water reabsorption in the cortical and outer medullary collecting duct without allowing urea to follow (since those segments are urea-impermeable), which concentrates urea in the tubular fluid. That concentrated urea is then reabsorbed in the inner medullary collecting duct (which is urea-permeable) into the interstitium, contributing directly to the high interstitial osmolarity at the papilla and helping recycle urea back into the tubule via the thin limbs of the loop of Henle.

incorrectas.A: Glucose is almost completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule under normal conditions and does not participate in generating the medullary interstitial osmotic gradient.
incorrectas.C: Phosphate reabsorption occurs mainly in the proximal tubule under PTH regulation and has no significant role in building the corticopapillary gradient, which depends specifically on NaCl handling in the loop of Henle and urea recycling in the medulla.
incorrectas.D: Bicarbonate is reabsorbed predominantly in the proximal tubule as part of acid-base regulation and does not contribute to the osmotic gradient used for urinary concentration in the medulla.

preguntas.q: In the presence of ADH, which collecting duct segments are permeable to water but impermeable to urea?

o.B: Thin descending limb and thin ascending limb
o.C: Cortical and outer medullary collecting ducts

e.correcta: With ADH present, the cortical and outer medullary collecting ducts become highly permeable to water (via aquaporin-2 insertion) but remain impermeable to urea. This mismatch is deliberate: as water leaves the tubular fluid in these segments, the urea left behind becomes progressively more concentrated, setting up the urea gradient that will later be exploited in the inner medullary collecting duct, where urea permeability finally increases and allows urea to move into the interstitium.

incorrectas.A: The inner medullary collecting duct is permeable to both water and urea in the presence of ADH — it is precisely where the urea concentrated upstream is finally allowed to diffuse into the interstitium, unlike the cortical and outer medullary segments.
incorrectas.B: The thin descending and ascending limbs of the loop of Henle have their own distinct permeability profiles (descending limb permeable to water, ascending limb impermeable to water) but are not the collecting duct segments described as water-permeable/urea-impermeable under ADH.
incorrectas.D: The proximal straight tubule reabsorbs water and solutes isosmotically early in the nephron and is not subject to ADH-dependent regulation of water or urea permeability, unlike the distal collecting system.

preguntas.q: With ADH present, how does the tubular fluid urea concentration ([TF]urea) change as fluid passes through the cortical and outer medullary collecting ducts?

o.A: It decreases due to urea secretion
o.C: It increases due to water reabsorption without urea
o.D: It decreases due to urea reabsorption

e.correcta: Because the cortical and outer medullary collecting ducts reabsorb water (under ADH) but remain impermeable to urea, urea gets left behind and becomes increasingly concentrated in the tubular fluid as it travels through these segments. This rising [TF]urea sets up a favorable concentration gradient so that once the fluid reaches the urea-permeable inner medullary collecting duct, urea can diffuse passively into the medullary interstitium, contributing to the corticopapillary gradient.

incorrectas.A: There is no active urea secretion into these collecting duct segments; the rise in tubular urea concentration results passively from water removal, not from added urea being secreted into the lumen.
incorrectas.B: [TF]urea does not stay constant — because water leaves the tubule while urea cannot follow in these segments, the urea concentration necessarily rises as the fluid volume shrinks around a relatively fixed amount of urea.
incorrectas.D: Urea reabsorption in these segments would require urea permeability, which is specifically absent in the cortical and outer medullary collecting ducts; urea reabsorption instead occurs later, in the inner medullary collecting duct.

preguntas.q: Which collecting duct segment is permeable to both water and urea in the presence of ADH?

e.correcta: The inner medullary collecting duct, unlike the cortical and outer medullary segments, is permeable to both water and urea when ADH is present. This dual permeability allows the urea that was concentrated upstream (as water left the urea-impermeable cortical/outer medullary collecting ducts) to now diffuse into the medullary interstitium along with water, directly contributing to the high osmolarity at the papilla and completing the urea recycling loop.

incorrectas.A: The cortical collecting duct is water-permeable but urea-impermeable under ADH, which is what allows urea to become concentrated in the tubular fluid rather than escaping into the interstitium at this level.
incorrectas.C: The outer medullary collecting duct shares the same permeability profile as the cortical collecting duct — permeable to water, impermeable to urea — continuing to concentrate urea in the lumen rather than allowing it to exit here.
incorrectas.D: The distal convoluted tubule is not a major site of ADH-regulated urea handling; its permeability characteristics relate mainly to NaCl reabsorption (cortical diluting segment) rather than the water/urea permeability switch seen in the collecting duct.

preguntas.q: What effect does the recycling of urea into the renal medullary interstitium have on interstitial fluid osmolarity?

o.D: It only affects cortical, not medullary, osmolarity

e.correcta: Urea recycling adds an osmotically active solute directly into the medullary interstitium, increasing its osmolarity. This is a key reason the deep medulla and papilla can reach osmolarities as high as 1200 mOsm/L — urea contributes roughly half of that total osmolarity, working alongside the NaCl gradient established by countercurrent multiplication in the loop of Henle. Without urea recycling, the kidney's maximal urine-concentrating ability would be substantially blunted, as seen clinically in protein-malnourished patients with low urea production.

incorrectas.A: Urea entering the interstitium adds osmotically active particles rather than removing them, so it raises rather than lowers interstitial osmolarity — a decrease would instead result if urea were being washed out of the medulla.
incorrectas.C: Urea recycling has a substantial, measurable effect — it accounts for a large fraction of the total medullary interstitial osmolarity, working in tandem with the NaCl gradient from the loop of Henle rather than being negligible.
incorrectas.D: Urea's osmotic contribution is concentrated specifically in the inner medulla/papilla, not the cortex, since that is where urea-permeable collecting duct segments allow urea to exit into the interstitium; it does not act primarily on cortical osmolarity.

preguntas.q: What effect does ADH have on activity of the urea recycling process in the inner medullary collecting duct?

o.C: ADH has no effect on urea handling
o.D: ADH shifts urea handling to the proximal tubule

e.correcta: ADH enhances the urea recycling process by increasing water reabsorption in the urea-impermeable cortical and outer medullary collecting ducts (concentrating luminal urea) and by increasing urea permeability (via UT-A1/UT-A3 transporters) in the inner medullary collecting duct, allowing that concentrated urea to move into the interstitium. This coordinated action deepens the corticopapillary gradient and allows for maximally concentrated urine during states of water conservation, such as dehydration.

incorrectas.A: ADH does not inhibit urea recycling — inhibition would blunt the medullary gradient and impair urine concentration, which runs counter to ADH's physiologic role of promoting water retention and concentrated urine formation.
incorrectas.C: ADH clearly affects urea handling by upregulating urea transporters in the inner medullary collecting duct in addition to its well-known effect on aquaporin-2-mediated water permeability; without ADH, urea recycling and the medullary gradient are both diminished.
incorrectas.D: Urea recycling occurs in the loop of Henle and inner medullary collecting duct, not the proximal tubule; ADH does not redirect urea handling to the proximal segment, which handles urea reabsorption passively and is not itself ADH-regulated.

preguntas.q: What is the approximate tubular fluid to plasma osmolarity ratio ([TF/P]osm) in the proximal tubule?

o.D: Undefined, since the proximal tubule has no measurable osmolarity

e.correcta: In the proximal tubule, [TF/P]osm equals 1 because reabsorption here is isosmotic — water and solutes (Na+, Cl-, glucose, amino acids, etc.) are reabsorbed together in proportional amounts, so the osmolarity of the remaining tubular fluid stays essentially identical to that of plasma throughout this segment. This reflects the proximal tubule's role as a bulk, non-selective reabsorptive segment rather than a site of fine urine concentration or dilution, which occurs further downstream in the loop of Henle and distal nephron.

incorrectas.A: A ratio less than 1 indicates the tubular fluid has become dilute relative to plasma, which happens in segments like the thick ascending limb and early distal tubule that reabsorb solute without water — not in the isosmotic proximal tubule.
incorrectas.C: A ratio greater than 1 indicates concentrated tubular fluid relative to plasma, which occurs in the medullary collecting duct when ADH is present and water is reabsorbed down the corticopapillary gradient — this does not happen in the proximal tubule.
incorrectas.D: The proximal tubule fluid absolutely has a measurable osmolarity; it is simply equal to that of plasma due to the isosmotic nature of proximal reabsorption, not undefined or absent.

preguntas.q: In the late distal tubule with high circulating ADH levels, what is the approximate [TF/P]osm ratio?

e.correcta: With high ADH, the late distal tubule becomes water-permeable via aquaporin-2 insertion, allowing the dilute tubular fluid (previously generated by NaCl reabsorption without water in the upstream diluting segments) to equilibrate osmotically with the surrounding isotonic cortical interstitium. Since the cortical interstitium sits at roughly the same osmolarity as plasma (~300 mOsm/L), the tubular fluid osmolarity rises back up to match plasma, giving a [TF/P]osm of 1 at this point — even though the fluid was hypotonic just upstream.

incorrectas.A: A ratio less than 1 would describe the state without ADH, where the late distal tubule remains impermeable to water and the dilute fluid generated upstream cannot equilibrate with the isotonic interstitium.
incorrectas.C: A ratio greater than 1 develops further downstream, in the medullary collecting duct, where the interstitium becomes progressively hypertonic due to the corticopapillary gradient; the late distal tubule sits in the cortex, where the interstitium is only isotonic, not hypertonic.
incorrectas.D: A ratio of zero would imply the tubular fluid has no osmotic solutes at all, which does not occur physiologically — the fluid always retains some solute even after extensive dilution in the upstream diluting segments.

preguntas.q: In the collecting duct with high ADH levels, what happens to the [TF/P]osm ratio as fluid moves toward the papilla?

o.D: It becomes undefined due to urea interference

e.correcta: With high ADH, the collecting duct becomes water permeable and, as it descends through the medulla, the tubular fluid progressively equilibrates with the increasingly hypertonic interstitium created by the corticopapillary gradient (up to ~1200 mOsm/L at the papilla). Because the interstitium here is hypertonic relative to plasma, the tubular fluid becomes correspondingly concentrated, producing a [TF/P]osm ratio greater than 1 — this is the physiologic basis for producing concentrated urine during water restriction or dehydration.

incorrectas.A: A ratio less than 1 describes dilute tubular fluid, which is what exists in the collecting duct in the absence of ADH (since the segment stays water-impermeable and cannot reabsorb water down the medullary gradient), not the high-ADH state.
incorrectas.B: A ratio equal to 1 describes fluid equilibrated with isotonic (not hypertonic) interstitium, as occurs in the late distal tubule within the cortex; it does not apply to the medullary collecting duct, which sits adjacent to progressively more concentrated interstitium.
incorrectas.D: Urea does not make the ratio undefined; rather, urea recycling is part of what makes the medullary interstitium hypertonic in the first place, directly contributing to (not confounding) the elevated [TF/P]osm ratio observed here.

preguntas.q: The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is also known by what functional name?

e.correcta: The thick ascending limb is called the diluting segment because it actively reabsorbs NaCl via the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter while remaining impermeable to water. Since solute leaves the tubular fluid without water following, the fluid becomes progressively hypotonic relative to plasma as it travels through this segment — a process that occurs whether or not ADH is present, since ADH does not alter this segment's water impermeability.

incorrectas.A: The concentrating function of the nephron happens downstream, in the medullary collecting duct, where ADH-driven water reabsorption down the corticopapillary gradient raises tubular fluid osmolarity — the opposite of what happens in the thick ascending limb.
incorrectas.C: The proximal tubule, not the thick ascending limb, is the isosmotic segment, since it reabsorbs water and solute in proportional amounts, keeping [TF/P]osm at 1 throughout.
incorrectas.D: The thick ascending limb is not primarily a secretory segment; while it does have some ion secretion via K+ recycling through ROMK, its defining functional role and eponym relate to dilution of the tubular fluid via solute reabsorption without water.

preguntas.q: The early distal tubule is also known by what functional name, reflecting its NaCl reabsorption without water?
