e.correcta: The early distal tubule is called the cortical diluting segment because, like the thick ascending limb, it reabsorbs NaCl (here via the Na+-Cl- cotransporter, the target of thiazide diuretics) without accompanying water reabsorption, further diluting the tubular fluid. It earns the "cortical" designation because, unlike the thick ascending limb which spans into the medulla, this segment is located entirely within the renal cortex.

incorrectas.A: There is no distinct "medullary diluting segment" — the analogous NaCl-without-water reabsorption occurring in the medulla is the thick ascending limb's function, which is simply termed the diluting segment (not medullary diluting segment) and lies in a different anatomic location than the early distal tubule.
incorrectas.C: The isosmotic segment refers to the proximal tubule, where water and solute are reabsorbed proportionally, maintaining [TF/P]osm at 1 — the opposite of the dilution occurring in the early distal tubule.
incorrectas.D: Concentration of the tubular fluid occurs later, in the medullary collecting duct under ADH, not in the early distal tubule, which is functionally defined by its dilutional, not concentrating, activity.

preguntas.q: In the absence of ADH, how is the corticopapillary osmotic gradient affected compared to when ADH is present?

e.correcta: Without ADH, the corticopapillary osmotic gradient becomes smaller because ADH normally amplifies both major contributors to the gradient: it increases NKCC2 activity in the thick ascending limb (boosting countercurrent multiplication) and increases urea permeability/recycling in the inner medullary collecting duct. When ADH is absent, both of these processes are attenuated, so less NaCl and urea accumulate in the medullary interstitium and the axial osmotic gradient is blunted, though it is not completely abolished.

incorrectas.A: The gradient becoming larger would require enhanced countercurrent multiplication and urea recycling, which are the effects specifically driven by ADH — removing ADH does the opposite, reducing rather than amplifying the gradient.
incorrectas.C: The gradient does not remain unchanged, because ADH has direct effects on both NKCC2 activity and urea transporter function that meaningfully modulate the magnitude of the medullary gradient; its absence measurably attenuates gradient formation.
incorrectas.D: The gradient does not reverse direction — osmolarity still increases from cortex to papilla even without ADH, since some baseline countercurrent multiplication persists; ADH modulates the magnitude of the gradient, not its overall directionality.

preguntas.q: What is the water permeability of the early distal tubule?

o.B: Permeable only when ADH is present
o.D: Permeable to water but impermeable to NaCl

e.correcta: The early distal tubule is impermeable to water regardless of ADH status, while remaining permeable to NaCl via the Na+-Cl- cotransporter. This combination — solute reabsorption without water — is exactly what allows this segment to dilute the tubular fluid, earning it the name "cortical diluting segment." Because water permeability here is never under ADH's control (unlike the more distal segments), the early distal tubule's dilutional function is a constant, ADH-independent feature of the nephron.

incorrectas.A: The early distal tubule is not permeable to water under any condition, including in the presence of ADH; ADH's water-permeability effects act on the late distal tubule and collecting duct, which express aquaporin-2, not on the early distal tubule.
incorrectas.B: Water permeability in this segment does not turn on even with ADH present — ADH-responsive water permeability applies to more downstream segments (late distal tubule and collecting duct), not the early distal tubule.
incorrectas.D: This describes the opposite permeability profile from reality; the early distal tubule is permeable to NaCl (which is actively reabsorbed) but impermeable to water, not the reverse.

preguntas.q: Without ADH, what is the water permeability of the late distal tubule and collecting ducts?

o.C: Permeable to water but not to solute
o.D: Permeable only to urea, not water

e.correcta: Without ADH, the late distal tubule and collecting ducts remain impermeable to water because aquaporin-2 channels are not inserted into the apical membrane of the principal cells. As a result, the dilute tubular fluid produced upstream (in the thick ascending limb and early distal tubule) passes through these segments without equilibrating with the surrounding interstitium, and dilute urine is excreted — this is the physiologic basis of water diuresis seen in central or nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

incorrectas.A: High water permeability describes the state when ADH IS present, when aquaporin-2 is inserted into the apical membrane; in its absence, these segments are specifically water-impermeable, allowing dilute urine to be excreted.
incorrectas.C: This segment's core issue in the absence of ADH is water impermeability, not solute impermeability — Na+ reabsorption via ENaC and K+ secretion continue to occur here independent of ADH status; it is specifically water movement that is blocked.
incorrectas.D: Urea permeability in the inner medullary collecting duct is regulated somewhat independently and also requires ADH for its full upregulation via urea transporters; without ADH, neither water nor urea permeability are substantially increased in this region.

preguntas.q: What is the [TF/P]osm relationship in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle?

o.D: TF/Posm cannot be determined without knowing ADH status

e.correcta: In the thick ascending limb, TF/Posm is less than 1 because this segment actively reabsorbs NaCl via the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter while remaining impermeable to water. As solute leaves the tubular fluid without water following, the remaining fluid becomes progressively hypotonic relative to plasma — a defining feature of this "diluting segment" that holds true regardless of ADH status, since ADH does not alter the water impermeability of this segment.

incorrectas.A: A ratio of 1 describes isosmotic fluid, characteristic of the proximal tubule where water and solute are reabsorbed proportionally — the thick ascending limb instead dilutes the fluid by removing solute without water.
incorrectas.B: A ratio greater than 1 would indicate concentrated tubular fluid, which occurs in the medullary collecting duct under ADH as fluid equilibrates with the hypertonic interstitium — the opposite process from what happens in the diluting thick ascending limb.
incorrectas.D: This ratio does not depend on ADH status; the thick ascending limb remains water-impermeable and continues diluting the tubular fluid whether or not ADH is present, unlike segments further downstream whose water permeability is ADH-dependent.

preguntas.q: What is the [TF/P]osm value in the early distal tubule?

e.correcta: In the early distal tubule, [TF/P]osm is less than 1 because NaCl continues to be reabsorbed via the Na+-Cl- cotransporter while the segment remains impermeable to water. This further dilutes the already hypotonic fluid delivered from the thick ascending limb, and this dilution occurs regardless of ADH status since ADH does not confer water permeability on this particular segment.

incorrectas.A: A ratio greater than 1 would indicate a concentrated tubular fluid, which requires water reabsorption into a hypertonic interstitium — something that only happens further downstream in the medullary collecting duct under ADH, not in the early distal tubule.
incorrectas.B: A ratio of 1 describes isosmotic fluid as seen in the proximal tubule; the early distal tubule instead actively dilutes the fluid by continuing to reabsorb NaCl without water.
incorrectas.D: A ratio of zero is not physiologically meaningful here — it would imply the tubular fluid has become completely solute-free, which does not occur; substantial solute (just proportionally less than plasma) remains in the fluid.

preguntas.q: In the late distal tubule when ADH levels are low, what is the expected [TF/P]osm value?

o.D: Exactly equal to plasma osmolarity of 300 mOsm/L multiplied by 2

e.correcta: With low ADH, [TF/P]osm in the late distal tubule remains less than 1 because this segment stays impermeable to water in the absence of ADH-driven aquaporin-2 insertion. The dilute fluid generated upstream in the thick ascending limb and early distal tubule therefore cannot equilibrate with the isotonic cortical interstitium, and the hypotonic fluid simply continues on toward the collecting duct — this is the physiologic mechanism by which the kidney excretes free water during states of water excess.

incorrectas.A: A ratio greater than 1 would require water reabsorption into a hypertonic interstitium, which cannot occur here both because ADH is low (no aquaporin-2) and because the late distal tubule sits within the cortex, where interstitial osmolarity is only isotonic, not hypertonic.
incorrectas.B: A ratio equal to 1 is what occurs in this same segment when ADH IS high, since water can then flow out to equilibrate with the isotonic cortical interstitium; with low ADH, that equilibration cannot happen and the fluid stays dilute.
incorrectas.D: This describes an arbitrary numeric relationship with no physiologic basis; the tubular fluid osmolarity in this low-ADH state is simply hypotonic relative to plasma, not a fixed multiple of the plasma value.

preguntas.q: In a patient with low ADH levels, the tubular fluid-to-plasma osmolality ratio [TF/P]osm in the collecting duct is which of the following?

e.correcta: With low ADH, the collecting duct principal cells insert few aquaporin-2 channels into the luminal membrane, so the duct remains relatively water-impermeable. Tubular fluid entering the collecting duct is already dilute from the thick ascending limb and early distal tubule, and without water reabsorption it cannot equilibrate osmotically with the hypertonic medullary interstitium, so [TF/P]osm stays below 1 and dilute urine is excreted — the basis of water diuresis.

incorrectas.A: A ratio of 1 would mean the tubular fluid has equilibrated exactly with plasma osmolality, which occurs at the end of the proximal tubule (isosmotic reabsorption) but not in the ADH-deficient collecting duct, where fluid remains dilute relative to plasma.
incorrectas.B: A ratio greater than 1 occurs when ADH IS present and the collecting duct becomes water-permeable, allowing water to be reabsorbed into the hypertonic medulla and concentrating the remaining tubular fluid above plasma osmolality — the opposite of the low-ADH state described.
incorrectas.D: Tubular flow does not stop in the absence of ADH; in fact, without water reabsorption more dilute filtrate is delivered to the renal pelvis, producing a large volume of dilute urine rather than no flow at all.

preguntas.q: Which term describes solute-free water generated by the nephron, conceptually equivalent to distilled water?

e.correcta: Free water is the portion of excreted water that carries no solute, generated when the thick ascending limb and early distal tubule (the diluting segments) actively pump NaCl out of the tubular fluid without allowing water to follow, since these segments are impermeable to water. This dilutes the remaining tubular fluid and is the physiological basis for how the kidney can excrete pure water separately from solute, which becomes clinically relevant when calculating free-water clearance to assess urine concentrating or diluting ability.

incorrectas.A: Osmotic diuresis refers to increased urine output caused by unreabsorbed solutes (such as glucose in uncontrolled diabetes) dragging water with them osmotically, which is a solute-driven process rather than the generation of solute-free water.
incorrectas.C: Isotonic filtrate describes fluid whose osmolality matches plasma, as occurs after proximal tubule reabsorption; this is the opposite concept of free water, which by definition is stripped of solute rather than osmotically matched to plasma.
incorrectas.D: Obligatory water loss refers to the minimum water excretion required to eliminate the daily solute load even when maximally concentrating urine, a distinct clinical concept from the diluting-segment mechanism that generates free water.

preguntas.q: Which renal parameter is calculated to estimate the kidney's ability to concentrate or dilute urine relative to plasma?

e.correcta: Free-water clearance (CH2O) equals urine flow rate minus osmolar clearance, and it quantifies how much solute-free water is being excreted or retained relative to an isosmotic urine. A positive CH2O indicates the kidney is diluting the urine (excreting excess free water, as in water diuresis), while a negative value indicates concentration (reabsorbing free water back into the body, as with ADH action), making it a direct functional readout of urinary diluting/concentrating capacity.

incorrectas.A: Fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) measures the percentage of filtered sodium that is excreted and is used clinically to distinguish prerenal azotemia from acute tubular necrosis, not to assess water handling.
incorrectas.B: Filtration fraction is the ratio of GFR to renal plasma flow, reflecting what fraction of plasma flowing through the glomerulus is filtered — a measure of glomerular hemodynamics, unrelated to urinary dilution or concentration.
incorrectas.D: Creatinine clearance approximates GFR by measuring how efficiently creatinine is cleared from plasma into urine; it tells you about filtration rate, not about the nephron's ability to separate water from solute.

preguntas.q: A patient taking which class of diuretics is most likely to have a free-water clearance (CH2O) of approximately 0?

e.correcta: Loop diuretics block the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, the primary diluting segment of the nephron responsible for generating both the dilute tubular fluid needed for water excretion and the medullary hypertonicity needed for water reabsorption. By disabling this transporter, loop diuretics prevent the kidney from either diluting or concentrating urine effectively, so urine osmolality approaches that of plasma and CH2O approaches zero.

incorrectas.A: Thiazide diuretics inhibit the Na+-Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, impairing urinary dilution (since the DCT is also a diluting segment) but they do not disrupt the medullary countercurrent gradient built by the thick ascending limb, so concentrating ability is relatively preserved and CH2O is not driven to zero the way loop diuretics do.
incorrectas.C: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors act in the proximal tubule to block bicarbonate reabsorption, causing a mild diuresis, but they do not act on the diluting segments and have minimal effect on the kidney's ability to dilute or concentrate urine.
incorrectas.D: Potassium-sparing diuretics act on the collecting duct (blocking ENaC or aldosterone's effects) to reduce potassium secretion, but they do not impair the loop's countercurrent multiplication, so urinary dilution/concentration capacity remains largely intact.

preguntas.q: Cholinomimetic drugs exert their effects by mimicking which endogenous neurotransmitter?

e.correcta: Cholinomimetics are drugs that mimic acetylcholine, either by directly binding and activating muscarinic or nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (direct agonists like bethanechol and pilocarpine) or by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase to increase endogenous acetylcholine levels at the synapse (indirect agonists like neostigmine). This class produces classic parasympathomimetic effects: increased secretions, smooth muscle contraction (bronchoconstriction, increased GI motility, bladder contraction), and bradycardia via M2 receptors in the heart.

incorrectas.B: Dopamine is the neurotransmitter targeted by drugs like levodopa and dopamine agonists used in Parkinson disease, and by dopamine receptor agonists/antagonists in cardiovascular and psychiatric pharmacology — a distinct pathway from the cholinergic system that cholinomimetics act on.
incorrectas.A: Norepinephrine is the primary neurotransmitter of the sympathetic nervous system, and drugs that mimic it (sympathomimetics like phenylephrine or albuterol) act on adrenergic receptors, producing effects largely opposite to the parasympathomimetic actions of cholinomimetics.
incorrectas.D: Serotonin is targeted by drugs such as SSRIs and triptans acting on serotonin receptors in the CNS and gut, an entirely separate neurotransmitter system from the acetylcholine-based mechanism that defines cholinomimetics.

preguntas.q: Which class of acetylcholine receptor is found predominantly in effector tissues such as the heart, smooth muscle, brain, and glands?

e.correcta: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors are metabotropic G-protein-coupled receptors (M1-M5) located on the effector organs innervated by postganglionic parasympathetic fibers — the heart, smooth muscle of the gut/bladder/airways, exocrine glands, and various sites in the CNS. Because they signal through second messenger cascades (Gq or Gi pathways) rather than direct ion flux, their effects tend to be slower in onset but modulate ongoing organ function, which is why the parasympathetic 'rest and digest' effects (slowed heart rate, increased secretions, smooth muscle tone) are mediated through these receptors.

incorrectas.A: Nicotinic Nm receptors are ligand-gated ion channels located at the neuromuscular junction on skeletal muscle, mediating fast, direct depolarization for muscle contraction — not the visceral effector tissues described in the question.
incorrectas.B: Nicotinic Nn receptors are ligand-gated ion channels found at autonomic ganglia (both sympathetic and parasympathetic) and the adrenal medulla, mediating fast synaptic transmission between pre- and postganglionic neurons, distinct from the slower metabotropic signaling in visceral effector organs.
incorrectas.D: Adrenergic alpha receptors respond to norepinephrine/epinephrine, not acetylcholine, and belong to the sympathetic (adrenergic) rather than cholinergic signaling system, so they are unrelated to the muscarinic receptors described here.

preguntas.q: The M1 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor is coupled to which G-protein subtype?

e.correcta: M1 receptors couple to Gq, which activates phospholipase C to cleave PIP2 into IP3 and DAG. IP3 triggers release of intracellular calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum while DAG activates protein kinase C, together increasing intracellular calcium and downstream signaling — the same Gq pathway shared by M1 and M3 receptors, which is a useful mnemonic pairing (the 'odd' muscarinic receptors M1 and M3 are Gq-coupled).

incorrectas.A: Gi is the G-protein used by the M2 muscarinic receptor (and alpha-2 adrenergic receptors), which inhibits adenylyl cyclase to lower cAMP — a different pathway from the PLC-driven calcium signaling of M1.
incorrectas.B: Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase to raise cAMP and is used by receptors like beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors and H2 histamine receptors, not by any muscarinic acetylcholine receptor.
incorrectas.D: Go is a less classically tested G-protein subtype involved in some neuronal signaling pathways, but it is not the G-protein taught for M1 receptor coupling in standard Step 1 muscarinic receptor pharmacology.

preguntas.q: The M2 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor found in cardiac tissue is coupled to which G-protein subtype?

e.correcta: M2 receptors couple to Gi, which inhibits adenylyl cyclase and thereby decreases intracellular cAMP. In the heart, this reduces the funny current (If) and calcium currents in the SA and AV nodes, slowing the rate of spontaneous depolarization and conduction velocity — the mechanism behind vagally-mediated bradycardia and AV nodal slowing, and part of why M2 is the 'even-numbered' exception among the Gq-coupled M1/M3/M5 receptors.

incorrectas.A: Gq is the G-protein used by M1, M3, and M5 muscarinic receptors, activating phospholipase C to raise intracellular calcium via IP3/DAG — the opposite signaling direction from the cAMP-lowering Gi pathway that defines M2.
incorrectas.B: Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase to increase cAMP, which would speed up cardiac conduction (as beta-1 adrenergic stimulation does) rather than slow it, so it is inconsistent with M2's bradycardic, cAMP-lowering effect.
incorrectas.D: G12/13 proteins typically signal through Rho-GTPase pathways affecting cytoskeletal rearrangement and are not part of the classic muscarinic receptor G-protein coupling scheme tested for M2.

preguntas.q: The M3 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor is coupled to which G-protein subtype?

e.correcta: M3 receptors are Gq-coupled, activating phospholipase C to cleave PIP2 into IP3 and DAG; IP3 releases intracellular calcium (driving smooth muscle contraction and glandular secretion) while DAG activates PKC. This is the same pathway used by M1, explaining why M3 activation produces bronchoconstriction, increased GI/bladder smooth muscle tone, and increased salivary, lacrimal, and sweat gland secretion — all classic muscarinic (SLUDGE-type) effects.

incorrectas.A: Gi, which inhibits adenylyl cyclase, is the pathway used by M2 receptors in the heart, not M3; using Gi for M3 would not explain the calcium-driven secretory and contractile effects M3 activation actually produces.
incorrectas.C: Gs increases cAMP via adenylyl cyclase stimulation, a pathway associated with receptors like beta-adrenergic and H2 histamine receptors, and does not match the PLC/calcium mechanism that drives M3-mediated smooth muscle contraction and secretion.
incorrectas.D: Gt (transducin) is the G-protein involved in phototransduction in retinal rod and cone cells, entirely unrelated to muscarinic acetylcholine receptor signaling in peripheral effector tissues.

preguntas.q: The M2 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor exerts its primary physiological effects on which organ?

e.correcta: M2 receptors are densely expressed in the heart, particularly at the SA and AV nodes, where vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation activates them to slow heart rate and AV conduction via Gi-mediated inhibition of adenylyl cyclase. This makes M2 the key mediator of parasympathetic cardiac control, distinguishing it functionally from the Gq-coupled M1/M3 receptors that act on glands and smooth muscle elsewhere in the body.

incorrectas.A: The bladder detrusor muscle is primarily under M3 receptor control, where Gq-mediated calcium signaling triggers detrusor contraction for voiding — a different receptor subtype and organ from M2's cardiac role.
incorrectas.C: Lacrimal (and salivary) gland secretion is driven by M3 receptors, which use Gq signaling to increase intracellular calcium and stimulate glandular secretion, not M2, which is concentrated in cardiac tissue.
incorrectas.D: Bronchial smooth muscle tone is regulated by M3 receptors, whose Gq-coupled activation causes bronchoconstriction; M2 receptors have comparatively minor effects on airway smooth muscle relative to their major cardiac role.

preguntas.q: Activation of M2 muscarinic receptors at the SA node produces which effect on heart rate?

e.correcta: M2 receptor activation at the SA node couples to Gi, inhibiting adenylyl cyclase and reducing cAMP, which slows the funny current (If) responsible for the pacemaker's spontaneous phase 4 depolarization. The net effect is a decreased rate of SA node firing and thus decreased heart rate — the physiological basis of vagally-mediated bradycardia, and why acetylcholinesterase inhibitor toxicity or cholinergic agonist overdose classically causes bradycardia.

incorrectas.A: Increased heart rate would result from sympathetic beta-1 adrenergic stimulation (Gs-coupled, raising cAMP), which is the opposite signaling direction from the Gi-mediated cAMP reduction produced by M2 activation.
incorrectas.B: M2 activation does produce a measurable, predictable physiological change (bradycardia) rather than no effect; parasympathetic tone via the vagus nerve is a major continuous regulator of resting heart rate.
incorrectas.D: The chronotropic effect of M2 activation is a consistent, mechanistically predictable decrease in rate rather than an irregular or unpredictable pattern, since it acts through a well-defined ion channel and cAMP pathway at the SA node.

preguntas.q: M2 muscarinic receptor activation at the AV node produces which effect on conduction velocity?

o.D: Conduction block only at supratherapeutic doses

e.correcta: M2 receptors at the AV node signal through Gi to lower cAMP and reduce calcium currents that normally support the slow conduction already characteristic of this node. This further slows conduction velocity through the AV node, prolonging the PR interval — the mechanism exploited therapeutically by drugs that increase vagal tone (e.g., digoxin) to control ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation, and the reason cholinergic toxicity can precipitate AV block.

incorrectas.A: Increased AV nodal conduction velocity would occur with sympathetic (beta-1, Gs-mediated) stimulation, which raises cAMP and calcium currents — the opposite of the Gi-mediated slowing produced by M2 activation.
incorrectas.B: M2 stimulation has a clear, dose-dependent slowing effect on AV conduction; it is not without effect, and this property is clinically exploited for rate control in supraventricular arrhythmias.
incorrectas.D: Even at therapeutic parasympathetic tone, M2 activation measurably slows AV conduction (increasing the PR interval); complete block is an extreme endpoint of excessive cholinergic activity, not the only level at which conduction is affected.

preguntas.q: M2 muscarinic receptor agonism produces which effect on atrial contractility?

o.D: Increased ventricular but not atrial contractility

e.correcta: M2 receptors, concentrated in the atria (particularly the SA and AV nodes), couple to Gi to reduce cAMP and calcium influx during the cardiac action potential, which decreases the force of atrial contraction alongside their well-known effects on heart rate and conduction velocity. This reflects the overall parasympathetic (vagal) dampening of cardiac activity, distinct from the sympathetic beta-1 pathway that increases contractility via Gs/cAMP.

incorrectas.B: M2 stimulation is not contractility-neutral in the atria; it has a real negative inotropic effect there, consistent with its Gi-mediated reduction of cAMP and calcium currents.
incorrectas.A: Increased contractility is the effect of sympathetic beta-1 stimulation (positive inotropy via Gs/cAMP/PKA-mediated calcium handling), which is functionally opposite to the negative inotropic effect produced by parasympathetic M2 activation.
incorrectas.D: M2 receptor density and functional parasympathetic innervation are much greater in the atria than the ventricles, and the effect described is a decrease, not an increase, so this option misrepresents both the chamber specificity and the direction of the effect.

preguntas.q: Which muscarinic acetylcholine receptor subtype is found on exocrine glands, the bladder detrusor, and smooth muscle throughout the body?

e.correcta: M3 receptors are Gq-coupled and widely distributed on smooth muscle (bladder detrusor, bronchi, GI tract, vasculature) and exocrine glands (salivary, lacrimal, sweat), where activation raises intracellular calcium via the IP3/DAG pathway to drive contraction or secretion. This broad distribution explains why M3 agonists like bethanechol are used for urinary retention (detrusor contraction) and why drugs like pilocarpine stimulate salivary and lacrimal secretion in conditions such as Sjögren syndrome.

incorrectas.A: M1 receptors are also Gq-coupled but are located mainly in the CNS, enteric nervous system ganglia, and gastric parietal cells (mediating acid secretion), not the broad glandular/smooth muscle distribution described for the bladder and generalized smooth muscle in this question.
incorrectas.B: M2 receptors are Gi-coupled and concentrated in the heart (SA and AV nodes), mediating bradycardia and slowed conduction rather than the glandular and generalized smooth muscle effects being asked about.
incorrectas.D: M4 receptors are located primarily in the CNS, particularly the striatum, where they modulate dopaminergic signaling, and are not the receptor responsible for peripheral glandular secretion or bladder/smooth muscle contraction.

preguntas.q: In a healthy patient with intact vascular endothelium, activation of endothelial M3 receptors indirectly produces which vascular effect, mediated by which molecule?

e.correcta: Acetylcholine acting on M3 receptors on healthy vascular endothelial cells activates endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), increasing nitric oxide production. NO diffuses into adjacent vascular smooth muscle, activates guanylate cyclase to raise cGMP, and causes smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation — an indirect endothelium-dependent mechanism, in contrast to the direct M3-mediated contraction seen in other smooth muscle like the bladder or bronchi.

incorrectas.A: Endothelin-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor released by endothelial cells in response to different stimuli (such as shear stress or angiotensin II), not the mediator of the cholinergic, NO-dependent vasodilation described here.
incorrectas.C: Thromboxane A2, produced mainly by platelets, promotes vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation, which is the opposite effect and an unrelated pathway to the NO-mediated vasodilation triggered by endothelial M3 activation.
incorrectas.D: Prostacyclin (PGI2) does cause vasodilation and is produced by endothelial cells, but the classic mechanism taught for acetylcholine/M3-mediated endothelium-dependent vasodilation is specifically through nitric oxide, not prostacyclin.

preguntas.q: In a patient with atherosclerosis and damaged vascular endothelium, M3 receptor activation on vascular smooth muscle directly produces which effect?

e.correcta: When the endothelium is damaged, as in atherosclerosis, it can no longer produce adequate nitric oxide in response to acetylcholine. Acetylcholine then acts directly on M3 receptors located on the underlying vascular smooth muscle itself, triggering Gq-mediated calcium release and direct smooth muscle contraction, producing paradoxical vasoconstriction — a phenomenon used clinically (acetylcholine provocation testing) to detect endothelial dysfunction in coronary arteries.

incorrectas.A: Nitric-oxide-mediated vasodilation requires an intact, functioning endothelium to convert acetylcholine's signal into NO production; in atherosclerotic vessels this endothelial step is impaired, so this protective pathway is lost rather than being the actual outcome.
incorrectas.B: There is a vascular effect in diseased vessels — it is simply reversed from the normal response; the smooth muscle's own M3 receptors are still stimulated directly, producing constriction rather than no response at all.
incorrectas.D: Prostacyclin-mediated vasodilation, like nitric oxide, depends on endothelial synthesis and release; damaged endothelium in atherosclerosis cannot reliably generate this dilatory signal, which is precisely why the unopposed direct smooth muscle M3 effect (constriction) predominates.

preguntas.q: Bethanechol, used to treat postoperative and neurogenic urinary retention, belongs to which drug class?

e.correcta: Bethanechol is a direct-acting muscarinic agonist (cholinomimetic) that is resistant to acetylcholinesterase degradation, allowing it to directly stimulate M3 receptors on the bladder detrusor muscle to promote contraction and voiding, as well as M1/M3 receptors elsewhere. Its selectivity for muscarinic over nicotinic receptors and resistance to breakdown make it useful specifically for urinary retention and, less commonly, GI hypomotility, without significant nicotinic (ganglionic/neuromuscular) side effects.

incorrectas.A: Anticholinesterases (like neostigmine or physostigmine) work indirectly by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase to raise endogenous acetylcholine levels, whereas bethanechol binds muscarinic receptors directly itself rather than acting through enzyme inhibition.
incorrectas.B: Muscarinic antagonists (like oxybutynin) block M3 receptors on the bladder to relax the detrusor and are used for the opposite condition — overactive bladder/urge incontinence — rather than for promoting bladder emptying like bethanechol does.
incorrectas.D: Alpha-1 adrenergic antagonists (like tamsulosin) relax smooth muscle in the bladder neck and prostate to relieve outlet obstruction in BPH; they act on the sympathetic adrenergic system rather than the cholinergic system bethanechol targets.

preguntas.q: Pilocarpine, used topically to treat closed-angle glaucoma and xerostomia, belongs to which drug class?

e.correcta: Pilocarpine is a direct-acting muscarinic agonist that predominantly stimulates M3 receptors, causing pupillary sphincter and ciliary muscle contraction (useful in closed-angle glaucoma to open the trabecular meshwork and lower intraocular pressure) and stimulating exocrine gland secretion (useful for dry mouth in Sjögren syndrome). Because it directly activates the receptor rather than relying on endogenous acetylcholine, its effects are more predictable and it penetrates tissues (including the cornea) well as a small tertiary amine.

incorrectas.B: Muscarinic antagonists like atropine or tropicamide dilate the pupil and relax the ciliary muscle (cycloplegia) — effects opposite to pilocarpine's — and would worsen rather than treat closed-angle glaucoma by further narrowing the anterior chamber angle.
incorrectas.C: Nicotinic ganglionic blockers act at autonomic ganglia to interrupt both sympathetic and parasympathetic transmission, producing widespread autonomic effects rather than the selective, direct M3-mediated ocular and glandular stimulation seen with pilocarpine.
incorrectas.D: Beta-adrenergic agonists (like timolol's opposite, or epinephrine) act on the sympathetic system and can be used in open-angle glaucoma (e.g., beta-blockers to reduce aqueous humor production), but they are pharmacologically and mechanistically distinct from muscarinic agonists like pilocarpine.

preguntas.q: Through its action on M3 receptors in exocrine glands, pilocarpine acts as a potent stimulator of which secretions, making it useful in Sjögren syndrome-related xerostomia?

e.correcta: Pilocarpine activates M3 receptors on lacrimal, sweat, and salivary glands, triggering the Gq/IP3/calcium pathway that drives glandular secretion. This makes it clinically useful for treating xerostomia (dry mouth) and dry eyes in Sjögren syndrome, where autoimmune destruction of exocrine glands reduces natural secretion — pilocarpine helps stimulate whatever residual glandular tissue remains functional.

incorrectas.A: Gastric acid secretion is influenced by M1 (and M3) receptors on parietal cells and enteric neurons, but this is not the classic clinical indication or the specific set of secretions (tears, sweat, saliva) that make pilocarpine useful in Sjögren syndrome.
incorrectas.C: While muscarinic stimulation can influence pancreatic exocrine secretion to some degree, this is not the primary or clinically relevant secretory effect being tested — pilocarpine's therapeutic use centers on lacrimal and salivary gland stimulation.
incorrectas.D: Bile secretion is regulated mainly by hormonal (CCK, secretin) and hepatic mechanisms rather than direct muscarinic stimulation of exocrine glands, and is not part of pilocarpine's recognized clinical effect profile.

preguntas.q: Carbachol, used in glaucoma and to induce miosis intraoperatively, acts as an agonist at which acetylcholine receptor type(s)?

o.D: Neither — it is a partial antagonist

e.correcta: Carbachol is a direct-acting cholinergic agonist that activates both muscarinic and nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, unlike more selective agents such as bethanechol (muscarinic-selective) or nicotine (nicotinic-selective). Its broad receptor activity makes it useful topically in ophthalmology to produce miosis and lower intraocular pressure (via M3 activation in the eye), while its nicotinic activity is less clinically exploited but explains its structural similarity to acetylcholine itself.

incorrectas.A: Restricting the answer to muscarinic-only would describe drugs like bethanechol or pilocarpine, which lack the nicotinic activity that distinguishes carbachol as an agonist at both receptor families.
incorrectas.B: Restricting the answer to nicotinic-only would describe a drug like nicotine itself, which lacks meaningful muscarinic activity, whereas carbachol's clinical ophthalmologic use depends specifically on its muscarinic (M3) agonism.
incorrectas.D: Carbachol is an agonist, not an antagonist, at cholinergic receptors — it directly activates rather than blocks receptor signaling, which is precisely why it produces cholinergic effects like miosis rather than blocking them.

preguntas.q: Methacholine, used diagnostically to provoke bronchoconstriction in suspected asthma, belongs to which drug class?

e.correcta: Methacholine is a direct-acting muscarinic agonist that predominantly activates M3 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, triggering the Gq/IP3/calcium pathway that causes bronchoconstriction. This property is harnessed diagnostically in the methacholine challenge test: patients with airway hyperreactivity (as in asthma) show an exaggerated bronchoconstrictive response and a significant drop in FEV1 at lower doses than would affect a healthy airway.

incorrectas.A: Beta-2 adrenergic agonists (like albuterol) relax bronchial smooth muscle via Gs/cAMP signaling and are used to treat, not provoke, bronchoconstriction — the pharmacologic opposite of what methacholine is used for.
incorrectas.C: Leukotriene receptor antagonists (like montelukast) block leukotriene-mediated bronchoconstriction and inflammation as asthma controller therapy; they do not provoke bronchoconstriction and work through an entirely different receptor system than muscarinic agonism.
incorrectas.D: Mast cell stabilizers (like cromolyn) prevent degranulation and mediator release to reduce allergic bronchoconstriction as a preventive therapy, which is a distinct mechanism from methacholine's direct muscarinic receptor activation used for diagnostic provocation.

preguntas.q: Which agent is administered by inhalation during pulmonary function testing to provoke bronchospasm and aid in diagnosing asthma?

e.correcta: Methacholine is inhaled during bronchoprovocation testing because it directly stimulates M3 muscarinic receptors on airway smooth muscle, inducing bronchoconstriction. In patients with underlying airway hyperresponsiveness, such as asthma, a much smaller dose produces a significant fall in FEV1 compared to individuals with normal airways, making the methacholine challenge test a sensitive tool to rule in or rule out reactive airway disease when spirometry is otherwise normal.

incorrectas.A: Ipratropium is a muscarinic antagonist that blocks M3 receptors to cause bronchodilation, used therapeutically in COPD and asthma exacerbations — it would relax, not provoke, bronchial smooth muscle, the opposite of what a provocation test requires.
incorrectas.B: Albuterol is a beta-2 agonist that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle via increased cAMP, used as rescue therapy for bronchospasm; it is a bronchodilator, so it could not be used to provoke bronchoconstriction for diagnostic testing.
incorrectas.D: Theophylline is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor that raises cAMP in airway smooth muscle, producing bronchodilation and used as adjunct asthma/COPD therapy — again a bronchodilating agent, not one used to provoke airway narrowing.

preguntas.q: Cholinomimetic drugs act on bronchial smooth muscle to produce which effect, potentially worsening asthma or COPD symptoms?

e.correcta: Cholinomimetics activate M3 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, triggering the Gq-PLC-IP3/DAG pathway that raises intracellular calcium and causes smooth muscle contraction (bronchoconstriction). In patients with reactive airway disease such as asthma or COPD, this cholinergic contraction can exacerbate airflow obstruction and worsen symptoms, which is why cholinesterase inhibitors and direct muscarinic agonists are used cautiously (or are contraindicated) in these populations, and why muscarinic antagonists are instead used therapeutically to relax the airway.

incorrectas.A: Relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle would result from beta-2 adrenergic stimulation (via Gs/cAMP) or from blocking muscarinic receptors with an antagonist, not from cholinomimetic (agonist) activity, which pushes airway tone in the opposite direction.
incorrectas.C: Cholinomimetics have a well-documented, clinically significant bronchoconstrictive effect through M3 receptors; this effect is precisely why they carry a caution or contraindication in obstructive airway disease, rather than being negligible.
incorrectas.D: Smooth muscle hypertrophy is a structural, chronic airway remodeling change seen in longstanding asthma, not an acute pharmacologic effect of cholinomimetic receptor activation, which instead produces immediate functional contraction.

preguntas.q: What is the normal range for arterial pH, and what is the outer range still considered compatible with life?

e.correcta: Normal arterial pH is tightly maintained between 7.35 and 7.45 (corresponding to a hydrogen ion concentration around 35-45 nmol/L, roughly 40 nmol/L at the midpoint) through buffering systems, respiratory compensation, and renal acid-base handling. The extreme outer limits still considered compatible with life are approximately 6.8 to 8.0, beyond which enzyme function and cellular processes are too severely disrupted to sustain life — a useful anchor for understanding just how narrow the truly normal range is compared to the survivable extremes.

incorrectas.B: This range is far too wide for both the normal physiologic range and the survivable extremes; actual buffering and compensatory systems cannot maintain function anywhere near pH 6.0 or 9.0, and the true survivable window is narrower (6.8-8.0).
incorrectas.C: This option shifts the compatible-with-life range narrower than it actually is (7.0-7.8) and widens the normal range beyond the tightly regulated 7.35-7.45 window, misrepresenting how narrowly pH is normally controlled.
incorrectas.D: While the normal range (7.35-7.45) is correct, restricting the survivable extreme to 7.0-7.6 is inaccurate — patients can survive (briefly) at more extreme derangements approaching 6.8 or 8.0, reflecting the buffering reserve and compensation mechanisms that extend well beyond the normal range.

preguntas.q: What is the normal average value for arterial pH?

e.correcta: The normal average arterial pH is 7.4, sitting at the midpoint of the tightly regulated normal range of 7.35-7.45, corresponding to a hydrogen ion concentration of about 40 nmol/L. This value reflects the balance achieved by the bicarbonate buffer system, respiratory CO2 elimination, and renal acid excretion/bicarbonate reabsorption working together, and it serves as the reference point from which acidemia (below 7.35) or alkalemia (above 7.45) is defined.

incorrectas.A: 7.35 represents the lower boundary of the normal range (the threshold for acidemia), not the average value; using it as 'the normal pH' would understate the typical resting value, which sits at the midpoint of 7.4.
incorrectas.C: 7.45 represents the upper boundary of the normal range (the threshold for alkalemia), not the average — like 7.35, it marks an edge of normal rather than the typical central value of 7.4.
incorrectas.D: 7.5 falls outside the normal reference range entirely and would be classified as alkalemia; it is neither the average nor even within the accepted normal range for arterial pH.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the reaction combining CO2 and H2O to form the weak acid H2CO3?

e.correcta: Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes the reversible hydration of CO2 into H2CO3, which then rapidly dissociates into H+ and HCO3-. This enzyme is present in red blood cells (for CO2 transport from tissues to lungs) and in renal tubular cells and brush border (for bicarbonate reabsorption and acid excretion), making it the central catalyst linking respiratory CO2 handling to renal acid-base regulation. Because the uncatalyzed reaction is slow, carbonic anhydrase speeds it up roughly a millionfold, which is why drugs like acetazolamide (a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) can produce a measurable metabolic acidosis.

incorrectas.B: Na+/K+-ATPase is the basolateral pump that maintains the Na+ gradient driving secondary active transport throughout the nephron, but it has no role in hydrating CO2 or forming carbonic acid.
incorrectas.C: Aldolase B is a glycolytic/fructose-metabolism enzyme in the liver (deficient in hereditary fructose intolerance) and is unrelated to CO2 hydration or acid-base buffering chemistry.
incorrectas.D: Lactate dehydrogenase interconverts pyruvate and lactate during anaerobic metabolism; it does not catalyze the CO2 + H2O to H2CO3 reaction that defines the bicarbonate buffer system.

preguntas.q: H2CO3 dissociates into which two ions in the bicarbonate buffer system?

e.correcta: Carbonic acid (H2CO3) is a weak acid that reversibly dissociates into a proton (H+) and bicarbonate (HCO3-). This equilibrium is the backbone of the bicarbonate buffer system: when H+ is added to the blood, the reaction shifts left (consuming H+ to form more H2CO3, then CO2), and when H+ is removed, it shifts right, releasing H+ from H2CO3 to minimize the pH change.

incorrectas.B: Carbonate (CO3^2-) is the doubly deprotonated form that would result from losing a second proton from HCO3-, but under physiologic pH this second dissociation is negligible — H2CO3 dissociates essentially completely to HCO3-, not CO3^2-.
incorrectas.C: Sodium is not a product of carbonic acid dissociation; Na+ is simply the common counterion paired with HCO3- in solution (e.g., NaHCO3), but it does not come from splitting H2CO3 itself.
incorrectas.D: Hydroxide (OH-) is generated from water autoionization or strong base dissociation, not from carbonic acid, which releases H+ (not OH-) upon dissociation.

preguntas.q: Non-volatile acids, which cannot be excreted as a gas by the lungs and must instead be buffered and excreted by the kidney, are also known by what other name?

e.correcta: Non-volatile acids are called "fixed" acids because, unlike carbonic acid (which can be converted to CO2 gas and eliminated by the lungs), they cannot leave the body as a gas — they are "fixed" in the blood and must be neutralized by buffers and ultimately excreted by the kidneys as titratable acid or ammonium. This distinction matters clinically because respiratory compensation can rapidly adjust volatile acid (CO2) but the kidney's excretion of fixed acid load takes much longer (hours to days), which is why metabolic acidosis from fixed acids resolves more slowly than respiratory acid-base disturbances.

incorrectas.B: Volatile acid refers specifically to carbonic acid (H2CO3), which is in equilibrium with CO2 gas and can be exhaled by the lungs — the opposite of a fixed/non-volatile acid, which has no gaseous form to expire.
incorrectas.C: Ketogenic describes amino acids or pathways that generate ketone bodies (a cause of fixed acid production in states like DKA), but it is not the general term for acids that cannot be exhaled.
incorrectas.D: A conjugate acid is the species formed when a base accepts a proton (a Bronsted-Lowry chemistry term describing acid-base pairs), not a classification based on whether an acid can be excreted via the lungs.

preguntas.q: Metabolism of sulfur-containing amino acids such as methionine and cysteine generates which non-volatile acid?

e.correcta: Catabolism of sulfur-containing amino acids (methionine and cysteine) liberates sulfate, which combines with water to form sulfuric acid, a strong fixed acid that dissociates completely and must be buffered and excreted renally. This is a major reason a high-protein diet increases the daily fixed acid load and urinary net acid excretion, since more sulfur-containing amino acids are catabolized.

incorrectas.B: Phosphoric acid is generated from phospholipid metabolism (releasing phosphate), a separate dietary/metabolic source of fixed acid distinct from the sulfur-containing amino acid pathway described here.
incorrectas.C: Lactic acid arises from anaerobic glycolysis, typically during strenuous exercise or tissue hypoperfusion, not from amino acid catabolism.
incorrectas.D: Acetoacetic acid is a ketone body produced from fatty acid oxidation/ketogenesis (e.g., in diabetic ketoacidosis or starvation), unrelated to sulfur amino acid breakdown.

preguntas.q: Metabolism of phospholipids generates which non-volatile acid that contributes to the daily fixed acid load?

e.correcta: Breakdown of phospholipids releases phosphate groups that combine with water to form phosphoric acid, one of the two major dietary-derived fixed (non-volatile) acids (alongside sulfuric acid) that the kidney must buffer and excrete daily. Phosphate itself also serves double duty as a urinary buffer (the H2PO4-/HPO4^2- pair, part of titratable acid), so phosphoric acid production and phosphate buffering are closely linked concepts in renal acid-base physiology.

incorrectas.B: Sulfuric acid comes from catabolism of sulfur-containing amino acids like methionine and cysteine, a different dietary source of fixed acid than phospholipid breakdown.
incorrectas.C: Formic acid is a toxic metabolite generated from methanol ingestion via alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase, unrelated to normal phospholipid metabolism.
incorrectas.D: Oxalic acid is produced from ethylene glycol metabolism (antifreeze ingestion) and can precipitate as calcium oxalate crystals in the kidney; it is not a product of phospholipid catabolism.

preguntas.q: A patient with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes develops a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Which non-volatile acids are characteristically elevated in this setting?

e.correcta: In type 1 diabetes, absolute insulin deficiency drives unrestrained lipolysis and hepatic fatty acid oxidation, producing the ketone bodies acetoacetic acid and beta-hydroxybutyric acid faster than they can be buffered or utilized. These ketoacids dissociate to release H+, consuming bicarbonate and producing the classic high anion gap metabolic acidosis of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), which is why urine and serum ketones are checked when DKA is suspected.

incorrectas.B: Sulfuric and phosphoric acid are the routine dietary fixed acids generated from protein and phospholipid metabolism in everyone, not the specific acids that spike in DKA — their production isn't driven by insulin deficiency or ketogenesis.
incorrectas.C: Lactic acid accumulates with tissue hypoperfusion or strenuous exercise (anaerobic glycolysis) and formic acid comes from methanol toxicity; neither is the hallmark acid of diabetic ketoacidosis, though lactic acidosis can coexist if a DKA patient is also hypoperfused.
incorrectas.D: Oxalic acid and glycolic acid are toxic metabolites of ethylene glycol (antifreeze) ingestion, producing a similar high anion gap picture but through a completely different toxicologic mechanism, not diabetic ketogenesis.

preguntas.q: Which non-volatile acid is characteristically elevated after strenuous exercise due to anaerobic metabolism?

e.correcta: During strenuous exercise, oxygen delivery to muscle can't keep pace with demand, so muscle shifts to anaerobic glycolysis, regenerating NAD+ by converting pyruvate to lactate via lactate dehydrogenase. The resulting lactic acid dissociates to release H+, producing a transient fixed-acid (high anion gap) metabolic acidosis that resolves once oxygen delivery is restored and lactate is cleared by the liver (Cori cycle).

incorrectas.B: Formic acid is a toxic byproduct of methanol metabolism (via alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenase), causing metabolic acidosis and retinal/optic nerve toxicity — unrelated to normal exercise physiology.
incorrectas.C: Salicylic acid accumulates in aspirin overdose, producing a mixed respiratory alkalosis (early, from direct respiratory center stimulation) and metabolic acidosis (late), not from exertion.
incorrectas.D: Sulfuric acid is a constant low-level fixed acid from sulfur amino acid catabolism (dietary protein turnover), not something that spikes specifically with anaerobic exercise the way lactate does.

preguntas.q: A patient presents several hours after an aspirin overdose. Which non-volatile acid accumulates and drives the (later) metabolic acidosis phase of the toxicity?

e.correcta: Aspirin is hydrolyzed to salicylic acid, which directly contributes a fixed acid load and also uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, impairing ATP production and promoting anaerobic metabolism and additional organic acid accumulation. The classic salicylate toxicity picture is biphasic: early direct stimulation of the medullary respiratory center causes hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis, while later salicylate and secondary organic acid accumulation produce a superimposed high anion gap metabolic acidosis, yielding a mixed acid-base disorder.

incorrectas.B: Formic acid results from methanol ingestion, a distinct toxic alcohol exposure that causes metabolic acidosis with visual disturbances, not from salicylate metabolism.
incorrectas.C: Oxalic acid results from ethylene glycol ingestion and is associated with calcium oxalate crystalluria and renal injury, a different toxic ingestion than aspirin.
incorrectas.D: Lactic acid can rise secondarily in severe salicylate toxicity due to uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation, but it is not the primary acid that defines aspirin overdose — salicylic acid itself is the direct causative fixed acid.

preguntas.q: Ingestion of methanol leads to accumulation of which toxic non-volatile acid metabolite?

e.correcta: Methanol is metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase to formaldehyde, then by aldehyde dehydrogenase to formic acid, which both produces a high anion gap metabolic acidosis and is directly toxic to the retina and optic nerve, causing the characteristic visual disturbances/blindness of methanol poisoning. Fomepizole (an alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor) is used to block this toxic conversion, the same rationale used in ethylene glycol poisoning.

incorrectas.B: Oxalic acid is the toxic metabolite of ethylene glycol (antifreeze), not methanol, and is notable for precipitating as calcium oxalate crystals in renal tubules.
incorrectas.C: Salicylic acid is the active/toxic metabolite in aspirin overdose, a different ingestion entirely from methanol poisoning.
incorrectas.D: Lactic acid rises with tissue hypoperfusion or anaerobic exercise; while severe methanol toxicity can secondarily elevate lactate, the specific acid metabolite that defines methanol poisoning is formic acid.

preguntas.q: Ingestion of ethylene glycol (antifreeze) leads to accumulation of which toxic non-volatile acid, which can also precipitate as crystals in the renal tubules?

e.correcta: Ethylene glycol is metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase into glycolic acid and ultimately oxalic acid, both contributing to a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Oxalic acid combines with calcium to form calcium oxalate crystals, which deposit in the renal tubules and cause acute kidney injury — a key diagnostic clue (calcium oxalate crystalluria) distinguishing this ingestion from other toxic alcohols.

incorrectas.B: Formic acid is the toxic metabolite specific to methanol ingestion, causing acidosis with retinal toxicity, not the crystal-forming acid seen with ethylene glycol.
incorrectas.C: Salicylic acid is the toxic species in aspirin overdose and does not form renal crystals or arise from antifreeze metabolism.
incorrectas.D: Acetoacetic acid is a ketone body from fatty acid oxidation in states like DKA or starvation, unrelated to ethylene glycol metabolism or renal crystal formation.

preguntas.q: What term describes a substance that minimizes the change in pH of a solution when H+ ions are added or removed?

e.correcta: A buffer is a weak acid/conjugate base pair (or weak base/conjugate acid pair) that can absorb added H+ (via the base component) or release H+ (via the acid component) to resist large swings in pH. Physiologic buffers — bicarbonate/CO2, phosphate, plasma proteins, and hemoglobin — work together to keep blood pH tightly controlled around 7.4 despite continuous acid production from metabolism.

incorrectas.B: A catalyst speeds up the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed (e.g., carbonic anhydrase speeding CO2 hydration), but it does not by itself resist pH change — that is the buffer's job, even though catalysts can accelerate buffer equilibration.
incorrectas.C: A chelator binds metal ions (e.g., EDTA binding calcium) to form stable complexes; this is a completely different chemical function from resisting pH change via proton exchange.
incorrectas.D: An osmolyte is a solute that affects the osmotic pressure/tonicity of a solution (e.g., urea, sorbitol) and has no inherent role in stabilizing pH against added or removed H+.

preguntas.q: Compared to a weak acid, a strong acid such as HCl has which relationship to its pK?

e.correcta: A strong acid dissociates almost completely in solution, meaning it has a large equilibrium (dissociation) constant K; since pK is the negative log of K, a larger K corresponds to a smaller (lower) pK. This inverse logarithmic relationship is why strong acids like HCl have very low (even negative) pK values, while weak acids like carbonic acid or acetic acid, which dissociate only partially, have higher pK values.

incorrectas.B: A higher pK would indicate a smaller dissociation constant, meaning the acid dissociates less completely — that describes a weak acid's behavior, the opposite of what defines a strong acid like HCl.
incorrectas.C: Strong and weak acids by definition have different tendencies to dissociate, which is precisely reflected in different (not equal) pK values; equal pK would mean equal acid strength.
incorrectas.D: Every acid, strong or weak, has a defined equilibrium constant and therefore a defined pK (even if extremely low for very strong acids); "no defined pK" is not a real chemical property.

preguntas.q: When the pH of a buffered solution equals which value are the concentrations of the acid [HA] and conjugate base [A-] forms equal?

e.correcta: This follows directly from the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, pH = pK + log([A-]/[HA]): when pH equals pK, the log term must equal zero, which only occurs when [A-]/[HA] = 1, i.e., the concentrations of conjugate base and acid are equal. This is also the point of maximum buffering capacity, since the buffer has equal reserves to neutralize either added acid or added base.

incorrectas.B: The isoelectric point is the pH at which a molecule (typically a protein or amino acid) carries no net electrical charge, a concept relevant to protein chemistry/electrophoresis, not to when [HA] equals [A-] in a simple acid-base buffer pair.
incorrectas.C: A pH of zero represents an extremely strong acidic solution, unrelated to the equilibrium condition where acid and conjugate base concentrations are equal; that condition depends on the buffer's specific pK, not on pH being zero.
incorrectas.D: The pH of pure water (7.0) is simply the neutral point where [H+] = [OH-]; it only equals the point of [HA] = [A-] for a buffer whose pK happens to be 7.0, which is not true for buffers like bicarbonate (pK 6.1) or phosphate (pK 6.8).

preguntas.q: Buffers are most effective at resisting pH change within approximately how many pH units of their pK?

e.correcta: A buffer works best within about ±1.0 pH unit of its pK, because in that range both the protonated (HA) and deprotonated (A-) forms are present in sufficient quantity (roughly between a 10:1 and 1:10 ratio) to absorb added acid or base without a large pH swing. Outside this range, one form becomes so scarce that the buffer's capacity to resist further pH change collapses — this is why the bicarbonate system (pK 6.1) is a relatively weak buffer at physiologic pH 7.4, yet remains effective because it is an open system continuously replenished by respiratory CO2 elimination and renal HCO3- regulation.

incorrectas.B: A range of only ±0.1 pH units would be far too narrow to describe practical buffering capacity — real buffers maintain meaningful reserve capacity over roughly a full pH unit on either side of the pK, not a tenth of a unit.
incorrectas.C: ±2.5 pH units is too wide; by that distance from the pK, the ratio of A- to HA (or vice versa) becomes so lopsided (over 300:1) that the solution's pH changes almost as if no buffer were present.
incorrectas.D: ±4.0 pH units is far beyond any meaningful buffering range for a single conjugate acid-base pair; buffering capacity is essentially exhausted well before reaching that distance from the pK.

preguntas.q: In the bicarbonate buffer system, which species represents the [A-] (conjugate base) form?

e.correcta: Bicarbonate (HCO3-) is the conjugate base [A-] of the buffer pair, formed when carbonic acid (H2CO3, the [HA] form) donates a proton. This pair — HCO3-/H2CO3 (with H2CO3 in rapid equilibrium with dissolved CO2) — is the principal extracellular buffer of the blood, and its concentration is regulated primarily by the kidney (reabsorption/regeneration of HCO3-).

incorrectas.B: CO2 is in equilibrium with carbonic acid and functionally serves as the [HA] (acid) side of the buffer pair since it is regulated by ventilation, not the conjugate base [A-] side.
incorrectas.C: H2CO3 (carbonic acid) is the protonated [HA] form of this buffer pair; it is what dissociates to release H+ and form HCO3-, so it is the acid, not the conjugate base.
incorrectas.D: H2PO4- is the acid [HA] form of the separate phosphate buffer pair (H2PO4-/HPO4^2-), a different buffer system entirely from the bicarbonate pair being described.

preguntas.q: In the bicarbonate buffer system, which species functionally represents the [HA] (acid) form, existing in equilibrium with H2CO3?

e.correcta: CO2 is in rapid equilibrium with carbonic acid (CO2 + H2O <-> H2CO3), and because carbonic anhydrase drives this equilibrium heavily toward CO2 (about a 400:1 ratio of CO2 to H2CO3), CO2 functionally serves as the [HA] (acid) reservoir of the bicarbonate buffer system. This is clinically crucial because it means the "acid" side of the body's most important buffer pair is under direct respiratory control — the lungs can rapidly adjust CO2 (and thus the HA/A- ratio) to compensate for metabolic acid-base disturbances.

incorrectas.B: HCO3- is the conjugate base [A-] of this buffer pair, not the acid form — it is what remains after H2CO3 (via CO2) donates a proton.
incorrectas.C: HPO4^2- is the conjugate base of the separate phosphate buffer pair (H2PO4-/HPO4^2-), unrelated to the bicarbonate/CO2 equilibrium described here.
incorrectas.D: NH4+ (ammonium) is the product of renal ammoniagenesis, an important vehicle for excreting fixed H+ in the urine, but it is not part of the HCO3-/CO2 buffer pair chemistry.

preguntas.q: What is the pK of the HCO3-/CO2 buffer pair?

e.correcta: The HCO3-/CO2 buffer pair has a pK of 6.1, which is more than a full pH unit below the normal blood pH of 7.4. On paper this makes it a mathematically weak buffer at physiologic pH (since [HA] is far less abundant than [A-]), yet it remains the dominant blood buffer because it is an open system: the lungs continuously regulate the CO2 (acid) side and the kidneys regulate the HCO3- (base) side, giving it enormous effective buffering capacity despite the unfavorable pK.

incorrectas.B: 6.8 is the pK of the phosphate buffer pair (H2PO4-/HPO4^2-), a separate buffer system that is quantitatively less important in plasma (present in lower concentration) but important intracellularly and in the urine.
incorrectas.C: 7.4 is the normal physiologic blood pH itself, not the pK of the bicarbonate buffer — the fact that pK (6.1) is lower than blood pH (7.4) is exactly why plasma HCO3- concentration so greatly exceeds CO2/H2CO3 concentration.
incorrectas.D: 4.2 is far too low for any of the physiologic buffer pairs discussed in acid-base physiology and does not correspond to the bicarbonate system.

preguntas.q: What is the pK of the H2PO4-/HPO4(2-) buffer pair?

e.correcta: The phosphate buffer pair (H2PO4-/HPO4^2-) has a pK of 6.8, which is much closer to physiologic urine pH than the bicarbonate system's pK of 6.1, making phosphate an effective urinary buffer for titratable acid excretion even though it is present in much smaller quantities in plasma. Because it is non-volatile (cannot be regenerated/eliminated via the lungs like the bicarbonate/CO2 pair), phosphate is not the primary blood buffer, but it plays an important role in buffering H+ secreted into the renal tubular lumen.

incorrectas.B: 6.1 is the pK of the bicarbonate/CO2 buffer pair, the dominant plasma buffer, not the phosphate pair.
incorrectas.C: 7.4 is the normal physiologic pH of blood, not the pK of any single buffer pair discussed here.
incorrectas.D: 9.2 is far higher than the phosphate buffer's actual pK and would make phosphate a poor buffer at physiologic or urinary pH ranges, which is not the case.

preguntas.q: Which plasma component can act as a buffer for H+, with changes in its buffering also affecting free Ca2+ levels?

e.correcta: Plasma proteins, particularly albumin, contain numerous histidine residues with side chains that can accept or donate protons, allowing them to act as buffers for H+ in the extracellular fluid. Because albumin also binds a significant fraction of circulating calcium, changes in H+ concentration alter the protein's net charge and calcium-binding affinity — acidosis tends to displace bound calcium (increasing ionized Ca2+), while alkalosis increases calcium binding to albumin (decreasing ionized Ca2+ and potentially causing symptomatic hypocalcemia, e.g., with hyperventilation).

incorrectas.B: Hemoglobin is the most important intracellular buffer, particularly in red blood cells (deoxyhemoglobin buffers H+ generated from CO2 transport), but it is not the plasma protein classically linked to calcium binding/buffering interactions.
incorrectas.C: Phosphate is a buffer present in smaller plasma quantities and is important intracellularly and in the urine, but it is not the buffer specifically tied to the calcium-binding relationship described here.
incorrectas.D: Bicarbonate is the principal extracellular buffer for CO2-derived acid, but it does not have the protein structure (histidine side chains, calcium-binding sites) that links buffering capacity to ionized calcium levels.

preguntas.q: What is the most significant intracellular buffer for H+ in the body?

e.correcta: Deoxyhemoglobin is the most important intracellular buffer for H+, largely because of its high concentration in red blood cells and its histidine residues, which have a pK favorable for buffering at physiologic pH once oxygen has been released to tissues. This buffering is functionally tied to the Bohr effect and CO2 transport: as red cells pick up CO2 in the tissues and generate H+ via carbonic anhydrase, hemoglobin releases O2 (facilitating tissue oxygen delivery) and simultaneously takes on a conformation that binds H+ more avidly, minimizing the local pH drop.

incorrectas.B: Albumin is an important extracellular (plasma) buffer with buffering histidine residues, but it does not match hemoglobin's dominance as the primary intracellular buffer given hemoglobin's far greater intracellular concentration within red blood cells.
incorrectas.C: Phosphate contributes to intracellular buffering to some degree and is important in the urine as a titratable acid buffer, but it is not the single most significant intracellular buffer overall — that role belongs to hemoglobin.
incorrectas.D: Oxyhemoglobin is actually a weaker buffer than deoxyhemoglobin because oxygen binding lowers the pK of hemoglobin's histidine residues, reducing its H+ binding affinity at physiologic pH — this is precisely why deoxyhemoglobin, not oxyhemoglobin, is the superior buffer.

preguntas.q: Which form of hemoglobin is the better buffer at physiologic pH: oxyhemoglobin or deoxyhemoglobin?

o.D: Neither form of hemoglobin buffers H+

e.correcta: Deoxyhemoglobin has a pK of about 7.9, much closer to physiologic pH (7.4) than oxyhemoglobin's pK of about 6.7, making deoxyhemoglobin the far more effective buffer for H+ at physiologic pH (recall buffers work best within about 1 pH unit of their pK). This is physiologically elegant: in peripheral tissues, hemoglobin releases O2 and converts to the deoxy form right as CO2-derived H+ is being generated locally, so the conformational change that releases oxygen simultaneously improves hemoglobin's capacity to buffer the incoming acid load (the structural basis of the Bohr effect).

incorrectas.B: Oxyhemoglobin has a pK (~6.7) that is farther from physiologic pH than deoxyhemoglobin's, making it a comparatively weaker buffer for H+ under normal blood pH conditions — the opposite of what is needed for effective buffering at 7.4.
incorrectas.C: The two forms do not buffer equally; their differing pK values (6.7 vs. 7.9) mean deoxyhemoglobin has a clear, physiologically important advantage in H+ buffering capacity near pH 7.4.
incorrectas.D: Both forms of hemoglobin can bind and buffer H+ via histidine residues; the difference is one of degree (better vs. worse buffering pK), not an all-or-nothing capability.

preguntas.q: In the lumen of the early proximal convoluted tubule (PCT), H2CO3 is converted to CO2 and H2O by which enzyme, located on the brush border?

e.correcta: Brush border (luminal, membrane-bound) carbonic anhydrase (type IV) rapidly dehydrates the H2CO3 formed in the tubular lumen (from secreted H+ combining with filtered HCO3-) back into CO2 and H2O, allowing CO2 to freely diffuse into the tubular cell. This luminal step is essential for efficient bicarbonate reabsorption in the PCT — without it, the reaction would proceed too slowly and much of the filtered HCO3- would be lost in the urine.

incorrectas.B: NHE3 is the luminal Na+/H+ exchanger that secretes H+ into the tubular lumen in exchange for reabsorbing Na+, providing the H+ that combines with filtered HCO3- to form H2CO3 in the first place — but NHE3 itself does not catalyze the H2CO3 to CO2/H2O conversion.
incorrectas.C: H+-ATPase is a luminal proton pump found more prominently in the collecting duct (intercalated cells), actively secreting H+ against a gradient; it does not catalyze the dehydration of H2CO3.
incorrectas.D: Aquaporin-1 is a water channel in the proximal tubule that allows passive water reabsorption; it has no enzymatic role in carbonic acid chemistry.

preguntas.q: Inside the cells of the early proximal convoluted tubule, H2CO3 is converted to CO2 and H2O by which form of carbonic anhydrase?

e.correcta: Within the PCT cell cytoplasm, intracellular carbonic anhydrase (type II) catalyzes the reverse reaction: CO2 that has diffused in from the lumen combines with H2O to reform H2CO3, which then dissociates into H+ (secreted back into the lumen via NHE3, continuing the cycle) and HCO3- (which exits across the basolateral membrane into the blood, completing net HCO3- reabsorption). This intracellular step is what actually regenerates the bicarbonate that ends up back in the plasma, distinguishing it from the brush border enzyme's job of breaking down luminal H2CO3.

incorrectas.B: Brush border carbonic anhydrase (type IV) works on the luminal side of the cell to dehydrate H2CO3 into CO2 and H2O so CO2 can enter the cell — it is a distinct, extracellularly-facing enzyme from the intracellular (cytoplasmic) form that generates H2CO3 inside the cell.
incorrectas.C: While mitochondrial carbonic anhydrase isoforms exist, the enzyme responsible for the described intracellular hydration reaction in proximal tubule bicarbonate handling is the cytoplasmic isoform, not one restricted to mitochondria.
incorrectas.D: Carbonic anhydrase is not membrane-bound on the basolateral surface in this pathway; the basolateral membrane instead contains the Na+/HCO3- cotransporter that moves the regenerated HCO3- into blood, while the enzymatic hydration step occurs freely in the cytoplasm.

preguntas.q: Does renal reabsorption of filtered HCO3- result in net secretion of H+ into the urine?

o.A: No — the H+ secreted is consumed reforming H2CO3/CO2 and is not net excreted
o.B: Yes — every H+ secreted during HCO3- reabsorption is excreted in the urine
o.C: Yes, but only in the distal nephron
o.D: No — HCO3- reabsorption does not involve H+ secretion at all

e.correcta: During bicarbonate reabsorption, secreted H+ combines with filtered HCO3- in the lumen to form H2CO3, which is broken down by brush border carbonic anhydrase into CO2 and H2O that diffuse back into the cell — the H+ is essentially recycled to regenerate intracellular HCO3-, not lost into the final urine. Because the H+ is consumed in this cycle rather than truly excreted, HCO3- reabsorption produces little to no net change in tubular fluid pH, in contrast to titratable acid and ammonium excretion, which do represent genuine net acid excretion.

incorrectas.B: This mistakes the mechanism: while H+ is indeed secreted into the lumen, it is captured by filtered HCO3- and converted back to CO2/H2O rather than passing through to the urine, so there is no meaningful net H+ excretion from this specific process.
incorrectas.C: The bicarbonate reabsorption mechanism using the H+/HCO3- cycle described occurs predominantly in the proximal tubule (accounting for the vast majority of filtered HCO3- reabsorption), not specifically or exclusively in the distal nephron, and regardless of segment it does not represent net H+ excretion.
incorrectas.D: HCO3- reabsorption absolutely depends on H+ secretion (via NHE3) into the tubular lumen to titrate filtered bicarbonate — the process could not occur without it; the key nuance is simply that this secreted H+ is not net excreted.

preguntas.q: Above what plasma bicarbonate concentration (mEq/L) do renal HCO3- reabsorption mechanisms become fully saturated, leading to excess HCO3- being excreted in the urine?

e.correcta: When plasma [HCO3-] rises above roughly 40 mEq/L (well above the normal ~24 mEq/L), the reabsorptive capacity of the proximal tubule (and downstream segments) becomes saturated, similar to a transport maximum (Tm)-limited process, so the excess filtered bicarbonate is no longer fully reabsorbed and spills into the urine (bicarbonaturia). This saturation phenomenon helps explain why severe metabolic alkalosis is partly self-limiting — the kidney begins dumping the excess base once its reabsorptive machinery is overwhelmed, although effective correction still requires addressing the underlying cause (e.g., volume/chloride depletion) since alkalosis often persists due to contraction and hypochloremia maintaining reabsorption below saturation.

incorrectas.B: 24 mEq/L is the normal (baseline) plasma bicarbonate concentration, not the elevated threshold at which the tubular reabsorptive mechanisms become saturated and begin spilling bicarbonate into urine.
incorrectas.C: 60 mEq/L overshoots the actual physiologic saturation threshold — reabsorptive capacity is exceeded well before plasma HCO3- reaches this level.
incorrectas.D: 15 mEq/L is actually below the normal plasma bicarbonate concentration (consistent with a mild metabolic acidosis), the opposite direction from the elevated level required to saturate and overwhelm reabsorption.

preguntas.q: ECF volume expansion has what effect on renal HCO3- reabsorption?

o.D: Reabsorption shifts entirely to the collecting duct

e.correcta: ECF volume expansion decreases isosmotic (Na+-linked) reabsorption in the proximal tubule, and since HCO3- reabsorption is tightly coupled to Na+ reabsorption via the Na+-H+ exchanger there, less filtered HCO3- gets reclaimed. This is part of the kidney's natural buffer against volume overload: the resulting mild bicarbonaturia and natriuresis help the body shed the excess fluid. It is the physiologic mirror image of contraction alkalosis.

incorrectas.A: Increased reabsorption is what happens with ECF volume contraction, not expansion — contraction concentrates the tubule's drive to reclaim Na+ (and with it HCO3-), the opposite of what volume expansion does.
incorrectas.C: Reabsorption is not static; the proximal tubule closely tracks ECF volume status, tightening or loosening isosmotic Na+/HCO3- reclamation as volume falls or rises.
incorrectas.D: There is no such compartmental shift — the change is a quantitative decrease in proximal tubule reabsorption, not a relocation of reabsorption machinery to a different nephron segment.

preguntas.q: A patient with severe vomiting develops ECF volume contraction. What effect does this have on renal HCO3- reabsorption, and what acid-base disturbance can result?

e.correcta: Volume contraction increases isosmotic proximal tubule reabsorption of Na+, and HCO3- rides along via the Na+-H+ exchanger, so more filtered HCO3- is reclaimed. Aldosterone (activated by the volume-depleted state) also stimulates H+-ATPase in the collecting duct, driving further H+ secretion and new HCO3- generation. The net effect is "contraction alkalosis" — a metabolic alkalosis that is maintained (not just caused) by the kidney's avid HCO3- retention as it tries to defend circulating volume.

incorrectas.A: Volume contraction increases, not decreases, HCO3- reabsorption, and the resulting acid-base disturbance is alkalosis (from bicarbonate retention), not acidosis.
incorrectas.C: This describes a primary respiratory process, but contraction alkalosis is a metabolic phenomenon driven by renal tubular handling of Na+ and HCO3-, not by a primary change in ventilation.
incorrectas.D: Renal tubular acidosis refers to defects in urinary acidification that cause acidosis, the opposite acid-base direction and opposite reabsorption pattern from what ECF contraction produces.

preguntas.q: Angiotensin II stimulates which transporter in the proximal tubule to promote Na+ and HCO3- reabsorption?

e.correcta: Angiotensin II upregulates the apical Na+-H+ exchanger (NHE3) in proximal tubule cells, which pulls Na+ into the cell in exchange for secreting H+ into the lumen. That secreted H+ combines with filtered HCO3- to form CO2 and water, which diffuse into the cell and regenerate HCO3- for reabsorption — so this single exchanger simultaneously drives both Na+ and HCO3- reclamation. This is a key mechanism by which the renin-angiotensin system defends both volume and, secondarily, contributes to alkalosis during states of volume depletion.

incorrectas.B: The Na+-glucose cotransporter (SGLT) reabsorbs glucose alongside Na+ but is not the mechanism angiotensin II uses to drive proximal HCO3- reabsorption; it is unrelated to acid-base handling.
incorrectas.A: The Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter is the target of loop diuretics and operates in the thick ascending limb, not the proximal tubule, and is not the transporter angiotensin II acts on here.
