This ratio becomes clinically useful precisely because it shifts predictably in different forms of azotemia — rising above 15:1 when tubular urea reabsorption is enhanced (as in prerenal states or early obstruction) and falling below 15:1 when tubular function itself is damaged (as in intrinsic renal disease or long-standing obstruction).

incorrectas.A: A ratio of ~5:1 is far too low to represent the normal baseline; ratios this low would suggest a process disproportionately raising creatinine relative to urea, not the normal physiologic state.
incorrectas.B: ~10:1 underestimates the normal ratio; the accepted baseline BUN:creatinine ratio in a healthy person is closer to 15:1.
incorrectas.C: ~25:1 is already in the range seen with enhanced urea reabsorption, such as in prerenal azotemia or early postrenal obstruction, not the normal baseline ratio.

preguntas.q: How does the BUN:creatinine ratio typically change in prerenal azotemia?

o.D: Becomes unmeasurable due to tubular necrosis

e.correcta: In prerenal azotemia, decreased renal perfusion triggers increased sodium and water reabsorption (via activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and ADH), and this enhanced tubular reabsorption drags urea passively along with it — but does not affect creatinine, which is not reabsorbed. The result is a disproportionate rise in BUN relative to creatinine, pushing the ratio above the normal 15:1, often exceeding 20:1, which is a key clue that hypoperfusion rather than intrinsic renal damage is driving the azotemia.

incorrectas.A: A ratio falling below 10:1 would suggest impaired urea reabsorption relative to creatinine handling, a pattern seen with tubular damage (as in intrinsic renal failure or long-standing obstruction), not the enhanced reabsorption state of prerenal azotemia.
incorrectas.C: The ratio does not stay at the normal 15:1 in prerenal azotemia — the entire diagnostic value of this ratio comes from its rise above baseline when tubular reabsorption of urea (but not creatinine) is enhanced by hypoperfusion.
incorrectas.D: Prerenal azotemia by definition does not yet involve tubular necrosis — the tubules are functioning normally (even hyperactively reabsorbing), which is exactly why the ratio remains measurable and characteristically elevated rather than becoming disrupted.

preguntas.q: In prerenal azotemia, what happens to tubular reabsorption of sodium and water?

e.correcta: Reduced renal perfusion in prerenal azotemia activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and ADH release, both of which act to increase tubular reabsorption of sodium and water in an attempt to restore intravascular volume and perfusion pressure. This appropriate, avid reabsorption is what produces the classic findings of prerenal azotemia: low urine sodium (<20 mEq/L), low FENa (<1%), and concentrated urine (osmolality >500 mOsm/kg) — all reflecting tubules that are working normally in response to perceived volume depletion.

incorrectas.A: Reabsorption is not decreased in prerenal azotemia — quite the opposite, the kidney's physiologic response to hypoperfusion is to reabsorb more sodium and water in an effort to conserve volume.
incorrectas.B: Reabsorption is not unchanged; the entire prerenal picture (concentrated urine, low urine Na+, low FENa) is generated by an active increase in tubular Na+/water reabsorption driven by RAAS and ADH activation.
incorrectas.D: Abolished reabsorption due to acute tubular necrosis describes intrinsic renal azotemia, not prerenal azotemia — in prerenal disease the tubules are intact and, if anything, reabsorbing more avidly than usual.

preguntas.q: What happens to the fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) in prerenal azotemia?

e.correcta: FENa measures the percentage of filtered sodium that ultimately appears in the urine, and because prerenal azotemia drives intact tubules to avidly reabsorb sodium (via RAAS/ADH activation in response to perceived hypoperfusion), very little filtered sodium escapes into the urine — giving a characteristically low FENa, typically <1%. This makes FENa one of the most useful bedside tools for distinguishing prerenal azotemia (low FENa, tubules intact and reabsorbing) from acute tubular necrosis (high FENa, damaged tubules that cannot reabsorb sodium properly).

incorrectas.B: A FENa >2% reflects impaired tubular sodium reabsorption, characteristic of intrinsic renal injury such as acute tubular necrosis, not prerenal azotemia where reabsorption is enhanced rather than impaired.
incorrectas.C: An intermediate FENa around 1-2% is sometimes described as an indeterminate zone but does not represent the classic prerenal pattern, which is defined by a low value below 1% reflecting avid sodium conservation.
incorrectas.D: FENa is readily calculable from paired serum and urine sodium and creatinine values and is, in fact, one of the standard clinical tests used specifically to help localize the cause of azotemia.

preguntas.q: What is the expected urine osmolality in prerenal azotemia?

e.correcta: Because tubular concentrating ability is preserved (in fact enhanced) in prerenal azotemia, the kidney responds to perceived volume depletion by maximally reabsorbing water under ADH stimulation, producing a highly concentrated urine with osmolality typically greater than 500 mOsm/kg. This concentrated, sodium-poor urine is the tubules working exactly as they should in response to hypoperfusion — a sharp contrast to acute tubular necrosis, where damaged tubules lose concentrating ability and produce isosmotic urine near plasma osmolality (~300 mOsm/kg).

incorrectas.A: Urine osmolality below 350 mOsm/kg suggests impaired concentrating ability, which points toward intrinsic tubular damage rather than the preserved, even enhanced, concentrating function seen in prerenal azotemia.
incorrectas.B: An isosmotic urine near 300-350 mOsm/kg (matching plasma) reflects a kidney that has lost its ability to concentrate urine — the hallmark of acute tubular necrosis, not prerenal azotemia, where the tubules are still fully capable of concentrating urine.
incorrectas.C: Urine osmolality is a routinely measurable lab value and is, in fact, one of the standard tests used to help distinguish prerenal azotemia from intrinsic renal failure.

preguntas.q: What is the expected urine sodium concentration in prerenal azotemia?

e.correcta: Enhanced RAAS-driven sodium reabsorption in response to perceived hypoperfusion means that very little filtered sodium reaches the final urine in prerenal azotemia, producing a characteristically low urine sodium, typically less than 20 mEq/L. This low urine Na+ (paired with a low FENa and concentrated urine) reflects intact tubules avidly conserving sodium, and is used clinically to distinguish prerenal azotemia from acute tubular necrosis, in which damaged tubules cannot reabsorb sodium and urine Na+ instead rises above 40 mEq/L.

incorrectas.A: A urine sodium above 100 mEq/L would be markedly elevated and inconsistent with the avid sodium conservation seen in prerenal azotemia; such high values instead suggest a tubule that cannot reabsorb sodium normally.
incorrectas.D: Urine sodium above 40 mEq/L is the pattern expected in intrinsic renal azotemia (e.g., acute tubular necrosis), where tubular damage prevents effective sodium reabsorption — the opposite physiology from prerenal azotemia.
incorrectas.C: 20-40 mEq/L falls in an intermediate/equivocal range rather than the clearly low value (<20 mEq/L) that reflects the avid tubular sodium reabsorption characteristic of prerenal azotemia.

preguntas.q: Which category of azotemia results from obstruction of the urinary tract downstream from the kidneys, such as from stones, benign prostatic hyperplasia, or neoplasia?

e.correcta: Postrenal azotemia occurs when an obstruction anywhere from the renal pelvis to the urethra blocks the outflow of urine, causing back-pressure that transmits upstream and ultimately reduces GFR. Classic causes include nephrolithiasis, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and pelvic or urethral neoplasia — all mechanical obstructions distal to the kidney parenchyma itself, distinguishing this category from problems with renal blood flow (prerenal) or the nephron tissue itself (intrinsic renal).

incorrectas.B: Prerenal azotemia results from reduced renal blood flow/perfusion (e.g., hypovolemia, heart failure), not from a mechanical blockage of urine outflow downstream from the kidney — the two categories have entirely different mechanisms even though both can raise BUN and creatinine.
incorrectas.C: Intrinsic (renal) azotemia arises from direct damage to the nephron itself — such as acute tubular necrosis, glomerulonephritis, or interstitial nephritis — rather than from an obstruction located outside the kidney in the collecting system or lower urinary tract.
incorrectas.D: "Functional azotemia" is not a standard clinical category distinct from prerenal, intrinsic, and postrenal azotemia, and does not describe the obstructive pathophysiology in question.

preguntas.q: For postrenal azotemia to develop in a patient with two normally functioning kidneys, at what level of the urinary tract must obstruction typically occur?

o.B: Obstruction at the level of a single major calyx
o.C: Any degree of partial obstruction, unilateral or bilateral

e.correcta: Because a single functioning kidney can compensate for the loss of the other, a rise in serum BUN/creatinine from postrenal obstruction in a patient with two kidneys generally requires bilateral obstruction (or obstruction at a common downstream point like the bladder outlet or urethra) — unless the patient has only one functioning kidney to begin with, in which case even unilateral obstruction is enough to cause azotemia.

incorrectas.A: Unilateral ureteral obstruction alone typically does not produce azotemia in a patient with two functioning kidneys, because the unobstructed contralateral kidney can maintain adequate overall GFR and clearance of BUN/creatinine — although it can still cause ipsilateral hydronephrosis and pain.
incorrectas.B: Obstruction limited to a single major calyx is a very localized, small-scale blockage that would not meaningfully reduce whole-kidney (let alone whole-body) GFR enough to produce systemic azotemia.
incorrectas.C: Mild partial or unilateral obstruction is generally insufficient to raise BUN/creatinine when the other kidney is intact and compensating; the obstruction needs to be bilateral (or affect a solitary/singly functioning kidney) to produce true postrenal azotemia.

preguntas.q: What is the effect of postrenal azotemia on GFR?

e.correcta: Obstruction to urine outflow causes pressure to build backward through the collecting system into Bowman's space, opposing the hydrostatic pressure that normally drives glomerular filtration. As this back-pressure rises, the net filtration pressure across the glomerulus falls, decreasing GFR — the shared final pathway by which prerenal, intrinsic, and postrenal causes all ultimately produce azotemia, even though the underlying mechanisms differ.

incorrectas.A: GFR does not increase with obstruction — rising intratubular/Bowman's space pressure from blocked outflow directly opposes filtration pressure, driving GFR down rather than up.
incorrectas.B: GFR is not unchanged in postrenal azotemia; a rise in BUN and creatinine (the defining feature of azotemia) only occurs because GFR has fallen due to the back-pressure effect of obstruction.
incorrectas.D: There is no initial-unchanged-then-increased pattern; obstruction produces a sustained decrease in GFR for as long as the outflow blockage persists (worsening further if tubular damage develops with prolonged obstruction).

preguntas.q: In early (acute) postrenal azotemia, how does the BUN:creatinine ratio typically appear?

o.A: >15, due to increased tubular pressure forcing urea back into the blood
o.C: Normal random ratio unrelated to obstruction

e.correcta: In the early phase of postrenal obstruction, the tubular epithelium is still intact, but the elevated back-pressure within the tubules forces filtered urea to passively diffuse back into the peritubular capillaries at a higher rate than creatinine (which is not reabsorbed), raising the BUN:creatinine ratio above 15 — mimicking the prerenal pattern even though the underlying cause is a distal mechanical obstruction rather than reduced perfusion.

incorrectas.B: A ratio below 15 reflecting tubular damage is the pattern seen in long-standing/chronic obstruction, once sustained back-pressure has actually injured the tubular epithelium — not in the early phase, when tubules are still intact and pressure-driven urea reabsorption dominates.
incorrectas.C: The ratio is not simply random or unrelated to obstruction — the elevated pressure from obstruction has a specific, predictable effect of enhancing passive urea reabsorption, producing a characteristically elevated (not random) ratio.
incorrectas.D: The BUN:creatinine ratio remains readily measurable in early postrenal azotemia; it is not undetectable — it is elevated above the normal 15:1 due to pressure-driven urea reabsorption.

preguntas.q: In early postrenal azotemia, before tubular damage has set in, what is the expected fractional excretion of sodium (FENa)?

o.B: <1% (normal), since tubular function is initially preserved

e.correcta: Because tubular epithelial function remains intact in the early phase of postrenal obstruction, the tubules can still reabsorb filtered sodium normally, so FENa stays low (<1%), just as it does in prerenal azotemia — even though the underlying mechanism (mechanical back-pressure rather than hypoperfusion) is completely different. This low FENa is what makes early obstruction look biochemically similar to a prerenal picture, which is why the clinical history and imaging (looking for hydronephrosis) are essential to distinguish the two.

incorrectas.A: A FENa >2% reflecting tubular injury is the pattern of long-standing, severe postrenal obstruction once sustained pressure has actually damaged the tubular epithelium — not the early phase, when tubular function (and sodium reabsorption) is still preserved.
incorrectas.C: An intermediate 1-2% value does not represent the early-obstruction pattern; with intact tubular function, FENa remains clearly low, similar to the prerenal pattern, rather than sitting in an indeterminate middle range.
incorrectas.D: Early obstruction, especially if unilateral or partial, does not necessarily cause anuria, and FENa remains measurable and low as long as some urine output continues and tubular reabsorptive function is preserved.

preguntas.q: In early postrenal azotemia, what is the expected urine osmolality?

o.C: >500 mOsm/kg (normal), since tubular concentrating ability is preserved

e.correcta: Because tubular function, including the countercurrent concentrating mechanism, is still intact early in postrenal obstruction, the kidney remains able to adequately reabsorb water and concentrate urine, keeping osmolality above 500 mOsm/kg — just as in prerenal azotemia. This preserved concentrating ability, alongside a low FENa and elevated BUN:creatinine ratio, is what makes early postrenal obstruction biochemically mimic a prerenal picture, even though its cause is a distal mechanical blockage rather than hypoperfusion.

incorrectas.A: Urine osmolality below 350 mOsm/kg indicates loss of concentrating ability, which reflects tubular damage — a finding of long-standing, not early, postrenal obstruction.
incorrectas.B: A fixed isosmotic urine at ~300 mOsm/kg (matching plasma) is the pattern of a kidney that has lost its concentrating ability due to tubular injury, which develops only with prolonged obstruction, not in the early phase when tubular function is preserved.
incorrectas.D: Urine osmolality remains a standard, measurable value in early postrenal obstruction as long as some urine is being produced — it is not rendered unassessable simply because obstruction is present.

preguntas.q: In long-standing (chronic) postrenal azotemia, how does the BUN:creatinine ratio compare to that seen in early obstruction?

o.D: Falls below 15:1, due to tubular damage impairing urea reabsorption and creatinine excretion

e.correcta: Prolonged obstruction eventually causes sustained back-pressure to injure the tubular epithelium itself, impairing both the passive reabsorption of urea and the normal handling of creatinine excretion. As tubular integrity breaks down, the BUN:creatinine ratio falls below the normal 15:1 — a shift from the elevated ratio of early obstruction to a reduced ratio that signals the obstruction has progressed to causing actual intrinsic renal damage, not just mechanical back-pressure.

incorrectas.A: The ratio does not stay elevated as in early obstruction — the whole point of this progression is that once tubular damage develops, the mechanism shifts from enhanced pressure-driven urea reabsorption (raising the ratio) to impaired tubular handling overall (lowering the ratio).
incorrectas.B: The ratio does not rise further above 20 in chronic obstruction; that pattern belongs to the early phase, when intact tubules are reabsorbing urea under increased pressure — chronic tubular damage instead drives the ratio down.
incorrectas.C: There is no fixed value of exactly 10:1 associated with chronic postrenal azotemia; the key teaching point is a directional shift to below the normal 15:1 as tubular damage sets in, not a specific fixed number.

preguntas.q: In long-standing (severe) postrenal azotemia, what happens to the fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) as tubular damage develops?

o.B: Rises above 2%, reflecting impaired tubular sodium reabsorption

e.correcta: As obstruction persists, sustained elevated pressure within the tubules eventually damages the tubular epithelium itself, impairing its ability to reabsorb filtered sodium. This causes FENa to rise above 2%, converting the biochemical picture from the low-FENa 'prerenal-mimicking' pattern of early obstruction to a high-FENa pattern resembling acute tubular necrosis — reflecting genuine tubular injury rather than simple mechanical back-pressure.

incorrectas.A: FENa staying below 1% describes early obstruction, when tubules are still intact and able to reabsorb sodium normally; long-standing obstruction is defined by tubular damage that impairs this reabsorption, pushing FENa up rather than keeping it low.
incorrectas.C: FENa remains a measurable value in long-standing obstruction (assuming there is still some urine output); it does not become undetectable — rather, it characteristically rises above 2% due to tubular injury.
incorrectas.D: The whole significance of this progression is that long-standing obstruction no longer mimics the prerenal pattern — sustained tubular damage causes FENa to rise above 2%, distinguishing it from the low-FENa prerenal-like pattern seen in early obstruction.

preguntas.q: In long-standing (chronic) postrenal azotemia caused by prolonged urinary tract obstruction, what happens to urine osmolality once tubular damage has occurred?

e.correcta: In early or acute postrenal obstruction, tubular function is often initially preserved, so urine can still be concentrated somewhat normally. But once obstruction persists long enough, back-pressure transmitted through the nephron damages the tubular epithelium and disrupts the medullary countercurrent concentrating mechanism, so the kidney loses its ability to concentrate urine. Osmolality falls below 350 mOsm/kg, mimicking the pattern seen in intrinsic acute tubular necrosis (ATN).

incorrectas.A: A high osmolality (>500 mOsm/kg) reflects an intact, ADH-responsive concentrating mechanism, as seen in prerenal azotemia or early postrenal obstruction before tubular injury develops — not the picture once chronic obstruction has damaged the tubules.
incorrectas.C: An intermediate value doesn't reflect the characteristic finding once obstruction has been prolonged enough to injure the tubular epithelium; the classic teaching point is a clearly low osmolality, not an ambiguous middle range.
incorrectas.D: Maximally concentrated urine indicates fully functioning tubules responding appropriately to ADH — essentially the opposite of what happens once chronic obstruction has impaired the kidney's concentrating ability.

preguntas.q: Once tubular damage has developed in postrenal azotemia, what is the characteristic urine sodium concentration?

e.correcta: Once obstruction has been present long enough to injure the tubular epithelium, the Na+/K+-ATPase-driven active reabsorption of sodium fails, so the kidney can no longer conserve sodium appropriately and urine Na+ rises above 40 mEq/L — the same pattern seen in ATN. (Note that the exact cutoff can vary somewhat in practice, but this elevated value is the classic teaching point.)

incorrectas.A: A low urine sodium (<20 mEq/L) reflects avid tubular sodium reabsorption by intact tubules responding to renal hypoperfusion — the pattern of prerenal azotemia, not the tubular damage that develops with chronic obstruction.
incorrectas.B: An intermediate value in the 20-40 range doesn't represent the classic, clearly elevated finding taught for tubular injury; the teaching cutoff is a value clearly above 40.
incorrectas.D: An even lower value (<10 mEq/L) would indicate even more aggressive sodium conservation than typical prerenal azotemia, which is the opposite of the sodium-wasting picture caused by damaged tubular epithelium.

preguntas.q: What is the most common cause of acute renal failure among hospitalized patients?

e.correcta: ATN, most often triggered by ischemic insults (sepsis, hypotension, major surgery) or nephrotoxins (contrast, aminoglycosides, other drugs) that are common in the inpatient setting, is the leading cause of intrinsic acute kidney injury in hospitalized patients. Critically ill patients frequently experience the very combination of hypoperfusion and toxin exposure that directly damages tubular epithelial cells.

incorrectas.A: Prerenal azotemia is extremely common but is a functional, reversible reduction in GFR from renal hypoperfusion with intact tubules; when severe or prolonged it often progresses into ATN itself, but as a distinct entity it is not the single leading identified cause of hospital-acquired AKI.
incorrectas.B: Acute interstitial nephritis, typically a hypersensitivity reaction to drugs like NSAIDs or penicillins, is an important but far less common cause of inpatient AKI than tubular necrosis.
incorrectas.C: Postrenal (obstructive) causes account for only a minority of AKI cases in hospitalized patients; most inpatient AKI arises from intrinsic tubular injury rather than mechanical outflow obstruction.

preguntas.q: What effect does acute tubular necrosis (ATN) have on glomerular filtration rate (GFR), and why?

o.A: Decreased, due to tubular obstruction by necrotic debris and back-leak of filtrate
o.B: Increased, due to loss of tubuloglomerular feedback
o.C: Unchanged, since the glomeruli remain structurally normal
o.D: Decreased only transiently, normalizing within hours

e.correcta: In ATN, sloughed necrotic tubular epithelial cells and debris form casts that obstruct the tubular lumen, raising intratubular pressure and opposing the pressure gradient that drives glomerular filtration. Loss of the tubular epithelial barrier also lets filtrate leak backward across the damaged epithelium into the interstitium. Both mechanisms sharply reduce GFR, which is why ATN presents as oliguric or non-oliguric renal failure.

incorrectas.B: GFR does not rise in ATN — in fact, increased distal solute delivery from injured tubules is sensed by the macula densa and triggers tubuloglomerular feedback that constricts the afferent arteriole, further lowering (not raising) GFR.
incorrectas.C: Although the glomeruli are histologically normal in ATN (the injury is tubular, not glomerular), GFR still falls markedly because tubular obstruction and back-leak physically impair net filtration despite intact glomeruli.
incorrectas.D: The GFR reduction in ATN is not brief — it persists throughout the maintenance phase (typically 1-3 weeks) until regenerating tubular epithelium restores function in the recovery phase.

preguntas.q: In acute tubular necrosis, how is the BUN:creatinine ratio characteristically affected?

e.correcta: In prerenal azotemia, intact tubules passively reabsorb urea along with sodium and water under ADH/aldosterone influence, disproportionately raising BUN relative to creatinine (ratio >20). In ATN, however, tubular epithelial damage impairs this passive urea reabsorption, so BUN rises roughly in proportion to creatinine, keeping the ratio low (<15). This lab distinction is a key clue used to separate prerenal azotemia from intrinsic ATN.

incorrectas.A: A ratio >20:1 is the classic finding in prerenal azotemia, where functioning tubules preferentially reabsorb urea — the opposite tubular status from the damaged epithelium of ATN.
incorrectas.C: A 'normal' ratio in the 15-20 range doesn't point clearly toward either prerenal or intrinsic disease and is not the characteristic finding taught for ATN, which is specifically low.
incorrectas.D: An even higher ratio (>40:1) would reflect an even more exaggerated urea-reabsorption pattern than typical prerenal azotemia — inconsistent with the failed tubular reabsorption seen in ATN.

preguntas.q: What is the characteristic fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) in acute tubular necrosis?

e.correcta: FENa measures how much filtered sodium ends up in the urine rather than being reabsorbed. Damaged proximal tubular cells in ATN lose the Na+/K+-ATPase-driven reabsorptive capacity that normally reclaims filtered sodium, so a much larger fraction escapes into the urine, pushing FENa above 2%. This elevated FENa is a hallmark used clinically to distinguish intrinsic ATN from prerenal azotemia.

incorrectas.A: A low FENa (<1%) reflects avid tubular sodium reabsorption in response to renal hypoperfusion — the pattern seen in prerenal azotemia, where tubules are still functioning appropriately, not ATN.
incorrectas.B: An indeterminate 1-2% range doesn't clearly distinguish prerenal from intrinsic disease, unlike the clearly elevated (>2%) FENa characteristic of ATN.
incorrectas.D: An even lower FENa (<0.1%) reflects an even more pronounced sodium-conserving state than typical prerenal azotemia, essentially the opposite of the failed tubular reabsorption seen in ATN.

preguntas.q: What is the characteristic urine osmolality in acute tubular necrosis?

e.correcta: The medullary concentrating gradient and ADH-driven water reabsorption in the collecting duct depend on intact tubular epithelium. In ATN, necrosis of tubular cells cripples this concentrating mechanism, so urine osmolality falls below 350 mOsm/kg regardless of hydration status or ADH levels — the urine becomes essentially isosthenuric, similar to plasma. This low, fixed osmolality helps separate ATN from prerenal azotemia.

incorrectas.B: An intermediate osmolality (350-500) doesn't reflect the severe concentrating defect produced by damaged tubular epithelium in established ATN.
incorrectas.C: Maximally concentrated urine (>800) indicates fully intact tubular function and a strong ADH response — essentially the opposite of the impaired concentrating ability that defines ATN.
incorrectas.D: A high osmolality (>500) reflects a still-functioning concentrating mechanism responding appropriately to ADH, characteristic of prerenal azotemia with intact tubules, not ATN.

preguntas.q: What is the characteristic urine sodium concentration in acute tubular necrosis?

e.correcta: Because ATN destroys the tubular epithelium that normally drives active sodium reabsorption via Na+/K+-ATPase, the kidney can no longer conserve sodium appropriately, so urine Na+ rises above 40 mEq/L. This elevated urine sodium, together with a FENa >2% and a low urine osmolality, forms the classic urinary triad that distinguishes ATN from prerenal azotemia.

incorrectas.B: A low urine sodium (<20 mEq/L) reflects intact tubular sodium reabsorption driven by renal hypoperfusion — the pattern of prerenal azotemia, inconsistent with the tubular epithelial destruction of ATN.
incorrectas.C: An intermediate value (20-40) doesn't reflect the clear tubular failure that occurs in established ATN.
incorrectas.D: An even lower value (<10) would represent an even more extreme sodium-conserving state, essentially the opposite of what happens when the tubular reabsorptive machinery is destroyed in ATN.

preguntas.q: Which mechanism of acute tubular necrosis results from decreased renal blood flow, as seen with hypotension, shock, sepsis, hemorrhage, or heart failure?

e.correcta: Ischemic ATN results from a prolonged reduction in renal blood flow, depriving the highly metabolically active proximal tubule and thick ascending limb of oxygen. These segments are especially vulnerable because they perform heavy active transport in the relatively low-oxygen-tension outer medulla, so sustained hypoperfusion from hypotension, shock, sepsis, hemorrhage, or heart failure causes frank tubular cell necrosis and sloughing.

incorrectas.A: Nephrotoxic ATN results from direct toxic injury to tubular cells by exogenous or endogenous substances (aminoglycosides, contrast, myoglobin, lead) rather than from a primary reduction in blood flow, though both mechanisms converge on tubular necrosis.
incorrectas.C: Obstructive uropathy is a postrenal cause of AKI from mechanical blockage of urine outflow, not a direct cause of tubular ischemia, though prolonged obstruction can secondarily injure tubules.
incorrectas.D: Acute interstitial nephritis is a hypersensitivity-mediated inflammatory infiltrate of the renal interstitium (classically drug-induced), a distinct pathologic process from ischemic tubular cell death.

preguntas.q: Ischemic acute tubular necrosis is most often preceded by which condition?

e.correcta: Prerenal azotemia and ischemic ATN exist on a continuum. Prerenal azotemia is a functional, reversible state of renal hypoperfusion with intact tubules that responds to volume repletion, but if the hypoperfusion is severe or prolonged enough, the tubular epithelial cells themselves become ischemic and die, converting reversible prerenal azotemia into established ATN that no longer improves with fluids alone.

incorrectas.A: AIN is a distinct drug-hypersensitivity process causing interstitial inflammation, not a precursor state on the hypoperfusion-to-necrosis continuum that precedes ischemic ATN.
incorrectas.B: Nephrotic syndrome is a glomerular disease characterized by heavy proteinuria, unrelated to the hemodynamic sequence of hypoperfusion progressing to tubular necrosis.
incorrectas.D: Postrenal obstruction is a separate category of AKI from mechanical outflow blockage; it is not the typical antecedent state to ischemic ATN, though chronic obstruction can independently cause tubular damage.

preguntas.q: Which mechanism of acute tubular necrosis is caused by direct injury from toxic substances such as aminoglycosides, contrast agents, lead, or cisplatin?

e.correcta: Nephrotoxic ATN occurs when exogenous agents (aminoglycosides, radiocontrast dye, cisplatin, lead) or endogenous pigments (myoglobin from rhabdomyolysis, hemoglobin from hemolysis) directly injure tubular epithelial cells — often through oxidative stress, direct cytotoxicity, or intratubular precipitation and obstruction — leading to cell death and sloughing distinct from a pure blood-flow problem.

incorrectas.A: Ischemic ATN results from inadequate renal perfusion (shock, sepsis, hypotension) rather than direct chemical or toxin-mediated cell injury, though both pathways converge on tubular necrosis histologically.
incorrectas.B: 'Obstructive injury' describes postrenal AKI from mechanical blockage of urine flow, not toxin-mediated tubular cell death.
incorrectas.C: Immune-mediated injury describes processes like acute interstitial nephritis or glomerulonephritis, which involve inflammatory or immune attack on renal structures, not direct toxic injury to tubular cells.

preguntas.q: In nephrotoxic acute tubular necrosis, which segment of the nephron is most commonly and severely affected?

o.B: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

e.correcta: The proximal tubule is the primary site of reabsorption and also the main site where filtered toxins, drugs, and pigments are concentrated and taken up via apical transporters (e.g., megalin-mediated endocytosis), exposing its epithelial cells to the highest intracellular toxin burden. Combined with its high metabolic and mitochondrial demand, this makes the proximal tubule the most vulnerable segment to direct nephrotoxic injury from agents like aminoglycosides, cisplatin, and contrast media.

incorrectas.B: The thick ascending limb is the segment most classically vulnerable to ischemic (not nephrotoxic) injury, because it performs heavy active NaCl transport in the relatively hypoxic outer medulla.
incorrectas.C: The distal convoluted tubule is less exposed to concentrated toxin burden than the proximal tubule, since most toxin reabsorption and uptake occurs proximally before fluid reaches this segment.
incorrectas.D: The collecting duct, mainly responsible for final urine concentration under ADH control, is not the characteristic site of nephrotoxic tubular injury in ATN.

preguntas.q: Which class of antimicrobials is a classic cause of nephrotoxic acute tubular necrosis?

e.correcta: Aminoglycosides (e.g., gentamicin, tobramycin) are taken up by proximal tubular cells via megalin-mediated endocytosis and accumulate in lysosomes, where they disrupt lysosomal membranes and cause direct cytotoxic tubular cell injury. This dose- and duration-dependent nephrotoxicity is one of the most common causes of drug-induced ATN, which is why aminoglycoside trough levels and renal function are closely monitored during therapy.

incorrectas.A: Fluoroquinolones are more classically associated with tendon rupture and QT prolongation than with direct tubular necrosis; they are not a leading cause of ATN.
incorrectas.C: Macrolides are primarily associated with GI upset, QT prolongation, and CYP450 drug interactions rather than direct tubular toxicity causing ATN.
incorrectas.D: Tetracyclines are associated with photosensitivity, tooth discoloration, and (with expired drug) Fanconi syndrome, but they are not a classic major cause of ATN the way aminoglycosides are.

preguntas.q: Acute tubular necrosis from heavy metal toxicity is classically associated with which metal?

e.correcta: Lead is directly toxic to proximal tubular epithelial cells, producing characteristic intranuclear inclusion bodies and interfering with mitochondrial function and heme synthesis (by inhibiting ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase). Chronic exposure classically causes both tubular injury contributing to ATN and a sideroblastic-type anemia with basophilic stippling, making lead the heavy metal most emphasized for renal tubular toxicity on boards.

incorrectas.A: Mercury is nephrotoxic as well, causing proximal tubular injury and membranous nephropathy, but it is not the heavy metal classically paired with ATN in standard board teaching the way lead is.
incorrectas.B: Arsenic toxicity classically causes peripheral neuropathy, a garlic breath odor, and skin changes (hyperkeratosis, hyperpigmentation) rather than being the prototypical heavy metal cause of ATN.
incorrectas.D: Cadmium exposure is linked to proximal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi-type wasting) and bone disease (itai-itai disease), but it is not the classically tested heavy metal cause of ATN in this context.

preguntas.q: Crush injuries can cause acute tubular necrosis through release of which substance from damaged skeletal muscle?

e.correcta: Crush injuries and severe muscle trauma cause massive release of myoglobin from damaged myofibers into the bloodstream and glomerular filtrate. Myoglobin is directly toxic to proximal tubular cells, precipitates with Tamm-Horsfall protein to form obstructing intratubular casts (especially in acidic urine), and its heme moiety generates reactive oxygen species — together producing rhabdomyolysis-induced ATN.

incorrectas.B: Hyperuricemia from massive cell turnover (as in tumor lysis syndrome) causes uric acid crystal precipitation and tubular obstruction, a distinct mechanism from muscle-derived myoglobin toxicity, though both cause intrarenal obstruction and ATN.
incorrectas.C: Bence Jones proteins (free immunoglobulin light chains) cause tubular injury and cast nephropathy in multiple myeloma, a different pathophysiology from muscle-breakdown-related myoglobin toxicity.
incorrectas.D: Hemoglobinuria from intravascular hemolysis can cause a similar pigment-induced ATN, but it is not specifically linked to crush injury — crush injury classically releases myoglobin from damaged skeletal muscle, not hemoglobin from lysed red cells.

preguntas.q: Which agent used in diagnostic imaging is a well-recognized cause of nephrotoxic acute tubular necrosis?

e.correcta: Radiocontrast-induced nephropathy causes ATN through a combination of direct tubular cytotoxicity, generation of reactive oxygen species, and renal medullary vasoconstriction that reduces blood flow to the already relatively hypoxic outer medulla — compounding ischemic and toxic injury. Risk is highest in patients with pre-existing renal insufficiency, diabetes, or volume depletion, which is why prophylactic IV hydration is used before contrast administration in at-risk patients.

incorrectas.A: Myoglobin causes pigment-induced ATN after rhabdomyolysis, a distinct exposure (muscle breakdown) rather than an iodinated contrast agent used for imaging.
incorrectas.B: Uric acid causes tubular obstruction in tumor lysis syndrome, unrelated to contrast media exposure.
incorrectas.C: Bence Jones protein causes cast nephropathy in multiple myeloma, a different clinical scenario entirely from contrast administration.

preguntas.q: In tumor lysis syndrome, acute tubular necrosis results from tubular precipitation of which substance?

e.correcta: In tumor lysis syndrome, rapid destruction of malignant cells (often after chemotherapy) releases massive amounts of intracellular purines, which are catabolized to uric acid. Under the relatively acidic conditions of the distal tubule and collecting duct, uric acid precipitates as crystals, directly obstructing tubules and inciting a crystal-mediated form of ATN — this is why prophylactic hydration, allopurinol, or rasburicase are used before treating high-tumor-burden malignancies.

incorrectas.A: Myoglobin causes pigment nephropathy following rhabdomyolysis or crush injury, an entirely different metabolic byproduct from purine catabolism in tumor lysis syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Oxalate crystal nephropathy is classically associated with ethylene glycol toxicity or primary hyperoxaluria, not tumor lysis syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Calcium phosphate precipitation can also occur in tumor lysis syndrome (from hyperphosphatemia), but the classically tested and dominant crystal-mediated ATN mechanism in tumor lysis is uric acid, not calcium phosphate.

preguntas.q: Which chemotherapeutic agent is classically associated with causing acute tubular necrosis?

e.correcta: Cisplatin and other platinum analogs (carboplatin, oxaliplatin) accumulate in proximal tubular cells via active transport, where they form DNA and protein adducts and generate oxidative stress, causing direct tubular cytotoxicity and cell death. This dose-limiting nephrotoxicity is why aggressive IV hydration (and sometimes mannitol) is used to protect the kidneys during cisplatin-based chemotherapy.

incorrectas.A: Methotrexate can cause AKI via crystallization and precipitation of the drug itself within renal tubules at high doses — a different mechanism from cisplatin's direct DNA-adduct cytotoxicity — and it is not the classic platinum-based nephrotoxic chemotherapeutic.
incorrectas.B: Doxorubicin's dose-limiting toxicity is dilated cardiomyopathy from free-radical-mediated cardiac injury, not renal tubular necrosis.
incorrectas.D: Vincristine's dose-limiting toxicity is peripheral neuropathy from microtubule disruption in axons, not nephrotoxicity.

preguntas.q: What is the first of the three classic stages of acute tubular necrosis?

e.correcta: The clinical course of ATN classically unfolds in three stages, the first being the inciting event — the initial ischemic or nephrotoxic insult that damages tubular epithelial cells. This stage may be clinically silent or show only a transient rise in creatinine before the full renal failure picture develops in the subsequent maintenance phase.

incorrectas.B: The maintenance phase is the second stage, characterized by sustained oliguria, a stable but markedly reduced GFR, and accumulation of nitrogenous waste — it follows, rather than defines, the initial inciting insult.
incorrectas.C: The recovery phase is the third and final stage, marked by tubular re-epithelialization and gradual return of renal function, not the initial insult.
incorrectas.D: 'Oliguric crisis' is not a formally named stage in the classic three-phase description of ATN; oliguria is a feature of the maintenance phase, not a separate named stage.

preguntas.q: What is the second of the three classic stages of acute tubular necrosis?

e.correcta: The maintenance phase is the second stage of ATN, lasting roughly 1-3 weeks, during which GFR remains persistently low due to ongoing tubular obstruction and back-leak while the quiescent tubular epithelial cells slowly regenerate. Clinically this phase is marked by oliguria, and it is when complications like hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, and uremia most often develop and require close monitoring, sometimes with dialysis.

incorrectas.A: The inciting event is the initial insult (ischemic or toxic) that precedes and triggers the maintenance phase — a distinct, earlier stage, not the sustained low-GFR period itself.
incorrectas.C: The recovery phase is the third stage, in which regenerating tubular epithelium re-establishes function and GFR begins improving, coming after (not during) the maintenance phase.
incorrectas.D: A diuretic phase can occur as the kidneys recover and newly regenerated tubules are not yet able to concentrate urine properly, but this is part of the recovery phase, not a separately named stage distinct from maintenance.

preguntas.q: During the maintenance phase of acute tubular necrosis, does urine output typically show oliguria or polyuria?

e.correcta: During the maintenance phase, ongoing tubular cell necrosis, cast formation, and back-leak of filtrate keep GFR persistently low, so urine output typically falls into the oliguric range (<400 mL/day), even though some cases of ATN are technically non-oliguric. This oliguria drives the fluid overload, hyperkalemia, and uremia risks that must be managed — sometimes with dialysis — during this stage.

incorrectas.A: Polyuria is characteristic of the later recovery phase, when regenerating tubules are numerous enough to filter but not yet mature enough to reabsorb and concentrate urine properly, producing an excessive diuresis rather than the low output of the maintenance phase.
incorrectas.B: Complete absence of urine output is unusual in typical ATN and should prompt consideration of an alternative diagnosis (e.g., complete urinary tract obstruction or bilateral renal artery occlusion) rather than being the expected maintenance-phase pattern.
incorrectas.C: While some cases of ATN are non-oliguric, the classic and most commonly tested maintenance-phase pattern is reduced, not normal, urine output.

preguntas.q: Approximately how long does the maintenance phase of acute tubular necrosis typically last?

e.correcta: Renal tubular epithelial cells are classified as stable (quiescent) cells — they normally reside in G0 but retain the capacity to re-enter the cell cycle and proliferate after injury, unlike permanent cells such as neurons or cardiac myocytes, which cannot regenerate. This regenerative process is not instantaneous, however: it takes roughly 1-3 weeks for surviving tubular cells to proliferate and re-epithelialize the denuded basement membrane, which is why the maintenance phase of ATN typically lasts that long before recovery begins.

incorrectas.B: This timeframe (24-48 hours) is far too short for stable-cell proliferation and tubular re-epithelialization to occur; it more closely approximates the timescale of the initial inciting event rather than the full maintenance phase.
incorrectas.C: A span of 1-3 days is also far too brief — it would not allow sufficient time for meaningful regeneration of the tubular epithelium, which requires sustained cellular proliferation over multiple weeks.
incorrectas.D: A duration of 2-3 months overstates the typical course; while severe cases can be prolonged, the classic teaching duration for the maintenance phase is measured in weeks (1-3), not months.

preguntas.q: During the maintenance phase of acute tubular necrosis, patients are at increased risk for which electrolyte disturbance?

e.correcta: With tubular cells necrotic and non-functional during the maintenance phase, the distal nephron loses its ability to secrete potassium via principal cell K+ channels, and the markedly reduced GFR further limits potassium filtration and excretion. Potassium — from both dietary intake and cellular release due to tissue injury and acidosis — accumulates in the blood, making hyperkalemia, and the arrhythmia risk it carries, one of the most dangerous complications of the maintenance phase, sometimes requiring urgent dialysis.

incorrectas.A: Hypokalemia is the opposite problem, seen with conditions of excess renal or GI potassium loss (e.g., diuretics, vomiting), not with the reduced excretory capacity of failing tubules in ATN.
incorrectas.B: Sodium handling is also impaired in ATN, tending toward natriuresis with elevated urine Na+, and volume and water balance disturbances more typically produce hyponatremia from impaired free water excretion rather than hypernatremia.
incorrectas.D: While calcium-phosphate handling can be disturbed in AKI, the specific electrolyte complication most emphasized and most immediately dangerous during the maintenance phase of ATN is hyperkalemia, not hypocalcemia.

preguntas.q: What acid-base disturbance is characteristically associated with the maintenance phase of acute tubular necrosis?

e.correcta: Failing tubules during the maintenance phase can no longer adequately excrete the daily fixed acid load generated by normal metabolism or regenerate bicarbonate through ammoniagenesis, so hydrogen ions accumulate in the blood. This produces a metabolic acidosis, which is one of the classic biochemical derangements — alongside hyperkalemia and uremia — that characterizes the maintenance phase and may prompt dialysis.

incorrectas.A: Respiratory acidosis results from primary alveolar hypoventilation and CO2 retention (e.g., COPD, opioid overdose), a pulmonary problem unrelated to the kidneys' failure to excrete acid in ATN.
incorrectas.C: Metabolic alkalosis would result from loss of acid (e.g., vomiting) or gain of bicarbonate — the opposite process from the acid retention that occurs when failing kidneys cannot excrete the daily acid load.
incorrectas.D: Respiratory alkalosis results from hyperventilation and excess CO2 loss, a primary respiratory disturbance that does not reflect the renal failure to excrete acid seen in ATN.

preguntas.q: What is the third and final stage of acute tubular necrosis?

e.correcta: The recovery phase is the third and final stage of ATN, during which surviving tubular epithelial cells proliferate and re-epithelialize the denuded basement membrane, gradually restoring tubular integrity and function. GFR improves as regeneration progresses, and patients often pass through a transient diuretic phase — excreting the fluid and solutes retained during the oliguric maintenance phase — before urine concentrating ability normalizes and renal function returns toward baseline, though some patients are left with residual chronic kidney disease.

incorrectas.A: The inciting event is the very first stage — the initial ischemic or toxic insult — occurring well before re-epithelialization begins, not the final regenerative stage.
incorrectas.B: The maintenance phase is the second stage, defined by persistently low GFR and oliguria while damage is ongoing, preceding the structural repair that defines the recovery phase.
incorrectas.C: 'Oliguric phase' is not one of the three formally named stages of ATN (inciting event, maintenance, recovery); oliguria is a feature associated with the maintenance phase, not a separate stage, and it resolves rather than defines the recovery phase.

preguntas.q: In the recovery (diuretic) phase of acute tubular necrosis, what characteristic change in urine output occurs?

e.correcta: ATN progresses through phases: an initial injury/maintenance phase with oliguria due to tubular obstruction by sloughed necrotic cells and casts and backleak of filtrate, followed by a recovery phase in which regenerating tubular cells restore glomerular filtration faster than their concentrating ability returns, producing marked polyuria. This diuretic surge risks hypokalemia and hyponatremia from ongoing urinary losses, so electrolytes must be monitored closely even as kidney function is improving.

incorrectas.A: Anuria describes near-complete absence of urine output, more typical of severe obstruction or the acute oliguric phase, not the recovery phase, in which output actually surges well above normal.
incorrectas.B: Oliguria is the hallmark of the initial/maintenance phase of ATN, when necrotic debris and casts obstruct the tubules and GFR falls; it is the opposite of what happens once tubular cells regenerate during recovery.
incorrectas.D: Hematuria is not a defining feature of ATN's phases; ATN classically produces muddy brown granular casts from sloughed epithelial cells, not gross or isolated hematuria, so this does not describe the recovery-phase urine pattern.

preguntas.q: As acute tubular necrosis enters its recovery phase, what happens to BUN and serum creatinine?

e.correcta: As regenerating tubular epithelium restores glomerular filtration and clears retained nitrogenous waste, BUN and creatinine—which had risen during the oliguric injury phase—begin trending back down toward baseline. This decline tracks the return of renal function even while urine output is still abnormally high during the polyuric diuretic phase.

incorrectas.A: Continued rise describes the trajectory during the initial oliguric/maintenance phase when GFR is still falling, not once regeneration is underway and filtration is being restored.
incorrectas.C: A plateau at peak values would reflect the maintenance phase of ATN, when tubular injury is stable and neither worsening nor improving, not the recovery phase, which is specifically defined by the resumption of clearance and falling retention values.
incorrectas.D: Becoming undetectable is unrealistic; creatinine and BUN gradually normalize toward baseline over days as function recovers, they do not disappear instantly or become undetectable.

preguntas.q: Acute tubular necrosis is intrinsically reversible, but patients often require which supportive intervention to manage dangerous electrolyte disturbances (e.g., hyperkalemia during the oliguric phase or hypokalemia as diuresis begins)?

e.correcta: Because tubular epithelium can regenerate, ATN itself often resolves without permanent scarring, but the intervening period of impaired filtration and shifting urine output can produce life-threatening electrolyte and volume derangements. Dialysis serves as a bridge that buys time for intrinsic renal recovery, correcting hyperkalemia, acidosis, and volume overload until the kidneys regain adequate function.

incorrectas.A: Peritoneal lavage is a technique for irrigating the peritoneal cavity, historically used in conditions like pancreatitis or overdose, not a standard renal replacement modality for the metabolic derangements of ATN.
incorrectas.B: Loop diuretics may be tried to convert oliguric to nonoliguric ATN in certain situations, but they do not correct life-threatening hyperkalemia or acidosis the way dialysis does, and are not the definitive supportive measure here.
incorrectas.D: Corticosteroids treat immune-mediated renal disease such as some glomerulonephritides or interstitial nephritis, but ATN results from ischemic or toxic tubular injury, not an inflammatory process that responds to steroids.

preguntas.q: Acute interstitial nephritis is characterized histologically by which finding in the connective tissue between renal tubules?

o.A: Granular immune complex deposits along the GBM

e.correcta: AIN is, by definition, an inflammatory reaction within the renal interstitium, typically triggered by a hypersensitivity response to a drug. Biopsy shows edema and an infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and often eosinophils in this interstitial space, generally sparing the glomeruli, which is what distinguishes it from a primary glomerular process.

incorrectas.A: Granular immune complex deposits along the GBM describe glomerular disease processes, such as membranous nephropathy or post-infectious GN, where the glomerular basement membrane is the site of injury, not the tubulointerstitial compartment affected in AIN.
incorrectas.C: Crescents in Bowman's space are the hallmark of rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, reflecting severe glomerular capillary injury with parietal cell proliferation, an entirely different anatomic compartment and disease category than AIN.
incorrectas.D: Diffuse tubular atrophy with fibrosis describes the chronic, irreversible endpoint of long-standing tubulointerstitial injury, not the acute inflammatory infiltrate that defines the active phase of AIN.

preguntas.q: A patient develops acute kidney injury with fever and rash days to weeks after starting a new antibiotic. Which combination of extrarenal findings classically accompanies this drug-induced hypersensitivity reaction?

e.correcta: AIN is a hypersensitivity reaction (typically type IV, sometimes type I) to an offending drug, classically penicillins, NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors, or sulfa drugs. The systemic allergic nature of this reaction commonly produces fever and a maculopapular rash alongside eosinophilia and eosinophiluria, appearing days to weeks after exposure, though many patients are actually asymptomatic aside from a rising creatinine.

incorrectas.B: Arthralgia and uveitis characterize tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis (TINU) syndrome, a distinct and much rarer entity, not the typical hypersensitivity presentation of drug-induced AIN.
incorrectas.C: Peripheral edema and hypertension are hallmarks of nephrotic or nephritic glomerular syndromes with sodium and water retention, not of a tubulointerstitial hypersensitivity reaction, which does not typically cause significant edema or hypertension.
incorrectas.D: Flank pain with gross hematuria suggests processes like nephrolithiasis, pyelonephritis, or papillary necrosis with sloughed tissue, rather than the classic fever-and-rash hypersensitivity picture of AIN.

preguntas.q: Which physical exam finding may be present in acute interstitial nephritis?

e.correcta: The interstitial inflammation and edema of AIN can stretch the renal capsule and irritate surrounding tissue, producing tenderness at the costovertebral angle on exam, similar to (though usually less pronounced than) the CVA tenderness classically taught with pyelonephritis. This is a reminder that CVA tenderness is a nonspecific sign of renal inflammation rather than being diagnostic of infection alone.

incorrectas.B: A costovertebral bruit would suggest a vascular abnormality such as renal artery stenosis, not the tubulointerstitial inflammatory process of AIN, which is not classically associated with an audible bruit.
incorrectas.C: Periorbital edema reflects significant proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia as seen in nephrotic syndrome, not the tubulointerstitial injury pattern of AIN, which typically does not cause heavy proteinuria or the resulting edema.
incorrectas.D: Abdominal striae are associated with rapid weight change or hypercortisolism (e.g., Cushing syndrome), and have no established relationship to AIN or renal inflammation.

preguntas.q: What is the most important step in treating drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis?

o.A: High-dose systemic corticosteroids as first-line therapy

e.correcta: Because AIN is a hypersensitivity reaction to a specific drug, the single most important intervention is identifying and stopping that agent. Renal function typically improves once the antigenic trigger is removed, and most cases resolve without any further specific therapy being needed.

incorrectas.A: Corticosteroids may be considered as an adjunct in severe or persistent cases after the drug has already been stopped and renal function fails to improve, but they are not first-line and do not substitute for removing the trigger.
incorrectas.C: Hemodialysis is reserved for AIN complicated by severe, refractory AKI (e.g., uremia, severe hyperkalemia), not used as the routine or primary treatment for a disease that is fundamentally reversible with drug withdrawal.
incorrectas.D: Cyclophosphamide is a potent immunosuppressant used for severe autoimmune or vasculitic renal disease, a far more aggressive and inappropriate therapy for a self-limited hypersensitivity reaction that typically resolves with drug cessation alone.

preguntas.q: Acute interstitial nephritis is less commonly caused by which category of illness, exemplified by Mycoplasma?

e.correcta: While most AIN is drug-induced, a minority of cases arise from direct or immune-mediated interstitial inflammation triggered by systemic infections such as Mycoplasma, Legionella, streptococcal infections, or certain viruses (CMV, EBV, HIV). Recognizing infectious AIN matters because management centers on treating the underlying infection rather than simply withdrawing a drug.

incorrectas.A: Autoimmune disease (e.g., Sjögren syndrome, SLE, sarcoidosis) is a separate, distinct minor cause of AIN, unrelated to the infectious mechanism exemplified by Mycoplasma.
incorrectas.C: Malignancy is not a recognized common cause of AIN the way infections and drugs are; paraneoplastic renal disease more classically presents as membranous nephropathy or minimal change disease rather than interstitial nephritis.
incorrectas.D: Metabolic disorders such as hypercalcemia or hyperuricemia can cause chronic tubulointerstitial damage over time, but this is a distinct mechanism from the acute hypersensitivity or infectious inflammatory process being described here.

preguntas.q: Acute interstitial nephritis is less commonly caused by which category of disease, exemplified by Sjögren syndrome, SLE, and sarcoidosis?

e.correcta: Systemic autoimmune conditions can directly infiltrate and inflame the renal interstitium as part of their broader immune dysregulation. Sjögren syndrome and sarcoidosis, in particular, are well-recognized (if uncommon) causes of AIN independent of any drug exposure, so a thorough autoimmune history and workup should be considered when no clear offending medication can be identified.

incorrectas.A: Infections such as Mycoplasma or Legionella represent a separate uncommon etiologic category for AIN, mechanistically distinct from the autoimmune-mediated interstitial inflammation of Sjögren, SLE, or sarcoidosis.
incorrectas.B: Drug hypersensitivity is actually the most common cause of AIN overall (e.g., penicillins, NSAIDs, PPIs), but it works through a different mechanism, type IV/I hypersensitivity to a specific agent, than the autoimmune systemic disease process being described.
incorrectas.D: Malignancy is not a well-established direct cause of AIN; paraneoplastic renal syndromes typically manifest as glomerular disease, such as minimal change disease with Hodgkin lymphoma, rather than tubulointerstitial nephritis.

preguntas.q: Acute interstitial nephritis may progress to which severe complication involving ischemic sloughing of the renal papillae?

e.correcta: Ongoing interstitial inflammation and edema in AIN can compress the vasa recta supplying the renal medulla, and if severe or prolonged enough, this ischemia can progress to renal papillary necrosis, in which the medullary papillae undergo coagulative necrosis and may slough into the collecting system, sometimes visible as tissue fragments in the urine.

incorrectas.A: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis is a distinct, severe glomerular process characterized by crescent formation and rapid loss of GFR, driven by glomerular capillary injury rather than the tubulointerstitial ischemia that leads to papillary necrosis.
incorrectas.B: Diffuse cortical necrosis results from severe, prolonged ischemia to the renal cortex, classically from obstetric catastrophes like placental abruption or shock, and destroys the entire cortex rather than the medullary papillae specifically.
incorrectas.D: Renal vein thrombosis is a vascular occlusive event, often associated with nephrotic syndrome and hypercoagulability, not a consequence of interstitial inflammation compressing medullary blood flow as occurs in AIN progressing to papillary necrosis.

preguntas.q: Which renal condition is characterized by sloughing of necrotic renal papillae, sometimes visible as tissue fragments in the urine?

e.correcta: Renal papillary necrosis results from ischemic or toxic injury specifically to the renal medullary papillae, the most vulnerable region of the kidney because of its relatively low blood flow. The necrotic papillary tissue can detach and pass into the collecting system and ureter, sometimes visible grossly as sloughed tissue fragments in the urine and occasionally causing ureteral obstruction.

incorrectas.A: Membranous nephropathy is a glomerular disease characterized by subepithelial immune complex deposits and GBM thickening causing nephrotic syndrome, with no relationship to papillary sloughing.
incorrectas.B: Medullary sponge kidney is a congenital anomaly with cystic dilation of the collecting ducts in the medulla, predisposing to stones and infection, but it does not itself cause papillary necrosis or sloughing.
incorrectas.C: Acute tubular necrosis involves necrosis of the tubular epithelial cells lining the nephron (proximal tubule and thick ascending limb), producing granular casts, not necrosis and sloughing of the papillary tip itself.

preguntas.q: In addition to hematuria, renal papillary necrosis may also present with which finding?

e.correcta: As necrotic papillary tissue and the associated tubulointerstitial injury disrupt normal nephron architecture and barrier function, some degree of proteinuria commonly accompanies the hematuria seen in renal papillary necrosis, reflecting the combined structural damage occurring alongside the ischemic papillary injury.

incorrectas.A: Ketonuria reflects a state of active fat metabolism or ketogenesis, as in diabetic ketoacidosis or starvation, not a finding related to renal papillary tissue injury.
incorrectas.B: Glucosuria typically indicates hyperglycemia exceeding the tubular reabsorptive threshold or a proximal tubular reabsorption defect (e.g., Fanconi syndrome), not a classic feature of papillary necrosis.
incorrectas.D: Isolated pyuria would suggest a primarily infectious or inflammatory urinary process, such as pyelonephritis or cystitis, rather than the hematuria-plus-proteinuria pattern typical of papillary necrosis.

preguntas.q: Renal papillary necrosis may be caused by chronic use of which class of drugs, such as long-term aspirin or phenacetin?

e.correcta: Chronic heavy use of analgesics, classically combinations containing phenacetin (now withdrawn) or long-term NSAID/aspirin use, can cause analgesic nephropathy, in which direct medullary toxicity combines with NSAID-mediated inhibition of vasodilatory prostaglandins to reduce medullary blood flow, leading to ischemic papillary necrosis.

incorrectas.A: Aminoglycosides are classically associated with proximal tubular toxicity leading to acute tubular necrosis, not the ischemic/toxic medullary papillary injury seen with analgesic-induced papillary necrosis.
incorrectas.C: Loop diuretics act on the thick ascending limb to block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter and are not established causes of papillary necrosis; they are used therapeutically, not implicated as a toxic cause.
incorrectas.D: Calcineurin inhibitors (e.g., cyclosporine, tacrolimus) cause a distinct pattern of nephrotoxicity via afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction and chronic interstitial fibrosis, not classically papillary necrosis from analgesic abuse.

preguntas.q: Renal papillary necrosis may be caused by which hematologic condition, even in trait form?

e.correcta: The renal medulla's hypoxic, hypertonic, and acidotic environment promotes sickling of red cells even in patients with sickle cell trait, and the resulting vaso-occlusion in the vasa recta causes ischemic injury to the papillae. This makes sickle hemoglobinopathies, both disease and trait, a classic cause of renal papillary necrosis, distinguishing them from most other hemolytic anemias.

incorrectas.A: Hereditary spherocytosis causes extravascular hemolysis due to a red cell membrane defect, but the abnormal cells do not undergo the vaso-occlusive sickling process responsible for medullary ischemia in papillary necrosis.
incorrectas.B: G6PD deficiency causes episodic oxidative hemolysis triggered by stressors like infections, certain drugs, or fava beans, a mechanism unrelated to vaso-occlusion of the medullary microvasculature.
incorrectas.D: Polycythemia vera increases blood viscosity and thrombotic risk, but it is not the classic hematologic cause taught for renal papillary necrosis; sickling hemoglobinopathies are the specific culprit because the hypoxic renal medulla promotes HbS polymerization.

preguntas.q: Renal papillary necrosis may be caused by which severe infectious process, in which interstitial edema compresses the medullary vasculature and causes ischemia?

e.correcta: In severe acute pyelonephritis, the intense interstitial inflammation and edema of the infected kidney can compress the delicate vasa recta supplying the medulla, producing ischemia that culminates in necrosis of the papillae. This is a mechanical/ischemic complication layered on top of the primary infectious process, and it is more likely with underlying risk factors like diabetes or urinary obstruction.

incorrectas.A: Chronic glomerulonephritis is a slow, progressive glomerular scarring process, mechanistically and anatomically distinct from the acute infectious/inflammatory medullary compression that causes papillary necrosis.
incorrectas.B: Renal artery stenosis causes chronic, global reduction in renal perfusion relevant to renovascular hypertension and ischemic nephropathy, not the acute focal medullary ischemia from interstitial edema seen with severe pyelonephritis.
incorrectas.C: Acute cystitis is a lower urinary tract infection confined to the bladder mucosa and does not involve the renal parenchyma or medullary blood supply, so it does not cause papillary necrosis.

preguntas.q: Which endocrine disorder is a classic cause of renal papillary necrosis?

e.correcta: Diabetes mellitus predisposes to renal papillary necrosis through a combination of microvascular disease causing small-vessel ischemia in the medulla, increased susceptibility to pyelonephritis and papillary infection, and frequent concurrent analgesic use for chronic pain. Along with sickle cell disease, analgesic abuse, and severe pyelonephritis, it is one of the classic causes to remember for this ischemic medullary complication.

incorrectas.A: Cushing syndrome causes hypercortisolism with hypertension, hyperglycemia, and immunosuppression, but is not a recognized direct cause of medullary ischemic papillary necrosis.
incorrectas.B: Primary hyperparathyroidism leads to hypercalcemia, which can cause nephrocalcinosis and chronic tubulointerstitial damage, but this is a distinct mechanism from the ischemic papillary necrosis associated with diabetes.
incorrectas.D: Hypothyroidism is not associated with renal papillary necrosis; it more classically causes generalized fluid retention and, rarely, a reversible reduction in GFR, not medullary ischemic necrosis.

preguntas.q: Nephrotic syndrome is classically associated with which lipid abnormality?

e.correcta: In nephrotic syndrome, heavy urinary protein loss lowers plasma oncotic pressure, which stimulates the liver to ramp up generalized lipoprotein synthesis in effect trying to restore that lost oncotic pressure, producing hyperlipidemia and hypercholesterolemia. This is compounded by decreased lipoprotein lipase activity and impaired clearance of circulating lipid particles, further worsening the lipid derangement.

incorrectas.A: Isolated hypertriglyceridemia with normal cholesterol understates the abnormality; while triglycerides can also rise, the hallmark and most consistent lipid finding in nephrotic syndrome is elevated cholesterol together with elevated lipids overall.
incorrectas.B: Hypolipidemia is the opposite of what actually occurs; hepatic overproduction of lipoproteins in response to low oncotic pressure drives lipid levels up, not down.
incorrectas.D: A normal lipid profile is inconsistent with the pathophysiology of nephrotic syndrome, in which the same protein loss that causes edema also triggers compensatory hepatic lipoprotein overproduction and impaired lipid clearance.

preguntas.q: What is the most common underlying cause of minimal change disease, which may be triggered by a recent URI, immunization, or insect bite?

o.A: Autoantibodies against the glomerular basement membrane

e.correcta: In the great majority of cases, no specific antigen or trigger is identified for minimal change disease; it is considered idiopathic, thought to involve T-cell dysfunction that releases a circulating permeability factor damaging the podocyte foot processes. Recent infections, vaccinations, or insect stings are recognized as occasional precipitants but do not represent a defined causal mechanism the way immune complex or antibody-mediated diseases do.

incorrectas.A: Anti-GBM antibodies define Goodpasture syndrome, a distinct antibody-mediated disease targeting type IV collagen in the GBM and alveolar basement membrane, not the mechanism behind minimal change disease.
incorrectas.C: Immune complex deposition characterizes diseases like membranous nephropathy, post-infectious GN, or lupus nephritis; minimal change disease is notable precisely because it lacks immune complex deposits on immunofluorescence and electron microscopy.
incorrectas.D: NSAID hypersensitivity can rarely trigger minimal change disease (and more classically causes AIN), but this is a specific secondary cause, not the most common idiopathic etiology being asked about here.

preguntas.q: Minimal change disease is rarely a paraneoplastic manifestation of which malignancy, attributed to massive cytokine release from Reed-Sternberg cells?

e.correcta: Reed-Sternberg cells in Hodgkin lymphoma secrete large quantities of cytokines, including factors resembling the circulating permeability factor implicated in idiopathic MCD, which can damage podocyte foot processes and produce a paraneoplastic nephrotic syndrome that looks histologically identical to minimal change disease. Recognizing this association matters clinically because treating the underlying lymphoma typically resolves the renal disease.

incorrectas.A: Renal cell carcinoma is more classically associated with paraneoplastic syndromes like polycythemia via ectopic EPO, hypercalcemia, and Stauffer syndrome, not minimal change disease.
incorrectas.B: Multiple myeloma classically causes renal injury through light-chain (cast) nephropathy, AL amyloidosis, or light-chain deposition disease, mechanistically very different from the cytokine-driven podocyte injury of paraneoplastic MCD.
incorrectas.C: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is more classically linked to membranous nephropathy as a paraneoplastic glomerular disease, whereas it is specifically Hodgkin lymphoma, via Reed-Sternberg cell cytokines, that is associated with minimal change disease.

preguntas.q: Minimal change disease is characterized by which finding on light microscopy?

o.A: Diffuse capillary wall thickening with a "spike and dome" pattern

e.correcta: The defining and somewhat paradoxical feature of minimal change disease is that despite massive proteinuria, the glomeruli appear entirely normal by light microscopy. The pathology is only visible on electron microscopy, which shows diffuse effacement of the podocyte foot processes, and this normal-LM/normal-IF/abnormal-EM triad is a classic testable pattern.

incorrectas.A: A "spike and dome" pattern refers to subepithelial immune deposits with intervening GBM spikes seen in membranous nephropathy on silver stain, a structural glomerular abnormality that is by definition absent in MCD.
incorrectas.B: Segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis is the defining light-microscopic lesion of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, a different podocytopathy in which some glomeruli show visible scarring, unlike the uniformly normal-appearing glomeruli of MCD.
incorrectas.D: Diffuse mesangial hypercellularity describes proliferative glomerular diseases such as IgA nephropathy or lupus nephritis, reflecting immune complex-driven mesangial cell proliferation, which is not a feature of minimal change disease.

preguntas.q: What is the typical immunofluorescence finding in minimal change disease?

e.correcta: Because minimal change disease is not mediated by antibody or immune complex deposition, immunofluorescence is essentially negative, with no significant deposits of immunoglobulin or complement. This is consistent with the disease's basis in a T-cell-derived circulating factor causing direct podocyte injury rather than immune complex-mediated glomerular damage.

incorrectas.A: "Lumpy-bumpy" granular deposits describe the coarse, irregular subepithelial immune complex deposits of post-infectious (poststreptococcal) glomerulonephritis, reflecting immune complex disease that MCD does not have.
incorrectas.B: Linear GBM staining is the hallmark of anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome), where autoantibodies bind uniformly along the basement membrane, in contrast to MCD, which shows no significant immunofluorescence positivity at all.
incorrectas.D: A "starry sky" granular mesangial pattern describes diseases like IgA nephropathy with mesangial immune complex deposition, again a fundamentally different, immune complex-driven process from the deposit-free picture of MCD.

preguntas.q: Which hematologic disease increases the risk of developing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis?

e.correcta: Chronic sickling and vaso-occlusion within the glomerular capillaries in sickle cell disease produces recurrent ischemic injury and compensatory glomerular hyperfiltration, which over time predisposes to secondary FSGS. This illustrates that FSGS is frequently a secondary, final-common-pathway lesion resulting from chronic hemodynamic or ischemic stress on glomeruli, not just idiopathic podocyte injury.

incorrectas.A: Thalassemia major causes iron-overload-related organ damage (e.g., cardiac, hepatic, endocrine) from chronic transfusions, but is not a classic risk factor for FSGS the way sickle cell disease is.
incorrectas.B: Polycythemia vera increases blood viscosity and thrombotic risk broadly, but it is not specifically linked to glomerular sclerosis in the way chronic sickling-induced ischemia predisposes to FSGS.
incorrectas.D: Hereditary spherocytosis causes extravascular hemolysis and splenic sequestration of abnormally shaped red cells, without the vaso-occlusive glomerular ischemia that links sickle cell disease to secondary FSGS.

preguntas.q: Which infectious disease is classically associated with a collapsing variant of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis?

e.correcta: HIV can directly infect renal epithelial cells, producing a distinct and aggressive form of FSGS known as HIV-associated nephropathy (HIVAN), typically the collapsing variant, characterized by rapid progression to renal failure and disproportionately affecting patients of African descent. This is an important secondary cause of FSGS to recognize since it changes both prognosis and management, including the role of antiretroviral therapy.

incorrectas.A: Hepatitis C is classically linked to membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, often via cryoglobulinemia, not FSGS, reflecting a different immune complex-mediated glomerular injury pattern.
incorrectas.C: Hepatitis B is classically associated with membranous nephropathy (and polyarteritis nodosa), an immune complex glomerular disease distinct from the direct viral podocyte injury seen in HIV-associated FSGS.
incorrectas.D: Streptococcus pyogenes causes post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, an immune complex-mediated proliferative and nephritic process, not the podocytopathy of FSGS.

preguntas.q: What is the typical immunofluorescence finding in focal segmental glomerulosclerosis?

o.A: Diffuse linear IgG deposition along the GBM
o.C: Negative, though nonspecific IgM and C3 may be seen in sclerotic segments

e.correcta: Like minimal change disease, FSGS is a primary podocytopathy rather than an immune complex-mediated disease, so immunofluorescence is generally negative for significant immune deposits. Nonspecific trapping of IgM and complement (C3, C1q) can be seen within the sclerotic segments themselves, reflecting passive entrapment of plasma proteins in damaged tissue rather than a true immune complex-mediated pathogenesis.

incorrectas.A: Linear IgG deposition is diagnostic of anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease, in which autoantibodies bind uniformly along the basement membrane, a completely different, antibody-driven mechanism from the podocyte-injury basis of FSGS.
incorrectas.B: "Lumpy-bumpy" subepithelial deposits describe post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, an immune complex-mediated proliferative disease, not the podocytopathy of FSGS, which lacks true immune complex deposition.
incorrectas.D: Dominant mesangial IgA is the defining immunofluorescence finding of IgA nephropathy, a distinct mesangial immune complex disease unrelated to the segmental sclerosis and largely negative immunofluorescence of FSGS.

preguntas.q: How does focal segmental glomerulosclerosis typically respond to corticosteroid therapy?

o.A: It is uniformly steroid-resistant and always requires transplantation
o.B: It responds identically to minimal change disease
o.D: It requires no treatment and resolves spontaneously

e.correcta: Unlike minimal change disease, which is usually highly steroid-responsive, FSGS shows a poor and inconsistent response to corticosteroids, with many patients partially or fully steroid-resistant. This contributes to its worse overall prognosis and higher rate of progression to chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease compared to MCD.
