incorrectas.A: Calling FSGS uniformly steroid-resistant and always requiring transplant overstates the case; while the response is poor and inconsistent, some patients do achieve partial or complete remission with steroids or other agents like calcineurin inhibitors, so it is not universally and immediately treatment-refractory.
incorrectas.B: An identical response to minimal change disease is incorrect and is actually the key clinical distinguishing feature between the two: MCD is classically steroid-responsive, while FSGS's poor, inconsistent response is a major reason the two entities, which can otherwise look similar clinically, are differentiated on biopsy.
incorrectas.D: Requiring no treatment is inaccurate; FSGS is a serious progressive disease that is actively treated with immunosuppressive regimens (steroids plus/minus calcineurin inhibitors) despite the incomplete response, since untreated disease tends to progress toward renal failure.

preguntas.q: A patient with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) who does not respond to treatment will most likely have his renal disease ultimately progress to which condition?

e.correcta: FSGS causes progressive scarring of segments of glomeruli; as more nephrons sclerose over time, irreversible loss of functioning nephron mass leads to progressive decline in GFR and ultimately chronic renal failure/ESRD, particularly in patients who are steroid-resistant (unlike minimal change disease, many FSGS patients do not respond well to steroids). This is why FSGS carries a worse long-term renal prognosis among the primary nephrotic syndromes.

incorrectas.A: Acute interstitial nephritis is typically a drug-hypersensitivity reaction causing tubulointerstitial inflammation, not the natural endpoint of glomerular scarring diseases like FSGS.
incorrectas.C: Renal artery stenosis is a vascular/renovascular disease causing hypertension and ischemic nephropathy from large-vessel narrowing, unrelated to the progressive segmental glomerular scarring seen in FSGS.
incorrectas.D: Acute tubular necrosis is an acute, often reversible tubular injury from ischemia or nephrotoxins, not the chronic, irreversible outcome of a glomerular scarring disease like FSGS.

preguntas.q: Membranous nephropathy occurring as a secondary phenomenon is classically associated with chronic infection by which pair of viruses?

e.correcta: Secondary membranous nephropathy results from circulating antigen-antibody immune complexes depositing in the subepithelial space of the glomerulus. Chronic hepatitis B and hepatitis C infections are classic triggers because viral antigens circulate persistently and form immune complexes that lodge along the GBM, activating complement and producing the granular subepithelial deposits characteristic of MN.

incorrectas.A: HIV nephropathy classically causes a collapsing variant of FSGS rather than membranous nephropathy, and CMV is not a classic trigger of secondary MN.
incorrectas.B: EBV and parvovirus B19 are not classic causes of secondary MN; parvovirus B19 has been linked to collapsing glomerulopathy in some reports, but neither generates the chronic circulating antigenemia typical of HBV/HCV-associated MN.
incorrectas.C: HSV and VZV do not typically produce chronic circulating immune complexes capable of depositing in glomeruli, so they are not associated with secondary membranous nephropathy.

preguntas.q: Which pattern of nephrotic syndrome is most commonly seen as a paraneoplastic manifestation of underlying solid tumors (e.g., lung, colon, breast carcinoma)?

e.correcta: Solid tumors can shed tumor antigens that circulate and form immune complexes, which deposit in the subepithelial space of the glomerulus, producing the same histologic and immunofluorescence pattern as idiopathic membranous nephropathy (granular subepithelial deposits, 'spike and dome' appearance on silver stain). This paraneoplastic association is why clinicians screen older adults with new-onset MN for occult malignancy.

incorrectas.A: Minimal change disease is the nephrotic syndrome classically linked to Hodgkin lymphoma via cytokine-mediated podocyte injury, not to solid tumors in general.
incorrectas.B: FSGS's secondary causes include HIV, heroin use, obesity, and reduced nephron mass, not typically solid-tumor-driven immune complex deposition.
incorrectas.D: Amyloidosis-related nephrotic syndrome arises from AL (plasma cell dyscrasia) or AA (chronic inflammation) amyloid deposition, a mechanistically distinct process from immune-complex-mediated tumor-associated membranous nephropathy.

preguntas.q: Immunofluorescence microscopy in membranous nephropathy classically shows which staining pattern along the capillary loops?

e.correcta: Membranous nephropathy is an immune-complex-mediated disease in which IgG and C3 deposit in a discontinuous, 'lumpy-bumpy' granular pattern along the subepithelial aspect of the GBM, corresponding to the 'spike and dome' appearance seen on silver stain and electron microscopy. This granular pattern reflects deposition of discrete immune complexes rather than a continuous antibody coating.

incorrectas.B: Linear IF staining is the hallmark of anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome), where antibodies bind directly and uniformly to a GBM antigen (type IV collagen), producing a smooth ribbon-like pattern distinct from MN's granular deposits.
incorrectas.C: Pauci-immune (minimal or absent) IF staining is characteristic of ANCA-associated vasculitides causing crescentic glomerulonephritis, reflecting an absence of immune complex deposition, the opposite of MN's immune-complex pattern.
incorrectas.D: Crescentic describes a histologic pattern of parietal epithelial cell proliferation seen in rapidly progressive GN, not an immunofluorescence staining pattern, and is not typical of uncomplicated membranous nephropathy.

preguntas.q: Compared to minimal change disease, membranous nephropathy typically shows what response to corticosteroid therapy?

e.correcta: Unlike minimal change disease, where nephrotic syndrome typically resolves dramatically with corticosteroids, membranous nephropathy responds poorly to steroids alone because the chronic subepithelial immune-complex deposits and associated GBM thickening are not rapidly reversed by steroid-mediated immunosuppression. Many patients require additional therapy (calcineurin inhibitors, rituximab) or still progress toward chronic kidney disease.

incorrectas.A: This describes minimal change disease, in which podocyte foot-process effacement driven by cytokine effects is highly steroid-responsive; MN is a structurally more chronic lesion that behaves very differently.
incorrectas.B: Some MN cases undergo spontaneous partial remission over time, but this is unpredictable and not the general rule, so expecting resolution without any treatment is not the standard clinical expectation.
incorrectas.C: MN is primarily a disease of adults, and the poor steroid responsiveness described applies regardless of age; this option incorrectly implies age determines the steroid response pattern.

preguntas.q: If unresponsive to therapy, membranous nephropathy most commonly progresses to which long-term outcome?

e.correcta: Persistent immune-complex deposition and complement-mediated podocyte injury in MN lead to ongoing proteinuria, progressive glomerulosclerosis, and tubulointerstitial fibrosis. A substantial share of untreated or refractory patients progress to chronic renal failure/ESRD over years, which is why patients with high-risk features (heavy proteinuria, declining GFR) are monitored closely and treated.

incorrectas.A: MN is fundamentally a nephrotic-syndrome process (heavy proteinuria, edema, hypoalbuminemia) rather than a nephritic process defined by hematuria; while mild hematuria can occur, this does not capture MN's chronic progressive course.
incorrectas.C: While a subset of patients spontaneously remit, this is not the typical trajectory in persistent or treatment-refractory disease; chronic progression toward renal failure is the concern that drives treatment decisions.
incorrectas.D: Acute kidney injury implies an acute, often reversible drop in renal function; MN's natural history is one of gradual, chronic decline rather than an acute reversible insult.

preguntas.q: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) is best classified as which type of glomerular disease?

o.A: A disorder that can present as nephritic, nephrotic, or a mixed/overlapping picture
o.D: A disease confined to isolated asymptomatic hematuria

e.correcta: MPGN is unusual among glomerular diseases in that its histologic pattern (mesangial proliferation with GBM splitting) can produce clinical features of nephrotic syndrome (heavy proteinuria), nephritic syndrome (hematuria, RBC casts, hypertension), or a combination of both, depending on the balance of proliferative versus membranous injury. This dual potential is a distinguishing exam point compared with diseases that fall cleanly into one category.

incorrectas.B: Classic purely nephrotic diseases like minimal change disease or FSGS lack the inflammatory/proliferative component and hematuria that MPGN frequently displays.
incorrectas.C: Classic purely nephritic diseases like poststreptococcal GN present with hematuria and hypertension without the heavy selective proteinuria that MPGN can also produce; MPGN is not restricted to a single pattern.
incorrectas.D: Isolated asymptomatic hematuria is more typical of IgA nephropathy or thin basement membrane disease; MPGN typically causes more overt disease with proteinuria, edema, and/or renal insufficiency rather than being silent.

preguntas.q: The characteristic 'tram-track' splitting of the glomerular basement membrane seen in MPGN is caused by which process?

o.A: Direct antibody binding to type IV collagen
o.B: Amyloid fibril deposition in the mesangium
o.D: Mesangial cell interposition and matrix ingrowth into the subendothelial space

e.correcta: In MPGN, immune complexes (e.g., IgG in Type I) deposited along the capillary wall trigger mesangial cells to proliferate and extend cytoplasmic processes between the endothelium and the GBM. This interposition, along with new basement-membrane-like matrix synthesis, splits the original GBM into two parallel layers visible on silver or PAS stain as the 'tram-track' sign, while the immune complexes also activate complement and drive the inflammatory, proliferative injury.

incorrectas.A: Direct linear antibody binding to type IV collagen is the mechanism of anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease, producing linear IF staining and crescents, not the tram-track splitting seen in MPGN.
incorrectas.B: Amyloid deposits produce apple-green birefringence with Congo red and a waxy, acellular expansion of the mesangium, not the cellular interposition and basement membrane duplication that creates tram-tracking.
incorrectas.C: Podocyte foot process effacement is the key ultrastructural finding in minimal change disease and FSGS, causing selective proteinuria, but by itself it does not create the double-layered GBM appearance, which specifically requires mesangial cell/matrix interposition.

preguntas.q: A renal biopsy showing subendothelial granular deposits positive for IgG and C1q on immunofluorescence, with evidence of classical complement pathway activation, is most consistent with which entity?

e.correcta: Type I MPGN is an immune-complex-mediated disease in which circulating antigen-antibody complexes (often IgG) deposit subendothelially and activate the classical complement pathway, producing granular IF staining for IgG and early complement components like C1q. This contrasts with Type II MPGN (dense deposit disease), which is driven by an autoantibody (C3 nephritic factor) that stabilizes the alternative pathway C3 convertase and is typically IgG-negative but C3-positive.

incorrectas.A: Type II MPGN/dense deposit disease shows intramembranous, ribbon-like electron-dense deposits that stain positive for C3 but are classically negative for IgG, the opposite immune-deposit pattern from what is described.
incorrectas.B: Minimal change disease shows no significant immune deposits on IF, since it is not immune-complex mediated; its pathology is confined to podocyte foot process effacement visible only on electron microscopy, so it would not show IgG/C1q granular staining.
incorrectas.D: Anti-GBM disease shows a smooth, linear (not granular) IF pattern for IgG along the GBM from direct antibody binding to type IV collagen, rather than discrete granular immune complex deposits.

preguntas.q: Which type of MPGN classically shows the 'tram-track' appearance on light microscopy (H&E/silver stain), seen in approximately 80% of cases of that subtype?

e.correcta: Type I MPGN, driven by subendothelial immune complex deposition and classical complement activation, most reliably produces mesangial cell interposition into the capillary wall, giving the tram-track double-contour appearance in roughly 80% of biopsies. Tram-tracking can occasionally be seen in other MPGN subtypes, but it is most classically and consistently linked to Type I; Type II (dense deposit disease) instead shows ribbon-like intramembranous dense deposits on electron microscopy.

incorrectas.A: Type II MPGN (dense deposit disease) is defined by dense, ribbon-like deposits within the GBM itself on electron microscopy, a different finding from the light-microscopic tram-track sign most strongly associated with Type I.
incorrectas.C: Type III MPGN is a rarer subtype with combined subendothelial and subepithelial deposits and a more complex basement membrane disruption pattern; it is not the subtype classically emphasized for the '80% tram-track' association.
incorrectas.D: Crescentic GN is defined by epithelial crescents from severe capillary wall rupture, a distinct histologic pattern from the double-contour tram-track appearance characteristic of MPGN.

preguntas.q: Type I membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, an immune-complex-mediated disease, is classically associated with chronic infection by which viruses?

e.correcta: Chronic hepatitis B and hepatitis C infections generate persistent circulating viral antigen-antibody immune complexes that deposit subendothelially, trigger classical complement pathway activation, and drive the mesangial proliferation and GBM splitting characteristic of Type I MPGN. This is the same viral association seen with membranous nephropathy, reflecting a shared immune-complex mechanism, though the resulting histologic pattern differs (proliferative in MPGN versus purely membranous in MN).

incorrectas.B: HSV and CMV are not classically linked to immune-complex-mediated MPGN, as they do not typically generate the chronic circulating antigenemia needed to drive persistent glomerular immune complex deposition.
incorrectas.C: EBV and HHV-8 are associated with lymphoproliferative disease and Kaposi sarcoma/primary effusion lymphoma, respectively, not with the classic viral triggers of Type I MPGN.
incorrectas.D: Influenza and RSV are acute respiratory viruses without a chronic carrier state, so they do not generate the sustained antigenemia required to produce chronic immune-complex glomerular disease like MPGN.

preguntas.q: Type II membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, characterized by ribbon-like intramembranous dense deposits on electron microscopy, is also known by which name?

e.correcta: Type II MPGN is called 'dense deposit disease' because its defining ultrastructural feature is a continuous ribbon of electron-dense material embedded within the GBM itself, rather than subendothelial or subepithelial deposits. This reflects uncontrolled alternative complement pathway activity driven by C3 nephritic factor, an autoantibody that stabilizes C3 convertase and causes persistent complement consumption.

incorrectas.A: IgA nephropathy is defined by mesangial IgA deposition and typically presents with episodic gross hematuria following mucosal infections, an entirely different mechanism and deposit location from the intramembranous dense deposits of Type II MPGN.
incorrectas.B: Diffuse proliferative GN is a pattern classically seen in lupus nephritis (Class IV), involving widespread endocapillary proliferation, not the specific intramembranous dense deposit finding that defines dense deposit disease.
incorrectas.C: Minimal change disease shows no deposits at all on light or immunofluorescence microscopy; its defining lesion is podocyte foot process effacement visible only by electron microscopy, unrelated to the dense deposit pattern of Type II MPGN.

preguntas.q: Type II MPGN (dense deposit disease) is characteristically associated with which serum complement finding, due to an autoantibody that stabilizes the alternative pathway C3 convertase?

e.correcta: In dense deposit disease, an autoantibody called C3 nephritic factor binds to and stabilizes the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb), preventing its normal inactivation and causing continuous, unregulated complement consumption. This results in persistently low serum C3 levels, often with a relatively normal C4 (since the classical pathway is not primarily involved), a lab clue that helps distinguish Type II from Type I MPGN and other complement-mediated diseases.

incorrectas.A: Elevated C3 would indicate increased complement production or decreased consumption, the opposite of what happens when C3 nephritic factor continuously drives C3 convertase activity and depletes circulating C3.
incorrectas.B: Low C4 more specifically implicates classical pathway activation, as in lupus nephritis or Type I MPGN with immune complexes, whereas dense deposit disease is driven by the alternative pathway, which does not consume C4 to the same degree.
incorrectas.D: Normal complement levels throughout the disease course would be inconsistent with the defining laboratory abnormality of dense deposit disease, which is a hallmark, persistent hypocomplementemia (low C3) used diagnostically.

preguntas.q: Compared to minimal change disease, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis typically shows what response to corticosteroid therapy?

o.C: Response occurs only in Type II disease
o.D: No relationship exists between steroids and MPGN outcomes

e.correcta: MPGN, whether Type I or Type II, generally responds poorly to corticosteroids because its pathology involves fixed structural changes (mesangial interposition, GBM duplication, ongoing complement-mediated injury) rather than the reversible podocyte dysfunction seen in minimal change disease. This poor steroid responsiveness is one reason MPGN carries a worse long-term prognosis and often requires other immunosuppressive or complement-targeted strategies.

incorrectas.A: This describes minimal change disease's classic behavior; MPGN's structural, proliferative injury does not resolve as readily with steroids the way MCD's isolated podocyte foot process effacement does.
incorrectas.C: Poor steroid response is a feature shared by both Type I and Type II MPGN, since both involve fixed proliferative or membranous injury, not something unique to Type II disease.
incorrectas.D: There is a well-established, if unfavorable, relationship: steroids generally fail to induce meaningful remission in MPGN, which is clinically important for guiding treatment expectations, so saying no relationship exists misrepresents the evidence.

preguntas.q: If untreated, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis most commonly follows which long-term clinical course?

o.D: Permanent but stable asymptomatic proteinuria without further decline

e.correcta: The ongoing mesangial proliferation, complement activation, and structural GBM remodeling in MPGN produce cumulative glomerular scarring over time. Without effective treatment, a substantial proportion of patients progress to chronic kidney disease and eventually end-stage renal disease, mirroring the poor natural history also seen with membranous nephropathy and FSGS when left unchecked.

incorrectas.B: Spontaneous resolution within weeks would be inconsistent with MPGN's chronic, proliferative pathology; unlike minimal change disease, MPGN does not typically remit rapidly or spontaneously.
incorrectas.C: MPGN and minimal change disease are histologically and mechanistically distinct entities, one proliferative and immune-complex-driven, the other an isolated podocyte disorder; one does not convert into the other over time.
incorrectas.D: While proteinuria can wax and wane, the natural history of untreated MPGN is progressive rather than a stable, indefinitely non-progressive state, given the ongoing complement-mediated glomerular injury.

preguntas.q: In a patient with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, chronically elevated serum glucose initiates renal injury by nonenzymatically modifying which structure, leading to its thickening and increased permeability?

e.correcta: Persistent hyperglycemia drives nonenzymatic glycosylation (glycation) of proteins within the glomerular basement membrane, forming advanced glycation end-products that cross-link GBM collagen. This thickens the membrane while paradoxically increasing its permeability to plasma proteins, marking the earliest structural lesion of diabetic nephropathy and setting the stage for later mesangial expansion and nodular sclerosis.

incorrectas.A: The renal tubular epithelium is affected later in diabetic kidney disease, such as tubular atrophy from chronic hyperfiltration injury, but the initiating glycation injury targets the glomerular filtration barrier, not tubular cells.
incorrectas.B: Bowman's capsule is not the primary site of glycation-driven injury in diabetic nephropathy; the pathologic process centers on the capillary basement membrane where filtration occurs.
incorrectas.C: The renal pelvis urothelium is part of the collecting system, unrelated to glomerular filtration, and is not a target of hyperglycemia-induced nonenzymatic glycosylation in diabetic nephropathy.

preguntas.q: Nonenzymatic glycosylation of vessel walls in diabetic nephropathy classically produces which type of arteriolar lesion?

o.D: Atherosclerotic plaque with a necrotic lipid core

e.correcta: Glycation of plasma proteins that leak into the arteriolar wall, along with associated endothelial injury, leads to deposition of homogeneous, pink, hyaline material within the vessel wall (hyaline arteriolosclerosis), which narrows the vessel lumen. This same lesion is also seen in benign hypertension, but in diabetes it characteristically affects both the afferent and efferent arterioles, unlike hypertension, which typically spares the efferent arteriole.

incorrectas.A: Fibromuscular dysplasia is a non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory arterial disease causing 'string of beads' stenoses, typically in renal or carotid arteries of young women, unrelated to glycation injury from diabetes.
incorrectas.C: Hyperplastic ('onion-skin') arteriolosclerosis is the lesion of malignant hypertension, produced by concentric smooth muscle proliferation from severe pressure-related endothelial injury, not by glycation of vessel wall proteins.
incorrectas.D: Atherosclerosis with a necrotic lipid core affects larger elastic and muscular arteries via lipid-laden plaque formation, a distinct process at a different vascular level from the small-vessel hyaline change caused by glycation in diabetic arterioles.

preguntas.q: In early diabetic nephropathy, nonenzymatic glycation initially and preferentially affects which renal arteriole?

e.correcta: Glycation-driven hyaline arteriolosclerosis initially narrows the efferent arteriole more than the afferent arteriole, increasing resistance to outflow from the glomerulus. Because the afferent arteriole remains comparatively less affected early on, glomerular capillary pressure rises, producing the hyperfiltration state characteristic of early diabetic nephropathy, before the afferent arteriole also becomes involved later in the disease.

incorrectas.B: The afferent arteriole is affected later in the disease course; early selective efferent involvement is what raises intraglomerular pressure and drives hyperfiltration, distinguishing this stage from more advanced disease.
incorrectas.C: Interlobular arteries are larger intrarenal vessels proximal to the arterioles; they are not the site of the microvascular glycation injury that determines glomerular filtration dynamics in early diabetic nephropathy.
incorrectas.D: The vasa recta are specialized capillaries supplying the renal medulla involved in the countercurrent mechanism, not the arterioles governing glomerular capillary pressure that are affected by diabetic glycation injury.

preguntas.q: Selective efferent arteriolar narrowing from glycation injury in early diabetic nephropathy has what net effect on glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?

o.A: GFR decreases due to reduced glomerular blood flow
o.B: GFR remains unchanged because afferent and efferent resistances balance
o.D: GFR becomes unmeasurable due to complete glomerular obliteration

e.correcta: Because efferent arteriolar resistance rises before afferent resistance does, blood entering the glomerulus is relatively unimpeded while its outflow is restricted, raising intraglomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure. This elevated pressure drives an early increase in GFR (hyperfiltration), which is paradoxically damaging over time because the sustained high pressure accelerates glomerular injury, mesangial expansion, and eventual sclerosis.

incorrectas.A: A GFR decrease would be expected if the afferent arteriole were the primary site of narrowing, reducing inflow, but early diabetic nephropathy's efferent-predominant lesion instead raises, rather than lowers, glomerular pressure and filtration.
incorrectas.B: Because the efferent and afferent arterioles are not equally affected early in the disease, their resistances do not simply balance out; the imbalance specifically favors increased intraglomerular pressure rather than a neutral net effect.
incorrectas.D: Complete glomerular obliteration and unmeasurable GFR describes end-stage, advanced nephropathy after years of progressive sclerosis, not the early hemodynamic stage being described here.

preguntas.q: If left untreated, does diabetic nephropathy remain confined to a nephrotic syndrome, or can it evolve further?

o.A: It always remains an isolated nephrotic syndrome
o.B: It converts directly into minimal change disease
o.C: It resolves without intervention once hyperfiltration subsides
o.D: It can progress to a nephritic syndrome

e.correcta: Diabetic nephropathy begins as a nephrotic-range proteinuric disease driven by GBM glycation and hyperfiltration injury, but as disease advances the afferent arteriole also develops hyaline arteriolosclerosis. This reduces renal blood flow, causing ischemic glomerular injury and infarction that produces hematuria and other features of a nephritic syndrome, so the clinical picture can evolve from a purely nephrotic to a mixed or nephritic pattern over time.

incorrectas.A: While early disease is nephrotic, assuming it always stays confined to this pattern ignores the later afferent arteriolar involvement and ischemic injury that can add nephritic features as the disease progresses.
incorrectas.B: Minimal change disease is a distinct, typically pediatric podocyte disorder that is mechanistically unrelated to diabetic glomerular injury; diabetic nephropathy does not transform into MCD.
incorrectas.C: Diabetic nephropathy does not resolve spontaneously; without glycemic and blood pressure control, and often ACE inhibitor therapy, it progresses rather than reversing once hyperfiltration begins.

preguntas.q: On light microscopy, diabetic glomerulonephropathy is characterized by which cellular change within the glomerulus?

o.B: Mesangial cell proliferation with increased matrix
o.C: Complete podocyte loss with capillary collapse

e.correcta: Chronic hyperglycemia and non-enzymatic glycation of mesangial cells stimulate them to proliferate and produce excess extracellular matrix, notably increased type IV collagen. This diffuse mesangial expansion progressively thickens the glomerular basement membrane and narrows capillary lumina, contributing to the characteristic light-microscopic findings of diabetic glomerulosclerosis, both diffuse mesangial expansion and, later, nodular Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions.

incorrectas.A: Crescent formation reflects severe capillary wall rupture with parietal epithelial cell proliferation, a feature of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, not the gradual mesangial matrix expansion typical of diabetic nephropathy.
incorrectas.C: While advanced diabetic nephropathy does involve podocyte loss and eventual glomerulosclerosis, 'complete podocyte loss with capillary collapse' better describes collapsing FSGS variants, not the defining early-to-mid light-microscopic mesangial proliferative pattern of diabetic disease.
incorrectas.D: Neutrophilic infiltration suggests an acute inflammatory or infectious glomerulonephritis, such as poststreptococcal GN, a very different acute inflammatory process from the chronic, metabolically driven mesangial proliferation of diabetes.

preguntas.q: Progressive glomerular hyperfiltration and mesangial matrix expansion in diabetic nephropathy can produce eosinophilic, nodular areas of glomerulosclerosis known by which eponym?

e.correcta: Sustained hyperfiltration injury and mesangial matrix accumulation in advanced diabetic nephropathy can coalesce into round, eosinophilic, laminated nodules within the mesangium, called Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules. This finding is highly specific for diabetic glomerulosclerosis and is a useful diagnostic clue on renal biopsy in a patient with long-standing diabetes and nephrotic-range proteinuria.

incorrectas.B: A Ghon complex refers to a calcified primary tuberculous lung lesion with associated hilar lymph node involvement, a completely unrelated pulmonary finding, not a renal one.
incorrectas.C: Aschoff bodies are granulomatous nodules with giant cells found in the myocardium in rheumatic fever, not a renal finding related to diabetic glomerular disease.
incorrectas.D: Councilman bodies are eosinophilic apoptotic hepatocyte remnants seen in viral hepatitis and yellow fever, a hepatic rather than renal histologic finding, unrelated to diabetic nodular glomerulosclerosis.

preguntas.q: Which class of medication is used to slow the progression of hyperfiltration-induced glomerular damage in diabetic nephropathy?

e.correcta: ACE inhibitors block the formation of angiotensin II, which normally constricts the efferent arteriole preferentially. By reducing this efferent constriction, ACE inhibitors lower intraglomerular capillary pressure and reduce hyperfiltration-mediated injury, slowing the progression of proteinuria and glomerulosclerosis; this renoprotective effect, independent of their blood-pressure-lowering effect, is why ACE inhibitors (or ARBs) are first-line therapy in diabetic nephropathy.

incorrectas.A: Loop diuretics manage volume overload and edema in nephrotic states but do not specifically reduce angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction or intraglomerular pressure, so they lack the same disease-modifying renoprotective effect.
incorrectas.B: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers preferentially dilate the afferent arteriole, which can actually increase glomerular capillary pressure and worsen hyperfiltration if used without concurrent renin-angiotensin blockade, making them a less ideal choice for this specific mechanism.
incorrectas.C: Beta-blockers reduce heart rate and cardiac output and can lower systemic blood pressure, but they do not specifically counteract angiotensin II's efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, so they do not target the hyperfiltration mechanism the way ACE inhibitors do.

preguntas.q: What is the most common cause of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) in the United States?

e.correcta: Diabetes mellitus, via the hyperfiltration-glycation-mesangial expansion cascade described in diabetic nephropathy, is the leading cause of ESRD in the U.S., reflecting the country's high prevalence of type 2 diabetes and the kidney's particular vulnerability to chronic hyperglycemic injury over decades. This makes glycemic control, blood pressure control, and ACE inhibitor/ARB therapy central public health priorities for preventing dialysis-dependence.

incorrectas.A: Hypertensive nephrosclerosis is the second most common cause of ESRD in the U.S., an important cause, but diabetes still outranks it as the single leading etiology.
incorrectas.B: IgA nephropathy is the most common cause of primary glomerulonephritis worldwide, but it is far less prevalent as a driver of ESRD in the U.S. population compared to diabetic nephropathy.
incorrectas.D: Polycystic kidney disease is an important inherited cause of ESRD, but it accounts for a much smaller proportion of cases nationally compared to the enormous burden contributed by diabetes.

preguntas.q: What is the earliest structural change that occurs in the kidney of a patient with diabetes mellitus?

o.B: Non-enzymatic glycosylation of the glomerular basement membrane

e.correcta: The diabetic renal cascade begins at the molecular level: chronic hyperglycemia nonenzymatically glycates proteins within the GBM, forming advanced glycation end-products that thicken the membrane and paradoxically increase its permeability to plasma proteins. This initiating biochemical change precedes and sets up the later downstream events, including efferent arteriolar hyalinosis, hyperfiltration, mesangial expansion, and eventually nodular sclerosis.

incorrectas.A: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules are a late finding, appearing only after years of hyperfiltration-driven mesangial matrix accumulation, not the initial change in the disease process.
incorrectas.C: Arteriolar hyaline sclerosis, particularly of the efferent arteriole first, occurs downstream of and later than the initial GBM glycation event, contributing to hyperfiltration rather than being the earliest change.
incorrectas.D: Tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis are late, chronic consequences of longstanding glomerular injury and reduced blood flow, occurring well after the initiating glomerular basement membrane glycation.

preguntas.q: In renal amyloidosis presenting with nephrotic syndrome, in which glomerular location does the amyloid protein most characteristically deposit?

e.correcta: Amyloid fibrils (AL or AA protein) infiltrate the mesangium and capillary walls of the glomerulus, expanding and stiffening the filtration barrier so that plasma proteins leak through in nephrotic-range amounts. On biopsy this deposition shows apple-green birefringence with Congo red stain under polarized light, which is the diagnostic hallmark. Because amyloidosis is a systemic disease, the kidney is one of several organs affected, but mesangial deposition is specifically what drives the nephrotic presentation.

incorrectas.A: The tubular basement membrane is not the primary site of amyloid deposition that causes nephrotic syndrome; tubulointerstitial pathology is more characteristic of processes like acute interstitial nephritis or chronic reflux nephropathy, not amyloid-related proteinuria.
incorrectas.C: The renal papillae are the site of injury in papillary necrosis, seen in conditions like sickle cell disease, diabetes, or analgesic nephropathy — a distinct process from the mesangial amyloid deposition that produces nephrotic syndrome.
incorrectas.D: The parietal layer of Bowman's capsule is where crescents form in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, a nephritic (not nephrotic) process driven by fibrin and macrophage accumulation, which is mechanistically unrelated to amyloid fibril deposition in the mesangium.

preguntas.q: How does nephritic syndrome typically affect urine output?

e.correcta: Nephritic syndrome is driven by inflammatory injury to the glomerulus (often immune-complex or antibody-mediated), which reduces the glomerular filtration rate by narrowing capillary lumens and triggering mesangial and endothelial proliferation. The resulting fall in GFR decreases the volume of filtrate reaching the tubules, producing oliguria alongside the classic triad of hematuria, hypertension, and azotemia. This is a key feature distinguishing the nephritic picture from nephrotic syndrome, in which GFR is typically preserved.

incorrectas.B: Polyuria suggests a tubular concentrating defect (as in diabetes insipidus or chronic tubulointerstitial disease) rather than glomerular inflammation reducing filtration — nephritic syndrome does the opposite, reducing urine output.
incorrectas.C: Urine output is not unchanged in nephritic syndrome; the hallmark physiology is a drop in GFR from glomerular inflammation, which directly reduces the amount of filtrate produced and thus urine output.
incorrectas.D: Anuria (essentially zero urine output) is a more extreme finding typically associated with complete urinary tract obstruction or acute cortical necrosis, not the moderate reduction in GFR seen in typical nephritic syndrome, which causes oliguria rather than total cessation of output.

preguntas.q: What change in BUN and creatinine is characteristically seen in nephritic syndrome, reflecting azotemia from reduced GFR?

e.correcta: Glomerular inflammation in nephritic syndrome impairs filtration, so nitrogenous waste products like urea (BUN) and creatinine, which are normally cleared by glomerular filtration, accumulate in the blood — this is azotemia. Both markers rise together because both depend on adequate GFR for clearance, and the degree of elevation roughly tracks the severity of glomerular injury. This distinguishes nephritic syndrome from nephrotic syndrome, where GFR and renal clearance are usually preserved.

incorrectas.A: Decreased BUN and creatinine would suggest improved renal clearance or reduced production (e.g., malnutrition or liver failure lowering urea synthesis), the opposite of what happens when glomerular filtration is impaired by inflammation.
incorrectas.B: Normal BUN and creatinine would imply preserved GFR, which contradicts the defining feature of nephritic syndrome — glomerular inflammation reducing filtration enough to cause measurable retention of nitrogenous waste.
incorrectas.D: BUN and creatinine rise together in glomerular azotemia because both depend on filtration for clearance; an isolated BUN rise with normal creatinine points instead toward a prerenal cause like dehydration or GI bleeding, not glomerulonephritis.

preguntas.q: Nephritic syndrome may present with hematuria and which type of urinary cast, indicating that the bleeding originates from the glomerulus itself?

e.correcta: RBC casts form when red blood cells that have leaked through damaged glomerular capillaries become trapped and molded within the tubular lumen by Tamm-Horsfall protein. Their presence is essentially pathognomonic for glomerular bleeding, distinguishing nephritic hematuria from lower urinary tract sources like cystitis or stones, which produce free RBCs without casts. This makes RBC casts a key diagnostic clue pointing directly to glomerulonephritis.

incorrectas.B: WBC casts indicate inflammation within the tubulointerstitium, classically seen in pyelonephritis or acute interstitial nephritis, not glomerular capillary bleeding — they reflect a different anatomic site of injury than the glomerulus.
incorrectas.C: Fatty casts (oval fat bodies with a 'Maltese cross' appearance under polarized light) result from lipiduria caused by heavy proteinuria, which is the hallmark of nephrotic, not nephritic, syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Waxy casts form in dilated tubules during chronic, advanced kidney disease and reflect long-standing tubular stasis rather than acute glomerular hemorrhage, so they are not the cast type specifically tied to nephritic hematuria.

preguntas.q: On renal biopsy, nephritic syndrome classically reveals which glomerular appearance?

o.C: Diffuse podocyte foot process effacement without hypercellularity
o.D: Glomeruli replaced by acellular hyaline sclerosis

e.correcta: In nephritic syndrome, immune-complex or antibody-mediated injury triggers proliferation of resident mesangial and endothelial cells along with infiltration by neutrophils and monocytes, producing glomeruli that look enlarged, crowded, and inflamed under the microscope. This hypercellularity is what narrows the capillary lumens, reduces GFR, and allows red cells to escape into the urinary space — tying the biopsy finding directly to the clinical picture of hematuria, oliguria, and azotemia.

incorrectas.A: Normal-appearing glomeruli on light microscopy is characteristic of minimal change disease, a nephrotic (not nephritic) condition where the defect is at the ultrastructural podocyte level rather than visible cellular proliferation or inflammation.
incorrectas.C: Isolated podocyte foot process effacement without hypercellularity is the electron microscopic signature of nephrotic syndromes like minimal change disease or early membranous nephropathy, not the proliferative, inflamed pattern seen in nephritic disease.
incorrectas.D: Glomeruli replaced by acellular hyaline sclerosis describes an end-stage or focal segmental glomerulosclerosis pattern, reflecting chronic scarring rather than the active hypercellular inflammation that defines acute nephritic syndrome.

preguntas.q: Immune-complex deposition in nephritic syndrome activates which pathway, generating a chemoattractant that recruits neutrophils to mediate glomerular damage?

e.correcta: Immune complexes lodged in the glomerulus fix and activate complement via the classical pathway, cleaving C3 and C5 to generate anaphylatoxins including C5a. C5a is a potent chemoattractant that recruits neutrophils and monocytes into the glomerulus, where they release proteases and reactive oxygen species that damage the capillary wall — this leukocyte-mediated injury is what produces the hypercellular, inflamed glomeruli and hematuria seen clinically. This complement-driven recruitment is the central mechanistic link between immune complex deposition and tissue damage in nephritic syndromes like PSGN.

incorrectas.B: The coagulation cascade can contribute secondarily to crescent formation in severe glomerulonephritis (via fibrin deposition in Bowman's space), but it is not the pathway directly activated by immune complexes to recruit neutrophils in typical nephritic injury.
incorrectas.C: The kinin-kallikrein system generates bradykinin and is involved in vascular permeability and pain signaling, not in the classical-pathway complement activation that immune complexes trigger to recruit neutrophils to the glomerulus.
incorrectas.D: Direct cytotoxic T-lymphocyte killing is a cell-mediated (type IV) mechanism relevant to processes like acute cellular transplant rejection, not the antibody/immune-complex-driven, complement-mediated injury (type III hypersensitivity) that characterizes nephritic syndromes such as PSGN.

preguntas.q: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) typically presents how long after a group A streptococcal infection?

e.correcta: PSGN is a type III hypersensitivity reaction, meaning the kidney damage requires time for circulating immune complexes (streptococcal antigen bound to antibody) to form and deposit in the glomerular basement membrane and mesangium before triggering complement activation and inflammation. This latent period is classically 2 to 4 weeks after the preceding pharyngitis or skin infection (impetigo), which helps distinguish PSGN from processes with a much shorter or longer latency and is a useful clue when a patient presents with cola-colored urine several weeks after a sore throat.

incorrectas.A: A latency of only hours would be far too short for antibody formation and immune complex deposition to occur; that time frame is more typical of an immediate (type I) hypersensitivity reaction, not the delayed immune-complex process of PSGN.
incorrectas.B: A few days is still too short for the adaptive immune response to generate sufficient antibody and form the immune complexes that must deposit and activate complement before nephritic symptoms appear in PSGN.
incorrectas.C: Months would be an unusually long latency for PSGN; by that point, the causative streptococcal infection would typically have long resolved, and other nephritic syndromes with a different time course (such as IgA nephropathy, which can flare within days of a mucosal infection) would be more likely considerations.

preguntas.q: What type of hypersensitivity reaction underlies post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?

e.correcta: In PSGN, antibodies form against streptococcal antigens (such as streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B), and the resulting antigen-antibody immune complexes circulate and deposit in the glomerular basement membrane and subepithelial space, producing the classic 'lumpy-bumpy' granular pattern on immunofluorescence. These trapped complexes activate complement and recruit neutrophils, causing the hypercellular, inflamed glomeruli seen on biopsy — this deposition-and-complement-activation sequence is the defining feature of a type III hypersensitivity reaction.

incorrectas.B: Type I hypersensitivity is IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation causing immediate reactions like anaphylaxis or allergic rhinitis; it does not involve immune complex deposition in the kidney and plays no role in PSGN pathogenesis.
incorrectas.C: Type II hypersensitivity involves antibodies binding directly to a fixed tissue antigen (as in Goodpasture syndrome, where anti-GBM antibodies bind the basement membrane itself), which produces a linear immunofluorescence pattern — distinct from the circulating immune complexes and granular pattern seen in PSGN.
incorrectas.D: Type IV hypersensitivity is a delayed, T-cell-mediated process (as in contact dermatitis or tuberculin skin testing) that does not depend on antibody or complement, unlike the antibody/complement-driven immune complex mechanism that defines PSGN.

preguntas.q: Which clinical finding, reflecting sodium and water retention from reduced GFR, may be seen in PSGN?

e.correcta: The glomerular inflammation of PSGN reduces GFR, which in turn decreases sodium and water excretion by the kidneys. This retained fluid expands the extracellular volume and, aided by gravity and loose periorbital tissue, manifests as peripheral edema (especially in the lower extremities) and characteristic periorbital puffiness, particularly noticeable in children on waking. This volume-overload edema, together with hematuria and hypertension, forms the classic nephritic triad.

incorrectas.A: Weight loss would suggest a catabolic or wasting process, the opposite of what happens in PSGN, where fluid retention from reduced GFR typically causes weight gain rather than loss.
incorrectas.B: Digital clubbing reflects chronic hypoxemia or certain chronic pulmonary, cardiac, or hepatobiliary diseases; it is not a feature of the acute volume-retention edema caused by glomerular inflammation in PSGN.
incorrectas.D: A malar (butterfly) rash is a classic finding in systemic lupus erythematosus, which can itself cause a form of nephritic syndrome (lupus nephritis), but it is not a feature of PSGN, which is triggered by a preceding streptococcal infection rather than autoimmune disease.

preguntas.q: What additional cardiovascular finding, resulting from sodium and water retention due to decreased GFR, is seen in PSGN?

e.correcta: As glomerular inflammation reduces GFR in PSGN, the kidneys retain sodium and water, expanding intravascular volume. This volume expansion raises cardiac preload and, through pressure-natriuresis feedback being overwhelmed, drives blood pressure up — producing the hypertension that is part of the classic nephritic triad alongside hematuria and edema. Recognizing this volume-mediated hypertension helps distinguish nephritic-syndrome physiology from hypotensive or volume-depleted states.

incorrectas.B: Hypotension would imply intravascular volume depletion, which is the opposite of the sodium and water retention that occurs when reduced GFR impairs the kidney's ability to excrete fluid in PSGN.
incorrectas.C: Orthostatic hypotension reflects inadequate compensatory vasoconstriction or volume depletion upon standing, which does not fit the volume-expanded, hypertensive physiology that reduced GFR produces in PSGN.
incorrectas.D: Blood pressure is not simply unaffected in PSGN; the retained sodium and water from decreased glomerular filtration characteristically elevate blood pressure, making hypertension one of the classic presenting features.

preguntas.q: Which demographic group is most commonly associated with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?

e.correcta: PSGN classically follows streptococcal pharyngitis or impetigo, infections that are especially common in school-age children, and the resulting immune-complex glomerulonephritis peaks around ages 6 to 10. Children with PSGN also tend to have a favorable prognosis, with the large majority recovering renal function fully, which contrasts with the disease's rarer but more severe course when it occurs in adults.

incorrectas.A: PSGN can occur in adults, but it is far less common than in children and — importantly — carries a worse prognosis in that age group, with a higher rate of progression to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis; the peak incidence itself remains in childhood, not old age.
incorrectas.C: Neonates are not the classic population for PSGN; the disease requires a preceding streptococcal infection and an adaptive immune response to generate the pathogenic immune complexes, a sequence more typically seen in school-age children with strep throat or skin infections.
incorrectas.D: Postmenopausal women are not the characteristic demographic for PSGN; the condition's epidemiology is driven by exposure to streptococcal pharyngitis/impetigo, which is most prevalent in childhood rather than tied to menopausal status.

preguntas.q: On light microscopy, PSGN characteristically shows glomeruli that are enlarged and display which finding?

o.C: Isolated basement membrane thickening without cellular proliferation

e.correcta: In PSGN, subepithelial immune complex deposits ('humps') trigger complement activation and neutrophil/monocyte infiltration along with proliferation of mesangial and endothelial cells, producing glomeruli that appear globally enlarged and diffusely hypercellular on light microscopy. This diffuse proliferative pattern, involving essentially all glomeruli, correlates with the acute nephritic presentation and is what distinguishes PSGN histologically from more focal or purely sclerosing glomerular diseases.

incorrectas.A: Segmental glomerulosclerosis describes scarring involving only part of some glomeruli, as seen in focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, a nephrotic-syndrome-associated lesion — not the diffuse, actively proliferative pattern that defines PSGN.
incorrectas.B: Crescents (accumulations of fibrin and proliferating parietal cells/macrophages in Bowman's space) are the hallmark of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and signal a more severe, aggressive course; while severe PSGN can rarely progress to RPGN with crescents, the classic finding in typical PSGN is diffuse hypercellularity, not crescent formation.
incorrectas.C: Isolated basement membrane thickening without cellular proliferation is characteristic of membranous nephropathy, a nephrotic disease driven by subepithelial immune deposits without the marked inflammatory hypercellularity that defines the acute proliferative pattern of PSGN.

preguntas.q: What is the standard treatment approach for post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?

e.correcta: PSGN is a self-limited disease in the great majority of cases, especially in children, because the immune complexes triggering glomerular inflammation are cleared once the underlying streptococcal infection resolves. Management is therefore supportive — controlling blood pressure and fluid overload with salt restriction and diuretics as needed — while the glomeruli recover on their own, reserving aggressive immunosuppression for the rare cases that progress to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

incorrectas.B: High-dose corticosteroids are reserved for glomerulonephritides with an ongoing, self-perpetuating immune or inflammatory process (such as lupus nephritis or vasculitis), not typical PSGN, which resolves as the triggering infection clears without needing immunosuppression.
incorrectas.C: Emergent plasmapheresis is used to rapidly remove pathogenic circulating antibodies in conditions like Goodpasture syndrome, where anti-GBM antibodies continuously drive tissue destruction; PSGN's immune complexes are transient and clear with time, so plasmapheresis is not standard therapy.
incorrectas.D: Cyclophosphamide plus corticosteroids is an aggressive immunosuppressive regimen used for severe, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (e.g., ANCA-associated vasculitis), which is disproportionate to the self-limited course of typical PSGN.

preguntas.q: What proportion of children with PSGN progress to chronic renal failure?

e.correcta: Because PSGN in children is typically a self-limited immune-complex disease that resolves once the triggering streptococcal antigens clear, the vast majority recover normal renal function, and only a very small fraction (around 1%) go on to develop chronic renal failure. This favorable pediatric prognosis is a key teaching point that distinguishes childhood PSGN from the disease in adults, where progression to renal failure or rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis is considerably more common.

incorrectas.A: A 50% progression rate would be far higher than what is actually observed in pediatric PSGN and would suggest a much more aggressive or chronic process, which is not consistent with the disease's generally excellent prognosis in children.
incorrectas.B: A 25% rate does apply to a related but distinct statistic — the proportion of adults with PSGN who develop rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis — but that adult figure should not be confused with the much lower (about 1%) progression rate seen in children.
incorrectas.D: A rate above 90% would essentially mean PSGN is almost always devastating in children, which contradicts the well-established fact that pediatric PSGN carries an excellent prognosis with supportive care alone.

preguntas.q: What percentage of adults with PSGN develop rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis?

e.correcta: Unlike children, in whom PSGN nearly always resolves with supportive care, adults with PSGN have a substantially worse prognosis — roughly 25% progress to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, and only about 60% of adult cases resolve completely. Increased age at presentation is considered the single most important poor prognostic factor in PSGN, so this statistic underscores why adult-onset nephritic syndrome following streptococcal infection warrants closer monitoring than the same disease in a child.

incorrectas.B: About 1% is the rate of progression to chronic renal failure seen in children with PSGN, a much more favorable figure that should not be conflated with the higher-risk course seen when PSGN occurs in adults.
incorrectas.C: A 75% rate would be a dramatic overstatement of adult PSGN's risk of progressing to RPGN; while adults do fare worse than children, the majority of adult cases (roughly 60%) still resolve completely rather than progressing.
incorrectas.D: Nearly 100% progression would mean adult PSGN is almost universally severe, which is inconsistent with the fact that most adult cases still recover, even though the risk of RPGN is meaningfully elevated compared to children.

preguntas.q: Diagnosis of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is supported by a positive result on which serologic test?

o.B: Anti-streptolysin O (ASO) and other streptococcal serologies

e.correcta: Because PSGN follows a documented or occult streptococcal infection, serologic evidence of recent exposure — elevated anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titers, anti-DNase B, or other streptococcal antibody panels — helps confirm the diagnosis, especially when the preceding pharyngitis or impetigo was mild or unrecognized. These titers, combined with a history of nephritic symptoms 2-4 weeks after infection and low complement levels, build a strong clinical case for PSGN without necessarily requiring a biopsy in classic pediatric presentations.

incorrectas.A: Anti-GBM antibody titers are used to diagnose Goodpasture syndrome, where antibodies attack the basement membrane directly (a type II hypersensitivity reaction), a fundamentally different immunologic mechanism than the immune-complex deposition of PSGN.
incorrectas.C: ANCA (antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody) titers are used to diagnose pauci-immune, ANCA-associated vasculitides such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis or microscopic polyangiitis, which cause glomerulonephritis without significant immune complex or immunoglobulin deposition — unlike PSGN.
incorrectas.D: Anti-dsDNA antibody titers are used to diagnose and monitor systemic lupus erythematosus, including lupus nephritis, but they have no role in confirming a streptococcal etiology, which is what distinguishes PSGN from other immune-complex nephritides.

preguntas.q: PSGN is characteristically associated with what change in serum complement levels?

e.correcta: In PSGN, circulating immune complexes deposit in the glomerulus and activate the classical complement pathway, consuming C3 and other complement components faster than the liver can replenish them. This produces measurably low serum complement (particularly C3) during the acute phase, which typically normalizes over several weeks as the immune complexes clear — making hypocomplementemia both a diagnostic clue and a marker that can be followed to track resolution.

incorrectas.B: Elevated complement would suggest ongoing synthesis without significant activation/consumption, which is inconsistent with the pathophysiology of PSGN, where immune complexes actively fix and consume complement in the glomerulus.
incorrectas.C: Complement levels are not simply normal in PSGN; the hallmark laboratory finding is transient hypocomplementemia from complement consumption, which is a useful distinguishing feature from other nephritic syndromes (like IgA nephropathy) that typically have normal complement.
incorrectas.D: Complement is not transiently elevated in PSGN — the direction of change is a decrease, not an increase, because activation and consumption of complement components outpaces production during the acute immune-complex-mediated injury.

preguntas.q: How is rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) defined in terms of its time course to renal failure?

e.correcta: RPGN is defined by an aggressive, fulminant course in which glomerular injury — often marked by crescent formation in Bowman's space — leads to a precipitous loss of renal function over a matter of days to weeks (some sources extend this to weeks to months). This rapid tempo distinguishes RPGN from the slow, insidious decline of chronic glomerulonephritis and demands urgent diagnosis and treatment (often including plasmapheresis or aggressive immunosuppression) to prevent irreversible end-stage renal disease.

incorrectas.B: Years to decades describes the slow, indolent progression typical of chronic kidney disease from causes like long-standing diabetes or hypertension, not the fulminant, crescent-driven injury of RPGN, which by definition progresses much faster.
incorrectas.C: Months to years is still far slower than the defining tempo of RPGN; while some sources allow a slightly extended window (weeks to months), the disease is characterized by its urgency and rapid loss of function, not a multi-year decline.
incorrectas.A: Hours would be an unrealistically fast time course even for RPGN; while RPGN is aggressive, the crescentic injury and functional decline still unfold over days to weeks, not within a single day.

preguntas.q: What is the general prognosis of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis if untreated?

o.A: Poor prognosis, often progressing to end-stage renal disease
o.C: Good prognosis with supportive care alone

e.correcta: RPGN is characterized histologically by crescents — proliferating parietal epithelial cells and infiltrating macrophages filling Bowman's space, often with fibrin deposition — which physically compress and destroy the glomerular tuft. Because this crescentic injury is aggressive and self-propagating, RPGN carries a poor prognosis and frequently progresses to irreversible end-stage renal disease within weeks to months if not treated promptly with immunosuppression (and sometimes plasmapheresis), regardless of the underlying etiology (anti-GBM disease, immune complex disease, or pauci-immune vasculitis).

incorrectas.B: Spontaneous resolution is not expected in RPGN; unlike a self-limited process such as childhood PSGN, the crescentic injury in RPGN tends to progress relentlessly unless actively treated, which is precisely why it is considered a nephrologic emergency.
incorrectas.C: Supportive care alone is inadequate for RPGN because the underlying crescent-forming process continues to destroy glomeruli; aggressive, disease-specific therapy (immunosuppression, plasmapheresis) is generally required to preserve renal function.
incorrectas.D: RPGN is not a self-limited disease; the rapid, crescentic destruction of glomeruli distinguishes it from more indolent or self-resolving nephritic syndromes, and without intervention it typically culminates in permanent renal failure.

preguntas.q: What type of hypersensitivity reaction underlies Goodpasture syndrome?

e.correcta: In Goodpasture syndrome, autoantibodies target the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen, an antigen present in both the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes. These antibodies bind directly to the fixed tissue antigen rather than forming circulating immune complexes, and this direct antibody-antigen binding activates complement and recruits inflammatory cells at the basement membrane itself — the defining mechanism of a type II hypersensitivity reaction. This also explains the linear (rather than granular) immunofluorescence pattern seen on biopsy.

incorrectas.A: Type I hypersensitivity involves IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation causing immediate reactions like anaphylaxis, which is unrelated to the direct antibody binding to basement membrane collagen that drives Goodpasture syndrome.
incorrectas.B: Type III hypersensitivity, as seen in PSGN, involves circulating immune complexes that deposit in tissue and produce a granular immunofluorescence pattern; Goodpasture syndrome instead involves antibodies binding directly to a fixed antigen, giving a linear pattern, which is the hallmark of type II rather than type III disease.
incorrectas.D: Type IV hypersensitivity is a delayed, T-cell-mediated process without a primary antibody component, unlike Goodpasture syndrome, which is driven by anti-GBM antibodies binding directly to basement membrane collagen.

preguntas.q: What two hallmark clinical features, reflecting simultaneous damage to the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, characterize Goodpasture syndrome?

e.correcta: The anti-GBM antibodies in Goodpasture syndrome target type IV collagen present in both the glomerular basement membrane and the alveolar basement membrane, so the antibody attack damages both organs simultaneously. Glomerular injury produces hematuria (often with RBC casts and progressive renal failure), while alveolar capillary injury causes pulmonary hemorrhage manifesting as hemoptysis — this combined renal-pulmonary presentation is the classic clue that should immediately raise suspicion for Goodpasture syndrome.

incorrectas.B: Nephrotic-range proteinuria and chronic cough describe a slower, less acute process more in keeping with a chronic nephrotic disease and an unrelated pulmonary complaint, not the acute hematuria and hemoptysis from simultaneous type IV collagen-targeted injury in Goodpasture syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Arthralgia and malar rash are classic features of systemic lupus erythematosus, a different autoimmune disease that can also cause glomerulonephritis (lupus nephritis) but through immune complex deposition rather than direct anti-basement-membrane antibody attack.
incorrectas.D: Sensorineural hearing loss paired with hematuria is characteristic of Alport syndrome, a hereditary type IV collagen defect (COL4A5 mutation) affecting the ear and kidney, which is a genetic structural disorder rather than the autoimmune antibody-mediated process of Goodpasture syndrome.

preguntas.q: Which demographic group is classically associated with Goodpasture syndrome?

e.correcta: Goodpasture syndrome has a bimodal age distribution but is classically described as affecting young adult males (often in their 20s-30s), a pattern that is frequently tested and helps distinguish it clinically from other causes of pulmonary-renal syndrome. Recognizing this typical demographic, together with the combination of hematuria and hemoptysis, should prompt urgent evaluation for anti-GBM antibodies.

incorrectas.A: Elderly women are not the classic demographic for Goodpasture syndrome; the disease is more typically described in young adult males, though a smaller second peak can occur in older individuals of either sex.
incorrectas.C: Prepubertal children are not the typical population for Goodpasture syndrome; this is primarily a disease of young adults, unlike PSGN, which more classically affects school-age children.
incorrectas.D: Postmenopausal women are not the characteristic demographic; Goodpasture syndrome's classic association is with young adult males, reflecting a different epidemiologic pattern than autoimmune diseases that more often favor women, such as lupus.

preguntas.q: What is the appropriate treatment for Goodpasture syndrome?

o.C: Observation alone, as it typically resolves spontaneously

e.correcta: Because Goodpasture syndrome is driven by continuously circulating pathogenic anti-GBM antibodies that keep attacking the basement membrane, emergent plasmapheresis is used to physically remove these antibodies from the plasma, typically combined with corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide to halt further antibody production. Prompt treatment is critical because ongoing antibody-mediated destruction of the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes can rapidly cause irreversible renal failure and life-threatening pulmonary hemorrhage if not addressed.

incorrectas.B: ACE inhibitor monotherapy addresses proteinuria and hypertension in chronic glomerular disease but does nothing to remove the actively pathogenic anti-GBM antibodies driving Goodpasture syndrome, so it is inadequate as sole therapy for this rapidly destructive disease.
incorrectas.C: Goodpasture syndrome does not resolve spontaneously; unlike self-limited PSGN, the antibody-mediated attack on basement membrane collagen persists and progresses without intervention, making observation alone dangerous.
incorrectas.D: High-dose diuretics can help manage fluid overload symptomatically but do not address the underlying autoimmune antibody production or ongoing basement membrane destruction, so they cannot substitute for plasmapheresis and immunosuppression in Goodpasture syndrome.

preguntas.q: RPGN with a granular ('lumpy-bumpy') immunofluorescence pattern is most commonly caused by which underlying disease?

e.correcta: A granular immunofluorescence pattern reflects immune complexes deposited in irregular clumps along the glomerular basement membrane and mesangium — the classic signature of type III hypersensitivity disease. Among the causes of RPGN that display this granular pattern, PSGN is by far the most common, occasionally progressing (especially in adults) to a crescentic, rapidly progressive course rather than resolving with the typical benign trajectory.

incorrectas.A: Goodpasture syndrome produces a linear, not granular, immunofluorescence pattern because anti-GBM antibodies bind directly and diffusely along the basement membrane rather than depositing as discrete immune complex clumps — this distinguishes it immunologically from the granular pattern of immune-complex diseases like PSGN.
incorrectas.B: ANCA-associated pauci-immune vasculitis is characterized by minimal to no immunoglobulin or complement deposition on immunofluorescence (hence 'pauci-immune'), which is essentially the opposite of a granular immune-complex pattern.
incorrectas.D: IgA nephropathy does show a granular pattern (mesangial IgA deposits) and can occasionally progress to RPGN, but it is a much less common cause of granular-pattern RPGN overall compared to PSGN, which remains the classic and most frequent culprit.

preguntas.q: Besides post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which less common condition can also cause RPGN with a granular immunofluorescence pattern?

o.B: Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (e.g., lupus nephritis class IV)

e.correcta: Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis, most classically seen as lupus nephritis class IV, is also an immune-complex-mediated disease, producing subendothelial and mesangial deposits that create a granular immunofluorescence pattern similar in character to PSGN, though driven by anti-dsDNA and other autoantibody-antigen complexes rather than a streptococcal antigen. While PSGN remains the more common cause of granular-pattern RPGN overall, diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis is an important less-common cause to recognize, particularly in a patient with other features of lupus.

incorrectas.A: PSGN is the more common (not the 'less common') cause of granular-pattern RPGN, so it does not fit the specific framing of this question, which asks for the less frequent alternative cause of the same granular immunofluorescence pattern.
incorrectas.C: Goodpasture syndrome causes RPGN with a linear, not granular, immunofluorescence pattern, since its anti-GBM antibodies bind diffusely along the basement membrane rather than forming discrete immune complex deposits — making it immunologically distinct from the granular-pattern diseases being contrasted here.
incorrectas.D: ANCA-associated vasculitis produces a pauci-immune pattern with little to no immunoglobulin deposition on immunofluorescence, essentially the opposite of a granular immune-complex pattern, so it does not belong among the granular-pattern causes of RPGN.

preguntas.q: Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis, a severe manifestation of lupus nephritis (WHO class IV), classically shows what pattern of immune deposits on immunofluorescence microscopy?

e.correcta: DPGN is an immune complex-mediated nephritis in which circulating and in situ immune complexes (containing anti-dsDNA and other autoantibodies in lupus) deposit throughout the glomerulus in a 'lumpy-bumpy' or granular pattern on immunofluorescence, staining positive for IgG, IgM, IgA, C3, and C1q (a 'full house' pattern). This granular pattern reflects deposition of discrete immune complex aggregates along the basement membrane and mesangium, distinguishing immune complex nephritides from other mechanisms of glomerular injury.

incorrectas.A: A linear pattern of IF staining is the hallmark of anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease (e.g., Goodpasture syndrome), where autoantibodies bind uniformly and continuously along the GBM itself rather than forming discrete immune complex deposits, producing a smooth ribbon-like line rather than the granular pattern seen in DPGN.
incorrectas.C: Pauci-immune GN shows little to no staining for immunoglobulin or complement on immunofluorescence because glomerular injury is mediated by ANCA-associated neutrophil activation and vasculitis rather than by immune complex deposition, the opposite of the immune-complex-rich granular pattern in DPGN.
incorrectas.D: 'Crescentic' describes a light microscopy finding (crescent-shaped proliferation of parietal epithelial cells and macrophages in Bowman's space) rather than an immunofluorescence staining pattern; crescents can occur in any severe RPGN regardless of whether the underlying IF pattern is linear, granular, or pauci-immune.

preguntas.q: A patient with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis undergoes renal biopsy; immunofluorescence shows no significant immunoglobulin or complement deposition. What type of RPGN does this represent?

e.correcta: Pauci-immune glomerulonephritis is defined by the absence of significant Ig or complement (C3) deposition on immunofluorescence and electron microscopy, because glomerular and capillary damage in this category is driven by ANCA-activated neutrophils attacking the vessel wall rather than by deposited antibody-antigen complexes. It is the most common overall cause of RPGN and is strongly associated with ANCA-associated vasculitides such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

incorrectas.A: Anti-GBM disease would instead show a strong, continuous linear pattern of IgG staining along the GBM, reflecting direct antibody binding to type IV collagen in the basement membrane — the opposite of the negative IF seen in pauci-immune GN.
incorrectas.B: Immune complex-mediated GN (e.g., lupus nephritis, post-infectious GN) shows granular 'lumpy-bumpy' deposits of Ig and complement on IF, since these diseases are driven by trapped antigen-antibody complexes rather than the complement-poor, deposit-poor injury of pauci-immune disease.
incorrectas.D: Post-infectious GN is itself a form of immune complex-mediated disease, typically showing granular IgG and C3 deposits ('starry sky' pattern on IF and subepithelial 'humps' on EM) following streptococcal or other infection, which contradicts the negative IF findings described.

preguntas.q: What is the most common cause of glomerulonephritis worldwide?

e.correcta: IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is the most common glomerulonephritis worldwide, caused by mesangial deposition of poorly galactosylated IgA1-containing immune complexes that trigger mesangial cell proliferation and complement activation. It classically presents with episodic gross or microscopic hematuria that occurs concurrently with or shortly after a mucosal infection (synpharyngitic hematuria), reflecting the mucosal origin of the abnormal IgA.

incorrectas.B: Post-streptococcal GN is a classic cause of nephritic syndrome, particularly in children, but it is far less common overall than IgA nephropathy and typically follows a distinct latent period (1-3 weeks) after streptococcal pharyngitis or skin infection rather than being the leading cause worldwide.
incorrectas.C: Membranous nephropathy is the most common cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in non-diabetic Caucasian adults, driven by subepithelial immune complex deposition (often anti-PLA2R antibodies), but it is a nephrotic rather than nephritic process and is not the most common glomerulonephritis globally.
incorrectas.D: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, characterized by diffuse podocyte foot process effacement without immune complex deposition, and is unrelated to the mesangial IgA deposition and hematuria that define IgA nephropathy.

preguntas.q: Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) causes renal injury that is histologically identical to which primary glomerular disease?

e.correcta: HSP is considered a systemic form of IgA nephropathy — both diseases share the same underlying mechanism of mesangial deposition of galactose-deficient IgA1 immune complexes, producing identical findings on renal biopsy (mesangial proliferation with IgA-dominant mesangial deposits). HSP additionally causes palpable purpura, arthralgias, and abdominal pain due to IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis outside the kidney, but the renal lesion itself is indistinguishable from isolated IgA nephropathy.

incorrectas.A: Post-streptococcal GN follows streptococcal infection and shows granular IgG/C3 deposits with subepithelial humps on EM, a different immunopathology from the IgA-dominant mesangial deposits that link HSP to IgA nephropathy.
incorrectas.C: Anti-GBM disease is caused by autoantibodies against type IV collagen producing linear IgG staining along the GBM, an entirely different antibody target and staining pattern from the IgA-mesangial process shared by HSP and IgA nephropathy.
incorrectas.D: Membranoproliferative GN is characterized by mesangial and subendothelial deposits with basement membrane duplication ('tram-track' appearance) and can be driven by complement dysregulation or chronic immune complex disease, but it is not the entity that shares a common pathogenesis with HSP.

preguntas.q: On light microscopy, IgA nephropathy characteristically shows expansion and hypercellularity of which glomerular compartment?

e.correcta: IgA nephropathy is fundamentally a disease of the mesangium: deposited IgA1 immune complexes stimulate mesangial cell proliferation and matrix expansion, which is visible on light microscopy as increased mesangial cellularity and matrix, sometimes with focal segmental sclerosis in more advanced disease. This mesangial-centered pathology correlates with the deposits seen in the same location on immunofluorescence and electron microscopy, tying together all three modalities into one coherent picture.

incorrectas.B: Subendothelial expansion is characteristic of diseases like lupus nephritis class III/IV or membranoproliferative GN, where immune complexes lodge between the endothelium and basement membrane, not the mesangial-predominant process of IgA nephropathy.
incorrectas.C: Subepithelial deposits and their associated 'spike and dome' basement membrane changes are the hallmark of membranous nephropathy, a nephrotic-syndrome-causing disease driven by deposits on the epithelial (podocyte) side of the GBM rather than in the mesangium.
incorrectas.D: Diffuse capillary loop thickening without notable mesangial proliferation is more typical of membranous nephropathy or diabetic glomerulosclerosis, not the mesangial hypercellularity that defines IgA nephropathy on light microscopy.

preguntas.q: On electron microscopy, where are the pathognomonic immune complex deposits located in IgA nephropathy?

e.correcta: Electron microscopy in IgA nephropathy shows electron-dense immune complex deposits confined to the mesangium, corresponding directly to the IgA-dominant staining seen on immunofluorescence and the mesangial hypercellularity seen on light microscopy. This consistent mesangial localization across all three modalities is what confirms the diagnosis and distinguishes IgA nephropathy from other glomerulonephritides that deposit complexes in different compartments.

incorrectas.A: Subendothelial deposits are typical of lupus nephritis (class III/IV) and membranoproliferative GN type I, reflecting immune complexes that have crossed the endothelium but not the GBM — a different ultrastructural location from the purely mesangial deposits of IgA nephropathy.
incorrectas.C: Subepithelial 'humps' or deposits are seen in post-streptococcal GN and membranous nephropathy, where complexes form or are trapped on the outer (epithelial) aspect of the GBM, contrasting with the inward mesangial location in IgA nephropathy.
