preguntas.q: In the United States, chronic irritation from which condition is a classic risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder, particularly in older women, alongside cigarette smoking?

e.correcta: Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder arises from squamous metaplasia of the normal transitional (urothelial) epithelium in response to chronic irritation and inflammation. Recurrent or chronic cystitis — often from repeated UTIs or long-term indwelling catheters — is the classic culprit in the US, especially in older women, and works alongside smoking (which delivers urothelial carcinogens via the urine) to drive this metaplastic-to-neoplastic transformation.

incorrectas.B: Schistosoma haematobium infection is the classic cause of bladder SCC worldwide (Egypt/Middle East, via egg deposition triggering chronic granulomatous inflammation), but it is not the risk factor specifically paired with cigarette smoking and older age in the US as described here.
incorrectas.C: Cyclophosphamide is metabolized to acrolein, which is toxic to the urothelium and classically causes hemorrhagic cystitis and an increased risk of transitional (urothelial) cell carcinoma, not the squamous metaplasia pattern driven by chronic infectious/inflammatory cystitis.
incorrectas.D: A persistent urachal remnant is the developmental anomaly linked to bladder adenocarcinoma (typically at the dome), not to squamous cell carcinoma from chronic mucosal irritation.

preguntas.q: Besides schistosomiasis and chronic cystitis, chronic irritation from long-standing presence of which condition is also a risk factor for bladder squamous cell carcinoma?

e.correcta: Bladder or urinary stones that persist for years mechanically abrade and chronically inflame the urothelium, and like chronic cystitis and Schistosoma infection, this sustained irritation predisposes the transitional epithelium to squamous metaplasia and eventually squamous cell carcinoma. The unifying theme across all bladder SCC risk factors is long-standing mucosal irritation/inflammation rather than a direct chemical carcinogen.

incorrectas.A: Aristolochic acid (found in some herbal remedies and linked to Balkan endemic nephropathy) is nephrotoxic and specifically associated with upper urinary tract urothelial carcinoma, not the chronic-irritation mechanism that produces bladder SCC.
incorrectas.B: Cyclophosphamide's toxic metabolite acrolein causes hemorrhagic cystitis and raises the risk of transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder through direct chemical mucosal injury, a distinct mechanism from the chronic mechanical/inflammatory irritation caused by stones.
incorrectas.D: Occupational exposure to aniline dyes (found in the rubber and dye industries) is a classic carcinogen exposure linked to transitional cell (urothelial) carcinoma of the bladder, not to the squamous metaplasia pathway associated with chronic stone-related irritation.

preguntas.q: Primary adenocarcinoma of the urinary tract most commonly arises in which location?

e.correcta: Although adenocarcinoma is a rare histologic subtype of urinary tract cancer (the vast majority being transitional/urothelial carcinoma), when it does occur it most often arises within the bladder itself — either from glandular metaplasia of chronically irritated urothelium (as in bladder exstrophy) or from a urachal remnant at the dome. This makes the bladder the site to remember when adenocarcinoma of the urinary tract is described on an exam.

incorrectas.A: The ureter is an uncommon site for any primary urinary tract malignancy, and when tumors do occur there they are overwhelmingly transitional cell carcinoma, not adenocarcinoma.
incorrectas.B: The renal pelvis, like the ureter, is lined by transitional epithelium and its cancers are typically urothelial (transitional cell) carcinomas rather than the glandular adenocarcinoma pattern.
incorrectas.C: The urethra can rarely develop adenocarcinoma (more often associated with periurethral glands), but it is a far less common site than the bladder for this histologic subtype.

preguntas.q: Adenocarcinoma arising from a persistent urachal remnant characteristically develops at which site in the bladder?

e.correcta: The urachus is the embryologic remnant of the allantois that connects the bladder to the umbilicus during development and normally involutes into the median umbilical ligament; when a segment of urachal epithelium persists, it sits at the bladder dome (the superior-most point, closest to the umbilicus) and can undergo glandular transformation into adenocarcinoma. Because the urachus is a midline structure running from the umbilicus to the dome, that anatomic location is the key clue for identifying a urachal-origin tumor.

incorrectas.B: The trigone, at the base of the bladder between the two ureteral orifices, is the classic site for the more common transitional cell carcinoma, not for urachal-remnant tumors, which track along the urachus toward the dome.
incorrectas.C: The lateral bladder wall has no embryologic connection to the urachus and is not the characteristic site for urachal adenocarcinoma.
incorrectas.D: The bladder neck, near the urethral outlet, is anatomically distant from the umbilical-to-dome course of the urachus and is not where urachal remnant tumors arise.

preguntas.q: Bladder adenocarcinoma may arise as a complication of which congenital anomaly, caused by failure of the caudal anterior abdominal and bladder walls to close?

e.correcta: Bladder exstrophy results from a defect in mesodermal migration that leaves the anterior abdominal wall and bladder open and exposed, so the bladder mucosa (normally protected transitional epithelium) is chronically exposed to air and irritation, undergoing glandular metaplasia over years. This long-standing metaplastic change is why exstrophy carries a markedly increased lifetime risk of bladder adenocarcinoma, making surgical closure in infancy essential.

incorrectas.A: Vesicoureteral reflux causes retrograde flow of urine from the bladder into the ureters, predisposing to recurrent pyelonephritis and renal scarring, but it does not expose the bladder mucosa to the outside world the way exstrophy does.
incorrectas.B: Posterior urethral valves are an obstructive congenital anomaly in male infants causing bladder outlet obstruction and hydronephrosis, not an open ventral defect of the bladder and abdominal wall, and they are not specifically linked to adenocarcinoma.
incorrectas.D: A patent urachus is a failure of urachal closure creating a fistulous connection between the bladder and umbilicus (causing urine leakage from the umbilicus); this is a different anomaly from exstrophy and is not the entity classically described as arising from failure of caudal abdominal/bladder wall closure.

preguntas.q: Acetazolamide and mannitol primarily exert their diuretic effects at which segment of the nephron?

o.B: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

e.correcta: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase, which is concentrated in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) and mediates most of the tubule's bicarbonate reabsorption there, while mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that is freely filtered and acts throughout the tubule but has its greatest effect in the highly water-permeable PCT and descending loop by limiting passive water reabsorption. Both drugs therefore share the PCT as their principal site of action, even though their mechanisms (enzyme inhibition vs. osmotic effect) differ.

incorrectas.B: The thick ascending limb is the site of action of loop diuretics like furosemide, which block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter — a different transporter and location from where acetazolamide and mannitol act.
incorrectas.C: The distal convoluted tubule is where thiazide diuretics inhibit the Na-Cl cotransporter; it is downstream of the PCT and not the primary site for either acetazolamide or mannitol.
incorrectas.D: The collecting duct is where potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g., spironolactone, amiloride) and ADH act on principal cells; it is not where carbonic anhydrase inhibition or the bulk of the osmotic diuretic effect occurs.

preguntas.q: On which membrane surface of renal tubular epithelial cells is the Na+/K+-ATPase located?

e.correcta: The Na+/K+-ATPase sits on the basolateral membrane, where it pumps 3 Na+ out of the cell into the interstitium/blood in exchange for 2 K+ into the cell, using ATP hydrolysis. This creates the low intracellular Na+ concentration and the electrochemical gradient that powers essentially all secondary active transport (like the apical Na+/H+ exchanger) across the tubular epithelium.

incorrectas.A: The apical (luminal) membrane instead houses transporters like the Na+/H+ exchanger, Na+/glucose cotransporter, and other channels that use the Na+ gradient generated by the basolateral pump — it is not itself the site of the ATPase.
incorrectas.C: The Na+/K+-ATPase is asymmetrically distributed to only the basolateral surface; this polarity is essential for establishing directional, vectorial transport of solutes from lumen to blood.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondria generate the ATP that fuels the Na+/K+-ATPase but do not themselves house this transporter on their membranes.

preguntas.q: In the proximal convoluted tubule, the Na+/H+ exchanger (NHE) responsible for bicarbonate reabsorption is located on which membrane?

e.correcta: The Na+/H+ exchanger sits on the apical (luminal) membrane of PCT cells, where it uses the inward Na+ gradient (established by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase) to secrete H+ into the tubular lumen while reabsorbing filtered Na+. This secreted H+ then combines with filtered HCO3- in the lumen, initiating the bicarbonate reabsorption cascade that acetazolamide blocks.

incorrectas.A: The basolateral membrane instead contains the Na+/K+-ATPase and the Na+/HCO3- cotransporter that moves reabsorbed bicarbonate into the blood — the opposite side from where H+ secretion occurs.
incorrectas.C: Paracellular tight junctions allow limited passive solute/water movement between cells, but they are not the site of active, transporter-mediated H+/Na+ exchange.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondria are intracellular organelles supplying ATP; they are not part of the plasma membrane transport machinery involved in luminal H+ secretion.

preguntas.q: In the PCT lumen, the H+ secreted by the apical Na+/H+ exchanger combines with which filtered ion to form carbonic acid (H2CO3)?

e.correcta: Secreted H+ combines with freely filtered bicarbonate (HCO3-) in the tubular lumen to form carbonic acid (H2CO3), which is then rapidly dehydrated by luminal (brush-border) carbonic anhydrase into CO2 and H2O — the CO2 diffuses back into the cell to regenerate intracellular H2CO3 and complete bicarbonate reabsorption. This reaction is the first step of the bicarbonate-reclamation pathway that acetazolamide interrupts by blocking carbonic anhydrase.

incorrectas.A: Chloride is not a substrate in the carbonic acid-forming reaction; it is instead reabsorbed largely via paracellular routes and other transporters later in the nephron.
incorrectas.B: Filtered sodium is reabsorbed in exchange for the secreted H+ via the Na+/H+ exchanger itself, but Na+ does not combine with H+ to form carbonic acid — that reaction is specific to bicarbonate.
incorrectas.D: Phosphate is an important urinary buffer (titratable acid) further along the nephron, but it is not the ion that reacts with secreted H+ to generate H2CO3 in this proximal bicarbonate-reabsorption pathway.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the interconversion of H2CO3 and CO2 + H2O, both in the PCT lumen and inside the tubular cell?

e.correcta: Carbonic anhydrase is present in two pools in the PCT — a brush-border (luminal) form that dehydrates H2CO3 into CO2 and H2O, and a cytoplasmic form that rehydrates CO2 and H2O back into H2CO3 inside the cell — and both reactions are essential steps in reclaiming filtered bicarbonate. This dual localization is exactly why acetazolamide, which inhibits carbonic anhydrase, blocks bicarbonate reabsorption at both the luminal and intracellular steps.

incorrectas.A: Na+/K+-ATPase is the basolateral pump that maintains the Na+ gradient driving proximal tubule transport, but it has no role in catalyzing the H2CO3/CO2+H2O interconversion.
incorrectas.C: H+/K+-ATPase is found in gastric parietal cells (and to a lesser extent in the collecting duct's intercalated cells) mediating H+ secretion, but it is not the enzyme responsible for carbonic acid hydration/dehydration.
incorrectas.D: Aldehyde dehydrogenase is involved in alcohol metabolism (oxidizing acetaldehyde to acetate) and has no role in renal acid-base handling of carbonic acid.

preguntas.q: Luminal (brush-border) carbonic anhydrase in the PCT converts carbonic acid (H2CO3) into which two products, which then diffuse into the tubular cell?

e.correcta: Brush-border carbonic anhydrase dehydrates the H2CO3 formed in the lumen into CO2 and H2O — both small, lipid-soluble, freely diffusible molecules that readily cross the apical membrane back into the tubular cell. Once inside, cytoplasmic carbonic anhydrase rehydrates them back into H2CO3, which dissociates into H+ (recycled for further secretion) and HCO3- (reabsorbed into blood), completing net bicarbonate reabsorption.

incorrectas.A: HCO3- and H+ are the products of H2CO3 dissociation that occurs inside the cell after CO2/H2O are rehydrated, not the products of the luminal dehydration reaction described here.
incorrectas.B: O2 is not generated or consumed in bicarbonate handling; this option confuses cellular respiration chemistry with the acid-base buffer reaction occurring in the tubule.
incorrectas.D: Ammonia (NH3) is produced from glutamine metabolism in the PCT as part of a separate acid-excretion pathway (ammoniagenesis), not from the breakdown of carbonic acid.

preguntas.q: Once CO2 and H2O diffuse into the proximal tubule cell, cytoplasmic carbonic anhydrase converts them back into which compound?

o.C: Carbonic acid dehydrated back to CO2

e.correcta: Inside the cell, cytoplasmic carbonic anhydrase catalyzes the hydration of CO2 and H2O into carbonic acid (H2CO3), the reverse of the dehydration reaction that occurred in the lumen. This intracellular H2CO3 then spontaneously dissociates into H+ (recycled back to the lumen via the Na+/H+ exchanger) and HCO3- (which exits across the basolateral membrane into the blood), completing the bicarbonate reabsorption cycle.

incorrectas.B: HCO3- is not formed directly from CO2 and H2O by carbonic anhydrase; the enzyme first produces H2CO3, which then dissociates nonenzymatically into H+ and HCO3-.
incorrectas.C: This describes the reverse (dehydration) reaction that happens in the lumen, not the hydration reaction that occurs inside the cell after CO2/H2O have diffused in.
incorrectas.D: Ammonium is generated separately from glutamine deamination in proximal tubule mitochondria as part of renal ammoniagenesis, unrelated to the carbonic anhydrase-catalyzed CO2/H2O hydration reaction.

preguntas.q: Intracellular carbonic acid (H2CO3) in PCT cells spontaneously dissociates into H+ and which base?

e.correcta: Carbonic acid is a weak acid that dissociates into a proton (H+) and its conjugate base, bicarbonate (HCO3-); this is simply the reverse of the reaction that formed it from CO2 and H2O. The regenerated H+ is pumped back into the lumen via the Na+/H+ exchanger to secrete more acid, while HCO3- exits basolaterally into the blood, net reabsorbing filtered bicarbonate.

incorrectas.B: Chloride is not a dissociation product of carbonic acid; it plays a separate role in tubular electroneutrality and is handled by distinct transporters later in the nephron.
incorrectas.C: Phosphate is a urinary buffer for titratable acid excretion in the distal nephron, unrelated to the carbonic acid dissociation reaction in the PCT.
incorrectas.D: Sulfate is a filtered anion with minimal reabsorption, unrelated to the H2CO3-to-H+/HCO3- reaction that underlies proximal bicarbonate handling.

preguntas.q: The H+ generated from intracellular H2CO3 dissociation in the PCT is transported into which compartment via the Na+/H+ exchanger?

e.correcta: The Na+/H+ exchanger on the apical membrane pumps the intracellularly generated H+ back out into the tubular lumen in exchange for reabsorbing filtered Na+, allowing that H+ to react with another filtered HCO3- and repeat the bicarbonate-reclamation cycle. This apical secretion step is the point acetazolamide indirectly disrupts, since without functional carbonic anhydrase, less H2CO3 (and thus less recyclable H+) is generated in the first place.

incorrectas.A: The renal interstitium is where reabsorbed HCO3- exits on the basolateral side, the opposite direction and compartment from where H+ is secreted.
incorrectas.C: Peritubular capillary blood receives reabsorbed solutes (like HCO3- and Na+) from the interstitium, but H+ itself is secreted into the lumen, not into the blood.
incorrectas.D: Lymphatics play no meaningful role in proximal tubular acid-base handling; solute movement here is between lumen, cell, interstitium, and peritubular capillaries.

preguntas.q: The HCO3- generated from intracellular H2CO3 dissociation in the PCT is transported into which compartment, completing bicarbonate reabsorption?

e.correcta: Newly formed intracellular HCO3- exits the cell across the basolateral membrane (via a Na+/HCO3- cotransporter) into the renal interstitium, from which it diffuses into peritubular capillary blood — this basolateral exit is the actual reabsorption step, since it returns bicarbonate to the systemic circulation. Acetazolamide blocks the upstream carbonic anhydrase reactions needed to generate this HCO3-, so less of it reaches the interstitium and more is lost in the urine.

incorrectas.A: The tubular lumen is where H+ is secreted and where the original filtered HCO3- came from — reabsorbed HCO3- moves in the opposite direction, out of the cell into the interstitium.
incorrectas.B: Bowman's space is the site of initial glomerular filtration upstream of the PCT, not a destination for reabsorbed solutes.
incorrectas.D: The loop of Henle lumen is a downstream nephron segment; the HCO3- reabsorbed in the PCT crosses the basolateral membrane locally rather than traveling further along the tubule.

preguntas.q: Acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, primarily prevents renal reabsorption of which ion?

e.correcta: By inhibiting both the luminal and cytoplasmic isoforms of carbonic anhydrase in the PCT, acetazolamide prevents the generation of H+ needed to titrate filtered bicarbonate in the lumen and prevents regeneration of intracellular bicarbonate for basolateral export — the net effect is that filtered HCO3- is not reabsorbed and instead spills into the urine. This is the defining pharmacologic action from which all of acetazolamide's other effects (alkaline urine, natriuresis, metabolic acidosis) follow.

incorrectas.B: Potassium wasting (hypokalemia) is a downstream consequence of acetazolamide — from increased distal Na+ delivery driving aldosterone-mediated K+ secretion — but K+ reabsorption is not the primary target of carbonic anhydrase inhibition.
incorrectas.A: Chloride handling is affected only secondarily, since blocked HCO3- reabsorption shifts the anion balance toward relative chloride retention (contributing to a hyperchloremic, normal anion gap acidosis), but Cl- reabsorption is not the enzyme's direct substrate pathway.
incorrectas.C: Phosphate reabsorption in the PCT occurs via a separate sodium-phosphate cotransporter unrelated to carbonic anhydrase activity, so acetazolamide does not primarily act on phosphate handling.

preguntas.q: By blocking bicarbonate reabsorption in the PCT, what effect does acetazolamide have on urine pH?

e.correcta: Because acetazolamide prevents reabsorption of filtered HCO3-, large amounts of bicarbonate — a base — are excreted in the urine, which raises (alkalinizes) urine pH. This property is exploited clinically to alkalinize the urine, for example to enhance excretion of certain weak acids (like aspirin) in overdose.

incorrectas.A: Acidification would occur if H+ excretion increased relative to base, but acetazolamide does the opposite — it impairs H+-driven bicarbonate reclamation, leaving more base (not acid) in the urine.
incorrectas.C: Urine pH does change substantially with acetazolamide use, since a major buffer (bicarbonate) is being dumped into the urine rather than reabsorbed.
incorrectas.D: The alkalinizing effect of acetazolamide is a predictable, mechanistically explained consequence of carbonic anhydrase inhibition, not a variable or unpredictable one.

preguntas.q: In addition to blocking HCO3- reabsorption, acetazolamide also impairs reabsorption of which other ion, contributing to its diuretic effect?

e.correcta: Because bicarbonate reabsorption in the PCT is tightly coupled to Na+/H+ exchange, blocking carbonic anhydrase also reduces the Na+ gradient-driven reabsorption of sodium (and the water that follows it osmotically), producing a true natriuretic diuresis in addition to bicarbonaturia. This dual loss of Na+ and HCO3- is why acetazolamide is classified as a diuretic and not merely an acid-base modifying agent.

incorrectas.A: Potassium is lost secondarily, downstream in the collecting duct, as a consequence of increased distal Na+ delivery and aldosterone activation — not because acetazolamide directly blocks K+ reabsorption in the PCT.
incorrectas.B: Magnesium reabsorption occurs predominantly in the thick ascending limb via a paracellular mechanism driven by the transepithelial voltage gradient, which is not the site or mechanism affected by acetazolamide.
incorrectas.D: Calcium reabsorption in the PCT is largely passive and paracellular, following sodium and water; it is Na+ itself, not Ca2+, that is classically named as co-lost with bicarbonate in this mechanism.

preguntas.q: Because acetazolamide blocks bicarbonate reabsorption in the PCT, what happens to urinary excretion of HCO3-?

e.correcta: With carbonic anhydrase inhibited, the tubule can no longer efficiently reclaim filtered bicarbonate, so a larger fraction of the filtered HCO3- load escapes reabsorption and is excreted in the urine — this bicarbonaturia is the direct, expected consequence of the drug's mechanism. Over time, sustained bicarbonate loss depletes plasma HCO3- stores, producing the drug's characteristic metabolic acidosis.

incorrectas.A: A decrease would be seen with a drug that enhances bicarbonate reabsorption, which is the opposite of what a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor does.
incorrectas.B: Excretion is not unchanged — inhibiting the enzyme central to the entire proximal bicarbonate-reclamation pathway has a clear, predictable, substantial effect on how much HCO3- reaches the urine.
incorrectas.C: The effect is not random or unpredictable; it follows directly and consistently from the known mechanism of carbonic anhydrase inhibition.

preguntas.q: Besides causing a type 2 (proximal) renal tubular acidosis, what other acid-base disturbance can result from chronic acetazolamide use?

e.correcta: Chronic bicarbonate wasting from carbonic anhydrase inhibition lowers plasma HCO3- while renal chloride reabsorption increases to maintain electroneutrality, so the anion gap stays normal (the lost HCO3- is replaced by retained Cl-) — this produces a hyperchloremic, normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, the same pattern classically seen with proximal (type 2) RTA. Recognizing this pairing (acetazolamide/RTA2 leading to normal anion gap acidosis) is a common exam link between renal physiology and acid-base pharmacology.

incorrectas.A: A high anion gap acidosis arises from accumulation of unmeasured acids (e.g., lactate, ketoacids, toxins), not from simple bicarbonate loss with compensatory chloride retention as seen with acetazolamide.
incorrectas.B: Metabolic alkalosis would result from bicarbonate retention or acid loss (e.g., vomiting, loop/thiazide diuretics), the opposite of acetazolamide's bicarbonate-wasting effect.
incorrectas.D: Respiratory acidosis results from CO2 retention due to hypoventilation, an entirely separate mechanism from acetazolamide's renal bicarbonate handling.

preguntas.q: Acetazolamide is used for the treatment and prophylaxis of which condition associated with rapid ascent to high elevation?

e.correcta: By inducing a mild metabolic acidosis, acetazolamide stimulates ventilation (via peripheral chemoreceptor and central respiratory drive), which helps compensate for the respiratory alkalosis of high-altitude hyperventilation and improves oxygenation, thereby preventing and treating the headache, nausea, and malaise of acute mountain sickness. This is a classic non-diuretic clinical use of the drug, taken prophylactically before ascent.

incorrectas.A: High-altitude pulmonary edema is a more severe, distinct high-altitude illness typically managed with descent, oxygen, and nifedipine rather than acetazolamide as first-line therapy, so restricting the answer to HAPE alone misses the broader and more classic indication of acute mountain sickness.
incorrectas.C: Decompression sickness ("the bends") results from nitrogen bubble formation during rapid ascent from underwater depths, an entirely different pathophysiology treated with recompression therapy, not acetazolamide.
incorrectas.D: Chronic mountain polycythemia is a maladaptive long-term response to chronic hypoxia at altitude, driven by excessive erythropoietin-stimulated red cell production, and is not the acute condition acetazolamide is used to prevent.

preguntas.q: What effect does acetazolamide have on serum potassium levels?

o.C: Effect depends only on underlying renal function

e.correcta: Inhibiting the apical Na+/H+ exchanger's coupled bicarbonate reabsorption leaves more Na+ (and HCO3-) undelivered upstream, so more Na+ reaches the collecting duct; this natriuresis causes mild volume contraction that activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and aldosterone in turn upregulates basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase and apical Na+ channels in principal cells, driving increased K+ secretion into the urine. The net result is hypokalemia, a clinically important adverse effect to monitor, especially when acetazolamide is combined with other potassium-wasting drugs.

incorrectas.A: Hyperkalemia would be expected from drugs that block aldosterone action or the collecting duct's K+ secretory pathway (e.g., potassium-sparing diuretics), which is the opposite of acetazolamide's effect of increasing distal Na+ delivery and stimulating K+ loss.
incorrectas.B: A significant effect on potassium is well documented and clinically relevant — hypokalemia is one of the more important adverse effects to watch for during acetazolamide therapy.
incorrectas.C: While the degree of hypokalemia can be influenced by baseline renal function and volume status, the drug has a predictable, mechanism-based tendency to cause potassium wasting regardless, not an effect that depends solely on renal function.

preguntas.q: By impairing proximal bicarbonate reabsorption, acetazolamide can cause which type of renal tubular acidosis?

e.correcta: Type 2 (proximal) RTA is defined by a defect in proximal tubular bicarbonate reabsorption, exactly the mechanism acetazolamide produces by inhibiting carbonic anhydrase — bicarbonate that should be reclaimed in the PCT is instead lost in the urine, causing a hyperchloremic, normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. This makes acetazolamide both a pharmacologic model for and a cause of proximal RTA.

incorrectas.A: Type 1 (distal) RTA results from a failure of the distal nephron's intercalated cells to secrete H+, impairing urinary acidification distally — a different defect from proximal bicarbonate wasting, and distal RTA classically presents with an inappropriately alkaline urine pH despite systemic acidosis, which is not acetazolamide's mechanism.
incorrectas.B: Type 4 RTA results from aldosterone deficiency or resistance, causing hyperkalemia that itself impairs ammoniagenesis and urinary acid excretion — a hormonal/potassium-driven mechanism entirely distinct from carbonic anhydrase inhibition.
incorrectas.D: "Type 3" RTA is a rare, less clinically emphasized overlap/mixed proximal-distal entity and is not the classic category associated with carbonic anhydrase inhibitor use.

preguntas.q: Which diuretic causes type 2 (proximal) renal tubular acidosis as an adverse effect?

e.correcta: Acetazolamide is the diuretic that directly targets the proximal tubule's carbonic anhydrase-dependent bicarbonate reabsorption pathway, so impairing this exact process reproduces the defect that defines type 2 RTA. Its use as a diuretic and its adverse effect of proximal RTA both stem from the same single mechanism — carbonic anhydrase inhibition — which is a useful way to remember the link.

incorrectas.A: Furosemide inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, causing volume contraction and a metabolic alkalosis (via enhanced distal H+ secretion and aldosterone activation), not a proximal bicarbonate-wasting acidosis.
incorrectas.B: Hydrochlorothiazide inhibits the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule and, like loop diuretics, tends to cause metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia rather than a proximal RTA.
incorrectas.C: Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing aldosterone antagonist acting on the collecting duct; if anything, it predisposes to hyperkalemia and a mild type 4-like acidosis, not the proximal bicarbonate-wasting acidosis characteristic of carbonic anhydrase inhibition.

preguntas.q: Acetazolamide belongs to which drug class, meaning patients with a history of sulfa allergy are at increased risk for adverse/allergic reactions?

e.correcta: Acetazolamide is chemically a sulfonamide derivative (it contains a sulfonamide moiety), placing it in the same broad hypersensitivity-risk category as sulfa antibiotics, thiazide and loop diuretics, and other sulfa-containing drugs — patients with a documented sulfa allergy should be used with caution or have this history flagged before starting acetazolamide. This cross-class risk is a frequently tested detail linking pharmacologic structure to clinical allergy screening.

incorrectas.A: Penicillins are a beta-lactam antibiotic class with their own distinct allergy profile (anaphylaxis, rash) unrelated to the sulfonamide moiety found in acetazolamide.
incorrectas.B: Aminoglycosides (e.g., gentamicin) are a separate antibiotic class known for nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, not sulfonamide hypersensitivity, and share no structural relationship with acetazolamide.
incorrectas.C: Fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin) are a distinct antibiotic class associated with tendon rupture and QT prolongation, with no sulfonamide component or cross-reactivity with acetazolamide's allergy risk.

preguntas.q: Which adverse effect of acetazolamide occurs because the drug alkalinizes the tubular fluid and reduces trapping of ammonium ion, allowing more ammonia to diffuse back into the circulation?

e.correcta: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, reducing H+ secretion into the lumen. With less H+ available, less NH3 is trapped as NH4+ (which cannot cross membranes back into blood), so more lipid-soluble NH3 diffuses back into the systemic circulation. This is especially dangerous in patients with cirrhosis or hepatic dysfunction who already have impaired ammonia clearance, risking precipitation of hepatic encephalopathy.

incorrectas.A: Hypokalemia does occur with acetazolamide from increased distal Na+ delivery driving K+ secretion, but this is a separate electrolyte effect unrelated to the ammonia-trapping mechanism described in the question.
incorrectas.C: Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis is the predictable, direct consequence of bicarbonate wasting from carbonic anhydrase inhibition, but it is a distinct primary adverse effect rather than the ammonia-specific toxicity being asked about here.
incorrectas.D: Paresthesias are a classic acetazolamide side effect linked to mild systemic acidosis affecting peripheral nerves, but they are not related to impaired renal ammonium trapping.

preguntas.q: Which neurological adverse effect is classically associated with acetazolamide, thought to relate to the mild systemic metabolic acidosis it induces?

e.correcta: Acetazolamide commonly causes paresthesias, a tingling sensation in the fingers, toes, and around the mouth, attributed to the drug's induced mild systemic metabolic acidosis altering the excitability of peripheral sensory nerve fibers. It is usually reversible with dose reduction or discontinuation and does not reflect structural nerve damage.

incorrectas.A: Seizures are not a typical acetazolamide adverse effect; in fact, acetazolamide is sometimes used as an adjunct anticonvulsant, the opposite of what this option implies.
incorrectas.B: Peripheral neuropathy implies structural axonal or demyelinating nerve injury, which is not what acetazolamide causes; that pattern is more characteristic of drugs like isoniazid or vincristine, not a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor.
incorrectas.D: Myoclonus is seen with other metabolic derangements such as uremia or serotonin syndrome, but it is not the classic sensory symptom described with acetazolamide use.

preguntas.q: A carbonic anhydrase inhibitor such as acetazolamide can be used to help correct which acid-base disorder, for example in diuretic-induced contraction alkalosis?

e.correcta: Acetazolamide blocks carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, preventing bicarbonate reabsorption and causing increased urinary bicarbonate excretion. This directly lowers plasma bicarbonate, correcting metabolic alkalosis, and it is used clinically for diuretic-induced contraction alkalosis as well as to induce a compensatory mild metabolic acidosis at high altitude.

incorrectas.A: Metabolic acidosis is actually a predictable adverse effect of acetazolamide itself (hyperchloremic, non-anion-gap) due to bicarbonate wasting, not a condition the drug is used to treat.
incorrectas.B: Respiratory alkalosis results from hyperventilation, such as at high altitude; acetazolamide helps altitude illness indirectly by inducing a metabolic acidosis that stimulates ventilation, but the acid-base disorder it directly treats is metabolic alkalosis, not primary respiratory alkalosis.
incorrectas.C: Respiratory acidosis results from hypoventilation and CO2 retention, and is managed by improving ventilation, not by inhibiting renal carbonic anhydrase.

preguntas.q: What effect does the osmotic diuretic mannitol have on urine output?

o.A: Increased urine flow via increased tubular fluid osmolarity
o.B: Decreased urine flow via increased ADH release
o.C: No significant change in urine flow
o.D: Increased urine flow via inhibition of the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter

e.correcta: Mannitol is freely filtered at the glomerulus but poorly reabsorbed by the tubule, so it raises the osmolarity of the tubular fluid, especially in the proximal tubule and descending limb. This opposes passive water reabsorption and osmotically retains water in the lumen, increasing urine flow. This mechanism underlies its use for cerebral edema, elevated intraocular pressure, and forced diuresis in certain toxic ingestions or rhabdomyolysis.

incorrectas.B: Mannitol does not work through ADH signaling; its diuretic effect is purely osmotic, and increased ADH would promote water reabsorption, the opposite of what mannitol produces.
incorrectas.C: Mannitol reliably increases urine output as its primary pharmacologic effect; this option contradicts its established clinical use as an osmotic diuretic.
incorrectas.D: Inhibition of the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter is the mechanism of loop diuretics like furosemide, which act on the thick ascending limb; mannitol's mechanism is purely osmotic and does not involve any specific transporter.

preguntas.q: Mannitol may be administered clinically to promote which of the following in the setting of certain drug overdoses?

o.A: Chelation of the drug in the bloodstream
o.B: Forced diuresis to enhance elimination of the offending drug
o.C: Induction of hepatic metabolism of the drug
o.D: Alkalinization of urine to trap the drug

e.correcta: Because mannitol produces a strong osmotic diuresis, it increases urine flow and can be used to promote forced diuresis in select overdose scenarios, enhancing the renal clearance of certain water-soluble toxins by flushing them through the tubules before extensive reabsorption can occur.

incorrectas.A: Chelation refers to binding metal ions with agents such as EDTA or dimercaprol to facilitate their excretion; mannitol has no chelating activity and works entirely through an osmotic mechanism.
incorrectas.C: Mannitol has no effect on hepatic drug-metabolizing enzymes; it acts exclusively at the level of the renal tubule to alter water handling.
incorrectas.D: Urinary alkalinization to trap weak acids like salicylates in an ionized, non-reabsorbable form is achieved with sodium bicarbonate, a completely different strategy from mannitol's osmotic diuresis.

preguntas.q: Mannitol is used therapeutically to reduce which of the following abnormally elevated parameters?

e.correcta: Mannitol creates an osmotic gradient that draws free water out of brain tissue and the vitreous/aqueous humor into the vasculature, lowering elevated intracranial pressure and intraocular pressure. This makes it useful in cerebral edema (e.g., after trauma or stroke) and in acute angle-closure glaucoma to rapidly reduce pressure.

incorrectas.A: Mannitol is not used as an antihypertensive agent; its transient effect is actually to expand intravascular volume before diuresis, which can transiently raise, not lower, blood pressure.
incorrectas.B: Central venous pressure is not a typical target of mannitol therapy; its clinically relevant pressure-lowering effects are localized to the brain and eye via the osmotic gradient, not systemic venous pressure.
incorrectas.D: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure reflects left atrial/ventricular filling pressures managed with diuretics like furosemide in heart failure; mannitol is not used for this purpose and can actually worsen volume overload transiently.

preguntas.q: Because mannitol initially draws water out of cells and transiently expands ECF volume before its diuretic effect takes hold, it can precipitate which pulmonary complication in susceptible patients?

e.correcta: Mannitol osmotically pulls water from the intracellular compartment into the extracellular fluid and plasma before the drug is filtered and excreted, transiently expanding intravascular volume. In patients with poor cardiac or pulmonary reserve, this early volume expansion can precipitate or worsen pulmonary edema before diuresis has a chance to correct the fluid shift.

incorrectas.A: Cerebral edema is actually reduced by mannitol, not caused by it, since the same osmotic gradient pulls water out of brain tissue into the vasculature; this is the opposite of what happens in this scenario.
incorrectas.B: Acute tubular necrosis is a separate, dose-related risk of mannitol from direct proximal tubular cell toxicity at high doses or in pre-existing renal impairment, not a consequence of the transient volume expansion described here.
incorrectas.C: Hyperkalemia is not the mechanism linked to mannitol's transient ECF volume expansion; the volume shift primarily threatens patients through fluid overload rather than potassium derangement.

preguntas.q: Mannitol-induced transient expansion of extracellular fluid volume, occurring before its diuretic effect begins, can exacerbate which pre-existing condition?

e.correcta: Before mannitol is filtered and excreted, it osmotically draws water from cells into the extracellular and intravascular space, transiently increasing venous return and cardiac preload. In a patient with an already failing heart, this added volume load can overwhelm limited cardiac reserve and precipitate acute decompensation, which is why mannitol is used cautiously, if at all, in patients with heart failure.

incorrectas.B: Hyperkalemia-driven arrhythmia is not the mechanism by which mannitol worsens cardiac status; the concern is volume-mediated preload increase, not a specific potassium disturbance.
incorrectas.C: Mannitol has no direct vasospastic effect on coronary arteries; its cardiac risk comes from transient volume expansion straining a compromised heart, not ischemia from vasospasm.
incorrectas.D: Pericardial effusion is a fluid accumulation around the heart from a separate inflammatory or malignant process; it is not a recognized consequence of mannitol's osmotic fluid shifts.

preguntas.q: Mannitol therapy can cause disturbances in serum sodium in which pattern?

e.correcta: Early on, mannitol sits in the tubular lumen and plasma as an osmotically active particle, and isotonic movement of fluid draws sodium along with water, transiently diluting plasma sodium and producing hyponatremia. Later, as the osmotic diuresis proceeds and free water is lost disproportionately during volume contraction, hypernatremia can develop, so mannitol can cause both disturbances depending on the phase of treatment.

incorrectas.A: Hyponatremia alone only captures the early phase driven by mannitol's osmotic pull of water and sodium into the vasculature; it misses the later hypernatremia that can follow sustained diuresis.
incorrectas.C: Hypernatremia alone only reflects the later diuretic phase with free water loss, ignoring the initial dilutional hyponatremia that occurs before significant diuresis has taken place.
incorrectas.D: Mannitol clearly perturbs sodium homeostasis through its osmotic effects on fluid shifts and diuresis; stating sodium is unaffected contradicts its well-documented biphasic electrolyte effects.

preguntas.q: Mannitol is contraindicated in patients with heart failure and which additional condition, because the kidneys cannot excrete the osmotic load?

o.D: Chronic kidney disease with preserved urine output

e.correcta: In an anuric patient, mannitol cannot be filtered and excreted into the urine, so its osmotic pull remains confined to the intravascular space, worsening volume overload without ever achieving the intended diuresis. Combined with heart failure, this trapped osmotic load can precipitate severe pulmonary edema, which is why anuria is an absolute contraindication.

incorrectas.A: Diabetes insipidus involves impaired water reabsorption due to ADH deficiency or resistance and is not a contraindication to mannitol; the two conditions involve different aspects of renal water handling.
incorrectas.B: Hyperkalemia is not the specific concern that makes mannitol dangerous in this context; the contraindication centers on the kidney's inability to excrete the osmotic load, not potassium handling.
incorrectas.D: Chronic kidney disease with preserved urine output still allows some renal excretion of the osmotic load, distinguishing it from anuria, where excretion is essentially impossible and the volume risk is far greater.

preguntas.q: Excessive use of which osmotic diuretic can lead to dehydration from substantial free water loss?

e.correcta: Mannitol is the prototypical osmotic diuretic: it produces a potent, purely osmotic diuresis that can lead to large volumes of urine output. If fluid intake or IV replacement does not keep pace with these losses, patients can develop significant dehydration and volume depletion, which is why fluid status must be monitored closely during mannitol therapy.

incorrectas.A: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb; while it can also cause volume depletion, its mechanism is transporter-based rather than osmotic, so it is not the answer to a question specifically about osmotic diuretics.
incorrectas.B: Hydrochlorothiazide inhibits the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule and is a comparatively weaker diuretic; dehydration is less classically associated with thiazides than with the potent osmotic effect of mannitol.
incorrectas.C: Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing aldosterone antagonist with relatively weak diuretic activity; it is not known for causing substantial dehydration and works through hormone receptor blockade, not osmotic force.

preguntas.q: What does the fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) represent?

o.A: Ratio of sodium excreted to sodium filtered
o.B: Ratio of sodium reabsorbed to sodium filtered
o.C: Ratio of sodium excreted to sodium reabsorbed
o.D: Ratio of water excreted to sodium filtered

e.correcta: FENa quantifies what fraction of the sodium filtered at the glomerulus ultimately appears in the urine rather than being reabsorbed by the tubules. Clinically, it helps differentiate prerenal azotemia (FENa less than 1%, since intact tubules avidly reabsorb sodium to conserve volume) from intrinsic acute tubular necrosis (FENa greater than 2%, since damaged tubules cannot reabsorb sodium normally).

incorrectas.B: The ratio of sodium reabsorbed to sodium filtered is essentially the complement of FENa (roughly 1 minus FENa), not the definition of FENa itself.
incorrectas.C: Sodium excreted relative to sodium reabsorbed is not the standard clinical ratio; FENa is specifically defined relative to the filtered load, not the reabsorbed amount.
incorrectas.D: FENa is a sodium-specific measure comparing excreted to filtered sodium; substituting water excretion changes the parameter entirely and does not reflect tubular sodium handling.

preguntas.q: Which formula correctly calculates the fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) when GFR is known directly?

e.correcta: FENa is defined as the sodium excretion rate divided by the filtered sodium load. The excretion rate is urine flow rate times urine sodium concentration (V × UNa), and the filtered load is GFR times plasma sodium concentration (GFR × PNa), giving FENa = (V × UNa) / (GFR × PNa), which directly follows from the definition of a fractional excretion for any filtered solute.

incorrectas.A: This arrangement is inverted, placing the filtered load in the numerator and the excretion rate in the denominator, which would actually calculate the reciprocal of FENa rather than FENa itself.
incorrectas.C: Swapping UNa and PNa into the wrong positions breaks the physiologic logic of comparing excreted sodium to filtered sodium, so this formula does not correctly represent FENa.
incorrectas.D: This arrangement does not correspond to any standard physiologic ratio and fails to correctly pair urine/plasma sodium concentrations with the appropriate flow terms.

preguntas.q: When GFR is not measured directly, which surrogate formula (using creatinine handling as a GFR estimate) is used to calculate FENa?

e.correcta: Since GFR can be estimated as (UCr × V) / PCr using creatinine clearance, substituting this into FENa = (V × UNa) / (GFR × PNa) allows the urine flow rate (V) to cancel out algebraically, leaving FENa = (PCr × UNa) / (UCr × PNa). This creatinine-based version is clinically useful because it avoids the need for a timed urine collection to directly measure V.

incorrectas.A: This arrangement is the mathematical inverse of the correct formula and would yield the reciprocal of FENa (essentially 1/FENa) rather than FENa itself.
incorrectas.B: Placing both urine terms (UCr and UNa) in the numerator does not correctly reflect the substitution derived from the GFR estimation formula, so the V term would not properly cancel.
incorrectas.D: Placing both plasma terms (PCr and PNa) in the numerator similarly breaks the correct algebraic substitution needed to eliminate the urine flow rate variable.

preguntas.q: Where along the nephron does the majority of filtered uric acid get reabsorbed?

e.correcta: Approximately 90% of filtered urate is reabsorbed in the early proximal convoluted tubule via the URAT1 transporter, with some urate then secreted back into the lumen further along the PCT. This transporter is a target of drugs like probenecid (uricosuric) and is affected by low-dose aspirin, thiazides, and pyrazinamide, which can alter serum uric acid and precipitate gout.

incorrectas.A: The loop of Henle is the site of the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter and countercurrent multiplication, generating the medullary concentration gradient, but it is not the major site of uric acid handling.
incorrectas.B: The distal convoluted tubule primarily handles Na+, Cl−, and Ca2+ reabsorption via the NCC cotransporter and is not where the bulk of filtered urate is reclaimed.
incorrectas.C: The collecting duct is responsible for principal and intercalated cell functions such as Na+/K+ balance, H+ secretion, and ADH-regulated water reabsorption, not urate handling, which occurs almost entirely in the proximal tubule.

preguntas.q: At which segment of the nephron is fluid reabsorption isotonic, meaning solute and water are reabsorbed in proportional amounts without changing luminal osmolarity?

o.B: Thin descending limb of the loop of Henle
o.C: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

e.correcta: The PCT reabsorbs roughly 65-70% of the filtered sodium load along with a proportional amount of water, keeping the tubular fluid isosmotic to plasma throughout this segment. This bulk, isotonic reabsorption is driven by Na+-coupled cotransport of glucose, amino acids, and other solutes on the apical membrane, with water following passively through both transcellular and paracellular pathways due to the osmotic gradient created by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase.

incorrectas.B: The thin descending limb is highly permeable to water but relatively impermeable to solute, so as fluid passes through it, water is reabsorbed and the luminal fluid becomes progressively hypertonic rather than remaining isotonic.
incorrectas.C: The thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs solute (via the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter) but is impermeable to water, so the tubular fluid becomes progressively hypotonic as it exits this segment, the opposite of isotonic reabsorption.
incorrectas.D: The distal convoluted tubule continues to reabsorb solute (via the Na-Cl cotransporter) while remaining relatively impermeable to water, further diluting the tubular fluid rather than maintaining isotonicity.

preguntas.q: Which transporter is located on the apical (luminal) membrane of β-intercalated cells in the collecting duct?

e.correcta: β-intercalated cells secrete bicarbonate into the urine, the opposite function of α-intercalated cells, and become active during states of systemic alkalosis. The apical Cl−-HCO3− exchanger, known as pendrin, moves luminal chloride into the cell in exchange for cytoplasmic bicarbonate secreted into the urine, while chloride is reclaimed, allowing the cell to dump base when the body needs to retain acid.

incorrectas.A: H+-ATPase is located on the basolateral membrane of β-intercalated cells (the reverse orientation compared to α-intercalated cells), pumping H+ into the blood rather than the lumen, so it is not the apical transporter being asked about here.
incorrectas.C: H+/K+-ATPase is found on the apical membrane of α-intercalated cells (and gastric parietal cells), where it secretes H+ into the lumen while reabsorbing K+; it is not characteristic of β-intercalated cells.
incorrectas.D: The Na+/H+ exchanger (NHE3) is a hallmark apical transporter of the proximal convoluted tubule, mediating bulk sodium and bicarbonate reabsorption, and is not found on collecting duct intercalated cells.

preguntas.q: Which pump is found on the basolateral membrane of β-intercalated cells in the collecting duct?

e.correcta: In β-intercalated cells, the basolateral H+-ATPase secretes H+ into the peritubular blood while the apical pendrin (Cl−-HCO3− exchanger) secretes bicarbonate into the urine. This is an inverse polarity compared to α-intercalated cells, which have H+-ATPase apically and the Cl−-HCO3− exchanger (AE1) basolaterally, allowing β-intercalated cells to respond appropriately to systemic alkalosis by excreting excess base.

incorrectas.A: Pendrin, the Cl−-HCO3− exchanger, is located on the apical membrane of β-intercalated cells, not the basolateral membrane, so this option has the correct transporter in the wrong location.
incorrectas.B: The Na+/K+-ATPase is a ubiquitous basolateral pump present in essentially all nephron segments to maintain the sodium gradient driving secondary active transport, but it is not the acid-base-specific pump that distinguishes β-intercalated cell function.
incorrectas.D: H+/K+-ATPase functions on the apical membrane of α-intercalated cells (and gastric parietal cells) to secrete H+ while reabsorbing K+, not on the basolateral membrane of β-intercalated cells.

preguntas.q: Global dysfunction of the proximal convoluted tubule, leading to increased urinary loss of amino acids, glucose, bicarbonate, and phosphate, describes which syndrome?

e.correcta: Fanconi syndrome reflects a generalized failure of proximal tubule reabsorptive machinery, affecting essentially all the solutes normally reclaimed there: glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate, phosphate, and uric acid. Clinically this produces type 2 (proximal) renal tubular acidosis, hypophosphatemia with resultant rickets or osteomalacia, and glucosuria despite normal serum glucose.

incorrectas.A: Bartter syndrome mimics chronic loop diuretic use, resulting from a defective Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, causing hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis, not the multi-solute proximal wasting described here.
incorrectas.B: Liddle syndrome is a gain-of-function mutation in the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) in the collecting duct, causing hypertension and hypokalemia from excess sodium reabsorption, unrelated to proximal tubule solute handling.
incorrectas.C: Gitelman syndrome mimics chronic thiazide use, resulting from a defective Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, causing hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and hypocalciuria, not the global proximal tubulopathy of Fanconi syndrome.

preguntas.q: What acid-base disturbance results from Fanconi syndrome due to impaired proximal bicarbonate reabsorption?

e.correcta: Loss of the proximal tubule's normal bicarbonate reabsorptive capacity, as occurs globally in Fanconi syndrome, causes ongoing urinary bicarbonate wasting. This produces a normal anion gap (hyperchloricemic) metabolic acidosis, which is classified specifically as type 2, or proximal, renal tubular acidosis.

incorrectas.B: Metabolic alkalosis would result from bicarbonate retention or acid loss, the opposite of what happens when the proximal tubule is wasting bicarbonate into the urine.
incorrectas.C: Respiratory acidosis arises from hypoventilation and CO2 retention, a pulmonary/ventilatory problem unrelated to renal tubular bicarbonate handling.
incorrectas.D: Respiratory alkalosis arises from hyperventilation and excess CO2 loss, which is also a ventilatory phenomenon and not a consequence of a renal tubular transport defect.

preguntas.q: Fanconi syndrome, when accompanied by systemic acidosis, causes which type of renal tubular acidosis?

e.correcta: Type 2 RTA results from defective proximal bicarbonate reabsorption, exactly the defect seen in Fanconi syndrome. Bicarbonate is wasted in the urine until plasma bicarbonate falls low enough that the reduced filtered load can once again be matched by the impaired reabsorptive capacity, at which point urine pH can appropriately acidify, distinguishing it from type 1 RTA where the urine can never be acidified.

incorrectas.A: Type 1 (distal) RTA is caused by failure of α-intercalated cells in the collecting duct to secrete H+, resulting in an inability to acidify urine below pH 5.5, a distal defect rather than the proximal bicarbonate wasting seen in Fanconi syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Type 4 RTA results from aldosterone deficiency or resistance, causing hyperkalemia that impairs ammoniagenesis, a mechanism entirely distinct from the global proximal tubular dysfunction of Fanconi syndrome.
incorrectas.D: "Type 3 RTA" is a rare, poorly characterized mixed variant and is not the classic type associated with Fanconi syndrome's proximal-only transport defect.

preguntas.q: Which genetic disorder of copper metabolism can cause Fanconi syndrome through copper deposition damaging the proximal tubule?

e.correcta: Wilson disease results from a mutation in ATP7B, which impairs biliary copper excretion and causes copper to accumulate in the liver, brain, cornea (producing Kayser-Fleischer rings), and kidney. Copper deposition and toxicity in proximal tubular cells can produce Fanconi syndrome as one of its renal manifestations, alongside the more classic hepatic and neuropsychiatric features.

incorrectas.A: Hemochromatosis involves iron overload affecting the liver, pancreas, heart, skin, and joints, not copper accumulation, and it is not classically associated with causing Fanconi syndrome.
incorrectas.B: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes liver cirrhosis and panacinar emphysema through accumulation of misfolded protein in hepatocytes, an entirely different mechanism unrelated to renal tubular copper toxicity.
incorrectas.D: Menkes disease is also a copper transport disorder (caused by ATP7A mutations) but produces copper deficiency rather than overload due to poor intestinal copper absorption, presenting with brittle "kinky" hair and neurodegeneration, not Fanconi syndrome.

preguntas.q: Which renal tubular defect can result from inherited metabolic diseases such as glycogen storage disease, tyrosinemia, and cystinosis?

e.correcta: Cystinosis (lysosomal cystine accumulation), tyrosinemia (toxic tyrosine metabolite buildup), and glycogen storage disease type I all directly injure or metabolically overload proximal tubular cells, producing hereditary or acquired Fanconi syndrome with global proximal reabsorptive failure. Cystinosis is in fact the most common cause of hereditary Fanconi syndrome in children.

incorrectas.A: Bartter syndrome arises from an inherited defect in the thick ascending limb's Na-K-2Cl cotransporter, an entirely different transport protein and nephron segment than the proximal tubule damage caused by these storage diseases.
incorrectas.B: Isolated renal glucosuria involves a selective defect in the SGLT2 transporter affecting only glucose reabsorption, not the multi-solute wasting of amino acids, phosphate, and bicarbonate seen with these metabolic diseases.
incorrectas.C: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus results from collecting duct unresponsiveness to ADH, a distinct water-handling problem in a different nephron segment, unrelated to the proximal solute reabsorption defects caused by these storage diseases.

preguntas.q: Which renal tubular defect can be caused by acquired insults such as ischemia, multiple myeloma (light chain toxicity), or lead poisoning?

e.correcta: In multiple myeloma, filtered free light chains are directly toxic to proximal tubular cells when reabsorbed, and similarly, ischemic injury and heavy metal toxicity from lead can damage the same cells. All of these insults converge on producing acquired Fanconi syndrome through direct proximal tubular cell injury, distinguishing it from the inherited metabolic causes of the syndrome.

incorrectas.B: Minimal change disease is a glomerular podocyte disorder causing nephrotic syndrome through loss of the glomerular filtration barrier's charge selectivity, not a tubular reabsorptive defect caused by these particular insults.
incorrectas.C: Membranous nephropathy is an immune-complex-mediated glomerular disease causing nephrotic-range proteinuria, a glomerular rather than tubular process, and is not linked to ischemia, myeloma light chains, or lead toxicity in this way.
incorrectas.D: Acute interstitial nephritis is typically a drug-induced hypersensitivity reaction causing interstitial inflammation with pyuria and eosinophiluria, a different pathologic process than the direct proximal tubular cell toxicity described here.

preguntas.q: Which renal tubular syndrome can be induced by nephrotoxic drugs such as ifosfamide, cisplatin, tenofovir, and expired tetracyclines?

o.A: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)

e.correcta: These drugs are directly toxic to proximal tubular epithelial cells through different mechanisms: ifosfamide and cisplatin cause mitochondrial and DNA damage, tenofovir causes mitochondrial toxicity via nucleotide analog incorporation, and degraded tetracycline byproducts are directly nephrotoxic. All converge on drug-induced Fanconi syndrome, with proximal wasting of glucose, amino acids, phosphate, and bicarbonate.

incorrectas.A: SIADH is typically caused by drugs like carbamazepine or SSRIs, or by ectopic ADH production from tumors, leading to water retention and hyponatremia, a completely different mechanism unrelated to proximal tubular solute handling.
incorrectas.C: Type 1 (distal) RTA results from failure of the collecting duct's α-intercalated cells to secrete H+, and is not the mechanism implicated by these proximal-toxic drugs, which instead damage the proximal tubule.
incorrectas.D: Hemolytic uremic syndrome is caused by endothelial injury, such as from Shiga toxin or certain drugs like cyclosporine, leading to microangiopathic hemolysis and thrombocytopenia, a vascular and glomerular process distinct from direct proximal tubular toxicity.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of Bartter syndrome?

e.correcta: Bartter syndrome is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, caused by loss-of-function mutations in transporters of the thick ascending limb (most commonly the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter NKCC2, but also ROMK or CLC-Kb channels). Because two defective alleles are needed for the phenotype to manifest, both parents are typically unaffected carriers, consistent with classic recessive inheritance patterns seen in many congenital tubulopathies.

incorrectas.A: Autosomal dominant inheritance requires only one mutant allele to produce disease, which is the pattern seen in Liddle syndrome (a gain-of-function ENaC mutation), not Bartter syndrome, which needs loss of both functional NKCC2/ROMK/CLC-Kb alleles.
incorrectas.C: X-linked recessive disorders map to genes on the X chromosome and predominantly affect males; Bartter syndrome genes (e.g., SLC12A1, KCNJ1, CLCNKB) are autosomal, so its recessive inheritance does not follow X-linked transmission.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance is maternally transmitted and affects organs with high energy demand (muscle, CNS); Bartter syndrome results from nuclear-encoded ion transporter defects, not mitochondrial DNA mutations.

preguntas.q: Which inherited renal tubular defect produces hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis that clinically mimic chronic loop diuretic use?

e.correcta: Bartter syndrome results from loss-of-function mutations in the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) or associated channels in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle — the same transporter that loop diuretics like furosemide pharmacologically inhibit. This shared mechanism produces an identical clinical picture of volume depletion, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and hypercalciuria, effectively making Bartter syndrome a genetic phenocopy of chronic furosemide use.

incorrectas.A: Gitelman syndrome results from loss-of-function mutations in the distal convoluted tubule Na+/Cl- cotransporter (NCC), the target of thiazide diuretics, not loop diuretics; it produces hypocalciuria rather than the hypercalciuria seen with loop-diuretic-like defects.
incorrectas.B: Liddle syndrome is caused by a gain-of-function mutation in ENaC in the collecting duct, mimicking a state of mineralocorticoid excess (hypertension, hypokalemia) rather than loop diuretic inhibition of NKCC2.
incorrectas.D: Syndrome of apparent mineralocorticoid excess results from 11beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 deficiency, causing unchecked cortisol activation of the mineralocorticoid receptor; this also mimics hyperaldosteronism, not loop diuretic use.

preguntas.q: What happens to serum potassium levels in a patient with Bartter syndrome?

e.correcta: Loss of NKCC2 function in Bartter syndrome impairs Na+ and Cl- reabsorption in the thick ascending limb, delivering a large sodium load to the distal nephron. This increased distal Na+ delivery drives enhanced Na+ reabsorption via ENaC in exchange for K+ secretion in the collecting duct, and the resulting volume contraction further activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, compounding renal potassium wasting and producing hypokalemia.

incorrectas.A: Serum potassium is not increased in Bartter syndrome; hyperkalemia would instead suggest a defect that impairs distal K+ secretion, such as a mineralocorticoid-deficient or ENaC-blocking state, the opposite of what occurs here.
incorrectas.C: Potassium levels are not unchanged — the increased distal sodium delivery and secondary hyperaldosteronism characteristic of Bartter syndrome reliably drive clinically significant renal potassium wasting.
incorrectas.D: There is no transient increase in Bartter syndrome; the hypokalemia is a chronic, sustained finding driven by ongoing NKCC2 dysfunction and persistent secondary hyperaldosteronism, not a self-correcting fluctuation.

preguntas.q: Which acid-base disturbance characteristically develops in Bartter syndrome?

e.correcta: Bartter syndrome causes chronic volume contraction (from NKCC2 dysfunction mimicking loop diuretic use) plus increased distal H+ secretion driven by secondary hyperaldosteronism and enhanced distal Na+ delivery. The combination of volume contraction, which stimulates proximal HCO3- reabsorption, and increased renal H+ excretion produces a contraction alkalosis, a hallmark of both Bartter syndrome and chronic loop diuretic therapy.

incorrectas.A: Metabolic acidosis would result from HCO3- loss or H+ retention (e.g., renal tubular acidosis), which is the opposite of the H+ wasting and volume-contraction-driven bicarbonate retention seen in Bartter syndrome.
incorrectas.B: Respiratory alkalosis arises from hyperventilation and primary CO2 loss through the lungs, not from a renal tubular ion transport defect; Bartter syndrome's acid-base disturbance originates in the kidney, not the respiratory system.
incorrectas.C: Respiratory acidosis results from hypoventilation and CO2 retention, an entirely separate mechanism from the renal salt-wasting and secondary hyperaldosteronism that drive Bartter syndrome's alkalosis.

preguntas.q: How is urinary calcium excretion affected in Bartter syndrome?

e.correcta: In the thick ascending limb, the lumen-positive potential generated by NKCC2-driven K+ recycling through ROMK normally drives paracellular reabsorption of Ca2+ and Mg2+. Loss of NKCC2 function in Bartter syndrome abolishes this lumen-positive gradient, so calcium reabsorption falls, producing hypercalciuria — a key feature that helps distinguish Bartter syndrome from Gitelman syndrome, where calcium handling is affected oppositely.

incorrectas.B: Hypocalciuria is the classic finding in Gitelman syndrome, where distal convoluted tubule NCC loss actually enhances calcium reabsorption at that segment; this is the opposite pattern from Bartter syndrome's thick ascending limb defect.
incorrectas.C: Calcium excretion is not unchanged — loss of the lumen-positive transepithelial voltage in the thick ascending limb directly impairs paracellular calcium reabsorption, producing a clinically significant increase in urinary calcium loss.
incorrectas.D: Calcium excretion does not become undetectable; hypercalciuria means excess, not absent, urinary calcium — this option describes a physiologically implausible extreme that does not reflect the actual defect.

preguntas.q: How are plasma renin and aldosterone levels affected in Bartter syndrome?

e.correcta: The chronic renal salt wasting in Bartter syndrome causes persistent volume contraction, which is sensed by the juxtaglomerular apparatus as reduced effective circulating volume. This triggers secondary activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, so both plasma renin and aldosterone rise — appropriately, since the kidney is trying (unsuccessfully) to compensate for ongoing salt loss, in contrast to primary hyperaldosteronism where renin is suppressed.

incorrectas.A: Both being decreased would occur only if the volume-sensing mechanism failed or if there were primary suppression of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis; instead, ongoing renal salt loss in Bartter syndrome robustly stimulates, not suppresses, this axis.
incorrectas.B: Renin and aldosterone move together because aldosterone secretion is driven by angiotensin II generated downstream of renin; an isolated rise in renin without a corresponding rise in aldosterone would be inconsistent with an intact renin-angiotensin-aldosterone cascade.
incorrectas.D: Both levels are not unchanged — the persistent volume contraction from NKCC2 dysfunction is a strong physiologic stimulus that reliably activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, producing measurably elevated levels of both hormones.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of Gitelman syndrome?

e.correcta: Gitelman syndrome is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, most commonly due to loss-of-function mutations in the SLC12A3 gene encoding the thiazide-sensitive Na+/Cl- cotransporter (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule. As with Bartter syndrome, two defective alleles are required for the tubulopathy to manifest clinically.

incorrectas.A: Autosomal dominant inheritance needs only a single mutant allele to cause disease, the pattern seen in Liddle syndrome's gain-of-function ENaC mutation, not in Gitelman syndrome's recessive NCC loss-of-function defect.
incorrectas.B: X-linked recessive disease maps to the X chromosome and predominantly affects males; the SLC12A3 gene responsible for Gitelman syndrome is located on an autosome, so its inheritance does not follow X-linked transmission.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance is maternally transmitted via mitochondrial DNA and typically affects tissues with high metabolic demand; Gitelman syndrome instead arises from a nuclear-encoded transporter mutation.

preguntas.q: Chronic thiazide diuretic use produces an electrolyte pattern that mimics which inherited renal tubular defect?

e.correcta: Gitelman syndrome results from loss-of-function mutations in the distal convoluted tubule Na+/Cl- cotransporter (NCC) — the exact molecular target that thiazide diuretics pharmacologically inhibit. This shared mechanism produces the same electrolyte signature in both conditions: hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypocalciuria, and hypomagnesemia, making Gitelman syndrome the genetic phenocopy of lifelong thiazide use.

incorrectas.A: Bartter syndrome affects the thick ascending limb NKCC2 cotransporter, the target of loop diuretics like furosemide, and produces hypercalciuria rather than the hypocalciuria characteristic of thiazide-like (Gitelman) physiology.
incorrectas.C: Liddle syndrome is caused by a gain-of-function ENaC mutation causing sodium retention and hypertension, mimicking mineralocorticoid excess rather than the salt-wasting picture produced by NCC inhibition.
incorrectas.D: Syndrome of apparent mineralocorticoid excess results from impaired cortisol inactivation and unchecked mineralocorticoid receptor stimulation, mimicking hyperaldosteronism, not thiazide-induced NCC blockade.

preguntas.q: Compared with Bartter syndrome, the clinical severity of Gitelman syndrome is generally:

o.D: Universally fatal in the neonatal period

e.correcta: Gitelman syndrome typically presents later in childhood or adulthood with milder symptoms (fatigue, cramps, mild salt craving) because the distal convoluted tubule NCC defect it involves has less impact on the kidney's overall concentrating and diluting capacity than the thick ascending limb NKCC2 defect in Bartter syndrome. Bartter syndrome, by contrast, often presents in infancy or childhood with more severe polyuria, growth failure, and volume depletion, since the loop of Henle plays a larger role in the countercurrent multiplication system.

incorrectas.B: Gitelman syndrome is not more severe than Bartter syndrome; the reverse is true because the thick ascending limb defect in Bartter syndrome disrupts a nephron segment central to the kidney's concentrating mechanism, producing more pronounced salt wasting and earlier, more severe presentation.
incorrectas.C: The two conditions differ meaningfully in severity and typical age of presentation — Bartter syndrome tends to present earlier and more severely (even antenatally in some forms), while Gitelman syndrome is often diagnosed later with milder symptoms, so they are not clinically equivalent.
incorrectas.D: Gitelman syndrome is not fatal in the neonatal period; it is generally a mild, chronic condition compatible with a normal lifespan, in contrast to antenatal Bartter syndrome, which can present with severe polyhydramnios and premature birth.

preguntas.q: What happens to serum potassium levels in Gitelman syndrome?

e.correcta: Loss of NCC function in the distal convoluted tubule increases sodium delivery to the collecting duct, where ENaC-mediated sodium reabsorption is coupled to potassium secretion. This enhanced distal K+ secretion, amplified by secondary hyperaldosteronism from chronic volume contraction, produces the hypokalemia characteristic of Gitelman syndrome, paralleling the mechanism seen in Bartter syndrome and in thiazide diuretic use.

incorrectas.A: Potassium is not increased in Gitelman syndrome; hyperkalemia would instead suggest impaired distal K+ secretion, such as with aldosterone deficiency or ENaC blockade, which is the opposite of the enhanced distal Na+/K+ exchange seen here.
incorrectas.B: Potassium levels are not unchanged — the increased distal sodium delivery and secondary hyperaldosteronism from chronic NCC loss reliably drive clinically significant renal potassium wasting in Gitelman syndrome.
incorrectas.D: There is no spontaneous normalization; the hypokalemia is a chronic, sustained consequence of the ongoing NCC defect and persistent secondary hyperaldosteronism, requiring potassium and magnesium supplementation rather than resolving on its own.

preguntas.q: How are serum magnesium levels affected in Gitelman syndrome?

e.correcta: Loss of NCC function in the distal convoluted tubule causes intracellular changes (thought to involve downregulation of the apical Mg2+ channel TRPM6) that impair active magnesium reabsorption in this segment, producing renal magnesium wasting and hypomagnesemia. This is a distinguishing feature from Bartter syndrome, where magnesium handling is typically less severely affected, and hypomagnesemia in Gitelman syndrome can itself worsen hypokalemia by impairing renal K+ conservation.

incorrectas.A: Magnesium is not increased in Gitelman syndrome; an elevated magnesium would suggest reduced renal excretion or excessive intake, not the renal magnesium-wasting defect that characterizes this disorder.
incorrectas.B: Magnesium levels are not unchanged — impaired distal convoluted tubule function in Gitelman syndrome directly reduces active magnesium reabsorption, producing a clinically relevant and often diagnostically useful drop in serum magnesium.
incorrectas.C: A markedly increased magnesium level is the opposite of what occurs; the DCT defect in Gitelman syndrome causes magnesium loss in the urine, not magnesium retention.

preguntas.q: Which acid-base disturbance is characteristic of Gitelman syndrome?

e.correcta: Loss of NCC function causes chronic renal salt wasting and volume contraction, which stimulates proximal tubule bicarbonate reabsorption, while the accompanying secondary hyperaldosteronism enhances distal H+ secretion via H+-ATPase in the collecting duct. Together, these mechanisms produce a contraction alkalosis, the same acid-base pattern seen with chronic thiazide use and in Bartter syndrome.

incorrectas.A: Respiratory acidosis results from hypoventilation and CO2 retention, an entirely separate pulmonary mechanism unrelated to the renal tubular salt-wasting defect that drives Gitelman syndrome's acid-base disturbance.
incorrectas.B: Metabolic acidosis would reflect bicarbonate loss or acid retention, the opposite process of the bicarbonate-conserving, H+-excreting state produced by volume contraction and secondary hyperaldosteronism in Gitelman syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Respiratory alkalosis arises from hyperventilation and primary CO2 loss through the lungs, not from a renal ion transport defect; Gitelman syndrome's alkalosis originates from renal, not respiratory, mechanisms.

preguntas.q: How is urinary calcium excretion affected in Gitelman syndrome?

e.correcta: Loss of NCC function in the distal convoluted tubule lowers intracellular Na+, which enhances basolateral Na+/Ca2+ exchange and increases apical Ca2+ entry, ultimately boosting transcellular calcium reabsorption at this segment. This produces hypocalciuria, a key feature that distinguishes Gitelman syndrome from Bartter syndrome (which causes hypercalciuria) and from thiazide diuretics, which share this same calcium-sparing mechanism.

incorrectas.A: Hypercalciuria is the hallmark of Bartter syndrome, where loss of the lumen-positive voltage in the thick ascending limb impairs paracellular calcium reabsorption — the opposite mechanism and opposite calcium finding from Gitelman syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Calcium excretion is not unchanged — the DCT defect in Gitelman syndrome actively enhances distal calcium reabsorption, producing a clinically useful decrease in urinary calcium that helps distinguish it from Bartter syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Calcium excretion does not become entirely absent; hypocalciuria refers to a reduced but still present amount of urinary calcium, not a complete absence, which would be physiologically implausible.

preguntas.q: How are plasma renin and aldosterone levels affected in Gitelman syndrome?

e.correcta: Chronic renal sodium and chloride wasting from NCC dysfunction causes persistent volume contraction, which the juxtaglomerular apparatus senses as reduced effective circulating volume, triggering secondary activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Both renin and aldosterone rise as the kidney attempts to compensate for ongoing salt loss, distinguishing this secondary hyperaldosteronism from primary hyperaldosteronism, where renin is suppressed.

incorrectas.A: Both being decreased would require primary suppression of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis; instead, the ongoing volume contraction from NCC loss is a potent physiologic stimulus that activates, rather than suppresses, this system.
incorrectas.B: Renin and aldosterone rise together because aldosterone secretion is driven by angiotensin II generated downstream of renin release; a fall in renin with a rise in aldosterone would be inconsistent with normal renin-angiotensin-aldosterone physiology.
incorrectas.D: Both levels are not unchanged — chronic salt wasting from the DCT defect provides a sustained stimulus to the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, reliably producing measurable elevations in both hormones.

preguntas.q: How does serum sodium change in Liddle syndrome?
