Loop diuretics like furosemide competitively block the Cl- binding site of NKCC2, abolishing this reabsorption; because the thick ascending limb normally reabsorbs roughly 25% of filtered Na+, this makes loop diuretics the most potent diuretic class and also collapses the countercurrent multiplier, impairing the kidney's ability to concentrate urine.

incorrectas.A: NCC is the target of thiazide diuretics and is located in the distal convoluted tubule, a different nephron segment downstream of the thick ascending limb — thiazides are far less potent than loop diuretics because the DCT reabsorbs a much smaller fraction of filtered Na+.
incorrectas.C: NHE3 mediates Na+/H+ exchange primarily in the proximal tubule (and contributes to bicarbonate reabsorption there); it is not the site of action of loop diuretics and is instead affected by drugs like acetazolamide.
incorrectas.D: ENaC is located in the principal cells of the collecting duct and is the target of potassium-sparing diuretics such as amiloride and triamterene, a segment and mechanism entirely distinct from loop diuretic action on NKCC2.

preguntas.q: The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is critical to the countercurrent multiplier because it is impermeable to which substance?

e.correcta: The thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs Na+, K+, and Cl- via NKCC2 but has essentially no water channels, so water cannot follow the reabsorbed solute out of the tubule. This dilutes the tubular fluid as it ascends (hence the segment is sometimes called the 'diluting segment') while simultaneously depositing solute into the medullary interstitium, which is the core mechanism generating the hypertonic medullary gradient the kidney relies on to concentrate urine later in the collecting duct.

incorrectas.A: Sodium is actively transported out of the tubular fluid in this segment via NKCC2 — it is reabsorbed, not excluded, and its movement (along with K+ and Cl-) is exactly what builds the medullary osmotic gradient.
incorrectas.B: Urea is largely impermeable in the thick ascending limb as well, but the defining, testable feature of this segment for the countercurrent multiplier is its water impermeability, which allows dilution of luminal fluid while solute is reabsorbed — urea's role is more relevant to the inner medullary collecting duct and urea recycling.
incorrectas.D: Chloride is actively reabsorbed here via NKCC2 alongside Na+ and K+, making it a transported solute rather than an excluded one — the opposite of water, which cannot cross at all.

preguntas.q: Furosemide, bumetanide, and torsemide all belong to which class of diuretics?

e.correcta: Furosemide, bumetanide, and torsemide are all loop diuretics that inhibit the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Blocking this transporter prevents reabsorption of roughly a quarter of filtered sodium, producing the most potent natriuresis and diuresis of any diuretic class, which is why these agents are the go-to choice for rapidly mobilizing fluid in conditions like pulmonary edema and severe volume overload.

incorrectas.A: Thiazide diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide and chlorthalidone act on the Na+/Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, a weaker and more distal site of Na+ reabsorption than the thick ascending limb targeted by these three drugs.
incorrectas.B: Potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, eplerenone, amiloride, triamterene) act on the collecting duct — either by blocking aldosterone receptors or ENaC directly — and are named for their tendency to cause hyperkalemia, the opposite electrolyte effect of loop diuretics.
incorrectas.C: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors like acetazolamide act in the proximal tubule by blocking bicarbonate reabsorption, producing a mild diuresis and metabolic acidosis, a very different mechanism and site from the NKCC2 blockade used by loop diuretics.

preguntas.q: Which class of diuretics produces the greatest degree of natriuresis and is considered the most efficacious?

e.correcta: Loop diuretics are the most potent diuretic class because they act on the thick ascending limb, the nephron segment responsible for reabsorbing roughly 25% of filtered Na+ — far more than the ~5-7% handled by the distal convoluted tubule (thiazide target) or the ~2-3% handled by the collecting duct (potassium-sparing diuretic target). Because so much Na+ (and accompanying water) escapes reabsorption downstream when NKCC2 is blocked, loop diuretics can produce dramatic fluid loss, making them the agents of choice when rapid, substantial diuresis is needed, such as in acute pulmonary edema.

incorrectas.B: Thiazide diuretics act more distally on the Na+/Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, a segment that reabsorbs a much smaller fraction of filtered Na+ than the thick ascending limb, so their maximal natriuretic effect is inherently smaller than that of loop diuretics.
incorrectas.C: Potassium-sparing diuretics act on the collecting duct, the most distal and lowest-capacity Na+-reabsorbing segment, giving them only a modest diuretic effect on their own — they are typically used adjunctively rather than for aggressive volume removal.
incorrectas.D: Osmotic diuretics like mannitol work by a different mechanism entirely, drawing water into the tubule by osmotic force throughout the nephron rather than blocking a specific transporter, and are used mainly to reduce intracranial or intraocular pressure rather than to achieve the potent natriuresis of loop diuretics.

preguntas.q: Ethacrynic acid, a drug that can be used safely in patients with a sulfa allergy, belongs to which diuretic class?

e.correcta: Ethacrynic acid is a loop diuretic that inhibits NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb just like furosemide, bumetanide, and torsemide, producing the same potent natriuretic and diuretic effect. What sets it apart within the class is its chemical structure — it is a phenoxyacetic acid derivative rather than a sulfonamide — which is why it is the loop diuretic of choice in patients with a documented sulfa allergy.

incorrectas.A: Thiazide diuretics act on the distal convoluted tubule via the Na+/Cl- cotransporter and are almost universally sulfonamide-derived (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide), making them a poor choice, not a substitute, for sulfa-allergic patients.
incorrectas.C: Potassium-sparing diuretics act on the collecting duct and are structurally and mechanistically unrelated to loop diuretics; ethacrynic acid's clinical niche specifically stems from its loop-diuretic potency combined with its non-sulfonamide structure, not from being a K+-sparing agent.
incorrectas.D: Osmotic diuretics such as mannitol are inert, non-absorbed molecules that create an osmotic pull of water rather than blocking a specific ion transporter, a completely different mechanism from ethacrynic acid's NKCC2 inhibition.

preguntas.q: Which electrolyte disturbance involving magnesium may occur as an adverse effect of loop diuretics?

e.correcta: Normally, the positive luminal potential generated by NKCC2-mediated K+ recycling in the thick ascending limb drives paracellular reabsorption of divalent cations like Mg2+ and Ca2+. When loop diuretics block NKCC2, this potential is lost, so paracellular Mg2+ reabsorption falls and Mg2+ is wasted in the urine, producing hypomagnesemia — a risk that is compounded in patients who already have marginal dietary magnesium intake.

incorrectas.A: Hypermagnesemia is the opposite finding and would instead be expected with impaired renal excretion (e.g., renal failure) or excessive magnesium intake, not with a drug that abolishes the driving force for Mg2+ reabsorption.
incorrectas.B: Hypernatremia is not a typical loop diuretic effect; loop diuretics cause natriuresis and volume contraction, and if anything free water losses can sometimes track with sodium losses depending on intake, but magnesium wasting specifically reflects loss of the paracellular divalent cation gradient, not sodium handling.
incorrectas.D: Hyperkalemia is the opposite of what loop diuretics cause — by increasing distal Na+ delivery to the collecting duct, they promote K+ secretion and typically cause hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.

preguntas.q: What effect do loop diuretics have on serum calcium, in contrast to thiazide diuretics?

e.correcta: Loop diuretics abolish the positive luminal potential in the thick ascending limb that normally drives paracellular Ca2+ reabsorption alongside Mg2+, so more Ca2+ is lost in the urine, producing a calciuric, hypocalcemic tendency. This is clinically useful — loop diuretics can be given (with saline) to help lower dangerously high calcium levels — and it is the opposite of thiazides, which enhance distal Ca2+ reabsorption and can cause mild hypercalcemia.

incorrectas.A: Hypercalcemia is the thiazide effect, not the loop diuretic effect — thiazides increase Ca2+ reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule via mechanisms linked to NCC inhibition, the reverse of what happens with loop diuretics.
incorrectas.B: Phosphate handling is not the primary electrolyte disturbance associated with loop diuretics; their signature electrolyte effects involve K+, Mg2+, and Ca2+ wasting via disruption of thick ascending limb transport, not phosphate.
incorrectas.C: Loop diuretics do have a clear effect on calcium — by eliminating the lumen-positive potential that drives paracellular Ca2+ reabsorption, they promote calciuria, which is significant enough to be a rare but real cause of hypocalcemia and is exploited therapeutically in hypercalcemia.

preguntas.q: Which class of drugs can blunt the renal-protective, prostaglandin-dependent vasodilatory effect of loop diuretics?

e.correcta: Loop diuretics partly rely on renal prostaglandins, which help maintain afferent arteriolar vasodilation and renal blood flow, particularly in states of reduced perfusion such as heart failure. NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase and thus prostaglandin synthesis, removing this protective vasodilatory tone; this both blunts the natriuretic/diuretic response to loop diuretics and increases the risk of acute kidney injury when the two drug classes are combined, especially in volume-depleted or heart failure patients.

incorrectas.B: ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction and can actually be used alongside loop diuretics in heart failure management; they do not blunt loop diuretic efficacy through a prostaglandin mechanism the way NSAIDs do (though the combination can still lower GFR through a different mechanism).
incorrectas.C: Beta-blockers reduce sympathetic drive to the heart and kidney but do not act through cyclooxygenase or prostaglandin pathways, so they do not interfere with the renal vasodilatory support that loop diuretics depend on.
incorrectas.D: Corticosteroids can cause sodium and fluid retention through mineralocorticoid-like effects, which could in theory oppose diuresis, but this is unrelated to the specific prostaglandin-mediated renal vasodilation that NSAIDs disrupt.

preguntas.q: Which class of diuretics is first-line for symptomatic treatment of acute decompensated heart failure with fluid overload?

e.correcta: In acute decompensated heart failure, the goal is rapid removal of excess extracellular fluid to relieve pulmonary and peripheral congestion, and loop diuretics achieve this fastest and most powerfully by blocking NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, the nephron segment with the greatest Na+-reabsorptive capacity. Intravenous loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) are therefore the standard first-line therapy for symptomatic relief in this setting, even though they do not address the underlying pump dysfunction.

incorrectas.A: Thiazide diuretics act on the distal convoluted tubule and produce a much weaker natriuretic effect than loop diuretics; they are sometimes added later for synergistic diuresis (sequential nephron blockade) but are not first-line for acute decompensation.
incorrectas.C: Potassium-sparing diuretics act on the collecting duct and produce only mild diuresis; they are used mainly for their aldosterone-antagonist mortality benefit in chronic heart failure (e.g., spironolactone) rather than for acute symptomatic fluid removal.
incorrectas.D: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors act in the proximal tubule and produce only modest, self-limited diuresis due to compensatory reabsorption downstream, making them far too weak for acute volume overload management.

preguntas.q: Loop diuretics are used to treat which acute complication of decompensated heart failure, characterized by fluid accumulation within the alveolar spaces?

e.correcta: When left ventricular function decompensates, hydrostatic pressure backs up into the pulmonary capillaries and fluid leaks into the alveolar spaces, causing pulmonary edema and the classic symptoms of dyspnea, orthopnea, and crackles on exam. Loop diuretics rapidly reduce intravascular volume and, through venodilation, lower pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure even before diuresis fully occurs, making them a mainstay of acute symptomatic management.

incorrectas.A: Pneumothorax is air in the pleural space from a ruptured bleb, trauma, or barotrauma — a mechanical process unrelated to fluid overload, and diuretics play no role in its treatment.
incorrectas.B: Pulmonary embolism results from thrombus obstruction of the pulmonary vasculature, treated with anticoagulation or thrombolysis, not diuresis; while it can coexist with heart failure, it is a distinct pathologic process from hydrostatic pulmonary edema.
incorrectas.D: Pleural fibrosis is a chronic scarring process (e.g., from prior effusion, asbestos exposure, or radiation) rather than an acute fluid-overload complication, and it does not respond to diuretic therapy.

preguntas.q: Regarding long-term outcomes in heart failure, what is true of loop diuretics compared to agents like ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers?

o.A: They reduce mortality similarly to ACE inhibitors
o.B: They increase survival by reducing preload
o.C: They reduce mortality only in HFpEF
o.D: They do not improve survival and are used only for symptomatic relief

e.correcta: Loop diuretics relieve the congestive symptoms of heart failure — edema, dyspnea, orthopnea — by reducing volume overload, but unlike ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, and aldosterone antagonists, they have not been shown to alter the neurohormonal and structural remodeling processes that drive disease progression, and so they do not prolong survival. They remain essential for quality of life and symptom control but are considered adjunctive rather than disease-modifying therapy.

incorrectas.A: ACE inhibitors do carry a proven mortality benefit in heart failure by blunting angiotensin II- and aldosterone-driven remodeling, a benefit loop diuretics — which act purely on tubular Na+ handling — do not share.
incorrectas.B: While loop diuretics do reduce preload, this hemodynamic effect improves symptoms rather than survival; large trials have not demonstrated a mortality reduction with loop diuretic use, distinguishing them from guideline-directed medical therapies.
incorrectas.C: There is no established loop diuretic mortality benefit specific to heart failure with preserved ejection fraction; their role there, as in HFrEF, remains symptomatic control of volume overload rather than a proven survival advantage.

preguntas.q: Loop diuretics, often combined with spironolactone, are used in the management of which complication of cirrhosis?

e.correcta: In cirrhosis, portal hypertension and hypoalbuminemia promote fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity, while secondary hyperaldosteronism (from decreased effective circulating volume activating the RAAS) drives renal Na+ and water retention that worsens it. Combining a loop diuretic with spironolactone addresses both the volume overload and the underlying aldosterone-driven Na+ retention, and this combination (often in a specific ratio) is standard therapy for cirrhotic ascites.

incorrectas.B: Hepatic encephalopathy results from accumulation of neurotoxic substances like ammonia due to impaired hepatic clearance and portosystemic shunting; it is managed with lactulose and rifaximin, not diuretics.
incorrectas.C: Esophageal variceal bleeding stems from ruptured portosystemic collateral vessels under portal hypertension and requires endoscopic banding, vasoactive drugs like octreotide, or beta-blocker prophylaxis — diuretics play no role in controlling variceal hemorrhage.
incorrectas.D: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is an infection of ascitic fluid treated with antibiotics (e.g., a third-generation cephalosporin); diuretics do not treat the infection, though ascites (the fluid diuretics help reduce) is the substrate in which SBP occurs.

preguntas.q: Loop diuretics can be used in the treatment of hypertension and are particularly useful when which comorbidity is also present?

e.correcta: Loop diuretics lower blood pressure primarily by reducing intravascular volume through potent natriuresis, which makes them especially valuable when hypertension coexists with heart failure and fluid overload — a single agent then addresses both the elevated blood pressure and the congestive symptoms. In uncomplicated hypertension without volume overload, thiazides are generally preferred because their longer duration of action and milder diuresis are better suited to chronic blood pressure control.

incorrectas.A: Diabetes without renal disease is actually a setting where thiazides are commonly favored (with attention to modest glucose effects); it does not create the volume-overload state that specifically favors loop diuretics over thiazides.
incorrectas.C: Osteoporosis is a scenario where thiazides are often preferred because they promote renal Ca2+ reabsorption and can modestly help bone density, the opposite of loop diuretics, which increase urinary Ca2+ loss.
incorrectas.D: Gout is a relative caution with both thiazides and loop diuretics, since both can raise uric acid levels by competing for proximal tubular organic anion secretion; it is not a reason to specifically favor loop diuretics for hypertension.

preguntas.q: Loop diuretics, through their calciuric effect, are used in the acute management of which electrolyte disorder?

e.correcta: By blocking NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, loop diuretics eliminate the lumen-positive potential that normally drives paracellular Ca2+ reabsorption, producing significant calciuria. Combined with aggressive IV saline hydration to replace volume losses, this calciuric effect is used to acutely lower dangerously elevated serum calcium (e.g., from malignancy or hyperparathyroidism) while definitive therapy is arranged.

incorrectas.A: Hypocalcemia is actually a potential adverse effect of loop diuretics due to their calciuric action, not an indication for their use — treating hypocalcemia requires calcium and/or vitamin D repletion, not a drug that increases urinary calcium loss.
incorrectas.B: Hyperkalemia is treated with measures like insulin/glucose, calcium gluconate for cardiac membrane stabilization, and potassium-wasting therapies; while loop diuretics do promote K+ excretion and can be adjunctive, the classic calcium-related use of loop diuretics is for hypercalcemia specifically.
incorrectas.D: Hypernatremia is managed by correcting free water deficits, not by loop diuretics, which cause isotonic or even hypotonic fluid loss depending on free water intake — they are not a standard therapy targeted at correcting elevated serum sodium.

preguntas.q: Loop diuretics may be used to reduce edema in which class of renal disorders, characterized by heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and generalized edema?

e.correcta: Nephrotic syndrome causes massive urinary protein loss, dropping plasma oncotic pressure and driving fluid out of the vasculature into the interstitium, producing significant edema (periorbital, peripheral, or even anasarca). Loop diuretics are used to promote natriuresis and reduce this fluid burden symptomatically, though because plasma proteins remain low, higher or more frequent doses are sometimes needed to overcome reduced diuretic delivery to its site of action when the drug is heavily protein-bound in circulation.

incorrectas.A: Nephritic syndrome is characterized more by hematuria, hypertension, and mild-to-moderate proteinuria from glomerular inflammation, with edema being a less dominant and less oncotic-pressure-driven feature than in nephrotic syndrome.
incorrectas.B: Acute tubular necrosis causes acute kidney injury with tubular cell death and can have an oliguric phase with volume overload, but its edema is driven by reduced GFR and fluid retention rather than the hypoalbuminemia-driven fluid shift of nephrotic syndrome, and diuretics are used cautiously (if at all) given the risk of worsening ischemic injury.
incorrectas.C: Renal tubular acidosis is a disorder of impaired acid excretion or bicarbonate handling, presenting with metabolic acidosis rather than the heavy proteinuria and edema that define nephrotic syndrome; it is not a classic indication for loop diuretic therapy.

preguntas.q: What effect do loop diuretics have on serum potassium, and by what mechanism?

o.A: Hypokalemia, due to increased distal Na+ delivery driving K+ secretion
o.D: Hyperkalemia, due to decreased distal Na+ delivery

e.correcta: By blocking Na+ reabsorption in the thick ascending limb, loop diuretics increase the amount of Na+ delivered to the collecting duct. There, principal cells reabsorb this excess Na+ through ENaC, and the resulting lumen-negative potential drives more K+ secretion into the tubular fluid (along with more H+ secretion by intercalated cells), producing hypokalemia — this is also why loop diuretics are often paired with a potassium-sparing diuretic or potassium supplementation in clinical practice.

incorrectas.B: Aldosterone antagonism describes the mechanism of spironolactone, a potassium-sparing diuretic, not loop diuretics; loop diuretics act on NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb and have no direct effect on the aldosterone receptor.
incorrectas.C: Loop diuretics have a well-documented and clinically significant effect on potassium — the increased distal Na+ delivery they cause reliably promotes urinary K+ wasting, which is one of their most important electrolyte side effects to monitor.
incorrectas.D: Decreased distal Na+ delivery would reduce K+ secretion and could cause hyperkalemia, but this is the opposite of what loop diuretics actually do — they increase, not decrease, Na+ delivery to the distal nephron, which is precisely why they cause hypokalemia rather than hyperkalemia.

preguntas.q: Which loop diuretic carries the highest risk of ototoxicity, particularly when combined with other ototoxic drugs like aminoglycosides?

e.correcta: All loop diuretics carry some risk of ototoxicity because NKCC transporters closely related to NKCC2 are also expressed in the stria vascularis of the inner ear, where their inhibition can disturb endolymph composition. Ethacrynic acid carries the highest risk among the loop diuretics, making it a drug generally reserved for patients who cannot take sulfonamide-based loop diuretics (e.g., due to sulfa allergy) rather than a first-choice agent, especially when other ototoxic drugs are on board.

incorrectas.A: Furosemide, the most commonly used loop diuretic, does carry some ototoxic risk (especially with rapid IV administration or renal impairment), but it is considered less ototoxic overall than ethacrynic acid, which is why furosemide remains first-line for most patients.
incorrectas.C: Bumetanide is a potent loop diuretic with a similar mechanism to furosemide and is not singled out as carrying the highest ototoxicity risk within the class; its adverse effect profile more closely parallels furosemide's than ethacrynic acid's.
incorrectas.D: Torsemide, like furosemide and bumetanide, has a more favorable ototoxicity profile than ethacrynic acid and is often chosen specifically because of better bioavailability and tolerability, not because of elevated ototoxic risk.

preguntas.q: Most loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide) share which structural feature that predisposes to cross-reactivity in sulfa-allergic patients?

e.correcta: Furosemide, bumetanide, and torsemide are all sulfonamide derivatives, meaning they share a chemical moiety with sulfa antibiotics and other sulfa-based drugs (including thiazide diuretics). This structural similarity is why patients with a true sulfa allergy can, in some cases, experience cross-reactive hypersensitivity reactions to these loop diuretics, prompting clinicians to consider a non-sulfonamide alternative when the allergy history is significant.

incorrectas.A: A phenoxyacetic acid backbone describes ethacrynic acid specifically, which is the exception within the loop diuretic class precisely because it lacks the sulfonamide group shared by the others — it is the answer to which loop diuretic is safe in sulfa allergy, not a shared feature of most loop diuretics.
incorrectas.B: Aminoglycosides are a separate antibiotic class (e.g., gentamicin) with no structural relationship to loop diuretics; the two drug classes are linked only functionally, since both carry ototoxic risk and can potentiate each other's toxicity, not by shared chemistry.
incorrectas.D: A thiazide ring structure describes thiazide diuretics, a related but distinct sulfonamide-containing class targeting the distal convoluted tubule — loop diuretics share the sulfonamide moiety with thiazides but are chemically and mechanistically a separate drug class.

preguntas.q: Which loop diuretic can be used safely in patients with a sulfonamide allergy because it is not a sulfonamide derivative?

e.correcta: Ethacrynic acid is a phenoxyacetic acid derivative rather than a sulfonamide, which distinguishes it structurally from the other loop diuretics. Because it still blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb just as effectively, it preserves the potent diuretic action of the class while avoiding the cross-reactivity risk that furosemide, bumetanide, and torsemide pose in patients with a genuine sulfa allergy — though it comes with a tradeoff of higher ototoxicity risk.

incorrectas.A: Furosemide is a sulfonamide-derived loop diuretic and, along with the other sulfa-based agents, carries a theoretical risk of cross-reactivity in sulfa-allergic patients, making it not the preferred choice in that population.
incorrectas.B: Bumetanide shares the sulfonamide structure common to most loop diuretics and is therefore in the same category as furosemide regarding sulfa cross-reactivity concerns, not the non-sulfonamide alternative.
incorrectas.C: Torsemide is likewise a sulfonamide derivative like furosemide and bumetanide; ethacrynic acid remains the classic exception within the loop diuretic class specifically because of its distinct phenoxyacetic acid chemistry.

preguntas.q: Which renal pathology, an idiosyncratic hypersensitivity reaction, may be caused by loop diuretics as with many sulfonamide-derived drugs?

e.correcta: Acute interstitial nephritis is a drug-induced hypersensitivity reaction in which immune cells infiltrate the renal interstitium, causing acute kidney injury often accompanied by fever, rash, and eosinophilia. Because most loop diuretics are sulfonamide derivatives, they belong to a broader group of drugs (alongside penicillins, NSAIDs, and sulfa antibiotics) known to trigger this idiosyncratic reaction, which is generally dose-independent and resolves with drug withdrawal.

incorrectas.B: Minimal change disease is a glomerular disease causing nephrotic-range proteinuria via podocyte foot process effacement, classically associated with NSAIDs or lymphoproliferative disorders rather than the tubulointerstitial hypersensitivity reaction seen with loop diuretics.
incorrectas.C: Membranous nephropathy involves subepithelial immune complex deposition along the glomerular basement membrane, associated with drugs like NSAIDs, penicillamine, or gold, and with underlying malignancy or infections — a different immune mechanism and anatomic site than the interstitial infiltrate of AIN.
incorrectas.D: Acute tubular necrosis results from direct ischemic or toxic injury to tubular epithelial cells (e.g., from aminoglycosides, contrast dye, or prolonged hypotension), producing tubular cell death rather than the immune-mediated interstitial inflammation characteristic of a hypersensitivity drug reaction.

preguntas.q: Which acid-base disturbance is classically caused by loop diuretics?

e.correcta: Loop diuretics inhibit the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, causing volume contraction that activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system; the resulting rise in aldosterone increases H+ and K+ secretion in the collecting duct, while the shrinking extracellular volume concentrates the existing bicarbonate ('contraction alkalosis'). Together these produce a hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.

incorrectas.B: Metabolic acidosis would result from bicarbonate loss or impaired bicarbonate reabsorption, as seen with carbonic anhydrase inhibitors like acetazolamide, which cause a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis in the proximal tubule - the opposite acid-base direction from loop diuretics.
incorrectas.C: Respiratory alkalosis arises from hyperventilation lowering PaCO2, a ventilatory process unrelated to loop diuretics' action on renal tubular NaCl transport and volume status.
incorrectas.D: Respiratory acidosis reflects hypoventilation and CO2 retention, a pulmonary problem with no connection to the renal contraction and aldosterone-driven mechanism that loop diuretics trigger.

preguntas.q: The potent natriuretic and diuretic effect of loop diuretics can lead to excessive fluid loss, resulting in which complication if not carefully monitored?

e.correcta: Loop diuretics inhibit the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, dramatically reducing reabsorption of the filtered load and producing a large, rapid diuresis; if fluid intake doesn't match losses, intravascular volume contracts, causing dehydration, prerenal azotemia, and hypotension - a common problem in elderly patients on aggressive diuretic regimens.

incorrectas.A: Hypervolemia is the opposite problem - excess fluid - and is actually the condition loop diuretics are used to treat (e.g., in heart failure or edematous states), not a complication of their diuretic action.
incorrectas.C: SIADH causes water retention and dilutional hyponatremia from excess ADH activity; it is not induced by NKCC2 inhibition, and loop diuretics actually impair the kidney's concentrating ability, working against an SIADH-like state.
incorrectas.D: Peripheral edema results from fluid accumulation (heart failure, venous insufficiency, low oncotic pressure) - the opposite direction of fluid balance from the volume depletion that loop diuretics produce.

preguntas.q: Ethacrynic acid, unlike other loop diuretics, lacks a sulfonamide moiety, making it a useful alternative in patients with an allergy to which class of drugs?

e.correcta: Furosemide, bumetanide, and torsemide are all sulfonamide-derivative loop diuretics that can trigger allergic or hypersensitivity reactions in sulfa-allergic patients. Ethacrynic acid is a phenoxyacetic acid derivative without a sulfonamide group, so it retains the NKCC2-blocking loop diuretic effect while avoiding this cross-reactivity, making it the preferred loop diuretic for patients with sulfa allergy.

incorrectas.A: Penicillin allergy involves reactivity to the beta-lactam ring and does not cross-react with the sulfonamide moiety found in most loop diuretics, so switching to ethacrynic acid is not done for a penicillin allergy.
incorrectas.C: Cephalosporin allergy similarly relates to a beta-lactam structure; ethacrynic acid's specific benefit is the absence of a sulfonamide group, not any consideration related to beta-lactam antibiotics.
incorrectas.D: Fluoroquinolone allergy is unrelated to sulfonamide chemistry, and there is no established cross-reactivity between fluoroquinolones and sulfonamide-based diuretics that would necessitate using ethacrynic acid.

preguntas.q: What effect do loop diuretics have on the hypertonicity of the renal medullary interstitium?

o.D: Hypertonicity confined to the cortex only

e.correcta: Loop diuretics block the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, which normally pumps NaCl into the medullary interstitium as the 'single effect' of the countercurrent multiplier system. Blocking this transporter abolishes the mechanism that builds the corticomedullary osmotic gradient, so medullary hypertonicity collapses.

incorrectas.A: An increase in medullary tonicity would require enhanced NKCC2 activity; loop diuretics do the opposite by inhibiting this transporter and washing out the gradient rather than reinforcing it.
incorrectas.B: The medullary gradient depends critically on active NaCl transport by the thick ascending limb, so removing this transport (as loop diuretics do) has a major, not negligible, effect on interstitial tonicity.
incorrectas.D: The corticomedullary gradient normally increases in tonicity from cortex to inner medulla; loop diuretics reduce tonicity throughout the outer and inner medulla by disabling the countercurrent multiplier, not selectively sparing the cortex.

preguntas.q: Loss of medullary hypertonicity (as seen with loop diuretic use) impairs the kidney's ability to do what?

e.correcta: Maximal urine concentration depends on a steep corticomedullary osmotic gradient established by the thick ascending limb's countercurrent multiplier, against which water is later reabsorbed via ADH-regulated aquaporins in the collecting duct. If that gradient is washed out, as with loop diuretics, the collecting duct has no osmotic driving force to pull water out, so urine cannot be concentrated above plasma osmolality even with maximal ADH.

incorrectas.B: Urine dilution occurs in the thick ascending limb and early DCT, segments that reabsorb NaCl without water; loop diuretics actually impair dilution too by blocking that same reabsorption, but the classically tested consequence of losing the medullary gradient is loss of concentrating ability, not dilution.
incorrectas.C: Glucose reabsorption occurs via SGLT transporters in the proximal tubule and is unrelated to medullary tonicity or the site of loop diuretic action in the thick ascending limb.
incorrectas.D: Potassium secretion occurs in principal cells of the collecting duct in exchange for Na+ reabsorption via ENaC, a process governed by aldosterone and distal Na+ delivery rather than by medullary interstitial osmolality.

preguntas.q: Which transporter, targeted by thiazide diuretics, is located on the luminal membrane of the distal convoluted tubule?

e.correcta: The Na+-Cl- cotransporter (NCC) sits on the apical membrane of DCT cells and reabsorbs roughly 5-10% of filtered NaCl without accompanying water, since this segment is water-impermeable. Thiazide diuretics bind and inhibit NCC directly, which is why thiazides increase distal Na+ delivery and, secondarily, promote Ca2+ reabsorption and K+ secretion downstream.

incorrectas.A: The Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) is the target of loop diuretics and resides in the thick ascending limb, not the DCT; it builds the medullary concentration gradient, a different segment and mechanism from thiazide action.
incorrectas.B: The epithelial Na+ channel (ENaC) is found on principal cells of the collecting duct and is the target of K+-sparing diuretics like amiloride, not thiazides, which act one segment upstream in the DCT.
incorrectas.D: The Na+/H+ exchanger (NHE3) is the major luminal Na+ transporter of the proximal convoluted tubule, mediating most bulk Na+ (and secondary bicarbonate) reabsorption, and is inhibited by carbonic anhydrase inhibitors rather than by thiazides.

preguntas.q: In which nephron segment is Ca2+ reabsorbed via an apical Ca2+ channel coupled to a basolateral Na+-Ca2+ exchanger, a process upregulated by PTH?

e.correcta: In the DCT, Ca2+ enters the cell passively through apical TRPV5 channels down its electrochemical gradient, then is extruded across the basolateral membrane by the Na+-Ca2+ exchanger (NCX1) and a Ca2+-ATPase. PTH upregulates these transporters to increase Ca2+ reabsorption, which is also why thiazide diuretics - acting just upstream on NCC in the same segment - secondarily enhance Ca2+ retention.

incorrectas.A: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs the majority of filtered Ca2+, but mostly passively via the paracellular route driven by bulk Na+/water reabsorption, not through a dedicated apical channel/basolateral exchanger system regulated by PTH.
incorrectas.B: In the thick ascending limb, Ca2+ (and Mg2+) reabsorption is largely paracellular, driven by the lumen-positive potential generated by ROMK-mediated K+ backleak, not by an apical channel-exchanger pair as in the DCT.
incorrectas.C: The collecting duct is the principal site of aldosterone- and ADH-regulated Na+, K+, and water transport, not the primary site of PTH-regulated transcellular Ca2+ reabsorption.

preguntas.q: What is the water permeability of the early distal convoluted tubule?

o.C: Permeable only in the presence of ADH

e.correcta: Like the thick ascending limb, the early DCT lacks aquaporin water channels and remains impermeable to water regardless of ADH status. NaCl is reabsorbed there via NCC without water following, which is why this segment (along with the thick ascending limb) is called a 'diluting segment' that helps produce hypotonic tubular fluid.

incorrectas.A: Free, ADH-independent water permeability describes the descending thin limb of the loop of Henle, which lacks NCC or NKCC2 and instead allows water to move passively out into the hypertonic medulla - not the early DCT.
incorrectas.C: ADH-dependent water permeability is a feature of the collecting duct (and to a lesser extent the late distal tubule), where ADH inserts aquaporin-2 channels; the early DCT has no aquaporins at all to be regulated in the first place.
incorrectas.D: Aquaporin-2 is expressed on principal cells of the collecting duct and is regulated by ADH-triggered trafficking to the membrane, not constitutively present in the early DCT, which lacks water channels entirely.

preguntas.q: What effect do thiazide diuretics have on the kidney's diluting capacity?

e.correcta: Thiazides inhibit NCC in the DCT, one of the two 'diluting segments' of the nephron (along with the thick ascending limb) that reabsorb NaCl without water to generate hypotonic urine. Blocking this transporter impairs the kidney's ability to dilute urine maximally, which is why thiazides can predispose to hyponatremia, especially in elderly patients who continue to drink free water.

incorrectas.A: An increase in diluting capacity would require enhanced NaCl reabsorption without water in the diluting segments; thiazides do the opposite by blocking NCC, reducing rather than boosting this capacity.
incorrectas.B: Because the DCT is one of the two major diluting segments, blocking its main transporter has a clinically meaningful effect on dilution (contributing to thiazide-induced hyponatremia), not a negligible one.
incorrectas.D: Thiazides do not enhance concentrating ability; unlike loop diuretics, which abolish the medullary gradient, thiazides act mainly in the cortex, and their key clinically relevant water effect is impaired dilution, not improved concentration.

preguntas.q: Hydrochlorothiazide belongs to which class of diuretics?

e.correcta: Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) is the prototypical thiazide diuretic, acting on the Na+-Cl- cotransporter in the DCT. It's widely used as first-line therapy for essential hypertension due to its mild natriuretic effect combined with a direct vasodilatory action, and its class-mates - chlorthalidone, indapamide, and metolazone - should be recognized as belonging to the same drug class.

incorrectas.A: Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide, ethacrynic acid) act on NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb and produce a much more potent diuresis than HCTZ, which acts downstream in the DCT with a smaller natriuretic effect.
incorrectas.B: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., acetazolamide) act in the proximal tubule by blocking bicarbonate reabsorption, producing a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis - a completely different mechanism and nephron site from HCTZ.
incorrectas.D: K+-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, amiloride, triamterene) act on the collecting duct to block aldosterone signaling or ENaC directly, whereas HCTZ acts upstream in the DCT and actually promotes K+ wasting rather than sparing it.

preguntas.q: Chlorthalidone, metolazone, and indapamide are classified as which type of diuretic?

e.correcta: Although structurally distinct from hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, metolazone, and indapamide are 'thiazide-like' diuretics that share the same fundamental mechanism - inhibition of the Na+-Cl- cotransporter in the DCT - and thus share the same indications (hypertension, mild edema) and side-effect profile (hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, hypercalcemia) as classic thiazides.

incorrectas.B: Loop diuretics inhibit NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb and produce a much greater natriuretic effect; none of chlorthalidone, metolazone, or indapamide act at that site or with that potency.
incorrectas.C: Osmotic diuretics like mannitol work by increasing tubular fluid osmolality throughout the nephron (especially the proximal tubule and descending limb) to limit water reabsorption - an entirely different, non-transporter-based mechanism from these agents.
incorrectas.D: Aldosterone antagonists (e.g., spironolactone) competitively block the mineralocorticoid receptor in the collecting duct's principal cells; the drugs listed instead act on the DCT's NCC transporter, unrelated to aldosterone signaling.

preguntas.q: What effect do thiazide diuretics have on renal Ca2+ handling?

e.correcta: By blocking NCC, thiazides reduce intracellular Na+ in DCT cells, which steepens the gradient for the basolateral Na+-Ca2+ exchanger to pull more Ca2+ out of the cell. This, combined with compensatory upstream proximal reabsorption from mild volume contraction, increases net Ca2+ reabsorption and lowers urinary Ca2+ excretion - the basis for using thiazides in idiopathic hypercalciuria and calcium stone prevention.

incorrectas.A: Increased Ca2+ excretion is actually the effect of loop diuretics, which inhibit the lumen-positive potential in the thick ascending limb that normally drives paracellular Ca2+ reabsorption - the opposite renal calcium effect from thiazides.
incorrectas.B: A decrease in Ca2+ reabsorption would raise urinary calcium losses; thiazides do the reverse by enhancing basolateral Ca2+ extrusion via NCX1 once NCC is blocked.
incorrectas.C: Thiazides have a well-documented, clinically exploited effect on calcium handling (increased reabsorption, decreased excretion) - this is not a neutral bystander effect but a mechanistically linked consequence of NCC inhibition.

preguntas.q: Thiazide diuretics can serve as adjunctive symptomatic therapy in which condition, even though loop diuretics remain first-line for that indication?

e.correcta: In decompensated heart failure, loop diuretics are first-line because their potent natriuretic effect (blocking NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, which handles a large fraction of filtered Na+) rapidly reduces volume overload. Thiazides can be added for 'sequential nephron blockade' when patients develop diuretic resistance, since blocking the DCT's NCC prevents compensatory Na+ reabsorption there once the loop segment is inhibited.

incorrectas.A: Thiazides help osteoporosis by promoting renal Ca2+ retention (indirectly reducing bone Ca2+ mobilization needs), an entirely separate use from volume management in heart failure and not a context where loop diuretics are 'first line.'
incorrectas.B: Idiopathic hypercalciuria is treated with thiazides for their calcium-retaining effect to prevent kidney stones, not because of a diuretic hierarchy with loop diuretics as first-line therapy.
incorrectas.D: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is treated with thiazides via a paradoxical mechanism (mild volume contraction increasing proximal water reabsorption) - a completely different clinical scenario that doesn't involve loop diuretics as first-line treatment.

preguntas.q: Which diuretic class may help attenuate bone loss in patients with osteoporosis due to enhanced renal Ca2+ reabsorption?

e.correcta: Thiazides increase Ca2+ reabsorption in the DCT via enhanced basolateral Na+-Ca2+ exchanger activity, which reduces urinary calcium losses and can modestly help preserve bone mineral density. This makes them a reasonable antihypertensive choice in patients who also have osteoporosis and need diuretic therapy.

incorrectas.A: Loop diuretics have the opposite effect on calcium - they increase urinary Ca2+ excretion by disrupting the paracellular reabsorption pathway in the thick ascending limb, and can worsen bone mineral loss with chronic use.
incorrectas.B: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors act in the proximal tubule on bicarbonate handling and have no meaningful calcium-conserving effect relevant to osteoporosis management.
incorrectas.C: K+-sparing diuretics act on the collecting duct to limit K+ and H+ secretion by blocking ENaC or aldosterone signaling, a mechanism unrelated to the DCT-based calcium retention seen with thiazides.

preguntas.q: Thiazide diuretics are useful in treating which condition characterized by excessive urinary calcium excretion?

e.correcta: Idiopathic hypercalciuria is a common cause of recurrent calcium-containing kidney stones. Because thiazides increase DCT Ca2+ reabsorption and lower urinary Ca2+ concentration, they are first-line pharmacologic therapy (alongside dietary sodium restriction) to reduce stone recurrence in these patients.

incorrectas.A: Hyperoxaluria (excess urinary oxalate, often from fat malabsorption or excessive oxalate intake) is treated with dietary oxalate restriction, calcium supplementation with meals, or cholestyramine - thiazides do not address the oxalate component of stone risk.
incorrectas.B: Struvite stones form from urease-producing bacterial infections (e.g., Proteus) and are managed with antibiotics and complete stone removal, not thiazide diuretics, since the underlying problem is infection-driven rather than calcium handling.
incorrectas.D: Uric acid stones are managed by urinary alkalinization (e.g., potassium citrate) and allopurinol to reduce uric acid production; thiazides do not correct the low urine pH or hyperuricosuria driving this stone type.

preguntas.q: Which electrolyte disturbance is a recognized adverse effect of thiazide diuretics, part of the 'hyperGLUC' mnemonic?

e.correcta: Thiazides enhance distal Ca2+ reabsorption (via upregulated Na+-Ca2+ exchanger activity once NCC is blocked), which can push serum calcium into a mildly elevated range - remembered by the 'hyperGLUC' mnemonic (hyperGlycemia, hyperLipidemia, hyperUricemia, hyperCalcemia). This effect can also unmask an underlying condition such as primary hyperparathyroidism.

incorrectas.A: Hyponatremia can occur with thiazides due to impaired urinary dilution, but that is a sodium-handling effect, not the calcium-related item captured by the 'hyperGLUC' mnemonic being asked about here.
incorrectas.B: Hypocalcemia would be expected if a diuretic increased calcium excretion, as loop diuretics do; thiazides instead cause the opposite - retained calcium leading to mild hypercalcemia.
incorrectas.C: Hyperkalemia is not a thiazide effect - thiazides increase distal Na+ delivery to the collecting duct, promoting K+ secretion and hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia, which is more typical of K+-sparing diuretics.

preguntas.q: What effect can thiazide diuretics have on serum glucose levels?

e.correcta: Thiazides can impair pancreatic beta-cell insulin secretion (partly through hypokalemia-mediated effects on beta-cell function) and may also reduce peripheral insulin sensitivity, producing mild hyperglycemia. This is part of the 'hyperGLUC' adverse effect profile and is a consideration when choosing antihypertensives in diabetic patients.

incorrectas.A: Hypoglycemia is not a thiazide effect; if anything, the hypokalemia thiazides cause impairs insulin release, pushing glucose up rather than down.
incorrectas.B: While the glucose elevation is often modest, it is a real, clinically recognized effect (part of the 'hyperGLUC' mnemonic) that can worsen glycemic control in diabetics, not a negligible one.
incorrectas.D: Thiazides do not enhance insulin secretion - they tend to impair it via hypokalemia, contributing to hyperglycemia rather than to better glucose control.

preguntas.q: What effect can thiazide diuretics have on serum lipid levels?

e.correcta: Thiazides can produce modest, dose-dependent increases in total cholesterol, LDL, and triglycerides, likely related to their metabolic effects on insulin sensitivity. This is part of the 'hyperGLUC' mnemonic (hyperGlycemia, hyperLipidemia, hyperUricemia, hyperCalcemia) and is a reason lower doses are now favored to minimize metabolic side effects while retaining antihypertensive benefit.

incorrectas.A: Thiazides do not selectively raise HDL - the recognized lipid effect is a mild rise in total cholesterol and triglycerides, not a favorable, isolated increase in HDL.
incorrectas.B: Thiazides do not lower LDL or triglycerides; the adverse metabolic effect goes in the opposite direction, which is why 'hyperGLUC' lists hyperlipidemia as a side effect to monitor.
incorrectas.C: The lipid effect, while generally modest, is real and reproducible enough to be a named part of the classic thiazide side-effect mnemonic, not a null finding.

preguntas.q: What effect can thiazide diuretics have on serum potassium levels?

e.correcta: By inhibiting NCC in the DCT, thiazides increase Na+ delivery to the collecting duct, where principal cells reabsorb more Na+ through ENaC and, to maintain electroneutrality, secrete more K+ into the tubular fluid. This potassium wasting is a hallmark thiazide side effect and a reason for co-administration with K+-sparing agents or K+ supplementation in some patients.

incorrectas.A: Hyperkalemia would result from reduced distal Na+ delivery or reduced aldosterone activity, as with K+-sparing diuretics or ACE inhibitors; thiazides instead increase distal Na+ delivery, driving K+ secretion in the opposite direction.
incorrectas.B: The potassium-wasting effect of thiazides is clinically significant and well documented (a leading cause of diuretic-induced hypokalemia), not a negligible or absent effect.
incorrectas.D: Thiazides do not cause a self-correcting, transient potassium rise; the hypokalemic effect persists as long as increased distal Na+ delivery and secretion continue, requiring ongoing monitoring or supplementation.

preguntas.q: Thiazide diuretics belong to which drug class, explaining their rare potential to cause allergic reactions in susceptible patients?

e.correcta: Thiazide diuretics contain a sulfonamide moiety in their chemical structure, shared with sulfonamide antibiotics, loop diuretics, and some other drug classes, which can rarely trigger hypersensitivity reactions - rash, photosensitivity, or, rarely, more severe reactions - in patients with sulfa allergies. This shared chemistry is why clinicians ask about sulfa allergy history before prescribing thiazides.

incorrectas.A: Penicillin allergy involves a beta-lactam ring structure entirely distinct from the sulfonamide group found in thiazides, so there is no expected cross-reactivity between the two.
incorrectas.B: Beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins) share a four-membered ring structure unrelated to the sulfonamide group; thiazides' allergy risk stems specifically from their sulfonamide component, not a beta-lactam structure.
incorrectas.D: Fluoroquinolones have a distinct quinolone-based structure without a sulfonamide group, so their allergy profile is unrelated to the sulfa cross-reactivity relevant to thiazide diuretics.

preguntas.q: What acid-base disturbance may result from thiazide diuretic use?

e.correcta: Similar to loop diuretics, thiazides cause volume contraction from natriuresis, which activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and increases aldosterone-mediated H+ and K+ secretion in the collecting duct. Concurrently, the contracted extracellular volume concentrates the existing bicarbonate ('contraction alkalosis'), together producing a hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.

incorrectas.B: Metabolic acidosis would occur with drugs that impair bicarbonate reabsorption or cause bicarbonate loss, such as carbonic anhydrase inhibitors; thiazides instead promote bicarbonate retention through the volume-contraction and aldosterone mechanisms described.
incorrectas.A: Respiratory acidosis reflects alveolar hypoventilation and CO2 retention, a pulmonary/ventilatory problem entirely unrelated to the renal tubular and volume effects of thiazide diuretics.
incorrectas.C: Respiratory alkalosis results from hyperventilation lowering PaCO2, not from renal electrolyte handling, so it is not a mechanism by which thiazides affect acid-base status.

preguntas.q: K+-sparing diuretics exert their effects at which site in the nephron?

e.correcta: K+-sparing diuretics act on principal cells of the cortical collecting tubule - spironolactone and eplerenone via mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism, and amiloride and triamterene via direct ENaC blockade. This is the site where aldosterone normally promotes Na+ reabsorption coupled to K+ and H+ secretion, and blocking that action produces a mild natriuresis while sparing potassium, the defining feature of this diuretic class.

incorrectas.A: The proximal convoluted tubule is the site of bulk Na+, water, glucose, and bicarbonate reabsorption, targeted instead by carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and osmotic diuretics, not by K+-sparing agents.
incorrectas.B: The thick ascending limb, where NKCC2 mediates Na+-K+-2Cl- reabsorption, is the target of loop diuretics; it is far more Na+-avid and unrelated to the aldosterone/ENaC axis that K+-sparing diuretics modulate downstream.
incorrectas.C: The distal convoluted tubule is where thiazide diuretics act on the Na+-Cl- cotransporter; K+-sparing diuretics act further downstream in the collecting tubule, a distinct segment with distinct transport machinery.

preguntas.q: Mineralocorticoids (e.g., aldosterone) exert their principal effects on which part of the nephron?

e.correcta: Aldosterone acts on principal cells of the collecting duct, upregulating ENaC and Na+/K+-ATPase to increase Na+ reabsorption (with obligate water) while promoting K+ and H+ secretion by intercalated cells. This is the physiologic basis for K+-sparing diuretics, which block this exact site and mechanism.

incorrectas.A: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs the bulk of filtered Na+, glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate largely independent of aldosterone regulation, driven instead by NHE3 and cotransporters responsive to filtered load.
incorrectas.B: The thin descending limb is permeable to water but has minimal active solute transport and is not a target of mineralocorticoid regulation; it functions passively within the countercurrent multiplication system.
incorrectas.C: While the DCT does have some late-segment aldosterone-sensitive Na+ channels, the classic, high-yield site of mineralocorticoid action is the collecting duct (specifically its principal cells), not the DCT.

preguntas.q: Which collecting duct cell type is the major site of Na+, K+, and water transport?

e.correcta: Principal cells of the collecting duct express ENaC and ROMK on their apical membrane and Na+/K+-ATPase basolaterally, mediating aldosterone-driven Na+ reabsorption coupled with K+ secretion, plus ADH-regulated aquaporin-2 water channels for water reabsorption. This makes them the primary site targeted by both K+-sparing diuretics and ADH/vasopressin analogs.

incorrectas.A: Intercalated cells (alpha and beta subtypes) are also found in the collecting duct but specialize in acid-base regulation, secreting H+ or bicarbonate via H+-ATPase and pendrin/AE1 exchangers, rather than mediating bulk Na+/K+/water transport.
incorrectas.B: Podocytes are specialized epithelial cells of the glomerular filtration barrier with foot processes and slit diaphragms; they participate in filtration, not in tubular reabsorption or secretion in the collecting duct.
incorrectas.D: Mesangial cells reside in the glomerulus, providing structural support and regulating glomerular capillary flow through contraction, entirely unrelated to collecting duct ion and water transport.

preguntas.q: Na+ is reabsorbed across the luminal membrane of collecting duct principal cells through which channel?

e.correcta: ENaC is a constitutively open apical sodium channel in principal cells whose expression and activity are upregulated by aldosterone. Na+ entry through ENaC creates a lumen-negative potential that drives K+ secretion through ROMK channels and H+ secretion by adjacent intercalated cells; this channel is the direct target of amiloride and triamterene (K+-sparing diuretics) and is pathologically overactive in Liddle syndrome.

incorrectas.A: Aquaporin-2 channels mediate water, not Na+, reabsorption in the same principal cells, under regulation by ADH rather than aldosterone; they explain the collecting duct's role in urine concentration, not sodium transport.
incorrectas.B: The Na+-Cl- cotransporter (NCC) is located in the DCT, one segment upstream of the collecting duct, and is the target of thiazide diuretics, not the channel responsible for luminal Na+ entry in principal cells.
incorrectas.D: The Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) is found in the thick ascending limb and is blocked by loop diuretics; it is a bulk, electroneutral transporter distinct from the single Na+ channel (ENaC) used by collecting duct principal cells.

preguntas.q: On the luminal (apical) membrane of collecting duct principal cells, K+ channels primarily perform which function?

o.A: They secrete K+ into the tubular lumen
o.B: They reabsorb filtered K+ into the cell
o.C: They exchange K+ for H+ across the membrane
o.D: They cotransport K+ with Na+ into the cell

e.correcta: Principal cells generate a high intracellular K+ concentration via the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase, and apical ROMK (renal outer medullary potassium) channels allow that K+ to diffuse down its electrochemical gradient into the tubular lumen. This apical K+ secretion is the main route of urinary potassium excretion and is amplified by aldosterone (which upregulates ENaC, Na+/K+-ATPase, and the K+ channels themselves) and by high distal tubular flow, which is why loop and thiazide diuretics cause kaliuresis.

incorrectas.B: Principal cells do not reabsorb luminal K+ back into the cell; there is no apical K+ reabsorptive transporter in this segment. The rare situation of net K+ reabsorption in the collecting duct is instead carried out by α-intercalated cells via an apical H+/K+-ATPase, a completely different cell type and mechanism.
incorrectas.C: H+/K+ exchange is the job of the H+/K+-ATPase found on α-intercalated cells (which reabsorb K+ while secreting H+), not the principal cell K+ channels, which simply allow passive efflux of K+ down its gradient.
incorrectas.D: There is no apical Na+-K+ cotransporter in principal cells; instead, Na+ enters through separate ENaC channels and K+ exits through separate ROMK channels, with the electrical gradient created by Na+ entry actually driving K+ secretion, not a shared carrier.

preguntas.q: Which cell type in the collecting duct is the major site of H+ secretion?

e.correcta: α-intercalated cells express an apical H+-ATPase (and H+/K+-ATPase) that actively pumps H+ into the tubular lumen, making them the major site of distal acid secretion and urinary acidification. This process is essential for regenerating bicarbonate that is returned to the blood via a basolateral Cl-/HCO3- exchanger, and it is the site targeted (via aldosterone stimulation) in the net acid excretion needed to maintain acid-base balance.

incorrectas.A: Principal cells are dedicated to Na+ reabsorption (via ENaC) and K+ secretion (via ROMK) under aldosterone control; they lack the H+-ATPase machinery and do not contribute meaningfully to acid secretion.
incorrectas.B: β-intercalated cells do the opposite job: they secrete bicarbonate into the lumen (via an apical Cl-/HCO3- exchanger) and reabsorb H+, which is important during states of alkalosis, rather than being the primary acid-secreting cell.
incorrectas.D: The proximal tubule reabsorbs the bulk (about 80-90%) of filtered bicarbonate via Na+/H+ exchange (NHE3), but it is not considered the major site of net H+ secretion for urinary acidification — that title belongs to the distal α-intercalated cells, which perform the fine-tuning that determines final urine pH.

preguntas.q: Which transporter on the luminal membrane of α-intercalated cells is primarily responsible for H+ secretion?

e.correcta: α-intercalated cells express an apical H+-ATPase that actively pumps H+ against its concentration gradient into the tubular lumen, independent of any Na+ gradient. A related apical H+/K+-ATPase also contributes to H+ secretion while simultaneously reabsorbing K+, which is clinically relevant because hypokalemia can drive additional H+ secretion through this pump and worsen metabolic alkalosis.

incorrectas.A: NHE3 is the dominant H+ secretory mechanism in the proximal tubule, where it couples H+ secretion to Na+ reabsorption to drive bulk bicarbonate reclamation, but it is not the transporter used by α-intercalated cells in the collecting duct.
incorrectas.C: The Cl-/HCO3- exchanger (AE1) sits on the basolateral membrane of α-intercalated cells, where it moves the bicarbonate generated intracellularly out into the blood in exchange for chloride; it does not secrete H+ into the lumen.
incorrectas.D: Na+/K+-ATPase is a basolateral pump found in nearly all nephron segments that maintains the low intracellular Na+ and high intracellular K+ needed to drive various transport processes, but it does not itself move H+ and is not located on the luminal membrane of intercalated cells.

preguntas.q: The mineralocorticoid receptor that mediates aldosterone's effects on principal cells is best classified as which type of receptor?

e.correcta: Aldosterone is a lipophilic steroid hormone that diffuses across the plasma membrane and binds its mineralocorticoid receptor in the cytoplasm; the hormone-receptor complex then translocates to the nucleus, where it acts as a transcription factor to increase expression of ENaC subunits, Na+/K+-ATPase, and apical K+ channels. Because this mechanism requires new protein synthesis, aldosterone's effects have a delayed onset (hours) compared to receptors that act through second messengers.

incorrectas.A: G protein-coupled receptors sit in the plasma membrane and signal through second messengers like cAMP or IP3 within seconds to minutes; steroid hormones like aldosterone instead bypass the membrane entirely and act on intracellular receptors that regulate gene transcription.
incorrectas.B: Receptor tyrosine kinases are membrane-spanning receptors activated by peptide growth factors (like insulin or EGF), which triggers autophosphorylation and downstream kinase cascades — an entirely different mechanism from a lipid-soluble steroid diffusing into the cell to bind a cytoplasmic receptor.
incorrectas.D: Ligand-gated ion channels open directly upon binding their ligand (e.g., nicotinic acetylcholine receptors) to allow ion flux across the membrane; aldosterone does not open a channel itself but instead changes the transcription of channel and pump genes over a slower time course.

preguntas.q: Aldosterone increases urinary potassium excretion primarily by upregulating which apical membrane component of principal cells?

e.correcta: Aldosterone increases transcription of apical ROMK channels in principal cells, providing more conduits through which intracellular K+ (concentrated there by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase) can diffuse into the lumen. Because aldosterone simultaneously boosts ENaC-mediated Na+ entry, which makes the lumen more electronegative, the net effect is a strong electrochemical driving force plus more channels — synergistically increasing K+ secretion, which is why hyperaldosteronism classically causes hypokalemia.

incorrectas.A: Na+/K+-ATPase is also upregulated by aldosterone and is essential for maintaining the intracellular K+ pool that gets secreted, but it is a basolateral pump, not the apical channel through which K+ actually exits into the urine — that specific step is answered by ROMK.
incorrectas.B: ENaC is aldosterone's other major target and mediates Na+ reabsorption; it indirectly promotes K+ secretion by making the lumen electrically negative (favoring K+ efflux), but ENaC itself conducts Na+, not K+, so it is not the direct answer to which channel secretes K+.
incorrectas.D: Aquaporin-2 is the antidiuretic hormone (ADH)-regulated water channel in principal cells that controls water reabsorption and urine concentration; it is unrelated to aldosterone's K+-secretory pathway.

preguntas.q: Aldosterone increases Na+ reabsorption in the collecting duct principal cells primarily by upregulating which apical transporter?

e.correcta: Aldosterone binding its intracellular receptor increases transcription of ENaC subunits on the apical membrane of principal cells, allowing passive Na+ entry down its electrochemical gradient from the lumen into the cell. This Na+ is then extruded basolaterally by the Na+/K+-ATPase (also upregulated by aldosterone), completing net Na+ reabsorption and making the lumen electronegative, which secondarily drives K+ and H+ secretion — the basis for amiloride and triamterene acting as K+-sparing diuretics by directly blocking ENaC.

incorrectas.B: NKCC2 is the target of loop diuretics and resides in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, a segment upstream of the aldosterone-sensitive principal cells; it reabsorbs Na+, K+, and 2 Cl- together and is not regulated by aldosterone in the way ENaC is.
incorrectas.C: NCC is the thiazide-sensitive Na+/Cl- cotransporter located in the distal convoluted tubule, a different nephron segment from the principal cells of the collecting duct, and its regulation is driven mainly by other pathways rather than being aldosterone's primary collecting-duct target.
incorrectas.D: NHE3 mediates most proximal tubule Na+/H+ exchange and drives bulk bicarbonate and Na+ reabsorption early in the nephron; it is not the aldosterone-regulated channel responsible for fine-tuning distal Na+ reabsorption in principal cells.

preguntas.q: Aldosterone acts on which basolateral transporter in principal cells to increase both Na+ reabsorption and K+ excretion?

e.correcta: Aldosterone upregulates the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase, which actively pumps Na+ out of the principal cell into blood (completing transcellular Na+ reabsorption started by apical ENaC) while pumping K+ into the cell, building the high intracellular K+ concentration that then diffuses out through apical ROMK channels into the urine. This single pump therefore links the two hallmark effects of aldosterone — Na+ retention and K+ wasting — and explains why aldosterone excess (e.g., primary hyperaldosteronism) produces both hypertension and hypokalemia.

incorrectas.A: A Ca2+-ATPase is a basolateral pump used to extrude calcium and maintain low intracellular Ca2+ in various epithelial cells (like in the distal convoluted tubule for calcium reabsorption), but it is not the pump aldosterone targets to drive Na+/K+ handling in principal cells.
incorrectas.C: H+/K+-ATPase is an apical (not basolateral) pump found in α-intercalated cells that secretes H+ while reabsorbing K+; it belongs to a different cell type and transport direction than the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase of principal cells.
incorrectas.D: The Cl-/HCO3- exchanger is a basolateral transporter in intercalated cells involved in acid-base handling, not in the Na+/K+ handling of principal cells that aldosterone primarily regulates.

preguntas.q: Aldosterone increases urinary acid excretion by upregulating which apical pump in α-intercalated cells?

e.correcta: In addition to its well-known effects on principal cells, aldosterone also stimulates the apical H+-ATPase of α-intercalated cells, directly increasing active H+ secretion into the tubular lumen. This is part of why hyperaldosteronism can cause a mild metabolic alkalosis (excess H+ loss) and why hypoaldosteronism (or K+-sparing diuretics that block aldosterone's effects) can produce a hyperkalemic, normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (type 4 RTA) from reduced H+ secretion.

incorrectas.B: Na+/K+-ATPase is aldosterone's basolateral target in principal cells (driving Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion), a distinct cell type and transporter from the apical H+-ATPase of α-intercalated cells that handles acid secretion.
incorrectas.C: Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes the intracellular hydration of CO2 to form H2CO3 (which dissociates to H+ and HCO3-), supplying the substrate for H+ secretion, but it is an enzyme, not the pump aldosterone upregulates to actively transport H+ across the apical membrane.
incorrectas.D: The Cl-/HCO3- exchanger sits on the basolateral membrane of α-intercalated cells and exports the bicarbonate generated during acid secretion into the blood; it works on the opposite membrane and moves bicarbonate/chloride, not H+, into the lumen.

preguntas.q: K+-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone and eplerenone are especially useful in treating which condition, often in combination with loop diuretics?

e.correcta: In heart failure, activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system drives pathologic cardiac remodeling and fibrosis in addition to Na+/water retention. Aldosterone antagonists like spironolactone and eplerenone block these deleterious mineralocorticoid receptor effects, and when combined with loop diuretics they also counteract the hypokalemia that loop diuretics cause, making the combination both symptomatically and prognostically beneficial in appropriately selected heart failure patients.

incorrectas.B: Acute kidney injury is not a standard indication for K+-sparing diuretics; in fact these drugs are often avoided or used cautiously in impaired renal function because reduced GFR predisposes to dangerous hyperkalemia.
incorrectas.C: Nephrotic syndrome is typically managed with loop diuretics (often at high doses due to albumin binding of the drug in the tubule) rather than K+-sparing agents as first-line therapy, and the edema of nephrotic syndrome is not primarily driven by the aldosterone pathway that these drugs target.
incorrectas.D: Hyperthyroidism is treated with antithyroid drugs, beta-blockers, or radioactive iodine/surgery; it has no direct relationship to the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis that K+-sparing diuretics act on.

preguntas.q: Do mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists such as spironolactone and eplerenone improve mortality in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?

o.A: No, they only provide symptomatic diuresis with no survival benefit
o.C: No, they increase mortality due to arrhythmia risk
o.D: Only in combination with digoxin do they reduce mortality

e.correcta: Landmark trials (such as RALES for spironolactone and EPHESUS/EMPHASIS-HF for eplerenone) demonstrated that mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists reduce mortality in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, beyond their diuretic effect. This benefit is attributed to blocking aldosterone-driven myocardial fibrosis, remodeling, and sympathetic activation, which is why these agents are now a guideline-directed medical therapy pillar for HFrEF, not merely a potassium-sparing add-on.

incorrectas.A: This understates their benefit — unlike most diuretics (including loop and thiazide agents), which primarily relieve congestion without proven mortality benefit, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists specifically have been shown in randomized trials to reduce death from cardiovascular causes.
incorrectas.C: The opposite is true when used appropriately with monitoring; the real risk with these drugs is hyperkalemia (since they block K+ excretion), not an inherent increase in mortality — appropriate patient selection and potassium monitoring mitigate this risk while preserving the mortality benefit.
incorrectas.D: The mortality benefit of mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists has been demonstrated as an independent effect in trials, not one that requires co-administration with digoxin, which itself only improves symptoms and hospitalization rates without a clear mortality benefit.

preguntas.q: K+-sparing diuretics are useful for correcting or preventing which electrolyte disturbance, often when it results from other diuretics?

e.correcta: K+-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, eplerenone, amiloride, triamterene) block aldosterone signaling or ENaC directly, reducing the electrochemical driving force for K+ secretion in the collecting duct's principal cells. This makes them useful both to treat existing hypokalemia and, more commonly, to counteract the kaliuresis produced by loop and thiazide diuretics when those agents are used together.

incorrectas.B: K+-sparing diuretics actually promote mild natriuresis (Na+ loss) rather than causing or treating hypernatremia; if anything, blocking ENaC/aldosterone reduces Na+ reabsorption, which would tend to lower, not raise, serum Na+.
incorrectas.C: These drugs have no specific calcium-raising mechanism; hypercalcemia is more associated with thiazide diuretics, which enhance distal calcium reabsorption — a distinct segment and mechanism from the K+-sparing diuretics' site of action.
incorrectas.D: K+-sparing diuretics act on collecting duct sodium and potassium transport and do not have a direct effect on phosphate handling, which is primarily regulated in the proximal tubule by PTH and FGF23.

preguntas.q: K+-sparing diuretics can cause which acid-base disturbance?

e.correcta: By blocking aldosterone's action (or ENaC directly), K+-sparing diuretics reduce the lumen-negative potential in the collecting duct that normally drives both K+ and H+ secretion; this impairs the apical H+-ATPase of α-intercalated cells, decreasing net acid excretion. Because bicarbonate and chloride handling are otherwise preserved (no unmeasured anion accumulates), the resulting acidosis has a normal anion gap and is accompanied by hyperkalemia — the classic picture of type 4 renal tubular acidosis.

incorrectas.B: A high anion gap metabolic acidosis results from accumulation of unmeasured acids (e.g., lactate, ketones, toxins, or uremic acids), not from a defect in distal H+ secretion; K+-sparing diuretics don't generate such acids, so their acidosis remains normal anion gap.
incorrectas.C: Metabolic alkalosis is instead the acid-base pattern seen with loop and thiazide diuretics, which cause volume contraction and enhanced distal H+/K+ secretion via a different mechanism (aldosterone-driven, not blocked) — the opposite direction from what K+-sparing diuretics produce.
incorrectas.D: Respiratory acidosis results from hypoventilation and CO2 retention, a pulmonary/respiratory problem unrelated to a renal tubular diuretic effect on acid secretion.

preguntas.q: K+-sparing diuretics can precipitate which type of renal tubular acidosis?

e.correcta: Type 4 RTA is caused by hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance, resulting in impaired distal Na+ reabsorption, reduced lumen-negative potential, and consequently decreased K+ and H+ secretion — producing the classic triad of hyperkalemia with a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. K+-sparing diuretics reproduce this physiology pharmacologically by blocking the mineralocorticoid receptor or ENaC directly, which is why they are grouped with type 4 RTA causes.

incorrectas.A: Type 1 (distal) RTA results from an inability of α-intercalated cells to secrete H+ (defective H+-ATPase or back-leak of H+), classically causing hypokalemia and a risk of nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis — a different mechanism and different potassium direction from the hyperkalemic picture caused by K+-sparing diuretics.
incorrectas.B: Type 2 (proximal) RTA is due to a defect in proximal tubule bicarbonate reabsorption (e.g., via a faulty Na+/HCO3- cotransporter), causing bicarbonate wasting until a new steady state is reached; it is unrelated to the aldosterone/ENaC-blocking mechanism of K+-sparing diuretics.
incorrectas.D: There is no clinically distinct 'type 3 RTA' as a combined category in standard classification (it historically referred to an overlap of types 1 and 2 in a rare pediatric condition), and it is not the entity produced by K+-sparing diuretics.

preguntas.q: Type 4 renal tubular acidosis is characteristically associated with which potassium abnormality?

o.C: Normal serum potassium with intracellular depletion

e.correcta: Type 4 RTA arises from hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance, which impairs the collecting duct's ability to secrete both K+ and H+. The resulting hyperkalemia is actually a key part of the mechanism (not just an association) — elevated K+ further inhibits ammoniagenesis in the proximal tubule, reducing urinary buffering capacity and worsening the accompanying normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, distinguishing type 4 from the other, hypokalemic forms of RTA.

incorrectas.A: Hypokalemia is instead the hallmark of type 1 (distal) and type 2 (proximal) RTA, where impaired H+ secretion or bicarbonate handling occurs without loss of aldosterone-driven K+ secretion, so more K+ is lost in the urine rather than retained.
incorrectas.C: Type 4 RTA does not present as a normal serum K+ with a hidden intracellular deficit — the defining laboratory finding is an overtly elevated serum K+, precisely because the aldosterone-dependent K+ secretory pathway is impaired at the collecting duct.
incorrectas.D: Type 4 RTA is a chronic, steady-state hyperkalemic condition rather than one that cycles between high and low potassium; such cycling is not a recognized feature of this disorder.

preguntas.q: Spironolactone's antiandrogen effects are partly due to inhibition of which steroidogenic enzyme in the testosterone synthesis pathway?

e.correcta: Spironolactone, in addition to antagonizing the mineralocorticoid and androgen receptors, also directly inhibits 17α-hydroxylase (and other steroidogenic enzymes), reducing the conversion of pregnenolone/progesterone intermediates into androgen precursors and ultimately testosterone. This multi-pronged antiandrogen action (receptor blockade plus decreased synthesis) is why spironolactone is repurposed clinically for hirsutism and acne in hyperandrogenic states like PCOS, despite being developed as a diuretic.

incorrectas.A: 5α-reductase converts testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone (DHT) and is the target of finasteride/dutasteride, not spironolactone's mechanism — spironolactone instead impairs an earlier step in androgen synthesis and blocks the androgen receptor itself.
