incorrectas.D: IDL is not classically included among apo C-II's three carriers; IDL clearance from the circulation is instead attributed largely to apo E-mediated hepatic receptor uptake rather than apo C-II activity.

preguntas.q: A biochemistry student is studying lipid transport. Apolipoprotein B-48 is a structural component found on which lipoprotein particle?

e.correcta: ApoB-48 is synthesized by intestinal enterocytes via mRNA editing of the APOB gene (a premature stop codon is introduced, producing a protein that is 48% the length of full-length apoB-100). It is the structural apolipoprotein of chylomicrons and remains on the particle even after it becomes a chylomicron remnant, serving as a lifelong marker of the particle's intestinal origin.

incorrectas.B: VLDL carries apoB-100, the full-length, unedited form of apolipoprotein B synthesized by the liver, not the truncated intestinal apoB-48 - the two forms mark the endogenous versus exogenous lipid transport pathways, respectively.
incorrectas.C: LDL retains a single copy of apoB-100 (inherited from VLDL/IDL processing), the hepatic apolipoprotein, distinguishing it from the intestinally-derived chylomicron particles that carry apoB-48.
incorrectas.D: HDL does not carry apoB at all; its major apolipoproteins are apoA-I (the LCAT activator) and apoA-II, reflecting its distinct role in reverse cholesterol transport rather than dietary lipid delivery.

preguntas.q: Apolipoprotein B-100, synthesized by the liver, is a structural component of which three lipoproteins?

e.correcta: ApoB-100 is the full-length form of apolipoprotein B translated from unedited APOB mRNA in hepatocytes. It is incorporated into nascent VLDL as it is secreted from the liver and remains on the particle as it is progressively delipidated into IDL and then LDL - each of these three particles carries exactly one copy of apoB-100, grouping them together as the hepatic (endogenous) lipoproteins in contrast to intestinal, apoB-48-containing chylomicrons.

incorrectas.A: Chylomicrons carry apoB-48, not apoB-100 - the intestinally-produced truncated form - so grouping chylomicrons with hepatic apoB-100 particles mixes the two separate pathways.
incorrectas.C: HDL does not carry apoB at all; it is built around apoA-I and apoA-II, and chylomicrons carry apoB-48 rather than apoB-100.
incorrectas.D: Chylomicron remnants carry apoB-48 (retained from the parent chylomicron) plus apoE, not apoB-100, and HDL again lacks apoB entirely.

preguntas.q: Before entering the bloodstream via the thoracic duct, nascent chylomicrons traveling through the lymphatics carry only which apolipoprotein on their surface?

e.correcta: Newly assembled chylomicrons are secreted from intestinal enterocytes into the lymphatics carrying only apoB-48, the structural apolipoprotein required for particle assembly and secretion. Only once the chylomicron reaches the bloodstream does it acquire apoC-II and apoE by transfer from circulating HDL, arming it with the apolipoproteins needed for lipoprotein lipase activation and later hepatic remnant clearance.

incorrectas.A: Apo E is acquired from HDL only after the chylomicron reaches the blood; it is needed later for hepatic receptor-mediated uptake of the remnant, not during lymphatic transit.
incorrectas.B: Apo C-II, the cofactor that activates lipoprotein lipase, is likewise picked up from HDL in the bloodstream, not while the particle is still confined to the lymph.
incorrectas.D: Apo A-I is the principal structural apolipoprotein of HDL and activates LCAT - it is not carried by chylomicrons at any stage of their life cycle.

preguntas.q: Chylomicrons transport dietary lipids from the intestine; which molecule makes up the largest proportion of their core?

e.correcta: Chylomicrons are the largest and least dense lipoproteins because their hydrophobic core is packed almost entirely with dietary triglycerides, with a much smaller amount of cholesterol ester; a surrounding phospholipid monolayer and surface apolipoproteins stabilize the particle. This triglyceride-dominant composition is why chylomicronemia classically causes markedly elevated serum triglycerides, eruptive xanthomas, and pancreatitis risk rather than pure hypercholesterolemia.

incorrectas.A: Cholesterol esters are present in chylomicrons but make up only a lesser fraction of the core lipid compared with triglyceride, in contrast to LDL, where cholesterol ester is the dominant core lipid.
incorrectas.B: Phospholipids form the amphipathic outer monolayer of the chylomicron (with free cholesterol and apolipoproteins), not the hydrophobic core, and are present in far smaller amounts than the triglyceride cargo.
incorrectas.C: Free (unesterified) fatty acids are not stored within lipoprotein particles; fatty acids are esterified into triglycerides for core packaging and only appear as free fatty acids after lipoprotein lipase acts at the tissue surface.

preguntas.q: After being assembled in intestinal enterocytes and secreted into the lymphatics, chylomicrons ultimately enter which compartment via the thoracic duct?

e.correcta: Because chylomicrons are far too large to cross directly into intestinal capillaries, they are packaged and released into intestinal lacteals, travel through the lymphatic system, and are finally emptied into systemic venous circulation at the junction of the thoracic duct with the left subclavian vein - only then do they reach the blood, bypassing the first-pass hepatic processing that portally-absorbed nutrients undergo.

incorrectas.B: The portal vein carries water-soluble absorbed nutrients (glucose, amino acids, short/medium-chain fatty acids) directly to the liver; chylomicrons, being lymphatic cargo, bypass the portal circulation entirely.
incorrectas.C: Hepatic sinusoids are where the liver later clears chylomicron remnants from systemic blood, but chylomicrons do not enter the hepatic sinusoids directly from the gut - they must first traverse the lymphatics and reach the venous blood.
incorrectas.D: The peritoneal cavity plays no role in lipid absorption or transport; lymphatic lacteals carrying chylomicrons drain toward the thoracic duct, not into the peritoneal space.

preguntas.q: Triglycerides carried within circulating chylomicrons are broken down into which products by lipoprotein lipase on the capillary endothelium near adipose and other peripheral tissue?

e.correcta: Lipoprotein lipase, anchored to capillary endothelium in adipose tissue, skeletal muscle, and cardiac muscle, hydrolyzes the core triglycerides of chylomicrons (and VLDL) into free fatty acids and glycerol. The liberated fatty acids are taken up locally for storage or oxidation, while the glycerol travels to the liver for gluconeogenesis; this enzyme requires apoC-II as a cofactor, which is why apoC-II deficiency mimics LPL deficiency with severe hypertriglyceridemia.

incorrectas.A: Glycerol is indeed a co-product of LPL-mediated hydrolysis, but it is the fatty acids that are preferentially taken up and utilized by the adjacent tissue - glycerol instead travels onward to the liver rather than being the answer sought here.
incorrectas.C: Cholesterol esters are a separate lipid component of the chylomicron core, hydrolyzed (if at all) by different enzymes, not the product of LPL action on triglyceride ester bonds.
incorrectas.D: Ketone bodies are produced in the liver from acetyl-CoA during fasting/starvation, not generated directly from LPL-mediated lipolysis of circulating triglycerides at peripheral capillaries.

preguntas.q: Once free fatty acids released from chylomicrons by lipoprotein lipase are taken up into adipocytes, they are re-esterified into which storage molecule?

e.correcta: Inside the adipocyte, free fatty acids liberated at the capillary surface are combined with glycerol-3-phosphate (generated from glucose via glycolysis, since adipocytes cannot directly reuse the glycerol released by LPL) and re-esterified into triglycerides for long-term storage. This step is why adipocyte fat storage depends on adequate glucose uptake and insulin signaling, both of which promote fatty acid uptake and glycerol-3-phosphate synthesis.

incorrectas.A: Phospholipids are membrane structural lipids, not the storage form fatty acids are converted into within adipocytes; triglyceride is the dedicated storage lipid of adipose tissue.
incorrectas.B: Cholesterol esters are formed by esterifying cholesterol (via ACAT intracellularly or LCAT in plasma), not by combining fatty acids with glycerol, and are not the primary storage product of adipocytes.
incorrectas.D: Ketone bodies are produced by the liver from fatty acid-derived acetyl-CoA during fasting, not synthesized within adipocytes, which store fat rather than generating ketones.

preguntas.q: As lipoprotein lipase progressively strips triglycerides from a circulating chylomicron, the shrinking, cholesterol-ester-enriched particle that remains is called a...?

e.correcta: As LPL removes the bulk of triglyceride from the chylomicron core, the particle shrinks and becomes relatively enriched in cholesterol esters, apoE, and apoB-48, forming the chylomicron remnant. This remnant is rapidly cleared by the liver via apoE-mediated receptor binding (LDL receptor and LRP1), delivering dietary cholesterol back to hepatocytes - a clearance step impaired in type III hyperlipoproteinemia due to defective apoE.

incorrectas.A: IDL is the analogous remnant particle formed from VLDL delipidation, not from chylomicrons - it is the endogenous (hepatic) pathway's equivalent, carrying apoB-100 and apoE rather than apoB-48.
incorrectas.B: LDL is the cholesterol-ester-rich end product of the endogenous (hepatic) pathway, formed from IDL after hepatic lipase removes remaining triglyceride; it is not derived from chylomicrons and carries only apoB-100.
incorrectas.C: Nascent HDL is a distinct, disc-shaped particle secreted by the liver and intestine that accepts free cholesterol from peripheral tissues via ABCA1, unrelated to the shrinking of a triglyceride-depleted chylomicron.

preguntas.q: After lipoprotein lipase has removed most of its triglyceride, the resulting chylomicron remnant displays which two apolipoproteins on its surface, having shed the others?

e.correcta: As the chylomicron is delipidated, its apoC-II is transferred back to HDL (no longer needed once LPL activation is complete), leaving the remnant displaying only apoB-48 (retained from intestinal assembly) and apoE. ApoE is essential at this stage because it is the ligand recognized by hepatic LDL receptors and LRP1, mediating rapid receptor-mediated clearance of the remnant by the liver.

incorrectas.B: ApoC-II is actually removed (recycled back to HDL) as the remnant forms, not retained - retaining apoC-II would describe the earlier, fully-armed circulating chylomicron rather than the remnant.
incorrectas.C: ApoB-100 is the hepatic form of apoB found on VLDL/IDL/LDL; chylomicrons and their remnants always carry the intestinally-derived apoB-48, never apoB-100.
incorrectas.D: ApoA-I is the principal HDL apolipoprotein (LCAT activator) and is not found on chylomicron remnants, which are characterized instead by apoB-48 and apoE.

preguntas.q: As a chylomicron loses its triglyceride core and is converted into a chylomicron remnant, what happens to the apoC-II that had been on its surface?

o.A: It is degraded by hepatic lysosomes
o.B: It is recycled back to HDL

e.correcta: ApoC-II is not a permanent part of the chylomicron - it was borrowed from HDL upon entering the bloodstream specifically to activate lipoprotein lipase. Once lipolysis is complete and the remnant no longer needs LPL activation, apoC-II is transferred back to HDL for reuse, illustrating the shuttle-like function of HDL as an apolipoprotein reservoir across both the exogenous and endogenous pathways.

incorrectas.A: ApoC-II is not degraded at this step; it is actively transferred back to HDL for reuse rather than destroyed, since HDL functions as an apolipoprotein recycling depot, not a disposal site.
incorrectas.C: If apoC-II remained on the remnant, that would contradict the remnant's actual composition (apoB-48 + apoE only) - apoC-II specifically leaves as the particle converts from an actively-lipolyzed chylomicron to a remnant awaiting hepatic clearance.
incorrectas.D: Biliary secretion is the route by which cholesterol and bile acids are eliminated from the body, not the mechanism by which apolipoproteins are exchanged between lipoprotein particles.

preguntas.q: When VLDL particles are first secreted from the liver into the bloodstream, which apolipoprotein do they initially carry alone?

e.correcta: VLDL is assembled in hepatocytes and secreted carrying only apoB-100, the full-length, unedited apolipoprotein B synthesized by the liver (in contrast to the intestinally-edited apoB-48 on chylomicrons). Just as with chylomicrons, VLDL then acquires apoC-II and apoE by transfer from circulating HDL once it enters the blood, arming it for lipoprotein lipase-mediated triglyceride hydrolysis and eventual remnant recognition.

incorrectas.A: Apo B-48 is the truncated apolipoprotein produced by intestinal mRNA editing and found on chylomicrons, not on VLDL, which is produced by hepatocytes using the full-length transcript.
incorrectas.B: Apo E is acquired from HDL after VLDL enters the bloodstream (needed later for IDL/remnant clearance), not present at the moment of initial hepatic secretion.
incorrectas.D: Apo C-II, the LPL activator, is likewise picked up from HDL in the circulation, not part of the initially-secreted VLDL particle.

preguntas.q: VLDL is the lipoprotein responsible for exporting endogenously synthesized lipid from the liver; what is the predominant lipid in its core?

e.correcta: Like chylomicrons, VLDL particles are built around a core that is predominantly triglyceride - in this case triglyceride synthesized de novo in the liver from excess carbohydrate, alcohol, or fatty acids - with a smaller proportion of cholesterol ester. This triglyceride-rich composition is why elevated VLDL (as in metabolic syndrome or excess alcohol intake) manifests primarily as hypertriglyceridemia and dominates type IV hyperlipoproteinemia.

incorrectas.A: Free (unesterified) cholesterol is found mainly at the particle surface along with phospholipids, not as the major core lipid; it is a minor structural component rather than the dominant cargo.
incorrectas.B: Cholesterol esters do make up part of the VLDL core, but in a lesser proportion than triglyceride - cholesterol ester instead becomes the dominant core lipid later, once VLDL is remodeled down to LDL.
incorrectas.C: Phospholipids form the outer amphipathic monolayer of the particle (with free cholesterol and apolipoproteins) rather than the hydrophobic triglyceride-rich core.

preguntas.q: Lipoprotein lipase acting on circulating VLDL near adipose tissue and other peripheral tissues hydrolyzes the particle's core triglycerides into which products for tissue uptake?

e.correcta: Just as with chylomicrons, VLDL triglycerides are hydrolyzed by endothelium-bound lipoprotein lipase (activated by apoC-II) into free fatty acids and glycerol at the capillary bed of adipose tissue, muscle, and other tissues. The fatty acids are taken up locally for storage or oxidation, while the delipidated VLDL remnant progressively shrinks toward IDL - this parallel handling of chylomicrons and VLDL by the same enzyme is a key unifying concept in lipid transport.

incorrectas.B: Ketone bodies are synthesized in hepatic mitochondria from fatty acid oxidation during fasting, not generated directly by LPL action on circulating lipoproteins.
incorrectas.C: Cholesterol esters are a separate lipid class within the VLDL core; they are not the hydrolysis product of triglyceride breakdown by lipoprotein lipase.
incorrectas.D: Amino acids come from protein digestion/catabolism and have no role in lipoprotein triglyceride metabolism; LPL acts specifically on triglyceride ester bonds, not peptide bonds.

preguntas.q: As lipoprotein lipase removes triglyceride from circulating VLDL, the shrinking particle is remodeled into which intermediate lipoprotein?

e.correcta: Progressive triglyceride removal from VLDL by lipoprotein lipase produces a smaller, relatively cholesterol-ester-enriched particle called intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL) - the structural analog of the chylomicron remnant, but arising from the endogenous (hepatic) rather than exogenous (dietary) pathway. IDL can then be taken up directly by the liver via apoE-mediated receptor binding or undergo further processing by hepatic lipase to become LDL.

incorrectas.A: A chylomicron remnant is the parallel product formed from a dietary chylomicron, not from hepatically-derived VLDL - the two remnant-generating pathways run in parallel even though both use lipoprotein lipase.
incorrectas.C: LDL is a later product formed after IDL undergoes additional triglyceride removal by hepatic triglyceride lipase and loses apoE - it is not the immediate product of VLDL delipidation by peripheral LPL.
incorrectas.D: HDL is an entirely separate particle class secreted by the liver and intestine for reverse cholesterol transport; it is not generated from VLDL remodeling.

preguntas.q: After VLDL is delipidated into IDL, which two apolipoproteins remain on its surface, having shed apoC-II back to HDL?

e.correcta: As VLDL loses its triglyceride and becomes IDL, its apoC-II is returned to HDL (mirroring the chylomicron-to-remnant transition), leaving IDL displaying apoB-100 (retained from the original VLDL) together with apoE. ApoE on IDL allows the particle to be recognized by hepatic apoE receptors (LDL receptor and LRP1) for direct hepatic uptake, or the particle can be remodeled further by hepatic lipase into LDL.

incorrectas.A: ApoB-48 is the intestinal form of apoB found on chylomicrons and their remnants; IDL, being derived from hepatically-secreted VLDL, carries apoB-100 instead.
incorrectas.B: ApoA-I is the major HDL apolipoprotein, not found on IDL, and apoC-II has already been recycled back to HDL by this stage rather than remaining on the particle.
incorrectas.D: ApoC-II is removed (recycled to HDL) as VLDL converts to IDL, so its continued presence on IDL contradicts the actual composition, which loses apoC-II and retains apoE instead.

preguntas.q: As VLDL is progressively delipidated by lipoprotein lipase and remodeled into IDL, what becomes of the apoC-II that had activated LPL on the VLDL surface?

o.B: It is degraded in the liver
o.D: It is transferred back to HDL

e.correcta: Mirroring the chylomicron pathway, apoC-II was only transiently borrowed by VLDL from HDL to activate lipoprotein lipase; once the bulk of triglyceride hydrolysis is complete, apoC-II is transferred back to HDL for reuse, while apoE (also originally from HDL) stays on the particle to mediate eventual hepatic recognition. This apolipoprotein shuttling via HDL is a recurring theme across both major lipid transport pathways.

incorrectas.A: If apoC-II remained on IDL, that would contradict IDL's actual apolipoprotein signature of apoB-100 plus apoE only - apoC-II is specifically removed at this transition, not retained.
incorrectas.B: ApoC-II is not degraded here; it is recycled intact back to HDL for future use activating LPL on newly secreted chylomicrons or VLDL, an efficient reuse mechanism rather than destruction.
incorrectas.C: Apolipoproteins are distinct polypeptides encoded by separate genes; apoC-II cannot chemically convert into apoE - each retains its own distinct structure and receptor-binding properties.

preguntas.q: Once in the vicinity of the liver, IDL may be cleared directly from circulation by binding which hepatic receptor via its apoB-100?

e.correcta: IDL carries both apoE and apoB-100, either of which can be recognized by the hepatic LDL receptor - apoE binds with especially high affinity, but apoB-100 also allows direct LDL receptor engagement, permitting the liver to clear a substantial fraction of circulating IDL directly (delivering its remaining cholesterol esters and triglyceride to hepatocytes) before the rest is converted to LDL by hepatic lipase.

incorrectas.B: Scavenger receptors (e.g., on macrophages) bind oxidized or modified LDL particles, playing a central role in atherosclerotic foam cell formation, not the physiologic clearance of normal IDL by hepatocytes.
incorrectas.C: LRP1 does participate in remnant/IDL clearance via apoE recognition, but the question specifically describes binding through apoB-100, which is the ligand recognized by the classic LDL receptor rather than LRP1 alone.
incorrectas.D: Toll-like receptors are pattern-recognition receptors of the innate immune system that detect pathogen- or damage-associated molecules; they play no role in lipoprotein particle uptake.

preguntas.q: Mature LDL, having lost its apoE during formation from IDL, carries a single copy of which apolipoprotein on its surface?

e.correcta: As IDL is further processed by hepatic triglyceride lipase, it loses its remaining triglyceride and its apoE, leaving LDL with exactly one copy of apoB-100 per particle. This single, non-exchangeable apolipoprotein is what allows LDL to be specifically recognized by the LDL receptor on peripheral cells and hepatocytes for cholesterol delivery, and it is the basis for LDL receptor/PCSK9-targeted cholesterol-lowering therapies.

incorrectas.A: ApoB-48 is the intestinally-derived, truncated form found on chylomicrons and their remnants, never on LDL, which arises exclusively from the hepatic VLDL/IDL processing pathway using apoB-100.
incorrectas.C: ApoA-I is the defining structural apolipoprotein of HDL and the activator of LCAT, unrelated to LDL, which is characterized by its single apoB-100 molecule.
incorrectas.D: ApoE is present on IDL (and chylomicron remnants) but is specifically lost as IDL is converted to LDL, which is why LDL is no longer recognized by apoE receptors and depends solely on apoB-100 for receptor binding.

preguntas.q: LDL is the primary carrier of cholesterol to peripheral tissues; which lipid predominates in its core, having become enriched as triglyceride was progressively stripped away?

e.correcta: Through the sequential action of lipoprotein lipase (on VLDL) and hepatic triglyceride lipase (on IDL), most of the original triglyceride cargo is removed, leaving LDL's core relatively enriched in cholesterol esters. This is why LDL is often called the cholesterol-carrying lipoprotein and why elevated LDL correlates with hypercholesterolemia and atherogenesis, in contrast to chylomicrons and VLDL, whose elevations manifest primarily as hypertriglyceridemia.

incorrectas.A: Triglycerides dominate the core of chylomicrons and VLDL, the precursor particles, but by the time VLDL has been remodeled into IDL and then LDL, most triglyceride has been removed, leaving cholesterol ester as the major core lipid instead.
incorrectas.B: Free fatty acids are not stored within lipoprotein cores; they are the products released by lipases at the tissue surface, not a structural component of the LDL particle itself.
incorrectas.D: Phospholipids occupy the outer monolayer of LDL along with free cholesterol and the single apoB-100 molecule, but they are not the dominant lipid of the hydrophobic core, which is cholesterol ester.

preguntas.q: Nascent, disc-shaped HDL particles that go on to collect peripheral cholesterol are synthesized and secreted by which two organs?

e.correcta: Nascent HDL is produced as a lipid-poor, discoid particle by both the liver and the small intestine; it circulates and acquires free cholesterol from peripheral cells via the ABCA1 transporter, which is then esterified by LCAT (activated by apoA-I) to form mature, spherical HDL. This dual hepatic/intestinal origin parallels the two apoB-containing lipoprotein systems, reinforcing that both organs contribute apolipoprotein-based particles to plasma lipid transport.

incorrectas.A: The pancreas is not a source of nascent HDL; its role in lipid metabolism is limited to secreting pancreatic lipase for luminal fat digestion, not lipoprotein particle synthesis.
incorrectas.B: The kidney does not synthesize lipoproteins; it is involved in lipid/lipoprotein filtration and reabsorption pathology (e.g., proteinuria-associated hyperlipidemia) rather than HDL production.
incorrectas.C: The spleen has no role in lipoprotein biogenesis; only the liver and intestine synthesize and secrete nascent HDL particles.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme transfers cholesterol esters from mature HDL to VLDL, IDL, and LDL in exchange for triglyceride?

e.correcta: CETP mediates a heterotypic lipid exchange, transferring cholesterol esters generated within HDL (by LCAT) to apoB-containing lipoproteins (VLDL, IDL, LDL) in exchange for triglyceride, redistributing cholesterol away from HDL toward particles that are ultimately returned to the liver or peripheral tissues. This is clinically relevant because CETP inhibitors were developed as a strategy to raise HDL cholesterol by blocking this transfer, and CETP deficiency itself causes markedly elevated HDL levels.

incorrectas.B: LCAT is the enzyme that actually esterifies free cholesterol into cholesterol ester within HDL (activated by apoA-I), generating the cargo that CETP then transfers - it does not itself move cholesterol ester between particles.
incorrectas.C: Hepatic lipase hydrolyzes remaining triglyceride (and some phospholipid) on IDL and HDL particles, contributing to LDL and HDL remodeling, but it does not shuttle cholesterol esters between lipoprotein classes.
incorrectas.D: Lipoprotein lipase hydrolyzes triglycerides within chylomicrons and VLDL at peripheral capillaries; it has no role in transferring cholesterol esters between HDL and apoB-containing particles.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme, secreted by the exocrine pancreas, is responsible for hydrolyzing dietary triglycerides within the lumen of the small intestine?

e.correcta: Pancreatic lipase, secreted into the duodenum along with colipase (which anchors the enzyme at the oil-water interface of bile-salt-emulsified fat droplets), hydrolyzes dietary triglycerides into monoglycerides and free fatty acids for absorption by enterocytes. This is the first digestive step in dietary lipid handling and is why pancreatic insufficiency (e.g., in cystic fibrosis or chronic pancreatitis) causes steatorrhea from unabsorbed dietary fat.

incorrectas.A: Lipoprotein lipase acts within the bloodstream at capillary endothelium, hydrolyzing triglycerides carried in circulating chylomicrons and VLDL - it plays no role in digesting dietary fat within the intestinal lumen.
incorrectas.C: Hepatic triglyceride lipase acts on circulating IDL and HDL particles at the liver, remodeling them further after they have already entered the bloodstream, not on luminal dietary fat.
incorrectas.D: Hormone-sensitive lipase mobilizes stored triglyceride from within adipocytes during fasting/lipolysis, an entirely intracellular process unrelated to luminal digestion of ingested fat.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme, anchored to capillary endothelium and activated by apoC-II, hydrolyzes the triglycerides carried within circulating chylomicrons and VLDL?

e.correcta: Lipoprotein lipase is expressed by adipocytes, myocytes, and cardiac muscle and displayed on the luminal surface of adjacent capillary endothelium, where circulating apoC-II-bearing chylomicrons and VLDL dock and have their core triglycerides hydrolyzed into fatty acids for local uptake. LPL deficiency (or apoC-II deficiency) causes type I hyperlipoproteinemia with severe chylomicronemia, eruptive xanthomas, and pancreatitis risk.

incorrectas.A: Pancreatic lipase acts within the intestinal lumen on dietary triglyceride before absorption, an entirely separate digestive step from the vascular hydrolysis of circulating lipoproteins performed by lipoprotein lipase.
incorrectas.B: Hepatic triglyceride lipase acts specifically on IDL and HDL at the liver surface, remodeling IDL into LDL - a distinct step further along the pathway from the peripheral LPL-mediated hydrolysis of chylomicrons and VLDL.
incorrectas.D: Hormone-sensitive lipase releases fatty acids from triglyceride stored within adipocytes during lipolysis (e.g., fasting, catecholamine stimulation), an intracellular process distinct from LPL's extracellular action on circulating lipoprotein particles.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme, expressed on hepatic endothelium, hydrolyzes the remaining triglyceride in IDL as it is remodeled into LDL?

e.correcta: Hepatic triglyceride lipase, anchored to the endothelial surface of hepatic sinusoids, removes the residual triglyceride (and some phospholipid) from IDL that was not already stripped by peripheral lipoprotein lipase, completing the conversion of IDL to cholesterol-ester-rich LDL (with loss of apoE in the process). This enzyme also converts HDL2 back to the smaller HDL3 particle, making it important in both apoB-lipoprotein remodeling and HDL cycling.

incorrectas.A: Lipoprotein lipase acts earlier in the pathway, at peripheral capillaries, hydrolyzing the bulk of triglyceride from chylomicrons and VLDL - the residual triglyceride left on IDL is specifically handled by hepatic lipase, not LPL.
incorrectas.B: Pancreatic lipase functions in the intestinal lumen on dietary fat prior to absorption, entirely unrelated to the vascular/hepatic remodeling of circulating IDL particles.
incorrectas.C: CETP transfers cholesterol esters (from HDL) and triglycerides (from apoB-lipoproteins) between particles rather than hydrolyzing triglyceride bonds - it moves lipids between particles rather than cleaving them.

preguntas.q: During fasting, which intracellular enzyme, activated by catecholamine-stimulated PKA phosphorylation, mobilizes triglycerides stored within adipocytes?

e.correcta: Hormone-sensitive lipase is the rate-limiting intracellular enzyme of adipocyte lipolysis; it is activated by PKA-mediated phosphorylation downstream of glucagon/epinephrine signaling (and inhibited by insulin), hydrolyzing stored triglyceride into free fatty acids and glycerol that are released into the blood for use by other tissues during fasting or exercise. This hormonal control is why insulin resistance or deficiency states are associated with excessive, unregulated lipolysis and elevated free fatty acid flux.

incorrectas.B: Lipoprotein lipase acts extracellularly, at the capillary endothelium, on circulating lipoprotein triglycerides, not on triglyceride stored within the adipocyte itself.
incorrectas.C: Pancreatic lipase digests dietary triglyceride within the intestinal lumen, an entirely separate digestive process unrelated to endogenous fat mobilization from adipose stores.
incorrectas.D: Hepatic triglyceride lipase remodels circulating IDL and HDL particles at the liver's endothelial surface, not intracellular adipocyte triglyceride stores mobilized during fasting.

preguntas.q: Which two lipoprotein classes carry the greatest amount of cholesterol by mass?

e.correcta: LDL and HDL are relatively triglyceride-poor and cholesterol-rich compared to the other lipoproteins. LDL delivers hepatic cholesterol to peripheral tissues, while HDL performs reverse cholesterol transport back to the liver; between them, these two particles carry the bulk of circulating cholesterol.

incorrectas.A: VLDL is predominantly triglyceride-rich (secreted by the liver to deliver endogenous TGs), and IDL is only a transient intermediate with less overall cholesterol content than LDL or HDL.
incorrectas.B: Chylomicrons and VLDL are the most triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, carrying dietary and hepatic triglycerides respectively — they are not the particles with the highest cholesterol content.
incorrectas.D: IDL is a short-lived remnant on its way to becoming LDL, and chylomicrons are overwhelmingly triglyceride-laden, so neither pair represents the lipoproteins with the greatest cholesterol mass.

preguntas.q: A lipoprotein assembled in intestinal enterocytes packages dietary triglycerides and travels via the lymphatics to deliver them to peripheral tissues such as adipose and muscle. Which lipoprotein is this?

e.correcta: Chylomicrons are synthesized by intestinal epithelial cells from absorbed dietary lipids, secreted into intestinal lacteals before entering systemic circulation, and carry ApoB-48. Lipoprotein lipase, activated by ApoC-II acquired from HDL, hydrolyzes their triglycerides for delivery to peripheral tissue.

incorrectas.A: VLDL is secreted by the liver (carrying ApoB-100) to deliver endogenously synthesized triglycerides, not triglycerides absorbed from the diet by intestinal cells.
incorrectas.C: IDL is a remnant particle formed after lipoprotein lipase strips triglyceride from VLDL; it is not a primary carrier of dietary lipid from the intestine.
incorrectas.D: LDL is derived from further degradation of IDL, is cholesterol-rich rather than triglyceride-rich, and never originates in the intestine.

preguntas.q: Which lipoprotein, synthesized and secreted by hepatocytes, transports endogenously synthesized triglycerides to peripheral tissues?

e.correcta: VLDL is assembled in the liver from hepatic triglycerides and cholesterol, carries ApoB-100, and delivers triglyceride to peripheral tissues via lipoprotein lipase. After progressive TG depletion it is converted first to IDL and then to LDL.

incorrectas.A: Chylomicrons carry dietary rather than hepatic triglyceride and originate in intestinal epithelial cells, not hepatocytes.
incorrectas.C: HDL is produced by the liver and intestine but functions mainly in reverse cholesterol transport, not in delivering triglyceride from liver to periphery.
incorrectas.D: IDL is a downstream degradation product of VLDL after partial triglyceride removal, not the initial hepatic secretory particle.

preguntas.q: As VLDL loses triglyceride through lipoprotein lipase activity, it is converted into an intermediate particle that delivers its remaining triglyceride and cholesterol back to the liver. What is this particle called?

e.correcta: IDL forms from partial lipoprotein lipase-mediated degradation of VLDL. Roughly half of IDL particles are taken up directly by the liver (via LDL receptor recognition of ApoE), while the remainder undergo further lipolysis to become LDL.

incorrectas.A: LDL is the further degradation product of IDL after additional triglyceride removal and loss of ApoE; it is cholesterol-rich and delivers cholesterol to peripheral tissue rather than returning it to the liver.
incorrectas.B: Chylomicron remnants are the analogous remnant particle formed from chylomicrons (not VLDL) after LPL action and are also cleared by the liver via ApoE, but they arise from dietary lipid processing, not from hepatic VLDL.
incorrectas.D: HDL is synthesized separately as small nascent discs by the liver and intestine; it is not a degradation product of VLDL.

preguntas.q: Which lipoprotein, formed from further degradation of IDL, is the major carrier of cholesterol from the liver to peripheral tissues?

e.correcta: LDL forms when IDL loses its remaining triglyceride and ApoE, leaving a cholesterol ester-rich particle recognized by peripheral and hepatic LDL receptors via ApoB-100. It is the principal vehicle delivering cholesterol to cells, and when oxidized it drives foam cell formation and atherogenesis.

incorrectas.A: HDL transports cholesterol in the opposite direction, from periphery back to the liver, as part of reverse cholesterol transport rather than from liver outward.
incorrectas.B: VLDL is the precursor several steps earlier in the pathway, still triglyceride-rich and destined to become IDL and then LDL, rather than being the terminal cholesterol-delivery particle itself.
incorrectas.D: IDL is the intermediate step immediately before LDL formation; it still carries ApoE and more triglyceride, and about half of it is cleared by the liver rather than reaching peripheral tissue as LDL.

preguntas.q: Which lipoprotein is primarily responsible for transporting cholesterol from peripheral tissues back to the liver for excretion or recycling?

e.correcta: HDL performs reverse cholesterol transport: nascent HDL picks up free cholesterol from peripheral cells (partly via ABCA1), esterifies it using LCAT (activated by ApoA-I), and delivers the cholesterol esters to the liver either directly via SR-B1 or indirectly by CETP-mediated transfer to VLDL/IDL/LDL.

incorrectas.A: LDL moves cholesterol in the opposite direction, from liver to peripheral tissues, and is the lipoprotein most implicated in atherogenesis when oxidized, rather than in cholesterol clearance back to the liver.
incorrectas.B: VLDL primarily delivers endogenous triglycerides to tissues; any role in reverse transport is indirect, occurring only after CETP transfers cholesterol esters from HDL onto it.
incorrectas.C: Chylomicrons deliver dietary triglycerides and fat-soluble vitamins from the gut to tissues, playing no role in returning peripheral cholesterol to the liver.

preguntas.q: Which lipoprotein serves as a circulating reservoir for apolipoproteins C-II and E, donating them to chylomicrons and VLDL as needed?

e.correcta: HDL particles carry a surface pool of ApoC-II (which activates lipoprotein lipase) and ApoE (which mediates hepatic remnant uptake). These apoproteins are transferred to nascent chylomicrons and VLDL in circulation, allowing those triglyceride-rich particles to be properly processed and cleared.

incorrectas.A: LDL carries mainly ApoB-100 as its structural apolipoprotein and does not function as a donor reservoir of ApoC-II or ApoE to other lipoproteins.
incorrectas.C: Chylomicrons are recipients of ApoC-II and ApoE from HDL, not the source; they acquire these apoproteins in circulation to become functional substrates for lipoprotein lipase.
incorrectas.D: VLDL, like chylomicrons, receives ApoC-II and ApoE from HDL in the bloodstream rather than storing and donating them to other particles.

preguntas.q: Regular moderate alcohol consumption has what effect on HDL synthesis, one proposed mechanism behind its association with reduced cardiovascular risk?

e.correcta: Moderate alcohol intake increases hepatic synthesis of HDL and ApoA-I, raising HDL levels. This is one proposed mechanism behind the epidemiologic association between light-to-moderate drinking and lower coronary risk, though heavier intake causes other harms (hypertriglyceridemia, hepatotoxicity) that outweigh this benefit.

incorrectas.A: Decreased synthesis is the opposite of alcohol's actual effect on hepatic HDL production and does not match the mechanism proposed for its cardioprotective association.
incorrectas.B: No significant effect is incorrect, since alcohol has a demonstrable stimulatory effect on hepatic ApoA-I/HDL production, distinguishing it from many other lifestyle factors with neutral lipid effects.
incorrectas.D: Increased degradation would lower HDL levels, which contradicts the observed rise in HDL seen with moderate alcohol use.

preguntas.q: After LDL binds its receptor on the cell surface, the receptor-ligand complex is internalized within specialized membrane invaginations coated by which protein?

e.correcta: LDL receptor-mediated endocytosis occurs through clathrin-coated pits: clathrin forms a lattice on the cytoplasmic face of the plasma membrane that helps deform it into a coated vesicle, internalizing the LDL-receptor complex for delivery to the endosomal system.

incorrectas.A: Caveolin coats caveolae, flask-shaped membrane invaginations involved in a distinct, largely clathrin-independent endocytic pathway, not the classic route used by the LDL receptor.
incorrectas.B: COPI coats vesicles mediating retrograde transport from the Golgi back to the ER and between Golgi cisternae, not endocytosis at the plasma membrane.
incorrectas.D: COPII coats vesicles that carry proteins anterograde from the rough ER to the Golgi, an intracellular trafficking step unrelated to receptor internalization at the cell surface.

preguntas.q: The clathrin-coated vesicle containing internalized LDL eventually fuses with which organelle, releasing free cholesterol from cholesterol esters?

e.correcta: After uncoating and passage through the endosomal system, the LDL-containing vesicle fuses with the lysosome, where lysosomal (acid) esterase hydrolyzes cholesteryl esters into free cholesterol and fatty acids, while the ApoB-100 protein component is degraded to amino acids.

incorrectas.A: The early endosome is an intermediate compartment where receptor and ligand dissociate (aided by acidic pH) before the LDL particle is routed onward; it is not itself the site of cholesterol ester hydrolysis.
incorrectas.B: Peroxisomes handle very-long-chain fatty acid beta-oxidation and other oxidative reactions, not the hydrolysis of endocytosed LDL cholesterol esters.
incorrectas.C: The Golgi apparatus modifies and sorts newly synthesized proteins and lipids destined for secretion or other compartments; it is not part of the LDL receptor's degradative endocytic pathway.

preguntas.q: Following dissociation from LDL in the endosome, what happens to the majority of internalized LDL receptors?

o.A: They are degraded in the lysosome along with the LDL
o.B: They are recycled back to the plasma membrane
o.C: They are marked for proteasomal degradation
o.D: They are transported to the Golgi for permanent storage

e.correcta: Most LDL receptors dissociate from their ligand in the acidified endosome and are recycled back to the cell surface to bind additional LDL particles, allowing a single receptor to be reused many times. Only a minority are degraded and must be replaced through new LDL-receptor gene transcription.

incorrectas.A: While the LDL particle itself proceeds to the lysosome for degradation, the receptor generally escapes this fate by dissociating and recycling rather than accompanying its ligand into the lysosome.
incorrectas.C: Proteasomal degradation targets cytosolic, typically ubiquitinated proteins, not the primary fate of the membrane LDL receptor, which is recycled through the endosomal pathway rather than the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
incorrectas.D: The Golgi is used for initial receptor synthesis and processing on the way to the cell surface, not as a long-term storage depot for receptors after endocytosis.

preguntas.q: As intracellular cholesterol concentration rises within a hepatocyte, what happens to LDL receptor gene expression?

o.A: It increases to clear more circulating LDL
o.D: It increases transiently before permanently shutting off

e.correcta: Rising intracellular cholesterol inhibits SREBP-mediated transcription of the LDL receptor gene (along with HMG-CoA reductase), reducing new receptor synthesis. This negative feedback protects the cell from cholesterol overload, but it also means less circulating LDL is cleared — one reason statins, which lower intracellular hepatocyte cholesterol, upregulate LDL receptors and improve LDL clearance.

incorrectas.A: An increase would represent a positive-feedback response that would allow unchecked cholesterol accumulation; instead, cells downregulate uptake machinery when cholesterol is already abundant.
incorrectas.B: Expression is not unchanged — LDL receptor transcription is actively regulated by intracellular sterol levels through the SREBP pathway, decreasing as cholesterol accumulates.
incorrectas.D: There is no described biphasic transient increase followed by permanent shutoff; regulation is a straightforward decrease in transcription proportional to intracellular cholesterol level.

preguntas.q: LDL that has undergone oxidative modification develops a defect in its apoB-100 and is no longer recognized by the standard LDL receptor. This altered particle is instead taken up by which cell type, a key early step in atherogenesis?

e.correcta: Oxidized LDL's damaged apoB-100 prevents recognition by the classic LDL receptor, but macrophages recognize and engulf it via scavenger receptors, becoming cholesterol-laden foam cells — the histologic hallmark of early atherosclerotic lesions (fatty streaks).

incorrectas.A: Neutrophils are acute inflammatory phagocytes central to bacterial killing and acute inflammation, not the primary cells implicated in lipid-driven foam cell formation in vessel walls.
incorrectas.C: Dendritic cells are antigen-presenting cells that link innate and adaptive immunity; they are not the principal scavenger cell responsible for oxidized LDL uptake and foam cell formation in atherosclerosis.
incorrectas.D: Hepatocytes normally clear native LDL and remnant particles via the LDL receptor and ApoE-mediated pathways, but they do not use scavenger receptors to consume oxidized LDL in the vessel wall the way macrophages do.

preguntas.q: Macrophages internalize oxidized LDL through which receptor, distinct from the classic apoB-100-recognizing LDL receptor?

e.correcta: Macrophages recognize the modified apolipoprotein and lipid components of oxidized LDL through scavenger receptor-A (SR-A), a pattern-recognition receptor that mediates uptake independent of ApoB-100 recognition. This unregulated uptake drives progressive cholesterol accumulation and foam cell transformation.

incorrectas.A: The LDL receptor recognizes native, unoxidized ApoB-100 on circulating LDL and is expressed on hepatocytes and peripheral cells generally, not the scavenger pathway macrophages use for damaged oxidized particles.
incorrectas.C: Scavenger receptor B-1 is the hepatocyte receptor that selectively takes up cholesterol esters from HDL during reverse cholesterol transport, a distinct process from macrophage oxidized LDL uptake.
incorrectas.D: Toll-like receptor 4 is an innate immune pattern-recognition receptor involved in sensing damage- and pathogen-associated molecular patterns and inflammatory signaling, not the main endocytic route responsible for loading macrophages with cholesterol to form foam cells.

preguntas.q: Unlike the classic LDL receptor, why does macrophage uptake of oxidized LDL via scavenger receptor-A continue unabated even as intracellular cholesterol accumulates?

o.A: Because SR-A expression is not down-regulated by rising intracellular cholesterol
o.B: Because SR-A is degraded and resynthesized at a fixed rate regardless of ligand
o.C: Because SR-A requires ApoB-100 recognition just like the LDL receptor
o.D: Because SR-A is down-regulated at the same rate as the LDL receptor

e.correcta: The LDL receptor is subject to negative feedback (via SREBP) that decreases its expression as intracellular cholesterol rises, protecting the cell from overload. Scavenger receptor-A lacks this feedback regulation, so macrophages continue taking up oxidized LDL unchecked, progressively accumulating cholesterol ester and transforming into foam cells — a key driver of atherosclerotic plaque growth.

incorrectas.B: The key mechanism isn't a fixed turnover rate for the receptor protein itself, but the absence of cholesterol-sensitive transcriptional downregulation, which is what permits continued unregulated uptake.
incorrectas.C: SR-A recognizes modified or oxidized lipoproteins and other polyanionic ligands through pattern recognition rather than native ApoB-100 — this is precisely what allows it to bind oxidized LDL that the ApoB-100-dependent LDL receptor can no longer recognize.
incorrectas.D: If SR-A were down-regulated like the LDL receptor, macrophages would stop accumulating cholesterol once intracellular levels rose, which would prevent rather than promote foam cell formation — the opposite of what actually occurs.

preguntas.q: Macrophages that become engorged with cholesterol after scavenging oxidized LDL take on a characteristic lipid-laden appearance and accumulate within the arterial subendothelium. What are these cells called?

e.correcta: These cholesterol- and lipid-engorged macrophages are called foam cells due to their frothy, vacuolated cytoplasm on histology. Their accumulation within the subendothelial space forms the fatty streak, the earliest visible lesion of atherosclerosis, which can progress to a fibrous plaque.

incorrectas.B: Touton giant cells are multinucleated cells with a wreath of nuclei surrounding central lipid-laden cytoplasm, seen in xanthomas and fat necrosis — histologically distinct from the mononuclear foam cells of early atherosclerotic lesions.
incorrectas.C: Langhans giant cells are multinucleated cells formed by fusion of activated macrophages in granulomatous inflammation (e.g., tuberculosis), a different pathologic process from lipid-driven foam cell formation in the vessel wall.
incorrectas.D: Xanthoma cells refers to lipid-laden macrophages that collect in the skin or tendons (as in familial hypercholesterolemia), not the specific term for subendothelial arterial foam cells in atherosclerosis.

preguntas.q: When cholesterol-laden foam cells within the arterial wall die and release precipitated cholesterol into the extracellular space, this process contributes to formation of what structure?

e.correcta: Death of foam cells releases their stored cholesterol extracellularly, contributing to a necrotic lipid core that, together with smooth muscle proliferation and a fibrous cap, constitutes the mature atherosclerotic plaque — the lesion responsible for luminal narrowing and, if it ruptures, thrombosis.

incorrectas.A: The fatty streak is the earlier, purely intracellular accumulation of living foam cells without a necrotic lipid core or fibrous cap, representing the initial rather than the mature lesion described here.
incorrectas.C: Xanthelasma refers to cholesterol deposits in the skin around the eyelids, a distinct extravascular finding rather than the intra-arterial plaque formed by foam cell death.
incorrectas.D: An Aschoff body is a granulomatous nodule with giant cells seen in rheumatic fever/myocarditis, unrelated to lipid accumulation and foam cell death in atherosclerosis.

preguntas.q: Cholesterol that has precipitated within the vessel wall can be picked up and esterified by which lipoprotein as part of reverse cholesterol transport?

e.correcta: HDL, via its surface ApoA-I activating the enzyme LCAT, esterifies free cholesterol it picks up (including cholesterol that has precipitated in the vessel wall) into cholesterol ester, which is then delivered directly to the liver or transferred via CETP to IDL, VLDL, or LDL for hepatic clearance.

incorrectas.A: VLDL delivers endogenous triglycerides outward from the liver to tissues; it does not scavenge precipitated vessel-wall cholesterol, though it may later receive cholesterol esters transferred from HDL via CETP.
incorrectas.B: IDL is a transient remnant of VLDL degradation en route to becoming LDL or being cleared by the liver; it plays no direct role in picking up cholesterol from the arterial wall.
incorrectas.D: LDL is the lipoprotein that delivers cholesterol to peripheral tissues (the reverse direction) and is actually one of the atherogenic particles implicated in depositing, rather than removing, arterial wall cholesterol.

preguntas.q: HDL can deliver cholesterol esters directly to hepatocytes without the whole particle being internalized and degraded, via which receptor?

e.correcta: Scavenger receptor B-1 (SR-B1) on hepatocytes selectively takes up cholesterol esters from HDL without internalizing and degrading the whole HDL particle, allowing HDL to be recycled back into circulation while its cholesterol cargo is delivered to the liver for bile acid synthesis or excretion.

incorrectas.A: The LDL receptor recognizes ApoB-100/ApoE-containing particles like LDL and remnants for whole-particle endocytosis, a different mechanism from SR-B1's selective lipid uptake from HDL.
incorrectas.B: CD36 is a scavenger receptor important in fatty acid uptake and macrophage recognition of oxidized LDL, not the primary hepatic receptor mediating HDL-cholesterol uptake in reverse cholesterol transport.
incorrectas.C: ABCA1 is a cholesterol efflux transporter on peripheral cells (including macrophages) that loads free cholesterol onto nascent HDL/ApoA-I, functioning at the opposite end of the reverse transport pathway from hepatic SR-B1 uptake.

preguntas.q: What is the pattern of inheritance for type I hyperlipoproteinemia (familial hyperchylomicronemia), caused by deficiency of lipoprotein lipase or its cofactor ApoC-II?

e.correcta: Type I hyperlipoproteinemia is autosomal recessive, requiring loss-of-function mutations in both alleles of LPL (or ApoC-II) to sufficiently impair chylomicron/VLDL triglyceride hydrolysis, leading to massive chylomicronemia; this contrasts with the autosomal dominant inheritance of types IIa and IV.

incorrectas.A: Autosomal dominant inheritance describes type IIa (familial hypercholesterolemia, LDL receptor defect) and type IV (hypertriglyceridemia), not type I, which requires biallelic loss of enzyme or cofactor function.
incorrectas.B: X-linked recessive inheritance is not a pattern seen in the classic familial dyslipidemias, which are autosomal disorders.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance applies to disorders of mitochondrial DNA-encoded proteins (e.g., certain myopathies), not to lipoprotein lipase or ApoC-II deficiency.

preguntas.q: Which serum lipoprotein accumulates to strikingly high levels in type I hyperlipoproteinemia due to deficient lipoprotein lipase activity?

e.correcta: Because LPL (or its activator ApoC-II) is deficient, chylomicrons cannot be hydrolyzed and cleared normally, so they accumulate massively in the plasma — so much so that the condition is also called familial chylomicronemia syndrome, with serum that appears creamy or lactescent after standing.

incorrectas.A: LDL is elevated in type IIa (familial hypercholesterolemia) due to LDL receptor dysfunction, not in type I, where the defect is in triglyceride-rich particle clearance rather than LDL receptor function.
incorrectas.B: IDL is markedly elevated in type III dysbetalipoproteinemia (due to defective ApoE), not type I, which involves the earlier chylomicron/VLDL processing step.
incorrectas.C: VLDL is the lipoprotein classically elevated in type IV hypertriglyceridemia and can be mildly elevated in type I as well, but the hallmark, massively elevated particle defining type I is the chylomicron, not VLDL.

preguntas.q: In type I hyperlipoproteinemia, accumulation of chylomicrons in serum leads to marked elevation of which lipid parameters?

e.correcta: Because chylomicrons carry both triglyceride and a smaller amount of cholesterol, their massive accumulation raises both serum triglycerides (often exceeding 1000 mg/dL) and total cholesterol, though the triglyceride elevation is proportionally far greater — this combination, along with lactescent plasma, is characteristic of the disorder.

incorrectas.A: While triglycerides are the dominant and most dramatically elevated lipid, chylomicrons also carry cholesterol, so cholesterol is elevated as well, making "triglycerides only" an incomplete description of the lipid profile.
incorrectas.B: LDL cholesterol elevation is the hallmark of type IIa (familial hypercholesterolemia) from LDL receptor dysfunction, not the pattern seen in type I, which reflects chylomicron rather than LDL accumulation.
incorrectas.D: HDL cholesterol is typically normal or even decreased in hyperchylomicronemia rather than elevated, since the underlying defect does not increase HDL production.

preguntas.q: Which familial dyslipidemia classically presents with recurrent acute pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas, and hepatosplenomegaly due to massive chylomicron accumulation?

e.correcta: Type I hyperlipoproteinemia's massive chylomicronemia (triglycerides often >1000 mg/dL) causes lipid accumulation in the pancreatic microvasculature (triggering pancreatitis), reticuloendothelial uptake in liver and spleen (hepatosplenomegaly), and eruptive cutaneous xanthomas, classically appearing after fatty meals and in childhood.

incorrectas.A: Type IIa presents with markedly elevated LDL, tendon xanthomas, corneal arcus, and premature atherosclerosis or MI, not the acute pancreatitis and hepatosplenomegaly picture driven by chylomicron overload.
incorrectas.B: Type III dysbetalipoproteinemia causes palmar and tuberoeruptive xanthomas along with premature atherosclerosis due to IDL/remnant accumulation, a different clinical picture from chylomicron-driven pancreatitis.
incorrectas.D: Type IV hypertriglyceridemia (elevated VLDL) can also cause pancreatitis at very high triglyceride levels, but it is not classically associated with hepatosplenomegaly; the full picture described here, driven by massive chylomicronemia, is characteristic of type I.

preguntas.q: Unlike most other familial dyslipidemias, type I hyperlipoproteinemia (hyperchylomicronemia) is notable for NOT increasing the risk of which condition?

e.correcta: Despite extremely high triglyceride levels, chylomicrons are too large to cross the arterial endothelium and be taken up in the vessel wall the way smaller, denser lipoproteins like LDL or IDL remnants can, so type I hyperlipoproteinemia does not confer increased atherosclerosis risk — unlike types IIa, III, and IV.

incorrectas.A: Acute pancreatitis is, if anything, a classic complication of type I due to lipid overload injuring pancreatic capillaries and acinar tissue from extremely elevated triglycerides, not a risk that is absent.
incorrectas.C: Eruptive xanthomas are a well-recognized cutaneous manifestation of type I from chylomicron accumulation in dermal macrophages, not a spared complication.
incorrectas.D: Hepatosplenomegaly does occur in type I from reticuloendothelial uptake of excess chylomicrons in liver and spleen, so this is not the complication that type I is notable for avoiding.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of type IIa familial dyslipidemia (familial hypercholesterolemia), caused by defective or absent LDL receptors?

e.correcta: Type IIa familial hypercholesterolemia is autosomal dominant, so heterozygotes with one defective LDL receptor allele already have markedly elevated LDL and premature atherosclerosis, while homozygotes with both alleles defective have even more severe, often fatal childhood disease — a dose-dependent phenotype typical of dominant disorders with partial gene-dosage effect.

incorrectas.A: Autosomal recessive inheritance describes type I hyperlipoproteinemia (LPL/ApoC-II deficiency), where heterozygous carriers of a single defective allele are typically unaffected, unlike the situation in type IIa.
incorrectas.C: X-linked dominant inheritance is not the pattern for LDL receptor gene mutations, which reside on an autosome (chromosome 19), not the X chromosome.
incorrectas.D: While common polygenic hypercholesterolemia exists in the general population, the classic familial (monogenic) type IIa disorder tested here follows a clear autosomal dominant single-gene inheritance pattern, not multifactorial/polygenic inheritance.

preguntas.q: Which serum lipoprotein is characteristically elevated in type IIa familial dyslipidemia?

e.correcta: Type IIa familial dyslipidemia (familial hypercholesterolemia) is caused by a defective or absent LDL receptor, most often due to autosomal dominant mutations in the LDLR gene, so LDL particles cannot be cleared from the plasma by hepatocytes. The result is a marked, isolated elevation in circulating LDL, which drives cholesterol deposition in tissues (xanthomas, corneal arcus) and accelerates atherosclerosis.

incorrectas.B: VLDL is the lipoprotein elevated in type IV familial dyslipidemia (familial hypertriglyceridemia), which reflects increased hepatic VLDL secretion rather than a defect in LDL receptor-mediated clearance.
incorrectas.C: Chylomicrons are elevated in type I familial dyslipidemia due to lipoprotein lipase or apoC-II deficiency, impairing chylomicron clearance from dietary fat — a distinct defect from the LDL receptor problem in type IIa.
incorrectas.D: HDL is not elevated in any of the classic familial dyslipidemias; it is the lipoprotein responsible for reverse cholesterol transport and is typically low, not high, in most dyslipidemic states.

preguntas.q: Which serum lipid is characteristically elevated in type IIa familial dyslipidemia?

e.correcta: Type IIa familial dyslipidemia results from defective LDL receptors, causing LDL particles — which are cholesterol-rich — to accumulate in the blood. This isolated elevation in serum cholesterol (with normal triglycerides) is exactly why the disease is also called familial hypercholesterolemia.

incorrectas.A: Triglycerides are the lipid elevated in type IV dyslipidemia (hypertriglyceridemia) due to increased VLDL production, not in type IIa, where triglyceride levels remain relatively normal.
incorrectas.C: Phospholipids are structural components of lipoprotein particle membranes but are not the lipid species used to classify or characterize familial dyslipidemias; cholesterol and triglycerides are the clinically measured markers.
incorrectas.D: Free fatty acids circulate bound to albumin and reflect adipose tissue lipolysis, not LDL receptor function; they are not the abnormality driving type IIa familial hypercholesterolemia.

preguntas.q: Which type of familial dyslipidemia classically presents with corneal arcus (a whitish ring in the peripheral cornea)?

e.correcta: Type IIa familial hypercholesterolemia causes chronically elevated LDL cholesterol that deposits in peripheral tissues, producing tendon xanthomas (especially Achilles), xanthelasma, and corneal arcus — a lipid ring at the corneal periphery from cholesterol deposition in Descemet's membrane. These findings, occurring at a young age, are a clinical clue pointing toward a genetic LDL receptor defect rather than an acquired dyslipidemia.

incorrectas.A: Type I dyslipidemia causes massive chylomicronemia from lipoprotein lipase or apoC-II deficiency, presenting with eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis, and pancreatitis rather than corneal arcus or accelerated atherosclerosis.
incorrectas.B: Type IV dyslipidemia is driven by VLDL overproduction and hypertriglyceridemia; it can cause eruptive xanthomas and pancreatitis at very high triglyceride levels but is not classically associated with corneal arcus.
incorrectas.D: Type III dysbetalipoproteinemia results from defective apoE (often apoE2/E2), causing accumulation of chylomicron and VLDL remnants and producing palmar and tuberoeruptive xanthomas rather than the classic corneal arcus of hypercholesterolemia.

preguntas.q: A young patient with type IIa familial hypercholesterolemia asks about cardiovascular risk. Which statement best describes the expected risk?

o.A: No increased risk, since only LDL cholesterol is affected and triglycerides remain normal
o.B: Risk only becomes relevant after age 60, similar to the general population
o.C: Risk is mitigated because HDL levels rise proportionally to compensate
o.D: Markedly increased risk, with accelerated atherosclerosis that can cause myocardial infarction before age 20

e.correcta: Because the LDL receptor defect causes lifelong, severe elevation in LDL cholesterol from birth, cholesterol deposition in arterial walls begins early and progresses rapidly. In homozygous or severe heterozygous cases, this accelerated atherosclerosis can cause myocardial infarction in childhood or the teenage years, making early lipid screening and aggressive LDL-lowering therapy essential once the diagnosis is suspected.

incorrectas.A: Isolated LDL elevation is precisely what drives atherogenesis — LDL is the lipoprotein most strongly linked to plaque formation, so a normal triglyceride level does not protect against cardiovascular risk in this disease.
incorrectas.B: The risk in familial hypercholesterolemia is present from early life, not delayed to older age, because the genetic receptor defect exposes vessel walls to high LDL burden for decades longer than in typical age-related atherosclerosis.
incorrectas.C: HDL levels do not rise to compensate in familial hypercholesterolemia; the disease is defined by an LDL receptor defect that affects LDL clearance specifically, and HDL metabolism is not protectively upregulated in response.

preguntas.q: A patient with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (allele frequency ~1:500) would be expected to have a total serum cholesterol of approximately what level?

e.correcta: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia involves one normal and one defective LDLR allele, so roughly half the normal number of functional LDL receptors remain, allowing partial LDL clearance. This produces a substantially elevated but not extreme cholesterol level, typically around 300 mg/dL, still high enough to cause premature coronary artery disease if untreated.

incorrectas.B: A cholesterol level of ~150 mg/dL is within the normal range and would not be expected in a patient with a defective LDL receptor allele, since even one nonfunctional allele meaningfully impairs LDL clearance.
incorrectas.C: ~500 mg/dL is higher than typical for the heterozygous state and would raise suspicion for an additional lipid abnormality or poor treatment adherence rather than representing the classic heterozygous FH phenotype.
incorrectas.D: Cholesterol levels of 700+ mg/dL are seen in the rare homozygous form of familial hypercholesterolemia, where both LDL receptor alleles are defective and essentially no functional receptor-mediated clearance remains — far more severe than the heterozygous case.

preguntas.q: A very rare patient with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia would be expected to have a total serum cholesterol of approximately what level?

e.correcta: In homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, both LDLR alleles are defective, so hepatocytes have essentially no functional LDL receptors to clear circulating LDL. This produces extreme cholesterol elevations, often 700 mg/dL or higher, along with severe cutaneous and tendon xanthomas and atherosclerosis so aggressive that myocardial infarction can occur in childhood.

incorrectas.A: ~300 mg/dL is the level expected in the heterozygous form, where one functional LDLR allele still permits partial LDL clearance — the homozygous form is far more severe because no functional receptor remains.
incorrectas.C: ~450 mg/dL would be an intermediate value that does not match either classic phenotype well; the homozygous state is defined by near-complete absence of functional LDL receptors and produces much higher levels.
incorrectas.D: ~200 mg/dL is only mildly elevated and is inconsistent with a complete absence of functional LDL receptors, which removes the primary mechanism for clearing LDL from plasma.

preguntas.q: What is the typical mode of inheritance of type IV familial dyslipidemia (familial hypertriglyceridemia)?

e.correcta: Type IV familial dyslipidemia follows an autosomal dominant pattern, meaning a single copy of the causative variant (affecting hepatic VLDL overproduction) is sufficient to produce the hypertriglyceridemic phenotype, often with variable expressivity influenced by diet, obesity, and alcohol use. This dominant inheritance means affected patients often have a parent or child who is also affected, which is useful for family screening.

incorrectas.A: Autosomal recessive inheritance would require two defective alleles to manifest disease; type IV dyslipidemia does not follow this pattern, unlike some rare recessive lipid disorders such as certain forms of type I hyperchylomicronemia.
incorrectas.B: X-linked recessive inheritance would predominantly affect males and show a distinct pedigree pattern with no male-to-male transmission; familial hypertriglyceridemia is not linked to the X chromosome.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance is transmitted exclusively through the maternal line and affects all offspring of an affected mother; this pattern does not apply to type IV dyslipidemia, which is a classic autosomal dominant lipid disorder.

preguntas.q: Which serum lipoprotein is characteristically elevated in type IV familial dyslipidemia?

e.correcta: Type IV familial dyslipidemia is driven by increased hepatic synthesis and secretion of VLDL, the triglyceride-rich lipoprotein produced by the liver to export endogenous fat. This VLDL overproduction raises plasma triglycerides substantially while LDL cholesterol often stays near normal, distinguishing it clinically from the LDL-driven type IIa pattern.

incorrectas.A: LDL is the lipoprotein elevated in type IIa familial hypercholesterolemia due to defective LDL receptors, a completely different mechanism from the VLDL overproduction seen in type IV.
incorrectas.B: Chylomicrons are elevated in type I dyslipidemia from lipoprotein lipase or apoC-II deficiency, reflecting impaired clearance of dietary (exogenous) fat rather than increased hepatic VLDL output.
incorrectas.C: HDL is not the lipoprotein elevated in any familial dyslipidemia; in fact, hypertriglyceridemic states like type IV are often associated with low HDL due to increased cholesteryl ester transfer protein-mediated exchange.

preguntas.q: Which serum lipid is characteristically elevated in type IV familial dyslipidemia?

e.correcta: Type IV dyslipidemia arises from excess hepatic VLDL secretion, and since VLDL is the primary carrier of endogenously synthesized triglycerides in the blood, the resulting lipid abnormality is a marked rise in serum triglycerides. This is why the condition is also known as familial hypertriglyceridemia, and very high levels also carry a risk of acute pancreatitis.

incorrectas.B: Cholesterol is the lipid elevated in type IIa familial hypercholesterolemia due to defective LDL receptors; type IV instead predominantly raises triglycerides while cholesterol may remain closer to normal.
incorrectas.C: Phospholipids form the outer monolayer of lipoprotein particles but are not the clinically measured or pathologically elevated lipid in type IV dyslipidemia.
incorrectas.D: Free fatty acids are released from adipose tissue by lipolysis and circulate bound to albumin; they are not the lipid species that defines the type IV hypertriglyceridemic phenotype, which is specifically about VLDL-carried triglycerides.

preguntas.q: Cholesterol synthesis begins with which starting molecule?

e.correcta: Cholesterol biosynthesis begins with acetyl-CoA, two molecules of which condense to form acetoacetyl-CoA, which then combines with a third acetyl-CoA to form HMG-CoA — the substrate for the rate-limiting enzyme HMG-CoA reductase. This pathway links cholesterol synthesis to the same acetyl-CoA pool used in fatty acid synthesis and the citric acid cycle, reflecting how central this two-carbon unit is to cellular metabolism.

incorrectas.A: Malonyl-CoA is the key building block for fatty acid synthesis, produced from acetyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA carboxylase, but it is not the starting molecule for the cholesterol synthesis pathway, which begins directly from acetyl-CoA condensation.
incorrectas.C: Glycerol-3-phosphate is the backbone used to synthesize triglycerides and phospholipids, not cholesterol, since cholesterol's structure is built from isoprenoid units derived from acetyl-CoA rather than a glycerol backbone.
incorrectas.D: Pyruvate is a central glycolytic end product that feeds into the citric acid cycle or gluconeogenesis, but it is not the direct precursor used to initiate cholesterol synthesis; acetyl-CoA itself is the required starting unit.

preguntas.q: In which cellular compartment does cholesterol synthesis primarily take place?

e.correcta: Cholesterol synthesis occurs in the cytoplasm, with key steps taking place on the cytosolic face of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, including the action of HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme embedded in the ER membrane facing the cytosol. This cytoplasmic localization contrasts with beta-oxidation and the citric acid cycle, which occur in the mitochondria, highlighting how anabolic lipid pathways and catabolic energy pathways are compartmentalized differently within the cell.

incorrectas.A: The mitochondrial matrix is the site of beta-oxidation and the citric acid cycle, both catabolic pathways, not cholesterol synthesis, which is an anabolic pathway occurring in a separate cellular compartment.
incorrectas.B: The nucleus houses DNA transcription and processing machinery, including the SREBP transcription factors that regulate cholesterol synthesis gene expression, but the actual enzymatic synthesis of cholesterol itself happens in the cytoplasm, not the nucleus.
incorrectas.D: The Golgi apparatus is involved in protein and lipid trafficking and post-translational modification, not in the enzymatic steps of cholesterol biosynthesis, which occur earlier in the cytosol and ER.

preguntas.q: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis?

e.correcta: HMG-CoA reductase converts HMG-CoA to mevalonate and is the committed, rate-limiting step of cholesterol biosynthesis. It is tightly regulated by cholesterol levels via SREBP-mediated transcription and by insulin/glucagon-driven phosphorylation, and it is the pharmacologic target of statin drugs, which competitively inhibit this exact enzyme to lower LDL cholesterol.

incorrectas.A: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme of fatty acid synthesis, converting acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA — a parallel but distinct lipid pathway from cholesterol synthesis, which does not use malonyl-CoA as an intermediate.
incorrectas.B: Citrate synthase catalyzes the first step of the citric acid cycle in the mitochondria, combining acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate; it has no regulatory role in the cytoplasmic cholesterol synthesis pathway.
incorrectas.C: HMG-CoA synthase catalyzes an earlier step, forming HMG-CoA from acetoacetyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA, but this step is not rate-limiting; the pathway's flux is controlled downstream at the HMG-CoA reductase step instead.

preguntas.q: HMG-CoA reductase requires two molecules of which cofactor to reduce HMG-CoA to mevalonate?

e.correcta: HMG-CoA reductase uses two molecules of NADPH to reduce HMG-CoA to mevalonate, consuming reducing equivalents generated largely by the pentose phosphate pathway. This reflects a general pattern in biosynthetic (anabolic) reactions, which typically rely on NADPH as the electron donor, in contrast to catabolic pathways that generate NADH and FADH2 for the electron transport chain.

incorrectas.B: NADH is generated primarily by catabolic pathways like glycolysis and the citric acid cycle and is used to fuel oxidative phosphorylation, not as the reducing cofactor for biosynthetic reactions like cholesterol synthesis.
incorrectas.C: FADH2 is generated in the citric acid cycle (e.g., by succinate dehydrogenase) and beta-oxidation and feeds electrons into complex II of the electron transport chain; it is not the cofactor used by HMG-CoA reductase.
incorrectas.D: ATP provides energy for many cellular processes but is not the specific reducing cofactor required by HMG-CoA reductase; the enzyme's reduction reaction specifically depends on NADPH, not high-energy phosphate bonds.

preguntas.q: Which intermediate of the cholesterol synthesis pathway is important for N-linked glycosylation of proteins?

e.correcta: Dolichol phosphate is a branch-point intermediate of the cholesterol synthesis pathway (derived from isoprenoid units) that serves as the lipid anchor on which oligosaccharide chains are assembled in the rough ER before being transferred en bloc to asparagine residues during N-linked glycosylation. This illustrates how the cholesterol pathway is not purely about making cholesterol — its isoprenoid intermediates are repurposed for other essential cellular functions.

incorrectas.A: Squalene is an intermediate further along the pathway toward cholesterol, formed from farnesyl pyrophosphate, but it is cyclized into sterols rather than being used for protein glycosylation.
incorrectas.C: Lanosterol is the first sterol formed after squalene cyclization and is a direct precursor to cholesterol itself, but it does not serve a role in attaching oligosaccharides to proteins.
incorrectas.D: Mevalonate is an early intermediate formed by HMG-CoA reductase and is the precursor to all downstream isoprenoids, but it is several steps removed from dolichol phosphate and is not itself used in glycosylation.

preguntas.q: Which substance is the primary regulator of cell membrane fluidity?

e.correcta: Cholesterol intercalates between phospholipid tails in the plasma membrane and acts as a fluidity buffer — at high temperatures it restricts phospholipid movement and decreases fluidity, while at low temperatures it prevents tight packing and maintains fluidity. This dual buffering effect is why cholesterol content is a key determinant of membrane rigidity and permeability across a range of physiological temperatures.

incorrectas.A: Phosphatidylcholine is a major structural phospholipid of the membrane bilayer, but it does not actively regulate fluidity across temperature changes the way cholesterol's rigid steroid ring structure does.
incorrectas.B: Sphingomyelin is a sphingolipid that contributes to membrane structure and is enriched in lipid rafts, but it is not the primary dynamic regulator of overall membrane fluidity; it works alongside cholesterol rather than replacing its regulatory role.
incorrectas.D: Ceramide is a sphingolipid backbone involved in signaling (e.g., apoptosis) and is a precursor to sphingomyelin and other sphingolipids, but it is not recognized as the primary modulator of bulk membrane fluidity.

preguntas.q: Which substance serves as the precursor to bile acids, steroid hormones, and vitamin D?

e.correcta: Cholesterol is the common structural precursor for bile acids (synthesized in the liver via 7-alpha-hydroxylase), all steroid hormones (via cytochrome P450 side-chain cleavage enzyme in steroidogenic tissues), and vitamin D3 (via UV-mediated conversion of 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin). This central role explains why cholesterol, despite its reputation in atherosclerosis, is biologically essential rather than purely harmful.

incorrectas.A: Acetyl-CoA is the initial building block that feeds into cholesterol synthesis, but it is several enzymatic steps removed from being the direct precursor of bile acids, steroids, or vitamin D — cholesterol itself is the immediate precursor.
incorrectas.B: Mevalonate is an early intermediate in the cholesterol synthesis pathway formed by HMG-CoA reductase, but downstream steps must still convert it to cholesterol before bile acids, steroids, or vitamin D can be made.
incorrectas.C: Squalene is a later intermediate that gets cyclized to lanosterol and then converted to cholesterol; it is not itself the molecule from which bile acids, steroid hormones, or vitamin D are directly synthesized.

preguntas.q: Approximately what percentage of plasma cholesterol is esterified by the enzyme LCAT (lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase)?

e.correcta: LCAT, activated by apoA-I on HDL particles, transfers a fatty acid from lecithin (phosphatidylcholine) to free cholesterol, converting it into cholesteryl ester that is sequestered in the hydrophobic core of HDL. This esterification of roughly two-thirds of plasma cholesterol is a key step in reverse cholesterol transport, allowing HDL to efficiently carry cholesterol from peripheral tissues back to the liver.
