incorrectas.B: Corneal clouding results from glycosaminoglycan deposition in the cornea and is characteristic of Hurler syndrome (and notably absent in Hunter syndrome), reflecting mucopolysaccharide accumulation rather than the sphingolipid-driven demyelination seen in Krabbe disease.
incorrectas.C: Cataracts are not a classic feature of Krabbe disease; they are more commonly associated with other metabolic or genetic conditions (e.g., galactosemia, Alport syndrome) and are not part of the globoid cell leukodystrophy phenotype.

preguntas.q: In addition to peripheral neuropathy, which neurodevelopmental feature is characteristic of infantile Krabbe disease?

e.correcta: Psychosine toxicity to oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells in Krabbe disease produces a globoid cell leukodystrophy affecting both the central and peripheral nervous systems, so infants classically present with irritability, developmental delay (with regression of previously acquired milestones), peripheral neuropathy, optic atrophy, and spasticity. This combined central and peripheral demyelination is a distinguishing feature of Krabbe disease compared with storage diseases confined to the CNS or reticuloendothelial system alone.

incorrectas.B: Precocious puberty is an endocrine phenomenon related to premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis (e.g., McCune-Albright syndrome, CNS tumors), not a feature of a demyelinating lysosomal storage disease like Krabbe disease.
incorrectas.C: Krabbe disease does not selectively spare hearing; it produces widespread neurodegeneration from global white matter damage, so isolated preserved hearing does not fit its clinical picture.
incorrectas.D: Macrocephaly can be seen in some other leukodystrophies (e.g., Canavan disease, Alexander disease) with relatively preserved early development, but Krabbe disease is instead characterized by progressive developmental delay/regression rather than isolated head enlargement with normal cognition.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme converts sulfatides to galactocerebroside, and is deficient in metachromatic leukodystrophy?

e.correcta: Arylsulfatase A normally removes the sulfate group from sulfatides (cerebroside sulfate), converting them to galactocerebroside for further degradation; when this enzyme is deficient, sulfatides accumulate within the myelin sheaths of the central and peripheral nervous systems, causing the progressive demyelination that defines metachromatic leukodystrophy. The accumulated sulfatide deposits stain metachromatically (a different color than the dye applied) on tissue biopsy, which is the origin of the disease's name.

incorrectas.A: Galactocerebrosidase is the enzyme deficient in Krabbe disease, where it normally degrades galactocerebroside — essentially the step downstream of the arylsulfatase A reaction — representing a distinct sphingolipidosis with a different accumulated substrate (psychosine/galactocerebroside rather than sulfatide).
incorrectas.C: Alpha-galactosidase A is deficient in Fabry disease, where its absence causes accumulation of ceramide trihexoside (globotriaosylceramide), an entirely different glycosphingolipid pathway from the sulfatide metabolism affected in metachromatic leukodystrophy.
incorrectas.D: Hexosaminidase A is deficient in Tay-Sachs disease, leading to GM2 ganglioside accumulation in neurons and the classic cherry-red macular spot, a distinct enzyme-substrate pair from arylsulfatase A and sulfatides.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of metachromatic leukodystrophy, caused by arylsulfatase A deficiency?

e.correcta: Metachromatic leukodystrophy is caused by biallelic mutations in the autosomal ARSA gene, following an autosomal recessive pattern typical of most lysosomal storage diseases — an affected child must inherit one nonfunctional allele from each carrier parent. This mirrors the pattern seen in Krabbe disease, Gaucher disease, Tay-Sachs disease, and Niemann-Pick disease, all grouped together as autosomal recessive sphingolipidoses, in contrast to the X-linked recessive Fabry disease and Hunter syndrome.

incorrectas.A: X-linked recessive inheritance applies to Fabry disease and Hunter syndrome because their causative genes (GLA and IDS) sit on the X chromosome; the ARSA gene responsible for metachromatic leukodystrophy is autosomal, not X-linked.
incorrectas.B: X-linked dominant inheritance would require only a single mutant allele to cause disease in either sex and is not the pattern seen in any of the classic lysosomal storage diseases, including metachromatic leukodystrophy.
incorrectas.D: Autosomal dominant inheritance is inconsistent with an enzyme-deficiency disorder like metachromatic leukodystrophy, since a single normal ARSA allele typically provides sufficient enzymatic activity to prevent overt disease.

preguntas.q: Deficiency of arylsulfatase A in metachromatic leukodystrophy leads to accumulation of which substrate?

e.correcta: Without functional arylsulfatase A, sulfatides (cerebroside sulfate) cannot be desulfated and degraded, so they accumulate within lysosomes of oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells, and other tissues, producing progressive demyelination of the central and peripheral nervous systems. The accumulated sulfatide deposits show characteristic metachromatic staining on biopsy, which both names the disease and helps confirm the diagnosis histologically.

incorrectas.A: Ceramide trihexoside (globotriaosylceramide) accumulates in Fabry disease due to alpha-galactosidase A deficiency, a distinct glycosphingolipid buildup unrelated to the sulfatide metabolism disrupted in metachromatic leukodystrophy.
incorrectas.B: GM2 ganglioside accumulates in Tay-Sachs disease from hexosaminidase A deficiency, producing neuronal lysosomal storage and a cherry-red macular spot, a different substrate and enzyme pathway than arylsulfatase A/sulfatide.
incorrectas.C: Glucocerebroside accumulates in Gaucher disease due to deficient glucocerebrosidase, forming the characteristic 'crumpled tissue paper' macrophages, unrelated to the sulfatide accumulation seen in metachromatic leukodystrophy.

preguntas.q: Hurler syndrome, caused by alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency, is inherited in what pattern?

e.correcta: Hurler syndrome results from mutations in the IDUA gene encoding alpha-L-iduronidase, located on an autosome, and follows an autosomal recessive pattern requiring two defective alleles. This is an important contrast to Hunter syndrome, the other major mucopolysaccharidosis, caused by deficiency of a different enzyme (iduronate-2-sulfatase) encoded on the X chromosome and therefore X-linked recessive — a classic exam pairing used to distinguish the two similarly presenting MPS disorders.

incorrectas.A: X-linked recessive inheritance describes Hunter syndrome, the milder mucopolysaccharidosis lacking corneal clouding, because its causative gene (IDS) lies on the X chromosome; Hurler syndrome's IDUA gene is autosomal.
incorrectas.C: Autosomal dominant inheritance would require only one mutant allele to produce the phenotype, which does not fit an enzyme-deficiency storage disorder like Hurler syndrome, where a single functional IDUA allele is generally adequate.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance is transmitted maternally through mitochondrial DNA and characterizes disorders like MELAS or Leigh syndrome, an entirely different genetic mechanism from the nuclear autosomal recessive defect causing Hurler syndrome.

preguntas.q: Deficiency of alpha-L-iduronidase in Hurler syndrome leads to lysosomal accumulation of which substrates?

e.correcta: Alpha-L-iduronidase is required to degrade the glycosaminoglycans heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate; without it, these mucopolysaccharides accumulate in lysosomes throughout connective tissue, viscera, and the CNS, producing the coarse facial features, corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly, airway obstruction, and developmental delay seen in Hurler syndrome. The identical substrates accumulate in Hunter syndrome as well, since both diseases disrupt sequential steps in the same glycosaminoglycan degradation pathway.

incorrectas.B: Keratan sulfate and chondroitin sulfate accumulate in other mucopolysaccharidoses (such as Morquio syndrome), which result from deficiency of different enzymes in the glycosaminoglycan degradation pathway, not alpha-L-iduronidase.
incorrectas.C: GM2 ganglioside and globotriaosylceramide are the accumulated substrates in Tay-Sachs disease and Fabry disease respectively — sphingolipidoses caused by entirely different enzyme defects than the mucopolysaccharide-processing defect in Hurler syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Glucocerebroside and sphingomyelin accumulate in Gaucher disease and Niemann-Pick disease respectively, both sphingolipidoses unrelated to the glycosaminoglycan accumulation that defines the mucopolysaccharidoses like Hurler syndrome.

preguntas.q: Which clinical feature is present in Hurler syndrome but characteristically absent in Hunter syndrome, helping distinguish the two mucopolysaccharidoses?

e.correcta: Hurler syndrome causes corneal clouding due to glycosaminoglycan deposition within corneal tissue, whereas Hunter syndrome characteristically spares the cornea — one of the classic bedside distinctions tested between the two mucopolysaccharidoses despite their shared accumulated substrates (heparan and dermatan sulfate). The mnemonic 'Hunters see clearly (no corneal clouding) but act aggressively' helps recall that Hunter syndrome also tends toward milder somatic disease but more behavioral/aggressive features than Hurler syndrome.

incorrectas.B: X-linked inheritance is actually the pattern seen in Hunter syndrome, not Hurler syndrome, which is autosomal recessive — the opposite pairing from what the question asks about clinical corneal findings.
incorrectas.C: Aggressive behavior is a feature more classically associated with Hunter syndrome, not Hurler syndrome, and does not represent the distinguishing corneal finding the question is asking about.
incorrectas.D: A cherry-red macular spot is a feature of the sphingolipidoses Tay-Sachs disease and Niemann-Pick disease, not the mucopolysaccharidoses Hurler or Hunter syndrome, which instead show corneal clouding (Hurler) or its absence (Hunter).

preguntas.q: Deposition of glycosaminoglycans in the tracheobronchial tissue of Hurler syndrome commonly leads to which complication, alongside developmental delay and hepatosplenomegaly?

e.correcta: Accumulated heparan and dermatan sulfate infiltrate soft tissues including the tonsils, adenoids, and tracheobronchial walls in Hurler syndrome, thickening and narrowing the airway; combined with a large tongue and coarse facial features, this produces airway obstruction that can manifest as obstructive sleep apnea and difficulty with intubation. Recognizing airway obstruction as a major cause of morbidity (and anesthesia risk) in Hurler syndrome is clinically important, since these patients often require careful airway management during any procedure.

incorrectas.A: Bronchiectasis refers to irreversible bronchial dilation typically from chronic infection or obstruction (e.g., cystic fibrosis), a structural airway disease distinct from the soft-tissue GAG infiltration causing obstruction in Hurler syndrome.
incorrectas.B: Spontaneous pneumothorax results from rupture of subpleural blebs or connective tissue fragility (e.g., in Marfan syndrome or COPD), a mechanism unrelated to the glycosaminoglycan deposition causing airway narrowing in Hurler syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Pulmonary fibrosis involves scarring of lung parenchyma from chronic inflammatory or interstitial lung disease, a different anatomic and pathologic process than the upper/central airway narrowing caused by GAG accumulation in Hurler syndrome.

preguntas.q: Hunter syndrome, caused by iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency, follows what pattern of inheritance?

e.correcta: Hunter syndrome results from mutations in the IDS gene encoding iduronate-2-sulfatase, located on the X chromosome, making the disease X-linked recessive — affected males are hemizygous and fully symptomatic, while carrier females are typically unaffected or only mildly affected. Along with Fabry disease, Hunter syndrome is one of the two classic X-linked recessive lysosomal storage diseases, standing out against the otherwise autosomal recessive pattern of most other storage diseases (including its close mimic, Hurler syndrome).

incorrectas.A: Autosomal recessive inheritance describes Hurler syndrome, the related mucopolysaccharidosis caused by deficiency of a different enzyme (alpha-L-iduronidase) encoded on an autosome, not the X-linked IDS gene responsible for Hunter syndrome.
incorrectas.B: Autosomal dominant inheritance is not seen in any of the classic lysosomal storage diseases, since a single functional enzyme allele is generally sufficient to prevent disease in these recessive enzyme-deficiency disorders.
incorrectas.C: Mitochondrial inheritance is transmitted exclusively through the maternal line via mitochondrial DNA, an entirely different genetic mechanism from the X-linked nuclear gene defect that causes Hunter syndrome.

preguntas.q: Iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency in Hunter syndrome causes lysosomal accumulation of which substrates?

e.correcta: Iduronate-2-sulfatase acts in the same glycosaminoglycan degradation pathway as alpha-L-iduronidase, so its deficiency in Hunter syndrome causes accumulation of the identical substrates seen in Hurler syndrome — heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate — within lysosomes of connective tissue and viscera. Despite sharing the same accumulated GAGs, Hunter syndrome tends to have a milder somatic phenotype without corneal clouding, illustrating how different enzymes acting on the same substrate pathway can still produce distinguishable clinical syndromes.

incorrectas.A: Cerebroside sulfate accumulates in metachromatic leukodystrophy and globotriaosylceramide accumulates in Fabry disease — both sphingolipids degraded through entirely different enzymatic pathways than the glycosaminoglycan processing disrupted in Hunter syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Keratan sulfate and chondroitin sulfate accumulate in other mucopolysaccharidoses (e.g., Morquio syndrome) that involve different sulfatase or glycosidase enzymes than iduronate-2-sulfatase.
incorrectas.D: GM2 ganglioside and glucocerebroside accumulate in Tay-Sachs disease and Gaucher disease respectively, both sphingolipidoses that are biochemically distinct from the glycosaminoglycan accumulation defining Hunter syndrome.

preguntas.q: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes Hunter syndrome from Hurler syndrome?

o.A: Hunter syndrome has no corneal clouding
o.B: Hunter syndrome has prominent corneal clouding
o.D: Hunter syndrome features a cherry-red macular spot

e.correcta: Unlike Hurler syndrome, Hunter syndrome characteristically does not cause corneal clouding, even though both diseases share accumulation of the same glycosaminoglycans (heparan and dermatan sulfate); this absence of corneal involvement, combined with more prominent aggressive behavior, is a key bedside differentiator between the two mucopolysaccharidoses. This distinction is high-yield because the two diseases otherwise look nearly identical biochemically.

incorrectas.B: Prominent corneal clouding is characteristic of Hurler syndrome, not Hunter syndrome — this option describes the opposite of Hunter syndrome's actual presentation.
incorrectas.C: Hunter syndrome is X-linked recessive, not autosomal recessive; autosomal recessive inheritance instead describes Hurler syndrome, making this an inversion of the correct inheritance pattern.
incorrectas.D: A cherry-red macular spot is a feature of sphingolipidoses like Tay-Sachs disease and Niemann-Pick disease, not of the mucopolysaccharidoses Hunter or Hurler syndrome, which instead affect connective tissue via glycosaminoglycan accumulation.

preguntas.q: Electron microscopy showing lysosomes with an 'onion skin' (whorled) appearance is characteristic of which lysosomal storage disease?

e.correcta: In Tay-Sachs disease, deficient hexosaminidase A allows GM2 ganglioside to accumulate progressively within neuronal lysosomes, and on electron microscopy this produces a characteristic whorled, concentric 'onion skin' lamellar pattern. This buildup drives the neurodegeneration responsible for progressive motor and cognitive decline, seizures, and the classic cherry-red macular spot, typically presenting in infancy without hepatosplenomegaly (unlike Niemann-Pick disease).

incorrectas.A: Niemann-Pick disease is characterized histologically by lipid-laden 'foam cells' (macrophages distended with sphingomyelin), a different lysosomal appearance than the onion-skin lamellar pattern seen with GM2 ganglioside in Tay-Sachs disease.
incorrectas.C: Gaucher disease shows macrophages with a 'crumpled tissue paper' cytoplasmic appearance due to glucocerebroside accumulation, histologically distinct from the onion-skin lysosomal pattern of Tay-Sachs disease.
incorrectas.D: Fabry disease can show lamellar inclusion bodies ('zebra bodies') in some tissues due to globotriaosylceramide accumulation, but the classically tested 'onion skin' lysosomal description belongs to Tay-Sachs disease's GM2 ganglioside accumulation.

preguntas.q: Which lysosomal storage disease is characterized by lipid-laden macrophages known as 'foam cells'?

e.correcta: Niemann-Pick disease results from deficient sphingomyelinase, causing sphingomyelin to accumulate within macrophages throughout the reticuloendothelial system and CNS; these lipid-engorged macrophages appear as characteristic 'foam cells' on histology. Clinically this manifests with hepatosplenomegaly, progressive neurodegeneration, and (in some cases) a cherry-red macular spot, distinguishing it from Tay-Sachs disease, which shares the cherry-red spot but lacks organomegaly.

incorrectas.A: Gaucher disease produces macrophages with a distinctive 'crumpled tissue paper' cytoplasmic appearance from glucocerebroside accumulation, a histologically different pattern from the foam cells of sphingomyelin-laden macrophages in Niemann-Pick disease.
incorrectas.B: Fabry disease causes globotriaosylceramide accumulation predominantly in vascular endothelium and other tissues, producing lamellar 'zebra bodies' rather than the classic macrophage foam cells seen in Niemann-Pick disease.
incorrectas.D: Hurler syndrome involves glycosaminoglycan accumulation in connective tissue and does not produce the lipid-laden foam cell macrophages characteristic of the sphingolipidosis Niemann-Pick disease.

preguntas.q: A cherry-red spot on the macula without hepatosplenomegaly is characteristic of which lysosomal storage disease?

e.correcta: Tay-Sachs disease results from hexosaminidase A deficiency, causing GM2 ganglioside to accumulate specifically within neurons (including retinal ganglion cells), which produces the classic cherry-red macular spot from the pale, lipid-laden ganglion cells surrounding the comparatively normal-colored fovea. Because the enzymatic defect in Tay-Sachs disease is largely confined to the CNS and does not affect visceral macrophages the way Niemann-Pick disease does, hepatosplenomegaly is characteristically absent — a key point used to distinguish the two conditions despite their shared retinal finding.

incorrectas.A: Niemann-Pick disease also produces a cherry-red macular spot but, unlike Tay-Sachs disease, it is accompanied by hepatosplenomegaly because sphingomyelin accumulates in macrophages throughout the reticuloendothelial system, not just in neurons.
incorrectas.B: Gaucher disease does not typically present with a cherry-red macular spot; instead it is characterized by hepatosplenomegaly, bone crises, and glucocerebroside-laden macrophages, a different clinical and biochemical picture than Tay-Sachs disease.
incorrectas.D: Krabbe disease presents with optic atrophy rather than a cherry-red macular spot, reflecting demyelination of the optic nerve from psychosine toxicity rather than the neuronal ganglioside accumulation seen in Tay-Sachs disease.

preguntas.q: A cherry-red spot on the macula together with hepatosplenomegaly is characteristic of which lysosomal storage disease?

e.correcta: Niemann-Pick disease is caused by sphingomyelinase deficiency, leading to sphingomyelin accumulation both within neurons (producing the cherry-red macular spot, similar in appearance to Tay-Sachs disease) and within macrophages of the liver and spleen (producing hepatosplenomegaly, which Tay-Sachs disease lacks). This combination of a cherry-red spot plus organomegaly is the key clinical clue that separates Niemann-Pick disease from Tay-Sachs disease on exams.

incorrectas.A: Tay-Sachs disease shares the cherry-red macular spot with Niemann-Pick disease but characteristically lacks hepatosplenomegaly, since hexosaminidase A deficiency causes GM2 ganglioside accumulation predominantly in neurons rather than in visceral macrophages.
incorrectas.C: Hurler syndrome causes hepatosplenomegaly from glycosaminoglycan accumulation but does not produce a cherry-red macular spot, since it is a mucopolysaccharidosis rather than a sphingolipidosis affecting retinal ganglion cells.
incorrectas.D: Gaucher disease also causes marked hepatosplenomegaly but is not associated with a cherry-red macular spot; its accumulated substrate, glucocerebroside, builds up in macrophages (producing 'crumpled tissue paper' cells) rather than in retinal neurons.

preguntas.q: Which lysosomal storage disease is the most common among the sphingolipidoses?

e.correcta: Gaucher disease, caused by deficient glucocerebrosidase (beta-glucosidase) leading to glucocerebroside accumulation in macrophages, is the most common lysosomal storage disease overall, with particularly high carrier frequency among Ashkenazi Jewish populations. Its relative prevalence (compared to the rarer Tay-Sachs, Niemann-Pick, and Fabry diseases) is part of why it's the sphingolipidosis for which enzyme replacement therapy was first developed and is most widely used.

incorrectas.A: Tay-Sachs disease, while also enriched in the Ashkenazi Jewish population, is considerably less common overall than Gaucher disease and presents with a distinct clinical picture (cherry-red spot, no organomegaly, uniformly fatal in infancy) rather than being the most prevalent lysosomal storage disease.
incorrectas.B: Niemann-Pick disease is rarer than Gaucher disease and is distinguished by hepatosplenomegaly plus a cherry-red macular spot from sphingomyelin accumulation, rather than being the most common lysosomal storage disorder.
incorrectas.D: Fabry disease, caused by alpha-galactosidase A deficiency, is less common than Gaucher disease and has a distinct X-linked inheritance pattern and clinical presentation (angiokeratomas, acroparesthesias, renal/cardiac disease) rather than being the most prevalent storage disease.

preguntas.q: Which lysosomal storage disease is classically treated with recombinant enzyme replacement therapy (e.g., recombinant glucocerebrosidase)?

e.correcta: Gaucher disease is amenable to enzyme replacement therapy because the deficient enzyme, glucocerebrosidase, primarily needs to reach macrophages in the reticuloendothelial system (spleen, liver, bone marrow) — tissues that are relatively accessible to intravenously infused recombinant enzyme. Recombinant glucocerebrosidase (imiglucerase) can reverse the hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, and bone disease of Gaucher disease, making it one of the first successful examples of enzyme replacement therapy for a lysosomal storage disease.

incorrectas.A: Tay-Sachs disease primarily affects the CNS, and because infused recombinant enzyme cannot effectively cross the blood-brain barrier, enzyme replacement therapy is not an effective strategy for this hexosaminidase A deficiency, unlike the more peripherally-affected Gaucher disease.
incorrectas.B: Krabbe disease also predominantly damages the central and peripheral nervous system through psychosine toxicity, and enzyme replacement is similarly limited by poor CNS penetration; hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, not enzyme infusion, is the mainstay intervention attempted in Krabbe disease.
incorrectas.D: Niemann-Pick disease (classic types A/B) does not have the same long-established, widely-used recombinant enzyme replacement therapy as Gaucher disease in classic teaching, since sphingomyelinase deficiency affects both visceral and neuronal tissue, limiting treatment efficacy compared to the largely macrophage-confined pathology of Gaucher disease.

preguntas.q: Macrophages resembling 'crumpled tissue paper' on histology are characteristic of which lysosomal storage disease?

e.correcta: In Gaucher disease, deficient glucocerebrosidase causes glucocerebroside to accumulate within macrophage lysosomes, giving these Gaucher cells a distinctive fibrillary, wrinkled cytoplasm classically described as resembling 'crumpled tissue paper' on light microscopy. These lipid-laden macrophages infiltrate the spleen, liver, and bone marrow, driving the hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and bone disease seen in the condition.

incorrectas.A: Niemann-Pick disease produces macrophages with a foamy, vacuolated appearance ('foam cells') from sphingomyelin accumulation, histologically distinct from the crumpled, fibrillary cytoplasm of Gaucher cells.
incorrectas.B: Fabry disease causes globotriaosylceramide accumulation predominantly within vascular endothelial and other tissue cells, producing lamellar 'zebra body' inclusions on electron microscopy rather than the crumpled tissue paper macrophages of Gaucher disease.
incorrectas.D: Hurler syndrome involves glycosaminoglycan accumulation in connective tissue and does not produce the lipid-laden macrophage morphology characteristic of the sphingolipidosis Gaucher disease.

preguntas.q: Osteoporosis, bone crises, avascular necrosis, and pancytopenia are most characteristic of which lysosomal storage disease?

e.correcta: In Gaucher disease, glucocerebroside-laden macrophages infiltrate the bone marrow, where they release proteolytic enzymes and inflammatory mediators that damage bone architecture, producing osteoporosis, painful bone crises, and avascular necrosis (classically of the femoral head). The same marrow infiltration by Gaucher cells, combined with splenic sequestration from massive splenomegaly, crowds out normal hematopoiesis and increases peripheral blood cell destruction, resulting in pancytopenia.

incorrectas.A: Fabry disease causes progressive renal failure and cardiovascular disease from globotriaosylceramide accumulation in vascular endothelium, not the bone marrow infiltration and hematologic compromise characteristic of Gaucher disease.
incorrectas.B: Hurler syndrome causes skeletal abnormalities (dysostosis multiplex) from glycosaminoglycan accumulation in connective tissue, but this differs mechanistically from the marrow-infiltrating macrophages and hypersplenism that cause pancytopenia and bone crises in Gaucher disease.
incorrectas.D: Niemann-Pick disease causes hepatosplenomegaly and neurodegeneration from sphingomyelin accumulation, but it is not classically associated with the bone crises and avascular necrosis that result from Gaucher cell infiltration of bone marrow.

preguntas.q: Progressive renal failure and cardiovascular disease in later life are characteristic late complications of which lysosomal storage disease?

e.correcta: In Fabry disease, progressive accumulation of globotriaosylceramide within vascular endothelium and other tissues of the kidney and heart over years leads to glomerulosclerosis and progressive renal failure, as well as left ventricular hypertrophy, arrhythmias, and increased risk of myocardial infarction and stroke. Because these complications typically develop later in life (after the earlier childhood/adolescent findings of angiokeratomas and acroparesthesias), renal and cardiac disease are the major causes of morbidity and mortality in adults with Fabry disease.

incorrectas.A: Gaucher disease causes hepatosplenomegaly, bone crises, and pancytopenia from macrophage infiltration, but it is not classically associated with progressive renal failure and cardiovascular disease as its defining late complication, unlike the vascular endothelial deposition seen in Fabry disease.
incorrectas.C: Metachromatic leukodystrophy causes progressive demyelination with motor and cognitive decline from sulfatide accumulation, a neurologic rather than renal/cardiovascular disease course, distinguishing it from Fabry disease.
incorrectas.D: Hunter syndrome causes glycosaminoglycan-related somatic and connective tissue disease (coarse features, joint stiffness, airway obstruction) but does not classically feature the progressive renal failure and cardiovascular disease seen as late Fabry disease complications, despite both being X-linked recessive lysosomal storage diseases.

preguntas.q: Which pair of lysosomal storage diseases are both inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern, in contrast to the autosomal recessive pattern of most other lysosomal storage diseases?

e.correcta: Fabry disease (alpha-galactosidase A deficiency, GLA gene) and Hunter syndrome (iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency, IDS gene) are the two classic lysosomal storage diseases whose causative genes reside on the X chromosome, making both X-linked recessive — a notable exception to the otherwise near-universal autosomal recessive inheritance of the other sphingolipidoses and mucopolysaccharidoses. Recognizing this pairing helps quickly rule in or out inheritance-pattern questions across the entire lysosomal storage disease group.

incorrectas.A: Tay-Sachs disease and Niemann-Pick disease are both autosomal recessive sphingolipidoses (hexosaminidase A and sphingomyelinase deficiencies, respectively), following the more typical inheritance pattern seen in most lysosomal storage diseases rather than the X-linked pattern the question asks about.
incorrectas.B: Gaucher disease and Krabbe disease are also both autosomal recessive (glucocerebrosidase and galactocerebrosidase deficiencies, respectively), fitting the general rule for lysosomal storage diseases rather than being exceptions like Fabry disease and Hunter syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Hurler syndrome and metachromatic leukodystrophy are likewise autosomal recessive conditions (alpha-L-iduronidase and arylsulfatase A deficiencies, respectively); Hurler syndrome in particular is often paired conceptually with Hunter syndrome but has the opposite (autosomal) inheritance pattern.

preguntas.q: A lysosomal storage disease caused by galactocerebrosidase deficiency shows characteristic multinucleated globoid cells on brain biopsy. Which disease is this?

e.correcta: Krabbe disease results from a deficiency of galactocerebrosidase (galactosylceramidase), causing accumulation of galactocerebroside and the toxic metabolite psychosine. Psychosine is directly toxic to oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells, destroying myelin-producing cells and recruiting multinucleated macrophages that engulf the debris, forming the characteristic globoid cells seen on histology. This severe central and peripheral demyelination presents in infancy with optic atrophy, peripheral neuropathy, developmental regression, and early death.

incorrectas.A: Metachromatic leukodystrophy is caused by arylsulfatase A deficiency with accumulation of cerebroside sulfate (sulfatide), producing metachromatically-staining granules in the brain and peripheral nerves, but it does not produce globoid cells — that histologic hallmark belongs specifically to Krabbe disease.
incorrectas.C: Tay-Sachs disease results from hexosaminidase A deficiency and accumulation of GM2 ganglioside in neurons, producing a cherry-red macular spot and progressive neurodegeneration without hepatosplenomegaly, but it has no globoid cell formation since it does not primarily attack myelin-producing cells the way Krabbe disease does.
incorrectas.D: Niemann-Pick disease is caused by sphingomyelinase deficiency, leading to sphingomyelin accumulation in macrophages (foam cells) with hepatosplenomegaly and a cherry-red spot; its characteristic cells are lipid-laden foam cells, not the globoid cells of Krabbe disease.

preguntas.q: An infant presents with optic atrophy, peripheral neuropathy, and progressive developmental regression. Deficiency of which enzyme is most likely responsible?

e.correcta: Krabbe disease is caused by a deficiency of galactocerebrosidase, which leads to buildup of psychosine, a metabolite toxic to oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells. This destroys myelin in both the central and peripheral nervous systems, producing the classic triad of optic atrophy, peripheral neuropathy, and developmental regression in infancy, along with globoid cells on brain biopsy.

incorrectas.A: Arylsulfatase A deficiency causes metachromatic leukodystrophy, which also demyelinates centrally and peripherally with ataxia and dementia, but it does not classically present with the globoid cell histology or the specific optic atrophy emphasis associated with Krabbe disease.
incorrectas.B: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency causes Fabry disease, an X-linked disorder with angiokeratomas, acroparesthesias, and progressive renal/cardiac disease from globotriaosylceramide accumulation — a very different clinical picture without early infantile demyelination.
incorrectas.D: Hexosaminidase A deficiency causes Tay-Sachs disease, presenting with a cherry-red macular spot, exaggerated startle response, and progressive neurodegeneration from GM2 ganglioside accumulation, but without the globoid cells or the peripheral neuropathy characteristic of Krabbe disease.

preguntas.q: A patient with progressive ataxia and dementia is found to have both central and peripheral demyelination due to arylsulfatase A deficiency. Which lysosomal storage disease is this?

e.correcta: Metachromatic leukodystrophy is caused by a deficiency of arylsulfatase A, leading to accumulation of cerebroside sulfate (sulfatide) within myelin-forming cells of both the central and peripheral nervous systems. The resulting demyelination produces the classic combination of ataxia, dementia, and peripheral neuropathy, with sulfatide granules that stain metachromatically on biopsy — the origin of the disease's name.

incorrectas.A: Krabbe disease is caused by galactocerebrosidase deficiency and psychosine accumulation, producing globoid cells and demyelination, but its enzyme defect and characteristic histology (globoid cells rather than metachromatic granules) differ from metachromatic leukodystrophy.
incorrectas.B: Fabry disease results from alpha-galactosidase A deficiency and globotriaosylceramide accumulation, causing angiokeratomas, painful acroparesthesias, and renal/cardiac disease — a systemic vasculopathy, not a primary central/peripheral demyelinating disease.
incorrectas.C: Gaucher disease is caused by glucocerebrosidase deficiency, leading to glucocerebroside accumulation in macrophages (Gaucher cells) with hepatosplenomegaly, bone crises, and pancytopenia, rather than the diffuse demyelination seen in metachromatic leukodystrophy.

preguntas.q: A child with coarse facial features, developmental delay, and hepatosplenomegaly is found on slit-lamp exam to have clouded corneas. Deficiency of which enzyme is most likely?

e.correcta: Hurler syndrome is caused by a deficiency of alpha-L-iduronidase, causing accumulation of heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate (mucopolysaccharides). This produces coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, developmental delay, and clouded corneas from glycosaminoglycan deposition in corneal stroma — a key exam feature that helps distinguish Hurler syndrome from the clinically similar but corneal-sparing Hunter syndrome.

incorrectas.B: Iduronate sulfatase deficiency causes Hunter syndrome, an X-linked mucopolysaccharidosis with a similar overall picture of coarse features and organomegaly, but it classically lacks corneal clouding and instead features aggressive behavior — the classic distinguishing point tested between Hurler and Hunter syndromes.
incorrectas.C: Hexosaminidase A deficiency causes Tay-Sachs disease, marked by GM2 ganglioside accumulation in neurons with a cherry-red macular spot and progressive neurodegeneration, but without coarse facies, organomegaly, or corneal clouding.
incorrectas.D: Sphingomyelinase deficiency causes Niemann-Pick disease, with sphingomyelin accumulation in macrophages producing hepatosplenomegaly and a cherry-red spot, but corneal clouding is not a typical feature of this sphingolipidosis.

preguntas.q: Which population has an increased carrier frequency for Tay-Sachs disease, Niemann-Pick disease, and some forms of Gaucher disease?

e.correcta: Ashkenazi Jewish populations have an increased carrier frequency for several autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease alleles (HEXA for Tay-Sachs, SMPD1 for Niemann-Pick, and GBA for type 1 Gaucher disease), attributable to founder effects and genetic drift within a historically isolated population. This is clinically relevant because it underlies targeted carrier-screening panels offered to individuals of this ancestry during genetic counseling and preconception testing.

incorrectas.A: Northern European ancestry is classically associated with increased carrier frequency for conditions like cystic fibrosis and hereditary hemochromatosis, not the sphingolipidoses highlighted here.
incorrectas.C: Sub-Saharan African ancestry is associated with increased carrier frequency for sickle cell trait/disease (owing to historical malaria selection pressure), not Tay-Sachs, Niemann-Pick, or Gaucher disease.
incorrectas.D: Southeast Asian ancestry is associated with increased frequencies of alpha-thalassemia and certain G6PD deficiency variants, not the lysosomal storage diseases enriched in the Ashkenazi Jewish population.

preguntas.q: Chronic kidney disease is staged based on incremental reductions in which parameter?

e.correcta: CKD is staged (stages 1 through 5) according to incremental declines in glomerular filtration rate, which directly reflects the kidney's actual filtering capacity. Because the relationship between GFR and serum creatinine is roughly hyperbolic, an equal drop in GFR causes a much larger rise in creatinine once GFR is already low than when it is near-normal — so staging is defined in terms of (estimated) GFR itself rather than raw creatinine values, which would understate early disease and overstate rapid decline late.

incorrectas.A: Serum creatinine is used to estimate GFR via prediction equations (e.g., CKD-EPI), but it is not itself the parameter that defines CKD stages, since creatinine is also influenced by muscle mass, age, and sex and changes nonlinearly relative to true filtration.
incorrectas.B: BUN reflects urea nitrogen and is affected by diet, hydration status, and GI bleeding in addition to filtration, making it a less specific marker that is not used to define the numeric stages of CKD.
incorrectas.D: Urine output is used to categorize acute kidney injury (e.g., oliguria, anuria) in the short term, but CKD staging requires a sustained measure of filtration capacity like GFR rather than a snapshot of urine volume.

preguntas.q: When an amino acid is catabolized, its amino group is removed to leave a carbon skeleton and which highly toxic byproduct?

e.correcta: Deamination or transamination of an amino acid strips off its amino group, releasing free ammonia (NH3) and leaving behind a carbon skeleton that can enter central metabolic pathways (glycolysis, TCA cycle, ketogenesis). Ammonia is highly neurotoxic — it disrupts glutamate signaling, depletes alpha-ketoglutarate in astrocytes, and impairs cerebral energy metabolism — which is why the body must promptly convert it into a safe, excretable form via the urea cycle.

incorrectas.A: Urea is the nontoxic, water-soluble product the liver synthesizes FROM ammonia via the urea cycle; it is the detoxified end product, not the immediate toxic byproduct released during amino acid catabolism.
incorrectas.B: Uric acid is generated from purine nucleotide catabolism via xanthine oxidase and causes gout when it accumulates, a completely separate pathway from the deamination of amino acids during protein catabolism.
incorrectas.C: Creatinine arises from the nonenzymatic breakdown of creatine and phosphocreatine in muscle and is used clinically as a renal filtration marker; it is unrelated to the amino group removed during amino acid catabolism.

preguntas.q: Ammonia generated by amino acid breakdown in skeletal muscle is transported to the liver mainly in the form of which molecule?

e.correcta: In muscle, ammonia produced from amino acid catabolism is transferred by alanine aminotransferase onto pyruvate (abundant from glycolysis) to form alanine — the glucose-alanine (Cahill) cycle. Alanine travels safely through the blood to the liver, where it is deaminated back to pyruvate (feeding gluconeogenesis) while releasing NH3 for urea synthesis, elegantly coupling muscle nitrogen disposal to hepatic glucose production during fasting or exercise.

incorrectas.A: Glutamine is the major ammonia carrier used by most other tissues, but muscle preferentially exports alanine because of its abundant pyruvate supply from active glycolysis, making the Cahill cycle the more efficient route.
incorrectas.C: Free ammonia is not exported directly from muscle in meaningful amounts because it is neurotoxic and would raise blood pH; it must first be incorporated into a carrier amino acid.
incorrectas.D: Urea is synthesized only in the liver as the final product of the urea cycle; muscle tissue does not export urea, since urea cycle enzymes are essentially restricted to hepatocytes.

preguntas.q: What class of enzymes catalyzes the transfer of an amino group between an amino acid and an alpha-keto acid during nitrogen metabolism?

e.correcta: Aminotransferases (transaminases), such as ALT and AST, transfer the amino group from an amino acid to an alpha-keto acid acceptor — typically alpha-ketoglutarate — generating a new amino acid (usually glutamate) and a new alpha-keto acid, with no net gain or loss of nitrogen. This transamination step is the crucial first move that funnels nitrogen from diverse amino acids toward glutamate, positioning it for either urea cycle disposal or entry into gluconeogenic pathways.

incorrectas.B: Dehydrogenases, such as glutamate dehydrogenase, catalyze oxidative deamination, actually releasing free ammonia from glutamate — a distinct reaction from the group transfer between two amino/keto acids that defines transamination.
incorrectas.C: Decarboxylases remove a carboxyl group as CO2 (e.g., converting histidine to histamine or glutamate to GABA), a completely different chemical transformation unrelated to nitrogen group transfer.
incorrectas.D: Hydroxylases add a hydroxyl group to a substrate, as in phenylalanine hydroxylase converting phenylalanine to tyrosine; this oxidative modification does not involve transferring an amino group between molecules.

preguntas.q: Which vitamin-derived cofactor is required by aminotransferase enzymes for their amino group transfer reaction?

e.correcta: Pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6, is the essential cofactor for aminotransferases (and amino acid decarboxylases). It forms a Schiff base with the amino acid substrate, allowing the amino group to be shuttled onto the alpha-keto acid acceptor during transamination. This is why B6 deficiency reduces ALT/AST activity, contributing to the elevated AST:ALT ratio sometimes seen in malnourished or alcoholic patients who are B6-deficient (ALT is more dependent on adequate cofactor for full activity than AST).

incorrectas.A: Thiamine pyrophosphate (from vitamin B1) is the cofactor for oxidative decarboxylation reactions such as pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, not for transamination reactions.
incorrectas.B: FAD (from vitamin B2) serves as a cofactor for oxidation-reduction flavoenzymes like succinate dehydrogenase, not for the amino group transfer catalyzed by transaminases.
incorrectas.D: Biotin is the cofactor for carboxylation reactions, such as those catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase, a chemically distinct process from transamination.

preguntas.q: In the liver, which amino acid undergoes oxidative deamination via glutamate dehydrogenase, donating its amino group to the urea cycle and regenerating alpha-ketoglutarate?

e.correcta: In hepatocyte mitochondria, glutamate dehydrogenase oxidatively deaminates glutamate, releasing free NH3 that feeds directly into the urea cycle's first step (via carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I) while regenerating alpha-ketoglutarate, which can re-enter the TCA cycle or accept another amino group through transamination. This reversible reaction is the key hub linking amino acid nitrogen disposal to both the urea cycle and central carbon metabolism.

incorrectas.A: Alanine carries ammonia from muscle to the liver via the Cahill cycle, but once there, its nitrogen is transferred by ALT onto alpha-ketoglutarate to FORM glutamate — it is glutamate, one step downstream, that then undergoes the oxidative deamination described here.
incorrectas.B: Glutamine is the principal systemic ammonia carrier from most tissues and is hydrolyzed by glutaminase to yield glutamate plus free NH3, but glutamine itself does not undergo the oxidative deamination reaction that regenerates alpha-ketoglutarate — that step happens to glutamate after glutaminase acts.
incorrectas.C: Aspartate contributes a second nitrogen atom to the urea cycle, but at a different step (combining with citrulline via argininosuccinate synthetase in the cytosol), not through the mitochondrial oxidative deamination reaction catalyzed by glutamate dehydrogenase.

preguntas.q: In the intestine, ammonia can be produced directly by which source acting on luminal urea and protein?

e.correcta: Colonic bacteria possess urease and amino acid-degrading enzymes that break down luminal urea and dietary/endogenous protein, releasing free ammonia that is absorbed into the portal circulation. This is clinically important because in liver failure or portosystemic shunting this gut-derived ammonia bypasses effective hepatic clearance and contributes to hepatic encephalopathy — the rationale for using nonabsorbable antibiotics like rifaximin to reduce colonic bacterial ammonia production in cirrhosis.

incorrectas.B: Pancreatic enzymes (such as trypsin and chymotrypsin) digest dietary protein into peptides and amino acids within the small intestinal lumen, but they do not themselves liberate free ammonia the way bacterial urease and deaminase activity does.
incorrectas.C: Gastric parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor to aid digestion and vitamin B12 absorption; they play no role in generating luminal ammonia.
incorrectas.D: Enterocytes do metabolize glutamine via glutaminase to generate some local ammonia as a fuel source, but this is a distinct route from the direct bacterial degradation of luminal urea and protein described in this question.

preguntas.q: Enterocytes and colonocytes generate ammonia by metabolizing which circulating amino acid, delivered from other tissues or from digested dietary protein?

e.correcta: Glutamine is a major fuel source for intestinal epithelial cells, which express glutaminase to hydrolyze it into glutamate plus free ammonia. This ammonia, together with that produced by luminal bacteria, is absorbed into the portal circulation for delivery to the liver, where it is normally cleared via the urea cycle — impaired hepatic clearance (cirrhosis, portosystemic shunts) allows this gut-derived nitrogen load to reach the systemic circulation and precipitate hepatic encephalopathy.

incorrectas.A: Alanine is the amino acid preferentially exported from skeletal muscle to carry ammonia to the liver (Cahill cycle), not the substrate that enterocytes locally catabolize to generate intestinal ammonia.
incorrectas.C: Glutamate is the direct product of glutaminase acting on glutamine (and can be further deaminated by glutamate dehydrogenase to release additional NH3), but it is glutamine itself that is delivered to and taken up by enterocytes as the initial substrate.
incorrectas.D: Asparagine can be hydrolyzed by asparaginase in some tissues to yield aspartate and ammonia, but it is not the amino acid classically described as the intestinal epithelium's preferred ammonia-generating fuel.

preguntas.q: Ammonia generated in the intestine (from bacterial and enterocyte metabolism) reaches the liver via the portal vein primarily in which form?

e.correcta: Unlike most peripheral tissues, which package ammonia into glutamine (or muscle, which uses alanine) before releasing it into the general circulation, the intestine drains directly into the portal vein with a short transit time straight to the liver. This anatomic shortcut allows ammonia generated by luminal bacteria and enterocyte glutaminase activity to be delivered as free, unconjugated NH3, relying on immediate first-pass hepatic extraction — exactly why portosystemic shunting or hepatic failure lets this ammonia spill into the systemic circulation.

incorrectas.A: Glutamine is how most other tissues safely export ammonia into the general circulation, since free ammonia would otherwise be toxic at a distance; the intestine's direct portal drainage is the exception that allows unconjugated transport.
incorrectas.B: Alanine is specific to skeletal muscle's method of ammonia export via the Cahill cycle and is not the form in which intestinally-generated ammonia travels to the liver.
incorrectas.D: Urea is the final detoxified product synthesized by hepatocytes from ammonia; it is not produced in the intestine and is not the form ammonia takes on its way to the liver.

preguntas.q: From most peripheral tissues (aside from muscle and the intestine), ammonia is transported through the bloodstream chiefly in which form?

e.correcta: Most tissues conjugate ammonia with glutamate via glutamine synthetase to form glutamine, a neutral, non-toxic carrier that does not perturb blood pH. The kidney and liver take up circulating glutamine and release its ammonia via glutaminase — the kidney for direct urinary excretion (important in acid-base regulation) and the liver for urea cycle disposal.

incorrectas.B: Alanine is the transport form specific to skeletal muscle, reflecting its high glycolytic pyruvate supply for the Cahill cycle, rather than the general systemic carrier used by most other tissues.
incorrectas.C: Free ammonia is toxic and would perturb acid-base balance if allowed to circulate broadly at high concentration, so the body avoids transporting it in free form except along the short portal route from the gut.
incorrectas.D: Glutamate is the amino group acceptor that becomes glutamine after incorporating a second ammonia molecule via glutamine synthetase; it is glutamine, not glutamate, that serves as the major inert systemic carrier because it can safely hold two nitrogens.

preguntas.q: Which tissue relies specifically on alanine, rather than glutamine, as its major vehicle for exporting ammonia?

e.correcta: Skeletal muscle has abundant pyruvate available from active glycolysis, allowing ALT to transaminate ammonia onto pyruvate to form alanine — the glucose-alanine (Cahill) cycle. Alanine travels to the liver, where it is deaminated back to pyruvate for gluconeogenesis while its nitrogen enters the urea cycle, a design that simultaneously disposes of muscle ammonia and recycles carbon for hepatic glucose production during fasting or exercise.

incorrectas.A: The liver is the destination organ that receives ammonia carriers (alanine, glutamine, and free NH3 from portal blood) and converts their nitrogen into urea; it does not export ammonia via alanine.
incorrectas.B: The kidney takes up glutamine and uses glutaminase to release ammonia directly into the urine as a buffering mechanism (especially important in metabolic acidosis), rather than exporting alanine.
incorrectas.C: The brain, like most other tissues besides muscle and intestine, detoxifies local ammonia by forming glutamine via glutamine synthetase for export, not alanine.

preguntas.q: Which organ is unique in delivering ammonia to the liver predominantly in its free, unconjugated form rather than as an amino acid carrier?

e.correcta: Because the intestine drains directly into the portal circulation with a short transit time straight to the liver, it can release the ammonia generated by luminal bacteria and enterocyte glutaminase activity as free NH3 without first conjugating it to a carrier amino acid. This shortcut depends entirely on rapid, efficient first-pass hepatic clearance — which is why conditions that impair this clearance (cirrhosis, portosystemic shunts) let intestinal ammonia reach the systemic circulation unchecked.

incorrectas.A: Skeletal muscle must conjugate its ammonia to alanine before export, since it releases nitrogen into the general systemic circulation, where free ammonia would be neurotoxic if not carried safely.
incorrectas.C: The kidney generates ammonia locally from glutamine for direct excretion into the urine as an acid-base buffering mechanism, rather than transporting ammonia to the liver in free form.
incorrectas.D: Adipose tissue is not a significant source or transporter of nitrogen/ammonia; its metabolism centers on lipid storage and mobilization, not amino acid catabolism.

preguntas.q: Unlike free ammonia, transport of nitrogen through the blood as glutamine has what effect on blood pH?

o.A: No significant change in blood pH

e.correcta: Glutamine carries two nitrogens in a neutral, chemically stable form that does not perturb plasma pH when it circulates. This is precisely why the body prefers packaging ammonia as glutamine (or, in muscle, as alanine) for long-distance transport rather than allowing free NH3/NH4+ to circulate, since free ammonia would both disturb acid-base balance and pose direct neurotoxic risk.

incorrectas.B: Glutamine does not act as a base that meaningfully raises blood pH; its molecular structure is specifically suited to being pH-neutral for safe systemic transport.
incorrectas.C: It is glutamate metabolism (not glutamine transport) that is linked to a fall in blood pH; glutamine itself, despite the similar name, does not acidify the blood — this distinction is a classic point of confusion worth memorizing.
incorrectas.D: Glutamine's effect on pH is not variable or dose-dependent — it is consistently pH-neutral, which is exactly the property that makes it suitable as the body's primary ammonia transport molecule.

preguntas.q: Why is glutamate not used as the body's primary long-distance carrier of ammonia, in contrast to glutamine?

o.A: Glutamate causes a rise in blood pH
o.C: Formation and metabolism of glutamate is linked to a decrease in blood pH

e.correcta: Glutamate carries a negative charge at physiologic pH, and reactions involving it — such as oxidative deamination by glutamate dehydrogenase, which releases NH4+ and a proton — tend to shift blood toward acidosis. This acidifying tendency makes glutamate unsuitable as the primary long-distance ammonia carrier; that role instead falls to glutamine, whose additional amide group neutralizes this effect, explaining why these two closely related molecules are handled so differently in nitrogen transport despite differing by only one amide.

incorrectas.A: Glutamate does not raise blood pH; if anything, reactions that release or process it in ammonia handling tend to be mildly acidifying, not alkalinizing.
incorrectas.B: Glutamate transport across membranes is well established via dedicated transporters (e.g., in astrocytes and hepatocytes); membrane impermeability is not the reason it is excluded as the systemic ammonia carrier — the acid-base effect is.
incorrectas.D: Glutamate is itself an amino acid bearing one amino group and does carry nitrogen; the problem is not an absence of nitrogen but the acidifying consequence of its metabolism compared to the pH-neutral glutamine.

preguntas.q: The urea cycle spans which cellular compartments?

o.B: Both the mitochondria and the cytosol

e.correcta: The urea cycle begins in the mitochondrial matrix, where carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and ornithine transcarbamylase produce citrulline. Citrulline is then exported to the cytosol, where argininosuccinate synthetase, argininosuccinate lyase, and arginase convert it through argininosuccinate and arginine into urea, regenerating ornithine, which shuttles back into the mitochondrion to restart the cycle — this compartmentalization is a frequently tested detail distinguishing it from purely cytosolic or purely mitochondrial pathways.

incorrectas.A: Restricting the cycle to mitochondria alone ignores that citrulline must exit into the cytosol for the argininosuccinate synthetase reaction and the subsequent steps leading to urea; only the first two enzymes are mitochondrial.
incorrectas.C: Restricting it to the cytosol alone ignores that the initial, rate-limiting step (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I) and ornithine transcarbamylase both occur in the mitochondrial matrix before citrulline is exported.
incorrectas.D: The endoplasmic reticulum has no role in the urea cycle; the correct compartments involved are the mitochondria and cytosol, not ER-associated pathways.

preguntas.q: The urea cycle's first two enzymatic steps — formation of carbamoyl phosphate and its conversion to citrulline — occur in which cellular compartment?

e.correcta: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I combines free ammonia, bicarbonate, and two ATP molecules to form carbamoyl phosphate in the mitochondrial matrix, and ornithine transcarbamylase then combines this with ornithine to form citrulline — still within the mitochondrion. Citrulline is subsequently exported to the cytosol to complete the remaining steps; keeping the ammonia-fixing reactions mitochondrial helps sequester highly reactive, toxic free ammonia away from the rest of the cell.

incorrectas.B: The cytosol houses the later urea cycle steps — argininosuccinate synthetase, argininosuccinate lyase, and arginase acting on citrulline through to urea and regenerated ornithine — not the initial ammonia-fixing reactions described here.
incorrectas.C: The nucleus has no enzymatic role in the urea cycle; nitrogen disposal chemistry occurs exclusively in the mitochondria and cytosol.
incorrectas.D: Peroxisomes house beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids and other oxidative reactions, not the urea cycle enzymes that begin this pathway.

preguntas.q: Most excess nitrogen from amino acid catabolism is excreted from the body in which chemical form?

e.correcta: The liver converts the toxic ammonia generated by transamination and deamination reactions throughout the body into urea via the urea cycle. Urea is water-soluble and non-toxic, allowing it to be readily filtered and excreted by the kidneys, which makes it the primary disposal form for nitrogenous waste in humans — reflected clinically by blood urea nitrogen (BUN) as a marker influenced by both production and renal clearance.

incorrectas.A: Free ammonia is the toxic precursor that must first be converted to urea before safe excretion; sustained elevations of circulating free ammonia cause hepatic encephalopathy, which is exactly why the body avoids excreting nitrogen in this form.
incorrectas.B: Uric acid is the excretory end product of purine nucleotide catabolism (via xanthine oxidase), notable clinically for causing gout and kidney stones, but it is a distinct pathway from the general disposal of amino acid nitrogen.
incorrectas.C: Creatinine is a waste product of muscle creatine/phosphocreatine breakdown used clinically as a filtration marker, but it is not the major route by which nitrogen from amino acid catabolism is excreted.

preguntas.q: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle, is allosterically activated by which molecule?

e.correcta: N-acetylglutamate, synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate by N-acetylglutamate synthase, is an obligate allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I. Its levels rise with increased protein intake or catabolism (arginine stimulates N-acetylglutamate synthase), ensuring the urea cycle ramps up its capacity to dispose of nitrogen precisely when the amino acid/ammonia load is high; N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency mimics a urea cycle disorder, producing hyperammonemia despite a structurally normal CPS I enzyme.

incorrectas.A: Citrulline is the direct product of the CPS I and ornithine transcarbamylase reactions (formed when carbamoyl phosphate combines with ornithine), not an upstream activator that switches the enzyme on.
incorrectas.C: Ornithine is the substrate that combines with carbamoyl phosphate to form citrulline and is later regenerated by arginase at the end of the cycle, but it does not allosterically activate CPS I.
incorrectas.D: Arginine does not directly activate CPS I; rather, it stimulates N-acetylglutamate synthase to produce more N-acetylglutamate, which is the actual allosteric activator — an important two-step distinction to keep straight.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of the urea cycle?

e.correcta: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step of the urea cycle, combining free ammonia, bicarbonate, and two ATP molecules to form carbamoyl phosphate within the mitochondrial matrix. Its activity is tightly controlled by the obligate allosteric activator N-acetylglutamate, making CPS I the key regulatory checkpoint that sets the overall flux of the urea cycle in response to dietary and catabolic nitrogen load.

incorrectas.B: Ornithine transcarbamylase catalyzes the second mitochondrial step, combining carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form citrulline; its deficiency is the most common urea cycle disorder, but OTC itself is not the allosterically-regulated, rate-limiting enzyme.
incorrectas.C: Argininosuccinate synthetase is a cytosolic enzyme that combines citrulline with aspartate to form argininosuccinate; it is an essential step but is not the rate-limiting one that governs overall cycle flux.
incorrectas.D: Arginase, the final cytosolic enzyme, cleaves arginine into urea and ornithine, completing the cycle, but it does not set the cycle's overall rate the way CPS I does.

preguntas.q: After arginase cleaves arginine into urea and ornithine in the final step of the urea cycle, what happens to the urea produced?

o.A: It re-enters the mitochondria to reform carbamoyl phosphate
o.B: It is converted back into ornithine for reuse
o.C: It is excreted in the urine
o.D: It is deaminated by glutamate dehydrogenase

e.correcta: Urea, generated by arginase acting on arginine in the cytosol, is released into the blood and filtered by the kidneys for excretion in the urine as the final disposal step for nitrogen waste. In contrast, ornithine — the other product of the arginase reaction — is recycled back into the mitochondrion to accept another carbamoyl phosphate molecule and restart the cycle, reflecting the pathway's efficient design of clearing nitrogen while regenerating its own carrier.

incorrectas.A: It is ornithine, not urea, that re-enters the mitochondria to combine with carbamoyl phosphate via ornithine transcarbamylase and continue the cycle; urea itself plays no further role in the pathway.
incorrectas.B: Urea is not converted back into ornithine — these are two distinct final products of the arginase reaction, and only ornithine is recycled, while urea is a metabolic dead-end product destined for excretion.
incorrectas.D: Glutamate dehydrogenase acts on glutamate to release or incorporate free ammonia via oxidative deamination; it has no role in further metabolizing the urea produced by arginase.

preguntas.q: In the urea cycle, arginase cleaves arginine into urea and ornithine. What happens to this ornithine molecule afterward?

o.A: It is excreted directly in the urine as a nitrogenous waste product
o.B: It is converted into arginine via the citric acid cycle
o.C: It is transported back into the mitochondria to combine with carbamoyl phosphate and continue the urea cycle
o.D: It is transaminated to alpha-ketoglutarate for use in gluconeogenesis

e.correcta: Ornithine produced by arginase is shuttled back into the mitochondrial matrix via an ornithine transporter, where it combines with carbamoyl phosphate (catalyzed by OTC) to reform citrulline, regenerating the urea cycle. This recycling makes the cycle catalytic rather than requiring a fresh ornithine molecule with every turn, which is essential since the body must continuously detoxify the ammonia generated by ongoing amino acid catabolism.

incorrectas.A: Ornithine is not excreted as waste — it is a nonstandard, cycle-internal intermediate that stays within the pathway; the actual nitrogenous waste product excreted in urine is urea itself, formed from the arginine that was just cleaved.
incorrectas.B: Ornithine is not converted to arginine via the TCA cycle; arginine is instead regenerated later in the urea cycle from argininosuccinate through argininosuccinate lyase, with the two cycles linked only via fumarate, not via ornithine.
incorrectas.D: Ornithine can be interconverted with glutamate semialdehyde in other pathways (e.g., proline/glutamate metabolism), but within the urea cycle it is conserved and recycled rather than diverted to alpha-ketoglutarate for gluconeogenesis.

preguntas.q: A patient with severe cirrhosis and hepatic synthetic dysfunction has an impaired urea cycle. How would you expect this patient's serum BUN to be affected?

e.correcta: Urea is synthesized almost exclusively by the liver's urea cycle; when hepatocyte function is impaired, as in cirrhosis or fulminant hepatic failure, the capacity to convert ammonia into urea falls, so less urea is produced and serum BUN decreases even as blood ammonia rises. This combination of low BUN with elevated ammonia should point toward a hepatic production problem rather than a renal clearance problem.

incorrectas.A: An increased BUN is the pattern seen with renal dysfunction, where urea is still made normally by the liver but cannot be cleared by failing kidneys — the opposite mechanism from liver failure, where production itself is reduced.
incorrectas.C: BUN is not unchanged in significant liver dysfunction, because urea synthesis capacity is directly tied to functioning hepatocytes and adequate urea cycle enzyme levels; loss of hepatic mass or function measurably lowers urea output.
incorrectas.D: There is no classic biphasic BUN pattern taught for liver failure; as long as hepatic synthetic function remains impaired, urea production stays reduced, producing a sustained low BUN rather than a transient rise followed by a fall.

preguntas.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease and a declining GFR undergoes routine labs. How would you expect this patient's serum BUN to be affected?

e.correcta: Urea is a small, water-soluble molecule normally filtered by the glomerulus and excreted in urine. As GFR falls in kidney disease, urea clearance decreases and it accumulates in the blood, raising BUN — which is why BUN, alongside creatinine, is used clinically as a marker of glomerular filtration.

incorrectas.B: BUN does not stay unchanged in significant renal impairment, because the kidney is the primary excretory route for urea; loss of filtration capacity directly causes retention and a rising BUN.
incorrectas.C: BUN becoming undetectable would require essentially no urea production, which is not what happens in kidney disease — hepatic urea production continues normally while renal excretion fails, so urea rises rather than disappears.
incorrectas.D: A decreased BUN would instead suggest reduced hepatic urea production (e.g., liver failure) rather than a renal problem, since kidney disease impairs excretion, not the liver's ability to synthesize urea.

preguntas.q: Disorders of the urea cycle impair the body's ability to eliminate which toxic nitrogenous compound?

e.correcta: The urea cycle exists specifically to convert free ammonia, generated from amino acid catabolism and gut bacterial activity, into water-soluble urea for renal excretion. When any urea cycle enzyme is deficient, ammonia cannot be incorporated into urea and accumulates in the blood, producing hyperammonemia with its characteristic neurotoxicity.

incorrectas.A: Uric acid is the end product of purine, not amino acid nitrogen, catabolism; its clearance is impaired in conditions like gout or tumor lysis syndrome, using pathways and enzymes entirely separate from the urea cycle.
incorrectas.B: Creatinine is a breakdown product of muscle creatine phosphate cleared by renal filtration; it is unrelated to nitrogen disposal via the urea cycle and is unaffected by urea cycle enzyme deficiencies.
incorrectas.D: Bilirubin is a heme breakdown product handled by hepatic conjugation and biliary excretion; its accumulation causes jaundice, a completely different pathway from the ammonia detoxification handled by the urea cycle.

preguntas.q: An infant with carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS1) deficiency is found to have elevated NH4+ levels and hyperammonemia. What is the underlying reason for this?

o.A: CPS1 deficiency causes excess renal ammonia reabsorption
o.B: CPS1 deficiency increases dietary protein absorption
o.C: CPS1 deficiency accelerates purine degradation to ammonia
o.D: CPS1 catalyzes the first, rate-limiting step of the urea cycle, and its loss prevents ammonia from entering the cycle at all

e.correcta: CPS1 catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting mitochondrial step of the urea cycle, combining free ammonia with CO2 and 2 ATP to form carbamoyl phosphate. Without this enzyme, ammonia cannot even begin to be converted into urea cycle intermediates, so NH4+/NH3 accumulates directly in the blood — this is why CPS1 deficiency produces hyperammonemia clinically indistinguishable from N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency, whose product is an obligate activator of CPS1.

incorrectas.A: The kidney does not meaningfully reabsorb ammonia in a way that would explain systemic hyperammonemia here; the defect is a block in hepatic mitochondrial ammonia fixation, not altered renal handling.
incorrectas.B: CPS1 deficiency does not increase dietary protein absorption; dietary protein is simply a source of amino groups that, once catabolized to ammonia, cannot be detoxified because the urea cycle is blocked at its very first step — the problem is downstream disposal, not intestinal uptake.
incorrectas.C: Purine degradation produces uric acid, not ammonia, and is unrelated to CPS1 or the urea cycle; conflating these pathways confuses two separate nitrogen-disposal systems.

preguntas.q: Why is serum glutamine elevated in patients with carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency?

o.A: CPS1 directly synthesizes glutamine from ornithine
o.B: Skeletal muscle and brain buffer excess ammonia by combining it with glutamate via glutamine synthetase, raising glutamine levels
o.C: Impaired glutaminase activity prevents glutamine breakdown
o.D: Excess urea is converted back into glutamine

e.correcta: When the urea cycle cannot dispose of ammonia, tissues such as skeletal muscle, brain, and liver use glutamine synthetase to combine free ammonia with glutamate, forming glutamine as a temporary, less toxic ammonia buffer and transport molecule. This compensatory reaction is why elevated serum glutamine is a sensitive downstream marker of hyperammonemia in urea cycle disorders.

incorrectas.A: CPS1 acts in the urea cycle to make carbamoyl phosphate from ammonia, bicarbonate, and ATP — it has no role in synthesizing glutamine, and ornithine is not a substrate for that reaction.
incorrectas.C: The rise in glutamine is not primarily due to a block in its breakdown by glutaminase; glutaminase is not the deficient enzyme here, and the glutamine elevation instead reflects increased production as the body tries to sequester excess ammonia.
incorrectas.D: Urea itself is not converted back to glutamine; in CPS1 deficiency, urea production is actually reduced (hence a low BUN), and the glutamine elevation arises from a separate ammonia-buffering reaction, not from urea being recycled.

preguntas.q: Would you expect serum BUN to be increased or decreased in a neonate with carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency, and why?

o.A: Increased, because ammonia is converted directly to urea by an alternate pathway
o.B: Increased, because renal excretion of urea is impaired
o.C: Decreased, because CPS1 catalyzes the first step of the urea cycle and its loss prevents urea from being synthesized
o.D: Unchanged, because urea synthesis does not depend on CPS1

e.correcta: BUN reflects how much urea the liver's urea cycle actually manufactures. Because CPS1 performs the first committed step of that cycle, its deficiency blocks urea synthesis from the very start, so less urea is made and BUN falls even as ammonia rises — a hallmark combination (low BUN plus high ammonia) that should raise suspicion for a proximal urea cycle defect.

incorrectas.A: There is no alternate enzymatic route that converts ammonia directly to urea bypassing the urea cycle; urea synthesis strictly requires the sequential CPS1 to OTC to argininosuccinate synthetase to argininosuccinate lyase to arginase pathway.
incorrectas.B: Renal excretion is not the problem in CPS1 deficiency — the kidneys work normally, but there is simply far less urea being produced by the liver for them to excrete, so BUN falls rather than rising from a clearance problem.
incorrectas.D: Urea synthesis is entirely dependent on CPS1 activity as the first enzyme of the pathway; without it, downstream steps have no carbamoyl phosphate substrate to work with, so urea output drops substantially.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency?

e.correcta: CPS1 deficiency is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, requiring two defective CPS1 alleles (one from each carrier parent) for disease to manifest. This distinguishes it from OTC deficiency, the only X-linked urea cycle disorder, even though both present with nearly identical hyperammonemic phenotypes.

incorrectas.A: X-linked recessive is the inheritance pattern of OTC deficiency, not CPS1 deficiency — a key distinguishing point, since the two conditions otherwise look clinically identical, but genetic counseling and carrier testing differ based on chromosome location.
incorrectas.C: Autosomal dominant inheritance would mean a single mutant allele causes disease, with an affected parent typically present in each generation; this is not the pattern seen in CPS1 deficiency, where both parents are usually unaffected heterozygous carriers.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance (maternal transmission) applies to disorders of mitochondrial DNA-encoded proteins; despite CPS1 functioning inside the mitochondrial matrix, the CPS1 gene itself is nuclear-encoded and follows autosomal recessive Mendelian inheritance, not mitochondrial inheritance.

preguntas.q: A neonate presents with hyperammonemia, elevated glutamine, and low BUN. Urine organic acids show no elevation in orotic acid. Which urea cycle enzyme deficiency is most consistent with this picture?

e.correcta: CPS1 deficiency blocks the very first step of the urea cycle, so carbamoyl phosphate is never made in the mitochondria in the first place — there is no excess carbamoyl phosphate to leak into the cytosol and feed pyrimidine synthesis, so orotic acid does not accumulate. This absence of orotic aciduria is the key lab feature that distinguishes CPS1 deficiency from OTC deficiency, which otherwise presents with an identical clinical picture.

incorrectas.A: OTC deficiency causes the opposite pattern — carbamoyl phosphate is still made normally by CPS1 but cannot be used by the deficient OTC enzyme, so it accumulates and diffuses into the cytosol, where it drives excess orotic acid production, causing orotic aciduria (unlike CPS1 deficiency).
incorrectas.B: Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency (classic citrullinemia) occurs further downstream, after carbamoyl phosphate has already been consumed to form citrulline; it presents with markedly elevated citrulline, not the absent orotic acid finding being tested here.
incorrectas.C: Hereditary orotic aciduria is a defect in de novo pyrimidine synthesis (UMP synthase), not a urea cycle enzyme; it causes orotic aciduria with megaloblastic anemia but without hyperammonemia — the reverse pattern from the one described in this vignette.

preguntas.q: N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency produces a clinical and biochemical picture nearly identical to which other urea cycle enzyme deficiency?

e.correcta: N-acetylglutamate is an obligate allosteric activator of CPS1; without it, CPS1 cannot function even though the enzyme protein itself is structurally normal. N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency therefore phenocopies primary CPS1 deficiency — both show hyperammonemia, elevated glutamine, low BUN, and no orotic aciduria, since carbamoyl phosphate production is blocked in either case.

incorrectas.A: OTC deficiency, unlike CPS1/NAGS deficiency, still allows carbamoyl phosphate to be made normally, and its buildup causes orotic aciduria — a lab finding absent in NAGS deficiency, making these two conditions distinguishable rather than identical.
incorrectas.B: Arginase deficiency occurs at the very last step of the urea cycle and presents differently, with progressive spasticity and hyperargininemia rather than the severe neonatal hyperammonemic crisis typical of NAGS/CPS1 deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency (argininosuccinic aciduria) presents with elevated argininosuccinate and trichorrhexis nodosa (brittle hair) — a distinct biochemical and clinical fingerprint different from the NAGS/CPS1 phenotype.

preguntas.q: In which age group does carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency classically present with poorly regulated respiration and body temperature, poor feeding, developmental delay, and intellectual disability?

e.correcta: CPS1 deficiency is a severe, complete urea cycle block that typically presents in the neonatal period, within the first days of life, once the infant begins protein feeding and generates a nitrogen load the cycle cannot handle. The resulting hyperammonemia causes lethargy, poor feeding, temperature and respiratory dysregulation, and, if untreated, cerebral edema and irreversible neurologic injury.

incorrectas.A: Presentation in school-age children would suggest a partial enzyme deficiency with residual activity, which is not the classic presentation of complete CPS1 deficiency — the severe neonatal crisis reflects near-total loss of enzyme function.
incorrectas.C: Adolescent onset is atypical for CPS1 deficiency and would be more consistent with a partial defect or a different diagnosis; the classic teaching point is the acute neonatal hyperammonemic crisis.
incorrectas.D: Adult-onset presentation is unusual for CPS1 deficiency and, if it occurred, would imply a mild partial deficiency; the disease as classically tested presents catastrophically in the neonatal period, not in adulthood.

preguntas.q: Which is the most common urea cycle disorder overall?
