e.correcta: OTC deficiency is the most common urea cycle disorder, in part because its X-linked recessive inheritance allows it to be transmitted broadly through carrier females, and because milder or partial forms exist that come to attention later in life, in addition to classic severe neonatal presentations in affected males.

incorrectas.B: Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency (citrullinemia) is a less common urea cycle disorder, distinguished biochemically by strikingly elevated plasma citrulline rather than by being the most prevalent defect.
incorrectas.C: Arginase deficiency is the rarest and mildest of the classic urea cycle disorders, presenting with a distinct chronic spastic diplegia picture rather than being the most frequent urea cycle enzyme defect.
incorrectas.D: CPS1 deficiency is autosomal recessive and, while it produces an identical clinical hyperammonemic picture to OTC deficiency, is considerably rarer overall in prevalence.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency?

e.correcta: OTC deficiency is the only X-linked recessive urea cycle disorder, all the others being autosomal recessive, so it predominantly affects males, while carrier females can have variable, sometimes significant, symptoms depending on the pattern of X-inactivation (lyonization).

incorrectas.B: Autosomal recessive is the inheritance pattern for CPS1 deficiency and most other urea cycle disorders, but OTC deficiency specifically breaks this pattern by being X-linked.
incorrectas.C: Autosomal dominant inheritance is not seen in any classic urea cycle disorder; these are loss-of-function enzyme deficiencies that require inheritance patterns consistent with recessive traits (or X-linked recessive for OTC).
incorrectas.D: X-linked dominant inheritance would mean heterozygous females are typically as severely affected as males, which does not reflect the more variable, often milder female carrier phenotype seen in OTC deficiency due to random X-inactivation.

preguntas.q: Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency classically presents within which timeframe of life, though later, milder presentations can also occur?

e.correcta: Classic, severe OTC deficiency in affected males typically presents within the first few days of life, as maternal nitrogen clearance via the placenta is lost and the newborn's own inadequate urea cycle fails to handle the nitrogen load from feeding, precipitating a rapid hyperammonemic crisis with lethargy, poor feeding, and potential progression to coma if unrecognized.

incorrectas.A: Presentation in the first few months would suggest a partial deficiency with some residual enzyme activity, which occurs but is not the classic, most heavily tested timeframe for OTC deficiency.
incorrectas.B: A presentation delayed to the first few years is seen in milder, partial OTC deficiency or in carrier females with skewed X-inactivation, but is not the classic teaching point, which emphasizes the acute neonatal crisis.
incorrectas.D: Adult-onset presentation, while described in some carrier females or very mild variants, is far from the classic teaching picture, which centers on early neonatal hyperammonemic crisis in affected males.

preguntas.q: Why does ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency, unlike carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency, present with orotic aciduria?

o.A: OTC deficiency directly increases activity of UMP synthase
o.B: Carbamoyl phosphate accumulates behind the block and is shunted into the cytosolic pyrimidine synthesis pathway, increasing orotic acid production
o.C: OTC deficiency impairs renal excretion of orotic acid
o.D: OTC deficiency causes excess pyrimidine breakdown

e.correcta: Because CPS1, the enzyme upstream of OTC, still functions normally, carbamoyl phosphate continues to be produced in the mitochondria. With OTC missing, this carbamoyl phosphate cannot be used to form citrulline and instead leaks into the cytosol, where it serves as a substrate for de novo pyrimidine synthesis, driving excess orotic acid production — the reverse of CPS1 deficiency, where carbamoyl phosphate is never made in the first place.

incorrectas.A: OTC deficiency does not act on UMP synthase directly; the orotic acid excess arises from substrate overflow (excess carbamoyl phosphate) feeding into the pyrimidine pathway, not from altered activity of the downstream pyrimidine synthesis enzyme itself.
incorrectas.C: The mechanism is increased production of orotic acid from excess substrate, not impaired renal clearance; renal handling of orotic acid is not the defect being tested in OTC deficiency.
incorrectas.D: There is no increase in pyrimidine breakdown in OTC deficiency; rather, there is increased synthesis of orotic acid due to a substrate pile-up feeding forward into pyrimidine biosynthesis.

preguntas.q: A male neonate with OTC deficiency develops hyperammonemia. What is the mechanistic basis for the rise in NH4+?

o.A: Ammonia that has been fixed into carbamoyl phosphate cannot proceed further in the urea cycle because citrulline formation is blocked, so nitrogen backs up as free ammonia
o.B: OTC deficiency increases dietary ammonia absorption in the gut
o.C: OTC deficiency accelerates glutaminase activity in the liver
o.D: OTC deficiency causes increased renal ammonia production

e.correcta: Even though CPS1 successfully fixes ammonia into carbamoyl phosphate, OTC deficiency prevents that carbamoyl phosphate from combining with ornithine to form citrulline, so the urea cycle stalls at that step. Nitrogen cannot continue toward urea, and ammonia accumulates in the blood, producing hyperammonemia essentially identical in severity and clinical impact to CPS1 deficiency, despite the defect being one step further downstream.

incorrectas.B: Increased gut ammonia absorption is not the primary mechanism of OTC-related hyperammonemia, though gut bacterial ammonia production does contribute to the total ammonia load in general; the core defect is the enzymatic block preventing hepatic processing of ammonia already generated.
incorrectas.C: Glutaminase activity, which releases ammonia from glutamine, is not upregulated as the cause of hyperammonemia in OTC deficiency; instead, glutamine synthesis actually increases as tissues attempt to buffer the excess ammonia, the opposite direction from what this option describes.
incorrectas.D: The kidney is not the source of the excess ammonia in OTC deficiency; the ammonia originates from normal amino acid catabolism throughout the body and simply cannot be processed by the blocked hepatic urea cycle.

preguntas.q: What accounts for the elevated serum glutamine seen in ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency?

o.A: OTC directly catalyzes glutamine formation from citrulline
o.C: Peripheral tissues combine excess ammonia with glutamate via glutamine synthetase to buffer neurotoxic ammonia
o.D: Renal glutamine reabsorption increases due to metabolic acidosis

e.correcta: Just as in CPS1 deficiency, when the urea cycle stalls (here at the OTC step) and free ammonia rises, skeletal muscle, liver, and brain tissue use glutamine synthetase to conjugate ammonia with glutamate, forming glutamine as a way to sequester and transport the toxic nitrogen. The resulting elevated serum glutamine is a useful downstream marker that a urea cycle defect, rather than isolated renal failure, is causing the hyperammonemia.

incorrectas.A: OTC's actual reaction combines carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to make citrulline — it has no direct role in glutamine synthesis, and citrulline is not converted to glutamine.
incorrectas.B: Decreased, not increased, glutaminase activity would tend to spare glutamine from breakdown, but the primary driver of elevated glutamine in OTC deficiency is increased synthesis via glutamine synthetase in response to hyperammonemia, not a defect in its breakdown.
incorrectas.D: OTC deficiency does not classically produce metabolic acidosis (unlike some organic acidemias), and renal glutamine handling is not the mechanism responsible for the elevated serum glutamine seen here.

preguntas.q: Why is serum BUN typically decreased in a patient with OTC deficiency, despite normal renal function?

o.A: OTC deficiency causes increased renal clearance of urea
o.B: The block in the urea cycle at the OTC step reduces overall urea production by the liver
o.C: OTC deficiency shifts urea synthesis to the kidney instead of the liver
o.D: OTC deficiency has no effect on urea production since CPS1 still functions normally

e.correcta: Even though CPS1 functions normally in OTC deficiency, the downstream block prevents citrulline, and therefore the rest of the urea cycle, from proceeding efficiently, so overall hepatic urea output falls. This produces the same low BUN plus hyperammonemia pattern seen with CPS1 deficiency, since both conditions ultimately impair net urea synthesis, just at different steps.

incorrectas.A: There is no increase in renal urea clearance in OTC deficiency; the kidneys function normally, but there is simply less urea being made by the liver for them to excrete, explaining the low BUN through reduced production rather than increased elimination.
incorrectas.C: Urea synthesis is not relocated to the kidney; the urea cycle is a hepatic pathway, and the kidney's job is only to excrete the urea the liver has already made, not to synthesize it.
incorrectas.D: OTC deficiency does reduce net urea production despite normal CPS1 activity, because the pathway is sequential — a block at OTC prevents carbamoyl phosphate from being converted onward into citrulline, arginine, and ultimately urea, so total urea output still falls.

preguntas.q: Increased orotic acid in the blood and urine in a patient with OTC deficiency results from excess accumulation of which upstream metabolite?

e.correcta: Carbamoyl phosphate is made normally by CPS1 but, because OTC is missing, cannot be conjugated with ornithine. The resulting mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate excess spills into the cytosol, where it is used as a substrate by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II in the de novo pyrimidine synthesis pathway, driving overproduction of orotic acid.

incorrectas.A: Ornithine itself does not accumulate to a degree that drives orotic acid overproduction; in fact, ornithine is the substrate that OTC would normally combine with carbamoyl phosphate, and its levels are not the source of the excess pyrimidine precursor.
incorrectas.B: Citrulline is the product OTC would normally form; in OTC deficiency, citrulline levels are actually low, not elevated, because the enzyme needed to produce it is deficient, so it cannot be the metabolite feeding orotic acid overproduction.
incorrectas.C: Argininosuccinate is formed later in the urea cycle from citrulline and aspartate; since citrulline production itself is impaired in OTC deficiency, argininosuccinate is not the accumulating precursor responsible for excess orotic acid.

preguntas.q: Does ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency cause megaloblastic anemia, in contrast to hereditary orotic aciduria?

o.A: Yes, both conditions impair DNA synthesis identically
o.B: Yes, excess orotic acid directly damages erythroid precursors
o.C: No, OTC deficiency causes orotic aciduria without megaloblastic anemia, since it is a urea cycle disorder, not a pyrimidine synthesis defect
o.D: No, OTC deficiency instead causes microcytic anemia from iron deficiency

e.correcta: Although OTC deficiency and hereditary orotic aciduria both cause elevated orotic acid, they arise from entirely different defects. OTC deficiency is a urea cycle enzyme block causing carbamoyl phosphate overflow into pyrimidine synthesis, whereas hereditary orotic aciduria is a defect in UMP synthase itself, directly impairing the conversion of orotic acid into UMP for nucleotide synthesis. Only the latter causes megaloblastic anemia, because only there is nucleotide synthesis itself defective; OTC deficiency's hallmark is hyperammonemia, not anemia.

incorrectas.A: The two conditions do not impair DNA synthesis identically — hereditary orotic aciduria directly blocks the conversion of orotic acid to UMP, impairing pyrimidine nucleotide availability for DNA synthesis, while OTC deficiency's orotic acid elevation is just a downstream overflow phenomenon that does not affect UMP synthase function or nucleotide production.
incorrectas.B: Excess orotic acid concentration itself is not directly cytotoxic to erythroid precursors; the megaloblastic anemia in hereditary orotic aciduria comes from insufficient UMP and pyrimidine synthesis for DNA replication, not from a toxic effect of orotic acid on bone marrow cells.
incorrectas.D: OTC deficiency is not associated with a classic microcytic, iron-deficiency-type anemia; its clinical picture is dominated by hyperammonemic encephalopathy (vomiting, lethargy, respiratory alkalosis, cerebral edema) rather than any particular anemia.

preguntas.q: Excess ammonia in hyperammonemia depletes which TCA cycle intermediate, thereby inhibiting the citric acid cycle?

e.correcta: Excess NH3 combines with alpha-ketoglutarate, via glutamate dehydrogenase forming glutamate and subsequently glutamine via glutamine synthetase, as the body attempts to buffer ammonia. This consumes alpha-ketoglutarate faster than it can be replenished, depleting a key TCA cycle intermediate and impairing oxidative energy metabolism — a major reason hyperammonemia is so toxic to the energy-hungry brain, contributing to the lethargy and altered mental status seen clinically.

incorrectas.A: Oxaloacetate is consumed in transamination reactions and gluconeogenesis, but the specific intermediate depleted by ammonia detoxification, via combination with an alpha-keto acid to form an amino acid, is alpha-ketoglutarate, not oxaloacetate.
incorrectas.C: Succinyl-CoA is not the intermediate consumed by ammonia buffering reactions; it participates in different reactions, such as heme synthesis and odd-chain fatty acid metabolism, unrelated to the glutamate dehydrogenase reaction that traps ammonia.
incorrectas.D: Citrate is the first intermediate of the TCA cycle, formed from oxaloacetate and acetyl-CoA; it is not directly depleted by ammonia detoxification reactions, which specifically act on alpha-ketoglutarate.

preguntas.q: As part of dietary management for hyperammonemia due to a urea cycle disorder, what is typically restricted?

e.correcta: Because ammonia is generated from the catabolism of amino acids, limiting dietary protein intake reduces the nitrogen load that the impaired urea cycle must handle, helping to prevent or lessen hyperammonemic crises. This is typically paired with providing enough calories from carbohydrates and fats to prevent catabolism of the body's own protein, which would itself generate more ammonia.

incorrectas.A: Dietary fat is not the primary source of the nitrogen that generates ammonia; adequate fat intake is actually encouraged in these patients to provide non-protein calories and help prevent the body from breaking down its own protein for energy.
incorrectas.B: Carbohydrate restriction is not part of urea cycle disorder management; carbohydrates provide calories without contributing nitrogen, so adequate carbohydrate intake actually helps spare protein from being catabolized for energy.
incorrectas.C: Dietary fiber has no direct role in nitrogen or ammonia metabolism and is not a targeted component of dietary management in urea cycle disorders; the key intervention is limiting protein, the source of the nitrogen burden.

preguntas.q: Which treatment for hyperammonemia works by acidifying the colonic lumen, converting NH3 to NH4+ and trapping it for fecal excretion?

e.correcta: Lactulose is a non-absorbable disaccharide metabolized by colonic bacteria into short-chain fatty acids, acidifying the gut lumen. This acidic environment favors conversion of freely diffusible NH3 into charged NH4+, which cannot easily cross back into the bloodstream and is instead trapped in the colon and excreted in stool, lowering systemic ammonia.

incorrectas.A: Rifaximin is a poorly absorbed antibiotic that reduces ammonia production by decreasing the population of colonic ammoniagenic bacteria — a different mechanism (reducing production) rather than lactulose's mechanism of trapping ammonia via pH-dependent ionization.
incorrectas.B: Sodium benzoate lowers ammonia by conjugating with glycine to form hippurate, which is excreted in urine, providing an alternative nitrogen excretion route entirely independent of the urea cycle — a different strategy from lactulose's gut-trapping mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Sodium phenylbutyrate is metabolized to phenylacetate, which conjugates with glutamine to form phenylacetylglutamine, excreted in urine as another alternative nitrogen-scavenging pathway, mechanistically distinct from lactulose's colonic acidification and trapping effect.

preguntas.q: Which treatment for hyperammonemia acts by decreasing the population of colonic ammoniagenic bacteria?

e.correcta: Rifaximin is a minimally absorbed oral antibiotic that reduces the number of urease-producing, ammonia-generating colonic bacteria, decreasing the amount of ammonia produced in the gut and absorbed into the portal circulation. It is often used together with lactulose for a complementary dual mechanism, less ammonia produced plus more efficient trapping and excretion, in hepatic encephalopathy management.

incorrectas.A: Lactulose does not primarily work by killing or reducing bacterial populations; its mechanism is acidifying the colon so that NH3 is converted to NH4+ and trapped for excretion, a chemical trapping effect rather than an antimicrobial one.
incorrectas.B: Sodium phenylbutyrate lowers ammonia by providing an alternative nitrogen excretion pathway, conjugation with glutamine excreted as phenylacetylglutamine, not by altering the gut bacterial population.
incorrectas.C: L-arginine can be used to help restart a partially functioning urea cycle in some urea cycle disorders by replenishing an intermediate depleted by the enzyme block, but it does not work by reducing colonic bacteria; its mechanism is entirely different from rifaximin's antimicrobial action.

preguntas.q: Which finding describes the characteristic flapping tremor seen in patients with hyperammonemia, alongside slurred speech, somnolence, vomiting, cerebral edema, and blurry vision?

e.correcta: Asterixis is the classic flapping tremor of hyperammonemic or hepatic encephalopathy, best elicited by asking the patient to extend their arms and dorsiflex their wrists, seen as an intermittent loss of postural tone. Mechanistically, excess ammonia causes astrocytes, which normally clear excess neurotransmitters and detoxify ammonia via glutamine synthetase, to become overloaded with glutamine, leading to astrocyte swelling and dysfunction, disrupted glutamate and GABA balance, and impaired CNS energy metabolism — collectively producing the encephalopathic picture that includes asterixis.

incorrectas.A: Chorea refers to involuntary, irregular, dance-like movements classically seen in disorders like Huntington disease or Sydenham chorea, driven by basal ganglia dysfunction, a distinct movement disorder from the metabolic, ammonia-induced flapping tremor of asterixis.
incorrectas.C: Myoclonus consists of brief, shock-like muscle jerks seen in various metabolic and neurodegenerative conditions, but it is not the specific term for the sustained postural lapse (flapping) tremor that characterizes hyperammonemic encephalopathy.
incorrectas.D: A resting tremor is the classic finding in Parkinson disease, caused by degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, a completely different pathophysiology from the astrocyte-mediated dysfunction underlying asterixis in hyperammonemia.

preguntas.q: A neonate with hyperphenylalaninemia has persistently elevated phenylalanine despite adequate dietary phenylalanine restriction, along with hyperprolactinemia and progressive neurologic decline. In addition to classic phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency, malignant PKU of this type is most commonly caused by a deficiency of which enzyme?

e.correcta: Dihydropteridine reductase (DHPR) regenerates tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) from BH2 using NADH; BH4 is the essential cofactor not only for phenylalanine hydroxylase but also for tyrosine hydroxylase and tryptophan hydroxylase. Because the defect lies in cofactor regeneration rather than in the hydroxylase enzyme itself, malignant PKU does not respond to dietary phenylalanine restriction the way classic PKU does. Loss of BH4 also cripples catecholamine and serotonin synthesis, producing hyperprolactinemia (from loss of dopaminergic inhibition of prolactin) and progressive neurologic deterioration even on a controlled diet.

incorrectas.B: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency is the enzyme defect of classic PKU, which directly converts phenylalanine to tyrosine and improves with dietary phenylalanine restriction; the scenario describes a case unresponsive to diet, pointing to a cofactor problem rather than PAH itself.
incorrectas.C: Tyrosine hydroxylase converts tyrosine to L-DOPA in catecholamine synthesis and does require BH4, so its function is secondarily impaired in malignant PKU, but it is not the primary enzyme deficiency that defines the diagnosis—that role belongs to DHPR (or a BH4 synthesis enzyme).
incorrectas.D: Homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency causes alkaptonuria, a distinct disorder of tyrosine catabolism further downstream, unrelated to phenylalanine hydroxylation or BH4 regeneration.

preguntas.q: In patients with phenylketonuria, which amino acid becomes conditionally essential and requires dietary supplementation because it can no longer be synthesized endogenously?

e.correcta: Tyrosine is normally synthesized from phenylalanine via phenylalanine hydroxylase. When this enzyme is deficient in PKU, that conversion cannot occur, so tyrosine can no longer be made endogenously and must come from the diet. Tyrosine is needed for synthesis of catecholamines, thyroid hormone, and melanin, so PKU management includes both phenylalanine restriction and tyrosine supplementation.

incorrectas.A: Phenylalanine is the amino acid that must be restricted, not supplemented, in PKU because it accumulates to neurotoxic levels when PAH is deficient; the question asks about the amino acid whose supply becomes inadequate, not the one that builds up.
incorrectas.C: Methionine metabolism is unrelated to the phenylalanine hydroxylase pathway; its conditionally essential status is relevant to disorders like homocystinuria, not PKU.
incorrectas.D: Tryptophan is a separate essential amino acid used for serotonin and niacin synthesis and is unaffected by the PAH block, so it is not rendered essential by PKU.

preguntas.q: In untreated phenylketonuria, elevated serum phenylalanine leads to excess urinary excretion of which class of compounds, giving the disease its name?

e.correcta: When phenylalanine hydroxylase is deficient, phenylalanine cannot be converted to tyrosine and instead is shunted through transamination into phenylpyruvate and related phenylketones (phenylacetate, phenyllactate), which spill into the urine. This excess urinary excretion of phenylketones is the source of the disease's name and also produces the classic musty or mousy body odor.

incorrectas.A: Homogentisic acid accumulates in alkaptonuria, a separate downstream defect in tyrosine catabolism caused by homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency, not by a block in phenylalanine hydroxylation.
incorrectas.B: Methylmalonic acid accumulates when methylmalonyl-CoA mutase or vitamin B12 is deficient, a pathway involving branched-chain amino acid and odd-chain fatty acid catabolism entirely unrelated to phenylalanine.
incorrectas.D: Orotic acid accumulates in urea cycle disorders such as OTC deficiency or in hereditary orotic aciduria from UMP synthase deficiency, neither of which involves phenylalanine metabolism.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of classic phenylketonuria (incidence approximately 1:10,000)?

e.correcta: Classic PKU is autosomal recessive, requiring both copies of the phenylalanine hydroxylase gene (on chromosome 12) to carry loss-of-function mutations. Heterozygous carriers, typically the unaffected parents, have enough residual enzyme activity to remain asymptomatic, which is why the disease appears in offspring of two unaffected carrier parents at the expected recessive incidence of roughly 1:10,000 births.

incorrectas.A: An autosomal dominant pattern would mean a single mutant allele produces disease, but enzyme deficiencies like PAH loss-of-function typically require both alleles affected, consistent with recessive rather than dominant inheritance.
incorrectas.B: X-linked recessive inheritance would cause PKU to affect males far more often than females, but PKU affects both sexes equally, consistent with an autosomal (not X-linked) gene location.
incorrectas.C: Mitochondrial inheritance is transmitted exclusively from the mother, but the PAH gene is nuclear-encoded on chromosome 12, so PKU follows standard Mendelian autosomal inheritance rather than maternal mitochondrial transmission.

preguntas.q: At what point after birth are newborns typically screened for phenylketonuria?

e.correcta: Newborn screening for PKU (the Guthrie test) is performed about 2-3 days after birth, once the infant has had adequate protein feeding (breast milk or formula) for phenylalanine to accumulate to detectable levels if PAH is deficient. Screening too early risks a false negative because maternal enzyme clearance during fetal life can keep the newborn's phenylalanine level artificially low right after delivery.

incorrectas.B: Testing immediately at birth from cord blood is unreliable because the mother's own functioning PAH enzyme has been clearing the fetus's phenylalanine throughout gestation, masking an affected infant's true enzyme status.
incorrectas.C: Waiting two weeks would unnecessarily delay diagnosis and treatment initiation; the standard protocol screens within the first few days precisely to catch the disease early enough to prevent irreversible neurologic injury.
incorrectas.D: A one-month delay would be far too late for a disease where early dietary intervention within the neonatal period is critical for preventing severe intellectual disability.

preguntas.q: Why is newborn screening for phenylketonuria performed 2-3 days after birth rather than immediately at delivery?

o.A: Neonatal kidney immaturity prevents phenylalanine from being excreted
o.B: Infants may appear biochemically normal at birth because maternal enzyme cleared phenylalanine during fetal life
o.C: Breast milk initially lacks any phenylalanine
o.D: Hepatic phenylalanine hydroxylase is not expressed until about one week of age

e.correcta: During gestation, the mother's own functioning phenylalanine hydroxylase metabolizes phenylalanine that crosses the placenta from the fetus, so even an affected infant can have a near-normal phenylalanine level at birth. Only after birth, once the neonate relies on its own (deficient) enzyme and begins ingesting dietary protein, does phenylalanine rise to detectable pathologic levels, which is why screening is timed to 2-3 days of age.

incorrectas.A: Renal immaturity is not the reason for the screening delay; the issue is that phenylalanine has not yet had time to accumulate because maternal clearance protected the fetus in utero, not a failure of the newborn kidney to excrete it.
incorrectas.C: Breast milk and formula do contain phenylalanine from the start; the delay in screening is not because the substrate is initially absent from feeds but because time and protein intake are needed for a true elevation to develop.
incorrectas.D: Phenylalanine hydroxylase is expressed in the fetal and neonatal liver from early on; the affected infant's enzyme is defective throughout, not simply unexpressed until a week of age—the confounder is maternal enzyme activity before birth, not delayed infant enzyme expression.

preguntas.q: Patients with phenylketonuria must avoid which artificial sweetener because it is metabolized to release phenylalanine?

e.correcta: Aspartame is a dipeptide ester composed of aspartate and the methyl ester of phenylalanine. When metabolized in the body, it releases free phenylalanine, which is dangerous for PKU patients whose deficient phenylalanine hydroxylase cannot clear the resulting load, risking further neurotoxic accumulation. This is why products containing aspartame carry a warning for phenylketonurics.

incorrectas.A: Saccharin is a sulfonamide-derived sweetener that is not metabolized into amino acids at all, so it poses no phenylalanine-related risk to PKU patients.
incorrectas.B: Sucralose is a chlorinated sucrose derivative that passes through the body largely unmetabolized and contains no phenylalanine, unlike aspartame.
incorrectas.D: Stevia is a plant-derived glycoside sweetener unrelated to amino acid chemistry, so it does not release phenylalanine on digestion and is safe for PKU patients.

preguntas.q: A woman with known phenylketonuria discontinues her phenylalanine-restricted diet before and during pregnancy. Her infant, who does not have PKU, is subsequently born with microcephaly, intellectual disability, and a congenital heart defect. What is this teratogenic condition called?

e.correcta: Maternal PKU syndrome occurs when a woman with PKU fails to maintain adequate phenylalanine restriction during pregnancy. Elevated maternal phenylalanine crosses the placenta and is directly teratogenic to the developing fetus, causing microcephaly, intrauterine growth restriction, congenital heart disease, and intellectual disability—even though the child may not have inherited PKU itself, since the damage is caused by in utero exposure rather than the infant's own enzyme status.

incorrectas.A: Classic PKU refers to an infant's own inherited phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency diagnosed by newborn screening, not to teratogenic damage from a mother's untreated disease during pregnancy.
incorrectas.B: Malignant PKU refers to a defect in BH4 synthesis or regeneration (e.g., DHPR deficiency) causing dietary-unresponsive hyperphenylalaninemia in the affected individual, not to fetal harm from maternal phenylalanine exposure.
incorrectas.C: Transient neonatal tyrosinemia is a benign, self-limited elevation of tyrosine seen in some premature infants due to immature tyrosine-metabolizing enzymes, unrelated to maternal phenylalanine levels or teratogenicity.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of alkaptonuria?

e.correcta: Alkaptonuria is caused by loss-of-function mutations in homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase, an enzyme in the tyrosine degradation pathway. Like most inborn errors of metabolism caused by deficient catabolic enzymes, it follows an autosomal recessive pattern, requiring both gene copies to be defective, with carrier parents typically unaffected.

incorrectas.B: An autosomal dominant pattern would require only a single mutant allele to cause disease, but a single functional homogentisate dioxygenase allele is generally sufficient to prevent buildup of homogentisic acid, consistent with recessive rather than dominant transmission.
incorrectas.C: X-linked recessive inheritance would produce a strong male predominance, but alkaptonuria affects both sexes roughly equally, consistent with an autosomal gene location rather than an X-linked one.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance is passed exclusively through the maternal line, but the homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase gene is nuclear, so alkaptonuria follows standard autosomal recessive Mendelian inheritance.

preguntas.q: Which metabolic disorder is classically associated with bluish-black discoloration of connective tissue and the sclerae?

e.correcta: Alkaptonuria results from homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency, causing homogentisic acid to accumulate and polymerize within collagen-rich tissues such as cartilage, tendons, and sclerae. This oxidized pigment deposition produces the bluish-black discoloration known as ochronosis, along with urine that darkens on standing when exposed to air.

incorrectas.A: Phenylketonuria results from phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency and causes intellectual disability, a musty body odor, and hypopigmentation (from reduced melanin synthesis), not the dark pigment deposition seen in alkaptonuria.
incorrectas.C: Homocystinuria, caused by defects such as cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, causes lens dislocation, a marfanoid habitus, and thromboembolism, but not connective tissue pigment deposition.
incorrectas.D: Maple syrup urine disease, from branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency, causes CNS toxicity and a characteristic sweet urine odor, with no association with tissue pigmentation.

preguntas.q: In alkaptonuria, deposition of oxidized homogentisic acid polymer in collagen produces bluish-black discoloration of connective tissue and sclerae. What is this finding termed?

e.correcta: Ochronosis refers to the bluish-black pigmentation that develops when homogentisic acid oxidizes and polymerizes within collagen-containing structures like cartilage (notably the ears), tendons, and sclerae in alkaptonuria. It develops gradually over years and is a hallmark clue linking the biochemical defect to its visible clinical sign.

incorrectas.A: Kernicterus is bilirubin deposition in the basal ganglia of neonates with severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, causing yellow staining and neurologic injury—an entirely different pigment and mechanism from homogentisic acid deposition.
incorrectas.B: Jaundice refers to yellow discoloration of skin and sclerae from hyperbilirubinemia, a different color and different underlying pigment than the bluish-black ochronotic deposits of alkaptonuria.
incorrectas.D: Cyanosis is a bluish discoloration of skin and mucous membranes caused by increased deoxygenated hemoglobin from hypoxemia, a functional vascular finding rather than a structural pigment deposition disorder.

preguntas.q: Alkaptonuria is usually a benign condition, but it may eventually present with which debilitating complication due to homogentisic acid toxicity to cartilage?

e.correcta: Homogentisic acid polymerizes and deposits within joint cartilage, where it is directly toxic and causes progressive degeneration of the cartilage matrix. Over decades this produces ochronotic arthropathy—debilitating arthralgias and joint destruction, particularly in large weight-bearing joints and the spine—which is the most clinically significant long-term complication of an otherwise largely benign metabolic disorder.

incorrectas.A: Seizures are not a feature of alkaptonuria; homogentisic acid accumulation does not directly affect central nervous system excitability the way toxic metabolites in disorders like MSUD or hyperammonemia can.
incorrectas.B: Hepatosplenomegaly is characteristic of storage diseases or hemolytic processes, not of homogentisic acid buildup, which targets connective tissue and cartilage rather than the reticuloendothelial organs.
incorrectas.C: Intellectual disability is a hallmark of disorders like PKU or MSUD that disrupt neurotransmitter synthesis or cause direct CNS toxicity; alkaptonuria patients have normal cognitive development since homogentisic acid deposition is limited to connective tissue.

preguntas.q: In the tyrosine degradation pathway, fumarylacetoacetate (derived from maleylacetoacetate) is cleaved by fumarylacetoacetase into acetoacetate and which compound that directly enters the Krebs cycle?

e.correcta: Fumarylacetoacetase hydrolyzes fumarylacetoacetate into two products: fumarate and acetoacetate. Fumarate is a genuine TCA cycle intermediate and feeds directly into the Krebs cycle, illustrating how an amino acid catabolic pathway can be glucogenic by funneling carbon skeletons into central energy metabolism.

incorrectas.B: Succinate is a distinct four-carbon TCA cycle intermediate, but it is not the direct product generated when fumarylacetoacetase cleaves fumarylacetoacetate; that reaction specifically yields fumarate, not succinate.
incorrectas.C: Acetoacetate is indeed the other product of the same cleavage reaction, but it is a ketone body precursor rather than a molecule that enters the Krebs cycle directly—the question specifically asks which product enters the TCA cycle, which is fumarate.
incorrectas.D: Oxaloacetate is a key TCA cycle intermediate, but it is not generated from tyrosine catabolism; it arises instead from pyruvate carboxylation or from malate dehydrogenase within the cycle itself.

preguntas.q: Maple syrup urine disease is characterized by blocked degradation of which category of amino acids?

e.correcta: MSUD results from deficiency of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, a mitochondrial enzyme complex structurally and functionally analogous to pyruvate dehydrogenase. This blocks the oxidative decarboxylation step in catabolism of the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine, and valine, causing both the amino acids and their corresponding toxic ketoacids to accumulate in blood and urine.

incorrectas.A: Aromatic amino acids (phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan) are affected in disorders like PKU, which involves a completely different enzyme (phenylalanine hydroxylase) and pathway, not the BCKD complex defective in MSUD.
incorrectas.C: Sulfur-containing amino acids like methionine and cysteine are relevant to homocystinuria, involving cystathionine beta-synthase or remethylation enzymes, an unrelated metabolic pathway from branched-chain amino acid catabolism.
incorrectas.D: Acidic amino acids such as aspartate and glutamate are not implicated in MSUD; their metabolism does not involve the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex at all.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of maple syrup urine disease?

e.correcta: MSUD is autosomal recessive, caused by mutations affecting subunits of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex. As with most inherited enzyme deficiencies, two defective alleles are needed for the disease to manifest, so affected infants typically have two unaffected carrier parents.

incorrectas.A: Autosomal dominant inheritance would mean a single mutant allele causes disease, but loss-of-function enzyme defects like BCKD deficiency generally require both alleles to be affected, consistent with recessive rather than dominant transmission.
incorrectas.B: X-linked recessive inheritance would cause a strong male predominance, but MSUD affects males and females at similar rates, consistent with an autosomal rather than X-linked gene location.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance is transmitted only from the mother, but the genes encoding BCKD complex subunits are nuclear-encoded, so MSUD follows classic autosomal recessive Mendelian inheritance.

preguntas.q: A newborn develops vomiting and poor feeding, with urine that has a distinctive sweet, burnt-sugar odor. Which condition does this presentation suggest?

e.correcta: Maple syrup urine disease results from deficient branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase activity, causing accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, valine, and their corresponding ketoacids. These accumulated ketoacids give the urine its characteristic sweet, maple syrup or burnt-sugar odor, accompanied in the neonatal period by vomiting, poor feeding, and lethargy that can progress rapidly to severe encephalopathy if untreated.

incorrectas.A: Phenylketonuria produces a musty or mousy body odor from accumulated phenylketones, a distinctly different smell from the sweet maple syrup odor described here, and usually presents more insidiously with developmental delay rather than acute neonatal vomiting.
incorrectas.B: Alkaptonuria typically presents later in life with darkening urine on standing and joint disease from ochronosis, not with an acute neonatal vomiting illness or a maple syrup odor.
incorrectas.C: Isovaleric acidemia is a distinct organic acidemia from isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (one step in leucine catabolism) that produces a "sweaty feet" odor rather than the maple syrup smell, and involves a different specific enzyme than the BCKD complex defective in MSUD.

preguntas.q: If maple syrup urine disease is left untreated, accumulated branched-chain amino acids and ketoacids are directly neurotoxic and can cause severe CNS defects and death. Which specific long-term complication commonly results in survivors?

e.correcta: The accumulated branched-chain amino acids and their toxic ketoacids impair cerebral energy metabolism and myelination during the critical period of infant brain development, causing cerebral edema and diffuse neuronal injury. Without prompt treatment—dietary restriction of leucine, isoleucine, and valine, sometimes combined with dialysis during acute crises—this results in irreversible global developmental delay and intellectual disability, alongside the risk of death from acute metabolic decompensation.

incorrectas.B: MSUD does not classically cause an isolated motor paralysis syndrome; its neurotoxicity manifests as diffuse encephalopathy and global developmental impairment rather than a discrete paralytic process like a peripheral neuropathy.
incorrectas.C: Sensorineural hearing loss is more characteristically associated with conditions like congenital rubella, Alport syndrome, or aminoglycoside toxicity, not with the branched-chain amino acid toxicity seen in MSUD.
incorrectas.D: A primary personality or psychotic disorder is not the classic long-term sequela of MSUD; the dominant complication is global intellectual and developmental impairment from diffuse neurotoxic injury, not an isolated psychiatric syndrome.

preguntas.q: Dietary intake of which amino acids must be restricted in patients with maple syrup urine disease?

e.correcta: Because branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase is deficient in MSUD, the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine, and valine cannot be properly degraded and accumulate along with their neurotoxic ketoacid derivatives. Dietary restriction of these three specific amino acids limits substrate buildup and prevents the toxic ketoacid accumulation responsible for CNS injury, analogous in principle to phenylalanine restriction in PKU.

incorrectas.A: Phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan are the aromatic amino acids whose metabolism is disrupted in disorders like PKU, not in MSUD, which involves an entirely separate branched-chain amino acid degradation pathway.
incorrectas.C: Methionine, cysteine, and homocysteine are relevant to sulfur amino acid metabolism disorders like homocystinuria, a distinct pathway from the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase defect underlying MSUD.
incorrectas.D: Lysine, arginine, and histidine are basic amino acids degraded through separate pathways unrelated to the BCKD complex, so their restriction is not part of MSUD dietary management.

preguntas.q: In addition to dietary restriction of branched-chain amino acids, treatment of maple syrup urine disease may include high-dose supplementation with which vitamin, since it serves as a cofactor for the deficient enzyme complex?

e.correcta: The branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, like pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, requires thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP, the active form of vitamin B1) as an essential cofactor. In a subset of MSUD patients with residual enzyme activity, high-dose thiamine supplementation can partially boost the function of the defective complex, following the same logic used for B6-responsive sideroblastic anemia—supplying extra cofactor to coax more activity out of a partially functional enzyme.

incorrectas.A: Pyridoxine (B6) is the cofactor relevant to conditions like B6-responsive sideroblastic anemia and to cystathionine beta-synthase in the homocystinuria pathway, not to the thiamine-dependent BCKD complex defective in MSUD.
incorrectas.B: Cobalamin (B12) is the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase, relevant to methylmalonic acidemia and homocystinuria, not to the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex.
incorrectas.D: Riboflavin (B2) is a cofactor for FAD-dependent enzymes such as succinate dehydrogenase and glutathione reductase, not the classic cofactor associated with BCKD complex function in MSUD.

preguntas.q: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase converts propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA as part of branched-chain amino acid and odd-chain fatty acid catabolism, using ATP and CO2. Which vitamin serves as the essential cofactor for this carboxylation reaction (as in the mnemonic "ABC carboxylase")?

e.correcta: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase is a biotin-dependent carboxylase—summarized by the mnemonic "ABC" for ATP, Biotin, CO2—that adds a carboxyl group derived from CO2 onto propionyl-CoA using ATP for energy, with biotin serving as the covalently bound carrier that shuttles the activated CO2 to the substrate. This same biotin-dependent carboxylation mechanism is shared by other carboxylases like pyruvate carboxylase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase, so biotin or biotinidase deficiency impairs all of them simultaneously.

incorrectas.A: Thiamine (as TPP) is the cofactor for alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complexes (pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, BCKD) that perform oxidative decarboxylation, a chemically different reaction from the carboxylation catalyzed by propionyl-CoA carboxylase.
incorrectas.B: Cobalamin (B12) is the cofactor for the next enzyme in this same pathway—methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA—but it is not the cofactor for propionyl-CoA carboxylase itself.
incorrectas.C: Folate participates in one-carbon transfer reactions such as purine and thymidylate synthesis and homocysteine remethylation, not in the biotin-dependent carboxylation step performed by propionyl-CoA carboxylase.

preguntas.q: If methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is dysfunctional (due to enzyme mutation or vitamin B12 deficiency), which compound accumulates in the blood and urine?

e.correcta: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, a cobalamin-dependent enzyme, normally converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA for entry into the TCA cycle. When this enzyme (or its B12 cofactor) is deficient, methylmalonyl-CoA and its associated metabolite methylmalonic acid accumulate in blood and urine, forming the basis of methylmalonic acidemia and making elevated urine methylmalonic acid a sensitive marker of B12 deficiency.

incorrectas.B: Propionic acid (from propionyl-CoA) accumulates one step upstream if the biotin-dependent enzyme propionyl-CoA carboxylase is deficient, not when the mutase downstream of it is affected.
incorrectas.C: Homocysteine accumulates when methionine synthase (also cobalamin-dependent) or cystathionine beta-synthase is impaired—a distinct cobalamin-dependent reaction separate from the methylmalonyl-CoA mutase pathway.
incorrectas.D: Orotic acid accumulates in urea cycle disorders like OTC deficiency or in hereditary orotic aciduria from UMP synthase deficiency, unrelated to the propionate/methylmalonate degradation pathway.

preguntas.q: Methionine combines with adenosine, using ATP, to form which activated compound?

e.correcta: Methionine adenosyltransferase catalyzes the ATP-dependent transfer of an adenosyl group onto the sulfur atom of methionine, producing S-adenosylmethionine (SAM). SAM is the body's principal activated methyl donor, supplying methyl groups for reactions such as norepinephrine-to-epinephrine conversion, DNA methylation, creatine synthesis, and phosphatidylcholine formation.

incorrectas.A: Homocysteine is formed later, after SAM has already donated its methyl group and been converted to S-adenosylhomocysteine, which is then hydrolyzed—it is not produced directly from methionine combining with adenosine.
incorrectas.C: Cystathionine is an intermediate formed when homocysteine condenses with serine via cystathionine beta-synthase, a separate downstream reaction in the transsulfuration pathway, not the product of methionine and adenosine combining.
incorrectas.D: Betaine is an alternative methyl donor that can remethylate homocysteine back to methionine via betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase; it is not the product formed when methionine reacts with adenosine.

preguntas.q: S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) primarily functions as a donor of which chemical group in biological methylation reactions?

e.correcta: SAM carries a highly reactive activated methyl group on its sulfonium sulfur, which it transfers to a wide variety of acceptor molecules including DNA, norepinephrine (forming epinephrine), phospholipids, and guanidinoacetate (forming creatine). This methyl-donating role makes SAM central to numerous biological methylation reactions throughout metabolism.

incorrectas.A: Acetyl group donation is the role of acetyl-CoA, used in reactions like histone acetylation and fatty acid synthesis; this is a distinct chemical function from SAM's methyl-donating role.
incorrectas.B: Carboxyl group addition is performed by biotin-dependent carboxylases such as pyruvate carboxylase and propionyl-CoA carboxylase, not by SAM, which transfers methyl rather than carboxyl groups.
incorrectas.D: Amino group transfer is the function of aminotransferases (transaminases) using pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor, a different chemical reaction from SAM's methylation chemistry.

preguntas.q: After S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) donates its methyl group to an anabolic acceptor molecule, what compound is formed?

e.correcta: Once SAM transfers its activated methyl group to an acceptor (such as DNA, a phospholipid, or a catecholamine), it becomes S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH). SAH is subsequently hydrolyzed by SAH hydrolase to release adenosine and homocysteine, completing one turn of the methionine (activated methyl) cycle.

incorrectas.A: Methionine is the starting molecule that gets converted to SAM before any methyl transfer occurs, not the product immediately following methyl donation—that product is SAH.
incorrectas.B: Cystathionine forms further downstream, only if the homocysteine eventually released from SAH goes on to condense with serine in the transsulfuration pathway, which is two steps beyond the immediate product of methyl donation.
incorrectas.C: Homocysteine is produced one step further downstream, after SAH is subsequently hydrolyzed by SAH hydrolase; the immediate demethylated product of SAM itself is SAH, not homocysteine directly.

preguntas.q: S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) is hydrolyzed by SAH hydrolase into adenosine and which compound, which then sits at a metabolic branch point between remethylation and transsulfuration pathways?

e.correcta: SAH hydrolase cleaves S-adenosylhomocysteine into adenosine and homocysteine. Homocysteine then sits at a metabolic crossroads: it can be remethylated back to methionine using methylcobalamin and folate (via methionine synthase) or transsulfurated by condensing with serine (via the B6-dependent enzyme cystathionine beta-synthase) to eventually form cysteine. Defects in either pathway cause homocystinuria, presenting with thromboembolism, lens dislocation, and a marfanoid habitus.

incorrectas.B: Methionine is regenerated FROM homocysteine via the remethylation pathway, but it is not the direct product of SAH hydrolysis itself—that reaction yields homocysteine, which may later become methionine again.
incorrectas.C: Cysteine is produced further downstream, only after homocysteine condenses with serine to form cystathionine, which is then cleaved into cysteine and alpha-ketobutyrate—two enzymatic steps beyond the immediate hydrolysis of SAH.
incorrectas.D: Serine is a substrate that combines WITH homocysteine (via cystathionine beta-synthase) in the transsulfuration pathway; it is not itself a product generated by the hydrolysis of SAH.

preguntas.q: Homocystinuria is a metabolic disorder characterized by an excess of which sulfur-containing amino acid metabolite in the blood and urine?

e.correcta: Homocystinuria results from impaired conversion of homocysteine downstream in its metabolic pathway (most classically due to cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, which normally condenses homocysteine with serine to form cystathionine). Because this and other salvage routes are blocked, homocysteine accumulates in blood and is excreted in urine, and it is directly toxic to vascular endothelium, connective tissue, and the lens of the eye, producing the disease's hallmark features (thromboembolism, marfanoid habitus, lens dislocation, intellectual disability).

incorrectas.A: Methionine is actually decreased or only mildly affected in classic CBS-deficient homocystinuria, since it lies downstream of homocysteine remethylation rather than being the metabolite that builds up and defines the disease — the diagnostic accumulation is of homocysteine itself, upstream of methionine.
incorrectas.C: Cystathionine is the product that cystathionine beta-synthase makes from homocysteine and serine; because this enzyme is the one that's deficient, cystathionine levels fall rather than rise, the opposite of what happens to its substrate homocysteine.
incorrectas.D: Cysteine is synthesized further downstream of cystathionine via cystathionine gamma-lyase, so with the pathway blocked at CBS, cysteine production actually decreases (making it a conditionally essential amino acid in these patients), rather than accumulating.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of homocystinuria?

e.correcta: Homocystinuria is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, most commonly from loss-of-function mutations in the gene encoding cystathionine beta-synthase. Affected individuals need two defective alleles (one from each carrier parent) to manifest disease, and the parents themselves are typically asymptomatic carriers.

incorrectas.A: X-linked recessive disorders (like Fabry disease or OTC deficiency) show a pattern where fathers cannot transmit to sons and heterozygous mothers are carriers, but homocystinuria's transmission instead requires two autosomal mutant alleles regardless of sex, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.
incorrectas.B: Autosomal dominant disease requires only one mutant allele to cause the phenotype and would show affected individuals in multiple generations; homocystinuria typically skips generations and clusters in siblings of unaffected parents, the classic recessive pattern.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance is transmitted exclusively through the maternal line to all offspring, a pattern not seen in homocystinuria, which follows nuclear autosomal recessive genetics tied to the CBS gene.

preguntas.q: Aside from enzyme mutations such as cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, homocystinuria can also result from deficiency of which class of nutrients that serve as cofactors in homocysteine metabolism?

e.correcta: Homocysteine metabolism depends on vitamin cofactors: pyridoxine (B6) is required by cystathionine beta-synthase in the transsulfuration pathway, while folate and B12 are required for methionine synthase to remethylate homocysteine back to methionine. Deficiency of any of these vitamins can produce a biochemical homocystinuria/hyperhomocysteinemia phenotype even without a primary enzyme gene mutation, which is why some patients respond to high-dose B6 (pyridoxine-responsive homocystinuria) or B12/folate supplementation.

incorrectas.B: Trace minerals such as zinc and copper are cofactors for other enzymes (e.g., copper for lysyl oxidase and ceruloplasmin) but are not required for the transsulfuration or remethylation reactions that clear homocysteine, so their deficiency does not cause homocystinuria.
incorrectas.C: Essential fatty acid deficiency causes dermatologic and growth abnormalities through altered eicosanoid and membrane lipid synthesis, an entirely separate pathway that does not intersect with homocysteine clearance.
incorrectas.D: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are absorbed with dietary lipids and support vision, bone mineralization, antioxidant defense, and coagulation factor synthesis respectively — none of them participate in the transsulfuration or remethylation reactions that keep homocysteine levels in check.

preguntas.q: In homocystinuria, lens subluxation (ectopia lentis) classically occurs in which direction, helping distinguish it from Marfan syndrome?

e.correcta: In homocystinuria, weakened zonular fibers (from impaired connective tissue cross-linking due to toxic homocysteine accumulation) cause the lens to sublux downward and inward (medially). This is a useful clinical discriminator, since Marfan syndrome — which can produce a similar marfanoid body habitus — instead causes upward and temporal lens subluxation from a primary fibrillin-1 defect in the suspensory ligament.

incorrectas.A: Upward and temporal subluxation is the classic direction seen in Marfan syndrome, where defective fibrillin-1 microfibrils fail to anchor the zonules superiorly and laterally — the opposite pattern from homocystinuria.
incorrectas.C: Downward and temporal is not the classic pairing taught for either condition; homocystinuria's downward displacement is paired with inward (nasal), not temporal, displacement.
incorrectas.D: Upward and nasal is not a classically taught direction for either disease; the two teaching patterns to remember are homocystinuria (down-and-in) versus Marfan syndrome (up-and-out/temporal).

preguntas.q: A patient with a marfanoid body habitus, lens subluxation, osteoporosis, and kyphosis is being evaluated for homocystinuria versus Marfan syndrome. Which additional finding favors homocystinuria over Marfan syndrome?

e.correcta: Both homocystinuria and Marfan syndrome can produce a tall, thin marfanoid habitus with long limbs and lens dislocation, but only homocystinuria typically also causes intellectual disability, along with osteoporosis, kyphoscoliosis, and a tendency toward thromboembolism from endothelial damage by excess homocysteine. This makes cognitive impairment a key clinical clue pointing away from a primary connective tissue disorder like Marfan syndrome and toward a metabolic one.

incorrectas.B: Aortic root dilation and dissection risk is a hallmark of Marfan syndrome, arising from weakened elastic fibers in the aortic media due to defective fibrillin-1 scaffolding for TGF-beta regulation; thrombosis (not aneurysm) is more typical of homocystinuria, so this does not favor it.
incorrectas.C: Arachnodactyly (long, slender fingers) is a shared connective tissue feature that can appear in both Marfan syndrome and homocystinuria due to overlapping skeletal overgrowth, so it does not help discriminate between them.
incorrectas.D: Joint hypermobility can be seen in Marfan syndrome from lax connective tissue, but it overlaps between the two conditions and is not the classic distinguishing feature — the discriminating clue emphasized for homocystinuria is intellectual disability, not joint laxity.

preguntas.q: A patient presents with sudden, severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back, and blood pressure measurements differ markedly between the two arms. Which diagnosis best explains this finding?

e.correcta: Aortic dissection occurs when blood tracks through a tear in the intima and dissects along the media, creating a false lumen that can compress or intermittently occlude branch arteries — including the subclavian arteries supplying each arm. Depending on which branch vessels are compromised by the dissection flap, one arm may receive markedly reduced flow compared to the other, producing the classic pulse and blood pressure discrepancy that should immediately raise suspicion for dissection in a patient with tearing chest/back pain, especially with a history of hypertension.

incorrectas.A: Acute MI classically presents with substernal pressure-like pain, sometimes radiating to the arm or jaw, and is diagnosed with ECG changes and troponin elevation — it does not produce differential limb blood pressures, since the pathology is in the coronary circulation, not a dissecting flap compromising great vessel branches.
incorrectas.B: Pulmonary embolism causes pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and hypoxia from a clot lodged in the pulmonary vasculature; it does not alter systemic arterial pressure differentially between the arms, since the embolus affects the pulmonary circuit rather than the aortic arch branches.
incorrectas.D: Cardiac tamponade presents with pulsus paradoxus (an exaggerated inspiratory drop in systolic pressure) and Beck's triad from pericardial fluid compressing the heart, but it affects overall cardiac output symmetrically rather than causing an asymmetric arm-to-arm blood pressure difference.

preguntas.q: Tetrahydrofolate (THF) functions in metabolism primarily as a carrier for which type of chemical group?

e.correcta: THF is the active, reduced form of folate that accepts, carries, and donates one-carbon units at various oxidation states — for example as formyl-THF, methenyl-THF, methylene-THF, or methyl-THF. These one-carbon transfers are essential for purine ring synthesis, thymidylate (dTMP) synthesis for DNA replication, and remethylation of homocysteine to methionine, which is why folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neural tube defects.

incorrectas.A: Acetyl group transfer is instead the job of coenzyme A (as acetyl-CoA), used in reactions like the TCA cycle and fatty acid synthesis, not a function of THF, whose chemistry is built around one-carbon units at various oxidation levels.
incorrectas.C: Amino group transfer (transamination) is carried out by pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6)-dependent aminotransferases, an entirely separate cofactor system from folate's one-carbon chemistry.
incorrectas.D: Phosphate group transfer is mediated by ATP and other high-energy phosphate compounds in kinase reactions, unrelated to THF's role as a one-carbon shuttle in nucleotide and methionine metabolism.

preguntas.q: What is the physiological role of methyl-THF (the reduced, methylated form of tetrahydrofolate)?

o.A: Active one-carbon donor for purine and thymidylate synthesis
o.C: Precursor absorbed directly from the diet
o.D: Inactive folate metabolite excreted in urine

e.correcta: Methyl-THF is considered the storage/circulating form of folate — it is the predominant form found in blood, and crucially cannot be converted back to other active THF derivatives until methionine synthase (a vitamin B12-dependent enzyme) transfers its methyl group to homocysteine, regenerating methionine and free THF. This creates the clinically important "methyl-folate trap": if B12 is deficient, methyl-THF accumulates because it can't be demethylated, functionally starving the cell of usable folate for DNA synthesis even when folate stores are adequate.

incorrectas.A: The active one-carbon donor forms used directly in purine ring assembly and dTMP synthesis are formyl-THF and methylene-THF, not methyl-THF — methyl-THF must first be demethylated by the B12-dependent methionine synthase reaction before its carbon can re-enter those other active pools.
incorrectas.C: Folate absorbed from the diet is taken up mainly as polyglutamated forms, then deconjugated and reduced in the intestine and liver before circulating as methyl-THF; it is not the form ingested directly from food.
incorrectas.D: Methyl-THF is not an inactive, excreted metabolite — it is biologically essential and actively participates in the methionine synthase reaction; true degraded folate breakdown products are handled differently and are not the main circulating folate species.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme uses methyl-THF as a methyl donor to convert homocysteine into methionine, simultaneously regenerating free tetrahydrofolate?

e.correcta: Methionine synthase (also called homocysteine methyltransferase) is a vitamin B12 (cobalamin)-dependent enzyme that transfers the methyl group from methyl-THF onto homocysteine, forming methionine and liberating free THF for reuse in other one-carbon reactions. This reaction is the only route by which methyl-THF is converted back to a form of folate usable for purine and thymidylate synthesis, which is why B12 deficiency causes a secondary "folate trap" and elevated homocysteine even when dietary folate is normal.

incorrectas.A: Cystathionine beta-synthase acts on the other branch of homocysteine metabolism, the transsulfuration pathway — it condenses homocysteine with serine to form cystathionine (a vitamin B6-dependent reaction), rather than remethylating homocysteine back to methionine using folate.
incorrectas.B: Dihydrofolate reductase reduces dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate (and is the target of methotrexate and trimethoprim), but it does not catalyze the methyl transfer from methyl-THF to homocysteine.
incorrectas.D: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is a separate vitamin B12-dependent enzyme that converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in odd-chain fatty acid and branched amino acid catabolism; its deficiency causes methylmalonic acidemia, a distinct pathway unrelated to homocysteine remethylation.

preguntas.q: What is the initial breakdown product formed when epinephrine is metabolized?

e.correcta: Epinephrine is first O-methylated by catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) to form metanephrine, which is the direct, initial breakdown product specific to epinephrine (as opposed to norepinephrine, whose analogous first metabolite is normetanephrine). Both metanephrines are later oxidized further to vanillylmandelic acid (VMA), which along with the metanephrines is measured clinically to screen for pheochromocytoma.

incorrectas.A: Normetanephrine is the analogous COMT-mediated breakdown product of norepinephrine, not epinephrine — the "nor-" prefix tracks with norepinephrine's lack of the N-methyl group that epinephrine has.
incorrectas.B: Homovanillic acid (HVA) is the downstream breakdown product of dopamine metabolism (via COMT and MAO), not of epinephrine, and is used clinically as a marker of dopamine turnover rather than adrenal catecholamine excess.
incorrectas.C: Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) is a further downstream metabolite formed after both metanephrine and normetanephrine are oxidized by monoamine oxidase (MAO), representing the common final breakdown product of both epinephrine and norepinephrine — not the initial one specific to epinephrine.

preguntas.q: Norepinephrine is broken down into which initial metabolite by the enzyme catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT)?

e.correcta: COMT methylates norepinephrine to produce normetanephrine, the norepinephrine-specific counterpart to the metanephrine formed from epinephrine. Normetanephrine (along with metanephrine) is later oxidized by monoamine oxidase to the common end product vanillylmandelic acid (VMA), and elevated plasma or urine normetanephrine/metanephrine levels are the key screening test for catecholamine-secreting tumors like pheochromocytoma.

incorrectas.A: Metanephrine is the COMT-derived metabolite of epinephrine specifically (which carries an extra N-methyl group added by PNMT in the adrenal medulla), not of norepinephrine.
incorrectas.B: Vanillylmandelic acid is a later, further-oxidized metabolite formed from both normetanephrine and metanephrine via monoamine oxidase — it is the shared downstream endpoint, not the initial COMT product being asked about here.
incorrectas.D: Homovanillic acid is the breakdown product of dopamine, a different catecholamine with its own distinct degradation pathway, not a metabolite of norepinephrine.

preguntas.q: Normetanephrine (from norepinephrine) and metanephrine (from epinephrine) are both further metabolized into which common downstream compound?

e.correcta: Both normetanephrine and metanephrine are oxidized by monoamine oxidase (MAO) into vanillylmandelic acid (VMA), the final common breakdown product of both norepinephrine and epinephrine metabolism. Urinary VMA (along with metanephrines) is measured as part of the workup for pheochromocytoma, since these tumors autonomously secrete excess catecholamines that get funneled down to this shared end-metabolite.

incorrectas.A: Homovanillic acid is the analogous final breakdown product of dopamine (via COMT and MAO), representing a parallel but separate degradation pathway from that of epinephrine/norepinephrine.
incorrectas.B: 5-Hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) is the breakdown product of serotonin, metabolized by MAO in a pathway relevant to carcinoid syndrome — an entirely different monoamine system, not the catecholamine pathway being asked about here.
incorrectas.C: Metanephrine itself is an intermediate metabolite of epinephrine that then gets further oxidized to VMA — it is not the final common product downstream of both catecholamines, but rather one of the two immediate precursors that feed into VMA formation.

preguntas.q: What is the final breakdown product of dopamine metabolism?

e.correcta: Dopamine is sequentially metabolized by COMT and monoamine oxidase (MAO) into homovanillic acid (HVA), its final urinary breakdown product. Elevated HVA (often alongside VMA) is used clinically as a tumor marker for neuroblastoma, a catecholamine-secreting tumor of neural crest origin seen in children.

incorrectas.A: Vanillylmandelic acid is the analogous final metabolite of epinephrine and norepinephrine breakdown, formed via a parallel but separate pathway (through metanephrine/normetanephrine) that does not apply to dopamine.
incorrectas.C: 5-HIAA is the breakdown product of serotonin via monoamine oxidase, part of an unrelated indoleamine degradation pathway used clinically to screen for carcinoid tumors, not catecholamine-secreting tumors.
incorrectas.D: Normetanephrine is an intermediate COMT-derived metabolite of norepinephrine (not dopamine), which is then further oxidized to VMA — it belongs to a different branch of catecholamine metabolism entirely.

preguntas.q: In a male fetus, regression of the müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts under the influence of anti-müllerian hormone leaves behind which vestigial remnant?

e.correcta: Sertoli cells in the fetal testis secrete anti-müllerian hormone (AMH), which causes regression of the paramesonephric (müllerian) ducts in males; the small remaining vestige at the superior pole of the testis is called the appendix testis (along with a smaller prostatic utricle remnant near the verumontanum). In females, by contrast, the absence of AMH allows these same ducts to persist and differentiate into the fallopian tubes, uterus, and upper vagina.

incorrectas.A: The gubernaculum is a distinct structure — a fibrous cord that guides testicular descent from the abdomen into the scrotum — and has no relationship to the müllerian duct system; it derives from mesenchyme unrelated to paramesonephric tissue.
incorrectas.B: The prostatic utricle is indeed another vestigial müllerian remnant in males, but it is the smaller structure found within the prostatic urethra near the verumontanum, distinct from the appendix testis at the testicular pole that is the classic answer here.
incorrectas.D: The epididymis develops from the mesonephric (wolffian) duct under the influence of testosterone, not from the regressing müllerian duct — it is part of the system that persists in males, the opposite of the structure being asked about.

preguntas.q: Which histologic type of lung carcinoma is most classically associated with central cavitary lesions on chest X-ray?

e.correcta: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung arises centrally near the hilum and has a strong tendency to undergo central necrosis as it outgrows its blood supply, producing a cavitary lesion visible on imaging. It is strongly linked to smoking and can also cause paraneoplastic hypercalcemia via PTHrP secretion, both classic testable associations alongside cavitation.

incorrectas.A: Adenocarcinoma tends to arise peripherally (and is now the most common lung cancer even in non-smokers), forming glandular structures and often presenting as a peripheral nodule rather than a centrally cavitating mass.
incorrectas.B: Small cell carcinoma is an aggressive, centrally located neuroendocrine tumor strongly tied to smoking and paraneoplastic syndromes (SIADH, Cushing syndrome, Lambert-Eaton), but it grows rapidly without the same tendency toward central cavitation seen in squamous cell carcinoma.
incorrectas.D: Large cell carcinoma is a poorly differentiated tumor that can occur centrally or peripherally and carries a poor prognosis, but cavitation is not its classic distinguishing radiographic feature the way it is for squamous cell carcinoma.

preguntas.q: In which cellular compartment does de novo synthesis of purine and pyrimidine nucleotides take place?

e.correcta: De novo purine and pyrimidine synthesis both occur in the cytoplasm, where the necessary enzymes (like PRPP synthetase, carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II, and the purine/pyrimidine biosynthetic enzyme complexes) are located, using cytoplasmic pools of amino acids, CO2, and PRPP as substrates. This cytoplasmic localization is distinct from the urea cycle's carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, which is mitochondrial — a common point of confusion since both enzymes make carbamoyl phosphate but for entirely different purposes.

incorrectas.A: Mitochondria house the urea cycle enzyme carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (which detoxifies ammonia) and oxidative phosphorylation machinery, but nucleotide synthesis itself takes place outside the mitochondria, in the cytoplasm.
incorrectas.B: The nucleus is where DNA replication and transcription occur using nucleotides as building blocks, but nucleotide synthesis itself (assembling the bases and sugars into nucleotides) happens in the cytoplasm before those nucleotides are transported into the nucleus.
incorrectas.D: The endoplasmic reticulum is the site of protein folding/synthesis for secretory pathways and lipid synthesis, not nucleotide biosynthesis, which relies on cytoplasmic enzyme complexes.

preguntas.q: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of de novo pyrimidine synthesis?

e.correcta: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II) catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step of de novo pyrimidine synthesis in the cytoplasm, combining glutamine, CO2, and ATP to form carbamoyl phosphate, which then condenses with aspartate to eventually form UMP. This is distinct from CPS I, the mitochondrial urea cycle enzyme with a similar name and reaction chemistry but an entirely different purpose (ammonia detoxification rather than pyrimidine building blocks).

incorrectas.A: PRPP synthetase generates 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate, a shared substrate needed for both purine and pyrimidine synthesis, but it is not itself the rate-limiting, committed step specific to the pyrimidine pathway.
incorrectas.B: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I is the mitochondrial enzyme of the urea cycle, using ammonia (not glutamine) as its nitrogen source to detoxify ammonia into urea — a completely separate metabolic role from CPS II's pyrimidine synthesis function, despite the similar name.
incorrectas.C: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase acts later in the pathway, oxidizing dihydroorotate to orotate, and is notably the target of the drug leflunomide, but it is not the initial, rate-limiting step of the pathway.

preguntas.q: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II, the rate-limiting enzyme of pyrimidine synthesis, is inhibited by negative feedback from which nucleotide?

e.correcta: UTP, the end product of the de novo pyrimidine synthesis pathway, feeds back to inhibit CPS II, throttling further carbamoyl phosphate production once pyrimidine nucleotide levels are adequate — a classic example of end-product feedback inhibition that keeps nucleotide pools balanced with cellular need. (Some sources cite UMP as the feedback inhibitor instead, but UTP is the answer most consistently tested for this regulatory step.)

incorrectas.A: ATP is actually a positive allosteric activator of CPS II (reflecting available energy and purine status to help balance nucleotide pools), not the inhibitory feedback signal for this pathway.
incorrectas.B: PRPP is a substrate shared by both purine and pyrimidine synthesis pathways, providing the ribose-phosphate backbone, but it is not the downstream pyrimidine product that exerts feedback inhibition on CPS II.
incorrectas.D: CTP is a downstream pyrimidine nucleotide (formed from UTP via CTP synthetase) that feeds back to inhibit CTP synthetase itself, a different regulatory step in the pathway than the CPS II feedback being asked about here.

preguntas.q: Which disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD), used to treat rheumatoid arthritis, works by inhibiting dihydroorotate dehydrogenase and thereby blocking pyrimidine synthesis?

e.correcta: Leflunomide inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, the enzyme that normally converts dihydroorotate to orotic acid in the de novo pyrimidine synthesis pathway. By blocking pyrimidine nucleotide production, it preferentially suppresses the proliferation of rapidly dividing lymphocytes involved in the autoimmune inflammation of rheumatoid arthritis, since these cells rely heavily on de novo nucleotide synthesis to support clonal expansion.

incorrectas.A: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking regeneration of tetrahydrofolate and thereby impairing both purine synthesis and thymidylate (dTMP) synthesis — a folate-pathway mechanism distinct from leflunomide's direct block of pyrimidine ring synthesis via dihydroorotate dehydrogenase.
incorrectas.B: Hydroxychloroquine works by a different mechanism entirely — it raises lysosomal pH within antigen-presenting cells, impairing antigen processing and toll-like receptor signaling — and has nothing to do with pyrimidine nucleotide synthesis.
incorrectas.C: Azathioprine is a purine analog (metabolized to 6-mercaptopurine) that is incorporated into DNA/RNA synthesis pathways to inhibit purine synthesis, not pyrimidine synthesis, and works through a different enzymatic target than dihydroorotate dehydrogenase.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of hereditary orotic aciduria (UMP synthase deficiency)?

e.correcta: Orotic aciduria is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of UMP synthase (which combines the activities of orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and OMP decarboxylase), blocking the final steps of de novo pyrimidine synthesis. Because two defective gene copies are required, unaffected carrier parents can have an affected child, distinguishing its inheritance pattern from X-linked disorders like OTC deficiency, which orotic aciduria can otherwise mimic biochemically (both cause elevated urinary orotic acid).

incorrectas.A: X-linked recessive is the inheritance pattern of ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency, a urea cycle disorder that also causes elevated orotic acid (by a completely different mechanism — buildup of carbamoyl phosphate shunted into the pyrimidine pathway) and can be confused with orotic aciduria, but the two are genetically distinct.
incorrectas.B: Autosomal dominant inheritance would require only one mutant allele and typically shows affected individuals in every generation, unlike orotic aciduria's recessive pattern requiring two defective UMP synthase alleles.
