incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance is maternally transmitted to all offspring; orotic aciduria instead follows nuclear autosomal recessive genetics, since UMP synthase acts in the cytoplasmic pyrimidine synthesis pathway, not within mitochondria.

preguntas.q: A patient with elevated urinary orotic acid is being evaluated for hereditary orotic aciduria (UMP synthase deficiency) versus ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency, both of which raise orotic acid levels. Which finding is expected in orotic aciduria but not in OTC deficiency?

e.correcta: Orotic aciduria results from a block in de novo pyrimidine synthesis at the level of UMP synthase, a pathway entirely separate from the urea cycle, so ammonia detoxification proceeds normally and serum ammonia stays normal. This is a key distinguishing feature from OTC deficiency, a urea cycle disorder in which impaired conversion of carbamoyl phosphate to citrulline causes ammonia to back up, producing hyperammonemia along with the same elevated orotic acid (because excess mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate leaks out and feeds the pyrimidine pathway).

incorrectas.A: Elevated serum ammonia is the hallmark of OTC deficiency, since the urea cycle block prevents nitrogen from being safely excreted as urea — orotic aciduria's defect lies downstream in pyrimidine synthesis, entirely outside the urea cycle, so ammonia does not accumulate.
incorrectas.C: Decreased BUN is actually seen in OTC deficiency (and other urea cycle disorders) because impaired urea synthesis means less urea nitrogen is produced overall — orotic aciduria, sparing the urea cycle, typically shows normal BUN rather than a decrease.
incorrectas.D: Hyperuricemia relates to purine metabolism disorders (like Lesch-Nyhan syndrome or gout), not to the pyrimidine synthesis defect seen in orotic aciduria, and is not the distinguishing lab finding used to separate it from OTC deficiency.

preguntas.q: OTC deficiency causes decreased BUN because the urea cycle is impaired. Does hereditary orotic aciduria (UMP synthase deficiency) also present with decreased BUN?

o.A: Yes, BUN is decreased just as in OTC deficiency
o.B: No, BUN is markedly elevated instead
o.D: No, BUN cannot be measured in this condition

e.correcta: Orotic aciduria does not impair the urea cycle at all — its defect is isolated to UMP synthase in the cytoplasmic de novo pyrimidine synthesis pathway — so urea production and BUN remain normal. This is another useful discriminator from OTC deficiency, in which impaired conversion of ammonia to urea both elevates ammonia and lowers BUN, since less nitrogen is being successfully converted to urea.

incorrectas.A: BUN is decreased specifically in urea cycle disorders like OTC deficiency, where the block prevents nitrogen from being converted to urea; because orotic aciduria's enzymatic defect lies entirely outside the urea cycle, it does not share this finding.
incorrectas.B: There is no mechanism by which orotic aciduria would elevate BUN — its pyrimidine synthesis defect does not affect nitrogen handling or urea production at all, so BUN is simply unaffected (normal), not elevated.
incorrectas.D: BUN is a routine, easily measured serum marker of urea cycle function in any patient, including those with orotic aciduria; the point being tested is that its value is normal in this condition, not that it is unmeasurable.

preguntas.q: Hereditary orotic aciduria (UMP synthase deficiency) can be treated with UMP or which other agent, both of which bypass the enzymatic block?

e.correcta: Because orotic aciduria results from a deficiency of UMP synthase, supplementing with a downstream pyrimidine product — either UMP itself or uridine triacetate, which is converted to uridine and then UMP — bypasses the blocked enzymatic step entirely. This restocks the pyrimidine nucleotide pool needed for DNA/RNA synthesis and also relieves the negative feedback that would otherwise keep driving orotic acid production, correcting both the megaloblastic anemia and the underlying biochemical abnormality.

incorrectas.B: Folinic acid (leucovorin) is a reduced folate derivative used to rescue cells from folate-pathway blockade (e.g., after methotrexate toxicity) or to treat folate deficiency, but it does not supply pyrimidine nucleotides to bypass a UMP synthase defect.
incorrectas.C: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase to lower uric acid production in conditions like gout or tumor lysis syndrome, working on purine catabolism — an unrelated pathway to the pyrimidine synthesis defect in orotic aciduria.
incorrectas.D: Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase to reduce DNA synthesis, used therapeutically in sickle cell disease and myeloproliferative disorders; it does not supply pyrimidine precursors and would not correct a UMP synthase deficiency.

preguntas.q: In the de novo pyrimidine synthesis pathway, UMP is phosphorylated to form which nucleotide?

e.correcta: UMP is sequentially phosphorylated by nucleoside monophosphate and diphosphate kinases to UDP, and then to UTP, which can subsequently be aminated by CTP synthetase to form CTP — completing the pyrimidine ribonucleotide pool needed for RNA synthesis. UDP also serves as a branch point, since ribonucleotide reductase can reduce it to dUDP, feeding into deoxyribonucleotide (DNA precursor) synthesis.

incorrectas.A: dUMP is a deoxyribonucleotide formed later, via reduction of UDP to dUDP by ribonucleotide reductase followed by dephosphorylation — it is not the direct, one-step phosphorylation product of UMP.
incorrectas.B: CDP is a cytidine nucleotide formed after UTP is first aminated to CTP and then dephosphorylated, a separate branch of the pathway that comes after UDP/UTP formation, not the immediate next step after UMP.
incorrectas.D: TMP (thymidylate) is formed much later in the pathway, from dUMP via thymidylate synthase using a methyl group donated by methylene-THF — several steps downstream of the simple UMP-to-UDP phosphorylation being asked about here.

preguntas.q: In pyrimidine deoxyribonucleotide synthesis, dUDP is dephosphorylated to form which compound, which then serves as the direct substrate for thymidylate synthase?

e.correcta: dUDP is dephosphorylated to dUMP, which then becomes the direct substrate for thymidylate synthase — the enzyme that methylates dUMP (using a one-carbon unit from methylene-THF) to produce dTMP for DNA synthesis. This dUMP-to-dTMP step is a major pharmacologic target, since drugs like 5-fluorouracil (whose active metabolite irreversibly inhibits thymidylate synthase) exploit this exact reaction to block DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells.

incorrectas.B: dTMP is the product formed one step later, after thymidylate synthase acts on dUMP — it is not the direct dephosphorylation product of dUDP itself.
incorrectas.C: UMP is a ribonucleotide (not a deoxyribonucleotide) that lies earlier in the pathway, upstream of the point where ribonucleotide reductase converts UDP to dUDP; it is not downstream of dUDP.
incorrectas.D: dCMP is a deoxycytidine nucleotide formed via a separate branch of pyrimidine metabolism (from dCDP, itself reduced from CDP), not part of the dUDP-to-dUMP-to-dTMP route being described here.

preguntas.q: During the conversion of dUMP to dTMP by thymidylate synthase, N5,N10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate donates a methyl group and is oxidized to which folate derivative?

e.correcta: Thymidylate synthase uses methylene-THF as both a one-carbon donor and a reducing agent, transferring a methyl group to dUMP to form dTMP while the folate itself is oxidized to dihydrofolate (DHF). This is the only step in folate metabolism where THF is oxidized rather than reduced, which is why dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) must immediately regenerate THF from DHF for the cycle to continue - explaining why antifolates like methotrexate (a DHFR inhibitor) and 5-FU (a thymidylate synthase inhibitor) both block DNA synthesis by disrupting this exact reaction.

incorrectas.B: THF is the reduced, active folate form that donates the methylene group in the first place; it is consumed as methylene-THF and only regenerated after DHF is reduced back by DHFR, making it a reactant/downstream product rather than the direct oxidation product of this reaction.
incorrectas.C: Folic acid is the fully oxidized dietary form of the vitamin that must be reduced (via DHFR, in two steps) to THF before it can participate in any one-carbon transfer; it is never regenerated directly by thymidylate synthase.
incorrectas.D: N5-methyl-THF is the folate form that donates a methyl group to homocysteine to regenerate methionine via methionine synthase, a B12-dependent reaction that is entirely separate from thymidylate synthesis.

preguntas.q: Besides glutamine, which amino acid contributes directly to the ring structure formed in de novo pyrimidine synthesis?

e.correcta: Pyrimidine synthesis begins with carbamoyl phosphate (made from glutamine, CO2, and ATP by CPS II), which combines with aspartate to form carbamoyl aspartate - the committed step catalyzed by aspartate transcarbamoylase. Aspartate thus supplies part of the pyrimidine ring's carbon/nitrogen skeleton itself, distinguishing pyrimidine synthesis from purine synthesis, where the ring is built atom-by-atom directly onto a PRPP scaffold using glycine, aspartate, and glutamine as separate contributors.

incorrectas.B: Glycine is incorporated whole into the purine ring (contributing carbons and a nitrogen) during de novo purine synthesis, not pyrimidine synthesis, where the ring is assembled first and only afterward attached to PRPP.
incorrectas.C: Glutamate is not a direct substrate in pyrimidine ring formation; it is glutamine, not glutamate, that donates its amide nitrogen to carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II, and confusing the two is a common exam trap.
incorrectas.D: Serine mainly functions as a one-carbon donor (via serine hydroxymethyltransferase, generating methylene-THF) that feeds into thymidylate synthesis, but it is not incorporated into the pyrimidine ring the way aspartate is.

preguntas.q: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle, is localized to which cellular compartment?

e.correcta: CPS I catalyzes the first, rate-limiting step of the urea cycle - combining ammonia, CO2, and ATP to form carbamoyl phosphate - in the mitochondrial matrix of hepatocytes, where ammonia delivered from amino acid catabolism is detoxified. A helpful mnemonic is "CPS1 = m1tochondria," which also distinguishes it from CPS II, the pyrimidine-synthesis enzyme that instead works in the cytosol.

incorrectas.B: The cytosol is where CPS II operates, using glutamine's amide nitrogen to make carbamoyl phosphate for pyrimidine synthesis, not the urea cycle; after CPS I acts in the mitochondrion, the resulting citrulline is exported to the cytosol for the remaining urea cycle steps.
incorrectas.C: The nucleus plays no role in either the urea cycle or nucleotide precursor synthesis; nucleotide synthesis intermediates are made in the cytosol/mitochondria, with only finished nucleotides used inside the nucleus for DNA/RNA synthesis.
incorrectas.D: The rough ER is the site of secretory and membrane protein synthesis, not nitrogen-handling metabolic enzymes like CPS I, which is a soluble mitochondrial matrix enzyme.

preguntas.q: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II, which initiates de novo pyrimidine synthesis using glutamine's amide nitrogen, is located in which cellular compartment?

e.correcta: CPS II works in the cytosol, using glutamine (rather than free ammonia) plus CO2 and ATP to generate carbamoyl phosphate destined for the pyrimidine ring. The mnemonic pair "CPS1 - mItochondria, CPS2 - cyTWOsol" highlights that although both enzymes catalyze a similar reaction, they use different nitrogen sources and feed entirely different pathways (urea cycle vs. pyrimidine synthesis).

incorrectas.B: The mitochondrial matrix is where CPS I operates in the urea cycle using free ammonia - a distinct enzyme and pathway from CPS II despite the similar name and reaction chemistry.
incorrectas.C: The nucleus is not a site of carbamoyl phosphate production; nucleotide precursor synthesis (both purine and pyrimidine) occurs in the cytosol, with finished nucleotides later transported into the nucleus for DNA/RNA synthesis.
incorrectas.D: The Golgi apparatus processes and sorts proteins and lipids for secretion; it has no role in nitrogen metabolism or nucleotide precursor synthesis.

preguntas.q: De novo purine synthesis begins with which molecule, which is first activated to PRPP before the purine ring is assembled onto it?

e.correcta: Ribose-5-phosphate, generated by the HMP shunt (pentose phosphate pathway), is the true starting material for both purine and pyrimidine synthesis. It is activated by PRPP synthetase to PRPP (adding a pyrophosphate group from ATP), and only then does purine ring assembly begin directly on the PRPP scaffold via glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase, the rate-limiting step of the pathway.

incorrectas.B: PRPP is the activated intermediate made from ribose-5-phosphate, not the initial starting material; it is the substrate onto which the purine ring is subsequently built, one step downstream of ribose-5-phosphate.
incorrectas.C: Ribulose-5-phosphate is the HMP shunt intermediate that gets isomerized to ribose-5-phosphate; it must first be converted to ribose-5-phosphate before it can enter nucleotide synthesis.
incorrectas.D: Fructose-6-phosphate is a glycolytic intermediate that can feed into the non-oxidative arm of the HMP shunt, but it is not itself the direct precursor converted to PRPP for purine synthesis.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting step of de novo purine synthesis, converting PRPP to 5-phosphoribosylamine?

e.correcta: Glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase transfers an amide nitrogen from glutamine onto PRPP, displacing the pyrophosphate group and forming 5-phosphoribosylamine - the first committed step of purine synthesis. This enzyme is feedback-inhibited by the eventual end products AMP and GMP, making it the pathway's key regulatory control point, and it is also indirectly targeted by purine-synthesis-inhibiting drugs like 6-mercaptopurine.

incorrectas.B: PRPP synthetase acts one step earlier, converting ribose-5-phosphate to PRPP using ATP; it sets up the substrate for the amidotransferase but does not itself add nitrogen to build the purine ring.
incorrectas.C: Adenylosuccinate synthetase acts much later, converting IMP to adenylosuccinate in the branch that specifically produces AMP, not the initial ring-forming step from PRPP.
incorrectas.D: IMP dehydrogenase also acts downstream of 5-phosphoribosylamine formation, converting IMP to xanthine monophosphate (XMP) toward GMP - it is the target of mycophenolate mofetil, but it does not initiate purine synthesis from PRPP.

preguntas.q: Which prodrug is metabolized in vivo to 6-mercaptopurine, thereby inhibiting de novo purine synthesis and providing immunosuppression?

e.correcta: Azathioprine is metabolized to 6-mercaptopurine, which is further converted to thio-IMP, inhibiting the amidotransferase and other enzymes of de novo purine synthesis and depleting purines needed for lymphocyte proliferation - the basis for its use in preventing transplant rejection and treating autoimmune disease. Because xanthine oxidase normally clears 6-MP, coadministration with allopurinol (a xanthine oxidase inhibitor) markedly increases azathioprine toxicity and requires dose reduction.

incorrectas.B: 6-Thioguanine is itself an active thiopurine antimetabolite used mainly in leukemia chemotherapy, not a prodrug that gets converted to 6-MP; it acts by a similar mechanism (conversion to thio-GMP and DNA/RNA incorporation) but through a separate metabolic route.
incorrectas.C: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking regeneration of THF and thus one-carbon transfers needed for both purine and thymidylate synthesis - a completely different mechanism from thiopurine incorporation, and it is not converted to 6-MP.
incorrectas.D: Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor used to lower uric acid in gout; it does not itself become 6-MP, but it dangerously potentiates azathioprine/6-MP toxicity by blocking their breakdown.

preguntas.q: 5-Phosphoribosylamine undergoes several enzymatic steps to form which common purine nucleotide intermediate, which then branches to either AMP or GMP?

e.correcta: Inosine monophosphate (IMP) is the first complete purine nucleotide formed in de novo synthesis, built up from 5-phosphoribosylamine through sequential ATP-dependent additions of glycine, formate (from THF), aspartate, and glutamine. IMP sits at the pathway's branch point: it can be converted to AMP (via adenylosuccinate, using aspartate and GTP) or to GMP (via XMP, using glutamine and ATP), making it the shared precursor of both purine nucleotides.

incorrectas.B: GMP is a downstream product formed from IMP (via XMP) using glutamine and ATP - it is one of the two end products of the pathway, not the intermediate that immediately follows 5-phosphoribosylamine.
incorrectas.C: AMP is the other downstream product of IMP, formed via adenylosuccinate using aspartate and GTP; like GMP, it is a branch endpoint rather than the shared intermediate preceding the branch point.
incorrectas.D: UMP is a pyrimidine nucleotide made by an entirely separate pathway (via orotate and PRPP), unrelated to the purine ring assembly that produces IMP.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme represents the rate-limiting and committed step of de novo purine synthesis?

e.correcta: Glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase catalyzes the first committed step of purine synthesis (PRPP to 5-phosphoribosylamine) and is allosterically inhibited by the pathway's end products, AMP and GMP, making it the key regulatory bottleneck of the entire cascade. This feedback control prevents wasteful overproduction of purines when cellular nucleotide pools are already adequate.

incorrectas.B: PRPP synthetase produces PRPP, the shared activated-ribose substrate used by both purine and pyrimidine synthesis; it is important but not specific to (or rate-limiting for) the purine pathway alone the way the amidotransferase is.
incorrectas.C: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II is the rate-limiting enzyme of pyrimidine synthesis, not purine synthesis - a common point of confusion given the similarly named CPS I of the urea cycle.
incorrectas.D: Adenylosuccinate lyase acts downstream, participating in ring closure and cleaving adenylosuccinate to form AMP, but it is not the pathway's regulated, rate-limiting step.

preguntas.q: Inosine is composed of ribose linked to which nitrogenous base?

e.correcta: Inosine is the nucleoside formed by hypoxanthine attached to ribose; it arises physiologically when adenosine is deaminated by adenosine deaminase or when AMP is further degraded, and its base, hypoxanthine, can be recycled back into IMP by HGPRT during purine salvage. Recognizing hypoxanthine as inosine's base clarifies why inosine sits at the crossroads of purine degradation and salvage.

incorrectas.B: Guanine paired with ribose forms guanosine, not inosine; guanosine is broken down to guanine and ribose in a separate step of the purine degradation pathway.
incorrectas.C: Adenine paired with ribose forms adenosine, the direct precursor of inosine; adenosine deaminase converts adenosine to inosine by removing an amino group and replacing it with a keto group, thereby converting the base from adenine to hypoxanthine.
incorrectas.D: Xanthine is a further-downstream oxidation product (formed when hypoxanthine is oxidized by xanthine oxidase); the ribose-containing nucleoside at the inosine step is built on hypoxanthine, not xanthine.

preguntas.q: AMP is enzymatically dephosphorylated into which nucleoside during purine catabolism?

e.correcta: AMP is dephosphorylated by 5'-nucleotidase to yield adenosine, the nucleoside form of adenine plus ribose. Adenosine is then deaminated by adenosine deaminase (ADA) to inosine, which is why ADA deficiency causes toxic accumulation of adenosine (and its phosphorylated derivative dATP) in lymphocytes, leading to severe combined immunodeficiency.

incorrectas.B: Inosine is the next downstream product, formed only after adenosine is deaminated by ADA; it is not the immediate breakdown product of AMP itself.
incorrectas.C: Hypoxanthine is the free base released when inosine is cleaved by purine nucleoside phosphorylase, two steps further down the degradation pathway from AMP.
incorrectas.D: Xanthine is formed even further downstream, when hypoxanthine is oxidized by xanthine oxidase; it is not a direct product of AMP breakdown.

preguntas.q: Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency is a major cause of which autosomal recessive immunodeficiency syndrome?

e.correcta: ADA deficiency causes toxic accumulation of adenosine and deoxyadenosine (converted to dATP), which is especially harmful to lymphocytes because dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, halting DNA synthesis and blocking both B- and T-cell development. This combined B- and T-cell defect produces one of the classic autosomal recessive forms of SCID, presenting in infancy with recurrent, severe infections from multiple organism types.

incorrectas.B: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton's) results from a BTK tyrosine kinase defect that arrests B-cell maturation, causing absent B cells and immunoglobulins but sparing T-cell function - a purely humoral defect unrelated to purine metabolism.
incorrectas.C: DiGeorge syndrome results from a 22q11 microdeletion causing thymic aplasia and a primarily T-cell deficiency, due to a developmental defect of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, not an enzymatic defect in purine salvage.
incorrectas.D: Chronic granulomatous disease results from defective NADPH oxidase in phagocytes, impairing the respiratory burst and predisposing to catalase-positive organism infections - a phagocyte defect, not a lymphocyte-depleting purine metabolism disorder.

preguntas.q: In adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency, which metabolite accumulates to toxic levels within lymphocytes?

e.correcta: Without ADA to deaminate adenosine and deoxyadenosine, deoxyadenosine is instead phosphorylated to dATP, which accumulates and allosterically inhibits ribonucleotide reductase. Since ribonucleotide reductase is essential for producing all deoxyribonucleotides needed for DNA replication, its inhibition is especially toxic to rapidly dividing lymphocyte precursors, explaining the severe combined B- and T-cell deficiency seen in ADA deficiency.

incorrectas.B: dGTP accumulates in purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) deficiency, a related but distinct purine salvage disorder that causes a predominantly T-cell immunodeficiency, not in ADA deficiency.
incorrectas.C: ATP is a normal, essential energy currency present in all cells at high levels; it is not the toxic species implicated in ADA deficiency, which specifically involves the deoxyribonucleotide dATP.
incorrectas.D: cAMP is a second messenger involved in signal transduction pathways (e.g., downstream of Gs-coupled receptors), entirely unrelated to purine degradation or the pathogenesis of ADA deficiency.

preguntas.q: GMP is broken down into which nucleoside during purine catabolism?

e.correcta: GMP is dephosphorylated to guanosine, the nucleoside pairing guanine with ribose, mirroring how AMP is dephosphorylated to adenosine. Guanosine can then be cleaved by purine nucleoside phosphorylase to release free guanine, which is either salvaged back to GMP by HGPRT or deaminated to xanthine for eventual excretion as uric acid.

incorrectas.B: Adenosine is the parallel breakdown product of AMP, not GMP, formed from adenine plus ribose rather than guanine plus ribose.
incorrectas.C: Inosine contains hypoxanthine, not guanine, and arises from deamination of adenosine rather than from GMP breakdown - guanine bases are never substrates for adenosine deaminase.
incorrectas.D: Xanthine is a purine base (not a nucleoside) formed later in catabolism, either from guanine deamination or from hypoxanthine oxidation, rather than being the direct dephosphorylation product of GMP.

preguntas.q: Which drug promotes uric acid excretion by inhibiting its reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule (a uricosuric agent)?

e.correcta: Probenecid inhibits the URAT1 transporter responsible for reabsorbing filtered uric acid in the proximal tubule, thereby increasing urinary uric acid excretion - useful for chronic gout management in patients who underexcrete uric acid. Because it also blocks tubular secretion of many organic anions, it has historically been paired with penicillin to prolong the antibiotic's half-life.

incorrectas.B: Allopurinol lowers uric acid by a different mechanism entirely - inhibiting xanthine oxidase to reduce uric acid production - rather than increasing renal excretion; it is preferred in patients who overproduce uric acid or who have kidney stones.
incorrectas.C: Colchicine treats acute gout flares by inhibiting microtubule polymerization in neutrophils, blunting the inflammatory response to urate crystals, but it has no effect on uric acid production or excretion.
incorrectas.D: Febuxostat, like allopurinol, is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that decreases uric acid synthesis; it does not act on renal urate transporters to increase excretion the way probenecid does.

preguntas.q: Hypoxanthine is salvaged back into IMP by which enzyme?

e.correcta: HGPRT transfers a phosphoribosyl group (from PRPP) onto hypoxanthine (or guanine) to regenerate IMP (or GMP), allowing cells to recycle purine bases instead of degrading them to uric acid. Deficiency of this enzyme underlies Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, in which unused PRPP accumulates and drives excessive de novo purine synthesis, ultimately causing uric acid overproduction.

incorrectas.B: APRT performs the analogous salvage reaction for adenine specifically (converting it to AMP), not hypoxanthine or guanine - the two enzymes salvage different bases and are encoded by separate genes.
incorrectas.C: Xanthine oxidase moves purine bases toward degradation, oxidizing hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid - the opposite direction from salvage back to IMP.
incorrectas.D: PRPP synthetase generates the PRPP substrate that HGPRT uses in the salvage reaction, but it does not itself catalyze the attachment of hypoxanthine to ribose-phosphate.

preguntas.q: Guanine is converted back to GMP via the purine salvage pathway by which enzyme?

e.correcta: HGPRT salvages both hypoxanthine and guanine, attaching a phosphoribosyl group from PRPP to regenerate IMP or GMP respectively, sparing the cell the energetic cost of de novo synthesis. This dual specificity (reflected in its full name, hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase) is why its deficiency in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome disrupts salvage of both bases at once, not just one.

incorrectas.B: APRT salvages adenine specifically, converting it to AMP; it does not act on guanine, which is why a separate enzyme (HGPRT) is required for guanine and hypoxanthine salvage.
incorrectas.C: Xanthine oxidase degrades purines toward excretion (oxidizing hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid); it plays no part in the salvage reaction that regenerates GMP from guanine.
incorrectas.D: Adenosine deaminase acts on adenosine, converting it to inosine - a completely different reaction from base salvage by phosphoribosyltransferases, and it has no role in guanine-to-GMP conversion.

preguntas.q: In Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, HGPRT deficiency leads to which change in uric acid production, and why?

o.A: Markedly increased, because unsalvaged hypoxanthine and guanine are instead degraded to uric acid while excess PRPP drives additional de novo purine synthesis
o.B: Decreased, because less purine base is available for degradation to uric acid
o.C: Unchanged, because salvage and degradation are independent, parallel pathways
o.D: Decreased, because HGPRT deficiency also inactivates xanthine oxidase

e.correcta: When HGPRT cannot salvage hypoxanthine and guanine, these bases accumulate and are instead shunted through xanthine oxidase to uric acid; simultaneously, the PRPP that would have been consumed in salvage builds up and accelerates the rate-limiting step of de novo purine synthesis, so more purine is made overall, only to be degraded. The net result is dramatic uric acid overproduction, producing gouty arthritis, urate nephrolithiasis, and the orange sodium urate "sand" classically seen in diapers of affected infants.

incorrectas.B: Uric acid production is actually increased, not decreased - failure to salvage bases means more of them (plus more newly synthesized purine) end up being degraded through xanthine oxidase to uric acid.
incorrectas.C: Salvage and de novo synthesis are not independent - they are reciprocally linked through the shared PRPP pool and feedback inhibition, so a block in salvage directly increases flux into degradation, making "unchanged" incorrect.
incorrectas.D: HGPRT and xanthine oxidase are unrelated enzymes; HGPRT deficiency does not affect xanthine oxidase activity, so oxidation of hypoxanthine/xanthine to uric acid proceeds normally, and in fact processes more substrate than usual.

preguntas.q: In Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, why does HGPRT deficiency lead to increased de novo purine synthesis?

o.A: Unused PRPP accumulates, both providing substrate for and relieving feedback inhibition of glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase
o.B: HGPRT normally inhibits glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase directly
o.C: Loss of hypoxanthine salvage increases glutamine availability for the amidotransferase reaction
o.D: Xanthine oxidase upregulation drives increased PRPP synthetase activity

e.correcta: Normally PRPP is consumed both by salvage (HGPRT, APRT) and by de novo synthesis; when HGPRT is deficient, the PRPP that would have been used for salvage instead accumulates. Since PRPP is itself a substrate for glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase (the rate-limiting enzyme of de novo synthesis) and also relieves purine-mediated feedback inhibition at that step, its buildup drives de novo purine synthesis into overdrive - explaining why Lesch-Nyhan patients simultaneously fail to salvage purines and overproduce them.

incorrectas.B: HGPRT does not directly inhibit the amidotransferase - the two enzymes are not in a direct regulatory relationship; their connection is indirect, mediated through shared consumption of the PRPP substrate pool.
incorrectas.C: Glutamine availability is not the limiting factor altered by HGPRT deficiency; the key change is excess PRPP substrate, not an increase in the nitrogen donor glutamine.
incorrectas.D: Xanthine oxidase acts in purine degradation (oxidizing hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid) and has no regulatory link to PRPP synthetase or to the rate of de novo purine ring assembly.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (HGPRT deficiency)?

e.correcta: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is caused by mutations in the HGPRT gene, which is located on the X chromosome, making it X-linked recessive - it affects males almost exclusively, presenting with intellectual disability, dystonia, self-mutilating behavior, and gout-like uric acid overproduction. This inheritance pattern places it among the classic X-linked recessive metabolic conditions tested on boards.

incorrectas.B: Autosomal recessive is the inheritance pattern of adenosine deaminase deficiency, a different purine metabolism disorder causing SCID, not Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, which is specifically X-linked.
incorrectas.C: Autosomal dominant conditions require only one mutated allele and affect both sexes roughly equally across generations; Lesch-Nyhan's near-exclusive occurrence in males reflects X-linked, not autosomal dominant, transmission.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance follows maternal transmission to all offspring and involves genes encoded in mitochondrial DNA; HGPRT is a nuclear, X-linked gene, so this pattern does not apply.

preguntas.q: The classic orange "sand" seen in the diapers of infants with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome represents crystals of which substance?

e.correcta: Overproduction of uric acid in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, driven by failed purine salvage and increased de novo synthesis, causes urate to crystallize as sodium urate in urine, producing an orange, sand-like precipitate in diapers - an early clinical clue that can appear before the neurologic features (dystonia, self-injurious behavior) become apparent. This finding directly reflects the same uric acid excess that causes gouty arthritis and urate nephrolithiasis in these patients.

incorrectas.B: Calcium oxalate crystals are the most common component of kidney stones in general and appear as envelope-shaped crystals, but they relate to oxalate/calcium metabolism, not purine overproduction, and are not the classic Lesch-Nyhan finding.
incorrectas.C: Calcium phosphate stones form in alkaline urine and are associated with conditions like renal tubular acidosis or hyperparathyroidism, not with defects in purine salvage.
incorrectas.D: Cystine crystals (hexagonal) occur in cystinuria, a defect in renal reabsorption of dibasic amino acids - an entirely unrelated transport disorder rather than a purine metabolism defect.

preguntas.q: Approximately how many kilocalories are produced per gram of protein or carbohydrate metabolized?

e.correcta: Both protein and carbohydrate yield about 4 kcal per gram when fully oxidized, a value used clinically to calculate caloric intake (e.g., for TPN formulations or dietary counseling). This is notably lower than fat's caloric density, reflecting fat's more reduced (hydrogen-rich) carbon backbone compared to the partially oxidized carbons of carbohydrate and the less energy-dense, nitrogen-containing structure of amino acids.

incorrectas.B: 9 kcal/g is the energy yield of fat, which is more calorically dense because its long hydrocarbon chains are highly reduced and yield more electrons for oxidative phosphorylation per gram than carbohydrate or protein.
incorrectas.C: 7 kcal/g is the value for alcohol (ethanol), which is metabolized via a different pathway (alcohol dehydrogenase) and sits between carbohydrate/protein and fat in caloric density.
incorrectas.D: 5 kcal/g does not correspond to any standard macronutrient caloric value; it does not match carbohydrate/protein (4), alcohol (7), or fat (9), the four values typically tested.

preguntas.q: Approximately how many kilocalories are produced per gram of fat metabolized?

e.correcta: Fat yields about 9 kcal per gram, more than double that of carbohydrate or protein, because triglycerides are composed of long, highly reduced hydrocarbon chains that generate large amounts of NADH and FADH2 during beta-oxidation, feeding extensively into the electron transport chain. This high energy density is why adipose tissue serves as the body's primary long-term energy reserve and why fat-rich diets are calorically dense.

incorrectas.B: 4 kcal/g is the yield for carbohydrate and protein, both of which are less energy-dense than fat because carbohydrates are already partially oxidized (carrying more oxygen atoms) and proteins carry nitrogen that is excreted as urea rather than contributing to ATP yield.
incorrectas.C: 7 kcal/g corresponds to alcohol, which sits between carbohydrate/protein and fat in caloric density owing to its intermediate degree of carbon reduction.
incorrectas.D: 5 kcal/g is not a recognized macronutrient value and does not correspond to any of the four standard energy-yielding substrates typically tested (carbohydrate/protein 4, alcohol 7, fat 9).

preguntas.q: Approximately how many kilocalories are produced per gram of alcohol (ethanol) metabolized?

e.correcta: Alcohol provides about 7 kcal per gram, placing it between carbohydrate/protein (4 kcal/g) and fat (9 kcal/g) in caloric density. This matters clinically because "empty" alcohol calories contribute significantly to total energy intake without providing the vitamins, minerals, or satiety of typical food macronutrients, which is relevant when counseling patients on alcohol use and weight management.

incorrectas.B: 4 kcal/g is the value for carbohydrate and protein, both metabolized through pathways (glycolysis/TCA cycle, or transamination/deamination followed by oxidation) that yield less energy per gram than ethanol oxidation via alcohol and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase.
incorrectas.C: 9 kcal/g corresponds to fat, the most calorically dense macronutrient owing to its highly reduced hydrocarbon structure; ethanol, though also calorie-dense, yields notably less energy per gram than fat.
incorrectas.D: 5 kcal/g is not a value associated with any standard energy-yielding substrate in human metabolism and does not match alcohol's actual caloric yield.

preguntas.q: What is the major source of energy for the body during a short fast between meals (e.g., overnight)?

e.correcta: In the early fasting state between meals, the liver's main contribution to maintaining blood glucose is breakdown of stored glycogen (glycogenolysis), which can rapidly release glucose without requiring new synthesis. This buys time before hepatic glycogen stores are depleted (roughly 12-24 hours of fasting), at which point the body must increasingly rely on gluconeogenesis and fat mobilization to sustain glucose and energy needs.

incorrectas.B: Hepatic gluconeogenesis becomes the dominant glucose source only once glycogen stores are significantly depleted, during more prolonged fasting or starvation, using substrates like lactate, alanine, and glycerol; it is only a minor contributor in the short interval between ordinary meals.
incorrectas.C: Adipose lipolysis releasing free fatty acids does occur to some degree between meals and becomes progressively more important the longer fasting continues, but it remains a secondary, minor source compared to glycogenolysis in the immediate post-absorptive period.
incorrectas.D: Muscle proteolysis, which supplies amino acids like alanine for gluconeogenesis, is a late-stage adaptation seen in prolonged starvation as the body tries to spare remaining protein while still supplying some gluconeogenic substrate - it is not a significant factor in the brief fasting interval between normal meals.

preguntas.q: Hepatic glycogen stores are typically exhausted after approximately how many hours of fasting?

e.correcta: Glycogenolysis depletes the limited hepatic glycogen reserve (roughly 70-100 g) within about 12-18 hours of fasting, and stores can stretch to about a day with reduced activity or minimal dietary contribution. This marks the transition point in starvation physiology where hepatic gluconeogenesis, rather than glycogen breakdown, becomes the dominant source of blood glucose.

incorrectas.A: 1-3 days describes the subsequent phase of starvation, during which gluconeogenesis (not glycogenolysis) supplies glucose and muscle/liver shift toward free fatty acid oxidation — by this point hepatic glycogen is already long gone.
incorrectas.C: 3-7 days is well into prolonged starvation, when ketone bodies have ramped up to become a major brain fuel; glycogen stores were exhausted days earlier, not at this time point.
incorrectas.D: 24-48 hours overstates the typical duration of hepatic glycogen reserves; classic teaching places depletion at 12-18 hours, with the outer edge closer to one day rather than two.

preguntas.q: Red blood cells cannot use ketone bodies for energy because they lack which cellular structure?

e.correcta: Converting ketone bodies back into usable acetyl-CoA (via succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase and thiolase) and then oxidizing that acetyl-CoA through the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation all require mitochondria. Mature red blood cells extrude their nucleus and mitochondria during erythropoiesis, so they cannot perform any oxidative metabolism at all and must rely exclusively on anaerobic glycolysis of glucose for ATP.

incorrectas.A: Peroxisomes handle very-long-chain fatty acid oxidation and bile acid synthesis; mature RBCs lack these too, but the organelle specifically required for oxidizing ketone bodies is the mitochondrion, not the peroxisome.
incorrectas.C: The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages proteins for secretion or membrane insertion; its absence in mature RBCs reflects general organelle loss but has nothing to do with the inability to oxidize ketones.
incorrectas.D: The endoplasmic reticulum is involved in protein folding and lipid synthesis; like the Golgi, its loss is part of RBC maturation but is irrelevant to why ketone bodies specifically cannot be used as fuel.

preguntas.q: Beta-oxidation of odd-chain fatty acids yields a 3-carbon product that can enter the TCA cycle and be used for gluconeogenesis. What is this product?

e.correcta: Propionyl-CoA is carboxylated (biotin-dependent) to methylmalonyl-CoA, then isomerized in a vitamin B12-dependent reaction to succinyl-CoA, a genuine TCA cycle intermediate that can be siphoned off toward oxaloacetate and ultimately glucose. This makes the propionyl-CoA generated from odd-chain fatty acid catabolism the only fatty-acid-derived carbon skeleton that is truly glucogenic.

incorrectas.A: Acetyl-CoA is the 2-carbon product from oxidizing even-chain fatty acids; although it enters the TCA cycle, its two carbons are lost as CO2 during the isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase steps, so it cannot be net converted into oxaloacetate or glucose.
incorrectas.C: Malonyl-CoA is not a beta-oxidation product at all — it's made from acetyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA carboxylase as the committed step of fatty acid synthesis, and it functions to inhibit CPT1, opposing rather than feeding gluconeogenesis.
incorrectas.D: Butyryl-CoA is a short-chain intermediate seen in fatty acid oxidation/synthesis cycles, not the terminal odd-chain oxidation product; it does not directly feed into the TCA cycle as succinyl-CoA does.

preguntas.q: After 1-3 days of fasting, which substrate becomes the predominant fuel source for skeletal muscle and liver, helping to spare glucose for the brain and red blood cells?

e.correcta: Falling insulin and rising glucagon/catecholamines activate adipose lipolysis, releasing free fatty acids that muscle and liver oxidize via beta-oxidation for ATP. This glucose-sparing shift is an early adaptive step in starvation, reserving the limited glucose supply (from gluconeogenesis) for obligate glucose users like the brain and RBCs.

incorrectas.A: Ketone bodies only become a major fuel source for the brain after several days of starvation, once hepatic ketogenesis has substantially ramped up — in the 1-3 day window it is free fatty acids, not ketones, driving the muscle/liver fuel shift.
incorrectas.C: Glycogen stores are already largely exhausted within the first 12-18 hours of fasting, so they cannot be the fuel shift described for the 1-3 day time frame.
incorrectas.D: Branched-chain amino acids from muscle protein breakdown become an important gluconeogenic substrate later in prolonged starvation, but this question is about the fuel muscle and liver themselves are burning, which is fatty acids, not amino acids.

preguntas.q: During the first 1-3 days of fasting, once hepatic glycogen is exhausted, what becomes the major source of blood glucose?

e.correcta: The liver synthesizes glucose de novo from lactate and alanine delivered by peripheral tissues (via the Cori and glucose-alanine cycles) and from glycerol and propionyl-CoA released by adipose tissue. This hepatic gluconeogenesis maintains blood glucose for the brain and RBCs during days 1-3 of starvation, before ketone bodies take over as the brain's dominant fuel later on.

incorrectas.A: Muscle glycogen cannot be released as free glucose into the blood because skeletal muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase; instead, muscle glycogenolysis yields lactate (via glycolysis) that is exported to the liver and feeds gluconeogenesis rather than directly supplying glucose.
incorrectas.C: Ketogenesis becomes the brain's major fuel source only after more prolonged starvation (generally after several days), not as the main immediate source of blood glucose within the first 1-3 days.
incorrectas.D: The kidney does not store meaningful glycogen for release, and while renal gluconeogenesis contributes modestly to blood glucose, it is a minor player compared to hepatic gluconeogenesis — and this option describes glycogenolysis, a process the kidney doesn't meaningfully perform.

preguntas.q: In prolonged starvation, once adipose triglyceride stores are exhausted, degradation of which vital substrate accelerates and ultimately leads to organ failure and death?

e.correcta: With fat depots emptied, the body has no choice but to catabolize functional and structural protein — first muscle, then visceral organ protein — for both energy and gluconeogenic substrate. This erosion of vital organ protein mass is what ultimately drives multiorgan failure, which is why the size of a person's excess adipose reserves is a major determinant of how long they can survive starvation.

incorrectas.B: Glycogen stores are exhausted within the first day or two of fasting, long before adipose triglycerides are depleted, so glycogen breakdown is not the process responsible for late-stage organ failure.
incorrectas.C: Ketone bodies are a fuel produced from fat breakdown, not a bodily store that gets "degraded"; in fact ketone levels remain elevated and are actively utilized throughout this period rather than being a substrate whose depletion causes organ damage.
incorrectas.D: Cholesterol is a structural lipid and steroid hormone precursor, not a major energy reserve; its levels are not what drives the organ failure seen in terminal starvation the way protein catabolism does.

preguntas.q: What is the primary energy source used by muscle during the first 2 seconds of intense exercise?

e.correcta: Muscle fibers keep a small reserve of ATP already bound within the myofibrils, immediately available for hydrolysis without requiring any biochemical conversion. This preformed ATP pool provides near-instantaneous energy for the very first contractions of exercise, before the creatine phosphate and glycolytic systems have time to ramp up.

incorrectas.A: Creatine phosphate regenerates ATP rapidly via creatine kinase, but it is tapped after the tiny stored-ATP pool runs out, covering roughly seconds 2-7 of exercise rather than the very first 2 seconds.
incorrectas.B: Anaerobic glycolysis takes longer to ramp up because it requires activation of glycolytic enzymes and mobilization of glucose/glycogen, making it dominant around the first minute of exercise — far too slow for the initial 2 seconds.
incorrectas.D: Aerobic metabolism depends on increased blood flow and oxidative phosphorylation, which take minutes to fully engage; it cannot account for the immediate, essentially instantaneous energy needed at the very start of exercise.

preguntas.q: Which high-energy compound serves as the primary energy source for muscle during roughly the first 2-7 seconds of exercise?

e.correcta: Creatine phosphate donates its phosphate group to ADP via creatine kinase, quickly regenerating ATP without requiring oxygen. This bridges the gap between the tiny initial stored-ATP pool (about the first 2 seconds) and the ramp-up of glycolysis, which is why creatine supplementation is popular for boosting short, explosive bursts of activity like sprinting or weightlifting.

incorrectas.A: Stored ATP provides energy only for the very first ~2 seconds of exercise before it is exhausted; it is too limited a reserve to power the 2-7 second window.
incorrectas.B: Anaerobic glycolysis becomes dominant around the first minute of exercise, after the phosphocreatine system, since building up glycolytic flux takes longer than tapping the pre-formed creatine phosphate reserve.
incorrectas.C: Aerobic metabolism only becomes the dominant energy pathway after several minutes, once oxygen delivery and mitochondrial oxidative capacity have caught up with demand — far too slow to explain the 2-7 second window.

preguntas.q: What is the predominant energy pathway used by muscle during roughly the first minute of high-intensity exercise?

e.correcta: Once the phosphocreatine reserve is used up, muscle shifts to anaerobic glycolysis, rapidly generating ATP from glucose and glycogen without requiring oxygen and producing lactate as a byproduct. This pathway covers roughly the first minute of intense exercise, until oxidative metabolism can be upregulated enough to sustain ongoing effort.

incorrectas.A: Aerobic metabolism only becomes the dominant pathway after several minutes, once cardiac output and mitochondrial oxidative capacity have increased enough to match demand — too slow to be the primary source during the first minute.
incorrectas.B: Creatine phosphate covers roughly seconds 2-7 of exercise and is already depleted by the time the one-minute mark is reached.
incorrectas.D: The stored ATP pool lasts only about the first 2 seconds of exercise, far too brief a window to account for energy production across the first minute.

preguntas.q: After several minutes of sustained exercise, what becomes the dominant source of ATP production in muscle?

e.correcta: As blood flow and oxygen delivery to muscle increase, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation — using glucose, fatty acids, and eventually ketone bodies as substrates — becomes the efficient, sustainable energy source. It yields far more ATP per glucose molecule than anaerobic glycolysis and supports prolonged, lower-intensity activity such as endurance exercise.

incorrectas.A: Anaerobic glycolysis dominates only in the first minute or so of intense effort, before oxygen delivery catches up; it is far less ATP-efficient per glucose molecule and generates lactate, making it unsustainable for prolonged exercise.
incorrectas.B: Creatine phosphate is a very short-term energy buffer lasting only a few seconds, completely depleted long before the multi-minute mark of sustained exercise.
incorrectas.D: Stored ATP is the smallest and most transient energy reserve in muscle, exhausted within about 2 seconds, making it irrelevant to energy production several minutes into exercise.

preguntas.q: Which set of vitamins is fat-soluble and therefore capable of accumulating in adipose tissue to the point of toxicity?

o.B: Vitamins A, D, E, and K

e.correcta: Vitamins A, D, E, and K require bile acids and micelle formation for absorption alongside dietary lipids and are then transported in chylomicrons and stored in adipose tissue and the liver. This lipid-dependent handling explains both why their deficiency develops slowly (unless fat malabsorption is present) and why excessive supplementation carries a real risk of toxic accumulation, unlike vitamins that are simply excreted in urine when in excess.

incorrectas.A: B-complex vitamins, vitamin C, and folate are water-soluble — they dissolve freely in plasma and are excreted renally once tissue needs are met, so they do not accumulate in fat and rarely cause toxicity the way fat-soluble vitamins can.
incorrectas.C: B1 (thiamine), B2 (riboflavin), and B6 (pyridoxine) are all water-soluble B vitamins that are cleared in the urine when consumed in excess, not stored in adipose tissue.
incorrectas.D: Vitamin C and B12 are both water-soluble; B12 is notably stored in meaningful amounts in the liver, but this storage is not fat-based, and neither vitamin fits the fat-soluble, adipose-accumulation profile being described.

preguntas.q: Vitamin toxicity from chronic excess intake is more commonly seen with which category of vitamins, given their tendency to accumulate in body tissue?

e.correcta: Because vitamins A, D, E, and K are stored in adipose tissue and the liver rather than being readily excreted, chronic overconsumption — often from supplement misuse — allows them to build up to toxic levels over time. This contrasts with vitamins that are cleared renally once the body's needs are met, which is why toxicity is emphasized much more for the fat-soluble group.

incorrectas.A: Water-soluble vitamins (the B-complex and vitamin C) are readily excreted in urine once the renal threshold is exceeded, making toxicity comparatively uncommon, though very high doses of niacin or B6 can still cause problems.
incorrectas.B: Trace minerals such as iron or copper can indeed cause toxicity with excess intake, but they are not vitamins and are not the category being contrasted in the classic water-soluble versus fat-soluble vitamin distinction.
incorrectas.D: Essential amino acids are not vitamins at all; excess intake is handled through nitrogen balance and urea cycle mechanisms, unrelated to the fat-based storage and toxicity pattern seen with fat-soluble vitamins.

preguntas.q: A patient using which substance as a laxative for constipation is at risk of developing fat-soluble vitamin deficiency?

e.correcta: Mineral oil is an indigestible hydrocarbon that coats the intestinal lumen and dissolves fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) within it, carrying them out in the stool before they can be absorbed. Chronic use for constipation therefore risks fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, in addition to the separate risk of lipoid pneumonia if it is aspirated.

incorrectas.A: Psyllium husk is a bulk-forming fiber laxative that absorbs water to increase stool bulk and stimulate peristalsis; it does not dissolve or sequester fat-soluble vitamins the way mineral oil's lipid-solubilizing action does.
incorrectas.B: Docusate sodium is a stool softener/surfactant that allows water and fat to penetrate the stool more easily, but it does not cause the vitamin malabsorption seen with mineral oil ingestion.
incorrectas.D: Bisacodyl is a stimulant laxative that increases colonic motility and fluid secretion through a completely different mechanism, and it is not linked to fat-soluble vitamin depletion.

preguntas.q: Fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies are classically seen in malabsorptive syndromes such as cystic fibrosis and celiac disease due to which process?

e.correcta: Pancreatic insufficiency in cystic fibrosis or mucosal damage in celiac disease impairs fat digestion and absorption, producing steatorrhea — fatty, foul-smelling stools in which fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K are lost along with the unabsorbed lipid instead of being packaged into chylomicrons for uptake.

incorrectas.A: Osmotic diarrhea results from unabsorbed solutes drawing water into the bowel lumen (as in lactose intolerance); it does not specifically describe the fat maldigestion mechanism responsible for fat-soluble vitamin loss in CF or celiac disease.
incorrectas.C: Achlorhydria reduces gastric acid production, which mainly impairs protein digestion and iron/B12 absorption; it is not the mechanism behind fat-soluble vitamin loss, which depends on bile acids, pancreatic lipase, and micelle formation.
incorrectas.D: Secretory diarrhea from bile acids reaching the colon typically follows ileal resection or disease, a distinct process from the primary fat maldigestion and steatorrhea driving vitamin loss in CF or celiac disease.

preguntas.q: Which vitamin is required for normal differentiation of epithelial cells into specialized tissues, such as pancreatic acinar cells and mucus-secreting goblet cells?

e.correcta: Vitamin A, via its active metabolite retinoic acid, binds nuclear retinoic acid receptors to regulate transcription of genes controlling epithelial cell differentiation. Deficiency causes squamous metaplasia of specialized epithelium — for instance, keratinization of the normally moist corneal and conjunctival epithelium in xerophthalmia — illustrating why vitamin A is essential for maintaining functional, differentiated epithelial linings throughout the body.

incorrectas.A: Vitamin D primarily regulates calcium and phosphate homeostasis and bone mineralization through VDR-mediated gene transcription, not the differentiation of epithelial cells into specialized secretory tissue.
incorrectas.B: Vitamin K is a cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins C and S; it has no established role in epithelial differentiation.
incorrectas.D: Vitamin E functions mainly as a lipid-soluble antioxidant that protects cell membranes from oxidative damage, not as a regulator of epithelial differentiation programs.

preguntas.q: Which vitamin, in its topical retinoid form, is used to treat wrinkles and acne?

e.correcta: Topical retinoids such as tretinoin are vitamin A derivatives that increase epidermal cell turnover, reduce keratin plugging of hair follicles (improving acne), and stimulate dermal collagen synthesis while reducing fine lines (improving wrinkles). This reflects vitamin A's broader physiologic role in driving epithelial cell differentiation and turnover throughout the body.

incorrectas.A: Vitamin E is sometimes marketed topically as an antioxidant or moisturizer, but it lacks the retinoic acid receptor-mediated mechanism that drives keratinocyte turnover and collagen synthesis, so it is not the classic agent for acne or wrinkles.
incorrectas.C: Topical vitamin D analogs (e.g., calcipotriene) are used for psoriasis by modulating keratinocyte proliferation, but this is a distinct indication from the retinoid-driven treatment of acne and wrinkles.
incorrectas.D: Topical vitamin K preparations are occasionally used for bruising or vascular concerns, not for acne or wrinkle treatment, and vitamin K has no role in epithelial turnover the way vitamin A does.

preguntas.q: Vitamin A deficiency has what effect on immune function, contributing to increased susceptibility to infections such as measles?

e.correcta: Vitamin A supports the normal differentiation and integrity of mucosal epithelial barriers and helps modulate T-cell and antibody responses; deficiency impairs both, producing a state of immunosuppression that increases susceptibility to infections, classically measles and diarrheal disease. This is precisely why vitamin A supplementation is used to reduce child mortality from infectious disease in deficient populations.

incorrectas.A: The opposite occurs — vitamin A deficiency actually impairs antibody (humoral) responses rather than enhancing them, since retinoic acid signaling supports normal B-cell and antibody function.
incorrectas.C: Vitamin A deficiency is not classically associated with triggering autoimmunity; retinoic acid signaling is actually implicated in promoting immune tolerance and regulatory T-cell development, so deficiency more typically causes generalized immune impairment rather than autoimmune activation.
incorrectas.D: Deficiency does not selectively enhance innate immune cell function; overall immune competence declines across multiple arms, including compromised epithelial barriers and cellular defenses, not an isolated improvement in neutrophil chemotaxis.

preguntas.q: Acute toxicity of which vitamin presents with nausea, vomiting, vertigo, and blurred vision?

e.correcta: Acute hypervitaminosis A — for example from excessive supplement use or ingesting large amounts of liver — raises intracranial pressure and produces direct toxic effects, causing nausea, vomiting, vertigo, and blurred vision resembling a pseudotumor cerebri-type picture. This toxicity profile reflects vitamin A's status as a fat-soluble vitamin that readily accumulates with excess intake.

incorrectas.A: Vitamin D toxicity classically presents with hypercalcemia symptoms — constipation, kidney stones, confusion, and bone pain ("stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones") — not the vertigo and blurred vision picture of vitamin A excess.
incorrectas.B: Vitamin K toxicity is rare and does not produce this symptom complex; excess vitamin K is more of a concern with synthetic forms in neonates (kernicterus) than with this constellation of symptoms in this context.
incorrectas.C: Vitamin E toxicity is more associated with impairing vitamin K-dependent clotting factor function and increasing bleeding risk, rather than causing the nausea, vertigo, and visual disturbance seen with vitamin A excess.

preguntas.q: Excess intake of which vitamin (and its derivative isotretinoin) is contraindicated during pregnancy due to teratogenic risk?

e.correcta: Isotretinoin, a vitamin A derivative used for severe acne, along with excess preformed vitamin A itself, is a potent teratogen causing craniofacial, cardiac, and CNS malformations. This is why women of childbearing age must use reliable contraception while on isotretinoin, and it is one of the classic teratogen associations tested on Step 1.

incorrectas.A: Vitamin K is not associated with teratogenicity; it is actually given therapeutically to neonates to prevent hemorrhagic disease and is considered safe during pregnancy.
incorrectas.B: Excess vitamin D is not classically taught as a major teratogen; if anything, vitamin D deficiency during pregnancy is more of a clinical concern, potentially causing neonatal rickets or hypocalcemia.
incorrectas.D: Vitamin E is not a recognized teratogen; excess vitamin E is more associated with an increased bleeding risk from impaired clotting than with structural birth defects.

preguntas.q: Vitamin A exerts its teratogenic effects during embryogenesis primarily by interfering with which class of developmental regulatory genes?

e.correcta: Retinoic acid, the active metabolite of vitamin A, normally binds nuclear retinoic acid receptors that regulate Hox gene expression along the embryo's anterior-posterior axis during development. Excess retinoic acid disrupts this tightly choreographed pattern of Hox expression, producing the characteristic craniofacial, cardiac, and limb malformations seen with isotretinoin or vitamin A embryopathy.

incorrectas.A: Tumor suppressor genes such as p53 and RB regulate cell cycle checkpoints and apoptosis in the context of carcinogenesis, an entirely different process from the body-axis patterning disrupted by teratogenic vitamin A excess.
incorrectas.B: Proto-oncogenes, when mutated or overactivated, drive uncontrolled cell proliferation in neoplasia; they are unrelated to the developmental patterning genes affected by retinoic acid signaling in the embryo.
incorrectas.D: DNA mismatch repair gene defects cause microsatellite instability and hereditary cancer syndromes such as Lynch syndrome — a completely different mechanism from the Hox gene disruption that underlies vitamin A's teratogenicity.

preguntas.q: What is the active coenzyme form of vitamin B1 (thiamine)?

e.correcta: Thiamine is phosphorylated in the body to form thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), the essential cofactor for enzymes that transfer 2-carbon (aldehyde) units — most notably pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase, and transketolase. Thiamine deficiency, as seen in chronic alcoholism or malnutrition, impairs all of these TPP-dependent reactions and underlies conditions such as Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and beriberi.

incorrectas.A: Pyridoxal phosphate is the active form of vitamin B6, functioning as a cofactor for transamination and decarboxylation reactions in amino acid metabolism — a different vitamin and different cofactor entirely.
incorrectas.B: FAD is the active form of vitamin B2 (riboflavin), used in redox reactions such as those catalyzed by succinate dehydrogenase; it is structurally and functionally distinct from TPP.
incorrectas.D: NAD+ is the active form of vitamin B3 (niacin), serving as a key electron carrier in redox reactions throughout metabolism, not the thiamine-derived coenzyme being asked about here.

preguntas.q: Thiamine pyrophosphate serves as a cofactor for which enzyme that converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, linking glycolysis to the TCA cycle?

e.correcta: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex uses TPP, along with lipoic acid, coenzyme A, FAD, and NAD+ (the "Tender Loving Care For Nancy" cofactors), to oxidatively decarboxylate pyruvate into acetyl-CoA inside the mitochondrion — the committed step linking cytosolic glycolysis to the TCA cycle. Thiamine deficiency impairs this step, causing pyruvate to be shunted to lactate instead, contributing to the lactic acidosis and neurologic findings seen in beriberi and Wernicke's encephalopathy.

incorrectas.A: Pyruvate carboxylase uses biotin, not TPP, to carboxylate pyruvate into oxaloacetate as the first committed step of gluconeogenesis — a distinct reaction from the oxidative decarboxylation to acetyl-CoA described here.
incorrectas.B: Pyruvate kinase is a glycolytic enzyme that catalyzes the final ATP-generating step converting phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate; it does not require TPP as a cofactor.
incorrectas.C: Lactate dehydrogenase interconverts pyruvate and lactate using NADH/NAD+ in an anaerobic reaction, with no TPP requirement at all.

preguntas.q: Thiamine pyrophosphate is required as a cofactor for which TCA cycle enzyme that converts α-ketoglutarate to succinyl-CoA?

e.correcta: α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is structurally and mechanistically analogous to pyruvate dehydrogenase, using the same set of cofactors (TPP, lipoic acid, coenzyme A, FAD, and NAD+) to oxidatively decarboxylate α-ketoglutarate into succinyl-CoA within the TCA cycle. Because it shares TPP as a cofactor, thiamine deficiency can impair this step as well, contributing to the energy deficit seen in beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

incorrectas.A: Citrate synthase condenses acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate to form citrate, the entry step of the TCA cycle; it does not use TPP as a cofactor.
incorrectas.B: Succinate dehydrogenase oxidizes succinate to fumarate while reducing FAD to FADH2, and doubles as Complex II of the electron transport chain — it does not require TPP.
incorrectas.D: Isocitrate dehydrogenase decarboxylates isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate using NAD+ as its cofactor, an earlier step in the cycle that does not depend on TPP.

preguntas.q: Thiamine pyrophosphate acts as a cofactor for which enzyme of the pentose phosphate (HMP shunt) pathway, whose impaired activity is linked to Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome?

e.correcta: Transketolase uses TPP to shuttle 2-carbon units between sugar phosphates in the non-oxidative phase of the HMP shunt. Because its activity directly depends on adequate thiamine, red blood cell transketolase activity is used clinically as an indirect assay of thiamine status, and impaired transketolase function in thiamine-deficient states such as chronic alcoholism contributes to the neurologic damage seen in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

incorrectas.A: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is the rate-limiting enzyme of the oxidative phase of the HMP shunt, generating NADPH using NADP+ as its cofactor rather than TPP; its deficiency causes hemolytic anemia (G6PD deficiency), a distinct clinical entity unrelated to thiamine.
incorrectas.C: Transaldolase also acts in the non-oxidative phase of the HMP shunt alongside transketolase, but unlike transketolase it does not require TPP as a cofactor.
incorrectas.D: Phosphofructokinase-1 is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis, regulated allosterically by ATP, citrate, AMP, and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate; it has no connection to the HMP shunt or to TPP-dependent reactions.

preguntas.q: Thiamine pyrophosphate is a required cofactor for which enzyme involved in branched-chain amino acid catabolism, whose deficiency causes maple syrup urine disease?

e.correcta: Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKDH) is a mitochondrial enzyme complex structurally analogous to pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, sharing the same cofactor requirements — TPP, lipoic acid, coenzyme A, FAD, and NAD+ — and it catalyzes oxidative decarboxylation of the ketoacids derived from leucine, isoleucine, and valine. Its deficiency causes maple syrup urine disease, in which accumulation of these branched-chain ketoacids produces the characteristic sweet-smelling urine and severe neurologic toxicity.

incorrectas.A: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase uses biotin, not TPP, to carboxylate propionyl-CoA into methylmalonyl-CoA during odd-chain fatty acid and some amino acid catabolism; its deficiency causes propionic acidemia, not maple syrup urine disease.
incorrectas.B: Homogentisate oxidase is deficient in alkaptonuria, causing accumulation of homogentisic acid (dark urine and ochronosis) — a tyrosine/phenylalanine degradation pathway defect unrelated to branched-chain amino acids or TPP.
incorrectas.C: Phenylalanine hydroxylase uses tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), not TPP, to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine; its deficiency causes phenylketonuria (PKU), a distinct condition from maple syrup urine disease.

preguntas.q: In the emergency department, a chronically malnourished alcoholic patient with suspected thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency is given IV fluids while thiamine is being obtained. Administration of which of the following, if given before thiamine, can precipitate acute worsening of ATP depletion and possibly acute Wernicke encephalopathy?

e.correcta: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is an essential cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase. When glucose is infused in a thiamine-deficient patient, the sudden increase in glucose metabolism consumes what little TPP-dependent enzymatic capacity remains, further crippling oxidative ATP production and can precipitate acute Wernicke encephalopathy or cardiovascular collapse. This is why thiamine should be given before or with glucose in any patient at risk of deficiency (e.g., alcoholics, malnourished patients).

incorrectas.A: Normal saline is an isotonic crystalloid that does not participate in glucose metabolism or place additional demand on thiamine-dependent enzymes, so it does not precipitate the same acute metabolic crisis that glucose does.
incorrectas.C: Insulin drives glucose and potassium into cells but does not itself increase the flux through TPP-dependent enzymes the way an actual glucose load does; the danger in thiamine deficiency specifically comes from ramping up glucose oxidation, not from insulin signaling.
incorrectas.D: Sodium bicarbonate corrects metabolic acidosis by buffering hydrogen ions and has no effect on glucose flux through pyruvate dehydrogenase or other thiamine-dependent enzymes, so it does not trigger the same worsening of ATP depletion.

preguntas.q: Which category of tissues is preferentially and earliest affected by vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency?

o.A: Tissues with low oxygen demand (e.g., adipose)
o.B: Tissues with high glycolytic capacity only (e.g., red blood cells)
o.C: Highly aerobic tissues with high oxidative ATP demand (e.g., brain, heart)
o.D: Tissues that rely primarily on fatty acid oxidation (e.g., resting skeletal muscle)

e.correcta: Thiamine pyrophosphate is required by pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, both central to aerobic oxidative metabolism feeding the TCA cycle. Tissues with the highest constant demand for oxidative ATP production, such as the brain and heart, are the most sensitive to any drop in these enzyme activities, which is why thiamine deficiency classically manifests as neurologic findings (Wernicke-Korsakoff) and high-output cardiac failure (wet beriberi).

incorrectas.A: Adipose tissue has comparatively low ongoing oxidative ATP demand and relies more on storage and slow turnover of triglycerides, so it is not preferentially vulnerable when thiamine-dependent oxidative enzymes falter.
incorrectas.B: Red blood cells lack mitochondria entirely and generate ATP purely through anaerobic glycolysis, so they do not depend on thiamine-requiring oxidative enzymes and are essentially unaffected by thiamine deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Resting skeletal muscle can shift substantially toward fatty acid oxidation and has lower baseline oxidative demand than brain or heart, making it comparatively less sensitive to early thiamine deficiency than these highly aerobic organs.

preguntas.q: A patient with Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is treated promptly with thiamine, resolving her confusion and ataxia. What is the expected course of the associated anterograde amnesia and confabulation (the Korsakoff component)?

o.A: It is permanent even with treatment
o.B: It fully resolves within days of thiamine repletion
o.C: It resolves completely but only after months of therapy
o.D: It never develops if thiamine is given early enough

e.correcta: The Korsakoff amnestic component reflects structural damage to the mammillary bodies and medial thalamus from thiamine deficiency, and once this damage has occurred, thiamine repletion cannot reverse it. This is why Wernicke-Korsakoff is described as having a reversible acute component (the Wernicke triad of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia) but a permanent chronic component (Korsakoff amnesia and confabulation) — early thiamine treatment can prevent progression but cannot undo the memory deficit once established.

incorrectas.B: Rapid resolution within days describes the acute Wernicke encephalopathy findings (confusion, ataxia, nystagmus/ophthalmoplegia), which do respond to thiamine, but the Korsakoff amnestic syndrome that follows is a distinct, fixed neurologic deficit.
incorrectas.C: Even prolonged thiamine therapy cannot restore the neurons lost in the mammillary bodies and thalamic nuclei once Korsakoff syndrome has developed; the amnesia is a structural, not purely metabolic, deficit.
incorrectas.D: While early thiamine administration can prevent progression from Wernicke encephalopathy to the Korsakoff state, once amnesia and confabulation are already present, they are already fixed regardless of how early treatment could theoretically have started.

preguntas.q: Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) is a metabolic precursor for which pair of redox coenzymes?

o.B: Coenzyme A and acyl carrier protein

e.correcta: Riboflavin is directly incorporated into flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) and flavin mononucleotide (FMN), the two flavin coenzymes that serve as electron carriers in numerous oxidoreductase reactions, including succinate dehydrogenase in the TCA cycle and the electron transport chain. Because these flavins are essential to core aerobic energy metabolism, riboflavin deficiency compromises cellular energy production broadly rather than one isolated pathway.

incorrectas.A: NAD+ and NADP+ are the nicotinamide-derived redox coenzymes synthesized from niacin (vitamin B3), not riboflavin — a distinct but analogous electron-carrier system.
incorrectas.B: Coenzyme A and acyl carrier protein are synthesized from pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) and function in acyl-group transfer during fatty acid metabolism, not in the flavin-based redox chemistry riboflavin supports.
incorrectas.C: Tetrahydrofolate derives from folate (vitamin B9) and methylcobalamin from vitamin B12; both function in one-carbon transfer reactions, an entirely different chemistry from the flavin redox coenzymes made from riboflavin.

preguntas.q: The flavin coenzymes derived from vitamin B2 (riboflavin), such as FAD in the succinate dehydrogenase reaction of the TCA cycle, primarily participate in which type of reaction?

e.correcta: FAD and FMN function as electron acceptors and donors, cycling between oxidized and reduced states (FAD/FADH2) as they shuttle electrons in reactions such as the conversion of succinate to fumarate by succinate dehydrogenase. This redox capacity is central to riboflavin's role in the electron transport chain and multiple dehydrogenase complexes throughout aerobic metabolism.

incorrectas.A: Carboxylation reactions, which add a carbon dioxide group to a substrate (e.g., the pyruvate carboxylase reaction), are driven by biotin (vitamin B7), a completely different cofactor chemistry from flavin-mediated electron transfer.
incorrectas.C: Transamination reactions, which transfer an amino group between an amino acid and a keto acid, require pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as the cofactor, not the flavin coenzymes derived from riboflavin.
incorrectas.D: Decarboxylation reactions removing a carboxyl group typically depend on thiamine pyrophosphate (vitamin B1) in enzymes like pyruvate dehydrogenase, distinct from the redox-cycling role that FAD and FMN play.

preguntas.q: A patient with vitamin B2 (riboflavin) deficiency develops inflammation of the lips with scaling and fissuring at the corners of the mouth. What is this finding called?

e.correcta: Cheilosis refers to the inflammation, scaling, and fissuring of the lips (including the angles of the mouth) that is a classic mucocutaneous finding of riboflavin deficiency, alongside corneal vascularization and normocytic anemia. It reflects the high turnover demand of epithelial tissue for FAD/FMN-dependent oxidative metabolism, making rapidly dividing mucosal surfaces especially sensitive to riboflavin deficiency.

incorrectas.B: Glossitis is inflammation and smoothing of the tongue's surface (loss of papillae), a finding more classically linked to niacin (B3), B12, or folate deficiency, and it targets the tongue rather than the corners of the mouth.
incorrectas.C: Aphthous stomatitis refers to painful shallow ulcers (canker sores) inside the oral mucosa, an idiopathic or immune-mediated process unrelated specifically to riboflavin deficiency and not localized to lip fissuring.
incorrectas.D: Leukoplakia is a white, adherent mucosal patch most associated with chronic irritation (e.g., tobacco use) that carries premalignant potential; it is a distinct pathologic entity, not a vitamin deficiency finding.

preguntas.q: Vitamin B3 (niacin) is a structural component of which pair of coenzymes essential to cellular redox chemistry?

o.B: Coenzyme A and acyl carrier protein

e.correcta: Niacin is incorporated into nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) and its phosphorylated form NADP+, which serve as the principal electron carriers for catabolic (NAD+/NADH, oxidative pathways like glycolysis and the TCA cycle) and anabolic (NADP+/NADPH, reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defense) reactions, respectively. This dual role explains why niacin deficiency broadly impairs both energy metabolism and reductive biosynthesis.

incorrectas.A: FAD and FMN are the flavin coenzymes derived from riboflavin (vitamin B2), a related but distinct redox cofactor system from the nicotinamide-based coenzymes made from niacin.
incorrectas.B: Coenzyme A and acyl carrier protein come from pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) and are used for acyl-group transfer in fatty acid metabolism, not for the electron-carrying chemistry of NAD+/NADP+.
incorrectas.D: Thiamine pyrophosphate (from vitamin B1) and lipoic acid are cofactors of decarboxylating dehydrogenase complexes like pyruvate dehydrogenase, functioning alongside — but chemically distinct from — the NAD+ that they ultimately help generate.

preguntas.q: Like the flavin coenzymes, the nicotinamide coenzymes derived from vitamin B3 (niacin) are primarily involved in which type of reaction?

e.correcta: NAD+/NADH and NADP+/NADPH cycle between oxidized and reduced states as they accept and donate electrons throughout metabolism — NAD+ predominantly in catabolic, energy-releasing reactions and NADPH in reductive biosynthesis and combating oxidative stress. This central redox role is why niacin deficiency (pellagra) causes widespread dysfunction across rapidly metabolizing tissues like skin, gut, and brain.
