incorrectas.A: Carboxylation reactions that fix CO2 onto a substrate, such as the pyruvate carboxylase reaction, depend on biotin (vitamin B7), not on the nicotinamide coenzymes made from niacin.
incorrectas.B: Acyl-group transfer reactions in fatty acid metabolism are mediated by coenzyme A, derived from pantothenic acid (vitamin B5), a separate cofactor chemistry from the electron-carrying NAD+/NADP+ system.
incorrectas.C: Transamination reactions transferring amino groups between amino acids and keto acids require pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6), not the redox-cycling nicotinamide coenzymes.

preguntas.q: Vitamin B3 (niacin) can be endogenously synthesized in the body from which amino acid?

e.correcta: Tryptophan can be converted into niacin via a pathway requiring vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate) as a cofactor, which is why conditions that impair tryptophan availability or metabolism (Hartnup disease, carcinoid syndrome, isoniazid-induced B6 deficiency) can secondarily cause niacin deficiency (pellagra) even when dietary niacin intake is adequate.

incorrectas.A: Phenylalanine is converted to tyrosine and feeds into catecholamine and melanin synthesis; it is not a precursor for niacin, so its metabolism is unrelated to pellagra risk.
incorrectas.C: Methionine is a key methyl-group donor (via S-adenosylmethionine) and, together with folate/B12/B6, participates in homocysteine metabolism, but it is not the amino acid precursor of niacin.
incorrectas.D: Histidine is decarboxylated to form histamine and is otherwise involved in protein structure and buffering, playing no role in endogenous niacin biosynthesis.

preguntas.q: Pharmacologic doses of which vitamin are used clinically to treat dyslipidemia by lowering VLDL and raising HDL levels?

e.correcta: High-dose niacin inhibits hepatic diacylglycerol acyltransferase, reducing hepatocyte triglyceride synthesis and VLDL secretion; because LDL is derived from VLDL, LDL falls as well, while niacin also reduces HDL catabolism, raising HDL levels. This lipid-modifying effect is a pharmacologic action distinct from niacin's role as a nutrient cofactor, and its main limiting side effect is prostaglandin-mediated cutaneous flushing.

incorrectas.B: Riboflavin has no established lipid-lowering pharmacologic use; its clinical relevance is limited to correcting deficiency states like cheilosis, glossitis, and corneal vascularization.
incorrectas.C: Pyridoxine (B6) is used pharmacologically to prevent isoniazid-induced neuropathy and in certain metabolic disorders, but it has no role in treating dyslipidemia.
incorrectas.D: Biotin (B7) has no clinically established use for lipid management; its cofactor role is limited to carboxylation reactions in gluconeogenesis and fatty acid synthesis, not to lowering VLDL or raising HDL.

preguntas.q: Which oral mucosal finding is most classically caused by even a mild deficiency of vitamin B3 (niacin)?

e.correcta: Glossitis, a smooth, beefy-red, swollen tongue from atrophy of the lingual papillae, is a hallmark early finding of niacin deficiency and reflects the high turnover rate of the tongue's mucosal epithelium, which depends heavily on NAD+/NADP+-driven metabolism for rapid cell renewal. Glossitis also occurs with B12 and folate deficiency, so in practice it is a nonspecific but useful clue that should prompt a broader nutritional workup.

incorrectas.A: Cheilosis (lip inflammation and fissuring at the mouth corners) is the classic finding of riboflavin (B2) deficiency, not niacin deficiency, though both vitamins can co-exist as deficiencies in malnourished patients.
incorrectas.B: Aphthous ulcers are recurrent, painful mucosal erosions with an idiopathic/immune-mediated etiology and are not a specific marker of niacin deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Leukoplakia is a premalignant, adherent white mucosal plaque linked to chronic irritation such as tobacco use, an entirely different process from the papillary atrophy seen in niacin-deficiency glossitis.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of Hartnup disease?

e.correcta: Hartnup disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in a neutral amino acid transporter (SLC6A19) in the small intestine and renal proximal tubule, meaning affected individuals must inherit a defective allele from each parent, while carriers (heterozygotes) are typically asymptomatic. This transporter defect impairs absorption/reabsorption of neutral amino acids like tryptophan, ultimately reducing the substrate available for endogenous niacin synthesis.

incorrectas.A: Autosomal dominant inheritance would require only one mutant allele to cause disease and typically shows the condition in multiple generations; Hartnup disease instead requires two defective alleles, consistent with a recessive pattern.
incorrectas.B: X-linked recessive conditions predominantly affect males and are transmitted through carrier mothers on the X chromosome, but the gene responsible for Hartnup disease (SLC6A19) is located on an autosome, not the X chromosome.
incorrectas.C: Mitochondrial inheritance follows maternal transmission because mitochondrial DNA comes only from the mother's oocyte; Hartnup disease follows classic Mendelian autosomal recessive inheritance instead, with the defective transporter gene on nuclear DNA.

preguntas.q: Which inherited disorder is characterized by defective neutral amino acid transport in the small intestine and kidney, leading to neutral aminoaciduria, decreased tryptophan absorption, and pellagra-like skin and neurologic findings?

e.correcta: Hartnup disease results from loss-of-function mutations in a neutral amino acid transporter, impairing gut absorption and renal reabsorption of neutral amino acids including tryptophan. Because tryptophan is a precursor for endogenous niacin synthesis, reduced tryptophan availability produces a secondary niacin deficiency, manifesting as intermittent pellagra-like photosensitive dermatitis and cerebellar ataxia that tends to improve with age.

incorrectas.B: Cystinuria involves a defective transporter for dibasic (not neutral) amino acids — cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine — in the proximal tubule, causing cystine kidney stones rather than pellagra-like symptoms.
incorrectas.C: Fanconi syndrome is a generalized proximal tubular dysfunction causing wasting of glucose, amino acids, phosphate, and bicarbonate broadly, rather than a selective defect in neutral amino acid transport tied to niacin deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Maple syrup urine disease results from a defect in branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase, causing accumulation of branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine), a distinct enzymatic block unrelated to intestinal/renal amino acid transport or niacin synthesis.

preguntas.q: Malignant carcinoid syndrome is characterized by increased metabolic diversion of which amino acid toward serotonin production, which can secondarily cause a niacin deficiency?

e.correcta: In carcinoid syndrome, neuroendocrine tumor cells shunt large amounts of dietary tryptophan toward serotonin synthesis rather than the normal kynurenine pathway that ultimately produces niacin. This diversion can deplete tryptophan stores enough to precipitate a secondary pellagra-like niacin deficiency, in addition to the classic flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm caused by excess serotonin and other vasoactive substances.

incorrectas.A: Histidine is decarboxylated to histamine, a mediator implicated in some carcinoid-related flushing, but it is not the amino acid whose diversion depletes niacin precursor stores in this syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Tyrosine is the precursor for catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) and thyroid hormone, an entirely separate pathway from the serotonin/niacin biochemistry disrupted in carcinoid syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Phenylalanine is converted to tyrosine and feeds into catecholamine and melanin pathways, not into serotonin or niacin synthesis, so it is not the amino acid implicated in carcinoid-associated niacin deficiency.

preguntas.q: Isoniazid therapy can indirectly cause a deficiency of which vitamin by first depleting vitamin B6, which is required for its synthesis?

e.correcta: Isoniazid structurally resembles pyridoxine and competitively inhibits pyridoxal kinase while also forming inactive hydrazones with pyridoxal phosphate, depleting functional vitamin B6. Because B6 (as PLP) is a required cofactor in the tryptophan-to-niacin synthetic pathway, isoniazid-induced B6 deficiency can secondarily reduce endogenous niacin production, contributing to pellagra-like symptoms in isoniazid-treated patients — which is why prophylactic pyridoxine is co-administered with isoniazid.

incorrectas.A: Riboflavin is not synthesized through a B6-dependent pathway, and isoniazid's well-known vitamin interaction is specifically with B6 depletion, not with riboflavin metabolism.
incorrectas.B: Vitamin B12 is absorbed via intrinsic factor and involved in methylmalonyl-CoA and homocysteine metabolism, an entirely separate pathway from the tryptophan-to-niacin conversion that depends on B6, and isoniazid does not deplete B12.
incorrectas.D: Folate metabolism intersects with B12 and methionine cycling for one-carbon transfers, but folate is not the vitamin whose synthesis depends on B6 in the way niacin's endogenous production does.

preguntas.q: Which change in bowel habits is one of the classic '3 D's' associated with pellagra (vitamin B3/niacin deficiency)?

e.correcta: Pellagra classically presents with the '3 D's': diarrhea, dementia, and dermatitis (sometimes a 4th D, death, is added if untreated). The diarrhea reflects the high-turnover, NAD+/NADP+-dependent metabolism of the rapidly dividing gut mucosal epithelium, which atrophies and becomes inflamed when niacin-dependent energy production is impaired, mirroring the mucosal effects seen in the mouth (glossitis) and skin (dermatitis).

incorrectas.A: Constipation reflects slowed gut motility and is not part of the classic pellagra triad; the gut mucosal injury from niacin deficiency instead produces increased, not decreased, bowel frequency.
incorrectas.B: Steatorrhea (fatty, foul-smelling stools) reflects fat malabsorption, typically from pancreatic insufficiency or bile salt deficiency, a different mechanism than the mucosal atrophy and inflammation driving pellagra-associated diarrhea.
incorrectas.C: Bloating and malabsorption are more characteristic of conditions like celiac disease or bacterial overgrowth affecting nutrient absorption broadly, rather than the specific diarrhea described in the mnemonic for pellagra.

preguntas.q: Which CNS complication is part of the classic triad seen in pellagra (vitamin B3/niacin deficiency)?

e.correcta: The '3 D's' of pellagra are diarrhea, dementia, and dermatitis, with dementia (which can include confusion, irritability, and hallucinations) resulting from impaired NAD+/NADP+-dependent oxidative metabolism in neurons, which are highly sensitive to energy deficits. This distinguishes pellagra's neuropsychiatric picture from the more focal ataxia and confabulation-based amnesia seen in thiamine (B1) deficiency.

incorrectas.B: Peripheral neuropathy is the classic neurologic finding of isoniazid-induced B6 deficiency (due to impaired myelin/neurotransmitter synthesis), not the CNS finding specifically highlighted in the pellagra triad.
incorrectas.C: Seizures are not a defining feature of the classic pellagra presentation; the mnemonic specifically highlights dementia as the CNS component alongside diarrhea and dermatitis.
incorrectas.D: Cerebellar ataxia is the hallmark cerebellar sign of Hartnup disease (and of thiamine deficiency/Wernicke encephalopathy), reflecting a different underlying mechanism than the diffuse cortical dysfunction causing dementia in pellagra.

preguntas.q: The dermatitis of pellagra (vitamin B3/niacin deficiency), which classically affects sun-exposed limbs (e.g., a 'Casal necklace' distribution), is characterized by which skin change?

e.correcta: Pellagra dermatitis produces a hyperpigmented, thickened, scaly rash in a symmetric distribution on sun-exposed skin (face, neck 'Casal necklace,' and dorsal hands/forearms), thought to result from impaired DNA repair and epidermal cell turnover in the setting of NAD+/NADP+ deficiency combined with photosensitization. This darkened, sunburn-like appearance is one of the '3 D's' (dermatitis) that, together with diarrhea and dementia, forms the classic clinical triad.

incorrectas.A: A vesiculobullous eruption with blistering is more characteristic of conditions like porphyria cutanea tarda or certain autoimmune blistering diseases, not the chronic hyperpigmented, scaly dermatitis of pellagra.
incorrectas.C: Hypopigmented patches (as in vitiligo or tinea versicolor) reflect loss of melanocyte function or activity, the opposite pigmentation change from the hyperpigmentation seen in pellagra's photo-distributed dermatitis.
incorrectas.D: A petechial rash suggests capillary fragility or a bleeding/platelet disorder (e.g., vitamin C deficiency or thrombocytopenia), a different mechanism entirely from the chronic photosensitive hyperpigmented dermatitis of niacin deficiency.

preguntas.q: The cutaneous flushing that occurs as a side effect of pharmacologic-dose niacin (vitamin B3) therapy is mediated primarily by which molecule?

e.correcta: High-dose niacin activates a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPR109A) on skin Langerhans cells and keratinocytes, triggering prostaglandin D2 (and E2) release, which causes cutaneous vasodilation and the characteristic flushing sensation. Because the mechanism is prostaglandin-mediated rather than histamine-mediated, pretreatment with aspirin (a cyclooxygenase inhibitor) or use of extended-release niacin formulations can blunt this flushing.

incorrectas.A: Serotonin release drives the flushing seen in carcinoid syndrome, a distinct clinical entity from niacin-induced flushing, which instead arises from prostaglandin release via GPR109A receptor activation.
incorrectas.B: Histamine mediates flushing and pruritus in conditions like mastocytosis or allergic reactions, but niacin-induced flushing is specifically prostaglandin-driven, which is why antihistamines are not the standard mitigation strategy — aspirin is.
incorrectas.D: Bradykinin mediates angioedema and is notably implicated in ACE inhibitor-induced swelling, not in the cutaneous flushing reaction triggered by niacin's activation of GPR109A.

preguntas.q: What is the active coenzyme form of vitamin B6?

e.correcta: Dietary pyridoxine is phosphorylated and oxidized to pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), the biologically active coenzyme form of vitamin B6. PLP serves as an essential cofactor for aminotransferase (transaminase) enzymes and numerous other reactions involving amino acid metabolism, which is why measuring PLP (rather than pyridoxine) reflects true vitamin B6 functional status.

incorrectas.A: Thiamine pyrophosphate is the active coenzyme form of vitamin B1 (thiamine), used by pyruvate dehydrogenase and related decarboxylating enzymes, not the coenzyme form of B6.
incorrectas.B: Tetrahydrofolate is the active coenzyme form of folate (vitamin B9), central to one-carbon transfer reactions in nucleotide synthesis, distinct from the transamination chemistry PLP supports.
incorrectas.C: Pyridoxine is the inactive dietary/precursor form of vitamin B6; it must be converted to pyridoxal phosphate through phosphorylation and oxidation before it becomes catalytically active.

preguntas.q: Which vitamin serves as a cofactor for transamination reactions, decarboxylation reactions, and glycogen phosphorylase?

e.correcta: Pyridoxal phosphate (the active form of vitamin B6) forms a Schiff base with amino acid substrates, enabling it to stabilize reaction intermediates for a remarkably wide range of processes — transamination (amino acid interconversion), decarboxylation (e.g., synthesis of neurotransmitters and histamine), and even an essential cofactor role for glycogen phosphorylase, which cleaves glucose units off glycogen during glycogenolysis. This versatility explains why B6 deficiency or depletion (as with isoniazid) has such broad downstream metabolic effects.

incorrectas.B: Thiamine pyrophosphate (B1) is the cofactor for oxidative decarboxylation reactions like pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, as well as transketolase, but it does not serve the transamination or glycogen phosphorylase roles that define B6's function.
incorrectas.C: FAD (from riboflavin, B2) functions in redox reactions such as succinate dehydrogenase, an entirely different chemical role from the Schiff-base-mediated transamination and decarboxylation chemistry of PLP.
incorrectas.D: Biotin (B7) is the cofactor for carboxylation reactions like pyruvate carboxylase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase, the chemical opposite of decarboxylation, and it plays no role in transamination or glycogen phosphorylase activity.

preguntas.q: Which vitamin acts as a cofactor for the synthesis of cystathionine, heme, histamine, and several neurotransmitters (including serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, and GABA)?

e.correcta: Pyridoxal phosphate is required by cystathionine beta-synthase (homocysteine to cystathionine, part of the transsulfuration pathway), ALA synthase (the rate-limiting step of heme synthesis), histidine decarboxylase (histamine synthesis), and the decarboxylase enzymes that generate serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine/epinephrine, and GABA from their amino acid precursors. This central role in decarboxylation reactions across such diverse pathways explains why B6 deficiency can cause sideroblastic anemia, seizures (from low GABA), and peripheral neuropathy.

incorrectas.A: Folate (B9) is essential for one-carbon transfers in nucleotide (purine and thymidine) synthesis and works with B12 in the methionine cycle, but it does not directly drive the decarboxylation reactions producing heme, histamine, or these neurotransmitters.
incorrectas.C: Vitamin B12 is required for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase reactions (fatty acid metabolism and remethylation of homocysteine), a different biochemical role from the PLP-dependent decarboxylations described here.
incorrectas.D: Niacin (B3) forms NAD+/NADP+, which function in redox reactions throughout metabolism, not in the decarboxylation and transsulfuration chemistry that pyridoxal phosphate performs for heme, histamine, and neurotransmitter synthesis.

preguntas.q: Vitamin B7 (biotin) functions as a cofactor for which class of reactions, in which it typically adds a carbon dioxide group to a substrate?

e.correcta: Biotin is covalently attached to carboxylase enzymes and acts as a mobile carrier of activated CO2, allowing it to add a one-carbon carboxyl group onto substrates such as pyruvate (forming oxaloacetate) or acetyl-CoA (forming malonyl-CoA). This carboxylation chemistry underlies biotin's essential roles in gluconeogenesis and fatty acid synthesis, and is why biotin deficiency (rare, but seen with excess raw egg white consumption due to avidin binding) impairs these pathways.

incorrectas.A: Decarboxylation reactions remove, rather than add, a carbon dioxide group and are typically catalyzed by thiamine pyrophosphate-dependent enzymes (like pyruvate dehydrogenase), the chemical reverse of what biotin-dependent carboxylases do.
incorrectas.B: Oxidation-reduction reactions involve electron transfer and are carried out by flavin (FAD/FMN, from B2) or nicotinamide (NAD+/NADP+, from B3) coenzymes, not by biotin, which instead handles carbon-group transfer.
incorrectas.D: Transamination reactions transfer amino groups between molecules and depend on pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6), a mechanistically distinct process from biotin's role in fixing CO2 onto substrates.

preguntas.q: Biotin (vitamin B7) serves as an essential cofactor for which enzyme, which converts pyruvate into oxaloacetate as an anaplerotic/gluconeogenic step?

e.correcta: Pyruvate carboxylase uses biotin as a covalently bound cofactor to carboxylate pyruvate (a 3-carbon molecule) into oxaloacetate (a 4-carbon molecule), replenishing TCA cycle intermediates and providing the first committed step of gluconeogenesis. This reaction is activated by acetyl-CoA, linking fatty acid oxidation status to the cell's gluconeogenic and anaplerotic capacity.

incorrectas.A: Pyruvate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA (a decarboxylation, oxidative step feeding the TCA cycle), the functional opposite of the gluconeogenic carboxylation performed by pyruvate carboxylase, and it depends on thiamine pyrophosphate/lipoic acid/FAD/NAD+, not biotin.
incorrectas.B: Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate, the step immediately after pyruvate carboxylase in gluconeogenesis, but this enzyme does not use biotin as its cofactor.
incorrectas.C: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase catalyzes a later step in gluconeogenesis (removing a phosphate from fructose-1,6-bisphosphate), a hydrolysis reaction that does not require biotin or carboxylation chemistry.

preguntas.q: Biotin (vitamin B7) serves as an essential cofactor for which enzyme, the rate-limiting step of fatty acid synthesis, that converts acetyl-CoA into malonyl-CoA?

e.correcta: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase uses biotin to add a carboxyl group (from CO2) onto acetyl-CoA, producing malonyl-CoA in the rate-limiting, committed step of fatty acid synthesis. Malonyl-CoA then serves as the 2-carbon-unit donor for chain elongation by fatty acid synthase, and it also allosterically inhibits carnitine acyltransferase I, coordinating fatty acid synthesis and oxidation so the two pathways don't run simultaneously.

incorrectas.B: Fatty acid synthase is the multi-enzyme complex that uses the malonyl-CoA produced by acetyl-CoA carboxylase to build the growing fatty acid chain, but its catalytic mechanism does not require biotin as a cofactor.
incorrectas.C: HMG-CoA reductase catalyzes the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis (HMG-CoA to mevalonate), an entirely separate lipid pathway from fatty acid chain synthesis, and does not use biotin.
incorrectas.D: Citrate synthase catalyzes the first step of the TCA cycle (combining acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate to form citrate), unrelated to the biotin-dependent carboxylation reactions of fatty acid synthesis and gluconeogenesis.

preguntas.q: Biotin (vitamin B7) serves as a cofactor for which enzyme that carboxylates propionyl-CoA (3 carbons) to form methylmalonyl-CoA (4 carbons) during odd-chain fatty acid and branched-chain amino acid catabolism?

e.correcta: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase is a biotin-dependent enzyme that uses biotin as a mobile CO2 carrier to add a carboxyl group onto propionyl-CoA, generating methylmalonyl-CoA. This reaction is the entry point by which odd-chain fatty acids, and the amino acids valine, isoleucine, methionine, and threonine, feed into the TCA cycle as succinyl-CoA. Because biotin is required, severe biotin deficiency (or biotinidase deficiency) impairs this step and can produce an organic acidemia with abnormal propionate metabolites.

incorrectas.B: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is also biotin-dependent, but it catalyzes the committed step of fatty acid synthesis (acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA), not the propionate degradation pathway described here.
incorrectas.C: Pyruvate carboxylase is likewise biotin-dependent, but it carboxylates pyruvate to oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis and anaplerosis, a distinct reaction from propionyl-CoA carboxylation.
incorrectas.D: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase catalyzes the very next step of this pathway (methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA), but it requires vitamin B12 (adenosylcobalamin) as its cofactor, not biotin.

preguntas.q: A patient develops a scaly periorificial dermatitis, enteritis, mental status changes, and lactic acidosis after chronic consumption of raw egg whites (which contain avidin, a biotin-binding protein). Which of the following is also a classic finding of this vitamin deficiency?

o.A: Photosensitive dermatitis with diarrhea and dementia
o.B: Peripheral neuropathy with subacute combined degeneration
o.C: Bleeding gums with corkscrew body hairs

e.correcta: Biotin (B7) is a cofactor for four carboxylases (pyruvate carboxylase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, propionyl-CoA carboxylase, and 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase); loss of their activity disrupts gluconeogenesis, fatty acid synthesis, and amino acid catabolism. Avidin in raw egg whites tightly binds biotin and blocks its intestinal absorption, producing deficiency with alopecia, a characteristic scaly dermatitis, and neurologic changes, often with lactic acidosis because impaired pyruvate carboxylase blocks conversion of lactate back to glucose.

incorrectas.A: This describes pellagra from niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency, classically presenting with diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia; biotin deficiency does not produce a photosensitive dermatitis.
incorrectas.B: This describes vitamin B12 deficiency, in which impaired myelin maintenance produces subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns, corticospinal tracts, and peripheral nerves; biotin deficiency does not damage myelin.
incorrectas.C: Bleeding gums and corkscrew (coiled) body hairs are features of vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) from defective collagen cross-linking, a completely different mechanism from biotin's role as a carboxylase cofactor.

preguntas.q: Which vitamin, in its active tetrahydro form, donates one-carbon units required for the synthesis of purine bases and thymidine used in DNA and RNA?

e.correcta: Folate is reduced to tetrahydrofolate (THF), which carries activated one-carbon units used for purine ring synthesis and for methylation of deoxyuridylate to thymidylate. Because rapidly dividing cells depend heavily on this one-carbon supply for DNA replication, folate deficiency impairs DNA synthesis first in the fastest-turnover tissues, such as bone marrow precursors, producing megaloblastic changes.

incorrectas.B: Vitamin B12 is needed to regenerate folate into its usable active form by acting as a cofactor for methionine synthase (converting 5-methyl-THF back to THF), so B12 deficiency secondarily traps folate, but B12 itself is not the direct one-carbon donor for base synthesis.
incorrectas.C: Niacin (as NAD+/NADP+) functions in redox reactions throughout metabolism, not in donating one-carbon units for nucleotide synthesis.
incorrectas.D: Riboflavin (as FAD/FMN) is also a redox cofactor for oxidation-reduction reactions (e.g., succinate dehydrogenase), unrelated to one-carbon transfer for base synthesis.

preguntas.q: Dietary folate (vitamin B9) is primarily absorbed in which segment of the small intestine?

e.correcta: Folate absorption occurs mainly in the proximal small bowel, specifically the jejunum, where dietary folate polyglutamates are hydrolyzed to monoglutamates and transported into enterocytes. This anatomic site matters clinically because diseases affecting the jejunum (e.g., celiac disease/sprue) predispose to folate deficiency, whereas disease limited to the terminal ileum spares folate absorption.

incorrectas.A: The duodenum is the primary site for iron, calcium, and fat-soluble vitamin absorption, not folate; folate uptake is concentrated further along in the jejunum.
incorrectas.C: The mid ileum is not the principal site of folate uptake; the relevant transporter and hydrolase activity are concentrated proximally in the jejunum.
incorrectas.D: The terminal ileum is the specific site of vitamin B12 absorption (via the intrinsic factor-B12 complex), a distinct anatomic location from folate absorption, which is why terminal ileal disease (e.g., Crohn disease) causes B12 rather than folate deficiency.

preguntas.q: Vitamin B9 (folate) is most abundant in which dietary source?

e.correcta: Folate is abundant in leafy green vegetables (as well as legumes and fortified grains) -- a useful mnemonic is that 'folate is in foliage.' Because folate stores are relatively small and turnover is fast, diets lacking green vegetables (e.g., in alcoholics with poor nutrition) can produce deficiency within weeks to months, much faster than the years it takes to deplete B12 stores.

incorrectas.B: Animal products such as organ meats and dairy are the major dietary source of vitamin B12, not folate -- plants, not animals, are the practical dietary source of folate.
incorrectas.C: Citrus fruits are best known as a rich source of vitamin C (ascorbic acid), important for collagen synthesis, not folate.
incorrectas.D: Fortified dairy products (and sunlight exposure) are the classic source of vitamin D, unrelated to folate, which is instead fortified into grain products in the U.S.

preguntas.q: What is the most common vitamin deficiency in the United States?

e.correcta: Folate deficiency is the most common vitamin deficiency in the U.S., largely because folate body stores are small (only a few months' worth) and are rapidly depleted by poor diet, alcoholism, or increased demand (e.g., pregnancy, hemolysis), unlike vitamins with larger hepatic reserves. This is why folate fortification of grain products was mandated in the U.S., both to reduce neural tube defects and to correct subclinical deficiency.

incorrectas.A: Vitamin B12 deficiency is less common than folate deficiency in the general U.S. population because the liver stores several years' worth of B12, so deficiency usually requires a specific cause (pernicious anemia, terminal ileal disease, strict veganism) rather than simple dietary insufficiency.
incorrectas.C: Thiamine deficiency is uncommon in the general U.S. population and mostly seen in specific at-risk groups such as alcoholics (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome), not the most common overall vitamin deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Vitamin D insufficiency is common in specific populations (limited sun exposure, dark skin, obesity) but is not classically cited as the single most common vitamin deficiency the way folate deficiency is in this context.

preguntas.q: What type of anemia results from vitamin B9 (folate) deficiency?

e.correcta: Folate deficiency impairs synthesis of thymidylate and purines needed for DNA replication, so erythroid precursors in the bone marrow undergo delayed nuclear maturation while cytoplasmic growth continues normally -- producing large, immature-appearing megaloblastic red cells and hypersegmented neutrophils. This nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony is the hallmark of megaloblastic anemia, distinguishing it from other macrocytic anemias without impaired DNA synthesis.

incorrectas.A: Microcytic, hypochromic anemia results from impaired hemoglobin synthesis, as in iron deficiency or thalassemia, which reflects a defect in globin/heme production rather than the DNA synthesis defect seen in folate deficiency.
incorrectas.B: Normocytic, normochromic anemia is typical of anemia of chronic disease or acute blood loss, where red cell size is unaffected because DNA synthesis and maturation are not primarily impaired.
incorrectas.D: Macrocytic, non-megaloblastic anemia occurs with liver disease, alcohol use, or hypothyroidism, where red cells enlarge due to membrane lipid changes rather than a defect in nuclear DNA synthesis, so hypersegmented neutrophils are typically absent.

preguntas.q: Which peripheral blood smear finding is characteristic of vitamin B9 (folate) deficiency?

e.correcta: Impaired DNA synthesis from folate deficiency delays nuclear maturation across all rapidly dividing marrow lineages, including granulocyte precursors, producing neutrophils with hypersegmented nuclei (more than 5 lobes). This finding, together with oval macrocytes, is one of the earliest and most specific peripheral blood clues to a megaloblastic process, often appearing before overt anemia develops.

incorrectas.A: Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear remnants seen in red cells after splenectomy or in functional asplenia (e.g., sickle cell disease), reflecting loss of splenic pitting function, not a defect in DNA synthesis.
incorrectas.B: Schistocytes are fragmented red cells produced by mechanical shearing in microangiopathic hemolytic processes (e.g., DIC, TTP, mechanical heart valves), unrelated to the megaloblastic changes of folate deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Target cells are seen in thalassemia, liver disease, and hemoglobinopathies due to an excess of membrane relative to hemoglobin content, not the nuclear maturation defect of folate deficiency.

preguntas.q: Which of the following distinguishes isolated folate (vitamin B9) deficiency from vitamin B12 deficiency, despite both causing megaloblastic anemia?

o.A: Folate deficiency also produces subacute combined degeneration
o.B: Folate deficiency uniquely elevates methylmalonic acid
o.C: Folate deficiency spares the bone marrow
o.D: Folate deficiency does not cause neurologic symptoms

e.correcta: Folate deficiency produces megaloblastic anemia through impaired DNA synthesis but does not affect the myelin-related reactions that depend on B12, so it characteristically does NOT cause neurologic symptoms. This is a key bedside distinction: a patient with macrocytic anemia plus neurologic findings should raise suspicion for B12 deficiency, whereas isolated folate deficiency should not have neurologic involvement.

incorrectas.A: Subacute combined degeneration (dorsal column, corticospinal tract, and peripheral nerve dysfunction) is a hallmark of vitamin B12 deficiency, not folate deficiency, because it results from disrupted myelin metabolism specific to the B12-dependent methylmalonyl-CoA mutase reaction.
incorrectas.B: Elevated methylmalonic acid is specific to vitamin B12 deficiency (since methylmalonyl-CoA mutase requires B12), while methylmalonic acid remains normal in isolated folate deficiency -- this is the opposite of what actually distinguishes folate deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Folate deficiency does affect the bone marrow -- megaloblastic changes and hypersegmented neutrophils are a direct consequence of impaired erythroid and granulocyte precursor DNA synthesis, so the marrow is not spared.

preguntas.q: A patient with megaloblastic anemia is found to have a normal serum methylmalonic acid level. Which vitamin deficiency does this finding suggest?

e.correcta: Methylmalonic acid (MMA) accumulates only when methylmalonyl-CoA mutase activity is impaired, and that enzyme specifically requires vitamin B12 (adenosylcobalamin) as its cofactor -- folate is not involved in this reaction. Therefore, a normal MMA level in a patient with megaloblastic anemia points away from B12 deficiency and toward folate deficiency, since folate deficiency impairs DNA synthesis without affecting the methylmalonyl-CoA pathway.

incorrectas.A: Vitamin B12 deficiency would be expected to raise, not normalize, methylmalonic acid, because B12 is required for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase to convert methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA; a normal MMA argues against this diagnosis.
incorrectas.B: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency causes a sideroblastic, microcytic anemia related to impaired heme synthesis (ALA synthase is B6-dependent), not megaloblastic anemia, and is unrelated to methylmalonic acid metabolism.
incorrectas.D: Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) deficiency causes glossitis, cheilosis, and dermatitis via impaired FAD-dependent redox reactions, not megaloblastic anemia or methylmalonic acid elevation.

preguntas.q: Which laboratory abnormality occurs in vitamin B9 (folate) deficiency due to impaired remethylation of homocysteine to methionine?

e.correcta: Methionine synthase uses 5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate as the methyl donor to convert homocysteine back to methionine; when folate is deficient, this methyl donor is unavailable and homocysteine accumulates. Elevated homocysteine is seen in both folate and B12 deficiency (since B12 is the other required cofactor for the same reaction), which is why homocysteine alone cannot distinguish between the two -- methylmalonic acid is needed for that distinction.

incorrectas.B: Methylmalonic acid is elevated specifically in vitamin B12 deficiency (due to impaired methylmalonyl-CoA mutase), a separate B12-dependent reaction that does not involve folate, so it remains normal in isolated folate deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Homocysteine increases, not decreases, with folate deficiency, since the methyl donor needed to clear homocysteine to methionine is missing.
incorrectas.D: Ammonia levels are not characteristically affected by folate deficiency; ammonia elevation instead relates to disorders of the urea cycle or severe liver dysfunction.

preguntas.q: Which nonspecific oral finding, described as a smooth, shiny, erythematous tongue, can be seen with folate (vitamin B9) deficiency as well as several other vitamin deficiencies (e.g., B3, B12)?

e.correcta: Glossitis -- a smooth, shiny, erythematous tongue from atrophy of the lingual papillae -- is a nonspecific mucosal finding that reflects the high turnover rate of the tongue's epithelium, making it especially sensitive to any deficiency that impairs cell division (folate, B12) or cellular redox metabolism (niacin, riboflavin). Its lack of specificity means glossitis alone cannot pinpoint which vitamin is deficient without additional clues like anemia type or neurologic findings.

incorrectas.A: Angular cheilitis (fissuring at the corners of the mouth) is classically associated with riboflavin (B2) deficiency, reflecting a different mucocutaneous pattern from the diffuse tongue atrophy of glossitis.
incorrectas.B: Leukoplakia is a white, premalignant mucosal patch typically related to chronic irritation (e.g., tobacco use), not a vitamin deficiency finding.
incorrectas.D: Bleeding gums are characteristic of vitamin C deficiency (scurvy), caused by defective collagen synthesis and fragile blood vessels, a distinct mechanism from the epithelial atrophy causing glossitis.

preguntas.q: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is found almost exclusively in which type of dietary source?

e.correcta: Vitamin B12 is found almost exclusively in animal products such as meat, fish, eggs, and dairy, because animals accumulate B12 that is originally synthesized by microorganisms. This is why strict vegans, who avoid all animal products, are at particular risk for dietary B12 deficiency, whereas lacto-ovo vegetarians who still consume dairy and eggs are largely protected.

incorrectas.A: Leafy green vegetables are a rich source of folate (vitamin B9), not B12 -- plants cannot synthesize B12 since only microorganisms have the enzymatic machinery to do so.
incorrectas.C: Citrus fruits are a source of vitamin C, unrelated to B12, which is not found in significant quantities in any plant food.
incorrectas.D: Whole grains provide B vitamins such as thiamine and niacin (and folate when fortified), but not meaningful amounts of B12.

preguntas.q: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) cannot be synthesized by plants or animals. Which organisms are the exclusive natural producers of vitamin B12?

e.correcta: Vitamin B12 synthesis requires a complex enzymatic pathway that exists only in certain bacteria and archaea; no plant, fungus, or animal cell can manufacture it de novo. Animals obtain B12 indirectly, either through symbiotic gut bacteria or by eating other animals/animal products further up the food chain, which is why B12 is essentially absent from unfortified plant foods.

incorrectas.A: Fungi, like plants and animals, lack the biosynthetic pathway for B12 and cannot produce it; this makes B12 deficiency a genuine risk in strictly plant/fungus-based diets.
incorrectas.B: Plants have no mechanism to synthesize B12 at all, which is precisely why leafy greens are a good folate source but not a B12 source.
incorrectas.D: Animal liver tissue stores large amounts of B12 (accumulated from the diet, ultimately of bacterial origin) but does not itself synthesize the vitamin -- it is simply a reservoir, not a producer.

preguntas.q: Which antibody test is diagnostic for pernicious anemia, the autoimmune cause of vitamin B12 deficiency?

e.correcta: Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies directly block the binding of intrinsic factor to B12 or its receptor in the terminal ileum, and their presence is highly specific for pernicious anemia, making them the diagnostic antibody of choice. This autoimmune destruction of intrinsic factor function (often alongside parietal cell destruction) prevents normal ileal absorption of dietary B12, leading to progressive deficiency.

incorrectas.B: Anti-parietal cell antibodies are also seen in pernicious anemia and reflect autoimmune gastritis, but they are more sensitive and less specific (they occur in other autoimmune gastritis without B12 deficiency), so anti-intrinsic factor antibodies are considered the more diagnostic test.
incorrectas.C: Anti-mitochondrial antibodies are the hallmark of primary biliary cholangitis, an autoimmune liver disease unrelated to vitamin B12 absorption.
incorrectas.D: Anti-smooth muscle antibodies are associated with autoimmune hepatitis, not pernicious anemia or B12 metabolism.

preguntas.q: Damage to or surgical resection of which structure is a recognized cause of vitamin B12 deficiency, as can occur in Crohn disease?

e.correcta: The B12-intrinsic factor complex is specifically absorbed via cubilin receptors located in the terminal ileum, so any disease process that damages or removes this segment -- such as Crohn disease (which classically affects the terminal ileum) or surgical resection -- disrupts B12 absorption regardless of adequate intake or intact intrinsic factor production. This is why terminal ileal disease produces the same downstream B12 deficiency as intrinsic factor loss, despite a completely different underlying mechanism.

incorrectas.A: The duodenum is important for iron, calcium, and fat-soluble vitamin absorption, but it is not the primary absorption site for B12, so duodenal disease alone would not typically cause B12 deficiency.
incorrectas.B: The jejunum is where folate is absorbed, not B12; jejunal disease (e.g., celiac sprue) more classically produces folate deficiency rather than B12 deficiency.
incorrectas.C: The stomach produces intrinsic factor (via parietal cells) and releases B12 from food proteins via acid and pepsin; gastric disease (e.g., atrophic gastritis, gastrectomy) causes B12 deficiency through loss of intrinsic factor production, a different mechanism than physical damage to the ileal absorption site itself.

preguntas.q: Insufficient dietary intake of vitamin B12 is most likely to develop in a patient who follows which type of diet?

e.correcta: Because B12 is found almost exclusively in animal products, a vegan diet -- which excludes all meat, dairy, and eggs -- removes essentially every dietary source of the vitamin, making insufficient intake a real risk without supplementation. Since hepatic B12 stores are large (years' worth), clinical deficiency in vegans typically takes years to manifest, but it remains the classic dietary cause of B12 insufficiency.

incorrectas.A: A lacto-ovo vegetarian diet still includes dairy and eggs, which contain B12, so this pattern of eating does not eliminate dietary intake of the vitamin the way a fully vegan diet does.
incorrectas.C: A gluten-free diet avoids wheat, barley, and rye but does not restrict animal products, so it does not predispose to B12 insufficiency from insufficient intake (though an underlying gluten-related enteropathy could separately cause malabsorption).
incorrectas.D: A low-fat diet limits dietary fat but not animal-derived protein sources such as lean meat, fish, or dairy, so it does not typically restrict B12 intake.

preguntas.q: Malabsorptive conditions such as sprue or enteritis are a recognized cause of deficiency of which vitamin?

e.correcta: Malabsorptive diseases affecting the small intestine (such as celiac sprue or infectious/inflammatory enteritis) can impair the mucosal surface needed for nutrient uptake, including the specific ileal receptor-mediated absorption pathway required for B12 bound to intrinsic factor. Because B12 absorption depends on this dedicated mechanism (unlike passive diffusion of many nutrients), even localized ileal mucosal disease can produce clinically significant B12 deficiency and megaloblastic anemia.

incorrectas.A: Vitamin D is fat-soluble and its absorption also depends on adequate small bowel and biliary/pancreatic function, so malabsorption syndromes can lower vitamin D as well -- but the vitamin classically linked to sprue/enteritis-induced ileal malabsorption and megaloblastic anemia in this context is B12.
incorrectas.B: Vitamin K, being fat-soluble, requires bile and pancreatic enzymes for absorption and can be affected in severe fat malabsorption, but its deficiency more classically presents with a bleeding diathesis rather than the anemia syndrome linked to B12 deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Vitamin A is also fat-soluble and can be affected by malabsorption, producing night blindness, but it is not the vitamin specifically associated with sprue/enteritis-induced megaloblastic anemia.

preguntas.q: A patient who regularly eats raw freshwater fish develops megaloblastic anemia. Which parasite, which competes with the host for dietary vitamin B12, is the likely cause?

e.correcta: Diphyllobothrium latum, the fish tapeworm acquired by eating undercooked or raw freshwater fish, resides in the small intestine and directly absorbs large amounts of dietary vitamin B12 for its own metabolism, depriving the host and producing a megaloblastic anemia similar to that of dietary B12 deficiency. This is a classic exception to the 'worms cause iron deficiency via blood loss' pattern, since D. latum instead causes vitamin depletion.

incorrectas.A: Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) is acquired from undercooked pork and is notable for causing cysticercosis (including neurocysticercosis) when larvae are ingested, not vitamin B12 competition or megaloblastic anemia.
incorrectas.C: Necator americanus (hookworm) attaches to the intestinal mucosa and causes chronic blood loss, leading to iron deficiency (microcytic) anemia, a fundamentally different mechanism from B12 competition.
incorrectas.D: Ascaris lumbricoides is a large roundworm that can cause intestinal obstruction or biliary/pancreatic duct obstruction, but it does not compete for vitamin B12 or cause megaloblastic anemia.

preguntas.q: Which test uses radiolabeled cobalamin to help determine whether vitamin B12 deficiency is due to dietary insufficiency, pernicious anemia, or another malabsorptive cause?

e.correcta: The Schilling test is a multi-stage test in which radiolabeled vitamin B12 is given orally with and without co-administered intrinsic factor, and urinary excretion of the label is measured to determine whether poor absorption corrects with intrinsic factor supplementation (suggesting pernicious anemia) or persists regardless (suggesting an intestinal/ileal cause). This staged approach allows clinicians to localize the cause of B12 deficiency beyond simply confirming a low serum level.

incorrectas.A: The D-xylose absorption test evaluates generalized proximal small bowel mucosal absorptive capacity (e.g., to distinguish pancreatic insufficiency from mucosal disease), but it is not used to differentiate the specific etiologies of B12 deficiency.
incorrectas.C: The direct Coombs test detects antibodies bound to red blood cells in autoimmune hemolytic anemia, an entirely different diagnostic question from localizing the cause of B12 malabsorption.
incorrectas.D: The Bernstein test is used to assess for esophageal acid sensitivity in evaluating chest pain/GERD, unrelated to vitamin B12 metabolism.

preguntas.q: What type of anemia is characteristically caused by vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency?

e.correcta: Like folate deficiency, B12 deficiency impairs DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing marrow precursors (B12 is needed to regenerate active folate via the methionine synthase reaction), causing the same nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony that produces megaloblastic, macrocytic red cells and hypersegmented neutrophils. Distinguishing B12 deficiency from folate deficiency as the cause of this megaloblastic picture requires additional clues, such as neurologic findings or elevated methylmalonic acid, both specific to B12.

incorrectas.B: Microcytic, hypochromic anemia reflects a hemoglobin synthesis defect (iron deficiency, thalassemia), a mechanism unrelated to the impaired DNA synthesis seen in B12 deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Normocytic, normochromic anemia is seen in conditions like anemia of chronic disease or acute hemorrhage, where red cell size and DNA synthesis are not primarily affected, unlike in B12 deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Aplastic anemia results from bone marrow failure with pancytopenia due to loss of hematopoietic stem cells (e.g., from toxins, radiation, or autoimmune destruction), a fundamentally different process from the megaloblastic changes of B12 deficiency.

preguntas.q: Which finding on peripheral blood smear is characteristic of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency?

e.correcta: As in folate deficiency, B12 deficiency impairs DNA synthesis in granulocyte precursors, producing neutrophils with more than five nuclear lobes (hypersegmentation). This finding, combined with oval macrocytes, is an early and sensitive smear clue to a megaloblastic process and often precedes overt anemia.

incorrectas.A: Target cells arise from an excess of red cell membrane relative to hemoglobin, as seen in thalassemia, liver disease, or hemoglobin C disease -- a membrane/hemoglobin content abnormality, not the nuclear maturation defect of B12 deficiency.
incorrectas.B: Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear remnants normally removed by the spleen, so they appear after splenectomy or in functional asplenia, unrelated to impaired DNA synthesis from B12 deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Basophilic stippling reflects residual ribosomal RNA aggregates classically seen in lead poisoning or thalassemia, a different pathophysiology from the megaloblastic changes of B12 deficiency.

preguntas.q: Unlike folate deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency characteristically causes which additional manifestation?

e.correcta: Vitamin B12 is required for the methylmalonyl-CoA mutase reaction, and disruption of this pathway leads to abnormal fatty acid incorporation into neuronal myelin, producing degeneration of the dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal tracts, and peripheral nerves -- a syndrome called subacute combined degeneration. Because folate deficiency does not involve this B12-dependent methylmalonate pathway, it does not cause these neurologic findings, making their presence a key clue pointing toward B12 rather than folate deficiency.

incorrectas.A: Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia) results from thiamine (B1) deficiency, classically in alcoholics, and is unrelated to B12's myelin-related mechanism.
incorrectas.B: Guillain-Barre syndrome is an autoimmune, often post-infectious demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy, a distinct immune-mediated process rather than a nutritional deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system with an immune-mediated pathophysiology distinct from the vitamin-deficiency-driven myelin damage of B12 deficiency, though the two can resemble each other on exam.

preguntas.q: Which laboratory finding is elevated in vitamin B12 deficiency but remains normal in isolated folate deficiency?

e.correcta: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase requires vitamin B12 (as adenosylcobalamin) to convert methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA; when B12 is deficient, this reaction cannot proceed and methylmalonic acid accumulates. Because folate plays no role in this particular reaction, methylmalonic acid stays normal in isolated folate deficiency, making it the key lab test to distinguish the two causes of megaloblastic anemia.

incorrectas.A: Homocysteine is elevated in both B12 and folate deficiency, since both vitamins are needed for the methionine synthase reaction that clears homocysteine, so it cannot by itself distinguish between the two.
incorrectas.B: Lactate dehydrogenase can be elevated in megaloblastic anemia due to ineffective erythropoiesis and intramedullary hemolysis, but this occurs with both folate and B12 deficiency and does not specifically differentiate them.
incorrectas.D: Indirect bilirubin may rise from ineffective erythropoiesis in either type of megaloblastic anemia, similarly to LDH, so it is likewise not a distinguishing marker between B12 and folate deficiency.

preguntas.q: Vitamin B12 acts as a cofactor for methionine synthase, which transfers a methyl group from 5-methyltetrahydrofolate to regenerate methionine from homocysteine. Which metabolite accumulates when B12 is deficient?

e.correcta: Without adequate B12, methionine synthase cannot transfer the methyl group from 5-methyl-THF to homocysteine, so homocysteine accumulates while methionine (and its downstream product S-adenosylmethionine) production falls. This same block also 'traps' folate in its 5-methyl-THF form (the methylfolate trap), which is why B12 deficiency secondarily worsens folate-dependent DNA synthesis, contributing to the megaloblastic anemia seen in B12 deficiency.

incorrectas.B: Methionine is the product of the methionine synthase reaction, so with B12 deficiency, methionine synthesis is impaired and its levels tend to fall, the opposite of what accumulates.
incorrectas.C: S-adenosylmethionine is the universal methyl donor generated from methionine; with B12 deficiency, less methionine is made, so SAM production would tend to decrease rather than accumulate.
incorrectas.D: Cystathionine is formed in the transsulfuration pathway (via cystathionine beta-synthase, a B6/PLP-dependent enzyme), a separate route for homocysteine disposal that is not directly affected by B12 deficiency.

preguntas.q: In vitamin B12 deficiency, correcting the deficiency reverses the megaloblastic anemia, but which type of damage may persist irreversibly if the deficiency has been prolonged?

e.correcta: B12 (cobalamin) is a required cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; when B12 is deficient, methylmalonic acid accumulates and disrupts normal fatty acid incorporation into neuronal membranes, contributing to demyelination of the dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal tracts, and peripheral nerves (subacute combined degeneration). Unlike the megaloblastic marrow changes, which resolve once B12 is repleted, damage to myelin and axons can become fixed and permanent if the deficiency persists too long — which is why B12 status is checked before giving folate, since folate corrects the anemia but not the neuropathy and can mask the underlying problem.

incorrectas.A: Megaloblastic bone marrow changes are reversible with B12 replacement, since they reflect impaired DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing erythroid precursors rather than fixed structural damage; the anemia resolves as new normal precursors are produced.
incorrectas.C: Glossitis is reversible mucosal inflammation of the tongue from impaired epithelial turnover, and it resolves with vitamin repletion rather than persisting as permanent damage.
incorrectas.D: Hepatic steatosis is not a typical feature of B12 deficiency at all; fatty liver relates to other metabolic or nutritional derangements, not to the classic neurologic pathology of cobalamin deficiency.

preguntas.q: Which vitamin acts as a cofactor for dopamine β-hydroxylase, the enzyme that converts dopamine to norepinephrine during catecholamine biosynthesis?

e.correcta: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a required cofactor for dopamine β-hydroxylase, a copper-containing enzyme in the secretory vesicles of noradrenergic neurons and adrenal chromaffin cells that hydroxylates dopamine to form norepinephrine. Ascorbate keeps the enzyme's copper in its reduced (Cu+) state, which is essential for catalysis; without it, norepinephrine (and downstream epinephrine) synthesis lags. This is one reason scurvy can be accompanied by fatigue and mood changes, beyond its better-known collagen-related effects.

incorrectas.A: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) is the cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase, the earlier, rate-limiting step converting tyrosine to L-DOPA, not the dopamine-to-norepinephrine reaction performed by dopamine β-hydroxylase.
incorrectas.B: Pyridoxal phosphate (active vitamin B6) is the cofactor for aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (DOPA decarboxylase), which converts L-DOPA to dopamine — one step upstream of the reaction that requires vitamin C.
incorrectas.D: S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) donates the methyl group used by phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT) to convert norepinephrine to epinephrine, the step that comes after, not the dopamine β-hydroxylase reaction itself.

preguntas.q: A diet deficient in which category of foods puts a patient at greatest risk for vitamin C deficiency (scurvy)?

e.correcta: Humans lack L-gulonolactone oxidase and cannot synthesize their own vitamin C, so it must come entirely from the diet — primarily citrus fruits, berries, tomatoes, and leafy or cruciferous vegetables. Populations with limited access to fresh produce (elderly patients living alone, people with alcohol use disorder, historically sailors on long voyages) are classically at risk for scurvy, tying the disease directly to this food group rather than to any single nutrient-dense food.

incorrectas.A: Whole grains and legumes are important sources of B vitamins (thiamine, folate) and fiber but contain little vitamin C, so lacking them raises risk for B-vitamin deficiencies rather than scurvy.
incorrectas.C: Organ meats and egg yolks are rich in vitamin A, vitamin D, and vitamin B12, but vitamin C content is low; missing these foods is more associated with those deficiencies.
incorrectas.D: Fortified dairy products are a major source of vitamin D (and calcium), not vitamin C, so lacking dairy affects bone mineral metabolism rather than collagen synthesis.

preguntas.q: Deficiency of which vitamin impairs hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues on procollagen, preventing formation of the collagen triple helix and causing the disease scurvy?

e.correcta: Vitamin C is a required cofactor for prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase, the enzymes that hydroxylate proline and lysine residues within procollagen's pro-α chains. Hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine are essential for the hydrogen bonding that stabilizes the collagen triple helix and for later cross-linking; without them, defective procollagen cannot fold properly and is degraded intracellularly instead of secreted, weakening connective tissue, vessel walls, and bone matrix — the basis for scurvy's bleeding gums, poor wound healing, and bone pain.

incorrectas.A: Vitamin D deficiency impairs intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, leading to poor bone mineralization (rickets/osteomalacia), but it does not affect the hydroxylation steps of collagen synthesis itself.
incorrectas.C: Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and squamous metaplasia of epithelium, reflecting its role in retinal pigments and epithelial differentiation, not procollagen hydroxylation.
incorrectas.D: Vitamin K deficiency impairs γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X in the liver, causing bleeding from factor dysfunction — a completely different mechanism from the connective tissue defect of scurvy.

preguntas.q: A malnourished patient presents with swollen, bleeding gums, perifollicular petechiae, easy bruising, and hemarthrosis. Which deficiency best explains this presentation?

e.correcta: Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) impairs hydroxylation of collagen, producing fragile, poorly cross-linked blood vessel walls and connective tissue. Subendothelial collagen normally helps activate platelets (via von Willebrand factor binding and contact activation of factor XII), so defective collagen leads to easy bleeding into skin (perifollicular petechiae, bruising), gums, and joints (hemarthrosis) even though platelet count and clotting factors are normal.

incorrectas.A: Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding from failure to γ-carboxylate clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, prolonging PT and PTT; it does not classically cause gum swelling or perifollicular petechiae, which are collagen/vessel-wall findings specific to scurvy.
incorrectas.B: Factor VIII deficiency (hemophilia A) causes deep tissue and joint bleeding from an intrinsic pathway clotting factor defect with a markedly prolonged PTT, but it does not produce the gum disease or perifollicular skin findings seen with vitamin C deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura causes mucocutaneous bleeding and petechiae from a low platelet count, but labs would show thrombocytopenia and it lacks the gum swelling and hemarthrosis pattern that points to a collagen/connective tissue problem like scurvy.

preguntas.q: Poor wound healing in scurvy is best explained by impaired synthesis of which structural molecule?

e.correcta: Proper wound healing depends on fibroblasts depositing new collagen to rebuild the extracellular matrix and give healing tissue tensile strength. Because vitamin C is required for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase activity during collagen synthesis, scurvy leads to unstable, poorly cross-linked collagen that cannot be secreted or properly organized, so wounds heal slowly, may dehisce, and old scars can even reopen ("scorbutic wound reopening").

incorrectas.B: Elastin provides recoil and elasticity to tissues like large arteries and lungs, but wound tensile strength during healing comes predominantly from collagen deposition, not elastin, so elastin synthesis is not the key defect in scorbutic wound healing.
incorrectas.C: Fibrin forms the initial clot scaffold during hemostasis and the early inflammatory phase of healing, but its formation depends on the coagulation cascade (vitamin K–dependent factors), not vitamin C, and it is not the long-term determinant of wound strength.
incorrectas.D: Fibronectin helps organize the provisional wound matrix and guides cell migration early in healing, but the vitamin C–dependent step that classically fails in scurvy is collagen hydroxylation, which underlies the long-term structural defect.

preguntas.q: "Corkscrew" hairs with surrounding perifollicular hemorrhage are a classic cutaneous finding in which vitamin deficiency?

e.correcta: In scurvy, defective collagen synthesis weakens hair follicle structure and the walls of tiny perifollicular capillaries, causing hair shafts to curl abnormally into a corkscrew shape and nearby vessels to rupture easily, producing visible perifollicular hemorrhage. This finding, along with hyperkeratotic follicular papules, is a distinctive skin sign that should prompt suspicion for vitamin C deficiency, especially in patients with poor intake of fruits and vegetables.

incorrectas.A: Vitamin A deficiency causes dry, scaly skin (phrynoderma) and night blindness from disrupted epithelial differentiation and retinal pigment function, not corkscrew hair or perifollicular bleeding.
incorrectas.B: Zinc deficiency causes acrodermatitis enteropathica–type lesions (perioral and acral dermatitis), hair thinning, and poor wound healing, but not the specific corkscrew hair and perifollicular hemorrhage pattern characteristic of scurvy.
incorrectas.C: Biotin deficiency causes alopecia, a scaly periorificial dermatitis, and neurologic symptoms (often from raw egg white ingestion or prolonged antibiotic use), but not the corkscrew hair deformity linked to defective collagen in scurvy.

preguntas.q: Which of the following best describes the effect of vitamin C deficiency on host defense?

o.A: Impaired immune response and increased susceptibility to infection

e.correcta: Vitamin C accumulates in leukocytes, particularly neutrophils, supporting chemotaxis, phagocytosis, and generation of reactive oxygen species used to kill ingested organisms, and it also helps regenerate other antioxidants that protect immune cells from oxidative damage during an immune response. In scurvy, low ascorbate blunts these neutrophil functions and overall immune competence, contributing to the poor wound healing and increased infection risk seen in severely deficient patients.

incorrectas.B: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia results from antibody-mediated destruction of red blood cells, a mechanism unrelated to vitamin C's role in leukocyte antioxidant support and collagen synthesis.
incorrectas.C: Selective IgA deficiency is a primary immunodeficiency from a defect in B-cell differentiation into IgA-producing plasma cells, an inherited immunologic disorder unrelated to ascorbate levels.
incorrectas.D: Eosinophilic tissue infiltration is typically driven by allergic, parasitic, or specific inflammatory conditions involving IL-5 and eosinophil recruitment, not by a nutritional antioxidant deficiency like scurvy.

preguntas.q: Vitamin C deficiency classically causes an increase in which bleeding parameter, helping distinguish it from clotting factor deficiencies such as vitamin K deficiency?

e.correcta: In scurvy, bleeding results from structurally weak, poorly hydroxylated collagen in vessel walls and impaired collagen-mediated platelet adhesion/activation, rather than from a deficiency of clotting factors. This produces a prolonged bleeding time, which reflects primary hemostasis (vessel wall and platelet function), while the clotting cascade itself remains essentially unaffected — a key clue that separates scurvy from coagulation factor disorders.

incorrectas.B: Prothrombin time (PT) measures the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways (factor VII and downstream), which depend on vitamin K–dependent clotting factors, not collagen integrity, so it is not the parameter classically elevated in scurvy.
incorrectas.C: Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) measures the intrinsic and common pathways (factors VIII, IX, XI, XII and downstream); deficiency of these factors, as in hemophilia or vitamin K deficiency, prolongs PTT, not a primary collagen defect.
incorrectas.D: INR is a standardized version of the PT used mainly to monitor warfarin therapy; like PT, it reflects vitamin K–dependent factor activity and is not the hemostatic value affected by defective collagen in scurvy.

preguntas.q: In vitamin C deficiency, which coagulation pattern is typically described, and how does it differ from the pattern seen in vitamin K deficiency?

o.D: Normal PT and PTT with normal bleeding time

e.correcta: Vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen-dependent hemostasis rather than the vitamin K–dependent clotting factor cascade, so PT (which reflects factor VII and the extrinsic pathway) stays normal. The classic teaching point is that PTT can be prolonged in this setting because defective, poorly cross-linked collagen fails to support normal contact activation/platelet interactions feeding into the intrinsic pathway, giving a normal PT with an elevated PTT — a pattern used to differentiate scurvy from vitamin K deficiency, which prolongs both PT and PTT.

incorrectas.A: A prolonged PT with normal PTT is more characteristic of early vitamin K deficiency or liver disease, where the short-half-life factor VII (extrinsic pathway) is affected first, not the pattern described for vitamin C deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Prolonged PT and PTT together are seen in vitamin K deficiency (which impairs synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, and X) or severe liver disease with global factor deficiency, not in isolated vitamin C deficiency, which does not affect γ-carboxylation of clotting factors.
incorrectas.D: A completely normal PT and PTT with normal bleeding time would not explain the clinical bleeding seen in scurvy; vitamin C deficiency does produce a hemostatic abnormality, attributed here to collagen dysfunction rather than to the intrinsic factor cascade alone.

preguntas.q: Excessive vitamin C supplementation increases the risk of which type of kidney stone?

e.correcta: Ascorbic acid is partially metabolized to oxalate, so very high vitamin C intake increases urinary oxalate excretion, which can combine with calcium to precipitate as calcium oxalate crystals and form kidney stones. This is why megadose vitamin C supplementation is generally discouraged in patients with a history of kidney stones or renal impairment, alongside milder toxicity symptoms like nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and fatigue.

incorrectas.A: Uric acid stones form from excess purine breakdown (e.g., gout or tumor lysis syndrome) and are favored by persistently acidic urine, a mechanism unrelated to vitamin C metabolism to oxalate.
incorrectas.B: Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones form in alkaline urine generated by urease-producing bacteria (e.g., Proteus) during chronic urinary tract infections, not from vitamin excess.
incorrectas.C: Cystine stones arise from an inherited defect in renal tubular reabsorption of cystine (cystinuria), a transporter defect unrelated to vitamin C intake or oxalate metabolism.

preguntas.q: Which form of vitamin D is obtained from dietary plant, fungal, and yeast sources (as opposed to being synthesized in the skin)?

e.correcta: Ergocalciferol (vitamin D2) is the plant/fungal/yeast-derived form of vitamin D, produced by UV irradiation of ergosterol, and it is absorbed from the diet like other fat-soluble vitamins. It is biologically similar to vitamin D3 and undergoes the same hepatic 25-hydroxylation and renal 1α-hydroxylation to become active, but its dietary/plant origin (versus D3's cutaneous or animal origin) is the classic distinguishing point tested for D2.

incorrectas.A: Cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) is synthesized in the skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol upon UV-B exposure, or obtained from animal sources like fish and egg yolk, not from plants or fungi.
incorrectas.B: Calcidiol (25-OH D3) is the hepatic hydroxylation product of either D2 or D3 and functions as the storage/circulating form used to assess vitamin D status; it is not itself a dietary source category.
incorrectas.D: Calcitriol (1,25-(OH)2 D3) is the fully activated hormone produced by renal 1α-hydroxylase; it is a metabolic product, not a form obtained directly from plant-based foods.

preguntas.q: UV-B–mediated conversion of 7-dehydrocholesterol into cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) occurs in which layer of the epidermis?

e.correcta: Keratinocytes of the stratum basale, the deepest, mitotically active layer of the epidermis, contain 7-dehydrocholesterol in their plasma membranes; upon UV-B exposure this precursor undergoes a photochemical reaction to form previtamin D3, which then thermally isomerizes to cholecalciferol. This cutaneous synthesis is the major natural source of vitamin D in humans, which is why individuals with limited sun exposure or heavily pigmented skin (more melanin absorbs UV-B) are at higher risk for deficiency.

incorrectas.A: The stratum corneum is the outermost, dead, keratinized layer that provides barrier function; it lacks the metabolically active cells and precursor lipid needed for vitamin D photosynthesis.
incorrectas.B: The stratum granulosum is where keratinocytes release lipid-filled lamellar bodies to help form the skin's water barrier, a process distinct from vitamin D precursor synthesis, which occurs deeper in the basal layer.
incorrectas.C: The stratum spinosum contributes structural keratin and desmosomal connections between keratinocytes but is not the principal site where 7-dehydrocholesterol is converted to previtamin D3.

preguntas.q: Which form of vitamin D, produced by an unregulated hepatic hydroxylation step, is used clinically as the best marker of a patient's vitamin D stores?

e.correcta: The liver converts vitamin D2 or D3 into 25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol) via 25-hydroxylase, a step that is not tightly hormonally regulated and instead reflects overall vitamin D intake and sun exposure. Because of this, and because calcidiol has a much longer half-life in circulation than the active hormone, serum 25-OH D is the standard lab test used to assess whether a patient is vitamin D deficient, insufficient, or replete.

incorrectas.A: Cholecalciferol (D3) is the initial substrate before hepatic hydroxylation; its serum level is not routinely measured because it fluctuates quickly with recent sun exposure or intake rather than reflecting stable body stores.
incorrectas.B: Ergocalciferol (D2) is likewise a precursor form (from plant/fungal sources) that must be hydroxylated before it reflects long-term vitamin D status, so it is not the storage form used for monitoring.
incorrectas.C: Calcitriol (1,25-(OH)2 D3) is the tightly regulated active hormone, controlled by PTH, phosphate, and calcitriol itself via negative feedback; because its production is regulated rather than reflecting total body stores, it is a poor and sometimes misleading marker of vitamin D status.

preguntas.q: Renal 1α-hydroxylase converts calcidiol into which hormonally active form of vitamin D, whose synthesis is stimulated by parathyroid hormone?

e.correcta: Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3) is produced when renal proximal tubule 1α-hydroxylase adds a second hydroxyl group to calcidiol; PTH stimulates this enzyme in response to low serum calcium, increasing calcitriol production, which then promotes intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption and bone resorption to raise serum calcium. Calcitriol feeds back to inhibit its own further synthesis (and suppresses PTH release), forming a tightly regulated hormonal axis central to calcium homeostasis.

incorrectas.A: Cholecalciferol is the unhydroxylated precursor formed in skin or absorbed from animal-derived diet; it requires two sequential hydroxylation steps (liver, then kidney) before becoming active, so it is not itself the PTH-stimulated active hormone.
incorrectas.B: Ergocalciferol is the plant-derived precursor analogous to cholecalciferol; like D3, it must undergo hepatic and renal hydroxylation before becoming biologically active, and it is not directly regulated by PTH.
incorrectas.C: Calcidiol (25-OH D3) is the intermediate hepatic product and circulating storage form; it still requires renal 1α-hydroxylation, the PTH-stimulated step, to become the active hormone calcitriol.

preguntas.q: A child presents with bowed legs, bone pain, and skeletal deformities from inadequate mineralization of growing bone and cartilage. This is characteristic of deficiency of which vitamin?

e.correcta: Vitamin D deficiency in children impairs intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate, leading to inadequate mineralization of growth plate cartilage and newly formed osteoid, which produces rickets — characterized by bowing of the legs, a rachitic rosary at the costochondral junctions, frontal bossing, and widened growth plates on X-ray. Because the growth plates are still open in children, the disease specifically affects the actively growing skeleton, distinguishing it from the analogous adult disease.

incorrectas.B: Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness, xerophthalmia, and immune impairment from disrupted retinal and epithelial function, not defective bone mineralization or the classic bowing deformities of rickets.
incorrectas.C: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, with bleeding gums, poor wound healing, and corkscrew hairs from defective collagen hydroxylation — a connective tissue disorder distinct from the mineralization defect of rickets.
incorrectas.D: Vitamin K deficiency impairs clotting factor carboxylation and causes a bleeding tendency, not a bone mineralization disorder; it has no direct role in calcium/phosphate handling like vitamin D does.

preguntas.q: An adult presents with diffuse bone pain and proximal muscle weakness due to defective mineralization of existing bone matrix (osteoid). Which vitamin deficiency is responsible?

e.correcta: In adults, whose growth plates have already fused, vitamin D deficiency still impairs calcium and phosphate absorption, but instead of the growth-plate deformities of rickets, the result is osteomalacia — accumulation of poorly mineralized osteoid throughout existing bone, causing bone pain, increased fracture risk (including pseudofractures/Looser zones), and often proximal muscle weakness from the effects of hypocalcemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

incorrectas.A: Vitamin K deficiency impairs γ-carboxylation of clotting factors, producing a bleeding tendency, not the bone pain and mineralization defect characteristic of osteomalacia.
incorrectas.C: Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) causes a collagen synthesis defect leading to bleeding gums, poor wound healing, and joint bleeding, but it does not primarily impair bone matrix mineralization the way vitamin D deficiency does.
incorrectas.D: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, presenting with paresthesias and ataxia rather than the diffuse bone pain and proximal weakness from defective mineralization seen in osteomalacia.

preguntas.q: Because breast milk contains very little of it, which vitamin should be given as an oral supplement to exclusively breastfed infants?

e.correcta: Breast milk is a poor source of vitamin D, and exclusively breastfed infants who receive little sun exposure are at real risk of developing rickets if not supplemented. Pediatric guidelines therefore recommend oral vitamin D supplementation (in addition to, not instead of, the vitamin K given by injection at birth) for breastfed infants until they are consuming enough vitamin D–fortified formula or food.

incorrectas.A: Vitamin K is also low in breast milk and newborns are relatively deficient in it, but that deficiency is addressed by a single intramuscular injection at birth to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn, not by ongoing oral supplementation — the distinction this question tests.
incorrectas.B: Vitamin B12 deficiency in exclusively breastfed infants is a concern mainly when the mother herself is B12 deficient (e.g., a vegan mother), not a routine universal supplementation issue the way vitamin D is.
incorrectas.C: Vitamin C is generally present in adequate amounts in breast milk (reflecting maternal intake) and is not the vitamin classically deficient enough to warrant routine oral supplementation in breastfed infants.

preguntas.q: Vitamin D toxicity causes hypercalcemia that can present with stupor along with which additional symptom?

e.correcta: Vitamin D excess drives excessive intestinal calcium absorption and bone resorption, producing hypercalcemia. Hypercalcemia classically causes gastrointestinal and neuropsychiatric symptoms summarized as "stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones" — including anorexia (decreased appetite), nausea, constipation, and altered mental status ranging from lethargy to stupor — because elevated calcium reduces neuromuscular excitability and disrupts normal GI motility and CNS function.

incorrectas.A: Increased appetite is not a feature of hypercalcemia from vitamin D toxicity; if anything, hypercalcemia typically suppresses appetite through its effects on the gastrointestinal tract and central nervous system.
incorrectas.C: Photophobia is not a classic symptom of vitamin D toxicity or hypercalcemia; it is more commonly associated with meningeal irritation, migraine, or ocular pathology, unrelated to calcium disturbances.
