incorrectas.D: Hyperactivity is inconsistent with the sedating, lethargic effects of hypercalcemia; vitamin D toxicity more typically causes lethargy or stupor rather than increased activity or agitation.

preguntas.q: Which vitamin functions primarily as a lipid-soluble antioxidant that protects red blood cell membranes and other lipid-rich structures from free radical damage?

e.correcta: Vitamin E (tocopherol/tocotrienol) is a fat-soluble antioxidant that inserts into cell membranes and neutralizes reactive oxygen species before they can propagate lipid peroxidation chain reactions. Because red blood cell membranes are especially rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids and constantly exposed to oxidative stress, vitamin E is particularly important for protecting them from oxidative hemolysis, which is why deficiency can present with a hemolytic anemia.

incorrectas.A: Vitamin A functions mainly in the visual cycle (as retinal, a component of rhodopsin) and in epithelial cell differentiation, not as the primary membrane antioxidant protecting red blood cells from oxidative damage.
incorrectas.B: Vitamin K's main role is as a cofactor for γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X in the liver, a function related to coagulation, not to antioxidant protection of cell membranes.
incorrectas.C: Vitamin C is a water-soluble antioxidant that works in the aqueous compartments of cells and plasma (and helps regenerate oxidized vitamin E), but it is vitamin E, being lipid-soluble, that specifically protects lipid membranes like those of red blood cells.

preguntas.q: Vitamin E deficiency can cause muscle weakness, a feature that helps distinguish it from which other vitamin deficiency with a similar neurologic presentation (ataxia, loss of proprioception)?

e.correcta: Both vitamin E deficiency and vitamin B12 deficiency can damage the posterior columns and spinocerebellar tracts, producing ataxia and loss of proprioception/vibration sense that can look quite similar clinically. However, vitamin E deficiency additionally causes skeletal muscle weakness (from oxidative membrane damage in myocytes, since vitamin E protects lipid membranes from free radical injury), a feature not typically seen in B12 deficiency, which instead is marked by megaloblastic anemia and hypersegmented neutrophils.

incorrectas.B: Thiamine (B1) deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (ataxia, confusion, ophthalmoplegia) and dry beriberi peripheral neuropathy, but its classic distinguishing companion findings are confusion/confabulation and cardiovascular effects (wet beriberi), not muscle weakness contrasted against B12 deficiency's anemia.
incorrectas.C: Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia similar to B12 deficiency but classically does NOT cause neurologic symptoms at all, making it an even less fitting comparison for a muscle-weakness-plus-ataxia presentation.
incorrectas.D: Vitamin B6 deficiency causes peripheral neuropathy (often in patients on isoniazid) and sideroblastic anemia, but it is not the vitamin whose overlapping ataxia/proprioceptive-loss picture with vitamin E deficiency is classically tested; that comparison is specifically drawn with B12.

preguntas.q: A patient has ataxia and loss of vibration/position sense resembling subacute combined degeneration, but has a hemolytic (not megaloblastic) anemia and no hypersegmented neutrophils or elevated methylmalonic acid. Which deficiency best fits this picture?

e.correcta: Vitamin E deficiency can mimic the posterior column/spinocerebellar findings of B12 deficiency (ataxia, impaired proprioception and vibration sense) because both vitamins are important for neuronal membrane integrity, but vitamin E deficiency is distinguished by the absence of the hematologic markers of B12 deficiency — no megaloblastic anemia, no hypersegmented neutrophils, and no elevated methylmalonic acid — and instead may cause hemolytic anemia from unchecked oxidative damage to red cell membranes, plus skeletal muscle weakness that B12 deficiency does not typically cause.

incorrectas.B: Folate deficiency produces the same megaloblastic anemia as B12 deficiency (elevated homocysteine, hypersegmented neutrophils) but characteristically lacks neurologic findings altogether, the opposite pattern from what is described here.
incorrectas.C: Vitamin B12 deficiency would be expected to show megaloblastic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils, and elevated methylmalonic acid alongside its neurologic findings — all of which are explicitly absent in this vignette, making B12 deficiency inconsistent with the description.
incorrectas.D: Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia) or dry beriberi neuropathy, but it does not produce the specific proprioceptive/vibratory loss pattern combined with hemolytic anemia that points to vitamin E deficiency.

preguntas.q: Vitamin K is also known by which of the following alternate names?

e.correcta: Vitamin K is also called phylloquinone (the plant-derived K1 form), as well as phytomenadione and phytonadione — names often encountered on medication labels for the injectable/oral form used clinically (e.g., given at birth or to reverse warfarin effect). Recognizing these synonyms is useful because vitamin K may appear under any of these names in pharmacy references or exam questions.

incorrectas.A: Retinol is the alcohol form of vitamin A, important for vision and epithelial differentiation, an entirely different vitamin from vitamin K.
incorrectas.C: Tocopherol is one of the chemical forms of vitamin E, the lipid-soluble antioxidant vitamin, unrelated to vitamin K's role in coagulation factor carboxylation.
incorrectas.D: Cobalamin is the chemical name for vitamin B12, the cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, a completely different vitamin from vitamin K.

preguntas.q: Vitamin K is synthesized endogenously by which source, in addition to being obtained from the diet?

e.correcta: Colonic (gut) bacteria synthesize a meaningful portion of the vitamin K (menaquinone, K2 form) that humans use, supplementing dietary intake of phylloquinone (K1) from leafy green vegetables. This is clinically important because prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotic use can wipe out these bacteria and precipitate or worsen vitamin K deficiency, and it is also why newborns — whose gut has not yet been colonized — are at particular risk and receive a vitamin K injection at birth.

incorrectas.A: Hepatocytes are where vitamin K is used as a cofactor by γ-glutamyl carboxylase to activate clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, but the liver does not synthesize vitamin K itself; it depends on dietary and bacterial sources.
incorrectas.C: Skin keratinocytes synthesize vitamin D (from 7-dehydrocholesterol) upon UV exposure, not vitamin K, so this is a distractor drawn from a different fat-soluble vitamin's synthesis pathway.
incorrectas.D: Renal tubular cells perform the 1α-hydroxylation step that activates vitamin D to calcitriol, again a vitamin D–related function, not a source of vitamin K production.

preguntas.q: Why is an injection of vitamin K routinely given to newborns shortly after birth?

o.A: To prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn

e.correcta: Newborns are relatively vitamin K deficient because vitamin K crosses the placenta poorly, breast milk contains very little of it, hepatic stores at birth are low, and the newborn gut has not yet been colonized by the bacteria that normally contribute to vitamin K synthesis. Without adequate γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, infants are at risk for hemorrhagic disease of the newborn (bleeding, including intracranial hemorrhage), so a single intramuscular vitamin K injection is given prophylactically at birth to prevent this.

incorrectas.B: Neonatal jaundice results from immature hepatic bilirubin glucuronidation and increased red cell turnover, a bilirubin-handling issue unrelated to vitamin K–dependent clotting factor synthesis.
incorrectas.C: Lung surfactant maturation depends on surfactant protein and phospholipid production by type II pneumocytes, promoted by factors like antenatal corticosteroids, not by vitamin K.
incorrectas.D: Neural tube defects are prevented by adequate maternal folate (folic acid) intake before and during early pregnancy, a completely different vitamin and mechanism from the coagulation factor role of vitamin K.

preguntas.q: Human breast milk is a poor source of which vitamin, making exclusively breastfed neonates dependent on an intramuscular injection at birth to prevent hemorrhagic complications?

e.correcta: Breast milk contains very little vitamin K, and newborns also have sterile guts (no colonic bacteria yet to synthesize vitamin K2) and immature hepatic clotting factor synthesis. This combination leaves exclusively breastfed infants at risk for hemorrhagic disease of the newborn, which is why a single intramuscular dose of vitamin K is given routinely at birth to activate the gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X.

incorrectas.A: Vitamin D is also relatively low in breast milk and infants are commonly supplemented for it, but its deficiency causes rickets and hypocalcemia, not the bleeding diathesis described here, so it is not the vitamin tied to the birth injection for hemorrhage prevention.
incorrectas.C: Vitamin B12 deficiency in breastfed infants occurs almost exclusively when the mother is severely B12-deficient (e.g., strict vegan diet), and it produces megaloblastic anemia and neurologic findings rather than a bleeding tendency at birth.
incorrectas.D: Vitamin C is present in adequate amounts in breast milk, and its deficiency causes scurvy (poor collagen cross-linking, gum bleeding, corkscrew hairs) rather than the coagulation factor deficiency that prompts routine neonatal prophylaxis.

preguntas.q: A newborn who did not receive vitamin K prophylaxis develops bleeding from the umbilical stump, GI tract, and circumcision site on day 3 of life. What is this classic presentation called?

e.correcta: Hemorrhagic disease of the newborn results from insufficient vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, so the infant cannot generate a stable fibrin clot. This manifests as diffuse bleeding from multiple sites — umbilicus, GI tract, circumcision or venipuncture sites — rather than a localized process, and it is prevented by early intramuscular vitamin K administration, which restores normal carboxylation and coagulation factor function.

incorrectas.B: Thrombosis is the opposite problem — it results from a procoagulant or antithrombotic deficiency (e.g., protein C/S deficiency), not from impaired synthesis of active clotting factors as seen with vitamin K deficiency.
incorrectas.A: Hemolytic anemia reflects red cell destruction (e.g., ABO/Rh incompatibility, G6PD deficiency) and presents with jaundice and anemia, not the multi-site bleeding from failure of the coagulation cascade seen in vitamin K deficiency.
incorrectas.D: A purely petechial rash without active bleeding would suggest a platelet-number or platelet-function problem (e.g., neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia) rather than the deep tissue and mucosal hemorrhage caused by a clotting factor deficiency.

preguntas.q: Which coagulation parameter typically remains normal in vitamin K deficiency, helping distinguish it from vitamin C deficiency (scurvy), which impairs collagen-dependent vascular integrity?

e.correcta: Bleeding time reflects platelet plug formation and vascular integrity, both of which are intact in vitamin K deficiency because the defect lies purely in the gamma-carboxylation of soluble clotting factors, not in platelets or vessel walls. This is a key distinguishing point from scurvy, where defective collagen synthesis weakens capillary walls and produces abnormal bleeding time and easy bruising despite a normal coagulation cascade.

incorrectas.A: PT (prothrombin time) is prolonged in vitamin K deficiency because factors II, VII, IX, and X (which PT/the extrinsic pathway is especially sensitive to via factor VII) require vitamin K-dependent carboxylation to function.
incorrectas.C: PTT (partial thromboplastin time) is also prolonged in vitamin K deficiency since the intrinsic pathway factors IX and X are likewise vitamin K-dependent, so both PT and PTT rise together rather than staying normal.
incorrectas.D: INR is a standardized derivative of the PT and is therefore elevated in vitamin K deficiency for the same reason PT is prolonged — impaired synthesis of functional factor VII and the other vitamin K-dependent factors.

preguntas.q: Which coagulation studies are prolonged in vitamin K deficiency, reflecting impaired carboxylation of both extrinsic and intrinsic pathway clotting factors?

e.correcta: Vitamin K is required for the gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, and X (as well as proteins C and S). Because factor VII (extrinsic pathway, measured by PT) and factors IX/X (intrinsic pathway, measured by PTT) are both affected, vitamin K deficiency prolongs both PT and PTT, unlike a selective factor VII deficiency or early warfarin effect, which initially prolongs PT alone due to factor VII's short half-life.

incorrectas.A: PT alone being prolonged would suggest an isolated extrinsic pathway problem, such as early warfarin therapy or isolated factor VII deficiency, before the intrinsic pathway factors are meaningfully depleted — not full vitamin K deficiency, which affects both pathways.
incorrectas.B: Neither test being prolonged would only occur before vitamin K stores are exhausted or in a purely platelet-mediated bleeding disorder; established vitamin K deficiency reliably prolongs both PT and PTT.
incorrectas.C: PTT alone being prolonged points toward an intrinsic pathway defect such as hemophilia (factor VIII or IX deficiency) or heparin effect, which spares the extrinsic pathway and factor VII, unlike vitamin K deficiency.

preguntas.q: Vitamin K deficiency can develop in adults after prolonged use of which class of medications?

e.correcta: Colonic bacteria synthesize a substantial portion of the body's vitamin K2 (menaquinone), supplementing dietary vitamin K1 intake. Prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotic use wipes out this gut flora, reducing endogenous vitamin K production and unmasking or worsening deficiency, particularly in patients with poor oral intake or malabsorption who depend more heavily on the bacterial contribution.

incorrectas.A: Proton pump inhibitors reduce gastric acid and can impair absorption of vitamin B12, calcium, and iron over the long term, but they do not disrupt colonic bacterial synthesis of vitamin K the way antibiotics do.
incorrectas.C: Loop diuretics act on the renal thick ascending limb to promote sodium and water excretion; they have no meaningful effect on gut flora or vitamin K metabolism.
incorrectas.D: Corticosteroids cause metabolic effects like hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, and immunosuppression, but they do not eliminate the intestinal bacteria responsible for endogenous vitamin K synthesis.

preguntas.q: Which trio of vitamins functions primarily as antioxidants, neutralizing free radicals and protecting cell membranes and tissues from oxidative damage?

e.correcta: Vitamins A, C, and E each scavenge reactive oxygen species through distinct mechanisms — vitamin E (a lipid-soluble molecule embedded in cell membranes) terminates lipid peroxidation chain reactions, vitamin C regenerates oxidized vitamin E and directly scavenges water-soluble radicals, and vitamin A (as beta-carotene and retinoids) also quenches singlet oxygen. Together they form a coordinated antioxidant defense system that limits oxidative damage to membranes, proteins, and DNA.

incorrectas.A: Vitamin B6, B12, and folate are essential cofactors in one-carbon metabolism and amino acid/nucleotide synthesis (e.g., homocysteine remethylation), not in neutralizing free radicals.
incorrectas.B: Vitamin D regulates calcium/phosphate homeostasis, vitamin K enables gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors, and B1 (thiamine) is a cofactor for decarboxylation reactions like pyruvate dehydrogenase — none of these three primarily function as antioxidants.
incorrectas.D: Vitamins B2 (riboflavin), B3 (niacin), and B5 (pantothenic acid) are precursors of the redox cofactors FAD, NAD, and coenzyme A respectively, supporting metabolic redox reactions, but they are not themselves the classic free-radical-scavenging antioxidant vitamins.

preguntas.q: Which trace mineral is a required cofactor for the catalytic activity of more than 100 different enzymes in the body?

e.correcta: Zinc is incorporated into the active sites of an enormous range of enzymes — including carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, DNA and RNA polymerases, alcohol dehydrogenase, and superoxide dismutase — stabilizing protein structure or directly participating in catalysis. Because it touches so many pathways, from nucleic acid synthesis to antioxidant defense, zinc deficiency produces a broad clinical picture including impaired wound healing, immune dysfunction, and dermatitis.

incorrectas.A: Copper is a cofactor for a smaller, more specific set of enzymes such as cytochrome c oxidase, lysyl oxidase, and ceruloplasmin, and its deficiency causes distinct findings like anemia and connective tissue fragility, not the broad 100+ enzyme dependency attributed to zinc.
incorrectas.C: Selenium is incorporated into a limited number of selenoproteins, most notably glutathione peroxidase, contributing to antioxidant defense, but it does not have the same breadth of enzymatic cofactor roles as zinc.
incorrectas.D: Manganese is a cofactor for enzymes like mitochondrial superoxide dismutase and pyruvate carboxylase, but its enzymatic footprint is far narrower than zinc's role across DNA/RNA synthesis, metabolism, and structural zinc-finger proteins.

preguntas.q: Zinc is essential for the formation of which structural motif commonly found in DNA-binding transcription factors?

e.correcta: Zinc fingers are protein domains in which a zinc ion is coordinated by cysteine and/or histidine residues, folding a small loop of amino acids into a rigid finger-like structure that inserts into the major groove of DNA. This motif is found in many transcription factors (including steroid hormone receptors) and allows sequence-specific DNA binding, which is why adequate zinc status is important for normal gene regulation.

incorrectas.B: Helix-turn-helix motifs achieve DNA binding through two alpha helices connected by a short turn, a structural strategy that does not require a metal ion cofactor the way zinc fingers do.
incorrectas.A: Leucine zippers mediate protein dimerization through a repeating leucine motif on adjacent alpha helices (as in bZIP transcription factors), a mechanism built from hydrophobic interactions rather than metal coordination.
incorrectas.D: Beta barrels are structural motifs formed by beta strands arranged in a closed, barrel-like sheet, commonly seen in membrane channel proteins, and are unrelated to zinc-dependent DNA-binding domains.

preguntas.q: Zinc deficiency delays wound healing primarily because zinc is a required cofactor for which enzyme involved in remodeling type III collagen into type I collagen at the wound site?

e.correcta: During wound healing, the initial type III collagen scaffold must be broken down and replaced with stronger type I collagen for proper scar maturation. Collagenase, a zinc-dependent matrix metalloproteinase, carries out this remodeling step, so zinc deficiency impairs collagen turnover and delays wound closure and tensile strength recovery.

incorrectas.A: Prolyl hydroxylase hydroxylates proline residues during collagen synthesis and requires vitamin C (and iron) as a cofactor, not zinc — its deficiency (as in scurvy) causes weak, poorly cross-linked collagen rather than a remodeling defect.
incorrectas.C: Lysyl hydroxylase similarly hydroxylates lysine residues in collagen synthesis using vitamin C as a cofactor, contributing to collagen cross-linking rather than the zinc-dependent breakdown of type III collagen during remodeling.
incorrectas.D: Alkaline phosphatase is important in bone mineralization and is used clinically as a marker of osteoblastic activity or biliary/liver disease, but it is not the zinc-dependent enzyme responsible for collagen remodeling in wound healing.

preguntas.q: An infant presents with periorificial and acral dermatitis, alopecia, and diarrhea due to an autosomal recessive defect in intestinal uptake of a trace mineral. What is the diagnosis?

e.correcta: Acrodermatitis enteropathica is caused by a mutation in the SLC39A4 gene, which encodes an intestinal zinc transporter, leading to impaired zinc absorption. The resulting zinc deficiency produces the classic triad of periorificial/acral dermatitis, alopecia, and diarrhea, and it responds dramatically to zinc supplementation, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

incorrectas.A: Pellagra results from niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency and classically causes the three D's — dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia — but it is not caused by a hereditary zinc transporter defect and typically involves sun-exposed skin rather than the periorificial/acral distribution described.
incorrectas.B: Biotin deficiency causes dermatitis, alopecia, and neurologic symptoms, often related to raw egg white (avidin) ingestion or genetic biotinidase deficiency, but it is a distinct cofactor deficiency unrelated to the zinc transporter defect in acrodermatitis enteropathica.
incorrectas.D: Essential fatty acid deficiency (e.g., linoleic acid deficiency) causes scaly dermatitis and impaired growth but is not linked to an autosomal recessive zinc transport defect or the specific periorificial/acral pattern described in this vignette.

preguntas.q: Zinc deficiency, which is common in chronic alcoholics, may predispose to which hepatic complication?

e.correcta: Chronic alcohol use both reduces dietary zinc intake and increases urinary zinc excretion, producing a state of relative zinc deficiency. Since zinc supports antioxidant defenses (e.g., as a cofactor for superoxide dismutase) and normal hepatocyte regeneration, its deficiency compounds alcohol-related oxidative liver injury and fibrosis, contributing to the progression toward cirrhosis in chronic alcoholics.

incorrectas.A: Wilson disease is a genetic disorder of copper accumulation due to defective ATP7B-mediated biliary copper excretion, an entirely separate mechanism from acquired zinc deficiency in alcoholics (in fact, zinc supplementation is used to treat Wilson disease by blocking copper absorption).
incorrectas.B: Budd-Chiari syndrome is caused by hepatic vein thrombosis, typically from an underlying hypercoagulable state, and is unrelated to trace mineral deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy results from a mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation defect (often LCHAD deficiency) that becomes apparent during pregnancy, a mechanism unrelated to alcohol-induced zinc deficiency.

preguntas.q: The peripheral edema seen in kwashiorkor results from decreased plasma oncotic pressure, which is a direct consequence of severe deficiency of which nutrient?

e.correcta: Kwashiorkor results from severe dietary protein deficiency despite often-adequate total caloric intake. Without sufficient amino acids, the liver cannot synthesize enough albumin, and low plasma albumin reduces the oncotic pressure that normally keeps fluid within the vasculature, allowing fluid to shift into the interstitium and produce the characteristic edema and swollen belly.

incorrectas.A: Carbohydrate intake is often relatively preserved in kwashiorkor (distinguishing it from marasmus, where total caloric intake including carbohydrates is severely restricted), so isolated carbohydrate deficiency does not explain the oncotic pressure drop.
incorrectas.C: Sodium deficiency would tend to cause hyponatremia and volume depletion rather than the low-oncotic-pressure edema seen in kwashiorkor, which is driven by low intravascular protein content, not electrolyte imbalance.
incorrectas.D: Fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies (A, D, E, K) can accompany malnutrition and contribute to other findings like skin changes or bleeding, but they do not directly lower plasma oncotic pressure, which is governed by circulating protein concentration.

preguntas.q: The fatty liver seen in kwashiorkor develops because inadequate protein intake impairs hepatic synthesis of which molecules needed to export triglycerides from hepatocytes?

e.correcta: Triglycerides are packaged into VLDL particles for export from the liver, and this packaging requires apolipoproteins (such as apoB-100), which are proteins that must be synthesized using dietary amino acids. In kwashiorkor, severe protein deficiency limits apolipoprotein production, so triglycerides accumulate inside hepatocytes instead of being exported, producing the fatty, enlarged liver characteristic of the disease.

incorrectas.A: Bile acids are synthesized from cholesterol and are involved in fat digestion and absorption in the intestine, not in packaging triglycerides for export from the liver, so their synthesis is not the mechanism behind kwashiorkor's fatty liver.
incorrectas.B: Albumin synthesis is also reduced in kwashiorkor and explains the hypoalbuminemia and edema, but it is not the protein responsible for exporting hepatic triglycerides as VLDL — that role belongs to the apolipoproteins.
incorrectas.D: Lipoprotein lipase acts extracellularly on capillary endothelium to hydrolyze triglycerides within circulating lipoproteins for tissue uptake; it does not function inside the hepatocyte to enable VLDL export, so its deficiency is not the cause of kwashiorkor's fatty liver.

preguntas.q: A young child from a famine-affected region presents with a swollen abdomen, peripheral edema, and a flaky skin rash despite seemingly adequate total caloric intake. Which malnutrition syndrome does this describe?

e.correcta: Kwashiorkor classically occurs when a child's diet is calorically sufficient (often carbohydrate-heavy, as after weaning onto a starchy diet) but severely deficient in protein. The resulting hypoalbuminemia causes the swollen, fluid-filled abdomen and peripheral edema, while impaired skin and hair protein turnover produces the flaky, depigmented 'flaky paint' dermatitis — a distinct picture from generalized caloric starvation.

incorrectas.A: Marasmus results from severe deficiency of total calories, including protein, producing generalized wasting, loss of subcutaneous fat, and a thin, wizened appearance without the edema or swollen belly seen in kwashiorkor.
incorrectas.B: Pellagra is a niacin (B3) deficiency causing dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia, typically with a photosensitive rash in sun-exposed areas, not the classic edema and abdominal swelling from hypoalbuminemia.
incorrectas.C: Beriberi results from thiamine (B1) deficiency and presents with either high-output cardiac failure and edema (wet beriberi) or peripheral neuropathy (dry beriberi), a different mechanism than the protein-deficiency-driven hypoalbuminemia of kwashiorkor.

preguntas.q: Which protein-energy malnutrition syndrome is characterized by severe overall caloric deficiency, producing emaciation, muscle wasting, and loss of subcutaneous fat, generally without significant edema?

e.correcta: Marasmus results from a global deficiency of calories, including both protein and non-protein energy sources, forcing the body to break down muscle and fat stores for fuel. Because total protein intake is proportionally reduced along with calories, plasma albumin is often relatively preserved compared to kwashiorkor, so patients present with a wasted, emaciated appearance rather than the edema seen when protein deficiency outpaces caloric deficiency.

incorrectas.A: Kwashiorkor occurs with relatively preserved caloric (often carbohydrate) intake but severe isolated protein deficiency, producing hypoalbuminemia, edema, and a swollen abdomen — the opposite pattern from the global caloric deprivation of marasmus.
incorrectas.C: Scurvy is caused by vitamin C deficiency impairing collagen synthesis, leading to bleeding gums, poor wound healing, and corkscrew hairs, a connective tissue problem rather than global caloric/protein wasting.
incorrectas.D: Pellagra results from niacin deficiency and causes dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia; it is a specific vitamin deficiency syndrome, not the generalized energy-wasting picture of marasmus.

preguntas.q: The neurologic manifestations of vitamin B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration) result from abnormal formation of which structure?

e.correcta: Vitamin B12 is required for the methylmalonyl-CoA mutase reaction that converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. When B12 is deficient, methylmalonyl-CoA (and its precursor propionyl-CoA derivatives) accumulates and gets incorporated into abnormal fatty acids that are used to synthesize myelin, producing structurally defective myelin sheaths. This underlies the demyelination of the dorsal columns, corticospinal tracts, and peripheral nerves seen in subacute combined degeneration, causing the combination of loss of vibration/proprioception, spasticity, and peripheral neuropathy.

incorrectas.A: Axonal microtubule and axonal transport defects are more characteristic of certain toxic or genetic neuropathies (e.g., vincristine toxicity), not the specific myelin abnormality driving B12 deficiency's neurologic syndrome.
incorrectas.B: Neurotransmitter vesicle formation and release are affected in disorders like botulism or Lambert-Eaton syndrome, which impair synaptic transmission, a mechanism distinct from the myelin synthesis defect of B12 deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Schwann cell nuclei themselves are not structurally abnormal in B12 deficiency; the defect lies in the biochemical composition of the myelin these cells produce, not in the Schwann cell nucleus.

preguntas.q: Which class of enzyme, exemplified by phosphofructokinase, catalyzes the transfer of a phosphate group from a high-energy donor molecule such as ATP onto a substrate?

e.correcta: Kinases use ATP (or another high-energy phosphate donor) as the phosphate source and transfer that phosphate group directly onto a substrate, often to regulate the substrate's activity or commit it to a metabolic pathway — as phosphofructokinase does in committing fructose-6-phosphate to glycolysis. Recognizing this ATP-dependent phosphate transfer is key to distinguishing kinases from other phosphate-modifying enzymes on exams.

incorrectas.A: Phosphatases do the opposite of kinases — they remove a phosphate group from a substrate via hydrolysis, releasing free inorganic phosphate rather than transferring one from ATP.
incorrectas.C: Phosphorylases add an inorganic phosphate group onto a substrate (such as cleaving glycogen), but they do so without consuming ATP, using free phosphate directly instead of transferring it from a high-energy donor.
incorrectas.D: Mutases relocate a functional group from one position to another within the same molecule; they do not add, remove, or transfer phosphate between separate molecules the way kinases do.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme class, exemplified by glycogen phosphorylase, adds an inorganic phosphate group onto a substrate without consuming ATP?

e.correcta: Phosphorylases cleave a bond in their substrate using free inorganic phosphate (phosphorolysis) rather than water (hydrolysis) or ATP-derived phosphate. Glycogen phosphorylase, for example, breaks the alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds of glycogen, releasing glucose-1-phosphate directly — an energetically efficient way to begin glycogen breakdown since the phosphate bond is created without spending ATP.

incorrectas.A: Kinases transfer a phosphate group from a high-energy donor like ATP onto a substrate, consuming ATP in the process, unlike phosphorylases, which use free inorganic phosphate without any ATP cost.
incorrectas.B: Phosphatases remove phosphate groups from substrates through hydrolysis, the reverse chemical direction from phosphorylases, which add phosphate onto their substrate.
incorrectas.D: Synthetases catalyze bond formation between two molecules using energy from ATP hydrolysis (as opposed to synthases, which do not require ATP), a different chemistry from the phosphate-addition reaction performed by phosphorylases.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme class, exemplified by fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, removes a phosphate group from a substrate?

e.correcta: Phosphatases catalyze the hydrolytic removal of a phosphate group from a substrate, releasing free inorganic phosphate. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase performs this exact reaction as a key regulated step in gluconeogenesis, reversing the kinase-catalyzed phosphorylation from glycolysis — a classic example of how kinase/phosphatase pairs can push a pathway in opposite directions at the same metabolic step.

incorrectas.A: Kinases perform the opposite chemistry — they add a phosphate group onto a substrate by transferring it from a high-energy donor like ATP, rather than removing one.
incorrectas.C: Phosphorylases also add phosphate onto a substrate (using free inorganic phosphate rather than ATP), which is the reverse direction of what a phosphatase does.
incorrectas.D: Carboxylases add a CO2 group onto a substrate, typically with biotin as a cofactor (as in pyruvate carboxylase), a completely different chemical modification from phosphate removal.

preguntas.q: Enzymes bearing the suffix '-dehydrogenase,' such as pyruvate dehydrogenase, catalyze which general type of chemical reaction?

e.correcta: Dehydrogenases catalyze redox reactions by removing (or adding) hydrogen atoms/electrons from a substrate and transferring them to a coenzyme acceptor such as NAD+ or FAD, generating NADH or FADH2. Pyruvate dehydrogenase, for instance, oxidatively decarboxylates pyruvate to acetyl-CoA while reducing NAD+ to NADH, linking glycolysis to the citric acid cycle and illustrating how dehydrogenase-driven redox chemistry captures energy as reduced electron carriers.

incorrectas.A: Phosphate transfer reactions, such as moving a phosphate from ATP to a substrate, are the domain of kinases, not dehydrogenases, which instead move electrons/hydrogens to redox cofactors.
incorrectas.B: Carboxylation reactions add a CO2 group onto a substrate and are catalyzed by carboxylases (often biotin-dependent), a distinct chemistry from the electron-transfer reactions performed by dehydrogenases.
incorrectas.D: Isomerization reactions rearrange atoms within a molecule without changing its overall formula and are catalyzed by isomerases (including mutases), not by dehydrogenases, which specifically mediate oxidation-reduction chemistry.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme class, exemplified by tyrosine hydroxylase, adds a hydroxyl group (-OH) onto its substrate?

e.correcta: Hydroxylases catalyze the addition of a hydroxyl group to a substrate, typically using molecular oxygen and often requiring cofactors such as tetrahydrobiopterin. Tyrosine hydroxylase performs the rate-limiting step of catecholamine synthesis by hydroxylating tyrosine to L-DOPA, illustrating how this enzyme class introduces new functional groups that are essential for downstream biosynthetic pathways.

incorrectas.A: Carboxylases add a CO2 group to a substrate (usually with biotin as a cofactor), which is a distinct chemical addition from the hydroxyl group added by hydroxylases.
incorrectas.B: Mutases relocate a functional group from one position to another within the same molecule rather than introducing an entirely new hydroxyl group from an external source.
incorrectas.C: Dehydrogenases catalyze oxidation-reduction reactions by transferring hydrogens/electrons to cofactors like NAD+ or FAD, a mechanistically different process from the direct addition of a hydroxyl group performed by hydroxylases.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme class, exemplified by pyruvate carboxylase, transfers a CO2 group onto a substrate and typically requires biotin as a cofactor?

e.correcta: Carboxylases add a carboxyl (CO2) group onto a substrate, and because activating CO2 for this transfer requires biotin as a covalently bound cofactor, biotin deficiency impairs the function of enzymes like pyruvate carboxylase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, and propionyl-CoA carboxylase. Pyruvate carboxylase specifically converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate, replenishing the citric acid cycle and serving as the first committed step of gluconeogenesis.

incorrectas.A: Decarboxylases catalyze the opposite reaction, removing a carboxyl group (releasing CO2) from a substrate, as seen in reactions like amino acid decarboxylation to form neurotransmitters, rather than adding CO2 the way carboxylases do.
incorrectas.C: Hydroxylases add a hydroxyl group to a substrate using molecular oxygen, a different chemical modification and cofactor requirement than the biotin-dependent CO2 transfer performed by carboxylases.
incorrectas.D: Mutases relocate an existing functional group within the same molecule rather than adding a new CO2 group from an external source, and they do not require biotin as a cofactor.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme class, exemplified by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, relocates a functional group from one position to another within the same molecule?

e.correcta: Mutases catalyze intramolecular rearrangements, moving a functional group to a different position on the same molecule rather than adding, removing, or transferring it between separate molecules. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, a vitamin B12-dependent enzyme, relocates a carbonyl-CoA group to convert methylmalonyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA, feeding odd-chain fatty acid and branched-chain amino acid metabolites into the citric acid cycle — which is why B12 deficiency causes methylmalonic acid buildup.

incorrectas.A: Kinases transfer a phosphate group from an external high-energy donor like ATP onto a substrate, an intermolecular phosphate transfer rather than the intramolecular rearrangement performed by mutases.
incorrectas.B: Hydroxylases introduce a new hydroxyl group onto a substrate from molecular oxygen, adding a functional group from an external source rather than repositioning one that is already present within the molecule.
incorrectas.D: Carboxylases add a CO2 group onto a substrate using biotin as a cofactor, which is the addition of a new group from an external source, unlike the internal relocation of an existing group carried out by mutases.

preguntas.q: Which heavy metal poisons glycolysis by acting as a phosphate analog that substitutes for inorganic phosphate at the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step, forming an unstable product that spontaneously hydrolyzes and yields zero net ATP?

e.correcta: Arsenite inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase (and other alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenases) by binding lipoic acid, while arsenate acts as a structural analog of inorganic phosphate and gets incorporated into 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate's normal position, forming 1-arseno-3-phosphoglycerate. This arsenate-containing compound is unstable and hydrolyzes spontaneously to 3-phosphoglycerate and free arsenate without ever generating ATP, so the substrate-level phosphorylation step that would normally produce ATP is short-circuited — net ATP yield from glycolysis becomes zero.

incorrectas.A: Lead poisoning classically inhibits ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase in heme synthesis, producing microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling, a mechanism entirely distinct from arsenate's phosphate-mimicking disruption of glycolysis.
incorrectas.B: Cyanide blocks cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) in the electron transport chain, halting oxidative phosphorylation and forcing cells into anaerobic metabolism, rather than directly sabotaging the substrate-level phosphorylation step of glycolysis itself.
incorrectas.C: Mercury toxicity primarily damages the kidneys and nervous system by binding sulfhydryl groups on various proteins, but it is not the classic phosphate-analog mechanism that specifically abolishes ATP yield during glycolysis.

preguntas.q: NAD+ is generally used as an electron carrier in which type of metabolic process?

e.correcta: NAD+ predominantly functions in catabolic (breakdown) pathways, accepting electrons and hydrogen as substrates are oxidized — for example in glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and fatty acid oxidation — and becoming reduced to NADH, which then carries those high-energy electrons to the electron transport chain to drive ATP synthesis. This is a useful mnemonic contrast with NADPH, which instead supplies reducing power for anabolic (biosynthetic) pathways like fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis.

incorrectas.A: Anabolic (biosynthetic) reactions typically rely on NADPH rather than NAD+ as the reducing agent — NADPH provides the electrons needed to build complex molecules like fatty acids, cholesterol, and nucleotides.
incorrectas.C: DNA replication depends on DNA polymerases, primers, and deoxynucleotide triphosphates, not directly on NAD+ as an electron carrier; NAD+ is not part of the core replication machinery.
incorrectas.D: Protein synthesis relies on ribosomes, tRNAs, and GTP hydrolysis for peptide bond formation and translocation, not on NAD+-mediated redox chemistry.

preguntas.q: NADPH is generally used as an electron carrier (donor of reducing equivalents) in which type of metabolic process?

e.correcta: NADPH, generated mainly by the HMP shunt (and to a lesser extent by malic enzyme and isocitrate dehydrogenase), supplies the reducing equivalents needed to build complex molecules from simpler ones — most notably fatty acid and steroid/cholesterol synthesis, and it also regenerates reduced glutathione for antioxidant defense. Because biosynthesis (anabolism) requires adding electrons/hydrogens to relatively oxidized precursors, cells keep a large pool of NADPH dedicated to this reductive biosynthetic work, separate from the NADH pool used for energy extraction.

incorrectas.A: Catabolic processes (like glycolysis and the TCA cycle) break down fuels and generate NADH and FADH2, which feed electrons into the electron transport chain to make ATP — this is the opposite direction (oxidative, energy-releasing) from what NADPH is used for.
incorrectas.C: Amphibolic pathways (like the TCA cycle) serve both catabolic and anabolic roles simultaneously, but the cycle's electron carrier is NADH, not NADPH, so this doesn't describe NADPH's role.
incorrectas.D: Anaplerotic reactions replenish TCA cycle intermediates (e.g., pyruvate carboxylase making oxaloacetate) and are not defined by electron carrier usage at all, making this an unrelated category to NADPH's biosynthetic reducing role.

preguntas.q: Which electron carrier serves as the reducing agent for the cytochrome P-450 mixed-function oxidase system in the liver?

e.correcta: Hepatic cytochrome P-450 enzymes use NADPH-cytochrome P-450 reductase to shuttle electrons from NADPH into the heme iron of the P-450 enzyme, enabling it to activate molecular oxygen and hydroxylate lipophilic substrates (drugs, steroids, xenobiotics) as phase I metabolism. This is a classic example of NADPH's broader role as the cell's dedicated reductive/detoxification electron donor, distinct from NADH's role in catabolic ATP generation.

incorrectas.A: NADH is the electron carrier generated by catabolic pathways (glycolysis, TCA cycle) and feeds directly into Complex I of the electron transport chain to drive ATP synthesis; it is not the cofactor used by microsomal P-450 reductase.
incorrectas.B: FADH2 similarly is a catabolic electron carrier that donates electrons to Complex II/the ETC for oxidative phosphorylation, not a reagent used in the liver's drug-metabolizing hydroxylation reactions.
incorrectas.D: FMN is a flavin cofactor found within certain flavoproteins (including as a component of some reductases and Complex I), but the electron donor that actually drives the P-450 system's chemistry is NADPH, not free FMN.

preguntas.q: What high-energy moiety does ATP carry in its activated form?

e.correcta: ATP's biological utility comes from its terminal high-energy phosphoanhydride bonds; transferring a phosphoryl group to a substrate (phosphorylation) or releasing it as inorganic phosphate drives countless reactions, from kinase-mediated substrate activation to muscle contraction and active transport. This is why ATP is classified among First Aid's 'activated carriers' as the universal phosphoryl group donor, distinct from carriers that shuttle electrons, acyl groups, or one-carbon units.

incorrectas.A: Acyl groups are carried by coenzyme A and lipoamide (e.g., acetyl-CoA), not by ATP — ATP can be used to activate a fatty acid into a CoA thioester, but ATP itself is not the acyl carrier.
incorrectas.B: Electrons are carried by NADH, NADPH, and FADH2; ATP does not participate in redox chemistry as an electron carrier, it is a phosphate-group energy currency instead.
incorrectas.C: One-carbon units are carried by tetrahydrofolate (and methyl groups specifically by SAM), a chemically distinct role from ATP's phosphoryl-group transfer function.

preguntas.q: NADH, NADPH, and FADH2 all function as activated carriers of which entity?

e.correcta: NADH, NADPH, and FADH2 are all dinucleotide cofactors that accept a hydride (effectively a pair of electrons plus a proton) during oxidation reactions in metabolism, becoming 'reduced' carriers of electrons. NADH and FADH2 later donate those electrons to the electron transport chain to generate a proton gradient for ATP synthesis, while NADPH instead donates its electrons for reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defense — same chemical function (electron carrier), different downstream purpose.

incorrectas.B: Phosphoryl groups are the currency carried by ATP, not by the NAD(P)H/FADH2 family, which are redox (electron) carriers rather than phosphate-transfer molecules.
incorrectas.C: Acyl groups are carried by CoA and lipoamide via thioester linkages, a completely different chemistry from the hydride-transfer redox reactions that define NAD(P)H and FADH2.
incorrectas.D: Aldehydes are carried by thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) during reactions like those catalyzed by pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase, not by the electron-carrying dinucleotides.

preguntas.q: Coenzyme A and lipoamide both serve as activated carriers of which chemical group?

e.correcta: Coenzyme A carries acyl groups via a high-energy thioester bond (e.g., forming acetyl-CoA, succinyl-CoA, fatty acyl-CoA), and lipoamide (lipoic acid attached to the E2 subunit of dehydrogenase complexes) also picks up and transfers acyl groups during oxidative decarboxylation reactions like those in pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Both are essential intermediates that funnel carbon skeletons into the TCA cycle or fatty acid metabolism as reactive acyl-thioester species.

incorrectas.A: One-carbon units are the domain of tetrahydrofolate, which carries formyl, methylene, and methenyl groups at various oxidation states — a distinct role from the acyl-group chemistry of CoA and lipoamide.
incorrectas.C: CO2 is carried by biotin during carboxylation reactions (e.g., pyruvate carboxylase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase), not by CoA or lipoamide, which handle acyl groups rather than a single-carbon gas.
incorrectas.D: Aldehydes are carried by thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), which works alongside lipoamide in the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex but performs a chemically different step — decarboxylating pyruvate to a hydroxyethyl-TPP intermediate before that group is handed off to lipoamide as an acyl group.

preguntas.q: Biotin functions as an activated carrier of which molecule during carboxylation reactions?

e.correcta: Biotin is covalently attached to carboxylase enzymes (like pyruvate carboxylase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase) and forms a carboxybiotin intermediate that temporarily holds and then transfers a CO2 molecule onto a substrate, adding a new carboxyl group. This is why biotin deficiency (rare, seen with excess raw egg white ingestion due to avidin binding biotin) impairs gluconeogenesis and fatty acid synthesis — both of which depend on biotin-mediated carboxylation steps.

incorrectas.B: Acyl groups are carried by CoA and lipoamide via thioester bonds, a different chemical handoff than biotin's carboxybiotin intermediate used for adding CO2 to a substrate.
incorrectas.C: Aldehydes are the province of thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), used in reactions like pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase, not in the carboxylation chemistry biotin performs.
incorrectas.D: Amino groups are transferred by aminotransferases using pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor, an entirely separate carrier system from biotin's CO2-carboxylation role.

preguntas.q: Tetrahydrofolate (THF) functions as an activated carrier for which chemical unit?

e.correcta: Tetrahydrofolate can carry one-carbon fragments at several different oxidation states — formyl, methenyl, methylene, and methyl groups — and shuttles them into reactions such as purine synthesis, thymidylate synthesis (dTMP), and formylation of initiator methionine. This versatility is what distinguishes THF from SAM, which carries only the fully reduced methyl group for biological methylation reactions.

incorrectas.A: Restricting THF to methyl groups only describes SAM's narrower role, not THF's — THF's biochemical importance actually comes from its ability to interconvert and donate one-carbon units at multiple oxidation states, most critically for thymidylate and purine synthesis.
incorrectas.B: Acyl groups are carried by CoA and lipoamide through thioester linkages, a completely different chemical function from THF's one-carbon transfer chemistry involving its N5 and N10 positions.
incorrectas.D: CO2 is specifically handled by biotin in carboxylation reactions; while THF does carry a formyl group (which is chemically related to a one-carbon unit derived from formate), it does not carry CO2 itself the way biotin does.

preguntas.q: S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) functions as an activated carrier of which group, used in reactions such as norepinephrine and phosphatidylcholine synthesis?

e.correcta: SAM is formed when methionine reacts with ATP, creating a high-energy sulfonium center that makes SAM an excellent methyl-group donor for methyltransferase reactions — including converting norepinephrine to epinephrine, phosphatidylethanolamine to phosphatidylcholine, and guanidinoacetate to creatine. After donating its methyl group, SAM becomes S-adenosylhomocysteine, which is then hydrolyzed to homocysteine and can be remethylated back to methionine using a methyl group from THF (via methionine synthase and B12), linking SAM's cycle tightly to folate metabolism.

incorrectas.B: One-carbon units at various oxidation states (formyl, methenyl, methylene) describe THF's broader carrying capacity, whereas SAM specifically donates only the fully reduced, single methyl group — a narrower but biologically critical role for methylation reactions.
incorrectas.C: Acyl groups are the domain of CoA and lipoamide, which form thioester bonds; SAM's chemistry instead centers on its reactive methyl-sulfonium bond, not acyl-group transfer.
incorrectas.D: Aldehydes are carried by thiamine pyrophosphate during reactions like those in the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, unrelated to SAM's role as the body's principal methyl donor.

preguntas.q: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), a cofactor for enzymes such as pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, functions as an activated carrier of which group?

e.correcta: TPP's reactive thiazole ring carbon forms a carbanion that attacks the carbonyl carbon of substrates like pyruvate, generating a covalent hydroxyethyl-TPP (an activated aldehyde-equivalent) intermediate after CO2 is released. This aldehyde-carrying step is essential in the multi-enzyme complexes of pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase, and transketolase — explaining why thiamine (B1) deficiency causes lactic acidosis and impairs energy metabolism, as seen in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and beriberi.

incorrectas.A: CO2 itself is carried by biotin in carboxylation reactions; TPP's job in the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is actually to catalyze the decarboxylation (release) of CO2 from pyruvate, generating the aldehyde-equivalent intermediate rather than carrying the CO2 onward.
incorrectas.B: Acyl groups are the acyl-thioester cargo of CoA and lipoamide; TPP hands its hydroxyethyl (aldehyde-derived) group off to lipoamide, which is what then becomes an acetyl group carried onward as acetyl-lipoamide/acetyl-CoA.
incorrectas.C: Electrons are carried by NADH, NADPH, and FADH2 in redox reactions; TPP's chemistry instead involves carbon-carbon bond formation/cleavage via its thiazole ring, not simple electron transfer.

preguntas.q: What is the most common mode of inheritance of pyruvate dehydrogenase (E1-alpha subunit) deficiency?

e.correcta: The gene encoding the E1-alpha subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is located on the X chromosome, making the most common form of this deficiency X-linked. Because of random X-inactivation (lyonization), heterozygous females can still express clinically significant disease depending on which X chromosome is silenced in affected tissues, giving the condition a quasi-dominant pattern in females even though it is fundamentally X-linked.

incorrectas.A: Autosomal recessive is the inheritance pattern for many other inborn errors of metabolism (like most urea cycle and glycogen storage diseases), but the E1-alpha subunit gene itself sits on the X chromosome, not an autosome, making this pattern incorrect for the most common PDH deficiency variant.
incorrectas.C: Autosomal dominant inheritance would require only one mutant autosomal allele to cause disease with each generation showing risk of transmission, but PDH deficiency's variable expression in females is explained by X-inactivation, not classic autosomal dominant transmission.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial (maternal) inheritance applies to diseases caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA itself (e.g., MELAS, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy); PDH deficiency, while affecting a mitochondrial enzyme complex, is caused by a nuclear (X-linked) gene defect, not a mitochondrial DNA mutation.

preguntas.q: In pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, accumulated pyruvate is redirected toward increased serum levels of which amino acid, starting in infancy?

e.correcta: When PDH cannot convert pyruvate to acetyl-CoA for entry into the TCA cycle, pyruvate backs up and is shunted toward alternative fates, including transamination by alanine aminotransferase (ALT), which adds an amino group from glutamate to pyruvate to form alanine. This produces the characteristic biochemical picture of elevated serum alanine (along with elevated lactate and pyruvate) presenting from infancy with neurologic dysfunction, since the brain is highly dependent on aerobic oxidation of glucose-derived pyruvate.

incorrectas.A: Glutamine is generated from glutamate via glutamine synthetase and functions as an ammonia-transport molecule and nitrogen donor in various pathways, but it is not the direct transamination product of accumulated pyruvate.
incorrectas.C: Glycine is a precursor for heme, purines, and glutathione, and is not derived from a buildup of pyruvate — its serum levels are not the classic finding in PDH deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Serine is synthesized from the glycolytic intermediate 3-phosphoglycerate and metabolically related to glycine, but it is not the amino acid classically elevated due to pyruvate transamination in PDH deficiency.

preguntas.q: Because patients with pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency cannot efficiently convert pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, dietary treatment focuses on increasing intake of which type of nutrients?

o.A: Ketogenic nutrients (high fat, or amino acids like lysine and leucine)

e.correcta: Because the PDH block prevents glucose-derived pyruvate from being efficiently used to generate acetyl-CoA, treatment bypasses this block by providing fuels that can be converted to acetyl-CoA or ketone bodies without needing PDH — namely dietary fat and the strictly/partially ketogenic amino acids lysine and leucine. This supplies the brain and other tissues with an alternative energy source (ketone bodies) that does not depend on the defective enzyme complex.

incorrectas.B: A high-carbohydrate (glucogenic) diet would actually worsen the problem, since it increases glucose flux into pyruvate that cannot be efficiently processed by the deficient PDH complex, exacerbating the lactic acidosis and pyruvate/alanine buildup.
incorrectas.C: A generic high-protein diet doesn't specifically address the metabolic block — only the ketogenic amino acids (lysine and leucine, which cannot be converted to glucose and instead feed into acetyl-CoA/ketone synthesis) are therapeutically useful, not protein intake as a whole.
incorrectas.D: A low-fat, high-carbohydrate diet is the opposite of what's needed — it would increase reliance on the pyruvate-to-acetyl-CoA step that is impaired, rather than providing the fat-derived acetyl-CoA and ketones the treatment aims to supply.

preguntas.q: Which amino acid serves as the substrate for nitric oxide synthase in the production of nitric oxide?

e.correcta: Nitric oxide synthase (NOS) oxidizes the guanidino nitrogen of arginine, converting it to citrulline and releasing nitric oxide (NO) as a byproduct, using NADPH and O2 as cosubstrates. NO then diffuses into adjacent vascular smooth muscle, activating guanylate cyclase to raise cGMP and cause vasodilation — a pathway targeted pharmacologically by nitrates and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, and disrupted in conditions of endothelial dysfunction.

incorrectas.B: Tyrosine is the precursor for catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) and thyroid hormone, a completely separate biosynthetic pathway from nitric oxide production.
incorrectas.A: Glutamine serves as a nitrogen shuttle and precursor for purine/pyrimidine synthesis and ammonia detoxification in the kidney, not as the direct substrate oxidized by nitric oxide synthase.
incorrectas.D: Glycine contributes to heme, purine, and glutathione synthesis, but it is not the amino acid whose guanidino group is oxidized to generate nitric oxide.

preguntas.q: Which amino acid, along with glycine and a methyl group from SAM, is a precursor in creatine synthesis?

e.correcta: Creatine synthesis begins when arginine transfers its amidino group to glycine to form guanidinoacetate, which is then methylated by SAM to yield creatine. Creatine (and its phosphorylated form, creatine phosphate) acts as a rapid-access energy buffer in skeletal muscle, regenerating ATP from ADP during short bursts of high-intensity activity — which is why creatine and its breakdown product creatinine are used clinically to assess muscle mass and renal function.

incorrectas.B: Glutamate is a precursor of GABA, glutathione, and participates broadly in amino acid transamination reactions, but it is not one of the two amino acids (arginine and glycine) that directly form the creatine backbone.
incorrectas.C: Histidine is decarboxylated to form histamine and participates in the histidine-buffering system, unrelated to the guanidinoacetate pathway that generates creatine.
incorrectas.D: Lysine, along with leucine, is one of the strictly ketogenic amino acids important in fueling ketone body production (notably relevant in PDH deficiency treatment), but it plays no role in creatine biosynthesis.

preguntas.q: Which amino acid serves as one of the precursors of the antioxidant tripeptide glutathione (along with cysteine and glycine)?

e.correcta: Glutathione is a tripeptide built from glutamate, cysteine, and glycine, with the gamma-carboxyl group of glutamate forming an unusual peptide bond to cysteine (gamma-glutamylcysteine) before glycine is added. Once assembled, glutathione's reactive cysteine thiol group allows it to neutralize reactive oxygen species and peroxides (using glutathione peroxidase, regenerated by glutathione reductase and NADPH), protecting cells — most notably red blood cells — from oxidative damage.

incorrectas.A: Aspartate is important in the urea cycle and purine/pyrimidine synthesis, contributing nitrogen atoms to those pathways, but it is not one of the three amino acids that make up glutathione.
incorrectas.B: Glutamine is the amidated form of glutamate and functions as a major nitrogen shuttle between tissues and a substrate for renal ammoniagenesis, but glutathione synthesis specifically requires glutamate itself, not its amidated derivative.
incorrectas.D: Arginine is the substrate for nitric oxide synthase and a precursor of creatine via guanidinoacetate, playing no direct role in the three-amino-acid backbone (glutamate-cysteine-glycine) of glutathione.

preguntas.q: Which amino acid is decarboxylated by glutamate decarboxylase (a vitamin B6-dependent enzyme) to form the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA?

e.correcta: Glutamate decarboxylase (GAD) removes a carboxyl group from glutamate using pyridoxal-5-phosphate (the active form of vitamin B6) as a cofactor, converting the principal excitatory neurotransmitter (glutamate) into the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter (GABA). This reaction is clinically relevant in autoimmune conditions like stiff person syndrome and type 1 diabetes, where anti-GAD antibodies are diagnostic markers, and in isoniazid toxicity/B6 deficiency, where impaired GABA synthesis can precipitate seizures.

incorrectas.B: Glycine itself acts as an inhibitory neurotransmitter (mainly in the spinal cord and brainstem) in its own right, but it is not converted into GABA — the two are distinct inhibitory neurotransmitters synthesized through separate pathways.
incorrectas.C: Tryptophan is the precursor for serotonin (via hydroxylation and decarboxylation) and niacin, an entirely different neurotransmitter pathway from the glutamate-to-GABA conversion.
incorrectas.D: Histidine is decarboxylated to form histamine, a mediator involved in allergic and inflammatory responses rather than the GABA-mediated inhibitory neurotransmission pathway.

preguntas.q: Which amino acid condenses with succinyl-CoA (via ALA synthase, using vitamin B6) to form the first committed intermediate in heme synthesis?

e.correcta: The rate-limiting step of heme synthesis is catalyzed by ALA synthase, which condenses glycine with succinyl-CoA (a TCA cycle intermediate) to form delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), using pyridoxal phosphate as a cofactor. Every carbon and nitrogen atom in the finished heme ring molecule ultimately traces back to either glycine or succinyl-CoA, which is why lead poisoning and porphyrias (which disrupt downstream steps of this pathway) produce accumulation of ALA and related precursors with characteristic clinical findings like microcytic anemia and abdominal pain.

incorrectas.A: Alanine is generated from pyruvate via transamination and is important in the Cahill (glucose-alanine) cycle shuttling nitrogen and carbon skeletons from muscle to liver, but it does not participate in the glycine/succinyl-CoA condensation that initiates heme synthesis.
incorrectas.B: Glutamate is central to transamination reactions and neurotransmitter synthesis (GABA) and nitrogen handling (via glutamine), but it is not the amino acid that combines with succinyl-CoA to start the heme synthesis pathway.
incorrectas.C: Serine can be converted to glycine (and vice versa) via serine hydroxymethyltransferase using THF, but it is glycine itself, not serine, that is the actual substrate condensed with succinyl-CoA by ALA synthase.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of cystinuria, a relatively common disorder (roughly 1 in 7,000 people) of renal amino acid transport?

e.correcta: Cystinuria is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, caused by mutations in genes encoding the PCT amino acid transporter (affecting the SLC3A1/SLC7A9 subunits) responsible for reabsorbing cystine and the dibasic amino acids (ornithine, lysine, arginine — remember 'COLA') in the proximal renal tubule. Its relatively high carrier frequency (about 1 in 7,000 affected) makes it one of the more common inherited aminoacidurias, presenting with recurrent cystine kidney stones, often in children or young adults.

incorrectas.A: X-linked recessive conditions (like Fabry disease or hemophilia) show a distinct pattern where affected fathers cannot transmit disease to sons and affected males are more common — cystinuria's transporter genes are located on autosomes, not the X chromosome.
incorrectas.B: Autosomal dominant inheritance would mean a single mutant allele from either parent causes disease in each generation, but cystinuria requires two defective transporter alleles (loss of both copies of the relevant amino acid transporter gene) to produce clinically significant cystine wasting.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance applies to diseases from mutations in mitochondrial DNA, transmitted only from the mother (e.g., MELAS, Leber optic neuropathy) — cystinuria instead results from nuclear gene mutations affecting a renal tubular transporter.

preguntas.q: Which treatment strategy for cystinuria helps prevent recurrent cystine kidney stones by increasing cystine's solubility in urine?

e.correcta: Cystine is poorly soluble in acidic urine but becomes markedly more soluble as urine pH rises, so alkalinizing the urine with agents like potassium citrate or acetazolamide (a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that promotes bicarbonate excretion) reduces the chance that cystine will precipitate and form stones. This approach is combined with high fluid intake to dilute urinary cystine concentration, and in refractory cases, chelating agents like penicillamine that bind cystine and increase its solubility further.

incorrectas.A: Urinary acidification would do the opposite of what's therapeutically needed — cystine solubility decreases at lower pH, so acidifying the urine would actually promote stone formation rather than prevent it.
incorrectas.B: Loop diuretics primarily promote sodium, potassium, and calcium excretion by blocking the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb; they do not target cystine solubility and are not the mainstay treatment for cystinuria-related stones.
incorrectas.C: A low-protein diet alone might slightly reduce cystine excretion but does not address the fundamental solubility problem, and it is insufficient on its own — urinary alkalinization and adequate hydration are the primary evidence-based interventions.

preguntas.q: Cystine is formed by a disulfide bond linking two molecules of which amino acid?

e.correcta: Cystine is generated when the thiol (-SH) side chains of two cysteine molecules are oxidized and joined by a disulfide (-S-S-) bond, forming a dimer. This disulfide bond is also the basis of tertiary protein structure stabilization (e.g., in extracellular and secreted proteins) and, in cystinuria, the reason cystine — rather than free cysteine — is the poorly soluble species that precipitates as kidney stones since the transporter defect fails to reabsorb the dimer efficiently.

incorrectas.B: Methionine is a sulfur-containing amino acid and the initiator amino acid in protein synthesis, and it is the metabolic precursor of cysteine via the transsulfuration pathway, but it is not itself the molecule joined to form cystine.
incorrectas.C: Serine lacks a sulfhydryl group entirely and instead contributes its hydroxymethyl group to one-carbon metabolism (interconverting with glycine); it cannot form the disulfide bond that defines cystine.
incorrectas.D: Threonine is an essential amino acid with a hydroxyl side chain, structurally and metabolically unrelated to the sulfur chemistry that allows cysteine molecules to dimerize into cystine.

preguntas.q: In the Cori cycle, the conversion of pyruvate to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase serves to regenerate which molecule needed to sustain glycolysis?

e.correcta: During anaerobic glycolysis (e.g., in exercising skeletal muscle or red blood cells lacking mitochondria), glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase consumes NAD+ and produces NADH; without a way to reoxidize that NADH back to NAD+, glycolysis would stall for lack of the oxidized cofactor it needs at that step. Lactate dehydrogenase solves this by transferring electrons from NADH back onto pyruvate to form lactate, regenerating NAD+ so glycolysis (and net ATP production) can continue even without oxygen.

incorrectas.A: ATP is generated directly by substrate-level phosphorylation steps within glycolysis itself (at the phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase steps), not by the pyruvate-to-lactate conversion, which instead serves a redox-balancing role.
incorrectas.C: NADH is actually consumed, not regenerated, in the pyruvate-to-lactate reaction — it's the electron donor that gets oxidized back to NAD+ as lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate.
incorrectas.D: Acetyl-CoA is produced from pyruvate by pyruvate dehydrogenase under aerobic conditions to feed the TCA cycle; the lactate pathway is instead an alternative anaerobic fate for pyruvate that bypasses acetyl-CoA formation entirely.

preguntas.q: Which of the following best describes the effect of the Cori cycle's pyruvate-to-lactate step on cytosolic redox balance in tissues undergoing anaerobic glycolysis?

o.A: It regenerates NAD+, allowing glycolysis to continue
o.B: It consumes NAD+ and therefore requires oxygen to proceed
o.C: It has no effect on the NAD+/NADH balance
o.D: It regenerates NADPH for biosynthetic reactions

e.correcta: Yes — the Cori cycle's defining biochemical feature is that lactate dehydrogenase reoxidizes the NADH generated during glycolysis back to NAD+, allowing glycolysis to continue producing ATP even when oxidative phosphorylation cannot keep pace (such as during intense exercise or in cells lacking mitochondria). The lactate produced is then transported to the liver, where it is reconverted to pyruvate and used for gluconeogenesis, completing the cycle and returning glucose to the bloodstream for peripheral tissues to use again.

incorrectas.B: This inverts the actual chemistry — the lactate-forming reaction consumes NADH (not NAD+) as it reduces pyruvate to lactate, and importantly this step does NOT require oxygen, which is precisely why it can sustain glycolysis under anaerobic conditions.
incorrectas.C: Saying there is no effect on NAD+/NADH balance misses the entire functional point of the reaction — regenerating cytosolic NAD+ is exactly why the pyruvate-to-lactate conversion exists as a metabolic strategy during anaerobic states.
incorrectas.D: NADPH regeneration is instead the job of the HMP shunt (via glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) for reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defense, a completely separate cofactor pool from the NAD+/NADH used in glycolysis and the Cori cycle.

preguntas.q: Compared to the Cori cycle, how does the Cahill (glucose-alanine) cycle affect cytosolic NAD+ regeneration in exercising muscle?

o.A: It regenerates NAD+ via lactate dehydrogenase, just like the Cori cycle
o.B: It does not regenerate NAD+, since transaminating pyruvate to alanine does not involve NADH oxidation
o.C: It regenerates NAD+ via alanine aminotransferase, which consumes NADH
o.D: It regenerates NADPH via transamination reactions

e.correcta: In the Cahill cycle, alanine aminotransferase transfers an amino group from glutamate onto pyruvate to form alanine — a transamination reaction that does not involve oxidizing NADH back to NAD+ the way lactate dehydrogenase does in the Cori cycle. Because of this, the Cahill cycle does not help regenerate the NAD+ that glycolysis needs to keep running, making it a less favorable route for sustaining ATP production during intense anaerobic exercise compared to lactate formation, even though it still serves the important role of shuttling amino groups and carbon skeletons from muscle to liver.

incorrectas.A: This describes the Cori cycle, not the Cahill cycle — lactate dehydrogenase (which does regenerate NAD+ by reducing pyruvate to lactate) is a distinct enzyme from alanine aminotransferase, which instead transfers an amino group without any NADH oxidation.
incorrectas.C: Alanine aminotransferase catalyzes a transamination (amino group transfer from glutamate to pyruvate), not an NADH-dependent redox reaction, so it does not consume NADH or regenerate NAD+ in the process.
incorrectas.D: NADPH regeneration is unrelated to either the Cori or Cahill cycles — it comes primarily from the HMP shunt — and transamination reactions like the one forming alanine do not generate or consume NADPH at all.

preguntas.q: Arsenic toxicity produces symptoms resembling pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency because arsenic inhibits which cofactor required for PDH complex activity?

e.correcta: Arsenic (as arsenite) binds to the vicinal sulfhydryl groups on lipoic acid, inactivating this cofactor and thereby impairing the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (as well as alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase), which mirrors the 'Tender Loving Care for Nancy' mnemonic cofactor list (TPP, Lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, NAD+) required for PDH function. Clinically, this manifests with vomiting, watery ('rice-water') diarrhea, garlic breath odor, QT prolongation, and characteristic skin findings (hyperpigmentation with hyperkeratosis), reflecting impaired cellular respiration and disrupted gluconeogenesis and glutathione metabolism.

incorrectas.A: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is also part of the PDH complex's required cofactors, but arsenic's specific toxic mechanism is binding the sulfhydryl groups of lipoic acid, not TPP — thiamine deficiency causes a different clinical picture (beriberi, Wernicke-Korsakoff), not arsenic poisoning.
incorrectas.C: Coenzyme A is a necessary PDH cofactor that accepts the final acetyl group, but it lacks the vicinal thiol structure that arsenic specifically targets — lipoic acid's dithiol groups are arsenic's actual binding site.
incorrectas.D: FAD is required to reoxidize the reduced lipoamide within the PDH complex, but it is not the direct target of arsenic; arsenic's toxicity centers specifically on inactivating lipoic acid's sulfhydryl groups upstream of FAD's role.

preguntas.q: Dietary iron is primarily absorbed by enterocytes in which segment of the small intestine?

e.correcta: Iron absorption occurs mainly in the duodenum, where enterocytes take up ferrous iron (Fe2+) via the divalent metal transporter DMT1 after gastric acid and duodenal reductases help convert dietary ferric iron (Fe3+) to the more absorbable ferrous form; iron then exits the enterocyte into the bloodstream via ferroportin, regulated by hepcidin. This anatomic localization explains why proximal small bowel disease (like duodenal resection or severe celiac disease affecting the proximal intestine) commonly causes iron deficiency anemia, while distal ileal disease more classically causes vitamin B12 or bile acid malabsorption instead.

incorrectas.A: The jejunum is the primary site for absorption of most macronutrients (folate, most vitamins, carbohydrates, fats) once they have already passed the duodenum, but it is not the principal site where dietary iron is taken up by enterocytes.
incorrectas.B: The ileum is the site of vitamin B12 (with intrinsic factor) and bile acid reabsorption, an entirely different transport system from iron uptake; ileal disease or resection is more classically linked to B12 deficiency and megaloblastic anemia, not iron deficiency.
incorrectas.D: The stomach contributes indirectly to iron absorption by secreting acid that helps solubilize and reduce dietary iron to its more absorbable ferrous state, but the actual transport of iron across the epithelium into the bloodstream occurs in the duodenum, not the stomach itself.

preguntas.q: Non-heme dietary iron is reduced to Fe2+ by duodenal cytochrome B (Dcytb) before crossing the apical membrane of the enterocyte. Which transporter mediates this uptake, functioning as an H+ co-transporter?

e.correcta: DMT1 sits on the apical (luminal) brush border membrane of duodenal enterocytes and co-transports Fe2+ together with H+, using the H+ gradient (favored by gastric acid and Dcytb-mediated reduction) to drive iron uptake into the cell. This is the rate-limiting step for absorbing non-heme iron and is why conditions that reduce gastric acid (e.g., PPI use, achlorhydria) can impair iron absorption.

incorrectas.A: Ferroportin is the exporter on the basolateral membrane that releases Fe2+ from the enterocyte into the bloodstream, the opposite direction and location from DMT1's apical uptake role, and it is the target inhibited by hepcidin.
incorrectas.C: Transferrin receptor 1 mediates receptor-mediated endocytosis of iron-loaded transferrin from plasma into cells throughout the body (e.g., erythroid precursors) — it acts on iron already in the blood bound to transferrin, not on luminal non-heme iron entering the gut.
incorrectas.D: ZIP14 can import non-transferrin-bound iron in some tissues like the liver, but it is not the primary apical transporter responsible for absorbing dietary non-heme iron in duodenal enterocytes.

preguntas.q: Which basolateral membrane transporter releases absorbed iron from duodenal enterocytes into the bloodstream?

e.correcta: Ferroportin is the sole known cellular iron exporter, located on the basolateral membrane of enterocytes; it releases Fe2+ into the portal circulation, where it is oxidized and bound to transferrin. Ferroportin is the key regulatory checkpoint of body iron balance because it is the direct target of hepcidin, which binds ferroportin and triggers its internalization/degradation, trapping iron inside enterocytes (and macrophages) during inflammation or iron excess.

incorrectas.A: DMT1 works at the opposite membrane and step — it imports Fe2+ into the enterocyte from the intestinal lumen, not out of the cell into blood.
incorrectas.C: Transferrin is the plasma carrier protein that binds Fe3+ after it leaves the enterocyte; it does not move iron across the basolateral membrane itself, it only picks it up afterward.
incorrectas.D: Hephaestin is a ferroxidase anchored near the basolateral membrane that oxidizes Fe2+ to Fe3+ as it exits (working alongside ferroportin), but it is not the transporter itself — it enables transferrin binding rather than performing membrane transport.

preguntas.q: Fe2+ exiting the enterocyte via ferroportin must be oxidized to Fe3+ before binding transferrin. Which class of copper-dependent enzymes performs this oxidation?

e.correcta: Ferroxidases such as hephaestin (membrane-bound, near enterocytes) and ceruloplasmin (circulating, copper-containing) oxidize Fe2+ to Fe3+ immediately after it exits cells via ferroportin. This step is essential because transferrin only binds the ferric (Fe3+) form; it also explains why copper deficiency or Wilson disease (low functional ceruloplasmin) can produce an iron-deficiency-like picture despite normal iron stores, since iron cannot be properly loaded onto transferrin.

incorrectas.B: Cytochrome b reductases (like duodenal cytochrome B) act at the opposite end of the pathway, reducing dietary Fe3+ to Fe2+ at the apical brush border so DMT1 can import it — the reverse reaction, in the reverse location.
