preguntas.q: In an elderly patient in the Western world, what should be assumed as the cause of new iron deficiency anemia until proven otherwise?

e.correcta: In elderly patients in developed nations, colorectal carcinoma (or a bleeding colonic polyp) must be assumed as the cause of new iron deficiency anemia until proven otherwise, because occult GI blood loss from a colonic neoplasm is common and potentially curable if caught early. This is why any elderly patient with new iron deficiency warrants colonoscopy.

incorrectas.A: Hookworm infection is the classic cause of elderly iron deficiency in developing regions with poor sanitation, but it is rare in the Western world.
incorrectas.C: Peptic ulcer disease is an important GI bleeding source but is more classically highlighted for younger adult men; in the elderly, malignancy takes diagnostic priority.
incorrectas.D: Poor diet can contribute to iron deficiency in elderly patients, but it is not the answer that must be ruled out first — occult malignancy takes precedence in this population.

preguntas.q: What is the most common cause of iron deficiency anemia in elderly patients in the developing world?

e.correcta: In the developing world, chronic hookworm infection is extremely common due to soil contamination and poor sanitation. The worms attach to the small intestinal mucosa with cutting mouthparts and cause continuous low-grade blood loss, making it the leading cause of iron deficiency anemia in elderly patients in these regions.

incorrectas.B: Colorectal carcinoma is the answer emphasized for elderly patients in the Western/developed world, where hookworm exposure is minimal, reflecting differing regional epidemiology.
incorrectas.C: Peptic ulcer disease is a more classic cause in adult men generally, not specifically highlighted for the elderly in endemic regions.
incorrectas.D: Menorrhagia is a female reproductive-age cause of blood loss and does not apply to elderly patients of either sex.

preguntas.q: Which two hookworm species are classically associated with causing iron deficiency anemia through chronic intestinal blood loss?

e.correcta: Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus are the two hookworm species that attach to the small intestinal wall using cutting mouthparts and feed on blood, causing chronic occult blood loss that leads to iron deficiency anemia. They are acquired via larval skin penetration from contaminated soil, classically in barefoot individuals in endemic regions.

incorrectas.A: Ascaris lumbricoides can cause intestinal obstruction or biliary/pancreatic duct obstruction, and Enterobius vermicularis causes perianal pruritus, but neither is a classic cause of chronic blood-loss anemia.
incorrectas.B: Strongyloides stercoralis is notable for autoinfection and life-threatening hyperinfection in immunosuppressed hosts, and Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) can cause dysentery or rectal prolapse with heavy infection, but hookworms specifically are the ones linked to iron deficiency anemia.
incorrectas.D: Taenia solium causes cysticercosis and Diphyllobothrium latum competes with the host for vitamin B12, causing megaloblastic anemia — neither causes iron deficiency through intestinal blood loss.

preguntas.q: Which surgical procedure predisposes to iron deficiency anemia because loss of gastric acid impairs conversion of dietary iron to its more absorbable form?

e.correcta: Gastric acid is needed to reduce dietary ferric iron (Fe3+) to the more absorbable ferrous form (Fe2+) and to liberate iron from food complexes. After gastrectomy, the loss of acid-secreting parietal cell mass (and, depending on reconstruction, bypass of the duodenum where iron is absorbed) impairs this process and reduces absorptive surface area, predisposing to iron deficiency anemia.

incorrectas.A: Cholecystectomy removes the gallbladder, affecting bile storage and fat digestion, not gastric acid secretion or the chemistry of iron reduction.
incorrectas.B: Splenectomy removes a major site of RBC destruction/recycling and increases susceptibility to encapsulated organism infections, but it does not impair dietary iron absorption.
incorrectas.C: Appendectomy removes the appendix, which plays no meaningful role in iron or other nutrient absorption.

preguntas.q: In iron deficiency anemia, what happens to the serum ferritin level?

e.correcta: In iron deficiency anemia, body iron stores are truly depleted, so ferritin (the storage protein found in macrophages and liver) is low. This is the most specific and useful single lab value for confirming true iron deficiency, in contrast to anemia of chronic disease, where ferritin is normal-to-high because inflammation both increases ferritin synthesis as an acute-phase reactant and traps iron within cells.

incorrectas.B: Increased ferritin would suggest iron overload or an acute-phase inflammatory response, essentially the opposite of what is seen in true iron deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Normal ferritin would not confirm iron deficiency and could instead suggest anemia of chronic disease, or a very early stage of iron deficiency before stores have fully dropped.
incorrectas.D: Ferritin does not fluctuate unpredictably in iron deficiency — it reliably falls as iron stores are progressively consumed, which is exactly why it is diagnostically useful.

preguntas.q: In iron deficiency anemia, what happens to total iron-binding capacity (TIBC)?

e.correcta: TIBC estimates the amount of transferrin available to bind iron. In iron deficiency, the liver upregulates transferrin production in an attempt to more efficiently scavenge any available iron, so TIBC rises even as iron stores fall. TIBC and ferritin characteristically move in opposite directions, a pattern that helps distinguish iron deficiency anemia from anemia of chronic disease, where TIBC is typically normal or decreased.

incorrectas.A: Decreased TIBC is the pattern seen in anemia of chronic disease, where inflammatory cytokines suppress transferrin synthesis — the opposite of what occurs in iron deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Normal TIBC would not fit the compensatory transferrin upregulation that characteristically occurs once the body senses depleted iron stores.
incorrectas.D: TIBC is never undetectable; it simply reflects transferrin's iron-carrying capacity and is always measurable, just elevated in this condition.

preguntas.q: In iron deficiency anemia, what happens to serum iron?

e.correcta: With depleted iron stores, there is less iron available to be released into circulation and bound to transferrin, so the serum iron concentration falls. Serum iron alone is a poor stand-alone diagnostic test, since it fluctuates with diet and time of day, so it is interpreted alongside ferritin, TIBC, and % saturation to build the full picture.

incorrectas.A: Increased serum iron would be expected in iron overload states such as hemochromatosis, hemolysis, or excess iron supplementation, not in deficiency.
incorrectas.B: Normal serum iron would not support a diagnosis of iron deficiency and might instead point toward another cause of microcytic or normocytic anemia.
incorrectas.D: Serum iron in iron deficiency does not behave unpredictably — it consistently trends downward as circulating iron becomes scarce, even though day-to-day values can fluctuate somewhat.

preguntas.q: In iron deficiency anemia, what happens to % transferrin saturation?

e.correcta: Since % saturation equals serum iron divided by TIBC, and in iron deficiency serum iron falls while TIBC rises (more empty transferrin), this ratio drops sharply — often below 15-20%. This combination of low % saturation with high TIBC is a hallmark of true iron deficiency, distinguishing it from anemia of chronic disease.

incorrectas.A: Increased % saturation would suggest an iron overload state, where abundant iron floods the available transferrin binding sites — essentially the opposite physiology.
incorrectas.B: Normal % saturation would not be diagnostic of a deficiency state and could be seen in early or mild cases, or in other types of anemia.
incorrectas.C: The change is not inconsistent or unpredictable — both the falling numerator (serum iron) and rising denominator (TIBC) reliably push % saturation downward in iron deficiency.

preguntas.q: In the earliest stage of iron deficiency, before iron stores are severely depleted, what is the characteristic MCV of the resulting anemia?

e.correcta: In the earliest phase of iron deficiency, the bone marrow initially compensates by producing fewer red cells that are still of normal size, since remaining iron stores can still adequately hemoglobinize each individual cell being produced. Only once iron stores are exhausted further does the marrow begin producing progressively smaller cells, transitioning into the classic microcytic picture.

incorrectas.B: Microcytic anemia is the later, more advanced stage of iron deficiency, appearing once iron stores can no longer support normal-sized RBC production — it is not present at the very onset.
incorrectas.C: Macrocytic anemia reflects impaired DNA synthesis from B12 or folate deficiency, an entirely different mechanism unrelated to iron availability.
incorrectas.D: A dimorphic (mixed cell size) population can appear transitioning between stages or with combined nutritional deficiencies, but it is not the term for the earliest single stage of iron deficiency.

preguntas.q: In the later, more advanced stage of iron deficiency, what is the characteristic MCV of the resulting anemia?

e.correcta: As iron stores become severely depleted over time, the bone marrow can no longer adequately hemoglobinize developing erythroblasts, so each successive generation of RBCs produced is smaller (low MCV) as well as fewer in number. This progression from normocytic to microcytic explains why chronic, longstanding iron deficiency produces the classic microcytic, hypochromic anemia seen on peripheral smear.

incorrectas.A: Macrocytic change is unrelated to iron deficiency and instead reflects megaloblastic processes such as B12 or folate deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Normocytic anemia is characteristic of the earlier stage of iron deficiency, before cell size itself becomes affected — by the later, advanced stage referenced here, cells have already become small.
incorrectas.D: A dimorphic population can appear during the transition between stages or with mixed etiologies, but the defining later-stage finding specifically named for iron deficiency is microcytosis.

preguntas.q: What morphologic change in RBC staining characterizes iron deficiency anemia on peripheral smear?

e.correcta: Because hemoglobin synthesis is impaired without adequate iron, red cells end up with less hemoglobin per cell, producing an enlarged area of central pallor on Wright-stained peripheral smear (normally central pallor occupies only about a third of the cell diameter). This hypochromia, together with microcytosis, is a defining morphologic feature of iron deficiency anemia.

incorrectas.A: Hyperchromia, or loss of central pallor, reflects an increased hemoglobin concentration relative to cell volume (as in spherocytes), essentially the opposite of what iron deficiency produces.
incorrectas.B: Normochromic cells have a normal amount of central pallor and are typical of anemias where hemoglobin synthesis is not impaired, such as acute blood loss or many hemolytic anemias, not chronic iron deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Polychromasia refers to bluish-gray immature reticulocytes on smear reflecting a robust marrow response to anemia, not a chromicity change related to iron content.

preguntas.q: What happens to red cell distribution width (RDW) in iron deficiency anemia, and how does this help distinguish it from thalassemia?

o.A: Decreased, unlike thalassemia which has an increased RDW
o.C: Highly variable and not useful for distinguishing the two
o.D: Increased, whereas thalassemia trait classically has a normal RDW

e.correcta: RDW measures variation in red cell size (anisocytosis). Because iron deficiency progresses through an initial normocytic phase followed by an increasingly microcytic phase, the blood contains a heterogeneous mix of normal-sized older cells and progressively smaller newer cells, producing a high RDW. This is a key feature distinguishing it from thalassemia trait, which is also microcytic but classically has a normal RDW because the small cell size is uniform and genetically determined from birth rather than a progressive nutritional deficiency.

incorrectas.A: Decreased RDW is not a recognized pattern in either condition, and thalassemia is actually the one with a normal (not increased) RDW.
incorrectas.B: A normal RDW is the classic finding in thalassemia trait, not in iron deficiency anemia — this is precisely the feature that helps tell the two apart.
incorrectas.C: RDW is quite useful here — it does not behave erratically in iron deficiency, reliably rising as anisocytosis develops during disease progression.

preguntas.q: Among the microcytic anemias, which one is classically associated with an increased RDW (anisocytosis)?

e.correcta: Iron deficiency anemia is the classic microcytic anemia with an elevated RDW, because it evolves through stages that produce a mixed population of normal and progressively smaller cells (anisocytosis) as stores are consumed over time, unlike other microcytic anemias that tend to produce a more uniformly sized cell population.

incorrectas.B: Thalassemia trait produces microcytosis from a genetic globin chain defect present from birth, yielding a uniformly small cell population and thus a normal RDW — a key point used to distinguish it from iron deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Anemia of chronic disease is typically normocytic to only mildly microcytic with a normal RDW, since hepcidin-driven iron trapping affects red cell production fairly uniformly rather than progressively.
incorrectas.D: Lead poisoning causes microcytic anemia by inhibiting heme synthesis enzymes and classically presents with basophilic stippling on smear, but an elevated RDW is not the hallmark feature emphasized for it the way it is for iron deficiency.

preguntas.q: What is the standard treatment for iron deficiency anemia?

e.correcta: Oral ferrous salts such as ferrous sulfate replenish iron stores by delivering iron in the more absorbable Fe2+ form. Treatment is typically continued for several months (often 6-12) beyond correction of hemoglobin to fully replete tissue iron stores (reflected by a normalized ferritin), and any underlying cause of blood loss or malabsorption must also be identified and treated.

incorrectas.A: Vitamin B12 treats megaloblastic anemia from B12 deficiency (e.g., pernicious anemia), a macrocytic process driven by impaired DNA synthesis, not the microcytic iron deficiency described here.
incorrectas.C: Folate similarly treats a different type of megaloblastic, macrocytic anemia and plays no role in repleting iron stores.
incorrectas.D: Erythropoietin stimulates RBC production in the marrow (used in anemia of CKD or chemotherapy-induced anemia), but without adequate iron substrate, EPO stimulation alone cannot correct hemoglobin synthesis in iron deficiency.

preguntas.q: Which anemia arises from hepcidin-mediated iron sequestration in the setting of malignancy or chronic inflammatory disease?

e.correcta: Anemia of chronic disease arises when chronic inflammatory states (malignancy, autoimmune disease like RA or SLE, chronic infection, CKD) drive hepcidin production. Hepcidin degrades ferroportin and traps iron within macrophages and enterocytes, making iron functionally unavailable for erythropoiesis even though total body iron stores (and ferritin) are normal or increased — a key distinguishing feature from true iron deficiency.

incorrectas.A: Iron deficiency anemia results from an actual depletion of total body iron stores (reflected by low ferritin), rather than iron being present but sequestered as in anemia of chronic disease.
incorrectas.B: Aplastic anemia results from bone marrow failure with pancytopenia due to loss of hematopoietic stem cells, an entirely different mechanism unrelated to iron handling.
incorrectas.D: Megaloblastic anemia results from impaired DNA synthesis due to B12 or folate deficiency, producing macrocytic cells, not the normocytic-to-mildly-microcytic picture seen in anemia of chronic disease.

preguntas.q: What is the most common type of anemia encountered in hospitalized patients?

e.correcta: Anemia of chronic disease is the most common anemia found in hospitalized patients because so many admitted patients have underlying chronic inflammatory, infectious, malignant, or renal conditions that drive hepcidin-mediated iron sequestration and a blunted erythropoietin response. It functions essentially as a marker of overall systemic illness burden rather than a primary hematologic disease.

incorrectas.A: Iron deficiency anemia is common in the general population, especially menstruating women, but it is not the anemia most characteristically tied to the hospitalized, systemically ill population as a whole.
incorrectas.B: Aplastic anemia is a relatively rare cause of pancytopenia from marrow failure and is far less common than anemia of chronic disease among hospitalized patients.
incorrectas.C: Hemolytic anemia encompasses various specific conditions (autoimmune, hereditary, etc.) but is not the most prevalent anemia type across the general hospitalized population.

preguntas.q: In addition to degrading ferroportin to trap iron in macrophages, hepcidin contributes to anemia of chronic disease by suppressing production of which hormone?

e.correcta: Beyond its primary action of degrading ferroportin (trapping iron in macrophages and enterocytes and blocking dietary iron absorption), hepcidin also blunts erythropoietin production/signaling during chronic inflammatory states, compounding the impaired erythropoiesis seen in anemia of chronic disease. This dual mechanism of iron restriction plus EPO suppression explains why anemia of chronic disease does not respond to iron supplementation alone.

incorrectas.B: Thrombopoietin regulates platelet production from megakaryocytes and is not part of the hepcidin-iron regulatory axis relevant to anemia of chronic disease.
incorrectas.C: Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid regulating sodium, potassium, and volume homeostasis via the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, unrelated to iron metabolism or erythropoiesis.
incorrectas.D: Renin initiates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone cascade that regulates blood pressure and volume, an entirely separate hormonal system from the hepcidin-erythropoietin axis involved in anemia of chronic disease.

preguntas.q: A 60-year-old man with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis develops a mild microcytic anemia. Which iron study finding helps distinguish anemia of chronic disease (ACD) from iron deficiency anemia (IDA)?

e.correcta: In ACD, chronic inflammation drives hepcidin production, which blocks ferroportin-mediated iron export from macrophages and enterocytes, trapping iron within storage sites. Because ferritin reflects intracellular iron stores (and is also an acute-phase reactant induced by inflammatory cytokines like IL-6), it rises even though iron is functionally unavailable for erythropoiesis — the opposite of true iron deficiency. This is the single most useful lab value for separating ACD from IDA when the two overlap on MCV.

incorrectas.A: Decreased ferritin reflects true depletion of iron stores and is the hallmark of iron deficiency anemia, not ACD — in ACD, iron is sequestered but stores are actually replete or even increased.
incorrectas.C: Increased TIBC (transferrin) is a compensatory hepatic response to low iron stores seen in IDA; in ACD, hepcidin and inflammatory cytokines suppress transferrin synthesis, so TIBC is characteristically decreased instead.
incorrectas.D: % transferrin saturation is decreased, not increased, in ACD because both serum iron and available iron for binding are low from macrophage sequestration; an increased saturation would instead suggest an iron-overload state such as hemochromatosis or sideroblastic anemia.

preguntas.q: Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) is characteristically decreased in anemia of chronic disease. Which of the following microcytic anemias instead shows an INCREASED TIBC?

e.correcta: In iron deficiency anemia, the liver senses low iron stores and low circulating iron and upregulates transferrin synthesis in an attempt to maximize iron capture from any available source, so TIBC rises. TIBC and ferritin move in opposite directions in essentially all microcytic anemias, so an elevated TIBC paired with low ferritin is a classic signature that points toward true iron deficiency rather than a disorder of iron distribution.

incorrectas.A: Anemia of chronic disease shows decreased TIBC because inflammatory cytokines and hepcidin suppress hepatic transferrin production even though iron stores (ferritin) are normal to high — the reverse pattern of IDA.
incorrectas.B: Sideroblastic anemia is an iron-overload state (iron accumulates in mitochondria and tissues), so the liver downregulates transferrin synthesis via the same feedback that occurs with high stores, giving a decreased, not increased, TIBC.
incorrectas.C: Thalassemia results from a globin chain synthesis defect, not a problem with iron handling — iron stores and TIBC are typically normal, distinguishing it from anemias where iron studies are deranged.

preguntas.q: In anemia of chronic disease, what happens to serum iron levels?

o.D: Markedly elevated with a normal ferritin

e.correcta: Serum iron is decreased in ACD because hepcidin, induced by inflammatory cytokines (especially IL-6), degrades ferroportin and traps iron inside macrophages and hepatocytes rather than releasing it into the circulation for erythropoiesis. This creates a state of functional iron deficiency despite normal or increased total body iron stores, which is why serum iron alone cannot distinguish ACD from true iron deficiency — ferritin and TIBC are needed to make that distinction.

incorrectas.B: An increased serum iron would instead suggest an iron-overload condition such as sideroblastic anemia or hemochromatosis, where iron is not being sequestered but rather accumulating in mitochondria or parenchymal tissue.
incorrectas.C: A normal serum iron would not fit the microcytic, iron-restricted picture of ACD; serum iron is consistently low in ACD due to hepcidin-mediated sequestration, similar in direction (though different in mechanism) to iron deficiency anemia.
incorrectas.D: A markedly elevated serum iron with a normal ferritin does not match any classic anemia of chronic disease pattern — ACD is defined by low serum iron together with a normal-to-high ferritin, the opposite combination described here.

preguntas.q: What is the expected % transferrin saturation in anemia of chronic disease?

e.correcta: % transferrin saturation (serum iron divided by TIBC) is decreased in ACD because serum iron falls due to hepcidin-mediated macrophage sequestration while TIBC also falls (inflammation suppresses transferrin synthesis) — but the drop in serum iron generally outpaces the drop in TIBC, so the ratio remains reduced. This mirrors iron deficiency anemia superficially, which is exactly why ferritin and TIBC direction are needed to separate the two conditions.

incorrectas.B: An undetectable or near-zero saturation is not typical of ACD; saturation is reduced but not to the near-total absence seen only in severe, prolonged true iron deficiency.
incorrectas.A: An increased % transferrin saturation would instead point to an iron-loading state, such as sideroblastic anemia or hereditary hemochromatosis, where excess iron overwhelms a normal or reduced binding capacity.
incorrectas.D: A normal % saturation would not fit ACD, which by definition produces some degree of functional iron restriction reflected in a reduced ratio of serum iron to binding capacity.

preguntas.q: In the early stages of anemia of chronic disease, before hepcidin-mediated iron sequestration substantially limits erythropoiesis, what is the characteristic red cell size pattern?

e.correcta: Early ACD is typically normocytic and normochromic because the initial driver of anemia is decreased erythropoietin responsiveness and mildly shortened RBC survival from inflammatory cytokines (like IL-1 and TNF-alpha), rather than a severe iron-restriction on hemoglobin synthesis. Only with more prolonged or intense inflammation does hepcidin-driven iron sequestration become severe enough to impair heme synthesis and shrink the MCV.

incorrectas.A: Microcytosis develops later in ACD, once iron sequestration becomes severe enough to limit hemoglobinization of developing red cells — it is not the earliest finding.
incorrectas.B: Macrocytosis is not a feature of ACD at any stage; it would instead suggest a coexisting cause such as B12/folate deficiency, alcohol use, or a bone marrow disorder.
incorrectas.C: A dimorphic population is more classically described when two processes coexist (e.g., concurrent iron deficiency and B12 deficiency) rather than as the expected early finding in isolated ACD.

preguntas.q: As anemia of chronic disease progresses and hepcidin-mediated iron sequestration becomes more pronounced, what does the anemia typically become?

e.correcta: With ongoing inflammation, hepcidin increasingly blocks ferroportin-mediated iron release, starving developing erythroblasts of iron needed for hemoglobin synthesis. Over time this iron-restricted erythropoiesis produces smaller, hypochromic red cells, converting the initially normocytic anemia into a microcytic one — mimicking iron deficiency anemia on CBC even though total body iron stores are preserved or increased.

incorrectas.A: Persistent normocytic anemia would suggest inflammation has not progressed to significantly impair iron delivery for hemoglobin synthesis, which contradicts the scenario of more pronounced iron sequestration described.
incorrectas.C: Macrocytic anemia is not a feature of chronic disease-related iron restriction; it points instead toward impaired DNA synthesis (B12/folate deficiency) or marrow disorders unrelated to hepcidin physiology.
incorrectas.D: A macrocyte-predominant dimorphic picture would suggest a second concurrent process (e.g., B12 deficiency) rather than the expected progression of ACD itself, which trends toward microcytosis, not macrocytosis.

preguntas.q: Which pair of microcytic anemias is characteristically associated with an INCREASED free erythrocyte protoporphyrin (FEP)?

o.C: Iron deficiency anemia and anemia of chronic disease

e.correcta: Both iron deficiency anemia and anemia of chronic disease involve a shortage of usable iron reaching developing erythroblasts (from true depletion in IDA, or hepcidin-mediated sequestration in ACD). Without enough iron to complete the final ferrochelatase-catalyzed step of heme synthesis, protoporphyrin IX accumulates upstream, raising FEP in both conditions — a useful clue that the defect is in iron delivery rather than globin or porphyrin synthesis itself.

incorrectas.A: Thalassemia results from a globin gene defect with normal heme synthesis machinery, so FEP is normal; sideroblastic anemia, though it does affect the heme pathway, is actually associated with normal to decreased FEP because iron is abundant (even trapped in mitochondria) and heme synthesis fails at an earlier enzymatic step, not from lack of iron.
incorrectas.B: Lead poisoning does elevate FEP (by inhibiting ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase), but sideroblastic anemia does not pair with it in the same direction — sideroblastic anemia's iron-replete, ALAS-deficient state keeps FEP normal to low rather than elevated.
incorrectas.D: Thalassemia's FEP is normal since its defect lies purely in globin chain production, so pairing it with lead poisoning (which does raise FEP) creates a mismatched, incorrect combination.

preguntas.q: What is the most effective overall treatment strategy for anemia of chronic disease?

o.A: Treat the underlying inflammatory, infectious, or neoplastic disorder
o.C: IV iron dextran regardless of the underlying cause

e.correcta: Because ACD arises from cytokine- and hepcidin-driven iron sequestration rather than true iron deficiency, the anemia resolves when the driving inflammatory, infectious, or malignant process is controlled — for example, treating chronic kidney disease with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents or controlling an underlying malignancy. Addressing the root cause removes the stimulus for hepcidin overproduction and allows normal iron trafficking and erythropoiesis to resume.

incorrectas.B: Oral iron supplementation is largely ineffective in ACD because the problem is not a lack of total body iron but its sequestration inside macrophages — giving more iron does not overcome the hepcidin-mediated block on ferroportin-dependent release.
incorrectas.C: IV iron dextran is reserved for situations with true iron deficiency or specific iron-refractory settings (e.g., dialysis patients on erythropoietin) and is not a general first-line approach for ACD, since indiscriminate iron loading in someone with normal-to-high stores risks harm without addressing the underlying cause.
incorrectas.D: Vitamin B12 treats megaloblastic (macrocytic) anemia from impaired DNA synthesis, an entirely different mechanism from the iron-trafficking problem underlying ACD, so it would not correct this anemia.

preguntas.q: In sideroblastic anemia, a relative deficiency of protoporphyrin prevents heme formation. Where does the resulting excess iron accumulate within developing erythroblasts?

e.correcta: Heme synthesis begins and ends in the mitochondrion (ALA synthase initiates the pathway there, and ferrochelatase inserts iron into protoporphyrin IX at the final step, also mitochondrial). When protoporphyrin production is impaired — as in ALAS deficiency, lead poisoning, or B6 deficiency — iron delivered to the mitochondrion has nowhere to go and accumulates there, forming iron-laden mitochondria that encircle the nucleus of the erythroblast, visualized as ringed sideroblasts with Prussian blue stain.

incorrectas.A: Iron transported into the erythroblast passes through the cytoplasm en route to the mitochondrion but does not pathologically accumulate there in sideroblastic anemia — the diagnostic accumulation is specifically perinuclear and mitochondrial.
incorrectas.C: The Golgi apparatus is involved in protein processing and secretion, not iron handling or heme synthesis, so it plays no role in the iron accumulation seen in sideroblastic anemia.
incorrectas.D: The nucleus is encircled by the iron-laden mitochondria (giving the classic 'ring' appearance) but the iron itself accumulates within the mitochondria, not inside the nucleus.

preguntas.q: Which histochemical stain is used on bone marrow biopsy to visualize iron deposits, such as those seen in ringed sideroblasts?

e.correcta: Prussian blue (Perls') stain reacts with ferric iron to produce a blue-colored precipitate, allowing pathologists to directly visualize iron granules within mitochondria that encircle the nucleus of erythroblasts — the defining feature of ringed sideroblasts on bone marrow biopsy in sideroblastic anemia.

incorrectas.B: Congo red stains amyloid fibrils and produces apple-green birefringence under polarized light; it has no affinity for iron and would not reveal ringed sideroblasts.
incorrectas.C: PAS stains glycogen and other polysaccharides/mucosubstances (useful in conditions like acute lymphoblastic leukemia or glycogen storage disease), not iron deposits.
incorrectas.D: Masson trichrome differentiates collagen (blue/green) from muscle and cytoplasm (red), useful for assessing fibrosis, but it does not specifically highlight iron.

preguntas.q: Congenital sideroblastic anemia is most commonly caused by a mutation in which enzyme of the heme synthesis pathway?

e.correcta: ALA synthase catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step of heme synthesis in the mitochondrion, condensing glycine and succinyl-CoA to form δ-aminolevulinic acid using pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor. The erythroid isoform ALAS2 is the one most commonly mutated in congenital (hereditary) sideroblastic anemia, and because this initial step is impaired, downstream porphyrin intermediates decrease while iron still enters the mitochondria and accumulates there unused.

incorrectas.A: ALA dehydratase acts one step after ALAS in the cytoplasm and is the enzyme classically inhibited in lead poisoning and ALA dehydratase deficiency porphyria, not the enzyme mutated in the most common congenital sideroblastic anemia.
incorrectas.B: Ferrochelatase catalyzes the final step of heme synthesis (inserting iron into protoporphyrin IX) in the mitochondrion and is deficient in erythropoietic protoporphyria and inhibited by lead, but ALAS2 mutations are the more common cause of the hereditary sideroblastic anemia phenotype.
incorrectas.C: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency causes porphyria cutanea tarda, a distinct disorder of porphyrin metabolism presenting with skin blistering and photosensitivity, not the classic congenital sideroblastic anemia picture.

preguntas.q: The gene encoding erythroid ALA synthase (ALAS2), when mutated, causes the most common form of congenital sideroblastic anemia. What is its inheritance pattern?

e.correcta: ALAS2 is located on the X chromosome, so its mutation causes an X-linked sideroblastic anemia that predominantly affects males, while female carriers may show milder or subclinical disease due to X-inactivation (lyonization) creating a mixed population of normal and affected erythroid precursors.

incorrectas.A: An autosomal dominant pattern would mean a single mutant copy on a non-sex chromosome causes disease regardless of sex, which does not match ALAS2's location and the male-predominant presentation actually observed.
incorrectas.B: Autosomal recessive inheritance would require two mutant copies on an autosome and would not explain the marked male predominance seen with ALAS2 mutations, since ALAS2 is X-linked, not autosomal.
incorrectas.D: While heme synthesis occurs partly in mitochondria, ALAS2 itself is a nuclear (X-linked) gene product imported into mitochondria — the disease is not transmitted via mitochondrial DNA inheritance.

preguntas.q: What is the most common reversible cause of acquired sideroblastic anemia?

e.correcta: Alcohol is a direct mitochondrial toxin that impairs ALA synthase and other mitochondrial enzymes involved in heme synthesis, producing ringed sideroblasts; because this toxicity is dose-related and not due to permanent structural damage in most cases, the anemia typically reverses with abstinence, making alcoholism the most common reversible acquired cause.

incorrectas.B: Isoniazid can cause sideroblastic anemia by antagonizing vitamin B6 (a cofactor for ALA synthase), and it is also reversible with cessation or B6 supplementation, but it is a much less common cause in the general population compared to alcohol use.
incorrectas.C: Lead poisoning causes sideroblastic anemia by inhibiting ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, and while removing the lead source can improve the anemia, lead toxicity is a far less common cause overall than chronic alcohol use.
incorrectas.D: Copper deficiency is a recognized but rare cause of sideroblastic anemia (copper is needed for enzymes involved in iron metabolism and mitochondrial function), occurring much less frequently than alcohol-related mitochondrial toxicity.

preguntas.q: Deficiency of which trace mineral can cause sideroblastic anemia by impairing copper-dependent enzymes involved in iron and mitochondrial metabolism?

e.correcta: Copper is a required cofactor for enzymes such as ceruloplasmin (which helps oxidize iron for loading onto transferrin) and cytochrome c oxidase in the mitochondrial electron transport chain; when copper is deficient — often from malabsorption, prolonged parenteral nutrition, or excess zinc intake displacing copper — mitochondrial and iron-handling dysfunction can produce ringed sideroblasts and a sideroblastic anemia picture.

incorrectas.A: Zinc deficiency does not classically cause sideroblastic anemia; in fact, excessive zinc intake is a recognized cause of copper deficiency (zinc induces intestinal metallothionein, which binds and blocks copper absorption), indirectly linking zinc excess — not zinc deficiency — to this condition.
incorrectas.B: Selenium deficiency is associated with cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease) and thyroid hormone metabolism abnormalities, not with sideroblastic anemia.
incorrectas.C: Manganese deficiency is not a recognized cause of sideroblastic anemia; manganese deficiency states are rare and typically linked to skeletal and connective tissue abnormalities rather than heme synthesis defects.

preguntas.q: Sideroblastic anemia, with its low free erythrocyte protoporphyrin, is classified under which red cell size category?

e.correcta: Impaired heme synthesis (from ALAS deficiency, lead toxicity, B6 deficiency, or alcohol) limits hemoglobinization of developing red cells, resulting in a microcytic anemia despite iron being present in abundance (indeed, trapped in mitochondria) — this places sideroblastic anemia alongside iron deficiency anemia, anemia of chronic disease, and thalassemia in the microcytic differential, even though its underlying mechanism (iron-replete, protoporphyrin-deficient) is the opposite of iron deficiency anemia.

incorrectas.A: Macrocytic anemia results from impaired DNA synthesis (e.g., B12/folate deficiency) rather than impaired hemoglobin synthesis, so it does not describe the mechanism or cell size seen in sideroblastic anemia.
incorrectas.B: While the smear may show variable cell sizes, sideroblastic anemia is classically grouped with the microcytic anemias in the standard MCV-based classification, not normocytic.
incorrectas.D: A dimorphic population (mix of normal and severely hypochromic microcytic cells) can be seen on peripheral smear in sideroblastic anemia, but this describes smear morphology rather than the overall MCV-based category, which is microcytic.

preguntas.q: What is the expected ferritin level in sideroblastic anemia?

o.D: Markedly decreased with a high TIBC

e.correcta: Sideroblastic anemia is fundamentally an iron-overload state at the cellular level: iron is delivered normally (or even in excess) to erythroblasts but cannot be incorporated into heme because of defective protoporphyrin synthesis, so it accumulates in mitochondria and eventually in body stores. This drives ferritin up, similar in direction to anemia of chronic disease but via a completely different mechanism (impaired heme synthesis rather than hepcidin-mediated sequestration).

incorrectas.B: A decreased ferritin is the hallmark of true iron deficiency anemia, which is mechanistically the opposite problem — insufficient iron delivery — compared to the iron-replete, protoporphyrin-deficient state of sideroblastic anemia.
incorrectas.C: A normal ferritin would understate the degree of iron accumulation that occurs in sideroblastic anemia, where ineffective erythropoiesis and unused mitochondrial iron drive stores upward over time, especially with repeated transfusions.
incorrectas.D: A markedly decreased ferritin paired with a high TIBC describes iron deficiency anemia, not sideroblastic anemia, which shows the opposite pattern of a high ferritin and low TIBC.

preguntas.q: What happens to total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) in sideroblastic anemia?

o.C: Markedly increased with a low ferritin

e.correcta: Because sideroblastic anemia is an iron-replete (even iron-loading) condition, the liver senses adequate-to-excess iron stores and downregulates transferrin production through the same feedback mechanism operative in any iron-overload state, causing TIBC to fall. This inverse relationship between ferritin and TIBC holds true whether the overload is due to sideroblastic anemia, hemochromatosis, or anemia of chronic disease.

incorrectas.A: An increased TIBC is the compensatory response seen when the liver detects low iron stores, as in iron deficiency anemia — the opposite physiologic signal from the iron-loaded state of sideroblastic anemia.
incorrectas.B: A normal TIBC would not reflect the iron-overloaded state that develops in sideroblastic anemia, where feedback suppression of transferrin synthesis is expected given elevated iron stores.
incorrectas.C: A markedly increased TIBC with a low ferritin describes iron deficiency anemia, the mirror-image iron study pattern compared to sideroblastic anemia's low TIBC and high ferritin.

preguntas.q: What is the expected serum iron level in sideroblastic anemia?

e.correcta: In sideroblastic anemia, iron is absorbed and delivered to erythroblasts normally (or in excess) but cannot be incorporated into heme due to impaired protoporphyrin synthesis, so it backs up into the circulation and mitochondria rather than being consumed for hemoglobin production, raising serum iron. This is a defining contrast with iron deficiency anemia, where serum iron is low because there simply isn't enough iron to begin with.

incorrectas.A: A decreased serum iron would instead suggest iron deficiency anemia or anemia of chronic disease, both of which limit the amount of iron reaching the plasma or erythroblasts — the opposite problem from sideroblastic anemia's iron-replete state.
incorrectas.C: A normal serum iron would understate the iron-loading physiology of sideroblastic anemia, where unused iron accumulates and raises circulating levels above normal.
incorrectas.D: An undetectable serum iron is inconsistent with any classic microcytic anemia pattern and specifically contradicts the iron-overload mechanism underlying sideroblastic anemia.

preguntas.q: What is the expected % transferrin saturation in sideroblastic anemia?

e.correcta: Since serum iron rises while TIBC (transferrin) falls in sideroblastic anemia — both consequences of the underlying iron-overload physiology — the ratio of serum iron to TIBC (% transferrin saturation) is increased. This combination of high serum iron, high ferritin, low TIBC, and high % saturation is essentially the same iron-study fingerprint seen in other iron-overload states like hereditary hemochromatosis.

incorrectas.A: A decreased % saturation is characteristic of iron deficiency anemia and, to a lesser degree, anemia of chronic disease — both states where either total iron or usable iron is reduced, unlike the iron-loaded state of sideroblastic anemia.
incorrectas.B: A normal % saturation would not capture the derangement produced when both serum iron rises and TIBC falls simultaneously, which pushes the ratio well above normal in sideroblastic anemia.
incorrectas.D: An undetectable % saturation would imply almost no circulating iron relative to binding capacity, which is the opposite of the iron-overloaded pattern actually seen in sideroblastic anemia.

preguntas.q: What is a first-line treatment for sideroblastic anemia caused by ALA synthase dysfunction or vitamin deficiency?

e.correcta: ALA synthase requires pyridoxal phosphate (the active form of vitamin B6) as an essential cofactor to catalyze the first step of heme synthesis; supplementing with pyridoxine can restore enzyme activity in B6-responsive congenital sideroblastic anemia and in acquired cases related to isoniazid therapy (which antagonizes B6), improving heme production and reducing mitochondrial iron accumulation.

incorrectas.B: Iron chelation therapy is used to manage the secondary iron overload that can develop from ineffective erythropoiesis or repeated transfusions in sideroblastic anemia, but it does not address the underlying enzymatic defect and is not the first-line treatment for the anemia itself.
incorrectas.C: Oral iron supplementation would be harmful in sideroblastic anemia, since the patient already has adequate-to-excess iron; the problem is a block in utilizing that iron for heme synthesis, not a lack of iron.
incorrectas.D: Folic acid corrects megaloblastic anemia from impaired DNA synthesis, an entirely different pathophysiology from the heme synthesis defect underlying sideroblastic anemia, so it would not correct this condition.

preguntas.q: Thalassemia classically produces a profoundly microcytic anemia, with MCV often falling below what threshold — out of proportion to the mildness of the anemia?

e.correcta: Because thalassemia results from a quantitative defect in globin chain production (rather than iron or heme availability), the bone marrow compensates by producing an increased number of very small red cells, often driving MCV below 70 fL even when hemoglobin is only mildly reduced. This mismatch — a strikingly low MCV relative to a mild degree of anemia, often with a normal or even increased RBC count — is a classic clue favoring thalassemia over iron deficiency anemia, where MCV reduction tends to track more proportionally with anemia severity.

incorrectas.A: 80–95 fL is the normal MCV range and would not reflect the classic microcytosis of thalassemia, which is typically far more pronounced than seen in most other microcytic anemias.
incorrectas.B: >100 fL describes macrocytosis, seen in conditions like B12/folate deficiency, and is essentially the opposite finding from the profound microcytosis characteristic of thalassemia.
incorrectas.C: 96–99 fL is within (or just above) the normal MCV range and does not represent the marked microcytosis expected in thalassemia, which is often more severe than in iron deficiency anemia at a comparable hemoglobin level.

preguntas.q: How does α-thalassemia with a single gene deletion typically present clinically?

e.correcta: With only one of the four α-globin genes deleted, the remaining three genes produce enough α-globin chains to maintain essentially normal hemoglobin synthesis and red cell indices, so affected individuals are asymptomatic silent carriers detected only through molecular testing or family screening — this represents the mildest point on the α-thalassemia severity spectrum.

incorrectas.A: A mild microcytic anemia (α-thalassemia trait) results from deletion of two of the four α-globin genes, not a single gene deletion, reflecting a greater reduction in α-globin output.
incorrectas.C: HbH disease, with its characteristic β4 tetramers and moderate-to-severe hemolytic anemia, results from deletion of three of the four α-globin genes — a much more severe genotype than the single-gene deletion described here.
incorrectas.D: Hydrops fetalis with Hb Barts (γ4 tetramers) occurs when all four α-globin genes are deleted, causing a complete absence of functional α-globin and is usually fatal in utero — far more severe than the asymptomatic single-gene deletion state.

preguntas.q: In α-thalassemia trait (two-gene deletion), which pattern of gene deletion carries a higher risk of producing severe thalassemia (HbH disease or hydrops fetalis) in the offspring of two carriers?

o.D: Compound heterozygous deletion of unrelated genes

e.correcta: In a cis deletion (--/αα), both missing α-globin genes are on the same chromosome, leaving one chromosome completely devoid of α-globin genes. If two carriers of the cis pattern (more common in Southeast Asian populations) have children, there is a real risk of inheriting a chromosome with zero α-genes from each parent, resulting in three-gene deletion (HbH disease) or four-gene deletion (Hb Barts hydrops fetalis) in the offspring.

incorrectas.B: In a trans deletion (-α/-α), one gene is missing from each of the two chromosomes, so every chromosome passed to offspring still carries at least one functional α-globin gene — this pattern (more common in African populations) essentially eliminates the risk of a fetus inheriting zero α-globin genes.
incorrectas.C: α-thalassemia deletions are not inherited in a classic autosomal dominant single-gene disease pattern; the risk to offspring depends specifically on which chromosomes carry the deletions (cis vs. trans), not simple dominant transmission.
incorrectas.D: The clinically important distinction is the cis/trans arrangement of deletions within the α-globin gene cluster on chromosome 16, not an unrelated compound heterozygous deletion of separate genes.

preguntas.q: Deletion of three of the four α-globin genes results in which condition, marked by excess β-globin chains forming an unstable tetramer?

e.correcta: With only one functional α-globin gene remaining, α-globin production falls so low that the excess unpaired β-globin chains associate with each other to form HbH (β4), an unstable tetramer with abnormally high oxygen affinity and poor tissue oxygen delivery; this produces a moderate-to-severe hemolytic, microcytic anemia known as HbH disease.

incorrectas.A: Hb Barts / hydrops fetalis results from deletion of all four α-globin genes, leading to excess γ-globin chains forming γ4 tetramers (Hb Barts), a condition far more severe than HbH disease and generally incompatible with life.
incorrectas.B: α-thalassemia trait, with only mild microcytic anemia and no significant hemolysis, results from a two-gene deletion — a milder genotype than the three-gene deletion described in this question.
incorrectas.D: Beta-thalassemia major results from mutations in the β-globin gene itself (on a different chromosome), not from α-globin gene deletions, and represents a completely separate genetic disorder from HbH disease.

preguntas.q: Patients with HbH disease (three-gene α-thalassemia deletion) retain a small amount of functional α-globin production from their single remaining gene. Why is this clinically significant?

o.A: It fully corrects the anemia so patients are asymptomatic
o.B: It causes iron overload requiring chelation therapy from birth
o.C: It converts the disease into a beta-thalassemia major phenotype
o.D: It allows formation of some HbF and HbA, preventing hydrops fetalis and lethality in utero

e.correcta: Even though three of four α-globin genes are deleted, the single remaining gene produces just enough α-globin to combine with γ-globin (forming HbF) and later β-globin (forming HbA) during fetal and postnatal life. This small but critical amount of normal hemoglobin is sufficient to prevent the complete absence of oxygen-carrying capacity seen with a four-gene deletion, allowing survival to birth and beyond — unlike Hb Barts hydrops fetalis, which is typically fatal in utero.

incorrectas.A: The residual α-globin production is enough to prevent fetal death but is far from sufficient to normalize hemoglobin synthesis — HbH disease still causes a clinically significant, moderate-to-severe hemolytic microcytic anemia, not a fully corrected, asymptomatic state.
incorrectas.B: Iron overload can develop over time in HbH disease from chronic hemolysis and increased erythropoietic drive (and especially with transfusions), but it is not an immediate, universal requirement for chelation from birth, and it is not the direct consequence of retaining a small amount of α-globin production.
incorrectas.C: Beta-thalassemia major is a distinct disease caused by β-globin gene mutations on a different chromosome; residual α-globin production in HbH disease does not convert the underlying genetic defect into a beta-globin disorder.

preguntas.q: Deletion of all four α-globin gene copies results in which fatal fetal condition?

e.correcta: With all four alpha-globin genes deleted, no alpha chains are produced, so no functional adult hemoglobin (HbA), fetal hemoglobin (HbF), or HbA2 can form since every one of them requires alpha chains as a partner. The excess gamma chains instead form Hb Barts (γ4) tetramers, which bind oxygen so tightly they cannot deliver it to tissues, causing severe intrauterine hypoxia, anasarca, and hydrops fetalis — a condition incompatible with life.

incorrectas.A: Beta-thalassemia major results from absent beta-globin production with normal alpha genes intact, and presents months after birth rather than in utero, because HbF (which does not require beta chains) is still protective at birth.
incorrectas.C: Hemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis) is caused by maternal antibodies against fetal Rh or ABO antigens crossing the placenta and destroying fetal RBCs, an immune mechanism unrelated to a globin gene deletion.
incorrectas.D: Hereditary spherocytosis results from defects in RBC membrane skeletal proteins such as spectrin or ankyrin, producing fragile spherical cells and extravascular hemolysis, a completely different mechanism from a globin gene deletion.

preguntas.q: In a fetus with deletion of all four alpha-globin gene copies, how much functional alpha-globin protein is produced?

o.B: Normal amounts, compensated by beta chains
o.D: Only in the bone marrow, not in peripheral blood

e.correcta: Because all four alpha-globin gene copies (two on each copy of chromosome 16) are deleted, there is no alpha-globin transcription at all, so zero functional alpha chains are made. Since every hemoglobin type — HbA, HbA2, and HbF — needs alpha chains as a partner, their complete absence means none of these hemoglobins can be assembled; excess gamma chains instead form the functionally useless Hb Barts (γ4), explaining why the condition presents as hydrops fetalis with ascites, effusions, and anasarca.

incorrectas.A: A reduced-but-present alpha-globin output describes the 1–3 gene deletion forms of alpha-thalassemia (silent carrier, trait, or HbH disease), where surviving alpha genes still permit some functional protein and a much milder phenotype.
incorrectas.B: Beta-globin chains cannot substitute for alpha-globin — a hemoglobin tetramer requires two alpha-like and two beta-like chains, so there is no compensatory pathway that rescues hemoglobin assembly when all alpha genes are lost.
incorrectas.D: Alpha-globin is a structural component of hemoglobin within mature circulating RBCs, not something confined to marrow precursors, so its complete absence affects oxygen-carrying capacity throughout the body, not just within the marrow.

preguntas.q: Which beta-globin genotype corresponds to the mildest, typically asymptomatic form of beta-thalassemia?

e.correcta: Beta-thalassemia minor (β/β+) retains one fully normal beta-globin allele, so enough HbA is still produced to prevent significant anemia. Patients are usually asymptomatic and are often discovered incidentally by an elevated RBC count with mild microcytosis, distinguishing this benign carrier state from the far more severe homozygous forms of the disease.

incorrectas.B: β0/β0 (beta-thalassemia major) means both alleles produce zero beta chains, causing severe, transfusion-dependent anemia presenting in infancy — the opposite end of the severity spectrum from minor.
incorrectas.C: β+/β+ still allows partial beta-chain output from both alleles, giving an intermediate phenotype that is more severe than heterozygous minor disease, since minor requires only one fully functional allele to stay largely asymptomatic.
incorrectas.D: A single alpha-globin gene deletion is the alpha-thalassemia silent carrier state, a completely separate gene locus and disease from beta-thalassemia, and does not describe beta-globin gene dosage at all.

preguntas.q: Which characteristic RBC morphology is seen on peripheral smear in beta-thalassemia?

e.correcta: In beta-thalassemia, decreased beta-globin chains create a relative excess of unpaired alpha chains and an imbalanced hemoglobin content per cell, leaving redundant RBC membrane surface area relative to the cell's volume. This redundancy produces a "bullseye" appearance on smear, with hemoglobin concentrated centrally and at the periphery but not in the mid-zone — the classic target cell.

incorrectas.A: Schistocytes are mechanically fragmented RBCs from microangiopathic processes like DIC or TTP, or from mechanical heart valves, reflecting physical shearing rather than a membrane surface excess from globin chain imbalance.
incorrectas.B: Spherocytes are small, dense, round cells that have lost membrane surface area (as in hereditary spherocytosis or warm autoimmune hemolysis) — essentially the opposite membrane change from the redundant membrane seen in thalassemia.
incorrectas.C: Sickle cells are crescent-shaped RBCs caused by polymerization of deoxygenated HbS, a structural point-mutation hemoglobinopathy rather than the quantitative chain-imbalance defect seen in thalassemia.

preguntas.q: Which beta-globin genotype produces the most severe form of beta-thalassemia, with severe anemia manifesting within the first few months of life?

e.correcta: The β0/β0 genotype means both beta-globin alleles are completely nonfunctional, producing no beta chains at all. As fetal hemoglobin (which doesn't need beta chains) declines during the first months of life, there is essentially no HbA to take its place, resulting in severe, transfusion-dependent anemia along with marked extramedullary hematopoiesis and skeletal remodeling.

incorrectas.A: β/β+ (minor) retains one fully normal beta allele, so enough HbA is still produced to keep patients asymptomatic or only mildly anemic — essentially the opposite severity extreme from major.
incorrectas.C: β+/β+ still permits some beta-chain output from both alleles, producing a milder, intermedia-like phenotype rather than the complete beta-chain absence and severity seen in β0/β0.
incorrectas.D: A single alpha-gene deletion is the alpha-thalassemia silent carrier state, clinically silent with normal hemoglobin, and unrelated to beta-thalassemia severity classification.

preguntas.q: Beta-thalassemia major typically becomes clinically apparent at what point in a child's life?

o.C: In utero, during the second trimester

e.correcta: At birth, HbF (α2γ2) still predominates and doesn't require beta-globin, so infants with the β0/β0 genotype are initially protected. As the normal physiologic switch from gamma- to beta-globin production occurs over the first several months of life, HbF declines and there is no HbA to replace it, so severe anemia typically emerges around 6 months of age.

incorrectas.B: Presentation immediately at birth would require the defect to affect a hemoglobin already dominant at birth (HbF), but beta-thalassemia specifically spares HbF production, delaying rather than causing immediate symptoms.
incorrectas.C: In utero, HbF dominates and does not depend on beta-globin, so a beta-chain defect does not manifest prenatally — this timing is more characteristic of severe alpha-thalassemia, where alpha chains needed for HbF itself are affected.
incorrectas.D: Adolescent onset is inconsistent with known globin switching physiology, since the gamma-to-beta transition is essentially complete by 6 months of age, meaning a beta-chain synthesis defect manifests in infancy, not years later.

preguntas.q: What explains why infants with beta-thalassemia major are not anemic immediately at birth?

o.A: High levels of fetal hemoglobin (HbF), which does not require beta-globin, are still protective
o.B: Maternal hemoglobin crosses the placenta and compensates
o.C: Alpha-globin synthesis is upregulated to compensate
o.D: Erythropoietin levels are physiologically low at birth, masking the defect

e.correcta: HbF is composed of two alpha and two gamma chains (α2γ2), so its production does not depend on beta-globin at all. Since HbF is still the dominant hemoglobin at birth, infants with a beta-globin defect are shielded from anemia until the normal postnatal gamma-to-beta switch depletes HbF and unmasks the underlying beta-chain deficiency several months later.

incorrectas.B: Maternal hemoglobin does not cross the placenta into fetal circulation — maternal and fetal blood compartments remain separate, and the fetus manufactures its own hemoglobin (HbF) throughout gestation.
incorrectas.C: Alpha-globin synthesis is not upregulated as a compensatory response in beta-thalassemia; rather, the excess unpaired alpha chains (from lack of beta partners) precipitate and damage RBC precursors, contributing to disease rather than protecting against it.
incorrectas.D: Erythropoietin physiology at birth is not the relevant protective mechanism here — protection comes specifically from which hemoglobin type is being made (HbF, not requiring beta chains), not from erythropoietin levels.

preguntas.q: In beta-thalassemia major, what abnormal hemoglobin species precipitates within RBC precursors and causes their destruction?

e.correcta: Because beta chains are absent or markedly reduced, the alpha chains that are produced have no beta partners to pair with. These unpaired alpha chains aggregate into insoluble α4 tetramers that precipitate within erythroid precursors in the marrow, damaging the cell membrane and triggering apoptosis — this ineffective erythropoiesis is a major driver of anemia and marrow expansion in beta-thalassemia major, distinct from peripheral hemolysis alone.

incorrectas.A: γ4 tetramers (Hb Barts) form in severe alpha-thalassemia when there is an excess of unpaired gamma chains due to absent alpha-globin — the mirror-image chain-imbalance problem to beta-thalassemia.
incorrectas.B: HbS polymers form in sickle cell disease from a structural point mutation in beta-globin (glutamic acid to valine) that causes deoxygenated hemoglobin to polymerize into rigid rods, a qualitative structural defect rather than a chain-imbalance problem.
incorrectas.D: Heinz bodies are precipitates of denatured, oxidized hemoglobin classically seen in G6PD deficiency after oxidative stress, a different mechanism entirely from the chain-imbalance precipitation seen in thalassemia.

preguntas.q: Which condition classically produces a "crewcut" appearance of the skull on X-ray due to marrow expansion?

e.correcta: In beta-thalassemia major, chronic severe anemia drives massive compensatory erythropoietin secretion and erythroid hyperplasia within the marrow. This expansion is especially pronounced in the flat bones of the skull, where new bone is laid down perpendicular to the skull surface, producing the characteristic "crewcut" or "hair-on-end" appearance on X-ray — reflecting the same marrow expansion process that also causes frontal bossing and maxillary overgrowth ("chipmunk facies").

incorrectas.A: Alpha-thalassemia trait (1–2 gene deletions) causes only mild microcytosis without significant anemia, so it does not generate the chronic erythropoietin drive needed to produce marrow expansion changes like crewcut skull.
incorrectas.B: Iron deficiency anemia causes microcytic anemia that typically develops more gradually and is usually less severe, and does not typically trigger the massive erythroid hyperplasia and skeletal remodeling seen in transfusion-dependent thalassemia major.
incorrectas.C: Aplastic anemia results from bone marrow failure with pancytopenia — a hypocellular marrow — the opposite process from marrow hyperplasia, so it would not cause expansile bony changes like crewcut skull.

preguntas.q: In beta-thalassemia major, which abdominal exam finding reflects extramedullary hematopoiesis compensating for ineffective erythropoiesis?

o.A: Isolated massive splenomegaly without hepatic involvement

e.correcta: Severe chronic hemolytic anemia in beta-thalassemia major drives extremely high erythropoietin levels, and when marrow capacity to expand is exceeded, the liver and spleen — organs with residual fetal hematopoietic potential — resume blood cell production. This extramedullary hematopoiesis, combined with the spleen's ongoing job of clearing damaged RBCs, causes both organs to enlarge, making hepatosplenomegaly a hallmark exam finding.

incorrectas.A: Isolated splenomegaly without hepatic involvement understates the process, since extramedullary hematopoiesis in beta-thalassemia major typically involves both the liver and spleen together, not the spleen alone.
incorrectas.C: Generalized lymphadenopathy is not a typical feature of thalassemia, since lymph nodes are not major sites of extramedullary hematopoiesis in this disease; their enlargement instead suggests infection or a lymphoproliferative process.
incorrectas.D: Parotid gland enlargement is associated with conditions like bulimia, sarcoidosis, or Sjögren syndrome, not with the erythropoietin-driven hematopoietic compensation seen in thalassemia.

preguntas.q: Which finding on peripheral blood smear reflects premature release of immature erythroid precursors from an overactive marrow in beta-thalassemia major?

e.correcta: In beta-thalassemia major, massive erythroid hyperplasia and ineffective erythropoiesis push the marrow to release erythroid precursors before they have fully matured and extruded their nucleus, so nucleated RBCs (normoblasts) appear in the peripheral blood — a marker of marrow stress and a high production/turnover state.

incorrectas.B: Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear DNA remnants retained within otherwise mature, enucleated RBCs, classically seen after splenectomy or functional asplenia (since the spleen normally clears them), not a marker of premature release of nucleated precursors.
incorrectas.C: Basophilic stippling reflects residual ribosomal RNA aggregates and is classically associated with lead poisoning or sideroblastic anemias; while it can co-occur in thalassemia, it does not represent release of whole nucleated precursors.
incorrectas.D: Reticulocytopenia (a low reticulocyte count) would indicate a hypoproliferative marrow, the opposite of what happens in beta-thalassemia major, where the marrow is markedly hyperproliferative, though ineffectively so.

preguntas.q: What term describes RBCs that are both abnormally shaped and unequal in size on peripheral smear, as seen in beta-thalassemia major?

e.correcta: "Anisocytosis" refers to unequal RBC size and "poikilocytosis" refers to abnormal RBC shape; when both features are present together, as commonly seen in the severely dysplastic, ineffective erythropoiesis of beta-thalassemia major, the combined term "anisopoikilocytosis" is used to capture the full range of morphologic abnormality on smear.

incorrectas.A: Anisocytosis alone describes only the variation in RBC size (reflected quantitatively as an elevated RDW) without addressing the shape abnormalities also seen in thalassemia, so it only captures part of the picture.
incorrectas.B: Poikilocytosis alone describes only abnormal shapes, such as target cells or teardrop cells, without addressing the size variation that is also prominent in thalassemia smears.
incorrectas.D: Polychromasia refers to RBCs that appear bluish-gray on Wright-Giemsa stain due to residual ribosomal RNA in young reticulocytes, reflecting increased marrow output rather than a description of size or shape variation.

preguntas.q: Hemoglobin electrophoresis in a patient with beta-thalassemia major would be expected to show which pattern?

o.B: Normal HbA with elevated Hb Barts
o.C: Elevated HbA with reduced HbF and HbA2
o.D: Little to no HbA, with compensatory increases in HbA2 and HbF

e.correcta: Because both beta-globin alleles are essentially nonfunctional in beta-thalassemia major (β0/β0), there is little to no HbA (α2β2) produced. The marrow compensates by upregulating the alternative hemoglobins that do not require normal beta-chains — HbA2 (α2δ2) and HbF (α2γ2) — so electrophoresis characteristically shows both of these elevated alongside a near-absent HbA band.

incorrectas.A: Predominant HbS reflects homozygous sickle cell disease, a structural beta-globin point mutation (HbSS) rather than the quantitative beta-chain absence of thalassemia; HbA is absent there for a different reason (both alleles make abnormal HbS, not zero beta protein).
incorrectas.B: Elevated Hb Barts (γ4) is seen in severe alpha-thalassemia when alpha chains are deficient, not in beta-thalassemia, and HbA would also not be "normal" in thalassemia major since beta-globin is essentially absent.
incorrectas.C: Elevated HbA would require adequate beta-globin production, precisely what is deficient in beta-thalassemia major, making this pattern physiologically inconsistent with the disease.

preguntas.q: As a general rule, most microcytic anemias are also associated with which additional RBC finding?

e.correcta: Microcytic anemias (iron deficiency, thalassemia, sideroblastic anemia, anemia of chronic disease) typically result from defective hemoglobin synthesis, whether from lack of iron, globin chain imbalance, or a heme synthesis defect. Since hemoglobin content is what gives RBCs their central color intensity, reduced hemoglobin production causes RBCs to appear pale centrally (increased central pallor) as well as small, so microcytic anemias are usually grouped together as "microcytic, hypochromic."

incorrectas.A: "Hyperchromia" (increased hemoglobin concentration per cell) is not a standard descriptor of typical RBC pathology, since hemoglobin concentration is capped by solubility; dense-appearing cells like spherocytes are described by their own term, not as hyperchromic.
incorrectas.C: Normal chromicity would imply normal hemoglobin content per cell, but the very defect causing microcytosis — reduced hemoglobin synthesis — is what also causes pallor, so a purely microcytic-but-normochromic pattern is not the typical association.
incorrectas.D: Macrocytosis (larger than normal RBCs) is the opposite size abnormality from microcytosis, seen in conditions like B12 or folate deficiency, and is not paired with microcytic anemias.

preguntas.q: Which two vitamins are essential cofactors for the synthesis of DNA precursors, such that their deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia?

e.correcta: Folate (as tetrahydrofolate) donates one-carbon units required for purine synthesis and for converting dUMP to dTMP (thymidylate synthesis), while vitamin B12 is required as a cofactor for methionine synthase, which simultaneously regenerates tetrahydrofolate from its methylated, "trapped" form. Deficiency of either vitamin impairs DNA synthesis, while RNA and protein synthesis continue, producing the enlarged, immature-appearing erythroid precursors that define megaloblastic anemia.

incorrectas.B: Thiamine (B1) and niacin (B3) function in energy metabolism as cofactors for pyruvate dehydrogenase and other dehydrogenase complexes; their deficiencies cause beriberi/Wernicke-Korsakoff and pellagra respectively, not megaloblastic anemia.
incorrectas.C: Pyridoxine (B6) is a cofactor for transamination and heme synthesis (ALA synthase), and biotin is a cofactor for carboxylation reactions; their deficiencies cause sideroblastic anemia and dermatitis/alopecia respectively, not the DNA-synthesis defect of megaloblastic anemia.
incorrectas.D: Riboflavin (B2) and pantothenic acid (B5) are cofactors in the electron transport chain and coenzyme A synthesis respectively, unrelated to nucleotide or DNA precursor synthesis.

preguntas.q: Deficiency of folate or vitamin B12 primarily impairs which cellular process, leading to megaloblastic anemia?

e.correcta: Both folate and B12 are required cofactors in one-carbon metabolism pathways that generate purines and thymidylate for DNA replication. When either vitamin is deficient, rapidly dividing cells like erythroid precursors cannot synthesize DNA fast enough to keep pace with cytoplasmic growth and hemoglobin accumulation, producing the nuclear-cytoplasmic maturation mismatch that defines megaloblastic change.

incorrectas.A: Heme synthesis requires iron, vitamin B6 as a cofactor for ALA synthase, and several enzymatic steps in the mitochondria and cytosol — it is not the pathway disrupted by folate or B12 deficiency, and defects here (B6 deficiency, lead poisoning) cause sideroblastic, not megaloblastic, anemia.
incorrectas.B: Globin chain synthesis defects, as in thalassemia, arise from gene mutations or deletions affecting globin protein translation, an entirely separate mechanism from the nucleotide synthesis defect of folate/B12 deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Iron absorption occurs in the duodenum via distinct transporters (DMT1, ferroportin) and is unrelated to folate or B12 metabolism; iron deficiency causes microcytic, not macrocytic, anemia.

preguntas.q: Impaired division of RBC precursors with continued cytoplasmic growth and enlargement leads to which type of anemia?

e.correcta: When DNA synthesis is impaired (as in folate or B12 deficiency) but RNA and protein synthesis continue relatively normally, erythroid precursors keep growing in cytoplasmic volume and accumulating hemoglobin without dividing on schedule. This mismatch produces abnormally large precursors and mature RBCs (megaloblasts and macro-ovalocytes), defining megaloblastic macrocytic anemia.

incorrectas.A: Microcytic hypochromic anemia results from impaired hemoglobin synthesis (iron deficiency, thalassemia), producing smaller, not larger, cells — the opposite defect from delayed nuclear maturation.
incorrectas.B: Normocytic normochromic anemia (as from acute blood loss or many chronic diseases) implies normal cell size and hemoglobin content, which would not result from a DNA synthesis defect that specifically causes cellular enlargement.
incorrectas.C: Aplastic anemia results from bone marrow failure with loss of hematopoietic stem cells and pancytopenia, a fundamentally different process from a nucleotide synthesis defect causing megaloblastic change in precursors that are still present.

preguntas.q: In megaloblastic anemia, maturation of which cellular component lags behind the other in erythroid precursors, producing nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony?

o.A: The cytoplasm lags behind nuclear maturation
o.B: The nucleus lags behind cytoplasmic maturation
o.C: Both mature at the same accelerated rate
o.D: Mitochondrial maturation lags behind ribosomal maturation

e.correcta: DNA synthesis (needed for nuclear maturation and cell division) depends on folate- and B12-driven nucleotide synthesis, so when these vitamins are deficient the nucleus remains immature-looking (open, fine chromatin) relative to the cytoplasm, which continues to mature and accumulate hemoglobin normally since RNA/protein synthesis is not folate/B12-dependent. This mismatch — "nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony" — is the defining cytologic feature of megaloblastic change on bone marrow biopsy.

incorrectas.A: If cytoplasmic maturation lagged behind the nucleus, small immature cytoplasm would be seen alongside an already-condensed nucleus — the reverse of what is actually observed, and inconsistent with a DNA synthesis defect.
incorrectas.C: Accelerated maturation of both components together would produce no asynchrony at all; the entire pathologic hallmark of megaloblastic anemia is the mismatch between the two compartments, not simultaneous acceleration.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial versus ribosomal maturation is not the relevant comparison in megaloblastic anemia; the clinically important asynchrony is specifically between nuclear (DNA-dependent) and cytoplasmic maturation.

preguntas.q: Megaloblastic anemia is classified under which broader category of anemia based on mean corpuscular volume (MCV)?

o.D: It does not fit standard MCV classification

e.correcta: Because impaired DNA synthesis allows erythroid precursors' cytoplasm to keep growing without proportional division, the resulting mature RBCs are abnormally large, giving an elevated MCV (typically >100 fL). This places megaloblastic anemia squarely in the macrocytic anemia category, alongside other macrocytic causes like liver disease and alcohol use, though it is distinguished by its characteristic megaloblastic precursor morphology.

incorrectas.B: Microcytic anemia (low MCV) reflects impaired hemoglobin synthesis, as in iron deficiency or thalassemia — a completely different mechanism (too little hemoglobin per cell) than the DNA synthesis defect underlying megaloblastic anemia.
incorrectas.C: Normocytic anemia (normal MCV) is typically seen in anemia of chronic disease, acute blood loss, or hemolysis without marked reticulocytosis, none of which describes the characteristically enlarged cells of megaloblastic anemia.
incorrectas.D: MCV classification is precisely how megaloblastic anemia is categorized clinically, as a subtype of macrocytic anemia, so this option incorrectly implies it falls outside standard anemia classification schemes.

preguntas.q: Which oral finding is classically associated with megaloblastic anemia due to folate or B12 deficiency?

e.correcta: Folate and B12 are needed for DNA synthesis in all rapidly dividing tissues, not just the bone marrow — the tongue's epithelium turns over quickly, so deficiency causes atrophy of the lingual papillae, producing a smooth, red, and often sore tongue known as glossitis, a classic extra-hematologic clue pointing toward megaloblastic anemia.

incorrectas.A: Aphthous ulcers (canker sores) are typically due to autoimmune, traumatic, or idiopathic mucosal breakdown and are not the classic tongue finding linked specifically to folate/B12 deficiency, unlike the diffuse atrophic glossitis seen there.
incorrectas.C: Leukoplakia is a white, often premalignant mucosal patch associated with chronic irritation such as tobacco or alcohol use, and is not a feature of vitamin-deficiency-related megaloblastic anemia.
incorrectas.D: Parotid gland swelling is seen in conditions like bulimia, mumps, or Sjögren syndrome, not as a classic finding of folate/B12 deficiency-related megaloblastic anemia.

preguntas.q: Besides RBC precursors, megaloblastic changes from folate/B12 deficiency are also seen in which other cell populations?

o.A: Only terminally differentiated, non-dividing cells like neurons
o.D: Other rapidly-dividing cells, such as intestinal epithelial cells

e.correcta: Because the underlying defect is impaired DNA synthesis rather than something specific to erythroid cells, any tissue with a high rate of cell turnover is vulnerable. This includes intestinal epithelium (leading to malabsorption and diarrhea that can further worsen the deficiency), oral/tongue mucosa (glossitis), and precursors of other hematopoietic lineages (contributing to hypersegmented neutrophils and sometimes mild leukopenia or thrombocytopenia in severe cases).

incorrectas.A: Neurons are actually affected in B12 (not folate) deficiency, but through a different mechanism — impaired methylmalonyl-CoA metabolism causing abnormal myelin synthesis (subacute combined degeneration) — not because neurons are dividing, since mature neurons do not divide at all.
incorrectas.B: Skeletal muscle cells are largely postmitotic in adults and are not classically affected by megaloblastic change, since muscle is not a preferentially high-turnover tissue the way marrow or gut epithelium are.
incorrectas.C: Mature circulating lymphocytes are not actively dividing in the periphery; it is the actively proliferating precursor pools in tissues like marrow and gut epithelium, not fully differentiated circulating cells, that show megaloblastic changes.

preguntas.q: Folate deficiency due to inadequate dietary intake typically develops over what time frame, given the body's folate stores?

o.D: It never develops from diet alone, only from malabsorption

e.correcta: The body's folate reserves, stored primarily in the liver, are relatively small and turn over quickly since folate participates continuously in one-carbon metabolism.
