incorrectas.B: Spherocytes do not disappear after splenectomy; what disappears is their premature destruction. The morphologic abnormality itself remains a permanent feature of this genetic disease.
incorrectas.C: Schistocytes are fragmented RBCs from mechanical shearing (e.g., microangiopathic hemolytic anemia or mechanical heart valves), a completely different process from the membrane skeleton defect that produces spherocytes; splenectomy does not convert one cell type into the other.

preguntas.q: What red blood cell inclusion characteristically appears on peripheral smear after splenectomy in a patient with hereditary spherocytosis?

e.correcta: Howell-Jolly bodies are small nuclear remnants (fragments of DNA) that persist in red cells because the spleen's macrophages normally pit them out during the cells' passage through splenic sinusoids. Once the spleen is removed (or nonfunctional, as in autosplenectomy from sickle cell disease), this quality-control mechanism is lost, so Howell-Jolly bodies accumulate and become a reliable marker of absent or hypofunctioning splenic tissue.

incorrectas.A: Basophilic stippling reflects residual ribosomal RNA aggregates and is classically associated with lead poisoning, thalassemia, or other disorders of hemoglobin synthesis, not specifically with loss of splenic pitting function.
incorrectas.C: Heinz bodies are denatured, precipitated hemoglobin (seen in G6PD deficiency) that are normally removed by splenic macrophages performing 'bite' removal, creating bite cells — but the finding classically taught for a post-splenectomy or asplenic smear is Howell-Jolly bodies, not persistent Heinz bodies.
incorrectas.D: Pappenheimer bodies are iron-containing (siderotic) granules seen in conditions of iron overload or sideroblastic anemia; they are not the classic marker of splenic absence that Howell-Jolly bodies represent.

preguntas.q: Sickle cell anemia typically causes anemia with which mean corpuscular volume (MCV) classification?

e.correcta: Sickle cell anemia is a hemolytic anemia caused by an abnormal hemoglobin molecule (HbS) rather than a defect in globin chain production or DNA synthesis, so the red cells that are made are of normal size — the MCV is typically normocytic. This places sickle cell anemia in the same broad category as other hemolytic anemias (like hereditary spherocytosis and G6PD deficiency), distinguishing it from anemias caused by impaired hemoglobin synthesis or impaired DNA synthesis.

incorrectas.B: Microcytic anemia results from defects in hemoglobin production, such as iron deficiency or the thalassemias (reduced globin chain synthesis); sickle cell disease does not reduce the amount of hemoglobin made per cell, so cells remain normal-sized.
incorrectas.C: Macrocytic anemia (non-megaloblastic) is seen in conditions like liver disease or alcohol use, reflecting altered membrane lipid content, not a feature of sickle hemoglobin polymerization.
incorrectas.D: Megaloblastic anemia is a subtype of macrocytic anemia caused by impaired DNA synthesis (B12 or folate deficiency), producing nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony; this is unrelated to the point mutation in beta-globin that causes sickle cell disease.

preguntas.q: Through which hemolytic mechanism(s) does sickle cell anemia destroy red blood cells?

e.correcta: Sickled cells repeatedly sickle and de-sickle as they pass through the microcirculation, and each cycle progressively damages the red cell membrane. Some of these damaged cells rupture directly within blood vessels (intravascular hemolysis, contributing to the low haptoglobin and hemoglobinuria seen in sickle cell disease), while others are recognized as abnormal and cleared by splenic and hepatic macrophages (extravascular hemolysis) — making this a combined mechanism, unlike diseases that are purely one or the other.

incorrectas.A: Purely intravascular hemolysis (as in PNH or mechanical hemolysis from a prosthetic valve) does not capture the full picture in sickle cell disease, where macrophage-mediated extravascular destruction of damaged sickled cells also plays a major role.
incorrectas.B: Sickle cell disease causes substantial hemolysis — shortened RBC lifespan, reticulocytosis, elevated indirect bilirubin, and low haptoglobin are all hallmark findings, so hemolysis is far from minimal.
incorrectas.D: Purely extravascular hemolysis (as classically emphasized in hereditary spherocytosis) understates sickle cell disease, where repeated membrane damage from sickling cycles also causes direct intravascular lysis.

preguntas.q: Sickle cell anemia results from a point mutation in which hemoglobin globin chain?

e.correcta: Adult hemoglobin (HbA) is composed of two alpha and two beta chains; sickle cell disease arises from a single point mutation in the beta-globin gene (HBB) on chromosome 11, which is why the disease does not manifest until beta-globin production ramps up after birth (as HbF, which contains gamma chains instead of beta chains, declines). This beta-chain specificity also explains why sickle cell trait/disease severity is modified by co-inherited alpha-thalassemia or persistent HbF production.

incorrectas.B: Alpha-globin gene defects cause the alpha-thalassemias (due to gene deletions), not sickle cell disease; alpha chains are shared by HbA, HbA2, and HbF, so an alpha chain mutation would affect fetal hemoglobin too, unlike sickle cell disease which spares HbF.
incorrectas.C: Gamma-globin chains pair with alpha chains to form HbF, the predominant hemoglobin in fetal life and early infancy; this is exactly why sickle cell disease is essentially asymptomatic at birth — HbF's gamma chains, not beta chains, dominate at that stage.
incorrectas.D: Delta-globin chains form the minor adult hemoglobin HbA2 (a2δ2); mutations here are irrelevant to sickle cell pathophysiology, which is specifically a beta-globin chain disorder.

preguntas.q: The point mutation causing sickle cell anemia replaces glutamic acid at position 6 of the beta-globin chain with which hydrophobic amino acid?

e.correcta: The HBB gene mutation (GAG→GTG) substitutes the negatively charged, hydrophilic glutamic acid with the small, nonpolar, hydrophobic amino acid valine at position 6 of the beta-globin chain. This creates a hydrophobic patch on deoxygenated HbS molecules that allows them to polymerize into rigid fibers, distorting the red cell into the classic sickle shape — the entire disease phenotype traces back to this single hydrophobic substitution.

incorrectas.A: Isoleucine is also a hydrophobic branched amino acid, but it is not the residue substituted in sickle hemoglobin; using it as a distractor tests whether you know the exact clinically relevant substitution rather than just 'any hydrophobic amino acid.'
incorrectas.C: Lysine substitution at this same position 6 (glutamic acid → lysine) actually defines a different disease, hemoglobin C (HbC), which causes a milder hemolytic anemia with target cells and HbC crystals — a useful contrast showing that the exact substituted residue, not just the position, determines the disease.
incorrectas.D: Leucine is another hydrophobic amino acid but is not the residue involved in the HbS mutation; the specific valine substitution is what confers the polymerization tendency unique to sickle hemoglobin.

preguntas.q: Approximately what percentage of African Americans carry the sickle cell (HbS) allele in heterozygous (trait) form?

e.correcta: About 8-10% of African Americans carry one copy of the HbS allele (sickle cell trait), a prevalence maintained at this relatively high level because heterozygous carriers gain a survival advantage against Plasmodium falciparum malaria — a classic example of heterozygote advantage/balanced polymorphism in population genetics.

incorrectas.A: A carrier rate of 1-2% would be far too low to explain the disease burden of sickle cell disease seen clinically and does not reflect the actual selective pressure malaria has exerted on this allele in populations of African descent.
incorrectas.B: 20-25% overstates the carrier frequency; while malaria-endemic regions do have meaningfully elevated HbS allele frequencies compared to non-endemic populations, this figure is higher than the commonly cited 8-10% for African Americans.
incorrectas.D: 40-50% would imply nearly half the population carries the trait, which is inconsistent with observed sickle cell disease incidence (since disease requires two copies) and greatly overstates the actual allele frequency.

preguntas.q: The high prevalence of the sickle cell allele in populations of African descent is thought to result from a protective effect against infection with which organism?

e.correcta: Plasmodium falciparum causes the most severe form of malaria and preferentially infects and matures within red blood cells; HbS polymerization under the low-oxygen conditions created by the parasite's metabolism promotes sickling of infected cells, which are then more readily cleared by the spleen before the parasite can complete its life cycle. This selective pressure explains why the HbS allele frequency tracks closely with historical P. falciparum-endemic regions of sub-Saharan Africa.

incorrectas.B: Plasmodium vivax causes a generally milder form of malaria and preferentially infects reticulocytes rather than mature RBCs broadly; the protective association with sickle trait is specifically strongest and best established for P. falciparum, the more lethal species.
incorrectas.C: Trypanosoma cruzi causes Chagas disease, a completely different vector-borne parasitic infection unrelated to red blood cell hemoglobin polymorphisms; it has no established relationship with the selection of the HbS allele.
incorrectas.D: Plasmodium malariae causes a milder, more chronic form of malaria and is not the species classically linked to the evolutionary selection pressure that maintains the sickle cell allele at high frequency.

preguntas.q: Does sickle cell trait (heterozygous, a single HbS allele) confer protection against malaria?

o.A: No, only homozygous sickle cell disease is protective
o.B: No, trait carriers have no protective advantage
o.C: Yes, but only against Plasmodium vivax
o.D: Yes, trait carriers are relatively protected

e.correcta: Sickle cell trait carriers make enough HbS that parasite-infected red cells are prone to sickling and premature splenic clearance, reducing the parasite's ability to replicate, while carriers make enough normal HbA to avoid the severe clinical manifestations of sickle cell disease. This heterozygote advantage is the textbook explanation for why the HbS allele persists at high frequency despite being harmful in homozygous form — a classic balanced polymorphism.

incorrectas.A: This gets the biology backwards: patients with full sickle cell disease actually suffer severe complications (functional asplenia, vaso-occlusion) that increase overall infection risk and mortality, so the evolutionary advantage is attributed to the heterozygous trait state, not homozygous disease.
incorrectas.B: If trait carriers had no advantage, there would be no selective pressure to maintain the allele at such high frequency in malaria-endemic regions; the entire balanced polymorphism model depends on trait carriers having a real, if partial, survival benefit.
incorrectas.C: The protective effect of sickle trait is classically attributed to Plasmodium falciparum, the most lethal and most red-cell-selective malaria species, not P. vivax.

preguntas.q: Sickle cell disease (as opposed to trait) arises from inheriting how many abnormal beta-globin genes, and what resulting proportion of hemoglobin in RBCs is HbS?

o.A: Two abnormal genes; greater than 90% HbS

e.correcta: Sickle cell disease requires inheriting the abnormal HBB allele from both parents (homozygous, HbSS), meaning essentially all of the beta-globin produced is the sickle variant, so more than 90% of the hemoglobin in each red cell is HbS. This near-total replacement of normal HbA is what makes disease-level sickling so much more frequent and severe than in trait carriers, whose cells contain a mix of roughly half HbA and half HbS.

incorrectas.B: One abnormal gene with ~40% HbS describes sickle cell trait, not disease — trait carriers retain enough normal beta-globin (HbA) to prevent significant sickling under normal physiologic conditions, which is why trait is usually clinically silent.
incorrectas.C: An even 50/50 mix of HbS and HbA is roughly what is seen in trait (heterozygotes), not disease; disease requires both beta-globin alleles to be abnormal, driving the HbS fraction much higher than 50%.
incorrectas.D: Humans only have two alleles of the beta-globin gene (one per chromosome 11), so 'three abnormal genes' is not biologically possible for this autosomal locus.

preguntas.q: Besides sickle cells, what other characteristic red blood cell morphology is seen on peripheral smear in sickle cell disease?

e.correcta: Target cells form when a red cell has excess membrane surface area relative to its hemoglobin content, giving it a 'bullseye' appearance on smear; in sickle cell disease this reflects the altered membrane and cell volume changes that accompany chronic sickling, and target cells are notably present in sickle cell disease but not typically in sickle cell trait, helping distinguish the two on smear.

incorrectas.A: Schistocytes are fragmented red cells produced by mechanical shearing forces, as seen in microangiopathic hemolytic anemias (TTP/HUS/DIC) or mechanical heart valves — a different mechanism from the membrane and hemoglobin-content changes that produce target cells in sickle cell disease.
incorrectas.C: Spherocytes arise from loss of membrane surface area relative to volume, the opposite membrane change from target cells, and are the hallmark of hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune hemolytic anemia rather than sickle cell disease.
incorrectas.D: Acanthocytes ('spur cells') have irregular spiky projections from abnormal membrane lipid composition, classically seen in liver disease or abetalipoproteinemia, not as a characteristic finding of sickle cell disease.

preguntas.q: How do infants with sickle cell disease typically present in the newborn period, and why?

o.A: Asymptomatic, because high HbF levels inhibit sickling
o.B: Symptomatic with severe hemolysis, because HbF is absent at birth
o.C: Symptomatic with vaso-occlusive crises from birth
o.D: Asymptomatic, because of a coexisting alpha-thalassemia trait

e.correcta: At birth, fetal hemoglobin (HbF, composed of alpha and gamma chains) still makes up the majority of hemoglobin, and because HbF does not participate in the polymerization that drives sickling, newborns with sickle cell disease are typically asymptomatic. As HbF production declines over the first several months of life and beta-chain-containing HbS increasingly predominates, sickling-related symptoms (vaso-occlusion, dactylitis, hemolysis) begin to emerge — which is also the physiologic rationale behind hydroxyurea therapy, which works partly by increasing HbF production.

incorrectas.B: This reverses the actual physiology — HbF is not absent at birth, it is the dominant hemoglobin, and its presence is precisely what protects against sickling in the newborn period rather than causing early hemolysis.
incorrectas.C: Vaso-occlusive crises are not typically seen immediately at birth; they emerge later in infancy as HbF declines and HbS becomes the predominant hemoglobin, allowing polymerization and sickling to occur under stress.
incorrectas.D: While co-inherited alpha-thalassemia can modify disease severity by reducing intracellular HbS concentration, the classic explanation for newborn asymptomatic status is the high HbF level, not an alpha-thalassemia trait.

preguntas.q: Which form of hemoglobin protects against polymerization and sickling in patients with sickle cell disease?

e.correcta: HbF (α2γ2) interferes with the polymerization of deoxygenated HbS because gamma chains do not participate efficiently in the same intermolecular contacts that HbS chains use to form rigid polymers. This is why elevated HbF — whether from young age, hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin, or pharmacologic induction with hydroxyurea — reduces sickling frequency and severity, and it's the mechanistic basis for one of the main disease-modifying treatments in sickle cell disease.

incorrectas.B: HbA (α2β2) is the normal adult hemoglobin that is markedly reduced or absent in sickle cell disease (since both beta-globin alleles are abnormal); it is not the protective hemoglobin variant being tested here, and in sickle trait it is the coexisting HbA that limits sickling, not HbF.
incorrectas.C: HbA2 (α2δ2) is a minor adult hemoglobin component (normally only a few percent of total hemoglobin) and does not play a significant protective role against HbS polymerization.
incorrectas.D: HbS itself is the polymerizing, disease-causing hemoglobin — it is not protective at any concentration; higher HbS concentration, not lower, increases the likelihood and severity of polymerization and sickling.

preguntas.q: In sickle cell anemia, chronic compensatory extramedullary hematopoiesis initially causes enlargement of which organs?

o.D: Bone marrow expansion only, without organ enlargement

e.correcta: Chronic hemolysis drives sustained erythropoietin secretion, which not only expands the bone marrow but also reactivates extramedullary hematopoiesis in the liver and spleen — organs that performed blood cell production during fetal life and retain the capacity to resume it under sufficient erythropoietic drive. Early in sickle cell disease this manifests as hepatosplenomegaly (with the spleen initially enlarged from macrophage hyperplasia), though later in the disease repeated splenic infarcts cause the spleen to shrink and fibrose (autosplenectomy) while the liver may remain enlarged.

incorrectas.A: The kidneys are not a site of extramedullary hematopoiesis; they are affected in sickle cell disease through a different mechanism — vaso-occlusive microinfarcts in the medulla causing papillary necrosis and impaired concentrating ability, not compensatory blood cell production.
incorrectas.B: The pancreas is not a classic site of extramedullary hematopoiesis in chronic hemolytic anemias; the liver and spleen are the organs that retain fetal hematopoietic potential and are recruited under chronic erythropoietin stimulation.
incorrectas.D: Extramedullary hematopoiesis by definition involves blood cell production occurring outside the bone marrow, in organs like the liver and spleen, which is exactly why those organs become enlarged — this option incorrectly denies that organ enlargement occurs.

preguntas.q: Expansion of hematopoiesis into the facial bones in sickle cell anemia (as in other chronic severe hemolytic anemias) produces what characteristic clinical finding?

e.correcta: Sustained erythropoietin drive from chronic hemolysis causes marrow hyperplasia that expands into the maxilla and other facial bones, producing the characteristic 'chipmunk facies' seen in severe chronic hemolytic anemias including sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia major. This is the clinical (physical exam) correlate of marrow expansion, distinct from the radiographic finding seen on imaging.

incorrectas.B: 'Crew-cut' skull X-ray appearance (thickened diploe with perpendicular striations) reflects the same underlying marrow expansion process but describes a radiographic finding on skull imaging, not the clinical facial appearance that 'chipmunk facies' specifically names.
incorrectas.C: Leontiasis ossea is a term more classically associated with fibrous dysplasia or advanced Paget disease of bone, referring to progressive facial bone enlargement from a different pathologic process (abnormal bone remodeling), not erythropoietin-driven marrow expansion.
incorrectas.D: Frontal bossing describes prominence of the forehead and is seen in various congenital and metabolic conditions (e.g., rickets, acromegaly), but it is not the specific term used for the marrow-expansion facial change of chronic hemolytic anemia.

preguntas.q: Irreversible sickling of red blood cells in sickle cell anemia produces microvascular complications through what underlying process?

e.correcta: Once red cells become irreversibly sickled, their rigid, elongated shape prevents them from deforming to pass through narrow capillaries, causing them to physically plug small vessels — vaso-occlusion. This process underlies most of the acute complications of sickle cell disease, including painful crises, dactylitis, acute chest syndrome, splenic infarction, and renal papillary necrosis, all stemming from downstream tissue ischemia at the site of the blockage.

incorrectas.A: Vasospasm refers to abnormal smooth muscle-mediated vessel constriction (as in Raynaud phenomenon or Prinzmetal angina), not physical blockage by misshapen cells; the mechanism in sickle cell disease is mechanical occlusion, not spasm.
incorrectas.C: Vasculitis is inflammation and damage of the vessel wall itself (as in ANCA-associated vasculitis or polyarteritis nodosa), a fundamentally different immune-mediated process from the mechanical plugging of vessels by rigid sickled cells.
incorrectas.D: Thrombotic microangiopathy involves platelet-rich microthrombi damaging small vessels (as in TTP/HUS), producing schistocytes and thrombocytopenia; sickle cell vaso-occlusion is caused by rigid cell shape blocking flow, not by a primary clotting/platelet-consumption process.

preguntas.q: Vaso-occlusive infarcts in the small bones of the hands and feet in a young child with sickle cell disease classically cause what presentation?

o.A: Dactylitis (painful swelling of the hands and feet)
o.D: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

e.correcta: In infants and young children, the metacarpals and metatarsals still contain active red marrow, making them vulnerable to vaso-occlusive infarction; the resulting painful, symmetric swelling of the hands and/or feet is termed dactylitis (or 'hand-foot syndrome') and is often the first clinical manifestation of sickle cell disease once fetal hemoglobin levels decline enough to permit sickling.

incorrectas.B: Osteomyelitis is bone infection, notably with Salmonella species in sickle cell disease (due to gut translocation combined with functional asplenia and ischemic bone from vaso-occlusion predisposing to infection), but it is a distinct complication from the acute vaso-occlusive infarction that directly causes dactylitis.
incorrectas.C: Acute chest syndrome results from vaso-occlusion within the pulmonary microcirculation, not the small bones of the extremities; it presents with chest pain, hypoxia, and new infiltrates rather than hand/foot swelling.
incorrectas.D: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head is a vaso-occlusive complication of sickle cell disease, but it typically presents later (often in adolescents or adults) as hip pain, and is a different anatomic site from the small bones affected in dactylitis.

preguntas.q: Repeated splenic infarctions over time in a patient with sickle cell disease lead to which complication?

e.correcta: Recurrent vaso-occlusive infarcts progressively destroy splenic tissue, leading over years to a small, shrunken, fibrotic, non-functional spleen — a process called autosplenectomy. The brownish color of the atrophic spleen reflects hemosiderin deposition from the repeated infarctions and hemorrhage, and functionally the patient becomes asplenic even though no surgery was performed.

incorrectas.B: While splenomegaly can be seen early in sickle cell disease (due to macrophage hyperplasia from extramedullary hematopoiesis and increased red cell destruction), repeated infarction over time causes progressive fibrosis and shrinkage rather than persistent enlargement into adulthood.
incorrectas.D: Splenic rupture is an acute, often traumatic or acute-sequestration-related event causing sudden hemorrhage, a different (and less typical) complication from the chronic, progressive fibrotic atrophy that defines autosplenectomy.
incorrectas.A: Splenic abscess results from infection seeding splenic tissue, a distinct infectious complication rather than the progressive ischemic fibrosis and atrophy caused directly by recurrent vaso-occlusive infarcts.

preguntas.q: Autosplenectomy in sickle cell disease increases susceptibility to infection with which category of organisms?

o.A: Encapsulated organisms (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae)

e.correcta: The spleen is critical for clearing encapsulated bacteria because these organisms rely on their polysaccharide capsule to resist phagocytosis unless first opsonized by antibody and complement — a process that depends heavily on splenic macrophages and marginal zone B cells for efficient antibody production and clearance. Once autosplenectomy occurs, patients (especially children) lose this defense and become highly susceptible to overwhelming infections with encapsulated organisms like S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae, which is why they require pneumococcal/Hib vaccination and often prophylactic penicillin.

incorrectas.B: Intracellular organisms like Listeria and Mycobacteria are primarily controlled by cell-mediated immunity (T cells and macrophage activation via interferon-gamma), a defense system that is not the specific function lost with splenectomy — the spleen's key protective role is against encapsulated, not intracellular, organisms.
incorrectas.C: Anaerobic infections are typically related to disruption of normal mucosal barriers or tissue necrosis (e.g., aspiration, abscesses) rather than to loss of splenic antibody-mediated clearance of capsulated bacteria.
incorrectas.D: Dimorphic fungi (e.g., Histoplasma, Coccidioides) cause disease primarily in the setting of impaired cell-mediated immunity, not from loss of splenic function; this is not the classic infectious risk associated with autosplenectomy.

preguntas.q: Which peripheral blood smear findings reflect loss of splenic function (autosplenectomy) in a patient with sickle cell disease?

e.correcta: With loss of splenic tissue from repeated infarction, the spleen can no longer perform its normal 'pitting' function of removing nuclear remnants from red cells, so Howell-Jolly bodies accumulate; target cells are also seen, reflecting the altered membrane surface-area-to-volume ratio characteristic of sickle cell disease. Together, these findings on smear serve as an indirect marker that a sickle cell patient has become functionally asplenic, prompting attention to infection prophylaxis.

incorrectas.A: Schistocytes and helmet cells result from mechanical red cell fragmentation in microangiopathic processes (like DIC or TTP/HUS), not from loss of the spleen's nuclear-remnant-clearing function.
incorrectas.C: Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin) and the bite cells produced when splenic macrophages remove them are actually markers of a working spleen actively processing damaged hemoglobin (as in G6PD deficiency) — the opposite of what you'd expect once splenic function is lost.
incorrectas.D: Spherocytes reflect a primary membrane cytoskeletal defect (as in hereditary spherocytosis) or antibody-mediated membrane loss, and reticulocytes simply reflect a compensatory bone marrow response to anemia — neither is the specific marker of absent splenic pitting function that Howell-Jolly bodies represent.

preguntas.q: Vaso-occlusion within the pulmonary microcirculation in a patient with sickle cell disease causes which life-threatening complication?

o.B: Pulmonary embolism from deep vein thrombosis

e.correcta: Acute chest syndrome occurs when sickled red cells occlude the pulmonary microvasculature (sometimes triggered or worsened by infection, fat embolism from bone marrow infarction, or postoperative atelectasis), producing localized hypoxia that promotes further local sickling in a vicious cycle. It presents with chest pain, hypoxemia, fever, and a new infiltrate on chest imaging, and is a leading cause of mortality in sickle cell disease requiring prompt treatment with oxygen, transfusion, and sometimes exchange transfusion.

incorrectas.A: Pneumothorax is a mechanical collapse of the lung from air in the pleural space, unrelated to microvascular occlusion by sickled cells; it is not a typical direct complication of sickle vaso-occlusion.
incorrectas.B: Pulmonary embolism from DVT involves a thrombus traveling from the venous system to the pulmonary arteries, a distinct large-vessel thromboembolic process, whereas acute chest syndrome arises from in-situ microvascular sickling and occlusion within the lung itself.
incorrectas.C: While infection can precipitate or coexist with acute chest syndrome, and the two can be difficult to distinguish clinically, a straightforward bacterial pneumonia is a primary infectious process rather than the vaso-occlusive, sickling-driven microvascular event that defines acute chest syndrome.

preguntas.q: A patient with sickle cell disease develops acute onset chest pain, shortness of breath, and a new pulmonary infiltrate on chest X-ray. Which complication is this?

e.correcta: Acute chest syndrome is defined by a new pulmonary infiltrate plus symptoms such as chest pain, fever, cough, or hypoxia in a patient with sickle cell disease. It results from a combination of pulmonary vaso-occlusion/in situ sickling, fat emboli released from infarcted bone marrow, and infection, and is a medical emergency that may require exchange transfusion in severe cases.

incorrectas.B: Community-acquired pneumonia can look identical and is actually one of the most common precipitants of ACS, but plain pneumonia doesn't capture the vaso-occlusive/infarctive component unique to sickle cell disease — by convention, this triad in a sickler is labeled acute chest syndrome regardless of whether an organism is identified.
incorrectas.C: Pulmonary embolism from venous thromboembolism can cause similar symptoms, but it results from a dislodged clot rather than the intravascular sickling and marrow fat emboli that define ACS.
incorrectas.D: Splenic sequestration crisis presents with sudden splenic enlargement, a rapidly falling hemoglobin, and hypovolemic shock, typically in young children — it reflects blood trapped in the spleen, not infiltrates in the lung.

preguntas.q: Which of the following is the most common precipitant of acute chest syndrome in patients with sickle cell disease?

e.correcta: Infection, especially pneumonia, is the most frequent trigger of acute chest syndrome. The resulting local hypoxia in lung tissue promotes sickling of RBCs within the pulmonary microvasculature, which worsens ventilation-perfusion mismatch and perpetuates a cycle of infarction and inflammation in the lung.

incorrectas.A: Reactive airway disease is common in sickle cell patients and can contribute to hypoxia that promotes sickling, but it is not the leading precipitant of ACS the way infection is.
incorrectas.C: Pulmonary embolism from venous thrombosis can mimic or coexist with ACS, but it is a distinct and less common trigger; the classic driver of ACS is infection-related hypoxia causing intrapulmonary sickling, not thromboembolic disease.
incorrectas.D: Aspiration pneumonitis is an uncommon precipitant compared with straightforward infectious pneumonia and does not carry the same epidemiologic weight as the leading cause of ACS.

preguntas.q: Which renal pathology is classically associated with sickle cell anemia and presents with gross hematuria and proteinuria?

e.correcta: The renal medulla's low oxygen tension, hypertonicity, and sluggish blood flow make it especially prone to RBC sickling, causing ischemic necrosis of the renal papillae. This renal papillary necrosis presents with gross hematuria and proteinuria and can appear on imaging as a classic 'ball-in-cup' defect, forming part of the broader sickle cell nephropathy that also includes hyposthenuria from medullary damage.

incorrectas.A: Renal medullary carcinoma is a rare, aggressive tumor associated with sickle cell trait (not full sickle cell disease) that presents as a renal mass with hematuria, but it is a distinct neoplastic process, not the ischemic microvascular injury of papillary necrosis.
incorrectas.B: FSGS can develop as a late complication of sickle cell disease from chronic glomerular hyperfiltration and hypertrophy, but it presents with proteinuria/nephrotic syndrome rather than the gross hematuria produced by papillary ischemia.
incorrectas.D: Minimal change disease is an idiopathic podocyte effacement disorder unrelated to sickle cell pathophysiology and is not a recognized complication of sickle hemoglobinopathies.

preguntas.q: Both sickle cell trait and sickle cell disease can cause microscopic hematuria. Which renal process is responsible?

e.correcta: The renal medulla is a uniquely hypoxic, hypertonic, low-flow environment, which is enough to promote sickling even in sickle cell trait, where the overall HbS fraction is low. Recurrent microinfarcts in the vasa recta and medullary interstitium damage the concentrating apparatus and cause microscopic — and sometimes gross — hematuria in both trait and full disease.

incorrectas.A: GBM thickening is a feature of diabetic nephropathy and certain glomerulopathies, not the microvascular ischemic injury that produces hematuria in sickle hemoglobinopathies.
incorrectas.B: Renal artery stenosis causes hypertension and ischemic nephropathy from large-vessel narrowing (e.g., atherosclerosis, fibromuscular dysplasia), not the small-vessel sickling injury confined to the medulla.
incorrectas.C: Acute interstitial nephritis is typically a hypersensitivity reaction to drugs or infection with white cell infiltration, not the ischemic sickling process that damages the medulla in sickle hemoglobinopathies.

preguntas.q: A young man with sickle cell disease presents with a prolonged, painful erection unrelated to sexual stimulation. Which genitourinary complication is this?

e.correcta: Priapism results from sickling and vaso-occlusion within the corpora cavernosa, trapping blood and preventing normal venous outflow. The resulting ischemia is painful and, if prolonged, can cause corporal fibrosis and erectile dysfunction, making it a urologic emergency that requires prompt hydration, exchange transfusion, or aspiration/irrigation.

incorrectas.B: Testicular torsion is a sudden twisting of the spermatic cord causing acute testicular pain and swelling — it is a vascular emergency of the testis itself, not the corpora cavernosa, and is not a recognized sickle cell complication.
incorrectas.C: Peyronie disease is fibrous scar tissue within the tunica albuginea causing penile curvature, typically from repeated trauma, and is unrelated to vaso-occlusive sickling.
incorrectas.D: Varicocele is dilation of the pampiniform venous plexus, usually asymptomatic or causing a dull scrotal ache, with no established link to sickle cell vaso-occlusion.

preguntas.q: What is the most common cause of death in children with sickle cell anemia?

e.correcta: Repeated splenic infarction from vaso-occlusion produces functional asplenia by early childhood, leaving these patients unable to mount an adequate antibody response to encapsulated organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. Overwhelming sepsis from these organisms is the leading cause of death in children with sickle cell disease, which is why prophylactic penicillin and pneumococcal/Hib vaccination are standard of care.

incorrectas.A: Splenic sequestration crisis is a life-threatening complication in young children (sudden pooling of blood in the spleen causing hypovolemic shock), but it is less common overall than death from overwhelming infection due to functional asplenia.
incorrectas.C: Acute chest syndrome is a major cause of morbidity and mortality, but it is the leading cause of death in adults rather than the top killer in children, where sepsis predominates.
incorrectas.D: Aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19 causes a transient, severe drop in reticulocyte count and worsening anemia that can be dangerous, but it is not the most common cause of death in pediatric sickle cell patients compared with sepsis from encapsulated organisms.

preguntas.q: What is the most common cause of death in adults with sickle cell anemia?

e.correcta: As patients survive into adulthood, aided by childhood prophylaxis against encapsulated organisms, recurrent vaso-occlusive lung injury culminating in acute chest syndrome becomes the leading cause of death. Repeated episodes cause progressive pulmonary fibrosis and chronic lung disease, and a severe episode can rapidly progress to fatal hypoxemic respiratory failure.

incorrectas.A: Infection with encapsulated organisms is the dominant killer in childhood, before prophylactic vaccination and penicillin have had decades to reduce this risk into adulthood.
incorrectas.B: Chronic renal failure from sickle cell nephropathy is a real long-term complication and contributor to morbidity, but it is not the leading cause of death in adult sickle cell patients.
incorrectas.D: Pulmonary hypertension is an increasingly recognized complication of chronic hemolysis (from nitric oxide scavenging by free hemoglobin) and contributes to mortality, but acute chest syndrome remains the single most common cause of death.

preguntas.q: What is the underlying cause of painful crises in patients with sickle cell anemia?

e.correcta: Painful (vaso-occlusive) crises occur when deoxygenated, sickled RBCs become rigid and clump together, obstructing small vessels in bones, muscles, and organs. The resulting ischemia and tissue infarction produce severe pain, classically in the long bones, back, and chest, and are precipitated by triggers such as hypoxia, dehydration, cold, and infection that promote HbS polymerization.

incorrectas.A: Autoimmune destruction of RBCs, as in autoimmune hemolytic anemia, involves antibody-mediated hemolysis — this is not the mechanism in sickle cell disease, where the RBC membrane itself is abnormal because of an intrinsic hemoglobin defect, not an antibody attack.
incorrectas.B: Increased osmotic fragility describes a defect seen in hereditary spherocytosis, from an abnormal membrane cytoskeleton — a distinct disease and mechanism from the hemoglobin polymerization behind sickle cell painful crises.
incorrectas.C: Extravascular hemolysis in the spleen contributes to the chronic anemia of sickle cell disease, but it is not what causes the acute pain of a vaso-occlusive crisis, which instead comes from microvascular obstruction and downstream ischemia.

preguntas.q: Sickle cell trait describes a patient who is heterozygous for the HbS mutation. How many mutated β-globin alleles does this genotype carry?

e.correcta: Sickle cell trait (HbAS) is the heterozygous carrier state, with one normal β-globin allele and one HbS allele. Because roughly half of the hemoglobin remains normal HbA, these patients usually do not sickle under normal physiologic conditions and are typically asymptomatic, unlike homozygous HbSS patients, who carry two mutated alleles and a much higher HbS burden.

incorrectas.B: Two mutated alleles describes homozygous sickle cell disease (HbSS), which produces predominantly HbS and the full clinical syndrome — not the milder carrier state of trait.
incorrectas.C: Zero mutated alleles would simply describe a person with normal hemoglobin (HbAA) and no HbS at all, which does not match the definition of sickle cell trait.
incorrectas.D: There are only two β-globin alleles per person, one inherited from each parent, so three is not a biologically possible number of mutated alleles at this locus.

preguntas.q: Approximately what percentage of hemoglobin is HbS in a person with sickle cell trait?

e.correcta: Because sickle cell trait carriers have one normal β-globin allele, less than half of their hemoglobin is HbS, with the rest being normal HbA. RBCs with under 50% HbS generally do not sickle at typical oxygen tensions in vivo, which is why trait carriers are usually asymptomatic except in the unusually hypoxic, hypertonic environment of the renal medulla.

incorrectas.A: Greater than 90% HbS is seen in homozygous sickle cell disease (HbSS), where nearly all hemoglobin is the abnormal form and severe, symptomatic sickling occurs — this is not the trait genotype.
incorrectas.C: 50-70% HbS would still mean mutant hemoglobin outweighs normal HbA, which does not fit the roughly even or lower distribution actually seen in trait.
incorrectas.D: 100% HbS is not seen in any clinical genotype, since even homozygous HbSS patients retain some HbF and HbA2, and trait carriers retain substantial HbA.

preguntas.q: How does sickle cell trait typically present clinically?

e.correcta: Because sickle cell trait carriers retain enough normal HbA — with HbS under 50% — to prevent significant polymerization and sickling under normal oxygen tensions, they typically have a normal hemoglobin level and no chronic hemolysis. Most people with trait are identified incidentally, such as on newborn screening or a metabisulfite test, rather than through symptoms, though they remain at risk for rare complications like renal medullary microinfarcts or exercise-related sickling under extreme hypoxia.

incorrectas.A: Recurrent painful vaso-occlusive crises are characteristic of full sickle cell disease (HbSS), where the high HbS percentage promotes sickling under everyday physiologic conditions — not trait.
incorrectas.B: Severe hemolytic anemia requiring transfusion reflects the ongoing extravascular hemolysis of sickle cell disease, not trait, where red cells function largely normally.
incorrectas.D: Chronic hemolytic anemia with jaundice is a hallmark of sickle cell disease from ongoing splenic destruction of sickled cells; trait carriers do not have chronic hemolysis because their cells rarely sickle in vivo.

preguntas.q: The extreme hypoxia and hypertonicity that predispose to sickling in patients with sickle cell trait are found in which renal structure?

e.correcta: The renal medulla's countercurrent multiplier system creates a hypertonic, low-oxygen environment even in healthy people, and blood flow through the vasa recta is sluggish. This combination is enough to trigger HbS polymerization and sickling even when the overall HbS fraction is low, as in sickle cell trait, leading to localized microinfarcts.

incorrectas.A: The glomerulus is a highly perfused, oxygen-rich filtering structure and is not the site where the hypoxic, hypertonic conditions needed to trigger sickling in trait carriers occur.
incorrectas.B: The renal cortex receives the bulk of renal blood flow and has much better oxygenation than the medulla, so it is not predisposed to sickling the way the medulla is.
incorrectas.C: The renal pelvis is a collecting structure for urine and does not have the hypertonic, hypoxic microenvironment of the medullary vasa recta that promotes sickling.

preguntas.q: Recurrent medullary microinfarcts in patients with sickle cell trait eventually impair which renal function?

o.B: Sodium reabsorption in the proximal tubule

e.correcta: Chronic ischemic injury to the vasa recta and medullary interstitium disrupts the countercurrent multiplication system needed to establish the medullary concentration gradient, producing hyposthenuria — an inability to maximally concentrate urine. This is why some patients with sickle cell trait or disease develop relative polyuria and nocturia over time.

incorrectas.B: Proximal tubule sodium reabsorption occurs in the cortex and depends on cortical blood flow and tubular integrity, not the medullary structures damaged by sickling-related infarcts.
incorrectas.C: Erythropoietin is produced by cortical peritubular fibroblasts in response to hypoxia; medullary microinfarcts do not primarily impair this cortical function, and EPO levels are typically appropriately elevated given the chronic anemia of sickle cell disease.
incorrectas.D: GFR is a glomerular (cortical) measure of filtration; medullary infarction primarily damages the concentrating mechanism of the loop of Henle and vasa recta rather than glomerular filtration itself, at least early in the disease course.

preguntas.q: Is the sodium metabisulfite screening test for RBC sickling positive in sickle cell trait, sickle cell disease, or both?

o.B: Both sickle cell disease and trait

e.correcta: The metabisulfite test works by deoxygenating the blood sample, which promotes HbS polymerization and induces sickling in any RBC that contains HbS, regardless of the percentage present. Since both sickle cell disease (high HbS) and sickle cell trait (lower HbS, but still present) carry the abnormal hemoglobin, both will show a positive result — making this a useful universal screen, though it cannot distinguish disease from trait, which requires hemoglobin electrophoresis.

incorrectas.A: Restricting a positive result to disease alone ignores that trait carriers also possess HbS, which will still polymerize and sickle under the deoxygenated test conditions, just less extensively than in disease.
incorrectas.C: The metabisulfite test does not require electrophoresis to give a result — it is a rapid, inexpensive screening test that turns positive in anyone carrying HbS; electrophoresis is a separate, more specific confirmatory test used to quantify hemoglobin types.
incorrectas.D: Limiting positivity to trait alone is incorrect, since sickle cell disease patients have an even higher HbS burden and will sickle at least as readily as trait carriers on this screen.

preguntas.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis of sickle cell anemia?

e.correcta: Hemoglobin electrophoresis separates hemoglobin species by charge, allowing precise quantification of HbA, HbS, HbF, and HbA2. This distinguishes homozygous sickle cell disease (predominant HbS, no HbA) from sickle cell trait (roughly half HbA, half HbS) and from other hemoglobinopathies, making it the definitive confirmatory test.

incorrectas.A: A peripheral smear showing sickled cells, Howell-Jolly bodies, and target cells is suggestive of sickle cell disease and prompts further workup, but it cannot definitively confirm the diagnosis or distinguish disease from trait the way electrophoresis can.
incorrectas.B: The osmotic fragility test assesses RBC membrane fragility and is used to diagnose hereditary spherocytosis, not hemoglobinopathies like sickle cell disease.
incorrectas.D: The metabisulfite screening test only shows whether HbS is present, positive in both disease and trait — it cannot quantify hemoglobin fractions or confirm the specific diagnosis the way electrophoresis does.

preguntas.q: A hemoglobin electrophoresis shows 90% HbS, 8% HbF, and 2% HbA2, with no HbA detected. Which condition does this represent?

e.correcta: The complete absence of HbA combined with a predominant HbS fraction indicates that both β-globin alleles produce the sickle variant, with no normal β-chain production at all — this is the electrophoretic signature of homozygous sickle cell disease (HbSS), with the small residual HbF and HbA2 reflecting the normal minor hemoglobin production that persists in every genotype.

incorrectas.A: Sickle cell trait would show substantial HbA, roughly half of total hemoglobin, alongside HbS, since one normal β-globin allele is still actively producing HbA — the complete absence of HbA here rules out trait.
incorrectas.B: HbSC disease is a compound heterozygous state producing both HbS and HbC (not HbA), so electrophoresis would show a significant HbC band rather than the pattern seen here, which lists no HbC and predominant HbS with no HbA.
incorrectas.C: Sickle β+-thalassemia retains some HbA production from the milder β+ allele, which still allows partial normal β-chain synthesis, so a total absence of HbA argues against this diagnosis in favor of true homozygous HbSS.

preguntas.q: A hemoglobin electrophoresis shows 55% HbA, 43% HbS, and 2% HbA2. Which condition does this represent?

e.correcta: The presence of a majority HbA fraction, roughly matching or exceeding HbS, reflects one normal β-globin allele still producing HbA alongside one HbS allele. This is the classic heterozygous pattern of sickle cell trait, in which under 50% of hemoglobin is HbS and the individual is generally asymptomatic.

incorrectas.B: Sickle cell disease (HbSS) would show little to no HbA, since both alleles produce HbS, which contrasts sharply with the roughly 55% HbA seen in this sample.
incorrectas.C: HbSC disease would show HbC on electrophoresis rather than HbA, since one allele produces HbS and the other produces HbC — the presence of substantial HbA instead of HbC rules this out.
incorrectas.D: Hemoglobin C trait would show HbC, not HbS, as the abnormal minor hemoglobin species alongside HbA; the abnormal band here is HbS, so this does not fit hemoglobin C trait.

preguntas.q: Along with adequate hydration, which medication is used to reduce the frequency of vaso-occlusive crises in sickle cell anemia?

e.correcta: Hydroxyurea is the mainstay disease-modifying therapy for sickle cell anemia. It increases fetal hemoglobin (HbF) production, which interferes with HbS polymerization, reducing the frequency of painful crises, transfusion requirements, and episodes of acute chest syndrome; hydration is used alongside it to help prevent the dehydration and hypertonicity that promote sickling.

incorrectas.A: Deferoxamine is an iron chelator used to treat transfusional iron overload, a complication of chronic transfusion therapy in sickle cell patients, not a drug that reduces sickling itself.
incorrectas.C: Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor used to prevent hyperuricemia/gout or tumor lysis syndrome and has no role in reducing HbS polymerization or vaso-occlusion.
incorrectas.D: Folic acid is given as a supportive supplement in chronic hemolytic anemias like sickle cell disease to support the high rate of RBC turnover, but it does not reduce the frequency of vaso-occlusive crises the way hydroxyurea does.

preguntas.q: Hydroxyurea reduces sickle cell disease complications primarily by raising the level of which hemoglobin, typically to above 15%?

e.correcta: Hydroxyurea increases synthesis of fetal hemoglobin (HbF), which does not participate in the polymer formation that drives sickling. Higher HbF levels effectively dilute the concentration of HbS within each red cell, raising the threshold at which polymerization and sickling occur — translating clinically into fewer painful crises, reduced transfusion needs, and fewer episodes of acute chest syndrome, even though the exact molecular mechanism by which hydroxyurea induces HbF remains incompletely understood.

incorrectas.A: HbA2 is a minor adult hemoglobin (α2δ2) present at low levels normally; it is not the hemoglobin species induced by hydroxyurea to reduce sickling.
incorrectas.B: HbC is the abnormal hemoglobin of hemoglobin C disease, an unrelated hemoglobinopathy — hydroxyurea's therapeutic mechanism in sickle cell disease does not involve HbC at all.
incorrectas.D: Raising HbS would worsen, not improve, sickling risk, since HbS is the abnormal hemoglobin that polymerizes under deoxygenated conditions; hydroxyurea instead works by increasing a different, fetal hemoglobin to dilute HbS's effect.

preguntas.q: What morphologic category of anemia does hemoglobin C disease cause?

e.correcta: Hemoglobin C disease causes a mild, chronic extravascular hemolytic anemia. Because red cell production and hemoglobin content per cell are not impaired, unlike in thalassemias or iron deficiency, the mean corpuscular volume remains normal, classifying it as a normocytic anemia, similar to other hemolytic anemias such as sickle cell disease and hereditary spherocytosis.

incorrectas.A: Macrocytic anemia, with an elevated MCV, is seen in conditions like B12/folate deficiency or marked reticulocytosis; HbC disease does not enlarge red cells and is not classified as macrocytic.
incorrectas.B: Microcytic anemia, with a low MCV, results from impaired hemoglobin synthesis, as in iron deficiency or thalassemia; HbC disease does not impair globin chain synthesis this way — it produces a structurally abnormal but normally sized hemoglobin molecule.
incorrectas.C: HbC disease does cause anemia, albeit typically mild, from chronic low-grade extravascular hemolysis of the HbC-crystal-containing red cells in the spleen.

preguntas.q: Hemoglobin C disease is primarily characterized by which type of hemolysis?

e.correcta: In HbC disease, the abnormal hemoglobin crystallizes within red cells, causing them to become rigid and dehydrated — forming the characteristic HbC crystals and target cells. These abnormal cells are recognized and removed by splenic macrophages, making this predominantly an extravascular hemolytic process, similar in location, though milder, to sickle cell disease's splenic clearance of rigid, sickled cells.

incorrectas.B: Intravascular hemolysis, as seen in conditions like G6PD deficiency, PNH, or mechanical hemolysis, involves red cell destruction directly within the bloodstream with free hemoglobin release; HbC disease's hemolysis instead occurs mainly in the spleen.
incorrectas.C: Complement-mediated hemolysis characterizes autoimmune or PNH-related processes in which complement activation directly lyses red cells; HbC disease's hemolysis is due to macrophage clearance of structurally rigid cells, not complement fixation.
incorrectas.D: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia involves red cell shearing by intravascular fibrin strands or damaged small vessels, as in TTP/HUS or DIC, producing schistocytes — this mechanical process is unrelated to the splenic clearance mechanism of HbC disease.

preguntas.q: A mutation in which hemoglobin chain causes hemoglobin C disease?

e.correcta: Like HbS, hemoglobin C results from a point mutation in the β-globin gene, at the same codon 6 affected in sickle cell disease but with a different amino acid substitution. This shared locus explains why HbC and HbS can combine in a single patient (HbSC disease) and why both conditions follow an autosomal recessive pattern affecting adult hemoglobin (HbA, α2β2).

incorrectas.A: The α-globin chain is affected in α-thalassemias (gene deletions) and in unstable hemoglobin variants involving α-chains, not in hemoglobin C disease, which specifically involves an abnormal β-chain.
incorrectas.C: The γ-globin chain makes up fetal hemoglobin (HbF, α2γ2) and is not the chain mutated in HbC disease, which is a disorder of adult hemoglobin's β-chain.
incorrectas.D: The δ-globin chain contributes to the minor adult hemoglobin HbA2 (α2δ2); it is not the site of the mutation responsible for hemoglobin C disease.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of hemoglobin C disease?

e.correcta: Hemoglobin C disease follows an autosomal recessive pattern, just like sickle cell disease, because the β-globin gene lies on an autosome (chromosome 11) and clinically significant disease requires two abnormal alleles (homozygous HbCC) or a second β-globin mutation in trans (e.g., HbSC). Heterozygous carriers, HbAC or 'HbC trait,' are generally asymptomatic.

incorrectas.A: X-linked recessive inheritance applies to conditions like G6PD deficiency or hemophilia, where the gene lies on the X chromosome; the β-globin gene responsible for HbC is autosomal, not X-linked.
incorrectas.B: Autosomal dominant inheritance would mean a single mutant allele alone produces significant disease; HbC requires two abnormal β-globin alleles, or interaction with another β-chain variant, to cause clinically significant hemolysis, consistent with recessive rather than dominant inheritance.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance applies to disorders caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA, transmitted only through the maternal line; hemoglobin C disease is a nuclear (autosomal) gene disorder, not a mitochondrial one.

preguntas.q: Hemoglobin C disease results from a point mutation causing which amino acid substitution in the β-globin chain?

o.B: Glutamic acid replaced by aspartic acid

e.correcta: Hemoglobin C arises from a missense mutation at codon 6 of the β-globin gene that substitutes lysine for glutamic acid — the same codon affected in sickle cell disease, but with a different resulting amino acid. This substitution promotes hemoglobin crystallization within red cells, visible as HbC crystals on smear, and red cell dehydration, producing a mild chronic hemolytic anemia.

incorrectas.A: Glutamic acid replaced by valine is the mutation that causes sickle cell disease (HbS), not hemoglobin C — both mutations occur at the same codon 6 position of β-globin, but they produce different substitutions and different phenotypes: polymerization/sickling in HbS versus crystallization/dehydration in HbC.
incorrectas.B: Glutamic acid replaced by aspartic acid is not the substitution seen in any major clinically significant hemoglobinopathy at this codon; aspartic acid and glutamic acid are both acidic residues, and this hypothetical change does not correspond to HbC (a basic lysine) or HbS (a nonpolar valine).
incorrectas.C: Lysine replacing glutamic acid describes the reverse direction of the actual mutation; in HbC it is glutamic acid that is replaced by lysine, not the other way around.

preguntas.q: Compared with patients homozygous for HbS (HbSS), how does disease severity typically differ in patients with HbSC disease (one HbS allele and one HbC allele)?

o.A: HbSC disease is typically milder than HbSS disease
o.B: HbSC disease is typically more severe than HbSS disease
o.C: HbSC disease has identical severity to HbSS disease
o.D: HbSC disease causes no clinical symptoms at all

e.correcta: In HbSC disease, only one allele produces the sickling HbS variant, while the other produces HbC, resulting in a lower overall concentration of HbS — the species that must polymerize to cause sickling — within each red cell. This means patients experience less frequent and less severe vaso-occlusive complications than homozygous HbSS patients, effectively behaving somewhat like a combination of sickle trait and HbC disease rather than full-blown sickle cell disease.

incorrectas.B: HbSC disease is not more severe than HbSS — having a second, HbS-independent hemoglobin (HbC) actually reduces the fraction of hemoglobin available to polymerize compared with pure HbSS, generally lowering rather than raising disease severity.
incorrectas.C: HbSC disease is clinically distinct from and generally milder than HbSS disease, though patients can still experience real complications such as retinopathy or avascular necrosis — it is not simply an identical phenotype to homozygous sickle cell disease.
incorrectas.D: HbSC disease is not asymptomatic; patients can still have vaso-occlusive events, splenomegaly, and other complications, just less frequently and typically less severely than in HbSS disease.

preguntas.q: Hepcidin is upregulated during infection and inflammation to prevent invading pathogens from accessing which nutrient essential for their growth?

e.correcta: Hepcidin acts by binding ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages, triggering its internalization and degradation so that stored iron cannot be released into the bloodstream. This is an evolved 'nutritional immunity' strategy, since many bacteria and other pathogens require circulating iron to proliferate; by trapping iron intracellularly, the host starves the invader. The same pathway, when chronically activated by inflammatory cytokines (like IL-6) in chronic disease states, causes functional iron sequestration and produces anemia of chronic disease even when total body iron stores are adequate.

incorrectas.A: Calcium homeostasis is governed by parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, and calcitonin, none of which are linked to the hepcidin-ferroportin axis, so restricting calcium is not the evolutionary purpose of hepcidin upregulation.
incorrectas.C: Vitamin B12 is transported via intrinsic factor and transcobalamin and is not regulated by hepcidin; B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia through impaired DNA synthesis, an entirely different mechanism from iron sequestration.
incorrectas.D: Glucose availability is controlled by insulin, glucagon, and other counter-regulatory hormones; while pathogens do use host glucose, hepcidin's specific evolutionary role is sequestering iron, not glucose.

preguntas.q: Which malignancy occurs with increased incidence in patients with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), developing in up to 10% of cases?

e.correcta: PNH arises from an acquired somatic mutation in the PIGA gene within a pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell, leading to loss of GPI-anchored complement regulators (CD55/CD59) on the surface of all blood cell lineages derived from that clone. Because the abnormal clone is a stem cell rather than a mature cell, it remains capable of acquiring additional oncogenic mutations over time, and roughly 10% of PNH patients progress to AML, reinforcing that PNH is fundamentally a clonal stem cell disorder rather than just a hemolytic anemia.

incorrectas.B: CML is driven by the BCR-ABL fusion from the t(9;22) translocation, a distinct oncogenic event unrelated to the PIGA mutation and complement dysregulation that defines PNH, so it is not the classically associated leukemia.
incorrectas.A: Hairy cell leukemia is a mature B-cell neoplasm driven by the BRAF V600E mutation; it has no established mechanistic link to the PNH stem cell clone or its complement-related surface defects.
incorrectas.D: Multiple myeloma is a malignancy of terminally differentiated plasma cells with no known association to the PIGA-mutant hematopoietic clone that characterizes PNH.

preguntas.q: Which medication used to treat paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria works as a terminal complement inhibitor?

e.correcta: Eculizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds complement protein C5, blocking its cleavage into C5a and C5b and thereby preventing assembly of the membrane attack complex (C5b-9). Because PNH red cells lack the GPI-anchored regulators CD55 and CD59 that normally restrain complement activation, they are exquisitely sensitive to complement-mediated lysis; halting the cascade at the terminal C5 step protects these cells from destruction and dramatically reduces intravascular hemolysis and transfusion needs.

incorrectas.A: Rituximab is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody that depletes B cells, useful in antibody-mediated hemolytic anemias or lymphoma, but it does not act on the complement cascade the way eculizumab does.
incorrectas.B: Infliximab is an anti-TNF-alpha antibody used in inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatologic conditions; it targets a cytokine, not the complement system, so it has no role in PNH.
incorrectas.C: Denosumab is an anti-RANKL antibody used to inhibit osteoclast activity in osteoporosis and bone metastases, a mechanism completely unrelated to complement inhibition in PNH.

preguntas.q: G6PD deficiency-related hemolysis, which preferentially affects older erythrocytes, results primarily from what abnormal property of the mutant enzyme?

e.correcta: Most common G6PD deficiency variants (such as G6PD A- and the Mediterranean variant) are missense mutations that destabilize the protein rather than abolishing its catalytic site outright, shortening the enzyme's functional half-life. Since mature RBCs are anucleate and cannot synthesize new protein, enzyme activity declines progressively as the cell ages, leaving the oldest RBCs with the least residual G6PD and the greatest vulnerability to oxidative injury — explaining the age-dependent pattern of hemolysis and why young reticulocytes are relatively spared.

incorrectas.A: Reduced substrate affinity would impair catalysis uniformly from the moment the RBC is made, rather than producing the progressive, age-dependent enzyme decline that is the hallmark of clinically significant G6PD variants.
incorrectas.B: This describes the opposite of what actually happens — mutant G6PD protein is more prone to degradation and has a shortened half-life, not increased resistance to proteolysis.
incorrectas.D: Complete loss of the NADPH binding site would abolish essentially all enzymatic activity immediately, producing severe, non-age-dependent hemolysis, which does not match the typically mild, episodic course seen with common G6PD variants.

preguntas.q: G6PD deficiency follows which pattern of inheritance?

e.correcta: The G6PD gene is located on the X chromosome, so hemizygous males express the deficiency fully whenever they inherit the mutant allele, while heterozygous females are typically mosaic due to random X-inactivation (Lyonization), giving them a mixed population of normal and deficient RBCs and usually a milder phenotype. This X-linked recessive pattern explains the strong male predominance of clinically significant hemolytic episodes and parallels other RBC disorders like hemophilia in its inheritance logic.

incorrectas.A: Autosomal recessive inheritance would require two mutant alleles on a non-sex chromosome and would affect males and females with equal frequency and severity, which does not match the male-predominant pattern actually observed in G6PD deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Autosomal dominant inheritance would mean a single mutant allele on an autosome causes full disease expression in either sex, which is inconsistent with G6PD deficiency's clear sex-linkage.
incorrectas.D: X-linked dominant inheritance would cause full disease expression in heterozygous females as well as hemizygous males, but carrier females are typically only mildly or variably affected due to X-inactivation mosaicism, not fully symptomatic.

preguntas.q: Red blood cells are normally exposed to ongoing oxidative stress, particularly from which reactive species generated as a byproduct of aerobic processes like hemoglobin autoxidation?

e.correcta: Hemoglobin autoxidation and other routine aerobic reactions continuously generate hydrogen peroxide inside RBCs. Because mature RBCs lack mitochondria, they depend entirely on the pentose phosphate (HMP shunt) pathway to produce NADPH, which is then used to regenerate reduced glutathione that neutralizes this H2O2 via glutathione peroxidase. This constant baseline oxidative load is precisely why any impairment in NADPH production, as occurs in G6PD deficiency, leaves RBCs chronically vulnerable to oxidative membrane and hemoglobin damage.

incorrectas.A: Nitric oxide is a signaling molecule important for vascular tone that hemoglobin also scavenges, but it is not the primary reactive species that RBCs must routinely detoxify via the glutathione/NADPH system.
incorrectas.B: Superoxide dismutase is actually an antioxidant enzyme that converts superoxide into hydrogen peroxide — it is a defense mechanism, not a reactive species the cell needs to be protected from.
incorrectas.C: Peroxynitrite forms from the reaction of nitric oxide with superoxide and is highly damaging, but it is not the everyday baseline oxidative stressor that RBCs handle through the HMP shunt/glutathione pathway.

preguntas.q: Hydrogen peroxide generated within red blood cells is neutralized primarily by which molecule, which itself becomes oxidized in the process?

e.correcta: Glutathione peroxidase uses reduced glutathione (GSH) as an electron donor to convert hydrogen peroxide into water, generating oxidized glutathione (GSSG) as a byproduct. GSSG must then be recycled back into GSH by glutathione reductase, a reaction that consumes NADPH supplied by the HMP shunt (via G6PD) — directly coupling this antioxidant cycle to G6PD activity and explaining why G6PD deficiency, with its limited NADPH supply, leads to hemolysis when this recycling loop fails under oxidative stress.

incorrectas.A: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is a water-soluble antioxidant important in collagen synthesis and enhancing dietary iron absorption, but it is not the enzymatically regenerated antioxidant central to the RBC's routine H2O2 defense.
incorrectas.C: Alpha-tocopherol (vitamin E) is a lipid-soluble antioxidant that protects membrane lipids from peroxidation, but it is not the molecule directly tied to the G6PD/NADPH cycle responsible for neutralizing intracellular H2O2.
incorrectas.D: Bilirubin, a heme breakdown product, has some incidental antioxidant properties, but it is not the primary, enzymatically-regenerated antioxidant that RBCs rely on to detoxify hydrogen peroxide.

preguntas.q: In G6PD deficiency, decreased NADPH and impaired regeneration of reduced glutathione leave red blood cells vulnerable to which type of cellular stress?

e.correcta: G6PD catalyzes the rate-limiting step of the HMP shunt, producing the NADPH needed to keep glutathione in its reduced, active form. When G6PD activity is deficient, NADPH and reduced glutathione levels fall, so the cell cannot adequately detoxify hydrogen peroxide and other oxidants; the resulting oxidation of hemoglobin (forming Heinz bodies) and membrane components triggers hemolysis, particularly during periods of increased oxidative demand such as infection or exposure to oxidant drugs.

incorrectas.A: Osmotic stress and fragility are the defining vulnerability in conditions like hereditary spherocytosis, where a membrane cytoskeletal defect makes cells rupture in hypotonic conditions — not the mechanism at play in G6PD deficiency.
incorrectas.B: Mechanical shear stress causing RBC fragmentation is characteristic of microangiopathic hemolytic anemias (e.g., DIC, TTP, mechanical heart valves), not the biochemical oxidant-detoxification failure seen in G6PD deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Hypoxic stress relates to oxygen delivery and is not the trigger for hemolysis in G6PD deficiency; the underlying problem is failure to neutralize oxidants, not a lack of oxygen itself.

preguntas.q: G6PD deficiency-related hemolytic anemia is typically classified under which red blood cell size (MCV) category?

e.correcta: Hemolytic anemias, including G6PD deficiency, are generally normocytic because the underlying pathology is premature destruction of otherwise normally-sized mature RBCs, rather than a defect in hemoglobin synthesis (which produces microcytosis) or impaired nuclear maturation (which produces macrocytosis). A brisk compensatory reticulocytosis can nudge the mean corpuscular volume up slightly, but the anemia is still categorized as normocytic overall.

incorrectas.A: Microcytic anemia reflects impaired hemoglobin synthesis, as seen in iron deficiency or thalassemia, which is a fundamentally different mechanism from the hemolytic destruction of normally-sized cells that occurs in G6PD deficiency.
incorrectas.B: Macrocytic anemia is characteristic of megaloblastic processes like B12 or folate deficiency, where impaired DNA synthesis delays nuclear maturation; G6PD deficiency does not share this mechanism and is classified as normocytic.
incorrectas.C: Variable or dimorphic RBC populations are seen in conditions with two coexisting processes (e.g., combined iron and B12 deficiency, or sideroblastic anemia), not in G6PD deficiency, which produces a single, normocytic RBC population.

preguntas.q: G6PD deficiency is characterized primarily by which type of hemolysis?

e.correcta: Oxidative injury in G6PD deficiency causes hemoglobin to denature and precipitate as Heinz bodies and damages the RBC membrane directly, leading to lysis of the cell within the bloodstream itself — producing hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, and decreased haptoglobin. Extravascular hemolysis also contributes, as splenic macrophages pluck out Heinz bodies (forming bite cells) or remove rigid, damaged cells, but the defining and predominant mechanism is intravascular destruction.

incorrectas.B: Describing the process as extravascular only ignores the defining intravascular component — direct oxidative lysis within the circulation — that distinguishes G6PD deficiency from purely extravascular processes like hereditary spherocytosis.
incorrectas.C: Splenic macrophage removal (an extravascular process producing bite cells) does contribute to the overall picture, but it is a secondary mechanism, not the primary or exclusive site of destruction in G6PD deficiency.
incorrectas.D: The liver is not a principal site of RBC destruction in G6PD deficiency; the relevant sites are the bloodstream itself (intravascular hemolysis) and, to a lesser extent, the spleen (extravascular hemolysis).

preguntas.q: The high carrier frequency of mutant G6PD alleles in certain populations is thought to reflect a protective effect against infection with which organism?

e.correcta: Similar to sickle cell trait and thalassemia traits, G6PD-deficiency alleles have been maintained at high frequency in historically malaria-endemic regions (Africa, the Mediterranean, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia) because the chronically oxidant-stressed intracellular environment of a G6PD-deficient RBC is relatively hostile to Plasmodium falciparum, which is more vulnerable to oxidative damage during its intraerythrocytic life cycle. This creates a balanced polymorphism: the survival advantage against severe falciparum malaria offsets the hemolytic risk, keeping the allele common in these populations.

incorrectas.A: While G6PD-deficient patients must be screened before receiving primaquine (used against P. vivax hypnozoites) because the drug itself can trigger hemolysis, the classic evolutionary selective pressure credited with maintaining high G6PD-deficiency allele frequency is protection against severe falciparum, not vivax, malaria.
incorrectas.C: Toxoplasma gondii is an intracellular protozoan that infects a broad range of nucleated cells, not primarily RBCs, and there is no established evolutionary relationship between it and G6PD-deficiency allele frequency.
incorrectas.D: Babesia microti is a tick-borne parasite that does infect RBCs, but it lacks the well-documented evolutionary selective relationship with G6PD deficiency that exists for P. falciparum.

preguntas.q: In G6PD deficiency, splenic macrophages remove Heinz bodies from circulating RBCs, producing which characteristic red cell morphology?

e.correcta: Heinz bodies (precipitated, denatured hemoglobin) adhere to the inner RBC membrane; as these cells pass through the spleen, macrophages 'bite' off the Heinz body along with a piece of adjacent membrane, leaving a characteristic semicircular defect known as a bite cell (or degmacyte). Seeing bite cells on a peripheral smear, especially after a recent oxidative stressor like infection, sulfa drugs, or fava beans, is a strong visual clue pointing toward G6PD deficiency.

incorrectas.A: Schistocytes are fragmented, helmet-shaped RBCs produced by mechanical shearing across fibrin strands or damaged small vessels (as in DIC or TTP) — a physical fragmentation process, not the macrophage-mediated Heinz body removal seen in G6PD deficiency.
incorrectas.B: Target cells show a central density surrounded by pallor and an outer ring of hemoglobin, arising from excess membrane relative to hemoglobin content (as in thalassemia, liver disease, or asplenia) rather than from Heinz body extraction.
incorrectas.C: Spherocytes form when macrophages remove membrane (not a Heinz body) from antibody-coated or intrinsically fragile RBCs, as in hereditary spherocytosis or warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia — a distinct process from the bite-cell mechanism of G6PD deficiency.

preguntas.q: What is the most common precipitant of hemolytic episodes in patients with G6PD deficiency?

e.correcta: Infections are the single most common trigger of hemolysis in G6PD deficiency because the inflammatory response activates neutrophils and macrophages that generate reactive oxygen species, which diffuse into nearby RBCs and overwhelm their already-limited antioxidant reserve. This is an important clinical point: even without any oxidant drug or dietary exposure, a febrile illness alone can precipitate a hemolytic crisis in a G6PD-deficient patient.

incorrectas.A: Fava bean ingestion (favism) is a well-known and classic dietary trigger, particularly with the Mediterranean variant, but across all G6PD-deficient patients it is less common overall as a precipitant than infection.
incorrectas.B: Sulfa drug exposure is an important and highly testable oxidant drug trigger, but infections remain the single most frequent overall cause of hemolytic episodes in G6PD-deficient patients.
incorrectas.D: Vigorous exercise is not a recognized major trigger of hemolysis in G6PD deficiency; that pattern is more relevant to other conditions such as paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria or exertional rhabdomyolysis.

preguntas.q: Ingestion of which food is a classic dietary trigger of hemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients, particularly those with the Mediterranean variant?

e.correcta: Fava beans contain oxidant compounds, vicine and convicine, that generate reactive oxygen species when metabolized, overwhelming the already-diminished antioxidant reserve of G6PD-deficient RBCs and precipitating acute intravascular hemolysis — a phenomenon historically called 'favism.' This association is classically described in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern populations, where both the G6PD A-/Mediterranean variant and fava bean consumption are common, creating a real-world clinical overlap.

incorrectas.B: Shellfish are not associated with oxidative RBC hemolysis; shellfish reactions are typically IgE-mediated allergic hypersensitivity, a completely different immunologic mechanism unrelated to G6PD physiology.
incorrectas.C: Aged cheese is relevant to tyramine-induced hypertensive crises in patients taking MAO inhibitors, an entirely separate pharmacologic interaction with no connection to G6PD-related oxidative stress.
incorrectas.D: Citrus fruit is not a recognized hemolytic trigger in G6PD deficiency; vitamin C is actually an antioxidant at typical doses, and only extremely high intravenous doses have been rarely implicated in issues, unlike the well-established fava bean trigger.

preguntas.q: Which class of antimicrobial drugs is contraindicated in patients with G6PD deficiency due to the risk of precipitating hemolysis?

e.correcta: Sulfonamide antibiotics (such as sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim) are potent oxidizing agents whose metabolism generates free radicals and hydrogen peroxide; RBCs with insufficient G6PD activity cannot regenerate enough reduced glutathione to neutralize this oxidative burden, resulting in Heinz body formation and hemolysis. This is a classic testable drug-disease interaction, grouped with other oxidant drugs like nitrofurantoin, dapsone, and the antimalarial primaquine.

incorrectas.A: Macrolides (e.g., azithromycin) work by inhibiting the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit and are not significant oxidant stressors, making them generally safe to use in patients with G6PD deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Tetracyclines inhibit bacterial protein synthesis via the 30S ribosomal subunit and do not carry a meaningful oxidative hemolytic risk in G6PD-deficient patients, unlike sulfonamides.
incorrectas.D: Aminoglycosides are bactericidal 30S ribosomal subunit inhibitors whose main toxicities are nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, not oxidative RBC damage, so they are not the class implicated in G6PD-related hemolysis.

preguntas.q: Which class of medications, including primaquine, can induce oxidative hemolysis and requires caution or G6PD screening before use in deficient patients?
