e.correcta: Primaquine and related 8-aminoquinoline antimalarials generate reactive oxygen species as part of their mechanism against Plasmodium hypnozoites, and this oxidative burden is poorly tolerated by G6PD-deficient RBCs, which cannot regenerate reduced glutathione quickly enough to keep pace, precipitating hemolysis. Because of this, patients are typically screened for G6PD deficiency before starting primaquine or tafenoquine for radical cure of P. vivax or P. ovale malaria.

incorrectas.A: Antifungal agents like amphotericin B are primarily associated with nephrotoxicity and infusion-related reactions, not with the oxidative RBC injury that defines the G6PD-antimalarial drug interaction.
incorrectas.B: Antiviral drugs such as acyclovir are mainly associated with nephrotoxicity and crystalluria at high doses, not with generating the reactive oxygen species that stress G6PD-deficient red cells.
incorrectas.C: Anthelmintic drugs like albendazole are primarily hepatotoxic and used to treat helminthic infections; they lack the oxidant mechanism relevant to hemolysis in G6PD-deficient RBCs.

preguntas.q: Which class of drugs, including dapsone and isoniazid, may induce oxidative stress and precipitate hemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients?

e.correcta: Dapsone (used for leprosy as well as PCP and toxoplasmosis prophylaxis) and isoniazid (a first-line antituberculous agent), along with nitrofurantoin, act as oxidant stressors on red blood cells. In G6PD-deficient patients, these drugs generate reactive oxygen species that exceed the diminished NADPH/glutathione antioxidant capacity, causing Heinz body formation and hemolysis, so clinicians should consider G6PD status before starting these agents in at-risk populations.

incorrectas.B: Antifungal drugs are generally associated with hepatotoxicity or nephrotoxicity (as with amphotericin B) rather than with the oxidative RBC injury that characterizes the dapsone/isoniazid-G6PD interaction.
incorrectas.C: Antiretroviral drugs primarily carry metabolic and mitochondrial toxicity risks, not the oxidant-hemolysis mechanism relevant to antimycobacterial agents in G6PD deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Anticoagulants act on coagulation cascade proteins and have no mechanistic relationship to oxidative red cell stress or G6PD deficiency.

preguntas.q: What is the most common enzymatic disorder affecting red blood cells worldwide?

e.correcta: G6PD deficiency is the most prevalent RBC enzymopathy in the world, affecting hundreds of millions of people, especially in regions with historical malaria endemicity such as Africa, the Mediterranean, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia, reflecting the heterozygote/hemizygote survival advantage against P. falciparum. Its X-linked inheritance pattern and typically mild, episodic (rather than constant) hemolytic presentation also contribute to its unusually high prevalence relative to other RBC enzyme defects.

incorrectas.A: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is the second most common RBC enzymopathy and an important autosomal recessive cause of hereditary nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia, but it is substantially less common than G6PD deficiency.
incorrectas.B: Hexokinase deficiency is a rare cause of hereditary nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia affecting an earlier step of glycolysis, and it occurs far less frequently than G6PD deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase deficiency is a rare enzyme defect that causes hemolytic anemia with basophilic stippling on smear, but it is much less prevalent than G6PD deficiency.

preguntas.q: Which laboratory test, using a crystal violet stain to visualize precipitated hemoglobin, is used to screen for G6PD deficiency?

e.correcta: The Heinz body preparation uses a supravital stain, such as crystal violet or new methylene blue, to visualize the denatured, precipitated hemoglobin aggregates (Heinz bodies) that form inside RBCs during oxidative stress in G6PD-deficient cells, making it a useful screening tool, particularly during or shortly after a hemolytic episode. Note that testing is best performed after the acute episode resolves, since the reticulocytes released during the compensatory response can have near-normal enzyme levels and falsely mask the deficiency; a quantitative G6PD enzyme assay is used for definitive diagnosis.

incorrectas.A: The osmotic fragility test assesses RBC membrane integrity by exposing cells to hypotonic saline and is useful for diagnosing hereditary spherocytosis, not for detecting the oxidized hemoglobin precipitates seen in G6PD deficiency.
incorrectas.C: The Coombs test detects antibody or complement bound to RBCs (direct) or circulating in serum (indirect) and is used to diagnose immune-mediated hemolytic anemias, not an enzymopathy like G6PD deficiency.
incorrectas.D: The sucrose hemolysis test is a screening test for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, detecting complement-mediated lysis in a low-ionic-strength sucrose solution, and is unrelated to G6PD deficiency's oxidative mechanism.

preguntas.q: Which condition is defined as antibody-mediated destruction of red blood cells?

e.correcta: Immune hemolytic anemia (IHA) occurs when autoantibodies, or in some cases alloantibodies or drug-induced antibodies, bind RBC surface antigens, marking the cells for destruction either through direct complement-mediated lysis or through opsonization and phagocytic removal by splenic and hepatic macrophages. It is further subclassified based on whether the responsible antibody is warm-reactive IgG or cold-reactive IgM, which determines the temperature dependence, typical smear findings, and clinical associations.

incorrectas.A: Hereditary spherocytosis results from an inherited defect in RBC membrane cytoskeletal proteins (such as spectrin or ankyrin), causing intrinsic membrane fragility and extravascular hemolysis, with no antibody involvement at all.
incorrectas.B: Thalassemia is a genetic defect in globin chain synthesis leading to ineffective erythropoiesis and hemolysis from abnormal hemoglobin, a mechanism entirely unrelated to antibody-mediated RBC destruction.
incorrectas.C: Sideroblastic anemia results from impaired heme synthesis, causing iron to accumulate within the mitochondria of erythroid precursors (forming ringed sideroblasts), not from an antibody-mediated hemolytic process.

preguntas.q: In immune hemolytic anemia, the pathogenic autoantibodies are typically of which two immunoglobulin classes?

e.correcta: Immune hemolytic anemia is classically divided based on which antibody class mediates RBC destruction: IgG causes warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, reacting optimally at body temperature and driving extravascular hemolysis via splenic macrophages, while IgM causes cold agglutinin disease, reacting optimally at cooler peripheral temperatures and fixing complement to cause intravascular hemolysis and agglutination. Identifying which class is involved has direct clinical implications for expected temperature dependence, direct Coombs test pattern, and treatment strategy.

incorrectas.B: IgE mediates type I hypersensitivity reactions like allergies and anaphylaxis via mast cell degranulation, and IgA functions mainly in mucosal immunity; neither is implicated in the two major subtypes of autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
incorrectas.C: While IgG is indeed correct for warm AIHA, IgD is a poorly understood immunoglobulin whose main role is as a B-cell surface receptor, not a mediator of hemolytic autoantibody disease.
incorrectas.D: IgM correctly represents cold agglutinin disease, but IgA is not the immunoglobulin class responsible for warm AIHA — that role is specifically played by IgG.

preguntas.q: Which class of autoantibody is responsible for warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, so named because it optimally binds RBCs at core body temperature (37°C)?

e.correcta: Warm AIHA is mediated by IgG autoantibodies that bind RBC surface antigens optimally at 37°C; splenic macrophages bearing Fc receptors then recognize these antibody-coated cells and partially phagocytose the membrane, converting the RBC into a spherocyte and driving predominantly extravascular hemolysis. This contrasts sharply with cold agglutinin disease, where IgM antibodies bind optimally at cooler peripheral temperatures and fix complement, producing agglutination and intravascular hemolysis.

incorrectas.A: IgM is responsible for cold agglutinin disease, binding optimally at low peripheral temperatures and activating complement — essentially the opposite temperature profile and mechanism from warm AIHA.
incorrectas.B: IgA is not a major mediator of either warm or cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia; its principal physiologic role is in mucosal secretory immunity, not RBC autoantibody responses.
incorrectas.D: IgE mediates type I hypersensitivity reactions, such as allergy and anaphylaxis via mast cell and basophil degranulation, and has no established role in autoimmune RBC destruction.

preguntas.q: In IgG-mediated (warm) autoimmune hemolytic anemia, partial phagocytic removal of antibody-coated RBC membrane by splenic macrophages produces which red cell morphology?

e.correcta: As IgG antibody-coated RBCs pass through the spleen, Fc receptor-bearing macrophages bite off portions of the tagged membrane without destroying the whole cell, and the RBC reseals with less membrane surface relative to its cytoplasmic volume, forcing it into a round shape with loss of central pallor. This produces spherocytes that are morphologically identical to those seen in hereditary spherocytosis, even though the underlying cause here is extrinsic and antibody-mediated rather than an intrinsic membrane protein defect — a key distinction tested between mechanism and morphology.

incorrectas.A: Schistocytes are fragmented RBCs produced by mechanical shearing forces, such as across fibrin strands in microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, not by the gradual macrophage-mediated membrane removal seen in warm AIHA.
incorrectas.C: Bite cells form when macrophages pluck out precipitated Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin) in conditions like G6PD deficiency, a mechanistically distinct process from the antibody-driven membrane loss of warm AIHA.
incorrectas.D: Elliptocytes are oval-shaped RBCs characteristic of hereditary elliptocytosis, caused by defects in membrane skeletal proteins like spectrin, and are unrelated to immune-mediated membrane removal.

preguntas.q: What is the most common underlying cause of IgG-mediated (warm) autoimmune hemolytic anemia?

e.correcta: Systemic lupus erythematosus is the most common identifiable cause of warm (IgG-mediated) autoimmune hemolytic anemia, reflecting the broader breakdown of self-tolerance and widespread autoantibody production characteristic of SLE, which can target RBC surface antigens in addition to nuclear antigens and other tissues. Warm AIHA can also arise idiopathically or secondary to other autoimmune diseases, certain drugs, and lymphoproliferative disorders, but SLE remains the classic and most frequently tested association.

incorrectas.A: Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection is classically associated with cold agglutinin disease (IgM-mediated, producing anti-I antibodies), placing it in the cold rather than warm AIHA category.
incorrectas.B: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV) is also classically linked to cold agglutinin production (anti-i antibodies), fitting the cold rather than the warm AIHA pattern described here.
incorrectas.C: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a recognized secondary cause of warm AIHA, but it is a less common etiology overall compared to SLE, which is the classic first-line association for IgG-mediated hemolytic anemia.

preguntas.q: Systemic lupus erythematosus is most commonly associated with which class of autoantibody-mediated hemolytic anemia?

e.correcta: SLE classically triggers warm-type (IgG-mediated) autoimmune hemolytic anemia, consistent with the broader systemic loss of B-cell tolerance in lupus that generates a wide range of IgG autoantibodies, including antinuclear, anti-dsDNA, and anti-RBC antibodies. The resulting IgG-coated RBCs undergo extravascular destruction by splenic macrophages, producing spherocytes on smear and a positive direct Coombs test for IgG, with or without complement (C3).

incorrectas.B: IgM (cold) agglutinin disease is typically triggered by Mycoplasma pneumoniae or EBV infection, or arises idiopathically or from a lymphoproliferative process — it is not a classic feature of SLE.
incorrectas.C: IgA-mediated hemolysis is not a recognized major category of autoimmune hemolytic anemia; IgA plays essentially no role in either the warm or cold AIHA classification schemes.
incorrectas.D: IgE mediates allergic and anaphylactic reactions through mast cell degranulation, not RBC destruction, and has no established connection to SLE-associated hemolytic anemia.

preguntas.q: A patient with warm (IgG-mediated) autoimmune hemolytic anemia is found on further workup to have an underlying lymphoproliferative malignancy. Which of the following is most classically associated with warm AIHA?

e.correcta: CLL is the classic B-cell malignancy associated with warm (IgG-mediated) autoimmune hemolytic anemia; the malignant B-cell clone produces autoantibodies (often IgG) against RBC surface antigens, and warm-reactive IgG opsonizes RBCs for extravascular destruction by Fc-receptor-bearing splenic macrophages. This warm AIHA can occur as a paraneoplastic phenomenon in CLL and is a key reason a Coombs test is checked in these patients.

incorrectas.B: Hairy cell leukemia is a B-cell neoplasm marked by cells with fine cytoplasmic projections, a dry tap on bone marrow aspiration, and TRAP positivity, but it is not classically linked to warm IgG-mediated hemolytic anemia the way CLL is.
incorrectas.C: CML is a myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by the BCR-ABL fusion and arises from the granulocytic lineage rather than B lymphocytes, so it is not the disease classically paired with autoantibody-mediated hemolysis.
incorrectas.D: Waldenström macroglobulinemia is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma that secretes monoclonal IgM, making it the classic cause of IgM-mediated (cold agglutinin) hemolytic anemia rather than warm IgG-mediated hemolysis.

preguntas.q: Which immunoglobulin isotype mediates drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia, such as when penicillin binds RBC membranes and triggers antibody formation?

e.correcta: Drug-induced hemolytic anemia is typically IgG-mediated: the drug haptenates onto the RBC membrane, and IgG antibodies form against this drug-RBC complex, opsonizing the cell for extravascular destruction by splenic macrophages. This warm-type mechanism is confirmed by a positive direct Coombs test.

incorrectas.A: IgM is the isotype responsible for cold agglutinin disease, where it binds RBCs at low temperatures and fixes complement — a distinct mechanism from the drug-hapten IgG process.
incorrectas.B: IgA is not a major mediator of hemolytic anemia; it functions mainly in mucosal immunity and is not implicated in the classic drug-induced hemolysis mechanism.
incorrectas.D: IgE mediates immediate hypersensitivity (type I) reactions like anaphylaxis and allergy via mast cell degranulation, not the opsonization of drug-hapten-coated RBCs seen in immune hemolytic anemia.

preguntas.q: A patient develops hemolytic anemia after starting a new antibiotic, with the drug covalently binding RBC membrane proteins and IgG antibodies subsequently targeting the drug-RBC complex. Which drug is the classic example of this hapten mechanism?

e.correcta: Penicillin is the classic drug that acts as a hapten, covalently binding to RBC membrane proteins; the immune system then generates IgG antibodies against this drug-modified RBC surface, leading to extravascular hemolysis. This is distinct from drugs that trigger a true autoantibody response independent of ongoing drug binding.

incorrectas.B: Methyldopa causes hemolytic anemia by a different mechanism — it induces true autoantibodies against intrinsic RBC antigens that persist even without ongoing drug presence, grouping it as an autoimmune-inducing drug rather than a hapten-forming one like penicillin.
incorrectas.C: Rifampin is more associated with drug-induced thrombocytopenia and other immune cytopenias via immune complex deposition, but it is not the prototypical hapten-type drug causing hemolytic anemia.
incorrectas.D: Quinidine classically causes drug-induced hemolysis and thrombocytopenia via an immune complex ("innocent bystander") mechanism, where drug-antibody complexes nonspecifically adsorb onto RBCs — a different mechanism from penicillin's direct hapten binding.

preguntas.q: Which drug is classically associated with inducing true autoantibodies against native RBC antigens (rather than acting as a hapten), resulting in IgG-mediated hemolytic anemia?

e.correcta: α-methyldopa induces production of genuine autoantibodies directed against intrinsic RBC membrane antigens (most often Rh antigens), independent of the drug remaining bound to the cell — distinguishing it from hapten-type drugs. This autoantibody-mediated mechanism produces a positive direct Coombs test and warm-type IgG hemolysis that can persist even after the drug is stopped, since true autoimmunity has already been triggered.

incorrectas.B: Penicillin causes hemolysis via a hapten mechanism, where the drug itself binds the RBC membrane and antibodies target the drug-RBC complex rather than native RBC antigens as with methyldopa.
incorrectas.C: Cephalosporins, like penicillin, typically act via a hapten mechanism binding RBC membranes, rather than by inducing autoantibodies against native RBC antigens.
incorrectas.D: Quinidine causes hemolysis through an immune complex ("innocent bystander") mechanism, in which drug-antibody complexes deposit nonspecifically on RBCs and fix complement, distinct from methyldopa's induction of true autoantibodies.

preguntas.q: Besides stopping the offending drug when applicable, which class of medication is first-line to slow antibody production in IgG-mediated (warm) hemolytic anemia?

e.correcta: Corticosteroids are first-line therapy for warm IgG-mediated hemolytic anemia because they suppress the immune system's production of the pathogenic autoantibody, reducing ongoing RBC destruction — this works upstream by dampening antibody synthesis rather than acting on already-coated RBCs.

incorrectas.A: Rituximab (anti-CD20) depletes B cells and is used as a second-line agent in refractory or steroid-dependent warm AIHA, but it is not the initial first-line treatment.
incorrectas.B: Plasmapheresis physically removes circulating antibody from plasma and is reserved for severe or refractory cases (more classically used in IgM-mediated disease), not as first-line therapy for warm AIHA.
incorrectas.D: IVIG can provide temporary relief by saturating splenic macrophage Fc receptors with donor immunoglobulin so autoantibody-coated RBCs are less readily phagocytosed, but this is a stopgap measure, not the first-line treatment aimed at reducing antibody production.

preguntas.q: In a patient with warm IgG-mediated hemolytic anemia refractory to steroids and rituximab, which procedure is considered a last-resort treatment?

e.correcta: Splenectomy removes the primary site where IgG-coated RBCs are recognized and destroyed by Fc-receptor-bearing macrophages, and is reserved as a last-resort treatment when medical therapy (steroids, IVIG, rituximab) fails to control warm AIHA. Removing the spleen eliminates the major organ of extravascular hemolysis, though it does not stop autoantibody production itself.

incorrectas.B: Bone marrow transplant is not standard treatment for autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which is a disorder of peripheral RBC destruction rather than a marrow failure state requiring stem cell replacement.
incorrectas.C: Plasmapheresis removes circulating antibody but provides only transient benefit since antibody production continues; it is used more for acute severe cases or IgM-mediated disease, not as the definitive last-resort step for warm AIHA.
incorrectas.D: IVIG offers temporary relief by blocking splenic Fc receptors but its effect is short-lived, making it a bridge therapy rather than the definitive last-resort intervention like splenectomy.

preguntas.q: Which subtype of autoimmune hemolytic anemia is also known as cold agglutinin disease?

e.correcta: IgM-mediated AIHA is called cold agglutinin disease because IgM antibodies bind RBC surface antigens optimally at temperatures below 30°C, causing agglutination in the cooler distal extremities (fingertips, ears, nose) — remember "cold weather is Miserable" for IgM. As blood recirculates to the warmer core, the IgM dissociates, but not before complement has often already been fixed.

incorrectas.A: IgA-mediated hemolytic anemia is not a recognized major clinical entity; IgA is not implicated in the cold agglutinin mechanism.
incorrectas.B: Cold agglutinin disease is actually defined by its heavy reliance on complement activation (IgM is an efficient complement fixer), so calling it "complement-independent" is incorrect — complement fixation is central to its pathophysiology.
incorrectas.D: IgG-mediated AIHA is "warm" AIHA, active at body temperature and causing extravascular hemolysis via splenic macrophages — the opposite thermal profile from cold agglutinin disease.

preguntas.q: When ambient temperature drops below 30°C, IgM antibodies in cold agglutinin disease bind RBCs and activate which system, leading to opsonization or, in severe cases, intravascular hemolysis?

e.correcta: IgM is a highly efficient activator of the classical complement pathway because its pentameric structure can engage C1q with a single molecule; once bound to cold-exposed RBCs, IgM fixes complement down to C3b, which coats the RBC as an opsonin for splenic macrophage clearance, while extensive activation can drive complement all the way to the membrane attack complex, causing intravascular hemolysis.

incorrectas.A: The kinin system generates bradykinin and mediates inflammation/vasodilation, unrelated to the antibody-mediated RBC destruction seen in cold agglutinin disease.
incorrectas.B: NADPH oxidase generates reactive oxygen species in phagocytes (the respiratory burst) and is unrelated to antibody-triggered complement fixation on RBCs.
incorrectas.C: The coagulation cascade generates fibrin clots and is not the system triggered by IgM binding to RBCs in cold agglutinin disease; hemolysis here is complement-mediated, not clot-mediated.

preguntas.q: In IgM-mediated (cold agglutinin) hemolytic anemia, RBCs inactivate most complement, but residual C3b opsonization leads splenic macrophages to remove part of the membrane. What RBC morphology results from this partial phagocytosis?

e.correcta: Splenic macrophages recognize C3b-opsonized RBCs and remove a portion of the membrane during partial phagocytosis (rather than destroying the whole cell), leaving a cell with reduced surface-area-to-volume ratio — a spherocyte. These spherocytes are then more susceptible to further extravascular destruction because they lack the deformability of normal biconcave RBCs.

incorrectas.A: Target cells show a central bullseye of hemoglobin and are seen in conditions like liver disease, thalassemia, and asplenia due to excess membrane relative to hemoglobin content, unrelated to the complement-opsonization process in cold AIHA.
incorrectas.B: Bite cells result from oxidative damage and removal of denatured hemoglobin (Heinz bodies) by splenic macrophages, classically seen in G6PD deficiency — a different mechanism from complement-mediated partial membrane loss.
incorrectas.D: Schistocytes are fragmented RBCs ("helmet cells") produced by mechanical shearing as cells pass through damaged or narrowed vessels (e.g., microangiopathic hemolytic anemia), not by macrophage-mediated partial phagocytosis via complement opsonization.

preguntas.q: IgM-mediated (cold agglutinin) hemolytic anemia can occur as a paraneoplastic phenomenon in which B-cell malignancy, even though this same malignancy is more classically linked to the IgG-mediated (warm) form?

e.correcta: CLL is most classically associated with warm (IgG-mediated) autoimmune hemolytic anemia, but it can less commonly present with cold agglutinin (IgM-mediated) hemolysis as well, reflecting the broader dysregulated antibody production by the malignant B-cell clone. Recognizing that CLL can drive either type of AIHA is a testable nuance distinguishing it from Waldenström macroglobulinemia, the prototypical cause of IgM-mediated cold agglutinin disease.

incorrectas.A: Hairy cell leukemia is characterized by pancytopenia, splenomegaly, and TRAP-positive cells with hairy projections, but it is not classically linked to either warm or cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
incorrectas.B: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm producing monoclonal immunoglobulin (often IgG or IgA) that causes lytic bone lesions and renal disease, not classically paired with cold agglutinin hemolytic anemia.
incorrectas.D: Follicular lymphoma is a common indolent B-cell lymphoma with a t(14;18) translocation, but it is not the malignancy classically linked to either warm or cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia in the way CLL is.

preguntas.q: A patient develops painful, bluish discoloration of the fingers and toes upon cold exposure due to RBC agglutination in the distal circulation. Which type of autoimmune hemolytic anemia does this represent?

e.correcta: Cold agglutinin disease is caused by IgM antibodies that bind RBC antigens optimally in cooler peripheral tissues (fingertips, toes, nose, ears), causing agglutination and vaso-occlusion that produces the painful, blue discoloration described; as blood returns to the warmer core, IgM dissociates, but repeated cold exposure reproduces the cycle.

incorrectas.A: Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria is caused by a biphasic IgG antibody (Donath-Landsteiner antibody) that binds RBCs in the cold and fixes complement upon rewarming, causing intravascular hemolysis and hemoglobinuria — a distinct entity from the IgM-mediated agglutination causing the digital vaso-occlusive symptoms described here.
incorrectas.B: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia results from mechanical RBC shearing in damaged small vessels (e.g., TTP, HUS, DIC), producing schistocytes, not temperature-dependent antibody-mediated agglutination in the distal extremities.
incorrectas.C: Warm AIHA is mediated by IgG that reacts at core body temperature, causing steady extravascular hemolysis rather than temperature-dependent peripheral agglutination and cold-induced digital symptoms.

preguntas.q: Which laboratory test is used to diagnose immune-mediated hemolytic anemia by detecting antibody or complement on the patient's RBCs?

e.correcta: The Coombs test (antiglobulin test) is the key diagnostic tool for immune hemolytic anemia — it detects whether antibody (IgG) or complement (C3) is bound to the patient's RBCs (direct Coombs) or present in the serum (indirect Coombs), confirming an immune-mediated hemolytic process rather than an intrinsic or mechanical one.

incorrectas.A: Ham's acid hemolysis test (and the related sucrose lysis test) evaluates complement-mediated lysis of complement-sensitive RBCs in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, a distinct disorder caused by a GPI-anchor deficiency rather than antibody-mediated hemolysis.
incorrectas.B: Hemoglobin electrophoresis separates hemoglobin variants to diagnose hemoglobinopathies like sickle cell disease or thalassemia, and does not detect antibody or complement on RBCs.
incorrectas.C: The osmotic fragility test assesses RBC membrane stability by exposing cells to hypotonic saline and is used to diagnose hereditary spherocytosis, not immune-mediated hemolysis.

preguntas.q: Which version of the Coombs test answers the question, "Are the patient's RBCs already coated with immunoglobulin or complement in vivo?"

e.correcta: The direct Coombs test (direct antiglobulin test) mixes the patient's own washed RBCs with anti-human globulin reagent; agglutination indicates that antibody or complement is already bound to the patient's RBCs in vivo, making it the most important confirmatory test for ongoing immune hemolytic anemia.

incorrectas.A: The indirect Coombs test instead detects free antibodies circulating in the patient's serum by mixing the serum with donor RBCs of known antigenicity, answering a different question about serum antibodies rather than what is already bound to the patient's own cells (used, for example, in prenatal antibody screening and crossmatching).
incorrectas.C: A cold agglutinin titer quantifies the level of cold-reactive IgM antibodies in serum and supports a diagnosis of cold agglutinin disease, but it does not directly test for antibody already bound to the patient's RBCs.
incorrectas.D: The Donath-Landsteiner test detects the biphasic hemolysin antibody responsible for paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria by observing complement-mediated lysis after cold-then-warm incubation, a specialized test distinct from the general direct Coombs test.

preguntas.q: Which version of the Coombs test answers the question, "Does the patient's serum contain free antibodies capable of binding RBC antigens?"

e.correcta: The indirect Coombs test mixes the patient's serum with reagent RBCs of known antigen composition and then adds anti-human globulin; agglutination reveals that the patient's serum contains free antibodies against RBC antigens, even if those antibodies aren't yet bound to the patient's own cells. This test is used clinically for prenatal antibody screening and pretransfusion compatibility testing.

incorrectas.A: The direct Coombs test instead detects antibody or complement already bound to the patient's own circulating RBCs, answering a different question about in vivo coating rather than free serum antibodies.
incorrectas.C: A peripheral blood smear can reveal morphologic clues like spherocytes or schistocytes suggestive of hemolysis, but it does not specifically detect free antibodies in the serum.
incorrectas.D: A reticulocyte count measures the bone marrow's compensatory response to hemolysis or blood loss, reflecting the degree of erythropoietic response rather than detecting circulating antibodies.

preguntas.q: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) is primarily driven by which mechanism of RBC destruction?

o.A: Osmotic lysis due to membrane defects

e.correcta: MAHA is caused by RBCs being physically sheared as they pass through partially occluded or abnormal small vessels (e.g., fibrin/platelet microthrombi in TTP, HUS, or DIC), producing fragmented cells (schistocytes) and releasing hemoglobin directly into the vasculature — this is intravascular hemolysis, in contrast to the macrophage-mediated extravascular clearance seen in AIHA.

incorrectas.A: Osmotic lysis due to membrane defects characterizes conditions like hereditary spherocytosis, where an intrinsic membrane skeleton abnormality makes RBCs fragile, not the mechanical shearing seen in MAHA.
incorrectas.B: Oxidative denaturation of hemoglobin (forming Heinz bodies) is the mechanism in G6PD deficiency, leading to bite cell formation via splenic macrophage removal, a different process from the vascular shearing injury of MAHA.
incorrectas.C: Extravascular hemolysis in the spleen is the mechanism behind antibody-mediated (Coombs-positive) hemolytic anemias like warm AIHA, where macrophages phagocytose antibody- or complement-coated RBCs — a distinct process from the mechanical fragmentation of MAHA.

preguntas.q: RBCs damaged by mechanical shearing as they pass through vessels obstructed by microthrombi (e.g., fibrin or platelet clots) are characteristic of which condition?

e.correcta: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia occurs when RBCs are forced through small vessels that are partially obstructed or narrowed — most often by fibrin or platelet microthrombi — causing mechanical shearing that fragments the cells into schistocytes and releases hemoglobin intravascularly. This mechanism links MAHA to underlying disorders that generate microthrombi, such as TTP, HUS, and DIC.

incorrectas.A: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia is caused by IgG antibody coating of RBCs leading to extravascular splenic phagocytosis, not by mechanical fragmentation from vascular obstruction.
incorrectas.C: Hereditary spherocytosis results from mutations in RBC membrane skeletal proteins (e.g., spectrin, ankyrin) causing progressive membrane loss and spherocyte formation, an intrinsic membrane defect rather than mechanical shearing from microthrombi.
incorrectas.D: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria results from a somatic PIGA mutation causing loss of GPI-anchored complement-regulatory proteins, making RBCs abnormally susceptible to complement-mediated lysis, not mechanical injury from vascular obstruction.

preguntas.q: A patient presents with schistocytes on smear, thrombocytopenia, and organ dysfunction. Which of the following classically causes microangiopathic hemolytic anemia through formation of microthrombi in small vessels?

e.correcta: TTP is a classic cause of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, driven by a deficiency of ADAMTS13 that leads to accumulation of ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers, excessive platelet aggregation, and widespread microthrombi that mechanically shear passing RBCs into schistocytes. This same mechanical hemolysis mechanism underlies other MAHA-associated conditions like HUS, DIC, HELLP syndrome, malignant hypertension, and SLE.

incorrectas.B: Hereditary spherocytosis is caused by an intrinsic RBC membrane skeleton defect (e.g., spectrin or ankyrin deficiency) leading to progressive membrane loss and extravascular splenic destruction, not microthrombus-induced mechanical shearing.
incorrectas.C: G6PD deficiency causes hemolysis via oxidative stress that denatures hemoglobin (Heinz bodies), leading to bite cell formation and splenic clearance, a mechanism unrelated to microthrombi or vascular obstruction.
incorrectas.D: Cold agglutinin disease causes hemolysis via IgM-mediated agglutination and complement fixation at low temperatures, not via mechanical fragmentation from microvascular thrombi.

preguntas.q: Which fragmented RBC morphology, sometimes called a "helmet cell," is characteristic of both micro- and macroangiopathic hemolytic anemia?

e.correcta: Schistocytes ("helmet cells") are irregularly shaped RBC fragments produced when cells are sheared by mechanical forces — either passing through fibrin/platelet microthrombi in small vessels (microangiopathic, e.g., TTP/HUS/DIC) or striking a damaged large vessel or prosthetic heart valve (macroangiopathic hemolysis) — and their presence on a peripheral smear is a key clue pointing toward a mechanical, rather than immune or intrinsic, cause of hemolysis.

incorrectas.B: Spherocytes are round RBCs lacking central pallor, formed either by hereditary membrane defects (hereditary spherocytosis) or partial macrophage phagocytosis of antibody/complement-coated cells (AIHA), not by mechanical vascular shearing.
incorrectas.C: Elliptocytes are oval-shaped RBCs classically seen in hereditary elliptocytosis, a membrane cytoskeletal disorder, and are not the fragment associated with mechanical hemolysis.
incorrectas.D: Acanthocytes ("spur cells") are RBCs with irregular thorny projections seen in liver disease and abetalipoproteinemia due to altered membrane lipid composition, distinct from the fragmentation pattern of schistocytes.

preguntas.q: Plasmodium species that cause malaria are transmitted to humans through the bite of which vector?

e.correcta: The female Anopheles mosquito is the definitive host and vector for Plasmodium species, transmitting sporozoites during a blood meal; the parasite then travels to the liver before infecting RBCs and causing the cyclic hemolysis characteristic of malaria. Recognizing Anopheles as the vector is key to understanding malaria's geographic distribution and prevention strategies (bed nets, mosquito control).

incorrectas.A: Ixodes ticks transmit Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease), Babesia, and Anaplasma, not Plasmodium — though Babesia causes a malaria-like hemolytic illness, its vector is different from that of Plasmodium.
incorrectas.B: Aedes mosquitoes transmit arboviruses such as dengue, Zika, yellow fever, and chikungunya, not Plasmodium malaria.
incorrectas.C: The reduviid (kissing) bug transmits Trypanosoma cruzi, the cause of Chagas disease, an entirely different parasite and vector from Plasmodium/Anopheles.

preguntas.q: A patient with malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum classically develops fever with which periodicity?

e.correcta: Plasmodium falciparum classically causes fever that can occur daily (quotidian) or every other day, reflecting a shorter and less strictly synchronized erythrocytic cycle compared to other Plasmodium species; it is also the most dangerous species because it can infect RBCs of any age, leading to high parasitemia and severe or complicated malaria (cerebral malaria, blackwater fever).

incorrectas.A: Strict tertian fever (every other day, i.e., a 48-hour cycle) is the classic pattern for P. vivax and P. ovale, which preferentially infect reticulocytes and have a more regular erythrocytic cycle than P. falciparum.
incorrectas.B: Quartan fever (every 72 hours) is classically associated with Plasmodium malariae, which has an even longer erythrocytic cycle than the tertian species.
incorrectas.D: Malaria fevers are cyclical and recurrent, corresponding to synchronized waves of RBC rupture releasing merozoites, not a single isolated fever episode.

preguntas.q: Malaria caused by Plasmodium vivax or Plasmodium ovale classically produces fever with which periodicity?

e.correcta: P. vivax and P. ovale preferentially infect reticulocytes and have a synchronized 48-hour erythrocytic cycle, producing classic tertian fever — spikes occurring every other day as merozoites are simultaneously released from ruptured RBCs. These two species also form hypnozoites in the liver, enabling relapse months to years after initial infection, a feature the quotidian-pattern P. falciparum does not share.

incorrectas.A: Daily (quotidian) fever is the pattern more typical of P. falciparum, whose less synchronized, shorter erythrocytic cycle can produce fevers every day rather than every other day.
incorrectas.C: Every-72-hour (quartan) fever is characteristic of P. malariae, reflecting its longer erythrocytic cycle compared to the 48-hour cycle of P. vivax/ovale.
incorrectas.D: Malaria fever is classically cyclical/paroxysmal, tied to synchronized RBC rupture, not continuous — a continuous pattern would be atypical for malaria and would suggest another process.

preguntas.q: Which tick-borne organism causes an illness with fever and hemolytic anemia that closely resembles malaria and can be confused with it on blood smear?

e.correcta: Babesia microti is an intraerythrocytic protozoan transmitted by the Ixodes tick (the same vector as Lyme disease, with which it can co-infect) that invades RBCs and causes fever, hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia mimicking malaria; on blood smear, Babesia can form a "Maltese cross" ring form tetrad that can be mistaken for Plasmodium, but Babesia lacks the pigment (hemozoin) seen with Plasmodium and has no mosquito vector.

incorrectas.A: Toxoplasma gondii is transmitted via cat feces or undercooked meat and causes congenital infection, encephalitis in immunocompromised hosts, or a mononucleosis-like illness, but it does not cause a malaria-mimicking hemolytic febrile illness via RBC invasion.
incorrectas.C: Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas disease) is transmitted by the reduviid bug and classically causes cardiomyopathy and megacolon/megaesophagus, not a malaria-like hemolytic febrile syndrome from RBC parasitization.
incorrectas.D: Leishmania donovani (visceral leishmaniasis/kala-azar) is transmitted by sandflies and infects macrophages (not RBCs), causing hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and fever — a different mechanism from the RBC-invasive hemolysis of Babesia.

preguntas.q: Anemia due to underproduction of RBCs can occur in patients with chronic kidney disease, primarily because of decreased production of which hormone?

e.correcta: The kidneys are the primary source of erythropoietin (EPO), a hormone that stimulates RBC production in the bone marrow in response to hypoxia; in chronic kidney disease, damaged peritubular interstitial cells produce less EPO, leading to a normocytic, normochromic anemia due to underproduction rather than hemolysis or blood loss. This is why exogenous EPO analogs (e.g., epoetin alfa) are used to treat anemia in dialysis patients.

incorrectas.A: Thrombopoietin stimulates platelet production and is made primarily by the liver, not the kidney, and its deficiency would cause thrombocytopenia rather than the anemia of chronic kidney disease.
incorrectas.B: Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid regulating sodium and potassium balance at the distal nephron; its levels are not the driver of the anemia seen in chronic kidney disease.
incorrectas.D: Renin is released by the juxtaglomerular apparatus to regulate blood pressure via the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and its reduced production is not the cause of chronic kidney disease-associated anemia.

preguntas.q: Parvovirus B19 causes anemia due to underproduction by infecting RBC progenitor cells and temporarily halting which process?

e.correcta: Parvovirus B19 has tropism for erythroid progenitor cells (via the P antigen receptor) and directly lyses these cells, temporarily halting erythropoiesis; in healthy individuals this causes only a transient, subclinical dip in RBC production, but in patients with an already shortened RBC lifespan (e.g., sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis), it can precipitate a severe aplastic crisis with a sudden drop in hemoglobin and reticulocyte count.

incorrectas.A: Hemoglobin synthesis defects (e.g., in thalassemia or iron deficiency) impair the quality of RBCs produced, but parvovirus B19's mechanism is direct destruction of the erythroid progenitor cells themselves, not impaired hemoglobin synthesis within surviving cells.
incorrectas.C: Iron absorption occurs in the duodenum and is regulated by hepcidin; parvovirus B19 does not act on iron absorption but rather directly infects and kills erythroid precursors in the bone marrow.
incorrectas.D: Reticulocyte maturation into RBCs is not specifically blocked by parvovirus B19; rather, the virus destroys the earlier progenitor cells needed to generate reticulocytes in the first place, causing reticulocytopenia.

preguntas.q: What is the appropriate treatment approach for an immunocompetent patient with acute parvovirus B19 infection?

o.A: Supportive care, as the infection is self-limited

e.correcta: In immunocompetent hosts, parvovirus B19 infection is typically self-limited, and the transient drop in erythropoiesis resolves on its own once the immune system clears the virus, so supportive care is all that's needed; the main exception is patients with chronic hemolytic anemias or immunosuppression, who may need transfusion support or (in chronic infection due to immunodeficiency) IVIG to help clear the virus.

incorrectas.B: IVIG plus corticosteroids is reserved for immunocompromised patients with chronic parvovirus B19 infection who cannot mount an adequate antibody response to clear the virus on their own, not for routine immunocompetent infection.
incorrectas.C: Acyclovir is an antiviral targeting herpesvirus DNA polymerase and has no activity against parvovirus B19, a non-enveloped DNA virus with a different replication mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Emergent RBC exchange transfusion is not indicated for typical parvovirus B19 infection; simple transfusion support might be considered only in the setting of a severe aplastic crisis in a patient with an underlying hemolytic disorder, not as routine management.

preguntas.q: Which type of anemia can be induced by radiation exposure and by drugs such as benzene, chloramphenicol, alkylating agents, and antimetabolites?

e.correcta: Aplastic anemia results from injury to hematopoietic stem cells, producing pancytopenia with a hypocellular, fatty bone marrow. Radiation and myelotoxic agents like benzene, chloramphenicol, alkylating agents, and antimetabolites directly damage or destroy these pluripotent stem cells rather than affecting a single cell lineage, which is why all three cell lines (RBCs, WBCs, platelets) fall together.

incorrectas.A: Megaloblastic anemia is caused by impaired DNA synthesis from folate or B12 deficiency, producing large, immature RBC precursors rather than marrow stem cell destruction — it is not a classic toxic/radiation-induced marrow failure.
incorrectas.B: Sideroblastic anemia results from defective heme synthesis (e.g., ALA synthase deficiency, lead poisoning, isoniazid), causing iron-laden ringed sideroblasts, not global marrow hypoplasia from stem cell injury.
incorrectas.D: Hemolytic anemia involves premature RBC destruction (intravascular or extravascular) rather than failure of marrow production, and is not the mechanism by which benzene or alkylating agents cause disease.

preguntas.q: Which anemia can be triggered by viral infections such as parvovirus B19, EBV, HIV, and hepatitis viruses?

e.correcta: Certain viruses can directly infect or trigger immune-mediated destruction of hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells, producing marrow failure. Parvovirus B19 classically infects erythroid progenitors (via the P antigen) causing transient pure red cell aplasia, while EBV, HIV, and hepatitis viruses (non-A, non-B, non-C) can precipitate broader aplastic anemia, likely through immune-mediated marrow suppression.

incorrectas.B: Megaloblastic anemia stems from nutritional deficiencies (folate/B12) impairing DNA synthesis, not from viral infection of marrow stem cells.
incorrectas.C: Sideroblastic anemia is due to defective mitochondrial heme synthesis (genetic, toxic, or drug-induced), unrelated to viral marrow suppression.
incorrectas.D: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia involves antibody-mediated destruction of mature circulating RBCs, a peripheral process distinct from viral-induced failure of marrow stem cell production.

preguntas.q: Fanconi anemia is caused by a defect in the repair of DNA double-strand breaks. This defect increases the risk of developing what?

e.correcta: Fanconi anemia is an autosomal recessive DNA repair disorder (FA/BRCA pathway) that impairs the cell's ability to fix DNA crosslinks/double-strand breaks. Because damaged DNA accumulates instead of being repaired, cells are prone to malignant transformation, giving patients a markedly increased lifetime risk of acute myeloid leukemia and squamous cell carcinomas, in addition to the bone marrow failure itself.

incorrectas.A: Fanconi anemia is not primarily an autoimmune disorder — its pathology stems from a DNA repair defect leading to marrow failure and malignancy, not antibody-mediated destruction of blood cells.
incorrectas.B: While pancytopenia can predispose to infection, the hallmark long-term complication tested on Step 1 for Fanconi anemia is malignancy risk from unrepaired DNA damage, not a primary immunodeficiency syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Iron overload is a feature of conditions like hereditary hemochromatosis or chronic transfusion therapy, not a direct consequence of the DNA repair defect that defines Fanconi anemia.

preguntas.q: Bone marrow biopsy in aplastic anemia classically shows a hypocellular, empty marrow with a "dry marrow tap." What replaces the normal hematopoietic marrow space?

e.correcta: In aplastic anemia, hematopoietic stem cells are destroyed or suppressed, so the marrow space that should contain proliferating precursor cells instead becomes replaced by fat, yielding a hypocellular marrow with normal cell morphology (the defect is in quantity, not quality). This fatty, empty marrow is why aspiration often yields a "dry tap" and biopsy is required for diagnosis.

incorrectas.A: Fibrotic replacement of marrow (myelofibrosis) is seen in primary myelofibrosis and some myelophthisic processes, where marrow is replaced by collagen deposition from megakaryocyte-derived cytokines, not the fatty change of aplastic anemia.
incorrectas.C: Granulomatous infiltration occurs with infections (e.g., TB, fungal) or sarcoidosis involving the marrow, a distinct inflammatory process rather than the passive fatty replacement seen when stem cells simply fail to proliferate.
incorrectas.D: Leukemic blast infiltration describes marrow packed with malignant immature cells (as in acute leukemia), which is the opposite picture from aplastic anemia's empty, hypocellular marrow.

preguntas.q: Which category of treatment for aplastic anemia includes agents like EPO, GM-CSF, and G-CSF?

e.correcta: Marrow-stimulating (hematopoietic growth) factors such as erythropoietin (EPO), granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) push residual stem/progenitor cells to proliferate and differentiate along the RBC and myeloid lineages, helping raise blood counts in aplastic anemia while definitive therapy (transplant or immunosuppression) is pursued.

incorrectas.A: Immunosuppressants (e.g., antithymocyte globulin, cyclosporine) are used in aplastic anemia, but they act by quieting an abnormal T-cell attack on stem cells, a different mechanism from directly stimulating growth factor receptors.
incorrectas.C: Anticoagulants prevent clot formation and have no role in stimulating hematopoiesis; they are not part of standard aplastic anemia management.
incorrectas.D: Iron chelators (e.g., deferasirox) are used to manage iron overload from chronic transfusions, not to stimulate marrow production of new blood cells.

preguntas.q: Beyond growth factors and immunosuppression, what supportive treatment is commonly used in aplastic anemia to manage symptomatic cytopenias?

e.correcta: Because aplastic anemia causes pancytopenia from failed marrow production, supportive transfusions of packed RBCs (for symptomatic anemia) and platelets (to prevent or treat bleeding) are used to bridge patients until marrow-stimulating therapy, immunosuppression, or transplant can restore hematopoiesis.

incorrectas.A: Plasmapheresis removes pathogenic antibodies or immune complexes from plasma and is used in conditions like TTP or Guillain-Barré syndrome, not to replace deficient blood cell counts in aplastic anemia.
incorrectas.B: Splenectomy is used in conditions with excessive splenic destruction of blood cells (e.g., hereditary spherocytosis, ITP), which is not the problem in aplastic anemia — here the marrow simply fails to produce cells in the first place.
incorrectas.D: Phlebotomy removes blood to reduce iron or RBC mass (as in hemochromatosis or polycythemia vera), the opposite of what a pancytopenic aplastic anemia patient needs.

preguntas.q: In idiopathic aplastic anemia thought to be driven by abnormal T-cell activation with cytokine-mediated marrow suppression, which treatment approach (e.g., antithymocyte globulin or cyclosporine) may be helpful?

e.correcta: Many idiopathic cases of aplastic anemia are now understood to be autoimmune, with activated cytotoxic T cells releasing cytokines (like IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha) that suppress hematopoietic stem cells. Immunosuppressive therapy — antithymocyte globulin (which depletes T cells) plus cyclosporine (which blocks T-cell activation via calcineurin inhibition) — removes this suppressive signal and allows marrow recovery, making it a mainstay treatment alongside transplant.

incorrectas.A: Iron chelation addresses iron overload from chronic transfusions rather than the underlying autoimmune T-cell attack on stem cells that drives idiopathic aplastic anemia.
incorrectas.B: Splenectomy would not address T-cell-mediated suppression of the bone marrow; it is more relevant to disorders of excessive splenic sequestration or destruction of blood cells.
incorrectas.C: Anticoagulation targets clot formation, a mechanism unrelated to cytokine-mediated stem cell suppression, and has no therapeutic role in aplastic anemia.

preguntas.q: What is considered a last-resort, definitive treatment for severe aplastic anemia?

e.correcta: Bone marrow (hematopoietic stem cell) transplant replaces the patient's damaged, failing stem cell pool with healthy donor stem cells, offering the only curative option for severe aplastic anemia. It is reserved as a last resort (especially in younger patients with a matched donor) because of the risks of graft-versus-host disease and transplant-related morbidity compared to growth factors or immunosuppression.

incorrectas.B: Chronic transfusion therapy is purely supportive — it replaces missing cells temporarily but does not fix the underlying marrow failure, and carries its own risk of iron overload with prolonged use.
incorrectas.C: High-dose corticosteroids are not a standard definitive therapy for aplastic anemia; immunosuppression in this disease relies primarily on antithymocyte globulin and cyclosporine rather than steroids alone.
incorrectas.D: Splenectomy does not restore marrow stem cell function and plays no role as a definitive treatment for aplastic anemia.

preguntas.q: A pathologic process that replaces bone marrow (such as metastatic cancer), impairing hematopoiesis and causing pancytopenia, is called what?

e.correcta: A myelophthisic process refers to space-occupying replacement of normal bone marrow architecture by an infiltrating pathologic tissue, classically metastatic carcinoma (also granulomas or fibrosis), which crowds out normal hematopoietic elements and impairs blood cell production, resulting in pancytopenia and characteristic teardrop cells/leukoerythroblastic smear.

incorrectas.A: Myelodysplastic syndrome involves intrinsically dysplastic, clonally abnormal hematopoietic stem cells that mature ineffectively, rather than marrow space being physically displaced by an infiltrating external process like metastasis.
incorrectas.B: Myelofibrosis is a specific type of marrow replacement by fibrous (collagen) tissue driven by megakaryocyte-derived cytokines (as in primary myelofibrosis), which is one cause of a myelophthisic picture but not the general umbrella term used here.
incorrectas.D: Extramedullary hematopoiesis is the compensatory response in which blood cell production shifts to the spleen and liver when marrow is compromised — it is a consequence of myelophthisis, not the process of marrow replacement itself.

preguntas.q: Hepatic failure and steroid use both alter thyroid-binding globulin (TBG) levels. What happens to the level of free (biologically active) thyroid hormone in these conditions?

e.correcta: Hepatic failure decreases TBG synthesis while steroid use can also lower TBG; total T4/T3 measured in blood falls because less hormone is bound. However, the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis senses and regulates only the free (unbound) hormone fraction via negative feedback, so the thyroid gland adjusts secretion to keep free T4/T3 — and therefore the patient's clinical thyroid status — normal despite the change in total hormone and binding protein levels.

incorrectas.A: Free hormone does not fall because the feedback loop targets free hormone concentration specifically; only total hormone level drops when TBG decreases, since less is bound but the free fraction is preserved by axis regulation.
incorrectas.B: Free hormone does not rise in this setting — a transient increase in free hormone when TBG first drops would suppress TSH and hence normalize the free level back down through feedback, not sustain an elevation.
incorrectas.D: Free thyroid hormone remains within the normal physiologic range and is not rendered undetectable; only the total (bound + free) hormone measurement is altered by changes in TBG.

preguntas.q: Pregnancy and oral contraceptive use both raise thyroid-binding globulin (TBG) levels via estrogen. What happens to the free thyroid hormone level as a result?

e.correcta: Estrogen increases hepatic synthesis of TBG, so more binding protein is available and total T4/T3 rises because more hormone is bound. But the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis regulates thyroid hormone secretion based on the free hormone fraction, so the thyroid compensates by secreting slightly more hormone to keep free T4/T3 (and TSH) within the normal range — the patient remains clinically euthyroid despite an elevated total T4.

incorrectas.B: Free hormone does not decrease; although more hormone becomes protein-bound, the axis compensates by increasing total secretion so the free, biologically active fraction stays constant.
incorrectas.C: It is the total hormone level that rises (due to more TBG binding sites), not the free hormone level — free hormone is kept normal by feedback regulation, which is the key physiologic point being tested.
incorrectas.D: The free hormone response is not unpredictable — it is a well-characterized, predictable homeostatic mechanism where the axis maintains a stable free hormone concentration despite changes in binding protein.

preguntas.q: In addition to delivering oxygen to peripheral tissues, what gas do erythrocytes transport back to the lungs?

e.correcta: Erythrocytes carry CO2 from peripheral tissues back to the lungs, largely as bicarbonate (generated via carbonic anhydrase inside the RBC) and partly bound to hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin, in addition to a small dissolved fraction. This reverse gas transport is essential for eliminating the CO2 produced by cellular metabolism and for buffering blood pH.

incorrectas.A: Nitric oxide is carried by hemoglobin (bound to cysteine residues) and helps regulate vascular tone, but it is a signaling molecule delivered to vessels, not the primary waste gas RBCs return to the lungs for exhalation.
incorrectas.B: Carbon monoxide can bind hemoglobin with very high affinity (forming carboxyhemoglobin) in cases of toxic exposure, but it is not a normal gas that RBCs physiologically transport back to the lungs as part of respiration.
incorrectas.D: Nitrogen is an inert gas that dissolves in blood (relevant in conditions like decompression sickness) but is not actively transported by RBCs as a metabolic waste product.

preguntas.q: Which granulocyte is highly phagocytic and serves as the primary first responder during acute bacterial infection and inflammation?

e.correcta: Neutrophils are the most abundant circulating leukocyte and are recruited rapidly to sites of acute inflammation, where they phagocytose and kill bacteria using granule contents (lysozyme, defensins) and oxidative burst mechanisms. Their multilobed nucleus and prominent role in acute pyogenic infections make them the hallmark cell of early innate immune response, and neutrophilia on a CBC is a classic sign of acute bacterial infection.

incorrectas.B: Basophils are the least common granulocyte and function mainly by releasing histamine and other mediators in allergic/hypersensitivity reactions; they are not the primary phagocytic responder in acute bacterial infection.
incorrectas.C: Mast cells are tissue-resident (not circulating) and, like basophils, mainly degranulate to release histamine and leukotrienes in allergic responses rather than acting as the principal phagocyte against bacteria.
incorrectas.D: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated B cells devoted to antibody production; they are not phagocytic and belong to the adaptive rather than innate immune response.

preguntas.q: Which type of leukocyte leaves the bloodstream and differentiates into macrophages within tissue?

e.correcta: Monocytes circulate in the blood for a limited time before migrating into tissues, where they differentiate into tissue macrophages (or dendritic cells), taking on organ-specific identities such as Kupffer cells in the liver or microglia in the CNS. This differentiation upregulates their phagocytic and antigen-presenting capacity for long-term tissue surveillance, unlike the short-lived, purely circulating role of most other granulocytes.

incorrectas.B: Eosinophils are granulocytes specialized for defense against helminthic parasites and modulation of allergic responses; they do not differentiate into macrophages in tissue.
incorrectas.A: Neutrophils are short-lived, terminally differentiated phagocytes that die at sites of acute infection (forming pus); they do not transform into a longer-lived tissue macrophage population.
incorrectas.D: Lymphocytes (B and T cells) are agranulocytes of the adaptive immune system that mature into effector or memory cells or plasma cells, not into macrophages.

preguntas.q: Which leukocyte is identified on peripheral smear by a large, kidney (bean)-shaped nucleus and gray-blue "frosted glass" cytoplasm?

e.correcta: Monocytes are the largest circulating leukocytes, recognized by their characteristic large, kidney- or horseshoe-shaped nucleus and abundant gray-blue cytoplasm that gives a ground-glass or "frosted glass" appearance on Wright-Giemsa stain. These morphologic features distinguish them from the segmented, multilobed nuclei of granulocytes and the scant cytoplasm of lymphocytes.

incorrectas.A: Lymphocytes have a round, densely staining nucleus that occupies nearly the entire cell with only a thin rim of cytoplasm, quite different from the monocyte's abundant frosted cytoplasm and kidney-shaped nucleus.
incorrectas.C: Neutrophils have a segmented nucleus with 3-5 lobes connected by thin chromatin strands and finely granular (not frosted-glass) cytoplasm, distinguishing them morphologically from monocytes.
incorrectas.D: Eosinophils have a bilobed nucleus and cytoplasm packed with large, eosinophilic (red-orange) granules, giving a very different appearance from the monocyte's smooth, frosted cytoplasm.

preguntas.q: Tissue macrophages arise from the differentiation of which circulating blood cell?

e.correcta: Circulating monocytes extravasate into tissues and mature into macrophages, acquiring enhanced phagocytic capacity and taking on tissue-specific forms (e.g., Kupffer cells in liver, osteoclasts in bone, alveolar macrophages in lung). This monocyte-to-macrophage transition is central to chronic inflammation, wound healing, and antigen presentation to T cells.

incorrectas.B: Dendritic cells are themselves a distinct antigen-presenting lineage (some arising from monocytes, others from separate precursors) specialized for activating naive T cells, not an intermediate that macrophages differentiate from.
incorrectas.C: Neutrophils are short-lived granulocytes that undergo apoptosis after their phagocytic burst in acute infection; they do not serve as the precursor to the longer-lived tissue macrophage population.
incorrectas.D: Lymphocytes belong to a separate hematopoietic lineage (lymphoid, not myeloid) and mature into T cells, B cells, or NK cells rather than into macrophages.

preguntas.q: Which leukocyte plays the primary defensive role against helminthic (parasitic worm) infections?

e.correcta: Eosinophils contain granules with major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein that are toxic to helminth parasites, and they are recruited to sites of parasitic infection under the direction of Th2 cytokines like IL-5. This makes peripheral eosinophilia a classic clue pointing toward parasitic infection (or allergic disease) on a differential.

incorrectas.A: Basophils release histamine and other mediators important in immediate hypersensitivity reactions and can contribute to anti-parasite immunity, but they are not the primary phagocyte/effector cell defending against helminths — eosinophils hold that role.
incorrectas.B: Monocytes/macrophages are generalist phagocytes important for bacteria, debris clearance, and antigen presentation, but they are not the specialized effector cell for extracellular parasitic worms.
incorrectas.C: Neutrophils are the principal responders to acute bacterial (pyogenic) infections, not the primary defense against multicellular helminthic parasites.

preguntas.q: Which leukocyte is characterized by a bilobed ("bilobulate") nucleus and large, red-orange cytoplasmic granules on H&E stain?

e.correcta: Eosinophils have a distinctive bilobed nucleus and cytoplasm packed with large granules that stain intensely eosinophilic (red-orange) due to their content of arginine-rich major basic protein, giving them a very recognizable appearance on peripheral smear associated with allergic and parasitic conditions.

incorrectas.B: Neutrophils have a multilobed (3-5 lobe) nucleus with fine, neutral-staining cytoplasmic granules, not the coarse bilobed and strongly eosinophilic granules of eosinophils.
incorrectas.C: Basophils have a bilobed-to-obscured nucleus that is often hidden by densely packed, deep purple-staining (basophilic) granules containing histamine and heparin, which stain quite differently from the red-orange eosinophil granules.
incorrectas.D: Monocytes have a single large, kidney-shaped nucleus and pale, ground-glass cytoplasm without the coarse, brightly staining granules seen in eosinophils.

preguntas.q: Eosinophils are highly phagocytic for which type of complex?

e.correcta: Eosinophils are notably efficient at phagocytosing antigen-antibody (immune) complexes, in addition to releasing cytotoxic granule proteins against parasites. This function ties them into clearance of immune complex deposits and links their activity to both allergic disease and helminthic infection, where antibody often coats the target.

incorrectas.A: Clearance of complement-opsonized debris is more classically a job of macrophages and neutrophils, which express complement receptors for efficient uptake, rather than being the signature phagocytic target of eosinophils.
incorrectas.C: Efferocytosis (clearance of apoptotic cells) is primarily performed by macrophages to resolve inflammation without triggering an immune response, not the defining phagocytic role of eosinophils.
incorrectas.D: Direct phagocytosis of bacterial cell wall fragments is characteristic of neutrophils and macrophages in acute bacterial infection, not the specialized function eosinophils are known for.

preguntas.q: Which leukocyte can synthesize and release leukotrienes "on demand" (via new synthesis) rather than relying solely on preformed granules?

e.correcta: Basophils are distinguished by their ability to rapidly synthesize and secrete leukotrienes on demand (via activation of membrane phospholipids and the 5-lipoxygenase pathway) in addition to releasing preformed histamine and heparin from their granules, giving them a dual immediate/delayed contribution to hypersensitivity reactions.

incorrectas.A: Mast cells also release histamine and leukotrienes in allergic responses, but the specific "on demand" leukotriene synthesis distinction (versus purely preformed granule release) is classically attributed to basophils in this context, since mast cells are tissue-resident rather than the circulating cell being tested here.
incorrectas.B: Eosinophils primarily release preformed cytotoxic granule proteins (major basic protein, eosinophil cationic protein) against parasites; leukotriene synthesis on demand is not their signature feature.
incorrectas.D: Neutrophils rely mainly on preformed granule contents (lysozyme, defensins) and oxidative burst for antimicrobial killing, not on synthesizing leukotrienes on demand.

preguntas.q: Basophils, the circulating counterpart to tissue mast cells, primarily mediate what type of reaction?

e.correcta: Basophils express high-affinity IgE receptors (FcεRI); when surface-bound IgE is cross-linked by allergen, they degranulate to release histamine, heparin, and leukotrienes, driving the immediate hypersensitivity (allergic) response seen in conditions like anaphylaxis, asthma, and urticaria.

incorrectas.A: Autoimmune reactions are typically driven by self-reactive T and B lymphocytes and autoantibodies, not by basophil degranulation, which is centered on IgE-mediated allergic pathways.
incorrectas.B: Antiviral defense relies mainly on cytotoxic T cells, NK cells, and type I interferon responses; basophils are not the principal effector cells against viral infection.
incorrectas.C: Antitumor immunity is largely mediated by cytotoxic T cells and NK cells recognizing abnormal or stressed cells, a function distinct from the IgE-driven allergic role of basophils.

preguntas.q: Mast cells, the tissue-resident analog of basophils, mediate what type of reaction locally within tissues?

e.correcta: Mast cells reside in connective tissue near blood vessels and mucosal surfaces and, like basophils, carry surface IgE via FcεRI receptors. Allergen-induced cross-linking of this IgE triggers degranulation with release of histamine, tryptase, and leukotrienes, producing local allergic manifestations such as urticaria, angioedema, and the wheal-and-flare response, as well as systemic anaphylaxis when widespread.

incorrectas.B: Granulomatous reactions are organized collections of activated macrophages (often with giant cells) walling off persistent antigens like mycobacteria or foreign material, a T cell/macrophage-driven process distinct from mast cell degranulation.
incorrectas.C: Autoimmune reactions involve self-reactive lymphocytes and autoantibodies attacking host tissue, which is mechanistically unrelated to IgE-mediated mast cell activation by allergens.
incorrectas.D: Antiviral responses depend on interferons, cytotoxic T cells, and NK cells rather than on mast cell histamine release, which is centered on allergic/hypersensitivity physiology.

preguntas.q: Which antigen-presenting cell serves as the critical link between the innate and adaptive immune systems by activating naive T cells?

e.correcta: Dendritic cells are the most potent professional antigen-presenting cells, capturing antigen in peripheral tissue and migrating to lymph nodes where they present it on MHC to prime naive T cells — a step required to initiate an adaptive immune response. This unique capacity to activate naive (not just previously primed effector) T cells is what makes dendritic cells the bridge between the innate system that first detects a pathogen and the adaptive system that mounts a specific response.

incorrectas.A: Macrophages present antigen and can restimulate previously activated (effector/memory) T cells, but they are generally not efficient at priming naive T cells the way dendritic cells are, making them a secondary rather than the initiating link to adaptive immunity.
incorrectas.C: B cells are also antigen-presenting cells, but like macrophages they primarily activate effector/memory T cells and receive T cell help for antibody responses, rather than serving as the principal primer of naive T cells.
incorrectas.D: Neutrophils are innate phagocytes focused on killing pathogens directly; they are not specialized antigen-presenting cells and do not activate T cells to link innate and adaptive immunity.

preguntas.q: Which cell type, terminally differentiated from activated B cells, produces large quantities of antibody specific to a single antigen?

e.correcta: Plasma cells arise when activated B cells differentiate into dedicated antibody factories, packed with rough endoplasmic reticulum to support high-volume secretion of immunoglobulin specific to the antigen that originally activated their parent B cell clone. This massive, focused antibody output is the effector arm of humoral immunity, in contrast to memory B cells, which stand ready to rapidly reactivate upon antigen re-exposure rather than actively secreting antibody.

incorrectas.A: Memory B cells persist long-term to enable a faster, stronger response on re-exposure to antigen, but they are not actively secreting large amounts of antibody in their resting memory state the way plasma cells do.
incorrectas.B: Dendritic cells present antigen to activate T and B cells but do not themselves produce antibody; their role is upstream of the antibody-secreting plasma cell stage.
incorrectas.D: Macrophages are phagocytic and antigen-presenting cells of the innate/adaptive interface, but antibody production is not part of their function — that is unique to the B cell/plasma cell lineage.

preguntas.q: Which cell is identified microscopically by a "clock-face" (spoke-wheel) chromatin pattern and an eccentrically placed nucleus?

e.correcta: Plasma cells have a characteristic "clock-face" (cartwheel) pattern of peripherally condensed chromatin and an eccentric nucleus pushed to one side by an abundant basophilic cytoplasm containing a prominent perinuclear pale zone (the Golgi apparatus, needed for immunoglobulin secretion). This distinctive morphology is a classic clue for plasma cell neoplasms like multiple myeloma when seen in excess on marrow biopsy.

incorrectas.A: Lymphocytes have a round, centrally placed nucleus with densely clumped (not clock-face) chromatin and minimal cytoplasm, lacking the eccentric nucleus and perinuclear clearing typical of plasma cells.
incorrectas.C: Monocytes have a large kidney-shaped (not clock-face) nucleus and abundant frosted-glass cytoplasm, morphologically distinct from the plasma cell's eccentric nucleus and cartwheel chromatin.
incorrectas.D: Macrophages are larger, more irregular cells with abundant vacuolated cytoplasm (often containing phagocytosed material) and lack the specific clock-face chromatin arrangement that defines plasma cells.

preguntas.q: Under normal, non-neoplastic conditions, in which anatomic compartment do fully differentiated plasma cells typically reside?

e.correcta: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated B cells that migrate out of the germinal center reaction and take up long-term residence in the bone marrow, where marrow stromal cells and cytokines like IL-6 support their survival for months to years, allowing sustained antibody secretion into the blood. This is why bone marrow biopsy is used to quantify plasma cells in disorders such as multiple myeloma and MGUS.

incorrectas.A: Although the antibody made by plasma cells enters the bloodstream, the plasma cells themselves do not normally circulate; they are sessile cells anchored in supportive niches such as marrow rather than free-floating in peripheral blood.
incorrectas.B: The thymic medulla houses maturing T cells undergoing negative selection, not antibody-secreting plasma cells, which are B-lineage cells with no relationship to thymic education.
incorrectas.D: The splenic white pulp germinal center is where naive B cells first encounter antigen and undergo class switching and affinity maturation before some daughter cells differentiate into plasma cells, but the germinal center itself is a transient site of B-cell activation, not the resting home of long-lived plasma cells, which move on to the bone marrow.

preguntas.q: Which of the following body compartments normally lacks circulating plasma cells?

e.correcta: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated, non-recirculating B cells that settle into fixed niches (bone marrow, lymph node medullary cords, mucosal lamina propria) to secrete antibody locally into blood or secretions; they do not themselves patrol the bloodstream the way lymphocytes do. This is why finding plasma cells on a peripheral smear is abnormal and raises concern for plasma cell leukemia, a rare aggressive variant of myeloma.

incorrectas.A: Bone marrow parenchyma is in fact one of the classic resident sites for long-lived plasma cells, supported by stromal-cell niches; it is the opposite of a site where they are normally absent.
incorrectas.B: Lymph node medullary cords are a well-described home for plasma cells after they leave the germinal center, so this is a normal residence site rather than one from which they are excluded.
incorrectas.D: The lamina propria of the gut hosts IgA-secreting plasma cells as part of mucosal immunity, so this too is a normal residence site, unlike peripheral blood.

preguntas.q: Which division of the nervous system is composed of the brain and spinal cord?

e.correcta: The central nervous system (CNS) is defined anatomically as the brain and spinal cord, the structures encased within the skull and vertebral column that integrate and process sensory input and generate motor output. Everything outside this axis, the nerves and ganglia, is classified separately as the peripheral nervous system.

incorrectas.A: The peripheral nervous system comprises the cranial and spinal nerves and their associated ganglia that lie outside the brain and spinal cord, carrying signals to and from the CNS rather than constituting the brain and cord themselves.
incorrectas.C: The autonomic nervous system is a functional subdivision of the nervous system that controls involuntary functions like heart rate and digestion via sympathetic and parasympathetic pathways; it is a functional category, not the anatomic brain-and-cord axis.
incorrectas.D: The enteric nervous system is the semi-autonomous network of neurons within the gut wall that regulates motility and secretion; it can function independently of the CNS and is not part of the brain or spinal cord.

preguntas.q: From which embryologic structure do neurons of the central nervous system arise?

e.correcta: The neural tube forms from neuroectoderm during neurulation and gives rise to the entire CNS, including its neurons, glia (except microglia), and ependymal lining. The neural tube's walls proliferate and differentiate into the brain and spinal cord, making it the direct embryologic source of CNS neurons.

incorrectas.A: Neural crest is a separate population of cells that delaminates from the dorsal neural tube and migrates peripherally to form PNS neurons, ganglia, and Schwann cells, among other structures; it is the source of PNS, not CNS, neurons.
incorrectas.B: Paraxial mesoderm forms somites, which give rise to skeletal muscle, dermis, and vertebrae, not any neural tissue.
incorrectas.D: Surface ectoderm remains outside the neural tube after neurulation and forms epidermis and structures like the lens and anterior pituitary, not neurons of the CNS.

preguntas.q: Which division of the nervous system comprises the cranial and spinal nerves that give rise to peripheral axons and neurons?

e.correcta: The peripheral nervous system (PNS) consists of the cranial nerves (arising from the brainstem) and spinal nerves (arising from the spinal cord), along with the neurons and axons that project outside the CNS to innervate muscles, glands, and sensory receptors. This distinguishes it from the CNS, which is confined to the brain and spinal cord itself.

incorrectas.A: The central nervous system is limited to the brain and spinal cord; the cranial and spinal nerves are, by definition, structures that carry information between the CNS and the periphery and are therefore classified outside it.
incorrectas.B: The enteric nervous system is the intrinsic neuronal network of the gastrointestinal tract wall, functioning largely autonomously to control peristalsis and secretion; it is not defined by the cranial and spinal nerve axons described here.
incorrectas.D: The limbic system is a functional and anatomic grouping of CNS structures (hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, etc.) involved in emotion and memory, unrelated to the peripheral nerve axons in question.

preguntas.q: Neurons of the peripheral nervous system are derived from which embryologic cell population?
