e.correcta: Neural crest cells delaminate from the dorsal margins of the neural tube during neurulation and migrate extensively throughout the embryo, giving rise to PNS neurons and their supporting glia (dorsal root ganglia, autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells) along with many non-neural derivatives like melanocytes and facial cartilage. Their broad migratory potential is why neural crest is sometimes called the "fourth germ layer."

incorrectas.A: The neural tube (neuroectoderm) remains in place and differentiates into the CNS (brain and spinal cord neurons and glia), not the migratory cells that populate the peripheral ganglia.
incorrectas.C: Intermediate mesoderm gives rise to the urogenital system (kidneys, gonads), entirely unrelated to neuronal lineages.
incorrectas.D: Endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the GI and respiratory tracts and associated glands, not neural tissue of any kind.

preguntas.q: What is the embryonic origin of the chromaffin cells that constitute the adrenal medulla?

e.correcta: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla are modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons derived from neural crest cells that migrate in and differentiate under the influence of cortisol from the surrounding (mesoderm-derived) adrenal cortex, which upregulates the enzyme PNMT to convert norepinephrine to epinephrine. This shared neural crest lineage explains why chromaffin cells function essentially as neuroendocrine cells, releasing catecholamines directly into the bloodstream in response to sympathetic preganglionic input.

incorrectas.A: Mesoderm gives rise to the adrenal cortex (the three zones producing steroid hormones), a completely distinct germ layer origin from the neural-crest-derived medulla it surrounds.
incorrectas.C: The neural tube (neuroectoderm) forms the CNS, not the migratory, peripherally located chromaffin cells; neural tube derivatives stay within the brain and spinal cord.
incorrectas.D: Endoderm forms gut and glandular epithelium, unrelated to the neuroendocrine chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.

preguntas.q: Neurulation, the process by which the neural tube forms from the neural plate, begins during which week of embryonic development?

e.correcta: Neurulation begins in the third week of development, when the notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate, which then folds and fuses into the neural tube. This early timing means the neural tube closes (rostral neuropore around day 25, caudal neuropore around day 27) before many women even know they are pregnant, which is why folic acid supplementation is recommended before conception to prevent neural tube defects.

incorrectas.A: Week 2 is the "week of twos," featuring formation of the bilaminar germ disc (epiblast and hypoblast), before gastrulation has even established the trilaminar embryo needed to induce neurulation.
incorrectas.C: Week 5 is well after neurulation is complete; by this time the neural tube has already differentiated into primary and secondary brain vesicles and limb buds are appearing.
incorrectas.D: Week 8 marks the end of the embryonic period and the transition to the fetal period, long after neural tube formation and closure have occurred.

preguntas.q: As the neural folds elevate and fuse to close the neural tube, which population of cells detaches from the crest of the folds and arises from neuroectoderm?

e.correcta: During closure of the neural folds, cells at the dorsal tips (the neural crest) separate from the neuroectoderm and become neural crest cells, a transient, highly migratory population that disperses throughout the embryo to form PNS ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes, and many craniofacial structures. Their origin right at the fusion line of the folds is what positions them to migrate laterally once the tube closes.

incorrectas.A: Notochord cells are mesoderm-derived and lie ventral to the neural tube; they induce neural plate formation but are not the cells arising from the neuroectoderm at the folding crest.
incorrectas.B: Surface ectoderm cells are the ectodermal cells that remain lateral to the neural folds and go on to form the epidermis, not the migratory crest cells budding from the neuroectoderm.
incorrectas.D: Mesenchymal somite cells derive from paraxial mesoderm, not neuroectoderm, and form muscle, vertebrae, and dermis, unrelated to the neural crest lineage.

preguntas.q: Early in development, the rostral neural tube first differentiates into how many primary brain vesicles?

e.correcta: The rostral neural tube initially forms three primary vesicles: the prosencephalon (forebrain), mesencephalon (midbrain), and rhombencephalon (hindbrain), before these further subdivide into five secondary vesicles (telencephalon and diencephalon from the forebrain, metencephalon and myelencephalon from the hindbrain) by week 5. Remembering the 3-then-5 vesicle sequence is key to mapping adult brain structures back to their embryonic origins.

incorrectas.A: Two undercounts the initial subdivisions; the rostral neural tube does not stop at two vesicles before further differentiation.
incorrectas.C: Four is not the classic staging; the standard framework describes three primary vesicles that later become five secondary vesicles, not four at either stage.
incorrectas.D: Five describes the number of secondary vesicles that the three primary vesicles subsequently divide into, not the initial primary count.

preguntas.q: Of the three primary brain vesicles, which one occupies the most rostral (superior) position?

e.correcta: The prosencephalon (forebrain) is the most rostral of the three primary vesicles and subsequently divides into the telencephalon (cerebral hemispheres) and diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus), placing its derivatives at the top of the neuraxis. Its rostral position reflects the general head-to-tail organization of the neural tube, with more complex integrative structures developing anteriorly.

incorrectas.A: The mesencephalon is the middle of the three primary vesicles, developing into the midbrain, positioned caudal to the forebrain and rostral to the hindbrain rather than at the most superior point.
incorrectas.B: The rhombencephalon is the most caudal (inferior) of the three primary vesicles, giving rise to the pons, cerebellum, and medulla, the opposite end of the neuraxis from the forebrain.
incorrectas.D: The myelencephalon is actually a secondary vesicle derived from the rhombencephalon, not one of the original three primary vesicles, and it goes on to form the medulla rather than sitting at the rostral end.

preguntas.q: Which of the three primary brain vesicles occupies the middle position, between the forebrain and hindbrain?

e.correcta: The mesencephalon (midbrain) is the middle primary vesicle and, unlike the forebrain and hindbrain, does not subdivide further into secondary vesicles; it simply matures directly into the adult midbrain, which houses structures like the cerebral aqueduct, superior and inferior colliculi, and substantia nigra. Its central position between the other two vesicles is why midbrain lesions can produce combined findings referable to both forebrain and hindbrain pathways.

incorrectas.A: The prosencephalon is the most rostral primary vesicle (forebrain), which further divides into telencephalon and diencephalon, not the vesicle sitting in the middle.
incorrectas.B: The diencephalon is actually a secondary vesicle derived from the prosencephalon (forming the thalamus and hypothalamus), not one of the three primary vesicles itself.
incorrectas.D: The rhombencephalon is the most caudal primary vesicle (hindbrain), positioned below the midbrain rather than between the forebrain and hindbrain.

preguntas.q: Which of the three primary brain vesicles is positioned most caudally (inferiorly), continuous with the spinal cord?

e.correcta: The rhombencephalon (hindbrain) is the most caudal of the three primary vesicles and sits directly continuous with the spinal cord; it later divides into the metencephalon (pons, cerebellum) and myelencephalon (medulla). Its caudal position places its derivatives closest to the spinal cord, which is why hindbrain structures house many of the cranial nerve nuclei and vital cardiorespiratory centers that interface with the cord.

incorrectas.A: The prosencephalon is the most rostral (superior) primary vesicle, forming the forebrain derivatives, the opposite end of the neuraxis from the caudal hindbrain.
incorrectas.B: The mesencephalon sits in the middle of the three primary vesicles, becoming the midbrain, positioned above the hindbrain rather than at the most caudal point.
incorrectas.D: The diencephalon is a secondary vesicle arising from the prosencephalon (thalamus and hypothalamus), not one of the three primary vesicles and not caudally located.

preguntas.q: The wall of the telencephalon, one of the secondary brain vesicles, gives rise to which adult structures?

e.correcta: The telencephalon, derived from the prosencephalon, develops into the cerebral hemispheres, including the cerebral cortex and the basal ganglia, which arise from proliferation of the telencephalic wall. This makes the telencephalon responsible for the most anatomically and functionally complex, "higher-order" structures of the adult brain.

incorrectas.A: The thalamus and hypothalamus arise from the diencephalon, the other forebrain-derived secondary vesicle, not the telencephalon.
incorrectas.B: The pons and cerebellum arise from the metencephalon, a hindbrain-derived secondary vesicle, anatomically and developmentally distant from the telencephalon.
incorrectas.D: The medulla oblongata arises from the myelencephalon, the most caudal secondary vesicle, derived from the hindbrain rather than the forebrain-derived telencephalon.

preguntas.q: The fluid-filled cavity within the telencephalon develops into which adult structure?

e.correcta: The cavity of the telencephalon expands into the paired lateral ventricles, which sit within each cerebral hemisphere and communicate with the third ventricle via the foramina of Monro. This mirrors the general embryologic rule that the neural tube's central cavity always becomes the corresponding adult ventricular space or canal at each level.

incorrectas.A: The third ventricle is the cavity derived from the diencephalon, sitting in the midline between the thalami, not from the telencephalon itself.
incorrectas.B: The cerebral aqueduct is the narrow channel derived from the cavity of the mesencephalon (midbrain), connecting the third and fourth ventricles, unrelated to the telencephalic cavity.
incorrectas.D: The fourth ventricle arises from the cavities of the metencephalon and myelencephalon (hindbrain derivatives), far removed developmentally from the telencephalon.

preguntas.q: The wall of the diencephalon gives rise to which pair of adult structures?

o.D: Medulla and lower fourth ventricle lining

e.correcta: The diencephalon, a secondary vesicle derived from the prosencephalon, gives rise to the thalamus and hypothalamus (as well as the epithalamus and the optic cup/retina), structures that together surround the third ventricle. The thalamus acts as the major relay station for sensory and motor information en route to the cortex, while the hypothalamus coordinates autonomic and endocrine function, reflecting the diencephalon's role as an integrative hub between forebrain and brainstem.

incorrectas.A: The cerebral hemispheres and basal ganglia arise from the telencephalon, the other forebrain-derived secondary vesicle, which forms the cortex rather than the thalamus and hypothalamus.
incorrectas.C: The pons and cerebellum arise from the metencephalon, a hindbrain-derived secondary vesicle, developmentally and anatomically distinct from the diencephalon.
incorrectas.D: The medulla and the lower fourth ventricle lining derive from the myelencephalon, the most caudal secondary vesicle, unrelated to the diencephalon's forebrain origin.

preguntas.q: The wall of the mesencephalon develops into which adult structure?

e.correcta: The mesencephalon does not subdivide into secondary vesicles the way the forebrain and hindbrain do; its wall simply matures directly into the adult midbrain, containing structures such as the superior and inferior colliculi, red nucleus, substantia nigra, and cranial nerve III and IV nuclei. This direct one-to-one correspondence (mesencephalon to midbrain) makes it the simplest vesicle-to-adult-structure mapping in neuroembryology.

incorrectas.A: The pons arises from the metencephalon, a secondary vesicle derived from the hindbrain (rhombencephalon), not from the mesencephalon.
incorrectas.B: The thalamus arises from the diencephalon, a forebrain-derived secondary vesicle, structurally and developmentally distinct from the midbrain.
incorrectas.D: The medulla arises from the myelencephalon, the most caudal hindbrain-derived secondary vesicle, not from the midbrain-forming mesencephalon.

preguntas.q: The cavity within the mesencephalon becomes which adult structure?

e.correcta: The narrow cavity of the mesencephalon becomes the cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius), the thin channel that connects the third ventricle above to the fourth ventricle below and carries CSF through the midbrain. Because it is so narrow, the aqueduct is a common site of obstruction (e.g., aqueductal stenosis), producing noncommunicating hydrocephalus with dilation of the lateral and third ventricles.

incorrectas.A: The lateral ventricles derive from the telencephalic cavity, not the midbrain, and are much larger, paired structures within the cerebral hemispheres.
incorrectas.B: The third ventricle derives from the diencephalic cavity, sitting rostral to the aqueduct, not from the mesencephalon itself.
incorrectas.D: The fourth ventricle derives from the cavities of the metencephalon and myelencephalon, caudal to the aqueduct, not from the midbrain.

preguntas.q: The wall of the metencephalon gives rise to which pair of adult structures?

o.D: Medulla oblongata and lower fourth ventricle lining

e.correcta: The metencephalon, a secondary vesicle derived from the rhombencephalon (hindbrain), develops into the pons and cerebellum. The pons serves as a relay and cranial nerve nucleus hub (CN V through VIII), while the cerebellum, arising from the rhombic lip of the metencephalic wall, coordinates movement and balance; together they flank the upper part of the fourth ventricle.

incorrectas.A: The thalamus and hypothalamus arise from the diencephalon, a forebrain-derived secondary vesicle, entirely distinct developmentally from the hindbrain-derived metencephalon.
incorrectas.B: The cerebral hemispheres and basal ganglia arise from the telencephalon, the most rostral secondary vesicle, far removed from the metencephalon both in position and germ vesicle lineage.
incorrectas.D: The medulla oblongata and lower fourth ventricle lining arise from the myelencephalon, the other hindbrain-derived secondary vesicle caudal to the metencephalon, not the metencephalon itself.

preguntas.q: The cavity of the metencephalon develops into which adult structure?

o.A: Lower part of the fourth ventricle
o.C: Upper part of the fourth ventricle

e.correcta: The metencephalon's cavity becomes the upper part of the fourth ventricle, situated between the pons anteriorly and the cerebellum posteriorly, the two structures that arise from the metencephalic wall. Together with the myelencephalon's cavity, which forms the lower fourth ventricle, this composes the full diamond-shaped fourth ventricle that drains via the foramina of Luschka and Magendie.

incorrectas.A: The lower part of the fourth ventricle arises from the cavity of the myelencephalon (medulla), the vesicle caudal to the metencephalon, not from the metencephalon itself.
incorrectas.B: The cerebral aqueduct is derived from the mesencephalic cavity, rostral to the fourth ventricle, connecting it to the third ventricle rather than being part of it.
incorrectas.D: The lateral ventricles derive from the telencephalic cavity within the cerebral hemispheres, anatomically and developmentally distant from the hindbrain-derived fourth ventricle.

preguntas.q: The wall of the myelencephalon develops into which adult structure?

e.correcta: The myelencephalon, the most caudal secondary vesicle (derived from the hindbrain), gives rise to the medulla oblongata, which houses vital cardiorespiratory centers and many cranial nerve nuclei (IX through XII) as it transitions into the spinal cord. This caudal position is why medullary lesions, such as lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, affect structures serving both cranial nerve and long-tract functions.

incorrectas.A: The pons arises from the metencephalon, the hindbrain-derived vesicle rostral to the myelencephalon, not from the myelencephalon itself.
incorrectas.B: The cerebellum also arises from the metencephalon, via the rhombic lip, alongside the pons, distinct from the myelencephalon's derivative.
incorrectas.C: The midbrain arises directly from the mesencephalon, a completely separate primary vesicle rostral to the entire hindbrain lineage.

preguntas.q: The cavity of the myelencephalon becomes which adult structure?

o.A: Upper part of the fourth ventricle
o.D: Lower part of the fourth ventricle

e.correcta: The cavity of the myelencephalon forms the lower part of the fourth ventricle, which is surrounded by the open (rostral) medulla; this is why an open medulla cross-section is recognized on imaging by the presence of the fourth ventricle overlying it. Together with the metencephalon's cavity (upper fourth ventricle), it completes the diamond-shaped ventricular space that drains into the subarachnoid space and spinal central canal.

incorrectas.A: The upper part of the fourth ventricle arises from the metencephalic cavity, bounded by the pons and cerebellum, rostral to the myelencephalon-derived lower part.
incorrectas.B: The cerebral aqueduct derives from the mesencephalic cavity, connecting the third and fourth ventricles, developmentally distinct from the myelencephalon.
incorrectas.C: The third ventricle derives from the diencephalic cavity in the forebrain, far removed from the hindbrain-derived myelencephalon.

preguntas.q: Which type of neuronal derivatives arise from the embryonic alar plate of the neural tube?

e.correcta: The alar plate is the dorsal portion of the neural tube (delineated from the basal plate by the sulcus limitans) and gives rise to sensory (afferent) neurons and interneurons that receive and relay incoming sensory information, consistent with the general rule that dorsal structures in the CNS are sensory. This dorsal-sensory, ventral-motor organization is a fundamental blueprint that persists throughout the spinal cord and brainstem.

incorrectas.A: Motor derivatives arise from the basal (ventral) plate, not the alar plate; motor neuron cell bodies sit ventrally and their axons exit ventrally to innervate muscle.
incorrectas.C: Combined motor and sensory describes the general spinal nerve after dorsal and ventral roots join distal to the ganglion, not the alar plate specifically, which contributes only the sensory component.
incorrectas.D: Visceral motor (autonomic preganglionic) neurons actually arise from a zone associated with the basal plate lineage in the thoracolumbar cord, not the alar plate, which is dedicated to sensory processing.

preguntas.q: Which type of neuronal derivatives arise from the embryonic basal plate of the neural tube?

e.correcta: The basal plate is the ventral portion of the neural tube and gives rise to motor (efferent) neurons whose axons exit ventrally to innervate skeletal muscle and, in appropriate segments, contribute preganglionic autonomic fibers, consistent with the classic ventral-equals-motor, dorsal-equals-sensory organization of the developing spinal cord. This organization explains why ventral horn lesions, such as poliomyelitis or ALS, produce pure lower motor neuron signs without sensory loss.

incorrectas.A: Sensory derivatives arise from the alar plate (dorsal), not the basal plate; the sensory neuron cell bodies actually reside in the dorsal root ganglia outside the neural tube, but the alar plate forms the sensory relay neurons and interneurons that receive their input.
incorrectas.C: Combined motor and sensory describes the mixed spinal nerve formed distal to the dorsal root ganglion, not the basal plate itself, which contributes only motor neurons.
incorrectas.D: Purely sensory association is not a basal plate function; association and interneuron sensory processing is a dorsal (alar plate) property, the functional opposite of the motor basal plate.

preguntas.q: Which embryonic structure forms the boundary that separates the alar plate from the basal plate within the neural tube?

e.correcta: The sulcus limitans is a longitudinal groove on the internal surface of the neural tube (and later the floor of the fourth ventricle) that marks the boundary between the dorsal alar plate (sensory) and the ventral basal plate (motor). This landmark persists into the adult brainstem, where it separates sensory nuclei laterally from motor nuclei medially in the floor of the fourth ventricle, a key anatomic principle for localizing cranial nerve nuclei.

incorrectas.A: The floor plate is the ventral midline signaling center of the neural tube (secreting Sonic hedgehog to pattern ventral structures), not the lateral groove that divides alar from basal plate.
incorrectas.B: The roof plate is the dorsal midline structure (secreting BMPs and Wnts to pattern dorsal structures) opposite the floor plate, also not the alar-basal boundary itself.
incorrectas.C: The central canal is the fluid-filled lumen running through the center of the neural tube and spinal cord, a cavity rather than the groove that separates the two plates.

preguntas.q: The autonomic nervous system (ANS) is classically divided into which two functional divisions?

e.correcta: The ANS is organized into sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions, which generally act as physiologic counterbalances on the same target organs (e.g., heart rate, pupil size, GI motility). The sympathetic division mediates the 'fight-or-flight' response while the parasympathetic mediates 'rest-and-digest' functions, and most viscera receive dual innervation from both so their net output reflects the balance between the two.

incorrectas.A: Afferent and efferent describe the direction of signal flow (sensory input versus motor output) in the nervous system broadly, not the two functional divisions of autonomic outflow itself — the ANS is entirely an efferent (motor) system to smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands.
incorrectas.C: Central and peripheral describe anatomic location (brain/spinal cord versus everything outside it) and apply to the nervous system as a whole, not to a division specific to autonomic function.
incorrectas.D: Somatic and autonomic are the two major divisions of the peripheral efferent nervous system as a whole, with the autonomic system itself then further split into sympathetic and parasympathetic — so this pair is one level too broad to answer what the ANS itself divides into.

preguntas.q: The autonomic nervous system typically reaches its target organ via how many neurons arranged in series?

e.correcta: Autonomic pathways typically use a two-neuron chain: a preganglionic neuron with its cell body in the CNS synapses onto a postganglionic neuron in a peripheral ganglion, and that second neuron then innervates the target organ. This two-neuron relay (with a few simplified exceptions, such as the adrenal medulla receiving direct preganglionic innervation) is a defining architectural feature that distinguishes the ANS from the somatic motor system.

incorrectas.A: One neuron describes the somatic motor pathway, where a single lower motor neuron cell body sits in the spinal cord/brainstem and its axon travels directly to skeletal muscle without an intervening ganglionic synapse.
incorrectas.B: Four neurons overstates the relay; no standard autonomic pathway requires that many sequential neurons to reach the effector organ.
incorrectas.D: Three neurons is also too many for the standard autonomic arrangement — even pathways with variable ganglion location (like the sympathetic chain) still complete the circuit in just two neurons, preganglionic and postganglionic.

preguntas.q: Where are the cell bodies of preganglionic autonomic neurons located?

e.correcta: Preganglionic autonomic neuron cell bodies reside within the CNS — in the intermediolateral cell column of the thoracolumbar spinal cord for sympathetics, or in specific brainstem nuclei and the sacral spinal cord for parasympathetics. Their axons then exit the CNS to synapse on postganglionic neurons in peripheral ganglia, marking the first leg of the two-neuron autonomic relay.

incorrectas.A: Peripheral ganglia house the cell bodies of postganglionic neurons, not preganglionic ones — this is where the preganglionic axon terminates and synapses, one step downstream of where the preganglionic soma actually sits.
incorrectas.B: Dorsal root ganglia contain the cell bodies of sensory (afferent) neurons carrying signals into the spinal cord, an entirely different pathway from the efferent autonomic outflow being described here.
incorrectas.C: The target organ is where the postganglionic axon terminals act on the effector tissue, not where any autonomic neuron cell body is located.

preguntas.q: Where are the cell bodies of postganglionic autonomic neurons located?

e.correcta: Postganglionic neuron cell bodies sit in autonomic ganglia within the peripheral nervous system — sympathetic chain or collateral ganglia for the sympathetic division, and ganglia near or within the target organ wall for the parasympathetic division. Their axons then travel the final short (parasympathetic) or long (sympathetic) distance to directly innervate the effector tissue.

incorrectas.B: Central nervous system is where preganglionic (not postganglionic) cell bodies are located — postganglionic neurons are, by definition, the peripheral second leg of the relay, situated beyond the CNS in ganglia.
incorrectas.C: Dorsal root ganglia hold sensory neuron cell bodies for somatic and visceral afferent fibers, an entirely separate circuit from the motor/efferent postganglionic autonomic neurons.
incorrectas.D: Target organs contain nerve terminals and receptors where postganglionic neurotransmitter acts, but the neuron's cell body itself lies upstream in a ganglion, not within the target tissue.

preguntas.q: Which neurotransmitter is released by ALL preganglionic neurons of the autonomic nervous system, regardless of division?

e.correcta: Every preganglionic autonomic neuron — sympathetic and parasympathetic alike — releases acetylcholine (ACh) onto its postganglionic neuron. This uniformity means the divergence between sympathetic and parasympathetic effects arises downstream, at the postganglionic neurotransmitter and receptor level, not at the ganglionic synapse itself.

incorrectas.A: Norepinephrine is the neurotransmitter released by most postganglionic sympathetic neurons at the target organ, not by preganglionic neurons at the ganglion.
incorrectas.C: Epinephrine is released mainly by chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla directly into the bloodstream, functioning as a hormone rather than as the preganglionic ganglionic neurotransmitter.
incorrectas.D: Dopamine is an important CNS neurotransmitter (and a minor renal vasodilator peripherally) but is not the transmitter used at the autonomic ganglionic synapse.

preguntas.q: Acetylcholine released from preganglionic autonomic neurons acts on which receptor type at the ganglionic synapse?

e.correcta: At the autonomic ganglion, ACh from the preganglionic neuron binds neuronal nicotinic (NN) receptors on the postganglionic neuron — ligand-gated cation channels that produce fast, direct depolarization (an EPSP) to propagate the signal to the next neuron in the chain. This is pharmacologically important because ganglionic blockers (like hexamethonium) act specifically at NN receptors and block both sympathetic and parasympathetic transmission simultaneously.

incorrectas.A: Muscarinic (M) receptors are G-protein-coupled receptors activated by ACh released from postganglionic parasympathetic neurons at the target organ, a different synapse than the ganglionic one described here.
incorrectas.B: Muscle nicotinic (NM) receptors are the nicotinic subtype found at the skeletal neuromuscular junction, distinct from the neuronal nicotinic receptors at autonomic ganglia — this distinction explains why some neuromuscular blockers spare ganglionic transmission.
incorrectas.D: Alpha-1 adrenergic receptors respond to norepinephrine/epinephrine, not acetylcholine, and are found on smooth muscle and other effector tissues rather than at the cholinergic ganglionic synapse.

preguntas.q: Acetylcholine released from postganglionic parasympathetic neurons acts on which receptor type at the target organ?

e.correcta: Postganglionic parasympathetic neurons release ACh onto muscarinic (M) receptors, a family of G-protein-coupled receptors (M1–M5) on smooth muscle, cardiac tissue, and glands that mediate effects like bradycardia, increased GI motility and secretions, and bronchoconstriction. This is the pharmacologic target of drugs like atropine (a muscarinic antagonist) and pilocarpine (a muscarinic agonist).

incorrectas.A: Neuronal nicotinic (NN) receptors are the ligand-gated ion channels found at the autonomic ganglion (preganglionic-to-postganglionic synapse), not at the postganglionic-to-effector synapse being asked about here.
incorrectas.B: Muscle nicotinic (NM) receptors mediate transmission at the skeletal neuromuscular junction, a somatic rather than parasympathetic pathway.
incorrectas.C: Beta-2 adrenergic receptors respond to epinephrine (and to a lesser extent norepinephrine), not acetylcholine, and are typically associated with sympathetic effects like bronchodilation and vasodilation in skeletal muscle.

preguntas.q: Which neurotransmitter is released by most postganglionic sympathetic neurons, acting on α1, α2, and β1 receptors at the target organ?

e.correcta: Most postganglionic sympathetic neurons release norepinephrine (NE), which acts on α1, α2, and β1 adrenergic receptors to produce classic sympathetic effects such as vasoconstriction, increased heart rate and contractility, and mydriasis. NE has relatively weak affinity for β2 receptors compared to epinephrine, which is a key pharmacologic distinction between the two catecholamines.

incorrectas.B: Epinephrine is released mainly by the adrenal medulla as a circulating hormone and additionally activates β2 receptors, which NE does not appreciably engage — this broader receptor profile is what distinguishes epinephrine from the neurally released NE described in the question.
incorrectas.C: Acetylcholine is the preganglionic neurotransmitter at all autonomic ganglia (and the postganglionic transmitter for sympathetic sweat glands specifically), not the typical postganglionic sympathetic transmitter acting on adrenergic receptors.
incorrectas.D: Dopamine is primarily a CNS neurotransmitter and a precursor in catecholamine synthesis; it is not the main effector neurotransmitter released by postganglionic sympathetic neurons onto adrenergic receptors.

preguntas.q: Which catecholamine, released mainly as a circulating hormone from the adrenal medulla, acts on α1, α2, β1, AND β2 receptors — a broader receptor profile than norepinephrine?

e.correcta: Epinephrine, secreted by chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla directly into the blood, activates all four major adrenergic receptor subtypes — α1, α2, β1, and β2 — giving it effects on the heart (β1), vasculature (α1 vasoconstriction in skin/gut but β2 vasodilation in skeletal muscle), and bronchial smooth muscle (β2 bronchodilation) that norepinephrine cannot fully replicate.

incorrectas.A: Norepinephrine, released from postganglionic sympathetic nerve terminals, has only weak β2 activity, so it lacks the marked bronchodilating and skeletal-muscle-vasodilating effects that distinguish epinephrine's broader receptor profile.
incorrectas.C: Acetylcholine acts on nicotinic and muscarinic cholinergic receptors, not adrenergic receptors, and is unrelated to the catecholamine receptor-selectivity distinction being tested here.
incorrectas.D: Dopamine acts on dopaminergic (D1) receptors at low doses and beta/alpha adrenergic receptors at progressively higher doses, but it is not the adrenal-medulla hormone classically described as hitting all four adrenergic subtypes equally.

preguntas.q: The adrenal medulla, essentially a modified sympathetic ganglion, exerts its postganglionic sympathetic effects via what mode of transmission?

e.correcta: The adrenal medulla is innervated directly by preganglionic sympathetic fibers (skipping the usual second neuron), and its chromaffin cells respond by releasing epinephrine and some norepinephrine straight into the bloodstream rather than across a discrete synaptic cleft. This neurohumoral (hormonal) mode of transmission allows the released catecholamines to act broadly and simultaneously on distant adrenergic receptors throughout the body, amplifying the systemic 'fight-or-flight' response.

incorrectas.A: Direct synaptic transmission describes the point-to-point release of neurotransmitter across a narrow synaptic cleft onto an adjacent postsynaptic neuron, which is how typical ganglionic and neuroeffector synapses work — but the adrenal medulla instead dumps its hormone into the circulation for widespread systemic action.
incorrectas.B: Gap junction electrical coupling allows direct ionic current flow between cells (as in cardiac or smooth muscle syncytium) and is not how chromaffin cells communicate their catecholamine release to the rest of the body.
incorrectas.D: Paracrine diffusion implies local action on nearby cells only, whereas the adrenal medulla's catecholamines travel through the bloodstream to reach distant target organs — a hallmark of endocrine/neurohumoral, not merely paracrine, signaling.

preguntas.q: In the parasympathetic division, are the preganglionic and postganglionic neurons long or short?

e.correcta: Parasympathetic ganglia lie near or within the wall of the target organ itself, so the preganglionic fiber must travel a long distance from the brainstem or sacral cord before synapsing, while the postganglionic fiber only has a short distance left to reach the effector cells. This anatomic arrangement produces more discrete, localized parasympathetic effects since each postganglionic neuron innervates a limited area near its ganglion.

incorrectas.A: Short preganglionic, long postganglionic describes the sympathetic arrangement, where ganglia (paravertebral chain or prevertebral) sit close to the spinal cord and postganglionic fibers travel long distances to reach peripheral targets — the opposite pattern from parasympathetics.
incorrectas.B: Both long is inaccurate because the parasympathetic postganglionic fiber is characteristically short, given that its ganglion is located right at or within the target organ.
incorrectas.C: Both short misses that the parasympathetic preganglionic fiber must actually travel a considerable distance from its cranial nerve nucleus or sacral cord origin all the way out to the organ wall before synapsing.

preguntas.q: In the sympathetic division, are the preganglionic and postganglionic neurons long or short?

e.correcta: Sympathetic ganglia (the paravertebral chain and prevertebral/collateral ganglia) are located close to the spinal cord, so the preganglionic fiber is short, while the postganglionic fiber must travel a long distance to reach peripheral targets such as the skin, blood vessels, and viscera. This wide anatomic reach helps explain why sympathetic activation tends to produce diffuse, body-wide effects rather than the more localized action typical of parasympathetic stimulation.

incorrectas.B: Long preganglionic, short postganglionic is the parasympathetic pattern, reflecting ganglia positioned near or within the target organ rather than near the spinal cord as in the sympathetic division.
incorrectas.C: Both short is incorrect because the sympathetic postganglionic fiber characteristically travels a long distance from the chain or collateral ganglion out to its often-distant target organ.
incorrectas.D: Both long is incorrect because the sympathetic preganglionic fiber is short, given how close the paravertebral/prevertebral ganglia sit to the spinal cord segments of origin.

preguntas.q: Unlike the autonomic nervous system, the somatic nervous system reaches its target (skeletal muscle) via how many neurons?

e.correcta: The somatic motor pathway uses a single lower motor neuron, whose cell body lies in the spinal cord ventral horn or a cranial nerve motor nucleus, with its axon extending uninterrupted all the way to skeletal muscle. This one-neuron design contrasts with the ANS's two-neuron relay and allows for faster, more direct voluntary motor control.

incorrectas.A: Two neurons describes the standard autonomic relay (preganglionic and postganglionic), not the somatic motor pathway, which reaches muscle without any intervening ganglionic synapse.
incorrectas.C: Three neurons overstates the somatic pathway; no ganglionic relay station exists between the motor neuron and the skeletal muscle fiber it innervates.
incorrectas.D: Four neurons is even further from correct — the defining feature of somatic motor control is its efficiency via a single, uninterrupted neuron to the effector.

preguntas.q: What neurotransmitter is used by somatic motor neurons innervating skeletal muscle?

e.correcta: Somatic motor neurons release acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, where it binds muscle nicotinic (NM) receptors to trigger depolarization and muscle contraction. This is the same transmitter used by preganglionic autonomic neurons, but the receptor it binds (NM versus NN) differs, which is clinically exploited by drugs like neuromuscular blockers that can be more selective for one synapse over the other.

incorrectas.A: Norepinephrine is the typical postganglionic sympathetic neurotransmitter acting on adrenergic receptors in viscera and vasculature, not the transmitter used at the skeletal neuromuscular junction.
incorrectas.B: GABA is a major inhibitory neurotransmitter within the CNS but is not released by peripheral somatic motor neurons onto skeletal muscle.
incorrectas.D: Epinephrine functions as a circulating adrenal hormone acting on adrenergic receptors, not as the direct synaptic transmitter released by somatic motor neurons at the neuromuscular junction.

preguntas.q: Acetylcholine released by somatic motor neurons acts on which receptor at the neuromuscular junction of skeletal muscle?

e.correcta: At the neuromuscular junction, ACh binds muscle nicotinic (NM) receptors, ligand-gated ion channels on the motor endplate that open to allow Na+ influx, depolarizing the muscle fiber and triggering excitation-contraction coupling. This receptor is the pathologic target in myasthenia gravis (antibodies against NM receptors impair transmission) and the pharmacologic target of neuromuscular blocking agents used in anesthesia.

incorrectas.A: Neuronal nicotinic (NN) receptors are the nicotinic subtype found at autonomic ganglia between pre- and postganglionic neurons, structurally and pharmacologically distinct from the NM receptors at the skeletal muscle endplate.
incorrectas.B: Muscarinic (M) receptors are G-protein-coupled receptors activated by ACh from postganglionic parasympathetic neurons on smooth muscle, cardiac tissue, and glands — not the ligand-gated ion channel used at the somatic NMJ.
incorrectas.C: Alpha-1 adrenergic receptors respond to norepinephrine and epinephrine, not acetylcholine, and are unrelated to cholinergic transmission at the neuromuscular junction.

preguntas.q: What tissue type is innervated by nerves of the somatic nervous system?

e.correcta: The somatic nervous system innervates skeletal (voluntary) muscle via lower motor neurons releasing acetylcholine onto NM receptors, mediating conscious, voluntary movement. This contrasts with the autonomic nervous system, which governs involuntary control of internal organs.

incorrectas.B: Smooth muscle, found in vessel walls, the GI tract, and other viscera, is innervated by the autonomic (not somatic) nervous system, mediated through both sympathetic adrenergic and parasympathetic muscarinic input.
incorrectas.C: Cardiac muscle receives autonomic innervation (sympathetic and parasympathetic) that modulates heart rate and contractility, and additionally has its own intrinsic conduction system — it is not a somatic nervous system target.
incorrectas.D: Glandular epithelium (e.g., salivary, sweat glands) is controlled by autonomic postganglionic fibers acting via muscarinic or adrenergic receptors, not by the voluntary somatic pathway.

preguntas.q: The parasympathetic nervous system is characterized by what anatomic distribution of its preganglionic neuron origins?

e.correcta: Parasympathetic preganglionic neurons originate in a craniosacral distribution — specific brainstem nuclei associated with cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X, plus the intermediate gray matter of spinal segments S2–S4. This split origin at the two ends of the neuraxis is a key anatomic mnemonic distinguishing parasympathetic outflow from the contiguous thoracolumbar sympathetic outflow.

incorrectas.A: Thoracolumbar describes the sympathetic distribution (spinal levels T1–L2/L3), the anatomic opposite of the craniosacral parasympathetic pattern being asked about.
incorrectas.C: Cervicothoracic is not a recognized autonomic outflow distribution; sympathetic fibers actually originate more caudally, starting around T1, not the cervical cord.
incorrectas.D: Lumbosacral is close to but not precisely correct — parasympathetic sacral outflow arises specifically from S2–S4, and there is no lumbar contribution to parasympathetic outflow (lumbar levels are actually sympathetic).

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerves carry parasympathetic fibers?

e.correcta: Cranial nerves III (oculomotor, to the pupillary sphincter and ciliary muscle), VII (facial, to lacrimal/salivary glands), IX (glossopharyngeal, to the parotid gland), and X (vagus, to thoracic and abdominal viscera) all carry parasympathetic fibers, forming the cranial component of craniosacral outflow. A useful mnemonic is that these are the only cranial nerves with a parasympathetic component, making 'III, VII, IX, X' worth memorizing as a set.

incorrectas.A: III, IV, VI, XII groups the oculomotor nerve (which does carry parasympathetics) with trochlear, abducens, and hypoglossal — all of which are purely motor nerves controlling extraocular or tongue muscles with no parasympathetic component.
incorrectas.B: V, VII, IX, XI substitutes the trigeminal nerve (primarily sensory/masticatory motor, no parasympathetic fibers of its own) and the spinal accessory nerve (purely motor to trapezius/sternocleidomastoid) for the correct oculomotor and vagus nerves.
incorrectas.D: II, III, IV, VI groups the optic nerve (purely sensory, vision) with three motor nerves to the extraocular muscles, none of which — aside from III's parasympathetic fibers — carry parasympathetic output.

preguntas.q: Which spinal segments give rise to the sacral parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic) outflow?

e.correcta: Sacral parasympathetic outflow arises from spinal cord segments S2–S4, forming the pelvic splanchnic nerves that supply parasympathetic innervation to the descending colon, rectum, bladder, and reproductive organs. This completes the craniosacral distribution alongside the cranial nerve III/VII/IX/X outflow, and 'S2, S3, S4 keep the pelvic organs off the floor' is a classic clinical mnemonic for these levels' importance in bladder and bowel function.

incorrectas.A: L1-L3 is actually part of the thoracolumbar sympathetic outflow, not parasympathetic — sympathetic preganglionic fibers extend from T1 down through about L2-L3.
incorrectas.B: T1-T4 lies within the sympathetic thoracolumbar range as well, contributing preganglionic sympathetic fibers to the head, neck, and thoracic viscera rather than any parasympathetic outflow.
incorrectas.C: S1-S2 captures only part of the true range; the pelvic splanchnic parasympathetic outflow specifically spans S2 through S4, not stopping at S2.

preguntas.q: The sympathetic nervous system is characterized by what anatomic distribution of its preganglionic neuron origins?

e.correcta: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons originate from the intermediolateral cell column spanning spinal levels T1 through about L2-L3 — a thoracolumbar distribution. These fibers exit via the ventral roots and white rami communicantes to reach the sympathetic chain, from which postganglionic fibers fan out widely to vessels, skin, and viscera throughout the body.

incorrectas.B: Craniosacral describes the parasympathetic distribution (brainstem nuclei of CN III, VII, IX, X plus S2–S4), the anatomic complement to the thoracolumbar sympathetic outflow, not the sympathetic pattern itself.
incorrectas.C: Cervicothoracic is not the standard term for sympathetic origin; although the sympathetic chain does extend up into the cervical region, the actual preganglionic cell bodies begin at T1, making 'thoracolumbar' the accurate descriptor.
incorrectas.D: Lumbosacral incorrectly shifts the range caudally — sympathetic preganglionic outflow starts more rostrally at T1 and the sacral segments belong to parasympathetic, not sympathetic, outflow.

preguntas.q: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons can synapse in which ganglia, potentially at a spinal level different from where the fiber originated?

o.A: Terminal ganglia near the target organ

e.correcta: All preganglionic sympathetic fibers can synapse within the paravertebral sympathetic chain, but a given fiber isn't restricted to synapsing at the ganglion at its own segmental level — it may travel up or down the chain before synapsing at a different vertebral level. This flexibility is what allows a limited number of thoracolumbar spinal segments (T1-L2/3) to distribute sympathetic output broadly to structures like the head and neck, which have no direct thoracolumbar segmental supply of their own.

incorrectas.A: Terminal ganglia located directly at the target organ are the parasympathetic arrangement, not the sympathetic chain synapse being described, and don't reflect the same-or-different-segmental-level flexibility unique to the paravertebral chain.
incorrectas.C: Collateral (prevertebral) ganglia — such as the celiac or mesenteric ganglia — are indeed an alternate synapse site for some preganglionic sympathetic fibers (mainly those supplying abdominal viscera), but restricting the answer to 'only' collateral ganglia excludes the paravertebral chain, which is the more universal option available to virtually all preganglionic sympathetic fibers.
incorrectas.D: Dorsal root ganglia contain sensory neuron cell bodies and are not a synaptic relay station for efferent preganglionic sympathetic fibers at all.

preguntas.q: The cavity of the diencephalon gives rise to which adult structure?

e.correcta: The diencephalon's central cavity becomes the third ventricle, bounded laterally by the thalamus, and it extends caudally to partially involve the rostral midbrain (its floor lying dorsal to the superior and inferior colliculi). Understanding this derivation helps localize lesions and hydrocephalus patterns, since obstruction between the third ventricle and the rest of the ventricular system produces a distinct pattern of dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal-sized fourth ventricle.

incorrectas.A: The fourth ventricle derives from the cavity of the rhombencephalon (hindbrain), not the diencephalon — it lies between the pons/medulla and cerebellum, a different neural tube segment entirely.
incorrectas.B: The lateral ventricles arise from the cavities of the telencephalon (the paired cerebral hemispheres), which develops from the prosencephalon alongside, but distinct from, the diencephalon.
incorrectas.D: The cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) is the derivative of the mesencephalon's (midbrain's) cavity, connecting the third and fourth ventricles — it is adjacent to, but not the same as, the third ventricle formed from the diencephalon.

preguntas.q: What term describes the non-neuronal supporting cells of the nervous system, which include astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells, and microglia?

e.correcta: Glial cells are the broad umbrella category of non-neuronal cells that support, protect, and maintain neurons — providing myelination (oligodendrocytes/Schwann cells), structural and metabolic support and blood-brain-barrier maintenance (astrocytes), and immune surveillance (microglia). Unlike neurons, most glial cells retain the capacity to divide, which is clinically relevant because most primary CNS tumors in adults (e.g., gliomas) arise from glial rather than neuronal cells.

incorrectas.A: Ependymal cells are actually one specific subtype of glial cell — ciliated cells lining the ventricles that help produce and circulate CSF — so this term is too narrow to capture the full non-neuronal category being described.
incorrectas.B: Neural crest cells are a transient embryonic cell population that gives rise to structures like Schwann cells, dorsal root ganglia neurons, and melanocytes, but the term refers to a developmental origin, not the general adult category of supporting nervous system cells.
incorrectas.C: Ganglion cells generally refers to neurons whose cell bodies cluster in a ganglion (e.g., retinal ganglion cells or dorsal root ganglion neurons) — these are neurons, the opposite of the non-neuronal glial cells the question asks about.

preguntas.q: Oligodendrocytes, the myelinating glial cells of the CNS, arise embryologically from which structure?

e.correcta: Oligodendrocytes derive from the neural tube (neuroectoderm), the same embryonic origin as CNS neurons and astrocytes, since the neural tube gives rise to essentially all of the central nervous system's parenchymal cells. This shared origin is why oligodendrocytes are confined to the CNS, in contrast to Schwann cells (their peripheral myelinating counterpart), which come from the separate neural crest lineage.

incorrectas.B: Neural crest gives rise to Schwann cells (the peripheral myelinating glia), along with dorsal root ganglia, autonomic ganglia, and melanocytes — but not oligodendrocytes, which are exclusively a central nervous system cell type.
incorrectas.C: Mesoderm forms connective tissue, muscle, bone, and the cardiovascular system, and plays no role in generating the neuroectoderm-derived glial cells of the CNS.
incorrectas.D: Surface ectoderm forms the epidermis, lens of the eye, and anterior pituitary (via Rathke's pouch), a separate ectodermal lineage from the neuroectoderm that folds inward to become the neural tube.

preguntas.q: Astrocytes arise embryologically from which structure?

e.correcta: Astrocytes, like oligodendrocytes and CNS neurons, develop from the neural tube (neuroectoderm), reflecting the fact that essentially the entire central nervous system parenchyma arises from this single embryonic structure. Astrocytes go on to provide structural scaffolding, maintain the blood-brain barrier, regulate extracellular ion and neurotransmitter levels, and contribute to glial scar formation after CNS injury.

incorrectas.A: Neural crest gives rise to peripheral structures such as Schwann cells, sensory and autonomic ganglia, and melanocytes, not astrocytes, which are exclusively found within the central nervous system and share the neural tube's neuroectodermal origin.
incorrectas.C: Mesoderm gives rise to connective tissue, muscle, and vasculature (including the endothelial cells that form the physical wall of CNS capillaries), but not to the astrocytes whose foot processes surround those vessels.
incorrectas.D: Surface ectoderm forms the epidermis and structures like the lens and anterior pituitary, a distinct ectodermal derivative that does not contribute cells to the neural parenchyma.

preguntas.q: According to cable theory, an increase in which axonal electrical property directly increases the conduction velocity of an action potential?

e.correcta: The length (space) constant, λ, describes how far a local, subthreshold change in membrane potential spreads passively along the axon before decaying to about 37% of its original amplitude; a larger λ means depolarizing current spreads further and faster between nodes of Ranvier before the next patch of membrane is triggered, which speeds saltatory conduction. Myelination increases λ by raising membrane resistance and lowering capacitance, which is exactly why demyelinating diseases like multiple sclerosis slow conduction velocity.

incorrectas.B: The time constant (τ) reflects how quickly the membrane potential rises toward its final value in response to a step of current, determined by membrane resistance and capacitance; it governs temporal summation and the speed of the local response, not how far the signal spreads along the length of the axon, so it doesn't directly determine conduction velocity the way λ does.
incorrectas.C: Threshold potential is the fixed voltage at which enough voltage-gated Na+ channels open to trigger a regenerative action potential; changing this value affects excitability (how easily a spike is generated) but is unrelated to the passive cable properties that determine how fast an already-triggered impulse propagates down the axon.
incorrectas.D: The absolute refractory period is the interval during which a just-fired patch of membrane cannot generate another action potential because its Na+ channels are inactivated; it limits the maximum firing frequency of a neuron but has no bearing on the passive spread of depolarization that sets conduction velocity.

preguntas.q: Schwann cells, which myelinate peripheral nerve axons, are derived embryologically from which structure?

e.correcta: Schwann cells arise from neural crest cells, the migratory population that buds off the dorsal neural tube during closure and gives rise to most of the peripheral nervous system, including dorsal root ganglia, autonomic ganglia, and the Schwann cells that myelinate peripheral axons. This shared origin explains why neural crest-derived tumors (e.g., schwannomas) and peripheral myelin disorders trace back to this same embryologic lineage.

incorrectas.A: The neural tube (neuroectoderm) gives rise to the CNS, including neurons, oligodendrocytes (the CNS myelinating cell), astrocytes, and ependymal cells — not Schwann cells, which are a peripheral rather than central structure.
incorrectas.C: Mesoderm gives rise to connective tissue, blood vessels, and, notably, microglia (via mesodermal/yolk sac monocyte precursors); it is not the source of Schwann cells, which are ectodermally derived through the neural crest.
incorrectas.D: Surface ectoderm forms the epidermis and structures like the lens and anterior pituitary (Rathke's pouch), a different ectodermal derivative pathway that does not contribute to peripheral nerve glia.

preguntas.q: Which glial cell type lines the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord in the adult CNS?

e.correcta: Ependymal cells form a single ciliated epithelial layer lining the ventricular system and central canal, where they are in direct contact with CSF; their cilia help propel CSF flow and their modified form (choroid plexus epithelium) actively secretes CSF, making them the defining glial cell of this location.

incorrectas.A: Astrocytes are star-shaped glia that support neurons, form the blood-brain barrier via foot processes on capillaries, and contribute to the glia limitans at the pial surface, but they do not form the epithelial lining that directly contacts CSF within the ventricles.
incorrectas.B: Oligodendrocytes myelinate multiple CNS axons, extending processes to wrap segments of several different neurons, but they have no role in lining ventricular surfaces or contacting CSF directly.
incorrectas.D: Microglia are the resident CNS phagocytes derived from mesodermal monocyte precursors; they patrol the parenchyma for damage and pathogens but do not form an epithelial-like lining of the ventricular system.

preguntas.q: What structural feature of ependymal cells allows them to help circulate CSF through the ventricular system?

e.correcta: Ependymal cells are ciliated, and the coordinated, whip-like beating of these cilia generates directional flow that helps propel CSF through the ventricles and central canal; this is analogous to how respiratory ciliated epithelium moves mucus, and impaired ciliary function (e.g., in primary ciliary dyskinesia) can contribute to hydrocephalus.

incorrectas.A: Microvilli increase surface area for absorption or secretion (as in choroid plexus cells) but are non-motile and do not generate fluid flow the way beating cilia do.
incorrectas.B: Tight junctions between ependymal cells (where present, as in the specialized ependyma of the choroid plexus) regulate paracellular permeability and barrier function, but they are static junctional structures, not motile organelles that drive CSF movement.
incorrectas.C: Gap junctions allow direct ionic and small-molecule communication between adjacent cells, coordinating cellular activity, but they play no direct role in generating the mechanical flow of CSF.

preguntas.q: Specialized ependymal cells that differentiate into the epithelium of the choroid plexus function to produce which fluid?

e.correcta: Choroid plexus epithelial cells are modified ependymal cells that actively secrete CSF by transporting ions (and water following osmotically) from plexus capillary blood into the ventricular lumen, while also forming the blood-CSF barrier via their tight junctions; this continuous production, balanced by reabsorption via arachnoid granulations, maintains normal CSF volume and pressure.

incorrectas.B: Aqueous humor is produced by the non-pigmented ciliary epithelium of the eye, an analogous secretory epithelium in a different fluid-filled compartment, but unrelated to the ventricular system.
incorrectas.C: Endolymph is secreted by the stria vascularis of the cochlea and dark cells of the vestibular labyrinth, filling the membranous labyrinth of the inner ear — a distinct fluid compartment from CSF.
incorrectas.D: Perilymph fills the bony labyrinth surrounding the membranous labyrinth of the inner ear and derives largely from filtration of blood plasma/CSF, but it is not produced by choroid plexus-derived ependymal cells.

preguntas.q: Ependymal cells, which line the ventricular system and give rise to choroid plexus epithelium, arise embryologically from which structure?

e.correcta: Ependymal cells differentiate from neuroepithelial cells of the neural tube (neuroectoderm), the same structure that gives rise to CNS neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes; this shared origin is why ependymal cells are classified as a type of CNS glial cell rather than a mesenchymal or epithelial derivative from another germ layer.

incorrectas.A: Neural crest cells migrate away from the neural tube to form the peripheral nervous system (Schwann cells, dorsal root ganglia, autonomic ganglia) — a lineage distinct from the ependymal cells that remain within the CNS lining the ventricles.
incorrectas.C: Mesoderm gives rise to microglia (via mesodermal/yolk sac monocyte precursors) and vascular structures, but the ependyma is a neuroectodermal, not mesodermal, derivative.
incorrectas.D: Surface ectoderm forms epidermis and related structures (lens, anterior pituitary) through a separate ectodermal pathway that does not contribute cells to the ventricular lining.

preguntas.q: Which glial cell type is derived from mesoderm-associated mononuclear phagocytes rather than neuroectoderm?

e.correcta: Microglia are unique among CNS glia in that they originate from yolk-sac-derived mesodermal monocyte/macrophage precursors that migrate into the CNS early in development, rather than from the neuroectodermal neural tube; this macrophage lineage is why microglia function as the resident immune cells and phagocytic scavengers of the CNS, mounting a response to injury or infection much like tissue macrophages elsewhere in the body.

incorrectas.A: Astrocytes are neuroectoderm-derived glia that provide structural and metabolic support to neurons and help form the blood-brain barrier, arising from the same neural tube lineage as neurons and oligodendrocytes, unlike the mesodermal microglia.
incorrectas.B: Oligodendrocytes are also neuroectodermal derivatives responsible for CNS myelination; they share a common progenitor lineage with astrocytes and neurons, in contrast to microglia's separate mesodermal/monocyte origin.
incorrectas.D: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and arise from neuroepithelial cells of the neural tube (neuroectoderm), placing them in the same broad lineage as astrocytes and oligodendrocytes rather than the mesodermal monocyte lineage of microglia.

preguntas.q: Resident CNS microglia become activated primarily in response to which stimulus?

e.correcta: Microglia continuously survey the CNS parenchyma with motile processes and become activated — proliferating, changing morphology, and upregulating phagocytic and antigen-presenting machinery — in response to tissue damage, infection, or protein aggregates, functioning as the CNS's resident innate immune sentinels. This activation underlies the microglial response seen from stroke and trauma to neurodegenerative diseases, where activated microglia clear debris but can also contribute to secondary injury through inflammatory mediators.

incorrectas.A: Hypoglycemia alters neuronal metabolism and can cause dysfunction or injury, but it is not itself the direct trigger recognized by microglial surveillance receptors; microglia respond to damage-associated signals released once injury has occurred, not to low glucose per se.
incorrectas.B: Hypercapnia affects cerebral blood flow and vascular tone (via vasodilation) rather than directly signaling microglia; it is a vascular/chemical stimulus, not a damage- or pathogen-associated signal that activates the CNS innate immune response.
incorrectas.C: Elevated intracranial pressure reflects a mechanical/volume problem within the closed cranial vault and is not itself a molecular danger signal; microglia activate in response to the tissue injury that may accompany elevated ICP, not the pressure reading itself.

preguntas.q: Which histologic stain, which highlights the rough endoplasmic reticulum (Nissl substance) of neuronal cell bodies, fails to reliably distinguish microglia from surrounding tissue?

e.correcta: Nissl stain (e.g., cresyl violet) binds RNA-rich rough endoplasmic reticulum, which is abundant in the cell bodies of neurons but scant in microglia; because microglia have little Nissl substance, they appear inconspicuous on Nissl-stained sections, so microglia are generally identified using other methods rather than routine Nissl histology.

incorrectas.B: Immunohistochemical staining for microglia/macrophage markers such as Iba-1 or CD11b specifically labels proteins expressed by microglia, making it an effective and commonly used method to visualize them — the opposite situation from Nissl stain, which cannot pick them out.
incorrectas.C: Silver impregnation techniques can outline cell processes and are sometimes used to visualize glial morphology (as in classical studies of "rod cells" in neurosyphilis), offering another way to visualize microglia that Nissl staining does not provide.
incorrectas.D: Prussian blue stain detects iron (hemosiderin), useful for identifying old hemorrhage or iron-laden macrophages, but it is not the stain being contrasted here — the point of the comparison is specifically Nissl's inability to reveal microglia.

preguntas.q: Unlike other CNS glial cells, microglia arise embryologically from which lineage?

e.correcta: Microglia are the exception among CNS glia: they derive from mesodermal yolk sac progenitors that differentiate into monocyte/macrophage-lineage cells and colonize the CNS during early development, rather than from the neuroectodermal neural tube. This mesenchymal, immune-cell origin explains their function as CNS-resident phagocytes and their molecular kinship to peripheral macrophages.

incorrectas.A: Neuroectoderm (neural tube) gives rise to neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and ependymal cells — the "true" glial and neuronal lineage — which is a different developmental pathway from the mesodermal monocyte lineage that produces microglia.
incorrectas.C: Neural crest cells give rise to peripheral structures such as Schwann cells and sensory/autonomic ganglia; while also outside the neural tube lineage, this is still a distinct pathway from the yolk-sac mesodermal origin of microglia.
incorrectas.D: Surface ectoderm forms skin and related structures (lens, anterior pituitary) via a separate ectodermal derivative pathway unrelated to either neural tissue or the mesodermal monocyte lineage that produces microglia.

preguntas.q: Which mural cell type wraps around CNS capillary endothelial cells and, along with tight junctions, the basement membrane, and astrocyte foot processes, contributes to the blood-brain barrier?

e.correcta: Pericytes are contractile mural cells embedded within the basement membrane surrounding CNS capillary endothelium; they help regulate capillary blood flow, support endothelial tight junction integrity, and contribute to blood-brain barrier formation and maintenance, working alongside (but distinct from) the astrocyte foot processes that also ensheathe the vessel.

incorrectas.A: Microglia are the CNS's resident mesoderm-derived phagocytes that patrol the parenchyma for damage and pathogens; despite occasionally being confused with pericytes due to a shared mesenchymal-type origin and immune-modulatory roles, microglia do not physically wrap capillaries as structural components of the BBB the way pericytes do.
incorrectas.B: Astrocytes contribute foot processes that ensheathe capillaries and help induce/maintain BBB properties, but they are a separate, neuroectoderm-derived glial cell type, not the mural cell embedded in the vascular basement membrane itself.
incorrectas.D: Fibroblasts are mesenchymal connective tissue cells found in the meninges and perivascular spaces, but they are not a recognized structural component of the blood-brain barrier the way pericytes, endothelial tight junctions, basement membrane, and astrocyte foot processes are.

preguntas.q: Which cytoskeletal filament type serves as the track along which motor proteins carry out anterograde and retrograde axonal transport?

e.correcta: Microtubules run longitudinally down the length of the axon and provide the polarized track (with a plus-end oriented toward the axon terminal) along which motor proteins like kinesin and dynein "walk" while carrying vesicles, organelles, and proteins — kinesin moving cargo anterogradely toward the plus end and dynein moving cargo retrogradely toward the minus end near the cell body. This system is essential for delivering synaptic components to the terminal and returning signals/damaged material to the soma for degradation or recycling.

incorrectas.A: Actin microfilaments are concentrated near the axon terminal (growth cone) and plasma membrane, supporting short-range movement and structural dynamics, but they are not the primary long-distance track used for bulk anterograde/retrograde transport — that role belongs to microtubules.
incorrectas.B: Neurofilaments (a type of intermediate filament) provide structural, tensile support to the axon and help determine axon caliber, but they are relatively stable, non-polarized structures that are not used as tracks for motor-protein-driven transport.
incorrectas.C: Spectrin forms a submembranous cytoskeletal lattice that provides mechanical support to the axolemma, but it does not serve as a track for kinesin/dynein-based transport of cargo.

preguntas.q: Which motor protein carries cargo from the neuronal cell body toward the axon terminal (anterograde transport) by moving along microtubules?

e.correcta: Kinesin is a plus-end-directed motor protein that uses ATP hydrolysis to "walk" along microtubules toward the axon terminal, carrying vesicles containing neurotransmitters, membrane components, and other cargo needed to sustain and build the synapse — this is anterograde transport, moving material away from the cell body.

incorrectas.B: Dynein is the motor responsible for the opposite direction — retrograde transport from the axon terminal back to the cell body — moving toward the microtubule minus end; it is not the motor used for anterograde delivery of cargo.
incorrectas.C: Myosin is an actin-based motor protein important for movements involving the actin cytoskeleton (e.g., growth cone motility, vesicle movement near the membrane), rather than the microtubule-based long-range anterograde axonal transport carried out by kinesin.
incorrectas.D: Dynactin is an accessory protein complex that helps activate and link dynein to its cargo and to microtubules, functioning as a cofactor for retrograde transport rather than serving as the anterograde motor itself.

preguntas.q: Which motor protein transports cargo — including retrogradely-transported pathogens such as rabies virus, herpes simplex virus, and tetanus toxin — from the axon terminal back to the neuronal cell body?

e.correcta: Dynein is a minus-end-directed motor protein that moves along microtubules toward the cell body, carrying cargo picked up at the axon terminal — including recycled synaptic vesicle components and, clinically important, neurotropic pathogens like rabies virus, herpes simplex virus, and tetanus toxin, which hijack this retrograde transport machinery to reach the CNS.

incorrectas.A: Kinesin moves in the opposite direction, carrying cargo from the cell body toward the axon terminal (anterograde transport) along the microtubule's plus end, making it the wrong motor for retrograde movement.
incorrectas.C: Myosin operates along actin filaments rather than microtubules and is involved in more localized movements (e.g., growth cone dynamics), not the long-distance retrograde transport of cargo along the axon.
incorrectas.D: Tubulin is the structural protein subunit that polymerizes to form the microtubule track itself, not a motor protein — it provides the road, not the vehicle, for axonal transport.

preguntas.q: Which barrier restricts diffusion of most circulating blood substances, such as bacteria and many drugs, from reaching the CSF and CNS parenchyma?

o.B: Blood-CSF barrier at the choroid plexus

e.correcta: The blood-brain barrier, formed by tight junctions between non-fenestrated CNS capillary endothelial cells along with the basement membrane and astrocyte foot processes, tightly restricts paracellular movement of circulating substances into the CNS parenchyma; only small nonpolar/lipid-soluble molecules cross freely by diffusion, while most bacteria, hydrophilic drugs, and large molecules are excluded unless the barrier is disrupted (e.g., by meningitis) or specific transporters exist.

incorrectas.A: The arachnoid mater barrier layer has tight junctions that prevent CSF from leaking into the subdural/extradural space, but it is a meningeal barrier separating CSF from the epidural venous system, not the endothelial barrier separating blood from brain parenchyma.
incorrectas.B: The blood-CSF barrier is formed by tight junctions between choroid plexus epithelial cells and regulates exchange between choroid plexus capillary blood and the CSF specifically within the ventricles, a related but anatomically distinct barrier from the blood-brain barrier covering the rest of the CNS microvasculature.
incorrectas.D: The perineurium is a connective tissue layer surrounding fascicles of peripheral nerve fibers that forms a diffusion barrier in the PNS, analogous in concept to the BBB but located outside the CNS entirely.

preguntas.q: Which structural feature of CNS capillary endothelial cells is considered the most important element establishing the blood-brain barrier?

o.D: Tight junctions between non-fenestrated endothelial cells

e.correcta: CNS capillaries are lined by continuous, non-fenestrated endothelial cells joined by extensive tight junctions (occludins, claudins), which seal the paracellular space and prevent free passage of solutes between cells; this is regarded as the single most important structural element of the blood-brain barrier, forcing most substances to cross transcellularly (by diffusion or specific transporters) rather than between cells.

incorrectas.A: Fenestrated capillaries, found in tissues requiring rapid filtration or hormone exchange (e.g., kidney glomeruli, endocrine glands), have pores spanned by diaphragms that allow much greater permeability — the opposite of the sealed, restrictive endothelium needed for the BBB.
incorrectas.B: Discontinuous (sinusoidal) capillaries, found in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow, have large gaps and incomplete basement membranes that allow free passage of cells and large proteins, which would be incompatible with the CNS's need to tightly control its microenvironment.
incorrectas.C: Gap junctions permit direct cytoplasmic communication between adjacent cells for ion and small-molecule exchange, but they do not function as the sealing structure that blocks paracellular movement of blood-borne substances — that role belongs to tight junctions.

preguntas.q: Along with endothelial tight junctions and astrocyte foot processes, which extracellular layer underlying the capillary endothelium also contributes to the blood-brain barrier?

e.correcta: The basement membrane (basal lamina) is a thin extracellular matrix layer secreted by endothelial cells and pericytes that surrounds the CNS capillary; it provides structural support, anchors the astrocyte foot processes and pericytes, and adds an additional physical barrier layer that substances must cross to move from blood into brain tissue, working together with tight junctions to constitute the BBB.

incorrectas.B: The tunica adventitia is the outermost connective tissue layer of larger blood vessels (arteries/veins), containing fibroblasts and collagen; capillaries, including CNS capillaries, are generally too small to have a distinct adventitial layer, so this is not a recognized BBB component.
incorrectas.C: The elastic lamina (internal/external) is found in the walls of arteries, providing elasticity to accommodate pulsatile blood flow; it is a feature of larger, muscular vessels, not of the thin-walled capillaries where the BBB is located.
incorrectas.D: The lamina propria is a layer of connective tissue underlying epithelium in mucosal surfaces (e.g., GI tract, respiratory tract), an entirely different anatomic structure unrelated to CNS capillary architecture.

preguntas.q: Which glial cell processes envelope CNS capillaries and contribute to inducing and maintaining the blood-brain barrier?

e.correcta: Astrocytes extend specialized end-feet, or foot processes, that closely ensheathe CNS capillaries; these processes release signaling molecules that help induce and maintain the tight junctions of the endothelium and contribute an additional physical layer around the vessel, making astrocytes a key inducer and structural component of the blood-brain barrier alongside endothelial tight junctions and the basement membrane.

incorrectas.B: Oligodendrocyte processes wrap around CNS axons to form myelin sheaths, a function related to conduction velocity rather than vascular ensheathment, so they do not contribute to the BBB.
incorrectas.C: Microglial processes are motile extensions used to survey the parenchyma for damage or pathogens as part of CNS immune surveillance; they are not a structural or inductive component of the blood-brain barrier itself.
incorrectas.D: Ependymal processes are minimal since ependymal cells form a simple epithelial lining of the ventricles facing CSF, not a process-based ensheathment of capillaries within the brain parenchyma.

preguntas.q: By what mechanism do small nonpolar, lipid-soluble molecules such as O2 and CO2 cross the blood-brain barrier?

o.D: Active transport via ATP-dependent efflux pumps

e.correcta: Because the BBB endothelium is continuous and tightly joined, the transcellular lipid bilayer route becomes the main path across it, and small nonpolar, lipid-soluble molecules like O2, CO2, and many lipophilic drugs can dissolve directly through the endothelial cell membrane by simple diffusion, moving down their concentration gradient without needing a transporter or energy input.

incorrectas.A: Receptor-mediated transcytosis is used for larger polar molecules such as insulin or transferrin, which bind specific receptors on the endothelial luminal membrane and are shuttled across in vesicles — an energy-dependent, receptor-specific process entirely different from the passive diffusion used by small lipid-soluble gases.
incorrectas.C: Facilitated diffusion via specific carriers such as GLUT1 is how polar but essential nutrients like glucose cross the BBB — glucose cannot simply diffuse through the lipid bilayer because it is hydrophilic, so it requires a dedicated transporter, unlike the small lipophilic gases that need no carrier.
incorrectas.D: Active efflux transport (e.g., by P-glycoprotein) pumps certain lipophilic drugs and xenobiotics back out of the endothelial cell into the blood, working against diffusion for some compounds, rather than being the mechanism that brings small gases like O2/CO2 across in the first place.

preguntas.q: By what mechanism do small polar ions such as Na+ and K+ cross the blood-brain barrier?

o.A: Simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer

e.correcta: Na+ and K+ are small but charged, polar ions that cannot cross the hydrophobic lipid bilayer of BBB endothelial cells by simple diffusion; instead, they move through specific ion channels (and associated transporters/pumps) embedded in the endothelial membrane, allowing tightly regulated ionic exchange that helps maintain the stable ionic composition of the CNS extracellular environment needed for normal neuronal signaling.

incorrectas.A: Simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer works for small nonpolar, lipid-soluble molecules like O2 and CO2, but charged ions like Na+/K+ are repelled by the hydrophobic membrane interior and cannot cross this way without a channel or transporter.
incorrectas.B: Receptor-mediated transcytosis is reserved for specific larger macromolecules (e.g., insulin, transferrin) that bind luminal receptors and are shuttled across in vesicles — a much larger-cargo, energy-dependent process distinct from the channel-mediated movement of small ions.
incorrectas.D: Bulk-phase pinocytosis nonspecifically engulfs extracellular fluid and its contents into vesicles; it is normally suppressed at the BBB precisely because it would allow uncontrolled, nonspecific entry of solutes, unlike the selective, regulated passage through dedicated ion channels.

preguntas.q: A destructive lesion to an axon is most likely to result in death of the parent neuron when it occurs closest to which structure?
