A lesion therefore produces contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation, beginning a couple of segments below the actual lesion level — a pattern classically tested with syringomyelia, which damages these crossing fibers directly.

incorrectas.A: Ipsilateral loss at the exact lesion level doesn't match spinothalamic anatomy, since these fibers cross early near their level of entry rather than remaining ipsilateral all the way to the medulla as the dorsal columns do.
incorrectas.C: Deficits appear below, not above, the lesion, because the interrupted ascending fibers were carrying information originating from spinal levels caudal to the lesion, not from levels above it.
incorrectas.D: Bilateral loss would suggest a process affecting both anterolateral systems or the decussating fibers at the midline itself (e.g., central cord syndrome/syringomyelia), rather than a typical unilateral tract lesion.

preguntas.q: How many orders of neurons make up the spinocerebellar tract pathway carrying unconscious proprioceptive information to the cerebellum?

e.correcta: Unlike the three-neuron DCML and spinothalamic pathways that relay through the thalamus to reach cortex for conscious perception, the spinocerebellar tracts use only two neurons — a 1st-order peripheral neuron synapses directly (via Clarke's nucleus or the external cuneate nucleus) onto a 2nd-order neuron that carries unconscious proprioceptive information straight to the cerebellum, entirely bypassing the thalamus and cerebral cortex.

incorrectas.A: Three neurons describes the conscious sensory pathways (DCML, spinothalamic) that require a thalamocortical relay for perception; the spinocerebellar tracts don't reach consciousness and therefore use one fewer synapse.
incorrectas.B: Four neurons overstates the relay — there is no extra intermediate synapse built into the standard spinocerebellar circuitry beyond the two orders described.
incorrectas.D: A single-neuron pathway could not span from peripheral proprioceptors all the way to the cerebellum; at least one central synapse is required en route.

preguntas.q: The dorsal (posterior) spinocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioceptive input from which body regions?

e.correcta: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract relays unconscious proprioceptive and mechanoreceptive information from the lower extremities and trunk. Its 1st-order neurons synapse in Clarke's nucleus (present T1-L2), and 2nd-order axons ascend ipsilaterally to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle — a pathway critical for coordinating gait and lower-limb movement.

incorrectas.A: Face and neck proprioception is conveyed through separate pathways involving trigeminal afferents (including the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus), not the dorsal spinocerebellar tract, which is dedicated to spinal-level input.
incorrectas.B: Upper extremities and trunk proprioception is instead carried by the cuneocerebellar tract, the analogous upper-body pathway, so this option describes the wrong tract's territory.
incorrectas.C: Upper extremities alone is inaccurate for either spinocerebellar tract, since both the dorsal spinocerebellar and cuneocerebellar tracts also carry trunk information alongside their respective limb input.

preguntas.q: The cuneocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioceptive input from which body regions?

e.correcta: The cuneocerebellar tract is the upper-body counterpart of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract — 1st-order neurons from the upper extremities and trunk synapse in the external cuneate nucleus of the medulla, and 2nd-order axons ascend ipsilaterally via the inferior cerebellar peduncle to relay unconscious proprioceptive information to the cerebellum, supporting fine motor coordination of the arms.

incorrectas.B: Lower extremity and trunk proprioception is instead carried by the dorsal spinocerebellar tract, which synapses in Clarke's nucleus rather than the external cuneate nucleus used by the cuneocerebellar tract.
incorrectas.C: Lower extremities alone describes neither spinocerebellar tract accurately, since both carry trunk information in addition to their respective limb input.
incorrectas.D: There is no tract carrying only bilateral lower extremity information in this fashion — the spinocerebellar pathways are ipsilateral, unlike what this distractor implies.

preguntas.q: The cell bodies of the 2nd-order neurons of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract, found in Clarke's nucleus, are located at which spinal cord levels?

e.correcta: Clarke's nucleus (nucleus dorsalis) is present in the spinal cord gray matter only from approximately T1 to L2. This limited distribution is why proprioceptive input entering below L2 (e.g., from sacral dermatomes) must first ascend a segment or two within the tract before it can find a Clarke's nucleus neuron to synapse with.

incorrectas.A: C1-T1 would place Clarke's nucleus in the cervical cord, but it is actually absent from cervical segments and is instead restricted to the thoracic-upper lumbar region, so this range is both too high and misses the actual span.
incorrectas.C: L2-S5 would place it in the lower lumbar and sacral cord — the opposite of its true thoracolumbar location — and would incorrectly exclude the thoracic segments where Clarke's nucleus is actually concentrated.
incorrectas.D: Clarke's nucleus is not present throughout the entire spinal cord; it is a discrete column limited to T1-L2, unlike some longer-spanning nuclei or tracts.

preguntas.q: The cell bodies of the 2nd-order neurons of the cuneocerebellar tract are located in which nucleus?

e.correcta: The external (accessory) cuneate nucleus, located in the medulla lateral to the main cuneate nucleus, is where 1st-order upper-extremity/trunk proprioceptive afferents synapse. Its 2nd-order axons travel via the inferior cerebellar peduncle to the cerebellum, functioning as the upper-body analog of Clarke's nucleus.

incorrectas.A: The nucleus gracilis is part of the DCML pathway, relaying lower-body fine touch and proprioception up to the thalamus for conscious perception — a different pathway entirely from the cerebellar-bound cuneocerebellar tract.
incorrectas.B: The nucleus cuneatus is likewise part of the DCML pathway for the upper body, projecting to the thalamus/cortex for conscious sensation, distinct from the external cuneate nucleus's role in unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum.
incorrectas.D: The inferior olivary nucleus gives rise to climbing fibers that also reach the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle, but it is not where cuneocerebellar 2nd-order proprioceptive neurons synapse; its input instead relates to motor error signaling and motor learning.

preguntas.q: The dorsal spinocerebellar and cuneocerebellar tracts enter the cerebellum through which structure?

e.correcta: Both tracts — the dorsal spinocerebellar tract for the lower body and the cuneocerebellar tract for the upper body — carry unconscious proprioceptive information and enter the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle, alongside other afferents such as vestibulocerebellar and olivocerebellar climbing fibers. A lesion here can produce ipsilateral ataxia and dysmetria.

incorrectas.A: The superior cerebellar peduncle is predominantly an efferent pathway carrying output from the deep cerebellar nuclei to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus (the ventral spinocerebellar tract is a notable exception that enters here), but it is not the entry route for the dorsal spinocerebellar or cuneocerebellar tracts.
incorrectas.B: The middle cerebellar peduncle carries afferent fibers from the contralateral pontine nuclei as part of the corticopontocerebellar pathway, not direct spinocerebellar proprioceptive input.
incorrectas.C: The cerebral peduncle is a midbrain structure containing descending corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers, entirely unrelated to cerebellar afferent pathways.

preguntas.q: On a cross-section of the spinal cord, the presence of both well-developed dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus) indicates the level is located where?

o.A: Above T5 (e.g., cervical or upper thoracic)
o.B: Below T5 (e.g., lower thoracic or lumbar)
o.D: At the level of the conus medullaris only

e.correcta: At cervical and upper thoracic levels (above roughly T5), both the fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus are present together, because upper-extremity fibers (fasciculus cuneatus) only join the ascending fasciculus gracilis once the cord has risen above the mid-thoracic level — a handy anatomic landmark for localizing an unlabeled spinal cord cross-section.

incorrectas.B: Below T5, only the fasciculus gracilis (lower-body information) is present, since upper-extremity fibers haven't yet entered the cord at these more caudal levels — the opposite finding from what's described in the question.
incorrectas.C: At the sacral level, the cord cross-section is dominated by gray matter with minimal white matter overall, and only a small fasciculus gracilis remains, not two fully developed dorsal columns.
incorrectas.D: The conus medullaris (the tapered terminal end of the cord, roughly L1-L2) is a specific anatomic landmark defined by cord termination, not one defined by the presence of both dorsal columns.

preguntas.q: If only a single dorsal column (fasciculus gracilis, without fasciculus cuneatus) is visible on a spinal cord cross-section, the level is most likely which of the following?

e.correcta: The fasciculus cuneatus (carrying upper-extremity information) only joins the dorsal columns above roughly T5-T6; below that level, only the fasciculus gracilis (lower-extremity/trunk information) is present. Seeing a single dorsal column on cross-section is therefore a reliable marker of a lower thoracic, lumbar, or sacral level.

incorrectas.A: Above T5, both the fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus are present together, so finding only one column would be inconsistent with a level above T5.
incorrectas.C: Cervical levels are well above T5 and contain both dorsal column components fully developed, since proprioceptive input from both the upper and lower body is represented that high in the cord, making a single visible column inconsistent with this level.
incorrectas.D: Upper thoracic levels (above about T5-T6) likewise still carry both dorsal column components together, so this level would also show two dorsal columns rather than one.

preguntas.q: The presence of a lateral horn (intermediolateral cell column) on a spinal cord cross-section indicates the level lies within which range?

e.correcta: The lateral horn contains preganglionic sympathetic neuron cell bodies of the intermediolateral cell column, which is present only from T1 to L2 — the thoracolumbar sympathetic outflow. This is precisely why the sympathetic nervous system is described as "thoracolumbar," and identifying a lateral horn on cross-section pinpoints the level to this specific range.

incorrectas.A: C1-T1 incorrectly extends the range into the cervical cord, where sympathetic outflow (and thus the lateral horn) has not yet begun, since the intermediolateral cell column doesn't start until T1.
incorrectas.B: L3-S5 corresponds roughly to where parasympathetic (sacral) outflow arises (S2-S4) rather than sympathetic outflow, and this region actually lacks a lateral horn, since the intermediolateral cell column terminates at L2.
incorrectas.D: The cervical enlargement (C4-T1) refers to a region with increased anterior horn size due to upper limb motor innervation — an unrelated landmark tied to motor neuron pools, not to the sympathetic lateral horn.

preguntas.q: Which spinal cord level shows the highest proportion of gray matter relative to white matter on cross-section?

e.correcta: At the sacral level, ascending sensory fibers from below have not yet accumulated (since this is the caudal-most part of the cord), and relatively little white matter is needed, while the sacral segments still contain their full complement of neuronal cell bodies for the lower limb and pelvic organs — giving the highest gray-to-white matter ratio of any spinal level, a useful clue for identifying a sacral cross-section.

incorrectas.A: Cervical levels show the opposite pattern — abundant white matter, since ascending tracts have accumulated fibers from the entire cord below and descending tracts haven't yet terminated, yielding a low gray-to-white ratio despite the cervical enlargement's larger anterior horns.
incorrectas.B: Thoracic levels have an intermediate amount of white matter (more than sacral, less than cervical) along with comparatively modest gray matter, since thoracic segments don't innervate limbs and lack an enlargement, so gray matter is not dominant here.
incorrectas.C: Lumbar levels have relatively larger gray matter due to the lumbosacral enlargement (limb innervation) but still carry a substantial amount of white matter accumulated from lower segments, so the gray:white ratio is not as extreme as at the sacral level.

preguntas.q: Before synapsing on 2nd-order neurons in the dorsal horn, incoming pain and temperature fibers travel 1-2 spinal segments up or down within which structure?

e.correcta: Lissauer's tract (also called the posterolateral tract or dorsolateral fasciculus) is a small bundle at the tip of the dorsal horn where incoming 1st-order pain and temperature afferents ascend or descend 1-2 spinal segments before synapsing on 2nd-order neurons. This short vertical spread explains why the clinically tested sensory level of a spinothalamic lesion can be slightly imprecise compared to the actual anatomic level of the lesion.

incorrectas.B: The fasciculus gracilis is part of the DCML pathway, carrying already-ascending 2nd-order axons (fine touch/proprioception from the lower body) toward the medulla — it is not a way-station for incoming pain fibers awaiting their first synapse.
incorrectas.C: The fasciculus cuneatus is likewise a DCML component carrying upper-body fine touch/proprioceptive fibers, entirely unrelated to the initial routing of pain and temperature afferents in the dorsal horn.
incorrectas.D: The anterior white commissure is where 2nd-order spinothalamic axons decussate after synapsing in the dorsal horn — a step that occurs after, not before, the initial synapse that Lissauer's tract fibers are traveling toward.

preguntas.q: A patient with tertiary syphilis and degeneration of the dorsal columns/dorsal roots (tabes dorsalis) is asked to stand with feet together, arms at sides, and then close their eyes. What Romberg sign result is expected?

o.C: The patient is unable to stand at all, even with eyes open
o.D: Romberg sign is not applicable in tabes dorsalis

e.correcta: Standing balance relies on three sensory inputs: vision, vestibular function (CN VIII), and proprioception (via the DCML pathway). In tabes dorsalis, degeneration of the dorsal columns and dorsal roots removes proprioceptive input, but the patient can still compensate visually with eyes open. Closing the eyes eliminates the remaining compensatory input and unmasks the deficit, causing swaying or falling — a positive Romberg sign that localizes the problem to a proprioceptive/dorsal column pathway rather than the cerebellum.

incorrectas.A: A negative Romberg sign (maintained balance with eyes closed) would be expected only if all three balance inputs were intact, which is not the case here given the destroyed proprioceptive pathway.
incorrectas.C: Patients with tabes dorsalis are not unable to stand at all; they compensate reasonably well using vision while their eyes remain open and only become unstable once that visual input is removed.
incorrectas.D: The Romberg test is in fact the classic bedside maneuver used specifically to unmask the proprioceptive deficit of tabes dorsalis, so it is highly applicable and diagnostic in this condition.

preguntas.q: Tabes dorsalis, caused by tertiary syphilis affecting the dorsal roots and dorsal columns, characteristically causes what change in deep tendon reflexes (DTRs)?

e.correcta: Deep tendon reflexes require an intact reflex arc, including a sensory afferent limb that travels through the dorsal root into the spinal cord. Because tabes dorsalis destroys the dorsal roots themselves, the afferent (sensory) limb of the reflex arc is interrupted, abolishing DTRs even though the efferent motor limb remains intact — a sensory disconnect rather than a true lower motor neuron lesion.

incorrectas.A: Hyperreflexia is typically seen with upper motor neuron lesions, where loss of descending inhibitory control disinhibits the stretch reflex — the opposite pattern from the interrupted afferent limb seen in tabes dorsalis.
incorrectas.B: Clonus, like hyperreflexia, signals upper motor neuron disease with disinhibited stretch reflexes, and is not consistent with the destroyed sensory afferent limb characteristic of tabes dorsalis.
incorrectas.D: Sensation and reflexes are not preserved in tabes dorsalis — the entire clinical picture centers on loss of proprioception, vibration sense, and reflexes from dorsal root/column degeneration, the opposite of what this option describes.

preguntas.q: Tabes dorsalis is classically associated with which pupillary finding?

o.B: Marcus Gunn pupil (relative afferent pupillary defect)
o.C: Anisocoria that worsens in dim light

e.correcta: Argyll Robertson pupils show light-near dissociation: they constrict normally with accommodation/convergence but fail to constrict in response to light (informally remembered as pupils that "accommodate but don't react"). This reflects selective damage to the pretectal nuclei in the midbrain, which mediate the pupillary light reflex but are not part of the separate accommodation reflex circuitry — a classic finding in neurosyphilis, including tabes dorsalis.

incorrectas.A: Fixed and dilated pupils bilaterally suggest a much more severe process, such as bilateral CN III/parasympathetic outflow failure or severe brainstem injury, not the selective light-near dissociation of Argyll Robertson pupils.
incorrectas.B: A Marcus Gunn pupil results from an afferent visual pathway lesion (e.g., optic nerve damage), producing paradoxical pupillary dilation when light swings from the unaffected to the affected eye — a completely different mechanism from the pretectal-specific damage of Argyll Robertson pupils.
incorrectas.C: Anisocoria worsening in dim light suggests a problem with pupillary dilation (e.g., a sympathetic lesion as in Horner syndrome), not the bilateral, symmetric light-near dissociation characteristic of tabes dorsalis.

preguntas.q: Patients with tabes dorsalis often experience brief, severe, shooting/stabbing episodes of pain ("lightning pains") in the legs or abdomen. What is the underlying mechanism?

o.A: Hypersensitization of sensory pain neurons in the degenerating dorsal roots
o.B: Ectopic firing from demyelinated corticospinal axons
o.C: Referred pain from autonomic dysfunction in the lateral horn
o.D: Central sensitization within the anterior horn motor neurons

e.correcta: In tabes dorsalis, the dorsal roots and dorsal columns undergo progressive degeneration from tertiary syphilis, and the damaged, dying sensory pain neurons become hyperexcitable and hypersensitive, misfiring spontaneously or in response to minor stimuli. This produces the characteristic paroxysmal, lightning-like pains, often felt in the legs, or as "gastric crises" that can mimic an acute abdomen.

incorrectas.B: The corticospinal tract is a descending motor pathway; its involvement would produce motor deficits such as weakness or spasticity, not the sensory paroxysmal pain phenomenon, which is rooted in sensory (dorsal root/column) pathology instead.
incorrectas.C: The lateral horn houses sympathetic preganglionic neurons, and while autonomic dysfunction can occur in some neuropathies, the classic lightning pains of tabes dorsalis are attributed specifically to the diseased sensory afferents, not to lateral horn/autonomic pathology.
incorrectas.D: The anterior horn contains motor neurons; sensitization here would affect motor output rather than sensory perception, and is not the accepted mechanism behind the paroxysmal pain of tabes dorsalis.

preguntas.q: A patient with tertiary neurosyphilis and loss of proprioception develops a swollen, deformed, painless knee joint after repeated unnoticed trauma. What is this joint complication called?

e.correcta: Charcot joint (neuropathic arthropathy) results when loss of proprioceptive and pain sensation from dorsal column/dorsal root degeneration in tabes dorsalis (tertiary syphilis) allows repeated unnoticed microtrauma to accumulate in weight-bearing joints, especially the knee. Because the protective pain/position feedback loop is broken, the joint progressively destructs, becomes swollen, unstable, and deformed without the patient reporting significant pain. This is a classic exam clue for any disease that destroys proprioception (also seen in diabetic neuropathy and syringomyelia).

incorrectas.B: Osteoarthritis is a degenerative 'wear and tear' arthritis from cartilage breakdown with age and mechanical stress, typically painful and slowly progressive, not driven by loss of protective sensation the way a neuropathic Charcot joint is.
incorrectas.C: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune, symmetric, inflammatory polyarthritis with pannus formation and morning stiffness, unrelated to sensory neuropathy — it is immune-mediated joint destruction, not the sensory-loss-driven microtrauma of tabes dorsalis.
incorrectas.D: Septic arthritis is caused by direct bacterial infection of the joint space, presenting acutely painful, hot, and swollen with fever, a distinct mechanism from the painless chronic destruction of a neuropathic joint.

preguntas.q: In tabes dorsalis, demyelination of the sensory neurons that convey bladder fullness leads to which type of urinary incontinence?

e.correcta: Tabes dorsalis destroys the dorsal columns and dorsal roots carrying sensory afferents from the bladder, so the patient loses the sensation of bladder fullness. The bladder progressively distends without the person feeling the urge to void, and once capacity is exceeded, urine dribbles out passively — this is overflow incontinence, a sensory/underactive-bladder problem rather than a motor or sphincter one.

incorrectas.A: Urge incontinence results from an overactive detrusor (an upper motor neuron-type problem, as in anterior spinal artery occlusion) causing sudden strong urges with leakage, the opposite physiology of the sensory deafferentation seen in tabes dorsalis.
incorrectas.C: Stress incontinence is due to weakened pelvic floor or sphincter mechanisms allowing leakage with increased intra-abdominal pressure (coughing, laughing), a structural problem unrelated to loss of bladder-fullness sensation.
incorrectas.D: Total incontinence implies continuous leakage from a fistula or complete sphincter failure, not the intermittent overflow pattern that follows from a bladder that can no longer sense when it is full.

preguntas.q: Tabes dorsalis, caused by tertiary syphilis affecting the dorsal columns and dorsal roots, most commonly affects which spinal levels?

e.correcta: Tabes dorsalis preferentially damages the lumbosacral dorsal roots and dorsal columns, which is why the classic findings — loss of proprioception and vibration, sensory ataxia (positive Romberg), absent deep tendon reflexes, and Charcot joints — predominate in the lower extremities. This lumbar predilection also explains why bladder dysfunction (loss of fullness sensation) is common, since lumbosacral sensory afferents are affected early.

incorrectas.A: Cervical levels are the classic site of onset for ALS (affecting anterior horn cells and corticospinal tracts), not the region primarily involved in tabes dorsalis.
incorrectas.B: Thoracic levels, particularly the mid-thoracic watershed zone, are most relevant to anterior spinal artery occlusion, a different vascular pathology rather than the syphilitic dorsal column/root degeneration of tabes dorsalis.
incorrectas.D: Sacral roots can be affected in tabes dorsalis to some degree, but the disease's hallmark predilection and classic teaching point is the lumbar region, not sacral levels in isolation.

preguntas.q: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) causes degeneration of which combination of motor neurons?

o.C: Both upper and lower motor neurons
o.D: Neither upper nor lower motor neurons

e.correcta: ALS is unique among the classic spinal cord syndromes in destroying both the anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons) and the corticospinal tracts/brainstem motor nuclei (upper motor neurons), which is why patients show a mixed picture: fasciculations, atrophy, and flaccid weakness (LMN) alongside spasticity, hyperreflexia, and pseudobulbar palsy (UMN), often in the same limb. This combination of UMN plus LMN signs without sensory or bladder/bowel involvement is the key pattern that distinguishes ALS from other spinal cord lesions.

incorrectas.A: Lower motor neurons only describes diseases like spinal muscular atrophy or polio, which spare the corticospinal tract and therefore never produce the spasticity or hyperreflexia that are prominent in ALS.
incorrectas.B: Upper motor neurons only would produce a purely spastic, hyperreflexic picture (as in primary lateral sclerosis, a rare ALS variant) without the atrophy and fasciculations that anterior horn cell loss causes in classic ALS.
incorrectas.D: Neither upper nor lower motor neurons is incorrect because ALS is fundamentally a motor neuron disease — it is defined by progressive degeneration of both motor neuron pools, which is exactly what produces its characteristic mixed UMN/LMN exam findings.

preguntas.q: ALS typically begins at which level of the spinal cord?

e.correcta: ALS characteristically begins in the cervical spinal cord, producing early atrophy and weakness in the hands and arms before spreading to other segments (bulbar, thoracic, lumbar) as the disease progresses. This is why early symptoms often include difficulty with fine hand movements, such as buttoning shirts or turning keys, rather than leg or bulbar symptoms.

incorrectas.B: Thoracic levels, especially T3-T8, form the classic watershed zone vulnerable to anterior spinal artery occlusion, not the typical site of ALS onset.
incorrectas.C: Lumbar levels are the predominant site of dorsal column/root involvement in tabes dorsalis, a different disease process from ALS's anterior horn/corticospinal degeneration.
incorrectas.D: Sacral levels are not the characteristic starting point for ALS; disease spread to sacral segments occurs later, and bladder/bowel function (largely sacral-mediated) is classically spared throughout the disease course.

preguntas.q: ALS classically presents with what pattern of limb weakness?

o.D: Purely bilateral and symmetric from onset

e.correcta: ALS typically begins asymmetrically — one hand or arm becomes weak and atrophic before the disease spreads to other limbs — reflecting the patchy, focal onset of anterior horn cell degeneration rather than a uniform, bilateral process. This asymmetry, combined with the mix of UMN and LMN signs and absence of sensory loss, helps distinguish ALS from symmetric peripheral neuropathies or myopathies.

incorrectas.A: Symmetric, proximal weakness is more typical of primary muscle diseases (myopathies) or neuromuscular junction disorders, not the asymmetric, distal-then-spreading pattern of anterior horn cell loss in ALS.
incorrectas.B: Symmetric, distal weakness suggests a length-dependent peripheral polyneuropathy (e.g., diabetic neuropathy), which would also produce sensory symptoms — unlike ALS, which is purely motor and asymmetric at onset.
incorrectas.D: A purely bilateral, symmetric pattern from the very start is atypical for ALS; the disease's hallmark is unilateral or asymmetric onset that spreads over time, not simultaneous bilateral involvement.

preguntas.q: An early sign of ALS is atrophy and weakness of which body part?

e.correcta: Because ALS classically begins at cervical spinal cord levels, the small muscles of the hands are often the first to show atrophy and weakness — patients notice clumsiness, trouble with fine motor tasks, or difficulty gripping objects before the weakness spreads proximally and to other limbs. This distal, hand-first pattern reflects early anterior horn cell loss in the cervical enlargement.

incorrectas.A: Foot weakness can occur as ALS progresses to lumbosacral segments, but it is not the classic earliest sign, since disease onset is typically cervical (hands) rather than lumbosacral.
incorrectas.C: Facial (bulbar) involvement causing dysarthria and dysphagia does occur in ALS from brainstem motor nuclei degeneration, but it represents a separate bulbar-onset presentation, not the classic early limb-onset sign of hand atrophy.
incorrectas.D: Proximal shoulder girdle weakness is more suggestive of a myopathy or neuromuscular junction disorder; ALS's motor neuron loss classically produces distal, hand-predominant weakness early on.

preguntas.q: What sensory deficits are typically found in ALS?

e.correcta: ALS is a pure motor neuron disease — it destroys anterior horn cells and corticospinal tracts but spares all sensory pathways, so patients have no objective sensory deficits despite significant weakness and atrophy. This absence of sensory findings is a key distinguishing feature used to differentiate ALS from other spinal cord syndromes like syringomyelia or anterior spinal artery occlusion, both of which do produce sensory deficits.

incorrectas.A: Loss of proprioception and vibration reflects dorsal column damage, as seen in tabes dorsalis or Friedreich ataxia — tracts that are entirely uninvolved in ALS, which affects only motor pathways.
incorrectas.B: Loss of pain and temperature reflects spinothalamic tract damage, characteristic of syringomyelia and anterior spinal artery occlusion, not ALS, which spares this tract along with all other sensory pathways.
incorrectas.D: Loss of all sensory modalities would suggest a complete cord transection or combined dorsal column plus spinothalamic involvement, which does not occur in ALS since the disease process is restricted to motor neurons.

preguntas.q: What bladder/bowel dysfunction is typically seen in ALS?

e.correcta: ALS spares the sacral parasympathetic nuclei (Onuf's nucleus) that control bladder and bowel sphincter function, so patients maintain normal continence throughout most of the disease course despite progressive limb and bulbar weakness. This preservation of autonomic/sphincter function, together with normal sensation, helps distinguish ALS from spinal cord lesions that do involve these pathways.

incorrectas.A: A spastic bladder (urge incontinence from an upper motor neuron lesion above the sacral cord) is seen in conditions like anterior spinal artery occlusion, which does damage descending pathways controlling the bladder — unlike ALS, which spares the relevant circuitry.
incorrectas.B: Overflow incontinence reflects loss of bladder-fullness sensation or an underactive detrusor, as in tabes dorsalis; ALS does not damage the sensory or autonomic pathways responsible for bladder sensation.
incorrectas.D: A flaccid, areflexic bladder would suggest damage to the sacral reflex arc or cauda equina, structures that ALS characteristically spares since the motor neurons of Onuf's nucleus are relatively resistant to the degenerative process.

preguntas.q: ALS is commonly known by what eponym, named after a famous baseball player diagnosed with the disease?

e.correcta: ALS is widely known as Lou Gehrig disease in the United States, named after the New York Yankees first baseman whose career and life were ended by the illness in the late 1930s, which brought public attention to this motor neuron disease. The eponym is a favorite exam detail since it links a recognizable name to the classic combined UMN/LMN degeneration described for ALS.

incorrectas.A: Werdnig-Hoffmann disease is the eponym for spinal muscular atrophy type I, a lower-motor-neuron-only disease of infancy caused by SMN1 mutations, distinct from the combined UMN/LMN pathology and adult onset of ALS.
incorrectas.B: Guillain-Barré syndrome is an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy causing ascending flaccid paralysis, a peripheral nerve disease unrelated to the central motor neuron degeneration of ALS.
incorrectas.D: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is a hereditary peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy causing distal muscle wasting and sensory loss, a different peripheral, sensorimotor disease from the central, purely motor pathology of ALS.

preguntas.q: Most cases of ALS are sporadic and typically arise in which age group?

e.correcta: The majority of ALS cases are sporadic (not familial) and typically present in middle-aged adults, usually in their 50s-60s, with progressive asymmetric limb weakness that evolves to include both UMN and LMN signs. Recognizing this typical age of onset helps distinguish ALS from motor neuron diseases of infancy, like spinal muscular atrophy, or the peak age ranges of other neurodegenerative conditions.

incorrectas.A: Children are affected by lower-motor-neuron-only diseases such as spinal muscular atrophy, not classic sporadic ALS, which has a much later, middle-aged onset.
incorrectas.B: Adolescents are not the typical population for ALS onset; this age group is more associated with hereditary conditions like Friedreich ataxia, which usually presents before age 25.
incorrectas.C: While ALS can occasionally occur in older adults, the classic and most commonly tested age of onset for sporadic ALS is middle age, not the extreme elderly range.

preguntas.q: Which drug decreases glutamate release from neurons and is used to modestly slow disease progression in ALS?

e.correcta: Riluzole is the classic disease-modifying drug for ALS; it decreases presynaptic glutamate release (and may also inhibit voltage-gated sodium channels), reducing excitotoxic damage to motor neurons and modestly prolonging survival, though it does not reverse existing weakness. It is a good example of targeting glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity as a therapeutic strategy in neurodegeneration.

incorrectas.A: Levodopa is a dopamine precursor used to treat Parkinson disease by replenishing dopaminergic neurotransmission in the substantia nigra, a mechanism unrelated to glutamate signaling and irrelevant to ALS's motor neuron degeneration.
incorrectas.B: Memantine is an NMDA receptor antagonist used in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease to reduce glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity in that context, but it is not the standard glutamate-release-inhibiting agent indicated for ALS.
incorrectas.C: Donepezil is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used to boost cholinergic transmission in Alzheimer disease, a completely different mechanism (enhancing acetylcholine rather than reducing glutamate) and not used for ALS.

preguntas.q: Anterior spinal artery occlusion produces which pattern of motor deficit below the level of the infarct, once the initial spinal shock phase resolves?

e.correcta: Below the level of an anterior spinal artery infarct, the lateral corticospinal tracts are damaged, producing bilateral upper motor neuron signs (spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign) once the initial flaccid spinal shock phase resolves over days to weeks. This reflects interruption of descending motor pathways traveling through the anterior two-thirds of the cord, which the anterior spinal artery supplies.

incorrectas.B: Bilateral lower motor neuron signs occur specifically at the level of the infarct, where the anterior horn cells themselves are destroyed, producing flaccid weakness — a distinct segment from the upper motor neuron pattern seen below the lesion.
incorrectas.C: Purely sensory ataxia would suggest isolated dorsal column damage, but the anterior spinal artery does not supply the dorsal columns (the posterior spinal arteries do), so proprioception and vibration are spared in anterior spinal artery occlusion.
incorrectas.D: Isolated cranial nerve palsies would suggest a brainstem lesion, not a spinal cord infarct; anterior spinal artery occlusion affects spinal levels below the medulla, not cranial nerve nuclei.

preguntas.q: Anterior spinal artery occlusion produces which pattern of motor deficit at the level of the infarct itself?

e.correcta: At the exact level of an anterior spinal artery infarct, the anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons) supplied by that segment are destroyed, producing flaccid paralysis, areflexia, and eventual atrophy confined to that spinal level — distinct from the upper motor neuron (spastic) signs seen below the lesion, where only the descending corticospinal tract fibers, not the cell bodies, are interrupted.

incorrectas.B: Bilateral upper motor neuron signs occur below the level of the infarct, where corticospinal tract axons traveling to more caudal segments are damaged, not at the level of the lesion itself where the anterior horn cell bodies are destroyed.
incorrectas.C: Contralateral hemiparesis would suggest a unilateral brain or brainstem lesion above the decussation of the corticospinal tracts, not a bilateral spinal cord infarct, which produces symmetric bilateral deficits.
incorrectas.D: Isolated distal sensory loss is not the mechanism at the level of the infarct; the anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior horns and spinothalamic tracts, not the dorsal columns, and the defining feature at the lesion level is motor (LMN), not purely sensory.

preguntas.q: What sensory deficit is characteristically seen with anterior spinal artery occlusion?

e.correcta: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, including the spinothalamic tracts, so its occlusion causes loss of pain and temperature sensation below the lesion while sparing the dorsal columns, which are supplied by the separate posterior spinal arteries, meaning vibration and proprioception remain intact. This dissociated sensory loss with preserved proprioception is a key feature distinguishing anterior spinal artery occlusion from lesions like tabes dorsalis or Friedreich ataxia that hit the dorsal columns instead.

incorrectas.A: Loss of vibration and proprioception results from dorsal column damage, which is supplied by the posterior spinal arteries, not the anterior spinal artery — this modality is classically preserved in anterior spinal artery occlusion, helping distinguish it from posterior cord syndromes.
incorrectas.C: Loss of light touch only does not reflect the actual anatomy — light touch is carried redundantly by both the anterior spinothalamic tract and dorsal columns, so isolated light-touch loss is not the characteristic finding; the hallmark is pain/temperature loss with sparing of touch and proprioception.
incorrectas.D: No sensory deficit is incorrect since the spinothalamic tracts, which mediate pain and temperature, run through the anterior cord territory supplied by the anterior spinal artery and are damaged by its occlusion.

preguntas.q: What bladder dysfunction is associated with anterior spinal artery occlusion?

e.correcta: Because anterior spinal artery occlusion damages descending pathways that normally inhibit the sacral micturition reflex (an upper motor neuron-type lesion above the sacral spinal segments), the bladder becomes spastic and hyperreflexic, leading to urge incontinence with frequent, uncontrolled voiding once spinal shock resolves. This contrasts with ALS, where bladder function is entirely spared, making bladder findings a useful way to distinguish these two conditions.

incorrectas.A: Overflow incontinence results from loss of bladder-fullness sensation or an underactive detrusor, as in tabes dorsalis, not from the upper-motor-neuron-type disinhibition of the micturition reflex seen in anterior spinal artery occlusion.
incorrectas.B: A flaccid, areflexic bladder is typical of acute spinal shock immediately after the infarct or of a lower motor neuron/sacral reflex arc lesion, but the chronic pattern that follows anterior spinal artery occlusion is a spastic, upper-motor-neuron bladder, not a persistently flaccid one.
incorrectas.D: No bladder dysfunction is the pattern seen in ALS, which spares autonomic/sacral pathways — anterior spinal artery occlusion, by contrast, does damage the descending tracts controlling bladder function and does produce dysfunction (spastic bladder).

preguntas.q: Which spinal cord segment supplied by the anterior spinal artery has the weakest collateral blood supply and is therefore most vulnerable to watershed infarction?

e.correcta: The mid-thoracic cord (roughly T3-T8) lies between two zones with strong collateral reinforcement — the cervical anterior spinal artery territory above, fed by branches of the costocervical trunk and vertebral arteries, and the lower thoracolumbar territory below, fed by the artery of Adamkiewicz — leaving this middle segment as a true watershed zone with minimal anastomotic backup. Consequently, it is the most vulnerable region to ischemia during hypotension or aortic surgery, producing deficits affecting the lower chest, trunk, and abdominal muscles.

incorrectas.A: The cervical region (C1-T2) is protected by robust collateral flow from branches of the costocervical trunk and vertebral arteries, making it comparatively resistant to watershed infarction relative to the mid-thoracic zone.
incorrectas.C: The lower thoracic-to-conus medullaris region (T9-conus) receives reinforcement from the artery of Adamkiewicz, which gives it collateral protection — unless that artery is also compromised (e.g., by trauma or aortic cross-clamping), in which case this zone, not the mid-thoracic one, becomes vulnerable.
incorrectas.D: Sacral segments are not typically described as the classic anterior spinal artery watershed zone; the well-established watershed territory that is tested is the mid-thoracic (T3-T8) region, between the cervical and Adamkiewicz-supplied territories.

preguntas.q: Syringomyelia (fluid-filled cavitation of the central spinal cord) most commonly occurs at which spinal levels?

e.correcta: Syringomyelia classically develops at the cervicothoracic junction, most commonly C8-T1, where the syrinx expands within the central canal and first destroys the crossing spinothalamic fibers near the anterior white commissure, producing the classic 'cape-like' loss of pain and temperature sensation over the shoulders and arms. This level correlates with the segmental distribution of the sensory deficits students are expected to recognize.

incorrectas.A: C1-C4 is a higher cervical level than the classic site of syrinx formation; syrinxes typically arise at the cervicothoracic junction (C8-T1) rather than the upper cervical cord.
incorrectas.C: T6-T10 is not the characteristic location for syringomyelia; this mid-thoracic range is instead associated with anterior spinal artery watershed infarction, a different pathologic process.
incorrectas.D: L1-L4 is well below the typical site of syrinx formation — syringomyelia's classic cervicothoracic (C8-T1) location is what produces the cape-like upper extremity sensory loss that is tested.

preguntas.q: Syringomyelia typically produces loss of pain and temperature sensation in which distribution?

e.correcta: As the syrinx expands within the central canal at the cervicothoracic cord, it first interrupts the decussating spinothalamic fibers crossing through the anterior white commissure at that level, producing a bilateral, symmetric 'cape-like' loss of pain and temperature sensation over the shoulders, arms, and upper trunk, while touch and proprioception, carried in the dorsal columns, remain intact. This dissociated sensory loss pattern, and its characteristic upper-body distribution, is a hallmark finding, and patients may present with unnoticed burns or cuts on their hands.

incorrectas.A: Lower extremity sensory loss would suggest a lumbosacral process rather than the cervicothoracic syrinx location classically tested, since the cavitation and its effect on crossing fibers occur at the level where the syrinx forms (C8-T1), affecting upper limb dermatomes.
incorrectas.B: Face and trunk loss does not fit the classic anatomy; facial sensation is carried by the trigeminal system, unaffected by a cervical spinal cord syrinx, and isolated trunk-only loss does not reflect the arm-predominant cape distribution.
incorrectas.D: A perianal 'saddle' distribution of sensory loss is characteristic of cauda equina or conus medullaris lesions, not syringomyelia, which affects the upper limbs and shoulders due to its cervicothoracic location.

preguntas.q: As a syrinx in syringomyelia expands to involve the anterior horn, what type of motor deficit results?

o.B: Lower motor neuron signs (flaccid weakness, atrophy)

e.correcta: When the expanding syrinx extends laterally into the anterior horn, it destroys the lower motor neuron cell bodies located there, producing segmental flaccid weakness, muscle atrophy, decreased tone, and diminished or absent reflexes in the muscles innervated at that level — the same LMN pattern seen with any anterior horn cell loss, such as polio or the LMN component of ALS. Damage to paravertebral muscle innervation can also cause a secondary scoliosis from asymmetric muscle weakness.

incorrectas.A: Upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia) would occur if the syrinx compressed the lateral corticospinal tracts instead, producing a different pattern below the lesion — this is separate from the flaccid LMN picture caused by direct anterior horn cell destruction.
incorrectas.C: Cerebellar ataxia would require involvement of the spinocerebellar tracts or cerebellum itself, structures not primarily destroyed by anterior horn expansion of a cervicothoracic syrinx.
incorrectas.D: Choreiform movements are a basal ganglia phenomenon (e.g., Huntington disease) related to disrupted GABAergic and dopaminergic circuits, entirely unrelated to the segmental lower motor neuron loss produced by anterior horn destruction in syringomyelia.

preguntas.q: Late-stage expansion of a cervicothoracic syrinx, disrupting the lateral horn (intermediolateral cell column), may produce which syndrome?

e.correcta: The intermediolateral cell column of the lateral horn, present at T1-L2, houses preganglionic sympathetic neurons; when a cervicothoracic syrinx expands enough to disrupt this region (classically at T1), it interrupts the sympathetic chain supplying the head and eye, producing Horner syndrome — ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis on the affected side. This is a helpful reminder that the lateral horn, not just the anterior or posterior horns, can become a target as a syrinx enlarges over time.

incorrectas.A: Adie tonic pupil results from damage to the ciliary ganglion or postganglionic parasympathetic fibers, causing a pupil that reacts poorly to light but shows tonic accommodation — a peripheral parasympathetic problem unrelated to the sympathetic chain disruption from a cervicothoracic syrinx.
incorrectas.B: Argyll Robertson pupil ('accommodates but does not react') is classically caused by neurosyphilis damage to the pretectal area, not by spinal cord lateral horn disruption — it reflects a midbrain lesion, not a sympathetic chain lesion from syringomyelia.
incorrectas.C: Marcus Gunn pupil (relative afferent pupillary defect) results from optic nerve damage causing paradoxical pupillary dilation when light is swung to the affected eye — an afferent visual pathway problem, distinct from the efferent sympathetic disruption that produces Horner syndrome.

preguntas.q: Which type of Chiari malformation is a congenital anomaly that is usually asymptomatic during childhood, often presenting later in life?

e.correcta: Chiari I malformation involves mild downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils, not the vermis, through the foramen magnum and is often clinically silent for years, since the herniation is relatively minor. Many patients remain asymptomatic through childhood and are diagnosed incidentally or present later in life with headaches or cerebellar symptoms, often when it becomes associated with a syrinx.

incorrectas.A: Chiari II malformation involves more extensive herniation of the cerebellar vermis and brainstem through the foramen magnum and is classically associated with a lumbosacral myelomeningocele, presenting in infancy with symptoms like hydrocephalus, not the largely silent childhood course typical of Chiari I.
incorrectas.C: Chiari III malformation is the most severe and rare form, involving herniation of the cerebellum into an occipital encephalocele, which is apparent and symptomatic at birth rather than being an asymptomatic incidental finding.
incorrectas.D: Dandy-Walker malformation involves agenesis of the cerebellar vermis with cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle and an enlarged posterior fossa, typically presenting with hydrocephalus in infancy — a distinct developmental anomaly from the tonsillar herniation of Chiari malformations.

preguntas.q: Chiari I malformation may present with paroxysmal occipital symptoms and cerebellar dysfunction due to tonsillar compression, classically worsened by which maneuver?

o.B: Headaches worsened only by lying supine
o.D: Headaches unaffected by any positional change

e.correcta: Chiari I malformation causes meningeal irritation and cerebellar tonsil compression at the foramen magnum, producing occipital headaches and ataxia that classically worsen with the Valsalva maneuver (coughing, straining, sneezing) because these actions transiently increase intracranial pressure and further impact the crowded posterior fossa/foramen magnum region. Recognizing a Valsalva-triggered occipital headache with cerebellar signs should prompt consideration of a Chiari malformation.

incorrectas.B: While positional changes can affect symptoms in some Chiari patients, the classic, specifically tested trigger is the Valsalva maneuver, which raises intracranial and intraspinal pressure, not simply lying supine in isolation.
incorrectas.C: Headaches relieved by standing is not the classic pattern for Chiari I malformation; if anything, activities that raise intracranial pressure, like Valsalva, worsen symptoms rather than postural changes toward standing.
incorrectas.D: Headaches unaffected by positional or pressure changes would be atypical and contrary to the classic teaching that Chiari I headaches are specifically provoked by maneuvers that raise intracranial pressure, like Valsalva.

preguntas.q: Which trinucleotide repeat disorder causes combined degeneration of the cerebellum, spinocerebellar tracts, dorsal columns, and lateral corticospinal tracts, producing ataxia, loss of vibration/proprioception, and muscle weakness with loss of reflexes?

e.correcta: Friedreich ataxia is caused by a GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the frataxin (FXN) gene, leading to impaired mitochondrial iron metabolism and progressive degeneration of multiple pathways: the cerebellum and spinocerebellar tracts (causing ataxia), the dorsal columns (loss of vibration and proprioception), and the lateral corticospinal tracts plus dorsal root ganglia (muscle weakness with loss of deep tendon reflexes). This multi-tract involvement, combined with typical onset before age 25 and association with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes, makes it a classic multisystem trinucleotide repeat disease distinct from single-pathway disorders.

incorrectas.A: Huntington disease is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene, causing degeneration of the caudate and putamen (GABAergic neurons) leading to chorea and dementia — a basal ganglia disease, not one involving the cerebellum and spinal cord tracts as in Friedreich ataxia.
incorrectas.C: Myotonic dystrophy results from a CTG repeat expansion in the DMPK gene, causing myotonia, muscle wasting, cataracts, and cardiac conduction defects primarily through a muscle/ion channel mechanism, not through cerebellar or spinal tract degeneration.
incorrectas.D: Fragile X syndrome is caused by a CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene, leading to intellectual disability, macroorchidism, and a long face — a neurodevelopmental disorder rather than a progressive ataxia/spinal tract degeneration disease like Friedreich ataxia.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of Friedreich ataxia?

e.correcta: Friedreich ataxia is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, caused by a GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in both copies of the FXN gene on chromosome 9, which reduces frataxin protein levels needed for proper mitochondrial iron-sulfur cluster assembly. This recessive inheritance, combined with its unstable GAA repeat (unlike the CAG or CGG repeats of many dominant or X-linked repeat disorders), makes it a notable exception among the trinucleotide repeat diseases, most of which are dominant or X-linked.

incorrectas.A: Autosomal dominant inheritance characterizes most other trinucleotide repeat disorders, like Huntington disease and myotonic dystrophy, but Friedreich ataxia is a recessive exception, requiring two mutated FXN alleles to cause disease.
incorrectas.B: X-linked recessive inheritance describes conditions like Fragile X syndrome, but Friedreich ataxia's FXN gene is located on an autosome (chromosome 9), not the X chromosome.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial (maternal) inheritance would apply to diseases caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA itself (e.g., MELAS, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy); although Friedreich ataxia impairs mitochondrial function via frataxin deficiency, the causative gene mutation itself is nuclear and follows autosomal recessive transmission.

preguntas.q: A mutation in the frataxin gene in Friedreich ataxia leads to impaired function of which cellular organelle?

e.correcta: Frataxin is a nuclear-encoded mitochondrial protein involved in iron-sulfur cluster assembly and mitochondrial iron homeostasis; the GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FXN gene silences its transcription, leading to iron accumulation within mitochondria, impaired oxidative phosphorylation, and increased free-radical damage. This mitochondrial dysfunction underlies the degeneration of the dorsal root ganglia, spinocerebellar tracts, and myocardium seen in the disease.

incorrectas.B: Lysosomal enzyme deficiencies cause lysosomal storage diseases (e.g., Tay-Sachs, Gaucher), which produce distinct patterns of neurodegeneration from accumulated substrates, not the iron-mediated oxidative damage seen with frataxin loss.
incorrectas.C: Peroxisomal dysfunction, as in adrenoleukodystrophy or Zellweger syndrome, impairs very-long-chain fatty acid beta-oxidation rather than iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis, producing a different clinical and biochemical picture than Friedreich ataxia.
incorrectas.D: The Golgi apparatus handles protein sorting and post-translational modification; frataxin's role is intramitochondrial iron handling, not Golgi trafficking, so Golgi dysfunction is not the mechanism implicated in this disease.

preguntas.q: What is the most common cause of death in patients with Friedreich ataxia?

e.correcta: Loss of frataxin causes iron accumulation and oxidative damage not only in neurons but also in cardiomyocytes, producing a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy that is the leading cause of death in Friedreich ataxia, often from arrhythmia or heart failure. This is why patients require serial echocardiographic monitoring even though the presenting complaints are neurologic, such as gait ataxia, dysarthria, and loss of proprioception.

incorrectas.B: Aspiration pneumonia is a common terminal event in many neurodegenerative diseases with bulbar dysfunction, but it is not the classically cited leading cause of death in Friedreich ataxia; cardiac disease is.
incorrectas.C: Friedreich ataxia primarily damages the dorsal columns, spinocerebellar tracts, and corticospinal tracts, and while dysarthria occurs, diaphragmatic or respiratory failure is not the characteristic fatal complication as it is in diseases like ALS.
incorrectas.D: The cardiomyopathy in Friedreich ataxia can occasionally progress to a dilated, poorly contractile phenotype late in disease, but the hallmark and classically tested cardiac finding and cause of death is the initial concentric hypertrophic pattern, not a primary dilated cardiomyopathy.

preguntas.q: Friedreich ataxia is associated with hammer toes and which characteristic high-arched foot deformity?

e.correcta: Pes cavus, an abnormally high medial longitudinal arch, develops in Friedreich ataxia from chronic denervation and muscle imbalance in the intrinsic foot muscles caused by the underlying peripheral neuropathy and spinocerebellar degeneration; it appears together with hammer toes as a classic exam finding. Pes cavus is not specific to Friedreich ataxia, however — it is also seen in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy), so other findings (cardiomyopathy, dysarthria, absent reflexes with extensor plantar responses) must be used to distinguish the two.

incorrectas.B: Pes planus (flat feet) results from collapse rather than exaggeration of the medial arch, reflecting ligamentous laxity or tibialis posterior dysfunction — the opposite deformity from what is seen in Friedreich ataxia.
incorrectas.C: Hallux valgus (bunion) is a lateral deviation of the great toe usually related to footwear and joint mechanics, not a neurogenic deformity from denervation of the intrinsic foot muscles.
incorrectas.D: Talipes equinovarus (clubfoot) is a congenital fixed deformity present at birth involving inversion and plantarflexion of the foot, distinct from the progressive, denervation-related arch deformity that develops later in life in Friedreich ataxia.

preguntas.q: Which eye movement abnormality is classically seen in patients with Friedreich ataxia?

e.correcta: Friedreich ataxia damages the cerebellum and its connections, producing cerebellar-type nystagmus (involuntary, rhythmic oscillation of the eyes) along with dysarthria and gait ataxia; this fits the pattern of diffuse spinocerebellar degeneration caused by frataxin loss. The nystagmus reflects dysfunction of the vestibulocerebellar pathways that normally stabilize gaze, rather than a discrete focal brainstem lesion.

incorrectas.B: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia results from a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (classically in multiple sclerosis), causing impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye with contralateral abducting nystagmus — a focal brainstem white-matter finding, not the diffuse cerebellar degeneration of Friedreich ataxia.
incorrectas.C: Oculomotor apraxia (difficulty initiating voluntary saccades, requiring compensatory head thrusts) is characteristic of ataxia-telangiectasia, another inherited ataxia, but is not the classic ocular finding taught for Friedreich ataxia.
incorrectas.D: Complete ophthalmoplegia implies paralysis of all extraocular movements, as seen in myasthenic crisis or combined CN III/IV/VI palsies, which is far more severe and mechanistically different from the cerebellar nystagmus of Friedreich ataxia.

preguntas.q: Elevated levels of which substance in the amniotic fluid serve as a confirmatory test for neural tube defects after an abnormal alpha-fetoprotein screen?

e.correcta: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) is normally confined to fetal CSF and neural tissue; when the neural tube fails to close, exposed neural tissue allows fetal AChE, along with AFP, to leak directly into the amniotic fluid. Because AChE is more specific to neural tissue than AFP (which can also rise with other defects like abdominal wall defects), a positive amniotic AChE assay is used to confirm a screening finding of elevated AFP before further work-up.

incorrectas.B: Alkaline phosphatase is a nonspecific enzyme found in liver, bone, and placenta; while placental ALP fractions are occasionally measured in obstetric contexts, it has no established role as a confirmatory marker for neural tube defects.
incorrectas.C: Creatine kinase is a marker of muscle injury (e.g., myocardial infarction, rhabdomyolysis, muscular dystrophies), not a substance released specifically from an open neural tube defect.
incorrectas.D: Lactate dehydrogenase is a nonspecific marker of cell turnover or hemolysis used in other contexts (e.g., tumor lysis syndrome, hemolytic anemia), not a specific confirmatory test tied to neural tube closure defects.

preguntas.q: Which neural tube defect is characterized by an open calvarium with absence of the skull and an absent forebrain?

e.correcta: Anencephaly results from failure of the rostral (cranial) neuropore to close during early gestation, leaving the forebrain undeveloped and the skull vault absent so that neural tissue is directly exposed to amniotic fluid (an open calvarium). It is uniformly fatal, usually resulting in stillbirth or death shortly after birth, and is a key example of a neural tube defect detectable prenatally via elevated AFP and AChE.

incorrectas.B: Encephalocele is a herniation of brain tissue and meninges through a focal defect in the skull (most often occipital), producing a covered sac rather than the complete, diffuse absence of the calvarium seen in anencephaly.
incorrectas.C: Spina bifida occulta is a caudal defect limited to failure of the posterior vertebral arch to close, with an intact dura and no exposed neural tissue, entirely different anatomically and in severity from anencephaly.
incorrectas.D: Meningocele is herniation of the meninges alone (without neural tissue) through a vertebral defect, a caudal neural tube abnormality — a completely different anatomic location and severity from the absent forebrain and calvarium of anencephaly.

preguntas.q: Failure of closure at the cranial (rostral) end of the neural tube results in which condition?

e.correcta: The neural tube closes in a zipper-like fashion outward from a central point, with the rostral neuropore normally sealing around day 24-26 of gestation; failure of this cranial closure produces anencephaly, in which the forebrain fails to develop and the overlying skull is absent. This is the cranial counterpart to spina bifida, which results from failure of the caudal neuropore instead.

incorrectas.B: Spina bifida results from failure of closure at the caudal (lower) end of the neural tube, affecting the vertebral arches over the spinal cord rather than the skull and forebrain.
incorrectas.C: Meningomyelocele is a severe subtype of spina bifida involving herniation of meninges and neural tissue through a caudal vertebral defect, again a caudal rather than cranial neural tube problem.
incorrectas.D: Holoprosencephaly arises from failure of the prosencephalon (forebrain) to divide into two hemispheres, a defect in forebrain cleavage rather than a failure of neural tube closure itself.

preguntas.q: Anencephaly is characteristically associated with which change in maternal serum and amniotic fluid alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)?

e.correcta: Because the neural tube fails to close in anencephaly, fetal AFP, normally confined largely within the closed neural tube and fetal circulation, leaks directly into the amniotic fluid and crosses into the maternal circulation, producing markedly elevated maternal serum and amniotic AFP. This elevation is the basis of second-trimester maternal serum screening for open neural tube defects and typically prompts a follow-up amniotic AChE assay and detailed ultrasound.

incorrectas.B: Reduced AFP is instead associated with chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), reflecting a completely different screening pattern than what is seen with open neural tube defects.
incorrectas.C: An unchanged AFP would be inconsistent with anencephaly, since the entire clinical utility of AFP screening rests on its characteristic elevation when neural tissue is exposed to amniotic fluid.
incorrectas.D: AFP is not undetectable in anencephaly; on the contrary, it is markedly increased, which is precisely what makes it a useful screening marker rather than an unhelpful one.

preguntas.q: Anencephaly is commonly associated with which amniotic fluid volume abnormality?

e.correcta: In anencephaly, the absent forebrain means the fetus lacks the neural centers that coordinate swallowing, so the fetus cannot swallow and reabsorb amniotic fluid normally; this impaired swallowing leads to accumulation of excess amniotic fluid, i.e., polyhydramnios. This is a useful clinical clue on prenatal ultrasound in a pregnancy already flagged by elevated maternal serum AFP.

incorrectas.B: Oligohydramnios (too little amniotic fluid) classically results from decreased fetal urine output, as in bilateral renal agenesis (Potter sequence) or severe urinary tract obstruction — the opposite mechanism from the failed swallowing that causes fluid excess in anencephaly.
incorrectas.C: Anhydramnios (near-complete absence of fluid) is an extreme form typically due to renal failure/agenesis or prolonged rupture of membranes, not a feature of anencephaly, where fluid actually accumulates.
incorrectas.D: Amniotic fluid volume is not normal in anencephaly; loss of the fetal swallowing reflex due to absent forebrain structures characteristically causes a volume abnormality (polyhydramnios), not an unaffected volume.

preguntas.q: Which congenital brain malformation results from failure of the developing cerebral hemispheres to separate into distinct left and right structures?

e.correcta: Holoprosencephaly occurs when the prosencephalon (forebrain) fails to cleave into two separate cerebral hemispheres during early gestation, most often due to disrupted sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling; severity ranges from mild (hypotelorism) to severe (cyclopia with a single fused ventricle), and it is associated with midline facial defects because the same signaling pathway patterns the face. It is also strongly associated with trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome).

incorrectas.B: Anencephaly is failure of closure of the rostral neural tube leading to absence of the forebrain and skull vault altogether, a different embryologic error (neural tube closure) than failure of hemispheric cleavage.
incorrectas.C: Lissencephaly is a disorder of neuronal migration resulting in a smooth brain surface lacking normal gyri and sulci, unrelated to the midline cleavage defect that defines holoprosencephaly.
incorrectas.D: Agenesis of the corpus callosum is a failure of the interhemispheric commissural fibers to form, but in this condition the hemispheres are still properly separated — it does not represent a failure of hemispheric cleavage as seen in holoprosencephaly.

preguntas.q: The left and right cerebral hemispheres normally separate during which weeks of embryonic development?

e.correcta: Cleavage of the prosencephalon into distinct cerebral hemispheres occurs early, during weeks 3 to 4 of gestation, driven largely by sonic hedgehog signaling that establishes midline patterning of the developing forebrain and face; disruption during this narrow window produces holoprosencephaly. This early timing, close to that of neural tube closure, is why insults very early in pregnancy (maternal diabetes, alcohol, cholesterol synthesis disorders) can cause this defect before many women even know they are pregnant.

incorrectas.B: Weeks 5-6 was an older, since-revised teaching point for this event; current First Aid (as of FA 2021) places hemispheric separation earlier, at weeks 3-4, making this an outdated rather than currently tested timing.
incorrectas.C: Weeks 7-8 corresponds to later stages of organogenesis (e.g., ongoing palatal fusion, cardiac septation), well after the forebrain has already begun cleaving into hemispheres, not the window in which that cleavage itself occurs.
incorrectas.D: Weeks 9-10 marks the transition to the fetal period, when most organ systems are essentially formed and the emphasis shifts to growth and maturation rather than the primary induction event of hemispheric separation.

preguntas.q: Mutations in which signaling pathway are classically implicated in holoprosencephaly?

e.correcta: Sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling from the prechordal plate establishes the midline of the developing forebrain and face; loss-of-function mutations in SHH or its downstream effectors impair this midline patterning, causing the hemispheres and midline facial structures to fail to separate properly, producing the spectrum of holoprosencephaly. This is a classic example of a developmental field defect, in which one disrupted signaling event in early gestation causes multiple, anatomically related malformations (brain and face) because both structures depend on the same midline induction signal.

incorrectas.B: Wnt/beta-catenin signaling is critical for many patterning processes (e.g., limb development, the intestinal crypt-villus axis) and its dysregulation is implicated in cancers like colorectal cancer, but it is not the pathway classically linked to holoprosencephaly.
incorrectas.C: Notch signaling mediates lateral inhibition and cell-fate decisions in tissues such as the developing pancreas and hematopoietic system, and mutations in Notch pathway genes are linked to conditions like Alagille syndrome, not holoprosencephaly.
incorrectas.D: BMP4 signaling contributes to dorsoventral patterning and skeletal/limb development, and it interacts with SHH in broader patterning networks, but it is not the specific pathway whose mutation is classically taught as the cause of holoprosencephaly.

preguntas.q: The moderate form of holoprosencephaly is classically associated with which facial finding?

e.correcta: Holoprosencephaly exists on a severity spectrum that parallels disrupted midline SHH signaling in both the brain and face; the moderate form manifests with cleft lip and/or cleft palate, reflecting incomplete fusion of the midline facial processes, while still allowing some separation of brain structures compared to the most severe form. This brain-face correlation is a key teaching point: the degree of facial midline defect roughly predicts the severity of the underlying brain malformation.

incorrectas.B: Cyclopia with a proboscis (a primitive nasal structure) represents the most severe end of the holoprosencephaly spectrum, with a single fused eye field and absent nasal septation — a far more extreme phenotype than the cleft lip/palate of the moderate form.
incorrectas.C: Isolated hypotelorism (abnormally close-set eyes) without cleft lip/palate is typically described as the mildest form of holoprosencephaly, reflecting subtler midline facial underdevelopment rather than the moderate phenotype.
incorrectas.D: Agenesis of the corpus callosum is a distinct malformation involving absence of the interhemispheric commissure and is not the facial finding used to define the moderate severity tier of holoprosencephaly.

preguntas.q: The most severe form of holoprosencephaly presents with which facial/ocular finding?

e.correcta: In the severe form of holoprosencephaly, the single eye field that normally splits into two separate orbits fails to divide, producing cyclopia (a single midline eye or partially fused orbits) along with a proboscis, a tubular vestigial nasal structure situated above the eye due to failure of normal nasal septal development. This extreme phenotype reflects a profound loss of SHH-mediated midline signaling and is typically incompatible with life.

incorrectas.B: Cleft lip/palate is the facial finding of the moderate form of holoprosencephaly, a less severe midline fusion defect than the complete failure of eye-field separation seen in the severe, cyclopic form.
incorrectas.C: Isolated hypotelorism without other severe facial defects corresponds to the mildest form of holoprosencephaly, reflecting only subtle underdevelopment of midline facial structures rather than the profound single-eye-field defect of the severe form.
incorrectas.D: Anophthalmia (absent eyes) without midline fusion is a distinct ophthalmologic finding from cyclopia, which specifically involves a single, fused (not absent) eye structure resulting from failed separation of the eye field.

preguntas.q: Spina bifida results from failure of closure of which vertebral structure?

e.correcta: Spina bifida arises from incomplete fusion of the posterior vertebral arch, the laminae that normally meet in the midline dorsal to the spinal cord, most commonly at the lumbosacral level; this leaves a gap through which meninges and/or neural tissue can potentially herniate, depending on severity. It is the caudal counterpart to the cranial defect seen in anencephaly, both arising from disrupted neural tube and vertebral closure.

incorrectas.B: The vertebral body forms the anterior weight-bearing portion of the vertebra and is not the structure whose failure to close produces spina bifida — abnormalities of the body instead relate to conditions like hemivertebrae or vertebral compression.
incorrectas.C: The intervertebral disc is a separate cartilaginous structure between vertebral bodies involved in conditions like disc herniation, not part of the posterior arch closure process relevant to spina bifida.
incorrectas.D: The anterior longitudinal ligament runs along the anterior vertebral column stabilizing it and has no role in the posterior neural arch closure that is disrupted in spina bifida.

preguntas.q: Disruption of the caudal end of the neural tube results in which condition?

e.correcta: The neural tube closes progressively, with the caudal neuropore normally sealing by around day 28 of gestation; failure of this caudal closure produces spina bifida, a spectrum of defects in the lower vertebral column and spinal cord ranging from asymptomatic spina bifida occulta to severe myelomeningocele. This mirrors the cranial defect (anencephaly) that results from failure of rostral neuropore closure.

incorrectas.B: Anencephaly results from failure of closure at the cranial (rostral), not caudal, end of the neural tube, producing absence of the forebrain and skull rather than a lower spine defect.
incorrectas.C: Holoprosencephaly is a defect in forebrain cleavage into hemispheres, unrelated to neural tube closure at either end, and does not involve the vertebral column.
incorrectas.D: Encephalocele is herniation of brain tissue through a cranial (usually occipital) bone defect, a cranial malformation rather than the caudal defect described by spina bifida.

preguntas.q: Which form of spina bifida involves failure of the bony spinal canal to close, without herniation of the meninges or neural tissue?

e.correcta: Spina bifida occulta is the mildest form of the spina bifida spectrum: only the bony vertebral arch fails to fuse, while the underlying dura and neural elements remain intact and contained, so there is no herniation of meninges or spinal cord through the defect. It is often an incidental finding, sometimes marked externally by a tuft of hair, dimple, or lipoma over the affected vertebral level.

incorrectas.B: Meningocele involves herniation of the meninges (but not neural tissue) through the vertebral defect, forming a fluid-filled sac — a more severe defect than the fully contained bony defect of spina bifida occulta.
incorrectas.C: Meningomyelocele (myelomeningocele) involves herniation of both meninges and neural tissue through the defect, typically causing significant neurologic deficits, unlike the asymptomatic occulta form.
incorrectas.D: Rachischisis refers to a complete failure of neural tube and posterior vertebral arch fusion along an extended segment, exposing the spinal cord widely to the surface — a much more severe and extensive defect than the contained bony defect of occulta.

preguntas.q: Spina bifida occulta is most commonly found at which region of the vertebral column?

o.D: It occurs with equal frequency at all levels

e.correcta: Spina bifida occulta most commonly occurs at the lower lumbosacral vertebral levels (classically around L5-S1), reflecting the region where caudal neural tube and posterior arch closure occurs last and is therefore most vulnerable to incomplete fusion. This lower-level predilection is consistent with the general pattern that spina bifida defects, as caudal neuropore closure failures, cluster in the lumbosacral spine.

incorrectas.B: Cervical-level involvement is not the characteristic location for spina bifida occulta; congenital cervical spine anomalies are more often associated with different conditions, such as Klippel-Feil syndrome.
incorrectas.C: While spina bifida defects can rarely occur elsewhere, the thoracic spine is not the classic or most common site; the pattern taught and tested is a lumbosacral predominance.
incorrectas.D: Occurrence is not uniform across levels — the lumbosacral region is disproportionately affected because it corresponds to the last-closing portion of the neural tube during embryogenesis.

preguntas.q: In spina bifida occulta, what is the status of the dura mater overlying the vertebral defect?

o.A: It is intact, containing the underlying neural elements
o.C: It herniates along with the meninges

e.correcta: A defining feature of spina bifida occulta is that, despite the bony defect in the posterior vertebral arch, the dura mater remains intact and continuous, keeping the spinal cord and nerve roots properly contained within the spinal canal. This is precisely why spina bifida occulta is usually asymptomatic and often discovered incidentally, in contrast to meningocele or meningomyelocele, where the dura (with or without neural tissue) protrudes through the defect.

incorrectas.B: The dura is not absent in spina bifida occulta; its intact presence is exactly what prevents herniation of the underlying contents and explains the benign course of this form.
incorrectas.C: Herniation of the dura and meninges through the vertebral defect is the defining feature of meningocele, not spina bifida occulta — in occulta, the dura specifically does not herniate.
incorrectas.D: Dural calcification or thickening is not a described feature of spina bifida occulta; the relevant anatomic point tested is that the dura remains intact and normally positioned, not that it undergoes some structural change.

preguntas.q: A tuft of hair or a skin dimple overlying a lumbosacral bony defect on physical exam is characteristic of which condition?

e.correcta: Spina bifida occulta is frequently a subtle, asymptomatic finding, and its presence over the affected vertebral level is often signaled externally by a cutaneous marker such as a tuft of hair, a dimple, a hemangioma, or a lipoma, reflecting the underlying incomplete fusion of the posterior vertebral arch with intact meninges beneath. Recognizing this skin sign is clinically important because it may prompt imaging to rule out an associated tethered cord even though the bony defect itself is otherwise benign.

incorrectas.B: Meningocele presents as a visible, often fluctuant midline sac due to herniated meninges protruding through the vertebral defect, a grossly apparent mass rather than the subtle cutaneous marker seen overlying an intact-dura occulta defect.
incorrectas.C: Meningomyelocele similarly presents as an obvious, often large sac containing both meninges and neural tissue, generally accompanied by significant neurologic deficits, not a subtle skin marker with no herniation.
