incorrectas.D: Anencephaly is a cranial defect involving absence of the skull and forebrain, an entirely different anatomic location and severity from the lumbosacral skin findings associated with spina bifida occulta.

preguntas.q: Compared to other neural tube defects, what is the characteristic maternal/amniotic AFP level in spina bifida occulta?

e.correcta: Because in spina bifida occulta the dura remains intact and no neural tissue is exposed to the amniotic fluid, fetal proteins like AFP are not released in excess, so maternal serum and amniotic AFP levels remain normal — this is the classic exception to the rule that open neural tube defects raise AFP. This distinction is clinically important because a normal AFP screen does not rule out spina bifida occulta, which is usually detected incidentally rather than through prenatal biochemical screening.

incorrectas.B: Elevated AFP is instead characteristic of open neural tube defects such as anencephaly or meningomyelocele, where exposed neural tissue allows leakage of fetal proteins into the amniotic fluid — a pattern that does not occur in the closed, dura-intact defect of spina bifida occulta.
incorrectas.C: There is no described pathological decrease in AFP associated with spina bifida occulta; the key teaching point is that AFP remains within the normal range, not that it drops below normal.
incorrectas.D: AFP is not undetectable in spina bifida occulta; it is simply unaffected (normal), since there is no exposed neural tissue causing either an increase or an artificial suppression of AFP.

preguntas.q: Which spina bifida subtype involves herniation of the meninges alone, without neural tissue, through the vertebral defect?

e.correcta: Meningocele occurs when the posterior vertebral arch fails to close and the meninges herniate outward through the defect, forming a CSF-filled sac covered by skin or a thin membrane, but the spinal cord and nerve roots remain in their normal position within the canal, so neurologic deficits are typically absent or mild. This distinguishes it from the more severe meningomyelocele, where neural tissue itself is displaced into the herniated sac.

incorrectas.B: Meningomyelocele involves herniation of both the meninges and the spinal cord/nerve roots into the sac, which usually produces significant neurologic deficits such as lower extremity weakness and bowel/bladder dysfunction, unlike the neurologically intact presentation of meningocele.
incorrectas.C: Spina bifida occulta involves no herniation at all — the dura remains intact and only the bony arch fails to fuse, making it a much milder defect than meningocele, which does involve dural/meningeal protrusion.
incorrectas.D: Encephalocele is a cranial (not spinal) defect in which brain tissue and meninges herniate through a skull defect, an entirely different anatomic location from the vertebral herniation of meningocele.

preguntas.q: Which spina bifida subtype involves herniation of both the meninges and neural tissue through the vertebral defect?

e.correcta: Meningomyelocele (myelomeningocele) is a severe form of spina bifida in which both the meninges and the spinal cord/nerve roots protrude through the posterior vertebral defect, typically producing significant neurologic deficits such as lower-extremity paralysis, sensory loss, and neurogenic bowel/bladder dysfunction. It is strongly associated with folate deficiency, which is a major reason folic acid supplementation is recommended before and during pregnancy.

incorrectas.B: Meningocele involves herniation of the meninges only, sparing the spinal cord and nerve roots, so it generally causes little to no neurologic deficit, in contrast to the significant deficits seen with meningomyelocele.
incorrectas.C: Spina bifida occulta has no herniation at all, with an intact dura covering an isolated bony arch defect, representing the mildest end of the spectrum rather than the severe combined meningeal/neural herniation of meningomyelocele.
incorrectas.D: Rachischisis describes a complete, extensive failure of neural tube and vertebral arch fusion along a segment of the spine with neural tissue widely exposed on the surface, an even more extensive/open defect than the localized sac of meningomyelocele.

preguntas.q: Congenital stenosis of the channel connecting the third and fourth ventricles, impairing CSF drainage, describes which condition?

e.correcta: The cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) is the narrow channel connecting the third and fourth ventricles; congenital stenosis of this aqueduct is the most common cause of congenital hydrocephalus, since it obstructs the normal one-way flow of CSF from the lateral and third ventricles toward the fourth ventricle and subarachnoid space. Because the obstruction lies within the ventricular system itself, this produces a noncommunicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus with dilation of the lateral and third ventricles but a normal-sized fourth ventricle.

incorrectas.B: Dandy-Walker malformation involves agenesis or hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis with cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle filling the posterior fossa, a structural cerebellar/posterior fossa anomaly rather than an isolated narrowing of the aqueduct itself.
incorrectas.C: Arnold-Chiari II malformation involves downward herniation of the cerebellar vermis and brainstem through the foramen magnum, usually associated with a myelomeningocele, a different anatomic problem (hindbrain herniation) from a primary aqueductal stenosis.
incorrectas.D: Foramen of Monro atresia would obstruct flow from the lateral ventricles into the third ventricle, causing lateral ventricular dilation alone, rather than the third-and-fourth-ventricle-connecting channel implicated in cerebral aqueduct stenosis.

preguntas.q: In cerebral aqueduct stenosis, what accumulates within the ventricular system proximal to the site of obstruction?

e.correcta: Because the aqueduct of Sylvius is the sole channel through which CSF passes from the third to the fourth ventricle, its stenosis blocks the normal downstream flow of CSF, causing it to accumulate and progressively dilate the lateral and third ventricles — the classic noncommunicating hydrocephalus. Clinically, this presents in infants as macrocephaly with a bulging fontanelle, or in older patients as signs of increased intracranial pressure such as headache, vomiting, and papilledema.

incorrectas.B: Blood accumulation would suggest intraventricular hemorrhage (e.g., germinal matrix bleeds in premature infants), a distinct process from the obstructive CSF buildup caused by a structural narrowing of the aqueduct.
incorrectas.C: Purulent exudate accumulating in the ventricles would suggest ventriculitis or meningitis with ventricular extension, an infectious process rather than the sterile CSF accumulation caused by a congenital anatomic obstruction.
incorrectas.D: Lipid-laden macrophages (gitter cells) are seen at sites of tissue necrosis or demyelination during phagocytic clean-up, not a feature of aqueductal stenosis, where the fluid that accumulates is simply CSF unable to drain past the narrowed channel.

preguntas.q: An infant is diagnosed with cerebral aqueduct stenosis causing obstructive hydrocephalus. Which physical finding would be expected due to the resulting ventricular dilation?

o.D: A normal head circumference with a sunken anterior fontanelle

e.correcta: In infants, the cranial sutures have not yet fused, so obstructive hydrocephalus from cerebral aqueduct stenosis (blocking CSF flow between the third and fourth ventricles) causes the ventricles to dilate and the skull to expand, producing macrocephaly with a bulging fontanelle. This is the classic presentation used to screen for congenital hydrocephalus and is why serial head circumference measurements are part of routine infant exams.

incorrectas.B: Microcephaly reflects a small brain/skull, as seen with congenital infections (e.g., CMV, Zika) or primary neurodevelopmental disorders — it is the opposite of what happens when CSF outflow is obstructed and pressure builds within the ventricular system.
incorrectas.C: Craniosynostosis is premature fusion of cranial sutures, which restricts rather than promotes skull growth and produces an abnormally shaped head, not the symmetric enlargement seen with hydrocephalus.
incorrectas.D: A sunken fontanelle suggests dehydration or low intracranial pressure, essentially the reverse of the bulging fontanelle and rising head circumference expected when ventricular dilation raises intracranial pressure.

preguntas.q: Hematopoiesis proceeds through stepwise maturation of pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells that are identified by which surface marker?

e.correcta: CD34 is the classic surface marker used to identify and isolate multipotent hematopoietic stem cells, which reside in the bone marrow and give rise to all myeloid and lymphoid blood cell lineages. This is why CD34+ selection is used clinically to harvest stem cells for bone marrow/stem cell transplantation.

incorrectas.B: CD117 (c-Kit, the stem cell factor receptor) is also expressed on hematopoietic progenitors and mast cells, but it is not the defining marker used to identify the earliest pluripotent stem cell population — that role belongs to CD34.
incorrectas.C: CD38 is expressed on more differentiated lymphoid cells (e.g., plasma cells) and is used in immunophenotyping of lymphoid malignancies, not as the primary marker of the multipotent hematopoietic stem cell.
incorrectas.D: CD3 is a T-cell lineage marker found on mature and developing T lymphocytes, marking a differentiated downstream lineage rather than the pluripotent stem cell itself.

preguntas.q: Which myeloid precursor cell matures directly into red blood cells?

e.correcta: Myeloid stem cells commit to the erythroid lineage by becoming erythroblasts, which undergo progressive hemoglobinization and nuclear condensation before enucleating to form reticulocytes and then mature RBCs. This lineage is driven mainly by erythropoietin acting on erythroid progenitors in the bone marrow.

incorrectas.B: Myeloblasts are the common precursor for granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils), not red cells — they differentiate along a distinct pathway driven by different cytokines (e.g., G-CSF, GM-CSF) than the erythroid line.
incorrectas.C: Monoblasts differentiate into monocytes, which circulate and later become tissue macrophages; this is a separate myeloid branch from the erythroid lineage that produces RBCs.
incorrectas.D: Megakaryoblasts mature into megakaryocytes, large polyploid cells that fragment into platelets — a distinct lineage from erythroid maturation despite sharing the same myeloid stem cell origin.

preguntas.q: Which precursor cell gives rise to granulocytes such as neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils?

e.correcta: Myeloblasts are the committed granulocytic precursors that mature into the three granulocyte types — neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils — under the influence of growth factors like G-CSF and GM-CSF. Recognizing myeloblasts is also clinically important because their uncontrolled proliferation, often marked by Auer rods, defines acute myeloid leukemia.

incorrectas.A: Erythroblasts are the red cell lineage precursor, maturing into RBCs through hemoglobin accumulation and enucleation — a completely separate differentiation pathway from granulocyte formation.
incorrectas.C: Monoblasts differentiate into monocytes rather than granulocytes; although both arise from the common myeloid progenitor, they follow distinct maturation programs driven by different transcription factor levels favoring monocytic differentiation.
incorrectas.D: Megakaryoblasts mature into megakaryocytes that fragment into platelets, a lineage devoted to hemostasis rather than the granulocyte-mediated innate immune response.

preguntas.q: Monocytes arise from which myeloid precursor cell?

e.correcta: Monoblasts are the myeloid precursors dedicated to the monocytic lineage; they mature into monocytes that circulate briefly before migrating into tissues to become macrophages or dendritic cells. This lineage is important in chronic inflammation and phagocytic clearance, and its malignant counterpart is seen in acute monocytic leukemia (a subtype of AML).

incorrectas.B: Myeloblasts differentiate into granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils), a parallel but distinct myeloid branch from the monocyte lineage.
incorrectas.C: Erythroblasts mature into RBCs via hemoglobin synthesis and enucleation, an entirely different maturation pathway focused on oxygen transport rather than phagocytic/immune function.
incorrectas.D: Megakaryoblasts give rise to platelet-producing megakaryocytes, a lineage geared toward hemostasis rather than monocyte/macrophage-mediated immunity.

preguntas.q: Platelet-producing megakaryocytes arise from which precursor cell?

e.correcta: Megakaryoblasts are large myeloid precursors that undergo endomitosis (repeated nuclear division without cytoplasmic division) to become polyploid megakaryocytes, which then shed cytoplasmic fragments as platelets. Thrombopoietin is the principal growth factor driving this maturation, analogous to erythropoietin's role in the red cell line.

incorrectas.B: Myeloblasts mature into granulocytes, not platelets — a distinct myeloid branch driven by different cytokine signals (G-CSF/GM-CSF) than the thrombopoietin-driven megakaryocytic line.
incorrectas.C: Monoblasts mature into monocytes and eventually tissue macrophages, serving an immune/phagocytic function unrelated to platelet production.
incorrectas.D: Erythroblasts mature into RBCs through hemoglobinization and enucleation, a lineage focused on oxygen transport rather than clot formation.

preguntas.q: Which lymphoid precursor matures into naive B cells and eventually plasma cells?

e.correcta: Lymphoid stem cells committed to the humoral immune lineage become B lymphoblasts, which mature in the bone marrow into naive B cells; upon antigen encounter and activation (often with T-cell help), these differentiate further into antibody-secreting plasma cells. This pathway underlies humoral immunity and is disrupted in B-cell malignancies like B-cell ALL.

incorrectas.B: T lymphoblasts are the precursor to T cells, which mature primarily in the thymus into CD4+ helper and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells — a cell-mediated immunity pathway distinct from the antibody-producing B-cell line.
incorrectas.C: Myeloblasts belong to the myeloid rather than lymphoid lineage and give rise to granulocytes, unrelated to antibody production.
incorrectas.D: Monoblasts are also myeloid-derived and mature into monocytes/macrophages, a phagocytic lineage rather than the adaptive humoral response carried out by B cells and plasma cells.

preguntas.q: Which lymphoid precursor matures into naive T cells and subsequently CD4+ or CD8+ T cells?

e.correcta: T lymphoblasts arise from lymphoid stem cells and migrate to the thymus, where positive and negative selection shape them into naive CD4+ helper or CD8+ cytotoxic T cells based on their T-cell receptor's affinity for self-MHC. This maturation step is essential for establishing a functional, self-tolerant cell-mediated immune repertoire, and its disruption underlies conditions like T-cell ALL and DiGeorge syndrome (thymic aplasia).

incorrectas.B: B lymphoblasts mature into naive B cells and then plasma cells, mediating humoral (antibody-based) immunity rather than the cell-mediated responses carried out by T cells.
incorrectas.C: Megakaryoblasts are myeloid-derived precursors of platelet-producing megakaryocytes, entirely unrelated to lymphocyte development.
incorrectas.D: Myeloblasts are also myeloid precursors that mature into granulocytes, a separate lineage from the lymphoid pathway that produces T and B cells.

preguntas.q: What is the approximate normal reference range for total white blood cell count in peripheral blood?

e.correcta: A normal total WBC count is roughly 5,000-10,000 cells/µL (5-10 K/µL), reflecting the balance of circulating neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils in a healthy individual. This range serves as the baseline against which leukopenia (below it) and leukocytosis (above it) are defined clinically.

incorrectas.B: A count of 1-4 K/µL falls below the normal range and would already represent leukopenia, not the expected normal reference range.
incorrectas.C: 10-20 K/µL exceeds the upper limit of normal and reflects leukocytosis, commonly seen with infection, inflammation, or a leukemoid reaction rather than baseline health.
incorrectas.D: 15-25 K/µL is even more elevated and would raise concern for a more severe leukocytosis or possible leukemic process, well outside the normal reference interval.

preguntas.q: A total WBC count below 5,000 cells/µL is termed what?

e.correcta: Leukopenia is the general term for a total white blood cell count falling below the normal reference range (< 5 K/µL), regardless of which specific cell line is reduced. It is an umbrella term that can result from decreased marrow production, increased peripheral destruction, or redistribution of any of the WBC subtypes.

incorrectas.B: Leukocytosis describes an elevated total WBC count (> 10 K/µL), the opposite abnormality from the low count described here.
incorrectas.C: Neutropenia specifically refers to a reduced absolute neutrophil count, a more specific finding than a generalized drop in total WBC count, though it often contributes to leukopenia.
incorrectas.D: Lymphopenia specifically refers to a reduced circulating lymphocyte count; like neutropenia, it is one possible contributor to overall leukopenia rather than the general term for a low total WBC count itself.

preguntas.q: A total WBC count above 10,000 cells/µL is termed what?

e.correcta: Leukocytosis is the general term for an elevated total white blood cell count (> 10 K/µL). Mild elevations (roughly < 50 K/µL) are usually reactive, reflecting an appropriate marrow response to infection, inflammation, or stress, whereas counts exceeding ~100 K/µL raise strong concern for a leukemic process rather than a benign reactive leukocytosis.

incorrectas.B: Leukopenia is the opposite finding — a total WBC count below the normal range — and would not apply to an elevated count.
incorrectas.C: Neutrophilia refers specifically to an increased absolute neutrophil count; it is one possible cause of leukocytosis but is not the general term for an elevated total WBC count across all cell lines.
incorrectas.D: Lymphocytosis refers specifically to an increased lymphocyte count (e.g., viral infections, CLL), which is a more specific finding than the general elevation in total WBC count described by leukocytosis.

preguntas.q: A decreased number of circulating neutrophils is termed what?

e.correcta: Neutropenia specifically denotes a low absolute neutrophil count (classically < 1500 cells/mm³), which is clinically important because neutrophils are the primary phagocytic defense against bacterial and fungal infections — severe reductions markedly increase infection risk.

incorrectas.B: Lymphopenia refers to a reduced lymphocyte count, affecting cell-mediated and humoral adaptive immunity rather than the innate phagocytic defense provided by neutrophils.
incorrectas.C: Eosinopenia refers to a reduced eosinophil count, a cell type primarily involved in defense against parasites and allergic/inflammatory modulation, not the frontline bacterial defense neutrophils provide.
incorrectas.D: Leukopenia is the broader term for any reduction in total WBC count and could result from a drop in neutrophils, lymphocytes, or other subtypes — it is not specific to the neutrophil line the way neutropenia is.

preguntas.q: Neutropenia due to bone marrow toxicity is most classically caused by which agent?

e.correcta: Cytotoxic chemotherapy damages rapidly dividing hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells in the bone marrow, decreasing production of all WBC lines but especially neutrophils (which have a short half-life and require constant marrow output), producing chemotherapy-induced neutropenia. This is the basis for monitoring counts and using growth factor support (e.g., G-CSF) after chemotherapy cycles.

incorrectas.B: Antihistamines are not classically associated with significant bone marrow suppression or clinically important neutropenia.
incorrectas.C: Aminoglycosides carry risks of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, not marrow suppression — they are not a classic cause of drug-induced neutropenia.
incorrectas.D: Beta-blockers affect cardiovascular and metabolic parameters (heart rate, blood pressure, glucose) but do not suppress bone marrow hematopoiesis or cause neutropenia.

preguntas.q: In a patient with overwhelming gram-negative sepsis, neutropenia can develop primarily through which mechanism?

o.A: Increased neutrophil migration out of the circulation into infected tissues
o.B: Decreased neutrophil production from chemotherapy-induced marrow toxicity

e.correcta: In severe infection, especially overwhelming gram-negative sepsis, neutrophils are rapidly recruited out of the bloodstream and into infected tissues (margination and extravasation) faster than the marrow can replace them, depleting the circulating pool despite normal or even increased marrow production. This 'consumptive' neutropenia is a poor prognostic sign in sepsis because it suggests the innate immune response is being overwhelmed.

incorrectas.B: Chemotherapy causes neutropenia by directly damaging marrow progenitors and reducing production — a distinct mechanism from the peripheral consumption/migration seen in severe sepsis.
incorrectas.C: Cortisol actually tends to increase circulating neutrophil counts (by demargination and delayed apoptosis), and its major suppressive effect is on lymphocytes and eosinophils, not the mechanism causing sepsis-related neutropenia.
incorrectas.D: Autoimmune neutrophil destruction (as in some drug-induced or autoimmune neutropenias) reflects antibody-mediated clearance, not the increased tissue migration driving neutropenia in severe infection.

preguntas.q: Besides drug toxicity and severe infection, neutropenia is also associated with which of the following conditions?

e.correcta: Aplastic anemia results from failure of the bone marrow to produce adequate numbers of all hematopoietic cell lines (pancytopenia), so it characteristically causes neutropenia along with anemia and thrombocytopenia — alongside SLE and radiation exposure, which are other recognized causes of decreased neutrophil counts.

incorrectas.B: Polycythemia vera is a myeloproliferative disorder marked by excessive RBC (and often WBC/platelet) production, the opposite marrow behavior from the hypoproliferative state seen in aplastic anemia.
incorrectas.C: Iron deficiency anemia impairs hemoglobin synthesis and causes microcytic anemia but does not typically suppress neutrophil production, since it reflects a nutrient deficiency for one lineage rather than global marrow failure.
incorrectas.D: Hemolytic anemia results from increased peripheral destruction of RBCs, not impaired marrow production of neutrophils, so it does not classically cause neutropenia.

preguntas.q: Which growth factors are administered to stimulate granulocyte production and reduce infection risk in neutropenic patients (e.g., after chemotherapy)?

e.correcta: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF, e.g., filgrastim) and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF, e.g., sargramostim) stimulate the bone marrow to accelerate production and release of neutrophils (and other granulocytes for GM-CSF), shortening the duration of severe neutropenia — typically defined as < 500 cells/mm³ — and lowering the risk of life-threatening infection after myelosuppressive chemotherapy.

incorrectas.B: Erythropoietin stimulates the erythroid lineage to boost RBC production (e.g., in chronic kidney disease anemia) and has no significant effect on neutrophil/granulocyte counts.
incorrectas.C: Thrombopoietin (and thrombopoietin receptor agonists like romiplostim) stimulate megakaryocyte and platelet production, addressing thrombocytopenia rather than neutropenia.
incorrectas.D: Interleukin-2 promotes T-cell and NK-cell proliferation and is used therapeutically in certain cancers (e.g., renal cell carcinoma, melanoma) for immune activation, not for stimulating granulocyte production.

preguntas.q: A decreased number of circulating lymphocytes is termed what?

e.correcta: Lymphopenia refers specifically to a reduced circulating lymphocyte count, impairing both cell-mediated (T-cell) and humoral (B-cell) adaptive immune responses. It can arise from immunodeficiency states, elevated cortisol, autoimmune destruction, or radiation exposure — lymphocytes are notably the most radiosensitive WBC line.

incorrectas.B: Neutropenia denotes a reduced neutrophil count, primarily compromising innate phagocytic defense against bacteria/fungi rather than adaptive immunity.
incorrectas.C: Eosinopenia denotes a reduced eosinophil count, most classically induced by corticosteroids via sequestration, and mainly affects antiparasitic/allergic-response capacity rather than adaptive immune function.
incorrectas.D: Leukopenia is the general term for any low total WBC count and does not specify which lineage (neutrophils, lymphocytes, eosinophils, etc.) is reduced.

preguntas.q: Lymphopenia occurring in the setting of HIV infection, DiGeorge syndrome, or SCID is best explained by which underlying mechanism?

e.correcta: HIV (which depletes CD4+ T cells via direct infection), DiGeorge syndrome (thymic aplasia impairing T-cell maturation), and SCID (combined defects in T- and/or B-cell development) all represent forms of immunodeficiency — one acquired, the others congenital — in which lymphocyte development or survival is directly impaired, producing lymphopenia through failure to generate or maintain a normal lymphocyte pool.

incorrectas.B: Cortisol-induced apoptosis (as with exogenous steroids or Cushing syndrome) is a distinct, hormonally mediated cause of lymphopenia that does not involve an intrinsic defect in lymphocyte development, unlike HIV, DiGeorge, or SCID.
incorrectas.C: Autoimmune destruction of lymphocytes (as can occur in SLE) reflects antibody- or immune-mediated peripheral clearance of otherwise normally developed lymphocytes, not the developmental/infectious failure seen in immunodeficiency syndromes.
incorrectas.D: Whole-body radiation causes lymphopenia by directly killing the highly radiosensitive lymphocyte population, a physical/cytotoxic mechanism unrelated to the genetic or infectious immunodeficiencies listed.

preguntas.q: A state of chronically elevated cortisol, such as Cushing syndrome or exogenous steroid use, causes lymphopenia primarily through which mechanism?

o.B: Direct viral destruction of CD4+ cells
o.C: Bone marrow failure to produce lymphoid precursors

e.correcta: Excess cortisol (whether from Cushing syndrome or exogenous corticosteroids) induces apoptosis in circulating lymphocytes and also promotes their redistribution out of the blood into lymphoid tissue, producing lymphopenia. This same anti-lymphocytic and anti-inflammatory action is why glucocorticoids are used therapeutically to suppress unwanted immune/inflammatory activity.

incorrectas.B: Direct viral destruction of CD4+ T cells is the mechanism of HIV-related lymphopenia, not a hormonally mediated one like cortisol excess.
incorrectas.C: Bone marrow failure to produce lymphoid precursors describes a marrow-level problem, as seen in aplastic anemia, rather than cortisol's action of promoting apoptosis/redistribution of already-formed circulating lymphocytes.
incorrectas.D: Antibody-mediated destruction is the mechanism behind autoimmune lymphopenia (e.g., in SLE), distinct from the direct pro-apoptotic and redistributive effect of glucocorticoids.

preguntas.q: What effect do corticosteroids have on circulating lymphocyte counts?

o.C: They have no significant effect on lymphocyte counts
o.D: They decrease lymphocyte counts only via bone marrow suppression

e.correcta: Corticosteroids lower circulating lymphocyte counts, producing lymphopenia, by triggering lymphocyte apoptosis and causing redistribution of lymphocytes out of the bloodstream into lymphoid tissue — a peripheral effect rather than a marrow production defect. This is one reason steroid therapy is immunosuppressive and why steroid-treated patients can show a relative lymphopenia on a CBC despite normal marrow function.

incorrectas.B: Corticosteroids do the opposite for neutrophils (causing neutrophilia by demargination), but for lymphocytes the net effect is a decrease, not an increase, so lymphocytosis is incorrect.
incorrectas.C: Corticosteroids have a well-documented, clinically significant suppressive effect on lymphocyte counts, so 'no significant effect' mischaracterizes a hallmark pharmacologic action of steroids.
incorrectas.D: The lymphopenic effect of corticosteroids is mediated mainly by peripheral apoptosis and redistribution rather than by suppressing bone marrow production of lymphoid precursors, so limiting the mechanism to marrow suppression is inaccurate.

preguntas.q: Lymphopenia occurring in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is most directly attributable to which mechanism?

e.correcta: In SLE, autoantibodies (including antilymphocyte antibodies) and immune complex-mediated processes can directly target and destroy circulating lymphocytes, producing lymphopenia that is itself one of the hematologic diagnostic criteria for SLE. This autoimmune consumption is distinct from lymphopenia caused by decreased production or hormonal suppression.

incorrectas.B: Cortisol-induced apoptosis is the mechanism behind steroid- or Cushing-related lymphopenia, a hormonal effect rather than the autoantibody-mediated destruction characteristic of SLE.
incorrectas.C: Whole-body radiation causes lymphopenia via direct cytotoxic injury to radiosensitive lymphocytes, an environmental/physical cause unrelated to the autoimmune process in SLE.
incorrectas.D: Primary immunodeficiency (e.g., SCID) reflects a genetic failure of lymphocyte development, not the acquired autoimmune destruction of otherwise normally developed lymphocytes seen in SLE.

preguntas.q: Following whole-body radiation exposure, which of the following typically occurs and is often the earliest hematologic change detected?

e.correcta: Lymphocytes are exquisitely radiosensitive because they undergo apoptosis (rather than simply failing to divide) in response to DNA damage, so lymphopenia is typically the earliest and most sensitive hematologic marker of radiation exposure, appearing within hours to days — even before neutrophil or platelet counts fall, which occurs later as marrow production wanes.

incorrectas.B: Neutropenia does eventually occur after significant radiation exposure due to marrow suppression, but neutrophils have a longer lifespan and their decline lags behind the rapid lymphocyte apoptosis, making lymphopenia the earlier change.
incorrectas.C: Thrombocytosis (an increased platelet count) is not an expected effect of radiation; if anything, platelet counts fall (thrombocytopenia) as marrow megakaryocyte production is suppressed, though this occurs later than the lymphocyte drop.
incorrectas.D: Polycythemia (an increased RBC mass) is not a radiation effect; radiation more typically leads to pancytopenia over time as it suppresses all marrow lineages, with RBCs affected later due to their longer lifespan.

preguntas.q: Which type of white blood cell is the most sensitive to radiation-induced cell death?

e.correcta: Lymphocytes are uniquely radiosensitive because ionizing radiation triggers apoptosis in these cells directly (an interphase death), rather than requiring them to attempt mitosis first, unlike most other rapidly dividing cells. This is why a falling lymphocyte count is used clinically as an early biodosimetry marker after suspected radiation exposure.

incorrectas.B: Neutrophils are affected by radiation mainly through impaired marrow production over time, but they are considerably less prone to direct interphase apoptosis than lymphocytes, so their decline is slower and less pronounced initially.
incorrectas.C: Eosinophils, like neutrophils, primarily depend on marrow production for their numbers and are not characterized by the same rapid, direct radiation-induced apoptosis seen in lymphocytes.
incorrectas.D: Monocytes also decline mainly via reduced marrow output following radiation rather than through the immediate apoptotic sensitivity that defines the lymphocyte response.

preguntas.q: A decreased number of circulating eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count < 30 cells/mm³) is termed what?

e.correcta: Eosinopenia specifically describes a reduced absolute eosinophil count, most classically induced by corticosteroids (via sequestration of eosinophils in lymph nodes) or acute stress response, distinguishing it from reductions in other WBC lines that have different characteristic causes.

incorrectas.B: Neutropenia refers to a reduced neutrophil count, primarily impairing bacterial/fungal defense, not the antiparasitic and allergic-modulation role served by eosinophils.
incorrectas.C: Lymphopenia refers to a reduced lymphocyte count, affecting adaptive immunity, and is most classically linked to radiation, immunodeficiency, or autoimmune disease rather than the corticosteroid-driven sequestration typical of eosinopenia.
incorrectas.D: Leukopenia is the nonspecific umbrella term for any reduced total WBC count and does not specifically denote the eosinophil line the way eosinopenia does.

preguntas.q: What effect do corticosteroids have on circulating eosinophil counts, and by what mechanism?

o.A: They decrease eosinophil counts (eosinopenia) by sequestering eosinophils in lymph nodes
o.B: They increase eosinophil counts (eosinophilia) by stimulating marrow release
o.C: They have no significant effect on eosinophil counts
o.D: They decrease eosinophil counts by inducing eosinophil apoptosis in the bloodstream

e.correcta: Corticosteroids produce eosinopenia by promoting the sequestration (trapping) of eosinophils within lymph nodes rather than primarily by killing them outright, removing them from the circulating pool measured on a CBC. This same effect is seen physiologically in Cushing syndrome and is a reason eosinopenia can be a clue to elevated cortisol states.

incorrectas.B: Corticosteroids do the opposite for neutrophils (increasing counts via demargination), but for eosinophils the well-documented effect is a decrease, not an increase, so eosinophilia is incorrect here.
incorrectas.C: The eosinopenic effect of corticosteroids is a reproducible, clinically used phenomenon (historically part of the 'Thorn test' for adrenal function), so 'no significant effect' misrepresents a real and specific pharmacologic action.
incorrectas.D: While cortisol does promote apoptosis in lymphocytes, the eosinopenic effect is attributed primarily to redistribution/sequestration into lymph nodes rather than direct apoptotic killing in the bloodstream.

preguntas.q: Which term describes an increase in the absolute number of circulating neutrophils in peripheral blood?

e.correcta: Neutrophilia is defined as an absolute increase in circulating neutrophils above the normal reference range, most commonly triggered by acute bacterial infection, tissue necrosis/inflammation, or corticosteroid/stress-induced demargination of the marginated pool. It is the most common form of leukocytosis encountered clinically and is often accompanied by a left shift when the marrow releases immature forms to keep up with demand.

incorrectas.B: Lymphocytosis refers to an increase in circulating lymphocytes, the expected response to most viral infections and some chronic bacterial infections (e.g., pertussis, TB), not the neutrophil-driven response being described here.
incorrectas.C: Monocytosis is an increase in circulating monocytes, seen in chronic inflammatory states, certain viral infections, and myeloid neoplasms, reflecting a different lineage than the one described.
incorrectas.D: Basophilia is a rare increase in circulating basophils, most often associated with chronic myeloid leukemia or other myeloproliferative neoplasms, not a general term for elevated neutrophils.

preguntas.q: What term describes the appearance of increased neutrophil precursors, such as band cells and metamyelocytes, in the peripheral blood?

e.correcta: A left shift indicates the bone marrow is releasing immature neutrophil precursors (bands, metamyelocytes) into circulation faster than usual, typically because ongoing infection or inflammation is outpacing the supply of mature segmented neutrophils. It is a marker of an active, demand-driven granulopoietic response and is commonly seen alongside neutrophilia in acute bacterial infection.

incorrectas.A: Toxic granulation refers to prominent, dark cytoplasmic granules within neutrophils seen in severe infection or inflammation — a morphologic change within the cell itself, not the appearance of immature precursor forms in blood.
incorrectas.C: A leukoerythroblastic reaction is a left shift accompanied by immature red cell precursors (nucleated RBCs) on smear, reflecting marrow infiltration or severe stress erythropoiesis — a distinct, more specific finding than a simple left shift.
incorrectas.D: There is no clinically named 'right shift' process describing increased precursor release; hypersegmented neutrophils (sometimes loosely called a right shift) instead reflect impaired DNA synthesis, as in megaloblastic anemia, not increased precursor release.

preguntas.q: A left shift accompanied by immature red blood cell precursors in the peripheral smear is termed a(n)?

e.correcta: A leukoerythroblastic reaction describes the combination of a neutrophilic left shift with circulating nucleated red cell precursors, signaling that something is forcibly pushing immature cells of both lineages out of the marrow. This occurs either as a physiologic response to severe anemia/hypoxia or, more concerningly, when marrow architecture is disrupted by fibrosis (myelofibrosis) or space-occupying tumor infiltration that displaces normal hematopoiesis.

incorrectas.A: Myelophthisic anemia refers to the anemia resulting from marrow infiltration or replacement (e.g., fibrosis, tumor, granulomas), which is often a cause of a leukoerythroblastic picture but is itself a diagnosis of anemia, not the name for the peripheral blood pattern described.
incorrectas.B: A leukemoid reaction is an exaggerated, benign neutrophilic leukocytosis with left shift that mimics leukemia in degree but lacks nucleated RBCs and resolves once the underlying trigger (severe infection, etc.) is treated, distinguishing it from a marrow-infiltrative leukoerythroblastic process.
incorrectas.D: Pelger-Huet anomaly is an inherited or acquired defect of neutrophil nuclear segmentation producing bilobed ('pince-nez') nuclei, a distinct morphologic abnormality unrelated to co-occurring immature myeloid and erythroid precursors in blood.

preguntas.q: A patient started on high-dose glucocorticoids develops an elevated neutrophil count with no evidence of infection. What is the primary mechanism responsible for this neutrophilia?

o.A: Increased granulopoiesis driven by G-CSF release
o.B: Impaired neutrophil apoptosis prolonging circulating lifespan
o.C: Demargination of the marginated neutrophil pool from vessel walls
o.D: Left shift with release of immature bands from the marrow

e.correcta: Glucocorticoids impair neutrophil adhesion molecule expression, causing neutrophils that are normally loosely adherent to vascular endothelium (the 'marginated pool') to detach and re-enter the actively circulating pool. This produces a rapid rise in the measured neutrophil count without any true increase in total body neutrophil number or new marrow production, which is why it can occur within hours of a steroid dose.

incorrectas.A: G-CSF-driven granulopoiesis does increase circulating neutrophils, but it does so over days by stimulating new marrow production, whereas steroid-induced neutrophilia is an immediate redistribution phenomenon rather than a demand-driven granulopoietic response.
incorrectas.B: Corticosteroids have some effect on neutrophil turnover, but the dominant, classically tested mechanism for steroid-induced neutrophilia is demargination, not delayed apoptosis, and this option does not explain the rapid onset seen clinically.
incorrectas.D: A left shift implies the marrow is releasing immature band forms because of increased demand, the pattern seen in bacterial infection, not the corticosteroid effect, which recruits already-mature marginated neutrophils rather than immature precursors.

preguntas.q: Which term describes an increase in the absolute number of circulating lymphocytes?

e.correcta: Lymphocytosis denotes an absolute rise in circulating lymphocytes above the normal range and is the expected leukocyte response to viral infections, certain intracellular bacteria, and lymphoproliferative disorders such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Recognizing which cell line is elevated helps narrow the differential, since lymphocytosis points toward a viral/lymphocyte-driven process rather than the acute bacterial/neutrophil-driven pattern of neutrophilia.

incorrectas.A: Monocytosis is an increase in circulating monocytes, associated with chronic infections (e.g., TB, endocarditis), autoimmune disease, and certain myeloid neoplasms — a different cell lineage than lymphocytes.
incorrectas.C: Neutrophilia is an increase in circulating neutrophils, the classic response to acute bacterial infection or stress/steroid states, not the lymphocyte-predominant pattern being described.
incorrectas.D: Eosinophilia is an increase in circulating eosinophils, typically driven by allergic disease, parasitic infection, or certain drug reactions, reflecting a distinct granulocyte lineage rather than lymphocytes.

preguntas.q: Lymphocytosis is most classically associated with which category of infectious agent?

e.correcta: Lymphocytosis occurs classically in viral infections because control of virally infected cells depends on cytotoxic T-lymphocyte responses; antigen-driven clonal expansion of T cells (and sometimes B cells) increases the absolute lymphocyte count. This is the mechanism behind the striking lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes seen in infectious mononucleosis.

incorrectas.A: Pyogenic bacterial infections classically drive neutrophilia with a left shift, since neutrophils are the first responders recruited to clear extracellular bacteria, not the lymphocyte-driven response of a viral infection.
incorrectas.B: Fungal infections do not have a single classic leukocyte signature the way viral or bacterial infections do; when a pattern is highlighted, it is more often neutrophilia or eosinophilia depending on the organism, not lymphocytosis.
incorrectas.D: Helminth (parasitic worm) infections classically provoke eosinophilia via a Th2-driven immune response, not the lymphocyte expansion characteristic of antiviral cytotoxic T-cell responses.

preguntas.q: Which organism produces a lymphocytosis-promoting factor that causes lymphocytosis by blocking circulating lymphocytes from entering lymph nodes?

e.correcta: Bordetella pertussis produces pertussis toxin, which acts as a lymphocytosis-promoting factor by inhibiting lymphocyte migration out of the bloodstream into lymph nodes, trapping them in circulation and producing a striking absolute lymphocytosis. This is a notable exception to the rule that bacterial infections cause neutrophilia, and marked lymphocytosis in a child with paroxysmal cough should raise suspicion for pertussis.

incorrectas.A: Corynebacterium diphtheriae produces diphtheria toxin, which inhibits protein synthesis via ADP-ribosylation of EF-2, causing pseudomembranous pharyngitis and myocarditis/neuropathy, not a lymphocyte-trapping lymphocytosis-promoting factor.
incorrectas.C: Mycobacterium tuberculosis can be associated with lymphocyte-predominant granulomatous inflammation, but it does not produce a specific toxin that blocks lymphocyte egress from blood into nodes the way pertussis toxin does.
incorrectas.D: Streptococcus pyogenes causes disease through mechanisms like M protein-mediated resistance to phagocytosis and exotoxins (e.g., streptolysin O), typically provoking neutrophilia rather than the pertussis-toxin-mediated lymphocytosis described here.

preguntas.q: A teenager presents with fever, pharyngitis, and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. Infectious mononucleosis in this setting is most commonly caused by which virus?

e.correcta: Epstein-Barr virus is by far the most common cause of infectious mononucleosis, infecting B lymphocytes via the CD21 receptor and triggering a vigorous CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell response against infected B cells that produces the classic triad of fever, pharyngitis, and lymphadenopathy along with atypical lymphocytes on smear. Most of the clinical findings of mono (lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes) actually reflect this host T-cell reaction rather than direct viral cytopathic effect.

incorrectas.A: Cytomegalovirus can cause a mononucleosis-like illness, but it is a much less common cause than EBV and typically produces a heterophile-antibody-negative presentation, making it the 'less common' cause rather than the classic one.
incorrectas.C: Human herpesvirus 6 causes roseola infantum in young children and can reactivate in immunocompromised adults, but it is not a typical cause of the classic adolescent mononucleosis syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Toxoplasma gondii can cause a mononucleosis-like syndrome with lymphadenopathy, but it is a protozoan parasite, not a virus, and is a far less common cause than EBV in this classic presentation.

preguntas.q: Which virus is recognized as a less common cause of an infectious mononucleosis-like syndrome, typically producing a heterophile-antibody-negative presentation?

e.correcta: Cytomegalovirus can cause a mononucleosis-like illness with fever, malaise, and atypical lymphocytosis that clinically resembles EBV mono, but it is encountered far less often and classically yields a negative monospot (heterophile antibody) test, requiring CMV-specific serology or PCR for confirmation. Distinguishing CMV from EBV mono matters because CMV mono tends to have less prominent pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy despite similar systemic symptoms.

incorrectas.A: Epstein-Barr virus is the classic and most common cause of infectious mononucleosis, the opposite of the 'less common' cause being asked about here.
incorrectas.B: Human herpesvirus 8 is associated with Kaposi sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma, particularly in immunocompromised patients, not with a mononucleosis-like febrile illness.
incorrectas.D: Adenovirus commonly causes pharyngitis and conjunctivitis (pharyngoconjunctival fever) but is not classically recognized as a cause of the mononucleosis syndrome the way CMV is.

preguntas.q: Epstein-Barr virus is classically transmitted between hosts via which route, earning infectious mononucleosis the nickname 'kissing disease'?

e.correcta: EBV is shed in saliva and spreads primarily through salivary contact, such as kissing or sharing utensils/cups, which is why infectious mononucleosis has earned the nickname 'kissing disease.' The virus establishes latency in B lymphocytes and oropharyngeal epithelial cells, both of which contribute to shedding into saliva that allows person-to-person spread.

incorrectas.A: Respiratory droplet transmission is the classic route for many airborne pathogens (e.g., influenza, pertussis), but EBV's defining transmission route emphasized clinically is direct salivary contact, not droplet spread.
incorrectas.C: Sexual contact is not the classic transmission route highlighted for EBV; that mode of spread is more associated with viruses like HIV, HSV-2, and HPV, not the salivary spread of mono.
incorrectas.D: Blood transfusion can rarely transmit EBV, but this is not the classic or common route responsible for the 'kissing disease' epidemiology seen in adolescents and young adults.

preguntas.q: Infectious mononucleosis due to primary EBV infection is classically most symptomatic in which age group?

e.correcta: While EBV infection is extremely common across all ages, primary infection in teenagers and young adults is the group most likely to produce the classic symptomatic mononucleosis syndrome (fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly), whereas infection at younger ages is usually subclinical or mild. This age-dependence relates to a more vigorous cytotoxic T-cell response in older children/young adults, since much of the symptomatology is immune-mediated rather than due to direct viral damage.

incorrectas.A: Neonates acquiring EBV would be unusual and is not the classically described demographic; congenital/perinatal viral mononucleosis-type illness is not a hallmark EBV presentation.
incorrectas.C: Elderly patients are not the group classically associated with primary symptomatic EBV mononucleosis; most older adults have already been infected in adolescence or young adulthood and carry the virus latently.
incorrectas.D: Young children (toddlers) who acquire EBV are typically asymptomatic or have only mild, nonspecific illness, in contrast to the more classic, symptomatic presentation seen in teenagers.

preguntas.q: The lymphocytosis of infectious mononucleosis is composed predominantly of which reactive cell population responding to EBV-infected B cells?

e.correcta: EBV infects B lymphocytes, and the body's control of this infection depends on a robust expansion of CD8+ cytotoxic T cells that recognize and kill infected B cells. These reactive/activated CD8+ T cells are the 'atypical lymphocytes' seen on peripheral smear in infectious mononucleosis, and their proliferation in lymph node paracortex and splenic PALS accounts for the lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly of the disease.

incorrectas.A: CD4+ helper T cells assist in orchestrating immune responses and provide help to B cells and CD8+ T cells, but the dominant expanded effector population directly responsible for the atypical lymphocytosis of mono is the CD8+ subset, not CD4+ cells.
incorrectas.C: Natural killer cells provide innate, non-antigen-specific cytotoxicity against virally infected cells, but the characteristic atypical lymphocytosis of EBV mononucleosis is driven by antigen-specific CD8+ T cells rather than NK cells.
incorrectas.D: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated antibody-secreting B cells; while EBV does infect B cells, the reactive proliferating population seen in peripheral blood and driving the clinical syndrome is the cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell response, not plasma cell expansion.

preguntas.q: In infectious mononucleosis, the CD8+ T-cell response classically produces prominent lymphadenopathy in which specific nodal group?

e.correcta: Infectious mononucleosis classically causes prominent posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, reflecting reactive T-cell hyperplasia in the nodes draining the oropharynx and Waldeyer ring, where EBV establishes its initial infection of B cells and epithelium. Posterior cervical adenopathy in a teenager with fever and pharyngitis is a classic clinical clue that should prompt consideration of mono over a simple bacterial pharyngitis.

incorrectas.A: Axillary lymphadenopathy is more typically associated with infections or malignancies of the upper extremity or breast, not the oropharyngeal drainage pattern characteristic of EBV mononucleosis.
incorrectas.B: Inguinal lymphadenopathy reflects drainage from the lower extremities or genital region (e.g., in sexually transmitted infections), unrelated to the pharyngeal site of EBV infection.
incorrectas.D: Supraclavicular lymphadenopathy is a classic red flag for intra-abdominal or intrathoracic malignancy (e.g., Virchow node), not the benign reactive pattern seen in infectious mononucleosis.

preguntas.q: The lymphadenopathy of infectious mononucleosis results from T-cell hyperplasia in which region of the lymph node?

e.correcta: The paracortex is the T-cell-dependent zone of the lymph node, located between the B-cell follicles and the medulla, and it is here that the massive expansion of reactive CD8+ T cells in response to EBV-infected B cells occurs, producing the nodal enlargement seen in mono. Knowing that the paracortex houses T cells (versus follicles housing B cells) helps predict which region expands in a given disease: viral/T-cell-driven processes expand the paracortex, while conditions like follicular hyperplasia (e.g., early HIV, rheumatoid arthritis) expand the follicles instead.

incorrectas.A: Follicular germinal centers are the B-cell proliferation zones of the lymph node cortex, expanding in humoral immune responses and follicular hyperplasia (e.g., early HIV infection), not in the T-cell-driven reaction of mononucleosis.
incorrectas.B: The subcapsular sinus is the peripheral channel where lymph first enters the node and macrophages sample antigen; it is not the site of the T-cell proliferation responsible for mono's lymphadenopathy.
incorrectas.C: The medulla contains medullary cords rich in plasma cells and macrophages involved in antibody secretion, not the site of the CD8+ T-cell hyperplasia driving mononucleosis lymphadenopathy.

preguntas.q: The CD8+ T-cell response in EBV infection classically leads to enlargement of which organ, presenting as left-upper-quadrant fullness or tenderness?

e.correcta: The same CD8+ T-cell proliferation that expands lymph nodes in mono also expands the spleen, specifically within the periarterial lymphatic sheath (PALS), the T-cell zone of the white pulp, producing splenomegaly. This splenic enlargement is clinically important because the capsule becomes stretched and friable, creating a real risk of splenic rupture with abdominal trauma or even vigorous physical activity.

incorrectas.A: The liver can show mild transaminase elevation in EBV mono due to hepatocyte involvement, but the organ classically enlarged by the T-cell hyperplastic reaction (and posing a rupture risk) is the spleen, not the liver.
incorrectas.C: The pancreas is not involved in the reactive lymphoid proliferation of infectious mononucleosis; pancreatic pathology is unrelated to this EBV-driven T-cell response.
incorrectas.D: The kidney is not a site of lymphoid hyperplasia in mononucleosis; renal involvement is not a feature of this disease's classic pathophysiology.

preguntas.q: Splenomegaly in infectious mononucleosis results from T-cell hyperplasia in which splenic compartment?

e.correcta: The periarterial lymphatic sheath (PALS) is the T-cell zone of the splenic white pulp, surrounding the central arteriole, and it is here that reactive CD8+ T cells proliferate in response to EBV-infected B cells, causing the spleen to enlarge. This mirrors the paracortical expansion seen in lymph nodes, since both PALS and paracortex are T-cell-dependent zones that expand together in mono.

incorrectas.A: The red pulp is composed of splenic cords and venous sinuses responsible for filtering aged/damaged red blood cells and clearing blood-borne pathogens, not for housing the proliferating T cells responsible for mono's splenomegaly.
incorrectas.B: The marginal zone, located between red and white pulp, contains specialized macrophages and B cells important for responding to blood-borne encapsulated organisms, not the T-cell compartment expanding in EBV mononucleosis.
incorrectas.D: Splenic (lymphoid) follicles are the B-cell zones of the white pulp, expanding in humoral immune responses, whereas the T-cell-driven expansion responsible for mono's splenomegaly occurs in the PALS, not the follicles.

preguntas.q: What abnormal-appearing cell is characteristically seen on peripheral blood smear in infectious mononucleosis?

e.correcta: The peripheral smear in infectious mononucleosis characteristically shows atypical lymphocytes -- reactive, activated CD8+ T cells with abundant pale-blue cytoplasm that scallops around adjacent red cells -- reflecting the vigorous cytotoxic T-cell expansion against EBV-infected B cells. These atypical lymphocytes accompany an overall elevated WBC count and are a key morphologic clue supporting the diagnosis alongside the clinical triad of fever, pharyngitis, and lymphadenopathy.

incorrectas.B: Smudge cells are fragile, ruptured lymphocytes seen on smear in chronic lymphocytic leukemia, an artifact of the cells' fragility during slide preparation, not the reactive, intact atypical lymphocytes of mono.
incorrectas.C: Auer rods are needle-like azurophilic granule aggregates seen in myeloblasts, most classically in acute promyelocytic leukemia, a completely different (myeloid neoplastic) process unrelated to reactive viral lymphocytosis.
incorrectas.D: Tear-drop cells (dacrocytes) are red blood cells with a teardrop shape seen in myelofibrosis and marrow infiltrative processes, reflecting an erythrocyte abnormality rather than the reactive lymphocyte morphology characteristic of mononucleosis.

preguntas.q: Which rapid screening test detects heterophile antibodies to aid diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis?

e.correcta: The Monospot test detects heterophile antibodies -- IgM antibodies produced during EBV infection that happen to agglutinate horse or sheep red blood cells despite not being directed against EBV antigens themselves -- providing a quick screening tool for mononucleosis. It has an important limitation: it carries roughly a 25% false-negative rate during the first week of illness (before heterophile antibodies rise sufficiently) and is often negative in CMV-associated mononucleosis-like illness, since CMV does not reliably generate heterophile antibodies.

incorrectas.A: The direct Coombs test detects antibodies or complement bound to a patient's own red blood cells, used in the workup of autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and has no role in screening for infectious mononucleosis.
incorrectas.C: The PPD skin test screens for prior exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis via a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction, unrelated to EBV serology or heterophile antibodies.
incorrectas.D: A rapid strep antigen test detects group A Streptococcus antigen from a throat swab to evaluate for streptococcal pharyngitis, a bacterial cause of sore throat that must be distinguished from, not used to diagnose, mononucleosis.

preguntas.q: A definitive diagnosis of EBV-associated infectious mononucleosis, especially when the Monospot test is negative, is made by serologic testing for which specific antigen?

e.correcta: Definitive, EBV-specific serologic diagnosis relies on detecting antibodies to the viral capsid antigen (VCA) -- IgM VCA antibodies indicate acute/recent infection, while IgG VCA antibodies persist for life -- making VCA serology far more specific than the nonspecific heterophile antibody test. This is particularly useful in atypical presentations or when the Monospot test is falsely negative, such as early in illness or in young children who mount a weaker heterophile response.

incorrectas.A: EBNA antibodies are useful too, but they characteristically appear months after acute infection and are used to identify past infection or distinguish acute from remote EBV exposure, not as the primary marker used for an immediate definitive diagnosis the way VCA IgM is.
incorrectas.C: Hepatitis B surface antigen is a marker of hepatitis B virus infection, an entirely different virus with no role in diagnosing EBV mononucleosis.
incorrectas.D: CMV pp65 antigen is used to detect active cytomegalovirus infection/reactivation (e.g., in transplant patients), not to confirm EBV as the cause of mononucleosis.

preguntas.q: Infectious mononucleosis carries an increased risk of which serious complication related to organ enlargement?

e.correcta: The marked splenomegaly of infectious mononucleosis stretches and thins the splenic capsule, making the organ unusually susceptible to rupture, even from relatively minor abdominal trauma or increased intra-abdominal pressure. Because rupture can cause life-threatening hemorrhage, patients are counseled to avoid contact sports and other activities that risk abdominal trauma while the spleen remains enlarged.

incorrectas.A: The liver can be mildly affected in mono (transaminitis), but it does not carry the marked rupture risk associated with the spleen's dramatic capsular stretching in this disease.
incorrectas.C: The kidneys are not enlarged or structurally weakened in infectious mononucleosis, so renal rupture is not a recognized complication of this disease.
incorrectas.D: The pancreas is not involved in the lymphoproliferative process of mononucleosis and is not at increased risk of rupture in this condition.

preguntas.q: Patients recovering from infectious mononucleosis are advised to avoid contact sports for approximately how long, given the risk of splenic rupture?

e.correcta: Because splenomegaly and the associated risk of rupture can persist for several weeks after acute infectious mononucleosis, patients are typically counseled to avoid contact sports and other activities risking abdominal trauma for about one month, or until splenomegaly has been confirmed to resolve on exam or imaging. This timeframe balances allowing the spleen to return to a safer size against unnecessarily prolonging activity restriction.

incorrectas.A: One week is too short an interval, since splenic enlargement and the associated fragility of the capsule typically persist well beyond the first week of illness.
incorrectas.B: Two weeks is still generally considered insufficient, as most guidance extends the restriction closer to a month to ensure adequate resolution of splenomegaly.
incorrectas.D: Six months is excessive for typical cases; while some clinicians individualize timing based on splenic size on exam or ultrasound, the standard general recommendation is closer to one month, not half a year.

preguntas.q: Acute leukemia is diagnosed when neoplastic blasts make up what minimum percentage of cells in the bone marrow?

e.correcta: Acute leukemia is defined by a neoplastic proliferation of blasts comprising greater than 20% of bone marrow cellularity, a threshold that distinguishes it from myelodysplastic syndromes (which have increased but still under 20% blasts) and marks the point at which normal hematopoiesis is critically crowded out, leading to cytopenias. This 20% cutoff (revised down from the older 30% criterion) is a key diagnostic feature because it directly separates acute leukemia from its 'pre-leukemic' precursor states.

incorrectas.A: A blast percentage above 10% is not the recognized diagnostic threshold for acute leukemia; blast counts in this lower range are more consistent with myelodysplastic syndrome with excess blasts, a pre-leukemic condition.
incorrectas.C: A threshold of greater than 30% was the older diagnostic criterion under earlier classification systems, but current (WHO) criteria define acute leukemia at the lower greater-than-20% blast threshold.
incorrectas.D: A threshold of greater than 50% is far higher than the actual diagnostic cutoff and would miss many true cases of acute leukemia that present with 20-50% marrow blasts.

preguntas.q: Peripheral blood counts in acute leukemia are typically characterized by which finding?

o.A: Decreased circulating WBCs in nearly all cases
o.C: Normal WBC count with isolated anemia

e.correcta: Acute leukemias typically present with an increased circulating white blood cell count, since neoplastic blasts spill out of the crowded bone marrow into peripheral blood, though the differential is dominated by blasts rather than functional mature leukocytes. This is why patients can have a very high WBC count yet still be functionally immunocompromised and prone to infection, since the circulating cells are largely non-functional blasts.

incorrectas.A: Rare cases of acute leukemia do present with a normal or decreased WBC count (aleukemic leukemia), but this is not the typical pattern and does not represent 'nearly all cases' as this option claims.
incorrectas.C: A normal WBC count with isolated anemia understates the disease; acute leukemia usually causes pancytopenia (anemia, thrombocytopenia, and often neutropenia of functional cells) alongside an elevated total count driven by blasts, not an isolated anemia picture.
incorrectas.D: Circulating blasts are actually a hallmark of acute leukemia on peripheral smear, so their absence would be atypical rather than the expected typical finding.

preguntas.q: Acute leukemia is subdivided into acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) based on which feature?

e.correcta: Acute leukemia is classified as ALL versus AML based on the immunophenotype (lineage) of the proliferating blasts, determined by flow cytometry markers such as TdT, CD10, and CD19 for lymphoblasts versus myeloperoxidase, CD13, and CD33 for myeloblasts. This distinction is critical because ALL and AML have different typical age distributions, cytogenetic associations, and treatment regimens, even though both meet the same greater-than-20% blast threshold for acute leukemia.

incorrectas.A: Age is a useful epidemiologic clue (ALL is more common in children, AML in older adults), but the actual diagnostic classification is based on blast immunophenotype, not age alone, since either leukemia can occur outside its 'classic' age group.
incorrectas.B: Absolute WBC count reflects disease burden and can be elevated in both ALL and AML; it does not distinguish which lineage the blasts belong to.
incorrectas.D: Lymphadenopathy can occur in either leukemia, especially ALL, but its presence or absence is not the defining criterion used to separate ALL from AML; that determination requires blast marker analysis.

preguntas.q: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is defined as a neoplastic accumulation of which cell type comprising more than 20% of the bone marrow?

e.correcta: ALL is defined by a clonal proliferation of lymphoblasts exceeding 20% of bone marrow cellularity -- immature lymphoid precursor cells identified by markers like TdT, CD10, and CD19 (B-lineage) or CD2-CD7 (T-lineage) -- distinguishing it from AML, which is driven by myeloblasts instead. ALL is the most common childhood leukemia and, unlike AML, frequently presents with lymphadenopathy and CNS involvement, reflecting the lymphoid lineage of the neoplastic cells.

incorrectas.A: Myeloblasts are the immature precursor cells that accumulate in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), not ALL; distinguishing myeloblasts from lymphoblasts by immunophenotype (e.g., myeloperoxidase positivity) is exactly how ALL and AML are differentiated.
incorrectas.C: Promyelocytes are a slightly more differentiated myeloid precursor stage, and their abnormal accumulation with characteristic Auer rods defines acute promyelocytic leukemia, a subtype of AML, not ALL.
incorrectas.D: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated, antibody-secreting B cells; their neoplastic accumulation defines multiple myeloma/plasma cell dyscrasias, a completely different disease from the lymphoblastic proliferation of ALL.

preguntas.q: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is most commonly diagnosed in which age group?

e.correcta: ALL is the most common malignancy of childhood, with peak incidence around 2-5 years of age, arising from a proliferation of TdT+ lymphoblasts. Its predominance in children contrasts sharply with AML, which is instead a disease of older adults.

incorrectas.B: Adults 20-40 do develop ALL, but this is not the classic peak; adult ALL is less common overall and typically carries a worse prognosis than the pediatric form.
incorrectas.C: Older adults over 60 are the characteristic population for AML, where myeloblasts (not lymphoblasts) accumulate in the marrow — the opposite epidemiologic pattern from ALL.
incorrectas.D: Congenital/neonatal leukemia is rare and, when it occurs, is often linked to specific genetic syndromes rather than representing the typical epidemiologic peak of ALL.

preguntas.q: ALL is subclassified into two major immunophenotypic subtypes based on lymphoblast surface markers. Which two subtypes are these?

o.C: Pre-B ALL and pre-T ALL only

e.correcta: ALL blasts are classified by lineage as B-ALL (precursor B-cell origin, expressing CD19, CD20, and CD10) or T-ALL (precursor T-cell origin, expressing markers spanning CD2 to CD8); both are TdT+, confirming their immature lymphoblastic nature. B-ALL is the more common subtype overall, while T-ALL classically presents with a mediastinal (thymic) mass in adolescent males.

incorrectas.B: "Myeloid ALL" is not a real category — ALL is by definition a lymphoid neoplasm; the myeloid/lymphoid split describes AML versus ALL, not the internal subclassification within ALL itself.
incorrectas.C: Pre-B and pre-T maturation stages are finer subdivisions within B-ALL and T-ALL, not the standard two-category classification of ALL that is tested — the umbrella terms are B-ALL and T-ALL.
incorrectas.D: CD10 status is a marker used to help distinguish B-ALL (CD10-positive) from T-ALL (CD10-negative), but it is a diagnostic feature, not the name given to the two ALL subtypes themselves.

preguntas.q: Between the two major subtypes of acute lymphoblastic leukemia, which one accounts for the majority of cases?

e.correcta: B-ALL, arising from precursor B lymphoblasts, makes up the large majority of ALL cases and is characterized by TdT+ blasts expressing CD10, CD19, and CD20. Its excellent chemosensitivity contributes to the high cure rates seen in pediatric ALL overall.

incorrectas.B: T-ALL is the less common subtype, arising from precursor T cells, often presenting with a mediastinal (thymic) mass in adolescent males, and notably lacking CD10 expression.
incorrectas.C: Mixed phenotype acute leukemia is a rare category in which blasts co-express both myeloid and lymphoid markers; it is far less common than typical B-ALL and represents a distinct diagnostic entity, not a form of B or T-ALL.
incorrectas.D: Burkitt leukemia/lymphoma is a mature B-cell neoplasm driven by c-myc translocations with a classic "starry sky" histologic pattern, biologically distinct from precursor B-ALL and much less frequent.

preguntas.q: Lymphoblasts in B-ALL are TdT+ and characteristically express which combination of surface markers?

e.correcta: B-ALL blasts express the B-lineage markers CD19 and CD20 along with CD10 (also called CALLA, the "common ALL antigen"), reflecting their origin from precursor B cells; TdT positivity in addition confirms their immature lymphoblastic nature. CD10 positivity is a key feature distinguishing B-ALL from T-ALL, which is CD10-negative.

incorrectas.B: CD2, CD5, and CD7 are pan-T-cell markers found on T-ALL blasts, reflecting T-lymphoid rather than B-lymphoid lineage commitment — the opposite lineage from what B-ALL represents.
incorrectas.C: CD13, CD33, and CD117 are myeloid markers characteristic of AML blasts, indicating myeloid rather than lymphoid differentiation, and would not be expected on B-ALL lymphoblasts.
incorrectas.D: CD3, CD4, and CD8 mark maturing/mature T cells, more consistent with T-ALL (though even T-ALL blasts remain CD10-negative) than with the B-lineage markers that define B-ALL.

preguntas.q: How does B-ALL typically respond to chemotherapy?

o.D: Response only achievable with allogeneic stem cell transplant

e.correcta: B-ALL, particularly in children, has one of the best chemotherapy responses of any leukemia, with combination regimens achieving high cure rates. This excellent chemosensitivity is a major reason pediatric ALL is often cited as a model of a highly curable cancer.

incorrectas.B: A poor response with rapid relapse is more characteristic of high-risk cytogenetic subtypes (e.g., Philadelphia chromosome-positive ALL) or adult-onset disease, not the typical, highly treatable pediatric B-ALL course.
incorrectas.C: B-ALL is not chemo-refractory — quite the opposite, it is among the most chemosensitive malignancies, unlike genuinely treatment-resistant leukemias.
incorrectas.D: Stem cell transplant is generally reserved for relapsed, refractory, or high-risk disease rather than needed as first-line therapy, since standard chemotherapy alone already produces an excellent response in most B-ALL cases.

preguntas.q: Lymphoblasts in T-ALL are TdT+ and express a range of markers most consistent with which lineage?

o.A: T-cell markers spanning CD2 to CD8
o.B: B-cell markers spanning CD10 to CD20
o.C: Myeloid markers spanning CD13 to CD33

e.correcta: T-ALL blasts express markers found on developing T cells across a range from CD2 through CD8 (e.g., CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD7, CD8), reflecting a thymocyte/precursor T-cell origin, while TdT positivity confirms their lymphoblastic (immature) nature. T-ALL classically presents with a mediastinal mass from thymic infiltration.

incorrectas.B: CD10 through CD20 markers (CD10, CD19, CD20) define B-ALL, not T-ALL; T-ALL is notably CD10-negative, which is a key distinguishing feature between the two subtypes.
incorrectas.C: CD13 and CD33 are myeloid antigens seen in AML, reflecting an entirely different (myeloid) lineage rather than the T-lymphoid lineage that defines T-ALL blasts.
incorrectas.D: CD16/CD56 mark NK cells and are not part of the T-ALL immunophenotype, which instead follows the sequential T-cell developmental marker pattern.

preguntas.q: Do the lymphoblasts of T-ALL typically express CD10 (CALLA)?

e.correcta: T-ALL blasts are characteristically CD10-negative, in contrast to B-ALL blasts, which are typically CD10-positive. This is a clinically useful distinguishing feature on flow cytometry when differentiating the two ALL subtypes at diagnosis.

incorrectas.B: CD10 positivity is the hallmark of B-ALL (hence the name "common ALL antigen"), not T-ALL; describing T-ALL as CD10-positive reverses the actual distinguishing pattern between the two subtypes.
incorrectas.C: CD10 expression is not something that appears specifically with relapse; T-ALL's CD10-negative status is intrinsic to its T-lymphoid immunophenotype from the time of initial diagnosis.
incorrectas.D: CD10 status in T-ALL does not depend on age of onset — T-ALL is CD10-negative in both pediatric and adult cases, since this reflects lineage commitment, not the patient's age.

preguntas.q: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is defined pathologically as a neoplastic accumulation of which cell type exceeding 20% of the bone marrow?

e.correcta: AML is defined by ≥20% myeloblasts in the bone marrow (or blood), reflecting a maturation arrest in the myeloid lineage that causes accumulation of immature, non-functional blasts. This crowds out normal hematopoiesis, producing anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia despite the high overall blast count.

incorrectas.B: Lymphoblasts exceeding 20% (with TdT+ B- or T-lineage markers) defines ALL, a distinct precursor lymphoid neoplasm — a completely different lineage from the myeloid blasts that define AML.
incorrectas.C: Promyelocytes are specifically increased in acute promyelocytic leukemia, a particular AML subtype with t(15;17), but promyelocyte accumulation is not the general diagnostic requirement for AML as a whole, which is based on myeloblast percentage.
incorrectas.D: Monocyte proliferation without myeloblast predominance would suggest acute monocytic leukemia (an AML subtype) or a chronic myelomonocytic process, not the general myeloblast-based definition used for AML overall.

preguntas.q: AML most commonly arises in which patient population?

e.correcta: AML is primarily a disease of older adults, with a median age at diagnosis around 65 years; it often arises de novo or secondary to a prior myelodysplastic syndrome or previous chemotherapy/radiation exposure. This contrasts with ALL, which peaks in early childhood.

incorrectas.B: Children under 5 represent the peak age group for ALL, not AML, reflecting the more common pediatric lymphoid malignancy rather than the myeloid leukemia typical of older adults.
incorrectas.C: Adolescence is not a characteristic AML peak; while AML can occur at any age, its incidence rises progressively with age rather than peaking during the teenage years.
incorrectas.D: Neonatal leukemia is rare overall and, when it occurs, is more often linked to specific genetic syndromes (e.g., Down syndrome-associated transient myeloproliferative disorder) rather than reflecting the typical epidemiologic peak of AML.

preguntas.q: The t(15;17) translocation characteristic of acute promyelocytic leukemia disrupts which receptor located on chromosome 17?

e.correcta: t(15;17) fuses the PML gene on chromosome 15 with the retinoic acid receptor alpha (RARA) gene on chromosome 17, producing a PML-RARA fusion protein that blocks normal myeloid differentiation at the promyelocyte stage, causing promyelocytes to accumulate. This is exactly why all-trans retinoic acid, a RAR ligand, can overcome the block and drive differentiation therapy.

incorrectas.B: The estrogen receptor plays no role in APL pathogenesis; the disease-defining fusion involves the retinoic acid receptor, not estrogen signaling.
incorrectas.C: The thyroid hormone receptor is a related nuclear receptor family member, but it is not the receptor disrupted in APL, and targeting it would not explain either the maturation block or the therapeutic response to ATRA.
incorrectas.D: The vitamin D receptor is unrelated to APL biology; the defining molecular lesion specifically targets the retinoic acid receptor, which is precisely why retinoids are the cornerstone of APL treatment.

preguntas.q: The abnormal promyelocytes in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) contain numerous primary granules that place patients at increased risk for which complication?

e.correcta: The primary (azurophilic) granules of APL promyelocytes, sometimes clustered as Auer rods in "faggot cells," contain procoagulant material that can activate the coagulation cascade when released, precipitating DIC with simultaneous bleeding and clotting. This risk is present at diagnosis and can transiently worsen when treatment causes blast lysis, which is why early ATRA initiation and close coagulation monitoring are critical in suspected APL.

incorrectas.B: Hemolytic uremic syndrome results from microangiopathic processes such as Shiga toxin exposure or complement dysregulation, not from granule contents released by leukemic promyelocytes, so it is not the classic APL-associated complication.
incorrectas.C: Polycythemia (elevated red cell mass) is not a feature of APL, which instead causes cytopenias from marrow replacement by blasts; the thrombotic risk in APL comes from DIC/coagulopathy, not hyperviscosity from excess red cells.
incorrectas.D: Tumor lysis syndrome can occur with any high-burden, rapidly proliferating leukemia during treatment, but it is a metabolic complication (hyperkalemia, hyperuricemia, hyperphosphatemia) distinct from the granule-driven coagulopathy that is the hallmark risk specifically highlighted in APL.

preguntas.q: All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) binds the altered retinoic acid receptor in APL and induces which effect on the leukemic blasts?

e.correcta: ATRA binds the abnormal PML-RARA fusion receptor and overcomes the maturation block it imposes, driving the leukemic promyelocytes to differentiate into mature neutrophils.
