This "differentiation therapy" is unique because it does not primarily kill cells directly but instead coaxes them to mature and undergo their natural lifespan, dramatically improving APL outcomes when paired with arsenic trioxide.

incorrectas.B: ATRA's mechanism is fundamentally about restoring differentiation rather than directly triggering apoptosis independent of maturation; any cell death that follows is a downstream consequence of the induced maturation, not a direct pro-apoptotic effect.
incorrectas.C: ATRA does not increase blast proliferation — by forcing terminal differentiation, it actually removes cells from the proliferative blast pool, reducing rather than expanding the leukemic population.
incorrectas.D: ATRA does not correct the underlying t(15;17) translocation or eliminate the PML-RARA fusion gene at the genetic level; it acts pharmacologically on the fusion protein's function, not on reversing the chromosomal abnormality itself.

preguntas.q: Which subtype of AML presents with a proliferation of monoblasts?

e.correcta: Acute monocytic leukemia is an AML subtype in which the neoplastic blasts (monoblasts) show monocytic rather than granulocytic differentiation. These blasts characteristically lack myeloperoxidase and are instead identified by nonspecific esterase positivity, and patients often develop gingival and skin (leukemia cutis) infiltration from the monocytic tumor cells.

incorrectas.B: Acute promyelocytic leukemia is defined by accumulation of abnormal promyelocytes with t(15;17), a granulocytic (not monocytic) lineage blast, and is associated with DIC risk rather than monoblast proliferation.
incorrectas.C: Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia involves proliferation of megakaryoblasts (the platelet precursor lineage), often associated with Down syndrome in infants — a completely distinct lineage from the monocytic blasts of acute monocytic leukemia.
incorrectas.D: Acute erythroid leukemia involves proliferation of abnormal erythroid (red cell) precursors, a different lineage entirely from the monocytic blasts described in this question.

preguntas.q: Do the monoblasts of acute monocytic leukemia typically stain positive for myeloperoxidase (MPO)?

o.D: Only when Auer rods are present

e.correcta: Monoblasts in acute monocytic leukemia are typically MPO-negative (or only weakly positive), reflecting their monocytic rather than granulocytic lineage. Instead, they are identified using nonspecific esterase staining, a key lab feature distinguishing this subtype from granulocytic AML forms that are strongly MPO-positive.

incorrectas.B: Strong MPO positivity is characteristic of granulocytic lineage blasts (such as in AML with maturation or APL), not monoblasts, which lack the primary granule myeloperoxidase content found in granulocytic precursors.
incorrectas.C: MPO status in monoblasts does not change based on whether disease is newly diagnosed or relapsed; the lineage-determined negativity is an intrinsic feature of the monocytic blasts themselves.
incorrectas.D: Auer rods, when present, are more typical of granulocytic or promyelocytic blasts and correlate with MPO positivity; their presence is not a prerequisite for or determinant of MPO status specifically in monoblasts, which remain characteristically MPO-negative.

preguntas.q: Which AML subtype presents with proliferation of megakaryoblasts?

e.correcta: Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia is an AML subtype driven by proliferation of megakaryoblasts, the precursors of platelet-producing megakaryocytes. It is notably associated with Down syndrome in young children and can be accompanied by myelofibrosis, since the abnormal megakaryoblasts release growth factors that stimulate marrow fibrosis.

incorrectas.B: Acute monocytic leukemia involves proliferation of monoblasts (monocytic lineage), a different precursor cell type from the megakaryocytic lineage seen in acute megakaryoblastic leukemia.
incorrectas.C: Acute promyelocytic leukemia involves abnormal promyelocytes of the granulocytic lineage carrying t(15;17), unrelated to the megakaryocyte/platelet lineage described here.
incorrectas.D: Chronic myeloid leukemia is a myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by the BCR-ABL fusion with excess mature granulocytes, an entirely different chronic disease process rather than an acute leukemia with megakaryoblast proliferation.

preguntas.q: Are the megakaryoblasts of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia typically positive for myeloperoxidase (MPO)?

o.C: Only in the presence of Down syndrome

e.correcta: Like monoblasts, megakaryoblasts are typically MPO-negative because they arise from a non-granulocytic lineage. Platelet-lineage markers (e.g., CD41, CD61) rather than MPO staining are used to identify these blasts on flow cytometry or immunohistochemistry.

incorrectas.B: Strong MPO positivity is a feature of granulocytic-lineage blasts, not megakaryoblasts, which lack the primary granules that contain myeloperoxidase.
incorrectas.C: MPO negativity in megakaryoblasts is a lineage-intrinsic feature and does not depend on the presence or absence of Down syndrome, even though Down syndrome is an important epidemiologic association with this leukemia subtype in young children.
incorrectas.D: MPO status is determined by cell lineage (megakaryocytic), not by age of onset; megakaryoblasts remain MPO-negative in both the transient myeloproliferative disorder of Down syndrome infants and any adult cases.

preguntas.q: AML may arise as a secondary neoplasm from which pre-existing hematologic condition?

e.correcta: Myelodysplastic syndromes are clonal stem cell disorders with ineffective hematopoiesis and dysplastic maturation defects across nonlymphoid cell lineages. A subset of MDS patients undergo clonal evolution with acquisition of additional mutations that push the blast percentage above 20%, transforming into overt AML ("secondary AML"), which tends to carry a worse prognosis than de novo AML.

incorrectas.B: Iron deficiency anemia is a nutritional/hematinic deficiency causing microcytic anemia, with no clonal stem cell abnormality and no established predisposition to transformation into AML.
incorrectas.C: Hereditary spherocytosis is an inherited RBC membrane defect causing hemolytic anemia, unrelated to myeloid stem cell clonality or leukemic transformation risk.
incorrectas.D: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura is an autoimmune platelet destruction disorder, not a clonal marrow stem cell disease, and it does not predispose to AML the way myelodysplastic syndrome's dysplastic clonal hematopoiesis does.

preguntas.q: Myelodysplastic syndromes are characterized by an increased blast percentage that remains below what threshold, distinguishing MDS from acute leukemia?

e.correcta: MDS is defined by dysplastic, ineffective hematopoiesis with blast counts elevated above normal but remaining under the 20% threshold that would otherwise define acute leukemia. The marrow is typically hypercellular, yet peripheral cytopenias persist because maturation of the abnormal clone is defective ("ineffective hematopoiesis").

incorrectas.B: Less than 5% blasts approximates a normal marrow blast percentage; MDS blast counts are elevated above this baseline, sometimes into double digits, just not high enough to cross into the acute leukemia range.
incorrectas.C: Less than 50% is far above the actual defining cutoff; the key numeric threshold separating MDS from acute leukemia is 20% blasts, not 50%.
incorrectas.D: MDS does involve an increase in blasts compared to a normal marrow, even though it remains below the acute leukemia threshold — describing it as having no increase at all misses the defining dysplastic/proliferative feature of the disease.

preguntas.q: Myelodysplastic syndrome may rarely progress into which acute leukemia?

e.correcta: MDS, a clonal myeloid stem cell disorder, can rarely transform into AML once additional oncogenic mutations accumulate and push the myeloblast percentage above 20%. Notably, most MDS patients actually die from complications of cytopenias, such as infection or bleeding, before this progression occurs, which is why transformation to AML is described as "rare" relative to the overall disease course.

incorrectas.B: ALL arises from lymphoid, not myeloid, precursors and is not the typical transformation pathway of MDS, which is a myeloid-lineage clonal disorder that would be expected to transform along myeloid lines if it transforms at all.
incorrectas.C: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a mature B-cell neoplasm of older adults, biologically unrelated to the myeloid stem cell clone driving MDS, and is not a recognized transformation outcome of MDS.
incorrectas.D: Hairy cell leukemia is a distinct mature B-cell neoplasm with characteristic "hairy" cytoplasmic projections and TRAP positivity, unrelated to the myeloid clonal evolution seen in MDS progression.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerves are NOT located within the brainstem?

e.correcta: CN I (olfactory) and CN II (optic) are unique among the cranial nerves in that their pathways bypass the brainstem entirely — CN I relays through the olfactory bulb/tract directly to the cerebral cortex, and CN II is technically an outgrowth of the diencephalon (retina and optic tract), not a true peripheral nerve arising from brainstem nuclei. Every other cranial nerve (III-XII) has its nucleus within the midbrain, pons, or medulla.

incorrectas.B: CN III and CN IV nuclei are located in the midbrain, one of the three brainstem subdivisions, making them very much brainstem nerves, unlike the truly extra-brainstem CN I and II.
incorrectas.C: CN V and CN VI nuclei are located in the pons, another brainstem subdivision, again placing them within (not outside) the brainstem in contrast to CN I and II.
incorrectas.D: CN IX and CN X nuclei are located in the medulla, the lowest brainstem subdivision, so they too are firmly within the brainstem rather than outside it.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerves are located above the level of the pons?

o.A: CN I, II, III, and IV
o.B: CN V, VI, VII, and VIII
o.C: CN IX, X, XI, and XII
o.D: CN III, IV, VI, and XII

e.correcta: CN I and II sit entirely above the brainstem (associated with the forebrain/diencephalon), while CN III (oculomotor) and CN IV (trochlear) nuclei reside in the midbrain, the most rostral brainstem segment. Together these four are the highest-positioned cranial nerves, all found at or above the midbrain level, above the pons.

incorrectas.B: CN V, VI, VII, and VIII nuclei are located in the pons itself, one level caudal to the midbrain grouping described, not above the pons.
incorrectas.C: CN IX, X, XI, and XII nuclei are located in the medulla, the lowest brainstem level, the opposite end of the brainstem from the group situated above the pons.
incorrectas.D: This combination mixes nuclei from different levels — CN III is midbrain, but VI is pons and XII is medulla — so it does not represent a single coherent "above the pons" grouping the way I, II, III, IV does.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerves have their nuclei located within the pons?

o.A: CN V, VI, VII, and VIII
o.D: CN IX, X, XI, and XII

e.correcta: The pons houses the nuclei of CN V (trigeminal), VI (abducens), VII (facial), and VIII (vestibulocochlear) — a useful grouping since these four nerves mediate facial sensation/mastication, lateral eye movement, facial expression, and hearing/balance, all functions localized to structures at the pontine level and often affected together by pontine lesions such as cerebellopontine angle tumors impacting VII and VIII.

incorrectas.B: CN I and II are not located in the brainstem at all, let alone specifically the pons; they relay through the forebrain/diencephalon instead, bypassing the brainstem entirely.
incorrectas.C: CN III and IV nuclei are located in the midbrain, rostral to the pons, not within the pons itself.
incorrectas.D: CN IX, X, XI, and XII nuclei are located in the medulla, caudal to the pons, representing a different brainstem level than the pontine group of V-VIII.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerves have their nuclei located within the medulla?

o.A: CN IX, X, XI, and XII
o.B: CN V, VI, VII, and VIII

e.correcta: The medulla, the most caudal brainstem segment, contains the nuclei for CN IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), XI (spinal accessory, whose nucleus actually lies proximal to, at the junction with, the medulla), and XII (hypoglossal). This grouping explains why medullary lesions such as lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome can produce dysphagia, hoarseness, and tongue deviation.

incorrectas.B: CN V, VI, VII, and VIII nuclei reside in the pons, the brainstem segment just rostral to the medulla, not within the medulla itself.
incorrectas.C: CN III and IV nuclei are in the midbrain, the most rostral brainstem segment, far from the medulla at the caudal end.
incorrectas.D: CN I and II are not located in the brainstem at all, unlike the medullary group of IX-XII, which are firmly brainstem structures.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve nuclei are classically located medially within the brainstem?

o.A: CN III, IV, VI, and XII
o.B: CN V, VII, IX, and X

e.correcta: CN III, IV, VI, and XII are remembered as the medially-located nuclei using the mnemonic "factors of 12, except 1 and 2" (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12 are factors of 12; excluding 1 and 2 leaves 3, 4, 6, and 12). These are all purely motor nerves (oculomotor, trochlear, abducens, hypoglossal), and medial brainstem lesions, such as medial medullary syndrome, classically affect these motor nuclei while sparing lateral sensory structures.

incorrectas.B: CN V, VII, IX, and X nuclei are positioned laterally in the brainstem because they carry mixed motor/sensory (or predominantly sensory) function — the opposite localization pattern from the medial, purely motor nuclei group.
incorrectas.C: CN I and II are not brainstem nuclei at all, so they cannot be classified as medial or lateral brainstem structures in the first place.
incorrectas.D: CN VIII (purely sensory, vestibulocochlear) is a laterally located nucleus, and CN XI's nucleus lies at the cervical cord/medulla junction rather than fitting the classic medial motor nuclei grouping of III, IV, VI, and XII.

preguntas.q: Cranial nerve nuclei that exit the brainstem laterally are typically what functional type?

e.correcta: The laterally-exiting cranial nerve nuclei — CN V, VII, VIII, IX, and X — are typically mixed (carrying both motor and sensory/autonomic components) or purely sensory, in contrast to the medially-exiting purely motor nuclei (III, IV, VI, XII, remembered via "factors of 12 except 1 and 2"). This anatomic split is a useful tool for localizing brainstem lesions based on which functions are affected.

incorrectas.B: Purely motor nuclei (III, IV, VI, XII) are the ones located medially, not laterally, making this the inverse of the correct lateral/mixed-sensory pattern.
incorrectas.C: Purely parasympathetic function is not how the lateral nuclei are functionally categorized; several lateral nerves (e.g., VII, IX, X) do carry parasympathetic fibers, but their defining group feature is their mixed/sensory character, not an exclusively parasympathetic role.
incorrectas.D: CN I and II carry special sensory (smell, vision) information but are not located in the brainstem at all, so they are excluded entirely from this classification of laterally-exiting brainstem nuclei.

preguntas.q: Which type of gaze is coordinated primarily by the superior colliculi in conjunction with midbrain gaze centers?

e.correcta: The superior colliculi, together with the rostral interstitial nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus and other midbrain vertical-gaze centers, coordinate conjugate vertical eye movements — moving both eyes together up or down. This contrasts with horizontal conjugate gaze, which is driven from the pons rather than the midbrain. Lesions near the superior colliculi (e.g., a pineal region tumor compressing the tectum) classically produce Parinaud syndrome, with paralysis of upward gaze.

incorrectas.B: Conjugate horizontal gaze is generated by the paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) working with the abducens nucleus and the contralateral oculomotor nucleus via the medial longitudinal fasciculus, a pontine circuit rather than the midbrain superior colliculus.
incorrectas.C: Smooth pursuit is mediated by cortical (frontal and parietal eye field) and cerebellar pathways that track a moving target, a distinct system from the superior colliculus's role in coordinating vertical gaze.
incorrectas.D: Vergence movements (convergence/divergence for near vision) depend on midbrain near-response circuitry linked to CN III's medial rectus and ciliary innervation, not on the superior colliculus's vertical gaze function.

preguntas.q: Which paired midbrain structures direct reflexive eye movements toward novel visual or auditory stimuli in the environment?

e.correcta: The superior colliculi sit in the midbrain tectum and integrate visual (and some auditory/somatosensory) input to generate rapid, reflexive saccades that orient the eyes toward a new stimulus, such as sudden movement in the peripheral visual field. They also participate in coordinating conjugate vertical gaze, tying orienting behavior and vertical eye movement to the same structure.

incorrectas.A: The inferior colliculi are the principal midbrain auditory relay nuclei, receiving ascending auditory input en route to the medial geniculate nucleus, but they do not themselves generate eye movements toward stimuli.
incorrectas.B: The red nuclei are involved in motor coordination (rubrospinal tract, cerebellar output relay) and limb movement, not in orienting the eyes toward sensory stimuli.
incorrectas.D: The substantia nigra is a basal ganglia structure central to dopaminergic modulation of voluntary movement, and its pars reticulata does help gate saccade initiation, but it is not itself the structure that directs the eyes toward a stimulus of interest.

preguntas.q: The inferior colliculi in the midbrain primarily serve which sensory/functional role?

e.correcta: The inferior colliculi are paired midbrain nuclei that serve as a major relay and processing station in the ascending auditory pathway, receiving input from the lateral lemniscus and projecting to the medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus before signals reach auditory cortex. The classic pairing to remember is 'inferior = hearing' and 'superior = seeing' for the corpora quadrigemina.

incorrectas.A: Visual orienting and reflexive saccades toward visual stimuli are functions of the superior colliculi, the paired structure just rostral to the inferior colliculi, not the inferior colliculi themselves.
incorrectas.B: Vestibular integration occurs mainly in the vestibular nuclei of the pons/medulla and the cerebellum, not in the midbrain tectum where the inferior colliculi reside.
incorrectas.C: Coordination of conjugate vertical gaze is a superior colliculus/midbrain vertical-gaze-center function, distinct from the inferior colliculi's dedicated auditory relay role.

preguntas.q: The olfactory nerve (CN I) is classified as which type of cranial nerve?

e.correcta: CN I carries only special sensory (olfactory) fibers from the olfactory epithelium to the olfactory bulb, with no motor component. In the mnemonic 'Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most,' which tracks which cranial nerves are sensory (S), motor (M), or both (B), CN I is an 'S.' Its purely sensory nature reflects that its receptor neurons project directly into the CNS rather than through a typical mixed peripheral nerve.

incorrectas.A: A purely motor classification would mean CN I innervates muscle, which it does not — CN I has no motor fibers at all, unlike nerves such as CN III, IV, VI, XI, and XII.
incorrectas.B: 'Both' describes mixed cranial nerves like CN V, VII, IX, and X, which carry both sensory and motor fibers; CN I lacks any motor component, so it does not fit this mixed category.
incorrectas.D: CN I does not carry parasympathetic (autonomic) fibers — that role belongs to nerves such as CN III, VII, IX, and X, none of which describes CN I's purely olfactory sensory function.

preguntas.q: What sensory modality does CN I (the olfactory nerve) transmit to the brain?

e.correcta: CN I transmits the special sense of smell, carrying signals from olfactory receptor neurons in the nasal epithelium through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb and ultimately to limbic and cortical olfactory areas. Because CN I uniquely bypasses the thalamus before reaching cortex, smell is tightly linked to memory and emotion via direct limbic connections, explaining why odors so powerfully evoke recollections.

incorrectas.A: Taste is carried by CN VII (anterior two-thirds of the tongue), CN IX (posterior third), and CN X (epiglottic region), not by CN I, even though smell and taste are perceptually intertwined.
incorrectas.B: Vision is transmitted by CN II (optic nerve), which carries visual information from the retina to the lateral geniculate nucleus and visual cortex — a completely separate special sense pathway from CN I's olfactory role.
incorrectas.C: Hearing is carried by CN VIII (vestibulocochlear nerve) via the cochlea and cochlear nuclei, an auditory pathway unrelated to CN I's olfactory function.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve is unique in that its sensory information reaches the cerebral cortex without first synapsing in the thalamus?

e.correcta: Nearly all ascending sensory modalities relay through the thalamus before reaching their cortical targets — except olfaction. Olfactory bulb output travels via the olfactory tract directly to primary olfactory (piriform) cortex and limbic structures like the amygdala, bypassing the thalamus, only reaching the thalamus (mediodorsal nucleus) secondarily for further processing. This direct limbic route helps explain smell's uniquely strong link to memory and emotion.

incorrectas.A: CN II carries visual information, which synapses in the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus before projecting to primary visual cortex, following the standard thalamic relay pattern that CN I alone skips.
incorrectas.B: CN VIII carries auditory and vestibular information, which relays through brainstem nuclei and the inferior colliculus before reaching the medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus and then auditory cortex — a full thalamic relay, unlike CN I.
incorrectas.D: CN V carries facial and oral sensory information that relays through the ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus of the thalamus before reaching somatosensory cortex, following the typical thalamic route that olfaction alone bypasses.

preguntas.q: The optic nerve (CN II) is classified as which type of cranial nerve?

e.correcta: CN II carries only special sensory (visual) fibers from the retina to the brain, with no motor fibers — it is actually considered an outgrowth of the diencephalon rather than a true peripheral nerve, wrapped in meninges instead of a typical nerve sheath. In the mnemonic 'Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most,' CN II is an 'S,' grouping it with CN I and CN VIII as purely sensory nerves.

incorrectas.B: A purely motor nerve carries efferent fibers to muscle, but CN II carries no motor fibers at all — eye movement is instead handled by CN III, IV, and VI, not CN II.
incorrectas.C: Mixed (both motor and sensory) nerves like CN V, VII, IX, and X carry both fiber types, but CN II is exclusively sensory with no motor component.
incorrectas.D: CN II carries no autonomic (parasympathetic or sympathetic) fibers; the pupillary light reflex's efferent parasympathetic limb runs through CN III, not CN II, which supplies only the afferent visual signal.

preguntas.q: What sensory function does CN II (the optic nerve) provide?

e.correcta: CN II transmits visual information from retinal photoreceptors, via retinal ganglion cell axons, through the optic chiasm and optic tracts to the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus and then to primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe. Because it also serves as the afferent (sensory) limb for the pupillary light reflex, lesions of CN II cause both visual field loss and an afferent pupillary defect.

incorrectas.B: Hearing is transmitted by CN VIII (vestibulocochlear nerve) through the cochlear pathway, a completely separate special sense from the vision carried by CN II.
incorrectas.C: Smell is the function of CN I (olfactory nerve), which bypasses the thalamus entirely — unlike CN II, which relays through the thalamus (lateral geniculate nucleus) on its way to cortex.
incorrectas.D: Balance (vestibular sense) is carried by the vestibular division of CN VIII, relying on the semicircular canals and otolith organs, not by CN II.

preguntas.q: A lesion of which cranial nerve abolishes the afferent (sensory) limb of the pupillary light reflex, so that light shone in the affected eye fails to constrict either pupil?

e.correcta: The pupillary light reflex has an afferent limb (retina to pretectal nucleus via CN II) and an efferent limb (Edinger-Westphal nucleus to sphincter pupillae via CN III). A CN II lesion knocks out the afferent limb, so light shone into the affected eye produces neither a direct nor a consensual response, while the response is preserved when light is shone in the healthy eye — the basis of a relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil).

incorrectas.A: CN III carries the efferent (motor) limb of the reflex via parasympathetic fibers to the sphincter pupillae; a CN III lesion causes loss of pupillary constriction when light hits either eye, but light detection itself is unaffected — the opposite pattern from a CN II lesion.
incorrectas.B: CN VII innervates facial muscles (including orbicularis oculi for eyelid closure) and has no role in detecting light or in pupillary constriction, so it does not participate in either limb of the light reflex.
incorrectas.C: CN VI innervates only the lateral rectus for eye abduction and has no sensory or parasympathetic role in the pupillary light reflex.

preguntas.q: Lesions of which cranial nerve produce visual field deficits (anopsia)?

e.correcta: CN II carries the entire visual pathway from retina to brain, so damage anywhere along it — the nerve itself, the chiasm, the optic tracts, or the radiations — produces a visual field deficit whose pattern (monocular, bitemporal, or homonymous) helps localize the lesion. Damage to the optic nerve proper specifically causes monocular vision loss in the affected eye.

incorrectas.A: CN III lesions impair extraocular movement, eyelid elevation, and pupillary constriction, causing diplopia, ptosis, and a 'down-and-out' eye, but they do not cause visual field cuts because CN III carries no visual sensory fibers.
incorrectas.B: CN IV lesions weaken the superior oblique, causing vertical/torsional diplopia worse on downgaze, not a loss of visual field, since CN IV is a purely motor nerve.
incorrectas.D: CN VI lesions weaken the lateral rectus, causing horizontal diplopia and impaired abduction, but they do not affect the visual field because CN VI carries no sensory fibers.

preguntas.q: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) is classified as which type of cranial nerve?

e.correcta: CN III carries somatic motor fibers to four of the six extraocular muscles (superior, inferior, and medial rectus, and inferior oblique) plus the levator palpebrae superioris, along with parasympathetic fibers to the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle, but no general sensory fibers. In the mnemonic 'Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most,' CN III is classified as 'M' (motor), grouping it with CN IV, VI, XI, and XII.

incorrectas.A: A purely sensory classification would mean CN III only carries afferent fibers, but in fact CN III supplies motor and parasympathetic efferents to eye muscles with no general sensory function.
incorrectas.C: 'Both' describes mixed nerves such as CN V, VII, IX, and X that carry substantial general sensory input from their territories; CN III has no general sensory component, so it is classified purely as motor rather than mixed.
incorrectas.D: CN III does not carry any special sensory modality (like vision, hearing, or smell) — that role belongs to nerves such as CN I, II, and VIII, not CN III.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve innervates the superior rectus muscle, allowing elevation of the eye?

e.correcta: CN III innervates the superior rectus (along with the inferior rectus, medial rectus, and inferior oblique), making it responsible for elevation of the eye, especially when the eye is abducted. Because CN III supplies four of the six extraocular muscles plus the levator palpebrae and pupillary sphincter, a complete CN III palsy produces the characteristic 'down-and-out' eye with ptosis and a dilated pupil.

incorrectas.A: CN IV innervates only the superior oblique, which primarily depresses the eye (especially when adducted) and assists with intorsion — a very different, more limited action than the superior rectus's elevation.
incorrectas.C: CN VI innervates only the lateral rectus, which abducts the eye; it plays no role in elevation and is entirely distinct from the muscles CN III controls.
incorrectas.D: CN VII is the facial nerve, supplying muscles of facial expression rather than any extraocular muscle, so it has no role in eye elevation.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve innervates the inferior rectus muscle, responsible for depression of the eye (best seen in abduction)?

e.correcta: CN III innervates the inferior rectus, which depresses the eye most effectively when the eye is already abducted (moved laterally), since in that position its pulling action is purely vertical. CN III also supplies the superior rectus, medial rectus, inferior oblique, levator palpebrae, and pupillary sphincter, so lesions of this nerve cause combined deficits in elevation, depression, adduction, lid position, and pupil size.

incorrectas.A: CN VI innervates only the lateral rectus (abduction) and has no role in vertical eye movement, unlike CN III's control of the inferior rectus.
incorrectas.B: CN IV innervates the superior oblique, which depresses the eye best when it is adducted (the opposite position from where the inferior rectus is most effective), reflecting a complementary but distinct depression mechanism from CN III's inferior rectus.
incorrectas.C: CN VII controls facial expression muscles, not any extraocular muscle, so it plays no part in vertical eye movement.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve innervates the medial rectus muscle, producing adduction of the eye?

e.correcta: CN III innervates the medial rectus, the muscle responsible for adducting the eye (moving it toward the nose), which is also essential for convergence during near vision. Along with its four other extraocular/levator targets and its parasympathetic pupillary fibers, a CN III palsy produces an eye that cannot adduct, elevate, or fully depress, resulting in an abducted, 'down-and-out' resting position.

incorrectas.B: CN IV innervates the superior oblique, which contributes to depression and intorsion of the eye, not adduction, making it functionally distinct from the medial rectus.
incorrectas.C: CN VI innervates the lateral rectus, which abducts the eye — the opposite movement from the medial rectus's adduction, and the two nerves work in balanced opposition during horizontal gaze.
incorrectas.D: CN II is the optic nerve, carrying only visual sensory information with no motor fibers to any extraocular muscle, so it has no role in adduction.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve innervates the inferior oblique muscle, contributing to elevation and extorsion of the eye?

e.correcta: CN III innervates the inferior oblique, which elevates and extorts the eye, acting most effectively when the eye is adducted. This complements the superior rectus (also CN III) for elevation in the abducted position, giving CN III control over the full range of upward eye movement across different gaze positions.

incorrectas.A: CN IV innervates the superior oblique, the inferior oblique's functional antagonist — the superior oblique depresses and intorts the eye rather than elevating and extorting it.
incorrectas.B: CN VI innervates only the lateral rectus for abduction, an entirely horizontal action with no torsional or elevating component like the inferior oblique's.
incorrectas.D: CN VII supplies facial expression muscles, not extraocular muscles, and thus has no role in elevating or torting the eye.

preguntas.q: CN III's parasympathetic fibers act on the sphincter pupillae to produce which pupillary response?

e.correcta: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers in CN III synapse in the ciliary ganglion, and postganglionic fibers innervate the sphincter pupillae, causing pupillary constriction (miosis) — the efferent limb of the pupillary light reflex and part of the near response. Because these parasympathetic fibers run along the outside of CN III, they are especially vulnerable to compression (e.g., an expanding posterior communicating artery aneurysm), which classically causes early pupillary dilation instead.

incorrectas.A: Pupillary dilation (mydriasis) is produced by sympathetic innervation of the dilator pupillae via the superior cervical ganglion, the opposite pathway from CN III's parasympathetic constriction of the sphincter pupillae.
incorrectas.B: A CN III lesion does change pupil size — loss of parasympathetic tone unopposed by intact sympathetics leads to a fixed, dilated pupil — so 'no change' is not the correct description of what CN III's parasympathetics normally do.
incorrectas.C: CN III's parasympathetics also control accommodation via the ciliary muscle, but the question specifically asks about the sphincter pupillae's action, which is constriction, not the separate accommodation function.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve innervates the levator palpebrae superioris, the muscle that elevates the upper eyelid?

e.correcta: CN III innervates the striated muscle component of the levator palpebrae superioris, which actively elevates the upper eyelid; a smooth-muscle component (the superior tarsal muscle) is separately controlled by sympathetic fibers. A CN III palsy therefore causes ptosis, which can sometimes mask the down-and-out eye position and dilated pupil that also result from the lesion.

incorrectas.A: CN VII innervates orbicularis oculi, the muscle that closes the eyelid, the functional opposite of the levator palpebrae's opening action; CN VII lesions (e.g., Bell palsy) cause inability to close the eye, not ptosis.
incorrectas.C: CN V provides sensory innervation to the face and cornea (and motor to the muscles of mastication), but it does not innervate any eyelid muscle.
incorrectas.D: CN IV innervates only the superior oblique, an extraocular muscle involved in eye depression and intorsion, with no role in eyelid position.

preguntas.q: In vasculopathic (e.g., diabetic) CN III palsy caused by ischemia of the nerve's core, which fiber type is preferentially affected first?

e.correcta: The blood supply to CN III comes from small vessels on the nerve's surface, so the centrally located motor fibers are most vulnerable to ischemia (as in diabetes or hypertension), while the peripherally located parasympathetic fibers are relatively spared from a purely vascular insult. This produces a 'pupil-sparing' CN III palsy — ptosis and impaired eye movement with a normal, reactive pupil — a classic feature distinguishing it from compressive lesions.

incorrectas.A: Parasympathetic fibers travel along the periphery of CN III, closer to the nerve's own surface vasculature, so they are relatively protected from central ischemia and are instead the fibers most vulnerable to external compression, not vascular disease.
incorrectas.B: CN III does not carry sympathetic fibers at all — sympathetic innervation to the eye travels separately via the long ciliary nerves and superior cervical ganglion, unrelated to this ischemia/compression distinction.
incorrectas.D: CN III carries no general somatic sensory fibers from the face or eye; that role belongs to CN V, so sensory fiber vulnerability is not part of this classic ischemia-versus-compression teaching point.

preguntas.q: In compressive CN III palsy (e.g., from a posterior communicating artery aneurysm or uncal herniation), which fiber type is affected first?

e.correcta: The parasympathetic fibers destined for the sphincter pupillae run superficially along the periphery of CN III, making them the first to be affected by an expanding mass such as a posterior communicating artery aneurysm or uncal herniation. This produces an early 'blown,' fixed, dilated pupil (with ptosis and ophthalmoplegia developing as compression worsens) — a red flag for a neurosurgical emergency, contrasting with the pupil-sparing pattern of vasculopathic CN III palsy.

incorrectas.B: Motor fibers lie centrally within CN III and are relatively protected from external compression initially, being more vulnerable to ischemic injury from compromised intrinsic blood supply — the opposite vulnerability pattern from parasympathetic fibers.
incorrectas.C: CN III does not carry general somatic sensory fibers, so this fiber type is not part of the compression-versus-ischemia distinction relevant to CN III palsy.
incorrectas.D: CN III does not carry special sensory fibers (like vision or hearing) — those travel in CN II and CN VIII respectively, unrelated to the fiber-vulnerability pattern seen in CN III lesions.

preguntas.q: A lesion of which cranial nerve abolishes the efferent (motor) limb of the pupillary light reflex, preventing pupillary constriction in response to light shone in either eye?

e.correcta: The efferent limb of the pupillary light reflex runs from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus through CN III's parasympathetic fibers to the sphincter pupillae. A CN III lesion abolishes this motor output, so the affected pupil fails to constrict whether light is shone directly into it or into the opposite (consensual) eye, even though light detection via CN II remains intact.

incorrectas.A: CN II carries the afferent (sensory) limb of the light reflex; a CN II lesion prevents the affected eye from detecting light at all, so neither pupil constricts when light hits that eye — a different pattern from the isolated motor loss seen with CN III lesions.
incorrectas.B: CN IV is a purely motor nerve to the superior oblique with no parasympathetic or pupillary function, so it plays no role in the light reflex at all.
incorrectas.C: CN VI is a purely motor nerve to the lateral rectus with no parasympathetic fibers, so it does not participate in either limb of the pupillary light reflex.

preguntas.q: A complete CN III palsy classically produces which pupillary finding?

o.C: A pinpoint pupil unresponsive to naloxone
o.D: Anisocoria that worsens in dim light only

e.correcta: Loss of CN III's parasympathetic input to the sphincter pupillae leaves the sympathetically innervated dilator pupillae unopposed, producing a fixed, 'blown,' dilated (mydriatic) pupil that does not constrict to light or accommodation. When this finding appears early and is accompanied by ptosis and ophthalmoplegia, it raises concern for a compressive lesion (aneurysm or herniation) rather than a purely ischemic one.

incorrectas.B: Miosis (pupillary constriction) would instead suggest a problem affecting sympathetic outflow (e.g., Horner syndrome) or preserved parasympathetic tone, the opposite of what unopposed sympathetic activity produces after CN III palsy.
incorrectas.C: A pinpoint, opioid-responsive pupil reflects opioid intoxication or a pontine lesion affecting descending sympathetics, an entirely different clinical picture from the mydriasis of CN III palsy.
incorrectas.D: Anisocoria that specifically worsens in dim light points toward a sympathetic lesion (Horner syndrome), where the affected pupil fails to dilate in the dark — the reverse of CN III palsy, where the affected pupil is already dilated and fails to constrict in light.

preguntas.q: A CN III palsy impairs the eye's ability to focus on near objects, a deficit termed cycloplegia, because it interrupts innervation to which structure?

e.correcta: CN III's parasympathetic fibers innervate the ciliary muscle, whose contraction relaxes the lens's zonular fibers and allows the lens to round up for near focus (accommodation). A CN III lesion disrupts this input, producing cycloplegia — loss of accommodation — alongside mydriasis, ptosis, and extraocular movement deficits, since all of these depend on structures CN III controls.

incorrectas.A: The dilator pupillae is controlled by sympathetic fibers, not CN III, and its dysfunction would affect pupil dilation rather than the lens-focusing function that defines cycloplegia.
incorrectas.B: The lateral rectus, which abducts the eye, is innervated by CN VI, not CN III, and its impairment causes horizontal diplopia rather than a focusing deficit.
incorrectas.D: The superior tarsal muscle is a smooth muscle innervated by sympathetic fibers that provides a small amount of eyelid elevation; its loss contributes to Horner syndrome-associated ptosis, not to cycloplegia, which specifically involves the ciliary muscle.

preguntas.q: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is classified as which type of cranial nerve?

e.correcta: CN IV is a purely motor nerve, supplying only the superior oblique muscle, with no sensory component. It is notable anatomically as the only cranial nerve to exit from the dorsal (posterior) surface of the brainstem and the one with the longest intracranial course, making it particularly vulnerable to head trauma. In the 'Some Say Marry Money...' mnemonic, CN IV is classified as 'M' for motor.

incorrectas.A: A sensory-only classification is inconsistent with CN IV's role, since it carries no afferent fibers at all — it exclusively drives contraction of the superior oblique.
incorrectas.B: Mixed nerves (both motor and sensory), like CN V, VII, IX, and X, carry substantial general sensory input in addition to motor fibers; CN IV has no sensory component, so it cannot be classified as mixed.
incorrectas.D: CN IV carries no special sensory modality such as vision, hearing, or smell — those belong to CN I, II, and VIII, not to the purely motor CN IV.

preguntas.q: Patients with a CN IV (trochlear) palsy often tilt their head in which direction to compensate for the deficit?

o.A: Toward the side of the lesion
o.B: The head remains upright with no tilt
o.D: Away from the side of the lesion

e.correcta: The superior oblique normally intorts the eye; without it, the affected eye tends to extort and drift upward, causing vertical/torsional diplopia. Patients compensate by tilting the head away from (contralateral to) the lesioned side, which reduces the demand for intorsion and realigns the images, easing the diplopia — an unexplained head tilt should prompt evaluation for a trochlear nerve palsy.

incorrectas.A: Tilting toward the lesioned side would actually worsen the extorsion-related image misalignment, since the compensatory tilt works by reducing the demand on the weakened superior oblique's intorting action, which requires tilting away from, not toward, the affected side.
incorrectas.B: Patients with CN IV palsy are not typically upright and tilt-free — the head tilt is a hallmark compensatory sign that helps clinicians recognize the palsy on physical exam.
incorrectas.C: Backward head extension is not the compensatory maneuver seen in trochlear palsy; the characteristic compensation is a lateral head tilt (often with a slight chin-down posture), not extension.

preguntas.q: A CN IV (trochlear) palsy causes the affected eye to deviate in which direction, most noticeably during contralateral (adducted) gaze?

e.correcta: The superior oblique's depressing action is strongest when the eye is adducted, as occurs in contralateral gaze, so loss of CN IV function unmasks upward deviation of the affected eye specifically in that position, since the unopposed inferior oblique (which elevates in adduction) is no longer counterbalanced. This is why the diplopia of a trochlear palsy classically worsens on downgaze and contralateral gaze, such as when reading or walking downstairs.

incorrectas.A: Downward deviation would be expected if the depressors were unopposed, but a superior oblique palsy removes a depressor, so the eye drifts upward (not downward) in the adducted position, the opposite of this option.
incorrectas.B: Medial deviation (adduction) is governed by the medial rectus (CN III), a muscle unaffected by a trochlear lesion, so adduction itself is preserved in CN IV palsy — the abnormality is vertical/torsional, not medial.
incorrectas.C: Lateral deviation (abduction) reflects lateral rectus (CN VI) function, which is unrelated to the superior oblique's vertical/torsional action and is not the deficit produced by a CN IV lesion.

preguntas.q: A patient reports increasing difficulty walking downstairs and reading, worse when looking down. Which cranial nerve lesion is most likely responsible?

e.correcta: CN IV innervates the superior oblique muscle, which is the primary depressor of the adducted eye and also contributes intorsion. A trochlear palsy causes vertical diplopia that worsens on downgaze, making tasks that require looking down - like walking downstairs or reading - especially difficult; patients often develop a compensatory head tilt away from the affected side to minimize the diplopia.

incorrectas.A: CN III palsy produces a "down and out" eye with ptosis and a dilated, poorly reactive pupil due to loss of most extraocular muscles and parasympathetic fibers; it does not selectively impair downgaze in the way an isolated superior oblique/CN IV lesion does.
incorrectas.C: CN VI palsy weakens the lateral rectus, causing horizontal diplopia and an inward-deviated eye (esotropia) that worsens on lateral gaze toward the affected side, not specifically downgaze.
incorrectas.D: The optic nerve carries visual information from the retina to the brain; a lesion causes visual field loss or blindness, not diplopia or extraocular muscle weakness, since CN II has no motor function.

preguntas.q: The abducens nerve (CN VI) is classified as which type of cranial nerve?

e.correcta: CN VI is a pure motor nerve that innervates only the lateral rectus muscle, mediating abduction of the eye. The mnemonic "Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most" tracks CN I-XII as Sensory, Motor, or Both - CN VI falls under "Motor," alongside III, IV, XI, and XII.

incorrectas.B: A purely sensory nerve carries only afferent information to the CNS; CN VI has no sensory component, unlike nerves such as CN I, II, or VIII, which relay smell, vision, and hearing/balance information.
incorrectas.C: "Both" nerves (like V, VII, IX, X) carry both efferent motor fibers and afferent sensory fibers; CN VI has only an efferent motor limb to the lateral rectus and no sensory fibers to reclassify it as mixed.
incorrectas.D: CN VI carries no autonomic/parasympathetic fibers at all - parasympathetic outflow from the brainstem travels with CN III, VII, IX, and X, not with the abducens nerve.

preguntas.q: Contraction of the lateral rectus muscle produces which movement of the eye?

e.correcta: The lateral rectus, innervated by CN VI, pulls the eye laterally away from the midline - abduction - because its fibers run straight back from the globe to the lateral orbital wall, giving it a pure horizontal vector with no vertical or torsional component.

incorrectas.A: Adduction (moving the eye toward the nose) is produced by the medial rectus, innervated by CN III, which pulls in the opposite horizontal direction from the lateral rectus.
incorrectas.C: Elevation is primarily produced by the superior rectus and inferior oblique (both CN III), which have vertical vectors quite different from the lateral rectus's purely horizontal pull.
incorrectas.D: Depression is primarily produced by the inferior rectus and superior oblique (CN III and CN IV respectively); the lateral rectus does not contribute meaningfully to vertical eye movement.

preguntas.q: Patients with a CN VI (abducens) palsy may partially close the eyelid on the affected side to reduce diplopia, mimicking which finding?

e.correcta: In CN VI palsy, the unopposed medial rectus pulls the eye into esotropia, and patients may squint or partially close the lid to blunt the resulting horizontal diplopia; because the levator palpebrae (CN III) is intact, this lid narrowing is not true paralytic ptosis but a compensatory "pseudo-ptosis."

incorrectas.A: True ptosis results from dysfunction of the levator palpebrae superioris (CN III) or Muller's muscle (sympathetics), not from a CN VI lesion, which has no motor supply to the eyelid at all.
incorrectas.C: Lagophthalmos is the inability to fully close the eyelid, classically from CN VII (facial nerve) palsy affecting the orbicularis oculi - the opposite problem of an eyelid that will not close, rather than one that is voluntarily narrowed.
incorrectas.D: Blepharospasm is involuntary, often bilateral spasmodic contraction of the orbicularis oculi, a distinct movement disorder unrelated to the voluntary lid-narrowing squint used to reduce diplopia in CN VI palsy.

preguntas.q: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is classified as which type of cranial nerve?

e.correcta: CN V carries somatosensory fibers from the face, scalp, cornea, and oral cavity via its three divisions (V1, V2, V3), and also carries motor fibers - exclusively through V3 - to the muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, pterygoids) plus tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini. Per "Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most," CN V is one of the four "Both" nerves along with VII, IX, and X.

incorrectas.A: Calling CN V purely sensory ignores its motor root, which travels with V3 to supply the muscles of mastication - a clinically important distinction tested by jaw deviation toward a weak side in V3 lesions.
incorrectas.B: Calling CN V purely motor ignores its much larger sensory role, providing general sensation to the entire face, cornea (afferent limb of corneal reflex), anterior tongue, and oral/nasal mucosa.
incorrectas.D: "Special sensory" refers to nerves carrying smell, vision, taste, hearing, or balance (e.g., CN I, II, VII taste, VIII); CN V's sensory fibers are general (touch/pain/temperature/proprioception), not special sensory.

preguntas.q: Which branch of the trigeminal nerve supplies general sensation to the forehead, scalp, and cornea?

e.correcta: The ophthalmic division (V1) exits through the superior orbital fissure and supplies sensory innervation to the upper face, scalp, and cornea, making it the afferent limb of the corneal (blink) reflex - loss of V1 sensation abolishes the corneal reflex on that side even though the motor (blink) response via CN VII remains intact.

incorrectas.B: The maxillary nerve (V2) exits through foramen rotundum and supplies the midface - upper lip, maxillary teeth, palate, and nasal cavity - not the forehead or cornea.
incorrectas.C: The mandibular nerve (V3) exits through foramen ovale and supplies the lower face, jaw, and mandibular teeth, along with motor fibers to mastication muscles; it has no role in corneal or forehead sensation.
incorrectas.D: The facial nerve (CN VII) provides motor innervation to facial expression muscles and taste to the anterior tongue, but general touch sensation to the face is a trigeminal (CN V), not facial nerve, function.

preguntas.q: Which branch of the trigeminal nerve supplies general sensation to the palate, nasal cavity, maxillary face, and maxillary teeth?

e.correcta: The maxillary nerve (V2) passes through the foramen rotundum into the pterygopalatine fossa and continues through the inferior orbital fissure to emerge on the face as the infraorbital nerve, along the way supplying the palate, nasal cavity, maxillary sinus/teeth, and midface skin.

incorrectas.A: V1 exits through the superior orbital fissure and supplies only the forehead, upper eyelid, and cornea - it does not extend down to the palate, nose, or maxillary teeth.
incorrectas.C: V3 exits through foramen ovale and supplies the lower face and mandibular teeth as well as the muscles of mastication; it is anatomically and functionally distinct from V2's maxillary distribution.
incorrectas.D: CN IX supplies the posterior third of the tongue, pharynx, and carotid body/sinus - it plays no role in facial or dental sensation, which is entirely a trigeminal function.

preguntas.q: Which branch of the trigeminal nerve supplies general sensation to the jaw and mandibular teeth?

e.correcta: The mandibular nerve (V3) exits the skull through foramen ovale and, via its inferior alveolar branch, enters the mandibular canal to supply the mandibular teeth before exiting through the mental foramen as the mental nerve to supply the chin. V3 is unique among the trigeminal divisions in also carrying the motor root to the muscles of mastication.

incorrectas.A: V1 exits through the superior orbital fissure and is limited to the upper face, scalp, and cornea - it has no distribution to the mandible or lower teeth.
incorrectas.B: V2 exits through foramen rotundum and supplies the midface, palate, and maxillary teeth, an entirely separate dental arch from the mandibular teeth supplied by V3.
incorrectas.D: CN VII supplies motor fibers to facial expression muscles and taste to the anterior tongue, but has no general sensory distribution to the jaw or teeth - that is exclusively trigeminal territory.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve provides general (touch/pain/temperature) sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?

o.A: Mandibular nerve, V3 (via the lingual nerve)

e.correcta: General somatosensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue travels via the lingual nerve, a branch of V3 (mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve). This is a classic Step 1 dissociation: the same anterior two-thirds of tongue receives its taste (special sensory) supply from a different nerve, CN VII's chorda tympani, which travels alongside the lingual nerve without being part of it.

incorrectas.B: CN VII supplies taste (not general touch/pain) to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via the chorda tympani, and also gives motor innervation to facial muscles - but general somatosensation there belongs to V3, not VII.
incorrectas.C: CN IX supplies both general sensation and taste to the posterior one-third of the tongue, the opposite territory from the anterior two-thirds tested here.
incorrectas.D: CN X supplies taste and general sensation only to the small area near the epiglottis/root of tongue, not the anterior two-thirds, which is trigeminal/facial territory.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve provides motor innervation to the muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids)?

e.correcta: The motor root of the trigeminal nerve travels exclusively with V3 to supply the four muscles of mastication - masseter, temporalis, and medial/lateral pterygoids - plus tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini. A unilateral V3 motor lesion causes jaw deviation toward the weak side on opening, because the unopposed contralateral lateral pterygoid pushes the jaw over.

incorrectas.B: CN VII innervates the muscles of facial expression (derived from the second pharyngeal arch), a completely separate muscle group from the first-arch-derived muscles of mastication supplied by V3.
incorrectas.C: CN XII is a pure motor nerve to the intrinsic and most extrinsic muscles of the tongue, not the muscles that move the mandible for chewing.
incorrectas.D: CN X supplies motor fibers to the pharynx, larynx, and palate (except tensor veli palatini, which is V3), but has no role in the muscles that elevate/protrude the jaw for chewing.

preguntas.q: A patient describes repetitive, unilateral, shooting facial pain in the CN V distribution, each episode lasting less than a minute and triggered by chewing or touching the face. What is the diagnosis?

e.correcta: Trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux) causes brief, severe, electric shock-like pain in one or more trigeminal divisions, classically triggered by light touch, chewing, or talking, often from vascular compression of the nerve root; first-line treatment is carbamazepine.

incorrectas.B: Cluster headache causes unilateral periorbital pain with autonomic features (lacrimation, rhinorrhea, ptosis) lasting 15 minutes to 3 hours, in clusters over weeks - a very different distribution and duration from the sub-minute, touch-triggered pain of trigeminal neuralgia.
incorrectas.C: Glossopharyngeal neuralgia produces similar brief, shock-like pain but in the distribution of CN IX - throat, tonsillar region, and ear - typically triggered by swallowing or coughing, not the CN V (facial) distribution described here.
incorrectas.D: Migraine with aura is a throbbing, often unilateral headache lasting hours to days, preceded by visual or sensory aura, and lacks the millisecond-to-second trigger-evoked shocks characteristic of trigeminal neuralgia.

preguntas.q: Individual episodes of trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux) typically last how long?

e.correcta: Trigeminal neuralgia produces paroxysms of severe, lancinating pain that last only seconds to under a minute per episode, though episodes can recur many times a day and tend to increase in frequency and intensity over time; carbamazepine is first-line therapy.

incorrectas.B: A 1-3 hour duration is characteristic of cluster headache attacks, not trigeminal neuralgia, which is defined by its extremely brief, shock-like paroxysms rather than sustained pain.
incorrectas.C: A 4-72 hour duration describes an untreated migraine attack, a fundamentally different, throbbing headache disorder rather than the brief neuralgic shocks of tic douloureux.
incorrectas.D: Trigeminal neuralgia pain does not persist continuously for days; between attacks patients are typically pain-free, which helps distinguish it from other chronic facial pain syndromes.

preguntas.q: The facial nerve (CN VII) is classified as which type of cranial nerve?

e.correcta: CN VII carries motor fibers to the muscles of facial expression (and stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior digastric), special sensory taste fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via the chorda tympani, general sensory fibers from a small area behind the ear, and parasympathetic fibers to the lacrimal, submandibular, and sublingual glands - making it a mixed ("Both") nerve like V, IX, and X in the "Some Say Marry Money..." mnemonic.

incorrectas.A: Restricting CN VII to "motor only" ignores its substantial sensory role in taste (chorda tympani) and small cutaneous patch behind the ear, both clinically tested findings in facial nerve lesions.
incorrectas.B: Restricting CN VII to "sensory only" ignores its primary, most clinically obvious function - motor innervation of facial expression muscles, whose loss produces the characteristic facial droop of Bell's palsy.
incorrectas.D: CN VII does carry parasympathetic fibers (to lacrimal and salivary glands), but it is not "parasympathetic only" since its dominant and most tested function is somatic motor control of facial muscles.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve carries special sensory taste fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?

o.A: Facial nerve (CN VII), via the chorda tympani

e.correcta: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the chorda tympani branch of CN VII, which joins the lingual nerve (a branch of V3) peripherally but carries its own special visceral afferent taste fibers back to the facial nerve's cell bodies in the geniculate ganglion - distinct from V3's general touch/pain fibers traveling the same physical path.

incorrectas.B: CN IX carries taste from the posterior one-third of the tongue, the opposite region from the anterior two-thirds tested here.
incorrectas.C: CN X carries taste only from a small area near the epiglottis and root of the tongue, not the anterior two-thirds.
incorrectas.D: CN V (via the lingual nerve, V3) carries general somatosensation (touch, pain, temperature) from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, but not taste - the classic dissociation is V3 for touch and VII for taste in that same region.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve provides motor innervation to the muscles of facial expression?

e.correcta: CN VII, arising from the second pharyngeal (branchial) arch, supplies all muscles of facial expression (frontalis, orbicularis oculi, orbicularis oris, buccinator, platysma, etc.). A peripheral (LMN) CN VII lesion, as in Bell's palsy, paralyzes the entire ipsilateral face including the forehead, whereas a central (UMN) lesion spares the forehead due to bilateral cortical innervation of the upper face.

incorrectas.B: V3 innervates the first-arch-derived muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, pterygoids), a completely separate muscle group from the second-arch facial expression muscles supplied by CN VII.
incorrectas.C: CN XII is a pure motor nerve to the tongue musculature, controlling tongue movement and shape, not facial expression.
incorrectas.D: CN X supplies the pharynx, larynx, and palate muscles (fourth/sixth arch derivatives) involved in swallowing and phonation, not the muscles that produce facial expressions.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve innervates the orbicularis oculi muscle, allowing forceful eyelid closure?

e.correcta: The orbicularis oculi is a muscle of facial expression, derived from the second pharyngeal arch and innervated by CN VII; its paralysis in a facial nerve lesion causes lagophthalmos (inability to fully close the eye), risking corneal drying and injury since the protective blink reflex is impaired.

incorrectas.B: CN III innervates the levator palpebrae superioris, which opens (elevates) the eyelid - the antagonist action to orbicularis oculi's closing function; a CN III lesion causes ptosis (droopy lid), not impaired closure.
incorrectas.C: V1 provides sensory innervation to the cornea and periorbital skin (the afferent limb of the corneal reflex) but has no motor fibers to any eyelid muscle.
incorrectas.D: CN VI is a pure motor nerve to the lateral rectus for eye abduction; it has no role in eyelid movement whatsoever.

preguntas.q: Cutaneous sensory branches of the facial nerve (CN VII) supply a small area of skin near which structure?

e.correcta: Beyond its dominant motor and taste functions, CN VII contributes a small general sensory branch to the skin of the posterior external ear/mastoid region - clinically relevant because herpes zoster oticus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome) can cause painful vesicles in this exact area alongside facial palsy and hearing changes.

incorrectas.B: The bridge of the nose is supplied by the ophthalmic (V1) and, more inferiorly, the maxillary (V2) divisions of the trigeminal nerve, not by CN VII.
incorrectas.C: The upper lip receives sensation from the infraorbital branch of the maxillary nerve (V2), a trigeminal territory unrelated to the facial nerve's small cutaneous patch.
incorrectas.D: The chin is supplied by the mental nerve, a branch of the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve, not by CN VII.

preguntas.q: The vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) is classified as which type of cranial nerve?

e.correcta: CN VIII is a purely sensory (special sensory) nerve, carrying auditory information from the cochlea and vestibular/balance information from the semicircular canals and otolithic organs to the brainstem; it has no efferent motor fibers, unlike mixed nerves such as V, VII, IX, and X.

incorrectas.A: CN VIII has no motor component at all - the small efferent olivocochlear fibers that modulate hair cell sensitivity are not classically taught as a "motor" function on Step 1, and the nerve overall is categorized as sensory.
incorrectas.C: Unlike CN V, VII, IX, and X, which genuinely carry both afferent and efferent fibers, CN VIII lacks any motor limb, so it does not belong in the "Both" category of the cranial nerve mnemonic.
incorrectas.D: CN VIII carries no autonomic/parasympathetic fibers; autonomic cranial nerve outflow is limited to III, VII, IX, and X.

preguntas.q: What are the two principal functions of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII)?

e.correcta: CN VIII has two divisions - the cochlear division, which transduces sound into neural signals for hearing, and the vestibular division, which relays head position/acceleration information from the semicircular canals and otoliths for balance and postural control - both are purely sensory functions.

incorrectas.B: Taste is carried by CN VII (anterior 2/3 tongue), IX (posterior 1/3), and X (epiglottis) - CN VIII carries no taste information at all.
incorrectas.C: While vestibular input from CN VIII does feed into reflexes like the vestibulo-ocular reflex, CN VIII itself does not control eye movement directly - that requires the motor cranial nerves III, IV, and VI acting on extraocular muscles.
incorrectas.D: Facial movement is a CN VII motor function; CN VIII is purely sensory and contributes nothing to facial muscle control.

preguntas.q: A lesion of which cranial nerve classically causes sensorineural hearing loss along with loss of balance?

e.correcta: CN VIII carries both cochlear (hearing) and vestibular (balance) fibers, so lesions - such as vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) at the cerebellopontine angle - classically produce unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo/imbalance together, reflecting damage to both divisions of the nerve.

incorrectas.A: CN VII lesions (e.g., Bell's palsy) cause facial weakness, loss of taste on the anterior tongue, and sometimes hyperacusis (due to stapedius paralysis), but not sensorineural hearing loss or vestibular imbalance, since VII carries no cochlear or vestibular fibers.
incorrectas.C: CN V lesions cause facial numbness, loss of the corneal reflex, and/or weakness of mastication, with no effect on hearing or balance, since the trigeminal nerve has no auditory or vestibular fibers.
incorrectas.D: CN IX lesions impair posterior tongue taste/sensation, pharyngeal sensation, and the gag reflex, but CN IX has no role in hearing or balance, which are exclusively CN VIII functions.

preguntas.q: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is classified as which type of cranial nerve?

e.correcta: CN IX carries motor fibers to stylopharyngeus and parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland, plus sensory fibers (taste and general sensation) from the posterior third of the tongue, pharynx/tonsils, and the carotid body/sinus - making it a "Both" nerve alongside V, VII, and X.

incorrectas.A: CN IX's motor contribution (to a single muscle, stylopharyngeus, plus parotid secretomotor fibers) is real but not its only function - it also carries substantial sensory input, so "motor only" is incomplete.
incorrectas.B: CN IX is not purely sensory - it does supply motor fibers to stylopharyngeus (which elevates the pharynx during swallowing) and parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland, in addition to its sensory roles.
incorrectas.D: "Special sensory only" would describe a nerve carrying just taste or another special sense; CN IX carries both special sensory (posterior tongue taste) and general sensory (pharyngeal touch/pain, baroreceptor/chemoreceptor input) fibers, plus motor fibers, so it doesn't fit this narrower category.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve carries taste sensation from the posterior one-third of the tongue?

e.correcta: CN IX supplies both taste and general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue (the region posterior to the sulcus terminalis), reflecting this portion of the tongue's embryologic origin from the third pharyngeal arch, which is innervated by the nerve of that arch, CN IX.

incorrectas.B: CN VII (chorda tympani) supplies taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, the region derived from the first arch, the opposite territory from the posterior third tested here.
incorrectas.C: CN X supplies taste only from a small area near the epiglottis/root of the tongue, distal to the posterior-third region that CN IX covers.
incorrectas.D: CN V provides general (not taste) sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via V3's lingual nerve branch; it carries no taste fibers to any part of the tongue.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve provides general somatosensation to the posterior one-third of the tongue, tonsillar region, and upper pharynx (the afferent limb of the gag reflex)?

e.correcta: CN IX carries both general sensation and taste from the posterior third of the tongue, and also innervates the tonsillar pillars and oropharyngeal mucosa, forming the afferent (sensory) limb of the gag reflex; the efferent (motor) limb of the gag reflex is carried by CN X to the pharyngeal muscles.

incorrectas.B: CN VII supplies taste (not general sensation) to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and has no role in pharyngeal or tonsillar sensation or the gag reflex's afferent limb.
incorrectas.C: CN X carries the motor (efferent) limb of the gag reflex to the pharyngeal muscles and supplies sensation to the larynx/lower pharynx, but the sensory trigger from the tonsils/oropharynx that initiates the reflex is CN IX's territory.
incorrectas.D: V3 provides general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and the lower face/jaw, an entirely different territory from the posterior tongue and pharynx supplied by CN IX.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve carries afferent signals from the carotid body chemoreceptors and carotid sinus baroreceptors?

e.correcta: CN IX (via its carotid sinus branch) carries chemoreceptor input (PO2, PCO2, pH from the carotid body) and baroreceptor input (blood pressure from the carotid sinus) to the medullary cardiovascular and respiratory centers, forming a key afferent arc for reflex control of blood pressure and ventilation.

incorrectas.B: CN X carries analogous chemoreceptor/baroreceptor information from the aortic arch and aortic bodies (not the carotid structures), a related but anatomically distinct reflex arc from the CN IX-mediated carotid pathway.
incorrectas.C: CN VIII is a purely sensory nerve for hearing and balance and has no connection to cardiovascular or respiratory chemoreceptor/baroreceptor reflexes.
incorrectas.D: CN V carries somatosensory information from the face and mouth; it plays no role in monitoring blood gases or blood pressure.

preguntas.q: The vagus nerve (CN X) is classified as which type of cranial nerve?

e.correcta: CN X carries motor fibers to the muscles of the pharynx, larynx, and palate (except stylopharyngeus and tensor veli palatini), extensive parasympathetic fibers to thoracic and abdominal viscera down to the splenic flexure, and sensory fibers from the larynx, pharynx, and thoracoabdominal organs - making it one of the "Both" mixed nerves alongside V, VII, and IX.

incorrectas.A: CN X is not motor only - it also carries major parasympathetic outflow (the primary source of parasympathetic tone to the heart, lungs, and GI tract) and sensory fibers from the larynx and viscera, so "motor only" undersells its role dramatically.
incorrectas.B: CN X is not sensory only - its motor fibers to the pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles are essential for swallowing and phonation, and a vagal lesion produces palatal/vocal cord weakness (e.g., uvula deviation, hoarseness), which a purely sensory nerve could never cause.
incorrectas.D: While CN X does carry extensive parasympathetic fibers, it is not "parasympathetic only" - it also has somatic motor fibers to skeletal muscle of the pharynx/larynx and general/visceral sensory fibers, making "Both" the accurate classification.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve carries afferent input from the aortic arch baroreceptors and aortic body chemoreceptors?

e.correcta: CN X (vagus) carries visceral afferents from the aortic arch baroreceptors and the aortic bodies (chemoreceptors sensing PaO2, PaCO2, and pH) to the nucleus tractus solitarius, enabling reflex regulation of blood pressure and respiration. This runs in parallel with CN IX's carotid sinus/body afferents, so together the two nerves form the cranial baro/chemoreceptor pathways, with the aortic arch specifically belonging to the vagus (mnemonic: aortic arch = arch-shaped X, carotid = C for CN IX).

incorrectas.A: Glossopharyngeal nerve carries afferents from the carotid sinus baroreceptors and carotid body chemoreceptors, which are anatomically and cranially distinct from the aortic arch/body input carried by the vagus.
incorrectas.C: The accessory nerve is purely motor, supplying the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; it carries no visceral sensory (baro- or chemoreceptor) fibers at all.
incorrectas.D: The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor to the tongue musculature and plays no role in cardiovascular or respiratory reflex sensing.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve provides taste sensation to the epiglottic and supraglottic mucosa?

e.correcta: CN X carries special visceral afferent (taste) fibers from the epiglottis and supraglottic region via the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve to the nucleus solitarius. This complements CN VII, which handles taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and CN IX, which handles the posterior third, so together the three nerves cover the entire taste map from tongue to larynx.

incorrectas.A: The facial nerve's chorda tympani supplies taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not the epiglottis or supraglottic mucosa, which lie outside its distribution.
incorrectas.B: Glossopharyngeal nerve supplies taste and general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue and oropharynx, but the epiglottis and supraglottic larynx are vagal territory, not glossopharyngeal.
incorrectas.D: The trigeminal nerve carries general somatic sensation (touch, pain, temperature) to the face and anterior tongue but has no taste fibers whatsoever.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve supplies parasympathetic innervation to the thoracic and abdominal viscera down to the splenic flexure?

e.correcta: CN X provides preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the heart, lungs, esophagus, stomach, and intestines up to the splenic flexure, synapsing on ganglia within or near the target organ walls to slow heart rate and stimulate secretions and peristalsis. Parasympathetic supply to the distal colon and rectum instead comes from the sacral (pelvic splanchnic) outflow, so the splenic flexure marks the vagus's caudal limit — a boundary that also corresponds to the embryologic midgut-hindgut junction.

incorrectas.B: CN IX provides parasympathetic fibers only to the parotid gland via the otic ganglion, not to the thoracoabdominal viscera.
incorrectas.C: Pelvic splanchnic nerves supply parasympathetic innervation to the hindgut (distal colon, rectum) and pelvic organs, taking over exactly where the vagus's coverage ends at the splenic flexure.
incorrectas.D: The accessory nerve is purely motor to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius and carries no parasympathetic fibers.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve is most responsible for swallowing and elevation of the soft palate?

e.correcta: CN X's motor fibers to the pharyngeal constrictors and levator veli palatini (via the pharyngeal plexus) drive both the pharyngeal phase of swallowing and elevation of the soft palate, which seals off the nasopharynx during the swallow. Vagal damage classically produces dysphagia along with palatal droop and uvula deviation away from the lesioned side.

incorrectas.A: CN IX contributes the stylopharyngeus muscle (pharyngeal elevation/widening) and sensory input to the swallow reflex, but the principal motor drive for pharyngeal constriction and palate elevation is vagal, not glossopharyngeal.
incorrectas.C: CN V's motor division innervates the tensor veli palatini and muscles of mastication, not the levator veli palatini or pharyngeal constrictors responsible for swallowing.
incorrectas.D: CN VII innervates the muscles of facial expression and the stapedius muscle, which are unrelated to pharyngeal swallowing or soft palate elevation.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve is most responsible for talking and coughing?

e.correcta: The vagus, via its recurrent and superior laryngeal branches, supplies the intrinsic laryngeal muscles that control vocal cord tension and closure — required both for phonation (talking) and for the forceful glottic closure and expulsion that make up a cough. Injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve produces hoarseness and a weak, breathy or 'bovine' cough, reflecting loss of this vagal motor control.

incorrectas.B: The hypoglossal nerve controls tongue movement, which contributes to articulation, but it does not control vocal cord function, so it is not the nerve most responsible for phonation or cough generation.
incorrectas.C: Glossopharyngeal nerve contributes the afferent (sensory) limb of the cough reflex from the oropharynx, but the motor output driving laryngeal closure and vocalization is vagal, not glossopharyngeal.
incorrectas.D: The phrenic nerve drives diaphragmatic contraction, providing the inspiratory and expulsive force behind a cough, but it does not control the larynx itself, which is essential for both talking and the explosive phase of coughing.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve is responsible for keeping the uvula in the midline?

e.correcta: CN X innervates the muscles of the soft palate (levator veli palatini, musculus uvulae) bilaterally, symmetrically pulling the uvula upward at the midline during phonation. A unilateral vagal lesion causes unopposed pull from the intact side, so the uvula deviates away from the side of the lesion — a classic bedside sign.

incorrectas.B: CN IX has minimal motor contribution to palate muscles; it is primarily sensory to the posterior tongue and pharynx, so it does not explain uvula deviation.
incorrectas.C: CN VII innervates the muscles of facial expression below the eyes and around the mouth, but not the intrinsic palate muscles that stabilize uvula position.
incorrectas.D: CN XII controls tongue muscles; a hypoglossal lesion causes tongue deviation toward the lesion side, not uvula deviation — a key distinguishing point between the two nerves on exam.

preguntas.q: What type of cranial nerve is the accessory nerve (CN XI)?

e.correcta: The accessory nerve (CN XI) is a purely motor cranial nerve, innervating the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, with no sensory or autonomic component. This fits the classic mnemonic grouping cranial nerves by function ('Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most'), in which CN XI is marked as Motor.

incorrectas.B: CN XI carries no general or special sensory fibers; sensation from the neck region is instead carried by cervical spinal nerves and other cranial nerves.
incorrectas.C: Several cranial nerves (V, VII, IX, X) are mixed motor and sensory, but CN XI is one of the 'pure motor' exceptions, grouped with III, IV, VI, and XII.
incorrectas.D: CN XI has no parasympathetic or other autonomic fibers; autonomic outflow via cranial nerves is limited to III, VII, IX, and X.

preguntas.q: When the left sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle contracts alone, to which side does it turn the head?

o.C: It does not rotate the head
