e.correcta: Each SCM originates on the sternum and clavicle and inserts on the mastoid process; unilateral contraction tilts the head toward the ipsilateral shoulder while rotating the chin to the contralateral side. Because of this contralateral rotation, a contracting left SCM turns the face to the right, which is why a left CN XI lesion produces weakness turning the head to the right — an important point when localizing accessory nerve palsies.

incorrectas.B: Turning the head to the left would instead require contraction of the right SCM, not the left; confusing this contralateral action is a common exam pitfall.
incorrectas.C: The SCM is a major mover of head rotation and lateral flexion, so ignoring its rotational action would miss the primary movement being tested by this nerve.
incorrectas.D: Bilateral SCM contraction, together with other neck muscles, contributes to neck flexion, and unilateral contraction produces rotation — not backward extension.

preguntas.q: What type of cranial nerve is the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)?

e.correcta: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is a purely motor cranial nerve, supplying the extrinsic and intrinsic muscles of the tongue with no sensory or autonomic fibers. It belongs with III, IV, VI, and XI as the 'pure motor' cranial nerves in the classic functional mnemonic ('Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most').

incorrectas.A: CN XII carries no sensory fibers at all; general sensation to the tongue is carried by CN V3 (anterior two-thirds) and CN IX (posterior third), not the hypoglossal nerve.
incorrectas.C: Nerves like V, VII, IX, and X are mixed motor and sensory, but CN XII is purely motor, without a sensory division.
incorrectas.D: CN XII has no parasympathetic fibers; autonomic cranial outflow is limited to CN III, VII, IX, and X.

preguntas.q: What is the primary function of CN XII (hypoglossal nerve)?

o.C: General sensation to the anterior tongue

e.correcta: CN XII innervates the extrinsic tongue muscles (genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus) and the intrinsic tongue muscles, controlling protrusion, retraction, and shape changes needed for speech, swallowing, and chewing. A notable exception worth remembering is the palatoglossus, which despite being a tongue muscle is actually innervated by CN X, not CN XII.

incorrectas.A: Taste to the posterior third of the tongue is carried by CN IX, not CN XII, which has no sensory component of any kind.
incorrectas.C: General (touch/pain/temperature) sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the lingual branch of CN V3, not the hypoglossal nerve.
incorrectas.D: Salivation is driven by parasympathetic fibers from CN VII (submandibular/sublingual glands) and CN IX (parotid gland), not CN XII, which is purely motor to muscle.

preguntas.q: In a patient with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and no history of chemotherapy or radiation exposure, what is the most likely underlying mechanism?

o.A: De novo somatic mutations in hematopoietic stem cells
o.C: Chronic viral infection of myeloid precursors
o.D: Autoimmune destruction of the bone marrow stroma

e.correcta: MDS is a clonal stem-cell disorder in which spontaneous, acquired ('de novo') somatic mutations accumulate in hematopoietic stem cells, producing dysplastic, ineffective hematopoiesis and cytopenias despite a normal or hypercellular marrow. The same clinical picture can also arise from known mutagenic exposures such as radiation, benzene, or alkylating chemotherapy, making MDS either primary (de novo) or secondary (therapy- or exposure-related).

incorrectas.B: Germline BRCA mutations predispose to breast, ovarian, and pancreatic cancers and some hematologic malignancies via DNA repair defects, but they are not the typical mechanism behind sporadic MDS, which is an acquired somatic process rather than an inherited one.
incorrectas.C: MDS is not driven by chronic viral infection of myeloid precursors; a virally driven hematologic malignancy mechanism is more characteristic of HTLV-1-associated adult T-cell leukemia, not myelodysplasia.
incorrectas.D: MDS is a clonal neoplastic stem cell disorder rather than primarily an autoimmune process; autoimmune marrow failure (as in aplastic anemia) is a distinct entity with a different underlying mechanism.

preguntas.q: Which exposure is most classically associated with pseudo-Pelger-Huet anomaly (bilobed, hyposegmented neutrophils)?

e.correcta: Pseudo-Pelger-Huet anomaly is an acquired dysplastic change in neutrophil nuclear segmentation (bilobed, 'pince-nez' or hyposegmented nuclei) seen after myelosuppressive chemotherapy or in myelodysplastic syndromes, reflecting disordered granulocyte maturation. It mimics the benign inherited Pelger-Huet anomaly in appearance, but arises from an acquired marrow insult rather than the germline lamin B receptor mutation that causes the true anomaly.

incorrectas.B: Iron deficiency causes microcytic, hypochromic anemia due to impaired hemoglobin synthesis; it does not alter neutrophil nuclear morphology.
incorrectas.C: Acute bacterial infection classically produces a left shift with increased band forms and toxic granulation, a distinct morphologic response from the dysplastic hyposegmentation seen in pseudo-Pelger-Huet anomaly.
incorrectas.D: B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic changes including hypersegmented neutrophils — the opposite nuclear pattern — along with macro-ovalocytes, not hyposegmentation.

preguntas.q: Which feature distinguishes chronic leukemias, such as CLL, from acute leukemias at the cellular level?

o.D: Rapid replacement of marrow by fibrosis

e.correcta: Chronic leukemias are neoplastic proliferations of mature-appearing, but functionally incompetent, lymphocytes that accumulate in blood and marrow, producing a high WBC count with a typically indolent, slower-onset course. This contrasts with acute leukemias, which are proliferations of immature blasts that rapidly crowd out normal hematopoiesis and present with a much faster clinical tempo.

incorrectas.B: Proliferation of undifferentiated blasts is the hallmark of acute leukemia (ALL/AML), not chronic leukemia, which by definition involves more mature-appearing malignant cells.
incorrectas.C: Auer rods are crystallized granule aggregates found in myeloblasts, a feature of acute myeloid leukemia, not a finding in mature lymphocyte-driven chronic leukemias.
incorrectas.D: Diffuse marrow fibrosis with rapid replacement is characteristic of primary myelofibrosis, a myeloproliferative neoplasm, not a defining feature that separates chronic from acute leukemia.

preguntas.q: Chronic leukemias, which have an insidious onset, are typically seen in which age group?

e.correcta: Chronic leukemias, particularly CLL, have a slow, often asymptomatic onset — frequently discovered incidentally on a routine CBC showing lymphocytosis — and predominantly affect older adults, typically over age 60. This reflects the gradual accumulation of a slowly proliferating malignant clone over decades, in sharp contrast to the abrupt presentation typical of acute leukemias.

incorrectas.B: Neonatal leukemias are exceedingly rare and, when they occur, are typically acute (often linked to specific genetic syndromes such as Down syndrome), not the indolent chronic pattern described here.
incorrectas.C: Childhood leukemia is overwhelmingly acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), which presents abruptly, unlike the insidious chronic leukemias that arise in older adults.
incorrectas.D: Young adults are not the typical demographic for chronic leukemias; CLL incidence rises sharply with age and is rare before age 50.

preguntas.q: Which is the most common leukemia among adults in Western countries?

e.correcta: CLL is the most common leukemia in adults in the Western world, typically presenting in older patients with lymphocytosis, smudge cells on peripheral smear, and a monoclonal population of CD5+ B cells. Its high prevalence largely reflects its indolent natural history, which allows many cases to accumulate and be detected over long clinical courses.

incorrectas.A: AML is the most common acute leukemia in adults and can present aggressively with Auer rods on smear, but it is overall less prevalent than the long-surviving, indolent CLL population.
incorrectas.C: ALL is primarily a childhood leukemia; although it can occur in adults, it is far less common in the adult population than CLL.
incorrectas.D: CML, associated with the BCR-ABL fusion from t(9;22), is less common than CLL and typically presents with marked leukocytosis and splenomegaly rather than being the most prevalent adult leukemia.

preguntas.q: Which immune abnormality in CLL predisposes patients to recurrent infections?

e.correcta: The malignant B cells in CLL are functionally incompetent and fail to properly differentiate into antibody-producing plasma cells, and their clonal expansion crowds out and suppresses normal B-cell populations, resulting in hypogammaglobulinemia (reduced levels of functional antibodies). This humoral immunodeficiency is the main driver of recurrent bacterial infections, which are in fact the leading cause of death in CLL.

incorrectas.B: CLL causes decreased, not increased, overall immunoglobulin production; an excess of IgA is not a recognized feature of this disease.
incorrectas.C: Complement deficiencies are distinct genetic or acquired disorders (e.g., terminal complement deficiency predisposing to Neisseria infections) and are not the mechanism underlying CLL-associated infection risk.
incorrectas.D: CLL primarily impairs humoral (antibody-mediated) immunity via B-cell dysfunction rather than neutrophil function, which distinguishes its infection risk pattern from conditions like chronic granulomatous disease.

preguntas.q: What is the most common cause of death in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia?

e.correcta: Because CLL cripples humoral immunity through hypogammaglobulinemia, most patients ultimately succumb to infections, often with encapsulated bacteria, rather than to direct effects of tumor bulk. This is why infection surveillance and prophylaxis (and sometimes IVIG) are central to long-term CLL management.

incorrectas.B: Hyperviscosity syndrome is classically associated with Waldenström macroglobulinemia (IgM paraproteinemia), not CLL, which does not typically produce a monoclonal protein at levels that cause hyperviscosity.
incorrectas.C: Tumor lysis syndrome is a risk during treatment of rapidly proliferating, highly chemosensitive tumors (such as Burkitt lymphoma or acute leukemias), not a typical spontaneous cause of death in the indolent course of CLL.
incorrectas.D: Richter transformation converts CLL into an aggressive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not Hodgkin lymphoma, and while serious, it is a less common cause of death overall compared to recurrent infection.

preguntas.q: Which autoimmune complication targeting erythrocytes can occur in CLL?

e.correcta: CLL is associated with autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA), often warm IgG-mediated, in which antibodies coat red cells and target them for destruction by splenic macrophages; this reflects broader immune dysregulation from the leukemic clone. It is confirmed by a positive direct Coombs test and is typically treated with corticosteroids in addition to CLL-directed therapy.

incorrectas.B: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura can also occur as an autoimmune complication of CLL, but it targets platelets rather than erythrocytes, so it does not answer a question specifically about red cell destruction.
incorrectas.C: Guillain-Barre syndrome is a demyelinating autoimmune neuropathy typically triggered by an antecedent infection (e.g., Campylobacter jejuni), and is unrelated to the immune dysregulation seen in CLL.
incorrectas.D: Autoimmune hepatitis targets hepatocytes and is not a recognized paraneoplastic or autoimmune complication of CLL.

preguntas.q: Richter transformation of CLL into diffuse large B-cell lymphoma classically presents clinically with which finding?

o.A: Rapidly enlarging lymph node or spleen

e.correcta: Richter transformation should be suspected when a CLL patient develops a disproportionately, rapidly enlarging lymph node, spleen, or extranodal mass along with systemic B symptoms such as fever, weight loss, and a rising LDH. This reflects a subclone transforming into an aggressive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, which requires biopsy for diagnosis and aggressive lymphoma-directed chemotherapy rather than standard CLL management.

incorrectas.B: Petechiae would suggest thrombocytopenia from marrow infiltration or immune destruction, not the classic mass-forming presentation of Richter transformation, which is a rapidly growing nodal or extranodal lesion.
incorrectas.C: Richter transformation does not cause resolution of lymphocytosis; the underlying CLL clone persists alongside the new aggressive lymphoma, and overall disease burden typically worsens.
incorrectas.D: Patients with Richter transformation typically experience clinical deterioration, including worsening performance status and systemic symptoms, given the aggressive nature of the transformed lymphoma, not improvement.

preguntas.q: Diagnosis of hairy cell leukemia today relies primarily on which test, having largely replaced the classic TRAP stain?

e.correcta: Flow cytometry immunophenotyping, detecting markers such as CD11c, CD25, CD103, and CD123 on the malignant B cells, is now the standard for diagnosing hairy cell leukemia. It offers greater sensitivity and reproducibility than the older tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) cytochemical stain, though the classic hairy cytoplasmic projections and TRAP positivity remain well-known teaching points.

incorrectas.B: Bone marrow biopsy in HCL often shows increased reticulin fibrosis, contributing to the classic 'dry tap,' but fibrosis grading is not the diagnostic test that has replaced TRAP staining.
incorrectas.C: Cytogenetic testing can identify the BRAF V600E mutation common in HCL, which is a supportive or confirmatory finding, but it is not the primary test that has replaced TRAP staining — that role belongs to flow cytometry.
incorrectas.D: Reticulocyte count assesses the marrow's erythropoietic response in anemia workups and plays no role in diagnosing or distinguishing hairy cell leukemia.

preguntas.q: Hairy cell leukemia characteristically lacks which clinical finding that is common in other lymphoproliferative disorders?

e.correcta: Unlike most lymphoid leukemias and lymphomas, hairy cell leukemia notably spares the lymph nodes — the malignant cells instead infiltrate the bone marrow (often causing a 'dry tap' due to associated fibrosis) and the splenic red pulp, producing massive splenomegaly without significant lymphadenopathy. This pattern is a classic distinguishing feature from CLL, which does typically cause lymphadenopathy.

incorrectas.B: Splenomegaly, often massive, is a hallmark of HCL due to red pulp infiltration by hairy cells — it is a prominent, characteristic finding, not something that is absent.
incorrectas.C: Pancytopenia is common in HCL due to marrow infiltration/fibrosis and splenic sequestration of blood cells, so it is a typical finding rather than an absent one.
incorrectas.D: Marrow infiltration by hairy cells is characteristic, often producing the classic 'dry tap' on aspiration, so it is present, unlike lymphadenopathy, which is classically absent.

preguntas.q: Hairy cell leukemia shows an excellent response to cladribine (2-CDA), whose mechanism involves inhibition of which enzyme?

e.correcta: Cladribine is a purine nucleoside analog that resists degradation by adenosine deaminase and, once phosphorylated intracellularly, accumulates as a toxic deoxyadenosine triphosphate analog that incorporates into DNA and disrupts repair. This causes preferential apoptosis of the relatively quiescent but adenosine-deaminase-dependent lymphoid cells in HCL, and a single course often produces durable remission, making it first-line therapy.

incorrectas.B: Dihydrofolate reductase is the target of methotrexate, which blocks folate-dependent nucleotide synthesis — a mechanism unrelated to cladribine's purine-analog toxicity via adenosine deaminase resistance.
incorrectas.C: Topoisomerase II is inhibited by drugs like etoposide or anthracyclines, which cause DNA strand breaks by a mechanism distinct from purine analog metabolism.
incorrectas.D: Ribonucleotide reductase is inhibited by hydroxyurea, a different class of antimetabolite acting on deoxyribonucleotide synthesis rather than adenosine deaminase resistance.

preguntas.q: In addition to cladribine, which other adenosine deaminase inhibitor is used to treat hairy cell leukemia?

e.correcta: Pentostatin (deoxycoformycin) is, like cladribine, a purine analog that inhibits adenosine deaminase, causing toxic accumulation of deoxyadenosine and dATP that is particularly damaging to lymphoid cells. It serves as an effective alternative or second-line agent to cladribine in the treatment of hairy cell leukemia.

incorrectas.B: Fludarabine is a purine analog used in CLL and other lymphoid malignancies that acts via inhibition of DNA polymerase and ribonucleotide reductase, but it is not an adenosine deaminase inhibitor and is not the classic second ADA-inhibiting drug used for HCL.
incorrectas.C: Azathioprine is a purine analog prodrug metabolized to 6-mercaptopurine and used as an immunosuppressant in transplant and autoimmune disease, not as a treatment for hairy cell leukemia, and it does not act as an adenosine deaminase inhibitor.
incorrectas.D: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, used to prevent gout and tumor lysis-associated hyperuricemia — a completely different enzyme target from adenosine deaminase, and it is not a chemotherapeutic agent for HCL.

preguntas.q: Hairy cell leukemia most typically affects which demographic group?

e.correcta: HCL classically presents in middle-aged to older adult men, with a median age around the 50s, reflecting its status as a rare, indolent B-cell neoplasm with a strong male predominance. This demographic pattern, combined with massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia without lymphadenopathy, helps distinguish it clinically from other chronic lymphoproliferative disorders.

incorrectas.B: HCL shows a strong male predominance rather than affecting young females; this demographic profile does not match the disease's known epidemiology.
incorrectas.C: HCL is a disease of adulthood, arising from accumulated somatic mutations (notably BRAF V600E) over a lifetime, not a neonatal or congenital condition.
incorrectas.D: HCL is rare in adolescents; its incidence rises with age and peaks in older adulthood, unlike leukemias such as ALL that predominate in children and teens.

preguntas.q: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, caused by HTLV-1 infection, is a neoplastic proliferation of which cell type?

e.correcta: ATLL arises from HTLV-1-infected CD4+ T lymphocytes; the viral Tax protein drives constitutive activation of pathways like NF-kB, promoting uncontrolled clonal proliferation of these CD4+ cells. The malignant cells characteristically show flower-shaped ('cloverleaf') nuclei on smear and the disease can present with hypercalcemia, skin lesions, and lytic bone lesions, all traceable to the CD4+ T-cell lineage being transformed.

incorrectas.B: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells are not the target lineage in ATLL; HTLV-1 preferentially infects and transforms CD4+ helper T cells, not CD8+ cells.
incorrectas.C: CD19+ B cells are the malignant lineage in B-cell neoplasms like CLL or ALL, but ATLL is a T-cell, not B-cell, malignancy driven by a retrovirus rather than typical B-cell oncogenic mutations.
incorrectas.D: Natural killer cells give rise to a distinct entity, extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (nasal type), typically associated with EBV, which differs from the HTLV-1-driven, CD4+ T-cell origin of ATLL.

preguntas.q: A patient with adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) develops erythematous skin lesions. What is the most likely explanation for this cutaneous finding?

o.A: Direct skin infiltration by neoplastic T cells

e.correcta: ATLL, caused by HTLV-1-infected CD4+ T cells, frequently involves direct infiltration of the dermis and epidermis by malignant lymphocytes, producing rash-like cutaneous lesions ranging from papules to exfoliative erythroderma. This skin tropism, together with hypercalcemia, lytic bone lesions, and generalized lymphadenopathy/hepatosplenomegaly, is a hallmark of the acute and lymphomatous subtypes of ATLL and reflects the same CD4+ T-cell clone that circulates in blood homing to the skin.

incorrectas.B: Paraneoplastic vasculitis is an immune-complex-mediated process seen with some malignancies, but it is not the mechanism behind ATLL's skin lesions; here the malignant T cells themselves physically infiltrate the skin rather than triggering vessel inflammation.
incorrectas.C: A graft-versus-host-like reaction requires transplanted immunocompetent donor lymphocytes attacking host tissue, which does not apply to ATLL, a primary malignancy of the patient's own HTLV-1-transformed T cells.
incorrectas.D: Immunosuppression from ATLL can predispose to infections, but the characteristic rash is due to the leukemic/lymphomatous process infiltrating skin, not a secondary bacterial infection.

preguntas.q: A patient presents with lytic bone lesions and hypercalcemia, and the differential includes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) versus multiple myeloma. Which additional clinical finding would point toward ATLL rather than multiple myeloma?

o.B: Monoclonal (M) spike on serum protein electrophoresis

e.correcta: Both ATLL and multiple myeloma can cause lytic bone lesions and hypercalcemia (myeloma via osteoclast-activating cytokines from plasma cells, ATLL via PTHrP-like humoral mechanisms from the malignant T cells), which is why they are a classic exam mimicker pair. The key discriminator is that ATLL, driven by HTLV-1-transformed CD4+ T cells, characteristically infiltrates the skin to produce a rash, a feature multiple myeloma (a plasma cell neoplasm) does not typically produce.

incorrectas.B: An M spike reflects a monoclonal immunoglobulin produced by a clonal plasma cell population and is the signature finding of multiple myeloma, not ATLL, which is a T-cell (not plasma cell) malignancy.
incorrectas.C: Rouleaux formation results from elevated serum immunoglobulins/paraproteins altering red cell interactions and is characteristic of multiple myeloma, not the T-cell process seen in ATLL.
incorrectas.D: Bence Jones proteinuria is free monoclonal light chain excreted by malignant plasma cells in multiple myeloma; ATLL does not produce a monoclonal immunoglobulin because it arises from T cells, not plasma cells.

preguntas.q: Mycosis fungoides is a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma composed of a neoplastic proliferation of which type of mature lymphocyte?

e.correcta: Mycosis fungoides is an indolent, slowly progressive cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) arising from mature, skin-homing CD4+ helper T cells that infiltrate the epidermis and superficial dermis. This CD4+ phenotype is why the disease can eventually spill into the blood as Sézary syndrome, a leukemic phase composed of the same malignant CD4+ clone, recognizable by their cerebriform nuclei (Sézary cells).

incorrectas.B: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells are not the neoplastic population in mycosis fungoides; the malignant clone is CD4+, part of why the disease behaves as an indolent helper-T-cell process rather than a cytotoxic one.
incorrectas.C: Naive B cells are the cell of origin for B-cell lymphomas such as follicular lymphoma, not mycosis fungoides, which is specifically a T-cell-derived cutaneous lymphoma.
incorrectas.D: Natural killer cells give rise to distinct NK-cell lymphomas (e.g., extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type) with very different clinical behavior, and are not the cell type involved in mycosis fungoides.

preguntas.q: An adult presents with chronic, slowly enlarging patches and plaques on the skin that on biopsy show malignant lymphocytes with Pautrier microabscesses. Where does this cutaneous T-cell lymphoma characteristically manifest first?

e.correcta: Mycosis fungoides is defined by its cutaneous localization: malignant CD4+ T cells home to and infiltrate the epidermis and dermis, producing scaly patches and plaques (and later, in more advanced disease, tumors and erythroderma) rather than presenting primarily as nodal or marrow disease. Skin biopsy showing lymphoid cells forming Pautrier microabscesses within the epidermis confirms the diagnosis.

incorrectas.B: A bulky mediastinal mass is the classic presentation of primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma or nodular sclerosing Hodgkin lymphoma, not mycosis fungoides, which is defined by skin, not nodal, disease at onset.
incorrectas.C: Marrow failure with pancytopenia is not how mycosis fungoides presents; it is a chronic, indolent cutaneous disease that involves the marrow late, if ever, and is diagnosed by skin biopsy.
incorrectas.D: Circulating malignant lymphocytes describe the leukemic phase (Sézary syndrome) that can develop after mycosis fungoides has been established in the skin, not the initial presentation itself.

preguntas.q: On skin biopsy of mycosis fungoides, neoplastic T cells characteristically aggregate within the epidermis to form which histologic finding?

e.correcta: Pautrier microabscesses are collections of malignant, cerebriform-nucleus CD4+ T cells that cluster within the epidermis in mycosis fungoides, a finding considered a diagnostic hallmark on skin biopsy. Their intraepidermal location reflects the epidermotropism of the malignant T-cell clone, distinguishing this cutaneous T-cell lymphoma from other dermatoses.

incorrectas.B: Councilman bodies are eosinophilic apoptotic hepatocytes seen in viral hepatitis and yellow fever, an unrelated hepatic finding with no connection to cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.
incorrectas.C: Civatte bodies are apoptotic keratinocytes seen in lichen planus and other interface dermatitides, reflecting basal keratinocyte death rather than a malignant lymphocyte infiltrate.
incorrectas.D: Langhans giant cells are multinucleated macrophages found in granulomatous inflammation (e.g., tuberculosis, sarcoidosis), a different pathologic process from the neoplastic T-cell aggregates of mycosis fungoides.

preguntas.q: When mycosis fungoides disseminates from the skin into the peripheral blood, producing widespread erythroderma and circulating malignant T cells, this leukemic phase is termed what?

o.D: Leukemic phase of hairy cell leukemia

e.correcta: Sézary syndrome represents the leukemic/erythrodermic progression of mycosis fungoides, in which the same malignant CD4+ T-cell clone spreads beyond the skin into the blood, producing circulating Sézary cells (lymphocytes with characteristic cerebriform nuclei) and diffuse, bright red erythroderma. It is essentially the systemic counterpart of mycosis fungoides, underscoring that the two conditions share a single neoplastic T-cell origin.

incorrectas.B: Richter transformation refers to CLL/SLL transforming into an aggressive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, a distinct B-cell process unrelated to the T-cell disease of mycosis fungoides.
incorrectas.C: Blast crisis describes the terminal accelerated phase of chronic myelogenous leukemia, in which myeloid or lymphoid blasts flood the marrow and blood, a different disease entirely from the T-cell lymphoma progression seen here.
incorrectas.D: Hairy cell leukemia is a distinct B-cell neoplasm marked by TRAP-positive cells with hairy cytoplasmic projections; its leukemic behavior is unrelated to the skin-to-blood spread characteristic of mycosis fungoides/Sézary syndrome.

preguntas.q: The substantia nigra grossly appears black to dark brown due to accumulation of which pigment within its dopaminergic neurons?

e.correcta: The substantia nigra pars compacta contains dopaminergic neurons that synthesize neuromelanin as a byproduct of catecholamine metabolism, giving the nucleus its characteristic dark/black gross appearance. Loss of these pigmented neurons, as occurs in Parkinson disease, causes visible pallor/depigmentation of the substantia nigra on gross or histologic examination, correlating with the disease's motor symptoms.

incorrectas.B: Hemosiderin is an iron-storage pigment that accumulates after hemorrhage or in iron-overload states; it is not the pigment responsible for the substantia nigra's normal dark coloration.
incorrectas.C: Lipofuscin is a 'wear-and-tear' pigment that accumulates with aging in various cell types, including neurons, but it is not what gives the substantia nigra its characteristic black color — that is due to neuromelanin, a distinct pigment tied to dopamine synthesis.
incorrectas.D: Ceroid is an oxidized lipid pigment associated with certain storage disorders and chronic tissue injury, not the pigment normally responsible for nigral coloration.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve is unique in that its fibers decussate within the brainstem before exiting?

e.correcta: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve whose fibers cross to the contralateral side before exiting the brainstem — they decussate within the superior medullary velum, so the CN IV nucleus innervates the contralateral superior oblique muscle. This unusual anatomy also explains why CN IV is the only cranial nerve to exit from the dorsal aspect of the brainstem and has the longest intracranial course, making it particularly vulnerable to trauma.

incorrectas.B: CN III (oculomotor) exits ventrally from the midbrain and innervates ipsilateral extraocular muscles without decussating, unlike the crossed trajectory of CN IV.
incorrectas.C: CN VI (abducens) arises from the caudal pons and travels ipsilaterally to the lateral rectus without any decussation, a straightforward ipsilateral course unlike CN IV.
incorrectas.D: CN VII (facial) fibers loop around the CN VI nucleus (forming the facial colliculus) within the pons, but this looping is not a midline decussation to the opposite side — the nerve still exits and innervates ipsilateral facial muscles.

preguntas.q: The nuclei of which cranial nerves are both located within the midbrain?

e.correcta: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) nucleus sits in the rostral midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus, while the trochlear nerve (CN IV) nucleus lies just caudal to it in the caudal midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus. Both nuclei govern extraocular movements, so midbrain lesions (e.g., from stroke or an expanding mass) can produce combined CN III/CN IV palsies.

incorrectas.B: CN V and VI have their nuclei in the pons (the trigeminal motor/main sensory nuclei and the abducens nucleus), not the midbrain.
incorrectas.C: CN VII and VIII nuclei (facial nucleus and vestibulocochlear nuclei) are located in the pons, a level caudal to the midbrain where CN III and IV reside.
incorrectas.D: CN IX and X nuclei (nucleus ambiguus, dorsal motor nucleus, nucleus solitarius) are situated in the medulla, well caudal to the midbrain.

preguntas.q: Which trigeminal nerve nucleus provides motor innervation to the muscles of mastication?

e.correcta: The trigeminal motor nucleus, located in the rostral pons medial to the main sensory nucleus, houses the cell bodies of motor neurons that travel with the mandibular division (V3) to innervate the muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, pterygoids), along with tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, and anterior digastric. It is the only purely motor nucleus among the trigeminal nuclear complex.

incorrectas.B: The main (chief/principal) sensory nucleus processes tactile and pressure sensation from the face, not motor output, and lies just lateral to the trigeminal motor nucleus.
incorrectas.C: The spinal trigeminal nucleus relays pain and temperature sensation from the face and extends from the pons down to the upper cervical cord; it has no motor role in mastication.
incorrectas.D: The mesencephalic nucleus of CN V contains proprioceptive neuron cell bodies (unusual in lying within the CNS rather than a peripheral ganglion) that relay stretch information from the muscles of mastication, but it does not itself provide their motor innervation.

preguntas.q: Which trigeminal nucleus receives tactile and pressure sensation from the face via CN V?

e.correcta: The main (chief/principal) sensory nucleus of CN V, located in the pons, receives discriminative touch and pressure sensation from the face and is functionally analogous to the dorsal column-medial lemniscus system used elsewhere in the body. This information ascends primarily via the trigeminothalamic tract to the VPM nucleus of the thalamus and then to sensory cortex.

incorrectas.B: The spinal trigeminal nucleus, which extends caudally into the upper cervical spinal cord, carries pain and temperature sensation from the face (analogous to the spinothalamic system), not fine touch/pressure.
incorrectas.C: The mesencephalic nucleus of CN V conveys proprioceptive information from the muscles of mastication and periodontal/temporomandibular structures, not cutaneous tactile/pressure sensation.
incorrectas.D: The trigeminal motor nucleus is a purely motor structure supplying the muscles of mastication; it plays no role in relaying sensory information.

preguntas.q: Which trigeminal nucleus carries pain and temperature sensation from the CN V distributions of the face?

e.correcta: The spinal trigeminal nucleus is the facial analog of the spinothalamic system, carrying pain and temperature sensation; it extends from the level of CN V's entry in the pons all the way down to the upper cervical spinal cord (around C2), becoming continuous with the substantia gelatinosa of the dorsal horn. This long craniocaudal extent explains why lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, which damages this nucleus and tract, causes loss of pain/temperature sensation on the ipsilateral face along with contralateral body loss from the damaged spinothalamic tract.

incorrectas.B: The main sensory nucleus handles fine touch and pressure, not pain and temperature, and is functionally analogous to the dorsal column system rather than the spinothalamic system.
incorrectas.C: The mesencephalic nucleus of CN V relays proprioceptive signals from the jaw muscles, unrelated to cutaneous pain/temperature sensation.
incorrectas.D: The trigeminal motor nucleus is exclusively motor, supplying the muscles of mastication, and carries no sensory information at all.

preguntas.q: Which brainstem nucleus lies immediately ventral to the facial nerve (CN VII) nucleus and integrates auditory input from both cochlear nuclei to enable sound localization?

e.correcta: The superior olivary nucleus, situated in the caudal pons just ventral to the facial nucleus, receives bilateral input from both the ipsilateral and contralateral cochlear nuclei, allowing it to compare interaural time and intensity differences — the basis for localizing sound in space. This bilateral convergence is also why unilateral lesions of the central auditory pathway above the cochlear nuclei rarely cause complete unilateral deafness, unlike lesions of the cochlea or CN VIII itself.

incorrectas.B: The inferior colliculus is a midbrain auditory relay station downstream of the superior olive, important for reflexive responses to sound, but it is not the pontine nucleus immediately ventral to the CN VII nucleus that first integrates bilateral cochlear input.
incorrectas.C: The nucleus ambiguus is a motor nucleus in the medulla supplying the pharynx, larynx, and esophagus via CN IX, X, and XI; it has no auditory function.
incorrectas.D: The medial vestibular nucleus processes vestibular (balance/equilibrium), not auditory, information, and is part of a separate sensory system from the cochlear/olivary auditory pathway.

preguntas.q: Which level of the brainstem houses the nuclei of CN V, VI, VII, and VIII?

e.correcta: The pons contains the trigeminal (V), abducens (VI), facial (VII), and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nuclei, making it (along with the medulla) one of the two richest cranial-nerve-nucleus levels of the brainstem. Lesions localized to the pons (e.g., a pontine stroke) classically produce combinations of ipsilateral facial weakness, lateral gaze palsy, facial sensory loss, and hearing/vestibular disturbance alongside contralateral long-tract signs.

incorrectas.B: The midbrain houses the nuclei of CN III and IV (oculomotor and trochlear), a rostral level distinct from the pontine nuclei of V, VI, VII, and VIII.
incorrectas.C: The medulla houses the nuclei of CN IX, X, and XII, a caudal level distinct from the pons where V, VI, VII, and VIII reside.
incorrectas.D: The upper cervical spinal cord contributes to the nucleus of CN XI (spinal accessory), not to CN V, VI, VII, or VIII, which are entirely brainstem (pontine) in origin.

preguntas.q: The dorsal motor nucleus in the medulla gives rise to preganglionic parasympathetic fibers that travel with which cranial nerve?

e.correcta: The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, located in the medulla, is the primary source of preganglionic parasympathetic outflow that travels within CN X to innervate thoracic and abdominal viscera (heart, lungs, and GI tract down to the splenic flexure). This vagal parasympathetic supply underlies the vagus nerve's broad role in slowing heart rate, promoting bronchoconstriction/secretion, and stimulating GI motility and secretion.

incorrectas.B: CN IX (glossopharyngeal) carries its own preganglionic parasympathetic fibers (to the otic ganglion for parotid secretion) originating from the inferior salivatory nucleus, a separate nucleus from the dorsal motor nucleus, which is specific to the vagus.
incorrectas.C: CN VII (facial) parasympathetic fibers arise from the superior salivatory nucleus, supplying the lacrimal, submandibular, and sublingual glands, distinct from the dorsal motor nucleus that supplies CN X.
incorrectas.D: CN XI (accessory) is a purely somatic motor nerve to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles and carries no parasympathetic fibers from the dorsal motor nucleus.

preguntas.q: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers that supply the heart, lungs, and upper GI tract via the vagus nerve originate from which medullary nucleus?

e.correcta: The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus is the medullary source of preganglionic parasympathetic fibers that travel in CN X to slow heart rate, promote bronchial secretions/constriction, and stimulate GI motility and glandular secretion through the upper gastrointestinal tract. It works alongside — but is functionally distinct from — the nucleus ambiguus, which provides the vagus's somatic motor (not autonomic) fibers to pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles.

incorrectas.B: Nucleus ambiguus is the source of somatic (branchial) motor fibers within CN IX, X, and XI that innervate the muscles of the pharynx, larynx, and upper esophagus for swallowing and phonation, not the visceral parasympathetic outflow to the heart and lungs.
incorrectas.C: Nucleus solitarius is a sensory (afferent) nucleus that receives visceral sensory input like taste and baroreceptor signals; it does not send efferent parasympathetic motor output to viscera.
incorrectas.D: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus is a midbrain parasympathetic nucleus that travels with CN III to mediate pupillary constriction and accommodation, an entirely different target (the eye) from the vagal parasympathetic supply to thoracoabdominal viscera.

preguntas.q: The nucleus solitarius receives sensory afferents carried by which cranial nerves?

e.correcta: The nucleus solitarius (nucleus tractus solitarius) receives visceral sensory afferents — including taste from the facial and glossopharyngeal nerves, and baroreceptor/chemoreceptor and general visceral sensation from the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves — making it the principal visceral sensory relay in the medulla for CN VII, IX, and X. This integration underlies reflexes such as the baroreceptor reflex and the sensory limb of the gag reflex.

incorrectas.B: CN XI (accessory) is a purely somatic motor nerve to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius and contributes no sensory fibers to the nucleus solitarius.
incorrectas.C: CN V (trigeminal) sensory input from the face is processed by the trigeminal sensory nuclei (main sensory and spinal trigeminal), not by the nucleus solitarius, which is dedicated to visceral sensation.
incorrectas.D: CN III (oculomotor) is a motor nerve to extraocular muscles and the pupil, carrying no visceral sensory afferents to the nucleus solitarius.

preguntas.q: Which medullary nucleus is the primary relay for visceral sensory information such as taste, baroreceptor signals, and gut distention?

e.correcta: The nucleus solitarius (solitarius = sensory) is the central visceral afferent relay, receiving taste fibers via CN VII and IX and general visceral sensory input, including baroreceptor and gastrointestinal stretch/distention signals, via CN IX and X. It then projects to autonomic control centers, such as the medullary cardiovascular and respiratory centers, to help mediate reflexes like the baroreceptor reflex.

incorrectas.B: Nucleus ambiguus (ambiguus = motor) is the motor counterpart, supplying somatic motor fibers to pharyngeal/laryngeal muscles via CN IX, X, and XI, not a sensory relay.
incorrectas.C: The dorsal motor nucleus is an efferent (motor) nucleus sending preganglionic parasympathetic fibers out via CN X to the viscera, the opposite direction of information flow from the sensory nucleus solitarius.
incorrectas.D: The spinal trigeminal nucleus relays facial pain and temperature sensation carried by CN V, an entirely different sensory modality and cranial nerve from the visceral afferents processed by the nucleus solitarius.

preguntas.q: The nucleus ambiguus provides motor fibers that travel within which cranial nerves?

o.A: CN IX, X, and XI (cranial portion)

e.correcta: The nucleus ambiguus, located in the medulla, gives rise to somatic (branchial) motor neurons whose axons travel within CN IX, X, and the cranial root of CN XI to supply the muscles of the pharynx, larynx, and upper esophagus, mediating swallowing, phonation, and palate elevation. Damage to this nucleus, as in lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, causes dysphagia, dysarthria, and hoarseness.

incorrectas.B: CN VII (facial) motor fibers arise from the facial motor nucleus, a separate pontine structure supplying facial expression muscles, not from the medullary nucleus ambiguus.
incorrectas.C: CN V motor fibers to the muscles of mastication arise from the trigeminal motor nucleus in the pons, distinct from the nucleus ambiguus and its pharyngeal/laryngeal targets.
incorrectas.D: CN III (oculomotor) motor fibers to the extraocular muscles arise from the oculomotor nucleus in the midbrain, an entirely different level and target from the nucleus ambiguus.

preguntas.q: Which medullary nucleus supplies motor innervation to the pharynx, larynx, and upper esophagus, mediating functions like swallowing and palate elevation?

e.correcta: Nucleus ambiguus (aMbiguus = Motor) houses the cell bodies of somatic motor neurons that travel via CN IX, X, and XI to innervate the striated muscles of the pharynx, larynx, and upper esophagus, driving swallowing, palate elevation, and vocal cord movement. Its damage classically produces the dysphagia and hoarseness seen in lateral medullary syndrome.

incorrectas.B: Nucleus solitarius (solitarius = Sensory) is the sensory counterpart, receiving visceral afferents like taste and baroreceptor input rather than sending motor output to pharyngeal/laryngeal muscles.
incorrectas.C: The dorsal motor nucleus sends autonomic (parasympathetic) fibers via CN X to smooth muscle and glands of the thoracoabdominal viscera, not somatic motor fibers to striated pharyngeal/laryngeal muscle.
incorrectas.D: The trigeminal motor nucleus, located in the pons, supplies the muscles of mastication via CN V, a completely different set of muscles from the pharynx/larynx supplied by the nucleus ambiguus.

preguntas.q: Before decussating to form the medial lemniscus, the axons of the nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus in the caudal medulla are termed what?

e.correcta: Second-order neurons of the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway synapse in the nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus, and their axons — called internal arcuate fibers — sweep ventromedially and cross the midline in the caudal medulla; once they have crossed, these same fibers ascend as the medial lemniscus toward the contralateral thalamus (VPL). This decussation is why fine touch, vibration, and proprioceptive deficits from a medullary lesion affecting these fibers present on the side of the body opposite the lesion.

incorrectas.B: External arcuate fibers are a separate set of medullary fibers (including those contributing to the inferior cerebellar peduncle) related to cerebellar input, not the pathway carrying dorsal column information across the midline.
incorrectas.C: Corticospinal fibers are descending motor fibers that decussate at the pyramidal decussation, a different tract, direction of travel, and level from the internal arcuate fibers of the dorsal column pathway.
incorrectas.D: Spinothalamic fibers carry pain and temperature and decussate at the level of the spinal cord, within a couple of segments of entry, not in the medulla, and never pass through the nucleus gracilis/cuneatus.

preguntas.q: Which level of the brainstem contains the nuclei of CN IX, X, and XII?

e.correcta: The medulla houses the nuclei serving CN IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), and XII (hypoglossal), along with contributions to CN XI, making it the most caudal cranial-nerve-bearing segment of the brainstem. This clustering explains why medullary lesions, such as lateral or medial medullary syndromes, often produce combined deficits in swallowing, phonation, palate/tongue function, and autonomic vagal output.

incorrectas.B: The pons contains the nuclei of CN V, VI, VII, and VIII, a level rostral to the medulla where IX, X, and XII actually reside.
incorrectas.C: The midbrain contains only the nuclei of CN III and IV, the most rostral brainstem cranial nerve nuclei, distinct from the caudal medullary nuclei of IX, X, and XII.
incorrectas.D: The upper cervical spinal cord contributes only to the nucleus of CN XI (spinal accessory), not to CN IX, X, or XII, whose nuclei are medullary.

preguntas.q: Where is the nucleus that gives rise to the spinal root of the accessory nerve (CN XI) located?

o.A: Upper cervical spinal cord (anterior horn, roughly C1-C5/C6)

e.correcta: Unlike the other cranial nerve nuclei, the nucleus of the spinal accessory nerve lies in the anterior (ventral) horn of the upper cervical spinal cord, roughly C1 through C5 or C6, not within the brainstem itself. Fibers from this nucleus ascend through the foramen magnum to briefly join the cranial rootlets before exiting the skull via the jugular foramen to innervate the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.

incorrectas.B: The medulla houses the nuclei of CN IX, X, and XII, not CN XI, whose motor neurons are located more caudally in the cervical spinal cord.
incorrectas.C: The pons houses the nuclei of CN V, VI, VII, and VIII, an entirely different, more rostral level from the spinal cord location of the CN XI nucleus.
incorrectas.D: The midbrain houses the nuclei of CN III and IV, the most rostral cranial nerve nuclei, unrelated to the spinal cord location of CN XI's nucleus.

preguntas.q: Because the fibers of the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) arise from anterior horn cells and ascend along the periphery of the spinal cord before exiting through the foramen magnum, they are characteristically spared by which type of pathology?

o.A: Intramedullary (central cord) lesions such as syringomyelia
o.B: Extramedullary compressive lesions at the jugular foramen
o.C: Skull base fractures involving the jugular foramen
o.D: Direct penetrating trauma to the posterior triangle of the neck

e.correcta: The lower motor neurons of CN XI sit in the anterior horn of the upper cervical cord, and their axons travel along the external/peripheral surface of the cord rather than through its central substance. Because of this superficial trajectory, processes that damage the center of the cord, like intramedullary syringomyelia, characteristically spare CN XI function, whereas lesions affecting the cord's surface, the foramen magnum region, or the jugular foramen (where CN XI actually passes) can readily damage it.

incorrectas.B: Extramedullary compressive lesions at the jugular foramen, such as a jugular foramen schwannoma or glomus tumor, directly compress CN XI as it exits the skull and are actually a classic cause of spinal accessory nerve palsy, unlike central intramedullary disease.
incorrectas.C: Skull base fractures through the jugular foramen can directly transect or compress CN XI fibers as they exit, again a real and recognized cause of CN XI injury, in contrast to the sparing seen with intramedullary lesions.
incorrectas.D: Penetrating trauma to the posterior triangle of the neck can injure CN XI peripherally after it has exited the skull (a common iatrogenic injury during lymph node biopsy in that region), which is unrelated to the sparing of CN XI from intramedullary cord disease.

preguntas.q: Within the medulla, which structure lies between and helps separate the exit zone of CN IX/X (dorsal) from the exit zone of CN XII (ventral to it)?

e.correcta: The olive (inferior olivary nucleus/eminence) is a prominent bulge on the ventrolateral surface of the medulla that sits between the more dorsal exit zone of CN IX and X and the more ventral exit zone of CN XII, which emerges between the olive and the pyramid. This anatomic landmark is clinically useful for localizing medullary lesions based on which combination of cranial nerve deficits and adjacent tract findings are present.

incorrectas.B: The pyramid is the ventral-most medullary structure containing the corticospinal tract, lying medial to CN XII's exit point, not the structure separating CN IX/X from CN XII.
incorrectas.C: The gracile tubercle is a dorsal medullary landmark overlying the nucleus gracilis (part of the dorsal column pathway), unrelated to the ventral cranial nerve exit zones being described.
incorrectas.D: The cuneate tubercle is likewise a dorsal medullary landmark overlying the nucleus cuneatus, a sensory relay structure with no role in separating the ventral exit points of CN IX/X and XII.

preguntas.q: The rootlets of which cranial nerves exit the medulla between the olive and the inferior cerebellar peduncle (the post-olivary sulcus)?

e.correcta: The glossopharyngeal (CN IX) and vagus (CN X) nerve rootlets emerge from the postolivary sulcus, the groove located dorsal to the olive and ventral to the inferior cerebellar peduncle. Along with the cranial root of the accessory nerve (CN XI), these rootlets line up in a vertical row at this location, which is why a lesion here (e.g., lateral medullary/Wallenberg syndrome) classically produces dysphagia, hoarseness, and loss of the gag reflex. Remembering the postolivary sulcus as the exit point for IX, X, and XI helps localize brainstem lesions on imaging or exam findings.

incorrectas.B: CN XII (hypoglossal) rootlets exit from the preolivary sulcus, between the pyramid and the olive — the opposite side of the olive from the postolivary exit point of IX and X — so a preolivary lesion produces tongue weakness (deviating toward the lesion) rather than the postolivary CN IX/X findings.
incorrectas.C: CN VII and CN VIII exit at the cerebellopontine angle, at the pontomedullary junction, a completely different level of the brainstem than the postolivary sulcus of the medulla; lesions there (e.g., vestibular schwannoma) cause facial weakness and hearing/balance loss, not dysphagia or hoarseness.
incorrectas.D: CN VI exits medially at the pontomedullary junction near the midline, not laterally at the medullary postolivary sulcus; its rootlets are vulnerable to compression from a different set of lesions (e.g., raised ICP causing abducens palsy) than those affecting IX and X.

preguntas.q: Rootlets of which cranial nerve exit the medulla between the olive and the medullary pyramid (the preolivary sulcus)?

e.correcta: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) rootlets emerge from the preolivary sulcus, the groove between the pyramid (which carries the corticospinal tract) and the olive (overlying the inferior olivary nucleus). Because the pyramid sits medially, a medial medullary syndrome (occlusion of the anterior spinal artery or a paramedian branch of the vertebral artery) damages both the pyramid and the exiting CN XII rootlets, causing contralateral body weakness plus ipsilateral tongue deviation. This preolivary/postolivary distinction is a classic way boards test localization of medullary strokes.

incorrectas.A: CN IX and CN X exit from the postolivary sulcus, on the dorsal side of the olive facing the inferior cerebellar peduncle — a different groove entirely from the preolivary sulcus where CN XII emerges — so lesions there produce dysphagia and hoarseness instead of tongue weakness.
incorrectas.C: CN VII and CN VIII exit at the cerebellopontine angle at the pontomedullary junction, well rostral to the medulla where the preolivary and postolivary sulci are found, so this option describes an entirely different brainstem level.
incorrectas.D: CN VI exits medially at the pontomedullary junction, not from the medullary preolivary sulcus; it is grouped with VII and VIII by level (pons) rather than with XII by medial position in the medulla.

preguntas.q: In the caudal medulla, the medial lemniscus is initially positioned in which orientation relative to the midline?

o.C: Medially, oriented vertically near the midline
o.D: Laterally, adjacent to the spinothalamic tract

e.correcta: As the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway decussates (as internal arcuate fibers) and re-forms the medial lemniscus in the caudal medulla, it initially sits close to the midline in a vertical orientation, just dorsal to the pyramids. This position reflects its recent crossing from the gracile and cuneate nuclei, which lie dorsally near the midline. Knowing this starting position is the anchor for tracking how the tract rotates as it ascends through the brainstem — a favorite "where is this tract at level X" board question.

incorrectas.A: The pyramids (carrying the corticospinal tract) are ventral structures separate from the medial lemniscus; while the medial lemniscus is near the midline in the caudal medulla, describing it as sitting directly with the pyramids conflates two distinct fiber systems that only share a general ventromedial neighborhood.
incorrectas.B: The dorsal medulla near the fourth ventricle is occupied by structures like the nucleus and tractus solitarius and vestibular nuclei, not the medial lemniscus, which lies more ventrally after its fibers cross and ascend from the dorsal column nuclei.
incorrectas.D: A lateral position is actually where the medial lemniscus ends up later, at the level of the midbrain, after it rotates during its ascent — in the caudal medulla itself it starts out medial, not lateral or already paired with the spinothalamic tract.

preguntas.q: As the medial lemniscus ascends from the medulla into the midbrain, its position within the brainstem shifts to become more:

e.correcta: The medial lemniscus progressively rotates and migrates laterally as it courses rostrally through the pons and into the midbrain, so that by the midbrain it lies laterally and comes to run alongside the spinothalamic tract. This convergence matters functionally: both pathways carry somatosensory information (fine touch/proprioception via the lemniscus, pain/temperature via the spinothalamic tract) and both terminate in the VPL nucleus of the thalamus, allowing the two modalities to be relayed together to the cortex. This lateral shift is a classic "tract position by level" fact tested on imaging-based brainstem questions.

incorrectas.A: Medial describes the tract's position back in the caudal medulla, not the midbrain; the whole point of this fact is that the lemniscus moves away from the midline as it ascends, ending up lateral rather than staying medial.
incorrectas.B: The medial lemniscus does not primarily shift dorsally; dorsal midbrain structures include the tectum (superior and inferior colliculi) and periaqueductal gray, which are distinct from the ventrolateral tegmental territory where the ascending medial lemniscus travels.
incorrectas.C: While the lemniscus is a tegmental structure and not purely dorsal, describing its key repositioning as "ventral" misses the defining lateral shift that brings it next to the spinothalamic tract — the ventral pyramidal/corticospinal fibers are a separate, more anterior system.

preguntas.q: Damage to the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), which coordinates the abducens and oculomotor nuclei during conjugate horizontal gaze, produces which clinical syndrome?

e.correcta: The MLF carries the signal from the contralateral abducens (CN VI) nucleus to the ipsilateral oculomotor (CN III) nucleus so that, on attempted lateral gaze, the medial rectus of the adducting eye contracts in sync with the lateral rectus of the abducting eye. When the MLF is damaged (classically by demyelination in multiple sclerosis in young patients, or stroke in older patients), the ipsilateral eye fails to adduct on attempted lateral gaze while the contralateral (abducting) eye shows nystagmus — this is internuclear ophthalmoplegia. Convergence is spared because it uses a different pathway that does not depend on the MLF, which is the key finding that localizes the lesion to the MLF rather than to CN III itself.

incorrectas.A: One-and-a-half syndrome results from a combined lesion of the MLF plus the ipsilateral abducens nucleus/paramedian pontine reticular formation, causing complete horizontal gaze palsy on one side (the "one") plus INO on the other (the "half") — a more extensive lesion than isolated MLF damage alone.
incorrectas.C: An isolated CN VI (abducens) palsy causes a purely abducens deficit — the ipsilateral eye cannot abduct, with horizontal diplopia worse on lateral gaze in that direction — but adduction of the other eye is unaffected, unlike INO where the abnormality is in adduction, not abduction.
incorrectas.D: A CN III (oculomotor) palsy produces ptosis, a "down and out" eye position, and often a dilated, unreactive pupil due to parasympathetic fiber involvement — findings not seen in INO, where pupillary function and eyelid position are normal because the oculomotor nerve itself, not just its MLF input, is spared.

preguntas.q: Throughout its course in the brainstem, the corticospinal tract occupies which position?

e.correcta: The corticospinal tract runs medially through the brainstem at every level — in the pyramids of the medulla, in the basis pontis, and in the crus cerebri of the midbrain — before decussating in the caudal medulla to form the lateral corticospinal tract in the spinal cord. This consistent medial position is why medial brainstem syndromes (e.g., medial medullary syndrome) combine corticospinal tract signs (contralateral hemiparesis) with damage to other medially-located structures, such as the exiting hypoglossal nerve rootlets or the medial lemniscus. Keeping track of which structures are medial versus lateral at each brainstem level is the key to localizing vascular brainstem syndromes.

incorrectas.B: A lateral position in the brainstem is occupied by structures like the spinothalamic tract, the corticobulbar fibers heading to certain cranial nerve nuclei, or the medial lemniscus in the midbrain — not the corticospinal tract, which stays medial until it crosses in the medulla.
incorrectas.C: Dorsal brainstem territory houses structures such as cranial nerve nuclei, the fourth ventricle, and ascending sensory pathways passing to the thalamus; the corticospinal tract is a ventral/basal structure (in the pyramids and crus cerebri), not a dorsal one.
incorrectas.D: Describing the tract as purely ventral but not medial misses the key teaching point — the corticospinal tract is specifically medial (within the midline pyramids/crus cerebri), which is exactly why it is grouped with other medial structures when localizing medial brainstem infarcts.

preguntas.q: The spinothalamic tract travels through the brainstem alongside which descending tract, such that a single lateral brainstem lesion damages both and produces contralateral pain/temperature loss plus an ipsilateral Horner syndrome?

e.correcta: The descending hypothalamospinal tract carries sympathetic fibers from the hypothalamus down through the lateral brainstem and spinal cord to the intermediolateral cell column, and it runs in close proximity to the ascending spinothalamic tract throughout this course. A lateral brainstem lesion (classically the lateral medullary/Wallenberg syndrome from PICA occlusion) therefore damages both simultaneously, producing contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation (spinothalamic) together with an ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) from interruption of the descending sympathetics. Recognizing this paired anatomy explains why these two seemingly unrelated deficits show up together on the same side of a single lesion.

incorrectas.A: The corticospinal tract runs medially in the brainstem (in the pyramids), not laterally alongside the spinothalamic tract, so a lateral lesion affecting the spinothalamic tract classically spares the corticospinal tract — this is precisely why lateral medullary syndrome does not cause limb weakness.
incorrectas.B: The medial lemniscus is a medially-positioned structure in the medulla (only becoming lateral higher up in the midbrain) and carries fine touch/proprioception, not sympathetic fibers; it is not the tract responsible for the Horner syndrome seen with lateral spinothalamic tract lesions.
incorrectas.D: The rubrospinal tract originates in the red nucleus and influences flexor tone in limb musculature; it is not a sympathetic pathway and does not explain the ipsilateral Horner syndrome that accompanies a lateral spinothalamic tract lesion.

preguntas.q: Muscle spindle afferents from the masseter that form the sensory (afferent) limb of the jaw jerk reflex synapse in which trigeminal nucleus?

e.correcta: The mesencephalic nucleus of CN V is unique among cranial nerve nuclei in that it houses the cell bodies of primary (first-order) proprioceptive afferents themselves — essentially a displaced dorsal root ganglion sitting inside the CNS — carrying muscle spindle information from the muscles of mastication, including the masseter. In the jaw jerk reflex, tapping the jaw stretches the masseter, the mesencephalic nucleus neurons detect this stretch, and they synapse directly onto the motor nucleus of CN V to drive a reflex jaw closure, analogous to a deep tendon reflex elsewhere in the body. Because this is a monosynaptic reflex arc mediated entirely by CN V (afferent and efferent), an exaggerated jaw jerk is a classic sign of an upper motor neuron (corticobulbar) lesion above the pons.

incorrectas.A: The main (chief) sensory nucleus of CN V processes discriminative touch and pressure from the face, not proprioceptive muscle spindle input from the muscles of mastication, so it is not the relay used for the jaw jerk's afferent limb.
incorrectas.B: The spinal trigeminal nucleus relays pain and temperature sensation from the face and extends down into the upper cervical spinal cord; it has no role in proprioceptive muscle spindle signaling from the masseter used in the jaw jerk.
incorrectas.C: The motor nucleus of CN V is the efferent (not afferent) limb of the jaw jerk reflex — it contains the lower motor neurons that innervate the masseter and other muscles of mastication, receiving input from the mesencephalic nucleus rather than generating the sensory signal itself.

preguntas.q: Second-order neurons carrying facial sensory information (pain, temperature, touch) synapse in which thalamic nucleus before projecting to the cortex?

e.correcta: The VPM nucleus of the thalamus is the trigeminal system's counterpart to the VPL: it receives second-order sensory fibers carrying facial pain, temperature, and touch from the trigeminal nuclei (spinal trigeminal and main sensory nucleus) and relays them to the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex), specifically to the face representation. This medial-to-lateral organization (VPM for face, VPL for body) mirrors the somatotopic map of the homunculus, which is a useful mnemonic — "M is for medial/face, L is for lateral/limbs."

incorrectas.B: The VPL nucleus relays somatosensory information from the body (via the dorsal column-medial lemniscus and spinothalamic pathways), not the face — facial sensory relay is specifically handled by the adjacent VPM nucleus.
incorrectas.C: The medial geniculate nucleus relays auditory information from the inferior colliculus to the primary auditory cortex; it has no role in somatosensory relay from the trigeminal system.
incorrectas.D: The ventral anterior nucleus is primarily a motor relay nucleus, receiving basal ganglia and cerebellar output and projecting to the motor and premotor cortex, rather than serving as a sensory relay for facial touch, pain, or temperature.

preguntas.q: A peripheral lesion of CN V causes facial sensory loss (pain/temperature via the spinal trigeminal nucleus, touch via the main sensory nucleus, and/or motor weakness) on which side relative to the lesion?

e.correcta: Because CN V is a peripheral nerve carrying uncrossed sensory and motor fibers from the face all the way into the brainstem nuclei, a lesion anywhere along CN V — the nerve trunk, its ganglion, or its brainstem nuclei themselves — produces deficits on the same (ipsilateral) side as the lesion. This is in contrast to lesions of central pathways beyond the point of decussation (e.g., a thalamic or cortical lesion), which produce contralateral deficits; testing which side is affected is a quick way to localize a lesion to the peripheral trigeminal apparatus versus a more central pathway.

incorrectas.A: Contralateral deficits would be expected from a lesion central to the decussation of trigeminothalamic fibers (e.g., in the thalamus or above), not from damage to CN V itself or its brainstem nuclei, which are ipsilateral to the affected side of the face.
incorrectas.C: Bilateral facial sensory loss would suggest either bilateral CN V lesions or a lesion affecting a structure that both sides pass through, such as certain brainstem or systemic processes, but a single unilateral CN V lesion produces strictly one-sided (ipsilateral) findings.
incorrectas.D: Restriction to only the lower face with contralateral involvement describes the pattern seen with facial nerve (CN VII) corticobulbar sparing of the forehead in central lesions, not the trigeminal sensory distribution, which covers the entire ipsilateral face via its three divisions (V1, V2, V3).

preguntas.q: Which descending tract provides upper motor neuron innervation to the lower motor neurons located in cranial nerve nuclei that supply skeletal muscle (e.g., CN V, VII, X, XI, XII)?

e.correcta: The corticobulbar tract originates from upper motor neurons in the primary motor cortex and descends to synapse on lower motor neurons within brainstem cranial nerve nuclei that innervate skeletal muscle, functioning as the cranial nerve equivalent of the corticospinal tract for the limbs and trunk. This means that damage to the corticobulbar tract (an UMN lesion, e.g., from a stroke) produces a different clinical picture (often milder, sometimes with sparing due to bilateral innervation) than direct damage to the cranial nerve nucleus or nerve itself (an LMN lesion), a distinction that is heavily tested for the facial nerve in particular.

incorrectas.A: The corticospinal tract is the analogous UMN pathway for spinal cord lower motor neurons controlling limb and trunk muscles — it does not synapse on brainstem cranial nerve nuclei, which is specifically the job of the corticobulbar tract.
incorrectas.B: The vestibulospinal tract originates from the vestibular nuclei and influences spinal cord motor neurons to maintain posture and balance; it is not a cortical UMN pathway and does not provide the primary voluntary motor drive to cranial nerve nuclei.
incorrectas.D: The rubrospinal tract arises from the red nucleus and modulates flexor tone via projections to spinal cord motor neurons, not cranial nerve nuclei, making it a distinct extrapyramidal pathway rather than the corticobulbar UMN system.

preguntas.q: Corticobulbar tract fibers, which supply upper motor neuron input to cranial nerve nuclei, arise from which cortical region?

e.correcta: The primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus), organized somatotopically as the motor homunculus, gives rise to corticobulbar fibers from its face and head representation area, just as it gives rise to corticospinal fibers from the more medial and lateral representations of the trunk and limbs. These fibers descend through the internal capsule (genu) and course through the brainstem to synapse on cranial nerve motor nuclei, delivering voluntary control over muscles like those of facial expression, tongue movement, and swallowing.

incorrectas.A: The premotor cortex contributes to motor planning and preparation, feeding into the primary motor cortex and other circuits, but it is not the principal direct origin of the corticobulbar tract's descending axons to brainstem nuclei.
incorrectas.B: The supplementary motor area is involved in planning and coordinating complex, internally-generated movement sequences and works upstream of the primary motor cortex; it is not the classic direct source of corticobulbar tract fibers tested in this context.
incorrectas.C: The primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus) receives sensory input via the thalamus (e.g., from VPM/VPL) rather than sending motor output; it plays no role as the origin of the corticobulbar tract, which is purely a motor pathway.

preguntas.q: The corticobulbar innervation pattern to lower motor neurons in most cranial nerve motor nuclei is predominantly:

o.D: Absent — these nuclei receive only spinal input

e.correcta: Most cranial nerve motor nuclei (e.g., those for the muscles of mastication, most facial muscles other than the lower face, the pharynx, larynx, and tongue in a bilateral fashion overall) receive corticobulbar input from both the ipsilateral and contralateral primary motor cortex. This bilateral redundancy means that a unilateral upper motor neuron lesion (e.g., a cortical stroke) typically causes only mild or no weakness in these muscles, because the intact hemisphere's corticobulbar fibers can still drive the nucleus — a key reason UMN facial palsy classically spares the forehead while LMN lesions (like Bell palsy) do not spare anything.

incorrectas.B: Purely contralateral-only innervation would mean a single UMN lesion completely knocks out function on the opposite side, which is not the typical pattern — most cranial nerve nuclei have redundant bilateral input specifically to protect against this vulnerability.
incorrectas.C: Purely ipsilateral-only innervation is not accurate either; while there is an ipsilateral contribution, the defining and clinically important feature of most cranial nerve nuclei is that they also receive contralateral input, making the overall pattern bilateral rather than exclusively ipsilateral.
incorrectas.D: Cranial nerve motor nuclei absolutely do receive corticobulbar (cortical) input for voluntary control — describing them as receiving "only spinal input" confuses the brainstem cranial nerve system with spinal cord lower motor neurons, which receive corticospinal (not corticobulbar) input.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve has a subset of lower motor neurons (those supplying the lower face) that receive corticobulbar innervation from only the contralateral motor cortex, explaining forehead-sparing in central lesions?

e.correcta: The facial nucleus is functionally split: the portion of the nucleus supplying the upper face (frontalis, orbicularis oculi) receives bilateral corticobulbar input, while the portion supplying the lower face (orbicularis oris, buccinator) receives input from only the contralateral motor cortex. This asymmetry is exactly why an upper motor neuron lesion (e.g., a stroke affecting the corticobulbar tract) causes contralateral lower facial weakness with a spared, wrinkling forehead, whereas a lower motor neuron lesion (e.g., Bell palsy, damaging the facial nerve or nucleus itself) causes complete ipsilateral facial paralysis, including forehead involvement — a hallmark distinction tested repeatedly on exams.

incorrectas.A: The trigeminal motor nucleus (supplying the muscles of mastication) receives predominantly bilateral corticobulbar input like most other cranial nerve nuclei, without the classic partial-contralateral-only exception that defines the facial nucleus's lower face representation.
incorrectas.C: The hypoglossal nucleus supplying tongue muscles receives mostly contralateral input overall for genioglossus in some descriptions, but the specific, heavily-tested upper/lower face split with forehead-sparing implications belongs to the facial nerve, not the hypoglossal nerve.
incorrectas.D: The vagus nerve's motor nuclei (nucleus ambiguus) generally receive bilateral corticobulbar innervation similar to most other cranial nerve nuclei, and it lacks the well-known asymmetric contralateral-only innervation to a specific muscle subgroup that characterizes the facial nucleus.

preguntas.q: What is the general clinical term for the syndrome resulting from either an upper or lower motor neuron lesion affecting CN VII?

e.correcta: Facial (nerve) palsy is the umbrella clinical term for weakness of the facial muscles arising from dysfunction anywhere along the CN VII pathway — whether the lesion is an upper motor neuron lesion (e.g., cortical stroke, which spares the forehead due to bilateral innervation) or a lower motor neuron lesion (damage to the facial nerve or nucleus itself, causing complete hemifacial weakness including the forehead). The severity and pattern (partial versus complete, upper-face sparing versus not) depend on exactly where along this pathway the lesion sits, making facial palsy a spectrum rather than a single specific diagnosis.

incorrectas.A: Trigeminal neuralgia is a completely different disorder — a pain syndrome caused by paroxysmal, often vascular, irritation of the sensory trigeminal nerve (CN V) — and is unrelated to facial motor weakness or CN VII dysfunction.
incorrectas.B: Horner syndrome results from disruption of the sympathetic pathway (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), not from facial motor nerve dysfunction, and is caused by lesions along the oculosympathetic chain rather than CN VII.
incorrectas.D: Bell palsy is a specific subtype of facial palsy — namely, the idiopathic form of lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy — rather than the general umbrella term that covers both upper and lower motor neuron facial nerve lesions.

preguntas.q: When facial nerve (CN VII) palsy occurs without an identifiable underlying cause, it is termed:

e.correcta: Bell palsy is, by definition, the idiopathic form of peripheral (lower motor neuron) facial nerve palsy — complete unilateral facial weakness, including the forehead, with no identifiable cause found on workup. Although it is idiopathic by definition, it is thought to often be related to herpes simplex virus reactivation causing inflammation and swelling of the facial nerve within its bony canal, and known secondary causes of similar-looking facial palsy (Lyme disease, herpes zoster/Ramsay Hunt, sarcoidosis, diabetes mellitus, or parotid tumors) must first be excluded before the label "Bell palsy" is applied.

incorrectas.A: Ramsay Hunt syndrome is a specific, identifiable cause of facial palsy due to varicella-zoster virus reactivation in the geniculate ganglion, presenting with facial weakness plus a vesicular rash in the ear canal or auricle — this is precisely the kind of identifiable etiology that excludes a diagnosis of idiopathic Bell palsy.
incorrectas.B: Central (UMN) facial palsy results from a lesion in the corticobulbar pathway above the facial nucleus (e.g., stroke), causing contralateral lower-face weakness with forehead sparing due to bilateral innervation of the upper face — a different pattern and mechanism from the complete, peripheral, idiopathic weakness of Bell palsy.
incorrectas.C: Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome is a rare condition featuring recurrent facial palsy, orofacial edema, and a fissured tongue; while it can cause facial nerve palsy, it is a distinct identifiable syndrome rather than the idiopathic diagnosis of exclusion that defines Bell palsy.

preguntas.q: Which portion of the ear is composed of the pinna (auricle) and the external auditory meatus (ear canal)?

e.correcta: The external ear consists of the pinna, which collects and funnels sound waves, and the external auditory meatus (canal), which channels those sound waves toward the tympanic membrane. This is the first of the three anatomically and functionally distinct segments of the ear (external, middle, inner), each of which serves a different role in the overall process of converting airborne sound into a neural signal, and knowing this division helps localize the anatomic level of pathology such as otitis externa versus otitis media.

incorrectas.B: The middle ear is the air-filled cavity housing the three auditory ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) that mechanically transmit and amplify vibrations from the tympanic membrane to the oval window — it does not include the pinna or ear canal, which belong to the external ear.
incorrectas.C: The inner ear consists of the bony and membranous labyrinth, containing the cochlea (hearing) and vestibular apparatus (balance) — these are fluid-filled sensory structures, entirely distinct from and much deeper than the external ear's cartilage-supported pinna and canal.
incorrectas.D: The tympanic cavity is another name for the space of the middle ear itself (containing the ossicles), not the external ear structures of pinna and ear canal, which lie external to the tympanic membrane rather than within the cavity behind it.

preguntas.q: The external ear transfers airborne sound waves to the middle ear by inducing what mechanical event at the eardrum?

o.C: Generation of a fluid traveling wave
o.D: Impedance matching between air and fluid

e.correcta: The pinna and external auditory canal funnel sound waves toward the tympanic membrane, causing it to vibrate in response to the pressure changes of the incoming sound wave. This vibration is the mechanical event that converts an airborne acoustic signal into a physical motion that can then be picked up and transmitted onward by the ossicular chain of the middle ear — the essential first mechanical step in the hearing pathway.

incorrectas.A: Amplification of sound pressure is primarily the job of the middle ear ossicles (via the lever action of the malleus-incus-stapes chain and the area ratio between the large tympanic membrane and small oval window), not a function performed by the external ear itself.
