e.correcta: As a vestibular schwannoma enlarges within the confined internal acoustic meatus, it eventually pushes medially out through the porus acusticus into the cerebellopontine angle cistern, the space bounded by the pons, cerebellum, and petrous temporal bone. This produces cerebellopontine angle syndrome as the enlarging mass also compresses CN V and CN VII along with the adjacent cerebellum.

incorrectas.A: The interpeduncular cistern lies between the cerebral peduncles anteriorly and contains the basilar artery bifurcation and oculomotor nerves; it is not anatomically contiguous with the internal acoustic meatus, so schwannomas do not extend there.
incorrectas.B: The cavernous sinus lies anterolateral to the sella turcica and contains CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI, and the internal carotid artery; lesions there (e.g., pituitary macroadenoma) cause ophthalmoplegia rather than the cerebellopontine angle triad.
incorrectas.D: Meckel cave in the middle cranial fossa houses the trigeminal ganglion; CN V schwannomas arise there, but vestibular schwannomas extend posteriorly into the cerebellopontine angle, not into Meckel cave.

preguntas.q: The absence of which finding in cerebellopontine angle syndrome helps localize the lesion outside the brainstem parenchyma?

e.correcta: Cerebellopontine angle syndrome results from an extra-axial mass compressing cranial nerves V, VII, and VIII as they cross the cistern, but because the lesion sits outside the brainstem itself, it does not directly damage the corticospinal, spinothalamic, or dorsal column tracts that run within the brainstem parenchyma. The absence of contralateral long-tract motor or sensory deficits, despite prominent cranial nerve findings, is the key clue that localizes the process extra-axially rather than to an intrinsic brainstem lesion like a stroke.

incorrectas.A: Ipsilateral facial weakness is actually a typical feature of cerebellopontine angle syndrome once CN VII becomes compressed by the growing mass, not a finding whose absence helps distinguish extra-axial from intra-axial disease.
incorrectas.B: Ipsilateral hearing loss from CN VIII compression is also a hallmark early finding of this syndrome, so its absence is not the discriminating feature; it is the coexistence of cranial nerve deficits without long tract signs that is diagnostic.
incorrectas.D: Ipsilateral ataxia can occur in cerebellopontine angle syndrome from cerebellar or peduncle compression, and its presence or absence is not the classic feature used to separate extra-axial from brainstem lesions.

preguntas.q: In cerebellopontine angle syndrome from a vestibular schwannoma, progressive hearing loss occurs on which side relative to the tumor?

e.correcta: Because the vestibular schwannoma directly compresses CN VIII on the same side as the tumor, before any central decussation of auditory pathways, the vertigo and progressive sensorineural hearing loss are ipsilateral to the mass. This slow, unilateral, progressive pattern (rather than sudden or bilateral onset) is an important clue pointing toward a schwannoma over other causes of hearing loss.

incorrectas.A: Contralateral hearing loss would suggest damage to central auditory pathways after they have already crossed (e.g., a pontine or midbrain lesion), not a peripheral compressive lesion of CN VIII itself.
incorrectas.C: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas do occur, but this is the hallmark of neurofibromatosis type 2, not sporadic disease, and even then each side's tumor still produces primarily ipsilateral symptoms rather than truly simultaneous symmetric onset.
incorrectas.D: This kind of side-switching progression is not characteristic of vestibular schwannoma, which evolves as a slow, unilateral process that remains referable to the side of the mass throughout its course.

preguntas.q: A patient presents with contralateral spastic hemiparesis (including the lower face) and ipsilateral oculomotor palsy with a down-and-out eye. Damage to which structure produces this presentation?

e.correcta: Weber syndrome results from infarction of the medial midbrain, which contains the descending corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts along with the exiting fibers of CN III. Damage here produces contralateral spastic hemiparesis of the body and lower face (an upper motor neuron pattern, since these tracts have not yet decussated) plus an ipsilateral CN III palsy from direct nerve involvement — this combination of crossed long-tract signs with an uncrossed cranial nerve deficit is the hallmark of medial brainstem syndromes.

incorrectas.B: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, from PICA territory infarction, spares the corticospinal tract and CN III entirely, instead producing ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, dysphagia, hoarseness, vertigo, and Horner syndrome — a very different pattern from Weber's hemiparesis and oculomotor palsy.
incorrectas.C: Medial medullary syndrome (anterior spinal artery territory) affects the corticospinal tract, medial lemniscus, and CN XII, causing contralateral hemiparesis with contralateral proprioceptive loss and ipsilateral tongue deviation; it does not involve CN III since the medulla lies caudal to the midbrain.
incorrectas.D: Lateral pontine syndrome (AICA territory) damages CN VII and VIII along with spinocerebellar and spinothalamic fibers, producing ipsilateral facial paralysis, hearing loss, and ataxia rather than the CN III palsy and hemiparesis seen in Weber syndrome.

preguntas.q: Parinaud syndrome (upward gaze palsy, light-near pupillary dissociation, convergence-retraction nystagmus) is classically caused by compression of the dorsal midbrain by a tumor arising from which structure?

e.correcta: The pineal gland sits immediately posterior to the midbrain tectum and superior colliculi, so pineal region tumors — most often germinomas — compress the dorsal midbrain and posterior commissure, producing Parinaud syndrome's triad of upward gaze paresis, pseudo-Argyll Robertson pupils, and convergence-retraction nystagmus. The pineal gland's tight anatomic relationship to the cerebral aqueduct also explains why these tumors frequently cause obstructive hydrocephalus.

incorrectas.A: Hypothalamic tumors (e.g., craniopharyngioma extension) more typically cause endocrine dysfunction, visual field defects, or diabetes insipidus rather than the dorsal midbrain compression that produces Parinaud syndrome.
incorrectas.B: Pituitary tumors expand into the suprasellar cistern and compress the optic chiasm, producing bitemporal hemianopia, not the vertical gaze and pupillary findings that require direct dorsal midbrain compression.
incorrectas.C: Thalamic lesions can affect sensory pathways or consciousness but do not produce the specific vertical gaze palsy and convergence-retraction nystagmus of Parinaud syndrome, which requires compression at the level of the tectum by an adjacent pineal mass.

preguntas.q: Which midbrain reticular formation nucleus surrounds the cerebral aqueduct and, rich in opioid receptors, sends descending projections that modulate pain transmission at the spinal dorsal horn?

e.correcta: The periaqueductal gray is a collection of neurons encircling the cerebral aqueduct in the midbrain that is densely populated with opioid receptors. When activated by endogenous opioids or exogenous opiates, it drives descending inhibitory projections — relayed largely through the rostral ventromedial medulla and raphe nuclei — that suppress nociceptive transmission at the dorsal horn, forming the core of the descending pain-modulation pathway that opioid analgesics exploit.

incorrectas.B: The locus ceruleus is the primary noradrenergic nucleus of the pons, involved in arousal, attention, and the stress response; it contributes some descending noradrenergic pain modulation, but it is not the aqueduct-surrounding structure containing the opioid receptors described here.
incorrectas.C: The raphe nuclei are serotonergic midline brainstem nuclei that do participate in descending pain inhibition, but they act downstream of, and are activated by, the periaqueductal gray rather than being the aqueduct-surrounding structure itself.
incorrectas.D: The nucleus ambiguus is a medullary motor nucleus supplying CN IX, X, and XI (pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles); it has no role in pain modulation and is unrelated to the periaqueductal gray.

preguntas.q: Which brain structure "fine-tunes" ongoing movement and coordinates balance, without itself initiating voluntary movement?

e.correcta: The cerebellum receives a copy of outgoing motor commands (efference copy) along with real-time proprioceptive, vestibular, and visual feedback, comparing intended versus actual movement to fine-tune coordination, timing, and balance. It does not initiate voluntary movement but corrects it in progress, which is why cerebellar lesions produce ataxia, dysmetria, and intention tremor rather than paralysis.

incorrectas.A: The basal ganglia modulate movement initiation and gating through direct and indirect pathways that influence thalamocortical output, and their dysfunction causes disorders of movement amount or character such as Parkinsonism or chorea, not the moment-to-moment coordination and balance correction that defines cerebellar function.
incorrectas.C: The thalamus relays motor and sensory signals to the cortex, including outputs from the cerebellum and basal ganglia, but it does not itself perform the comparison of intended versus actual movement that underlies coordination.
incorrectas.D: The primary motor cortex generates the voluntary descending command for movement via the corticospinal tract; it initiates movement rather than fine-tuning its execution, which is the cerebellum's role.

preguntas.q: Which cerebellar division spans through the vermis and lateral hemispheres and, via vestibular nuclei input, plays a key role in vestibulo-ocular control?

e.correcta: The flocculonodular lobe (archicerebellum, or vestibulocerebellum) is the phylogenetically oldest cerebellar division. It receives direct input from the vestibular nuclei and projects back to them, allowing it to coordinate the vestibulo-ocular reflex and postural/balance control; lesions here classically produce truncal ataxia and nystagmus without prominent limb dysmetria.

incorrectas.B: The anterior lobe is part of the spinocerebellum, receiving spinocerebellar proprioceptive input that regulates limb and trunk muscle tone and gait, rather than vestibular or eye movement control.
incorrectas.C: The posterior lobe comprises much of the neocerebellum (cerebrocerebellum), which plans and coordinates fine, skilled voluntary movements through connections with the cerebral cortex, not vestibular reflexes.
incorrectas.D: The cerebellar tonsil is a posteroinferior projection near the foramen magnum, best known clinically for its risk of herniation ("coning") with elevated intracranial pressure, not for a role in vestibulo-ocular control.

preguntas.q: Which cerebellar structure controls truncal and proximal limb musculature, such that midline lesions produce truncal ataxia and a wide-based gait?

e.correcta: The vermis is the midline portion of the cerebellum belonging to the spinocerebellum, receiving proprioceptive input primarily from axial and proximal limb muscles. Because it projects to medial descending motor pathways such as the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts, vermal lesions classically cause truncal instability and a broad-based, staggering gait rather than distal limb clumsiness.

incorrectas.A: The lateral hemisphere is part of the cerebrocerebellum and governs motor planning of skilled voluntary limb movements through connections with the cerebral cortex; damage here produces limb dysmetria and ataxia, not truncal instability.
incorrectas.B: The intermediate hemisphere (paravermal zone) controls distal limb musculature via corticospinal-linked circuits, so lesions there impair fine distal movements rather than trunk control.
incorrectas.D: The flocculonodular lobe governs vestibulo-ocular reflexes and balance via vestibular nuclei connections, producing nystagmus and disequilibrium rather than the truncal ataxia caused by vermal damage.

preguntas.q: Which cerebellar region primarily controls distal limb musculature, allowing fine motor control of the hands and feet?

e.correcta: The intermediate (paravermal) hemisphere is a transitional zone of the spinocerebellum that receives proprioceptive feedback from distal limb muscles and projects via the interposed nuclei to influence the rubrospinal and corticospinal pathways, allowing it to fine-tune the more distal, precise components of ongoing limb movement.

incorrectas.A: The vermis governs axial and proximal trunk musculature, so its damage produces truncal ataxia rather than the distal limb dysfunction attributed to the intermediate zone.
incorrectas.C: The lateral hemisphere belongs to the cerebrocerebellum and is involved in higher-order planning of skilled movement in conjunction with the cerebral cortex, rather than the online correction of distal limb execution handled by the intermediate zone.
incorrectas.D: The flocculonodular lobe manages vestibular and ocular motor reflexes rather than limb musculature, so lesions there produce disequilibrium and nystagmus rather than distal limb ataxia.

preguntas.q: Damage to which cerebellar structure produces ipsilateral ataxia due to impaired motor planning of a limb?

e.correcta: The lateral hemispheres constitute the cerebrocerebellum, the phylogenetically newest and largest cerebellar division, which communicates reciprocally with the cerebral cortex (via the dentate nucleus and thalamus) to plan and sequence complex, skilled voluntary movements before they are executed. Because the effective outflow of cerebellar pathways ends up controlling the ipsilateral limb (the cerebellum's double decussation restores ipsilateral control), damage here produces ipsilateral limb ataxia and dysmetria.

incorrectas.A: The vermis handles axial and truncal control rather than the planning of limb movements, so its damage produces truncal, not limb, ataxia.
incorrectas.B: The intermediate hemisphere fine-tunes ongoing distal limb execution using proprioceptive feedback rather than pre-movement planning, so it is not the region responsible for motor planning deficits.
incorrectas.C: The flocculonodular lobe is dedicated to vestibulo-ocular and balance functions, unrelated to the cortical-cerebellar loop that plans limb movements.

preguntas.q: Which cerebellar lobe receives input from the vestibular nuclei and is responsible for controlling balance and eye movements?

e.correcta: As the vestibulocerebellum, the flocculonodular lobe receives direct primary and secondary vestibular afferents from the vestibular nuclei and inner ear, and its Purkinje cell output projects back onto the vestibular nuclei to coordinate the vestibulo-ocular reflex, gaze stabilization, and postural balance. Lesions here (e.g., medulloblastoma in children) cause truncal instability, wide-based gait, and nystagmus.

incorrectas.A: The vermis is concerned with axial and trunk motor control through spinocerebellar proprioceptive circuits, not vestibular input, so vermal damage produces truncal ataxia without the prominent nystagmus of flocculonodular lesions.
incorrectas.B: The lateral hemisphere participates in higher cortical-cerebellar loops for planning skilled limb movement, unrelated to vestibular processing.
incorrectas.D: The intermediate hemisphere fine-tunes distal limb movement via somatosensory feedback rather than vestibular input, so it is not implicated in balance or eye movement control.

preguntas.q: Which is the outermost layer of the cerebellar cortex, containing the dendritic arbors of Purkinje cells along with stellate and basket cell interneurons?

e.correcta: The molecular layer is the outermost of the three cerebellar cortical layers and is relatively cell-sparse, consisting mainly of the extensive dendritic trees of Purkinje cells plus the parallel fibers of granule cell axons that synapse onto them, along with the inhibitory stellate and basket cell interneurons. This is where most of the synaptic integration shaping Purkinje cell output occurs.

incorrectas.B: The Purkinje cell layer is the thin middle layer containing just a single row of large Purkinje cell bodies, distinct from the outer molecular layer where their dendrites extend.
incorrectas.C: The granule cell layer is the innermost, densely cellular layer packed with small granule cell bodies whose axons ascend past the Purkinje layer into the molecular layer as parallel fibers; it is deep to, not superficial to, the Purkinje layer.
incorrectas.D: There is no distinct "white matter layer" within the cerebellar cortex proper — the white matter (arbor vitae) lies beneath the three-layered cortex and carries afferent/efferent fibers, but it is not one of the cortical layers itself.

preguntas.q: Stellate and basket cells of the cerebellar cortex, located in the molecular layer, use which neurotransmitter to inhibit Purkinje cell dendrites and soma, respectively?

e.correcta: Stellate and basket cells are inhibitory interneurons of the molecular layer that use GABA as their neurotransmitter; stellate cells synapse onto Purkinje cell dendrites while basket cells form specialized "basket" synapses around the Purkinje cell soma and axon initial segment, both providing feed-forward inhibition that sharpens and times Purkinje cell output. In fact, every neuron of the cerebellar cortex is GABAergic except the granule cell, which is the sole excitatory (glutamatergic) cell type.

incorrectas.A: Glutamate is the excitatory neurotransmitter used by granule cells (via parallel fibers) and by climbing and mossy fiber afferents entering the cerebellum, not by the inhibitory stellate and basket interneurons.
incorrectas.C: Acetylcholine is not a principal neurotransmitter within intrinsic cerebellar cortical circuitry; it is more relevant to the neuromuscular junction and autonomic ganglia.
incorrectas.D: Serotonin is supplied by raphe nuclei projections that provide diffuse modulatory input to the cerebellum, but it is not the neurotransmitter used by stellate or basket cells themselves.

preguntas.q: Which layer forms the thin middle layer of the cerebellar cortex, situated between the molecular and granule cell layers?

e.correcta: The Purkinje cell layer is a single-cell-thick middle layer of the cerebellar cortex containing the large, flask-shaped Purkinje cell bodies, whose dendrites extend upward into the overlying molecular layer and whose axons are the sole output leaving the cerebellar cortex, descending through the granule layer to reach the deep cerebellar or vestibular nuclei.

incorrectas.A: The molecular layer is the outer, most superficial layer, containing Purkinje cell dendrites and inhibitory interneurons rather than the Purkinje cell bodies themselves.
incorrectas.B: The granule cell layer is the innermost layer, deep to the Purkinje layer, densely packed with small granule cells whose axons ascend as parallel fibers into the molecular layer.
incorrectas.D: "Golgi cell layer" is not a recognized distinct layer of the cerebellar cortex — Golgi cells actually reside within the granule cell layer, not as a separate stratum.

preguntas.q: All extrinsic and intrinsic circuitry within the cerebellar cortex ultimately converges to modulate the firing of which single output cell type?

e.correcta: Purkinje cells are the sole output neuron of the cerebellar cortex, so every afferent pathway — climbing fibers from the inferior olive providing powerful one-to-one excitatory input, and mossy fiber–granule cell–parallel fiber circuits providing more diffuse excitatory drive, further shaped by inhibitory Golgi, stellate, and basket cells — exists ultimately to regulate simple and complex spike firing of Purkinje cells, since their axons alone carry the cortex's computed output onward.

incorrectas.A: Granule cells are intrinsic excitatory relay neurons that receive mossy fiber input and, via their parallel fiber axons, help shape Purkinje cell firing, but they are themselves an intermediate step in the circuit rather than the final convergence point.
incorrectas.B: Golgi cells are inhibitory interneurons that regulate granule cell activity through a feedback loop limiting parallel fiber excitation, meaning their influence on cerebellar output is indirect, acting upstream of Purkinje cells rather than being the endpoint of cerebellar processing.
incorrectas.C: Basket cells provide feed-forward inhibition onto Purkinje cell bodies, which is one of the many inputs converging onto Purkinje cells rather than the ultimate target of cerebellar circuitry itself.

preguntas.q: Which cerebellar cortical neurons give rise to the only axons that exit the cerebellar cortex to synapse on the deep cerebellar or vestibular nuclei?

e.correcta: Purkinje cells are unique among cerebellar cortical neurons in sending their axons out of the cortex — through the underlying white matter to synapse on and inhibit (via GABA) the deep cerebellar nuclei, or in the case of the flocculonodular lobe, directly on the vestibular nuclei. Every other neuron type in the cerebellar cortex (granule, Golgi, stellate, basket) is a local interneuron whose processes stay confined within the cortex.

incorrectas.B: Granule cells send their axons only as far as the molecular layer, where they bifurcate into parallel fibers that run within the cortex to synapse on Purkinje, Golgi, stellate, and basket cell dendrites — they never leave the cortex.
incorrectas.C: Golgi cells are inhibitory interneurons confined to the granule cell layer, where their axons and dendrites remain local, providing feedback inhibition onto granule cells rather than projecting out of the cortex.
incorrectas.D: Basket cells are molecular layer interneurons whose axons travel only short distances to encircle nearby Purkinje cell bodies; like other interneurons, they do not send projections beyond the cerebellar cortex.

preguntas.q: What neurotransmitter do Purkinje cells release onto the deep cerebellar nuclei to inhibit their tonic firing?

e.correcta: Purkinje cells are inhibitory GABAergic neurons — the only output of the cerebellar cortex — and they tonically inhibit the deep cerebellar nuclei (and vestibular nuclei), meaning cerebellar cortical processing largely works by modulating how much of this inhibition is released rather than by direct excitation of downstream targets. This GABAergic output is consistent with the rule that every cerebellar cortical neuron except the granule cell is inhibitory.

incorrectas.A: Glutamate is the excitatory transmitter of granule cells (parallel fibers) and of the climbing and mossy fiber afferents that drive cerebellar cortical activity, not the transmitter Purkinje cells use for their inhibitory output.
incorrectas.B: Acetylcholine is not a major neurotransmitter in cerebellar cortical output circuitry, making it an implausible choice for Purkinje cell signaling.
incorrectas.C: Dopamine is used predominantly in nigrostriatal, mesolimbic, and mesocortical pathways involved in movement initiation and reward, not in the cerebellar cortex's regulation of the deep nuclei.

preguntas.q: Which is the innermost of the three layers of the cerebellar cortex, densely packed with small neurons?

e.correcta: The granule cell layer is the deepest of the cerebellum's three cortical layers, containing enormous numbers of tightly packed small granule cells (the most numerous neuron type in the entire CNS). Their axons ascend past the Purkinje layer into the molecular layer, where they bifurcate into parallel fibers that synapse on Purkinje cell dendrites.

incorrectas.B: The molecular layer is the outermost, cell-poor layer containing Purkinje dendrites and interneurons, the opposite end of the cortex from the granule layer.
incorrectas.C: The Purkinje cell layer is a thin, single-cell-body-thick layer sandwiched between the molecular and granule layers, not the innermost layer itself.
incorrectas.D: The arbor vitae is the white matter core beneath the three-layered cortex, carrying myelinated afferent and efferent fibers rather than being a cortical cell layer.

preguntas.q: Which is the only neuron with its cell body located in the cerebellar cortex that provides excitatory output within that circuitry?

e.correcta: The granule cell is the sole excitatory, glutamatergic neuron of the cerebellar cortex — every other cortical neuron (Purkinje, Golgi, stellate, basket) is inhibitory and GABAergic. Granule cells receive excitatory mossy fiber input and relay it via their parallel fibers to excite Purkinje cells, Golgi cells, and molecular layer interneurons, making them the critical excitatory link in the cortical circuit.

incorrectas.A: The Golgi cell is an inhibitory GABAergic interneuron in the granule layer that provides negative feedback onto granule cells, the opposite excitatory/inhibitory role from what the question describes.
incorrectas.C: The basket cell is an inhibitory GABAergic interneuron of the molecular layer that inhibits Purkinje cell bodies, not an excitatory neuron.
incorrectas.D: The stellate cell is likewise an inhibitory GABAergic interneuron of the molecular layer, acting on Purkinje cell dendrites rather than providing excitatory drive.

preguntas.q: What neurotransmitter do Golgi cells use to inhibit granule cells as part of a negative feedback loop?

e.correcta: Golgi cells are inhibitory GABAergic interneurons residing in the granule cell layer; they receive excitatory input from granule cell parallel fibers and mossy fibers, and in turn inhibit those same granule cells, forming a negative feedback loop that limits and times excitatory granule cell output to the molecular layer — consistent with the rule that every cerebellar cortical neuron besides the granule cell is inhibitory.

incorrectas.A: Glutamate is the excitatory neurotransmitter released by granule cells and by incoming mossy and climbing fibers, the opposite of the inhibitory signal Golgi cells send back onto granule cells.
incorrectas.B: Acetylcholine is not a significant neurotransmitter within intrinsic cerebellar cortical microcircuitry.
incorrectas.D: Glycine is an inhibitory neurotransmitter used prominently in the spinal cord and brainstem (e.g., Renshaw cells), not the transmitter employed by cerebellar Golgi cells, which are GABAergic.

preguntas.q: Granule cells, the only excitatory neurons of the cerebellar cortex, use which neurotransmitter to excite Purkinje cells via parallel fibers?

e.correcta: Granule cells release glutamate from their parallel fiber axons (formed after ascending through the molecular layer) onto the dendritic spines of Purkinje cells, Golgi cells, and molecular layer interneurons, providing the sole excitatory drive within the intrinsic cerebellar cortical circuit; this fits the broader rule that granule cells are the only glutamatergic neuron type in an otherwise GABAergic cortex.

incorrectas.B: GABA is the inhibitory neurotransmitter used by every other cerebellar cortical neuron (Purkinje, Golgi, basket, stellate cells), the opposite of the excitatory signal granule cells provide.
incorrectas.C: Serotonin is supplied to the cerebellum diffusely by raphe nuclei projections for modulatory purposes, not the point-to-point excitatory signaling of granule cell parallel fibers.
incorrectas.D: Dopamine has minimal direct involvement in intrinsic cerebellar cortical microcircuitry, making it an implausible transmitter for granule cells.

preguntas.q: Golgi cells within the cerebellar granule cell layer form inhibitory synapses primarily onto which cell type, closing a negative feedback loop?

e.correcta: Golgi cells receive excitatory input from granule cell parallel fibers (and mossy fibers) and project their inhibitory GABAergic output back onto those very granule cells, forming a classic negative feedback circuit that regulates the timing, gain, and spatial pattern of granule cell/parallel fiber activity reaching the molecular layer.

incorrectas.A: Purkinje cells receive their inhibitory modulatory input directly from basket and stellate cells in the molecular layer, not from Golgi cells, which act one synaptic step earlier at the level of the granule cell layer.
incorrectas.C: Basket cells are themselves inhibitory interneurons of the molecular layer targeting Purkinje cell somata; they are not the target of Golgi cell inhibition, and they operate in a different layer altogether.
incorrectas.D: Climbing fibers are excitatory afferents from the inferior olive that synapse directly onto Purkinje cell dendrites; they are an input to the cerebellar cortex, not a postsynaptic target of Golgi cell axons.

preguntas.q: Within the cerebellar cortex, granule cells (via parallel fibers), stellate cells, and basket cells all converge to influence which single cell type?

o.D: Climbing fiber neurons of the inferior olive

e.correcta: Purkinje cells are the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex, and essentially all cortical circuitry converges on them: granule cells excite Purkinje cells (and Golgi cells) via parallel fibers, while stellate and basket cells provide feedforward inhibition onto Purkinje cell dendrites and soma/axon initial segment, respectively. This convergence lets the cerebellar cortex fine-tune the timing and gain of the single inhibitory GABAergic signal that Purkinje cells then send on to the deep cerebellar nuclei.

incorrectas.A: Golgi cells are themselves part of the cortical circuit - they receive input from parallel fibers and mossy fibers and feed back inhibition onto granule cells - but they are not the shared downstream target described here; that role belongs to Purkinje cells.
incorrectas.C: The deep cerebellar nuclei are downstream of Purkinje cells, receiving inhibitory Purkinje output plus collaterals from mossy and climbing fibers, but granule, stellate, and basket cells do not synapse directly on them within the cortex.
incorrectas.D: Climbing fiber neurons of the inferior olive are the presynaptic source of climbing fibers that synapse onto Purkinje cells; they are an input to the circuit, not a downstream convergence point for these local interneurons.

preguntas.q: Purkinje cells are the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex. Their inhibitory (GABAergic) axons project primarily to which structure?

e.correcta: Purkinje cells integrate excitatory input from parallel fibers (granule cells) and climbing fibers (inferior olive), then send an inhibitory GABAergic signal to the deep cerebellar nuclei (dentate, interposed, fastigial), which serve as the true output relay of the cerebellum to the thalamus and brainstem. This arrangement means the deep nuclei are tonically active on their own, and it is the Purkinje cell inhibition that sculpts and times their firing to coordinate movement.

incorrectas.A: The inferior olive is upstream of Purkinje cells - it sends climbing fibers to Purkinje cells and receives feedback indirectly via the deep nuclei - but Purkinje cells are not primarily projecting to it.
incorrectas.C: Pontine nuclei relay cortical input to the cerebellum via mossy fibers entering through the middle cerebellar peduncle; they are an input source to the cerebellum, not the target of Purkinje cell output.
incorrectas.D: The red nucleus receives input from the deep cerebellar nuclei (interposed nuclei) to form the rubrospinal tract, one synapse downstream of where Purkinje cells actually project.

preguntas.q: Climbing fibers arising from the inferior olivary nucleus provide powerful, monosynaptic excitatory input directly onto which cell type?

e.correcta: Each Purkinje cell receives input from a single climbing fiber that wraps around its dendritic tree and fires a powerful complex spike whenever it discharges, in contrast to the many weak parallel-fiber inputs it also receives. This olivary climbing fiber input is thought to encode error signals used in motor learning, helping calibrate the strength of parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses over time.

incorrectas.B: Granule cells receive their excitatory input from mossy fibers, not climbing fibers; granule cell axons then ascend and bifurcate into parallel fibers, which provide the other (weaker, more numerous) excitatory input onto Purkinje cells.
incorrectas.C: Golgi cells are inhibitory interneurons driven mainly by parallel fibers and mossy fiber collaterals, providing feedback/feedforward inhibition onto granule cells; they are not the direct monosynaptic target of climbing fibers.
incorrectas.D: Basket cells are inhibitory interneurons activated by parallel fibers that in turn inhibit Purkinje cell somata, but they do not receive the powerful monosynaptic climbing fiber input themselves.

preguntas.q: Which afferent fiber type enters the cerebellum from numerous and diverse sources - including the pontine nuclei, spinal cord, and vestibular nuclei - in contrast to the single-source climbing fibers from the inferior olive?

e.correcta: Mossy fibers are the major and most numerous cerebellar afferent, arising from many different origins - pontine nuclei relaying cerebral cortical information, spinocerebellar tracts carrying proprioceptive data, and vestibular nuclei - and synapsing on granule cells within cerebellar glomeruli. This diversity lets the cerebellum integrate motor plans, proprioceptive feedback, and balance information within the same circuit, in contrast to climbing fibers, which come exclusively from the inferior olive and carry a much more specific error signal.

incorrectas.A: Parallel fibers are the axons of granule cells themselves, formed after mossy fiber input excites the granule cells - they are an internal cerebellar cortex element, not an extracerebellar afferent fiber type.
incorrectas.B: Climbing fibers arise from a single source, the contralateral inferior olivary nucleus, and synapse directly onto Purkinje cells; this is the opposite of the multi-source mossy fiber system described here.
incorrectas.C: Corticospinal fibers are descending upper motor neuron axons that travel from the motor cortex to the spinal cord; they are not an afferent input into the cerebellum at all.

preguntas.q: Mossy fibers form excitatory synapses on which cerebellar cortical cell type, whose axons then ascend to become parallel fibers?

e.correcta: Granule cells are the most numerous neurons in the entire brain and receive excitatory mossy fiber input within cerebellar glomeruli. Their thin, unmyelinated axons ascend into the molecular layer and bifurcate in a T-shape to form parallel fibers, which run for millimeters and provide widespread, weak excitatory input onto many Purkinje, stellate, basket, and Golgi cells - this is how a single mossy fiber signal gets distributed across a broad population of Purkinje cells.

incorrectas.A: Purkinje cells receive parallel fiber input (from granule cells) and climbing fiber input (from the inferior olive) but are not the direct target of mossy fibers themselves; they sit one synapse downstream of the mossy fiber-granule cell relay.
incorrectas.C: Golgi cells receive excitatory drive from parallel fibers and mossy fiber collaterals and provide inhibitory feedback onto granule cells, but they are not the primary, defining first-order target of mossy fibers in this classic relay.
incorrectas.D: Basket cells are inhibitory interneurons activated by parallel fibers (i.e., downstream of granule cells), not direct mossy fiber targets.

preguntas.q: The output of Purkinje cells onto the deep cerebellar nuclei is always which type of signal?

o.C: Mixed, excitatory or inhibitory depending on the target nucleus

e.correcta: Purkinje cells are unusual among principal neurons in that they use GABA and are exclusively inhibitory, regardless of which deep nucleus (dentate, interposed, or fastigial) or vestibular nucleus they target. This means the tonic firing of the deep cerebellar nuclei, which drives thalamic and brainstem motor output, is continuously sculpted by how much Purkinje inhibition is superimposed on it - increased Purkinje firing suppresses the nuclei, while pauses in Purkinje firing allow bursts of nuclear output, a mechanism central to fine motor coordination.

incorrectas.B: Excitatory (glutamatergic) output describes granule cells and climbing fiber (inferior olive) neurons, which excite Purkinje cells - the reverse direction of what Purkinje cells themselves do to their targets.
incorrectas.C: A mixed excitatory/inhibitory output would require Purkinje cells to release different transmitters depending on target, but they are uniformly GABAergic no matter which nucleus they synapse on.
incorrectas.D: Dopaminergic modulation is characteristic of nigrostriatal neurons in the basal ganglia circuit, not of Purkinje cells, which act via fast GABA-A-mediated inhibition rather than slow dopaminergic modulation.

preguntas.q: Neurons of the ventral lateral (VL) nucleus of the thalamus, which relay basal ganglia and cerebellar output, synapse onto upper motor neurons located in which structure?

e.correcta: The VL nucleus of the thalamus is the final relay station through which processed basal ganglia and cerebellar output reaches the cerebral cortex, and its principal target is the primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus, where upper motor neurons originate. Those UMNs then send descending axons (e.g., via the corticospinal tract) to influence lower motor neurons, completing the loop by which subcortical motor centers shape voluntary movement.

incorrectas.A: Premotor cortex is involved in planning movement and receives some thalamic input as well, but the classic VL relay to the UMNs that then descend via the corticospinal tract is to primary motor cortex, the structure specifically tested here.
incorrectas.B: The supplementary motor area contributes to sequencing and bilateral coordination of movement and receives some basal ganglia-thalamic input, but it is not the site containing the UMNs whose corticospinal axons are the focus of this classic pathway.
incorrectas.D: The postcentral gyrus is primary somatosensory cortex, receiving sensory (not motor) thalamic relay from the VPL/VPM nuclei; it does not contain the upper motor neurons of the corticospinal tract.

preguntas.q: Upper motor neurons in the motor cortex that receive VL thalamic input send their descending axons to lower motor neurons via which contralateral tract?

e.correcta: The corticospinal tract is the direct pathway by which upper motor neurons in the precentral gyrus, having received VL thalamic input reflecting basal ganglia/cerebellar processing, project to lower motor neurons in the spinal cord, decussating at the caudal medulla (pyramidal decussation) to control the contralateral body. This tract is the principal pathway for fine, voluntary movement in humans, especially of the distal limbs.

incorrectas.A: The vestibulospinal tract originates from vestibular nuclei (not motor cortex) and mainly controls axial/postural muscles and balance reflexes, not the fine voluntary movement pathway described from cortical UMNs.
incorrectas.B: The reticulospinal tract arises from the reticular formation in the brainstem and modulates muscle tone and gross postural movements; it is not the tract carrying descending axons from the VL-recipient motor cortex neurons.
incorrectas.C: The rubrospinal tract originates from the red nucleus (which itself receives cerebellar interposed nucleus input), not from motor cortex UMNs, so it is a separate descending pathway from the one described here.

preguntas.q: Neurons of the red nucleus that receive input from the emboliform and globose (interposed) cerebellar nuclei send descending axons via which contralateral tract?

e.correcta: The interposed nuclei (emboliform and globose) of the cerebellum project to the contralateral red nucleus in the midbrain, which in turn gives rise to the rubrospinal tract; this tract crosses again shortly after leaving the red nucleus, a double decussation that results in a net ipsilateral effect on limb flexor tone, mainly of the upper extremity. This pathway works in parallel with the corticospinal tract to modulate distal limb movement, particularly flexor muscle activity.

incorrectas.B: The corticospinal tract arises from upper motor neurons in the motor cortex (relayed via the VL thalamic nucleus), not from red nucleus neurons receiving cerebellar interposed nucleus input; it is a separate descending pathway.
incorrectas.C: The vestibulospinal tract originates in the vestibular nuclei, which receive input more from the flocculonodular lobe and fastigial nucleus for balance, not from the emboliform/globose nuclei that feed the red nucleus.
incorrectas.D: The reticulospinal tract arises from brainstem reticular formation nuclei, which are influenced by different cerebellar and cortical inputs, not specifically by the interposed nuclei-to-red nucleus circuit described.

preguntas.q: The major efferent (outflow) pathway of the cerebellum, carrying deep cerebellar nuclei output to the thalamus and red nucleus, travels through which peduncle?

e.correcta: The superior cerebellar peduncle (brachium conjunctivum) is predominantly an efferent pathway, carrying axons from the deep cerebellar nuclei (mainly dentate and interposed) to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus (VL nucleus), which then relays to motor cortex - making it the chief route by which the cerebellum influences voluntary movement. This is a useful anchor point: of the three cerebellar peduncles, the superior is the one that is mostly "cerebellum-out" rather than "into cerebellum."

incorrectas.A: The middle cerebellar peduncle (brachium pontis) is the largest peduncle but is purely afferent, carrying mossy fiber input from the contralateral pontine nuclei into the cerebellum - the opposite direction of the major outflow described.
incorrectas.C: The inferior cerebellar peduncle (restiform body) carries mostly afferent fibers into the cerebellum (spinocerebellar, vestibulocerebellar, olivocerebellar), along with only a modest efferent component, so it is not considered the major outflow tract.
incorrectas.D: The cerebral peduncle is an entirely different midbrain structure carrying descending corticospinal, corticobulbar, and corticopontine fibers from the cerebral cortex; it has nothing to do with cerebellar output despite the similar-sounding name.

preguntas.q: A patient develops a movement abnormality in which the hand shows a slow, zigzag oscillation as it approaches a target during finger-to-nose testing. Which movement disorder is this?

e.correcta: Intention tremor is a cardinal sign of cerebellar (especially lateral hemisphere) dysfunction and appears or worsens as the limb approaches its target during goal-directed movement, reflecting impaired online error correction normally provided by cerebellar circuits that fine-tune trajectory via feedback through the deep nuclei and red nucleus/thalamus. It is classically elicited with finger-to-nose or heel-to-shin maneuvers and is often accompanied by other lateral cerebellar signs like dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia.

incorrectas.A: Resting tremor occurs at rest and diminishes with voluntary movement; it is characteristic of basal ganglia dopaminergic dysfunction (Parkinson disease), the opposite pattern of a tremor that worsens on approaching a target.
incorrectas.B: Essential tremor is a postural/action tremor present throughout a movement (and with sustained posture) rather than specifically worsening near the endpoint, and it typically improves with alcohol - a distinct entity from the endpoint-worsening intention tremor of cerebellar disease.
incorrectas.D: Myoclonus consists of sudden, brief, shock-like muscle jerks, not a smooth oscillating zigzag tremor that builds as a target is approached, so it does not match the finding described.

preguntas.q: Patients with a lesion of the lateral cerebellar hemisphere characteristically fall toward which side when walking?

e.correcta: Because each cerebellar hemisphere coordinates ipsilateral limb movement (cerebellar efferents cross once via the superior cerebellar peduncle/red nucleus/thalamus pathway to reach contralateral motor cortex, whose corticospinal output then crosses again to affect the side ipsilateral to the cerebellum), a lateral hemispheric lesion produces limb ataxia and a tendency to veer or fall toward the same (ipsilateral) side as the lesion. This "double decussation" logic is a classic testable point distinguishing cerebellar lesions from cerebral hemisphere lesions, which cause contralateral deficits.

incorrectas.B: Falling toward the contralateral side would be expected from a cerebral hemisphere (cortical or corticospinal) lesion causing contralateral hemiparesis, not from a cerebellar hemisphere lesion, which produces ipsilateral limb and gait ataxia due to the double-crossing circuitry.
incorrectas.C: Falling straight backward without lateral preference is more typical of midline (vermian/flocculonodular) or basal ganglia disease causing postural instability, not the lateralized ataxia produced by a lateral hemispheric lesion.
incorrectas.D: Falling forward without lateralization does not reflect the lateralized limb/gait ataxia caused by a unilateral lateral cerebellar lesion.

preguntas.q: A patient overshoots the target and cannot stop the movement at the intended point during finger-to-nose testing. What is this cerebellar sign called?

e.correcta: Dysmetria refers specifically to the inability to judge distance and stop a movement at the correct point, producing overshoot (hypermetria) or undershoot as the limb approaches a target - a hallmark sign of lateral cerebellar hemisphere dysfunction because the lateral cerebellum normally fine-tunes the amplitude and endpoint of a planned movement using ongoing proprioceptive feedback. It is classically demonstrated with finger-to-nose or heel-to-shin testing.

incorrectas.A: Intention tremor is a rhythmic oscillation that appears or worsens as the limb nears the target, which can co-occur with dysmetria, but it describes a tremor pattern rather than the specific failure to stop the movement at the right point.
incorrectas.B: Dysdiadochokinesia is the reduced ability to perform rapid alternating movements (like forearm pronation/supination), a distinct cerebellar sign testing rhythmic reciprocal motion rather than the endpoint accuracy of a single reaching movement.
incorrectas.C: Ataxia is a broad umbrella term for uncoordinated movement in general (which can include dysmetria, gait instability, and tremor); it is not the precise name for the specific overshoot phenomenon being described here.

preguntas.q: A patient has a reduced ability to perform rapid alternating movements, such as pronation and supination of the forearm. What is this cerebellar finding called?

e.correcta: Dysdiadochokinesia describes impaired ability to perform rapid alternating (agonist-antagonist) movements, classically tested by having the patient rapidly pronate and supinate the forearm or tap alternating surfaces of the hand; it results from a lateral cerebellar hemisphere lesion disrupting the fine temporal coordination between opposing muscle groups. It is a distinct clinical test from dysmetria, though both localize to the lateral cerebellum.

incorrectas.A: Dysmetria refers to inaccurate distance/endpoint control during a single targeted movement (overshoot or undershoot), not the specific slowing/clumsiness of rapidly alternating reciprocal movements being described here.
incorrectas.C: Intention tremor is an oscillation that worsens as a limb approaches a target during a single reaching movement, a different phenomenon from the rhythmic alternating-movement task used to test dysdiadochokinesia.
incorrectas.D: Dysarthria refers to impaired articulation of speech due to muscular incoordination, not to limb movement, so it does not describe difficulty with alternating forearm movements.

preguntas.q: A patient with a cerebellar lesion divides words into syllables when speaking, due to asynergy of the muscles of speech. What is this finding called?

e.correcta: Scanning dysarthria (ataxic dysarthria) results from cerebellar dysfunction disrupting the fine coordination ("synergy") between the muscles of respiration, phonation, and articulation, causing speech to come out slow, irregular, and broken into syllables as if being scanned or read robotically. It is grouped with other lateral cerebellar signs like dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, reflecting a shared underlying deficit in coordinating the timing and amplitude of sequential muscle contractions.

incorrectas.B: Spastic dysarthria results from bilateral upper motor neuron (corticobulbar) damage causing a strained, strangled voice quality with slow, effortful speech, a different mechanism (spasticity) from the cerebellar asynergy causing syllabic scanning.
incorrectas.C: Flaccid dysarthria arises from lower motor neuron or neuromuscular junction disease causing weak, breathy, hypernasal speech due to muscle weakness, not incoordination of otherwise strong speech muscles as in cerebellar disease.
incorrectas.D: Hypokinetic dysarthria is characteristic of Parkinson disease, producing soft, monotone, rapid speech from reduced movement amplitude (bradykinesia), a basal ganglia dopaminergic problem rather than a cerebellar coordination deficit.

preguntas.q: Which lateral cerebellar hemisphere sign involves the eyes overshooting and correcting when trying to fixate on a target, often producing nystagmus?

e.correcta: Just as the limbs can overshoot a target (limb dysmetria), the extraocular system can show an analogous deficit called gaze dysfunction or ocular dysmetria, where the eyes overshoot a target during saccades and must correct with small back-and-forth movements, often manifesting clinically as nystagmus. This reflects the cerebellum's broader role in fine-tuning the amplitude and timing of movement across many effector systems, not just skeletal muscle.

incorrectas.A: Scanning dysarthria is the speech analog of cerebellar asynergy (dividing words into syllables), a different effector system (speech muscles) than the oculomotor system being tested here.
incorrectas.B: Dysdiadochokinesia refers to impaired rapid alternating limb movements (e.g., forearm pronation/supination), not to eye movement control, so it does not match the ocular fixation problem described.
incorrectas.D: Dysmetria of the limbs describes overshoot/undershoot during limb-targeted movements like finger-to-nose testing; while it shares the same underlying mechanism as gaze dysfunction, it refers to a different body part (limbs, not eyes).

preguntas.q: Lesions of which region of the cerebellum classically produce nystagmus and head tilting, given its connections through the vermal cortex, fastigial nucleus, and flocculonodular lobe?

e.correcta: The medial cerebellum - comprising the vermis, flocculonodular lobe, and fastigial nucleus - is heavily connected to the vestibular system and is responsible for maintaining truncal/axial balance and coordinating eye movements with head position; damage here produces nystagmus, head tilting, and a wide-based ("truncal") gait ataxia, in contrast to the limb-predominant dysmetria and intention tremor seen with lateral hemisphere lesions. This medial/lateral distinction is a classic way exams test localization within the cerebellum.

incorrectas.A: The lateral cerebellar hemispheres control ipsilateral limb coordination and produce signs like dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and intention tremor of the limbs, rather than the axial/vestibular findings of nystagmus and head tilting described here.
incorrectas.B: The superior cerebellar peduncle is a white matter outflow tract (not a functional "region" with its own localized syndrome) carrying deep nuclear output to the red nucleus and thalamus; damage there does not specifically map onto nystagmus/head tilting.
incorrectas.C: The dentate nucleus is part of the lateral cerebellar output system (relaying lateral hemisphere processing to the thalamus for voluntary movement planning), not the vestibularly connected medial structures responsible for nystagmus and head tilting.

preguntas.q: A patient with a cerebellar lesion is asked to stand with feet together. Under which condition(s) does the resulting truncal ataxia cause them to sway?

o.A: Both with eyes open and eyes closed
o.D: They do not sway in either condition

e.correcta: Cerebellar (especially vermian/medial) lesions impair postural coordination through proprioceptive and vestibular integration that does not depend on vision, so patients sway with both eyes open and eyes closed - visual input can partially compensate but does not correct the ataxia. This is a key distinguishing feature from a positive Romberg sign, which is specific to dorsal column (proprioceptive) lesions.

incorrectas.B: Swaying only with eyes closed describes a positive Romberg sign, which localizes to dorsal column/proprioceptive pathway lesions where vision was compensating for lost proprioception - closing the eyes removes that compensation. Cerebellar ataxia is different because it is not primarily a proprioceptive-input problem that vision can fix.
incorrectas.C: Swaying only with eyes open would be an unusual, non-classic pattern not associated with either cerebellar or dorsal column disease; vision generally helps stability rather than worsening it.
incorrectas.D: Cerebellar lesions of the vermis/flocculonodular system characteristically DO cause postural sway/truncal ataxia; the patient does not maintain normal balance in either condition.

preguntas.q: A patient sways markedly when standing with eyes closed but not with eyes open (a positive Romberg sign). This localizes to a lesion of which pathway?

e.correcta: A positive Romberg sign - swaying specifically when the eyes are closed - indicates loss of proprioceptive input carried by the dorsal columns (e.g., in tabes dorsalis or subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency), because the patient had been using vision to compensate for lost joint-position sense; removing vision unmasks the imbalance. This contrasts with cerebellar disease, where patients sway with both eyes open and closed, since cerebellar ataxia is not simply a proprioceptive-input deficit that vision can correct for.

incorrectas.A: A lateral cerebellar hemisphere lesion produces ataxia that persists with both eyes open and closed (not just closed), because the cerebellum's role in coordinating movement is not corrected by visual compensation, unlike a pure proprioceptive deficit.
incorrectas.C: Vestibular nuclei lesions cause vertigo, nystagmus, and imbalance that is often worsened by head movement, but the classic pure "sways only with eyes closed" pattern specifically defines dorsal column disease, not vestibular pathology.
incorrectas.D: The corticospinal tract carries voluntary motor command output; a lesion here causes upper motor neuron weakness and spasticity, not the sensory ataxia and Romberg sign associated with proprioceptive loss.

preguntas.q: Which structure initiates and provides gross, background control over skeletal muscle movement, working with the cortex to select and scale voluntary motor programs?

e.correcta: The basal ganglia (striatum, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra) act via parallel direct and indirect pathways to modulate thalamocortical output, effectively gating which motor programs are allowed to proceed and providing the gross initiation and scaling of voluntary movement; dysfunction here produces disorders of movement initiation and amplitude like Parkinson disease (hypokinesia) or Huntington disease (hyperkinesia/chorea). This is distinct from fine online correction of ongoing movement, which is the cerebellum's job.

incorrectas.A: The cerebellum's role is to fine-tune the timing, coordination, and accuracy of movements already underway, via comparison of intended versus actual movement using proprioceptive feedback, rather than to initiate or provide gross control over movement, which is the basal ganglia's role.
incorrectas.B: The reticular formation contributes to modulating muscle tone and gross postural/locomotor patterns via the reticulospinal tracts, but it is not the structure classically credited with initiating and providing gross voluntary control, a role attributed to the basal ganglia-thalamocortical loop.
incorrectas.D: The thalamus (particularly the VL/VA nuclei) is a relay station passing basal ganglia and cerebellar output to the cortex; it does not itself initiate movement but transmits the processed signal from structures like the basal ganglia.

preguntas.q: The globus pallidus, a key basal ganglia output nucleus, is divided into which two segments?

e.correcta: The globus pallidus is anatomically and functionally split into an internal segment (GPi), which along with the substantia nigra pars reticulata serves as a major basal ganglia output nucleus projecting inhibitory GABAergic fibers to the thalamus, and an external segment (GPe), which is an interneuron-like relay within the indirect pathway that projects to the subthalamic nucleus. This internal/external distinction is essential for understanding the differing roles of GPi and GPe in the direct versus indirect pathways.

incorrectas.A: Rostral and caudal segments is not the anatomical division used to describe the globus pallidus; this terminology does not correspond to the actual GPi/GPe subdivision used in basal ganglia circuitry.
incorrectas.B: Medial and lateral segments is not accurate terminology for globus pallidus subdivisions; the standard nomenclature is internal (GPi) and external (GPe), reflecting their nested position relative to each other rather than a simple medial-lateral split.
incorrectas.C: Dorsal and ventral segments likewise does not describe the actual globus pallidus subdivision; the correct terms internal/external reflect the nucleus's layered structure, with GPi lying medial/internal to GPe.

preguntas.q: Which basal ganglia component is located in the diencephalon, distinguishing it anatomically from the striatum and globus pallidus (which arise from the telencephalon)?

e.correcta: The subthalamic nucleus is embedded in the diencephalon, specifically ventral to the thalamus, unlike the caudate, putamen, and globus pallidus, which are telencephalic structures. Functionally, the subthalamic nucleus is a key excitatory (glutamatergic) node in the indirect pathway, driving the GPi/SNr to inhibit the thalamus, and its dysfunction (e.g., a contralateral lesion) classically produces hemiballismus, a testable clinical correlate.

incorrectas.B: The putamen is a telencephalic structure that, together with the caudate nucleus, forms the striatum - the main input nucleus of the basal ganglia - and it is not located in the diencephalon.
incorrectas.C: The caudate nucleus is likewise a telencephalic structure and, with the putamen, comprises the striatum receiving cortical glutamatergic input; it is not the diencephalic component being asked about.
incorrectas.D: The globus pallidus (both GPi and GPe) is a telencephalic structure serving as an output/relay nucleus of the basal ganglia, not the diencephalic component described in the question.

preguntas.q: Which basal ganglia pathway facilitates and helps initiate voluntary movement through net disinhibition of the thalamus?

e.correcta: In the direct pathway, cortical glutamatergic input excites striatal neurons that inhibit the GPi/SNr; since the GPi/SNr tonically inhibits the thalamus, inhibiting the inhibitor results in net disinhibition (activation) of the thalamus, which then excites the motor cortex - overall facilitating movement. This double-negative logic ("inhibit the inhibitor") is the key concept for understanding why the direct pathway is pro-movement, while the indirect pathway (net effect: more inhibition of the thalamus) is anti-movement.

incorrectas.A: The nigrostriatal pathway refers to dopaminergic projections from the substantia nigra pars compacta to the striatum, which modulate the balance between the direct and indirect pathways (dopamine loss, as in Parkinson disease, shifts the balance toward the indirect/anti-movement pathway); it is not itself "the pathway" that facilitates movement.
incorrectas.C: The indirect pathway has the opposite net effect: striatal neurons inhibit the GPe, which normally inhibits the subthalamic nucleus, so disinhibiting the subthalamic nucleus increases its excitatory drive on the GPi/SNr, ultimately increasing thalamic inhibition and suppressing movement.
incorrectas.D: The hyperdirect pathway is a faster route from cortex directly to the subthalamic nucleus (bypassing the striatum) that rapidly increases GPi/SNr output to broadly suppress movement, functioning more like an emergency "stop" signal than a movement-facilitating pathway.

preguntas.q: In the basal ganglia circuit, the motor cortex releases which neurotransmitter onto the striatum to drive both the direct and indirect pathways?

e.correcta: The cortex sends excitatory, glutamatergic projections onto striatal medium spiny neurons, which express either D1 receptors (direct pathway) or D2 receptors (indirect pathway) that respond differently to dopaminergic modulation from the substantia nigra. This shared glutamatergic cortical input is the trigger that starts the entire basal ganglia processing loop, regardless of which specific pathway is ultimately favored.

incorrectas.A: Acetylcholine is used by striatal cholinergic interneurons that locally modulate medium spiny neuron activity, not by the cortical projection neurons that initiate the direct/indirect pathways from the cortex.
incorrectas.B: GABA is the neurotransmitter released by the striatal output neurons themselves (onto GPi/GPe/SNr) and by globus pallidus neurons, representing a downstream step in the pathway, not the initial cortex-to-striatum signal.
incorrectas.D: Dopamine is released by substantia nigra pars compacta neurons onto the striatum as a modulatory input (via the nigrostriatal pathway) that biases the direct versus indirect pathways, but it is not the excitatory signal that motor cortex itself uses to drive the striatum.

preguntas.q: In the direct basal ganglia pathway, striatal neurons project to the GPi/SNr releasing which neurotransmitters?

e.correcta: Direct pathway striatal medium spiny neurons (expressing D1 dopamine receptors) co-release GABA (inhibitory) along with the neuropeptide substance P onto the GPi/SNr, inhibiting these tonically active output neurons and thereby disinhibiting the thalamus to facilitate movement. Substance P release is a useful pathway-specific marker: direct pathway neurons release GABA/substance P, while indirect pathway neurons release GABA/enkephalin, a classic distinguishing detail tested on exams.

incorrectas.A: Dopamine and glutamate are not co-released by striatal projection neurons; dopamine instead arrives at the striatum from the substantia nigra pars compacta as a modulatory input, while glutamate is the cortical input onto the striatum, not the striatal output transmitter.
incorrectas.B: Glutamate and acetylcholine are not the striatal output transmitters either - glutamate is the excitatory cortical afferent to the striatum, and acetylcholine is used locally by striatal cholinergic interneurons, not projected to the GPi/SNr.
incorrectas.C: GABA and enkephalin is the neurotransmitter combination released by indirect pathway striatal neurons (D2-expressing) projecting to the GPe, not by the direct pathway neurons targeting the GPi/SNr described in the question.

preguntas.q: In both the direct and indirect basal ganglia pathways, which neurotransmitter is released by the globus pallidus internus (GPi) onto its downstream target?

e.correcta: The GPi is the inhibitory output nucleus of the basal ganglia and tonically inhibits the thalamus via GABA. The direct pathway works by inhibiting the GPi (disinhibiting the thalamus and facilitating movement), while the indirect pathway net-excites the GPi (increasing thalamic inhibition and suppressing movement) — both pathways converge on modulating the strength of this same GABAergic output rather than changing its transmitter.

incorrectas.A: Glutamate is the excitatory transmitter released by the subthalamic nucleus onto the GPi/GPe in the indirect pathway, and by cortex onto the striatum — it is an input to basal ganglia circuitry, not what the GPi itself releases.
incorrectas.C: Dopamine is released by the substantia nigra pars compacta onto the striatum to modulate D1/D2 receptor balance between the two pathways; it is not the output transmitter of the GPi.
incorrectas.D: Acetylcholine is used by striatal cholinergic interneurons to modulate local circuitry, not by GPi projection neurons, which are GABAergic.

preguntas.q: Which of the two basal ganglia pathways functions to inhibit movement, helping suppress unwanted motor activity?

e.correcta: The indirect pathway (striatum → GPe → STN → GPi) ultimately increases GPi inhibitory output onto the thalamus, further suppressing thalamocortical excitation and thus movement. This makes it useful for suppressing unwanted or extraneous movements, complementing the direct pathway's movement-facilitating role, and the two must stay balanced for smooth, purposeful motor output.

incorrectas.A: The direct pathway has striatal neurons directly inhibiting the GPi/SNr, which disinhibits the thalamus and net-facilitates movement — the opposite effect of the indirect pathway.
incorrectas.B: The corticospinal tract is the descending pathway carrying voluntary movement commands from motor cortex to spinal motor neurons; it executes movement rather than being part of the basal ganglia circuitry that suppresses it.
incorrectas.D: The nigrostriatal pathway is the dopaminergic projection from the substantia nigra pars compacta to the striatum that modulates the balance between the direct and indirect pathways, but it does not itself directly inhibit movement.

preguntas.q: In the indirect basal ganglia pathway, which neurotransmitters are released by striatal neurons projecting onto the globus pallidus externus?

e.correcta: Indirect-pathway striatal (medium spiny) neurons express D2 dopamine receptors and co-release GABA plus enkephalin onto the GPe, inhibiting it. This disinhibits the subthalamic nucleus, which then increases its glutamatergic drive onto the GPi, increasing GPi inhibition of the thalamus and suppressing movement.

incorrectas.A: Substance P is co-released with GABA by direct-pathway (D1-expressing) striatal neurons onto the GPi/SNr, not by the indirect-pathway projection to the GPe; glutamate is not released by striatal projection neurons at all.
incorrectas.C: Dopamine is supplied to the striatum from the substantia nigra to modulate which pathway predominates, but it is not released by striatal neurons onto the GPe.
incorrectas.D: Acetylcholine is used by striatal interneurons and glutamate is used by cortical and subthalamic afferents onto the striatum/GPi, neither of which describes the striato-pallidal (GPe-directed) projection itself.

preguntas.q: Which neurotransmitter does the globus pallidus externus (GPe) release onto the subthalamic nucleus in the indirect basal ganglia pathway?

e.correcta: The GPe tonically inhibits the subthalamic nucleus (STN) via GABA. In the indirect pathway, GABA/enkephalin-releasing striatal neurons inhibit the GPe, which removes this GABAergic brake on the STN (disinhibition); the STN then fires more and increases its excitatory glutamate output to the GPi, which increases GPi inhibition of the thalamus — net suppression of movement. A useful memory hook is that the pathway has two inhibitory GABA links in a row (striatum→GPe, GPe→STN), so inhibiting an inhibitor disinhibits the STN.

incorrectas.B: Glutamate is what the STN releases onto the GPe and GPi, the reverse direction of transmission from what the GPe itself releases.
incorrectas.C: Dopamine is supplied by the substantia nigra pars compacta to the striatum to set pathway balance; it is not released by the GPe.
incorrectas.D: Serotonin is not part of the basal ganglia direct/indirect motor circuitry; it is primarily released from raphe nuclei projections that modulate mood and arousal.

preguntas.q: In the indirect basal ganglia pathway, which excitatory neurotransmitter does the subthalamic nucleus release onto the globus pallidus internus?

e.correcta: The subthalamic nucleus is the only excitatory nucleus in the basal ganglia circuit and uses glutamate to excite the GPi (and GPe), which increases the GPi's inhibitory GABAergic output onto the thalamus, net-suppressing movement. This is why a lesion of the STN (classically a lacunar stroke) removes this excitatory drive, disinhibits the thalamus, and produces the excessive, uncontrolled movements of hemiballismus.

incorrectas.A: GABA is the inhibitory transmitter used by the GPe onto the STN and by the GPi onto the thalamus, not the transmitter the STN itself uses.
incorrectas.B: Dopamine is released by the substantia nigra pars compacta onto the striatum, not by the STN, and it modulates striatal input rather than acting directly on the GPi.
incorrectas.D: Acetylcholine is used by striatal cholinergic interneurons and is unrelated to the STN-to-GPi glutamatergic projection.

preguntas.q: Which basal ganglia structure sends dopaminergic projections to the striatum to modulate activity of both the direct and indirect pathways?

e.correcta: The substantia nigra pars compacta sends the nigrostriatal dopaminergic projection to the striatum, acting on excitatory D1 receptors on direct-pathway neurons (facilitating movement) and inhibitory D2 receptors on indirect-pathway neurons (also reducing indirect-pathway suppression) — so net dopamine release promotes movement. Degeneration of these neurons is the pathologic basis of Parkinson disease, producing bradykinesia and rigidity.

incorrectas.A: The globus pallidus externus is a GABAergic relay nucleus of the indirect pathway that targets the STN; it is not a source of dopamine to the striatum.
incorrectas.B: The subthalamic nucleus is the glutamatergic excitatory nucleus of the indirect pathway and does not send dopaminergic input to the striatum.
incorrectas.D: The ventral tegmental area is also dopaminergic but projects via the mesolimbic and mesocortical pathways to the nucleus accumbens and prefrontal cortex, not the nigrostriatal pathway to the striatum.

preguntas.q: A patient presents with sudden, wild, involuntary flailing movements of one arm and the ipsilateral leg. Which movement disorder is this?

e.correcta: Hemiballismus results from a lesion (classically a lacunar infarct) of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus, which removes its excitatory glutamatergic drive on the GPi. This reduces GPi inhibitory output to the thalamus, disinhibiting thalamocortical motor circuits and producing the large-amplitude, violent flinging/flailing movements of the limbs contralateral to the lesion.

incorrectas.B: Chorea consists of rapid, irregular, dance-like movements classically seen in Huntington disease from loss of indirect-pathway striatal neurons; it is smaller-amplitude and more continuous than the violent, large-amplitude flinging of hemiballismus, though the two lie on a related spectrum.
incorrectas.C: Athetosis produces slow, writhing, snake-like movements, often affecting the distal extremities, and is typically seen in cerebral palsy or kernicterus rather than from an acute focal subthalamic lesion.
incorrectas.D: Dystonia involves sustained abnormal postures from simultaneous co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles, a different mechanism than the discrete unilateral basal ganglia circuit lesion that causes flailing movements.

preguntas.q: Hemiballismus is most strongly associated with which underlying risk factor, given its predisposition to lacunar stroke affecting the subthalamic nucleus?

e.correcta: Chronic hypertension causes lipohyalinosis of small penetrating arteries, predisposing to lacunar infarcts, and a lacunar stroke affecting the contralateral subthalamic nucleus is the classic cause of hemiballismus. Because of this link, blood pressure control is central to preventing recurrence.

incorrectas.B: Hyperlipidemia mainly contributes to large-vessel atherosclerosis and embolic or large-territory strokes, rather than the small-vessel lipohyalinosis specifically implicated in the lacunar infarcts that cause hemiballismus.
incorrectas.C: Atrial fibrillation predisposes to cardioembolic strokes that typically affect larger cortical or subcortical territories, not the small, discrete lacunar infarct mechanism classically responsible for hemiballismus.
incorrectas.D: Diabetes insipidus is a disorder of antidiuretic hormone action and water balance, unrelated to cerebrovascular disease risk or stroke.

preguntas.q: Which region of the retina has the highest visual acuity?

e.correcta: The macula lutea is the central retina, densely packed with cone photoreceptors, which gives it the sharpest spatial resolution and best color vision of any retinal region; within the macula, the fovea is the point of peak cone density and thus peak acuity.

incorrectas.A: The optic disc is the "blind spot" where retinal ganglion cell axons exit as the optic nerve and where retinal vessels enter — it contains no photoreceptors at all, so acuity there is effectively zero.
incorrectas.C: The ora serrata is the peripheral edge where the retina transitions into the ciliary body; photoreceptors there are sparse, so it is not a site of high acuity.
incorrectas.D: The peripheral retina is dominated by rod photoreceptors, which favor light sensitivity and motion detection over fine spatial resolution, making acuity there comparatively low.

preguntas.q: Which depression within the macula is the point of maximal light focus and highest visual acuity?

e.correcta: The fovea centralis is a thinned pit within the macula containing almost exclusively cone photoreceptors, with minimal overlying retinal layers and vasculature, so incoming light strikes the cones with little scatter or obstruction — this is what gives the fovea the sharpest acuity in the retina.

incorrectas.B: The optic disc is a separate, distinct structure elsewhere on the retina (the blind spot where the optic nerve exits) and has no relation to the fovea's high-acuity function.
incorrectas.C: The ciliary body is an anterior segment structure that produces aqueous humor and adjusts lens shape via the zonular fibers during accommodation; it is not part of the retina.
incorrectas.D: The pars plana is the posterior portion of the ciliary body commonly used as a surgical entry site, unrelated to macular or foveal vision.

preguntas.q: The lens is suspended and anchored to the ciliary body by which structures?

e.correcta: Zonular fibers (suspensory ligaments) anchor the equator of the lens to the ciliary body. Contraction of the ciliary muscle relaxes tension on these fibers, allowing the lens to round up for near accommodation, while ciliary muscle relaxation increases zonular tension and flattens the lens for distance vision.

incorrectas.B: Vitreous strands are not a real anchoring structure for the lens; the vitreous humor is a gel filling the posterior segment and does not physically suspend the lens.
incorrectas.C: The trabecular meshwork is the drainage structure at the iridocorneal angle responsible for aqueous humor outflow, unrelated to lens support.
incorrectas.D: Descemet membrane is the basement membrane of the corneal endothelium, part of the cornea rather than a structure suspending the lens.

preguntas.q: What are the two types of photoreceptor cells responsible for vision in the retina?

e.correcta: Rods and cones are the true light-transducing photoreceptors: they convert photons into electrical signals through phototransduction cascades involving rhodopsin (rods) or photopsins (cones), then relay that signal to bipolar cells.

incorrectas.B: Bipolar and horizontal cells are retinal interneurons that relay and modulate signals between photoreceptors and ganglion cells; neither type directly senses light.
incorrectas.C: Amacrine cells modulate signals laterally in the inner plexiform layer, and ganglion cells are the retina's output neurons whose axons form the optic nerve — neither directly transduces light.
incorrectas.D: Müller cells are retinal glia providing structural and metabolic support, and pigment epithelial cells absorb stray light and recycle vitamin A, but neither converts light into a neural signal.

preguntas.q: Which photoreceptor type is primarily responsible for vision in low-light (nighttime) conditions?

e.correcta: Rods contain rhodopsin, a highly light-sensitive pigment capable of responding even to single photons, and many rods converge onto a single bipolar cell, summing weak signals together — this convergence enables scotopic (night) vision at the cost of spatial resolution.

incorrectas.A: Cones require brighter light to activate and mediate photopic (daytime) and color vision; their low convergence ratio makes them poorly suited to detecting dim light.
incorrectas.C: Ganglion cells are the output neurons of the retina that relay processed signals to the brain via the optic nerve; they are not primary light detectors themselves.
incorrectas.D: Horizontal cells are lateral interneurons that modulate photoreceptor output to sharpen contrast, but they do not perform light detection.

preguntas.q: Which photoreceptor is most sensitive to low-intensity light stimuli?

e.correcta: High convergence of many rods onto a single bipolar cell allows summation of weak signals, and the biochemistry of rhodopsin allows rods to respond even to dim or single-photon stimuli, giving them far greater sensitivity than cones — at the expense of spatial acuity.

incorrectas.A: Cones require more photons to activate because of their lower convergence ratio onto bipolar cells and different phototransduction kinetics; they are instead adapted for high-acuity, color vision in bright light.
incorrectas.B: Bipolar cells are relay neurons that receive input from photoreceptors; they are not primary sensors of light intensity themselves.
incorrectas.D: Amacrine cells are modulatory interneurons within the inner retina and are not primary phototransducers.

preguntas.q: Rods are best characterized by which combination of visual properties?

e.correcta: Because many rods converge onto a single bipolar cell, activation of any one rod in the group can trigger that bipolar cell, which is excellent for detecting faint light (high sensitivity) but poor for distinguishing fine spatial detail since signals from many separate rods get pooled together (low acuity).

incorrectas.A: High acuity with low sensitivity describes cones, which have a low convergence ratio (near 1:1 with bipolar cells in the fovea), preserving spatial detail but requiring more light to activate.
incorrectas.C: No photoreceptor achieves both high acuity and high sensitivity simultaneously; there is an inherent tradeoff between convergence-driven sensitivity and single-cell spatial resolution.
