incorrectas.D: Rods are specifically defined by their strong sensitivity due to convergent summation, so "low sensitivity" is inaccurate — only the acuity half of this pairing is correct for rods.

preguntas.q: Cones are best characterized by which combination of visual properties?

e.correcta: Few cones converge onto each bipolar cell, often approaching a 1:1 ratio in the fovea, which preserves fine spatial information (high acuity) but makes cones harder to activate under dim light (low sensitivity) since there is little signal summation — this is why cones dominate photopic (daylight) vision.

incorrectas.A: Low acuity with high sensitivity describes rods, whose high convergence ratio pools signals to boost sensitivity at the cost of spatial resolution.
incorrectas.C: This combination is incorrect for cones, which specifically retain high acuity precisely because of their minimal convergence onto bipolar cells.
incorrectas.D: Photoreceptors show an inherent tradeoff between convergence-based sensitivity and single-cell resolution, so no photoreceptor type achieves both high acuity and high sensitivity at once.

preguntas.q: Which photoreceptor type mediates daytime and color vision?

e.correcta: Cones contain photopsins (three subtypes tuned to red, green, and blue wavelengths) that function best in bright light, giving photopic vision its color discrimination and high spatial resolution; they are concentrated in the fovea and macula, which is why sharp color vision is best when looking directly at an object.

incorrectas.A: Rods contain a single photopigment (rhodopsin), so they cannot distinguish wavelengths or colors, and they function best in scotopic (dim) rather than daytime conditions.
incorrectas.C: Ganglion cells relay processed visual signals to the brain via the optic nerve; while a small intrinsically photosensitive subset contributes to circadian light detection, they are not the primary color/day-vision photoreceptors.
incorrectas.D: Pigment epithelium absorbs stray light and supports photoreceptor metabolism and vitamin A recycling, but it does not itself detect light for vision.

preguntas.q: Which photoreceptor requires higher-intensity light in order to become activated?

e.correcta: Cones have a higher activation threshold than rods because of their lower convergence onto bipolar cells and different phototransduction kinetics, meaning they need brighter light to generate a usable signal — this is why cones mediate photopic (daytime) rather than scotopic vision.

incorrectas.A: Rods are the opposite: they are exquisitely sensitive to dim light and actually saturate (bleach) in bright light, which is why they contribute little to daytime vision.
incorrectas.B: Horizontal cells are lateral interneurons that adjust photoreceptor signaling to enhance contrast; they are not primary detectors with an intrinsic light-intensity threshold.
incorrectas.D: Bipolar cells are relay neurons downstream of photoreceptors, so their activity simply reflects rod/cone input rather than possessing their own light-intensity threshold.

preguntas.q: Which photoreceptor type predominates in the fovea?

o.D: Neither (the fovea is avascular and cell-free)

e.correcta: The fovea is packed almost exclusively with cones, with rods essentially absent, which maximizes spatial resolution and color vision at the point of central gaze — this is why acuity is best when looking directly at an object using the fovea rather than viewing it peripherally.

incorrectas.A: Rods are essentially absent from the fovea and instead populate the peripheral retina, which explains why dim objects are sometimes seen better "out of the corner of the eye" using peripheral rod vision.
incorrectas.C: There is a sharp cone predominance and rod-free zone specifically at the fovea, not an equal mixture of the two photoreceptor types.
incorrectas.D: The fovea is indeed avascular (nourished instead by the underlying choroid), but it is densely populated with cone photoreceptor cells rather than being devoid of cells.

preguntas.q: Which layer of the retina absorbs stray light to prevent scatter and improve image clarity?

e.correcta: The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) contains melanin that absorbs photons not captured by the photoreceptors, preventing internal reflection and scatter much like the black backing of a camera. It also recycles retinal (vitamin A metabolism) and phagocytoses shed photoreceptor outer segments, supporting overall photoreceptor health.

incorrectas.A: The outer nuclear layer contains the photoreceptor cell bodies and nuclei, the site of phototransduction machinery, not a light-absorbing/anti-glare layer.
incorrectas.C: The inner plexiform layer is a synaptic layer where bipolar, amacrine, and ganglion cells connect and process signal, unrelated to stray-light absorption.
incorrectas.D: The nerve fiber layer consists of ganglion cell axons converging to form the optic nerve — a conduction pathway, not a pigmented or light-absorbing layer.

preguntas.q: The cell bodies (nuclei) of the rod and cone photoreceptors are located in which retinal layer?

e.correcta: The outer nuclear layer contains the nuclei of rods and cones, positioned just internal to the photoreceptor outer/inner segments and the retinal pigment epithelium. Because the retina is "inverted," light must pass through the inner retinal layers before finally reaching the photoreceptors housed here.

incorrectas.A: The inner nuclear layer houses the cell bodies of bipolar, horizontal, and amacrine cells — the interneurons — not the photoreceptors themselves.
incorrectas.C: The ganglion cell layer contains ganglion cell bodies, the retina's output neurons, positioned closest to the vitreous and farthest from the photoreceptors.
incorrectas.D: The nerve fiber layer consists of ganglion cell axons traveling toward the optic disc, not photoreceptor cell bodies.

preguntas.q: Bipolar cells of the retina relay visual signals by synapsing onto which output neurons?

e.correcta: Bipolar cells receive input from photoreceptors in the outer plexiform layer and synapse onto ganglion cells in the inner plexiform layer. Ganglion cells are the sole output neurons of the retina, and their axons form the optic nerve that carries visual information to the brain.

incorrectas.A: Horizontal cells synapse laterally with photoreceptors and bipolar cells in the outer plexiform layer to modulate contrast and surround inhibition, but they are not the retina's final output target.
incorrectas.B: Amacrine cells modulate signal transfer within the inner plexiform layer between bipolar and ganglion cells, functioning as interneurons rather than the final relay cell.
incorrectas.D: Photoreceptors are upstream of bipolar cells (bipolar cells receive input from, rather than synapse onto, photoreceptors), so this option reverses the actual direction of signal flow.

preguntas.q: Regeneration of 11-cis-retinal from all-trans-retinal in the visual cycle requires adequate levels of which vitamin?

e.correcta: Vitamin A (retinol) is the precursor from which 11-cis-retinal is synthesized and regenerated, then recombined with opsin to reform functional rhodopsin after light bleaches it to all-trans-retinal; part of this recycling occurs in the retinal pigment epithelium. Because rods depend heavily on rapid pigment turnover, vitamin A deficiency impairs rod function first, producing night blindness (nyctalopia).

incorrectas.B: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration and megaloblastic anemia; it is unrelated to the retinoid visual cycle.
incorrectas.C: Vitamin D regulates calcium and phosphate homeostasis and bone metabolism, not photopigment regeneration.
incorrectas.D: Vitamin E is a fat-soluble antioxidant important for preventing lipid peroxidation and can cause neuromuscular problems when deficient, but it is not involved in the retinal visual cycle.

preguntas.q: Which fluid fills the anterior and posterior chambers of the eye (the anterior segment)?

e.correcta: Aqueous humor, produced by the nonpigmented epithelium of the ciliary body, fills the anterior and posterior chambers of the anterior segment. It nourishes avascular structures such as the cornea and lens and helps maintain intraocular pressure, ultimately draining through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm canal.

incorrectas.A: Vitreous humor is a gel that fills the posterior segment behind the lens; unlike aqueous humor, it is not continuously secreted and reabsorbed, and it does not fill the anterior/posterior chambers.
incorrectas.C: Perilymph is fluid within the bony labyrinth of the inner ear (scala vestibuli and scala tympani), unrelated to ocular anatomy.
incorrectas.D: Endolymph is fluid within the membranous labyrinth (scala media, semicircular canals) of the inner ear, also unrelated to the eye's chambers.

preguntas.q: Aqueous humor is produced in the posterior chamber and flows through the pupil into which chamber before draining at the iridocorneal angle?

e.correcta: Aqueous humor is secreted by the ciliary processes into the posterior chamber (between iris and lens), flows anteriorly through the pupil into the anterior chamber (between iris and cornea), and then drains via the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm canal (conventional pathway) or the uveoscleral pathway. Obstruction of this outflow, such as at the trabecular meshwork or in a narrowed angle, raises intraocular pressure and causes glaucoma.

incorrectas.B: The vitreous chamber lies behind the lens in the posterior segment and is filled with vitreous gel; it is not part of the aqueous humor's normal anterior circulation pathway.
incorrectas.C: The suprachoroidal space is a potential space between the choroid and sclera, relevant in choroidal detachment or hemorrhage, not in normal aqueous humor flow.
incorrectas.D: The subretinal space is the potential space between the neurosensory retina and the retinal pigment epithelium, relevant in retinal detachment, not in aqueous humor circulation.

preguntas.q: Timolol, a topical beta-blocker used to treat open-angle glaucoma, lowers intraocular pressure by decreasing aqueous humor production. This effect is best explained by which receptor action?

e.correcta: Beta receptors on the ciliary body epithelium normally stimulate aqueous humor secretion via a Gs/cAMP pathway. Blocking these receptors with a beta-antagonist like timolol reduces cAMP-driven fluid secretion by the ciliary processes, lowering intraocular pressure without changing pupil size or outflow — which is why beta-blockers are a mainstay first-line option for open-angle glaucoma that avoids the miotic side effects of cholinergic drugs.

incorrectas.B: Alpha-2 agonists such as brimonidine also decrease aqueous production, but through a different receptor family (Gi-coupled alpha-2 receptors that lower cAMP), which is the opposite pharmacologic strategy from blocking beta receptors.
incorrectas.C: M3 agonists like pilocarpine work by an entirely different mechanism — contracting the sphincter and ciliary muscle to open the trabecular meshwork and increase aqueous OUTFLOW, rather than reducing its production the way beta-blockade does.
incorrectas.D: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide, dorzolamide) block the enzyme needed for bicarbonate-dependent fluid secretion in the ciliary epithelium — a non-adrenergic, enzyme-based pathway distinct from beta-receptor blockade.

preguntas.q: Brimonidine, an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, is used in glaucoma management to lower intraocular pressure by decreasing aqueous humor production. Which receptor mediates this effect?

e.correcta: Alpha-2 agonists bind Gi-coupled alpha-2 receptors on the ciliary epithelium, lowering intracellular cAMP and thereby reducing aqueous secretion; brimonidine also has the added benefit of increasing uveoscleral outflow, giving it a dual mechanism that makes it useful when other agents fail.

incorrectas.A: M3 agonists like pilocarpine act on the sphincter and ciliary muscle to increase aqueous OUTFLOW via miosis and trabecular meshwork opening, rather than acting through the Gi-coupled alpha-2 pathway that reduces production.
incorrectas.C: Beta-blockers reduce aqueous production by antagonizing Gs-coupled beta receptors — an opposite receptor family and an opposite pharmacologic action (antagonist rather than agonist) compared to an alpha-2 agonist.
incorrectas.D: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide, dorzolamide) reduce bicarbonate-transport-dependent fluid formation through direct enzyme inhibition, a mechanism entirely unrelated to adrenergic receptor signaling.

preguntas.q: Acetazolamide and dorzolamide reduce intraocular pressure in glaucoma by decreasing aqueous humor production. Which enzyme do these drugs inhibit to achieve this effect?

e.correcta: Carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary epithelium catalyzes CO2 + H2O to form HCO3- and H+, supplying the bicarbonate that drives sodium and fluid secretion into the posterior chamber. Inhibiting the enzyme (dorzolamide topically, acetazolamide systemically) reduces this bicarbonate-dependent fluid formation and lowers intraocular pressure, and acetazolamide's systemic use is also exploited to prevent altitude sickness.

incorrectas.A: Adenylate cyclase produces cAMP downstream of beta-adrenergic stimulation; inhibiting it would mimic the effect of beta-blockade, but that is not the enzyme these carbonic anhydrase inhibitors act on.
incorrectas.B: Acetylcholinesterase breaks down acetylcholine at cholinergic synapses; inhibiting it (e.g., echothiophate) increases cholinergic tone causing miosis and increased outflow, a completely different target and mechanism from carbonic anhydrase inhibition.
incorrectas.D: Monoamine oxidase metabolizes catecholamines and is relevant to depression and Parkinson disease pharmacology, not to aqueous humor formation in the ciliary body.

preguntas.q: Which gel-like fluid fills the vitreous chamber (posterior segment) of the eye, providing structural support and maintaining ocular shape?

e.correcta: Vitreous humor is the transparent, avascular gel occupying the space between the lens and the retina in the posterior segment. Composed mostly of water, collagen, and hyaluronic acid, it maintains the eye's spherical shape and keeps the retina pressed against the underlying choroid, and unlike aqueous humor it is not continuously produced and drained.

incorrectas.A: Aqueous humor instead fills the anterior and posterior chambers of the anterior segment (between cornea and lens), and unlike static vitreous humor it is continuously produced by the ciliary body and drained through the trabecular meshwork.
incorrectas.B: Perilymph is the fluid within the bony labyrinth of the inner ear (cochlea and vestibular apparatus), important for sound and balance transduction — it has nothing to do with ocular anatomy.
incorrectas.C: Tears are an aqueous secretion from the lacrimal gland that lubricates the corneal surface externally; they do not fill any internal chamber of the eye.

preguntas.q: Which autonomic receptor predominates on the pupillary sphincter muscle, such that its stimulation produces miosis?

e.correcta: Parasympathetic postganglionic fibers from the ciliary ganglion release acetylcholine onto Gq-coupled M3 receptors on the circularly-arranged sphincter muscle, contracting it to constrict the pupil. This mechanism underlies pilocarpine's use in glaucoma and physostigmine's ability to reverse anticholinergic-induced mydriasis.

incorrectas.B: Alpha1 receptors instead mediate contraction of the radially-oriented pupillary DILATOR muscle, producing mydriasis — the opposite muscle and the opposite pupillary effect from the sphincter.
incorrectas.C: Beta2 receptors are Gs-coupled and typically relax smooth muscle (as in bronchodilation or vasodilation); they are not the predominant receptor governing iris muscle tone.
incorrectas.D: Nicotinic receptors mediate fast synaptic transmission at autonomic ganglia and neuromuscular junctions (i.e., the preganglionic-to-postganglionic synapse), not the receptor on the smooth muscle target itself.

preguntas.q: Which receptor predominates on the pupillary dilator muscle, whose stimulation produces mydriasis?

e.correcta: Sympathetic postganglionic fibers release norepinephrine onto Gq-coupled alpha1 receptors on the radially-arranged dilator muscle, contracting it to widen the pupil. This is the pharmacologic basis for using phenylephrine eye drops to achieve mydriasis during fundoscopic examination.

incorrectas.A: M3 muscarinic receptors instead mediate parasympathetic-driven contraction of the sphincter (miosis) and ciliary muscle (accommodation) — the opposite muscle and effect from dilation.
incorrectas.C: Alpha2 receptors act mainly as presynaptic autoreceptors limiting further norepinephrine release, and in the eye alpha2 agonists reduce aqueous humor production rather than directly contracting the dilator muscle.
incorrectas.D: Beta1 receptors are primarily found in the heart (increasing rate and contractility) and the juxtaglomerular apparatus (renin release); they are not the receptor responsible for iris dilator contraction.

preguntas.q: Which receptor predominates on the ciliary muscle, mediating contraction for near-vision accommodation?

e.correcta: Parasympathetic acetylcholine acting on M3 receptors contracts the circular ciliary muscle, relaxing zonular fiber tension and allowing the lens to become more rounded for near vision. Relaxation of this muscle flattens the lens for distance vision, and antimuscarinic cycloplegics like atropine exploit this pathway to paralyze accommodation for eye examinations.

incorrectas.A: Alpha1 stimulation instead contracts the pupillary dilator muscle to produce mydriasis — an unrelated iris muscle that plays no role in lens shape or accommodation.
incorrectas.B: Beta2 receptors relax smooth muscle in other systems (bronchi, vasculature, uterus) and are not the primary mediator of ciliary muscle tone.
incorrectas.D: Nicotinic receptors act at the ganglionic synapse within the parasympathetic pathway (preganglionic to postganglionic fiber in the ciliary ganglion), not on the ciliary muscle itself, which responds to muscarinic input.

preguntas.q: The pupillary sphincter (constrictor) muscle, responsible for miosis, is under which branch of autonomic control?

e.correcta: The sphincter muscle receives parasympathetic innervation via CN III (Edinger-Westphal nucleus, then ciliary ganglion, then short ciliary nerves), with acetylcholine acting on M3 receptors to constrict the pupil in bright light or during the near reflex. This is why compressive lesions of CN III's parasympathetic fibers classically cause a dilated, poorly reactive ('blown') pupil.

incorrectas.A: Sympathetic innervation instead targets the pupillary DILATOR muscle via alpha1 receptors, causing mydriasis — the opposing muscle and pathway.
incorrectas.B: Somatic (voluntary) motor control governs skeletal muscle such as the extraocular muscles that move the globe, not the smooth muscle of the iris, which is autonomically controlled.
incorrectas.C: The enteric nervous system governs gastrointestinal motility and secretion largely independently of central control and has no role in pupillary function.

preguntas.q: In the pupillary light reflex pathway, after light stimulates the retina and the signal travels via CN II, to which midbrain structure does the afferent signal project next?

e.correcta: Retinal ganglion cell axons carrying light information travel via the optic nerve and tract, branching off before reaching the lateral geniculate nucleus to synapse in the pretectal nuclei of the midbrain. From there, the pretectal neurons relay bilaterally to the Edinger-Westphal nuclei, initiating the consensual parasympathetic response.

incorrectas.B: The superior colliculus receives some visual fibers to coordinate reflexive eye and head movement toward visual stimuli, but it is not the initial relay station for the pupillary light reflex.
incorrectas.C: The lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus is the main relay for conscious visual perception, sending fibers via the optic radiations to the visual cortex — a separate pathway from the reflex circuit described here.
incorrectas.D: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus is correct further downstream in the circuit (receiving bilateral input from the pretectal nuclei), but it is not the first midbrain structure the afferent signal reaches.

preguntas.q: In the pupillary light reflex, cells in the pretectal nuclei send bilateral projections to which structure to initiate the parasympathetic efferent limb?

e.correcta: Pretectal neurons project bilaterally to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, the parasympathetic component of CN III — this bilateral crossing is exactly why shining light in one eye constricts both pupils (the consensual reflex). The Edinger-Westphal nucleus then sends preganglionic parasympathetic fibers via CN III to the ciliary ganglion.

incorrectas.A: The ciliary ganglion is the next station further downstream, receiving preganglionic fibers FROM the Edinger-Westphal nucleus rather than directly from the pretectal nuclei.
incorrectas.C: The superior colliculus participates in visuomotor reflexes for orienting the eyes and head, not in the parasympathetic efferent chain of the pupillary light reflex.
incorrectas.D: The superior cervical ganglion belongs to the SYMPATHETIC pathway supplying the dilator muscle, an entirely separate circuit from the parasympathetic light reflex involving the Edinger-Westphal nucleus.

preguntas.q: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus travel via CN III to synapse in which ganglion?

e.correcta: Edinger-Westphal preganglionic parasympathetic fibers run within CN III to the ciliary ganglion, located just behind the eye in the orbit, where they synapse onto postganglionic neurons. These postganglionic fibers then travel via the short ciliary nerves to the pupillary sphincter and ciliary muscle to complete the reflex.

incorrectas.A: The pterygopalatine ganglion carries parasympathetics from CN VII, supplying the lacrimal gland and nasal/palatine mucosal secretion — a completely different cranial nerve and target from the pupillary pathway.
incorrectas.B: The otic ganglion relays CN IX parasympathetics to the parotid gland to drive salivation, unrelated to any ocular structure.
incorrectas.D: The submandibular ganglion relays CN VII parasympathetics to the submandibular and sublingual glands, again a salivary target rather than the eye.

preguntas.q: Postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the ciliary ganglion reach the pupillary sphincter muscle via which nerves, producing bilateral (consensual) pupillary constriction?

e.correcta: Postganglionic parasympathetic fibers exit the ciliary ganglion as the short ciliary nerves, which pierce the sclera to innervate the pupillary sphincter (and the ciliary muscle). Because both Edinger-Westphal nuclei were activated bilaterally, this completes the efferent limb of the light reflex on both sides, producing the consensual response.

incorrectas.A: Long ciliary nerves instead carry SYMPATHETIC fibers (traveling with the nasociliary nerve, not originating from the ciliary ganglion) to the pupillary dilator muscle — an entirely different autonomic branch and target.
incorrectas.B: The nasociliary nerve is a sensory branch of CN V1 that also transmits sympathetic fibers to the globe, but it does not carry the parasympathetic output of the ciliary ganglion.
incorrectas.C: The lacrimal nerve, another CN V1 branch, supplies sensation to the lacrimal gland region and conveys parasympathetics to it (from the pterygopalatine ganglion), unrelated to pupillary constriction.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve carries the afferent (sensory) limb of the pupillary light reflex from the retina to the brainstem?

e.correcta: Light detected by retinal photoreceptors generates signals carried by retinal ganglion cell axons that form CN II, which travel to the pretectal nuclei to initiate the reflex. A lesion of CN II abolishes both the direct and consensual pupillary responses when light is shone specifically in the affected eye — the hallmark of an afferent pupillary defect.

incorrectas.B: CN III carries the EFFERENT parasympathetic output that constricts the pupil, not the incoming visual signal; a CN III lesion instead produces a dilated, poorly reactive pupil rather than an afferent defect.
incorrectas.C: CN V provides corneal and facial sensation and forms the afferent limb of the corneal reflex, but it plays no role in transmitting the retinal light information used by the pupillary reflex.
incorrectas.D: CN VI innervates the lateral rectus muscle for eye abduction — a purely motor nerve for eye movement, unrelated to the pupillary light reflex.

preguntas.q: Which cranial nerve carries the efferent (motor) limb of the pupillary light reflex, causing pupillary constriction?

e.correcta: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus sends preganglionic parasympathetic axons within CN III to the ciliary ganglion, whose postganglionic fibers then constrict the sphincter muscle. Compressive lesions of CN III (uncal herniation, posterior communicating artery aneurysm) classically produce a dilated, unreactive 'blown pupil' because these parasympathetic fibers run superficially on the nerve and are compressed before the motor fibers are affected.

incorrectas.A: CN II is the AFFERENT nerve carrying the light signal from the retina to the brainstem, not the motor output responsible for pupillary constriction.
incorrectas.C: CN IV innervates the superior oblique muscle for eye movement (intorsion and depression in adduction), carrying no autonomic fibers relevant to pupil size.
incorrectas.D: CN VI innervates the lateral rectus for abduction — also a purely somatic motor nerve with no involvement in pupillary constriction.

preguntas.q: The ciliary muscle, whose contraction enables lens accommodation for near vision, is under which branch of autonomic control?

e.correcta: Parasympathetic fibers travel via CN III to the ciliary ganglion and short ciliary nerves to innervate the ciliary muscle; its contraction relaxes zonular fiber tension, allowing the lens to round up for near vision, while relaxation (from reduced parasympathetic tone or cycloplegic antimuscarinic drugs) flattens the lens for distance vision.

incorrectas.A: Sympathetic input to the eye instead targets the pupillary dilator muscle to produce mydriasis; it contributes only a minor relaxing influence on accommodation rather than driving ciliary muscle contraction.
incorrectas.B: Somatic motor control governs skeletal muscles such as the extraocular muscles that move the globe, not the smooth ciliary muscle, which is under autonomic (parasympathetic) control.
incorrectas.D: The enteric nervous system controls gastrointestinal motility and secretion independently and has no involvement in ocular accommodation.

preguntas.q: The pupillary dilator muscle, whose contraction produces mydriasis, is under which branch of autonomic control?

e.correcta: Sympathetic fibers originate in the hypothalamus, descend through the brainstem and spinal cord to the ciliospinal center of Budge (C8-T2), then travel via the sympathetic chain to the superior cervical ganglion and long ciliary nerves, acting on alpha1 receptors of the radially arranged dilator muscle to widen the pupil. Because this is a long three-neuron pathway, a lesion anywhere along its course (as in Horner syndrome) impairs pupillary dilation.

incorrectas.A: Parasympathetic fibers instead innervate the pupillary SPHINCTER and ciliary muscle via CN III, producing miosis and accommodation respectively — the opposite muscle and effect.
incorrectas.B: Somatic motor neurons control skeletal muscle such as the extraocular muscles, not the smooth muscle of the iris.
incorrectas.C: The enteric nervous system is confined to the gastrointestinal tract and does not participate in pupillary control.

preguntas.q: Sympathetic axons from the ciliospinal center of Budge exit the spinal cord at T1 and ascend the cervical sympathetic chain to synapse in which ganglion before reaching the eye?

e.correcta: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers from the ciliospinal center (C8-T2) exit at T1 and ascend near the lung apex and subclavian vessels through the cervical sympathetic chain to synapse in the superior cervical ganglion. Postganglionic fibers then travel with the carotid plexus and long ciliary nerves to the dilator muscle, also innervating Muller's muscle of the eyelid and facial sweat glands — which explains why a lesion anywhere along this course (such as a Pancoast tumor) produces the full Horner triad of ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis.

incorrectas.B: The ciliary ganglion is a PARASYMPATHETIC relay station for CN III fibers, an entirely separate ganglion from the sympathetic chain being described here.
incorrectas.C: The stellate ganglion (fused inferior cervical and first thoracic ganglion) lies lower in the neck and mainly supplies cardiac and upper limb sympathetics rather than serving as the primary relay for oculosympathetic fibers to the eye.
incorrectas.D: The celiac ganglion is an abdominal sympathetic ganglion serving gastrointestinal and other visceral organs, unrelated to the head and neck oculosympathetic pathway.

preguntas.q: Postganglionic sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion reach the pupillary dilator muscle via which nerves?

e.correcta: Postganglionic sympathetic fibers travel with the internal carotid plexus, join the nasociliary nerve (CN V1), and reach the globe as the long ciliary nerves to innervate the dilator muscle (while also carrying some sensory fibers). These same sympathetic fibers also supply the eyelid's Muller muscle and facial sweat glands, tying dilator innervation to the broader oculosympathetic pathway disrupted in Horner syndrome.

incorrectas.A: Short ciliary nerves instead carry PARASYMPATHETIC postganglionic fibers from the ciliary ganglion to the sphincter and ciliary muscle — the opposite autonomic branch and target.
incorrectas.C: The infraorbital nerve is a sensory branch of CN V2 supplying the lower eyelid, cheek, and upper lip; it plays no role in autonomic innervation of intraocular muscles.
incorrectas.D: The zygomatic nerve is another CN V2 sensory branch supplying skin over the zygomatic and temporal region, not a conduit for sympathetic fibers to the iris.

preguntas.q: A patient with tertiary neurosyphilis has pupils that constrict normally with accommodation but fail to constrict in response to light. What is this finding called?

e.correcta: The Argyll-Robertson pupil (sometimes called the 'prostitute's pupil' because it accommodates but does not react) results from bilateral lesions in the midbrain pretectal area that damage the light reflex pathway while sparing the near/accommodation pathway, which travels via different, more ventral fibers. It is classically seen in neurosyphilis (and occasionally diabetic neuropathy), reflecting the differential vulnerability of these two anatomically distinct circuits.

incorrectas.A: Marcus Gunn pupil (relative afferent pupillary defect) shows decreased constriction when light is swung to the affected eye due to a damaged optic nerve or retina, not a dissociation between the light and accommodation responses.
incorrectas.B: Adie (tonic) pupil is a unilaterally dilated pupil with a sluggish light response but a slow, tonic accommodation response, due to ciliary ganglion damage; it is unilateral and dilated rather than the typically bilateral, small-pupil picture of Argyll-Robertson pupil.
incorrectas.D: Horner syndrome causes miosis (with ptosis and anhidrosis) from sympathetic disruption, but both light and accommodation reflexes remain intact, unlike the specific light-near dissociation of Argyll-Robertson pupil.

preguntas.q: When a light is swung from the unaffected eye to the affected eye, both pupils show decreased constriction (appearing to paradoxically dilate) compared to shining light in the unaffected eye. What is this finding called?

e.correcta: The Marcus Gunn pupil (relative afferent pupillary defect, RAPD) reflects a weakened afferent signal from one eye due to optic nerve or severe retinal disease. On the swinging-flashlight test, moving the light to the damaged eye produces less bilateral constriction (and apparent relative dilation) compared to the healthy eye, because the efferent CN III pathway and its bilateral projections remain fully intact — the deficit is purely on the input side.

incorrectas.A: Argyll-Robertson pupil shows dissociation between an absent light reflex and a preserved accommodation reflex, not a relative difference in the light response between the two eyes on the swinging-flashlight test.
incorrectas.B: Adie pupil is a unilaterally dilated pupil with a tonic, sluggish reaction to light and slow redilation after near focus, caused by a ciliary ganglion lesion, not by an afferent conduction deficit.
incorrectas.C: Horner pupil is a small, sympathetically denervated pupil accompanied by ptosis and anhidrosis, with entirely normal light and accommodation reflexes — it does not produce the swinging-flashlight asymmetry characteristic of RAPD.

preguntas.q: The 'Marcus Gunn pupil' is another name for which clinical sign?

e.correcta: 'Marcus Gunn pupil' and 'relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD)' are synonymous terms describing the same finding: an asymmetric, decreased pupillary light response detected on the swinging-flashlight test due to unilateral damage along the afferent (optic nerve or retinal) pathway.

incorrectas.B: The consensual light reflex refers to the normal bilateral pupillary constriction produced by shining light in only one eye — a healthy phenomenon that becomes diminished (not the same thing as) the Marcus Gunn finding.
incorrectas.C: The accommodation reflex is the near-response triad (miosis, convergence, lens rounding) triggered by near focus, a separate reflex from the light-reflex pathway tested for RAPD.
incorrectas.D: The Argyll-Robertson sign describes light-near dissociation with an ABSENT light reflex but preserved accommodation — a distinct clinical entity from the relative afferent defect of the Marcus Gunn pupil.

preguntas.q: A relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil) most commonly results from damage to which structure?

e.correcta: Because the defect lies in the AFFERENT limb of the light reflex, it arises from optic nerve pathology (such as optic neuritis in multiple sclerosis) or severe retinal injury or disease that reduces the amount of light signal reaching the brainstem, weakening pupillary constriction when light is directed at the affected eye relative to the healthy one.

incorrectas.A: Ciliary ganglion damage affects the EFFERENT parasympathetic supply to the sphincter and ciliary muscle (as in Adie pupil), not the incoming visual signal tested by RAPD.
incorrectas.C: Edinger-Westphal nucleus lesions would impair the efferent motor output bilaterally rather than producing a relative, eye-specific afferent deficit.
incorrectas.D: Superior cervical ganglion lesions disrupt the SYMPATHETIC pathway to the dilator muscle (Horner syndrome), unrelated to the light-reflex afferent limb tested in RAPD.

preguntas.q: A young woman presents with a unilaterally dilated pupil that reacts sluggishly to light but constricts more readily with accommodation. Which condition is this?

e.correcta: Adie pupil results from denervation of the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves (often idiopathic or post-viral, and more common in women), leading to aberrant reinnervation such that the light reflex is weak and tonic while the near/accommodation response — mediated by relatively more fibers to the ciliary muscle — is comparatively preserved, though slow; it is often accompanied by diminished deep tendon reflexes (Holmes-Adie syndrome).

incorrectas.A: Marcus Gunn pupil (RAPD) reflects an AFFERENT (optic nerve or retinal) problem detected by comparing the two eyes' light response, not an isolated tonic pupil with light-near dissociation from a ciliary ganglion lesion.
incorrectas.B: Argyll-Robertson pupil is typically bilateral, small (miotic), and shows an essentially absent light reflex with preserved accommodation, arising from a midbrain pretectal lesion (classically neurosyphilis) — a different location, mechanism, and pupil size than the dilated Adie pupil.
incorrectas.D: Horner pupil is a small (miotic) pupil with ptosis and anhidrosis from sympathetic denervation, not a dilated pupil with a sluggish light response.

preguntas.q: Visual images from an object located in a person's nasal (medial) visual hemifield will stimulate photoreceptors on which portion of the ipsilateral retina?

e.correcta: Because the eye's optics (cornea and lens) invert and reverse the image, light from the nasal visual field crosses the optical axis and strikes the temporal (lateral) half of the retina, while light from the temporal visual field strikes the nasal retina. This retinotopic inversion is the anatomic basis for visual field defects, since nasal retinal fibers (representing the temporal field) cross at the optic chiasm while temporal retinal fibers (representing the nasal field) remain ipsilateral.

incorrectas.A: The nasal retina is instead stimulated by light from the TEMPORAL (lateral) visual field — the opposite hemifield from the one described in the question.
incorrectas.B: The eye's optics also invert the image vertically, but superior retina corresponds to the inferior visual field; this is a different axis of inversion than the nasal-temporal relationship being asked about here.
incorrectas.C: Similarly, inferior retina corresponds to the superior visual field via the vertical axis of optical inversion, not the nasal-temporal relationship the question addresses.

preguntas.q: Most fibers in the optic tract synapse in which thalamic nucleus before continuing on to the primary visual cortex?

e.correcta: The majority of optic tract axons terminate in the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the thalamus, which relays visual information via the optic radiations to the primary (striate) visual cortex in the occipital lobe for conscious visual perception. The LGN's six cellular layers also segregate magnocellular from parvocellular input, important for processing motion and depth versus color and fine detail respectively.

incorrectas.B: A smaller subset of fibers branches off to the pretectal nuclei (not the LGN) to mediate the pupillary light reflex, a reflex pathway rather than the main route carrying the majority of fibers for conscious vision.
incorrectas.C: Another small subset of fibers projects to the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus to entrain circadian rhythms to the light-dark cycle — a non-image-forming function distinct from the dominant geniculate relay.
incorrectas.D: Some fibers also reach the superior colliculus to coordinate reflexive eye and head movements toward visual stimuli, but this represents a minor branch compared to the dominant projection to the lateral geniculate nucleus.

preguntas.q: A child is found to have galactose accumulation and early cataracts but normal cognitive development, and is diagnosed with galactokinase deficiency. What is the inheritance pattern of this disorder?

e.correcta: Galactokinase deficiency, like classic galactosemia (GALT deficiency), is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern - both copies of the GALK1 gene must be nonfunctional for the enzyme deficiency to manifest. Because galactokinase acts earlier in the pathway than GALT, galactose-1-phosphate cannot accumulate, sparing the liver and brain and explaining why patients develop cataracts (from galactitol accumulating in the lens via aldose reductase) without the hepatomegaly or intellectual disability seen in classic galactosemia.

incorrectas.B: If galactokinase deficiency were autosomal dominant, a single mutant allele would cause disease and it would appear in nearly every generation of an affected family; instead, unaffected carrier parents can have an affected child, the hallmark of a recessive trait.
incorrectas.C: X-linked recessive disorders (like G6PD deficiency or Fabry disease) predominantly affect males with no male-to-male transmission, but galactokinase deficiency affects both sexes equally because GALK1 is an autosomal gene, not located on the X chromosome.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance shows transmission only from affected mothers to all of their children with no paternal transmission, a pattern seen in disorders like MELAS, not in enzyme deficiencies encoded by nuclear autosomal genes such as GALK1.

preguntas.q: The plasma anion gap (Na+ minus [Cl- + HCO3-], normally about 8-12 mEq/L) is most clinically useful for narrowing the differential diagnosis of which acid-base disturbance?

e.correcta: The anion gap represents unmeasured anions (mainly albumin) that balance the difference between measured cations and anions, and it rises when an acid other than HCl accumulates (e.g., lactate, ketoacids, or toxic acid metabolites) because the added anion isn't chloride and isn't part of the gap calculation. This lets clinicians split metabolic acidosis into anion-gap causes (MUDPILES: methanol, uremia, DKA, propylene glycol, iron/isoniazid, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol, salicylates) versus normal-gap/hyperchloremic causes (diarrhea, RTA), which is the main diagnostic use of the gap.

incorrectas.B: Metabolic alkalosis is instead classified by volume status (saline-responsive vs. saline-resistant) and urine chloride, not by the anion gap, since it involves a rise rather than a consumption of HCO3-.
incorrectas.C: Respiratory acidosis results from primary CO2 retention (hypoventilation), and its workup centers on causes of impaired ventilation such as COPD or opioid overdose, not on anion-gap calculations, which are specific to metabolic acid-base disorders.
incorrectas.D: Respiratory alkalosis arises from primary hyperventilation (e.g., anxiety, salicylate stimulation of the respiratory center, high altitude), and like respiratory acidosis it is evaluated through its ventilatory cause rather than the anion gap.

preguntas.q: Which laboratory value is defined as the difference between the measured plasma osmolarity and the calculated (estimated) plasma osmolarity, and becomes markedly elevated in toxic alcohol ingestions such as methanol or ethylene glycol?

e.correcta: The osmolar gap compares the osmolarity actually measured in the lab (by freezing point depression) to the value estimated from the standard formula (2xNa + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8); a large positive gap means an osmotically active substance is present that the formula doesn't account for. Toxic alcohols like methanol and ethylene glycol are small, uncharged, osmotically active molecules not included in the estimation equation, so their ingestion produces a markedly elevated osmolar gap even before they are metabolized into the toxic acids that later widen the anion gap.

incorrectas.B: The anion gap measures unmeasured anions in the plasma (Na - [Cl + HCO3]) and rises later, after toxic alcohols are metabolized into their acidic byproducts (formic acid, glycolic/oxalic acid); it does not reflect the parent alcohol itself the way the osmolar gap does.
incorrectas.C: The delta-delta ratio compares the rise in anion gap to the fall in bicarbonate to determine whether a mixed acid-base disorder is present in anion-gap metabolic acidosis; it has nothing to do with osmolarity or toxic alcohol screening.
incorrectas.D: The A-a gradient is a respiratory physiology value comparing alveolar and arterial oxygen tension to assess causes of hypoxemia, unrelated to plasma osmolarity or toxic ingestions.

preguntas.q: A primary decrease in serum bicarbonate (HCO3-) concentration is the defining feature of which acid-base disturbance?

e.correcta: Metabolic acidosis is defined by a primary fall in plasma HCO3-, either because bicarbonate is consumed buffering an excess acid load (e.g., ketoacids, lactic acid) or because it is lost directly from the body (e.g., diarrhea, renal tubular acidosis). The drop in this key buffer lowers the HCO3-/PCO2 ratio in the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, which lowers pH and defines the acidemia.

incorrectas.A: Metabolic alkalosis is the opposite process, a primary rise in HCO3- (from acid loss as in vomiting, or diuretic-induced contraction), which raises pH rather than lowering it.
incorrectas.C: Respiratory acidosis is driven by a primary rise in PCO2 from hypoventilation, not a primary change in HCO3-; any rise in HCO3- seen there is a secondary renal compensation, not the initiating problem.
incorrectas.D: Respiratory alkalosis is caused by a primary fall in PCO2 from hyperventilation; HCO3- changes in that setting are again a compensatory renal response, not the primary abnormality.

preguntas.q: A primary decrease in serum HCO3- (metabolic acidosis) has what immediate effect on arterial pH, before any respiratory compensation occurs?

o.D: pH decreases only after several days

e.correcta: Per the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship, pH is proportional to the ratio [HCO3-]/PCO2; when HCO3- falls while PCO2 is initially unchanged, this ratio drops and pH must fall accordingly, producing acidemia. This is the direct chemical link between losing or consuming the body's main extracellular buffer and the resulting drop in blood pH, independent of any compensatory mechanism.

incorrectas.A: pH would only increase if HCO3- rose or PCO2 fell; a fall in HCO3- can only push the HCO3-/PCO2 ratio down, not up, so an increase in pH is the opposite of what mass action predicts here.
incorrectas.C: The pH does change - it falls immediately, because the buffer ratio is disturbed the instant HCO3- decreases; this is not a system that can hold pH constant on its own.
incorrectas.D: The pH falls immediately, not after a delay - it is the subsequent respiratory compensation (hyperventilation lowering PCO2) that takes time to develop and only partially restores pH, but the initial fall in pH is instantaneous with the HCO3- change.

preguntas.q: In metabolic acidosis, once arterial pH falls, what respiratory response occurs and how does it affect PCO2?

e.correcta: The fall in pH in metabolic acidosis is sensed by peripheral (carotid body) and central chemoreceptors, which drive an increase in respiratory rate and depth (hyperventilation); this blows off more CO2, lowering PCO2 and raising the HCO3-/PCO2 ratio back toward normal, partially correcting the pH. This immediate respiratory compensation is why a well-compensated metabolic acidosis shows both low HCO3- and low PCO2 together.

incorrectas.B: Hypoventilation with a rising PCO2 would push the pH even lower, compounding rather than compensating for the acidosis - the opposite of what the chemoreceptor-driven response actually produces.
incorrectas.C: Hyperventilation by definition increases minute ventilation and CO2 elimination, so it necessarily lowers, not raises, PCO2; pairing hyperventilation with increased PCO2 is physiologically contradictory.
incorrectas.D: Hypoventilation would raise, not lower, PCO2, since less CO2 is exhaled; this pairing is internally inconsistent and describes the opposite compensatory direction needed to counter acidemia.

preguntas.q: Which combination of arterial pH, HCO3-, and PCO2 values is characteristic of a well-compensated metabolic acidosis?

o.A: pH increased, HCO3- increased, PCO2 increased
o.B: pH decreased, HCO3- increased, PCO2 increased
o.C: pH decreased, HCO3- decreased, PCO2 decreased
o.D: pH increased, HCO3- decreased, PCO2 decreased

e.correcta: In compensated metabolic acidosis, the primary problem is a low HCO3-, and the body's respiratory compensation (hyperventilation) secondarily lowers PCO2 to try to restore the HCO3-/PCO2 ratio; the net result is that all three values move together in the low direction - pH stays below normal since compensation is never complete, while HCO3- and PCO2 are both low. Recognizing that all three values fall together is the classic pattern-recognition shortcut for metabolic acidosis on an ABG.

incorrectas.A: This everything-elevated pattern describes compensated metabolic alkalosis, where a primary rise in HCO3- is partly offset by hypoventilation raising PCO2, the mirror image of metabolic acidosis.
incorrectas.B: A low pH with high HCO3- and high PCO2 describes compensated respiratory acidosis, where the primary problem is CO2 retention and the kidneys secondarily retain HCO3-; here HCO3- and PCO2 move together in the high direction rather than both being low as in metabolic acidosis.
incorrectas.D: A high pH with low HCO3- and low PCO2 describes compensated respiratory alkalosis, where hyperventilation primarily lowers PCO2 and the kidneys secondarily excrete HCO3- to compensate - the opposite primary process from metabolic acidosis.

preguntas.q: What term describes the deep, labored hyperventilation pattern that serves as respiratory compensation for severe metabolic acidosis, classically seen in diabetic ketoacidosis?

e.correcta: Kussmaul breathing is the deep, rapid, labored respiratory pattern driven by chemoreceptor sensing of severe metabolic acidosis (classically DKA); it maximizes CO2 elimination to raise the HCO3-/PCO2 ratio and blunt the fall in pH, making it a visible clinical sign of significant acidemia that demands urgent correction of the underlying cause.

incorrectas.A: Cheyne-Stokes breathing is a crescendo-decrescendo pattern with periods of apnea, typically seen in heart failure or CNS injury from delayed feedback in the respiratory control loop, not a direct chemoreceptor response to a fixed acid load like Kussmaul breathing.
incorrectas.C: Biot (ataxic) breathing is an irregular pattern with variable rate and depth interspersed with apneic periods, associated with brainstem damage or opioid effects, not with the regular deep hyperventilation used to compensate for metabolic acidosis.
incorrectas.D: Agonal breathing refers to irregular gasping respirations seen near death (e.g., during cardiac arrest), reflecting brainstem failure rather than a purposeful compensatory hyperventilation for acid-base correction.

preguntas.q: Respiratory compensation for a metabolic acid-base disturbance (adjusting ventilation and PCO2) occurs on what time scale relative to the primary metabolic disturbance?

o.D: Only after dialysis or bicarbonate therapy

e.correcta: Because ventilation is controlled by chemoreceptors that respond to blood pH and PCO2 in real time, the respiratory system can adjust breathing rate and depth within minutes of a metabolic acid-base disturbance, making it the fastest compensatory mechanism available. This immediate responsiveness is why an ABG drawn shortly after an acute metabolic insult already shows a compensatory PCO2 change, unlike the much slower renal compensation.

incorrectas.A: A 3-5 day time course describes renal (metabolic) compensation for a respiratory acid-base disorder, which requires upregulating ammoniagenesis and titratable acid excretion - a much slower process than adjusting minute ventilation.
incorrectas.C: Respiratory compensation does occur reliably in metabolic acid-base disorders (assuming intact lung/chemoreceptor function); it just does not fully normalize pH, but it is not absent - the body always mounts some ventilatory response.
incorrectas.D: Respiratory compensation is a physiologic reflex mediated by chemoreceptors, not a consequence of a specific treatment like dialysis or bicarbonate infusion; it begins as soon as the metabolic disturbance alters blood pH/PCO2, independent of any therapy.

preguntas.q: A primary increase in serum bicarbonate (HCO3-) concentration is the defining feature of which acid-base disturbance?

e.correcta: Metabolic alkalosis is defined by a primary rise in plasma HCO3-, most often from loss of acid (e.g., vomiting, nasogastric suction) or diuretic-induced volume contraction that increases HCO3- reabsorption. The elevated HCO3-/PCO2 ratio raises pH, producing alkalemia, and is the mirror-image process to the HCO3- consumption seen in metabolic acidosis.

incorrectas.A: Respiratory alkalosis results from a primary fall in PCO2 due to hyperventilation, not a primary rise in HCO3-; any HCO3- change seen there is a secondary renal compensation (excreting HCO3-), the opposite direction of the primary disturbance in metabolic alkalosis.
incorrectas.B: Respiratory acidosis is caused by a primary rise in PCO2 from hypoventilation; the renal compensation there raises HCO3- secondarily, but the primary abnormality is CO2 retention, not a bicarbonate-driven process.
incorrectas.C: Metabolic acidosis is the opposite condition, a primary fall (not rise) in HCO3- from acid accumulation or bicarbonate loss, which lowers rather than raises pH.

preguntas.q: A primary increase in HCO3- (metabolic alkalosis) has what immediate effect on arterial pH, before respiratory compensation occurs?

o.D: pH increases only after renal correction

e.correcta: By the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship, pH tracks the ratio of [HCO3-] to PCO2; when HCO3- rises while PCO2 is initially unchanged, this ratio increases, so pH rises immediately, producing alkalemia. This direct mass-action link between a rising buffer concentration and rising pH is why any process that adds or retains bicarbonate (vomiting, diuretics, bicarbonate administration) causes alkalemia right away, before any compensatory mechanism engages.

incorrectas.A: A fall in pH would require the HCO3-/PCO2 ratio to decrease, which is the opposite of what happens when HCO3- rises; a decreasing pH is the pattern seen in metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis.
incorrectas.C: The pH does change immediately - the buffer equilibrium shifts the instant HCO3- rises, so pH cannot remain static; only the eventual degree of compensation (not the initial pH change) develops over time.
incorrectas.D: The rise in pH is immediate, driven directly by the increased HCO3-/PCO2 ratio; the renal system is actually what caused the elevated HCO3- to begin with, not a delayed cause of the pH rise itself.

preguntas.q: In metabolic alkalosis, once arterial pH rises, what respiratory response occurs and how does it affect PCO2?

e.correcta: Chemoreceptors sensing the elevated pH of metabolic alkalosis blunt the drive to breathe, producing compensatory hypoventilation; this allows PCO2 to rise, which lowers the HCO3-/PCO2 ratio back toward normal and partially corrects the alkalemia. This compensatory hypoventilation is limited by the competing need to maintain adequate oxygenation, which is why respiratory compensation for alkalosis is generally less complete than for acidosis.

incorrectas.A: Hyperventilation would lower PCO2 further, widening rather than narrowing the elevated HCO3-/PCO2 ratio, worsening the alkalemia instead of compensating for it - the opposite direction needed here.
incorrectas.C: Hypoventilation, by definition, reduces CO2 elimination and raises PCO2, so labeling this response hyperventilation while pairing it with a rising PCO2 is internally contradictory; the correct pairing is hypoventilation with increased PCO2.
incorrectas.D: Hypoventilation raises, not lowers, PCO2 because less CO2 is exhaled per minute; pairing hypoventilation with a falling PCO2 misstates the basic relationship between ventilation and CO2 elimination.

preguntas.q: Which combination of arterial pH, HCO3-, and PCO2 values is characteristic of a well-compensated metabolic alkalosis?

o.A: pH decreased, HCO3- decreased, PCO2 decreased
o.B: pH increased, HCO3- decreased, PCO2 decreased
o.C: pH increased, HCO3- increased, PCO2 increased
o.D: pH decreased, HCO3- increased, PCO2 increased

e.correcta: In compensated metabolic alkalosis, the primary abnormality is an elevated HCO3-, and compensatory hypoventilation secondarily raises PCO2 in an attempt to restore the normal HCO3-/PCO2 ratio; the net result is that pH, HCO3-, and PCO2 are all elevated together, since compensation is never complete. This everything-elevated pattern is the classic ABG signature that lets you identify metabolic alkalosis at a glance.

incorrectas.A: A pattern with all three values decreased describes compensated metabolic acidosis, the mirror-image disorder in which a primary low HCO3- is met by compensatory hyperventilation lowering PCO2.
incorrectas.B: A high pH with low HCO3- and low PCO2 describes compensated respiratory alkalosis, where the primary process is hyperventilation lowering PCO2 and the kidneys secondarily excrete HCO3- - the opposite primary abnormality from metabolic alkalosis.
incorrectas.D: A low pH with high HCO3- and high PCO2 describes compensated respiratory acidosis, where CO2 retention is primary and renal HCO3- retention is the compensation; here pH is low rather than high, unlike in metabolic alkalosis.

preguntas.q: In a patient with metabolic alkalosis, what additional hemodynamic change increases proximal tubular HCO3- reabsorption and thereby perpetuates the disorder as 'contraction alkalosis'?

e.correcta: When effective circulating volume falls (e.g., from diuretic use or vomiting), the kidney responds by avidly reabsorbing Na+ (and with it HCO3-) in the proximal tubule to defend volume status, even though this comes at the cost of worsening the existing alkalosis. This contraction alkalosis illustrates how the kidney prioritizes volume homeostasis over acid-base homeostasis, and explains why volume repletion with saline (when appropriate) is often required to correct the alkalosis by removing the stimulus for HCO3- retention.

incorrectas.A: ECF volume expansion would suppress renal sodium (and bicarbonate) reabsorption via mechanisms like increased GFR and reduced aldosterone, tending to promote HCO3- excretion rather than retention - the opposite effect needed to worsen alkalosis.
incorrectas.C: Hyperkalemia is not the classic driver of contraction alkalosis; in fact, hypokalemia (from volume contraction and secondary hyperaldosteronism) typically accompanies and perpetuates this alkalosis by driving H+ into cells and increasing renal H+ secretion.
incorrectas.D: Hypoalbuminemia affects the anion gap and oncotic pressure but is not the mechanism linking volume status to bicarbonate handling in contraction alkalosis; it does not directly drive proximal HCO3- reabsorption.

preguntas.q: What is the primary ventilatory disturbance in respiratory acidosis, and what happens to arterial CO2 as a result?

e.correcta: Respiratory acidosis begins with hypoventilation - inadequate alveolar ventilation from causes like COPD, opioid overdose, or neuromuscular weakness - which prevents CO2 from being exhaled at a normal rate, so it accumulates in the blood as increased PCO2. Since CO2 combines with water to form carbonic acid, this CO2 retention is the direct cause of the acidemia that defines respiratory acidosis.

incorrectas.A: Hyperventilation increases CO2 elimination and would lower, not raise, PCO2, producing respiratory alkalosis instead - the opposite of the process that defines respiratory acidosis.
incorrectas.C: Hypoventilation reduces CO2 elimination, so it necessarily raises, not lowers, PCO2; pairing hypoventilation with decreased CO2 misrepresents the basic ventilation-CO2 relationship.
incorrectas.D: Hyperventilation, by definition, increases minute ventilation and CO2 clearance, so it lowers rather than raises PCO2; this pairing is internally inconsistent with how increased ventilation affects CO2.

preguntas.q: A primary rise in arterial CO2 (respiratory acidosis) has what immediate effect on arterial pH?

e.correcta: CO2 combines with water via carbonic anhydrase to form carbonic acid (H2CO3), which dissociates into H+ and HCO3-; a rise in PCO2 therefore directly increases H+ concentration and lowers pH, per the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship in which pH falls as the HCO3-/PCO2 ratio decreases. This is the immediate chemical basis for the acidemia in respiratory acidosis, occurring within minutes of hypoventilation, well before any renal compensation begins.

incorrectas.A: A rise in pH would require the HCO3-/PCO2 ratio to increase; since PCO2 itself is rising here, the ratio falls rather than rises, so pH cannot rise - this describes the opposite scenario.
incorrectas.B: The pH does not stay unchanged - it falls immediately as carbonic acid formation increases with the rising CO2; equilibrium chemistry dictates an instantaneous shift, not a static value.
incorrectas.D: The fall in pH is immediate, not delayed; the 3-5 day time course refers to the renal compensatory rise in HCO3- that partially corrects (but does not cause) the pH change, a distinct, slower process.

preguntas.q: In respiratory acidosis, the initial rise in PCO2 shifts the CO2 + H2O <-> H2CO3 <-> H+ + HCO3- equilibrium by mass action, causing what immediate change in serum HCO3-?

e.correcta: By simple mass action on the bicarbonate buffer equation, adding more CO2 pushes the equilibrium toward more carbonic acid formation and thus more H+ and HCO3- production, so plasma HCO3- rises immediately (a small, non-renal chemical rise) even before any renal compensatory mechanism engages. This acute chemical buffering blunts the fall in pH somewhat, but is much less effective than the later renal compensation that further raises HCO3- over days via increased ammoniagenesis and titratable acid excretion.

incorrectas.A: A fall in HCO3- would occur if the equilibrium shifted away from carbonic acid formation, which is the opposite of what happens when CO2 (a reactant) increases; by Le Chatelier's principle, more CO2 drives the reaction forward, raising HCO3-, not lowering it.
incorrectas.C: HCO3- does not stay unchanged - the equilibrium reaction is directly coupled to PCO2, so any rise in CO2 immediately shifts bicarbonate production upward, even if the magnitude is modest compared to renal compensation.
incorrectas.D: There is no initial fall in HCO3- followed by rebound; the acute mass-action effect of rising CO2 is a straightforward, immediate increase in HCO3-, not a biphasic response.

preguntas.q: Unlike compensated metabolic acid-base disorders (where all values move in the same direction), which combination of arterial pH, HCO3-, and PCO2 is seen in compensated respiratory acidosis?

o.A: pH decreased, HCO3- decreased, PCO2 decreased
o.B: pH decreased, HCO3- increased, PCO2 increased
o.C: pH increased, HCO3- increased, PCO2 increased
o.D: pH increased, HCO3- decreased, PCO2 decreased

e.correcta: In compensated respiratory acidosis, the primary problem is CO2 retention (high PCO2), and renal compensation raises HCO3- over several days (via increased ammoniagenesis and titratable acid excretion) to partially restore the HCO3-/PCO2 ratio; the pH remains below normal since compensation is never complete, giving the distinctive pattern of low pH with both HCO3- and PCO2 elevated - not all three values moving together the way they do in the metabolic disorders.

incorrectas.A: A pattern with all three values decreased describes compensated metabolic acidosis, where the primary process is a low HCO3- met by hyperventilation lowering PCO2 - a fundamentally different primary abnormality (renal/metabolic vs. ventilatory).
incorrectas.C: A pattern with all three values elevated describes compensated metabolic alkalosis, where a primary rise in HCO3- is met by hypoventilation raising PCO2; here pH is elevated rather than depressed, unlike in respiratory acidosis.
incorrectas.D: A pattern with all three values decreased alongside an elevated pH describes compensated respiratory alkalosis, where primary hyperventilation lowers PCO2 and the kidneys secondarily excrete HCO3-, the opposite primary ventilatory disturbance from respiratory acidosis.

preguntas.q: Chronic renal compensation for respiratory acidosis increases excretion of excess fixed acid mainly in which two urinary buffered forms?

e.correcta: The kidney cannot excrete meaningful amounts of free H+ (urine pH would become dangerously low), so it instead buffers secreted H+ onto phosphate and other buffers to form titratable acid, and separately generates ammonia (NH3) in the proximal tubule that combines with secreted H+ to form NH4+, which is then trapped in the urine. Chronic respiratory acidosis upregulates both of these pathways (titratable acid and NH4+ excretion) to eliminate the excess fixed acid load and generate new HCO3- for the blood, the basis of the slow (3-5 day) renal compensation.

incorrectas.A: Free H+ excretion alone is quantitatively minor and would require an impossibly acidic urine to matter; the kidney relies on buffered forms (titratable acid and NH4+), and filtered HCO3- is reabsorbed rather than excreted during compensation, so this option misdescribes both mechanisms.
incorrectas.B: NH4+ excretion is indeed one correct mechanism, but 'free H+' is not a meaningful quantitative excretory pathway on its own; the missing partner mechanism is titratable acid excretion, not free H+ excretion.
incorrectas.D: Filtered HCO3- is reabsorbed (not excreted) during compensation for respiratory acidosis - excreting it would worsen rather than help the acidosis, so pairing it with titratable acid misstates the direction of the renal response.

preguntas.q: Renal compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis raises plasma HCO3- primarily through which mechanism?

o.A: Increased reabsorption of 'new' HCO3- generated via renal ammoniagenesis

e.correcta: In the proximal tubule, glutamine metabolism (ammoniagenesis) generates NH4+ (excreted in urine) along with 'new' HCO3- that is not simply reabsorbed filtered bicarbonate but newly synthesized bicarbonate added to the blood; chronic respiratory acidosis upregulates this pathway, gradually raising plasma HCO3- over several days to partially normalize the HCO3-/PCO2 ratio. This generation of new HCO3- paired with NH4+ excretion is distinct from, and more important than, simple reabsorption of already-filtered bicarbonate.

incorrectas.B: Compensation for respiratory acidosis involves increased, not decreased, excretion of titratable acid, since more fixed acid needs to be eliminated to allow new HCO3- generation; decreased excretion would work against compensation.
incorrectas.C: Compensation requires increased, not decreased, NH4+ excretion, since ammoniagenesis is upregulated specifically to handle the excess acid load and generate new bicarbonate; reducing NH4+ excretion would blunt rather than support compensation.
incorrectas.D: Increasing excretion of already-filtered HCO3- would lower, not raise, plasma bicarbonate, the opposite of what is needed to compensate for respiratory acidosis; compensation depends on reabsorbing/generating new HCO3-, not excreting existing bicarbonate.

preguntas.q: Renal (metabolic) compensation for a respiratory acid-base disturbance occurs on what time scale, in contrast to the immediate respiratory compensation for metabolic disturbances?

e.correcta: Renal compensation requires upregulating slow cellular processes - increased proximal tubular ammoniagenesis, generation of new HCO3-, and titratable acid excretion - that take roughly 3-5 days to fully develop, in contrast to the chemoreceptor-mediated respiratory compensation that begins within minutes. This is why acute respiratory acid-base disturbances (e.g., acute CO2 retention from opioid overdose) show little to no metabolic compensation, while chronic respiratory disorders (e.g., COPD) show a fully compensated bicarbonate level.

incorrectas.A: A within-minutes time course describes the respiratory compensation for metabolic disorders (via chemoreceptor-driven changes in ventilation), not the renal compensation for respiratory disorders, which is a much slower cellular adaptation.
incorrectas.C: Renal compensation does occur reliably, just slowly; it is not absent - patients with chronic respiratory acidosis or alkalosis do show a compensatory HCO3- shift once enough time has passed for renal adaptation.
incorrectas.D: Renal compensation is markedly slower, not faster, than respiratory compensation; the lungs adjust ventilation within minutes while the kidneys need days to alter acid/ammonia handling.

preguntas.q: What is the primary ventilatory disturbance in respiratory alkalosis, and what happens to arterial CO2 as a result?

e.correcta: Respiratory alkalosis begins with hyperventilation - excessive alveolar ventilation from causes like anxiety, pain, high altitude, or salicylate toxicity stimulating the respiratory center - which blows off more CO2 than is being produced, lowering PCO2. Because less carbonic acid is formed from CO2, this fall in PCO2 directly raises pH, producing the alkalemia that defines respiratory alkalosis.

incorrectas.A: Hypoventilation reduces CO2 elimination and would raise, not lower, PCO2, producing respiratory acidosis rather than alkalosis - the opposite ventilatory disturbance from what defines this condition.
incorrectas.C: Hyperventilation, by definition, increases CO2 clearance and lowers PCO2, so pairing it with 'CO2 increases' is internally contradictory and misstates the direct relationship between ventilation and CO2 elimination.
incorrectas.D: Hypoventilation decreases CO2 elimination, so it raises rather than lowers PCO2; this option incorrectly pairs reduced ventilation with a falling CO2 level.

preguntas.q: A primary fall in arterial CO2 due to hyperventilation (respiratory alkalosis) has what immediate effect on arterial pH?

o.D: pH increases only after renal compensation

e.correcta: With less CO2 available to combine with water and form carbonic acid, H+ concentration falls and the HCO3-/PCO2 ratio rises, directly increasing pH per the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship. This immediate rise in pH is what defines the alkalemia of respiratory alkalosis, occurring within minutes of hyperventilation, well before the kidneys mount any compensatory response.

incorrectas.A: A fall in pH would require the HCO3-/PCO2 ratio to decrease; since PCO2 is falling here (raising the ratio), pH must rise, not fall - this describes the opposite scenario, respiratory acidosis.
incorrectas.B: The pH does not remain static - it rises immediately because the carbonic acid/bicarbonate equilibrium shifts the instant PCO2 falls; this is a direct chemical effect, not one requiring further physiologic input.
incorrectas.D: The rise in pH is immediate, not delayed until renal compensation; the kidneys instead work over days to lower HCO3- and bring pH back toward normal (compensation), but the initial pH increase happens right away as PCO2 falls.

preguntas.q: In respiratory alkalosis, decreased PCO2 shifts the CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3- equilibrium. By mass action, what happens to plasma HCO3- concentration acutely, before any renal compensation occurs?

e.correcta: According to the bicarbonate buffer equilibrium, when PCO2 falls (from hyperventilation), the reaction CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3- is driven to the left as substrate (CO2) is removed, pulling H+ and HCO3- back toward forming H2CO3/CO2. This consumes HCO3-, so plasma bicarbonate falls modestly even before the kidneys compensate — this immediate, non-renal drop is the acute 'buffering' component of respiratory alkalosis, distinct from the larger renal compensatory decline that follows over days.

incorrectas.B: An increase in HCO3- would occur if the equilibrium were being driven to generate more bicarbonate, which is what happens in respiratory acidosis (CO2 excess pushes the reaction right, generating H+ and HCO3-) — the opposite direction from what falling PCO2 produces.
incorrectas.C: HCO3- does change immediately, even before renal compensation; the acute mass-action effect on the bicarbonate buffer system is essentially instantaneous chemistry, not a slower excretory adjustment.
incorrectas.D: There is no biphasic rise-then-fall; the acute chemical effect of hypocapnia on HCO3- is a straightforward decrease from the moment PCO2 drops, with any further decline over days reflecting a separate, slower renal compensatory mechanism rather than a reversal of the acute change.

preguntas.q: A patient with chronic hyperventilation undergoes an arterial blood gas after several days. Which pattern of pH, PCO2, and HCO3- is most consistent with renally compensated respiratory alkalosis?

o.A: pH increased, PCO2 decreased, HCO3- decreased
o.B: pH decreased, PCO2 increased, HCO3- increased
o.C: pH increased, PCO2 decreased, HCO3- increased
o.D: pH normal, PCO2 increased, HCO3- increased

e.correcta: In respiratory alkalosis, primary hyperventilation lowers PCO2, which by mass action modestly lowers HCO3- and raises pH acutely. Over roughly 3-5 days the kidneys compensate by excreting less fixed acid as titratable acid and NH4+ and reabsorbing less filtered HCO3-, driving plasma HCO3- down further; this brings pH back toward (but not fully to) normal while PCO2 stays low and HCO3- stays low — the hallmark compensated triad of increased pH, decreased PCO2, decreased HCO3-.

incorrectas.B: This pattern (decreased pH, increased PCO2, increased HCO3-) describes compensated respiratory ACIDOSIS, where hypercapnia drives the primary acidemia and the kidneys respond by generating and retaining new HCO3- — the reverse process from respiratory alkalosis.
incorrectas.C: An increased HCO3- alongside decreased PCO2 would suggest a concurrent metabolic alkalosis rather than renal compensation for respiratory alkalosis; true renal compensation pushes HCO3- down, not up, since the kidney reduces acid excretion and bicarbonate reclamation.
incorrectas.D: A normal pH with increased PCO2 and increased HCO3- describes full renal compensation of chronic respiratory ACIDOSIS, not respiratory alkalosis; the direction of the PCO2 change marks this as the opposite primary disorder.

preguntas.q: As part of the renal compensatory response to sustained respiratory alkalosis, what happens to renal excretion of fixed acid as titratable acid and ammonium (NH4+)?

o.A: It increases, generating new HCO3- to raise plasma bicarbonate
o.B: It decreases, allowing plasma HCO3- to fall further
o.C: It is unchanged, while HCO3- reabsorption alone decreases
o.D: It increases for NH4+ specifically but decreases for titratable acid

e.correcta: Chronic hypocapnia reduces the intracellular CO2 available to the tubular cell's carbonic anhydrase, lowering the H+ available for apical secretion into the lumen; because both titratable acid excretion (H+ buffered by phosphate) and NH4+ excretion (from ammoniagenesis) depend on this same H+ secretion, both fall in parallel. Less new HCO3- is generated and returned to the blood, so plasma HCO3- is driven down further — this is the true renal compensation for respiratory alkalosis, distinct from the immediate mass-action drop in HCO3-.

incorrectas.A: Increased excretion of fixed acid with generation of new HCO3- is the renal compensatory response to respiratory ACIDOSIS (hypercapnia), where the kidney needs to raise HCO3- to offset acidemia — the opposite adjustment needed in respiratory alkalosis.
incorrectas.C: Titratable acid/NH4+ excretion and HCO3- reabsorption are not independent; both are driven by the same apical Na+/H+ exchanger activity in the proximal tubule, so a change in one accompanies a parallel change in the other rather than one staying fixed.
incorrectas.D: Titratable acid and NH4+ excretion move together because both are downstream of the same driving force (luminal H+ secretion) rather than being independently regulated in opposite directions.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of sickle cell disease?

e.correcta: Sickle cell disease results from a homozygous point mutation in the beta-globin gene (HBB) on chromosome 11 (Glu6Val), and clinical disease requires two abnormal beta-globin alleles, making it autosomal recessive. Heterozygous carriers (sickle trait) are generally asymptomatic — the classic pattern of a recessive disorder where carriers are protected and even gain some relative resistance to falciparum malaria.

incorrectas.A: An autosomal dominant disorder causes disease with only one copy of the mutant allele, but sickle trait carriers with one HBB mutant allele are clinically normal under most conditions, ruling out a dominant pattern.
incorrectas.B: X-linked recessive disorders (like hemophilia or G6PD deficiency) map to genes on the X chromosome and predominantly affect males; the beta-globin gene is autosomal (chromosome 11), and sickle cell disease affects males and females equally.
incorrectas.D: X-linked dominant conditions are rare and show a distinct sex-linked transmission pattern (affected fathers cannot pass the trait to sons); sickle cell disease follows autosomal transmission with equal sex distribution, inconsistent with X-linked dominant inheritance.

preguntas.q: In cerebellopontine angle syndrome caused by an enlarging vestibular schwannoma, initial CN VIII dysfunction (hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo) is followed by compression of CN V, and — as the tumor continues to expand — which additional cranial nerve is next affected?

e.correcta: The cerebellopontine angle is the anatomic space where CN VII and CN VIII travel together (with CN V nearby) before entering the internal auditory meatus. A vestibular schwannoma arises from CN VIII (usually its vestibular division) and, as it enlarges, compresses adjacent CN V and then CN VII given their close anatomical proximity, producing facial hypesthesia followed by facial nerve weakness.

incorrectas.A: CN VI (abducens) travels near the pons but exits at the pontomedullary junction and runs through Dorello's canal, a different course from the cerebellopontine angle, so it is not the nerve classically compressed by an expanding vestibular schwannoma.
incorrectas.B: CN IX (glossopharyngeal) exits via the jugular foramen, more inferiorly and posteriorly than the CPA; it can be affected by very large tumors extending into that region, but it is not the nerve classically listed as being compressed next after CN V in CPA syndrome.
incorrectas.C: CN X (vagus) also exits through the jugular foramen rather than the cerebellopontine angle itself; involvement would suggest a much larger or more inferiorly extending mass than the classic CPA syndrome triad of CN V, VII, and VIII.

preguntas.q: Due to the optics of the eye and the crossing of neural pathways to the visual cortex, what is the orientation of a visual image by the time it reaches the primary visual cortex?

e.correcta: The lens inverts and reverses the image on the retina, so an object in the superior visual field lands on the inferior retina and an object in the temporal visual field lands on the nasal retina. This inverted, reversed retinal image is preserved as it travels via the optic nerve, chiasm (where nasal fibers cross), optic radiations, and into the primary visual cortex, so the raw image the brain initially receives is upside-down and left-right reversed before higher cortical processing reconstructs our perceived, upright view of the world.

incorrectas.B: The image is not merely left-right reversed while staying right-side up; the same optical inversion that flips left-right also flips top-to-bottom, so vertical orientation is inverted too, not preserved.
