incorrectas.C: The image is not just upside down without left-right reversal; the convex lens of the eye inverts the image in both the vertical and horizontal axes simultaneously, so left-right reversal necessarily accompanies the vertical inversion.
incorrectas.D: If the image reaching the cortex were right-side up and not reversed, no optical inversion would have occurred at all, which contradicts basic lens optics — any real image formed by a converging lens onto a screen (the retina) is inverted in both axes.

preguntas.q: Compared to lesions of the optic chiasm or postchiasmal pathways, a lesion of the optic nerve itself (before the chiasm) produces what pattern of visual field loss?

e.correcta: Each optic nerve carries all visual information from one eye only, and this occurs before any fibers cross at the chiasm, so a lesion of the optic nerve affects only the eye on the same (ipsilateral) side — producing monocular, ipsilateral visual loss. This is a key localizing principle: monocular symptoms point to a prechiasmal (retina or optic nerve) lesion, whereas binocular, patterned deficits point to chiasmal or postchiasmal disease.

incorrectas.A: Binocular, homonymous, contralateral deficits are the hallmark of postchiasmal lesions (optic tract, radiations, or visual cortex), where fibers from both eyes carrying the same contralateral hemifield travel together after crossing at the chiasm — this requires the lesion to be beyond the optic nerve, not within it.
incorrectas.C: Bitemporal, bilateral loss is the classic pattern of a chiasmal lesion (e.g., pituitary adenoma) that damages the crossing nasal retinal fibers from both eyes simultaneously, which cannot happen with a lesion confined to one prechiasmal optic nerve.
incorrectas.D: Monocular deficits are correct for optic nerve lesions, but the deficit is ipsilateral (same eye as the lesion) since the nerve has not yet crossed at the chiasm — there is no mechanism for a prechiasmal, single-nerve lesion to produce a contralateral-eye deficit.

preguntas.q: A patient develops sudden, complete monocular blindness in one eye due to a central retinal artery occlusion, which effectively knocks out that entire optic nerve's input. What is this visual deficit called?

o.D: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

e.correcta: Because the entire optic nerve of one eye is knocked out before the chiasm, all visual input from that eye is lost while the fellow eye is completely unaffected — this total loss of vision in one eye, on the same side as the lesion, is termed ipsilateral (monocular) anopia. It is the most complete but also most localized visual field defect in the chain of prechiasmal-to-cortical lesions, reflecting damage isolated to a single, uncrossed nerve.

incorrectas.A: Bitemporal hemianopia requires damage to the crossing (nasal retinal) fibers from BOTH eyes at the optic chiasm, such as from a pituitary mass — a lesion confined to one optic nerve, before the chiasm, cannot produce a bilateral field cut.
incorrectas.B: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia results from postchiasmal lesions (optic tract, radiations, cortex) affecting the crossed and uncrossed fibers representing the same hemifield from both eyes; a single prechiasmal optic nerve lesion instead produces total loss in just one eye, not a shared hemifield defect in both eyes.
incorrectas.D: Macular sparing with contralateral homonymous hemianopia is specific to lesions of the primary visual (occipital) cortex, where collateral MCA blood flow spares the macular representation; this is unrelated to a prechiasmal optic nerve occlusion, which destroys the entire eye's visual field including the macula.

preguntas.q: A medially expanding internal carotid artery aneurysm compresses the optic nerve just before it joins the optic chiasm. What visual field defect results?

e.correcta: A lesion at the junction of the optic nerve and chiasm selectively damages the temporal retinal fibers of that eye, and since the temporal retina subserves the nasal visual field, this produces an ipsilateral nasal hemianopia — a partial, localized defect that helps distinguish a prechiasmal-junction lesion from a lesion fully within the nerve or squarely at the chiasm.

incorrectas.B: Bitemporal hemianopia results from damage to the crossing nasal retinal fibers of BOTH eyes at the body of the chiasm; a lesion positioned just before the chiasm, affecting only one nerve's temporal fibers, produces a unilateral nasal — not bilateral temporal — defect.
incorrectas.C: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia arises from postchiasmal damage to fibers from both eyes representing the same visual hemifield; this requires the lesion to be beyond the point where fibers have already crossed, not at the prechiasmal optic nerve-chiasm junction.
incorrectas.D: Ipsilateral monocular anopia implies total loss of vision in that eye, requiring destruction of the whole optic nerve; a lesion isolated to the fibers near the chiasm junction selectively damages only the temporal retinal fibers, sparing the rest of the nerve and leaving partial (nasal field) vision intact.

preguntas.q: A pituitary adenoma expands superiorly and compresses the central portion of the optic chiasm. What visual field defect characteristically results?

e.correcta: The optic chiasm is where the nasal retinal fibers from each eye (which subserve the temporal visual fields) cross to the opposite side; a midline chiasmal lesion like a pituitary adenoma compresses these crossing fibers from both eyes, producing loss of the temporal visual field in each eye — bitemporal hemianopia. Pituitary adenomas classically compress from below, affecting the inferior chiasmal fibers first and causing a superior bitemporal quadrantanopia before progressing to a full bitemporal hemianopia, while craniopharyngiomas compress from above, causing inferior quadrant defects first.

incorrectas.A: Ipsilateral nasal hemianopia results from a more lateral, prechiasmal lesion affecting only one nerve's uncrossed temporal fibers; a pituitary adenoma compressing the central chiasm affects the crossing fibers from both eyes, producing a bilateral (bitemporal), not unilateral, defect.
incorrectas.B: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia is a postchiasmal finding, arising after fibers from both eyes representing the same hemifield have already joined together in the optic tract; a chiasmal lesion instead selectively hits only the crossing fibers, sparing the uncrossed fibers and producing the distinct bitemporal pattern.
incorrectas.C: Monocular anopia implies complete unilateral visual loss from destruction of an entire optic nerve; a chiasmal mass compresses fibers from both eyes symmetrically at the midline, producing a bilateral, partial (temporal field) defect rather than total loss in one eye.

preguntas.q: As one moves along the visual pathway from the optic tract through the optic radiations to the visual cortex — any lesion location posterior to the optic chiasm — what general pattern of visual field deficit is produced?

e.correcta: After the optic chiasm, fibers carrying information from the same (contralateral) visual hemifield — the crossed nasal fibers from one eye and the uncrossed temporal fibers from the other eye — travel together through the optic tract, lateral geniculate body, optic radiations, and visual cortex. Because of this pairing, any postchiasmal lesion affects both eyes' representation of the same hemifield simultaneously, producing binocular, homonymous, contralateral deficits — a pattern used to localize a lesion to somewhere behind the chiasm, with exact location narrowed further by whether the defect is a full hemianopia or a specific quadrantanopia.

incorrectas.A: Monocular, ipsilateral deficits are the signature of a prechiasmal optic nerve lesion, where only uncrossed fibers from one eye are involved; postchiasmal structures instead contain fibers from both eyes already recombined by hemifield, so a postchiasmal lesion cannot produce a purely monocular defect.
incorrectas.C: Bitemporal deficits specifically implicate the chiasm itself, where the crossing nasal fibers from both eyes are damaged together; postchiasmal fibers have already sorted by hemifield rather than by nasal/temporal origin, so a postchiasmal lesion does not reproduce the bitemporal pattern.
incorrectas.D: The defect from postchiasmal lesions is contralateral to the lesion, not ipsilateral, reflecting the crossing of nasal fibers at the chiasm before the pathway reaches postchiasmal structures.

preguntas.q: A lesion of the optic tract (or lateral geniculate body) produces contralateral homonymous hemianopia, similar to a lesion of the primary visual cortex. Which additional finding helps localize the lesion specifically to the optic tract rather than the visual cortex?

e.correcta: Fibers subserving the pupillary light reflex branch off from the visual pathway before the lateral geniculate body, heading instead to the pretectal nucleus in the midbrain. A lesion of the optic tract, being proximal to this branch point, damages both the visual fibers and the pupillary afferents together, producing a mildly diminished pupillary light reflex alongside the contralateral homonymous hemianopia — a finding absent when the lesion is at or distal to the lateral geniculate body, since the pupillary fibers have already diverged by that point.

incorrectas.A: Macular sparing is a feature that localizes a hemianopia to the primary visual cortex (via MCA collateral flow to the occipital pole), not a way to distinguish an optic tract lesion from a lateral geniculate lesion, both of which typically lack macular sparing.
incorrectas.B: Superior quadrantanopia points to a Meyer's loop (temporal lobe) lesion rather than either the optic tract or lateral geniculate body, both of which classically produce a full hemianopia rather than an isolated quadrant defect.
incorrectas.D: Bitemporal field loss is a chiasmal finding, occurring well before the optic tract or lateral geniculate body in the visual pathway; neither of these postchiasmal structures produces a bitemporal pattern since their fibers have already sorted by hemifield.

preguntas.q: A patient develops a lesion of Meyer's loop in the temporal lobe (e.g., from an inferior division MCA stroke). What visual field defect, classically nicknamed 'pie in the sky,' results?

o.C: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

e.correcta: Meyer's loop carries optic radiation fibers from the inferior retina, which represents the superior visual field, looping through the temporal lobe on their way to the inferior bank of the calcarine cortex. Damage here (e.g., from a temporal lobe lesion or inferior-division MCA stroke) knocks out these fibers, producing a contralateral homonymous superior quadrantanopia — the classic 'pie in the sky' defect, an important localizer to temporal lobe pathology.

incorrectas.B: Contralateral homonymous inferior quadrantanopia ('pie on the floor') results from damage to Baum's loop in the parietal lobe, which carries fibers from the superior retina (representing the inferior visual field) — the anatomically and functionally opposite pathway from Meyer's loop.
incorrectas.C: Macular sparing with contralateral homonymous hemianopia localizes to the primary visual (occipital) cortex, typically from a PCA infarct with MCA collateral flow protecting the macula — this is a full hemianopia pattern, not the isolated superior quadrant defect produced by a Meyer's loop lesion.
incorrectas.D: Ipsilateral nasal hemianopia is a prechiasmal finding from a lesion near the optic nerve-chiasm junction affecting one eye's temporal retinal fibers; Meyer's loop is a postchiasmal, bilaterally-represented structure and produces a binocular, homonymous defect instead.

preguntas.q: A parietal lobe lesion (e.g., from a superior-division MCA stroke) damages Baum's loop, the dorsal optic radiation. What visual field defect, nicknamed 'pie on the floor,' results?

o.D: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

e.correcta: Baum's loop (the dorsal/parietal optic radiation) carries fibers from the superior retina, which represents the inferior visual field, running a relatively direct course through the parietal lobe to the superior bank of the calcarine cortex. A parietal lesion damaging this pathway knocks out these fibers, producing a contralateral homonymous inferior quadrantanopia — the 'pie on the floor' defect, which localizes disease to the parietal lobe as opposed to the temporal lobe.

incorrectas.A: Contralateral homonymous superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky') is produced by a lesion of Meyer's loop in the temporal lobe, which carries the opposite (inferior retina/superior field) fibers — the reciprocal pathway and defect from a Baum's loop lesion.
incorrectas.C: Bitemporal hemianopia is a chiasmal finding due to damage of crossing nasal retinal fibers from both eyes; Baum's loop is a postchiasmal parietal structure carrying fibers already sorted by hemifield, so it cannot produce the bitemporal pattern.
incorrectas.D: Macular sparing with full hemianopia is characteristic of primary visual cortex (occipital) lesions with collateral MCA supply protecting the macula, not a partial quadrant defect from parietal (Baum's loop) damage, which affects only the inferior quadrant rather than the whole hemifield.

preguntas.q: A patient suffers a posterior cerebral artery occlusion damaging the primary visual cortex. Which visual field defect is classically seen, distinguished from other postchiasmal lesions by sparing of central vision?

o.D: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

e.correcta: The primary visual cortex (occipital lobe) is supplied mainly by the PCA, but the occipital pole (which represents the macula) also receives collateral blood flow from the middle cerebral artery; a PCA infarct therefore destroys most of the contralateral visual field but spares the macula, producing a contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. This macular sparing is the key distinguishing feature from other postchiasmal lesions (optic tract, Meyer's/Baum's loop), and in the dominant hemisphere may be accompanied by alexia without agraphia if the splenium of the corpus callosum is also involved.

incorrectas.A: Superior quadrantanopia (sparing the inferior field entirely, not just the macula) is the pattern from a temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) lesion, a different anatomic level from primary visual cortex damage, and lacks the specific macular-sparing feature of a cortical/PCA lesion.
incorrectas.B: Inferior quadrantanopia is produced by a parietal lobe (Baum's loop) lesion, not by damage to the visual cortex itself; it also does not carry the classic macular-sparing feature that specifically points to a cortical, PCA-territory lesion.
incorrectas.C: Bitemporal hemianopia is a chiasmal (not postchiasmal cortical) finding from damage to crossing nasal fibers of both eyes; it has nothing to do with macular sparing, which is a cortical-collateral-blood-flow phenomenon specific to occipital lobe infarcts.

preguntas.q: During a posterior cerebral artery infarct affecting the occipital visual cortex, the macula is characteristically spared. This sparing is attributed to collateral blood supply from which artery?

e.correcta: The occipital pole, where the macula is cortically represented, sits at a vascular watershed and receives dual blood supply: primarily from the PCA but also from collateral branches of the middle cerebral artery. When the PCA is occluded, this MCA collateral flow can keep the occipital pole (and therefore central/macular vision) perfused even while the rest of the calcarine cortex infarcts, producing the classic finding of macular sparing in PCA-territory strokes.

incorrectas.B: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes (and the leg-dominant motor/sensory cortex), not the occipital pole, so it does not provide the collateral flow responsible for macular sparing.
incorrectas.C: The anterior choroidal artery supplies structures like the optic tract, internal capsule, and medial temporal lobe (hippocampus); it is relevant to optic tract lesions and their pupillary findings, but it is not the source of the occipital pole's protective collateral supply.
incorrectas.D: The basilar artery gives rise to the posterior cerebral arteries themselves and supplies the brainstem and cerebellum; it is upstream of the PCA rather than a separate collateral source that specifically protects the macular-representing occipital pole.

preguntas.q: A patient with age-related macular degeneration (or ethambutol toxicity) develops a lesion isolated to the macula. What visual field defect results?

e.correcta: The macula is the retinal region responsible for central, high-acuity vision, and it is particularly vulnerable to processes like age-related degeneration, trauma, and certain toxins (e.g., ethambutol-associated optic/retinal toxicity). Damage isolated to the macula knocks out central vision while peripheral vision remains intact, producing a central scotoma — a focal blind spot in the middle of the visual field, distinct from the hemifield or quadrant patterns seen with lesions elsewhere in the visual pathway.

incorrectas.A: Bitemporal hemianopia results from damage to the crossing nasal retinal fibers of both eyes at the chiasm, a structure well removed from the macula itself; a macular lesion affects central vision, not a temporal hemifield in both eyes.
incorrectas.B: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia is a postchiasmal pattern from lesions in the optic tract, radiations, or cortex affecting an entire hemifield; an isolated macular lesion produces a focal central defect rather than loss of an entire half of the visual field.
incorrectas.D: Ipsilateral nasal hemianopia arises from a prechiasmal lesion near the optic nerve-chiasm junction affecting one eye's temporal retinal fibers, a very different location and mechanism from a lesion confined to the macula itself.

preguntas.q: Both an optic tract lesion and a lateral geniculate body lesion can produce contralateral homonymous hemianopia. Which finding helps distinguish a tract lesion from a geniculate lesion?

e.correcta: The afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex diverges from the main visual pathway before reaching the lateral geniculate body, traveling instead to the pretectal nucleus. A lesion of the optic tract, being proximal to this divergence, damages both the visual fibers and the pupillary afferents together, causing a mildly diminished pupillary light reflex alongside the visual field defect — a finding absent when the lesion is at or distal to the lateral geniculate body, since the pupillary fibers have already branched off by that point.

incorrectas.A: Macular sparing is a feature that localizes a hemianopia to the primary visual cortex (via MCA collateral flow to the occipital pole), not a way to distinguish an optic tract lesion from a lateral geniculate lesion, both of which typically lack macular sparing.
incorrectas.C: Superior quadrantanopia points to a Meyer's loop (temporal lobe) lesion rather than either the optic tract or lateral geniculate body, both of which classically produce a full hemianopia rather than an isolated quadrant defect.
incorrectas.D: Bitemporal visual loss is a chiasmal finding, occurring well before the optic tract or lateral geniculate body in the visual pathway; neither of these postchiasmal structures produces a bitemporal pattern since their fibers have already sorted by hemifield.

preguntas.q: Myeloproliferative neoplasms (e.g., CML, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, primary myelofibrosis) are best defined by which process?

o.A: Neoplastic proliferation of mature cells of the myeloid lineage
o.B: Clonal proliferation of immature myeloid blasts
o.C: Ineffective, dysplastic hematopoiesis with peripheral cytopenias
o.D: Neoplastic proliferation of mature lymphoid cells

e.correcta: Myeloproliferative neoplasms arise from a clonal hematopoietic stem cell that retains the ability to differentiate, so the bone marrow overproduces relatively mature, functional cells of one or more myeloid lineages (granulocytes, red cells, platelets) rather than accumulating immature blasts. The specific disorder is classified by which mature lineage dominates — granulocytes in CML, red cells in polycythemia vera, platelets in essential thrombocythemia — and all carry a risk of progressing to marrow fibrosis or transforming into acute leukemia.

incorrectas.B: Clonal proliferation of immature blasts defines acute leukemias (like AML), which by definition halt differentiation and accumulate a high percentage of blasts in the marrow — the opposite of myeloproliferative disorders, where cells mature relatively normally but are overproduced.
incorrectas.C: Ineffective, dysplastic hematopoiesis with cytopenias describes myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), a related but distinct category in which cell production is impaired and dysplastic rather than proliferative and excessive; MDS patients are typically cytopenic, whereas myeloproliferative disorders typically show elevated cell counts.
incorrectas.D: Neoplastic proliferation of mature lymphoid cells describes chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma, a lymphoid neoplasm arising from a different hematopoietic lineage than the myeloid-lineage disorders grouped as myeloproliferative neoplasms.

preguntas.q: Chronic myeloproliferative disorders (CML, PV, ET, primary myelofibrosis) most commonly present in which age group?

e.correcta: Myeloproliferative neoplasms are acquired clonal disorders driven by somatic mutations (e.g., BCR-ABL in CML, JAK2 V617F in the others) that accumulate with age, so incidence rises substantially later in life, with most patients presenting in their 50s to 60s. This is a useful epidemiologic clue on exams: an older patient with an isolated elevation in one myeloid cell line (RBCs, platelets, or granulocytes) should raise suspicion for a myeloproliferative neoplasm.

incorrectas.A: Childhood presentation is far more typical of acute leukemias, particularly ALL, which peaks around ages 2-5; chronic myeloproliferative disorders are diseases of acquired somatic mutation accumulation and are rare in children.
incorrectas.B: Adolescence is not a typical age of onset for myeloproliferative neoplasms; these disorders require accumulation of driver mutations over time and their incidence increases with advancing age rather than clustering in the teenage years.
incorrectas.C: While myeloproliferative disorders can occasionally occur in younger adults, their peak incidence is not in the 20s-30s; the classic epidemiologic association taught for boards is a later peak in the 50s-60s, reflecting age-related mutation accumulation.

preguntas.q: Chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms carry a risk of long-term disease progression through which marrow change, in addition to transformation to acute leukemia?

e.correcta: Sustained overproduction of myeloid cells and their associated growth factors (e.g., PDGF, TGF-beta released by proliferating megakaryocytes) stimulates reactive fibroblast proliferation in the bone marrow stroma over time, leading to progressive marrow fibrosis — most classically seen as the natural evolution of polycythemia vera or essential thrombocythemia into a myelofibrotic picture ('spent phase'), with resulting cytopenias and extramedullary hematopoiesis such as splenomegaly. This, along with transformation to acute leukemia, represents the two major long-term complications monitored in these patients.

incorrectas.A: Marrow hypoplasia/aplasia (as in aplastic anemia) reflects loss of hematopoietic stem cells and marrow fat replacement, essentially the opposite process from a myeloproliferative disorder, which is characterized by cellular overproduction, not marrow failure.
incorrectas.B: Granulomatous replacement of the marrow is a feature of infections (e.g., disseminated TB, fungal infection) or sarcoidosis, not a recognized natural progression pathway of chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms.
incorrectas.D: Amyloid deposition in the marrow is associated with plasma cell dyscrasias like multiple myeloma (AL amyloidosis) or chronic inflammatory states (AA amyloidosis), not a typical long-term complication of myeloproliferative neoplasms.

preguntas.q: A JAK2 V617F point mutation is characteristically found across which category of hematologic neoplasms, with the notable exception of CML?

o.A: Chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms (PV, ET, primary myelofibrosis)

e.correcta: JAK2 is a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase that transduces signals from cytokine receptors (like the erythropoietin, thrombopoietin, and G-CSF receptors) that lack intrinsic kinase activity; the V617F mutation locks JAK2 in a constitutively active state, making myeloid progenitors hypersensitive to growth factors even at low levels. This drives the excessive, relatively mature cell proliferation seen in polycythemia vera (nearly all cases), essential thrombocythemia, and primary myelofibrosis (roughly half of cases) — the classic 'Philadelphia-chromosome-negative' myeloproliferative neoplasms.

incorrectas.B: CML is specifically the exception because its driver mutation is the BCR-ABL fusion (Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22)) producing a constitutively active tyrosine kinase through a completely different mechanism than JAK2 activation, which is why CML is treated with BCR-ABL inhibitors like imatinib rather than JAK inhibitors.
incorrectas.C: Myelodysplastic syndromes are characterized by a variety of cytogenetic and molecular abnormalities (e.g., deletions of chromosome 5q, 7, or 20q) related to ineffective hematopoiesis, but JAK2 V617F is not their defining or characteristic mutation the way it is for the Philadelphia-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms.
incorrectas.D: Acute myeloid leukemia is defined by a distinct set of mutations (e.g., FLT3, NPM1, core-binding factor translocations) driving a block in differentiation with blast accumulation, a different molecular and clinical entity from the JAK2-driven, maturation-preserving myeloproliferative neoplasms.

preguntas.q: Chronic myeloid leukemia responds well to targeted therapy exemplified by imatinib. What is the mechanism of this drug class?

o.D: Differentiation induction via retinoic acid receptor agonism

e.correcta: CML is driven by the BCR-ABL fusion protein, produced by the t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome translocation, which is a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that drives unchecked myeloid proliferation. Imatinib (and related agents like dasatinib and nilotinib) is a small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor that binds the ATP-binding pocket of BCR-ABL, blocking its kinase activity and shutting down the abnormal proliferative signal — producing excellent control of chronic-phase CML, though not typically curative, so allogeneic stem cell transplant remains an option after treatment failure or progression.

incorrectas.A: Proteasome inhibitors (like bortezomib) work by blocking degradation of pro-apoptotic regulatory proteins, a mechanism used in multiple myeloma treatment, not the mechanism by which imatinib controls CML.
incorrectas.C: Anti-CD20 antibodies (like rituximab) target a surface marker on B lymphocytes and are used in B-cell lymphomas and CLL; CML is a myeloid, not lymphoid, neoplasm and does not express CD20 as a therapeutic target.
incorrectas.D: Differentiation-inducing retinoic acid receptor agonists (like all-trans retinoic acid) are the mechanism used to treat acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), a distinct acute leukemia with a PML-RARA fusion, not the mechanism behind imatinib's action in chronic-phase CML.

preguntas.q: What physical exam finding is characteristic of chronic myeloid leukemia, reflecting extramedullary hematopoiesis and leukemic cell infiltration?

e.correcta: In CML, the BCR-ABL-driven clonal myeloid proliferation leads to markedly increased numbers of circulating and marrow granulocytic precursors, which seed the spleen and drive extramedullary hematopoiesis there; this produces massive splenomegaly, often the most prominent physical exam finding and sometimes causing early satiety or left upper quadrant discomfort. The degree of splenomegaly is also clinically useful — a spleen that continues enlarging despite therapy raises concern for transformation to accelerated phase or blast crisis.

incorrectas.A: Generalized lymphadenopathy is more typical of lymphoid neoplasms like CLL or lymphoma, where malignant lymphocytes accumulate in lymph nodes; CML is a myeloid proliferation that preferentially infiltrates the spleen (and marrow) rather than causing prominent widespread lymph node enlargement.
incorrectas.B: Hepatomegaly can occur in CML from myeloid infiltration of the liver, but it is not the dominant or classic finding; splenomegaly is typically far more pronounced and clinically prominent than isolated liver enlargement.
incorrectas.C: Gum hypertrophy (gingival infiltration) is a classic finding in acute monocytic/myelomonocytic leukemia (AML subtypes M4/M5), where malignant monocytic cells infiltrate the gums; this is not a feature of chronic myeloid leukemia.

preguntas.q: A patient with known chronic-phase CML on imatinib is found to have a rapidly enlarging spleen on follow-up exam. What does this finding most likely suggest?

o.A: Progression to accelerated phase or blast crisis
o.B: An excellent response to tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy
o.D: Onset of an autoimmune hemolytic process

e.correcta: An enlarging spleen in a patient with previously stable or treated CML is a red flag for disease progression, since accelerating clonal evolution (often with additional cytogenetic abnormalities layered onto the original BCR-ABL translocation) drives renewed, more aggressive extramedullary proliferation in the spleen. This finding should prompt evaluation for accelerated phase or frank blast crisis (transformation toward acute leukemia, either myeloid or lymphoid), which typically follows shortly after and carries a much worse prognosis than chronic phase.

incorrectas.B: A good response to tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy is instead expected to shrink the spleen toward normal size as the leukemic burden falls with effective BCR-ABL inhibition; an enlarging, not shrinking, spleen is the opposite of what a good treatment response looks like.
incorrectas.C: Iron deficiency anemia is unrelated to splenic size in CML and would present with microcytic anemia findings rather than a change in spleen size; it is not the expected explanation for splenomegaly progression in a CML patient.
incorrectas.D: Autoimmune hemolysis would more typically present with jaundice, elevated LDH/indirect bilirubin, and reticulocytosis rather than being signaled specifically by an enlarging spleen in the context of known CML; splenomegaly progression in this setting is classically interpreted as disease progression, not a new autoimmune process.

preguntas.q: Blast crisis in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) most commonly transforms into which type of acute leukemia?

e.correcta: About two-thirds of CML blast crises differentiate along the myeloid lineage into AML, reflecting that the underlying BCR-ABL1 mutation arises in a pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell capable of giving rise to myeloid precursors that then acquire additional mutations blocking normal differentiation. This myeloid predominance is the more common of the two blast transformation patterns, which is why CML patients are monitored closely with serial CBCs and marrow evaluation for signs of transformation.

incorrectas.B: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia does occur in CML blast crisis, but only in about one-third of cases — less common than myeloid transformation — because although the pluripotent stem cell can differentiate toward lymphoid precursors, myeloid differentiation predominates numerically in blast crisis.
incorrectas.C: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a distinct AML subtype defined by the t(15;17) PML-RARA translocation, a completely separate genetic event from the BCR-ABL1 fusion of CML, and is not the typical blast crisis pathway.
incorrectas.D: Acute monocytic leukemia is a subtype of AML (M5) but is not specifically the pattern described for CML blast transformation; the transformation is typically classified simply as myeloid versus lymphoid lineage rather than by a specific AML subtype.

preguntas.q: Roughly one-third of CML blast crises transform into which type of acute leukemia, illustrating that the causative mutation arises in a multipotent hematopoietic stem cell?

e.correcta: Because the BCR-ABL1 translocation occurs in a pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell that gives rise to both myeloid and lymphoid lineages, CML can transform not only into AML but also into ALL, accounting for roughly one-third of blast crisis cases. This dual lineage potential is a key concept distinguishing CML (a stem-cell-derived myeloproliferative neoplasm) from leukemias confined to a single lineage.

incorrectas.A: Acute myeloid leukemia is actually the more common blast crisis transformation (about two-thirds of cases), not the minority (one-third) pathway being described here.
incorrectas.C: Hairy cell leukemia is a distinct B-cell neoplasm characterized by TRAP-positive cells with hairy cytoplasmic projections and pancytopenia with splenomegaly; it is unrelated to BCR-ABL1 or CML blast transformation.
incorrectas.D: Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia is a specific AML subtype (M7) associated with Down syndrome and myelofibrosis, not the classic lymphoid blast transformation seen in a subset of CML cases.

preguntas.q: A patient has marked neutrophilic leukocytosis. Which peripheral blood finding helps distinguish chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) from a benign leukemoid reaction?

e.correcta: Basophilia is a hallmark of CML because BCR-ABL1-driven myeloproliferation expands multiple granulocytic lineages including basophils, which are essentially never elevated in a benign leukemoid reaction. Along with a low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score and Philadelphia chromosome positivity, basophilia helps separate true CML from reactive neutrophilia triggered by infection or inflammation.

incorrectas.A: Eosinophils can be mildly increased in CML as well, but basophilia is the more specific and classically tested distinguishing feature; isolated eosinophilia is not the discriminator highlighted between CML and leukemoid reaction.
incorrectas.B: Toxic granulations and Döhle bodies are morphologic clues seen in a leukemoid reaction (reflecting a reactive response to infection or inflammation), the opposite pattern of what identifies CML.
incorrectas.C: Lymphocytes are not typically increased in either CML (a myeloid, granulocyte-predominant process) or a leukemoid reaction (also neutrophil-predominant), so lymphocyte counts do not help differentiate the two.

preguntas.q: Polycythemia vera arises from a JAK2 V617F mutation intrinsic to myeloid progenitor cells themselves. Based on this mechanism, polycythemia vera is classified as which type of polycythemia?

e.correcta: In PV, the JAK2 V617F mutation makes myeloid progenitors hypersensitive to growth factors independent of EPO signaling, so red cell (and often white cell/platelet) overproduction is intrinsic to the marrow itself rather than a response to an outside stimulus — this defines primary polycythemia. Because the defect is autonomous marrow proliferation, EPO levels are actually suppressed via negative feedback, in contrast to the secondary forms of polycythemia driven by elevated EPO.

incorrectas.B: Secondary (appropriate) polycythemia is driven by physiologic hypoxia (e.g., COPD, high altitude) causing an appropriate rise in EPO and RBC production — the opposite of PV, where the marrow proliferates autonomously and EPO is low.
incorrectas.C: Relative polycythemia reflects hemoconcentration from a decreased plasma volume (e.g., dehydration) with a normal total RBC mass, unlike PV where the RBC mass itself is markedly increased due to true marrow overproduction.
incorrectas.D: Secondary (inappropriate) polycythemia results from ectopic EPO secretion (e.g., renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma) without hypoxia; PV does not involve elevated EPO at all, since the mutation acts downstream of the EPO receptor pathway.

preguntas.q: A patient with polycythemia vera reports blurry vision and headache. These symptoms are best explained by which physiologic consequence of the disease?

e.correcta: The markedly elevated red cell mass in PV raises whole blood viscosity, which increases vascular resistance and can produce headache and visual disturbances via increased pressure transmitted to the CNS and retinal vasculature (engorged retinal veins on funduscopy). Hyperviscosity is also why patients develop stasis-related thrombosis in addition to these direct symptoms of sluggish flow.

incorrectas.A: Splenomegaly with sequestration can occur in myeloproliferative disorders, but it does not directly cause headache or visual disturbances — those symptoms trace back to increased blood viscosity affecting cerebral and retinal circulation.
incorrectas.B: Thrombocytosis in PV contributes to thrombotic risk (e.g., digital ischemia, erythromelalgia) but is not the direct mechanism behind headache and blurry vision, which are attributed to blood viscosity and vascular engorgement rather than platelet number itself.
incorrectas.D: Hyperuricemia results from increased cell turnover in myeloproliferative states and predisposes to gout, not to headache or visual symptoms, which are hemodynamic rather than metabolic in origin.

preguntas.q: What is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with polycythemia vera?

e.correcta: The markedly increased RBC mass and often elevated platelet count in PV raise blood viscosity and promote stasis, leading to thrombosis at both venous sites (e.g., Budd-Chiari from hepatic vein thrombosis, portal vein thrombosis, DVT, dural venous sinus thrombosis) and arterial sites (stroke, MI). This thrombotic burden — not leukemic transformation or fibrosis — is the dominant driver of morbidity and mortality, which is why antiplatelet therapy and phlebotomy to lower hematocrit are central to management.

incorrectas.A: Myelofibrosis can be a late complication of PV ('spent phase'), but it is a less common long-term outcome and is not the principal cause of early morbidity and mortality compared with thrombosis.
incorrectas.B: Although PV can paradoxically cause bleeding (via acquired platelet dysfunction or acquired von Willebrand syndrome at very high platelet counts), thrombosis — not hemorrhage — is the more common and more consequential complication overall.
incorrectas.C: Transformation to acute leukemia occurs in a minority of PV patients, particularly with certain treatments, but it is a rarer event than the vascular thrombotic complications that dominate the clinical course.

preguntas.q: A patient with polycythemia vera develops episodes of severe burning pain and red discoloration in the distal extremities due to microvascular platelet-mediated clotting. What is this finding called?

e.correcta: Erythromelalgia results from episodic microvascular thrombosis in the distal extremities in the setting of thrombocytosis and hyperviscosity, producing the classic triad of burning pain, erythema, and warmth in the hands or feet. It is a relatively rare but characteristic complication of PV and essential thrombocythemia, and it often responds to aspirin, which reduces platelet-mediated microthrombosis.

incorrectas.A: Livedo reticularis is a mottled, lace-like purplish skin discoloration typically from cutaneous vasospasm or embolic/vasculitic disease (e.g., antiphospholipid syndrome), not the burning red pain of microvascular thrombosis described here.
incorrectas.C: Acrocyanosis is persistent, painless blue discoloration of the hands/feet from peripheral vasoconstriction, lacking the burning pain and episodic thrombotic mechanism that defines erythromelalgia.
incorrectas.D: Raynaud phenomenon involves episodic vasospasm-induced pallor and cyanosis of the digits triggered by cold or stress, a vasospastic (not thrombotic) process typically without the burning erythema seen in erythromelalgia.

preguntas.q: Low-dose aspirin is used in polycythemia vera to reduce thrombosis risk, though it carries a theoretical risk of worsening which associated condition by inhibiting renal OAT-mediated uric acid transport?

e.correcta: Low-dose aspirin (unlike high-dose aspirin) paradoxically reduces renal excretion of uric acid by inhibiting organic anion transporters (OATs) that normally move uric acid into proximal tubule cells for secretion, raising serum urate. Because PV already predisposes to hyperuricemia and gout from high cell turnover, this pharmacologic side effect can compound an existing risk, so clinicians must weigh the clear antithrombotic benefit of aspirin against this modest gout risk.

incorrectas.A: Budd-Chiari syndrome is a thrombotic complication of PV that aspirin is meant to help prevent, not something aspirin's OAT-inhibiting effect would exacerbate.
incorrectas.C: Peptic ulcer disease/GI bleeding is a recognized aspirin side effect via COX-1 inhibition reducing protective gastric prostaglandins, but it is not the specific interaction with OAT-mediated uric acid transport referenced here.
incorrectas.D: Erythromelalgia is actually a complication that low-dose aspirin helps treat (by reducing platelet-mediated microthrombosis), not a condition it worsens.

preguntas.q: In polycythemia vera, the marrow's autonomous overproduction of red cells expands intravascular volume. What happens to plasma volume as a result, and how does this manifest clinically?

o.A: Plasma volume increases, contributing to hypertension and facial plethora
o.C: Plasma volume stays normal while only RBC mass rises
o.D: Plasma volume decreases, causing orthostatic hypotension

e.correcta: In true (absolute) polycythemia vera, the expanded red cell mass is accompanied by an increase in total plasma/blood volume as the vasculature engorges, producing hypertension, facial plethora (ruddy, red complexion), and — via increased pressure transmitted through the optic nerve meninges — headache and visual disturbances with dilated retinal veins on funduscopy. This distinguishes PV's volume physiology from relative polycythemia, where it is a drop in plasma volume (not a rise) that concentrates a normal red cell mass.

incorrectas.B: A decrease in plasma volume causing hemoconcentration is the mechanism of relative polycythemia (e.g., from dehydration or burns), the opposite of what happens in PV, where total blood volume actually expands.
incorrectas.C: While RBC mass is indeed markedly elevated in PV, plasma volume also rises rather than staying flat — the combined expansion of both compartments is what produces the plethora and hypertension seen clinically.
incorrectas.D: PV causes hypertension from volume expansion, not orthostatic hypotension from volume depletion; a falling plasma volume with hypotension would instead suggest a relative/hemoconcentration process.

preguntas.q: A patient with polycythemia vera has a hemoglobin of 20 g/dL (normal ~15) and a hematocrit of 60%. What underlies these findings?

o.A: A modest, EPO-driven rise in RBC mass appropriate to chronic hypoxia
o.B: An EPO-secreting tumor driving inappropriate RBC production
o.C: A markedly increased total RBC mass from autonomous marrow proliferation
o.D: Hemoconcentration from a normal RBC mass with reduced plasma volume

e.correcta: PV is defined by a true, often dramatic, expansion of total RBC mass because the JAK2-mutated myeloid progenitors proliferate independent of normal EPO regulation, pushing hemoglobin and hematocrit well above normal (e.g., Hgb ~20 g/dL, Hct ~60%). This distinguishes PV from relative polycythemia, where the RBC mass itself is normal and only appears elevated due to reduced plasma volume.

incorrectas.A: A modest, appropriately EPO-driven RBC rise describes secondary (appropriate) polycythemia from chronic hypoxia (e.g., COPD, high altitude); PV's RBC elevation is autonomous and typically more pronounced, occurring with low (not high) EPO.
incorrectas.B: An EPO-secreting tumor driving RBC overproduction describes secondary (inappropriate) polycythemia (e.g., renal cell carcinoma); PV's proliferation is intrinsic to the marrow and actually suppresses EPO via negative feedback.
incorrectas.D: Hemoconcentration with a normal RBC mass describes relative polycythemia (e.g., dehydration), not PV — in PV the RBC mass itself is truly and markedly elevated, not just concentrated.

preguntas.q: Measuring serum erythropoietin (EPO) is a key step in distinguishing polycythemia vera from secondary causes of polycythemia. What is the expected EPO level in polycythemia vera, and why?

o.B: Normal, because the process is independent of the EPO axis
o.C: Increased, due to ectopic tumor secretion
o.D: Decreased, due to negative feedback from the expanded RBC mass

e.correcta: In PV, the JAK2 V617F mutation causes red cell overproduction independent of the normal EPO signaling pathway, so the body's oxygen-sensing feedback loop responds to the resulting elevated oxygen-carrying capacity by suppressing renal EPO production. A low EPO level in the setting of polycythemia is therefore a key laboratory clue pointing toward PV rather than a secondary cause, where EPO would instead be elevated.

incorrectas.A: An increased EPO from tissue hypoxia describes secondary (appropriate) polycythemia (e.g., COPD, high altitude), the opposite of PV, where oxygen delivery is actually enhanced by the excess RBCs, suppressing EPO.
incorrectas.B: EPO is not simply 'normal and irrelevant' in PV — while the disease process bypasses EPO signaling, the resulting RBC excess actively suppresses EPO via negative feedback, making a low EPO level a meaningful diagnostic clue.
incorrectas.C: An increased EPO from ectopic tumor secretion describes secondary (inappropriate) polycythemia (e.g., renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma), not PV, whose autonomous marrow proliferation lowers EPO instead.

preguntas.q: A dehydrated patient has an elevated hematocrit despite a normal total red cell mass. What change in plasma volume accounts for this apparent polycythemia?

o.C: Normal plasma volume with increased RBC production
o.D: Decreased plasma volume plus decreased RBC mass

e.correcta: Relative polycythemia occurs when plasma volume contracts (e.g., from dehydration, burns, vomiting, diarrhea, or diuretics) while the total red cell mass stays the same, so the RBCs become more concentrated in a smaller volume of plasma — raising hematocrit and hemoglobin concentration without any true increase in red cell number. This is why it's also called hemoconcentration, and correcting the underlying fluid deficit normalizes the hematocrit.

incorrectas.A: An increased plasma volume would dilute, not concentrate, the red cell population, lowering hematocrit rather than producing the apparent polycythemia described here.
incorrectas.C: A normal plasma volume with increased RBC production would represent a true (absolute) polycythemia rather than relative polycythemia — here it is the plasma volume that changes while RBC mass is unchanged, not the reverse.
incorrectas.D: The RBC mass in relative polycythemia is normal, not decreased — only the plasma volume drops, which is precisely what distinguishes it from other causes of volume contraction with actual red cell loss.

preguntas.q: What happens to total RBC mass in relative polycythemia (hemoconcentration), and why is this clinically important?

o.A: RBC mass is decreased, masked by volume loss
o.B: RBC mass is markedly increased, as in polycythemia vera
o.C: RBC mass remains normal, distinguishing it from true polycythemias
o.D: RBC mass is increased due to elevated EPO

e.correcta: In relative polycythemia, total RBC mass is normal — the elevated hematocrit reflects a shrunken plasma volume concentrating a normal number of red cells, not true erythrocyte overproduction. Recognizing that RBC mass is unchanged is the key distinguishing feature from the absolute polycythemias (PV, and secondary appropriate/inappropriate forms), where RBC mass is genuinely elevated.

incorrectas.A: RBC mass is not decreased in relative polycythemia; total red cell number is unchanged, and it is specifically the plasma compartment that shrinks — a decreased RBC mass would instead suggest true anemia complicated by volume contraction.
incorrectas.B: A markedly increased RBC mass describes polycythemia vera, a true (absolute) polycythemia from autonomous marrow proliferation, not the hemoconcentration mechanism of relative polycythemia.
incorrectas.D: Increased EPO driving RBC production describes secondary (appropriate) polycythemia; relative polycythemia involves no true change in RBC production or mass at all.

preguntas.q: In relative polycythemia from hemoconcentration, why is the serum EPO level typically normal rather than elevated?

o.A: Because negative feedback from excess RBCs suppresses EPO
o.B: Because an ectopic source is secreting EPO at baseline levels
o.C: Because oxygen delivery is unaffected, so there is no hypoxic stimulus to raise EPO
o.D: Because the JAK2 mutation suppresses EPO independent of oxygen status

e.correcta: Since relative polycythemia reflects a contracted plasma volume rather than a true change in red cell number, the actual oxygen-carrying capacity and tissue oxygenation are unaffected — there is no hypoxia to stimulate renal EPO production, so EPO remains normal. This is a useful distinguishing point from the appropriate secondary polycythemias, where genuine hypoxia does raise EPO.

incorrectas.A: Negative feedback suppression of EPO by excess RBCs is the PV mechanism; in relative polycythemia, the RBC mass itself is normal, so there is no true excess to trigger feedback suppression — EPO is normal because nothing is actually driving it up or down.
incorrectas.B: Ectopic EPO secretion at baseline levels describes secondary (inappropriate) polycythemia from tumors like renal cell carcinoma, not the hemoconcentration mechanism of relative polycythemia, where EPO production is unaltered because there's no true RBC excess.
incorrectas.D: JAK2 V617F suppressing EPO via negative feedback is the mechanism in polycythemia vera (a true, autonomous overproduction of RBCs), not in relative polycythemia, which has no primary marrow mutation at all.

preguntas.q: A patient presents with an elevated hematocrit in the setting of severe dehydration from prolonged vomiting. Which category of polycythemia does this represent?

e.correcta: Dehydration, burns, prolonged vomiting or diarrhea, diuretic use, and conditions like dengue hemorrhagic fever all cause fluid loss that contracts plasma volume, concentrating a normal RBC mass — this is relative polycythemia (hemoconcentration). Because RBC mass and EPO are both normal here, fluid resuscitation (not phlebotomy or myelosuppressive therapy) is the appropriate treatment.

incorrectas.A: Secondary (appropriate) polycythemia results from chronic hypoxia (e.g., COPD, high altitude) driving a true, EPO-mediated increase in RBC mass, not from a volume shift as seen with dehydration or burns.
incorrectas.B: Polycythemia vera is a primary myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by JAK2 V617F with autonomous marrow proliferation and low EPO — an entirely different, intrinsic marrow process rather than a response to fluid loss.
incorrectas.C: Secondary (inappropriate) polycythemia results from ectopic EPO secretion (e.g., by a renal or hepatic tumor) without hypoxia, which is unrelated to the volume contraction seen with vomiting, burns, or dehydration.

preguntas.q: A patient with severe COPD and chronic hypoxemia develops a true increase in circulating RBC mass as a compensatory response. How is this form of polycythemia classified?

e.correcta: Chronic hypoxemia (from COPD, obstructive sleep apnea, congenital heart disease, high altitude, etc.) triggers a physiologically appropriate rise in renal EPO, which drives real erythropoiesis and increases total RBC mass — this is secondary appropriate polycythemia, an adaptive response aimed at improving tissue oxygen delivery. Unlike PV, both EPO and RBC mass are elevated together here, tracking the underlying hypoxic stimulus.

incorrectas.A: Polycythemia vera is an autonomous JAK2-driven marrow proliferation with low EPO, the opposite pattern of the EPO-driven, hypoxia-appropriate RBC rise described in this scenario.
incorrectas.C: Relative polycythemia involves no true increase in RBC mass at all — only a contracted plasma volume concentrating a normal red cell number, unlike the true erythrocytosis driven by chronic hypoxia here.
incorrectas.D: Secondary (inappropriate) polycythemia also involves elevated EPO and RBC mass, but the EPO arises from ectopic/pathologic secretion (e.g., renal cell carcinoma) in the absence of true hypoxia, rather than as an appropriate response to genuine tissue hypoxia as in COPD.

preguntas.q: In a patient with chronic hypoxemia from high altitude, why is serum EPO elevated alongside the increased RBC mass, and what does this indicate diagnostically?

o.A: EPO remains normal because the RBC rise is due to hemoconcentration
o.B: EPO is suppressed by negative feedback from RBC excess
o.C: EPO rises due to ectopic tumor production unrelated to oxygen status
o.D: EPO rises appropriately in response to hypoxia, distinguishing this from polycythemia vera

e.correcta: Chronic hypoxia stimulates renal peritubular cells to increase EPO production as a normal physiologic response aimed at boosting oxygen-carrying capacity, and the resulting elevated EPO together with elevated RBC mass is the hallmark of secondary (appropriate) polycythemia. This elevated-EPO pattern is an important distinguishing lab feature from polycythemia vera, where EPO is suppressed despite (or because of) the elevated RBC mass.

incorrectas.A: EPO does not stay normal in this scenario — hemoconcentration with normal EPO describes relative polycythemia, whereas high-altitude polycythemia involves a true, EPO-driven increase in RBC mass in response to real hypoxia.
incorrectas.B: EPO suppression by negative feedback from RBC excess is the pattern seen in polycythemia vera, the opposite of what occurs here, where a genuine hypoxic stimulus is actively driving EPO upward.
incorrectas.C: Ectopic tumor-driven EPO production unrelated to oxygen status describes secondary (inappropriate) polycythemia (e.g., renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma), not the hypoxia-driven appropriate response occurring at high altitude.

preguntas.q: Which category of polycythemia is associated with conditions like COPD, obstructive sleep apnea, congenital heart disease, high altitude, and low birth weight?

e.correcta: All of these conditions share chronic tissue hypoxia as their common mechanism (impaired gas exchange in lung disease/OSA, right-to-left shunting in congenital heart disease, low ambient oxygen at altitude, or relative intrauterine hypoxia with low birth weight), which appropriately raises EPO and drives a true, compensatory increase in RBC mass — defining secondary appropriate polycythemia. This is a physiologic adaptation to improve oxygen delivery, unlike the pathologic, EPO-independent proliferation of PV.

incorrectas.A: Relative polycythemia results from plasma volume contraction (e.g., dehydration), not from the sustained hypoxia-driven true RBC overproduction seen in chronic lung or heart disease and high-altitude living.
incorrectas.B: Essential thrombocythemia is a myeloproliferative neoplasm defined by isolated platelet overproduction, unrelated to hypoxia or the erythrocytosis conditions listed here.
incorrectas.D: Secondary (inappropriate) polycythemia is driven by ectopic EPO secretion from tumors or renal lesions without any true hypoxic drive, not by the hypoxia-based mechanisms shared by lung disease, OSA, congenital heart disease, and high altitude.

preguntas.q: A patient with a renal cell carcinoma secreting ectopic erythropoietin develops a true increase in RBC mass without any hypoxic stimulus. How is this form of polycythemia classified?

e.correcta: When a tumor or renal lesion secretes EPO independent of any real oxygen deficit, the resulting RBC overproduction is termed secondary inappropriate polycythemia because the EPO rise (and consequent RBC mass increase) is not a physiologically justified response to hypoxia — it's a paraneoplastic or ectopic phenomenon. Classic causes include renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, hydronephrosis/renal cysts, and exogenous EPO doping.

incorrectas.B: Polycythemia vera is characterized by autonomous marrow proliferation with low EPO from negative feedback, the opposite lab pattern from this scenario, where EPO is elevated and driving the RBC excess.
incorrectas.C: Relative polycythemia involves no true RBC mass increase at all, only hemoconcentration from reduced plasma volume, unlike the genuine erythrocytosis produced by ectopic EPO here.
incorrectas.D: Secondary (appropriate) polycythemia also involves elevated EPO and RBC mass, but the rise in EPO is a genuine physiologic response to real tissue hypoxia (e.g., COPD, high altitude), not ectopic tumor secretion as in this scenario.

preguntas.q: Why is serum EPO elevated in a patient with polycythemia due to a paraneoplastic process (e.g., renal cell carcinoma), and how does this help distinguish the condition from polycythemia vera?

o.A: EPO falls due to negative feedback, as in PV
o.B: EPO is secreted ectopically by the tumor independent of oxygen status, whereas EPO is low in PV
o.C: EPO is normal in both conditions
o.D: EPO rises appropriately due to tissue hypoxia, whereas EPO is low in PV

e.correcta: In secondary inappropriate polycythemia, the source tissue (tumor, cyst, or dysfunctional kidney) secretes EPO in an unregulated, ectopic fashion unrelated to actual oxygen levels, driving RBC overproduction; measuring an elevated EPO in this setting is a key distinguishing feature from PV, where the autonomous JAK2-driven proliferation instead suppresses EPO via negative feedback. This EPO level is therefore central to working up any patient with polycythemia to sort true marrow disease from a secondary/ectopic cause.

incorrectas.A: A falling EPO from negative feedback is the PV pattern, not the paraneoplastic pattern — in inappropriate secondary polycythemia, EPO is elevated because it is the ectopic source itself driving RBC production, unchecked by normal feedback.
incorrectas.C: EPO is not normal in either condition being contrasted — it is elevated in secondary inappropriate polycythemia (from ectopic secretion) and low in PV (from negative feedback suppression); the EPO level is precisely what differentiates them.
incorrectas.D: Appropriate, hypoxia-driven EPO elevation describes secondary appropriate polycythemia (e.g., COPD, high altitude), not the ectopic, hypoxia-independent EPO secretion characteristic of a paraneoplastic process like renal cell carcinoma.

preguntas.q: Which category of polycythemia is caused by ectopic EPO production from malignancy, hydronephrosis/renal cysts, or exogenous EPO use (e.g., blood doping)?

e.correcta: These causes share a common feature: EPO is elevated (endogenously ectopic or exogenously administered) without any genuine hypoxic drive, so the resulting RBC overproduction is termed secondary inappropriate polycythemia. Hydronephrosis, for example, causes localized peritubular hypoxia that triggers renal fibroblasts to secrete EPO even though the patient is not systemically hypoxic — illustrating how 'inappropriate' here refers to a mismatch between EPO secretion and true oxygen need at the whole-body level.

incorrectas.A: Polycythemia vera arises from an intrinsic JAK2 mutation in marrow progenitors with low EPO, an entirely different (and EPO-independent) mechanism from the ectopic or exogenous EPO sources described here.
incorrectas.B: Secondary (appropriate) polycythemia is driven by genuine systemic hypoxia (e.g., COPD, high altitude) appropriately raising EPO, not by ectopic tumor/cyst secretion or exogenous EPO administration as described here.
incorrectas.C: Relative polycythemia involves no change in EPO or true RBC mass, only plasma volume contraction, unlike the genuinely elevated EPO and RBC mass caused by ectopic secretion or doping.

preguntas.q: Compared to other chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms, what is the risk of marrow fibrosis or transformation to acute leukemia in essential thrombocythemia (ET)?

o.A: High risk, similar to CML blast crisis
o.B: Moderate risk, similar to polycythemia vera
o.C: Low/rare risk, one of the more indolent myeloproliferative neoplasms
o.D: Universal progression, as in primary myelofibrosis

e.correcta: Essential thrombocythemia is generally the most indolent of the classic myeloproliferative neoplasms — marrow fibrosis and transformation to acute leukemia are rare, and many patients have a near-normal life expectancy if thrombotic/hemorrhagic complications are managed. This favorable natural history contrasts with primary myelofibrosis (where fibrosis is intrinsic to the disease) and with CML (which has a well-defined, more frequent blast crisis phase).

incorrectas.A: CML has a defined and relatively common blast crisis phase (transformation to AML or ALL in a substantial minority of patients), a much higher transformation risk than the rare occurrence seen in ET.
incorrectas.B: Polycythemia vera carries a real, non-trivial risk of both fibrotic transformation ('spent phase') and, less commonly, leukemic transformation, which is somewhat higher than the rare risk seen in ET.
incorrectas.D: Primary myelofibrosis is defined by progressive marrow fibrosis as its core pathology, essentially the opposite natural history from ET, which rarely progresses to significant fibrosis.

preguntas.q: Unlike polycythemia vera, why does essential thrombocythemia (ET) carry little risk of hyperuricemia and gout despite high cell turnover?

o.A: ET is associated with low, not high, platelet turnover
o.B: ET patients have enhanced renal urate clearance
o.C: ET does not actually involve increased cell turnover
o.D: Platelets lack nuclei, so their turnover does not generate the purine breakdown products that raise uric acid

e.correcta: Hyperuricemia and gout in myeloproliferative neoplasms result from increased purine degradation as nucleated cells turn over rapidly; because mature platelets are anucleate cell fragments with no DNA/RNA to break down into purines, even a very high platelet count in ET does not meaningfully raise uric acid production. This is why gout risk is much more closely tied to PV (with its nucleated RBC precursors and overall myeloid hypercellularity) than to ET.

incorrectas.A: ET is actually characterized by markedly increased platelet turnover/production (that's the defining feature of the disease) — the low gout risk comes from platelets lacking nuclei, not from a low turnover rate.
incorrectas.B: There's no evidence of enhanced renal urate clearance in ET; the reason gout risk is low is a lack of purine substrate from anucleate platelets, not a compensatory increase in excretion.
incorrectas.C: ET does involve increased cell turnover — megakaryocytes and platelets are markedly overproduced — but because platelets are non-nucleated, this turnover simply doesn't generate the purine byproducts responsible for hyperuricemia.

preguntas.q: In primary myelofibrosis, what do proliferating megakaryocytes overproduce that drives the characteristic marrow fibrosis?

o.A: Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and IL-6

e.correcta: In myelofibrosis, neoplastic megakaryocytes secrete excess PDGF and TGF-beta, which stimulate marrow fibroblasts to proliferate and deposit collagen, progressively replacing normal hematopoietic marrow with fibrous tissue. This fibrotic replacement is what forces hematopoiesis to relocate to extramedullary sites like the spleen and liver, producing the disease's characteristic massive splenomegaly.

incorrectas.A: VEGF and IL-6 are implicated in angiogenesis and inflammatory signaling in various myeloid neoplasms, but the specific fibrogenic drivers classically attributed to megakaryocytes in myelofibrosis are PDGF and TGF-beta.
incorrectas.C: BCR-ABL1 is the defining fusion protein of CML, not myelofibrosis (which instead is associated with JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutations), and IL-3 is a general hematopoietic growth factor, not the specific fibrogenic signal from megakaryocytes.
incorrectas.D: Erythropoietin and thrombopoietin are physiologic growth factors regulating red cell and platelet production respectively; they are not the fibrogenic cytokines responsible for the marrow scarring seen in myelofibrosis.

preguntas.q: A patient with primary myelofibrosis presents with massive splenomegaly. What is the primary mechanism behind this finding?

o.A: Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia from chronic inflammation
o.B: Splenic vein thrombosis causing congestive splenomegaly
o.C: Extramedullary hematopoiesis compensating for fibrotic marrow replacement
o.D: Direct infiltration of the spleen by BCR-ABL1-positive clones

e.correcta: As progressive marrow fibrosis (driven by megakaryocyte-derived PDGF and TGF-beta) destroys the normal hematopoietic niche, blood cell production shifts to extramedullary sites — most prominently the spleen (and to a lesser extent the liver) — causing it to enlarge dramatically as it takes over hematopoietic function. This massive splenomegaly is a hallmark clinical clue for myelofibrosis and can be complicated by symptoms of splenic infarction or early satiety from mass effect.

incorrectas.A: Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia reflects an immune/inflammatory response to infection or antigenic stimulation, not the marrow failure-driven extramedullary hematopoiesis that characterizes myelofibrosis-associated splenomegaly.
incorrectas.B: Splenic vein thrombosis causing congestive splenomegaly is a vascular mechanism seen in conditions like portal hypertension, distinct from the hematopoietic compensatory mechanism that enlarges the spleen in myelofibrosis.
incorrectas.D: BCR-ABL1 is the hallmark fusion protein of CML, not myelofibrosis, which is instead associated with mutations like JAK2 V617F, CALR, or MPL; myelofibrosis splenomegaly is due to extramedullary hematopoiesis, not a specific clonal infiltration process tied to BCR-ABL1.

preguntas.q: Which peripheral blood smear finding is characteristic of myelofibrosis?

o.A: A leukoerythroblastic pattern (nucleated RBCs and immature granulocytes)

e.correcta: In myelofibrosis, marrow scarring destroys the normal hematopoietic architecture, forcing extramedullary hematopoiesis in the spleen and liver. Because splenic sinusoids do not filter immature cells as effectively as bone marrow does, nucleated RBCs and immature granulocyte forms spill into the peripheral blood, producing the classic leukoerythroblastic smear that signals a myelophthisic process.

incorrectas.B: Microcytic hypochromic anemia points to iron deficiency or thalassemia, reflecting a defect in hemoglobin synthesis rather than the myelophthisic marrow replacement seen in myelofibrosis, which instead produces a normocytic anemia with teardrop cells.
incorrectas.C: Schistocytes and helmet cells arise from mechanical shearing of RBCs in microangiopathic hemolytic processes (TTP, HUS, DIC), a fragmentation injury unrelated to the fibrotic marrow and extramedullary hematopoiesis driving myelofibrosis.
incorrectas.D: Target cells with basophilic stippling suggest hemoglobinopathies (thalassemia) or lead poisoning, reflecting altered membrane surface-to-volume ratio or defective heme synthesis, not marrow fibrosis and extramedullary blood cell release.

preguntas.q: Myelofibrosis increases the risk of infection, thrombosis, and bleeding primarily because of which hematologic abnormality?

e.correcta: Progressive marrow fibrosis (driven by megakaryocyte-released cytokines like PDGF and TGF-beta) replaces the hematopoietic space, and the spleen's compensatory extramedullary hematopoiesis cannot fully make up for the deficit. The result is pancytopenia — low neutrophils raise infection risk, and low or dysfunctional platelets contribute to both bleeding and, paradoxically, thrombosis via abnormal platelet activation.

incorrectas.A: Early myelofibrosis can transiently show leukocytosis, but it is the later fall in blood counts as fibrosis progresses — not an elevated WBC — that actually drives the infection, bleeding, and thrombosis risk described here.
incorrectas.C: Polycythemia (elevated red cell mass) is the hallmark of polycythemia vera, a different JAK2-driven myeloproliferative neoplasm; myelofibrosis instead typically causes progressive anemia as fibrotic tissue replaces functional marrow.
incorrectas.D: Thrombocytosis characterizes essential thrombocythemia; in myelofibrosis, platelet counts usually fall (thrombocytopenia) as fibrotic marrow fails to sustain adequate megakaryocyte output, contributing to bleeding rather than resulting from platelet excess.

preguntas.q: What pathologic red blood cell morphology is classically associated with myelofibrosis?

e.correcta: Teardrop cells (dacrocytes) form when RBCs are physically deformed as they squeeze through a stiff, fibrotic bone marrow on their way into circulation. Their presence on a smear is a strong morphologic clue pointing toward a myelophthisic process like myelofibrosis, especially when paired with a leukoerythroblastic picture.

incorrectas.A: Schistocytes are fragmented RBCs produced by mechanical shearing in the microvasculature during processes like TTP, HUS, or DIC — a reflection of intravascular trauma, not of cells being extruded through scarred marrow.
incorrectas.B: Spherocytes are round, dense RBCs that have lost membrane surface area, typically from immune-mediated membrane loss (autoimmune hemolytic anemia) or a membrane skeleton defect (hereditary spherocytosis), unrelated to marrow fibrosis.
incorrectas.D: Target cells reflect an increased membrane-to-volume ratio and are seen in thalassemia, liver disease, and hemoglobin C disease — a membrane/hemoglobin content issue, not the marrow scarring that produces teardrop cells in myelofibrosis.

preguntas.q: In polycythemia vera, in addition to erythrocytosis, what typically happens to the white blood cell count?

o.C: It increases only after transformation to the spent (fibrotic) phase

e.correcta: Polycythemia vera arises from a single hematopoietic stem cell clone carrying a JAK2 V617F (or exon 12) mutation that drives cytokine-independent proliferation across all myeloid lineages, not just erythroid precursors. This panmyeloproliferation means leukocytosis (and often thrombocytosis) accompanies the erythrocytosis and is part of the WHO diagnostic criteria from the outset.

incorrectas.A: A decreased WBC count would suggest a failing or aplastic marrow process, the opposite of the proliferative biology that defines PV.
incorrectas.B: An unchanged WBC count would be expected if PV involved only the erythroid lineage, but because the disease arises from a multipotent JAK2-mutated stem cell, all myeloid lineages — including granulocytes — are typically overproduced.
incorrectas.C: Leukocytosis is present from early, proliferative-phase PV as a core diagnostic feature, not something that only appears once the disease transforms into the late myelofibrotic 'spent phase.'

preguntas.q: In polycythemia vera, in addition to erythrocytosis, what typically happens to the platelet count?

e.correcta: Because PV originates from a JAK2-mutated multipotent stem cell clone, proliferation is not confined to the erythroid line — megakaryocytes are also driven to overproduce platelets. Thrombocytosis alongside erythrocytosis and leukocytosis reflects this panmyeloid clonal expansion and contributes to the thrombotic risk that makes PV clinically dangerous.

incorrectas.B: A decreased platelet count would instead suggest a failing marrow state, such as late spent-phase transformation to myelofibrosis, rather than the proliferative early/mid course of PV.
incorrectas.C: An unchanged platelet count would be expected only if PV selectively affected the erythroid lineage, but the clonal process involves all myeloid lineages, so platelets are typically elevated too.
incorrectas.D: Thrombocytosis in PV arises directly from the underlying clonal proliferative process and is usually present at diagnosis, not something that depends on a prior splenectomy.

preguntas.q: Polycythemia vera is characterized by activating mutations in which gene, found in the vast majority (~95%) of cases?

e.correcta: PV is driven almost universally by a JAK2 mutation (classically V617F, or an exon 12 mutation in JAK2-V617F-negative cases), which locks the JAK-STAT signaling pathway downstream of the erythropoietin receptor into a constitutively active state. This makes erythroid progenitors proliferate independent of normal EPO regulation, explaining why serum EPO is typically low in PV despite marked erythrocytosis.

incorrectas.A: BCR-ABL1 is the fusion oncogene created by the Philadelphia chromosome translocation t(9;22), the defining molecular lesion of CML, not PV, and PV patients are BCR-ABL1 negative by definition.
incorrectas.C: CALR (calreticulin) mutations are found in a subset of JAK2-negative essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis, not typically in PV, where JAK2 mutation dominates.
incorrectas.D: MPL mutations (affecting the thrombopoietin receptor) are also seen in a minority of JAK2-negative ET and myelofibrosis cases, not as the primary driver of PV.

preguntas.q: In essential thrombocythemia, JAK2 V617F mutations are found in approximately what proportion of cases?

e.correcta: Unlike polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia is molecularly heterogeneous — JAK2 V617F accounts for only roughly 30-50% of cases, with the remainder driven by CALR mutations, MPL mutations, or occasionally no identifiable driver (triple-negative disease). This genetic diversity is a key distinguishing feature of ET compared to PV, where JAK2 mutation is present in nearly all patients.

incorrectas.A: A ~95% JAK2 mutation rate describes polycythemia vera, not ET; ET's molecular landscape is considerably more heterogeneous, split among JAK2, CALR, and MPL mutations.
incorrectas.B: Less than 5% would essentially exclude JAK2 as a meaningful driver in ET, but JAK2 V617F is actually one of the three major recognized driver mutations in this disease, present in roughly a third to half of cases.
incorrectas.D: 100% would imply JAK2 is the sole driver in ET, but CALR and MPL mutations (and rare triple-negative cases) account for a substantial share of ET, unlike the near-uniform JAK2 positivity seen in PV.

preguntas.q: Unlike CML, which is defined by the BCR-ABL1 fusion, primary myelofibrosis is associated with JAK2 V617F mutations in approximately what fraction of cases?

e.correcta: Primary myelofibrosis shares its molecular heterogeneity with essential thrombocythemia: JAK2 V617F is found in roughly 30-50% of cases, while the rest are driven by CALR mutations, MPL mutations, or are triple-negative. This mixed driver profile distinguishes myelofibrosis and ET from polycythemia vera, where JAK2 mutation is nearly universal.

incorrectas.A: A ~95% mutation rate describes polycythemia vera's relationship with JAK2, not the more heterogeneous mutation profile of primary myelofibrosis.
incorrectas.B: Virtually 0% would essentially describe CML, which lacks JAK2 mutations entirely and is instead driven by the BCR-ABL1 fusion; myelofibrosis is a Philadelphia-chromosome-negative, JAK2-associated myeloproliferative neoplasm, unlike CML.
incorrectas.C: More than 90% overstates JAK2's contribution to myelofibrosis; like ET, myelofibrosis has a mixed molecular profile including CALR and MPL mutations and a triple-negative subset.

preguntas.q: Which molecular abnormality is characteristic of chronic myeloid leukemia, distinguishing it from the JAK2-associated myeloproliferative neoplasms (PV, ET, myelofibrosis)?

o.A: BCR-ABL1 fusion via the t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome

e.correcta: CML is defined by the reciprocal translocation t(9;22)(q34;q11), which fuses the ABL1 tyrosine kinase gene (chromosome 9) to BCR (chromosome 22), creating the Philadelphia chromosome and a constitutively active BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase that drives uncontrolled myeloid proliferation. This is the molecular target of imatinib and related tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and it sets CML apart from the classic Philadelphia-negative, JAK2-mutated MPNs.

incorrectas.B: JAK2 V617F is the hallmark mutation of the Philadelphia-chromosome-negative MPNs (PV, ET, myelofibrosis), not CML, which is instead defined by its BCR-ABL1 fusion.
incorrectas.C: CALR mutations occur in a subset of JAK2-negative ET and myelofibrosis, an entirely separate molecular pathway from CML's fusion oncogene.
incorrectas.D: MPL mutations occur in a subset of JAK2-negative ET and myelofibrosis as well, unrelated to the BCR-ABL1 fusion that defines CML.

preguntas.q: Lymphomas are classified into Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin types. Which type accounts for the majority (~60%) of cases?

e.correcta: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is a heterogeneous group of B- and T-cell neoplasms that together make up about 60% of lymphomas, and unlike Hodgkin lymphoma's bimodal age distribution, NHL can occur across all age groups, from children through older adults, reflecting the diverse cells of origin and genetic drivers that fall under the NHL umbrella.

incorrectas.A: Hodgkin lymphoma accounts for the remaining ~40% of cases and is defined by the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells within a reactive background, along with a characteristic bimodal age distribution (young adulthood and again after age 55).
incorrectas.C: Burkitt lymphoma is a specific aggressive subtype within the NHL category (driven by a MYC translocation), not itself the broader ~60% category being described here.
incorrectas.D: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell dyscrasia, not a lymphoma at all — it involves monoclonal immunoglobulin production and lytic bone lesions, a distinct disease process from either Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

preguntas.q: Which lymphoma is a neoplastic proliferation of small CD20+ B cells that characteristically forms follicle-like nodules?

e.correcta: Follicular lymphoma arises from germinal center B cells and retains the germinal center program (expressing markers like Bcl-6 and CD10) while acquiring t(14;18)-driven BCL2 overexpression. Because the neoplastic cells still recapitulate the germinal center architecture, they form nodular, back-to-back follicles composed mainly of small cleaved centrocytes admixed with variable numbers of larger centroblasts.

incorrectas.A: Mantle cell lymphoma arises from naive B cells of the mantle zone (CD5+, with cyclin D1 overexpression from t(11;14)) and grows in a vaguely nodular but monotonous pattern that does not recapitulate true germinal center follicles the way FL does.
