It is distinguished from mechanical speech disorders because the deficit lies in generating or comprehending language, not in the physical articulation of words.

incorrectas.A: Dysarthria is a motor disorder of articulation due to weakness or incoordination of the speech muscles; language content and comprehension are intact, unlike in aphasia.
incorrectas.C: Apraxia is the inability to carry out a learned motor task despite intact strength and comprehension; when it affects speech it impairs motor planning, not the language faculty itself.
incorrectas.D: Agnosia is the inability to recognize objects, faces, or stimuli despite intact sensation, a perceptual recognition failure rather than a language deficit.

preguntas.q: What term describes a purely motor inability to speak, arising from weakness or incoordination of the muscles used for articulation?

e.correcta: Dysarthria is a motor speech disorder caused by impaired control of the muscles responsible for articulation (from CNS, cranial nerve, neuromuscular junction, or muscle pathology), producing slurred or poorly formed speech. Crucially, the language content itself is normal, distinguishing it from aphasia, in which the core language faculty is affected.

incorrectas.A: Aphasia is a higher-order cortical language deficit affecting comprehension or word generation, not the mechanical articulation of intact language.
incorrectas.C: Aphonia is the complete loss of voice, typically from a laryngeal or vocal cord problem, rather than a disorder of articulating words that can still be phonated.
incorrectas.D: Dysphagia is difficulty swallowing; although it shares neuromuscular substrates with dysarthria, it concerns bolus transit, not speech production.

preguntas.q: Broca (expressive) aphasia is characterized by what quality of speech?

o.C: Normal fluent speech with paraphasic errors

e.correcta: Broca aphasia produces nonfluent, effortful, agrammatic speech because the frontal motor speech center that assembles words into grammatical output is damaged. Patients typically manage only short, telegraphic phrases and, because comprehension is preserved, are aware of and frustrated by their difficulty.

incorrectas.A: Fluent speech is the hallmark of Wernicke and conduction aphasias, where the frontal output apparatus is intact; it is the opposite of the effortful output seen in Broca aphasia.
incorrectas.C: Fluent speech riddled with paraphasic (word-substitution) errors describes Wernicke aphasia, not Broca aphasia, where output is sparse and effortful rather than fluent.
incorrectas.D: Completely absent phonation describes mutism or aphonia; Broca patients can produce some speech, just haltingly and agrammatically.

preguntas.q: In Broca (expressive) aphasia, comprehension is typically:

e.correcta: In Broca aphasia comprehension is intact because Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe (the comprehension center) is spared; only the frontal motor speech center is damaged. This preserved understanding is exactly why these patients recognize their own errors and appear frustrated, a classic clinical clue.

incorrectas.B: Impaired comprehension is the defining feature of Wernicke aphasia, where the temporal comprehension center is destroyed; it is not the pattern seen in Broca aphasia.
incorrectas.C: Comprehension in Broca aphasia is reliably preserved rather than fluctuating; a waxing-and-waning course would suggest a metabolic or seizure-related process instead.
incorrectas.D: Comprehension of both spoken and written language is retained in Broca aphasia; there is no selective loss of reading comprehension.

preguntas.q: In Broca (expressive) aphasia, the ability to repeat phrases is:

e.correcta: Repetition is impaired in Broca aphasia because repeating a phrase requires intact motor speech output, which is precisely the function that is lost. As a rule, any aphasia involving Broca's area, Wernicke's area, or the connecting arcuate fasciculus will impair repetition, so both perisylvian centers must be spared for repetition to be preserved.

incorrectas.A: Intact repetition would point to a transcortical aphasia, where the perisylvian language loop is spared; it is not seen in classic Broca aphasia.
incorrectas.C: Echolalia (compulsive repetition) is characteristic of transcortical aphasias with a preserved repetition circuit, the opposite of the impaired repetition in Broca aphasia.
incorrectas.D: Repetition failure in Broca aphasia is global for phrases and words, not selectively limited to numbers.

preguntas.q: A stroke patient produces sparse, effortful, telegraphic speech but clearly understands spoken commands and is frustrated by his errors; repetition is impaired. Which aphasia is this?

e.correcta: The triad of nonfluent speech, intact comprehension, and impaired repetition defines Broca (expressive) aphasia, caused by a lesion of the inferior frontal gyrus in the dominant hemisphere. Because comprehension is preserved, patients understand language yet can only manage limited, often one-syllable output and characteristically appear frustrated by their inability to express themselves.

incorrectas.A: Wernicke aphasia features fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension and patients who are typically unaware of their deficit, the near-mirror image of this presentation.
incorrectas.B: Conduction aphasia spares both fluency and comprehension, with the deficit isolated to repetition; it does not produce the nonfluent, effortful output seen here.
incorrectas.D: Global aphasia impairs fluency, comprehension, and repetition together, so the preserved comprehension in this patient rules it out.

preguntas.q: Wernicke (receptive) aphasia is characterized by what quality of speech?

e.correcta: Wernicke aphasia produces fluent speech with normal rate and melody because the frontal motor output apparatus is intact; the lesion is in the temporal comprehension center. However, the fluent output lacks meaning, being filled with paraphasias and neologisms, so patients speak effortlessly but say little of sense and are usually unaware of the problem.

incorrectas.B: Nonfluent speech results from frontal (Broca) lesions; in Wernicke aphasia the frontal output region is spared, so speech remains fluent.
incorrectas.C: Effortful, telegraphic speech is the signature of Broca aphasia, the opposite of the smooth but empty output in Wernicke aphasia.
incorrectas.D: Complete mutism implies no speech output, whereas Wernicke patients characteristically produce copious fluent speech, just without meaningful content.

preguntas.q: In Wernicke (receptive) aphasia, comprehension is typically:

o.C: Intact for speech but lost for reading

e.correcta: Comprehension is impaired in Wernicke aphasia because the lesion destroys the temporal-lobe center that decodes language into meaning. As a result patients cannot understand spoken or written language and, lacking insight into their deficit, often produce confident but nonsensical fluent speech.

incorrectas.A: Intact comprehension characterizes Broca and conduction aphasias, where the temporal comprehension center is preserved; it is not seen in Wernicke aphasia.
incorrectas.C: Comprehension of both spoken and written language is impaired in Wernicke aphasia, not selectively lost for reading alone.
incorrectas.D: Comprehension is diminished, never enhanced; a language center lesion can only degrade understanding.

preguntas.q: In Wernicke (receptive) aphasia, the ability to repeat phrases is:

e.correcta: Repetition is impaired in Wernicke aphasia because meaningful repetition depends on comprehending the phrase and on an intact perisylvian language loop, both of which are disrupted. Any classic aphasia involving Wernicke's area, Broca's area, or the arcuate fasciculus connecting them will impair repetition.

incorrectas.A: Intact repetition would indicate a transcortical aphasia with a spared repetition circuit, not the classic Wernicke pattern.
incorrectas.C: Repetition failure in Wernicke aphasia is not limited to long phrases; even short items cannot be reliably repeated because comprehension itself is lost.
incorrectas.D: Selective sparing of repetition defines transcortical sensory aphasia, distinguishing it from Wernicke aphasia, in which repetition is impaired.

preguntas.q: A patient speaks fluently with normal rhythm but produces sentences full of made-up words and word substitutions, cannot follow commands, cannot repeat phrases, and seems unaware anything is wrong. Which aphasia is this?

e.correcta: Fluent speech, impaired comprehension, and impaired repetition together define Wernicke (receptive) aphasia, from a lesion of the superior temporal gyrus in the dominant hemisphere. The output is fluent but empty (paraphasias and neologisms), and because comprehension is lost the patient characteristically lacks awareness of the deficit, unlike the frustrated Broca patient.

incorrectas.A: Broca aphasia produces nonfluent, effortful speech with intact comprehension, the opposite of this patient's fluent but meaningless output.
incorrectas.C: Conduction aphasia spares comprehension; the deficit is isolated to repetition, so the impaired comprehension here excludes it.
incorrectas.D: Transcortical sensory aphasia resembles Wernicke aphasia but preserves repetition, whereas this patient cannot repeat phrases.

preguntas.q: Conduction aphasia is characterized by what quality of speech?

e.correcta: Conduction aphasia produces fluent speech because both cortical language centers (Broca and Wernicke) are intact; the lesion is confined to the arcuate fasciculus connecting them. Speech flows normally and comprehension is preserved, so the only prominent deficit is a striking inability to repeat.

incorrectas.A: Nonfluent speech reflects a frontal (Broca) lesion; in conduction aphasia the frontal output center is spared, leaving speech fluent.
incorrectas.C: Effortful, agrammatic speech is the Broca pattern, whereas conduction aphasia leaves output fluent and grammatically normal.
incorrectas.D: Mutism implies no speech output; conduction patients speak fluently, merely failing at repetition.

preguntas.q: In conduction aphasia, comprehension is typically:

e.correcta: Comprehension is intact in conduction aphasia because Wernicke's area, the temporal comprehension center, is undamaged; the lesion lies only in the arcuate fasciculus linking the two language centers. Thus patients understand language and speak fluently, and the isolated failure of repetition is the diagnostic hallmark.

incorrectas.B: Impaired comprehension indicates a Wernicke's area lesion; in conduction aphasia that region is spared, so understanding is preserved.
incorrectas.C: Comprehension of both spoken and written language is preserved in conduction aphasia; there is no selective loss for reading.
incorrectas.D: Comprehension is fully retained, not absent; the deficit is limited to repetition, not understanding.

preguntas.q: In conduction aphasia, the ability to repeat phrases is:

e.correcta: Repetition is impaired in conduction aphasia and is in fact its defining feature, because the arcuate fasciculus that relays decoded language from Wernicke's area to Broca's area for output is severed. Comprehension and fluency remain normal, so a patient who understands and speaks well yet cannot repeat a spoken phrase points squarely to a conduction lesion.

incorrectas.A: Intact repetition would exclude conduction aphasia entirely, since impaired repetition is its cardinal sign.
incorrectas.C: Repetition cannot be enhanced by an arcuate fasciculus lesion; disconnection of the two centers only degrades the ability to repeat.
incorrectas.D: Repetition failure in conduction aphasia applies broadly, not just to unfamiliar phrases; even familiar items are hard to repeat.

preguntas.q: A patient has fluent speech and intact comprehension but is strikingly unable to repeat phrases. Which type of aphasia does this describe?

e.correcta: Fluent speech, intact comprehension, and isolated impairment of repetition define conduction aphasia, caused by damage to the arcuate fasciculus connecting Wernicke's and Broca's areas. Because both cortical centers are spared, the patient understands and produces language normally but cannot route the information between them to repeat what was heard.

incorrectas.A: Broca aphasia is nonfluent with impaired repetition; the preserved fluency here rules it out.
incorrectas.B: Wernicke aphasia impairs comprehension, whereas this patient understands language normally, excluding it.
incorrectas.D: Global aphasia impairs fluency, comprehension, and repetition together, so the retained fluency and comprehension exclude it.

preguntas.q: Damage to which white-matter structure, the large fiber bundle connecting Broca's area with Wernicke's area, causes conduction aphasia?

e.correcta: The arcuate fasciculus is the association tract that links Wernicke's area to Broca's area, carrying decoded language forward for spoken output and thereby enabling repetition. When it is lesioned, the two intact cortical centers are disconnected, producing conduction aphasia with fluent speech, preserved comprehension, and impaired repetition.

incorrectas.B: The corpus callosum connects the two cerebral hemispheres; its section causes disconnection syndromes but not the specific repetition deficit of conduction aphasia.
incorrectas.C: The internal capsule carries motor and sensory projection fibers between cortex and brainstem/spinal cord; lacunar lesions there cause pure motor or sensory strokes, not conduction aphasia.
incorrectas.D: The broader superior longitudinal fasciculus system serves many parietal-frontal connections, but it is the arcuate component specifically bridging the two language centers whose lesion produces conduction aphasia.

preguntas.q: Global aphasia is characterized by what quality of speech?

o.D: Normal speech with isolated naming difficulty

e.correcta: Global aphasia is nonfluent because it results from a large dominant-hemisphere lesion (typically a proximal MCA occlusion) that destroys both Broca's and Wernicke's areas along with the connecting tracts. With the motor speech center wiped out, output is sparse and effortful, and comprehension and repetition are impaired as well, making it the most severe aphasia.

incorrectas.A: Fluent speech requires an intact frontal Broca's area, which is destroyed in global aphasia, so output is nonfluent.
incorrectas.C: Fluent speech with preserved repetition describes a transcortical sensory aphasia, the opposite extreme from the sweeping deficits of global aphasia.
incorrectas.D: Isolated naming difficulty with otherwise normal speech describes anomic aphasia, the mildest form, not the severe nonfluent picture of global aphasia.

preguntas.q: In global aphasia, comprehension is typically:

o.C: Intact for spoken but not written language

e.correcta: Comprehension is impaired in global aphasia because the extensive dominant-hemisphere lesion destroys Wernicke's comprehension center along with Broca's area and their connections. All major language functions (fluency, comprehension, and repetition) are lost together, reflecting the large territory of damage and carrying a poor prognosis for recovery.

incorrectas.A: Intact comprehension would require sparing of Wernicke's area, which is destroyed in global aphasia; preserved comprehension instead points toward Broca or conduction aphasia.
incorrectas.C: Both spoken and written comprehension are impaired in global aphasia; there is no selective sparing of one modality.
incorrectas.D: Global aphasia does not selectively preserve emotional or automatic speech comprehension; the deficit spans all language functions.

preguntas.q: In global aphasia, what is the status of the patient's ability to repeat words and phrases?

e.correcta: Global aphasia is the most severe aphasia and results from a large dominant-hemisphere lesion destroying Broca's area, Wernicke's area, AND the arcuate fasciculus connecting them. Because all three core language regions are damaged, every language function fails: speech is nonfluent, comprehension is impaired, and repetition is impaired. Repetition specifically requires an intact Broca-arcuate fasciculus-Wernicke loop, so with all of it destroyed the patient cannot repeat.

incorrectas.A: Intact repetition is the hallmark of the transcortical aphasias, where the perisylvian repetition loop (Broca, Wernicke, arcuate fasciculus) is spared and only the surrounding watershed cortex is injured; global aphasia by definition destroys that loop.
incorrectas.C: Category-selective naming deficits (e.g., loss of nouns) point to focal anomic or degenerative processes, not the broad language collapse of global aphasia, in which all output including repetition is lost.
incorrectas.D: Fluent output with paraphasic errors but preserved repetition describes anomic or conduction-related pictures, not global aphasia, which produces sparse nonfluent speech and failed repetition.

preguntas.q: A patient has nonfluent speech, impaired comprehension, and impaired repetition following a large left-hemisphere stroke. Which type of aphasia is this?

e.correcta: The combination of nonfluent speech, impaired comprehension, AND impaired repetition defines global aphasia, which results from a large lesion (typically a proximal MCA occlusion) destroying Broca's area, Wernicke's area, and the arcuate fasciculus together. Because every language node is lost, all three functions fail simultaneously. It is the only classic aphasia in which fluency, comprehension, and repetition are all impaired.

incorrectas.A: Broca (expressive) aphasia is nonfluent with impaired repetition, but comprehension is relatively PRESERVED because Wernicke's area is intact; the impaired comprehension here excludes it.
incorrectas.B: Wernicke (receptive) aphasia has impaired comprehension and repetition, but speech is FLUENT (paraphasic, nonsensical); the nonfluent output here rules it out.
incorrectas.D: Conduction aphasia (arcuate fasciculus lesion) has fluent speech and intact comprehension with disproportionately impaired repetition, so it fails to match the nonfluent, poorly comprehending picture described.

preguntas.q: Damage to Broca's area, Wernicke's area, and the arcuate fasciculus simultaneously produces which aphasia?

e.correcta: Global aphasia occurs when a single large lesion knocks out all three perisylvian language components at once: Broca's area (production), Wernicke's area (comprehension), and the arcuate fasciculus (the fiber tract linking them). This is why fluency, comprehension, and repetition are all lost. Such lesions usually reflect a large MCA-territory infarct and often carry contralateral hemiplegia because adjacent motor cortex is involved.

incorrectas.B: Transcortical mixed aphasia injures the watershed cortex AROUND Broca, Wernicke, and the arcuate fasciculus while sparing those structures themselves, so repetition is preserved rather than lost; global aphasia destroys the structures directly.
incorrectas.C: Conduction aphasia is a selective lesion of the arcuate fasciculus alone, leaving Broca and Wernicke areas intact, so fluency and comprehension are preserved and only repetition suffers.
incorrectas.D: Transcortical motor aphasia spares Broca's area and involves cortex just anterior/superior to it, producing nonfluent speech with intact comprehension and repetition, not the total language loss of global aphasia.

preguntas.q: What is the character of speech output in transcortical motor aphasia?

o.D: Fluent with intact grammar but empty content

e.correcta: Transcortical motor aphasia is a nonfluent aphasia because the lesion sits in the watershed cortex just anterior and superior to Broca's area, disconnecting it from the supplementary motor area that initiates speech. Broca's area itself is spared, so repetition remains intact, but spontaneous speech initiation is markedly reduced, giving sparse, effortful, nonfluent output. The key teaching point is nonfluent speech WITH preserved repetition.

incorrectas.A: Fluent output with normal prosody characterizes the sensory-type aphasias (Wernicke, transcortical sensory), where speech production drive is intact; transcortical motor aphasia specifically impairs speech initiation.
incorrectas.C: Fluent speech littered with neologisms is the signature of Wernicke aphasia, reflecting damage to the comprehension cortex, not the reduced initiation seen when the pre-motor watershed zone is injured.
incorrectas.D: Fluent but empty (semantically hollow) speech points to transcortical sensory or anomic aphasia; transcortical motor aphasia produces reduced, halting, nonfluent output rather than fluent empty speech.

preguntas.q: In transcortical motor aphasia, what happens to language comprehension?

e.correcta: Comprehension is intact in transcortical motor aphasia because Wernicke's area and the temporal comprehension cortex lie outside the lesion, which is confined to the frontal watershed zone near (but not including) Broca's area. The deficit is one of speech INITIATION, not understanding. This mirrors Broca aphasia in its nonfluency but is distinguished by preserved repetition due to sparing of the perisylvian language loop.

incorrectas.B: Severely impaired comprehension indicates a Wernicke-area or transcortical sensory lesion in the temporal lobe; transcortical motor aphasia leaves the comprehension cortex untouched.
incorrectas.C: A selective written-comprehension deficit describes alexia, a disconnection of visual input from language cortex, which is a different lesion from the frontal watershed injury of transcortical motor aphasia.
incorrectas.D: Fluctuating comprehension is not a defining feature of any classic aphasia and would suggest a metabolic or attentional process; transcortical motor aphasia has consistently intact comprehension.

preguntas.q: What is the status of repetition in transcortical motor aphasia?

o.C: Repetition intact only for single words

e.correcta: Repetition is intact in ALL transcortical aphasias, and transcortical motor is no exception, because the perisylvian repetition loop (Broca's area, arcuate fasciculus, Wernicke's area) is spared and only the surrounding watershed cortex is damaged. Preserved repetition despite nonfluent spontaneous speech is precisely what separates transcortical motor aphasia from Broca aphasia. Patients may even show echolalia, involuntarily repeating what they hear.

incorrectas.A: Impaired repetition occurs when the repetition loop itself is damaged, as in Broca, Wernicke, conduction, or global aphasia; the transcortical aphasias are defined by the OPPOSITE, preserved repetition.
incorrectas.C: Repetition in transcortical motor aphasia is not limited to single words; the spared perisylvian arc allows repetition of phrases and sentences as well.
incorrectas.D: Transcortical motor aphasia is nonfluent, not fluent, and its repetition is preserved rather than failing, so this option contradicts both features of the syndrome.

preguntas.q: A patient has nonfluent speech, intact comprehension, and intact repetition. Which aphasia does this describe?

e.correcta: Nonfluent speech with intact comprehension AND intact repetition is the defining triad of transcortical motor aphasia. The lesion sits in the frontal watershed cortex near Broca's area, impairing speech initiation while sparing the perisylvian loop that permits repetition and the temporal cortex that permits comprehension. The preserved repetition is the single feature that distinguishes it from Broca aphasia.

incorrectas.A: Broca aphasia shares the nonfluent speech and intact comprehension, but repetition is IMPAIRED because Broca's area and the arcuate fasciculus are directly damaged; the intact repetition here points away from it.
incorrectas.B: Global aphasia would show impaired comprehension and impaired repetition in addition to nonfluent speech, since all language regions are destroyed; that does not match the preserved functions described.
incorrectas.D: Transcortical sensory aphasia is FLUENT with impaired comprehension (repetition intact); the nonfluent, well-comprehending profile here is the opposite pattern.

preguntas.q: Damage to the watershed cortex surrounding Broca's area, with Broca's area itself spared, produces which aphasia?

e.correcta: Transcortical motor aphasia arises from injury to the frontal watershed cortex just anterior/superior to Broca's area (often from anterior-MCA/ACA borderzone hypoperfusion), while Broca's area itself is preserved. Because Broca's area and the arcuate fasciculus stay intact, repetition is retained even though spontaneous, self-generated speech is nonfluent. The sparing of Broca's area is exactly why repetition survives.

incorrectas.A: Broca aphasia requires damage to Broca's area ITSELF (not just the surrounding cortex), which is why repetition is lost; this stem explicitly spares Broca's area.
incorrectas.C: Conduction aphasia is caused by a lesion of the arcuate fasciculus, producing fluent speech with impaired repetition, not the nonfluent output of a frontal watershed lesion.
incorrectas.D: Transcortical mixed aphasia requires watershed damage around BOTH Broca and Wernicke areas plus the arcuate fasciculus, giving impaired comprehension as well; damage confined near Broca alone gives the motor subtype.

preguntas.q: What is the character of speech in transcortical sensory aphasia?

e.correcta: Transcortical sensory aphasia is a FLUENT aphasia because the lesion lies in the posterior watershed cortex around Wernicke's area, leaving the speech-production apparatus in the frontal lobe untouched. Output flows freely but is semantically empty because comprehension is impaired, much like Wernicke aphasia; the crucial difference is that repetition is preserved. Think of it as a Wernicke-type picture with intact repetition.

incorrectas.B: Nonfluent, effortful speech reflects frontal (Broca or transcortical motor) lesions that impair speech production; transcortical sensory aphasia spares that region, so speech remains fluent.
incorrectas.C: Muteness implies severe damage to speech-initiation networks (as in acute global or severe transcortical motor aphasia), not the posterior comprehension-zone lesion of the sensory subtype.
incorrectas.D: Telegraphic, agrammatic output is the classic description of Broca aphasia; transcortical sensory speech is grammatically fluent though semantically hollow.

preguntas.q: What happens to comprehension in transcortical sensory aphasia?

o.C: Impaired only for spoken but not written language

e.correcta: Comprehension is impaired in transcortical sensory aphasia because the lesion involves the posterior watershed cortex surrounding Wernicke's area, disconnecting word forms from their meanings. The patient produces fluent but empty speech and cannot understand language, closely resembling Wernicke aphasia. The one distinguishing feature is that repetition remains intact because Wernicke's area and the arcuate fasciculus themselves are spared.

incorrectas.A: Intact comprehension characterizes the motor-type aphasias (Broca, transcortical motor), where the temporal comprehension cortex is undamaged; the sensory subtype specifically impairs understanding.
incorrectas.C: A deficit selective for spoken versus written input describes pure word deafness or alexia, distinct disconnection syndromes, not the general comprehension failure of transcortical sensory aphasia.
incorrectas.D: Comprehension of complex commands is typically the FIRST to fail, not the last to be preserved; transcortical sensory aphasia broadly impairs comprehension.

preguntas.q: What is the status of repetition in transcortical sensory aphasia?

e.correcta: Repetition is intact in transcortical sensory aphasia, which is the hallmark that separates it from Wernicke aphasia. The lesion spares Wernicke's area and the arcuate fasciculus (the perisylvian repetition loop) and instead damages the surrounding posterior watershed cortex, so patients can echo back words and phrases even though they cannot understand them. This preserved-repetition-with-poor-comprehension pattern is the defining clue.

incorrectas.A: Impaired repetition would indicate direct damage to the perisylvian loop, as in Wernicke, conduction, or global aphasia; the transcortical aphasias are precisely those in which repetition is spared.
incorrectas.C: Repetition in transcortical sensory aphasia is preserved for phrases and sentences too, not just single words, because the intact loop can relay full utterances.
incorrectas.D: Paraphasic substitutions during repetition point to conduction aphasia (arcuate fasciculus damage); in the transcortical sensory subtype repetition is faithfully preserved.

preguntas.q: A patient has fluent speech, impaired comprehension, and intact repetition. Which aphasia is this?

e.correcta: Fluent speech with impaired comprehension but INTACT repetition defines transcortical sensory aphasia. The posterior watershed lesion spares Wernicke's area and the arcuate fasciculus (so repetition works) while disconnecting the surrounding cortex needed to attach meaning to words (so comprehension fails). The intact repetition is what separates it from Wernicke aphasia, which shares the fluency and comprehension deficit.

incorrectas.A: Wernicke aphasia matches the fluent speech and impaired comprehension but has IMPAIRED repetition because Wernicke's area and the arcuate fasciculus are directly damaged; the preserved repetition here excludes it.
incorrectas.B: Conduction aphasia has fluent speech but intact comprehension with disproportionately impaired repetition, the reverse of the comprehension/repetition pattern described.
incorrectas.D: Transcortical motor aphasia is nonfluent with intact comprehension; the fluent, poorly comprehending profile here is the opposite.

preguntas.q: Damage to the watershed cortex around Wernicke's area, with Wernicke's area itself spared, produces which aphasia?

e.correcta: Transcortical sensory aphasia results from injury to the posterior temporo-parietal watershed cortex encircling Wernicke's area, while Wernicke's area itself is preserved. Because Wernicke's area and the arcuate fasciculus survive, the repetition loop is intact, but the surrounding cortex that links words to meaning is lost, so comprehension fails despite fluent speech. Sparing of Wernicke's area is exactly why repetition is retained.

incorrectas.A: Wernicke aphasia requires damage to Wernicke's area ITSELF, which abolishes repetition; this stem explicitly spares Wernicke's area, so repetition is preserved.
incorrectas.C: Conduction aphasia is due to an arcuate fasciculus lesion, producing intact comprehension with impaired repetition, not the impaired comprehension of a posterior watershed lesion.
incorrectas.D: Anomic aphasia is a milder, focal naming deficit with otherwise preserved fluency, comprehension, and repetition, not the broad comprehension loss produced by peri-Wernicke watershed injury.

preguntas.q: What is the character of speech in transcortical mixed aphasia?

e.correcta: Transcortical mixed aphasia is nonfluent because the lesion encompasses the watershed cortex around BOTH Broca's and Wernicke's areas, so speech initiation (a frontal function) is impaired just as in transcortical motor aphasia. It essentially combines the transcortical motor and sensory syndromes: nonfluent, poorly comprehending, but with strikingly intact repetition because the perisylvian loop is islanded and spared. Patients often only echo (echolalia).

incorrectas.A: Fluent output would require an intact frontal speech-initiation zone; transcortical mixed aphasia damages the peri-Broca watershed cortex, rendering speech nonfluent.
incorrectas.C: Neologistic fluent speech is the signature of Wernicke aphasia; the mixed transcortical picture is dominated by sparse, nonfluent, often echolalic output.
incorrectas.D: Circumlocutory fluent speech (talking around words) suggests anomic aphasia; it does not fit the nonfluent, initiation-poor output of transcortical mixed aphasia.

preguntas.q: What happens to comprehension in transcortical mixed aphasia?

e.correcta: Comprehension is impaired in transcortical mixed aphasia because the lesion involves the posterior watershed cortex around Wernicke's area in addition to the frontal watershed zone. This is why the syndrome resembles global aphasia in having nonfluent speech AND impaired comprehension, yet is distinguished by one preserved function: repetition, because the perisylvian core is spared. It is essentially a global aphasia with intact repetition.

incorrectas.A: Intact comprehension would occur if only the frontal watershed near Broca were involved (transcortical motor aphasia); the mixed subtype additionally damages the peri-Wernicke cortex, impairing comprehension.
incorrectas.C: Comprehension in transcortical mixed aphasia is broadly impaired, not selectively preserved for single words; even simple understanding is compromised.
incorrectas.D: A deficit limited to written material describes alexia, a disconnection syndrome, not the generalized comprehension failure caused by widespread watershed injury.

preguntas.q: What is the status of repetition in transcortical mixed aphasia?

o.D: Repetition abolished along with all output

e.correcta: Repetition is intact in transcortical mixed aphasia, and this is the single feature that separates it from global aphasia despite otherwise identical nonfluent speech and impaired comprehension. The widespread watershed lesion encircles but spares the perisylvian language core (Broca, arcuate fasciculus, Wernicke), leaving that isolated 'island of language' able to repeat. These patients often produce little except echolalic repetition of what they hear.

incorrectas.A: Impaired repetition would make this global aphasia, in which the perisylvian core is destroyed; the defining trait of the mixed transcortical syndrome is that repetition survives.
incorrectas.C: Repetition in transcortical mixed aphasia occurs spontaneously and even compulsively (echolalia), not only with external cueing.
incorrectas.D: Although spontaneous propositional speech is minimal, repetition specifically remains preserved, so it is not abolished along with other output.

preguntas.q: A patient has nonfluent speech, impaired comprehension, and intact repetition. Which aphasia does this represent?

e.correcta: Nonfluent speech and impaired comprehension WITH intact repetition define transcortical mixed aphasia. Widespread borderzone (watershed) injury surrounds the perisylvian language core but spares it, so both frontal (production) and temporal (comprehension) watershed functions fail while the islanded repetition loop keeps working. It looks like global aphasia except that repetition is preserved.

incorrectas.A: Global aphasia has the same nonfluent speech and impaired comprehension but ALSO impaired repetition because the perisylvian core is destroyed; the intact repetition here rules it out.
incorrectas.C: Transcortical motor aphasia is nonfluent with intact comprehension; the impaired comprehension described exceeds that syndrome, indicating additional peri-Wernicke involvement.
incorrectas.D: Wernicke aphasia is fluent with impaired comprehension and impaired repetition; both the nonfluency and preserved repetition here contradict it.

preguntas.q: Ischemic injury to the watershed cortex surrounding (but not including) Broca's area, Wernicke's area, and the arcuate fasciculus produces which aphasia?

e.correcta: Transcortical mixed aphasia results from widespread watershed (borderzone) infarction encircling Broca's area, Wernicke's area, and the arcuate fasciculus while leaving that perisylvian core intact, an isolation-of-the-speech-area picture. Classic causes are severe hypotension or bilateral carotid disease producing borderzone hypoperfusion. Because the core is spared, repetition (often only echolalia) survives amid otherwise nonfluent, poorly comprehended language.

incorrectas.A: Global aphasia destroys Broca, Wernicke, and the arcuate fasciculus THEMSELVES, abolishing repetition; the mixed transcortical lesion spares those structures, preserving repetition.
incorrectas.C: Conduction aphasia is a focal arcuate fasciculus lesion causing fluent speech with impaired repetition, not the broad watershed isolation pattern described.
incorrectas.D: Transcortical sensory aphasia is confined to the peri-Wernicke watershed and produces fluent speech; involvement of the peri-Broca zone as well makes this the nonfluent mixed subtype.

preguntas.q: A patient develops agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and left-right disorientation after a dominant parietal lobe stroke. What is this syndrome called?

e.correcta: Gerstmann syndrome is the classic tetrad of agraphia (inability to write), acalculia (inability to do arithmetic), finger agnosia (inability to identify individual fingers), and left-right disorientation, produced by a lesion of the DOMINANT (usually left) inferior parietal lobule near the angular gyrus. The angular gyrus integrates the cross-modal associations underlying these skills, which is why they cluster together. Recognizing the tetrad localizes the lesion to the dominant parietal cortex.

incorrectas.B: Balint syndrome (bilateral parieto-occipital lesions) is a triad of optic ataxia, oculomotor apraxia, and simultanagnosia, a visuospatial syndrome unrelated to the writing/calculation/finger deficits of Gerstmann.
incorrectas.C: Anton syndrome is cortical blindness with denial of blindness from bilateral occipital (visual cortex) damage, not a dominant-parietal syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker is a rare inherited prion disease causing progressive ataxia and dementia; despite the shared eponym it is entirely distinct from the parietal Gerstmann syndrome.

preguntas.q: An anterior-circulation stroke causes paralysis and sensory loss of the face and upper limb accompanied by cortical signs such as aphasia and neglect. Which vessel is occluded?

e.correcta: A middle cerebral artery (MCA) stroke produces contralateral face and upper-limb weakness/sensory loss because it supplies the lateral cortex where the face and arm are represented on the motor and sensory homunculus. Crucially, because the MCA feeds the cortical SURFACE, it also causes cortical signs: aphasia (if dominant hemisphere) and hemineglect (if nondominant). The presence of cortical signs is what flags a cortical (MCA) rather than a deep lacunar stroke.

incorrectas.A: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial cortex where the LOWER limb is represented, so its stroke causes contralateral leg weakness/sensory loss, not a face-and-arm pattern.
incorrectas.C: The lenticulostriate arteries supply deep subcortical structures (internal capsule, basal ganglia) and cause a pure motor lacunar stroke of the face and arm WITHOUT cortical signs; the aphasia/neglect here indicates cortical involvement.
incorrectas.D: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital cortex, so its occlusion produces contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, not a face-and-arm sensorimotor deficit.

preguntas.q: An anterior-circulation stroke causes paralysis and sensory loss of the face and upper limb WITHOUT any cortical signs such as aphasia or neglect. Which vessel is occluded?

e.correcta: The lenticulostriate arteries are small deep penetrating branches of the MCA that supply the internal capsule and basal ganglia. Occlusion (classically from chronic hypertension causing lipohyalinosis) produces a lacunar pure motor or sensorimotor stroke of the contralateral face and arm, but because the injury is deep and subcortical it lacks cortical signs like aphasia or neglect. The ABSENCE of cortical signs is the clue that distinguishes a lacunar lenticulostriate stroke from a cortical MCA stroke.

incorrectas.A: A middle cerebral artery stroke damages the cortical surface, so it produces the SAME face/arm deficit but WITH cortical signs (aphasia, neglect); the absence of those signs points deeper.
incorrectas.C: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial motor/sensory cortex for the lower limb, producing contralateral leg weakness, not a face-and-arm pattern.
incorrectas.D: The ophthalmic artery supplies the retina; its occlusion causes monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax), not a sensorimotor deficit of the face and limb.

preguntas.q: Which system is a collection of neural structures involved in emotion, long-term memory, olfaction, behavior modulation, and autonomic function?

e.correcta: The limbic system is the group of interconnected structures (hippocampus, amygdala, fornix, mammillary bodies, cingulate gyrus, and related areas) that governs emotion, long-term memory formation, olfaction, and modulation of behavior and autonomic output. A useful memory aid is the 'famous 5 F's': feeding, fleeing, fighting, feeling, and sex, capturing its role in primal drives and 'animal instincts.' Its close tie to olfaction reflects its evolutionary origins.

incorrectas.A: The reticular activating system, in the brainstem, controls arousal, wakefulness, and the sleep-wake cycle, not the emotional/memory/olfactory functions attributed to the limbic system.
incorrectas.C: The extrapyramidal system (basal ganglia and connections) modulates involuntary movement and motor tone; it is a motor-control network, not an emotion-and-memory system.
incorrectas.D: The dorsal column system is a sensory pathway carrying fine touch, vibration, and proprioception to the cortex, unrelated to emotion, memory, or autonomic regulation.

preguntas.q: The hippocampus, amygdala, fornix, mammillary bodies, and cingulate gyrus are all components of which system?

e.correcta: These structures form the core of the limbic system: the hippocampus (memory encoding), amygdala (fear and emotion), cingulate gyrus (emotional processing), and the mammillary bodies linked to the hippocampus via the fornix. The fornix is the bundle of axons arising from the hippocampal subiculum that projects to the mammillary bodies, a key relay in the Papez circuit for memory. Together they subserve emotion, memory, and autonomic drive.

incorrectas.A: The basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra) are a motor-modulating network; none of the listed limbic structures belong to them.
incorrectas.C: Cerebellar circuitry (Purkinje cells, deep cerebellar nuclei, peduncles) coordinates movement and balance and does not include the hippocampus, amygdala, or cingulate gyrus.
incorrectas.D: While the thalamus interconnects with limbic structures, the thalamocortical relay system refers to sensory/motor relay nuclei projecting to cortex, not this specific set of emotion-and-memory structures.

preguntas.q: Fracture of which structure is the classic cause of post-traumatic olfactory deficits (anosmia)?

o.A: Cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone
o.B: Petrous portion of the temporal bone
o.C: Sella turcica of the sphenoid bone
o.D: Foramen magnum of the occipital bone

e.correcta: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone is perforated by the olfactory nerve (CN I) fibers passing from the nasal epithelium to the olfactory bulb. A head injury that fractures this thin plate shears those delicate fila olfactoria, causing anosmia (loss of smell). This is why anosmia is a classic clue to anterior skull-base (cribriform) trauma.

incorrectas.B: The petrous temporal bone houses the inner ear and CN VII/VIII; its fracture causes hearing loss, vertigo, or facial palsy, not olfactory loss.
incorrectas.C: The sella turcica cradles the pituitary gland; injury there affects endocrine function or the optic chiasm, not the olfactory nerve.
incorrectas.D: The foramen magnum transmits the spinal cord/brainstem junction and vertebral arteries; it has no relation to the olfactory pathway.

preguntas.q: Besides anosmia, cribriform plate fractures classically cause leakage of what fluid from the nose?

e.correcta: The olfactory bulb is an outgrowth of the central nervous system and is therefore covered by meninges (dura/arachnoid) and surrounded by CSF. A cribriform plate fracture can tear these meningeal coverings, creating a communication between the subarachnoid space and the nasal cavity, so CSF leaks out as CSF rhinorrhea. This carries a real risk of ascending meningitis and can be confirmed by testing the fluid for beta-2 transferrin.

incorrectas.B: Purulent nasal discharge indicates infectious sinusitis, not a traumatic dural tear; it lacks the CSF markers and does not signal a skull-base fracture.
incorrectas.C: Aqueous humor is intraocular fluid of the anterior chamber of the eye and has no anatomic route to the nasal cavity via the cribriform plate.
incorrectas.D: Perilymph is inner-ear fluid; its leakage (perilymph fistula) relates to temporal bone/otic capsule injury, not to the anterior skull base.

preguntas.q: Which structure of the limbic system is primarily responsible for the formation of new declarative (learning and) memories?

e.correcta: The hippocampus is the limbic structure essential for consolidating short-term experience into long-term declarative memory, and bilateral hippocampal damage produces profound anterograde amnesia. Synaptic plasticity here (long-term potentiation) underlies memory formation, and the retrograde messenger nitric oxide is thought to help strengthen these new synaptic connections.

incorrectas.A: The amygdala assigns emotional significance (especially fear) to stimuli and modulates the emotional coloring of memories, but it is not the site where the memory trace itself is encoded and consolidated.
incorrectas.C: The mammillary bodies are a relay in the Papez circuit (via the fornix), and their degeneration in thiamine deficiency causes Korsakoff amnesia, but memory encoding itself is a hippocampal function rather than a mammillary one.
incorrectas.D: The cingulate gyrus participates in emotional processing, motivation, and integrating behavior with emotion, but it does not carry out the encoding of new declarative memories the way the hippocampus does.

preguntas.q: Which part of the limbic system is responsible for attaching emotional significance, particularly fear, to a sensory stimulus?

e.correcta: The amygdala is the limbic center that evaluates the emotional salience of stimuli and generates fear and aggression responses, linking sensory input to autonomic and behavioral output. Bilateral amygdala destruction produces the placidity and loss of fear seen in Kluver-Bucy syndrome, underscoring its role in emotional tagging.

incorrectas.A: The hippocampus encodes and consolidates new declarative memories, so it stores the factual content of an experience rather than assigning the emotional weight that the amygdala provides.
incorrectas.B: The mammillary bodies serve as a memory relay in the Papez circuit and are damaged in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome; they are not the structure that appraises the emotional meaning of a stimulus.
incorrectas.D: The nucleus accumbens is central to reward and reinforcement (the mesolimbic dopamine pathway), which concerns pleasure and motivation rather than the fear-based emotional tagging carried out by the amygdala.

preguntas.q: A patient develops disinhibited behavior including hyperphagia, hypersexuality, and hyperorality after bilateral lesions of the anterior temporal lobes. Which syndrome does this describe?

e.correcta: Kluver-Bucy syndrome results from bilateral destruction of the amygdalae, usually in the anterior temporal lobes, and classically presents with disinhibition, hyperphagia, hypersexuality, hyperorality, and docility. A frequent cause is HSV-1 encephalitis, which has a predilection for the temporal lobes.

incorrectas.B: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome results from thiamine deficiency damaging the mammillary bodies and thalamus, producing confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confabulatory amnesia rather than the hyperoral/hypersexual disinhibition of amygdala loss.
incorrectas.C: Frontotemporal dementia causes progressive behavioral change and disinhibition, but it is a slowly progressive degenerative disease with Pick bodies rather than the acute amygdala-lesion picture defined by hyperphagia, hypersexuality, and hyperorality.
incorrectas.D: Gerstmann syndrome results from a dominant parietal (angular gyrus) lesion and consists of agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and left-right disorientation, which is unrelated to the temporal-lobe behavioral triad described.

preguntas.q: In a chronically malnourished, alcohol-dependent patient, administering which of the following without first replacing thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy?

e.correcta: Thiamine (B1) is an essential cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase, all needed for glucose metabolism. Giving a glucose load to a thiamine-deficient patient forces these enzymes to work and consumes the last remaining thiamine, precipitating or worsening Wernicke encephalopathy, so thiamine must be given before or with glucose.

incorrectas.B: Magnesium is actually a required cofactor for thiamine-dependent reactions, and hypomagnesemia can blunt the response to thiamine repletion; magnesium administration does not itself trigger Wernicke encephalopathy.
incorrectas.C: Folate deficiency is common in alcoholics and causes megaloblastic anemia, but replacing folate does not drive the thiamine-dependent metabolic pathways that precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.
incorrectas.D: Isotonic saline restores volume and electrolytes without imposing a carbohydrate load on thiamine-dependent enzymes, so it does not precipitate acute Wernicke encephalopathy the way a glucose infusion can.

preguntas.q: Meningitis is defined pathologically as inflammation of which of the following?

e.correcta: Meningitis refers to inflammation of the leptomeninges, which comprise the pia mater and arachnoid mater (leptos = thin/light) and the CSF-filled subarachnoid space between them. Because the pathogen and inflammatory cells reside in this space, sampling CSF by lumbar puncture is the diagnostic test.

incorrectas.A: The dura mater is the tough outer pachymeninx; its involvement is termed pachymeningitis and is uncommon, whereas the clinical entity of meningitis specifically involves the pia-arachnoid layer.
incorrectas.B: Inflammation of the brain parenchyma itself is encephalitis, which produces altered mental status and focal deficits rather than the meningeal signs that define meningitis.
incorrectas.D: The choroid plexus produces CSF and can be a route of pathogen entry, but inflammation confined to it (choroid plexitis/ventriculitis) is not the definition of meningitis, which centers on the subarachnoid space.

preguntas.q: The pia mater and arachnoid mater are together referred to by which term?

e.correcta: The pia and arachnoid are collectively the leptomeninges (leptos = thin), the delicate inner coverings that enclose the CSF-containing subarachnoid space. This is the compartment inflamed in meningitis and sampled during lumbar puncture.

incorrectas.A: Pachymeninx (thick meninx) is the term for the dura mater alone, the tough outermost covering, and is contrasted with the thin leptomeninges rather than being synonymous with them.
incorrectas.C: The tela choroidea is a fold of pia mater and ependyma that gives rise to the choroid plexus in the ventricles; it is a specialized structure, not the general name for the pia-arachnoid pair.
incorrectas.D: The dural venous sinuses are venous channels located between layers of dura that drain cerebral blood; they are part of the dura, not the combined pia-arachnoid leptomeninges.

preguntas.q: A 5-day-old neonate presents with fever, poor feeding, and a bulging fontanelle. Which organism is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in this age group?

e.correcta: Group B streptococcus (S. agalactiae) is the leading cause of neonatal meningitis, acquired during passage through a colonized birth canal, which is why intrapartum screening and penicillin prophylaxis are standard. E. coli and Listeria monocytogenes round out the classic neonatal triad.

incorrectas.A: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of meningitis in adults and the elderly, but neonates have not yet developed the antibody responses and are instead colonized peripartum by vaginal flora such as GBS.
incorrectas.B: Neisseria meningitidis typically causes meningitis in adolescents and young adults living in close quarters, not neonates, whose infections reflect vertically transmitted organisms.
incorrectas.D: Haemophilus influenzae type B was historically a major cause in unvaccinated infants and young children, but it is uncommon in the immediate neonatal period and has largely been eliminated by the Hib vaccine.

preguntas.q: An 18-year-old college freshman living in a dormitory develops fever, headache, neck stiffness, and a petechial rash. Which organism is the most common cause of meningitis in this age group?

e.correcta: Neisseria meningitidis is the classic cause of meningitis in teenagers and young adults, especially in crowded settings such as dormitories and military barracks. Its polysaccharide capsule allows it to evade alternative-pathway complement and survive in the bloodstream, and it uses pili to breach the blood-brain barrier; the associated meningococcemia produces the petechial/purpuric rash.

incorrectas.B: Group B streptococcus is the predominant neonatal pathogen acquired at birth, not the organism responsible for meningitis in an otherwise healthy adolescent.
incorrectas.C: Listeria monocytogenes causes meningitis in neonates, the elderly, pregnant women, and the immunocompromised, but it is not the typical cause in a healthy teenager.
incorrectas.D: Cryptococcus neoformans causes fungal meningitis chiefly in immunocompromised hosts such as AIDS patients, and would not be expected in an immunocompetent college student with a petechial rash.

preguntas.q: Which organism is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in adults and the elderly?

e.correcta: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults and the elderly. It is a lancet-shaped, alpha-hemolytic, optochin-sensitive diplococcus whose polysaccharide capsule is its major virulence factor, and asplenic patients are at particularly high risk.

incorrectas.A: Neisseria meningitidis predominates in adolescents and young adults in crowded living conditions, and although it can affect adults, it is not the single most common adult cause overall.
incorrectas.C: Haemophilus influenzae type B is associated with meningitis in unvaccinated young children, not with the adult and elderly population where pneumococcus dominates.
incorrectas.D: Group B streptococcus is the leading neonatal pathogen and can also affect the elderly, but S. pneumoniae remains the most common overall cause in adults.

preguntas.q: Which organism is a common cause of meningitis specifically in an unvaccinated young child?

e.correcta: Haemophilus influenzae type B was historically a leading cause of meningitis in children 6 months to 5 years old, and it remains an important cause in the unvaccinated. Its type b polysaccharide (polyribosylribitol phosphate) capsule is the virulence factor targeted by the conjugate Hib vaccine, which has dramatically reduced incidence in immunized populations.

incorrectas.A: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a common cause of meningitis across many age groups, but the key teaching point here is that Hib specifically re-emerges when a child is unvaccinated.
incorrectas.B: Listeria monocytogenes affects neonates, the elderly, pregnant women, and immunocompromised patients, not immunocompetent unvaccinated toddlers as the characteristic group.
incorrectas.D: Neisseria meningitidis is more characteristic of adolescents and young adults in close quarters, whereas the classic vaccine-preventable childhood organism is Hib.

preguntas.q: A patient with AIDS and a CD4 count of 30 develops subacute headache and fever. A CSF India ink stain is ordered. Which organism is the most common cause of fungal meningitis in HIV-positive patients?

e.correcta: Cryptococcus neoformans is the classic cause of fungal meningitis in HIV-positive patients, typically once the CD4 count falls below 100. It is an encapsulated yeast identified by India ink or a latex agglutination test for capsular antigen, and its thick polysaccharide capsule is its main virulence factor; fungal meningitis in general is far more common in immunocompromised hosts.

incorrectas.A: Candida albicans can cause CNS infection in neonates and severely immunocompromised or catheterized patients, but it is not the characteristic cause of meningitis in AIDS the way Cryptococcus is.
incorrectas.C: Histoplasma capsulatum causes disseminated disease in AIDS patients and can involve the CNS, but it is a much less common cause of isolated fungal meningitis than Cryptococcus and is geographically restricted.
incorrectas.D: Aspergillus fumigatus tends to cause invasive angioinvasive disease in profoundly neutropenic patients, producing abscesses and infarcts rather than the classic cryptococcal meningitis of AIDS.

preguntas.q: Which enterovirus is the most common cause of viral (aseptic) meningitis?

e.correcta: Coxsackievirus, a member of the enterovirus genus of the Picornaviridae, is the most common cause of viral meningitis, which typically follows a milder, self-limited course than bacterial meningitis. Enteroviruses are non-enveloped, single-stranded positive-sense RNA viruses transmitted by the fecal-oral route, and viral meningitis characteristically shows a lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose.

incorrectas.B: Rotavirus is a reovirus that causes infantile gastroenteritis with watery diarrhea; it is not an enterovirus and does not cause meningitis.
incorrectas.C: Rhinovirus is also a picornavirus but, being acid-labile and confined to the upper respiratory tract, it causes the common cold rather than meningitis.
incorrectas.D: Hepatitis A virus is a picornavirus as well, but it targets the liver via fecal-oral spread and is not a recognized cause of aseptic meningitis.

preguntas.q: Besides Streptococcus pneumoniae and gram-negative rods, which organism is a characteristic cause of bacterial meningitis in the elderly?

e.correcta: Listeria monocytogenes is a characteristic cause of meningitis in the elderly (as well as neonates, pregnant women, and the immunocompromised) because waning cell-mediated immunity permits this intracellular organism to invade. It is a gram-positive, facultative intracellular rod with tumbling motility, and empiric therapy in older adults adds ampicillin specifically to cover it.

incorrectas.A: Group B streptococcus is chiefly a neonatal pathogen acquired at birth; although it can occasionally affect older adults, Listeria is the organism classically added for the elderly alongside pneumococcus and gram-negative rods.
incorrectas.C: Neisseria meningitidis predominates in adolescents and young adults in crowded settings rather than being a hallmark elderly pathogen.
incorrectas.D: Haemophilus influenzae type B is associated with unvaccinated young children, not the elderly population highlighted here.

preguntas.q: The definitive diagnosis of meningitis is made by which of the following procedures?

e.correcta: Lumbar puncture is the diagnostic procedure for meningitis because it samples CSF from the subarachnoid space, allowing measurement of opening pressure, cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, and culture. The needle is placed at the L4-L5 interspace (identified along the line between the iliac crests) because this is safely below the conus medullaris, which ends near L1-L2.

incorrectas.A: Blood cultures should be drawn and are useful for identifying the organism in bacteremic patients, but they do not sample the CSF and cannot by themselves establish the diagnosis of meningeal inflammation.
incorrectas.B: CT of the head is sometimes obtained before LP to exclude a mass or raised pressure, but it does not analyze CSF and therefore cannot diagnose meningitis itself.
incorrectas.D: Electroencephalography records cortical electrical activity and may help in evaluating encephalitis or seizures, but it provides no information about CSF and is not the diagnostic test for meningitis.

preguntas.q: During a lumbar puncture, what is the deepest meningeal layer the needle normally crosses to reach the CSF?

e.correcta: During an LP the needle passes through skin, subcutaneous tissue, the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, the ligamentum flavum, the epidural space, the dura mater, and finally the arachnoid mater to enter the CSF-filled subarachnoid space. The arachnoid is therefore the deepest layer crossed, and the pia is left undisturbed because it adheres directly to the spinal cord and roots.

incorrectas.A: The dura mater is pierced just before the arachnoid, but it is not the deepest layer; the needle must still traverse the arachnoid to reach the CSF.
incorrectas.C: The pia mater is not normally pierced because it is closely applied to the surface of the cord and nerve roots, which float within the subarachnoid CSF that the needle enters.
incorrectas.D: The ligamentum flavum is a ligament, not a meninx, and is crossed relatively superficially before the epidural space and dura, so it is not the deepest meningeal layer.

preguntas.q: During a routine lumbar puncture, is the pia mater normally pierced by the needle?

o.A: Yes, it is the final layer crossed
o.B: No, the pia is not normally pierced
o.D: Only in the lateral decubitus position

e.correcta: The pia mater is not normally pierced during a lumbar puncture. The needle enters the subarachnoid space after passing through the dura and arachnoid, and the pia remains intact because it is firmly adherent to the surface of the spinal cord and nerve roots, which are bathed in the CSF the needle samples.

incorrectas.A: The final meningeal layer crossed is the arachnoid, not the pia; the CSF lies in the subarachnoid space superficial to the pia-covered neural tissue.
incorrectas.C: The dura is indeed pierced, but the pia is not, so a combined dura-plus-pia answer is incorrect; the arachnoid, not the pia, accompanies the dura in being traversed.
incorrectas.D: Patient positioning affects the ease and landmarks of the procedure but does not change the layers traversed, so the pia is spared regardless of decubitus or sitting position.

preguntas.q: On lumbar puncture, what is the characteristic opening (CSF) pressure finding in bacterial meningitis?

e.correcta: Bacterial meningitis characteristically produces an increased CSF opening pressure. Intense purulent inflammation of the subarachnoid space raises CSF protein and cellular content and impairs CSF resorption at the arachnoid granulations, so fluid accumulates and pressure rises.

incorrectas.B: Decreased CSF pressure is seen with CSF leaks or overdrainage, not with the inflammatory, high-protein state of bacterial meningitis, which raises pressure.
incorrectas.C: A normal opening pressure would argue against florid bacterial meningitis; the brisk neutrophilic inflammation typically drives the pressure up.
incorrectas.D: Undetectable pressure would suggest a complete block or dry tap and is not a recognized feature of bacterial meningitis, which characteristically shows elevated pressure.

preguntas.q: Bacterial meningitis is associated with a markedly increased CSF concentration of which cell type?

e.correcta: Bacterial meningitis characteristically produces a marked CSF neutrophilic (PMN) pleocytosis, often into the thousands, reflecting the acute pyogenic inflammatory response to the organism. This neutrophil predominance, together with high protein and low glucose, distinguishes bacterial meningitis from viral, fungal, and TB causes, which show only moderate, lymphocyte-predominant cell increases.

incorrectas.A: A lymphocytic predominance is typical of viral, fungal, and tuberculous meningitis, not the acute pyogenic bacterial process that recruits neutrophils.
incorrectas.B: CSF eosinophilia points toward parasitic (e.g., neurocysticercosis, Angiostrongylus) or certain fungal infections, not routine bacterial meningitis.
incorrectas.D: Plasma cells are not the hallmark CSF finding in acute bacterial meningitis; the acute pyogenic response is dominated by neutrophils rather than antibody-secreting cells.

preguntas.q: How is the CSF protein concentration altered in bacterial meningitis?

e.correcta: CSF protein is increased in bacterial meningitis. Intense inflammation disrupts the blood-brain barrier and allows plasma proteins to leak into the subarachnoid space, and the accumulation of bacteria, inflammatory cells, and debris further raises the protein level.

incorrectas.B: Decreased CSF protein is not a feature of meningitis; inflammatory barrier breakdown drives protein up, not down.
incorrectas.C: An unchanged, normal protein would be atypical for bacterial meningitis, where the inflamed, leaky barrier characteristically elevates protein.
incorrectas.D: CSF normally contains a small amount of protein and it is never truly absent; in bacterial meningitis the level actually rises above normal.

preguntas.q: How is the CSF glucose concentration typically altered in bacterial meningitis?

e.correcta: CSF glucose is decreased in bacterial meningitis. The metabolically active bacteria and infiltrating neutrophils consume glucose, and inflammation also impairs glucose transport across the blood-brain barrier, so the CSF-to-serum glucose ratio falls below the normal ~0.6.

incorrectas.A: CSF glucose does not rise in bacterial meningitis; the heavy metabolic demand of bacteria and leukocytes drives it down.
incorrectas.C: An unchanged glucose is more typical of viral meningitis, whereas the bacterial process characteristically produces hypoglycorrhachia (low CSF glucose).
incorrectas.D: The change is not unpredictable; low CSF glucose is a consistent and diagnostically useful hallmark of bacterial (and also fungal/TB) meningitis.

preguntas.q: A CSF analysis shows decreased glucose and a markedly increased neutrophil (PMN) count. Which category of meningitis does this pattern indicate?

e.correcta: The combination of low CSF glucose and a neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis (with elevated protein and pressure) is the classic signature of bacterial meningitis. Bacteria and neutrophils consume glucose while the acute pyogenic response floods the CSF with PMNs, distinguishing this from other causes.

incorrectas.A: Viral meningitis typically shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose, the opposite of the low-glucose, neutrophilic pattern described.
incorrectas.B: Fungal meningitis also lowers glucose but characteristically produces a lymphocytic rather than a neutrophilic pleocytosis, so the PMN predominance points to bacteria.
incorrectas.D: Tuberculous meningitis likewise lowers glucose but is marked by lymphocytes and very high protein with a subacute course, not the acute PMN surge of bacterial infection.

preguntas.q: On lumbar puncture, what is the typical CSF opening pressure finding in fungal or tuberculous meningitis?

e.correcta: Fungal and tuberculous meningitis characteristically produce an increased CSF opening pressure, similar to bacterial meningitis. The chronic inflammatory exudate raises protein and cell content and can obstruct CSF flow and resorption at the arachnoid granulations, particularly at the basal cisterns in TB, elevating pressure.

incorrectas.B: Decreased pressure occurs with CSF leaks or overdrainage, not with the inflammatory exudative process of fungal or TB meningitis.
incorrectas.C: A normal opening pressure would be atypical, since the chronic meningeal inflammation and impaired CSF resorption generally raise the pressure.
incorrectas.D: Negative CSF pressure is not a recognized finding in these infections; the exudative inflammation drives pressure upward.

preguntas.q: Fungal and tuberculous meningitis are associated with an increased CSF concentration of which cell type?

e.correcta: Fungal and tuberculous meningitis characteristically produce a lymphocyte-predominant CSF pleocytosis, reflecting the chronic, cell-mediated (granulomatous) immune response these organisms elicit. This lymphocytic pattern, along with low glucose and high protein, helps distinguish them from the acute neutrophilic picture of bacterial meningitis.

incorrectas.A: Neutrophils dominate in acute bacterial meningitis; a PMN predominance would argue against the chronic fungal/TB process (though very early TB can occasionally be neutrophilic).
incorrectas.C: Eosinophilic pleocytosis suggests parasitic infection or certain fungi like Coccidioides, but the typical fungal/TB pattern tested here is lymphocytic.
incorrectas.D: Basophils are essentially never the predominant CSF cell in meningitis; the characteristic chronic-infection response is lymphocytic.

preguntas.q: How is the CSF protein concentration typically altered in fungal or tuberculous meningitis?

e.correcta: CSF protein is increased in fungal and tuberculous meningitis. The chronic inflammatory exudate disrupts the blood-brain barrier and adds cells and debris to the CSF; in TB the protein elevation can be especially striking and may cause a fibrin web (pellicle) to form on standing.

incorrectas.B: Decreased CSF protein is not seen in these infections; chronic meningeal inflammation raises protein rather than lowering it.
incorrectas.C: An unchanged, normal protein would be atypical because the exudative process characteristic of fungal/TB meningitis elevates protein.
incorrectas.D: CSF always contains some protein, and in fungal/TB meningitis the concentration is elevated, so an absent-protein answer is incorrect.

preguntas.q: How is the CSF glucose concentration typically altered in fungal or tuberculous meningitis?

e.correcta: CSF glucose is decreased in fungal and tuberculous meningitis, mirroring the low glucose seen in bacterial meningitis. The metabolic activity of the organisms and inflammatory cells consumes glucose, and impaired glucose transport across the inflamed blood-brain barrier lowers the CSF-to-serum ratio; the lymphocytic pleocytosis distinguishes these from bacterial causes.

incorrectas.A: CSF glucose does not rise in fungal or TB meningitis; ongoing consumption by organisms and leukocytes drives it down.
incorrectas.C: Unchanged (normal) glucose is more typical of viral meningitis, whereas fungal and TB meningitis characteristically lower CSF glucose.
incorrectas.D: CSF glucose is normally about two-thirds of serum and never exceeds serum levels; in fungal/TB meningitis it falls further below normal rather than rising above serum.

preguntas.q: A patient with suspected meningitis has a lumbar puncture showing decreased CSF glucose and a lymphocytic pleocytosis. Which category of meningitis does this CSF profile most strongly suggest?

e.correcta: Fungal and tuberculous meningitis classically produce a lymphocyte-predominant pleocytosis together with a LOW CSF glucose. The low glucose reflects that the organisms (and the host inflammatory response) consume glucose, while the chronic/granulomatous nature of the infection recruits lymphocytes rather than neutrophils. This combination of low sugar plus lymphocytes is the fingerprint that separates fungal/TB from viral disease.

incorrectas.A: Viral meningitis also shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis, but its CSF glucose is characteristically NORMAL because viruses do not consume glucose the way fungi/mycobacteria do; the normal sugar is the key discriminator against fungal/TB.
incorrectas.C: Acute bacterial meningitis does cause low CSF glucose, but the cellular response is a neutrophil (PMN) predominance, not lymphocytes, and the opening pressure and protein are markedly elevated.
incorrectas.D: Drug-induced/chemical aseptic meningitis typically produces a neutrophilic or mixed pleocytosis with normal glucose and is a diagnosis of exclusion, not the low-glucose lymphocytic pattern described.

preguntas.q: During a lumbar puncture on a patient with viral (aseptic) meningitis, what is the expected CSF opening pressure?

o.D: Immeasurably low due to CSF leak

e.correcta: In viral meningitis the CSF opening pressure is typically normal or only mildly increased. The relatively modest inflammatory response does not obstruct CSF flow or arachnoid granulation reabsorption to the degree seen with pyogenic bacterial infection, so pressures stay closer to the normal range (roughly 5-20 cm H2O).

incorrectas.A: A markedly decreased pressure is not a feature of meningitis; very low pressures suggest a CSF leak or prior over-drainage, not viral inflammation.
incorrectas.C: Uniformly very high pressures are more characteristic of acute bacterial meningitis, where purulent exudate impairs CSF reabsorption; viral disease is usually only mildly elevated at most.
incorrectas.D: An immeasurably low pressure indicates a dural leak or blocked needle, which is unrelated to the inflammatory physiology of viral meningitis.

preguntas.q: Which cell type predominates in the CSF pleocytosis of viral meningitis?

e.correcta: Viral meningitis produces a lymphocyte-predominant pleocytosis. Viruses trigger a cell-mediated immune response, recruiting lymphocytes rather than the neutrophils mobilized against pyogenic bacteria. This lymphocytic profile, combined with normal glucose, is the classic aseptic-meningitis picture.

incorrectas.A: Neutrophils dominate in acute bacterial (pyogenic) meningitis, where the innate response to extracellular bacteria mobilizes PMNs; a neutrophilic count argues against a viral cause (though very early viral cases can transiently show PMNs).
incorrectas.B: Eosinophilic pleocytosis is unusual and points toward parasitic infection (e.g., Angiostrongylus, cysticercosis) or certain fungal/hypersensitivity processes, not typical viral meningitis.
incorrectas.D: Plasma cells are not the predominant CSF cell in acute viral meningitis; while they can appear in some chronic CNS processes, the hallmark of viral meningitis is a lymphocytic pleocytosis.

preguntas.q: What is the expected CSF protein level in viral meningitis?

e.correcta: Viral meningitis is associated with a normal or only mildly elevated CSF protein. The blood-brain barrier is disrupted far less than in pyogenic infection, so relatively little serum protein leaks into the CSF. This modest protein rise contrasts sharply with bacterial meningitis, where protein is often markedly high.

incorrectas.B: A markedly decreased CSF protein is not a recognized meningitis pattern; inflammatory processes raise protein rather than lower it.
incorrectas.C: Extremely high protein (often several hundred mg/dL) is characteristic of bacterial or TB meningitis due to heavy barrier breakdown and exudate, not the milder viral process.
incorrectas.D: CSF normally contains a small amount of protein (roughly 15-45 mg/dL); it is never truly undetectable, and viral meningitis raises it slightly if anything.

preguntas.q: Which CSF glucose finding helps distinguish viral meningitis from bacterial and fungal/TB meningitis?

e.correcta: Viral meningitis characteristically leaves the CSF glucose NORMAL. Because viruses do not metabolize glucose (and the inflammatory burden is lower), the CSF-to-serum glucose ratio is preserved. This normal sugar is the single most useful discriminator from bacterial and fungal/TB meningitis, both of which drive glucose down.

incorrectas.B: Low CSF glucose (hypoglycorrhachia) is the hallmark of bacterial and fungal/TB meningitis, where organisms and inflammatory cells consume glucose; finding low glucose argues against a purely viral cause.
incorrectas.C: Markedly elevated CSF glucose is not a meningitis pattern; high CSF glucose simply reflects hyperglycemia in the blood, not an inflammatory process.
incorrectas.D: CSF glucose is normally about two-thirds of serum glucose and does not exceed serum levels; a value above serum would be physiologically implausible.

preguntas.q: A patient's CSF shows normal glucose with an increased lymphocyte count. Which category of meningitis does this profile most strongly indicate?

e.correcta: Normal glucose plus a lymphocytic pleocytosis is the classic profile of viral (aseptic) meningitis. The lymphocytes reflect a cell-mediated antiviral response, and the preserved glucose reflects that viruses do not consume it. Together these separate viral disease from the low-glucose lymphocytic picture of fungal/TB meningitis.

incorrectas.A: Acute bacterial meningitis shows a neutrophilic pleocytosis with LOW glucose and very high protein, essentially the opposite of the normal-glucose, lymphocyte-predominant picture described.
incorrectas.B: Fungal meningitis also produces lymphocytes, but its CSF glucose is typically LOW; the normal glucose here points away from a fungal etiology.
incorrectas.D: Tuberculous meningitis likewise gives a lymphocytic pleocytosis but with characteristically LOW glucose and high protein, so a normal glucose makes TB much less likely than a viral cause.

preguntas.q: Bacterial meningitis can be fatal when severe cerebral edema raises intracranial pressure. What is the immediate mechanism of death in this setting?

e.correcta: In bacterial meningitis, purulent exudate and pus provoke marked cerebral edema, raising intracranial pressure. When the pressure gradient becomes severe, brain tissue is forced across rigid dural or bony boundaries (uncal, tonsillar, or subfalcine herniation), compressing the brainstem and its cardiorespiratory centers, which is the acute cause of death. This is why elevated ICP in meningitis is a neurologic emergency.

incorrectas.B: Communicating hydrocephalus is a chronic complication caused by fibrosis of arachnoid granulations; it develops over time and does not cause the acute death from edema described here.
incorrectas.C: Diffuse cortical liquefactive necrosis is the tissue outcome of ischemic infarction, not the acute pressure-driven mechanism by which meningitis-related edema kills.
incorrectas.D: Sagittal sinus thrombosis can complicate infection, but the scenario specifies death from cerebral edema, which acts through herniation and brainstem compression rather than venous thrombosis.

preguntas.q: Bacterial meningitis can lead to communicating hydrocephalus, hearing loss, and seizures. Which pathologic process of the arachnoid granulations underlies the resulting high-pressure hydrocephalus?

e.correcta: Inflammation from bacterial meningitis causes fibrosis (scarring) of the arachnoid granulations, the structures that reabsorb CSF into the venous sinuses. When these granulations are scarred, CSF continues to be produced but cannot be reabsorbed, producing a communicating (non-obstructive) hydrocephalus with elevated pressure. This is why meningitis is a classic cause of communicating hydrocephalus.

incorrectas.B: Calcification of arachnoid granulations is an incidental aging finding, not the post-inflammatory scarring that blocks CSF reabsorption after meningitis.
incorrectas.C: Neoplastic infiltration (leptomeningeal carcinomatosis) can also impair CSF reabsorption, but the mechanism after bacterial meningitis is inflammatory fibrosis, not tumor spread.
