o.A: Aphasia, reflecting dominant frontal lobe involvement
o.B: Dysarthria from CN XII palsy, reflecting medullary involvement
o.C: Apraxia of speech, reflecting parietal lobe involvement

e.correcta: Scanning speech is a form of ataxic dysarthria seen in MS when demyelinating plaques involve the brainstem and cerebellar pathways; it is characterized by slow, halting speech with abnormal separation and stress of syllables, and along with vertigo and nystagmus it can resemble alcohol intoxication because both processes disrupt cerebellar coordination of speech and balance. Recognizing this presentation helps localize brainstem/cerebellar plaques as the anatomic basis for these symptoms in MS.

incorrectas.A: Aphasia is a disorder of language content (production or comprehension) from dominant hemisphere (usually left frontal/temporal) cortical damage, not a motor speech articulation problem from brainstem/cerebellar disease, so it does not describe the scanning speech pattern seen here.
incorrectas.B: Isolated CN XII (hypoglossal) palsy causes tongue deviation and dysarthria from tongue weakness, but this is a distinct, focal lower cranial nerve/medullary problem rather than the diffuse cerebellar-type ataxic dysarthria described as scanning speech in MS.
incorrectas.C: Apraxia of speech is a motor planning disorder usually from dominant frontal cortical or subcortical injury, affecting the ability to program articulatory movements, which is different from the cerebellar-pattern ataxic dysarthria of scanning speech.

preguntas.q: In a patient with multiple sclerosis and cerebral white matter (periventricular) plaques, which of the following symptoms can occur — hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, or both?

o.A: Both hemiparesis and hemisensory symptoms can occur
o.B: Only hemiparesis occurs, since MS spares sensory pathways
o.C: Only hemisensory symptoms occur, since MS spares motor pathways
o.D: Neither occurs, since cerebral plaques cause only visual symptoms

e.correcta: MS plaques in the cerebral white matter, particularly the periventricular regions, can disrupt both descending corticospinal (motor) fibers and ascending sensory pathways as they course through this white matter, so patients can present with pyramidal weakness (hemiparesis), sensory disturbances affecting the trunk or one or more limbs, or both together depending on which tracts a given plaque involves. This reflects that a single anatomic region of periventricular white matter carries fibers serving multiple different functional systems.

incorrectas.B: MS is not restricted to motor pathways — it commonly involves ascending sensory tracts as well, so sensory symptoms (numbness, paresthesias) are a very common presenting complaint, not something the disease spares.
incorrectas.C: MS is not restricted to sensory pathways either — corticospinal tract demyelination causing pyramidal weakness is a classic MS finding, so motor involvement is just as characteristic as sensory involvement.
incorrectas.D: Cerebral periventricular plaques are not limited to producing only visual symptoms (optic neuritis is a separate, classic MS presentation from optic nerve involvement); periventricular white matter plaques can cause a wide range of motor and sensory deficits depending on location.

preguntas.q: A patient with multiple sclerosis and spinal cord demyelination above the sacral segments develops urinary urgency with frequent voiding of small amounts. What is the underlying mechanism?

o.A: Direct destruction of the sacral micturition center causing an atonic, areflexic bladder from the onset
o.B: Peripheral pudendal nerve injury causing sphincter weakness and stress incontinence
o.C: Loss of higher center inhibitory control over the sacral micturition reflex, causing detrusor hyperreflexia
o.D: Autonomic neuropathy causing bladder outlet obstruction from sphincter spasm alone

e.correcta: Early in MS, demyelinating plaques in the spinal cord above the sacral segments interrupt descending pathways that normally provide voluntary, cortical inhibition of the sacral micturition reflex; without this higher-center control, the detrusor muscle becomes hyperreflexic, contracting involuntarily and producing urinary urgency with frequent voiding of small volumes. As MS progresses and lower segments become more involved, the bladder can eventually become atonic and overflow, so the clinical picture evolves over the disease course rather than being fixed from onset.

incorrectas.A: An atonic, areflexic bladder from the onset would suggest direct destruction of the sacral micturition center itself or its peripheral connections, but the initial mechanism in MS is loss of higher inhibitory control producing a hyperreflexic (not areflexic) bladder; the atonic pattern is a later development, not the starting point.
incorrectas.B: MS is a CNS demyelinating disease, not a peripheral nerve injury; the urinary symptoms arise from disrupted central pathways controlling the micturition reflex rather than a peripheral pudendal nerve lesion causing sphincter weakness and stress incontinence.
incorrectas.D: The problem in early MS bladder dysfunction is unrestrained detrusor contraction from loss of central inhibition, not a fixed sphincter spasm causing outlet obstruction; framing it purely as an obstructive process misses the detrusor hyperreflexia mechanism that actually drives the urgency/frequency symptoms.

preguntas.q: What is the gold-standard imaging modality for diagnosing multiple sclerosis?

e.correcta: MRI is the imaging modality of choice for MS because it provides superior soft tissue contrast to visualize demyelinating plaques, especially as hyperintense periventricular lesions on T2/FLAIR sequences, and can demonstrate lesions disseminated in space and time needed for diagnosis, as well as gadolinium enhancement of active, inflamed lesions. Its sensitivity for white matter changes far exceeds other imaging modalities, making it essential for both diagnosis and monitoring of disease activity.

incorrectas.A: CT can detect large structural abnormalities and hemorrhage but has poor soft tissue and white matter contrast compared with MRI, making it insensitive for detecting the subtle demyelinating plaques characteristic of MS.
incorrectas.C: PET imaging assesses metabolic activity and is useful in oncology and some neurodegenerative disease workups, but it is not the standard modality for identifying or monitoring MS plaques, which are better characterized structurally by MRI.
incorrectas.D: Ultrasound cannot adequately image intracranial or spinal cord white matter through the skull and vertebral column, making it entirely unsuitable for detecting CNS demyelinating lesions in MS.

preguntas.q: What characteristic MRI finding, also known as 'Dawson fingers,' is associated with multiple sclerosis?

e.correcta: MS classically produces periventricular white matter plaques that, when oriented perpendicular to the ventricles along the path of medullary veins, create the finger-like projections known as Dawson fingers on MRI. These lesions are hyperintense on T2 and FLAIR sequences and histologically show oligodendrocyte loss with reactive gliosis, with early preservation but late destruction of axons; their periventricular distribution and orientation are a highly characteristic imaging clue supporting the MS diagnosis.

incorrectas.A: Lacunar infarcts are small subcortical infarcts from occlusion of penetrating arterioles, typically from chronic hypertension or diabetes, producing small round cavitary lesions in a vascular (not periventricular perpendicular) distribution, unrelated to demyelination.
incorrectas.B: Ring-enhancing lesions on MRI are classically associated with processes like brain abscess, toxoplasmosis, or high-grade glioma/metastasis, reflecting a necrotic center with peripheral enhancement, a very different appearance from the periventricular Dawson fingers of MS.
incorrectas.C: Diffuse cortical atrophy is a nonspecific finding seen in many neurodegenerative conditions and normal aging, and it does not represent the characteristic focal periventricular white matter lesion pattern used to identify MS on MRI.

preguntas.q: Multiple sclerosis is associated with increased levels of which immunoglobulin in the CSF, often detected as oligoclonal bands?

e.correcta: MS is associated with intrathecal synthesis of IgG, reflected by elevated CSF IgG levels and the presence of oligoclonal bands on CSF electrophoresis that are not present in matched serum; this indicates a localized, chronic B-cell/plasma-cell-driven immune response within the CNS itself. Along with MRI findings of disseminated lesions, elevated CSF IgG/oligoclonal bands serve as a supportive laboratory finding for the diagnosis of MS.

incorrectas.B: IgA is the predominant antibody of mucosal immunity (found in secretions like saliva, tears, and breast milk) and is not the immunoglobulin classically elevated in the CSF of MS patients.
incorrectas.C: IgM is the first antibody produced in an acute immune response and is largely confined to the intravascular space due to its large pentameric size; it is not the immunoglobulin whose elevated intrathecal synthesis and oligoclonal banding are characteristic of MS.
incorrectas.D: IgE mediates immediate hypersensitivity (allergic) and antiparasitic responses, and it is not associated with the chronic intrathecal humoral response measured in the CSF for the diagnosis of MS.

preguntas.q: A 30-year-old woman with relapsing neurologic deficits undergoes lumbar puncture. Which protein is characteristically elevated in the CSF, reflecting active destruction of the myelin sheath?

e.correcta: In multiple sclerosis, autoimmune attack strips oligodendrocyte myelin from CNS axons, releasing myelin basic protein (MBP)—a major structural component of the sheath—into the CSF. Elevated MBP is a marker of active demyelination, and alongside oligoclonal IgG bands and elevated protein it supports the diagnosis. Its level tends to rise during acute relapses, mirroring ongoing myelin breakdown.

incorrectas.A: Tau protein is a microtubule-associated protein that accumulates intracellularly in neurofibrillary tangles of Alzheimer disease; it reflects neuronal cytoskeletal pathology, not the myelin destruction that defines MS.
incorrectas.C: 14-3-3 protein in the CSF is a marker of rapid neuronal destruction seen in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, not the demyelinating process of MS.
incorrectas.D: Amyloid beta is the cleavage product of amyloid precursor protein that aggregates into extracellular plaques in Alzheimer disease; it is unrelated to the myelin sheath breakdown occurring in MS.

preguntas.q: CSF analysis in a patient with multiple sclerosis is expected to show what change in the lymphocyte count?

e.correcta: MS is a T-cell-mediated autoimmune disease, so activated lymphocytes traffic across the blood-brain barrier into the CNS, producing a mild lymphocytic pleocytosis in the CSF (typically <50 cells/µL). This reflects the inflammatory, immune-driven nature of the demyelination. The finding accompanies elevated protein, oligoclonal bands, and increased myelin basic protein.

incorrectas.B: A markedly decreased lymphocyte count is not a feature of MS; the immune-mediated inflammation drives cells into the CSF rather than depleting them.
incorrectas.C: Complete absence of lymphocytes would argue against an active inflammatory CNS process; MS characteristically produces a modest lymphocytic pleocytosis.
incorrectas.D: A neutrophil-predominant CSF suggests acute bacterial meningitis, not the mononuclear/lymphocytic inflammation of MS.

preguntas.q: A woman with multiple sclerosis notes that her leg weakness and blurred vision transiently worsen after a hot shower or exercise. Exposure to which of the following triggers this phenomenon?

e.correcta: This is Uhthoff phenomenon: a rise in body temperature (hot shower, exercise, fever) transiently worsens MS symptoms. Elevated temperature slows conduction and can cause conduction block along already-demyelinated axons, whose exposed membranes are exquisitely temperature-sensitive. The deficit is reversible once the patient cools down, distinguishing it from a true relapse.

incorrectas.A: Cold does not provoke Uhthoff phenomenon; if anything, cooling can transiently improve conduction in demyelinated fibers, which is why patients often feel better after cooling down.
incorrectas.C: Bright light does not affect axonal conduction velocity in demyelinated nerves; the trigger is a rise in core body temperature, not visual stimulation.
incorrectas.D: Loud noise has no effect on the temperature-dependent conduction block that underlies symptom worsening in MS.

preguntas.q: A patient with multiple sclerosis presents with an acute relapse of optic neuritis. What is the first-line treatment to shorten the acute attack?

e.correcta: Acute MS relapses are treated with high-dose corticosteroids (e.g., IV methylprednisolone), which rapidly suppress the inflammatory demyelinating attack and hasten recovery. Steroids shorten the duration of the acute exacerbation but do not alter the long-term course of the disease. They work by dampening the T-cell-mediated inflammation and reducing blood-brain barrier permeability during the flare.

incorrectas.B: Interferon beta is a disease-modifying therapy used chronically to reduce relapse frequency; it does not act quickly enough to abort an acute attack in progress.
incorrectas.C: Natalizumab is a long-term disease-modifying monoclonal antibody that prevents future relapses, not a rescue agent for an ongoing exacerbation.
incorrectas.D: Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist used for symptomatic relief of spasticity; it has no effect on the underlying inflammatory attack.

preguntas.q: Long-term disease-modifying therapies for multiple sclerosis, such as interferon beta, glatiramer, and natalizumab, primarily aim to accomplish which of the following?

e.correcta: Disease-modifying therapies reduce the frequency of relapses and slow accumulation of disability rather than curing MS. Each acts on the immune process: interferon beta decreases blood-brain barrier permeability, glatiramer is a myelin basic protein analog that shifts the T-cell response from a Th1 to a Th2 (anti-inflammatory) phenotype, and natalizumab is an alpha-4-integrin inhibitor that blocks T-cell extravasation into the CNS. Together they blunt the recurrent immune assaults that drive progression.

incorrectas.A: These agents cannot reverse axonal loss that has already occurred; once demyelinated axons degenerate, the deficit is largely permanent, which is why early treatment matters.
incorrectas.B: MS has no cure; disease-modifying therapy controls disease activity but does not eliminate the underlying autoimmune predisposition.
incorrectas.D: Acute pain and other symptoms are managed with symptomatic drugs (TCAs, anticonvulsants), not with disease-modifying immunotherapies.

preguntas.q: An MS patient develops urinary retention and incomplete emptying managed with intermittent catheterization and muscarinic antagonists. This bladder dysfunction is best classified as which type?

e.correcta: MS lesions interrupt the spinal pathways coordinating bladder filling and voiding, producing a neurogenic bladder with detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia and impaired emptying. Management targets the disordered neural control: catheterization empties retained urine, and muscarinic antagonists reduce detrusor overactivity. This is one of the most common and disabling symptomatic problems in MS.

incorrectas.B: Stress incontinence results from pelvic floor/urethral sphincter weakness with leakage on exertion; it is a mechanical failure, not the central neural dysregulation seen in MS.
incorrectas.C: Obstructive uropathy is caused by a physical blockage (e.g., stones, prostate) impeding outflow, whereas the MS problem is a nerve-signaling failure of the bladder.
incorrectas.D: Interstitial cystitis is a chronic inflammatory bladder pain syndrome, unrelated to the demyelinating disruption of bladder innervation in MS.

preguntas.q: In an MS patient, baclofen or other GABA-B receptor agonists are used to provide symptomatic relief of which problem?

e.correcta: Spasticity—velocity-dependent increased muscle tone from loss of descending inhibitory control—is treated with baclofen, a GABA-B receptor agonist. By activating presynaptic and postsynaptic GABA-B receptors in the spinal cord, baclofen reduces excitatory reflex transmission and relaxes hypertonic muscles. Tizanidine (an alpha-2 agonist) is an alternative used for the same indication.

incorrectas.B: Neuropathic pain in MS is treated with TCAs and anticonvulsants that modulate abnormal sensory signaling, not with GABA-B-mediated reduction of muscle tone.
incorrectas.C: Fatigue is managed with agents such as amantadine or modafinil; baclofen would not address the pathologic tiredness of MS and can even worsen sedation.
incorrectas.D: Depression is treated with antidepressants; baclofen targets spinal motor reflex arcs, not mood.

preguntas.q: Tricyclic antidepressants and anticonvulsants are used in MS patients to provide symptomatic relief of which of the following?

e.correcta: Neuropathic pain in MS is managed with tricyclic antidepressants and anticonvulsants (e.g., gabapentin, carbamazepine). These drugs dampen aberrant neuronal firing—anticonvulsants stabilize neuronal membranes through sodium-channel blockade, and TCAs modulate descending pain pathways via monoamine reuptake inhibition. This makes them effective for the burning, shooting dysesthesias that demyelinated sensory tracts generate.

incorrectas.A: Spasticity is treated with baclofen (GABA-B agonist) or tizanidine, which reduce muscle tone rather than modulate pain pathways.
incorrectas.C: Neurogenic bladder is managed with catheterization and muscarinic antagonists, targeting detrusor function rather than nociceptive signaling.
incorrectas.D: Intention tremor and other cerebellar symptoms are not the target of TCAs/anticonvulsants, which are specifically directed at neuropathic pain.

preguntas.q: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a late complication of measles infection, involves which region(s) of the brain?

e.correcta: SSPE is a panencephalitis, meaning it affects both gray and white matter diffusely (the prefix pan- signals whole-brain involvement). Persistent defective measles virus incites chronic inflammation with neuronal (gray matter) and myelin (white matter) destruction, producing viral inclusion bodies in both neurons and oligodendrocytes. This widespread involvement causes the progressive dementia, myoclonus, and seizures that characterize the disease.

incorrectas.A: Restriction to gray matter alone would not qualify as a panencephalitis; SSPE damages neurons and myelinated tracts alike.
incorrectas.B: Pure white-matter (demyelinating) involvement describes disorders like PML or MS; SSPE additionally destroys neuronal gray matter.
incorrectas.D: SSPE clearly produces extensive parenchymal damage, so neither being affected is incorrect.

preguntas.q: A child who had measles in infancy develops progressive cognitive decline and myoclonus. How long after the original measles infection does subacute sclerosing panencephalitis typically present?

e.correcta: SSPE presents years after the primary measles infection—infection occurs in infancy, but neurologic signs emerge during later childhood or adolescence. During this long latent interval, defective measles virus persists and slowly replicates within CNS neurons before triggering the fatal chronic encephalitis. This delayed onset is a key clue distinguishing SSPE from acute post-measles encephalitis.

incorrectas.A: Onset within days would suggest acute measles encephalitis or another acute process, not the slowly evolving SSPE.
incorrectas.B: A few-week interval is too short; SSPE has a characteristically prolonged latency measured in years.
incorrectas.C: Even a few months underestimates the latency; the classic teaching is that SSPE surfaces years after the initial infection.

preguntas.q: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) arises from reactivation of latent JC virus in which patient population?

e.correcta: PML occurs almost exclusively in immunosuppressed patients—classically those with AIDS (seen in 2-4%), leukemia, or on immunomodulators like natalizumab. Loss of T-cell surveillance allows latent JC (John Cunningham) virus to reactivate and lytically infect oligodendrocytes, destroying myelin in multiple white-matter foci. The result is progressive focal neurologic deficits such as visual loss, weakness, and cognitive decline.

incorrectas.B: Healthy individuals with intact immunity suppress latent JC virus and do not develop PML; competent T-cell surveillance keeps the virus dormant.
incorrectas.C: Pregnancy involves relative immune modulation but is not the setting for JC virus reactivation and PML; the disease requires substantial cellular immunodeficiency.
incorrectas.D: Controlled hypertension carries no immunosuppression and is unrelated to JC virus reactivation.

preguntas.q: Which of the following best describes the typical clinical course of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy?

e.correcta: PML is rapidly progressive and usually fatal. JC virus lytically destroys oligodendrocytes, producing expanding, non-inflammatory demyelinating lesions and rapidly worsening deficits—visual loss (common), weakness, and dementia—over weeks to months. Because it occurs in immunocompromised hosts who cannot mount an effective response, outcomes are generally poor unless immune function can be restored.

incorrectas.B: PML is not reversible; the demyelination reflects irreversible destruction of oligodendrocytes, and progression is fast rather than slow.
incorrectas.C: PML does not self-resolve; without immune reconstitution it advances relentlessly to death.
incorrectas.D: A static course is the opposite of PML's aggressive, deteriorating trajectory.

preguntas.q: Osmotic demyelination syndrome, often triggered by overly rapid correction of hyponatremia, characteristically causes massive demyelination in which structure?

e.correcta: Osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis) targets the pons. When chronic hyponatremia is corrected too quickly, the brain—which had lowered its intracellular osmolytes to adapt—cannot re-accumulate them fast enough, so water shifts out of neurons and glia, shearing myelin. The densely packed, tightly myelinated fibers of the pons are especially vulnerable to this abrupt osmotic gradient.

incorrectas.A: The cerebellum is not the classic site; while extrapontine myelinolysis can occur, the hallmark lesion of ODS is central pontine.
incorrectas.C: The frontal cortex is gray matter and is not the characteristic target; ODS strikes the heavily myelinated pontine white matter.
incorrectas.D: The hippocampus is associated with anoxic/ischemic and seizure-related injury, not the osmotic myelinolysis that defines this syndrome.

preguntas.q: Osmotic demyelination syndrome most classically occurs in patients with which underlying condition?

e.correcta: ODS classically strikes severely malnourished patients, especially alcoholics and those with liver disease. These patients are prone to profound chronic hyponatremia and have depleted brain osmolytes, making the pons highly susceptible to injury when sodium is corrected too rapidly. Recognizing this risk group is why sodium must be raised slowly (no more than ~8 mEq/L per 24 hours).

incorrectas.B: Uncontrolled hypertension predisposes to hemorrhagic and lacunar strokes, not to the osmotic myelinolysis of ODS.
incorrectas.C: Chronic constipation has no relationship to sodium homeostasis or pontine demyelination.
incorrectas.D: Iron overload causes end-organ damage in the liver, heart, and pancreas (hemochromatosis) but is unrelated to osmotic demyelination.

preguntas.q: A malnourished alcoholic develops acute paralysis, dysarthria, and dysphagia after rapid sodium correction. This presentation of osmotic demyelination syndrome is classically described as which syndrome?

e.correcta: Destruction of the pontine corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts produces 'locked-in' syndrome: quadriplegia with loss of voluntary facial, mouth, and tongue movement, while consciousness is preserved. Patients can typically communicate only through vertical eye movements and blinking. Other features include dysarthria, dysphagia, diplopia, and depressed consciousness in severe cases.

incorrectas.B: Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome results from posterior inferior cerebellar artery/vertebral occlusion, causing crossed sensory loss, vertigo, and dysphagia—not the pontine quadriplegia of ODS.
incorrectas.C: Horner syndrome is a triad of ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis from disrupted sympathetic innervation, unrelated to central pontine demyelination.
incorrectas.D: Guillain-Barré is an acute ascending peripheral demyelinating polyneuropathy; ODS is a central (CNS) demyelinating lesion of the pons.

preguntas.q: Locked-in syndrome from stroke is most typically caused by occlusion of which artery?

e.correcta: Locked-in syndrome results from basilar artery occlusion, which infarcts the ventral pons. This damages the pons, medulla, lower midbrain, corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, ocular cranial nerve nuclei, and the PPRF, producing quadriplegia with preserved consciousness. The basilar artery supplies the pontine base, so its occlusion selectively destroys the descending motor pathways while sparing the dorsal reticular activating system.

incorrectas.B: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial frontal and parietal cortex; its occlusion causes contralateral leg-predominant weakness, not pontine locked-in syndrome.
incorrectas.C: The middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral cortex, causing face/arm-predominant weakness and aphasia—cortical, not brainstem, deficits.
incorrectas.D: The PICA supplies the lateral medulla (Wallenberg syndrome); it does not infarct the ventral pons responsible for locked-in syndrome.

preguntas.q: Locked-in syndrome presents with loss of voluntary facial, mouth, and tongue movement together with which motor finding?

e.correcta: Locked-in syndrome causes quadriplegia because the ventral pontine lesion destroys the corticospinal tracts bilaterally, cutting off voluntary motor output to all four limbs. Simultaneous corticobulbar tract damage abolishes voluntary control of the face, mouth, and tongue. The patient is fully awake but almost completely paralyzed, able to move only the eyes vertically and to blink.

incorrectas.B: Isolated monoparesis reflects a small focal cortical or peripheral lesion, not the bilateral tract destruction that produces global paralysis in locked-in syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Hemiballismus is a wild flinging movement from a subthalamic nucleus lesion—a hyperkinetic basal ganglia sign, opposite to the paralysis of locked-in syndrome.
incorrectas.D: A resting tremor is a hallmark of Parkinsonism (basal ganglia/nigrostriatal pathology), unrelated to the corticospinal tract injury here.

preguntas.q: In a patient with locked-in syndrome, which movements typically remain possible?

e.correcta: Patients with locked-in syndrome retain vertical eye movements and blinking, which serve as their only means of communication. The ventral pontine lesion spares the midbrain centers controlling vertical gaze, while horizontal gaze is lost because the pontine PPRF and CN VI/III connections are destroyed. This preserved vertical gaze and blinking, combined with intact awareness, defines the syndrome.

incorrectas.A: Horizontal eye movement is lost due to damage to the PPRF (horizontal gaze center) and abducens pathways in the pons, so it is precisely the movement that is abolished.
incorrectas.C: Finger flexion requires intact corticospinal output, which is destroyed—hence the quadriplegia; voluntary limb movement is not possible.
incorrectas.D: Tongue protrusion depends on corticobulbar control of CN XII, which is disrupted, so voluntary tongue movement is lost.

preguntas.q: Despite near-total paralysis, patients with locked-in syndrome characteristically retain which of the following?

e.correcta: Consciousness is preserved in locked-in syndrome because the reticular activating system (RAS), located in the dorsal pons and midbrain tegmentum, is spared by the ventral pontine lesion. The patient is fully awake and aware but unable to move or speak. This dissociation—intact cognition trapped in a paralyzed body—is the defining and clinically crucial feature, distinguishing it from coma.

incorrectas.B: Voluntary limb movement is lost; the corticospinal tracts are destroyed, producing quadriplegia.
incorrectas.C: Speech is abolished because corticobulbar control of the bulbar muscles is disrupted, causing anarthria.
incorrectas.D: Horizontal gaze is lost due to PPRF damage; only vertical eye movement and blinking are preserved.

preguntas.q: Degeneration of neurons in which region of the brain characteristically produces dementia, as seen in Alzheimer disease?

e.correcta: Dementia arises from degeneration of cerebral cortex neurons, which subserve memory, language, judgment, and higher cognition. In Alzheimer disease, cortical atrophy—especially of the hippocampus and association cortices—accompanies neurofibrillary tangles and amyloid plaques, producing progressive global cognitive decline. This contrasts with subcortical structures whose degeneration yields movement disorders rather than dementia.

incorrectas.B: Basal ganglia degeneration produces movement disorders (e.g., Parkinson's, Huntington's), not the cortical cognitive loss that defines dementia.
incorrectas.C: Cerebellar degeneration causes ataxia, dysmetria, and coordination deficits, not dementia.
incorrectas.D: Anterior horn cell degeneration (as in ALS or polio) causes lower motor neuron weakness, with cognition typically spared.

preguntas.q: Degeneration of neurons in the brainstem and which other structure characteristically leads to movement disorders such as Parkinson's and Huntington's disease?

e.correcta: Movement disorders arise from degeneration of the basal ganglia (and associated brainstem nuclei), which regulate the initiation and modulation of movement. In Parkinson's, dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra degenerate; in Huntington's, GABAergic neurons of the caudate are lost. Disruption of these circuits produces the hypokinetic rigidity of Parkinson's or the hyperkinetic chorea of Huntington's.

incorrectas.B: Cortical neuron degeneration produces dementia (e.g., Alzheimer's), not the extrapyramidal movement abnormalities of basal ganglia disease.
incorrectas.C: The thalamus is a sensory relay; its degeneration is not the classic substrate of Parkinson's or Huntington's motor features.
incorrectas.D: The hippocampus governs memory formation; its loss causes amnestic dementia rather than a movement disorder.

preguntas.q: Decreased cognitive ability, memory, or function with intact consciousness best defines which of the following?

e.correcta: Dementia is defined as a decline in cognitive ability, memory, or function while consciousness (level of arousal/alertness) remains intact. This preserved consciousness is the key distinction from delirium, which involves a fluctuating, clouded sensorium. Dementia is typically chronic and progressive, reflecting underlying neurodegeneration.

incorrectas.A: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and consciousness, often reversible and triggered by illness or drugs—the impaired consciousness distinguishes it from dementia.
incorrectas.C: Coma is a state of profound unresponsiveness with loss of consciousness, the opposite of the preserved awareness in dementia.
incorrectas.D: Aphasia is a focal language deficit, not a global decline in cognition and memory; consciousness and other cognitive domains may be intact.

preguntas.q: What is the most common cause of dementia in the elderly?

e.correcta: Alzheimer disease is the most common cause of dementia in the elderly. It is characterized pathologically by extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau, with widespread cortical and hippocampal atrophy. Clinically it produces insidious, progressive memory loss beginning with short-term recall.

incorrectas.A: Vascular dementia is the second most common cause; it produces stepwise decline related to cumulative infarcts, but is less frequent than Alzheimer disease overall.
incorrectas.B: Lewy body dementia features fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism, and is less common than Alzheimer disease.
incorrectas.D: Frontotemporal dementia tends to occur at a younger age with early personality/behavioral or language changes and is far less common than Alzheimer disease.

preguntas.q: Which pattern best describes the onset and progression of memory loss in Alzheimer disease?

o.A: Slow onset, short-term loss progressing to long-term loss
o.B: Abrupt onset with immediate global amnesia
o.D: Rapidly progressive over days to weeks

e.correcta: Alzheimer disease has a slow, insidious onset with memory loss that begins with short-term (recent) memory and gradually progresses to involve long-term memory. This reflects early degeneration of the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex, which encode new memories, before spreading to broader association cortices. The gradual, continuous decline over years is a hallmark distinguishing it from vascular or rapidly progressive dementias.

incorrectas.B: Abrupt global amnesia suggests an acute event such as transient global amnesia or a strategic infarct, not the gradual course of Alzheimer disease.
incorrectas.C: Stepwise decline with discrete drops is characteristic of vascular dementia caused by recurrent infarcts, not the smooth progression of Alzheimer's.
incorrectas.D: Rapid progression over days to weeks points toward prion disease (Creutzfeldt-Jakob) rather than the slowly evolving Alzheimer disease.

preguntas.q: Are focal neurologic deficits typically present in early Alzheimer disease?

o.A: No, they are characteristically absent early
o.B: Yes, hemiparesis is an early sign
o.C: Yes, early cranial nerve palsies are typical
o.D: Yes, early sensory level loss is expected

e.correcta: Early Alzheimer disease characteristically lacks focal neurologic deficits—the presentation is a diffuse cognitive/memory decline without motor, sensory, or cranial nerve signs. This absence of focal findings is an important distinguishing feature from disorders like Parkinson's and Huntington's, which show prominent movement abnormalities, and from vascular dementia, where infarct-related focal deficits appear. Focal signs in Alzheimer's, if any, emerge only very late.

incorrectas.B: Hemiparesis indicates a focal motor tract lesion (e.g., stroke); it is not a feature of early Alzheimer disease, which spares the motor system initially.
incorrectas.C: Cranial nerve palsies point to focal brainstem or nerve pathology, not the diffuse cortical degeneration of early Alzheimer's.
incorrectas.D: A sensory level suggests a spinal cord lesion; this focal finding is unrelated to the global cortical process of Alzheimer disease.

preguntas.q: The overwhelming majority (>90%) of Alzheimer disease cases fall into which category?

e.correcta: More than 90% of Alzheimer disease is sporadic and late-onset, arising in elderly patients without a single identifiable Mendelian mutation; incidence roughly doubles every 5 years after age 60. The strongest genetic risk factor in this sporadic group is the ε4 allele of ApoE on chromosome 19, but this is a risk modifier rather than a deterministic mutation.

incorrectas.B: Autosomal dominant familial Alzheimer accounts for only about 5-10% of cases; it involves highly penetrant mutations (APP, presenilin-1, presenilin-2) and presents at a much earlier age than the common sporadic form.
incorrectas.C: Down syndrome greatly raises Alzheimer risk (due to an extra copy of the APP gene on chromosome 21), but trisomy 21 patients are a small minority of all Alzheimer cases, not the >90% majority.
incorrectas.D: Prion disease (e.g., Creutzfeldt-Jakob) is a separate, rapidly progressive dementia caused by misfolded PrP protein and spongiform change, entirely distinct from the amyloid/tau pathology of Alzheimer disease.

preguntas.q: Compared with sporadic Alzheimer disease, familial cases (roughly 10%) typically present with what feature?

e.correcta: Familial (autosomal dominant) Alzheimer disease is driven by highly penetrant mutations in APP, presenilin-1, or presenilin-2 that accelerate amyloid-β generation, so symptoms appear at an earlier age—often in the 40s or 50s—than the typical elderly sporadic case. Recognizing early-onset dementia with a strong family history should prompt consideration of these inherited mutations.

incorrectas.A: A later age of onset is characteristic of the common sporadic form, whose risk climbs steeply with advancing age; the inherited mutations do the opposite by front-loading amyloid accumulation.
incorrectas.C: The ages are not identical—the defining clinical distinction of familial Alzheimer is precisely its earlier presentation relative to sporadic disease.
incorrectas.D: Familial Alzheimer still produces progressive cortical dementia; a pure movement disorder without dementia points instead to conditions like Parkinson or Huntington disease.

preguntas.q: Patients with which chromosomal disorder have a markedly increased, early risk of developing Alzheimer disease?

e.correcta: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) carries three copies of the APP gene, which resides on chromosome 21; the extra gene dosage means more amyloid precursor protein and more amyloid-β deposition over time, so nearly all these patients develop Alzheimer pathology by middle age. This directly links the location of APP to the pathogenesis of Alzheimer disease.

incorrectas.A: Turner syndrome (45,XO) causes short stature, streak ovaries, and cardiovascular anomalies such as coarctation, but it does not carry the extra chromosome 21 dosage that drives amyloid accumulation.
incorrectas.B: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) produces hypogonadism and tall stature from an extra X chromosome; it does not increase APP gene dosage or accelerate Alzheimer pathology.
incorrectas.D: Fragile X results from a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in FMR1 on the X chromosome, causing intellectual disability and macroorchidism, not the trisomy-21 amyloid mechanism.

preguntas.q: By approximately what age do most individuals with Down syndrome develop Alzheimer disease?

e.correcta: Because the extra copy of chromosome 21 provides an additional APP gene, amyloid-β accumulates faster in Down syndrome, and nearly all patients show Alzheimer pathology and clinical decline by about age 40. This decades-earlier onset compared with the general population underscores how gene dosage of APP accelerates the disease.

incorrectas.A: Age 20 is too early—significant amyloid plaque burden and clinical dementia have generally not yet developed, even with the extra APP copy accelerating the process.
incorrectas.C: Age 60 corresponds to when sporadic Alzheimer risk begins climbing in the general population, but Down syndrome patients characteristically present roughly two decades sooner.
incorrectas.D: Age 80 reflects typical late sporadic disease; the whole point of the Down syndrome association is that dementia appears far earlier, around 40.

preguntas.q: Mutations in which pair of genes are classically associated with familial (early-onset) Alzheimer disease?

e.correcta: Autosomal dominant familial Alzheimer is linked to mutations in presenilin-1 and presenilin-2, which are catalytic components of the γ-secretase complex; abnormal γ-secretase activity increases production of the aggregation-prone amyloid-β 42 fragment. Along with APP mutations, these presenilin defects drive the accelerated amyloid deposition and early-onset dementia of familial disease.

incorrectas.B: Huntingtin (CAG repeat expansion) and ataxins cause Huntington disease and spinocerebellar ataxias—trinucleotide repeat movement disorders, not the amyloid-driven pathology of Alzheimer.
incorrectas.C: SOD1 and TDP-43 mutations are associated with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (and TDP-43 with frontotemporal dementia), not with familial Alzheimer disease.
incorrectas.D: MECP2 mutations cause Rett syndrome and FMR1 expansions cause fragile X; neither relates to the γ-secretase/amyloid pathway of familial Alzheimer.

preguntas.q: On gross examination, the brain in Alzheimer disease characteristically shows what change to the cerebral cortex?

e.correcta: Progressive neuronal loss in Alzheimer disease produces diffuse cortical atrophy, most pronounced in the hippocampus and temporal/parietal association cortices. This shrinkage manifests as narrowed gyri, widened sulci, and compensatory ventricular enlargement (hydrocephalus ex vacuo).

incorrectas.B: Cortical hypertrophy with thickened gyri is the opposite of what occurs; Alzheimer is a neurodegenerative, atrophic process, not one of tissue overgrowth.
incorrectas.C: Focal hemorrhagic necrosis suggests infarction or a vascular event, whereas Alzheimer atrophy is diffuse and non-hemorrhagic, reflecting slow neuronal dropout.
incorrectas.D: Cerebellar vermis degeneration is seen in chronic alcohol use and paraneoplastic syndromes; Alzheimer preferentially targets the cerebral cortex and hippocampus, sparing the cerebellum.

preguntas.q: The cortical atrophy of Alzheimer disease produces what characteristic change in the sulci?

e.correcta: As cortical neurons are lost, brain volume decreases and the sulci (grooves) widen while the intervening gyri narrow. This sulcal widening, together with ventricular enlargement, is the hallmark gross imaging finding of Alzheimer-related atrophy.

incorrectas.A: Effacement (flattening) of sulci indicates the opposite process—cerebral edema or increased intracranial pressure that compresses the grooves, not the tissue loss of Alzheimer.
incorrectas.C: Calcification of sulci is not a feature of Alzheimer; intracranial calcifications occur in conditions such as congenital infections or certain tumors.
incorrectas.D: The sulci definitely change—their widening is precisely the visible consequence of the underlying cortical atrophy.

preguntas.q: The atrophy of Alzheimer disease produces what corresponding change in the gyri?

e.correcta: Loss of cortical neurons thins the gyri, so they appear narrowed while the sulci between them widen. This combination of narrow gyri and wide sulci is the classic gross picture of neurodegenerative cortical atrophy in Alzheimer disease.

incorrectas.B: Broadening of gyri would imply added cortical tissue, the reverse of the atrophic neuronal loss that defines Alzheimer.
incorrectas.C: Polymicrogyria (many small, abnormal gyri) is a developmental malformation of cortical formation, not an acquired degenerative change in an elderly brain.
incorrectas.D: Lissencephaly (smooth brain lacking gyri) is a congenital neuronal migration defect; Alzheimer gyri are narrowed but still present, not absent.

preguntas.q: What type of hydrocephalus is characteristically seen in Alzheimer disease?

e.correcta: Hydrocephalus ex vacuo is passive ventricular dilation that follows loss of surrounding brain parenchyma; as Alzheimer atrophy destroys cortical tissue, the ventricles enlarge to fill the space. Crucially, CSF pressure is normal here—the ventriculomegaly is a consequence of atrophy, not of impaired CSF flow.

incorrectas.B: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is an active accumulation of CSF causing the triad of gait apraxia, urinary incontinence, and dementia; it is treatable with shunting, unlike the passive ex vacuo dilation of Alzheimer.
incorrectas.C: Noncommunicating hydrocephalus results from a physical obstruction of CSF flow (e.g., aqueductal stenosis) and raises intracranial pressure, whereas Alzheimer ventricular enlargement occurs at normal pressure without obstruction.
incorrectas.D: Communicating hydrocephalus from meningitis reflects impaired CSF resorption at the arachnoid granulations after inflammation, a different mechanism from the atrophy-driven enlargement of Alzheimer.

preguntas.q: Which histologic feature, found in the gray matter, is characteristic of Alzheimer disease?

e.correcta: Alzheimer disease is defined histologically by extracellular neuritic (senile) plaques in the gray matter, composed of a central core of amyloid-β surrounded by dystrophic neuritic processes, alongside intracellular neurofibrillary tangles. These plaques reflect the abnormal aggregation of amyloid-β cleaved from APP.

incorrectas.B: Lewy bodies are intracytoplasmic α-synuclein aggregates seen in Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies, not the extracellular amyloid plaques of Alzheimer.
incorrectas.C: Negri bodies are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions found in neurons infected with rabies virus, unrelated to Alzheimer pathology.
incorrectas.D: Spongiform vacuolation of the neuropil is the hallmark of prion diseases such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob, a distinct cause of rapidly progressive dementia.

preguntas.q: The neuritic plaques of Alzheimer disease are composed primarily of which substance?

e.correcta: Neuritic (senile) plaques are extracellular deposits of amyloid-β (Aβ) surrounded by entangled dystrophic neuritic processes. Aβ is generated when amyloid precursor protein is cleaved by β- and γ-secretase, producing an aggregation-prone peptide that deposits in the cortex and, when in vessel walls, causes cerebral amyloid angiopathy predisposing to lobar hemorrhage.

incorrectas.B: Hyperphosphorylated tau is the component of the intracellular neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer, not of the extracellular neuritic plaques—the two lesions are distinct.
incorrectas.C: α-synuclein forms Lewy bodies in Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies, not the amyloid plaques of Alzheimer.
incorrectas.D: Prion protein (PrPsc) accumulates in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and can form amyloid-like plaques, but it is not the constituent of Alzheimer's neuritic plaques.

preguntas.q: Amyloid precursor protein (APP) is normally cleaved by which pathway, yielding a non-pathogenic product?

e.correcta: In the normal (non-amyloidogenic) pathway, APP is cleaved by α-secretase, which cuts within the amyloid-β region and therefore precludes formation of an intact, aggregation-prone Aβ peptide. The resulting soluble fragment is harmless, so α-cleavage is the protective default processing route.

incorrectas.B: Beta (β-secretase) cleavage is the pathogenic pathway: cutting at the β site, followed by γ-secretase, releases the full amyloid-β peptide that aggregates into plaques.
incorrectas.C: Caspase cleavage relates to apoptotic protein processing and is not the physiologic route of APP metabolism that determines amyloid formation.
incorrectas.D: Calpain is a calcium-dependent protease involved in various cellular processes but is not the secretase responsible for the benign versus amyloidogenic fate of APP.

preguntas.q: Cleavage of APP by which enzyme produces the amyloid-β peptide that aggregates in Alzheimer disease?

e.correcta: When APP is cleaved by β-secretase (BACE1) and then γ-secretase, the intact amyloid-β peptide is released; this fragment misfolds and aggregates into the neuritic plaques of Alzheimer disease. This amyloidogenic route contrasts with α-secretase cleavage, which cuts within the Aβ sequence and prevents plaque-forming peptide from being generated.

incorrectas.B: Alpha (α-secretase) cleavage is the non-amyloidogenic pathway; by cutting within the amyloid-β domain it precludes formation of an intact Aβ peptide.
incorrectas.C: Neprilysin is a protease that degrades amyloid-β and helps clear it, so it reduces rather than produces amyloid burden.
incorrectas.D: Insulin-degrading enzyme also participates in amyloid-β clearance/degradation; it does not generate the pathogenic peptide from APP.

preguntas.q: The tau protein that aggregates into neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer disease normally functions as what kind of protein?

o.C: A motor protein for vesicle transport

e.correcta: Tau is normally a microtubule-associated protein that stabilizes the microtubule cytoskeleton and supports axonal transport in neurons. In Alzheimer disease it becomes hyperphosphorylated, detaches from microtubules, and aggregates into intracellular neurofibrillary tangles, losing its stabilizing function and disrupting the neuron.

incorrectas.B: Intermediate filament proteins (e.g., neurofilaments, GFAP) form a separate cytoskeletal system; tau specifically binds and stabilizes microtubules rather than intermediate filaments.
incorrectas.C: Motor proteins such as kinesin and dynein actively transport vesicles along microtubules; tau does not generate movement, it stabilizes the tracks themselves.
incorrectas.D: Synaptic vesicle membrane proteins like synaptophysin function in neurotransmitter release; tau is a cytoskeletal-associated protein, not a vesicle membrane component.

preguntas.q: The number of neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer disease correlates most closely with the degree of what?

e.correcta: The burden of intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (hyperphosphorylated tau) tracks with the severity of cognitive decline in Alzheimer disease, making tangle density a better correlate of dementia than plaque count. This reflects that tau pathology closely mirrors the neuronal dysfunction and loss driving clinical deterioration.

incorrectas.B: Cerebellar ataxia arises from cerebellar pathology; Alzheimer preferentially affects the cortex and hippocampus and does not characteristically cause ataxia.
incorrectas.C: Peripheral neuropathy is a disorder of peripheral nerves (e.g., from diabetes or B12 deficiency), unrelated to the central cortical tau pathology of Alzheimer.
incorrectas.D: Resting tremor is a cardinal feature of Parkinson disease, tied to nigrostriatal dopamine loss, not to cortical neurofibrillary tangle burden.

preguntas.q: Alzheimer disease is characterized by an alteration in which neurotransmitter, providing the rationale for its pharmacologic treatment?

e.correcta: Alzheimer disease features a marked decrease in acetylcholine due to degeneration of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert and hippocampus, regions rich in cholinergic signaling important for memory. This deficit is why acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) are used to boost synaptic acetylcholine and modestly improve cognition.

incorrectas.B: Decreased dopamine (from substantia nigra degeneration) characterizes Parkinson disease and its motor symptoms, not the cholinergic memory deficit of Alzheimer.
incorrectas.C: Glutamate is targeted in Alzheimer therapy via the NMDA antagonist memantine to limit excitotoxicity, but the disease is not defined by increased glutamate synthesis; the core neurotransmitter loss is cholinergic.
incorrectas.D: Decreased GABA is a feature of Huntington disease, where loss of striatal GABAergic neurons produces chorea, distinct from the acetylcholine deficit of Alzheimer.

preguntas.q: A definitive diagnosis of Alzheimer disease is established by what method?

e.correcta: A definitive diagnosis of Alzheimer requires histologic confirmation of neuritic plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, which in practice is achieved at autopsy. During life the diagnosis is presumptive—made clinically after excluding reversible and alternative causes of dementia.

incorrectas.B: Serum amyloid-β is not a validated confirmatory test; blood levels do not reliably reflect the cortical plaque and tangle pathology that defines the disease.
incorrectas.C: Head CT during life may show atrophy and help exclude other causes (tumor, hydrocephalus, infarcts), but atrophy is nonspecific and cannot confirm the microscopic hallmark lesions.
incorrectas.D: ApoE4 genotyping identifies a risk factor for sporadic Alzheimer, not a diagnostic marker; many carriers never develop disease and many patients are non-carriers.

preguntas.q: Which type of dementia results from multiple arterial infarcts and/or chronic ischemia (e.g., from hypertension, atherosclerosis, or vasculitis)?

e.correcta: Vascular dementia is caused by cumulative brain injury from multiple infarcts or chronic hypoperfusion, with major risk factors being hypertension, atherosclerosis, and vasculitis. It is the second most common cause of dementia and characteristically produces a stepwise decline tied to discrete ischemic events.

incorrectas.B: Alzheimer dementia is a primary neurodegenerative disease driven by amyloid plaques and tau tangles with gradual decline, not by discrete vascular infarcts.
incorrectas.C: Lewy body dementia is defined by α-synuclein Lewy bodies and features fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism—not an ischemic, vascular mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Frontotemporal dementia arises from focal frontal/temporal degeneration (tau or TDP-43) causing behavioral or language changes, unrelated to arterial infarcts.

preguntas.q: Vascular dementia classically causes a stepwise cognitive decline with what timing of memory impairment relative to Alzheimer disease?

o.C: No memory impairment at any stage
o.D: Simultaneous global memory loss from onset

e.correcta: Vascular dementia typically produces a stepwise decline reflecting successive infarcts, with memory impairment tending to appear relatively late; early deficits often involve executive function and processing speed instead. This contrasts with Alzheimer disease, where insidious, gradually progressive memory loss is an early and prominent feature.

incorrectas.B: Early-onset memory impairment is more characteristic of Alzheimer disease, whose hippocampal pathology impairs new memory formation from the outset.
incorrectas.C: Vascular dementia does eventually impair memory; it simply tends to do so later than Alzheimer, so "no memory impairment" is incorrect.
incorrectas.D: The decline in vascular dementia is stepwise and patchy rather than a simultaneous global loss, mirroring the discrete territories damaged by individual infarcts.

preguntas.q: What is the second most common cause of dementia in the elderly?

e.correcta: Vascular dementia is the second most common cause of dementia in older adults, after Alzheimer disease. It stems from cerebrovascular injury (multiple infarcts, chronic ischemia) and is strongly associated with hypertension and atherosclerosis, making risk-factor control an important preventive strategy.

incorrectas.B: Alzheimer disease is the single most common cause of dementia, so it ranks first, not second.
incorrectas.C: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a rare prion disorder causing rapidly progressive dementia; it accounts for a very small fraction of cases, not the second-leading cause.
incorrectas.D: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is an important reversible cause of dementia but is far less common than vascular dementia and does not rank second overall.

preguntas.q: On MRI or CT, vascular dementia is characterized by the presence of what finding?

o.C: Caudate atrophy with ex vacuo dilation of the frontal horns

e.correcta: Neuroimaging in vascular dementia shows multiple cortical and/or subcortical infarcts, reflecting the cumulative ischemic injury responsible for the stepwise decline. Identifying these lesions on MRI or CT helps distinguish vascular dementia from the diffuse atrophy of Alzheimer disease.

incorrectas.B: Symmetric hippocampal atrophy is more suggestive of Alzheimer disease, reflecting its predilection for memory-related structures rather than discrete vascular infarcts.
incorrectas.C: Caudate atrophy with dilated frontal horns (the "boxcar" ventricles) is the imaging signature of Huntington disease, not vascular dementia.
incorrectas.D: Cerebellar tonsillar herniation is an acute finding of raised intracranial pressure or a Chiari malformation, unrelated to the multifocal infarcts of vascular dementia.

preguntas.q: Which ubiquitinated inclusion may be seen histologically in frontotemporal dementia (Pick disease)?

e.correcta: Frontotemporal dementia (Pick disease) can show ubiquitinated TDP-43 inclusions, in addition to the classic tau-positive Pick bodies. This TDP-43 pathology overlaps with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, which is why FTD may co-occur with an ALS-like motor disorder.

incorrectas.B: Amyloid-β plaques are the extracellular hallmark of Alzheimer disease, not a feature of frontotemporal dementia.
incorrectas.C: Lewy bodies are α-synuclein aggregates seen in Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies; frontotemporal dementia is instead characterized by tau or TDP-43 pathology.
incorrectas.D: Cowdry A intranuclear inclusions are seen with herpesvirus infection and certain other conditions, not in the degenerative process of frontotemporal dementia.

preguntas.q: In addition to behavioral and language changes, frontotemporal dementia may be associated with which category of accompanying disorder?

e.correcta: Frontotemporal dementia can be accompanied by movement disorders, including parkinsonism and an ALS-like syndrome with combined upper and lower motor neuron degeneration. This reflects shared underlying tau or TDP-43 pathology that can extend into motor pathways beyond the frontal and temporal lobes.

incorrectas.B: Peripheral sensory neuropathy involves the peripheral nerves and is characteristic of metabolic or toxic causes; it is not the classic motor-predominant association of frontotemporal dementia.
incorrectas.C: Optic neuritis is an inflammatory demyelinating lesion of the optic nerve seen in multiple sclerosis, unrelated to the degenerative movement features of frontotemporal dementia.
incorrectas.D: Isolated autonomic dysfunction points to conditions like multiple system atrophy; frontotemporal dementia's classic association is with parkinsonism and ALS-type motor neuron disease, not autonomic-only failure.

preguntas.q: On gross examination, Parkinson disease is characterized by what change in the substantia nigra pars compacta?

e.correcta: Parkinson disease causes loss of the dopaminergic, neuromelanin-containing neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta, so the normally dark structure appears grossly depigmented (pale). This nigral cell loss reduces dopaminergic input to the striatum, producing the resting tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia of the disease.

incorrectas.B: Hyperpigmentation is the opposite of what occurs; the neuromelanin-bearing neurons are being destroyed, so the region loses its dark color rather than gaining it.
incorrectas.C: Cystic cavitation indicates prior infarction or tissue necrosis, not the selective neuronal dropout that pales the substantia nigra in Parkinson disease.
incorrectas.D: Calcification of basal ganglia structures occurs in disorders such as Fahr disease or hypoparathyroidism, not as the gross hallmark of Parkinson disease.

preguntas.q: What is the single greatest risk factor for developing Parkinson disease?

e.correcta: Aging is the strongest risk factor for Parkinson disease, which affects roughly 2% of older adults, as cumulative loss of substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons compounds over time. While genetic and environmental factors contribute, advancing age is the dominant driver of incidence.

incorrectas.B: Female sex is not the major risk factor; if anything Parkinson disease is somewhat more common in men, and age far outweighs sex as a determinant.
incorrectas.C: Hypertension is a key risk factor for vascular dementia and stroke, but it is not the principal risk factor for the neurodegenerative process of Parkinson disease.
incorrectas.D: Cigarette smoking is actually associated epidemiologically with a lower risk of Parkinson disease, making it the opposite of a risk factor.

preguntas.q: A cluster of young adults developed rapid-onset parkinsonism after using a synthetic street drug. Which contaminant is historically responsible for this drug-induced Parkinson disease?

e.correcta: MPTP (1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine) is a byproduct of illicit meperidine-analog synthesis that is taken up by dopaminergic neurons and oxidized by MAO-B to MPP+. MPP+ inhibits complex I of the electron transport chain, selectively destroying the substantia nigra pars compacta and producing rapid, irreversible parkinsonism. This accident became a landmark model for studying Parkinson pathophysiology.

incorrectas.B: Chronic manganese exposure (as in welders or miners) does cause a parkinsonian syndrome, but it targets the globus pallidus rather than the substantia nigra and is an occupational, not illicit-drug, exposure.
incorrectas.C: Carbon monoxide poisoning can produce delayed parkinsonism through bilateral globus pallidus necrosis, but it is a toxic gas exposure, not a contaminant of illicit drugs.
incorrectas.D: Rotenone is a pesticide and complex I inhibitor used experimentally to model Parkinson disease in animals, but it is not the historical illicit-drug contaminant that caused human cases.

preguntas.q: Which movement disorder is characterized by uncontrolled shaking of the distal extremities at rest that improves with intentional, purposeful movement?

e.correcta: A resting tremor is most prominent when the limb is relaxed and supported, and it characteristically dampens or disappears with voluntary movement. The classic example is the 4-6 Hz pill-rolling tremor of the hands in Parkinson disease, which reflects dysfunction of the nigrostriatal dopaminergic pathway and basal ganglia.

incorrectas.A: An intention tremor is the opposite pattern: it is absent at rest and worsens as the hand approaches a target, reflecting cerebellar dysfunction rather than basal ganglia disease.
incorrectas.C: Essential tremor is a postural/action tremor that appears when holding a posture or acting, often improves with alcohol, and is worsened (not relieved) by movement, distinguishing it from a resting tremor.
incorrectas.D: Asterixis is not a true tremor but a negative myoclonus (brief lapses in posture) seen with metabolic encephalopathies such as hepatic failure, not a rest-predominant shaking relieved by movement.

preguntas.q: In the neurotransmitter imbalance of Parkinson disease, the level of acetylcholine is best described as which of the following?

e.correcta: Parkinson disease involves loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, which normally inhibit striatal cholinergic interneurons. With dopamine reduced, this cholinergic activity is released from inhibition, so acetylcholine is relatively increased. This dopamine-low/ACh-high imbalance explains why anticholinergics (e.g., benztropine) help tremor, especially in younger patients.

incorrectas.B: Acetylcholine is not decreased in Parkinson disease; decreased cholinergic tone is instead a feature of Alzheimer disease, which is why cholinesterase inhibitors are used there.
incorrectas.C: The neurotransmitter balance is not preserved; the whole basis of Parkinson pharmacology is the relative rise in acetylcholine accompanying the fall in dopamine.
incorrectas.D: Acetylcholine is relatively elevated, not eliminated; cholinergic interneurons remain functional and are in fact overactive due to loss of dopaminergic inhibition.

preguntas.q: The core neurochemical deficit responsible for the motor symptoms of Parkinson disease is a change in which neurotransmitter?

e.correcta: Parkinson disease is defined by progressive degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, causing decreased dopamine delivery to the striatum. Loss of this nigrostriatal input disrupts the direct and indirect basal ganglia pathways, producing bradykinesia, rigidity, and resting tremor. Treatment centers on restoring dopamine with levodopa/carbidopa.

incorrectas.A: Dopamine is decreased, not increased; excess dopaminergic signaling is instead associated with conditions like Huntington disease and with the hyperkinetic side effects of Parkinson therapy.
incorrectas.C: Altered GABA is central to Huntington disease (loss of GABAergic striatal neurons), not the defining lesion of Parkinson disease.
incorrectas.D: Glutamate excitotoxicity is a mechanism emphasized in Huntington disease and other neurodegeneration, not the primary neurochemical deficit driving Parkinson motor signs.

preguntas.q: Beyond dopamine loss, Parkinson disease is also associated with which change in serotonin levels, contributing to nonmotor symptoms such as depression?

e.correcta: Parkinson disease causes decreased serotonin in addition to decreased dopamine, reflecting degeneration that extends beyond the nigrostriatal system to include serotonergic raphe nuclei. This helps explain the high prevalence of depression and other nonmotor features in Parkinson patients. The overall picture is one of low dopamine, low serotonin, and relatively high acetylcholine.

incorrectas.A: Serotonin is reduced, not increased; a rise in serotonergic tone is not a feature of Parkinson pathology and would not explain its depressive symptoms.
incorrectas.B: Serotonin does not remain at normal levels; its decline is part of the widespread monoaminergic depletion in Parkinson disease.
incorrectas.D: There is no marked elevation of serotonin; the disease is characterized by depletion of multiple monoamines including serotonin.

preguntas.q: In classic Parkinson disease, dementia most characteristically emerges at which point in the clinical course?

e.correcta: In Parkinson disease, cognitive decline and dementia typically appear late, after years of established motor symptoms. This temporal sequence is a key distinguishing feature from dementia with Lewy bodies, where dementia precedes or coincides with parkinsonism. By convention, when dementia follows established Parkinson disease by at least a year, it is termed Parkinson disease dementia.

incorrectas.A: Dementia preceding motor symptoms is the hallmark of dementia with Lewy bodies, not classic Parkinson disease, in which motor signs come first.
incorrectas.C: Cognitive impairment developing at the same time as the tremor points toward Lewy body dementia; in Parkinson disease the motor and cognitive features are separated by years.
incorrectas.D: Dementia does eventually develop in a substantial fraction of long-standing Parkinson patients, so saying it never occurs is incorrect.

preguntas.q: An elderly patient develops progressive dementia early in his course, accompanied by parkinsonian features and visual hallucinations. Which diagnosis is most likely?

e.correcta: Dementia with Lewy bodies is defined by early dementia that develops before or within a year of parkinsonism, along with characteristic fluctuating cognition and vivid visual hallucinations. This early cognitive onset is precisely what distinguishes it from Parkinson disease, where dementia appears only late. The pathology is intracellular alpha-synuclein (Lewy body) aggregation involving the cortex.

incorrectas.B: In Parkinson disease dementia the motor disease clearly precedes cognitive decline by years, whereas here dementia and parkinsonism emerge together, favoring Lewy body dementia.
incorrectas.C: Alzheimer disease presents with early memory loss but not the prominent early parkinsonism and visual hallucinations, and it lacks cortical Lewy bodies as its defining lesion.
incorrectas.D: Vascular dementia produces stepwise decline linked to cerebrovascular events and focal deficits, not the fluctuating cognition, hallucinations, and parkinsonism of Lewy body dementia.

preguntas.q: In dementia with Lewy bodies, the intracellular Lewy bodies are found predominantly in which region of the brain?

e.correcta: In dementia with Lewy bodies, alpha-synuclein aggregates (Lewy bodies) are distributed diffusely throughout the cerebral cortex, which correlates with the prominent early cognitive impairment. This cortical distribution contrasts with Parkinson disease, where Lewy bodies are concentrated in subcortical structures such as the substantia nigra. The cortical burden is what drives the dementia-predominant presentation.

incorrectas.A: Concentration of Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra is characteristic of Parkinson disease, whose motor-first presentation reflects that subcortical, nigrostriatal involvement.
incorrectas.B: The cerebellar cortex is not the site of Lewy body accumulation; cerebellar pathology would produce ataxia and intention tremor, not the cognitive syndrome described.
incorrectas.D: Anterior horn cell pathology characterizes motor neuron disease (e.g., ALS), not the cortical alpha-synuclein deposition of Lewy body dementia.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of Huntington disease?

e.correcta: Huntington disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene on chromosome 4. Because a single mutant allele is sufficient to cause disease, each child of an affected parent has a 50% risk. The expanded polyglutamine tract produces a toxic gain-of-function huntingtin protein.

incorrectas.A: Autosomal recessive inheritance would require two mutant alleles and typically skip generations, which does not match Huntington's vertical transmission from a single affected parent.
incorrectas.B: X-linked recessive inheritance predominantly affects males and is transmitted through carrier mothers, whereas Huntington affects both sexes equally and is passed by either parent.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance is transmitted exclusively through the mother to all offspring, unlike the autosomal, either-parent pattern of Huntington disease.

preguntas.q: Further expansion of the CAG repeats in Huntington disease, causing anticipation in offspring, occurs predominantly during which process in affected males?

e.correcta: In Huntington disease, the unstable CAG repeat tends to expand further during spermatogenesis, so paternal transmission is associated with larger repeat numbers in offspring. Because a greater repeat count correlates with earlier and more severe disease, children who inherit the mutation from their father often present at a younger age. This progressive worsening across generations is called anticipation.

incorrectas.B: Repeat expansion is comparatively stable during oogenesis, so maternal transmission tends not to drive the marked anticipation seen with paternal inheritance.
incorrectas.C: Fertilization simply combines the parental gametes; the repeat instability arises during gamete formation, not at the moment of fertilization.
incorrectas.D: While somatic instability exists, the intergenerational expansion responsible for anticipation occurs in the germline during spermatogenesis, not in postmitotic neurons.

preguntas.q: Which hyperkinetic movement disorder is characterized by sudden, rapid, jerky, purposeless movements and is classically seen in Huntington disease?

e.correcta: Chorea consists of sudden, brief, jerky, purposeless movements that flow randomly from one body part to another, reflecting damage to the basal ganglia (especially the caudate). It is the hallmark movement disorder of Huntington disease and is also seen in Sydenham chorea following acute rheumatic fever. The shared feature is disruption of striatal circuitry that normally suppresses unwanted movement.

incorrectas.A: Athetosis refers to slow, continuous, writhing snake-like movements, which is a different tempo from the sudden, rapid jerks of chorea (though both can coexist in Huntington disease).
incorrectas.C: Myoclonus is a very brief, shock-like muscle twitch, not the flowing, dance-like, migrating movements that define chorea.
incorrectas.D: Dystonia involves sustained muscle co-contraction producing twisting postures and is not the fleeting, purposeless jerking that characterizes chorea.

preguntas.q: Which movement disorder is characterized by slow, continuous, writhing snake-like movements, especially of the fingers?

e.correcta: Athetosis describes slow, involuntary, writhing (snake-like) movements that are most conspicuous in the distal extremities such as the fingers, and it results from basal ganglia dysfunction. It can be seen in Huntington disease and often blends with chorea (choreoathetosis). The key descriptor is the slow, continuous, twisting quality that distinguishes it from faster hyperkinetic disorders.

incorrectas.A: Chorea consists of sudden, rapid, jerky movements rather than the slow, continuous writhing that defines athetosis, though the two frequently overlap.
incorrectas.B: Hemiballismus produces violent, large-amplitude flinging movements of one side of the body, classically from a subthalamic nucleus lesion, not slow distal writhing.
incorrectas.D: Tics are stereotyped, repetitive movements that can be briefly suppressed and are relieved by performance, unlike the involuntary continuous writhing of athetosis.

preguntas.q: The symptoms of Huntington disease most characteristically manifest within which age range?

e.correcta: Huntington disease classically becomes clinically apparent between ages 20 and 50, typically presenting in mid-adulthood with chorea, behavioral changes, and progressive cognitive decline. This adult onset, combined with autosomal dominant inheritance, means many patients have already had children before symptoms appear. Larger CAG repeat expansions shift onset earlier within (and occasionally before) this window.

incorrectas.B: Onset in early childhood is atypical; juvenile Huntington (Westphal variant) is uncommon and occurs with very large repeat expansions, not the usual presentation.
incorrectas.C: While symptoms can occasionally begin later, the characteristic window is mid-adulthood (20-50), not the 60-80 range typical of many other neurodegenerative dementias.
incorrectas.D: The 10-15 year range describes rare juvenile-onset disease rather than the typical adult manifestation between ages 20 and 50.

preguntas.q: Because early Huntington disease often presents with behavioral changes, irritability, and abnormal movements, it may initially be mistaken for which of the following?

e.correcta: Early Huntington disease frequently begins with psychiatric and behavioral disturbances such as irritability, personality change, and disinhibition, along with subtle involuntary movements. These features can be misattributed to substance abuse, particularly in a young adult before the family history or genetic diagnosis is recognized. Recognizing this pitfall helps avoid delayed diagnosis of an inherited neurodegenerative disease.

incorrectas.B: Multiple sclerosis presents with relapsing focal neurologic deficits (optic neuritis, sensory or motor symptoms) reflecting CNS demyelination, not the behavioral change and chorea that mimic substance abuse.
incorrectas.C: Migraine is an episodic headache disorder and would not produce the progressive behavioral and movement abnormalities of early Huntington disease.
incorrectas.D: Bell palsy is an acute peripheral facial nerve palsy, an entirely different presentation from the psychiatric and hyperkinetic features of early Huntington disease.

preguntas.q: The neurotransmitter changes in Huntington disease include which alteration in GABA?

e.correcta: Huntington disease preferentially destroys the GABAergic medium spiny neurons of the caudate and putamen, so GABA levels are decreased. Loss of these inhibitory striatal neurons disrupts the indirect pathway that normally suppresses unwanted movement, producing the characteristic chorea. The neurotransmitter profile is decreased GABA and acetylcholine with relatively increased dopamine.

incorrectas.A: GABA is decreased, not increased; a rise in inhibitory GABAergic tone would tend to reduce movement rather than cause the hyperkinetic chorea of Huntington disease.
incorrectas.C: GABA does not remain normal; degeneration of striatal GABAergic neurons is a defining biochemical feature of the disease.
incorrectas.D: GABA is not converted to glutamate in this process; rather the GABAergic neurons are lost, and glutamate excitotoxicity is a separate contributor to neuronal death.

preguntas.q: In addition to reduced GABA, Huntington disease is characterized by which change in acetylcholine?

e.correcta: In Huntington disease, striatal cholinergic interneurons are lost along with GABAergic neurons, so acetylcholine is decreased. This differs from Parkinson disease, where acetylcholine is relatively increased. The overall Huntington signature is low GABA, low acetylcholine, and relatively high dopamine, which underlies the hyperkinetic movements.

incorrectas.A: Increased acetylcholine is the pattern of Parkinson disease, not Huntington disease, and helps explain why the two disorders have opposite therapeutic approaches.
incorrectas.B: Acetylcholine is not preserved at normal levels; loss of striatal cholinergic interneurons reduces it as part of the neurodegeneration.
incorrectas.D: Acetylcholine is reduced but not entirely absent; some cholinergic signaling persists even as neurons are progressively lost.

preguntas.q: The relative neurotransmitter imbalance in Huntington disease includes which change in dopamine?

e.correcta: Huntington disease features a relative increase in dopamine, because the inhibitory GABAergic and cholinergic striatal neurons degenerate while dopaminergic input is comparatively preserved. This dopamine excess relative to the depleted inhibitory circuitry drives the hyperkinetic chorea. Accordingly, dopamine-depleting agents like tetrabenazine and dopamine antagonists are used to control the movements.

incorrectas.A: Decreased dopamine characterizes Parkinson disease and produces hypokinesia, the opposite of the hyperkinetic chorea of Huntington disease.
incorrectas.C: Dopamine is not simply unchanged; its relative excess compared with the lost GABA and acetylcholine is central to the movement disorder.
incorrectas.D: Dopamine is relatively increased, not undetectable; the nigrostriatal dopaminergic system is comparatively spared in Huntington disease.

preguntas.q: Neuronal death in Huntington disease is mediated in part by NMDA receptor binding and excitotoxicity from which neurotransmitter?

e.correcta: In Huntington disease, excessive glutamate acting on NMDA receptors drives calcium influx into striatal neurons, triggering excitotoxic cell death. This glutamate excitotoxicity, combined with the toxic mutant huntingtin protein, accounts for the selective loss of medium spiny neurons in the caudate and putamen. Excitotoxicity is a recurring mechanism of neurodegeneration on Step 1.

incorrectas.A: GABA is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter and its striatal neurons are the ones being destroyed; it does not cause excitotoxic death via NMDA receptors.
incorrectas.C: Glycine is an inhibitory neurotransmitter (and an NMDA co-agonist), but the primary excitotoxic driver here is glutamate acting on NMDA receptors.
incorrectas.D: Serotonin modulates mood and other functions but is not the excitatory transmitter responsible for NMDA-mediated excitotoxicity in Huntington disease.

preguntas.q: The caudate and putamen atrophy of Huntington disease produces which type of ventricular enlargement on imaging?

o.D: Communicating hydrocephalus from impaired CSF absorption
