preguntas.q: Which component of GI innervation is capable of independently coordinating peristalsis and secretion even when extrinsic sympathetic and parasympathetic input is removed?

e.correcta: The enteric nervous system, organized into the myenteric and submucosal plexuses within the gut wall, functions as a self-contained network with its own sensory neurons, interneurons, and motor neurons capable of generating reflex peristalsis and secretory responses autonomously. Extrinsic sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers only modulate -- speed up or slow down -- this intrinsic activity rather than being required to initiate it, which is why isolated bowel segments can still contract rhythmically even without external innervation.

incorrectas.B: The somatic nervous system innervates skeletal muscle, such as the external anal sphincter, under voluntary control, and plays no role in coordinating the involuntary smooth muscle motility and secretion of the GI tract.
incorrectas.C: The sympathetic chain alone generally inhibits GI motility and secretion; it is not capable of generating the coordinated peristaltic reflex on its own -- that intrinsic coordinating capacity belongs to the enteric plexuses.
incorrectas.D: The vagus nerve enhances GI motility and secretion, but it works by modulating the enteric plexuses; when extrinsic innervation including the vagus is removed, the enteric nervous system alone still sustains basic gut function.

preguntas.q: Which enteric plexus, located between the mucosa and the muscularis, primarily regulates GI secretion and local mucosal blood flow?

e.correcta: The submucosal (Meissner) plexus lies within the submucosa, close to the epithelium and mucosal glands, positioning it to sense luminal conditions and regulate epithelial secretion, absorption, and local mucosal blood flow. This contrasts with the myenteric plexus, which sits between the muscle layers and is dedicated primarily to controlling motility.

incorrectas.A: The myenteric (Auerbach) plexus is located between the inner circular and outer longitudinal muscle layers and primarily governs motility (peristaltic contractions), not the secretory and mucosal blood flow functions of the submucosal plexus.
incorrectas.B: The celiac plexus is an extrinsic prevertebral sympathetic ganglion outside the gut wall that relays sympathetic outflow to abdominal viscera; it is not an intrinsic enteric plexus regulating local secretion.
incorrectas.D: The pelvic plexus carries parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic) and sympathetic fibers to pelvic organs and the hindgut; it is an extrinsic autonomic plexus, not the intrinsic submucosal plexus responsible for local secretomotor regulation.

preguntas.q: Which enteric plexus, situated between the inner circular and outer longitudinal muscle layers of the gut wall, primarily governs GI motility?

e.correcta: The myenteric (Auerbach) plexus lies between the inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle layers, a position that lets it directly coordinate the contractile activity of both layers to generate peristalsis -- increasing tone, contraction velocity, and rhythmic contraction rate. Loss of this plexus, as in Hirschsprung disease (from failure of neural crest cell migration), causes functional obstruction from absent peristalsis in the aganglionic segment.

incorrectas.A: The submucosal (Meissner) plexus is located in the submucosa, not between the muscle layers, and its main role is regulating secretion and blood flow rather than driving the muscular contractions of motility.
incorrectas.C: The hypogastric plexus is an extrinsic autonomic plexus carrying sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers to pelvic organs; it is not an intrinsic enteric plexus embedded in the gut wall muscle layers.
incorrectas.D: The celiac (solar) plexus is a prevertebral sympathetic ganglion supplying postganglionic fibers to abdominal viscera; it lies outside the gut wall and is not the intrinsic motility-controlling plexus found between the muscle layers.

preguntas.q: How does serum gastrin level typically change with chronic proton pump inhibitor (PPI) use?

o.A: It decreases due to feedback inhibition

e.correcta: Chronic PPI use profoundly reduces gastric acid secretion by irreversibly inhibiting the H+/K+-ATPase on parietal cells, raising intragastric pH. Because gastric acid normally suppresses gastrin release from G cells via negative feedback, this alkalinization removes that brake and drives compensatory hypergastrinemia -- which matters clinically because abrupt PPI withdrawal can unmask the built-up gastrin drive, causing rebound acid hypersecretion and reflux symptoms as previously blocked parietal cell pumps become overstimulated.

incorrectas.A: Gastrin does not decrease with PPI use; the physiology runs the opposite direction -- loss of acid-mediated negative feedback on G cells causes gastrin to rise, not fall.
incorrectas.B: Gastrin levels are not unchanged; chronic acid suppression is a potent, well-documented stimulus for increased gastrin secretion, significant enough to sometimes complicate the workup for a suspected gastrinoma.
incorrectas.D: Gastrin does not become undetectable; the opposite occurs -- PPI-induced hypochlorhydria is a classic cause of markedly elevated, not absent, serum gastrin.

preguntas.q: A patient with recurrent, atypical peptic ulcers and diarrhea is found to have a gastrin-secreting pancreatic/duodenal tumor (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome). How does serum gastrin in this condition compare to the mild elevation seen with chronic PPI use?

o.C: It remains normal, since the tumor is autonomous
o.D: It is decreased due to tumor consumption of gastrin

e.correcta: In Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, a gastrinoma autonomously secretes gastrin independent of normal feedback inhibition by gastric acid, producing gastrin levels that are markedly, often dramatically, elevated -- typically far higher than the modest rise seen with PPI-induced hypochlorhydria. This massive gastrin drive causes continuous parietal cell stimulation, leading to severe acid hypersecretion, multiple or atypically located peptic ulcers, and diarrhea from acid-mediated mucosal injury and enzyme inactivation.

incorrectas.B: PPI-induced hypergastrinemia is typically mild-to-moderate because it results from removal of a physiologic feedback brake, whereas a gastrinoma is an autonomous tumor unrestrained by any feedback, producing a substantially greater elevation -- a distinction used clinically to help separate the two.
incorrectas.C: Gastrin is far from normal in ZES; it is one of the defining biochemical features of the disease, used diagnostically (often with a secretin stimulation test) to confirm a gastrinoma.
incorrectas.D: Gastrinomas increase, not decrease, gastrin -- they are neuroendocrine tumors that actively oversecrete the hormone rather than consuming it.

preguntas.q: Abdominal pain in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome most directly results from which process caused by massive gastrin-driven acid hypersecretion?

o.A: Acute pancreatitis from pancreatic ductal obstruction
o.D: Peptic ulcer disease, including atypical distal ulcers

e.correcta: The extreme gastrin elevation in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome drives massive, continuous gastric acid hypersecretion that overwhelms mucosal defenses throughout the proximal GI tract, producing multiple, often refractory, and atypically distal peptic ulcers (extending beyond the duodenal bulb into the jejunum). These ulcers are the direct source of the abdominal pain and should raise suspicion for ZES when ulcers are multiple, recurrent despite therapy, or unusually located.

incorrectas.A: Acute pancreatitis is not the mechanism of pain in ZES; although gastrinomas can arise within the pancreas, the abdominal pain of ZES comes from acid-driven mucosal ulceration, not pancreatic ductal obstruction or enzyme autoactivation.
incorrectas.B: Cholelithiasis relates to bile composition and gallbladder stasis, an unrelated process to the acid-hypersecretory ulcer disease that characterizes ZES.
incorrectas.C: Mesenteric ischemia results from compromised bowel blood supply, not from acid hypersecretion, and is not a recognized mechanism of the abdominal pain seen in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

preguntas.q: A patient with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome develops steatorrhea. What is the primary mechanism behind this fat malabsorption?

o.A: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic acinar cells
o.C: Bile acid deconjugation by bacterial overgrowth
o.D: Direct tumor invasion of the small bowel mucosa

e.correcta: The massive gastric acid hypersecretion driven by unchecked gastrin in ZES delivers abnormally low-pH chyme into the duodenum that overwhelms the bicarbonate-buffering capacity of pancreatic secretions. Pancreatic lipase is highly pH-sensitive and becomes denatured/inactivated in this excessively acidic environment, impairing triglyceride digestion and producing steatorrhea, even though the pancreas itself is structurally normal and secreting adequate lipase.

incorrectas.A: ZES-related steatorrhea is not due to autoimmune destruction of the pancreas, as seen in chronic pancreatitis or type 1 diabetes; the pancreatic parenchyma and enzyme output are intact -- the problem is enzyme inactivation by excess acid, not a loss of enzyme production.
incorrectas.C: Bacterial overgrowth causing bile acid deconjugation is the mechanism of steatorrhea in conditions like small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, not the acid-driven lipase inactivation that is the hallmark mechanism in ZES.
incorrectas.D: Gastrinomas are neuroendocrine tumors that cause disease through hormone secretion, not through direct invasive destruction of small bowel mucosa; the steatorrhea is a functional consequence of the hormonal/acid effect, not physical tumor invasion.

preguntas.q: In a patient with suspected Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, what happens to serum gastrin levels after intravenous secretin is administered during a secretin stimulation test?

o.D: Gastrin levels normalize to the baseline range

e.correcta: Secretin normally suppresses gastrin release from antral G cells via a physiologic negative feedback loop, but gastrinoma cells lack this inhibitory response and instead paradoxically increase gastrin secretion when exposed to secretin. This paradoxical rise (typically an increase of at least 200 pg/mL above baseline) is highly specific for gastrinoma and is the basis of the confirmatory secretin stimulation test. Everywhere else in GI physiology secretin turns gastrin off; in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome it paradoxically turns it further on.

incorrectas.B: A fall in gastrin is the expected response in a person without a gastrinoma, since secretin normally inhibits antral G-cell gastrin release — this pattern would argue against, not for, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
incorrectas.C: An unchanged gastrin level is considered a negative test; because gastrinoma cells retain functioning secretin receptors that drive additional gastrin release, a truly unresponsive tumor would be atypical and does not support the diagnosis.
incorrectas.D: Normalization to baseline is not the pattern seen — gastrin is already elevated at baseline in gastrinoma from autonomous tumor secretion, and secretin exaggerates that elevation further rather than correcting it.

preguntas.q: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma) occurs sporadically in most cases, but when it occurs as part of an inherited multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome, which one is it associated with?

e.correcta: About 20-25% of gastrinomas arise as part of MEN1, an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by mutation of the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene (menin) that classically produces tumors of the '3 P's' — Parathyroid (hyperplasia/adenoma causing hypercalcemia), Pituitary (typically prolactinoma), and Pancreas (islet cell tumors, most commonly gastrinoma). Screening for hypercalcemia and pituitary hormone excess is warranted whenever a gastrinoma is diagnosed, because finding a coexisting parathyroid or pituitary tumor points to MEN1 and changes management (parathyroidectomy is pursued first, which alone can improve gastrin levels).

incorrectas.A: MEN2B features mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus, medullary thyroid carcinoma, and pheochromocytoma from RET mutations — it does not include gastrinomas or pancreatic islet tumors, so it is not the syndrome linked to Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
incorrectas.C: MEN2A involves medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and primary hyperparathyroidism, also from RET mutations, but like MEN2B it has no pancreatic islet cell tumor component and is unrelated to gastrinoma.
incorrectas.D: Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (VHL gene mutation) predisposes to hemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma, and pheochromocytoma; while it can rarely cause pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, it is not the classic syndrome associated with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome the way MEN1 is.

preguntas.q: Which pancreatic secretory function does cholecystokinin (CCK) stimulate, acting in part through neural muscarinic pathways?

o.A: Secretion of digestive enzymes by acinar cells
o.B: Secretion of bicarbonate by ductal cells
o.C: Secretion of insulin by pancreatic beta cells
o.D: Secretion of glucagon by pancreatic alpha cells

e.correcta: CCK is released by duodenal I cells in response to fatty acids and amino acids in chyme, and it binds CCKA receptors on pancreatic acinar cells (and also acts indirectly via vagal afferent-efferent muscarinic pathways) to trigger exocytosis of zymogen granules containing lipase, amylase, and proteases. This matches digestive enzyme output to the fat/protein content of a meal, making CCK the dominant stimulus for the enzymatic (acinar) component of pancreatic secretion, complementing secretin's control of the bicarbonate (ductal) component.

incorrectas.B: Bicarbonate secretion by pancreatic ductal cells is primarily driven by secretin acting through a cAMP-mediated pathway, not by CCK; CCK's main pancreatic target is the acinar cell rather than the ductal cell.
incorrectas.C: Insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells is regulated mainly by circulating glucose and incretins like GLP-1 and GIP, not by CCK, which functions here as an exocrine (not endocrine) pancreatic secretagogue.
incorrectas.D: Glucagon release from alpha cells responds chiefly to hypoglycemia and sympathetic stimulation; CCK does not act on the endocrine islets to modulate glucagon secretion.

preguntas.q: What effect does cholecystokinin (CCK) have on the gallbladder to promote delivery of bile into the duodenum?

o.A: It increases relaxation of the gallbladder
o.B: It increases contraction of the gallbladder
o.C: It has no effect on gallbladder tone

e.correcta: CCK released from duodenal I cells in response to dietary fat and protein binds CCKA receptors on gallbladder smooth muscle, triggering coordinated contraction that squeezes stored bile out of the gallbladder. This is paired with CCK-induced relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi, so the two effects work together to open the biliary 'gate' and propel bile into the duodenal lumen exactly when fat needs to be emulsified for digestion.

incorrectas.A: Relaxation of the gallbladder would be the opposite of what's needed to expel bile; CCK's job is to contract the gallbladder, while it is the sphincter of Oddi (not the gallbladder itself) that CCK relaxes.
incorrectas.C: CCK is one of the most potent physiologic stimulants of gallbladder motor activity — clinically, a CCK-stimulated HIDA scan uses synthetic CCK to provoke gallbladder contraction and measure ejection fraction, showing this is far from a 'no effect.'
incorrectas.D: Decreased emptying would impair fat digestion and predispose to bile stasis and gallstone formation, the opposite of CCK's physiologic role; this inhibitory pattern is more characteristic of somatostatin, which does suppress gallbladder contraction.

preguntas.q: What effect does cholecystokinin (CCK) have on the sphincter of Oddi to facilitate bile flow into the duodenum?

o.A: It causes relaxation of the sphincter
o.B: It causes contraction/spasm of the sphincter
o.C: It has no measurable effect on sphincter tone
o.D: It causes rhythmic peristaltic contractions of the sphincter

e.correcta: CCK relaxes the sphincter of Oddi at the same time it contracts the gallbladder, so bile released from the gallbladder encounters an open passage into the duodenum rather than a closed valve. This coordinated dual action — gallbladder squeezing while the sphincter opens — is what actually delivers bile (and pancreatic enzymes, since the sphincter also guards the pancreatic duct in most people) into the gut lumen in response to a fatty meal.

incorrectas.B: Contraction or spasm of the sphincter of Oddi would trap bile in the biliary tree rather than release it, and is instead associated with pathologic sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, not with the normal postprandial CCK response.
incorrectas.C: CCK has a clear, reproducible effect on the sphincter — its relaxation is a core part of the coordinated biliary emptying reflex, not an inert bystander effect.
incorrectas.D: The sphincter of Oddi does not undergo CCK-driven peristalsis; it functions as a tonic valve that is either relatively closed (interdigestive state) or relaxed open (postprandial, CCK-mediated), not as a peristaltic pump.

preguntas.q: What effect does cholecystokinin (CCK) have on the rate of gastric emptying?

o.B: It has no effect on gastric emptying
o.D: It only affects emptying of liquids, not solids

e.correcta: CCK slows gastric emptying by increasing pyloric tone and reducing antral motility, keeping chyme in the stomach longer whenever the duodenum senses fat. This delay gives the pancreas and gallbladder time — through CCK's other actions of enzyme secretion and bile release — to deliver the enzymes and bile salts needed to digest that fat before more chyme is dumped into the duodenum, preventing the small intestine from being overwhelmed.

incorrectas.A: Increasing emptying would push undigested fat into the duodenum faster than it could be processed; this is the opposite of CCK's actual feedback role, which is to slow gastric emptying in response to fat.
incorrectas.B: CCK is actually one of the more potent inhibitors of gastric emptying among the GI hormones — describing it as having no effect ignores its central role in the fat-sensing feedback loop between duodenum and stomach.
incorrectas.D: CCK's inhibitory effect on gastric emptying is not restricted to liquid-phase emptying; it slows the overall rate at which gastric contents, including the solid/chyme phase, are delivered to the duodenum.

preguntas.q: Cholecystokinin (CCK) potentiates the action of secretin on which pancreatic ductal secretion?

e.correcta: Although CCK's own primary target is the acinar cell (enzyme output), CCK also amplifies secretin's stimulation of bicarbonate-rich fluid secretion from pancreatic ductal cells, so the two hormones act synergistically rather than independently after a meal. This potentiation ensures that when both fat/protein (via CCK) and acid (via secretin) are present in the duodenum, bicarbonate output is boosted enough to neutralize gastric acid quickly, protecting the duodenal mucosa and creating the near-neutral pH pancreatic enzymes need to work.

incorrectas.B: Chloride secretion is not the classically tested ductal output potentiated by CCK-secretin synergy; the physiologically emphasized and clinically tested effect is on bicarbonate output.
incorrectas.C: Enzyme secretion is CCK's own direct acinar effect, largely independent of secretin, not something CCK 'potentiates' in secretin — the potentiation described here specifically concerns the ductal bicarbonate response to secretin.
incorrectas.D: Gastric acid secretion is suppressed, not potentiated, by these two hormones; it is not the ductal bicarbonate pathway being described here.

preguntas.q: Which cholecystokinin receptor subtype is selective for CCK, showing little response to gastrin?

e.correcta: The CCKA receptor (CCK1) is expressed on pancreatic acinar cells, gallbladder smooth muscle, and vagal afferents, and it is highly selective for CCK over gastrin despite the structural similarity between the two peptides. This selectivity is what allows CCK to exert its own distinct set of effects — enzyme secretion, gallbladder contraction, sphincter of Oddi relaxation, delayed gastric emptying — largely independent of circulating gastrin levels.

incorrectas.A: The CCKB receptor (CCK2) is the one that is roughly equally sensitive to both CCK and gastrin, because the two hormones share the same active C-terminal amino acid sequence recognized by that receptor — the opposite selectivity pattern from what the question describes.
incorrectas.B: The secretin receptor is a distinct class of GI hormone receptor activated by secretin, not by CCK or gastrin, so it plays no role in CCK/gastrin selectivity.
incorrectas.D: The motilin receptor mediates the effects of motilin (and motilin agonists like erythromycin) on GI motility; it is unrelated to CCK or gastrin signaling.

preguntas.q: Which cholecystokinin receptor subtype responds with roughly equal sensitivity to both gastrin and CCK?

e.correcta: The CCKB receptor (CCK2) binds both CCK and gastrin with similar affinity because gastrin and CCK share an identical five-amino-acid C-terminal sequence, the minimal region required for receptor recognition and biologic activity. CCKB receptors are found on gastric parietal and ECL cells, which is why gastrin — acting through this shared receptor family — can stimulate acid secretion despite being structurally related to CCK.

incorrectas.A: The CCKA receptor is the selective one — it responds strongly to CCK but only weakly to gastrin, the reverse of the equal sensitivity described in the question.
incorrectas.B: The secretin receptor recognizes secretin, a structurally distinct hormone from the secretin/glucagon family, and does not bind CCK or gastrin at all.
incorrectas.C: Somatostatin receptors bind somatostatin, not CCK or gastrin, and mediate an inhibitory (not stimulatory) signal on many GI cell types.

preguntas.q: What is the minimum fragment of cholecystokinin (CCK) required for full biologic activity?

e.correcta: The C-terminal heptapeptide of CCK contains the receptor-binding and activating domain sufficient to reproduce essentially all of CCK's physiologic effects, even though native CCK circulates in several longer forms (CCK-33, CCK-58). This is why synthetic CCK analogs used clinically, such as sincalide for gallbladder-stimulated imaging or CCK provocation testing, are built around this minimal active fragment rather than the full-length peptide.

incorrectas.A: The N-terminal portion of CCK is not the biologically active region; activity resides at the C-terminus, so an N-terminal fragment alone would not reproduce CCK's actions.
incorrectas.B: The full 33-amino-acid form (CCK-33) is one of the naturally circulating forms of CCK, but it is not the 'minimum' fragment needed — a much shorter C-terminal fragment retains full activity.
incorrectas.D: A pentapeptide is one residue too short — CCK and gastrin actually share an identical C-terminal pentapeptide sequence, which is why a pentapeptide alone cannot reproduce CCK-specific activity; the heptapeptide is the accepted minimum for full bioactivity.

preguntas.q: Secretin's principal action on the exocrine pancreas is to increase secretion of which substance from ductal cells?

e.correcta: Secretin is released from duodenal S cells when luminal pH drops below about 4.5, and it acts on pancreatic ductal cells via a cAMP-dependent pathway to drive secretion of a bicarbonate-rich, low-enzyme fluid. This bicarbonate neutralizes the acidic chyme entering the duodenum from the stomach, raising luminal pH into the range at which pancreatic enzymes (secreted mainly under CCK's control) are enzymatically active, so secretin and CCK together create the conditions digestion actually requires.

incorrectas.B: Amylase, like other digestive enzymes, is secreted by pancreatic acinar cells primarily under CCK's control, not secretin's — secretin's hallmark effect is on the ductal bicarbonate component, not the enzymatic component.
incorrectas.C: Secretin actually decreases gastric acid secretion, by inhibiting gastrin release and directly dampening parietal cell activity, which is the opposite of an increase — its major positive effect is on pancreatic bicarbonate, not gastric acid.
incorrectas.D: Insulin secretion is governed by glucose and incretins such as GLP-1 and GIP; secretin is not a primary regulator of endocrine islet hormone release.

preguntas.q: What effect does secretin have on bile secretion by the biliary ductal epithelium?

o.B: It has no effect on bile flow
o.D: It only affects bile composition, not volume

e.correcta: Secretin acts on cholangiocytes lining the bile ducts to stimulate secretion of a bicarbonate-rich fluid into bile, expanding bile volume in the same way it expands pancreatic ductal secretion — an effect sometimes called hydrocholeresis. This choleretic action increases the fluidity and bicarbonate content of bile delivered to the duodenum, complementing CCK's role in physically expelling stored bile from the gallbladder.

incorrectas.A: A decrease would run counter to secretin's known choleretic (bile-flow-increasing) action; secretin's bicarbonate-driven fluid secretion by bile duct epithelium raises, not lowers, bile output.
incorrectas.B: Secretin has a well-documented and clinically relevant effect on bile duct secretion — enough that secretin-stimulated MRCP is used clinically to enhance visualization of the biliary and pancreatic ductal system, so 'no effect' is inaccurate.
incorrectas.D: The change is primarily a volume/fluid effect, more bicarbonate-rich fluid secreted into bile, not merely a compositional change with fixed volume — secretin measurably increases bile flow.

preguntas.q: What combination of effects does secretin have on gastric physiology, helping to protect the duodenum from further acid exposure after a meal?

o.A: Decreases gastric acid secretion and increases pyloric sphincter contraction
o.B: Increases gastric acid secretion and decreases pyloric sphincter contraction
o.C: Decreases gastric acid secretion and decreases pyloric sphincter contraction
o.D: Increases gastric acid secretion and increases pyloric sphincter contraction

e.correcta: Secretin reduces gastric acid output both directly, by dampening parietal cell H+ secretion, and indirectly, by inhibiting gastrin release from antral G cells, while simultaneously increasing tone of the pyloric sphincter to slow further delivery of acidic chyme into the duodenum. Together these actions form a negative-feedback 'off switch' that engages once duodenal pH has already dropped, preventing ongoing acid injury to the duodenal mucosa while bicarbonate (also secretin-driven) has time to neutralize what has already entered.

incorrectas.B: This pairing is essentially the reverse of secretin's real actions — secretin does not increase gastric acid output, and relaxing rather than tightening the pylorus would let more acid flood the duodenum, worsening rather than protecting against acid injury.
incorrectas.C: Secretin does inhibit acid secretion correctly here, but it increases, not decreases, pyloric sphincter contraction — tightening the pylorus is part of how secretin limits further acid delivery to an already-acidified duodenum.
incorrectas.D: Increasing acid secretion is opposite to secretin's actual inhibitory effect on parietal cells and gastrin release; secretin's overall physiologic theme is acid suppression, not stimulation.

preguntas.q: Which macronutrients, when present in the gut lumen, stimulate secretion of glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP)?

e.correcta: GIP is unique among the GI regulatory hormones in that it is released from duodenal K cells in response to all three major macronutrients — oral glucose, fatty acids, and amino acids — rather than being triggered by just one class of nutrient. Once released, GIP's most clinically important role is as an incretin: it potentiates glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, which is why oral glucose produces a greater insulin response than an equivalent IV glucose load (the 'incretin effect').

incorrectas.A: Glucose alone does stimulate GIP release, but restricting the trigger to glucose only misses that fat and protein are equally effective secretagogues for this hormone — GIP is the broadest-acting nutrient sensor among the gut hormones.
incorrectas.B: Fat is indeed one of the stimuli for GIP, but fat alone does not capture the full picture; GIP is distinguished precisely because it also responds robustly to glucose and protein, unlike most other GI hormones that are more nutrient-specific.
incorrectas.D: Protein does stimulate GIP secretion, but limiting the answer to protein alone misses GIP's hallmark feature of responding to all three macronutrient classes, which is the detail most often tested.

preguntas.q: GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide) has what exocrine effect on the stomach, consistent with its older name 'gastric inhibitory peptide'?

o.C: Has no effect on gastric acid output
o.D: Increases pepsinogen secretion only, without affecting acid

e.correcta: GIP's exocrine (non-insulin-related) action is to inhibit gastric acid secretion by parietal cells and reduce gastric motility, which is exactly why it was originally named 'gastric inhibitory peptide' before its far more clinically prominent incretin (insulinotropic) role was discovered. Remembering this dual identity — inhibits gastric acid/motility on one hand, potentiates insulin release on the other — helps reconcile why the same molecule carries two seemingly unrelated names.

incorrectas.A: An increase in acid secretion would contradict the 'inhibitory' part of GIP's original name; GIP's exocrine gastric effect is suppressive, not stimulatory, on parietal cell acid output.
incorrectas.C: GIP has a measurable inhibitory effect on gastric acid secretion — well established enough to have originally named the hormone — so 'no effect' misrepresents its physiology.
incorrectas.D: GIP's inhibitory effect is on gastric acid (H+) secretion broadly, not selectively on pepsinogen while sparing acid; the classic teaching point is inhibition of H+ output itself.

preguntas.q: Motilin is secreted by the small intestine predominantly during which state?

o.A: The fed state, immediately after a meal
o.C: Equally during fed and fasting states
o.D: Only during REM sleep, regardless of feeding status

e.correcta: Motilin is released in cyclic bursts from the duodenum and jejunum during fasting, where it triggers phase III of the migrating motor complex (MMC) — a powerful, sweeping wave of peristalsis that clears residual food, secretions, and debris from the stomach and small intestine between meals. This 'intestinal housekeeper' function explains why motilin levels rise during prolonged fasting and fall after eating, the opposite pattern from hormones like CCK and secretin that respond to a meal.

incorrectas.A: The fed state is actually when motilin secretion is suppressed, not stimulated; feeding interrupts the migrating motor complex that motilin drives, so motilin activity is lowest right after a meal.
incorrectas.C: Motilin secretion is not steady across states — it shows a distinct fasting-predominant, cyclic pattern with surges roughly every 90-120 minutes between meals, rather than being equally active whether or not a person has eaten.
incorrectas.D: Motilin's cyclic release is tied to the fasting/interdigestive state generally, not specifically to REM sleep; its pattern persists during fasting whether the person is awake or in any sleep stage.

preguntas.q: Which antibiotic can be used off-label as a motilin receptor agonist to stimulate GI motility, for example in diabetic gastroparesis?

e.correcta: Erythromycin, a macrolide antibiotic, happens to bind and activate motilin receptors on GI smooth muscle, mimicking motilin's normal action of triggering the migrating motor complex and increasing gastric and intestinal peristalsis. This off-label prokinetic effect is used clinically, typically at lower sub-antimicrobial doses, to accelerate gastric emptying in conditions like diabetic gastroparesis, though tolerance can develop with prolonged use as receptors downregulate.

incorrectas.A: Azithromycin is also a macrolide but has much weaker motilin receptor agonist activity than erythromycin and is not used clinically as a prokinetic; erythromycin remains the macrolide specifically exploited for this off-label GI motility effect.
incorrectas.B: Clindamycin is a lincosamide antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis; it has no meaningful motilin receptor agonist activity and is not used as a prokinetic.
incorrectas.D: Metronidazole is a nitroimidazole active against anaerobes and protozoa; it does not act on motilin receptors and has no established role as a GI prokinetic agent.

preguntas.q: What are the two principal effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) on pancreatic islet hormone secretion?

o.A: Increases insulin secretion and decreases glucagon secretion
o.B: Decreases insulin secretion and increases glucagon secretion
o.C: Increases both insulin and glucagon secretion
o.D: Decreases both insulin and glucagon secretion

e.correcta: GLP-1, released from intestinal L cells after a meal, is a glucose-dependent incretin hormone — it potentiates insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells specifically when glucose is elevated (minimizing hypoglycemia risk), while simultaneously suppressing glucagon release from alpha cells. This dual action lowers postprandial blood glucose from both directions, more insulin to drive glucose uptake and less glucagon to limit hepatic glucose output, which is exactly why GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide and liraglutide are used to treat type 2 diabetes.

incorrectas.B: This is the reverse of GLP-1's actual physiology; increasing glucagon while decreasing insulin would raise blood glucose, whereas GLP-1's whole purpose as an incretin is to lower postprandial glucose.
incorrectas.C: Increasing both hormones simultaneously would work against each other in terms of net glucose control, since insulin lowers and glucagon raises glucose; GLP-1 specifically increases insulin while decreasing glucagon so their glucose-lowering effects are additive, not both up.
incorrectas.D: Suppressing both hormones would remove insulin's glucose-lowering action along with glucagon's glucose-raising action; GLP-1's defining feature is that it pushes insulin and glucagon in opposite directions, not down together.

preguntas.q: Secretion of somatostatin by gastric D cells is stimulated by which luminal condition?

o.A: High (alkaline) pH in the GI mucosa
o.B: Low (acidic) pH in the GI mucosa

e.correcta: Falling luminal pH (increasing acidity) directly stimulates antral D cells to release somatostatin, which then acts in a paracrine fashion to inhibit further gastrin release from neighboring G cells and to directly suppress parietal cell acid secretion. This creates a local negative-feedback loop: as the stomach becomes more acidic, somatostatin release increases to rein in further acid production, protecting the mucosa from excessive acidification.

incorrectas.A: A high (alkaline) pH would not provide the acid-sensing trigger that D cells respond to; it is the drop toward acidity, not a rise toward alkalinity, that activates somatostatin release as part of the feedback-inhibition loop.
incorrectas.C: Somatostatin release is not restricted to a neutral pH condition — its release scales with how acidic the luminal environment becomes, with lower (more acidic) pH producing a stronger stimulatory signal.
incorrectas.D: Somatostatin secretion is, in fact, pH-dependent — luminal acidity is one of its principal physiologic triggers, central to how the stomach self-regulates acid output.

preguntas.q: What effect does vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation have on somatostatin secretion from gastric D cells?

o.C: Vagal stimulation has no effect on somatostatin secretion
o.D: Vagal stimulation converts somatostatin-secreting D cells into G cells

e.correcta: Vagal (cholinergic) input inhibits somatostatin release from D cells, which removes somatostatin's normal inhibitory brake on both gastrin release from G cells and acid secretion from parietal cells. This is part of why the cephalic phase of gastric acid secretion, triggered by sight, smell, and thought of food and mediated through vagal outflow, is so effective at ramping up acid production — the vagus simultaneously stimulates acid-promoting pathways directly and disinhibits them further by suppressing somatostatin.

incorrectas.A: An increase would dampen acid secretion right when the body is preparing to digest a meal, which is physiologically counterproductive; vagal stimulation actually removes the somatostatin brake rather than reinforcing it.
incorrectas.C: Vagal input has a clear, functionally important inhibitory effect on D cells; describing it as 'no effect' misses a key mechanism behind the cephalic phase's potent stimulation of gastric acid secretion.
incorrectas.D: Vagal stimulation does not change D cells into a different cell type — it modulates D-cell secretory activity, specifically suppressing somatostatin release, without altering cell identity.

preguntas.q: What effect does somatostatin have on gastric acid secretion?

o.D: Increases secretion only at high pH

e.correcta: Somatostatin is one of the most broadly inhibitory hormones in the gut, acting directly on parietal cells to suppress acid output and indirectly by inhibiting gastrin release from G cells and histamine release from ECL cells, both of which are themselves stimulants of acid secretion. This makes somatostatin a physiologic master brake on gastric acid production, which is why octreotide, a somatostatin analog, is used clinically to reduce GI secretions and treat conditions like variceal bleeding.

incorrectas.A: An increase would contradict somatostatin's fundamental identity as an inhibitory GI hormone; virtually all of its major actions across the gut, on acid, enzymes, hormones, and motility, are suppressive, not stimulatory.
incorrectas.B: Somatostatin's suppression of acid secretion is substantial and clinically exploited, as with octreotide for acid-related or secretory conditions, so describing it as having no significant effect understates a core, well-established action.
incorrectas.D: There is no meaningful pH-dependent reversal of somatostatin's action; its inhibitory effect on acid secretion is consistent rather than conditional on high pH.

preguntas.q: What effect does somatostatin have on pancreatic and small intestinal fluid secretion?

o.C: No effect on fluid secretion, only on enzyme content
o.D: Increases fluid but decreases bicarbonate content specifically

e.correcta: Somatostatin inhibits pancreatic exocrine secretion, both the ductal bicarbonate-rich fluid and the acinar enzyme component, as well as small intestinal fluid secretion, consistent with its role as a global inhibitor of GI secretory activity. This broad anti-secretory effect is exploited therapeutically with octreotide to reduce output in conditions such as high-output fistulas, pancreatitis-related secretions, and severe diarrhea from neuroendocrine tumors.

incorrectas.A: An increase would be inconsistent with somatostatin's overall physiologic role as an inhibitory hormone that dampens virtually every GI secretory process it touches, including pancreatic and intestinal fluid output.
incorrectas.C: Somatostatin's inhibitory effect is not limited to enzyme content — it reduces the overall volume of pancreatic and intestinal fluid secretion as well, central to why octreotide is effective at reducing high-volume secretory states.
incorrectas.D: Somatostatin does not selectively spare fluid while cutting bicarbonate — it broadly suppresses the secretory process, reducing both fluid volume and its bicarbonate/enzyme content together rather than dissociating the two.

preguntas.q: What effect does somatostatin have on gallbladder contraction, and what is a clinical consequence of this effect?

o.A: It increases contraction, protecting against gallstones
o.B: It decreases contraction, increasing the risk of gallstones due to bile stasis
o.C: It has no effect on the gallbladder
o.D: It relaxes the sphincter of Oddi but does not affect the gallbladder itself

e.correcta: Somatostatin inhibits gallbladder smooth muscle contraction, opposing CCK's stimulatory effect and allowing bile to stagnate within the gallbladder for longer periods. Clinically, this matters because patients on long-term somatostatin analog therapy, such as octreotide used for acromegaly or neuroendocrine tumors, are at increased risk of developing gallstones and biliary sludge due to this chronic inhibition of gallbladder emptying.

incorrectas.A: Increased contraction would actually protect against stasis-related gallstones, but this is the opposite of somatostatin's real effect — somatostatin inhibits, rather than promotes, gallbladder emptying, which is why it raises, not lowers, gallstone risk.
incorrectas.C: Somatostatin has a well-documented inhibitory effect on the gallbladder that is clinically significant enough to cause a recognized adverse effect (cholelithiasis) with long-term analog use, so 'no effect' is inaccurate.
incorrectas.D: Somatostatin's inhibitory action is not limited to the sphincter of Oddi — it directly reduces gallbladder smooth muscle contraction itself, and this gallbladder-specific inhibition is what drives the clinical stasis and gallstone risk.

preguntas.q: What effect does somatostatin have on secretion of insulin and glucagon from pancreatic islet cells?

o.A: It increases secretion of both hormones
o.B: It selectively increases glucagon while decreasing insulin
o.C: It decreases secretion of both hormones
o.D: It has no effect on islet hormone secretion, only on exocrine secretion

e.correcta: Somatostatin is produced locally by pancreatic islet D cells and acts in a paracrine fashion to inhibit secretion of both insulin (from beta cells) and glucagon (from alpha cells), in addition to inhibiting gastrin release in the stomach. This broad suppressive action across multiple islet cell types is consistent with somatostatin's general physiologic theme as an inhibitor of virtually all GI and pancreatic hormone secretion, which is why somatostatinomas, rare somatostatin-secreting tumors, can present with diabetes, gallstones, and steatorrhea from this combined inhibition.

incorrectas.A: Increasing both hormones would contradict somatostatin's identity as a broadly inhibitory regulator; somatostatinomas, in fact, cause disease specifically because they suppress rather than boost islet hormone output.
incorrectas.B: Somatostatin does not selectively spare or favor glucagon over insulin — it suppresses both alpha- and beta-cell secretion together, unlike GLP-1, for example, which does move insulin and glucagon in opposite directions.
incorrectas.D: Somatostatin's inhibitory reach extends beyond the exocrine pancreas to the endocrine islets as well; its paracrine inhibition of both insulin and glucagon secretion is a well-established, clinically relevant action, as in somatostatinoma syndrome.

preguntas.q: Ghrelin, secreted by gastric cells, has what effect on appetite?

o.B: It has no significant effect on appetite, only on growth hormone release
o.D: It increases appetite only in the fed state

e.correcta: Ghrelin is released mainly from the stomach, predominantly the fundus, during fasting and acts on the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus to stimulate appetite, making it the primary orexigenic ('hunger') signal among the gut-brain hormones — essentially the physiologic counterpart to leptin, which signals satiety from adipose stores. Ghrelin levels rise before meals and fall after eating, and it also stimulates growth hormone release from the pituitary, giving it a dual role in energy balance and growth hormone regulation.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in appetite would make ghrelin an anorexigenic signal, a role played by hormones like leptin and PYY, not ghrelin; ghrelin's defining physiologic role is to stimulate, not suppress, hunger.
incorrectas.B: Ghrelin does stimulate growth hormone release, acting as a growth hormone secretagogue, but this is in addition to, not instead of, its major and well-established appetite-stimulating effect — describing it as having no significant effect on appetite ignores its primary clinical and physiologic significance.
incorrectas.D: Ghrelin's appetite-stimulating action is most prominent during fasting/preprandial states, when its levels peak, rather than being restricted to the fed state; levels actually fall after eating.

preguntas.q: Ghrelin, a peptide hormone secreted from the stomach (mainly the fundus), is released predominantly during which physiologic state?

e.correcta: Ghrelin is the 'hunger hormone' — it rises during fasting and just before expected meals, acting on the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus to stimulate NPY/AgRP neurons and drive appetite, then falls sharply after eating. This orexigenic signal helps explain the pre-meal hunger pangs people feel and is one of the few gut hormones that stimulates rather than suppresses food intake.

incorrectas.A: The fed (postprandial) state is when ghrelin levels fall, not rise, as gastric distention and nutrient absorption suppress its secretion — this is the opposite pattern from what actually happens.
incorrectas.C: Ghrelin does show mild circadian variation, but its dominant physiologic driver is meal timing (fasting vs. fed), not sleep state per se, so this doesn't capture the key regulatory trigger tested here.
incorrectas.D: Exercise is not the classic stimulus for ghrelin release; the hormone's secretion is tied to the fasting/feeding cycle around meals rather than physical activity.

preguntas.q: Prader-Willi syndrome, caused by loss of the paternally-expressed genes at chromosome 15q11-13, is associated with what abnormality in ghrelin levels?

o.C: Normal ghrelin with compensatory elevated leptin

e.correcta: Patients with Prader-Willi syndrome have paradoxically elevated ghrelin levels, which is thought to be a major driver of the hyperphagia and severe obesity that characterize the disorder despite hypotonia and reduced muscle mass in infancy. This is clinically important because it links a genetic imprinting disorder to a specific gut-hormone mechanism of uncontrollable appetite, distinguishing PWS from simple obesity.

incorrectas.B: Decreased ghrelin would be expected to suppress appetite, which is the opposite of the hyperphagia and food-seeking behavior that defines Prader-Willi syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Leptin resistance/elevation is seen in common obesity from fat mass expansion, but the hallmark endocrine finding specific to Prader-Willi syndrome is elevated ghrelin, not a leptin-driven mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Ghrelin secretion is not absent in Prader-Willi syndrome — quite the opposite, it is abnormally high, which is precisely why these patients have such intense, difficult-to-control hunger.

preguntas.q: What happens to circulating ghrelin levels after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery?

e.correcta: Gastric bypass removes or bypasses the fundus, the main site of ghrelin production, so circulating ghrelin falls markedly after surgery. This drop in the 'hunger hormone' is one reason bypass patients experience reduced appetite and better sustained weight loss compared to purely restrictive procedures that leave the fundus intact.

incorrectas.B: Ghrelin does not stay unchanged — its levels fall significantly because the gastric fundus, its primary source, is surgically excluded from the nutrient stream, which is part of why bypass suppresses hunger more effectively than diet alone.
incorrectas.A: An increase would work against weight loss by driving hunger; this is the opposite of what is observed and would not explain the appetite suppression seen clinically after bypass.
incorrectas.D: There is no well-described transient rise-then-normalize pattern for ghrelin after bypass; the physiologically important and tested finding is a sustained decrease due to fundic exclusion.

preguntas.q: Leptin, secreted by adipocytes in proportion to fat mass, acts on the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus to produce what net effect on appetite?

e.correcta: Leptin signals long-term energy stores to the brain: as fat mass rises, leptin rises and inhibits NPY/AgRP orexigenic neurons while stimulating POMC/CART anorexigenic neurons in the arcuate nucleus, producing satiety and increased energy expenditure. This is the mirror-image counterpart to ghrelin — leptin reports fullness of fat stores, while ghrelin reports gastric emptiness — and leptin resistance in obesity is a key reason high leptin levels fail to suppress appetite in that setting.

incorrectas.A: Increasing appetite is the role of orexigenic signals like ghrelin or NPY, not leptin — leptin's physiologic action is anorexigenic (appetite-suppressing), which is why leptin deficiency causes severe early-onset obesity.
incorrectas.B: Leptin clearly has a potent central effect on feeding behavior and energy balance; claiming no effect ignores its well-established role as the primary long-term adiposity signal to the hypothalamus.
incorrectas.C: Leptin's action is not restricted to fasting — it continuously reports adipose stores to the brain and tends to fall during fasting/weight loss (permitting increased hunger), which is the opposite pairing implied here.

preguntas.q: Peptide YY (PYY), secreted by ileal and colonic L cells after a meal, has what effect on appetite?

o.D: Has no known effect on appetite

e.correcta: PYY is released by L cells in the distal small bowel and colon in proportion to caloric intake, and it acts on the hypothalamus (via Y2 receptors on NPY neurons, among other sites) to suppress appetite and slow gastric emptying — part of the 'ileal brake' that signals nutrients have already reached the distal gut. It works alongside GLP-1, which is co-secreted by the same L cells, to promote post-meal satiety.

incorrectas.A: An appetite-stimulating action would make PYY orexigenic like ghrelin, but PYY's physiologic role is the opposite — it is released after eating to help terminate the meal and promote satiety.
incorrectas.C: PYY does not stimulate gastric acid secretion; if anything, it slows gastric emptying and motility, which is a very different action from the acid-stimulating role of hormones like gastrin.
incorrectas.D: PYY has a clearly defined satiety-promoting effect that is well characterized in GI physiology and is one reason it has been studied as a target for obesity therapeutics; saying it has no known effect misses this established role.

preguntas.q: Vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) is secreted from neurons of which division within the gallbladder, small intestine, and sphincters?

e.correcta: VIP is a neuropeptide released from parasympathetic (and enteric) neurons that innervate GI smooth muscle, and its release parallels parasympathetic activation of the gut — for example during distention or vagal stimulation. Functionally it complements acetylcholine: while ACh from parasympathetic fibers often contracts sphincters, VIP co-released from these same pathways relaxes smooth muscle and sphincters, allowing coordinated relaxation ahead of a peristaltic wave.

incorrectas.B: Sympathetic input actually suppresses VIP release rather than being its source — adrenergic stimulation decreases VIP secretion, the reverse of the relationship described in the question.
incorrectas.C: Somatic motor neurons innervate skeletal muscle (such as the striated upper esophagus) via acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction; they are not the source of VIP acting on smooth muscle sphincters.
incorrectas.D: Interstitial cells of Cajal are the electrical pacemakers that generate slow waves in GI smooth muscle, not neurons that release the neuropeptide VIP — they set rhythm, they don't secrete this hormone.

preguntas.q: VIP acting on GI smooth muscle and sphincters, including the lower esophageal sphincter, produces what effect?

e.correcta: VIP relaxes GI smooth muscle and sphincters, including the LES, by increasing intracellular cAMP in smooth muscle cells, which lowers intracellular calcium and reduces actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling. This relaxant action is why VIP is considered one of the main inhibitory neurotransmitters of the enteric nervous system, working opposite to excitatory transmitters like acetylcholine and substance P.

incorrectas.A: Contraction of GI smooth muscle is more typical of excitatory mediators like acetylcholine, motilin, or gastrin — VIP's cAMP-mediated signaling produces the opposite effect, smooth muscle relaxation.
incorrectas.B: VIP has a well-documented and clinically important relaxant effect (its deficiency is implicated in achalasia, where LES relaxation fails), so 'no effect' does not reflect its actual physiologic role.
incorrectas.D: Phasic rhythmic contractions are a pattern seen in areas like the gastric antrum driven by slow waves and excitatory input, not the sustained smooth-muscle relaxation that VIP produces.

preguntas.q: Through activation of adenylate cyclase and increased intracellular cAMP in intestinal epithelial cells (which opens CFTR chloride channels), VIP has what effect on intestinal water and electrolyte secretion?

o.C: Increases absorption only, with no effect on secretion

e.correcta: VIP raises cAMP in intestinal epithelial cells, which opens CFTR chloride channels on the apical membrane; chloride efflux into the lumen creates an electrochemical gradient that drags sodium and water along with it, producing net intestinal secretion. This exact mechanism explains why VIP-secreting tumors (VIPomas) cause profuse secretory (watery) diarrhea, since the pathway mimics the same cAMP-CFTR mechanism exploited pathologically by cholera toxin.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in secretion would be the opposite of what elevated cAMP and open CFTR channels produce — this pathway drives fluid loss into the gut lumen, not fluid conservation.
incorrectas.B: VIP clearly has a potent secretory effect on intestinal epithelium — strong enough that VIPomas cause the debilitating diarrhea of WDHA syndrome — so 'no effect' contradicts the well-established mechanism.
incorrectas.C: VIP promotes net secretion, not absorption; the cAMP-driven chloride efflux described here is the defining mechanism of a secretory, not absorptive, process.

preguntas.q: VIP secretion from enteric neurons is increased in response to which stimuli?

e.correcta: VIP release rises with intestinal distention (mechanical stretch activating enteric reflex arcs) and with vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation, both of which are physiologic signals that the gut needs to relax and accommodate a meal or an advancing peristaltic bolus. This fits VIP's broader role as an inhibitory neurotransmitter recruited whenever the parasympathetic/enteric nervous system needs to coordinate smooth muscle relaxation.

incorrectas.A: Sympathetic (adrenergic) stimulation actually decreases VIP secretion rather than increasing it, and fasting is not a classic trigger for VIP release the way a meal-related distention signal is.
incorrectas.C: Luminal acidification is a stimulus for other regulatory peptides, such as secretin release from S cells, but it is not the classic trigger described for VIP secretion.
incorrectas.D: Somatostatin is broadly inhibitory to many GI hormones (including VIP) rather than being a stimulus that increases VIP release — it works in the opposite direction.

preguntas.q: What effect does adrenergic (sympathetic) input have on VIP secretion from enteric neurons?

o.C: Has no effect on VIP secretion

e.correcta: Adrenergic input suppresses VIP release, consistent with the broader antagonism between the sympathetic and parasympathetic/enteric nervous systems in gut regulation — sympathetic activation generally favors gut quiescence (reduced motility, sphincter contraction, vasoconstriction) rather than the smooth-muscle-relaxing, secretion-promoting actions driven by VIP. This reciprocal relationship mirrors how sympathetic tone slows digestion overall ('rest and digest' vs. 'fight or flight').

incorrectas.B: An increase would run counter to the general sympathetic effect of dampening enteric neurotransmitter release and gut activity; adrenergic input inhibits, not stimulates, VIP secretion.
incorrectas.C: Adrenergic input has a clear inhibitory effect on VIP release rather than no effect — this reciprocal regulation is part of how the autonomic nervous system balances gut motility and secretion.
incorrectas.D: VIP and secretin are distinct, structurally related but separately synthesized peptide hormones; adrenergic stimulation does not chemically convert one into the other.

preguntas.q: A pancreatic islet cell tumor secretes excess VIP, producing watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome). This tumor arises from which cell type?

e.correcta: A VIPoma arises from non-α, non-β, non-δ pancreatic islet cells and secretes VIP, which drives massive cAMP-mediated intestinal chloride and fluid secretion, producing the classic triad of Watery Diarrhea, Hypokalemia, and Achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome, also called pancreatic cholera). The achlorhydria results because VIP inhibits gastric acid secretion while the profuse secretory diarrhea causes severe potassium loss, distinguishing it clinically from osmotic diarrheas that improve with fasting.

incorrectas.A: α cells give rise to glucagonomas, which cause the 4 D's — diabetes, DVT, dermatitis (necrolytic migratory erythema), and depression — a very different clinical picture from the secretory diarrhea of WDHA syndrome.
incorrectas.B: β cells give rise to insulinomas, which cause fasting hypoglycemia with Whipple's triad, not the watery diarrhea and hypokalemia driven by VIP-induced intestinal chloride secretion.
incorrectas.D: δ cells give rise to somatostatinomas, which classically cause the triad of diabetes, cholelithiasis (gallstones), and steatorrhea due to global inhibition of pancreatic and biliary secretion — a different mechanism than VIP-driven secretory diarrhea.

preguntas.q: Which type of GI smooth muscle contraction consists of periodic contractions followed by complete relaxation, and is seen in the esophagus, gastric antrum, and small intestine?

e.correcta: Phasic contractions are periodic, rhythmic contractions that occur in bursts and are followed by full relaxation of the muscle, generated in coordination with the underlying slow-wave electrical rhythm of the ICC pacemaker cells. They are the contraction pattern responsible for propulsive movements — peristalsis in the esophagus and small intestine and mixing/grinding in the gastric antrum — as opposed to sustained baseline tone.

incorrectas.A: Tonic contractions maintain a sustained, constant level of contraction without regular periods of relaxation, which is the opposite pattern — tonic contraction is seen in sphincters and the orad stomach, not in the propulsive segments described here.
incorrectas.B: Segmentation is a specific pattern of phasic contractions used for mixing chyme in the small intestine, but it is a subtype/example rather than the general term for the periodic-contraction-then-relaxation pattern being asked about across the esophagus, antrum, and small intestine.
incorrectas.C: The migrating motor complex is a specific interdigestive (fasting-state) motility pattern that sweeps the gut every ~90 minutes between meals; it is not the general descriptive term for periodic contraction-relaxation cycles occurring during digestion.

preguntas.q: Which type of GI smooth muscle contraction maintains a constant baseline level of tone without regular periods of relaxation, as seen in the orad stomach and the lower esophageal, ileocecal, and internal anal sphincters?

e.correcta: Tonic contractions are sustained states of partial contraction maintained continuously, without the rhythmic on/off pattern of phasic activity — this is exactly what sphincters need functionally, since they must remain closed most of the time to prevent reflux or premature emptying, relaxing only transiently to allow passage of contents. The orad (upper) stomach also uses tonic tone to generate the baseline pressure that pushes contents toward the antrum for mixing.

incorrectas.A: Phasic contractions are periodic bursts followed by full relaxation, seen in propulsive segments like the esophageal body, gastric antrum, and small intestine — the opposite pattern from the sustained tone described in sphincters.
incorrectas.C: Peristaltic contractions are a specific propulsive wave pattern (a type of phasic activity) that moves a bolus forward, not the sustained baseline tone that keeps a sphincter closed between swallows or boluses.
incorrectas.D: Segmenting contractions are localized phasic contractions used to mix luminal contents in the small intestine, distinct from the continuous, non-relaxing tone that defines tonic sphincter contraction.

preguntas.q: Spontaneous, rhythmically oscillating membrane potentials that are intrinsic to GI smooth muscle cells and set the rhythm for potential contractions are called what?

e.correcta: Slow waves are subthreshold oscillations in resting membrane potential generated by the interstitial cells of Cajal and propagated to smooth muscle via gap junctions; they don't directly cause contraction but instead set the maximum frequency and timing at which action potentials — and therefore contractions — can occur if threshold is reached. This is why the frequency of slow waves differs by GI segment (about 3/min in the stomach vs. 12/min in the duodenum) and dictates the pace of motility in each region.

incorrectas.B: Action potentials are the rapid depolarizations that actually trigger calcium entry and contraction, riding on top of slow waves when threshold is reached — they are the downstream event, not the intrinsic oscillating rhythm itself.
incorrectas.C: This is a distractor phrase rather than a standard physiologic term; the actual pacemaker rhythm in GI smooth muscle is specifically termed the slow wave, generated by interstitial cells of Cajal.
incorrectas.D: Plateau potentials refer to a different electrophysiologic phenomenon (a sustained depolarized phase seen in cells like cardiac myocytes or certain neurons), not the intrinsic rhythmic subthreshold oscillation described here.

preguntas.q: What is the approximate frequency of slow waves in the stomach?

e.correcta: The stomach has the slowest slow-wave frequency in the GI tract, at approximately 3 waves per minute, which corresponds to its role in prolonged mixing and grinding of food into chyme rather than rapid propulsion. This low frequency reflects the relatively sparse density and slower intrinsic rhythm of interstitial cells of Cajal in gastric smooth muscle compared with the duodenum.

incorrectas.A: 12 waves/minute is the frequency in the duodenum, the fastest-paced segment of the upper GI tract, not the stomach — mixing up these numbers is a common trap on this exact fact.
incorrectas.B: 8-9 waves/minute corresponds to the ileum, an intermediate frequency between the duodenum's faster rate and the stomach's much slower rate.
incorrectas.D: 20 waves/minute exceeds any physiologic slow-wave frequency documented in the human GI tract; the fastest region (duodenum) tops out around 12/minute.

preguntas.q: What is the approximate frequency of slow waves in the duodenum?

e.correcta: The duodenum has the fastest slow-wave frequency in the GI tract, roughly 12 waves per minute, reflecting the need for relatively rapid mixing of chyme with pancreatic and biliary secretions immediately as it exits the stomach. This is the opposite end of the spectrum from the stomach's slow ~3/minute rhythm, illustrating how slow-wave frequency is tuned regionally to the functional demands of each GI segment.

incorrectas.A: 3 waves/minute is the stomach's rate, the slowest in the GI tract — this is essentially the inverse extreme from the duodenum, which has the fastest rate.
incorrectas.B: 8-9 waves/minute corresponds to the ileum, which sits between the duodenum's fast rhythm and slower rhythms more distally/proximally.
incorrectas.C: 6 waves/minute does not correspond to any of the classically taught GI slow-wave frequencies (stomach ~3, ileum ~8-9, duodenum ~12); it's a plausible-sounding but incorrect intermediate value.

preguntas.q: What is the approximate frequency of slow waves in the ileum?

e.correcta: The ileum has an intermediate slow-wave frequency of about 8-9 waves per minute — slower than the duodenum's 12/minute but faster than the stomach's 3/minute. This creates a gradient of decreasing slow-wave frequency moving distally along the small intestine, which helps propel luminal contents forward toward the colon (since more proximal segments can, in principle, contract at a higher rate than more distal ones).

incorrectas.A: 3 waves/minute is the frequency found in the stomach, the slowest-paced region of the GI tract, quite different from the intermediate ileal rate.
incorrectas.C: 12 waves/minute is the duodenum's frequency, the fastest in the small intestine — the ileum's rate is somewhat slower than this as you move distally.
incorrectas.D: 15 waves/minute exceeds the physiologic maximum described in the GI tract (topped by the duodenum at ~12/minute), so it does not correspond to any real segment's slow-wave frequency.

preguntas.q: Which segment of the GI tract has the lowest frequency of slow waves, and therefore the lowest rate of potential contractions?

e.correcta: The stomach has the lowest slow-wave frequency of the GI tract, about 3 waves per minute, which matches its physiologic job of prolonged mechanical mixing and grinding of food into chyme rather than fast, frequent contractions. Because contraction frequency cannot exceed the underlying slow-wave frequency, the stomach's slow intrinsic rhythm caps how often it can contract, unlike the much faster duodenum just downstream.

incorrectas.B: The duodenum actually has the highest slow-wave frequency in the GI tract (about 12/minute), the opposite extreme from what the question is asking about.
incorrectas.C: The ileum has an intermediate frequency (about 8-9/minute) — faster than the stomach but slower than the duodenum, so it is not the lowest.
incorrectas.D: The jejunum's slow-wave frequency also falls in an intermediate range along the gradient from duodenum to ileum, and is not the segment with the lowest rate — that distinction belongs to the stomach.

preguntas.q: Which segment of the GI tract has the highest frequency of slow waves, and therefore the highest potential rate of contractions?

e.correcta: The duodenum has the highest slow-wave frequency in the GI tract, about 12 waves per minute, reflecting the need to rapidly mix acidic chyme arriving from the stomach with alkaline pancreatic and biliary secretions and move it along efficiently. This fast pacemaker rhythm sets the ceiling for how often duodenal smooth muscle can contract, in contrast to the much slower, more deliberate rhythm of the stomach.

incorrectas.A: The stomach has the lowest slow-wave frequency (about 3/minute) of the segments discussed, exactly the opposite extreme from the duodenum's fast rhythm.
incorrectas.B: The ileum's frequency (about 8-9/minute) is faster than the stomach's but still slower than the duodenum's, so it does not hold the highest rate.
incorrectas.D: The colon has its own distinct, generally slower and less regular motility pattern compared to the small intestine, and is not classically cited as having the highest slow-wave frequency in the GI tract.

preguntas.q: Slow waves in GI smooth muscle originate from which specialized pacemaker cells?

e.correcta: Interstitial cells of Cajal (ICC) are specialized pacemaker cells interposed between enteric neurons and smooth muscle that spontaneously generate rhythmic slow-wave depolarizations and propagate them to adjacent smooth muscle through gap junctions. Because they set the baseline electrical rhythm, damage or dysfunction of ICC (as seen in some cases of gastroparesis) directly impairs coordinated GI motility even when the muscle itself is otherwise intact.

incorrectas.B: The myenteric (Auerbach) plexus regulates motility through its neural circuitry and neurotransmitter release, modulating the amplitude and pattern of contractions, but it does not generate the intrinsic slow-wave rhythm itself — that is the specific job of ICC.
incorrectas.A: Enterochromaffin cells are neuroendocrine cells that secrete serotonin and other signaling molecules in response to luminal stimuli, playing a role in reflexes like the vomiting response, but they are not the electrical pacemakers of GI smooth muscle.
incorrectas.C: The submucosal (Meissner) plexus primarily regulates secretion, local blood flow, and epithelial function rather than generating motility-driving slow waves, a role that instead belongs to the myenteric plexus and ICC network.

preguntas.q: During swallowing, which structure is pulled upward to prevent food from entering the nasopharynx?

e.correcta: During the pharyngeal phase of swallowing, the soft palate (along with the uvula) elevates and tenses to seal off the nasopharynx, preventing retrograde reflux of the food bolus into the nasal cavity. This action is coordinated by cranial nerves IX and X and is why damage to these nerves (e.g., in bulbar palsy) can cause nasal regurgitation of food or liquid.

incorrectas.A: The epiglottis protects the airway by covering the laryngeal inlet to prevent aspiration into the trachea — a separate protective mechanism from the nasopharyngeal seal formed by the soft palate.
incorrectas.C: The larynx elevates as a whole during swallowing (partly to help tuck under the epiglottis and protect the airway), but it is the soft palate specifically, not the larynx, that seals the nasopharynx.
incorrectas.D: The cricopharyngeus muscle functions as the upper esophageal sphincter, relaxing to allow the bolus to pass into the esophagus and normally staying contracted to keep air out — it has no role in sealing the nasopharynx.

preguntas.q: During swallowing, which structure moves to cover the laryngeal inlet, preventing food from entering the trachea?

e.correcta: The epiglottis folds downward/backward over the laryngeal opening during the pharyngeal phase of swallowing, working together with laryngeal elevation and vocal cord closure to divert the bolus posteriorly into the esophagus rather than into the airway. This mechanical protection is one of several redundant airway-protective reflexes, so its failure (e.g., after certain neurologic injuries) significantly raises the risk of aspiration pneumonia.

incorrectas.B: The soft palate seals off the nasopharynx to prevent nasal regurgitation, a different structure protecting a different route (nose, not trachea) during swallowing.
incorrectas.C: Vocal cord adduction does contribute to airway closure, but it acts as one part of a coordinated reflex alongside laryngeal elevation and epiglottic closure — it is not, by itself, the structure classically described as covering the laryngeal inlet.
incorrectas.D: The upper esophageal sphincter (cricopharyngeus) relaxes to let the bolus enter the esophagus; it does not physically cover the larynx and its main job is regulating the esophageal entrance, not airway protection.

preguntas.q: The pharynx and upper third of the esophagus are composed of which type of muscle?

o.D: An equal mixture of smooth and striated muscle throughout

e.correcta: The pharynx and upper third of the esophagus are made of striated skeletal muscle under voluntary/somatic motor control (innervated by cranial nerves IX and X acting on skeletal muscle fibers), which allows the initial, voluntarily-initiated phase of swallowing to proceed rapidly and forcefully. This is clinically relevant because disorders affecting skeletal muscle or its motor neurons (e.g., myasthenia gravis, ALS, bulbar palsy) classically impair this upper esophageal/pharyngeal phase of swallowing.

incorrectas.A: Smooth muscle characterizes the lower two-thirds of the esophagus, not the upper third — this is the opposite muscle type from what the question describes for the pharynx and proximal esophagus.
incorrectas.B: Cardiac muscle is unique to the heart and is never found in the esophagus at any level; it is not a relevant option for esophageal histology.
incorrectas.D: The transition is not an even mixture throughout — rather, there is a proximal-to-distal transition where the upper third is purely striated, the middle third has a mix, and the lower third is purely smooth muscle.

preguntas.q: The lower two-thirds of the esophagus are composed of which type of muscle?

o.C: Skeletal muscle innervated only by the vagal motor nucleus

e.correcta: The lower two-thirds of the esophagus are composed of smooth muscle under involuntary autonomic control, primarily via the vagus nerve acting on enteric neurons rather than directly on skeletal-type neuromuscular junctions. This distal smooth muscle segment generates the coordinated peristaltic waves that carry the bolus into the stomach and forms the physiologic basis of the lower esophageal sphincter's tone; disorders here (like achalasia) reflect dysfunction of smooth muscle/enteric innervation rather than skeletal muscle disease.

incorrectas.A: Striated (skeletal) muscle characterizes the pharynx and upper third of the esophagus, not the lower two-thirds — this is the reverse of the correct anatomic distribution.
incorrectas.B: Cardiac muscle is exclusive to the heart and is never a component of esophageal wall histology at any level.
incorrectas.C: While the vagus does innervate this region, it does so via enteric neurons acting on smooth muscle (not by direct skeletal-type innervation), and the muscle type itself here is smooth muscle, not skeletal muscle.

preguntas.q: Which sphincter's tonic contraction primarily prevents air from entering the esophagus during normal respiration?

e.correcta: The upper esophageal sphincter (formed mainly by the cricopharyngeus muscle) maintains tonic contraction at rest, keeping the entrance to the esophagus closed so that air moving through the pharynx during breathing does not pass into the esophagus and stomach (which would otherwise cause aerophagia and bloating). It relaxes only transiently and in a coordinated fashion during swallowing to admit a food bolus.

incorrectas.A: The lower esophageal sphincter sits at the gastroesophageal junction and prevents reflux of gastric contents back into the esophagus — a different structure guarding a different junction, unrelated to keeping air out of the esophagus from above.
incorrectas.C: The pyloric sphincter regulates the rate at which gastric chyme empties into the duodenum; it has no role in preventing air entry at the top of the esophagus.
incorrectas.D: The ileocecal sphincter/valve regulates flow between the terminal ileum and cecum, preventing colonic reflux into the small bowel — far removed anatomically and functionally from air entry into the esophagus.

preguntas.q: Which sphincter, when competent, prevents reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus?

e.correcta: The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) is a physiologic (not fully anatomic) high-pressure zone at the gastroesophageal junction that stays tonically contracted between swallows, preventing acidic gastric contents from refluxing into the esophagus. It relaxes transiently during swallowing (mediated by vagal VIP/NO release) to allow the bolus to pass, then recontracts; when this tone is chronically reduced (e.g., in GERD) or relaxes inappropriately, reflux esophagitis results.

incorrectas.A: The upper esophageal sphincter (cricopharyngeus) sits at the pharyngoesophageal junction and prevents air from entering the esophagus during breathing and reflux of esophageal contents into the pharynx, but it plays no role in guarding against gastric reflux at the distal end.
incorrectas.C: The pyloric sphincter regulates the rate at which gastric chyme empties into the duodenum and helps prevent duodenogastric reflux of bile and pancreatic secretions, not gastroesophageal reflux.
incorrectas.D: The ileocecal valve separates the terminal ileum from the cecum, preventing retrograde flow of colonic bacteria into the small intestine; it has no anatomic or functional relationship to the esophagus.

preguntas.q: During swallowing, release of which neurotransmitter from inhibitory neurons mediates relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter?

e.correcta: VIP (along with nitric oxide) is released from inhibitory neurons of the myenteric plexus onto LES smooth muscle, activating pathways that increase cGMP and cause smooth muscle relaxation. This transient LES relaxation, triggered by the swallowing center via the vagus nerve, allows the food bolus to pass into the stomach before the sphincter regains its resting tone.

incorrectas.B: Acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors is the excitatory neurotransmitter of the enteric nervous system that increases smooth muscle contraction and sphincter tone; it would not explain the relaxation needed to let a bolus pass through the LES.
incorrectas.C: Substance P is an excitatory tachykinin that promotes smooth muscle contraction (increasing motility) rather than sphincter relaxation, making it inconsistent with the relaxation phase of the swallowing reflex.
incorrectas.D: Norepinephrine, released from sympathetic fibers, generally has variable and comparatively minor effects on GI smooth muscle tone compared to the dominant inhibitory role of VIP/NO in mediating LES relaxation during swallowing.

preguntas.q: As the lower esophageal sphincter relaxes during swallowing, the orad stomach also relaxes to accommodate the incoming bolus. What is this vagally mediated phenomenon called?

e.correcta: Receptive relaxation is a vagovagal reflex in which afferent vagal fibers sense distension/swallowing and efferent vagal fibers (via VIP/NO-releasing neurons) relax the smooth muscle of the orad stomach (fundus and proximal body), allowing it to accommodate a large volume of ingested food with only a small rise in intragastric pressure. Loss of this reflex (e.g., after vagotomy) causes early satiety and dumping symptoms because the stomach can no longer stretch to store food.

incorrectas.A: The migrating motor complex is a cyclic pattern of strong peristaltic waves that sweeps through the stomach and small intestine during the fasting state to clear residual debris, unrelated to the gastric accommodation that occurs with a swallow.
incorrectas.B: Segmentation refers to localized, back-and-forth mixing contractions of the small intestine that mix chyme with digestive secretions; it does not describe the fundic relaxation that occurs with swallowing.
incorrectas.D: Haustration describes the segmental sacculations of the colon produced by the teniae coli and circular muscle, a large-intestine phenomenon unrelated to gastric accommodation after swallowing.
