preguntas.q: Which region of the stomach is thin-walled and comprises the fundus and proximal body?

e.correcta: The orad ('toward the mouth') stomach — the fundus and proximal body — has thin smooth muscle walls specialized for receptive relaxation and tonic contraction, allowing it to store ingested food and gradually push it toward the distal stomach without generating strong peristaltic waves. Because it primarily functions as a reservoir rather than a mixing chamber, its muscle layer is comparatively thin and its contractions are tonic rather than phasic.

incorrectas.B: The caudad stomach (distal body and antrum) is thick-walled, generating the strong, rapid peristaltic contractions responsible for mechanically mixing and grinding food into chyme — the opposite muscular arrangement from the thin-walled, storage-oriented orad stomach.
incorrectas.C: The pyloric antrum is part of the caudad stomach; it is thick-walled and generates forceful contractions to mix and propel chyme through the pylorus, not a thin-walled storage region.
incorrectas.D: The duodenal bulb is the first part of the duodenum just distal to the pylorus, anatomically outside the stomach entirely, so it cannot be the thin-walled gastric reservoir being described.

preguntas.q: Which region of the stomach is thick-walled and comprises the distal body and antrum?

e.correcta: The caudad stomach — the distal body and antrum — has a thick muscular wall (including a prominent third oblique muscle layer) that generates strong, rapid peristaltic contractions used to mechanically mix food with gastric secretions and grind it into chyme before propelling it toward the pylorus. This muscular power contrasts with the thin, tonically contracted orad stomach, which is built for storage rather than grinding.

incorrectas.A: The fundus is part of the orad stomach — thin-walled and specialized for receptive relaxation and storage, not the thick, forcefully contracting region described here.
incorrectas.C: The cardia is the small transitional zone immediately surrounding the gastroesophageal junction; it is not the thick-walled, actively mixing region of the stomach referred to as caudad.
incorrectas.D: The orad stomach (fundus and proximal body) is thin-walled and tonically contracted for storage, the functional and structural opposite of the thick-walled caudad stomach.

preguntas.q: Which region of the stomach generates the strong contractions responsible for mixing food with gastric secretions?

e.correcta: The caudad stomach (distal body and antrum) has thick, powerful musculature that produces strong peristaltic contractions, mechanically breaking down food and mixing it with gastric acid and pepsin to form chyme. These contractions also propel chyme against the closed pylorus, causing retropulsion that further grinds solid particles before small amounts are released into the duodenum.

incorrectas.A: The orad stomach is thin-walled and undergoes tonic (sustained), not strong phasic, contractions — it functions mainly to store food via receptive relaxation rather than to mix it.
incorrectas.B: The fundus, part of the orad stomach, participates in storage and tonic contraction, not the vigorous mixing contractions that occur more distally in the caudad stomach.
incorrectas.C: The cardia is simply the narrow zone at the gastroesophageal junction and does not generate the forceful mixing contractions characteristic of the distal, thick-walled stomach.

preguntas.q: Which segment of the GI tract is primarily responsible for digestion and absorption of nutrients?

e.correcta: The small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum) is where the vast majority of chemical digestion (via pancreatic enzymes and bile) and nutrient absorption (via its extensive villous and microvillous surface area) take place. Its combination of segmentation contractions for mixing and a huge absorptive surface area make it the principal site for extracting carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals from chyme.

incorrectas.B: The stomach mainly stores food, initiates protein digestion via pepsin, and mechanically breaks food into chyme, but it absorbs very little (mainly some water, alcohol, and a few lipophilic drugs) compared with the small intestine.
incorrectas.C: The large intestine primarily absorbs water and electrolytes and hosts bacterial fermentation of undigested material, but it does not perform the bulk of nutrient digestion and absorption, which has already occurred by the time chyme reaches it.
incorrectas.D: The esophagus is a purely conduit organ that propels the bolus from the pharynx to the stomach via peristalsis; it has no digestive or absorptive function.

preguntas.q: Which type of intestinal contraction mixes luminal contents back-and-forth without producing net forward movement?

e.correcta: Segmentation contractions are localized, rhythmic contractions of circular smooth muscle that divide and mix the intestinal contents locally, exposing chyme to the mucosal surface and digestive enzymes/bile without propelling it appreciably down the tract. This mixing pattern predominates in the fed state and is driven by intrinsic slow waves originating from the interstitial cells of Cajal.

incorrectas.A: Peristalsis is a coordinated, propagating wave of contraction behind the bolus and relaxation ahead of it that produces net forward (aboral) movement of contents, the opposite motility pattern from the stationary mixing of segmentation.
incorrectas.C: The migrating motor complex is a cyclic, propagating pattern of strong contractions that occurs during fasting to sweep residual debris and bacteria distally through the GI tract — it produces net forward movement, unlike segmentation.
incorrectas.D: Receptive relaxation refers to fundic smooth muscle relaxation that accommodates an incoming meal, a storage-related phenomenon in the stomach, not a mixing contraction pattern of the small intestine.

preguntas.q: Which type of contraction propels chyme forward along the small intestine toward the large intestine?

e.correcta: Peristaltic contractions consist of a ring of contraction proximal to the bolus and relaxation distal to it, coordinated by the enteric nervous system, that produces net aboral (forward) propulsion of luminal contents. This differs from segmentation, whose back-and-forth contractions mix contents locally without significant net forward movement.

incorrectas.A: Segmentation contractions mix intestinal contents locally through repeated back-and-forth division of the lumen, but by design they do not propel chyme forward the way peristalsis does.
incorrectas.C: Haustration describes the sacculated appearance and slow mixing movements of the colon produced by its teniae coli, a large-intestine phenomenon distinct from small-intestinal peristalsis.
incorrectas.D: Mass movements are powerful, infrequent peristaltic-like contractions of the colon (often triggered by the gastrocolic reflex) that push contents toward the rectum; they occur in the large intestine, not the small intestine.

preguntas.q: Binding of which substance to intrinsic primary afferent neurons (IPANs) in the gut wall triggers the peristaltic reflex?

e.correcta: Enterochromaffin cells in the intestinal mucosa release serotonin (5-HT) in response to mechanical or chemical stimulation by luminal contents; 5-HT binds 5-HT receptors on intrinsic primary afferent neurons (IPANs) of the enteric nervous system, initiating the peristaltic reflex — contraction proximal to the bolus and relaxation distal to it. This 5-HT signaling pathway is the pharmacologic target of drugs like 5-HT4 agonists (prokinetics) and 5-HT3 antagonists (antiemetics).

incorrectas.B: Acetylcholine is an excitatory motor neurotransmitter released by enteric motor neurons onto smooth muscle to cause contraction, but it is not the mucosal signal that initially activates IPANs to trigger the peristaltic reflex.
incorrectas.C: Substance P is co-released with acetylcholine at excitatory motor neuron endings to help drive smooth muscle contraction during peristalsis, but it is not the primary mucosal trigger that activates the sensory IPANs.
incorrectas.D: VIP is an inhibitory neurotransmitter that mediates smooth muscle relaxation (e.g., receptive relaxation, LES relaxation), the opposite role from the excitatory mucosal signal (5-HT) that initiates the peristaltic reflex via IPANs.

preguntas.q: What is the term for the reflex increase in colonic mass movements triggered by the presence of food in the stomach?

e.correcta: The gastrocolic reflex is triggered by gastric distension (and mediated by gastrin, CCK, and extrinsic autonomic pathways) and produces mass movements — strong, sweeping colonic contractions that propel contents toward the rectum, often prompting the urge to defecate shortly after eating. This reflex is typically stronger after the first meal of the day and is often exaggerated in conditions like irritable bowel syndrome.

incorrectas.A: The enterogastric reflex is the opposite-direction signal: distension or acidic/fatty chyme in the duodenum inhibits gastric motility and secretion, slowing gastric emptying — it does not describe stomach-to-colon signaling.
incorrectas.B: The migrating motor complex is an intrinsic fasting-state motility pattern that clears the stomach and small intestine of residual debris between meals; it is not triggered specifically by food entering the stomach nor does it act on the colon.
incorrectas.C: The gastroileal reflex increases motility and relaxes the ileocecal sphincter to move ileal contents into the cecum in response to a meal, which is related but distinct from the gastrocolic reflex's effect on colonic mass movements.

preguntas.q: By what transport process do ductal cells of the salivary gland add K+ and HCO3- to the initially isotonic, plasma-like saliva produced by acinar cells?

e.correcta: Salivary ductal cells actively secrete K+ and HCO3- into the luminal fluid while simultaneously reabsorbing Na+ and Cl- (via active transport, exceeding the secretion of K+/HCO3-), progressively modifying the initial isotonic acinar secretion into a hypotonic final saliva enriched in K+ and HCO3- relative to plasma. Because the ducts are relatively impermeable to water, this ion modification occurs without proportional water movement, which is what makes final saliva hypotonic.

incorrectas.A: Reabsorption describes what ductal cells do to Na+ and Cl- (removing them from the lumen back into the interstitium), the opposite ionic movement from the active secretion of K+ and HCO3- into the saliva.
incorrectas.C: Facilitated diffusion is passive, carrier-mediated movement down a concentration gradient; ductal modification of saliva is an active, energy-requiring process capable of moving ions against their gradients, not simple facilitated diffusion.
incorrectas.D: Filtration (bulk flow driven by hydrostatic/oncotic pressure differences, as in glomerular filtration) is not how salivary ducts modify fluid composition — ductal modification is achieved through active ion transport across the ductal epithelium.

preguntas.q: Compared with plasma, how do the K+ and HCO3- concentrations in final saliva compare?

e.correcta: Ductal cells actively secrete K+ and HCO3- into the saliva while reabsorbing Na+ and Cl-, so the final saliva that reaches the mouth has higher K+ and HCO3- concentrations than plasma, especially at low (resting) flow rates when the ducts have more contact time to modify the fluid. This bicarbonate-rich, potassium-rich profile helps neutralize oral acids and buffer the mouth's pH.

incorrectas.B: Lower-than-plasma concentrations describe Na+ and Cl- in saliva (which are reabsorbed by the ducts), not K+ and HCO3-, which are actively secreted and therefore end up elevated relative to plasma.
incorrectas.C: Saliva is not simply isotonic/equal to plasma in composition — only the initial acinar secretion is plasma-like; ductal modification actively changes the ionic composition, raising K+/HCO3- and lowering Na+/Cl- relative to plasma.
incorrectas.D: K+ and HCO3- are not absent from saliva — they are actively added by the ductal cells and are, in fact, present at higher concentrations than in plasma.

preguntas.q: Compared with plasma, how do the Na+ and Cl- concentrations in final saliva compare?

e.correcta: Ductal cells actively reabsorb Na+ and Cl- from the luminal fluid (via active transport) while secreting K+ and HCO3-, so final saliva ends up with lower Na+ and Cl- concentrations than plasma. This reabsorption is most complete at low flow rates, when the fluid has more time in contact with the ducts, making resting saliva the most hypotonic and Na+/Cl--poor.

incorrectas.A: Saliva is not compositionally equal to plasma; only the initial acinar secretion resembles plasma before ductal modification changes its ion content substantially.
incorrectas.B: Higher-than-plasma concentrations describe K+ and HCO3-, which are actively secreted by ductal cells — the opposite ionic behavior from Na+ and Cl-, which are reabsorbed and thus reduced relative to plasma.
incorrectas.D: Na+ and Cl- reabsorption is governed mainly by ductal transport and flow rate (with parasympathetic stimulation driving flow), not specifically by sympathetic activity, and the relative reduction versus plasma holds under normal physiologic conditions, not just with sympathetic input.

preguntas.q: Overall, how does the tonicity of final saliva compare with that of plasma?

o.D: Tonicity is unrelated to flow rate

e.correcta: Because ductal reabsorption of Na+ and Cl- exceeds the secretion of K+ and HCO3-, and the ducts are relatively impermeable to water, saliva ends up hypotonic relative to plasma — most markedly at low (resting) flow rates. At very high flow rates there is less time for ductal modification, so saliva approaches (but typically does not exceed) plasma osmolarity, but it never becomes hypertonic under normal physiology.

incorrectas.A: Saliva is never hypertonic to plasma; the net effect of ductal transport (net solute removal without matching water removal) always drives saliva toward a lower, not higher, osmolarity than plasma.
incorrectas.C: Saliva is not isotonic to plasma except transiently in the acinar secretion before ductal modification; the final saliva that exits the ducts is measurably hypotonic due to net ion reabsorption exceeding secretion.
incorrectas.D: Salivary tonicity is directly related to flow rate — at high flow rates saliva is closer to isotonic (less time for ductal modification), while at low flow rates it becomes markedly more hypotonic, so flow rate is a key determinant, not an unrelated variable.

preguntas.q: Which salivary enzyme initiates digestion of dietary carbohydrates in the mouth?

e.correcta: Salivary α-amylase (ptyalin), secreted by the parotid and other salivary glands, begins hydrolyzing internal α-1,4-glycosidic bonds in starch (amylose and amylopectin) in the mouth, producing shorter oligosaccharides and maltose even before food reaches the stomach. Its action is later halted by the low gastric pH, with carbohydrate digestion resuming in the duodenum via pancreatic amylase.

incorrectas.B: Pepsin is a gastric protease, secreted as pepsinogen by chief cells and activated by acid in the stomach, that begins protein (not carbohydrate) digestion — it has no role in oral starch breakdown.
incorrectas.C: Trypsin is a pancreatic protease released into the duodenum that continues protein digestion; it is not present in saliva and does not act on carbohydrates.
incorrectas.D: Lingual lipase, though also secreted in the mouth, targets dietary triglycerides (fat digestion), not carbohydrates — the enzyme responsible for initial starch breakdown is α-amylase.

preguntas.q: Which salivary enzyme begins the initial digestion of dietary fats in the mouth?

e.correcta: Lingual lipase, secreted by serous glands at the base of the tongue, begins hydrolyzing dietary triglycerides into free fatty acids and diglycerides while food is still in the mouth and stomach — it is particularly important in infants (who rely on it more heavily due to lower pancreatic lipase activity) and remains active in the acidic gastric environment, unlike salivary amylase.

incorrectas.A: Pancreatic lipase is the major fat-digesting enzyme, but it is secreted by the exocrine pancreas into the duodenum, not by salivary glands, and acts later in digestion than lingual lipase.
incorrectas.B: α-amylase is the salivary enzyme responsible for initiating carbohydrate (starch) digestion, not fat digestion.
incorrectas.C: Pepsin is a gastric protease that begins protein digestion in the stomach; it plays no role in fat digestion.

preguntas.q: Which salivary enzyme cleaves kininogen to release bradykinin, a potent vasodilator that increases blood flow to active salivary glands?

e.correcta: Kallikrein, released by salivary gland cells (especially with parasympathetic stimulation), proteolytically cleaves kininogen into bradykinin, which vasodilates local blood vessels and increases glandular blood flow to support the increased metabolic demand of active secretion. This is a classic example of a local paracrine feedback loop that couples secretory activity to its own blood supply.

incorrectas.A: Renin is a proteolytic enzyme released by the kidney's juxtaglomerular cells that cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, part of the RAAS system for blood pressure regulation — unrelated to salivary kinin generation.
incorrectas.C: α-amylase is the salivary enzyme that digests starch into smaller carbohydrates; it has no proteolytic action on kininogen.
incorrectas.D: Lingual lipase digests dietary triglycerides in the mouth and stomach; it does not cleave kininogen or generate bradykinin.

preguntas.q: At which salivary flow rate condition does saliva composition most closely resemble plasma (high Na+ and Cl-, low K+)?

o.D: Flow rate does not affect composition

e.correcta: At the highest flow rates (strong parasympathetic stimulation), saliva passes through the ducts too quickly for the ductal cells to fully reabsorb Na+/Cl- or secrete K+/HCO3-, so the final secretion more closely resembles the isotonic, plasma-like fluid initially produced by the acinar cells. This is why copious salivation (e.g., with a meal) yields saliva with relatively higher Na+/Cl- and lower K+ than the more concentrated, hypotonic saliva produced at rest.

incorrectas.B: At the lowest (resting) flow rates, saliva has the most time for ductal modification, making it the most dissimilar to plasma (highest K+, lowest Na+/Cl-) — the opposite of what this question describes.
incorrectas.C: Composition changes progressively with flow rate rather than only at some intermediate range; the extremes (highest vs. lowest flow) are what produce the most plasma-like and least plasma-like saliva, respectively.
incorrectas.D: Flow rate is actually the key determinant of salivary composition because it controls how much time ductal cells have to modify the fluid — it strongly, not negligibly, affects ion concentrations.

preguntas.q: At which salivary flow rate condition is saliva composition most dissimilar to plasma (high K+, low Na+ and Cl-)?

o.D: Flow rate has no effect on composition

e.correcta: At the lowest, resting flow rates, saliva remains in contact with the ductal epithelium the longest, allowing maximal reabsorption of Na+/Cl- and maximal secretion of K+/HCO3-. This produces the most hypotonic saliva with the greatest deviation from plasma composition — high K+ and low Na+/Cl- — compared with the near-plasma-like composition seen at high flow rates.

incorrectas.B: At the highest flow rates, saliva passes through the ducts too quickly for full ionic modification, so it actually resembles plasma most closely — the opposite of maximal dissimilarity.
incorrectas.C: Sleep is associated with markedly reduced (near-resting) salivary flow, but the determining physiologic variable is flow rate itself, not sleep as a distinct state — the same low-flow composition occurs any time flow is low, awake or asleep.
incorrectas.D: Flow rate is the principal determinant of salivary ionic composition; higher flow yields more plasma-like saliva and lower flow yields more modified, dissimilar saliva.

preguntas.q: How does the concentration of HCO3- in saliva change as salivary flow rate increases?

o.D: It fluctuates unpredictably with no clear pattern

e.correcta: Unlike Na+ and Cl- (whose ductal handling is relatively flow-independent in direction), HCO3- secretion by ductal cells is selectively upregulated when salivary secretion is stimulated, so HCO3- concentration rises as flow rate increases. This increase helps neutralize the extra acid load and provides greater buffering capacity in the mouth precisely when more saliva (e.g., with eating) is being produced.

incorrectas.A: A decrease would be the pattern seen for K+ concentration as flow rate rises toward the plasma-like profile at high flow, but HCO3- behaves oppositely — its secretion is actively increased with higher flow, not decreased.
incorrectas.C: HCO3- concentration is not constant — it is one of the ions most sensitively regulated by flow rate, rising specifically because ductal HCO3- secretion is stimulated along with overall salivary flow.
incorrectas.D: The change in HCO3- with flow rate is not random — it follows a predictable, physiologically purposeful pattern of increasing secretion as flow rate rises to meet the buffering needs of a more actively secreting gland.

preguntas.q: What effect does parasympathetic stimulation have on salivary gland secretion, and via which receptor?

e.correcta: Parasympathetic fibers (from the facial and glossopharyngeal nerves) release acetylcholine onto M3 muscarinic receptors on acinar and ductal cells, activating a Gq-PLC-IP3-Ca2+ pathway that strongly increases the volume of watery, enzyme-rich saliva. This is the dominant driver of salivary secretion, which is why anticholinergic drugs (e.g., antihistamines, TCAs) classically cause dry mouth.

incorrectas.A: Parasympathetic (muscarinic) stimulation increases, not decreases, salivary secretion — this is the primary physiologic drive for copious saliva production, such as at the sight or smell of food.
incorrectas.B: Muscarinic, not nicotinic, receptors mediate the postganglionic parasympathetic effect on salivary acinar/ductal cells; nicotinic receptors are involved in ganglionic transmission along the autonomic pathway, not the end-organ effect on the gland itself.
incorrectas.C: Parasympathetic input is actually the single most important driver of salivary flow — far from having no effect, it produces the largest increases in secretion of any autonomic input to the gland.

preguntas.q: What effect does sympathetic stimulation have on salivary gland secretion, and via which receptor?

e.correcta: Sympathetic fibers release norepinephrine that acts on β-adrenergic receptors on salivary acinar cells, which — somewhat unusually compared with sympathetic effects elsewhere — also increases secretion, though it produces a smaller volume of thicker, more protein/mucus-rich saliva compared with the large watery output driven by parasympathetic stimulation. Both autonomic limbs therefore stimulate salivation, unlike in most other exocrine glands where sympathetic and parasympathetic effects oppose each other.

incorrectas.B: Sympathetic stimulation actually increases, not decreases, salivary secretion via β receptors, even though it yields a thicker, lower-volume secretion compared with the parasympathetic response.
incorrectas.C: α1 receptors on salivary gland vasculature primarily mediate vasoconstriction (reducing blood flow), while it is β receptors on the acinar cells themselves that drive the direct secretory effect described here.
incorrectas.D: Sympathetic input does have a measurable effect on salivary glands — it increases secretion of a thick, protein-rich saliva via β receptors, distinct from the larger watery response to parasympathetic stimulation.

preguntas.q: In the first step of gastric acid secretion by parietal cells, which enzyme catalyzes the combination of CO2 and H2O to form H2CO3?

e.correcta: Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes the hydration of CO2 (diffusing in from blood or generated by cellular metabolism) with H2O to form carbonic acid (H2CO3) inside the parietal cell. This H2CO3 rapidly dissociates into H+ (which is then pumped into the gastric lumen) and HCO3- (which exits across the basolateral membrane into blood via the Cl-/HCO3- exchanger, producing the postprandial 'alkaline tide').

incorrectas.A: The H+/K+ ATPase is the pump on the apical (luminal) membrane that actively secretes the H+ generated from H2CO3 dissociation into the gastric lumen in exchange for K+ — it acts after, not during, the carbonic anhydrase step.
incorrectas.B: The Cl-/HCO3- exchanger on the basolateral membrane moves the HCO3- byproduct of H2CO3 dissociation out of the cell into the blood in exchange for Cl-; it is a later step, not the enzyme that forms H2CO3 from CO2 and H2O.
incorrectas.D: Adenylate cyclase generates cAMP as a second messenger downstream of histamine binding to H2 receptors on the parietal cell, part of the signaling cascade that stimulates acid secretion — it is not the enzyme responsible for CO2 hydration.

preguntas.q: Through which transporter is H+ secreted from the parietal cell into the gastric lumen?

e.correcta: The H+/K+ ATPase ('proton pump'), located on the apical (canalicular) membrane of the parietal cell, actively pumps H+ into the gastric lumen in exchange for K+, using ATP hydrolysis to move H+ against a massive concentration gradient (luminal pH can drop below 1). This pump is the definitive target of proton pump inhibitors like omeprazole, which irreversibly block it to suppress gastric acid secretion.

incorrectas.A: The Cl-/HCO3- exchanger sits on the basolateral membrane and moves HCO3- out of the cell into the blood in exchange for Cl- (which then exits the apical membrane into the lumen); it does not itself transport H+ into the lumen.
incorrectas.C: The Na+/K+ ATPase maintains the parietal cell's basic ionic gradients (low intracellular Na+, high intracellular K+) on the basolateral membrane, supporting the cell's overall ion transport machinery, but it is not the apical pump that secretes H+ into the gastric lumen.
incorrectas.D: Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes formation of H2CO3 from CO2 and H2O, generating the H+ that will be secreted, but the actual transport of H+ across the apical membrane into the lumen is performed by the H+/K+ ATPase, not carbonic anhydrase.

preguntas.q: In the gastric parietal cell, Cl- follows H+ into the lumen by diffusing through which type of transport protein on the apical (luminal) membrane?

e.correcta: Cl- channels on the apical membrane allow passive diffusion of Cl- into the gastric lumen, where it combines with the H+ actively secreted by the H+/K+-ATPase to form HCl. The electrochemical gradient established by active H+ secretion is what drives this passive Cl- efflux, so the channel itself requires no direct energy input.

incorrectas.B: The H+/K+-ATPase is the primary active transporter that pumps H+ into the lumen in exchange for K+ using ATP hydrolysis; it does not carry Cl-, which instead crosses through the separate passive Cl- channel described here.
incorrectas.C: The Na+/K+-ATPase is a basolateral pump that maintains the ionic gradients supporting the overall secretory process, but it does not directly move Cl- into the gastric lumen.
incorrectas.D: The Cl--HCO3- exchanger sits on the basolateral membrane and moves Cl- INTO the cell in exchange for HCO3- leaving to the blood (the alkaline tide) — the opposite membrane and direction from the apical Cl- channel that lets Cl- exit into the lumen.

preguntas.q: During gastric acid secretion, the HCO3- generated from carbonic acid within the parietal cell is transported into the blood via which basolateral transporter?

e.correcta: Carbonic anhydrase converts CO2 and H2O into H2CO3, which dissociates into H+ (secreted apically) and HCO3-. The HCO3- exits the parietal cell into the blood via the basolateral Cl--HCO3- exchanger, which simultaneously imports Cl- destined for apical secretion; this HCO3- efflux is what produces the postprandial 'alkaline tide' seen in venous blood pH after a meal.

incorrectas.A: The Na+/H+ exchanger is more classically associated with intracellular pH regulation and Na+ handling in tissues like the renal proximal tubule, not with the parietal cell's route for exporting HCO3- to the blood.
incorrectas.C: The H+/K+-ATPase is the apical pump that actively secretes H+ into the lumen in exchange for K+; it operates on the opposite membrane and has no role in basolateral HCO3- export.
incorrectas.D: The Na+/K+-ATPase is a basolateral pump that maintains the Na+/K+ gradients supporting other transporters, but it does not itself move HCO3- from the cell into the blood.

preguntas.q: Gastrin directly stimulates gastric acid secretion by binding to which receptor on parietal cells?

e.correcta: Gastrin binds CCKB (also called CCK2) receptors on parietal cells, a Gq-coupled receptor that triggers the IP3/Ca2+ signaling cascade to stimulate H+/K+-ATPase-mediated acid secretion. This direct action is real but modest compared to gastrin's larger indirect effect via ECL-cell histamine release, which is why H2 blockers so effectively blunt gastrin-driven acid output.

incorrectas.A: The CCKA receptor primarily mediates cholecystokinin's effects on gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion, not gastrin's direct action on gastric parietal cells.
incorrectas.B: The M3 receptor is the muscarinic receptor for acetylcholine on parietal cells; like CCKB it is Gq-coupled, but it is activated by vagal ACh release during the cephalic and gastric phases, not by gastrin.
incorrectas.D: The H2 receptor is the histamine receptor, Gs-coupled and linked to cAMP; it mediates the major indirect (ECL-histamine) route of gastric stimulation, not gastrin's direct receptor binding.

preguntas.q: Which hormone indirectly promotes gastric acid secretion primarily by stimulating histamine release from enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells?

e.correcta: Gastrin acts on CCKB receptors on ECL cells to trigger histamine release, and that histamine then diffuses to adjacent parietal cells to bind H2 receptors, amplifying acid secretion through the cAMP pathway. This indirect ECL-mediated route actually accounts for a larger share of gastrin's acid-stimulating effect than its direct action on parietal cells.

incorrectas.A: Secretin is released from duodenal S cells in response to acidic chyme and inhibits gastric acid secretion while stimulating pancreatic bicarbonate release — the opposite effect of stimulating ECL histamine release.
incorrectas.B: Cholecystokinin is released in response to fatty acids and amino acids in the duodenum and mainly stimulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion; it has only a minor, largely inhibitory role on gastric acid rather than driving ECL histamine release.
incorrectas.C: Somatostatin inhibits acid secretion by suppressing gastrin release, ECL histamine release, and parietal cell activity directly, the opposite of stimulating the ECL-histamine pathway.

preguntas.q: Gastrin's stimulatory effect on gastric acid secretion occurs primarily through actions on which cell type, rather than through direct action on parietal cells?

e.correcta: Although gastrin can bind CCKB receptors directly on parietal cells, its dominant mechanism is stimulating enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells to release histamine, which then acts locally on parietal cell H2 receptors. This explains why H2 blockers so effectively suppress gastrin-driven acid secretion — they interrupt the major amplification step rather than gastrin's minor direct effect.

incorrectas.B: D cells are the source of somatostatin, an inhibitor of acid secretion, and are not the target cell type through which gastrin exerts its stimulatory effect.
incorrectas.C: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and gastric lipase; they are not part of the ECL-mediated amplification pathway that underlies gastrin's main acid-stimulating action.
incorrectas.D: G cells are the antral cells that SECRETE gastrin in the first place, not a downstream target cell that gastrin acts upon to stimulate acid secretion.

preguntas.q: What type of signaling mechanism does gastrin use to reach and act on parietal cells?

e.correcta: Gastrin is a true hormone released from antral G cells into the bloodstream, allowing it to travel systemically and reach parietal cells throughout the stomach. This endocrine mode of signaling is why gastrin can act at a distance from its site of release, unlike locally acting mediators such as histamine.

incorrectas.A: Paracrine signaling involves local diffusion to nearby cells, which describes histamine's action on adjacent parietal cells, not gastrin, which travels through the bloodstream as a true endocrine hormone.
incorrectas.C: Autocrine signaling occurs when a cell acts on itself via receptors it also expresses; this does not apply to gastrin, which is released by G cells but acts on distant parietal cells.
incorrectas.D: Neurocrine signaling involves neurotransmitter release from nerve terminals, such as acetylcholine from vagal fibers; gastrin instead reaches its target cells through the circulation as a blood-borne hormone.

preguntas.q: What type of signaling mechanism does histamine use to reach parietal cells from nearby ECL cells?

e.correcta: Histamine released from ECL cells diffuses through the local interstitium to act on immediately adjacent parietal cells — a classic paracrine mechanism that depends on close physical proximity rather than release into the bloodstream. This local action is precisely why H2 blockers are so effective: they target a short-range, high-concentration signal rather than a diluted systemic hormone.

incorrectas.A: Endocrine signaling describes gastrin's bloodstream-based route to distant cells, not histamine's local, diffusion-based action on adjacent parietal cells.
incorrectas.B: Neurocrine signaling involves neurotransmitter release from nerve terminals (such as vagal acetylcholine), which is distinct from histamine's release by ECL cells acting on nearby, non-neuronal targets.
incorrectas.D: Autocrine signaling would mean the ECL cell acting on itself; instead, ECL-released histamine targets neighboring parietal cells, making this a paracrine, not autocrine, interaction.

preguntas.q: Binding of gastrin to CCKB receptors on parietal cells activates which second messenger pathway?

e.correcta: CCKB receptors are Gq-coupled, activating phospholipase C to generate IP3 and DAG; IP3 releases Ca2+ from intracellular stores, and the resulting rise in intracellular Ca2+ activates kinases that stimulate H+/K+-ATPase-mediated acid secretion. This is the same Gq/IP3 pathway used by acetylcholine acting on M3 receptors, distinguishing it from histamine's Gs/cAMP route.

incorrectas.A: cAMP is the second messenger generated by Gs-coupled receptors such as the H2 histamine receptor — a separate signaling pathway from gastrin's Gq/IP3 cascade, even though both ultimately increase acid secretion.
incorrectas.B: cGMP is produced via guanylate cyclase activation (for example, by nitric oxide or natriuretic peptides) and is not part of the CCKB receptor's signaling cascade in parietal cells.
incorrectas.C: Ras/MAPK is a growth-factor-associated cascade typically downstream of receptor tyrosine kinases, not the mechanism by which the Gq-coupled CCKB receptor stimulates acid secretion.

preguntas.q: Binding of histamine to H2 receptors on parietal cells increases which second messenger?

e.correcta: H2 receptors are Gs-coupled, activating adenylate cyclase and raising intracellular cAMP, which activates protein kinase A and drives insertion and activation of the H+/K+-ATPase at the apical membrane. This cAMP pathway is exactly why H2 blockers such as cimetidine and ranitidine effectively reduce acid secretion.

incorrectas.B: IP3/Ca2+ is the second messenger pathway used by Gq-coupled receptors such as gastrin's CCKB receptor and acetylcholine's M3 receptor, not by the Gs-coupled H2 receptor.
incorrectas.C: cGMP is produced via a separate guanylate cyclase pathway and is unrelated to histamine's Gs/adenylate cyclase/cAMP signaling on parietal cells.
incorrectas.D: DAG is generated together with IP3 by phospholipase C downstream of Gq-coupled receptors, not by the Gs-coupled H2 receptor, which signals exclusively through cAMP.

preguntas.q: Which phase of gastric acid secretion, triggered by the sight, smell, taste, chewing, and swallowing of food, accounts for approximately 30% of total HCl secreted per meal?

e.correcta: The cephalic phase is triggered by sensory and cognitive cues — sight, smell, taste, chewing, and swallowing — processed through the vagus nerve, which stimulates parietal cells both directly via acetylcholine and indirectly via gastrin-releasing peptide-driven gastrin release from G cells. It contributes roughly 30% of total meal-stimulated acid output, priming the stomach even before food physically arrives.

incorrectas.A: The gastric phase is triggered once food is actually in the stomach (via distention and luminal amino acids/peptides) and contributes the largest share of secretion (~60%), rather than the anticipatory, pre-ingestion cephalic response.
incorrectas.C: The intestinal phase occurs after chyme reaches the duodenum and contributes only a small fraction (roughly 5-10%) of total acid secretion, and is largely inhibitory once acid delivery increases — distinct from the stimulatory, anticipatory cephalic phase.
incorrectas.D: The basal (interdigestive) phase refers to the ongoing, low-level acid secretion that occurs between meals following a circadian rhythm, unrelated to meal-anticipation cues like smell or taste.

preguntas.q: Which phase of gastric acid secretion, triggered by gastric distention and the presence of amino acids/peptides in the stomach, accounts for approximately 60% of total HCl secreted per meal?

e.correcta: The gastric phase begins once food actually enters the stomach: distention activates vagovagal and local enteric reflexes, while luminal peptides and amino acids directly stimulate G cells to release gastrin. Together these mechanisms drive the largest share of a meal's total acid secretion, roughly 60%.

incorrectas.A: The cephalic phase is the anticipatory response driven by sensory cues (sight, smell, taste) before food reaches the stomach, and contributes a smaller share (~30%) compared to the gastric phase.
incorrectas.B: The intestinal phase occurs after chyme enters the duodenum and contributes only a minor fraction of total acid secretion, with a net inhibitory effect once acid delivery to the duodenum increases, unlike the strongly stimulatory gastric phase.
incorrectas.D: The basal phase describes the low baseline secretion that occurs between meals, not the large distention- and amino-acid-driven response characteristic of the gastric phase.

preguntas.q: Acid secretion during the gastric phase is mediated by which two mechanisms in response to stomach distention and luminal amino acids?

o.D: Vagal stimulation and direct gastrin release

e.correcta: Gastric distention activates a vagovagal (long) reflex and local enteric reflexes that release acetylcholine onto parietal and G cells, while luminal amino acids and peptides directly stimulate G cells to release gastrin into the blood. Both mechanisms converge on the parietal cell to substantially boost acid secretion during the gastric phase.

incorrectas.A: Secretin and CCK are released from duodenal S and I cells during the intestinal phase in response to acid and fat/protein in the duodenum, and they largely inhibit or modulate gastric emptying and stimulate pancreatic secretion rather than driving gastric-phase acid output.
incorrectas.B: Somatostatin and prostaglandins both inhibit acid secretion by lowering parietal cell cAMP — the opposite of the stimulatory processes that actually characterize the gastric phase.
incorrectas.C: Motilin regulates the interdigestive migrating motor complex between meals, and vagal inhibition would reduce rather than increase acid secretion, contrary to the genuinely stimulatory vagal role during the gastric phase.

preguntas.q: What effect do alcohol and caffeine have on gastric HCl secretion?

e.correcta: Alcohol and caffeine both stimulate gastric acid secretion. Caffeine acts partly by inhibiting phosphodiesterase, raising intracellular cAMP in a manner that mimics histamine's stimulatory effect, while alcohol directly irritates the gastric mucosa and promotes gastrin and histamine release; this is why both are counseled against in patients with peptic ulcer disease or GERD.

incorrectas.B: Decreased secretion is the opposite of the actual effect — agents that genuinely decrease acid secretion include somatostatin and prostaglandins, not alcohol or caffeine.
incorrectas.C: No significant effect is inaccurate; both substances have well-documented stimulatory actions on parietal cell acid output rather than being neutral.
incorrectas.D: Describing the effect as occurring 'only via somatostatin suppression' mischaracterizes the mechanism — alcohol and caffeine directly stimulate acid secretion (via mucosal irritation and cAMP elevation), rather than acting indirectly by suppressing an inhibitory hormone.

preguntas.q: Somatostatin inhibits gastric acid secretion primarily by decreasing which second messenger in parietal cells, via a Gi-coupled receptor?

e.correcta: Somatostatin, released from D cells in response to luminal acid, binds Gi-coupled receptors on parietal cells (and also inhibits G cells and ECL cells), decreasing adenylate cyclase activity and thus lowering cAMP. This counteracts the stimulatory cAMP rise driven by histamine/H2 signaling, forming a negative feedback loop that limits further acid secretion once luminal pH becomes very low.

incorrectas.A: IP3 is increased, not decreased, by stimulatory Gq-coupled pathways such as gastrin/CCKB and acetylcholine/M3 signaling — it is not the messenger targeted by somatostatin's inhibitory Gi mechanism.
incorrectas.C: Intracellular Ca2+ rises with Gq-pathway stimulation via IP3; it is not the second messenger directly decreased by somatostatin's Gi-cAMP inhibitory action.
incorrectas.D: cGMP is produced through a separate guanylate cyclase pathway and is not the second messenger modulated by somatostatin's Gi-coupled receptor on parietal cells.

preguntas.q: What effect do prostaglandins (e.g., PGE2) have on gastric acid secretion?

e.correcta: Prostaglandins, particularly PGE2 and PGI2, inhibit gastric acid secretion while also stimulating mucus and bicarbonate secretion and increasing mucosal blood flow, together producing a protective effect on the gastric lining. This is precisely why NSAIDs, which block prostaglandin synthesis via COX inhibition, predispose patients to peptic ulcers.

incorrectas.A: Increased secretion is the opposite of prostaglandins' actual protective, inhibitory role on parietal cell acid output.
incorrectas.B: No effect is inaccurate, since prostaglandins have a well-established Gi-mediated inhibitory action on parietal cell cAMP and acid secretion.
incorrectas.D: Prostaglandins' gastric action is consistently inhibitory and cytoprotective across physiologic conditions, not a dose-dependent effect that reverses direction.

preguntas.q: Prostaglandins inhibit gastric acid secretion by activating a Gi-coupled receptor on parietal cells and decreasing levels of which second messenger?

e.correcta: Prostaglandin E2 binds an EP3-type Gi-coupled receptor on parietal cells, inhibiting adenylate cyclase and lowering intracellular cAMP, directly opposing the stimulatory cAMP rise produced by histamine's H2/Gs signaling. This mirrors somatostatin's inhibitory mechanism and is a key reason NSAID-induced loss of prostaglandins increases the risk of acid-related mucosal injury.

incorrectas.A: IP3 is increased by stimulatory Gq-coupled receptors such as gastrin and acetylcholine, not the messenger decreased by prostaglandin's Gi-mediated inhibitory pathway.
incorrectas.B: cGMP is produced through a distinct guanylate cyclase pathway unrelated to prostaglandin's Gi/adenylate cyclase signaling in parietal cells.
incorrectas.C: Ca2+ rises with Gq/IP3 stimulatory signaling, not with prostaglandin's inhibitory Gi/cAMP mechanism, which instead lowers cAMP.

preguntas.q: Which is the only secretion of the stomach that is essential for survival?

e.correcta: Intrinsic factor, secreted by parietal cells, is required for binding vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum for absorption via cubam receptors. Unlike acid or pepsinogen, which have redundant or non-essential contributions to digestion, there is no alternate pathway for B12 absorption without intrinsic factor, which is why patients after total gastrectomy require lifelong parenteral or very high-dose oral B12.

incorrectas.B: Pepsinogen is activated to pepsin for protein digestion, but its loss can largely be compensated by pancreatic proteases, so it is not essential for survival the way intrinsic factor is.
incorrectas.C: Gastric acid aids digestion, iron absorption, and killing of ingested pathogens, but patients on long-term acid suppression or after partial gastrectomy can survive without significant acid secretion.
incorrectas.D: Mucus protects the gastric mucosa from autodigestion, but its absence does not cause the specific, irreversible nutritional deficiency that loss of intrinsic factor does.

preguntas.q: Mucus is secreted into the GI tract by which cell type, found in the stomach, duodenum, salivary glands, and pancreas?

e.correcta: Mucous cells (called foveolar or mucous neck cells in the stomach) line the surface and glands of multiple GI organs and secrete a protective mucus layer rich in mucin. This is distinct from goblet cells, which are the dedicated mucus-secreting cells specifically of the intestinal and respiratory epithelium.

incorrectas.A: Goblet cells secrete mucus specifically within the small and large intestinal (and respiratory) epithelium, not the broader set of mucous cells found across the stomach, duodenum, salivary glands, and pancreas described here.
incorrectas.C: Chief cells, located in gastric glands, secrete pepsinogen and gastric lipase — digestive products, not mucus.
incorrectas.D: Paneth cells, located at the base of small intestinal crypts, secrete antimicrobial peptides such as defensins and lysozyme as part of innate immunity, not mucus.

preguntas.q: Mucus in the duodenum is secreted primarily by which glandular structures located in the submucosa?

e.correcta: Brunner glands are submucosal glands unique to the duodenum that secrete an alkaline, mucus-rich fluid to protect the duodenal mucosa from acidic chyme and help neutralize gastric acid as it enters the small intestine. Their hypertrophy is classically associated with peptic ulcer disease due to chronic acid exposure.

incorrectas.A: Crypts of Lieberkuhn are intestinal glands found throughout the small and large intestine that house stem cells, Paneth cells, and various secretory cells, but they are not the alkaline mucus-secreting glands specific to the duodenal submucosa.
incorrectas.B: Peyer patches are lymphoid tissue found mainly in the ileum, involved in mucosal immune surveillance, and are unrelated to mucus secretion.
incorrectas.D: Foveolar cells are the mucous cells of the gastric pits in the stomach, not the submucosal glands specific to the duodenum.

preguntas.q: The mucus layer covering the gastric epithelium protects the mucosa by trapping which substance, which neutralizes any HCl that penetrates the mucus barrier?

e.correcta: Gastric surface mucous (foveolar) cells secrete both mucus and bicarbonate; the mucus gel traps a layer of HCO3- against the epithelial surface, creating a local pH gradient that neutralizes any hydrogen ions diffusing in from the highly acidic lumen. This mucus-bicarbonate barrier is a key defense that protects epithelial cells from autodigestion.

incorrectas.A: Pepsin is a proteolytic enzyme active in the acidic lumen; mucus limits pepsin's access to the epithelial surface, but pepsin itself is not the buffering substance trapped within the mucus to neutralize acid.
incorrectas.B: Intrinsic factor is a glycoprotein secreted by parietal cells for vitamin B12 absorption, unrelated to the mucus-bicarbonate barrier that buffers acid at the epithelial surface.
incorrectas.C: K+ is secreted apically as part of the H+/K+-ATPase cycle in parietal cells, not the buffering ion trapped within the protective mucus layer.

preguntas.q: How do the concentrations of Na+ and K+ in pancreatic secretions compare to plasma concentrations?

o.A: Similar to plasma, regardless of flow rate
o.D: Similar only at low flow rates

e.correcta: Unlike Cl- and HCO3-, whose concentrations vary reciprocally with secretory flow rate as ductal cells modify the fluid, Na+ and K+ concentrations in pancreatic juice remain essentially equal to their plasma concentrations across all flow rates, since the ductal epithelium does not substantially alter cation content.

incorrectas.B: Much higher than plasma is inaccurate — pancreatic secretion is essentially isonatric and isokalemic with plasma, not concentrated relative to it.
incorrectas.C: Much lower than plasma is also inaccurate for the same reason: the ductal cells do not substantially dilute Na+ or K+ relative to plasma.
incorrectas.D: It is Cl- and HCO3- concentrations, not Na+ and K+, that change with flow rate; Na+ and K+ remain approximately constant and similar to plasma across the entire physiologic flow range.

preguntas.q: Pancreatic secretions are isotonic relative to plasma across what range of secretory flow rates?

e.correcta: Pancreatic secretion remains isotonic to plasma at all flow rates: although the relative proportions of HCO3- and Cl- shift with flow (ductal cells increasingly secrete HCO3- and absorb Cl- as flow rises), total osmolarity is maintained by paracellular water movement that keeps pace. This differs from salivary secretion, which starts isotonic but becomes hypotonic because ductal Na+/Cl- reabsorption outpaces water permeability.

incorrectas.A: Isotonicity is not restricted to high flow rates — pancreatic secretion is isotonic across the entire physiologic range, not just at peak secretion.
incorrectas.C: Isotonicity also is not restricted to low (basal) flow rates; low basal secretion is just as isotonic as high-flow secretion, for the same reason of matched water movement.
incorrectas.D: The tonicity of pancreatic secretion is a constant property across flow rates and is not tied to a specific neurohormonal phase of stimulation such as the cephalic phase.

preguntas.q: The enzyme-rich component of pancreatic secretion is produced by which cell type?

e.correcta: Pancreatic acinar cells synthesize and secrete digestive enzymes and zymogens, such as trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, amylase, and lipase, via zymogen granules into the acinar lumen. This forms the enzyme-rich component of pancreatic juice, which is subsequently diluted and alkalinized by the separate aqueous ductal secretion.

incorrectas.A: Ductal cells secrete the aqueous, bicarbonate-rich component of pancreatic juice, stimulated primarily by secretin, rather than the digestive enzymes produced by acinar cells.
incorrectas.B: Centroacinar cells, located at the junction between acini and ducts, contribute to the aqueous/bicarbonate secretion alongside ductal cells rather than producing digestive enzymes.
incorrectas.D: Islet cells (alpha, beta, delta) are endocrine cells that secrete hormones such as insulin and glucagon directly into the blood, entirely separate from the exocrine enzyme secretion delivered into the ductal system.

preguntas.q: The aqueous, bicarbonate-rich component of pancreatic secretion is produced by which cell types?

e.correcta: Ductal and centroacinar cells, stimulated primarily by secretin acting through cAMP, secrete a bicarbonate-rich fluid via the CFTR channel and the Cl--HCO3- exchanger. This aqueous secretion dilutes and alkalinizes the enzyme-rich acinar secretion, neutralizing acidic chyme as it enters the duodenum.

incorrectas.A: Acinar cells produce the enzyme-rich, not aqueous/bicarbonate, component of pancreatic secretion — functionally the counterpart to the ductal/centroacinar aqueous component.
incorrectas.B: Islet beta cells are endocrine cells that secrete insulin directly into the bloodstream, entirely unrelated to the exocrine ductal secretion delivered into the pancreatic duct.
incorrectas.C: Goblet cells are mucus-secreting cells of the intestinal and respiratory epithelium, not part of the pancreatic ductal system that produces the aqueous, bicarbonate-rich secretion.

preguntas.q: As pancreatic secretion flows through the ducts, ductal cells modify its composition primarily by which process involving Cl-?

o.A: Absorption of Cl- from the lumen
o.B: Secretion of Cl- into the lumen
o.C: Co-transport of Cl- with Na+ into the lumen
o.D: Passive diffusion of Cl- with no net movement

e.correcta: As the initial acinar secretion flows through the ducts, ductal cells absorb Cl- from the lumen via the CFTR-linked Cl--HCO3- exchanger, secreting HCO3- into the lumen in exchange. This reciprocal exchange means that at higher flow rates the secretion becomes progressively richer in HCO3- and lower in Cl- (while Na+ and K+ remain constant), producing the classic inverse Cl-/HCO3- concentration curves seen with increasing flow rate.

incorrectas.B: Secretion of Cl- into the lumen describes the reverse of what actually happens — ductal cells reabsorb Cl- from the lumen (via the CFTR-linked exchanger) while secreting HCO3-, not the other way around.
incorrectas.C: Co-transport of Cl- with Na+ into the lumen does not describe the actual ductal mechanism, which relies on a Cl--HCO3- antiporter (an exchange, not a cotransport) to move Cl- out of the lumen as HCO3- moves in.
incorrectas.D: Passive diffusion with no net movement is incorrect, since there is substantial net Cl- absorption (coupled to HCO3- secretion) as flow rate increases, not an equilibrium state with no net transport.

preguntas.q: As pancreatic ductal cells modify the initial acinar secretion, which process do they carry out to raise its HCO3- concentration?

o.A: Reabsorption of HCO3- from the lumen
o.B: Secretion of HCO3- into the lumen
o.C: Secretion of Cl- into the lumen
o.D: Reabsorption of Na+ from the lumen

e.correcta: Pancreatic ductal cells actively secrete HCO3- into the lumen via an apical Cl-/HCO3- exchanger that is fueled by CFTR recycling Cl- back into the lumen, along with carbonic anhydrase generating HCO3- intracellularly from CO2 and water. At high secretory flow rates this ductal HCO3- secretion dominates, so the final pancreatic juice becomes progressively more alkaline (approaching plasma-like HCO3- concentrations) and less chloride-rich than the initial acinar fluid. This alkaline fluid neutralizes acidic chyme entering the duodenum, protecting the mucosa and creating the optimal pH for pancreatic enzyme activity.

incorrectas.A: Reabsorption of HCO3- would lower, not raise, the luminal HCO3- concentration, which is the opposite of what ductal cells actually do; ductal modification pushes pancreatic juice toward higher HCO3- as flow increases, not lower.
incorrectas.C: Cl- is actually reabsorbed (via the apical Cl-/HCO3- exchanger), not secreted, as ductal cells modify the acinar secretion; Cl- moves out of the lumen in exchange for the HCO3- being secreted in.
incorrectas.D: Sodium and water follow the osmotic gradient created by HCO3- transport but are not themselves the process that ductal cells use to raise luminal HCO3-; the defining ductal modification is bicarbonate secretion, not sodium handling.

preguntas.q: Vagal parasympathetic stimulation acting on pancreatic acinar and ductal cells has what net effect on pancreatic secretion?

o.D: Selective inhibition of the aqueous component only

e.correcta: Parasympathetic (vagal) fibers release acetylcholine, which binds M3 muscarinic receptors on acinar cells to trigger IP3/Ca2+ signaling and stimulate enzyme secretion, while also potentiating the ductal response to secretin. This vagal input increases both the enzymatic and aqueous components of pancreatic secretion, especially during the cephalic and gastric phases of digestion, priming the pancreas even before food reaches the duodenum.

incorrectas.B: Decreased secretion is the effect of sympathetic, not parasympathetic, stimulation; sympathetic fibers release norepinephrine that inhibits acinar and ductal output and also reduces blood flow to the gland.
incorrectas.C: The vagus has a clear, well-documented stimulatory effect on the exocrine pancreas rather than no effect; this is the basis for the cephalic phase of pancreatic secretion triggered by the sight and smell of food.
incorrectas.D: Parasympathetic stimulation is not selective for the aqueous component - it also strongly stimulates acinar cells to release digestive enzymes, so this pathway augments both components rather than affecting only one.

preguntas.q: Sympathetic innervation of the exocrine pancreas has what net effect on pancreatic secretion?

o.D: Selective stimulation of enzyme secretion only

e.correcta: Sympathetic postganglionic fibers release norepinephrine, which acts on alpha-adrenergic receptors to inhibit acinar and ductal cell secretion and to constrict pancreatic vasculature, reducing blood flow to the gland. This is the physiologic counterbalance to vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation, and it reflects the general pattern where the sympathetic nervous system suppresses digestive/absorptive ('rest-and-digest') functions in favor of fight-or-flight priorities.

incorrectas.A: Increased secretion describes the effect of parasympathetic input, not sympathetic; the two divisions have opposing effects on the exocrine pancreas, and sympathetic activation reliably suppresses output.
incorrectas.B: Sympathetic stimulation is not neutral - it actively inhibits secretion and reduces glandular blood flow, consistent with sympathetic suppression of digestive processes throughout the gut.
incorrectas.D: Sympathetic stimulation does not selectively boost enzyme output; if anything it globally suppresses pancreatic secretion, the opposite of a selective stimulatory effect.

preguntas.q: Release of the aqueous, HCO3--rich component of pancreatic secretion is primarily stimulated by which hormone?

e.correcta: Secretin is released from S cells of the duodenum in response to luminal acid (pH <4.5) and acts on ductal cells via a Gs-coupled receptor to raise cAMP, driving HCO3--rich fluid secretion that neutralizes acidic chyme. This is a classic negative-feedback loop: acid entering the duodenum triggers secretin release, and the resulting bicarbonate secretion raises duodenal pH, which then turns off further secretin release.

incorrectas.A: CCK is released in response to fatty acids and amino acids in the duodenum and primarily stimulates the enzymatic (zymogen-rich) component of pancreatic secretion from acinar cells, not the aqueous HCO3- component from ductal cells.
incorrectas.B: Gastrin is released from G cells in the stomach mainly in response to luminal peptides and vagal input, and its main target is parietal cell acid secretion, not pancreatic ductal bicarbonate secretion.
incorrectas.D: Motilin is released cyclically during fasting to trigger migrating motor complexes that clear the gut between meals; it does not drive pancreatic bicarbonate secretion.

preguntas.q: Binding of secretin to its receptor on pancreatic ductal cells activates which second messenger pathway?

e.correcta: Secretin binds a Gs-protein-coupled receptor, activating adenylyl cyclase to raise intracellular cAMP, which in turn activates PKA to open apical CFTR channels and drive the Cl-/HCO3- exchange responsible for bicarbonate-rich ductal secretion. This cAMP pathway is characteristic of secretin family hormones (secretin, VIP, glucagon), in contrast to the IP3/Ca2+ pathway used by CCK and gastrin.

incorrectas.A: IP3/Ca2+ is the second messenger pathway used by CCK acting on CCKA receptors on acinar cells, not by secretin, which instead couples to Gs and raises cAMP.
incorrectas.B: cGMP is the second messenger for guanylate cyclase-linked receptors, such as those for ANP or guanylin, and is not part of secretin's signaling pathway in pancreatic ductal cells.
incorrectas.D: DAG/PKC arises from phospholipase C activation downstream of Gq-coupled receptors like the CCKA receptor, not the Gs-coupled secretin receptor, which signals through cAMP instead.

preguntas.q: Release of the enzyme-rich component of pancreatic secretion from acinar cells is primarily stimulated by which hormone?

e.correcta: CCK is secreted by I cells of the duodenum and jejunum in response to fatty acids and amino acids, and it binds CCKA receptors on pancreatic acinar cells to trigger IP3/Ca2+ signaling, causing exocytosis of zymogen granules containing digestive enzymes (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, lipase, amylase). CCK also stimulates gallbladder contraction and sphincter of Oddi relaxation, coordinating enzyme delivery with bile flow for efficient lipid and protein digestion.

incorrectas.A: Secretin acts on ductal cells to stimulate the aqueous, bicarbonate-rich component of pancreatic secretion, not the enzymatic component, which is driven by CCK acting on acinar cells.
incorrectas.C: Gastrin's principal target is the gastric parietal cell, driving acid secretion; while it shares a similar C-terminal sequence to CCK and can weakly cross-react with CCK receptors, it is not the primary physiologic stimulus for pancreatic enzyme release.
incorrectas.D: Somatostatin is broadly inhibitory in the GI tract and suppresses secretion of gastrin, CCK, and pancreatic output rather than stimulating enzyme release.

preguntas.q: Binding of cholecystokinin to CCKA receptors on pancreatic acinar cells activates which second messenger pathway?

e.correcta: The CCKA receptor is Gq-coupled, activating phospholipase C to generate IP3 and DAG; IP3 releases Ca2+ from the endoplasmic reticulum, and this rise in intracellular calcium triggers exocytosis of zymogen granules from acinar cells. This IP3/Ca2+ pathway is shared by other Gq-coupled GI hormone receptors such as gastrin, in contrast to the Gs/cAMP pathway used by secretin and VIP.

incorrectas.A: cAMP is the second messenger generated downstream of Gs-coupled receptors such as the secretin receptor on ductal cells, not the Gq-coupled CCKA receptor on acinar cells.
incorrectas.C: cGMP signaling is used by receptor guanylate cyclases (e.g., ANP, guanylin) or soluble guanylate cyclase activated by nitric oxide, and is not part of the CCKA receptor's signaling cascade.
incorrectas.D: Nitric oxide/cGMP signaling mediates smooth muscle relaxation (e.g., in the sphincter of Oddi or vasculature) rather than the calcium-driven exocytotic response CCK elicits in acinar cells.

preguntas.q: Which hepatic secretion is composed of bile salts, phospholipids, cholesterol, bilirubin, water, and ions?

e.correcta: Bile is the fluid secreted by hepatocytes into the biliary canaliculi and is made up of bile salts (for lipid emulsification), phospholipids (mainly lecithin), cholesterol, bilirubin (the pigment giving bile its color), water, and electrolytes. It is stored and concentrated in the gallbladder between meals and released into the duodenum in response to CCK, where it aids fat digestion, cholesterol excretion, and elimination of lipophilic waste products like bilirubin.

incorrectas.A: Gastric juice is secreted by parietal, chief, and mucous cells of the stomach and consists mainly of HCl, pepsinogen, and mucus/intrinsic factor - it does not contain bile salts, phospholipids, or bilirubin.
incorrectas.B: Pancreatic juice is an exocrine secretion of acinar and ductal cells containing digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, proteases) and a bicarbonate-rich aqueous fluid, distinct from the bile-salt-and-pigment mixture that defines bile.
incorrectas.D: Saliva is produced by the salivary glands and contains water, electrolytes, mucus, and enzymes like salivary amylase and lingual lipase, but it has no bile salts, cholesterol, or bilirubin.

preguntas.q: Which pigment, derived from heme catabolism, is the major coloring component of bile?

e.correcta: Bilirubin is produced when heme oxygenase converts heme (from senescent RBCs) to biliverdin, which is then reduced to bilirubin; hepatocytes conjugate it with glucuronic acid to make it water-soluble before excreting it into bile. As the major bile pigment, conjugated bilirubin gives bile its characteristic yellow-green color, and downstream gut bacterial metabolism of bilirubin produces urobilinogen and stercobilin, which color urine and stool respectively.

incorrectas.A: Biliverdin is the intermediate breakdown product of heme that is rapidly reduced to bilirubin by biliverdin reductase; it is not the pigment that predominates in secreted bile.
incorrectas.B: Urobilinogen is formed by gut bacterial reduction of bilirubin after it reaches the intestine, and part of it is reabsorbed and excreted in urine - it is a downstream metabolite, not the major pigment within bile itself.
incorrectas.C: Stercobilin is the oxidized derivative of urobilinogen that gives stool its brown color; it is formed in the colon, not secreted as a component of hepatic bile.

preguntas.q: What is the physiologic purpose of hepatocytes conjugating bile acids (with glycine or taurine) before secreting them into bile?

o.A: To increase their lipid solubility for easier diffusion across membranes
o.B: To increase their water solubility, keeping them ionized in the acidic duodenal environment
o.C: To decrease their molecular weight for renal filtration
o.D: To inactivate them so they do not emulsify dietary lipids until reaching the colon

e.correcta: Conjugation with glycine or taurine lowers the pKa of bile acids, so they remain ionized (as bile salts) even in the relatively acidic proximal duodenum, which keeps them water-soluble and able to form micelles that emulsify dietary lipids. This ionized, amphipathic form is also what allows efficient reabsorption by the specific Na+-bile acid transporter in the terminal ileum as part of enterohepatic circulation, rather than being passively lost across the gut lining.

incorrectas.A: Conjugation does the opposite of increasing lipid solubility - it makes bile acids more polar and water-soluble, which is exactly why conjugated bile salts stay in solution in the aqueous intestinal lumen rather than diffusing back across the mucosa.
incorrectas.C: Conjugation adds glycine or taurine, slightly increasing (not decreasing) molecular weight, and bile acid elimination occurs mainly through enterohepatic recycling and fecal loss, not primarily renal filtration.
incorrectas.D: Conjugated bile salts are the active emulsifying form used throughout the small intestine, not an inactivated form; their detergent (amphipathic) properties are what allow them to solubilize lipids for micelle formation right where digestion occurs.

preguntas.q: What chemical property of bile salts and phospholipids allows them to emulsify dietary lipids in the aqueous intestinal lumen?

o.A: They are amphipathic, having both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions
o.D: They carry no net charge under any pH condition

e.correcta: Bile salts and phospholipids are amphipathic - they have a hydrophobic steroid or fatty-acid tail alongside hydrophilic hydroxyl/conjugated groups. This dual nature lets them orient at the surface of lipid droplets, breaking large fat globules into smaller ones (emulsification) and then packaging free fatty acids, monoglycerides, and cholesterol into mixed micelles that can diffuse through the unstirred water layer to reach the enterocyte brush border for absorption.

incorrectas.B: A purely hydrophobic molecule would coalesce with lipids but could not interface with the surrounding water, so it could not disperse fat into stable, small droplets suspended in the aqueous lumen.
incorrectas.C: A purely hydrophilic molecule would dissolve in the aqueous phase but could not associate with lipid droplets at all, so it would be unable to emulsify fat or form micelles that carry lipids.
incorrectas.D: Bile salts do carry charge (their conjugated, ionized carboxylate or sulfonate groups are what keep them soluble at duodenal pH); it is precisely this combination of charged and nonpolar regions - not charge neutrality - that gives them their emulsifying, amphipathic character.

preguntas.q: Which organ is responsible for the synthesis of bile?

e.correcta: Hepatocytes synthesize bile acids from cholesterol (via the rate-limiting enzyme 7α-hydroxylase/CYP7A1) and secrete bile salts, phospholipids, cholesterol, bilirubin, water, and ions into the bile canaliculi, which drain into the intrahepatic and then extrahepatic bile ducts. This continuous hepatic production is distinct from the gallbladder's role, which is simply to store and concentrate the bile the liver makes.

incorrectas.A: The gallbladder does not synthesize bile - it stores bile produced by the liver between meals and concentrates it by actively absorbing water and ions, then releases it in response to CCK.
incorrectas.B: The pancreas produces digestive enzymes and a bicarbonate-rich fluid, but it plays no role in bile acid synthesis, which is a hepatocyte-specific process using cholesterol as the precursor.
incorrectas.D: The duodenum is where bile acts (emulsifying lipids) and where its hormonal triggers (CCK, secretin) originate, but the duodenum itself does not synthesize any component of bile.

preguntas.q: Which organ stores and concentrates bile between meals?

e.correcta: Between meals, hepatic bile flows into the gallbladder, where the epithelium actively transports Na+, Cl-, and HCO3- out of the lumen, and water follows osmotically, concentrating the bile up to 5-10 fold. When a meal (especially one with fat) enters the duodenum, CCK triggers gallbladder contraction and sphincter of Oddi relaxation, delivering this concentrated bile into the intestine to emulsify lipids.

incorrectas.A: The liver is where bile is synthesized and continuously secreted, but it is not the site of storage/concentration between meals - that role belongs to the gallbladder downstream.
incorrectas.B: The common bile duct is simply a conduit that carries bile from the liver and gallbladder to the duodenum; it does not actively concentrate bile the way the gallbladder epithelium does.
incorrectas.D: The duodenum receives and uses concentrated bile for digestion but has no storage or concentrating function for bile itself.

preguntas.q: Which hormone provides the major stimulus for bile ejection from the gallbladder into the duodenum?

e.correcta: CCK, released from duodenal I cells in response to fatty acids and amino acids, causes contraction of the gallbladder smooth muscle and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi, together propelling concentrated bile into the duodenum in coordination with pancreatic enzyme release (which CCK also stimulates). This dual action ensures bile salts and digestive enzymes arrive together to efficiently emulsify and digest a fatty meal.

incorrectas.A: Secretin's major role is stimulating pancreatic ductal bicarbonate secretion in response to duodenal acid; while it has some minor potentiating effects on bile flow, it is not the primary trigger for gallbladder contraction.
incorrectas.B: Gastrin mainly drives gastric acid secretion from parietal cells and has only weak, non-primary effects on gallbladder contraction compared with CCK.
incorrectas.D: Somatostatin is inhibitory throughout the GI tract, suppressing gallbladder contraction and other hormone release rather than triggering bile ejection.

preguntas.q: Most secreted bile salts are returned to the liver for reuse via which physiologic process?

e.correcta: Roughly 95% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum by an active Na+-bile acid cotransporter, enter the portal circulation, and are taken back up by hepatocytes to be resecreted into bile - this recycling loop is called enterohepatic circulation. Because the total bile acid pool is small relative to the amount needed per meal, this efficient recycling (several times per meal) allows the body to conserve bile acids and minimize new synthesis, which is why interruption of the terminal ileum (e.g., in Crohn disease or resection) causes bile acid malabsorption and steatorrhea.

incorrectas.A: Portal-systemic shunting refers to blood bypassing the liver (as seen in cirrhosis with varices), which is unrelated to the normal recycling pathway that returns bile salts specifically to hepatocytes.
incorrectas.C: Bile salt reabsorption occurs via an active transporter into the portal venous blood, not via lymphatic drainage, distinguishing it from the lymphatic route used for absorbed long-chain fatty acids packaged as chylomicrons.
incorrectas.D: Bile salts are absorbed via a dedicated active transport mechanism concentrated in the terminal ileum, not by passive diffusion across the colon, which is downstream of where most bile salt reabsorption actually occurs.

preguntas.q: Which segment of the small intestine is responsible for active reabsorption of bile salts?

e.correcta: The terminal ileum expresses a specific Na+-dependent bile acid transporter (ASBT) on its apical membrane that actively reabsorbs bile salts, returning them to the liver via the portal vein as part of enterohepatic circulation. Restricting reabsorption to this distal site keeps bile salt concentrations high throughout the entire length of the small intestine, maximizing the time available for lipid digestion and absorption before the bile salts are recycled; disease or resection of the terminal ileum (e.g., Crohn disease) therefore causes bile acid malabsorption, steatorrhea, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.

incorrectas.A: The duodenum is where bile is delivered and lipid emulsification begins, but it lacks the dedicated bile acid transporter needed for reabsorption - absorbing bile salts this early would shorten their available action time along the gut.
incorrectas.B: The jejunum is the primary site for absorption of most digested nutrients (monosaccharides, amino acids, fatty acids) but not for bile salt reabsorption, which is reserved for the more distal terminal ileum.
incorrectas.D: The cecum is part of the colon, downstream of the small intestine; any bile salts not reabsorbed in the terminal ileum that reach the colon are deconjugated by bacteria and largely lost in stool rather than actively reabsorbed there.

preguntas.q: What is the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic bile acid synthesis from cholesterol?

e.correcta: 7α-hydroxylase (CYP7A1) catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step in the classic bile acid synthesis pathway, converting cholesterol into 7α-hydroxycholesterol, the precursor to cholic acid and other primary bile acids. Because this enzyme is the pathway's bottleneck, it is also the point of negative feedback regulation: rising bile salt levels returning via enterohepatic circulation suppress 7α-hydroxylase activity, keeping the bile acid pool in balance.

incorrectas.A: HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme for de novo cholesterol synthesis itself (and the target of statins), not for the downstream conversion of cholesterol into bile acids.
incorrectas.C: Cholesterol esterase hydrolyzes dietary cholesteryl esters into free cholesterol and fatty acids during digestion in the small intestine; it is a digestive enzyme, not part of the hepatic bile acid synthesis pathway.
incorrectas.D: LCAT esterifies free cholesterol on HDL particles in plasma lipoprotein metabolism, which is unrelated to the hepatic pathway converting cholesterol into bile acids.

preguntas.q: 7α-hydroxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme of bile acid synthesis, is subject to negative feedback inhibition by which substance?

e.correcta: As bile salts are reabsorbed through enterohepatic circulation and return to the liver via the portal vein, rising hepatocyte bile salt levels suppress 7α-hydroxylase (CYP7A1) transcription, reducing further conversion of cholesterol into new bile acids. This negative feedback loop matches bile acid synthesis to the amount actually being lost (mainly in feces), preventing wasteful overproduction when the recycled pool is already adequate.

incorrectas.A: Cholesterol is the substrate for the bile acid synthesis pathway (acted upon by 7α-hydroxylase), not the feedback signal that shuts the enzyme down; rising cholesterol would not be expected to suppress its own conversion into bile acids.
incorrectas.B: CCK regulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme release, not the transcriptional feedback control of hepatic bile acid synthesis enzymes.
incorrectas.D: Secretin regulates pancreatic ductal bicarbonate secretion and has no role in feedback inhibition of hepatic 7α-hydroxylase.

preguntas.q: Bile plays a key physiologic role in the digestion and absorption of which nutrient class?

e.correcta: Bile salts and phospholipids emulsify dietary triglycerides and cholesterol into small droplets, increasing the surface area available for pancreatic lipase, and then package the resulting fatty acids, monoglycerides, and cholesterol into mixed micelles that ferry them across the unstirred water layer to the enterocyte brush border. Because this process is essential for lipid absorption, bile is also required for absorbing the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K, which travel within the same micelles.

incorrectas.A: Protein digestion depends on gastric pepsin and pancreatic proteases (trypsin, chymotrypsin) plus brush-border peptidases, not on bile, which has no emulsifying role for peptides.
incorrectas.C: Carbohydrate digestion relies on salivary and pancreatic amylase plus brush-border disaccharidases (lactase, sucrase); bile salts play no part in breaking down or absorbing sugars.
incorrectas.D: Nucleic acid digestion is handled by pancreatic nucleases and intestinal nucleotidases/nucleosidases, a pathway entirely independent of bile's lipid-emulsifying function.

preguntas.q: Besides aiding lipid digestion, bile serves as the body's primary route for eliminating excess which substance?

e.correcta: The liver excretes excess cholesterol into bile both directly (as free cholesterol solubilized within mixed micelles/bile salts) and indirectly after conversion into bile acids, making biliary excretion the body's principal pathway for eliminating cholesterol that cannot be catabolized by cells. When bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol relative to bile salts and phospholipids, cholesterol can precipitate and form gallstones, a direct clinical consequence of this excretory function.

incorrectas.B: Glucose is not excreted via bile - excess glucose is stored as glycogen or converted to fat, and any renal loss occurs via filtration once the tubular reabsorption threshold is exceeded, not through biliary excretion.
incorrectas.C: Urea is the nitrogenous waste product of the urea cycle and is eliminated primarily by renal filtration and excretion, not by secretion into bile.
