Painlessness is why patients often do not seek care until the mass has grown noticeably, and it also helps distinguish tumors from acutely inflamed or infected glands.

incorrectas.A: Pain and overlying erythema suggest an acute inflammatory or infectious process (such as bacterial sialadenitis or an abscess) rather than the classic slow, painless growth of a salivary neoplasm; pain in a known tumor should instead raise concern for aggressive or nerve-invasive malignancy.
incorrectas.C: A fluctuant mass implies a fluid-filled collection such as an abscess, not the firm, solid character typical of a salivary gland neoplasm.
incorrectas.D: Rapid growth with fixation to the skin is a red flag for an aggressive, invasive malignant process, which is the exception rather than the classic presentation of most salivary gland tumors at diagnosis.

preguntas.q: What is the most common tumor of the salivary glands overall?

e.correcta: Pleomorphic adenoma is the single most common salivary gland tumor overall and the most common benign tumor of the parotid gland. Histologically it shows a mixture of epithelial (ductal) and mesenchymal (myoepithelial/stromal) elements, giving it a heterogeneous, "mixed tumor" appearance, which is reflected in its name.

incorrectas.A: Warthin tumor is the second most common benign salivary tumor, distinguished by its cystic, papillary architecture with a dense lymphoid stroma, but it occurs far less frequently than pleomorphic adenoma.
incorrectas.B: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common malignant salivary gland tumor, but malignant tumors as a category are less common than the single most frequent tumor type, pleomorphic adenoma.
incorrectas.D: Adenoid cystic carcinoma is a malignant tumor notable for perineural invasion and late recurrences, but it is considerably less common than pleomorphic adenoma.

preguntas.q: Pleomorphic adenoma of the salivary gland is classified as which of the following?

e.correcta: Pleomorphic adenoma is a benign salivary gland tumor, composed of a mix of epithelial and stromal/myoepithelial tissue. Importantly, although benign, it carries a real risk of malignant transformation over time (into carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma), particularly with long tumor duration or multiple recurrences, which is why complete surgical excision with margins is preferred over simple enucleation.

incorrectas.A: Pleomorphic adenoma itself is not malignant at diagnosis; malignant transformation is a possible but distinct late complication, not the tumor's baseline classification.
incorrectas.B: Salivary tumors are not classified using an "uncertain malignant potential" category; pleomorphic adenoma is definitively categorized as benign on histology, even though it has malignant potential over time.
incorrectas.C: There is no age-based rule that converts pleomorphic adenoma to malignant; while risk of malignant transformation increases with the duration the tumor has been present, it is not an automatic reclassification tied to a specific age.

preguntas.q: Which salivary gland tumor is notorious for a high rate of local recurrence after resection, owing to its irregular, incompletely encapsulated growth pattern?

e.correcta: Pleomorphic adenoma often has a thin, incomplete capsule with small finger-like (pseudopod) projections of tumor extending into surrounding normal tissue. If the tumor is simply enucleated (shelled out) rather than excised with a margin of normal tissue (e.g., via superficial parotidectomy), these microscopic extensions can be left behind, leading to a high rate of local recurrence, sometimes with multiple recurrent nodules over time.

incorrectas.B: Warthin tumor is well encapsulated with a smooth, cystic architecture, and does not have the pseudopod-like capsular breaches of pleomorphic adenoma, so it does not carry the same classic reputation for high post-resection recurrence.
incorrectas.C: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is a malignant tumor that can recur due to its invasive growth and potential for regional spread, but the specific teaching point about recurrence from an incomplete capsule and pseudopod extensions is characteristic of pleomorphic adenoma, not this malignant tumor.
incorrectas.D: Acinic cell carcinoma is a generally low-grade malignant tumor without the classic incomplete-capsule recurrence pattern that defines pleomorphic adenoma's surgical challenge.

preguntas.q: What is the most common malignant tumor of the salivary glands?

e.correcta: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common malignant salivary gland tumor, composed of a mixture of mucus-secreting and squamous (epidermoid) cells, most often arising in the parotid gland. Its clinical behavior ranges from low-grade (better prognosis, less invasive) to high-grade (more aggressive with nerve and tissue invasion), and it is a key cause of malignant salivary masses presenting with facial nerve symptoms when it invades the parotid parenchyma.

incorrectas.A: Adenoid cystic carcinoma is the second most common malignant salivary tumor and is especially notorious for perineural invasion, causing pain and nerve deficits, along with a tendency toward late recurrence and metastasis, but it is less common overall than mucoepidermoid carcinoma.
incorrectas.B: Acinic cell carcinoma is a generally low-grade malignant tumor of serous acinar differentiation, occurring less frequently than mucoepidermoid carcinoma.
incorrectas.D: Carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma refers to malignant transformation arising within a long-standing pleomorphic adenoma; it is a less common route to salivary malignancy compared with primary mucoepidermoid carcinoma.

preguntas.q: Malignant salivary gland tumors classically present with damage to which cranial nerve, reflecting its anatomic course through the affected gland?

e.correcta: The facial nerve (CN VII) runs directly through the substance of the parotid gland, dividing it anatomically into superficial and deep lobes before branching to innervate the muscles of facial expression. A malignant tumor that invades or compresses this nerve as it infiltrates surrounding tissue produces facial nerve palsy (e.g., facial droop), which is a critical red flag distinguishing a malignant, invasive process from a benign tumor that simply displaces the nerve without damaging it.

incorrectas.A: The trigeminal nerve provides facial sensation and motor innervation to the muscles of mastication but does not course through the parotid gland, so it is not the nerve classically compromised by parotid malignancy.
incorrectas.B: The hypoglossal nerve innervates the muscles of the tongue and runs near the submandibular region, not through the parotid gland, so it is not the nerve associated with facial droop from parotid tumor invasion.
incorrectas.C: The glossopharyngeal nerve contributes to pharyngeal sensation, taste on the posterior third of the tongue, and parotid gland secretomotor function via the otic ganglion, but it is not the nerve whose compression classically produces the visible facial weakness associated with malignant parotid tumors.

preguntas.q: What congenital anomaly is defined by an abnormal connection between the esophagus and the trachea?

e.correcta: A tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) results from abnormal partitioning of the foregut into separate respiratory (tracheal) and digestive (esophageal) tubes during the fourth week of embryonic development; incomplete or malpositioned division of the tracheoesophageal septum leaves an abnormal communication between the two structures. TEF frequently occurs together with esophageal atresia (a blind-ending esophageal segment), and the various anatomic combinations of atresia and fistula location produce distinct clinical presentations that are classic exam material.

incorrectas.B: An esophageal duplication cyst is a separate congenital foregut malformation forming a fluid-filled cystic structure adjacent to, but not communicating with, the esophagus or trachea, unlike the direct fistulous connection defining TEF.
incorrectas.C: A laryngeal cleft results from failure of fusion of the posterior cricoid lamina and interarytenoid tissue, creating a communication at the laryngeal level between the airway and esophagus, which is anatomically distinct from a tracheoesophageal fistula lower in the foregut.
incorrectas.D: A bronchogenic cyst arises from abnormal budding of the developing tracheobronchial tree, forming a mediastinal or pulmonary cyst that does not directly connect the esophagus and trachea the way a TEF does.

preguntas.q: The most common tracheoesophageal anomaly (about 85% of cases) is proximal esophageal atresia combined with which type of fistula?

o.A: Isolated esophageal atresia without any fistula

e.correcta: The most common tracheoesophageal anomaly is a blind-ending proximal esophageal pouch (atresia) with the distal esophageal segment instead connecting to the trachea via a fistula. This configuration explains the classic clinical picture: the infant cannot swallow (proximal pouch is blind, so feeds and saliva back up, causing drooling and choking), yet air can still pass from the trachea into the stomach through the distal fistula, producing a gas-filled, distended abdomen on imaging.

incorrectas.A: Isolated (pure) esophageal atresia without any fistula is a much rarer variant, and it produces a gasless abdomen on x-ray, because no fistula exists that would let air enter the stomach.
incorrectas.C: A proximal fistula (with the upper pouch connecting to the trachea instead of the lower segment) is a rare pattern and carries a high aspiration risk from swallowed material entering the airway, but it is not the most common anomaly.
incorrectas.D: H-type fistula describes a fistula connecting an otherwise continuous, patent esophagus and trachea without any atresia at all, which is a distinct and less common subtype than atresia with distal fistula.

preguntas.q: Esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula classically presents prenatally with which finding on obstetric ultrasound?

e.correcta: Normally the fetus swallows amniotic fluid throughout gestation, which is absorbed in the gut and helps regulate amniotic fluid volume. When esophageal atresia creates a blind-ending upper esophageal pouch, the fetus cannot swallow fluid effectively, so fluid accumulates in the amniotic sac, producing polyhydramnios—an important prenatal clue that should prompt evaluation for esophageal atresia after delivery.

incorrectas.A: Oligohydramnios occurs when fetal urine output is impaired (e.g., renal agenesis or a urinary tract obstruction), since fetal urine becomes the major contributor to amniotic fluid volume in the second half of pregnancy; it is the opposite of what is seen with esophageal atresia, which impairs fluid removal, not production.
incorrectas.B: Fetal ascites is a sign of fetal hydrops, typically from severe anemia, cardiac failure, or other systemic causes, and is not the mechanism by which esophageal atresia affects amniotic fluid dynamics.
incorrectas.D: Increased nuchal translucency is a first-trimester ultrasound marker used to screen for chromosomal abnormalities like trisomy 21, not a finding directly caused by a blocked esophagus later in gestation.

preguntas.q: A newborn with esophageal atresia and a distal tracheoesophageal fistula presents with drooling and choking, and which symptom during the first feeding attempt?

e.correcta: Because the proximal esophageal segment ends in a blind pouch, swallowed milk cannot reach the stomach and is immediately regurgitated back up, causing vomiting with the very first feed. This occurs alongside excessive drooling (the infant cannot swallow its own saliva either) and choking or coughing, since overflow from the blind pouch can spill into the airway and cause aspiration.

incorrectas.A: Diarrhea reflects abnormal intestinal motility or absorption further down the GI tract, which is not the mechanism at play when the esophagus itself is a blind-ending pouch obstructing swallowed feeds.
incorrectas.B: Hematemesis implies bleeding into the upper GI tract, which is not the expected presentation of a structural, non-hemorrhagic obstruction like esophageal atresia.
incorrectas.C: Constipation relates to lower gastrointestinal transit and stool passage, which is unrelated to the proximal esophageal obstruction seen in esophageal atresia.

preguntas.q: Esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula may present with abdominal distention due to which mechanism, visible on chest/abdominal x-ray?

o.A: Air entering the stomach through the distal fistula

e.correcta: In esophageal atresia with a distal fistula, the lower esophageal segment (which connects to the stomach) is fused instead to the trachea, so with each breath, air moves directly from the airway into the stomach and bowel through this abnormal connection. This produces a gas-filled, distended stomach and bowel visible on imaging—an important distinguishing feature from pure esophageal atresia without any fistula, which instead shows a completely gasless abdomen because no route exists for air to reach the GI tract.

incorrectas.B: Meconium ileus results from abnormally thick, inspissated meconium obstructing the distal ileum, classically seen in cystic fibrosis, a completely different mechanism unrelated to a tracheoesophageal connection.
incorrectas.C: Volvulus is a mechanical twisting of bowel around its mesentery, typically related to intestinal malrotation, and is not the mechanism by which esophageal atresia with a distal fistula causes abdominal gas distention.
incorrectas.D: Ascites from portal hypertension is a hepatic and vascular problem causing fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity, unrelated to the direct airway-to-gut air passage seen with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula.

preguntas.q: Esophageal atresia is confirmed at the bedside by failure to pass which device into the stomach?

e.correcta: Because the proximal esophagus in esophageal atresia ends as a blind pouch, an attempt to pass a nasogastric (or orogastric) tube down into the stomach will meet resistance and coil back in the pouch, typically confirmed by an x-ray showing the tube curled in the upper chest rather than reaching the stomach. This simple bedside maneuver is a key diagnostic step in a newborn suspected of having esophageal atresia, often prompted by excessive oral secretions or a failed feeding attempt.

incorrectas.A: An endotracheal tube is placed into the trachea for airway management and ventilation, not to assess esophageal patency, so it is not the device used to confirm esophageal atresia.
incorrectas.C: A Foley catheter is used for urinary bladder catheterization and has no role in evaluating the esophagus or upper gastrointestinal tract.
incorrectas.D: A central venous catheter provides vascular access for medications or fluids and is unrelated to assessing whether the esophagus is patent down to the stomach.

preguntas.q: Which tracheoesophageal anomaly, in which the esophagus remains anatomically continuous and connects to the trachea via a separate fistulous tract, resembles the letter "H" on contrast imaging?

o.A: Esophageal atresia with proximal tracheoesophageal fistula
o.B: Esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula

e.correcta: In the pure, or "H-type," tracheoesophageal fistula, there is no esophageal atresia at all—both the esophagus and trachea remain intact, continuous tubes, but an abnormal fistulous tract connects them laterally, which on a contrast esophagram resembles the two vertical strokes and connecting bar of the letter H. Because the esophagus is otherwise patent, infants with this variant can often feed initially but develop recurrent coughing, choking with feeds, or repeated aspiration pneumonia, so it may present later than the atresia-associated forms.

incorrectas.A: Esophageal atresia with a proximal fistula involves a blind-ending distal esophageal segment and a fistula from the proximal pouch to the trachea, an anatomic pattern quite different from the intact, dual-tube "H" configuration of the pure H-type fistula.
incorrectas.B: Esophageal atresia with distal fistula (the most common variant) involves a blind proximal pouch and a separate distal esophageal segment fused to the trachea, which does not create the continuous double-tube "H" appearance seen when there is no atresia at all.
incorrectas.D: Esophageal atresia without any fistula (pure atresia) has no connection at all between the esophagus and trachea, so it cannot produce the H-shaped connecting tract seen on imaging in the H-type variant.

preguntas.q: Which tracheoesophageal anomaly, lacking any communication with the trachea, characteristically produces a gasless abdomen on chest/abdominal x-ray?

o.A: Esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula
o.B: Esophageal atresia with both proximal and distal fistulas

e.correcta: In pure esophageal atresia, the esophagus ends blindly with no fistulous connection to the trachea at all, so there is no route by which swallowed or inspired air can reach the stomach and intestines. This produces a completely gasless abdomen on imaging, in direct contrast to atresia with a distal fistula, where air passes through the fistula into the GI tract and produces a distended, gas-filled stomach.

incorrectas.A: Esophageal atresia with a distal fistula allows air to enter the stomach through the fistula, producing a gas-filled distended abdomen rather than a gasless one.
incorrectas.B: When both proximal and distal fistulas are present, the distal fistula still permits air to pass into the stomach and bowel, so the abdomen would again show gas rather than being gasless.
incorrectas.C: H-type fistula preserves a continuous, patent esophagus connected normally to the stomach, so swallowed air reaches the GI tract normally; it does not produce the gasless abdomen seen with pure atresia.

preguntas.q: What esophageal lesion consists of a thin membrane of mucosa and submucosa protruding into the lumen, most often located in the upper esophagus?

e.correcta: An esophageal web is a thin, eccentric protrusion of mucosa and submucosa into the esophageal lumen, most commonly located in the upper esophagus, and it can cause dysphagia to solids as well as an increased risk of food impaction and aspiration. It is classically associated with Plummer-Vinson syndrome (esophageal webs, iron deficiency anemia, and glossitis/atrophic glossitis), which itself carries an increased risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, making web recognition clinically important beyond the dysphagia itself.

incorrectas.B: Zenker diverticulum is an outpouching of pharyngoesophageal mucosa through a weak point (Killian's triangle) at the pharyngoesophageal junction, caused by increased intraluminal pressure against a dysfunctional cricopharyngeus muscle, rather than a thin intraluminal membrane like a web.
incorrectas.C: A peptic stricture is a circumferential narrowing from chronic fibrosis due to long-standing GERD, typically located in the distal esophagus near the gastroesophageal junction, a different mechanism and location than the thin upper esophageal web.
incorrectas.D: A Schatzki ring is a mucosal ring located at the gastroesophageal junction (distal esophagus), classically causing intermittent dysphagia to solids ("steakhouse syndrome"), which differs both in location and clinical pattern from an upper esophageal web.

preguntas.q: A patient with an esophageal web develops dysphagia. Ingestion of which type of food is most likely to precipitate her symptoms?

o.D: Any food, chewed or unchewed, equally

e.correcta: Esophageal webs are thin, eccentric membranes of mucosa and submucosa that partially occlude the lumen; because the lumen is narrowed but not completely blocked, symptoms are typically provoked by large or poorly chewed boluses that cannot pass through the narrowed segment, producing intermittent solid-food dysphagia. This mechanical, size-dependent pattern distinguishes a structural lesion like a web from a motility disorder such as achalasia, in which both solids and liquids cause trouble from the start.

incorrectas.B: Liquids readily pass through a narrowed but still patent web-like lumen, so isolated liquid dysphagia would instead suggest a motility disorder like achalasia or a near-complete obstruction, not a typical esophageal web.
incorrectas.C: Pureed food, like liquids, generally flows through the fixed anatomic narrowing of a web without difficulty; it is specifically larger, poorly chewed solid boluses that catch at the web.
incorrectas.D: Esophageal webs cause a size-dependent mechanical obstruction — small or well-chewed boluses pass while large, poorly chewed ones do not — so dysphagia is not equal across all food consistencies.

preguntas.q: Which syndrome presents as a triad of iron deficiency anemia, esophageal web, and atrophic glossitis (beefy-red tongue), classically in middle-aged women?

e.correcta: Plummer-Vinson syndrome (mnemonic "Plumbers DIE": dysphagia, iron deficiency anemia, esophageal webs) classically occurs in middle-aged women and combines iron deficiency anemia with an esophageal web causing dysphagia, plus atrophic glossitis, in which chronic iron deficiency damages the tongue mucosa to produce a smooth, beefy-red appearance. Iron deficiency is thought to impair epithelial turnover and contribute to web formation, and the syndrome also carries an increased long-term risk of postcricoid esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

incorrectas.A: Mallory-Weiss syndrome is a mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction from forceful retching or vomiting, causing painful hematemesis; it has no association with chronic iron deficiency anemia or glossitis.
incorrectas.C: Zenker diverticulum is an outpouching of pharyngeal mucosa above the cricopharyngeus, typically in elderly men, causing halitosis and regurgitation of undigested food, not anemia or a beefy-red tongue.
incorrectas.D: Boerhaave syndrome is a full-thickness esophageal rupture from violent retching, presenting acutely with chest pain and pneumomediastinum — a surgical emergency unrelated to chronic anemia or glossitis.

preguntas.q: Because it involves herniation of only mucosa and submucosa through the pharyngeal constrictor muscles (Killian triangle), how is a Zenker diverticulum classified?

e.correcta: A Zenker diverticulum is a false (pulsion) diverticulum because only the mucosa and submucosa herniate outward through a weak point in the pharyngeal wall (Killian triangle, between the cricopharyngeus and inferior pharyngeal constrictor) — the muscular layer is not part of the outpouching. This distinguishes it from a true diverticulum, which contains all wall layers, and explains why it readily traps food debris, leading to halitosis and aspiration risk.

incorrectas.A: A true diverticulum contains all layers of the wall — mucosa, submucosa, and muscularis — unlike Zenker diverticulum, where only mucosa and submucosa protrude through a defect in the muscular wall.
incorrectas.B: Traction diverticula form when external inflammation, such as mediastinal lymphadenitis, pulls all layers of the esophageal wall outward, making them true diverticula typically located in the mid-esophagus — a different mechanism and location from the pulsion-type Zenker diverticulum.
incorrectas.D: Zenker diverticulum is an acquired lesion related to age-related pharyngeal wall weakening and increased intraluminal pressure against the cricopharyngeus, not a congenital malformation present from birth.

preguntas.q: Beyond oropharyngeal dysphagia and obstruction, which symptom is classically caused by food debris retained within a Zenker diverticulum?

o.D: Chest pain radiating to the back

e.correcta: Because a Zenker diverticulum is an outpouching just above the cricopharyngeus that traps swallowed food and secretions, the retained material decomposes within the pouch and produces halitosis; patients may also regurgitate this undigested food, sometimes hours after eating, and can develop recurrent aspiration pneumonia if pouch contents spill into the airway.

incorrectas.A: Odynophagia (painful swallowing) suggests active mucosal inflammation or ulceration, such as infectious or pill esophagitis, rather than the painless retention of food typical of a Zenker diverticulum.
incorrectas.C: Hematemesis points to an actively bleeding source such as esophageal varices or a Mallory-Weiss tear; Zenker diverticulum instead causes regurgitation of undigested food and halitosis, not vomiting of blood.
incorrectas.D: Chest pain radiating to the back with an abnormal CXR is characteristic of Boerhaave syndrome (esophageal rupture), a surgical emergency very different from the chronic, indolent course of a Zenker diverticulum.

preguntas.q: Zenker diverticulum most characteristically affects which patient population?

e.correcta: Zenker diverticulum results from age-related weakening of the pharyngeal wall combined with increased pressure against a poorly relaxing cricopharyngeus, so it typically presents in elderly patients with a male predominance — quite different from the demographic pattern of Plummer-Vinson syndrome, which favors middle-aged women.

incorrectas.B: Young women are not the typical population for Zenker diverticulum; this is an age-related, acquired condition seen predominantly in elderly men, reflecting decades of cumulative pharyngeal wall stress.
incorrectas.C: Middle-aged women are the classic demographic for Plummer-Vinson syndrome (iron deficiency anemia, esophageal web, glossitis), not Zenker diverticulum, which skews older and male.
incorrectas.D: Zenker diverticulum is an acquired, degenerative condition of aging pharyngeal musculature; it is not seen in infants or toddlers, who have not accumulated the decades of mechanical stress needed to produce it.

preguntas.q: The mucosal tears of Mallory-Weiss syndrome occur at the gastroesophageal junction because of a rapid rise in which pressure, typically triggered by forceful retching or vomiting?

e.correcta: Forceful retching or vomiting causes a sudden, sharp rise in intraabdominal pressure that is transmitted to the gastroesophageal junction; because this junction is a relatively fixed, less distensible point, the abrupt pressure surge tears the mucosa and submucosa longitudinally, producing the linear lacerations characteristic of Mallory-Weiss syndrome. This pressure-driven mechanism explains the syndrome's strong link to retching, for example in alcoholics or patients with bulimia, rather than to a chronic mucosal disease process.

incorrectas.A: Intrathoracic pressure changes occur with straining and coughing, but the tear in Mallory-Weiss syndrome is specifically attributed to the abdominal-side pressure surge generated during retching or vomiting, not primarily thoracic pressure.
incorrectas.B: Portal venous pressure elevation is the mechanism behind esophageal varices, which bleed from dilated submucosal veins rather than from a mechanical mucosal tear; Mallory-Weiss syndrome is unrelated to portal hypertension.
incorrectas.D: Intracranial pressure has no role in the mechanism of Mallory-Weiss tears; this is a purely mechanical gastroesophageal junction injury driven by abdominal pressure, not an intracranial process.

preguntas.q: Which symptom is characteristic of Mallory-Weiss syndrome and can be painful, reflecting the mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction?

e.correcta: The longitudinal mucosal tear of Mallory-Weiss syndrome disrupts submucosal vessels at the gastroesophageal junction, so patients typically vomit blood (hematemesis), often after an initial bout of forceful, non-bloody retching or vomiting; because the injury is a fresh mucosal laceration, this hematemesis can be accompanied by pain, unlike the classically painless bleeding of esophageal varices.

incorrectas.A: Melena without hematemesis suggests a slower upper GI bleed that has time to be digested as it transits the gut; a Mallory-Weiss tear typically causes visible fresh hematemesis because the bleeding source sits right at the gastroesophageal junction.
incorrectas.C: Hemoptysis is coughing up blood from a pulmonary or airway source, not vomiting blood from the GI tract, so it does not describe the presentation of a gastroesophageal junction tear.
incorrectas.D: Hematochezia (bright red blood per rectum) usually indicates a lower GI bleed or a very brisk upper GI bleed passing quickly through the bowel, not the direct vomiting of blood seen with a proximal mucosal tear like Mallory-Weiss syndrome.

preguntas.q: Is the hematemesis of Mallory-Weiss syndrome typically painful or painless, a feature that helps distinguish it from bleeding esophageal varices?

o.D: Painful only in patients with cirrhosis

e.correcta: Because Mallory-Weiss syndrome involves an acute mechanical tear of the mucosa and submucosa, the resulting hematemesis is typically painful — a key clinical clue distinguishing it from bleeding esophageal varices, which classically produce painless hematemesis since the varices are simply ruptured dilated veins without an accompanying tissue injury.

incorrectas.A: Painless hematemesis is the hallmark of bleeding esophageal varices, where blood loss occurs from ruptured dilated veins without an acute mucosal laceration; this is the opposite of the painful presentation expected with a Mallory-Weiss tear.
incorrectas.C: The pain associated with Mallory-Weiss syndrome is a reliable, testable distinguishing feature rather than something unpredictable, precisely because it reflects a genuine mechanical tissue tear, unlike the painless bleeding of varices.
incorrectas.D: The pain in Mallory-Weiss bleeding comes from the mechanical tear itself, not from underlying cirrhosis; cirrhosis and portal hypertension instead set the stage for painless variceal bleeding, a separate condition.

preguntas.q: Boerhaave syndrome, a full-thickness esophageal rupture, classically presents with subcutaneous emphysema and which finding on imaging?

e.correcta: In Boerhaave syndrome, the full-thickness esophageal tear allows swallowed air (and esophageal contents) to escape directly into the mediastinum, producing pneumomediastinum on CXR or CT along with subcutaneous emphysema as air tracks into the neck and chest wall tissues. This abnormal imaging finding, combined with excruciating retrosternal chest pain after violent retching, is a key distinguishing feature from Mallory-Weiss syndrome, which does not involve full-thickness perforation and shows a normal CXR.

incorrectas.A: A pleural effusion, often left-sided from spillage of esophageal contents, can develop secondarily in Boerhaave syndrome, but it is not the hallmark finding directly explained by air escaping through the rupture — that is pneumomediastinum.
incorrectas.B: Pneumothorax may occur as a complication if the pleura is also breached, but the classic, defining imaging finding of rupture into the mediastinal space is pneumomediastinum, not primary pneumothorax.
incorrectas.D: Pericardial effusion is not a typical feature of esophageal rupture; Boerhaave syndrome affects the esophagus and adjacent mediastinal space, not the pericardial sac directly.

preguntas.q: Boerhaave syndrome, characterized by full-thickness esophageal rupture, is most often precipitated by which event?

e.correcta: Boerhaave syndrome results from a sudden, severe increase in intraesophageal pressure during violent retching or vomiting, often after a large meal or heavy alcohol intake, which is enough to blow out the full thickness of the esophageal wall, most commonly at the left posterolateral distal esophagus. This is a surgical emergency, presenting with excruciating retrosternal chest pain, and is distinguished from the more superficial mucosal tear of Mallory-Weiss syndrome by its full-thickness nature and abnormal chest imaging.

incorrectas.A: Chronic acid reflux (GERD) can cause strictures or Barrett esophagus over time, but it does not produce the sudden, catastrophic full-thickness rupture seen in Boerhaave syndrome, which requires an acute pressure surge.
incorrectas.B: Foreign body ingestion can cause esophageal perforation, but this occurs through direct mechanical injury or erosion at the impaction site, a distinct mechanism from the pressure-driven blowout of violent retching in classic Boerhaave syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Caustic ingestion causes chemical injury and necrosis of the esophageal wall that can lead to perforation, but this is a distinct chemical mechanism, whereas Boerhaave syndrome is specifically defined by a pressure-related rupture from forceful retching.

preguntas.q: Esophageal varices are best described as which of the following?

o.A: Dilated submucosal veins in the lower third of the esophagus
o.B: Thin mucosal/submucosal membranes narrowing the lumen
o.C: Full-thickness outpouchings of the esophageal wall

e.correcta: Esophageal varices are dilated, tortuous submucosal veins located in the distal (lower) third of the esophagus, formed when portal hypertension forces blood through portosystemic collaterals — specifically the left gastric (coronary) vein anastomosing with esophageal veins that drain into the azygos system. Because these veins sit just beneath a thin mucosal layer, they are fragile and prone to rupture, causing painless but potentially massive hematemesis.

incorrectas.B: A thin mucosal/submucosal membrane narrowing the lumen describes an esophageal web, a distinct structural lesion associated with Plummer-Vinson syndrome, not the vascular dilation seen in varices.
incorrectas.C: A full-thickness outpouching of the wall describes a true diverticulum, such as a traction diverticulum, which is an anatomic herniation rather than the venous dilation that defines esophageal varices.
incorrectas.D: Squamous-to-columnar metaplasia describes Barrett esophagus, a response to chronic GERD injury — a completely different, epithelial rather than vascular, pathologic process from esophageal varices.

preguntas.q: Esophageal varices develop as a direct consequence of which underlying condition?

o.D: Isolated portal vein thrombosis without cirrhosis

e.correcta: Esophageal varices arise secondary to portal hypertension, most often from cirrhosis, in which increased resistance to portal blood flow forces blood to seek alternative low-resistance pathways through portosystemic anastomoses; the left gastric vein-to-esophageal vein connection is one such route, and the resulting engorgement of submucosal esophageal veins produces varices that are fragile and prone to life-threatening rupture.

incorrectas.B: Systemic arterial hypertension affects the systemic arterial circulation and has no direct mechanistic link to portal venous congestion or the formation of esophageal varices, which are a venous, portal-system phenomenon.
incorrectas.C: Pulmonary hypertension affects the pulmonary vascular bed and right heart, an entirely separate circulatory system from the portal venous circulation responsible for esophageal varices.
incorrectas.D: Portal vein thrombosis can raise portal pressure and contribute to varices, but the classic and by far most common cause of clinically significant portal hypertension driving esophageal varices is cirrhosis with increased intrahepatic resistance, not isolated portal vein thrombosis.

preguntas.q: In portal hypertension, backup of blood through which vein into the esophageal venous plexus produces esophageal varices?

e.correcta: The left gastric (coronary) vein normally drains into the portal vein, but in portal hypertension, elevated pressure causes retrograde flow through this vein into the esophageal venous plexus, which drains into the azygos system of the systemic circulation — this portosystemic anastomosis is precisely what produces esophageal varices in the distal esophagus.

incorrectas.A: The splenic vein contributes to portal hypertension-related splenomegaly and can be involved in gastric varices via short gastric veins if thrombosed, but the specific vessel that backs up to form esophageal varices is the left gastric vein, not the splenic vein directly.
incorrectas.C: The superior mesenteric vein joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein and drains the midgut, but it is not the vessel directly connecting to the esophageal venous plexus; that portosystemic link runs through the left gastric vein.
incorrectas.D: The inferior mesenteric vein drains the hindgut and is involved in a different portosystemic anastomosis, around the rectum, contributing to internal hemorrhoids, not the one responsible for esophageal varices.

preguntas.q: Rupture of esophageal varices classically presents with which finding?

o.B: Painful hematemesis with retrosternal chest pain

e.correcta: Because esophageal varices are dilated veins without an accompanying acute tissue tear, their rupture produces painless hematemesis that can be sudden and massive given the high pressure within the portal system feeding these vessels. This painless quality is a key clinical clue distinguishing variceal bleeding from the painful hematemesis of a Mallory-Weiss tear, and it constitutes a medical emergency requiring urgent endoscopic management, such as banding, given the risk of hemorrhagic shock.

incorrectas.A: Odynophagia and fever suggest an inflammatory or infectious esophagitis, not the acute, painless hemorrhage typical of a ruptured varix.
incorrectas.B: Painful hematemesis with chest pain is more consistent with a mechanical injury such as a Mallory-Weiss tear or Boerhaave rupture, not the painless bleeding characteristic of esophageal varices.
incorrectas.D: Melena without hematemesis suggests a slower, more distal or lower-volume bleed; ruptured varices typically cause overt, often large-volume hematemesis given the high-pressure, high-flow nature of the dilated venous plexus.

preguntas.q: Is the hematemesis caused by bleeding esophageal varices typically painful or painless — a feature useful for distinguishing it from Mallory-Weiss syndrome?

o.D: Painful only when varices are actively inflamed

e.correcta: Bleeding esophageal varices classically present with painless hematemesis because the bleeding arises from rupture of dilated submucosal veins rather than from an acute mucosal tear; this lack of pain, together with a history of liver disease or portal hypertension, helps differentiate variceal bleeding from the painful hematemesis of a Mallory-Weiss tear.

incorrectas.A: Painful hematemesis is characteristic of Mallory-Weiss syndrome, where an actual mucosal laceration occurs; esophageal varices bleed painlessly because there is no comparable tissue tear, only rupture of a thin-walled dilated vein.
incorrectas.C: The painless nature of variceal hemorrhage is a consistent, testable teaching point rather than something that varies with variceal size; the mechanism, venous rupture without tissue laceration, is the same regardless of variceal caliber.
incorrectas.D: Esophageal varices are not typically described as becoming inflamed; the defining clinical feature tested here is that variceal rupture is painless, independent of any inflammatory state.

preguntas.q: Primary achalasia results from autoimmune destruction of the ganglion cells in which structure?

o.B: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus

e.correcta: Primary achalasia is caused by autoimmune destruction of the inhibitory ganglion cells, which normally release nitric oxide and VIP, within the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus of the esophageal wall. Loss of these inhibitory neurons removes the signal needed for lower esophageal sphincter relaxation and coordinated peristalsis, resulting in a persistently high-pressure LES with uncoordinated or absent peristalsis; this autoimmune process has been associated with HLA-DQB1/DQw1 haplotypes, supporting a genetic susceptibility component.

incorrectas.A: The submucosal (Meissner) plexus primarily regulates local blood flow, secretions, and mucosal activity rather than coordinating the peristaltic wave and LES tone that are disrupted in achalasia; the myenteric plexus is the one responsible for motility control.
incorrectas.B: The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus is a central brainstem nucleus providing efferent parasympathetic outflow to the gut, but achalasia is caused by destruction of the peripheral, intramural ganglion cells of the myenteric plexus itself, not a central brainstem lesion.
incorrectas.D: The celiac ganglion is part of the sympathetic prevertebral ganglia supplying abdominal viscera; it is not the structure whose inhibitory neurons are destroyed in achalasia, which specifically involves the intrinsic myenteric plexus of the esophagus.

preguntas.q: Secondary achalasia can result from destruction of myenteric ganglion cells by which infectious disease?

e.correcta: Chagas disease, caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma cruzi, can destroy the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus ganglion cells throughout the GI tract, producing secondary achalasia with the same loss of LES relaxation and peristalsis seen in the primary autoimmune form. It should be suspected in patients with achalasia-like symptoms and a history of residence in or travel to endemic areas of Latin America, and it may also cause megacolon and cardiomyopathy from the same underlying neuronal destruction elsewhere in the body.

incorrectas.A: Toxoplasmosis, caused by Toxoplasma gondii, classically affects the brain and eyes and can cause congenital infection, but it is not a recognized cause of myenteric plexus destruction leading to secondary achalasia.
incorrectas.C: Schistosomiasis causes granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis, classically affecting the liver (periportal fibrosis) and bladder, but it is not associated with destruction of esophageal myenteric ganglia or achalasia.
incorrectas.D: Cytomegalovirus can cause esophagitis with linear ulcers in immunocompromised patients, but this is an infectious mucosal inflammation, not a cause of ganglion cell destruction producing achalasia's motility disorder.

preguntas.q: Achalasia characteristically causes dysphagia for which food consistencies, distinguishing it from a mechanical obstruction (which typically affects solids only)?

o.D: Neither — achalasia causes odynophagia rather than dysphagia

e.correcta: Because achalasia is a motility disorder, with failure of LES relaxation and impaired peristalsis, rather than a fixed anatomic narrowing, it causes dysphagia for both solids and liquids from the outset. This is an important distinguishing feature from mechanical obstructions such as strictures, rings, or tumors, which typically cause dysphagia for solids first and progress to liquids only as the lumen narrows further over time.

incorrectas.A: Dysphagia for solids only is the classic pattern of a mechanical/structural obstruction, such as a stricture, web, or malignancy, where a fixed narrowing initially only impedes larger boluses; achalasia, being a motility disorder, affects both solids and liquids together.
incorrectas.B: Isolated liquid dysphagia is not a typical presentation of achalasia or of most esophageal disorders; achalasia's hallmark is that both solids and liquids are affected simultaneously.
incorrectas.D: Achalasia's defining symptom is dysphagia, not odynophagia (painful swallowing), which is more typical of infectious or pill esophagitis; patients with achalasia may also regurgitate undigested food, but dysphagia is present, not absent.

preguntas.q: On esophageal manometry, achalasia is characterized by which resting lower esophageal sphincter (LES) pressure?

e.correcta: In achalasia, loss of the inhibitory nitric oxide/VIP-releasing neurons of the myenteric plexus removes the normal relaxation signal to the LES, so the sphincter remains persistently contracted, producing a high resting LES pressure on manometry that fails to relax appropriately with swallowing. This contrasts with sclerodermal esophageal dysmotility, in which fibrosis and smooth muscle atrophy instead produce a weak, low-pressure, incompetent LES prone to reflux.

incorrectas.A: A low LES pressure is the manometric finding in scleroderma-related esophageal dysmotility, where smooth muscle atrophy and fibrosis weaken sphincter tone, leading to severe GERD — essentially the opposite pattern from the elevated pressure seen in achalasia.
incorrectas.B: A normal LES pressure would not explain the impaired bolus transit seen in achalasia; the entire pathophysiology hinges on the LES failing to relax and maintaining an abnormally high pressure.
incorrectas.D: LES pressure is measurable and is in fact elevated, not absent, in achalasia; an "absent" pressure would suggest a completely incompetent sphincter, which is not the finding in this disorder.

preguntas.q: Besides elevated LES pressure, esophageal manometry in achalasia shows which pattern of esophageal body motor activity?

o.C: Increased-amplitude peristaltic waves throughout the body

e.correcta: In achalasia, the same loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons that impairs LES relaxation also disrupts the coordinated sequential contractions needed for normal peristalsis, so manometry shows uncoordinated or completely absent peristalsis in the esophageal body. Together with the elevated LES pressure and a "bird's beak" tapering on barium swallow, this triad supports the diagnosis of achalasia.

incorrectas.A: Normal, coordinated peristalsis is precisely what is lost in achalasia; if peristalsis were normal, the diagnosis of achalasia would not be supported, since impaired peristalsis is a defining manometric criterion.
incorrectas.C: Increased-amplitude peristaltic waves are seen in disorders like diffuse esophageal spasm or hypercontractile ("jackhammer") esophagus, which are distinct motility disorders from achalasia's pattern of weak, disorganized, or absent contractions.
incorrectas.D: Achalasia primarily affects the lower esophageal sphincter and esophageal body, not the upper esophageal sphincter; isolated UES hypertonicity is not the characteristic manometric finding in this condition.

preguntas.q: Which type of hiatal hernia increases the risk of developing GERD by displacing the gastroesophageal junction and LES above the diaphragm?

e.correcta: In a sliding hiatal hernia, the gastroesophageal junction itself slides upward through the esophageal hiatus into the thorax, disrupting the normal anti-reflux barrier formed by the diaphragmatic crura and intra-abdominal LES positioning. This loss of the normal high-pressure zone predisposes to reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus, making it the most common type of hiatal hernia associated with GERD, accounting for roughly 95% of hiatal hernias.

incorrectas.A: In a paraesophageal hiatal hernia, the gastroesophageal junction remains in its normal position while the fundus of the stomach herniates alongside the esophagus; because the GE junction and LES stay properly positioned, GERD is less consistently a feature, though strangulation risk is a separate concern.
incorrectas.C: A Morgagni hernia is a congenital diaphragmatic hernia through the anterior parasternal defect, typically presenting in infancy or as an incidental finding, and has no specific relationship to GERD risk.
incorrectas.D: A Bochdalek hernia is a congenital posterolateral diaphragmatic defect, the most common congenital diaphragmatic hernia causing neonatal respiratory distress, and is unrelated to acquired GERD risk from GE junction displacement.

preguntas.q: GERD often presents with which symptom that can mimic cardiac chest pain, sometimes complicating the initial clinical evaluation?

e.correcta: GERD classically presents with heartburn, a burning, substernal discomfort caused by reflux of acidic gastric contents into the esophagus, which can closely mimic the substernal pressure or burning of cardiac ischemia, sometimes leading to unnecessary cardiac workups before a GI cause is identified. This overlap is why cardiac causes of chest pain must be excluded before attributing symptoms to reflux, especially in patients with cardiac risk factors.

incorrectas.A: Odynophagia (pain with swallowing) suggests active esophageal mucosal injury such as infectious esophagitis or a pill-induced ulcer, and is not the symptom classically described as mimicking cardiac chest pain in GERD.
incorrectas.B: Globus sensation is the feeling of a lump in the throat and can be associated with reflux, but it is not the classic symptom described as mimicking cardiac chest pain — that role belongs to heartburn.
incorrectas.C: Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) can occur with GERD-related strictures over time, but it is a mechanical symptom of impaired bolus transit, not the burning chest discomfort that is mistaken for cardiac pain.

preguntas.q: GERD can present with chronic cough and which pulmonary condition due to microaspiration or vagally-mediated bronchospasm?

e.correcta: Refluxed gastric contents can trigger adult-onset asthma through microaspiration of acid into the airways and through vagally-mediated reflex bronchoconstriction when acid contacts the distal esophagus, even without frank aspiration. GERD is an important and often under-recognized contributor to chronic cough and new-onset wheezing in adults, and it may also cause laryngopharyngeal reflux presenting with hoarseness.

incorrectas.A: Bronchiectasis is irreversible bronchial dilation typically resulting from recurrent infections or chronic inflammatory airway damage, not a classic extraesophageal manifestation of GERD in the way adult-onset asthma is.
incorrectas.C: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a progressive fibrosing lung disease of unclear primary etiology; it is not the classic GERD-associated respiratory presentation tested here, which is asthma-like bronchospasm rather than fibrosis.
incorrectas.D: COPD is primarily caused by chronic exposure to inhaled irritants, especially cigarette smoke, and involves fixed airflow obstruction from emphysema and bronchitis — a different process from the reversible, reflux-triggered bronchospasm associated with GERD.

preguntas.q: Chronic GERD can cause damage to which dental structure due to repeated acid exposure in the mouth?

e.correcta: In chronic GERD, refluxed gastric acid can reach the oral cavity and erode the enamel, the hard, mineralized outer surface of the teeth that normally protects against acid and mechanical wear. This acid-related enamel erosion is a recognized extraesophageal complication of GERD and typically affects the posterior and lingual tooth surfaces most exposed to refluxed acid.

incorrectas.A: The periodontal ligament anchors the tooth root to the alveolar bone and is affected by periodontal disease, a bacterial and inflammatory process, not by the acid erosion from reflux, which instead targets the exposed enamel surface.
incorrectas.B: The gingiva (gum tissue) is primarily affected by plaque-related inflammation such as gingivitis or periodontitis, not by the chemical acid erosion process that characterizes GERD-related dental damage, which targets hard tooth enamel.
incorrectas.C: Acid erosion in GERD begins at and primarily damages the enamel, the outermost layer; dentin becomes exposed only secondarily once enamel is significantly eroded, so enamel — not dentin exclusively — is the structure classically cited as damaged.

preguntas.q: What term describes a fixed narrowing of the esophageal lumen, which can result from chronic GERD, caustic ingestion, or radiation injury?

e.correcta: An esophageal stricture is a fixed, often circumferential narrowing of the esophageal lumen that develops when chronic injury, most commonly long-standing GERD but also caustic ingestion, radiation, or eosinophilic esophagitis, triggers fibrosis and scarring of the esophageal wall. This produces progressive dysphagia, typically for solids initially, and may require endoscopic dilation to relieve symptoms.

incorrectas.A: An esophageal web is a thin, eccentric mucosal/submucosal membrane rather than a longer segment of circumferential fibrotic narrowing; webs are associated with Plummer-Vinson syndrome, a different structural lesion from a stricture.
incorrectas.B: A Schatzki ring is a specific thin mucosal ring located at the gastroesophageal junction (the squamocolumnar junction), distinct from the longer, fibrotic segmental narrowing that defines a true stricture.
incorrectas.C: A diverticulum is an outpouching of the esophageal wall, such as a Zenker or traction diverticulum — the opposite structural change from a stricture, which is a narrowing rather than an outpouching.

preguntas.q: Which condition is characterized by specialized intestinal metaplasia of the lower esophageal mucosa?

e.correcta: Barrett's esophagus is the metaplastic replacement of the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the distal esophagus with columnar epithelium containing goblet cells (specialized intestinal metaplasia), an adaptive response to chronic acid reflux. This is a premalignant change that increases the risk of progression to dysplasia and adenocarcinoma, which is why patients with long-standing GERD undergo surveillance endoscopy with biopsy.

incorrectas.B: Eosinophilic esophagitis is an allergen-driven inflammatory condition marked by dense eosinophilic infiltration of the esophageal mucosa, not by metaplasia of the epithelial cell type — its histology shows eosinophils, not columnar/goblet cells replacing squamous epithelium.
incorrectas.C: Esophageal adenocarcinoma is the malignant proliferation of glandular epithelium that can arise from Barrett's esophagus after it undergoes dysplastic transformation, but the metaplastic (non-malignant) precursor lesion itself is Barrett's esophagus.
incorrectas.D: Achalasia is a motility disorder caused by failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax due to loss of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus; it does not involve any change in the epithelial lining.

preguntas.q: Barrett's esophagus develops in approximately 10% of patients with which chronic condition?

e.correcta: Barrett's esophagus develops in about 10% of patients with chronic GERD as the distal esophageal squamous epithelium is repeatedly exposed to refluxed gastric acid and adapts by transforming into more acid-resistant intestinal-type columnar epithelium. Because only a minority of GERD patients develop this change, risk stratification (duration/severity of symptoms, age, obesity) helps decide who needs screening endoscopy.

incorrectas.B: Achalasia causes dysphagia and regurgitation from impaired LES relaxation rather than acid reflux, and it is not the classic antecedent condition linked to the 10% Barrett's esophagus figure.
incorrectas.C: Eosinophilic esophagitis is an allergic condition that can mimic GERD symptoms but is driven by food/aeroallergen-triggered eosinophilic inflammation, not chronic acid exposure, and is not the condition associated with Barrett's metaplasia.
incorrectas.D: Esophageal varices result from portal hypertension causing dilated submucosal veins; they carry a risk of catastrophic bleeding but have no relationship to metaplastic transformation of the esophageal lining.

preguntas.q: Which type of esophageal cancer is associated with obesity, GERD, and Barrett's esophagus?

e.correcta: Esophageal adenocarcinoma arises from glandular metaplasia (Barrett's esophagus) that develops secondary to chronic GERD, and obesity contributes both by increasing intra-abdominal pressure (worsening reflux) and through metabolic/inflammatory effects. The sequence of chronic acid injury leading to intestinal metaplasia, then dysplasia, then adenocarcinoma makes glandular transformation, not squamous injury, the driving mechanism, and it typically affects the lower third/gastroesophageal junction.

incorrectas.A: Squamous cell carcinoma arises from direct injury to the native squamous epithelium (e.g., alcohol, smoking, hot liquids, caustic ingestion) rather than through a glandular metaplasia pathway, and it is not the type linked to obesity/GERD/Barrett's.
incorrectas.C: Leiomyosarcoma is a rare malignant smooth muscle tumor of the esophageal wall, unrelated to epithelial metaplasia or reflux-driven carcinogenesis.
incorrectas.D: Small cell carcinoma of the esophagus is a rare, aggressive neuroendocrine tumor, not the common epithelial malignancy associated with the obesity-GERD-Barrett's pathway.

preguntas.q: Which esophageal malignancy is defined histologically as a malignant proliferation of glands?

e.correcta: Adenocarcinoma is defined histologically by malignant cells forming gland-like structures that recapitulate glandular epithelium, reflecting its origin from the columnar/glandular metaplastic epithelium of Barrett's esophagus. This glandular architecture on biopsy (often with mucin production) is what distinguishes it microscopically from other esophageal tumors and confirms its origin in the intestinalized mucosa rather than native squamous tissue.

incorrectas.A: Leiomyoma is a benign smooth muscle tumor arising from the muscularis propria, not an epithelial malignancy, and shows spindle cell morphology rather than gland formation.
incorrectas.C: Squamous cell carcinoma is composed of malignant squamous cells, often showing keratinization and intercellular bridges, reflecting its origin from native stratified squamous epithelium rather than glandular tissue.
incorrectas.D: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor arises from the interstitial cells of Cajal and is a mesenchymal (not epithelial) neoplasm, characterized by spindle or epithelioid cells with KIT/CD117 positivity, not gland formation.

preguntas.q: Esophageal adenocarcinoma most commonly arises from which pre-existing condition?

e.correcta: Esophageal adenocarcinoma most commonly arises through the metaplasia-dysplasia-carcinoma sequence beginning with Barrett esophagus, in which chronic acid exposure drives intestinal metaplasia that can progressively accumulate genetic alterations leading to low-grade dysplasia, high-grade dysplasia, and ultimately invasive adenocarcinoma. This stepwise progression is why patients with Barrett esophagus require periodic surveillance biopsies to catch dysplasia before it becomes cancer. Other risk factors such as chronic GERD, obesity, smoking, and achalasia contribute to but do not replace this central metaplastic pathway.

incorrectas.A: Achalasia predisposes mainly to squamous cell carcinoma (via chronic stasis and irritation of retained food against native squamous mucosa), not adenocarcinoma, since it doesn't create glandular metaplasia.
incorrectas.B: Esophageal webs (as in Plummer-Vinson syndrome) increase risk for squamous cell carcinoma of the upper esophagus, not adenocarcinoma, because they do not involve columnar metaplasia.
incorrectas.D: Eosinophilic esophagitis causes chronic inflammation and stricture formation but is not established as a precursor lesion for adenocarcinoma the way Barrett esophagus is.

preguntas.q: Esophageal adenocarcinoma most commonly affects which portion of the esophagus?

e.correcta: Esophageal adenocarcinoma characteristically arises in the lower third of the esophagus, near the gastroesophageal junction, because this is the site where Barrett metaplasia develops in response to reflux of acidic gastric contents. Its location mirrors the distribution of chronic acid exposure and explains why it is often difficult to distinguish from a proximal gastric cardia cancer.

incorrectas.A: The middle third is the classic site for squamous cell carcinoma related to more diffuse mucosal injury (alcohol, smoking), not the reflux-driven glandular metaplasia that produces adenocarcinoma.
incorrectas.C: The upper third is typically involved by squamous cell carcinoma, often related to caustic injury or esophageal webs, rather than adenocarcinoma.
incorrectas.D: Esophageal adenocarcinoma has a distinct predilection for the distal esophagus rather than uniform involvement, reflecting the localized nature of acid-induced metaplasia at the gastroesophageal junction.

preguntas.q: Which esophageal malignancy arises from malignant proliferation of squamous cells?

e.correcta: Squamous cell carcinoma is defined by malignant proliferation of squamous cells, typically showing keratin pearl formation and intercellular bridges on histology, reflecting its origin from the native stratified squamous epithelium that lines most of the esophagus. This origin explains why risk factors are things that directly injure squamous mucosa (alcohol, tobacco, hot liquids, caustic substances) rather than chronic acid reflux.

incorrectas.A: Adenocarcinoma is composed of malignant glandular cells arising from columnar (Barrett) metaplasia, histologically and mechanistically distinct from a squamous cell malignancy.
incorrectas.B: Barrett esophagus is a benign but premalignant metaplastic change (squamous to columnar epithelium), not itself a malignant proliferation of any cell type.
incorrectas.D: Esophageal leiomyoma is a benign smooth muscle tumor of the muscularis propria, an entirely different (mesenchymal, non-epithelial) tissue origin from squamous cell carcinoma.

preguntas.q: Which type of esophageal cancer is associated with esophageal webs, as in Plummer-Vinson syndrome?

e.correcta: Squamous cell carcinoma is associated with esophageal webs, classically in Plummer-Vinson syndrome (iron deficiency anemia, esophageal web, and dysphagia), because the chronic mucosal irritation and altered epithelial turnover from the web and underlying iron deficiency predispose the native squamous epithelium to malignant transformation. Recognizing this association is high yield because Plummer-Vinson syndrome itself is a marker of increased SCC risk requiring surveillance.

incorrectas.A: Adenocarcinoma arises from glandular (Barrett) metaplasia related to chronic acid reflux, a mechanism unrelated to esophageal webs or iron deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor is a mesenchymal neoplasm of the interstitial cells of Cajal, with no established link to esophageal webs or Plummer-Vinson syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Esophageal lymphoma is a rare malignancy of lymphoid tissue, not associated with the mucosal web/iron deficiency mechanism that predisposes to SCC in Plummer-Vinson syndrome.

preguntas.q: Which type of esophageal cancer is associated with consumption of very hot beverages (e.g., hot tea)?

e.correcta: Squamous cell carcinoma is associated with thermal injury from very hot beverages such as tea, because repeated thermal insult to the native squamous mucosa causes chronic irritation and increases the likelihood of malignant transformation, similar to how alcohol and tobacco act as direct mucosal irritants. This fits the broader pattern that SCC risk factors are things that directly damage squamous epithelium rather than promote glandular metaplasia.

incorrectas.A: Adenocarcinoma is linked to chronic acid reflux and Barrett metaplasia, not to thermal injury from hot beverages, since it arises from glandular rather than squamous epithelium.
incorrectas.B: Esophageal leiomyoma is a benign smooth muscle tumor with no established relationship to thermal injury from hot liquids.
incorrectas.D: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor arises from the interstitial cells of Cajal and has no known association with thermal mucosal injury.

preguntas.q: Which type of esophageal cancer is associated with esophageal injury from caustic ingestion (e.g., lye)?

e.correcta: Squamous cell carcinoma is associated with esophageal injury from caustic ingestion (e.g., lye), because severe chemical burns to the squamous mucosa cause chronic scarring, stricture formation, and ongoing epithelial regeneration that increases the risk of malignant transformation years to decades later. This is why patients with a history of caustic ingestion require long-term surveillance even after the acute injury has healed.

incorrectas.A: Barrett esophagus is a metaplastic response to chronic acid reflux, not to a single caustic chemical injury, and represents a different (glandular) transformation pathway.
incorrectas.C: Eosinophilic esophagitis is an allergen-driven eosinophilic inflammatory condition unrelated to caustic chemical injury.
incorrectas.D: Adenocarcinoma arises from glandular (Barrett) metaplasia due to chronic reflux, a distinct mechanism from the direct squamous mucosal scarring caused by caustic ingestion.

preguntas.q: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma most commonly affects which portion of the esophagus?

e.correcta: Squamous cell carcinoma characteristically affects the upper two-thirds of the esophagus, which is lined by native stratified squamous epithelium and is exposed to the classic SCC risk factors (alcohol, tobacco, hot liquids, caustic injury, esophageal webs) that directly injure this squamous mucosa. This proximal-to-mid distribution contrasts with adenocarcinoma's predilection for the distal esophagus.

incorrectas.A: The lower third is the classic site for adenocarcinoma arising from Barrett metaplasia near the gastroesophageal junction, not the typical location for squamous cell carcinoma.
incorrectas.B: Restricting involvement to the gastroesophageal junction describes the adenocarcinoma/gastric cardia cancer distribution, not the broader upper two-thirds distribution typical of SCC.
incorrectas.D: Describing the distal third as exclusive is inaccurate for SCC, and this description instead better fits the distal predilection of adenocarcinoma.

preguntas.q: What is the general prognosis of esophageal carcinoma, and why?

o.A: Excellent, because it is usually detected early via screening
o.B: Poor, because it typically presents late
o.D: Variable, primarily determined by patient age alone

e.correcta: Esophageal carcinoma generally carries a poor prognosis because the esophagus lacks a serosa and has rich submucosal lymphatic drainage, allowing early local spread, and because symptoms (progressive dysphagia) typically don't appear until the tumor has significantly narrowed the lumen, by which point the disease is often locally advanced or metastatic. This combination of anatomic vulnerability and delayed symptom onset is why routine screening isn't standard except in high-risk groups like Barrett's esophagus patients.

incorrectas.A: There is no routine population-wide screening program for esophageal carcinoma (unlike colorectal cancer), so it is not typically caught early, contributing to its poor rather than excellent prognosis.
incorrectas.C: Esophageal carcinoma frequently metastasizes early via the submucosal lymphatic network and direct extension given the lack of a serosal barrier, rather than rarely spreading.
incorrectas.D: While age can influence outcomes, the dominant driver of poor prognosis is late-stage presentation due to anatomic features and lack of early symptoms, not age alone.

preguntas.q: A patient with esophageal carcinoma reports difficulty swallowing that started with solid foods and has progressed to include liquids, along with weight loss and pain. What symptom pattern is this?

o.A: Dysphagia to liquids only, with solids preserved
o.C: Intermittent dysphagia unrelated to food consistency

e.correcta: Esophageal carcinoma classically causes progressive mechanical dysphagia that begins with solids and progresses to liquids as the tumor grows and increasingly narrows the esophageal lumen. This progressive pattern (as opposed to dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the onset) is a hallmark of a structural/obstructive lesion and, together with weight loss, chest pain, and hematemesis from tumor ulceration, should prompt urgent endoscopic evaluation.

incorrectas.A: Dysphagia to liquids with solids preserved is atypical for a mechanical obstruction and would be unusual for a growing luminal mass, which progressively narrows the lumen and affects solids first.
incorrectas.C: Intermittent dysphagia unrelated to food consistency is more characteristic of a motility disorder like esophageal spasm, not the steadily progressive, consistency-dependent pattern seen with a structural malignancy.
incorrectas.D: Odynophagia (painful swallowing) without dysphagia would suggest a primarily inflammatory/infectious esophagitis process rather than the progressive mechanical obstruction typical of carcinoma.

preguntas.q: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma invading which structure classically causes hoarseness?

e.correcta: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma can directly invade the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which runs in close proximity to the esophagus in the tracheoesophageal groove, causing vocal cord paralysis and resultant hoarseness. This finding is clinically significant because it indicates local invasion beyond the esophageal wall and often signals a less favorable prognosis.

incorrectas.A: The phrenic nerve innervates the diaphragm; its involvement would cause diaphragmatic paralysis (and possibly hiccups or dyspnea), not hoarseness.
incorrectas.B: The superior laryngeal nerve mainly affects pitch control via the cricothyroid muscle, producing subtle voice changes rather than the classic hoarseness from vocal cord paralysis seen with recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion.
incorrectas.D: The vagus nerve trunk gives rise to the recurrent laryngeal nerve among many other branches, but it is specifically the recurrent laryngeal branch, not the vagal trunk broadly, that runs adjacent to the esophagus and is classically invaded to produce hoarseness.

preguntas.q: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma invading which adjacent structure classically causes cough?

e.correcta: Direct invasion of the trachea by esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, particularly tumors in the upper/middle esophagus which lies close to the posterior trachea, can cause cough, and in severe cases a tracheoesophageal fistula with coughing during swallowing (due to aspiration) or recurrent pneumonia. This anatomic proximity is why upper and mid-esophageal tumors are more prone to airway complications than distal tumors.

incorrectas.A: Recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion causes hoarseness from vocal cord paralysis, not cough from airway involvement.
incorrectas.C: Thoracic duct invasion could theoretically cause chylothorax from lymphatic fluid leakage, not a cough related to tracheal involvement.
incorrectas.D: Azygos vein involvement would relate more to venous drainage or potential hemorrhage, not to the airway irritation and cough produced by tracheal invasion.

preguntas.q: Esophageal carcinoma located in the upper third of the esophagus characteristically metastasizes to which lymph nodes?

e.correcta: Esophageal carcinoma in the upper third drains to cervical lymph nodes, reflecting the lymphatic drainage pattern of the proximal esophagus, which parallels drainage of the pharynx and larynx. Knowing this site-specific drainage (upper third to cervical, middle third to mediastinal/tracheobronchial, lower third to celiac/gastric nodes) helps predict metastatic spread and guides staging workup based on tumor location.

incorrectas.A: Mediastinal/tracheobronchial nodes are the classic drainage site for tumors of the middle third of the esophagus, an intermediate location distinct from the upper third's cervical drainage.
incorrectas.B: Celiac and gastric lymph nodes are the classic drainage sites for tumors of the lower third of the esophagus, which lies close to the stomach, not the upper third.
incorrectas.D: Para-aortic nodes are not the classically taught primary drainage site for any specific third of the esophagus in the standard teaching of esophageal lymphatic drainage.

preguntas.q: Barrett esophagus is characterized by proximal extension of which anatomic landmark into the esophageal mucosa?

e.correcta: Barrett esophagus is defined by proximal extension of the squamocolumnar junction (the Z-line, where esophageal squamous epithelium meets gastric columnar epithelium) into the tubular esophagus, replacing the normal squamous lining with metaplastic columnar epithelium containing goblet cells. Endoscopically this appears as tongues or a circumferential band of salmon-colored (columnar) mucosa extending above the gastroesophageal junction into the normally pale, glistening squamous esophagus.

incorrectas.A: The lower esophageal sphincter is a functional/anatomic zone of tonic smooth muscle contraction; its position is not what defines the histologic diagnosis of Barrett esophagus, which is based on the epithelial transition line.
incorrectas.C: The gastroesophageal junction muscularis refers to muscle layers, not the mucosal boundary between epithelial types, and is not the structure whose displacement defines Barrett esophagus.
incorrectas.D: The diaphragmatic hiatus is the anatomic opening through which the esophagus passes into the abdomen; it is relevant to hiatal hernia, not to the mucosal metaplasia that defines Barrett esophagus.

preguntas.q: Eosinophilic esophagitis classically presents with dysphagia and food impaction triggered by exposure to what?

e.correcta: Eosinophilic esophagitis is a T(H)2-mediated allergic condition in which exposure to food allergens (and sometimes aeroallergens) triggers eosinophil recruitment and infiltration of the esophageal mucosa, leading to chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and stricture/ring formation that manifest as dysphagia and food impaction, especially in patients with a personal or family history of atopy (asthma, eczema, allergic rhinitis). This allergic mechanism is why elimination diets and topical steroids, rather than acid suppression, are central to management.

incorrectas.A: Acid reflux is the driver of GERD-related esophagitis, but eosinophilic esophagitis is characteristically unresponsive to acid suppression, underscoring that its inflammation is allergen- rather than acid-driven.
incorrectas.C: Viral infection causes infectious esophagitis (e.g., HSV, CMV), typically in immunocompromised patients, presenting with discrete ulcers rather than the diffuse eosinophilic infiltration and food impaction pattern of EoE.
incorrectas.D: Caustic chemical exposure causes direct corrosive injury with acute necrosis and later stricture, a distinct mechanism from the chronic allergen-driven eosinophilic inflammation of EoE.

preguntas.q: Does eosinophilic esophagitis typically respond to standard GERD therapy such as PPIs?

o.C: No, symptoms persist despite acid suppression

e.correcta: Eosinophilic esophagitis does not reliably respond to standard GERD therapy such as PPIs because its underlying pathology is allergen-driven eosinophilic inflammation rather than acid-mediated injury; management instead centers on dietary allergen elimination and topical (swallowed) corticosteroids. That said, a PPI trial is still part of the diagnostic workup, since a subset of patients with eosinophilic infiltration do have PPI-responsive esophageal eosinophilia, and persistence of eosinophils despite an adequate PPI trial supports the EoE diagnosis and the need for endoscopy with biopsy.

incorrectas.A: Claiming PPIs fully resolve symptoms mischaracterizes EoE; since the inflammation is allergen- rather than acid-driven, most patients do not achieve full symptom resolution with acid suppression alone.
incorrectas.B: EoE occurs in both children and adults, and the general lack of PPI responsiveness is not limited to pediatric patients.
incorrectas.D: Antibiotics have no role in eosinophilic esophagitis, which is an allergic, not infectious, inflammatory condition, so combining them with PPIs would not be expected to help.

preguntas.q: Which infectious cause of esophagitis classically presents with punched-out ulcers on endoscopy?

e.correcta: HSV-1 esophagitis classically produces multiple small, discrete punched-out ulcers on endoscopy, reflecting the virus's cytopathic effect on esophageal squamous epithelial cells (with characteristic multinucleated giant cells and Cowdry A intranuclear inclusions on biopsy). Distinguishing this punched-out appearance from CMV's linear ulcers is a classic testable contrast in infectious esophagitis.

incorrectas.A: CMV esophagitis classically produces linear, longitudinal ulcers rather than the punched-out lesions of HSV-1, reflecting infection of endothelial and stromal (not primarily epithelial) cells.
incorrectas.B: HIV itself can cause idiopathic esophageal ulcers in advanced disease, but these are a diagnosis of exclusion and not the classic punched-out ulcer description tested for infectious esophagitis.
incorrectas.D: Candida esophagitis characteristically presents with white plaques/pseudomembranes rather than discrete ulcers, reflecting a fungal, adherent-plaque pattern of infection distinct from viral ulceration.

preguntas.q: Which infectious cause of esophagitis classically presents with linear ulcers on endoscopy?

e.correcta: CMV esophagitis classically causes linear, longitudinal ulcers, reflecting CMV's tropism for endothelial cells and fibroblasts in the esophageal submucosa, with characteristic large cells containing both intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusions ("owl's eye" inclusions) on biopsy. This occurs mainly in severely immunocompromised patients (e.g., advanced HIV/AIDS, transplant recipients) and is distinguished from HSV-1's punched-out ulcers.

incorrectas.A: HSV-1 classically causes punched-out ulcers due to its cytopathic effect on squamous epithelial cells, a distinct endoscopic pattern from the linear ulcers of CMV.
incorrectas.C: Candida esophagitis presents with white pseudomembranes/plaques rather than ulcers, reflecting fungal colonization of the mucosal surface rather than deep ulceration.
incorrectas.D: HIV can cause idiopathic esophageal ulcers as a diagnosis of exclusion once infectious causes like CMV and HSV are ruled out, but it is not itself the organism producing the classic linear ulcer pattern.

preguntas.q: Which infectious cause of esophagitis presents with white pseudomembranes on endoscopy?

e.correcta: Candida esophagitis classically presents with white, adherent pseudomembranes/plaques on endoscopy, corresponding to fungal colonization with pseudohyphae and yeast forms visible on biopsy or brushing. It is the most common cause of infectious esophagitis overall and typically occurs in immunocompromised patients (e.g., HIV/AIDS with low CD4 counts, diabetes, or those on inhaled/systemic corticosteroids).

incorrectas.A: HSV-1 causes punched-out ulcers from direct viral cytopathic injury to squamous epithelium, not the adherent white plaques characteristic of fungal (Candida) infection.
incorrectas.B: Aspergillus can cause esophageal disease in severely immunocompromised hosts but is not the classic organism associated with white pseudomembranes in standard infectious esophagitis teaching; that is Candida.
incorrectas.D: CMV causes linear ulcers from endothelial/stromal cell infection, a very different endoscopic appearance from the plaque-like pseudomembranes of Candida.

preguntas.q: Infectious esophagitis (e.g., due to Candida, HSV-1, or CMV) is typically seen in which patient population?

o.C: Patients with normal immune function and no risk factors

e.correcta: Infectious esophagitis (Candida, HSV-1, CMV) is typically seen in immunocompromised patients, such as those with HIV/AIDS, on chemotherapy, or post-transplant on immunosuppressive therapy, because a healthy immune system normally keeps these opportunistic and latent pathogens in check. A low CD4 count in HIV patients, for example, is a classic clinical clue that should raise suspicion for one of these infectious causes when a patient presents with odynophagia.
