incorrectas.A: Pregnancy is not a classic risk factor for infectious esophagitis; the immune changes of pregnancy do not typically predispose to opportunistic esophageal infections the way significant immunosuppression does.
incorrectas.B: Healthy young athletes have intact immune systems and are not the population at risk for opportunistic infectious esophagitis, which requires a compromised immune defense to allow these organisms to invade.
incorrectas.C: Patients with normal immune function and no risk factors are precisely the group in whom infectious esophagitis would be unusual, since these are opportunistic pathogens that exploit reduced host immune surveillance.

preguntas.q: Which connective tissue disease is associated with esophageal dysmotility due to smooth muscle atrophy and fibrous replacement?

e.correcta: Scleroderma (systemic sclerosis) causes esophageal dysmotility through atrophy of the muscularis, particularly in the lower two-thirds (smooth muscle portion), with replacement by collagenous fibrous tissue, leading to weak or absent peristalsis and a hypotensive lower esophageal sphincter. This produces the 'E' (esophageal dysmotility) in CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia) and predisposes patients to severe GERD and its complications, including stricture and Barrett esophagus.

incorrectas.A: Systemic lupus erythematosus is an autoimmune disease with diverse multi-organ manifestations, but esophageal dysmotility from smooth muscle atrophy and fibrosis is not its classic hallmark the way it is for scleroderma.
incorrectas.B: Dermatomyositis primarily causes proximal muscle weakness and characteristic skin findings (heliotrope rash, Gottron papules); while it can affect striated muscle in the pharynx/upper esophagus, it is not classically associated with the smooth muscle atrophy and fibrous replacement of the lower esophagus seen in scleroderma.
incorrectas.C: Rheumatoid arthritis primarily targets synovial joints and is not classically associated with esophageal smooth muscle atrophy or dysmotility, distinguishing it from scleroderma's well-known GI involvement.

preguntas.q: On esophageal manometry, scleroderma-associated esophageal dysmotility characteristically shows what change in lower esophageal sphincter (LES) pressure?

o.A: Markedly elevated LES pressure with impaired relaxation on swallowing
o.C: Normal LES pressure with simultaneous, non-peristaltic contractions
o.D: Elevated LES pressure that relaxes normally with swallowing

e.correcta: In systemic sclerosis, fibrous replacement of the smooth muscle in the distal two-thirds of the esophagus weakens both peristalsis and sphincter tone, producing a hypotensive (low-pressure) LES on manometry. This is the opposite pattern from achalasia, where loss of inhibitory (NO/VIP-releasing) neurons in the myenteric plexus causes the LES to fail to relax and remain persistently high-pressure. Recognizing this contrast is a classic Step 1 distinguishing point, since both conditions cause dysphagia but arise from opposite mechanisms.

incorrectas.A: A markedly elevated LES pressure with failed relaxation is the hallmark of achalasia, caused by degeneration of inhibitory myenteric neurons, not of sclerodermal esophageal disease, where fibrosis instead weakens the sphincter.
incorrectas.C: Normal LES pressure with simultaneous, non-propulsive contractions describes diffuse esophageal spasm, a disorder of dysregulated peristaltic coordination rather than the fibrotic, low-pressure sphincter seen in scleroderma.
incorrectas.D: An elevated LES pressure that relaxes normally would not explain dysphagia from sphincter dysfunction and does not match either scleroderma (low pressure) or the classic achalasia pattern (elevated, non-relaxing) taught for these motility disorders.

preguntas.q: In systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), the loss of lower esophageal sphincter tone most directly predisposes patients to which complication, which may progress to stricture, Barrett esophagus, or aspiration?

e.correcta: Fibrotic weakening of the LES in scleroderma removes the normal barrier that keeps gastric acid in the stomach, so acid refluxes freely into the esophagus. Chronic reflux then damages the squamous epithelium, and over time this can lead to peptic stricture, Barrett metaplasia (a precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma), or aspiration pneumonia if reflux reaches the airway, especially with the impaired clearance from concurrent poor peristalsis.

incorrectas.B: Esophageal varices arise from portal hypertension causing dilation of submucosal veins, an entirely separate mechanism from LES hypotonia and unrelated to scleroderma's fibrotic esophageal involvement.
incorrectas.C: Diffuse esophageal spasm is a primary motility disorder of uncoordinated, simultaneous contractions; it is not a consequence of low LES pressure but a distinct disease process affecting the esophageal body.
incorrectas.D: Achalasia results from loss of LES relaxation due to myenteric neuron degeneration, producing a hypertensive, non-relaxing sphincter — the opposite physiology of the hypotensive LES caused by scleroderma.

preguntas.q: A newborn is found to have loops of bowel freely protruding through a defect in the anterior abdominal wall, typically located to the right of the umbilicus, with no covering membrane. What is this congenital defect called?

e.correcta: Gastroschisis is a full-thickness paraumbilical abdominal wall defect, classically just to the right of an intact umbilical cord, through which loops of bowel herniate directly into the amniotic fluid without any covering membrane. It is thought to result from a vascular insult (disruption of the right umbilical vein or omphalomesenteric artery) rather than a failure of physiologic midgut herniation to return, which distinguishes its embryologic mechanism from omphalocele.

incorrectas.A: Omphalocele involves herniation through the umbilical ring itself (not lateral to it) and the herniated viscera remain covered by peritoneum and amnion, unlike the naked, exposed bowel of gastroschisis.
incorrectas.C: An umbilical hernia is a postnatal defect where abdominal contents protrude through an incompletely closed umbilical ring, usually skin-covered and often resolving spontaneously — a very different entity from the exposed bowel seen at birth in gastroschisis.
incorrectas.D: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia involves herniation of abdominal viscera into the thoracic cavity through a diaphragmatic defect (most often the foramen of Bochdalek), not through the anterior abdominal wall.

preguntas.q: Which congenital abdominal wall defect features herniated abdominal contents that are NOT covered by peritoneum or amniotic membrane?

e.correcta: Gastroschisis results from a vascular disruption of the abdominal wall lateral to an otherwise normal umbilical cord, so the extruded bowel loops sit directly exposed to amniotic fluid with no peritoneal or amniotic covering. This exposure predisposes the bowel to chemical irritation, edema, and matting from prolonged amniotic fluid contact, which is why these infants often need prompt surgical closure.

incorrectas.A: Omphalocele occurs when the midgut fails to return to the abdominal cavity after physiologic herniation, but the herniated viscera remain enclosed by peritoneum internally and amnion externally, giving it a translucent covering absent in gastroschisis.
incorrectas.B: An umbilical hernia is covered by skin and subcutaneous tissue since it results from incomplete closure of the umbilical ring after cord separation, not a lack of covering membrane.
incorrectas.D: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia involves abdominal organs herniating into the thorax through a diaphragmatic defect; the question of a peritoneal covering over herniated bowel does not apply to this distinct thoracoabdominal defect.

preguntas.q: Which congenital defect is defined by persistent herniation of abdominal viscera into the base of the umbilical cord, covered by peritoneum and amnion?

e.correcta: Normally, the midgut physiologically herniates into the umbilical cord around week 6 and returns to the abdominal cavity by week 10 as the abdomen enlarges. Omphalocele occurs when this return fails, leaving bowel (and sometimes liver) persistently herniated within the cord, covered by peritoneum internally and amnion externally, giving it the characteristic membranous sac seen on prenatal ultrasound or at birth.

incorrectas.B: Gastroschisis is a separate, lateral abdominal wall defect from vascular disruption, and its herniated bowel is uncovered — the opposite of the membrane-covered herniation defining omphalocele.
incorrectas.C: Meckel diverticulum results from incomplete obliteration of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct, producing a true diverticulum of the ileum — an entirely different embryologic error unrelated to abdominal wall herniation.
incorrectas.D: An umbilical hernia is a postnatal, skin-covered protrusion through a weak umbilical ring, not the persistence of the embryonic physiologic midgut herniation described here.

preguntas.q: Omphalocele results from failure of which normal embryologic process?

o.A: Failure of the physiologic midgut herniation to return to the abdominal cavity by week 10
o.B: Failure of the vitelline duct to obliterate
o.C: Failure of the midgut to complete its normal 270-degree counterclockwise rotation
o.D: Failure of the lateral body wall folds to fuse in the ventral midline

e.correcta: Between weeks 6 and 10, the rapidly growing midgut normally herniates through the umbilical ring into the extraembryonic coelom (the umbilical cord) because the abdominal cavity is temporarily too small to hold it, then retracts back into the abdomen by week 10 as the liver and kidneys shrink relatively and the abdominal cavity enlarges. Omphalocele occurs when this retraction fails, so the bowel remains herniated within the cord, covered by peritoneum and amnion.

incorrectas.B: Failure of the vitelline duct to obliterate produces a Meckel diverticulum, a persistent outpouching of the ileum — a distinct embryologic error involving duct regression, not abdominal wall or midgut return.
incorrectas.C: Failure of normal midgut rotation causes malrotation (with risk of volvulus), which involves the orientation of the bowel around the SMA axis rather than failure of the herniated gut to return to the abdominal cavity.
incorrectas.D: Failure of lateral body wall fold fusion is a proposed mechanism for some ventral wall defects broadly, but omphalocele specifically is attributed to failed return of the physiologic midgut herniation, not a primary fusion defect of the folds themselves.

preguntas.q: Which congenital abdominal wall defect is characteristically covered by both peritoneum and the amnion of the umbilical cord?

e.correcta: Because omphalocele arises from failure of the physiologically herniated midgut to return through the umbilical ring, the protruding viscera remain enveloped by the peritoneal lining internally and the amniotic membrane of the umbilical cord externally. This membranous sac is a key distinguishing feature on exam and imaging, and its presence is also why omphalocele is more often associated with other congenital anomalies (it reflects a primary developmental arrest rather than an isolated vascular accident).

incorrectas.A: Gastroschisis results from a vascular disruption lateral to the cord, so the herniated bowel is directly exposed to amniotic fluid with no peritoneal or amniotic covering, unlike omphalocele.
incorrectas.C: An umbilical hernia is covered by skin, not by peritoneum-and-amnion in the way described; it develops postnatally from incomplete closure of the umbilical ring rather than from persistence of the embryonic midgut herniation.
incorrectas.D: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia involves abdominal viscera entering the thoracic cavity through a diaphragmatic defect, a location and covering (or lack thereof) unrelated to the peritoneum/amnion-covered umbilical cord herniation of omphalocele.

preguntas.q: Congenital hypertrophy of the pyloric smooth muscle, causing narrowing of the gastric outlet in infants, is known as what condition?

e.correcta: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is caused by hyperplasia and hypertrophy of the circular and longitudinal smooth muscle layers of the pylorus, which thickens the muscular wall and narrows the gastric outlet lumen. On exam this can produce a palpable, firm, mobile 'olive'-shaped mass in the epigastrium, and the mechanical obstruction is the direct cause of the projectile vomiting seen in affected infants.

incorrectas.A: Duodenal atresia results from failure of the duodenal lumen to recanalize during development, producing a complete obstruction distal to the stomach (classically with the 'double bubble' sign), a distinct congenital defect from pyloric muscle hypertrophy.
incorrectas.C: Annular pancreas occurs when the ventral pancreatic bud fails to rotate properly and encircles the duodenum, causing extrinsic duodenal compression rather than intrinsic pyloric muscle thickening.
incorrectas.D: Malrotation with volvulus results from abnormal midgut rotation during development, predisposing the bowel to twist around the superior mesenteric artery; it causes obstruction through vascular compromise and twisting, not through hypertrophied pyloric muscle.

preguntas.q: What is the most common cause of gastric outlet obstruction in infants, occurring in roughly 1 in 600 live births?

e.correcta: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is the leading cause of gastric outlet obstruction in infancy, with an incidence of about 1 in 600 live births and a strong male predominance. Progressive hypertrophy of the pyloric muscularis narrows the outlet over the first weeks of life, so, unlike other congenital GI obstructions, symptoms are typically absent at birth and emerge only after the muscle has had time to thicken.

incorrectas.B: Annular pancreas is a much rarer cause of duodenal obstruction from an encircling band of pancreatic tissue, and it more often presents in the neonatal period or even prenatally, unlike the delayed presentation of pyloric stenosis.
incorrectas.A: Duodenal atresia, while classically associated with Down syndrome and presenting with bilious vomiting shortly after birth, is considerably less common than pyloric stenosis as an overall cause of infant gastric outlet or upper GI obstruction.
incorrectas.D: Malrotation with volvulus is a surgical emergency causing obstruction with possible bowel ischemia, but it is far less common than pyloric stenosis and typically presents with bilious vomiting rather than the classic nonbilious, projectile vomiting of pyloric stenosis.

preguntas.q: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis classically occurs most often in which demographic group?

o.D: Later-born males with an affected older sibling

e.correcta: Pyloric stenosis has a well-documented predilection for first-born male infants, reflecting a combination of genetic (polygenic, with increased risk if a parent was affected, especially the mother) and possibly hormonal or environmental influences on pyloric muscle development. This demographic pattern is a classic testable association that helps prioritize the diagnosis in the appropriate clinical vignette.

incorrectas.B: While female infants can develop pyloric stenosis, the condition shows a male predominance (roughly 4-6:1), so 'first-born females' does not reflect the classically taught highest-risk group.
incorrectas.C: Prematurity is not the classic risk factor emphasized for pyloric stenosis; the condition is primarily associated with birth order (first-born) and male sex rather than gestational age at birth.
incorrectas.D: Later-born infants are actually at somewhat lower baseline risk than first-born infants, even though having an affected sibling does raise familial risk — the single best-known demographic association remains first-born male.

preguntas.q: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis typically becomes symptomatic at what age, a timing that helps distinguish it from intestinal atresia (which presents with bilious vomiting in the first 1-2 days of life)?

o.A: Within the first 24 hours of life
o.D: In utero, detected on routine prenatal ultrasound

e.correcta: Because pyloric stenosis results from progressive postnatal hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle rather than a fixed structural defect present at birth, it takes time — typically about 2 to 6 weeks — for the muscle to thicken enough to cause a clinically significant obstruction. This delayed onset is a key distinguishing feature from intestinal atresia, which is a fixed anatomic obstruction present from birth and therefore causes bilious vomiting within the first day or two of life.

incorrectas.A: Vomiting within the first 24 hours of life is much more characteristic of a fixed congenital obstruction like intestinal or duodenal atresia, present from birth, rather than pyloric stenosis, which requires time for muscular hypertrophy to develop.
incorrectas.C: By 6 to 12 months, pyloric stenosis would be an unusually late presentation; the muscle hypertrophy and resulting obstruction almost always become apparent within the first two months of life.
incorrectas.D: Pyloric stenosis is a postnatal, progressive process of muscle hypertrophy and is not typically detected on prenatal ultrasound, unlike some structural anomalies (e.g., duodenal atresia's double bubble) that can be seen before birth.

preguntas.q: The projectile vomiting characteristic of pyloric stenosis is typically described as which of the following, a feature that helps distinguish it from intestinal atresia?

e.correcta: Because the obstruction in pyloric stenosis is proximal to the ampulla of Vater (at the gastric outlet), bile from the duodenum cannot reflux back into the stomach and vomitus, so the projectile vomiting is characteristically nonbilious. This contrasts with obstructions distal to the ampulla, such as intestinal (duodenal) atresia, where bile mixes with the vomitus, making the bilious versus nonbilious distinction a high-yield localizing clue.

incorrectas.A: Bilious vomiting implies an obstruction distal to the entry of the common bile duct, which is the pattern seen in duodenal or intestinal atresia and malrotation with volvulus, not in pyloric stenosis where the block is proximal to the ampulla.
incorrectas.C: Bloody vomiting (hematemesis) would suggest mucosal injury or bleeding, such as from severe esophagitis or a Mallory-Weiss tear, and is not a classic feature of uncomplicated pyloric stenosis.
incorrectas.D: Feculent vomiting suggests a very distal, long-standing bowel obstruction allowing bacterial overgrowth and reflux of colonic contents, a picture far more advanced and distal than the proximal gastric outlet obstruction of pyloric stenosis.

preguntas.q: Physical examination of an infant with pyloric stenosis may reveal which visible finding on the abdomen?

o.A: Visible peristaltic waves moving across the epigastrium

e.correcta: As the stomach contracts forcefully against the narrowed, hypertrophied pylorus in an attempt to push contents through the obstruction, these strong peristaltic contractions can sometimes be seen as waves moving left to right across the upper abdomen, especially right after feeding. Combined with a palpable olive-shaped mass and nonbilious projectile vomiting, visible peristalsis rounds out the classic clinical triad taught for pyloric stenosis.

incorrectas.B: Caput medusae refers to dilated, engorged periumbilical veins seen in portal hypertension from recanalized paraumbilical veins, an entirely different finding related to portosystemic shunting rather than gastric outlet obstruction.
incorrectas.C: Cullen sign (bluish discoloration around the umbilicus) reflects retroperitoneal or intra-abdominal hemorrhage tracking to the umbilicus, classically seen in hemorrhagic pancreatitis or ruptured ectopic pregnancy, not pyloric stenosis.
incorrectas.D: Grey Turner sign (flank ecchymosis) similarly indicates retroperitoneal hemorrhage, again most classically associated with severe hemorrhagic pancreatitis, and has no relationship to the muscular hypertrophy causing pyloric stenosis.

preguntas.q: Exposure to which drug class, whether given directly to an infant or transmitted through breast milk, is associated with an increased risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?

e.correcta: Macrolide antibiotics (such as erythromycin) are motilin receptor agonists, and this same prokinetic action on smooth muscle is thought to contribute to pyloric smooth muscle hypertrophy when infants are exposed either directly (e.g., treatment for pertussis or eye prophylaxis) or indirectly through a breastfeeding mother taking the drug. This association is why macrolide use in young infants is approached cautiously, with counseling about watching for pyloric stenosis symptoms.

incorrectas.A: Penicillins act on bacterial cell wall synthesis and have no recognized motilin-receptor or smooth muscle hypertrophic effect linking them to pyloric stenosis risk.
incorrectas.C: Aminoglycosides work by inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis at the 30S ribosome and are notable for nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, not for any association with pyloric muscle hypertrophy.
incorrectas.D: Tetracyclines are protein synthesis inhibitors best known for effects on bone and teeth in children (discoloration, growth inhibition), not for a motilin-agonist effect on gastric smooth muscle like macrolides.

preguntas.q: Persistent vomiting of gastric contents in an infant with pyloric stenosis classically produces which acid-base and electrolyte disturbance?

e.correcta: Repeated vomiting of hydrochloric acid–rich gastric secretions directly removes acid and chloride from the body, driving a metabolic alkalosis with hypochloremia. Volume contraction from ongoing fluid losses activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and aldosterone-driven renal potassium wasting (to preserve sodium and water) compounds this into hypokalemia, producing the classic hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis of pyloric stenosis.

incorrectas.A: Hyperkalemic metabolic acidosis would be expected with conditions causing acid retention or impaired renal acid excretion (such as renal failure or aldosterone deficiency), the opposite of the acid- and chloride-losing picture from vomiting gastric contents.
incorrectas.C: While hyponatremia can occur to some degree with volume depletion, the defining and classically tested disturbance in pyloric stenosis is a metabolic alkalosis (from acid loss), not a metabolic acidosis.
incorrectas.D: Respiratory alkalosis arises from hyperventilation-driven CO2 loss, an entirely different mechanism from the metabolic (renal/GI electrolyte) alkalosis caused by vomiting acidic gastric contents in pyloric stenosis.

preguntas.q: What is the definitive treatment for infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?

o.C: Endoscopic balloon dilation of the pylorus
o.D: Nasogastric decompression until the hypertrophy spontaneously resolves

e.correcta: Pyloromyotomy involves surgically incising the hypertrophied pyloric muscle (typically the Ramstedt procedure, splitting the muscularis down to but not through the mucosa) to relieve the mechanical obstruction while preserving the mucosal lining. Since the underlying problem is a fixed muscular hypertrophy rather than a reversible acid-mediated process, mechanical relief of the obstruction — after first correcting the metabolic alkalosis and dehydration — is curative and rapidly restores normal feeding.

incorrectas.B: Proton pump inhibitors reduce gastric acid secretion but do nothing to relieve the mechanical narrowing caused by hypertrophied pyloric muscle, so they have no role as definitive therapy for this structural obstruction.
incorrectas.C: Balloon dilation is used for some acquired strictures but is not the standard approach for congenital pyloric muscle hypertrophy in infants, where surgical division of the muscle is both safer and definitive.
incorrectas.D: Unlike some transient neonatal conditions, pyloric muscle hypertrophy does not spontaneously resolve with conservative decompression alone; without surgical intervention the obstruction and its complications (dehydration, alkalosis, failure to thrive) persist.

preguntas.q: Acute gastritis results from which underlying process affecting the gastric mucosa?

o.C: Acidic damage to the mucosa from disrupted mucosal defenses
o.D: Neoplastic transformation of surface epithelial cells

e.correcta: Acute gastritis occurs when something disrupts the mucosa's normal protective mechanisms — such as severe burns (Curling ulcer), NSAIDs (which inhibit protective prostaglandin synthesis), alcohol, increased intracranial pressure (Cushing ulcer), shock, or chemotherapy killing rapidly dividing mucosal cells — allowing gastric acid to directly injure the epithelium. Because the damage is acid-mediated and the insult is typically identifiable and often reversible, this is fundamentally different from the chronic, ongoing inflammatory processes seen in chronic gastritis.

incorrectas.A: Chronic H. pylori infection causes a persistent, ongoing inflammatory infiltrate that defines chronic (not acute) gastritis, developing over months to years rather than the abrupt, insult-driven injury of the acute form.
incorrectas.B: Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells describes autoimmune (type A) chronic gastritis, which leads to achlorhydria, B12 deficiency, and pernicious anemia — a distinct, antibody-mediated chronic process rather than acute acid-mediated mucosal injury.
incorrectas.D: Neoplastic transformation refers to the development of gastric cancer, an entirely different long-term process from the acute, reversible mucosal injury caused by acid exposure in acute gastritis.

preguntas.q: The pathophysiology of acute gastritis is best explained by which mechanism?

o.A: An imbalance between mucosal protective defenses and the acidic gastric environment
o.B: Progressive glandular atrophy from chronic autoimmune attack
o.C: Intestinal metaplasia of the gastric epithelium
o.D: Chronic active inflammation driven by H. pylori colonization

e.correcta: The stomach normally maintains a delicate balance between aggressive factors (acid, pepsin) and protective mechanisms (mucus-bicarbonate layer, epithelial tight junctions, prostaglandin-driven blood flow and secretion, and rapid cell turnover). Acute gastritis develops when this balance tips toward injury — either because defenses are weakened (e.g., NSAID-induced prostaglandin inhibition) or acid exposure is overwhelming (e.g., severe stress states) — allowing acid to damage the mucosa faster than it can be repaired.

incorrectas.B: Progressive glandular atrophy from autoimmune attack describes chronic autoimmune gastritis, a slowly evolving process targeting parietal cells over years, not the acute defense-versus-acid imbalance that defines acute gastritis.
incorrectas.C: Intestinal metaplasia is a longer-term adaptive/premalignant change seen in chronic gastritis after prolonged mucosal injury, not the mechanism underlying the acute process itself.
incorrectas.D: Chronic active inflammation from H. pylori is, by definition, the chronic form of gastritis developing over a sustained period, distinct from the acute mucosal-defense-versus-acid imbalance driving acute gastritis.

preguntas.q: Which component of gastric mucosal defense functions by delivering nutrients and oxygen to the mucosa while removing acid that has leaked back into the tissue?

o.C: Tight junctions between surface epithelial cells

e.correcta: A healthy submucosal blood supply is essential to gastric mucosal defense because it continuously delivers oxygen and nutrients needed for epithelial cell turnover and repair, while also washing away any acid that has diffused back through the epithelium (back-diffusion), preventing it from accumulating and causing further injury. This is why states of hypoperfusion, such as shock or severe burns, are classic causes of acute gastritis and stress ulcers — the protective 'clearance' function of blood flow is lost.

incorrectas.A: The mucus-bicarbonate layer forms a physical and chemical barrier that traps a neutral pH microenvironment against the epithelial surface, but it does not itself perform the nutrient-delivery and acid-clearance role that is specifically attributed to mucosal blood flow.
incorrectas.C: Tight junctions between epithelial cells prevent acid from freely diffusing between cells into the submucosa, contributing to barrier integrity, but they do not deliver nutrients or actively remove leaked acid the way blood flow does.
incorrectas.D: Prostaglandins stimulate bicarbonate and mucus secretion and help maintain mucosal blood flow, but the specific defense mechanism of nutrient delivery and acid washout described here is a direct function of blood supply itself, not of prostaglandin signaling per se.

preguntas.q: A gastric (stress) ulcer arising in the setting of severe burns is known by what eponym?

e.correcta: Curling ulcer refers to acute gastric mucosal ulceration occurring after severe burns, resulting from hypovolemia and reduced mucosal blood flow (splanchnic hypoperfusion as the body shunts blood to vital organs), which impairs the mucosa's ability to clear back-diffused acid and repair itself. The mnemonic 'you get Curling ulcers from being burned by a curling iron' helps link the eponym to burns, and prophylactic PPI or H2-blocker therapy is often given to at-risk burn patients to prevent this complication.

incorrectas.A: Cushing ulcer is the analogous stress ulcer associated with increased intracranial pressure (from trauma, tumor, or hemorrhage), thought to result from vagal stimulation driving excess acid secretion — a different trigger and mechanism than the hypoperfusion of burns.
incorrectas.C: A marginal ulcer occurs at the anastomotic margin after gastric bypass or gastrojejunostomy surgery, a mechanically and anatomically distinct entity unrelated to burns or systemic hypoperfusion.
incorrectas.D: A Dieulafoy lesion is a dilated, aberrant submucosal artery that erodes through the overlying epithelium and can cause sudden, massive GI bleeding; it is a vascular malformation, not a stress-related mucosal ulcer from burns.

preguntas.q: Gastric ulcers that occur secondary to increased intracranial pressure are known by what eponym?

e.correcta: Cushing ulcer describes acute gastric (and sometimes duodenal) ulceration that develops in the setting of elevated intracranial pressure, such as from head trauma, brain tumor, or intracranial hemorrhage. The proposed mechanism is increased vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation from raised ICP, which directly increases gastric acid secretion and overwhelms mucosal defenses, in contrast to the hypoperfusion-driven mechanism of Curling ulcers from burns — a helpful mnemonic is that Cushing 'cushions' (protects) the brain but attacks the stomach via the vagus.

incorrectas.A: Curling ulcer is the stress ulcer associated with severe burns, driven by hypovolemic hypoperfusion of the gastric mucosa rather than by vagally mediated acid hypersecretion from elevated intracranial pressure.
incorrectas.C: A marginal ulcer develops at a surgical gastrojejunal anastomosis, an anatomically localized complication of bariatric or gastric surgery that has no relationship to intracranial pressure.
incorrectas.D: A Dieulafoy lesion is a structurally abnormal, unusually large submucosal artery prone to erosion and bleeding, a vascular anomaly unrelated to the acid-hypersecretion mechanism of Cushing ulcers.

preguntas.q: Acute gastritis occurring in the setting of systemic shock is best explained by which mechanism, producing multiple stress ulcers?

o.A: Direct corrosive injury from NSAID-mediated prostaglandin inhibition

e.correcta: In shock, the body preferentially shunts blood away from the splanchnic circulation to preserve perfusion to the brain and heart, leaving the gastric mucosa relatively ischemic. Without adequate blood flow, the mucosa cannot clear back-diffused acid or maintain the rapid epithelial turnover needed for repair, so multiple superficial stress ulcers can develop rapidly across the stomach — this is why critically ill, hypotensive patients are often placed on stress ulcer prophylaxis.

incorrectas.A: NSAID-mediated prostaglandin inhibition is a distinct cause of acute gastritis (reducing mucus and bicarbonate secretion), relevant to medication-induced injury, but it is not the mechanism specifically implicated in shock-related stress ulceration.
incorrectas.C: Autoimmune injury to parietal cells describes a chronic, antibody-mediated process (autoimmune gastritis) unfolding over years, not the acute ischemic insult that develops rapidly during an episode of shock.
incorrectas.D: Chronic H. pylori-mediated inflammation develops over a prolonged period through bacterial colonization and immune response, which is unrelated to the acute hemodynamic hypoperfusion driving stress ulcers in shock.

preguntas.q: Chronic gastritis, in contrast to acute gastritis, is defined by which underlying process?

o.A: A single acute episode of acid-mediated mucosal injury
o.B: Chronic, ongoing inflammation of the gastric mucosa
o.D: Acute ischemic injury from transient hypoperfusion

e.correcta: Chronic gastritis reflects sustained, long-term inflammation of the gastric mucosa, most often driven by chronic H. pylori infection (the most common cause worldwide) or by autoimmune destruction of parietal cells. Unlike acute gastritis, which results from a discrete acid-mediated insult and can resolve once the trigger is removed, chronic gastritis involves persistent immune cell infiltration that can progress over years to glandular atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, and increased cancer risk.

incorrectas.A: A single acute episode of acid-mediated injury describes acute gastritis, which is by definition a shorter-term, insult-driven process rather than the persistent inflammation that characterizes the chronic form.
incorrectas.C: Neoplastic transformation refers to the development of gastric adenocarcinoma or lymphoma, which can be a long-term consequence of untreated chronic gastritis but is not itself the definition of chronic gastritis.
incorrectas.D: Acute ischemic injury from transient hypoperfusion describes the mechanism behind acute stress-related gastritis (as in shock), not the sustained inflammatory process that defines the chronic form.

preguntas.q: Long-standing chronic gastritis characteristically leads to which structural change in the gastric mucosa?

o.C: Squamous metaplasia of the surface epithelium
o.D: Hyperplastic polyp formation without any glandular loss

e.correcta: Persistent chronic inflammation, whether from H. pylori or autoimmune destruction of parietal and chief cells, progressively destroys the normal glandular architecture of the stomach, leading to thinning and loss of the specialized gastric glands — atrophic gastritis. This atrophy reduces acid and intrinsic factor production (contributing to hypochlorhydria and, in autoimmune disease, B12 deficiency), and is a key step on the pathway toward intestinal metaplasia and increased gastric cancer risk.

incorrectas.A: Hypertrophy (thickening) of the gastric glands is not the characteristic long-term outcome of chronic inflammation; the process instead progressively destroys glandular tissue, producing atrophy rather than growth.
incorrectas.C: Squamous metaplasia is not a recognized adaptive change of the gastric mucosa in chronic gastritis; the mucosa instead tends toward intestinal metaplasia (columnar epithelium resembling intestinal mucosa with goblet cells), not squamous change.
incorrectas.D: While hyperplastic polyps can occur in the setting of chronic gastritis, they are a focal secondary finding, not the defining structural change of the mucosa overall — the hallmark change is diffuse glandular atrophy.

preguntas.q: Chronic gastritis can lead to a histologic change in which the gastric epithelium is replaced by tissue resembling intestinal mucosa, complete with goblet cells, and which increases the risk of gastric adenocarcinoma. What is this change called?

e.correcta: In response to prolonged chronic inflammation, the normal gastric columnar epithelium can undergo an adaptive change in which it is replaced by epithelium resembling small intestinal mucosa, including goblet cells and sometimes Paneth cells — this is intestinal metaplasia. It is considered a premalignant change because it marks a step toward dysplasia and intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma, making its identification on biopsy clinically important for cancer risk stratification and surveillance.

incorrectas.A: Squamous metaplasia is not a recognized response pattern of gastric mucosa to chronic injury; metaplastic change in the stomach characteristically produces intestinal-type epithelium, not squamous epithelium.
incorrectas.B: Barrett metaplasia refers specifically to replacement of the normal squamous epithelium of the distal esophagus with intestinal-type columnar epithelium in response to chronic acid reflux — an esophageal, not gastric, process, even though it shares the intestinal metaplasia theme.
incorrectas.D: Pseudopyloric metaplasia (also called antralization) refers to fundic (oxyntic) glands being replaced by mucous glands resembling antral/pyloric glands, a different metaplastic change from the goblet-cell-containing intestinal metaplasia described here.

preguntas.q: In chronic gastritis (whether autoimmune or H. pylori-related), what happens to gastric acid (HCl) secretion over time?

o.A: It increases due to compensatory parietal cell hyperplasia
o.B: It remains within normal limits throughout the disease course
o.C: It transiently increases before normalizing with treatment
o.D: It decreases, progressing toward achlorhydria or hypochlorhydria

e.correcta: Chronic gastritis, whether autoimmune or H. pylori-driven, causes progressive glandular atrophy of the acid-secreting oxyntic mucosa (body/fundus) and often intestinal metaplasia. As functional parietal cell mass is lost, HCl output steadily falls, eventually producing hypochlorhydria or frank achlorhydria. This decline in acid removes the normal negative feedback on antral G cells, which is why hypergastrinemia so reliably accompanies chronic gastritis.

incorrectas.A: Parietal cells are the cells being destroyed or atrophying in chronic gastritis, not proliferating — the compensatory hyperplasia that does occur is in antral G cells (gastrin-producing), which respond to falling acid levels, not in the acid-secreting parietal cell mass itself.
incorrectas.B: Chronic gastritis is defined by ongoing mucosal injury that, over years, produces glandular atrophy; acid output does not remain static but declines in parallel with loss of parietal cells.
incorrectas.C: There is no transient increase-then-normalization pattern in chronic gastritis; the trajectory is a gradual, progressive decline in acid secretion as atrophic changes accumulate, not a self-correcting fluctuation.

preguntas.q: What happens to serum gastrin levels in chronic gastritis?

o.A: Increased (hypergastrinemia), driven by loss of acid-mediated feedback inhibition
o.B: Decreased, due to destruction of antral G cells
o.C: Unchanged, because gastrin release is independent of gastric pH
o.D: Increased only when Zollinger-Ellison syndrome coexists

e.correcta: Gastrin release from antral G cells is normally suppressed by low gastric pH (acid provides negative feedback via somatostatin release from D cells). As chronic gastritis destroys parietal cells and acid output falls, this feedback inhibition is lost, so G cells are chronically disinhibited and undergo hyperplasia, producing sustained hypergastrinemia. This is a useful clinical clue — a patient with unexplained hypergastrinemia and low acid output points toward atrophic gastritis rather than a gastrin-secreting tumor, where acid is typically high.

incorrectas.B: Antral G cells are not the cells destroyed in chronic gastritis — in autoimmune gastritis it is parietal cells (body/fundus) that are targeted, and G cells actually increase in activity and number as a compensatory response to low acid.
incorrectas.C: Gastrin secretion is directly regulated by luminal pH; low acid is precisely the stimulus that drives G cells to secrete more gastrin, so gastrin levels are very much dependent on, not independent of, gastric acidity.
incorrectas.D: Hypergastrinemia in chronic gastritis occurs on its own as a physiologic response to hypochlorhydria; Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is a separate, tumor-driven cause of hypergastrinemia associated with high (not low) acid output, and its presence is not required for gastritis-related hypergastrinemia.

preguntas.q: Which historical classification term is used for chronic autoimmune gastritis?

e.correcta: In the older ABC classification of chronic gastritis, "Type A" designates autoimmune gastritis, a helpful mnemonic being "A for autoimmune." It targets the body and fundus, destroys parietal cells, and produces achlorhydria, hypergastrinemia, and often pernicious anemia from loss of intrinsic factor.

incorrectas.A: Type B gastritis refers to bacterial (H. pylori-associated) gastritis, which predominantly affects the antrum and is a distinct entity from the autoimmune process, distinguished by its infectious rather than autoimmune etiology.
incorrectas.C: "Type AB" is not a standard designation in this classification scheme; the ABC system separates autoimmune (A) from bacterial (B) gastritis rather than blending them into a combined category.
incorrectas.D: "Type C" gastritis in some classifications refers to chemical/reactive gastropathy (e.g., from NSAIDs or bile reflux), not the autoimmune process, so it does not describe autoimmune destruction of parietal cells.

preguntas.q: Which historical classification term is used for chronic H. pylori gastritis?

e.correcta: "Type B" gastritis denotes bacterial gastritis caused by H. pylori — "B for bacterial" — which is the most common cause of chronic gastritis overall. It typically begins in the antrum and, with chronicity, may spread proximally to the body, in contrast to the fundus/body-predominant autoimmune (Type A) form.

incorrectas.A: Type A gastritis is the autoimmune form, caused by immune-mediated destruction of parietal cells in the body/fundus, not by bacterial infection of the antrum — a different mechanism and distribution entirely.
incorrectas.B: "Type AB" is not part of the standard ABC nomenclature; the classification keeps autoimmune and bacterial gastritis as separate categories (A and B) rather than combining them.
incorrectas.C: "Type C" gastritis refers to chemical/reactive gastropathy from agents like NSAIDs, alcohol, or bile reflux, a non-infectious mechanism distinct from H. pylori-driven inflammation.

preguntas.q: Chronic autoimmune gastritis results from autoantibody- and T-cell-mediated destruction of which gastric cell type?

e.correcta: In autoimmune gastritis, autoreactive T cells and autoantibodies (anti-parietal cell and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies) target and destroy parietal cells located in the body and fundus. Loss of parietal cells eliminates both HCl and intrinsic factor production, explaining the combination of achlorhydria/hypergastrinemia and vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia) seen in this disease.

incorrectas.B: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and are found alongside parietal cells in the oxyntic mucosa, but they are not the primary autoimmune target in this disease — the defining autoantibodies and clinical consequences (achlorhydria, B12 deficiency) trace back to parietal cell loss.
incorrectas.C: Mucous neck cells produce protective mucus within gastric glands but are not the cells targeted by the autoimmune attack in this condition; their loss would not explain the hallmark achlorhydria and intrinsic factor deficiency.
incorrectas.D: ECL cells secrete histamine and can become hyperplastic secondary to chronic hypergastrinemia (a downstream consequence of parietal cell loss), but they are not themselves the initial target of the autoimmune destruction.

preguntas.q: Which regions of the stomach are primarily affected in chronic autoimmune gastritis?

e.correcta: Autoimmune gastritis selectively affects the body and fundus because that is where parietal cells (the autoimmune target) are concentrated. This distribution explains why acid- and intrinsic-factor-producing mucosa is lost while the antrum, which houses gastrin-producing G cells, is relatively spared — helping distinguish it from H. pylori gastritis, which starts in the antrum.

incorrectas.A: The antrum and pylorus are the regions preferentially involved in H. pylori (Type B) gastritis, not autoimmune gastritis; autoimmune disease spares the antrum because it lacks the parietal cells that are the autoimmune target.
incorrectas.B: The cardia is a small transitional zone near the esophagogastric junction and is not the principal site of autoimmune injury; the disease process is centered on the acid-producing body and fundus mucosa.
incorrectas.D: Autoimmune gastritis is regionally selective, not diffuse — it targets parietal-cell-rich body/fundus mucosa specifically, sparing the antrum, rather than affecting the stomach uniformly.

preguntas.q: Chronic autoimmune gastritis is best classified as which type of hypersensitivity reaction?

e.correcta: Autoimmune gastritis is primarily driven by CD4+ T-cell-mediated (Type IV, delayed-type) autoimmune destruction of parietal cells, with cytotoxic T cells and cytokine-mediated injury as the actual cause of mucosal damage. The characteristic autoantibodies against parietal cells and intrinsic factor are present and useful diagnostically, but they are considered a consequence/marker of the T-cell-driven injury rather than the primary mechanism of tissue destruction.

incorrectas.A: Type I hypersensitivity is IgE-mediated, immediate degranulation-based injury (e.g., allergic reactions, anaphylaxis) and has no role in the chronic, cell-mediated destruction of parietal cells seen in autoimmune gastritis.
incorrectas.C: Type II hypersensitivity involves antibody-mediated destruction of cells (e.g., via complement or ADCC) as the direct cause of injury; while anti-parietal cell antibodies exist here, current understanding attributes the actual tissue destruction primarily to T cells, making this predominantly a Type IV process.
incorrectas.D: Type III hypersensitivity involves immune complex deposition causing inflammation (e.g., serum sickness, lupus nephritis) — there is no significant immune complex deposition mechanism driving autoimmune gastritis.

preguntas.q: What is the most common cause of chronic gastritis, accounting for roughly 90% of cases?

e.correcta: Chronic H. pylori infection accounts for roughly 90% of chronic gastritis cases, making it by far the most common cause. The organism's urease and proteases erode the protective mucus layer and provoke chronic inflammation, and if untreated, the infection can persist for decades, predisposing to peptic ulcers, atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, and gastric cancer.

incorrectas.A: Autoimmune gastritis is a much less common cause of chronic gastritis than H. pylori infection; it is an important entity because of its association with pernicious anemia, but it does not account for the majority of cases.
incorrectas.B: NSAID-induced injury more classically causes acute erosive gastropathy or contributes to peptic ulcers via prostaglandin inhibition, but it is a distinctly less common and mechanistically different cause of chronic gastritis than H. pylori.
incorrectas.D: Bile reflux gastropathy is a recognized but minor contributor to chemical gastritis, typically seen after gastric surgery altering pyloric function; it is far less prevalent than H. pylori as a cause of chronic gastritis.

preguntas.q: Chronic H. pylori gastritis initially and predominantly affects which region of the stomach?

e.correcta: H. pylori preferentially colonizes and initially infects the antrum, where it is well adapted to the local mucous environment and where its urease-mediated ammonia production helps it survive. With longstanding infection the inflammation can extend proximally into the body (pangastritis) as well, but the antrum is where disease begins and is heaviest.

incorrectas.B: The fundus is part of the acid-secreting oxyntic mucosa and is a later, not initial, site of H. pylori-related inflammation as chronic infection spreads proximally.
incorrectas.C: The body (like the fundus) is oxyntic mucosa that is typically involved only with longstanding, more extensive H. pylori gastritis, not the initial site of colonization.
incorrectas.D: The cardia is a small transitional region near the esophagogastric junction and is not the primary or initial region where H. pylori establishes infection.

preguntas.q: Does H. pylori invade the gastric epithelium/mucosa to cause disease?

o.A: Yes — it invades the lamina propria directly
o.B: Yes — it replicates intracellularly within epithelial cells
o.C: Yes — it disseminates hematogenously to the submucosa
o.D: No — it remains on the mucosal surface, embedded within the overlying mucus layer

e.correcta: H. pylori is a noninvasive extracellular organism that colonizes the mucus layer overlying the gastric epithelium rather than penetrating into or beneath the epithelial cells. It causes damage indirectly — its urease neutralizes local acid to permit survival, while proteases, cytotoxins (e.g., CagA, VacA), and the resulting host inflammatory response injure the mucosa from the surface, without the bacterium itself invading tissue.

incorrectas.A: H. pylori does not breach the epithelial barrier to reach the lamina propria; its pathogenic effects are mediated from the luminal surface via toxins and induced inflammation, not by physical tissue invasion.
incorrectas.B: Unlike genuinely intracellular pathogens, H. pylori is an extracellular organism that adheres to gastric epithelial cells and lives in the overlying mucus, rather than replicating inside epithelial cells.
incorrectas.C: H. pylori infection remains localized to the gastric mucosal surface; it does not enter the bloodstream or disseminate to the submucosa or other tissues.

preguntas.q: Chronic H. pylori gastritis increases the risk of developing which condition?

e.correcta: Chronic H. pylori gastritis is the leading risk factor for peptic ulcer disease, since chronic mucosal inflammation, mucus barrier breakdown, and (in antral-predominant disease) loss of somatostatin-producing D cells all favor unopposed acid secretion and epithelial injury that can progress to ulceration in the duodenum or stomach. Eradicating the infection is a cornerstone of ulcer treatment and prevention of recurrence.

incorrectas.A: Eosinophilic esophagitis is an allergen/immune-driven eosinophilic infiltration of the esophagus unrelated to H. pylori infection or gastric acid pathology; it has a distinct atopic pathophysiology.
incorrectas.C: Achalasia results from loss of inhibitory neurons in the esophageal myenteric plexus causing impaired lower esophageal sphincter relaxation, a motility disorder with no established link to H. pylori-driven gastric inflammation.
incorrectas.D: Celiac disease is an autoimmune reaction to gluten causing small bowel villous atrophy, a completely separate disease process from H. pylori-associated gastric injury.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme produced by H. pylori alkalinizes its local environment by hydrolyzing urea into ammonia and CO2, enabling survival in gastric acid?

e.correcta: Urease is the key enzyme that allows H. pylori to survive in the highly acidic gastric lumen — it hydrolyzes host urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, and the ammonia locally neutralizes acid around the bacterium, creating a more hospitable microenvironment. This same enzyme is exploited diagnostically in the urea breath test and rapid urease (CLO) test.

incorrectas.A: Catalase helps some bacteria neutralize reactive oxygen species from host immune cells, but it is not the enzyme responsible for locally alkalinizing the gastric environment to permit acid survival.
incorrectas.B: Proteases produced by H. pylori help degrade the protective mucus layer and contribute to mucosal injury, but they do not neutralize gastric acid the way urease's ammonia production does.
incorrectas.D: CagA is a virulence factor injected into host cells that disrupts signaling and contributes to inflammation and carcinogenesis, but it plays no role in acid neutralization — that function belongs specifically to urease.

preguntas.q: Which noninvasive test detects active H. pylori infection by measuring labeled CO2 exhaled after ingestion of labeled urea?

e.correcta: The urea breath test has patients ingest urea labeled with a nonradioactive carbon isotope (13C); if H. pylori (with its urease) is present, the urea is hydrolyzed into labeled CO2, which is absorbed and exhaled and can be measured in breath samples, along with ammonia. It is noninvasive and also useful for confirming eradication after treatment, since it reflects active, current infection.

incorrectas.A: The stool antigen test also detects active infection (by detecting H. pylori antigens in stool) and is a valid noninvasive alternative, but it works through antigen detection, not through metabolism of labeled urea into exhaled CO2 as described.
incorrectas.B: Serum IgG antibody testing detects prior exposure to H. pylori but can remain positive long after successful eradication, so it cannot reliably distinguish active from past infection the way a breath test measuring live bacterial urease activity can.
incorrectas.C: The rapid urease (CLO) test is also urease-based but requires an endoscopic biopsy specimen placed in a reagent, rather than analysis of a patient's exhaled breath after ingesting labeled urea — it is invasive, unlike the breath test.

preguntas.q: Is intestinal metaplasia associated with H. pylori gastritis reversible?

o.A: Yes, it typically resolves after successful eradication of the infection
o.B: No, it is permanent once established
o.C: Only in autoimmune gastritis, not H. pylori gastritis
o.D: No, it progresses to gastric cancer even after eradication

e.correcta: Intestinal metaplasia arising from chronic H. pylori gastritis can regress after the infection is eradicated, particularly if treatment occurs before metaplasia has become extensive or long-standing. This is one of the key reasons early detection and treatment of H. pylori matter — removing the chronic inflammatory stimulus allows at least partial reversal of the adaptive metaplastic change and reduces the downstream risk of progression toward dysplasia and gastric adenocarcinoma.

incorrectas.B: While longstanding, extensive metaplasia may be less likely to fully reverse, the metaplastic change associated with H. pylori gastritis is not considered fixed and permanent — eradication therapy is specifically pursued because it can lead to at least partial regression.
incorrectas.C: Intestinal metaplasia is a well-described consequence of H. pylori-associated chronic gastritis, not something restricted to autoimmune gastritis; both entities can lead to atrophic and metaplastic mucosal changes over time.
incorrectas.D: Intestinal metaplasia is a risk factor for future gastric cancer, but it does not inevitably progress to malignancy — eradicating the underlying H. pylori infection is precisely the intervention shown to reduce that progression risk, not something that occurs regardless of treatment.

preguntas.q: What is the most common cause of duodenal ulcers, accounting for approximately 90% of cases?

e.correcta: H. pylori accounts for roughly 90% of duodenal ulcers. The organism preferentially infects the antrum, where it disrupts somatostatin-producing D cells; loss of somatostatin removes an inhibitory brake on gastrin (and thus acid) secretion, so excess acid is delivered into the duodenum, overwhelming its bicarbonate-buffering capacity and causing mucosal ulceration.

incorrectas.A: NSAID use is an important cause of peptic ulcers overall (via COX inhibition and loss of protective prostaglandins), but it is a less common cause of duodenal ulcers specifically compared to H. pylori, which dominates at roughly 90%.
incorrectas.C: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is a genuine but rare cause of duodenal (and even more distal) ulcers due to autonomous gastrin secretion from a neuroendocrine tumor; it accounts for only a small minority of cases compared to H. pylori.
incorrectas.D: Crohn disease can rarely cause duodenal inflammation or ulceration as part of its patchy transmural involvement of the GI tract, but it is not a common or classic cause of duodenal peptic ulcers, which are overwhelmingly attributable to H. pylori.

preguntas.q: Which rare gastrin-secreting tumor syndrome can cause duodenal ulcers, often extending unusually far past the duodenal bulb?

e.correcta: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, caused by a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma), is a rare but classic cause of duodenal ulcers. Because acid delivery is markedly excessive and not adequately neutralized by the time it reaches the duodenal papilla, ulcers in this syndrome often occur unusually distal to the duodenal bulb and can even extend into the jejunum, which should raise clinical suspicion when seen.

incorrectas.A: MEN1 is an important association with gastrinomas (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome can occur as part of MEN1), but MEN1 itself is a multi-tumor endocrine syndrome, not the specific gastrin-driven mechanism directly responsible for causing duodenal ulcers described here.
incorrectas.B: Carcinoid syndrome results from serotonin and other vasoactive substances secreted by neuroendocrine tumors, causing flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm — it is not associated with excess gastric acid production or duodenal ulceration.
incorrectas.D: VIPoma causes a syndrome of watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome) due to excess vasoactive intestinal peptide — its hallmark is actually reduced, not increased, gastric acid secretion, the opposite of what drives Zollinger-Ellison-associated ulcers.

preguntas.q: Duodenal ulcers most commonly arise in which wall of the duodenum?

e.correcta: Duodenal ulcers arise more commonly in the anterior wall of the duodenal bulb. This anatomic detail is clinically relevant because anterior ulcers are more prone to perforation into the peritoneal cavity (since there is free peritoneal space anteriorly), whereas posterior ulcers are more likely to erode into the gastroduodenal artery and cause bleeding.

incorrectas.A: Posterior duodenal ulcers are less common than anterior ones, but they carry a distinct danger of eroding into the gastroduodenal artery, causing brisk hemorrhage, rather than perforating freely as anterior ulcers tend to do.
incorrectas.B: The duodenal bulb's ulcer predilection is described in terms of anterior versus posterior wall involvement rather than a superior location, which is not the classic anatomic distinction taught for duodenal ulcers.
incorrectas.C: "Lateral" is not the standard anatomic classification used for duodenal ulcer location — the clinically important distinction is anterior (usual site, perforation risk) versus posterior (bleeding risk).

preguntas.q: What is the most common cause of gastric ulcers, accounting for approximately 70% of cases?

e.correcta: H. pylori causes roughly 70% of gastric ulcers, somewhat less than its dominant role in duodenal ulcers (~90%). In gastric ulcers, the mechanism is more directly local: H. pylori's proteases and ureases produce cytotoxic damage to the gastric mucosa itself, rather than the antral D-cell/somatostatin loss mechanism that predominates in duodenal ulcer pathogenesis.

incorrectas.B: NSAIDs are an important but less common cause of gastric ulcers than H. pylori, acting through inhibition of protective prostaglandin synthesis (via COX-1 inhibition) rather than direct bacterial mucosal injury.
incorrectas.C: Bile reflux is a recognized but minor contributor to gastric mucosal injury, typically more relevant after gastric surgery that disrupts normal pyloric function, and accounts for a much smaller proportion of gastric ulcers than H. pylori.
incorrectas.D: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome can cause gastric ulcers via markedly excessive gastrin-driven acid secretion, but it is a rare tumor-related cause, far less common than H. pylori infection.

preguntas.q: Besides H. pylori, which of the following is a recognized (though less common) cause of gastric ulcers?

e.correcta: Beyond H. pylori (the dominant cause), NSAIDs and bile reflux are recognized secondary causes of gastric ulcers. NSAIDs impair the gastric mucosa's protective mechanisms by inhibiting COX-1-derived prostaglandins, which normally stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion and maintain mucosal blood flow — removing this protection makes the epithelium vulnerable to acid-peptic injury even without infection.

incorrectas.A: Autoimmune parietal cell destruction underlies autoimmune (Type A) gastritis and its associated achlorhydria and pernicious anemia, but it is not classically described as a cause of gastric ulcers in the way NSAIDs and bile reflux are.
incorrectas.B: Crohn disease can rarely involve the stomach as part of its patchy transmural GI involvement, but it is not among the classically taught "less common causes" of gastric ulcers alongside H. pylori.
incorrectas.C: Viral gastritis (e.g., CMV) is a recognized entity, particularly in immunocompromised patients, but it is not part of the standard teaching of common or less-common causes of typical gastric peptic ulcer disease.

preguntas.q: What is the most common location for a gastric ulcer?

e.correcta: The most common site for a gastric ulcer is the lesser curvature, specifically at the transition zone between the acid-secreting body and the gastrin-secreting antrum. This border region is thought to be an optimal microenvironment for H. pylori colonization, since it sits at the interface of the two functionally distinct mucosal types, making it particularly susceptible to the combined effects of acid exposure and bacterial injury.

incorrectas.B: The greater curvature is a much less typical site for peptic ulcers; the disease process concentrates instead along the lesser curvature at the body-antrum junction.
incorrectas.C: The fundus, part of the oxyntic (acid-producing) mucosa, is not the classic site of ulceration; ulcers cluster instead near the antral-body transition on the lesser curvature.
incorrectas.D: The cardia is a small transitional zone near the esophagogastric junction and is not the characteristic location for typical gastric peptic ulcers.

preguntas.q: A gastric ulcer on the lesser curvature erodes through the stomach wall. Bleeding from which artery is most likely?

e.correcta: Because the classic gastric ulcer location is the lesser curvature, a deeply eroding ulcer there is most likely to perforate into the left gastric artery, which runs along the lesser curvature and supplies that region. Bleeding from this vessel can be brisk and clinically significant, making location-based prediction of bleeding source a useful clinical reasoning tool.

incorrectas.A: The right gastroepiploic artery runs along the greater curvature, not the lesser curvature, so it is not the vessel typically eroded by a lesser-curvature gastric ulcer.
incorrectas.C: The splenic artery is more classically associated with erosion from pancreatic pseudocysts or pancreatitis-related pathology rather than lesser-curvature gastric ulcers.
incorrectas.D: The gastroduodenal artery lies posterior to the duodenal bulb and is the vessel classically eroded by posterior duodenal ulcers, not by lesser-curvature gastric ulcers.

preguntas.q: Which type of peptic ulcer, gastric or duodenal, is more likely to be malignant?

o.B: Neither — peptic ulcers are never malignant
o.D: Both are equally likely to be malignant

e.correcta: Gastric ulcers carry a meaningfully higher risk of harboring or representing malignancy than duodenal ulcers, which is why endoscopic biopsy and follow-up to confirm healing are routinely performed for gastric ulcers but not typically required for duodenal ulcers. Duodenal carcinoma is exceedingly rare, so the diagnostic vigilance for malignancy is concentrated on the stomach.

incorrectas.A: Duodenal ulcers are essentially always benign, since primary duodenal carcinoma is extremely rare — this is precisely why biopsy of duodenal ulcers to rule out cancer is not routinely necessary, unlike for gastric ulcers.
incorrectas.B: While most peptic ulcers overall are benign, gastric ulcers specifically can arise from or coexist with gastric adenocarcinoma, so malignancy is a real and important consideration that must be excluded, particularly for gastric lesions.
incorrectas.D: The risk of malignancy is not equal between the two locations — gastric ulcers carry a substantially higher likelihood of malignant transformation or coexisting cancer than duodenal ulcers, which is why clinical practice treats them differently (routine biopsy and repeat endoscopy for gastric ulcers).

preguntas.q: A gastric ulcer biopsy shows a small (<3 cm), sharply demarcated, "punched-out" lesion surrounded by radiating mucosal folds. Which of the following best describes this ulcer?

o.C: Indeterminate, requiring repeat biopsy regardless of appearance

e.correcta: Small size (<3 cm), a sharply demarcated "punched-out" appearance, and surrounding radiating mucosal folds are classic gross features of a benign gastric ulcer. These features reflect a well-defined, non-infiltrative ulcer crater with mucosa that retains a relatively organized architecture around the defect, in contrast to the disorganized, infiltrative appearance of malignant lesions.

incorrectas.A: Malignant ulcers, even early ones, tend to have irregular, heaped-up or nodular margins rather than the sharply demarcated, punched-out edges and organized radiating folds described here, which are the hallmark of a benign process.
incorrectas.B: Borrmann type IV (linitis plastica) refers to a diffusely infiltrative malignant pattern causing a rigid, thickened "leather bottle" stomach — a very different gross appearance from the small, well-circumscribed, punched-out lesion with radiating folds described in this case.
incorrectas.C: The gross features described (small size, sharp demarcation, radiating folds) are specific enough to be classically taught as benign; while biopsy is still standard practice to confirm this clinically, the morphology itself is a recognized textbook description of a benign ulcer rather than an ambiguous one.

preguntas.q: A gastric ulcer is large, irregular, and has heaped-up, everted margins. Which of the following best describes this ulcer?

o.D: NSAID-induced ulcer with normal healing margins

e.correcta: A large, irregular ulcer with heaped-up, everted margins is a classic gross description of a malignant gastric ulcer, reflecting infiltrative tumor growth disrupting the normal mucosal architecture at the ulcer edge. This contrasts sharply with the small, sharply demarcated, punched-out appearance with radiating folds typical of benign ulcers, which is why gross and endoscopic appearance, along with biopsy, helps guide suspicion for malignancy.

incorrectas.B: Benign gastric ulcers characteristically appear small and sharply demarcated with radiating mucosal folds, the opposite of the large, irregular, heaped-up margins described here, which instead point toward malignancy.
incorrectas.C: Curling ulcers are stress ulcers associated with severe burns, typically located in the proximal duodenum/stomach and related to mucosal ischemia rather than malignant infiltration; they do not classically present with large, irregular, heaped-up margins as their defining feature.
incorrectas.D: NSAID-induced ulcers, when healing, tend to show a more regular, less infiltrative appearance; heaped-up, irregular margins are not a feature of straightforward NSAID-related mucosal injury but rather raise concern for malignant transformation.

preguntas.q: Gastric ulcers, unlike duodenal ulcers, should always undergo biopsy of the ulcer margins prior to treatment. What is the primary reason for this practice?

o.A: To rule out underlying gastric malignancy
o.B: To confirm the presence of Helicobacter pylori
o.C: To assess the depth of ulcer penetration into the muscularis
o.D: To identify the ulcer as chronic versus acute

e.correcta: Gastric ulcers carry a real risk of being (or overlying) a gastric adenocarcinoma, so endoscopic biopsy of the ulcer margins — where malignant cells are most likely to be sampled — is mandatory to exclude cancer before assuming the lesion is benign peptic disease. Duodenal ulcers, in contrast, are almost never malignant, so routine biopsy for cancer screening is not required there.

incorrectas.B: H. pylori status is usually assessed with rapid urease testing, histology special stains, or noninvasive breath/stool antigen testing rather than being the specific reason margin biopsies are mandated; the defining concern with a gastric ulcer is ruling out cancer, not confirming the infection.
incorrectas.C: Endoscopic biopsy samples mucosal tissue for histology; it does not reliably assess the depth of wall penetration, which is better evaluated by imaging or intraoperative findings, and depth of penetration is not why gastric ulcers specifically require biopsy.
incorrectas.D: Chronicity is inferred from clinical history, ulcer appearance, and healing pattern, not from a targeted margin biopsy, and this is not the reason gastric ulcers are biopsied while duodenal ulcers typically are not.

preguntas.q: What is the most common complication of peptic ulcer disease, occurring with similar frequency in both gastric and duodenal ulcers?

e.correcta: Hemorrhage from erosion of the ulcer base into submucosal or, in deeper ulcers, named arteries is the most frequent complication of peptic ulcer disease overall, presenting as hematemesis, melena, or occult blood loss with anemia. Because both gastric and duodenal mucosa are richly vascularized, bleeding is more common than perforation or obstruction.

incorrectas.B: Perforation is a dramatic and dangerous complication, particularly of anterior duodenal ulcers, but it occurs less frequently overall than hemorrhage, which can result from more superficial erosion without full-thickness wall breakdown.
incorrectas.C: Gastric outlet obstruction results from scarring and edema narrowing the pyloric channel after recurrent ulceration, but it is a comparatively uncommon, late complication rather than the most frequent one.
incorrectas.D: Penetration occurs when an ulcer erodes through the bowel wall into a contiguous structure (e.g., pancreas) without free perforation into the peritoneal cavity; it is a recognized but less common complication than bleeding.

preguntas.q: Which location of duodenal ulcer is most commonly associated with major hemorrhage, due to its proximity to the gastroduodenal artery?

e.correcta: Posterior duodenal ulcers erode toward the retroperitoneum, where the gastroduodenal artery runs directly behind the duodenal bulb; deep posterior ulcers can erode through the vessel wall and cause massive, sometimes life-threatening hemorrhage. This posterior relationship to a major artery is why posterior ulcers are the classic cause of significant duodenal ulcer bleeding.

incorrectas.A: Anterior duodenal ulcers face the relatively free peritoneal cavity rather than a major artery, so when they erode through the full thickness of the wall they classically cause perforation with free air, not the massive arterial hemorrhage seen with posterior ulcers.
incorrectas.C: Prepyloric ulcers sit at the gastric outlet and can bleed or obstruct, but they are not the classic teaching example for major hemorrhage from arterial erosion the way posterior duodenal bulb ulcers are.
incorrectas.D: The apex of the duodenal bulb is not the anatomic hallmark used in this classic anterior/posterior distinction; the key point is that posterior wall ulcers overlie the gastroduodenal artery, not a specific apex location.

preguntas.q: A patient with longstanding peptic ulcer disease develops recurrent vomiting of undigested food and early satiety due to scarring of the gastric outlet. Which complication does this represent?

e.correcta: Chronic or recurrent ulceration near the pylorus or duodenum causes scarring and fibrosis that progressively narrow the channel, producing gastric outlet obstruction with postprandial vomiting, early satiety, and a succussion splash. This mechanical narrowing is distinct from acute bleeding or free perforation.

incorrectas.B: Hemorrhage presents with hematemesis, melena, or anemia from a bleeding ulcer base, not with the mechanical vomiting and outlet narrowing described, which instead reflect scar-related stricture.
incorrectas.C: Perforation is an acute, catastrophic event with sudden severe pain and peritonitis from free rupture of the bowel wall, not the gradual, scarring-related narrowing that produces obstructive symptoms over time.
incorrectas.D: Fistula formation would create an abnormal connection between the GI tract and another structure (e.g., gastrocolic fistula), which is a different complication from simple luminal narrowing due to scar tissue at the pylorus/duodenum.

preguntas.q: Perforation of a duodenal ulcer is classically associated with which location on the duodenal wall?

o.D: Lateral wall near the gallbladder fossa

e.correcta: Anterior duodenal ulcers face the peritoneal cavity rather than a retroperitoneal structure, so when they erode through the full wall thickness, they perforate freely into the peritoneum rather than eroding into a vessel. This produces sudden severe abdominal pain, peritonitis, and free air on imaging.

incorrectas.B: Posterior wall ulcers lie against the retroperitoneal gastroduodenal artery and pancreas, so deep erosion there tends to cause hemorrhage (from the artery) or penetration into the pancreas rather than free intraperitoneal perforation.
incorrectas.C: The medial wall near the ampulla is not the classic site referenced in the anterior/posterior teaching distinction for duodenal ulcer complications, and ulcers there are not specifically linked to perforation risk in this framework.
incorrectas.D: The lateral wall near the gallbladder fossa is not the anatomically relevant surface in this classic teaching point; the key distinction is anterior (perforation) versus posterior (bleeding/penetration).

preguntas.q: An anterior duodenal ulcer erodes through the full thickness of the bowel wall. Chest and abdominal imaging reveal free air beneath the diaphragm. Which complication does this represent?

e.correcta: Free intraperitoneal air (pneumoperitoneum) on an upright chest or abdominal film is the classic radiographic sign of a perforated hollow viscus; an anterior duodenal ulcer that erodes through the full wall thickness releases air and luminal contents into the peritoneal cavity, producing this finding along with acute peritonitis. This is a surgical emergency requiring prompt repair.

incorrectas.B: Hemorrhage produces hematemesis or melena and drops in hemoglobin, not free intraperitoneal air; it results from erosion into a blood vessel rather than a full-thickness break with air escaping into the peritoneal cavity.
incorrectas.C: Obstruction causes a dilated, air- and fluid-filled stomach proximal to a narrowed outlet, not free air outside the bowel lumen; it reflects a mechanical blockage rather than a breach of the wall.
incorrectas.D: Penetration means the ulcer has eroded into an adjacent solid organ (commonly the pancreas) without spilling contents freely into the peritoneal cavity, so it does not produce the pneumoperitoneum seen with true perforation.

preguntas.q: A patient with a perforated anterior duodenal ulcer reports pain radiating to which site, due to irritation of the diaphragm and referred pain via the phrenic nerve?

e.correcta: The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) innervates the diaphragm and shares spinal cord segments with the cutaneous sensory supply to the shoulder region, so irritation of the diaphragm by free air or spilled gastric/duodenal contents after perforation is perceived as referred shoulder pain (analogous to Kehr sign with splenic irritation). Recognizing this pattern helps identify diaphragmatic irritation from an intra-abdominal source rather than a primary shoulder problem.

incorrectas.B: Lower back pain is a classic referred pain pattern for posterior-penetrating ulcers eroding into the pancreas (a retroperitoneal structure), not for diaphragmatic irritation from perforation, which follows the phrenic nerve distribution instead.
incorrectas.C: Groin pain is not part of the phrenic referred pain pattern; it is more typical of processes involving the genitofemoral or ilioinguinal nerves, such as renal colic or inguinal pathology, unrelated to diaphragmatic irritation.
incorrectas.D: Flank pain classically suggests retroperitoneal or renal pathology, not diaphragmatic irritation; the phrenic nerve's shared cervical segments with the shoulder are what produce the referred pain in perforation, not a flank distribution.

preguntas.q: What is the most common histologic classification of gastric carcinoma, accounting for the large majority of cases?

e.correcta: Gastric adenocarcinoma, arising from the glandular epithelium of the stomach, is by far the most common gastric malignancy and is further subdivided into intestinal and diffuse types with distinct morphology, risk factors, and behavior. The other stomach malignancies exist but occur far less frequently.

incorrectas.B: Gastric MALT lymphoma is a recognized malignancy strongly associated with chronic H. pylori infection and can regress with antibiotic eradication, but it arises from mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue rather than epithelium and is much less common than adenocarcinoma.
incorrectas.C: GI stromal tumors (GISTs) arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal, typically driven by KIT mutations, and behave as mesenchymal tumors rather than epithelial cancers; they are an important but comparatively rare gastric neoplasm.
incorrectas.D: Carcinoid (well-differentiated neuroendocrine) tumors of the stomach arise from enterochromaffin-like cells, often in the setting of chronic atrophic gastritis or Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, but they represent a small minority of gastric tumors compared to adenocarcinoma.

preguntas.q: Of the two major histologic subtypes of gastric adenocarcinoma, which one — characterized by gland-forming tumor cells resembling intestinal epithelium — is more common overall?

e.correcta: Intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma forms cohesive, gland-like structures similar to colonic adenocarcinoma and typically develops through a stepwise sequence of chronic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia, and carcinoma, often linked to H. pylori infection and dietary factors. It is the more common of the two subtypes and tends to occur in older patients as a discrete ulcerating mass, usually on the lesser curvature.
