incorrectas.B: Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma consists of discohesive signet ring cells that infiltrate the gastric wall individually rather than forming glands, producing linitis plastica; it is less common than the intestinal type and is not linked to the same metaplasia-dysplasia sequence.
incorrectas.C: Signet ring cells are the characteristic cell of the diffuse type, not a separate subtype in the intestinal/diffuse (Lauren) classification, and diffuse-type tumors overall are less common than intestinal-type.
incorrectas.D: While tumors with overlapping intestinal and diffuse features exist, the Lauren classification's two dominant subtypes are intestinal and diffuse, and it is the intestinal type — not a mixed category — that predominates numerically.

preguntas.q: Intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma most commonly arises at which site within the stomach?

o.D: Diffusely throughout the entire stomach wall

e.correcta: Intestinal-type adenocarcinoma typically develops as a localized, ulcerating mass with heaped-up margins on the lesser curvature of the gastric antrum, the region most affected by chronic H. pylori-related gastritis and subsequent intestinal metaplasia. Its discrete, mass-forming growth pattern there contrasts with the diffusely infiltrating pattern of diffuse-type cancer.

incorrectas.B: The greater curvature and fundus are less typically the site of the classic intestinal-type lesion; chronic gastritis and metaplasia driving intestinal-type cancer preferentially affect the antrum and lesser curvature.
incorrectas.C: Gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma is a distinct clinical entity often linked to Barrett esophagus and reflux disease rather than the antral intestinal-type cancer arising from H. pylori-driven gastritis.
incorrectas.D: Diffuse involvement of the entire stomach wall with a thickened, non-distensible 'leather bottle' appearance (linitis plastica) is the hallmark of diffuse-type carcinoma, not the localized lesser-curvature mass typical of intestinal-type.

preguntas.q: Chronic Helicobacter pylori infection, via induction of chronic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia, predisposes most strongly to which histologic subtype of gastric adenocarcinoma?

e.correcta: H. pylori-induced chronic gastritis drives the antral mucosa through a metaplasia-dysplasia-carcinoma sequence, and this pathway is specifically the mechanism behind intestinal-type adenocarcinoma, which forms recognizable glandular structures similar to intestinal mucosa. This is why intestinal-type cancer's incidence tracks closely with H. pylori prevalence and declines with eradication programs.

incorrectas.B: Diffuse-type adenocarcinoma, with its discohesive signet ring cells, is thought to arise more from genetic factors (such as CDH1/E-cadherin mutations) than from the H. pylori-driven metaplasia pathway that produces intestinal-type cancer, so it is not the subtype classically linked to chronic H. pylori infection.
incorrectas.C: Signet ring cells are the defining cell type of diffuse-type carcinoma, which is not the subtype tied to H. pylori-associated chronic gastritis and metaplasia; that association belongs to the intestinal type.
incorrectas.D: The two subtypes have distinct pathogeneses — intestinal type is environmentally driven (H. pylori, metaplasia) while diffuse type is more associated with germline E-cadherin loss — so H. pylori is not equally implicated in both.

preguntas.q: A patient with longstanding chronic gastritis and gastric intestinal metaplasia is at increased risk of developing which histologic subtype of gastric adenocarcinoma?

e.correcta: Intestinal metaplasia — replacement of gastric epithelium with intestinal-type glandular epithelium in response to chronic gastritis — is a direct precursor lesion in the stepwise pathway to intestinal-type adenocarcinoma, which is named for its histologic resemblance to intestinal glands. This progression (chronic gastritis to metaplasia to dysplasia to carcinoma) is a key concept linking chronic inflammation to cancer risk.

incorrectas.B: Diffuse-type carcinoma does not arise through the intestinal metaplasia pathway; it develops from normal gastric mucosa via loss of cell adhesion (often E-cadherin dysfunction) rather than a metaplastic precursor lesion.
incorrectas.C: Signet ring cells characterize diffuse-type tumors, which are not the subtype linked to the chronic gastritis-metaplasia-dysplasia sequence described in this scenario.
incorrectas.D: Neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors arise from enterochromaffin-like cells, sometimes in the setting of atrophic gastritis with hypergastrinemia, but this is a distinct tumor lineage from adenocarcinoma and not what is meant by the intestinal-type designation here.

preguntas.q: Gastric adenocarcinoma most often follows which clinical course before diagnosis?

o.A: It remains largely asymptomatic and is diagnosed late, after weight loss, early satiety, and anemia have developed
o.B: It causes early, localized epigastric pain that prompts diagnosis before significant tumor growth
o.C: It presents acutely with sudden hematemesis as the first symptom
o.D: It is typically detected incidentally on screening endoscopy in asymptomatic patients

e.correcta: Gastric adenocarcinoma tends to grow silently for an extended period because the stomach can accommodate a slowly enlarging mass without producing specific early symptoms, so most patients present late with nonspecific findings such as unintentional weight loss, early satiety, vague abdominal pain, and iron-deficiency anemia from chronic occult blood loss. This late presentation is a major reason gastric cancer often carries a poor prognosis at diagnosis in Western countries, where routine screening endoscopy is not standard practice.

incorrectas.B: Early, well-localized epigastric pain that reliably prompts early diagnosis is not typical; symptoms are usually vague and nonspecific, mimicking benign dyspepsia, which contributes to diagnostic delay rather than early detection.
incorrectas.C: While bleeding can occur, acute hematemesis as the initial presenting symptom is uncommon; more often, blood loss is chronic and occult, manifesting as iron-deficiency anemia rather than an acute bleeding episode.
incorrectas.D: Routine screening endoscopy for gastric cancer is standard practice in high-incidence countries like Japan, allowing earlier detection there, but it is not the typical route to diagnosis in most Western settings, where the disease usually presents late as described.

preguntas.q: Distant metastasis of gastric adenocarcinoma most commonly involves which organ?

e.correcta: Gastric adenocarcinoma commonly spreads hematogenously via the portal venous drainage of the stomach, which empties directly into the liver, making the liver the most frequent site of distant metastasis. Hepatic metastases can present with hepatomegaly, abnormal liver function tests, or be found incidentally on staging imaging.

incorrectas.B: Lung metastases can occur in advanced gastric cancer through systemic hematogenous spread after tumor cells reach the pulmonary circulation, but this is a less common site than the liver, which is reached more directly via portal venous drainage.
incorrectas.C: Bone metastases are a recognized but less common site of spread for gastric cancer compared with the liver, and are not the classic teaching answer for the most frequent metastatic destination.
incorrectas.D: Brain metastases from gastric adenocarcinoma are relatively uncommon compared with other primary tumors known for CNS spread (like lung or breast cancer), and are far less frequent than hepatic metastases in gastric cancer.

preguntas.q: A Krukenberg tumor — a metastatic ovarian mass composed of mucin-secreting signet ring cells — most commonly originates from which subtype of gastric adenocarcinoma?

e.correcta: Krukenberg tumors are metastatic ovarian tumors characteristically composed of mucin-filled signet ring cells, which are the defining cell morphology of diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma. The discohesive nature of diffuse-type cells allows them to seed transperitoneally or via lymphatic/hematogenous routes to the ovaries, producing this classic metastatic pattern.

incorrectas.B: Intestinal-type adenocarcinoma forms cohesive gland-like structures rather than discohesive signet ring cells, and is instead more classically linked to distant spread patterns like the Sister Mary Joseph nodule rather than to Krukenberg tumors.
incorrectas.C: Papillary architecture is not the defining feature of the tumor type associated with Krukenberg metastasis; the essential link is the signet ring cell morphology of diffuse-type carcinoma.
incorrectas.D: Tubular growth patterns are more characteristic of gland-forming, intestinal-type adenocarcinoma, not of the discohesive signet ring cells that characterize diffuse-type tumors and their ovarian metastases.

preguntas.q: Ménétrier disease produces markedly thickened gastric rugae due to which change in the surface mucous cells of the gastric mucosa, occurring alongside atrophy of the parietal and chief cells?

e.correcta: In Ménétrier disease, excessive TGF-alpha signaling drives hyperplasia of the surface mucous (foveolar) cells lining the stomach, producing grossly enlarged, thickened rugae, while the acid- and enzyme-secreting parietal and chief cells atrophy. The combination of foveolar hyperplasia with glandular atrophy explains both the characteristic endoscopic appearance and the resulting hypochlorhydria.

incorrectas.B: Dysplasia refers to cytologic and architectural atypia representing a precancerous change, not the benign proliferative overgrowth of normal-appearing mucous cells that defines Ménétrier disease's rugal hypertrophy.
incorrectas.C: Intestinal metaplasia is the replacement of gastric epithelium with intestinal-type glands seen in chronic H. pylori gastritis and a precursor to intestinal-type cancer, which is a different process from the foveolar cell hyperplasia driving Ménétrier disease.
incorrectas.D: Squamous metaplasia is not a recognized feature of Ménétrier disease; the gastric mucosa remains glandular but with excessive hyperplastic mucous cell proliferation rather than a squamous change.

preguntas.q: Which gastric disorder is characterized by massively hypertrophied rugae that give the mucosa an appearance resembling brain gyri on endoscopy?

e.correcta: Ménétrier disease causes such pronounced foveolar cell hyperplasia that the gastric rugae become massively enlarged and convoluted, producing an endoscopic appearance often described as resembling brain gyri or cerebriform folds. This distinctive gross appearance, combined with protein-losing hypertrophic gastropathy, is a classic identifying feature of the disease.

incorrectas.B: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome involves a gastrin-secreting tumor that causes marked acid hypersecretion and can thicken gastric folds due to parietal cell hyperplasia, but the classic 'brain gyri' cerebriform rugal appearance is specifically associated with Ménétrier disease, not ZES.
incorrectas.C: Chronic atrophic gastritis typically causes thinning and flattening of the gastric mucosa with loss of rugal folds as glands atrophy, the opposite of the massive rugal hypertrophy seen in Ménétrier disease.
incorrectas.D: Gastric lymphoma can cause localized mucosal thickening or mass lesions, but it does not classically produce the diffuse cerebriform rugal hypertrophy that defines Ménétrier disease.

preguntas.q: Ménétrier disease leads to excessive gastric mucus production with associated loss of which serum component, resulting in edema and giving the condition its designation as a hypoproteinemic gastropathy?

e.correcta: The hyperplastic, mucus-hypersecreting gastric epithelium in Ménétrier disease leaks large amounts of protein into the gastric lumen, producing a protein-losing enteropathy that lowers serum albumin and other proteins. The resulting hypoalbuminemia drops plasma oncotic pressure and causes peripheral and facial edema, which is why the condition is also called hypoproteinemic hypertrophic gastropathy.

incorrectas.B: Potassium loss is not the mechanism behind the edema seen in Ménétrier disease; the defining process is loss of protein (particularly albumin) into the gut lumen, lowering oncotic pressure rather than causing an electrolyte-driven problem.
incorrectas.C: Bicarbonate is not the substance lost in this condition; the pathologic mucus and protein leakage from hyperplastic foveolar cells is what drives hypoalbuminemia and edema, not a bicarbonate deficit.
incorrectas.D: Intrinsic factor is produced by parietal cells and its loss (as these cells atrophy) can contribute to vitamin B12 malabsorption, but it is protein loss — not intrinsic factor loss — that explains the hypoproteinemia and edema characteristic of Ménétrier disease.

preguntas.q: Ménétrier disease is characterized by atrophy of which gastric cell type, resulting in decreased gastric acid secretion?

e.correcta: Parietal cells, which secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, undergo atrophy in Ménétrier disease as the hyperplastic foveolar (surface mucous) cell compartment expands at their expense, resulting in hypochlorhydria or achlorhydria. This acid-reducing atrophic change occurs alongside the massive rugal hypertrophy that defines the disease's characteristic endoscopic appearance.

incorrectas.B: Chief cells, which secrete pepsinogen, also atrophy in Ménétrier disease, but they are not the acid-producing cell type; the question specifically concerns the cell responsible for decreased gastric acid secretion, which is the parietal cell.
incorrectas.C: G cells secrete gastrin to stimulate acid secretion and are located in the antrum; they are not the atrophying cell type responsible for reduced acid production in Ménétrier disease, and gastrin levels are not the primary abnormality described.
incorrectas.D: Mucous neck cells are precursor cells in the gastric gland neck region, not the acid-secreting cells; the loss of gastric acid output in Ménétrier disease is specifically attributed to parietal cell atrophy.

preguntas.q: Is Ménétrier disease considered a premalignant condition with respect to gastric cancer risk?

o.A: Yes — it is a precancerous lesion associated with increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma
o.B: No — there is no established association between Ménétrier disease and gastric cancer
o.C: Only in pediatric-onset cases, which are typically self-limited
o.D: Yes, but only for gastric lymphoma, not adenocarcinoma

e.correcta: Ménétrier disease is regarded as a premalignant condition, with the chronic hyperplastic and dysregulated epithelial proliferation in the gastric mucosa carrying an increased long-term risk of progression to gastric adenocarcinoma. This risk is one reason patients with Ménétrier disease require ongoing surveillance rather than being managed as having a purely benign, static condition.

incorrectas.B: There is in fact a recognized, clinically important association between Ménétrier disease and gastric cancer risk, which is why surveillance is recommended; denying any association would miss a key clinical implication of the diagnosis.
incorrectas.C: Pediatric-onset Ménétrier disease is often distinct in that it is frequently transient and self-limited (sometimes linked to cytomegalovirus infection), but the malignant potential concern classically applies to the adult form of the disease, not exclusively to self-limited pediatric cases.
incorrectas.D: The increased malignancy risk in Ménétrier disease is specifically for gastric adenocarcinoma arising from the hyperplastic epithelium, not gastric lymphoma, which has its own distinct association with chronic H. pylori-driven MALT tissue.

preguntas.q: A newborn presents with abdominal distention and vomiting shortly after birth. The vomitus is bilious. Which diagnosis is most consistent with this finding, and how does it differ from pyloric stenosis in this respect?

o.A: Intestinal atresia (e.g., duodenal, jejunal, or ileal), which classically causes bilious vomiting because the obstruction is distal to the ampulla of Vater
o.B: Pyloric stenosis, which also classically causes bilious vomiting
o.C: Intestinal atresia, but vomiting is classically nonbilious because the obstruction is proximal to the ampulla of Vater
o.D: Malrotation without volvulus, which never causes bilious vomiting

e.correcta: Intestinal atresia (duodenal, jejunal, or ileal) typically causes an obstruction distal to the ampulla of Vater, so bile mixes with the gastric and proximal intestinal contents before the blockage, producing bilious vomiting — a key clinical clue that helps localize the level of obstruction and distinguishes it from more proximal processes. This bilious quality, combined with abdominal distention, should prompt urgent evaluation for a surgical cause of neonatal obstruction.

incorrectas.B: Pyloric stenosis causes obstruction proximal to the ampulla of Vater (at the level of the pylorus, before bile enters the GI tract), so its hallmark is nonbilious, projectile vomiting — the opposite of the bilious vomiting used to distinguish it from intestinal atresia.
incorrectas.C: This reverses the actual anatomy: because atresia sites (duodenal beyond the ampulla, jejunal, ileal) are distal to where bile enters the gut, the vomiting is bilious, not nonbilious; nonbilious vomiting is the pattern seen with pyloric stenosis instead.
incorrectas.D: Malrotation with volvulus is itself a surgical emergency that classically presents with bilious vomiting due to obstruction distal to the ampulla, so it is inaccurate to say it never causes bilious vomiting.

preguntas.q: Intestinal atresia (e.g., duodenal, jejunal, or ileal) typically becomes clinically apparent within what time frame after birth?

o.C: 2-3 weeks after birth, similar to pyloric stenosis

e.correcta: Because intestinal atresia is a complete or near-complete congenital luminal obstruction, affected neonates typically develop symptoms — bilious vomiting and abdominal distention — very early, generally within the first one to two days of life, prompting rapid clinical recognition and surgical evaluation. This early presentation contrasts with conditions that develop gradually over weeks.

incorrectas.B: While atresia is a congenital anomaly present from fetal development (and can cause antenatal findings like polyhydramnios), overt clinical symptoms such as vomiting and distention manifest after birth, not as an in-utero presentation in the newborn nursery sense.
incorrectas.C: A presentation delayed to 2-3 weeks of age with progressive nonbilious projectile vomiting is the classic timeline for pyloric stenosis, which develops as the pyloric muscle hypertrophies over time — quite different from the near-immediate postnatal presentation of atresia.
incorrectas.D: A delay of several months would be atypical for a complete congenital luminal obstruction like atresia, which nearly always presents in the immediate newborn period due to the inability to pass intestinal contents.

preguntas.q: Duodenal atresia results from a congenital failure of which embryologic process during development of the duodenum?

o.A: Recanalization (failure of the solid duodenal epithelial cord to canalize into a hollow lumen)
o.B: Rotation of the midgut around the superior mesenteric artery
o.C: Fusion of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds
o.D: Closure of the physiologic umbilical herniation

e.correcta: During normal development, the duodenal epithelium proliferates and transiently obliterates the lumen before it recanalizes to form a patent tube; duodenal atresia results when this recanalization fails to occur, leaving a blind, obstructed segment. This distinguishes it mechanistically from malrotation, which involves an error in intestinal positioning rather than a failure of the lumen itself to form.

incorrectas.B: Abnormal rotation of the midgut around the superior mesenteric artery describes malrotation, a different congenital anomaly that predisposes to volvulus, not the failure of luminal recanalization that specifically causes duodenal atresia.
incorrectas.C: Abnormal fusion of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds can produce anomalies like annular pancreas, which may itself cause extrinsic duodenal obstruction, but this is a distinct embryologic error from the failure of duodenal recanalization that defines atresia.
incorrectas.D: Failure of the physiologic umbilical herniation to return to the abdominal cavity produces omphalocele-related anomalies, an unrelated embryologic process from the intraluminal recanalization defect responsible for duodenal atresia.

preguntas.q: Duodenal atresia in a fetus is classically associated with which finding on prenatal ultrasound, reflecting impaired fetal swallowing of amniotic fluid?

e.correcta: Amniotic fluid volume is regulated in part by fetal swallowing and intestinal absorption; when duodenal atresia obstructs the proximal bowel, the fetus cannot adequately swallow and process amniotic fluid, causing it to accumulate and produce polyhydramnios. This finding, often combined with the classic 'double bubble' sign on ultrasound (distended stomach and proximal duodenum), raises prenatal suspicion for duodenal atresia and its association with Down syndrome.

incorrectas.B: Oligohydramnios is the pattern seen with impaired fetal urine production or output (e.g., renal agenesis or severe urinary tract obstruction), which is the opposite mechanism from the impaired swallowing/absorption that produces the fluid excess seen in duodenal atresia.
incorrectas.C: Normal amniotic fluid volume would not be expected, because the obstructed, non-functional bowel disrupts the normal fetal swallowing/absorption pathway that helps regulate amniotic fluid turnover, leading instead to fluid accumulation.
incorrectas.D: Amniotic band syndrome refers to fibrous bands from a ruptured amnion entangling and constricting fetal parts, an entirely separate process from bowel obstruction and unrelated to the amniotic fluid volume abnormality seen with duodenal atresia.

preguntas.q: Jejunal and ileal atresia most often result from a vascular accident in utero. Disruption of which vessels is responsible for the resulting ischemic necrosis and segmental bowel resorption?

e.correcta: Jejunal and ileal atresia are thought to arise from an intrauterine vascular accident in which the mesenteric vessels supplying a segment of midgut are compromised (e.g., due to volvulus, gastroschisis, or intussusception around a mesenteric defect), producing focal ischemia. The necrotic segment is resorbed, leaving a blind proximal bowel end and a distal segment that classically coils around its ileocolic vessel, unlike duodenal atresia, which results from failed recanalization of the gut lumen rather than a vascular insult.

incorrectas.A: The umbilical vessels carry blood between the fetus and placenta and are not the arcades that directly perfuse the jejunum and ileum; their compromise causes different problems (e.g., single umbilical artery associations) rather than the focal ischemic bowel necrosis seen in jejunoileal atresia.
incorrectas.C: Portal vein branches drain nutrient-rich blood from the gut to the liver rather than supplying arterial flow to the bowel wall, so their disruption would not produce the arterial ischemia and segmental necrosis characteristic of jejunoileal atresia.
incorrectas.D: The vitelline duct connects the midgut to the yolk sac and its persistence causes anomalies like Meckel diverticulum or vitelline fistula, but it is not the arterial supply whose disruption causes jejunoileal atresia; that mechanism is a separate embryologic story.

preguntas.q: The most severe form of jejunal atresia, resulting from a mesenteric vascular accident that compromises the superior mesenteric artery distribution, produces which classic appearance of the distal small bowel?

e.correcta: In the 'apple peel' (or Christmas tree) variant of jejunal atresia, occlusion of the distal superior mesenteric artery leads to loss of a long segment of midgut; the remaining distal ileum receives collateral blood supply only from the ileocolic artery and coils around it in a spiral fashion resembling a peeled apple. This is the most severe form of intestinal atresia and is often associated with a shortened, malrotated bowel and significant risk of short bowel syndrome after resection.

incorrectas.B: The double bubble sign refers to a distended stomach and proximal duodenum on imaging, classically seen in duodenal atresia (often associated with Down syndrome), not the vascular disruption pattern seen in jejunoileal atresia.
incorrectas.C: The bird's beak sign is a radiographic finding of sigmoid or cecal volvulus, where the twisted, tapering bowel loop resembles a bird's beak on contrast imaging — an entirely different pathology from the vascular jejunal atresia described here.
incorrectas.D: The string of pearls sign describes small pockets of gas trapped between valvulae conniventes in a dilated, fluid-filled small bowel loop on imaging, seen in mechanical small bowel obstruction, not the gross morphologic appearance of atretic bowel from a vascular accident.

preguntas.q: Meckel diverticulum is classified as a true diverticulum. This classification is based on the outpouching containing which layers of the bowel wall?

o.C: All three layers: mucosa, submucosa, and muscularis propria

e.correcta: A true diverticulum, by definition, involves herniation of the full thickness of the bowel wall — mucosa, submucosa, and muscularis propria — because it originates from a persistent embryologic structure (the vitelline duct) rather than from mucosa pushing through weak points in the muscular wall. This full-thickness composition is why Meckel diverticulum can contain ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue capable of causing peptic ulceration and bleeding, unlike acquired false diverticula.

incorrectas.A: An outpouching of mucosa alone would not constitute any recognized diverticulum type; false diverticula (pseudodiverticula) still carry mucosa and submucosa together, just without the muscular layer, which already distinguishes them from a mucosa-only herniation.
incorrectas.B: Mucosa and submucosa without muscularis propria describes a false diverticulum (pseudodiverticulum), such as those seen in colonic diverticulosis or Zenker diverticulum, which form by herniation through weak points in the muscular wall — the opposite of Meckel diverticulum's full-thickness, true composition.
incorrectas.D: Serosa alone cannot herniate as a diverticulum without the underlying layers; diverticula are defined by mucosal (and in true diverticula, muscular) outpouching, not by serosal changes.

preguntas.q: A Meckel diverticulum is discovered incidentally during laparotomy. Based on its embryologic origin from the vitelline duct, how should this diverticulum be classified?

o.A: False diverticulum, because it lacks a muscular layer
o.B: True diverticulum, because it contains all layers of the bowel wall
o.C: Pseudodiverticulum, because it forms from mucosal herniation through a weak point
o.D: Pulsion diverticulum, because it forms from increased intraluminal pressure

e.correcta: Because Meckel diverticulum develops from incomplete obliteration of the vitelline duct rather than from acquired herniation through a weak spot in the bowel wall, it retains all three layers of the intestinal wall — mucosa, submucosa, and muscularis propria — making it a true diverticulum. This distinguishes it from the much more common acquired false diverticula of the colon, which are pulsion-type outpouchings of mucosa and submucosa only.

incorrectas.A: Meckel diverticulum does have a muscular layer, since it is a true diverticulum formed from a congenital, full-thickness embryologic remnant rather than an acquired mucosal herniation, so this description is the opposite of its actual anatomy.
incorrectas.C: Pseudodiverticula (false diverticula) arise from mucosa and submucosa herniating through points of weakness in the muscularis, typically at sites where vasa recta penetrate the colon wall — a mechanism unrelated to the vitelline duct remnant that produces Meckel diverticulum.
incorrectas.D: Pulsion diverticula, like most colonic diverticula, form when elevated intraluminal pressure pushes mucosa through a weakened muscular wall; Meckel diverticulum instead results from a developmental failure of duct obliteration, not from a pressure-driven herniation process.

preguntas.q: Meckel diverticulum arises embryologically from incomplete obliteration of which structure?

e.correcta: The vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct normally connects the midgut to the yolk sac during early development and obliterates by around the seventh week of gestation. When a portion of this duct near the ileal end fails to regress, it persists as a true diverticulum arising from the antimesenteric border of the ileum — the Meckel diverticulum — which can carry ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue from its origin along the primitive gut tube.

incorrectas.B: The urachus connects the fetal bladder to the allantois; its failure to obliterate produces urinary anomalies such as a urachal fistula, cyst, or sinus with urine leakage from the umbilicus — a genitourinary problem, not a bowel outpouching like Meckel diverticulum.
incorrectas.C: The allantois is an extraembryonic membrane involved in early waste exchange and forms part of the urachus; its persistence is linked to urachal anomalies, not to true diverticula of the ileum.
incorrectas.D: The cloacal membrane separates the hindgut from the future perineum, and its abnormal breakdown or persistence causes anorectal malformations, not Meckel diverticulum, which is a vitelline duct remnant located in the small bowel.

preguntas.q: What is the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract, affecting approximately 2% of the population?

e.correcta: Meckel diverticulum, a remnant of the vitelline duct, is the most common congenital GI anomaly, present in roughly 2% of the population. Most cases are asymptomatic and found incidentally, but its ectopic gastric or pancreatic mucosa can cause painless lower GI bleeding, and it can serve as a lead point for intussusception or volvulus in symptomatic patients.

incorrectas.A: Hirschsprung disease is a congenital absence of ganglion cells in the distal colon causing functional obstruction, but it is far less common than Meckel diverticulum and represents a neural crest migration defect rather than a vitelline duct remnant.
incorrectas.B: Duodenal atresia, often associated with Down syndrome, results from failed recanalization of the duodenal lumen and is a well-known but much rarer congenital anomaly than Meckel diverticulum.
incorrectas.C: Intestinal malrotation results from abnormal rotation of the midgut around the superior mesenteric artery during development; it predisposes to volvulus but occurs far less frequently than the 2% prevalence of Meckel diverticulum.

preguntas.q: The classic features of Meckel diverticulum (prevalence, distance from the ileocecal valve, length, and typical age of symptomatic presentation) are traditionally remembered using a mnemonic built around which number?

e.correcta: Meckel diverticulum is remembered by the 'rule of 2s': it occurs in about 2% of the population, is typically located about 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, is roughly 2 inches long, is about 2 times more common in males, and most often becomes symptomatic within the first 2 years of life. This mnemonic bundles several otherwise disconnected facts into one easily recalled framework for board exams.

incorrectas.B: There is no established 'rule of 3s' mnemonic for Meckel diverticulum; using 3 for any of its features (prevalence, length, distance) would misstate the actual figures, which all cluster around the number 2.
incorrectas.C: A 'rule of 5s' is not the mnemonic associated with Meckel diverticulum; substituting 5 for the true values (2% prevalence, 2 feet, 2 inches) would give inaccurate figures for its clinical features.
incorrectas.D: No 'rule of 7s' exists for Meckel diverticulum; while the vitelline duct does normally obliterate around week 7 of gestation, that developmental timing is a separate fact from the 'rule of 2s' used to summarize the diverticulum's clinical characteristics.

preguntas.q: Regarding the sex distribution of Meckel diverticulum, which statement is correct?

o.A: It occurs with equal frequency in males and females
o.C: It is approximately twice as common in males as in females
o.D: It is approximately twice as common in females as in males

e.correcta: Meckel diverticulum shows a male predominance, occurring roughly twice as often in males as in females — one of the features bundled into the 'rule of 2s.' While the diverticulum itself forms at similar rates embryologically, males appear to be at higher risk of becoming symptomatic (e.g., bleeding, obstruction), which is why the male-to-female ratio is emphasized clinically.

incorrectas.A: An equal sex distribution would contradict the well-documented male predominance of Meckel diverticulum and would not fit the 'rule of 2s' framework, which specifically calls out the roughly 2:1 male-to-female ratio.
incorrectas.B: Meckel diverticulum is not exclusive to males — it can occur and become symptomatic in females as well — it is simply more common and more often symptomatic in males, not restricted to one sex.
incorrectas.D: The sex predominance runs in the opposite direction from this option: Meckel diverticulum is more common in males, not females, so reversing the ratio misstates the established epidemiology.

preguntas.q: Meckel diverticulum is typically what length?

e.correcta: Meckel diverticulum is classically about 2 inches long, another component of the 'rule of 2s' used to recall its features. This size, combined with its full-thickness wall and potential ectopic mucosa, is relevant when it becomes a lead point for intussusception or undergoes torsion/volvulus.

incorrectas.A: 1 inch underestimates the typical size; the classically cited length for Meckel diverticulum in the 'rule of 2s' is twice that, at approximately 2 inches.
incorrectas.C: 6 inches substantially overstates the usual size of a Meckel diverticulum; a diverticulum that large would be atypical and does not match the standard teaching figure of about 2 inches.
incorrectas.D: 12 inches is far larger than any typical Meckel diverticulum; this length would be inconsistent with the compact, finger-like outpouching described in the classic 'rule of 2s.'

preguntas.q: Meckel diverticulum is typically located in the small bowel at what distance from the ileocecal valve?

e.correcta: Meckel diverticulum is classically found about 2 feet proximal to the ileocecal valve, arising from the antimesenteric border of the ileum — again fitting the 'rule of 2s.' Knowing this location helps explain why it is found near the terminal ileum during surgery for suspected appendicitis, since the two conditions can mimic each other clinically.

incorrectas.A: 6 inches is much closer to the ileocecal valve than the classically taught distance; the standard teaching figure for Meckel diverticulum's location is about four times that distance, at roughly 2 feet.
incorrectas.B: 1 foot is half the classically cited distance; the well-established teaching point places Meckel diverticulum about 2 feet, not 1 foot, from the ileocecal valve.
incorrectas.C: 5 feet is farther from the ileocecal valve than Meckel diverticulum is typically located; this distance would place it well up into the jejunum rather than the distal ileum where it classically arises.

preguntas.q: When Meckel diverticulum becomes symptomatic, it most commonly does so during which period of life?

e.correcta: Symptomatic Meckel diverticulum most commonly presents within the first 2 years of life, consistent with the 'rule of 2s.' Painless lower GI bleeding from ectopic gastric mucosa-induced ulceration is the classic presentation in this age group, though it can also present later with intussusception, volvulus, or diverticulitis mimicking appendicitis.

incorrectas.B: While Meckel diverticulum can occasionally present later in childhood or adolescence, this is not the classically taught peak; the 'rule of 2s' specifically emphasizes presentation within the first 2 years of life.
incorrectas.C: Young adulthood is not the typical age of symptomatic presentation for Meckel diverticulum; most clinically significant cases declare themselves much earlier, in infancy or early childhood.
incorrectas.D: Presentation after age 60 would be atypical for Meckel diverticulum, which is a congenital lesion that most often causes symptoms early in life rather than remaining silent for six decades before manifesting.

preguntas.q: What is the typical clinical course of Meckel diverticulum in the general population?

o.A: It usually causes chronic watery diarrhea
o.B: It is usually asymptomatic and found incidentally
o.D: It usually causes recurrent biliary colic

e.correcta: The overwhelming majority of Meckel diverticula are asymptomatic and are discovered incidentally during imaging or surgery for unrelated reasons. When symptoms do occur, they result from complications such as ectopic gastric mucosa causing peptic ulceration and painless bleeding, or the diverticulum acting as a lead point for volvulus, intussusception, or obstruction, sometimes producing a palpable lump in the umbilical area.

incorrectas.A: Chronic watery diarrhea is not a typical presentation of Meckel diverticulum; it is more characteristic of malabsorptive or secretory processes elsewhere in the gut, whereas Meckel diverticulum, when symptomatic, more classically causes painless bleeding or mechanical complications like obstruction.
incorrectas.C: Progressive dysphagia relates to esophageal pathology (e.g., strictures, motility disorders, malignancy), not to an ileal diverticulum located far from the esophagus; this is not a recognized presentation of Meckel diverticulum.
incorrectas.D: Recurrent biliary colic reflects gallbladder or biliary tract pathology from gallstones, not an ileal remnant of the vitelline duct; Meckel diverticulum has no direct connection to the biliary system.

preguntas.q: The vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct normally undergoes obliteration by which week of gestation?

e.correcta: The vitelline duct, which connects the developing midgut to the yolk sac, normally obliterates by around week 7 of gestation as the midgut returns to the abdominal cavity and no longer requires this connection. Failure of complete obliteration by this point can leave behind a spectrum of anomalies, from a fully patent fistula to a partially patent Meckel diverticulum or an isolated vitelline cyst, depending on which portion of the duct persists.

incorrectas.A: Week 4 is too early; at this stage the midgut is still herniating through the vitelline duct connection to the yolk sac as part of normal physiologic herniation, well before the duct is expected to close.
incorrectas.B: Week 12 is later than the normal timing of vitelline duct obliteration; by this point the duct should already have regressed, as physiologic midgut herniation itself typically resolves by around week 10-11.
incorrectas.D: Week 20 is far past the expected window for vitelline duct closure; using this timepoint would suggest a much longer persistence of the embryonic connection than is developmentally normal.

preguntas.q: A newborn is noted to pass meconium from the umbilicus shortly after birth, reflecting complete failure of the vitelline duct to obliterate. What congenital anomaly does this represent?

e.correcta: When the vitelline duct fails to close along its entire length, it leaves a direct, patent connection between the ileal lumen and the umbilicus — a vitelline (omphalomesenteric) fistula. Because this tract communicates freely with the bowel, meconium and later stool can drain from the umbilicus, a finding that distinguishes it from a patent urachus, where urine (not stool) leaks from the umbilicus due to a persistent bladder-to-umbilicus connection.

incorrectas.B: Meckel diverticulum results from only partial closure of the vitelline duct, leaving a blind outpouching attached to the ileum without an open connection to the umbilicus, so it would not cause meconium to drain externally the way a full fistula does.
incorrectas.C: A vitelline cyst forms when the middle portion of the duct remains patent while both ends obliterate, creating an isolated cystic remnant with no open connection to either the bowel lumen or the umbilical surface, so it cannot produce external meconium discharge.
incorrectas.D: Omphalocele is a distinct anterior abdominal wall defect in which abdominal viscera herniate into the umbilical cord and remain covered by peritoneum and amnion; it is unrelated to vitelline duct patency and does not present with meconium draining from an otherwise intact umbilicus.

preguntas.q: Partial closure of the vitelline duct, in which the duct remains patent only near its ileal attachment while the umbilical end obliterates, results in which anomaly?

e.correcta: When only the segment of vitelline duct closest to the ileum stays patent, it produces a blind-ending outpouching attached to the antimesenteric border of the ileum — a Meckel diverticulum. A fibrous remnant (the vitelline ligament) often still connects the obliterated portion of the duct to the umbilicus, explaining why Meckel diverticulum can sometimes be associated with volvulus around this fibrous band.

incorrectas.A: A vitelline fistula results from failure of the entire duct to close, creating an open communication all the way from the ileum to the umbilicus, unlike the partial, ileal-end-only patency described here that produces a blind diverticulum instead.
incorrectas.B: A vitelline cyst arises when the central portion of the duct remains patent while both the ileal and umbilical ends close off, an entirely different pattern of partial closure from the ileal-end persistence that produces Meckel diverticulum.
incorrectas.C: Patent urachus involves failure of the urachus (a derivative of the allantois connecting the bladder to the umbilicus) to close, an entirely separate embryologic structure from the vitelline duct and unrelated to Meckel diverticulum's formation.

preguntas.q: Cystic dilation of a persistent middle segment of the vitelline duct, with both the ileal and umbilical ends obliterated, produces which anomaly?

e.correcta: If the central portion of the vitelline duct remains patent while both its ileal and umbilical ends close normally, the isolated segment can dilate into a fluid-filled sac beneath the umbilicus known as a vitelline cyst (or enterocyst). Because it has no open connection to the bowel lumen or the skin surface, it typically presents as a palpable mass rather than with drainage, and it is usually still tethered by fibrous bands that can serve as a point around which bowel can twist.

incorrectas.A: A vitelline fistula requires the entire duct to remain open from ileum to umbilicus, producing external drainage of meconium/stool, which is the opposite pattern from the isolated, closed-off cystic segment described here.
incorrectas.C: Meckel diverticulum results from persistence of the ileal end of the duct only, forming a blind outpouching attached to the bowel, not an isolated cyst arising from the mid-portion of the duct with both ends closed.
incorrectas.D: A urachal cyst is a similar concept but involves the urachus (bladder-to-umbilicus allantoic remnant), not the vitelline duct; it is a genitourinary anomaly rather than a gastrointestinal one and arises from an entirely different embryologic structure.

preguntas.q: A newborn presents with meconium discharge from the umbilicus, in contrast to another infant with urine discharge from the umbilicus due to a patent urachus. What congenital anomaly explains the meconium-discharging infant?

e.correcta: Meconium discharge from the umbilicus indicates a direct, patent communication between the bowel lumen and the umbilicus — a vitelline (omphalomesenteric) fistula, caused by complete failure of the vitelline duct to obliterate. This is contrasted with a patent urachus, which instead connects the bladder to the umbilicus and therefore leaks urine rather than stool, helping distinguish the two umbilical drainage anomalies clinically.

incorrectas.A: Meckel diverticulum is a blind-ending outpouching of the ileum without any open connection to the umbilical skin, so it cannot produce meconium discharge externally the way a fully patent fistula can.
incorrectas.B: A vitelline cyst is an isolated, closed-off remnant of the mid-portion of the duct with no communication to either the bowel lumen or the umbilicus, so it would present as a mass rather than with any drainage.
incorrectas.D: An umbilical hernia is a defect in the abdominal wall fascia allowing abdominal contents to protrude at the umbilicus; it is a structural fascial defect unrelated to vitelline duct patency and does not cause meconium drainage.

preguntas.q: Which condition is defined by twisting of a loop of bowel around its mesentery, which can compromise blood supply and lead to ischemia?

e.correcta: Volvulus occurs when a segment of bowel twists around its own mesenteric axis, which can both obstruct the lumen and, more dangerously, kink the mesenteric vessels supplying that segment, leading to ischemia and potential infarction if not promptly corrected. This mesenteric twisting mechanism is what distinguishes volvulus from simple luminal obstruction and makes it a surgical emergency.

incorrectas.B: Intussusception occurs when one segment of bowel telescopes into an adjacent segment, dragging its mesentery along with it, which is a different mechanical process from a bowel loop twisting around its own mesenteric axis as in volvulus.
incorrectas.C: An incarcerated inguinal hernia involves bowel or other abdominal contents becoming trapped within a hernia defect, potentially compressing the bowel wall and its blood supply at the hernia neck, but this is a herniation problem rather than mesenteric twisting of a bowel loop in situ.
incorrectas.D: Adhesive small bowel obstruction results from fibrous bands (adhesions), often from prior surgery, kinking or compressing the bowel externally, which is mechanically distinct from a loop of bowel rotating around its own mesenteric pedicle as occurs in volvulus.

preguntas.q: Volvulus involving the midgut, typically related to underlying malrotation, is most commonly seen in which population?

e.correcta: Midgut volvulus classically occurs in infants and young children, most often as a complication of intestinal malrotation, in which an abnormally narrow, poorly fixed mesenteric attachment predisposes the midgut to twist around the superior mesenteric artery. Because this twisting can compromise the entire SMA distribution at once, it is a surgical emergency in this age group, presenting with bilious vomiting and possible signs of ischemia.

incorrectas.A: Elderly adults are the population classically affected by sigmoid volvulus, related to an acquired, redundant, elongated sigmoid colon with a narrow mesenteric base, not by midgut volvulus, which is tied to congenital malrotation presenting early in life.
incorrectas.B: While pregnancy can occasionally be associated with volvulus due to anatomic displacement of bowel by the gravid uterus, this is not the classic epidemiologic association for midgut volvulus, which is predominantly a disease of infants and children with malrotation.
incorrectas.C: Young to middle-aged adults are the population classically associated with cecal volvulus rather than midgut volvulus, which instead occurs early in life as a consequence of congenital malrotation.

preguntas.q: Volvulus of the cecum is most commonly seen in which population?

e.correcta: Cecal volvulus classically occurs in young adults, often related to a congenitally mobile cecum with an incompletely fixed mesentery that allows it to twist. This contrasts with sigmoid volvulus, which is the more common form of colonic volvulus overall and is instead classically seen in elderly, often debilitated or chronically constipated patients with a redundant sigmoid colon.

incorrectas.A: Infants are the population associated with midgut volvulus from malrotation, not cecal volvulus, which requires a mobile, incompletely fixed cecum that is more characteristically an adult anatomic variant.
incorrectas.C: Elderly patients are classically linked to sigmoid volvulus, arising from an acquired redundant sigmoid colon, whereas cecal volvulus is instead associated with a younger population who have a congenitally mobile cecum.
incorrectas.D: Neonates would be expected to present with midgut volvulus from malrotation if volvulus occurs at all, rather than cecal volvulus, which is a condition of a mobile adult cecum rather than a neonatal anatomic anomaly.

preguntas.q: In children, what is the most common cause of intussusception?

o.A: Meckel diverticulum acting as a lead point
o.C: Lymphoid hyperplasia (e.g., from rotavirus or adenovirus infection)

e.correcta: In children, the most common cause of intussusception is lymphoid hyperplasia of Peyer patches in the terminal ileum, typically triggered by a preceding viral infection such as rotavirus or adenovirus. The hypertrophied lymphoid tissue acts as a lead point that the peristalsing bowel telescopes around, dragging the proximal segment (and its mesentery) into the distal segment and increasing the risk of ischemia if not reduced promptly.

incorrectas.A: Meckel diverticulum is an important pathologic lead point for intussusception, but it is much less common overall than lymphoid hyperplasia and is more classically implicated in older children, especially those with recurrent intussusception, rather than being the most common cause across all pediatric cases.
incorrectas.B: Intraluminal tumors are a common lead point for intussusception in adults, where malignancy must be ruled out, but tumors are a rare cause of pediatric intussusception, which is instead dominated by lymphoid hyperplasia.
incorrectas.D: Henoch-Schönlein purpura can cause a submucosal hematoma that acts as a lead point for intussusception, and this is a recognized but comparatively uncommon cause; it does not account for the majority of pediatric cases the way viral-triggered lymphoid hyperplasia does.

preguntas.q: In children older than 2 years, especially those with recurrent episodes, what is the most common pathologic lead point for intussusception?

e.correcta: While lymphoid hyperplasia from viral infection is the overall most common trigger for intussusception in young children, in children older than 2 — particularly those with recurrent intussusception — a true pathologic lead point such as Meckel diverticulum should be suspected. Its ileal location and, in some cases, ectopic tissue make it a structural point around which the bowel can telescope, and this possibility should prompt further workup rather than assuming a self-limited, infection-related cause.

incorrectas.B: Lymphoid (Peyer patch) hyperplasia is the most common overall cause of intussusception in the general pediatric population (usually under age 2) but is not the pathologic lead point specifically associated with older children or recurrent cases, where a structural lesion like Meckel diverticulum becomes more likely.
incorrectas.C: Intraluminal polyps can occasionally serve as lead points for intussusception, but they are not the classically emphasized structural cause in older children with recurrent intussusception the way Meckel diverticulum is.
incorrectas.D: An appendiceal stump is not a recognized lead point for intussusception; the appendix itself is not typically implicated in this condition, unlike a true pathologic lesion such as Meckel diverticulum.

preguntas.q: In adults, intussusception is far less common than in children and is more often due to an identifiable pathologic lesion. What is the most common lead point in this age group?

e.correcta: In adults, intussusception is uncommon and, unlike in children, is usually secondary to an identifiable structural lesion — most often an intraluminal mass or tumor (benign or malignant) that serves as the physical lead point the bowel telescopes around. Because malignancy is a real concern in this age group, adult intussusception generally warrants prompt surgical evaluation and resection rather than the non-operative reduction often used in children.

incorrectas.A: Lymphoid hyperplasia from viral infection is the dominant cause of intussusception in young children, but it is not the typical mechanism in adults, whose intestinal lymphoid tissue is not the usual driver of this condition.
incorrectas.B: Meckel diverticulum can be a lead point at any age, including adulthood, but it is not the single most common cause in adults; that distinction belongs to intraluminal masses and tumors, which are more frequently responsible overall in this population.
incorrectas.C: An appendiceal fecalith is a cause of appendiceal obstruction leading to appendicitis, not a recognized lead point for intussusception; this option confuses two distinct GI pathologies.

preguntas.q: Where in the GI tract does intussusception most commonly occur?

e.correcta: Intussusception most commonly occurs at the ileocecal junction, where the terminal ileum telescopes into the cecum, often around a lead point such as hypertrophied Peyer patches or, in older children, a Meckel diverticulum. This location is emphasized because it explains the classic presentation of colicky abdominal pain, a palpable sausage-shaped abdominal mass, and currant jelly stools.

incorrectas.A: The duodenojejunal junction (ligament of Treitz) is not a typical site for intussusception; this location is more relevant to other conditions, such as certain forms of obstruction or the anatomic landmark used to define upper versus lower GI bleeding.
incorrectas.C: The gastroesophageal junction is the site of reflux disease and hiatal hernia, structurally very different from the ileocecal region and not a recognized location for intussusception to occur.
incorrectas.D: The rectosigmoid junction is the classic site for sigmoid volvulus in elderly patients, a distinct mechanical problem from intussusception, which instead most often centers on the ileocecal region.

preguntas.q: Intussusception is classically diagnosed on abdominal ultrasound by identification of which finding?

e.correcta: On ultrasound, intussusception produces a 'bull's-eye' or 'target' sign in cross-section, formed by the concentric rings of bowel wall as one segment telescopes inside another (the layers of the outer and inner intussuscepted bowel loops nested together). Ultrasound is the preferred initial imaging modality for suspected intussusception because it is fast, radiation-free, and highly sensitive for this characteristic appearance.

incorrectas.A: The double bubble sign reflects gas distension of the stomach and proximal duodenum, classically from duodenal atresia or annular pancreas, not the concentric bowel-within-bowel appearance seen in intussusception.
incorrectas.B: The string sign describes a thin column of contrast passing through a severely narrowed, inflamed segment of bowel, classically discussed in strictures such as those from Crohn disease, rather than the telescoping bowel loops of intussusception.
incorrectas.D: The coffee bean sign describes a markedly distended, twisted loop of sigmoid colon on abdominal X-ray in sigmoid volvulus, an entirely different radiographic pattern from the target sign used to diagnose intussusception on ultrasound.

preguntas.q: Acute mesenteric ischemia that progresses to transmural bowel infarction and perforation is most likely to result in which life-threatening complication?

e.correcta: Transmural necrosis breaks down the bowel wall barrier, allowing perforation with translocation of gut bacteria and endotoxin into the peritoneal cavity and bloodstream; the resulting overwhelming infection and inflammatory cascade produces septic (distributive) shock. This is why acute mesenteric ischemia with perforation carries such high mortality and demands emergent surgical intervention.

incorrectas.B: Cardiogenic shock arises from pump failure (e.g., after a large myocardial infarction) reducing cardiac output; although a cardiac embolus can be the cause of the ischemia itself, the shock that follows bowel perforation is due to sepsis, not primary heart failure.
incorrectas.C: Neurogenic shock results from loss of sympathetic vascular tone, classically after spinal cord injury, leading to hypotension with bradycardia — an entirely different mechanism than bacterial translocation from a perforated gut.
incorrectas.D: Anaphylactic shock is an IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation response to an allergen, causing vasodilation and capillary leak; it has no relationship to bowel wall necrosis or bacterial peritoneal contamination.

preguntas.q: A patient presents with abdominal pain that is markedly out of proportion to physical exam findings, small bowel necrosis, bloody diarrhea, and decreased bowel sounds. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?

e.correcta: In acute mesenteric ischemia, sudden (often embolic) loss of blood flow causes severe visceral ischemic pain signaled by nociceptive afferents well before peritoneal signs develop on exam, producing the classic 'pain out of proportion to exam' finding; ongoing hypoperfusion leads to small bowel necrosis, bloody diarrhea, and hypomotility (decreased bowel sounds).

incorrectas.A: Chronic mesenteric ischemia presents with recurrent, predictable postprandial pain over weeks to months ('intestinal angina') and weight loss from food aversion, not sudden pain with acute small bowel necrosis.
incorrectas.C: Ischemic colitis affects watershed regions of the colon (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid) and typically causes milder, self-limited bloody diarrhea with LLQ pain, not the severe pain-out-of-proportion picture with small bowel necrosis seen here.
incorrectas.D: Sigmoid volvulus is a mechanical large bowel obstruction from colonic twisting, presenting with distention and obstipation; it is not primarily a small bowel ischemic-necrotic process.

preguntas.q: Which stool finding, also classically described in intussusception, may be seen in acute mesenteric ischemia due to mucosal sloughing and bleeding?

e.correcta: Currant jelly stool refers to a thick mixture of blood and sloughed mucus/mucosa passed per rectum, reflecting mucosal necrosis and hemorrhage into the bowel lumen; it appears in both acute mesenteric ischemia and intussusception because both involve compromised blood flow damaging the mucosal lining.

incorrectas.C: Melena is black, tarry stool produced when upper GI blood is degraded by gastric acid and gut bacteria during transit; it reflects a different bleeding source and appearance than the mucus-blood mixture of currant jelly stool.
incorrectas.A: Rice-water stool is the classic finding in cholera, a secretory toxin-mediated watery diarrhea without blood or mucus, mechanistically unrelated to ischemic mucosal sloughing.
incorrectas.D: Steatorrhea is greasy, foul-smelling stool from fat malabsorption (e.g., pancreatic insufficiency, celiac disease), not a feature of ischemic bleeding.

preguntas.q: Because chronic mesenteric ischemia involves a gradual, partial reduction rather than complete occlusion of blood flow, it typically produces infarction limited to which layer of the bowel wall?

e.correcta: The mucosa is the most metabolically active layer and lies farthest from the extramural blood supply, making it the most vulnerable to chronic, partial hypoperfusion; slowly progressive narrowing therefore tends to cause mucosal injury rather than the full-thickness damage seen with sudden complete occlusion.

incorrectas.A: Transmural (full-thickness) infarction, with its risk of perforation, is characteristic of acute mesenteric ischemia from abrupt, complete vessel occlusion, not the gradual chronic form.
incorrectas.B: The serosa is the outermost layer and is relatively well protected by collateral perfusion, so it is rarely the primary site of ischemic injury in either acute or chronic disease.
incorrectas.D: Submucosal involvement implies a deeper degree of injury than typically seen with chronic partial ischemia, which classically spares deeper layers and stays limited to the oxygen-hungry mucosa.

preguntas.q: Which type of mesenteric ischemia, often likened to stable angina of the gut, is most commonly caused by atherosclerotic narrowing of the mesenteric vasculature?

e.correcta: Just as fixed coronary atherosclerotic plaques cause predictable, exertional stable angina, atherosclerotic narrowing of the celiac, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric arteries produces chronic mesenteric ischemia — reproducible postprandial pain when digestive demand exceeds the fixed, reduced blood supply.

incorrectas.B: Embolic occlusion from a cardiac source causes sudden, complete blockage typical of acute mesenteric ischemia, not the gradual, exertional (postprandial) pattern of the chronic form.
incorrectas.C: Mesenteric venous thrombosis causes venous congestion and often subacute, vague abdominal pain from outflow obstruction, a different mechanism than fixed arterial narrowing.
incorrectas.D: Vasculitis is a less common cause of mesenteric ischemia and does not classically produce the gradual atherosclerotic 'intestinal angina' pattern that defines the chronic form.

preguntas.q: In chronic mesenteric ischemia, epigastric pain classically occurs at which point relative to meals, reflecting a mismatch between metabolic demand and fixed blood supply?

o.D: Only at night, unrelated to meals

e.correcta: Digestion sharply increases splanchnic metabolic demand, which narrowed, atherosclerotic mesenteric vessels cannot meet, producing postprandial pain ('intestinal angina') analogous to exertional cardiac angina; over time this causes food aversion and significant weight loss.

incorrectas.A: Pain occurring before eating does not fit the demand-supply mismatch mechanism, since the ischemic trigger is the increased metabolic demand that digestion itself imposes.
incorrectas.B: Fasting lowers splanchnic metabolic demand, so pain should be minimal or absent during that period rather than provoked by it.
incorrectas.D: Nocturnal pain unrelated to meals would not reflect the postprandial demand-ischemia mechanism that defines and is used to diagnose this condition clinically.

preguntas.q: Which modifiable risk factor is most strongly associated with the development of a Warthin tumor of the parotid gland?

e.correcta: Cigarette smoking significantly increases the risk of Warthin tumor (papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum), a benign salivary gland tumor thought to arise from a metaplastic/proliferative response of entrapped ductal epithelium and associated lymphoid tissue to tobacco carcinogens; it is frequently bilateral and almost always occurs in the parotid gland.

incorrectas.A: Alcohol use is a risk factor for several head and neck squamous cell carcinomas, but it is not the classic modifiable risk factor linked to Warthin tumor specifically.
incorrectas.C: HPV infection drives a subset of oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinomas through viral oncoproteins, an entirely different tumor category from the benign, smoking-associated Warthin tumor.
incorrectas.D: EBV infection is associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma and Burkitt lymphoma, not with benign salivary gland tumors like Warthin tumor.

preguntas.q: In Boerhaave syndrome, dissection of air from the ruptured esophagus into the soft tissues of the neck and chest wall produces a crackling sensation on palpation. What is this physical exam finding called?

e.correcta: Full-thickness esophageal rupture allows air to track from the esophageal lumen into the mediastinum and then into subcutaneous tissue planes of the neck and chest wall; the trapped gas produces a palpable, crackling sensation known as subcutaneous (surgical) emphysema, often accompanying the Hamman sign, severe chest/upper abdominal pain, and rapid progression to sepsis if the diagnosis is delayed.

incorrectas.A: Pneumothorax is air within the pleural space causing dyspnea and diminished breath sounds on auscultation, not a palpable crackling in the skin and soft tissue.
incorrectas.C: Pleural effusion is fluid accumulation in the pleural space, detected by dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds, not gas-related crepitus.
incorrectas.D: Hemothorax refers to blood within the pleural cavity, presenting with dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds, mechanistically unrelated to air dissecting through subcutaneous tissue.

preguntas.q: Along with tetracyclines, NSAIDs, iron, and potassium chloride, which drug class classically causes pill-induced esophagitis if taken without adequate water or while lying down?

e.correcta: Bisphosphonates (e.g., alendronate) are directly caustic to esophageal mucosa if the tablet lingers in contact with the wall, which is why patients are instructed to take them with a full glass of water and remain upright for at least 30 minutes; prolonged mucosal contact leads to localized chemical injury and pill-induced esophagitis.

incorrectas.A: Proton pump inhibitors reduce gastric acid production and are used to treat esophagitis, not cause it through direct mucosal contact injury.
incorrectas.C: H2 receptor blockers similarly decrease acid secretion for therapeutic benefit and are not associated with caustic pill-esophagitis.
incorrectas.D: Antacids neutralize existing acid and are protective for the esophageal mucosa, the opposite of the mucosa-damaging mechanism described for pill-induced esophagitis.

preguntas.q: Achalasia results from loss of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus, leading to failure of lower esophageal sphincter relaxation. Loss of which two mediators is implicated?

e.correcta: Nitric oxide and VIP are normally released by inhibitory myenteric neurons to relax the LES between swallows; their loss (from autoimmune destruction of ganglion cells in idiopathic achalasia, or from Chagas disease) leaves excitatory cholinergic tone unopposed, causing sustained LES contraction and impaired relaxation — the classic 'bird's beak' narrowing seen on barium swallow.

incorrectas.A: Acetylcholine and substance P are excitatory mediators that increase LES tone; losing them would cause a hypotensive sphincter, the opposite problem from the elevated, non-relaxing LES tone of achalasia.
incorrectas.C: Norepinephrine and epinephrine are sympathetic mediators not primarily responsible for the parasympathetic-associated inhibitory relaxation pathway that is disrupted in achalasia.
incorrectas.D: Serotonin and dopamine participate in GI motility regulation broadly, but they are not the specific inhibitory neurotransmitters whose loss defines achalasia's pathophysiology.

preguntas.q: The original rotavirus vaccine formulation was withdrawn due to an increased risk of which GI pathology, a concern that still shapes the age-restricted dosing schedule of current vaccines?

e.correcta: An increased risk of intussusception — telescoping of a proximal bowel segment into a distal one, classically ileocolic, causing colicky pain, a palpable sausage-shaped mass, and currant jelly stools — was linked to rotavirus vaccination, particularly when the first dose was given after 15 weeks of age; current schedules restrict initial dosing to before that age to minimize this risk.

incorrectas.A: Pyloric stenosis is a congenital hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle in infants causing projectile non-bilious vomiting, an anatomic condition unrelated to vaccine timing.
incorrectas.B: Meckel diverticulum is a congenital remnant of the vitelline duct present from birth, not an acquired complication associated with vaccination.
incorrectas.D: Volvulus is bowel twisting typically related to malrotation or a redundant colon segment, not a recognized complication of rotavirus vaccine administration.

preguntas.q: Lactose intolerance results from decreased activity of which brush-border enzyme in small intestinal enterocytes?

e.correcta: Lactase is the brush-border disaccharidase that hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose for absorption; its deficiency — whether the common primary genetic decline after weaning or a secondary loss from mucosal injury — leaves lactose undigested and osmotically active in the intestinal lumen.

incorrectas.A: Sucrase-isomaltase deficiency is a distinct, much rarer congenital condition causing malabsorption of sucrose and starch-derived sugars, not the milk-sugar intolerance being described.
incorrectas.B: Trehalase deficiency causes intolerance to trehalose, a sugar found in mushrooms and certain insects, an unrelated and uncommon enzyme deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Maltase deficiency would impair digestion of maltose derived from starch breakdown, not the specific milk disaccharide lactose.

preguntas.q: A patient develops abdominal distention and diarrhea after drinking milk because undigested sugar in the bowel lumen osmotically draws in water and is fermented by colonic bacteria. Which condition does this describe?

e.correcta: Undigested lactose remains osmotically active within the gut lumen, drawing water in to cause osmotic diarrhea and bloating, while colonic bacteria ferment the sugar to generate gas and further distention; the tight temporal link to dairy consumption is the key clinical clue pointing to lactose intolerance rather than a chronic malabsorptive disease.

incorrectas.A: Celiac disease is an autoimmune reaction to gluten causing chronic villous injury and malabsorption; symptoms relate to gluten-containing foods (wheat, barley, rye) rather than being specifically tied to milk ingestion.
incorrectas.B: Tropical sprue is an acquired malabsorption syndrome of uncertain (likely infectious/environmental) etiology seen in people from tropical regions, without a specific dairy trigger.
incorrectas.C: Whipple disease results from infection with Tropheryma whipplei infiltrating macrophages in the intestinal lamina propria, presenting with arthralgias, weight loss, and diarrhea unrelated to a specific milk-ingestion trigger.

preguntas.q: On small bowel biopsy, primary (age-related) lactose intolerance is typically characterized by which villous appearance, distinguishing it from disorders such as celiac disease?

e.correcta: In primary lactase deficiency, the enterocytes and overall villous architecture remain structurally normal, because the enzyme deficiency is a functional/genetically programmed decline rather than the result of mucosal destruction; biopsy therefore appears unremarkable, in contrast to immune-mediated conditions that physically damage the mucosa.

incorrectas.A: Blunted, flattened villi describe the histology of celiac disease, resulting from gluten-triggered T-cell mediated mucosal injury, not the intact architecture seen in primary lactase deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia is the classic Marsh-classification finding in celiac disease, reflecting ongoing immune injury with compensatory crypt proliferation — not a feature of isolated lactase deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Subtotal villous atrophy again describes an intermediate degree of celiac-type mucosal damage, inconsistent with the structurally normal mucosa found in primary lactose intolerance.

preguntas.q: Secondary (acquired) lactase deficiency, causing temporary lactose intolerance, most commonly follows which insult to the small bowel?

o.A: Small bowel viral infection (e.g., viral enteritis)

e.correcta: Lactase sits at the very tip of the intestinal villi, making it especially exposed and metabolically vulnerable; viral enteritis (e.g., rotavirus, norovirus) damages these villous tips, transiently wiping out lactase activity even after the infection itself resolves, until the brush border regenerates over subsequent weeks.

incorrectas.B: Proton pump inhibitor use decreases gastric acid, which affects pepsin activation and calcium/B12 absorption in the stomach, not the villous-tip enzyme content of the small bowel targeted in secondary lactase deficiency.
incorrectas.C: H. pylori gastritis is a stomach-localized infection causing gastritis and peptic ulcers; it does not directly injure the small intestinal villous tips where lactase is expressed.
incorrectas.D: Cholecystectomy removes the gallbladder and affects bile storage and fat digestion, an unrelated process to small intestinal brush-border enzyme injury.

preguntas.q: In lactose intolerance, colonic bacterial fermentation of undigested lactose into short-chain fatty acids typically causes which change in stool pH?

e.correcta: Colonic bacteria ferment the unabsorbed lactose into short-chain fatty acids and gas (hydrogen, carbon dioxide, methane), which acidifies the stool; a decreased (acidic) stool pH is therefore a useful supportive laboratory clue for carbohydrate malabsorption such as lactose intolerance.

incorrectas.A: An increased or alkaline stool pH would point toward a different process, such as protein fermentation or a secretory diarrhea, rather than carbohydrate malabsorption with short-chain fatty acid production.
incorrectas.B: Bacterial fermentation of the excess undigested sugar substrate actively generates acidic byproducts, so 'no change' does not reflect the underlying pathophysiology of lactose malabsorption.
incorrectas.D: A strongly alkaline stool pH is not characteristic of carbohydrate fermentation; short-chain fatty acid production from fermented sugar drives pH down, not into a strongly alkaline range.

preguntas.q: Which noninvasive test is used to diagnose lactose intolerance by measuring gas produced from bacterial fermentation of unabsorbed sugar?

e.correcta: After an oral lactose load, colonic bacteria ferment any undigested lactose and release hydrogen gas, which is absorbed into the bloodstream and exhaled; measuring the rise in breath hydrogen after this lactose challenge is the standard noninvasive diagnostic test for lactose intolerance.

incorrectas.A: The D-xylose test distinguishes mucosal (small bowel) causes of malabsorption from pancreatic exocrine insufficiency by measuring urinary/blood xylose absorption, not fermentation gas production.
incorrectas.B: The secretin stimulation test evaluates exocrine pancreatic bicarbonate secretion, used when chronic pancreatitis or gastrinoma is suspected, not for diagnosing lactose intolerance.
incorrectas.C: The Schilling test historically assessed vitamin B12 absorption to evaluate pernicious anemia or ileal disease, an entirely different diagnostic purpose than testing for carbohydrate malabsorption.

preguntas.q: On lactose hydrogen breath testing, a rise in breath hydrogen of greater than how many ppm above baseline after lactose ingestion is considered diagnostic of lactose malabsorption?

e.correcta: A rise of more than 20 ppm above baseline breath hydrogen after an oral lactose load reflects clinically significant bacterial fermentation of unabsorbed lactose in the colon, and this cutoff is the accepted threshold for a positive test.

incorrectas.A: A threshold of only 5 ppm would be overly sensitive and nonspecific, since small physiologic fluctuations in breath hydrogen can occur normally without true malabsorption.
incorrectas.B: 10 ppm falls below the validated diagnostic cutoff and risks false-positive results from minor fermentation of other substrates unrelated to significant lactose malabsorption.
incorrectas.D: A 50 ppm threshold would be overly conservative, potentially missing patients with clinically meaningful lactose malabsorption whose breath hydrogen rise falls below that higher cutoff.

preguntas.q: Celiac disease shows a strong genetic association with which HLA class II alleles, whose absence has strong negative predictive value for the diagnosis?

e.correcta: Nearly all patients with celiac disease carry HLA-DQ2 and/or HLA-DQ8, class II molecules on antigen-presenting cells that bind deamidated gliadin peptides and present them to CD4+ T cells, triggering the autoimmune mucosal injury characteristic of the disease; because the association is so strong, a negative HLA-DQ2/DQ8 test carries substantial negative predictive value.

incorrectas.A: HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 are classically associated with type 1 diabetes mellitus, not the primary alleles linked to celiac disease susceptibility.
incorrectas.B: HLA-B27 is a class I allele associated with the seronegative spondyloarthropathies (ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, IBD-associated arthritis), unrelated to celiac disease genetics.
incorrectas.D: HLA-DR2 is associated with conditions such as Goodpasture syndrome and narcolepsy, not with celiac disease susceptibility.

preguntas.q: Which malabsorption syndrome, characterized by immune-mediated small bowel villous injury, is strongly associated with HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8?

e.correcta: Celiac disease is the classic HLA-DQ2/DQ8-linked autoimmune enteropathy triggered by gluten (gliadin) exposure, in which HLA-restricted presentation of deamidated gliadin activates CD4+ T cells that drive villous atrophy and malabsorption, predominantly in the proximal small bowel.

incorrectas.A: Tropical sprue is an acquired, likely infectious/environmental malabsorption syndrome seen in people from tropical regions, without the strong HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genetic association seen in celiac disease.
incorrectas.C: Crohn disease is a transmural inflammatory bowel disease with patchy 'skip lesions' that can occur anywhere along the GI tract, and its genetic risk is more strongly tied to genes like NOD2, not HLA-DQ2/DQ8.
incorrectas.D: Whipple disease results from infection with Tropheryma whipplei infiltrating macrophages in the lamina propria — an infectious process, not an HLA-linked autoimmune one.

preguntas.q: Gluten is composed of several protein fractions. Which component is considered the most pathogenic in triggering celiac disease?

e.correcta: Gliadin, the alcohol-soluble prolamin fraction of wheat gluten, is rich in proline and glutamine residues that resist complete digestion by intestinal proteases, allowing immunogenic peptide fragments to cross the epithelium, be deamidated by tissue transglutaminase, and trigger the adaptive immune response that defines celiac disease.

incorrectas.A: Glutenin is the other major wheat gluten protein fraction, responsible mainly for dough elasticity; it is not the primary immunogenic trigger implicated in celiac disease pathogenesis.
incorrectas.B: Hordein is the analogous prolamin found in barley and can cross-react immunologically, but wheat-derived gliadin is the classically described most pathogenic gluten component.
incorrectas.D: Avenin is the oat prolamin, generally much less immunogenic than wheat gliadin and tolerated by many (though not all) patients with celiac disease.

preguntas.q: After absorption across the intestinal epithelium, gliadin is deamidated by which enzyme, enhancing its immunogenicity and binding to HLA-DQ2/DQ8?
