e.correcta: Tissue transglutaminase converts specific glutamine residues in gliadin into glutamic acid (deamidation), which increases the peptide's negative charge and boosts its binding affinity for the HLA-DQ2/DQ8 groove on antigen-presenting cells, strengthening CD4+ T-cell activation; anti-tTG antibodies produced against this same enzyme are also the key serologic marker used to diagnose celiac disease.

incorrectas.A: Sucrase-isomaltase is a brush-border disaccharidase that digests sucrose and starch-derived oligosaccharides, unrelated to modifying gliadin's immunogenicity.
incorrectas.C: Trypsin is a pancreatic protease that breaks down dietary protein generally, but it does not perform the specific deamidation reaction that enhances gliadin's HLA-DQ2/DQ8 binding.
incorrectas.D: Lactase hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose, an entirely unrelated brush-border function with no role in gluten peptide processing.

preguntas.q: In celiac disease pathogenesis, which specific antigen is presented by antigen-presenting cells via MHC class II to activate CD4+ T cells?

e.correcta: After tissue transglutaminase deamidates gliadin, the modified peptide binds with high affinity to the HLA-DQ2/DQ8 groove on antigen-presenting cells and is presented to CD4+ helper T cells, which then drive the inflammatory cascade (cytokine release, B-cell activation) responsible for damaging the villous mucosa.

incorrectas.A: Native gliadin has much lower affinity for the HLA-DQ2/DQ8 groove prior to deamidation, so it is the modified (deamidated) peptide, not the native form, that is efficiently presented to T cells.
incorrectas.B: Anti-tTG antibody is a downstream serologic marker produced later by activated B cells, not the antigen being presented to T cells in the initiating step of the immune response.
incorrectas.D: Endomysial antigen refers to the target of anti-endomysial antibodies (which is also tTG-related) — another downstream serologic marker rather than the primary antigen driving initial T-cell activation.

preguntas.q: Which immune cell type is primarily responsible for mediating the mucosal tissue damage seen in celiac disease?

e.correcta: CD4+ helper T cells recognize deamidated gliadin presented via HLA-DQ2/DQ8 on antigen-presenting cells, then release proinflammatory cytokines (such as IFN-gamma) that recruit and activate other immune cells, driving the villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia characteristic of celiac disease — this HLA-restricted adaptive T-cell response is central to disease pathogenesis, even though B cells are the ones producing the diagnostic antibodies.

incorrectas.A: Cytotoxic CD8+ intraepithelial lymphocytes do increase in celiac disease and contribute to epithelial injury, but the primary orchestrating response that drives tissue damage is the CD4+ helper T-cell reaction to HLA-DQ2/DQ8-presented antigen.
incorrectas.C: NK cells are part of the innate immune system and are not the main effector cells responsible for the adaptive, HLA-restricted damage characteristic of celiac disease.
incorrectas.D: B cells produce the anti-tTG and anti-endomysial antibodies used for diagnosis, but the destructive mucosal T-cell response driving villous atrophy is primarily attributed to helper T cells, not B cells directly.

preguntas.q: Classic celiac disease presenting with abdominal distention, steatorrhea, and failure to thrive is most typical of which age group?

e.correcta: Classic pediatric celiac disease manifests after gluten-containing foods are introduced into the diet, causing malabsorption of fat (steatorrhea) and nutrients severe enough to impair growth (failure to thrive), along with abdominal distention from bloating and malabsorption — a full-blown presentation less commonly seen in adult-onset disease, which tends to be subtler or atypical.

incorrectas.A: Elderly adults with celiac disease more often present atypically with iron-deficiency anemia, osteoporosis, or nonspecific GI complaints rather than the classic pediatric triad of distention, steatorrhea, and failure to thrive.
incorrectas.B: Adolescents can certainly have celiac disease, but the classic distention/steatorrhea/failure-to-thrive presentation is most characteristically described in younger children shortly after gluten is introduced.
incorrectas.C: Middle-aged adults more commonly present with silent or atypical celiac disease (fatigue, anemia, infertility) rather than overt failure to thrive, which is specifically a pediatric growth-related finding.

preguntas.q: Celiac disease classically presents with chronic steatorrhea and bloating in which age group?

e.correcta: Celiac disease in adults classically presents with chronic, insidious symptoms of malabsorption—steatorrhea (bulky, foul-smelling, fat-laden stools), abdominal bloating, and flatulence—reflecting years of gradual villous damage in the proximal small bowel. This subtler presentation contrasts with earlier-onset disease, where growth failure dominates; recognizing the adult pattern matters because celiac disease is now diagnosed more often in adulthood, sometimes with only atypical or extraintestinal findings such as anemia, osteoporosis, or dermatitis herpetiformis.

incorrectas.A: Infants typically develop symptoms only once gluten-containing foods are introduced (usually 6-24 months), and when celiac disease does present in infancy it tends to show as failure to thrive, irritability, and abdominal distension rather than the chronic steatorrhea/bloating pattern classically emphasized for adults.
incorrectas.C: Toddlers can develop celiac symptoms once gluten exposure begins, but classic teaching separates a pediatric pattern (growth failure, irritability, abdominal distension) from the adult pattern of chronic steatorrhea and bloating, so this age group is not the one highlighted for that presentation.
incorrectas.D: Neonates have not yet been exposed to dietary gluten in the first weeks of life, so celiac disease cannot present at this age at all; symptoms require prior gluten ingestion to trigger the immune-mediated mucosal injury.

preguntas.q: Celiac disease is classically associated with which ancestral/ethnic background?

e.correcta: Celiac disease shows a strong association with the HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 haplotypes, which are most prevalent in populations of northern European descent; this genetic predisposition, combined with early and heavy dietary gluten exposure, explains why celiac disease is classically taught as a disease of people with northern European ancestry (e.g., Irish, Scandinavian) and why it is comparatively rare where these HLA alleles are less common.

incorrectas.B: Mediterranean populations do carry some HLA-DQ2/DQ8 alleles and celiac disease occurs there, but the classic epidemiologic teaching point highlights northern European ancestry as having the highest prevalence, not Mediterranean.
incorrectas.C: East Asian populations have a markedly lower prevalence of celiac disease, partly due to lower frequency of HLA-DQ2/DQ8 haplotypes and different dietary staples (rice-based rather than wheat-based), making this population the opposite of the classic association.
incorrectas.D: Sub-Saharan African populations similarly have lower reported rates of celiac disease, again related to lower frequency of the predisposing HLA alleles and historically lower gluten consumption, contrasting with the northern European association classically tested.

preguntas.q: In dermatitis herpetiformis associated with celiac disease, which immunoglobulin deposits at the tips of the dermal papillae?

e.correcta: Dermatitis herpetiformis is caused by IgA immune complexes (cross-reacting with tissue transglutaminase) depositing at the tips of the dermal papillae, triggering a neutrophilic inflammatory response that produces the intensely pruritic, grouped vesicles typical of the rash. Because the underlying driver is the same gluten-triggered IgA response seen in celiac disease, dermatitis herpetiformis resolves with a strict gluten-free diet, just like the intestinal disease.

incorrectas.A: IgG is not the immunoglobulin implicated in dermatitis herpetiformis; IgG anti-tTG/anti-endomysial antibodies are instead used diagnostically in celiac patients who are IgA-deficient, not as the mediator of the skin lesions.
incorrectas.B: IgE mediates type I hypersensitivity reactions such as urticaria and anaphylaxis, not the granular dermal papillary deposits of dermatitis herpetiformis, so it is not the correct immunoglobulin here.
incorrectas.C: IgM is not the immunoglobulin deposited in dermatitis herpetiformis; the disease is specifically defined by granular IgA deposits at the dermal papillary tips, distinguishing it from other immunobullous diseases.

preguntas.q: In a patient with selective IgA deficiency who also has celiac disease, which class of antibodies against endomysium, tTG, or gliadin should be used for serologic diagnosis?

e.correcta: Because standard celiac serologies (anti-tTG, anti-endomysial, anti-gliadin) are IgA-based, a patient with concurrent selective IgA deficiency will have falsely negative IgA antibody tests despite having active celiac disease. In this setting, IgG-based versions of these same antibodies (e.g., IgG anti-tTG) are used instead to avoid a false-negative workup — a classic testing pitfall on exams, which is why total IgA should always be checked before interpreting celiac serology as negative.

incorrectas.A: IgA antibodies are the ones that will be falsely low or absent in a patient with selective IgA deficiency, which is exactly why they cannot be relied upon for diagnosis in this scenario and why the IgG alternative is needed.
incorrectas.B: IgE is not used in celiac serologic testing; it is relevant to type I hypersensitivity reactions, not to the antibody panel used to diagnose celiac disease.
incorrectas.D: IgM is not the standard alternative immunoglobulin class used for celiac serology in IgA-deficient patients; clinical practice specifically substitutes IgG-based tTG, endomysial, and gliadin antibodies.

preguntas.q: Celiac disease patients have an increased incidence of deficiency of which immunoglobulin?

e.correcta: Selective IgA deficiency occurs at a higher rate in patients with celiac disease than in the general population, a clinically important association because it can cause false-negative IgA-based celiac serologies (anti-tTG, anti-endomysial antibodies) and necessitates either checking a total IgA level or using IgG-based alternative tests.

incorrectas.B: IgG deficiency is not the immunoglobulin deficiency classically linked to celiac disease; IgG-based tests are actually the backup assay used when the truly associated deficiency (IgA) is present.
incorrectas.C: IgM deficiency is not part of the classic celiac disease association; the well-documented immunodeficiency link is specifically with selective IgA deficiency.
incorrectas.D: IgE deficiency is not a recognized or clinically relevant association with celiac disease; IgE relates to allergic and parasitic immune responses, not to celiac disease's immunodeficiency association.

preguntas.q: Celiac disease is characterized histologically by an increase in which intraepithelial cell type, along with villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia?

e.correcta: The classic histologic triad of celiac disease is villous blunting/atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (predominantly CD8+ T cells) infiltrating the surface epithelium, reflecting the T-cell-mediated immune response to gluten-derived gliadin peptides presented by HLA-DQ2/DQ8. This intraepithelial lymphocytosis is one of the earliest histologic changes and can be seen even before overt villous atrophy develops.

incorrectas.A: Eosinophils are the hallmark intraepithelial infiltrate of eosinophilic esophagitis/gastroenteritis, not celiac disease, which is defined by lymphocytic rather than eosinophilic infiltration.
incorrectas.C: Neutrophils suggest an acute infectious or active inflammatory process (such as active colitis or an abscess), not the chronic T-cell-mediated injury pattern seen in celiac disease.
incorrectas.D: Plasma cells are normally present in the lamina propria and increase in various chronic inflammatory conditions, but the specific diagnostic finding in celiac disease is increased lymphocytes within the epithelium itself, not plasma cells.

preguntas.q: Celiac disease characteristically affects which segment(s) of the small bowel most severely?

o.C: Entire small bowel diffusely, including the ileum

e.correcta: Celiac disease preferentially damages the proximal small bowel — the distal duodenum and proximal jejunum — because these segments receive the highest concentration of dietary gluten before it is further digested; villous atrophy is therefore most severe proximally and can taper off more distally in milder disease, which is why duodenal biopsies are the standard diagnostic sampling site.

incorrectas.A: The terminal ileum is classically spared in celiac disease (in contrast to tropical sprue, which can involve the ileum), so ileal involvement is not the expected finding and its presence should prompt consideration of another diagnosis.
incorrectas.B: The stomach and duodenal bulb are not the primary sites of celiac injury; celiac disease is a small bowel mucosal disease affecting the distal duodenum onward, not the stomach.
incorrectas.C: Celiac disease does not diffusely and uniformly involve the entire small bowel including the ileum in typical cases; that pattern of more extensive small bowel involvement is a distinguishing feature of tropical sprue rather than celiac disease.

preguntas.q: Which malabsorption syndrome primarily affects the proximal small bowel (distal duodenum and proximal jejunum)?

e.correcta: Celiac sprue is defined by an immune reaction to gluten that damages the proximal small bowel mucosa first and most severely, since that is where ingested gluten peptides are most concentrated; this proximal predominance, with relative sparing of the ileum, is a key distinguishing feature from tropical sprue, which can involve the bowel more diffusely.

incorrectas.A: Tropical sprue classically affects the small bowel more diffusely and can extend to involve the ileum over time, which is precisely why proximal predominance is used to distinguish celiac disease from tropical sprue rather than describing tropical sprue itself.
incorrectas.B: Whipple disease is a systemic infection by Tropheryma whipplei that infiltrates the lamina propria of the small bowel (along with joints, heart valves, and CNS) with PAS-positive macrophages, not a disease defined by proximal small bowel-predominant villous injury.
incorrectas.D: Pancreatic insufficiency causes malabsorption due to a lack of digestive enzymes reaching the small bowel lumen, a functional/luminal problem rather than a mucosal disease with a specific proximal small bowel predilection.

preguntas.q: Celiac disease increases the long-term risk of small bowel adenocarcinoma and which type of lymphoma?

e.correcta: Longstanding, poorly controlled celiac disease increases the risk of enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL), thought to arise from chronic intraepithelial T-cell stimulation and proliferation in the damaged mucosa. It should be suspected in a celiac patient who develops refractory symptoms (weight loss, abdominal pain) despite strict dietary adherence, since ongoing symptoms despite good dietary control is a red flag for malignant transformation rather than simple non-adherence.

incorrectas.B: Mantle cell lymphoma is a B-cell neoplasm associated with cyclin D1 overexpression from t(11;14) and is not part of the celiac disease-associated malignancy spectrum.
incorrectas.C: B-cell lymphomas (e.g., MALT lymphoma) are classically associated with other GI conditions such as H. pylori-associated gastric lymphoma, not with the intraepithelial T-cell-driven process of celiac disease.
incorrectas.D: NK-cell lymphomas are more classically associated with EBV infection and conditions like nasal NK/T-cell lymphoma, not with the T-cell lineage lymphoma that arises specifically from celiac-associated intraepithelial lymphocytosis.

preguntas.q: Celiac disease is associated with what change in bone density, due to chronic fat-soluble vitamin D malabsorption?

e.correcta: Because celiac disease damages the proximal small bowel mucosa needed to absorb fat and fat-soluble vitamins, chronic vitamin D malabsorption leads to reduced calcium absorption and secondary hyperparathyroidism, resulting in decreased bone mineral density (osteopenia/osteoporosis) over time; this is one of the extraintestinal complications that can prompt bone density screening in celiac patients.

incorrectas.A: Increased bone density would not be expected from a malabsorptive state; chronic deficiency of vitamin D and impaired calcium absorption drives bone loss, not bone gain.
incorrectas.B: Bone density is not unaffected in celiac disease — it is a well-recognized extraintestinal complication precisely because fat-soluble vitamin D malabsorption impairs calcium homeostasis and bone mineralization over time.
incorrectas.D: While severity can vary by disease duration and control, the classic teaching point is a consistent direction of decreased bone density from chronic malabsorption, not an unpredictable or fluctuating pattern.

preguntas.q: What is the definitive treatment for celiac disease?

e.correcta: The treatment for celiac disease is strict, lifelong avoidance of dietary gluten (found in wheat, barley, and rye), which removes the antigenic trigger for the immune-mediated mucosal damage. With adherence, the small bowel villi typically heal and symptoms resolve, while continued gluten exposure perpetuates inflammation and raises the long-term risk of complications like EATL.

incorrectas.A: Antibiotics are the treatment for tropical sprue (and address the infectious component of Whipple disease), not celiac disease, which is an immune-mediated reaction to a dietary protein rather than an infection.
incorrectas.C: Pancreatic enzyme replacement is used for pancreatic insufficiency (e.g., chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis) to compensate for a lack of digestive enzymes, not for celiac disease, where the problem is mucosal immune injury rather than enzyme deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Corticosteroids are not first-line or definitive therapy for celiac disease; they may occasionally be used in refractory celiac disease, but the cornerstone and essentially curative treatment is dietary gluten elimination.

preguntas.q: In celiac disease, urinary excretion of D-xylose after an oral load is typically:

e.correcta: D-xylose is a pentose sugar absorbed passively across the proximal small bowel mucosa without requiring pancreatic enzymes, so its urinary excretion after an oral load directly tests mucosal integrity. Because celiac disease damages the proximal small bowel mucosa itself, D-xylose absorption — and therefore its urinary excretion — is decreased, which helps distinguish a mucosal malabsorptive process like celiac disease from a purely pancreatic enzyme deficiency, where D-xylose excretion remains normal.

incorrectas.A: Increased D-xylose excretion would suggest normal or even excessive absorption, the opposite of what happens when the absorptive mucosa itself is damaged, as in celiac disease.
incorrectas.B: Normal D-xylose excretion is the expected finding in pancreatic insufficiency, where the mucosa is intact and enzymes — not mucosal absorptive surface — are lacking; it is specifically abnormal (decreased) in mucosal diseases like celiac disease.
incorrectas.C: Excretion is decreased, not completely undetectable or absent; the test still shows some xylose absorption and excretion, just at a reduced quantity reflecting the degree of mucosal damage.

preguntas.q: Which malabsorption syndrome is characterized by small bowel villous damage attributed to an unidentified infectious organism, typically following a bout of infectious diarrhea in a tropical region?

e.correcta: Tropical sprue is a malabsorptive disease seen in residents of, or travelers to, tropical regions, thought to result from an unidentified infectious agent (possibly with bacterial overgrowth) that damages small bowel villi, often triggered by a preceding episode of acute infectious diarrhea. Unlike celiac disease, it responds to antibiotics plus folate/B12 supplementation rather than gluten avoidance.

incorrectas.A: Celiac disease is an immune-mediated reaction to dietary gluten in genetically susceptible individuals (HLA-DQ2/DQ8), not a disease attributed to an unidentified infectious organism, and it is not specifically linked to tropical geography.
incorrectas.B: Whipple disease is caused by a specific, identified organism — Tropheryma whipplei — and produces PAS-positive foamy macrophage infiltration of the lamina propria, in contrast to tropical sprue's presumed-but-unidentified infectious trigger.
incorrectas.D: Crohn disease is an idiopathic inflammatory bowel disease with transmural granulomatous inflammation and skip lesions, not a malabsorptive syndrome attributed to an infectious agent following diarrhea.

preguntas.q: Which malabsorption disorder is more common in patients living in or having traveled to tropical regions such as the Caribbean, India, or Southeast Asia?

e.correcta: Tropical sprue occurs predominantly in residents of, and travelers to, tropical/subtropical regions (e.g., Caribbean, India, Southeast Asia), which is reflected directly in its name; this geographic clustering supports an infectious or environmental trigger (such as chronic bacterial overgrowth) rather than the genetic/immune mechanism seen in celiac disease.

incorrectas.A: Celiac sprue occurs worldwide and is actually classically associated with northern European ancestry rather than tropical geography, the opposite epidemiologic pattern from tropical sprue.
incorrectas.B: Whipple disease is caused by Tropheryma whipplei and, while it can occur anywhere, it is not defined by a tropical geographic distribution the way tropical sprue is; it is instead notable for affecting older men.
incorrectas.C: Pancreatic insufficiency results from disorders like chronic pancreatitis or cystic fibrosis and has no particular tropical geographic predilection; its distribution follows the underlying pancreatic disease, not travel or residence in tropical regions.

preguntas.q: Tropical sprue classically develops after an episode of which preceding illness?

e.correcta: Tropical sprue classically arises following a bout of acute infectious diarrhea (gastroenteritis), which is thought to trigger persistent small bowel bacterial overgrowth and ongoing mucosal villous damage even after the initial infection clears; this temporal link to preceding enteric infection, combined with a tropical geographic setting, is a key part of its classic history.

incorrectas.B: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV) is not the preceding illness linked to tropical sprue; it causes pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly, not a small bowel malabsorptive trigger.
incorrectas.C: Viral hepatitis affects the liver and is not the classic antecedent infection associated with tropical sprue, which is specifically tied to an enteric/diarrheal illness affecting the gut.
incorrectas.D: A urinary tract infection is an infection of the urinary tract with no established link to triggering small bowel villous damage, unlike the enteric infectious diarrhea classically implicated in tropical sprue.

preguntas.q: Which type of sprue can affect any part of the small bowel, including the ileum, distinguishing it from the more proximally restricted disease?

e.correcta: Tropical sprue characteristically begins in the duodenum and jejunum but, unlike celiac disease, can progress to involve the ileum over time; this ileal involvement is a key distinguishing clinical clue, since ileal disease can cause additional vitamin B12 malabsorption (via loss of the terminal ileal absorption site) on top of the folate deficiency seen with proximal disease.

incorrectas.A: Celiac sprue is characteristically restricted to the proximal small bowel (distal duodenum and proximal jejunum) with relative sparing of the ileum, the opposite pattern from the diffuse involvement seen in tropical sprue.
incorrectas.C: Whipple disease involves lamina propria infiltration by PAS-positive macrophages as part of a systemic infection, but it is not the entity classically taught as extending to 'any part of the small bowel including the ileum' to distinguish it from celiac disease — that distinguishing feature belongs to tropical sprue.
incorrectas.D: Pancreatic insufficiency is a functional deficiency of digestive enzymes rather than a mucosal disease with a defined anatomic distribution of villous damage, so it does not fit the comparison being made about mucosal segment involvement.

preguntas.q: Tropical sprue may be associated with which type of anemia, related to folate (and later B12) deficiency?

e.correcta: Because tropical sprue damages the small bowel and can extend to the ileum, it impairs absorption of folate (early) and later vitamin B12, both of which are required for DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells. The resulting defective DNA synthesis produces megaloblastic anemia, characterized by large, immature-appearing red cell precursors and hypersegmented neutrophils.

incorrectas.A: Microcytic anemia results from impaired hemoglobin synthesis (e.g., iron deficiency, thalassemia), not from folate/B12 deficiency, which instead impairs DNA synthesis and produces macrocytic, megaloblastic changes.
incorrectas.B: Normocytic anemia is typical of anemia of chronic disease or acute blood loss, not the DNA synthesis defect from folate/B12 deficiency, which specifically enlarges red cell precursors.
incorrectas.C: Hemolytic anemia results from increased red cell destruction (e.g., autoimmune, hereditary spherocytosis), a different mechanism entirely from the impaired DNA synthesis caused by folate/B12 malabsorption in tropical sprue.

preguntas.q: In tropical sprue, urinary excretion of D-xylose after an oral load is typically:

e.correcta: Tropical sprue damages the small bowel mucosa (and can promote bacterial overgrowth), impairing the passive absorption of D-xylose across the epithelium; this results in decreased urinary D-xylose excretion, similar to celiac disease, reflecting a mucosal absorptive defect rather than an isolated enzyme deficiency.

incorrectas.A: Increased excretion would indicate preserved or enhanced mucosal absorption, which is inconsistent with the villous damage and bacterial overgrowth seen in tropical sprue.
incorrectas.B: Excretion is decreased, not completely absent; some xylose is still absorbed and excreted, just less than normal, proportional to the degree of mucosal injury and bacterial overgrowth.
incorrectas.D: Normal D-xylose excretion would be expected if the mucosa were intact and only pancreatic enzymes were deficient (as in pancreatic insufficiency); tropical sprue instead damages the absorptive mucosa itself, causing decreased excretion.

preguntas.q: Tropheryma whipplei, the causative organism of Whipple disease, is an intracellular organism with which Gram stain characteristic?

e.correcta: Tropheryma whipplei is a gram-positive, intracellular actinomycete that infects macrophages, which then accumulate in the lamina propria and other tissues; its gram-positive, intracellular nature underlies the classic PAS-positive, foamy macrophage histology seen in Whipple disease, since PAS stains the bacterial glycoprotein cell walls within the macrophage cytoplasm.

incorrectas.B: Tropheryma whipplei is not gram-negative; gram-negative organisms have a different cell wall structure (thin peptidoglycan layer with an outer membrane) than the gram-positive cell wall of T. whipplei.
incorrectas.C: T. whipplei is not classified as acid-fast; acid-fast staining identifies organisms with mycolic acid-rich cell walls such as Mycobacterium species, a different diagnostic stain from the Gram/PAS approach used for Whipple disease.
incorrectas.D: T. whipplei has a consistent gram-positive cell wall, not a variable staining pattern; it is simply difficult to culture using standard methods, which is different from having gram-variable staining.

preguntas.q: Which malabsorption syndrome is diagnosed by finding PAS-positive, foamy macrophages infiltrating the small bowel lamina propria?

e.correcta: Whipple disease is diagnosed histologically by PAS-positive, foamy macrophages packed with Tropheryma whipplei organisms infiltrating the small bowel lamina propria, distorting the villi and impairing nutrient (especially fat, via lymphatic obstruction) absorption; this macrophage-laden pattern is distinct from the epithelial lymphocytic infiltrate of celiac disease or the villous blunting of tropical sprue.

incorrectas.A: Celiac disease shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, not PAS-positive macrophage infiltration of the lamina propria, which is specific to Whipple disease.
incorrectas.C: Tropical sprue shows nonspecific villous blunting and inflammation of the small bowel mucosa but does not feature the characteristic PAS-positive foamy macrophages that define Whipple disease histologically.
incorrectas.D: Pancreatic insufficiency is a functional/enzymatic deficiency without any specific small bowel mucosal histologic finding like PAS-positive macrophages; the bowel mucosa itself is typically structurally normal in this condition.

preguntas.q: Whipple disease classically involves infiltration of which layer of the small bowel wall by PAS-positive macrophages?

e.correcta: In Whipple disease, PAS-positive macrophages laden with Tropheryma whipplei characteristically infiltrate the lamina propria of the small bowel — the loose connective tissue layer beneath the epithelium containing the villous core — distorting normal villous architecture and impairing lymphatic drainage of absorbed fat. The same organism-laden macrophages can also be found in extraintestinal sites like the synovium (arthritis), cardiac valves, lymph nodes, and CNS.

incorrectas.A: The muscularis mucosae is a thin smooth muscle layer separating the mucosa from the submucosa; it is not the site of the characteristic macrophage infiltration in Whipple disease, which occurs in the adjacent lamina propria.
incorrectas.B: The serosa is the outermost layer of the bowel wall and is not the site of the disease-defining macrophage infiltrate seen in Whipple disease, which is a mucosal/lamina propria process.
incorrectas.C: The submucosa lies beneath the muscularis mucosae, and while inflammation can extend more deeply in severe disease, the classic and diagnostic site of PAS-positive macrophage accumulation in Whipple disease is the lamina propria within the mucosa itself.

preguntas.q: Which group of lymph nodes is commonly affected in Whipple disease, reflecting spread from the infected small bowel?

e.correcta: Because Tropheryma whipplei infects macrophages in the small bowel and can spread via lymphatics, the mesenteric lymph nodes — which drain the small bowel — are commonly involved in Whipple disease, becoming enlarged and infiltrated with the same PAS-positive foamy macrophages seen in the bowel wall; this reflects the disease's tendency toward systemic dissemination from its GI origin.

incorrectas.B: Axillary nodes drain the upper limb and lateral breast/chest wall, not the small bowel, so they are not the classically affected nodal group in Whipple disease.
incorrectas.C: Cervical nodes drain head and neck structures and are not anatomically positioned to be the primary nodal group involved by a small bowel-based infection like Whipple disease.
incorrectas.D: Inguinal nodes drain the lower limb and external genitalia/perineum, not the small bowel, making them an unlikely site for the mesenteric lymphatic spread characteristic of Whipple disease.

preguntas.q: Whipple disease most classically affects which demographic group?

e.correcta: Whipple disease classically affects older, middle-aged to elderly men, a demographic pattern noted in classic teaching though the exact reason for the male predominance is not fully established. Recognizing this typical patient profile — an older man with malabsorption, arthralgias, and sometimes neurologic or cardiac symptoms — helps raise suspicion for this rare but treatable infectious disease.

incorrectas.A: Young women are not the demographic classically associated with Whipple disease; this disease shows a distinct predilection for older men rather than younger patients of either sex.
incorrectas.B: Children are essentially not affected by Whipple disease in classic teaching; it is described as a disease of older adults, particularly men, not a pediatric condition.
incorrectas.D: While Whipple disease can rarely occur in women, the classic demographic emphasized is older men, not elderly women specifically, reflecting the disease's recognized male predominance.

preguntas.q: Pancreatic insufficiency causes malabsorption of dietary fat, fat-soluble vitamins, and which additional water-soluble vitamin?

e.correcta: Vitamin B12 absorption requires pancreatic proteases to cleave B12 off of R-proteins (haptocorrin) so that it can bind intrinsic factor for absorption in the terminal ileum. Without adequate pancreatic enzyme secretion, as in chronic pancreatitis or cystic fibrosis, this cleavage step fails and B12 malabsorption occurs alongside the more obviously expected fat and fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) malabsorption.

incorrectas.A: Folate absorption occurs in the proximal jejunum via a brush-border process that does not require pancreatic enzymes, so folate deficiency is not the classic pancreatic insufficiency-associated water-soluble vitamin deficiency the way B12 is.
incorrectas.C: Vitamin C absorption is an active transport process in the small intestine that is not dependent on pancreatic enzyme secretion, so it is not the vitamin classically linked to pancreatic insufficiency.
incorrectas.D: Thiamine (B1) absorption also does not depend on pancreatic proteolytic cleavage from a carrier protein, unlike B12, so it is not the water-soluble vitamin classically taught as impaired in pancreatic insufficiency.

preguntas.q: Which test is used to indirectly assess exocrine pancreatic function in suspected pancreatic insufficiency?

e.correcta: Fecal elastase is a stool-based test that indirectly assesses exocrine pancreatic function by measuring the concentration of pancreatic elastase enzyme in stool; low fecal elastase indicates reduced pancreatic enzyme secretion, and because it is noninvasive and doesn't require duodenal intubation, it is used far more commonly in practice than direct pancreatic function tests.

incorrectas.A: The secretin stimulation test is a direct test of pancreatic function — it measures bicarbonate output collected via duodenal intubation after IV secretin administration — rather than the noninvasive indirect stool-based approach that fecal elastase represents.
incorrectas.B: The D-xylose test assesses mucosal absorptive integrity, not pancreatic enzyme output; it is classically normal in pancreatic insufficiency (since the mucosa is intact) and abnormal in mucosal diseases like celiac disease, making it useful to distinguish the two rather than to assess pancreatic function directly.
incorrectas.C: The Schilling test evaluates the cause of vitamin B12 malabsorption (e.g., pernicious anemia vs. ileal disease vs. pancreatic insufficiency) through staged administration of labeled B12, not a general indirect screening test for pancreatic exocrine function like fecal elastase.

preguntas.q: In a patient with exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (e.g., chronic pancreatitis or cystic fibrosis), what happens to fecal elastase-1 excretion?

e.correcta: Fecal elastase-1 is a proteolytic enzyme secreted by pancreatic acinar cells that survives intestinal transit largely intact. When acinar cell mass and secretory output fall, as in chronic pancreatitis or cystic fibrosis, less elastase reaches the stool, so fecal elastase-1 is decreased. This makes it a convenient noninvasive screening test for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency without requiring pancreatic stimulation testing.

incorrectas.B: There is no physiologic mechanism by which loss of pancreatic acinar function would increase elastase output; secretion tracks with functioning acinar mass, so insufficiency can only lower, not raise, the amount reaching stool.
incorrectas.C: A normal fecal elastase level argues against pancreatic insufficiency and instead points toward a mucosal or other non-pancreatic cause of malabsorption, such as celiac disease, since the test is specifically measuring pancreatic secretory capacity.
incorrectas.D: Fecal elastase falls proportionally with the degree of acinar cell loss rather than becoming instantly undetectable; mild-to-moderate insufficiency often shows reduced but still measurable levels, with very low or absent levels reserved for severe disease.

preguntas.q: In pancreatic insufficiency, decreased pancreatic bicarbonate secretion has what effect on duodenal luminal pH?

e.correcta: Pancreatic ductal cells normally secrete a bicarbonate-rich fluid that neutralizes the acidic gastric chyme entering the duodenum. When exocrine function is impaired, less bicarbonate is delivered, so duodenal pH decreases (becomes more acidic). This acidic environment further impairs digestion because pancreatic lipase and other enzymes function optimally near neutral pH and because bile acids can precipitate at low pH, compounding fat malabsorption.

incorrectas.A: An increase in duodenal pH would require more acid neutralization, which is the opposite of what happens when bicarbonate secretion falls; alkalinization is not a feature of pancreatic insufficiency.
incorrectas.C: Duodenal pH is not independent of pancreatic secretion — bicarbonate output is the principal buffer of gastric acid in the proximal small bowel, so losing it necessarily shifts pH, it does not leave it unchanged.
incorrectas.D: The pH change described is a local luminal phenomenon in the duodenum, not a systemic acid-base disturbance; pancreatic insufficiency does not directly cause a measurable change in systemic blood pH via this mechanism.

preguntas.q: A patient with confirmed pancreatic insufficiency undergoes a D-xylose absorption test. What result is expected?

e.correcta: D-xylose is a pentose sugar absorbed across the proximal small bowel mucosa by passive and facilitated diffusion, a process that does not require pancreatic enzymatic digestion. Because pancreatic insufficiency leaves the intestinal mucosa itself intact, D-xylose absorption and subsequent urinary excretion remain normal, which is exactly why the test is used to distinguish pancreatic (normal xylose test) from mucosal (abnormal xylose test) causes of malabsorption.

incorrectas.A: Decreased excretion reflects a defect in the absorptive surface itself, such as celiac disease or extensive mucosal damage, or consumption of xylose by overgrown bacteria — not a pancreatic enzyme deficiency, since xylose absorption bypasses the need for pancreatic digestion.
incorrectas.B: Absent excretion would imply essentially no functional small bowel mucosa, a far more severe and different scenario than isolated exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, where the mucosa itself is normal.
incorrectas.D: There is no mechanism by which pancreatic insufficiency would increase D-xylose absorption or excretion; the test result in this condition is expected to be unchanged from normal, not elevated.

preguntas.q: Which stain is used to screen stool for excess neutral fat when malabsorption is suspected?

e.correcta: Sudan III (or Sudan IV) stain binds neutral lipids, allowing fat globules in a stool smear to be visualized directly under the microscope. A positive qualitative Sudan stain supports steatorrhea and prompts confirmatory quantitative testing (72-hour fecal fat), making it a fast first-line screen for malabsorption syndromes such as pancreatic insufficiency, celiac disease, and bile acid deficiency.

incorrectas.A: Prussian blue stains ferric iron (hemosiderin), classically used on bone marrow aspirates to assess iron stores, and has nothing to do with lipid detection in stool.
incorrectas.B: Congo red stains amyloid deposits, producing apple-green birefringence under polarized light; it is used to diagnose amyloidosis, not to detect fecal fat.
incorrectas.C: PAS (periodic acid-Schiff) stains glycogen and neutral mucopolysaccharides, and is notably used to highlight PAS-positive macrophages in Whipple disease, but it does not selectively mark neutral lipid the way Sudan stain does.

preguntas.q: Fat malabsorption in abetalipoproteinemia results from defective formation of which apoB-48-containing lipoprotein particle in enterocytes?

e.correcta: Abetalipoproteinemia is caused by mutations in microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP), which is required to lipidate apolipoprotein B within enterocytes and hepatocytes. Without functional MTP, enterocytes cannot package absorbed dietary triglycerides and cholesterol with apoB-48 into chylomicrons, so absorbed lipid cannot be exported from the intestinal cell into lymphatics — producing fat malabsorption, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, acanthocytosis, and later ataxia and retinitis pigmentosa from vitamin E deficiency.

incorrectas.B: VLDL is also affected by loss of MTP (since it requires apoB-100 and is assembled in the liver), but VLDL is a hepatic export particle for endogenous lipid, not the intestinal particle responsible for absorbing dietary fat, which is what drives the malabsorption.
incorrectas.C: LDL is generated in the circulation from VLDL catabolism rather than being directly assembled in enterocytes or hepatocytes; its absence in abetalipoproteinemia is a downstream consequence of low VLDL, not the primary defect causing dietary fat malabsorption.
incorrectas.D: HDL is synthesized independently of MTP-mediated apoB lipidation and functions in reverse cholesterol transport; it is not involved in packaging dietary lipid for intestinal absorption, so it is unaffected in the way chylomicron formation is.

preguntas.q: Which autosomal recessive disorder presents with absent plasma VLDL and LDL because hepatocytes cannot properly lipidate apoB-100?

e.correcta: Abetalipoproteinemia results from loss-of-function mutations in microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP), which is needed to lipidate both apoB-48 in enterocytes and apoB-100 in hepatocytes. Because hepatic VLDL assembly requires apoB-100 lipidation, VLDL (and the LDL derived from it) is essentially absent from plasma, contributing to the classic clinical triad of fat malabsorption, acanthocytosis, and neurologic/ophthalmologic findings from fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.

incorrectas.A: Familial hypercholesterolemia is caused by a defective or absent LDL receptor, which impairs LDL clearance and produces markedly elevated, not absent, plasma LDL — essentially the opposite lipid pattern.
incorrectas.C: Tangier disease is caused by ABCA1 mutations that impair cholesterol efflux and nascent HDL formation, leading to very low or absent HDL, not absent VLDL/LDL, and does not involve defective apoB lipidation.
incorrectas.D: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency impairs hydrolysis of triglycerides within circulating chylomicrons and VLDL, causing these particles to accumulate (increase) in plasma rather than disappear, the reverse of the abetalipoproteinemia pattern.

preguntas.q: Carcinoid tumors are a low-grade malignant proliferation of which cell type?

e.correcta: Carcinoid tumors arise from neuroendocrine cells that are scattered throughout the gastrointestinal (and bronchopulmonary) mucosa as part of the diffuse neuroendocrine system. These cells contain dense-core secretory granules and can synthesize bioactive amines and peptides, most notably serotonin, which underlies carcinoid syndrome once tumor burden is high enough. Because they are well-differentiated, carcinoid tumors typically behave as low-grade malignancies with slower growth than conventional adenocarcinomas, though they retain metastatic potential.

incorrectas.A: Goblet cells are mucin-secreting epithelial cells of the intestinal lining; their malignant transformation gives rise to mucinous adenocarcinomas, not neuroendocrine tumors like carcinoid.
incorrectas.B: Paneth cells reside in the crypts of the small intestine and secrete antimicrobial peptides such as defensins and lysozyme; they are not the cell of origin for carcinoid tumors.
incorrectas.D: Interstitial cells of Cajal are the pacemaker cells of the GI tract's smooth muscle layer, and their neoplastic proliferation produces gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs), a completely different tumor lineage from carcinoid.

preguntas.q: Which immunohistochemical marker of neurosecretory granules stains positive in carcinoid tumor cells, alongside synaptophysin?

e.correcta: Chromogranin A is a protein packaged within the dense-core secretory granules of neuroendocrine cells. Immunohistochemical positivity for chromogranin A, together with synaptophysin, confirms neuroendocrine differentiation of a tumor and is a standard diagnostic marker used to identify carcinoid tumors and other neuroendocrine neoplasms.

incorrectas.A: CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen) is a nonspecific tumor marker elevated in colorectal and other adenocarcinomas; it reflects glandular epithelial differentiation, not the neurosecretory granule content that defines neuroendocrine tumors.
incorrectas.B: CA 19-9 is classically associated with pancreatic and biliary tract adenocarcinomas and has no relationship to the secretory granule proteins found in neuroendocrine cells.
incorrectas.C: Alpha-fetoprotein is a marker for hepatocellular carcinoma and yolk sac tumors, reflecting a completely different cell lineage and is not a component of neuroendocrine secretory granules.

preguntas.q: Although carcinoid tumors may arise anywhere along the gut, they most commonly originate in which location?

e.correcta: The small bowel, particularly the ileum, is the most common site along the gastrointestinal tract for carcinoid tumors, where they classically grow as a submucosal, polyp-like nodule. Small bowel carcinoids are also the subtype most likely to cause mesenteric fibrosis, bowel obstruction, and to metastasize to the liver, making them the ones most often responsible for producing carcinoid syndrome.

incorrectas.B: The appendix is a very common site for incidentally discovered carcinoid tumors, often found in appendectomy specimens, but these tend to be small and behave more indolently, making them less often the answer when asked about the overall most common site along the gut.
incorrectas.C: Gastric carcinoids do occur, often in the setting of chronic atrophic gastritis or Zollinger-Ellison syndrome with ECL-cell hyperplasia, but they are considerably less common overall than small bowel carcinoids.
incorrectas.D: Rectal carcinoids are frequently found incidentally on colonoscopy and tend to be small and low-risk, but they do not represent the most common site for GI carcinoid tumors as a whole.

preguntas.q: What is the most common malignant tumor of the small intestine?

e.correcta: Carcinoid tumor, a well-differentiated neuroendocrine neoplasm, is the most common malignancy of the small intestine overall. Histologically these tumors classically show nests of uniform cells arranged in rosette-like patterns, reflecting their neuroendocrine origin, and they can produce serotonin and other secretory products that drive carcinoid syndrome once metastatic.

incorrectas.A: Adenocarcinoma is the dominant malignancy in the stomach and colon, and does occur in the small bowel (especially the duodenum), but it is less common there than carcinoid tumor, reversing the pattern seen in the rest of the GI tract.
incorrectas.C: Small bowel lymphoma does occur, including MALT-type lymphoma and lymphoma associated with untreated celiac disease, but it is encountered less frequently than carcinoid tumor as the leading small intestinal malignancy.
incorrectas.D: GISTs arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal and can occur throughout the GI tract including the small bowel, but they are overall less common there than carcinoid tumors.

preguntas.q: Which neurotransmitter/hormone is most classically secreted by carcinoid tumors?

e.correcta: Carcinoid tumor cells derive from enterochromaffin (neuroendocrine) cells and characteristically secrete serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) as their predominant bioactive product. Once serotonin escapes hepatic and pulmonary metabolism to reach the systemic circulation, it drives the classic features of carcinoid syndrome: flushing, secretory diarrhea, bronchospasm, and right-sided cardiac valve fibrosis.

incorrectas.A: Dopamine is the characteristic secretory product of tumors such as pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma and neuroblastoma, not the primary mediator classically tested for carcinoid tumors.
incorrectas.B: Norepinephrine excess is the hallmark of pheochromocytoma, producing episodic hypertension, tachycardia, and diaphoresis, distinct from the serotonin-driven presentation of carcinoid syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Histamine can be co-secreted by some carcinoid tumors, particularly gastric ECL-cell-derived ones, and can contribute to flushing, but serotonin remains the classic, predominant secretory product associated with carcinoid tumors as a group.

preguntas.q: Carcinoid syndrome is characterized by increased urinary excretion of which serotonin metabolite?

e.correcta: Serotonin released by carcinoid tumor cells is broken down by monoamine oxidase, largely in the liver, into 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), which is then excreted in the urine. Measuring 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA is the classic diagnostic test for carcinoid syndrome, since elevated levels reflect the high serotonin turnover characteristic of an active, systemically secreting tumor.

incorrectas.A: Homovanillic acid is the breakdown product of dopamine and is used mainly in the workup of neuroblastoma, not in evaluating serotonin-secreting carcinoid tumors.
incorrectas.B: Vanillylmandelic acid is a catecholamine (epinephrine/norepinephrine) metabolite classically elevated in pheochromocytoma, reflecting a different amine pathway than serotonin metabolism.
incorrectas.C: Metanephrines, like VMA, are catecholamine metabolites used to screen for pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma; they do not reflect serotonin turnover and are not the test used for carcinoid syndrome.

preguntas.q: In carcinoid syndrome, hepatic metastasis of a GI carcinoid tumor allows serotonin to reach the systemic circulation by bypassing which process?

e.correcta: Serotonin released by a GI carcinoid tumor normally drains via the portal vein directly to the liver, where monoamine oxidase metabolizes it before it can enter the systemic circulation — this is hepatic first-pass metabolism. When the tumor metastasizes to the liver itself, serotonin is secreted straight into the hepatic veins, bypassing this protective clearance step and reaching systemic circulation in high enough concentrations to produce flushing, diarrhea, bronchospasm, and right-sided valvular fibrosis.

incorrectas.B: Renal filtration is relevant to excreting the serotonin metabolite 5-HIAA into urine, not to the mechanism that normally clears active serotonin from the blood before it can act systemically.
incorrectas.C: Pulmonary MAO does provide a secondary clearance mechanism for serotonin (explaining why left-sided valve lesions are typically spared), but the specific first-pass step bypassed by hepatic metastasis is hepatic, not pulmonary, metabolism.
incorrectas.D: Enterohepatic recirculation describes the recycling of substances like bile acids and bilirubin between the gut and liver via bile, which is a different physiologic circuit than the direct hepatic metabolism of portal venous serotonin.

preguntas.q: Why are left-sided cardiac valve lesions typically absent in carcinoid syndrome, in the absence of a right-to-left shunt or a primary lung carcinoid?

o.A: The left heart valves lack serotonin receptors
o.B: The lungs contain MAO that metabolizes serotonin before it reaches the left heart
o.C: Serotonin is degraded by hepatic first-pass metabolism before reaching the left heart
o.D: The pulmonic valve is inherently more susceptible to fibrosis than the mitral or aortic valve

e.correcta: Serotonin-laden venous blood from a metastatic GI carcinoid reaches the right heart first, depositing fibrous plaques on the tricuspid and pulmonic valves. Before that blood can reach the left heart, it must pass through the pulmonary circulation, where monoamine oxidase in the lung further metabolizes and inactivates serotonin — sparing the left-sided valves from the same chronic exposure. This is precisely why left-sided valve lesions in a carcinoid patient should raise suspicion for either a primary bronchopulmonary carcinoid or a right-to-left cardiac shunt allowing serotonin to bypass pulmonary clearance.

incorrectas.A: The valve lesions of carcinoid heart disease result from direct chronic exposure of endocardial tissue to serotonin causing plaque-like fibrous deposition, not from differences in receptor expression between right- and left-sided valves.
incorrectas.C: Hepatic first-pass metabolism is already bypassed in metastatic disease — that is precisely why systemic serotonin levels rise enough to cause syndrome symptoms in the first place; it explains why the syndrome occurs at all, not why the left-sided valves specifically are spared.
incorrectas.D: The pattern of valve involvement is explained by differential serotonin exposure due to circulatory anatomy, not by an intrinsic difference in fibrosis susceptibility among the valves themselves.

preguntas.q: A patient has a carcinoid tumor confined to the small bowel with no hepatic or other distant metastases. Is carcinoid syndrome expected to develop?

o.A: Yes, because GI carcinoid tumors always secrete directly into systemic veins
o.B: Yes, because serotonin is not metabolized in the liver
o.C: No, because serotonin undergoes hepatic first-pass metabolism via the portal circulation
o.D: No, because tumors confined to the GI tract cannot produce serotonin

e.correcta: When a carcinoid tumor is confined to the GI tract, its venous drainage passes through the portal vein to the liver before entering the systemic circulation, and hepatic monoamine oxidase efficiently metabolizes the secreted serotonin during this first pass. As a result, carcinoid syndrome typically requires either hepatic metastases (which bypass this clearance) or a primary tumor whose venous drainage does not route through the liver, such as an ovarian or bronchial carcinoid.

incorrectas.A: GI carcinoid tumors drain via the portal venous system to the liver, not directly into the systemic circulation, which is exactly why isolated GI tumors usually do not cause systemic symptoms.
incorrectas.B: The liver is in fact highly effective at metabolizing serotonin via monoamine oxidase; this hepatic clearance is the very reason serotonin from a localized GI tumor fails to reach the systemic circulation in sufficient quantity to cause syndrome symptoms.
incorrectas.D: The tumor does produce and secrete serotonin regardless of location; the issue is not production but that hepatic first-pass metabolism clears it before it can act systemically when the tumor and its drainage remain confined to the gut.

preguntas.q: Malignant carcinoid syndrome can precipitate a deficiency of which vitamin, potentially leading to pellagra?

e.correcta: Carcinoid tumors consume large amounts of dietary tryptophan to synthesize serotonin in excess. Because tryptophan is also the metabolic precursor used by the body to synthesize niacin (vitamin B3), this diversion in malignant carcinoid syndrome can deplete tryptophan stores enough to cause niacin deficiency, manifesting as pellagra with its classic triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia.

incorrectas.A: Thiamine deficiency produces Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome or beriberi and is unrelated to the tryptophan-diversion mechanism that links carcinoid tumors to niacin deficiency.
incorrectas.B: Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anemia and neural tube defects in pregnancy, but it is not mechanistically tied to tryptophan consumption by an overactive serotonin-producing tumor.
incorrectas.C: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord; its metabolism does not intersect with the tryptophan-to-serotonin pathway responsible for niacin depletion in carcinoid syndrome.

preguntas.q: Besides surgical resection, carcinoid syndrome may be treated medically with which class of drug that inhibits release of the tumor's bioactive peptides?

e.correcta: Somatostatin analogs such as octreotide bind somatostatin receptors expressed on neuroendocrine tumor cells, suppressing the release of serotonin and other vasoactive peptides from the tumor. This makes them a mainstay of medical management for controlling flushing, diarrhea, and other symptoms of carcinoid syndrome, particularly when curative surgical resection is not feasible.

incorrectas.B: Proton pump inhibitors block the gastric H+/K+ ATPase to reduce acid secretion, which is useful for peptic ulcer disease and GERD but has no effect on neuroendocrine peptide release from a carcinoid tumor.
incorrectas.C: Beta-blockers reduce heart rate and myocardial contractility via adrenergic receptor blockade; they do not suppress tumor peptide secretion and could theoretically aggravate bronchospasm in a carcinoid patient.
incorrectas.D: SSRIs increase synaptic serotonin availability by blocking its reuptake, which would be counterproductive in carcinoid syndrome, where the goal is to reduce, not increase, serotonin activity.

preguntas.q: Carcinoid tumors are classically associated with which epidemiologic teaching mnemonic describing their tendency toward multiplicity, metastasis, and association with a second malignancy?

e.correcta: The "rule of thirds" for carcinoid tumors is a teaching approximation that roughly one-third are multiple, one-third metastasize, and one-third are associated with a second primary malignancy. It captures the somewhat unpredictable behavior of these tumors despite their overall classification as low-grade, well-differentiated neuroendocrine neoplasms.

incorrectas.A: The "rule of 2s" is the classic mnemonic for Meckel diverticulum (occurs in about 2% of the population, located within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve, about 2 inches long, often presents by age 2), an entirely different embryologic entity from carcinoid tumor.
incorrectas.C: The "70-20-10 rule" is not an established or standard teaching mnemonic for carcinoid tumor behavior in USMLE-level material.
incorrectas.D: The "triple A rule" is not a recognized medical mnemonic associated with carcinoid tumors; no standard teaching uses this term.

preguntas.q: By definition, what is appendicitis?

o.A: Chronic inflammation of the terminal ileum
o.C: Acute inflammation of the vermiform appendix
o.D: Ischemic necrosis of the appendix without preceding inflammation

e.correcta: Appendicitis is defined as acute inflammation of the vermiform appendix, most often initiated by luminal obstruction that raises intraluminal pressure, promotes bacterial overgrowth, and triggers an inflammatory response. Left untreated, this inflammatory cascade can progress to ischemia, gangrene, and perforation, and it classically presents with pain migrating from the periumbilical region to McBurney point, along with fever and leukocytosis.

incorrectas.A: Chronic inflammation of the terminal ileum describes Crohn disease, a distinct chronic granulomatous inflammatory bowel disease with a very different time course and pathology from appendicitis.
incorrectas.B: Acute inflammation of the cecum is termed typhlitis (neutropenic enterocolitis), typically seen in immunocompromised or neutropenic patients, and is anatomically and clinically distinct from appendicitis.
incorrectas.D: Ischemia and necrosis are late secondary complications that can follow unchecked inflammation and luminal obstruction in appendicitis, not the primary defining process; appendicitis begins as an inflammatory, not primarily ischemic, condition.

preguntas.q: In children, appendicitis is most often triggered by luminal obstruction due to what process?

e.correcta: The appendiceal wall in children and young adults contains abundant lymphoid follicles. Viral or other infections can trigger reactive lymphoid hyperplasia, which narrows and obstructs the appendiceal lumen, setting off the cascade of rising intraluminal pressure, bacterial overgrowth, and inflammation that produces appendicitis — making lymphoid hyperplasia the characteristic pediatric mechanism.

incorrectas.A: Fecalith (hardened, calcified fecal material) is the more typical cause of obstruction in adults, reflecting differences in appendiceal lymphoid content and stool consistency compared with children, rather than the classic pediatric mechanism.
incorrectas.B: Appendiceal carcinoid tumor is actually the most common tumor of the appendix and can rarely obstruct it, but it is not the typical or common cause of obstruction specifically in children.
incorrectas.C: Foreign body impaction is an uncommon cause of appendiceal obstruction overall and is not the characteristic mechanism taught for pediatric appendicitis.

preguntas.q: In adults, appendicitis is most commonly caused by luminal obstruction due to what structure?

e.correcta: In adults, appendiceal lymphoid tissue is relatively less prominent than in childhood, and obstruction is more commonly caused by a fecalith — a hardened, calcified mass of fecal material — becoming impacted in the lumen. This obstruction triggers the same downstream cascade of increased intraluminal pressure, bacterial overgrowth, ischemia, and inflammation that defines appendicitis.

incorrectas.B: Lymphoid hyperplasia is the more typical mechanism in children and young adults, when appendiceal lymphoid follicles are more abundant and reactive to infection, rather than the classic adult mechanism.
incorrectas.C: Carcinoid tumor is the most common neoplasm of the appendix and can occasionally obstruct it, but it is an uncommon cause of obstruction overall compared with fecalith in the general adult population.
incorrectas.D: Parasitic worms such as Enterobius vermicularis are only a rare cause of appendiceal obstruction, occasionally noted incidentally in appendectomy specimens, not the typical adult mechanism.

preguntas.q: Rupture of an inflamed appendix leads to peritonitis, classically presenting with guarding and which additional physical exam finding?

e.correcta: Rebound tenderness — pain elicited when pressure over the abdomen is rapidly released — indicates peritoneal irritation. When an inflamed appendix ruptures and spills infected contents into the peritoneal cavity, this produces localized or diffuse peritonitis, and guarding plus rebound tenderness are the classic findings that prompt urgent surgical evaluation.

incorrectas.A: Murphy sign is inspiratory arrest triggered by palpation of the right upper quadrant during deep inspiration, a finding associated with acute cholecystitis, not appendiceal rupture or peritonitis.
incorrectas.C: Grey Turner sign is flank ecchymosis seen with retroperitoneal hemorrhage, such as in hemorrhagic pancreatitis, and is unrelated to appendiceal perforation.
incorrectas.D: Cullen sign is periumbilical ecchymosis, also associated with retroperitoneal or intra-abdominal hemorrhage (e.g., hemorrhagic pancreatitis or ruptured ectopic pregnancy), not with appendicitis-related peritonitis.

preguntas.q: Which physical exam sign for appendicitis is elicited by passive flexion and internal rotation of the right hip?

e.correcta: The obturator sign is positive when passive flexion and internal rotation of the hip stretches the obturator internus muscle, which lies adjacent to a pelvic or retrocecal inflamed appendix, reproducing the patient's pain. A positive test suggests inflammation near the obturator internus, supporting an appendiceal or other pelvic inflammatory process located low in the pelvis.

incorrectas.A: The psoas sign is elicited by passive extension of the hip (or active hip flexion against resistance), which stretches the iliopsoas muscle and is associated with a retrocecal appendix or psoas abscess — a distinct maneuver from hip flexion with internal rotation.
incorrectas.B: Rovsing sign is elicited by palpating the left lower quadrant and observing referred pain in the right lower quadrant, reflecting peritoneal irritation, not a hip movement maneuver at all.
incorrectas.D: McBurney point tenderness is direct palpation tenderness at a fixed anatomic point (roughly one-third of the distance from the ASIS to the umbilicus), not a passive hip movement test.

preguntas.q: The psoas sign, elicited by passive extension of the right hip, is a sensitive finding for appendicitis but has a key limitation. What is it?

o.A: It is only positive in children
o.B: It requires CT confirmation before it is considered clinically valid
o.C: It is caused exclusively by psoas abscess and never by appendicitis
o.D: It is nonspecific, as it can be positive with any retroperitoneal or psoas muscle irritation/inflammation

e.correcta: The psoas sign reflects irritation of the iliopsoas muscle, which sits in the retroperitoneum. A retrocecal, retroperitoneally positioned inflamed appendix can trigger it, but so can any other process irritating that space, such as a primary psoas abscess or other retroperitoneal inflammation — making the sign sensitive for retroperitoneal irritation broadly but not specific to appendicitis.

incorrectas.A: The sign is not restricted to children; it is used across age groups and reflects an anatomic relationship between the iliopsoas muscle and a retrocecal appendix or adjacent retroperitoneal process, not an age-dependent physiologic response.
incorrectas.B: The psoas sign is a bedside physical exam maneuver that can raise clinical suspicion on its own; imaging such as CT or ultrasound may be used separately to confirm a diagnosis, but the sign itself does not require CT to be clinically meaningful.
incorrectas.C: The sign is not exclusive to psoas abscess — its very lack of specificity comes from the fact that it can be triggered by either a retrocecal appendicitis or a true psoas abscess, rather than being caused by only one of these conditions.

preguntas.q: Which appendicitis sign is elicited by palpating the left iliac fossa and observing pain referred to the right iliac fossa?

e.correcta: The Rovsing sign is positive when palpation of the left lower quadrant produces pain in the right lower quadrant. Pressure on the left side shifts bowel contents and gas, indirectly increasing pressure and traction on the already-inflamed peritoneum overlying the appendix on the right, reproducing referred pain and supporting a diagnosis of appendicitis.

incorrectas.B: The obturator sign is elicited by passive hip flexion with internal rotation, testing for obturator internus muscle irritation from a pelvic or retrocecal appendix, a distinct maneuver from cross-abdominal palpation.
incorrectas.C: The psoas sign is elicited by passive hip extension, testing for iliopsoas irritation from a retrocecal appendix, and does not involve palpating the contralateral abdomen.
incorrectas.D: Murphy sign involves palpation of the right upper quadrant during inspiration to test for gallbladder inflammation (cholecystitis) and is unrelated to appendiceal pathology or the crossed-palpation technique of Rovsing sign.

preguntas.q: A patient with appendicitis develops a localized, walled-off collection of pus adjacent to the appendix. What is this complication called?

e.correcta: When appendicitis progresses beyond simple luminal obstruction and inflammation, the appendix can perforate in a contained fashion, with adjacent tissues and omentum walling off the resulting collection of pus into a periappendiceal abscess. This is distinguished from free perforation because the body's peritoneal defenses (omentum, adjacent bowel loops) manage to localize the infection, producing a palpable mass with fever and localized peritoneal signs rather than diffuse peritonitis. Recognizing this complication matters clinically because a walled-off abscess is often managed with image-guided percutaneous drainage and interval appendectomy rather than emergent surgery.

incorrectas.B: A phlegmon is an inflammatory mass of solid, edematous, inflamed tissue without a discrete, drainable pus collection, in contrast to an abscess, which has a defined fluid-filled cavity that can be aspirated or drained. Phlegmons are typically managed with antibiotics alone since there is no collection to drain.
incorrectas.C: Generalized peritonitis results when the appendix perforates freely into the peritoneal cavity without being walled off, spreading infection diffusely rather than localizing it into a discrete collection; this presents with diffuse rebound and guarding rather than a localized mass.
incorrectas.D: Pylephlebitis is septic thrombophlebitis of the portal venous system, a rare complication in which infection tracks from the appendix (or other abdominal source) into the portal vein, causing fever and potentially liver abscesses; it is a vascular complication rather than a localized soft-tissue collection like a periappendiceal abscess.

preguntas.q: Inflammatory bowel disease classically presents with recurrent bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain in which demographic group?

e.correcta: IBD, particularly ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease, classically presents in young adulthood, with a modest female predominance. Because the presenting symptoms—recurrent bloody diarrhea and cramping abdominal pain—overlap heavily with infectious colitis, irritable bowel syndrome, and other causes of bowel inflammation, IBD is often considered a diagnosis of exclusion once these mimics have been ruled out. Recognizing the typical demographic helps raise clinical suspicion early in a young woman with recurrent, unexplained bloody diarrhea.

incorrectas.A: While IBD certainly occurs in young men, the classic epidemiologic pattern taught for IBD leans toward a female predominance in the young-adult-onset peak, making this a less accurate description of the typical presenting demographic.
incorrectas.C: IBD has a bimodal age distribution with a second smaller peak later in life, but the classic, most commonly tested presentation is in young adulthood rather than in elderly men, and the elderly-onset peak does not carry the same female predominance.
incorrectas.D: IBD can begin in adolescence, but the demographic classically emphasized on Step 1 is young women in their teens to thirties, not specifically adolescent boys.

preguntas.q: Which form of inflammatory bowel disease is characterized by ulceration limited to the mucosa and submucosa, without transmural involvement?

e.correcta: Ulcerative colitis is defined pathologically by inflammation that is confined to the mucosa and submucosa, producing continuous, superficial ulcers without deeper wall involvement. Because the inflammation does not penetrate the muscularis propria or serosa, UC does not form fistulas or abscesses the way transmural Crohn disease does, but the superficial ulceration and crypt abscesses account for the bloody diarrhea that is a hallmark of the disease. This mucosal-only pattern is also why UC carries a distinct risk for toxic megacolon, since the thinned, inflamed wall dilates and is prone to perforation.

incorrectas.A: Crohn disease involves transmural inflammation that extends through the full thickness of the bowel wall, from mucosa to serosa, which is why it produces deep fissures, fistulas, and abscesses—findings that do not occur with a purely mucosal/submucosal process like UC.
incorrectas.B: Microscopic colitis causes chronic watery (non-bloody) diarrhea with a grossly normal-appearing colon; the diagnosis requires biopsy to see lymphocytic or collagenous inflammation, and it does not produce visible mucosal or submucosal ulcers the way UC does.
incorrectas.D: Ischemic colitis results from reduced blood flow to watershed areas of the colon (e.g., splenic flexure), causing mucosal injury and bloody diarrhea, but it is an acute vascular insult rather than a chronic autoimmune process confined to the mucosa/submucosa like UC.

preguntas.q: Which form of IBD is characterized by transmural inflammation with deep, linear 'knife-like' fissures?

e.correcta: Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation that extends through the entire bowel wall, and the deep linear ulcers that penetrate toward the serosa are classically described as 'knife-like' fissures. These fissures are the anatomic basis for Crohn's tendency to form fistulas and sinus tracts, since a fissure that fully penetrates the wall creates a channel that can connect to adjacent organs or skin. This full-thickness pattern also explains why Crohn causes strictures and a thickened, cobblestoned bowel wall, unlike the superficial disease of ulcerative colitis.

incorrectas.A: Ulcerative colitis is limited to the mucosa and submucosa, producing continuous superficial ulceration rather than the deep, knife-like transmural fissures seen in Crohn disease, which is why UC does not typically cause fistulas.
incorrectas.B: Microscopic colitis shows a grossly normal colon with only microscopic lymphocytic or collagenous inflammation on biopsy, the opposite of the grossly visible, deep transmural fissuring that defines Crohn disease.
incorrectas.C: Pseudomembranous colitis, caused by Clostridioides difficile toxin, produces adherent yellow-white mucosal plaques (pseudomembranes) from superficial mucosal damage, not the deep transmural fissures characteristic of Crohn disease.

preguntas.q: Which form of IBD is characterized by continuous colonic lesions that always involve the rectum?

e.correcta: Ulcerative colitis begins in the rectum and extends proximally in a continuous, uninterrupted fashion without skip lesions, which is why the rectum is essentially always involved in UC. This continuous rectal-based pattern is a key distinguishing feature from Crohn disease, which characteristically produces skip lesions and often spares the rectum. Recognizing that UC always involves the rectum is clinically useful on colonoscopy and helps explain the tenesmus and urgency that UC patients often report.

incorrectas.B: Crohn disease is characterized by skip lesions—discontinuous patches of inflammation with intervening normal mucosa—and classically spares the rectum, the opposite of the continuous, rectum-involving pattern of UC.
incorrectas.C: Ischemic colitis typically affects watershed regions like the splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction due to reduced perfusion, but it is an acute, patchy vascular process rather than a continuous, rectum-originating chronic inflammatory disease like UC.
incorrectas.D: Diverticulitis reflects inflammation/infection of colonic diverticula, most often in the sigmoid colon, and is a focal process rather than the continuous, rectum-based mucosal inflammation seen in ulcerative colitis.

preguntas.q: Crohn disease most commonly involves which segment of the GI tract?

e.correcta: Crohn disease can affect any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus, but it most commonly involves the terminal ileum, which is why patients often present with right lower quadrant pain that can mimic appendicitis. The terminal ileum is also the primary site of vitamin B12 and bile acid absorption, so Crohn disease affecting this region can cause B12 deficiency and bile acid malabsorption diarrhea. This ileal predilection, combined with skip lesions, is a key distinguishing feature from ulcerative colitis, which never involves the small bowel (except for rare 'backwash ileitis').

incorrectas.A: The rectum is classically spared in Crohn disease (in contrast to ulcerative colitis, which always involves it), so it is not the most common site of Crohn involvement.
incorrectas.C: The duodenum can rarely be involved in Crohn disease, but it is far less commonly affected than the terminal ileum and is not the classic site emphasized for Crohn disease.
incorrectas.D: The sigmoid colon can be affected in Crohn disease as part of a skip-lesion pattern, but the terminal ileum is the single most commonly and classically involved segment, which is why the disease is sometimes still colloquially linked to ileitis.

preguntas.q: Which form of inflammatory bowel disease typically spares the rectum?

e.correcta: Crohn disease characteristically produces skip lesions with discontinuous segments of inflamed bowel, and the rectum is typically spared even when other regions of the colon are severely diseased. This rectal sparing, combined with the tendency toward terminal ileal involvement, is one of the classic gross features used to distinguish Crohn disease from ulcerative colitis on endoscopy and imaging. Clinically, rectal sparing also means Crohn patients are less likely to present with the tenesmus and urgency typical of UC, since the rectal mucosa is often relatively preserved.

incorrectas.A: Ulcerative colitis always involves the rectum as the site where the disease begins, extending proximally in continuity, which is the opposite of the rectal-sparing pattern seen in Crohn disease.
incorrectas.B: Microscopic colitis causes chronic watery diarrhea with a normal-appearing colon on gross endoscopic examination, so the concept of 'sparing' a particular segment doesn't apply the way it does to the patchy, skip-lesion pattern of Crohn disease.
incorrectas.D: Diversion colitis occurs in a segment of colon that has been surgically excluded from the fecal stream (e.g., after colostomy), causing inflammation due to lack of short-chain fatty acids, which is an unrelated process from Crohn disease's chronic autoimmune skip-lesion pattern.

preguntas.q: Which form of IBD always causes bloody diarrhea?

e.correcta: Ulcerative colitis produces continuous mucosal ulceration and crypt abscesses beginning in the rectum, and because this superficial ulceration directly involves the highly vascular mucosal surface, bloody diarrhea is essentially a universal feature of active UC. This is a key distinguishing point from Crohn disease, where diarrhea may or may not be bloody depending on which segment of bowel is involved. The reliability of bloody diarrhea in UC also makes it a useful clinical clue when trying to differentiate the two major forms of IBD at the bedside.

incorrectas.A: Crohn disease can cause bloody or non-bloody diarrhea depending on the site and depth of involvement, since its transmural, skip-lesion pattern doesn't guarantee mucosal ulceration everywhere, unlike the mucosal disease of UC which reliably bleeds.
incorrectas.B: Microscopic colitis classically causes chronic watery, non-bloody diarrhea, since the inflammation is subtle and lymphocytic/collagenous rather than ulcerative, distinguishing it clearly from the reliably bloody diarrhea of UC.
