incorrectas.B: A cyst is a dormant, resistant form used by organisms like Giardia or Entamoeba to survive harsh environments, a completely different life-cycle concept from the two-stage elementary/reticulate body system used by Chlamydia.
incorrectas.C: A trophozoite is the actively feeding, motile form of certain protozoan parasites, not a term applicable to the bacterial Chlamydia life cycle, which instead uses elementary body/reticulate body terminology.

preguntas.q: Which stage of the Chlamydia life cycle exists extracellularly and is responsible for transmitting infection to new host cells?

e.correcta: The elementary body is the compact, environmentally stable, infectious form that exists extracellularly between hosts or host cells; because it is metabolically inactive, it can survive outside a cell long enough to attach to and be taken up by a new epithelial cell, where it converts into the replicating reticulate body — this EB-to-RB-to-EB cycle is central to how Chlamydia spreads and reinfects tissue.

incorrectas.A: The reticulate body exists only intracellularly, within the protective inclusion vacuole of the host cell, where it replicates; it lacks the environmental stability needed to survive extracellularly, unlike the elementary body.
incorrectas.C: An inclusion body is the intracellular compartment containing developing reticulate and elementary bodies, a structural feature of the infected host cell rather than an independent extracellular infectious particle.
incorrectas.D: A persistent body refers to an aberrant, dormant intracellular form Chlamydia can adopt under stress, such as antibiotic exposure or immune pressure, associated with chronic/latent infection, but it is an intracellular stress-response state, not the extracellular transmissible form.

preguntas.q: During the biphasic developmental cycle of Chlamydia spp., which form resides and multiplies inside the host cell after entry?

e.correcta: The reticular body (RB) is the intracellular, metabolically active form of Chlamydia. After the infectious elementary body (EB) is endocytosed into the host cell, it reorganizes into the larger, non-infectious RB, which resides within a cytoplasmic inclusion vacuole and uses host ATP (Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular energy parasite) to replicate by binary fission. This EB-to-RB-to-EB cycle is the hallmark of the chlamydial life cycle and explains why the organism cannot be cultured on artificial media.

incorrectas.A: The elementary body is the small, dense, infectious form that is metabolically inactive and adapted for extracellular survival; it is the form that initiates infection by attaching to and entering host cells, not the form that lives and divides intracellularly.
incorrectas.C: Endospores are dormant, highly resistant survival structures formed by genera like Bacillus and Clostridium in response to nutrient deprivation; Chlamydia has no endospore stage and instead alternates between two distinct developmental forms, neither of which is a true spore.
incorrectas.D: A trophozoite is the actively feeding, motile form of protozoan parasites such as Giardia or Entamoeba, not a bacterial developmental form; Chlamydia's intracellular replicative form is specifically termed the reticular body.

preguntas.q: Which developmental form of Chlamydia divides by binary fission while inside the host cell's cytoplasmic inclusion?

e.correcta: The reticular body is the replicating intracellular form; once the elementary body converts to a reticular body inside the inclusion vacuole, it repeatedly divides by binary fission, generating many daughter reticular bodies that eventually condense back into infectious elementary bodies before the cell lyses.

incorrectas.B: The elementary body is metabolically dormant and non-replicating; it is specialized for extracellular survival and cell entry, not division, which is why it must convert to a reticular body before any replication can occur.
incorrectas.C: Endospores are dormant survival forms produced by spore-forming genera like Bacillus and Clostridium under stress, not a replicative stage; Chlamydia does not form endospores at any point in its cycle.
incorrectas.D: L-forms are bacteria that have lost their cell wall (spontaneously or under antibiotic pressure) but remain viable; this is unrelated to Chlamydia's normal biphasic life cycle, which involves two structurally distinct forms rather than a wall-deficient variant.

preguntas.q: What event triggers reticular bodies within the chlamydial inclusion to condense back into infectious elementary bodies and be released to infect new cells?

e.correcta: As the intracellular infection matures, reticular bodies asynchronously reorganize back into elementary bodies, and ultimately the host cell lyses, releasing infectious elementary bodies that go on to infect neighboring cells. This lysis step completes the developmental cycle and is the mechanism by which Chlamydia spreads from cell to cell within an infected host.

incorrectas.B: Antibodies target extracellular elementary bodies and help limit spread of released organisms, but antibody binding is not the intracellular trigger that converts reticular bodies back into elementary bodies within the inclusion.
incorrectas.C: Complement can help opsonize and neutralize free elementary bodies in the extracellular space, but Chlamydia's intracellular inclusion is largely shielded from complement, and complement is not what drives the RB-to-EB conversion.
incorrectas.D: Chlamydia actually prevents phagolysosomal fusion so its inclusion escapes the normal acidified, degradative environment; it is host cell lysis at the end of the cycle, not phagolysosomal acidification, that releases the newly formed elementary bodies.

preguntas.q: Which form of Chlamydia is the small, metabolically inactive, infectious particle responsible for initiating a new infection?

e.correcta: The elementary body (EB) is the small, electron-dense, extracellular form of Chlamydia that is metabolically inert but highly resistant to environmental stress, allowing it to survive outside a host cell. It is the EB that attaches to and is endocytosed by susceptible epithelial cells, after which it reorganizes into the replicating reticular body, so the EB is specifically the infectious particle while the RB is the intracellular replicating form.

incorrectas.A: The reticular body is the larger, metabolically active intracellular form responsible for replication, not infectivity; it is fragile outside the host cell and cannot initiate a new infection.
incorrectas.B: A trophozoite is the motile, feeding form of protozoan parasites (e.g., Giardia), not a term that applies to Chlamydia's bacterial developmental cycle.
incorrectas.D: Chlamydia does not form true endospores; that dormant, highly resistant structure is characteristic of spore-forming genera like Bacillus and Clostridium, not the chlamydial infectious particle.

preguntas.q: On microscopic examination, cells infected with Chlamydia spp. characteristically show which finding?

o.B: Cytoplasmic inclusion bodies containing reticulate bodies

e.correcta: Chlamydia replicates within a membrane-bound cytoplasmic vacuole, and the accumulation of reticulate/elementary bodies inside this vacuole forms a visible intracytoplasmic inclusion on light microscopy (classically highlighted with Giemsa or fluorescent antibody stains). Finding these inclusions in conjunctival or cervical epithelial cells is a classic diagnostic clue for chlamydial infection.

incorrectas.A: Negri bodies are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions found in neurons infected with rabies virus, reflecting viral nucleocapsid aggregates, a completely different pathogen and cell type than chlamydial epithelial inclusions.
incorrectas.C: Councilman bodies are apoptotic hepatocyte remnants seen in viral hepatitis (e.g., yellow fever), representing individual cell death, not an intracellular colony of replicating organisms like the chlamydial inclusion.
incorrectas.D: Psammoma bodies are laminated, calcified concretions seen in certain neoplasms (e.g., papillary thyroid carcinoma, meningioma, serous ovarian carcinoma) and have nothing to do with intracellular bacterial replication.

preguntas.q: Which stain is classically used to detect intracytoplasmic Chlamydia inclusions in infected cells?

e.correcta: Giemsa staining highlights the intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies formed by Chlamydia within infected epithelial cells, making it a classic method for detecting chlamydial infection, historically used on conjunctival or cervical scrapings before molecular tests became standard.

incorrectas.B: Chlamydia lacks a typical peptidoglycan-rich cell wall and does not reliably take up the Gram stain, which is why it is often described as effectively unstainable by standard Gram technique; Giemsa is used instead to visualize inclusions.
incorrectas.C: Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) staining detects mycolic-acid-containing cell walls of organisms like Mycobacterium and Nocardia; Chlamydia's cell envelope does not have this acid-fast property, so this stain would not reveal chlamydial inclusions.
incorrectas.D: India ink is used to visualize the polysaccharide capsule of Cryptococcus neoformans against a dark background; it has no role in detecting the intracellular inclusions formed by Chlamydia.

preguntas.q: What is the most commonly reported bacterial sexually transmitted infection in the United States?

e.correcta: Chlamydia trachomatis (serotypes D-K) causes the most commonly reported bacterial STI in the US, largely because infections are frequently asymptomatic (especially in women), allowing silent transmission and delayed treatment until complications like pelvic inflammatory disease or infertility arise. Its high prevalence and often subclinical presentation are why routine screening of sexually active young women is recommended.

incorrectas.A: Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes gonorrhea, the second most commonly reported bacterial STI in the US; it tends to be more symptomatic (purulent discharge) than chlamydia, which contributes to a somewhat lower reported incidence despite frequent co-infection with chlamydia.
incorrectas.C: Treponema pallidum causes syphilis, which, while a major public health concern with rising rates, is reported far less frequently than chlamydia in the US.
incorrectas.D: Haemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid, a painful genital ulcer disease that is comparatively rare in the United States, nowhere near as commonly reported as chlamydial infection.

preguntas.q: Which C. trachomatis serotypes are responsible for causing sexually transmitted infection, as opposed to trachoma?

e.correcta: C. trachomatis serotypes D-K cause the common urogenital STI (urethritis, cervicitis, and neonatal conjunctivitis/pneumonia acquired during vaginal delivery), while serotypes L1-L3 cause lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), an invasive STI affecting lymphatics and lymph nodes. Together D-K and L1-L3 represent the sexually transmitted disease-causing serotypes, distinct from the ocular serotypes A-C that cause trachoma.

incorrectas.A: Serotypes A-C cause trachoma, a chronic conjunctival infection spread by direct/fomite contact (not sexual contact) that is a leading infectious cause of blindness worldwide, the opposite of the STI-causing serotypes asked about here.
incorrectas.C: Serotypes L1-L3 do cause the STI lymphogranuloma venereum, but this option omits serotypes D-K, which cause the far more common chlamydial urethritis/cervicitis; the complete STI-causing set requires both groups.
incorrectas.D: Serotypes D-K do cause urogenital chlamydial infection, but this option omits L1-L3, which cause LGV; both serotype groups together are responsible for sexually transmitted chlamydial disease.

preguntas.q: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), caused by C. trachomatis serotypes L1-L3, is treated with which antibiotic?

e.correcta: LGV requires a prolonged course of doxycycline (typically about three weeks) because the organism invades lymphatic tissue and causes deep, granulomatous lymphadenitis (buboes) that is harder to eradicate than superficial mucosal chlamydial infection; the short course used for uncomplicated urethritis/cervicitis is inadequate for LGV.

incorrectas.B: Single-dose azithromycin is effective for uncomplicated urogenital chlamydia (D-K serotypes) but is not the standard regimen for LGV, which needs the longer doxycycline course to clear the invasive lymphatic infection.
incorrectas.C: Intramuscular penicillin G is the treatment for syphilis (Treponema pallidum), a spirochete unrelated to Chlamydia; it has no role in treating LGV.
incorrectas.D: Ceftriaxone is used to treat gonorrhea (Neisseria gonorrhoeae), not chlamydial infections including LGV, since Chlamydia lacks the cell wall target that beta-lactams like ceftriaxone act on.

preguntas.q: Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes A, B, and C cause trachoma, which is recognized as which of the following?

o.A: The most common infectious cause of diabetic vision loss
o.B: A late complication of untreated congenital syphilis
o.C: The most common infectious cause of blindness worldwide
o.D: A viral cause of hemorrhagic conjunctivitis

e.correcta: Trachoma, caused by chronic conjunctival infection with C. trachomatis serotypes A-C, is classically taught as the leading infectious cause of blindness worldwide, driven by repeated infection causing conjunctival scarring, in-turned eyelashes (trichiasis), and corneal damage. It remains endemic in resource-limited regions of Africa, reflecting poor access to the hygiene and treatment resources needed to interrupt transmission.

incorrectas.A: Diabetic retinopathy is a vascular, non-infectious complication of chronic hyperglycemia damaging retinal microvasculature; it is unrelated to chlamydial infection and is not what trachoma refers to.
incorrectas.B: Congenital syphilis produces its own distinctive findings (Hutchinson teeth, saddle nose, interstitial keratitis), but trachoma is a separate, unrelated ocular disease caused by C. trachomatis serotypes A-C acquired through direct or fomite spread, not congenitally via T. pallidum.
incorrectas.D: Trachoma is a bacterial (chlamydial), not viral, conjunctival disease, and while it causes scarring conjunctivitis, its hallmark clinical significance is being a leading infectious cause of blindness, not an acute hemorrhagic presentation.

preguntas.q: Trachoma caused by C. trachomatis serotypes A-C must be treated with macrolides given by which route to be effective?

e.correcta: Oral macrolides (e.g., erythromycin or azithromycin) are required to treat trachoma because topical therapy alone does not achieve adequate tissue concentrations to eradicate the chronic, recurrent conjunctival infection; systemic dosing ensures the drug reaches infected conjunctival and tarsal tissue thoroughly enough to prevent the scarring and trichiasis that lead to blindness.

incorrectas.B: Topical eye drops alone are insufficient for trachoma because the chronic, deeply seated conjunctival infection is not reliably cleared by local application; oral therapy is needed for adequate systemic and tissue drug levels.
incorrectas.C: Intravenous macrolide administration is not standard for trachoma treatment; oral dosing achieves sufficient levels for this outpatient-managed, chronic ocular infection without the need for IV access.
incorrectas.D: Subconjunctival injection is not part of standard trachoma management; treatment relies on systemic oral macrolide therapy (often via mass drug administration programs in endemic areas), not local injection.

preguntas.q: Because co-infection is common, a patient diagnosed with chlamydia has classically also been empirically treated for which other sexually transmitted infection?

e.correcta: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae frequently co-infect the same patient because they share transmission routes and risk factors, and gonococcal infection can also be under-detected on initial testing. Historical practice has therefore been to empirically cover gonorrhea when treating chlamydia (and vice versa) to avoid missing a concurrent infection, though current guidelines increasingly favor confirmed dual testing over blanket empiric treatment.

incorrectas.A: Syphilis (T. pallidum) is an important STI to screen for, but the classic teaching about empiric dual coverage in chlamydia treatment specifically pairs chlamydia with gonorrhea, not syphilis, reflecting their particularly high rates of true co-infection.
incorrectas.C: Trichomonas vaginalis causes vaginitis with a different treatment (metronidazole/tinidazole), and while it should be considered in the differential of vaginal discharge, it is not the STI classically linked with empiric co-treatment of chlamydia the way gonorrhea is.
incorrectas.D: HSV-2 causes genital herpes, a viral infection requiring antiviral (not antibiotic) therapy; it is not part of the classic empiric antibiotic co-treatment paired with chlamydia.

preguntas.q: What is the characteristic morphology of Treponema pallidum?

e.correcta: Treponema pallidum is a thin, tightly coiled spirochete, a helical bacterium whose spiral shape and motility (via periplasmic flagella/axial filaments) allow it to penetrate mucosal surfaces and disseminate through tissue, underlying syphilis's characteristic progression from a localized chancre to systemic secondary disease. Its thinness also explains why it is too narrow to be seen with standard light microscopy or Gram stain, requiring darkfield microscopy instead.

incorrectas.A: A comma-shaped curved rod describes organisms like Vibrio cholerae, not Treponema pallidum, which has a much more tightly coiled, elongated spiral morphology characteristic of spirochetes.
incorrectas.B: Branching filamentous morphology is characteristic of Actinomyces or Nocardia, which grow as filamentous, sometimes beaded structures; this is a completely different bacterial architecture from the coiled spirochete form of T. pallidum.
incorrectas.C: Club-shaped rods with metachromatic (Babes-Ernst) granules describe Corynebacterium diphtheriae on special stains; T. pallidum does not share this morphology or staining pattern.

preguntas.q: Because Treponema pallidum is too thin to be seen with standard light microscopy or Gram stain, which technique is needed for its direct visualization?

e.correcta: Darkfield microscopy illuminates the specimen from the side so that only light scattered by the thin, coiled treponemes reaches the observer's eye, making the organism visible against a dark background despite being below the resolution normally needed for standard bright-field viewing. This technique allows direct visualization of motile spirochetes from a chancre swab, providing rapid diagnosis of primary syphilis before serologic tests may even turn positive.

incorrectas.B: Gram stain relies on differential retention of crystal violet based on cell wall peptidoglycan content and organism thickness; T. pallidum is too thin to be reliably visualized this way, which is precisely why darkfield microscopy is required instead.
incorrectas.C: Giemsa stain is useful for visualizing structures like malaria parasites or chlamydial inclusions, but it does not provide adequate resolution or contrast to directly visualize the very thin treponemal spirochetes.
incorrectas.D: Ziehl-Neelsen acid-fast staining detects mycolic-acid-containing organisms like Mycobacterium; T. pallidum is not acid-fast and this stain would not reveal it.

preguntas.q: A positive nontreponemal screening test for syphilis (VDRL or RPR) is confirmed using which test?

o.D: PCR for Treponema pallidum DNA from blood

e.correcta: FTA-ABS specifically detects antibodies directed against Treponema pallidum antigens, making it a confirmatory treponemal test used after a positive nontreponemal screen (VDRL/RPR), which instead detects nonspecific antibodies against cardiolipin and can give false positives (e.g., in SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome, or other infections). Because FTA-ABS targets the organism itself, it remains reactive lifelong even after successful treatment, functionally distinguishing it from the nontreponemal tests used to track disease activity.

incorrectas.A: Western blot is the classic confirmatory test used for HIV diagnosis after a reactive screening ELISA, not for confirming syphilis; syphilis confirmation instead relies on treponemal-specific tests like FTA-ABS or TP-PA.
incorrectas.B: ELISA for HIV antibodies screens for a completely different infection (HIV); it plays no role in confirming a positive syphilis screening test, though HIV testing is often appropriately offered alongside syphilis testing given shared risk factors.
incorrectas.D: While treponemal PCR exists in research/reference settings, it is not the standard confirmatory test in clinical practice for a positive VDRL/RPR; FTA-ABS (antibody-based) remains the classic confirmatory treponemal test taught for this purpose.

preguntas.q: How is secondary syphilis best characterized in terms of disease distribution?

o.A: A localized infection confined to the site of the primary chancre
o.B: A systemic disease, no longer localized to the genital region
o.C: A disease limited to the central nervous system
o.D: A disease confined to regional lymph nodes only

e.correcta: Secondary syphilis reflects hematogenous and lymphatic dissemination of Treponema pallidum from the primary chancre, producing systemic manifestations such as a diffuse maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles, condyloma lata, generalized lymphadenopathy, and constitutional symptoms. This systemic spread distinguishes secondary syphilis from the localized primary chancre and underscores why untreated secondary syphilis can seed distant sites, setting the stage for later tertiary disease.

incorrectas.A: A lesion confined to the site of inoculation describes primary syphilis (the painless chancre), which precedes secondary syphilis; by the secondary stage the organism has already disseminated well beyond the original genital lesion.
incorrectas.C: Confinement to the CNS describes neurosyphilis, which can occur at any stage but is a specific manifestation, not a description of secondary syphilis as a whole, which involves widespread mucocutaneous and systemic findings, not an isolated CNS process.
incorrectas.D: While lymphadenopathy is part of secondary syphilis, the disease is not limited to lymph nodes; it involves skin, mucous membranes, and other organ systems simultaneously, reflecting true systemic dissemination rather than regional lymphatic confinement.

preguntas.q: Gummas, granulomatous lesions that can occur on the skin, bones, or internal organs, are a hallmark of which stage of syphilis?

e.correcta: Gummas are chronic granulomatous lesions with central necrosis that develop years after untreated infection, representing a delayed-type hypersensitivity response to residual Treponema pallidum antigens; they are a hallmark of tertiary syphilis, alongside cardiovascular complications (aortitis, aortic aneurysm) and neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis, general paresis). Their granulomatous, destructive nature in skin, bone, and viscera reflects the chronic immune-mediated damage that defines this late stage of disease.

incorrectas.A: Primary syphilis is defined by the painless chancre at the site of inoculation, occurring weeks after exposure, long before the chronic granulomatous gumma formation that characterizes tertiary disease years later.
incorrectas.B: Secondary syphilis presents with disseminated mucocutaneous findings like rash, condyloma lata, and lymphadenopathy from active systemic spread, not the chronic granulomatous gummas that only appear after years of untreated latent infection.
incorrectas.D: Congenital syphilis produces its own characteristic findings (Hutchinson teeth, saddle nose, saber shins, rhagades) from transplacental transmission, distinct from the granulomatous gummas that develop in adults with longstanding untreated tertiary disease.

preguntas.q: The high-stepping gait with foot-slapping seen in tabes dorsalis results from loss of which sensory modality?

e.correcta: Tabes dorsalis results from syphilitic degeneration of the dorsal columns and dorsal roots, which carry proprioceptive input needed to sense limb and joint position. Without this feedback, patients cannot sense where their feet are in space, so they compensate by lifting their legs unusually high and slapping their feet down forcefully to get tactile confirmation of foot placement, producing the classic high-stepping, slapping gait.

incorrectas.A: Pain and temperature sensation travels via the spinothalamic tract, which is not the primary pathway damaged in tabes dorsalis; the gait disturbance specifically reflects dorsal column proprioceptive loss, not loss of spinothalamic modalities.
incorrectas.C: Motor strength is carried by the corticospinal tract and is classically preserved in tabes dorsalis, which is a sensory (dorsal column) disorder; the gait abnormality is due to sensory ataxia, not weakness.
incorrectas.D: While fine touch does travel with proprioception in the dorsal columns, isolating it as 'fine touch only' misses that the specific deficit driving this gait is loss of proprioceptive/position sense, which the patient compensates for visually and by forceful heel strike.

preguntas.q: Loss of deep tendon reflexes (DTRs) in tabes dorsalis occurs due to degeneration of which structure?

e.correcta: Tabes dorsalis is caused by chronic syphilitic inflammation and degeneration of the dorsal (posterior) nerve roots and dorsal columns, which carry the afferent limb of the deep tendon reflex arc. Because DTRs depend on intact sensory input from muscle spindles traveling through these dorsal roots, their degeneration interrupts the reflex arc and produces loss of DTRs, alongside the proprioceptive and vibratory sensory loss also caused by this same pathology.

incorrectas.A: Anterior horn cells house the lower motor neurons that form the efferent limb of the reflex arc; their degeneration (as in poliomyelitis or ALS) would cause flaccid weakness and areflexia through a motor mechanism, not the sensory dorsal root pathology specific to tabes dorsalis.
incorrectas.B: The lateral corticospinal tract carries descending voluntary motor commands and its damage produces upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia), essentially the opposite reflex change from the hyporeflexia/areflexia seen in tabes dorsalis.
incorrectas.C: Peripheral motor nerve degeneration would primarily impair the motor (efferent) limb of reflexes and cause weakness; tabes dorsalis instead selectively damages the sensory dorsal roots and columns, disrupting reflexes via the afferent limb.

preguntas.q: A positive Romberg sign in tabes dorsalis (worsened imbalance with eyes closed) reflects loss of which sensory modality?

e.correcta: The Romberg test isolates proprioceptive deficits: patients with tabes dorsalis rely on visual input to compensate for lost dorsal column proprioceptive feedback about limb and trunk position, so they can stand steadily with eyes open but become markedly unsteady or fall when vision is removed. A positive Romberg sign therefore localizes the problem to proprioceptive (dorsal column) pathways rather than to the cerebellum or vestibular system, which would cause instability even with eyes open.

incorrectas.B: Vestibular dysfunction typically causes imbalance and nystagmus regardless of whether the eyes are open, since the vestibular system provides its own independent input about head position; this is not the sensory deficit isolated by the Romberg maneuver in tabes dorsalis.
incorrectas.C: Visual acuity loss would impair vision itself but would not selectively worsen balance only when the eyes are closed in the specific way that identifies a proprioceptive Romberg sign; the test specifically removes the visual compensation to unmask a dorsal column deficit.
incorrectas.D: Cerebellar ataxia causes unsteadiness and incoordination that is present with both eyes open and closed (a negative or non-lateralizing Romberg), different from the tabetic pattern where instability appears specifically once visual compensation is removed.

preguntas.q: Charcot joints (neuropathic joint destruction) in tabes dorsalis develop as a consequence of loss of which protective sensory function?

o.C: Local blood supply to the joint
o.D: Vibratory sense only, with intact position sense

e.correcta: Loss of proprioceptive feedback in tabes dorsalis means patients cannot sense abnormal joint positioning or the microtrauma of everyday mechanical stress, so joints are repeatedly overused and injured without the protective reflexes that would normally limit damaging movements. Over time this unnoticed repetitive trauma leads to progressive joint destruction, effusion, and instability, the neuropathic (Charcot) joint, classically affecting the knees in tabes dorsalis.

incorrectas.A: Motor strength to the muscles around a joint is generally preserved in tabes dorsalis, since it is primarily a sensory (dorsal column/root) disease; Charcot joints arise from loss of protective sensory feedback, not from motor weakness destabilizing the joint.
incorrectas.C: Charcot joints are a neuropathic, not vascular, process; local blood supply is not primarily impaired in tabes dorsalis, and joint destruction results from repeated unnoticed mechanical trauma rather than ischemia.
incorrectas.D: Isolated vibratory loss with intact position sense would not produce the severe unnoticed joint trauma seen in Charcot joints; it is the combined loss of proprioception (and pain sensation) that removes the protective feedback needed to prevent repetitive joint injury.

preguntas.q: Hutchinson's teeth (notched, widely spaced incisors) are a classic finding in which congenital infection?

e.correcta: Hutchinson's teeth, small, notched, peg-shaped or widely spaced permanent incisors, are part of the Hutchinson triad of late congenital syphilis (along with interstitial keratitis and CN VIII sensorineural deafness), resulting from transplacental transmission of Treponema pallidum that disrupts normal tooth development. This dental finding, together with other stigmata like saddle nose and saber shins, is a classic finding pointing specifically to congenital syphilis rather than other TORCH infections.

incorrectas.A: Congenital CMV classically presents with periventricular calcifications, sensorineural hearing loss, chorioretinitis, and microcephaly; it does not cause the notched incisor dental abnormality that is specific to congenital syphilis.
incorrectas.B: Congenital toxoplasmosis classically causes the triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial (diffuse) calcifications, not dental notching, which is a distinguishing feature of congenital syphilis instead.
incorrectas.D: Congenital rubella syndrome classically presents with cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and patent ductus arteriosus (and a 'blueberry muffin' rash), not the notched Hutchinson incisors that specifically identify congenital syphilis.

preguntas.q: Mulberry molars, characterized by abnormal enamel outgrowth on the molar surface, are a classic dental finding in which condition?

e.correcta: Mulberry molars, first molars with abnormal, rounded, mulberry-like enamel projections instead of normal cusps, arise from disrupted dentin and enamel formation caused by transplacental Treponema pallidum infection, and are grouped with Hutchinson's teeth as classic dental stigmata of congenital syphilis. Along with the Hutchinson triad, these findings reflect the organism's ability to interfere with normal odontogenesis during fetal development.

incorrectas.B: Congenital rubella syndrome is defined by cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and cardiac defects like PDA, not by a specific molar enamel abnormality; the mulberry molar is a syphilis-specific finding.
incorrectas.C: Congenital CMV is associated with periventricular calcifications, hearing loss, and microcephaly, not dental enamel changes; mulberry molars are not part of the CMV phenotype.
incorrectas.D: Congenital toxoplasmosis presents with chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications; it does not produce the distinctive mulberry molar dental finding associated with congenital syphilis.

preguntas.q: Congenital sensorineural hearing loss due to CN VIII damage, as part of the Hutchinson triad, is classically caused by which congenital infection?

e.correcta: Congenital syphilis can damage cranial nerve VIII, producing progressive sensorineural hearing loss that, together with Hutchinson's teeth and interstitial keratitis, forms the classic Hutchinson triad of late congenital syphilis. This deafness typically develops later in childhood, reflecting ongoing inflammatory injury from transplacentally acquired Treponema pallidum rather than an immediate neonatal finding.

incorrectas.A: Congenital toxoplasmosis classically causes chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications rather than the CN VIII-mediated hearing loss that is part of the syphilis-specific Hutchinson triad.
incorrectas.B: Congenital rubella syndrome does cause sensorineural hearing loss, making it a reasonable-sounding distractor, but the hearing loss described here as part of the 'Hutchinson triad' is specifically the syphilis-associated finding, distinguished by its co-occurrence with Hutchinson teeth and interstitial keratitis rather than cataracts and PDA as in rubella.
incorrectas.C: Congenital CMV is actually the most common infectious cause of congenital sensorineural hearing loss overall, but the hearing loss described here as part of the Hutchinson triad (with notched teeth and keratitis) is specifically attributed to congenital syphilis, not CMV.

preguntas.q: Rhagades, linear scars radiating from the angle of the mouth, are a classic finding in which condition?

e.correcta: Rhagades are linear fissures/scars at the corners of the mouth (and sometimes nose) that result from healed perioral skin lesions caused by congenital syphilis, often following the fissuring rash seen in early congenital infection. They are one of several late stigmata of congenital syphilis, alongside saddle nose, saber shins, and the Hutchinson triad, reflecting the destructive mucocutaneous effects of untreated transplacental Treponema pallidum infection.

incorrectas.A: Congenital HSV typically presents with vesicular skin lesions, keratoconjunctivitis, and potentially disseminated or CNS disease acquired around delivery, not the linear perioral scarring (rhagades) characteristic of congenital syphilis.
incorrectas.C: Congenital varicella syndrome causes limb hypoplasia, cutaneous scarring in a dermatomal distribution, and CNS/eye abnormalities from first-trimester maternal varicella infection, a different scarring pattern and mechanism than the perioral rhagades of congenital syphilis.
incorrectas.D: Congenital rubella syndrome is characterized by cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and cardiac defects, not the linear perioral scars caused by healed syphilitic skin lesions.

preguntas.q: A patient with syphilis at any stage (primary, secondary, latent, or tertiary) who is not penicillin-allergic should receive which first-line treatment?

e.correcta: Benzathine penicillin G, given intramuscularly, remains the treatment of choice for all stages of syphilis because Treponema pallidum has never developed clinically significant resistance to penicillin despite decades of use, and its long-acting depot formulation maintains treponemicidal levels over the days-to-weeks needed to kill the slow-dividing spirochete. Because penicillin is so reliably effective and safe, even penicillin-allergic patients are preferentially desensitized and then treated with it rather than switched to an alternative, particularly in pregnant women and in neurosyphilis, where alternatives are inadequately studied or penetrate poorly.

incorrectas.B: Doxycycline is a reasonable alternative for early syphilis in truly penicillin-allergic, non-pregnant patients, but it is not first-line and is specifically avoided in pregnancy (tetracyclines affect fetal bone/teeth) and in neurosyphilis, unlike penicillin, which remains preferred and safe in these situations.
incorrectas.C: Ceftriaxone has some anti-treponemal activity and is occasionally used off-label when penicillin truly cannot be given, but it lacks the extensive clinical outcome data and guideline endorsement that make penicillin G the default across all stages.
incorrectas.D: Azithromycin has been used in some settings for early syphilis, but resistance-conferring mutations in T. pallidum have emerged and compromised its reliability, so it is not recommended as first-line therapy.

preguntas.q: The TORCH complex mnemonic refers to pathogens capable of crossing the placenta to cause congenital infection. Which of the following organisms is classically included in TORCH?

e.correcta: Toxoplasma gondii is the "To" in TORCH (ToRCHeS), a protozoan parasite acquired from undercooked meat or cat feces that can cross the placenta and cause the classic congenital triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications. The TORCH group as a whole (Toxoplasma, Rubella, CMV, HIV, Herpes, Syphilis, VZV, Parvovirus B19) is unified not by organism class but by the shared ability to cross the placental barrier and infect the fetus in utero, unlike organisms that infect the neonate during passage through the birth canal.

incorrectas.A: Group B Streptococcus is a major cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis, but it is acquired by ascending infection or passage through a colonized birth canal during delivery, not by transplacental spread, so it is not part of the TORCH group.
incorrectas.C: Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) from direct contact with infected cervical secretions during vaginal delivery, again a peripartum rather than transplacental route, so it falls outside TORCH.
incorrectas.D: Chlamydia trachomatis similarly causes neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia via intrapartum exposure to the birth canal rather than transplacental crossing, distinguishing its transmission mechanism from the TORCH organisms.

preguntas.q: Which early finding in congenital syphilis presents as a persistent mucopurulent, blood-tinged nasal discharge teeming with spirochetes?

e.correcta: "Snuffles" refers to the profuse, often blood-tinged rhinorrhea seen in early congenital syphilis, caused by direct spirochetal invasion and inflammation of the nasal mucosa; the discharge is highly infectious because it is loaded with live Treponema pallidum. It typically appears within the first few weeks of life and, if untreated, is one of the earliest clues prompting evaluation for congenital syphilis alongside hepatosplenomegaly and a desquamating rash.

incorrectas.A: Saddle nose deformity is a late (not early) manifestation of congenital syphilis, resulting from destruction of nasal cartilage after chronic untreated infection, structurally different from the acute infectious discharge of snuffles.
incorrectas.C: Choanal atresia is a congenital structural anomaly (failure of posterior nasal passage canalization) present from birth regardless of infection, unrelated to spirochetal invasion or infectivity.
incorrectas.D: Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to environmental allergens, a common pediatric condition unrelated to congenital infection and not associated with spirochete-laden discharge.

preguntas.q: The genetic material (DNA or RNA) of a virus is directly surrounded by which protein structure?

e.correcta: The capsid is the protein shell, built from repeating protein subunits, that directly encloses and protects the viral genome; it is typically arranged in an icosahedral or helical geometry. Together the capsid plus enclosed genome make up the nucleocapsid, and in some viruses an additional lipid envelope derived from host membrane surrounds this structure.

incorrectas.A: The envelope is an optional outer lipid bilayer, acquired from host cell membranes as the virus buds out, that surrounds the capsid in "enveloped" viruses — it is external to, not the structure directly enclosing, the genome.
incorrectas.B: A capsomere is a single structural subunit (typically an oligomer of capsid protein) that assembles together with many other capsomeres to build the complete capsid, so it is a building block rather than the whole enclosing shell.
incorrectas.D: The nucleocapsid is the combined unit of the capsid plus the genome it encloses, a broader term than capsid alone, which specifically refers only to the protein shell itself.

preguntas.q: Which of the following statements correctly explains why viral (as opposed to bacterial) meningitis does not typically cause a decreased CSF glucose level?

o.A: Viruses actively metabolize glucose to fuel their replication
o.B: Viruses lack independent metabolic activity and cannot consume host glucose
o.C: Viruses possess their own ribosomes that consume glucose for protein synthesis
o.D: Viruses generate ATP via viral mitochondria

e.correcta: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites with no independent metabolism — they carry no ribosomes, no enzymes for ATP generation, and cannot consume glucose on their own; they simply hijack the host cell's existing metabolic and synthetic machinery to replicate. Because nothing in viral meningitis is actively consuming CSF glucose the way metabolically active bacteria do, CSF glucose typically remains normal, a key lab clue that helps distinguish viral from bacterial meningitis.

incorrectas.A: Viruses have no metabolic enzymes of their own and therefore cannot actively ferment or metabolize glucose; this is precisely why CSF glucose is preserved in viral infections, in contrast to bacteria, which do consume glucose and thereby cause hypoglycorrhachia.
incorrectas.C: Viruses do not possess their own ribosomes — they depend entirely on hijacking the host cell's ribosomes to translate viral mRNA, so there is no independent viral protein synthesis machinery consuming glucose.
incorrectas.D: Viruses have no organelles at all, including mitochondria; they are acellular particles that rely completely on the host cell's ATP-generating machinery, so there is no viral ATP production consuming glucose.

preguntas.q: Aside from icosahedral, what is the other most common geometric shape of viral capsids?

e.correcta: Helical capsids form when identical protein subunits assemble in a repeating spiral around the coiled nucleic acid, producing a rod-like structure (as in the tobacco mosaic virus or paramyxoviruses); together with icosahedral symmetry, these are the two most common capsid architectures among viruses. Helical capsids are found only in enveloped viruses, since the flexible helical arrangement lacks the mechanical stability to survive outside a protective lipid membrane.

incorrectas.A: Complex capsids, seen in viruses like poxviruses and many bacteriophages, have an irregular, multi-layered structure that does not fit simple icosahedral or helical symmetry, making them a distinct third (much less common) category rather than one of the two "most common" shapes.
incorrectas.C: Filamentous is a descriptive term sometimes applied to elongated helical virions, but it is not the standard name used alongside "icosahedral" for the two major capsid symmetry classes taught in virology.
incorrectas.D: Prolate refers to an elongated icosahedral variant (an icosahedron stretched along one axis, as in some bacteriophage heads) rather than an independent third major capsid shape category.

preguntas.q: Viruses that lack a host-cell-derived lipid membrane surrounding their capsid are called "naked," while those that possess one are called what?

e.correcta: "Enveloped" describes viruses whose capsid is wrapped in an additional lipid bilayer acquired from the host cell membrane (or nuclear membrane) as the virus buds out of the cell. This envelope typically carries viral glycoproteins used for receptor binding and cell entry, but it also makes enveloped viruses more fragile — sensitive to desiccation, heat, and detergents — compared to naked viruses.

incorrectas.A: Pleomorphic describes variability in virion shape (seen in some enveloped viruses like influenza), not the presence or absence of an envelope itself, so it isn't the correct term for this distinction.
incorrectas.B: Encapsidated refers to the genome being packaged within a capsid, a step common to all viruses (enveloped or not), not specifically to the presence of an outer lipid membrane.
incorrectas.D: Lysogenic describes a bacteriophage life cycle state in which viral DNA integrates into the host genome as a prophage, an entirely different concept unrelated to capsid or envelope structure.

preguntas.q: All non-enveloped ("naked") viruses share which capsid shape, a geometry stable enough to survive in the environment without a protective lipid membrane?

e.correcta: The icosahedral shape — a symmetric 20-faced polyhedron built from repeating capsomere subunits — is mechanically stable and resistant to environmental stresses like desiccation and pH changes, which is why every naked virus uses this architecture rather than the more fragile helical form. This inherent durability is also why naked viruses (e.g., picornaviruses, adenoviruses, papillomaviruses) tend to spread efficiently via the fecal-oral route or fomites, surviving outside a host without an envelope to protect them.

incorrectas.A: Helical capsids are more flexible and mechanically less robust, so they are found exclusively among enveloped viruses, which rely on the lipid membrane for structural protection rather than capsid rigidity.
incorrectas.B: Complex capsids (as in poxviruses) have irregular, multilayered architecture and are not a feature of naked viruses generally, representing a distinct minority structural category.
incorrectas.D: Filamentous is a description sometimes used for elongated helical virions, not a shape adopted by naked viruses, which are uniformly icosahedral.

preguntas.q: Which capsid shape is found among enveloped viruses but never among naked (non-enveloped) viruses?

e.correcta: Helical capsids are seen only in enveloped viruses because the loosely coiled protein-nucleic acid helix lacks the rigidity to withstand the environment on its own; the surrounding lipid envelope provides the structural protection that a naked helical virus would otherwise lack. In contrast, naked viruses are restricted to the more mechanically stable icosahedral shape, which is why "helical implies enveloped" is a useful high-yield rule of thumb.

incorrectas.A: Icosahedral capsids are found in both enveloped viruses (e.g., herpesviruses) and naked viruses (e.g., adenoviruses), so this shape does not distinguish enveloped from naked viruses.
incorrectas.B: Complex capsids, as in poxviruses, are a separate irregular structural category found in select enveloped viruses, but they are not the shape that is exclusive to enveloped viruses in the icosahedral-versus-helical framework being tested here.
incorrectas.D: Spherical is a loose descriptive term sometimes applied to the overall envelope shape of a virion, not a formal capsid symmetry class distinguishing enveloped from naked viruses.

preguntas.q: The lipid bilayer that forms a virus's envelope is typically derived from which source?

e.correcta: Enveloped viruses acquire their outer lipid membrane by budding through a host cell membrane — commonly the plasma membrane, but sometimes the nuclear or Golgi membrane depending on the virus — incorporating host phospholipids studded with viral glycoproteins into the envelope as the virion exits the cell. This "stolen" membrane origin is clinically important because it makes enveloped viruses susceptible to disruption by lipid solvents like alcohol, ether, and detergents, unlike naked viruses.

incorrectas.B: Viruses do not synthesize their own phospholipids — they lack the metabolic machinery for lipid biosynthesis entirely and instead co-opt pre-existing host cell membrane during the budding process.
incorrectas.C: Bacterial cell walls are made of peptidoglycan, not lipid bilayer, and animal viruses infecting human cells have no access to a bacterial structure at all, making this an inapplicable source.
incorrectas.D: The capsid is a protein structure (not a lipid structure) that lies internal to the envelope; the envelope surrounds the capsid rather than being derived from it.

preguntas.q: What is the typical structural configuration of RNA virus genomes?

e.correcta: The overwhelming majority of RNA viruses carry a single-stranded, linear RNA genome — the major exception being the Reoviridae (e.g., rotavirus), which are segmented and double-stranded. This single-stranded, linear format is directly relevant to replication strategy, since it determines whether the genome must first be converted to a usable form (negative-sense) or can be translated immediately (positive-sense).

incorrectas.A: Double-stranded, circular genomes are a hallmark of certain DNA viruses (e.g., papillomavirus, polyomavirus) and some bacteriophages, not the typical configuration of RNA virus genomes.
incorrectas.C: Single-stranded circular genomes are unusual and more characteristic of small subviral agents like the hepatitis D virus or plant viroids, not the general RNA virus population.
incorrectas.D: Double-stranded, linear genomes describe most herpesviruses and adenoviruses (DNA viruses), the opposite structural pattern from the single-stranded RNA genomes typical of RNA viruses.

preguntas.q: Where in the host cell do most RNA viruses carry out their replication?

e.correcta: Most RNA viruses replicate entirely within the cytoplasm using virally encoded RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, since human cells lack an enzyme capable of copying RNA into RNA — the virus must supply its own. This cytoplasmic localization is a key distinguishing feature from most DNA viruses, which typically replicate in the nucleus using host DNA polymerase (with notable exceptions like poxviruses, a DNA virus that replicates in the cytoplasm because it carries its own polymerase).

incorrectas.A: The nucleus is where most DNA viruses replicate, taking advantage of host DNA polymerase and the nuclear replication machinery; RNA viruses generally avoid the nucleus since they don't need host DNA-copying enzymes, with retroviruses being a notable exception that must enter the nucleus to integrate.
incorrectas.B: Mitochondria contain their own small genome and replication machinery for organelle maintenance, but they are not hijacked as a site of viral genome replication by RNA viruses.
incorrectas.D: The Golgi apparatus is involved in post-translational modification and trafficking of viral envelope glycoproteins for some viruses, not in genome replication itself.

preguntas.q: RNA viruses are broadly classified based on which genomic property, which determines whether the genome can be translated directly by host ribosomes upon cell entry?

e.correcta: Polarity, or "sense," describes whether the RNA genome reads in the same orientation as mRNA (positive-sense, directly translatable) or in the complementary orientation (negative-sense, requiring conversion by RNA-dependent RNA polymerase before translation can occur). This distinction fundamentally shapes each virus's replication strategy — positive-sense viruses can begin producing protein immediately upon cell entry, while negative-sense viruses must first bring in (or synthesize) polymerase to make a usable positive-sense copy.

incorrectas.A: Capsid symmetry (icosahedral vs. helical) describes the geometric arrangement of the protein shell, an entirely separate structural property from how the genome's nucleotide sequence relates to mRNA.
incorrectas.B: Segmentation refers to whether the genome is divided into multiple separate RNA pieces (as in influenza) versus a single continuous molecule; this affects reassortment potential but not whether the genome itself needs to be converted before translation.
incorrectas.D: Envelope status refers to the presence or absence of a lipid membrane, a structural feature unrelated to the sense/orientation of the RNA genome.

preguntas.q: A positive-sense RNA viral genome is structurally analogous to which host cell molecule, allowing it to be translated directly by ribosomes?

e.correcta: Positive-sense RNA has the same 5' to 3' orientation and coding sequence as messenger RNA, meaning host ribosomes can bind and translate it immediately upon entry into the cytoplasm without any need for a polymerase to first generate a complementary strand. This head start makes positive-sense RNA viruses (e.g., picornaviruses, flaviviruses) inherently infectious as naked RNA — injecting the purified genome alone into a cell can initiate infection.

incorrectas.A: tRNA functions as an adaptor molecule that delivers specific amino acids to the ribosome during translation; it is not itself translated and bears no structural resemblance to a positive-sense viral genome.
incorrectas.C: rRNA is a structural and catalytic component of the ribosome itself, not a template that gets translated, making it functionally distinct from an mRNA-like positive-sense genome.
incorrectas.D: Genomic DNA must first be transcribed into mRNA before translation can occur; it cannot be read directly by ribosomes, unlike positive-sense RNA, which mimics mRNA's ready-to-translate form.

preguntas.q: Which RNA genome polarity can be used immediately by host ribosomes for protein synthesis as soon as it enters the cytoplasm, without requiring a prior polymerase step?

e.correcta: Positive-sense RNA is functionally identical in orientation to mRNA, so host ribosomes can immediately translate it into viral proteins the moment it reaches the cytoplasm — no intermediate conversion step is needed. This gives positive-sense RNA viruses a replication head start and also explains why their isolated genomic RNA alone is infectious if introduced into a susceptible cell.

incorrectas.A: Ambisense genomes (seen in some bunyaviruses and arenaviruses) contain both positive- and negative-sense regions on the same strand, so only part of the genome is immediately translatable while the rest still requires polymerase-mediated conversion first.
incorrectas.B: Negative (-) sense RNA is the exact complement of mRNA and cannot be read by ribosomes at all; it must first be transcribed into a positive-sense copy by a virally supplied RNA-dependent RNA polymerase before any translation can occur.
incorrectas.C: Double-stranded RNA cannot be directly translated by ribosomes either — it must be transcribed into single-stranded mRNA-equivalent segments by a viral RNA polymerase, similar in principle to negative-sense RNA.

preguntas.q: A positive-sense RNA genome is oriented in which direction, matching the orientation required for direct ribosomal translation?

e.correcta: Positive-sense RNA runs 5' to 3', the same directionality ribosomes use to read mRNA during translation, which is precisely why it can be translated immediately without modification. This is a defining structural feature that distinguishes it from negative-sense RNA, which runs in the opposite orientation relative to a readable message and must be flipped by RNA polymerase first.

incorrectas.A: A 3' to 5' orientation (relative to a translatable message) describes negative-sense RNA, which is the complementary strand to mRNA and cannot be read directly by ribosomes — the opposite of the positive-sense genome being asked about here.
incorrectas.C: RNA viral genomes are not generally described as circular with no fixed polarity; virtually all RNA viruses have a defined linear polarity (positive, negative, or ambisense) that dictates their replication strategy.
incorrectas.D: "Bidirectional" is not a recognized category of RNA genome orientation; each strand of RNA has a single defined 5' to 3' polarity, even though ambisense genomes contain regions of opposite sense on the same strand.

preguntas.q: A negative-sense RNA genome is oriented 3' to 5' relative to a readable message, and therefore requires which enzyme to be brought into the cell before viral proteins can be made?

e.correcta: Because negative-sense RNA is the exact complement of mRNA, host ribosomes cannot read it directly — the virus must carry its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (packaged within the virion) to transcribe the negative-sense genome into a usable positive-sense mRNA copy immediately upon entry. This is why negative-sense RNA viruses (e.g., influenza, rabies, measles) are not infectious as naked, purified RNA — without the pre-packaged polymerase, the genome alone cannot initiate protein synthesis.

incorrectas.A: DNA polymerase synthesizes DNA from a DNA template and has no ability to transcribe an RNA genome into mRNA, so it cannot fulfill the role needed by negative-sense RNA viruses.
incorrectas.B: Reverse transcriptase converts RNA into DNA and is the defining enzyme of retroviruses, a completely different replication strategy from the RNA-to-RNA transcription needed by standard negative-sense RNA viruses.
incorrectas.D: Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling tension in DNA during replication and transcription; it plays no role in generating a translatable message from a negative-sense RNA genome.

preguntas.q: Which class of RNA viruses is unique for carrying a diploid genome (two identical copies of single-stranded RNA) and using reverse transcriptase to generate a DNA intermediate?

e.correcta: Retroviruses, including HIV, are atypical among RNA viruses because they package two identical copies of single-stranded RNA (making them functionally diploid) along with the enzyme reverse transcriptase, which converts their RNA genome into double-stranded DNA that then integrates into the host genome. This "backwards" flow of genetic information (RNA to DNA rather than DNA to RNA) is the origin of the name "retrovirus" and allows the provirus to persist indefinitely within infected host cells, a key reason HIV infection cannot currently be cured.

incorrectas.A: Picornaviruses (e.g., poliovirus, rhinovirus, hepatitis A) are small, naked, positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses with a single (haploid) genome copy and no reverse transcriptase — a conventional RNA virus replication strategy, unlike retroviruses.
incorrectas.C: Orthomyxoviruses (e.g., influenza) have a segmented, negative-sense single-stranded RNA genome divided into multiple distinct segments, which is a different structural strategy from the diploid, reverse-transcribing genome of retroviruses.
incorrectas.D: Flaviviruses (e.g., dengue, Zika, hepatitis C) are enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses with a single haploid genome and no reverse transcriptase, replicating entirely through RNA intermediates rather than a DNA provirus stage.

preguntas.q: DNA viral genomes can be either circular or linear, but the vast majority are structurally which of the following?

e.correcta: Most DNA viruses carry a double-stranded DNA genome, mirroring the structure of host cellular DNA, which allows many of them to exploit host DNA polymerase and repair machinery for replication (typically within the nucleus). This double-stranded structure also confers relative genomic stability compared to single-stranded genomes, which are more susceptible to damage.

incorrectas.A: Single-stranded DNA is actually the exception among DNA viruses — Parvoviridae (e.g., parvovirus B19) is the classic example of the one DNA virus family with a single-stranded genome, highlighting just how atypical this configuration is.
incorrectas.C: RNA-DNA hybrid genomes are not a recognized category of viral genome; viruses use either pure RNA or pure DNA genomes (with retroviruses undergoing RNA-to-DNA conversion via reverse transcriptase, but the packaged genome itself is RNA, not a hybrid).
incorrectas.D: Triple-stranded nucleic acid structures (triplex DNA) are not used as a viral genome format; this is not a genome architecture found in any human viral pathogen.

preguntas.q: Which is the only DNA virus family with a single-stranded (rather than double-stranded) genome?

e.correcta: Parvovirus (including parvovirus B19, the cause of erythema infectiosum and aplastic crisis in sickle cell disease) is the sole DNA virus family that packages a single-stranded DNA genome, making it a frequently tested exception to the general rule that DNA viruses are double-stranded. This unusual structure is part of why parvovirus B19 is also notable for being one of the smallest, simplest human DNA viruses, requiring actively dividing host cells (like erythroid precursors) to help replicate its genome.

incorrectas.A: Adenovirus has a linear, double-stranded DNA genome, consistent with the typical DNA virus pattern, and is a common cause of respiratory and conjunctival infections rather than the ssDNA exception.
incorrectas.B: Herpesviruses (e.g., HSV, VZV, CMV, EBV) all carry large, linear, double-stranded DNA genomes, fitting the standard dsDNA pattern seen in most DNA virus families.
incorrectas.D: Papillomavirus has a circular, double-stranded DNA genome, again following the typical dsDNA structure of DNA viruses rather than the single-stranded exception seen in parvovirus.

preguntas.q: Among dsDNA, positive-sense RNA, and negative-sense RNA viral genomes, which type is NOT infectious on its own if introduced directly into a host cell?

e.correcta: A negative-sense RNA genome cannot be translated by host ribosomes because it is the complementary sequence to mRNA, so purified negative-sense RNA alone cannot initiate infection — the virion must also deliver its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase to first generate a translatable positive-sense copy. This is why negative-sense RNA viruses always package their polymerase within the virion, unlike positive-sense RNA viruses, whose genome alone is sufficient to start an infection.

incorrectas.A: Positive-sense RNA is directly readable by host ribosomes, just like mRNA, so purified positive-sense genomic RNA introduced into a cell is by itself sufficient to initiate translation and infection.
incorrectas.B: Double-stranded DNA can be transcribed into mRNA using host (or in some cases viral) RNA polymerase machinery already present in the nucleus, so dsDNA genomes are generally infectious on their own once inside a cell.
incorrectas.D: Single-stranded DNA (as in parvovirus) can also be converted to a replicative double-stranded form and transcribed using host cell enzymes, so it, too, remains capable of initiating infection without requiring a pre-packaged viral polymerase.

preguntas.q: The modern Hepatitis B vaccine is produced using recombinant technology to generate which viral antigen?

e.correcta: The current Hepatitis B vaccine is made by inserting the gene for HBsAg (hepatitis B surface antigen) into yeast cells, which then produce this surface protein in large quantities for use as the immunogen — eliciting protective anti-HBs antibodies without any risk of transmitting live virus. This recombinant approach replaced the older plasma-derived vaccine and is why a patient's serologic pattern of anti-HBs positive with all other markers negative indicates vaccination rather than natural infection (which would also show anti-HBc).

incorrectas.A: HBeAg is a secreted marker of active viral replication and high infectivity during natural infection, but it is not the antigen manufactured in the vaccine, and vaccinated individuals never develop anti-HBe.
incorrectas.B: HBcAg is the core antigen found only within the intact virion and infected hepatocytes (never detectable free in serum) — the vaccine deliberately avoids using it, which is why a vaccinated (as opposed to naturally infected) patient never develops anti-HBc antibodies.
incorrectas.D: HBV DNA polymerase is the viral enzyme responsible for genome replication, not a structural antigen used to generate a protective antibody response, and is not part of the vaccine formulation.

preguntas.q: Which structural feature does HIV possess that enables its gp120/gp41 glycoproteins to mediate fusion with host CD4+ T cells?

e.correcta: HIV is an enveloped retrovirus — its capsid is surrounded by a host-cell-derived lipid bilayer studded with the viral glycoproteins gp120 (which binds CD4 and a chemokine coreceptor) and gp41 (which mediates membrane fusion). Because these glycoproteins are embedded in the envelope itself, the presence of an envelope is a structural prerequisite for HIV's receptor-mediated entry mechanism; without it, there would be no membrane in which gp120/gp41 could be anchored.

incorrectas.A: A naked icosahedral capsid, as seen in viruses like adenovirus, lacks any lipid membrane, so there is no surface for anchoring fusion glycoproteins like gp120/gp41 — this describes a fundamentally different, non-enveloped viral architecture from HIV.
incorrectas.C: A naked helical capsid is not a real combination seen in nature (helical capsids require envelope support for stability), and in any case a naked virus by definition lacks the lipid membrane needed to display gp120/gp41.
incorrectas.D: A polysaccharide capsule is a bacterial virulence factor (e.g., in Streptococcus pneumoniae or Neisseria meningitidis) that helps evade phagocytosis; it is not a viral structure and has nothing to do with HIV's envelope or fusion machinery.

preguntas.q: HIV, like other retroviruses, packages how many identical copies of its single-stranded RNA genome within each virion?

e.correcta: HIV carries two identical copies of its single-stranded RNA genome, making it functionally diploid — an unusual feature among RNA viruses, most of which are haploid. This diploid arrangement, along with the two packaged copies of reverse transcriptase, is thought to promote genetic recombination between the two RNA strands during reverse transcription, contributing to HIV's remarkable capacity for rapid genetic diversification and immune/drug-resistance evolution.

incorrectas.A: A single haploid RNA copy is the typical arrangement for most other RNA viruses (e.g., picornaviruses, flaviviruses), but retroviruses like HIV are a specific exception that package two copies rather than one.
incorrectas.C: Three copies is not the packaging number for any well-described human retrovirus; HIV specifically packages a defined pair (two copies) of its genome.
incorrectas.D: Four copies would exceed the diploid packaging characteristic of retroviruses; HIV's genome content is specifically two identical RNA strands, not four.

preguntas.q: Which HIV envelope glycoprotein is the transmembrane protein responsible for mediating fusion of the viral envelope with the host cell membrane and inducing syncytia formation?

e.correcta: gp41 is the transmembrane component of the HIV envelope glycoprotein complex; after gp120 binds CD4 and a coreceptor (CCR5 or CXCR4) and undergoes a conformational change, gp41 inserts its fusion peptide into the host cell membrane, drawing viral and cell membranes together to allow fusion and, in infected cells expressing HIV envelope proteins on their surface, fusion with neighboring cells to form multinucleated syncytia. This fusion step is the target of the antiretroviral drug enfuvirtide, which blocks gp41 to prevent viral entry.

incorrectas.A: gp120 is the surface (not transmembrane) glycoprotein that noncovalently associates with gp41 and is responsible for initial receptor binding to CD4 and a chemokine coreceptor — a necessary first step, but it is gp41, not gp120, that actually executes membrane fusion.
incorrectas.B: p24 is the HIV capsid protein that forms the conical core enclosing the viral RNA genome and enzymes; it is a structural matrix/capsid protein with no role in membrane fusion, and it also serves as a useful early serologic marker of acute HIV infection.
incorrectas.C: Reverse transcriptase is the enzyme that converts the HIV RNA genome into DNA after the virus has already entered the cell; it acts intracellularly during replication and plays no role in the membrane fusion event itself.

preguntas.q: Which HIV envelope glycoprotein binds host CD4 and a chemokine coreceptor (CCR5 or CXCR4) to mediate viral attachment and entry?

e.correcta: gp120 is the outer envelope glycoprotein of HIV, noncovalently associated with the transmembrane gp41 anchor. gp120 binds CD4 on macrophages/T cells first, undergoing a conformational change that exposes a coreceptor-binding site for CCR5 (macrophages, early/M-tropic strains) or CXCR4 (T cells, late/T-tropic strains). This sequential CD4-then-coreceptor binding determines HIV's cellular tropism and is the target of entry inhibitors like maraviroc (a CCR5 antagonist).

incorrectas.B: gp41 is the transmembrane glycoprotein that pairs with gp120; after gp120 engages CD4 and coreceptor, gp41 undergoes its own conformational change to drive fusion of viral and host membranes, but it does not itself bind CD4/CCR5/CXCR4.
incorrectas.C: p24 is the capsid (core) protein forming the conical shell around the viral RNA genome and is used as a serologic marker in combination Ag/Ab immunoassays, not a receptor-binding envelope protein.
incorrectas.D: Integrase is a pol-encoded enzyme that inserts reverse-transcribed proviral DNA into the host genome after entry has already occurred, playing no role in attachment or receptor binding.

preguntas.q: HIV is classified as a ToRCHeS pathogen because it can be transmitted to the fetus by crossing which structure?

e.correcta: The ToRCHeS group of congenital infections (Toxoplasma, Rubella, CMV, HSV/HIV, Syphilis) share the ability to cross the placental barrier and infect the fetus in utero, in addition to intrapartum or postpartum transmission (e.g., breastfeeding for HIV). Recognizing the placenta as the anatomic route ties HIV to the same vertical-transmission framework used for the other ToRCHeS organisms and explains why perinatal prophylaxis (antiretrovirals, cesarean delivery in select cases) reduces transmission.

incorrectas.A: The amniotic membrane surrounds the amniotic fluid and fetus but is not the maternal-fetal exchange interface; pathogens reach the fetus via the placental villi, not by traversing the amniotic sac itself.
incorrectas.C: The umbilical cord carries fetal blood vessels connecting fetus to placenta; it is a conduit for blood flow, not the site where maternal pathogens cross into fetal circulation.
incorrectas.D: The cervix is relevant to intrapartum transmission during vaginal delivery (exposure to genital secretions), but it is not the structure implicated in transplacental (in utero) transmission.

preguntas.q: Early in infection, HIV preferentially infects which cell type using CCR5 as its coreceptor?

e.correcta: Early, transmitted HIV strains are M-tropic (macrophage-tropic), using CCR5 to infect macrophages and dendritic cells at mucosal entry sites; macrophages then act as a reservoir that disseminates virus to lymphoid tissue. This is why CCR5-Δ32 mutations, which impair macrophage infection, confer resistance early in exposure, and why CCR5 antagonists like maraviroc are used therapeutically.

incorrectas.A: CD4+ T cells become the dominant target later in infection once the virus shifts to CXCR4-using, T-tropic strains; they are not typically the first cell type infected.
incorrectas.B: B lymphocytes do not express CD4 and are not directly infected by HIV; their dysfunction in HIV disease is indirect, related to loss of CD4+ T cell help.
incorrectas.D: Neutrophils lack CD4 and the relevant chemokine coreceptors, so they are not targets of HIV infection at any stage.

preguntas.q: As HIV disease progresses, the virus shifts tropism and preferentially infects which cell type via CXCR4?

e.correcta: Over the course of infection, HIV quasispecies evolve from CCR5-using (M-tropic) to CXCR4-using (T-tropic) variants, shifting the dominant target from macrophages to CD4+ helper T cells. Progressive infection and destruction of CD4+ T cells is the central pathogenic event in HIV disease, driving the decline in CD4 count that defines progression to AIDS.

incorrectas.A: Macrophages are the primary target earlier in infection (via CCR5); they remain infectable but are no longer the dominant, disease-driving target once T-tropic strains predominate.
incorrectas.B: Dendritic cells can capture and transmit HIV to T cells (in trans) but are not the principal cell destroyed as disease progresses; the hallmark of progression is CD4+ T cell depletion.
incorrectas.C: NK cells lack CD4 and are not infected by HIV; their function is altered indirectly during chronic infection but they are not a viral target.

preguntas.q: In untreated HIV infection, the clinical latency period during which the patient remains largely asymptomatic typically lasts approximately how long?

e.correcta: After acute retroviral syndrome resolves, untreated HIV enters a clinical latency phase lasting roughly 10 years on average, during which the virus continues to replicate at a low but steady level (seeding lymphoid tissue) while CD4 counts gradually decline. This latency is clinical, not virologic — the virus is never truly dormant — and the length of this phase is a major reason HIV can go undiagnosed for years before progressing to AIDS.

incorrectas.B: Two years is far shorter than the typical latency period and would represent unusually rapid progression, sometimes seen with especially virulent strains or an ineffective immune response, but not the average course.
incorrectas.C: Twenty years overstates the typical latency period; while a minority of long-term nonprogressors can remain asymptomatic for two decades or more due to unusually effective immune control, this is not the average timeline taught for untreated HIV.
incorrectas.D: One year is far too short and does not reflect the natural history of untreated HIV, which by definition includes a prolonged asymptomatic period before AIDS-defining illnesses appear.

preguntas.q: Which stage of untreated HIV infection corresponds to acute retroviral syndrome, characterized by high-level viremia and wide dissemination of virus to lymphoid organs?

e.correcta: Stage 1 of untreated HIV infection is the acute phase, occurring weeks after exposure, marked by a burst of high-titer viremia, a mononucleosis-like flu syndrome, and widespread seeding of virus into lymphoid organs (which become the major long-term viral reservoir). Recognizing this stage matters clinically because patients are highly infectious during this window and antibody tests may still be negative (the window period), making viral load or Ag/Ab combo testing important.

incorrectas.A: Stage 3 (AIDS) is defined by a CD4 count under 200 cells/mcL or an AIDS-defining illness, reflecting years of immune depletion — the opposite end of the disease course from the dissemination event described.
incorrectas.C: Stage 2, clinical latency, follows the acute stage and is characterized by low-level ongoing viral replication with a gradually falling CD4 count, not the initial wide dissemination event.
incorrectas.D: There is no formally separate Stage 4 in the standard CDC 3-stage classification of untreated HIV (acute, clinical latency, AIDS); this option does not correspond to a recognized stage.

preguntas.q: Individuals who are homozygous for the CCR5-Δ32 mutation typically show which outcome regarding HIV infection?

o.D: No change compared to wild-type individuals

e.correcta: The CCR5-Δ32 deletion produces a nonfunctional, truncated CCR5 coreceptor that fails to reach the cell surface; individuals homozygous for this allele lack functional CCR5 on macrophages and are therefore highly resistant to infection by CCR5-tropic (M-tropic) strains of HIV, which represent the vast majority of transmitted virus. This principle underlies the mechanism of maraviroc (a CCR5 antagonist) and was demonstrated by the 'Berlin patient,' who was functionally cured after a bone marrow transplant from a CCR5-Δ32 homozygous donor.

incorrectas.A: Slower progression, not resistance, is the phenotype seen in heterozygotes, who retain one functional CCR5 allele and can still be infected but control the virus somewhat better.
incorrectas.B: Increased susceptibility is the opposite of the actual effect; loss of functional CCR5 removes the main entry coreceptor used by transmitted HIV strains, reducing rather than increasing infection risk.
incorrectas.D: Homozygous CCR5-Δ32 individuals are not equivalent to wild-type; they show a clear, clinically significant reduction in HIV acquisition risk, which is why this genotype is studied as a model for HIV resistance and cure strategies.

preguntas.q: Individuals heterozygous for the CCR5-Δ32 mutation who become infected with HIV typically show which clinical course?

o.C: No difference from CCR5 wild-type individuals

e.correcta: Heterozygotes express reduced levels of functional CCR5 on the cell surface (one normal allele, one nonfunctional Δ32 allele), which partially limits viral entry and replication efficiency. This does not prevent infection outright but is associated with a measurably slower decline in CD4 count and delayed progression to AIDS compared with individuals who are CCR5 wild-type on both alleles.

incorrectas.A: Complete resistance is seen only in homozygotes, who lack functional CCR5 entirely; heterozygotes retain enough receptor expression to be infected, just with a more favorable disease course.
incorrectas.B: Accelerated progression is the opposite of the actual effect; reduced CCR5 expression impairs, rather than enhances, viral entry and replication.
incorrectas.C: There is a real, reproducible difference in progression rate between CCR5 heterozygotes and wild-type individuals, which is why this genotype has been studied as a modifier of HIV natural history.

preguntas.q: HIV transmission between individuals occurs primarily through contact with which of the following?

o.A: Bodily fluids (blood, semen, vaginal secretions, breast milk)

e.correcta: HIV is transmitted through direct contact with infected bodily fluids that contain sufficient viral load and access to susceptible cells — chiefly blood, semen, vaginal/rectal secretions, and breast milk — via sexual contact, needle sharing, occupational exposure, or perinatal transmission. It is not transmitted through casual contact because the virus is fragile outside the body and requires direct mucosal or bloodstream exposure to infected fluid to establish infection.

incorrectas.B: Unlike respiratory viruses (e.g., influenza, SARS-CoV-2), HIV is not spread by airborne or droplet transmission; it cannot establish infection via the respiratory route.
incorrectas.C: HIV does not survive well on surfaces and is not transmitted through fomites or casual/social contact such as sharing utensils or touching; this is a common but incorrect public misconception.
incorrectas.D: HIV is not a gastrointestinal pathogen and is not transmitted via the fecal-oral route, unlike enteric viruses such as hepatitis A or norovirus.

preguntas.q: ELISA and western blot testing for HIV can yield false-positive results in infants born to HIV-positive mothers because maternal IgG against which HIV antigen crosses the placenta?
