e.correcta: Maternal IgG antibodies, including those directed against the envelope glycoprotein gp120, cross the placenta during pregnancy to confer passive immunity to the newborn; in an HIV-exposed infant, these maternal anti-gp120 antibodies are detected by antibody-based assays even if the infant is not actually infected, producing a false-positive result. Because of this, antibody-based tests cannot reliably diagnose HIV in neonates, and direct detection of the virus itself via nucleic acid amplification is required instead.

incorrectas.A: p24 is a capsid protein and is a target of antigen-detection assays rather than the antibody highlighted here crossing the placenta; while anti-p24 antibodies also cross, the classic teaching point for this false-positive phenomenon centers on anti-gp120 (envelope) antibody.
incorrectas.C: Reverse transcriptase is an internal viral enzyme, not a major target of the antibody response measured by standard ELISA/western blot, and is not the antigen implicated in this maternal-antibody crossover phenomenon.
incorrectas.D: gp41 is the transmembrane envelope protein and is also immunogenic, but it is gp120 that is specifically highlighted in this classic teaching point about maternal antibody transfer causing false-positive neonatal testing.

preguntas.q: Because maternal antibodies cross the placenta and confound antibody-based testing, which method is used to diagnose HIV infection in neonates born to HIV-positive mothers?

o.C: HIV RNA/DNA nucleic acid amplification testing (PCR)

e.correcta: Because maternal IgG (including anti-gp120/anti-p24 antibodies) crosses the placenta and can persist in an infant's blood for up to 18 months regardless of whether the infant is actually infected, antibody-based assays like ELISA and western blot are unreliable in this age group. Instead, HIV RNA or DNA nucleic acid amplification testing directly detects the virus's genetic material, providing a reliable diagnosis in neonates and young infants independent of maternal antibody status.

incorrectas.A: Waiting to repeat ELISA at 18 months, once maternal antibody has cleared, is impractical for early diagnosis and treatment initiation, and delays care during a period when early antiretroviral therapy significantly improves outcomes.
incorrectas.B: Western blot, like ELISA, is an antibody-detection method and suffers from the same limitation — maternal antibody crossing the placenta — so it is not used for neonatal diagnosis (and is in fact no longer recommended even in adults).
incorrectas.D: CD4 count reflects immune status and disease staging but does not establish whether an infant is infected with HIV; it is not a diagnostic test for the virus itself.

preguntas.q: Which HIV regulatory protein promotes nuclear export of unspliced and singly spliced viral RNA transcripts to the cytoplasm?

e.correcta: Rev binds the Rev response element (RRE) on unspliced/incompletely spliced HIV mRNA and shuttles these transcripts out of the nucleus via the host's nuclear export machinery, allowing them to be translated into structural proteins (Gag, Pol, Env) or packaged as genomic RNA. A helpful mnemonic distinction: Rev = REgulates viral RNA export, while Tat = Transactivator of Transcription; both proteins are essential for productive replication.

incorrectas.A: Nef ('negative factor') downregulates CD4 and MHC I expression on infected cells to help evade immune detection, but it does not participate in RNA nuclear export.
incorrectas.B: Tat enhances transcriptional elongation from the HIV LTR promoter by binding the TAR RNA element, increasing the amount of viral RNA made — a distinct step from Rev's role in exporting that RNA out of the nucleus.
incorrectas.C: Vpu promotes degradation of CD4 in the endoplasmic reticulum and enhances release of virions from the cell surface (tetherin antagonism); it has no role in RNA transport.

preguntas.q: Which HIV regulatory protein binds the TAR RNA element to transactivate transcription from the viral LTR promoter?

e.correcta: Tat (transactivator of transcription) binds the TAR (trans-activation response) stem-loop RNA element near the 5' end of nascent HIV transcripts and recruits host transcriptional machinery (including P-TEFb) to dramatically increase the rate of RNA polymerase II elongation from the LTR promoter. Without Tat, transcription initiates but stalls early, producing only short abortive transcripts, so Tat is essential for generating full-length viral mRNA.

incorrectas.B: Rev acts downstream of transcription, exporting already-made unspliced/partially spliced RNA from the nucleus to the cytoplasm; it does not activate transcription itself.
incorrectas.C: Vif (viral infectivity factor) counteracts the host restriction factor APOBEC3G, preventing hypermutation of viral DNA during reverse transcription; it has no role in LTR-driven transcriptional activation.
incorrectas.D: Gag is a structural polyprotein cleaved by protease into matrix, capsid, and nucleocapsid proteins forming the virion core; it is a structural gene product, not a regulatory transcription factor.

preguntas.q: Which two HIV regulatory proteins are essential (non-redundant) for productive viral replication?

e.correcta: Among HIV's several regulatory/accessory proteins, Tat and Rev are considered essential for replication because they control obligatory steps — Tat drives efficient transcription of viral RNA from the LTR, and Rev enables export of unspliced/singly spliced RNA needed to make structural proteins and genomic RNA. Accessory proteins like Nef, Vif, Vpr, and Vpu enhance pathogenicity and immune evasion but are dispensable for replication in vitro, distinguishing them from the truly essential Tat/Rev pair.

incorrectas.A: Gag and Pol are structural/enzymatic genes (encoding capsid/matrix proteins and reverse transcriptase/integrase/protease, respectively), not regulatory proteins; they are necessary but belong to a different category than the essential Tat/Rev regulatory pair being tested.
incorrectas.C: Vif and Vpr are accessory proteins that enhance viral fitness (Vif counters APOBEC3G; Vpr arrests the cell cycle and aids nuclear import of the preintegration complex) but are not strictly required for basic replication the way Tat and Rev are.
incorrectas.D: Env is a structural gene encoding gp160 (cleaved into gp120/gp41), and Nef is an accessory protein that downregulates CD4/MHC I; neither is the essential regulatory pair referenced by this question.

preguntas.q: Once inside a host cell, which HIV enzyme converts the single-stranded viral RNA genome into double-stranded DNA before integration?

e.correcta: Reverse transcriptase, encoded by the pol gene, uses the viral RNA genome as a template to synthesize a complementary DNA strand (via its RNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity) and then degrades the RNA template (via its RNase H activity) before completing a double-stranded DNA copy. This proviral dsDNA is the substrate that integrase subsequently inserts into the host genome, and reverse transcriptase's high error rate (lacking proofreading) is a major driver of HIV's rapid mutation and drug resistance.

incorrectas.A: Protease, also pol-encoded, cleaves the Gag and Gag-Pol polyprotein precursors into individual structural and enzymatic proteins during virion maturation — a step that occurs after assembly, not RNA-to-DNA conversion.
incorrectas.B: Integrase acts after reverse transcription is complete, inserting the newly made double-stranded proviral DNA into the host cell's chromosomal DNA; it does not itself synthesize DNA from RNA.
incorrectas.D: Host RNA polymerase II transcribes the integrated proviral DNA back into viral mRNA/genomic RNA later in the replication cycle; it is a host enzyme used for transcription, not the viral enzyme that reverse-transcribes the incoming RNA genome.

preguntas.q: Which class of antiretroviral drugs, exemplified by zidovudine, traditionally forms the backbone of combination antiretroviral therapy (HAART/cART) for HIV?

e.correcta: Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) such as zidovudine were the first class of anti-HIV drugs developed and remain the traditional backbone of combination regimens, typically paired with a drug from a second class (an NNRTI, protease inhibitor, or integrase inhibitor) to suppress viral replication from multiple angles and reduce the risk of resistance. NRTIs are nucleoside/nucleotide analogs that get incorporated into the growing viral DNA chain by reverse transcriptase, terminating further elongation.

incorrectas.A: Protease inhibitors block polyprotein cleavage during virion maturation and are commonly combined with an NRTI backbone, but they are not themselves the backbone class referenced by this question.
incorrectas.B: Integrase strand transfer inhibitors (e.g., dolutegravir) block proviral DNA insertion into the host genome and are increasingly used as a preferred third agent, but are a newer class, not the traditional backbone.
incorrectas.C: NNRTIs (non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors) also inhibit reverse transcriptase but by a different, non-competitive mechanism (binding an allosteric site rather than causing chain termination); they are typically added to, rather than defining, the NRTI backbone.

preguntas.q: Which NRTI, when given to HIV-positive pregnant patients, has been shown to reduce vertical (mother-to-fetus) transmission of HIV by approximately two-thirds?

e.correcta: Zidovudine (AZT) was the first antiretroviral shown in clinical trials to significantly reduce perinatal HIV transmission — administered to the mother during pregnancy and labor and to the neonate after birth, it lowers vertical transmission by roughly two-thirds compared to no treatment. This landmark finding (from the ACTG 076 trial) established the principle that antiretroviral prophylaxis around pregnancy and delivery dramatically reduces mother-to-child transmission, a strategy now extended to combination regimens.

incorrectas.B: Tenofovir is a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor commonly used in modern combination regimens and in pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), but it is zidovudine that carries the classic historical association with the two-thirds reduction in vertical transmission tested here.
incorrectas.C: Lamivudine is another NRTI frequently paired with zidovudine in combination regimens, but it is not the specific agent credited with the landmark two-thirds reduction in perinatal transmission.
incorrectas.D: Nevirapine is an NNRTI (not an NRTI) that has also been studied for prevention of mother-to-child transmission in resource-limited settings, but it is a different drug class from the one specified in this question, and zidovudine remains the classically referenced agent for this statistic.

preguntas.q: Which class of antiretrovirals acts by being incorporated directly into the growing viral DNA chain during reverse transcription, thereby halting further chain elongation?

e.correcta: NRTIs are nucleoside/nucleotide analogs lacking a proper 3'-hydroxyl group; reverse transcriptase mistakes them for natural nucleotides and incorporates them into the elongating DNA strand, but because no further nucleotides can be added at that 3' end, DNA synthesis terminates prematurely (obligate chain termination). This directly competitive, incorporation-based mechanism distinguishes NRTIs from NNRTIs, which inhibit the same enzyme by a completely different, non-competitive mechanism.

incorrectas.A: NNRTIs inhibit reverse transcriptase by binding a hydrophobic pocket near, but distinct from, the enzyme's active site, causing an allosteric conformational change that blocks its function — they are not incorporated into the DNA chain themselves.
incorrectas.C: Protease inhibitors act at a later stage of the viral life cycle, blocking cleavage of Gag-Pol polyproteins during virion maturation, and have no role in DNA synthesis or chain termination.
incorrectas.D: Fusion inhibitors (e.g., enfuvirtide) block gp41-mediated fusion of the viral and host cell membranes at the entry step, acting well before reverse transcription even begins.

preguntas.q: Which class of antiretroviral drugs inhibits the viral enzyme responsible for cleaving Gag and Gag-Pol polyproteins into mature structural and enzymatic proteins during virion assembly?

e.correcta: HIV protease, encoded by pol, cleaves the large Gag and Gag-Pol polyprotein precursors into individual functional proteins (matrix, capsid, nucleocapsid, reverse transcriptase, integrase, protease itself) as new virions bud from the cell — a maturation step required for released particles to become infectious. Protease inhibitors (e.g., ritonavir, lopinavir) block this active site, causing production of immature, non-infectious viral particles, and are typically 'boosted' with low-dose ritonavir to inhibit hepatic CYP3A4 metabolism and increase drug levels.

incorrectas.A: Integrase inhibitors block insertion of proviral DNA into the host genome, an earlier step in the replication cycle that occurs well before polyprotein cleavage during virion maturation.
incorrectas.B: NRTIs inhibit reverse transcriptase during the DNA synthesis step of the life cycle, unrelated to the proteolytic processing of structural polyproteins that occurs later during virion assembly and budding.
incorrectas.D: CCR5 antagonists (e.g., maraviroc) block viral entry by preventing gp120 from engaging the CCR5 coreceptor, acting at the very first step of infection rather than at polyprotein maturation.

preguntas.q: Most DNA viruses replicate within which cellular compartment, an important exception being the poxviruses?

e.correcta: Most DNA viruses replicate in the host cell nucleus because they rely on host nuclear DNA polymerases and other nuclear machinery for genome replication; this is a key distinguishing feature from RNA viruses, most of which replicate in the cytoplasm using their own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. The major exception is the Poxviridae family, which are large enough to encode their own complete DNA replication machinery and therefore replicate entirely within the cytoplasm.

incorrectas.A: The cytoplasm is where most RNA viruses replicate (since it contains ribosomes and lacks host DNA polymerase); it is also where the exceptional poxviruses replicate, but it is not the site used by the majority of DNA viruses.
incorrectas.B: Mitochondria contain their own small circular genome and replication machinery for mitochondrial DNA, but they are not a site exploited by DNA viruses for their replication.
incorrectas.C: The Golgi apparatus is involved in protein processing, glycosylation, and trafficking (relevant to envelope glycoprotein maturation for some enveloped viruses), not in genome replication.

preguntas.q: Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), consistent with most DNA viruses, replicates its genome in which cellular compartment?

e.correcta: HSV is a large double-stranded DNA virus that, like most DNA viruses (except poxviruses), replicates its genome within the host cell nucleus, using host machinery alongside several virally encoded replication proteins (including its own DNA polymerase and helicase-primase). This nuclear replication is also why herpesvirus-infected cells characteristically show intranuclear inclusion bodies (Cowdry type A bodies) on histology.

incorrectas.B: The cytoplasm is where most RNA viruses (and the exceptional poxviruses among DNA viruses) replicate; HSV does not fit this pattern since it depends on nuclear machinery for genome synthesis.
incorrectas.C: The rough endoplasmic reticulum is involved in synthesis and glycosylation of viral envelope glycoproteins as part of virion assembly, but it is not where HSV's DNA genome is replicated.
incorrectas.D: Peroxisomes are involved in lipid metabolism and reactive oxygen species detoxification and play no role in herpesvirus genome replication.

preguntas.q: Cowdry type A inclusion bodies, a histologic hallmark of HSV-infected cells, are found in which part of the cell?

e.correcta: Cowdry type A bodies are eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions seen in cells infected by herpesviruses (HSV, VZV, CMV), reflecting accumulation of viral proteins and altered chromatin at the site of nuclear viral replication and assembly. Their intranuclear location directly parallels the fact that HSV, like most DNA viruses, replicates its genome in the nucleus, making the inclusion bodies a histologic clue that corresponds to the virus's replication site.

incorrectas.A: Cytoplasmic inclusion bodies are characteristic of viruses that replicate outside the nucleus, such as rabies virus (Negri bodies) or poxviruses (Guarnieri bodies), not HSV.
incorrectas.C: The cell membrane is where viral envelope glycoproteins are inserted before budding for some viruses, but it is not a site where inclusion bodies form; inclusion bodies reflect intracellular accumulation of replication complexes, not membrane assembly.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondria are not a site of herpesvirus replication or inclusion body formation; HSV depends on host nuclear, not mitochondrial, machinery for genome synthesis.

preguntas.q: What is the term for passage of a pathogen from mother to infant immediately before, during, or shortly after birth?

e.correcta: Vertical transmission refers specifically to mother-to-child spread of an infection — occurring transplacentally in utero, during passage through the birth canal (intrapartum), or postnatally (e.g., through breastfeeding) — and is the mechanism by which the ToRCHeS group of pathogens (Toxoplasma, Rubella, CMV, HSV/HIV, Syphilis) cause congenital or perinatal infection. Understanding vertical transmission underlies practices like prenatal screening, antiretroviral prophylaxis, and decisions about cesarean delivery in select maternal infections.

incorrectas.A: Horizontal transmission describes spread between individuals within the same generation (e.g., person-to-person contact, respiratory droplets, sexual contact) and does not specifically denote the mother-to-child route.
incorrectas.B: Fomite transmission refers to spread via contaminated inanimate objects (e.g., doorknobs, shared utensils) and is unrelated to the maternal-fetal or maternal-neonatal route described here.
incorrectas.D: Nosocomial transmission refers to infections acquired within a healthcare setting, a different concept entirely from mother-to-child transmission around the time of birth.

preguntas.q: In addition to saliva and sexual contact, HSV can be transmitted vertically from mother to fetus by crossing which structure?

e.correcta: As a member of the ToRCHeS group, HSV can cross the placenta to infect the fetus in utero, though intrapartum transmission during vaginal delivery through an actively shedding genital lesion is actually the more common route for neonatal HSV. Recognizing the placenta as a potential route reinforces why maternal HSV serostatus and lesion history matter for delivery planning, since untreated neonatal HSV carries a high risk of disseminated disease and encephalitis.

incorrectas.A: The amniotic sac contains the fetus and amniotic fluid but is not the interface across which maternal pathogens gain access to fetal circulation; that exchange occurs at the placental villi.
incorrectas.B: The umbilical cord is the conduit for blood flow between fetus and placenta once transmission has occurred, not the site where the virus initially crosses from mother to fetus.
incorrectas.C: The cervix is relevant to intrapartum exposure during vaginal delivery (contact with genital lesions/secretions), a distinct transmission route from transplacental (in utero) spread.

preguntas.q: Which HSV serotype is classically described as being confined to the upper half of the body, causing oral lesions and gingivostomatitis?

e.correcta: HSV-1 is traditionally associated with orolabial infection (gingivostomatitis, herpes labialis, keratoconjunctivitis) affecting structures above the waist, while HSV-2 is traditionally associated with genital infection below the waist; both serotypes are now frequently found at either site due to oral-genital sexual contact, but the above/below-the-waist distinction remains the classic teaching framework tested on exams. Both serotypes establish latency in sensory ganglia (trigeminal for HSV-1, sacral for HSV-2), consistent with the anatomic site of primary infection.

incorrectas.B: VZV (varicella-zoster virus) causes chickenpox and shingles with a dermatomal distribution that can occur anywhere on the body, not a serotype specifically confined to the upper half like classic HSV-1.
incorrectas.C: HSV-2 is the serotype classically associated with the lower half of the body (genital herpes), the reciprocal pattern to the one described in this question.
incorrectas.D: CMV is a different herpesvirus (HHV-5) that causes congenital infection, mononucleosis-like illness, and retinitis in immunocompromised hosts; it is not characterized by an upper/lower body distribution pattern the way HSV-1/HSV-2 are.

preguntas.q: Genital and lower-body herpetic lesions transmitted primarily through sexual contact are most classically associated with which herpes simplex virus serotype?

e.correcta: HSV-2 is transmitted predominantly through sexual contact and classically infects the skin and mucosa below the waist, causing genital herpes. Overlap with HSV-1 has become common due to oral-genital contact, but the classic below-the-waist pattern is attributed to HSV-2.

incorrectas.A: HSV-1 is classically transmitted via oral secretions and kissing, causing oral/facial lesions above the waist; although it increasingly causes genital disease via oral sex, that is not its classic anatomic pattern.
incorrectas.C: VZV causes chickenpox and shingles in a dermatomal distribution and is not defined by an above/below-the-waist split based on route of sexual transmission.
incorrectas.D: CMV is a herpesvirus causing congenital infection and a mononucleosis-like illness in immunocompetent hosts, not a virus classically divided by upper versus lower body location.

preguntas.q: Painful vesicular and ulcerative lesions of the gums and oral mucosa, often the first clinical manifestation of primary HSV-1 infection in young children, describe which condition?

e.correcta: Primary HSV-1 infection classically presents in young children as gingivostomatitis - painful vesicles and ulcers on the gingiva, tongue, and buccal mucosa, often with fever and cervical lymphadenopathy. This is typically the first visible sign of infection before the virus establishes latency in the trigeminal ganglion.

incorrectas.A: Herpangina is caused by coxsackievirus A and produces vesicular lesions on the posterior oropharynx and soft palate rather than the gingiva, making it a distinct enteroviral disease rather than a herpes simplex presentation.
incorrectas.C: Aphthous stomatitis causes recurrent shallow ulcers of unclear or autoimmune etiology; it is not caused by primary viral infection and lacks the systemic prodrome (fever, adenopathy) typical of HSV gingivostomatitis.
incorrectas.D: Oral candidiasis (thrush) is a fungal infection producing white plaques that wipe off, typically in immunocompromised or antibiotic-treated patients, not a vesicular/ulcerative viral gingival disease.

preguntas.q: Reactivation of latent HSV-1 from the trigeminal ganglion during periods of stress or immunosuppression classically manifests as which recurrent lesion?

e.correcta: HSV-1 establishes lifelong latency in the trigeminal ganglion after primary oral infection. Stress, UV exposure, or immunosuppression can reactivate the virus, which travels back down the nerve to the perioral skin, producing herpes labialis (cold sores) - the most common recurrent manifestation and the classic teaching point that this is the most common viral infection of the mouth.

incorrectas.A: Herpes zoster results from reactivation of VZV, not HSV-1, from a dorsal root or cranial nerve ganglion, producing a painful dermatomal vesicular rash rather than perioral cold sores.
incorrectas.B: Herpetic whitlow is an HSV infection of the finger typically from direct inoculation (e.g., healthcare workers or thumb-sucking children), not the classic site reached via stress-triggered trigeminal reactivation.
incorrectas.D: Eczema herpeticum is a severe, disseminated HSV infection superimposed on atopic dermatitis, a complication of a compromised skin barrier rather than the typical benign perioral reactivation lesion caused by stress.

preguntas.q: A patient presents with fever, seizures, and altered mental status, with MRI showing temporal lobe involvement. What is the most common cause of sporadic (non-epidemic) encephalitis in the United States?

e.correcta: HSV-1 is the most common cause of sporadic, non-epidemic encephalitis in the US, with a predilection for the temporal and inferior frontal lobes. It produces a hemorrhagic, necrotizing encephalitis and is a medical emergency treated empirically with IV acyclovir while awaiting PCR confirmation, because delayed treatment carries high mortality.

incorrectas.A: West Nile virus is an important cause of epidemic, seasonal, mosquito-borne encephalitis, but it does not outrank HSV-1 as the leading overall cause of sporadic encephalitis.
incorrectas.C: Enterovirus more commonly causes aseptic meningitis than true encephalitis, and its outbreaks tend to be seasonal and epidemic rather than representing the leading sporadic cause.
incorrectas.D: Rabies virus causes an almost universally fatal encephalitis, but it is exceedingly rare in the US due to vaccination and animal control programs, making it a distant statistical cause compared to HSV-1.

preguntas.q: In HSV-1 temporal lobe encephalitis, seizures and aphasia are classically accompanied by which additional clinical feature?

e.correcta: HSV-1 encephalitis preferentially damages the temporal and inferior frontal lobes, producing a classic triad of focal seizures (from temporal lobe irritation), aphasia (from involvement of dominant temporal/language areas), and altered mental status or personality change from limbic system involvement - reflecting the virus's anatomic route of spread from the trigeminal-associated pathways into these specific brain regions.

incorrectas.A: Bilateral leg weakness suggests a spinal cord or bilateral corticospinal tract process, not the localized temporal/frontal lobe pathology characteristic of HSV encephalitis.
incorrectas.C: Diplopia implies brainstem or cranial nerve III, IV, or VI involvement, structures that are not primarily affected by the temporal lobe predilection of HSV-1 encephalitis.
incorrectas.D: Resting tremor is a basal ganglia/extrapyramidal finding characteristic of parkinsonism, unrelated to the limbic and temporal lobe destruction seen in HSV encephalitis.

preguntas.q: After primary oral infection, HSV-1 establishes lifelong latency in which anatomic site?

e.correcta: HSV-1 travels retrograde along sensory axons from the oral mucosa to establish latency in the trigeminal (Gasserian) ganglion, consistent with its tropism for the face and mouth. Reactivation travels back down the same nerve to cause perioral lesions such as herpes labialis, which is why HSV-1 disease is normally confined to the face.

incorrectas.A: The sacral ganglion is the latency site for HSV-2, which is acquired through genital mucosa innervated by sacral sensory nerves, not the site reached by HSV-1 following oral infection.
incorrectas.B: The geniculate ganglion houses sensory fibers of the facial nerve (CN VII) and is the site of VZV reactivation causing Ramsay Hunt syndrome, not the site of HSV-1 latency.
incorrectas.D: The celiac ganglion is an autonomic sympathetic ganglion supplying abdominal viscera, unrelated to sensory innervation of the oral mucosa or herpesvirus latency.

preguntas.q: Following primary genital infection, HSV-2 establishes lifelong latency in which structure?

e.correcta: HSV-2 ascends sensory nerves from the genital mucosa to establish latency in the sacral (S2-S4) dorsal root ganglia, mirroring the sacral dermatomal innervation of the genital region. Reactivation travels back down these same nerve roots to cause recurrent genital lesions.

incorrectas.A: The trigeminal ganglion is the latency site for HSV-1 after oral infection, reflecting facial rather than genital sensory innervation.
incorrectas.B: Dorsal root ganglia in general can harbor latent herpesviruses at the dermatome corresponding to the original infection, but the genital mucosa is innervated by sacral, not cervical, sensory roots, so cervical ganglia are not the correct site for HSV-2.
incorrectas.D: The geniculate ganglion is associated with facial nerve sensation and VZV reactivation (Ramsay Hunt syndrome), unrelated to genital HSV-2 latency.

preguntas.q: Painful genital vesicles and ulcers with a tendency toward recurrent outbreaks are most commonly caused by which virus?

e.correcta: HSV-2 is the classic cause of herpes genitalis, producing painful grouped vesicles that ulcerate, with recurrences driven by reactivation from the sacral ganglia. Although HSV-1 increasingly causes genital disease via oral-genital contact, HSV-2 remains the serotype most strongly associated with genital herpes and its pattern of frequent recurrence.

incorrectas.A: HSV-1 classically causes oral/facial disease; while it can cause genital herpes via oral sex, it is not the serotype traditionally and most strongly linked to recurrent genital disease.
incorrectas.B: VZV causes chickenpox and shingles with a dermatomal distribution, not genital mucosal vesicles acquired through sexual transmission.
incorrectas.D: HPV causes genital warts (condyloma acuminatum) and cervical dysplasia through a very different, non-vesicular, proliferative mechanism driven by the E6/E7 oncoproteins, not painful ulcerative lesions.

preguntas.q: A neonate develops skin vesicles, encephalitis, and disseminated disease after passing through an infected birth canal. Which pathogen classically causes this presentation?

e.correcta: HSV-2 is the classic cause of neonatal herpes, acquired intrapartum through contact with maternal genital lesions or secretions during vaginal delivery. It can cause localized skin/eye/mouth disease, CNS disease, or fulminant disseminated multi-organ infection, which is why active maternal genital lesions at term often prompt cesarean delivery.

incorrectas.A: CMV is a TORCH pathogen but is transmitted transplacentally in utero rather than primarily intrapartum, causing sensorineural hearing loss, periventricular calcifications, and microcephaly rather than the acute vesicular/disseminated picture of neonatal HSV.
incorrectas.B: HSV-1 can rarely cause neonatal herpes, but the genital, intrapartum route of transmission is classically attributed to HSV-2 since HSV-1 more often causes oral disease in the mother rather than genital lesions.
incorrectas.C: Rubella virus is a TORCH pathogen causing congenital defects such as cataracts, cardiac malformations, and deafness from early transplacental infection, not the acute intrapartum vesicular/disseminated disease seen with neonatal HSV.

preguntas.q: Which antiviral is preferred for once-daily oral chronic suppressive therapy to reduce the frequency of recurrent HSV outbreaks?

e.correcta: Valacyclovir, the prodrug of acyclovir, has improved oral bioavailability that allows convenient once-daily dosing for chronic suppressive therapy of recurrent HSV outbreaks. Like acyclovir, it is selectively phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase and then inhibits viral DNA polymerase, but its dosing convenience makes it the preferred agent when patients need long-term suppression.

incorrectas.A: Foscarnet is a pyrophosphate analog that directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase without requiring activation by viral thymidine kinase; it is reserved for acyclovir-resistant HSV/CMV due to significant nephrotoxicity, not used as a first-line oral suppressive agent.
incorrectas.B: Ganciclovir is used primarily for CMV infections (e.g., in transplant or HIV patients) and carries greater myelosuppressive toxicity, making it an unsuitable choice for routine oral HSV suppression.
incorrectas.D: Cidofovir is a nucleotide analog reserved mainly for CMV retinitis and other resistant viral infections, requiring IV administration with probenecid and hydration due to nephrotoxicity, not a convenient oral option for HSV suppression.

preguntas.q: What is the current gold-standard laboratory test for diagnosing HSV infection, including HSV encephalitis?

o.C: PCR of CSF or lesion fluid

e.correcta: PCR detection of HSV DNA, whether from CSF in suspected encephalitis or from lesion swabs in mucocutaneous disease, is the current gold standard because of its high sensitivity, specificity, and rapid turnaround. It has largely replaced older, less sensitive methods for confirming the diagnosis, especially in time-critical scenarios like encephalitis.

incorrectas.A: A Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells suggestive of herpesvirus infection but cannot distinguish HSV-1 from HSV-2 or VZV, and it has much lower sensitivity than PCR.
incorrectas.B: Viral culture was historically used but is slower and less sensitive, particularly for CSF samples in encephalitis, and has largely been supplanted by PCR-based testing.
incorrectas.D: Serologic antibody testing detects prior exposure or seroconversion but is not useful for diagnosing acute infection or encephalitis in real time, since antibody titers take time to rise and don't confirm active CNS disease.

preguntas.q: Recurrent superficial Candida infections of the skin, nails, and mucous membranes (chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis) are most classically associated with a deficiency in which arm of the immune system?

e.correcta: T cells, particularly Th17 cells producing IL-17, are critical for mucosal antifungal defense against Candida. T-cell deficiencies (e.g., DiGeorge syndrome, HIV/AIDS, IL-17 pathway defects) predispose to chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, characterized by recurrent, difficult-to-clear superficial infections of the skin, nails, and mucosa without hematogenous spread.

incorrectas.A: B-cell/humoral immunity deficiencies, such as X-linked agammaglobulinemia, predispose mainly to recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria and enteroviruses, not the classic mucocutaneous candidiasis pattern tied to defective cellular immunity.
incorrectas.B: Neutropenia predisposes to invasive, disseminated hematogenous candidiasis rather than the chronic superficial mucocutaneous pattern, since neutrophils are the primary defense against tissue invasion and bloodstream dissemination, not mucosal surveillance.
incorrectas.D: Complement deficiencies predispose mainly to infections with Neisseria species and other encapsulated organisms via impaired opsonization and membrane attack complex formation, not to mucocutaneous fungal disease.

preguntas.q: Hematogenous, disseminated candidiasis (candidemia with multi-organ seeding) is most classically seen in patients with which underlying condition?

e.correcta: Neutrophils are the primary cellular defense preventing Candida from invading the bloodstream and disseminating to organs. Neutropenic patients, such as those undergoing chemotherapy or with hematologic malignancy, are at high risk for candidemia and disseminated disease with seeding of the liver, spleen, eyes, and other organs, in contrast to the localized mucocutaneous pattern seen with T-cell defects.

incorrectas.A: T-cell deficiency predisposes to chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, a superficial, localized infection of skin and mucosa, not the invasive hematogenous dissemination associated with neutrophil dysfunction.
incorrectas.B: Asplenia increases the risk of overwhelming infection with encapsulated bacteria (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis) due to loss of splenic clearance of opsonized organisms, not specifically disseminated candidiasis.
incorrectas.C: Complement deficiency predisposes to infections with Neisseria and other organisms cleared via complement-mediated lysis and opsonization, not the neutrophil-dependent containment of Candida.

preguntas.q: Which DNA virus family is unusual among enveloped viruses in synthesizing its own envelope within the cytoplasm rather than acquiring it by budding through a host cell membrane?

e.correcta: Poxviruses replicate entirely in the host cell cytoplasm and synthesize their own envelope de novo rather than budding through the host plasma or nuclear membrane like most other enveloped viruses. This reflects their unusually large, complex, self-sufficient replication machinery, which encodes most of the enzymes needed for replication without relying on host nuclear enzymes.

incorrectas.A: Herpesvirus replicates in the nucleus and acquires its envelope by budding through the host nuclear membrane, the more typical mechanism used by enveloped DNA viruses.
incorrectas.C: Adenovirus is a naked, non-enveloped DNA virus, so the concept of envelope acquisition does not apply to it at all.
incorrectas.D: Papillomavirus is also a naked, non-enveloped DNA virus, distinguishing it entirely from the enveloped, self-enveloping poxvirus.

preguntas.q: Which virus has a distinctive 'dumbbell-shaped' core visible on electron microscopy?

e.correcta: Poxviruses have a complex structure with a biconcave, dumbbell-shaped core containing the viral DNA and enzymes, flanked by lateral bodies and enclosed within a complex, brick-shaped or ovoid envelope. This distinctive morphology reflects the unusually large and complex virion architecture of poxviruses compared to other DNA viruses.

incorrectas.A: Adenovirus has an icosahedral capsid with characteristic fiber projections at each vertex, not a dumbbell-shaped core.
incorrectas.B: Herpesvirus has an icosahedral capsid surrounding a linear dsDNA genome, with a surrounding tegument and envelope, but it lacks the dumbbell-shaped core structure unique to poxviruses.
incorrectas.D: Papillomavirus has a small, naked icosahedral capsid, a structurally simple virion that bears no resemblance to the complex poxvirus core morphology.

preguntas.q: Which is the largest DNA virus that infects humans?

e.correcta: Poxviruses are the largest and most complex DNA viruses infecting humans, with a genome and virion large enough to encode many of their own replication enzymes. This size and complexity are what allow poxviruses to replicate entirely in the cytoplasm, independent of host nuclear machinery, unlike smaller DNA viruses that depend heavily on host cell enzymes.

incorrectas.A: Adenovirus is a medium-sized, naked icosahedral DNA virus, considerably smaller and structurally simpler than poxviruses.
incorrectas.B: Papillomavirus is one of the smallest DNA viruses, with a small circular genome, far from being the largest human DNA virus.
incorrectas.C: Herpesvirus is a moderately large enveloped DNA virus, but it is still smaller and less complex than the poxvirus family.

preguntas.q: A patient has a diffuse vesicular rash in which all lesions appear to be at the same stage of development. This finding is classically associated with which infection?

e.correcta: Smallpox lesions characteristically appear synchronously, so all lesions are at the same stage of development (macule, papule, vesicle, pustule, or crust) at any given time. This distinguishes it from chickenpox, where lesions appear in successive crops, producing lesions of different ages seen simultaneously - a bedside distinction historically used to differentiate the two diseases.

incorrectas.A: Chickenpox (VZV) classically shows lesions in different stages of development at the same time, because new crops of vesicles continue to erupt over several days while older ones crust over - the opposite of the synchronous smallpox pattern.
incorrectas.C: Molluscum contagiosum presents as flesh-colored, umbilicated papules without the macule-to-pustule progression of a true poxvirus/varicella-type rash, so staging synchrony is not a relevant diagnostic feature.
incorrectas.D: Herpes zoster presents as a dermatomal vesicular rash from VZV reactivation, generally confined to a single dermatome, rather than a diffuse rash characterized by synchronous versus asynchronous lesion staging.

preguntas.q: A rash with lesions in different stages of development simultaneously - some vesicular, some crusted - is classically described in which infection?

e.correcta: Chickenpox, primary VZV infection, produces successive crops of lesions over several days, so at any given time the rash contains macules, vesicles, and crusted lesions together, often described as 'dew drops on a rose petal' in varying stages. This is the opposite of smallpox, where lesions erupt synchronously and are all in the same stage at once.

incorrectas.A: Smallpox classically produces lesions that are all at the same stage of development simultaneously, the opposite of the varied lesion staging seen in chickenpox.
incorrectas.C: Hand-foot-mouth disease, caused by coxsackievirus, presents with oral ulcers and vesicles on the hands, feet, and mouth, but it is not classically used in the synchronous-versus-asynchronous staging distinction that separates smallpox from chickenpox.
incorrectas.D: Molluscum contagiosum presents as umbilicated papules without a vesicle-to-crust progression, so staging variability is not the defining diagnostic feature of that disease.

preguntas.q: Compared to smallpox, chickenpox (varicella) lesions are classically described as being located at what depth within the skin?

e.correcta: Chickenpox lesions are classically superficial, involving primarily the epidermis, which is why they tend to heal without significant scarring. This contrasts with smallpox lesions, which are deep, involving the dermis, and much more likely to leave permanent scars after healing.

incorrectas.A: A deep, dermal location describes the classic depth of smallpox lesions, not chickenpox, and is a key differentiating feature historically used at the bedside between the two poxvirus-family rashes.
incorrectas.C: Neither chickenpox nor smallpox lesions are classically described as subcutaneous; both are dermal/epidermal skin-level processes rather than extending into the subcutaneous fat.
incorrectas.D: Intramuscular is not a relevant depth for either viral exanthem; both are cutaneous infections, not muscular ones.

preguntas.q: Smallpox skin lesions are classically described as being centered at what depth, contributing to their tendency to leave scars?

e.correcta: Smallpox lesions are classically deep, involving the dermis, which is why they tend to leave permanent, pitted scars after healing - a key bedside differentiator from the more superficial, less scarring lesions of chickenpox.

incorrectas.A: A superficial, epidermal location describes the classic depth of chickenpox lesions, which heal with minimal scarring, the opposite of the deep, scarring smallpox lesions.
incorrectas.C: Subcutaneous fat involvement is not classically described for either smallpox or chickenpox; both remain within the skin layers proper rather than extending into deeper fat.
incorrectas.D: Smallpox involves the skin diffusely and can involve mucosa, but the classic teaching point about lesion depth and scarring refers specifically to the dermal skin lesions, not to an exclusively mucosal distribution.

preguntas.q: Varicella (chickenpox) lesions classically show which distribution pattern on the body?

e.correcta: Chickenpox has a classic centripetal distribution, with lesions concentrated on the trunk and face while relatively sparing the distal extremities. This contrasts with other viral exanthems, such as hand-foot-mouth disease, that are more peripherally distributed, and helps distinguish varicella clinically at the bedside.

incorrectas.A: A peripheral distribution sparing the trunk describes a centrifugal pattern, which is more characteristic of smallpox (denser on the face and extremities) than the centripetal, trunk-predominant chickenpox rash.
incorrectas.C: Palms and soles predominance is characteristic of infections like secondary syphilis, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, or hand-foot-mouth disease, not the classic chickenpox distribution.
incorrectas.D: Chickenpox is a diffuse rash that spreads well beyond the face, with the trunk actually being the area of highest lesion density, not the face alone.

preguntas.q: Localized vesicular skin lesions ('milkmaid's blisters') acquired through direct contact with infected cow udders are caused by which virus?

e.correcta: Cowpox virus is transmitted through direct contact with infected cattle, classically the udders during milking, producing localized vesicular and pustular skin lesions historically termed 'milkmaid's blisters.' This same exposure led Edward Jenner to observe that milkmaids who developed cowpox were protected from smallpox, the historical basis for the first vaccine.

incorrectas.A: Molluscum contagiosum virus causes flesh-colored umbilicated papules via direct skin-to-skin (often sexual or fomite) contact between humans, not through contact with cattle udders.
incorrectas.C: Orf virus is a related parapoxvirus causing similar localized vesicular lesions, but it is transmitted through contact with infected sheep or goats, not cows.
incorrectas.D: Vaccinia virus is the virus used in the smallpox vaccine, related to cowpox but not itself the naturally occurring, cattle-transmitted pathogen described in this classic exposure history.

preguntas.q: Molluscum contagiosum, a common cause of localized skin infection especially in children and immunocompromised patients, belongs to which viral family?

e.correcta: Molluscum contagiosum virus is a member of the Poxviridae family, sharing the large, complex, cytoplasmic-replicating structure typical of poxviruses. It spreads by direct skin contact or fomites and causes localized, self-limited papular skin lesions rather than systemic disease, unlike many other poxviruses such as smallpox.

incorrectas.A: Herpesviridae includes HSV, VZV, CMV, and EBV, which replicate in the nucleus and cause distinct disease patterns (vesicular eruptions, mononucleosis, congenital infection) rather than the umbilicated papules of molluscum.
incorrectas.B: Papillomaviridae includes HPV, a small naked DNA virus causing warts and cervical dysplasia through a very different oncogenic mechanism (E6/E7 oncoproteins), structurally and clinically distinct from molluscum contagiosum virus.
incorrectas.D: Picornaviridae is a family of small RNA viruses (e.g., coxsackievirus, poliovirus, rhinovirus), completely unrelated to the large DNA poxvirus responsible for molluscum contagiosum.

preguntas.q: Flesh-colored, dome-shaped skin papules with central umbilication are diagnostic of which infection?

e.correcta: Molluscum contagiosum classically presents with flesh-colored, dome-shaped, waxy papules that have a characteristic central umbilication (dimple). This distinctive finding results from the poxvirus's cytopathic effect within the epidermis and is often diagnostic on clinical inspection alone, without need for biopsy.

incorrectas.A: Verruca vulgaris (common wart) is caused by HPV and presents as rough, hyperkeratotic papules without central umbilication, reflecting a very different epithelial growth pattern than the smooth, dimpled molluscum lesion.
incorrectas.C: Herpes zoster presents as grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a dermatomal distribution, not as discrete umbilicated flesh-colored papules.
incorrectas.D: Chickenpox presents as diffuse vesicles ('dew drops on a rose petal') at varying stages, not the waxy, umbilicated papules characteristic of molluscum contagiosum.

preguntas.q: Umbilicated papules concentrated on the trunk of a child are most consistent with which diagnosis?

e.correcta: Molluscum contagiosum classically presents as multiple small, flesh-colored, umbilicated papules that favor the trunk and flexural areas in children, spread by direct skin contact or fomites such as shared towels or swimming pools. The central umbilication is a key clinical clue that distinguishes it from other papular skin conditions in this age group.

incorrectas.A: Chickenpox produces vesicular lesions in different stages of development diffusely across the body, not the discrete waxy umbilicated papules seen with molluscum.
incorrectas.B: Impetigo is a superficial bacterial skin infection (Staph/Strep) causing honey-colored crusted lesions, not umbilicated papules.
incorrectas.D: Scabies is caused by a mite infestation, producing intensely pruritic burrows and papules typically in the finger webs, wrists, and flexural areas, without the characteristic central umbilication seen in molluscum.

preguntas.q: Diffuse or extensive molluscum contagiosum lesions in an adult patient should prompt evaluation for which underlying condition?

e.correcta: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a poxvirus and in an immunocompetent adult usually produces a few localized, often sexually-transmitted lesions; when lesions become numerous, large, and widespread (sparing only the palms and soles), this pattern signals impaired cell-mediated immunity, most classically from HIV/AIDS, and should trigger HIV testing. Extensive disease reflects the host's diminished ability to contain a normally self-limited cutaneous poxvirus infection.

incorrectas.B: Diabetes mellitus predisposes to certain skin/soft tissue infections (e.g., mucormycosis, necrotizing fasciitis, recurrent candidiasis) but is not the classic association taught for diffuse molluscum contagiosum; the hallmark trigger for widespread molluscum is cellular immunodeficiency, particularly HIV.
incorrectas.C: Iron deficiency anemia can cause glossitis, koilonychia, and pica, but it has no recognized link to poxvirus containment or to the spread of molluscum contagiosum.
incorrectas.D: Primary hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcemia-related findings (bone disease, kidney stones, GI/psychiatric symptoms) and is not associated with impaired control of cutaneous viral infections like molluscum contagiosum.

preguntas.q: In an adult, molluscum contagiosum presenting as a single lesion or a few localized lesions (rather than diffuse disease) is most commonly acquired through which route?

e.correcta: In adults, molluscum contagiosum virus is usually spread by direct skin-to-skin contact during sexual activity, producing a limited number of pearly, umbilicated papules concentrated on the genitals, lower abdomen, and inner thighs; this pattern differs from the diffuse disease seen with immunosuppression. Recognizing sexual transmission is important because it should prompt screening for other sexually transmitted infections.

incorrectas.A: Fecal-oral spread is the classic route for viruses like hepatitis A and many enteroviruses, not for molluscum contagiosum, which requires direct skin contact with infected epithelium or fomites rather than ingestion.
incorrectas.C: Respiratory droplet transmission is how the related poxvirus smallpox spreads, but molluscum contagiosum is transmitted by direct contact, not inhalation of secretions.
incorrectas.D: Vertical transmission across the placenta is described for organisms like the TORCH pathogens, not for molluscum contagiosum, which in adults is overwhelmingly acquired through direct sexual or skin contact.

preguntas.q: On skin biopsy, molluscum contagiosum characteristically shows which histologic finding, and where is it located?

o.A: Eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion bodies within keratinocytes
o.B: Basophilic nuclear inclusion bodies within keratinocytes
o.C: Eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion bodies within dermal fibroblasts
o.D: Basophilic cytoplasmic inclusion bodies within melanocytes

e.correcta: Molluscum contagiosum virus, a poxvirus, replicates exclusively in the cytoplasm (poxviruses carry their own DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, so they do not need the nucleus), producing large eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions called molluscum (Henderson-Patterson) bodies within infected keratinocytes of the epidermis. Seeing cytoplasmic rather than nuclear inclusions is a useful clue that distinguishes poxviruses from most other DNA viruses, such as herpesviruses or adenovirus, which replicate in the nucleus and form intranuclear inclusions instead.

incorrectas.B: Basophilic nuclear inclusions are the pattern seen with viruses that replicate in the nucleus, such as CMV (owl's-eye nuclear inclusions) or adenovirus, not poxviruses, which lack dependence on nuclear replication machinery and stay in the cytoplasm.
incorrectas.C: The inclusions of molluscum are found in keratinocytes of the epidermis, the cell type the virus actually infects, not in dermal fibroblasts, which are not the target cell for this epidermotropic poxvirus.
incorrectas.D: Melanocytes are not infected by molluscum contagiosum virus, and the inclusions described are eosinophilic rather than basophilic; this combination does not match the actual histology of molluscum bodies.

preguntas.q: Smallpox (variola virus) is primarily transmitted between people by which route?

o.B: Ingestion of contaminated food or water

e.correcta: Variola virus, the poxvirus that causes smallpox, is spread mainly by inhalation of airborne respiratory droplets or aerosolized secretions from an infected person, as well as by contact with skin lesions or contaminated fomites; this respiratory route, combined with high mortality, is what made smallpox so devastating before its eradication through vaccination. This contrasts with molluscum contagiosum, a related poxvirus that spreads by direct skin contact rather than respiratory secretions.

incorrectas.B: Ingestion of contaminated food or water is the transmission route for fecal-oral pathogens such as hepatitis A or many enteroviruses; smallpox is a respiratory/contact-transmitted virus, not an enteric one.
incorrectas.C: Sexual contact is the classic route for molluscum contagiosum in adults, but smallpox spreads primarily via the respiratory route, reflecting its ability to cause explosive epidemics through airborne transmission.
incorrectas.D: Smallpox is not an arboviral disease and has no insect vector; mosquito-borne transmission characterizes viruses like dengue, Zika, or yellow fever, not variola virus.

preguntas.q: What type of vaccine has historically been used to prevent smallpox, and what is it called?

o.A: Live attenuated vaccine using vaccinia virus
o.B: Inactivated whole-virus vaccine using variola virus
o.D: mRNA vaccine encoding variola surface antigens

e.correcta: The smallpox vaccine uses live, attenuated vaccinia virus, a related but distinct poxvirus (the origin of the term "vaccine" itself, from vacca, Latin for cow, referencing Jenner's use of cowpox). Because vaccinia is antigenically similar to variola but far less virulent, it induces protective immunity against smallpox without causing the disease itself in most recipients, and this same platform underlies modern vaccinia-based vaccines used against mpox.

incorrectas.B: The vaccine does not use variola virus itself, whether inactivated or otherwise; using the actual smallpox-causing virus, even killed, was never how the classic smallpox vaccine was made, since a safe related virus, vaccinia, was used instead.
incorrectas.C: Subunit/recombinant protein vaccines, like the hepatitis B vaccine, present isolated viral proteins rather than a whole live virus; the classic smallpox vaccine instead uses a live, replicating virus (vaccinia) to generate robust immunity.
incorrectas.D: mRNA vaccines are a modern platform, seen in some COVID-19 vaccines, that did not exist when the smallpox vaccine was developed; the traditional smallpox vaccine is a live-virus vaccine, not a nucleic acid-based one.

preguntas.q: Human papillomavirus (HPV) primarily infects and establishes itself in which layer of the squamous epithelium?

e.correcta: HPV infects the stratum basale, the deepest layer of the epidermis/cervical epithelium where undifferentiated keratinocytes are actively dividing; the virus gains access to these basal cells through microabrasions and relies on the host cell's replication machinery as keratinocytes differentiate and migrate upward, with viral gene expression and virion assembly increasing as cells move toward the surface. This basal-layer tropism explains why HPV requires epithelial trauma to initiate infection and why persistent infection of these long-lived basal stem cells underlies chronic or recurrent disease and oncogenic potential.

incorrectas.A: The stratum spinosum lies above the basal layer and is where HPV gene expression later increases as infected cells differentiate, but the virus must first establish infection in the basal layer's replicating stem cells, not the spinosum.
incorrectas.C: The stratum corneum is the outermost, dead, keratinized layer where mature virions are ultimately shed, not where the virus initially infects or establishes itself, since these cells lack the replicative machinery the virus depends on.
incorrectas.D: The stratum granulosum is an intermediate differentiating layer involved in late stages of the HPV life cycle, such as capsid assembly, but it is not the site of initial infection, which requires access to the actively dividing basal cells.

preguntas.q: Staphylococcus epidermidis infections are classically associated with which of the following?

o.A: Native, non-prosthetic heart valves in intravenous drug users
o.B: Community-acquired skin abscesses in healthy children
o.C: Indwelling medical devices such as prosthetic joints, urinary catheters, and prosthetic heart valves
o.D: Hematogenous native joint infections in young athletes

e.correcta: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a coagulase-negative staphylococcus and a normal skin commensal that becomes pathogenic mainly when it gains access to foreign material, where it forms a protective biofilm on the surface of prosthetic joints, indwelling urinary or vascular catheters, and prosthetic heart valves. Because the organism itself is low-virulence, these device-associated infections are the clinical context in which it truly matters, and management usually requires removing or replacing the infected hardware in addition to antibiotics.

incorrectas.A: Native valve endocarditis in IV drug users is the classic scenario for Staphylococcus aureus (often right-sided, tricuspid valve), a far more virulent organism than S. epidermidis that does not require a foreign device to invade.
incorrectas.B: Community-acquired skin abscesses in healthy children are typically caused by Staphylococcus aureus, including MRSA strains, which possess virulence factors for invading intact skin; S. epidermidis is low-virulence and rarely causes disease without a prosthetic nidus.
incorrectas.D: Hematogenous seeding of native joints in young, healthy patients is more typical of Neisseria gonorrhoeae (disseminated gonococcal infection) or S. aureus, not S. epidermidis, which needs a foreign surface like a prosthetic joint to establish infection.

preguntas.q: Which organism most commonly causes endocarditis involving a prosthetic heart valve?

e.correcta: Staphylococcus epidermidis, a coagulase-negative staphylococcus and normal skin flora, is the leading cause of prosthetic valve endocarditis because it can be introduced onto the valve at the time of surgery or via catheter-associated bacteremia, after which it forms a protective biofilm on the foreign material that resists both host immune clearance and many antibiotics. This differs from native valve endocarditis, where more virulent organisms like S. aureus or viridans streptococci predominate.

incorrectas.A: Streptococcus viridans classically causes subacute native valve endocarditis, particularly on previously damaged valves, following dental procedures and transient bacteremia, but it is not the leading cause of infection on prosthetic valves specifically.
incorrectas.B: Enterococcus faecalis causes endocarditis typically after GI or GU procedures or manipulation and can affect native or prosthetic valves, but it is not the most common organism implicated in prosthetic valve endocarditis; that distinction belongs to biofilm-forming S. epidermidis.
incorrectas.D: Staphylococcus aureus is a major cause of acute, aggressive native valve endocarditis, especially in IV drug users, and can also infect prosthetic valves, but the organism most classically and most commonly associated with prosthetic valve endocarditis is S. epidermidis.

preguntas.q: What virulence factor allows Staphylococcus epidermidis to colonize prosthetic devices and resist both host defenses and antibiotics?

e.correcta: S. epidermidis produces an extracellular polysaccharide matrix that forms a biofilm on synthetic surfaces such as catheters, joint prostheses, and heart valves; the biofilm physically shields the bacteria from phagocytes and antibodies and impairs antibiotic penetration, allowing the organism to persist on hardware despite treatment. This is why device-associated S. epidermidis infections are notoriously difficult to eradicate without removing the infected material.

incorrectas.A: Protein A is a virulence factor of Staphylococcus aureus that binds the Fc portion of IgG to inhibit opsonization and phagocytosis; it is not the key factor explaining S. epidermidis's ability to colonize prosthetic devices.
incorrectas.C: Coagulase is the enzyme that defines S. aureus (coagulase-positive) and helps it form a protective fibrin clot; S. epidermidis is coagulase-negative, and its device tropism is explained by biofilm formation, not coagulase activity.
incorrectas.D: Exfoliative toxin is produced by certain S. aureus strains and causes staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome by cleaving desmosomal proteins; it has no role in S. epidermidis's colonization of prosthetic material.

preguntas.q: A prosthetic device infection is suspected to be caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus epidermidis. Which antibiotic should be used empirically?

e.correcta: Because methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative staphylococci, like MRSE, carry an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a via the mecA gene) that renders essentially all beta-lactams ineffective, vancomycin, a glycopeptide that inhibits cell wall synthesis by binding D-ala-D-ala termini rather than PBPs, is the empiric treatment of choice until susceptibilities return.

incorrectas.A: Nafcillin is a beta-lactamase-resistant penicillin used for methicillin-sensitive staphylococci, but it works by binding penicillin-binding proteins that are structurally altered in methicillin-resistant strains, making it ineffective against MRSE.
incorrectas.B: Cefazolin is a first-generation cephalosporin, also a beta-lactam, and shares the same vulnerability to PBP2a-mediated resistance seen in methicillin-resistant staphylococci, so it will not reliably treat MRSE.
incorrectas.D: Ampicillin is a beta-lactam antibiotic with activity against susceptible gram-positive and some gram-negative organisms, but like other beta-lactams it is rendered ineffective against methicillin-resistant staphylococci by the altered PBP2a target.

preguntas.q: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a normal inhabitant of which body site, explaining why it can easily contaminate specimens or seed prosthetic devices during procedures?

e.correcta: S. epidermidis is one of the dominant organisms of normal skin flora, colonizing essentially everyone; this ubiquity is precisely why it so easily contaminates blood cultures drawn through skin and why it can be introduced into surgical wounds or onto catheters and prosthetic devices during placement, later forming biofilm-protected infections.

incorrectas.A: The gut lumen is dominated by organisms like Bacteroides, E. coli, and Enterococcus as part of the normal gastrointestinal flora, not S. epidermidis, which is a skin commensal rather than an enteric one.
incorrectas.C: The oropharynx harbors viridans streptococci and various anaerobes as its dominant normal flora; S. epidermidis is not characteristically described as a major oropharyngeal commensal.
incorrectas.D: The vagina is more classically associated with Staphylococcus saprophyticus (and lactobacilli) as part of its normal flora, whereas S. epidermidis is specifically the organism found ubiquitously on the skin.

preguntas.q: Staphylococcus epidermidis, as normal skin flora, is a frequent contaminant of which type of clinical specimen?

e.correcta: Because S. epidermidis heavily colonizes the skin, needle puncture during venipuncture can inadvertently introduce it into the blood culture bottle even when the patient has no true bacteremia; interpreting a positive blood culture for S. epidermidis therefore requires clinical correlation, such as multiple positive bottles, presence of a line or device, and signs of sepsis, to distinguish true infection from contamination.

incorrectas.A: Sputum cultures are more often confounded by oropharyngeal flora, such as viridans streptococci and Neisseria species, contaminating the sample as it passes through the mouth, not primarily by skin flora like S. epidermidis.
incorrectas.B: CSF is obtained via lumbar puncture through skin that is sterilized first, and while skin flora contamination can occur, the classic teaching point about S. epidermidis contamination centers on blood cultures drawn by venipuncture.
incorrectas.D: Stool cultures reflect the gut microbiota, dominated by anaerobes and enteric gram-negative rods, not skin flora, so S. epidermidis is not the classic contaminant discussed for stool specimens.

preguntas.q: What is the catalase test result for Staphylococcus epidermidis?

e.correcta: All Staphylococcus species, including S. epidermidis, S. aureus, and S. saprophyticus, are catalase-positive, meaning they produce the enzyme catalase that breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, visualized as bubbling when H2O2 is added to a colony. This catalase positivity is the key test that separates staphylococci from streptococci and enterococci, which are catalase-negative, in the initial workup of gram-positive cocci in clusters.

incorrectas.A: A negative catalase result is characteristic of streptococci and enterococci (gram-positive cocci in chains or pairs), not staphylococci; S. epidermidis reliably produces catalase and would test positive.
incorrectas.C: Catalase positivity is not variable among staphylococcal strains — it is a consistent, defining biochemical feature of the entire Staphylococcus genus, used precisely because it is reliable enough to separate staphylococci from streptococci.
incorrectas.D: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a facultative anaerobe, not an obligate anaerobe, and the catalase test is a standard, easily performed assay for this organism, indeed how staphylococci are first distinguished from streptococci in the lab.

preguntas.q: Like other members of its genus, what is the catalase test result for Staphylococcus saprophyticus?

o.A: Weakly positive only under strict aerobic conditions
o.D: Positive only after 48 hours of incubation

e.correcta: Catalase positivity is a genus-defining trait shared by all Staphylococcus species — S. aureus, S. epidermidis, and S. saprophyticus alike — reflecting their shared enzymatic breakdown of hydrogen peroxide. Clinically, this test is used early in identifying gram-positive cocci in clusters as staphylococci (catalase-positive) versus streptococci or enterococci (catalase-negative), before further tests like coagulase are used to speciate within Staphylococcus.

incorrectas.A: The catalase reaction in staphylococci is a straightforward positive or negative result performed under standard conditions, not a weak reaction confined to strict aerobiosis; S. saprophyticus gives a clear positive result like the rest of the genus.
incorrectas.B: A negative catalase result would instead suggest a streptococcus or enterococcus, not a staphylococcus; S. saprophyticus, being a Staphylococcus species, is catalase-positive.
incorrectas.D: The catalase test produces an immediate visible reaction (bubbling) within seconds of adding hydrogen peroxide to a colony; it does not require prolonged incubation to become positive.

preguntas.q: What is the coagulase test result for Staphylococcus saprophyticus?

o.D: Cannot be determined without additional biochemical panels

e.correcta: Staphylococcus saprophyticus, like S. epidermidis, is coagulase-negative, meaning it lacks the enzyme that clots plasma; Staphylococcus aureus is the only clinically significant coagulase-positive staphylococcus. The coagulase test is the key step used to distinguish S. aureus from the coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus, once catalase positivity has already identified an organism as a Staphylococcus.

incorrectas.A: A positive coagulase result is the defining feature of Staphylococcus aureus, which uses the enzyme to convert fibrinogen to fibrin and cloak itself in a protective clot; S. saprophyticus lacks this enzyme and is coagulase-negative.
incorrectas.B: Coagulase status is not strain-variable within a species — it is a stable, species-defining characteristic used reliably in the laboratory to separate S. aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci like S. saprophyticus.
incorrectas.D: The coagulase test is itself a simple, standard biochemical assay, mixing the organism with plasma and observing for clot formation, that directly and reliably answers this question without needing additional panels.

preguntas.q: Staphylococcus saprophyticus infections are typically spread by which route?

e.correcta: S. saprophyticus is part of the normal perineal, rectal, and vaginal flora and is transmitted via close contact with bodily fluids, most notably through sexual activity, which is why it is a classic cause of UTI/cystitis in young, sexually active women. This contact-based spread, combined with its proximity to the urethra as normal flora, explains its predilection for ascending into the bladder.

incorrectas.A: Fecal-oral transmission characterizes enteric pathogens spread by ingestion of contaminated material, such as hepatitis A or norovirus; S. saprophyticus causes disease through ascension of local flora via contact, not by being swallowed.
incorrectas.B: Respiratory droplet spread applies to airborne pathogens like influenza or tuberculosis; S. saprophyticus is a urogenital commensal transmitted through bodily/sexual contact, not respiratory secretions.
incorrectas.D: Tick-borne transmission is the route for vector-borne organisms like Borrelia burgdorferi or Rickettsia; S. saprophyticus has no arthropod vector and spreads through direct contact.

preguntas.q: On Gram stain, how does Staphylococcus saprophyticus appear?

e.correcta: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a gram-positive coccus that, like other staphylococci, appears in clusters on Gram stain (from the Greek "staphyle," meaning bunch of grapes), reflecting its thick peptidoglycan cell wall that retains crystal violet stain. This gram-positive, cluster-forming morphology, together with catalase positivity and coagulase negativity, places it within the coagulase-negative staphylococci alongside S. epidermidis.

incorrectas.A: Gram-negative rods describes organisms like E. coli or Proteus, common gram-negative uropathogens, but S. saprophyticus has a thick peptidoglycan wall that retains crystal violet stain, making it gram-positive, not gram-negative.
incorrectas.C: Gram-negative coccobacilli describes organisms like Haemophilus influenzae or Acinetobacter, not staphylococci; S. saprophyticus is a gram-positive coccus, distinguished by a completely different cell wall structure and stain retention.
incorrectas.D: Gram-variable filamentous morphology is seen in organisms like Gardnerella or Nocardia under certain conditions, not in staphylococci, which reliably and consistently stain gram-positive as clustered cocci.

preguntas.q: On Gram stain, how does Staphylococcus epidermidis appear?

e.correcta: S. epidermidis, like all staphylococci, is a gram-positive coccus that classically clusters in grape-like arrangements on Gram stain due to its cell division pattern in multiple planes and its thick peptidoglycan wall retaining crystal violet stain. This gram-positive, catalase-positive, coagulase-negative profile places it in the coagulase-negative staphylococcus group alongside S. saprophyticus, distinct from the coagulase-positive S. aureus.

incorrectas.B: Gram-negative diplococci describes organisms like Neisseria species, which have a thin peptidoglycan wall and an outer membrane that does not retain crystal violet; S. epidermidis is gram-positive with a thick peptidoglycan wall.
incorrectas.C: Gram-positive rods in chains describes organisms like Bacillus or Listeria (or Corynebacterium, which forms palisades); S. epidermidis is a coccus, not a rod, and clusters rather than forming chains.
incorrectas.D: Gram-negative bacilli describes enteric organisms like E. coli or Klebsiella; S. epidermidis has a thick peptidoglycan cell wall that retains crystal violet, making it gram-positive, not gram-negative.

preguntas.q: A young sexually active woman presents with dysuria, urinary frequency, and lower abdominal discomfort due to Staphylococcus saprophyticus infection. Which clinical entity does this most likely represent?

e.correcta: S. saprophyticus is a well-known cause of uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection (cystitis) in young, sexually active women, second only to E. coli; the organism ascends from perineal/vaginal flora into the bladder, producing classic cystitis symptoms of dysuria, urinary frequency, and suprapubic or abdominal discomfort, without the flank pain or systemic toxicity that would suggest upper tract (kidney) involvement.

incorrectas.A: Pyelonephritis is upper urinary tract infection involving the kidneys and typically presents with flank pain, fever, and costovertebral angle tenderness in addition to lower urinary symptoms; the presentation described is limited to lower tract (bladder) symptoms, consistent with cystitis rather than pyelonephritis.
incorrectas.C: Chlamydial urethritis presents with dysuria and often mucopurulent discharge from urethral, not bladder, inflammation, typically without the bacterial growth pattern of S. saprophyticus on urine culture; this vignette specifically implicates S. saprophyticus infection of the bladder, i.e., cystitis.
incorrectas.D: Vulvovaginal candidiasis presents with vulvar itching or irritation and thick discharge, not primarily with dysuria and urinary frequency from a bacterial urinary pathogen; the scenario described is a bacterial cystitis caused by S. saprophyticus, not a fungal vaginal infection.

preguntas.q: What is the nitrate reductase test result for Staphylococcus saprophyticus, distinguishing it from many gram-negative uropathogens?

o.C: Weakly positive only in acidic urine

e.correcta: S. saprophyticus is nitrate reductase-negative, meaning it cannot convert urinary nitrate to nitrite; this is why urine nitrite testing, which is positive with organisms like E. coli that are nitrate reductase-positive, is not a reliable screening tool when S. saprophyticus is the causative UTI pathogen, and diagnosis instead relies on urinalysis (pyuria) and culture.

incorrectas.A: A positive nitrate reductase result is characteristic of many gram-negative enteric uropathogens like E. coli, which is why urine nitrite is used as a dipstick screening marker for UTI; S. saprophyticus lacks this enzyme activity and would give a negative result.
incorrectas.C: The nitrate reductase reaction is not urine-pH dependent in the way described; S. saprophyticus is straightforwardly negative for this enzyme regardless of urine acidity.
incorrectas.D: Nitrate reductase status is a stable, reproducible biochemical characteristic of S. saprophyticus, consistently negative, not a variable trait that differs unpredictably between strains.

preguntas.q: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is part of the normal flora at which anatomic sites in up to 10% of females?

e.correcta: S. saprophyticus colonizes the rectum and vagina as normal flora in up to about 10% of women; from this periurethral reservoir it can ascend into the bladder, which is why it is a recognized cause of cystitis particularly in young, sexually active women, second in frequency only to E. coli among community-acquired UTI pathogens.

incorrectas.A: The skin and nares are the classic colonization sites for Staphylococcus aureus and S. epidermidis, not the specific reservoir cited for S. saprophyticus, whose relevant normal flora sites are the rectum and vagina.
incorrectas.B: The oropharynx and skin are colonized predominantly by viridans streptococci and S. epidermidis respectively, not by S. saprophyticus, whose clinically relevant colonization sites are the lower GI/genital tract.
incorrectas.D: While the vagina is indeed one relevant site, the urethra itself is not typically described as a normal colonization reservoir for S. saprophyticus; the paired sites classically taught are the rectum and vagina, from which the organism can subsequently ascend into the urethra and bladder.

preguntas.q: Streptococcus pyogenes is also known by which designation based on the Lancefield classification system?

e.correcta: Streptococcus pyogenes is classified as group A streptococcus (GAS) under the Lancefield grouping system, which categorizes beta-hemolytic streptococci by cell-wall carbohydrate antigens; GAS is responsible for pharyngitis, impetigo, scarlet fever, necrotizing fasciitis, and the post-streptococcal sequelae of rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis.

incorrectas.A: Group B streptococcus (GBS) refers to Streptococcus agalactiae, a distinct organism important in neonatal sepsis and meningitis and in colonization screening during pregnancy, not to S. pyogenes.
incorrectas.C: Group D streptococcus historically included organisms like Streptococcus bovis/gallolyticus and enterococci, which are separate from S. pyogenes and associated with different clinical entities, such as colon cancer association or endocarditis.
incorrectas.D: Viridans streptococci, such as S. mutans and S. sanguinis, are alpha-hemolytic organisms associated with dental caries and subacute native valve endocarditis; they are a distinct group from the beta-hemolytic group A S. pyogenes.

preguntas.q: What is the hemolysis pattern of Group A streptococcus (S. pyogenes) on blood agar?

o.D: Hemolysis pattern is strain-variable and unpredictable

e.correcta: S. pyogenes is beta-hemolytic, meaning it completely lyses red blood cells on blood agar due to the pore-forming toxins streptolysin O and streptolysin S, producing a clear zone around colonies; this complete hemolysis is a key initial lab clue, along with bacitracin sensitivity, used to identify group A strep in a throat or wound culture.

incorrectas.A: Alpha-hemolysis is partial lysis producing a greenish discoloration around colonies, characteristic of Streptococcus pneumoniae and viridans streptococci, not S. pyogenes, which causes complete (beta) hemolysis.
incorrectas.B: Gamma-hemolysis refers to no hemolysis at all, as seen with most enterococci; this does not describe S. pyogenes, whose toxins cause complete red cell lysis (beta-hemolysis).
incorrectas.D: Beta-hemolysis is a stable, defining laboratory characteristic of S. pyogenes, not a variable or unpredictable trait; this consistency is exactly why hemolysis pattern is used diagnostically.
